text: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency (SRD5A2) — 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, SRD5A2 deficiency, steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency, 46,XY DSD due to 5-alpha-reductase deficiency Partial androgen insensitivity syndrome Disorders of testosterone biosynthesis Gonadal dysgenesis in 46,XY individuals 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency Ovotesticular disorder of sex development Karyotype confirming 46,XY Baseline and stimulated testosterone and dihydrotestosterone with calculation of their ratio Anti-Mullerian hormone and gonadotropins to assess testicular function Pelvic and genital imaging to define internal anatomy and gonadal position Molecular genetic testing of SRD5A2 An autosomal recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by mutations in SRD5A2 The enzyme converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, which drives external genital virilisation Affected 46,XY newborns typically have undervirilised or ambiguous external genitalia despite normal testes Wolffian-derived internal structures are usually formed because they depend on testosterone rather than dihydrotestosterone Marked virilisation often occurs at puberty as testosterone levels rise, sometimes prompting a change in perceived sex An elevated ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, especially after stimulation, supports the diagnosis Prostate development and typical male-pattern balding are reduced because these are dihydrotestosterone dependent Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment Rapid virilisation at puberty causing distress or prompting reconsideration of sex of rearing Undescended or intra-abdominal gonads needing evaluation and monitoring Diagnostic uncertainty that risks incorrect early sex assignment Confusing the condition with partial androgen insensitivity without measuring the testosterone to dihydrotestosterone ratio Making irreversible early decisions about sex of rearing before the diagnosis is clarified Underestimating the degree of virilisation that can occur at puberty Neglecting psychological support during evaluation and management Dihydrotestosterone is the principal androgen responsible for masculinising the external genitalia and prostate during fetal development, and it is produced from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase type 2. In SRD5A2 deficiency, reduced enzyme activity limits dihydrotestosterone formation, so the external genitalia of a 46,XY fetus are incompletely virilised even though testes and testosterone are present. Testosterone-dependent Wolffian structures develop, and anti-Mullerian hormone still causes Mullerian regression. At puberty the surge in testosterone can partially overcome the deficiency and produce substantial virilisation. Prognosis is generally favourable with multidisciplinary care; fertility may be possible in some individuals, and management, including any decisions about hormone therapy or surgery, should be individualised and guided by the person's gender identity.

Achalasia — achalasia cardia, esophageal achalasia, cardiospasm, failure of LES relaxation, esophageal aperistalsis, megaesophagus Distal esophageal spasm and other esophageal motility disorders Gastroesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture Esophageal or gastric cardia malignancy causing pseudoachalasia Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi infection) Eosinophilic esophagitis Scleroderma-related esophageal dysmotility Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) causing destruction of myenteric plexus with achalasia-like esophageal dysfunction Barium esophagram — shows esophageal dilation with distal 'bird's beak' tapering and poor emptying High-resolution esophageal manometry — confirms diagnosis via absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation, and subtypes achalasia (I–III) Upper endoscopy — mandatory to exclude a mechanical or malignant cause (pseudoachalasia) at or near the gastroesophageal junction Endoscopic ultrasound or CT chest/abdomen — used selectively when pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration is suspected Serology for Trypanosoma cruzi — considered in patients from endemic regions to exclude Chagas disease Timed barium swallow — assesses esophageal emptying and is useful for monitoring treatment response Chest imaging — may incidentally reveal a dilated, air/fluid-filled esophagus or absent gastric air bubble Peptic or malignant esophageal stricture Esophageal or gastroesophageal junction carcinoma (pseudoachalasia) Diffuse esophageal spasm Scleroderma esophagus Eosinophilic esophagitis Progressive dysphagia to both solids AND liquids from the outset is the classic clue distinguishing achalasia from a mechanical stricture or malignancy, where solid-food dysphagia usually predominates and progresses later to liquids. Regurgitation of undigested food (especially at night, with risk of aspiration) and slow, gradual weight loss are common accompanying features. Retrosternal chest pain/discomfort with meals occurs in a subset of patients, more often early in the disease course. Patients often learn compensatory maneuvers — eating slowly, holding arms overhead, or performing repeated swallows/Valsalva — to help push food through the non-relaxing lower esophageal sphincter. Barium esophagram classically shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth 'bird's beak' narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. Manometry is the gold standard: it shows absent/incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation together with loss of normal peristalsis in the esophageal body. New-onset 'achalasia-like' symptoms in an older adult, especially with rapid weight loss, should prompt evaluation for pseudoachalasia from a malignancy at the gastroesophageal junction. Chagas disease should be considered in patients from or with travel history to endemic areas of Latin America presenting with an achalasia-like picture. Rapid symptom onset or significant weight loss in an older patient, raising concern for pseudoachalasia due to malignancy Recurrent aspiration pneumonia from nocturnal regurgitation Severe odynophagia or evidence of esophageal perforation Marked, progressive esophageal dilation (megaesophagus) with risk of retained food and aspiration New or worsening symptoms despite treatment, warranting re-evaluation for an underlying malignant cause Attributing dysphagia to reflux disease and delaying manometry, since achalasia can be misdiagnosed as GERD for years Failing to perform endoscopy to exclude a malignant or infiltrative cause before treating for idiopathic achalasia Overlooking Chagas disease in patients with relevant epidemiologic exposure Assuming a normal-caliber esophagus on barium study excludes achalasia; early disease may show minimal dilation despite abnormal manometry Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophagus, leading to loss of coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax appropriately with swallowing. The cause is usually idiopathic, though an autoimmune or postviral inflammatory process targeting these neurons is suspected in many cases. Similar clinical pictures can arise secondarily from infiltrative or destructive processes affecting the myenteric plexus, such as Chagas disease or tumor invasion at the gastroesophageal junction (pseudoachalasia). With appropriate treatment (pneumatic dilation, surgical myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy), most patients achieve durable symptomatic improvement, though the underlying esophageal aperistalsis is not reversed and long-term surveillance is often needed. Untreated or longstanding disease carries risk of progressive esophageal dilation, aspiration, malnutrition, and a modestly increased long-term risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Acute Bronchitis — None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for atypical course, prolonged symptoms, or red-flag features suggesting pneumonia. Chest X-ray (only if pneumonia cannot be excluded clinically) — To rule out consolidation if exam findings are equivocal or symptoms persist beyond expected course. Community-acquired pneumonia (distinguished by a new infiltrate on chest radiography and focal exam findings) (p.1024). Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis / COPD (p.1024). Heart failure (p.1024). Pulmonary embolism (p.1024). Influenza and nonspecific upper respiratory infection, which overlap clinically with lower-tract infection (p.252). Pneumonia (cough plus sputum, dyspnea, chest pain, fever, and a new infiltrate point to pneumonia rather than bronchitis) (p.1537, p.1024). Influenza (overlapping cough and systemic features; can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection) (p.1537). Pertussis / subacute postinfectious tracheobronchitis (a frequent cause of cough persisting 3-8 weeks) (p.272). Chest radiography should be obtained whenever pneumonia is suspected, to confirm the absence of an infiltrate that defines acute bronchitis (p.1537). Specific viral diagnosis is generally unnecessary but, when needed, RT-PCR/multiplex respiratory panels are the most sensitive tests; results must be interpreted cautiously because viral genome can persist for weeks after a resolved infection (p.1537). Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction presenting as cough and dyspnea, illustrated by a fatal case in which exertional dyspnea and chest heaviness were prematurely labeled acute bronchitis (p.21). Cough-variant asthma (p.272). Gastroesophageal reflux (p.272). Rhinosinusitis with postnasal drainage (p.272). ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (p.272). Inhalation of noxious chemicals or smoke, and aspiration, as causes of acute cough (p.272). Defined as a dry or productive cough lasting <3 weeks, occurring without clinical or radiographic signs of pneumonia; it is most common during winter (p.1537). Sputum purulence does not distinguish viral from bacterial cause; in acute bronchitis the cough is predominantly viral, whereas bacteria play a larger role in chronic bronchitis (p.1537). Among acute respiratory infections, only acute otitis media, sinusitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, and pneumonia warrant antibiotics; acute bronchitis is not on that list (p.252). Acute bronchitis and sinusitis are common at all stages of HIV infection, with more severe disease at lower CD4+ counts (p.1595). An individual episode of acute bronchitis does not typically cause lasting reductions in pulmonary function (p.1537 context; long-term lung-function data p. respiratory infections section). Dyspnea, especially exertional dyspnea or chest heaviness/pain, which should trigger consideration of cardiac or thromboembolic disease rather than acute bronchitis (p.21). Cough accompanied by sputum, fever, chest pain, or focal chest signs suggesting pneumonia, prompting chest radiography (p.1537). Hemoptysis or weight loss (raising concern for malignancy or other serious pulmonary disease) (p.272). Cough persisting beyond a few weeks, warranting reassessment and chest radiography for serious causes (sarcoidosis, lymphoma, lung cancer, tuberculosis) (p.272-273). Prescribing antibiotics for acute bronchitis is inappropriate stewardship; roughly half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for acute respiratory infections are unnecessary, and antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile infection, microbiome disruption, and resistance (p.252). Treating purulent sputum as evidence of bacterial infection is a mistake, since purulence does not reliably indicate bacterial etiology in acute bronchitis (p.1537). Premature closure: relying on a rapid 'URI/bronchitis' protocol can cause clinicians to miss life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction; a patient who does not look 'sick' may be wrongly assumed to have a benign illness (p.21). Not eliciting a full dyspnea history (exertional onset, chest heaviness, relief with rest) can lead to a dangerous misdiagnosis of acute bronchitis (p.21). Acute bronchitis is predominantly a viral infection of the lower airways below the vocal cords, caused by common respiratory viruses; the inflammatory airway response produces cough that may be dry or productive, without parenchymal consolidation. Bacterial involvement is uncommon, in contrast to chronic bronchitis where bacteria contribute more prominently (p.1537). Acute bronchitis is a self-limited illness; the cough usually resolves within about 3 weeks, and antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications in most acute respiratory infections. A dry, irritative postbronchitic cough may linger for more than 2 months, particularly in winter, and a residual subacute cough of 3-8 weeks is common after tracheobronchitis (p.252, p.272-273).

(INR generally above 1.5) and any degree of encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing chronic liver disease, developing within about 26 weeks of illness onset Speed of onset matters clinically: hyperacute presentations (encephalopathy within roughly a week or two of jaundice) are typically from acetaminophen toxicity or viral hepatitis and, despite dramatic cerebral edema risk, often carry better spontaneous recovery odds than slower subacute forms Acetaminophen overdose and drug-induced liver injury are the leading causes in resource-rich settings, while viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis B and E) dominates in many other regions Cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure are the most feared early complications and a major cause of death, particularly in hyperacute presentations Coagulopathy in ALF reflects a rebalanced but fragile hemostatic state rather than pure bleeding tendency; INR is used mainly for prognosis and monitoring, not as a routine transfusion trigger Early transfer to a liver transplant center should be considered as soon as ALF is recognized, since deterioration can be rapid and unpredictable Look actively for a treatable cause (acetaminophen, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease, HELLP/acute fatty liver of pregnancy, vascular causes) since specific therapy can be life-saving Infection and sepsis are common complications during the course of ALF and should be surveilled for proactively rather than only when clinically obvious Any new alteration in mental status or asterixis in a patient with acute severe liver injury — signals encephalopathy and true liver failure Rapidly rising INR with jaundice — suggests impending or established failure requiring urgent transplant center contact Signs of raised intracranial pressure (hypertension with bradycardia, pupillary changes, posturing) — medical emergency Hemodynamic instability, oliguria, or lactic acidosis — herald multiorgan involvement Grade III–IV encephalopathy — generally warrants intensive care and consideration of airway protection Any suspicion of acetaminophen ingestion, even with a vague or denied history — treatable and time-sensitive Assuming a normal or mildly elevated bilirubin excludes liver failure — hyperacute acetaminophen-related ALF can present with striking coagulopathy and encephalopathy before marked jaundice develops Using INR alone to guide prophylactic correction with plasma products — this does not reflect true bleeding risk in the rebalanced coagulopathy of ALF and can complicate assessment of hepatic synthetic recovery Delaying transfer to a transplant-capable center while pursuing additional outpatient-type workup — deterioration can be abrupt Overlooking a treatable etiology (Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, pregnancy-related liver disease) because acetaminophen or viral hepatitis seems statistically likely Massive hepatocyte necrosis or dysfunction outstrips the liver's regenerative capacity, causing simultaneous failure of synthetic function (coagulation factors, albumin), detoxification (ammonia, other neurotoxins), and metabolic homeostasis. Accumulating ammonia and inflammatory mediators drive astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema, producing hepatic encephalopathy and raised intracranial pressure. The systemic inflammatory response and impaired hepatic clearance of pathogens also predispose to circulatory dysfunction, renal impairment, and secondary infection, contributing to a multiorgan failure picture. Outcome depends heavily on etiology and speed of onset: hyperacute presentations from acetaminophen or hepatitis A/E often have a better chance of spontaneous recovery than subacute presentations, which have lower native-liver survival. Emergency liver transplantation substantially improves survival in appropriately selected patients who do not recover spontaneously.

truncal and on proximal limbs, non-pruritic, and often elicited or worsened by scratching (Koebner-like phenomenon) Sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy are common early features and can mimic infection Markedly elevated ferritin, often more than five times normal, is a strong clue but not specific Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are typically negative, helping distinguish AOSD from other connective tissue diseases Neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift and elevated inflammatory markers accompany the fever spikes Diagnosis is one of exclusion after infections, malignancy, and other rheumatologic diseases are ruled out Watch for macrophage activation syndrome, a life-threatening complication marked by falling counts and rapidly rising ferritin Cytopenias, coagulopathy, or precipitous rise in ferritin suggesting macrophage activation syndrome Hepatic failure or disseminated intravascular coagulation Cardiac tamponade from serositis Adult respiratory distress syndrome from pulmonary involvement Persistent fever despite broad antimicrobial coverage without an identified infectious source Treating as fever of unknown origin with prolonged empiric antibiotics before considering an autoinflammatory cause Missing the diagnosis because the evanescent rash is absent at the time of examination Anchoring on markedly elevated ferritin as diagnostic without excluding lymphoma and macrophage activation syndrome Delaying immunosuppressive therapy while pursuing an exhaustive infectious workup in a clinically deteriorating patient AOSD is an autoinflammatory disorder driven by innate immune activation rather than autoantibody-mediated disease, with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumor necrosis factor. This cytokine storm produces the systemic febrile illness, marked acute-phase response, and hyperferritinemia seen clinically. The absence of a clear autoantibody or defined trigger, along with strong similarity to systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, supports its classification as an autoinflammatory rather than autoimmune condition. Course is variable: some patients have a self-limited monophasic illness, others a chronic intermittent pattern, and a subset develop chronic destructive polyarthritis. Most patients respond well to anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy, though macrophage activation syndrome significantly increases morbidity and mortality.

Amoebic Liver Abscess — Abdominal ultrasound or CT — Characterizes the abscess (typically single, right lobe, in amoebic disease) and guides the decision on aspiration. Amoebic serology (IgG) — Highly sensitive for invasive amoebiasis and useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive. Stool microscopy for E. histolytica (trophozoites/cysts) — Supportive if positive, but a substantial proportion of liver abscess patients have negative stool studies at the time of presentation. Diagnostic aspiration (if no improvement in 5-7 days, large/left-lobe abscess, or diagnostic uncertainty) — Classic 'anchovy paste' aspirate supports amoebic etiology; also allows bacterial culture to exclude/identify a pyogenic or mixed process. Pyogenic liver abscess (the most important imaging-based distinction once a hepatic abscess is identified) (p.1801) Malaria (p.1801) Typhoid/enteric fever (p.1801) Pulmonary disease (p.1801) Gallbladder disease (p.1801) Any febrile illness with few localizing signs / fever of unknown origin, since 10-15% present with fever alone (p.1799, p.1801) Pyogenic liver abscess (p.1801) Malaria (p.1801) Typhoid (enteric) fever (p.1801) Serum alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases (enzymes often normal/minimally elevated; raised aminotransferases suggest acute disease or complication) (p.1800) Full blood count for leukocytosis >10,000/uL, present in about three-quarters of patients, especially with acute or complicated disease (p.1800) Enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin antigen, usable on stool and on liver-abscess aspirates (p.1800) Multiplex PCR for E. histolytica DNA (near 100% sensitivity/specificity) (p.1800) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) on abscess pus as a low-cost molecular option (p.1800) Diagnostic aspirate sent for Gram stain and bacterial culture when distinguishing amebic from pyogenic abscess (p.1801) Gallbladder disease (p.1801) Pulmonary disease presenting with right-sided pleural/pleuritic findings (p.1801) Most patients are febrile with right-upper-quadrant pain that may be dull or pleuritic and may radiate to the shoulder; point tenderness over the liver and a right-sided pleural effusion are common, whereas jaundice is rare (p.1799). Although the colon is the initial site of infection, fewer than one-third of patients with an amebic abscess have active diarrhea at presentation (p.1799). Strongly age- and sex-dependent: men aged 30-60 are infected at a rate roughly 10-12 times that of women in the same age group; testosterone-modulated NK-T-cell interferon-gamma signaling is implicated experimentally (p.1798). Young patients tend to present acutely with prominent symptoms of under 10 days' duration, while older patients from endemic areas more often follow a subacute course over months with weight loss and hepatomegaly; only about one-third of those with chronic presentations are febrile (p.1799). Of travelers who develop an amebic liver abscess after leaving an endemic area, 95% do so within 5 months (p.1799). Amebic liver abscesses are always preceded by intestinal colonization, which may be entirely asymptomatic (p.1799). On imaging, more than 80% of patients symptomatic for over 10 days have a single right-lobe abscess, but about 50% of those symptomatic for under 10 days have multiple abscesses (p.1800). The classic necrotic 'anchovy paste' contents are variable in color and bacteriologically sterile, composed of granular debris with few or no cells; amebae, when present, sit near the abscess capsule rather than in the aspirable necrotic center (p.1799). Liver enzymes are usually normal or only minimally elevated even with large abscesses; alkaline phosphatase is the most commonly elevated value, while aminotransferase elevation suggests acute disease or a complication (p.1800). Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1800). Pleuropulmonary involvement (reported in 20-30%, the most frequent complication): contiguous spread or frank rupture into the pleural space, the latter requiring drainage (p.1799). Large abscess (>10 cm) in the superior right lobe, which may rupture into the pleural space (p.1800). Left-lobe abscess, which may rupture into the pericardium, the complication carrying the gravest prognosis and able to occur even during medical therapy (p.1799-1800). Rupture into the peritoneum, presenting as an indolent leak or as an acute abdomen (p.1799). Hepatobronchial fistula causing cough productive of large amounts of necrotic material (p.1799). Lack of clinical response within 3-5 days or threat of imminent rupture (p.1801). Expecting concurrent dysentery: fewer than one-third of patients have active diarrhea, so a negative stool examination or absent diarrhea does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1799). Trophozoites are rarely recovered from liver aspirates because they reside in the abscess capsule, not in the necrotic center that is actually aspirated (p.1799). Up to 10% of patients with acute amebic liver abscess have negative serology early; titers usually become positive within a week (p.1799). Microscopy cannot distinguish E. histolytica cysts from non-pathogenic E. dispar, E. moshkovskii, or E. bangladeshi; species-specific diagnosis on microscopy requires seeing trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes (p.1799). In endemic areas serology may stay positive for years (indirect hemagglutination up to ~10 years), complicating interpretation (p.1799). Follow-up imaging may be confusing because abscesses resolve slowly and can transiently enlarge despite a good clinical response (p.1800). Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade colonic mucosal venules and travel via the portal venous system to the liver; the organism is resistant to complement-mediated lysis, which is critical to its survival in the bloodstream. An early acute infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils) is followed by lysis of those neutrophils on contact with amebae, and the released neutrophil toxins are thought to contribute to hepatocyte necrosis. The liver parenchyma is progressively replaced by necrotic material surrounded by a thin rim of congested liver tissue, producing the classically described (but variably colored) 'anchovy paste' that is sterile and largely acellular, with amebae found mainly at the capsule. Genetically, a leptin-receptor substitution (Q223R) increases the risk of amebic liver abscess in adults (p.1798-1799). With early diagnosis and treatment, mortality from uncomplicated amebic liver abscess is under 1%, and over 90% of patients respond dramatically with reduced pain and fever within 72 hours; recurrence is rare. Abscesses resolve slowly and may even enlarge despite clinical improvement, so follow-up ultrasonography can be misleading; complete resolution within 6 months is expected in about two-thirds of patients, while roughly 10% have persistent imaging abnormalities for up to a year. A hepatobronchial fistula carries a good prognosis, whereas pericardial rupture (usually from left-lobe abscesses) carries the gravest prognosis (p.1799-1801).

Aspiration Pneumonia — Chest X-ray — Aspiration classically affects dependent lung segments (posterior upper lobes if aspirated supine, basal segments of lower lobes if upright) — helpful in confirming the diagnosis. Swallowing assessment (if recurrent or ongoing risk) — Identifies the underlying mechanism (dysphagia, reduced consciousness) to prevent recurrence. CBC, CRP — Supports severity assessment and baseline for response monitoring. Foreign-body/food aspiration causing major-airway obstruction with atelectasis and nonspecific inflammation, managed by removal rather than antibiotics (p.1418) Chemical (acid) pneumonitis, e.g., Mendelson syndrome from regurgitated gastric contents (p.1418) Pneumococcal pneumonia, distinguished by its more acute presentation (p.1418) Lung abscess (subacute anaerobic infection) as a related/overlapping entity (p.1072, p.1418) Pneumococcal pneumonia presenting more acutely than indolent anaerobic aspiration infection (p.1418) Chest radiography looking for consolidation in dependent lung segments (basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright; posterior segment of the upper lobe or superior segment of the lower lobe if supine) (p.1418) Gram stain of sputum, which characteristically shows a mixed bacterial population with many polymorphonuclear leukocytes (p.1418) Bronchoscopic protected-brush specimens or bronchoalveolar lavage, which may recover anaerobes from the lower tract with less oropharyngeal contamination (role still being defined) (p.1418) Assessment of dentition/oral hygiene, given the association of severe dental disease with aspiration pneumonia (p.1418) Chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from aspiration of acidic gastric juices, with rapid alveolar injury and pulmonary edema, often without fever and frequently needing no antibiotics (p.1418) Foreign-body/food aspiration with airway obstruction and atelectasis (p.1418) Aspiration pneumonia is best viewed as a point on a continuum that also includes community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia, defined by a phenotype with macroaspiration risk factors and involvement of characteristic gravity-dependent lung locations (p.1066). Aspiration pneumonia is estimated to account for roughly 5-15% of community-acquired pneumonia cases; reliable figures for the hospital-acquired setting are not available (p.1066). The historical view that aspiration pneumonia is caused mainly by anaerobes has shifted: when acquired in the community or hospital, the likely pathogens mirror those of CAP or HAP, with anaerobes still relevant mainly in poor dentition, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or empyema (p.1067). Anaerobic aspiration infections tend to follow an indolent course, a clinical clue that helps separate them from more acutely presenting conditions such as chemical pneumonitis or pneumococcal pneumonia (p.1418). Sputum in bacterial aspiration pneumonia is characteristically NOT malodorous unless the process has been ongoing for at least about a week (p.1418). Expectorated sputum is unreliable for anaerobic culture because of inevitable contamination by normal oral microbiota; reliable anaerobic specimens historically required transtracheal or transthoracic aspiration, techniques rarely used now (p.1418). In CAP overall, no specific etiology is identified in more than half of cases despite careful history, examination, and imaging (p.1067). Gross hemoptysis suggesting necrotizing pneumonia (p.1067) Progression to respiratory failure; in chemical pneumonitis a chest x-ray can evolve from normal to a complete bilateral whiteout within 8-24 hours (p.1067, p.1418) Septic shock and organ failure in severe pneumonia (p.1067) Weight loss and anemia indicating a more chronic process (p.1418) Development of lung abscess or complicated/empyematous pleural effusion (pleural fluid pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, or LDH >1000 U/L, or organisms seen/cultured indicates need for drainage) (p.1072) Failing to distinguish chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from bacterial aspiration pneumonia: chemical pneumonitis is a non-infectious acid injury that usually resolves with supportive care and does NOT warrant antibiotics unless bacterial superinfection develops (p.1418). Routinely covering anaerobes for all aspiration pneumonia: anaerobic coverage is unnecessary unless dentition is poor or there is lung abscess or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1070). Expecting an acute, foul-smelling presentation: bacterial aspiration pneumonia evolves over days to weeks and sputum is usually not malodorous until the process has lasted about a week (p.1418). Relying on expectorated sputum for anaerobic culture, which is invalid because of oral-flora contamination (p.1418). Macroaspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents delivers a high microbial burden directly into the lower airways; lung involvement reflects this rather than invasion of a sterile space, since the lungs normally harbor a microbiota. Mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, branching airways, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) reduce but do not fully block bacterial access to the lower respiratory tract. Bacterial aspiration pneumonia develops over several days to weeks (not hours) through a combination of increased bacterial burden, increased virulence of aspirated organisms, and potential airway damage from aspirated gastric fluid. This contrasts with chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome), where aspirated acidic gastric juice causes rapid, direct destruction of the alveolar lining with fluid transudation into the alveolar space within hours (p.1066, p.1418).

hepatic/uremic encephalopathy) Hashimoto (steroid-responsive) encephalopathy Central nervous system vasculitis Non-convulsive status epilepticus from other causes Subacute (days to a few weeks) behavioral change, memory decline, psychiatric symptoms, seizures, or movement disorder should prompt consideration of autoimmune encephalitis, especially in young adults or children. Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis classically evolves through a viral-like prodrome, then psychiatric/behavioral disturbance, followed by seizures, movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias), autonomic instability, and decreased consciousness. Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are a highly characteristic, near-pathognomonic sign of anti-LGI1 encephalitis and often precede overt cognitive decline. Always search for an underlying tumor (ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDAR disease, thymoma, small-cell lung cancer) since paraneoplastic triggers are common and tumor removal aids recovery. MRI can be normal or show only subtle mesial temporal T2/FLAIR signal change; a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis. CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands; antibody testing should be sent on both serum and CSF since CSF sensitivity is higher for some antibodies (e.g., NMDAR). Response to immunotherapy can be slow (weeks to months), and early aggressive treatment plus tumor removal improves long-term outcome. Relapses occur in a meaningful proportion of patients, particularly with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, warranting longitudinal follow-up. Rapid decline in consciousness, autonomic instability (labile blood pressure, arrhythmia, central hypoventilation) requiring ICU-level monitoring Refractory or super-refractory seizures/status epilepticus Faciobrachial dystonic seizures with rapidly progressive cognitive decline (LGI1 encephalitis) New psychiatric presentation in a young woman with subsequent neurologic signs — evaluate urgently for ovarian teratoma and anti-NMDAR encephalitis Failure to improve or worsening despite first-line immunotherapy — consider escalation and repeat tumor search Signs suggesting an alternative treatable infectious cause (fever, meningismus) that must be excluded/treated empirically first Misdiagnosing early psychiatric or behavioral presentations as a primary psychiatric disorder, delaying immunotherapy Excluding the diagnosis because MRI or initial antibody testing is negative — antibody testing can be falsely negative early, and CSF testing may be more sensitive than serum Failing to empirically treat for herpes simplex encephalitis while autoimmune work-up is pending Overlooking the need for repeated or interval tumor screening, since a causative tumor may not be apparent at initial presentation Autoimmune encephalitis results from antibody-mediated or T-cell-mediated attack on neuronal surface or intracellular antigens, producing limbic or diffuse cortical dysfunction. Surface-antigen antibodies (e.g., against the NMDA receptor, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B receptor) directly disrupt synaptic receptor function and are often reversible with immunotherapy, whereas antibodies against intracellular (onconeural) antigens reflect cytotoxic T-cell-mediated neuronal injury and are less responsive to treatment. A subset is paraneoplastic, triggered by tumor expression of neuronal antigens (e.g., ovarian teratoma expressing NMDA receptors), while others arise post-infection (e.g., following herpes simplex encephalitis) or without any identifiable trigger. Many patients, particularly those with anti-NMDAR or anti-LGI1 encephalitis, achieve substantial or full recovery with prompt immunotherapy and tumor removal when applicable, though recovery may take many months and some residual cognitive or behavioral deficits can persist. Relapses occur in a meaningful minority, and outcomes are generally worse with delayed treatment, intracellular (onconeural) antibody syndromes, or need for prolonged intensive care.

Autoimmune hepatitis — autoimmune hepatitis, AIH, lupoid hepatitis, chronic active hepatitis (autoimmune), autoimmune chronic hepatitis Drug-induced liver injury Viral hepatitis (acute or chronic hepatitis B or C) Wilson disease Primary biliary cholangitis Primary sclerosing cholangitis Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis Acute viral hepatitis A, B, C, or E Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus hepatitis ANA and anti-smooth-muscle antibody — supports type 1 AIH diagnosis Anti-LKM1 antibody — supports type 2 AIH, more typical in pediatric cases Serum IgG level — characteristic hypergammaglobulinemia aids diagnosis and monitoring Liver biopsy — confirms interface hepatitis and plasma cell infiltrate, stages fibrosis Viral hepatitis serologies (hepatitis B and C) — exclude viral etiology Ceruloplasmin and copper studies — exclude Wilson disease, especially in younger patients Alkaline phosphatase and antimitochondrial antibody — screen for overlap with primary biliary cholangitis Standardized AIH scoring system (simplified diagnostic criteria) — integrates autoantibodies, IgG, histology, and viral exclusion Drug-induced or toxin-induced hepatitis Wilson disease Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease/steatohepatitis Primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis overlap Consider AIH in any patient with unexplained acute or chronic hepatocellular injury, especially young to middle-aged women, but it can occur at any age and in either sex. Presentation is highly variable, from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant acute liver failure or established cirrhosis at diagnosis. Marked hypergammaglobulinemia (especially elevated IgG) out of proportion to the degree of liver injury is a classic clue. Two broad serologic patterns exist: type 1 (ANA and/or anti-smooth-muscle antibody positive) and type 2 (anti-LKM1 positive, more common in children). Concurrent autoimmune conditions (autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, ulcerative colitis) support the diagnosis. Liver biopsy showing interface hepatitis with a dense plasma cell infiltrate is characteristic and helps confirm diagnosis and grade severity. A dramatic biochemical response to immunosuppressive therapy is itself supportive of the diagnosis and is used as a diagnostic criterion when the picture is ambiguous. Overlap syndromes with primary biliary cholangitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis occur and should be considered when cholestatic features coexist. Acute presentation with coagulopathy or encephalopathy suggesting evolution to acute liver failure Jaundice with rapidly rising bilirubin and synthetic dysfunction Evidence of established cirrhosis or portal hypertension at initial presentation Lack of biochemical response after an adequate trial of immunosuppression, raising concern for an alternate or overlapping diagnosis Signs of decompensation (ascites, variceal bleeding) warranting hepatology and transplant center referral Attributing transaminase elevation solely to another cause (e.g., fatty liver or medication) without considering AIH, delaying treatment Relying on autoantibody titers alone; seronegative AIH exists, and titers do not reliably track disease activity Missing an overlap syndrome with cholestatic liver disease when only hepatocellular pattern is evaluated Discontinuing therapy too early without confirming sustained biochemical and histologic remission, risking relapse AIH results from a breakdown in immune self-tolerance leading to T-cell-mediated attack on hepatocytes in a genetically susceptible host, often triggered by an environmental factor such as a viral infection or drug exposure. Autoantibody production (ANA, anti-smooth-muscle antibody, or anti-LKM1) accompanies the T-cell-driven injury but is thought to be a marker rather than the primary mediator of hepatocyte damage. Chronic interface hepatitis with ongoing necroinflammation can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis if untreated. With timely immunosuppressive treatment, most patients achieve biochemical remission and have a favorable long-term prognosis, though relapse after treatment withdrawal is common and many require long-term maintenance therapy. Untreated or refractory disease can progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, and the need for liver transplantation.

Brain Abscess — Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI brain — Confirms the diagnosis, localizes the abscess, and is essential for surgical planning; MRI is more sensitive, particularly for early/cerebritis-stage lesions. Stereotactic aspiration or surgical drainage with culture — Provides definitive microbiological diagnosis and is often therapeutic, particularly for abscesses >2.5cm. Blood cultures — May identify the organism in hematogenous spread, supporting de-escalation. Echocardiography (if hematogenous spread suspected) — Screens for infective endocarditis as the source, which would change the overall management plan significantly. HIV testing (if risk factors or atypical presentation) — Relevant given the broader differential (e.g., toxoplasmosis) in immunocompromised hosts. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Subdural empyema Bacterial meningitis Viral meningoencephalitis Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Primary or metastatic brain tumor (the major consideration when fever is absent) Cerebral infarction or hematoma (can resemble abscess on CT/MRI) Neurocysticercosis Tuberculoma (a major cause of focal CNS mass lesions in India and East Asia) Subdural empyema Bacterial meningitis Viral meningoencephalitis Cerebral toxoplasmosis (reactivation, mainly in immunocompromised/HIV hosts) Neurocysticercosis Tuberculoma Nocardial, Aspergillus, Candida, or Cryptococcus CNS lesions in immunocompromised hosts MRI is preferred over CT, being superior for detecting early (cerebritis-stage) lesions and posterior fossa abscesses (p.1178). Diffusion-weighted imaging with apparent diffusion coefficient mapping to separate abscess (restricted diffusion) from tumor (p.1178). Gram stain plus aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures of abscess material obtained by CT-guided stereotactic needle aspiration (p.1179). Inflammatory markers: peripheral leukocytosis in about half, elevated ESR in about 60%, and elevated C-reactive protein in about 80% of patients (p.1179). Serum IgG antibody to Toxoplasma gondii when imaging suggests toxoplasmosis (p.1181). Enzyme-linked immunotransfer blot as a confirmatory test for neurocysticercosis, plus funduscopic examination in suspected cases (p.1181). Primary or metastatic brain tumor Cerebral infarction Intracerebral hematoma Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis The classic triad of headache, fever, and a focal neurologic deficit is present in fewer than half of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1178). Headache is the single most common symptom (more than 75% of patients), typically a constant, dull ache that becomes progressively more severe and refractory to treatment (p.1178). Fever is present in only about half of patients at diagnosis; its absence should not be used to rule out a brain abscess (p.1178). Most patients present a relatively long time after symptom onset (commonly around 11-12 days), and a brain abscess usually behaves like an expanding mass lesion rather than an obvious infection (p.1178). Meningismus is generally absent unless the abscess has ruptured into the ventricle or infection has reached the subarachnoid space (p.1178). Diffusion-weighted MRI helps distinguish abscess from tumor: an abscess shows restricted diffusion (high DWI signal, low ADC) within the cavity, whereas necrotic tumors typically do not (p.1178). Lesion location predicts the source and the deficit: otogenic abscesses favor the temporal lobe and cerebellum, while sinus and dental abscesses favor the frontal lobes (p.1179). New-onset partial seizures are the most common manifestation of neurocysticercosis, an important focal CNS lesion in patients from Latin America (p.1181). Lumbar puncture should NOT be performed when a focal intracranial infection such as abscess or empyema is known or suspected, because CSF analysis adds nothing and LP increases the risk of herniation (p.1179). Signs of raised intracranial pressure (papilledema, nausea/vomiting, drowsiness or confusion) can dominate the presentation, particularly with cerebellar abscesses (p.1178). Rupture of an abscess into the ventricle (heralded by new meningismus) is an ominous development (p.1178). High risk (about 35%) of focal or generalized seizures (p.1180). Glucocorticoids and prior treatment can alter the CT/MRI appearance of the capsule, potentially masking or modifying the imaging picture (p.1178). Relying on the classic triad: headache, fever, and focal deficit coexist in fewer than half of patients (p.1178). Excluding the diagnosis because the patient is afebrile - fever is absent in roughly half of cases (p.1178). Performing a lumbar puncture in a patient with a suspected focal intracranial infection, risking herniation without diagnostic benefit (p.1179). Misreading a ring-enhancing lesion as tumor when diffusion-weighted imaging would point to abscess (p.1178). Forgetting that glucocorticoid therapy can alter the imaging appearance of the abscess capsule (p.1178). Overlooking cerebral toxoplasmosis, which characteristically reactivates and causes ring-enhancing lesions in HIV-infected and other immunocompromised patients (p.1181). Dismissing a cryptogenic abscess as having no source - many are in fact attributable to occult dental infection (p.1179). Intact brain parenchyma is relatively resistant to infection; bacterial invasion generally requires preexisting or concomitant ischemia, necrosis, or hypoxemia in brain tissue. Abscesses arise by direct contiguous spread (sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis, dental infection), by inoculation after penetrating trauma or neurosurgery, or by hematogenous seeding from a distant focus; about a quarter are cryptogenic with no identified source. Hematogenous abscesses are often multiple, frequently lie at the gray-white junction in the middle cerebral artery territory, and tend to be poorly encapsulated. Once established, the lesion evolves through stages: early cerebritis (days 1-3, perivascular inflammation around a core of coagulative necrosis with marked edema), late cerebritis (days 4-9, expanding necrotic center with macrophage/fibroblast infiltrate and a developing thin capsule), early capsule formation (days 10-13, capsule better formed on the cortical than ventricular side, correlating with the ring-enhancing appearance on imaging), and late capsule formation (day 14 onward, dense collagenous capsule, regressing edema, and surrounding gliosis with reactive astrocytes that may underlie later seizures). In right-to-left cardiac or pulmonary shunts, bacteria bypass the pulmonary capillary filter while shunt-related hypoxemia and polycythemia create ischemic nidi favoring abscess formation (p.1178-1179). With modern neuroimaging, stereotactic aspiration, and improved antibiotics, mortality has fallen to typically less than 15% in recent series. However, significant sequelae - including seizures, persisting weakness, aphasia, or mental impairment - occur in at least 20% of survivors (p.1180). Harrison describes a staged histopathologic/radiologic evolution rather than a clinical severity score: early cerebritis (days 1-3), late cerebritis (days 4-9), early capsule formation (days 10-13, when ring enhancement appears), and late capsule formation (day 14 and beyond) (p.1178).

Bronchiectasis Exacerbation — Sputum culture (every exacerbation) — Tracks colonization status over time and directly informs both current and future empiric choices. Chest X-ray (if new symptoms or to exclude complications) — Excludes pneumonia or other acute complications superimposed on chronic bronchiectatic changes. Pulse oximetry — Assesses for hypoxia, particularly relevant in patients with significant structural lung disease. COPD - airflow obstruction on pulmonary function testing overlaps with bronchiectasis at presentation (Harrison 22e p.2243) Asthma - may coexist; ABPA should be considered in refractory asthma (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243) Cystic fibrosis - should be excluded early in any diffuse bronchiectasis workup (Harrison 22e p.2243) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (central-airway-predominant) (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243) Nontuberculous mycobacterial (especially MAC) airway infection - organisms may be colonisers rather than true pathogens, complicating interpretation of positive cultures (Harrison 22e p.2243) Active or reactivated tuberculosis (in endemic areas, a cause and mimic of recurrent airway infection) (Harrison 22e p.2242) High-resolution chest CT - imaging modality of choice; more specific than chest radiograph; look for airway dilation as 'tram tracks' or the 'signet-ring sign' (airway diameter at least 1.5x the adjacent vessel), lack of bronchial tapering, bronchial wall thickening, and inspissated secretions in a 'tree-in-bud' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2243) Bronchoscopy - almost always required in focal bronchiectasis to exclude airway obstruction by mass or foreign body; consider with BAL in diffuse disease if no pathogen is identified (Harrison 22e p.2243) Pulmonary function testing - functional assessment, typically showing mild-to-moderate airflow obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2243) Etiologic workup for diffuse disease: sputum stains/cultures for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi; immunoglobulin levels and CBC with differential; HIV testing; sweat chloride and genetic testing for CF; alpha-1 antitrypsin level; nasal/respiratory brush or biopsy for ciliary dyskinesia; autoimmune serologies; ABPA workup (Aspergillus skin test/precipitins, serum IgE, eosinophils); swallowing/neuromuscular assessment (Harrison 22e p.2242) Traction bronchiectasis from underlying lung fibrosis (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, post-radiation fibrosis) - dilated airways from parenchymal distortion rather than active infection (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243) Autoimmune/rheumatologic airway disease (rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease) (Harrison 22e p.2242) Recurrent aspiration (e.g., from esophageal motility disorders such as scleroderma) (Harrison 22e p.2242) Bronchiectasis is irreversible airway dilation, classically categorised as cylindrical/tubular (most common), varicose, or cystic; it may be focal or diffuse (Harrison 22e p.2242). An acute exacerbation is defined primarily by a change in sputum character - increased volume and increased purulence - rather than by classic infection signs; fever and new infiltrates may be absent (Harrison 22e p.2243). The usual clinical picture between exacerbations is a persistent productive cough with thick, tenacious sputum, often with crackles, wheeze, and sometimes digital clubbing (Harrison 22e p.2243). Pseudomonas aeruginosa preferentially colonises damaged airways and evades host defences; its colonisation marks more severe disease and worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243, p.2244). The pattern of lung-field involvement on imaging hints at the underlying cause: upper-zone in CF and post-radiation fibrosis, lower-zone in chronic aspiration/end-stage fibrosis/immunodeficiency, midlung in NTM (MAC) and dyskinetic cilia syndrome, and central-airway in ABPA (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243). MAC-related bronchiectasis classically affects nonsmoking women over 50 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2242). Up to 25-50% of patients referred for bronchiectasis have idiopathic disease after workup (Harrison 22e p.2242). Hemoptysis - bronchiectatic airways are dilated, inflamed, and highly vascular (supplied by the high-pressure bronchial circulation), so exacerbations can produce massive, life-threatening hemoptysis (Harrison 22e p.2243-2244, p.1408 hemoptysis chapter) Massive hemoptysis - may require intubation to stabilise the patient, protection of the nonbleeding lung, and bronchial artery embolisation or surgery (Harrison 22e p.2244) Emergence of antibiotic-resistant organisms after recurrent infections and repeated antibiotic courses (Harrison 22e p.2244) Expecting classic infection signs: an exacerbation may lack fever or new infiltrates, so reliance on these can miss it - the defining change is sputum volume and purulence (Harrison 22e p.2243). Chest radiographs lack sensitivity for bronchiectasis; a normal or unremarkable film does not exclude it, and CT is needed for confirmation (Harrison 22e p.2243). Positive NTM cultures may reflect colonisation rather than true infection; consensus diagnostic criteria (e.g., two positive sputum cultures, or one positive BAL, plus symptoms and radiographic findings) should be applied before attributing disease (Harrison 22e p.2243). Focal bronchiectasis should prompt bronchoscopy to exclude an obstructing mass or foreign body rather than being attributed to infection alone (Harrison 22e p.2243). The dominant mechanism of infectious bronchiectasis is the 'vicious cycle hypothesis': susceptibility to infection plus impaired mucociliary clearance permits microbial colonisation of the bronchial tree; the persistent microbial presence incites chronic inflammation that damages the airway wall, which further impairs secretion and microbial clearance, perpetuating the infectious-inflammatory cycle. Some organisms, notably Pseudomonas aeruginosa, are especially adept at colonising damaged airways and evading host defences. Impaired mucociliary clearance may be inherited (e.g., cystic fibrosis, dyskinetic cilia syndrome), and a single severe infection such as Bordetella pertussis or Mycoplasma pneumoniae can cause enough airway damage to seed the cycle. Pathologically there is small-airway wall inflammation with larger-airway wall destruction and dilation, and loss of elastin, smooth muscle, and cartilage; inflammatory cells release proteases, reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokines that damage larger airways while ongoing small-airway inflammation produces airflow obstruction. Antiproteases such as alpha-1 antitrypsin help neutralise neutrophil elastase, and bronchiectasis/emphysema occur in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Molecular endotypes with distinct inflammatory and microbiome signatures may correlate with exacerbation risk. Noninfectious mechanisms include immune-mediated bronchial wall damage (e.g., Sjogren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis) and traction from parenchymal fibrosis. (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243) Outcomes vary widely with the underlying etiology and comorbidities, and are influenced by exacerbation frequency and, in infectious disease, the specific pathogens involved - Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation is associated with worse outcomes. Lung-function decline in non-CF bronchiectasis can resemble that of COPD, with FEV1 falling roughly 50-55 mL/year versus 20-30 mL/year in healthy controls. (Harrison 22e p.2244)

Community Acquired Pneumonia (non-severe) — Chest X-ray — Confirms presence and pattern of consolidation; supports diagnosis and baseline for response assessment. CBC — Leukocytosis with neutrophilia supports a bacterial process and provides a baseline. CRP — Elevated CRP supports bacterial etiology and can track response. Pulse oximetry — Screens for hypoxia which would reclassify severity and site of care. Acute bronchitis (Harrison 22e p.1068) Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis/COPD (Harrison 22e p.1068) Tuberculosis (suggested by an upper-lobe cavitating lesion) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Sputum Gram stain and culture (recommended chiefly for hospitalized patients, particularly severe cases or those at risk for MRSA or P. aeruginosa; an adequate specimen needs >25 neutrophils and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Blood cultures (reserved for high-risk patients such as neutropenia, asplenia, complement deficiency, chronic liver disease, or severe CAP, and those at risk for MRSA/P. aeruginosa; yield only ~5-14% in hospitalized CAP) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen tests (reserved for severe cases or relevant epidemiology; Legionella test detects only serogroup 1) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Multiplex respiratory PCR / nasopharyngeal swab PCR (standard for viral diagnosis including influenza and coronaviruses; can also detect Legionella, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, mycobacteria) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein (adjuncts for stewardship only; PCT is not accurate enough to diagnose bacterial CAP or to withhold initial antibiotics, and CRP is even less sensitive) (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069) CT chest (for suspected loculated effusion, cavitary disease, or postobstructive pneumonia from tumor or foreign body) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Diagnostic pleural fluid sampling for a significant effusion (Harrison 22e p.1072) Follow-up chest radiograph ~4-6 weeks after hospitalization (not routinely needed in well, nonsmoking outpatients whose symptoms resolve in 5-7 days) (Harrison 22e p.1072) Heart failure / pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.1068, p.1072) Pulmonary embolism / pulmonary infarction (Harrison 22e p.1068, p.1072) Lung carcinoma (consider with relapse or recurrence in the same segment, raising concern for underlying neoplasm) (Harrison 22e p.1072) Radiation pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1072) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1072) Connective tissue disease involving the lungs (Harrison 22e p.1072) Typical and atypical pathogens cannot be reliably separated on clinical or radiographic grounds because both can produce overlapping syndromes; atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) are not seen on Gram stain or grown on standard media and are intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams (Harrison 22e p.1067). In more than half of CAP cases no specific pathogen is identified despite history, examination, and imaging; in one large emergency-department series an etiology was established in under 8% (Harrison 22e p.1068). Physical examination has limited diagnostic accuracy in pneumonia (sensitivity ~58%, specificity ~67%), so a compatible clinical picture plus a new infiltrate on chest film remains the diagnostic standard (Harrison 22e p.1068). In the elderly the presentation may be subtle, manifesting as new or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (Harrison 22e p.1068). Gross hemoptysis raises concern for necrotizing pneumonia, such as that caused by community-associated MRSA (Harrison 22e p.1067). Up to about 20% of patients have gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) in addition to constitutional and pulmonary findings (Harrison 22e p.1067-1068). Aspiration pneumonia sits on a continuum with CAP/HAP and accounts for roughly 5-15% of CAP cases; modern organisms mirror the usual CAP/HAP flora, with anaerobes mainly relevant in poor dentition, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or empyema (Harrison 22e p.1066-1067). Epidemiologic exposures can flag specific organisms (e.g. birds for Chlamydia psittaci/Histoplasma, recent hotel or cruise stay for Legionella, local influenza activity for influenza/pneumococcus/S. aureus) (Harrison 22e p.1067). CAP can be complicated by cardiovascular events (heart failure, arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, stroke), especially in the elderly with pneumococcal or influenza pneumonia, attributed to increased myocardial load and inflammation-driven plaque destabilization, and these events may occur acutely or up to a year later (Harrison 22e p.1072). Septic shock requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (major severe-CAP criteria mandating direct ICU admission) (Harrison 22e p.1069) Room-air oxygen saturation <92% (Harrison 22e p.1069) Confusion or disorientation, including new or worsening confusion in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069) Respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min (Harrison 22e p.1069) Multilobar infiltrates (Harrison 22e p.1069) Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation (Harrison 22e p.1069) Gross hemoptysis suggesting necrotizing pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1067) Failure to improve by ~day 3 of therapy, prompting reassessment for resistant or unexpected pathogen, sequestered focus (abscess/empyema), or a noninfectious mimic (Harrison 22e p.1072) Treating a macrolide as adequate empirical monotherapy where high-level pneumococcal macrolide resistance is prevalent risks treatment failure (Harrison 22e p.1069). Relying on chest radiography or clinical features to determine etiology is unreliable; imaging often cannot distinguish CAP from other conditions and seldom yields a specific organism (Harrison 22e p.1068). Using procalcitonin or CRP in isolation to decide on or withhold antibiotics is inappropriate, as neither is sufficiently accurate for diagnosing bacterial CAP (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069). Neither PSI nor CURB-65 is designed to determine the need for ICU admission, so they should not be used for that purpose (Harrison 22e p.1069). Delayed ICU transfer of a deteriorating ward patient is associated with higher mortality than initial ICU monitoring of equally ill patients (Harrison 22e p.1069). Inability to expectorate sputum may reflect dehydration rather than absence of disease; rehydration can yield a productive sample and a more apparent infiltrate (Harrison 22e p.1068). Pneumonia that relapses or recurs in the same lung segment should prompt evaluation for an underlying neoplasm or focal abnormality such as bronchiectasis (Harrison 22e p.1072). Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli together with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract chiefly by microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, but also by inhalation and direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, branching airways, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are imperfect barriers. Rather than simple invasion of a sterile space, current models view pneumonia as an emergent disturbance of the lung microbiota driven by self-reinforcing positive-feedback loops: an inciting epithelial/endothelial injury (often a viral infection plus microaspiration) releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively favor growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, amplifying inflammation. When innate and adaptive immunity fail to contain this, mediators (IL-6 and TNF cause fever; IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils) drive an alveolar-capillary leak producing hypoxemia and radiographic infiltrates. Bacterial toxins amplify inflammation, and some pathogens blunt hypoxic vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia; reduced compliance, increased secretions, raised respiratory drive, and intrapulmonary shunting cause dyspnea and, when severe, respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1066). Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia passes through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution; a bronchopneumonia pattern predominates in nosocomial disease while a lobar pattern is more typical of bacterial CAP, and viral pneumonias are alveolar rather than interstitial processes (Harrison 22e p.1066). Outcome depends on age, comorbidities, and site of care. Young patients without comorbidity generally recover fully in about 2 weeks, whereas older patients or those with comorbid illness may take several weeks longer. Overall mortality is under 5% for outpatients but ranges from roughly 12% to 40% for hospitalized patients depending on the patient category and the timeliness of appropriate antibiotics; in older patients the 1-year mortality after CAP exceeds the 30-day mortality. Fever and leukocytosis typically resolve in 2-4 days in otherwise healthy patients, while chest radiographic clearance is slowest (4-12 weeks). About 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month (Harrison 22e p.1067, p.1072). Two validated tools guide the site-of-care decision. The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) is a prognostic model using 20 variables (age, comorbidities, abnormal exam and laboratory findings) that stratifies patients into five classes with rising mortality (class 1 ~0.1%, class 2 ~0.6%, class 3 ~2.8%, class 4 ~8.2%, class 5 ~29.2%); classes 1-2 are generally suitable for outpatient care and class 3 for an observation unit. CURB-65 scores one point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, low Blood pressure (systolic <=90 or diastolic <=60 mmHg), and age >=65: a score of 0 (30-day mortality ~1.5%) suggests outpatient treatment, 1-2 generally warrants admission (unless driven only by age >=65), and >=3 (mortality ~22%) may need ICU care. PSI is better validated and more discriminating but harder to compute. Severe CAP (Harrison/IDSA-ATS criteria) is defined by either major criterion (invasive mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, or septic shock requiring vasopressors), mandating ICU admission; presence of at least 3 of 9 minor criteria (RR >=30/min; PaO2/FiO2 <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia with BUN >=20 mg/dL; leukopenia <4000/uL; thrombocytopenia <100,000/uL; hypothermia <36 degrees C; hypotension needing aggressive fluids) warrants ICU or high-level monitoring. Independent of these scores, inability to maintain oral intake, concerns about compliance (e.g. cognitive impairment, homelessness), or room-air O2 saturation <92% are indications for hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.1069).

bronchial and other extra-intestinal primaries can bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism and cause symptoms without liver metastases Right-sided (and occasionally left-sided) valvular heart disease from fibrotic plaque deposition is a hallmark late complication and a major driver of morbidity/mortality Flushing is usually dry, reddish-violet, and involves face/neck/upper trunk, lasting minutes; triggers include alcohol, certain foods, emotional stress, and palpation of the tumor Niacin deficiency (pellagra-like features) can occur because tryptophan is diverted toward serotonin synthesis rather than niacin production Carcinoid crisis — profound flushing, bronchospasm, and hemodynamic instability — can be precipitated by anesthesia, tumor manipulation, or invasive procedures and requires pre-procedural prophylaxis Signs of carcinoid heart disease (new murmur, right heart failure symptoms) warrant urgent echocardiography and cardiology referral Pre-procedural or pre-anesthetic patients with known/suspected carcinoid require prophylaxis to prevent carcinoid crisis Acute severe flushing with hypotension or bronchospasm suggests evolving carcinoid crisis and needs emergent management Bowel obstruction or ischemia from mesenteric fibrosis/desmoplastic reaction is a surgical emergency Refractory diarrhea causing dehydration or electrolyte derangement needs prompt correction Attributing episodic flushing/diarrhea to anxiety, menopause, or irritable bowel syndrome, delaying diagnosis for years Obtaining urinary 5-HIAA without dietary restriction (serotonin-rich foods) or accounting for interfering medications, leading to false results Overlooking carcinoid heart disease until advanced right heart failure develops Failing to anticipate and prevent carcinoid crisis before surgery, biopsy, or anesthesia in a patient with known tumor Carcinoid syndrome arises from a neuroendocrine tumor (most often midgut origin) that secretes serotonin and other vasoactive substances (histamine, tachykinins, prostaglandins, kallikrein) directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic inactivation once liver metastases develop or when the primary tumor drains outside the portal system. These circulating mediators produce the characteristic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchoconstriction, while chronic exposure to serotonin and related factors promotes fibrous plaque deposition on cardiac valves, producing carcinoid heart disease. Prognosis depends primarily on tumor grade, extent of metastatic disease, and presence of carcinoid heart disease; with modern somatostatin analog therapy and multidisciplinary management, many patients experience prolonged survival and symptom control, though cardiac involvement significantly worsens outcomes if untreated.

Castleman disease — castleman, angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia, castleman's disease, unicentric castleman disease, multicentric castleman disease, HHV-8 associated multicentric castleman disease, giant lymph node hyperplasia Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) Autoimmune/rheumatologic disease with lymphadenopathy (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis) IgG4-related disease Reactive lymphadenopathy from chronic infection POEMS syndrome Kaposi sarcoma / HHV-8-associated disease Tuberculous lymphadenitis HIV-associated persistent generalized lymphadenopathy Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) Cat-scratch disease Excisional lymph node biopsy — required for definitive histopathologic diagnosis and subtype classification HIV serology and HHV-8 testing (blood PCR or tissue staining) — identifies virus-associated multicentric disease Complete blood count — screens for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or thrombocytosis seen in multicentric/TAFRO variants Serum IL-6 and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) — supports the systemic inflammatory phenotype Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulin levels — assesses hypergammaglobulinemia and screens for paraproteins/POEMS Cross-sectional imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) — defines extent of nodal disease and organomegaly, distinguishes unicentric from multicentric involvement Renal and liver function testing — evaluates end-organ involvement from systemic cytokine excess Bone marrow examination — helps exclude lymphoma or plasma cell dyscrasia when systemic disease is suspected Lymphoma Sarcoidosis IgG4-related disease Autoimmune lymphoproliferative conditions Plasma cell dyscrasias (e.g., POEMS-associated) Consider Castleman disease when lymphadenopathy (localized or generalized) is accompanied by unexplained constitutional symptoms, cytopenias, or hypergammaglobulinemia. Unicentric disease is usually indolent, presenting as a single enlarged lymph node mass, and is often curable with excision. Multicentric disease is a systemic illness with fevers, weight loss, organomegaly, and multi-organ dysfunction driven by excess IL-6 signaling. HHV-8 infection drives most multicentric cases in HIV-positive patients; idiopathic multicentric disease occurs without HHV-8 or HIV. POEMS syndrome and TAFRO syndrome are important clinical variants/associations that change management and prognosis. Excisional lymph node biopsy with expert hematopathology review is essential — needle biopsies are often non-diagnostic. Multicentric disease carries an increased risk of progression to lymphoma and of concurrent Kaposi sarcoma in HHV-8-positive/HIV-positive patients. Rapidly progressive multi-organ failure (renal, hepatic) suggesting TAFRO syndrome Severe cytopenias or bleeding diathesis Concurrent Kaposi sarcoma or hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like picture New neurologic findings or organomegaly suggesting POEMS syndrome Rapid nodal growth or B symptoms raising concern for transformation to lymphoma Attributing lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms solely to infection or malignancy without considering Castleman disease, delaying diagnosis Relying on core needle biopsy alone, which frequently yields non-diagnostic or misleading architecture compared to excisional biopsy Failing to test for HIV and HHV-8 in patients with multicentric disease, missing a treatable driver Overlooking associated syndromes (POEMS, TAFRO) that substantially alter prognosis and treatment approach Castleman disease is a heterogeneous group of lymphoproliferative disorders characterized by distinctive lymph node architectural changes, most driven by dysregulated interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling. In unicentric disease the process is localized and follicular/vascular changes predominate, while multicentric disease reflects a systemic cytokine-driven process, frequently linked to lytic HHV-8 infection in immunocompromised hosts, producing viral IL-6 and human IL-6 that fuel plasmablast proliferation and systemic inflammation. Idiopathic multicentric disease lacks HHV-8 but shares a similar IL-6-driven inflammatory phenotype, sometimes with an associated clonal or autoimmune-like process. Unicentric Castleman disease has an excellent prognosis after complete surgical excision, with cure in most cases. Multicentric disease, particularly HHV-8-associated or TAFRO-variant forms, follows a more relapsing and potentially life-threatening course, with outcomes improved by IL-6-pathway-targeted therapy but still carrying elevated risk of lymphoma and organ dysfunction.
