anticoagulation Mistaking catastrophic APS for straightforward sepsis-related multi-organ failure or DIC and delaying antibody testing Withholding anticoagulation and immunosuppression while awaiting confirmatory biopsy in a rapidly deteriorating patient Failing to identify and treat the precipitating trigger (e.g., untreated infection) alongside the antibody-driven process Overlooking coexisting thrombotic microangiopathy, which may require additional therapies beyond standard APS management Catastrophic APS represents an accelerated, disseminated form of antiphospholipid antibody-mediated thrombosis affecting predominantly small vessels and multiple organs simultaneously, rather than the single medium/large-vessel thrombi seen in classic APS. Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant) activate endothelium, platelets, and complement, driving a systemic thrombo-inflammatory cascade that resembles disseminated intravascular coagulation but with predominant thrombosis rather than bleeding. A triggering event (infection, surgery, trauma, or abrupt anticoagulant discontinuation) is thought to initiate a self-amplifying cytokine storm and complement activation, leading to a vicious cycle of endothelial injury and microthrombosis across organs. This results in a systemic inflammatory response with multi-organ failure occurring within days to weeks. Catastrophic APS carries a high mortality rate even with aggressive combination treatment, though survival has improved with earlier recognition and multimodal therapy. Survivors remain at risk for recurrent thrombotic events and organ damage, requiring long-term anticoagulation and monitoring.

Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection — Urine culture (from newly placed catheter if replacing, or freshly collected sample) — Essential given the high resistance burden and biofilm-related polymicrobial colonization in this population — guides definitive therapy. Blood cultures (if systemically unwell) — CA-UTI can be a source of bacteremia/urosepsis; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement. Renal function tests — Baseline assessment, particularly relevant if upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) is suspected. Asymptomatic bacteriuria / catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing or systemic symptoms attributable to UTI) Complicated UTI extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) Candiduria representing colonization rather than true infection in a catheterized patient Other infectious or noninfectious source of fever or altered mentation in a catheterized patient, which must be systematically excluded before attributing symptoms to CAUTI Asymptomatic bacteriuria with incidental pyuria Candida colonization of the catheter/urine without invasive infection Another concurrent infection (e.g., respiratory, intra-abdominal, bloodstream) causing the fever or systemic findings Urine culture collected from a freshly placed catheter (after exchanging/removing the indwelling catheter) to reflect bladder rather than biofilm microbiology, with susceptibilities to guide therapy Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis, interpreted with awareness that pyuria and bacteriuria are expected in catheterized patients Systematic workup to exclude alternative infectious and non-infectious causes of fever or altered mental status before settling on CAUTI Delirium from non-infectious causes (e.g., metabolic, medication-related) in an older patient, mistaken for UTI-related encephalopathy Pyuria due to urinary stasis from an obstructed catheter rather than active infection Hematuria or local irritation from catheter trauma CAUTI is diagnosed only when localizing urinary and/or systemic symptoms (e.g., fever) are present together with pyuria and bacteriuria; bacteriuria and pyuria alone do not establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1090). Because the catheter is a conduit for bacterial entry, bacteriuria is essentially inevitable with catheterization, so an abnormal urinalysis alone should not be the endpoint of evaluating a febrile catheterized patient (Harrison 22e p.1090). The accepted bacteriuria threshold for CAUTI is at least 10^3 colony-forming units per mL of urine (Harrison 22e p.1090). Typical UTI features (pain, urgency, dysuria, fever, peripheral leukocytosis) have lower predictive value in catheterized patients than in non-catheterized patients (Harrison 22e p.1090). The catheter should be exchanged or, if feasible, removed during treatment to clear biofilm-associated organisms; ideally the exchange precedes urine culture collection so results reflect bladder rather than catheter-wall microbiology (Harrison 22e p.1094). Very high pyuria levels are common with urinary stasis (e.g., end-stage renal disease, obstructed catheters) and the degree of pyuria should not influence the distinction between asymptomatic bacteriuria and true UTI in an asymptomatic patient (Harrison 22e p.1089). Candiduria is common in catheterized patients, especially after antimicrobial therapy for CAUTI or inappropriate treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria; removal of the catheter alone resolves candiduria in over a third of asymptomatic cases (Harrison 22e pp.1088, 1095). Urine nitrite is detectable only with Enterobacterales and adequate accumulation, so it can be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales pathogens (e.g., enterococci, Pseudomonas, Candida) that are prominent in CAUTI (Harrison 22e pp.1090-1091). Fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, or flank/costovertebral angle pain suggesting infection has extended beyond the bladder (pyelonephritis or bloodstream) Signs of sepsis in a catheterized patient with systemic symptoms Isolation of S. aureus from urine, which should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia Persistent fever and/or bacteremia despite appropriate therapy, suggesting renal/perinephric abscess or obstruction requiring drainage Treating catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria: apart from pregnancy (and pre-urologic-procedure screening), urine culture and treatment are not indicated for asymptomatic catheterized patients, and treating it does not reduce subsequent infection (Harrison 22e pp.1147, 1095). Attributing nonspecific symptoms such as confusion in an elderly catheterized patient to bacteriuria without excluding other time-sensitive causes of delirium, leading to premature diagnostic closure (Harrison 22e pp.1089, 1147). Improper treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria followed by repeat 'test-of-cure' cultures, driving a vicious cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance (Harrison 22e p.1147). Sending urine cultures in catheterized patients lacking signs/symptoms of UTI (poor diagnostic stewardship), which promotes overdiagnosis and overtreatment (Harrison 22e pp.1089, 1147). Sampling urine through the existing biofilm-laden catheter rather than from a newly placed catheter, yielding culture results that reflect the catheter wall rather than the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1094). Routinely using antimicrobial (silver- or nitrofurazone-impregnated) catheters to prevent CAUTI, which has not shown significant clinical benefit (Harrison 22e p.1094). Urinary catheters and other foreign bodies (stones, stents, nephrostomy tubes) provide an inert surface for bacterial colonization and formation of a persistent biofilm, and catheterization dramatically increases bacterial entry into the urinary tract. The catheter serves as a conduit allowing organisms to ascend into the bladder, making bacteriuria nearly universal during catheterization. Biofilm on the catheter shelters organisms and acts as a nidus for reinfection, which is why catheter exchange or removal is central to clearing infection. The microbiology is more diverse than in uncomplicated cystitis; while E. coli remains predominant, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, enterococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida are important additional pathogens (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088, 1094). Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in catheterized and elderly patients but does not itself increase risk of infection or death, which argues against treating it. In the absence of anatomic abnormalities (e.g., reflux, obstruction), recurrent urinary infection does not lead to chronic pyelonephritis or renal failure; however, with underlying renal abnormalities such as obstructing stones, infection can accelerate renal parenchymal damage. A randomized trial found more relapses with 3 versus 14 days of therapy, supporting longer treatment than for uncomplicated cystitis (Harrison 22e pp.1094-1095). CAUTI falls within the complicated UTI category, defined by infection in the setting of intermittent or indwelling urinary catheterization. Severity ranges from localized symptomatic infection to infection extending beyond the bladder (pyelonephritis, bacteremia) signaled by fever, rigors, flank pain, and systemic toxicity (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087, 1089).

malabsorption Testing serology after the patient has already started a gluten-free diet, producing false-negative results Relying on serology alone without confirmatory duodenal biopsy, or biopsying too few sites reducing diagnostic yield Missing the diagnosis in atypical presentations (isolated anaemia, infertility, elevated liver enzymes) because classic diarrhoea is absent Failing to screen at-risk relatives or patients with associated autoimmune conditions Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (from wheat, barley, and rye) in genetically susceptible individuals, most of whom carry HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Deamidation of gluten peptides by tissue transglutaminase enhances their binding to these HLA molecules, driving an aberrant T-cell response that damages small intestinal enterocytes. The resulting villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis impair mucosal absorptive surface area, leading to malabsorption of macronutrients and micronutrients. Most patients respond well to strict, lifelong adherence to a gluten-free diet, with resolution of symptoms and mucosal healing over months to years. A small subset develops refractory disease or, rarely, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, particularly with prolonged undiagnosed or poorly controlled disease.

Cellulitis — None routinely required for typical mild-moderate cellulitis — Diagnosis is clinical; cultures of intact cellulitic skin have low yield. Blood cultures (if systemically unwell or immunocompromised) — Identifies bacteremic spread in more severe presentations. Wound/abscess culture (if purulent drainage present) — Identifies organism and susceptibility, particularly important given variable MRSA prevalence. CBC, CRP — Supports severity assessment and provides a baseline to track response. Erysipelas (S. pyogenes superficial dermal/lymphatic infection with sharply demarcated, raised, indurated borders and abrupt fiery-red swelling) (Harrison 22e p.1095) Necrotizing fasciitis / deeper necrotizing soft-tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1095) Purulent cellulitis associated with a focal staphylococcal lesion such as a furuncle, carbuncle, or abscess (Harrison 22e p.1095) Herpes zoster (dermatomal vesicular eruption may be mistaken for cellulitis early) (Harrison 22e p.93) Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or identifiable portal of entry when present, for definitive etiology (Harrison 22e p.1095) Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy of involved skin in selected cases, recognizing low (~20%) culture yield (Harrison 22e p.1095) Stasis dermatitis, which when acutely inflamed with crusting and exudate is easily confused with cellulitis; symmetric bilateral leg involvement favors stasis dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428, p.436) Eczema (Harrison 22e p.93) Lymphedema (Harrison 22e p.93) Contact dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428) Non-purulent cellulitis (no associated abscess, focal purulence, or drainage) is a rapidly spreading, diffuse process typically due to S. pyogenes, often accompanied by lymphangitis and fever; purulent cellulitis arising from a focal lesion (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, surgical wound) is more likely staphylococcal (Harrison 22e p.1095). Even with needle aspiration of the advancing edge or punch biopsy of involved tissue, cultures are positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and that much of the spreading erythema is driven by extracellular toxins and host inflammatory mediators (Harrison 22e p.1095). When a draining wound or visible portal of entry is present, Gram stain and culture of that material can give a definitive microbiologic diagnosis, unlike cultures of intact cellulitic skin (Harrison 22e p.1095). A careful exposure/epidemiologic history is diagnostically valuable because many less common causative organisms occupy characteristic ecological niches (e.g., cat/dog bite, freshwater laceration, fish/swine handling, aquarium water) (Harrison 22e p.1095). Bilateral, symmetric lower-leg involvement favors a mimic such as stasis dermatitis, whereas true cellulitis is usually unilateral (Harrison 22e p.428). Purple/hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis, or cutaneous anesthesia suggesting loss of vascular integrity and possible necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1095) Pain or tenderness disproportionate to visible skin findings, or unexplained fever with deep soft-tissue pain even without overt skin inflammation (Harrison 22e p.1095) Brawny edema, dark-red induration, skin friability with bluish/maroon/black discoloration, or systemic toxicity/shock indicating deep necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095) Routine cultures of intact cellulitic skin are frequently negative (positive in only ~20% even with aspiration or biopsy), so negative cultures do NOT exclude cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1095). When patients labeled 'cellulitis' are reviewed by dermatology, roughly one-third have an alternative diagnosis (e.g., eczema, lymphedema), so an overcall risks unnecessary hospitalization and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.93). Bilateral symmetric lower-extremity erythema is more likely stasis dermatitis than cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.428). Early necrotizing fasciitis may present with pain or unexplained fever as the only manifestation; do NOT rely on overt cutaneous inflammation to exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1095). Bacteria reach the dermis and subcutaneous soft tissue after disruption of the epidermal barrier by cracks, abrasions, cuts, burns, insect bites, surgical incisions, IV catheters, trauma, tinea/fungal infection, or pressure and venous-stasis ulcers. Organisms already colonizing the skin (notably S. aureus and group A streptococci) most readily exploit such breaks, though many exogenous bacteria can be introduced. Streptococcal disease characteristically spreads diffusely via lymphatics, producing lymphangitis, whereas staphylococcal disease spreads from a central focus such as an abscess or infected foreign body. Much of the expanding erythema reflects the action of bacterial extracellular toxins and host-derived inflammatory mediators rather than high bacterial burden. Progression to deeper structures with loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia) signals possible necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095, p.1007). Harrison distinguishes non-purulent cellulitis (diffuse, spreading, typically streptococcal, often with lymphangitis and fever) from purulent cellulitis (associated with a focal lesion such as furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, or surgical wound, typically staphylococcal, the FDA-preferred term for these). Loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia, systemic toxicity) marks progression toward necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095).

infectious, or inflammatory trigger in every confirmed case Rapidly declining consciousness or signs of impending herniation New or worsening papilledema with visual field loss threatening vision Extensive bilateral hemorrhagic venous infarction on imaging Status epilepticus or recurrent seizures at presentation Clinical deterioration despite anticoagulation, suggesting need for endovascular or surgical intervention Dismissing headache as migraine or tension-type without considering CVST in at-risk patients (pregnancy, postpartum, hormonal contraception, thrombophilia) Withholding anticoagulation because of hemorrhagic venous infarction, which is generally still an indication for treatment rather than a contraindication Relying on a normal non-contrast CT to exclude the diagnosis instead of obtaining dedicated venous imaging Attributing bilateral or non-arterial-territory deficits to a psychiatric or functional cause rather than pursuing venous imaging Thrombosis of a dural venous sinus or cortical vein obstructs cerebral venous drainage, raising venous and capillary pressure. This leads to impaired CSF resorption with intracranial hypertension, and can progress to vasogenic edema, venous congestion, and eventually venous infarction with secondary hemorrhage. Because venous drainage territories overlap and are variable between individuals, resulting deficits are often atypical for a single vascular distribution. Most patients who receive timely anticoagulation have a favorable outcome with good functional recovery, though a minority develop persistent neurological deficits, chronic intracranial hypertension, or, rarely, death from extensive venous infarction or herniation. Recurrence risk depends on the presence and persistence of underlying prothrombotic risk factors.

Chikungunya — Chikungunya IgM serology / RT-PCR (early illness) — Confirms the diagnosis; RT-PCR is most sensitive in the first few days, IgM becomes detectable slightly later. Dengue NS1/serology (concurrent testing) — Co-circulation with dengue is common and clinical distinction is imperfect — concurrent testing avoids missing dengue, which has different monitoring needs. CBC — Typically shows lymphopenia rather than the thrombocytopenia more characteristic of dengue, supporting clinical distinction. Dengue (co-circulating Aedes-borne flavivirus; may coinfect) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060) Zika virus infection (Aedes-borne; can also cause joint manifestations) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060) Other arthritogenic alphaviruses with clinically similar presentations: Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus, Sindbis virus, o'nyong-nyong virus, Mayaro virus (Harrison 22e p.1712) Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes (yellow-fever and Asian tiger) mosquitoes; after a 2-10 day incubation it causes abrupt high fever, sometimes with a saddleback pattern, plus severe arthralgia (Harrison 22e p.1712). Migratory polyarthritis predominantly involves the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, though larger joints may also be affected; periarticular swelling and immobility are common, while frank effusions are less frequent (Harrison 22e p.1712). A rash appears at onset or several days in, often coinciding with defervescence around day 2-3, is most intense over trunk and limbs, and may desquamate; children more often develop a bullous rather than maculopapular/petechial rash (Harrison 22e p.1712). Although petechiae and epistaxis are occasionally seen, CHIKV should not be classified as a cause of viral hemorrhagic fever; older reports of 'chikungunya hemorrhagic fever' largely reflected concurrent dengue coinfection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706). A recovery period of weeks is common, and a substantial proportion of middle-aged to older patients go on to develop chronic, sometimes disabling arthritis or arthralgia syndromes typically involving the same joints (Harrison 22e p.1712). Pregnant women are not at increased risk of severe disease, but there is a high risk of maternal-fetal transmission, especially intrapartum, which has occasionally led to fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712). A live-attenuated chikungunya vaccine was approved in the United States in 2023 for adults at increased exposure risk and is contraindicated in immunocompromised persons; about 12% of recipients developed chikungunya-like symptoms in trials (Harrison 22e p.1060). Cardiorespiratory, neurologic, renal, or ocular complications in severe acute disease (uncommon but reported, typically in hospitalized patients) (Harrison 22e p.1712) Pregnancy near delivery, given high risk of intrapartum maternal-fetal transmission and reported fetal death (Harrison 22e p.1712) Do not label CHIKV as a viral hemorrhagic fever despite occasional petechiae/epistaxis; apparent 'hemorrhagic' cases historically reflected concurrent dengue infection (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1706). Do not assume severe disease in pregnancy; the principal pregnancy concern is intrapartum vertical transmission rather than maternal severity (Harrison 22e p.1712). Do not consider the live-attenuated vaccine safe in immunocompromised persons, in whom it is contraindicated (Harrison 22e p.1060). CHIKV is an arthropod-borne alphavirus (family Togaviridae) spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It produces an acute febrile illness with prominent joint involvement; rheumatic manifestations span arthralgia with or without inflammatory signs (periarticular redness, swelling, immobility). Adults experience more severe and articular-predominant disease than children. Chronic musculoskeletal sequelae are thought to relate to host factors, with increased risk in patients who have preexisting osteoarthritis, severe acute disease, or the HLA-B27 subtype, and may be associated with cryoglobulins (Harrison 22e p.1712). Life-threatening illness is rare; most patients recover, though recovery may take weeks. A significant fraction of middle-aged to older patients develop chronic, potentially disabling arthritis/arthralgia. Deaths have been reported, typically in the setting of large outbreaks. Children generally have milder disease and are less frequently hospitalized (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060).

Acute Cholangitis — Blood cultures — Frequently positive in cholangitis and identifies organism/susceptibility for de-escalation. Liver function tests — Cholestatic pattern (elevated bilirubin, ALP, GGT) supports the diagnosis and tracks resolution after drainage. Abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to identify biliary dilation and the level of obstruction. MRCP or CT abdomen (if ultrasound inconclusive) — Better characterizes the cause and location of obstruction (stone, stricture, malignancy) to guide definitive drainage strategy. Bile culture (at time of ERCP/drainage) — Identifies the causative organism directly from the infected source for the most targeted de-escalation. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Biliary colic / choledocholithiasis without infection Acute cholecystitis Gallstone pancreatitis Obstructive jaundice from malignancy of the pancreatic head, bile ducts, or ampulla of Vater (often painless jaundice) Primary sclerosing cholangitis with superimposed bacterial cholangitis Acute cholecystitis Hepatic (pyogenic) abscess Septic shock from another occult source (e.g., pneumonia, pyelonephritis) presenting before the biliary source is evident Serum alkaline phosphatase (almost always elevated in biliary obstruction; rise may precede clinical jaundice) Serum aminotransferases (two- to tenfold elevation, especially with acute obstruction) ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy as the preferred initial procedure for both definitive diagnosis and therapeutic drainage EUS as a less invasive alternative for detecting duct stones when the pretest probability of a persistent stone is lower Biliary colic from choledocholithiasis (pain without fever or rigors) Painless obstructive jaundice from neoplastic biliary obstruction IgG4-associated (sclerosing) cholangitis, which causes biliary stricturing and is glucocorticoid-responsive Gallstone pancreatitis The classic presentation is Charcot's triad: biliary pain, jaundice, and spiking fevers with rigors; it is present in roughly 70% of patients with ascending cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735). Addition of shock and confusion to Charcot's triad constitutes Reynolds's pentad, which signals high mortality and should trigger urgent biliary drainage (Harrison 22e p.2489). Bile cultures are positive in approximately 75% of patients with acute cholangitis early in the symptomatic course, and blood cultures are frequently positive (Harrison 22e p.2735). Most acute cholangitis is the nonsuppurative form, which often responds relatively quickly to supportive care and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2735). Initial medical management (fluids and IV antibiotics) usually stabilizes the patient and buys a window of about 24 hours within which biliary drainage should be established, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489). The bile duct may not yet be dilated on early ultrasound during acute biliary obstruction, so a normal-caliber duct does not exclude cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2489). Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) indicating suppurative cholangitis and high mortality Mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock signaling suppurative cholangitis with pus under pressure Failure to respond to antibiotics, which in suppurative disease is associated with multiple hepatic abscesses Delay in establishing biliary drainage beyond the ~24 h stabilization window, risking recrudescent sepsis Relying on antibiotics alone in suppurative cholangitis; biliary decompression is required because antibiotic response is poor and mortality is very high without it. Excluding cholangitis because the bile duct appears non-dilated on early ultrasound, which can occur in acute obstruction. Awaiting the full Charcot's triad before acting, since not all patients display all three components. Mistaking the relentless toxicity of suppurative disease for simple sepsis without recognizing the need for urgent source control. Acute cholangitis arises from infection within an obstructed biliary tree, most often due to choledocholithiasis (common duct stones complicate about 10-15% of cholelithiasis). At least partial obstruction to bile flow combined with bacterial colonization of bile produces inflammation; rising intrabiliary pressure in an obstructed system promotes translocation of organisms into the bloodstream, causing bacteremia and biliary sepsis. In suppurative cholangitis, pus accumulates under pressure within a completely obstructed duct, driving severe toxicity (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735). Nonsuppurative acute cholangitis generally responds well to antibiotics and supportive care. Suppurative acute cholangitis carries a far worse prognosis: response to antibiotics alone is poor and mortality approaches 100% unless prompt endoscopic or surgical relief of the obstruction with drainage of infected bile is achieved. Reynolds's pentad and undue delay in drainage both predict increased morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735). Harrison distinguishes nonsuppurative acute cholangitis (the more common, milder form responsive to antibiotics) from suppurative acute cholangitis (pus under pressure in a completely obstructed duct, with severe toxicity, bacteremia, septic shock, and very high mortality without drainage). Clinically, Charcot's triad (pain, jaundice, fever/rigors) defines the typical syndrome, and progression to Reynolds's pentad (adding shock and confusion) marks the severe/suppurative end of the spectrum requiring urgent biliary decompression (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).

Acute Cholecystitis — Abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging — gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid support the diagnosis. Liver function tests — Typically mildly elevated; significant jaundice should prompt consideration of choledocholithiasis or cholangitis instead. CBC — Leukocytosis supports the diagnosis and tracks response. Blood cultures (if systemically unwell) — May identify bacteremia and guide de-escalation. Choledocholithiasis / common bile duct stone (suggested by elevated bilirubin and/or alkaline phosphatase with biliary pain) (Harrison 22e p.2731) Peptic ulcer disease, especially perforated peptic ulcer (Harrison 22e p.113, p.155) Gastritis / GERD (Harrison 22e p.113) Hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.113) Right lower-lobe pneumonia / pleurisy / subdiaphragmatic abscess (Harrison 22e p.113) Mirizzi's syndrome (cystic-duct/gallbladder-neck stone compressing the CBD with obstruction and jaundice) (Harrison 22e p.2732) Acute cholangitis (overlapping fever, RUQ pain, leukocytosis; empyema of the gallbladder may clinically resemble cholangitis) (Harrison 22e p.2733) Hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.113) Right-sided pneumonia / empyema / subdiaphragmatic abscess presenting as RUQ pain (Harrison 22e p.113) Ultrasound demonstrates calculi in about 90-95% of cases and shows signs of inflammation: gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and bile-duct dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2732). Radionuclide (HIDA/DISIDA) biliary scan can be confirmatory when bile-duct imaging is seen without gallbladder visualization, indicating cystic-duct obstruction; useful when ultrasound is equivocal (Harrison 22e p.2730, p.2732). WBC count typically shows leukocytosis around 10,000-15,000/uL with a left shift (Harrison 22e p.2732). Serum bilirubin is mildly elevated (<5 mg/dL [85.5 umol/L]) in fewer than half of patients; about one-fourth have modest aminotransferase elevations (usually <5-fold) (Harrison 22e p.2732). CT or ultrasound showing a large, tense, static, stone-free gallbladder with poor emptying can support acalculous cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2733). Plain abdominal film may reveal gas within the gallbladder lumen/wall or pericholecystic tissues in emphysematous cholecystitis, and pneumobilia in cholecystoenteric fistula/gallstone ileus (Harrison 22e p.2733). Acute pancreatitis (HIDA scanning can help differentiate acute cholecystitis or biliary colic from acute pancreatitis; serum amylase may rise in cholecystitis as well) (Harrison 22e pp.114-115, p.155) Uncomplicated biliary colic / symptomatic cholelithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2731) Acalculous cholecystopathy (gallbladder dysmotility causing recurrent biliary-type RUQ pain without stones) (Harrison 22e p.2733) Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction causing recurrent RUQ pain (Harrison 22e p.2733) Myocardial infarction / pericarditis (epigastric/RUQ overlap in the acute abdomen differential) (Harrison 22e p.113) Acute cholecystitis usually opens as an attack of biliary pain that progressively worsens and becomes more generalized in the right upper abdomen; pain may radiate to the interscapular area, right scapula, or shoulder (Harrison 22e p.2732). Roughly 60-70% of patients recall prior self-limited biliary attacks before the index episode of acute cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2732). Biliary pain that persists beyond about 5 hours should raise suspicion of acute cholecystitis rather than uncomplicated biliary colic (Harrison 22e p.2731). Fever or rigors accompanying biliary pain generally signal a complication such as cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or cholangitis (Harrison 22e p.2731). Murphy's sign: deep inspiration or cough during subcostal palpation of the RUQ produces increased pain with inspiratory arrest, a characteristic bedside finding (Harrison 22e p.2732). An enlarged, tense gallbladder is palpable in only about 25-50% of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2732). Generalized peritoneal signs and abdominal rigidity are usually absent in uncomplicated acute cholecystitis; their presence should prompt concern for perforation (Harrison 22e p.2732). About 75% of medically treated patients remit within 2-7 days, but roughly 25% develop a complication despite conservative management, and recurrence is common (about 25% within 1 year) (Harrison 22e p.2732). In empyema or free perforation the picture may mimic cholangitis with high fever, severe RUQ pain, marked leukocytosis, and prostration (Harrison 22e p.2733). A sudden transient relief of RUQ pain (gallbladder decompression) followed by generalized peritonitis suggests free perforation (Harrison 22e pp.2733-2734). Generalized peritoneal signs / abdominal rigidity (suggests perforation) (Harrison 22e p.2732) High fever, severe RUQ pain, marked leukocytosis, and prostration resembling cholangitis (suggests empyema of the gallbladder, which carries high risk of gram-negative sepsis and perforation) (Harrison 22e p.2733) Gas in the gallbladder lumen/wall on imaging (emphysematous cholecystitis; considerable morbidity/mortality) (Harrison 22e p.2733) Transient relief of RUQ pain followed by generalized peritonitis (free perforation) (Harrison 22e pp.2733-2734) Acute cholecystitis arising in the setting of severe critical illness (trauma, burns, prolonged fasting, major non-biliary surgery) suggesting acalculous disease with a higher complication rate (Harrison 22e p.2733) Vague post-fatty-meal symptoms (epigastric fullness, dyspepsia, eructation, flatulence) are nonspecific and should not be misread as biliary pain (Harrison 22e p.2731). Jaundice is unusual early in acute cholecystitis; when present it may reflect bile-duct involvement or a coexisting CBD stone rather than simple cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2732). Leukocytosis alone should never be the single deciding factor for operation, and a normal WBC count does not exclude a surgical abdomen including perforation (Harrison 22e p.155). Clinical features of acalculous cholecystitis are indistinguishable from calculous disease; diagnosis depends on recognizing the critically ill setting and using imaging (Harrison 22e p.2733). Emphysematous cholecystitis presents essentially like nongaseous cholecystitis clinically and is identified by imaging, not by a distinct clinical picture; it favors elderly men and diabetics (Harrison 22e p.2733). Acalculous cholecystitis can occur with unusual organisms (e.g., Leptospira, Salmonella, Vibrio cholerae) or systemic disease, so failure to find stones at surgery does not exclude cholecystitis (Harrison 22e p.2733). Acute cholecystitis is acute inflammation of the gallbladder wall that usually follows obstruction of the cystic duct by a stone. Three mechanisms drive the inflammatory response: mechanical inflammation from increased intraluminal pressure and distention producing mucosal/wall ischemia; chemical inflammation from release of lysolecithin (via phospholipase action on biliary lecithin) and other local tissue factors; and bacterial inflammation, which contributes in roughly 50-85% of cases. Chronic cholecystitis is almost always associated with gallstones and results from repeated bouts of subacute/acute inflammation or persistent mechanical irritation of the wall by stones (Harrison 22e pp.2732-2733). Most medically treated patients (about 75%) achieve remission of acute symptoms within 2-7 days, but roughly 25% develop a complication requiring prompt surgery. Among those who remit, about 25% recur within 1 year and 60% within 6 years, so early surgery is preferred. Mortality for emergency cholecystectomy is about 1-3%, versus about 0.5% for early elective cholecystectomy in patients under 60, rising with age and comorbidity. Acalculous and emphysematous forms carry higher complication and mortality rates, and free perforation has a mortality of roughly 30% (Harrison 22e pp.2732-2734).

HIV, or other systemic association that should be screened for Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory compromise mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome requires urgent evaluation and monitoring multifocal motor neuropathy rather than CIDP Coexisting monoclonal gammopathy warrants hematologic workup to exclude POEMS syndrome or malignancy Lack of any response to appropriate first-line immunotherapy should trigger diagnostic reconsideration Mistaking CIDP for a slowly evolving Guillain-Barre syndrome, or vice versa, based solely on time course without full electrodiagnostic correlation Over-reliance on CSF protein elevation alone, which is nonspecific and can be seen in diabetes and other conditions Missing an underlying paraproteinemia or nodopathy antibody profile that changes expected treatment response Attributing residual deficits solely to inadequate treatment when secondary axonal degeneration has already occurred CIDP results from a T-cell and antibody-mediated autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin and, in some cases, the nodal/paranodal region, producing segmental demyelination and secondary remyelination with onion-bulb formation. Some patients harbor antibodies against paranodal proteins (e.g., neurofascin, contactin-1), which behave more like a nodopathy than classic demyelination and may predict differential treatment response. Chronic or repeated inflammatory injury can eventually cause secondary axonal degeneration, which correlates with residual disability. Most patients improve substantially with timely immunotherapy, though relapses are common and some require long-term maintenance treatment. Delayed diagnosis or predominant axonal involvement is associated with greater residual disability.

CNS Tuberculosis (TB Meningitis) — Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis, AFB smear, CBNAAT/Xpert, and culture — CSF in TB meningitis classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, and high protein; CBNAAT provides faster confirmation and rifampicin resistance status than culture. MRI brain with contrast — Identifies basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas, infarcts, and hydrocephalus — all characteristic complications requiring specific management. Chest X-ray — Concurrent or prior pulmonary TB is common and supports the diagnosis. HIV testing — TB meningitis is disproportionately seen in HIV co-infection, which changes overall management and prognosis. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Fungal (subacute/chronic) meningitis, e.g. Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis (p.1124, 1127) Listeria monocytogenes meningoencephalitis (p.1124) Syphilitic (Treponema pallidum) meningitis (p.1127) Neoplastic / carcinomatous meningitis (p.1124) Neurosarcoidosis (p.1124) Cryptococcal meningitis (lymphocytic CSF with low glucose) (p.1124, 1127) Histoplasma and Coccidioides meningitis (p.1127) Listeria meningoencephalitis (p.1124) Neurosyphilis (p.1127) Viral meningitis due to mumps, LCMV, HSV-2, VZV or enteroviruses, which can occasionally cause low CSF glucose and mimic the TB profile (p.1124) CSF AFB smear taken from the last LP tube, or from any pellicle/cobweb clot - but smears are positive in only ~10-40% of adult cases (p.1127). Mycobacterial CSF culture - gold standard, but takes 4-8 weeks and is positive in only ~50% to up to 80% of cases (p.1127, 1389). CSF nucleic acid amplification testing - Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra or Xpert MTB/RIF; in the TB chapter the Xpert MTB/RIF assay has sensitivity up to 80% and is the preferred initial diagnostic option, with treatment started immediately on a positive result; a negative result does not exclude TB (p.1127, 1389). CSF opening pressure measurement (characteristically elevated) (p.1127). Repeat lumbar puncture to increase diagnostic yield, since AFB are infrequently seen on a single direct smear (p.1389). CT/MRI brain looking specifically for hydrocephalus and abnormal enhancement of the basal cisterns or ependyma; contrast-enhanced ring lesions on CT/MRI suggest tuberculoma (biopsy needed to confirm) (p.1389). Neoplastic / neoplastic (carcinomatous) meningitis (p.1124) Neurosarcoidosis (p.1124) Typically evolves over 1-2 weeks (subacute) - a longer course than typical bacterial meningitis; often begins as headache plus subtle mental changes after a prodrome of weeks of low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia and irritability (p.1389). Because meningeal involvement is most pronounced at the base of the brain, cranial nerve palsies (ocular nerves in particular) are a frequent finding (p.1389). Involvement of cerebral arteries at the skull base can produce focal ischemia/infarction (p.1389). Untreated, the disease progresses toward coma with hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension (p.1389). In more than half of cases, evidence of old pulmonary lesions or a miliary pattern is found on chest radiograph (p.1389). CNS TB accounts for roughly 5% of extrapulmonary TB cases; it is seen most often in young children but also in adults, especially those with HIV (p.1389). The last tube of CSF collected at lumbar puncture is the best tube to send for an AFB smear; if a pellicle or cobweb-like clot forms on the fluid surface, AFB are best demonstrated in a smear of that clot/pellicle (p.1127). Empiric anti-tuberculous therapy is often started on a high index of clinical suspicion without adequate laboratory support, given the poor smear yield and slow culture (p.1127). A lymphocytic pleocytosis with low CSF glucose should prompt consideration of fungal or tuberculous meningitis, Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1124). Declining level of consciousness / progression toward coma (p.1389) New cranial nerve palsies, especially ocular nerves, indicating basal meningeal involvement (p.1389) Focal neurologic deficit suggesting arteritic cerebral infarction (p.1389) Clinical or imaging evidence of hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure (p.1389) Acute deterioration with severe headache, confusion, lethargy, altered sensorium and neck rigidity in a previously subacute presentation (p.1389) Low CSF smear yield (AFB seen on direct smear in only ~10-40% of adult cases) and slow culture (4-8 weeks) mean diagnosis cannot wait for microbiologic confirmation - empiric anti-TB therapy is appropriately started on high clinical suspicion (p.1127). Any one of the classic CSF parameters (cell count, protein, glucose) can be within the normal range, so a normal value does not exclude TB meningitis (p.1389). A negative CSF Xpert MTB/RIF result does not exclude TB and requires further diagnostic workup (p.1389). Early in the course CSF may show a neutrophil predominance rather than lymphocytes, which can mislead toward bacterial meningitis (p.1389). Delayed recognition allows the subacute illness to evolve acutely (severe headache, confusion, altered sensorium, neck rigidity) and is the main driver of death and of the ~25% rate of neurologic sequelae (p.1389). Tuberculous meningitis in adults does not arise acutely from direct hematogenous seeding of the meninges. Rather, during hematogenous dissemination of primary infection, miliary (millet seed-sized) tubercles form in the brain parenchyma; these enlarge and usually caseate. Whether a caseous focus produces meningitis depends on its proximity to the subarachnoid space (SAS) and how quickly it becomes fibrous-encapsulated. Subependymal caseous foci discharge bacilli and mycobacterial antigens into the SAS; rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space is a recognized route. The mycobacterial antigens trigger an intense inflammatory reaction producing a thick exudate that fills the basilar cisterns and encases the cranial nerves and the major blood vessels at the base of the brain - explaining the basal enhancement, cranial nerve palsies, arteritic infarcts and obstructive hydrocephalus seen clinically. Meningitis can also result from hematogenous spread of primary or postprimary pulmonary TB, and is a particular concern in very young children and immunocompromised persons (e.g., people living with HIV) (p.1127, 1389). If unrecognized, tuberculous meningitis is uniformly fatal. The disease responds to chemotherapy, but neurologic sequelae are documented in about 25% of treated cases - most often when the diagnosis was delayed. Adjunctive glucocorticoids may speed resolution of CSF abnormalities and raised CSF pressure and lower rates of death or severe disability and relapse; in one trial adjunctive dexamethasone improved survival in patients >14 years but did not reduce the frequency of neurologic sequelae. Among people living with HIV, a placebo-controlled study showed no survival or secondary-endpoint benefit from a 6-8 week tapering course of adjunctive dexamethasone (p.1389). Pharmacogenomic data suggest only a subset of patients benefit from steroids: those homozygous for the proinflammatory LTA4H allele were most helped, whereas those homozygous for the anti-inflammatory allele may be harmed (p.1026). Harrison describes a clinical continuum that maps to the British MRC staging used for TB meningitis: an early stage with headache and slight mental changes after a prodrome of low-grade fever/malaise/anorexia, evolving (if unrecognized) to severe headache, confusion, lethargy and altered sensorium with neck rigidity, and ultimately to coma with hydrocephalus and intracranial hypertension; outcome worsens markedly with more advanced stage at presentation/diagnostic delay (p.1389).

Complicated Urinary Tract Infection — Urine culture and sensitivity — Essential in complicated UTI given higher rates of resistant organisms — guides definitive therapy. Renal function tests — Assesses baseline renal function, particularly relevant if structural abnormality or obstruction is suspected. Renal ultrasound (if recurrent or treatment failure) — Evaluates for obstruction, stones, or structural abnormality contributing to complicated infection. Acute bacterial prostatitis (consider in men with UTI plus systemic symptoms and no other clear anatomic source) (p.1132) Chronic bacterial prostatitis (consider with recurrent UTI in men, especially outside catheterization) (p.1132) Pyelonephritis with or without urinary obstruction (p.1132-1133) Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (not associated with bacteriuria, not improved by antibiotics) (p.1132) Sexually transmitted infection / cervicitis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) presenting with dysuria (p.1133) Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) (p.1133) Herpetic urethritis (p.1133) Urethritis from STI pathogens (gonococcal, chlamydial, Mycoplasma genitalium); urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt STI evaluation (p.1130, p.1133) CT or ultrasound imaging in men with febrile UTI to evaluate for anatomic abnormality or obstruction (p.1132) Blood cultures when complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, or systemic features are present (p.1134 diagnostic algorithm) Urine dipstick (nitrite and leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tools mainly useful for ruling out UTI when the clinical diagnosis is unclear (p.1133-1135) Imaging to identify renal calculi or other nidus, plus assessment for urinary retention, in recurrent UTI (p.1138) Serum creatinine monitoring (a rapid rise may be the first sign of bilateral papillary necrosis) (p.1133) Asymptomatic bacteriuria misclassified as UTI, especially in older patients with isolated altered mentation; degree of pyuria should not drive the distinction (p.1132) Interstitial cystitis (p.1133) Noninfectious vaginal or vulvar irritation (p.1133) Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (p.1132) Harrison defines complicated UTI as infection extending beyond the bladder (e.g., prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or UTI occurring in the setting of intermittent or indwelling catheterization; this is a shift from the older approach that automatically labeled any UTI in men, diabetics, the immunocompromised, or those with anatomic abnormalities as complicated (p.1129-1130). Recurrent UTI is not inherently complicated; individual episodes may be uncomplicated and managed as such (p.1130). Fever, rigors, and unilateral back or flank pain are incompatible with infection confined to the bladder and should trigger evaluation for infection beyond the bladder (kidney, prostate, or bloodstream) (p.1132). In men, UTI is uncommon outside the context of catheterization/instrumentation or obstructive uropathy from prostatic hypertrophy; a urine culture should be obtained in every case of male UTI (p.1132). Men with febrile UTI, even at first episode, should undergo imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, specifically to assess for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (p.1132). Predictors of a surgically correctable disorder in men with febrile UTI include urinary retention symptoms, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties; men with none of these had normal urinary tracts on workup (p.1132). Early recurrence within 2 weeks is regarded as relapse rather than reinfection and may signal a sequestered focus of ongoing infection that needs evaluation (p.1130). Foreign bodies such as stones, stents, and catheters provide an inert surface for bacterial colonization and persistent biofilm formation, serving as a nidus for recurrent infection (p.1130-1131). Initial evaluation of recurrent cystitis should include imaging to identify renal calculi or another nidus of infection and assessment for urinary retention (p.1138). Fever, rigors, nausea/vomiting, and flank pain suggesting severe pyelonephritis or infection beyond the bladder (p.1133) Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy, suggesting intraparenchymal renal abscess (p.1133) Failure to respond clinically within 72 h, prompting evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (p.1137) Gas in renal/perinephric tissues (emphysematous pyelonephritis), almost exclusive to poorly controlled diabetes (p.1133) Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter complicating pyelonephritis (p.1133) Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine, raising concern for concomitant bacteremia / hematogenous seeding (p.1131) Symptoms of urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, or voiding difficulty in men with febrile UTI (predict surgically correctable disease) (p.1132) Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings: it does not reduce future UTI and may even increase risk, possibly by promoting colonization with more virulent/resistant pathogens (p.1129, p.1136). Ending the workup of a febrile catheterized patient at an abnormal urinalysis: bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable with catheterization, so other infectious and noninfectious causes must be systematically excluded before diagnosing CAUTI (p.1133-1134). Premature diagnostic closure in elderly patients with isolated delirium; collateral history is needed and a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB (p.1132). Relying on a negative urine dipstick to rule out bacteriuria in pregnancy; it is not sensitive enough and culture-based ASB screening is required (p.1135). Using nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin as if they treat tissue-invasive disease; they do not achieve adequate renal tissue levels and should not be used for pyelonephritis, and nitrofurantoin is inactive against many Proteus, Providencia, Morganella, Pseudomonas, Serratia, and some Klebsiella/Enterobacter (knowledge of intrinsic resistance) (p.1136-1137). Interpreting a mixed-flora urine culture as infection; it usually represents contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula (p.1135). Most UTIs arise by ascent of bacteria from the urethra to the bladder, with further ascent up the ureter producing renal parenchymal infection; the hematogenous route accounts for under 2% of cases and typically involves virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella (isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia). Whether bladder entry leads to symptomatic infection depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. Conditions causing urinary stasis or obstruction (vesicoureteral reflux, ureteral obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy, neurogenic bladder, urinary-diversion surgery) and foreign bodies that support biofilm all predispose to infection. Uropathogenic E. coli virulence factors include P fimbriae (mediating binding to renal epithelial receptors and important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion) and type 1 pili (mediating mannose binding and initiating bladder infection), plus toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilm formation, and capsules. Candiduria is pathogenetically distinct in that the hematogenous route is more common, and in non-instrumented immunocompetent patients its presence implies either genital contamination or possible widespread visceral dissemination (p.1131). Most simple cystitis carries a low risk of serious complication, but tissue-invasive complicated disease (pyelonephritis and beyond) carries greater risk and patients are often systemically ill. Pyelonephritis may be complicated by acute papillary necrosis with obstruction (requiring relief of obstruction to preserve renal function), perinephric or renal cortical abscess (often requiring percutaneous drainage), emphysematous pyelonephritis (a severe form, almost exclusive to poorly controlled diabetes), and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (suppurative renal destruction associated with chronic obstruction, often by staghorn calculi, that can mimic renal malignancy and frequently requires nephrectomy). Bilateral papillary necrosis is rare but may present with a rapid rise in creatinine (p.1133, p.1137). Harrison frames the practical categorization around whether infection is confined to the bladder (uncomplicated cystitis) versus extends beyond it (complicated UTI: prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) and whether catheter-associated (CAUTI). The key bedside questions are whether the patient is stable for outpatient management, whether a recalcitrant/recurrent source (e.g., obstructing calculi) must be identified, and whether the chosen agent must reach adequate blood and renal-tissue levels in addition to urine. Pyelonephritis itself ranges from mild (low-grade fever +/- back or costovertebral angle pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain) (p.1130, p.1133).

Acute COPD Exacerbation — Pulse oximetry / ABG — Assesses for hypoxia or hypercapnic respiratory failure, which determines need for ventilatory support and site of care. Chest X-ray — Excludes pneumonia, pneumothorax, or other alternative/complicating diagnoses presenting similarly. Sputum culture (if frequent exacerbator or treatment failure) — Identifies resistant or atypical organisms (e.g., Pseudomonas) in patients with recurrent exacerbations. Pneumonia - the most frequent abnormal finding on chest imaging in this setting; about 25% of x-rays obtained for moderate-to-severe exacerbations in severe COPD are abnormal (p.2301). Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, altered mental status (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as PCO2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2301). Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal examination findings (p.2301). C-reactive protein, as part of emerging expert-consensus objective criteria (combining dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases) to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity, mainly of use in the emergency department (p.2301-2302). Pulmonary embolism - should be actively considered because the incidence of PE is increased during COPD exacerbations (p.2301). Congestive heart failure - a common alternative or contributing finding on imaging in patients presenting as an exacerbation (p.2301). Pneumothorax - asymmetry on chest examination may indicate pneumothorax (or large-airway obstruction) mimicking an exacerbation (p.2301). An exacerbation is defined clinically as an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or a change in sputum volume and character), usually evolving over fewer than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2301). COPD exacerbation is a clinical diagnosis; no single test confirms it, and measurement of pulmonary function (unlike in asthma) has not been shown to aid diagnosis or management of a COPD exacerbation (p.2301). The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a history of a previous exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization is a history of a previous hospitalization (p.2301). The cardinal symptoms of a bacterial exacerbation are increased cough with increased sputum production, sputum purulence, and increased dyspnea relative to baseline; nontypeable H. influenzae exacerbations typically show only low-grade fever and no infiltrate on chest x-ray (p.1305-1307). Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens: patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients are not frequent exacerbators (p.2301). A target oxygen saturation of 88-92% is used; in patients with acute or chronic hypercarbia, supplemental O2 does not reduce minute ventilation but may modestly raise arterial PCO2 by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships - this should not deter giving the oxygen needed to correct hypoxemia (p.2302). Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PCO2 >45 mmHg, pH <=7.35) - an indication for noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation, which reduces mortality, need for intubation, complications, and length of stay (p.2302). Severe respiratory distress, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis despite noninvasive ventilation, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest, or hemodynamic instability - indications for invasive mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube (p.2302). New or worsening hypoxemia, severe underlying COPD, or significant comorbidity such as heart failure - features suggesting the need for inpatient treatment (p.2301). Inability to speak in complete sentences, accessory muscle use, perioral or peripheral cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, altered mental status, or paradoxical abdominal wall motion on examination (p.2301). Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention is an error; oxygen should be titrated to 88-92% saturation to correct hypoxemia despite a possible modest PCO2 rise (p.2302). Contraindications to noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation that must be screened for include cardiovascular instability, impaired mental status, inability to cooperate, copious or unclearable secretions, and craniofacial abnormality or trauma preventing mask fit (p.2302). M. catarrhalis is easily mistaken for commensal Neisseria species on respiratory culture and was historically overlooked as a pathogen, so culture interpretation requires care (p.1308). A variety of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation with increased respiratory symptoms. Viral respiratory infection, once thought less common than bacterial infection, is detected by PCR-based studies in over half of exacerbations; acquisition of a new bacterial strain is associated with increased near-term exacerbation risk. Non-infective contributors include air pollution, allergens, and environmental/Aspergillus sensitization, and in a significant minority no specific precipitant is identified (p.1756, p.2301). Mortality for patients requiring mechanical ventilatory support during a COPD exacerbation is 17-49% for that hospitalization. After any hospitalization for COPD, about 20% are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, and mortality is approximately 20% in the year after discharge. Because of the high mortality of invasive ventilation, advance directives (e.g., resuscitation preferences) should be discussed in the outpatient setting (p.2302). Assessment should grade both the severity of the acute exacerbation and the severity of preexisting COPD; the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission. An expert consensus has proposed more objective criteria to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity using dyspnea, vital signs, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases, although this schema is more useful in the emergency department than the outpatient setting (p.2301-2302).

Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis — Urinalysis — Confirms pyuria and supports the diagnosis before starting therapy. Urine culture (only if treatment failure, recurrence, or atypical features) — Not routinely needed in straightforward uncomplicated cystitis, but useful if symptoms persist or recur. Cervicitis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) presenting with dysuria (p.1090) Urethritis, including gonococcal/chlamydial and herpetic urethritis (p.1087, p.1090) Sexually transmitted infection mistaken for UTI, especially with multiple partners or inconsistent condom use; vaginal discharge should prompt STI consideration (p.1090-1091) Vaginitis due to Candida albicans or Trichomonas vaginalis causing dysuria (p.1090) Sexually transmitted urethritis/cervicitis (gonococcal, chlamydial, Mycoplasma genitalium) (p.1087, p.1090) Acute or chronic bacterial prostatitis in men presenting as cystitis-like symptoms (p.1089) Urine dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase as point-of-care testing, used mainly to help rule out UTI when the clinical diagnosis is unclear (p.1091) Microscopic urinalysis (white and red cell counts); pyuria is present in nearly all cystitis and hematuria in about 30% (p.1092) Urine culture when a resistant organism is suspected, in recurrent UTI, after prior treatment failure, or in all male UTI; a colony count threshold of >10^2 bacteria/mL is more sensitive than 10^5/mL for diagnosing cystitis in symptomatic women (p.1089, p.1092) STI screening / pelvic examination in women with risk factors for STI or with vaginal discharge (p.1090-1091) Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (p.1090) Noninfectious vaginal or vulvar irritation (p.1090) Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (not associated with bacteriuria, not improved by antibiotics) (p.1089) Bacteria in the urine without related symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), not UTI; ASB usually needs no treatment and the diagnosis of cystitis requires symptoms, not merely a positive culture or pyuria (p.1086-1087). In an otherwise healthy non-pregnant woman with typical symptoms and no complicating factors, cystitis can be diagnosed and treated on history alone, with no dipstick or culture required (p.1089, p.1091). Patient self-diagnosis of recurrent cystitis is highly accurate, which underlies the success of patient-initiated treatment for recurrent UTI (p.1090). Fever, rigors, or unilateral back/flank pain are inconsistent with uncomplicated cystitis and should prompt evaluation for infection beyond the bladder (kidney, prostate, or bloodstream) (p.1089). A dipstick negative for both nitrite and leukocyte esterase should prompt consideration of non-UTI causes for symptoms, but a small fraction can be falsely negative and a negative dipstick does not fully exclude UTI in a symptomatic woman (p.1089, p.1092). Avoid sending urine cultures in patients lacking urinary or systemic symptoms (diagnostic stewardship) to reduce overdiagnosis of UTI and inappropriate treatment of ASB (p.1089). In older patients presenting only with altered mentation and chronic cognitive deficits, distinguishing true UTI from incidental ASB is difficult; clinicians should look for sepsis, seek collateral history, and rule out other time-sensitive causes of delirium before attributing it to UTI (p.1089). A reported history of recurrent UTIs in an elderly patient may actually reflect persistent ASB rather than true infection (p.1089). Fever, rigors, or unilateral back/costovertebral or flank pain suggesting pyelonephritis or other extension beyond the bladder (p.1089) Perineal, pelvic, or prostatic pain in a man, suggesting prostatitis (p.1089, p.1091) Recurrent cystitis in a man, warranting evaluation for a prostatic focus and for urinary retention (p.1089) Vaginal discharge raising concern for STI rather than UTI (p.1090-1091) Early recurrence within 2 weeks (relapse), suggesting a sequestered focus of ongoing infection (p.1087) Treating ASB as if it were UTI; the degree of pyuria in an asymptomatic patient should not drive a UTI diagnosis, and very high pyuria is common with urinary stasis (e.g., end-stage renal disease, obstructed catheters) (p.1089). Relying on nitrite: only Enterobacterales convert nitrate to nitrite, so it can be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales organisms or with frequent voiding from high fluid intake, and can be positive in Enterobacterales ASB (p.1091-1092). Treating an STI (especially C. trachomatis) as UTI because symptoms overlap; women at risk for UTI are often also at risk for STI (p.1090-1091). Assuming a negative dipstick excludes infection; it is not sensitive enough to rule out bacteriuria in pregnancy, where culture-based ASB screening is required (p.1092). The >10 WBC/HPF pyuria cutoff has poor specificity (about 36%) for UTI; a much higher count may correlate better with symptoms, though >10/HPF remains the accepted standard (p.1092). Misinterpreting a mixed-flora culture as infection; mixed growth usually indicates contamination except with long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or a urinary-enteric/genital fistula (p.1092). Most cystitis arises by ascending infection: gut flora (typically E. coli) colonize the vaginal introitus and periurethral area, then ascend the urethra into the bladder. Introduction of bacteria into the bladder does not inevitably cause sustained symptomatic infection; normal voiding and innate bladder defenses often clear organisms (e.g., after intercourse). Outcome reflects the interplay of host, organism, and environmental factors. Anything that increases bacterial entry or retention raises risk. The shorter female urethra is considered the primary anatomic reason cystitis predominates in young women over young men. Uropathogenic E. coli express virulence factors including type 1 pili (fimbriae) that bind mannose on bladder uroepithelium and initiate bladder infection (P fimbriae are more relevant to pyelonephritis/bloodstream invasion); toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilm formation, and capsules also contribute. Disruption of the normal vaginal lactobacilli (e.g., by spermicide/nonoxynol-9, or estrogen loss after menopause) permits Gram-negative colonization and bacteriuria. Hematogenous spread accounts for under 2% of UTIs. Intracellular bacterial communities within bladder epithelium are demonstrated in models but their clinical significance in humans is unclear (p.1088). Uncomplicated cystitis generally responds promptly and favorably to appropriately chosen modern antimicrobials. About 20-30% of women who have one UTI develop recurrent episodes, and recurrences may cluster after an initial infection; recurrence likelihood decreases as time since the last infection increases. Withholding effective antimicrobial therapy (e.g., treating with NSAIDs alone, or strict delayed therapy) prolongs discomfort and carries a small increased risk of progression to pyelonephritis (p.1087, p.1092). Uncomplicated UTI is infection confined to the bladder in a woman or man without a urinary catheter; complicated UTI is infection extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or occurring with intermittent/indwelling catheterization (CAUTI). Recurrent UTI is not inherently complicated, since individual episodes may be uncomplicated and treated as such. This contrasts with the older approach that automatically classified UTI in men, diabetics, those with anatomic abnormalities, or the immunocompromised as complicated (p.1086-1087).

Clostridioides difficile Infection — Stool C. difficile toxin EIA and/or PCR (per local two-step algorithm) — Confirms the diagnosis; testing only symptomatic patients (not all diarrhea, and never asymptomatic patients) avoids overdiagnosis of colonization. Abdominal X-ray or CT (if severe/fulminant presentation suspected) — Screens for toxic megacolon or ileus, which would change management to include surgical involvement. CBC, renal function, albumin — Supports severity classification (e.g., leukocytosis >15,000, rising creatinine define severe disease per IDSA criteria) which guides treatment intensity. Only diarrhoeal (unformed) stool should be tested; testing of asymptomatic patients is not recommended except for epidemiologic study (Harrison 22e p.1084). NAAT/PCR for the toxin gene is rapid and sensitive but may detect mere colonisation in a patient whose diarrhoea is due to another cause; toxin EIA is specific but insensitive (Harrison 22e p.1084). Recommended multi-step algorithms: NAAT followed by toxin EIA on NAAT-positive results, or GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase common-antigen) plus toxin EIA with NAAT as arbiter when the two disagree; confirming actual toxin in stool is favoured to avoid over-diagnosing colonisation (Harrison 22e p.1084). Empirical treatment is appropriate if stool testing is delayed (Harrison 22e p.1084). Endoscopy (sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy) is highly specific only if pseudomembranes are seen but is insensitive (pseudomembranes visible in only ~50% of culture/toxin-positive diarrhoea); a negative endoscopy does NOT exclude CDI. It is most useful as a rapid test in the seriously ill patient with an acute abdomen and no diarrhoea (Harrison 22e p.1084). Abdominal CT in colitis shows bowel-wall thickening (significantly more prominent than in other colitides), wall oedema, mesenteric stranding and ascites (Harrison 22e p.640, p.1085). CDI is the most commonly diagnosed hospital-acquired diarrhoeal illness and the leading health care-associated infection; it follows ingestion of spores that germinate and produce toxins once the normal colonic microbiota has been disrupted (Harrison 22e p.1082). Almost any antibiotic can precipitate CDI, including vancomycin itself; clindamycin, ampicillin, cephalosporins (especially 2nd/3rd generation), and fluoroquinolones carry the highest risk, whereas penicillin/beta-lactamase-inhibitor combinations carry notably less (Harrison 22e p.1082). Proton pump inhibitors are at most a modest risk factor; the data are weak and PPIs have not been clearly implicated in patients not already on antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1082). Asymptomatic faecal carriage rises with length of hospital stay (often >=20% after 2 weeks inpatient) versus only 1-3% in community residents; neonates and infants are very frequently colonised yet almost never develop disease, attributed to absent mucosal toxin receptors early in life (Harrison 22e p.1082-1083). Stools in CDI are essentially never grossly bloody and have a characteristic odour, ranging from soft/unformed to watery or mucoid (Harrison 22e p.1084). Recurrence after treatment occurs in roughly 15-30% of cases and may be either relapse with the same strain or reinfection with a new one, driven by ongoing disruption of the faecal microbiota by the treating antibiotic; a first recurrence raises the risk of a second (Harrison 22e p.1084-1085). Serum IgG antibody to toxins A and B from prior colonisation/childhood exposure helps determine who develops symptomatic disease versus remains an asymptomatic carrier and protects against recurrence (Harrison 22e p.1083). Spores persist on environmental surfaces for months and on the hands of staff; alcohol hand gels are NOT sporicidal, so soap-and-water hand washing is required during outbreaks (Harrison 22e p.1083, p.1086). Unexplained leukocytosis with WBC >=15,000/uL, especially when stool passage has ceased due to adynamic ileus (ileus seen on x-ray in ~20%) - a clue to unsuspected CDI and a marker of high risk for toxic megacolon and sepsis (Harrison 22e p.1084). Marked leukocytosis >=20,000 WBCs/uL with an acute abdomen suggests fulminant CDI (Harrison 22e p.1085). Fulminant disease may present WITHOUT diarrhoea, mimicking an acute surgical abdomen, with sepsis (hypotension, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis), obstruction/ileus, colon-wall thickening and ascites - include CDI in the differential of acute abdomen, sepsis or toxic megacolon in anyone given antibiotics in the prior 2 months (Harrison 22e p.1085). Toxic megacolon, colonic perforation, shock and the need for colectomy denote fulminant/complicated disease; a rising serum lactate (aim to operate before it reaches 5 mmol/L) signals the need for surgery (Harrison 22e p.1085-1086). Even a single recurrence carries an ~11% risk of serious complications (shock, megacolon, perforation, colectomy or death within 30 days) (Harrison 22e p.1085). Do not perform a 'test of cure' after treatment: >50% of patients keep harbouring the organism and its toxin after diarrhoea resolves, and results do not predict recurrence; such results must not be used to restrict long-term-care or nursing-home placement (Harrison 22e p.1084). Distinguish colonisation from infection - a positive NAAT/PCR in a patient with diarrhoea from another cause may simply reflect colonisation; treating asymptomatic carriers is not indicated (Harrison 22e p.1084). In adynamic ileus the diagnosis is frequently overlooked because stool passage stops - look for unexplained leukocytosis (Harrison 22e p.1084). A negative endoscopy does not rule out CDI, and pseudomembranes are absent in roughly half of confirmed cases (Harrison 22e p.1084). Antiperistaltic agents and opiates may mask symptoms and possibly worsen disease and should generally be avoided (Harrison 22e p.1084). Ingested spores of toxigenic C. difficile survive gastric acid, germinate in the small bowel, and colonise the lower gut once antibiotic exposure has disrupted the protective microbiota. There they elaborate two large clostridial toxins: toxin A (an enterotoxin and potent neutrophil chemoattractant) and toxin B (a cytotoxin). Both glucosylate Rho-family GTP-binding proteins that regulate the actin cytoskeleton, causing loss of cell shape, adherence and tight junctions, with epithelial barrier breakdown, fluid leakage, diarrhoea and pseudomembrane formation. Toxin B appears to be the dominant virulence factor: disease occurs with toxin A-negative but not toxin B-negative strains. A third (binary) toxin, CDT, is present in all NAP1/BI/027 epidemic isolates but its pathogenic role is undefined. Disease typically requires at least three events: antibiotic exposure establishing susceptibility, acquisition of a toxigenic strain, and an inadequate host (anamnestic antibody) immune response. Notably, patients colonised by (often nontoxigenic) strains who have not previously had CDI actually have a DECREASED, not increased, risk of subsequent CDI (Harrison 22e p.1082-1084). Most patients recover, but recurrences are common (~15-30%). Attributable mortality, historically 0.6-3.5%, has reached ~6.9% in recent epidemic-strain outbreaks and rises progressively with increasing age (Harrison 22e p.1086). Harrison applies the IDSA/SHEA-aligned severity tiers as treatment-decision markers: SEVERE disease is indicated by leukocytosis >=15,000 WBCs/uL and/or a serum creatinine >=1.5 mg/dL; FULMINANT (severe complicated) disease is severe CDI plus hypotension/shock, ileus, or toxic megacolon, often with leukocytosis >=20,000/uL and a rising lactate. Mild-to-moderate disease lacks these features (Harrison 22e p.1084-1085).

Dengue Fever — NS1 antigen (early, days 1-5 of fever) — Detects dengue viral antigen early in illness before antibody response develops. Dengue IgM/IgG serology (later in illness) — Confirms diagnosis when NS1 is negative or testing occurs later in the course; IgG pattern can also suggest primary vs. secondary infection. CBC with platelet count (serial) — Tracks thrombocytopenia and hematocrit trends, central to monitoring for plasma leakage and bleeding risk. Hematocrit (serial) — A rising hematocrit with falling platelets signals plasma leakage and impending severe dengue — the single most important trend to follow. Liver function tests — Transaminitis is common in dengue and severe elevation can indicate more severe disease. Zika virus disease (often misdiagnosed as dengue; low-grade fever, itchy maculopapular rash, arthralgia/myalgia, nonpurulent conjunctivitis) Influenza Other arboviral fevers presenting as fever-and-myalgia syndrome Chikungunya Zika virus infection Yellow fever Leptospirosis Other viral hemorrhagic fevers Antigen-detection ELISA or RT-PCR (nucleic acid amplification) during the acute phase, useful within roughly the first 5 days of illness (p.1714, 1721) Combination point-of-care testing pairing NS1 antigen with IgM antibody assay, increasingly used clinically (p.1721) Paired (acute and convalescent) serology during recovery (p.1714) Serum AST (often modestly elevated without true hepatic synthetic dysfunction) (p.1714) Tourniquet test as a bedside marker of microvascular fragility (p.1714) Symptomatic dengue evolves through three phases: febrile, critical (plasma leakage), and recovery; most patients never enter the critical phase, but the possibility must be actively considered in every case (p.1714). The critical/plasma-leakage phase characteristically begins around the time fever subsides (defervescence, roughly days 3-5), so worsening at this transition - not at peak fever - signals deterioration (p.1721). A 'saddle-back' fever pattern (recurrence of fever after defervescence and a brief remission) can occur in a subset of patients (p.1714). Most primary DENV infections are subclinical, and only about 25% of the ~400 million annual infections cause clinical illness (p.1711). Incubation is approximately 4-7 days (p.1714). A positive tourniquet test (>=10 new petechiae per square inch on the upper arm after BP-cuff inflation for 5 min) reflects microvascular damage and is more often linked to severe dengue (p.1714). Near defervescence a maculopapular rash typically starts on the trunk and spreads to the extremities and face; a separate transient macular rash may appear at illness onset (p.1714). During recovery a patchy erythematous pruritic rash that desquamates may develop as extravascular fluid and effusions are reabsorbed (p.1722). Early IgG appearing about 4 days after onset and rising rapidly suggests a secondary (rather than primary) infection, where IgG otherwise appears later and at much lower titers (p.1721). Onset of restlessness or lethargy together with thrombocytopenia (<100,000/uL) and hemoconcentration 2-5 days into illness, typically at defervescence (p.1721) Signs of plasma leakage: rising hematocrit/hemoconcentration, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal effusions (pleural effusion, ascites) (p.1721) Circulatory compromise with narrowed pulse pressure, hepatomegaly, and cyanosis progressing to shock (p.1721) Severe or spontaneous bleeding in the absence of a predisposing lesion (p.1721) Severe organ dysfunction: altered mental status or seizures (CNS), arrhythmias (cardiac), acute kidney injury (renal), hepatic injury (p.1721) Respiratory distress from plasma leakage (p.1721) Anchoring on the febrile phase and missing the critical phase, which paradoxically begins as fever declines rather than at its peak (p.1721). Serologic cross-reactivity with antigenically similar orthoflaviviruses (yellow fever, Zika, Japanese encephalitis virus) - including after vaccination - can confound serologic diagnosis (p.1721). Relying on antigen/nucleic-acid tests outside their acute-phase window: after about day 5 diagnosis must shift to serology (p.1721). Failing to distinguish secondary from primary infection: early, rapidly rising IgG points to secondary infection and higher severe-disease risk (p.1721).
