Dengue is caused by the four flavivirus (orthoflavivirus) serotypes DENV-1 to DENV-4, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti (and the secondary vector Aedes albopictus), which bite during the day. After infection of one serotype, the cross-protection against a different (heterotypic) serotype is only transient and wanes within weeks to a few weeks of convalescence; subsequent heterotypic infection can produce classic dengue or, less often, severe dengue. The progression to severe disease centers on immune-mediated enhancement, in which enhancing, non-neutralizing antibodies are implicated, whereas neutralizing antibodies are associated with lower viremia on reinfection. The hallmark of severe dengue is a vascular-leak syndrome producing increased capillary permeability, intravascular volume depletion, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal (pleural, ascitic) effusions; recent evidence assigns the DENV NS1 protein a key role in this vascular leak. Host/viral risk modifiers include age (susceptibility to severe dengue drops markedly after 12 years), the specific sequence and timing of serotype infections (e.g., DENV-1 then DENV-2 tends to be more severe), and viral-variant heterogeneity (p.1711, 1721). Most patients with uncomplicated dengue recover from the acute illness within 7-10 days, though convalescence may be prolonged and post-acute fatigue and depression are recognized sequelae. Among the millions of annual DENV infections, about 500,000 progress to severe dengue, with an overall case-fatality rate near 2.5%; with early recognition and good supportive care most patients with severe dengue respond well, and CFR at experienced tropical centers can be as low as ~1% (p.1714, 1721-1722). Harrison endorses the WHO pragmatic categories that replaced the older 'dengue fever / dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome' terminology: dengue without warning signs, dengue with warning signs (which directs inpatient management), and severe dengue. Severe dengue is defined as confirmed or presumptive dengue plus at least one of: (1) plasma leakage severe enough to cause shock or respiratory distress, (2) severe bleeding, or (3) severe organ dysfunction. Every patient with presumptive dengue of any severity should be assessed up front for warning signs and for the criteria of severe dengue, with the provisional diagnosis of severe dengue made clinically (p.1704, 1721).

Device-Related Infection (CIED / Vascular Catheter) — Blood cultures (peripheral and through each catheter lumen if not removed) — Differential time-to-positivity (catheter culture positive significantly earlier than peripheral) supports a catheter-related source. Catheter tip culture (if removed) — Confirms the device as the source when growth matches blood culture results. Echocardiography (if S. aureus bacteremia, prosthetic valve, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for endocarditis, a serious complication of device-related bacteremia, particularly with S. aureus. Repeat blood cultures after line removal/initiation of therapy — Confirms clearance of bacteremia, especially important for S. aureus where persistent positivity changes management significantly. Left-sided native-valve or prosthetic-valve endocarditis (may coexist with or be mistaken for CIED-IE) (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1084) Bloodstream infection from an extracardiac focus (e.g., gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia) not arising from the device (Harrison 22e p.1084) Remote-site metastatic infection complicating bacteremic CIED infection, such as vertebral osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1084) Non-device bloodstream infection from a separate source presenting with fever and sepsis in a CIED patient (Harrison 22e p.1084) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): detects vegetations in >90% of patients with definite IE; an initial study may be falsely negative in a minority, so a negative TEE when IE is likely should be repeated in 7-10 days rather than used to exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1083). Three or more separate blood culture sets (two-bottle, ~10 mL per bottle) from different venipuncture sites; if negative at 48-72 h, obtain additional sets and consult the lab for optimal techniques (Harrison 22e p.1082-1083). FDG-PET/CT: less sensitive than TEE for intracardiac pathology in CIED-IE but useful for assessing CIED pocket and lead infection and extracardiac/remote complications (Harrison 22e p.1083). Aspiration of any pyogenic collection at the device/pocket site, combined with blood cultures, to establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1201). Echocardiographic assessment is specifically indicated in monomicrobial S. aureus bacteremia when an intracardiac device is present (Harrison 22e p.1084). CIED-related endocarditis (CIED-IE) involves either the device hardware itself or the endothelium at points of device contact, and occasionally coexists with concurrent valvular infection (Harrison 22e p.1078). The timing of CIED-IE is split roughly into thirds: about one-third present within 3 months of implantation or manipulation, one-third between 3 and 12 months, and one-third more than a year afterward (Harrison 22e p.1078). CIED infection can be obvious from a generator pocket infection (especially within 6 months of device manipulation) or cryptic, arising through bacteremic seeding without any visible pocket involvement (Harrison 22e p.1082). Risk of device-associated endocarditis is reported as higher on implanted defibrillators and resynchronization devices than on permanent pacemakers (Harrison 22e p.1078). In a patient with a CIED, an unexplained Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (and persistent coagulase-negative staphylococcal bacteremia) without another source is likely to indicate CIED-IE or valvular IE and should be investigated and managed as such (Harrison 22e p.1084). Relapse of bloodstream infection after a course of antimicrobial therapy in a CIED patient increases the likelihood that the device is the source and warrants treatment as CIED-IE (Harrison 22e p.1084). S. aureus device-related infections tend to be acute with both local and systemic manifestations and to progress more rapidly than the indolent course seen in non-S. aureus staphylococcal infections; a pyogenic collection at the device site is relatively common (Harrison 22e p.1200-1201). S. aureus bacteremia in a patient with a CIED with no alternative source (Harrison 22e p.1084) Persistent or relapsing bacteremia after antimicrobial therapy in a device patient (Harrison 22e p.1084) Generator pocket inflammation/pyogenic collection at the device site (Harrison 22e p.1082, p.1201) Lead vegetation >2 cm, which carries a risk of pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.1085) Treating an infected CIED with antibiotics alone (salvage/suppression) usually fails and should not be the default approach (Harrison 22e p.1084). Using a negative TEE to rule out CIED-IE when clinical suspicion is high, rather than repeating the study in 7-10 days (Harrison 22e p.1083). In critically ill patients already on antibiotics for other indications, blood cultures may be negative and device-related endocarditis missed (Harrison 22e p.1200-1201). Assuming every bloodstream infection in a CIED patient indicates the device: gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia from an extracardiac focus may not be device-related, though relapse afterward raises suspicion for CIED-IE (Harrison 22e p.1084). Cardiac implantable electronic devices (pacemakers, implantable defibrillators, cardiac resynchronization devices) and other prosthetic intravascular hardware provide an avascular foreign surface that organisms colonize and on which they persist. Infection localizes to the generator pocket and/or the intravascular leads, and may extend to the endothelium at points of lead contact, producing endocarditis (CIED-IE). Staphylococci dominate because skin flora is the principal portal; S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci cause the majority of CIED-IE cases. Once organisms establish on the foreign material, antimicrobial therapy alone usually fails to eradicate them, because the retained device continues to act as a nidus for persistent or recurrent infection (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1201). Removal of the infected CIED during the initial hospitalization is associated with increased 30-day and 1-year survival compared with antibiotic therapy and device retention. Attempted salvage of an infected device with antibiotics alone plus long-term suppressive therapy is usually unsuccessful and is reserved only for patients whose devices cannot be removed or who decline removal; left in place, the device remains a nidus for persistent or recurrent infection (Harrison 22e p.1084, p.1085, p.1201). Harrison distinguishes generator pocket infection without bacteremia (more localized) from bacteremic CIED infection and CIED-IE (more severe, with risk of coincident left-sided valve infection or remote metastatic foci); complete hardware removal is required across the spectrum of established CIED-IE and pocket or intracardiac lead infection (Harrison 22e p.1084, p.1085).

Diabetic Foot Infection — Deep tissue/bone culture (avoid superficial swab alone) — Superficial swabs poorly correlate with the true infecting organism; deep culture better guides targeted therapy. Plain X-ray of the foot — Screens for osteomyelitis and gas in soft tissue. MRI (if osteomyelitis suspected and X-ray inconclusive) — More sensitive for early osteomyelitis than plain films. HbA1c and glycemic control assessment — Poor glycemic control impairs healing and infection clearance; relevant to overall management. Vascular assessment (ABI/Doppler) — Peripheral arterial disease impairs healing and antibiotic delivery to tissue — relevant to overall treatment plan and need for revascularization. Charcot neuroarthropathy (neuropathic joint disease) — can mimic or coexist with foot osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272) Purely neuropathic ulcer without infection (p.3272) Cellulitis without underlying ulceration (p.3272) Probe-to-bone test with a blunt sterile instrument as a bedside clinical assessment (p.92, 1112, 3272) Bone biopsy with culture (preferred basis for diagnosing/treating osteomyelitis given poor swab-to-bone correlation) (p.1112) Cultures taken from the debrided ulcer base, purulent drainage, or wound aspiration rather than superficial swabs (p.3272) MRI when pretest probability is lower or imaging needed (sensitivity 80-100%, specificity 80-90%) (p.1112) Nuclear medicine studies (PET, CT/SPECT) or labeled white-cell scans as alternatives to MRI (p.3272) Ankle-brachial index screening for peripheral arterial disease in diabetics >50 years with risk factors (p.3272) Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy with bony deformity, which can radiographically and clinically resemble osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272) Callus or pressure changes from abnormal foot biomechanics (p.3271) A wound that probes to bone (rock-hard, gritty base without intervening soft tissue) strongly predicts underlying osteomyelitis; the probe-to-bone test has a positive predictive value of ~90% in high-pretest-probability populations (p.1112). In a hospitalized diabetic patient with a chronic deep foot ulcer, the pretest probability of osteomyelitis is high (~65%), so a positive probe-to-bone test can often establish the diagnosis clinically without imaging (p.91, 1112). A negative probe-to-bone test lowers the likelihood of osteomyelitis (likelihood ratio ~0.2) (p.92). An infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis; superficial swab cultures recover multiple organisms of uncertain significance and correlate poorly with bone biopsy (only ~24% concordance in one study) (p.1111-1112, 3271-3272). Culture-pathogen concordance between deep samples and bone is best for S. aureus (40-50%) and poorest for coagulase-negative staphylococci, anaerobes, and gram-negative bacilli (p.1112). About 34% of people with diabetes develop a foot ulcer in their lifetime; among those with an ulcer, ~5% per year progress to foot osteomyelitis (p.1111). Gas gangrene-like findings may occur in a diabetic foot wound even in the absence of clostridial infection (p.3272). Wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) (p.1112, 3272) Chronic ulcer failing to respond to therapy (prompt plain radiographs to assess for osteomyelitis) (p.3272) Underlying peripheral arterial insufficiency / ischemic limb (contributes to non-healing and amputation risk) (p.3272) Charcot foot deformity complicated by chronic osteomyelitis (p.1111) Do NOT rely on superficial swab cultures to guide therapy — they grow contaminants/colonizers and correlate poorly with bone culture (p.1112, 3272). Plain x-rays have limited sensitivity (30-90%) for diabetic foot osteomyelitis and are mainly useful for follow-up of confirmed cases, not for early diagnosis (p.1112). A negative probe-to-bone test does not fully exclude osteomyelitis, especially when pretest probability is low — pursue MRI (p.1112). Antiseptic agents should be avoided and topical antibiotics are of limited value in wound care (p.3272). Diabetic foot infection arises from the interaction of peripheral sensory, motor, and autonomic neuropathy with abnormal foot biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and impaired wound healing. Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain sensation, allowing unrecognized repetitive or major trauma; impaired proprioception causes abnormal weight-bearing and callus/ulcer formation. Motor and sensory neuropathy produce structural deformities (hammer/claw toe, prominent metatarsal heads, Charcot joint). Autonomic neuropathy causes anhidrosis with dry, fissured skin. Peripheral arterial disease and poor healing then allow minor skin breaks to enlarge and become infected. Foot osteomyelitis is almost always acquired by the exogenous (contiguous) route, progressing from skin/soft-tissue infection into bone, and can also follow deep wound infection after foot surgery (p.1111, 3271). Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation. Diabetic foot osteomyelitis increases amputation risk; a foot ulcer (or subsequent ulceration) carries a 14-24% risk of eventual amputation. Adequate management of early-stage infection lowers the amputation rate, and wound debridement combined with antibiotics makes amputation unnecessary in roughly two-thirds of patients (p.1111-1112, 3271). Harrison references the IWGDF/IDSA 2023 guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of diabetes-related foot infections but does not reproduce the detailed IDSA/IWGDF grading scale in this text. Infections are described broadly as mild/non-limb-threatening versus more severe (p.1112, 3272).

Disseminated (Miliary) Tuberculosis — Chest X-ray / CT chest — Classic miliary pattern (diffuse small nodules) supports the diagnosis, though it may be subtle or absent early. Blood culture for mycobacteria (if available) and AFB smear of any accessible fluid/tissue — May provide microbiological confirmation; mycobacterial blood culture has reasonable yield in disseminated disease, particularly in HIV co-infection. Liver or bone marrow biopsy (if hepatosplenomegaly/cytopenias and other tests inconclusive) — Can provide histological confirmation (caseating granulomas, AFB on staining) when other less invasive tests are unrevealing. HIV testing — Essential given the strong association between disseminated TB and immunosuppression, with direct treatment implications. Lumbar puncture (if any neurological signs) — Screens for concurrent CNS involvement, which would extend treatment duration. Disseminated fungal infection (a differential when miliary or interstitial pulmonary infiltrates and multi-organ involvement are present) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Dilated fundoscopic eye examination for choroidal tubercles (pathognomonic, up to ~30% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy for improved bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390) Full blood count for hematologic clues (anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis/leukemoid reactions, polycythemia; pancytopenia in nonreactive form; DIC reported) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Liver function tests including alkaline phosphatase (elevated with hepatic involvement) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Tuberculin skin test (may be falsely negative in up to half of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial test when TB meningitis is suspected; positive results prompt immediate treatment (Harrison 22e p.1393) Presentation is notoriously nonspecific and protean, varying with the organs predominantly seeded; constitutional features (fever, night sweats, anorexia, weakness, weight loss) dominate in most patients (Harrison 22e p.1390). Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopic eye examination are pathognomonic of miliary TB and are present in up to roughly 30% of cases, so dilated fundoscopy is a high-yield bedside step (Harrison 22e p.1390). A high index of suspicion is essential; the diagnosis is easily missed and untreated miliary TB is lethal, whereas early treatment is curative (Harrison 22e p.1390). Sputum-smear microscopy is negative in most cases, so a negative smear does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1390). The tuberculin skin test may be negative in up to half of patients, with reactivity sometimes returning during chemotherapy; a negative TST therefore cannot rule out disease (Harrison 22e p.1390). In adults miliary TB may arise from either recent infection or reactivation of old disseminated foci, whereas in children it more often follows primary infection (Harrison 22e p.1390). Granulomas are often found on liver or bone-marrow biopsy, and bronchoalveolar lavage with transbronchial biopsy improves bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390). Meningismus, present in fewer than 10% of cases, signals possible concurrent tuberculous meningitis and warrants urgent CNS evaluation (Harrison 22e p.1390). Pancytopenia with an acute septicemic course suggests nonreactive miliary TB, a rare and rapidly fatal form from massive dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1390). Disseminated intravascular coagulation has been reported and indicates severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1390). Relying on sputum-smear microscopy or the tuberculin skin test to exclude the diagnosis, since both are frequently negative in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390). Expecting a typical chest radiograph: early in the course, and especially among people living with HIV, the CXR may show no abnormality; findings may instead be large or interstitial infiltrates or pleural effusion rather than the classic miliary reticulonodular pattern (Harrison 22e p.1390). Overlooking cryptic miliary TB in elderly patients with only mild intermittent fever and anemia (Harrison 22e p.1390). Miliary/disseminated TB results from hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis when an acquired immune response fails to contain infection. Bacilli carried to regional lymph nodes reach the central venous return and the systemic circulation, seeding multiple organs with innumerable small (1-2 mm) yellowish granulomas resembling millet seeds. Occult hematogenous dissemination commonly follows primary infection; in the very young and the immunocompromised (including people living with HIV), insufficient immunity allows progression to fatal miliary disease or tuberculous meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1386, 1390). Unrecognized miliary TB is lethal, but with proper early treatment it is amenable to cure. Cryptic miliary TB (seen in the elderly) runs a chronic course with mild intermittent fever and anemia, ultimately progressing to meningeal involvement before death. The nonreactive (acute septicemic) form is rapidly fatal with multiple necrotic, nongranulomatous lesions at postmortem. Glucocorticoid therapy has not proved beneficial in miliary TB (Harrison 22e p.1390).

DRESS syndrome — dress syndrome, drug reaction eosinophilia, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, drug hypersensitivity syndrome, drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome, DIHS, DRESS Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis Viral exanthem (e.g., EBV, CMV, HHV-6 primary infection) Hypereosinophilic syndrome Serum sickness-like reaction Autoimmune connective tissue disease with rash and organ involvement Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) Primary CMV infection Acute HIV seroconversion Measles or other viral exanthems Complete blood count with differential — assesses eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytosis Liver function tests — screens for hepatitis, the most common visceral involvement Serum creatinine and urinalysis — evaluates renal involvement Chest imaging — assesses for pulmonary infiltrates or pneumonitis Skin biopsy — supports diagnosis and helps exclude other severe cutaneous adverse reactions HHV-6 (and other herpesvirus) serology/PCR — assesses viral reactivation contributing to disease course Cardiac enzymes/echocardiography if myocarditis suspected — detects cardiac involvement Thyroid function tests at follow-up — late autoimmune thyroiditis can occur after recovery Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis Hypereosinophilic syndrome Lymphoma with paraneoplastic skin findings Autoimmune/connective tissue disease flare Onset is classically delayed, typically 2-8 weeks after starting the culprit drug, distinguishing it from more immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Look for the triad of fever, widespread morbilliform (often confluent and edematous) rash, and facial edema, especially periorbital swelling. Systemic involvement is the hallmark: lymphadenopathy plus at least one internal organ (liver most common, also kidney, lung, heart) helps separate DRESS from simple drug rash. Peripheral eosinophilia and/or atypical lymphocytosis on blood smear strongly support the diagnosis but may lag behind skin findings. Common culprits include aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, and certain antibiotics — always take a careful medication history covering the prior 2 months. Symptoms can worsen for days to weeks even after the offending drug is stopped, and relapses/flares are common during the recovery phase. Human herpesvirus-6 reactivation is frequently detected during the illness and may contribute to prolonged or relapsing disease course. Cross-reactivity exists among structurally related anticonvulsants, so the entire drug class should generally be avoided going forward. Evidence of fulminant hepatitis or rising transaminases suggesting hepatic failure Signs of myocarditis (chest pain, arrhythmia, heart failure) or interstitial pneumonitis Acute kidney injury with rising creatinine Rapidly progressive skin involvement raising concern for overlap with SJS/TEN Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like features (cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hepatosplenomegaly) Attributing the rash only to the most recently started drug while missing a culprit introduced weeks earlier due to the characteristic delayed onset. Discontinuing suspected culprit and expecting immediate improvement — worsening despite drug withdrawal is common and should not prompt reinstatement. Underestimating disease severity because eosinophilia or organ involvement may be absent or delayed at initial presentation. Failing to screen for and monitor internal organ involvement once the skin findings are recognized, since mortality is driven by visceral disease, not the rash itself. DRESS is a severe, delayed T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction, thought to arise from impaired drug detoxification pathways or specific HLA associations that lead to a robust immune response against drug-modified proteins. The resulting systemic activation of eosinophils and lymphocytes drives multi-organ inflammation. Reactivation of latent herpesviruses, particularly HHV-6, is commonly observed and may amplify and prolong the immune response, contributing to the characteristic waxing-waning course. DRESS carries a mortality risk of roughly 5-10%, primarily related to fulminant hepatic, cardiac, or pulmonary involvement. Even after recovery, patients can develop delayed autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, or other autoimmune conditions over the following months to years, warranting longitudinal follow-up.

Dysentery (Invasive Bacterial Diarrhea) — Stool culture — Identifies the causative organism and susceptibility, the basis for de-escalation or confirmation of empiric choice. Stool microscopy for ova and parasites — Excludes or confirms Entamoeba histolytica, which requires different therapy (metronidazole). CBC — Assesses degree of inflammatory response and any hemolysis (relevant if EHEC/HUS is suspected). Renal function tests — Screens for hemolytic uremic syndrome, particularly important if Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli is suspected. Shigella species (bacillary dysentery; prototypic invasive cause) Shiga toxin-producing / enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (STEC/EHEC, e.g. O157:H7) Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC; shigellosis-like dysentery, shares ancestry with Shigella) Campylobacter jejuni (inflammatory diarrhoea, ~10% grossly bloody in adults) Non-typhoidal Salmonella (inflammatory diarrhoea; full dysentery uncommon) Yersinia enterocolitica (terminal ileitis/right-sided pain mimicking appendicitis) Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery; subacute, travel/endemic exposure) Vibrio parahaemolyticus (can cause dysentery; shellfish exposure) Clostridioides difficile (cytotoxin-mediated colitis; antibiotic/healthcare exposure) Klebsiella oxytoca (antibiotic-associated haemorrhagic colitis) Clostridioides difficile colitis (consider with recent or current antibiotic use, hospitalisation/long-term care; can also be community-acquired without prior antibiotics) Enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica) - penetrating organisms that can present with fever and abdominal pain; fecal mononuclear leukocytes rather than frank dysentery Schistosomiasis and other invasive parasitic colitides in endemic exposure Sexually transmitted proctocolitis (gonococcal, syphilitic, chlamydial/LGV) presenting with bloody mucoid rectal discharge and tenesmus Fecal leukocyte smear (methylene blue wet mount) - suggests inflammatory disease, though predictive value is debated (p.1078-1079) Fecal lactoferrin (latex agglutination or ELISA) - more sensitive surrogate marker of fecal leukocytes than microscopy; fecal calprotectin similarly used (p.306, p.1079) Specific/selective stool culture with isolate retention for Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter (MacConkey/Salmonella-Shigella/selenite media; Campylobacter on selective medium at 42C microaerophilic); sampling the bloody/mucopurulent portion or a rectal swab improves Shigella yield (p.1079-1080, p.1367) Dedicated Shiga toxin / Shiga toxin-gene testing AND culture in ALL community-acquired diarrhoea (inflammatory or not), because bloody stool and fecal leukocytes are not reliably present with STEC/EHEC; O157 screened as sorbitol non-fermenters on sorbitol-MacConkey (p.1080, p.1288-1289) Culture-independent multiplex nucleic acid amplification panels (e.g. detecting STEC, ETEC, EPEC, EAEC, EIEC) - faster and more sensitive than culture, but a positive result should be followed by attempted culture isolation for susceptibility testing and outbreak surveillance (p.1080-1081, p.1289) Stool examination for ova and parasites with E. histolytica-specific rapid antigen detection (microscopy is less sensitive/specific); definitive amoebic diagnosis requires hematophagous trophozoites, as cysts cannot be distinguished from E. dispar/E. moshkovskii/E. bangladeshi; examine at least three fresh specimens (p.1080, p.1756) Amoebic serology (ELISA) - positive in >90% of amoebic colitis/ameboma/liver abscess and useful before starting glucocorticoids when IBD is considered (p.1756) CBC and peripheral smear (microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, schizocytes, thrombocytopenia signalling HUS), renal function/creatinine, and LDH when STEC/EHEC or S. dysenteriae 1 is suspected (p.1288, p.1366) Sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy with biopsy - reserved for uncharacterised persistent diarrhoea or suspected IBD; endoscopic biopsy may not distinguish Campylobacter colitis from IBD, and is hazardous during fulminant amoebic colitis (perforation risk) (p.307, p.1306, p.1756) Inflammatory bowel disease - a first flare of ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease can be clinically indistinguishable from invasive bacterial dysentery, particularly in industrialised settings; travel history and stool studies help discriminate, and IBD should not be diagnosed until invasive infection (e.g. Campylobacter, amoebiasis) is excluded (p.1366, p.1306) Ischaemic colitis - typically age >50, acute lower abdominal pain preceding watery then bloody diarrhoea, with inflammation of the sigmoid/left colon and rectal sparing (p.306) Colonic diverticulitis (p.307) Graft-versus-host disease of the gut (p.307) Intussusception (can mimic afebrile bloody diarrhoea, especially in children) (p.1288) Drug-induced colitis (e.g. NSAIDs and other medication-related diarrhoea) (p.306) Dysentery is bloody diarrhoea arising from mucosal invasion or cytotoxin injury to the colon, not from secretory/enterotoxin mechanisms; the triad of high fever, abdominal pain and grossly bloody stool points to invasive disease rather than toxin-mediated watery diarrhoea (p.306, p.1077). The single most useful initial distinction is inflammatory vs noninflammatory diarrhoea: grossly bloody or mucoid stool, plus fecal leukocytes or a positive fecal lactoferrin/calprotectin, defines the inflammatory (dysenteric) category and a colonic/distal small-bowel locus (p.1079, p.1077). Tenesmus (painful rectal spasm with a strong urge but little stool passage) signals proctitis and is characteristic of the distal-colonic involvement of shigellosis and amoebiasis (p.1078). Bloody diarrhoea with a low-grade fever or no fever is a clinical clue to Shiga toxin-producing/enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC, e.g. O157:H7), which can be mistaken for noninfectious disease such as ischaemic or inflammatory bowel disease (p.1081, p.1288). Unlike most watery diarrhoeal syndromes, dysenteric illness rarely presents with major dehydration; in shigellosis the stools are small-volume and dehydration is uncommon (p.1366). Shigellosis classically evolves through four phases: incubation (usually 1-4 days), initial watery diarrhoea, then dysentery with frequent small bloody mucopurulent stools, tenesmus and cramps, followed by a postinfectious phase (p.1366). On stool microscopy, abundant PMNs in every field favour bacterial enteroinvasive disease (especially Shigella), whereas erythrophagocytic trophozoites with few PMNs favour Entamoeba histolytica (p.1366). Fewer than ~40% of patients with amoebic dysentery are febrile, in contrast to bacterial dysentery; nearly all have heme-positive stools, and amoebic colitis typically has a more gradual onset over 2-6 weeks (p.1754). EHEC/STEC stools are commonly grossly bloody with abdominal pain and fecal leukocytes in ~70% of cases, yet fever is characteristically absent (p.1288). An appendicitis-like presentation (right-sided pain, tenderness) should raise Yersinia enterocolitica, which invades the terminal ileum and proximal colon; Campylobacter and amoebic caecal involvement can similarly mimic appendicitis (p.306, p.1078). Grossly bloody diarrhoea with low-grade or absent fever - suspect STEC/EHEC and the risk of haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (p.1081, p.1288) Falling urine output, pallor, irritability, edema, or new neurological signs after several days of diarrhoea - developing HUS (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute renal failure) (p.1288, p.1366) Abdominal distension and tenderness with loss of haustration / dilated transverse colon - toxic megacolon, a complication of severe Shigella (and severe amoebic) colitis (p.1366) Signs of perforation or peritonitis (rebound, free air) (p.1366) Altered consciousness, seizures or coma - seen especially in children under 5 with severe shigellosis and carries a poor prognosis (p.1366) Severe dehydration (lethargy, feeble pulse, hypotension, shock) (p.1078) High fever (>=38.5C), profuse diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain in patients over 50, or illness in the elderly (>=70) or immunocompromised - warrant prompt stool microbiological evaluation (p.306) Rectal prolapse in a child with dysentery (a recognised complication of severe shigellosis) (p.1367) Do NOT give antibiotics for suspected enterohaemorrhagic/Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (grossly bloody diarrhoea, often afebrile) - antibiotics induce Shiga toxin-producing phage replication, can increase toxin production roughly 20-fold, and raise the risk of HUS; this caution applies especially to children (p.1081, p.1289). Avoid antimotility/antiperistaltic agents (e.g. loperamide, diphenoxylate-atropine) in febrile or bloody dysentery - they may prolong fever and shedding in Shigella, increase the risk of toxic megacolon, and have been implicated in HUS in EHEC-infected children (p.349, p.1077, p.1367). Do not diagnose inflammatory bowel disease before excluding invasive infection - Campylobacter and amoebic colitis can closely mimic and even be histologically confused with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease (p.1306, p.1755). Exclude amoebiasis (stool studies plus serology) before giving glucocorticoids for presumed IBD - unsuspected amoebic colitis can become fulminant or develop toxic megacolon on steroids (p.1755-1756, p.1757). A negative fecal leukocyte/lactoferrin test or absence of fever does NOT rule out invasive disease - STEC/EHEC frequently lacks reliable fecal leukocytes and fever, which is why both Shiga toxin testing and culture are recommended in all community-acquired diarrhoea (p.1080, p.1289). Shigella is fragile and is easily lost in transport (temperature/pH changes); inoculate promptly or use a holding medium (Cary-Blair) and sample the bloody/mucopurulent stool portion or use a rectal swab to maximise yield (p.1367). Microscopy cannot distinguish E. histolytica cysts from non-pathogenic E. dispar (and E. moshkovskii/E. bangladeshi); a microscopic species diagnosis of E. histolytica requires demonstrating trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes (use antigen/molecular testing) (p.1080, p.1756). Empirical antimotility therapy should be avoided more broadly with febrile dysentery; bismuth subsalicylate should be avoided in immunocompromised or renally impaired patients (bismuth encephalopathy risk) (p.349). Dysentery results from injury to the colonic (and distal small-bowel) mucosa by two overlapping mechanisms. (1) Bacterial invasion: Shigella and enteroinvasive E. coli invade mucosal epithelial cells, multiply intracellularly and spread cell-to-cell, producing acute colitis mainly of the distal colon and rectum with edematous, hemorrhagic, ulcerated mucosa. (2) Cytotoxin production: organisms such as Shigella dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin-producing/enterohaemorrhagic E. coli and Vibrio parahaemolyticus elaborate cytotoxins that destroy mucosal cells; Shiga toxins inhibit the 60S ribosomal subunit, shut off protein synthesis, and after systemic translocation injure renal and cerebral microvascular endothelium. The resulting mucosal destruction yields small-volume bloody, mucopurulent stools containing inflammatory cells. Salmonella invades the bowel mucosa and causes inflammatory diarrhoea but generally does not destroy enterocytes or produce the full dysentery syndrome. Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites adhere via the Gal/GalNAc lectin, degrade mucus and extracellular matrix with proteases, and kill epithelial and inflammatory cells by contact-dependent (apoptosis, trogocytosis, pore-forming peptides) and contact-independent cytotoxicity, producing characteristic flask-shaped colonic ulcers and bloody diarrhoea, and can invade the portal venous system to seed the liver (p.306, p.1076-1077, p.1366, p.1754-1755). Most invasive bacterial dysentery is self-limited: shigellosis usually resolves within about a week (faster with appropriate therapy), and STEC/EHEC illness typically lasts 5-10 days. Severe outcomes and death cluster in children under 5 (especially the malnourished) and the elderly. Adverse prognostic features in clinically severe shigellosis include nonbloody diarrhoea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteraemia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, rectal prolapse, and altered consciousness. Haemolytic-uraemic syndrome occurs in roughly 15% of infected children under 10 with STEC/EHEC; with dialysis support its mortality is under 10%, but survivors often have persisting renal and neurological dysfunction; acute renal failure complicates 55-70% of HUS cases yet renal function recovers in most. Postinfectious sequelae include reactive arthritis (after Shigella flexneri, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) and, after Campylobacter, Guillain-Barre syndrome; postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome may follow, particularly after Campylobacter (p.306, p.1288, p.1306, p.1366). Harrison frames severity primarily by the inflammatory vs noninflammatory distinction and by host/feature risk rather than a single formal dysentery score. Inflammatory (dysenteric) disease is defined by grossly bloody/mucoid stool with fecal leukocytes/lactoferrin and a colonic locus. Indications that mark an episode as severe and warranting evaluation/empirical therapy include profuse diarrhoea with dehydration, overtly bloody stools, fever >=38.5C (>=101F), duration >48 h without improvement, severe abdominal pain in patients over 50, and elderly (>=70) or immunocompromised hosts. Dehydration is graded clinically as mild (thirst, dry mouth, decreased urine output), moderate (orthostatic hypotension, skin tenting, sunken eyes/fontanelle), and severe (lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, shock). For shigellosis, severe disease is signalled by features such as bacteraemia, altered consciousness/seizures, toxic megacolon, perforation, severe dehydration, and occurrence in malnourished young children or the elderly (p.306, p.1077-1078, p.1366).

Encephalitis — CSF PCR for HSV (and other relevant viruses) — Definitive test to confirm or exclude HSV encephalitis and guide duration of acyclovir. MRI brain — Temporal lobe involvement is characteristic of HSV encephalitis and supports the diagnosis pending PCR results. EEG — May show characteristic findings (e.g., periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges) supporting HSV encephalitis and helps detect non-convulsive seizures. CSF routine analysis, Gram stain, culture — Evaluates for bacterial meningoencephalitis as an overlapping or alternative diagnosis. Serology for regional arboviruses (e.g., Japanese encephalitis IgM) where endemic — Identifies regionally relevant viral causes that change counseling and prognosis even though treatment is supportive. Southeast Asian outbreaks) SARS-CoV-2 - true viral CNS encephalitis (rare) versus encephalopathy from systemic/hyperinflammatory illness Mycobacteria (tuberculous meningitis/meningoencephalitis) Fungi Rickettsiae Listeria monocytogenes (including rhombencephalitis) Mycoplasma Bartonella and other bacteria Neurosyphilis Naegleria fowleri primary amebic meningoencephalitis (neutrophilic CSF, low glucose, motile trophozoites in warm fresh CSF; warm freshwater exposure) Acanthamoeba / Balamuthia mandrillaris granulomatous amebic encephalitis (can mimic acute viral encephalitis; near-100% mortality) Baylisascaris procyonis (raccoon roundworm) encephalitis - usually children, dirt/raccoon-feces exposure, eosinophilia Leptospirosis Lyme disease and cat-scratch disease Diffusion-weighted and FLAIR MRI sequences in addition to standard MRI - increase sensitivity for HSV temporal-lobe lesions (detect ~90% when added) Repeat CSF HSV PCR if the initial test is obtained within the first ~72 h and clinical suspicion of HSV remains high (early PCR can be falsely negative) CSF virus-specific IgM / intrathecal antibody synthesis (IgG index) - especially West Nile CSF IgM (diagnostic), and VZV CSF IgM as complementary to PCR; HSV CSF antibody testing useful when illness >1 week and PCR negative Store frozen CSF (collect ~20 mL, freeze 5-10 mL) for later virus-specific PCR or metagenomic next-generation sequencing, as many neuroinvasive viruses are only transiently present in CSF Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of CSF/brain for obscure or immunocompromised-host cases Autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody panel in serum and CSF (e.g. NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, AMPAR, GABA-R, GAD65; onconeural antibodies) when infectious workup is negative Brain biopsy - reserved for patients with focal MRI abnormality, negative CSF PCR, no autoimmune serology, who deteriorate despite aciclovir and supportive care Autoimmune anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis - young women/children, viral-like prodrome then psychiatric symptoms, insomnia, reduced verbal output, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability and hypoventilation; MRI often normal; can follow HSV encephalitis (NMDAR antibodies in up to 25% of HSV recoveries) and may be initially mistaken for primary psychosis (p.746-747, p.1114) Other antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitides - LGI1/CASPR2 (anti-VGKC complex), AMPA receptor, GABA receptor, GAD65 (p.1114) Paraneoplastic encephalitis with onconeural antibodies (anti-Hu, Yo, Ma2, amphiphysin, CRMP5/CV2) Hashimoto's encephalopathy (anti-thyroglobulin / anti-thyroperoxidase antibodies) Prion disease Acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis Metabolic/toxic encephalopathy (e.g. hyperammonemia, hepatic failure, intoxication) Encephalitis differs from meningitis by the presence of altered brain function itself - altered consciousness (confusion, behavioural change, lethargy to coma) and focal or diffuse neurologic signs - whereas uncomplicated meningitis spares brain parenchymal function (p.1111). Seizures (focal or generalized) occur in many patients with encephalitis, and prophylactic anticonvulsant therapy may be considered given the high seizure frequency in severe cases (p.1111, p.1115). Clinical features alone cannot reliably establish the specific viral cause; presentations overlap too much, so etiology rests on CSF PCR, serology, imaging and epidemiologic clues (p.1111). Features pointing to inferomedial frontotemporal involvement - prominent olfactory or gustatory hallucinations, anosmia, bizarre behaviour or personality change, and memory disturbance - should specifically raise HSV encephalitis (p.1114). HSV is the single most common cause of sporadic encephalitis and the chief treatable cause, so the central diagnostic task once non-viral causes are excluded is to distinguish HSV from other viruses (p.1112, p.1114). A CSF pleocytosis (>5 cells/uL) occurs in >95% of immunocompetent patients with viral encephalitis; severely immunocompromised patients (HIV, glucocorticoids/immunosuppressants, chemotherapy, lymphoreticular malignancy) may fail to mount this response (p.1112). CSF cell counts exceed 500/uL in only about 10% of cases; counts >1000/uL should prompt consideration of non-viral infection or other inflammatory processes (p.1112). A low CSF glucose is distinctly unusual in viral encephalitis and should suggest bacterial, fungal, tuberculous, parasitic, leptospiral, syphilitic, sarcoid or neoplastic disease instead (p.1112). Prominent brainstem involvement suggests flaviviruses (West Nile, St. Louis, Japanese encephalitis), HSV, enterovirus A71, rabies or Listeria; deep grey matter (basal ganglia/thalamus) involvement with movement disorders suggests flavivirus infection (p.1114). Persisting CSF neutrophilia should prompt consideration of bacterial infection, leptospirosis, amebic infection, and non-infectious acute hemorrhagic leukoencephalitis (p.1112). Empiric aciclovir for suspected HSV should be started immediately on clinical suspicion (especially with focal features) while awaiting diagnostic studies, and is more effective the earlier it is given (p.1115; principle only - no dose). Focal neurologic findings on examination, neuroimaging, or EEG in suspected encephalitis - strongly suggest HSV and mandate immediate empiric aciclovir while testing proceeds Severely depressed or declining level of consciousness / coma (Glasgow Coma Scale ~6 at start of therapy predicts death or severe sequelae) Seizures, particularly status or recurrent seizures Signs of severely raised intracranial pressure (a relative contraindication to lumbar puncture) Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction (temperature dysregulation, diabetes insipidus, SIADH) Acute flaccid paralysis accompanying encephalitis (West Nile, EV-A71/D68) Do not wait for CSF PCR confirmation before starting aciclovir in suspected HSV encephalitis - early treatment improves outcome, and PCR can be falsely negative in the first ~72 h (start empirically, repeat PCR if needed) (p.1112-1115). A negative HSV CSF PCR reduces but does not exclude HSV encephalitis; interpret against pretest probability, timing, and prior antiviral use, and consider repeat testing or CSF antibody studies (p.1112-1113). Worsening neurologic or psychiatric symptoms in the weeks after recovery from HSV encephalitis are often post-HSV anti-NMDA-receptor autoimmune encephalitis (needing immunotherapy), not aciclovir-resistant HSV - test for NMDAR antibodies (p.1114, p.1116). Detecting NMDAR antibodies does not exclude HSV - they appear in up to 25% of HSV-encephalitis recoveries, so still test and treat for HSV when indicated (p.1114). Negative CSF viral culture does not exclude HSV or EBV encephalitis (culture is insensitive; >95% of HSV cases have negative CSF culture) (p.1113). A positive EBV CSF PCR may be non-specific, reflecting reactivation in lymphocytes entering the CNS during an unrelated process - corroborate before attributing encephalitis to EBV (p.1113). Up to ~10% of PCR-proven HSV encephalitis cases have a normal MRI, and CT is normal in 20-35% - normal imaging does not exclude HSV (p.1113). Discontinue aciclovir once HSV encephalitis is excluded (with possible exception of severe VZV or EBV encephalitis) (p.1115). Serum HSV serology alone has no diagnostic value because of high background seroprevalence (p.1114). Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain parenchyma, usually viral (or from a primary autoimmune process). Neurotropic viruses tend to injure characteristic CNS regions, producing the clinical pattern. Associated meningeal inflammation (meningoencephalitis) is common, and spinal cord or nerve-root involvement may co-occur (encephalomyelitis, encephalomyeloradiculitis). HSV has a predilection for the inferomedial frontotemporal/limbic regions, producing the characteristic temporal-lobe imaging and EEG changes and a hemorrhagic/necrotizing process; punctate microhemorrhages explain CSF red cells in some cases. Flaviviruses such as West Nile and Japanese encephalitis virus preferentially involve deep grey structures (thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem). VZV tends to produce a CNS vasculopathy with hemorrhagic and ischemic infarction rather than a true parenchymal encephalitis. Some viral encephalitides (notably HSV, and Japanese encephalitis) can trigger a subsequent antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis, e.g. anti-NMDA-receptor antibodies after HSV (p.1111-1114, p.746). Outcome varies widely by etiology and host factors. For HSV encephalitis treated with aciclovir, roughly 81% survive but only about half of survivors have no or minor sequelae; outcome is directly related to patient age and to the level of consciousness at the start of therapy - younger patients with good neurologic function do markedly better, while those comatose (GCS ~6) at treatment initiation die or survive with severe deficits. Eastern equine encephalitis carries very high sequelae rates (~80% of survivors severely impaired), whereas EBV, California (La Crosse) and Venezuelan equine encephalitis rarely cause severe sequelae. West Nile survivors frequently have prolonged cognitive impairment, weakness, tremor, myoclonus and parkinsonism, with recovery taking many months. Japanese encephalitis case-fatality in hospitalized patients is high (~20-30%) with common long-term neurologic disability; rabies is almost invariably fatal. (p.1115-1117, p.1671)

Enteric Fever (Typhoid) — Blood culture — Gold standard for diagnosis and the only reliable way to confirm S. Typhi/Paratyphi and obtain susceptibility data. CBC — Typically shows leukopenia or normal counts in enteric fever, supporting the diagnosis and distinguishing from other causes of prolonged fever. Liver function tests — Mild transaminitis is common and helps support the diagnosis. Stool/urine culture — May identify the organism, particularly useful for detecting chronic carriers. Malaria Viral hepatitis Bacterial enteritis Dengue fever Rickettsial infection Leptospirosis Amebic liver abscess Acute HIV infection Malaria Dengue fever Leptospirosis Rickettsial infection Viral hepatitis Acute (primary) HIV infection Amebic liver abscess Bacterial enteritis / other Salmonella gastroenteritis Buffy-coat (centrifuged blood) culture — speeds isolation because most S. Typhi reside in the mononuclear-cell/platelet fraction, though it does not raise overall sensitivity (p.1360). Bone marrow culture — about 80% sensitive and, unlike blood culture, its yield is not reduced by up to 5 days of prior antibiotics (p.1360). Culture of intestinal/duodenal secretions (noninvasive duodenal string test) — can be positive even when bone marrow culture is negative; combining blood, marrow and intestinal-secretion cultures gives a yield over 90% (p.1360). Stool culture — often negative in the first week (negative in 60-70%) but may turn positive by the third week in untreated patients (p.1360). Culture of rose-spot punch biopsies (p.1360). Rapid immunodiagnostic serologic tests (e.g., Tubex, Typhidot detecting IgM/IgG to O and H antigens) — point-of-care, low cost, but only ~70-80% sensitive and ~80-90% specific, so insufficient to replace blood culture (p.1360). Blood PCR for S. Typhi/S. Paratyphi — reported sensitivity ~40-100% depending on gene target (p.1360). Both 'enteric fever' and 'typhoid fever' refer to the same systemic illness caused by dissemination of S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi; the names are used interchangeably (p.1358). The classic 'hallmarks' of fever plus abdominal pain are actually variable: fever is present at presentation in over three-quarters of cases, but abdominal pain is reported in only about 30-40% (p.1358). Prolonged fever (roughly 38.8-40.5 C) is the most prominent symptom and can persist up to about 4 weeks if untreated (p.1359). Mean incubation for S. Typhi is about 10-14 days (range 5-21), shortened by larger ingested inoculum (p.1359). Relative bradycardia at the peak of high fever is described in under half of patients (p.1359). Rose spots are faint, salmon-colored, blanching maculopapular lesions on the trunk/chest, appearing in about 30% near the end of the first week and fading in 2-5 days; they are hard to see in highly pigmented skin and Salmonella can be cultured from punch biopsies of them (p.1359-1360). Headache (~80%) and coated/furred tongue are among the most common symptoms/signs; in a Nepal series S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A infections were clinically indistinguishable even though Paratyphi A is generally thought milder and more GI-predominant (p.1359). Diarrhea is somewhat more common than constipation in enteric fever, contrary to older teaching (p.1359). Up to ~10% of treated patients have a mild relapse, typically 2-3 weeks after fever resolves, with the same strain and susceptibility profile (p.1360). Chronic asymptomatic carriage (S. Typhi shed in stool or urine for over a year) develops in 2-5% and is more common in women, infants, and those with biliary disease; organisms persist by forming biofilms on gallstones (p.1360). Gastrointestinal hemorrhage (~6%) — most often in the third and fourth weeks; life-threatening, needs fluid resuscitation and possible surgery (p.1360). Intestinal (ileal) perforation (~1%) — from necrosis/ulceration of ileocecal Peyer's patches, typically weeks 3-4; requires urgent surgery and broadened cover for polymicrobial peritonitis (p.1360). Neuropsychiatric deterioration ('muttering delirium' or 'coma vigil', picking at bedclothes/imaginary objects) (p.1360). Neurologic complications — meningitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, neuritis (p.1360). Shock and obtundation, marking critically ill / severe typhoid (p.1361). Disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemophagocytic syndrome, myocarditis/pericarditis/endocarditis, severe pneumonia, or hemolytic-uremic syndrome as uncommon severe complications (p.1360). No single laboratory test other than a positive culture is diagnostic; the presentation is nonspecific, so a high index of suspicion is needed in any febrile returning traveler from an endemic region (notably the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, or Africa) (p.1358, p.1360). Blood culture sensitivity is only ~40-60% and falls further with low sample volume, prior antibiotics, or sampling in the first week, because very few organisms (<15/mL) circulate — a negative blood culture does not exclude enteric fever (p.1360). Rapid serologic/immunodiagnostic tests are not accurate enough to replace blood culture for diagnosis (p.1360). Leukopenia/neutropenia occur in only ~15-25%; counts can instead be normal or, especially in children or with perforation/secondary infection, show leukocytosis — so the WBC count is unreliable for ruling the diagnosis in or out (p.1360). The textbook triad is fluid: abdominal pain is present in only ~30-40% and splenomegaly/hepatosplenomegaly are documented in a minority on exam, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1358-1359). Fluoroquinolones should no longer be used empirically in regions with high decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility prevalence (Indian subcontinent, parts of Africa); travel from Pakistan raises concern for XDR/ceftriaxone-resistant strains (p.1361). After ingestion (infectious dose ~200 to 10^6 CFU; lower gastric acidity or impaired intestinal integrity raises susceptibility), S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi traverse the small-bowel mucosa via M cells overlying Peyer's patches, using a type III secretion system to induce membrane ruffling and bacterium-mediated endocytosis. Crossing the epithelium, they are phagocytosed by macrophages but survive the intracellular environment by remodeling their surface (e.g., via the PhoP/PhoQ regulatory system) and by delivering effector proteins across the phagosome to remodel the Salmonella-containing vacuole for survival and replication. Carried within macrophages, the organisms disseminate via lymphatics and colonize reticuloendothelial tissue (liver, spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow); the patient is largely asymptomatic during this incubation. Fever and abdominal pain emerge once a critical bacterial load triggers macrophage/epithelial cytokine release recognized by innate immune receptors; hepatosplenomegaly reflects mononuclear-cell recruitment and acquired cell-mediated immunity. Recruitment of mononuclear cells and lymphocytes to Peyer's patches over subsequent weeks causes marked enlargement and necrosis, the basis for later intestinal complications. Many S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A strains also produce a toxin within host cells that is exported extracellularly and probably contributes to systemic and neuropsychiatric features. This contrasts with the mononuclear (rather than neutrophilic) bowel infiltrate that distinguishes enteric fever from nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis (p.1358-1359). Overall case-fatality is about 2.5%, rising to ~4.5% in hospitalized patients and to 10-30% in untreated disease; prompt appropriate antibiotics prevent severe complications and cut mortality to under 1%. Complications occur in roughly 27% of hospitalized patients and correlate with longer symptom duration before admission, host factors, strain virulence/inoculum, and antibiotic choice. Chronic S. Typhi carriage carries an increased long-term risk of gallbladder cancer, especially in endemic regions like the Indian subcontinent (p.1360-1361). Harrison does not give a formal grading scale; it distinguishes uncomplicated enteric fever (manageable at home with oral therapy) from disease warranting hospitalization (persistent vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal distension) and from critically ill / severe typhoid characterized by shock and obtundation, plus complicated disease with GI hemorrhage, intestinal perforation, or other end-organ involvement (p.1360-1361).

Eosinophilic oesophagitis — eosinophilic esophagitis, eosinophilic oesophagitis, EoE, allergic esophagitis, eosinophilic esophageal disease, food impaction-associated esophagitis Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with secondary esophageal eosinophilia Achalasia and other esophageal motility disorders Eosinophilic gastroenteritis with esophageal involvement Infectious esophagitis (candidal, viral) Pill-induced esophagitis Esophageal webs, Schatzki ring, or peptic stricture from other causes Candida esophagitis Herpes simplex virus esophagitis Cytomegalovirus esophagitis Upper endoscopy with multiple esophageal biopsies (proximal and distal) — required to confirm eosinophil-predominant inflammation and exclude mimics Histology quantifying peak eosinophil count per high-power field — supports diagnostic threshold for EoE Trial of acid suppression before/around diagnostic biopsy — helps distinguish reflux-related eosinophilia from primary EoE Barium esophagram — useful to characterize strictures, rings, or narrow-caliber esophagus, particularly pre-dilation Allergy evaluation (skin prick/patch or specific IgE testing) — may help guide elimination diet strategy though imperfect at predicting food triggers Esophageal functional/impedance-pH testing — considered when reflux contribution is uncertain Peripheral eosinophil count and total IgE — sometimes elevated but neither sensitive nor specific Repeat endoscopy with biopsy after treatment — used to assess histologic response to dietary or pharmacologic therapy GERD-related reflux esophagitis Pill-induced esophageal injury Achalasia Eosinophilic gastroenteritis Hypereosinophilic syndrome with esophageal involvement Crohn disease affecting the esophagus Consider EoE in young adults (often male) presenting with recurrent solid-food dysphagia or food bolus impaction, especially with a personal or family history of atopy, asthma, or allergic rhinitis. In children, presentation is often less specific — feeding difficulty, vomiting, abdominal pain, or failure to thrive rather than classic dysphagia. Endoscopy may show characteristic esophageal rings ('trachealization'), linear furrows, whitish exudates/plaques, and mucosal fragility ('crepe-paper' esophagus), but can appear normal in a subset of patients. Diagnosis requires both compatible clinical symptoms and esophageal biopsies showing eosinophil-predominant inflammation, after excluding other causes of esophageal eosinophilia. Proton pump inhibitor-responsive esophageal eosinophilia exists on the same clinical spectrum and no longer excludes an EoE diagnosis; PPIs are considered a treatment option rather than purely a diagnostic exclusion test. Take multiple biopsies (typically several from proximal and distal esophagus) since eosinophilic infiltration can be patchy. Dietary elimination approaches (empiric or allergy-testing-directed) and topical swallowed corticosteroids are mainstay therapies alongside consideration of PPIs. Esophageal dilation may be needed for fibrostenotic disease but carries a higher perforation risk than in other esophageal strictures due to mucosal fragility. Acute food bolus impaction causing complete dysphagia — requires urgent endoscopic evaluation and possible removal Suspected esophageal perforation, especially after dilation given increased mucosal fragility Progressive weight loss or failure to thrive in pediatric patients Signs of a tight fibrostenotic stricture on imaging/endoscopy before attempting dilation Unexplained esophageal eosinophilia not responding to standard measures — reconsider alternative diagnoses (hypereosinophilic syndrome, Crohn disease) Assuming a normal-appearing esophagus on endoscopy excludes EoE — mucosal appearance can be unremarkable despite significant histologic eosinophilia. Relying on a single biopsy site, missing patchy involvement and underestimating eosinophil counts. Treating all esophageal eosinophilia as pure GERD without considering the overlapping PPI-responsive EoE spectrum. Performing aggressive dilation without recognizing the higher perforation risk from mucosal fragility and lack of prior gentle approach. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic, immune/antigen-mediated condition in which food and aeroallergens drive a Th2-skewed inflammatory response leading to dense eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa. Persistent inflammation promotes epithelial barrier dysfunction and, over time, subepithelial fibrosis and smooth muscle remodeling, producing the strictures, rings, and narrow-caliber esophagus seen in longstanding disease. It is closely linked to atopic disease and shares overlapping pathways with asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis. EoE is a chronic, relapsing condition requiring long-term management; without maintenance therapy, symptoms and inflammation typically recur. Untreated or undertreated disease can progress to fibrostenotic remodeling with strictures and recurrent food impactions, but sustained dietary or pharmacologic control can maintain remission and reduce complications.

Erysipelas — None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical based on the characteristic appearance; cultures of intact skin have low yield. Blood cultures (if systemically unwell) — May identify bacteremic spread in more severe presentations. Cellulitis (deeper dermal/subcutaneous involvement, with less sharply demarcated borders) (Harrison 22e p.1210) Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis, which can produce a similar appearance, especially when the lesion is atypical, less intensely red, fades into surrounding skin, or arises around a wound or ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211) Abrupt onset of fiery-red swelling of the face or extremities, with well-defined indurated margins (notably along the nasolabial fold), rapid progression, and intense pain (Harrison 22e p.1052). The sharply demarcated, raised border distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis and reflects involvement limited to the superficial (upper) dermis and superficial lymphatics rather than the deeper subcutaneous tissue (Harrison 22e p.1051, p.1210). A peau d'orange (orange-peel) texture of the skin is characteristic and is thought to reflect involvement of superficial lymphatics (Harrison 22e p.1210). Lesion typically develops over a few hours and is accompanied by fever and chills; flaccid superficial blebs/bullae may appear on the second or third day (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210). Classic distribution is the malar area of the face (often extending over the bridge of the nose to the contralateral malar region) or the lower extremities (Harrison 22e p.1210). Infants and elderly adults are most commonly affected, and the severity of systemic toxicity varies (Harrison 22e p.1052). Desquamation of the involved skin occurs roughly 5-10 days into the illness (Harrison 22e p.1052). Classic cases with typical features are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci, usually group A and occasionally group C or G (Harrison 22e p.1210). Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia suggests loss of vascular integrity and necessitates exploration of deeper structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1051). Unexplained fever with disproportionate pain and tenderness in soft tissue, even without acute cutaneous inflammation, should raise suspicion for a deeper necrotizing process (Harrison 22e p.1051). Atypical erysipelas may involve an unusual anatomic site, appear less intensely red, fade into surrounding skin, or cause only mild systemic illness, in which case a specific clinical diagnosis cannot reliably be made and broader empirical coverage (including S. aureus) is prudent (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211). Extension to deeper soft tissues is rare in true erysipelas; if present, reconsider the diagnosis and exclude a deeper or necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1052). In most parts of the world, acute rheumatic fever is NOT a sequela of streptococcal skin infection (unlike pharyngitis), though post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis may follow either skin or throat infection (Harrison 22e p.1210). Streptococcus pyogenes infecting the epidermis is translocated laterally to deeper structures via lymphatics, producing the characteristic rapid superficial spread of erysipelas. Subsequent engorgement or obstruction of lymphatics causes flaccid edema of the epidermis. The infection is confined to the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics (in contrast to cellulitis, which involves deeper subcutaneous tissue), and extension to deeper soft tissues is rare (Harrison 22e p.1051-1052, p.1210). Generally responds well to therapy; with appropriate treatment, fever, pain, and the intense red color diminish, although swelling may continue to progress initially. Recurrence at the same site (sometimes years later) is not uncommon, particularly where normal lymphatic drainage has been disrupted (Harrison 22e p.1052, p.1210-1211).

Erythema nodosum — erythema nodosum, EN, septal panniculitis, nodular erythema Nodular vasculitis / erythema induratum (lobular panniculitis, often with ulceration, seen more on posterior calves) trauma Streptococcal pharyngitis-associated panniculitis Tuberculosis-related erythema nodosum (erythema induratum can mimic classic EN) Deep fungal infection (coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis) streptococcal infection, the most common identifiable trigger Chest radiograph — evaluate for hilar lymphadenopathy suggesting sarcoidosis or for findings of tuberculosis Complete blood count and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) — assess systemic inflammatory activity, often markedly elevated Stool studies or IBD-directed workup if gastrointestinal symptoms present — assess for inflammatory bowel disease Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay — evaluate for underlying tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions Medication history review — identify possible drug-induced etiology Skin biopsy (deep incisional, including subcutaneous fat) — confirms septal panniculitis when diagnosis is uncertain or lesions are atypical Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age — pregnancy is a recognized trigger Sarcoidosis (with or without Löfgren syndrome triad of EN, hilar adenopathy, and arthritis) Inflammatory bowel disease-associated panniculitis Drug hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., to sulfonamides, oral contraceptives) Behçet syndrome with nodular lesions Pregnancy-associated erythema nodosum Malignancy-associated panniculitis (rare, e.g., lymphoma) Presents as tender, erythematous, non-ulcerating nodules typically over the bilateral pretibial surfaces, sometimes extending to knees, ankles, or extensor forearms Lesions evolve in color like a bruise (bright red to violaceous to yellow-green) over 1-2 weeks without ulcerating or scarring Often accompanied by fever, malaise, arthralgia, and sometimes frank arthritis of ankles/knees Far more common in women, with peak incidence in the second to fourth decades of life Most cases are idiopathic or post-streptococcal, but a broad secondary workup is warranted, especially with atypical features Lesions are typically bilateral and symmetric; unilateral or ulcerating nodules should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis Represents a hypersensitivity reaction pattern rather than a single disease, so the search for an underlying trigger is central to management Usually self-limited, resolving over 3-6 weeks even without treatment of an identifiable cause Ulcerating, unilateral, or persistent nodules beyond 6-8 weeks, suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as nodular vasculitis or vasculitic panniculitis Significant weight loss, chronic cough, or night sweats raising concern for tuberculosis or malignancy Bloody diarrhea or chronic abdominal symptoms suggesting undiagnosed inflammatory bowel disease Marked hilar adenopathy on imaging warranting evaluation for sarcoidosis or lymphoma Recurrent or refractory episodes despite removal of an identified trigger, warranting rheumatologic referral Assuming erythema nodosum is always idiopathic without pursuing a directed search for streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, tuberculosis, or drug causes Confusing erythema nodosum with nodular vasculitis/erythema induratum, which favors the posterior calf and can ulcerate, changing management implications Overlooking Löfgren syndrome (EN plus bilateral hilar adenopathy and arthritis) as a distinct, generally self-limited sarcoid presentation with a favorable prognosis Performing a superficial punch biopsy instead of a deep incisional biopsy, which may miss the septal panniculitis needed for histologic confirmation Erythema nodosum is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction resulting in inflammation centered on the subcutaneous fat septae (septal panniculitis), triggered by circulating immune complexes or antigen-driven T-cell responses to a variety of infectious, inflammatory, or drug antigens. The septal inflammatory infiltrate initially contains neutrophils and later becomes predominantly lymphohistiocytic with multinucleated giant cells, without primary vasculitis. The overlying epidermis and dermis are typically spared, which explains the absence of ulceration or scarring despite the deep tenderness. Erythema nodosum is typically self-limited, with lesions resolving spontaneously over 3-6 weeks without scarring, though it may recur if the underlying trigger persists or recurs. Prognosis is generally excellent and closely tied to management of any identified underlying condition.

Febrile Neutropenia — Blood cultures (peripheral and from each lumen of central line if present) — Identifies bacteremia and distinguishes line-associated infection, both common and consequential in this population. CBC with differential (serial) — Tracks neutrophil recovery, which determines duration of antibiotics and risk stratification. Chest X-ray — Screens for pulmonary source even when respiratory symptoms are minimal, since neutropenic patients may lack typical localizing signs. Urinalysis and urine culture — Screens for urinary source even in the absence of typical symptoms. MASCC risk index calculation — Stratifies low- versus high-risk febrile neutropenia, which determines candidacy for oral/outpatient therapy versus mandatory inpatient IV therapy. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) presenting as abdominal pain and fever in chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression (Harrison 22e p.154) Serial absolute neutrophil count (band forms plus mature neutrophils) to track depth and duration of neutropenia (Harrison 22e p.499) Skin examination for ecthyma gangrenosum suggesting Pseudomonas bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.186) Cross-sectional abdominal imaging when neutropenic enterocolitis/typhlitis is suspected, with serial clinical examination for perforation (Harrison 22e p.154) Acute graft-versus-host disease, which should be considered when a marrow-suppressed/transplant patient develops abdominal pain and fever (Harrison 22e p.154) Drug fever and chemotherapy-related fever in the absence of demonstrable infection Susceptibility to infection rises sharply once the neutrophil count drops below 1000/uL, and worsens markedly at lower thresholds (Harrison 22e p.499). When the absolute neutrophil count falls below 500/uL, the host's ability to contain its own endogenous flora from sites such as the mouth and gut becomes impaired (Harrison 22e p.499). Acute neutropenia from cancer chemotherapy carries a substantially higher infection risk than chronic neutropenia of months-to-years duration, which is often better tolerated (Harrison 22e p.499). After conventional chemotherapy doses, the neutrophil nadir typically occurs about 6-14 days later, defining the window of highest infection risk (Harrison 22e p.617). Certain agents (nitrosoureas, dacarbazine, temozolomide, procarbazine) can cause delayed marrow toxicity that may not appear until roughly 6 weeks after dosing (Harrison 22e p.617). Ecthyma gangrenosum is a characteristic skin lesion of Pseudomonas bacteremia that occurs predominantly in neutropenic patients and is reported in up to roughly a quarter of Pseudomonas bacteremia cases (Harrison 22e p.186). Even highly experienced clinicians may have no advantage over a junior physician in managing the neutropenic patient with fever and hypotension, underscoring the need for protocolized rapid response rather than reliance on intuition (Harrison 22e). Hypotension or hemodynamic instability accompanying fever and neutropenia (Harrison 22e) Ecthyma gangrenosum skin lesions, signaling probable Pseudomonas bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.186) Abdominal pain and fever suggesting neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) with risk of bowel perforation (Harrison 22e p.154) Classic signs of infection and inflammation are blunted or absent in profound neutropenia (local inflammatory response is essentially lost below ANC 200/uL), so the usual physical findings of focal infection may be missing despite serious infection (Harrison 22e p.499). The infecting organisms are frequently the patient's own endogenous mouth and gut flora rather than exogenous pathogens, so absence of an obvious external source does not exclude bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.499). A single normal neutrophil count is insufficient; a falling count or failure to mount a neutrophil response to challenge is what defines risk and warrants attention (Harrison 22e p.499). Most cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents suppress bone marrow function, and polymorphonuclear neutrophils, with their very short circulating half-life of roughly 6-8 hours, are the cell line most rapidly and severely depleted. As the neutrophil count falls, the host loses the first-line cellular defense that normally contains commensal flora at mucosal surfaces; below an ANC of 500/uL control of endogenous mouth and gut organisms is impaired, and below 200/uL the local inflammatory response is essentially absent, so signs of infection are blunted. The combination of profound neutropenia and chemotherapy-induced mucosal barrier injury allows translocation and rapid dissemination of bacteria from the patient's own gut and oral flora. Neutropenia is most commonly iatrogenic, arising from cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy. (Harrison 22e p.499-500, p.617) Risk of serious infection is driven by both the depth and the expected duration of neutropenia; acute chemotherapy-induced neutropenia is more dangerous than chronic neutropenia, and the deepest risk corresponds to the post-chemotherapy nadir at roughly 6-14 days. Pseudomonas bacteremia in this setting is associated with rapidly progressive illness and characteristic ecthyma gangrenosum. (Harrison 22e p.499, p.617, p.186) Febrile neutropenia is defined by fever together with neutropenia (granulocytes below ~1500/uL, with clinically significant risk concentrated at ANC <500/uL and severe impairment of host defense at ANC <200/uL) (Harrison 22e p.499, p.617). Risk stratification for management intensity is performed with validated tools such as the MASCC risk index, which separates low-risk from high-risk febrile neutropenia (referenced in existing curated investigations; specific scoring not detailed in this Harrison excerpt).

Outcomes vary widely by FSGS subtype: primary FSGS achieving remission (spontaneous or treatment-induced) has a favorable long-term renal outlook, whereas resistant primary disease and most secondary/collapsing forms carry a substantial risk of progression to kidney failure over years.
