Presents with abrupt-onset heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema; renal function and blood pressure are typically preserved at onset. Light microscopy is essentially normal ('minimal change'); diagnosis relies on electron microscopy showing diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement. Excellent response to corticosteroids is characteristic and considered almost diagnostic in children; failure to respond should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Frequent relapses and steroid dependence are common, often requiring steroid-sparing agents over time. Can be triggered or associated with recent upper respiratory infection, atopy/allergy, immunizations, NSAID use, or (in adults) underlying lymphoproliferative disease (especially Hodgkin lymphoma). Selective proteinuria (predominantly albumin, low IgG) on urine protein electrophoresis supports the diagnosis. Thromboembolic risk and increased infection susceptibility parallel the severity of nephrotic syndrome regardless of underlying cause. Steroid resistance or failure to achieve remission — reconsider diagnosis (likely FSGS) and pursue biopsy Significant hematuria, hypertension, or renal impairment at presentation — atypical for minimal change disease, suggests alternative diagnosis Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, chest pain, dyspnea) given hypercoagulable state of nephrotic syndrome Severe hypovolemia or acute kidney injury from aggressive diuresis in the setting of low oncotic pressure Signs of serious infection (peritonitis, cellulitis, sepsis) due to functional hypogammaglobulinemia and immunosuppressive therapy New systemic symptoms (weight loss, lymphadenopathy, night sweats) in adults raising concern for occult malignancy Assuming a normal light microscopy biopsy excludes glomerular disease without electron microscopy to assess podocyte foot processes Delaying biopsy in adults presenting with nephrotic syndrome, where minimal change disease is less common and other etiologies must be excluded Misclassifying steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome as minimal change disease when it more likely represents FSGS or another glomerulopathy Overlooking secondary causes (drugs, malignancy) in adult-onset minimal change disease Minimal change disease is thought to result from a circulating permeability factor or T-cell/immune dysregulation that injures podocytes, causing effacement of their foot processes and loss of the glomerular filtration barrier's charge/size selectivity without structural glomerular damage visible by light microscopy. This leads to massive selective loss of albumin into the urine, producing hypoalbuminemia, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, and edema, along with compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidemia. The glomerular basement membrane and capillary architecture otherwise remain intact, distinguishing it from other primary glomerulopathies. Minimal change disease has an excellent overall prognosis, with the large majority of children and most adults achieving remission with corticosteroid therapy and rarely progressing to chronic kidney disease. However, relapses are common and some patients become steroid-dependent or frequently relapsing, necessitating steroid-sparing immunosuppressive strategies.

Mixed Malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) — Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) confirming both species — Definitive method to confirm mixed infection and quantify parasitemia of each species, directly determining treatment approach and monitoring intensity. Rapid diagnostic test (combination P.f/P.v if available) — Can support or suggest mixed infection rapidly, though smear remains the definitive confirmatory test. G6PD testing — Mandatory before primaquine administration to avoid precipitating hemolysis in deficient patients. CBC, renal function, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and escalated care. Urgent antimalarial therapy required (NOT an antibiotic) Single-species P. falciparum malaria with an undetected coexisting vivax/ovale component (the central diagnostic trap of mixed infection) P. knowlesi infection, which on RDT/microscopy may be misidentified as P. falciparum and can reach dangerously high densities (24-h cycle) Recrudescent falciparum vs. true vivax/ovale relapse vs. reinfection as the cause of recurrent fever after treatment Dengue (myalgia typically more severe than in malaria) Leptospirosis (tender muscles, unlike malaria) Typhus Viral hemorrhagic fevers (petechiae/rash, which are very rare in malaria) Bacterial sepsis with incidental parasitemia (concomitant bacteremia coexists with severe malaria and is hard to distinguish, especially in children) Thick and thin Giemsa-stained blood films examined immediately for parasite demonstration AND species identification; examine 100-200 fields before calling a thick film negative PCR amplification for definitive speciation and genotyping when mixed infection is suspected (more sensitive than microscopy/RDT for detecting and distinguishing species) Combination RDT carrying a P. falciparum-specific antigen plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band Quantification of parasitemia (RDTs do not quantify) and assessment of parasite maturity/pigment for prognostic stratification G6PD status (knowledge basis for safe hypnozoite-directed therapy of the vivax component) — testing rationale only Mixed infections (most commonly P. falciparum together with P. vivax) are frequently under-detected by light microscopy and rapid antigen tests; PCR is the most sensitive method and is increasingly used specifically for speciation and genotyping in mixed infections (p.1767). Because microscopy and RDTs may detect only the dominant species, a smear or RDT reported as single-species (especially P. falciparum) does not exclude a coexisting vivax/ovale component carrying dormant liver-stage hypnozoites. P. vivax + P. falciparum is recognized as a distinct co-circulating pattern in endemic mapping, with roughly equal prevalence of the two species in Oceania (p.1761-1762). Standard combination RDTs typically carry one P. falciparum-specific band plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band; this design distinguishes falciparum from the 'less dangerous' malarias but is not optimized to flag concurrent dual infection (p.1766). RDTs may miss low-level P. vivax (and P. ovale/P. malariae) parasitemia and PfHRP2-based tests can be falsely negative where parasites carry HRP2/3 gene deletions — both failure modes can mask one component of a mixed infection (p.1766). The classic regularly-spaced febrile paroxysm at presentation suggests P. vivax or P. ovale (often relapse); its presence in a patient with confirmed falciparum should raise suspicion of a coexisting vivax/ovale component. Apparent vivax/ovale relapses arising after treatment of a mixed infection reflect persistence of liver-stage hypnozoites, which are not cleared by standard blood-stage schizonticides. Coma, obtundation, delirium, or abnormal behavior (cerebral malaria) — attributable to the falciparum component Repeated or generalized convulsions (>2 in 24 h) Respiratory distress / acidotic deep breathing (acidosis, lactate >=5 mmol/L) Hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L) Shock / hypotension with impaired perfusion Severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%) and/or spontaneous bleeding / DIC Hemoglobinuria (black/brown/red urine) Acute kidney injury (creatinine >265 umol/L) Hyperparasitemia (>2% indicates increased risk; >5-10% defines severe disease) — a falciparum-driven marker Prostration / inability to sit or stand unaided Treating an apparently single-species falciparum infection as if vivax were absent: the coexisting vivax hypnozoite reservoir is not cleared by blood-stage drugs and later causes relapse — manage mixed infection as falciparum AND provide hypnozoite-directed coverage for vivax. Relying on microscopy or RDT alone to exclude a second species — both under-detect the minor component; PCR is needed to confirm/exclude mixed infection. Misreading PfHRP2 RDT positivity that persists for weeks after a prior infection as evidence of the current species mix. Mistaking persistent P. falciparum gametocytemia after treatment for treatment failure or active infection. Attributing all post-treatment fever to falciparum recrudescence when it may be a true vivax/ovale relapse from the mixed-infection liver reservoir. Misidentifying P. knowlesi as P. falciparum on microscopy/RDT, distorting the apparent species picture. Sporozoites inoculated by anopheline mosquitoes reach the liver and undergo pre-erythrocytic schizogony; a single sporozoite yields thousands of merozoites that invade RBCs and multiply (every 48 h for P. falciparum and P. vivax). In P. vivax (and P. ovale) infection, a fraction of intrahepatic forms do not divide but persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, later reactivating to cause relapses — a feature absent in P. falciparum. In a mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection, the falciparum component drives the risk of severe disease through cytoadherence (PfEMP1 binding endothelial receptors), rosetting, and agglutination, causing sequestration of mature parasites in vital organs; only ring forms circulate, so peripheral parasitemia underestimates true burden. P. vivax preferentially invades young reticulocytes and produces lower parasitemia (seldom >2%), while P. falciparum invades RBCs of all ages and can reach very high densities. The simultaneous presence of a vivax hypnozoite reservoir means blood-stage cure of both species does not prevent later vivax relapse (p.1760-1763). Promptly treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds ~2%. In a mixed infection the falciparum component dictates the severe-disease prognosis; cerebral malaria carries ~20% mortality in adults and ~15% in children even with treatment, and ~10% of child survivors have residual neurologic deficits (most improving within 6 months). Poor-prognosis features include hyperparasitemia (>100,000/uL), predominance of mature pigment-containing parasites (>20%), pigment in >5% of neutrophils, hypoglycemia, hyperlactatemia, acidemia, and coagulopathy. The vivax component does not usually drive mortality but, if its hypnozoite reservoir is not addressed, predisposes to later relapse and recurrent anemia (p.1763-1767). Severity is governed by the P. falciparum component per Harrison Table 231-2 (Manifestations of Severe Falciparum Malaria): major criteria include unarousable coma/cerebral malaria, acidosis (arterial pH <7.25 / lactate >=5 mmol/L), severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%), renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS, hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L), hypotension/shock, bleeding/DIC, and repeated convulsions; other criteria include hemoglobinuria, prostration, and hyperparasitemia (>5% nonimmune, >10% any patient). Uncomplicated disease = patient can sit/stand unaided and swallow, with no vital-organ dysfunction and parasitemia <2% (p.1763-1764).

Necrotizing Fasciitis — Urgent surgical exploration (diagnostic AND therapeutic) — The definitive diagnostic test — direct visualization of necrotic fascia confirms the diagnosis and simultaneously allows debridement; imaging should not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high. Blood cultures and intraoperative tissue/fluid cultures — Identifies the causative organism(s) to guide de-escalation. CT or MRI (only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable enough to tolerate delay) — May show fascial thickening/gas, but should never delay surgery in a patient with high clinical suspicion. CPK — Markedly elevated levels suggest muscle involvement (myonecrosis), affecting the extent of surgical debridement needed. LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) — Can support clinical suspicion using CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose, though it should not override strong clinical suspicion if score is low. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy) Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle) Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing) Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) — a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate) Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis) Aeromonas soft-tissue infection (freshwater laceration exposure) Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas, neutropenic hosts) Clostridial myonecrosis Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess — most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists) Lactate, d-dimer, coagulation, liver and renal function as markers of systemic toxicity/organ failure Thrombophlebitis (a common early misdiagnosis) Muscle strain or contusion (the minor trauma at the deep nidus) Pain out of proportion to physical findings is the classic early clue: physical signs may be minimal (only soft-tissue edema and mild erythema) while pain and fever are severe; this disparity helps distinguish NF from superficial cellulitis, where skin appearance is more abnormal but pain is only mild-to-moderate. Early disease is frequently misdiagnosed (e.g., as thrombophlebitis) and patients may be sent home with analgesics, especially in the strep type that begins deep at a site of non-penetrating minor trauma (bruise, muscle strain) with no visible portal of entry. Classic late signs evolve sequentially: swelling and brawny edema/tenderness, then dark-red (violaceous) induration, then bullae filled with blue/purple fluid, then friable bluish-maroon-to-black skin; thrombosis of dermal-papillae vessels is extensive by this stage. Paradoxical decrease in pain or progression to anesthesia over the involved area is an ominous sign reflecting thrombosis of small vessels and infarction of cutaneous nerves. GAS NF can be preceded by varicella, childbirth, or muscle strain, and most patients deny an antecedent streptococcal infection. The inoculation site may be inapparent and remote from clinical involvement (e.g., minor hand trauma manifesting as infection over the shoulder or chest). Myositis/myonecrosis coexists with NF in roughly 20-50% of cases and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) may be markedly elevated, signaling deeper muscle involvement. Pain out of proportion to examination findings Rapidly progressing lesion with signs of systemic inflammatory response / toxicity Violaceous (blue/purple) bullae, skin sloughing, dusky/mottled erythema Progression of tenderness to anesthesia over the lesion (cutaneous nerve infarction) Crepitus or gas in deep tissue (suggests mixed/clostridial infection) Renal impairment that may precede shock, plus hypotension/multiorgan failure Urgent surgical exploration supersedes other diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers — debridement is life-saving and must not be delayed Early physical findings are minimal relative to pain/fever, leading to underestimation of severity and misdiagnosis as thrombophlebitis or simple cellulitis. Absence of gas does NOT exclude NF: gas is usually absent when the cause is GAS or MRSA and is seen mainly with mixed/clostridial infection. Normal or nonspecific imaging does NOT rule out NF — CT/MRI may show only soft-tissue swelling and are not specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis. A negative aspirate or frozen-section biopsy does NOT exclude NF (negative in ~80% of cases). Decreasing pain should not be reassuring — it can signal nerve infarction and disease progression rather than improvement. Do not wait for imaging or cultures when NF is suspected with systemic toxicity; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic. NF is infection of the superficial and/or deep fascia investing the muscles of an extremity or trunk, with extensive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and via venous channels and lymphatics, typically sparing the muscle itself in pure fasciitis. Two main microbiologic patterns: a mixed aerobic-anaerobic (type I) process beginning with a breach of a mucosal barrier (GI/GU tract), and a monomicrobial group A streptococcal (type II) process. In GAS disease, organisms reach deep fascia either by transient bacteremic seeding at a site of minor non-penetrating trauma (no portal) or by spread from cutaneous infection/penetrating trauma. Thrombosis of dermal vessels produces progressive skin necrosis; infarction of cutaneous nerves causes the characteristic late anesthesia. NF caused by Clostridium perfringens or extending into muscle (clostridial/streptococcal myonecrosis) carries very high systemic toxicity with hemolysis. PVL-producing MRSA strains have been reported as a cause. Mortality for NF is roughly 11-34% overall and rises substantially when associated with toxic shock syndrome. GAS/clostridial fascial-muscle infection historically carried 20-50% mortality with penicillin alone. Survivors of GAS NF often require repeated surgeries including amputation. Clostridial NF/myonecrosis is far more lethal: spontaneous (nontraumatic) myonecrosis mortality exceeds 65% (often C. septicum with underlying malignancy); trunk infection ~63% vs limb ~12% mortality. Any delay in surgery increases the risk of death; early aggressive surgery markedly improves outcomes. Microbiologic/clinical typing: Type I = mixed aerobic-anaerobic, begins at a mucosal-barrier breach (GI/GU), common in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, surgery, or abdominal penetrating injury; Fournier gangrene is the perineal/scrotal form. Type II = monomicrobial group A streptococcal (GAS implicated in ~60% of NF cases), can occur in otherwise healthy hosts, two presentations (with vs without a defined portal of entry). PVL-producing MRSA is a recognized monomicrobial cause. NF qualifies as soft-tissue necrosis under the CDC streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (hypotension plus >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, hepatic impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous desquamating rash, soft-tissue necrosis/NF/myositis/gangrene). (LRINEC score not described in this source.)

Acute Pharyngitis — Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) or throat culture — Confirms or excludes Group A Streptococcus before committing to antibiotics, directly preventing unnecessary use in viral pharyngitis. Acute infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — marked cervical adenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, palatine petechiae, gelatinous uvula, splenomegaly (Harrison 22e p.301-302) Non-group-A streptococcal pharyngitis (group C and group G streptococci) (Harrison 22e p.302) Gonococcal pharyngitis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) (Harrison 22e p.302) Mycoplasma pneumoniae pharyngitis (persistent sore throat with bronchopulmonary symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.300) Chlamydia pneumoniae pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.302) Haemophilus influenzae pharyngitis (cough and otitis media) (Harrison 22e p.300) Arcanobacterium haemolyticum (scarlatiniform rash) (Harrison 22e p.300) Acute HIV infection (Harrison 22e p.302) Acute epiglottitis/supraglottitis — sore throat with dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, stridor or tachypnea, drooling; airway emergency (Harrison 22e p.302) Peritonsillar abscess — fever, dysphagia, profound throat pain with drooling, trismus, 'hot potato voice', unilateral palate bulge and uvular deviation (Harrison 22e p.302) Retropharyngeal abscess — post-URI in children with sore throat, dysphagia, deep neck pain, neck stiffness, trismus, drooling; severe cases with dyspnea/stridor (Harrison 22e p.302) Submandibular abscess / Ludwig angina — swelling of the floor of the mouth displacing the tongue posteriorly, usually after dental infection or extraction (Harrison 22e p.302) Lemierre syndrome — septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic infection (Harrison 22e p.302) Candida pharyngitis — cottage-cheese exudate that scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface (Harrison 22e p.300) Rapid GAS antigen test: sensitivity ~80%, specificity ~95%; proper technique (swabbing tonsils/pharynx and any exudate or ulceration) is essential to sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.301) Throat culture: single-swab sensitivity ~85-90%; can be falsely positive in carriers; not recommended for routine adult evaluation given 24-48 h delay (Harrison 22e p.301) Heterophil antibody test for EBV mononucleosis (low early sensitivity, rises by week 3) (Harrison 22e p.302) CBC for atypical lymphocytosis in mononucleosis (absolute lymphocytes >4000/uL or relative >50% with >10% atypical morphology) (Harrison 22e p.302) CT imaging for suspected head and neck abscess (except obvious peritonsillar abscess) (Harrison 22e p.302) Lateral neck radiograph in epiglottitis may show the 'thumb sign' (not required for diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.302) Gastroesophageal reflux / laryngopharyngeal reflux (Harrison 22e p.300) Postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300) Head and neck tumors (Harrison 22e p.300) Thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.300) Leukoplakia mimicking exudate (cannot be scraped off) (Harrison 22e p.300) Sore throat is not synonymous with pharyngitis: it may also arise from submandibular/retropharyngeal/peritonsillar space infections, thyroiditis, gastroesophageal reflux, tumors, or postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300). Pharyngeal erythema is most commonly seen with viral infection (common cold, influenza), not bacterial disease (Harrison 22e p.300). Pharyngeal exudate can be mimicked by Candida (cottage-cheese appearance, scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface) or leukoplakia (cannot be scraped off) — do not equate exudate with bacterial pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.300). GAS is the only common cause of sore throat that warrants antibiotics; most non-GAS pharyngitis is viral and self-limited (Harrison 22e p.300). About 10% of adults with sore throat have GAS; in children the prevalence may reach ~35%, peaking at ages 5-15 years, and is higher in winter and early spring (Harrison 22e p.300). Risk of GAS pharyngitis is elevated in health care and child care workers, teachers, parents of young children, and contacts of known strep cases; clinicians should watch for local outbreaks in military and institutional settings (Harrison 22e p.300). GAS carriage is common (up to ~20% of schoolchildren, ~5% of adolescents/young adults); rapid antigen tests and culture cannot distinguish true infection from carriage (Harrison 22e p.301). In adults meeting zero or one Centor criterion, a positive GAS test is very likely a false positive and/or represents carriage; indiscriminate testing of adults with sore throat is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.301). Lower the threshold to test/treat GAS in patients with a history of acute rheumatic fever, documented strep exposure in the past week, those in a community strep epidemic, and diabetic or immunocompromised patients (Harrison 22e p.301). In children the Centor criteria are less specific, so GAS pharyngitis should be confirmed by testing; children with pharyngitis but no viral signs (conjunctivitis, runny nose, cough, hoarseness, nonexudative oral lesions) warrant testing (Harrison 22e p.301). In developed countries the prevalence of rheumatic fever is extremely low, and antibiotic treatment does not prevent poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.300). Full-blown infectious mononucleosis (EBV) appears in only about one-fourth of cases and is a triad of clinical, hematologic, and serologic findings; new EBV causes 1-6% of pharyngitis in young adults and is rare over age 40 (Harrison 22e p.301). Heterophil antibody is detectable in only ~40% of mononucleosis patients in the first week but in 80-90% by the third week, so an early negative test does not exclude EBV (Harrison 22e p.302). Gonococcal pharyngitis is more often asymptomatic than symptomatic; suspect it with persistent sore throat unresponsive to presumptive strep treatment and relevant sexual exposure (Harrison 22e p.302). Diphtheria produces only mild pharyngitis beneath its characteristic grayish pseudomembrane (Harrison 22e p.302). Acute HIV infection causes sore throat in roughly half of cases; consider it when sore throat accompanies headache, fever, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia, and rash (Harrison 22e p.302). Shaking chills/rigors, neck swelling beyond lymphadenopathy, trouble swallowing, drooling, or symptoms persisting >5 days without improvement should prompt urgent re-evaluation (Harrison 22e p.301) Stridor, dyspnea, hoarseness, or tripod/forward-leaning posture with drooling — suggests epiglottitis and impending airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.302) Non-GAS pharyngitis that is not resolving in a teenager/young adult with rigors, neck pain or swelling, or extrapharyngeal symptoms — suspect Lemierre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.302) Trismus, 'hot potato voice', and unilateral palate bulge with uvular deviation — peritonsillar abscess (Harrison 22e p.302) Grayish pharyngeal pseudomembrane in a traveler from an endemic area — suspect diphtheria (Harrison 22e p.300, 302) Prescribing antibiotics to the majority of adults with sore throat despite only ~10% having GAS — most cases are viral (Harrison 22e p.300). Testing adults who meet zero or one Centor criterion: 40-60% of adults with pharyngitis fall here, and a positive test is highly likely to be false-positive or carriage (Harrison 22e p.301). Relying on throat culture or rapid test to distinguish active infection from GAS carriage — neither can (Harrison 22e p.301). Applying adult Centor criteria to children, in whom they are less specific (Harrison 22e p.301). Mistaking Candida or leukoplakia for bacterial pharyngeal exudate (Harrison 22e p.300). Attempting to examine or swab the posterior pharynx in suspected epiglottitis — this can provoke laryngospasm and should only be done in a controlled setting (Harrison 22e p.302). Assuming antibiotic treatment of GAS prevents poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — it does not (Harrison 22e p.300). A negative early heterophil antibody test does not rule out EBV mononucleosis (Harrison 22e p.302). Acute pharyngitis (symptoms generally present for days) is most often caused by respiratory viruses; group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) are a frequent bacterial cause, with other contributors including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, non-group-A streptococci (groups C and G), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Complications of GAS pharyngitis arise from both suppurative spread (e.g., peritonsillar abscess, sinusitis, other invasive GAS infection) and nonsuppurative immune-mediated sequelae (acute rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, scarlet fever) (Harrison 22e p.300-301). Both streptococcal and nonstreptococcal pharyngitis should resolve within 3-5 days. Nonsuppurative complications are rare, and even streptococcal pharyngitis is self-limited in the vast majority of cases; outside the U.S., because complications are rare, some guidelines do not recommend routine GAS testing or antibiotic treatment of sore throat (Harrison 22e p.301). Centor criteria (4 findings, 1 point each): history of fever, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate or swelling. For an adult pretest probability of ~10%, post-evaluation probability of GAS is ~2% at 0 points, ~3% at 1, ~8% at 2, ~19% at 3, and ~41% at 4 points (area under the curve 0.79). Conceptually: 0-1 criteria -> neither test nor treat; 2-3 -> rapid antigen test to guide management; 4 -> rapid test or empirical treatment. (Harrison 22e p.300-301).

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — paroxysmal nocturnal, PNH, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, Marchiafava-Micheli syndrome, PIGA mutation clone, complement-mediated hemolytic anemia Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm or cold antibody type) Aplastic anemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome Hereditary spherocytosis or other membrane defects G6PD deficiency and other hemolytic enzymopathies Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (FLAER, CD55, CD59) on granulocytes and erythrocytes — confirms and sizes the PNH clone Complete blood count with reticulocyte count — documents hemolysis and identifies coexisting cytopenias LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin — supports intravascular hemolysis Urinalysis for hemoglobinuria and urinary hemosiderin — evidence of chronic intravascular hemolysis Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — should be negative, helping exclude autoimmune hemolysis Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with cytogenetics — assesses for underlying aplastic anemia or MDS Iron studies — chronic hemoglobinuria can cause iron deficiency despite hemolysis Imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT/MR venography) if thrombosis at an atypical site is suspected Autoimmune hemolytic anemia Microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (TTP/HUS, DIC) Aplastic anemia without a PNH clone Budd-Chiari syndrome from other hypercoagulable states Cold agglutinin disease Acquired clonal stem-cell disorder from a somatic PIGA gene mutation, leading to loss of GPI-anchored surface proteins (including CD55 and CD59) that normally protect red cells from complement attack. Classic triad is intravascular hemolysis, marrow failure/cytopenias, and a marked thrombotic tendency, though most patients present with only one or two of these features. Morning hemoglobinuria is a well-known feature but is actually seen in only a minority of patients; hemolysis is often chronic and low-grade rather than dramatically episodic. Thrombosis is the leading cause of death and characteristically occurs at unusual sites — hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal, mesenteric, cerebral (dural sinus), and dermal veins. Consider PNH in any patient with unexplained hemolysis plus cytopenia, or with venous thrombosis at an atypical site, especially with a normal or low platelet count. PNH clones frequently coexist with, precede, or follow aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, reflecting a shared marrow-failure background. Smooth muscle dystonia (esophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain) results from free-hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging rather than mechanical obstruction. Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., FLAER, CD55/CD59) on granulocytes and red cells is the diagnostic test of choice, replacing older Ham's and sucrose lysis tests. Sudden abdominal pain, ascites, or hepatomegaly suggesting Budd-Chiari or mesenteric venous thrombosis New neurologic deficit or severe headache raising concern for cerebral or dural venous sinus thrombosis Rapidly worsening cytopenias suggesting evolution to aplastic anemia or MDS/leukemia Severe abdominal or chest pain with hemolysis flare, which may signal smooth-muscle dystonia or thrombotic event Pregnancy in a known PNH patient, which carries substantially increased maternal thrombotic and fetal risk Acute kidney injury from massive hemoglobinuria or renal vein thrombosis Assuming hemoglobinuria must be present and grossly visible; many patients have only subclinical or intermittent hemolysis Missing the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained thrombosis at an atypical site because cytopenias are mild or absent Relying on outdated Ham's/sucrose lysis tests instead of flow cytometry, which is far more sensitive and specific Overlooking a coexisting or antecedent marrow failure syndrome (aplastic anemia, MDS) when a PNH clone is found PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a hematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor required to display several surface proteins. Loss of the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) leaves the abnormal red cell clone vulnerable to unchecked complement-mediated intravascular lysis. The clonal population expands, often in the setting of an immune-mediated marrow injury that gives PIGA-mutant cells a relative survival advantage, producing the combination of hemolysis, cytopenias, and a pro-thrombotic state linked to platelet and microparticle complement activation. Historically PNH carried significant mortality, largely from thrombosis and marrow failure, but complement-inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival and quality of life. Long-term outcome also depends on clone size and any associated bone marrow failure syndrome, with a small risk of progression to MDS or acute leukemia over time.

POEMS syndrome — poems, osteosclerotic myeloma, Crow-Fukase syndrome, Takatsuki syndrome, PEP syndrome, polyneuropathy organomegaly endocrinopathy M-protein skin changes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) without associated plasma cell disorder Multiple myeloma with peripheral neuropathy Waldenström macroglobulinemia / IgM-related neuropathy Castleman disease (may overlap with or occur alongside POEMS) Amyloidosis (AL) with neuropathy and organomegaly Diabetic or other systemic causes of sensorimotor polyneuropathy Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — detects and characterizes the monoclonal (typically lambda) protein Serum free light chain ratio — supports clonality assessment Serum VEGF level — supports diagnosis and can track disease activity Skeletal survey and/or whole-body imaging (CT or PET) — identifies characteristic sclerotic or mixed bone lesions Nerve conduction studies/EMG — confirms demyelinating polyneuropathy pattern Bone marrow biopsy — quantifies clonal plasma cells and excludes overt myeloma Endocrine panel (thyroid, gonadal, adrenal, glucose) — screens for associated endocrinopathies Echocardiography and pulmonary function testing — assesses for pulmonary hypertension and extravascular volume overload CIDP (idiopathic) Amyloid neuropathy Diabetic polyneuropathy with unrelated monoclonal gammopathy (MGUS) Castleman disease without POEMS features Hypothyroid-associated neuropathy Rare paraneoplastic disorder driven by an underlying clonal plasma cell process, almost always with lambda light-chain restriction. Peripheral polyneuropathy is typically the presenting and most disabling feature — usually a symmetric, ascending, demyelinating sensorimotor pattern resembling CIDP. Suspect POEMS when 'CIDP' fails to respond to standard immunotherapy, especially if accompanied by systemic features. Sclerotic bone lesions (solitary or multiple) are common and often visible on skeletal survey or CT even without lytic disease typical of myeloma. Papilledema, extravascular volume overload (ascites, edema, effusions), and thrombocytosis/erythrocytosis are distinctive clues that separate POEMS from typical myeloma or CIDP. Markedly elevated serum VEGF is a hallmark biomarker reflecting disease activity. Endocrinopathies (commonly hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, or glucose intolerance) are frequent but nonspecific, and should not be over-interpreted alone. Skin changes (hyperpigmentation, thickening, hypertrichosis, glomeruloid hemangiomas) support the diagnosis when present alongside neuropathy. Rapidly progressive neuropathy with respiratory or bulbar involvement New papilledema suggesting raised intracranial pressure Signs of extravascular volume overload (ascites, pleural effusion, peripheral edema) indicating advancing systemic disease Evidence of pulmonary hypertension or thrombotic events, which portend higher morbidity Rapid rise in serum VEGF or new osteolytic transformation suggesting progression or evolution toward myeloma Misdiagnosing as idiopathic CIDP and treating with standard immunotherapy (e.g., IVIG/plasma exchange) alone, which is typically ineffective since the underlying plasma cell clone is not addressed Overlooking sclerotic bone lesions on imaging because they lack the classic lytic appearance of multiple myeloma Failing to check serum VEGF or overinterpreting an isolated endocrinopathy without considering the full multisystem picture Anchoring on a single feature (e.g., organomegaly) rather than recognizing the required combination of core diagnostic criteria POEMS syndrome arises from an underlying monoclonal, lambda-restricted plasma cell disorder that drives systemic overproduction of proinflammatory and proangiogenic cytokines, most notably vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). This cytokine excess is thought to underlie the vascular, neurologic, and organ-based manifestations rather than direct tumor infiltration, distinguishing the disease from classic multiple myeloma. The resulting syndrome combines a chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy with multisystem involvement including bone, endocrine, dermatologic, and extravascular fluid abnormalities. With clone-directed therapy, many patients achieve meaningful and durable improvement in neuropathy and systemic features, and overall survival is generally more favorable than multiple myeloma. However, residual neurologic deficits are common, and relapse or progression can occur, warranting long-term surveillance of the monoclonal marker and VEGF level.

(apparent mineralocorticoid excess) Liddle syndrome Diuretic-induced hypokalemia with secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism Renal artery stenosis with secondary hyperaldosteronism Chronic laxative abuse or bulimia causing hypokalemia Consider in any hypertensive patient with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia, treatment-resistant hypertension, or an incidentally found adrenal from bilateral disease before considering surgery, since imaging alone is unreliable in this regard Correcting the underlying aldosterone excess improves blood pressure control and reduces the excess cardiovascular and renal risk associated with this condition beyond what is expected from hypertension alone Severe or refractory hypokalemia with muscle weakness, cramps, or cardiac arrhythmia Resistant hypertension requiring three or more antihypertensive agents including a diuretic Adrenal incidentaloma with hypertension or hypokalemia raising concern for functioning adenoma or carcinoma Very young age of hypertension onset or hypertensive stroke in a young relative, suggesting a familial syndrome Large or irregular adrenal mass on imaging raising concern for adrenocortical carcinoma Failing to correct hypokalemia and withdraw interfering drugs (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, high-dose diuretics) before aldosterone-to-renin ratio testing, leading to false results Relying on adrenal CT alone to decide unilateral versus bilateral disease instead of adrenal vein sampling, risking inappropriate or missed surgery Assuming normokalemia excludes the diagnosis and therefore not screening appropriately hypertensive patients Misattributing resistant hypertension to poor adherence or essential hypertension without screening for secondary causes Autonomous, renin-independent overproduction of aldosterone from one or both adrenal glands leads to sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, and volume-mediated hypertension. The excess mineralocorticoid activity suppresses plasma renin and can produce hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, though many patients remain normokalemic. Beyond hemodynamic effects, chronic aldosterone excess produces direct pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory effects on the heart, vasculature, and kidney that account for disproportionate target-organ damage relative to blood pressure alone. With correct subtype classification, unilateral disease treated surgically often achieves cure or major improvement of hypertension and hypokalemia, while bilateral disease managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists generally achieves good blood pressure control. Untreated or unrecognized disease carries excess risk of cardiovascular events, stroke, and chronic kidney disease compared with blood-pressure-matched essential hypertension.
