cranial nerves, hypothalamic-pituitary axis, brain parenchyma, or spinal cord. The granulomas provoke a perivascular and leptomeningeal inflammatory response that can cause direct compressive or infiltrative neurologic deficits, hydrocephalus from impaired CSF flow, or vasculopathy. Because it is part of a systemic multisystem granulomatous disease, isolated CNS presentations without other organ involvement are diagnostically challenging. Course is variable — many patients respond to immunosuppressive therapy with partial or complete resolution, but a subset experience chronic, relapsing, or progressive disease, particularly with parenchymal brain or spinal cord involvement, which carries a worse functional outcome.

Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis — Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — Defines the diagnosis (neutrophil count ≥250/mm³) and identifies the organism for targeted therapy — essential before committing to a full antibiotic course where feasible. Blood cultures — Frequently positive and may identify the organism even when ascitic fluid culture is negative (culture-negative neutrocytic ascites). Renal function tests — Guides decision on adjunctive albumin and assesses for hepatorenal syndrome, a major complication of SBP. Liver function tests and coagulation profile — Establishes baseline severity of underlying liver disease, relevant to prognosis and overall management. Secondary bacterial peritonitis from a perforated or inflamed viscus or intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071) Hepatic encephalopathy from other precipitants (GI bleed, volume depletion, hyponatremia, constipation) when SBP presents as altered mentation (Harrison 22e p.2716-2717) Acute kidney injury / hepatorenal syndrome from non-infectious causes when SBP presents as renal deterioration (Harrison 22e p.329, 2716) Secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforated viscus, ruptured appendix/diverticulum/ulcer, intraabdominal abscess) (Harrison 22e p.1071-1072) Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax (Harrison 22e p.330) Tuberculous peritonitis (ascitic lymphocytosis; can complicate or mimic infected ascites) (Harrison 22e p.373) Ascitic fluid PMN/neutrophil count (>=250/microL is diagnostic) (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070) Ascitic fluid inoculated into blood-culture bottles at the bedside (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070) Gram stain of ascitic fluid (often negative; does not exclude SBP) (Harrison 22e p.1070) Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and ascitic total protein to characterize the underlying ascites and assess risk (Harrison 22e p.372) Ascitic glucose and LDH when secondary peritonitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.373) Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to seek an intraabdominal source / exclude secondary peritonitis (Harrison 22e p.1070-1071) Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air (perforation) when abdominal pain is present (Harrison 22e p.1070) Repeat paracentesis at 48 hours to confirm >=25% fall in ascitic PMN count (Harrison 22e p.329) Peritoneal carcinomatosis / malignant ascites (low-SAAG ascites; SBP is rare in malignant ascites) (Harrison 22e p.372-373) Pancreatic ascites (high ascitic amylase, typically >1000) (Harrison 22e p.373) Worsening uncomplicated tense ascites with increased girth but no infection (Harrison 22e p.329) An ascitic-fluid PMN (neutrophil) count of at least 250/microL is diagnostic of SBP, irrespective of whether cultures grow an organism (Harrison 22e p.329, 372, 1070). Fever is the single most common manifestation, present in roughly 80% of cases; abdominal pain, acute onset, and peritoneal signs aid diagnosis but their absence does not rule SBP out (Harrison 22e p.1070). Abdominal tenderness is found in only about 40% of patients and rebound tenderness is uncommon, so a benign abdomen does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329). SBP can present with no abdominal symptoms at all, instead manifesting as new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, altered mental status, jaundice, or acute kidney injury without another explanation (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715). In any cirrhotic patient hospitalized with ascites who deteriorates or shows signs of infection, a diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory; tapping within 12 hours of admission lowers mortality through early SBP detection (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715). Ascitic fluid should be injected directly into blood-culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield, and blood cultures drawn simultaneously, since the organism burden in the fluid is low and bacteremia frequently coexists (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070). Culture samples should be obtained before antibiotics are started to maximize recovery of the organism (Harrison 22e p.1070). SBP is almost always monomicrobial; a single isolate is the rule (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070). Gram stain of ascitic fluid is frequently negative in SBP and a negative result should not deter treatment (Harrison 22e p.1070). SBP virtually always arises on a background of preexisting ascites, which predates the infection (Harrison 22e p.1070). A repeat paracentesis after 48 hours of therapy should confirm at least a 25% fall in the ascitic PMN count from baseline; failure to fall, or persistent ascitic leukocytosis after treatment, should prompt a search for an alternative or secondary diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071). New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy or altered mental status in a cirrhotic with ascites (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715) Unexplained acute kidney injury, jaundice, or nonlocalizing malaise/fatigue in a susceptible patient (Harrison 22e p.1070) Multiple organisms recovered from ascitic fluid, especially with anaerobes, suggesting secondary peritonitis requiring source control (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071) Free air under the diaphragm on imaging, signaling perforation (Harrison 22e p.1070) Concurrent GI/variceal bleeding, which markedly increases SBP frequency (Harrison 22e p.330, 2716) Failure of the ascitic PMN count to fall, or persistence of WBCs after therapy, indicating treatment failure or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071) Diagnosis rests on the ascitic PMN count >=250/microL, not on a positive culture; ascitic cultures are often negative because the organism burden is low (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070). Recovery of more than one organism (a mixed flora, especially with anaerobes) alongside an elevated PMN count points to SECONDARY peritonitis from a ruptured viscus or abscess, not SBP, and demands a search for a surgical source (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071). Multiple organisms WITHOUT an elevated PMN count suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle rather than true infection (Harrison 22e p.329). Failing to perform a diagnostic paracentesis in a decompensated cirrhotic who deteriorates (encephalopathy, AKI, sepsis) misses SBP, since the abdomen may be benign and tenderness is present in only ~40% (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715). A low ascitic total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL) reflects low opsonic activity and identifies patients at higher risk for SBP; this group warrants heightened suspicion (Harrison 22e p.330, 1071). The 250/microL PMN threshold is specific to SBP and should not be applied to secondary peritonitis or to peritoneal-dialysis peritonitis, where lower leukocyte cutoffs are used (Harrison 22e p.1070, p.2486 context). Gastric acid suppression (e.g., proton-pump inhibitors) has been associated with increased SBP risk in observational data (Harrison 22e p.1071). SBP is spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid in the absence of an intraabdominal surgical source. The presumed mechanism is bacterial translocation: gut flora cross an edematous, leaky intestinal wall into mesenteric lymph nodes, producing bacteremia that seeds the ascites, which is a good growth medium. Susceptibility in cirrhosis reflects impaired hepatic filtration from a diseased liver and altered portal circulation, low ascitic complement levels (lower than in non-cirrhotic ascites), and diminished opsonic and phagocytic function of PMNs in advanced liver disease. Cirrhosis is also associated with gut dysbiosis (increased Enterobacteriaceae), small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, reduced Paneth-cell defensins, decreased intestinal motility, reduced pancreatobiliary secretions, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy, all of which promote pathologic translocation. SBP occurs in up to ~30% of hospitalized cirrhotics with ascites but is an uncommon event overall, affecting 10% or fewer of cirrhotic patients. (Harrison 22e p.1070, 2715) SBP is a common and potentially lethal complication of cirrhotic ascites and carries significant morbidity and mortality, largely because it tends to occur in patients with the most advanced liver disease. In-hospital mortality is roughly 17-25%; one tertiary-center series reported ~23% mortality at 30 days and ~37% at 90 days. Recurrence is high, with up to ~70% of patients having another episode within a year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within about 72 hours. The underlying prognosis of cirrhosis with ascites is itself poor, with under 50% surviving 2 years after ascites onset in some series, so SBP should prompt consideration of liver transplantation. (Harrison 22e p.1071, 2715-2716, 373) Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system specific to SBP. Risk stratification is framed around predictors of poor outcome and renal injury: higher SBP risk in patients with low ascitic-fluid total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL), impaired renal function (creatinine >=1.2 mg/dL, BUN >=25 mg/dL, or serum sodium <=130 mEq/L), and advanced liver failure (Child-Turcotte-Pugh score >=9, bilirubin >=3 mg/dL); these are used to identify candidates for prophylaxis. The greatest benefit of adjunctive albumin is seen in those presenting with serum creatinine >=1 mg/dL, BUN >=30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >=5 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.1071)

Scrub Typhus — Careful skin examination for eschar — Eschar (a painless, often overlooked necrotic lesion at the chigger bite site) is highly specific for scrub typhus when found — actively look in skin folds, axillae, groin. Scrub typhus IgM ELISA / Weil-Felix (less specific) — Confirms diagnosis serologically, though treatment should not wait for results when clinical suspicion is high. CBC, LFTs, renal function — Assesses organ involvement; transaminitis and thrombocytopenia are common supportive findings. Chest X-ray (if respiratory symptoms) — Screens for ARDS, a recognized complication of severe/delayed scrub typhus. Other rickettsioses presenting with eschar, rash, fever and headache (e.g., Mediterranean spotted fever, African tick-bite fever, rickettsialpox, murine and epidemic typhus) (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456). Atypical/community-acquired pneumonia, given the cough and dyspnea of pulmonary involvement (Harrison 22e p.1126). Other undifferentiated tropical febrile illnesses with thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. Serology is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis: indirect fluorescent antibody, indirect immunoperoxidase, enzyme immunoassays, and rapid lateral-flow chromatographic tests (Harrison 22e p.1460). PCR amplification of Orientia genes is effective when performed on eschar material, but is less sensitive on blood (Harrison 22e p.1460). Platelet count: thrombocytopenia is a characteristic laboratory finding in scrub typhus (as in other rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455). WBC count is typically normal or low (Harrison 22e p.1455). Serum sodium: hyponatremia is a recognized associated finding across the rickettsioses (Harrison 22e p.1455). Hepatic aminotransferases: mild to moderate elevation is commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.1455). The classic triad of an inoculation eschar at the chigger feeding site, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash is the textbook description, but these signs are seldom seen in indigenous (local endemic) patients (Harrison 22e p.1460). Among returning travelers, fewer than 50% develop an eschar and fewer than 40% develop a rash; when a rash does appear it typically emerges on day 4-6 of illness (Harrison 22e p.1460). Eschar formation occurs at the site of mite/chigger feeding and may develop during the incubation period; an eschar is a useful diagnostic clue that should prompt consideration of scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1455). Onset after a 6-21 day incubation is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms; some patients recover spontaneously after a few days while others progress to severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1460). Chigger bites may be asymptomatic, so the absence of a recalled bite does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3773). Immunity to scrub typhus is short-lived: protection against the homologous strain wanes over 1-3 years, and the organism's marked antigenic diversity means cross-protective immunity can be lost in as little as 1 month, so reinfection is possible (Harrison 22e p.1460). Altered mental status / encephalitis (meningoencephalitis is a feature of severe disease) (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455). Interstitial pneumonia / pneumonitis with dyspnea or progression toward respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460). Myocarditis (Harrison 22e p.1035). Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1035). Renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1035). Progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (a severe-disease pattern shared by the rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455). Relying on the classic triad: eschar, rash, and lymphadenopathy are frequently absent (eschar <50% and rash <40% of travelers; signs seldom seen in indigenous patients), so a negative skin exam does not exclude scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1460). Expecting a recalled bite: chigger bites may be asymptomatic and the mites are tiny and rarely noticed (Harrison 22e p.3773). Assuming geographic exclusion: although classically eastern/southern Asia, northern Australia, and Pacific/Indian Ocean islands, emerging and reemerging foci (e.g., Chile, parts of South/Central America, Africa, Arabian peninsula via related Orientia species) challenge the traditional epidemiology (Harrison 22e p.1460, p.3773). Note that PCR on blood is less sensitive than PCR on eschar material (Harrison 22e p.1460). Some Thai isolates are poorly responsive to doxycycline or chloramphenicol (Harrison 22e p.1460). Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). The organism is maintained in nature by transovarial transmission within trombiculid mites; infected larval mites (chiggers, the only mite stage that feeds on a vertebrate host) inoculate the organism into the skin during feeding. Severe disease reflects widespread vascular injury, producing the encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia that characterize advanced cases. Closely related Orientia species (O. chuto, Candidatus O. chiloensis) cause scrub typhus-like illness in newly recognized foci (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456, p.1460, p.3773). Illness ranges from mild and self-limiting to fatal. The case-fatality rate for untreated classic cases is about 6% and would likely be lower if all mild cases were captured; overall reported mortality varies widely by location (cited as 1% to 70%). Risk of death rises with increasing age and with the presence of myocarditis, delirium, pneumonitis, or signs of hemorrhage. Recognized in time, the disease responds well to appropriate antibiotic therapy (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460). Harrison does not give a formal severity score; it contrasts mild/self-limiting illness with severe disease. Severe scrub typhus is marked by encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and interstitial pneumonia due to vascular injury, and may progress to myocarditis, DIC, renal failure, hypotension, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455, p.1460).

Sepsis — Blood cultures (x2, before antibiotics if feasible) — Identifies the causative organism and susceptibility for de-escalation. Lactate — Core Sepsis-3/Surviving Sepsis Campaign marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides resuscitation and risk-stratification toward septic shock. Source-specific cultures (urine, sputum, wound, CSF as guided by clinical exam) — Identifies and confirms the infectious source to allow targeted therapy. CBC, renal function, liver function, coagulation profile — Assesses organ dysfunction (SOFA components) and supports staging severity. Imaging directed by suspected source (CXR, abdominal ultrasound/CT) — Localizes the source and identifies any need for source control (drainage, debridement). Immediate empiric antibiotics required Sepsis mimics, retrospectively found in ~25% of ICU 'sepsis' admissions; continuous reevaluation for an alternative diagnosis is imperative when infection is not confirmed (p.2320) Distributive shock from non-septic causes (e.g., neurogenic shock from brain/spinal-cord injury disrupting vascular autonomic tone) (p.2311) Serum procalcitonin / point-of-care pathogen testing where available to support diagnosis (p.2320) Repeat/serial lactate to gauge response to resuscitation, not just a single value (p.2313) Arterial (or venous) blood gas for acid-base assessment; arterial sampling if hypoxemia present (p.2313) Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) as a surrogate of oxygen-delivery adequacy in refractory shock (p.2313) Echocardiography / point-of-care ultrasound for sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, volume responsiveness, and to exclude mimics (tamponade, PE, pulmonary edema, pneumothorax) (p.2293-2294, 2322) EEG, brain imaging, or lumbar puncture if seizure, stroke, or meningoencephalitis is suspected in a septic patient with neurologic findings (p.2321-2322) Coagulation profile / DIC and sepsis-induced-coagulopathy (SIC) markers - platelets, PT/INR, fibrinogen, fibrin split products (p.2323) Abdominal ultrasound in the septic patient with elevated bilirubin to look for biliary obstruction, cholecystitis, or cholangitis (p.2323) Noninfectious inflammatory febrile syndromes - connective tissue diseases and vasculitides (p.2320) Heart failure and other noninfectious causes of pneumonitis or lung injury (the commonest mimic category in one ICU series was cardiovascular, e.g., heart failure, cardiac arrest) (p.2320) Noninfectious abdominal syndromes - mesenteric ischemia and inflammatory bowel disease (p.2320) Acute pancreatitis (a recognized noninfectious cause of distributive/high-output shock) (p.2293, 2311) Adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis (distributive shock from cortisol/aldosterone deficiency, unmasked by stress of infection or surgery) (p.2293, 2311) Severe burns (distributive shock with cellular hypoxia from reduced SVR) (p.2311) Acute liver failure (high-output hypotension) (p.2293, 2311) Anaphylaxis (IgE-mediated distributive shock with rapid plasma extravasation) (p.2311) Thyrotoxicosis and large peripheral arteriovenous shunts (other causes of high-output hypotension) (p.2293) Hypovolemia and autonomic dysfunction as noninfectious causes of hypotension (p.2320) Pulmonary embolism / obstructive shock (acute chest pain, dyspnea, hypoxia in the immobile or malignancy patient) (p.2313) Sepsis-3 (2016) reframes sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, not merely a systemic inflammatory state; the older SIRS-based criteria and the term 'severe sepsis' were discarded for poor specificity (p.2316). Operationally, sepsis is identified by an acute rise of >=2 points in the SOFA score over baseline in a patient with suspected or confirmed infection (p.2320). Septic shock is the subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg PLUS lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, reflecting circulatory, cellular, and metabolic derangement that markedly raises mortality (p.2310, 2320). qSOFA (>=2 of: respiratory rate >=22/min, altered mentation/GCS <15, systolic BP <=100 mmHg) flags infected patients at high risk of poor outcome; it is more specific but less sensitive than SIRS and was NOT designed or endorsed as a standalone diagnostic/screening test for sepsis (p.2292, 2320). There is NO gold-standard diagnostic test for sepsis; the diagnosis is a synthesis of epidemiologic, clinical, laboratory, imaging, and microbiologic data (p.2320). Presentation is frequently nonspecific (fever, tachycardia, lethargy, myalgias) and may lack localizing features; the CNS, kidneys, and skin act as accessible 'windows' onto early organ hypoperfusion (altered mentation, oliguria, mottling/delayed capillary refill) (p.2320, 2312). Hypotension or an isolated low BP reading does not by itself define sepsis/shock; interpret BP against the patient's baseline and look for evidence of organ hypoperfusion, since hypertensive patients can decompensate at 'normal' pressures (p.2312). Absence of tachycardia does not exclude sepsis: nodal-blocking drugs or conduction disease can blunt the compensatory heart-rate response (p.2312). Sepsis is the commonest cause of distributive (high-cardiac-output, low-SVR) shock and of high-output hypotension overall; warm extremities with a wide pulse pressure suggest this physiology (p.2310, 2293). Lactate is central to risk-stratifying sepsis: elevation reflects tissue hypoperfusion/anaerobic metabolism, correlates with worse outcome, and serial measurements help track response to resuscitation (p.2313). Most sepsis is community-onset (~88%); the urinary tract is the single most common primary site, followed by respiratory, intra-abdominal, and skin/soft-tissue sources (p.2316). Hospital-onset sepsis tends to involve sicker, more comorbid patients with more intra-abdominal infection and bacteremia from Enterococcus, Candida, and Pseudomonas, and carries higher ICU admission and mortality (p.2317). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (reduced LVEF, dilated LV, RV impairment) affects up to half of septic-shock patients and can convert initial distributive shock into a mixed distributive-cardiogenic picture (p.2311, 2322). qSOFA >=2 (RR >=22, altered mentation, SBP <=100) in suspected infection - identifies the most acutely ill subset with higher mortality and ICU need (p.2292, 2320) Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors plus lactate >2 mmol/L after adequate fluids = septic shock, with mortality up to ~40% (p.2310, 2316) New altered mental status / encephalopathy or new oliguria as early signs that compensatory mechanisms are exhausted (p.2312) Skin mottling, prolonged capillary refill, cool clammy skin - hypoperfusion (p.2312, 2322) Every hour of delay in appropriate antibiotics in bacterial septic shock raises mortality (estimated 7-8% per hour after shock recognition) - empiric antibiotics within 1 h of shock recognition (p.2320-2321) An infection source needing urgent control (intra-abdominal abscess, bowel perforation, cholangitis, obstructed/infected urinary tract, necrotizing soft-tissue infection, infected indwelling catheter/endovascular infection) - source control as fast as possible (p.2321) Failure to confirm infection should prompt active search for a mimic rather than indefinite empiric antibiotics (antibiotic stewardship: stop antibiotics when sepsis is excluded) (p.2315, 2320) Treating sepsis as a single pathogen rather than a syndrome - empiric therapy and workup must be driven by the most likely source (p.2316). Relying on SIRS criteria or a single abnormal vital sign to rule sepsis in or out - poor specificity led to their abandonment in Sepsis-3 (p.2316). Using qSOFA as a diagnostic test - it is a risk-stratification/screening prompt, not a diagnostic criterion (p.2292, 2320). Being falsely reassured by a normal heart rate (beta-blockade/conduction disease) or by a low BP reading in a chronically hypotensive patient (p.2312). Anchoring on 'sepsis' when infection is unconfirmed - up to a quarter of presumed-sepsis ICU cases are mimics; failure to reevaluate delays the correct diagnosis (p.2320). Continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics once infection is excluded, undermining stewardship and risking C. difficile, allergy, and AKI (p.2315, 2321). Over-resuscitation with fluid - excess volume is likely harmful; targeted, dynamically reassessed resuscitation is the goal (p.2294). Attributing all altered mentation to sepsis-associated encephalopathy without excluding seizure, stroke, or CNS infection (p.2321-2322). Missing sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, which can turn distributive shock into mixed shock and change management (p.2311, 2322). Sepsis arises when an infection provokes a dysregulated, self-amplifying host response rather than a contained local one. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g., LPS, bacterial cell-wall components, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g., histones, HMGB1, S100 proteins, mitochondrial/double-stranded DNA, ATP released from injured cells) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD-like receptors) on innate immune and parenchymal cells. This triggers exuberant release of cytokines and chemokines and upregulation of vascular adhesion molecules. Myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, M1 macrophages, dendritic cells) drive injury through phagocytosis, degranulation, reactive oxygen/nitrogen species, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), while emergency granulopoiesis releases immature neutrophils (a poor-prognosis marker). Lymphoid responses are dysregulated, with lymphocyte apoptosis, exhaustion, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells producing a state of immunosuppression that predisposes survivors to secondary infection. The endothelium is activated and injured: glycocalyx breakdown, loss of VE-cadherin/tight junctions, and apoptosis cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and a widened oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic shift (increased tissue factor, vWF, PAI-1; depleted antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and protein C; complement activation with C3a/C5a and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex) generates microvascular thrombi and, once clotting factors and platelets are consumed, bleeding. Excess nitric oxide drives systemic vasodilation. The net result is impaired oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization; even when oxygen delivery is adequate, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction impairs ATP generation and ion homeostasis, producing multiorgan cellular injury and dysfunction (p.2317-2319). Overall in-hospital mortality is roughly 15% among hospitalized adults with sepsis, rising to up to ~40% with septic shock; globally an estimated ~11 million sepsis-related deaths occur yearly (about one in five deaths worldwide). Mortality climbs with age and is higher in men. Elevated SOFA scores and machine-learning-defined phenotypes track population-level outcome (e.g., alpha/beta/gamma/delta phenotypes with ~2%/5%/15%/32% mortality) but cannot reliably predict an individual patient's outcome. Survivorship carries a heavy long-term burden: physical (prolonged fatigue, muscle loss, weakness, reduced functional capacity), cognitive (cognitive decline, dementia), and psychological (depression, reduced quality of life) sequelae, plus increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. About half of survivors are rehospitalized within a year and roughly one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated death risk persisting up to ~2 years (p.2316-2317, 2324). No FDA-approved host-targeted/immunomodulatory therapy exists for sepsis (p.2324). Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) is the current framework: (1) Infection (suspected or confirmed) without organ dysfunction is not sepsis. (2) Sepsis = suspected/confirmed infection with an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score from baseline (life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response). The SOFA score grades six systems 0-4: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP / vasopressor requirement), CNS (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine / urine output). (3) Septic shock = sepsis with vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. qSOFA (>=2 of RR >=22/min, altered mentation, SBP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside risk-stratification prompt for poor outcome in suspected infection, not a diagnostic criterion. The prior 1991/1992 SIRS-based definitions and the term 'severe sepsis' are obsolete under Sepsis-3 (p.2292, 2316, 2320).

Arterial blood gas — Assesses acid-base status and oxygenation in the context of shock. Central venous/arterial line monitoring as per unit protocol — Guides hemodynamic management alongside antibiotic therapy. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Other causes of distributive shock: pancreatitis, severe burns, liver failure, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock from brain/spinal cord injury, and adrenal insufficiency/adrenal crisis (p.2353-2354) Cardiogenic shock (myocardial infarction, myocarditis, arrhythmia, acute valvular failure) (p.2353-2354) Hypovolemic shock (hemorrhagic from trauma or GI bleeding; point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS, e.g. RUSH/ACES protocols) helps classify undifferentiated and mixed shock (p.2356) SOFA score components for severity (GCS, MAP/vasopressor use, PaO2/FiO2, bilirubin, creatinine, platelets) (p.2317) Noninfectious inflammatory febrile syndromes including connective tissue diseases and vasculitides (p.2320) Heart failure and cardiac arrest (the most common cardiovascular mimics in ICU series, where ~25% of presumed septic patients were later judged to have a mimic) (p.2320) Noninfectious chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation (common respiratory mimic) (p.2320) Hypotension from noninfectious causes: hypovolemia, autonomic dysfunction, and adrenal insufficiency (p.2320) Septic shock under Sepsis-3 is a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic derangements that carry a higher mortality than sepsis alone; sepsis itself is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection (p.2316). Sepsis-3 abandoned the older SIRS criteria (used by Sepsis-1/2) because of poor specificity for distinguishing infection from other inflammatory states, and eliminated the term 'severe sepsis' (p.2316). Sepsis is operationalized as an acute rise of at least 2 points in the SOFA score from baseline in a patient with suspected or confirmed infection (p.2320). qSOFA (respiratory rate >=22/min, altered mentation with GCS <15, systolic BP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside screen; a score >=2 is more specific but less sensitive than SIRS and flags patients at higher risk of death, ICU admission, and longer stay (p.2313, p.2320). Sepsis presentation can be nonspecific (fever, tachycardia, lethargy, myalgias) with or without localizing findings; there is no single gold-standard diagnostic test, so the diagnosis integrates clinical, laboratory, microbiologic, and imaging data (p.2320). Approximately 88% of sepsis cases are community onset (detected within 48 h of admission); hospital-onset sepsis (after 48 h) tends to involve more comorbidities, intraabdominal infection, and Enterococcus/Candida/Pseudomonas, with higher ICU admission and mortality (p.2316-2317). Among culture-positive community-onset sepsis, the most common primary sites are urinary tract (~49%), respiratory tract (~33%), intraabdominal (~14%), and skin/soft tissue (~10%) (p.2316). About 53% of US sepsis cases are bacterial culture positive with a roughly even gram-positive / gram-negative split; common gram-positives are S. aureus, Streptococcus, and Enterococcus, and common gram-negatives are E. coli, Klebsiella, and P. aeruginosa (p.2316). Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation defines septic shock and marks the highest-mortality end of the spectrum (p.2320, p.2354) Acute rise of >=2 SOFA points from baseline with suspected infection indicates new organ dysfunction (p.2320) qSOFA >=2 (RR>=22, GCS<15, SBP<=100) signals high risk of death and ICU need (p.2313, p.2320) Elevated and rising serial lactate, which correlates with worse outcome and reflects tissue hypoperfusion (p.2356) Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (altered consciousness, cognition, or behavior) signaling CNS organ dysfunction (p.2319) New oliguria / acute kidney injury, occurring in up to two-thirds of septic patients (p.2319) Signs of coagulopathy/DIC with consumption of platelets and clotting factors and bleeding risk (p.2319) Relying on SIRS criteria to define or exclude sepsis: SIRS lacks specificity, which is why Sepsis-3 replaced it (p.2316). Treating shock as a single entity: distributive (septic) shock has low SVR with high cardiac output and low filling pressures, the opposite hemodynamic profile of cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock, so misclassification leads to wrong resuscitation (p.2353-2354). Assuming a single shock type: sepsis frequently coexists with a cardiogenic component (sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy) or hypovolemia, producing mixed shock that POCUS can help dissect (p.2355). A normal hemoglobin/hematocrit early in concurrent hemorrhage, or a normal WBC, does not exclude the relevant process; leukocytosis is suggestive but not diagnostic of infection (p.2356). Anchoring on sepsis when infection is not confirmed: about 25% of presumed septic ICU patients had a mimic, so alternative diagnoses must be continually reconsidered (p.2320). Failure to identify and control the source (e.g. infected catheter, abscess, endocarditis) undermines management even with appropriate antibiotics (p.2321). Septic shock is the most common form of distributive shock, in which the primary hemodynamic derangement is a fall in systemic vascular resistance (vasoplegia) rather than a primary loss of preload or pump function. The vasodilatory profile is distinctive: SVR is reduced, cardiac output is typically increased as a compensatory response, and both central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tend to be low (p.2353-2354). Arterial and venous vasodilation is mediated in part by excess nitric oxide; vasopressin deficiency may also contribute to refractory hypotension. The dysregulated host response begins when pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g. LPS, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g. histones, HMGB1, mitochondrial DNA, ATP) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD receptors) on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and parenchymal cells, triggering proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine release and upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecules. Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); endothelial activation/injury, glycocalyx degradation, and loss of VE-cadherin tight junctions cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and increased oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic state arises from tissue-factor-driven coagulation, platelet/vWF microthrombi, complement activation (C3a, C5a, C5b-9 membrane attack complex), reduced anticoagulants (antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, activated protein C), and impaired fibrinolysis (elevated PAI-1); consumption of clotting factors and platelets can then produce hemorrhage. The net effect is hypotension (from vasodilation, myocardial depression, and hypovolemia), microcirculatory dysfunction, and mitochondrial/metabolic failure, so that oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization are all impaired and cellular injury occurs even when bulk oxygen delivery appears adequate (p.2317-2320). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy can add a cardiogenic component, producing mixed shock (p.2355). Septic shock carries up to ~40% mortality, far higher than the ~15% overall mortality among US hospitalized adults with sepsis (p.2316). In emergency-department shock cohorts, septic and cardiogenic shock have the highest 90-day mortality (reported ~56% and ~52% respectively), and septic shock predominates among ICU shock (~62% of ICU shock patients in one multicenter series), whereas hypovolemic shock has lower mortality (p.2355). Mortality rises with age and is higher in men; comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, neurologic/respiratory/cardiac disease, renal or hepatic insufficiency, cancer, and immunosuppression worsen outcomes (p.2317). SOFA scores predict mortality at the population level but not for individual patients; proposed clinical 'phenotypes' (alpha/beta/gamma/delta) carried roughly 2%, 5%, 15%, and 32% mortality (p.2317). Survivors face substantial long-term sequelae: physical (fatigue, muscle loss, weakness), cognitive and psychological (cognitive decline, dementia, depression), and increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. Roughly half of survivors are rehospitalized within 1 year and about one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated risk persisting up to 2 years (p.2321). Sepsis-3 spectrum: (1) Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalized as an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score in a patient with suspected/confirmed infection. (2) Septic shock = a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities and higher mortality, operationally defined as a septic patient who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, requires vasopressors to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND has serum lactate >2 mmol/L. qSOFA (RR>=22, GCS<15, SBP<=100; score >=2) is a rapid risk-stratification screen, not a diagnosis. The historical Sepsis-1/2 terms 'severe sepsis' and SIRS-based septic shock (SBP<90 or drop >=40 mmHg) have been superseded (p.2316, p.2320).

Severe Community Acquired Pneumonia — Blood cultures (x2) — Bacteremia rate is higher in severe CAP; identifies organism and susceptibility for de-escalation. Sputum culture and Gram stain — Helps target and de-escalate empiric therapy. Urinary antigen (pneumococcal and Legionella) — Rapid, useful for severe presentations to guide targeted therapy. ABG — Quantifies hypoxia/hypercapnia and guides ventilatory support decisions. Chest X-ray / CT chest — Defines extent (multilobar disease, effusion, cavitation) which affects prognosis and management. Lactate — Screens for tissue hypoperfusion and helps gauge severity/sepsis overlap. Patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors or acute respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation meet a major criterion and should be admitted directly to an ICU (p.1026). Presence of three or more of the nine minor severe-CAP criteria warrants admission to an ICU or high-level monitoring unit (p.1026). Late or delayed ICU admission is associated with increased mortality; less-ill patients placed on a general ward who then deteriorate fare worse than equally ill patients monitored in the ICU from the outset (p.1026). In ICU-admitted CAP specifically, treatment directed at an identified pathogen may be superior to empirical therapy, so etiologic workup carries more weight in severe disease (p.1025). The microbial spectrum of severe (ICU) CAP differs from milder CAP: Legionella tends to cause more serious disease, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli become more prominent (p.1024). Prior respiratory-tract isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa within the past year is a stronger (more robust) risk factor for these pathogens than recent hospitalization plus parenteral antibiotic exposure (p.1028). Procalcitonin (PCT) is insufficiently accurate to diagnose bacterial CAP and must NOT be used as a basis for withholding initial antibiotics; CRP is even less sensitive than PCT (p.1026). If only a viral pathogen (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2) is found and no bacterial pathogen is evident, antibacterial therapy can be stopped — BUT in severe illness, bacterial-viral co-infection must still be considered (p.1028). Gross hemoptysis suggests necrotizing pneumonia, e.g., due to CA-MRSA (p.1024). In the elderly, severe CAP may present atypically as new-onset or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (p.1025). Recent data show a mortality benefit for corticosteroids in severe CAP, particularly when there is a high level of systemic inflammation (CRP >15 mg/dL) (p.1029). Septic shock requiring vasopressors (major criterion - direct ICU admission) Acute respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation (major criterion - direct ICU admission) Three or more minor severe-CAP criteria (warrants ICU/high-level monitoring) O2 saturation <92% on room air (mandates hospitalization) Multiorgan failure Multilobar infiltrates or cavitation on imaging (increased severity) Gross hemoptysis (suggests necrotizing pneumonia, e.g., CA-MRSA) Failure to improve / deterioration by ~day 3 of therapy Using PSI or CURB-65 to decide ICU admission - neither is accurate for that purpose (p.1026). Withholding initial antibiotics based on a low procalcitonin - PCT is too inaccurate to exclude bacterial CAP (p.1026). Assuming hospitalization alone is a significant risk factor for MRSA or P. aeruginosa - it is no longer considered so; severity plus specific risk factors drive coverage decisions (p.1028). Requiring all three drug-resistance risk factors (recent hospitalization, recent oral/IV antibiotics, local validation) before considering resistant pathogens - any can apply (p.1028). Stopping antibacterials when a virus is identified in a severely ill patient without considering bacterial-viral co-infection (p.1028). Attributing failure to improve to the wrong cause: consider resistant or unexpected pathogen (CA-MRSA, M. tuberculosis, fungus), a sequestered focus (lung abscess, empyema), wrong drug/dose, or nosocomial superinfection (p.1029). Routinely covering anaerobes in aspiration-related severe CAP - unnecessary unless poor dentition, lung abscess, or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1027). Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli combined with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract by inhalation, microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, or direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, the branching airway, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are insufficient to fully exclude bacteria, and the lung is now understood to harbor a microbiota rather than being sterile. An inflammatory/epithelial-endothelial injury event releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively promote growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, generating a positive-feedback loop; in CAP the trigger is often a viral infection compounded by microaspiration. Inflammatory mediators (IL-6, TNF) cause fever, while IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils; mediators from macrophages and neutrophils produce alveolar-capillary leak with impaired oxygenation, hypoxemia, and radiographic infiltrates. Some pathogens interfere with hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia. Reduced compliance from capillary leak, increased respiratory drive and secretions, and intrapulmonary shunting drive worsening dyspnea, and when severe, reductions in lung volume/compliance and shunting can precipitate respiratory failure. Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia evolves through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution phases. Prognosis depends on age, comorbidities, and site of treatment. For hospitalized CAP, overall mortality ranges from 12% to 40%, the higher end reflecting ICU-level disease and care-process factors such as timely administration of appropriate antibiotics (vs <5% for outpatients). CURB-65 scores >=3 carry an overall ~22% mortality and may indicate ICU admission; PSI class 5 has a ~29.2% mortality. CAP is a leading infectious cause of death in patients >65 years; about 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month, and recent data show 1-year mortality after CAP (especially in older patients) exceeds 30-day mortality. Severe-CAP complications (respiratory failure, shock, multiorgan failure) and pneumonia-associated cardiovascular events worsen outcomes. IDSA/ATS severe-CAP criteria (Harrison 22e Table 131-3, p.1026). MAJOR criteria (either qualifies for ICU): (1) respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation; (2) septic shock requiring vasopressors. MINOR criteria (>=3 warrant ICU/high-level monitoring): respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia (BUN >=20 mg/dL); leukopenia (WBC <4000/uL); thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/uL); hypothermia (core temperature <36 C); and hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation. Prognostic tools PSI (5 mortality classes, class 5 ~29.2%) and CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, RR >=30, SBP <=90 or DBP <=60 mmHg, age >=65; score >=3 ~22% mortality) assess severity/site of care but are NOT accurate for determining ICU need.

Acute Sinusitis (Rhinosinusitis) — None routinely required — Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is reserved for suspected complications (orbital/intracranial extension) or recurrent/chronic disease. Sinus transillumination is NOT accurate for diagnosing sinusitis and should not be relied upon (p. 299). Noncontrast CT is the preferred imaging modality when imaging is indicated (e.g., failure to improve, suspected complication, or alternative diagnosis) (p. 300). Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the preferred imaging modality when invasive fungal sinusitis is suspected (p. 299). Nasal endoscopy with biopsy is part of the evaluation for suspected invasive fungal sinusitis (p. 299). Direct rhinoscopy may reveal excess mucus or purulence on examination (p. 299). In recurrent acute sinusitis, consider nasal culture during episodes, imaging between episodes to identify predisposing anatomic abnormalities, and allergic/immunologic evaluation (p. 300). Autoimmune disease such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (p. 298) Allergic rhinitis and other noninfectious rhinitides (p. 298) Structural causes such as deviated nasal septum or nasal polyps (noted in chronic disease, p. 300) The vast majority of acute sinusitis cases are caused by respiratory viruses; fewer than 2% of episodes are bacterial, yet antibiotics are prescribed at over 70% of office visits, making sinusitis a leading driver of unnecessary antibiotic use in adults (p. 299). By guideline criteria, no more than about 50% of adults (and probably closer to 20%) with sinusitis actually meet thresholds for antibiotic prescribing (p. 299). Symptoms are classified by duration: acute (<4 weeks), subacute (4-12 weeks), and chronic (>=12 weeks) (p. 298). Common features are purulent nasal discharge, facial congestion/fullness, and facial pain or pressure; additional symptoms include fever, hyposmia or anosmia, ear pressure/pain, postnasal drip, halitosis, maxillary toothache, cough, and fatigue (p. 299). Risk factors include age 45-65 years, smoking, asthma, air travel, and allergies (p. 299). For an individual patient with a nonspecific upper respiratory illness, an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication such as bacterial sinusitis (p. 296). Recurrent acute sinusitis is defined as four or more episodes of acute sinusitis in a year with no signs or symptoms between episodes (p. 299). Nosocomial sinusitis occurs in critically ill patients, often those who are nasotracheally intubated, and should be suspected in hospitalized patients with fever lacking another identifiable source (p. 299). Relying on sinus transillumination, which is inaccurate for diagnosis (p. 299). Prescribing a macrolide for sinusitis - specifically not recommended because of high rates of macrolide-resistant S. pneumoniae (p. 300). Missing invasive fungal sinusitis in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with rapidly progressive disease - delay can be fatal (p. 299). Overlooking nosocomial sinusitis as a hidden source of unexplained fever in nasotracheally intubated ICU patients (p. 299). In children, failing to consider a nasal foreign body as the cause of sinus symptoms (p. 298). Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses; when the nasal passages are also involved the term rhinosinusitis is used. Most acute disease begins as a viral process. Bacterial sinusitis, when it occurs, is usually a secondary superinfection of the obstructed/inflamed sinus and is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or M. catarrhalis. Invasive fungal disease arises when host defenses are impaired (uncontrolled diabetes, transplant/immunocompromise), allowing Mucorales or Aspergillus to invade tissue and spread beyond the sinus (pp. 298-299). Most acute sinusitis is viral and self-limited. Symptoms of the underlying upper respiratory illness generally peak early but can persist up to about 14 days (p. 296). Complications of sinusitis can be dramatic but are extremely rare (p. 299). Invasive fungal sinusitis is an emergency: in immunocompromised hosts it can progress within days from rhinosinusitis to cranial nerve involvement, orbital and ophthalmic involvement, and critical illness (p. 299). Antibiotic-prescribing indications (Harrison Table 37-2, p. 299): Persistent = symptoms lasting >=10 days; Severe = fever >102 degrees F with either purulent nasal discharge or nasal pain for at least 3-4 consecutive days; Worsening = new fever, headache, or increased nasal discharge following an upper respiratory infection that had lasted 5-6 days and was initially improving (double-sickening). Duration-based: acute <4 weeks, subacute 4-12 weeks, chronic >=12 weeks (p. 298).

proconvulsant drug toxicity) Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury Eclampsia in pregnancy Defined operationally as a single seizure lasting beyond the time most seizures of that type would normally stop (roughly 5 minutes for convulsive seizures) or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness in between. Treat convulsive status epilepticus as a time-critical emergency — earlier treatment initiation strongly predicts easier termination and better outcome. Airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and thiamine should be addressed simultaneously with, not after, anticonvulsant therapy. Always check a bedside glucose early; hypoglycemia is a rapidly reversible cause that mimics or precipitates status epilepticus. Non-convulsive status epilepticus should be suspected in any patient with unexplained persistent altered consciousness, especially after a convulsive seizure has been treated but the patient fails to wake up. Continuous EEG monitoring is essential once convulsions have stopped to confirm electrographic seizure resolution, particularly in patients who remain unresponsive. Refractory status epilepticus (persisting despite adequate first- and second-line therapy) generally requires escalation to continuous anesthetic infusions with EEG guidance in an ICU setting. Identifying and treating the underlying etiology is as important as stopping the seizure itself, since ongoing precipitants (e.g., infection, toxin, structural lesion) will otherwise perpetuate the episode. Seizure activity continuing beyond the expected duration without response to initial therapy — escalate treatment promptly Persistent unresponsiveness after convulsions have visibly stopped — evaluate for non-convulsive status epilepticus Hemodynamic instability, hyperthermia, or severe acidosis during prolonged seizure activity Focal neurologic signs or papilledema suggesting an acute structural intracranial process Fever with meningismus suggesting an infectious CNS cause requiring urgent antimicrobial coverage Failure to respond to first- and second-line agents, indicating refractory status epilepticus requiring ICU-level anesthetic therapy Assuming convulsions have stopped means the seizure is over — non-convulsive status epilepticus can persist electrographically with only subtle clinical signs. Delaying anticonvulsant administration while awaiting imaging or laboratory results, which worsens the chance of terminating the seizure. Underdosing initial therapy out of caution about respiratory depression, which increases the risk of treatment failure and need for escalation. Failing to search for and treat the underlying precipitant, allowing the episode to recur despite initial seizure control. Status epilepticus arises from a failure of the mechanisms that normally terminate seizure activity, leading to sustained abnormal neuronal hypersynchronization. This results from a relative excess of excitatory (glutamatergic) neurotransmission and depletion or dysfunction of inhibitory (GABAergic) signaling, with progressive receptor trafficking changes that make prolonged seizures increasingly resistant to GABA-acting drugs over time. Prolonged seizure activity can itself cause excitotoxic neuronal injury independent of the underlying cause, and is accompanied by systemic derangements including hyperthermia, acidosis, hypoxia, and autonomic instability that compound neuronal damage. Outcome depends heavily on etiology, age, and duration of status before treatment, with prolonged or refractory episodes carrying substantially higher morbidity and mortality. Even with successful seizure termination, patients face risk of cognitive sequelae and recurrent epilepsy, particularly when status is due to an acute severe brain insult.

Toxic shock syndrome — toxic shock, TSS, staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, STSS, menstrual TSS, tampon-associated shock Kawasaki disease (especially in children with fever, rash, and mucosal changes) Necrotizing fasciitis without full toxic shock physiology Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsial infections Severe scarlet fever Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or Stevens-Johnson spectrum Septic shock from another gram-negative or gram-positive source Kawasaki disease Scarlet fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever Leptospirosis (Weil syndrome) Meningococcemia Blood cultures (times two) — often negative in staphylococcal TSS but essential to identify streptococcal bacteremia and guide therapy Wound, vaginal, or device-site cultures — to isolate toxin-producing S. aureus or S. pyogenes and confirm source Complete metabolic panel with renal and hepatic function — documents multi-organ involvement required for diagnosis Complete blood count with differential — assesses for thrombocytopenia and left shift Creatine kinase — elevated with muscular involvement/myositis component Coagulation studies (PT/INR, fibrinogen) — screens for evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation Imaging (CT/MRI or bedside ultrasound) of suspected soft-tissue focus — evaluates for necrotizing infection requiring surgical debridement Serologic/toxin studies where available — can support etiology in atypical or culture-negative presentations Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis Drug hypersensitivity reaction (DRESS) Systemic lupus erythematosus flare with vasculitic rash Adult-onset Still disease Consider TSS in any acute febrile illness with diffuse macular erythroderma, hypotension, and multi-organ involvement, even without an obvious focal infection source. A retained tampon, nasal packing, surgical wound packing, or postpartum/post-surgical site should always be actively sought and removed as part of initial assessment. Streptococcal TSS typically presents with a clear, severe, deep soft-tissue focus (necrotizing fasciitis or bacteremia) and is far more often bacteremic than the staphylococcal form. Desquamation of the palms and soles is a late finding, occurring one to two weeks after illness onset, and should never be relied upon to make the initial diagnosis. Hypotension plus involvement of three or more organ systems (renal, hepatic, hematologic, mucosal, CNS, muscular/GI) in a febrile diffuse-rash illness supports the syndromic diagnosis. Early aggressive fluid resuscitation is often required because of profound capillary leak, and volume needs can be extreme in the first 24-48 hours. Source control (removing foreign material, draining/debriding infected tissue) is as critical as antimicrobial therapy and delays worsen outcomes. Blood cultures are frequently negative in staphylococcal TSS since the syndrome is toxin-mediated rather than driven by bloodstream invasion. Refractory hypotension unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation, suggesting need for vasopressors and ICU-level care Rapidly spreading pain, swelling, or crepitus over a soft-tissue site raising concern for necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent surgical exploration Evolving coagulopathy or falling platelet count concerning for disseminated intravascular coagulation Altered mental status or new organ dysfunction indicating rapid progression to multi-organ failure Any retained foreign material (tampon, packing, prosthetic material) not yet identified or removed Dismissing the diagnosis because blood cultures are negative — staphylococcal TSS is toxin-mediated and frequently culture-negative. Waiting for classic desquamation before considering the diagnosis, which delays treatment since desquamation occurs late in the course. Failing to perform a thorough examination for retained foreign bodies (vaginal, nasal, surgical) as the driving source. Underestimating streptococcal TSS severity because the cutaneous findings can be subtler than staphylococcal disease despite higher mortality. TSS results from exotoxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus (notably TSST-1) or by Streptococcus pyogenes acting as superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the conventional antigen groove. This bypasses normal antigen processing and triggers massive, non-specific polyclonal T-cell activation with a resulting cytokine storm (IL-1, IL-2, TNF, interferon-gamma). The surge in inflammatory mediators produces capillary leak, vasodilation, hypotension, and secondary multi-organ dysfunction, explaining why the clinical picture can be severe even with a small, localized focus of infection or colonization. Staphylococcal TSS has a lower mortality (roughly a few percent) when recognized early and the source is controlled, whereas streptococcal TSS carries a substantially higher mortality, often cited around 30-70%, particularly when associated with necrotizing soft-tissue infection or bacteremia. Prompt source control, resuscitation, and antimicrobial therapy are the main determinants of outcome.
