acid and/or calcium phosphate precipitation in renal tubules Cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia is the most immediately life-threatening complication Aggressive risk stratification and prophylaxis before chemotherapy is far more effective than treating established syndrome Oliguria or rising creatinine suggesting evolving acute kidney injury ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS, QT prolongation) indicating hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia Symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia) Rapidly rising potassium or phosphate despite supportive measures High tumour bulk with elevated baseline LDH and uric acid before therapy initiation Need for urgent renal replacement therapy in refractory metabolic derangement Assuming TLS only occurs after chemotherapy — spontaneous lysis can precede any treatment in highly proliferative tumours Correcting hypocalcemia aggressively without addressing hyperphosphatemia first, which can worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation Underestimating risk in patients with bulky, chemosensitive tumours and pre-existing renal impairment or dehydration Delaying prophylactic measures until after laboratory abnormalities appear rather than initiating them proactively Rapid destruction of malignant cells releases large quantities of intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the circulation. Nucleic acid catabolism generates a surge of uric acid that can precipitate in the relatively acidic, low-flow environment of the renal tubules, producing obstructive nephropathy. Hyperphosphatemia from cell lysis exceeds the solubility product for calcium phosphate, causing tissue and renal deposition and consequent hypocalcemia. The resulting acute kidney injury further impairs excretion of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, creating a self-amplifying metabolic crisis. With prompt recognition, risk stratification, and preventive management, most cases resolve without permanent renal impairment; outcomes worsen substantially once oliguric acute kidney injury or refractory hyperkalemia develops, occasionally requiring dialysis.

Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (common cold) — None required — Diagnosis is clinical and investigations rarely change management in uncomplicated URTI. Influenza (more prominent myalgias and systemic symptoms) COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 can cause virtually any upper respiratory symptom; new loss of taste or smell appears specific for COVID-19) Measles (cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis) Acute HIV infection (sore throat and rash often predominate) Allergic, inflammatory, autoimmune, or neoplastic causes of upper respiratory symptoms Influenza COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) Acute HIV infection Measles Streptococcal pharyngitis Acute bacterial sinusitis Acute otitis media No specific viral testing is needed for diagnosis; multiplex RT-PCR panels exist but are often unnecessary and may be falsely positive due to recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296) Allergic rhinitis / allergic upper respiratory symptoms Other inflammatory upper respiratory conditions Autoimmune causes of upper respiratory symptoms Neoplastic causes of upper respiratory symptoms The nonspecific URI ('common cold') is defined as a respiratory tract infection in which no single symptom predominates, distinguishing it clinically from more localized syndromes such as pharyngitis, sinusitis, or otitis media (Harrison 22e p.296). The overwhelming majority of acute respiratory infections are caused by common respiratory viruses and are self-limited; antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications, which is why at least half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for these infections are inappropriate (Harrison 22e p.295). Nasal mucus in a viral URI can range anywhere from watery to frankly purulent, so purulent or discolored nasal discharge by itself does not indicate bacterial infection or warrant antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.296). Symptoms typically begin gradually after a 2-8 day incubation, peak early, and usually last 5-10 days but may persist up to 14 days; patients remain infectious as long as symptoms are present (Harrison 22e pp.296-297). Adults average 2-4 URIs per year and children 6-10 per year; reinfection is common because immunity to the many rhinovirus and adenovirus serotypes is serotype-specific and immunity to coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, and metapneumovirus is weak or short-lived (Harrison 22e pp.295-296). Myalgias may occur but are usually less prominent than in influenza, a useful bedside discriminator from influenza (Harrison 22e p.296). Making a specific viral diagnosis is not practical, cost-effective, or necessary; multiplex RT-PCR panels may be overly sensitive and yield false positives from recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296). URI can be reduced by hand hygiene, physical distancing, masking, isolation of ill persons, and environmental cleaning (Harrison 22e p.295). Fever above 102 degrees F (38.9 C) Chest pain not attributable to a pulled muscle Shortness of breath Dizziness Confusion New ear or sinus pain (suggesting otitis media or bacterial sinusitis complication) Symptoms lasting longer than 14 days New loss of taste or smell where SARS-CoV-2 is circulating (suggests COVID-19) Prescribing antibiotics for a viral URI: they do not shorten illness or prevent complications and risk adverse drug effects, microbiome disruption, C. difficile infection, increased cost, and antibiotic resistance (Harrison 22e p.295). Interpreting purulent nasal discharge as evidence of bacterial infection; viral URI mucus normally ranges from watery to purulent (Harrison 22e p.296). Drivers of inappropriate prescribing include time pressure, fear of missing a rare bacterial diagnosis, concern about a rare complication, low salience of antibiotic harms, and the mistaken belief that patients demand antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.295). Delayed antibiotic prescriptions are conceptually flawed for self-limited respiratory infections, shift decision-making to patients, and send a mixed message; they should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.296). Procalcitonin testing has been ineffective and CRP testing not durable for reducing inappropriate ambulatory antibiotic use (Harrison 22e p.296). Many popular cold remedies are ineffective, of questionable benefit, or harmful, including echinacea, zinc, inhaled steam, vitamin C, vitamin D, garlic, antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, saline nasal irrigation, and antiviral drugs (Harrison 22e p.296). Cough and cold medicines should not be used in children under 6 years because of the risk of adverse effects (Harrison 22e p.296). Nonspecific URI is an acute infection of the respiratory tract above the vocal cords, most commonly caused by respiratory viruses acquired through direct contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, and large and small respiratory droplets. Susceptibility depends on prior exposure and immunity, general health, genetics, microbiome factors, and psychosocial factors including stress. Because immunity is serotype-specific (rhinovirus, adenovirus) or weak/short-lived (coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, metapneumovirus), reinfection is frequent (Harrison 22e pp.295-296). Nonspecific URI is self-limited. Symptoms peak early and generally resolve within 5-10 days, though some last up to 14 days. Although the cold can occasionally be complicated by otitis media or bacterial sinusitis, for any individual patient an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication (Harrison 22e pp.296-297).

Ventilator Associated Pneumonia — Quantitative endotracheal aspirate or BAL culture — Gold standard to identify causative organism and guide de-escalation in VAP. Blood cultures — Detects bacteremic spread. Chest X-ray (serial) — Tracks new or progressive infiltrate. Procalcitonin (serial) — Supports shortened duration of therapy when trending down with clinical improvement. Immediate empiric antibiotics required Purulent tracheobronchitis (especially in chronic ventilator units, where it can impede weaning) (p.1030) Fungal pneumonia (requires different antibiotics from those used for bacterial VAP) (p.1031) Viral pneumonia (requires different antibiotics from those used for bacterial VAP) (p.1031) Quantitative deep respiratory tract cultures to separate colonization from true infection: more distal sampling is more specific and uses a lower growth threshold; endotracheal aspirate threshold is 10^6 cfu/mL and protected specimen brush threshold is 10^3 cfu/mL, but sensitivity falls with more distal blind sampling (p.1031). Gram stain of respiratory specimen, differential cell counts, staining for intracellular organisms, and detection of locally elevated infection-related protein levels to increase diagnostic yield (p.1031). Molecular diagnostic methods, which can exclude a suspected MDR pathogen as a therapy target when results are negative (p.1031). Serial procalcitonin and other biomarkers, used together with the initial clinical response to help guide therapy duration (p.1032). Atypical pulmonary edema (p.1031) Pulmonary contusion (p.1031) Alveolar hemorrhage (p.1031) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (p.1031) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (p.1031) Pulmonary infarction / pulmonary embolism (p.1031) Non-pulmonary causes of fever and/or leukocytosis: antibiotic-associated diarrhea, central line-associated infection, sinusitis, urinary tract infection, pancreatitis, and drug fever (p.1031) VAP is defined as pneumonia with onset at or beyond 48 h after the start of mechanical ventilation; the same principles extend to ventilated HAP and to non-ICU HAP (p.1029). About 35% of all HAP patients require mechanical ventilation, which marks ventilated HAP as a distinct entity; roughly 70% of HAP is acquired outside the ICU and 30% within it (p.1029). Three sequential steps drive VAP: oropharyngeal colonization with pathogens, aspiration of these organisms into the lower airway, and compromise of host defenses; almost all intubated patients are at least transiently colonized, yet only about one-third go on to develop VAP (p.1030). Colony counts often rise to high levels days before clinical pneumonia appears, supporting the idea that the final step is overwhelming of host defenses by a large bacterial inoculum (p.1030). Serial changes in oxygenation may detect VAP earlier than other clinical findings and can also be used to track response to therapy (p.1030). Clinical manifestations of HAP and VAP are nonspecific: fever, leukocytosis, increased respiratory secretions, consolidation on examination, and a new or changing radiographic infiltrate (p.1030). Absence of bacteria on a Gram stain of an endotracheal aspirate makes pneumonia an unlikely cause of fever or infiltrates, and absence of an MDR pathogen on culture supports de-escalation of empirical therapy (p.1031). Clinical improvement, when it occurs, is usually evident within 48-72 h of starting therapy, typically as improved oxygenation; chest radiographs often worsen early in treatment and are therefore less useful than clinical criteria for judging response (p.1033). P. aeruginosa essentially never causes infection in patients without prior antibiotic exposure; antibiotic exposure is by far the greatest risk factor for replacement of normal oropharyngeal flora by pathogens (p.1030). On any given day in the ICU, an average of about 10% of patients have pneumonia, the overwhelming majority of which is VAP; reported prevalence ranges from 6 to 52 cases per 100 patients depending on the population (p.1030). Worsening oxygenation, tachypnea, tachycardia, and increased minute ventilation in a ventilated patient (p.1030). Septic shock accompanying suspected VAP (favors broader empirical and combination coverage) (p.1031-1032). Colony counts above the diagnostic threshold while already on antibiotics, suggesting current therapy is ineffective (p.1031). Necrotizing pneumonia (e.g., P. aeruginosa or S. aureus) causing significant pulmonary hemorrhage or empyema (p.1032). VAP complicating COVID-19, which carries higher attributable mortality than other forms of VAP (p.1033). Applying clinical criteria designed for community-acquired pneumonia consistently overdiagnoses VAP, because of frequent tracheal colonization in intubated patients, multiple alternative causes of radiographic infiltrates, and the high frequency of other fever sources in critically ill patients (p.1030-1031). No single set of criteria is reliably diagnostic of pneumonia in a ventilated patient, which undermines both prevention and treatment efforts and even estimates of VAP attributable mortality (p.1030). Recently effective antibiotics given in the 24-48 h before sampling can cause false-negative quantitative cultures; with susceptible organisms a single dose can drop colony counts below threshold, and operating characteristics only normalize after about 3 days (p.1031). Quantitative cultures can also fall below threshold if obtained very early in infection or if delayed until an effective host response has reduced bacterial counts; the specimen should ideally be taken as soon as VAP is suspected and before antibiotics are started or changed (p.1031). Recurrent VAP with the same pathogen can occur because endotracheal-tube biofilm allows persistence and reintroduction; however, about half of recurrent Pseudomonas cases are actually due to a new strain (p.1032). Aggressive early extubation can lead to reintubation and increased aspiration (raising VAP risk), while heavy continuous sedation also increases VAP risk and undersedation risks self-extubation, so tradeoffs must be balanced (p.1033). The endotracheal tube is the single most important risk factor for VAP. While it blocks large-volume aspiration, it worsens microaspiration of secretions that pool above the cuff, and the tube plus suctioning damages tracheal mucosa and promotes tracheal colonization. Pathogenic bacteria form a glycocalyx biofilm on the tube surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defenses; suctioning can dislodge organisms that reinoculate the trachea, and biofilm fragments can embolize to distal airways carrying bacteria. Ventilator circuit tubing can harbor organisms that wash back if manipulated, so circuits are changed only when soiled or with a new patient. In critically ill patients, normal oropharyngeal flora is replaced by pathogens, driven mainly by antibiotic selection pressure, cross-infection, severe systemic illness, and malnutrition. Severely ill patients with sepsis or trauma appear to enter a state of immunoparalysis several days after ICU admission, coinciding with peak VAP risk; the mechanism is unclear but hyperglycemia and frequent transfusions adversely affect immunity (p.1029-1030). Crude mortality rates for VAP are reported as high as 50-70%, but the clinically meaningful figure is attributable mortality, since many patients have underlying diseases that would be fatal regardless. Attributable mortality exceeded 25% in one matched-cohort study, while more recent estimates are lower (5-10%); VAP complicating COVID-19 has higher attributable mortality. Mortality varies with patient type and ICU; VAP in trauma patients is generally not associated with attributable mortality (these patients were often previously healthy). The causative pathogen matters: MDR pathogens carry significantly greater attributable mortality than non-MDR pathogens, and infection with organisms such as S. maltophilia mainly marks a severely immunocompromised host at high risk. Beyond death, the major complication is prolonged mechanical ventilation with longer ICU and hospital stays; long-term sequelae of necrotizing infection include bronchiectasis and parenchymal scarring with recurrent pneumonia, prolonged oxygen need, a catabolic state, and (in the elderly) loss of independent function (p.1032-1033). Harrison does not present a formal VAP severity score in this text. Empirical-therapy decisions are instead stratified by (1) the presence of risk factors for MDR pathogens and (2) the predicted risk of death, with a mortality risk of <=15% considered low risk (p.1031).

Acute Viral Hepatitis — Liver function tests — Marked transaminase elevation (often >10x upper limit of normal) with hyperbilirubinemia is characteristic of acute viral hepatitis and helps distinguish it from other causes of jaundice. Hepatitis A IgM, Hepatitis E IgM — Confirms the most likely causes in this setting; both are the standard first-line serologic tests for acute fecal-oral hepatitis. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), IgM anti-HBc — Identifies acute Hepatitis B, which has different counseling, monitoring, and contact-tracing/vaccination implications than A or E. Coagulation profile (PT/INR) — A rising INR is the key early warning sign of evolving acute liver failure and should be tracked closely. Mental status assessment (serial) — Screens for hepatic encephalopathy, the clinical hallmark of progression to acute liver failure requiring urgent escalation of care. Autoimmune hepatitis (suggested by repeated unexplained episodes of acute hepatitis; can also be triggered after self-limited acute hepatitis A, B, or C) (p.2660) Alcohol-associated hepatitis (aminotransferases usually below ~400 IU/mL with a heavy-drinking history, unlike viral hepatitis) (p.2660) Drug-induced/toxin-induced liver injury, including acetaminophen, and anesthetic-agent hepatotoxicity (p.2660) Acute biliary disease: acute cholecystitis, common-duct stone, or ascending cholangitis (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice overlap) (p.2660) Obstructive jaundice from common-duct stone or pancreatic carcinoma (viral hepatitis in the elderly is often misdiagnosed as this) (p.2660) Wilson disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (genetic/metabolic liver disorders) (p.2660) Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD/MASH, formerly NAFLD/NASH) (p.2660) Ischemic (hypoxic) liver injury (a leading cause of aminotransferases >=1000 IU/L, along with drug injury and acute viral hepatitis) (p.2660) Infectious mononucleosis / Epstein-Barr virus (p.2660) Cytomegalovirus hepatitis (p.2643, p.2660) Herpes simplex virus (p.2660) Adenovirus (including the unexplained severe pediatric acute hepatitis linked to adenovirus type 41) (p.2643, p.2660) Coxsackievirus infection (p.2660) Toxoplasmosis (p.2660) SARS-CoV-2 (aminotransferase elevations in ~10% of cases and up to half of severe cases) (p.2660) Leptospirosis (p.2660) Brucellosis (p.2660) Disseminated candidiasis (p.2660) Mycobacterial infection (p.2660) Pneumocystis infection (p.2660) Anti-HCV antibody plus HCV RNA (HCV RNA is the gold standard; needed when anti-HCV is undetectable or in immunosuppressed patients where antibody may be absent) (p.2657-2658) Anti-HDV (IgM/IgG) and/or HDV RNA in HBsAg-positive patients who are at high risk or have severe/fulminant disease (p.2658, p.2659) IgM anti-HEV / HEV RNA when standard A/B/C tests are negative and enteric risk factors are present (specialized labs/CDC) (p.2658) HBeAg and anti-HBe to assess relative infectivity and replication in chronic HBV (p.2656, p.2659) Quantitative HBV DNA (PCR) to gauge replication level and risk of cirrhosis, decompensation, and HCC in chronic HBV (p.2656-2657) Serum albumin (a fall is uncommon in uncomplicated acute hepatitis; signals severe disease) (p.2656) Blood glucose (hypoglycemia can occur in severe hepatitis) (p.2656) Complete blood count / differential (transient neutropenia and lymphopenia, then relative lymphocytosis with 2-20% atypical lymphocytes) (p.2656) Serum bilirubin with conjugated/unconjugated fractions (levels >20 mg/dL persisting late suggest severe disease) (p.2655-2656) Liver biopsy only when the diagnosis is in doubt or chronic/autoimmune hepatitis is suspected; it is rarely needed in acute viral hepatitis (p.2658) Passive hepatic congestion / hypoperfusion from right ventricular failure, shock, severe hypotension, or severe left ventricular failure (p.2660) Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein occlusion) and hepatic veno-occlusive disease (p.2660) Constrictive pericarditis or right atrial myxoma impeding venous return (p.2660) Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (p.2660) Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (p.2660) Eclampsia (p.2660) HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver tests, low platelets) (p.2660) Liver metastases mimicking acute or even fulminant hepatitis (rare) (p.2660) Five hepatotropic viruses cause almost all acute viral hepatitis: HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV (delta), and HEV. All are RNA viruses except HBV, which is a DNA virus that replicates via reverse transcription like a retrovirus (p.2643). All five types produce a clinically similar acute illness, so the type cannot be reliably distinguished by clinical or epidemiologic features alone; specific serologic testing is the accurate way to tell them apart (p.2643, p.2651). Only the bloodborne agents (HBV, HCV, HDV) can become chronic and progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; HAV and HEV do not cause chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts (p.2643, p.2659-2660). Hepatitis A is diagnosed during acute illness by detecting IgM anti-HAV; IgM persists ~3 months (rarely 6-12). IgG anti-HAV appears in convalescence, remains detectable indefinitely, and confers lifelong immunity to reinfection (p.2643-2644, p.2656). The serologic/virologic course of acute hepatitis E mirrors hepatitis A: brief fecal shedding and viremia, an early IgM anti-HEV response dominating ~the first 3 months, then long-lasting IgG anti-HEV (p.2658). Acute hepatitis can be evaluated with five serologic tests: HBsAg, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HBc, anti-HCV, and HCV RNA (p.2657-2658). HBsAg positive plus IgM anti-HBc indicates acute (or acute reactivation) hepatitis B; HBsAg positive with IgG anti-HBc (IgM negative) indicates chronic HBV (p.2657-2658). In about 1-5% of acute HBV infections HBsAg is below the detection threshold; in that window the presence of IgM anti-HBc establishes the diagnosis of acute hepatitis B (p.2646, p.2656). The anti-HBc 'window' period (HBsAg already cleared, anti-HBs not yet detectable) is now rarely encountered because of higher-sensitivity HBsAg/anti-HBs assays (p.2646). Isolated anti-HBc usually represents remote past HBV infection (IgG class); rarely it reflects low-level viremia with HBsAg below detection, or a false-positive (p.2646). IgM anti-HBc can reappear with high titer during acute flares of chronic hepatitis B, so IgM vs IgG anti-HBc does not always reliably separate de novo acute hepatitis B from an exacerbation of chronic HBV; history and serial follow-up help (p.2646-2647, p.2657). HBeAg is a qualitative marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity; HBV DNA is the quantitative marker. HBeAg-positive HBsAg-positive mothers transmit to >90% of offspring versus only 10-15% if anti-HBe positive (p.2645-2646). Precore/core-promoter mutant HBV cannot make HBeAg, producing HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis with detectable HBV DNA and anti-HBe; it can run a more aggressive course and is the predominant form in the Mediterranean and Europe (p.2646-2647). Anti-HCV (IgG) is the available antibody marker (no clinically useful IgM anti-HCV exists); with contemporary assays it is detectable early in acute hepatitis C and persists after recovery and during chronic infection (p.2657). HCV RNA is the most sensitive test and the diagnostic gold standard; it appears before aminotransferase rise and before anti-HCV. Detectable anti-HCV with negative HCV RNA signifies cleared/cured infection (p.2657-2658). Recovery from hepatitis C leaves persistent anti-HCV but does NOT protect against reinfection; in people who inject drugs, anti-HCV plus HCV RNA may indicate reinfection rather than chronic infection (p.2657-2658). Serum aminotransferase levels do not correlate well with the degree of liver cell damage; peak ALT/AST does not predict severity (p.2655-2656). A low-grade fever (38-39 C) is more typical of hepatitis A and E than of B or C, except when hepatitis B presents with a serum sickness-like syndrome (p.2655). HDV is a defective virus that requires HBV (HBsAg envelope) for replication; negative HBV serology excludes hepatitis D, and the duration of HDV infection cannot outlast HBV infection (p.2646-2647, p.2658). In acute hepatitis with HBsAg and anti-HDV, the anti-HBc class clarifies the relationship: IgM anti-HBc indicates simultaneous acute HBV-HDV co-infection, whereas IgG anti-HBc indicates HDV superinfection on chronic HBV (p.2658). Among healthy adults, acute hepatitis B is self-limited in ~95-99%, whereas acute hepatitis C is self-limited in only ~15-20% (chronicity is the rule for HCV) (p.2655-2656). Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, disorientation, somnolence, progression to coma) - hallmark of fulminant hepatitis with very high mortality (>80% in deep coma without transplant) (p.2659) Markedly prolonged prothrombin time / INR (reflects severe synthetic failure and extensive hepatocellular necrosis) (p.2656, p.2658-2659) Rapidly shrinking liver size with rapidly rising bilirubin even as aminotransferases fall - indicates massive hepatic necrosis (p.2659) Ascites and peripheral edema at presentation (poorer prognosis) (p.2658-2659) Hypoglycemia and falling serum albumin in acute hepatitis (severe hepatocellular disease) (p.2656, p.2658-2659) Very high or persistently rising serum bilirubin (>20 mg/dL late in the course) (p.2655-2656, p.2659) Pregnancy with acute hepatitis E - up to 10-20% risk of fulminant hepatitis and death (p.2659, p.2661) HDV superinfection of chronic hepatitis B - clinical deterioration with substantially increased risk of fulminant hepatitis and death (mortality >20% in 'Labrea fever' outbreaks) (p.2659) Advanced age or serious underlying disease, especially pre-existing chronic liver disease (raises risk of severe and fulminant course) (p.2658-2659) Acute hepatitis E or other insult superimposed on chronic liver disease (acute-on-chronic liver failure) (p.2659-2660) Relying on HBsAg alone can miss acute hepatitis B: in ~1-5% of cases HBsAg is below detection and only IgM anti-HBc reveals the diagnosis (p.2656, p.2657-2658). IgM anti-HBc can re-emerge during an acute exacerbation of chronic HBV, so it does not always distinguish true acute hepatitis B from a chronic flare (p.2646-2647, p.2657). False-positive IgM anti-HAV occurs in rheumatologic disease (rheumatoid factor) and rarely in EBV infection; false-positive IgM anti-HBc occurs with high-titer rheumatoid factor (p.2656). Anti-HCV immunoassays can be falsely positive (low pretest probability, rheumatoid factor); confirm with HCV RNA (p.2657). In immunosuppressed patients anti-HCV may be undetectable, so HCV RNA testing is required to diagnose hepatitis C (p.2655, p.2657). HBsAg titer does not reflect disease severity - an inverse correlation exists, with very low HBsAg in fulminant hepatitis (p.2656-2657). Coexisting HBsAg and anti-HBs in chronic HBV does not signal imminent HBsAg clearance; these patients still have chronic HBV infection (p.2646, p.2657). A normal or only mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and normal albumin are expected in uncomplicated acute hepatitis; abnormal values suggest an alternative or complicated course (p.2656). The serum sickness-like prodrome of acute hepatitis B (arthralgia, rash, angioedema) is often misdiagnosed as a rheumatologic disease before jaundice appears (p.2659). Retrospective diagnosis of self-limited simultaneous acute HBV-HDV co-infection is difficult because anti-HDV is often transient and disappears once HBsAg clears (p.2658). Patients with acute viral hepatitis tolerate surgery poorly; biliary disease should be excluded clinically and with imaging before any operation (p.2660). None of the hepatitis viruses is ordinarily directly cytopathic to hepatocytes; the clinical manifestations and outcome of acute liver injury are largely determined by the host immune (chiefly cell-mediated/cytolytic T-cell) response to infected hepatocytes. In hepatitis B the existence of inactive carriers with normal histology and the more severe disease seen with defective cellular immunity support an immune-mediated mechanism; in immunocompetent adults the degree of liver injury correlates with the level of HBV replication (HBV DNA). HBV enters hepatocytes via the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor and replicates through reverse transcription of a pregenomic RNA, forming covalently closed circular DNA in the nucleus. HDV likewise enters via NTCP but depends on HBV helper function for complete virions and liver injury (p.2643-2645, p.2651). Hepatitis A and acute hepatitis B in previously healthy persons usually resolve completely (HBV self-limited in ~95-99% of healthy adults; HAV essentially always), with an overall case-fatality of ~0.1% (1% among hospitalized acute hepatitis B). Hepatitis A and E cause no chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts. Acute hepatitis C becomes chronic in ~85-90%; among chronic HCV, cirrhosis develops in up to ~20% over 10-20 years, with an annual decompensation risk ~4% and annual HCC risk ~1-4% (about 3.36%) once cirrhotic - rates declining with effective direct-acting antiviral therapy. Chronic hepatitis B carries an enhanced HCC risk, especially with infection in infancy/childhood and high HBV DNA/HBeAg; risk of cirrhosis and HCC rises with the level of HBV replication. Waterborne hepatitis E (genotypes 1 and 2) in India/Asia has a case-fatality of 1-2%, rising to 10-20% in pregnant women. Acute HBV-HDV co-infection mortality is usually similar to HBV alone (~5% in some injection-drug-user outbreaks), but HDV superinfection of chronic HBV markedly worsens outcome (annual cirrhosis rate ~4% in chronic hepatitis D; annual HCC ~3% once cirrhotic) (p.2658-2660). No formal grading system for acute viral hepatitis is given; severity is judged clinically. Features indicating severe hepatocellular disease warranting prompt hospital admission include prolonged prothrombin time, low serum albumin, hypoglycemia, and very high serum bilirubin; presenting ascites, edema, or encephalopathy indicate a poorer prognosis. Progression to fulminant hepatitis (massive hepatic necrosis) is marked by encephalopathy with rapidly shrinking liver size, rapidly rising bilirubin, and markedly prolonged PT even as aminotransferases fall (p.2658-2659).

Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis — Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture — The decisive test distinguishing viral from bacterial meningitis and guiding the decision to continue or stop empiric antibacterial therapy. CSF viral PCR (enterovirus, HSV) — Identifies the specific viral cause; HSV PCR specifically changes management since HSV meningitis/encephalitis is treated with acyclovir. Blood cultures — Performed alongside LP workup to support the broader diagnostic picture, particularly if bacterial meningitis cannot yet be excluded. Arthropod-borne (arbovirus) meningitis, notably West Nile virus; consider when meningitis/encephalitis clusters occur in a restricted region in summer/early fall (p.1167-1168) Epstein-Barr virus (may produce aseptic meningitis with or without infectious mononucleosis; atypical lymphocytes in CSF/blood are suggestive) (p.1168) Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) (p.1167) Cytomegalovirus (notably in immunocompromised hosts, where it may cause PMN pleocytosis with low glucose) (p.1167) HSV-1 (less common cause of meningitis than HSV-2) (p.1167) Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) (p.1167, 1169) Mumps (late winter/early spring, male predominance ~3:1) (p.1167, 1168-1169) Zika and other non-WNV arboviruses (p.1167) Human parechovirus (included on the FilmArray ME panel) (p.1167) Untreated or partially treated bacterial meningitis (a key pitfall when CSF shifts toward lymphocytic predominance) (p.1167) Early fungal meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis common; hypoglycorrhachia may be absent early) (p.1167) Early mycobacterial / tuberculous meningitis (p.1167) Neurosyphilis (Treponema pallidum) (p.1167) Mycoplasma pneumoniae CNS infection (p.1166-1167) Listeria spp. (p.1167) Brucella spp. (p.1167) Coxiella spp. (p.1167) Leptospira spp. (p.1167) Rickettsia spp. (p.1167) Parameningeal infections (p.1167) CSF reverse transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) for enteroviruses: diagnostic procedure of choice, highest sensitivity if done within 48 h of symptom onset, falling rapidly after day 5 (p.1166, 1168) FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis multiplex PCR panel covering HSV-1, HSV-2, enteroviruses, VZV, HHV-6, and human parechovirus (does NOT include CMV, WNV, LCMV, or EBV) (p.1166) WNV-specific CSF IgM (more sensitive than CSF RT-PCR for WNV; RT-PCR ~70% sensitive, useful mainly in immunocompromised patients with poor antibody response) (p.1166, 1168) Arboviral serology demonstrating CSF viral-specific IgM or seroconversion; repeat testing if early study is negative and suspicion is high (p.1168) Throat washing and stool PCR/culture to support enteroviral (and Mycoplasma) diagnosis (stool/throat shedding may persist for weeks) (p.1166-1167) Demonstration of intrathecal HSV-specific or VZV-specific antibody synthesis (less sensitive/specific than PCR; may take >1 week to become positive) (p.1168) Routine bloods: complete blood count with differential, liver and renal function tests, ESR, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, glucose, creatine kinase, aldolase, amylase, and lipase (p.1167) Neuroimaging (MRI preferred over CT) when there is altered consciousness, seizures, focal signs, atypical CSF profile, or immunocompromise (not mandatory in uncomplicated viral meningitis) (p.1167) Serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL as a clue favoring bacterial over aseptic meningitis (p.1167) Neoplastic meningitis (p.1167) Medication-induced hypersensitivity (drug-induced) meningitis (p.1167) Systemic lupus erythematosus and other rheumatologic diseases (p.1167) Sarcoidosis (p.1167) Behcet's syndrome (p.1167) Uveomeningitic syndromes (p.1167) Profound alterations in consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion), seizures, focal neurologic signs, or neuroimaging evidence of parenchymal involvement do NOT occur in viral meningitis; their presence points instead to encephalitis or another CNS process (p.1166). Headache is almost invariably present, often frontal or retroorbital, with photophobia and pain on eye movement; nuchal rigidity is usually present but may be mild, appearing only near the limit of neck anteflexion (p.1166). A specific viral cause is identified in 60-90% of cases using combined CSF PCR, culture, and serology; roughly two-thirds of culture-negative 'aseptic' meningitis cases have a viral etiology found by CSF PCR (p.1166). Enteroviruses account for >85% of cases with an identified etiology and predominate in summer and fall, especially in children <15 years (p.1167-1168). HSV-2 causes most adult uncomplicated HSV meningitis (HSV-1 causes ~90% of HSV encephalitis); ~20% of HSV meningitis patients develop recurrent attacks, and most recurrent/'aseptic' meningitis, including cases formerly called Mollaret's meningitis, is due to HSV (p.1168). Many HSV meningitis patients give no history and show no active genital herpes lesions at presentation, so absence of genital lesions does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168). VZV is increasingly recognized as a cause of meningitis even WITHOUT rash, so absence of chickenpox or shingles does not exclude it (p.1168). Cranial nerve palsies (most often V, VII, or VIII) are more common in HIV meningitis than in other viral meningitides; HIV seroconversion may be delayed, so seronegative suspected cases warrant repeat testing (p.1168). Mumps meningitis is suggested by parotitis, orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, or raised serum amylase/lipase, but their absence does not exclude it; a documented prior mumps infection (lifelong immunity) does exclude it (p.1168-1169). Consider LCMV when aseptic meningitis occurs in late fall/winter with exposure to house mice or pet/laboratory rodents or their excreta, particularly when accompanied by leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal liver function tests (p.1169). Depressed or markedly altered consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion) — suggests encephalitis or alternative diagnosis, not simple viral meningitis (p.1166) Seizures (p.1166) Focal neurologic signs/symptoms or neuroimaging abnormalities indicating parenchymal brain involvement (p.1166) CSF PMN pleocytosis without an established diagnosis — should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (p.1166-1167) Lymphocytic pleocytosis WITH low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) — should raise suspicion of fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1167) Atypical CSF profile or immunocompromising condition/treatment — warrants hospitalization and neuroimaging (p.1167) Failing to recognize partially or incompletely treated bacterial meningitis, which can produce a lymphocytic-predominant CSF that mimics viral meningitis (p.1167) Up to 15% of enteroviral meningitis patients (most often young infants) have a NORMAL CSF leukocyte count, so a normal cell count does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168) PMNs may predominate during the first 48 h of viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps); WNV PMN pleocytosis occurs in ~45% and can persist a week or more before shifting to lymphocytes — do not assume early neutrophilia means bacterial infection (p.1167-1168) Treating a normal CSF glucose as ruling out viral meningitis is wrong, but conversely low CSF glucose can occur in 10-30% of mumps or LCMV and rarely with enteroviruses, HSV-2, or VZV (p.1167) CSF viral culture has generally poor sensitivity for viral meningitis (unlike its utility in bacterial infection), so reliance on culture alone underdiagnoses (p.1167) Enterovirus detected in stool is NOT diagnostic of acute CNS infection — it may reflect residual shedding from a prior infection or asymptomatic carriage during epidemics (p.1167) Enteroviral RT-PCR has low sensitivity for EV71; specific testing may be required (p.1168) EBV CSF PCR false-positives may reflect viral reactivation or latent viral DNA in recruited lymphocytes rather than true EBV meningitis (p.1168) Routine serology is unhelpful for high-seroprevalence viruses (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) (p.1167) Viral meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, most often caused by enteroviruses, with a self-limited course in immunocompetent hosts. Inflammation is largely confined to the meninges, producing meningeal irritation without the parenchymal brain involvement that characterizes encephalitis; preservation of higher cerebral function distinguishes meningitis from encephalitis. CSF oligoclonal IgG bands directed against viral proteins can occur, though they are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.1166-1167). In adults the prognosis for full recovery from viral meningitis is excellent; treatment of almost all cases is primarily symptomatic. Rare adult patients have persisting headache, mild mental impairment, incoordination, or generalized asthenia for weeks to months. Outcome is less certain in infants and neonates (<1 year), in whom intellectual impairment, learning disabilities, hearing loss, and other lasting sequelae have been reported. Enteroviral meningitis outside the neonatal period is usually benign with recovery without sequelae, but chronic/severe infection can occur in neonates and in people with hypo- or agammaglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.1168-1169). Harrison does not give a formal severity grading for viral meningitis; it instead frames disposition by risk. Immunocompetent patients with a classic CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain), no focal signs, and no significant alteration in consciousness may not require hospitalization if home monitoring and follow-up are assured. Hospitalization is indicated for immunocompromised patients, those with significant alteration in consciousness, seizures, or focal signs suggesting encephalitis/parenchymal involvement, and those with an atypical CSF profile (Harrison 22e p.1169).

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia — macroglobulinaemia, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia, WM, IgM lymphoma, IgM monoclonal gammopathy-associated lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraproteinemia Multiple myeloma (IgM myeloma is rare but distinguishable by lytic bone lesions and different marrow morphology) IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma Marginal zone lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation Other B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas with paraproteinemia Amyloidosis (AL) presenting with neuropathy and paraproteinemia Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation — identifies and characterizes the monoclonal IgM spike Serum viscosity — quantifies hyperviscosity risk when symptomatic Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with immunophenotyping — confirms lymphoplasmacytic infiltration MYD88 L265P mutation testing (allele-specific PCR) — supports diagnosis and distinguishes from other lymphomas CXCR4 mutation testing — informs prognosis and response to certain targeted therapies Complete blood count — assesses cytopenias from marrow infiltration Anti-MAG antibody testing — when peripheral neuropathy is present CT imaging of chest/abdomen/pelvis — evaluates lymphadenopathy and organomegaly IgM MGUS Multiple myeloma Chronic lymphocytic leukemia Marginal zone lymphoma Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis from other causes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) unrelated to paraproteinemia Consider WM in an older adult with fatigue, weight loss, and an incidental monoclonal IgM spike on protein electrophoresis. Hyperviscosity symptoms (visual blurring, headache, mucosal bleeding, dizziness) reflect the very large size of the pentameric IgM molecule rather than tumor burden alone. Bone lesions are characteristically absent, unlike multiple myeloma, which helps distinguish the two at the bedside. Peripheral neuropathy (often demyelinating, anti-MAG antibody mediated) can be a presenting or dominant feature. Cold agglutinin disease and cryoglobulinemia are important IgM-related complications that can cause hemolysis or vasculitis-like skin findings. Bone marrow involvement by small lymphoplasmacytic cells with a mast-cell-rich infiltrate is a classic morphologic clue. MYD88 L265P mutation is present in the great majority of cases and is a useful diagnostic and prognostic marker. Asymptomatic patients with low IgM levels can often be observed without treatment (watch-and-wait). Visual disturbance, headache, confusion, or mucosal bleeding suggesting hyperviscosity syndrome requiring urgent plasmapheresis Rapidly progressive peripheral neuropathy Evidence of cryoglobulinemia with skin ulceration, digital ischemia, or renal involvement Cold agglutinin-mediated hemolysis with severe anemia Marked cytopenias suggesting extensive marrow replacement Transformation to a more aggressive (diffuse large B-cell) lymphoma Attributing an incidental IgM paraprotein to benign MGUS without adequate marrow and clinical evaluation when other features are present Delaying plasmapheresis in symptomatic hyperviscosity while awaiting definitive chemoimmunotherapy Missing WM as a cause of unexplained demyelinating peripheral neuropathy in older adults Confusing WM with IgM myeloma or misinterpreting lytic bone lesions as consistent with WM (they are not typical) Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in which clonal B-lymphoplasmacytic cells infiltrate the bone marrow (and sometimes lymph nodes and spleen) and secrete large quantities of monoclonal IgM. The pentameric structure of IgM raises serum viscosity disproportionately to its molar concentration, producing the hyperviscosity syndrome, and the paraprotein may also deposit in nerves, precipitate in the cold (cryoglobulinemia), or bind red cells (cold agglutinin disease). Somatic activating mutations in MYD88 (and often CXCR4) drive NF-κB signaling and are central to disease pathogenesis. The disease course is typically indolent with survival often measured in many years, and asymptomatic low-burden disease can be observed safely. Prognosis is influenced by age, cytopenias, beta-2-microglobulin level, and genetic features such as CXCR4 mutation status, with most patients eventually requiring treatment for symptomatic progression.

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) — zollinger, gastrinoma, ZES, gastrin-secreting tumor, gastrinoma syndrome, hypergastrinemic peptic ulcer disease, pancreatic gastrinoma, duodenal gastrinoma Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease Idiopathic gastric acid hypersecretion Antral G-cell hyperplasia Other causes of chronic secretory diarrhea (VIPoma, carcinoid syndrome) Retained gastric antrum syndrome after prior gastric surgery Helicobacter pylori peptic ulcer disease Fasting serum gastrin — markedly elevated levels raise suspicion for gastrinoma Gastric pH measurement — low pH with high gastrin confirms inappropriate acid-driven hypergastrinemia Secretin stimulation test — paradoxical rise in gastrin supports the diagnosis when basal levels are equivocal Upper endoscopy — assesses ulcer burden, location, and mucosal complications Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET/CT) — preferred for primary tumor and metastasis localization Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI abdomen) — evaluates tumor size, local invasion, and hepatic metastases Endoscopic ultrasound — useful for detecting small pancreatic/duodenal lesions Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone, prolactin — screen for coexisting MEN1 NSAID-induced ulcer disease Idiopathic gastric acid hypersecretion VIPoma (pancreatic cholera) Carcinoid syndrome Antral G-cell hyperplasia Suspect ZES in patients with severe, recurrent, or refractory peptic ulcers, ulcers in unusual locations (distal duodenum, jejunum), or ulcers with prominent diarrhea that improves with acid suppression. Chronic secretory diarrhea plus peptic ulcer disease is a classic combination that should prompt gastrin testing. About 20-30% of gastrinomas occur as part of MEN1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1) — screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumors. Most gastrinomas arise within the 'gastrinoma triangle' bounded by the cystic duct, junction of the pancreatic head/neck, and duodenal junction. Fasting serum gastrin should be measured off proton pump inhibitors when clinically feasible, since acid suppression can falsely elevate gastrin. A markedly elevated fasting gastrin with an inappropriately low gastric pH strongly supports the diagnosis. Roughly half of gastrinomas are malignant with a tendency for lymph node and hepatic metastases at diagnosis. Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET) is the preferred modality for tumor localization given high sensitivity. Multiple or recurrent ulcers despite adequate acid-suppressive therapy Ulcers in atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum) Evidence of hepatic or nodal metastases at diagnosis Signs of MEN1 (hypercalcemia, pituitary symptoms) suggesting hereditary syndrome Complications of ulcer disease such as perforation or bleeding Severe secretory diarrhea causing dehydration or electrolyte derangement Failing to hold proton pump inhibitors (when safe to do so) before gastrin testing, leading to false-positive hypergastrinemia Attributing recurrent ulcers solely to H. pylori or NSAIDs without considering gastrinoma in refractory cases Overlooking associated MEN1 features, delaying recognition of a hereditary tumor syndrome Relying on gastrin level alone without confirming inappropriate acid hypersecretion Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), most often located in the duodenum or pancreas, that drives unregulated gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting profound acid load overwhelms mucosal defenses and inactivates pancreatic enzymes, producing severe/recurrent peptic ulceration and secretory diarrhea with malabsorption. A substantial minority of cases occur in association with MEN1, reflecting a hereditary predisposition to multiple endocrine tumors. Prognosis depends primarily on tumor biology and extent of disease at diagnosis; localized, resectable gastrinomas carry a favorable long-term outlook, while metastatic disease (especially hepatic spread) is associated with reduced survival. Effective acid suppression has greatly reduced ulcer-related morbidity, shifting long-term outcome toward tumor-related factors.

Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — Bedside aortic ultrasound / CT Crossmatch; vascular surgery NOW Hypotension + back pain + pulsatile mass = surgical emergency Acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA embolism/thrombosis) — also causes severe diffuse abdominal pain, classically pain out of proportion to exam findings (p.154). Thoracic / thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, which is often contiguous with infradiaphragmatic disease (p.2208). Mycotic (infective) aortic aneurysm from staphylococcal, streptococcal, Salmonella, or fungal seeding — typically saccular and often with positive blood cultures (p.2209). Syphilitic aortitis — uncommon cause, predominantly involves the ascending aorta/arch rather than the abdominal aorta (p.2209). Tuberculous aneurysm — typically affects the thoracic aorta via contiguous spread from hilar nodes or abscess (p.2209). Abdominal ultrasound — delineates transverse and longitudinal dimensions, can detect mural thrombus, and is the tool for serial size surveillance and screening (p.2211). Plain abdominal radiograph — may show a calcified aneurysm outline, but ~25% are non-calcified and not visualized (p.2211). Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI — accurate for location and size and for planning open or endovascular repair (p.2211). Contrast aortography may underestimate true diameter when mural thrombus reduces luminal size, and carries risks of bleeding, allergy, and atheroembolism (p.2211). Renal/ureteric colic — rupturing AAA pain radiating to flank or genitalia can mimic urolithiasis (p.154). Rectus sheath hematoma — abdominal wall mass and pain, especially on anticoagulants (p.154). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and are found as an incidental imaging finding or as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass on routine abdominal exam (p.2211). New aneurysmal pain is usually a harbinger of rupture and constitutes a medical emergency; however, acute rupture more often occurs without any prior warning (p.2211). Acute pain plus hypotension is the presentation of frank rupture and mandates emergency open or endovascular repair (p.2211). At least 90% of abdominal aortic aneurysms >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic, and most lie below the level of the renal arteries (infrarenal) (p.2211). Cigarette smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor; incidence rises with age and the condition is more common in men (p.2211). Mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac can be a source of peripheral (distal) embolization (p.2211). New or worsening aneurysmal pain (abdomen, lower back, chest, or scrotum) signals impending rupture (p.2211). Abdominal pain radiating to sacrum, flank, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a rupturing AAA (p.154). Acute pain with hypotension indicates rupture — emergency repair required (p.2211). A rupturing AAA can be misattributed to renal/ureteric colic when pain radiates to the flank or genitalia (p.154). Plain x-ray cannot exclude an aneurysm because roughly a quarter are non-calcified (p.2211). Aortography may underestimate aneurysm diameter when mural thrombus narrows the lumen (p.2211). Premonitory pain may persist for several days before rupture and collapse, so an evolving symptomatic aneurysm should not be dismissed (p.154). Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of the aortic wall; a true aneurysm involves all three wall layers, versus a pseudoaneurysm in which intima and media are disrupted and the dilated segment is contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are degenerative and atherosclerotic. Wall failure results from degradation or abnormal production of the structural matrix proteins elastin and collagen, driven by inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis, and biomechanical wall stress. B- and T-lymphocytes, macrophages, inflammatory cytokines, and matrix metalloproteinases degrade elastin and collagen, reducing tensile strength and the aorta's ability to tolerate pulsatile stretch; histology shows elastin/collagen destruction, loss of vascular smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation (p.2208). Prognosis depends on aneurysm size and on the severity of coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Rupture risk rises sharply with diameter: the 5-year rupture risk is roughly 1-2% for aneurysms <5 cm versus 20-40% for aneurysms >5 cm. At smaller diameters the rupture risk is higher in women than in men (p.2211-2212). Rupture-risk stratification is driven by maximal aortic diameter. Per Harrison: a true abdominal aortic aneurysm is dilation 50% greater than the adjacent normal segment; aneurysms >=4.0 cm affect 1-2% of men >50. 5-year rupture risk is ~1-2% for <5 cm and ~20-40% for >5 cm. Repair thresholds: any size if rapidly expanding or symptomatic; for asymptomatic aneurysms repair is indicated at >=5.5 cm in men and >=5.0 cm in women, with smaller aneurysms followed by ultrasound surveillance (p.2210-2212).

Progressive ataxia, neuropathy or visual loss indicating advancing fat-soluble vitamin deficiency Coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency with bleeding risk Severe failure to thrive in infancy from fat malabsorption Retinal degeneration threatening irreversible visual impairment Overlooking acanthocytes and a strikingly low cholesterol as clues to the diagnosis Under-dosing vitamin E, which is the key intervention to protect the nervous system and retina Attributing the neurological picture to a primary ataxia without checking lipids and vitamin E Confusing the condition with chylomicron retention disease without appropriate genetic and lipid testing Abetalipoproteinaemia is caused by loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, encoded by MTTP, which is required to lipidate apolipoprotein B during assembly of chylomicrons in the intestine and VLDL in the liver. Without functional MTTP, apoB-containing lipoproteins cannot be assembled or secreted, so dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins are not exported from enterocytes and accumulate as lipid droplets within the cells. The result is severe fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea, extremely low plasma lipids, and progressive deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K. Chronic vitamin E deficiency underlies the spinocerebellar degeneration, neuropathy and retinopathy, while red-cell membrane lipid abnormalities produce acanthocytosis. When diagnosed early and treated with fat restriction and lifelong high-dose vitamin E and other fat-soluble vitamins, the disabling neurological and retinal complications can be largely prevented. Late or untreated disease leads to progressive, often irreversible, neurological and visual deterioration.

woman with lifelong heavy periods Not sampling the endometrium in women with risk factors for hyperplasia or cancer Treating presumed dysfunctional bleeding without excluding structural lesions Normal menstruation depends on cyclical ovulation producing coordinated oestrogen and progesterone effects, followed by orderly progesterone withdrawal and controlled endometrial shedding with effective local haemostasis. Abnormal bleeding arises when this is disrupted: structural lesions (polyps, adenomyosis, fibroids, hyperplasia or cancer) distort the endometrium and its vasculature; anovulation leads to unopposed oestrogen with an unstable proliferative endometrium that sheds erratically; systemic coagulopathy impairs haemostasis; and local disturbances of endometrial prostaglandins and fibrinolysis increase menstrual loss. Most abnormal uterine bleeding is benign and responds well to medical or targeted surgical treatment, with good symptom control and correction of anaemia. Prognosis in structural or malignant causes depends on the underlying diagnosis, so timely investigation to identify hyperplasia or carcinoma is key to a favourable outcome.

Acatalasaemia — Takahara disease, Catalase deficiency, Acatalasia, CAT Necrotising (ulcerative) gingivitis and periodontitis of other cause Immunodeficiency-related oral ulceration and gangrene (for example neutropenia) Other inherited antioxidant enzyme deficiencies Noma (cancrum oris) from severe malnutrition and infection Aggressive periodontal disease Oral manifestations of haematological malignancy Erythrocyte catalase activity assay, which is absent or markedly reduced Simple bedside test observing lack of frothing when blood meets hydrogen peroxide CAT molecular genetic testing Full blood count to exclude neutropenia as a cause of oral gangrene Dental and periodontal assessment of the extent of oral disease Screening for associated oxidative-stress conditions where clinically indicated Acatalasaemia is an autosomal recessive deficiency of the antioxidant enzyme catalase, encoded by CAT, which normally decomposes hydrogen peroxide within peroxisomes It was first described in Japan (Takahara disease) and is often clinically silent, discovered incidentally when blood fails to froth on contact with hydrogen peroxide The best-known manifestation is progressive oral gangrene (Takahara disease), where hydrogen peroxide from oral bacteria is not detoxified, leading to painful ulcerating gum and alveolar lesions Many individuals, especially those with residual enzyme activity (hypocatalasaemia), remain entirely asymptomatic throughout life Reduced antioxidant defence has been linked epidemiologically to increased susceptibility to oxidative-stress-related conditions such as diabetes mellitus in some populations Diagnosis is by demonstrating absent or markedly reduced erythrocyte catalase activity, confirmed by CAT gene analysis Management centres on scrupulous oral hygiene and prompt treatment of oral infection; no specific enzyme replacement exists Progressive oral gangrene with tissue necrosis and secondary infection Spreading orofacial infection threatening deeper structures Severe periodontal destruction with tooth loss Systemic sepsis arising from an oral focus Assuming all affected individuals develop oral disease, when the majority are asymptomatic Overlooking catalase deficiency as a cause of unexplained recurrent oral gangrene Failing to distinguish acatalasaemia from neutropenic or malnutrition-related oral necrosis Not recognising the residual-activity (hypocatalasaemia) state, which is milder and often silent Acatalasaemia results from recessive loss-of-function mutations in CAT, the gene encoding catalase, a haem-containing peroxisomal enzyme that catalyses the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. When catalase activity is largely absent, hydrogen peroxide generated by cellular metabolism or, in the mouth, by peroxide-producing bacteria is inadequately cleared. The accumulating hydrogen peroxide oxidises haemoglobin and damages tissue, and in the oral cavity it causes local ischaemia and ulceration that manifests as the characteristic gangrenous stomatitis. In most tissues, alternative antioxidant systems such as glutathione peroxidase partly compensate, which explains why many individuals are asymptomatic. The prognosis is generally excellent, since most individuals are asymptomatic; where the oral (Takahara) form occurs, outcome is good with meticulous oral hygiene and infection control, and severity tends to lessen after adolescence.
