cognitive decline or new psychiatric symptoms Poorly controlled diabetes with metabolic decompensation Severe or disabling involuntary movements Signs of significant hepatic iron-related dysfunction Confusing the low serum copper and caeruloplasmin with Wilson disease and giving copper-directed therapy while missing the iron-overload picture Overlooking the systemic clues of diabetes and retinopathy that point to the diagnosis Failing to consider a treatable iron-chelation opportunity when NBIA is suspected Not measuring ferritin, which is characteristically high and helps separate this from copper disorders Aceruloplasminaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in CP, which encodes caeruloplasmin, a ferroxidase that oxidises ferrous to ferric iron to enable iron export and loading onto transferrin. Without functional caeruloplasmin, iron cannot be released normally from cells, so it accumulates within the brain and visceral organs including the pancreas, liver, and retina. The resulting iron-mediated oxidative injury produces neurodegeneration concentrated in the basal ganglia and cerebellum together with diabetes and retinopathy, distinguishing this from copper-overload disorders such as Wilson disease. Untreated, the disorder is progressive with worsening neurological disability, diabetes, and retinopathy, but because iron-lowering therapy can retard progression, prognosis is more favourable with early diagnosis than for most other NBIA subtypes.

Achilles tendinopathy — Achilles tendinosis, Achilles tendinitis, mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, insertional Achilles tendinopathy Complete or partial Achilles tendon rupture Retrocalcaneal or superficial calcaneal bursitis Haglund deformity Posterior ankle impingement or os trigonum Calcaneal stress fracture Sural nerve irritation Systemic enthesitis from seronegative spondyloarthropathy Largely a clinical diagnosis Ultrasound to show tendon thickening, hypoechoic areas, neovascularity, and to detect partial tears MRI for detailed assessment in refractory or surgical cases and to characterise insertional pathology Plain radiographs for insertional disease to identify calcification, a Haglund deformity, or spur Consider metabolic and inflammatory screening in atypical, bilateral, or young patients Presents with posterior heel or lower-calf pain and stiffness that is worst on starting activity and after rest, with local tendon thickening and tenderness It is divided into mid-portion disease (a few centimetres above the insertion) and insertional disease at the calcaneal attachment, which are managed differently The mid-portion tendon has a relatively hypovascular zone that predisposes it to degenerative failure under repetitive load It is a degenerative tendinopathy with disorganised collagen and neovascularisation rather than true tendinitis Always distinguish tendinopathy from a complete rupture; a positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test and a palpable gap indicate rupture and need urgent referral Progressive eccentric or heavy slow-resistance calf loading is the cornerstone of treatment for mid-portion disease Insertional disease may respond less well to full-range eccentric loading and often needs modified, reduced-dorsiflexion exercises and heel lifts Corticosteroid injection into or around the tendon is generally avoided because of the risk of rupture Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with tendinopathy and tendon rupture and should be considered in the history Sudden pain with a palpable gap and positive Thompson test indicating tendon rupture Recent fluoroquinolone use raising rupture risk Night pain, systemic symptoms, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour Inflammatory or bilateral enthesitis suggesting spondyloarthropathy Missing a tendon rupture by not performing the Thompson test Injecting corticosteroid into or around the tendon and precipitating rupture Applying mid-portion eccentric protocols to insertional disease and worsening symptoms Advancing loading too quickly and provoking flares, or ignoring contributory training errors Achilles tendinopathy is an overuse condition in which repetitive loading exceeds the tendon's capacity to adapt, causing microtears and a failed healing response. Histology shows collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance, and neovascularisation with accompanying nerve ingrowth rather than inflammatory cells. The mid-portion watershed zone of relative hypovascularity is vulnerable, while insertional disease involves the enthesis and may be associated with a Haglund deformity or retrocalcaneal bursitis. Most patients improve over three to six months with structured loading, though symptoms can be slow to settle and recurrence is common; insertional disease is generally more resistant to conservative treatment than mid-portion disease.

Achondrogenesis — achondrogenesis type 1A (TRIP11), achondrogenesis type 1B (SLC26A2), achondrogenesis type 2 (COL2A1) Thanatophoric dysplasia (FGFR3, lethal short-limbed dysplasia) Osteogenesis imperfecta type II (fractures, poor ossification) Hypophosphatasia, perinatal lethal form Hypochondrogenesis (milder end of the COL2A1 spectrum) Short-rib polydactyly syndromes Fibrochondrogenesis and atelosteogenesis Detailed prenatal ultrasound and, where appropriate, fetal MRI to characterise limb, trunk and thoracic size Postnatal or postmortem skeletal radiographs demonstrating the ossification pattern Molecular testing of TRIP11, SLC26A2 and COL2A1 to define the subtype Histopathology of the cartilage growth plate Placental and fetal examination in perinatal death for diagnostic confirmation Genetic counselling with consideration of parental carrier or gonadal mosaicism testing A group of lethal skeletal dysplasias defined by extreme micromelia (very short limbs), a short trunk and severe deficiency of endochondral ossification Type 1A (Houston-Harris) is caused by TRIP11 mutations and type 1B (Fraccaro) by SLC26A2 mutations, both autosomal recessive; type 2 (Langer-Saldino) is caused by dominant COL2A1 mutations, usually de novo Presents prenatally or at birth with a large head, extremely short limbs, a narrow chest and hydrops or marked soft-tissue oedema The small, poorly compliant thorax causes pulmonary hypoplasia and lethal respiratory failure in the perinatal period Radiographs show virtually absent ossification of the vertebral bodies and sacrum, short ribs (with fractures in type 1A) and severely shortened, poorly modelled long bones Type 2 belongs to the type II collagenopathy spectrum, at the severe end of a continuum that includes hypochondrogenesis and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Diagnosis rests on the radiographic pattern, histology of the growth plate and molecular confirmation Because the condition is lethal, care centres on accurate diagnosis, recurrence-risk counselling and compassionate perinatal support Severe pulmonary hypoplasia causing respiratory failure at birth Hydrops fetalis detected antenatally A markedly small thorax on prenatal imaging predicting lethality Recurrence in a subsequent pregnancy indicating recessive inheritance or gonadal mosaicism Confusing it with other lethal short-limbed dysplasias without radiographic and molecular characterisation Assuming a de novo dominant cause and understating recurrence risk in the recessive types Not securing tissue or molecular confirmation before counselling about future pregnancies Overlooking gonadal mosaicism as an explanation for recurrence in type 2 Achondrogenesis is a disorder of cartilage and endochondral bone formation with several molecular causes. Type 1A involves TRIP11, encoding a Golgi protein needed for normal cartilage matrix processing. Type 1B involves SLC26A2, a sulphate transporter required to sulphate cartilage proteoglycans, so undersulphated matrix cannot support normal skeletal growth. Type 2 arises from dominant-negative mutations in COL2A1, the gene for type II collagen, the principal structural collagen of cartilage. In each case, disordered cartilage matrix prevents normal growth-plate function and ossification, producing the profound skeletal deficiency. Achondrogenesis is generally lethal before or shortly after birth because of pulmonary hypoplasia; the value of diagnosis lies in accurate classification, recurrence-risk counselling and support for the family rather than in curative treatment.

Achondroplasia — FGFR3, ACH, rhizomelic short-limbed dwarfism Hypochondroplasia Thanatophoric dysplasia Pseudoachondroplasia Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia Cartilage-hair hypoplasia SHOX-related short stature Skeletal survey demonstrating rhizomelic shortening and characteristic pelvic and spinal changes Targeted FGFR3 molecular testing to confirm the diagnosis Craniocervical MRI and neurological assessment to evaluate foramen magnum stenosis in infancy Polysomnography for suspected central or obstructive sleep apnoea Serial head circumference and disproportionate growth charting on condition-specific curves Spinal imaging for symptomatic canal stenosis or kyphosis The most common non-lethal skeletal dysplasia, characterised by disproportionate short stature with rhizomelic (proximal) limb shortening Nearly all cases arise from a recurrent gain-of-function variant in FGFR3; inheritance is autosomal dominant with high de novo rates, and paternal age is a risk factor Typical features include macrocephaly with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia, a trident hand configuration, and thoracolumbar kyphosis in infancy Radiographs show short tubular bones, narrowing rather than widening of the interpedicular distance descending the lumbar spine, squared iliac wings, and champagne-glass pelvis Foramen magnum stenosis is a critical early complication that can cause cervicomedullary compression, central apnoea, and sudden death in infancy Later complications include spinal canal stenosis, obstructive sleep apnoea, recurrent otitis media, and genu varum A targeted FGFR3-modulating therapy is now available to promote linear growth, alongside multidisciplinary surveillance Signs of cervicomedullary compression such as central apnoea, hypotonia, or long-tract signs in infancy Rapidly progressive hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure Progressive neurogenic claudication or myelopathy from spinal stenosis Severe fixed thoracolumbar kyphosis with neurological involvement Attributing infant apnoea or hypotonia to benign causes and missing foramen magnum compression Plotting growth on standard rather than condition-specific charts Assuming developmental delay when early gross-motor milestones are expectedly slow due to body proportions Overlooking recurrent middle-ear disease and its impact on hearing and speech Achondroplasia is caused by an activating variant in FGFR3, the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene. Constitutive receptor signalling suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation in the growth plate, impairing endochondral ossification. Because long bones grow chiefly through endochondral ossification while membranous ossification is relatively spared, the result is disproportionate shortening of the limbs with a relatively normal trunk length and a large skull. The same mechanism underlies the characteristic craniofacial and spinal features, including a small foramen magnum and narrow spinal canal. Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal with appropriate surveillance, though foramen magnum stenosis raises early infant mortality if unrecognised. Adult stature is markedly reduced, and morbidity later relates chiefly to spinal stenosis, sleep-disordered breathing, and joint problems.

Achromatopsia — rod monochromatism, complete achromatopsia, incomplete achromatopsia, CNGB3, CNGA3, congenital cone dysfunction Blue-cone monochromatism Leber congenital amaurosis Cone or cone-rod dystrophy Congenital stationary night blindness Ocular or oculocutaneous albinism Bilateral optic nerve or foveal hypoplasia Full-field electroretinography demonstrating absent cone with preserved rod responses Detailed colour vision testing (e.g. Hardy-Rand-Rittler or arrangement tests) Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography of the fovea Fundus autofluorescence imaging Molecular genetic testing (CNGB3, CNGA3 and related genes) Assessment of best-corrected acuity and refraction under controlled lighting Autosomal recessive congenital cone dysfunction most often caused by mutations in CNGB3 or CNGA3, and less commonly GNAT2, PDE6C, or PDE6H Presents in early infancy with pendular nystagmus, marked photophobia (day blindness), poor visual acuity, and absent or severely defective colour vision The full-field electroretinogram shows absent or grossly reduced photopic (cone) responses with preserved scotopic (rod) responses The fundus often appears near-normal in infancy, which can lead to delayed diagnosis despite abnormal function Optical coherence tomography typically reveals disruption or loss of the foveal cone photoreceptor layer and outer retinal changes Complete (typical) achromatopsia has total colour blindness, whereas incomplete forms retain some residual cone function and colour discrimination Management is supportive with tinted or red-tinted lenses to reduce photophobia and low-vision aids, and it is a leading candidate condition for gene-replacement therapy trials Nystagmus and photophobia in infancy requiring prompt paediatric ophthalmology and genetics referral Progressive loss of foveal cone structure on imaging Missed diagnosis attributed to a normal-looking fundus delaying appropriate support Attributing infantile nystagmus and poor vision to a normal fundus and missing the electrophysiological diagnosis Confusing achromatopsia with albinism or Leber congenital amaurosis Overlooking the photophobia burden and failing to prescribe appropriate tinted lenses Assuming complete colour blindness in all cases when incomplete forms retain partial function Achromatopsia arises from loss of function of the cone phototransduction cascade. Mutations most commonly affect the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel subunits CNGB3 and CNGA3, and less often the cone transducin GNAT2 or phosphodiesterase subunits, disrupting the cones' ability to respond to light. Rod-mediated (scotopic) vision remains functional, so vision is relatively better in dim conditions, while bright light saturates the rods and produces disabling photophobia. Because central vision depends on the cone-rich fovea, cone dysfunction causes reduced acuity, nystagmus from lack of a stable foveal fixation signal, and impaired or absent colour perception. Progressive cone photoreceptor structural loss may occur at the fovea over time. Vision is stable in most patients with typically low but non-progressive acuity, though photophobia and colour blindness persist lifelong; the condition is generally non-degenerative, and emerging gene therapies offer future therapeutic promise.

Acinetobacter Infections — Acinetobacter baumannii infection, A. baumannii infection, Acinetobacter calcoaceticus-baumannii complex infection, MDR Acinetobacter, Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRAB) Ventilator-associated/hospital-acquired pneumonia due to other nosocomial gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterobacterales) Stenotrophomonas maltophilia or Burkholderia infection in the ventilated/immunocompromised host Catheter-related bloodstream infection from other nosocomial pathogens Necrotizing fasciitis or other necrotizing soft tissue infection from streptococcal, clostridial, or polymicrobial causes following trauma Bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis (similar gram-negative paired cocci on CSF Gram stain) Neisseria meningitidis on CSF Gram stain (both appear as gram-negative diplococci/paired cocci) Other nonfermenting gram-negative nosocomial pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for species-level identification Quantitative real-time PCR for identification of A. baumannii Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide definitive therapy (given extensive and variable resistance) Respiratory cultures interpreted in clinical context to distinguish colonization from pneumonia Blood cultures (assessing for polymicrobial growth in suspected bacteremia) Rectal surveillance cultures for outbreak detection and infection-control purposes Molecular typing of isolates to differentiate outbreak from nonoutbreak strains Airway colonization without true pneumonia (positive respiratory culture not equating to active infection) Wound colonization rather than soft tissue infection, particularly in burns and trauma Acinetobacter are gram-negative, oxidase-negative, nonmotile, nonfermenting coccobacilli readily grown on standard media; A. baumannii is the most clinically relevant species. Phenotypic differentiation between species is difficult, so molecular methods such as MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry or quantitative real-time PCR are often needed for accurate identification. A. baumannii can survive environmental desiccation for weeks, allowing it to persist on hospital surfaces and equipment - a key reason it drives health care-associated outbreaks. A. baumannii is a notorious cause of nosocomial pneumonia, especially with prolonged mechanical ventilation; onset tends to be later than with other gram-negative bacilli, and the usual clues are fever and increased sputum production. Airway colonization with A. baumannii does not by itself confirm pneumonia, but it is a recognized risk factor for subsequent infection - distinguishing colonization from true infection is a recurring clinical challenge. On a CSF Gram stain, Acinetobacter can mimic Neisseria meningitidis since both appear as gram-negative paired cocci; a petechial rash was described in up to 30% of one meningitis case series. Bloodstream infection most often arises in ICU patients with a central venous catheter or as a secondary complication of ventilator-associated/hospital-acquired pneumonia; fever occurs in over 95% of cases and polymicrobial growth is reported in roughly 20-36% of bacteremia episodes. In combat-trauma soft tissue infection, the described clinical evolution progresses from an edematous peau d'orange appearance to a sandpaper appearance with overlying vesicles, then to a necrotizing process with hemorrhagic bullae; necrotizing fasciitis has been reported. Community-acquired Acinetobacter pneumonia is relatively rare but severe, with fever, prominent respiratory symptoms, multi-organ dysfunction, lobar consolidation on imaging, and mortality exceeding 50%. A. baumannii is an important burn-unit pathogen; large burns provide ideal growth conditions, facilitate patient-to-patient transmission, and wound colonization is a risk factor for bloodstream infection. Risk factors for health care-associated colonization/infection include nursing home residence, prolonged ICU stay, central venous catheterization, tracheostomy, mechanical ventilation, enteral feeding, and prior third-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, or carbapenems; carbapenem-resistant strains are most common after carbapenem exposure. Urinary tract infection is infrequent and usually catheter-associated, reflecting biofilm formation on devices; rare community-acquired cases occur with nephrolithiasis or after renal transplantation. Less common manifestations include contact lens-associated keratitis and native- or prosthetic-valve endocarditis. Septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation, each reported in roughly 25-30% of bloodstream infection cases Infection caused by carbapenem-resistant (extremely drug-resistant) isolates, where delayed adequate therapy drives poor outcomes Evolving necrotizing soft tissue picture (hemorrhagic bullae, necrotizing fasciitis) after combat or disaster-related trauma New A. baumannii in a long-term ventilated ICU patient with fever and rising sputum Multi-organ dysfunction with severe community-acquired pneumonia Treating positive respiratory or wound cultures as proof of infection when they may represent colonization, leading to overtreatment. Underestimating environmental persistence: failure to address desiccation-resistant contamination of surfaces and equipment perpetuates outbreaks. Mistaking Acinetobacter for Neisseria meningitidis on CSF Gram stain. Assuming susceptibility - intrinsic and acquired beta-lactamases (including OXA-type carbapenemases) make empirical choices unreliable without local epidemiology and susceptibility testing. Overlooking Acinetobacter in the differential of soft tissue infection following exposure to tropical/subtropical environments or natural disasters. A. baumannii has greater virulence potential than other Acinetobacter species, partly through its ability to grow at 37 degrees C and resist macrophage uptake. Colonization is facilitated by adherence to surfaces and human cells and by biofilm formation, which is linked to exopolysaccharide production and pilus formation; a quorum-sensing molecule encoded by the abaI autoinducer synthase gene contributes to biofilm on abiotic surfaces. The organism modifies its lipid A structure to survive harsh environments, decreasing susceptibility to antibiotics and antimicrobial peptides and enhancing desiccation survival. An extracellular capsule protects against complement-mediated killing and can be upregulated in the presence of subinhibitory antibiotic levels, producing a hypervirulent phenotype. Phospholipase C and D act as cytotoxic virulence factors aiding epithelial invasion, and siderophore-based iron-acquisition systems permit growth despite host iron limitation. Multiple protein-secretion systems (type II with the LipA lipase substrate, type V trimeric autotransporter mediating biofilm and matrix adherence, and a type VI system secreting antibacterial toxins) plus outer-membrane vesicles carrying OmpA, proteases, and phospholipases contribute to pathogenesis and innate immune activation. Antimicrobial resistance arises from reduced porin expression, overexpressed efflux pumps (removing quinolones, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, disinfectants, and tigecycline), and beta-lactamases including intrinsic AmpC cephalosporinases (upregulated when the ISAba1 insertion sequence is placed next to the AmpC gene) and acquired serine and metallo-beta-lactamases. Carbapenem resistance is mostly tied to Ambler class D oxacillinases (group 2d), some intrinsic/chromosomal (e.g., OXA-51-like) and others acquired (e.g., OXA-23-, 24-, 58-, 143-, 235-like). The small A. baumannii core genome with a large accessory genome confers high genomic plasticity and ready uptake of resistance genes by horizontal gene transfer. Infections carry high mortality, driven largely by the severity of the patient's underlying illness and by drug resistance of the infecting strain. Crude mortality with nosocomial pneumonia has been reported as high as 65%, though attributable mortality is hard to establish because affected patients are typically debilitated. Community-acquired pneumonia mortality exceeds 50%. Crude bloodstream infection mortality reaches about 40% overall and as high as 70% with carbapenem-resistant isolates. Wound colonization/infection contributes to healing delays and graft loss in burn patients. No formal disease-specific severity score is provided in the source. Severity is gauged clinically by site and host factors: presence of septic shock or DIC in bloodstream infection (~25-30%), need for prolonged mechanical ventilation in pneumonia, and carbapenem/extreme drug resistance, all of which predict markedly higher mortality.

Anterior cruciate ligament injury — ACL tear, ACL rupture, anterior cruciate ligament rupture, cruciate ligament injury Meniscal tear Collateral (medial or lateral) ligament injury Posterior cruciate ligament injury Patellar dislocation Osteochondral fracture or tibial spine avulsion Knee dislocation with multiligament injury Extensor mechanism rupture MRI of the knee to confirm the tear and detect associated meniscal, chondral, and ligamentous injury Clinical stability testing (Lachman, anterior drawer, pivot-shift) Plain radiographs to exclude fracture, including a Segond fracture as an indirect sign Aspiration of a tense haemarthrosis for symptom relief and diagnostic information where appropriate Assessment for associated multiligament injury if a knee dislocation is suspected Typically follows a non-contact pivoting, twisting, or deceleration injury, often in sport, with the patient reporting a 'pop' and rapid swelling of the knee A tense, blood-filled effusion (haemarthrosis) developing within hours of injury strongly suggests an ACL rupture (or other significant intra-articular injury) The Lachman test is the most sensitive clinical examination; the anterior drawer and pivot-shift tests also demonstrate anterior tibial translation and rotational instability MRI confirms the diagnosis and, importantly, identifies associated meniscal tears, collateral ligament injury, and bone bruising Symptomatic instability with the knee 'giving way' during turning or pivoting is the key indication for reconstruction Management is individualised: reconstruction (usually with a tendon graft) is favoured for young, active, or pivoting-sport patients, while rehabilitation-led treatment suits lower-demand individuals Rehabilitation to restore quadriceps strength and neuromuscular control is essential whether or not surgery is performed Untreated instability predisposes to recurrent meniscal tears and secondary osteoarthritis over time Features of knee dislocation with multiligament injury requiring urgent vascular and neurological assessment (risk to the popliteal artery and peroneal nerve) A locked knee suggesting a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear needing prompt treatment Signs of neurovascular compromise after significant knee trauma Open injury or associated fracture Missing an ACL rupture by not recognising the significance of an acute haemarthrosis Failing to identify associated meniscal or collateral ligament injury Overlooking a knee dislocation that has spontaneously reduced, with its vascular risk Proceeding to surgery on a stiff, poorly rehabilitated knee, increasing the risk of postoperative stiffness The anterior cruciate ligament runs from the posterior femoral intercondylar notch to the anterior tibial plateau and is the principal restraint to anterior translation of the tibia and a key stabiliser against rotational and pivoting forces. Sudden deceleration, landing, or a valgus-external rotation force with the foot planted overloads the ligament, causing partial or complete rupture, frequently near its femoral origin. Because the ligament is intra-articular and vascular, rupture produces a rapid haemarthrosis. The ACL has poor intrinsic healing capacity, so complete tears generally do not reunite. Persistent instability increases shear on the menisci and articular cartilage, accelerating degenerative change. Outcomes depend on activity demands and associated injuries; reconstruction restores stability and enables return to pivoting sport in most, while appropriately selected patients do well with rehabilitation alone, but chronic instability and untreated meniscal damage increase the long-term risk of osteoarthritis regardless of treatment.

Acne vulgaris — acne, common acne, pimples Rosacea (lacks comedones, features flushing and telangiectasia) Perioral dermatitis Folliculitis (bacterial or fungal) Keratosis pilaris Drug-induced acneiform eruptions (e.g. corticosteroids) Hidradenitis suppurativa when lesions involve flexures Clinical diagnosis; investigations rarely needed for typical presentations Hormonal workup (androgens, and related endocrine tests) when hyperandrogenism or polycystic ovary syndrome is suspected Pregnancy testing and lipid and liver monitoring before and during systemic retinoid therapy Swabs when Gram-negative folliculitis or resistant infection is suspected A disorder of the pilosebaceous unit affecting the face, chest, and back, typically beginning around puberty The hallmark non-inflammatory lesion is the comedo (open blackheads and closed whiteheads); its presence distinguishes acne from other papulopustular eruptions like rosacea Inflammatory lesions range from papules and pustules to deep nodules and cysts, and severe forms lead to scarring and post-inflammatory pigmentation Treatment is chosen by severity: topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide for comedonal and mild inflammatory disease, adding topical or oral antibacterials for moderate disease Combining benzoyl peroxide with antibacterials reduces bacterial resistance, and antibacterials should not be used as prolonged monotherapy Systemic retinoid therapy is reserved for severe, nodulocystic, or scarring acne resistant to other measures and requires careful monitoring and strict pregnancy precautions given teratogenicity Hormonal therapy can help women with acne linked to androgen excess; consider investigating for hyperandrogenism when there are virilising features or menstrual irregularity Sudden severe nodular acne with fever and joint pain (acne fulminans) is a systemic emergency needing urgent specialist care Acne fulminans: abrupt severe ulcerating nodular acne with fever, malaise, and arthralgia Signs of underlying endocrine disorder such as virilisation or rapid-onset severe acne Extensive scarring or psychological distress requiring escalation of care Suspected retinoid-associated mood disturbance during systemic treatment Prolonged antibacterial monotherapy promoting resistance and relapse Under-treating scarring or nodular acne and delaying referral for systemic retinoid therapy Overlooking the significant psychological burden and risk of low mood Failing to enforce pregnancy prevention during teratogenic systemic retinoid use Acne results from four interacting processes within the pilosebaceous unit: increased sebum production driven by androgens, abnormal keratinisation of the follicular lining producing microcomedones, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. Trapped sebum and keratin form comedones; bacterial activity and the host immune response generate inflammatory mediators that produce papules, pustules, and deeper nodules. Rupture of the follicular wall extends inflammation into the dermis, and disordered wound healing can result in atrophic or hypertrophic scarring. Hormonal influences, genetic predisposition, and certain drugs modulate severity. Acne usually improves after adolescence but may persist into adulthood, particularly in women; early effective treatment limits permanent scarring and psychosocial impact.

between observation with serial imaging, stereotactic radiosurgery, and microsurgical excision, depending on size, growth, symptoms, hearing and age Unilateral or asymmetrical sensorineural hearing loss or tinnitus mandating MRI to exclude the tumour Facial numbness or an absent corneal reflex suggesting trigeminal involvement by a larger tumour Headache, ataxia, vomiting or altered consciousness suggesting brainstem compression or raised intracranial pressure (an emergency) Sudden sensorineural hearing loss, which can occasionally be the presenting feature Bilateral tumours or a family history suggesting neurofibromatosis type 2 Attributing unilateral hearing loss or tinnitus to age or noise without imaging Overlooking disproportionately poor speech discrimination as a retrocochlear clue Assuming prominent vertigo must be present, when balance symptoms are often mild Missing the significance of facial numbness or an absent corneal reflex Failing to consider neurofibromatosis type 2 in young or bilateral cases Acoustic neuroma is a benign neoplasm of Schwann cells, most often originating at the transition zone of the vestibular nerve within or near the internal auditory canal. As it grows it first fills the canal, compressing the cochlear and vestibular fibres and their blood supply to produce sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. Continued expansion into the cerebellopontine angle displaces and stretches adjacent structures: the trigeminal nerve above, the facial nerve alongside, and eventually the brainstem and cerebellum. Large tumours can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and raise intracranial pressure. Most cases are sporadic and unilateral, while bilateral tumours are the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2. Because the tumour is benign and usually slow growing the prognosis is generally good, and small tumours may simply be observed; treatment outcomes depend on tumour size at diagnosis, with hearing preservation and facial nerve function being more achievable when tumours are small.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica — SLC39A4, ZIP4 deficiency, hereditary zinc deficiency, AE Acquired zinc deficiency from poor intake, malabsorption or parenteral nutrition Biotinidase and other the dermatitis Autosomal recessive disorder of intestinal zinc uptake caused by SLC39A4 variants affecting the ZIP4 transporter Classic triad is periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia and diarrhoea, often emerging when breast-feeding is stopped Skin lesions are sharply demarcated, scaly, erythematous or vesiculobullous around the mouth, nappy area and over the hands and feet Associated features include irritability, poor growth, recurrent infections and impaired wound healing A low serum zinc with reduced alkaline phosphatase (a zinc-dependent enzyme) supports the diagnosis Acquired zinc deficiency from inadequate intake or malabsorption can mimic the inherited disorder and must be considered Skin, gut and growth abnormalities respond rapidly and dramatically to zinc replacement Extensive erosive or secondarily infected skin disease Severe failure to thrive and immune compromise with recurrent infections Rapid clinical deterioration in an untreated infant Persistent symptoms despite replacement suggesting non-adherence or an alternative diagnosis Not distinguishing inherited ZIP4 deficiency from acquired zinc deficiency, which alters duration of treatment Falsely low or high zinc levels from sample contamination or handling Misdiagnosing the rash as candidiasis or eczema and delaying zinc therapy Stopping zinc prematurely in the genetic form, allowing relapse Acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by variants in SLC39A4, which encodes the intestinal zinc transporter ZIP4 responsible for zinc uptake at the enterocyte apical membrane. Impaired transport leads to systemic zinc deficiency. Zinc is a cofactor for numerous metalloenzymes and is essential for epithelial integrity, immune function and cell proliferation, so its deficiency produces the characteristic dermatitis at sites of friction and around orifices, hair loss, impaired healing and immune dysfunction, together with malabsorptive diarrhoea. Because human milk contains a zinc-binding ligand that aids absorption, symptoms often surface after weaning from breast milk. The inherited form requires lifelong zinc replacement but carries an excellent prognosis once treatment is established, with rapid resolution of skin, gastrointestinal and growth abnormalities. Untreated disease can be life-threatening.

Acromegaly — growth hormone excess, GH excess, somatotroph adenoma, gigantism (if before epiphyseal fusion) Constitutional large body habitus or familial coarse features Pachydermoperiostosis and other causes of acral enlargement Hypothyroidism causing coarse features and soft-tissue changes Other pituitary masses causing mass effect without GH excess Ectopic GHRH or GH secretion from a neuroendocrine tumour Serum IGF-1 interpreted against age-matched reference ranges as the initial screen Oral glucose tolerance test with GH measurement to confirm non-suppression Pituitary MRI to define adenoma size and relation to the optic chiasm Formal visual field assessment when a macroadenoma abuts the chiasm Evaluation of remaining anterior pituitary axes for co-secretion or hypopituitarism Screening for complications including echocardiography, sleep study, and colonoscopy Insidious onset means diagnosis is often delayed by years; comparing old photographs can reveal the gradual coarsening of features Characteristic findings include enlarging hands and feet, coarse facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, and interdental spacing Soft-tissue overgrowth commonly causes carpal tunnel syndrome, arthralgia, excessive sweating, and obstructive sleep apnoea Systemic complications include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and an increased risk of colonic polyps Because GH secretion is pulsatile, a random GH level is not reliable; IGF-1 is the preferred screening test as it reflects integrated secretion Biochemical confirmation rests on failure of GH to suppress during an oral glucose load Most cases arise from a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, so pituitary MRI and assessment of other pituitary axes and visual fields are essential Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the usual first-line treatment, with medical therapy or radiotherapy for residual disease Visual field loss or new headache suggesting chiasmal compression by a macroadenoma Features of pituitary apoplexy such as sudden severe headache with ophthalmoplegia Signs of heart failure from acromegalic cardiomyopathy Coexisting hypopituitarism, particularly unrecognised adrenal insufficiency Relying on a single random GH level, which is uninterpretable given pulsatile secretion Attributing carpal tunnel syndrome, sleep apnoea, or new diabetes to common causes without considering acromegaly Missing coexisting hypopituitarism when focusing on GH excess Overlooking the need for long-term surveillance for cardiovascular disease and colonic polyps Acromegaly is caused by chronic excess of growth hormone, almost always from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma, and rarely from ectopic GH or GHRH secretion. Excess GH stimulates hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediates most of the peripheral growth effects on bone, cartilage, and soft tissue. When GH excess occurs before epiphyseal fusion it produces gigantism; after fusion it produces the acral and soft-tissue overgrowth of acromegaly. The expanding pituitary mass may also compress the optic chiasm and impair other pituitary hormone axes, while GH's counter-regulatory metabolic effects promote insulin resistance and cardiovascular disease. Biochemical control that normalises IGF-1 and GH restores life expectancy toward normal and improves soft-tissue and metabolic features, whereas persistent disease increases cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic mortality and the risk of colonic neoplasia.

Acute coronary syndrome — 12-lead ECG (serial) Troponin Aspirin + cardiology referral STEMI → immediate reperfusion pathway Stable angina (chronic, exertional) Esophageal spasm (can closely mimic angina and may respond to nitroglycerin) Gastroesophageal reflux / peptic ulcer disease Costochondritis / chest wall (musculoskeletal) syndromes Cervical radiculitis / disk disease Panic disorder and related psychiatric conditions (up to ~10% of ED chest pain) High-sensitivity cardiac troponin at presentation, repeated at 1-3 h (1-2 h rapid rule-out possible with hs-assays); conventional troponin repeated at 3-6 h Right-sided ECG leads when ischemia is suspected but standard 12-lead is nondiagnostic Chest radiograph (often normal in ACS; may show pulmonary edema; helps exclude pneumothorax, wide mediastinum) Echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality, mechanical complications, or tamponade when diagnosis is uncertain or there is hemodynamic instability Coronary CT angiography for low-intermediate probability (high negative predictive value; also excludes dissection, effusion, PE) Stress nuclear perfusion imaging or stress echocardiography for intermediate-risk patients eligible for further testing Cardiac MRI to characterize troponin elevation without definite CAD and to discriminate ischemic from non-ischemic injury B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer as adjuncts (for heart failure and PE exclusion respectively) Acute pericarditis (pleuritic pain, relieved by sitting forward, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression) Acute myocarditis (non-ischemic myocardial injury; troponin may rise but should not be labeled MI) Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (abrupt chest pain/dyspnea after emotional or physical stress; may show ST elevation and elevated biomarkers mimicking MI) Acute aortic syndrome / aortic dissection (sudden tearing or knifelike pain, may radiate to back) Pulmonary embolism (massive PE can cause substernal pain mimicking MI) Pulmonary hypertension (anginal-quality chest pain) Tension pneumothorax Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave) / Mallory-Weiss ACS encompasses unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI, and the term is generally reserved for ischemia precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis (Harrison 22e p.145). Unstable ischemic heart disease is sub-classified by whether acute myocardial injury is detectable and whether ST-segment elevation is present: unstable angina = no detectable acute injury; NSTEMI/STEMI = acute injury without/with ST elevation (Harrison 22e p.145). Type 1 MI (acute coronary thrombosis) is distinguished from type 2 MI, which results from another imbalance of myocardial oxygen supply and demand; type 2 may be driven by anemia, hypoxia, hypotension, or intense psychological stress (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150). An ECG is recommended within 10 minutes of presentation, primarily to identify ST-segment elevation candidates for immediate reperfusion (Harrison 22e p.150). Resting ECG sensitivity for ischemia is poor (as low as ~20%), so a normal ECG does not exclude ACS; serial ECGs every 30-60 min are recommended early in suspected ACS (Harrison 22e p.150). Physical examination findings may be entirely normal in unstable ischemic heart disease, so an unremarkable exam is not reassuring (Harrison 22e p.149). Relief of pain by nitroglycerin is neither sensitive nor specific for ischemia (esophageal spasm also responds); relief delayed beyond ~10 min suggests either a non-ischemic cause or severe ischemia such as acute MI (Harrison 22e p.149). Chest wall tenderness on palpation does not exclude myocardial ischemia (Harrison 22e p.150). ST-segment elevation on ECG (candidate for immediate reperfusion) ST-segment depression or symmetric T-wave inversions >=0.2 mV (higher risk of death or recurrent ischemia) Hypotension and significant tachycardia (suggest cardiogenic shock or other severe cause) New murmur of mitral regurgitation or ventricular septal defect (mechanical complication of STEMI) Pulmonary edema / S3 / rales (high-risk LV dysfunction) Pain prolonged >=30 min and not relieved by rest (suggests MI rather than stable angina) Syncope or presyncope with chest pain (consider ischemic arrhythmia, also PE and dissection) Relying on a normal resting ECG or unremarkable physical exam to exclude ACS - both can be normal in unstable ischemic heart disease (Harrison 22e p.149-150). Treating nitroglycerin response as diagnostic - esophageal spasm also responds and ischemic relief is non-specific (Harrison 22e p.149). Attributing pain to the chest wall because palpation reproduces it - tenderness does not exclude ischemia (Harrison 22e p.150). Some patients with ischemia deny 'pain' and report only dyspnea or vague anxiety; women and the elderly may present with anginal equivalents (dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue, faintness) (Harrison 22e p.149). Inferior MI may present with nausea/vomiting (vagal / Bezold-Jarisch reflex), simulating a GI disorder (Harrison 22e p.149). High-sensitivity troponin detects injury in many non-ACS cardiopulmonary conditions; without a dynamic rise/fall and clinical correlation, a single elevated value can be misinterpreted as MI - chronic elevation occurs with structural heart disease, end-stage renal disease, or interfering antibodies (Harrison 22e p.150). Non-ischemic injury (e.g., myocarditis) can raise troponin but should not be labeled MI (Harrison 22e p.150). Confusing diagnostic decision-aids (HEART, EDACS) with prognostic risk scores (TIMI, GRACE), which are intended for patients with already-established ACS, not for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.151). Myocardial ischemia (angina pectoris) arises from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand (raised by heart rate, ventricular wall stress, and contractility) and oxygen supply (set by coronary blood flow and arterial oxygen content). ACS is typically precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis. When ischemia is sufficiently severe and prolonged (as little as ~20 min), irreversible cellular injury and MI occur. Symptoms can also be driven predominantly by increased demand (e.g., intense psychological stress) or reduced delivery (anemia, hypoxia, hypotension), underlying the type 2 MI concept (Harrison 22e p.145). Among unselected ED chest-pain populations, only ~10-20% (as low as 5%) are ultimately diagnosed with ACS, while gastrointestinal causes predominate; historically 2-6% of patients discharged with presumed non-ischemic pain were later found to have had a missed MI. In patients stratified as low risk (excluding ST elevation or definite noncardiac pain), the estimated 30-day major cardiovascular event rate was ~2.5%. Validated clinical decision pathways combining ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin can achieve ACS miss rates <0.5%, and a single very low hs-troponin >2-3 h after symptom onset carries a negative predictive value >99% for MI (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150-151). ACS is categorized along two clinical decision-making lines. (1) Diagnostic/disposition risk in undifferentiated chest pain uses clinical decision pathways such as the HEART score (history, ECG, age, risk factors; low risk 0-3) and EDACS, combined with serial high-sensitivity troponin, to classify patients as low/intermediate/high risk. (2) Prognostic risk in established ACS uses the TIMI and GRACE risk scores to estimate event risk - these are explicitly not intended for diagnostic use. Common high-risk elements across tools: typical ACS symptoms, older age, known/atherosclerotic risk factors, ischemic ECG changes, and elevated troponin (Harrison 22e p.151).

Actinic Keratosis — AK, solar keratosis, senile keratosis Squamous cell carcinoma (invasive) Bowen's disease (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) Superficial basal cell carcinoma Seborrhoeic keratosis Discoid lupus erythematosus Localised patch of eczema or psoriasis Largely a clinical and dermoscopic diagnosis Skin biopsy when a lesion is thick, indurated, tender, or otherwise suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma Full skin examination to assess overall field damage and detect other skin cancers Closer surveillance protocols for immunosuppressed and transplant patients Presents as rough, scaly, erythematous macules or thin papules on chronically sun-exposed skin such as the face, scalp of balding men, ears, forearms, and backs of hands Lesions are often more easily felt than seen, giving a sandpaper-like texture to palpation They are markers of cumulative ultraviolet damage and indicate field change, so surrounding skin often harbours further subclinical lesions A minority progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and the risk rises with the number of lesions and degree of sun damage Features that raise concern for progression include thickening, tenderness, induration, rapid growth, bleeding, or ulceration Management options span lesion-directed treatments such as cryotherapy and curettage and field-directed topical therapies, with photoprotection central to prevention Immunosuppressed patients, particularly organ transplant recipients, develop more numerous and aggressive lesions and need closer surveillance Sun-protection advice and regular skin self-examination reduce the development of new lesions and help detect malignant change early Rapid growth, induration, tenderness, ulceration, or bleeding suggesting progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma A lesion that recurs quickly or fails to respond to appropriate treatment Numerous or aggressive lesions in an immunosuppressed or organ transplant patient A hyperkeratotic horn-like lesion with a firm, tender base warranting histology Dismissing an indurated or growing lesion as a simple actinic keratosis when it is an invasive squamous cell carcinoma Treating individual visible lesions while ignoring the wider field of sun damage Underestimating risk and undertreating in immunosuppressed patients Neglecting to reinforce sun protection and self-examination, allowing recurrent disease Actinic keratosis is an intraepidermal proliferation of atypical, dysplastic keratinocytes driven by cumulative ultraviolet radiation. UV exposure induces characteristic DNA mutations, including in the TP53 tumour-suppressor gene, that impair repair and apoptosis and allow clonal expansion of abnormal keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. The result is disordered maturation and hyperkeratosis producing the palpable scale. Because the whole photo-damaged area shares this mutational burden (field cancerisation), multiple lesions and recurrences are common, and continued genetic damage can lead to full-thickness dysplasia and invasion characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma. Individual actinic keratoses are common and most remain stable or regress, but they mark significant sun damage and carry a small per-lesion risk of transforming into squamous cell carcinoma; with a high lesion burden the cumulative risk becomes clinically important, so treatment and long-term photoprotection and surveillance are worthwhile.

Actinomycosis — Actinomyces infection, lumpy jaw, cervicofacial actinomycosis Malignancy / solid tumor (most common misdiagnosis given mass-like, tissue-plane-crossing behavior) Tuberculosis Nocardiosis Inflammatory bowel disease (when abdominal sinus tracts/fistulas develop) Endometriosis (in pelvic disease) Bacterial pneumonia or lung neoplasm (in thoracic disease) Tuberculosis Nocardiosis Mycetoma due to Nocardia or Actinomadura species Botryomycosis (chronic suppurative bacterial infection forming granule-like clumps) Bacterial pneumonia/empyema from usual organisms Microscopic identification of sulfur granules in pus or tissue (most common diagnostic means; yield improves with additional histopathologic sections and positively charged slides) Anaerobic culture—isolation maximized under anaerobic conditions, typically requiring 5–7 days and potentially up to 2–4 weeks; even a single antibiotic dose can preclude recovery 16S rRNA gene amplification and sequencing to enhance sensitivity and specificity MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry (databases still being optimized) Histologic stains: periodic acid–Schiff (PAS), Grocott methenamine silver (GMS), and Gram stains to identify actinomycotic aggregates CT and MRI for lesion characterization and monitoring; FDG-PET may demonstrate hypermetabolism CT/ultrasound-guided aspiration or biopsy to obtain material in a minimally invasive fashion; endometrial biopsy for pelvic disease Malignant neoplasm / solid tumor Endometriosis Inflammatory bowel disease Lung neoplasm An uncommon, indolent, slowly progressive infection caused by anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria—primarily Actinomyces species—that normally colonize the mouth, colon, and vagina; it has been called one of the most frequently misdiagnosed diseases (Harrison 22e p.1363). Three classic presentations should trigger suspicion: a chronic mass-like lesion that crosses tissue planes and mimics malignancy, a sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs, and a refractory or relapsing infection after a short course of therapy (Harrison 22e p.1363). Most infections are polymicrobial; companion organisms such as Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Eikenella corrodens, Enterobacteriaceae, Fusobacterium, and Bacteroides are commonly co-isolated, though their pathogenic contribution is uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1363). Disease spreads contiguously, ignoring tissue planes; the characteristic chronic phase produces single or multiple indurated lesions with fibrotic walls classically described as wooden (Harrison 22e p.1364). Central necrosis containing neutrophils and sulfur granules is virtually diagnostic; over time, sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone develop (Harrison 22e p.1364). Lymphatic spread with lymphadenopathy and distant hematogenous seeding are uncommon—an important contrast with malignancy and tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1364). Oral–cervicofacial disease is the most frequent presentation, typically at the angle of the jaw, often precipitated by dental disease or procedures (Harrison 22e p.1364). Pelvic actinomycosis is strongly associated with intrauterine contraceptive devices (IUDs) and other foreign bodies such as surgical mesh; risk increases the longer the device remains in place and is low when in place under one year (Harrison 22e p.1364-1365). Sulfur granules represent an in vivo matrix of bacteria, calcium phosphate, and host material; on hematoxylin-eosin staining they may be surrounded by a radiating fringe of eosinophilic clubs (Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon) (Harrison 22e p.1365). Foreign bodies (especially IUDs) and immunocompromising states—HIV, transplantation, common variable immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, and certain immunosuppressive therapies—are recognized predisposing factors (Harrison 22e p.1364). FDG-PET may show hypermetabolism in actinomycotic lesions, potentially compounding confusion with malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1365). Chronic mass-like lesion crossing tissue planes and mimicking cancer Sinus tract that spontaneously resolves and recurs Refractory or relapsing infection after a short antibiotic course Lesions crossing fissures/pleura, extending into mediastinum, bone, or chest wall (empyema necessitatis) Wound or fistula that fails to heal, or recurrent abdominal disease CNS involvement (brain abscess, meningitis, cavernous sinus syndrome)—a critical-site presentation Diagnosis is rarely considered prospectively—actinomycosis is often first identified by the pathologist after extensive (and avoidable) surgery (Harrison 22e p.1365). Prior antibiotic exposure or failure to obtain appropriate anaerobic cultures frequently precludes microbiologic identification; even a single antibiotic dose can prevent isolation (Harrison 22e p.1365). Because actinomycetes are normal oral and genital-tract flora, their detection in sputum, bronchial washings, or cervicovaginal secretions without sulfur granules may reflect colonization rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.1365). Detection of Actinomyces-like organisms on Papanicolaou smear in IUD users has low positive predictive value; in an asymptomatic patient this warrants education and follow-up, not routine IUD removal (Harrison 22e p.1365). Isolation of Actinomyces from blood cultures without a defined focus may represent contamination or transient bacteremia from a mucosal site (Harrison 22e p.1366). Elevated CA-125 in pelvic disease and FDG-PET hypermetabolism can reinforce a mistaken cancer diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1365). The etiologic agents are members of the normal oral, gastrointestinal, and female genital flora. The critical initiating step is disruption of the mucosal barrier, allowing local infection. Once established, the infection spreads contiguously in a slow, progressive fashion that disregards normal tissue planes. Although acute inflammation may occur initially, the hallmark is a chronic indolent phase with indurated lesions, central necrosis (neutrophils plus sulfur granules), and dense fibrotic walls. Sinus tracts to skin, adjacent organs, or bone may develop over time. Foreign bodies, particularly IUDs, facilitate infection, and ulcerative mucosal infections (e.g., HSV, CMV) may promote disease (Harrison 22e p.1364). Actinomycosis is usually curable with medical therapy alone, even in extensive disease, and an awareness of its clinical spectrum can expedite diagnosis and minimize unnecessary surgery, morbidity, and mortality. Cure of established disease requires prolonged treatment, and relapse is a clinical hallmark if therapy is stopped too early; refractory disease has been described in HIV-infected individuals (Harrison 22e p.1363, p.1366).

Acute abdomen — surgical abdomen, acute abdominal pain, peritonitis Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm Mesenteric ischaemia or infarction Perforated viscus (peptic ulcer, diverticulum, appendix) Bowel obstruction with or without strangulation Ectopic pregnancy or other gynaecological emergency Inferior myocardial infarction or lower-lobe pneumonia mimicking abdominal pain Erect chest and abdominal radiographs to detect free air or obstruction Bedside ultrasound and CT abdomen for definitive assessment when stable Serum lactate as a marker of ischaemia or hypoperfusion Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age Amylase/lipase, renal and liver function, and inflammatory markers as part of the workup The immediate task is to identify the patient who needs urgent surgery from among the many with self-limiting abdominal pain Assess airway, breathing, and circulation first, since perforation, ischaemia, or bleeding can cause rapid haemodynamic collapse The character, onset, and migration of pain guide the diagnosis; sudden severe pain suggests perforation, rupture, or vascular catastrophe Peritonism (guarding, rigidity, rebound, pain on movement) indicates peritoneal irritation and a likely surgical cause Pain out of proportion to examination findings should raise concern for mesenteric ischaemia Always consider extra-abdominal and vascular causes such as myocardial infarction, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, and ectopic pregnancy Serial examination and reassessment are valuable when the diagnosis is uncertain, as the picture often evolves Resuscitate, provide analgesia, and involve surgery early rather than delaying for prolonged investigation in the unstable patient Sudden severe pain with peritonism suggesting perforation or vascular rupture needing immediate surgery Haemodynamic instability indicating haemorrhage, ischaemia, or septic shock Pain disproportionate to findings, raising suspicion of mesenteric ischaemia A pulsatile mass or back pain with collapse suggesting ruptured aortic aneurysm Rapidly progressive distension, fever, and toxicity signalling advancing peritonitis Withholding analgesia for fear of masking signs, which is not supported and delays comfort Attributing pain to a benign cause in the elderly, in whom signs are often muted despite serious disease Overlooking vascular and extra-abdominal causes such as aortic aneurysm or myocardial infarction Delaying surgery to complete imaging in an unstable patient Failing to reassess when the initial diagnosis is uncertain Acute abdomen results from inflammation, obstruction, perforation, ischaemia, or haemorrhage of intra-abdominal organs. Visceral pain is initially poorly localised because of autonomic innervation, but once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum the pain becomes sharp and localised. Perforation releases luminal contents causing chemical then bacterial peritonitis; obstruction causes distension, third-space fluid loss, and potential strangulation; and vascular occlusion causes bowel ischaemia and infarction. These processes can precipitate hypovolaemia, sepsis, and shock, making the acute abdomen a potentially life-threatening presentation. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and the speed of definitive treatment. Early recognition and surgery for perforation, ischaemia, or haemorrhage improve survival, while delay allows sepsis, bowel infarction, or exsanguination with markedly higher mortality.

hypoxia or hypoglycaemia demanding immediate correction Fluctuating consciousness or new focal neurology suggesting a serious intracranial cause Agitation in a trauma patient indicating possible hypoxia or shock and prompting reassessment Autonomic instability with hyperthermia suggesting a severe toxidrome or serotonin/neuroleptic syndrome Rapid physical exhaustion during prolonged struggle, risking sudden collapse Labelling agitation as psychiatric or drug-related before excluding hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, and head injury Sedating the patient without monitoring, risking airway obstruction and respiratory depression Using prolonged or unmonitored physical restraint Failing to reassess the trauma patient whose agitation reflects worsening shock or hypoxia Overlooking withdrawal states that can escalate dangerously Acute agitation is a final common pathway of many disturbances of brain function. Global cerebral dysfunction (delirium) arises from hypoxia, hypoperfusion, hypoglycaemia, metabolic derangement, sepsis, drug intoxication or withdrawal, and structural brain injury, all of which impair the neural networks governing attention and behaviour. In the trauma setting, agitation may be the earliest external sign of inadequate cerebral oxygen delivery from hypoxia or haemorrhagic shock. Primary psychiatric illness and severe pain also contribute, but organic causes must be excluded because they are frequently reversible and can be fatal if missed. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause. When a reversible medical precipitant is identified and treated, agitation usually resolves, but a missed organic cause such as hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, or intracranial pathology can be rapidly fatal.

Acute and Chronic Myocarditis — Myocarditis, Inflammatory cardiomyopathy, Viral myocarditis, Giant cell myocarditis, Eosinophilic myocarditis, Cardiac sarcoidosis, Lyme carditis, Chagas cardiomyopathy, Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (shared chest pain, ECG, troponin) and MINOCA Genetic dilated or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (overlapping CMR fibrosis patterns) Stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy and other dilated cardiomyopathies Pericarditis and other COVID-associated cardiac involvement Sepsis-related reversible myocardial depression from systemic inflammatory response Sepsis with reversible systemic-inflammation-mediated myocardial depression (mimics myocarditis but is generally reversible if the patient survives) Chagas cardiomyopathy presenting as dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disease Lyme carditis (Borrelia burgdorferi) presenting with conduction block Granulomatous infections such as tuberculosis or histoplasmosis that must be excluded before immunosuppression for presumed sarcoidosis Cardiac troponin (often elevated) and B-type natriuretic peptide Cardiac MRI showing myocardial edema plus nonischemic late gadolinium enhancement (typical mid-wall location) ECG (ST elevation mimicking infarction, conduction block, tachyarrhythmias, nonspecific ST-T changes) Coronary artery imaging to exclude infarction Eosinophil count (hypereosinophilia in most eosinophilic myocarditis); creatine phosphokinase and C-reactive protein Respiratory viral panel; selected serologies for HIV, Chagas, CMV, dengue, Lyme, and systemic autoimmune disease (viral titers rarely guide initial therapy) Endomyocardial biopsy (with immunohistochemistry) when ventricular arrhythmias, conduction block, eosinophilia, or autoimmune disease suggest a specific etiology Chest CT (mediastinal lymphadenopathy) and whole-chest FDG-PET for active sarcoid lesions; PCR for T. cruzi in acute Chagas Cardiac sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas; may mimic arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy) Giant cell myocarditis Eosinophilic myocarditis / hypereosinophilic syndrome with Loeffler endocarditis Systemic autoimmune disease: polymyositis/dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus (which also causes accelerated CAD, sterile endocarditis, pericarditis, vasculitis) Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis and vaccine-associated myocarditis Myocarditis is inflammation of heart muscle that can present acutely, subacutely, or insidiously, with outcomes ranging from full resolution to a relapsing course or progression to chronic cardiomyopathy; it is termed acute when symptoms have lasted under a month, often only days (p.2011). Chest pain is the most common symptom of acute myocarditis, occurring in more than 80% of patients, who frequently also have dyspnea or arrhythmias; fever is present in over half of cases and a viral prodrome may precede onset by days to weeks (p.2011). Acute myocarditis in adults typically occurs between roughly 30 and 45 years and is more common in men, whereas women tend to present after age 45 (p.2011). At presentation about one-fourth of acute myocarditis cases have an LVEF below 0.50, ventricular arrhythmias, or shock; fulminant myocarditis (circulatory shock) is reported in about 3-9% of cases (p.2011). Diagnosis can now be made noninvasively when a typical symptomatic presentation is accompanied by elevated troponin plus cardiac MRI showing both myocardial edema and nonischemic injury without another cause; biopsy is no longer strictly required for a 'definite' diagnosis (p.2011-2012). Because chest pain, ECG changes, and elevated troponin overlap between acute myocarditis and myocardial infarction, coronary imaging is often the first differential step; myocarditis is later diagnosed in up to one-third of patients with MINOCA (myocardial infarction with nonobstructed coronary arteries) (p.2011). Eosinophil counts should be checked routinely because hypereosinophilia is present in most cases of eosinophilic myocarditis; right bundle branch block should raise suspicion for sarcoidosis or Chagas rather than typical cardiomyopathies, in which left bundle branch block predominates (p.2011, p.2013, p.2014). Around one in five patients with inflammatory myocarditis carry genetic variants considered pathogenic for cardiomyopathy, and 20-40% of dilated cardiomyopathy patients have variants sufficient to explain their disease; CMR fibrosis patterns once attributed to prior viral myocarditis are now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy too (p.2011, p.2012). Giant cell myocarditis accounts for 10-20% of biopsy-proven myocarditis, occurs equally in men and women (typically older than viral cases), is more often linked to systemic autoimmune disease, and usually presents acutely with rapidly progressive heart failure and tachyarrhythmias (p.2014). Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is the most common infective cause of cardiomyopathy worldwide; after a usually silent initial infection patients enter an 'indeterminate phase' lasting decades, during which persistent low-level parasitemia is now recognized as the major driver of progression to chronic heart failure (p.2013). Diphtheria toxin (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) interferes with cardiac protein synthesis and especially affects the conduction system; cardiac involvement is the most common cause of death in this infection, and clinical suspicion alone justifies giving antitoxin with higher priority than antibiotics (p.2013). Combined immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis is the most dramatic noninfectious form: troponin is often elevated, biopsy shows extensive lymphocytic infiltration, and it should be suspected immediately with any acute cardiac presentation in a treated patient; CCU admission is recommended for elevated troponin with ECG changes (p.2014). Fulminant presentation with cardiogenic shock or need for high-dose inotropes/mechanical circulatory support (3-9% of cases) Ventricular arrhythmias or syncope, which may precede sudden cardiac death (inflammatory myocarditis found in 3-10% of sudden deaths in previously healthy young adults) New conduction block, especially right bundle branch block (suggests sarcoidosis or Chagas) LVEF <0.50 at presentation (marks higher-risk 'complicated' course and chronic cardiomyopathy risk) Hypereosinophilia (suggests eosinophilic myocarditis, a cause of fulminant disease) Acute cardiac symptoms in a patient on immune checkpoint inhibitors, often with concurrent involvement of other organs Assuming any chest pain/ECG change/troponin elevation is infarction can miss myocarditis, which underlies up to one-third of MINOCA cases (p.2011). Sarcoid granulomas are scattered and commonly missed on endomyocardial biopsy, so a negative biopsy does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (p.2014). Eosinophilic myocarditis may be overlooked in milder presentations if hypereosinophilia is not assessed (p.2014). Viral titers and detection of viral genome fragments or anticardiac antibodies in chronic cardiomyopathy are of uncertain significance, as the same viruses (e.g., parvovirus B19, HHV6) are also found in normal control hearts and these assays are not in routine clinical use (p.2011, p.2012). There are no data supporting routine immunosuppression for presumed viral acute myocarditis, and immunosuppression for nonspecific lymphocytic chronic myocarditis has not shown convincing benefit (p.2012). Initial care of suspected checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis should generally not be delayed to obtain endomyocardial biopsy (p.2014). Infectious agents injure the myocardium both by direct cellular invasion (disrupting normal cellular processes) and by activating immune responses, with or without persistent infection. Viral myocarditis has classically been described in three phases from murine enterovirus (coxsackie B) models: (1) direct myocardial invasion, with viral entry sometimes enhanced by coxsackie/adenovirus receptor variants and enteroviral protease degrading dystrophin to trigger apoptosis and impair autophagy; (2) host immune response to conserved antigenic patterns, activating macrophages and expanding T- and B-cell populations, which can produce 'virally triggered' myocarditis even without direct viral injury, possibly via molecular mimicry between viral and cardiac antigens; and (3) progression to chronic cardiomyopathy, demonstrated in animal models. Direct genome entry occurs with enteroviruses, HIV, and dengue, but most common viruses do not appear to damage the heart directly, and early injury is often driven by cytokine storm and nonspecific immune activation. Notably, this initial immune response appears crucial to recovery, since early immunosuppression worsened viral replication and cardiac injury in animals. Viral 'hijacking' of cellular machinery to produce extracellular vesicles carrying viral RNA may allow protected spread to other cells. In Chagas disease, acute infection produces dense parasitic pseudocysts that rupture and cause diffuse myocyte necrosis, while chronic disease reflects persistent parasitemia plus depopulation of cardiac and gastrointestinal parasympathetic neurons. Noninfective inflammatory myocarditis (sarcoid granulomas, giant cell, eosinophilic, autoimmune, checkpoint inhibitor) reflects antigen-driven, dysregulated immune attack on myocardium; the paradigm is cardiac transplant rejection, which showed that antibodies and cytokines, not only lymphocytes, mediate reversible myocardial depression and that antigens are exposed by prior injury or infection (p.2011-2014). Prognosis is good for 'uncomplicated' acute myocarditis (LVEF >=0.50 without ventricular arrhythmias or shock), which represents about three-fourths of patients; spontaneous recovery is common, almost all retain LVEF >=0.50 on follow-up, and they survive without transplantation at 5 years. Among the one-fourth with complicated presentations, roughly 18% die or undergo transplantation over the next 5 years. In fulminant myocarditis, more than half of affected patients recover to near-normal LVEF despite presenting with refractory cardiogenic shock. Reduced LVEF at presentation predicts chronic cardiomyopathy. Chagas cardiomyopathy has lower survival than other cardiomyopathies once overt heart failure develops, and LVEF improvement is uncommon. Most patients with giant cell myocarditis in cardiogenic shock require urgent mechanical support or transplant. Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis fatality was initially very high but is improving with earlier recognition and treatment (p.2011-2014). Harrison distinguishes uncomplicated acute myocarditis (LVEF >=0.50, no ventricular arrhythmias, no shock; ~75% of cases, good prognosis) from complicated acute myocarditis (LVEF <0.50, ventricular arrhythmias, or shock; ~25%, higher 5-year death/transplant rate). Fulminant myocarditis (~3-9%) denotes circulatory shock requiring high-dose inotropes or mechanical circulatory support. Diagnostically, 'probable myocarditis' requires at least one symptom plus one supporting finding (elevated troponin, consistent ECG, or reduced LVEF/wall-motion abnormality on imaging), while 'definite myocarditis' historically required a positive endomyocardial biopsy with lymphocytic infiltrate (p.2011).

normal pressure once the acute attack settles without confirming the angle is open In predisposed eyes with a shallow anterior chamber and short axial length, the peripheral iris crowds the drainage
