When the pupil becomes mid-dilated, relative pupillary block impedes aqueous flow from the posterior to the anterior chamber, so pressure builds behind the iris and bows it forward against the trabecular meshwork. This apposition abruptly obstructs aqueous outflow, causing a rapid and severe rise in intraocular pressure that compromises the optic nerve head and corneal endothelium if not relieved promptly. Prompt reduction of pressure and timely iridotomy usually preserve vision, but delayed treatment can cause permanent optic nerve damage and irreversible loss of sight.

Acute Appendicitis and Peritonitis — appendicitis, peritonitis Crohn's disease Cholecystitis or other gallbladder disease Diverticulitis Ectopic pregnancy Endometriosis Gastroenteritis or colitis Gastric or duodenal ulceration Hepatitis Kidney disease including nephrolithiasis Liver abscess Meckel's diverticulitis Mittelschmerz Mesenteric adenitis Omental torsion Pancreatitis Lower lobe pneumonia Pelvic inflammatory disease Ruptured ovarian cyst or other cystic ovarian disease Small-bowel obstruction Urinary tract infection Ovarian torsion (Harrison 22e p.2596) Gastroenteritis or colitis (nausea precedes pain, unlike appendicitis) (Harrison 22e p.2595) Pelvic inflammatory disease (Harrison 22e p.2596) Urinary tract infection / genitourinary infection (Harrison 22e p.2596) Mesenteric adenitis (Harrison 22e p.2595) Hepatitis / liver abscess (Harrison 22e p.2595) Lower lobe pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2595) COVID-19 infection occasionally coincident (Harrison 22e p.2595) In immunocompromised patients: atypical infections from mycobacteria, Cytomegalovirus, or fungi, and neutropenic enterocolitis (Harrison 22e p.2596) WBC count: only mildly to moderately elevated (~10,000-18,000 cells/uL) in ~70% of simple appendicitis; laboratory testing alone does not identify patients with appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596). A left shift toward immature polymorphonuclear leukocytes is present in >95% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2596). Serum amylase and lipase should be measured; sickle cell preparation may be prudent in patients of African, Spanish, Mediterranean, or Indian ancestry (Harrison 22e p.2596). Urinalysis to help exclude genitourinary mimics; a few red or white cells may be a nonspecific finding, and an inflamed appendix abutting the ureter or bladder may cause sterile pyuria or hematuria (Harrison 22e p.2596). Pregnancy test in every woman of childbearing age; cervical cultures if PID is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2596). Anemia and guaiac-positive stools should raise concern for other disease or complications such as cancer (Harrison 22e p.2596). Ultrasonography: highly operator dependent; overall sensitivity ~0.86 and specificity ~0.81; appendix may not be visualized even in skilled hands; especially useful (including intravaginal techniques) for pelvic pathology in women. Suggestive findings: wall thickening, increased appendiceal diameter, free fluid (Harrison 22e p.2596). CT: sensitivity at least 0.94 and specificity at least 0.95; high negative predictive value; suggestive findings include dilatation >6 mm with wall thickening, a lumen that does not fill with enteric contrast, and periappendiceal fatty stranding or air. Presence of luminal air or contrast is NOT consistent with appendicitis; nonvisualization of the appendix is nonspecific and should NOT be used to rule out appendiceal/periappendiceal inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2596). Plain abdominal films are rarely helpful and not routinely obtained; <5% show an opaque fecalith, and a fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596). For peritonitis: in stable patients with ascites, diagnostic paracentesis is indicated with testing of fluid for protein and LDH and a cell count; radiographs may show bowel dilatation and wall edema, and free air or other leakage may represent a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.2597). Ectopic pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.2596) Ovarian torsion (Harrison 22e p.2596) Ruptured ovarian cyst / cystic ovarian disease (Harrison 22e p.2595) Mittelschmerz (Harrison 22e p.2595) Endometriosis (Harrison 22e p.2595) Nephrolithiasis / ureterolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2595-2596) Small-bowel obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2595) Omental torsion (Harrison 22e p.2595) Pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2595) Appendiceal tumors / neoplasms (incidence increasing) (Harrison 22e p.2594) Classic history is migration of vague, intermittent, crampy epigastric or periumbilical pain to the right lower quadrant over 12-24 h, where it becomes sharper and localizes as transmural inflammation irritates the parietal peritoneum (p.2595). Maximal tenderness is classically at or near McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant, about one-third of the way along a line from the anterior iliac spine to the umbilicus (p.2596). Nausea, if present, characteristically follows the onset of abdominal pain (helping distinguish appendicitis from gastroenteritis, in which nausea precedes pain); emesis is typically mild and scant and also occurs after pain onset (p.2595). Anorexia is so common that the diagnosis of appendicitis should be questioned in its absence (p.2595). Rovsing's sign: palpation/gentle pressure in the left lower quadrant elicits pain in the right lower quadrant (p.2596). Iliopsoas sign: extending the right hip causes pain along the posterolateral back and hip, suggesting a retrocecal appendix (p.2596). Obturator sign: internal rotation of the hip causes pain, suggesting an inflamed appendix located in the pelvis (p.2596). Patients with appendicitis tend to lie quite still to avoid peritoneal irritation; some report discomfort with a bumpy car ride, coughing, sneezing, or Valsalva-type maneuvers. Parietal peritoneal irritation is often best elicited by gentle percussion, jiggling the bed/gurney, or mildly bumping the feet (p.2596). Simple appendicitis patients usually appear only mildly ill with pulse and temperature only slightly above normal; temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors should raise concern for another process or for complications such as perforation, phlegmon, or abscess (p.2596). Examine the entire abdomen systematically, starting in a non-tender area; all patients should have a rectal examination, and a pelvic examination in women is mandatory to exclude PID, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian torsion (p.2596). Appendicitis should be included in the differential diagnosis of abdominal pain for every patient of any age unless it is certain the appendix has been previously removed (p.2595). Free perforation normally causes severe (generalized) peritonitis; perforation risk is ~10-20% and is significantly higher in patients <5 or >65 years of age (Harrison 22e p.2594). Temperature >38.3 C (~101 F) or rigors suggest a complication (perforation, phlegmon, abscess) or another diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2596). Persistent symptoms not improved over 48 h are more likely to perforate or develop other complications (Harrison 22e p.2595). Rare but dreaded complication: infective suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein and its tributaries with intrahepatic abscesses, with very poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2595). Diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding and rigidity indicates generalized peritonitis; tachycardia, hypotension/volume depletion, significant leukocytosis, and severe acidosis are signs of serious disease (Harrison 22e p.2597). In pregnancy, perforation raises fetal mortality fourfold (from ~5% to ~20%) (Harrison 22e p.2596). Postoperative fever and leukocytosis persisting beyond 5 days should raise concern for an intraabdominal abscess (Harrison 22e p.2597). Atypical presentations and pain patterns are common, especially in the very old and very young; signs and symptoms can be subtle in the elderly, who may not react vigorously, with nausea/anorexia/emesis predominating (Harrison 22e p.2596). Retrocecal or pelvic (below the pelvic brim) appendix may prompt very little anterior abdominal wall tenderness; pelvic appendicitis may present with dysuria, urinary frequency, diarrhea, or tenesmus and only suprapubic or rectal/pelvic-exam tenderness (Harrison 22e p.2596). Appendiceal location varies widely (right lower quadrant, pelvis, right flank, right upper quadrant, or even the left side with malrotation/redundant colon), influencing presentation; delay in diagnosis is more likely when the appendix is unusually positioned (Harrison 22e p.2595). Diagnosing appendicitis in children is challenging (dramatic response to stimulation, difficult history); the smaller pediatric omentum may be less able to wall off a perforation (Harrison 22e p.2596). Pregnancy: appendicitis is the most common extrauterine general surgical emergency in pregnancy; early symptoms (nausea, anorexia) may be overlooked and the enlarging/gravid uterus may displace the appendix higher and obscure typical findings (Harrison 22e p.2596). Immunocompromised patients may present with only mild tenderness; do not be overly cautious and delay operation in those believed to have appendicitis (Harrison 22e p.2596). Laboratory testing alone does not identify appendicitis, and no currently available decision tool obviates the need for expert clinical opinion (Harrison 22e p.2596). A fecalith is not diagnostic of appendicitis, though its presence in an appropriate location with pain is suggestive and associated with greater likelihood of complications (Harrison 22e p.2596). Etiology is not completely understood. Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen (by fecaliths/appendicoliths, incompletely digested food residue, lymphoid hyperplasia, intraluminal scarring, tumors, bacteria, viruses, or inflammatory bowel disease) is believed, though not proven, to be an important early step at least in some cases. Obstruction leads to bacterial overgrowth and luminal distension with increased intraluminal pressure that can inhibit lymph and blood flow; vascular thrombosis and ischemic necrosis with perforation of the distal appendix may then follow. Perforation near the base of the appendix should raise concern for another disease process. Appendicoliths are found in ~50% of patients with gangrenous appendicitis who perforate but are rarely seen in simpler disease, suggesting differing underlying pathophysiology. Uncomplicated appendicitis does not always progress to perforation; some cases of simple acute appendicitis may temporarily resolve or be managed with antibiotics, though at least one-third will subsequently require appendectomy. When perforation occurs, the leak may be contained by omentum or surrounding tissues to form an abscess, whereas free perforation normally causes severe peritonitis (p.2594-2595). Mortality from simple appendicitis is currently <1%, and for uncomplicated nonperforated appendicitis the operative mortality rate is 0.1-0.5% (approximating the risk of general anesthesia). Mortality for perforated or otherwise complicated disease is much higher, ranging from ~3% overall to as high as 15% in the elderly. For acute peritonitis, mortality can be <10% in reasonably healthy patients with relatively uncomplicated, localized disease but >40% in the elderly or immunocompromised (Harrison 22e p.2597). No formal grading scale is presented; disease is broadly distinguished as simple/uncomplicated appendicitis (without gangrenous necrosis, appendicoliths, perforation, or tumors) versus complicated disease (gangrene, perforation, phlegmon, abscess). Peritonitis is classified as secondary (most commonly from perforation of a hollow viscus, e.g., appendix, colonic diverticula, stomach/duodenum) versus primary or spontaneous (no identifiable intraabdominal source; >90% occur in patients with ascites or hypoproteinemia <1 g/L), and either type may be localized or diffuse; aseptic/chemical peritonitis (e.g., from gastric juice, bile, pancreatic enzymes, blood, or urine) is also distinguished (Harrison 22e p.2595-2597).

Acute Epiglottitis — epiglottitis, supraglottitis, acute supraglottitis Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) Bacterial tracheitis Retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscess Foreign body aspiration Anaphylaxis with airway angioedema Diphtheria (in unimmunised populations) Direct laryngoscopy under controlled conditions to confirm the diagnosis and secure the airway Blood cultures and epiglottic surface cultures after the airway is protected Lateral neck radiograph only if the child is stable and it will not delay care Full blood count and inflammatory markers once safe to obtain Hib and other relevant serological or PCR testing where indicated A rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures that can cause sudden complete airway obstruction. Historically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b; its incidence has fallen dramatically since Hib immunisation, so other organisms and unimmunised children now feature prominently. Classic presentation is abrupt onset of high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, and difficulty swallowing, usually without the barking cough of croup. The child characteristically sits upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with the neck extended to maximise the airway. This is an airway emergency: keep the child calm, avoid distressing procedures such as throat examination or venepuncture, and do not lay the child flat. Definitive airway management is secured in a controlled setting, ideally the operating theatre with experienced anaesthetic and ENT support, before other interventions. Once the airway is secure, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics targeting likely pathogens are given. A lateral neck radiograph may show the classic 'thumbprint' sign, but imaging must never delay airway management and is unnecessary in an unstable child. Direct visualisation of a cherry-red swollen epiglottis confirms the diagnosis but should only be performed where the airway can be immediately secured. Stridor, drooling, and respiratory distress indicating imminent obstruction Tripod positioning and refusal to lie flat Cyanosis, exhaustion, or decreasing level of consciousness Muffled voice with inability to swallow secretions Rapid clinical deterioration Examining the throat or performing painful procedures that can precipitate obstruction Laying the child supine or forcing separation from a caregiver Delaying airway management to obtain imaging or bloods Assuming the diagnosis is excluded in an immunised child, since non-Hib causes still occur Bacterial invasion of the supraglottic tissues produces intense inflammation and oedema of the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, and surrounding structures. Because these tissues sit at the laryngeal inlet, swelling rapidly narrows the airway, and the loose submucosa allows oedema to accumulate quickly. Progressive obstruction, worsened by agitation and secretions, can culminate in acute total airway occlusion. With prompt airway control and antibiotics, recovery is usually rapid and complete; outcomes are poor if the airway obstructs before it is secured, making early recognition critical.

Acute Glomerulonephritis (Child) — acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, APSGN, acute nephritic syndrome, paediatric acute glomerulonephritis IgA nephropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Henoch-Schonlein (IgA) vasculitis nephritis Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease Urinalysis and microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells Serum complement (C3 and C4) Evidence of streptococcal infection (ASO, anti-DNase B, throat or skin swab) Renal function and electrolytes Urine protein quantification Renal biopsy if the course is atypical, complement stays low, or renal function deteriorates The classic nephritic picture is gross haematuria (often described as tea- or cola-coloured urine), oedema, and hypertension. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the most common cause in children and typically follows a group A streptococcal throat infection by about 1-2 weeks or a skin infection by 3-6 weeks. Although labelled non-infective as a glomerular process, it is an immune-mediated sequela of a preceding streptococcal infection rather than active kidney infection. Look for evidence of recent streptococcal infection with elevated antibody titres (such as ASO) and a low serum C3 that typically normalises within 6-8 weeks. Fluid overload from sodium and water retention can precipitate hypertension, pulmonary oedema, and hypertensive encephalopathy. Urinalysis characteristically shows red blood cells, red cell casts, and mild to moderate proteinuria. Management is largely supportive with salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension; the condition is generally self-limiting in children. Persistently low complement beyond 8 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis such as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis. Severe hypertension or hypertensive encephalopathy (headache, seizures, altered consciousness) Pulmonary oedema or respiratory distress from volume overload Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Oligoanuria or features of acute kidney injury requiring dialysis Hyperkalaemia with associated arrhythmia risk Assuming all paediatric nephritis is post-streptococcal and missing lupus or membranoproliferative disease when complement stays persistently low Overlooking hypertension, which may be asymptomatic yet dangerous, by not measuring blood pressure Fluid overloading a child with impaired filtration Attributing dark urine to dehydration rather than examining the urine sediment Immune complexes involving streptococcal antigens deposit in or form within the glomerular basement membrane, activating the complement cascade (predominantly the alternative pathway). This drives glomerular inflammation with endothelial and mesangial proliferation and neutrophil influx, reducing the glomerular filtration surface. The result is a fall in filtration rate, sodium and water retention, haematuria, and proteinuria producing the nephritic syndrome. The great majority of children with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis recover completely, with resolution of gross haematuria within weeks and normalisation of complement within about two months; microscopic haematuria may persist for a year or more. A small minority develop chronic kidney impairment.

Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction — AHTR, acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction Bacterial contamination of the component with septic shock Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction Immediate clerical recheck of patient identity and unit labelling Direct antiglobulin test and repeat ABO grouping on pre- and post-transfusion samples Inspection of plasma and urine for free haemoglobin Haemolysis markers including lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, and haptoglobin Coagulation screen and renal function to detect DIC and acute kidney injury, with cultures if sepsis is possible A life-threatening emergency caused by immune destruction of transfused red cells, most severely from ABO incompatibility due to clerical or identification errors Symptoms begin during or soon after transfusion and include fever, chills, back or flank pain, pain along the infusion vein, dyspnoea, hypotension, and dark urine In an unconscious or anaesthetised patient, unexplained hypotension, haemoglobinuria, and diffuse bleeding from disseminated intravascular coagulation may be the only clues The immediate action is to stop the transfusion, keep the intravenous line open with saline, and recheck all patient and unit identifiers The mechanism is largely intravascular haemolysis from complement-fixing IgM antibodies, releasing free haemoglobin and triggering DIC, shock, and acute kidney injury Investigation includes repeat clerical checks, a direct antiglobulin test, inspection of plasma and urine for free haemoglobin, and haemolysis markers, with return of the unit to the transfusion service Management is supportive with aggressive fluids to maintain renal perfusion and urine output, treatment of hypotension, and correction of coagulopathy, while prevention rests on rigorous bedside identification Fever, hypotension, back or flank pain, and dark urine during transfusion, indicating an acute haemolytic emergency Unexplained intraoperative hypotension, oozing, and haemoglobinuria under anaesthesia Evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation or oliguric acute kidney injury Cardiovascular collapse requiring resuscitation Skipping or rushing the bedside identity check, the commonest root cause Dismissing early fever or discomfort as a benign febrile reaction and continuing the transfusion Failing to maintain intravenous access and fluids after stopping, delaying renal protection Overlooking haemolysis in an anaesthetised patient where classic symptoms are masked Acute haemolytic transfusion reactions occur when recipient antibodies bind antigens on transfused red cells, most dangerously when preformed anti-A or anti-B react with ABO-incompatible cells. These IgM antibodies activate complement fully, causing rapid intravascular lysis and release of free haemoglobin. Complement fragments and cytokines produce fever, vasodilatation, and hypotension, while the reaction activates coagulation and can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation. Free haemoglobin, hypotension, and renal vasoconstriction combine to cause acute kidney injury. The severity relates to the volume of incompatible cells infused, so early recognition and cessation are critical. Prognosis depends on the volume of incompatible blood transfused and the speed of response; stopping early limits harm, whereas large-volume ABO-incompatible transfusion can cause fatal shock, DIC, and renal failure.

Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning — acute infectious diarrhea, acute gastroenteritis, bacterial food poisoning, infectious diarrhea Noninflammatory watery diarrhea: enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative E. coli, Vibrio cholerae, Clostridium perfringens, Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus, Aeromonas hydrophila, Plesiomonas shigelloides, rotavirus, norovirus, enteric adenovirus, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, microsporidia Inflammatory diarrhea/dysentery: Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, enterohemorrhagic E. coli, enteroinvasive E. coli, Yersinia enterocolitica, Listeria monocytogenes, Vibrio parahaemolyticus, Clostridioides difficile, Entamoeba histolytica, Klebsiella oxytoca Enteric fever (penetrating): Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica Traveler's diarrhea: most often enterotoxigenic and enteroaggregative E. coli, with Campylobacter jejuni notably common in Asia Nonbacterial / noninfectious food poisoning: capsaicin (hot peppers) and fish/shellfish toxins Malaria (fever and diarrhea, and prominent vomiting, may occur with infection outside the GI tract) Clostridioides difficile / antibiotic-associated colitis in patients on or recently on antibiotics Yersinia enterocolitica infection presenting as an appendicitis-like (pseudoappendicitis) syndrome Stool examination for gross blood/mucus and a fecal leukocyte smear (thin smear + methylene blue wet mount) to identify inflammatory disease, although its predictive value is debated Fecal lactoferrin (latex agglutination or ELISA) - a more sensitive marker of fecal leukocytes than the WBC smear Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter in febrile inflammatory diarrhea (MacConkey/Salmonella-Shigella agar/selenite broth; Campylobacter requires 42 degrees C microaerophilic culture) Selective culture for V. cholerae on TCBS or TTG agar, plus rapid diagnostic tests when cholera is suspected Sorbitol-MacConkey culture and/or Shiga toxin/PCR testing of visibly bloody stools for E. coli O157:H7 C. difficile toxin A/B testing (enzyme immunoassay, latex agglutination, or PCR) for nosocomial or antibiotic-associated diarrhea Rapid antigen, immunofluorescence, or PCR (and less sensitive microscopy) for Giardia, Cryptosporidium, and Entamoeba histolytica Multiplex nucleic acid amplification panels for viral/bacterial/parasitic pathogens - faster and more sensitive than culture, but may detect multiple organisms and complicate interpretation; CDC advises follow-up culture to allow susceptibility testing and outbreak typing Inflammatory bowel disease (acute diarrheal illness may be its initial presentation or an exacerbation, sometimes precipitated by traveler's diarrhea) Intestinal obstruction (vomiting prominent) Colonic diverticulitis Graft-versus-host disease Noninfectious food poisoning from capsaicin and fish/shellfish toxins Irritable bowel syndrome (postinfectious) Diarrhea is defined as the passage of three or more loose or watery stools (conforming to the shape of the container) within a 24-hour period; illness lasting more than 2 weeks is generally classified as chronic and shifts the likely differential away from typical acute infectious causes (Harrison 22e p.1078, 1079). The first practical step is to separate noninflammatory from inflammatory disease: watery diarrhea with no fecal leukocytes and minimal/no fecal lactoferrin points to proximal small-bowel enterotoxin-mediated disease, whereas fecal polymorphonuclear leukocytes and high fecal lactoferrin point to colonic invasion or cytotoxin (dysentery/inflammatory diarrhea) (Harrison 22e p.1077-1079). Infective dose varies enormously and shapes transmission: as few as 10-100 organisms/cysts of Shigella, enterohemorrhagic E. coli, Giardia, or Entamoeba cause infection and allow person-to-person spread, while 10^5-10^8 Vibrio cholerae must be ingested, often requiring growth in food first (Harrison 22e p.1076). Neurotoxin-mediated food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus emetic form) is caused by toxin preformed outside the host, giving the shortest incubation (1-6 h), prominent vomiting, and usually no fever (Harrison 22e p.1076-1077, 1080). Stool appearance is diagnostically informative: bloody/mucoid stool suggests large-bowel ulceration/inflammation; profuse rice-water stools suggest cholera or a similar toxigenic process; bulky white/gray stools suggest a malabsorptive small-bowel process (Harrison 22e p.1078). Bloody stools WITHOUT fecal leukocytes should specifically raise suspicion for Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli (e.g., O157:H7) (Harrison 22e p.1078). Severity is judged largely by dehydration: thirst and dry mouth indicate mild dehydration; orthostatic blood-pressure fall, skin tenting, and sunken eyes/fontanelle indicate moderate dehydration; lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock indicate severe dehydration (Harrison 22e p.1078). Recent or current antibiotic use shifts suspicion toward Clostridioides difficile; C. difficile is the predominant cause of nosocomial diarrhea in U.S. adults, and stool culture for other pathogens in the hospital setting is low-yield (Harrison 22e p.1078-1080). Host defenses against enteric pathogens include the intestinal microbiota (colonization resistance, >99% anaerobic colonic flora with acidic pH/volatile fatty acids), gastric acid, peristalsis, the mucus barrier, mucosal/secretory IgA immunity, and host genetics (Harrison 22e p.1077). Blood group O confers increased susceptibility to disease from V. cholerae, Shigella, E. coli O157, and norovirus (Harrison 22e p.1077). Salmonella Typhi and Yersinia enterocolitica can penetrate intact mucosa, multiply in Peyer patches/lymph nodes, and disseminate to cause enteric fever - fever, headache, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, splenomegaly, and leukopenia (Harrison 22e p.1077). Cholera toxin is the prototype enterotoxin: its A subunit ADP-ribosylates a GTP-binding protein, persistently activating adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, increasing Cl- secretion and decreasing Na+ absorption to drive secretory diarrhea; E. coli LT acts identically, while ST acts via guanylate cyclase and cyclic GMP (Harrison 22e p.1076-1077). Signs of severe dehydration: lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock Fever, which often signals invasive disease Bloody or mucoid stools (dysentery) indicating large-bowel ulceration Bloody stools without fecal leukocytes - alert for Shiga toxin-producing enterohemorrhagic E. coli and risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome Diarrhea in an immunocompromised host (cell-mediated immunity defects/AIDS, hypogammaglobulinemia, cancer), where infection can be life-threatening with persistent infection, bacteremia, and metastatic seeding Profuse rice-water stools suggesting cholera, with risk of rapid life-threatening volume loss Diarrhea in infants <2 years with moderate dehydration, fever >24 h, bloody stools, or prolonged duration Relying on the fecal leukocyte smear alone - its predictive value is debated, and fecal lactoferrin is more sensitive (Harrison 22e p.1079). Routine stool culture cannot distinguish pathogenic E. coli from normal flora, and enterotoxin assays are unavailable in most clinical labs, so a negative routine culture does not exclude E. coli disease (Harrison 22e p.1080). Sending broad stool cultures for nosocomial diarrhea is low-yield and not cost-effective; initial workup should focus on C. difficile (Harrison 22e p.1080). Antimotility agents (e.g., diphenoxylate-atropine) and opioids can prolong fever and organism shedding in Shigella infection and increase bacteremia risk in Salmonella - impaired motility favors bacterial overgrowth (Harrison 22e p.1077). Multiplex NAAT panels may detect multiple pathogens, complicating interpretation, and the absence of an isolate prevents susceptibility testing and outbreak typing - CDC advises follow-up culture (Harrison 22e p.1080). Reheating/frying contaminated fried rice may not destroy preformed heat-stable B. cereus toxin or its heat-resistant spores (Harrison 22e p.1080). Missing infection outside the GI tract (e.g., malaria) as a cause of fever and diarrhea/vomiting (Harrison 22e p.1078). Acute infectious diarrhea results from a contest between ingested enteric pathogens and host defenses. Pathogens overcome defenses through small infective inoculum, adherence/colonization factors (e.g., V. cholerae toxin-coregulated pilus; enterotoxigenic E. coli colonization factor antigen; attaching-effacing lesions of enteropathogenic and enterohemorrhagic E. coli), and the elaboration of toxins or direct invasion. Three broad mechanisms produce three clinical patterns: (1) Noninflammatory enterotoxin-mediated disease in the proximal small bowel causes watery diarrhea without fecal leukocytes - the cholera-toxin/LT pathway elevates cyclic AMP (increased Cl- secretion, decreased Na+ absorption) and ST elevates cyclic GMP. (2) Inflammatory disease in the colon/distal small bowel results from cytotoxins (e.g., Shiga toxin of S. dysenteriae type 1 and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, V. parahaemolyticus, C. difficile) or from mucosal invasion (Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Salmonella), producing dysentery with fecal leukocytes and blood. (3) Penetrating organisms (Salmonella Typhi, Y. enterocolitica) traverse intact mucosa, multiply in lymphoid tissue, and disseminate to cause enteric fever. Neurotoxins (staphylococcal, B. cereus emetic) are typically preformed outside the host and act on the nervous system to cause rapid-onset vomiting. Host protection depends on the intestinal microbiota's colonization resistance, gastric acidity, intestinal motility/peristalsis, the mucin barrier, mucosal and systemic immunity, and genetic factors; impairment of any of these (achlorhydria/acid suppression, antimotility drugs, antibiotic-altered flora, immunocompromise) raises infection risk and severity. Most acute diarrheal episodes are mild and self-limited. Traveler's diarrhea is typically self-limited, lasting 1-5 days, and Clostridium perfringens food poisoning rarely lasts more than 24 h; toxin-mediated staphylococcal/B. cereus emetic illness generally lasts under 12 h. Globally, however, acute diarrheal disease remains a leading cause of illness, associated with an estimated 1.57 million deaths per year, and in low- and middle-income countries it accounts for about one in ten deaths in children under 5; recurrent intestinal infection contributes to stunting, wasting, micronutrient deficiency, and malnutrition. Outcome is worse in immunocompromised hosts, where dehydration can also compromise renal function and increase immunosuppressive drug toxicity. Postdiarrhea complications include chronic diarrhea (~1% of travelers; protozoa account for about one-third), postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome (~10% of those with traveler's diarrhea), reactive arthritis (especially after Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Yersinia), hemolytic-uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin-producing bacteria), and Guillain-Barre syndrome (especially after Campylobacter). Severity is graded clinically by degree of dehydration (Harrison 22e p.1078). Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, decreased axillary sweat, decreased urine output, slight weight loss. Moderate dehydration: orthostatic fall in blood pressure, skin tenting, sunken eyes (or sunken fontanelle in infants). Severe dehydration: lethargy, obtundation, feeble pulse, hypotension, and shock. The complementary classification is mechanistic/syndromic per Table 138-1: noninflammatory (enterotoxin, proximal small bowel, watery diarrhea, no fecal leukocytes), inflammatory (invasion or cytotoxin, colon/distal small bowel, dysentery, fecal PMNs and high lactoferrin), and penetrating (distal small bowel, enteric fever, fecal mononuclear cells).

investigations or surgery without carbohydrate cover Acute intermittent porphyria results from partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase, the third enzyme of the haem biosynthetic pathway, which condenses porphobilinogen molecules. When hepatic haem demand rises, the rate-limiting enzyme ALA synthase is induced; the downstream bottleneck causes accumulation of the early precursors ALA and PBG. These precursors, particularly ALA, are thought to be neurotoxic and underlie the neurovisceral manifestations. Because no photoreactive porphyrins accumulate, the skin is spared. Enzyme activity is typically around half of normal, so most carriers remain asymptomatic unless exposed to precipitating factors that upregulate hepatic haem synthesis. With prompt recognition, trigger avoidance and treatment most attacks resolve, though recovery from severe neuropathy can be slow and incomplete. Recurrent attacks, chronic pain, and long-term risks including hypertension, renal impairment and hepatocellular carcinoma may complicate the course.

Acute Intestinal Obstruction — Bowel obstruction, Mechanical bowel obstruction, Small-bowel obstruction, Large-bowel obstruction, Ileus, Pseudo-obstruction Postoperative ileus (functional obstruction following intraabdominal surgery) Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) Obstructive colon cancer (may mimic small-bowel obstruction when the ileocecal valve is incompetent) Crohn's disease and other inflammatory strictures Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to findings) Complete blood count and serum electrolytes/creatinine with serial assessment (mild hemoconcentration and slight leukocytosis are common in simple obstruction) Upright/cross-table lateral abdominal radiographs ('staircasing' of dilated small-bowel loops >2.5 cm, air-fluid levels, 'coffee bean' shadow in volvulus) CT with enteral and IV contrast (location, closed-loop, and ischemia features such as altered wall enhancement, mesenteric venous gas, pneumatosis, pneumoperitoneum) Markers possibly suggestive of strangulation: serum D-lactate, creatine kinase BB isoenzyme, intestinal fatty acid binding protein Contrast enema or colonoscopy for suspected colonic obstruction; ultrasound when radiation is contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy) Adynamic ileus from metabolic/electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, uremia, severe hyperglycemia) Drug-induced dysmotility (opiates, antihistamines, anticholinergics, some psychotropics) Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) Intestinal ischemia presenting with functional dysmotility Collagen vascular disease (e.g., lupus, scleroderma) causing visceral dysmotility The cardinal features are colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distention, emesis, and obstipation; distal obstruction tends to produce more distention and later, sometimes feculent, vomiting, whereas proximal obstruction produces more pronounced vomiting with less distention (Harrison 22e p.2591). Obstruction is characterized as partial, high grade, or complete, which generally tracks with the risk of complications and the urgency of intervention; it is termed simple versus strangulated when vascular insufficiency and ischemia are present (Harrison 22e p.2589). Roughly 80% of cases involve the small bowel, and about one-third of small-bowel cases show significant ischemia; obstruction accounts for about 1-3% of hospitalizations and a quarter of urgent/emergent general surgery admissions (Harrison 22e p.2589). Postoperative adhesions are the single most common cause (>50% overall), followed by neoplasms (~20%) and hernias (~10%); lower abdominal operations (appendectomy, colorectal, gynecologic) are especially adhesiogenic (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590). Classic early small-bowel obstruction produces high-pitched 'musical' tinkling bowel sounds and peristaltic rushes (borborygmi), which later become absent or hypoactive; in ileus/pseudo-obstruction sounds are typically absent or hypoactive from the start (Harrison 22e p.2591). A tender abdominal or groin mass strongly suggests an incarcerated hernia; pain out of proportion to physical findings can mimic acute mesenteric ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2591). Carcinomatosis causing obstruction most often originates from the ovary, but can arise from the pancreas, stomach, or colon, and rarely from distant sites such as breast or skin (Harrison 22e p.2589). In adult intussusception the lead point is typically a polyp or tumor; in gallstone 'ileus' the most common obstruction site is the ileum (~60%), with the stone usually entering via a cholecystoduodenal fistula (Harrison 22e p.2590, 2593). Sigmoid colon volvulus comprises about two-thirds of all volvulus cases and ~4% of large-bowel obstruction; risk factors include institutionalization, neuropsychiatric conditions on psychotropics, chronic constipation, and advanced age (seventies-eighties) (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590). Stasis raises bacterial counts in the jejunum and ileum; organisms such as Escherichia coli, Streptococcus faecalis, and Klebsiella may be recovered from intestinal cultures, mesenteric nodes, and blood (Harrison 22e p.2590). CT is the most frequently used modality, with sensitivity ~95% (78-100%) and specificity ~96% for high-grade obstruction, but accuracy for closed-loop obstruction is much lower (~60%) (Harrison 22e p.2592). Contrast appearing within the cecum 4-24 h after oral water-soluble contrast predicts improvement with high (~95%) sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.2592). Fever, which raises concern for strangulation or systemic inflammation Severe localized pain or peritoneal signs, suspicious for strangulated or closed-loop obstruction Leukocytosis with immature forms plus metabolic acidosis, worrisome for ischemic necrosis and sepsis Cecal diameter exceeding 10-12 cm in distal colonic obstruction with a competent ileocecal valve (impending ischemic perforation) Free intraperitoneal air in a patient who has not recently had surgery (perforation) Oliguria, hypotension, and tachycardia indicating severe intravascular volume depletion Barium should never be given orally until obstruction is excluded; in significant obstruction it may form concretions and renders later cross-sectional imaging or angiography uninterpretable (Harrison 22e p.2592-2593). No laboratory test reliably distinguishes simple from strangulated obstruction; reliance on labs may delay needed intervention (Harrison 22e p.2592). Bowel sounds are notoriously unreliable for diagnosis, and pain may be out of proportion to physical findings, masking strangulation or mimicking mesenteric ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2591). Distal colonic obstruction with an incompetent ileocecal valve can present late and mimic distal small-bowel obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2591). Imaging intervention should not be delayed when signs strongly suggest high-grade/complete obstruction or bowel compromise (Harrison 22e p.2592). Acute obstruction is either mechanical (extrinsic, intrinsic bowel-wall, or intraluminal lesions) or functional (dysmotility without blockage). Increased contractility proximal and distal to the block is characteristic; peristalsis then slows as proximal bowel dilates and fills with secretions and swallowed air, with additional luminal gas from fermentation and CO2 production. Rising intraluminal pressure exceeding venous pressure impairs venous and lymphatic drainage, producing wall edema and proximal hypoxemia, with epithelial necrosis identifiable within 12 h. Progressive arterial compromise can cause full-thickness ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. Inflammatory edema generates reactive oxygen species and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, disrupting secretory and neuromotor function. Loss of absorptive capacity plus fluid sequestration in the bowel wall and peritoneum causes dehydration; anorexia and emesis worsen volume depletion, and high-grade distal obstruction with vomiting causes loss of gastric potassium, hydrogen, and chloride while dehydration drives proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption (metabolic alkalosis). Closed-loop obstruction, in which both ends of a segment are occluded (e.g., volvulus, hernia), is the most common precursor to strangulation and carries high risk of vascular insufficiency and irreversible ischemia (Harrison 22e p.2590-2591). Overall morbidity and mortality appear to be decreasing. The mortality rate for patients with strangulation operated on within 24-30 h of symptom onset is about 8% but roughly triples thereafter. Most postoperative adhesive obstructions are partial and resolve spontaneously, and about 60-80% of selected mechanical obstructions can be managed conservatively; recurrence requiring readmission within 10 years occurs in ~20% of conservatively treated and 5-30% of operatively managed patients. Major complications after operation occur in roughly 12-47%, with higher risk for resection therapies and for patients with ASA class III or higher (Harrison 22e p.2589, 2593). Mechanical obstruction is graded as partial, high grade, or complete, correlating with complication risk and urgency. It is further classified as simple versus strangulated when vascular insufficiency and ischemia supervene, and closed-loop when both ends of a segment are occluded (highest risk of strangulation) (Harrison 22e p.2589-2590).

Acute leukaemia — CBC + peripheral smear (blasts) Bone marrow Coagulation (APML risk) Febrile neutropenia / leukostasis are emergencies Acute myeloid leukaemia vs acute lymphoblastic leukaemia - distinguished by morphology (Auer rods imply AML), cytochemistry, flow-cytometric immunophenotype and genetics (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844) Myelodysplastic syndrome or myeloproliferative neoplasm evolving to acute leukaemia (antecedent haematologic disorder) (Harrison 22e p.828) Therapy-related (secondary) acute leukaemia after alkylating agents (4-6 yr) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (1-3 yr) (Harrison 22e p.826) Peripheral blood smear (Wright-Giemsa) with manual differential - essential at presentation; look for blasts and Auer rods (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844) Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for morphology, cytochemistry, flow-cytometric immunophenotyping, cytogenetics and molecular studies (Harrison 22e p.829, p.844) Cytogenetics/karyotype and molecular panel at diagnosis (NPM1, FLT3-ITD/TKD, CEBPA, TP53, IDH1/IDH2, RUNX1 etc.) - the most important prognostic data in AML (Harrison 22e p.827-828) Serum uric acid, electrolytes including potassium, phosphate and calcium, creatinine/BUN, and LDH to assess and monitor tumour-lysis risk (Harrison 22e p.829, p.593) Coagulation panel - PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer - to detect DIC, especially when APL is suspected (Harrison 22e p.829) Measurable (minimal) residual disease assessment by multiparameter flow cytometry or molecular methods (e.g. PCR for PML-RARA in APL) for response monitoring (Harrison 22e p.827, p.834, p.847) Lumbar puncture/CSF cytology in ALL (and AML with neurologic symptoms) to detect CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.845) Urinalysis for uric acid crystals; urinary uric acid:creatinine ratio >1 supports acute uric-acid nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.593) AML accounts for ~31% of new acute leukaemias but ~62% of leukaemic deaths; it is the commonest acute leukaemia in older adults (median age ~69), whereas ALL peaks in young children (age 3-4) and again in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.825, p.844). Presentation is usually nonspecific and reflects marrow failure: fatigue (often the first symptom), anorexia/weight loss, bleeding/easy bruising, and fever; about half of AML patients have symptoms for 3 months or less before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.828). Auer rods (rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules) on the blood film establish a myeloid lineage with certainty and are not seen in ALL (Harrison 22e p.828). Gum (gingival) hypertrophy and skin/soft-tissue infiltration are characteristic of monocytic AML subtypes and KMT2A-rearranged disease (Harrison 22e p.828). A myeloid sarcoma (chloroma) is a tissue mass of myeloid blasts (skin, lymph node, GI tract, soft tissue, testis); isolated myeloid sarcoma rapidly progresses to marrow/blood involvement and cannot be cured by local therapy alone (Harrison 22e p.828). Median presenting WBC in AML is ~15,000/uL; 20% present with >100,000/uL and <5% have no circulating blasts. In ALL ~40% have normal or low WBC and 8% have no circulating blasts, so an automated count can miss the diagnosis - always review the smear (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844). Diagnosis requires examination of blood AND bone marrow; biopsy distinguishes AML from ALL, and cytochemistry, flow-cytometric immunophenotyping, cytogenetics and molecular studies are all needed for subtyping (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844). Diagnosis no longer rests on the historical >=20% blast threshold alone - the 2022 WHO classification removed the blast-percent requirement for AML defined by specific genetic lesions such as t(15;17), t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation (Harrison 22e p.826). DIC and coagulopathy are classically associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (t(15;17)/PML-RARA); APL bleeding can be catastrophic (GI, intrapulmonary, intracranial), and paradoxically thrombosis can also occur (Harrison 22e p.828). CSF examination is routine in ALL: CNS leukaemia is defined by >=5 cells/uL or blasts on morphology; CNS involvement is present at diagnosis in 5-10% of adults (higher in mature B-ALL and T-ALL). Defer/limit lumbar puncture if platelets <20 x10^9/L or active bleeding (Harrison 22e p.844-845). Suspected APL (ecchymoses/oozing from IV sites, DIC) - a haematologic emergency; coagulopathy can be rapidly fatal and warrants prompt differentiation therapy (Harrison 22e p.828, p.834) Hyperleukocytosis with blast count >100,000/uL and leukostasis - brain (stupor, headache, visual change, confusion, coma, sudden death) or lung (dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, respiratory failure); a potentially fatal emergency, especially in AML (Harrison 22e p.591) Tumour lysis syndrome - hyperkalaemia (risk of fatal arrhythmia), hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia (tetany), hyperuricaemia and acute kidney injury (Harrison 22e p.592-593) Febrile neutropenia (fever with granulocytes <1500/uL) - medical emergency requiring urgent empirical antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.575) CNS symptoms - headache, visual change, focal/non-focal neurologic deficit - may indicate CNS leukaemia or intracranial bleed (Harrison 22e p.829-830) Relying on an automated blood count can miss acute leukaemia - 8% of ALL patients (and <5% of AML) have no circulating blasts; review the smear (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844). In hyperleukocytosis, arterial blood gas oxygen tension can be spuriously low because the high WBC mass consumes plasma oxygen in the sample; use pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation (Harrison 22e p.591). High leukocyte and platelet counts can cause pseudohyperkalaemia from cell lysis after the blood is drawn (no ECG changes) - follow plasma rather than serum potassium (Harrison 22e p.593). Avoid unnecessary RBC transfusion and intravascular volume depletion in hyperleukocytosis - both raise blood viscosity and can worsen leukostasis (Harrison 22e p.591). Urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is no longer recommended for tumour-lysis prophylaxis (Harrison 22e p.593). Even minor bleeding in a thrombocytopenic leukaemia patient justifies immediate platelet transfusion because qualitative platelet dysfunction and infection increase bleeding risk independent of the count (Harrison 22e p.829). Acute leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of immature, poorly differentiated haematopoietic precursors (blasts) that infiltrate marrow, blood and other tissues; AML arises from myeloid progenitors and ALL from lymphoid (B- or T-lineage) progenitors. Genome sequencing indicates most AML arises from a small number of mutations that accumulate with age - up to 5-6% of normal people over 70 carry premalignant clones (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, CHIP, commonly DNMT3A/TET2/ASXL1), which carries a ~10-fold increased risk of haematologic malignancy though additional 'hits' are required to progress to overt leukaemia. Genetic lesions drive both phenotype and behaviour: for example t(15;17)/PML-RARA defines APL and predisposes to DIC, while NPM1 and FLT3 mutations associate with high leukocyte counts. Marrow replacement by blasts produces anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, accounting for the dominant clinical features (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.844). Outcome is dominated by age and genetics. In AML, cytogenetic/molecular findings at diagnosis are the strongest predictors: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), core-binding-factor AML (t(8;21), inv(16)) is favourable (~55% cured), normal-karyotype AML is intermediate (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3) or monosomy 7 are adverse with little chance of cure without transplant. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favourable, whereas FLT3-ITD is adverse. Advancing age, poor performance status, antecedent haematologic disorder/preceding cytopenias, therapy-related disease and high presenting WBC all worsen outcome; only ~32% of AML patients survive 5 years overall. In ALL, outcome is strongly age-dependent - cure rates ~90% in children falling to <10% in elderly/frail adults; achievement of molecular complete remission (MRD negativity) is the most important on-treatment prognostic factor (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.846-847). AML is classified by the WHO 2022 system primarily on defining genetic abnormalities (e.g. PML-RARA, RUNX1-RUNX1T1, CBFB-MYH11, KMT2A rearrangement, NPM1 or CEBPA mutation) and, where genetics are absent, by differentiation; the historical >=20%-blast diagnostic threshold has been removed for genetically defined entities. Prognostic risk is stratified by the 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) scheme into favourable, intermediate and adverse categories based on cytogenetic and molecular findings at diagnosis (APL is risk-stratified separately, low- vs high-risk by presenting WBC, threshold 10,000/uL). ALL is subtyped immunologically into B-lineage and T-lineage, with risk stratification (standard vs high) using age, WBC count, immunophenotype, cytogenetics/molecular lesions (notably Ph/BCR-ABL) and MRD status (Harrison 22e p.826-827, p.834, p.846-847).
