Acute Lymphoid Leukemia — Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia, ALL Acute myeloid leukemia (distinguished by marrow biopsy, cytochemistry, and immunophenotype) Biphenotypic/mixed-phenotype acute leukemia (markers of both lymphoid and myeloid lineages on the same cells) Bilineage leukemia (two separate blast populations, lymphoid and myeloid) Lymphoblastic lymphoma (e.g., precursor T- or B-lymphoblastic lymphoma) Chronic myeloid leukemia in lymphoid blast crisis Aplastic anemia or other marrow failure presenting with pancytopenia Peripheral blood count with Wright-Giemsa-stained differential smear at presentation Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for morphology, immunophenotype, cytogenetics, and molecular markers Cytochemical stains and immunologic marker panel to assign B- versus T-lineage Standard cytogenetics, FISH, and RT-PCR to detect t(9;22)/BCR-ABL1, t(4;11)/MLL, t(1;19)/PBX-E2A and other entities Gene expression profiling, SNP array, array-CGH, and next-generation sequencing to identify ETP-ALL and Ph-like ALL Lumbar puncture with CSF examination for CNS leukemia (diagnostic if >=5 cells/uL or blasts on morphology) MRD assessment by flow cytometry or RT-qPCR/NGS/ddPCR with collection of patient-specific markers at diagnosis Acute myeloid leukemia Lymphoblastic lymphoma with marrow involvement Marrow failure syndromes presenting as pancytopenia In ALL the malignant clone arises from hematopoietic progenitors in marrow or lymphatic tissue, producing immature nonfunctioning blasts; marrow infiltration causes anemia, granulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia, so fatigue, infection, and hemorrhage (rather than tumor bulk) are usually the presenting complaints. Tumor-bulk features such as lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly from leukemic infiltration, and CNS involvement (meningeosis leukemica) may occur but are less often the reason a patient first seeks care. ALL is the most frequent neoplasm of childhood with an early peak at age 3-4 years; in adults the incidence ranges from about 0.7 to 1.8 per 100,000 per year, higher in adolescents/young adults and rising again in the elderly. The WBC count is normal or reduced in roughly 40% of patients, and in about 8% no circulating blasts are seen, so automated counters may fail to flag the diagnosis; only about 16% present with WBC above 100 x 10^9/L. Bone marrow is typically heavily packed, with more than 90% blasts in about 70% of patients and near-absent normal hematopoiesis; a biopsy is essential to confirm acute leukemia and distinguish ALL from AML. Immunophenotyping is the principal tool for subclassification: more than 70% of adult ALL is B-lineage (common ALL being most frequent, CD10+), while about 25% is T-lineage (all express CD7 and cytoplasmic/surface CD3). An immunologic marker is considered positive when more than 20% of cells stain with the monoclonal antibody. Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL (t(9;22), BCR-ABL1) is seen in roughly half of elderly B-lineage patients; subtype frequencies shift substantially with age. Minimal residual disease detected by flow cytometry, RT-qPCR for clonal Ig/TCR rearrangements or fusion transcripts (limit ~0.1-0.001%, lower with NGS/ddPCR) is the most important prognostic factor during therapy; patient-specific markers should be banked from diagnostic marrow. Achieving a molecular complete remission after induction predicts disease-free survival around 70% versus under 40% for MRD-positive patients, the single most relevant independent prognostic factor in both pediatric and adult ALL. Mature B-ALL (Burkitt leukemia, ~3-4% of adults) expresses surface IgM, shows L3 morphology, and has short relapse kinetics (up to ~1-1.5 years) with frequent organ and CNS involvement. Down syndrome carries a roughly 20-fold increased leukemia risk (ALL predominating in childhood, AML at older age), and other congenital disorders raising risk include Klinefelter, Fanconi anemia, Bloom syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, and neurofibromatosis. Platelet count below 20 x 10^9/L, signaling high bleeding risk Neutropenia with neutrophils below 0.5 x 10^9/L, signaling high infection risk Hemoglobin below 7-8 g/dL (present in nearly one-third of patients) Hyperleukocytosis (WBC above 100 x 10^9/L), more common in t(4;11) and T-ALL CNS involvement at diagnosis (5-10% overall, higher in mature B-ALL and T-ALL) Large mediastinal mass in T-ALL (frequent, up to ~60%) with potential airway/vascular compromise Risk of tumor lysis syndrome at treatment initiation given high tumor burden Because the WBC is normal or low in about 40% of patients and roughly 8% have no circulating blasts, automated blood counts may miss the diagnosis; a manual smear and marrow biopsy are required. Failing to bank diagnostic marrow for patient-specific markers compromises later MRD follow-up. Assuming an MRD-negative result guarantees cure: 20-30% of MRD-negative adults still relapse, attributable to loss of assay sensitivity, evolving subclones, or extramedullary disease. Performing lumbar puncture without an adequate platelet count (>20 x 10^9/L) or in the presence of clinical hemorrhage; potentially seeded blasts should be addressed with intrathecal therapy at the first tap. Overlooking that L1/L2 FAB morphology has no clinical bearing while only L3 morphology indicates mature B-ALL. Misclassifying Ph-like ALL as Ph-positive: Ph-like ALL is BCR-ABL1 negative despite similar genetic lesions and requires molecular testing to identify. Malignant transformation of lymphoid progenitor cells in the bone marrow or lymphatic system produces a clone of immature, nonfunctioning lymphoblasts. Progressive marrow infiltration crowds out normal hematopoiesis, yielding anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Blasts may also infiltrate lymph nodes, liver, spleen, mediastinum, and the central nervous system (a pharmacologic sanctuary site). Subtypes correspond to arrest at defined stages of B-cell or T-cell differentiation and carry characteristic cytogenetic/molecular lesions such as t(9;22)/BCR-ABL1, t(4;11)/MLL-AF4, t(1;19)/PBX-E2A, and t(8;14) in mature B-ALL, as well as newer entities including early T-precursor (ETP) ALL and Ph-like (BCR-ABL1-like) ALL driven by IKZF1 deletion, CRLF2 overexpression, and tyrosine kinase-activating rearrangements (ABL1, JAK2, PDGFRB). Outcome is strongly age-dependent, with cure rates around 90% in children falling to under 10% in elderly or frail patients. Prognostic stratification rests on age, WBC count at diagnosis, immunophenotype, cytogenetic/genetic lesions, and especially MRD response: molecular complete remission after induction predicts disease-free survival near 70% versus under 40% if MRD-positive. The greatest relapse risk is within the first 2 years and is much lower after 5 years. Relapse kinetics vary by subtype, being short (up to ~1-1.5 years) in mature B-ALL, intermediate (~3-4 years) in T-ALL, and prolonged (up to 5-7 years) in common ALL. CNS relapse, usually accompanied by marrow involvement, carries a dismal outcome. Lineage/immunophenotypic subtyping (EGIL-type) divides ALL into B-lineage (pro-B, common, pre-B, mature B/Burkitt) and T-lineage (early/ETP, cortical-thymic, mature) categories. MRD-based response categories (Harrison Table 111-3) include complete hematologic remission (<5% marrow blasts), complete molecular remission/MRD negativity (<=0.01%, i.e. <=1 leukemic cell in 10,000 marrow cells), molecular failure/MRD positivity (>0.01% with hematologic remission), molecular relapse, and hematologic relapse (>5% blasts in marrow or blood). Risk stratification assigns standard-risk patients (no risk factors) versus high-risk patients (one or more of advanced age, high WBC, adverse immunophenotype, or adverse cytogenetic/genetic lesions).

Acute Meningitis — Bacterial meningitis, Viral meningitis, Aseptic meningitis, Meningoencephalitis Herpes simplex virus encephalitis (HSV-1) and other viral meningoencephalitides (Harrison 22e p.1121) Rickettsial disease, notably Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii), and ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1121) Focal suppurative CNS infections: subdural or epidural empyema and brain abscess (Harrison 22e p.1121) Subarachnoid hemorrhage (the major noninfectious consideration) and pituitary apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.1121-1122) Subacute meningitis from M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis, and Treponema pallidum (Harrison 22e p.1122) Mycoplasma pneumoniae CNS infection, which can mimic viral meningitis/encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1124) HSV encephalitis presenting with headache, fever, altered consciousness, focal deficits, and seizures (Harrison 22e p.1121) Rocky Mountain spotted fever with high fever, headache, and a rash evolving from maculopapular to petechial/purpuric, easily confused with meningococcemia (Harrison 22e p.1121) Ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis with fever, headache, confusion, and leukopenia/thrombocytopenia with elevated transaminases (Harrison 22e p.1121) Untreated or partially treated bacterial meningitis mimicking aseptic meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123) Early fungal, mycobacterial, or syphilitic (T. pallidum) meningitis with lymphocytic pleocytosis and not-yet-low glucose (Harrison 22e p.1123) Meningitis due to Mycoplasma, Listeria, Brucella, Coxiella, Leptospira, and Rickettsia species (Harrison 22e p.1123) CSF examination is the diagnostic cornerstone; classic bacterial findings are PMN pleocytosis >100/uL (90%), low glucose <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL) and/or CSF/serum glucose ratio <0.4 (~60%), elevated protein >0.45 g/L (90%), and raised opening pressure >180 mmH2O (90%) (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121) CSF Gram stain positive in >60% and bacterial culture positive in >70-80%; culture remains required for susceptibility testing (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121) Blood cultures should be obtained immediately when bacterial meningitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1120) CSF multiplex PCR (e.g., FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis panel) detects S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, E. coli, L. monocytogenes, H. influenzae, S. agalactiae, plus HSV-1/2, enteroviruses, VZV, HHV-6, and parechovirus, but does not replace culture (Harrison 22e p.1121, p.1124) Neuroimaging before LP (CT or MRI) when immunocompromised, recent head trauma, depressed consciousness, papilledema, or focal deficits; MRI preferred for edema/ischemia and shows diffuse meningeal enhancement after gadolinium (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121) For suspected viral meningitis: CBC with differential, liver and renal function, ESR, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, glucose, creatine kinase, aldolase, amylase, and lipase; CSF PCR is the diagnostic procedure of choice for enteroviral and HSV CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.1124) Biopsy of petechial skin lesions may reveal organisms on Gram stain in meningococcemia (Harrison 22e p.1121) Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1121) Medication-induced hypersensitivity meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1121) Chemical meningitis from rupture of tumor contents (cystic glioma, craniopharyngioma, epidermoid or dermoid cyst) into CSF (Harrison 22e p.1121) Carcinomatous or lymphomatous (neoplastic) meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1121) Inflammatory disorders: sarcoidosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1121-1122) Uveomeningitic syndromes including Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and pituitary apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.1122) The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity each occurs in more than 80% of adults with acute bacterial meningitis, but the complete triad is frequently absent; a depressed level of consciousness is seen in over 75% (Harrison 22e p.1119). Acute presentation can be either fulminant over hours or subacute over several days; nausea, vomiting, and photophobia are common (Harrison 22e p.1119). Nuchal rigidity is the pathognomonic sign of meningeal irritation; Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are classic but of uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in the very young, elderly, immunocompromised, or obtunded (Harrison 22e p.1119-1120). S. pneumoniae (~50%) and N. meningitidis (~25%) are the leading causes of community-acquired bacterial meningitis; group B streptococci (~15%) and L. monocytogenes (~10%) follow, with H. influenzae type b now <10% (Harrison 22e p.1118). Petechial or purpuric skin lesions are an important clue to meningococcal infection; the rash starts as a maculopapular eruption resembling a viral exanthem then becomes petechial on trunk, extremities, mucosae, conjunctivae, and sometimes palms/soles (Harrison 22e p.1118, p.1120). Listeria meningitis should be considered in neonates, pregnant women, those over 60, and immunocompromised hosts; infection is acquired from contaminated foods such as soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk, deli meats, and uncooked hotdogs (Harrison 22e p.1119). Seizures occur in 15-40% of bacterial meningitis cases; focal seizures suggest focal ischemia/infarction, cortical venous thrombosis with hemorrhage, or focal edema, while generalized seizures may reflect hyponatremia or cerebral anoxia (Harrison 22e p.1120). More than 90% of bacterial meningitis patients have a CSF opening pressure above 180 mmH2O, and 20% exceed 400 mmH2O; raised ICP is the major cause of obtundation/coma (Harrison 22e p.1120). Viral meningitis is distinguished from encephalitis by the absence of stupor, coma, marked confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic signs; their presence points toward encephalitis or another process (Harrison 22e p.1123). Profound CNS depression, seizures, or focal deficits should never be attributed to uncomplicated viral meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123). A lymphocytic pleocytosis combined with a low CSF glucose should raise suspicion for fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningitis or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis rather than typical viral meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1124). Neurologic injury in bacterial meningitis can progress even after CSF sterilization because much of the damage stems from the host inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial injury (Harrison 22e p.1119). Petechial or purpuric rash suggesting meningococcemia, which can be fulminant and fatal within hours of symptom onset (Harrison 22e p.1118) Deteriorating consciousness, papilledema, dilated poorly reactive pupils, sixth nerve palsy, decerebrate posturing, or the Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, irregular respirations) indicating raised ICP (Harrison 22e p.1120) Cerebral herniation, the most disastrous complication of raised ICP, reported in 1-8% of bacterial meningitis cases (Harrison 22e p.1120) Focal neurologic findings, which mandate prompt MRI to detect focal suppurative infection (Harrison 22e p.1121) Seizures or status epilepticus at presentation (Harrison 22e p.1120) Stupor, coma, or marked confusion in a presumed viral meningitis, which instead suggest encephalitis or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1123) Awaiting LP or neuroimaging to start therapy: blood cultures and empirical treatment must not be delayed in suspected bacterial meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1120) Assuming antibiotics given a few hours before LP invalidate the CSF; they do not significantly alter WBC count or glucose, nor reliably prevent Gram stain or PCR detection (Harrison 22e p.1120) Relying on multiplex PCR alone: it omits S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and many gram-negatives, and cannot provide susceptibility data (Harrison 22e p.1121) Interpreting meningeal enhancement on MRI as diagnostic of meningitis; it occurs in any condition with increased blood-brain barrier permeability (Harrison 22e p.1121) Overreliance on Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, which have uncertain sensitivity/specificity and may be absent in vulnerable groups; cervical spine disease in the elderly can cause false-positive nuchal rigidity (Harrison 22e p.1119-1120) Misreading an early PMN pleocytosis in viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps) as bacterial; a PMN-predominant CSF without a diagnosis should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (Harrison 22e p.1123-1124) Forgetting that giving IV 50% glucose before LP can take hours to alter CSF glucose, so it rarely confounds early sampling (Harrison 22e p.1120-1121) Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the subarachnoid space accompanied by a CNS inflammatory reaction that may cause decreased consciousness, seizures, raised ICP, and stroke, with meninges, subarachnoid space, and parenchyma often jointly involved (meningoencephalitis). The leading organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) colonize the nasopharynx, cross or bypass epithelial tight junctions to enter the bloodstream, evade neutrophil phagocytosis and complement via a polysaccharide capsule, then reach the CSF through the choroid plexus or cerebral capillary endothelium. Bacteria multiply readily in CSF given its scarce leukocytes, complement, and immunoglobulin, which impair opsonization. Lysis of bacteria releases cell-wall components (LPS of gram-negatives, teichoic acid and peptidoglycan of pneumococci) that drive microglia, astrocytes, monocytes, and endothelium to produce TNF-alpha and IL-1 beta; these cytokines synergistically increase blood-brain barrier permeability (vasogenic edema, protein leakage), and the proteinaceous leukocytic exudate obstructs CSF flow and arachnoid resorption causing hydrocephalus and interstitial edema. Leukocyte adhesion and degranulation, excitatory amino acids, and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species produce cytotoxic edema and cell death (notably in the hippocampal dentate gyrus). Loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, basal arterial narrowing/vasculitis with thrombosis, and venous/sinus thrombosis cause ischemia and infarction; combined interstitial, vasogenic, and cytotoxic edema raise ICP and may produce herniation (Harrison 22e p.1118-1120). Viral (aseptic) meningitis produces meningeal irritation with a CSF inflammatory profile but, by definition, does not produce the parenchymal dysfunction of encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1123). Mortality from bacterial meningitis varies by organism: about 3-7% for H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, or group B streptococci; ~15% for L. monocytogenes; and ~20% for S. pneumoniae. Risk of death rises with decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age in infancy or over 50, comorbidities such as shock or need for mechanical ventilation, and delayed treatment; very low CSF glucose (<2.2 mmol/L) and very high CSF protein (>3 g/L) also predict worse outcomes. Moderate-to-severe sequelae occur in roughly 25% of survivors, including impaired intellect, memory loss, seizures, hearing loss, dizziness, and gait disturbance. In adults, recovery from viral meningitis is excellent, with only rare lingering headache, mild cognitive complaints, or asthenia; outcomes in infants/neonates under 1 year are less certain, with reported intellectual impairment, learning disability, and hearing loss (Harrison 22e p.1123, p.1125). No single formal grading scale is given for acute meningitis; instead Harrison enumerates prognostic risk factors for death in bacterial meningitis (decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, raised ICP, age <1 or >50, shock or need for ventilation, treatment delay, CSF glucose <2.2 mmol/L, CSF protein >3 g/L). For distinguishing bacterial from aseptic meningitis, a prospectively validated bacterial meningitis score yields a negative predictive value of about 99.7% in children, and CSF protein >0.5 g/L and serum procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL favor bacterial over aseptic meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1123-1125).

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) — AML Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) - distinguished by flow cytometry/immunophenotype; presence of Auer rods confirms AML and excludes ALL Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) - may precede/evolve into AML; AML-MR is defined by antecedent MDS or MDS/MPN and/or specific cytogenetic/molecular features Myeloproliferative neoplasm (including chronic myeloid leukemia) - antecedent hematologic disorder that can transform to AML Therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML - after alkylating agents (4-6 yr latency) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (1-3 yr latency) CBC with manual differential (anemia normocytic normochromic; median presenting WBC ~15,000/uL; platelets <100,000/uL in ~75%) Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, and molecular studies (cornerstone of diagnosis and classification) Cytogenetics and molecular testing at diagnosis (NPM1, FLT3-ITD/TKD, CEBPA bZIP, TP53, IDH1/IDH2, RUNX1, ASXL1 and others) for ELN risk stratification Peripheral blood smear for blasts and Auer rods; peroxidase staining Chemistry including uric acid, LDH, phosphorus, calcium, creatinine/BUN (tumor lysis screen); ~50% have mild-moderate uric acid elevation Coagulation studies - PT, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer (screen for DIC, especially APL) Cryopreservation of viable leukemia cells for future testing HLA typing for potential allogeneic HCT; echocardiogram/MUGA for cardiac function; chest radiograph Infection screen including SARS-CoV-2 and other viruses in patients with respiratory symptoms before chemotherapy Measurable residual disease (MRD) assessment by flow cytometry or quantitative RT-PCR (e.g., NPM1, RUNX1-RUNX1T1, CBFB-MYH11, PML-RARA transcripts) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Aplastic anemia / marrow failure syndromes (also present with pancytopenia) Myeloproliferative neoplasms (e.g., CML in blast crisis) AML is a clonal neoplasm characterized by infiltration of blood, bone marrow, and other tissues by proliferative, poorly differentiated myeloid cells (myeloblasts); historically the diagnosis required a marrow or blood myeloid blast count of >=20%, though the 2022 WHO classification eliminated the blast-percent requirement for cases with specific defining genetic aberrations (Harrison 22e p.825, p.826). Most cases are idiopathic; genome sequencing suggests the majority arise from a limited number of mutations that accumulate with age. AML is the most common acute leukemia in older patients (median age at diagnosis 69 years) and causes 62% of leukemic deaths; only ~32% of patients survive 5 years (Harrison 22e p.825). Auer rods are abnormal rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules; they are NOT uniformly present, but when seen they establish AML (and exclude acute lymphocytic leukemia) with certainty. AML blasts show fine lacy chromatin with one or more nucleoli and primary (nonspecific) cytoplasmic granules (Harrison 22e p.829). Presentation is usually nonspecific and gradual (sometimes abrupt), reflecting marrow failure: fatigue (frequent first symptom) and anemia, abnormal hemostasis/bleeding and easy bruising from thrombocytopenia, and fever +/- infection from neutropenia/leukocyte dysfunction. Fever is the initial symptom in ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e p.828). Multiparameter flow cytometry helps distinguish AML from acute lymphoblastic leukemia and identify subtypes (e.g., myeloid antigens CD13/CD117 in minimally differentiated AML; platelet antigens CD41/CD61 in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia); it has only a supportive role for WHO subtyping given the paramount importance of genetics, and is increasingly used to measure measurable residual disease (MRD) (Harrison 22e p.827). Cytogenetic/molecular testing at diagnosis provides the most important prognostic information and drives risk stratification (European LeukemiaNet 2022 categories: favorable, intermediate, adverse). All AML cells contain genetic mutations, most recurring; the majority of patients now have a genetic lesion that can be specifically targeted (Harrison 22e p.826, p.827). Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), defined by t(15;17)(q22;q12) / PML-RARA fusion, is a distinct, highly curable subtype (~85% long-term survival) treated uniquely with tretinoin (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide; it is excluded from the ELN risk table and is a coagulopathy emergency (Harrison 22e p.826, p.833). Myeloid sarcoma is a tumor mass of myeloid blasts at sites other than marrow (commonly skin, lymph node, GI tract, soft tissue, testis); it may precede or coincide with blood/marrow involvement, is associated with t(8;21), and patients with isolated myeloid sarcoma typically develop blood/marrow disease quickly and cannot be cured by local therapy alone (Harrison 22e p.828). Infiltration of gingiva, skin, soft tissues, or meninges with leukemic blasts at diagnosis is characteristic of the monocytic subtypes and those with KMT2A chromosomal abnormalities; gum hypertrophy is a classic monocytic finding (Harrison 22e p.828, p.830). Infectious complications during neutropenia are the major cause of morbidity and death during induction and postremission chemotherapy; fever develops in most patients but infection is documented in only about half of febrile patients, and empiric broad-spectrum antibacterial/antifungal therapy at onset of neutropenic fever has substantially reduced infectious deaths (Harrison 22e p.832). Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, t[15;17]/PML-RARA): coagulopathy/DIC emergency - presents with DIC-associated hemorrhage (may include significant GI, intrapulmonary, or intracranial bleeding); requires immediate recognition and ATRA-based therapy Disseminated intravascular coagulation - classically in APL but also in monocytic AML and with extreme leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia; note thrombosis is also a recognized feature of DIC in APL Hyperleukocytosis (WBC >100,000/uL, seen in ~20% at presentation) with pulmonary leukostasis and early CNS bleeding - associated with poor outcomes Intracranial hemorrhage / CNS bleed - headache, vision changes, nonfocal neurologic abnormalities Febrile neutropenia - fever in a neutropenic patient mandates immediate evaluation and empiric broad-spectrum antibacterials covering gram-negative organisms Tumor lysis syndrome / uric acid nephropathy - hyperuricemia (aggravated by initiating chemotherapy); allopurinol/hydration started at diagnosis, rasburicase for severe cases (avoid in G6PD deficiency) APL differentiation syndrome - within first 3 weeks of ATRA (or less commonly ATO): fever, fluid retention, dyspnea, chest pain, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural/pericardial effusions, hypoxemia; ~10% mortality if unrecognized Auer rods are not uniformly present in AML, so their absence does NOT exclude AML; their presence, however, confirms AML over ALL Diagnosis based on blast percent alone is outdated - cases with defining genetic abnormalities (e.g., t[15;17], t[8;21], inv[16], KMT2A rearrangement, NPM1 mutation) qualify as AML even with <20% blasts; genetic/cytogenetic testing is mandatory for precise diagnosis APL must be recognized urgently - delay or treating it like ordinary AML risks fatal DIC; high-risk APL (WBC >10,000/uL) requires immediate cytoreduction because ATRA can precipitate life-threatening differentiation syndrome and rapidly rising leukocyte count Even infirm older patients generally benefit from treatment over supportive care alone - age and comorbidity should not automatically exclude therapy Even patients with undetectable MRD remain at risk for relapse; without postremission therapy virtually all CR patients eventually relapse, and there is no consensus on the optimal MRD technique or its use to direct therapy NPM1 prognostic favorability is negated by co-existing FLT3-ITD; prognostic mutations are not mutually exclusive (>80% of patients carry two or more) Anemia at diagnosis is usually present but not typically severe and is normocytic normochromic - a 'mild' blood count abnormality can still herald AML AML results from clonal proliferation of poorly differentiated myeloid progenitor (blast) cells that infiltrate the marrow, blood, and tissues, crowding out normal hematopoiesis and producing pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia/leukocyte dysfunction, thrombocytopenia). Leukemogenesis is driven by accumulating somatic mutations; clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), most often involving epigenetic regulators DNMT3A, TET2, and ASXL1, carries a ~10-fold increased risk of hematologic malignancy, though additional 'hits' are required to progress to leukemia. Recurrent genetic lesions define disease biology and presentation: fusion genes (e.g., PML-RARA from t[15;17]; RUNX1-RUNX1T1 from t[8;21]; CBFB-MYH11 from inv[16]/t[16;16] core-binding-factor AML; MLLT3-KMT2A; DEK-NUP214) and gene mutations (NPM1, present in ~30% of AML and ~60% of cytogenetically normal AML; FLT3, activating ITD or TKD mutations in ~30%; CEBPA; TP53; IDH1/IDH2 producing the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate that disrupts epigenetic processes). KMT2A rearrangements and monocytic differentiation favor extramedullary/tissue infiltration; t(15;17) APL drives DIC. Untreated AML is uniformly fatal; overall only ~32% of US patients survive 5 years. Cytogenetic/molecular risk is the dominant prognostic determinant: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), t(8;21) and inv(16) (core-binding-factor AML) a good prognosis (~55% cured), cytogenetically normal AML an intermediate outcome (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3), or monosomy 7 confer adverse risk with very poor outcomes and virtually no cure without transplantation. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favorable; in-frame bZIP CEBPA mutation is favorable; FLT3-ITD carries negative prognostic impact. Clinical adverse factors include advancing age (the most important clinical factor), poor performance status, high presenting leukocyte count, antecedent hematologic disorder (MDS/MPN) or prolonged preceding cytopenias, and therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML. Achievement of complete remission (CR) and MRD-negative status predict longer survival. Risk stratification per 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) by genetics at diagnosis (APL excluded): Favorable - t(8;21)/RUNX1-RUNX1T1, inv(16) or t(16;16)/CBFB-MYH11, mutated NPM1 without FLT3-ITD, in-frame bZIP-mutated CEBPA. Intermediate - mutated NPM1 with FLT3-ITD, wild-type NPM1 with FLT3-ITD (without adverse lesions), t(9;11)/MLLT3-KMT2A, and abnormalities not classified as favorable or adverse. Adverse - t(6;9)/DEK-NUP214, KMT2A rearrangements, t(9;22)/BCR-ABL1, inv(3)/t(3;3) MECOM(EVI1), -5/del(5q), -7, -17/abn(17p), complex or monosomal karyotype, mutated ASXL1/BCOR/EZH2/RUNX1/SF3B1/SRSF2/STAG2/U2AF1/ZRSR2, and mutated TP53 (>=10% VAF). Classification (2022 WHO): AML with defining genetic abnormalities versus AML defined by differentiation; the >=20% blast requirement is removed for cases with specific defining genetic aberrations.

Acute otitis media — AOM, acute suppurative otitis media, acute middle ear infection Otitis externa Otitis media with effusion Referred otalgia from teeth, throat or temporomandibular joint Bullous myringitis Early mastoiditis Furuncle of the external auditory canal Otoscopy to assess drum colour, position, mobility and integrity Tuning fork tests and audiometry to characterise conductive hearing loss Tympanometry where effusion or Eustachian tube dysfunction is suspected Culture of ear discharge in severe, recurrent or non-resolving cases Imaging of the temporal bone if intratemporal or intracranial complications are suspected Most common in infants and young children because of a shorter, more horizontal Eustachian tube; often follows an upper respiratory tract infection Presents with ear pain, fever, irritability and conduction-type hearing loss; young children may only tug at the ear or feed poorly Otoscopy progresses through stages: initial hyperaemia, then a bulging congested drum, then perforation with discharge, and finally resolution Sudden relief of pain accompanied by ear discharge usually signals spontaneous perforation of the tympanic membrane Common organisms include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis Management principles centre on analgesia and appropriate antibiotics; myringotomy is considered when the drum is bulging, pain is severe, or complications threaten Watchful waiting without immediate antibiotics may be appropriate in older children with mild, non-severe disease Recurrent episodes or persistent effusion warrant assessment for adenoid hypertrophy and Eustachian tube dysfunction Postauricular swelling, tenderness or a protruding pinna suggesting acute mastoiditis Persistent high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness or altered consciousness indicating intracranial spread Facial nerve weakness or vertigo suggesting facial canal or labyrinthine involvement Failure to improve despite adequate treatment Mistaking otitis externa or referred otalgia for middle ear infection Overlooking early mastoiditis in a child who is not improving Assuming a red drum alone confirms the diagnosis without assessing bulging and mobility Failing to follow up to ensure resolution of effusion and return of hearing Acute otitis media is an acute suppurative inflammation of the middle ear cleft, usually arising when Eustachian tube dysfunction (commonly from a viral upper respiratory infection or adenoid obstruction) impairs middle ear ventilation and drainage. Negative middle ear pressure and mucosal oedema allow pathogens to ascend from the nasopharynx and proliferate, producing an inflammatory exudate that becomes purulent. Rising pressure causes the tympanic membrane to bulge and may lead to necrosis and perforation with discharge, after which the process typically resolves. Untreated or aggressive infection can extend to adjacent structures. Most cases resolve completely with prompt treatment and restoration of normal hearing, but neglected or recurrent infection can progress to chronic otitis media, persistent effusion, or intratemporal and intracranial complications.

Acute pain management — acute postoperative pain, perioperative pain control, acute pain Pain from a surgical complication such as bleeding, ischaemia, or infection Compartment syndrome presenting as disproportionate pain Neuropathic pain from nerve injury Referred pain from another organ system Anxiety or distress amplifying pain report Undiagnosed acute cardiac or abdominal event Regular pain scoring at rest and on movement Assessment for sedation and respiratory rate when opioids are used Evaluation for a surgical or vascular cause when pain is severe or escalating Assessment for compartment syndrome when pain is disproportionate Review of the analgesic regimen and its effectiveness and side effects Effective acute pain control improves comfort, supports early mobilisation and recovery, and reduces complications such as respiratory compromise and the risk of persistent postsurgical pain A multimodal approach combines analgesics with different mechanisms (paracetamol, anti-inflammatories, regional or neuraxial techniques, and opioids when needed) to improve relief while limiting side effects Opioid-sparing strategies reduce nausea, sedation, ileus, and respiratory depression, and are central to enhanced recovery pathways Regular assessment using pain scores at rest and on movement guides titration, and analgesia should be tailored to the individual and the surgical procedure Regional and neuraxial techniques provide excellent targeted analgesia but require monitoring for block-related complications and, with neuraxial opioids, delayed respiratory depression Opioid therapy demands vigilance for oversedation and respiratory depression, particularly in the elderly, those with sleep apnoea, and when combined with other sedatives Special populations, including opioid-tolerant patients, those with substance use disorders, children, and the elderly, need individualised plans and often specialist input Poorly controlled acute pain is a risk factor for developing chronic postsurgical pain, so proactive, adequate management has longer-term benefits Pain that is severe, escalating, or disproportionate, suggesting compartment syndrome or a surgical complication Excessive sedation or a falling respiratory rate indicating opioid-induced respiratory depression New neurological deficit after neuraxial or regional analgesia Pain accompanied by signs of ischaemia, sepsis, or haemorrhage Relying on opioids alone rather than a multimodal, opioid-sparing plan Missing compartment syndrome or a surgical complication behind disproportionate pain Underestimating opioid respiratory-depression risk in vulnerable patients Failing to reassess and titrate analgesia to individual response Neglecting the special needs of opioid-tolerant patients and those with substance use disorders Acute pain after surgery or injury arises from tissue damage that activates peripheral nociceptors and releases inflammatory mediators, sensitising both peripheral nerves and central pathways. Nociceptive signals travel via the dorsal horn to higher centres, where they are modulated by descending inhibitory and facilitatory systems. Peripheral and central sensitisation lower pain thresholds and amplify responses, contributing to hyperalgesia. Because pain is transmitted and modulated at multiple sites, combining agents that act at different points in these pathways (peripheral inflammation, nerve conduction, spinal transmission, and central perception) produces additive or synergistic relief with fewer dose-related adverse effects. Most acute pain resolves as healing progresses, and good multimodal control aids recovery; inadequate management increases complications and the likelihood of chronic postsurgical pain.

Acute respiratory failure — ARF, respiratory failure, acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure Acute respiratory distress syndrome Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema Severe pneumonia or aspiration Acute exacerbation of asthma or COPD Pulmonary embolism Neuromuscular weakness or central respiratory depression Arterial blood gas to classify the type of failure and assess acid-base status Chest radiograph to identify consolidation, oedema, effusion, or pneumothorax Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography where available Bedside lung and cardiac ultrasound to differentiate causes CT pulmonary angiography if embolism is suspected Recognise failure clinically before blood gases confirm it: rising respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, altered consciousness, and inability to speak in full sentences are early warnings Type 1 (hypoxaemic) failure reflects a problem with oxygenation, whereas type 2 (hypercapnic) failure reflects inadequate ventilation and carbon dioxide clearance Secure the airway and support oxygenation and ventilation as the first priority, in parallel with seeking the cause A falling respiratory rate or conscious level in a tiring patient can herald impending arrest rather than improvement Non-invasive ventilation can be effective in selected causes, but a deteriorating or obtunded patient needs intubation without delay Titrate oxygen to a target saturation, being mindful of the risk of worsening hypercapnia in chronic carbon dioxide retainers Arterial blood gases distinguish the type of failure and reveal the acid-base disturbance guiding urgency Treat the reversible precipitant (e.g. bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax) alongside respiratory support Exhaustion with a falling respiratory rate or rising carbon dioxide indicating impending respiratory arrest Deteriorating conscious level or inability to protect the airway Refractory hypoxaemia despite maximal oxygen therapy Silent chest or minimal air entry in severe bronchospasm Haemodynamic instability accompanying the respiratory compromise Mistaking a tiring patient's slowing respiratory rate for clinical improvement Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen worsening hypercapnia in chronic retainers Persisting with non-invasive ventilation in a patient who needs intubation Treating the numbers on the blood gas without addressing the underlying cause Underestimating fatigue and delaying escalation of respiratory support Respiratory failure occurs when gas exchange fails to maintain adequate oxygenation or carbon dioxide elimination. Hypoxaemic (type 1) failure arises mainly from ventilation-perfusion mismatch and shunt, as in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, and acute respiratory distress syndrome, where alveoli are filled or collapsed. Hypercapnic (type 2) failure results from reduced alveolar ventilation due to depressed respiratory drive, neuromuscular weakness, increased airway resistance, or chest wall problems, so carbon dioxide accumulates. Both cause tissue hypoxia; hypercapnia additionally produces respiratory acidosis. Fatigue of the respiratory muscles can convert a compensated state into rapid decompensation and arrest. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and reversibility. Prompt recognition and support of oxygenation and ventilation with treatment of the precipitant allow recovery in many cases, whereas established acute respiratory distress syndrome and multi-organ involvement carry substantial mortality.

Acute Rheumatic Fever — ARF Always request: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), and streptococcal serology (antistreptolysin O [ASO] and anti-DNase B [ADB]) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Echocardiography should be performed on all possible cases to aid diagnosis (including detection of subclinical carditis/valvulitis) and to establish baseline carditis severity; auscultation is poorly sensitive and specific for RHD in asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.2855, p.2857). Because most cases lack a positive throat swab culture or rapid antigen test, serologic evidence of preceding group A strep infection is usually needed (ASO and anti-DNase B titers), ideally with locally derived age-specific reference ranges (Harrison 22e p.2856). In relevant situations: throat swab, skin sore swab, blood cultures, synovial fluid aspirate (cell count, microscopy, culture, gonococcal PCR), pregnancy test, and creatinine/UEC (since NSAIDs can affect renal function) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Tests to exclude alternative diagnoses (per clinical presentation/local endemic infections): autoantibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-CCP antibodies; urine molecular testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; serology for viral hepatitis, Yersinia, CMV, parvovirus B19, respiratory viruses, Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus (Harrison 22e p.2857). Inflammatory markers should be monitored every 1-2 weeks until normalized (usually within 4-6 weeks), and a repeat echocardiogram performed after 1 month to assess for progression of carditis (Harrison 22e p.2858). ARF is a multisystem autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal infection; almost all manifestations resolve completely, the major exception being cardiac valvular damage (rheumatic heart disease, RHD), which may persist after other features disappear (Harrison 22e p.2854). Mainly a disease of children aged 5-14 years; initial episodes are rare in persons aged >30 years, whereas recurrent episodes remain relatively common in adolescents and young adults. RHD prevalence peaks between 25 and 40 years (Harrison 22e p.2854). There is no clear gender association for ARF, but RHD more commonly affects females, sometimes up to twice as often as males (Harrison 22e p.2854). Latent period of ~3 weeks (range 1-5 weeks) between the precipitating group A streptococcal infection and onset of ARF; the exceptions are chorea and indolent (low-grade) carditis, which may follow prolonged latent periods of up to 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2855). Most common clinical features are polyarthritis (60-75% of cases) and carditis (50-75%); chorea prevalence varies from <2% to 30% between populations; erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules are now rare, found in <5% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2855). Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD; the mitral valve is almost always affected, sometimes with the aortic valve. Isolated aortic valve involvement is rare. The characteristic manifestation of carditis in previously unaffected individuals is mitral regurgitation, sometimes with aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2855). ARF arthritis is typically a migratory polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, hips, elbows), asymmetric, severe and disabling, and highly responsive to salicylates/NSAIDs (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856). Sydenham's chorea often occurs in the absence of other manifestations, follows a prolonged latent period, and is found mainly in females; more than 50% of patients presenting with chorea will have carditis, so echocardiography should be part of the workup (Harrison 22e p.2856). Erythema marginatum is an evanescent serpiginous rash (pink macules clearing centrally) usually on the trunk, sometimes the limbs, but almost never on the face. Subcutaneous nodules are painless, mobile, occur over bony prominences, appear 2-3 weeks after onset, and are commonly associated with carditis (Harrison 22e p.2856). Revised Jones criteria (2015 AHA): for all populations with evidence of preceding group A strep infection, initial ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations; recurrent ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor OR 3 minor manifestations. Separate, more sensitive criteria apply to moderate/high-risk populations versus low-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857). Major manifestations: carditis (clinical and/or subclinical), arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules; in moderate/high-risk populations arthritis includes monoarthritis and polyarthralgia (Harrison 22e p.2857). Secondary prevention with long-term penicillin prophylaxis is the mainstay of controlling ARF and RHD, best delivered through a register-based RHD control program; patients should be entered on an ARF registry, educated, and linked to follow-up before discharge (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858). Severe carditis causing congestive heart failure; treatment of heart failure may be lifesaving (Harrison 22e p.2857). Myocardial inflammation affecting conduction, causing P-R interval prolongation (first-degree AV block, rarely higher-level block) (Harrison 22e p.2855). More than 50% of patients presenting with chorea have underlying carditis, mandating echocardiographic workup (Harrison 22e p.2856). Advanced RHD complications: heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, and infective endocarditis (Harrison 22e p.2856). The preceding group A streptococcal infection is commonly subclinical, so the absence of a reported sore throat or a negative throat swab/rapid antigen test does not exclude ARF; serologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856). Diagnosis of ARF is often missed, particularly in resource-poor settings, so children, adolescents, and young adults may have undiagnosed RHD; echocardiographic screening can detect these cases (Harrison 22e p.2855). Early commencement of anti-inflammatory medication before the typical migratory pattern is established may produce an atypical presenting picture such as aseptic monoarthritis (Harrison 22e p.2856). Recurrence of fever, joint manifestations, and elevated acute-phase reactants up to 3 weeks after stopping anti-inflammatory medication does NOT indicate a true ARF recurrence and is managed by briefly recommencing anti-inflammatory agents (Harrison 22e p.2857). Glucocorticoid use in ARF carditis remains controversial; two meta-analyses failed to demonstrate benefit over placebo or salicylates, though included studies were >40 years old and used outdated medications (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858). Salicylates/NSAIDs are of no proven value in the treatment of carditis or chorea (they treat arthritis, arthralgia, and fever) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Medications to control choreiform movements do NOT alter the duration or outcome of chorea; IVIg shows no benefit on short- or long-term carditis outcome and is not recommended except in severe chorea refractory to other treatments (Harrison 22e p.2858). ARF results from an autoimmune reaction to group A streptococcal infection, classically of the upper respiratory tract, with increasing evidence for a role of streptococcal skin infection. The most widely accepted theory is molecular mimicry: an immune response to streptococcal antigens (mainly the M protein) cross-reacts with human tissues. Antigen-presenting cells of the innate immune system present streptococcal antigens to T cells, activating humoral and cellular immunity; cross-reactive antibodies bind heart-valve endothelial cells, activating VCAM-1 with recruitment of activated lymphocytes and complement-mediated lysis, releasing peptides (laminin, keratin, tropomyosin) that activate cross-reactive T cells invading the heart, amplifying damage and causing epitope spreading. An alternative hypothesis proposes initial damage from streptococcal invasion of epithelial surfaces with M-protein binding to type IV collagen, rendering it immunogenic but not through molecular mimicry. Susceptibility is inherited (~3-6% of a population susceptible; 44% concordance in monozygotic vs 12% in dizygotic twins; heritability ~60%), with associations to HLA class II alleles, TNF and mannose-binding-lectin polymorphisms, the IGH locus (IGHV4-61*02), and complement factor H (Harrison 22e p.2854-2855). Untreated, ARF lasts on average 12 weeks; with treatment, patients are usually discharged within 1-2 weeks. Almost all non-cardiac manifestations resolve completely. Inflammatory markers usually normalize within 4-6 weeks. Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD, the long-term consequence being valvular damage; people with RHD are often asymptomatic for many years before progression to cardiac failure. There is no treatment proven to alter the likelihood or severity of RHD; apart from heart-failure management, treatment of ARF is symptomatic. RHD is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in low- and middle-income countries and a major cause of adult mortality and morbidity, with >40 million people affected worldwide and >300,000 deaths annually (Harrison 22e p.2854, p.2857-2858). RHD detected by echocardiography is staged (2023 World Heart Federation guidelines) into: Stage A (minimal echocardiographic criteria for RHD, individuals aged <=20 years, mild MR or AR without morphologic features); Stage B (mild RHD, mild valvular regurgitation plus morphologic feature(s)); Stage C (advanced RHD at risk of clinical complications - moderate/severe MR or AR, any MS or AS, pulmonary hypertension, decreased LV systolic function); Stage D (advanced RHD with established clinical complications such as cardiac surgery, heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, infective endocarditis). The 2015 revised Jones criteria additionally separate low-risk populations (ARF incidence <=2 per 100,000 school-age children, or all-age RHD prevalence <=1 per 1000) from moderate/high-risk populations, applying more sensitive criteria to the latter (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857).

three days up to one month after the trauma Symptoms span intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal, including intrusive memories, distressing dreams, flashbacks, and a sense of risk and provide practical support, safety, and psychoeducation as part of early management Suicidal or self-harm ideation following the trauma Ongoing exposure to danger, such as continuing abuse or violence Severe dissociation impairing safety or the ability to seek help Concurrent physical injury or head trauma requiring medical attention Providing single-session psychological debriefing, which is ineffective and potentially harmful Prescribing benzodiazepines, which may impair recovery Assuming all acutely distressed trauma survivors will develop a chronic disorder Overlooking suicide risk or ongoing danger to the patient Missing concurrent physical or head injury from the traumatic event Acute stress disorder reflects the immediate dysregulation of fear and stress-response systems following trauma, with heightened amygdala-driven threat processing, altered prefrontal regulation, and disturbed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and noradrenergic activity. Impaired encoding and contextualisation of the traumatic memory, together with dissociative responses, are thought to underlie the intrusive and dissociative symptoms, modulated by prior vulnerability and severity of exposure. Many individuals with acute stress disorder recover within weeks, but a significant proportion progress to post-traumatic stress disorder, and the acute diagnosis identifies people who may benefit from early, evidence-based support. Prognosis is better with early trauma-focused intervention, safety, and social support, and worse with severe or ongoing trauma, prominent dissociation, and prior psychiatric illness.

Acute tonsillitis — acute tonsillopharyngitis, acute sore throat, tonsillar infection Viral pharyngitis Infectious mononucleosis Peritonsillar abscess Diphtheria Candidal or other fungal pharyngitis Agranulocytosis or leukaemic infiltration presenting with sore throat Throat examination to assess tonsillar size, exudate and membrane Throat swab or rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus where indicated Full blood count and monospot or heterophile antibody test when mononucleosis is suspected Assessment for splenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy Blood glucose and further workup if recurrent or atypical infection suggests immunosuppression Presents with sore throat, painful swallowing, fever, malaise and tender enlarged jugulodigastric lymph nodes The follicular (spotted) form shows yellowish exudate at the tonsillar crypt openings, while the membranous form has a coalescent whitish membrane Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus is the most important bacterial cause because of its non-suppurative sequelae Viral causes are common; features such as prominent cough, coryza and conjunctivitis point away from streptococcal infection Consider infectious mononucleosis when there is marked tonsillar enlargement, membrane formation, generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly Management principles include adequate hydration, analgesia and antibiotics when streptococcal infection is likely, avoiding aminopenicillins if glandular fever is suspected because of the rash Non-suppurative complications of streptococcal infection include rheumatic fever and acute glomerulonephritis, which justify appropriate antibiotic treatment Recurrent tonsillitis meeting frequency criteria, or complications such as abscess, may warrant tonsillectomy Trismus, drooling, muffled voice or unilateral swelling suggesting peritonsillar or deep neck abscess Stridor or respiratory difficulty from airway obstruction A grey adherent membrane bleeding on removal, raising concern for diphtheria Persistent unilateral tonsillar enlargement or ulceration suggesting malignancy Prescribing ampicillin-type antibiotics in undiagnosed glandular fever and precipitating a rash Missing a developing peritonsillar abscess in a patient with worsening unilateral symptoms Treating all sore throats as bacterial when many are viral Overlooking a haematological cause in unusually severe or persistent cases Acute tonsillitis is acute inflammation of the palatine tonsils, usually from viral or bacterial infection of the tonsillar crypts and parenchyma. Pathogens invade the crypt epithelium, provoking an inflammatory response with hyperaemia, oedema and crypt exudate. Streptococcal infection can trigger immune-mediated sequelae elsewhere in the body. Local spread of infection beyond the tonsillar capsule can produce peritonsillar or deep neck space abscesses, and marked tonsillar and adenoid enlargement may compromise the airway. Most episodes are self-limiting or resolve promptly with treatment; complications such as abscess formation and, in streptococcal disease, rheumatic and renal sequelae are largely preventable with appropriate management.

Acute urinary retention — AUR, acute retention of urine, acute bladder outlet obstruction Benign prostatic hyperplasia with decompensation Prostate cancer causing outlet obstruction Urethral stricture Blood clot retention (clot from haematuria) Neurogenic bladder / cauda equina syndrome Constipation or pelvic mass causing extrinsic compression Drug-induced retention (anticholinergics, opioids, sympathomimetics) Bladder ultrasound to confirm distension and measure retained volume Urinalysis and culture to identify infection Serum creatinine and electrolytes to detect obstructive renal impairment Renal tract ultrasound to assess for hydronephrosis in suspected chronic retention PSA (interpreted with caution, as retention and catheterisation raise levels) Neurological assessment and spinal imaging when cauda equina or cord compression is suspected Presents as the sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a palpable, tender, distended bladder that is dull to percussion In men the commonest precipitant is benign prostatic obstruction, often triggered by infection, constipation, alcohol, immobility, or anticholinergic and sympathomimetic drugs Immediate management is urgent bladder decompression with a urethral catheter; suprapubic catheterisation is used when urethral access fails or is contraindicated Painless retention with a grossly distended bladder suggests chronic-on-acute (high-pressure or high-residual) retention rather than a purely acute event Record the drained volume; a large residual and any renal impairment point toward chronic high-pressure retention with risk of post-obstructive diuresis Post-obstructive diuresis after decompression can cause marked fluid and electrolyte losses, requiring monitoring of urine output, weight, and electrolytes A trial without catheter, often facilitated by an alpha-blocker, is appropriate once the precipitant is treated; failure indicates need for ongoing catheterisation or definitive surgery Always exclude and treat urinary infection, and consider spinal cord compression or cauda equina when neurological features accompany retention Acute urinary retention is itself a urological emergency requiring immediate bladder decompression High-pressure chronic retention with hydronephrosis and renal impairment Post-obstructive diuresis causing dehydration and electrolyte disturbance after decompression Retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, or bowel dysfunction suggesting cauda equina syndrome Associated fever or urosepsis in an obstructed system Delaying catheterisation and allowing prolonged painful overdistension Missing high-pressure chronic retention by not measuring residual volume or checking renal function Failing to anticipate and monitor for post-obstructive diuresis Overlooking neurological causes such as cauda equina compression Rapid complete decompression without awareness of possible haematuria ex vacuo Acute urinary retention is the abrupt failure to empty the bladder, arising from mechanical obstruction (most often prostatic enlargement, but also urethral stricture, clot, or stone), increased outlet tone, impaired detrusor contractility, or neurogenic causes. Bladder overdistension raises intravesical pressure and, in high-pressure chronic retention, is transmitted to the upper tracts causing hydronephrosis and renal impairment. Precipitating factors such as anticholinergic drugs, alpha-agonists, infection, pain, and prostatic congestion tip a compensated bladder into decompensation and acute failure to void. Prompt decompression relieves symptoms rapidly; many men can eventually void after a trial without catheter and treatment of precipitants, but recurrent retention often signals the need for definitive prostatic surgery, and delayed relief risks lasting renal damage.

Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency — APRT deficiency, 2,8-dihydroxyadenine urolithiasis, 2,8-DHA stone disease, DHA crystal nephropathy Uric acid urolithiasis (also radiolucent but pH-responsive) Hereditary xanthinuria and other radiolucent stone disorders Cystinuria and calcium-based stone disease Other crystalline nephropathies (e.g. oxalate, drug crystals) Idiopathic chronic kidney disease of unknown cause Recurrent idiopathic urolithiasis Stone analysis and urine microscopy for characteristic 2,8-DHA crystals Infrared spectroscopy or capillary electrophoresis to confirm 2,8-DHA composition Erythrocyte APRT enzyme activity measurement Molecular genetic testing of the APRT gene Renal function and urinalysis to assess crystal nephropathy Renal tract imaging for radiolucent calculi Autosomal recessive deficiency of adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme of the purine salvage pathway Loss of salvage diverts adenine to oxidation by xanthine oxidase, producing the highly insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (2,8-DHA) 2,8-DHA precipitates as radiolucent urinary stones and as intratubular crystals, causing renal colic, haematuria, recurrent stones and crystal nephropathy It is a major under-recognised cause of chronic kidney disease and can present with graft dysfunction after kidney transplantation if undiagnosed 2,8-DHA stones are radiolucent and can be mistaken for uric acid stones, but unlike uric acid they do not dissolve with urinary alkalinisation Diagnosis rests on identifying 2,8-DHA in stone or crystal analysis (round brown crystals on urine microscopy), enzyme assay or APRT gene testing Management is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor to block 2,8-DHA formation, together with high fluid intake and dietary purine moderation; urinary alkalinisation does not help Progressive or unexplained chronic kidney disease, especially with crystals on biopsy Acute kidney injury from crystal obstruction Early graft dysfunction after renal transplantation from recurrent crystal deposition Recurrent stone disease from infancy or childhood Misclassifying 2,8-DHA stones as uric acid stones and prescribing ineffective alkalinisation Failing to diagnose the condition before kidney transplantation, risking rapid graft injury Overlooking crystalline nephropathy as a cause of unexplained chronic kidney disease Not maintaining lifelong therapy, as crystal formation resumes if treatment stops Missing the diagnosis in adults because it can present at any age Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase normally salvages free adenine by combining it with phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate to form adenosine monophosphate. When the enzyme is deficient, adenine cannot be recycled and is instead oxidised by xanthine oxidase, first to 8-hydroxyadenine and then to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine. This end product is extremely insoluble across the physiological urinary pH range, so it crystallises within the renal tubules and urinary tract, producing stones and progressive crystalline tubulointerstitial damage. Because the enzyme block lies upstream, inhibiting xanthine oxidase effectively prevents 2,8-DHA generation. With early diagnosis and continuous xanthine oxidase inhibitor therapy the prognosis is excellent and renal function can be preserved; delayed diagnosis may lead to irreversible chronic kidney disease or loss of a transplanted kidney.

hypertrophy Choanal atresia (particularly if present from birth) Nasopharyngeal mass such as an angiofibroma in adolescent males Foreign body in the nose (unilateral obstruction) Nasopharyngeal tumour in adults with apparent adenoid tissue Nasal endoscopy to visualise and grade the adenoid pad Lateral soft tissue radiograph of the nasopharynx to estimate adenoid size Tympanometry and audiometry to a mass of lymphoid tissue at the back of the nasopharynx that normally enlarge in early childhood and regress toward puberty Hypertrophy commonly causes nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, snoring and a characteristic hyponasal (blocked) voice Long-standing obstruction and mouth breathing can produce the adenoid facies, with an open mouth, pinched nose, high-arched palate and dull expression By blocking the Eustachian tube openings the adenoids predispose to recurrent otitis media and persistent middle ear effusion with conductive hearing loss They also contribute to recurrent or chronic rhinosinusitis and postnasal discharge Sleep-disordered breathing, ranging from snoring to obstructive sleep apnoea, is an important consequence and can affect growth and behaviour Assessment uses history, examination, and either nasal endoscopy or a lateral nasopharyngeal radiograph to gauge the size of the adenoid pad Adenoidectomy, often combined with grommet insertion or tonsillectomy, is indicated for significant obstruction, sleep apnoea or recurrent middle ear disease not responding to conservative measures Features of obstructive sleep apnoea such as witnessed apnoeas, restless sleep and daytime effects, which need timely evaluation Strictly unilateral nasal obstruction or bloody discharge suggesting a mass or foreign body rather than adenoids In an adolescent boy, profuse epistaxis with a nasopharyngeal mass suggesting juvenile angiofibroma Apparent adenoid enlargement in an adult, which is unusual and should prompt exclusion of a nasopharyngeal tumour Failure to thrive or significant growth and behavioural disturbance from chronic obstruction Assuming any nasopharyngeal fullness in an adult is benign adenoid tissue and missing a tumour Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea and its effect on growth and behaviour Attributing nasal obstruction solely to adenoids while missing allergy, septal deviation or a foreign body Failing to assess and treat coexisting middle ear effusion and hearing loss Neglecting the possibility of juvenile angiofibroma in an adolescent boy with obstruction and bleeding The adenoid (nasopharyngeal tonsil) is part of Waldeyer's ring and undergoes physiological enlargement with repeated exposure to inhaled and ingested antigens in childhood. Recurrent infection and allergy drive lymphoid hyperplasia so the pad enlarges enough to obstruct the posterior nasal choanae and the nasopharyngeal openings of the Eustachian tubes. Choanal obstruction forces mouth breathing and impairs sinus drainage, while Eustachian tube dysfunction interferes with middle ear ventilation, favouring effusion and recurrent otitis media. Chronic mouth breathing during the years of facial growth alters craniofacial and dental development, and narrowing of the upper airway during sleep produces snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea. The adenoid tissue can also act as a reservoir of infection and biofilm. Adenoid tissue tends to regress naturally with age, so many children improve over time, and adenoidectomy gives prompt and lasting relief of obstruction, sleep-disordered breathing and associated ear disease in those who need surgery.

Adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency — ADSL deficiency, adenylosuccinase deficiency, succinylpurinaemic autism, ADSL gene deficiency Idiopathic autism spectrum disorder Non-specific syndromic intellectual disability Early-onset epileptic encephalopathies of other causes Other inborn errors of purine or pyrimidine metabolism Mitochondrial disorders with developmental delay and seizures calculation of their ratio Molecular genetic testing of ADSL Enzyme activity assay in fibroblasts or liver Electroencephalography and brain MRI to characterise seizures and structural change Developmental and behavioural assessment Autosomal recessive disorder of purine synthesis caused by variants in ADSL, encoding adenylosuccinate lyase The enzyme acts at two steps of purine metabolism, so its deficiency causes accumulation of the dephosphorylated succinylpurines SAICA-riboside and succinyladenosine in body fluids The biochemical hallmark is elevated succinylpurines in urine and cerebrospinal fluid, detectable with a modified Bratton-Marshall test or by chromatography Clinical phenotypes range from a severe neonatal form with seizures and encephalopathy to childhood forms with psychomotor delay, epilepsy and autistic behaviour Prominent autistic features and self-injurious or stereotyped behaviour are characteristic of the milder phenotypes The ratio of succinyladenosine to SAICA-riboside broadly correlates with clinical severity Muscle wasting, growth impairment and epilepsy are common accompanying features There is no established curative treatment, and management is supportive Neonatal seizures with encephalopathy and profound hypotonia Developmental regression with epilepsy Marked autistic and self-injurious behaviour with global delay Failure to thrive with muscle wasting Missing the diagnosis by not screening urine for succinylpurines in unexplained autism with epilepsy Attributing the presentation solely to idiopathic autism or cerebral palsy Overlooking milder phenotypes with predominantly behavioural features Assuming a normal metabolic screen excludes the disorder without specific purine testing Adenylosuccinate lyase catalyses two reactions in purine metabolism: the conversion of SAICAR to AICAR in de novo purine synthesis, and the conversion of adenylosuccinate to AMP in the purine nucleotide cycle. Enzyme deficiency blocks these steps, leading to accumulation of the phosphorylated precursors, which are dephosphorylated to the succinylpurines SAICA-riboside and succinyladenosine. These accumulated metabolites are thought to be neurotoxic and to impair normal purine nucleotide availability, disrupting cerebral development and function. The degree of residual enzyme activity and the relative accumulation of each metabolite influence the severity of the neurological phenotype. The neonatal-onset form is severe and often fatal in early life. Childhood-onset forms cause variable but usually significant intellectual disability, epilepsy and behavioural problems that persist, as no disease-modifying therapy is currently available.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder — ADHD, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADD, hyperkinetic disorder Anxiety disorders Mood disorders including bipolar disorder Oppositional defiant disorder and conduct disorder Learning disorders and intellectual disability Autism spectrum disorder Sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea Thyroid dysfunction Substance use disorder in adolescents and adults Standardised rating scales completed by multiple informants across settings Developmental, educational, and collateral history Baseline cardiovascular assessment before stimulant initiation Screening for comorbid learning, mood, anxiety, and sleep disorders Growth, blood pressure, and heart rate monitoring during treatment A neurodevelopmental disorder defined by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development Several symptoms must be present before around age twelve and across more than one setting, such as home and school or work Presentations are described as predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, or combined Inattentive features include distractibility, disorganisation, forgetfulness, and difficulty sustaining attention; hyperactive-impulsive features include restlessness, excessive talking, and interrupting Diagnosis relies on history and collateral information from multiple informants and standardised rating scales, not a single test Management principles combine behavioural and educational interventions with pharmacotherapy; stimulants are first-line, with non-stimulant options available, all described here without dosing Screen cardiovascular history before stimulant treatment and monitor growth, blood pressure, and heart rate during therapy Comorbidities are common, including learning disorders, oppositional and conduct problems, anxiety, depression, and tics Cardiac symptoms or family history of sudden death before or during stimulant therapy Emerging psychosis, mania, or marked mood instability Stimulant misuse or diversion, especially in adolescents and adults Significant growth suppression during treatment in children Diagnosing on the basis of symptoms in a single setting or from one informant Overlooking comorbid conditions such as anxiety, sleep disorders, or learning difficulties that mimic or worsen inattention Starting stimulants without assessing cardiovascular history Attributing normal age-appropriate activity to a disorder Failing to reassess ongoing need for medication and monitor growth and vital signs Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a highly heritable neurodevelopmental condition involving dysregulation of dopaminergic and noradrenergic signalling in fronto-striatal and fronto-cerebellar circuits that support attention, executive function, and response inhibition. Delayed maturation of these networks and gene-environment interactions, including prematurity and prenatal exposures, contribute to the phenotype. Symptoms, particularly hyperactivity, often lessen with age, but many individuals continue to experience inattention and functional difficulties into adulthood. Outcomes improve with treatment and support, while untreated ADHD is associated with academic underachievement, accidents, and increased risk of substance use.
