renal failure Simple renal cysts Tuberous sclerosis or von Hippel-Lindau associated cystic disease Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease Medullary cystic disease Renal ultrasound applying age-adjusted cyst count criteria Cross-sectional imaging and total kidney volume measurement to assess prognosis Blood pressure monitoring and assessment of renal function Urinalysis for haematuria, proteinuria, and infection Liver imaging for hepatic cysts when relevant Targeted cerebral vascular imaging for aneurysm screening in high-risk patients; genetic testing when the diagnosis is uncertain ADPKD is the most common inherited kidney disease and is characterised by progressive bilateral cyst formation that gradually replaces functioning renal tissue Most cases result from mutations in one of two genes, with the more common mutation generally causing earlier and more severe disease than the other Common presentations include hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, haematuria, kidney stones, urinary infections, and a family history of kidney disease Diagnosis is usually established by ultrasound using age-adjusted criteria for the number of cysts, with a positive family history strengthening the diagnosis Extrarenal manifestations are important and include hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valve abnormalities, and abdominal wall hernias Screening for intracranial aneurysms is targeted rather than universal, focusing on those with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage or high-risk occupations Blood pressure control with renin-angiotensin system blockade and generous water intake are core management principles, and a vasopressin antagonist can slow cyst growth in selected rapidly progressing patients Total kidney volume and the specific genotype help predict the rate of progression and identify candidates for disease-modifying therapy Sudden severe headache suggesting rupture of an intracranial aneurysm Cyst infection or haemorrhage causing fever and severe flank pain Rapidly declining renal function or refractory hypertension Obstructing or infected kidney stones Applying uniform ultrasound cyst criteria without adjusting for the patient's age Recommending universal aneurysm screening rather than targeting high-risk patients Missing a cyst infection because it can present without the usual urinary findings Failing to identify rapidly progressing patients who might benefit from disease-modifying therapy ADPKD is caused by mutations in genes encoding polycystin proteins, which are located in the primary cilium and are important for sensing tubular flow and regulating tubular cell proliferation and differentiation. Loss of normal polycystin function disrupts intracellular calcium signalling and increases cyclic AMP, promoting abnormal epithelial proliferation and fluid secretion into forming cysts. Cysts arise from tubular segments, enlarge progressively, and detach from the parent tubule, expanding relentlessly and compressing adjacent normal parenchyma. Vasopressin-driven cyclic AMP signalling is a key driver of cyst fluid secretion and growth, which underlies the therapeutic role of vasopressin blockade. Progressive cyst expansion, interstitial inflammation, and fibrosis gradually reduce functioning nephron mass, while activation of the renin-angiotensin system contributes to the early and often severe hypertension. ADPKD typically progresses over decades, with many patients reaching end-stage kidney disease in mid to later adult life, though the rate varies widely with genotype and total kidney volume. Blood pressure control, treatment of complications, and disease-modifying therapy in appropriate patients can slow progression, and outcomes on dialysis and after transplantation are generally good. Intracranial aneurysm rupture is a serious extrarenal risk in susceptible individuals.

Adrenal crisis — Random cortisol Electrolytes (Na↓ K↑) Empiric hydrocortisone Give IV hydrocortisone if suspected Other causes of distributive/endocrine shock (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) (p.2353) Hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock (p.2353) Acute abdomen-like presentation with abdominal tenderness, nausea, vomiting and fever can mimic an intra-abdominal infection (p.3111) Baseline serum cortisol AND plasma ACTH drawn before starting steroids, with formal testing deferred (p.3111) Short cosyntropin (ACTH stimulation) test once stabilised — failure cutoff roughly cortisol <450-500 nmol/L (16-18 ug/dL) at 30-60 min (p.3111) Plasma renin to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary disease (p.3111) Adrenal steroid autoantibodies to assess for autoimmune adrenalitis (p.3111) Adrenal CT for hemorrhage, infiltration or masses if autoantibodies negative (p.3111) Very-long-chain fatty acids in autoantibody-negative males to exclude X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (p.3111) Hypothalamic-pituitary MRI when ACTH is inappropriately low (secondary cause) (p.3111) Associated labs: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, raised creatinine, normochromic anaemia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia (p.3110) Acute abdomen / surgical abdomen (abdominal pain, tenderness, nausea, vomiting) (p.3111) Primary neurologic disease — decreased responsiveness progressing to stupor and coma (p.3111) Adrenal crisis typically emerges after a prolonged prodrome of nonspecific complaints rather than appearing out of the blue (p.3111). Crisis is more frequent in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency because both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion are lost (p.3111). Postural hypotension can progress to frank hypovolaemic shock (p.3111). Prospective data: about 8.3 adrenal crises per 100 patient-years and roughly 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years (p.3111). Adrenal crisis is classified as a form of endocrine/distributive shock (p.2353). In suspected crisis, it is reasonable to draw a baseline cortisol (and ACTH), start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing — diagnostic testing must never delay treatment (p.3111). Starting thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient can precipitate adrenal crisis, because thyroid hormone shortens cortisol half-life; screen for adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism in possible polyendocrine syndrome (p.3133). Refractory or postural hypotension progressing to hypovolaemic shock (p.3111) Decreased responsiveness, stupor or coma (p.3111) Hyperpigmentation suggesting underlying primary adrenal insufficiency (p.3110) Do NOT let diagnostic testing delay treatment in suspected crisis (p.3111). Random/baseline serum cortisol has limited diagnostic value because levels may be coincidentally low from normal diurnal rhythm, and many secondary cases have near-normal baseline cortisol that only fails on stimulation testing (p.3111). Do NOT start thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency — it can precipitate crisis (p.3133). Hyperthyroidism increases glucocorticoid inactivation and can trigger crisis (p.3111). Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by concurrent primary hypothyroidism, which prolongs cortisol half-life (p.3133). Acute adrenal insufficiency reflects an absolute or relative deficiency of cortisol, in primary disease compounded by loss of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decompensate into hypovolaemic shock. Crisis is usually unmasked by a stressor that exceeds the inadequate cortisol reserve — intercurrent illness, surgery or other stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation as in hyperthyroidism (p.3111). Acute adrenal insufficiency is potentially lethal (p.636). Even with established care, crises and crisis-related deaths continue to occur (~8.3 crises and ~0.5 deaths per 100 patient-years) (p.3111).

Normal/high ACTH = ACTH-dependent -> pituitary MRI plus dynamic tests (high-dose dexamethasone, CRH or desmopressin); pituitary MRI can be normal in up to 40% because microadenomas are small. (p.3061, p.3064) CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase) deficiency causes 90-95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia; it impairs glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid synthesis and drives ACTH-mediated adrenal androgen excess. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker steroid. Severity spans classic salt-wasting (neonatal), simple virilizing, to nonclassic (presents in adolescence/adulthood). severe alkalosis causing tetany Classic salt-wasting CAH in male neonates presenting as life-threatening adrenal crisis in the first weeks of life Performing imaging or surgery before biochemically confirming Cushing's beyond doubt - pituitary/adrenal nodules are common incidental findings and lead to misdiagnosis Forgetting to exclude exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid use as the cause before working up endogenous Cushing's Dexamethasone test pitfalls: false non-suppression from oral estrogens/contraceptives (raise CBG/total cortisol; retest after 4-6 weeks off estrogen) and rapid dexamethasone inactivation by CYP3A4 inducers (antiepileptics, rifampicin); antibody-based urinary free cortisol assays have specificity problems improved by tandem mass spectrometry Not normalizing potassium before, or failing to stop MR antagonists (4-6 weeks) before, ARR testing; beta-blockers give false-positive and ACE inhibitors/ARBs false-negative ARR results Relying on the ARR alone when renin is very low increases false positives; only 10-40% of primary aldosteronism patients are hypokalemic, so normokalemia does not exclude it Using random serum cortisol to diagnose adrenal insufficiency - baseline levels may be coincidentally low (diurnal rhythm), and secondary insufficiency often shows near-normal baseline cortisol that fails only on stimulation Stopping exogenous glucocorticoids abruptly can precipitate iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency even though the patient still looks cushingoid Judging adrenal mass attenuation on post-contrast CT - Hounsfield-unit discrimination of benign vs malignant only applies to unenhanced CT; lipid-poor adenomas (high HU) overlap with ACC and pheochromocytoma Mistaking testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) in CAH for testicular neoplasms The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids (cortisol, zona fasciculata under HPA/ACTH control), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone, zona glomerulosa under renin-angiotensin-aldosterone control), and adrenal androgens. Cushing's syndrome reflects chronic glucocorticoid excess: ~90% of endogenous cases are ACTH-dependent (mostly a pituitary corticotrope adenoma = Cushing's disease, or ectopic ACTH from carcinoid/small-cell lung cancer), ~10% are ACTH-independent adrenal causes (adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral macronodular/pigmented nodular hyperplasia). Cortisol excess upregulates gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and protein catabolism, and when 11beta-HSD2 is overwhelmed cortisol activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema. Primary mineralocorticoid excess (primary aldosteronism) is autonomous aldosterone production by the zona glomerulosa (bilateral hyperplasia or unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma/Conn's); MR over-activation causes sodium retention with volume expansion, potassium and hydrogen loss (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis), and direct cardiac/renal damage. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) is destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex (most often autoimmune adrenalitis, also TB, adrenoleukodystrophy, hemorrhage, infiltration, CAH), causing combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency; secondary insufficiency is HPA/pituitary-hypothalamic failure (tumor, surgery, irradiation, apoplexy/Sheehan's, or iatrogenic glucocorticoid suppression) with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency. CAH results from inherited steroidogenic enzyme defects (commonly CYP21A2) causing glucocorticoid deficiency, loss of feedback, raised ACTH, and adrenal androgen excess, with mineralocorticoid deficiency or excess depending on the enzymatic block. After successful removal of an ACTH- or cortisol-producing tumor the HPA axis remains suppressed and may take months to years (or never) to recover; recovery rates differ by cause - ectopic ACTH best (~80%, median ~7 months), Cushing's disease intermediate (~60%, ~17 months), adrenal Cushing's lowest (~40%, ~30 months). Even after cure, long-term quality of life can remain impaired with increased cardiovascular and osteoporotic-fracture risk depending on duration and degree of cortisol excess. Primary aldosteronism carries increased osteoporosis, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive dysfunction. Adrenal crisis is potentially lethal, with prospective data of 8.3 crises and 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years. MACS is associated with increased mortality. In CAH, fertility may be compromised (anovulation in women, testicular adrenal rest tumors and fibrosis in men). Adrenal insufficiency is classified as primary (Addison's, combined glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid deficiency, high ACTH) vs secondary/central (isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, low/inappropriate ACTH), with acute adrenal crisis as the life-threatening acute form. Endogenous Cushing's is classified as ACTH-dependent (~90%; Cushing's disease vs ectopic ACTH) vs ACTH-independent (~10%; adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Cortisol excess severity ranges from overt Cushing's to mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS). Primary aldosteronism is divided into unilateral (adenoma/Conn's, surgically curable) vs bilateral (hyperplasia, medical therapy). CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency) is graded by severity into classic salt-wasting, simple virilizing, and nonclassic forms. Adrenocortical carcinoma is staged by the ENSAT/TNM system (Stage I T1 <=5 cm to advanced/metastatic).

reason, and its evaluation centres on two questions: is it functional, and is it malignant Every incidentaloma should be screened biochemically for cortisol excess, phaeochromocytoma, and, in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients, primary aldosteronism Unenhanced CT attenuation is key: a lipid-rich lesion with low Hounsfield values strongly favours a benign adenoma, while high attenuation warrants further characterisation Large size and imaging features such as irregular margins, heterogeneity, and delayed contrast washout raise concern for adrenocortical carcinoma Phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before any biopsy or surgery to avoid a catastrophic hypertensive crisis Surgery (usually laparoscopic adrenalectomy) is indicated for functional tumours, lesions with malignant features, and masses above a threshold size, while smaller non-functioning benign lesions are monitored Biopsy of an adrenal mass is rarely helpful and is reserved for suspected metastasis or infiltrative disease after phaeochromocytoma has been ruled out Undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma before intervention, risking a life-threatening hypertensive crisis on biopsy or induction Large or rapidly enlarging mass with heterogeneous, high-attenuation, poorly washing-out features suggesting adrenocortical carcinoma Severe or resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia indicating a functioning tumour Known extra-adrenal malignancy with a new adrenal lesion suggesting metastasis Proceeding to biopsy or surgery without first excluding a phaeochromocytoma Labelling a mass non-functioning without complete biochemical screening, missing subclinical cortisol excess Underestimating malignant potential by relying on size alone and ignoring washout and morphology Inadequate perioperative alpha- (then beta-) blockade when operating on a catecholamine-secreting tumour Failing to plan perioperative glucocorticoid cover when removing a cortisol-secreting adenoma with a suppressed contralateral gland Adrenal incidentalomas are a heterogeneous group. Most are benign non-functioning cortical adenomas, but the differential spans hormonally active adenomas (secreting cortisol or aldosterone), phaeochromocytomas arising from the adrenal medulla, adrenocortical carcinoma, myelolipomas, cysts, and metastatic deposits. Functional lesions cause disease through autonomous hormone secretion: cortisol excess produces subclinical or overt Cushing syndrome, aldosterone excess produces hypertension and hypokalaemia, and catecholamine excess from a phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension and its complications. Malignant potential correlates with size, growth rate, and imaging characteristics reflecting lipid content and vascularity. Most incidentalomas are benign and non-functioning with an excellent outlook and stable behaviour on surveillance. Functional lesions generally do well after adrenalectomy with resolution or improvement of hormone excess, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma carries a poor prognosis, strongly influenced by stage and completeness of resection.

unexplained adrenal insufficiency in a boy or man should prompt VLCFA testing Female carriers can develop a mild myelopathy in later life, so heterozygotes are not always asymptomatic Elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids is the key biochemical screening test, confirmed by ABCD1 mutation analysis The disorder is increasingly detected through newborn screening programmes, allowing presymptomatic identification and timely monitoring for cerebral disease and adrenal failure There is no reliable phenotype-genotype correlation, so the same mutation within a family can produce very different clinical courses A previously well boy with rapid cognitive, behavioural, or visual decline suggesting active cerebral demyelination Unexplained primary adrenal insufficiency, especially with hyperpigmentation or adrenal crisis Rapidly enhancing white matter lesions on MRI indicating an inflammatory, aggressive cerebral phase Progressive gait failure with sphincter involvement in an adult male Attributing early cerebral disease in a boy to a behavioural or psychiatric disorder and delaying imaging Overlooking coexisting adrenal insufficiency, which can be life-threatening if untreated Assuming female carriers are always asymptomatic Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening once a proband is identified Adrenoleukodystrophy results from loss-of-function mutations in ABCD1, which encodes a peroxisomal membrane transporter needed for the import and beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids. Impaired degradation leads to accumulation of these fatty acids in tissues, particularly cerebral white matter, spinal cord long tracts, adrenal cortex, and testis. In the cerebral form, an inflammatory demyelinating process destroys white matter, whereas adrenomyeloneuropathy is characterised by a slowly progressive distal axonopathy of the spinal cord. Adrenocortical cells accumulate abnormal lipid and undergo dysfunction, producing primary adrenal insufficiency. The childhood cerebral form is often relentlessly progressive once inflammatory demyelination is established, whereas adrenomyeloneuropathy advances slowly over years to decades. Early identification through screening allows monitoring and consideration of disease-modifying options in appropriate candidates, and adrenal insufficiency can be effectively treated with hormone replacement, but neurological outcomes remain variable.

constitutional decline raising concern for occult malignancy Diagnosing it before adequately excluding infection and malignancy Missing evolving macrophage activation syndrome when cytopenias develop Dismissing the diagnosis because the transient rash is absent at the time of review Over-reliance on ferritin alone, which is nonspecific Failing to escalate to cytokine-directed therapy in corticosteroid-refractory disease Adult-onset Still disease is a systemic autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulation of the innate immune system rather than autoantibody-mediated autoimmunity. Activation of macrophages and neutrophils with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, particularly interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumour necrosis factor, produces the fever, rash, arthritis, and hyperferritinaemia. Interleukin-18 and macrophage activation underlie the extreme ferritin elevation and the propensity to macrophage activation syndrome. A genetic predisposition combined with an infectious or other environmental trigger is thought to initiate the process. The course is variable: some have a self-limiting monocyclic illness, others a polycyclic relapsing course, and a subset develop chronic destructive arthritis; macrophage activation syndrome is the principal cause of mortality.

Intracranial haemorrhage or other major spontaneous bleeding Spontaneous splenic rupture or intra-abdominal haemorrhage Thrombotic events, which can occur despite the bleeding phenotype Pregnancy complications including recurrent miscarriage and placental abruption Confusing afibrinogenaemia with dysfibrinogenaemia by relying on a single test rather than both activity and antigen Forgetting that these patients can thrombose as well as bleed Overlooking fibrinogen replacement to sustain pregnancy Attributing grossly abnormal clotting times to DIC or liver disease without measuring fibrinogen Fibrinogen is the soluble plasma protein that thrombin converts to fibrin, the structural scaffold of the clot, and it also supports platelet aggregation by bridging activated platelets. Congenital afibrinogenaemia results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in one of the three fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, FGG), abolishing production or secretion of the protein. Without fibrinogen, no fibrin clot can form and platelet aggregation is impaired, so all fibrin-dependent coagulation assays are markedly prolonged and haemostasis fails, producing bleeding that frequently manifests at birth. The same molecule is required for placental integrity, so its absence causes recurrent pregnancy loss and abruption. A coexisting thrombotic tendency reflects loss of fibrinogen's normal role in binding and clearing thrombin, leaving unbound thrombin free to act elsewhere. With fibrinogen concentrate replacement, bleeding episodes can be controlled and pregnancies supported, giving a reasonable outlook, though patients face lifelong risks of both haemorrhage and thrombosis requiring specialist management.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum — ACC, callosal agenesis, corpus callosum dysgenesis, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum Holoprosencephaly with absent corpus callosum Interhemispheric cyst with callosal dysgenesis Septo-optic dysplasia Aicardi syndrome Secondary callosal thinning from destructive or hypoxic-ischaemic injury Chromosomal syndromes with callosal involvement Brain MRI to confirm complete or partial agenesis and detect associated malformations Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected antenatally Chromosomal microarray and, where indicated, exome sequencing Metabolic screening for disorders that include callosal agenesis such as certain organic acidaemias Ophthalmological examination, particularly to evaluate for Aicardi syndrome Developmental assessment and electroencephalography if seizures occur Complete or partial absence of the corpus callosum, the major commissure connecting the cerebral hemispheres, and one of the most common brain malformations It may be isolated or, more often clinically significant, part of a wider syndrome, chromosomal disorder, or metabolic condition, so a careful search for associated anomalies is essential Characteristic MRI features include widely spaced parallel lateral ventricles, colpocephaly (dilated occipital horns), a high-riding third ventricle, and radiating medial gyri (the sunburst sign) When complete agenesis is present, longitudinal Probst bundles run anteroposteriorly along the medial ventricular walls instead of crossing the midline Outcome depends heavily on associated malformations and the underlying cause; truly isolated agenesis may be compatible with near-normal development Clinical manifestations when present include developmental delay, epilepsy, and subtle deficits in interhemispheric transfer, and some syndromes such as Aicardi syndrome combine it with distinctive eye and seizure features Diagnosis is by prenatal ultrasound and foetal or postnatal MRI, supplemented by genetic and metabolic testing to identify a cause Seizures, including infantile spasms, especially in the context of Aicardi syndrome Features suggesting an underlying metabolic disorder such as decompensation or regression Multiple associated malformations pointing to a syndromic or chromosomal cause Progressive macrocephaly from an associated interhemispheric cyst or hydrocephalus Labelling the malformation isolated without thorough imaging, genetic, and metabolic evaluation for associated conditions Failing to consider Aicardi syndrome in a girl with callosal agenesis, seizures, and chorioretinal lacunae Giving overly pessimistic prognosis for truly isolated cases Confusing an associated interhemispheric cyst or colpocephaly with hydrocephalus requiring shunting The corpus callosum forms in the first half of gestation as axons from cortical neurons cross the midline, guided by midline glial structures and molecular cues. Agenesis results when these guidance mechanisms fail, so callosal axons cannot cross and instead run longitudinally as Probst bundles along the medial ventricular walls. The malformation can arise from single-gene disorders, chromosomal imbalances, metabolic diseases, or disruptions of midline development, and it frequently coexists with other cerebral and systemic anomalies that determine the clinical picture. Isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum can be compatible with normal or near-normal neurodevelopment, though subtle cognitive and social deficits may emerge. When it is part of a syndromic, chromosomal, or metabolic disorder, the prognosis is dictated by the associated condition.

ganglia calcification solely to prior infection or metabolic causes Failing to consider genetic counselling given both recessive and dominant inheritance patterns Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome is a genetically determined type I interferonopathy in which defects in intracellular nucleic-acid metabolism cause self-derived DNA and RNA to accumulate or to be misrecognised as foreign. The causative genes encode nucleases and nucleic-acid-editing or sensing proteins (for example the exonuclease TREX1, the ribonuclease H2 complex, the deoxynucleotide-regulating enzyme SAMHD1, the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, and the cytosolic RNA sensor encoded by IFIH1). When these fail, endogenous nucleic acids trigger innate immune sensors and drive chronic overproduction of type I interferon. Sustained interferon signalling produces the inflammatory encephalopathy, intracranial calcification, white matter injury and systemic features that characterise the disorder. The classic early-onset form often causes severe, permanent neurological disability with significant early mortality, though a wide clinical spectrum exists including milder later-onset presentations; interferon-directed therapies offer the prospect of attenuating disease activity, particularly the systemic and skin manifestations.

excluding pre- and post-renal causes points to an intrinsic parenchymal disease (p.340). Reduced renal perfusion (prerenal) accounts for roughly 40-80% of cases and is typically readily reversible if perfusion is restored promptly (p.340). Urinary tract obstruction (postrenal) accounts for under 5% of cases but is usually reversible and should be excluded early, generally with renal ultrasound looking for ureteric/pelvic dilatation (p.340). Ischaemic and toxic acute tubular necrosis (ATN) together account for about 90% of intrinsic AKI (p.340). Prerenal azotaemia and ATN lie on a spectrum of hypoperfusion: prerenal reverses promptly with restored perfusion, whereas ATN involves structural tubular injury (p.340). Microscopic examination of urine sediment is a key bedside test in AKI; dark (muddy-brown) granular casts and/or tubular epithelial cells strongly suggest ATN (p.340). Because a single kidney can clear adequately, complete obstructive AKI requires bladder-outlet/urethral obstruction, bilateral ureteric obstruction, or unilateral obstruction in a solitary kidney (p.340). RBC casts in the urine indicate glomerular disease (acute nephritic picture) and are an indication for early renal biopsy; they are highly specific but very insensitive for glomerulonephritis (p.341). The kidney is particularly vulnerable to toxic injury because it receives about 25% of cardiac output and concentrates and metabolises toxins (p.340). Distinguishing acute from chronic kidney disease can be difficult because anaemia, hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia occur in both; small echogenic kidneys with cortical thinning on ultrasound and radiographic renal osteodystrophy favour chronicity (p.339-340). Oliguria (24-h output under 400 mL) or anuria (under 100 mL); oliguria is never normal as at least ~400 mL of maximally concentrated urine is needed to excrete the daily osmolar load (p.341) Anuria suggesting complete bilateral obstruction, vascular catastrophe (dissection/arterial occlusion), renal vein thrombosis, myeloma cast nephropathy, cortical necrosis, severe ATN, severe rapidly progressive GN, combined NSAID+ACEi/ARB, or shock (p.341) RBC casts or dysmorphic red cells (acute nephritic/glomerular emergency warranting urgent biopsy) (p.341) Dialysis-indication complications of AKI (refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, refractory volume overload/pulmonary oedema, uraemic complications) (existing entry; supported p.2330 RRT criteria for overload/acidosis/hyperkalaemia) Failing to exclude obstruction early; ultrasound can be falsely negative very early in obstruction or when ureters cannot dilate (tumour encasement, retroperitoneal fibrosis) (p.340) Measuring urine eosinophils to diagnose interstitial nephritis: eosinophiluria is raised in many causes of AKI, has no diagnostic utility, and is no longer recommended (p.340) Assuming FENa over 1% always means ATN: it may be under 1% in mild nonoliguric ATN (e.g., rhabdomyolysis) and in prerenal-like states such as CHF, cirrhosis or hepatorenal syndrome (p.340) Over-relying on creatinine-based eGFR: muscle mass, sex, race assumptions can mislead (e.g., a bodybuilder with high creatinine) (p.339) Attributing RBC casts to interstitial nephritis: their presence should instead prompt a search for glomerular disease (p.340-341) In prerenal states, a fall in true or effective arterial volume lowers mean arterial pressure and triggers sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vasopressin release; GFR is sustained by prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. Once mean arterial pressure falls below about 80 mmHg, GFR declines steeply. This autoregulation explains why NSAIDs (which block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs (which reduce efferent constriction) can precipitate hemodynamically mediated AKI when volume or perfusion pressure is already reduced, and why patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis of a solitary kidney) are especially susceptible to a precipitous GFR fall on ACEi/ARBs. Sustained hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic ATN. Nephrotoxic ATN results from a combination of intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct tubular toxicity, and intratubular obstruction (p.340). Prerenal AKI is usually readily reversible when perfusion is restored, and postrenal AKI is usually reversible once obstruction is relieved if recognised early. In nephrotoxic ATN, stopping the offending agent and stabilising blood pressure often suffice, with regeneration of tubular cells and recovery without dialysis. Nonoliguric ATN tends to have less severe potassium and acid-base disturbance and a more rapid recovery than oliguric AKI (p.340-341). AKI severity is staged by the KDIGO criteria (referenced as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes; p.341, line ref to KDIGO Controversies Conference). Detailed KDIGO stage cut-offs (serum creatinine rise and urine-output thresholds for stages 1-3) are not specified in this source excerpt and are therefore not reproduced. The source's working framework classifies AKI anatomically into prerenal, intrinsic (renal), and postrenal categories, with supporting urinary indices distinguishing prerenal azotaemia from oliguric ATN (Table 55-2, p.340).

proceeding to unnecessary Kasai portoenterostomy Underestimating vascular risk, including intracranial aneurysms and bleeding Assuming absence of the classic facies or one feature excludes the Alagille syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of the Notch signalling pathway, most commonly through mutations in the ligand JAG1 and occasionally the receptor NOTCH2. Notch signalling is essential for the differentiation and branching morphogenesis of intrahepatic bile ducts, as well as for cardiac, vascular, renal, skeletal, and ocular development. Impaired signalling leads to progressive loss (paucity) of the interlobular bile ducts, causing chronic intrahepatic cholestasis with retention of bile acids and cholesterol, alongside the syndrome's characteristic extrahepatic malformations. Expressivity is highly variable even within families. Outcome is largely determined by the severity of cardiac and vascular anomalies and the progression of liver disease; many patients do well, but a subset develops end-stage cholestatic liver disease requiring transplantation, and vascular events can cause sudden morbidity or mortality.

one typical drink raises the blood ethanol level by about 0.02 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3675). Behavioral, psychomotor and cognitive impairment appears at only 0.02-0.04 g/dL (one to two drinks); 'legal intoxication' in most U.S. states is 0.08 g/dL, with 0.04 g/dL applied to pilots and to drivers in some countries (Harrison 22e p.3676). In a person without tolerance, light coma with depressed vital signs occurs around 0.30 g/dL and death between 0.30 and 0.40 g/dL; alcohol probably causes more overdose deaths than any other drug (Harrison 22e p.3676). Heavy drinking while fasting can cause transient hypoglycemia within 6-36 h by suppressing gluconeogenesis, producing temporarily abnormal glucose tolerance that can be misread as diabetes until 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675). Most ethanol is metabolized in the liver: the cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase pathway generates acetaldehyde (then cleared by aldehyde dehydrogenase), while the microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS) handles >=10% at high blood levels (Harrison 22e p.3675). Blackouts (temporary anterograde amnesia while awake) occur in about 35% of drinkers, with en bloc blackouts at levels >0.20 and fragmentary blackouts at >0.12 (Harrison 22e p.3676). Alcohol disrupts sleep architecture, reducing early-night REM and deep sleep and relaxing pharyngeal muscles to worsen snoring and apnea; sleep apnea symptoms occur in about 75% of men with AUD aged >=60 (Harrison 22e p.3676). DSM-5 diagnoses AUD when >=2 of 11 criteria cluster in the same 12-month period; severity is mild (2-3), moderate (4-5) or severe (>=6 items) (Harrison 22e p.3677-3678). Roughly 60% of the risk for AUD is genetic; a flushing response (ALDH variant seen in Japanese, Chinese and Korean individuals) lowers risk, while a low level of response to alcohol predicts future heavy drinking and problems (Harrison 22e p.3678). Useful blood markers of regular heavy intake are GGT (>35 U) and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%), with the combination more accurate than either alone; high-normal MCV (>=91) and elevated uric acid also support the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3678-3679). Continued heavy drinking shortens life span by about 10 years, with leading causes of early death being heart disease, cancer, accidents and suicide (Harrison 22e p.3678). 'Holiday heart' refers to atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, especially paroxysmal tachycardia, occurring temporarily after heavy drinking in people with no other evidence of heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3677). light coma near 0.30 g/dL and death 0.30-0.40 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.3676, 3679) Gastrointestinal bleeding from hemorrhagic gastritis or a Mallory-Weiss tear after violent vomiting (Harrison 22e p.3677) Pregnancy: any drinking risks fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; complete abstinence advised (Harrison 22e p.3677) Misreading alcohol-induced transient hypoglycemia/abnormal glucose tolerance as diabetes before 2-4 weeks of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3675) Misdiagnosing alcohol ketoacidosis as diabetic ketosis (Harrison 22e p.3675) Treating substance-induced psychiatric symptoms with long-term medication when they typically resolve within days to ~4 weeks of abstinence (only short-term antipsychotics for substance-induced psychosis are usually needed) (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677) Giving routine IV fluids in withdrawal - most patients are normally hydrated or mildly overhydrated, so fluids should be avoided unless there is a specific medical indication, bleeding, vomiting or diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.3680) Relying on questionnaires (e.g., AUDIT) alone - they are screening tools and a face-to-face interview is required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3679) A false-negative tuberculin skin test from impaired delayed-hypersensitivity in chronic heavy drinkers (Harrison 22e p.3677) Assuming AUD spares affluent or professional patients - lifetime risk among physicians is similar to the general population (Harrison 22e p.3678) Ethanol is a CNS depressant that acutely enhances GABA activity (notably at GABA-A receptors) and inhibits postsynaptic NMDA excitatory glutamate receptors; chronic exposure produces compensatory downregulation of GABA-related activity and upregulation of NMDA receptor subunits. Falling blood levels after chronic use therefore unmask a hyperexcitable state, explaining withdrawal phenomena. Acute alcohol raises dopamine in the ventral tegmentum and nucleus accumbens, releases beta-endorphins, and increases serotonin and stress hormones (cortisol, ACTH), driving reward, craving and relapse. Cellular (pharmacodynamic), metabolic (up to ~30% faster hepatic metabolism after 1-2 weeks) and learned/behavioral mechanisms contribute to acquired tolerance. Cellular adaptations may take weeks to resolve, so rapid drops in blood level produce withdrawal that is most intense in the first 5 days but with protracted symptoms (disturbed sleep, anxiety) lasting up to 4-6 months (Harrison 22e p.3675-3676). With at least a year of follow-up after treatment, more than half of people with AUD achieve a marked reduction in drinking and related problems or full abstinence, and even without formal treatment or self-help groups there is at least a 20% chance of spontaneous long-term remission. DSM-5 alcohol use disorder severity by number of criteria endorsed in a 12-month period: mild = 2-3 items, moderate = 4-5 items, severe = >=6 of the 11 items (Harrison 22e p.3678). Effects of blood alcohol levels without tolerance: 0.02 decreased inhibitions; 0.08 reduced complex cognition and motor performance; 0.20 slurred speech, incoordination, poor judgment; 0.30 light coma with depressed vital signs; 0.40 death (Harrison 22e p.3676).

Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease — alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, ALD Viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B or C) Wilson's disease Severe autoimmune liver disease Drug-induced liver injury (DILI), including amiodarone-related pseudoalcoholic injury Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) and MetALD Hemochromatosis Ischemic hepatitis Biliary obstruction Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Viral hepatitis (hepatitis B or C) producing aminotransferase elevation that can be confused with ALD Liver function tests with AST, ALT (AST/ALT ratio), GGT, bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Inventory Test) to identify alcohol use disorder Abdominal ultrasound, MRI, or CT to detect steatosis, nodularity, and signs of portal hypertension Controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) or MR proton density fat fraction (MR-PDFF) for noninvasive hepatic fat quantification Transient elastography / liver stiffness measurement (e.g., FibroScan) for fibrosis staging Fib-4 score (age, AST, ALT, platelets) to exclude advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis (threshold <3.25) Transjugular liver biopsy when confounding factors are present (to confirm alcohol-associated hepatitis) Imaging to exclude biliary obstruction and HCC; AFP and ultrasonography for HCC surveillance in cirrhosis Infection workup: chest x-ray plus blood, urine, and ascites cultures in alcohol-associated hepatitis MASLD/NAFLD (key distinction: ALD typically shows AST/ALT >2:1, whereas NAFLD usually has ALT >= AST) Amiodarone hepatotoxicity producing pseudoalcoholic liver injury (steatosis to alcoholic-hepatitis-like neutrophilic infiltration with Mallory-Denk bodies) Wilson's disease Autoimmune hepatitis Hemochromatosis Ischemic hepatitis ALD is a spectrum: alcohol-associated fatty liver (steatosis) and steatohepatitis progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis; acute alcohol-associated hepatitis is an acute-on-chronic form associated with liver failure and high mortality (p.2697). Characteristic biochemical signature: AST/ALT ratio >1 (commonly cited as >2:1 for alcoholic liver disease), with serum AST rarely exceeding 300 IU/L; in alcohol-associated hepatitis AST and ALT do not exceed 400 IU/L and the AST/ALT ratio is >1.5 with serum bilirubin >3 mg/dL (p.2699). Steatosis and steatohepatitis are clinically silent; symptoms typically appear only when alcohol-associated cirrhosis decompensates or alcohol-associated hepatitis develops (p.2699). Alcohol-associated hepatitis is defined clinically by heavy drinking (>40 g/d women, >50-60 g/d men) for >6 months with <60 days abstinence before symptom onset, presenting with rapid-onset jaundice (bilirubin >3 mg/dL), often with fever, malaise, and tender hepatomegaly (p.2698). Prolonged alcohol abstinence is the most effective therapy to reduce progression and reverse ALD; steatosis and steatohepatitis are reversible with cessation of alcohol consumption (p.2699). There are currently NO approved drugs for treatment of alcohol-associated steatosis or steatohepatitis with or without fibrosis (p.2699). Severity of alcohol-associated hepatitis is stratified by Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) and MELD: severe disease (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) carries high short-term mortality (~30% at 3 months) and may benefit from glucocorticoids; moderate disease (MDF <32 or MELD <=20) still carries ~20% 1-year mortality (p.2700). Lille score >=0.45 after 7 days of glucocorticoid treatment identifies non-responders unlikely to benefit from continued therapy; glucocorticoids should be stopped and early liver transplantation considered (p.2700). Liver transplantation for alcohol-associated decompensated cirrhosis or HCC is the leading indication for liver transplantation in the United States (p.2699-2700). In confirmed cirrhosis, HCC surveillance with liver ultrasonography and serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months and upper GI endoscopy to screen for varices are recommended (p.2699). Only 10-20% of individuals with alcohol-induced hepatic steatosis develop progressive liver disease and cirrhosis; women develop ALD at a lower daily alcohol intake (p.2698). Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) - high short-term mortality (~30% at 3 months) Rapid-onset jaundice with serum bilirubin >3 mg/dL, fever, and tender hepatomegaly Clinical signs of hepatic decompensation: ascites, variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy Bacterial infection (occurs in 12-26% of severe alcohol-associated hepatitis at admission) Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) Acute kidney injury / hepatorenal syndrome Lille score >=0.45 at day 7 (glucocorticoid non-response) - high 30-day mortality Multiorgan failure and shock Diagnosis of ALD requires exclusion of other liver diseases in heavy drinkers; do not attribute liver disease to alcohol without ruling out viral hepatitis, Wilson's disease, autoimmune liver disease, and DILI. Atypical laboratory values (AST <50 IU/L or >400 IU/L, or AST/ALT ratio <1.5) argue against alcohol-associated hepatitis and warrant transjugular liver biopsy - 10-20% of clinically diagnosed cases have a different disease on biopsy. Do not give glucocorticoids when contraindications are present: uncontrolled infection/sepsis, AKI/hepatorenal syndrome, uncontrolled upper GI bleeding, concomitant viral hepatitis/HCC/pancreatitis/DILI/active TB/HIV, multiorgan failure, or shock; glucocorticoids may be used only once infection, sepsis, and GI bleeding are adequately controlled. Liver biopsy is rarely needed to diagnose simple steatosis or steatohepatitis - reserve invasive biopsy for confounding/atypical cases. Distinguish ALD from NAFLD/MASLD by the AST/ALT pattern (ALD favors AST/ALT >2:1). Ethanol is rapidly absorbed in the upper GI tract and metabolized predominantly in the liver, reaching it via the portal vein. Most ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase 1 (ADH1) to acetaldehyde in hepatocytes; chronic consumption also induces CYP2E1, which similarly generates acetaldehyde. Beyond direct acetaldehyde toxicity, ethanol metabolism generates reactive oxygen species causing hepatocyte injury through lipid peroxidation and DNA damage. Acetaldehyde is then oxidized to acetate by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH); inherited ALDH2 deficiency (common in Asian populations) causes acetaldehyde accumulation with nausea and cutaneous flushing. Steatosis arises because acetate becomes acetyl-CoA feeding fatty acid/triglyceride synthesis, alcohol upregulates lipogenic genes (partly epigenetically) while suppressing fatty acid transport/oxidation, and the increased NADH/NAD+ ratio reduces mitochondrial beta-oxidation; alcohol also mobilizes fatty acids from adipose and intestine into the liver. A subset develop gut dysbiosis and increased intestinal permeability, allowing microbial components (e.g., bacterial LPS) to reach the liver via the portal vein, driving inflammation, hepatocyte death, and fibrotic pathway activation; sustained alcohol use progresses to cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Impaired liver regeneration may contribute to acute alcohol-associated hepatitis arising in underlying cirrhosis (p.2698). Steatosis and steatohepatitis are reversible with abstinence, but only 10-20% of those with steatosis progress to cirrhosis. In alcohol-associated hepatitis, short-term mortality is predicted by MDF, MELD, or ABIC scores: moderate disease (MDF <32 or MELD <=20) carries ~20% 1-year mortality, whereas severe disease (MDF >=32 or MELD >20) carries ~30% 3-month mortality. Glucocorticoids reduce risk of death in severe disease within 28 days but not over the following 6 months. While short-term prognosis depends on disease severity at presentation, long-term prognosis (>1 year) largely depends on alcohol abstinence and underlying cirrhosis. Non-responders to medical therapy have high 30-day mortality (p.2700). Alcohol-associated hepatitis severity: Moderate AH = MDF <32 or MELD <=20 (~20% 1-year mortality); Severe AH = Maddrey discriminant function (MDF) >=32 or MELD >20 (~30% 3-month mortality), candidates for glucocorticoids if no contraindication. MDF = 4.6 x (prothrombin time prolongation above control in seconds) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). Day-7 Lille score >=0.45 defines glucocorticoid non-response. Cirrhosis prognosis assessed by Child-Pugh-Turcotte (CPT) and MELD (or sodium-MELD). Fibrosis staging by liver stiffness: <6 kPa normal, >8 kPa indicates >=F3 advanced fibrosis, >12.5 kPa indicates F4 cirrhosis.

Alcohol withdrawal syndrome — alcohol withdrawal, delirium tremens, DTs, alcohol withdrawal delirium Delirium from other causes (infection, metabolic derangement) Sedative-hypnotic or benzodiazepine withdrawal Stimulant intoxication Thyroid storm Sepsis or central nervous system infection Wernicke encephalopathy Hepatic encephalopathy Validated withdrawal severity scale to guide symptom-triggered treatment Electrolytes including magnesium and phosphate, glucose, and renal function Liver function tests and full blood count Assessment for infection and other precipitants of delirium Thiamine status and evaluation for Wernicke encephalopathy Occurs on reduction or cessation of heavy, sustained alcohol use, with symptoms typically emerging within hours to a few days Early features include tremor, anxiety, agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension; insomnia and irritability are common Withdrawal seizures (typically generalised tonic-clonic) tend to occur early, usually within the first day or two Alcoholic hallucinosis produces hallucinations, often visual, with an otherwise clear sensorium, distinguishing it from delirium tremens Delirium tremens is a later, life-threatening complication with clouded consciousness, disorientation, severe autonomic hyperactivity, and hallucinations, usually appearing after a couple of days Management principles rest on benzodiazepine-based regimens, often symptom-triggered using a standardised withdrawal scale, in a supportive monitored setting Give thiamine before or with glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy, and correct fluid and electrolyte disturbances Assess withdrawal severity and complication risk with a validated instrument and identify high-risk patients for closer monitoring Delirium tremens with severe autonomic instability, a medical emergency with appreciable mortality if untreated Withdrawal seizures or status epilepticus Signs of Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) Hyperthermia, marked tachycardia, and haemodynamic instability Giving glucose before thiamine and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy Underestimating severity and under-dosing benzodiazepines in early withdrawal Attributing agitation solely to withdrawal while missing infection, bleeding, or metabolic causes Failing to identify patients at high risk of seizures or delirium tremens Not addressing underlying alcohol use disorder after acute treatment Chronic alcohol exposure enhances inhibitory gamma-aminobutyric acid signalling and suppresses excitatory glutamatergic (NMDA receptor) activity; the brain adapts by downregulating GABA and upregulating glutamate systems. When alcohol is withdrawn, this adaptation leaves a state of central nervous system hyperexcitability and autonomic overactivity, producing the tremor, seizures, and delirium of the withdrawal syndrome. Uncomplicated withdrawal usually resolves within several days with appropriate treatment. Delirium tremens carries significant mortality if unrecognised but is greatly reduced with timely benzodiazepine therapy and supportive care. Long-term prognosis depends on engagement with relapse prevention and treatment of alcohol use disorder.

Krabbe disease Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies Brainstem glioma (for adult brainstem-predominant presentations) Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating disease in adults GFAP gene sequencing as the definitive diagnostic test Brain and spinal cord MRI to identify characteristic white matter and brainstem patterns EEG in patients with seizures Developmental and neurocognitive assessment in children Historically brain biopsy demonstrating Rosenthal fibres, now rarely required A rare astrocytic leukodystrophy caused predominantly by de novo dominant mutations in the GFAP gene encoding glial fibrillary acidic protein The infantile form presents with macrocephaly, developmental delay or regression, seizures, and spasticity in the first years of life Juvenile and adult forms tend to present with bulbar and brainstem signs, ataxia, and spasticity, often with a more indolent course The pathological hallmark is widespread deposition of Rosenthal fibres, eosinophilic inclusions within astrocytes MRI often shows a frontal-predominant white matter abnormality with involvement of basal ganglia and brainstem, and characteristic patterns aid recognition Most cases arise from spontaneous mutations rather than inherited transmission, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis Adult-onset disease can mimic other conditions with prominent brainstem and cerebellar signs and may show tadpole-like atrophy of the medulla and cervical cord on imaging Genetic testing for GFAP mutations is the principal confirmatory investigation and has largely replaced biopsy Rapid developmental regression with seizures and progressive macrocephaly in an infant Progressive bulbar dysfunction threatening airway and swallowing safety Brainstem atrophy with respiratory or autonomic compromise Acute deterioration superimposed on a chronic course Excluding the diagnosis because there is no family history, despite the predominance of de novo mutations Misreading adult brainstem-predominant disease as a tumour or demyelinating disorder Overlooking the diagnostic value of characteristic MRI patterns Delaying genetic testing while pursuing invasive investigations Alexander disease is caused by gain-of-function mutations in GFAP, the gene for the main intermediate filament protein of astrocytes. Mutant protein accumulates and forms Rosenthal fibres within astrocytes, disturbing astrocyte function and secondarily impairing myelin maintenance, producing a leukodystrophy. The astrocytic dysfunction is considered the primary event, distinguishing this from disorders that primarily affect oligodendrocytes or myelin, and the distribution of pathology accounts for the frontal-predominant cerebral and brainstem clinical features. The infantile form generally carries the poorest prognosis with progressive deterioration over a few years, whereas juvenile and adult forms often follow a slower, more variable course; management remains supportive as no curative therapy exists.

ALG6-CDG (CDG type Ic) — ALG6 deficiency, dolichyl-P-Glc:Man9GlcNAc2-PP-dolichyl glucosyltransferase deficiency, CDG-Ic, ALG6 PMM2-CDG and other type 1 CDGs (shared transferrin screening pattern) Genetic/idiopathic epilepsy with developmental delay Mitochondrial disorders Inherited thrombophilias and bleeding disorders Congenital hypotonia of neuromuscular origin Congenital ichthyosis syndromes Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing/mass spectrometry (type 1 pattern) Lipid-linked oligosaccharide (LLO) analysis in fibroblasts ALG6 gene sequencing for confirmation Coagulation panel including antithrombin, protein C and protein S Brain MRI and EEG for epilepsy and structural anomalies Ophthalmological assessment for retinopathy Liver function and glucose monitoring Second most common type 1 CDG after PMM2-CDG, caused by biallelic ALG6 variants Generally milder than PMM2-CDG, with developmental delay, hypotonia and epilepsy predominating Cerebellar hypoplasia is typically less prominent than in PMM2-CDG Features may include failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and a coagulopathy with low antithrombin and protein C/S Some patients have retinopathy, deep vein thrombosis or ichthyosiform skin changes; virilisation/genital anomalies have been described Serum transferrin analysis shows a type 1 pattern reflecting loss of whole N-glycan chains at the assembly stage Definitive diagnosis rests on lipid-linked oligosaccharide analysis and ALG6 gene sequencing Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; no proven disease-modifying therapy exists Poorly controlled or status epilepticus in infancy Thromboembolic events including deep vein thrombosis Bleeding tendency complicating procedures Acute metabolic or systemic deterioration during intercurrent illness Progressive failure to thrive with feeding failure Stopping the workup at the transferrin screen without identifying the specific CDG subtype Neonatal or infection-related false transferrin patterns misleading interpretation Overlooking coagulation abnormalities before surgery or anticoagulation Assuming a benign course given the milder label and under-monitoring multisystem complications Missing retinopathy or thrombotic risk on long-term follow-up ALG6-CDG is a defect in the endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor used for N-glycosylation. The ALG6 enzyme is the dolichyl-phosphate glucosyltransferase that adds the first glucose residue to the Man9GlcNAc2 dolichol-linked structure. When this step is impaired, an incompletely glucosylated precursor is transferred less efficiently to nascent proteins, producing hypoglycosylation with loss of complete glycan chains and hence a type 1 serum transferrin pattern. As with other N-glycosylation defects the deficiency affects multiple organ systems, but the neurological phenotype tends to be less severe than PMM2-CDG. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The phenotype is generally milder than PMM2-CDG with better survival, but most patients have persisting intellectual disability, epilepsy and variable multisystem involvement.

Alkaptonuria — AKU, homogentisic aciduria, homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency, ochronosis Other causes of dark urine (haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, porphyria, drug effects) Tyrosinemia (other tyrosine pathway disorders) Osteoarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis for the arthropathy Exogenous ochronosis (e.g. from hydroquinone or phenol exposure) Degenerative disc and joint disease of other cause Urinary homogentisic acid quantification (diagnostic) Simple test of urine darkening on standing or alkalinisation Molecular testing of the HGD gene Imaging of the spine and large joints for ochronotic arthropathy and disc calcification Echocardiography for valvular involvement in adults Assessment for renal and prostate stones where indicated A rare autosomal recessive defect in tyrosine catabolism caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, allowing homogentisic acid to accumulate The classic and often earliest sign is urine that turns dark brown or black on standing or on alkalinisation, sometimes noticed as dark-staining nappies in infancy Ochronosis, the bluish-black pigmentation of connective tissue, becomes apparent in adulthood, notably in the ear cartilage and the sclerae A severe, early-onset degenerative arthropathy, particularly of the spine and large joints, is the major cause of morbidity Deposition of ochronotic pigment can also affect heart valves (aortic stenosis and valve calcification), cause pigmented renal and prostate stones, and stiffen tendons Diagnosis is confirmed by markedly elevated urinary homogentisic acid, and the disorder is usually benign in childhood with complications emerging over decades Management is largely symptomatic with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint care; nitisinone, which reduces homogentisic acid production, is being used to slow disease progression It is one of the original inborn errors of metabolism described by Garrod but is not a routine newborn screening target, being clinically mild early in life Symptomatic aortic valve stenosis or significant valve calcification requiring cardiac assessment Severe, disabling spinal or large-joint arthropathy Obstructing pigmented renal or prostatic stones Rapid functional decline from progressive joint destruction in adulthood Dismissing dark urine as a benign curiosity and missing the underlying diagnosis Attributing the arthropathy to ordinary osteoarthritis without recognising ochronosis Overlooking cardiac valve and renal stone complications during long-term follow-up Confusing endogenous ochronosis with exogenous pigmentation from topical or occupational exposure Alkaptonuria results from deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, an enzyme in the pathway that degrades tyrosine and phenylalanine. The block causes homogentisic acid to accumulate and be excreted in large amounts in urine, where it oxidises and polymerises to a dark pigment, explaining the darkening of urine. Over years, oxidised homogentisic acid deposits as ochronotic pigment in collagen-rich connective tissues, particularly cartilage, tendons, sclerae and heart valves. This pigment makes cartilage brittle and provokes a progressive degenerative arthropathy, and its deposition in other tissues underlies the cardiac, renal and cutaneous manifestations. Alkaptonuria is compatible with a normal lifespan and is largely asymptomatic in childhood, but progressive ochronotic arthropathy and, less often, cardiac and renal complications cause substantial disability in later adult life; disease-modifying therapy aims to slow this progression.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — ABPA, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergillus hypersensitivity Poorly controlled asthma without ABPA Cystic fibrosis exacerbation Eosinophilic pneumonia Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) Bronchiectasis of other cause Invasive or semi-invasive aspergillosis and aspergilloma Total serum IgE, which is characteristically very high and useful for monitoring Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG (precipitins) and skin testing for sensitisation Peripheral blood eosinophil count High-resolution CT to detect central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction Sputum examination for Aspergillus and eosinophils ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonising the airways, occurring almost exclusively in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis Suspect it in poorly controlled asthma with recurrent exacerbations, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, and expectoration of brownish mucus plugs Markedly elevated total serum IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG, with peripheral eosinophilia, support the diagnosis A positive immediate skin test or specific IgE to Aspergillus reflects the underlying sensitisation Imaging classically shows central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction, sometimes with transient infiltrates Treatment centres on suppressing the immune and inflammatory response with corticosteroids, with antifungal therapy used to reduce fungal burden in selected cases The disease evolves through stages including acute presentation, remission, exacerbation, and, if untreated, fibrotic end-stage lung disease It is a hypersensitivity phenomenon rather than tissue-invasive infection, distinguishing it from invasive aspergillosis and aspergilloma Progressive fixed airflow obstruction or fibrosis indicating advanced disease Frequent severe asthma exacerbations unresponsive to standard therapy Features suggesting invasive aspergillosis in an immunocompromised patient Massive mucoid impaction causing lobar collapse Mistaking ABPA for ordinary difficult asthma and missing the diagnosis Confusing this hypersensitivity condition with invasive aspergillosis and mismanaging treatment Failing to monitor total IgE to gauge disease activity and treatment response Overlooking ABPA as a treatable cause of bronchiectasis In predisposed patients, inhaled Aspergillus fumigatus spores germinate and persist within the viscid airway mucus rather than being cleared. Fungal antigens provoke a vigorous combined type I (IgE-mediated) and type III (immune-complex) hypersensitivity response, with strong Th2 activation, eosinophil recruitment, and high IgE production. The resulting intense airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and mucoid impaction damage the bronchial walls, leading to central bronchiectasis. Recurrent inflammatory episodes can ultimately produce fibrosis and irreversible loss of lung function. With early recognition and appropriate immunosuppressive treatment, exacerbations can be controlled and lung damage limited; however, repeated undertreated flares lead to progressive bronchiectasis and fibrosis with permanent loss of lung function, so long-term monitoring of symptoms and IgE is important.

medicamentosa from overuse of decongestant sprays Nasal polyps Structural causes such as deviated nasal septum Hormonal or drug-induced rhinitis Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to assess mucosa and exclude polyps Skin prick testing to identify causative allergens Serum allergen-specific IgE testing where skin testing is unsuitable Nasal smear for eosinophils in selected cases Assessment for coexisting asthma and sinus disease An IgE-mediated hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa presenting with sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, nasal itching and congestion Often classified as seasonal (pollen-driven) or perennial (dust mite, animal dander, mould), and by severity and effect on quality of life Commonly associated with allergic conjunctivitis, asthma and eczema as part of clinical, supported by skin prick testing or specific IgE assays to identify triggers Management principles begin with allergen avoidance and saline measures, then intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines according to severity Poorly controlled disease contributes to sinusitis, otitis media with effusion, sleep disturbance and reduced school or work performance Immunotherapy may be considered for confirmed single-allergen sensitivity that is inadequately controlled by standard therapy Unilateral nasal symptoms, bleeding or a mass suggesting a tumour or foreign body Progressive obstruction with facial pain and purulent discharge indicating complicated sinusitis Anosmia or orbital or visual symptoms requiring further evaluation Symptoms of poorly controlled coexisting asthma Missing coexisting asthma that needs concurrent treatment Encouraging prolonged use of topical decongestants leading to rebound rhinitis Attributing unilateral or bloodstained symptoms to allergy rather than investigating for tumour or foreign body Underusing intranasal corticosteroids, the most effective agents, in moderate to severe disease Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated inflammatory response of the nasal mucosa to inhaled allergens. On re-exposure, allergen cross-links IgE bound to mast cells, triggering an early-phase release of histamine and other mediators that produce sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea and congestion within minutes. A late-phase reaction, driven by recruited eosinophils, basophils and T cells, sustains mucosal inflammation and congestion hours later and heightens nasal reactivity. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema and hyperresponsiveness, and shared airway inflammation links the condition to asthma. Allergic rhinitis is generally a chronic but benign condition; with allergen avoidance and appropriate pharmacotherapy most patients achieve good symptom control, though it may persist for years and contribute to comorbidities.

Alopecia Areata — AA, patchy hair loss, alopecia totalis, alopecia universalis Tinea capitis (scaly, inflamed, often with broken hairs and positive mycology) Trichotillomania (irregular patches with hairs of varying length) Telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding rather than discrete patches) Traction alopecia at sites of chronic tension Early scarring alopecias such as lichen planopilaris or discoid lupus Secondary syphilis producing a moth-eaten pattern Usually a clinical diagnosis aided by dermoscopy showing exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots, and black dots Mycology (scrapings or culture) when tinea capitis cannot be excluded Thyroid function and autoantibody testing when clinically indicated Scalp biopsy reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases Screening for associated autoimmune disease guided by symptoms Presents as sudden, sharply bordered round or oval bald patches on otherwise normal-appearing scalp skin, without scarring or scale Look for exclamation-mark hairs at the margins of active patches, where the shaft narrows towards the scalp A positive hair-pull test at the periphery indicates ongoing disease activity Extensive forms include loss of all scalp hair (totalis) and loss of all body hair (universalis); the ophiasis pattern along the occipital and temporal rim tends to respond poorly Nail involvement such as fine regular pitting or roughening may accompany more severe or persistent disease Associations with thyroid disease, vitiligo, atopy, and other autoimmune conditions warrant a focused history and examination Regrowth often begins as fine depigmented or white hairs that later regain colour Management ranges from watchful waiting in limited disease to intralesional or topical anti-inflammatory therapy, contact immunotherapy, and newer targeted systemic agents for extensive involvement; psychological impact should be addressed directly Rapidly progressive or extensive loss suggesting evolution towards totalis or universalis Scarring, scale, or follicular destruction indicating a different, potentially permanent alopecia Significant psychological distress or impact on functioning requiring support Diffuse hair loss with systemic symptoms prompting evaluation for an underlying disorder Confusing non-scarring alopecia areata with a scarring alopecia and missing the window for treatment Overlooking tinea capitis in children by not performing mycology Attributing patchy loss to alopecia areata when hair-length variation points to trichotillomania Underestimating the psychological burden and failing to offer support or counselling Alopecia areata is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which the immune privilege of the hair follicle breaks down, allowing a T-cell-mediated attack focused on the anagen-phase follicular bulb. Interferon-gamma and other cytokines signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway drive a peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate classically likened to a swarm of bees. Affected follicles prematurely enter catagen and telogen and produce dystrophic hairs, but the follicular stem-cell compartment is preserved, which is why regrowth remains possible even after long-standing loss. A polygenic predisposition interacts with environmental triggers, and there is overlap with other autoimmune diseases. Outcome is variable and unpredictable; limited single patches frequently regrow spontaneously within months, whereas early onset, extensive involvement, the ophiasis pattern, nail changes, and atopy predict a more prolonged and relapsing course.

Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome — Alpers syndrome, Alpers disease, Progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood, POLG Other mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes Leigh syndrome Non-metabolic causes of intractable childhood epilepsy with regression Wilson disease and other metabolic liver diseases Acute viral or autoimmune hepatitis with encephalopathy Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis POLG molecular testing as the definitive diagnostic step Liver function tests with coagulation profile to detect synthetic hepatic failure EEG to characterise occipital and multifocal epileptiform activity Brain MRI looking for occipital, thalamic and cerebellar signal change and volume loss Cerebrospinal fluid protein and lactate Blood lactate and, where indicated, quantification of mitochondrial DNA content or muscle respiratory-chain enzymology The classic clinical triad is intractable epilepsy (often with epilepsia partialis continua), psychomotor regression and liver disease progressing to failure It is an autosomal recessive nuclear disorder caused by biallelic mutations in POLG, the gene for the catalytic subunit of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, leading to mitochondrial DNA depletion Sodium valproate must be avoided because it can precipitate or accelerate fulminant hepatic failure in POLG disease, and this warning applies whenever POLG is suspected before genetic confirmation Seizures are frequently occipital in onset, drug-resistant, and can evolve into status epilepticus Liver involvement may be present at onset or emerge later, sometimes only after valproate exposure, and includes microvesicular steatosis and eventual cirrhosis Cerebrospinal fluid protein is often raised, and MRI may show occipital and thalamic changes; EEG can show high-amplitude, low-frequency activity with polyspikes Management is supportive, targeting seizure control with mitochondria-sparing agents, nutritional and hepatic support, avoiding hepatotoxic and mitochondrial-toxic drugs Refractory seizures or status epilepticus, including epilepsia partialis continua Rising transaminases, coagulopathy or jaundice indicating hepatic failure Recent valproate exposure with clinical deterioration Rapid neurological regression or coma Giving sodium valproate for the epilepsy before excluding POLG disease, risking fatal hepatotoxicity Attributing the liver failure to the anticonvulsant alone and missing the underlying mitochondrial disorder Waiting for liver disease before considering the diagnosis, since hepatic involvement can be delayed Considering liver transplantation without recognising the systemic, progressive neurological disease Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is caused by recessive mutations in POLG, which encodes the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase gamma, the sole polymerase responsible for replicating and repairing mitochondrial DNA. Defective enzyme activity leads to quantitative depletion and qualitative errors of mitochondrial DNA, particularly in post-mitotic tissues with high energy demand such as neurons and hepatocytes. The resulting failure of oxidative phosphorylation causes progressive neuronal loss, spongiform change in grey matter and hepatocellular injury. Valproate further inhibits mitochondrial function and fatty acid oxidation, which explains its propensity to trigger catastrophic liver failure in these patients. Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is relentlessly progressive with a poor prognosis; most affected children deteriorate over months to a few years, and liver failure, often accelerated by valproate, is a major cause of death.

Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency — pulmonary/emphysema focus — A1AT deficiency, AAT deficiency, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, SERPINA1, PiZZ emphysema Usual smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Asthma with fixed airflow obstruction Bronchiectasis Other causes of basal lung disease Cystic fibrosis in younger patients Congenital lobar or bullous lung disease Serum alpha-1-antitrypsin level Alpha-1-antitrypsin phenotyping or SERPINA1 genotyping Pulmonary function tests demonstrating airflow obstruction and reduced gas transfer High-resolution chest computed tomography showing basal panacinar emphysema Liver function tests and hepatic assessment for associated liver disease Family screening and genetic counselling for relatives Suspect in emphysema presenting at a young age, in a never-smoker or light smoker, or with a strong family history The emphysema is classically panacinar and basal (lower-zone) predominant, in contrast to the upper-zone centrilobular pattern of typical smoking-related disease The severe deficiency genotype is most often PiZZ, and testing includes serum alpha-1-antitrypsin level with phenotyping or genotyping Smoking dramatically accelerates lung destruction, so smoking cessation is the single most important intervention Coexisting liver disease can occur because the abnormal Z protein polymerises and is retained within hepatocytes Intravenous augmentation therapy with pooled human alpha-1-antitrypsin is the specific disease-directed treatment for emphysema in suitable deficient patients All patients with COPD should be tested at least once, as recommended by guidelines, since the condition is under-recognised Rapidly declining lung function or frequent exacerbations Signs of chronic liver disease such as jaundice, ascites, or deranged synthetic function Continued smoking in a confirmed deficient patient Severe breathlessness or hypoxaemia indicating advanced emphysema Not testing for the deficiency in every patient diagnosed with COPD Attributing early or basal emphysema solely to smoking Overlooking coexisting liver disease Failing to offer family screening once an index case is identified Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor made in the liver that protects the lung from neutrophil elastase. In the common Z variant of SERPINA1, the abnormal protein misfolds and polymerises within hepatocytes, so little is secreted into the circulation. The resulting deficiency leaves the lung interstitium unprotected against elastase, particularly when neutrophil recruitment is amplified by cigarette smoke, leading to progressive destruction of alveolar walls and panacinar emphysema. Hepatic retention of the polymerised protein separately drives liver injury. Prognosis depends heavily on smoking status and baseline lung function; non-smokers may have near-normal life expectancy, whereas smokers with severe deficiency can develop disabling emphysema early, and augmentation therapy may slow the rate of lung tissue loss in selected patients.

The liver phenotype is highly variable: many PiZZ individuals never develop significant hepatic disease, while others progress to cirrhosis in childhood or adulthood with a raised risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Avoidance of smoking and alcohol, and liver transplantation for end-stage disease, substantially improve outcomes.

This enzyme cleaves terminal mannose residues during the ordered degradation of N-linked glycoproteins. Its deficiency causes accumulation of mannose-rich oligosaccharides within lysosomes throughout the body and their excretion in the urine. Storage affects the central nervous system, producing cognitive impairment; the inner ear, causing sensorineural deafness; the skeleton, causing dysostosis multiplex; and the immune system, contributing to recurrent infections. In the kidney, defective collagen disrupts the glomerular basement membrane, producing progressive nephritis with haematuria and eventual renal failure. The same collagen is present in basement membranes of the cochlea, and its abnormality is thought to impair the mechanical and metabolic environment of the organ of Corti, causing progressive high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Prognosis is dominated by the renal disease, which in more severe (often X-linked male) cases progresses to end-stage renal failure requiring dialysis or transplantation; the sensorineural hearing loss is progressive but manageable with amplification, and does not itself threaten life.

structural component of specialised basement membranes. Defective assembly of the collagen IV network weakens the glomerular basement membrane, which progressively thickens, thins, splits, and develops the characteristic basket-weave lamellation seen on electron microscopy. The abnormal membrane cannot maintain a normal filtration barrier, leading to haematuria, progressive proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and interstitial fibrosis. Because the same collagen chains are found in the cochlea and the lens and retina, the disorder also produces sensorineural hearing loss and ocular changes. Inheritance is most often X-linked, with autosomal recessive and dominant forms accounting for the remainder and influencing severity and sex distribution. In classic X-linked disease, affected males commonly progress to end-stage kidney disease by early to middle adulthood, whereas female carriers and some autosomal forms have a more variable and often milder course. Early renin-angiotensin blockade can delay progression. Transplantation is generally successful, though a small number of patients develop anti-GBM disease in the graft against the previously absent collagen antigen.
