Altitude Illness — Acute mountain sickness, AMS, High-altitude cerebral edema, HACE, High-altitude pulmonary edema, HAPE, Mountain sickness, Altitude sickness Exhaustion Dehydration Hypothermia Alcoholic hangover Hyponatremia Migraine Anxiety attack (for HAPE) Pneumonia (for HAPE) Pneumothorax (for HAPE) Pulmonary embolism (for HAPE) Respiratory tract infection / viral illness (HAPE historically misdiagnosed as viral pneumonia or as a viral illness in reentry HAPE) Pneumonia (HAPE radiographic opacities simulating pneumonic consolidation) Bacterial or Giardia enteric infection (high-altitude GI bloating/distension must be distinguished from infectious diarrhea) Clinical assessment with Lake Louise Scoring System (used chiefly for research uniformity) Pulse oximetry (oxygen saturation; arterial blood gas usually not necessary for HAPE) Chest radiography (patchy/localized opacities or streaky interstitial edema in HAPE; Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are NOT seen) Electrocardiography (may show right ventricular strain or hypertrophy in HAPE) Brain MRI (T2 signal change in white matter and splenium of corpus callosum confirmatory of HACE; hemosiderin deposits as footprints) Echocardiography (recommended when HAPE occurs below 3000 m or when predisposing cardiopulmonary abnormality is suspected) Lung ultrasound comet-tail/B-line scoring (sensitive but not specific for HAPE) Cardiogenic pulmonary edema / heart failure (HAPE was historically mistaken for heart failure) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (another noncardiogenic edema, but lung architecture is preserved in HAPE) Pulmonary embolism Pneumothorax Anxiety/panic attack Stroke or TIA unrelated to altitude illness Subarachnoid hemorrhage, transient global amnesia, delirium, cranial nerve palsy occurring at altitude outside altitude sickness Altitude illness encompasses a spectrum: acute mountain sickness (AMS, the benign form) and the two life-threatening forms, high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) (Harrison 22e p.3754). AMS is a clinical diagnosis presenting 6-12 h after ascent with nonspecific symptoms (headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness) and few physical findings; the Lake Louise Scoring System is used for research uniformity (Harrison 22e p.3755). AMS and HACE are viewed as opposite ends of one neurologic continuum; HACE (not AMS) is an encephalopathy whose hallmarks are ataxia and altered consciousness with diffuse cerebral involvement, typically without focal deficits, and progression can be rapid (Harrison 22e p.3755). The two most important risk factors for altitude illness are a rapid rate of ascent and a prior history of high-altitude illness; exertion is a risk factor, but lack of physical fitness is not (Harrison 22e p.3755). Illness is likely above 2500 m but has been documented at 1500-2500 m; in the Everest region about 50% of trekkers ascending above 4000 m over 5+ days develop AMS, rising to 84% with direct flight to 3860 m, whereas HACE and HAPE incidence is far lower (roughly 0.1-4%) (Harrison 22e p.3754). HAPE is primarily a pulmonary disorder and need not be preceded by AMS; it develops within 2-4 days of arrival and rarely after 4-5 days at the same altitude owing to vascular remodeling and adaptation (Harrison 22e p.3757). HAPE is a noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with normal pulmonary artery wedge pressure, driven by patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing regional overperfusion, capillary pressures above 18 mmHg, and capillary stress failure (Harrison 22e p.3757). Retinal hemorrhages are common at altitudes of 5000 m or more even without AMS/HACE symptoms; most resolve on descent, but macular hemorrhage can cause devastating, occasionally permanent visual loss (Harrison 22e p.3755, 3759). Gradual ascent with time for acclimatization is the best preventive measure; a conservative target above 3000 m is graded gain of no more than ~300 m per sleeping-altitude night with an extra acclimatization day every third day of gain (Harrison 22e p.3756). Sickle cell disease is one of the rare exposures in which altitude can provoke vaso-occlusive crisis, reported even at passes as low as 2500 m; thalassemia has not been linked to high-altitude problems (Harrison 22e p.3759). Hypertensive patients are not more prone to altitude illness, and most with well-controlled hypertension can be reassured that blood pressure stays relatively stable; antihypertensives should be continued at altitude (Harrison 22e p.3759). High-altitude cough can be severe enough to cause rib fracture above 5000 m; it is multifactorial (cold dry air plus hypoxia and respiratory water loss), and infection is generally not a common cause (Harrison 22e p.3758). Ataxia or altered consciousness (hallmarks of HACE) - mandates immediate descent Any hint of HAPE or HACE mandates descent Tachypnea and tachycardia at rest as HAPE progresses Blood-tinged sputum following a dry persistent cough Disproportionate fall in exercise tolerance, or fatigue/dyspnea at rest as the only initial HAPE signs Debilitating fatigue consistent with severe AMS on descent from a summit (important risk factor for death in mountaineers) Papilledema or retinal hemorrhages, especially macular hemorrhage with visual loss Worsening symptoms despite halting ascent Treating AMS as trivial - symptoms overlap with exhaustion, dehydration, hypothermia, hangover, and hyponatremia, and it can progress to life-threatening HACE. Relying on pulse oximetry alone to predict AMS during a trek - readings should not be used predictively unless guided by clinical signs. Assuming HAPE is always preceded by AMS - it is primarily pulmonary and may present without headache or nausea, sometimes only as fatigue and rest dyspnea. Misreading HAPE chest opacities as pneumonia (cold) or as heart failure - Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are absent in HAPE. Confusing sudden neurologic events (TIA, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cranial nerve palsy) at altitude with altitude illness - AMS evolves gradually whereas these typically occur suddenly. Mistaking reentry HAPE in returning highlanders for a viral illness. Injudicious prophylactic glucocorticoid use by climbers to boost performance - can be tragic owing to severe side effects, especially with prolonged use. Overhydration - adequate (not excessive) hydration is intended; potent diuretics such as furosemide should be avoided in HAPE. Comet-tail/B-line lung ultrasound is sensitive but not specific, since B-lines also appear in individuals who never develop clinical HAPE - clinical correlation is essential. Ascent lowers barometric pressure and thus the partial pressure of inspired oxygen, reducing the pressure gradient driving oxygen diffusion along the oxygen cascade. Hypobaric hypoxia is the central trigger for all forms of altitude illness. The normal struggle response is increased ventilation (the cornerstone of acclimatization) mediated by the carotid bodies; this can produce marked respiratory alkalosis (arterial pH may exceed 7.7 at extreme altitude) and dehydration, with alkalosis blunting ventilatory drive in sleep and causing periodic breathing and hypoxemia. Early acclimatization includes renal carbonic-anhydrase suppression with dilute alkaline urine to correct pH, plus increased sympathetic tone, rising erythropoietin/hemoglobin and red cell mass, greater tissue capillary density and mitochondrial numbers, and elevated 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Hypoxia-inducible factor governs transcriptional hypoxia responses; the EPAS1 gene (HIF-2alpha) and EGLN1/PPARA influence adaptation in Tibetan highlanders (lower hemoglobin than Han Chinese or Andeans). In AMS/HACE, raised intracranial pressure, increased sympathetic activity, relative hypoventilation, fluid retention/redistribution, and impaired gas exchange contribute; MRI evidence points to vasogenic (interstitial) cerebral edema, especially in the splenium of the corpus callosum, that may become cytotoxic in severe HACE, with hemosiderin deposits as long-lasting footprints. Impaired cerebral autoregulation with hypoxic vasodilation, altered blood-brain-barrier permeability via histamine, arachidonic acid, and VEGF, and venous outflow obstruction raising capillary pressure all promote edema. HAPE results from patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with regional overperfusion and capillary stress failure at normal wedge pressure; endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide availability and elevated endothelin-1, exaggerated sympathetic drive (pulmonary venoconstriction), and impaired transepithelial alveolar fluid clearance are implicated. Inflammation in HAPE is regarded as an epiphenomenon rather than the primary cause, although inflammatory/viral respiratory processes can predispose to it. AMS is benign and usually self-limited; once symptoms abate (with or without acetazolamide) the patient may reascend gradually. HACE and HAPE are life-threatening but generally reversible with prompt recognition and descent. In HAPE the lung architecture is typically well preserved with rapid reversibility (radiographic opacities can clear in about 2 days), allowing some patients to reascend slowly after a few days of descent and rest; after HACE, reascent within the same trip may be inadvisable. Severe AMS-related debilitating fatigue on descent is an important predictor of death in mountaineers, and macular hemorrhage can rarely cause permanent visual loss. HACE complicated by globus pallidus lesions has been reported to lead to parkinsonism. AMS is graded clinically as mild versus moderate, a subjective judgment based on headache severity and the presence/severity of nausea, fatigue, and dizziness (the Lake Louise Scoring System, without the sleep score, is used for research). The overall spectrum runs from benign AMS to the life-threatening forms HACE (neurologic, the severe end of the AMS-HACE continuum) and HAPE (pulmonary), which can coexist.

Preclinical biomarker changes may precede clinical symptoms by 20 years or more, creating a window for early treatment and prevention (Harrison 22e p.3476). Core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) are considered necessary and sufficient for biological diagnosis of AD under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria; tau PET is a core 2 biomarker used for staging (Harrison 22e p.3477). A negative amyloid PET scan in a patient with dementia makes an AD diagnosis unlikely; a positive scan can establish eligibility for amyloid-lowering therapy (Harrison 22e p.3477). Decreases in the CSF Abeta42/Abeta40 ratio and increases in p-Tau181 or p-Tau217 correlate with AD pathology; plasma biomarkers show high concordance with amyloid PET and are entering clinical use (Harrison 22e p.3477). ApoE epsilon4 is the most important genetic risk factor for sporadic AD: one allele raises risk ~2-3 fold (higher in women), two alleles raise it ~10-15 fold; each allele shifts onset ~10 years earlier (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3479-3480). Lecanemab (anti-Abeta protofibril) and donanemab (anti-pyroglutamate Abeta) are FDA-approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies for early-stage AD, showing ~22-27% slowing of clinical decline; restricted to MCI/mild dementia with biomarker-confirmed Abeta pathology (Harrison 22e p.3480-3481). Antiamyloid antibodies carry risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA-E edema, ARIA-H microhemorrhage/siderosis); risk rises with each ApoE epsilon4 allele and is highest in epsilon4 homozygotes, prompting an FDA box warning (Harrison 22e p.3481). Treatment with lecanemab or donanemab should be considered a contraindication to peripheral thrombolysis, as catastrophic multifocal hemorrhages and death have been reported when antiamyloid-treated patients received thrombolytics for stroke (Harrison 22e p.3482). Medications with strong anticholinergic effects (e.g., diphenhydramine sleep aids, oxybutynin) should be vigilantly avoided in AD (Harrison 22e p.3482). Typical symptomatic duration is 8-10 years (range 1-25 years); death often results from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, heart disease, or, most commonly, aspiration (Harrison 22e p.3476). Rapid progression over weeks to months with rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than AD (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482) Early prominent gait disturbance with mild memory loss suggests vascular dementia or normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.3476) Early focal seizure suggests a metastatic or primary brain neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.3476) Loss of joint position/vibration sense with Babinski signs suggests vitamin B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.3476) Stroke-like symptoms in a patient on anti-Abeta monoclonal antibody require immediate MRI to differentiate acute stroke from ARIA before any thrombolysis (Harrison 22e p.3482) Seizures (focal or generalized) can herald AD and occur even before dementia onset, especially in younger patients and autosomal dominant mutation carriers (Harrison 22e p.3476) Failing to exclude reversible/treatable mimics early in the course - vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and depression-related cognitive impairment should be excluded before attributing dementia to AD (Harrison 22e p.3476). A clinical diagnosis of AD is confirmed at autopsy only ~70-80% of the time; misdiagnoses are usually LATE (with or without hippocampal sclerosis), PART, Lewy body disease, vascular pathology, or FTLD (Harrison 22e p.3476). Amyloid PET positivity is not specific: ~25% of cognitively unimpaired older adults have positive scans, and a positive scan can reflect comorbid (incidental) AD pathology rather than the primary cause of impairment (Harrison 22e p.3476). A completely negative tau PET does not rule out early neurofibrillary pathology (Braak stages I-III) (Harrison 22e p.3477). Increased total tau in CSF is nonspecific - seen in AD but also other neurodegeneration (Harrison 22e p.3477). Plasma Abeta and p-Tau concentrations can be altered by comorbidities (reduced creatinine clearance, elevated BMI), causing false-positive or false-negative results near the threshold (Harrison 22e p.3477). ApoE epsilon4 is neither necessary nor sufficient to cause AD - many AD patients lack epsilon4 and many epsilon4 carriers never develop dementia (Harrison 22e p.3479-3480). Estrogen, statins, vitamin E, ginkgo biloba, and NSAIDs appeared protective in observational studies but did NOT show efficacy in randomized controlled trials; consumer 'memory-enhancing' supplements lack evidence (Harrison 22e p.3478, p.3482). Antipsychotics carry an FDA black box warning in elderly dementia patients (increased risk of death) and should be used with caution for neuropsychiatric symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3482). AD is characterized by extracellular neuritic plaques containing amyloid beta (Abeta) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) of hyperphosphorylated tau, with Abeta also accumulating in cortical and leptomeningeal blood vessel walls (amyloid angiopathy). Abeta is a 39-42 amino acid peptide cleaved from amyloid precursor protein (APP) by beta and gamma secretases; excess production of Abeta42 is a key initiator of cellular damage, and soluble oligomers are thought to be the early toxic species before fibril/plaque formation. Hyperphosphorylated tau can no longer stabilize microtubules and redistributes from axon to cytoplasm and dendrites, with prion-like templating proposed to drive tau spread. Earliest and most severe degeneration is in the medial temporal lobe (entorhinal/perirhinal cortex, hippocampus), inferolateral temporal cortex, and nucleus basalis of Meynert; atrophy spreads to temporoparietal and frontal cortices. Biochemically there is depletion of acetylcholine (degeneration of cholinergic nucleus basalis of Meynert neurons) plus noradrenergic and serotonergic loss from locus coeruleus and dorsal raphe. Genetic contributors include autosomal dominant mutations in APP (chromosome 21), PSEN-1 (chromosome 14, most common cause of early-onset familial AD), and PSEN-2 (chromosome 1), plus the ApoE epsilon4 risk allele (chromosome 19) and >40 minor GWAS risk variants in innate immunity, lipid metabolism, and synaptic pathways (e.g., CLU, PICALM, CR1, TREM2). (Harrison 22e p.3475, p.3478-3480) Typical duration of symptomatic AD is 8-10 years, with a course ranging from 1 to 25 years. Some patients decline steadily while others have prolonged plateaus. Late stages bring rigidity, mutism, incontinence, and a bedridden state with dependence for eating, dressing, and toileting; hyperactive tendon reflexes and myoclonic jerks may occur. Death most commonly results from aspiration, and also from malnutrition, secondary infections, pulmonary emboli, or heart disease. Approved disease-modifying antiamyloid antibodies slow but do not halt clinical decline (~22-27% slowing over the trial periods). (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3480-3481) Clinical staging is performed independent of biomarkers, based on functional impairment along a continuum: preclinical AD (biomarker evidence of amyloid pathology without symptoms) -> subjective cognitive decline -> mild cognitive impairment / early symptomatic AD (functionally compensated) -> dementia stages (early/middle/late/end-stage). Biological staging under the revised Alzheimer's Association criteria uses core 1 biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF/plasma Abeta and p-Tau) for diagnosis and tau PET (core 2) for biomarker-based disease staging. (Harrison 22e p.3476-3478)

Amblyopia — lazy eye, strabismic amblyopia, anisometropic amblyopia, deprivation amblyopia Uncorrected refractive error without amblyopia Structural ocular disease (e.g. optic nerve or macular pathology) causing reduced vision Retinoblastoma or other intraocular tumour presenting with poor vision Cortical visual impairment Functional (non-organic) visual loss Age-appropriate best-corrected visual acuity testing, ideally with crowded (linear) optotypes Cycloplegic refraction to detect anisometropia or significant refractive error Cover testing and motility assessment to detect associated strabismus Dilated fundus and media examination to exclude a structural or deprivational cause Amblyopia is reduced best-corrected visual acuity in one or both eyes due to abnormal visual development, in the absence of a structural cause that fully explains the deficit The main types are strabismic (from ocular misalignment), anisometropic or refractive (from unequal or high refractive error), and stimulus deprivation (from media opacity such as congenital cataract or ptosis) It develops only during the sensitive period of visual development in early childhood, which is why early detection through vision screening is critical It is usually unilateral but can be bilateral, for example with high symmetrical refractive error or bilateral media opacity A crowding phenomenon is characteristic, with worse acuity for lines of letters than for single optotypes Deprivation amblyopia from causes such as congenital cataract is the most severe and least responsive type and needs urgent treatment Management is to correct any refractive error and to treat the underlying cause, then to encourage use of the amblyopic eye with occlusion (patching) or pharmacological penalisation of the better eye Treatment is most effective when started young; response diminishes with increasing age although some improvement can still occur in older children An identifiable structural lesion (e.g. cataract, retinoblastoma, optic nerve disease) that could account for reduced vision and must not be attributed to amblyopia alone Deprivation amblyopia from congenital cataract or dense media opacity requiring urgent intervention Failure of vision to improve with adequate treatment, prompting re-evaluation for organic pathology Poor vision persisting beyond the sensitive period with no prior treatment Diagnosing amblyopia without excluding a structural cause of visual loss Delaying treatment beyond the sensitive period when response is greatly reduced Failing to prescribe full refractive correction before or alongside occlusion therapy Poor compliance with patching leading to treatment failure or reverse amblyopia in the occluded eye Amblyopia results from abnormal visual experience during the critical period of cortical visual development. When the two eyes receive unequal or degraded input (from misalignment, unequal refractive error, or media opacity), competitive cortical mechanisms favour the better eye and suppress the input from the affected eye. This leads to persistent cortical under-development of that eye's pathway and reduced acuity that is not correctable by optical means alone once the sensitive period has passed, though it remains treatable if addressed early. The prognosis depends on the type of amblyopia and the age at which treatment begins; anisometropic and strabismic amblyopia treated early in childhood often recover good acuity, whereas deprivation amblyopia and late-treated cases have a more guarded outcome. Untreated amblyopia results in lifelong reduced vision in the affected eye and vulnerability if the better eye is later lost.

Amniotic Fluid Embolism — amniotic fluid embolism, AFE, anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy Pulmonary thromboembolism Eclampsia Haemorrhagic shock from obstetric haemorrhage Anaphylaxis to drugs administered peripartum Myocardial infarction or peripartum cardiomyopathy Septic shock High neuraxial block or local anaesthetic toxicity Air or venous embolism Arterial blood gases to quantify hypoxaemia and acidosis Full blood count and urgent coagulation studies including fibrinogen to confirm and monitor DIC Cross-match and activation of a massive transfusion pathway Electrocardiogram and echocardiography where feasible to assess right and left ventricular function Continuous haemodynamic and oxygen saturation monitoring Investigations principally to exclude alternative diagnoses, as no specific confirmatory test exists Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare, unpredictable, and catastrophic obstetric emergency in which entry of amniotic fluid and fetal material into the maternal circulation triggers sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and coagulopathy The classic presentation is abrupt hypoxia, hypotension or cardiac arrest, and disseminated intravascular coagulation occurring during labour, delivery, or the immediate postpartum period Premonitory features may include breathlessness, chest pain, agitation, a sense of impending doom, and altered mental state before collapse It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion made on the characteristic sudden presentation; no confirmatory test exists in the acute setting Management is supportive and immediate: high-quality resuscitation, airway and oxygenation support, circulatory support, and aggressive correction of coagulopathy with blood products If maternal cardiac arrest occurs undelivered, perimortem caesarean delivery is undertaken promptly to aid maternal resuscitation and salvage the fetus Because coagulopathy is often severe and early, activation of a massive transfusion protocol and involvement of haematology are key Risk associations include advanced maternal age, multiparity, placental abnormalities, operative delivery, and induction of labour, though the condition is essentially unpreventable Care is best delivered by a rapidly assembled multidisciplinary team including obstetrics, anaesthesia, intensive care, and haematology OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: sudden peripartum cardiorespiratory collapse or cardiac arrest requiring immediate resuscitation Rapid-onset severe hypoxia and hypotension during or just after delivery Disseminated intravascular coagulation with uncontrolled haemorrhage Maternal cardiac arrest with an undelivered fetus mandating perimortem caesarean delivery Premonitory breathlessness, agitation, or sense of impending doom preceding collapse Delaying resuscitation while seeking a confirmatory test that does not exist Underestimating the speed and severity of the coagulopathy and transfusing too late Failing to perform timely perimortem caesarean delivery during maternal arrest Anchoring on pulmonary embolism or haemorrhage and missing the diagnosis Not mobilising a full multidisciplinary team early in the event Amniotic fluid and fetal cellular debris gain access to the maternal circulation, usually through breaches in the uteroplacental interface or endocervical veins. Rather than simple mechanical embolic obstruction, the syndrome is thought to reflect an abnormal host response resembling anaphylaxis and systemic inflammatory activation. This provokes intense pulmonary vasoconstriction and acute right ventricular failure, causing profound hypoxaemia and cardiovascular collapse, often followed by left ventricular dysfunction. Simultaneous activation of the coagulation cascade produces rapid, severe disseminated intravascular coagulation with consumption of clotting factors and life-threatening haemorrhage. Amniotic fluid embolism carries high maternal mortality and a substantial risk of permanent neurological injury among survivors, with outcome strongly dependent on the speed and quality of resuscitation. Perinatal outcome is likewise poor when collapse occurs before delivery. Prompt recognition, immediate resuscitation, perimortem delivery when indicated, and early correction of coagulopathy improve survival, and recent outcomes have improved with organised team-based care.

Amoebiasis (Intestinal) — Entamoeba histolytica infection, amebic dysentery Bacterial dysentery / inflammatory diarrhea (Campylobacter, enteroinvasive E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella, Vibrio) Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease) Carcinoma of the colon (especially when an ameboma mass is present) Acute appendicitis (with cecal involvement) Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) Campylobacter colitis Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli infection Salmonella enterocolitis Vibrio enteritis Examination of at least three fresh stool specimens (wet mount, iodine-stained concentrate, trichrome-stained preparation) for cysts/trophozoites Stool test for occult blood (heme) and microscopy for neutrophils Stool antigen detection assay (monoclonal anti-Gal/GalNAc lectin enzyme immunoassay) Stool multiplex PCR / nucleic acid amplification for GI protozoa Serology (ELISA / indirect hemagglutination) for invasive amebiasis Sigmoidoscopy with biopsy of the edge of ulcers if stool studies negative (avoid in fulminant colitis) Biopsy of a colonic mass to confirm ameboma and exclude carcinoma Stool culture for bacterial pathogens to exclude bacterial dysentery Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis / Crohn disease) Colonic carcinoma (mimicked by ameboma on barium studies) Acute appendicitis Amebiasis is infection with Entamoeba histolytica, an intestinal protozoan; ~90% of infections are asymptomatic cyst passage and only ~10% are invasive (p.1753). Symptomatic amebic colitis develops 2-6 weeks after ingestion of infectious cysts, with gradual-onset lower abdominal pain and mild diarrhea progressing to malaise, weight loss, and dysentery (p.1755). In full-blown dysentery patients may pass 10-12 stools per day consisting mainly of blood and mucus with little fecal material; virtually all have heme-positive stools (p.1755). In contrast to bacterial diarrhea, fewer than 40% of patients with amebic dysentery are febrile and stools show a paucity of neutrophils (p.1755). Cecal involvement may mimic acute appendicitis (p.1755). Definitive diagnosis of amebic colitis requires demonstration of hematophagous (erythrocyte-ingesting) trophozoites of E. histolytica; this is the only way microscopy can identify the species (p.1756). Because trophozoites are rapidly killed by water, drying, or barium, at least three fresh stool specimens should be examined; wet mounts, iodine-stained concentrates, and trichrome-stained preparations confirm diagnosis in 75-95% of cases (p.1756). Stool antigen detection (Gal/GalNAc lectin EIA, sensitivity 87%, specificity >90%) and multiplex PCR (sensitivity/specificity approaching 100%) are more sensitive, specific, and rapid than microscopy (p.1757). Serology (ELISA) is positive in >90% of cases of colitis, ameboma, or liver abscess; results usually revert to negative within 6-12 months, so positivity with a compatible syndrome suggests active disease (p.1756). E. histolytica infection is widespread in the Indian subcontinent, Africa, parts of East Asia, and Central/South America, often affecting children under 5 in areas of poor sanitation; in developed countries returning travelers, immigrants, MSM, military personnel, and institutional inmates are the main at-risk groups (p.1753). Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1757). Fulminant intestinal infection with severe abdominal pain, high fever, and profuse diarrhea (rare; predominantly in children) Toxic megacolon with severe bowel dilation and intramural air Full-thickness necrosis and bowel perforation Patients receiving glucocorticoids are at risk for severe amebiasis E. histolytica cannot be distinguished microscopically from the non-pathogenic commensal E. dispar (nor from E. moshkovskii or E. bangladeshi); most asymptomatic carriers actually harbor E. dispar, which is incapable of invasive disease and does not warrant treatment, so species-specific antigen detection or PCR is needed (p.1754, p.1756). Cysts must also be differentiated from non-pathogenic Entamoeba hartmanni, Entamoeba coli, and Endolimax nana, which do not cause disease (p.1756). Amebiasis must be excluded before starting glucocorticoid therapy for suspected inflammatory bowel disease; unsuspected amebiasis treated with steroids can precipitate severe colitis or toxic megacolon (p.1755-1757). An ameboma can be mistaken for cancer on barium studies; positive serology or biopsy can prevent unnecessary surgery (p.1755). Sigmoidoscopy/biopsy and barium studies are dangerous during fulminant or acute colitis because of the risk of perforation (p.1756-1757). Trophozoites are rapidly killed by water, drying, and barium and may be confused with neutrophils, so examination must use multiple fresh specimens with experienced microscopy (p.1756). E. histolytica is acquired by ingesting viable cysts from fecally contaminated water, food, or hands (food-borne exposure being most common). Motile trophozoites excyst in the small intestine; in most patients they remain as harmless commensals in the large bowel and re-encyst, shedding infectious cysts in stool. In some patients trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa (causing colitis) or enter the portal bloodstream (causing distant abscesses, most often hepatic). Trophozoites attach to colonic mucus and epithelium via the Gal/GalNAc adherence lectin and release glycosidases, proteases, and cysteine proteinases that degrade mucus, collagen, elastin, immunoglobulins, and complement anaphylatoxins; mucosal damage follows via contact-dependent cytotoxicity (apoptosis, trogocytosis, lysis of inflammatory and epithelial cells) and contact-independent mechanisms (inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandin E2). Resistance to reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and to complement-mediated lysis are virulence factors. The earliest lesions are mucosal microulcerations of the cecum, sigmoid, or rectum; submucosal extension beneath viable surface mucosa produces the classic 'flask-shaped' ulcer with trophozoites at the margins. Human infection is notable for a paucity of inflammatory cells (in part because trophozoites kill neutrophils) (p.1753-1755). Outcome relates to the clinical syndrome: about 90% of infections are asymptomatic and self-limited, and uncomplicated amebic colitis responds well to therapy with ulcers characteristically healing with little or no scarring. Fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, and perforation are rare but carry a poor prognosis. Treated colitis generally resolves, but severe disease (notably in those given glucocorticoids or in children with fulminant infection) markedly worsens outcome (p.1755-1756). Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading scheme: (1) asymptomatic cyst passage (~90% of infections); (2) symptomatic amebic colitis/dysentery with bloody mucoid stools; and (3) rare fulminant intestinal infection (severe pain, high fever, profuse diarrhea, predominantly in children) that may progress to toxic megacolon, full-thickness necrosis, or perforation (p.1753, p.1755).

Amputation care and rehabilitation — amputee rehabilitation, residual limb management, prosthetic rehabilitation, post-amputation care Residual limb wound infection or dehiscence Ischaemia of the residual limb requiring revision to a higher level Neuroma causing focal residual limb pain Phantom limb pain Heterotopic ossification in the residual limb Contralateral limb ischaemia or ulceration Vascular assessment to evaluate healing potential and select amputation level Wound and skin inspection with monitoring for infection and pressure areas from the socket Assessment of proximal joint range of motion and strength for prosthetic candidacy Imaging of the residual limb where neuroma, bony spur, or heterotopic ossification is suspected Cardiopulmonary and functional evaluation to inform realistic mobility goals Amputation rehabilitation is a continuum spanning preoperative counselling, surgical level selection, postoperative residual limb care, prosthetic prescription and training, and long-term follow-up The surgical level is chosen to balance healing potential against function, with more distal levels generally allowing better function and lower energy cost of walking Early postoperative care focuses on wound healing, oedema control with compression or rigid dressings, residual limb shaping, and prevention of contracture through positioning and stretching Preventing hip and knee flexion contractures is essential, as these can prevent successful prosthetic fitting and mobility Distinguish and manage the different pain types that occur, including surgical wound pain, residual limb pain from causes such as neuroma, and phantom limb pain Prosthetic prescription is individualised to the patient's level, goals, cognition, cardiovascular fitness, and skin condition, and requires ongoing socket fit review as the limb volume changes The energy expenditure of walking rises with more proximal amputation and with bilateral or dysvascular amputations, which must be considered when setting mobility goals Ongoing skin surveillance of the residual limb and the contralateral limb is vital, particularly in patients with diabetes or peripheral vascular disease who are at risk of further amputation Psychological support and addressing body image, mood, and social reintegration are integral to successful rehabilitation Signs of residual limb infection, wound dehiscence, or systemic sepsis Critical ischaemia of the residual or contralateral limb New non-healing ulcer on the remaining foot in a diabetic or vascular patient Rapidly worsening pain suggesting deep infection or ischaemia Severe mood disturbance or suicidal ideation after limb loss Allowing flexion contractures to develop through poor positioning, jeopardising prosthetic fitting Fitting a prosthesis before the wound has healed or the limb volume has stabilised Neglecting the contralateral limb in patients at high risk of further amputation Failing to distinguish and treat the different sources of residual and phantom pain Setting unrealistic mobility goals without accounting for the raised energy cost of walking Most amputations in adults result from complications of peripheral vascular disease and diabetes, with trauma, malignancy, and infection accounting for others. After surgery the residual limb undergoes healing, oedema resolution, and progressive volume reduction and reshaping over weeks to months. Loss of the limb alters biomechanics and substantially increases the metabolic cost of locomotion, while neural changes from severed nerves and central reorganisation give rise to phantom phenomena and neuroma-related pain. Successful prosthetic use depends on a well-healed, appropriately shaped, and pain-free residual limb with adequate proximal joint mobility and strength. Functional outcome depends on amputation level, cause, age, comorbidity, and the state of the contralateral limb. Younger traumatic amputees often achieve high levels of prosthetic function, whereas older dysvascular patients, especially with bilateral or proximal amputations, may have limited walking potential and rely more on wheelchair mobility. Diligent skin care and vascular risk management are key to preventing further amputation.

Amyloidosis — AL amyloidosis, ATTR amyloidosis, AA amyloidosis Multiple myeloma and other plasma cell dyscrasias (AL arises from the same clonal disorder) Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) and smoldering myeloma Hypertensive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (vs amyloid cardiomyopathy) Other causes of nephrotic syndrome / proteinuric renal disease Other causes of length-dependent peripheral and autonomic neuropathy AA amyloidosis is driven by chronic infections such as tuberculosis, osteomyelitis, or subacute bacterial endocarditis, which may be the presenting or underlying illness Congo red staining of aspirated abdominal subcutaneous fat (positive in >80%); if negative, biopsy of involved organ (kidney, heart, liver, tongue, GI tract) Amyloid typing: laser-capture microdissection with tandem mass spectrometry is the diagnostic standard (sensitivity ~88%, specificity ~96%); immunoelectron microscopy more reliable than immunohistochemistry Serum/urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) and nephelometric serum free light chain assay with kappa/lambda ratio (>90% of AL patients have a detectable monoclonal light chain) Bone marrow examination for clonal plasma cells (kappa/lambda clonality by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or in situ hybridization) Cardiac biomarkers NT-proBNP/BNP and troponin for staging, prognosis, and disease monitoring; ECG (low voltage, pseudo-infarct pattern) and echocardiography (concentric thickening, diastolic dysfunction, abnormal global longitudinal strain) Cardiac MRI showing increased wall thickness and characteristic delayed subendocardial gadolinium enhancement DNA/gene sequencing for hereditary (TTR and other AF) mutations CT imaging plus serologic/microbiologic studies in AA disease to identify underlying tumor, inflammation, or infection Electron microscopy of paraformaldehyde-fixed tissue to visualize 10-nm fibrils Hypertensive concentric left ventricular hypertrophy mimicking amyloid cardiomyopathy Hereditary (AF) amyloidoses from variant fibrinogen, lysozyme, gelsolin, or apolipoproteins can clinically mimic AL disease Idiopathic or other axonal/autonomic neuropathies mimicking ATTR neuropathy Amyloidosis is a group of protein-misfolding disorders defined by extracellular deposition of insoluble polymeric protein fibrils with a common antiparallel beta-pleated-sheet structure; nomenclature is AX, where A = amyloidosis and X = the fibril precursor protein (p.895). AL amyloidosis (formerly primary systemic amyloidosis) is composed of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains from a clonal B-cell/plasma-cell disorder and is the most common systemic type in North America; it can occur with myeloma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (p.895, p.897). In AL amyloidosis the kidneys are involved in 60-70% (proteinuria, often nephrotic range, with hypoalbuminemia) and the heart in 70-80%; cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death (p.897). Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic signs of AL amyloidosis but each is seen in only about 10% of patients (p.897). Easy bruising in AL amyloidosis is due to amyloid deposits in capillaries or to acquired factor X deficiency from binding of factor X to amyloid fibrils (p.897). ATTR amyloidosis is the most prevalent hereditary amyloidosis and derives from wild-type or mutated transthyretin (TTR); it targets the peripheral and autonomic nerves and the heart (p.895, p.899). The TTR variant V122I occurs in nearly 4% of African-American and Afro-Caribbean populations and causes late-onset cardiac amyloidosis; suspect it in African-American patients with concentric cardiac hypertrophy and diastolic heart failure, especially without hypertension or valvular disease (p.899). Wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt, formerly senile systemic amyloidosis) is a disease of aging, not inheritance; it predominates in men from the seventh decade and is found at autopsy in 25% of hearts of men >=80 years, and is now the most prevalent and fastest-growing form of amyloidosis worldwide (p.899). Carpal tunnel syndrome, tendinopathy, and spinal stenosis (soft-tissue disease) can precede ATTR nerve or heart disease by one to two decades, and ATTRwt patients frequently report bicipital, patellar, or Achilles tendon rupture (p.899). AA amyloidosis arises from the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA) in chronic inflammatory or infectious disease and typically begins in the kidneys; cardiomyopathy is a late manifestation in about 10-25% (p.895, p.899). Abdominal subcutaneous fat aspiration is the most accessible diagnostic tissue, positive in >80% of systemic amyloidosis, avoiding surgical biopsy (p.895). Amyloid deposits show characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light when stained with Congo red, whereas other regular protein structures such as collagen appear white (p.895). Macroglossia or periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses (pathognomonic of AL) Concentric ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction plus low-voltage ECG (voltage-mass mismatch) Easy bruising or bleeding diathesis from acquired factor X deficiency Multisystem involvement (unexplained nephropathy, cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, enteropathy) in a patient with fatigue/weight loss Serum albumin <2 g/dL with pedal edema or anasarca from nephrotic-range proteinuria Atrial contractile dysfunction even in sinus rhythm, with risk of atrial thrombi and thromboembolism Amyloid typing pitfall: commercial immunohistochemistry antibodies may be inaccurate and some AL deposits bind light-chain antibodies nonspecifically; accurate typing (mass spectrometry / immunoelectron microscopy / genetic testing) is essential because therapy differs by type (p.895, p.899). Serum and urine protein electrophoresis are NOT useful screening tests for AL because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce a detectable M-spike; immunofixation and free light chain assays are required (p.897). A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; conversely, AF carriers may have a coincidental monoclonal gammopathy, so screen for BOTH plasma-cell disorder and protein mutations (p.897, p.899). Renal insufficiency can falsely elevate cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP, troponin) and nonspecifically raise both free light chain isotypes, so the free light chain ratio (not just absolute level) must be examined (p.896, p.897). In amyloid cardiomyopathy digitalis, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers are relatively contraindicated because they interact with amyloid fibrils and can cause heart block and worsening heart failure (p.899). Interstitial (rather than glomerular) renal amyloid can cause azotemia WITHOUT proteinuria (p.897). Apparent sporadic ATTRv (no family history) often reflects incomplete penetrance rather than a true spontaneous case (p.899). Mass spectrometry detects amino-acid sequence variation but does not definitively identify specific protein variants; DNA sequencing is the standard for hereditary (AF) mutations (p.899). Genetic mutation, abnormal processing, or aging-related decline in protein quality control causes precursor proteins to undergo reversible unfolding/misfolding. Misfolded subunits adopt a common antiparallel beta-pleated-sheet conformation and assemble into oligomers, higher-order polymers, and ultimately 10-nm fibrils that deposit extracellularly in tissues/organs. Soluble oligomeric intermediates are thought to be the most toxic species (generating reactive oxygen species and stress signaling), while fibrillar deposits mechanically interfere with organ function. Fibrils co-deposit accessory molecules including serum amyloid P component, apolipoproteins E and A-IV, glycosaminoglycans, and metal ions. Precursors include monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL; lambda subtypes predominate), transthyretin (ATTR; wild-type or >130 described mutations), and the hepatic acute-phase protein serum amyloid A (AA) (p.895, p.897, p.899). AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive; historically untreated median survival was only ~1-2 years, but outcomes have improved markedly over four decades with newer plasma-cell-directed therapy. Cardiac stage (Mayo system based on NT-proBNP and troponin) is the strongest determinant of management and survival; very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts better outcome regardless of cardiac stage. High-risk patients (~15-20%) with advanced cardiac stage IIIb or NYHA III-IV heart failure are largely excluded from trials. ATTR cardiac disease is better tolerated than AL: untreated median survival from heart failure presentation is ~42-48 months for ATTR versus ~6 months for AL. Untreated ATTR survival after onset ranges 4-15 years depending on predominant cardiac versus neurologic involvement (p.897, p.899). AL amyloidosis is staged primarily by the Mayo 2004 cardiac staging system (NT-proBNP and cardiac troponins), modified by European investigators to identify very-high-risk patients; the Mayo 2012 revision adds clonal burden via dFLC (difference between involved and uninvolved free light chains). A Boston University system uses BNP and troponin I. A separate renal staging system based on 24-h urine protein and eGFR predicts progression to dialysis at 2 years. ATTR cardiac involvement is graded by stage (e.g., advanced stage IIIb) and NYHA functional class (p.897).

Amyloidosis and Other Restrictive Cardiomyopathies — Cardiac amyloidosis, Restrictive cardiomyopathy, RCM, AL amyloid cardiomyopathy, Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, ATTR cardiomyopathy, ATTRwt, ATTRv Constrictive pericardial disease (the classic and most important differential, sharing dominant right-sided failure, edema, ascites, elevated JVP and Kussmaul sign; echocardiography readily distinguishes the two today) (Harrison 22e p.2020-2022) Hypertensive heart disease (usually shows LVH on ECG and requires years of severe uncontrolled hypertension to reach amyloid-degree wall thickening) (Harrison 22e p.2021) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (rarely presents with peripheral edema and usually has LVH on ECG; distinction from amyloidosis is usually fairly clear) (Harrison 22e p.2021) Fabry disease and other infiltrative cardiomyopathies (may have typical skin manifestations and usually LVH on ECG) (Harrison 22e p.2021-2022) Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (echocardiographic appearance can mimic amyloidosis but with distinct noncardiac features such as maternally inherited diabetes, deafness, and recurrent strokes) (Harrison 22e p.2022) Advanced diabetic heart disease with heavy proteinuria (obvious diabetes history and echocardiogram lacking amyloid features) (Harrison 22e p.2022) Echocardiography showing increased LV wall thickness without dilation, frequent biatrial enlargement, increased RV free-wall thickness, restrictive diastolic filling pattern, and a small transmitral A wave (the latter associated with increased thromboembolic risk) (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023) Longitudinal strain imaging demonstrating apical-sparing 'bull's-eye' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023) Cardiac magnetic resonance with extracellular volume measurement, abnormal myocardial nulling, and extensive late gadolinium enhancement (Harrison 22e p.2023-2024) Bone-avid radionuclide imaging (technetium PYP, DPD, or HMDP) with SPECT and ideally cardiac CT to confirm myocardial rather than blood-pool uptake (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026) Serum free light chains plus serum and urine protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect or exclude a plasma cell dyscrasia (immunofixation is more sensitive than electrophoresis for the low paraprotein levels of AL amyloidosis) (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026) Tissue biopsy (subcutaneous fat pad aspirate or deep-skin biopsy first; endomyocardial biopsy if needed, positive in well over 90% of cardiac amyloid cases) with amyloid typing ideally by mass spectrometry (Harrison 22e p.2024-2026) TTR gene sequencing to distinguish familial (variant) from wild-type TTR when AL is not clearly established (Harrison 22e p.2026) NT-proBNP (often disproportionately high for the degree of heart failure, frequently 1000-2000 pg/mL even with mild symptoms) and high-sensitivity troponin (frequently mildly elevated, risking misdiagnosis as ischemic disease) (Harrison 22e p.2023-2024) ECG, which may show abnormally low voltage (particularly in AL) though not invariably (Harrison 22e p.2022) Constrictive pericarditis Hypertensive heart disease with left ventricular hypertrophy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (including sarcomere-variant forme fruste presenting as RCM) Fabry disease and other infiltrative or storage cardiomyopathies Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy Hemochromatosis (iron storage) Restrictive cardiomyopathy is dominated by abnormal diastolic function in a noncompliant ventricle with usually only mildly reduced contractility; ejection fraction is often 30-50% and both atria are typically enlarged, sometimes massively (Harrison 22e p.2020). Despite biventricular elevation of filling pressures, restrictive disease and cardiac amyloidosis tend to present with predominantly right-sided symptoms such as peripheral edema, abdominal discomfort, and ascites (Harrison 22e p.2020-2021). In sinus rhythm a fourth heart sound is more typical than a third in RCM generally, but in cardiac amyloidosis both an S3 and an S4 are unusual because restrictive physiology impairs relaxation and the infiltrated atrium generates little contractile pressure; jugular venous pressure is elevated and may rise paradoxically on inspiration (positive Kussmaul sign) (Harrison 22e p.2020-2021). The two precursor proteins causing most cardiac amyloidosis are transthyretin (TTR, produced in the liver) and light chains (produced by abnormal plasma cells); precise typing of the precursor is essential because therapy is type-specific and incorrect typing leads to inappropriate treatment (Harrison 22e p.2020). Periorbital purpura is virtually pathognomonic of AL amyloidosis (occurring in about 20-30% of cases) and macroglossia occurs in roughly 10%; an unusually hard liver may reflect amyloid hepatic infiltration, which occurs in AL but not TTR amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2021). A history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or a ruptured biceps tendon — often 5-8 years before heart failure — points toward TTR amyloidosis, reflecting TTR's predilection for ligaments and tendons (Harrison 22e p.2021-2022). Longitudinal strain imaging classically shows relatively preserved apical strain with severely impaired basal strain, producing a 'bull's-eye' color pattern highly suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023). On cardiac MRI, abnormal nulling of the myocardium with poor myocardium-to-cavity distinction plus extensive transmural late gadolinium enhancement and markedly increased extracellular volume are near-pathognomonic of amyloid infiltration (Harrison 22e p.2022-2024). Bone-avid tracers (technetium pyrophosphate/PYP, DPD, HMDP) are normally not taken up by the heart but show avid myocardial uptake in TTR amyloidosis; a positive scan with a negative plasma cell dyscrasia workup confirms TTR amyloidosis without biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026). In the United States the most common variant causing TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy is Val122Ile, present in about 3.5% of people of African descent, presenting as a late-onset restrictive cardiomyopathy usually from the seventh decade with incomplete penetrance (Harrison 22e p.2022). Wild-type TTR amyloidosis (ATTRwt) is now considered the most common form of amyloidosis, affecting predominantly older men (men roughly 20 times more likely than women); the heart is usually the sole clinically involved organ, though lung and gut deposits are often found histologically (Harrison 22e p.2022). Atrial arrhythmia, especially atrial fibrillation or flutter, is a common presenting feature (particularly in TTR amyloidosis) and its onset often precipitates or worsens heart failure; refractory atrial arrhythmia in a patient in the mid-60s or older without other cause should raise suspicion for TTR cardiac amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2021-2027). Heart failure with a thick left ventricle but without a history of severe hypertension and without LVH on ECG Disproportionately elevated NT-proBNP relative to clinical heart failure severity Periorbital purpura or macroglossia (suggesting AL amyloidosis) Refractory atrial fibrillation/flutter in a patient in the mid-60s or older without other cause (suggesting TTR amyloidosis) Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or ruptured biceps tendon preceding heart failure (suggesting TTR amyloidosis) Abnormal postural blood-pressure drop indicating autonomic neuropathy (AL or some variant TTR forms) Unexplained nonpostural dizziness or syncope with bifascicular or left bundle branch block in TTR amyloidosis, indicating risk of high-degree atrioventricular block Significant proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia (renal AL involvement) Mildly elevated high-sensitivity troponin may lead to misdiagnosis as ischemic heart disease (Harrison 22e p.2023-2024). AL amyloidosis can occasionally show myocardial uptake on bone-avid tracer scans, so a positive nuclear scan must never be interpreted as diagnostic of TTR without first excluding a plasma cell dyscrasia (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026). Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is common in older patients and not uncommonly coexists with TTR amyloidosis, so abnormal plasma cell dyscrasia testing does not automatically equal AL amyloidosis and may require hematology input (Harrison 22e p.2023-2026). Serum and urine protein electrophoresis may miss the low-level paraprotein of AL amyloidosis; immunofixation is more sensitive and should be performed (Harrison 22e p.2024). The sedimentation rate is usually normal or only minimally elevated in AL amyloidosis, unlike the marked elevation in multiple myeloma, so a normal ESR does not exclude AL amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2024). Immunohistochemical typing of amyloid is fraught with diagnostic uncertainty and can be misleading; typing is ideally done by mass spectrometry (Harrison 22e p.2024-2026). There is no definitive noninvasive test for AL cardiac amyloidosis, so a tissue biopsy is always required to confirm it (Harrison 22e p.2024). Rare variant TTR forms can have negative bone-tracer imaging, so a negative scan does not entirely exclude amyloidosis when clinical suspicion remains high (Harrison 22e p.2026). Restrictive cardiomyopathy results from a noncompliant ventricle with markedly impaired diastolic filling; most cases are 'infiltrative,' due to deposition of abnormal substances between myocytes (amyloid being the most common), with additional causes from intramyocyte storage of metabolic products (e.g., iron in hemochromatosis, Fabry disease, glycogen storage disease) or acquired fibrosis (radiation, scleroderma, endomyocardial/hypereosinophilic injury, carcinoid). In amyloidosis, fibrillar proteinaceous material is deposited extracellularly; amyloid stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light, and electron microscopy reveals nonbranching fibrils about 10 nm in diameter. Extracellular amyloid deposition expands the extracellular space, increasing heart mass and ventricular wall thickness while reducing compliance; the left ventricular cavity may be relatively small (restrictive physiology) and both atria dilate from chronically elevated biventricular filling pressures. AL amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder closely related to multiple myeloma in which excess abnormal free light chains (more often lambda than kappa) deposit in multiple organs, with heart and kidney most commonly affected. TTR amyloidosis arises from liver-produced transthyretin, either wild-type (ATTRwt) or from a destabilizing genetic variant (ATTRv); variant TTR is generally considered less stable than wild-type. Both wild-type and variant TTR cardiomyopathy have a subclinical phase of probably several years, and by the time heart failure occurs 30-50% of the involved heart weight may be amyloid (Harrison 22e p.2020-2022). Prognosis depends heavily on amyloid type. AL cardiac amyloidosis is aggressive and, with cardiac involvement, carries the worst survival, with median survival from onset of heart failure to death of about 6 months in untreated patients, underscoring the urgency of diagnosis. Among TTR forms, untreated Val122Ile variant disease tends to progress relatively rapidly with median survival of 2-3 years from onset of heart failure, whereas wild-type TTR amyloidosis has an untreated median survival of about 4-5 years, with death usually from progressive congestive heart failure rather than sudden death; wild-type disease occurring in women tends to present later and follow a more indolent course. There is a high risk of thromboembolism in cardiac amyloidosis, and sudden cardiac death may occur (more common in advanced AL disease). Overall, cardiac amyloidosis is now recognized as far more common than previously appreciated, and earlier diagnosis with the advent of disease-modifying therapy has improved outlook (Harrison 22e p.2021-2028). Harrison does not provide a single formal staging scale within this chapter; severity is gauged clinically and prognostically by amyloid type and stage of cardiac involvement. Adverse markers include disproportionately elevated NT-proBNP (often 1000-2000 pg/mL even with mild heart failure) and elevated high-sensitivity troponin, with the proportion of heart weight composed of amyloid reaching 30-50% by the time heart failure occurs in TTR disease. AL cardiac involvement confers the worst prognosis among the types (Harrison 22e p.2022-2024).

deficiency of folate, vitamin B12, vitamin E, copper or zinc Heavy metal / toxin intoxication (lead, aluminum) Kennedy's disease (spinobulbar muscular atrophy) ALS is the most common progressive motor neuron disease and ultimately causes progressive loss of BOTH upper (corticospinal) and lower motor neurons; in the absence of clear involvement of both motor neuron types, the diagnosis of ALS is questionable (p.3519-3520). Lower motor neuron features: insidious asymmetric weakness usually first distal in one limb, progressive wasting/atrophy, and fasciculations (spontaneous twitching of motor units); in the hands a preponderance of extensor over flexor weakness is common (p.3521). Upper (corticospinal) motor neuron features: hyperactive muscle-stretch reflexes (tendon jerks), spastic resistance to passive movement, and muscle stiffness often out of proportion to weakness (p.3521). Bulbar onset presents with difficulty chewing, swallowing, and moving the face and tongue; corticobulbar degeneration causes dysarthria and pseudobulbar affect (involuntary excess weeping or laughing) (p.3521). World Federation of Neurology criteria: simultaneous upper AND lower motor neuron involvement with progressive weakness and exclusion of all alternative diagnoses; 'definite' when 3-4 regions involved (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral), 'probable' when 2, 'possible' when 1 (p.3521). Elevated CSF/serum neurofilament light chains (Nfl) or phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chains are markers of neurodegeneration in most cases; higher levels correlate with more aggressive disease and more rapid progression (p.3521). About 10% of cases are inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (familial ALS); FALS is clinically indistinguishable from sporadic ALS apart from its inheritance. C9orf72 is the most common genetic cause (~45-50% of FALS), followed by SOD1 (~20%) (p.3521). ALS may arise concurrently with frontotemporal dementia (particularly in familial cases), with early behavioral abnormalities reflecting frontal lobe dysfunction (p.3520-3521). Respiratory involvement: weakness of the muscles of respiration may rarely cause death before the disease is advanced elsewhere; the illness is relentlessly progressive, leading to death from respiratory paralysis - respiratory failure determines prognosis. Bulbar dysfunction (difficulty chewing/swallowing) risks aspiration pneumonia and compromised nutrition/hydration. Atypical features warranting search for a remediable mimic: restriction to only upper OR only lower motor neurons, involvement of non-motor neurons, or evidence of motor conduction block on electrophysiology. Because ALS is currently untreatable, it is imperative to exclude potentially remediable mimics - especially cervical cord compression/cervical spondylotic myelopathy, which can produce weakness, wasting, fasciculations in the arms and leg spasticity that closely resembles ALS. Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMCB) must be excluded: unlike ALS it lacks corticospinal signs, often has elevated anti-GM1 antibodies, and may respond dramatically to IVIG or chemotherapy. Diagnosing ALS without clear involvement of BOTH upper and lower motor neurons is questionable - reconsider the diagnosis. Features favoring ALS over a compressive mimic: absence of pain or sensory changes, normal bowel and bladder function, and normal spinal radiology and CSF. Sensory, sphincter, ocular-motility, and cognitive functions are preserved even late (except when concurrent frontotemporal dementia is present). Motor neuron degenerative disorder marked by death of lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and their brainstem bulbar homologues) and upper/corticospinal motor neurons (layer-five motor cortex neurons descending via the pyramidal tract). Affected neurons shrink and accumulate lipofuscin; the motor neuron cytoskeleton is affected early, with proximal axonal 'spheroids' composed of neurofilament accumulations. Both sporadic and familial ALS show ubiquitin-positive aggregates frequently associated with the protein TDP43, plus astroglial/microglial proliferation (neuroinflammation). Loss of cortical motor neurons thins the corticospinal tracts; lateral-column fiber loss and fibrillary gliosis impart firmness (lateral sclerosis), while muscle denervation and atrophy give rise to the term amyotrophy. Neuronal cell death is strikingly selective: the sensory apparatus, cerebellar coordination structures, ocular-motility neurons, and the sacral parasympathetic sphincter neurons (nucleus of Onuf) are characteristically spared. Familial ALS most commonly involves mutations in C9orf72, SOD1, TDP43, and FUS/TLS (p.3519-3521). Relentlessly progressive; median survival is 3 to 5 years, with death typically from respiratory paralysis. Stabilization or regression is very rare. Higher serum/CSF neurofilament light chain levels correlate with more aggressive disease and more rapid progression. No treatment arrests the underlying pathologic process (p.3521, 3524). World Federation of Neurology diagnostic categories based on number of body regions with combined upper and lower motor neuron involvement (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral): 'definite' ALS = 3-4 regions; 'probable' = 2 regions; 'possible' = 1 region. Exception: progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs at one site plus a SOD1 mutation also qualifies (p.3521).

anal lesion attributed to haemorrhoids A firm or ulcerated anal mass with associated pain Enlarged inguinal lymph nodes suggesting nodal spread New anal symptoms in an immunosuppressed or HIV-positive patient Diagnosing haemorrhoids without examining or biopsying a persistent anal lesion Confusing anal squamous cell carcinoma with rectal adenocarcinoma and applying the wrong treatment pathway Proceeding to primary radical surgery instead of first-line chemoradiotherapy Overlooking HIV status and immunosuppression that influence management and prognosis Most anal cancers develop from squamous or transitional epithelium of the anal canal, driven by persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus. Viral oncoproteins inactivate tumour suppressor pathways, producing progressive squamous intraepithelial lesions (anal intraepithelial neoplasia) that can advance to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Immunosuppression, especially from HIV, impairs viral clearance and accelerates this process. Tumours spread locally into the sphincter complex and surrounding tissues and metastasise to inguinal, perirectal, and pelvic lymph nodes. Localised anal squamous cell carcinoma has a favourable prognosis with organ-preserving chemoradiotherapy and high rates of local control; outcome worsens with larger tumours, nodal involvement, and metastatic disease.

Anal fissure — fissure-in-ano, anal fissure, chronic anal fissure Thrombosed external haemorrhoid or perianal haematoma Anorectal abscess Fistula-in-ano Crohn's disease or ulcerative proctitis Anal carcinoma Sexually transmitted infection (herpes, syphilis) Pruritus ani with excoriation Gentle inspection of the anal verge, often with the patient positioned to allow the fissure to be seen Examination under anaesthesia when pain precludes assessment or the diagnosis is unclear Endoscopic evaluation and biopsy for atypical, multiple, or non-healing fissures Investigations for inflammatory bowel disease or infection when clinically suspected Presents with severe, sharp anal pain during and often for a prolonged period after defaecation, frequently with a small amount of bright red blood on the paper Most fissures occur in the posterior midline; anterior fissures are more common in women, and fissures away from the midline should raise suspicion of underlying disease Pain and reflex internal sphincter spasm create a cycle of ischaemia that impairs healing and perpetuates the fissure A chronic fissure shows a triad of a sentinel skin tag, exposed internal sphincter fibres in the base, and a hypertrophied anal papilla Examination is often too painful for a digital rectal examination, which may need to be deferred or performed under anaesthesia First-line management aims to break the spasm-ischaemia cycle with stool softening, fibre, and topical agents that relax the internal sphincter such as glyceryl trinitrate or a calcium channel blocker Refractory fissures may be treated with botulinum toxin injection or lateral internal sphincterotomy, the latter carrying a small risk of incontinence Multiple, lateral, or atypical fissures warrant investigation for Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, sexually transmitted infection, or malignancy Atypical, lateral, or multiple fissures suggesting Crohn's disease, infection, or malignancy A non-healing indurated ulcer that may represent anal carcinoma Associated perianal sepsis, abscess, or fistula Systemic features of inflammatory bowel disease or immunosuppression Forcing a digital or instrumental examination through severe pain rather than deferring or examining under anaesthesia Overlooking Crohn's disease or malignancy in atypical or non-healing fissures Proceeding to sphincterotomy without considering continence risk, especially in women and older patients Failing to address ongoing constipation, allowing recurrence An anal fissure is a longitudinal tear in the anoderm of the distal anal canal, usually initiated by the passage of a hard or bulky stool. Resulting pain triggers spasm and hypertonia of the internal anal sphincter, which raises resting anal pressure and reduces blood flow to the relatively poorly perfused posterior midline. This local ischaemia impairs mucosal healing, converting an acute tear into a chronic non-healing ulcer. Persistent inflammation produces the sentinel tag, papilla hypertrophy, and exposure of sphincter fibres seen in chronic fissures. Acute fissures commonly heal with conservative treatment and stool softening. A substantial proportion of chronic fissures heal with topical sphincter-relaxing therapy, and most of the remainder respond to botulinum toxin or sphincterotomy, though a small risk of minor incontinence follows surgery.

Anaphylaxis — Clinical diagnosis Serum tryptase IM adrenaline immediately Systemic mastocytosis (elevated baseline tryptase; spindle-shaped mast cells on bone marrow) (p. 2813) Pheochromocytoma (elevated urine metanephrines) (p. 2813) Carcinoid syndrome (elevated urine 5-HIAA) (p. 2813) Hereditary angioedema (decreased C4 during attacks) (p. 2813) Acquired angioedema (decreased C1q) (p. 2813) Systemic capillary leak syndrome (severe hypotension with poor response to first-line agents) (p. 2813) Serum tryptase peaks 60-90 min after onset and remains measurable for up to about 5 h; apply the '20% + 2' rule (an acute level >20% above the patient's baseline plus 2 ng/mL is diagnostic of clinically significant mast-cell activation) (p. 2813) Repeat tryptase once the patient is stable to establish the individual baseline, since baseline serum tryptase varies widely and can be raised by hereditary alpha-tryptasemia or high environmental allergen exposure (p. 2813) Serum histamine is of limited use acutely - its measurable window expires within about 1 h of onset (p. 2813) Allergen-specific skin testing or serum-specific IgE to confirm a suspected drug or food trigger (p. 2813) Baseline tryptase in sting-induced anaphylaxis to screen for underlying systemic mastocytosis (p. 2813) Scombroid poisoning (ingested histamine from improperly stored histidine-rich fish such as tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi); clinically mimics anaphylaxis but tryptase is NOT elevated because histamine is exogenous, and skin test/oral challenge to fish are negative (p. 2813) Direct (pseudoallergic) mast-cell degranulation from opiates, neuromuscular blocking agents, vancomycin, or CT radiocontrast (e.g., via MRGPRX2) - clinically indistinguishable from IgE-mediated reactions but occurs without prior sensitization (p. 2813) Vasovagal (neurally mediated) syncope - provoked by emotion, pain, or orthostatic stress and accompanied by bradycardia, in contrast to the tachycardia and urticaria/angioedema of anaphylaxis (p. 2813; cf. p. 156-157) Onset is typically within seconds to minutes of exposure to the trigger; an exception is the delayed (about 3-6 h) reaction to mammalian meat seen in alpha-gal syndrome (p. 2812-2813). Most episodes (about 80-90%) are uniphasic, but roughly 10-20% are biphasic, with symptoms recurring an hour or more after the initial reaction has resolved (p. 2812). Cutaneous features (urticaria, flushing, generalized warmth) are the most common manifestation, present in over 90% of cases (p. 2812). Cross-linking of allergen with IgE bound to FcepsilonRI receptors on mast cells and basophils is the usual initiating mechanism; sensitization requires prior exposure, so repeated exposure to the antigen is a key risk factor (p. 2812-2813). Some severe reactions are non-IgE-mediated and can occur on first known exposure, because direct mast-cell activation needs no prior sensitization (e.g., via the MRGPRX2 receptor with neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, and icatibant) (p. 2813). Severe Hymenoptera sting anaphylaxis, especially with prominent hypotension, may be the first presentation of underlying systemic mastocytosis; checking a baseline tryptase screens for this (p. 2812-2813). Failure to give epinephrine within the first 20 minutes of symptoms is a risk factor for poor outcomes (p. 2813). About 6% of Western populations carry hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, an extra TPSAB1 allele giving a high baseline tryptase that can confound interpretation and may itself be a risk factor for severe reactions (p. 2813). Hypotension or hypoxia - the most dangerous features, risking cardiovascular collapse or respiratory failure (p. 2812) Laryngeal edema (sensation of a lump in the throat, hoarseness, stridor) or angioedema of the epiglottis/larynx threatening mechanical airway obstruction (p. 2812) Bronchial obstruction (chest tightness, wheezing), especially severe in patients with underlying asthma, who have increased mortality (p. 2812) Underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease - predisposes to more rapid decompensation (p. 2812) Severe GI involvement (vomiting, crampy abdominal pain); bowel-wall angioedema can deplete intravascular volume enough to cause cardiovascular collapse (p. 2812) Treat with epinephrine first - antihistamines, glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators are ancillary agents for residual urticaria/angioedema and bronchospasm once the patient is hemodynamically stable, not initial therapy (p. 2813). Biphasic reactions in 10-20% recur an hour or more after apparent recovery, so a period of observation is needed after initial resolution (p. 2812). A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis - it is not elevated in scombroid poisoning (exogenous histamine), and an acutely 'normal' value may still be diagnostic relative to a low individual baseline (apply the 20% + 2 rule) (p. 2813). Non-IgE-mediated reactions can occur on first exposure, so the absence of prior exposure does not rule out an anaphylactic reaction (p. 2813). Beta blockers can blunt the response to epinephrine; consider an alternative antihypertensive in patients at high risk of needing emergency epinephrine (p. 2813). Skin/serum specific-IgE testing to foods has relatively poor predictive value, so a positive test alone does not confirm clinical reactivity (p. 2814). Anaphylaxis is driven by mediators released chiefly from mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. The most common mechanism is allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation. Preformed granule contents include histamine, proteases (tryptase, chymase), proteoglycans (heparin, chondroitin sulfate), and TNF-alpha; newly generated arachidonic-acid products include cysteinyl leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, and platelet-activating factor (PAF). Histamine produces flushing, urticaria, pruritus and, at high levels, hypotension and tachycardia; cysteinyl leukotrienes and PGD2 cause bronchoconstriction and increased microvascular permeability, with PGD2 also recruiting eosinophils and basophils. Serum PAF correlates with severity and is inversely related to PAF acetylhydrolase. Tryptase and chymase activate complement (generating the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a) and the kallikrein-kinin system, with mediator effects likely additive or synergistic. Reactions can also be non-IgE-mediated: direct mast-cell activation (e.g., via MRGPRX2 by neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, icatibant; or opiates, vancomycin, radiocontrast, NSAIDs), complement activation (e.g., Cremophor-solubilized paclitaxel), or contact-system/bradykinin generation (e.g., oversulfated chondroitin sulfate heparin contaminant). (p. 2812-2813) Severe and even fatal complications can develop within minutes of symptom onset, making early recognition critical; deaths occur via airway/bronchial obstruction, laryngeal angioedema, or vascular collapse. Delaying epinephrine beyond the first 20 minutes worsens outcomes. Risk is higher with underlying asthma or cardiovascular disease. Natural history varies by trigger: most childhood egg, milk, soy, and wheat allergy resolves, whereas about 80% of peanut allergy persists for life. (p. 2812-2813)

variable Under-appreciating arrhythmic risk because the ventricular tachycardia is often asymptomatic Prescribing QT-prolonging drugs without recognising the underlying repolarisation abnormality Andersen-Tawil syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in KCNJ2, which encodes the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1. This channel stabilises the resting membrane potential and shapes the terminal phase of repolarisation in both skeletal and cardiac muscle. Reduced Kir2.1 current, often through a dominant-negative effect on the tetrameric channel, destabilises the resting potential of skeletal muscle to produce periodic paralysis, and prolongs and destabilises cardiac repolarisation to generate the prominent U waves, QU prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias. The same channel and related developmental signalling pathways are implicated in the skeletal and craniofacial dysmorphism that completes the triad. Life expectancy is usually near normal because the ventricular arrhythmias are frequently well tolerated, but syncope and, rarely, sudden cardiac death can occur, so cardiac surveillance is essential and the periodic paralysis and dysmorphic features add variable long-term morbidity.
