autosomal dominant, caused by heterozygous mutations or deletions of the PAX6 gene on chromosome 11p13 Characterised by partial or near-complete absence of the iris, though the underlying problem affects the whole eye, not just the iris Associated features include foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia, nystagmus, photophobia, and reduced visual acuity from birth Aniridia-associated keratopathy from limbal stem cell deficiency, cataract, and glaucoma are important vision-threatening complications that develop over time Sporadic aniridia due to larger 11p13 deletions can involve the adjacent WT1 gene, causing WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of intellectual disability) Children with sporadic aniridia require renal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour until the risk period has passed and WT1 involvement is excluded Lifelong monitoring for glaucoma and keratopathy is essential, and coloured or occlusive contact lenses can reduce glare and photophobia New or uncontrolled raised intraocular pressure indicating glaucoma Progressive corneal opacification from limbal stem cell deficiency Abdominal mass, haematuria, or genitourinary anomaly suggesting Wilms tumour in sporadic aniridia Treating aniridia as an isolated iris defect and missing the panocular and systemic implications Failing to arrange Wilms tumour surveillance in a child with apparently sporadic aniridia Overlooking insidious glaucoma or progressive keratopathy on routine review Not offering genetic counselling given the dominant inheritance and reproductive risk Aniridia results from haploinsufficiency of PAX6, a master transcription factor that orchestrates development of the eye and parts of the central nervous system and pancreas. Reduced PAX6 dosage disrupts formation of multiple ocular structures, producing iris hypoplasia together with foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia, and predisposing to limbal stem cell deficiency, cataract, and abnormal anterior chamber angle development. The result is a spectrum of structural and functional deficits present from birth. In sporadic cases caused by contiguous gene deletions of 11p13, loss of the neighbouring WT1 tumour-suppressor gene confers a high risk of Wilms tumour, defining the WAGR association. Visual acuity is typically reduced from birth due to foveal hypoplasia and often declines further with progressive glaucoma, cataract, and keratopathy; prognosis in WAGR cases is additionally determined by the outcome of Wilms tumour.

Ankle sprain — lateral ligament sprain, inversion injury, ATFL sprain, twisted ankle Lateral malleolus, fifth metatarsal base, or other foot/ankle fracture Maisonneuve fracture (proximal fibula) Osteochondral lesion of the talus Peroneal tendon subluxation, tear, or dislocation Syndesmotic (high ankle) injury Subtalar or midfoot (Lisfranc) injury Deltoid ligament injury Apply the Ottawa ankle and foot rules to select patients for plain radiographs Weight-bearing or stress radiographs if syndesmotic disruption or instability is suspected MRI for suspected osteochondral lesions, occult injury, or persistent symptoms Ultrasound to assess peroneal tendon and ligament integrity Consider proximal fibula imaging when a Maisonneuve injury is suspected The typical mechanism is an inversion and plantarflexion injury damaging the lateral ligament complex, with the anterior talofibular ligament injured first Sprains are graded from mild ligament stretch (grade I) through partial tear (grade II) to complete rupture with instability (grade III) Use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide on radiographs and reduce unnecessary imaging Always palpate the proximal fibula, base of the fifth metatarsal, navicular, and medial malleolus to avoid missing associated fractures A high ankle (syndesmotic) sprain from an external rotation injury causes pain above the joint line, is confirmed by the squeeze and external rotation tests, and has a longer recovery Marked medial-sided pain or a positive external rotation test raises concern for a Maisonneuve injury with a proximal fibular fracture Early functional management with relative rest, compression, elevation, and progressive weight-bearing and mobilisation is preferred over prolonged immobilisation Rehabilitation with proprioceptive and balance training and peroneal strengthening reduces the risk of recurrent sprains and chronic instability Most sprains recover well, but a significant minority develop chronic instability or persistent symptoms if inadequately rehabilitated Inability to bear weight and bony tenderness meeting Ottawa criteria, indicating possible fracture Proximal fibular tenderness suggesting a Maisonneuve fracture Gross instability, deformity, or neurovascular compromise Persistent locking, catching, or effusion suggesting an osteochondral lesion Missing associated fractures such as the fifth metatarsal base or a Maisonneuve injury Failing to identify a syndesmotic sprain and underestimating recovery time Prolonged immobilisation leading to stiffness and deconditioning Omitting proprioceptive rehabilitation, increasing the risk of recurrent sprains An ankle sprain is a ligamentous injury, most often to the lateral complex (anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular, and posterior talofibular ligaments), caused by forced inversion. Excessive load tears collagen fibres, causing bleeding, swelling, and loss of mechanical restraint. Syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains involve the distal tibiofibular ligaments from external rotation. Impaired ligament healing and proprioceptive deficits can lead to mechanical and functional instability. Most low-grade lateral sprains recover within weeks with functional treatment, but up to a third develop residual symptoms or chronic instability; syndesmotic injuries recover more slowly and unstable injuries may require surgery.

Ankylosing spondylitis — AS, radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, Bechterew disease Mechanical or degenerative low back pain Psoriatic arthritis with axial involvement Reactive arthritis Arthritis associated with inflammatory bowel disease Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) Infective sacroiliitis or vertebral osteomyelitis MRI of the sacroiliac joints to detect early active inflammation before radiographic change Plain radiographs of the pelvis and spine for sacroiliitis, syndesmophytes, and ankylosis HLA-B27 typing to support the diagnosis in the right clinical context Inflammatory markers (CRP and ESR), which may be normal despite active disease Assessment of extra-articular features including ophthalmology review for uveitis Typically presents in young adults, more often men, with insidious chronic low back pain and stiffness that improves with activity and worsens with rest, especially in the second half of the night Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes and buttock pain from sacroiliitis are characteristic inflammatory back pain features Progressive loss of spinal mobility can be assessed with the modified Schober test and chest expansion measurement Enthesitis (notably at the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia) and asymmetric large-joint peripheral arthritis are common Extra-articular manifestations include acute anterior uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and psoriasis Strongly associated with HLA-B27, though a positive test alone is neither diagnostic nor required Early sacroiliitis is often better seen on MRI (bone marrow oedema) before radiographic changes such as sclerosis, erosions, and eventual ankylosis appear Management combines a regular exercise and physiotherapy programme with NSAIDs first-line, escalating to biologic therapy (TNF or IL-17 inhibitors) for inadequate control Acute painful red eye suggesting anterior uveitis requiring urgent ophthalmology assessment New or worsening neurological deficit, or acute severe pain after minor trauma, raising concern for spinal fracture through a rigid fused spine Cauda equina syndrome from arachnoiditis Symptoms of cardiac conduction block or aortic regurgitation from cardiac involvement Restrictive lung disease or apical pulmonary fibrosis Attributing chronic back pain in a young adult to mechanical causes and delaying diagnosis for years Relying on HLA-B27 as a diagnostic test rather than a supportive finding Assuming normal inflammatory markers exclude active disease Overlooking the high fracture risk of a rigid, osteoporotic spine after minor trauma Neglecting extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, bowel disease, and cardiac involvement Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton and the prototype of the seronegative spondyloarthritides. Inflammation centres on the entheses (sites where ligaments and tendons attach to bone) and the sacroiliac joints. A strong genetic association with HLA-B27 implicates aberrant antigen presentation and dysregulated IL-23/IL-17 pathway signalling. Chronic enthesitis and osteitis drive a cycle of erosion followed by reactive new bone formation, leading to syndesmophyte development, bony bridging across vertebrae, and ultimately spinal fusion (the 'bamboo spine'). Disease course is variable; many patients maintain good function with exercise and modern therapy, but persistent inflammation can lead to progressive spinal ankylosis, fixed kyphotic deformity, and increased fracture risk. Early diagnosis and biologic therapy have improved symptom control and quality of life.

Anorectal abscess — perianal abscess, ischiorectal abscess, perirectal abscess, intersphincteric abscess Thrombosed external haemorrhoid Pilonidal abscess Bartholin abscess (in women) Hidradenitis suppurativa Perianal Crohn's disease Anal or rectal malignancy with sepsis Fournier's gangrene (necrotising perineal infection) Clinical examination and, where pain permits, digital rectal examination to assess deeper spaces Examination under anaesthesia to fully assess and drain the collection and look for a fistula MRI pelvis or endoanal ultrasound for complex, recurrent, or supralevator disease Blood glucose and screening for immunosuppression, and blood cultures if systemically septic Consideration of investigations for Crohn's disease in recurrent or atypical abscesses Presents with acute, constant, throbbing perianal or rectal pain, often with a tender fluctuant swelling, fever, and malaise Classified by anatomical space into perianal, ischiorectal, intersphincteric, and supralevator abscesses, each with characteristic examination findings Most arise from infection of the anal glands opening into the crypts at the dentate line (the cryptoglandular theory) A superficial perianal abscess is visibly red and fluctuant, whereas a deeper ischiorectal or supralevator abscess may cause deep pain and systemic upset with little external sign Treatment is prompt surgical incision and drainage; antibiotics alone are inadequate and delay is dangerous A significant proportion of drained abscesses are associated with, or later develop, a fistula-in-ano Diabetes, immunosuppression, and Crohn's disease predispose to abscess formation and to more aggressive, spreading infection Spreading perianal sepsis with systemic toxicity may herald necrotising infection (Fournier's gangrene), which is a surgical emergency Spreading cellulitis, crepitus, skin necrosis, or disproportionate pain suggesting Fournier's gangrene (surgical emergency) Systemic sepsis with tachycardia, hypotension, or confusion Immunocompromise or poorly controlled diabetes with rapid progression Deep or supralevator sepsis with minimal external signs but severe pain and toxicity Relying on antibiotics instead of prompt incision and drainage Missing a deep ischiorectal or supralevator abscess because external signs are minimal Failing to recognise early Fournier's gangrene in a diabetic or immunosuppressed patient Overzealous probing for a fistula at the time of acute drainage, risking a false track Anorectal abscesses usually begin with obstruction and infection of an anal gland at the base of an anal crypt (cryptoglandular infection). Pus tracks along planes of least resistance from the intersphincteric space into the perianal, ischiorectal, or supralevator spaces, and can extend circumferentially in a horseshoe pattern. The causative organisms are typically gut flora, including coliforms and anaerobes. Underlying conditions such as Crohn's disease, diabetes, and immunosuppression predispose to formation and to more extensive spread. Persistence of the primary gland infection after drainage creates the epithelialised track of a fistula-in-ano. Simple abscesses drained promptly resolve well, but recurrence and fistula formation are common. Delayed treatment, deep spaces, immunosuppression, or necrotising infection markedly worsen outcomes and can be life-threatening.

Anorexia nervosa — anorexia, AN Bulimia nervosa Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder Major depressive disorder with appetite loss Hyperthyroidism Malabsorption and gastrointestinal disease Malignancy or chronic infection causing weight loss Body dysmorphic disorder Weight, height, and body mass index with growth trajectory in young people Electrolytes including potassium, phosphate, and magnesium ECG to assess for bradycardia and QT prolongation Full blood count, renal and liver function, and glucose Bone density assessment in prolonged illness Assessment for refeeding risk before and during nutritional rehabilitation Characterised by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain, and a disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced Two patterns are recognised: a restricting type and a binge-eating/purging type Physical consequences include amenorrhoea, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, and osteopenia Purging behaviours can cause electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis, and dental erosion Management principles centre on structured nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration alongside psychotherapy, with family-based treatment favoured for adolescents Medical stabilisation takes priority in severe cases; feeding must be advanced cautiously to avoid refeeding syndrome Comorbid depression, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive features are common, and suicide risk is elevated Weigh patients and monitor electrolytes and cardiac status, since bradycardia and QT prolongation can be dangerous Severe bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, or arrhythmia indicating cardiac instability Dangerous electrolyte derangement, particularly hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia Refeeding syndrome during nutritional restoration Rapid or extreme weight loss and very low body mass index Suicidal ideation Refeeding too rapidly and precipitating life-threatening refeeding syndrome Focusing on weight alone while neglecting electrolyte and cardiac monitoring Underestimating suicide risk Being reassured by a normal weight in the binge-purge type despite dangerous electrolyte disturbance Delaying medical stabilisation while awaiting psychiatric transfer Anorexia nervosa arises from an interaction of genetic and temperamental vulnerability (perfectionism, anxiety, harm avoidance), sociocultural pressures, and neurobiological factors including altered reward and interoceptive processing and serotonergic and dopaminergic dysregulation. Starvation itself perpetuates the disorder through neuroendocrine and cognitive changes, and complications reflect the systemic effects of chronic malnutrition. Anorexia nervosa has one of the highest mortality rates among psychiatric disorders, from both medical complications and suicide. Many patients recover, particularly with early intervention in adolescence, but a substantial proportion follow a chronic or relapsing course.

Anterior uveitis — iritis, iridocyclitis, acute anterior uveitis, AAU Acute angle-closure glaucoma Bacterial or viral conjunctivitis Bacterial keratitis or corneal ulcer Scleritis and episcleritis Endophthalmitis Acute red eye from subconjunctival haemorrhage Slit-lamp examination to grade anterior chamber cells and flare and identify keratic precipitates Intraocular pressure measurement to detect secondary glaucoma Dilated fundus examination to exclude intermediate/posterior involvement and macular oedema HLA-B27 typing and targeted systemic workup in recurrent or bilateral disease Investigations for infective or granulomatous causes (e.g. syphilis, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis) when indicated Presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, tearing, and blurred vision, typically with circumcorneal (ciliary) injection rather than diffuse redness The pupil is often small (miotic) and may be irregular if posterior synechiae have formed Slit-lamp examination shows cells and flare in the anterior chamber; a hypopyon (layered pus) indicates severe inflammation Keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium help characterise the inflammation as granulomatous or non-granulomatous Strongly associated with HLA-B27 and its related systemic conditions (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis) Management principles are topical corticosteroids to suppress inflammation and cycloplegic/mydriatic drops to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent or break synechiae Recurrent, bilateral, or granulomatous uveitis warrants investigation for underlying systemic or infective causes Hypopyon or severe inflammation suggesting aggressive or infective uveitis, or endophthalmitis Marked pain with a red eye and raised intraocular pressure requiring differentiation from angle closure Bilateral, recurrent, or granulomatous disease pointing to serious systemic illness Progressive visual loss from macular oedema or dense synechiae Prescribing topical steroids without excluding herpetic or other infective keratitis, which steroids can worsen Failing to use a cycloplegic, allowing painful ciliary spasm and permanent posterior synechiae Missing raised intraocular pressure or steroid-induced pressure rise during treatment Not investigating recurrent or bilateral cases for an underlying systemic cause Anterior uveitis is inflammation of the iris and ciliary body (anterior uveal tract). Breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier allows inflammatory cells and protein to leak into the anterior chamber, seen clinically as cells and flare. The process may be immune-mediated (often HLA-B27 associated or linked to systemic autoimmune disease), infective, or triggered by trauma. Inflammatory adhesions can form between the iris and lens (posterior synechiae) or the iris and trabecular meshwork (peripheral anterior synechiae), and secondary complications include raised intraocular pressure, cataract, and macular oedema. Most acute, non-granulomatous, HLA-B27-associated episodes respond well to prompt topical treatment, but recurrent or chronic uveitis can lead to cataract, glaucoma, and macular oedema with lasting visual loss.

Anthrax — Bacillus anthracis infection, cutaneous anthrax, inhalational anthrax, woolsorter's disease Staphylococcal or streptococcal skin and soft-tissue infection with eschar Necrotising fasciitis Plague (bubonic or pneumonic) Tularaemia Community-acquired pneumonia or mediastinitis for the inhalational form Severe cellulitis with lymphadenitis Brown recluse spider bite with necrotic eschar Rickettsial eschar (e.g. scrub typhus) Ecthyma gangrenosum Orf or other zoonotic skin lesions Gram stain and culture of skin lesion fluid, blood, pleural fluid or CSF Blood cultures in systemic disease Chest imaging looking for a widened mediastinum and pleural effusions in inhalational anthrax PCR and toxin/antigen detection for rapid confirmation Notification to and testing by a reference/public-health laboratory Caused by the spore-forming Gram-positive rod Bacillus anthracis, a zoonosis of herbivores acquired through contact with infected animals or contaminated animal products Cutaneous anthrax is the commonest form and presents as a painless papule that ulcerates into a characteristic black eschar with marked surrounding oedema Inhalational (pulmonary) anthrax follows spore inhalation and causes a fulminant illness with a widened mediastinum from haemorrhagic lymphadenitis and rapidly fatal shock Gastrointestinal and oropharyngeal forms follow ingestion of contaminated meat and carry high mortality It is a recognised agent of bioterrorism, so clustered or unexplained inhalational cases warrant urgent public-health alert Prompt antibacterial therapy is effective for cutaneous disease, while systemic forms also require antitoxin and intensive supportive care In endemic parts of India it occurs sporadically among people handling livestock, hides and wool Diagnosis rests on Gram stain and culture of lesion, blood or other fluids, with PCR and toxin assays as confirmatory tests Widened mediastinum with dyspnoea and shock indicating inhalational anthrax, a medical emergency Extensive oedema of the head and neck threatening the airway in cutaneous or oropharyngeal disease Signs of meningitis (anthrax meningoencephalitis is often haemorrhagic and rapidly fatal) A cluster of unexplained severe febrile respiratory illnesses suggesting deliberate release Incising or debriding a cutaneous anthrax lesion, which can worsen dissemination Mistaking early inhalational anthrax for ordinary influenza or community-acquired pneumonia and delaying therapy Failing to consider occupational or bioterrorism exposure history Overlooking the need for antitoxin and public-health notification in systemic disease Bacillus anthracis spores enter through skin abrasions, inhalation or ingestion, germinate, and multiply while producing a poly-D-glutamic acid capsule that resists phagocytosis and a tripartite toxin. Protective antigen mediates entry of lethal factor and oedema factor into cells; lethal factor is a protease that disrupts intracellular signalling and triggers massive inflammatory and cytotoxic effects, while oedema factor raises cyclic AMP causing the striking tissue oedema. Systemic dissemination produces toxaemia, vascular leak, haemorrhage and shock, which drive the high mortality of non-cutaneous disease. Cutaneous anthrax usually responds well to timely antibacterial treatment with low mortality, though the eschar heals with scarring. Inhalational, gastrointestinal and meningeal forms are frequently fatal even with treatment, and outcome depends critically on how early therapy and antitoxin are started.

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis — anti-NMDAR encephalitis, NMDA receptor antibody encephalitis, anti-GluN1 encephalitis, anti-NR1 encephalitis Primary psychiatric illness such as a first psychotic episode or catatonia Viral (including herpes simplex) or other infective encephalitis Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome Other antibody-mediated encephalitides (LGI1, GABA-B, CASPR2) Drug intoxication or withdrawal states Status epilepticus of other cause Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other rapidly progressive encephalopathies Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands, and paired serum/CSF NMDA receptor antibodies Electroencephalography, which may show the extreme delta brush pattern or diffuse slowing MRI of the brain with contrast to exclude alternative structural or inflammatory causes Pelvic and abdominal imaging (ultrasound, MRI or CT) to search for an ovarian teratoma Whole-body tumour screening in older patients or when teratoma is not found Screening for herpes simplex virus, which can precede antibody-mediated relapse Typically evolves through a viral-like prodrome into a florid psychiatric phase (agitation, delusions, disorganised behaviour) that frequently reaches psychiatry before neurology The mature syndrome combines seizures, orofacial and limb dyskinesias, mutism, memory failure, a reduced level of consciousness, and autonomic instability Autonomic dysfunction (labile blood pressure, cardiac arrhythmia, hyperthermia, central hypoventilation) is a leading cause of intensive-care need and death Antibodies target the GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor; diagnosis rests on detecting these antibodies, with cerebrospinal fluid testing more sensitive and specific than serum An ovarian teratoma is a common trigger in young women, so pelvic imaging and tumour screening are mandatory even when the initial scan is unremarkable MRI is often normal or only subtly abnormal, so a normal scan must not dissuade from the diagnosis in a compatible clinical picture Management combines tumour removal where a teratoma is found with first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange) and escalation to second-line agents such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide Recovery is often slow and stepwise over many months, typically reversing the order in which deficits appeared Autonomic instability with cardiac arrhythmia, blood-pressure swings, or central hypoventilation requiring critical care Refractory seizures or status epilepticus Rapidly declining consciousness and the need for airway protection New or recurrent psychiatric decompensation after apparent recovery, suggesting relapse or an undetected tumour Attributing the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder and delaying immunological investigation Excluding the diagnosis because MRI is normal Testing serum alone and missing antibodies detectable only in cerebrospinal fluid Failing to search repeatedly for an ovarian teratoma when the first imaging is negative Prematurely stopping escalation of therapy in patients who respond slowly The disorder is driven by immunoglobulin G antibodies against the GluN1 subunit of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. Antibody binding causes reversible cross-linking and internalisation of surface receptors, reducing NMDA-mediated synaptic transmission particularly across frontostriatal and limbic circuits, which is thought to underlie the psychiatric, movement, and memory features. Because the mechanism is functional receptor loss rather than fixed neuronal destruction, deficits are potentially reversible once antibody production is suppressed. In a substantial proportion of young women the immune response is triggered by neural tissue within an ovarian teratoma, while other cases follow herpes simplex encephalitis or arise without an identified trigger. Most patients improve substantially with tumour removal and immunotherapy, though recovery frequently takes many months and cognitive or behavioural sequelae may persist. Early treatment and identification of an associated teratoma are associated with better outcomes, while relapses occur in a minority and warrant repeat tumour surveillance.

Antiphospholipid Syndrome — APS, Hughes syndrome Inherited or acquired thrombophilias including factor V Leiden and other causes Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia Thrombocytopenia of other cause Atherosclerosis Polyarteritis nodosa SLE Cryoglobulinemia Lymphomas Myeloproliferative disorders Hypercholesterolemia For catastrophic APS: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic-uremic syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Lupus anticoagulant testing as a three-step procedure: screening with activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and dilute Russell viper venom test (DRVVT), mixing study, and confirmation Anticardiolipin and anti-beta2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies by standardized ELISA Antiphosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibodies when APS features are present without classical aPL Repeat aPL testing 12 weeks apart to confirm persistence Assessment per 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (>=3 points from clinical domains and >=3 points from laboratory domains) Renal biopsy for suspected aPL-nephropathy (thrombotic microangiopathy in acute phase; fibrous intima hyperplasia, fibrous/fibrocellular arteriolar occlusions, focal cortical atrophy in chronic phase) Cardiac MRI or histology for suspected myocardial disease; imaging for adrenal hemorrhage; BAL or pathology for pulmonary hemorrhage Other inherited or acquired thrombophilias (e.g., factor V Leiden) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Hemolytic-uremic syndrome Disseminated intravascular coagulation Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Livedo reticularis from vascular-wall disease (atherosclerosis, polyarteritis nodosa, SLE, cryoglobulinemia, lymphomas) or vascular-lumen disease (myeloproliferative disorders, hypercholesterolemia) APS is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia defined by recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis, microvascular manifestations, and/or pregnancy morbidity; it affects primarily young females (Harrison 22e p.2837). APS may occur alone (primary) or in association with other autoimmune diseases, mainly SLE; about one-third of SLE patients carry aPL antibodies and 10-15% of those develop APS (Harrison 22e p.2837). Diagnosis should be seriously considered with thrombosis, cerebrovascular accidents in individuals younger than 55 years, or pregnancy morbidity, particularly in the presence of livedo reticularis or thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2838). The three classical laboratory antibodies are lupus anticoagulant (LA), anticardiolipin (aCL), and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I (anti-beta2GPI); higher-risk profiles include triple positivity, IgG isotype, moderate-to-high titers, and persistent positivity (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839). Laboratory criteria require persistence: moderate (40-79 units) or high (>=80 units) aCL/anti-beta2GPI titers confirmed on two occasions 12 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839). In patients receiving anticoagulation, LA test positivity should be interpreted with caution; when features are highly reminiscent of APS but classical aPL are absent, antiphosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibody testing may have a diagnostic role (Harrison 22e p.2837). Deep venous thrombosis occurs primarily in the lower extremities and often causes pulmonary emboli; cerebral venous thrombosis may present with intracranial hypertension and focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.2837). Arterial thrombosis most commonly affects cerebral arteries, manifesting as transient ischemic attack, stroke, migraine, or cognitive dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2837). Libman-Sacks endocarditis (small, usually <1 cm, organized platelet-fibrin valve vegetations) and valve thickening are characteristic cardiac manifestations (Harrison 22e p.2837). Thrombocytopenia and autoimmune hemolytic anemia are the main hematologic manifestations of APS (Harrison 22e p.2837). DOACs have recently been shown to increase the risk of arterial events, especially in patients with triple positivity or previous arterial thrombosis, and a meta-analysis found prior thrombosis type did not change this increased arterial risk versus VKAs (Harrison 22e p.2839). Catastrophic APS (CAPS): a rare, life-threatening, rapidly progressive thromboembolic disease simultaneously involving three or more organs, typically with microvascular thrombosis developing in less than a week Thrombotic microangiopathy (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with severe thrombocytopenia) as a typical CAPS finding Cerebrovascular accident in an individual younger than 55 years Acute limb ischemia or digital gangrene from peripheral arterial thrombosis Budd-Chiari syndrome from hepatic vein thrombosis Pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary arterial thrombosis Paradoxical pitfall: lupus anticoagulant prolongs in vitro clotting tests (e.g., aPTT) yet is associated with thrombosis in vivo, not bleeding; the prolongation is NOT corrected by mixing with normal plasma, distinguishing it from a factor deficiency. aPTT has variable sensitivity to lupus anticoagulant depending on the reagent used; aPTT prolongation is not specific because factor deficiencies or other inhibitors also prolong it, so confirmation requires lack of correction on mixing and correction with added phospholipids (Harrison 22e p.~700). In patients receiving anticoagulation, lupus anticoagulant positivity should be interpreted with caution. Classification requires that clinical manifestations with other equally or more likely explanations than APS not be counted toward the criteria. aPL antibodies are frequently transiently positive, so persistence must be confirmed (titers on two occasions 12 weeks apart) before attributing disease. APS is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia. The major autoantibodies target phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, chiefly beta2-glycoprotein I (beta2GPI, a 43-kDa apolipoprotein of 326 amino acids in five domains) and prothrombin; anti-domain I IgG is associated with increased thrombotic risk, while the antithrombotic function of beta2GPI depends on its fifth domain. Lupus anticoagulant is a separate group of antibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins that prolongs in vitro clotting time which is not corrected by adding normal plasma. Antibody induction is thought to begin with endothelial injury (from infections, oxidative stress, or major physical stress such as surgery or trauma) in a permissive genetic background (HLA associations), driving increased endothelial apoptosis, autoantigen presentation, and an autoimmune response. Binding of aPL to disrupted endothelium produces a proinflammatory, prothrombotic state with monocyte and platelet activation, adhesion molecules and proinflammatory cytokines, complement and neutrophil activation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and thrombus formation. Type I interferon pathway activation and an imbalance between type I and III interferons have recently been proposed as mechanisms of thrombosis and obstetric complications (Harrison 22e p.2837). Thrombotic and obstetric event risk is closely tied to the underlying aPL profile, depending on antibody type (IgG high risk vs IgM low risk), number of antibodies (two or three classical autoantibodies confer higher risk than a single antibody), titer (moderate-high vs low), and persistence on repeated measurements. Catastrophic APS is life-threatening and rapidly progressive. APS antibodies increase with age, though it is questionable whether they induce thrombotic events in elderly individuals (Harrison 22e p.2837-2839). 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria require at least 3 points from clinical domains AND at least 3 points from laboratory domains. Clinical domains: (1) venous thromboembolism, (2) arterial thrombosis, (3) microvascular events, (4) obstetric complications, (5) cardiac valve disease, (6) hematologic manifestations. Laboratory domains: (1) lupus anticoagulant, (2) anticardiolipin, and/or (3) anti-beta2GPI antibodies at moderate (40-79 units) or high (>=80 units) titers on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Definite CAPS requires all four: thrombosis in >=3 organs/systems; development in less than a week; histologic small-vessel thrombosis in at least one organ; and aPL presence (probable CAPS when a combination is present) (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).

Antisynthetase syndrome — anti-Jo-1 syndrome, anti-tRNA synthetase syndrome, anti-synthetase syndrome, anti-PL-7 / anti-PL-12 / anti-EJ / anti-OJ syndrome Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis and dermatomyositis) without synthetase antibodies Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Systemic sclerosis and overlap connective tissue disease Rheumatoid arthritis with lung involvement Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease Drug-induced or hypersensitivity pneumonitis Myositis-specific and myositis-associated antibody panel including anti-Jo-1 and other anti-synthetase antibodies Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes to assess myositis activity High-resolution CT of the chest to characterise interstitial lung disease Pulmonary function tests including gas transfer to quantify and monitor lung involvement MRI of muscle and/or electromyography and muscle biopsy to confirm myositis Nailfold capillaroscopy and autoimmune screen to define overlap features Defined by antibodies to aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (most commonly anti-Jo-1) together with a characteristic clinical constellation The typical features are inflammatory myositis, interstitial lung disease, non-erosive arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and 'mechanic's hands' Interstitial lung disease is frequently the dominant and prognosis-determining manifestation and may occur without overt muscle weakness (amyopathic presentations) Mechanic's hands describes hyperkeratotic, fissured, roughened skin along the radial and palmar aspects of the fingers Non-anti-Jo-1 antibodies (anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12, anti-EJ, anti-OJ) may present with more prominent lung disease and less myositis Creatine kinase is usually elevated when myositis is active, and myositis-specific antibody panels aid diagnosis Management centres on systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppression, tailored to the severity of lung and muscle involvement Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with worsening dyspnoea and hypoxaemia Respiratory failure requiring urgent immunosuppression Severe or rapidly progressive muscle weakness including respiratory or bulbar muscles Pulmonary hypertension complicating chronic lung disease Missing the diagnosis in amyopathic patients who present with lung disease and normal creatine kinase Failing to test the full anti-synthetase antibody panel when anti-Jo-1 is negative Underestimating interstitial lung disease, the main determinant of outcome Attributing mechanic's hands to occupational or eczematous skin change Not screening for pulmonary hypertension in longstanding lung disease Antisynthetase syndrome is an autoimmune connective tissue disease characterised by autoantibodies directed against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzymes, which normally catalyse the attachment of amino acids to their transfer RNA during protein synthesis. In genetically predisposed individuals, an environmental trigger is thought to provoke an immune response against these cytoplasmic enzymes, generating both a humoral (antibody) and cell-mediated attack. The resulting inflammation targets skeletal muscle, the lung interstitium, joints, and skin, producing myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and mechanic's hands. Prognosis is largely determined by the severity and progression of interstitial lung disease; many patients stabilise with immunosuppression, but rapidly progressive lung disease carries significant mortality, and relapses are common on treatment reduction.

Antithrombin deficiency — AT deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, ATIII deficiency, hereditary antithrombin deficiency Protein C deficiency Protein S deficiency Factor V Leiden and activated protein C resistance Prothrombin gene mutation Antiphospholipid syndrome Acquired antithrombin loss (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, DIC) Functional antithrombin activity assay as the key diagnostic test Antithrombin antigen level to distinguish type I from type II deficiency A broader thrombophilia panel (protein C, protein S, factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid antibodies) Repeat testing away from acute thrombosis and heparin therapy to confirm a persistent defect Renal and liver assessment to exclude acquired causes Family testing of first-degree relatives once a hereditary defect is confirmed An inherited thrombophilia in which reduced antithrombin activity removes a key brake on coagulation, producing a strong predisposition to venous thromboembolism Among the heritable thrombophilias it confers one of the highest relative risks of thrombosis, often presenting at a young age or in unusual sites such as mesenteric or cerebral veins Thrombosis is frequently provoked by additional risk factors including pregnancy, the postpartum period, surgery, immobility, and oestrogen-containing contraception A characteristic clue is apparent resistance to unfractionated heparin, because heparin works by potentiating antithrombin, which is deficient Diagnosis uses a functional antithrombin activity assay; levels can be lowered acutely by active clot, heparin therapy, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, and disseminated intravascular coagulation Testing is best deferred until after the acute event and away from anticoagulant interference to avoid misclassification, and family screening is worthwhile Acute venous thromboembolism is treated with anticoagulation, and antithrombin concentrate may be used in high-risk situations such as surgery or delivery when heparin alone is inadequate Long-term anticoagulation is considered after unprovoked or recurrent thrombosis given the high recurrence risk Acute venous thromboembolism, including extensive deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism Thrombosis at unusual sites such as cerebral, mesenteric, or hepatic veins Apparent heparin resistance with failure to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation Pregnancy or the peripartum period, when thrombotic risk is greatly increased and needs proactive management Interpreting a low antithrombin level measured during acute thrombosis or heparin therapy as hereditary deficiency without confirmatory repeat testing Failing to recognise heparin resistance as a clue to the diagnosis Overlooking acquired causes such as nephrotic syndrome or liver disease Not providing intensified prophylaxis or antithrombin support during pregnancy, surgery, or delivery Omitting family counselling and screening after a hereditary defect is identified Antithrombin is a circulating serine protease inhibitor that neutralises thrombin and factor Xa (and other activated clotting factors), acting as a principal natural anticoagulant; its activity is greatly accelerated by heparin and endothelial heparan sulphate. Inherited deficiency, usually autosomal dominant, arises from mutations that reduce either the amount (type I) or the function (type II) of the protein. With less effective inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa, coagulation proceeds unchecked, tipping haemostatic balance towards thrombosis. Acquired reductions occur through loss (nephrotic syndrome), reduced synthesis (liver disease), or consumption (acute thrombosis, DIC, heparin therapy). Antithrombin deficiency carries a high lifetime and recurrence risk of venous thromboembolism relative to other inherited thrombophilias; with appropriate anticoagulation, risk-situation prophylaxis, and use of antithrombin concentrate when indicated, most affected individuals can be managed effectively.

Antley-Bixler syndrome — trapezoidocephaly-synostosis syndrome, POR-related disordered steroidogenesis, ABS Pfeiffer syndrome (FGFR craniosynostosis) Crouzon syndrome (FGFR2) Fluconazole embryopathy (medication phenocopy) Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (disordered cholesterol synthesis) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (for the steroidogenic abnormality) Other congenital radioulnar/radiohumeral synostosis syndromes Molecular testing of POR and FGFR2 to establish the underlying cause Adrenal and sex-steroid profiling, including precursors, to detect disordered steroidogenesis Three-dimensional cranial CT to define suture fusion Skeletal survey to document radiohumeral synostosis, bowing and fractures Airway and choanal assessment, including nasal endoscopy or imaging for choanal atresia Detailed maternal medication history focused on antifungal exposure in pregnancy Characterised by craniosynostosis (often bicoronal), midface hypoplasia and, distinctively, radiohumeral or radioulnar synostosis limiting elbow movement Two aetiologies exist: a recessive form from cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR) deficiency, and cases associated with FGFR2 mutations The POR-deficiency form causes a disorder of steroidogenesis, so ambiguous genitalia and abnormal steroid profiles can occur, and it may be associated with maternal virilisation in pregnancy Fluconazole exposure in pregnancy produces a phenocopy, so a medication history is important Additional features include arachnodactyly, joint contractures, femoral bowing and fractures, and choanal atresia or stenosis Choanal atresia and midface hypoplasia together create a substantial neonatal airway risk Distinguishing POR deficiency is critical because it requires assessment of adrenal steroid synthesis and potential steroid support Care is multidisciplinary, combining craniofacial surgery, orthopaedic management and endocrine evaluation Neonatal airway obstruction from choanal atresia with midface hypoplasia Adrenal insufficiency or salt-wasting crisis in the POR-deficiency form Raised intracranial pressure from craniosynostosis Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent endocrine and multidisciplinary assessment Failing to distinguish POR deficiency and thereby missing a treatable steroidogenic disorder Overlooking maternal azole exposure as a cause of a phenocopy Underestimating the neonatal airway risk from combined choanal and midface anomalies Not evaluating genital and adrenal status when steroid synthesis may be affected Antley-Bixler syndrome is genetically heterogeneous. The recessive form is caused by deficiency of cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR), the electron-donor enzyme required by multiple microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes, including those of steroid and sterol synthesis; impaired activity disrupts steroidogenesis (causing genital and hormonal abnormalities) and sterol-dependent developmental signalling, producing the skeletal malformations. Other cases arise from activating FGFR2 mutations that cause premature suture fusion. Prenatal exposure to certain azole antifungals inhibiting sterol synthesis can mimic the skeletal phenotype. Neonatal outcome is dominated by airway and, in POR deficiency, endocrine risks; with early airway management, endocrine support and staged craniofacial and orthopaedic surgery, survival and function can be good, though outcomes vary with severity and subtype.

Antrochoanal polyp — Killian polyp, ACP, maxillary antrochoanal polyp Bilateral ethmoidal inflammatory nasal polyps Inverted papilloma Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in an adolescent male Nasal or nasopharyngeal malignancy Rhinosporidiosis Encephalocoele or meningocoele in a midline mass Nasal endoscopy to characterise the polyp and its posterior extension Computed tomography of the sinuses to confirm the antral origin and define anatomy for surgery Biopsy or histology of the excised specimen to confirm the benign nature and exclude neoplasia Assessment for coexisting sinus disease or allergy where relevant A solitary benign polyp that arises from the maxillary antrum, passes through its ostium (usually the accessory ostium), and extends back into the choana and nasopharynx It is most common in children and young adults and is typically unilateral, unlike bilateral ethmoidal inflammatory polyps Presents with progressive unilateral nasal obstruction that may become bilateral, and a large polyp can be seen or felt in the nasopharynx and occasionally hangs behind the soft palate It has three parts, an antral part, a part in the nasal cavity, and a choanal part, which explains its dumbbell shape Nasal endoscopy shows a smooth pale polyp, and computed tomography demonstrates the antral origin and opacified maxillary sinus The definitive treatment is complete removal including the antral origin, as leaving the maxillary attachment leads to recurrence Endoscopic sinus surgery with removal of the antral component has largely replaced simple avulsion because it lowers recurrence A unilateral nasal mass should always be evaluated to exclude more sinister pathology before assuming it is an antrochoanal polyp A unilateral nasal mass that bleeds readily, particularly in an adolescent male, suggesting angiofibroma rather than a benign polyp Rapid growth, bony destruction, orbital or neurological signs suggesting malignancy A midline mass that could be a meningocoele or encephalocoele before any biopsy Recurrent unilateral polyp raising suspicion of inverted papilloma or missed antral attachment Assuming a unilateral mass is a simple polyp and biopsying a vascular angiofibroma or a meningocoele Removing only the nasal part and leaving the antral origin, leading to recurrence Overlooking malignancy in an adult with a unilateral nasal mass Failing to obtain cross-sectional imaging before surgery An antrochoanal polyp is thought to originate from a cystic or oedematous swelling of the maxillary antral mucosa, often related to chronic inflammation or an antral cyst. The polyp enlarges within the antrum and then prolapses through the maxillary ostium, most often a widened accessory ostium, into the nasal cavity. Continued growth carries it posteriorly through the choana into the nasopharynx, producing its characteristic dumbbell configuration with a narrow neck at the ostium. It is a benign, single, unilateral lesion and, unlike multiple inflammatory polyps, is only loosely linked to allergy. The lesion is benign and the outlook is very good after complete surgical removal; recurrence is uncommon when the antral origin is fully excised but is more frequent after simple avulsion that leaves the maxillary attachment behind.

Aortic dissection — CT aortogram (urgent) BP in both arms Control HR & BP Tearing chest/back pain with pulse/BP differential — emergency imaging Acute myocardial infarction / acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, and dissection can occlude a coronary ostium) (Harrison 22e p.2169) Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.108) Pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.106) Esophageal pain / spasm, which can mimic angina (Harrison 22e p.106) CT (with contrast) — most commonly used given proximity of scanners to emergency rooms and rapidity; sensitivity and specificity >90% for the intimal flap and extent (Harrison 22e p.2169) MRI — highly accurate for intimal flap, extent, intramural hemorrhage and penetrating ulcers; sensitivity and specificity >90% (Harrison 22e p.2169) Transesophageal echocardiography — ~98% sensitivity and ~90% specificity for ascending and descending dissection (but not the arch); also assesses aortic regurgitation and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169) Transthoracic echocardiography — rapid bedside test, overall sensitivity 60-85% (>80% for proximal ascending dissection), less useful for arch and descending aorta (Harrison 22e p.2169) Chest x-ray — may show widened superior mediastinum and/or pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169) ECG — to look for ischemia and help differentiate from MI (Harrison 22e p.2169) Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168) Acute intramural hematoma of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168) Aortic rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168) Pain characteristically migrates as the dissection propagates, often shifting to the interscapular region of the back (Harrison 22e p.2169). Systemic hypertension coexists in about 70% of patients with aortic dissection (Harrison 22e p.2168). Peak incidence is in the sixth and seventh decades, with men affected about twice as often as women (Harrison 22e p.2169). A normal ECG showing no ischemia helps distinguish dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain, though dissection can rarely involve a coronary ostium and cause an actual MI (Harrison 22e p.2169). On chest x-ray, ascending dissection often produces a widened superior mediastinum; a pleural effusion (usually left-sided) may appear and is typically serosanguineous rather than a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169). Although 'tearing' or 'ripping' pain is classic, acute aortic emergencies also commonly present with knifelike pain (Harrison 22e p.106). Stanford type A or B classification is more practical for management than DeBakey, because DeBakey types I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168). Sudden, very severe tearing chest or interscapular back pain with diaphoresis, especially when it migrates (Harrison 22e p.2169) New aortic regurgitation murmur (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur along the right sternal border) in a patient with chest pain — common (>50%) in proximal dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169) Pulse deficit or loss of pulses (Harrison 22e p.2169) Hypotension with hemopericardium / cardiac tamponade signs (suggests retrograde type A dissection) (Harrison 22e p.2169) Acute neurologic deficit — hemiplegia/hemianesthesia (carotid involvement) or paraplegia (spinal cord ischemia) (Harrison 22e p.2169) Acute pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.2169, p.107) Falling hematocrit with hypotension and pleural effusion (suggests rupture) (Harrison 22e p.2169) Aortic dissection is a classic disease that is misdiagnosed as acute myocardial infarction — a dangerous error because anticoagulant/thrombolytic therapy for presumed MI can be catastrophic (Harrison 22e p.102, p.2169). A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and does not by itself indicate rupture unless there is accompanying hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169). Transthoracic echocardiography is insensitive for arch and descending dissections, so a negative TTE does not exclude dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169). Dissection begins with a tear of the intima, most often along the high-shear right lateral wall of the ascending aorta or in the descending thoracic aorta just below the ligamentum arteriosum. Pulsatile flow dissects along the elastic lamellar plates of the media to create a false lumen; the initiating event may be a primary intimal tear with secondary dissection into the media, or a medial hemorrhage that secondarily disrupts the intima. The dissection usually propagates distally (sometimes proximally), may be limited distally by atherosclerotic plaque, and can re-enter the true lumen through a secondary distal intimal disruption. Underlying medial degeneration and conditions that raise aortic wall stress predispose to dissection. Two related radiologic/pathologic variants are intramural hematoma (rupture of vasa vasorum bleeding into the wall, without an intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (plaque erosion into the media); both can progress to dissection and rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168-2169). In-hospital mortality after surgical treatment of dissection is reported at about 15-25%; for medically treated uncomplicated type B dissection it is about 12%. Major perioperative causes of death and morbidity include myocardial infarction, paraplegia, renal failure, tamponade, hemorrhage, and sepsis. With careful follow-up the long-term outlook after discharge is generally good, with roughly 60% 10-year survival; patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for post-dissection complications (Harrison 22e p.2170). Stanford classification: type A involves the ascending aorta (proximal dissection) regardless of tear site or distal extension; type B is limited to the arch and/or descending aorta (distal dissection). DeBakey classification: type I — intimal tear in ascending aorta with propagation to arch, descending and possibly abdominal aorta; type II — limited to the ascending aorta; type III — tear in the descending aorta with distal propagation. Stanford A/B is more practical for management since DeBakey I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).

Aortic Regurgitation — AR, aortic insufficiency Aortic stenosis (a mid-systolic ejection murmur and systolic thrill are frequently audible in isolated AR and do not necessarily signify coexisting AS) Combined aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation (coexistence of hemodynamically significant AS with AR occurs almost exclusively in rheumatic or congenital disease) Mitral regurgitation (contrasted hemodynamically; severe AR can also coexist with MR) ECG: LV hypertrophy signs in chronic severe AR, with ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5, V6 ('LV strain'); left axis deviation and/or QRS prolongation may be present (p.2044) Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE): cornerstone of longitudinal follow-up; assesses LV size/function and cause/severity of AR; LV global longitudinal strain (GLS) by speckle tracking may detect systolic dysfunction before EF falls (p.2044) Color flow Doppler: with severe AR the central jet width exceeds 65% of the LV outflow tract, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50%, and there is diastolic flow reversal in the proximal descending thoracic aorta; continuous-wave Doppler shows rapid deceleration time in acute severe AR (p.2044) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): detailed anatomic assessment of valve, root, and portions of the aorta (p.2044) Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR): accurate LV volumes and aortic size/contour when TTE is limited; can screen for increased LV interstitial (extracellular volume fraction) and replacement fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement) (p.2044) Cardiac CT: detailed assessment of aortic valve, root, and thoracic aortic anatomy; coronary CT angiography can provide preoperative coronary information (p.2044-2045) Chest X-ray: downward and leftward apex displacement, posterior LV displacement encroaching on the spine, and possible aneurysmal aortic dilation when root disease is the cause (less sensitive than echo/CMR/CT for root/ascending aortic enlargement) (p.2045) Cardiac catheterization with contrast aortography: confirms magnitude of regurgitation and LV status when needed; coronary angiography routinely before surgery in those at coronary risk (p.2045) Chronic severe AR can have a long latent period, with patients remaining relatively asymptomatic for 10-15 years; exertional dyspnea is usually the first symptom of diminished cardiac reserve, followed by orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (p.2044). A wide arterial pulse pressure (systolic hypertension plus low diastolic pressure) is characteristic of chronic severe AR, producing peripheral signs such as the water-hammer (Corrigan's) pulse, Quincke's capillary pulsations, Traube's pistol-shot femoral sounds, and Duroziez's sign (p.2043-2044). The murmur of chronic AR is a high-pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur heard best in the third intercostal space along the left sternal border; it is best appreciated with the patient sitting up, leaning forward, breath held in forced expiration (p.2044). A diastolic murmur louder along the right sternal border suggests AR caused by aneurysmal dilation of the aortic root rather than primary valvular disease (p.2044). The Austin Flint murmur is a soft, low-pitched rumbling mid-to-late diastolic murmur in severe AR, probably from diastolic displacement of the anterior mitral leaflet by the regurgitant stream; it is NOT associated with hemodynamically significant mitral obstruction (p.2044). Anginal chest pain can occur in severe AR even without coronary artery disease and even in younger patients, may occur at rest, and often responds poorly to sublingual nitroglycerin (p.2044). On echocardiography, a rapid high-frequency diastolic fluttering of the anterior mitral leaflet, produced by the impact of the regurgitant jet, is a characteristic finding (p.2044). Auscultatory features of AR are intensified by sustained handgrip, which augments systemic vascular resistance and increases LV afterload (p.2044). In acute severe AR, the elevated LV end-diastolic pressure leads to early (premature) closure of the mitral valve, a soft S1, and a soft, short early diastolic murmur (p.2044). Acute severe AR (as in infective endocarditis, aortic dissection, or trauma): the LV cannot dilate enough to maintain stroke volume, LV diastolic pressure rises rapidly with marked LA and PA wedge pressure elevation, and pulmonary edema and/or cardiogenic shock may develop rapidly - a surgical emergency requiring operation usually within 24 h (prompt 24-48 h surgery may be lifesaving) (p.2044, p.2046-2047). Acute severe AR may show only slight widening of pulse pressure and invariably presents with tachycardia (heart rate increases to preserve cardiac output), unlike the wide pulse pressure of chronic AR (p.2044). In acute severe AR, intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation is contraindicated and beta blockers are best avoided (p.2045). Onset of symptoms or LV systolic dysfunction in chronic severe AR is an indication for surgery (p.2045). Sphygmomanometer diastolic pressure can be hard to read because systolic sounds may persist with the cuff fully deflated; the muffling point (Korotkoff phase IV) corresponds reasonably to true intra-arterial diastolic pressure (p.2044). As chronic AR progresses and LV end-diastolic pressure rises, the arterial diastolic pressure may actually rise (aortic diastolic pressure cannot fall below LV end-diastolic pressure), so a less-wide pulse pressure does not exclude severe disease (p.2044). A mid-systolic ejection murmur and systolic thrill in isolated AR can be loud without signifying aortic valve obstruction and do not necessarily indicate coexisting AS (p.2044). Deterioration of LV function often precedes the development of symptoms, so waiting for symptoms risks irreversible dysfunction; serial noninvasive follow-up is essential to time surgery (p.2043-2044, p.2046). Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is NOT recommended for patients with severe AR who are surgical candidates (technical success limited by annular dilation and paucity of valvular/annular calcium) (p.2046). The total LV stroke volume (effective forward stroke volume plus regurgitant volume) is increased; in severe AR the regurgitant volume may equal the effective forward stroke volume. Unlike MR, the entire LV stroke volume is ejected into the high-pressure aorta. The major compensation is an increase in LV end-diastolic volume (increased preload); dilation and eccentric hypertrophy allow a larger stroke volume without increased myofibril shortening, so severe AR can occur with a normal effective forward stroke volume and normal LVEF together with elevated LV end-diastolic pressure and volume. By Laplace's law LV dilation increases systolic wall tension, so chronic AR is a state of both increased preload and afterload. Adaptive measures eventually fail; deterioration of LV function often precedes symptom onset. Considerable LV wall thickening occurs and hearts can weigh >1000 g. The reverse aorta-to-LV diastolic pressure gradient decreases through diastole, accounting for the decrescendo murmur. In acute severe AR the LV is unprepared for the volume load, compliance is normal or reduced, diastolic pressures rise rapidly (occasionally >40 mmHg), and the reversed pressure gradient closes the mitral valve prematurely. Myocardial ischemia may occur because of elevated oxygen demand (LV dilation, hypertrophy, increased systolic tension) combined with reduced coronary perfusion (most coronary flow is diastolic, when aortic pressure is low), affecting particularly the subendocardium even without epicardial CAD (p.2043-2044). Operative and late mortality risks depend largely on disease stage and myocardial function at operation. Overall operative mortality for isolated AVR for pure AR is ~1-2%; the risk doubles when aortic surgery is added. Patients with marked cardiac enlargement and established LV dysfunction have an operative mortality of ~5-10% and a late mortality of ~3-5% per year from LV failure despite technically satisfactory operation; nonetheless, because of the very poor prognosis with medical management, even patients with advanced LV systolic dysfunction should be considered for operation. If surgery is delayed too long (>1 year from onset of symptoms or LV dysfunction), it often does not restore normal LV size and function (p.2046-2047). Severe AR is characterized by central jet width >65% of the LV outflow tract on color Doppler, vena contracta >0.6 cm, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50%, effective regurgitant orifice >=0.3 cm2, and holodiastolic flow reversal in the proximal descending thoracic aorta. AHA/ACC staging (per Fig. 273-2): asymptomatic (Stage C, with C2 denoting LV dysfunction EF <=55%) versus symptomatic (Stage D). Surgical thresholds for asymptomatic severe AR include LVEF <55%, LV end-systolic dimension >50 mm (>25 mm/m2), or LV end-diastolic dimension >65 mm on serial studies (p.2044, p.2046).

Aortic stenosis (syncope) — Echocardiogram ECG Examine for ejection systolic murmur Exertional syncope is a red flag Aortic sclerosis (focal leaflet thickening/calcification without obstruction; Doppler jet velocity 2.5 m/s or less) can produce a grade 2-3 midsystolic murmur acoustically identical to AS (Harrison 22e p.1908). Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (subvalvular dynamic outflow obstruction) (Harrison 22e p.328, 1934). Subaortic membrane (fixed subvalvular obstruction that can mimic valvular AS) (Harrison 22e p.1934). Supravalvular aortic stenosis (exceedingly rare) (Harrison 22e p.1934). Pulmonic stenosis (midsystolic murmur, second left interspace) (Harrison 22e p.329). Atrial septal defect with increased pulmonic flow producing a midsystolic murmur with fixed splitting of S2 (Harrison 22e p.329). Mitral regurgitation, given the apical Gallavardin transmission of the AS murmur (Harrison 22e p.328). Transthoracic echocardiography to assess valve anatomy (tricuspid/bicuspid, leaflet calcification, excursion), stenosis severity, LV size/wall thickness/function, and aortic root and proximal ascending aorta (Harrison 22e p.329, 1933). Doppler estimation of transvalvular peak velocity and pressure gradient (Harrison 22e p.1933). Continuity-equation estimation of aortic valve area, the most accurate echo technique, especially when gradients are underestimated by LV dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). Dobutamine stress echocardiography to evaluate low-flow/low-gradient AS and determine whether the valve can open further (Harrison 22e p.1934). Cardiac MRI for quantitative assessment of severity (Harrison 22e p.1933). Carotid pulse examination for parvus et tardus contour (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905). Hyperdynamic flow murmurs without structural disease (fever, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, anemia, normal childhood/adolescence) can produce midsystolic murmurs (Harrison 22e p.1908). The murmur of AS is a crescendo-decrescendo (midsystolic/ejection) murmur, usually loudest in the second right intercostal space and radiating into the carotids; it is the most common midsystolic murmur in adults (Harrison 22e p.328). Apical transmission of the AS murmur, where it becomes higher-pitched, is common (Gallavardin effect) and may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation; the AS murmur intensifies in the beat following a premature beat and varies directly with cardiac output, whereas the MR murmur stays constant beat-to-beat (Harrison 22e p.328). Auscultatory features pointing to severe AS include a soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, a late-peaking systolic murmur, an apical S4, and (at normal output) a systolic thrill and a grade 4 or louder murmur (Harrison 22e p.328). An early ejection sound (click) in children/young adults signifies a flexible, noncalcified bicuspid valve and localizes obstruction to the valvular level rather than sub- or supravalvular (Harrison 22e p.328). Bicuspid aortic valve is one of the most common congenital anomalies and predisposes to both aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.1933). AS can precipitate myocardial ischemia and anginal chest pain even without obstructive coronary atherosclerosis, by creating extreme myocardial oxygen demand with impaired endocardial blood flow (type 2 ischemia mechanism) (Harrison 22e p.285). Heyde's syndrome is the association of aortic stenosis with bleeding gastrointestinal vascular ectasias (acquired von Willebrand disease); such patients appear to benefit from aortic valve replacement (Harrison 22e p.361). A weak and delayed carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905). Soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, late-peaking murmur, and an apical S4 indicate severe AS (Harrison 22e p.328). A softening AS murmur in the setting of heart failure/low cardiac output is misleading and does not indicate mild disease (Harrison 22e p.328). Syncope (including reflex/exertional) from AS reflects structural compromise of cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.203-204). Avoid aggressive preload/afterload reduction: aggressive treatment of cardiac failure with diuretics and/or vasodilators can precipitate orthostatic hypotension in patients with structural disease such as AS (Harrison 22e p.203). Transvalvular pressure gradients underestimate severity in severe LV dysfunction; rely on valve area by continuity equation (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). In low-flow/low-gradient AS the valve may behave stenotic simply because of the low gradient; provocative dobutamine testing is needed to distinguish true severe stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1934). The carotid parvus-et-tardus sign is less discriminatory in older patients with stiffened arteries (Harrison 22e p.329). Aortic sclerosis can produce a murmur indistinguishable on auscultation from significant AS (Harrison 22e p.1908). Aortic stenosis is most often caused by gradual progression of valvular calcification of either normal trileaflet or congenitally bicuspid valves, producing fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction. The pressure overload drives left ventricular hypertrophy, which manifests on the ECG as LVH that increases with severity. The combination of increased myocardial oxygen demand and impaired endocardial perfusion can cause ischemia/angina even with normal coronaries. Syncope in AS reflects a structural disorder compromising cardiac output, and inappropriate reflex vasodilation may be provoked by increased ventricular contractility against the fixed obstruction (Harrison 22e p.203-204, 285, 329, 1933). Patients with good left ventricular function can tolerate severe AS for a considerable period, so valve area or gradient alone should not dictate timing of surgery, which remains a clinical decision (Harrison 22e p.1934). Echo: peak instantaneous velocities of 3.0 m/s or higher (often >4.0 m/s) correspond to gradients of ~36 and ~64 mmHg and indicate at least moderate AS; aortic valve area <1.0 cm2 is generally severe and <0.6 cm2 critical (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). Catheterization: a valve area <1.0 cm2 with a mean gradient >40 mmHg indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.1950). Aortic sclerosis (non-obstructive) is defined by a Doppler jet velocity of 2.5 m/s or less (Harrison 22e p.1908).

Aortoiliac occlusive disease — aortoiliac occlusive disease, Leriche syndrome, inflow disease, aortoiliac atherosclerosis Femoropopliteal or infrapopliteal occlusive disease Spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication Hip or lumbar spine osteoarthritis Nerve root or sciatic pathology Chronic venous disease Buerger disease Ankle-brachial index with segmental pressures to localise the level of disease Arterial duplex ultrasound of the aortoiliac and femoral segments CT or MR angiography, or catheter angiography, for reconstructive planning Cardiovascular risk assessment including lipids, glucose, and smoking status Cardiac and functional assessment before major open reconstruction Represents atherosclerotic inflow disease of the distal aorta and iliac arteries and often coexists with more distal (femoropopliteal) disease The classic Leriche triad comprises buttock, hip, and thigh claudication, diminished or absent femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction in men Because obstruction is proximal, claudication is typically felt in the buttocks and thighs rather than the calves alone Well-developed collateral pathways can maintain limb viability despite extensive occlusion, so rest pain is less common than in multilevel disease Duplex ultrasound, CT angiography, or MR angiography define the pattern and length of disease to guide endovascular versus open reconstruction Focal iliac stenoses are well suited to endovascular treatment, while extensive aortoiliac occlusion may require aortobifemoral bypass or extra-anatomic reconstruction Risk-factor modification, particularly smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, and statins, underpins all management Presence of aortoiliac disease signals widespread atherosclerosis with a high burden of coronary and cerebrovascular risk Rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene indicating limb-threatening ischaemia and urgent vascular referral Acute-on-chronic occlusion with sudden severe limb ischaemia, a limb-threatening emergency Rapidly progressive symptoms or tissue loss Concurrent features of severe cardiovascular disease Misattributing buttock and thigh claudication to hip or spinal disease Overlooking coexisting infrainguinal disease that limits the benefit of inflow correction alone Underestimating cardiovascular risk and omitting systemic prevention Failing to recognise Leriche syndrome in men presenting with erectile dysfunction and claudication Aortoiliac occlusive disease is caused by progressive atherosclerotic plaque within the infrarenal aorta and common and external iliac arteries, reducing arterial inflow to the pelvis and lower limbs. Because the obstruction is proximal, symptoms involve the buttocks and thighs and, in men, erectile function through compromise of the internal iliac supply. Gradual stenosis stimulates collateral development via lumbar, mesenteric, and pelvic pathways, which can preserve limb perfusion. When inflow disease coexists with infrainguinal disease (multilevel disease), the additive resistance more readily precipitates rest pain and tissue loss. Isolated aortoiliac disease with good collateral flow often has a favourable limb outlook, and revascularisation, whether endovascular or bypass, provides durable symptom relief in appropriately selected patients. Overall survival is chiefly limited by concurrent coronary and cerebrovascular atherosclerosis.

endocrine function tests (calcium, parathyroid hormone, adrenal axis, thyroid, glucose) Fungal cultures and clinical assessment of mucocutaneous candidiasis Periodic screening for evolving autoimmune components Surveillance for oral squamous cell carcinoma in chronic oral candidiasis APECED is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene, which governs central immune tolerance in the thymus It is classically defined by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with diagnosis usually requiring two of the three Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is often the earliest feature and is driven by autoantibodies against Th17-related cytokines (such as IL-17 and IL-22) The candidiasis reflects immune dysregulation rather than a classical phagocyte or T-cell deficiency, and is largely limited to skin, nails, and mucosa without systemic dissemination A wide range of additional autoimmune conditions can occur, including gonadal failure, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, hepatitis, pernicious anaemia, and vitiligo A useful diagnostic marker is the presence of high-titre autoantibodies against type 1 interferons, which are highly characteristic of the condition Chronic oral candidiasis carries a long-term risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma, warranting Adrenal crisis from unrecognised or undertreated primary adrenal insufficiency requiring emergency treatment Symptomatic hypocalcaemia from hypoparathyroidism New oral lesions raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma Autoimmune hepatitis progressing to liver failure Emergence of a new autoimmune endocrinopathy needing prompt recognition Treating individual endocrinopathies in isolation without recognising the unifying syndrome Missing evolving components, since the full picture develops over years Overlooking adrenal insufficiency, with the danger of a precipitated crisis Failing to survey chronic oral candidiasis for malignant change Confusing APECED with IPEX, which is X-linked, FOXP3-related, and presents in infancy APECED results from biallelic mutations in AIRE (the autoimmune regulator), a transcriptional regulator expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells that drives the display of tissue-specific self antigens during T-cell development. Defective AIRE function impairs negative selection, allowing autoreactive T cells to escape into the periphery and mount organ-specific autoimmune attacks. The result is progressive autoimmune destruction of endocrine and other tissues. The characteristic mucocutaneous candidiasis is explained by the generation of neutralising autoantibodies against Th17 cytokines that are essential for mucosal antifungal defence, and neutralising autoantibodies against type 1 interferons serve as a highly specific biomarker. With appropriate hormone replacement and antifungal therapy the prognosis is generally reasonable, but outcome is shaped by the cumulative burden of autoimmune organ damage, the risk of unrecognised adrenal crisis, and the long-term risk of oral malignancy, so lifelong monitoring is required.

bony and soft-tissue syndactyly of the hands and feet, often a 'mitten' or 'sock' fusion involving digits two to four Midface retrusion narrows the airway and choanae, so obstructive sleep apnoea and feeding difficulty are common and should be screened for early A cleft or high-arched palate, acne, and hyperhidrosis are frequently seen, and variable intellectual disability occurs Raised cranial vault expansion, midface advancement and hand reconstruction over childhood Prenatal or postnatal diagnosis is confirmed by FGFR2 sequencing when the phenotype is characteristic Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema, headache or developmental regression Severe obstructive sleep apnoea or airway compromise from midface hypoplasia Corneal exposure and ulceration from marked proptosis Progressive hydrocephalus requiring neurosurgical intervention Attributing feeding problems or noisy breathing to reflux rather than recognising airway narrowing from midface hypoplasia Missing raised intracranial pressure because early signs can be subtle in infants Confusing Apert with Crouzon when the hands are not carefully examined for the characteristic syndactyly Underestimating the need for staged, lifelong multidisciplinary care Apert syndrome results from constitutive activation of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2). The gain-of-function change increases receptor signalling that normally regulates the balance between proliferation and differentiation in cranial suture mesenchyme and in developing limb tissue. Excess signalling drives premature ossification and fusion of the calvarial sutures (especially the coronal sutures) and disturbs apoptosis in the interdigital tissue, so the digits fail to separate and instead fuse. The same disordered signalling underlies the midface hypoplasia and other skeletal features. With coordinated craniofacial, neurosurgical and hand surgery, survival and functional outcomes are good, though cognitive outcome is variable and many children have some degree of learning difficulty. Lifelong follow-up is needed for airway, vision, hearing and intracranial pressure.
