disease Dismissing a persistent solitary ulcer as aphthous when it may be malignant Failing to screen for haematinic deficiency or coeliac disease in severe or new-onset cases Confusing herpetiform aphthae with herpes simplex infection Overlooking systemic disease such as Behcet when extra-oral features are present The precise cause is not fully understood, but recurrent aphthous stomatitis is considered a T-cell mediated immune reaction directed at the oral epithelium, producing focal ulceration. A genetic predisposition is common, and episodes are triggered by factors such as local trauma, stress, hormonal fluctuation, and specific foods. Systemic contributors, including deficiencies of iron, folate, or vitamin B12, and gastrointestinal or systemic inflammatory conditions, can precipitate or worsen ulceration. The lesions represent localised epithelial destruction with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate that heals as the immune response subsides. Most patients have self-limiting recurrent episodes that heal without scarring and can be controlled symptomatically, though major aphthae may scar and some cases reflect a treatable underlying systemic condition.

Aplastic anaemia — aplastic anemia, AA, bone marrow aplasia, hypoplastic anaemia Hypoplastic myelodysplastic syndrome Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Acute leukaemia (particularly hypocellular presentations) Marrow infiltration or fibrosis causing pancytopenia Severe megaloblastic anaemia (B12 or folate deficiency) Overwhelming infection or hypersplenism causing peripheral cytopenias Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film to confirm pancytopenia and exclude abnormal cells Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to demonstrate hypocellularity and exclude infiltration or dysplasia Cytogenetic and molecular studies to differentiate from myelodysplasia Peripheral blood flow cytometry for a PNH clone Chromosomal fragility testing and telomere length in suspected inherited syndromes Viral serology (including hepatitis) and screening for autoimmune disease Defined by pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow in the absence of abnormal infiltrating cells or fibrosis, reflecting failure of the haematopoietic stem cell compartment Presentation reflects the affected lineages: fatigue and breathlessness from anaemia, mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae from thrombocytopenia, and infections from neutropenia Most cases are acquired and immune-mediated, with T-cell attack on stem cells; drugs, chemicals (e.g. benzene), viral hepatitis (seronegative), and radiation are recognised triggers Inherited causes such as Fanconi anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita should be considered in younger patients or those with characteristic physical or family features Severity is graded by degree of neutropenia, reticulocytopenia, and thrombocytopenia; very severe disease carries the highest risk of early death from infection or haemorrhage Definitive management is either allogeneic stem cell transplant (favoured in younger patients with a matched sibling donor) or immunosuppressive therapy combining antithymocyte globulin and a calcineurin inhibitor A thrombopoietin receptor agonist can augment haematopoietic recovery when added to immunosuppression Overlap exists with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and hypoplastic myelodysplasia, so flow cytometry for PNH clones and marrow cytogenetics are important at diagnosis Severe neutropenia with fever, indicating potentially fatal sepsis requiring urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics Profound thrombocytopenia with mucosal bleeding or signs of intracranial haemorrhage Rapidly falling counts defining very severe aplastic anaemia and the need for prompt referral to a transplant centre Emergence of dysplastic or cytogenetic abnormalities suggesting clonal evolution to MDS or leukaemia Attributing pancytopenia to a peripheral cause and omitting a marrow biopsy that would reveal hypocellularity Overlooking a coexisting PNH clone or evolving myelodysplasia Delaying HLA typing and transplant referral in young patients with severe disease Failing to recognise an inherited marrow failure syndrome, which changes treatment and family counselling Giving platelet or red cell transfusions without irradiation or leucodepletion in a potential transplant candidate Aplastic anaemia results from destruction or profound suppression of pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells, leaving an empty (hypocellular) marrow and peripheral pancytopenia. In most acquired cases the mechanism is autoimmune: activated cytotoxic T lymphocytes and their cytokines (interferon-gamma, tumour necrosis factor) drive stem cell apoptosis. Environmental exposures, certain drugs, and viral illness can initiate this immune attack, while inherited marrow failure syndromes reflect defects in DNA repair or telomere maintenance that exhaust the stem cell pool. Clonal disorders such as PNH and MDS can emerge from a damaged marrow because surviving abnormal clones gain a survival advantage. Untreated severe aplastic anaemia is frequently fatal from infection or bleeding, but outcomes have transformed with early allogeneic transplantation and effective immunosuppression; younger patients with matched sibling donors have high survival, while older patients rely on immunosuppressive therapy with a meaningful risk of relapse and late clonal disease.

Apparent Life-Threatening Event — ALTE, BRUE, brief resolved unexplained event Gastro-oesophageal reflux with laryngospasm Respiratory infection (including pertussis, RSV) Seizure or other neurological event Cardiac arrhythmia or structural heart disease Inborn error of metabolism Non-accidental injury or inflicted harm Airway anomaly or feeding-related aspiration Thorough history and examination to risk-stratify and seek an underlying cause Observation and pulse oximetry as appropriate ECG when a cardiac cause or arrhythmia is a concern Targeted testing (e.g. for infection, reflux, or seizures) guided by history rather than routinely Evaluation for non-accidental injury when the history is inconsistent or concerning Metabolic screening only if clinical features suggest it The older term ALTE described a frightening episode in an infant involving some combination of apnoea, colour change, altered tone, and choking or gagging as perceived by the observer. Because ALTE was poorly defined, it has largely been replaced by the concept of a brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) in infants under one year. A BRUE applies only when the infant is asymptomatic on presentation, the episode was brief and has fully resolved, and no explanation is found after appropriate history and examination. A qualifying event involves one or more of: cyanosis or pallor, absent, decreased, or irregular breathing, marked change in tone, or altered responsiveness. The main clinical task is to distinguish low-risk infants, who need little or no intervention, from higher-risk infants requiring evaluation. Low-risk criteria generally include age over about two months, no prematurity, a single brief event, no need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a reassuring history and examination. A careful history and examination frequently reveal an underlying explanation such as reflux, a respiratory infection, a seizure, or feeding difficulty, in which case the event is not a BRUE. Extensive investigation is often unnecessary in low-risk infants, and shared decision-making with caregivers, including reassurance and safety advice, is central to management. Age under two months or history of prematurity Recurrent or multiple events, or a prolonged episode Cardiopulmonary resuscitation required by a trained provider Abnormal examination findings, ongoing symptoms, or failure to return to baseline History inconsistent with the injury or features suggesting non-accidental harm Family history of sudden unexplained death or a sibling with a similar event Applying the BRUE label when the infant is symptomatic or an explanation exists Over-investigating and hospitalising clearly low-risk infants Under-investigating higher-risk infants who need closer evaluation Missing non-accidental injury when the history does not fit the presentation Failing to provide caregiver reassurance, safety advice, and clear follow-up guidance These events are a clinical presentation rather than a single disease, and reflect a transient disturbance of cardiorespiratory or neurological control in the infant. Immature regulation of breathing, airway protective reflexes, and arousal can be perturbed by triggers such as gastro-oesophageal reflux, airway obstruction, infection, seizure activity, or autonomic instability, producing a brief episode that resolves as the infant recovers. When no cause is identified despite adequate assessment, the event is classified as unexplained. Most infants meeting low-risk BRUE criteria have an excellent outcome with a very low risk of recurrence or serious underlying disease, whereas higher-risk infants and those with an identified cause have a prognosis that depends on the specific diagnosis.

Apparent mineralocorticoid excess — AME, HSD11B2 deficiency, 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 deficiency, cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid excess Liddle syndrome (ENaC gain-of-function) Primary hyperaldosteronism Licorice or carbenoxolone ingestion (acquired AME) Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism Cushing syndrome Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with mineralocorticoid excess (11-beta or 17-alpha hydroxylase types) Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed) Serum potassium and bicarbonate to document hypokalaemic alkalosis Urinary steroid metabolite profile showing an increased cortisol-to-cortisone ratio Screening for licorice, carbenoxolone and other enzyme-inhibiting exposures Renal and cardiac end-organ assessment given severe hypertension Molecular genetic testing of HSD11B2 Apparent mineralocorticoid excess is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in HSD11B2, encoding 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 This enzyme normally converts cortisol to inactive cortisone within mineralocorticoid target cells, protecting the mineralocorticoid receptor from being activated by cortisol When it fails, cortisol floods and activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, producing a mineralocorticoid-excess state despite normal aldosterone The hallmark is severe low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and both renin and aldosterone are suppressed An elevated urinary cortisol-to-cortisone metabolite ratio is characteristic and helps confirm the diagnosis The acquired phenocopy is heavy licorice or carbenoxolone ingestion, which inhibits the same enzyme Management combines mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade and sometimes an ENaC blocker with salt restriction; suppressing endogenous cortisol may be considered in selected cases Severe hypertension presenting in childhood or young adulthood Profound hypokalaemia with weakness or arrhythmia Hypertensive end-organ damage including nephrocalcinosis and left ventricular hypertrophy Failure to thrive or growth restriction in affected children Hypertensive crisis or stroke Attributing the picture to primary hyperaldosteronism despite the suppressed aldosterone Missing a dietary licorice or carbenoxolone cause of an identical biochemical picture Relying on aldosterone antagonism alone when severe disease may also need ENaC blockade and salt restriction Overlooking the recessive inheritance and the need to evaluate siblings Apparent mineralocorticoid excess arises from deficiency of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, an enzyme expressed in aldosterone-responsive tissues that inactivates cortisol to cortisone. Cortisol binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with affinity similar to aldosterone, but is normally circulating at far higher concentrations; the enzyme provides tissue specificity by locally clearing cortisol so that only aldosterone reaches the receptor. When the enzyme is deficient, intracellular cortisol accumulates and inappropriately activates the mineralocorticoid receptor in the distal nephron, driving sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen loss. The resulting volume expansion causes low-renin hypertension and hypokalaemic alkalosis, while the same volume expansion suppresses aldosterone, so the biochemistry shows mineralocorticoid effects without a raised mineralocorticoid hormone. Outlook depends on how early treatment begins; poorly controlled disease leads to severe hypertensive complications and chronic kidney damage, whereas mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade with salt restriction can achieve reasonable control.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) — ARDS Cardiogenic (hydrostatic) pulmonary edema Bilateral pneumonia Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Acute interstitial lung disease (e.g., acute interstitial pneumonitis) Acute immunologic injury (e.g., hypersensitivity pneumonitis) Toxin injury (e.g., radiation pneumonitis) Neurogenic pulmonary edema Bilateral pneumonia (may also coexist with ARDS) Arterial blood gas to determine PaO2/FiO2 ratio for Berlin severity grading Chest radiograph (bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, often involving >=three-quarters of lung fields) Echocardiography to exclude hydrostatic/cardiac etiology when no ARDS risk factor is present Chest CT (shows bilateral infiltrates with heterogeneous, often dependent lung involvement) Lung ultrasound permitted as an alternative imaging modality under proposed 2023 Berlin updates, especially in resource-limited settings Cardiogenic pulmonary edema Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Acute interstitial pneumonitis Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Radiation pneumonitis Neurogenic pulmonary edema ARDS is a clinical syndrome of severe dyspnea of rapid onset, hypoxemia, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure, caused by diffuse lung injury (Harrison 22e p.2299). By 2012 expert consensus, ARDS is graded as mild, moderate, or severe by the degree of hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), and these stages correlate with mortality risk and duration of mechanical ventilation in survivors (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300). Most cases (>80%) arise from a small number of disorders: pneumonia and sepsis (~40-60%), followed by aspiration of gastric contents, trauma, multiple transfusions, and drug overdose; risk rises with more than one predisposing condition (Harrison 22e p.2299). The natural history has three phases - exudative (first ~7 days), proliferative (~day 7-21), and fibrotic - each with characteristic clinical and pathologic features (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2301). Cornerstone of management is recognizing and treating the underlying trigger (pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, trauma) plus standardized bundled ICU care, rather than ARDS-specific drug therapy (Harrison 22e p.2302). Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) and limited plateau pressure (<=30 cmH2O) significantly lowers mortality versus conventional higher tidal volumes; this is the only therapy graded by the strongest evidence (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303). Prone positioning early in severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150 mmHg) reduced 28-day mortality in a randomized trial; it requires a team experienced in proning because repositioning critically ill patients can be hazardous (Harrison 22e p.2302). A conservative fluid strategy - reducing left atrial filling pressure with fluid restriction and diuretics - shortens ICU stay and duration of ventilation, limited only by hypotension and organ hypoperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2302). Mortality in ARDS is largely due to nonpulmonary causes, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure accounting for >80% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2303). Progressive hypoxemia and increasing work of breathing leading to respiratory fatigue and respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg) carrying the highest mortality Concurrent sepsis or multiorgan failure, which account for most ARDS deaths Lung biopsy evidence of pulmonary fibrosis in any phase, associated with increased mortality ARDS radiographic findings are characteristic but not specific and can be indistinguishable from cardiogenic pulmonary edema; unlike cardiogenic edema, ARDS often lacks cardiomegaly, pleural effusions, or pulmonary vascular redistribution. Hydrostatic edema must not be the primary cause - if no ARDS risk factor is present, objective evaluation (e.g., echocardiography) is required to exclude a cardiac etiology (Harrison 22e p.2300, p.2301). Mechanical ventilation, though life-saving, can aggravate lung injury via volutrauma (alveolar overdistention from excess tidal volume), barotrauma (high alveolar pressure), and atelectrauma (recurrent alveolar collapse); because ARDS lung is heterogeneous, fully inflating consolidated regions can overdistend and injure more normal lung (Harrison 22e p.2302). Routine glucocorticoids are NOT supported by current evidence for ARDS itself; recruitment maneuvers combined with higher baseline PEEP increased mortality in one study; routine early neuromuscular blockade is not beneficial in all moderate-to-severe ARDS (reserve for ventilatory dyssynchrony despite sedation); surfactant replacement and inhaled vasodilators (e.g., inhaled nitric oxide) do not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.2302, p.2303). Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones, so correlation with PaO2 should be considered when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2300). ARDS results from diffuse lung injury, either direct (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, toxic inhalation, pulmonary contusion) or indirect (e.g., sepsis, severe trauma, multiple transfusions, pancreatitis). It evolves through three phases. In the EXUDATIVE phase (first ~7 days), alveolar capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes are injured, the tight alveolar barrier is lost, and protein-rich edema fluid accumulates in the interstitial and alveolar spaces. Proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and lipid mediators recruit neutrophils, and condensed plasma proteins plus cellular debris and dysfunctional surfactant form hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage). Pulmonary vascular injury occurs early with microthrombi. Dependent alveolar collapse reduces lung compliance, producing intrapulmonary shunting, hypoxemia, and increased work of breathing; microvascular occlusion raises dead space and pulmonary vascular resistance, so hypercapnia and pulmonary hypertension can also occur. The PROLIFERATIVE phase (~day 7-21) brings lung repair, organization of exudates, a shift from neutrophil- to lymphocyte-predominant infiltrates, and proliferation of type II pneumocytes that regenerate surfactant and differentiate into type I cells; most patients recover. Some progress to the FIBROTIC phase, with alveolar-duct and interstitial fibrosis, emphysema-like bullae, vascular occlusion and pulmonary hypertension, increased pneumothorax risk, reduced compliance, and increased dead space (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300, p.2301, p.2302). Hospital mortality in the LUNG SAFE study was approximately 34.9% for mild, 40.3% for moderate, and 46.1% for severe ARDS, with a trend toward improved outcomes over time. Increasing Berlin-defined severity predicts higher mortality. Most deaths are nonpulmonary, with sepsis and nonpulmonary organ failure causing >80%. Major mortality risk factors are nonpulmonary: advanced age (~60% mortality in patients >75 vs ~20% in those <45), preexisting organ dysfunction (chronic liver disease, chronic alcohol abuse, chronic immunosuppression); direct lung injury carries nearly twice the death risk of indirect injury. Among survivors, the lung has notable resolving power: most regain nearly normal lung function, usually within 6 months, and more than a third have normal spirometry and diffusion capacity one year after extubation. However, exercise limitation and reduced physical quality of life are often documented at 5 years despite near-normal pulmonary function, and survivors and family caregivers carry a substantial burden of depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (Harrison 22e p.2303, p.2304). Berlin definition (2012): severity is graded by oxygenation (PaO2/FiO2 assessed on at least 5 cmH2O PEEP) - Mild: 200 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=300 mmHg; Moderate: 100 mmHg < PaO2/FiO2 <=200 mmHg; Severe: PaO2/FiO2 <=100 mmHg. Onset must be acute (within 1 week of a clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms), chest imaging must show bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules, and respiratory failure must not be primarily due to hydrostatic (cardiogenic) edema (objective evaluation such as echocardiography required if no ARDS risk factor present). Proposed 2023 updates extend criteria to nonintubated patients on high-flow nasal oxygen or noninvasive ventilation, add SpO2/FiO2 (S/F) ratios, permit ultrasound imaging, and allow application in resource-limited settings. A more recent global definition has also been proposed that does not rely on arterial blood gases, chest radiography, or PEEP (Harrison 22e p.2299, p.2300).

low arginine Urine orotic acid (typically raised) Blood gas to assess for respiratory alkalosis of hyperammonaemia ASL gene sequencing or enzyme assay in erythrocytes/fibroblasts Liver function tests and hepatic imaging/elastography for fibrosis Blood pressure monitoring for systemic hypertension Second most common urea cycle disorder, caused by biallelic ASL variants (argininosuccinate lyase deficiency) Neonatal-onset form presents with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy: poor feeding, vomiting, tachypnoea, lethargy and coma in the first days of life Biochemical hallmark is markedly raised plasma and urine argininosuccinic acid, with raised citrulline and low arginine Late-onset disease may present with episodic hyperammonaemia, developmental delay, learning difficulties or chronic liver involvement Distinctive features include trichorrhexis nodosa (brittle, fragile hair) and a tendency to hepatomegaly and hepatic fibrosis Systemic hypertension and neurocognitive impairment can occur even with good ammonia control, reflecting nitric oxide deficiency Confirm with plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid, enzyme assay in fibroblasts/red cells and ASL sequencing Management combines protein restriction, arginine supplementation and nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate/phenylbutyrate), with haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency ammonia removal Rapidly rising ammonia with encephalopathy at any age Cerebral oedema complicating severe hyperammonaemia Progressive hepatic dysfunction or fibrosis Uncontrolled systemic hypertension Delaying ammonia measurement and treatment in an encephalopathic neonate Assuming normal ammonia control prevents all complications, missing hypertension and liver disease Overlooking argininosuccinate on amino acid analysis and misclassifying the urea cycle defect Neglecting arginine supplementation, which is required to correct the downstream deficiency Failing to prepare an emergency regimen for catabolic illness or surgery Argininosuccinic aciduria is caused by deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase, the urea cycle enzyme that cleaves argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. The block prevents completion of ureagenesis, so waste nitrogen cannot be efficiently converted to urea and ammonia accumulates. Argininosuccinate itself builds up to high levels in blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, while arginine (a downstream product) becomes deficient. Because arginine is also the substrate for nitric oxide synthesis, chronic arginine deficiency and argininosuccinate accumulation are thought to contribute to the hypertension, hepatic disease and neurocognitive problems that can persist despite adequate ammonia control, distinguishing this disorder from other urea cycle defects. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Early recognition and prompt control of hyperammonaemia improve survival, but neurocognitive impairment, hypertension and hepatic disease may develop even with satisfactory metabolic control, so outcome is more variable than in some other urea cycle disorders.

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — ARVC, ARVD, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, PKP2-related cardiomyopathy Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract tachycardia Cardiac sarcoidosis Brugada syndrome Dilated cardiomyopathy with predominant right ventricular involvement Athlete's heart with physiological right ventricular remodelling Myocarditis 12-lead ECG for right precordial T-wave inversion, epsilon waves and prolonged terminal activation Signal-averaged ECG to detect late potentials Cardiac MRI to assess right ventricular size, wall motion and fibrofatty infiltration Echocardiography for right ventricular dilatation and regional dysfunction Ambulatory monitoring and exercise testing to quantify ventricular arrhythmia Genetic testing for desmosomal gene variants and cascade family screening A genetic cardiomyopathy in which fibrofatty tissue progressively replaces right ventricular myocardium, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death Typically presents in young adults with palpitations, syncope, or exertional ventricular arrhythmia, and is an important cause of sudden death in athletes Most cases are autosomal dominant and caused by variants in desmosomal proteins, particularly plakophilin-2 (PKP2), desmoplakin, desmoglein-2 and desmocollin-2 The resting ECG may show T-wave inversion in the right precordial leads and an epsilon wave (a low-amplitude terminal QRS deflection) Diagnosis uses the Task Force Criteria, combining imaging, ECG, arrhythmic, tissue and family/genetic categories into major and minor criteria Cardiac MRI demonstrates right ventricular dilatation, regional wall-motion abnormalities and fibrofatty infiltration; left ventricular involvement is increasingly recognised Management centres on arrhythmia risk reduction with exercise restriction, beta-blockers, antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk patients Intense endurance exercise accelerates disease progression, so activity counselling is a key part of care Syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death, particularly during exertion Sustained ventricular tachycardia of left bundle branch block morphology Progressive right or biventricular failure Family history of premature sudden death or confirmed ARVC Mislabelling the arrhythmia as benign idiopathic outflow tract tachycardia and missing the underlying cardiomyopathy Confusing physiological athlete's heart remodelling with early ARVC Permitting competitive or endurance exercise, which hastens disease progression Relying on right ventricular imaging alone and overlooking left-dominant or biventricular variants Underestimating arrhythmic risk in gene-positive relatives with subtle findings ARVC is caused predominantly by variants in genes encoding desmosomal proteins that maintain mechanical junctions between cardiomyocytes. Impaired cell-cell adhesion, aggravated by mechanical stress such as vigorous exercise, leads to myocyte detachment and death, with progressive replacement of myocardium by fibrous and fatty tissue. This begins in the right ventricle but can extend to the left. The scarred, electrically heterogeneous myocardium forms re-entry circuits that generate ventricular arrhythmias, while progressive myocardial loss can cause right and eventually biventricular dysfunction. The clinical course is variable; with risk stratification, exercise restriction and appropriate defibrillator therapy many patients do well, but the condition is progressive and carries an ongoing risk of life-threatening arrhythmia and, in advanced cases, heart failure.

Arterial and Venous Thrombosis — Thrombosis, Venous thromboembolism, VTE, Arterial thrombosis, Pathologic thrombosis Atherosclerotic plaque rupture causing acute coronary syndrome Embolism (cardiac source) versus in-situ thrombosis Aortic or arterial dissection Vasculitis causing arterial occlusion Postthrombotic syndrome as sequela of DVT Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after PE Thrombophilia evaluation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiencies) in selected patients, recognizing many older genetic associations are being questioned in larger contemporary studies Antiphospholipid antibody testing when autoimmune prothrombotic state suspected Plasma homocysteine and MTHFR considerations as historically reported independent risk factors Assessment of acquired risk factors: malignancy screening, recent surgery/trauma, pregnancy status, hormonal therapy use Markers reflecting inflammation-thrombosis crosstalk (e.g., soluble CD40 ligand) noted as research-relevant Acute limb ischemia from arterial embolism rather than local thrombosis Superficial venous thrombophlebitis Lymphedema or cellulitis mimicking DVT-related limb swelling Extrinsic venous compression mimicking thrombotic obstruction Thrombosis is essentially hemostasis occurring in the wrong place at the wrong time; the same processes that protect against hemorrhage can, under certain conditions, produce pathologic arterial or venous occlusion. Hemostasis and thrombosis arise from interplay among three elements: the vessel wall, the coagulation/fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. Arterial thrombosis is dominated by platelet adhesion to an injured vessel wall and the state of the wall itself, whereas venous thrombosis is driven mainly by activation of the coagulation cascade in the setting of stasis or hypercoagulability. Platelets are small anucleate cells (1-5 microns) circulating at roughly 200,000-400,000/microL with a 7-10 day lifespan, derived from marrow megakaryocytes under the control of thrombopoietin. The platelet GPIb-IX-V complex binds exposed subendothelial von Willebrand factor to initiate adhesion, and signaling converts the GPIIb/IIIa integrin from a low-affinity to a high-affinity fibrinogen receptor that cross-links platelets into an aggregate. Inflammation and infection transiently raise thrombotic risk: acute upper respiratory infection, bacterial and viral infections (including SARS-CoV-2, HIV, hepatitis C, dengue) are linked to increased myocardial infarction, stroke, and VTE. Roughly 5-8% of the U.S. population carries a genetic risk factor predisposing to venous thrombosis, and multiple risk factors frequently coexist in a single patient. Cancer confers an approximately fourfold increased risk of VTE compared with the general population, and VTE in cancer patients is associated with reduced survival. Although factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A mutation are established risk factors for DVT and PE, their contribution to arterial thrombotic events such as acute coronary syndromes is not well established. Loss-of-function CYP2C19 polymorphisms are the strongest single determinant of reduced antiplatelet response to clopidogrel (a prodrug requiring hepatic activation) but account for only about 5-12% of the variability in ADP-induced platelet aggregation. Antithrombin reactions governed by normal endothelium become pivotal in limiting clot extension into adjacent uninjured vessel once a protective clot has formed; antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, heparin cofactor II, and protein C/protein S all restrain thrombin generation. Sudden death from pulmonary embolism (a substantial fraction of new VTE cases die early, with high 30-day mortality) PE in the setting of cancer carries roughly a 25% fatality rate Homozygous protein C or protein S deficiency can produce fatal purpura fulminans Coagulation abnormalities and increased PE/DVT/peripheral thrombosis in hospitalized COVID-19 patients (noted in nearly 20%) Calf-vein thrombus extension into popliteal and proximal veins, where fragments can embolize to the lungs Assuming hypercoagulable (thrombophilic) states that drive venous thrombosis are equally important for arterial events; their role in acute coronary syndromes is poorly defined and often not clinically significant. Genotyping to optimize aspirin therapy is not currently clinically indicated, as ex vivo studies have not firmly established a pharmacogenetic interaction between aspirin and COX1. Over-relying on CYP2C19 genotype for clopidogrel decisions, since loss-of-function alleles explain only a small fraction (about 5-12%) of antiplatelet response variability and genetics do not appreciably affect outcomes with prasugrel or ticagrelor. Forgetting that up to 10% of venous thromboembolic events occur outside the lower extremities and lungs. Treating many older single-gene thrombophilia associations as definitive when larger contemporary studies have called several into question. Thrombus formation reflects dysregulated hemostasis involving the vessel wall, coagulation and fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. In arterial thrombosis, vessel-wall damage exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor; the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex mediates adhesion, platelets are activated through seven-transmembrane receptors (thrombin/PAR1, PAR4, ADP receptors P2Y1 and P2Y12, prostaglandin and lipid receptors), release thromboxane A2, serotonin, and ADP from granules, and undergo a calcium-dependent conformational change in GPIIb/IIIa that allows high-affinity fibrinogen binding and irreversible aggregation. Most arterial thrombi are superimposed on disrupted atherosclerotic plaque whose thrombogenic core triggers platelet-rich thrombus. In venous thrombosis, the coagulation cascade is initiated chiefly by exposure of tissue factor: factor VII/VIIa-tissue factor complex activates factor X (directly or via factor IX/VIIIa), FXa with cofactor FVa converts prothrombin to thrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin and activates FXIII to cross-link the clot. Amplification lets a small stimulus generate large amounts of fibrin. Venous thrombi typically originate in valve cusps of calf deep veins or muscular sinuses where sluggish flow lowers oxygen delivery, activating endothelial cells that express adhesion molecules; tissue-factor-bearing leukocytes and microvesicles adhere, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) provide a scaffold that binds and activates platelets and activates factor XII, and impaired clearance of activated clotting factors worsens local thrombosis. Hypercoagulability (heritable or acquired), stasis, and vascular dysfunction (Virchow's elements) underlie venous events. Inflammation links the two: platelet P-selectin binds leukocyte PSGL-1, induces monocyte tissue factor and CD40 ligand expression, and Toll-like receptors (TLR2/3/4, TLR7/8) connect infection to platelet-dependent thrombosis. Thrombosis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Coronary disease and stroke account for a large share of deaths; arterial thrombosis underlies most acute MI, ischemic stroke, and limb gangrene. For VTE, up to 30% of patients die within 30 days, about one-fifth experience sudden death from PE, and roughly 30% develop recurrent VTE within 10 years. The ARIC study reported a 9% 28-day fatality from DVT and 15% from PE; cancer-associated PE carries about 25% fatality. Incidence of first DVT rises sharply with age (from about 2-3 per 10,000 person-years at 30-49 years to about 20 per 10,000 at 70-79 years). Increasing age, obesity, malignancy, and acute extremity paresis independently predict recurrence.

provocative maneuvers (abduction/external rotation, scalene, costoclavicular, hyperabduction) Serologic and hematologic workup for secondary Raynaud (connective tissue disease, cold agglutinins, cryoglobulins, cryofibrinogen) Erythromelalgia (warm, erythematous, painful extremity with preserved pulses, opposite trigger to ischemia) Acrocyanosis (persistent, non-episodic cyanosis with normal pulses, no blanching, distinguishing it from Raynaud) Atheroembolic 'blue toe' confined to one or two digits, not to be confused with Raynaud phenomenon Spinal/neurogenic causes (intervertebral disk disease, syringomyelia, complex regional pain syndrome) mimicking vasospasm Myeloproliferative disorders and hyperviscosity states presenting with digital ischemia or erythromelalgia Peripheral artery disease (PAD) means stenosis or occlusion of the aorta or limb arteries; atherosclerosis is the dominant cause in patients over 40, while thrombosis, embolism, vasculitis, fibromuscular dysplasia, entrapment, cystic adventitial disease, and trauma account for the remainder. Risk factors mirror those for coronary and cerebral atherosclerosis: cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, elevated lipoprotein(a), hypertension, and renal insufficiency; prevalence is similar between sexes but greater in Black than non-Hispanic white persons and in lower socioeconomic groups. More than half of PAD patients are asymptomatic; the classic symptom is intermittent claudication (pain, ache, cramp, numbness, or fatigue in muscle that appears with exertion and resolves with rest), and the symptomatic muscle group lies distal to the obstructing lesion (e.g., buttock/hip/thigh with aortoiliac disease, calf with femoral-popliteal disease). Chronic limb-threatening ischemia produces rest pain or a cold/numb foot that worsens at night when legs are horizontal and improves with dependency; signs include hair loss, thickened nails, shiny atrophic skin, coolness, pallor or cyanosis, and ultimately ulcers or gangrene. Ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the key noninvasive test: normal 1.00-1.40, borderline 0.91-0.99, and abnormal/diagnostic of PAD at 0.90 or below; values above 1.40 indicate noncompressible, calcified vessels (as in diabetes or chronic kidney disease). When the ABI is unreliable because of medial calcification, a toe-brachial index of 0.70 or below is considered abnormal and supports the diagnosis. A drop in ABI immediately after treadmill exercise helps confirm PAD when resting findings are equivocal; MRA, CTA, and catheter angiography are reserved for revascularization planning, not routine diagnosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-inflammatory hyperplastic arteriopathy of medium and small (sometimes large) arteries, predominant in women, classically renal and carotid/vertebral, with a multifocal 'string of beads' or focal pattern, and can cause stenosis, dissection, aneurysm, or thrombosis. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is an inflammatory occlusive disorder of distal small and medium arteries and veins, strongly linked to tobacco, typically in men under 40, presenting with a triad of distal claudication, Raynaud phenomenon, and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis; brachial and popliteal pulses are normal while distal pulses are reduced or absent. Acute limb ischemia is sudden cessation of limb blood flow most often from cardiac embolism (atrial fibrillation, MI, ventricular aneurysm, endocarditis, prosthetic valves, atrial myxoma), in-situ thrombosis, dissection, or trauma; emboli lodge at bifurcations, most commonly the femoral artery in the leg. Atheroembolism (cholesterol/fibrin/platelet debris from proximal plaque or aneurysm) classically spares large vessels, so distal pulses remain palpable; it causes the painful 'blue toe' syndrome, livedo reticularis, and may show cholesterol crystals on skin or muscle biopsy. Raynaud phenomenon is episodic digital ischemia with sequential pallor (vasospasm), cyanosis (deoxygenated blood in dilated capillaries), and rubor (reactive hyperemia) after cold or emotional stress; over half of cases are primary/idiopathic, with women affected roughly five times more often and onset typically between ages 20 and 40. Rest pain, ulceration, or gangrene indicating chronic limb-threatening ischemia Sudden severe pain, paresthesia, numbness, coldness, pallor, and pulselessness within an hour signaling acute limb ischemia Paralysis, loss of sensation, and absent Doppler signal in both arteries and veins, marking a nonviable limb requiring amputation Blue toe syndrome with progressive digital necrosis suggesting ongoing atheroembolism Ischemic fingertip ulcers progressing to gangrene and autoamputation in scleroderma-associated Raynaud Subclavian/axillary vein thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter) in venous thoracic outlet syndrome High-output cardiac failure and cardiomegaly from a large arteriovenous fistula Relying on the ABI in calcified, noncompressible vessels (ABI above 1.40) where it falsely appears normal or high; use the toe-brachial index instead. Ordering routine MRA/CTA/angiography for diagnosis when history, examination, and ABI usually suffice and imaging is meant for revascularization planning. Confusing atheroembolic digital ischemia (often one or two digits, palpable distal pulses) with Raynaud phenomenon. Mistaking acrocyanosis for Raynaud phenomenon; acrocyanosis is persistent rather than episodic, extends proximally from the digits, and lacks a blanching phase. Missing the strong tobacco link in Buerger disease and overlooking it in young male smokers presenting with distal ischemia and Raynaud features. Overlooking secondary causes of Raynaud (scleroderma, SLE, blood dyscrasias, drugs, vibration injury) and labeling the disease primary prematurely. Failing to perform provocative maneuvers in suspected thoracic outlet or popliteal entrapment syndromes, where the resting examination is often normal. Applying massage, ice water, or extreme heat to frostbite, which are contraindicated; rewarming should use a 40-44 C water bath. In atherosclerotic PAD, segmental plaques with calcium deposition, medial thinning, patchy loss of muscle and elastic fibers, fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, and platelet-fibrin thrombi narrow large and medium vessels, preferentially at branch points where turbulence, altered shear stress, and intimal injury occur. Principal sites are the abdominal aorta/iliac arteries (about 30% of symptomatic patients), femoral/popliteal arteries (80-90%), and tibial/peroneal vessels (40-50%); distal disease predominates in the elderly and in diabetics. Hemodynamically significant stenoses lower distal systolic pressure (reflected in a reduced ABI). During exercise, vasodilation distal to a stenosis drops perfusion pressure below interstitial tissue pressure generated by working muscle, producing claudication. Buerger disease shows early neutrophilic infiltration of vessel walls with a preserved internal elastic lamina and a cellular inflammatory luminal thrombus, evolving to mononuclear/giant-cell infiltration, then perivascular fibrosis, organized thrombus, and recanalization. Raynaud phenomenon reflects digital arterial vasospasm; inherited erythromelalgia involves gain-of-function SCN9A (Nav1.7 sodium channel) mutations in sensory/sympathetic nerves. PAD natural history is driven largely by coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease: roughly one-third to one-half of symptomatic patients have clinical/ECG evidence of CAD and over half have significant disease on coronary angiography. PAD carries a 15-25% 5-year mortality and a two- to fourfold increased risk of cardiovascular death, with the highest mortality in those with most severe disease. Over 5 years the ABI worsens in nearly 40% and symptoms progress in about 20-25%; roughly 11% of symptomatic patients ultimately develop chronic limb-threatening ischemia, and without revascularization about 25% of those with chronic limb-threatening ischemia undergo amputation within a year. Prognosis is worse in continued smokers and diabetics. In thromboangiitis obliterans the outlook is worse in continued smokers and remains discouraging even after cessation. Primary Raynaud disease is generally mild, with fewer than 1% losing part of a digit, spontaneous improvement in about 15%, and progression in about 30%; primary acrocyanosis and benign livedo reticularis have favorable outcomes without ulceration or gangrene. PAD severity is graded hemodynamically by ABI: normal 1.00-1.40, borderline 0.91-0.99, abnormal/diagnostic at 0.90 or below, and noncompressible above 1.40 (toe-brachial index 0.70 or below abnormal). Clinically the spectrum runs from asymptomatic disease, to intermittent claudication, to chronic limb-threatening ischemia (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene). Acute limb ischemia is assessed for limb viability by presence of sensation, motor function, and Doppler-detectable arterial and venous flow; loss of all three defines a nonviable limb.

ulceration Missing an acquired fistula after penetrating trauma or vascular procedures Overlooking high-output cardiac failure as a consequence of a large chronic shunt Confusing a fistula with a pseudoaneurysm and choosing the wrong treatment Underestimating distal ischaemia caused by arterial steal An arteriovenous fistula creates a low-resistance channel that diverts arterial blood directly into the venous system, bypassing the capillary bed. This produces a steal effect that can reduce distal arterial perfusion, while transmission of arterial pressure into the veins causes venous hypertension, dilatation, and secondary tissue changes. The reduced systemic vascular resistance increases venous return, stroke volume, and cardiac output; a large chronic shunt can lead to cardiac chamber enlargement and high-output heart failure. Congenital lesions reflect abnormal vascular development, whereas acquired fistulae follow penetrating trauma, procedures, or erosion between an adjacent artery and vein. Small fistulae may remain asymptomatic and be safely observed, while large or high-flow lesions can progressively cause limb complications or cardiac strain and generally require intervention. Outcomes after embolisation or surgical repair are favourable when the lesion is anatomically suitable, though congenital malformations can recur.

seizures or deficits to other causes without vascular imaging A cerebral arteriovenous malformation is a congenital vascular anomaly in which feeding arteries drain directly into veins through a nidus of abnormal channels, bypassing the normal capillary network. The absence of intervening capillaries exposes the draining veins to high arterial pressures and flow, causing vessel wall changes and predisposing to rupture. Diversion of blood through the low-resistance shunt can reduce perfusion of surrounding brain (vascular steal), while venous hypertension and gliosis contribute to seizures and focal deficits. Haemorrhage results from rupture of the fragile nidus, draining veins, or associated aneurysms. Prognosis depends on whether the malformation has bled, its size and location, and its venous drainage; haemorrhage carries significant morbidity and a risk of recurrent bleeding, whereas complete obliteration by surgery, radiosurgery, or embolisation can substantially reduce future haemorrhage risk.

In hemochromatosis, arthropathy may be the FIRST clinical clue: degenerative-type involvement that characteristically starts at the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints (joints generally spared by routine OA), often with hooklike MCP osteophytes and frequent calcium pyrophosphate deposition. An early hemochromatosis diagnosis is suggested by a high serum transferrin saturation, which is more sensitive than ferritin elevation; dominant 2nd/3rd MCP findings warrant ferritin and iron/total iron-binding capacity testing. Hemophilic recurrent spontaneous hemarthrosis (factor VIII or IX deficiency) typically begins after age 1 when the child walks/runs and targets knees, ankles, elbows, shoulders, and hips, progressing to chronic fibrotic deforming arthropathy. Hemarthrosis is characteristic of hemophilia but NOT of von Willebrand disease, factor V deficiency, oral anticoagulation, or thrombocytopenia. Low-grade temperature can accompany acute hemarthrosis, but fever above 38.3 C (101 F) should raise concern for joint infection and prompt aspiration; clotting factor should be corrected before arthrocentesis. Sickle cell dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in children under 5 produces diffuse swelling/tenderness of hands and feet from marrow and cortical bone infarction and is rarely seen after age 5; it generally resolves without residual damage. Distinguishing osteomyelitis from bone infarction in sickle cell disease is clinically difficult; Salmonella is a notably associated cause of osteomyelitis, whereas S. aureus and Streptococcus are the more common organisms in sickle cell septic arthritis. Up to ~40% of sickle cell patients are hyperuricemic (urate overproduction plus interstitial renal disease) and can develop acute, sometimes polyarticular, gouty arthritis; arthrocentesis distinguishes gout from infection or synovial infarction. Achilles tendinitis and migratory large-joint arthritis can be the first clinical sign of familial hypercholesterolemia, preceding the appearance of tendinous xanthomas; synovial fluid is noninflammatory and crystal-negative. Neuropathic (Charcot) joint disease arises from loss of pain sensation and/or proprioception with impaired protective reflexes; diabetes mellitus is the most frequent cause, classically affecting the tarsal and tarsometatarsal joints. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy combines digital clubbing with periosteal new-bone formation; secondary HOA points to intrathoracic malignancy, suppurative/hypoxemic lung disease, congenital heart disease, or hepatopulmonary disease and may precede the underlying illness. Relying on ferritin alone for early hemochromatosis when transferrin saturation is the more sensitive marker. Mistaking acute hemarthrosis for septic arthritis (or vice versa) in hemophilia; failing to correct clotting factor before aspirating. Aspirating a hemophilic intramuscular cyst, which can provoke further bleeding (relatively contraindicated unless secondarily infected, and then only after factor repletion). Using a technetium bone scan to try to separate osteomyelitis from neuropathic arthritis, since uptake is increased in both. Overlooking that nonselective NSAIDs impair platelet function and should be avoided where feasible in hemophilic bleeding. Treating isolated clubbing as benign and missing an associated malignancy or lung/cardiac disease. These arthritides share the theme of an underlying systemic disorder injuring joints rather than a primary autoimmune synovitis. In acromegaly, excess growth hormone and IGF-I stimulate cartilage, periarticular connective tissue, and bone, producing hypertrophic then degenerating cartilage that is prone to fissuring, with ligamentous laxity worsening joint discomfort. In hemochromatosis, parenchymal iron deposition damages cartilage: iron catalyzes superoxide-dependent lipid peroxidation, interferes with collagen formation, increases lysosomal enzyme release from synovium, and inhibits synovial pyrophosphatase, favoring chondrocalcinosis. Hemophilic arthropathy results from repeated intraarticular bleeding; blood persists because intrinsic clotting factors and tissue thromboplastin are absent in the synovium, and recurrent hemarthrosis leads to chronic noninflammatory fibrotic joints. Sickle cell musculoskeletal disease stems from vasoocclusion and marrow/cortical bone infarction, splenic dysfunction predisposing to osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, and avascular necrosis (notably femoral head); marrow hyperplasia widens medullary cavities and thins cortices. In neuropathic joints, loss of deep pain/proprioception plus dysregulated autonomic blood flow leads to bone resorption, repeated microtrauma, ligament tears, and fractures with progressive disorganization. HOA pathogenesis centers on circulating cells/platelet particles and growth factors (PDGF, VEGF) bypassing pulmonary clearance and stimulating peripheral connective tissue and periosteal proliferation, with endothelial activation reflected by elevated von Willebrand factor antigen. Outcomes are determined largely by the underlying disorder. Acromegalic joint pain may persist even after the acromegaly is treated. In hemochromatosis, established arthritis and chondrocalcinosis often progress despite phlebotomy. Hemophilic hemarthrosis usually resolves with joint function returning to baseline over about two weeks, but recurrent bleeding causes chronic fibrotic, flexion-deformed, function-limiting arthropathy. Sickle cell dactylitis resolves without residual damage, but avascular necrosis (about 5% femoral head involvement) and osteomyelitis carry greater morbidity. Neuropathic joints can disorganize rapidly and are largely unaffected by treating the underlying disease; early recognition and offloading of a diabetic Charcot foot can prevent severe disease. In primary HOA, symptoms typically disappear on reaching adulthood. No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by the staging of the underlying arthropathy. Hemophilic arthropathy progresses radiographically from capsular distention, to juxtaarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions and subchondral cysts, to late joint-space narrowing with osteoarthritis-like bony overgrowth. Neuropathic arthritis evolves from early osteoarthritis-like changes (joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, effusions) to marked destructive/hypertrophic disorganization. HOA progresses from periostitis with a radiolucent zone between new periosteal bone and cortex to multilayered cortical thickening.

CSF; tissue, thrombus, or autopsy specimens in HPS) Metagenomic / high-throughput sequencing of CSF for arboviral encephalitis CSF analysis (typically modest WBC elevation, early PMN then monocyte predominance, usually normal glucose; lymphocyte counts in the thousands with low glucose in LCM) CBC for thrombocytopenia, leukopenia or leukocytosis with left shift, and circulating atypical lymphocytes/immunoblasts (HPS) Hematocrit/hemoconcentration, serum albumin, lactate, and arterial blood gas in suspected HPS Renal panel (creatinine, potassium), liver transaminases (AST/ALT), and urinalysis for proteinuria in VHF Chest radiography for interstitial then bilateral central alveolar edema with normal cardiac size in HPS Anti-NMDA receptor and other autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitides Metabolic encephalopathy (hyperammonemia, liver failure) Toxic/intoxication states Brain abscess and cerebrovascular events (stroke) Oncologic CNS disease Surgical abdomen / acute pyelonephritis (mimicking the febrile prodrome of HPS) Most arthropod-borne (arbovirus) and rodent-borne zoonotic viral infections in humans are subclinical or unrecognized; humans are usually accidental, dead-end hosts and are not important amplifiers of these viruses (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665). Recognized illness usually falls into one of five overlapping syndromic categories: fever and myalgia (F&M), arthritis and rash (A&R), encephalitis, pulmonary disease, and viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF); a single virus may cause several of these (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665). Fever and myalgia is by far the most common and most benign syndrome, with abrupt fever, chills, intense myalgia, malaise, anorexia, and headache with photophobia/retroorbital pain; true arthritis is absent and physical findings are minimal (Harrison 22e p.1665-1666). A history of tick bite has more diagnostic significance than a history of mosquito exposure; clinical and epidemiologic clues may allow presumptive diagnosis in epidemics, but laboratory confirmation is required in all cases (Harrison 22e p.1664). Arthropod vectors acquire arboviruses from viremic vertebrate blood meals; the virus must disseminate to the salivary glands (extrinsic incubation, typically 1-3 weeks in mosquitoes) before the vector can transmit; transovarial transmission to progeny is an alternative maintenance mechanism (Harrison 22e p.1664). Rodent-borne viruses are maintained by chronically infected rodents; humans are typically infected by inhalation of or contact with aerosolized rodent excreta/secreta, and most show a high degree of rodent-virus specificity (Harrison 22e p.1664). Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is acquired from the house mouse and classically causes a biphasic illness with a febrile phase followed by a CNS (meningeal) phase; patients with neuroinvasive LCM, including frank encephalitis, almost always recover fully, but the virus can cause fetal microcephaly and has been transmitted by organ transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1666-1667). Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) begins after a 2-3 week incubation with a nonspecific 3-4 day prodrome, then rapidly progresses to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemic respiratory failure; coincident thrombocytopenia, circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes), and a left shift are considered almost diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.1673). In suspected HPS, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is hazardous because of widespread capillary leak and depressed cardiac output; management is hemodynamic/respiratory support, with ECMO for the most critically ill (Harrison 22e p.1673). Lassa fever: most Lassa virus infections are subclinical or mild, onset is gradual (characteristic of mammarenavirus VHFs), and overt hemorrhage occurs in only about 15-30% of patients; about 30% of survivors develop sensorineural deafness (Harrison 22e p.1675-1676). Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is the most significant VHF today, with over 100,000 severe cases annually in Asia; major agents are Hantaan (Eastern Asia), Dobrava (the Balkans), and Puumala (Europe) (Harrison 22e p.1676). Arboviral CNS disease can leave residual deficits; spinal/motor-neuron (poliomyelitis-like) disease has been documented after West Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis virus infection, and difficulty concentrating, fatigability, tremor, and personality change are common during recovery (Harrison 22e p.1671). Altered mental status, seizures, focal neurologic signs, or coma indicating neuroinvasive disease New dry cough, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and early pulmonary edema heralding the HPS cardiopulmonary phase Hypotension, hemoconcentration, and marked thrombocytopenia with left shift Mucosal/overt hemorrhage, marked thrombocytopenia, and CNS dysfunction in suspected VHF CNS features, facial/neck edema, hypotension, hemorrhage, or jaundice in Lassa fever (markers of fatal outcome) Pregnancy, especially the last trimester, in Lassa fever (very high case fatality and ~90% fetal death) Oliguria and rising creatinine signaling acute kidney injury in HPS/VHF Marked confusion, tremor, and cerebellar signs in South American mammarenavirus hemorrhagic fevers Anchoring on the most severe known phenotype of a virus; many agents most commonly cause mild F&M rather than their eponymous severe disease (e.g., West Nile, Venezuelan equine encephalitis, Rift Valley fever). Treating the F&M syndrome as benign and self-limited without watching for evolution into A&R, neuroinvasive, pulmonary, or VHF syndromes for which it can be a prodrome. Using acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) in these febrile illnesses, given the risk of exacerbated bleeding and Reye syndrome. Giving aggressive IV fluids in HPS, which worsens noncardiogenic pulmonary edema because of capillary leak and depressed cardiac output. Relying on a negative CSF RT-PCR to exclude arboviral encephalitis; viruses generally cannot be isolated from blood or CSF and RT-PCR cannot rule out the diagnosis. Misreading the gradual onset of mammarenavirus VHF (Lassa, Argentinian/Bolivian) and expecting prominent early hemorrhage, which is often absent or late. Treating a single positive heterotypic IgG cross-reaction as diagnostic in HPS serology given very low background seroprevalence. Overlooking person-to-person/nosocomial transmission risk (Lassa virus, Andes virus, mammarenaviruses) and sexual transmission during early convalescence. These taxonomically diverse zoonotic RNA viruses (Togaviridae/Alphavirus; Flaviviridae/Orthoflavivirus; the bunyaviricete families Arenaviridae, Hantaviridae, Nairoviridae, Peribunyaviridae, Phenuiviridae; Orthomyxoviridae; Bornaviridae and Rhabdoviridae; and the reovirus families) circulate in nature between arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies, midges) or chronically infected rodents and vertebrate reservoirs. Arboviruses establish chronic systemic infection of the vector after a blood meal and reach the salivary glands during extrinsic incubation (1-3 weeks in mosquitoes); vertical transovarial transmission also maintains some viruses. In arboviral encephalitis, an initial lymphoid-origin viremia seeds multifocal CNS entry, presumably via olfactory neuroepithelium/cribriform plate or brain capillary endothelium; CNS injury results partly from direct neuronal infection and partly from edema, inflammation, and host immune response, with focal neuronal necrosis, glial nodules, and perivascular lymphoid cuffing. LCM meningitis is T-cell-mediated immunopathology. VHF agents share a core pathophysiology of disrupted vascular function, stability, and integrity producing multisystem organ dysfunction and capillary leak; in HPS, widespread pulmonary capillary leak with depressed cardiac output produces noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and shock. Outcome depends heavily on syndrome and specific virus. The F&M syndrome generally resolves completely within 2-5 days, though prolonged asthenia may follow LCMV or dengue infection. A&R illness resolves over days, but joint pain/arthritis may persist for months to years without deformity. Encephalitis ranges from full recovery (often slow, over weeks to months) to permanent deficits or death. HPS carries a case-fatality rate of approximately 30-40% even with appropriate care, though most patients surviving the first 48 hours of hospitalization recover without long-term sequelae. Argentinian and Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can reach case-fatality rates over 50% in individual outbreaks. About 20% of Lassa virus infections become Lassa fever; survivors have roughly a 30% rate of (usually bilateral) sensorineural deafness, and pregnancy markedly worsens prognosis. No single unified severity scale; severity is framed by syndrome. The five-syndrome heuristic (F&M, arthritis and rash, encephalitis, pulmonary disease, viral hemorrhagic fever) stratifies expected severity, with F&M most benign and encephalitis/pulmonary/VHF most severe. Encephalitis severity grades clinically from asymptomatic through febrile headache and aseptic meningitis to full encephalitis with coma. HPS is staged by progression from nonspecific prodrome to the cardiopulmonary phase with respiratory failure and shock. Lassa fever severity/fatality is predicted by high viral load, high serum creatinine and AST, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, CNS features, face/neck swelling, hypotension, hemorrhage, jaundice, and pregnancy.

a documented occupational history for compensation Assuming a short exposure excludes disease when latency is prolonged Inhaled asbestos fibres that reach the distal airways and alveoli are incompletely cleared and provoke chronic macrophage-driven inflammation with release of reactive oxygen species and fibrogenic mediators. Ascariasis — Ascaris lumbricoides infection, roundworm infection, giant intestinal roundworm Other intestinal helminth infections (hookworm, Trichuris, Strongyloides) Non-parasitic causes of eosinophilic pneumonia Mechanical bowel obstruction of other cause Gallstone disease or other biliary obstruction Pancreatitis of other aetiology Asthma or allergic bronchopulmonary disease during the pulmonary phase Drug or allergic eosinophilic pneumonitis Functional abdominal pain in children Stool microscopy for Ascaris eggs Full blood count for eosinophilia, especially during larval migration Abdominal ultrasound or imaging to detect worms in bowel or biliary tree Chest imaging if eosinophilic pneumonitis is suspected Endoscopic evaluation for hepatobiliary or pancreatic complications The most common soil-transmitted helminth worldwide, acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs from faecally contaminated food, water or soil Most infections are light and asymptomatic; heavy worm loads, especially in children, cause malnutrition and growth impairment During larval lung migration patients may develop a transient eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loeffler syndrome) with cough, wheeze and pulmonary infiltrates Heavy intestinal burdens can cause bowel obstruction, particularly in children, and adult worms can migrate into the biliary or pancreatic ducts causing obstruction, cholangitis or pancreatitis It is highly prevalent in parts of India with inadequate sanitation and is targeted by school-based mass deworming programmes Diagnosis is usually by detecting characteristic eggs on stool microscopy; adult worms may be seen passed in stool or vomit or on imaging Antiparasitic (anthelmintic) therapy is highly effective for uncomplicated intestinal infection Biliary or obstructive complications may require endoscopic or surgical intervention in addition to anthelmintics Features of intestinal obstruction (distension, vomiting, absent stool/flatus), particularly in a child Biliary obstruction, cholangitis or pancreatitis from worm migration Respiratory distress during the pulmonary migratory phase Signs of peritonitis suggesting bowel perforation from a heavy worm bolus Overlooking ascariasis as a cause of paediatric bowel obstruction in endemic areas Missing biliary or pancreatic migration as the cause of acute abdominal pain Attributing migratory pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia to asthma alone Neglecting sanitation and re-treatment, allowing reinfection Ingested Ascaris eggs hatch in the small intestine; larvae penetrate the gut wall, travel via the portal circulation to the liver and then the lungs, break into the alveoli, ascend the tracheobronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature into large adult worms in the small intestine. The pulmonary phase provokes an eosinophilic hypersensitivity reaction. In the gut, large numbers of worms can form a bolus that obstructs the lumen, and individual worms may migrate into the biliary tree, pancreatic duct or appendix, producing obstructive and inflammatory complications. Chronic infection contributes to malabsorption and nutritional deficits. Uncomplicated infection has an excellent prognosis and responds promptly to anthelmintic treatment. Morbidity arises from heavy infections causing nutritional compromise in children and from obstructive complications, which can occasionally be life-threatening if not treated in time.

intellectual decline after relatively normal early development Emerging psychiatric or behavioural disturbance in adolescence or adulthood Recurrent infections Accelerated deterioration in adulthood Attributing the slow cognitive decline to a static intellectual disability and missing the progressive storage disorder Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the oligosaccharide pattern Overlooking the diagnosis outside the Finnish population where it also occurs Failing to consider it in adults presenting with new psychiatric symptoms and intellectual disability Aspartylglucosaminuria is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in AGA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme aspartylglucosaminidase (glycosylasparaginase). This enzyme hydrolyses the bond between N-acetylglucosamine and asparagine, a late step in the degradation of N-linked glycoproteins. Its deficiency causes accumulation of aspartylglucosamine and related glycoasparagines within lysosomes across many tissues, with excretion of aspartylglucosamine in the urine. Progressive storage in the central nervous system underlies the characteristically slow intellectual decline, while systemic accumulation contributes to the coarse features, connective tissue laxity, and skeletal changes. A single founder variant accounts for most Finnish cases. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The disorder is slowly progressive, with many patients reaching adulthood before a phase of more rapid cognitive decline; life expectancy is reduced but survival into middle adulthood is common. Management is supportive, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been explored in selected cases.

only 10-30% of invasive cases have a positive culture Fluconazole is commonly used for prophylaxis but has NO activity against Aspergillus species No prophylactic regimen is completely successful Antifungal therapy reduces the sensitivity of antigen detection Aspergillus IgG may not be positive on initial testing in subacute/nonneutropenic invasive disease A positive respiratory culture may represent only noninvasive disease or airway colonization, not invasion Contrast CT of the brain is often contraindicated by poor renal function and unenhanced CT is usually nonspecific; MRI is the most useful immediate investigation for cerebral disease Surgery is problematic in chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis and often causes serious complications; bronchial artery embolization is preferred for problematic hemoptysis Aspergillus is a ubiquitous hyaline septate branching mold whose conidia (spores) are inhaled from indoor/outdoor air; only species growing at 37C cause invasive disease. Disease form depends on host immunity. Invasive disease arises with profound neutropenia, glucocorticoid use, phagocyte dysfunction (CGD, advanced HIV, relapsed leukemia) and underlying respiratory disease, with angioinvasion and hemorrhagic infarction; from the lungs (>80% of cases) it may disseminate hematogenously (most often to brain). Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis occurs in apparently immunocompetent hosts with prior lung disease and a suboptimal TH1-like inflammatory response. Allergic forms (ABPA, SAFS) reflect a TH2-like hypersensitivity response to A. fumigatus, classically complicating asthma and cystic fibrosis. Multiple gene variants underlie susceptibility to each form (Harrison 22e p.1713-1714). Invasive aspergillosis is curable if immune reconstitution occurs, whereas allergic and chronic forms are not curable. Mortality of invasive aspergillosis is 30-70% if treated but ~100% if the diagnosis is missed; cerebral aspergillosis, Aspergillus endocarditis, bilateral extensive invasive pulmonary disease, late-stage AIDS, relapsed uncontrolled leukemia, and liver failure carry very poor outcomes. Untreated chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis causes clinical deterioration in ~70%; with antifungal treatment mortality is 15-20% in the first year, ~40% over 5 years, and 50-60% over 10 years, with treatment failure in ~30% (more with azole resistance). ABPA/SAFS respond to glucocorticoids and antifungals (~60% to itraconazole, ~80% to voriconazole/posaconazole) but relapse after discontinuation is common (Harrison 22e p.1717). By disease category: INVASIVE (acute course <=1 month, subacute 1-3 months) - angioinvasive/nonangioinvasive/granulomatous pulmonary, invasive sinusitis, tracheobronchitis, disseminated, cerebral, endocarditis, cutaneous, keratitis/endophthalmitis. CHRONIC - chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis, chronic fibrosing pulmonary aspergillosis (destroyed lung), Aspergillus bronchitis, Aspergillus nodule, chronic invasive and chronic granulomatous sinusitis. SAPROPHYTIC - aspergilloma (single fungal ball), airway colonization, maxillary sinus fungal ball. ALLERGIC - ABPA, severe asthma with fungal sensitization (SAFS), allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1714-1715).

Aspiration pneumonitis — Mendelson's syndrome, perioperative pulmonary aspiration, acid aspiration syndrome Bronchospasm from asthma or anaphylaxis Pulmonary oedema (cardiogenic or negative-pressure) Pulmonary embolism Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Airway obstruction or laryngospasm Bacterial aspiration pneumonia (later infective complication) Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia Chest radiograph or CT to identify infiltrates, often in dependent lung zones Bronchoscopy to clear particulate material when obstruction is suspected Sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage culture if secondary infection is suspected Serial observation for progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome Results from inhalation of gastric contents, most often during induction, emergence, or in patients with impaired airway protection Chemical injury from acidic gastric fluid produces a rapid inflammatory pneumonitis, which is distinct from later bacterial aspiration pneumonia Risk is highest with a full stomach, delayed gastric emptying, bowel obstruction, pregnancy, obesity, reflux, and emergency or difficult airway situations Signs include hypoxaemia, wheeze or bronchospasm, cough, tachypnoea, and diffuse crackles, sometimes with visible gastric material in the airway Immediate management is to position to limit further soiling, apply suction, secure the airway, and provide oxygen and supportive ventilation with lung-protective strategies Routine antibiotics and corticosteroids are not indicated for pure chemical pneumonitis; antibiotics are reserved for established infection or high-risk contamination Prevention centres on appropriate fasting, rapid-sequence induction with cricoid pressure in at-risk patients, and airway protection with a cuffed tube Aspiration prophylaxis with agents that reduce gastric volume and acidity may be considered in high-risk patients Witnessed massive aspiration with rapid desaturation and airway soiling Progressive hypoxaemia or rising oxygen requirement suggesting evolving acute respiratory distress syndrome Severe bronchospasm with difficult ventilation Haemodynamic instability or the need for escalating respiratory support Giving prophylactic antibiotics and steroids for uncomplicated chemical pneumonitis Underestimating aspiration risk and omitting rapid-sequence induction in at-risk patients Attributing hypoxaemia solely to aspiration and missing another cause Failing to protect the airway promptly and allowing continued soiling Assuming a normal early chest radiograph excludes significant aspiration Aspiration occurs when protective airway reflexes are obtunded, allowing gastric contents to enter the tracheobronchial tree. Acidic fluid causes rapid chemical burn of the alveolar-capillary membrane, triggering an inflammatory cascade with increased permeability, alveolar oedema, surfactant dysfunction, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch that produces hypoxaemia. Particulate matter can cause mechanical obstruction and atelectasis. The initial insult is sterile, but secondary bacterial infection may supervene, and severe injury can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome. Severity depends on the volume, acidity, and particulate content of the aspirate. Mild chemical pneumonitis often resolves within days with supportive care, but large-volume acidic or particulate aspiration can cause severe respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and death.
