mechanism noted elsewhere in text) An exacerbation is an episode of acute bronchospasm that may be severe enough to require emergency care or hospitalization and can be fatal (p.2216). During an acute attack patients typically show tachypnea, tachycardia and accessory-muscle use, with wheezing and a prolonged expiratory phase (p.2222). As airway obstruction worsens the chest may become 'silent' with loss of breath sounds, indicating a more dangerous attack rather than improvement (p.2222). Most patients in an attack are hypocapnic from a high respiratory rate; a normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic signals impending respiratory failure (p.2227). PEFR, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC are reduced in obstruction, but these may appear normal during an attack or after recent bronchodilator use, so a normal value does not exclude severe disease (p.2222-2223). In urgent care, PEFR/FEV1 should be measured; patients with PEFR >60% predicted often respond to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h should prompt hospital admission (p.2227). Severe exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids may themselves accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221). More than one-third of patients carrying a physician diagnosis of asthma do not actually meet diagnostic criteria, so consider mimics when an 'asthmatic' fails to respond (p.2222). Some patients cannot distinguish an anxiety attack from an asthma attack, which can confound assessment of an apparent exacerbation (p.2222). Silent chest with loss of breath sounds (life-threatening) (p.2222) Normal or near-normal PaCO2 in a distressed asthmatic, or a rising PaCO2 - signals impending respiratory failure and possible need for mechanical ventilation (p.2227) Respiratory exhaustion / failure to respond to repeated beta2-agonists (p.2227) Failure to achieve PEFR >60% predicted or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h (warrants admission) (p.2227) Need for hourly beta2-agonists for several hours despite treatment (p.2227) Status asthmaticus: severe attack in which mechanical ventilation is difficult due to high airway resistance/pressures (p.2227) Interpreting a 'silent chest' or quieting wheeze as improvement when it actually signals worsening, life-threatening obstruction (p.2222). Being reassured by a normal/normalizing PaCO2 - in a distressed asthmatic this is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure, not stability (p.2227). Relying on PFT/PEF values that may look normal during an attack or shortly after bronchodilator use (p.2222-2223). Overlooking mimics such as vocal-cord dysfunction, heart failure or COPD in 'difficult' or treatment-refractory presentations - over one-third of diagnosed asthmatics do not meet criteria (p.2222). Missing precipitants such as beta-blockers (including ophthalmic drops), aspirin/NSAIDs in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, or ACE-inhibitor cough (p.2221). Giving antibiotics routinely in an exacerbation - they should be used only if there are signs of infection (p.2227). Asthma is characterized by episodic, usually reversible airway obstruction with airway hyperresponsiveness, generally accompanied by airway inflammation (most often eosinophilic, sometimes neutrophilic, occasionally with no obvious inflammation). Exacerbations are episodes of acute bronchospasm driven by luminal narrowing from airway smooth-muscle constriction, airway edema and mucus secretion, superimposed on chronic airway inflammation. Triggers activate mast cells/basophils and inflammatory cells (releasing bronchoconstrictors and mediators) and stimulate sensory nerves acting on smooth muscle. Allergen exposure can cause an immediate (early) bronchospasm and a late response 2-24 h later with airway narrowing and inflammation. Structural airway-wall thickening (smooth-muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, subepithelial collagen deposition, edema, mucosal inflammation) increases the tendency to narrow disproportionately. In severe airflow obstruction there may be air trapping with dynamically elevated FRC and increased residual volume; mild hypoxemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch (oxygen-responsive) is common (p.2216-2217, p.2221, p.2222-2223). Asthma causes significant morbidity and mortality; roughly 3000-4000 people die from asthma each year in the United States. Death can occur even in mild asthma (at lower rates than severe asthma). Mortality in patients over 65 is about five times that of younger cohorts. High-risk features for asthma death include prior ICU admission or intubation for asthma, illicit drug use, depression, a new diagnosis within the past year, two or more emergency visits in the past 6 months, severe psychosocial problems, lower socioeconomic status, and being on daily prednisone before admission. Severe exacerbations may accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221, p.2227). Harrison stratifies acute deteriorations practically rather than by a fixed table. Mild-to-moderate deteriorations can initially be managed with frequent beta2-agonists; failure to control with hourly beta2-agonists for several hours warrants urgent care. In urgent/ED care, PEFR or FEV1 guides severity: PEFR >60% predicted usually responds to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach PEFR >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h indicates a severe attack needing admission. Life-threatening / near-fatal features include silent chest, respiratory exhaustion, and a normal or rising PaCO2 signaling impending respiratory failure; status asthmaticus denotes a severe refractory attack with high airway resistance making ventilation difficult (p.2227).

recurrent infection and aspiration Immunodeficiency raising the risk of severe infection Exposing patients to standard-dose radiation before recognising the diagnosis Attributing early ataxia to Ataxia-telangiectasia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ATM gene, which encodes a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and coordinates the cellular response, including cell-cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis. Loss of ATM function leaves cells unable to respond properly to DNA damage, causing genomic instability, heightened sensitivity to ionising radiation, and a strong predisposition to malignancy. Progressive death of cerebellar Purkinje and granule cells produces the characteristic neurodegeneration and ataxia, while impaired lymphocyte development and class-switching cause the combined immunodeficiency. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The condition is progressive, with most affected individuals becoming wheelchair-dependent by adolescence and life expectancy reduced, chiefly due to malignancy and chronic respiratory disease.

anti-Ri opsoclonus-myoclonus with breast/lung cancer and neuroblastoma) Anti-GAD65 antibody-associated progressive ataxia without underlying cancer Gluten/antigliadin antibody-associated ataxia (HLA DQB1*0201, may have villus atrophy on small-bowel biopsy) Hyponatremia-associated ataxia Vitamin E deficiency states (abetalipoproteinemia/Bassen-Kornzweig and ataxia with vitamin E deficiency) The core ataxic syndrome is gait impairment, scanning (unclear) speech, blurred vision from nystagmus, limb incoordination, and tremor on movement, reflecting disease of the cerebellum and its afferent/efferent pathways including the spinocerebellar and frontopontocerebellar tracts (p.3533). True cerebellar ataxia is an unsteady, imbalanced gait without vertigo, light-headedness, or sense of movement; vestibular/labyrinthine disorders by contrast produce gait disturbance accompanied by prominent dizziness (p.3533). Sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia can mimic cerebellar imbalance but is distinguished because instability worsens markedly when visual input is removed (positive Romberg sign); rarely proximal leg weakness also mimics cerebellar disease (p.3533). The tempo and pattern of onset guide etiology: gradual, bilateral, symmetric progression points to genetic, metabolic, immune, or toxic causes, whereas focal unilateral signs with headache and depressed consciousness, ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies, and contralateral weakness suggest a space-occupying cerebellar lesion (p.3533). Acute, reversible symmetric ataxias commonly follow intoxication with alcohol, phenytoin, lithium, or barbiturates and exposures such as toluene, gasoline/glue sniffing, methyl mercury, or bismuth (p.3533-3534). Subacute symmetric ataxia raises suspicion of alcoholic-nutritional vermal degeneration (thiamine/B12 deficiency), paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, immune-mediated ataxia, or a prion disorder (p.3533-3534). Friedreich's ataxia is the most common inherited ataxia, accounting for about half of all hereditary ataxias, and is autosomal recessive (p.3536). Friedreich's ataxia features onset before age 25 with progressive staggering gait, areflexia, extensor plantar responses, loss of vibratory/proprioceptive sensation, and frequently pes cavus and scoliosis (p.3536). Among the dominant ataxias, the polyglutamine SCAs (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3/Machado-Joseph, SCA6, SCA7, SCA17) arise from expanded CAG triplet repeats; genotype, not phenotype, is the diagnostic gold standard because clinical pictures overlap (p.3534). Retinal pigmentary degeneration (blue-yellow color blindness progressing to macular degeneration and visual loss) is the distinguishing feature of SCA7 among the spinocerebellar ataxias (p.3535-3536). Episodic ataxia type 1 causes brief (minutes-long) attacks of ataxia with myokymia and nystagmus, while type 2 produces longer attacks lasting hours to days; type 2 stems from CACNA1A mutations (the same calcium-channel gene as SCA6 and familial hemiplegic migraine) (p.3536). A treatable mimic to always exclude in chronic symmetric gait ataxia is hypothyroidism; infectious causes to consider include meningovascular syphilis/tabes dorsalis and Lyme disease (p.3534). Acute focal ataxia with headache, depressed consciousness, and ipsilateral pontine/cranial nerve signs suggesting cerebellar infarction or hemorrhage with brainstem compression Rapidly worsening focal cerebellar signs raising concern for posterior fossa hematoma, abscess, or tumor at risk of rostral (tentorial) or downward (foramen magnum/tonsillar) herniation, which can be devastating and may require emergent surgical decompression Subacute progressive ataxia as the presenting feature of an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndrome) Cardiac symptoms in Friedreich's ataxia (cardiomegaly, hypertrophy, conduction defects), since cardiac involvement occurs in about 90% of patients Recurrent pulmonary infections and lymphoreticular malignancy risk in ataxia-telangiectasia Mislabeling vestibular or sensory (proprioceptive) imbalance as cerebellar ataxia; absence of vertigo and a positive Romberg sign help distinguish them. Overlooking readily treatable and reversible causes such as hypothyroidism, vitamin E/B1/B12 deficiency, and intoxications. Relying on clinical phenotype alone to classify inherited ataxias, since SCA phenotypes overlap and genotype is the diagnostic gold standard. In Machado-Joseph disease type I, the stiff broad-based lurching gait results from spasticity rather than true ataxia and lacks truncal titubation, which can be misread. Failing to recognize an acute focal cerebellar lesion as a neurosurgical emergency because of herniation risk. Forgetting that some SCAs have prominent non-cerebellar features (e.g., retinal degeneration in SCA7, parkinsonism/extrapyramidal signs in SCA1/SCA2, peripheral neuropathy in MJD type III). Ataxia results from dysfunction of the cerebellum and the pathways connecting it to the rest of the nervous system, including the spinocerebellar tracts and the frontopontocerebellar pathway arising in the rostral frontal lobe. In the inherited polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias, expanded CAG triplet repeats produce mutant ataxin proteins with abnormally long polyglutamine tracts (generally toxic beyond ~40 glutamines); these proteins misfold into beta-pleated aggregates, are abnormally transported into the nucleus, bind and impair other polyglutamine proteins such as TATA-binding protein and CREB-binding protein, disrupt the ubiquitin-proteasome protein-turnover system, and trigger neuronal apoptosis, yielding a relatively disease-specific pattern of neuronal loss and gliosis. Longer repeats correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease across generations (anticipation). In Friedreich's ataxia, an expanded GAA repeat in the first intron of the frataxin gene silences frataxin expression; frataxin is a mitochondrial protein involved in iron homeostasis, so its loss causes mitochondrial iron accumulation, deficiency of iron-sulfur cluster enzymes, reduced ATP production, oxidative injury, and irreversible cell death, with predominant degeneration of the spinal cord (spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, posterior columns), dorsal root ganglia, and peripheral nerves. Prognosis depends on cause: several acquired ataxias (intoxications, postinfectious ataxia, hypothyroidism, vitamin deficiencies) are reversible, whereas the inherited degenerative ataxias progress relentlessly. In Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) deficits invariably progress to death from debilitation within about 15 years of onset (especially types I and II), with intellect usually preserved. Friedreich's ataxia has a median age of death around 35 years, and women have a significantly better prognosis than men. Larger triplet-repeat expansions correlate with earlier onset and more aggressive disease, and anticipation produces earlier, more severe disease in successive generations. No single formal severity score is given; etiologic and temporal frameworks are used instead. Cerebellar ataxia is categorized as symmetric/progressive versus focal/ipsilateral, each subdivided by tempo into acute (hours to days), subacute (days to weeks), or chronic (months to years) per Table 450-1. Inherited ataxias are classified genomically by mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant (SCAs, DRPLA, episodic ataxias), autosomal recessive (Friedreich's ataxia, ataxia-telangiectasia, RFC1-related CANVAS), and mitochondrial. Machado-Joseph disease is further graded into clinical types I (ALS-parkinsonism-dystonia), II (ataxic, most common), and III (ataxic-amyotrophic).

itch is the cardinal symptom and often precedes visible changes Distribution shifts with age: face and extensor surfaces in infants, flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae) in older children and adults Look for supporting features such as dry skin (xerosis), keratosis pilaris, and a personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis) The disease reflects impaired skin barrier plus immune dysregulation, so consistent emollient use is the foundation of every management plan Flares are treated with topical corticosteroids of potency matched to site and severity, or with topical calcineurin inhibitors on delicate areas Sudden worsening with weeping, crusting, or painful clustered vesicles suggests bacterial superinfection or eczema herpeticum, which needs prompt antiviral treatment Identify and reduce trigger exposure (soaps, heat, sweat, aeroallergens, stress) and consider phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators for severe refractory disease Eczema herpeticum: rapidly spreading painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions with systemic upset Extensive secondary bacterial infection or signs of sepsis Erythroderma with widespread inflammation and impaired thermoregulation Failure to thrive or recurrent severe infection suggesting underlying immunodeficiency Under-treating flares with insufficiently potent topical steroids while over-worrying about steroid side effects Neglecting regular generous emollient use, the cornerstone of maintenance Missing eczema herpeticum and treating it as a routine bacterial flare Attributing all disease to food allergy and pursuing unnecessary elimination diets Atopic dermatitis arises from the interplay of a defective epidermal barrier and a skewed type-2 immune response. Loss-of-function variants in the filaggrin gene and reduced barrier lipids increase transepidermal water loss and allow penetration of allergens and microbes. This drives activation of type-2 cytokines (including interleukins 4, 13, and 31) that promote inflammation, further barrier breakdown, and the sensation of itch. Scratching perpetuates an itch-scratch cycle, causing lichenification, and the barrier defect predisposes to colonisation and infection with Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus. Many children improve substantially or clear by adolescence, but a proportion have persistent or adult-onset disease; a relapsing course is typical and long-term control depends on barrier maintenance and trigger avoidance.

damage is advanced Transferrin is the plasma glycoprotein that binds iron and delivers it to cells, especially erythroid precursors, via the transferrin receptor. In congenital atransferrinaemia the near-absence of transferrin means dietary and recycled iron cannot be transported to the bone marrow, so haemoglobin synthesis is impaired and a microcytic anaemia develops even though total body iron is high. The excess iron, unable to be handled by the normal transferrin pathway, is absorbed avidly from the gut and deposited as haemosiderin in parenchymal organs, producing progressive hepatic, cardiac and endocrine iron toxicity that resembles other iron-overload states. Early recognition with transferrin or plasma replacement to support haematopoiesis and control of iron overload can markedly improve outcome; untreated disease progresses to organ damage from iron deposition, particularly cardiac and hepatic, which determines long-term prognosis.

Atrial fibrillation / arrhythmia — 12-lead ECG Electrolytes, TSH Echocardiogram Rate/rhythm control; anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 distinct P-wave morphologies with clear isoelectric intervals and a slower atrial rate than AF; typically in chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness) (p.1989). Other supraventricular tachycardias including atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia, AV nodal reentry, and AV reciprocating tachycardia, distinguished by 12-lead ECG appearance and response to AV nodal blockade (p.1976-1977). Preexcited (accessory-pathway) AF, presenting as an irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, beat-to-beat-variable QRS morphology (p.1985-1986). Transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion when AF duration is >48 h or unknown (p.1992). Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-acquisition imaging as an alternative to TEE for left atrial appendage thrombus detection, with high sensitivity and specificity (p.1992). Ambulatory ECG monitoring, implantable loop recorders, or wearable/home ECG devices to capture intermittent or subclinical episodes (p.1991, 1993). AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia; prevalence rises steeply with age (~20% of those over 80), and the lifetime risk for a 40-year-old man is roughly one in four (p.1990). On the ECG, AF shows absence of organized atrial activity (no P waves) with an irregularly irregular ventricular response; the chaotic atrial activity is often best seen in lead V1 (p.1990, 1991). The conducted ventricular rate is variable and usually rapid (commonly 110-160/min), but may exceed 200/min, or be inappropriately slow when there is high vagal tone or AV nodal conduction disease (p.1990). Many patients are unaware of the irregular heartbeat, so AF is frequently asymptomatic; absence of AF on intermittent monitoring does not establish low risk (p.1990, 1993). AF is categorized by temporal pattern: paroxysmal (self-terminating, usually within 7 days), persistent (continuous >7 days but <1 year), and long-standing persistent (>1 year); these patterns correlate with progressive left atrial enlargement and scar burden (p.1990, 1991). Stroke and bleeding risks are estimated as concepts using the CHA2DS2-VASc score (stroke risk: congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, sex) and HAS-BLED score (bleeding risk), respectively (p.1993). AF burden does not predict stroke risk; the approach to paroxysmal AF is the same as for persistent AF, and even apparently infrequent episodes carry risk because asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993). Subclinical AF detectable only on long-term continuous monitoring is associated with roughly 2.5-fold increased stroke risk (p.1993). AF detected after cryptogenic stroke using insertable cardiac monitors in up to ~8.9% of patients within 6 months, supporting prolonged rhythm monitoring in this setting (p.1990). Acute AF with significant haemodynamic compromise, pulmonary oedema, or evidence of coronary ischaemia indicates need for emergent cardioversion (p.1992). Preexcited AF over an accessory pathway with very rapid repetitive conduction (minimum R-R <250 ms occurs in ~25% of preexciting pathways) is potentially life-threatening, predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (p.1985-1986). Syncope or presyncope from bradycardia/pauses, including offset pauses on spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm, suggesting coexisting sinus node dysfunction (tachy-brady syndrome) (p.1992). Sustained uncontrolled rapid ventricular rates risk precipitating heart failure and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1990, 1992). Relying on AF burden or symptom frequency to gauge stroke risk is mistaken; anticoagulation decisions should rest on the risk-factor profile, not how often AF is documented (p.1993). A normal intermittent monitor does not exclude clinically important AF, since asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993). Cardioverting AF of >48 h (or unknown) duration without anticoagulation or thrombus exclusion risks thromboembolism, which can occur even days later because of post-conversion atrial stunning (delayed recovery of mechanical function) (p.1992). Nonvalvular AF (AF without mitral stenosis) differs in management from valvular AF; rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical valves carry especially high thromboembolic risk (p.1993). AF is characterized by disorganized, rapid, irregular atrial electrical activation with loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction; the AV node filters these impulses to produce an irregular ventricular rate. The pathophysiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with a proposed 'final common pathway' in which risk factors (age, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing) drive electrophysiologic changes in atrial tissue. Altered membrane channel regulation produces abnormal excitability; pulmonary vein musculature (and other foci such as the posterior left atrial wall, superior vena cava, coronary sinus, vein of Marshall) shows enhanced automaticity generating ectopic beats that initiate AF. Progressive cellular and tissue remodeling shortens atrial refractory periods and creates functional reentry, with eventual fibrosis and left atrial enlargement, explaining the typical progression from paroxysmal to persistent to long-standing persistent disease. Loss of atrial systole reduces cardiac output, and variable ventricular filling produces variable stroke volume (p.1990-1992). AF is not benign: it carries a 1.5- to 1.9-fold increased mortality after adjusting for underlying cardiac disease, and causes approximately 25% of all strokes. It increases the risk of dementia, MRI-detected silent embolic infarcts, congestive heart failure, and cardiomyopathy. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is generally reversible once ventricular rate is controlled. AF tends to be progressive, with no definitive durable cure, and patients maintaining sinus rhythm generally have better survival than those who remain in AF (p.1990, 1992, 1994). By temporal pattern: paroxysmal AF (self-terminates or is cardioverted within 7 days; normal-to-mildly enlarged left atrium, low scar burden), persistent AF (continuous >7 days but <1 year; mild-to-severe LA enlargement, moderate scar), and long-standing persistent AF (>1 year; severely enlarged LA, high scar burden). A newer staged framework (at risk of AF, pre-AF, AF, permanent AF) reframes AF as a disease continuum. Mitral stenosis defines valvular versus nonvalvular AF for risk purposes (p.1991, 1993, 1996).

Atrial Myxoma and Other Cardiac Tumors — Cardiac myxoma, Left atrial myxoma, Primary cardiac tumor, Cardiac sarcoma, Cardiac neoplasm Mitral stenosis Mitral regurgitation Subaortic or subpulmonic (outflow tract) stenosis from a ventricular tumor Restrictive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (mimicked by pediatric rhabdomyoma/fibroma) Pericardial constriction Infective endocarditis (myxoma with embolic phenomena, fever, and constitutional symptoms is frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis) Valvular vegetation Transthoracic echocardiography (initial modality; tumor location, size, attachment site, impact on valves/pericardium) Transesophageal echocardiography (improved characterization and spatial resolution; aids surgical planning) Cardiac MRI with gadolinium (tissue characterization, local invasion, differentiating tumor from thrombus) Gated cardiac CT (anatomic and tissue assessment, calcified lesions, extracardiac involvement; useful when MRI not feasible) Nuclear imaging including FDG-PET (extracardiac disease; some tumor types) and 131I-MIBG scanning for paraganglioma Echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives when myxoma is familial/syndromic Pericardiocentesis with cytology for malignant pericardial effusion (reported sensitivity ~67-92%) Intracardiac thrombus Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor Myocardial hypertrophy mistaken for a mass Collagen vascular disease (mimicked by myxoma constitutional/laboratory picture) Paraneoplastic syndrome Cardiac tumors are broadly divided into primary tumors (arising in the heart) and metastatic tumors from a distant source; metastatic involvement is far more common and is seen in up to roughly 20% of patients with end-stage metastatic cancer. Primary cardiac tumors are rare (about 1 in 2000 in autopsy series); roughly three-quarters are histologically benign, and most of those benign tumors are myxomas, while malignant primaries (almost all sarcomas) make up about 25%. Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, comprising one-third to one-half of cases at postmortem and about three-quarters of surgically treated tumors; it favors the third through sixth decades with a female predilection. Roughly 90% of myxomas are sporadic; the remainder are familial (autosomal dominant), often as part of the Carney complex (cardiac/skin/breast myxomas, lentigines or pigmented nevi, and endocrine overactivity), associated in about 70% of cases with inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A tumor-suppressor gene. Sporadic myxomas are typically solitary, pedunculated on a fibrovascular stalk, and arise from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, most often in the left atrium; familial/syndromic myxomas occur in younger patients, are often multiple, may be ventricular, and recur more often. Myxomas most commonly produce obstructive features mimicking mitral valve disease (stenosis from prolapse into the mitral orifice, or regurgitation from valvular trauma); symptoms may be sudden or positional because of gravitational effects on tumor position. A characteristic low-pitched early or mid-diastolic 'tumor plop' may be heard, attributed to the tumor striking the mitral valve or ventricular wall. Myxomas can cause peripheral or pulmonary embolic events (tumor fragments or associated thrombus) and constitutional/cytokine-mediated features (often interleukin-6), so they are frequently misdiagnosed as endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome. Papillary fibroelastomas are the most common tumors of the cardiac valves (friable, frond-like, usually solitary) and, although often silent, may embolize to cause TIA, stroke, or myocardial infarction. Rhabdomyomas and fibromas are the most common cardiac tumors of infants and children, usually ventricular; rhabdomyomas occur in about 50% of children with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations) and tend to regress, whereas fibromas (PTCH1) tend to grow. Malignant primaries are almost all sarcomas (angiosarcoma most common in adults, rhabdomyosarcoma in children), frequently right-sided, rapidly growing, and often invade the pericardium; about one-third are metastatic at diagnosis, usually to the lungs. Tissue histology remains the gold standard for diagnosis; echocardiography is the usual initial test, with cardiac MRI (gadolinium) helping differentiate tumor from thrombus and benign from malignant lesions. Syncope or positional symptoms suggesting intermittent obstruction by a mobile tumor Embolic events (stroke, TIA, peripheral or pulmonary embolism) as the presenting feature Cardiac tamponade or large pericardial effusion (especially with metastatic disease) Rapidly progressive heart failure or chamber/vena caval obstruction suggesting sarcoma New heart block or conduction disturbance (tumors near the AV node, e.g., hemangioma/mesothelioma, can cause sudden death) Misdiagnosing myxoma as infective endocarditis, collagen vascular disease, or a paraneoplastic syndrome because of fever, embolism, and laboratory abnormalities (e.g., elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia). Catheterizing the chamber harboring a tumor, which risks tumor embolization; angiography/catheterization is no longer mandatory when noninvasive imaging is adequate and coronary disease is unlikely. Failing to screen first-degree relatives of young patients with multiple myxomas or syndromic features. Attributing cardiac symptoms in cancer patients solely to the tumor when radiotherapy/chemotherapy-induced myocarditis, pericarditis, or cardiomyopathy can produce identical findings. Overlooking that a left-sided sarcoma may be mistaken for a myxoma. Cardiac tumors are classified as primary (benign, chiefly myxoma; or malignant, chiefly sarcoma) or secondary/metastatic. Myxomas are gelatinous masses of myxoma cells in a glycosaminoglycan-rich stroma, usually arising from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis and most often projecting into the left atrium on a fibrovascular stalk. Clinical effects arise from three mechanisms: mechanical obstruction or valvular interference (mimicking mitral stenosis/regurgitation, or outflow obstruction for ventricular tumors), embolization of tumor fragments or associated thrombus, and constitutional effects from tumor-secreted cytokines such as interleukin-6. Familial myxomas relate to PRKAR1A inactivation within the Carney complex. Metastatic tumors reach the heart by hematogenous or lymphangitic spread or direct invasion, most often involving the pericardium, then myocardium of any chamber, and rarely the endocardium or valves. Benign myxoma is generally cured by surgical excision; recurrence is about 1-2% in sporadic cases but 12-22% in familial cases (multifocal disease or incomplete resection). Malignant primary tumors carry a poor prognosis: sarcomas typically progress rapidly to death within weeks to months from hemodynamic compromise, local invasion, or metastasis, and respond poorly to radiotherapy/chemotherapy. The notable exception is primary cardiac lymphoma, the most chemotherapy-sensitive primary cardiac malignancy, with long-term survival in about 40% of treated patients. Metastatic cardiac involvement usually occurs with advanced disease, is clinically apparent only about 10% of the time, is rarely the cause of death, and carries an overall poor prognosis.

Atrial Septal Defect — ASD, atrial septal defects Ventricular septal defect Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return Atrioventricular septal defect (primum type) Innocent pulmonary flow murmur Pulmonary valve stenosis Patent foramen ovale (a normal variant, not a true defect) Echocardiography to define defect type, size, and right heart volume overload Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings in significant shunts Electrocardiogram, often showing right axis deviation and right ventricular volume overload (rsR' pattern) Transoesophageal echocardiography or advanced imaging when transthoracic views are inadequate Cardiac catheterisation if pulmonary hypertension needs assessment A communication in the atrial septum permitting left-to-right shunting; the secundum type in the region of the fossa ovalis is the most common form. Most children are asymptomatic and are detected through an incidental murmur or, later, right heart enlargement; heart failure in infancy is uncommon. The characteristic auscultatory finding is a widely and fixedly split second heart sound, accompanied by a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border from increased pulmonary flow. A larger shunt may produce a mid-diastolic rumble at the lower left sternal border from increased flow across the tricuspid valve. The murmur reflects increased flow through the pulmonary valve rather than turbulent flow across the defect itself, which is low-velocity and inaudible. Echocardiography defines the defect type and size, direction of shunt, and degree of right atrial and right ventricular volume overload. Small secundum defects frequently close spontaneously in early childhood; a defect must be distinguished from a normal patent foramen ovale. Significant defects are closed, often by transcatheter device for suitable secundum defects, to prevent later right heart enlargement, arrhythmias, and pulmonary vascular disease. Untreated large defects may lead in adulthood to atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, and, rarely, paradoxical embolism. Signs of significant right heart volume overload or pulmonary hypertension Development of atrial arrhythmias Failure to thrive or heart failure in an infant, suggesting an additional or larger lesion New cyanosis suggesting shunt reversal in longstanding, untreated disease Paradoxical embolic events Mistaking a normal patent foramen ovale for a true atrial septal defect Dismissing the subtle findings and missing a significant defect until right heart enlargement is advanced Attributing fixed splitting of the second heart sound to a benign murmur Assuming all defects require closure when many small secundum defects close spontaneously Overlooking associated anomalous pulmonary venous drainage An opening in the atrial septum allows blood to shunt from the higher-compliance left atrium toward the right atrium, the direction favoured because the right ventricle is more compliant than the left. This left-to-right shunt volume-loads the right atrium, right ventricle, and pulmonary circulation while the left-sided output is maintained by the shunt returning through the lungs. Chronic volume overload dilates the right heart; over many years a minority develop elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary hypertension, and the resulting right atrial stretch predisposes to atrial arrhythmias. Isolated secundum defects, whether closed spontaneously, by device, or surgically, have an excellent outlook when addressed before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Late, unrepaired large defects carry increasing risk of arrhythmia and pulmonary hypertension in adulthood.

change Failing to investigate secondary causes when disease is unilateral or atypical In atrophic rhinitis the respiratory epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia and the seromucinous glands, cilia, and nerve endings are lost, while the turbinate bone resorbs. The nasal cavity therefore widens abnormally and loses its normal humidifying and self-cleaning function, so secretions dry into thick crusts that are colonised by organisms (classically Klebsiella ozaenae) producing the foetid odour. Proposed contributors include chronic infection, nutritional deficiency, endocrine and hereditary factors, and autonomic imbalance; secondary forms follow destruction of mucosa by surgery, radiotherapy, trauma, or granulomatous disease. The condition is chronic and tends to persist for years; symptoms can be well controlled with diligent nasal hygiene and moisturising measures, and surgical narrowing helps selected refractory cases, but complete cure of primary disease is uncommon and secondary disease depends on treating its cause.

awaiting genetic results Confusing it with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and mismanaging accordingly Attributing the picture to typical HUS and withholding complement-directed therapy Forgetting meningococcal vaccination and prophylaxis considerations before complement inhibition Underestimating the risk of recurrence in a kidney transplant Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is driven by uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway on endothelial surfaces. Under normal conditions, regulatory proteins such as complement factor H, factor I and membrane cofactor protein restrain complement amplification; loss-of-function variants in these regulators, or gain-of-function variants in the C3 convertase components C3 and factor B, allow persistent complement activation and generation of the terminal membrane attack complex. The resulting endothelial injury, particularly in the renal microvasculature, promotes platelet activation and microthrombus formation, which mechanically shears red cells to produce microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, consumes platelets to cause thrombocytopenia, and obstructs glomerular capillaries to cause acute kidney injury. A genetic predisposition typically requires an environmental trigger such as infection or pregnancy to precipitate an episode. Before complement-targeted therapy many patients progressed to end-stage kidney disease or died; terminal complement inhibition has greatly improved renal and overall outcomes, though prognosis still depends on the underlying genetic variant and the promptness of treatment.

Autism Spectrum Disorder — ASD, autism, autistic spectrum disorder, pervasive developmental disorder Global developmental delay or intellectual disability Isolated language disorder or hearing impairment Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Social (pragmatic) communication disorder Anxiety disorders and selective mutism Rett syndrome and other genetic or metabolic syndromes Severe early deprivation or attachment disorder Formal audiology assessment to exclude hearing loss Structured diagnostic observation and developmental history Genetic evaluation (chromosomal microarray, fragile X testing, targeted panels) Assessment of cognitive and adaptive functioning Screening for co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy or sleep disorders Metabolic testing when clinical features suggest an inborn error A neurodevelopmental disorder defined by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction together with restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests, or activities. Symptoms are present from early development, though they may become fully apparent only when social demands exceed the child's capacities. It is more frequently diagnosed in boys and shows a strong genetic contribution, with increased recurrence risk in siblings. Early signs include reduced eye contact, limited joint attention and pointing, absent or delayed social smiling, and lack of response to name. Repetitive behaviours may include hand-flapping, lining up objects, insistence on routines, and unusual sensory responses. Diagnosis is clinical and based on developmental history and structured observation rather than a laboratory test. Routine developmental surveillance and autism-specific screening in toddlerhood aid early identification. Early intensive behavioural and educational intervention improves functional outcomes. Common co-occurring conditions include intellectual disability, ADHD, anxiety, epilepsy, sleep problems, and gastrointestinal symptoms, and no evidence links vaccines to autism. Regression or loss of previously acquired language or social skills Absence of babbling, pointing, or other gestures by around 12 months No single words by 16 months or no two-word phrases by 24 months Seizures or focal neurological signs suggesting an underlying disorder Concern for self-injurious behaviour or safety Attributing early social and language concerns to shyness and delaying referral Failing to test hearing before attributing delay to autism Overlooking treatable co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy, anxiety, or sleep disturbance Assuming intellectual ability from verbal fluency alone Autism arises from atypical early brain development influenced by a strong and heterogeneous genetic basis, including many single-gene syndromes, copy number variants, and polygenic risk, interacting with prenatal and perinatal factors. These influences alter neuronal connectivity, synaptic function, and the balance of excitation and inhibition during critical periods, affecting circuits underlying social cognition, language, and behavioural flexibility. No single mechanism or biomarker accounts for all cases, reflecting the disorder's biological heterogeneity. Outcomes vary widely; language ability and cognitive level are important predictors, and early intervention improves adaptive functioning, though most individuals have lifelong needs requiring ongoing support.

Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome — ALPS, Canale-Smith syndrome Lymphoma and other lymphoproliferative malignancies Common variable immunodeficiency with autoimmune features Evans syndrome from other causes Chronic viral infection causing lymphadenopathy (for example EBV) Other immune dysregulation syndromes such as activated PI3K-delta syndrome Flow cytometry to quantify alpha-beta double-negative T cells Full blood count and direct antiglobulin test for autoimmune cytopenias Serum vitamin B12, IL-10, and soluble FAS ligand as supportive biomarkers In vitro lymphocyte apoptosis assays Genetic testing (FAS, FASLG, CASP10 and related genes) Imaging and, where indicated, lymph node biopsy to exclude lymphoma Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome is a disorder of defective lymphocyte apoptosis, most often caused by mutations in the FAS (TNFRSF6) pathway Impaired programmed cell death allows autoreactive lymphocytes to accumulate, producing chronic non-malignant lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly A hallmark laboratory finding is an expanded population of 'double-negative' T cells (CD3-positive, TCR alpha-beta-positive, but CD4- and CD8-negative) Autoimmune cytopenias are characteristic, particularly autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia Unlike most primary immunodeficiencies, the dominant clinical problem is immune dysregulation and autoimmunity rather than recurrent infection, though hyposplenism after splenectomy raises infection risk Supportive biomarkers include raised serum vitamin B12, elevated IL-10 and soluble FAS ligand, and increased IgG There is a substantially increased lifetime risk of lymphoma, warranting long-term surveillance Treatment targets the autoimmune manifestations with immunosuppression and, in refractory cases, agents such as sirolimus or mycophenolate; splenectomy is generally avoided because of infection risk and often incomplete benefit Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric, or hard lymph nodes or systemic B symptoms suggesting lymphoma and needing urgent evaluation Severe autoimmune cytopenia (profound anaemia or thrombocytopenia) causing symptomatic disease Overwhelming infection risk if the patient is asplenic, requiring vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis Massive splenomegaly at risk of rupture Mistaking the chronic lymphadenopathy for lymphoma and vice versa, delaying correct management Performing splenectomy for cytopenias without recognising the resulting infection risk and often limited durable benefit Overlooking the diagnostic value of double-negative T cells and supportive biomarkers Attributing recurrent cytopenias to isolated Evans syndrome without investigating for ALPS Neglecting long-term lymphoma surveillance Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome results from defects in the FAS-mediated (extrinsic) apoptotic pathway that normally deletes activated and autoreactive lymphocytes at the end of an immune response. Germline or somatic mutations in FAS, or in FAS ligand or caspase-10, impair this death signal, so lymphocytes fail to undergo apoptosis and accumulate. This produces the chronic lymphoproliferation (lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly) and the expansion of the unusual alpha-beta double-negative T-cell population. The persistence of autoreactive clones and disturbed immune homeostasis drives autoimmune cytopenias and other autoimmune features, and the impaired deletion of proliferating lymphocytes underlies the elevated risk of lymphoma. Many patients do well with control of autoimmune complications, and lymphoproliferation may lessen with age, but the markedly increased risk of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma means lifelong surveillance is essential and largely determines long-term outcome.

FAS ligand and caspase-10 defects also occur, and somatic FAS mutations are recognised Supportive biomarkers include raised vitamin B12, soluble FAS ligand, interleukin-10 and interleukin-18 There is a substantially increased lifetime risk of Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma Immunosuppression targeting the autoimmune cytopenias is used rather than routine splenectomy, which carries added sepsis risk in these patients Rapidly enlarging, asymmetric or B-symptom-associated lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma transformation Severe autoimmune haemolysis or thrombocytopenia with bleeding Overwhelming sepsis, particularly if the spleen has been removed New cytopenias or organomegaly warranting re-evaluation for malignancy Misdiagnosing the lymphoproliferation as lymphoma and administering unnecessary chemotherapy Performing splenectomy for cytopenias without recognising the heightened post-splenectomy sepsis risk Overlooking the diagnosis in a child labelled as having idiopathic Evans syndrome Failing to arrange long-term lymphoma surveillance Autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome results from impaired programmed cell death (apoptosis) of lymphocytes through the FAS receptor pathway. Under normal circumstances, activated lymphocytes that are no longer needed, including autoreactive clones, are removed when FAS engages its ligand and triggers a caspase-dependent death signal. Mutations affecting FAS, its ligand, or downstream caspase-10 disrupt this deletion, so lymphocytes accumulate, producing chronic lymphoproliferation and a characteristic expansion of immature double-negative T cells. The persistence of autoreactive cells drives autoimmunity, predominantly directed at blood cells, and the failure of a key tumour-suppressive apoptotic checkpoint underlies the elevated lymphoma risk. Many patients have a chronic but manageable course with autoimmune cytopenias controlled by immunosuppression and lymphoproliferation that may lessen with age, but the persistently raised risk of lymphoma requires lifelong surveillance and tempers the overall outlook.

Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes — APS, APS-1, APS-2, APECED, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome, polyglandular deficiency syndrome Isolated autoimmune Addison's disease without polyglandular involvement Isolated autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis or Graves' disease Isolated type 1 diabetes mellitus Idiopathic/isolated hypoparathyroidism IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, X-linked) Insulin autoimmune syndrome (Hirata's syndrome) Adult combined pituitary hormone deficiency with anti-Pit1 autoantibodies (anti-Pit1 syndrome) POEMS syndrome Kearns-Sayre and DIDMOAD (Wolfram) syndromes as causes of multiple endocrine deficiencies Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis from primary immunodeficiencies other than APS-1 (e.g., STAT1 gain-of-function) Congenital rubella associated with thyroiditis and/or diabetes AIRE gene sequencing in suspected APS-1 Anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies (identify nearly 100% of APS-1) Anticytokine antibodies to IL-17 and IL-22 (support candidiasis of APS-1) Anti-21-hydroxylase (and anti-17-hydroxylase) autoantibodies for Addison's disease risk Morning ACTH and cortisol; cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test if abnormal Serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH for hypoparathyroidism TSH with anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin and anti-TSH receptor antibodies Islet autoantibodies (insulin, GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) and hemoglobin A1c for type 1 diabetes Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies for celiac disease Vitamin B12, CBC, and anti-parietal cell/intrinsic factor antibodies for pernicious anemia Peripheral blood smear for Howell-Jolly bodies to detect asplenism (with splenic ultrasound if positive) Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced endocrinopathies producing multiple gland failure Sequential isolated autoimmune endocrinopathies occurring by chance Trisomy 21 and Turner's syndrome associated autoimmune endocrine disease Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (APS) are divided into two principal categories: APS type 1 (APS-1) and APS type 2 (APS-2); some authors further split APS-2 into APS-3 and APS-4, but this added subdivision adds little to understanding pathogenesis or guiding management (Harrison 22e p.3089). Although the underlying autoimmunity predominantly targets endocrine glands, many nonendocrine tissues can be affected, so a range of nonendocrine disorders is recognized as part of these syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3089). APS-1 (APECED) is defined by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison's disease; the diagnosis is usually made clinically when two of these three major components are present (Harrison 22e p.3089). APS-1 is rare (<500 reported cases) and classically is autosomal recessive, caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21; AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells where it drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens such as insulin (Harrison 22e p.3089). Anticytokine autoantibodies are characteristic of APS-1: anti-IL-17A, anti-IL-17F, and anti-IL-22 underlie the mucocutaneous candidiasis, while detection of anti-interferon alpha and anti-interferon omega antibodies identifies nearly 100% of APS-1 cases and is not seen in other autoimmune disorders (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090). APS-1 typically begins in infancy with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (mouth and nails more than skin/esophagus), followed by hypoparathyroidism (>85% of cases) and then Addison's disease (nearly 80%); the interval between components can be many years and the order is variable (Harrison 22e p.3089-3090). APS-2 is more common (prevalence 1-2 per 100,000), shows a female predominance (at least 3:1), has multigenerational inheritance, and usually presents in adulthood with peak incidence between 20 and 60 years (Harrison 22e p.3090). APS-2 is defined by two or more of: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, 50-70%), Graves' disease or autoimmune thyroiditis (15-69%), type 1 diabetes (40-50%), and primary hypogonadism; associated conditions include celiac disease, myasthenia gravis, vitiligo, alopecia, serositis, and pernicious anemia (Harrison 22e p.3090). Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by coexisting primary hypothyroidism because low thyroid hormone prolongs the half-life of cortisol; patients with hypothyroidism and possible APS should be screened for adrenal insufficiency, since starting thyroid hormone first can precipitate an adrenal crisis (Harrison 22e p.3090). Antibody screening can detect risk years before clinical disease: anti-21-hydroxylase antibodies are highly predictive of future adrenal insufficiency, and presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is defined as stage 1 type 1 diabetes with a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical disease (Harrison 22e p.3091). About 50% of patients with Addison's disease develop another autoimmune disorder during their lifetime, so a new diagnosis of Addison's should prompt broader screening for linked conditions (Harrison 22e p.3091). New thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient with adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis Treatment of mucocutaneous candidiasis with ketoconazole in a patient with subclinical adrenal insufficiency may also precipitate adrenal crisis Hyperpigmentation, unexplained hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, or hypotension signaling evolving Addison's disease Tetany or seizures from hypocalcemia indicating hypoparathyroidism Howell-Jolly bodies on smear indicating functional asplenism and increased infection risk in APS-1 Refractory diarrhea or obstipation suggesting autoimmune destruction of enterochromaffin(-like) cells Chronic oral candidiasis with leukoplakia-like atrophic change carrying a risk of future carcinoma Initiating thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency, precipitating adrenal crisis Failing to recognize that one component disorder warrants screening for others, and that siblings of an APS-1 patient should be considered affected even with a single component Attributing chronic candidiasis purely to local infection rather than recognizing it as a marker of APS-1 Missing functional asplenism (Howell-Jolly bodies) in APS-1, which raises infection risk Overlooking subclinical/preclinical disease detectable only by autoantibodies and physiologic testing APS-1 is a monogenic, classically autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene on chromosome 21. AIRE is most highly expressed in thymic medullary epithelial cells, where it promotes expression of tissue-specific self-antigens; its loss reduces this expression and is thought to allow autoreactive T cells to escape central (thymic) deletion. Over 100 mutations are described, with higher frequency in certain ethnic groups (Iranian Jews, Sardinians, Finns, Norwegians, Irish). Newly recognized autosomal dominant mutations cluster in the PHD1 domain and tend to cause later-onset, less aggressive disease. Patients develop anticytokine autoantibodies (anti-IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, and type 1 interferons). In contrast, APS-2 is polygenic, with the dominant risk in the HLA complex on chromosome 6: Addison's disease in APS-2 is strongly linked to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4, with additional contributions from HLA-B8, DQ2, DQ8, and DRB1 subtypes. Non-HLA immune genes including MIC-A (the 5.1 allele strongly associated with Addison's), PTPN22, CTLA4, and IL-2R-alpha variants further modulate susceptibility. Organ damage in both syndromes is mediated by organ-specific autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells against targets such as 21-hydroxylase, GAD65, thyroid peroxidase, transglutaminase, and intrinsic factor (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091). These are chronic, progressive disorders in which individual component diseases continue to emerge over years to decades, so cumulative prevalence rises with age and lifelong surveillance is required. APS-1 typically presents earliest (often infancy) and its chronic candidiasis is nearly always present and poorly responsive to treatment. In APS-2, autoantibodies can precede clinical disease by many years, allowing early detection; about half of patients with Addison's disease develop an additional autoimmune disorder over their lifetime, and individuals with two or more islet autoantibodies have a near-100% lifetime risk of clinical type 1 diabetes. With timely hormone replacement and monitoring, prognosis for individual endocrinopathies is generally favorable, but unrecognized adrenal insufficiency or precipitated adrenal crisis is potentially fatal (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091). No formal severity grading is defined; classification is by type (APS-1 vs APS-2, with proposed APS-3/APS-4 subtypes) based on the constellation of component autoimmune disorders. For type 1 diabetes risk within APS-2, presence of two or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance is staged as stage 1 disease (Harrison 22e p.3089-3091).

Autoimmunity and Autoimmune Diseases — Autoimmune disease, AD, Loss of immune tolerance, Autoimmunity Organ-specific AD (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia/autoimmune gastritis, myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, vitiligo, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis) (p.2822) Systemic AD (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, primary antiphospholipid syndrome, Sjogren syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, mixed connective tissue disease) (p.2822) Systemic vasculitides (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, IgA/Henoch-Schonlein vasculitis, Behcet disease) (p.2822) Paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes (Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic pemphigus, dermatomyositis, anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis with ovarian cancer) (p.2826) Drug-induced lupus (antihistone-antibody positive) and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related immune adverse events (p.2826) Infections that trigger or mimic autoimmune flares: group A streptococcal infection underlying rheumatic fever via M-protein/myosin cross-reactivity (p.2825) Coxsackievirus (myocarditis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, T1DM) and influenza A (T1DM, IgA vasculitis) as proposed autoimmune triggers (p.2825) Epstein-Barr virus linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren syndrome (p.2825) SARS-CoV-2-associated myocarditis, antiphospholipid syndrome, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre syndrome (p.2826) Disease-specific autoantibody panels: anti-dsDNA and anti-RNP (SLE); anti-Ro/anti-La and rheumatoid factor (Sjogren); ACPA, anti-carbamylated antibodies, rheumatoid factor (RA); anti-MPO and anti-PR3 (ANCA-associated vasculitis); anti-type IV collagen (Goodpasture) (p.2825) Anti-TSH-receptor antibodies (Graves); anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin (Hashimoto) (p.2825) Islet-related antibodies in T1DM: anti-insulin, anti-GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase), anti-protein-tyrosine-phosphatase/IA-2; antibodies to multiple targets confer higher risk of progression (p.2825) Anti-parietal cell antibodies in pernicious anemia (present in 70-90% of patients) and antimitochondrial antibodies (anti-pyruvate dehydrogenase) in primary biliary cholangitis (p.2825) Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, anti-Mi2, anti-MDA5, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-HMGCR, anti-cN1A) for risk stratification in inflammatory myopathies (p.2825) Antihistone antibodies for suspected drug-induced lupus (p.2826) Serum tryptase, 24-h urinary 5-HIAA, and metanephrines to exclude mast-cell, carcinoid, and pheochromocytoma mimics when relevant (contextual) (p.2821) Paraneoplastic syndromes presenting before a cancer diagnosis (e.g., dermatomyositis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia, vitiligo, thyroiditis) (p.2826) Drug-induced autoimmunity from antibiotics, antihypertensives, antiarrhythmics, TNF inhibitors, antiseizure agents (p.2826) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia and mast-cell activation disorders presenting with multisystem symptoms (contextual, adjacent chapter) (p.2821) Autoimmunity (development of autoantibodies or autoreactive T-cell responses against self-antigens) is present in essentially all individuals and tends to increase with age; it does not by itself imply disease. Autoimmune disease (AD) arises only when a loss of tolerance produces clinically relevant, pathogenic responses (p.2821-2822). Roughly 150 organ-specific and systemic ADs have been described; in 2009 the U.S. prevalence was estimated at 7.6-9.4% of the population (about 25-31 million people), likely an underestimate, with an apparent ongoing rise in incidence and prevalence (p.2822). ADs predominantly affect women and, as a group, rank among the top 10 leading causes of death in women; an affected person carries a higher risk of developing a second autoimmune condition, of autoimmunity in relatives, and of certain cancers and premature cardiovascular disease (p.2822). AD is a multistep process: genetic and environmental factors drive immune dysregulation and loss of tolerance, and autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical symptoms appear (p.2822-2825). HLA haplotype is considered the best single predictor of AD risk; specific HLA-DR types, complement-component deficiencies, and genes in the type I interferon and B-/T-cell pathways raise risk, and many susceptibility genes (e.g., STAT4, PTPN22) are shared across several ADs (p.2822-2823). Autoantibodies serve as diagnostic tools and, in some diseases, as markers of activity or worse outcome; however, for several autoantibodies a specific pathogenic role has not been established, and the relevant autoantigens of many ADs remain unknown (p.2825). Natural autoantibodies are mainly IgM, encoded by unmutated V(D)J genes with moderate self-affinity, and are not pathogenic; the harmful autoantibodies of AD are high-affinity, somatically mutated IgG generated by somatic hypermutation, class switching, and antigen-driven clonal selection (p.2824-2825). Dysregulated type I interferon signaling is implicated across SLE, primary Sjogren syndrome, and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies; neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation externalizes modified autoantigens and is implicated in SLE, ANCA-associated vasculitis, myopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome, and RA (p.2823-2824). Many ADs are female-predominant; two X chromosomes (women, and men with Klinefelter XXY) increase expression of X-linked immunity genes such as TLR-7/8 and IRAK-1, and breakdown of X-inactivation has been linked to autoimmunity (p.2823). Infections can both trigger AD and provoke flares via molecular mimicry, epitope spreading, bystander/adjuvant effects, release of hidden self-antigens, and epigenetic changes; EBV is linked to SLE, MS, RA, celiac disease, and Sjogren, and SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with myocarditis, new APS, MIS-C, Kawasaki disease, and Guillain-Barre (p.2825-2826). Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) cause immune-related adverse events in up to 85% of treated patients (dermatitis, arthritis, thyroiditis, colitis among the most common); most are mild and overall survival/time to progression is generally not influenced by their occurrence (p.2826). Drug-induced lupus is a well-recognized iatrogenic AD characterized by antihistone antibodies; in many cases discontinuing the offending drug is sufficient to abate symptoms (p.2826). New autoimmune-pattern symptoms in a patient on an immune checkpoint inhibitor (irAE such as colitis, thyroiditis, arthritis, dermatitis) — can be severe and may persist after stopping therapy (p.2826) Sudden new autoimmunity or autoantibody synthesis following SARS-CoV-2 or other viral infection (APS, myocarditis, MIS-C, Guillain-Barre) (p.2826) Autoimmune presentation that may herald an occult malignancy (paraneoplastic syndromes often precede cancer diagnosis) (p.2826) Anti-Ro-positive pregnancy: IgG anti-Ro crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus and congenital heart block in the fetus (p.2825) Multiple positive autoantibody specificities (e.g., several islet antibodies in at-risk individuals) signaling high likelihood of progression to overt disease (p.2825) Equating autoimmunity with autoimmune disease: autoantibodies/autoreactivity occur in healthy individuals (and relatives) and increase with age without necessarily causing disease (p.2821-2822, p.2825). Assuming any detected autoantibody is pathogenic — several are used only as diagnostic or activity/outcome markers without a proven causal role (p.2825). Overlooking that classification criteria (e.g., for SLE) were designed for clinical-trial enrollment, not for individual diagnosis (contextual, p.2827). Attributing AD to infection on circumstantial grounds — causality is often unproven and supported mainly by animal models (p.2825-2826). Missing iatrogenic causes: failing to recognize drug-induced lupus (antihistone antibodies) or checkpoint-inhibitor irAEs, where stopping the agent may resolve symptoms (p.2826). Autoimmune disease reflects a failure of self-tolerance in a genetically predisposed host exposed to environmental and stochastic 'hits'. Central tolerance (deletion of autoreactive T cells in the thymus and high-affinity autoreactive B cells in the marrow) and peripheral tolerance (anergy from lack of costimulation, regulatory lymphocyte suppression, inhibitory costimulation, removal of autoreactive cells) normally restrain autoreactivity; impairment of these mechanisms allows pathogenic autoimmune responses. Susceptibility is largely polygenic (HLA-DR types, complement deficiencies, type I IFN-pathway and B-/T-cell genes such as STAT4 and PTPN22), with rare monogenic forms, and epigenetic programming (histone modifications, altered DNA methylation, trained immunity) further shapes risk. On the innate side, dysregulated or proinflammatory cell death (apoptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis, NETosis) plus impaired clearance of dead-cell debris and defective nucleases prolong exposure of modified nucleic-acid autoantigens; endosomal TLR-7/8/9 and cytosolic sensors then drive type I interferon production and inflammasome activation. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (major IFN-alpha producers), conventional dendritic cells, neutrophils/low-density granulocytes with aberrant NET formation, monocytes/macrophages with defective phagocytosis, and NK cells are all implicated. On the adaptive side, autoreactive CD4/CD8 T cells, Treg deficiency, and imbalance between costimulatory and inhibitory pathways (PD-1, CTLA-4) and cytokines (IL-2, IL-6, IL-17, IL-33) promote disease; pathogenic high-affinity IgG autoantibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissue, fix complement, opsonize, engage activating Fc receptors, and drive type I IFN production. Inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-17, type I IFNs) sustain and amplify tissue injury. Female sex (sex hormones, X-chromosome dosage) and immune aging (inflammaging with senescent, proinflammatory cells) further potentiate autoimmunity. ADs are described as chronic, incurable conditions that significantly impair quality of life and, in many cases, carry accelerated mortality; as a group they are among the top 10 leading causes of death in women. An individual with one AD has elevated risk of additional autoimmune conditions, certain cancers, and premature cardiovascular disease. Autoantibodies (e.g., ACPA in RA, islet antibodies in T1DM, antimitochondrial antibodies in PBC) may precede clinical disease by years to a decade and can mark worse prognosis. Better understanding of pathophysiology is hoped to enable primary or secondary prevention (e.g., trials of oral insulin in T1DM-autoantibody-positive infants and at-risk RA studies), though more data are needed (p.2822, p.2825-2826). No single unifying severity grading exists for autoimmunity as a whole; severity and classification are disease-specific and covered in the individual disease chapters. Autoantibody breadth/titer (e.g., number of islet antibodies in T1DM risk) and specific specificities (e.g., anti-TIF1-gamma marking cancer-associated myositis, anti-HMGCR statin-induced myositis, anti-cN1A inclusion body myositis) help stratify risk and outcome (p.2825).

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (PKD1/PKD2) — ADPKD, PKD1, PKD2, polycystin, adult polycystic kidney disease Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease Simple renal cysts or acquired cystic disease of chronic kidney disease Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal cysts and angiomyolipomas Von Hippel-Lindau disease with renal cysts and tumours Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies Renal ultrasound applying age-specific cyst-number diagnostic criteria MRI or CT for total kidney volume measurement and prognostication Blood pressure assessment and renal function monitoring Urinalysis for haematuria, proteinuria and infection MR angiography screening for intracranial aneurysm in selected patients (family history or high-risk occupation) Genetic testing of PKD1 and PKD2 when imaging is inconclusive or for family or reproductive planning The commonest inherited kidney disease, characterised by progressive bilateral renal cyst formation and enlarging kidneys Most disease results from mutations in PKD1 (encoding polycystin-1); PKD2 (polycystin-2) disease is generally milder with later kidney failure Typical presentations include hypertension, flank or abdominal pain, haematuria, urinary tract infection, stones, or an incidental family finding Extrarenal features include hepatic cysts, intracranial aneurysms, cardiac valve abnormalities and abdominal wall or inguinal hernias Diagnosis is usually by ultrasound using age-adjusted cyst-count criteria in an at-risk individual, with genetic testing where imaging is equivocal Total kidney volume is a validated marker of disease progression and helps identify rapid progressors Blood pressure control with renin-angiotensin blockade and, in selected rapidly progressing patients, a vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist can slow decline Sudden severe headache suggesting rupture of an intracranial aneurysm Cyst infection or haemorrhage with fever, severe pain or sepsis Rapidly rising blood pressure or accelerating decline in renal function Gross haematuria with clot colic or haemodynamic compromise Applying adult ultrasound cyst criteria to young at-risk relatives, in whom absence of cysts does not exclude disease Undertreating hypertension, a major modifiable driver of cardiovascular risk and progression Offering aneurysm screening indiscriminately rather than to those with family history or specific risk Missing cyst infection because standard imaging and cultures can be unremarkable ADPKD is caused by heterozygous mutations in PKD1 or PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 and polycystin-2, proteins that localise to the primary cilium and regulate tubular cell proliferation, differentiation and fluid secretion. A somatic second hit in individual tubular cells is thought to trigger focal cyst initiation, and cysts then expand through cell proliferation and fluid secretion driven in part by cyclic AMP and vasopressin signalling. Progressive cyst growth distorts and compresses the surrounding parenchyma, causing interstitial fibrosis, activation of the renin-angiotensin system, hypertension and gradual loss of glomerular filtration over decades. Progression is variable, with many PKD1 patients reaching end-stage kidney disease in mid-to-late adulthood while PKD2 disease progresses more slowly; blood pressure control and, in rapid progressors, vasopressin antagonism can delay kidney failure.

children Failing to arrange surveillance for portal hypertension and cholangitis ARPKD results from biallelic mutations in PKHD1, encoding fibrocystin (polyductin), a protein of the primary cilium and basal body of renal and biliary epithelium. Defective fibrocystin disrupts normal tubular and ductal development, producing non-obstructive fusiform dilatation of the renal collecting ducts and abnormal remodelling of the biliary tree (ductal plate malformation) with congenital hepatic fibrosis. Massive kidney enlargement in utero can restrict lung growth and amniotic fluid, while progressive tubular and interstitial injury impairs renal concentrating ability and glomerular filtration, and hepatic fibrosis leads to portal hypertension. Outcome depends heavily on surviving the neonatal period, since perinatal respiratory failure is a major early risk; children who survive infancy can live into adulthood but face progressive kidney failure and complications of congenital hepatic fibrosis requiring lifelong specialist care.

psychological harm including post-traumatic stress Risk factors include use of neuromuscular blockade (which masks movement), difficult airway management, haemodynamic instability limiting anaesthetic depth, and certain high-risk settings such as obstetric, cardiac, and trauma anaesthesia Total intravenous techniques carry particular risk if drug delivery fails or is interrupted, so vigilance over the infusion is essential Prevention includes confirming delivery and adequate dosing of anaesthetic, monitoring end-tidal volatile concentration, checking equipment, and considering processed EEG depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring in high-risk cases When paralysed, patients cannot signal distress, so clinical signs of light anaesthesia (movement, autonomic changes) may be blunted and must be interpreted with care If awareness is suspected or reported, a compassionate response, honest explanation, and structured psychological support and follow-up are important Documentation and use of a structured interview help confirm the event and guide support and any formal reporting Reports of explicit recall with pain or the sensation of paralysis Evidence of severe psychological distress or post-traumatic stress after surgery Recognised anaesthetic delivery failure during a paralysed case Signs of inadequate anaesthesia in a paralysed patient at high risk Relying on movement to gauge depth in a neuromuscularly blocked patient Failing to notice interrupted or failed intravenous anaesthetic delivery Dismissing or disbelieving a patient's report of awareness Not offering timely psychological support and follow-up Omitting depth monitoring in recognised high-risk situations General anaesthesia suppresses consciousness by acting on the brain, and adequate depth depends on delivering sufficient anaesthetic to the effect site relative to individual requirement and surgical stimulation. Awareness occurs when brain anaesthetic concentration is inadequate to prevent consciousness while the patient is unable to communicate, often because neuromuscular blockade prevents movement. Contributing mechanisms include underdosing to protect a compromised circulation, equipment or infusion failure, increased anaesthetic requirement, and pharmacokinetic variability. Explicit memory formation during light anaesthesia can lead to conscious recall and psychological sequelae. Many episodes are brief with limited recall, but distressing awareness can cause persistent anxiety, sleep disturbance, and post-traumatic stress disorder; early acknowledgement and psychological support improve outcomes.

infant suggesting early glaucoma Family history of anterior segment anomalies and glaucoma indicating dominant inheritance Regarding posterior embryotoxon or iris changes as benign and not screening for glaucoma Assuming the glaucoma is a one-off, when lifelong surveillance is required Overlooking the systemic dental and umbilical features that support the diagnosis Failing to examine and counsel relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome results from abnormal development of neural-crest-derived tissues forming the anterior segment of the eye, driven by mutations in developmental transcription-factor genes such as PITX2 and FOXC1. Faulty migration and differentiation of these cells produces incomplete regression and anomalous development of structures at the iridocorneal angle and iris, giving the characteristic angle strands, prominent Schwalbe line and iris defects. Maldevelopment of the trabecular meshwork and drainage angle impairs aqueous outflow, leading to raised intraocular pressure and glaucoma. The same transcription factors act in the development of teeth, the umbilicus and midface, explaining the associated systemic features. The ocular anomalies themselves are static, but glaucoma is common, may be difficult to control, and is the principal threat to vision; with early detection and effective pressure control the visual prognosis is good, whereas late or refractory glaucoma can cause irreversible optic nerve damage.
