Babesiosis — Babesia Lyme disease (concurrent or co-transmitted by the same tick) Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) Borrelia miyamotoi infection HELLP syndrome in pregnant women at risk of tick exposure (babesiosis is an imitator) Other causes of febrile hemolytic anemia Malaria (Plasmodium falciparum and others) — intraerythrocytic febrile illness most readily confused with babesiosis Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum) Borrelia miyamotoi infection Giemsa-stained thin blood smear (microscopy) — definitive diagnosis; trophozoites appear as ring/ameboid forms, and merozoites arranged in tetrads form the pathognomonic 'Maltese cross' Real-time PCR amplifying the parasite 18S rRNA gene (detects 1–10 parasites/uL; allows speciation; used to monitor low-grade infection and relapse risk) Complete blood count (anemia, often severe thrombocytopenia preceding severe anemia; WBC may be low, normal, or high) and reticulocyte count Hemolysis markers: low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, elevated total bilirubin Liver enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, AST, ALT) and renal function (BUN, creatinine) Urinalysis (urobilinogen, hemoglobinuria, proteinuria) Indirect fluorescent antibody serology (IgM and IgG titers) — a single positive result is NOT sufficient for diagnosis because antibodies can persist for over a year CT for suspected splenic infarction or rupture HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) in pregnancy Other hemolytic anemias / thrombotic microangiopathies presenting with hemolysis and thrombocytopenia Emerging tick-borne infection caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia that invade and lyse red blood cells; most U.S. cases are due to Babesia microti, transmitted by the deer tick Ixodes scapularis, with ~90% presenting June through August (p.1775, 1777). Presents as a flu-like illness: gradual-onset fatigue/malaise followed within days by fever (can reach 40.9 C) with chills, night sweats, headache, myalgia, and anorexia; dark urine and jaundice raise suspicion of severe hemolytic anemia (p.1777). Because the same I. scapularis tick co-transmits Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum, co-infection is common: about one-half of patients diagnosed with babesiosis are also infected with B. burgdorferi, so a babesiosis diagnosis should prompt evaluation for Lyme disease, and vice versa (p.1778). Most symptomatic patients (~80%) are 50 years or older; hospitalized patients are roughly a decade older (median 68 years) (p.1777). Splenic complications (infarction, subcapsular hematoma, rupture) can occur even with low-grade parasitemia (median ~1%) and typically affect young, healthy patients (p.1777, 1780). Severe disease especially in asplenic (congenital, functional, or post-splenectomy), elderly, and immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS, transplant, malignancy, B-cell-depleting/rituximab therapy) patients Dark urine and jaundice indicating severe hemolytic anemia, with scleral icterus on examination Left-sided abdominal pain, unexplained hypotension with tachycardia, or hemodynamic instability suggesting splenic infarction or rupture Acute renal failure (leading complication, ~20%) and acute respiratory failure (~7%); also DIC, shock, arrhythmia, heart failure Parasitemia >4% (risk factor for severe, complicated disease; can reach 30–40% in immunocompromised patients) Diagnosis delayed >7 days after symptom onset predisposes to severe complicated disease Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from massive phagocytosis of blood cells (fatal) Misidentifying Babesia as malaria on the blood smear: distinguish by absence of central brownish hemozoin pigment, presence of extracellular merozoites, absence of gametocytes and schizonts, and the pathognomonic tetrad ('Maltese cross'); a negative BinaxNOW malaria test helps rule out falciparum malaria when microscopy is ambiguous (p.1779). Relying on a single positive serology for diagnosis — antibodies persist for over a year after the parasite is cleared (p.1779). Missing co-infection: failing to evaluate for Lyme disease (and other tick-borne pathogens) when babesiosis is diagnosed, or for babesiosis when Lyme symptoms worsen or fail to abate on appropriate antibiotics (p.1778). Overlooking splenic complications, which can occur with low-grade parasitemia and in young, otherwise healthy patients (p.1777, 1780). Routine follow-up PCR is not recommended in immunocompetent patients (parasite DNA detectable up to 3 months) since relapse is unlikely, and persistent fatigue alone does not warrant extending or resuming therapy (p.1779). Babesia parasites invade and lyse red blood cells. RBC debris from hemolysis can accumulate in the renal vasculature and cause renal failure. Free hemoglobin is complexed by haptoglobin, then the oxidized heme group by hemopexin; excess free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide, promoting thrombus formation and vascular inflammation. RBC lysis in splenic capillaries can trigger localized necrosis and splenic infarction; oxidatively stressed, poorly deformable RBCs are filtered and phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, and erythrophagocytosis with the immune response contributes to splenomegaly and rupture. Fever, chills, and sweats reflect a systemic inflammatory response to RBC lysis, and excessive inflammation drives end-organ (renal and pulmonary) damage. The spleen is the immunodominant organ, explaining why asplenia is a major risk factor for severe disease; protective immunity involves CD4+ Th1 cells (severe disease in AIDS and transplant recipients), and B cells/antibodies appear critical for clearance in some patients (relapsing disease after rituximab). Persistent anemia after infection clears has been attributed to autoantibodies tagging RBCs for clearance (p.1778). With first-line atovaquone plus azithromycin, a fatal outcome is rare; of 7612 CDC-reported cases in 2011–2015, 46 (0.6%) ended in death. Older regimens (clindamycin plus quinine) had fatality rates of 5–9%. Death is more frequent in those 65 years or older. Among Medicare recipients diagnosed 2006–2013, ~1% died within 30 days; fatality was ~3% among hospitalized patients. Fatality is high in immunocompromised patients (~20%) and in those with splenic rupture or infarction (~6%). Fatigue may persist for weeks to months after treatment. Highly immunocompromised patients are at risk of persistent, relapsing infection (p.1778). Severe babesiosis requires hospital admission (median stay 4 days). Severe, complicated babesiosis is defined as illness requiring ICU admission; complicated by ARDS, heart failure, or shock; or requiring dialysis, intubation, or RBC exchange. Diarrhea and nausea/vomiting are strong predictors of severe disease, and asplenia and autoimmune disorders predispose to it. Parasitemia is typically 0.1–10% in immunocompetent patients (up to 30–40% in immunocompromised); parasitemia >4% is a risk factor for severe complicated disease (p.1777-1778).

Bacterial keratitis — microbial keratitis, bacterial corneal ulcer, infective keratitis, corneal ulcer Herpes simplex (dendritic) keratitis Fungal keratitis Acanthamoeba keratitis Marginal (hypersensitivity) keratitis Sterile contact-lens-related infiltrates Anterior uveitis or acute angle-closure glaucoma (for the red painful eye) Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining to define the infiltrate and epithelial defect Corneal scraping for Gram stain, culture, and sensitivities Contact lens and lens case cultures where relevant Measurement of infiltrate size and assessment of corneal thinning Confocal microscopy or specialised staining if Acanthamoeba or fungal infection is suspected Presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, watering, discharge, and reduced vision, usually developing over hours to days Examination shows a focal white or grey corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein; a hypopyon may be present in severe cases Contact lens wear (especially overnight or poor hygiene) is the leading risk factor, alongside corneal trauma, ocular surface disease, and previous surgery Pseudomonas is an important and rapidly destructive pathogen in contact lens wearers; Staphylococci and Streptococci are also common Corneal scraping for Gram stain and culture should ideally be taken before starting intensive treatment in significant ulcers Management is with intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotics, initially given very frequently, and stopping contact lens use Central ulcers, large infiltrates, or delayed treatment risk scarring, perforation, and permanent visual loss Sight-threatening — central or large ulcers can scar the visual axis or perforate the cornea Rapid progression, especially in a contact lens wearer, suggesting Pseudomonas Hypopyon, corneal thinning, or descemetocele indicating impending perforation Worsening despite treatment raising suspicion of fungal or Acanthamoeba infection Prescribing topical steroids or a patch that can worsen infection, particularly with undiagnosed herpetic or fungal disease Failing to scrape a significant ulcer for culture before starting treatment Underestimating the aggressiveness of contact-lens-associated Pseudomonas keratitis Missing Acanthamoeba in a contact lens wearer with pain out of proportion to signs Bacterial keratitis develops when the corneal epithelial barrier is breached (by trauma, contact lens wear, dry eye, or surgery), allowing bacteria to invade the corneal stroma. Bacterial proliferation and the release of enzymes and toxins, together with the host inflammatory response and recruited neutrophils, cause stromal necrosis and an infiltrate. Collagen-degrading enzymes can rapidly thin the cornea, leading to ulceration, descemetocele formation, and perforation. Healing occurs with scarring that reduces corneal clarity, particularly when the visual axis is involved. Prompt intensive antibiotic treatment usually controls infection, but a central scar, large ulcer, or delayed care can leave permanent visual impairment; perforation may require corneal grafting.

anaerobes rather than a single infecting pathogen The characteristic feature is a thin, homogeneous, greyish-white discharge with a fishy odour that is often most noticeable after intercourse It is Amsel criteria combines discharge characteristics, raised vaginal pH, a positive whiff test with potassium hydroxide, and clue cells on microscopy Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria and are a hallmark microscopic finding Treatment targets anaerobes with agents such as metronidazole or clindamycin, but recurrence is common and reflects failure to re-establish a lactobacillus-dominant flora In pregnancy it is associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, late miscarriage, and postpartum endometritis, so symptomatic pregnant women are treated It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections including HIV and to post-procedural pelvic infection Symptomatic bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy given the association with preterm birth and miscarriage Signs of ascending infection such as pelvic pain, fever, or cervical motion tenderness suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease Bacterial vaginosis before termination or intrauterine procedures, increasing post-procedure infection risk Persistent atypical discharge not responding to treatment, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Coexisting features of a sexually transmitted infection Mistaking it for candidiasis and treating with antifungals Overtreating asymptomatic women outside pregnancy or pre-procedure settings Failing to consider it in recurrent or malodorous discharge with minimal inflammation Not screening for concurrent sexually transmitted infections when risk exists Overlooking its role in preterm birth in symptomatic pregnant women The healthy vagina is dominated by lactobacilli that produce lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide, maintaining an acidic environment that suppresses other organisms. In bacterial vaginosis this population is depleted and replaced by a polymicrobial overgrowth of anaerobes such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Atopobium, often organised into a biofilm on the epithelium. The resulting rise in vaginal pH and production of amines generates the typical odour and discharge, while the biofilm contributes to treatment resistance and recurrence. Symptoms usually respond well to appropriate antibiotic therapy, but recurrence within months is frequent because the protective lactobacillus flora and the biofilm are difficult to eradicate permanently. It is not itself a serious infection but its associations with adverse pregnancy outcomes, post-procedural infection, and enhanced susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections give it clinical importance.

brain tumour Cerebral abscess Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis MRI of the brain, ideally showing the characteristic concentric lamellated lesion, with behaves as a relapsing demyelinating disease Rapidly progressive focal deficits or declining consciousness Mass effect with raised intracranial pressure Radiological features that cannot be confidently separated from tumour or infection Steroid-refractory deterioration requiring escalation Mistaking the lesion for a neoplasm and proceeding to unnecessary aggressive intervention Assuming an inevitably fatal outcome and withholding active treatment Overlooking evolution into typical multiple sclerosis requiring long-term therapy Omitting antibody testing for alternative demyelinating disease Balo concentric sclerosis is an inflammatory demyelinating process in which bands of myelin loss alternate with bands of preserved or partially preserved myelin, producing the concentric lamellated pattern. The rings are thought to arise from a tissue preconditioning mechanism in which hypoxia-like metabolic stress and protective upregulation at the advancing lesion edge spare a rim of myelin, so that successive waves of demyelination leave alternating layers. Oligodendrocyte injury with relative axonal preservation in the earlier layers underlies the potential for recovery, and the disorder is considered part of the multiple sclerosis spectrum. Outcome is variable; some patients recover well and follow a relapsing-remitting course while others sustain significant deficits, and the historically fulminant fatal form is now less commonly seen with modern treatment.

With surveillance and early treatment of tumours the outlook is favourable.

Barth syndrome — TAZ deficiency, tafazzin deficiency, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria type II, X-linked cardioskeletal myopathy with neutropenia, BTHS Other genetic dilated cardiomyopathies and left ventricular non-compaction Primary mitochondrial cardiomyopathies and other causes of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria Congenital or cyclical neutropenia of other causes Congenital myopathies and muscular dystrophies Viral or other acquired myocarditis Glycogen storage disease with cardiac involvement (for example Pompe disease) Cardiolipin analysis with the monolysocardiolipin-to-cardiolipin ratio in blood spots or tissue Molecular genetic testing of TAZ Urine organic acids showing raised 3-methylglutaconic acid Serial full blood counts to characterise cyclical or persistent neutropenia Echocardiography and cardiac assessment for cardiomyopathy and non-compaction Creatine kinase and assessment of skeletal muscle function X-linked recessive disorder caused by variants in TAZ (also called TAFAZZIN), encoding the enzyme tafazzin, so it almost exclusively affects males Tafazzin remodels cardiolipin, the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, so its deficiency impairs mitochondrial structure and oxidative phosphorylation The core clinical triad is cardiomyopathy (often dilated, sometimes with left ventricular non-compaction), skeletal myopathy with proximal weakness, and cyclical or persistent neutropenia Growth delay is common in childhood, sometimes with a characteristic catch-up growth in later adolescence Recurrent bacterial infections result from the neutropenia and can be life-threatening A useful biochemical clue is raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid (a form of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria) and an abnormal monolysocardiolipin-to-cardiolipin ratio Cardiomyopathy may present in utero, in infancy or later, and can fluctuate in severity Diagnosis is confirmed by cardiolipin analysis and TAZ genetic testing; management is supportive with attention to cardiac failure and infection risk Heart failure from dilated cardiomyopathy in an infant or child Serious or recurrent bacterial infection during neutropenic episodes Ventricular arrhythmia or sudden deterioration in cardiac function Severe hypotonia and weakness impairing feeding or breathing Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy with dilated cardiomyopathy by not checking for neutropenia or 3-methylglutaconic aciduria Attributing recurrent infections to an unrelated immune problem Assuming the cardiomyopathy is static, when it can fluctuate and worsen Missing the raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid as a diagnostic clue Barth syndrome is caused by deficiency of tafazzin, a transacylase that remodels immature cardiolipin into its mature form containing predominantly unsaturated fatty acyl chains. Mature cardiolipin is concentrated in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it stabilises the respiratory chain complexes and supports oxidative phosphorylation, membrane curvature and cristae structure. Loss of tafazzin leaves an abnormal cardiolipin profile with accumulation of the intermediate monolysocardiolipin, destabilising the respiratory chain and impairing energy production. Tissues with high energy demand, particularly cardiac and skeletal muscle, are most affected, and mitochondrial dysfunction in the bone marrow contributes to the neutropenia. The disturbed leucine and mitochondrial metabolism underlies the 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. Historically Barth syndrome carried high early mortality from heart failure and infection, but with modern cardiac care, monitoring and management of neutropenia many patients now survive into adulthood. Prognosis depends largely on the severity and course of the cardiomyopathy and on preventing serious infections.

Most Bartholin abscesses resolve well after adequate drainage, and techniques that create a lasting drainage tract, such as catheter placement or marsupialisation, substantially lower recurrence. Bartonellosis — cat scratch disease, Bartonella infection, bacillary angiomatosis, Carrion's disease Mycobacterial lymphadenitis (tuberculous or atypical) Lymphoma and other causes of regional lymphadenopathy Toxoplasmosis Pyogenic bacterial lymphadenitis Other causes of culture-negative endocarditis (e.g. Coxiella) Kaposi sarcoma (for the vascular lesions of bacillary angiomatosis) Tuberculous lymphadenitis Toxoplasmosis Coxiella (Q fever) endocarditis Pyogenic lymphadenitis Bartonella serology (indirect immunofluorescence or EIA) as a first-line test PCR of blood, lymph node aspirate, or tissue for Bartonella DNA Histopathology of affected nodes or skin lesions, with special stains such as Warthin-Starry silver stain Echocardiography and repeated cultures when endocarditis is suspected HIV testing and immune status assessment when bacillary angiomatosis is considered Bartonella species cause a spectrum of illness; Bartonella henselae is the usual agent of cat scratch disease, typically following a scratch or bite from a young cat or flea exposure Cat scratch disease classically presents with a papule or pustule at the inoculation site followed by regional lymphadenopathy that is often tender and can suppurate Most immunocompetent patients have a self-limiting illness, and management is often supportive with antibiotics reserved for more severe or systemic disease In immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV, Bartonella can cause bacillary angiomatosis with vascular proliferative skin and visceral lesions Bartonella is an important cause of culture-negative endocarditis, so it should be considered when blood cultures remain sterile Atypical presentations include prolonged fever of unknown origin, hepatosplenic granulomatous disease, neuroretinitis with a macular star, and encephalopathy Diagnosis relies on serology, PCR, or special stains and histology, as the organism is fastidious and difficult to culture by routine methods Culture-negative endocarditis with embolic phenomena or heart failure Neuroretinitis with visual loss, or encephalopathy and seizures Disseminated vascular lesions (bacillary angiomatosis) in an immunocompromised patient Persistent high fever, hepatosplenic lesions, or systemic deterioration Overlooking Bartonella as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis Failing to elicit a history of cat or flea exposure in regional lymphadenopathy Not assessing immune status when vascular proliferative lesions are found Draining or excising nodes unnecessarily in what is often a self-limiting illness Bartonella are fastidious, facultatively intracellular Gram-negative bacteria that infect erythrocytes and endothelial cells. Transmission occurs through animal scratches or bites and arthropod vectors such as fleas and lice depending on species. In immunocompetent hosts the infection typically provokes a granulomatous immune response producing localised lymphadenitis. The bacterium's ability to invade endothelium and stimulate vascular proliferation underlies bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis seen in immunocompromised patients, and its persistence within red cells and on cardiac valves accounts for bacteraemia and endocarditis. Cat scratch disease in immunocompetent people usually resolves spontaneously over weeks to months, while endocarditis, disseminated disease, and complications in immunocompromised hosts require prolonged antibiotic therapy and carry greater morbidity.

the eruptive phase is supported by histology of skin lesions and serology or PCR Asymptomatic carriage occurs and sustains transmission, and immunity after infection modifies the presentation in endemic residents versus travellers Treatment differs by phase, using antibiotics effective against Bartonella; severe Oroya fever requires cover for concurrent bacteraemias and supportive transfusion Severe haemolytic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise in Oroya fever Signs of secondary bacteraemia or sepsis (e.g. Salmonella) Neurological involvement or altered consciousness Profound immunosuppression during the acute phase Failure to improve on antibiotics suggesting concurrent infection Attributing febrile haemolysis to malaria alone and missing the blood-smear bacilli Overlooking secondary Salmonella or other bacteraemia in acute-phase patients Mistaking verruga peruana nodules for pyogenic granuloma, Kaposi sarcoma or bacillary angiomatosis Using the same treatment approach for both phases without accounting for their differences Underestimating transfusion and supportive needs in severe anaemia Bartonella bacilliformis is inoculated during the bite of an infected sandfly. The bacterium invades and multiplies within erythrocytes, causing massive intravascular and extravascular haemolysis that produces the profound anaemia of the acute Oroya fever phase; immunosuppression during this phase predisposes to superimposed infections. After the acute illness resolves the organism persists and, in the eruptive phase, stimulates vascular endothelial proliferation, producing the angiomatous cutaneous nodules of verruga peruana. Cell-mediated immunity governs progression between phases, and partial immunity in endemic populations attenuates disease. Untreated Oroya fever has a high mortality from haemolysis and secondary infection, whereas prompt antibiotic and supportive treatment greatly improves survival; the eruptive verruga phase is generally benign and self-limiting though lesions can bleed and persist.

hypokalaemia causing arrhythmia or profound weakness Marked volume depletion and dehydration, especially in neonates Failure to thrive or growth retardation in children Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function Mistaking surreptitious diuretic or laxative abuse for a genetic tubulopathy without appropriate screening Confusing Bartter with Gitelman syndrome by not checking urinary calcium and serum magnesium Overlooking the diagnosis in a normotensive patient with unexplained hypokalaemic alkalosis Inadequate potassium and magnesium repletion leaving the patient symptomatic Bartter syndrome comprises a group of autosomal recessive defects in the ion transporters of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the site of action of loop diuretics. Loss of function in the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter or its associated potassium and chloride channels impairs sodium chloride reabsorption, causing renal salt and water wasting. The resulting volume contraction activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, and the combination of increased distal sodium delivery and high aldosterone drives potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Because the transporter normally contributes to the electrochemical gradient favouring calcium reabsorption, its loss leaves calcium excretion normal or elevated. Overproduction of prostaglandins amplifies the salt wasting and the activation of renin. With consistent electrolyte and fluid replacement and prostaglandin inhibition, most patients maintain reasonable growth and function, though lifelong therapy is required. Severe antenatal forms carry higher perinatal risk, and chronic hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis can gradually impair renal function.

dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Profound hypokalaemia risking cardiac arrhythmia Failure to thrive with growth restriction Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function Mistaking the presentation for surreptitious diuretic use, or vice versa Confusing it with Gitelman syndrome, which characteristically causes hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia rather than hypercalciuria nephrocalcinosis surveillance and cumulative renal injury Antenatal Bartter syndrome results from inherited loss of salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where the NKCC2 cotransporter (SLC12A1) and the apical ROMK channel (KCNJ1) normally drive sodium, potassium and chloride uptake and recycle potassium back into the tubular lumen. When these fail, sodium chloride is lost in the urine, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increasing distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion, which produces hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Impaired salt handling also dissipates the transepithelial voltage that normally drives paracellular calcium reabsorption, causing hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Compensatory renal prostaglandin synthesis amplifies polyuria and systemic vasodilatation, explaining the severe fetal and neonatal phenotype and the benefit of prostaglandin inhibition. With early salt and potassium replacement and prostaglandin inhibition, many children stabilise and grow, though nephrocalcinosis and a degree of chronic kidney impairment may persist. Long-term outcome depends on the genetic subtype and on avoiding recurrent severe electrolyte crises.

nose, ears) where local destruction threatens vital structures Numerous or early-onset tumours suggesting an inherited cancer syndrome or prior radiotherapy Mistaking a morphoeic BCC for a scar and underestimating its true extent Treating a superficial BCC as eczema or psoriasis and delaying diagnosis Choosing a non-surgical or narrow-margin approach for high-risk or recurrent facial tumours Failing to arrange ongoing skin surveillance after a first diagnosis Basal cell carcinoma is a malignancy of the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis and follicular structures, driven predominantly by ultraviolet-induced DNA damage. Aberrant activation of the Hedgehog signalling pathway, commonly through inactivating mutations in the PTCH1 tumour-suppressor gene or activating changes in SMO, is central to tumour development, alongside UV signature mutations in TP53. The tumour grows as nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a surrounding fibromyxoid stroma. Its behaviour is locally invasive rather than metastatic, and infiltrative or morphoeic patterns spread with subclinical extension that explains higher recurrence when margins are inadequate. The prognosis is excellent because metastasis is exceedingly rare, and appropriately treated tumours are usually cured; however, incompletely excised or high-risk subtypes recur and can cause significant local morbidity, and patients remain at higher lifetime risk of further skin cancers requiring ongoing surveillance.

Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System — Cardiovascular system biology, Cardiac and vascular cell biology, Cardiovascular developmental biology Flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery by ultrasound (cuff occlusion/release) to assess endothelial vasodilator function in vivo The heart arises from crescent-shaped fields of lateral splanchnic mesoderm; a primary (first) heart field forms the linear heart tube while a second heart field, marked by Islet-1 expression, later adds myocardium to the inflow/outflow poles and contributes much of the right ventricle and outflow tract. Neural crest cells are required for aortic arch remodeling and truncus arteriosus septation; because these cells are sensitive to vitamin A and folic acid, maternal deficiency of these vitamins is associated with congenital defects of aortic arch remodeling. Coronary arteries depend on epicardial cells derived from the proepicardial organ (a septum transversum derivative that also forms the fibrous diaphragm and contributes to the liver), which supply coronary smooth muscle and help pattern the vessels. The cardiac conduction system differentiates from cardiomyocyte precursors into slow-conducting proximal components (SA and AV nodes) and fast-conducting distal components (His bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers); developmental defects can produce congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White). Decremental conduction across the AV node delays atrial-to-ventricular impulse transmission to allow sequential contraction and protects the ventricle by limiting transmission of rapid atrial rates. The endothelium is a selectively permeable barrier and a major homeostatic organ: under physiologic conditions it favors vasodilation, an antithrombotic/profibrinolytic state, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; endothelial dysfunction reverses each of these (vasoconstriction, prothrombotic, proinflammatory, prooxidant, impaired barrier). Endothelium-derived vasodilators include nitric oxide (NO), prostacyclin, endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor, and hydrogen peroxide; flow-mediated dilatation (brachial artery cuff occlusion/release with ultrasound) is used to assess endothelial vasodilator function in humans. Excess reactive oxygen species (e.g., superoxide generated under high angiotensin II exposure) inactivate NO, and inflammatory stimuli/endotoxin/angiotensin II drive endothelial production of PAI-1 and tissue factor, shifting balance toward thrombosis (contributing to DIC in sepsis and to hyperglycemia-related prothrombotic states). Vascular smooth-muscle contraction is governed by cytosolic calcium and the balance of myosin light chain kinase (calcium/calmodulin-activated) versus myosin light chain phosphatase; voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels and IP3-triggered sarcoplasmic reticulum release raise intracellular calcium. Cardiac contraction follows the sliding-filament model: an L-type calcium current during the action potential plateau triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the SR via the ryanodine receptor RyR2; calcium binds troponin C, relieving troponin-tropomyosin inhibition so actin and myosin cross-bridge cycling (ATP-dependent) can occur. Relaxation depends on lowering cytosolic calcium by SR reuptake via SERCA2A (regulated by phospholamban) and sarcolemmal Na+/Ca2+ exchange; PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds reuptake and produces the lusitropic (enhanced relaxation) effect. Cytoplasmic calcium is the principal determinant of inotropic state: positive inotropes such as digitalis glycosides and beta-adrenergic agonists act by raising cytosolic calcium (beta agonists via Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cyclic AMP-PKA phosphorylation of sarcolemmal calcium channels). Ventricular stroke volume is set by three factors: preload (muscle length at contraction onset), afterload (tension developed during contraction), and contractility; contractile force is optimal near a sarcomere length of about 2.2 micrometers, the structural basis of the Frank-Starling relationship. Inherited or acquired disturbances of SR calcium handling (RyR2/regulatory protein abnormalities) can impair contraction and predispose to heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias. Mutations in sarcomeric and cytoskeletal proteins (including titin, dystrophin/dystroglycan complex) cause Mendelian cardiomyopathies and sensitize the heart to toxic insults such as alcohol or chemotherapy and to inflammatory or peripartum cardiomyopathy. Developmental conduction-system defects may present as congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White). Treating these molecular and developmental concepts as purely theoretical: shared embryonic origins of cardiovascular cell types explain syndromic associations between congenital heart disease and extracardiac anomalies. Overlooking that true regeneration of a complete three-layered blood vessel does not normally occur in adult mammals, so adult arteriogenesis/angiogenesis reflects growth and collateral expansion rather than new full-thickness vessel formation. Assuming adult vascular smooth-muscle cells are quiescent; they proliferate and migrate after injury or inflammatory activation, contributing to atherosclerotic stenosis, hypertensive arteriolar remodeling, and restenosis. The cardiovascular system develops from cardiac progenitors in lateral splanchnic mesoderm that fuse into a linear heart tube of endocardium and spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes, then undergo asymmetric looping and chamber specification with continued addition of second-heart-field cells (Islet-1 positive). Septation separates the cardiac chambers and divides the truncus arteriosus into aorta and pulmonary artery; endocardial cushions, rich in hyaluronic-acid 'cardiac jelly', undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transformation to form valves. Neural crest cells direct aortic arch remodeling and supply smooth muscle to the great vessels, while proepicardial cells form coronary vasculature. Blood vessels share a trilaminar architecture (intimal endothelium, smooth-muscle media, fibroblast-rich adventitia), with capillaries reduced to an endothelial tube and pericytes and large vessels nourished by vasa vasorum. The endothelium maintains vascular homeostasis through balanced production of vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (endothelin), regulation of leukocyte adhesion, and modulation of coagulation; loss of these functions underlies atherosclerosis, hypertension, capillary-leak states, and immune-mediated vascular injury. Vascular smooth-muscle tone is set by intracellular calcium and myosin light chain phosphorylation, integrated through sympathetic, parasympathetic, and nonadrenergic/noncholinergic (nitrergic, peptidergic) autonomic signaling. In the myocardium, the sarcomere is the contractile unit; excitation-contraction coupling links the action potential and T-tubular calcium entry to RyR2-mediated SR calcium release, troponin C activation, and actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling, with relaxation driven by SERCA2A reuptake and Na+/Ca2+ exchange. Cardiac output reflects the interplay of preload, afterload, and contractility (Frank-Starling mechanism). As a foundational chapter, prognosis is framed at the level of mechanism: increased arterial stiffness with aging or disease raises left ventricular afterload and portends a poor outcome, and sustained high-flow states (e.g., left-to-right shunts) drive pulmonary smooth-muscle proliferation and pulmonary hypertension. Outcomes in specific cardiovascular diseases are detailed in their respective chapters.

with different prognoses Beals syndrome is caused by variants in FBN2, a gene closely related to FBN1 that encodes fibrillin-2, a component of the microfibrils that form during early elastic-fibre assembly. Fibrillin-2 is expressed prominently in developing tissues, so its deficiency chiefly disturbs early skeletal and joint development, producing congenital contractures, long slender digits, and a tall marfanoid build. Because fibrillin-2 has a more limited role in the mature aortic wall and lens zonules than fibrillin-1, the severe progressive aortopathy and ectopia lentis of Marfan syndrome are generally absent, which is the key clinical distinction. The outlook is generally good, with contractures often improving over childhood and a life expectancy usually within the normal range. Kyphoscoliosis is the main source of long-term morbidity, and the aorta, when involved, is usually only mildly affected.

Repeated contraction-induced sarcolemmal damage leads to calcium influx, fibre necrosis, and progressive replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue, but at a slower rate than in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Progression is slower than in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and many patients remain ambulant well into adulthood with a substantially longer life expectancy. Cardiomyopathy is often the main determinant of prognosis, so cardiac surveillance and timely heart-failure treatment are essential.

Behçet Syndrome — Behçet's disease, Behcet syndrome, Behcet disease Crohn's disease (gastrointestinal Behçet can be clinically and endoscopically indistinguishable; distinction often relies on extraintestinal features) Recurrent aphthous stomatitis / ordinary canker sores Acne vulgaris (papulopustular lesions are indistinguishable in appearance and pathology) Other systemic vasculitides Inflammatory bowel disease more broadly Herpetic and other infectious genital/oral ulceration causing recurrent ulcers Diagnosis is clinical; no specific laboratory, imaging, or histologic test confirms it, so investigations mainly serve to exclude mimics. International Study Group (ISG) criteria: recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 times in 12 months) plus two of recurrent genital ulcers, skin lesions, eye lesions, or a positive pathergy test (sensitivity ~95%, specificity ~96%). Pathergy test: dermal insertion of a 20-gauge (20-21 gauge) needle, read at 24-48 h. HLA-B*51 testing may support but cannot establish the diagnosis. Endoscopy for suspected gastrointestinal involvement (ulcers typically single or fewer than five, deep, round, confined to the ileocecal area, prone to perforation). Vascular and neuroimaging when vascular or CNS involvement is suspected (e.g., pulmonary artery aneurysm, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, parenchymal CNS lesions). Crohn's disease (especially with ileocecal ulcers) Acne vulgaris Recurrent aphthous stomatitis A systemic vasculitis presenting with various combinations of oral and genital ulcers, skin lesions, uveitis, arthritis, large vessel (arterial and venous) disease, and gastrointestinal and neurologic involvement, with manifestations appearing in differing sequences over time. Oral ulcers occur in essentially all patients (~98%) and are usually the first manifestation; they are typically multiple, resemble ordinary canker sores, last about 10 days, and recur unless treated, with only the uncommon major ulcers tending to scar. Genital ulcers are the most specific lesion, most often on the scrotum or labia; they are larger, deeper, slower to heal than oral ulcers, and tend to scar. The pathergy reaction (a papule or pustule forming 24-48 h after a needle prick) is a fairly unique nonspecific skin hyperreactivity and is part of the diagnostic criteria. Hypopyon (intense anterior chamber inflammation), seen in about 10% of patients with eye disease, is quite specific for Behçet syndrome. Superficial thrombophlebitis often occurs in men and is associated with deep-vein thrombosis; its presence should prompt a workup for other vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm. HLA-B*51 is positive in up to 50-60% of patients depending on geographic origin, but it is not diagnostic because roughly 20% of the normal population also carries it. Most prevalent in Turkey (about 1 in 250 adults); patients are most commonly from the Middle East, Mediterranean, and Far East. Onset before the late teens or after age 50 is uncommon. Sexes are affected roughly equally, but males tend to have more severe disease and worse outcomes; eye involvement may reach ~70% in males. Ocular disease (most often bilateral panuveitis) usually appears within the first 2 years after diagnostic criteria are met, is most severe early, then tends to abate. Most new manifestations appear within the first 5 years, and the natural history for most patients is one of diminishing symptoms that may culminate in remission. Superficial thrombophlebitis in a male should trigger evaluation for deeper vascular involvement including pulmonary artery aneurysm. Pulmonary artery aneurysms carry a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%. Subacute severe headache with cranial nerve palsy, dysarthria, ataxia, or hemiparesis suggests parenchymal CNS involvement (telencephalic-diencephalic junction, brainstem, spinal cord). Deep, round ileocecal ulcers are prone to perforation. Clustering thrombotic events (deep-vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, IVC syndrome, intracardiac thrombosis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis). Diagnosis may take months to years as the full constellation of features evolves; a tentative diagnosis often precedes a definitive one. HLA-B*51 is not a diagnostic test because it is common in the general population. Gastrointestinal Behçet is easily mistaken for Crohn's disease unless extraintestinal manifestations are evident. Pathergy and eye lesions each occur in only about half of patients, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Regional variation matters: gastrointestinal involvement is common in Japan and seen in ~30% of US patients but rare in Turkey. The cause and pathogenesis are unknown. Family studies suggest a possible genetic predisposition, and heightened inflammation with involvement of both innate and adaptive immunity is implicated. Neutrophil hyperreactivity is present, though it is unclear whether this is primary or secondary to cytokine-driven activation. The disorder sits between classic autoimmune and autoinflammatory conditions: unlike typical autoimmune disease it is not generally associated with autoantibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, Sjögren's syndrome, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, photosensitivity, serosal involvement, or increased risk of other autoimmune diseases; unlike classic autoinflammatory disease it tends to abate over time, lacks the mutations seen in autoinflammatory syndromes, and is more prevalent than disorders such as familial Mediterranean fever. Retrospective cohort data suggest distinct disease clusters (e.g., acne lesions clustering with arthritis and enthesitis) that may have differing pathogeneses. Most patients follow a course of diminishing symptoms over time with potential remission, often eventually requiring no ongoing medication, and most new manifestations emerge within the first 5 years. Young male patients tend to have worse outcomes. Poor ocular prognostic factors include male sex, posterior involvement, frequent attacks (>3 per year), strong vitreous opacity, and macular edema. Pulmonary artery aneurysms are associated with a 5-year mortality of about 20-25%. No formal severity grade; management and outlook are stratified by the type and severity of organ involvement (mucocutaneous, ocular, vascular, gastrointestinal, neurologic), with young male sex and posterior/severe eye disease marking higher-risk disease.

neurological symptoms to other causes rather than neuro-Behçet Assuming absence of pathergy or HLA-B51 excludes the diagnosis Behçet disease is a chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder classified as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can affect vessels of any size and type, both arterial and venous. Its cause is uncertain but involves genetic susceptibility (notably HLA-B51) and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity with prominent neutrophil hyperactivity, elevated Th1/Th17 responses, and inflammation triggered in predisposed individuals. Vascular inflammation produces thrombosis, aneurysm formation, and tissue damage, while immune-mediated inflammation drives the recurrent mucocutaneous, ocular, neurological, and gastrointestinal lesions. Course is relapsing and remitting and tends to be more severe in young men. Mucocutaneous disease is troublesome but not dangerous, whereas ocular, neurological, and major vascular involvement drive the risk of blindness, disability, and death. Early aggressive treatment of organ-threatening disease improves outcome.

Bejel — endemic syphilis, Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum, non-venereal endemic syphilis, dichuchwa, njovera Venereal syphilis (serologically identical) Yaws and pinta (other endemic treponematoses) Aphthous or herpetic stomatitis Oral candidiasis or other causes of mucous patches Nutritional angular stomatitis Other causes of destructive nasopharyngeal lesions (e.g. leishmaniasis, rhinoscleroma) Dark-field microscopy of mucosal or skin lesion exudate for spirochaetes Non-treponemal serology (e.g. RPR/VDRL) for activity and follow-up Treponemal serology (e.g. TPPA/TPHA) for confirmation PCR of lesion material where available to support subspecies context Radiographs for osteoperiostitis in symptomatic bones Assessment of household and community contacts Bejel is a chronic non-venereal treponematosis caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum, occurring in dry, arid regions such as the Sahel, parts of the Middle East and Central Asia Transmission is non-sexual, by mouth-to-mouth contact or by sharing drinking and eating utensils, mainly among children in dry rural communities The primary lesion is often unnoticed; disease typically presents in the secondary stage with mucous patches of the mouth and oropharynx and moist condyloma-like lesions in skin folds Secondary features include angular stomatitis (split papules at the mouth angles), laryngitis and generalised skin lesions, with osteoperiostitis of long bones Late (tertiary) bejel produces gummatous destruction of skin, nasopharynx and bone, including gangosa, similar to late yaws Serology and dark-field microscopy are indistinguishable from those of venereal syphilis and the other endemic treponematoses Treatment of the endemic treponematoses uses benzathine penicillin, with a macrolide alternative for penicillin-allergic patients and mass-treatment campaigns Destructive nasopharyngeal (gangosa) lesions causing disfigurement Airway or swallowing compromise from laryngeal or oropharyngeal involvement Extensive gummatous bone destruction with deformity Difficulty distinguishing from venereal syphilis in adolescents or adults Reappearance of lesions after treatment Misinterpreting positive treponemal serology as venereal syphilis, with inappropriate social and clinical implications Overlooking the largely unnoticed primary stage and only recognising disease when secondary lesions appear Failing to treat contacts and address shared-utensil transmission Confusing bejel with yaws or pinta without geographic and clinical context Neglecting nutritional and hygiene factors in affected communities Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum is transmitted through direct mucosal contact or shared utensils in communities with limited hygiene. After entering through the oral mucosa or skin the treponeme multiplies locally and disseminates, producing mucosal and cutaneous secondary lesions and bone involvement over weeks to months. A latent phase may be followed years later by destructive tertiary gummatous lesions of skin, bone and the nasopharynx. As with yaws, the cardiovascular and neurological complications and congenital transmission characteristic of venereal syphilis are not features of bejel. Early bejel responds well to penicillin with full recovery, but untreated late disease may cause permanent, disfiguring destruction of the oronasopharynx and bone; the endemic treponematoses are targets for elimination programmes.

or slow to recover for an underlying structural lesion Bell's palsy is an acute mononeuropathy of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve, widely attributed to inflammation and oedema of the nerve, often linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus. Swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal causes compression, ischaemia, and demyelination, producing unilateral weakness of all facial muscles on the affected side. Depending on the segment involved, taste, lacrimation, and stapedius function may also be impaired. Most patients with Bell's palsy recover well, and the majority regain normal or near-normal function, particularly with early corticosteroid treatment and when weakness is incomplete. A minority, especially those with complete paralysis, are left with residual weakness, synkinesis, or contracture. Recovery beginning within the first few weeks predicts a favourable outcome.

Benign familial neonatal epilepsy is caused by autosomal dominant loss-of-function variants in KCNQ2 or KCNQ3, which together form the Kv7 potassium channel generating the neuronal M-current. Modest reduction of this stabilising current transiently increases neuronal excitability in the maturing neonatal brain, producing seizures that resolve as channel expression and network development mature. The milder functional impact compared with the dominant-negative variants of KCNQ2 encephalopathy explains the self-limited course and favourable developmental outcome. The prognosis is generally excellent, with seizures remitting within weeks to months and normal neurodevelopment in most children. A minority develop later seizures, so long-term outcome is favourable but not uniformly seizure-free.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia — BPH, benign prostatic enlargement, BPE, prostatic hyperplasia Prostate cancer Urethral stricture Bladder neck stenosis or contracture Neurogenic bladder / detrusor dysfunction Overactive bladder Urinary tract infection or prostatitis Bladder stone or bladder tumour Urinalysis to exclude infection and haematuria Serum creatinine and renal function assessment PSA measurement with counselling about interpretation Post-void residual volume by bladder ultrasound Uroflowmetry to assess flow rate and obstructive pattern Renal and bladder ultrasound to assess upper tracts, bladder wall, and residual urine Pressure-flow urodynamics in equivocal or complex cases Typically affects men over 50 and presents with lower urinary tract symptoms that are grouped into voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining, incomplete emptying) and storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia) categories Symptom severity correlates poorly with prostate size, so a large gland may be asymptomatic while a small gland can cause significant obstruction Digital rectal examination usually reveals a smooth, firm, symmetrically enlarged gland; nodularity, asymmetry, or a hard area should raise suspicion of malignancy The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is useful for quantifying symptom burden and monitoring response to treatment Medical management principles include alpha-blockers to relax prostatic smooth muscle for rapid symptom relief and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors to shrink the gland over months in larger prostates Absolute surgical indications include refractory retention, recurrent urinary infection, bladder stones, recurrent haematuria, and upper tract dilatation or renal impairment from obstruction Transurethral resection of the prostate remains the reference surgical standard, with newer minimally invasive and laser techniques offering alternatives PSA may be mildly elevated due to gland volume, but a significantly raised or rising level warrants evaluation for prostate cancer Acute urinary retention, a urological emergency requiring prompt catheterisation Obstructive uropathy with hydronephrosis and renal impairment Recurrent urinary infection or urosepsis associated with an obstructed, incompletely emptying bladder Gross or persistent haematuria requiring exclusion of malignancy Hard, nodular, or asymmetric prostate on examination suggesting cancer Attributing all lower urinary tract symptoms to the prostate and missing bladder dysfunction, cancer, or stricture Overlooking chronic high-residual retention presenting with overflow incontinence and silent renal impairment Relying on prostate size alone to judge the need for treatment Failing to counsel that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors lower PSA and take months to act Missing prostate cancer masked by a benign clinical picture Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a proliferation of glandular epithelial and stromal cells in the transition zone of the prostate, driven by ageing and androgen (dihydrotestosterone) activity. The enlarging gland produces a static component of obstruction by mechanical narrowing of the prostatic urethra and a dynamic component from increased smooth muscle tone mediated by alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. Chronic outflow obstruction leads to detrusor muscle hypertrophy, trabeculation, and eventually detrusor decompensation, incomplete emptying, and rising post-void residual volumes, with risk of upper tract dilatation and renal impairment in advanced cases. BPH is a slowly progressive condition; many men remain stable or improve with medical therapy, but a subset progress to retention or complications requiring surgery, which generally produces durable symptom relief.

recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis arises from partial-function mutations in the same canalicular transport proteins implicated in progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis: the aminophospholipid flippase FIC1 (ATP8B1) in type 1 and the bile salt export pump BSEP (ABCB11) in type 2. Because residual transporter function is retained, hepatocyte bile acid secretion is only intermittently impaired, typically when an additional stress such as infection, hormonal change, or a drug tips the balance. During an episode, bile acids and conjugated bilirubin accumulate and cholestasis with pruritus develops, but between episodes bile flow normalises and the liver recovers without lasting structural injury. The normal or low gamma-glutamyl transferase reflects that, as in the corresponding PFIC subtypes, the underlying lesion does not damage the bile duct epithelium. The condition is benign with a normal life expectancy; episodes are self-limiting and, by definition, do not progress to chronic liver disease or cirrhosis, although attacks can be prolonged and debilitating during the cholestatic phase.

Benzodiazepine overdose — benzodiazepine poisoning, benzodiazepine toxicity, sedative overdose Opioid overdose Alcohol or other sedative-hypnotic intoxication Hypoglycaemia Structural or metabolic causes of coma Carbon monoxide or other toxic causes of reduced consciousness Capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia Pulse oximetry and, if indicated, arterial blood gas for hypoventilation Paracetamol and salicylate levels and an ECG to screen for co-ingestants Urine or serum toxicology where it will change management CT head if reduced consciousness is unexplained or focal signs are present Produces a sedative-hypnotic toxidrome of drowsiness, slurred speech, ataxia, and depressed consciousness, typically with preserved or only mildly depressed vital signs Taken alone, benzodiazepines rarely cause death; serious respiratory depression usually reflects co-ingestion of alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, or the parenteral route The mainstay of care is supportive - airway protection, breathing support, and observation - rather than any specific antidote in most cases Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist that reverses sedation, but its use is limited because it can precipitate seizures and a withdrawal state, particularly in chronic users or mixed overdoses Flumazenil is especially hazardous when a proconvulsant (such as a tricyclic antidepressant) has been co-ingested, as it removes the seizure threshold-raising effect of the benzodiazepine Marked or fluctuating conscious level, disproportionate hypotension, or significant respiratory depression should prompt a search for a co-ingested agent Activated charcoal offers little benefit and risks aspiration in a drowsy patient, so it is generally not recommended Consider alternative causes of coma (hypoglycaemia, head injury, other intoxicants) if the clinical picture does not fit a pure benzodiazepine effect Significant respiratory depression or hypoxaemia Deep or fluctuating coma suggesting a co-ingested agent Hypotension out of proportion to isolated benzodiazepine effect Loss of airway protective reflexes with aspiration risk Seizures, which should raise concern for a proconvulsant co-ingestant rather than benzodiazepine alone Reflexively giving flumazenil and precipitating seizures or acute withdrawal, especially in chronic users or mixed overdose Attributing deep coma or hypotension to benzodiazepines alone and missing a co-ingestant Overlooking hypoglycaemia or another treatable cause of reduced consciousness Administering charcoal to a drowsy patient and causing aspiration Benzodiazepines enhance the inhibitory action of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA-A receptor by increasing the frequency of chloride channel opening, producing central nervous system depression. Because they modulate rather than directly open the channel, there is a ceiling to their respiratory depressant effect when taken alone, which explains their relatively wide margin of safety in isolated overdose. When combined with other central depressants such as opioids or alcohol, this ceiling is lost and dangerous synergistic respiratory depression can occur. Isolated benzodiazepine overdose usually has an excellent prognosis with supportive care, but outcome worsens considerably with co-ingestion of other central depressants or when aspiration or prolonged hypoxia occurs.

confirmation may be slow Acute high-output cardiac failure or cardiovascular collapse (fulminant wet beriberi) Wernicke encephalopathy, a medical emergency requiring immediate thiamine Rapid deterioration in an infant with suspected infantile beriberi Glucose administration in an at-risk patient without prior thiamine Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine in an at-risk patient and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy Failing to recognise high-output failure as a treatable nutritional cardiomyopathy Waiting for laboratory confirmation before treating in suspected Wernicke encephalopathy Overlooking deficiency after bariatric surgery, in hyperemesis, or on prolonged parenteral nutrition Thiamine, as thiamine pyrophosphate, is a cofactor for key enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism including pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. Deficiency impairs oxidative energy production and causes accumulation of pyruvate and lactate, hitting tissues with high energy demand such as heart, peripheral nerves, and brain. Cardiovascular (wet) disease reflects impaired myocardial energetics and peripheral vasodilatation producing high-output failure, while neural (dry) disease and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome reflect neuronal energy failure. Carbohydrate loading raises thiamine demand and can unmask or worsen deficiency. Cardiac and early neurological features often improve rapidly with thiamine, but delayed treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy risks permanent Korsakoff amnesia, and severe peripheral neuropathy may recover only partially.

compromise Uncontrolled peri-operative or post-traumatic bleeding Platelet refractoriness from alloimmunisation Misdiagnosing the low platelet count as immune thrombocytopenia and treating with immunosuppression Automated analysers undercounting the giant platelets, exaggerating the apparent thrombocytopenia Confusing the ristocetin defect with von Willebrand disease without a mixing (normal plasma) study Overusing platelet transfusion and provoking alloimmunisation Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in GP1BA, GP1BB or GP9, which encode subunits of the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex. This complex is the receptor through which platelets bind von Willebrand factor on exposed subendothelium, the first step of platelet adhesion under high shear. When the complex is deficient or defective, platelets cannot tether to the vessel wall, so primary haemostasis is impaired. The same molecular defect disturbs normal megakaryocyte and platelet development, producing mild thrombocytopenia and abnormally large platelets, and the combined adhesion failure and low platelet number underlie the bleeding phenotype. With appropriate supportive care and bleeding prophylaxis around procedures, most patients do well, although serious spontaneous or provoked bleeds can occur and repeated transfusion carries a risk of alloimmunisation.

Removal from exposure and immunosuppression can slow progression, but the disease is not curable.

cause of acute visual loss Failing to screen at-risk family members given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity Best vitelliform macular dystrophy results from mutations in BEST1, which encodes bestrophin-1, a calcium-activated chloride channel located on the basolateral membrane of retinal pigment epithelial cells. Dysfunction of this channel disturbs ion and fluid transport across the retinal pigment epithelium and impairs the standing potential of the eye, which underlies the abnormal electro-oculogram. Lipofuscin-like material accumulates within and beneath the retinal pigment epithelium in the subretinal space at the macula, forming the characteristic vitelliform lesion. Over time this deposited material breaks down and disperses, leading to photoreceptor loss, geographic atrophy, and sometimes fibrous scarring, with the risk of secondary choroidal neovascularisation. Prognosis is generally favourable, with many patients retaining good central vision into later life; however, the fellow eye is usually affected and vision can decline significantly if atrophy, scarring, or choroidal neovascularisation develops.

Seizures in more severely affected individuals Missing the diagnosis because urinary oligosaccharide screening can appear near-normal Assuming a phenotype identical to alpha-mannosidosis Overlooking peripheral neuropathy as part of the disorder Attributing behavioural symptoms solely to a primary neurodevelopmental disorder Beta-mannosidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in MANBA, encoding lysosomal beta-D-mannosidase. This enzyme catalyses the final step in the degradation of N-linked glycoprotein oligosaccharides, cleaving the terminal beta-linked mannose. Its deficiency leads to accumulation and urinary excretion of small mannose-containing disaccharides and related oligosaccharides. Because the accumulated substrate is small and the metabolic block is at the very end of the degradation pathway, the biochemical and clinical picture is often milder and more variable than that of alpha-mannosidosis. The mechanisms underlying the neurological features, including peripheral neuropathy and behavioural problems, remain incompletely understood. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The prognosis is variable and generally less severe than alpha-mannosidosis, with many patients surviving into adulthood, though intellectual disability, hearing loss, and neuropathy cause chronic morbidity. No disease-modifying therapy is established, so care is supportive.

protein-associated neurodegeneration is caused by variants in WDR45, an X-linked gene encoding WIPI4, a beta-propeller scaffolding protein essential for autophagosome formation during macroautophagy. Defective autophagy is thought to impair clearance of damaged organelles and proteins, driving progressive neuronal dysfunction. As the disease advances, iron accumulates in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, situating it within the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation spectrum. The gene's location on the X chromosome, combined with somatic mosaicism and presumed male lethality, accounts for the predominance of affected females. The early phase is characterised by developmental delay and epilepsy that may appear relatively static for years, but a later neurodegenerative phase brings progressive dystonia-parkinsonism and dementia, usually with substantial disability. Overall the condition shortens life expectancy, though the pace of the second phase varies.

Beta Thalassaemia — beta-thalassaemia major, Cooley anaemia, beta-thalassaemia intermedia, beta thalassemia Iron deficiency anaemia Alpha thalassaemia Sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies Anaemia of chronic disease Sideroblastic anaemia Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia Full blood count with red cell indices (low MCV and MCH) Peripheral blood film Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC quantifying HbA, HbA2, and HbF Reticulocyte count Iron studies and serum ferritin to distinguish iron deficiency and monitor overload Genetic mutation analysis of the beta-globin gene Serial ferritin and cardiac/hepatic MRI (T2*) to monitor iron burden An inherited disorder of reduced or absent beta-globin chain production, most common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Southeast Asian populations. Beta-thalassaemia major typically presents in the second half of the first year of life as protective fetal haemoglobin declines, with progressive pallor, poor growth, and hepatosplenomegaly. The blood film shows a severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia with marked anisopoikilocytosis, target cells, and nucleated red cells. Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC demonstrates elevated HbF and often raised HbA2, with little or no HbA in the major form. Chronic transfusion is required in transfusion-dependent disease to sustain growth and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis. Repeated transfusion inevitably causes iron overload, so iron chelation is essential to prevent cardiac, hepatic, and endocrine damage. Untreated or under-transfused children develop characteristic skeletal changes from marrow expansion, including frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth. Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers a potential cure, and newer gene-based therapies are emerging. Splenomegaly may lead to hypersplenism and rising transfusion requirements; genetic counselling and antenatal screening are important for at-risk families. Symptomatic severe anaemia with cardiac decompensation Signs of iron overload cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia Rapidly enlarging spleen with falling counts (hypersplenism) Growth failure and delayed puberty from chronic anaemia or endocrine iron toxicity Features of extramedullary masses causing compressive symptoms Misdiagnosing microcytic anaemia as simple iron deficiency and giving unnecessary iron Under-transfusing and allowing marrow expansion and skeletal deformity to progress Neglecting or delaying iron chelation, leading to preventable organ damage Overlooking endocrine complications such as hypothyroidism, diabetes, and delayed puberty Mutations in the beta-globin gene reduce (beta+) or abolish (beta0) beta-chain synthesis, creating an imbalance with relatively excess alpha-globin chains. Unpaired alpha chains precipitate within red cell precursors, causing their destruction in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and shortened survival of circulating red cells (haemolysis). The resulting chronic anaemia drives erythropoietin-mediated marrow expansion and extramedullary haematopoiesis, while increased gastrointestinal iron absorption and transfusional iron together produce progressive tissue iron overload. With regular transfusion and effective iron chelation, survival into adulthood with good quality of life is achievable; outcomes are limited chiefly by iron-related cardiac and endocrine complications, and stem cell transplant can be curative in selected patients.

monitor respiratory function because ambulation is preserved Missing the connective-tissue skin clues that point to collagen VI disease Assuming normal collagen VI immunostaining excludes the diagnosis, as it can be normal or only subtly abnormal in milder cases Bethlem myopathy is caused by mutations in one of the three genes encoding the alpha chains of collagen VI, a microfibrillar extracellular-matrix protein that forms a network in the interstitium around muscle fibres and connects the basement membrane to the surrounding connective tissue. Defective assembly or secretion of collagen VI disrupts this network, impairing the mechanical and signalling interactions between muscle fibres and their matrix and contributing to fibre dysfunction, abnormal mitochondrial regulation and apoptosis. Because collagen VI is also important in tendon, skin and joint connective tissue, the disorder produces the combination of muscle weakness, the distinctive laxity-and-contracture joint phenotype, and characteristic skin abnormalities. Bethlem myopathy is slowly progressive and most patients retain independent ambulation well into adult life, though a minority require walking aids later and respiratory involvement can develop, so lifespan is usually near normal with appropriate surveillance.
