spectrometry, which is the key diagnostic test Many respond dramatically to oral primary bile acid replacement (e.g. cholic acid or chenodeoxycholic acid), which restores bile flow, suppresses toxic intermediates and can avert liver transplantation Progressive neonatal or infantile cholestasis with coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency Advancing liver disease or failure without an identified structural cause Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency with bleeding, rickets or neurological signs Delay in starting bile acid replacement in a potentially treatable liver disease Overlooking the diagnosis because serum bile acids are low rather than high, which seems counterintuitive in cholestasis Not sending specialist urinary bile acid analysis in unexplained neonatal cholestasis Confusing a treatable synthesis defect with untreatable cholestatic disease Missing fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and associated coagulopathy Failing to consider these disorders in the low-GGT cholestasis group alongside transporter defects The synthesis of primary bile acids from cholesterol requires a sequence of enzymatic modifications to the sterol ring and side chain. In these inborn errors, deficiency of a specific enzyme in the pathway prevents formation of normal cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid and causes accumulation of upstream sterol and bile acid intermediates. The lack of normal bile acids reduces the osmotic driving force for bile flow, producing cholestasis and malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins, while the abnormal intermediates that build up are themselves hepatotoxic and drive progressive liver injury. Because the accumulating intermediates fail to suppress the pathway through feedback, provision of primary bile acids both downregulates their production and restores bile flow. Several of these disorders are highly treatable, and timely primary bile acid replacement can normalise liver biochemistry and prevent progression to cirrhosis or transplantation; delayed diagnosis may allow irreversible liver failure to develop.

Biliary Atresia — extrahepatic biliary atresia, EHBA Neonatal (idiopathic) hepatitis Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency Choledochal cyst Alagille syndrome and other intrahepatic cholestatic syndromes Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis Inspissated bile / bile plug syndrome Congenital infection (TORCH) Fractionated (total and conjugated) serum bilirubin Liver function tests including GGT and aminotransferases Abdominal ultrasound (gallbladder, triangular cord sign, exclusion of choledochal cyst) Hepatobiliary scintigraphy assessing excretion into the intestine Percutaneous liver biopsy Intraoperative cholangiogram to confirm the diagnosis Studies to exclude alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and metabolic causes The most common cause of neonatal cholestasis leading to liver transplantation, resulting from progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts. Classic presentation is a term infant with prolonged jaundice, pale (acholic) stools, and dark urine, usually with otherwise good early growth. Any infant jaundiced beyond about two weeks of age should have a fractionated bilirubin measured; a raised conjugated (direct) fraction signals cholestasis and needs urgent evaluation. Early diagnosis is critical because the success of surgery falls sharply with age, ideally before about 8 weeks (60 days) of life. The Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy aims to restore bile drainage; the earlier it is performed, the better the chance of clearing jaundice. Even after a successful Kasai procedure, many children progress to cirrhosis and ultimately require liver transplantation. A subset have the biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome with situs and other congenital anomalies. Ultrasound may show an absent or small gallbladder and the 'triangular cord' sign; a hepatobiliary scan shows hepatic uptake without excretion into the bowel. Acholic (pale, clay-coloured) stools Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia at any age in an infant Jaundice persisting beyond two weeks of life Signs of coagulopathy or vitamin K deficiency bleeding Hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, or other features of advanced liver disease Dismissing prolonged neonatal jaundice as physiological or breast-milk jaundice without checking a split bilirubin Failing to inspect stool colour Delaying referral and surgery beyond the window where the Kasai procedure is most effective Relying on a normal ultrasound to exclude the diagnosis Overlooking associated congenital anomalies in the splenic malformation syndrome A fibro-obliterative process destroys the extrahepatic and often intrahepatic bile ducts, obstructing bile flow. Retained bile causes progressive hepatocellular injury, portal tract inflammation, and bile ductular proliferation, leading to fibrosis and, if untreated, biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension and liver failure. The initiating cause is uncertain and probably heterogeneous, involving developmental, immune, and possibly viral mechanisms. Outcome depends heavily on the age at surgery; early Kasai portoenterostomy can restore bile flow and delay or avoid transplantation, but many children eventually progress to end-stage liver disease. Overall long-term survival is good when transplantation is available.

Biliary colic / cholelithiasis — Abdominal ultrasound LFTs Fever/jaundice → cholecystitis/cholangitis (infective) Acute cholecystitis (pain >5 h, fever, Murphy's sign) — represents biliary pain that fails to resolve as the cystic duct stays obstructed (p.2731-2732) Choledocholithiasis with cholangitis — CBD stone causing biliary pain plus jaundice and spiking fevers/chills (Charcot's triad) (p.2735) Gallstone pancreatitis — stone-related obstruction at the ampulla; pain is severe and persists for days, not hours (p.2461, p.2735) Peptic ulcer disease / functional dyspepsia — ulcer pain is intermittent over weeks-months and may be relieved by eating, unlike the sudden hours-long onset of colic (p.2461) Irritable bowel syndrome and other disorders of gut-brain interaction — common causes of abdominal pain, exacerbated by stress rather than fatty meals (p.2460-2461) Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction / biliary dyskinesia — biliary-type pain without stones, may follow cholecystectomy (p.2734) Acalculous cholecystopathy — disordered gallbladder motility producing recurrent biliary pain in the absence of stones (p.2732) Right-lower-lobe pneumonia, mesenteric ischemia, or right renal colic as non-biliary causes of RUQ/flank pain (p.2460) Right-upper-quadrant ultrasound is the procedure of choice: rapid, not limited by jaundice or pregnancy, and >95% accurate for gallstones, identifying calculi as small as ~1.5 mm by their acoustic shadowing and gravity-dependent movement (p.2729-2730) Ultrasound also distinguishes biliary sludge (low-echogenicity layer that shifts with position but casts NO acoustic shadow) from true stones, and can assess gallbladder emptying (p.2728-2730) Serum bilirubin and/or alkaline phosphatase elevation during a biliary attack suggests a common-duct stone rather than simple colic (p.2731) Cholescintigraphy (HIDA/DISIDA scan): non-visualization of the gallbladder indicates cystic-duct obstruction and supports acute cholecystitis (p.2730) MRCP, EUS, or ERCP for suspected choledocholithiasis; ERCP is the gold standard and also therapeutic, MRCP often the initial test (p.325) Plain abdominal film detects only the radiopaque minority of stones (~10-15% of cholesterol, ~50% of pigment) and has low yield (p.2730) Functional dyspepsia / non-ulcer dyspepsia presenting with post-prandial epigastric discomfort (p.2461) Gastroesophageal reflux / pill esophagitis (biliary colic itself can be mistaken for unexplained upper-GI symptoms) (p.2728) Irritable bowel syndrome (most common cause of abdominal pain alongside functional dyspepsia) (p.2461) Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction and acalculous cholecystopathy (biliary-type pain without calculi) (p.2732, p.2734) Cardiac/precordial referral — gallbladder pain may occasionally be referred to the precordium (p.2728) Biliary colic is the most specific symptom of gallstone disease, yet 'colic' is a misnomer: the pain is steady rather than waxing-and-waning, reflecting non-relievable distention of the gallbladder/duct against a stone obstructing the cystic duct or CBD (p.2731). A typical episode begins abruptly and lasts roughly 30 minutes to 5 hours before easing; pain that persists beyond ~5 hours should prompt suspicion of acute cholecystitis rather than uncomplicated colic (p.2731). Pain is characteristically a severe steady ache or fullness in the epigastrium or right upper quadrant, often radiating to the interscapular region, right scapula, or shoulder (p.2731). Attacks may be triggered by a fatty meal, a large meal after prolonged fasting, or even a normal meal, and are frequently nocturnal, occurring within a few hours of going to bed (p.2731). Nausea and vomiting commonly accompany the pain, but fever/chills are NOT features of uncomplicated colic and signal a complication (p.2731). Vague short-lived epigastric fullness, dyspepsia, belching, or flatulence after fatty food are nonspecific and occur with or without gallstones; they should not be equated with true biliary pain (p.2731). Most asymptomatic gallstones stay silent: 60-80% remain symptom-free over follow-up up to 25 years, so incidentally found stones without referable symptoms generally do not warrant intervention (p.2731). Once colic occurs, the disease has 'declared' itself; complications requiring surgery are far more common in patients who have developed biliary pain than in the asymptomatic group, and most patients who develop complications had prior warning symptoms (p.2731). Sudden awakening from sleep by pain favors an organic cause such as biliary colic over a functional gut-brain disorder (p.2461). Pain persisting beyond ~5 hours — suspect acute cholecystitis (p.2731) Fever, chills, or rigors with biliary pain — implies a complication (cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis), not uncomplicated colic (p.2731) Jaundice and/or rising bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase — suggests common-bile-duct stone or obstruction (p.2731) Charcot's triad (biliary pain + jaundice + spiking fever/chills) — acute cholangitis (p.2735) Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) with RUQ tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis — acute cholecystitis (p.323, p.2732) Severe pain persisting for days, with confusion/sepsis features — suggests pancreatitis or suppurative cholangitis (p.2461, p.2735) Treating the term 'colic' literally and expecting intermittent crampy pain — biliary colic is steady, and waiting for it to fluctuate can delay recognition (p.2731). Attributing nonspecific fatty-food dyspepsia, belching, or bloating to gallstones; these symptoms are equally common in people without stones and do not establish a biliary cause (p.2731). Assuming an incidental gallstone explains a patient's symptoms — most stones are silent, and a coexisting non-biliary disorder (e.g., reflux, peptic ulcer, IBS) may be the true cause (p.2731, p.2735). Missing that fever or jaundice has converted 'colic' into a complication requiring different (often urgent) management (p.2731). Relying on a plain abdominal film, which misses most cholesterol stones, instead of ultrasound (p.2730). Overlooking acalculous causes of biliary-type pain (sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, acalculous cholecystopathy) when ultrasound shows no stones (p.2732, p.2734). Biliary colic results from transient obstruction of the cystic duct (or common bile duct) by a gallstone migrating out of the gallbladder. The obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and distends the viscus; because repetitive biliary contractions cannot overcome or relieve the blockage, a steady visceral pain is generated. When the stone disimpacts or falls back, pressure normalizes and the pain resolves spontaneously, so an uncomplicated episode is self-limited and is NOT accompanied by inflammation, fever, or sustained cholestasis. Underlying stones are usually cholesterol stones (>90% in Western populations), which form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, cholesterol monohydrate crystals nucleate, and gallbladder hypomotility allows stasis and stone growth; gallbladder emptying is frequently impaired in stone formers. Distinct mechanisms (mechanical, chemical from lysolecithin, and bacterial) convert simple obstruction into acute cholecystitis when the cystic duct stays blocked (p.2727-2732). Uncomplicated biliary colic is self-limited; the individual attack resolves once the transient obstruction clears. The natural history of the underlying gallstones is generally favorable: 60-80% of asymptomatic stone carriers stay symptom-free for up to 25 years, the chance of developing symptoms is only ~2-4% per year in the first 5 years after diagnosis (falling to 1-2% thereafter), and the yearly incidence of complications is only ~0.1-0.3%. The cumulative risk of death from gallstone disease under expectant management is small. However, once biliary pain has occurred, the likelihood of recurrent attacks and of complications requiring intervention rises substantially; younger patients at diagnosis are more likely to become symptomatic than those over 60 (p.2731). Harrison frames the spectrum by clinical course rather than a formal grading scale: uncomplicated biliary colic = transient cystic-duct obstruction giving self-limited pain (30 min-5 h) WITHOUT fever, inflammation, or jaundice; progression/complication is signalled by pain >5 h, fever/chills, or jaundice, and corresponds to acute cholecystitis (sustained cystic-duct obstruction with inflammation), choledocholithiasis with cholangitis (CBD obstruction + infection, Charcot's triad), or gallstone pancreatitis. Acute cholecystitis is itself triaged by complications (e.g., empyema, gangrene, perforation, Mirizzi's syndrome) (p.2731-2735).

which mediates thiamine uptake into cells. Because thiamine (as thiamine pyrophosphate) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase, transporter failure produces intracellular thiamine deficiency and impaired oxidative energy metabolism. The basal ganglia, with high metabolic demand, are especially vulnerable, so metabolic stress such as fever or fasting precipitates acute energy crises with cytotoxic oedema and neuronal injury. Supraphysiological biotin and thiamine are thought to drive residual transporter activity and alternative uptake pathways, restoring intracellular thiamine. Prognosis depends critically on how early treatment begins; when high-dose biotin and thiamine are started promptly, recovery from acute crises can be near-complete. Delayed or missed episodes cause cumulative basal ganglia damage with residual dystonia, dysarthria and cognitive impairment.

the cofactor for several carboxylase enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis and amino acid catabolism. Biotinidase cleaves biocytin to release free biotin, recycling it, and also frees biotin bound to dietary protein. When biotinidase is deficient, biotin is progressively lost and cannot be adequately reused, producing a functional deficiency that impairs the biotin-dependent carboxylases (pyruvate carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase). The resulting metabolic block causes lactic acidosis and abnormal organic acid accumulation, while the neurological, cutaneous, ophthalmological and auditory features reflect tissue biotin deficiency. Supplemental free biotin bypasses the recycling defect. Prognosis is excellent when biotin supplementation is started early, and screen-detected infants treated before symptoms usually develop normally; however, hearing loss, optic atrophy and neurological damage that occur before diagnosis may not fully reverse, underscoring the value of early detection.

Episodes are often precipitated by sleep disruption, stress, or substances acting on an underlying biological vulnerability. Bipolar disorder is a lifelong, recurrent illness with substantial risk of functional impairment and elevated suicide rate. Prognosis improves with early diagnosis, mood-stabiliser adherence, and relapse-prevention strategies, whereas repeated episodes, substance misuse, and poor adherence worsen outcomes.

Bladder & Urinary Tract Cancer — urothelial carcinoma, transitional cell carcinoma Hematuria from malignancy in females is frequently mistaken for a urinary tract infection (Harrison 22e p.691). Urine cytology (detects cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers) (Harrison 22e p.691). Cystoscopy for direct bladder visualization; blue light or narrow-band imaging cystoscopy improves detection of small or flat noninvasive tumors and is used routinely in monitoring (Harrison 22e p.691). CT urogram (or MR urogram if renal function is impaired) for the kidneys and upper tract (Harrison 22e p.691). Adjunct urine molecular tests (FISH for chromosomal changes, nuclear mitotic proteins, bladder tumor-associated antigens) used mainly for detecting recurrence, as they can be falsely positive (Harrison 22e p.691). Ureteroscopy or retrograde pyelography when upper-tract tumors are suspected with a normal bladder (Harrison 22e p.691). Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) or endoscopic resection of upper tract tumors for histologic diagnosis and staging (Harrison 22e p.691). Genomic sequencing of tumor tissue and/or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) recommended in all metastatic patients (Harrison 22e p.690). In females, malignant hematuria may be misattributed to menstrual bleeding (Harrison 22e p.691). Intravesical BCG side effects (dysuria, urinary frequency, bladder spasms, hematuria) overlap with infection/cystitis, and in <5% a systemic inflammatory response can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692). Painless hematuria, either gross or microscopic, is the initial manifestation of urinary tract cancer in most patients; in males painless hematuria is almost always abnormal and must be worked up (Harrison 22e p.691). In females, hematuria due to malignancy is often mistaken for a urinary tract infection or menstrual bleeding; antibiotics are warranted if a concurrent UTI is found, but persistent hematuria still requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691). Initial investigation in either sex includes urine cytology plus visual examination of the bladder by cystoscopy, together with radiographic evaluation of the kidneys and upper tract by CT urogram (MR urogram if renal function is poor) (Harrison 22e p.691). Smoking of tobacco products is the overwhelming leading risk factor; 90% of new bladder cancer diagnoses occur in current or former smokers, and roughly one-third of cases could be prevented by smoking cessation (Harrison 22e p.692). Urothelial carcinoma (formerly transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common histology, seen in about 90% of cases; nonurothelial variants (squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, small-cell, carcinosarcoma) collectively account for 10% or less (Harrison 22e p.690-691). Disease is divided into non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC: carcinoma in situ, Ta, or T1 not reaching the muscularis propria; ~75% at presentation) and muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC: T2 invasion of muscularis propria and beyond) (Harrison 22e p.691-692). Urothelial carcinoma shows a biphasic phenotype: low-grade papillary tumors that frequently recur but rarely invade or metastasize, and high-grade often flat tumors that invade early and lead to lethal metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.691). Painless gross or microscopic hematuria warrants investigation for urothelial cancer; in males it is almost always abnormal (Harrison 22e p.691). Persistent hematuria despite treatment of a concurrent UTI requires further workup (Harrison 22e p.691). Flank pain with an upper tract renal pelvis/ureter cancer, or hydronephrosis from a bladder tumor obstructing the ureteral orifice (Harrison 22e p.691). Cachexia and widespread metastatic disease at presentation (rare) (Harrison 22e p.691). Urine cytology is insensitive, identifying cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers, so a negative cytology does not exclude malignancy (Harrison 22e p.691). Treating presumed UTI without follow-up risks missing malignancy; persistent hematuria after antibiotics still requires workup (Harrison 22e p.691). Adjunct urine molecular tests may be abnormal in patients without cancer (false positives) and are best reserved for surveillance of known cancer (Harrison 22e p.691). Systemic inflammatory reaction after intravesical BCG can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692). Urothelial carcinoma arises from the lining of the bladder, renal pelvis, ureter, and urethra and displays a biphasic clinical behavior. Loss of portions of chromosomes 9q and 9p (loss of heterozygosity) is an early molecular event in both phenotypes; candidate genes in these regions include CDKN2A and TSC1. Low-grade papillary tumors are characterized by RAS/RAF pathway alterations with activating FGFR3 mutations or fusions in 60-80% of patients, whereas the high-grade invasive phenotype features early deleterious TP53 and RB1 mutations, CDH1 (E-cadherin) alterations, and increased VEGFR2 expression. Chronic inflammatory states drive squamous-type bladder cancer, classically chronic schistosomiasis infection and chronic indwelling catheters in paraplegic patients. Carcinogenic exposures include aromatic amines (benzidine, beta-naphthylamine) in industrial dyes and arsenic-contaminated drinking water. The Cancer Genome Atlas defined five intrinsic molecular subtypes (luminal papillary, luminal infiltrated, luminal, basal squamous, neuronal) resembling breast cancer subclasses (Harrison 22e p.691-692). Outcomes correlate closely with stage at diagnosis. About 75% present with non-muscle-invasive disease, 18% with muscle-invasive disease, and only 3% with metastatic spread. 5-year overall survival is 70-90% for disease confined to the bladder (stage I-II), 39-50% for disease penetrating through the bladder or involving regional lymph nodes (stage III), and only 8% for metastatic disease (stage IV) (Harrison 22e p.692). Staging is driven primarily by depth of invasion (T stage). NMIBC: Tis (CIS) and Ta (epithelial layer only) or T1 (into connective tissue/lamina propria below urothelium but not muscularis propria). MIBC: T2 (into muscularis propria), T3 (through muscularis propria to serosa), T4 (adjacent pelvic organs - rectum, prostate, vagina, cervix). Nodal: N1 (single true pelvic node), N2 (two true pelvic nodes), N3 (common iliac nodes); disease beyond common iliac nodes or distant spread is M1. Stages 0a-II are defined by T stage alone without nodal/metastatic disease; regional pelvic or common iliac nodal involvement is stage III; any distant metastasis is stage IV (Harrison 22e p.691-692).

wounds Enclosed-space exposure with combined burns, inhalation, and toxic effects Considering only the visible wounds and missing primary blast injury to lung or bowel Assuming intact eardrums exclude significant blast exposure Aggressive positive-pressure ventilation aggravating blast lung and air embolism Failing to anticipate delayed bowel perforation Underestimating severity of injuries sustained in enclosed spaces An explosion generates a high-pressure blast wave that transmits energy across tissue interfaces of differing density. Where gas meets fluid or solid, as in the alveoli, middle ear, and gut, shearing and implosion-reexpansion forces rupture delicate structures, producing pulmonary haemorrhage and oedema (blast lung), tympanic perforation, and bowel contusion or perforation. Secondary injury results from fragments propelled by the blast causing penetrating wounds, tertiary injury from the body being thrown, and quaternary effects from burns, crush, inhalation, and toxic exposure. Blast lung can allow air to enter pulmonary veins, producing systemic air embolism to the brain or coronary circulation. Prognosis depends on the dominant mechanism and injury burden. Blast lung and multi-mechanism injuries carry significant early mortality, while many fragment and displacement injuries are survivable with prompt trauma care; delayed presentations such as bowel perforation add later risk.

A primary fungal pathogen: it infects persons with intact as well as impaired immune systems (p.1699). Endemic mainly in North America (Mississippi/Ohio and St. Lawrence River basins, Great Lakes states, southeastern states) but of global importance with cases in Africa and Asia; outbreaks linked to construction, soil excavation, water sports, compost piles, and beaver dams (p.1699-1700). Yeast form (37 degrees C) is a broad-based budding yeast, 4-29 micrometers, with a doubly refractile cell wall, allowing distinction from other fungi (p.1700, 1702). After a 3-week to 3-month incubation, about 50% of those exposed develop symptomatic infection; the long incubation means cases present year-round (p.1701). Pulmonary disease occurs in 69-93% of symptomatic patients (most common feature) and may present as asymptomatic infection, influenza-like illness, acute pneumonia, chronic pneumonia, or ARDS (p.1701). Disseminated disease occurs in 15-48%; skin is the most common site (papules, ulcers, verrucous lesions, abscesses), followed by bone (osteomyelitis of spine, long bones, ribs) (p.1701). CNS (meningitis/abscess/mass), laryngeal, and genitourinary (prostate, epididymis) dissemination each occur in fewer than 10%, usually with concurrent lung or skin involvement (p.1701). Diagnosis combines microscopy of stained specimens, fungal culture, and antigen testing; serology (complement fixation 9%, immunodiffusion 28%) is diagnostically dispensable, though a newer anti-BAD1 antibody test has higher sensitivity/specificity (p.1702). Urine galactomannan antigen testing (sensitivity 85-93% urine, 57-82% serum) has supplanted older serology and can monitor treatment response as levels decline (p.1702-1703). Treatment is recommended for ALL patients because there are no criteria to identify which untreated cases will self-resolve; antifungals are amphotericin B formulations and triazoles (p.1699, 1703). Unexplained respiratory failure or ARDS in a person from or visiting an endemic area; 4-15% of pulmonary cases develop ARDS with a fulminant course and 40-89% mortality (p.1701) Pneumonia that fails to improve despite antibiotics, or pneumonia with extrapulmonary features (skin lesions, osteomyelitis, CNS involvement) (p.1701) Skin ulcers unresponsive to standard therapy (p.1701) AIDS with CD4+ count <100/microliter: increased risk of CNS dissemination (p.1702) B. helicus infection (commonly causes fungemia, usually in immunosuppressed hosts, high mortality ~71%) (p.1702) Called 'the great pretender' because it mimics infectious and noninfectious diseases; pulmonary blastomycosis is commonly misdiagnosed, and patients often receive two or three antibiotic courses before diagnosis (p.1701). No distinctive radiographic features differentiate blastomycosis from other pulmonary diseases (consolidation, mass, nodules, miliary, cavitary patterns all possible); a mass lesion can mimic malignancy (p.1701). Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and a detailed exposure history (about 50-60% of patients have environmental risk factors); failure to consider Blastomyces in the differential delays treatment (p.1701). Serology by complement fixation/immunodiffusion has poor sensitivity and is diagnostically dispensable (p.1702). Echinocandins are ineffective (minimal beta-(1,3)-glucan in the yeast cell wall) and should not be used (p.1703). Antigen testing cross-reacts with other dimorphic fungi, notably H. capsulatum which shares the same endemic region (p.1703). Blastomyces is a thermally dimorphic species complex (including B. dermatitidis, B. gilchristii, B. helicus, B. percursus, B. emzantsi). In soil at 22-25 degrees C it grows as septate hyphae producing infectious conidia; inhalation into the lungs and conversion at the mammalian core temperature of 37 degrees C yields a pathogenic broad-based budding yeast that upregulates yeast-phase virulence factors and downregulates host immune defenses, eliciting pyogranulomatous inflammation. Shared virulence traits with other dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Sporothrix, Paracoccidioides) include thermotolerance at 37 degrees C, intracellular survival, and the ability to infect immunocompetent hosts. Blastomyces can also replicate outside macrophages. Notably, immunosuppression has only minimal influence on dissemination, suggesting fungal virulence factors outweigh host defenses; the infecting species and duration of pulmonary symptoms (and concomitant AIDS) influence dissemination, with B. dermatitidis more likely to disseminate than B. gilchristii. (p.1700-1702) Overall mortality ranges from 5 to 13% (7.9% in 11,776 U.S. hospital admissions, 2010-2020), with most deaths from respiratory failure due to ARDS. Mortality is higher in older patients and those with COPD or concomitant solid/hematologic malignancy, and is increased when diagnosis is delayed. The vast majority who recover from pulmonary blastomycosis do not have long-term loss of pulmonary function; cutaneous blastomycosis typically heals with scarring. (p.1703) Harrison does not give a formal numeric severity scale. Severe blastomycosis is operationally defined as disease requiring hospitalization (medical ward, intermediate care, or ICU). Risk factors for severe pulmonary disease include diabetes, solid organ transplantation, immunosuppression, and multilobar pneumonia; ARDS (in 4-15%) represents the most severe pulmonary form with high mortality. Special high-risk/severity categories warranting intensified management include CNS, severe pulmonary, and severe disseminated disease. (p.1701-1703)

is an autosomal dominant granulomatous disorder caused by gain-of-function mutations in NOD2 (also called CARD15), an intracellular pattern-recognition receptor that senses bacterial peptidoglycan fragments. The disease-causing mutations lie in the nucleotide-binding domain and render the receptor constitutively active, driving ligand-independent activation of the pro-inflammatory transcription factor NF-kB and dysregulated innate immune signalling. This sustained activation promotes formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in the joints, skin and eyes. The mutations are mechanistically and topographically distinct from the Crohn-disease-associated NOD2 variants, which impair rather than enhance receptor function. The joint and skin disease are often manageable, but the chronic uveitis is the principal threat to long-term outcome and can lead to visual loss if not aggressively monitored and treated; systemic involvement in atypical cases can broaden morbidity.

Blepharitis — anterior blepharitis, posterior blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, lid margin inflammation Dry eye disease Allergic or bacterial conjunctivitis Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid (in atypical, unilateral disease) Rosacea-associated ocular surface disease Demodex lash infestation Contact dermatitis of the eyelids Slit-lamp examination of the lid margins, lashes, and meibomian gland orifices Assessment of tear film stability and ocular surface staining for associated dry eye Lid margin or lash swab in severe or atypical cases Lid margin biopsy when malignancy is suspected (unilateral disease with lash loss and induration) A common, chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins presenting with burning, grittiness, crusting, and redness that is typically bilateral and worse in the mornings Divided into anterior blepharitis (affecting the lash bases, often staphylococcal or seborrhoeic) and posterior blepharitis (meibomian gland dysfunction) Anterior staphylococcal disease shows hard crusts and collarettes around the lashes, with lash loss and misdirection in chronic cases Posterior disease shows capped, plugged, or inspissated meibomian orifices and a poor-quality, foamy tear film with associated evaporative dry eye Strongly associated with rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis; recurrent chalazia and styes are common complications The mainstay of management is lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid margin cleaning; topical antibiotic ointment helps anterior disease and oral tetracyclines help refractory meibomian dysfunction Recurrent, unilateral, or asymmetrical lid margin disease with lash loss should raise suspicion of eyelid malignancy such as sebaceous gland carcinoma Patients should be counselled that it is a chronic, relapsing condition controlled rather than cured Unilateral or markedly asymmetrical disease with localised lash loss and lid thickening suggesting sebaceous gland carcinoma Associated corneal involvement (marginal keratitis or ulceration) threatening vision Failure to respond to appropriate treatment prompting re-evaluation of the diagnosis Recurrent chalazia at the same site raising concern for malignancy Expecting a cure rather than long-term control and stopping lid hygiene prematurely Missing sebaceous gland carcinoma masquerading as recurrent unilateral blepharitis or chalazion Overlooking associated dry eye and rosacea that require concurrent management Prolonged unmonitored topical steroid use with risk of raised intraocular pressure Blepharitis is chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins with overlapping mechanisms. Anterior blepharitis involves bacterial (chiefly staphylococcal) colonisation of the lash bases and an inflammatory reaction to bacterial products, or seborrhoeic changes with excessive scaling. Posterior blepharitis reflects meibomian gland dysfunction, in which altered and inspissated meibomian secretions block the glands, destabilise the lipid layer of the tear film, and promote evaporative dry eye. Bacterial lipases and inflammatory mediators contribute to ocular surface irritation, and the condition is frequently linked to rosacea. Blepharitis is a chronic relapsing condition that is generally controlled well with sustained lid hygiene, though symptoms recur if treatment lapses; complications such as recurrent chalazia and evaporative dry eye can be troublesome but vision is usually preserved.

reconsideration Functional visual impairment from inability to open the eyes Overlooking treatable ocular surface disease driving reflex eye closure Misdiagnosing unilateral hemifacial spasm as blepharospasm Failing to identify drug-induced dystonia from a reversible cause Missing associated oromandibular dystonia in Meige syndrome Blepharospasm is a focal cranial dystonia in which abnormal function of basal ganglia and brainstem circuits controlling blink and eyelid movement leads to excessive, involuntary orbicularis oculi contraction. Reduced inhibition within the blink reflex pathway and abnormal sensorimotor integration are implicated, and dopaminergic and other neurotransmitter systems are thought to be involved. Ocular surface irritation can trigger or worsen symptoms through the reflex arc, and the disorder can extend to adjacent facial and jaw muscles in segmental forms. Blepharospasm is usually chronic and can fluctuate but is not life-threatening; most patients gain substantial and repeatable relief from botulinum toxin, though the condition generally requires ongoing treatment.

progressive growth failure in infancy Using standard-dose radiotherapy or DNA-damaging chemotherapy without accounting for the extreme treatment sensitivity Attributing early growth restriction to nutritional causes and missing the underlying diagnosis Failing to maintain a low threshold for investigating possible malignancy Overlooking associated immunodeficiency and diabetes in ongoing care Bloom syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in BLM, which encodes a RecQ-family DNA helicase essential for maintaining genomic stability during DNA replication and repair, particularly in resolving recombination intermediates and stalled replication forks. Loss of BLM function leads to excessive homologous recombination and a striking increase in sister chromatid exchanges, the cytogenetic signature of the disorder. This genomic instability drives the profound cancer predisposition and contributes to the growth failure and other systemic features. The condition is more frequent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population owing to a founder variant. Life expectancy is significantly reduced, largely because of the exceptionally high and early risk of multiple cancers, which are the leading cause of death. Infections, diabetes and chronic pulmonary disease add to morbidity, and management is supportive with intensive cancer awareness and cautious use of DNA-damaging treatments.

1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia Tumor-induced osteomalacia mimicking idiopathic chronic bone pain and myopathy Milk-alkali syndrome mimicking other hypercalcemic states with renal impairment Bone is continuously remodeled by a basic multicellular unit: osteoblasts (mesenchymal origin) lay down and mineralize osteoid, osteoclasts (hematopoietic/macrophage lineage) resorb matrix, and long-lived embedded osteocytes coordinate both and act as mechanosensors (Harrison 22e p.3259). Roughly half of total serum calcium is ionized; the rest is bound to albumin/immunoglobulins or complexed to anions, so total calcium must be interpreted with the serum protein level. A useful correction adds about 0.8 mg/dL to total calcium for each 1 g/dL the albumin is below normal, but in acute illness measure ionized calcium directly with a calcium-selective electrode (Harrison 22e p.3261-3262). Acidosis raises ionized calcium by reducing calcium binding to protein; alkalosis does the opposite, which helps explain tetany seen with respiratory alkalosis (Harrison 22e p.3262). Serum phosphate varies by up to 50% over a day with a morning nadir, and IV dextrose, insulin, or alkalosis can drop it acutely, so phosphate should be measured fasting and in the basal state (Harrison 22e p.3262-3263). Because only about 1% of body magnesium is in the extracellular fluid, a normal serum magnesium does not exclude significant total-body magnesium depletion (Harrison 22e p.3266-3267). Hypomagnesemia frequently causes refractory hypocalcemia and hypokalemia; at very low serum magnesium (below roughly 0.4 mmol/L) PTH secretion is impaired and there is cellular PTH resistance, so calcium and potassium will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3267). FGF23, secreted by osteocytes, is a phosphaturic hormone that both lowers proximal-tubule phosphate reabsorption and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase (lowering 1,25(OH)2D); excess FGF23 underlies XLH, ADHR, and tumor-induced osteomalacia, whereas deficient/inactive FGF23 causes tumoral calcinosis (Harrison 22e p.3263-3265). Vitamin D is effectively a hormone, not a true vitamin: skin synthesizes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UV light, the liver performs unregulated 25-hydroxylation (25(OH)D is the storage/measured form), and the kidney performs the tightly regulated 1-alpha-hydroxylation to active 1,25(OH)2D (Harrison 22e p.3268). Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and hypophosphatemia and suppressed by calcium, FGF23, and 1,25(OH)2D itself; granuloma/lymphoma macrophages express an unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase, explaining hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.3268). Optimal intestinal calcium absorption requires gastric acid; achlorhydria, proton pump inhibitors, or post-bariatric surgery impair absorption of poorly dissociable salts like calcium carbonate, so calcium citrate or dosing with meals is preferred (Harrison 22e p.3262). Active vitamin D-dependent transcellular calcium and phosphate absorption uses specific apical channels/transporters (TRPV6 and Npt2b in the gut, TRPV5 in the distal tubule); thiazides lower urinary calcium (useful in hypercalciuria) while loop diuretics and saline promote calciuresis (Harrison 22e p.3262). Serious neuromuscular sequelae of hypophosphatemia (seizures, paralysis, rhabdomyolysis) occur mainly when phosphate falls below about 0.25 mmol/L, reflecting ATP depletion; up to 30% of patients with acute hypophosphatemia have CPK elevations peaking 1-2 days after the phosphate nadir (Harrison 22e p.3264). Severe hypophosphatemia below about 0.25 mmol/L (0.8 mg/dL): risk of seizures, ascending paralysis, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory and cardiac failure, coma Acute severe hyperphosphatemia: widespread calcium-phosphate precipitation with tetany, seizures, acute renal failure, and pulmonary/cardiac calcification including heart block Hypermagnesemia above ~2 mmol/L: refractory hypotension, neuromuscular blockade, hyporeflexia progressing to respiratory failure, heart block, and asystole near 10 mmol/L Severe hypomagnesemia: tetany, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, prolonged QT and enhanced digitalis toxicity Very high calcium intake or milk-alkali syndrome: hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, progressive renal failure Relying on total serum calcium without correcting for albumin, or on corrected calcium during acute illness, can mislead; ionized calcium should be measured directly when accuracy matters A normal serum magnesium does not exclude total-body magnesium depletion because the extracellular pool is tiny The body phosphate deficit cannot be predicted from a single serum phosphate; repletion must be empirical and monitored, since the nadir often occurs hours into insulin/glucose therapy Giving IV magnesium alone to a patient with combined hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia can worsen hypophosphatemia by abruptly restoring PTH secretion; give calcium and magnesium together Failing to recognize that hypocalcemia and hypokalemia are refractory until magnesium is repleted Overlooking 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia from granulomatous disease or lymphoma, where calcium does not suppress the ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase Phosphate measured non-fasting or after IV dextrose can be spuriously low; rapid phosphate correction risks heterotopic calcification if the calcium-phosphorus product is allowed to rise Mineral homeostasis is maintained by integrated handling of calcium, phosphate, and magnesium across gut, kidney, and bone under hormonal control by PTH, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, and FGF23. Bone provides both mechanical support and the major reservoir of these ions; it is constantly remodeled, with osteoblasts (mesenchymal lineage, driven by Runx2, osterix, Ihh, Wnt and BMP signaling) forming and mineralizing type I collagen matrix and osteoclasts (hematopoietic lineage, driven by M-CSF and RANK ligand, opposed by osteoprotegerin) resorbing it via acidification and proteases such as cathepsin K. Osteocytes sense mechanical load, secrete the Wnt inhibitor sclerostin and the phosphaturic hormone FGF23, and orchestrate remodeling. Ionized calcium in the extracellular fluid is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells and renal tubule; low calcium raises PTH, which mobilizes bone calcium, enhances distal renal calcium reabsorption, lowers renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make 1,25(OH)2D, which in turn increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Phosphate balance is governed largely by proximal tubular NaPi-2a/2c transporters, which are downregulated by PTH and FGF23; FGF23 from osteocytes additionally suppresses 1,25(OH)2D synthesis. Vitamin D is produced in skin or absorbed from diet, 25-hydroxylated in liver, and 1-alpha-hydroxylated in kidney, with 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) providing inactivation. Disturbances at any node (dietary extremes, renal failure, hormone deficiency/excess, intestinal disease, or genetic transporter/enzyme defects) disrupt the narrow regulation of ionized calcium and lead to skeletal and systemic disease. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying disorder rather than on bone and mineral metabolism per se. Acute redistributive electrolyte derangements (hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia) are typically reversible with appropriate repletion, and respiratory/cardiac dysfunction from severe hypophosphatemia improves with phosphate replacement. Tumor-induced osteomalacia resolves within hours to days after successful tumor resection. Chronic renal phosphate-wasting disorders (XLH, ADHR) generally cannot be fully normalized but can be controlled. Persistent dysregulation, as in chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism and hyperphosphatemia, leads to progressive skeletal and vascular consequences. Hypophosphatemia is graded by serum phosphate (mild-moderate ~0.5-0.8 mmol/L [1.5-2.5 mg/dL] with mainly musculoskeletal/reversible cardiorespiratory effects; severe <0.5 mmol/L [<1.5 mg/dL]; life-threatening <0.25 mmol/L [<0.8 mg/dL] with paralysis, seizures, rhabdomyolysis). Hyperphosphatemia in adults is defined as fasting phosphate >1.8 mmol/L (5.5 mg/dL). Hypomagnesemia is usually asymptomatic above ~0.5 mmol/L; defects in PTH secretion appear below ~0.4 mmol/L. Hypermagnesemia produces vasodilation/neuromuscular blockade above ~2 mmol/L, coma and hyporeflexia above ~4 mmol/L, and asystole near 10 mmol/L.

hypocellular marrow with <25% hematopoietic cells supports aplastic anemia Peripheral smear and reticulocyte count (look for absent reticulocytes, large red cells, immature myeloid forms or nucleated red cells suggesting MDS/myelophthisis) Flow cytometry for a PNH clone Chromosome breakage testing with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C for Fanconi anemia (children and younger adults) Peripheral blood leukocyte telomere length measurement for telomere biology disorders Bone marrow cytogenetics and FISH (abnormal in MDS, expected normal in typical aplastic anemia) Next-generation sequencing germline panels (50+ genes) for constitutional syndromes and myeloid neoplasm somatic panels (~100 genes) for MDS/AML, including spliceosome and cohesin genes Serologies for EBV, HIV and viral hepatitis Vitamin B12, folate and serum copper levels Spinal MRI may demonstrate fatty marrow replacement in aplastic anemia Parvovirus B19 DNA detection in suspected PRCA Chest imaging to seek thymoma in PRCA and to exclude miliary tuberculosis Megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency Copper deficiency (and zinc or alcohol toxicity) causing dysplastic marrow with vacuolated precursors Alcohol-related marrow suppression Hypersplenism / splenomegaly of cirrhosis Metastatic carcinoma infiltrating marrow Anorexia nervosa or starvation Sarcoidosis Drug-induced cytopenias (idiosyncratic reactions and chemotherapy) Marrow failure cytopenias reflect deficient production, distinguishing them from peripheral destruction (hemolysis, ITP, immune leukopenia, hypersplenism); the syndromes are categorized by the dominant marrow morphology, with aplastic anemia (fatty/empty marrow), MDS (dysplastic marrow), and single-lineage aplasias forming a related spectrum. Immune (acquired) aplastic anemia is classically a young person's disease with abrupt pancytopenia in a previously well adolescent or young adult; the age distribution is biphasic with peaks in the teens-twenties and again in older adults. In aplastic anemia bleeding (bruising, gum oozing, epistaxis, menorrhagia, petechiae) is typically the earliest symptom, whereas infection as a first symptom is unusual; lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are highly atypical and should prompt search for another cause of pancytopenia. Clues to an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome: short stature and cafe au lait spots with thumb/radial anomalies (Fanconi anemia); dystrophic nails, mucosal leukoplakia and reticular hyperpigmentation (dyskeratosis congenita); premature hair graying plus a family history of pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis (telomere biology disorders); recurrent warts and unusual infections (GATA2 deficiency). A detectable PNH clone by flow cytometry is found in up to half of patients at presentation of aplastic anemia and strongly suggests immune-mediated pathophysiology and likely responsiveness to immunosuppression; patients can later cross over between aplastic and hemolytic PNH phenotypes. MDS is predominantly a disease of older adults (mean onset over 70) with a slight male predominance; anemia (often macrocytic) dominates the early course and at least half of patients are asymptomatic, discovered incidentally on routine blood counts. Persistent parvovirus B19 infection is a treatable cause of pure red cell aplasia; the marrow shows giant pronormoblasts (the cytopathic signature), and diagnosis requires detection of viral DNA because IgG/IgM antibodies are commonly absent in immunodeficient hosts. B19 parvovirus uses the erythrocyte P antigen as its receptor; in patients with underlying hemolysis it can precipitate a transient aplastic crisis with abrupt worsening of anemia from arrested erythropoiesis. Macrocytosis (elevated MCV) is a frequent finding across marrow failure states; in aplastic anemia the smear shows large red cells with a paucity of platelets and granulocytes, near-absent reticulocytes, and the elevated MCV often persists even after recovery. Marrow blast percentage is the strongest morphologic prognostic determinant in MDS; the WHO threshold of 20% marrow blasts separates AML from MDS, and blasts should be enumerated manually on smear and by flow cytometry. 5q deletion MDS arises from heterozygous loss of a ribosomal protein gene, effectively mimicking constitutional red cell aplasia; SF3B1 mutation is strongly associated with ring sideroblasts and a relatively favorable outcome. Severity grading in aplastic anemia and recovery thresholds are defined by blood counts (see severity criteria); absolute reticulocyte and lymphocyte numbers are better predictors of treatment response than the classic severity definition in the immunosuppression era. Profound neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count <500/uL) with fever mandates urgent empirical broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics without awaiting cultures Persistent or recrudescent fever despite antibacterials implies invasive fungal disease (Candida, Aspergillus) Severe thrombocytopenia with central nervous system or retinal bleeding can be catastrophic (intracranial or retinal hemorrhage) Platelet count below 5000/uL sharply increases risk of gut bleeding Systemic symptoms, weight loss, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly point away from simple aplastic anemia toward malignancy or systemic disease Emergence of new cytogenetic abnormalities, rising blasts, marrow fibrosis or abrupt worsening of pancytopenia signals clonal evolution to MDS/leukemia Family history of AML/MDS or unexplained cytopenias should trigger evaluation for an inherited predisposition syndrome Clinical drug/chemical and viral associations with aplastic anemia are not proof of causation; the implicated agent may merely have been used to treat the earliest symptoms (antibiotics for fever, NSAIDs causing petechiae in an already thrombocytopenic patient). Marrow cellularity correlates imperfectly with disease severity: 'empty' biopsies can occur in moderate disease and focal 'hot spots' of hematopoiesis can be seen in severe aplasia, so a single small or dilute sample can mislead (a dry tap suggests fibrosis or myelophthisis rather than aplasia). Distinguishing acquired from constitutional aplastic anemia is essential; constitutional marrow is usually morphologically indistinguishable and physical anomalies may be subtle or absent (adults with telomere disorders can present without anomalies, only premature graying). Hypocellular MDS can be mistaken for aplastic anemia; the boundary with low-risk MDS is blurred (del 13q/20q may respond to immunosuppression, and DNMT3A/ASXL1 mutations occur in both). Dysplastic marrow changes are not specific to MDS, occurring with vitamin deficiencies, copper deficiency, drug effects, alcohol and acute viral infection; interobserver agreement on dysplasia morphology is imperfect. Germline genomic panel results may take weeks to return, a problem in the severely pancytopenic patient who needs prompt management. In transplant-eligible aplastic anemia patients, transfusing blood from family members risks alloimmunization and should be avoided; HLA typing should be ordered as soon as the diagnosis is made. Glucocorticoids are not effective primary therapy for aplastic anemia and increase fungal infection risk. Bone marrow failure results from severe damage to the hematopoietic cell compartment. In aplastic anemia the marrow is replaced by fat, CD34+ early hematopoietic cells are greatly diminished, and the stem cell pool in severe disease may be reduced to about 1% or less of normal. Three principal mechanisms underlie an empty marrow: physical/chemical damage (high-dose radiation, benzene and its reactive hydroquinone/quinolone metabolites, cytotoxic chemotherapy), immune-mediated stem cell destruction, and constitutional genetic defects. Acquired aplastic anemia is most often immune: activated cytotoxic T cells suppress hematopoietic progenitors, type 1 cytokines including interferon-gamma upregulate Fas on CD34+ cells driving apoptosis, and immune selection can produce HLA-loss and PNH clones. Genetically determined immune-response features (HLA, cytokine and T-cell polarization gene polymorphisms) likely convert a normal response into sustained autoimmunity, explaining why aplasia is rare despite common exposures. Idiosyncratic drug-induced aplasia is attributed to abnormal generation of or failure to detoxify reactive electrophilic drug intermediates that bind cellular macromolecules. Constitutional syndromes are intrinsic stem cell defects: Fanconi anemia involves a DNA interstrand cross-link repair pathway (most often FANCA; the gene products monoubiquitinate FANCD2), telomere biology disorders involve telomerase complex (DKC1, TERC, TERT) or shelterin (TINF2) defects that limit replicative capacity, and GATA2/RUNX1 mutations disrupt hematopoietic transcriptional regulation; Diamond-Blackfan and Shwachman-Diamond syndromes are ribosomopathies. MDS is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder of aging marrow characterized by disordered proliferation, impaired differentiation and ineffective hematopoiesis producing cytopenias plus risk of leukemic progression; both chromosomal instability (non-random losses of 5, 7, 20, trisomy 8) and accumulating somatic mutations in ~100 recurrently mutated myeloid genes drive disease, with clonal succession of founder clones acquiring further mutations during evolution to AML. Untreated severe aplastic anemia deteriorates rapidly and is fatal; spontaneous recovery is rare. The dominant prognostic factor is the blood count: severe disease has historically required two of three of an absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelets <20,000/uL and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocytes <60,000/uL), while in the immunosuppression era higher absolute reticulocytes (>25,000/uL) and lymphocytes (>1000/uL) better predict response and survival. A PNH clone, very short telomeres and somatic myeloid mutations (e.g., ASXL1) further influence outcome and risk of clonal evolution. Clonal evolution to MDS or leukemia occurs in roughly 10-15% of immunosuppression-treated patients over a decade. In MDS, median survival ranges from years (5q- or sideroblastic anemia) to only months (high blast count disease); the IPSS-R and emerging molecularly informed IPSS-M stratify risk. Even lower-risk MDS carries meaningful morbidity and mortality; most patients die of complications of pancytopenia rather than leukemic transformation, and about a third die of unrelated comorbidities. Therapy-related MDS has an extremely poor prognosis with rapid progression to refractory AML. Pure red cell aplasia is generally compatible with long-term survival with supportive care, and persistent parvovirus B19 PRCA almost always responds to immunoglobulin. Severe aplastic anemia has historically been defined by the presence of at least two of three criteria: absolute neutrophil count <500/uL, platelet count <20,000/uL, and corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocyte count <60,000/uL). In the immunosuppressive-therapy era, absolute reticulocyte count >25,000/uL and absolute lymphocyte count >1000/uL are better predictors of response and long-term outcome. For MDS, prognostic severity is assessed by the Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R), which integrates marrow blast percentage (categories at <=2%, >2-<5%, 5-10%, >10-30%), refined cytogenetic risk groups, depth of cytopenias (hemoglobin, platelets, neutrophils), and additional features (age, performance status, ferritin, LDH, beta-2-microglobulin) into five risk categories; the molecularly enhanced IPSS-M is emerging as the current standard.

Post-traumatic stress disorder and complex trauma presentations Other personality disorders such as histrionic or narcissistic Substance use disorders causing affective and behavioural instability Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder with impulsivity Longitudinal history and collateral information to establish the enduring pattern Structured suicide and self-harm risk assessment with a crisis plan Screening for comorbid mood, anxiety, eating, and substance use disorders Trauma history taken sensitively Standardised personality assessment tools where appropriate The disorder is a pervasive pattern of instability in relationships, self-image, and affect, together with marked impulsivity, beginning by early adulthood and evident across contexts Characteristic features include frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, intense and unstable relationships that swing between idealisation and devaluation, identity disturbance, and chronic feelings of emptiness Recurrent self-harm and suicidal behaviour, affective instability, transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation, and difficulty controlling anger are common and clinically important Self-harm and suicide attempts are frequent, so ongoing risk assessment and a clear crisis plan are essential parts of care Structured evidence-based psychotherapies, such as dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based treatment, are the mainstay of management Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive and targets specific symptoms or comorbidities rather than the disorder itself, and polypharmacy should be avoided A consistent, validating, and boundaried therapeutic stance reduces crises and helps prevent unhelpful splitting among care providers Comorbid mood, anxiety, eating, and substance use disorders are common and should be identified and treated Acute suicidal ideation, escalating self-harm, or a recent attempt Rapid escalation of impulsive behaviour placing the patient at serious risk Emergence of psychotic-level symptoms beyond transient stress-related phenomena Severe comorbid substance misuse increasing danger during crises Reacting to crises with escalating polypharmacy rather than psychotherapy and structure Dismissing chronic suicidality and thereby missing genuine acute risk Allowing splitting to divide the treating team through inconsistent boundaries Misdiagnosing affective instability as bipolar disorder Overlooking comorbid trauma and substance use disorders Borderline personality disorder is understood through a biosocial model in which a heritable predisposition to emotional vulnerability and impulsivity interacts with an invalidating or traumatic developmental environment. Neurobiological findings include altered function of limbic structures such as the amygdala and of prefrontal regulatory regions, contributing to heightened emotional reactivity and impaired regulation, with disturbances in serotonergic and stress-response systems. Contrary to older pessimistic views, many patients with borderline personality disorder show substantial improvement over time, with reduced impulsivity and self-harm and often remission of full criteria, though interpersonal and functional difficulties can persist. Prognosis is better with engagement in structured psychotherapy and stable support, and worse with severe early trauma, persistent substance misuse, and repeated high-lethality self-harm.

Botulism — Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) Myasthenia gravis Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome Tick paralysis Basilar stroke producing nonlateralizing/symmetric bulbar palsies Tetrodotoxin or shellfish poisoning Antimicrobial-associated paralysis Guillain-Barre syndrome following Campylobacter jejuni or viral infection Detailed neurologic examination (the key to clinical diagnosis, uncovering invariable cranial nerve deficits) Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis (protein usually normal in botulism, in contrast to GBS; may help distinguish) Electromyography by an experienced operator (neuromuscular junction blockage with normal axonal conduction and potentiation on rapid repetitive stimulation) Brain imaging (normal in botulism; helps exclude basilar stroke) Serologic antibody tests and rapid nerve stimulation tests (to evaluate myasthenia gravis) Mouse bioassay (gold standard for BoNT identification and serotyping in clinical or food specimens) Detection of BoNT in serum or stool, or isolation of BoNT-producing Clostridium from stool or wound cultures; toxin in suspected food In vitro assays: real-time PCR for bont genes, Endopep mass spectrometry, immune-based and cell-based assays Myasthenia gravis Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (proximal limb weakness, often with advanced cancer) Tick paralysis Basilar stroke Intoxication from alcohol or other substances (ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can be misattributed) Classic syndrome: bilateral cranial nerve palsies followed by symmetric, descending flaccid paralysis, in a patient who is afebrile and fully conscious with normal sensorium (Harrison 22e p.1235). First neurologic manifestation is usually ptosis, which can be striking; ocular findings include blurred/fuzzy vision or diplopia from extraocular palsies of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI (Harrison 22e p.1235). Bulbar onset: dysarthria, difficulty swallowing, and nasal/oral regurgitation reflect cranial nerve involvement; descending weakness then spreads to neck, shoulders, and limbs, with proximal groups affected before distal (Harrison 22e p.1235). Paralysis descends symmetrically and distal tendon reflexes diminish symmetrically; constipation from intestinal paralysis develops in almost all patients (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236). In a U.S. series of 332 cases, the most common reported symptoms were difficulty swallowing (86%), fatigue (85%), blurred vision (80%), and slurred speech (78%); signs included afebrile temperature (99%), descending paralysis (93%), alert/oriented status (93%), and ptosis (81%) (Harrison 22e p.1236). BoNTs irreversibly block acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, so paralysis persists for weeks to months until nerve endings regenerate; the clinical approach is the same for all toxin types causing human illness (Harrison 22e p.1234, p.1236). Four naturally occurring forms (foodborne, infant, wound, adult intestinal colonization) plus iatrogenic and inhalational forms; the neurologic syndrome is essentially identical across all forms and all ages (Harrison 22e p.1233-1235). Every case of foodborne botulism is a public health emergency, as it may be the first in an outbreak; clinicians should contact the state health department emergency line to reach a CDC botulism consultant (Harrison 22e p.1235, p.1237). More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the U.S. recover, and the infant botulism survival rate is near 100% (Harrison 22e p.1236). Pharyngeal muscle flaccidity causing airway collapse and respiratory arrest early in the course Falling vital capacity / diaphragmatic and accessory muscle weakness signaling impending respiratory failure Rapidly progressive descending paralysis (especially BoNT type A or F) A placid, expressionless appearance masking the agitation expected with respiratory distress Autonomic dysfunction producing hemodynamic instability Two or more patients with the same syndrome (near-pathognomonic and signals an outbreak / public health emergency) Misclassifying the paralysis as ascending: botulism is a DESCENDING (cranial-first, then downward) symmetric flaccid paralysis, whereas GBS presents as an ASCENDING paralysis in about 95% of cases - this descending-versus-ascending distinction is central, though the Miller Fisher GBS variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia) may resemble early descending paralysis (Harrison 22e p.1236). Mistaking intact sensorium for altered consciousness: cranial nerve palsies, ptosis, dysarthria, and gait instability can give a false impression of obtundation or be wrongly attributed to alcohol/substance intoxication, even though patients remain fully conscious (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236). Sporadic (lone) cases are commonly misdiagnosed because of the rarity of botulism and clinician unfamiliarity; an incomplete neurologic examination is a frequent cause of delayed or missed diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1236). Waiting for laboratory confirmation: confirmation may take >=24 h, so treatment must rely on rapid clinical diagnosis rather than awaiting lab results (Harrison 22e p.1236-1237). Assuming normal CSF excludes GBS too early: in GBS, CSF protein elevation may lag symptom onset by days, so a normal early CSF must be interpreted with symptom duration and the lumbar puncture may need repeating (Harrison 22e p.1236). Reported paresthesias are not explained by the known activity of botulinum toxin, and GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting) are seen in foodborne but have NOT been reported in wound botulism (Harrison 22e p.1235-1236). Disease is caused by botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs) produced by Clostridium botulinum (rarely C. butyricum or C. baratii), gram-positive, spore-forming, anaerobic bacteria whose heat-resistant spores are ubiquitous in soil. Serotypes A, B, E, and F cause human disease. BoNT is a metalloprotease whose heavy chain mediates neurospecific binding and internalization and whose light chain enters the cytosol and cleaves SNARE-family proteins (e.g., SNAP-25, VAMP), disrupting synaptic vesicle fusion and blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles. Toxin binding is effectively irreversible, so recovery requires regeneration of nerve endings over weeks to months. Routes differ by form: foodborne (ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly preserved foods, often home-canned low-acid vegetables), wound (spore germination in wounds/necrotic tissue, notably from black tar heroin injection), infant and adult intestinal colonization (in situ toxin production by colonizing Clostridium), iatrogenic (high-dose therapeutic BoNT injection), and inhalational (aerosolized toxin as a bioweapon). (Harrison 22e p.1233-1234) More than 95% of noninfant botulism patients in the United States recover, often after protracted intensive care and rehabilitation, even without antitoxin; the survival rate for infant botulism is near 100%. Paralysis lasts weeks to months while affected nerve endings regenerate. Serotype A is associated with more rapid progression, more frequent respiratory compromise and mechanical ventilation, and longer-duration paralysis; type B is milder and shorter; type F progresses rapidly but recovers faster. Untreated, early death results from airway obstruction and inadequate tidal volume from respiratory muscle paralysis. (Harrison 22e p.1236) Harrison does not provide a formal numeric severity score; severity is described as varying greatly between patients and is probably governed by toxin dose. At the mild end, some untreated patients progress no further than ptosis and mild palsy of one or two cranial nerves; at the severe end, others develop fulminant cranial nerve palsies and rapidly progressive descending flaccid paralysis affecting most or all voluntary muscles with respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation within hours. (Harrison 22e p.1236)

Bowel obstruction — Erect/supine abdominal X-ray or CT NG decompression Surgical review Strangulation / perforation → emergency surgery Adynamic / paralytic ileus (loss of peristalsis with absent bowel sounds) rather than mechanical obstruction Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) — colonic dilatation without a mechanical lesion Severe constipation / fecal impaction causing abdominal distension and discomfort Sigmoid or cecal volvulus as a cause of colonic obstruction Gastric outlet obstruction (malignancy or chronic peptic stenosis of the pylorus) presenting with vomiting of partially digested food hours after eating Esophageal obstruction by impacted food bolus / foreign body (proximal obstruction mimic) Low-dose CT is preferred over plain abdominal radiography when the indication for surgical/medical intervention is unclear in nontraumatic acute abdominal pain Plain upright/lateral-decubitus abdominal radiographs can show dilated bowel loops suggesting obstruction or ileus, but have limited utility and may be unnecessary when the cause (e.g., strangulated external hernia) is already evident Water-soluble contrast enema can be diagnostic in suspected colonic obstruction without perforation; oral barium sulfate should be avoided if colonic obstruction is suspected Serum amylase may be raised by strangulating intestinal obstruction (also by perforated ulcer, cholecystitis), so an elevation neither confirms nor excludes the need for operation Leukocytosis is non-specific (a WBC >20,000/uL may follow perforation but also pancreatitis, cholecystitis, infarction) and should never be the sole determinant of operative need; a normal count does not exclude perforation Endoscopy can diagnose and often manage gastroduodenal and colonic obstruction/pseudo-obstruction, but small-bowel obstruction from surgical adhesions is generally neither diagnosed nor treated endoscopically Acute mesenteric arterial occlusion — early diffuse cramping pain from hyperperistalsis with 'pain out of proportion to physical findings' can mimic early obstruction; tenderness and rigidity may be absent until vascular collapse Porphyria and lead colic — severe hyperperistalsis makes the pain difficult to distinguish from intestinal obstruction Diabetic ketoacidosis — can both precipitate and mimic an acute abdomen; if pain does not resolve with metabolic correction, suspect an organic cause such as obstruction Irritable bowel syndrome — functional pain with altered bowel habit, but nausea/vomiting are rare and localized tenderness/spasm inconsistent (a non-obstructive mimic of altered bowel habit) Small-bowel obstruction characteristically produces poorly localized, intermittent peri-/supra-umbilical colicky pain; as the bowel progressively dilates and loses muscular tone the colicky quality of the pain may actually diminish, which can be falsely reassuring (p.110). Colonic obstruction tends to cause lower-intensity colicky pain located in the infraumbilical area, often radiating to the lumbar region, in contrast to the more periumbilical pain of small-bowel obstruction (p.110). High-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds are characteristic of mechanical obstruction, whereas loss of bowel sounds points toward ileus; however, once proximal bowel becomes markedly distended and edematous, peristaltic sounds may become weak or absent even without peritonitis. Auscultation is one of the least revealing parts of the abdominal exam: a strangulating small-intestinal obstruction can occur with normal-sounding peristalsis, so normal bowel sounds do not exclude a catastrophe (p.113). Patients with obstructive colic tend to be restless and may thrash about, in contrast to the peritonitic patient who lies still to avoid movement — a useful bedside discriminator when ischaemia/perforation supervenes (p.110). Inability to pass stool or flatus combined with nausea/vomiting and increasing abdominal girth suggests bowel obstruction (or severe constipation/ileus); retained feces in the colon itself adds to the distension (p.327). Continuous diffuse pain with absent tenderness/rigidity ('pain out of proportion to findings') in a patient at vascular risk — suspect superior mesenteric artery occlusion / intestinal ischaemia Spread of pain to the lower lumbar region — may indicate strangulating obstruction with traction on the mesenteric root Truly silent abdomen with sudden severe pain — suggests chemical peritonitis from a perforated viscus Catastrophic intra-abdominal events may present with minimal or no pain/muscle spasm in obtunded, debilitated, immunosuppressed, or elderly patients — a slowly developing process also attenuates guarding Relying on auscultation or bowel-sound quality: strangulating obstruction can occur with normal peristaltic sounds, and distended/edematous proximal bowel may be quiet even without peritonitis (p.113). Interpreting waning colicky pain as improvement — pain may diminish simply because the dilated bowel has lost muscular tone (p.110). Using leukocytosis or serum amylase as a deciding factor for surgery — both are non-specific in obstruction and infarction (p.113). Giving oral barium when colonic obstruction is possible (risk of inspissation above the obstruction); use water-soluble contrast instead. Missing intestinal ischaemia, which classically elicits severe pain but little tenderness (GI evaluation chapter). Mechanical obstruction of a hollow viscus classically elicits intermittent (colicky) pain that is less well localized than the parietal pain of peritoneal irritation; distension of the viscus may also produce steady pain with only occasional paroxysms. With superimposed strangulating obstruction, traction on the root of the mesentery can refer pain to the lower lumbar region. As the obstructed proximal bowel progressively dilates it loses muscular tone, so colicky pain may wane and peristaltic sounds may weaken. Obstruction must be distinguished from adynamic ileus (loss of peristalsis) and from colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), in which the bowel is dilated without a mechanical lesion (Harrison 22e pp.110-113, p.327).

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — BPPV, positional vertigo, benign positional vertigo Vestibular neuritis Meniere's disease Central positional vertigo from posterior fossa pathology Vestibular migraine Orthostatic hypotension Perilymph fistula Dix-Hallpike test for posterior canal involvement Supine roll (head-turn) test for suspected horizontal canal disease Otoscopy and hearing assessment to exclude other otological causes Neurological examination to exclude central causes Imaging of the brain and posterior fossa only if central pathology is suspected The most common cause of peripheral vertigo, characterised by brief spinning episodes triggered by changes in head position Typical triggers include rolling over in bed, lying down, looking up or bending forward Each episode is short-lived, usually lasting seconds to under a minute, and there is no associated hearing loss or tinnitus The posterior semicircular canal is most often involved because of its dependent position The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces symptoms and elicits characteristic positional nystagmus with a brief latency and fatigability Management principles rely on canalith repositioning manoeuvres such as the Epley manoeuvre rather than long-term drug therapy Vestibular sedatives are generally unhelpful and may hinder central compensation if used long term Recurrences are common but usually respond again to repositioning; atypical or persistent features should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis Atypical nystagmus that is purely vertical, direction-changing or non-fatiguing suggesting a central cause Associated neurological signs, severe headache or gait ataxia Accompanying hearing loss or tinnitus pointing to alternative inner ear disease Persistent continuous vertigo rather than brief positional episodes Mistaking central positional vertigo for BPPV and missing serious pathology Relying on vestibular suppressant drugs instead of repositioning manoeuvres Failing to identify the affected canal, leading to ineffective treatment Overlooking coexisting hearing loss that indicates a different diagnosis Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by displacement of otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) from the utricular macula into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal. In the common canalithiasis form, these free-floating particles move under gravity when the head changes position, creating abnormal endolymph flow that deflects the cupula and generates a transient, mismatched sensation of rotation. The brief latency, short duration and fatigability of symptoms reflect the settling of the particles. A less common cupulolithiasis form, with particles adherent to the cupula, produces more persistent positional nystagmus. The condition is benign and often self-limiting, with excellent response to repositioning manoeuvres, although recurrences over time are common and occasionally require repeat treatment.

Brachial neuritis — neuralgic amyotrophy, Parsonage-Turner syndrome, idiopathic brachial plexopathy, acute brachial plexus neuropathy Cervical radiculopathy from disc or spondylosis Rotator cuff disease or other primary shoulder pathology Compressive or traumatic brachial plexopathy Neoplastic or radiation-induced plexopathy Thoracic outlet syndrome Mononeuritis multiplex from vasculitis
