structural lesions Cervical spine MRI when radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis Basic inflammatory and infective screen when a systemic cause is suspected Consideration of genetic testing (SEPT9) in recurrent or familial cases Characterised by abrupt, severe pain around the shoulder and upper arm, followed within days to weeks by patchy weakness and wasting as the pain subsides The distribution is often patchy and does not conform to a single nerve or root, reflecting involvement of individual nerves or plexus branches The long thoracic nerve is frequently affected, producing scapular winging, and the anterior interosseous and suprascapular nerves are also commonly involved Often follows an antecedent trigger such as infection, immunisation, surgery, or physical stress Sensory symptoms are usually less prominent than the motor deficit and the early pain A hereditary recurrent form exists (linked to SEPT9), so a family history and recurrent episodes should be explored Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by electromyography showing multifocal denervation, with imaging used to exclude structural or compressive lesions Management is mainly supportive with analgesia and physiotherapy, as most patients recover over months Progressive or non-resolving deficit suggesting a compressive, neoplastic, or infiltrative plexopathy A history of cancer or radiotherapy raising concern for malignant or radiation plexopathy Bilateral or systemic features suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as vasculitis Rapidly worsening weakness that warrants urgent structural imaging Mistaking the initial severe pain for a primary shoulder or rotator cuff problem and delaying diagnosis Confusing it with cervical radiculopathy because both cause arm pain and weakness Overlooking scapular winging from long thoracic nerve involvement Failing to consider a hereditary recurrent form in patients with repeated attacks Assuming a compressive lesion and pursuing unnecessary surgery in a self-limiting inflammatory condition Brachial neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) is thought to be an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the brachial plexus and its branches, often triggered by antecedent infection, vaccination, surgery, or other immunological stressors. Inflammation causes multifocal axonal damage to individual nerves or fascicles, sometimes with focal nerve constrictions or torsions demonstrable on high-resolution imaging. The predominantly axonal injury explains the muscle wasting and the protracted recovery as reinnervation occurs. A hereditary form associated with SEPT9 mutations produces recurrent attacks. Most patients recover useful function over many months to a few years, though recovery can be incomplete with residual weakness or scapular winging, and the hereditary form tends to recur.

HV interval for His-Purkinje ≤55 ms) reserved for selected/uncertain cases; SNRT/SACT rarely used and NOT an absolute pacing indication Drug/medication effect (beta blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone and other antiarrhythmics, clonidine, lithium, etc.) Hypothyroidism and other endocrine disease Hyperkalemia/electrolyte disturbance Increased vagal tone (sleep, well-conditioned athlete, cough/micturition/vasovagal, carotid sinus hypersensitivity) Sleep apnea (high vagal tone during apneic events) Hypothermia, hypoxia, raised intracranial pressure Infiltrative cardiomyopathy (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis) Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy, Kearns-Sayre, Lamin A/C cardiomyopathy) Iatrogenic: cardiac/valve surgery, TAVR, alcohol septal ablation, catheter ablation injury, spinal cord injury, post heart transplant Sinus node dysfunction (SND), also termed sick sinus syndrome, typically presents with fatigue, exercise intolerance, dyspnea, or syncope from a slow rate or pauses; the key diagnostic step is correlating symptoms with bradycardia/pauses on ECG or ambulatory monitoring (p.1917-1918). Tachycardia-bradycardia (tachy-brady) syndrome is a subset of SND: high rates (most commonly atrial fibrillation) alternating with symptomatic bradycardia or offset pauses after the tachycardia terminates; the drugs needed for rate control often worsen the bradycardia, frequently prompting pacemaker implantation (p.1919). AV block is classified on ECG: first-degree = fixed PR prolongation >200 ms with all impulses conducted; second-degree = intermittent failure of conduction (Mobitz I/Wenckebach with progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat vs Mobitz II with fixed PR before a dropped beat); third-degree = complete AV dissociation with ventricular rate slower than atrial rate (p.1925-1926). Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block typically involves the AV node, is hemodynamically stable, and in the absence of symptoms does NOT usually warrant pacing; Mobitz II is usually infranodal, associated with QRS widening and a less reliable escape rhythm, carries a risk of sudden death, and requires permanent pacing even when asymptomatic (p.1925). Escape morphology localizes block: a narrow QRS escape implies AV-nodal/proximal-His block with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape implies distal His or bundle-branch block with a slower, less reliable rhythm (p.1926). AV block from acute MI is more common with inferior MI but is usually proximal (AV node), with a stable narrow escape >40/min and often reversible; AV block in anterior MI is usually distal/infranodal, gives wide unstable escape rhythms, and carries a worse prognosis with high mortality (p.1926-1927). Lyme carditis is a classic reversible infectious cause of AV block (usually nodal, narrow junctional escape >40/min) that typically resolves within about a week of antibiotic therapy; AV block with infective endocarditis should raise concern for a perivalvular abscess requiring urgent surgical consultation (p.1927). AV block that develops at a younger age (≤60 years) warrants advanced imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, or FDG-PET) to evaluate for infiltrative disease such as sarcoidosis, since age-related progressive conduction-system fibrosis is otherwise the most common cause (p.1928). Permanent pacing is the only reliable long-term therapy for symptomatic irreversible bradycardia; there is NO established heart-rate threshold below which pacing is automatically indicated, and the decision is driven by symptom-bradycardia correlation (p.1917, p.1922). Initial management of any bradyarrhythmia is to identify and eliminate reversible causes and assess the safety/reliability of the escape rhythm before deciding on temporary or permanent pacing (p.1922, p.1929). Missing reversible causes (drugs, hypothyroidism, hyperkalemia/electrolytes, ischemia, sleep apnea, increased vagal tone, hypothermia, raised ICP) before committing to permanent pacing. Overlooking Lyme carditis as a reversible cause of AV block (typically resolves within ~1 week of antibiotics) - a treatable cause that should not lead to an unnecessary permanent pacemaker. Failing to suspect a perivalvular abscess when AV block develops during infective endocarditis. Treating Mobitz II or high-grade/complete infranodal block as benign - it requires pacing even without symptoms, unlike Mobitz I. In 2:1 AV block, ECG cannot reliably distinguish Mobitz I from Mobitz II; clues (PR <160 ms with wide QRS suggesting infranodal) or EP study may be needed. Missing chronotropic incompetence because a patient achieves a normal maximum heart rate on standard exercise testing despite inadequate rate during daily activity. Misjudging a normal heart-transplant resting rate (~90-110/min due to denervation) as normal when it may represent chronotropic incompetence. Bradyarrhythmias arise from abnormalities of the specialized conduction tissues. The sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker (resting rate 60-100/min); its pacemaker cells have no true resting potential and depolarize spontaneously in phase 4 driven by the funny current (If) plus T- and L-type calcium currents, with calcium (not sodium) carrying the slow phase-0 upstroke. SA node function is dominated by parasympathetic tone at baseline (intrinsic heart rate ~100-110/min after autonomic blockade); intrinsic rate declines ~5-6 beats/min per decade of age. SA node dysfunction reflects problems of impulse formation (sinus arrest) or impulse conduction (sinoatrial exit block), and is most often due to age-related fibrosis and loss of pacemaker myocytes. In the AV node, conduction is decremental and depends on L-type calcium current; the node and proximal His are richly innervated by autonomic input, whereas the His bundle and distal conduction system are NOT influenced by autonomic tone. Acquired AV conduction disease is most commonly due to fibrosis/sclerosis/calcification of the conduction system (~50% of cases: senile degeneration/Lev's disease, Lenegre's disease, aortic-annular calcification). Block is anatomically nodal (vagally modulated, stable narrow escape) or infranodal (His-Purkinje, unstable wide escape, higher risk). Asymptomatic sinus bradycardia has NOT been associated with adverse outcomes and generally does not warrant pacing; symptomatic SND is benign in terms of mortality and is treated to relieve symptoms. AV block prognosis depends critically on the level of block: AV-nodal (Mobitz I) block tends to be stable with a reliable junctional escape and good prognosis, whereas infranodal block (Mobitz II, distal third-degree) has unreliable escape rhythms and risk of sudden death. AV block complicating anterior MI carries high mortality, while inferior-MI nodal block is often transient and reversible. With appropriate permanent pacing, symptomatic bradyarrhythmias have an excellent prognosis. An HV interval >100 ms predicts ~10% annual progression to complete block. ECG-based AV block grading: First-degree (PR >200 ms, all impulses conducted, usually AV-nodal delay) -> Second-degree (intermittent failure; Mobitz I/Wenckebach = progressive PR prolongation before dropped beat, usually nodal/stable; Mobitz II = fixed PR before dropped beat, usually infranodal/wide QRS/unstable) -> Third-degree/complete (complete AV dissociation, ventricular rate slower than atrial). SND subtypes: sinus arrest, sinoatrial exit block (type I, type II Mobitz I/II), tachy-brady syndrome, chronotropic incompetence. Pacing-indication classes (ACC/AHA/HRS): Class I (complete/high-grade or acquired Mobitz II block when irreversible - pace regardless of symptoms; symptomatic irreversible 2nd/3rd-degree block), Class IIa/IIb (symptom- or disease-dependent for milder block), Class III: Harm (asymptomatic physiologic bradycardia/pauses).

Brain tumour / mass lesion — MRI brain with contrast Refer neuro-oncology Progressive headache, morning vomiting, papilloedema Metastatic brain tumour - three times more common than all primary brain tumours combined in adults; commonest sources lung and breast, with melanoma having the greatest propensity to metastasize to brain (p.716, p.723) Diffuse glioma - the most common malignant PRIMARY brain tumour; subdivided into IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and IDH wild-type glioblastoma (p.717-718) Meningioma - now the most common primary brain tumour overall (~35%); extra-axial dural-based lesion, WHO grades I-III (p.720-721) Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) - ~9% of primary brain tumours, presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus/dizziness (p.721) Primary CNS lymphoma - densely enhancing, often periventricular/basal ganglia/corpus callosum; associated with immunosuppression and EBV in HIV (p.720) Pituitary adenoma - amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea with headache suggests a prolactinoma (p.157, p.721) Pineal-region tumour presenting with Parinaud's syndrome and hydrocephalus (p.720) Colloid cyst of the third ventricle - intermittent hydrocephalus, rarely sudden death (p.722) Brain abscess - shares a ring-enhancing radiographic appearance with metastasis and high-grade glioma (p.723) Cerebral toxoplasmosis - in immunocompromised patients, multiple ring-enhancing lesions can be hard to distinguish from PCNSL or metastases (p.721) MRI with gadolinium is the preferred test; CT only if MRI cannot be done (p.716) Neuroimaging is often the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumour; laboratory tests are rarely useful (p.716) FLAIR sequences to detect non-enhancing low-grade gliomas (p.716, p.718) Functional MRI for presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex (p.716) PET, MR perfusion and MR spectroscopy to assess metabolic activity and help separate tumour progression from radiation/treatment necrosis (p.716) CSF cytology / flow cytometry when leptomeningeal involvement is suspected (gold standard but positive in only ~50% on first LP, still misses ~10% after three samples) (p.720, p.724) Stereotactic biopsy for histologic diagnosis when imaging is insufficient; in suspected PCNSL withhold glucocorticoids until biopsy because they are cytolytic and can render tissue non-diagnostic (p.720) HIV testing and body PET/CT, spine MRI, CSF and slit-lamp eye exam to stage suspected PCNSL (p.720-721) Serum tumour markers (e.g. beta-hCG) occasionally elevated in metastatic disease (p.716) Demyelinating lesion - can mimic the nonspecific appearance of a brain metastasis (p.723) Neurosarcoidosis - listed among lesions resembling metastatic disease on imaging (p.723) Radiation necrosis in a previously irradiated patient - mimics tumour and may need PET/MR perfusion to distinguish recurrence from treatment effect (p.716, p.723) Presenting features split into general (raised-ICP) symptoms - headache +/- nausea/vomiting, cognitive change, personality change, gait disorder - and focal/lateralizing signs such as hemiparesis, aphasia or visual field loss; many patients have both (p.716). The classic morning-predominant headache that eases through the day occurs in only a minority of patients; brain-tumour headache is more often a nondescript dull ache, and migraine produces this pattern far more often than tumour (p.716, p.157). Vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumours, and headache disturbs sleep in about 10% (p.157). Seizures from a brain tumour always have a focal onset whether or not this is clinically apparent (p.716). New de novo headache in a patient with known malignancy should raise suspicion of cerebral metastases or carcinomatous (leptomeningeal) meningitis (p.157). On MRI, malignant tumours (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, have central necrosis and surrounding white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen as increased signal on FLAIR (p.716). Meningiomas and vestibular schwannomas are extra-axial, densely enhancing lesions; a meningioma characteristically shows a dural tail and compresses but does not invade brain (p.716, p.721). Leptomeningeal disease produces multilevel neuraxis signs (radiculopathies, cranial neuropathies, seizures, confusion, raised-ICP encephalopathy); isolated focal deficits like hemiparesis are rarely from it unless brain is directly infiltrated (p.724). Parinaud's syndrome (impaired upgaze and accommodation) points to a pineal-region mass (p.720). Progressive, subacute focal/lateralizing deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field loss) (p.716) New-onset focal-onset seizures (p.716) Morning-predominant headache or headache with raised-ICP features (nausea/vomiting, worse with exertion or position change) (p.716, p.157) Vomiting preceding headache by weeks - suggests a posterior fossa mass (p.157) New de novo headache in a patient with known systemic cancer (p.157) Personality change/apathy that may be mistaken for depression (p.716) A ring-enhancing lesion is non-specific - the differential includes brain abscess, toxoplasmosis, PCNSL, demyelination, sarcoidosis, radiation necrosis and primary brain tumour, so do not assume tumour without context (p.721, p.723). Withholding the diagnosis of glioma can be hard for diffusely infiltrative non-enhancing tumours (formerly gliomatosis cerebri), which often present only with cognitive decline and confluent FLAIR signal without mass effect (p.718). Do not give glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL - their cytolytic effect can yield non-diagnostic tissue (p.720). Prophylactic antiepileptic drugs have no role in tumour patients who have not had a seizure (only perioperative use is sometimes appropriate) (p.716). A normal or migrainous headache pattern is far more often migraine than tumour - tumour headache is frequently nondescript (p.157). Imaging-negative leptomeningeal disease is common; a single negative CSF cytology does not exclude it (positive in only ~50% on first LP) (p.724). General/raised-ICP symptoms arise as the enlarging tumour plus surrounding vasogenic edema raises intracranial pressure or obstructs CSF circulation, producing hydrocephalus; focal deficits reflect local invasion or compression (p.716). Primary tumours develop through stepwise acquisition of genetic changes - loss of tumour-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of oncogenes such as EGFR and PDGFR - and glioblastomas in particular show marked molecular heterogeneity (p.717). The 2021 WHO CNS classification integrates molecular markers (e.g. IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion) with histology into the diagnosis (p.717-718). Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the grey-white junction in watershed territory, so distribution follows blood flow (~85% supratentorial, ~15% posterior fossa) (p.723). Outcome is tumour-specific. Low-grade (grade 2) IDH-mutant astrocytoma usually transforms to higher grade with median survival around 10 years; high-grade IDH-mutant astrocytoma roughly 3-9 years (p.718). Oligodendrogliomas (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted) are more therapy-responsive with median survival in excess of 10 years (p.718). Glioblastoma (IDH wild-type) is the most common malignant primary tumour and invariably recurs; with standard combined therapy median survival is ~15-18 months and 5-year survival ~10%; adverse factors include older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor performance status and unresectable tumour (p.718-719). Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered carries a poor prognosis (~1 year) regardless of grade (p.719). Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1) and completely resected meningiomas/ependymomas can be cured (p.719-721). Brain metastases treated with WBRT have median survival of only ~4-6 months, though SRS achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure (p.724). WHO CNS grading (2021 integrated histologic + molecular classification): diffuse gliomas graded 2-4 by histologic malignancy and molecular markers, with CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion conferring grade 4 to otherwise lower-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas; pilocytic astrocytoma is grade 1. Meningiomas are graded I (benign), II (atypical) and III (malignant) by increasing aggressiveness (p.717-718, p.720-721).

Branchial cyst — branchial cleft cyst, branchial cleft anomaly, second branchial cleft cyst Cervical lymphadenopathy or reactive node Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) Cystic metastatic lymph node (in older patients) Dermoid or epidermoid cyst Tuberculous or atypical mycobacterial lymphadenitis Neck ultrasound to characterise the cystic lesion CT or MRI to map the tract and its relationship to the carotid vessels before excision Fine-needle aspiration when malignancy or nodal metastasis is a concern, particularly in adults Fistulography in cases with a discharging sinus or fistula Inflammatory markers and cultures if infection is present A lateral neck swelling arising from incomplete regression of the embryological branchial (pharyngeal) apparatus, most commonly from the second cleft The typical location is along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the upper to mid neck It often becomes clinically apparent in older children or young adults, sometimes enlarging after an upper respiratory infection Anomalies may take the form of a cyst, sinus, or fistula; a fistulous opening at the lower neck that discharges may indicate a tract to the pharynx Infected cysts present as tender, inflamed, sometimes fluctuant masses and should have infection controlled before elective excision Ultrasound is a useful first-line study, with cross-sectional imaging helping to define the tract before surgery Definitive management is complete surgical excision of the cyst and any associated tract to prevent recurrence In adults, a persistently cystic lateral neck mass should raise suspicion of a cystic nodal metastasis rather than a benign branchial cyst A cystic lateral neck mass in an older patient that may represent metastatic squamous carcinoma Acute infection with abscess formation requiring drainage Rapid enlargement or solid components suggesting an alternative or malignant diagnosis Airway or vascular compromise from a large or deep lesion Assuming a lateral neck cyst in an adult is benign without excluding malignancy Incomplete excision of the tract, leading to recurrence Operating during acute infection, increasing the risk of incomplete removal and complications Injuring adjacent nerves or vessels because the tract's course was not defined preoperatively The branchial apparatus of clefts, arches, and pouches contributes to head and neck development and normally regresses. Failure of obliteration of a cleft or its associated structures leaves an epithelial-lined remnant that can form a cyst, a blind-ending sinus, or a complete fistula connecting skin to pharynx. Second cleft anomalies characteristically pass between the internal and external carotid arteries toward the tonsillar fossa. Retained secretions distend the cyst, and communication with the pharynx or skin predisposes to recurrent infection. Benign branchial anomalies have an excellent prognosis after complete excision, with recurrence mainly seen when a tract is incompletely removed or when surgery is undertaken during active infection. Long-term outlook is worse only when a presumed cyst proves to be a cystic malignancy.

Branchio-oto-renal syndrome — BOR syndrome, EYA1, SIX1, SIX5, Melnick-Fraser syndrome Isolated branchial cleft cyst, sinus or fistula Isolated preauricular pit or sinus without syndromic features Other syndromic hearing loss such as Pendred or Waardenburg syndrome CHARGE syndrome with ear and other anomalies Townes-Brocks syndrome with ear, anal and limb anomalies Isolated congenital renal dysplasia or agenesis Audiometry to characterise the type and severity of hearing loss Renal ultrasound and further imaging to detect dysplasia, agenesis or collecting-system anomalies High-resolution CT or MRI of the temporal bones for inner-ear malformation Clinical assessment for branchial fistulae, sinuses and preauricular pits Molecular genetic testing of EYA1 and related genes with family screening Characterised by branchial anomalies, otological abnormalities with hearing loss, and renal malformations Branchial defects include lateral cervical fistulae, sinuses or cysts along the line of the second branchial cleft Otological features include preauricular pits, malformed pinnae, and hearing loss that may be sensorineural, conductive or mixed Most commonly caused by mutations in EYA1, with SIX1 and SIX5 also implicated; inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity Renal anomalies range from mild dysplasia to agenesis and can significantly affect prognosis, so renal imaging is essential Temporal-bone imaging often shows cochlear hypoplasia or other inner-ear malformations Preauricular pits with hearing loss should prompt evaluation for the full syndrome including the kidneys Signs of renal impairment or a solitary or absent kidney requiring nephrology input Recurrent infection or discharge from a branchial fistula or sinus Progressive hearing loss threatening speech development in a child Family history of hearing loss with renal or branchial anomalies indicating dominant inheritance Treating a preauricular pit or branchial fistula in isolation without evaluating hearing and kidneys Assuming normal renal function without imaging, given the wide range of renal involvement Underestimating variability within a family and missing mildly affected relatives Overlooking inner-ear malformations that influence surgical and rehabilitation planning Branchio-oto-renal syndrome results from mutations in transcription-factor and cofactor genes, most often EYA1 and the SIX family, which regulate development of structures derived from the branchial apparatus, the otic placode and the metanephric kidney. Disruption of this shared developmental network during embryogenesis produces the coexisting branchial (cleft-derived), otological (external, middle and inner ear) and renal abnormalities. Because expression is variable, affected individuals within a family can show markedly different combinations and severities of features, and penetrance is incomplete. Prognosis is largely determined by the severity of renal involvement, which can range from clinically silent to end-stage renal failure; hearing loss is managed with amplification or surgery, and branchial anomalies are treated surgically when symptomatic.

antibiotics alone rarely cure a collection Breastfeeding or expression from the affected side should generally continue to relieve stasis in lactational cases A non-lactational or non-resolving abscess, particularly in an older woman, requires exclusion of inflammatory breast cancer and other malignancy Recurrent periareolar abscess with a mammary duct fistula may need duct excision once inflammation settles Non-resolving or recurrent inflammatory changes suggesting inflammatory breast cancer Overlying skin necrosis or spreading cellulitis with systemic sepsis Immunosuppression or diabetes with rapidly progressive infection A persistent mass after treatment requiring triple assessment Treating with antibiotics alone and failing to drain an established collection Missing inflammatory breast cancer masquerading as a non-resolving abscess Advising cessation of breastfeeding unnecessarily, worsening milk stasis Not addressing smoking in recurrent non-lactational disease A breast abscess is a localised collection of pus within breast tissue. In lactating women, milk stasis and nipple trauma allow skin organisms, chiefly Staphylococcus aureus, to enter and proliferate, progressing from mastitis to a walled-off abscess. In non-lactating women, periductal mastitis, strongly linked to smoking, causes duct damage, squamous metaplasia, and duct obstruction, with secondary infection by mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms producing periareolar collections and sometimes a mammary duct fistula. Untreated collections enlarge, may point to the skin, and can cause tissue necrosis. Most breast abscesses resolve fully with timely drainage and appropriate antibiotics. Non-lactational and smoking-related disease is prone to recurrence and mammary duct fistula, and outcome improves with smoking cessation and, when indicated, duct excision.

Breast Cancer — breast carcinoma Inflammatory breast cancer is sometimes confused with mastitis or other breast infection (Harrison 22e p.638). Benign breast pathology such as atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia (raises risk about four- to fivefold) and lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS, raises risk 7- to 12-fold) (Harrison 22e p.633). Mastitis or other breast infection can be mimicked by inflammatory breast cancer, which presents with rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast; breast or skin biopsy is critical when breast inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638). Image-guided core biopsy for pathologic confirmation, tumor grade/morphology, and biomarker testing (ER, PR, HER2 protein, and potentially HER2 gene amplification) (Harrison 22e p.634). Diagnostic breast imaging: mammography, ultrasonography, and MRI if indicated; bilateral breast imaging because up to 3% have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634). Germline panel testing for breast cancer susceptibility mutations on DNA from peripheral blood or saliva after appropriate counseling (not recommended for the general population) (Harrison 22e p.633). For symptoms or findings of advanced disease (large tumor, skin changes, extensive adenopathy): CT and radionuclide bone scanning to look for overt metastatic disease, with biopsy of suspicious lesions to confirm metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635). Genomic transcriptional profiling assays for early-stage ER-positive disease (Oncotype Dx 21-gene, MammaPrint 70-gene, ProSigna 50-gene, EndoPredict 12-gene, Breast Cancer Index) to inform adjuvant chemotherapy decisions; ordering more than one per case is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.636). Skin biopsy showing dermal lymphatic invasion with tumor cells supports diagnosis of inflammatory breast cancer (Harrison 22e p.638). Evolving changes in the pregnant breast can make diagnosis of breast cancer during pregnancy difficult, so suspicious lumps or skin or nipple changes still require formal evaluation (Harrison 22e p.638). Most common nonskin cancer in women worldwide; predominantly a disease of prolonged estrogen exposure, with female gender and increasing age the most common risk factors (about 70% diagnosed at 55 years or older, median age 63) (Harrison 22e p.632). Clinical signs and symptoms suggestive of breast cancer may include a breast lump, skin or nipple changes, or palpable regional nodes; with mammographic screening many patients are asymptomatic and present only with an imaging abnormality (mass, distortion, or suspicious microcalcifications) (Harrison 22e p.634). Diagnosis rests on pathologic confirmation, generally by image-guided core biopsy, which also assesses tumor grade and morphology and performs biomarker evaluation for estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 protein expression and potentially HER2 gene amplification (the triple assessment of clinical/imaging/pathology with biomarkers) (Harrison 22e p.634). Suspicious axillary nodes should be biopsied via image-guided techniques, and both breasts should be imaged because up to 3% of women with newly diagnosed breast cancer have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634). Invasive breast cancer is divided into at least four molecular subtypes: luminal A and luminal B (both ER positive; luminal B has reduced PR or higher Ki67 proliferation and worse outcome), HER2 subtype (high HER2 expression, benefits from HER2-targeted therapy), and basal/triple-negative (TNBC, lacking ER, PR, and HER2) (Harrison 22e p.636). Most invasive breast cancers are ductal; about 10-15% are lobular, which are usually ER positive and HER2 negative, distinguished by absence of E-cadherin, and have a propensity to spread to serosal surfaces (omentum, pleura, meninges) and parenchyma (ovaries, GI tract) (Harrison 22e p.636). Family history is a critical risk factor, yet only 20% of women diagnosed with breast cancer have a family history; a first-degree relative with breast cancer doubles the risk (Harrison 22e p.633). Inflammatory breast cancer: rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast (a subset of locally advanced disease); breast inflammation failing to resolve after antibiotics warrants breast or skin biopsy, and up to one-third have detectable metastasis at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.638). Any unexplained mass or lesion palpable on physical examination needs further assessment including biopsy where warranted; a normal mammogram does NOT rule out cancer in a woman with a palpable breast lump (Harrison 22e p.45). Locally advanced features: large primary tumor, involvement of skin or chest wall, or fixed tumor or axillary nodes (Harrison 22e p.638). A common disease-specific diagnostic pitfall is ordering a mammogram for a woman with a palpable breast lump and, when it returns normal, reassuring her that cancer has been ruled out; any unexplained palpable mass needs further testing and biopsy where warranted (Harrison 22e p.45). Lobular cancers can recur at unusual sites (serosal surfaces, ovaries, GI tract), producing atypical presentations that may delay diagnosis if metastatic disease is not considered (Harrison 22e p.636). Up to 3% of newly diagnosed patients have unsuspected contralateral disease, so both breasts must be imaged (Harrison 22e p.634). Inflammatory breast cancer may be mistaken for mastitis or infection; biopsy is critical when inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638). Germline panel testing can yield variants of unknown significance (VUS) and includes genes with poorly defined clinical risk, causing patient confusion and discomfort (Harrison 22e p.633). Breast cancer is predominantly a disease resulting from prolonged exposure of the breast to estrogen. Most breast cancers begin in epithelial cells within the lobules or ducts and proceed through a conceptual continuum of atypia and hyperplasia to in situ malignancy, then invasion into surrounding tissue, intravasation into lymph and blood channels, spread to regional lymph nodes, and distant metastases (though not all cancers progress through every stage). Hereditary breast cancer susceptibility genes account for 5-10% of cases; these genes participate in DNA damage repair, and inherited autosomal dominant mutations generally cause protein truncation and loss of function of DNA repair proteins. The most common are BRCA1 (chromosome 17q21) and BRCA2 (chromosome 13q12), conferring a 50-80% lifetime risk of invasive breast cancer by age 80 and a 30% risk of ovarian cancer; other germline mutations include TP53 (Li-Fraumeni), PALB2, ATM, STK11 (Peutz-Jeghers), and PTEN (Cowden). Ashkenazi Jews have a higher BRCA mutation incidence (Harrison 22e p.632-633). 5-year relative survival in the United States is currently about 91%. Outcomes are directly related to stage at presentation (and vary by race/ethnicity): 5-year relative survival is over 99% for stage I, about 93% for stage II, about 75% for stage III, and about 29% for stage IV. Less than 10% present with de novo metastatic (M1) disease. Luminal B tumors carry a poorer outcome than luminal A; TNBC carries a poorer prognosis; mucinous and pure medullary cancers have very favorable prognoses with local therapy only; higher Nottingham grade is associated with poorer prognosis. About 20-25% of patients treated for early breast cancer subsequently develop metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635-638). Staging follows the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) eighth edition TNM (tumor-node-metastasis) system, which has evolved to incorporate molecular biomarkers (ER, PR, HER2) and certain genomic tests (e.g., Oncotype 21-gene assay). Conceptually, stages I and II are early-stage disease confined to breast and ipsilateral nodes; stage III is locally advanced disease; and stage IV (M1) is metastatic disease. Staging may be clinical (c), pathologic after surgery (p), or post-neoadjuvant (y prefix). Common metastatic sites are soft tissues, lung, bone, liver, and brain (Harrison 22e p.634-635).

Breast fibroadenoma — fibroadenoma, breast mouse, FAD, benign breast fibroadenoma Phyllodes tumour Breast cyst Fibrocystic change Breast carcinoma (particularly in older patients) Hamartoma of the breast Lipoma or other benign stromal lesion Breast ultrasound as first-line imaging in younger women Mammography in older patients or where imaging is indeterminate Core needle biopsy for histological confirmation and to exclude phyllodes tumour or malignancy Fine-needle aspiration cytology in selected settings as part of triple assessment Clinical follow-up imaging for lesions managed conservatively Fibroadenoma is the commonest benign solid breast lump in young women, typically presenting as a smooth, firm, well-defined, highly mobile mass, hence the nickname breast mouse It is usually painless and often discovered incidentally; multiple and bilateral lesions occur in a minority Assessment follows triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound in younger women, with mammography added in older patients), and needle biopsy where indicated Ultrasound characteristically shows a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, oval lesion with a benign appearance Core biopsy is used to confirm the diagnosis and, importantly, to distinguish a fibroadenoma from a phyllodes tumour, which can behave more aggressively Many small, biopsy-proven fibroadenomas can be safely observed, as a proportion regress, while excision is offered for large, enlarging, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesions or patient preference A giant fibroadenoma or a rapidly enlarging lesion should prompt careful exclusion of a phyllodes tumour Rapid growth or a large (giant) lesion suggesting a phyllodes tumour Irregular, hard, or fixed features or suspicious imaging raising concern for malignancy New solid breast mass in an older woman requiring careful exclusion of cancer Discordance between clinical, imaging, and pathology findings on triple assessment Assuming a solid mass in an older woman is a fibroadenoma without excluding carcinoma Failing to distinguish a phyllodes tumour from a fibroadenoma, leading to inadequate excision margins Ignoring discordance within triple assessment and falsely reassuring the patient Over-treating small, biopsy-proven, asymptomatic fibroadenomas that could be safely observed Neglecting follow-up of a lesion managed conservatively that later enlarges A fibroadenoma is a benign biphasic tumour arising from the breast lobule, composed of both epithelial and stromal (fibrous) elements that proliferate together. It is regarded as an aberration of normal breast development and involution rather than a true neoplasm, and its growth is hormonally responsive, which explains its predominance in the reproductive years, occasional enlargement during pregnancy, and tendency to regress after the menopause. The lesion is well encapsulated and mobile within the breast tissue. The main clinical distinction is from phyllodes tumours, which share stromal and epithelial components but have greater stromal cellularity and a spectrum of behaviour from benign to malignant. The prognosis is excellent; fibroadenomas are benign, a significant proportion regress or remain stable, and they carry little or no increase in subsequent breast cancer risk in the usual simple form. Recurrence after complete excision is uncommon, though new fibroadenomas may develop elsewhere.

cause exercise-induced contractures Brody myopathy is caused by mutations in ATP2A1, which encodes SERCA1, the calcium ATPase of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in fast-twitch (type II) muscle fibres. SERCA1 pumps calcium from the cytoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to terminate contraction and allow relaxation. When SERCA1 activity is deficient, cytoplasmic calcium is cleared too slowly after a contraction, so relaxation is delayed and repeated contractions cause cumulative stiffness, particularly during sustained or rapid exercise and in the cold. Because the impaired relaxation results from defective calcium reuptake rather than abnormal membrane excitability, the phenomenon is electrically silent, distinguishing it from the true myotonias. Brody myopathy is generally non-progressive and compatible with a normal lifespan, and although exercise-induced stiffness can be functionally limiting, most patients manage well with pacing of activity, warming-up and avoidance of cold.

Bronchiectasis — bronchiectasis, non-CF bronchiectasis, chronic suppurative lung disease Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic bronchitis Cystic fibrosis Chronic asthma with mucus hypersecretion Pulmonary tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Chronic aspiration High-resolution CT of the chest to confirm and map the extent of airway dilatation Sputum culture including for mycobacteria and fungi to guide targeted therapy Immunoglobulin levels and other immune workup to detect underlying immunodeficiency Testing for cystic fibrosis and, where suspected, ciliary function studies Aspergillus-specific serology and total IgE to evaluate for ABPA Defined by permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi, presenting with chronic productive cough, copious purulent sputum, and recurrent chest infections Haemoptysis, breathlessness, and coarse crackles with occasional wheeze are common, and clubbing may be present in advanced disease High-resolution CT is the diagnostic standard, showing airway dilatation greater than the accompanying vessel (signet-ring sign), lack of tapering, and airway wall thickening Causes include prior severe infection, cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, ABPA, and obstruction; a cause should be actively sought Sputum microbiology guides therapy; chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation is associated with more frequent exacerbations and worse outcomes Airway clearance techniques and pulmonary rehabilitation are cornerstones of long-term management Exacerbations are treated with appropriately targeted antimicrobials guided by prior culture results, and long-term suppressive strategies are considered in frequent exacerbators Assessment for treatable contributors such as immunoglobulin deficiency or ABPA can meaningfully change management Massive or recurrent haemoptysis requiring urgent intervention Rapid clinical decline or systemic sepsis during an exacerbation New isolation of resistant organisms or non-tuberculous mycobacteria Progressive respiratory failure or features of cor pulmonale Treating recurrent chest infections symptomatically without imaging to establish the diagnosis Failing to search for a reversible or treatable underlying cause Neglecting airway clearance in favour of antibiotics alone Not obtaining sputum cultures before escalating antimicrobial therapy A vicious cycle of airway injury drives bronchiectasis: an initial insult (infection, impaired mucociliary clearance, immune deficiency, or obstruction) impairs clearance of secretions, allowing bacterial colonisation. Persistent bacterial presence provokes chronic neutrophilic inflammation with release of proteases and reactive oxygen species that progressively damage the bronchial wall, weakening and dilating the airways. The damaged, dilated airways clear secretions still less effectively, perpetuating infection and inflammation and leading to further structural destruction. Prognosis varies widely with the underlying cause and disease extent; many patients remain stable for years with good airway clearance and infection control, but frequent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas colonisation, and extensive disease predict faster decline in lung function and higher mortality.

Bronchiolitis — acute bronchiolitis, RSV bronchiolitis, viral bronchiolitis Viral-induced wheeze / early asthma Pneumonia Congenital heart disease with heart failure Foreign body aspiration Gastro-oesophageal reflux with aspiration Pertussis Pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation Nasopharyngeal viral testing (mainly for cohorting or in severe/atypical cases) Chest radiograph only if diagnosis is unclear or deterioration is unexplained Blood gas in severe respiratory distress or impending failure Capillary or venous blood tests only when a bacterial complication is suspected A common lower respiratory tract infection of infants, typically under 2 years and peaking around 2-6 months, most often caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Begins with upper respiratory symptoms (coryza, cough, low-grade fever) that progress over a few days to tachypnoea, wheeze, crackles, and increased work of breathing. Diagnosis is clinical; routine viral testing, chest radiographs, and blood tests are usually unnecessary and can be misleading. Management is supportive: ensure adequate hydration and feeding, maintain oxygenation, and provide gentle nasal suction as needed. Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics are generally not beneficial in typical bronchiolitis and are not routinely recommended. Apnoea can be an early and sometimes presenting sign, particularly in young or premature infants. Risk factors for severe disease include prematurity, age under 2-3 months, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease, and immunodeficiency. Most cases are self-limiting over 1-2 weeks, though cough can persist longer. Apnoea or episodes of colour change Persistent hypoxaemia or rising oxygen requirement Severe respiratory distress: marked recession, grunting, nasal flaring, head bobbing Inability to feed or signs of dehydration Exhaustion, lethargy, or signs of impending respiratory failure Overusing bronchodilators, steroids, or antibiotics that provide no benefit in typical disease Relying on transient oxygen desaturation readings and over-treating stable, feeding infants Missing apnoea as a presenting feature in very young infants Ordering routine chest radiographs, which may prompt unnecessary antibiotics for atelectasis mistaken for infiltrate Viral infection of the small airway epithelium causes inflammation, oedema, and necrosis of epithelial cells with increased mucus production. Sloughed cellular debris and mucus, together with airway wall swelling, partially or completely obstruct the small bronchioles. Because infant airways are narrow, this obstruction produces air trapping, hyperinflation, atelectasis, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch, leading to wheeze, hypoxaemia, and increased work of breathing. Most previously healthy infants recover fully within one to two weeks; a minority, especially high-risk infants, require hospitalisation, and some children have recurrent wheeze afterwards.

Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia — BPD, chronic lung disease of prematurity, chronic lung disease of infancy Recurrent aspiration Congenital heart disease with left-to-right shunt or pulmonary oedema Pulmonary hypertension from other causes Recurrent or persistent lower respiratory infection Interstitial lung disease of infancy Tracheobronchomalacia Chest radiograph showing hyperinflation, cystic or coarse interstitial changes Pulse oximetry and, where indicated, blood gas analysis Echocardiography to screen for pulmonary hypertension Assessment of growth and nutritional status Selected infants may need chest CT or bronchoscopy for airway evaluation A chronic lung disease of prematurity, usually defined by a persisting need for supplemental oxygen or respiratory support at around 36 weeks postmenstrual age. Occurs mainly in very preterm, very-low-birth-weight infants, often those who required prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen for respiratory distress syndrome. The modern ('new') form reflects arrested alveolar and pulmonary vascular development rather than the severe fibrotic airway injury seen historically. Contributing factors include oxygen toxicity, ventilator-induced volutrauma and barotrauma, inflammation, infection, and a patent ductus arteriosus. Lung-protective strategies, such as early CPAP, gentle ventilation targeting acceptable gas exchange, and judicious oxygen targeting, help prevent it. Management emphasises adequate nutrition and calories for lung growth, careful fluid balance, and weaning of respiratory support as tolerated. Systemic corticosteroids can facilitate extubation but carry neurodevelopmental risks, so their use is weighed carefully and generally limited. Affected infants are prone to recurrent wheeze, respiratory infections, and pulmonary hypertension, and benefit from RSV prophylaxis and immunisation. Caffeine therapy for apnoea of prematurity is associated with a lower rate of bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Escalating oxygen or ventilatory requirement Signs of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale Failure to gain weight despite adequate calories Frequent acute deteriorations or hypoxaemic spells Recurrent lower respiratory tract infections requiring hospitalisation Using liberal oxygen targets that worsen lung and retinal injury Overlooking pulmonary hypertension as a cause of persistent oxygen need Excess fluid administration precipitating pulmonary oedema Prolonged or high-dose systemic steroid courses despite neurodevelopmental risk Underestimating nutritional needs required for lung repair and growth In the immature lung, the combination of oxidative stress from supplemental oxygen, mechanical injury from positive-pressure ventilation, inflammation, and antenatal or postnatal infection disrupts normal alveolar septation and pulmonary microvascular growth. The result is fewer, larger, simplified alveoli with an abnormal vascular bed, variable airway smooth-muscle and interstitial changes, and impaired gas exchange. Pulmonary vascular remodelling can lead to pulmonary hypertension. Most infants gradually improve as the lung grows during early childhood, but many have increased respiratory morbidity, exercise limitation, and abnormal lung function later; severe disease with pulmonary hypertension carries higher mortality and long-term risk.

Brucellosis — undulant fever, Malta fever Tuberculosis is the most important differential for vertebral osteomyelitis or septic arthritis; vertebral destruction or spinal cord impingement is rare in brucellosis and usually suggests tuberculosis (p.1333). Typhoid fever and malaria as causes of fever in endemic areas (p.1333). Glandular fever-like illness (EBV, Toxoplasma, cytomegalovirus, HIV, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis) when hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy is present (p.1333). Mumps and surgical conditions such as testicular torsion when epididymo-orchitis occurs (p.1333). Neurotuberculosis, atypical leptospirosis, and noninfectious conditions when lymphocytic meningoencephalitis develops (p.1333). Tuberculosis Typhoid fever Malaria Leptospirosis Epstein-Barr virus infection Cytomegalovirus infection Toxoplasmosis HIV infection Mumps Blood, CSF, bone marrow, joint fluid, or tissue aspirate/biopsy culture under containment conditions for dangerous pathogens; alert the laboratory when brucellosis is suspected (p.1333). Standard tube/plate/microagglutination serology as the mainstay, with complement fixation, Coombs antiglobulin, and ELISA tests; repeat after 2-4 weeks to detect a rising titer (p.1334). Peripheral blood PCR / nucleic acid amplification (e.g., targeting rrs-rrl spacer, outer-membrane protein genes, IS711, BCSP31) which is more sensitive and quicker than culture and avoids biohazard risk (p.1334). MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for identification in well-resourced laboratories, with the caveat that earlier implementations often failed to identify Brucella correctly (p.1333). Isotope bone scanning, more sensitive than plain x-ray for bony disease (p.1333). CSF/joint fluid analysis showing lymphocytosis and low glucose; tissue biopsy may show noncaseating granulomas without acid-fast bacilli (p.1333). Noninfectious causes of lymphocytic meningoencephalitis Chronic fatigue syndromes (in the context of a suspected chronic brucellosis state) Other causes of excessive sweating such as alcohol abuse and obesity A bacterial zoonosis caused by Brucella species, transmitted directly or indirectly from infected animals, predominantly domesticated ruminants and swine; B. melitensis (sheep, goats, camels) is the most common cause of symptomatic human disease, with B. abortus (cattle/buffalo), B. suis (swine), and B. canis (dogs) also implicated (p.1331). Human infection is usually associated with occupational or domestic animal exposure (farmers, shepherds, goatherds, veterinarians, slaughterhouse and meat-processing workers, laboratory staff); travelers and urban residents typically acquire it through contaminated food (p.1332). Dairy products, especially soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk, and ice cream, are the most frequently implicated sources; acquisition may occur by ingestion, inhalation, or mucosal/percutaneous exposure (p.1332). Almost invariably causes fever, which may be accompanied by profuse sweats, especially at night; untreated, the fever classically shows an undulating pattern persisting for weeks before an afebrile period that may be followed by relapse (p.1332-1333). Fever is associated with musculoskeletal symptoms and signs in about half of patients; nonspecific features include apathy, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, myalgia, headache, and chills (p.1333). Presentation often fits one of three patterns: a typhoid-like febrile illness but less severe; fever with acute monoarthritis (typically hip or knee) in a young child; and long-lasting fever with misery and low-back or hip pain in an older person, especially men (p.1333). Focal musculoskeletal involvement is the most common complication (~40%): osteomyelitis favors lumbar and low thoracic vertebrae, and septic arthritis most often affects knee, hip, sacroiliac, shoulder, and sternoclavicular joints, as monoarthritis or polyarthritis (p.1333). Roughly one-quarter of patients have hepatosplenomegaly and 10-20% have significant lymphadenopathy; up to 10% of men develop acute epididymo-orchitis (p.1333). Endocarditis occurs in about 1% of cases, most often affecting the aortic valve (native or prosthetic), and is the usual cause of death when the outcome is fatal (p.1333, p.1335). Diagnosis rests on a history of potential exposure, a compatible presentation, and supporting laboratory findings, because the clinical picture is not distinctive (p.1333). Isolation of brucellae from blood, CSF, bone marrow, joint fluid, or a tissue aspirate/biopsy is definitive and succeeds in about 50-70% of cases; modern automated blood culture systems (e.g., Bactec) usually turn positive within 7 days (p.1333). Serology often provides the only positive laboratory finding; in endemic or occupationally exposed settings agglutinin titers of 1:320-1:640 or higher are considered diagnostic, while in nonendemic areas a titer of at least 1:160 is significant, with no single universal cutoff (p.1334). Endocarditis, most often of the aortic valve (native or prosthetic), the leading cause of death in fatal cases (p.1333, p.1335). Neurobrucellosis: lymphocytic meningoencephalitis mimicking neurotuberculosis, and rarely intracerebral abscess, cranial nerve deficits, or ruptured mycotic aneurysms (p.1333). Vertebral osteomyelitis (spondylitis) and sacroiliitis (p.1333). Disseminated intravascular coagulation with raised fibrinogen degradation products and thrombocytopenia (p.1333). Increased fetal loss in infected pregnant women (though teratogenicity has not been described and abortion is much less pronounced in humans than in animals) (p.1333). The clinical picture is not distinctive and definitive diagnostic signs may be lacking, so exposure history and laboratory support are essential (p.1331, p.1333). Routine biochemistry is usually normal; peripheral leukocyte counts are typically normal or low with relative lymphocytosis, so normal blood counts do not exclude the disease (p.1333). Brucella may be misidentified by gallery strips as Agrobacterium, Ochrobactrum, or Psychrobacter (Moraxella) phenylpyruvicus; after taxonomic changes Ochrobactrum isolates may now be reported as a Brucella subspecies despite completely different management, so culture reports should be confirmed with the laboratory before therapeutic decisions (p.1333-1334). Rough strains such as B. canis and B. ovis do not react in conventional serologic tests and will give false-negative results; consult the laboratory if B. canis is suspected (p.1334). Serologic cross-reactions occur with other gram-negative bacteria including Yersinia enterocolitica O:9, E. coli O157, Francisella tularensis, Salmonella enterica group N, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Vibrio cholerae (p.1334). Live B. abortus vaccine strain RB51 does not elicit antibody in tests using smooth antigens, which must be considered when following accidental vaccine exposures (p.1334). Elevated CSF adenosine deaminase cannot be used to distinguish tubercular meningitis, as it may also be raised in brucellosis (p.1333). Existence of a prolonged chronic brucellosis state after successful treatment remains controversial; evaluation requires careful exclusion of malingering, chronic fatigue syndromes, and other causes of sweating such as alcohol abuse and obesity (p.1335). Brucellae are small, gram-negative, unencapsulated, nonsporulating coccobacilli that behave as facultative intracellular parasites. Following entry by ingestion, inhalation, or mucosal/percutaneous exposure, initial replication is presumed to occur within cells of the lymph nodes draining the entry point, with subsequent hematogenous spread that can establish chronic localizing infection at almost any site, most often the reticuloendothelial system, musculoskeletal tissues, and genitourinary system. The macrophage is the key target cell; Brucella is a "stealth" pathogen that evades innate immunity and survives within monocytic cells by restricting fusion of type IV secretion system-dependent Brucella-containing vacuoles with lysosomes, inhibiting apoptosis of infected cells, and preventing dendritic cell maturation and T-cell activation. Smooth LPS has low endotoxin activity and contributes to pyrogenicity and resistance to phagocytosis and serum killing. Antibodies aid clearance of extracellular organisms but alone cannot eradicate infection; control depends on macrophage activation and IFN-gamma/TH1 responses. Tissue responses range from acute and chronic inflammation to granuloma formation, with or without necrosis and caseation, and abscesses may develop in chronic localized infection (p.1332). Fewer than 1% of patients die of brucellosis; when fatal, death is usually due to cardiac involvement and, more rarely, severe neurologic disease. Despite low mortality, recovery is slow and the illness can cause prolonged inactivity. Relapse occurs in up to 30% of poorly compliant patients, so clinical follow-up for up to 2 years is recommended; relapse responds to a prolonged repeat course of the original therapy. General well-being and body weight are better guides to absence of relapse than serology, since IgG agglutination titers can stay in the diagnostic range for more than 2 years after cure. Immunity is not solid and reinfection can occur after repeated exposures (p.1335). Harrison distinguishes acute nonfocal brucellosis (duration under about 1-2 months) from complex or focal disease (e.g., spondylitis, neurobrucellosis, endocarditis), the latter requiring more prolonged and tailored therapy. Patterns by species are also noted: B. melitensis tends toward a more acute, aggressive presentation, B. suis toward focal abscess formation, and B. abortus toward a more insidious onset that is more likely to become chronic (p.1333-1334).

Brugada syndrome — Brugada, Brugada pattern, SCN5A channelopathy, sudden unexpected nocturnal death syndrome Right bundle branch block Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy Acute right precordial ST elevation from ischaemia or pericarditis Electrolyte disturbance mimicking a Brugada pattern Early repolarisation variants Drug-induced or fever-induced phenocopies of the pattern 12-lead ECG including high right precordial lead placement to detect the coved pattern Sodium-channel-blocker provocation testing under monitoring when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic Assessment during febrile illness given fever-induced unmasking Genetic testing and cascade family screening Echocardiography or cardiac imaging to exclude structural disease such as ARVC Electrophysiology study in selected cases for risk stratification Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmia disorder characterised by a distinctive coved ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads and a risk of polymorphic ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death in a structurally normal heart Only the type 1 coved pattern is diagnostic; the saddleback type 2 pattern is suggestive and may need provocation or repositioned high leads to confirm Arrhythmic events characteristically occur at rest or during sleep and may be triggered by fever, which can unmask the pattern Certain drugs (including some sodium-channel blockers, and various psychotropic and anaesthetic agents) can precipitate or accentuate the pattern and should be avoided It disproportionately affects young to middle-aged men and can present as syncope, nocturnal agonal breathing, or aborted sudden death Diagnosis integrates the ECG pattern with clinical and family history, and a drug provocation test may be used when the resting ECG is non-diagnostic An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is the mainstay of protection in high-risk patients, and prompt treatment of fever is advised Family screening and genetic counselling are important given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expression MEDICAL EMERGENCY: polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation causing syncope, cardiac arrest, or sudden death Syncope or nocturnal agonal respiration in a patient with a type 1 pattern indicating high arrhythmic risk Spontaneous (not drug-induced) type 1 pattern, which carries greater risk Fever in a known patient, which can precipitate malignant arrhythmia Treating a non-diagnostic saddleback pattern as definitive Brugada syndrome Failing to place high right precordial leads or to consider provocation when suspicion is high Prescribing drugs that can precipitate the pattern or omitting prompt fever control Neglecting family screening after a diagnosis Brugada syndrome is most often linked to loss-of-function mutations in the cardiac sodium channel gene SCN5A, reducing inward sodium current. The leading explanation involves heterogeneity of repolarisation and depolarisation predominantly in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing a transmural voltage gradient that generates the characteristic ST-segment changes and a substrate for phase 2 reentry. This can trigger polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Factors that reduce sodium current or increase transient outward current, such as fever and specific drugs, accentuate the abnormality and increase arrhythmic risk, which is why events cluster at rest, during sleep, and with febrile illness. Asymptomatic individuals with only a drug-induced pattern generally have a low event rate, whereas those with a spontaneous type 1 pattern and prior syncope or aborted arrest are at substantially higher risk; defibrillator therapy and avoidance of triggers markedly improve outcomes in high-risk patients.

other causes with portal hypertension Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease) Portal vein thrombosis Malignant infiltration of the liver or vena cava Fulminant hepatitis of other aetiology Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava as the initial test CT or MR venography to map the site and length of obstruction and assess caudate lobe changes Thrombophilia and myeloproliferative neoplasm workup, including JAK2 mutation testing Liver function tests, coagulation profile, and assessment for encephalopathy to gauge severity Ascitic fluid analysis and, where needed, liver biopsy or hepatic venography Caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow anywhere from the small hepatic veins to the junction of the inferior vena cava and right atrium, producing hepatic congestion The classic triad is abdominal pain, ascites, and hepatomegaly, though presentation ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant liver failure An underlying prothrombotic state is present in most patients, most notably myeloproliferative neoplasms (including JAK2-associated disease), so a thrombophilia workup is essential Doppler ultrasound is the usual first-line test, with CT or MR venography to define the level and extent of the obstruction The caudate lobe often drains directly into the inferior vena cava and is characteristically spared and hypertrophied while the rest of the liver is congested Management is stepwise: anticoagulation for essentially all patients, then angioplasty or stenting of short-segment stenoses, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunting, and finally liver transplantation for refractory or fulminant cases Acute presentation with rapid-onset jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy represents acute liver failure and is a medical emergency Chronic outflow obstruction leads to congestive fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis with portal hypertension Acute liver failure with jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy requiring emergency specialist and transplant assessment Rapidly worsening liver function or tense refractory ascites Concurrent inferior vena cava obstruction with lower-limb oedema and renal impairment Evidence of an aggressive underlying myeloproliferative disorder Attributing ascites and hepatomegaly to more common cirrhosis and missing outflow obstruction Failing to search for and treat an underlying prothrombotic disorder, allowing rethrombosis Delaying escalation from anticoagulation to interventional or transplant options in deteriorating patients Misinterpreting caudate lobe hypertrophy as a mass lesion Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow raises sinusoidal pressure and causes hepatic congestion, hypoxic injury to hepatocytes, and centrilobular necrosis. The resulting portal hypertension produces ascites and, over time, congestive fibrosis progressing to cirrhosis. Most cases stem from thrombosis on a background prothrombotic disorder, commonly a myeloproliferative neoplasm, inherited thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, pregnancy, or oral contraceptive use; in some regions membranous webs of the inferior vena cava predominate. The caudate lobe, with its independent venous drainage into the vena cava, escapes congestion and hypertrophies. Speed and completeness of obstruction determine whether the course is fulminant, acute, or chronic. Outcome depends on the rapidity and extent of obstruction and the response to a staged treatment strategy. Many patients do well with anticoagulation and interventional or shunt procedures, but fulminant presentations carry high mortality without transplantation, and untreated chronic disease progresses to cirrhosis.

Buerger disease — thromboangiitis obliterans, TAO, Buerger's disease Premature atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease Embolic occlusion from a cardiac or proximal arterial source Systemic vasculitides (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa) Connective tissue disease with digital ischaemia (e.g. scleroderma) Thrombophilia or hypercoagulable states Ergotism or vasospastic disorders Angiography vasculitis serology to exclude systemic vasculitis and connective tissue disease Thrombophilia screening where clinically indicated Tobacco use assessment including confirmatory testing when abstinence is claimed A non-atherosclerotic segmental inflammatory occlusive disease of small and medium arteries and veins of the distal limbs Overwhelmingly affects young tobacco users, typically men under forty, with a strong and causal relationship to smoking Presents with distal ischaemia including digital pain, claudication of the foot or hand, cold sensitivity, ulceration, and gangrene of or an embolic source Complete and permanent tobacco cessation is the single most effective intervention and can halt progression and prevent amputation Standard revascularisation is often not feasible because of the distal small-vessel pattern, so wound care and abstinence are central Rest pain, ulceration, or digital gangrene indicating critical ischaemia and threatened tissue loss Rapidly progressive digital necrosis, particularly with continued smoking Ascending infection of an ischaemic digit Involvement of multiple limbs signalling extensive disease Diagnosing atherosclerotic disease in a young smoker and missing thromboangiitis obliterans Underemphasising that continued smoking, including any tobacco or nicotine exposure, drives progression Pursuing revascularisation where the distal small-vessel pattern makes it unsuitable Failing to exclude an embolic source or systemic vasculitis before settling on the diagnosis Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a segmental non-atherosclerotic vasculitis affecting small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities. There is an inflammatory, highly cellular thrombus with relative sparing of the vessel wall and internal elastic lamina, distinguishing it histologically from atherosclerosis and other vasculitides. Tobacco exposure is central to pathogenesis, likely through an immune-mediated and endothelial mechanism, and continued use drives progression. Occlusion of distal vessels produces critical ischaemia of the digits with limited collateral compensation. Prognosis is closely tied to smoking behaviour: complete cessation usually arrests the disease and greatly reduces amputation risk, whereas continued tobacco use commonly leads to recurrent ischaemia and progressive tissue loss. Life expectancy is generally near normal, but limb and digit loss is the major morbidity.

Bulimia nervosa — bulimia, BN Anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type Binge-eating disorder Major depressive disorder Borderline personality disorder with impulsive eating Gastrointestinal causes of vomiting Kleine-Levin syndrome and other causes of hyperphagia Electrolytes, particularly potassium, with bicarbonate and chloride to detect metabolic alkalosis ECG where electrolyte disturbance or arrhythmia is suspected Renal function assessment Dental examination for enamel erosion Screening for comorbid depression, substance use, and self-harm Defined by recurrent episodes of binge eating with a sense of loss of control, followed by compensatory behaviours to prevent weight gain Compensatory behaviours include self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight, and patients are typically of normal or near-normal weight, unlike in anorexia nervosa Physical signs may include salivary gland enlargement, dental enamel erosion, and Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting) Purging can cause dangerous electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, with risk of cardiac arrhythmia First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for eating disorders; SSRIs (notably fluoxetine) are the pharmacological principle of choice Comorbid depression, anxiety, substance use, and impulsivity are common, and suicide risk should be assessed Behaviours are often concealed, so specific, non-judgemental enquiry is needed to detect them Severe hypokalaemia or other electrolyte disturbance with arrhythmia risk Haematemesis or oesophageal tear (Mallory-Weiss or Boerhaave) from forceful vomiting Suicidal ideation or self-harm Marked dehydration and haemodynamic instability from purging Assuming a normal body weight excludes serious medical risk from purging Missing dangerous hypokalaemia and its arrhythmic potential Not asking directly about purging behaviours that patients tend to conceal Overlooking comorbid depression and suicide risk Failing to offer evidence-based cognitive behavioural therapy Bulimia nervosa involves interacting genetic, temperamental, and sociocultural factors, with dysregulation of serotonergic systems affecting satiety, mood, and impulse control. Dietary restraint promotes binge episodes, and the binge-purge cycle is maintained by both physiological drives and psychological reinforcement, while overvaluation of shape and weight sustains the disorder. Bulimia nervosa often has a fluctuating course, but many patients improve substantially with cognitive behavioural therapy. Comorbid substance use, personality disorder, and persistent purging are associated with a more chronic course and greater medical risk.

Bullous pemphigoid — pemphigoid, BP Pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid blisters, mucosal erosions, intraepidermal split) Dermatitis herpetiformis Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita Bullous drug eruption Bullous impetigo Urticaria or eczema during the non-bullous prodromal phase Lesional skin biopsy showing a subepidermal blister with eosinophils Perilesional direct immunofluorescence showing linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone Serum indirect immunofluorescence and ELISA for BP180 and BP230 antibodies Salt-split skin studies to localise antibody binding when distinguishing from related disorders Review of medication history for possible drug-induced pemphigoid The commonest autoimmune blistering disease, typically affecting older adults Classically produces large, tense, fluid-filled blisters on an erythematous or urticarial base, favouring the trunk, flexures, and limbs Blisters are tense and relatively robust because the split is subepidermal, unlike the fragile flaccid blisters of pemphigus A prodromal phase of intense itch with urticarial or eczematous plaques may precede blistering by weeks or months and is easily misdiagnosed Mucosal involvement is uncommon and usually mild, which helps distinguish it from pemphigus vulgaris Diagnosis is confirmed by subepidermal blistering on histology and linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence Management uses potent topical corticosteroids for localised disease and systemic corticosteroids or steroid-sparing immunomodulators for widespread involvement Consider a drug trigger, since certain medications (including some diabetes and immunotherapy agents) can precipitate pemphigoid Extensive blistering with widespread skin barrier loss and secondary infection risk Signs of sepsis or systemic deterioration, particularly in frail elderly patients Complications of systemic corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy Rapidly progressive disease unresponsive to initial treatment Missing the non-bullous urticarial or eczematous prodrome and delaying diagnosis Confusing it with pemphigus vulgaris and misjudging prognosis and mucosal risk Over-reliance on high-dose systemic steroids in frail patients when potent topical steroids may suffice Failing to identify a drug trigger that could be withdrawn Bullous pemphigoid is caused by autoantibodies directed against hemidesmosomal proteins of the dermal-epidermal junction, principally BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230. Antibody binding activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells, particularly eosinophils, which release proteases that degrade the anchoring structures holding the epidermis to the dermis. This produces a subepidermal split, giving tense blisters with an intact epidermal roof. The urticarial prodrome reflects the inflammatory phase before frank blistering. Disease predominates in the elderly and may be associated with neurological disease and, in some cases, drug exposure. Bullous pemphigoid is often a self-limiting disease over months to a few years and generally responds to treatment, but morbidity and mortality are notable in elderly patients, largely driven by comorbidity and treatment-related complications.
