inhalation injury until airway swelling makes intubation difficult Failing to reassess deep dermal burns, which may convert to full thickness and need grafting Neglecting hypothermia, analgesia, and nutrition during the acute phase Missing the need for escharotomy in circumferential deep burns A burn causes coagulative tissue necrosis whose severity depends on temperature and contact time. Jackson described three zones: a central zone of coagulation (irreversible necrosis), a surrounding zone of stasis with compromised perfusion that can be salvaged or progress to necrosis, and an outer zone of hyperaemia. Large burns trigger a systemic inflammatory response with release of mediators that increase capillary permeability, causing fluid shift from the intravascular space into the interstitium and burn oedema. This produces hypovolaemia (burn shock) and, if inadequately treated, organ hypoperfusion. Loss of the skin barrier impairs thermoregulation and fluid balance and predisposes to infection and hypermetabolism. Outcome depends on burn size and depth, age, inhalation injury, and comorbidity. Superficial and superficial partial thickness burns generally heal without surgery and with minimal scarring, whereas deep dermal and full thickness burns require grafting and are prone to hypertrophic scarring and contracture. Timely resuscitation, early excision, infection control, and rehabilitation markedly improve survival and functional recovery.

Buruli ulcer — Mycobacterium ulcerans infection, Bairnsdale ulcer, Daintree ulcer, Searls ulcer Tropical phagedenic ulcer Cutaneous leishmaniasis Venous or arterial leg ulcer Pyoderma gangrenosum Squamous cell carcinoma (including within chronic ulcers) Other mycobacterial or deep fungal infection Necrotising bacterial infection PCR for the IS2404 sequence on swab or tissue (most sensitive confirmatory test) Ziehl-Neelsen microscopy of swab or tissue for acid-fast bacilli Culture of M. ulcerans (slow-growing, requires lower incubation temperature) Histopathology showing necrosis with clumps of extracellular acid-fast bacilli Imaging to assess deep or bone involvement in extensive disease Assessment of functional impairment where lesions cross joints Caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, an environmental mycobacterium associated with slow-moving or stagnant water; most cases occur in West and Central Africa, with foci in Australia and elsewhere The organism produces the toxin mycolactone, which causes tissue necrosis and local immunosuppression, explaining the characteristically painless lesion Early disease presents as a painless nodule, plaque or oedematous area; without treatment it progresses to a painless ulcer with widely undermined edges The undermined, deeply excavated ulcer with necrotic base extending beyond the visible skin margin is the hallmark of established disease Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR for the IS2404 insertion sequence, supported by microscopy for acid-fast bacilli, culture and histopathology Because lesions are painless, patients often present late with extensive tissue loss, and disease over joints can cause disabling contractures Treatment combines prolonged rifampicin-based anti-mycobacterial therapy with wound care, and surgery or skin grafting for larger lesions; physiotherapy prevents contractures Rapidly enlarging or oedematous lesions suggesting aggressive disease Lesions crossing joints with impending contracture and disability Bone involvement (osteomyelitis) Malignant transformation in a long-standing chronic ulcer Extensive tissue loss requiring reconstructive surgery Attributing a painless chronic ulcer to trivial trauma and delaying diagnosis Underestimating the true extent of necrosis, which extends beyond the visible ulcer margin Relying on surgery alone without anti-mycobacterial therapy, risking recurrence Neglecting physiotherapy, allowing preventable contractures Missing malignant change in long-standing ulcers Mycobacterium ulcerans is acquired from aquatic environments, though the precise mode of transmission remains uncertain. Once in subcutaneous tissue it secretes mycolactone, a diffusible lipid toxin that induces coagulative necrosis of fat and dermis while suppressing local immune and pain responses, accounting for the painless, minimally inflamed lesion. Necrosis spreads laterally in the subcutaneous plane, producing ulcers whose undermined edges extend well beyond the surface defect. As anti-mycobacterial therapy reduces bacillary load, the local immunosuppressive effect lifts and healing can proceed, sometimes with a paradoxical inflammatory reaction. Early nodular disease can heal with antibiotics alone and minimal scarring, but late, extensive ulceration frequently leaves disfiguring scars, contractures and functional disability; relapse is uncommon with adequate combination therapy.

C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary angioedema types I and II) — hereditary angioedema, HAE, C1-INH deficiency, SERPING1, C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, HAE type I, HAE type II Histaminergic (mast-cell/allergic) angio-oedema with or without urticaria ACE-inhibitor-induced angio-oedema Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor (e.g. factor XII or plasminogen mutations) Idiopathic recurrent angio-oedema Gastrointestinal or surgical causes of recurrent abdominal pain Complement C4 level as an initial screen C1-inhibitor antigenic (quantitative) level C1-inhibitor functional assay to distinguish type II C1q level to help separate hereditary from acquired deficiency SERPING1 genetic testing when biochemistry is equivocal or for family studies Investigation for underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease if acquired deficiency is suspected Causes recurrent non-pruritic, non-urticarial angio-oedema of the skin, gastrointestinal tract and upper airway, with attacks that are bradykinin-mediated Type I (about 85 percent) has low antigenic and functional C1 inhibitor; type II has normal or high antigenic level but reduced C1-inhibitor function A persistently low complement C4 is a useful screening clue between and during attacks Attacks lack the wheals of histaminergic angio-oedema and characteristically do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline Laryngeal oedema can be fatal, and unexplained abdominal attacks may mimic a surgical abdomen Attacks are triggered by trauma, dental or surgical procedures, infection, oestrogens and ACE inhibitors Management separates on-demand attack treatment, short-term procedural prophylaxis, and long-term prophylaxis using C1-inhibitor concentrate or bradykinin-pathway-directed agents rather than antihistamines/steroids Laryngeal or tongue swelling with any voice change, stridor or difficulty swallowing Rapidly progressive facial or neck oedema threatening the airway Severe unexplained abdominal attacks that could be mistaken for an acute surgical abdomen Attacks provoked or worsened by an ACE inhibitor or oestrogen therapy Treating bradykinin-mediated attacks as allergic and relying on antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline, which do not work for hereditary angioedema attacks Being falsely reassured by a normal C1-inhibitor antigenic level in type II, where function is the abnormal parameter Continuing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing therapy that provoke attacks Overlooking short-term prophylaxis before dental or surgical procedures Hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by SERPING1 mutations that reduce the quantity (type I) or function (type II) of C1 inhibitor. C1 inhibitor is the principal brake on the contact (kallikrein-kinin) system as well as on the classical complement and fibrinolytic pathways. When it is deficient, unrestrained activation of plasma kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to release bradykinin, a potent vasodilator that increases vascular permeability. The resulting fluid extravasation produces the localised, self-limiting but potentially life-threatening swelling, and the mechanism explains why the swelling is bradykinin-driven rather than histamine-driven and does not respond to antiallergic therapy. With accurate diagnosis and access to modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy the outlook is good and quality of life can be near normal, but untreated laryngeal attacks carry a real risk of asphyxiation, making airway attacks the principal cause of mortality.

acquired partial lipodystrophy Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents Nephrotic-range proteinuria with declining renal function Severe hypertension Progression toward end-stage kidney disease Recurrence in a kidney transplant Misclassifying it as immune-complex membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis without careful immunofluorescence Overlooking an underlying monoclonal gammopathy driving complement dysregulation in older patients Failing to perform a complement functional and genetic workup once the biopsy pattern is recognised Not anticipating disease recurrence in the allograft Confusing it with atypical HUS, which shares complement dysregulation but presents as thrombotic microangiopathy C3 glomerulopathy results from persistent activation and dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway in the fluid phase, leading to deposition of C3 breakdown products within the glomerulus. Normally the alternative-pathway C3 convertase is tightly regulated by proteins such as factor H and factor I; in this disease acquired autoantibodies (notably C3 nephritic factor, which stabilises the convertase) or genetic abnormalities in complement regulators or activators allow uncontrolled convertase activity and continuous C3 turnover. The resulting C3 fragments accumulate along the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium, producing the characteristic complement-dominant, immunoglobulin-poor staining. This drives glomerular inflammation and a membranoproliferative pattern of injury, manifesting clinically as haematuria, proteinuria and progressive loss of kidney function, with correspondingly low circulating C3. C3 glomerulopathy is frequently progressive, with a substantial proportion of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease over years, and it commonly recurs after transplantation; outcome varies with histological severity and the underlying complement abnormality.

definitive CADASIL results from mutations in the NOTCH3 gene, which is expressed in vascular smooth muscle cells of small and medium arteries. or over-replacing glucocorticoid, risking either androgen excess or iatrogenic Cushingoid effects Failing to arrange sensitive multidisciplinary care for ambiguous genitalia 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis caused by variants in CYP11B1, which encodes the enzyme catalysing the final step of cortisol synthesis in the zona fasciculata. Because cortisol cannot be produced efficiently, the loss of negative feedback increases pituitary ACTH secretion, driving adrenal hyperplasia and diverting accumulated precursors down the androgen pathway; the resulting androgen excess produces virilisation, presenting as ambiguous genitalia in genetic females and early virilisation in males. At the same time, the enzyme block causes accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone, a steroid with intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity, which drives sodium retention and volume-dependent, low-renin hypertension often accompanied by hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. This mineralocorticoid excess distinguishes the condition from the salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase form. With glucocorticoid replacement to control ACTH-driven androgen and precursor overproduction, virilisation and hypertension can be managed and growth optimised, though long-standing or poorly controlled disease may leave residual hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency — CYP17A1 deficiency, 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency, combined 17-hydroxylase deficiency, 17-OHD 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency (hypertension but with virilisation) 21-hydroxylase deficiency (salt wasting and virilisation) Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (primary amenorrhoea in 46,XY) Gonadal dysgenesis and other disorders of sex development Primary hyperaldosteronism Constitutional or hypogonadotrophic delayed puberty Adrenal steroid profile showing raised 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone with low cortisol and sex steroids Serum gonadotrophins (elevated) and sex hormones (low) Plasma renin and aldosterone (both typically suppressed) Serum electrolytes for hypokalaemic alkalosis and blood pressure assessment Karyotype and pelvic/gonadal imaging to clarify sexual development Molecular genetic testing of CYP17A1 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by loss-of-function variants in CYP17A1 The enzyme is required for both cortisol synthesis and, through its 17,20-lyase activity, for adrenal and gonadal sex-steroid synthesis, so both cortisol and sex steroids are deficient Steroid production is shunted into the mineralocorticoid pathway, with accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone producing low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis Cortisol is low but overt adrenal crisis is uncommon because corticosterone provides some glucocorticoid activity Sex-steroid deficiency causes absent or delayed puberty; genetic females present with primary amenorrhoea and lack of secondary sexual characteristics, and genetic males (46,XY) typically have undervirilised or female-appearing external genitalia Diagnosis rests on the combination of hypertension with hypokalaemia, low sex steroids and cortisol, raised mineralocorticoid precursors, and elevated gonadotrophins Management combines glucocorticoid replacement to suppress the mineralocorticoid excess and control hypertension with appropriate sex-hormone replacement at puberty Severe hypertension with hypokalaemia in a young person Primary amenorrhoea and absent puberty prompting evaluation Cardiac arrhythmia from profound hypokalaemia Undervirilised genitalia in a 46,XY individual requiring multidisciplinary care Intra-abdominal gonads with potential malignancy risk Missing the diagnosis in a phenotypic female presenting with hypertension and delayed puberty Attributing the hypertension to primary hyperaldosteronism despite suppressed aldosterone Overlooking the need for sex-hormone replacement at the expected age of puberty Failing to identify and manage intra-abdominal gonads in 46,XY individuals Over- or under-replacing glucocorticoid when balancing blood-pressure control against iatrogenic effects 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency results from autosomal recessive variants in CYP17A1, whose enzyme carries out two activities: 17-alpha-hydroxylation, needed for cortisol synthesis, and 17,20-lyase activity, needed to generate androgen and oestrogen precursors in the adrenal and gonad. Loss of both activities lowers cortisol and sex steroids, and the reduced cortisol removes negative feedback so ACTH rises and drives steroidogenesis into the intact mineralocorticoid pathway. Accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, both with mineralocorticoid activity, causes sodium retention, volume expansion and low-renin hypertension with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, while the raised corticosterone provides enough glucocorticoid effect to usually prevent adrenal crisis. Sex-steroid deficiency impairs sexual development, producing hypogonadism with absent puberty and, in 46,XY individuals, undervirilised or female-appearing genitalia because androgen synthesis fails. With glucocorticoid therapy to reverse the mineralocorticoid excess and control blood pressure and potassium, plus sex-hormone replacement to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, patients can do well; fertility is impaired and long-term outcome depends on blood-pressure control and adherence.

Circulatory collapse during intercurrent illness or under-replacement Failure to thrive in infancy Confusing it with 21-hydroxylase deficiency and misinterpreting the steroid profile Failing to recognise that both males and females can have genital abnormalities (undervirilisation versus mild virilisation) Missing impending adrenal crisis and not stress-dosing glucocorticoid during illness dehydrogenase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in HSD3B2, encoding the type 2 isoenzyme that catalyses an early, shared step converting delta-5 steroids to delta-4 steroids in the adrenal and gonad. Because this step lies upstream of the mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid and androgen branches, deficiency reduces aldosterone and cortisol production, leading to salt wasting with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis and to cortisol insufficiency with risk of adrenal crisis. Loss of cortisol feedback raises ACTH and causes accumulation of delta-5 precursors such as dehydroepiandrosterone; these are only weak androgens, so genetic males are incompletely virilised while genetic females may show mild virilisation from peripheral conversion. The elevated delta-5 to delta-4 steroid ratio provides the biochemical signature, and unlike the hypertensive CAH variants there is no mineralocorticoid excess. With prompt glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement and salt supplementation, the salt-wasting crises and cortisol deficiency can be managed and children grow well; long-term outcome depends on adherence, crisis prevention during illness, and appropriate management of the disorder of sex development.

as warfarin Rapidly enlarging necrotic ulcers with surrounding cellulitis and systemic sepsis Severe pain disproportionate to visible skin changes signalling early disease Truncal or proximal (central) lesions carrying a worse prognosis Signs of overwhelming infection in an immunocompromised or dialysis-dependent patient Dismissing severe pain before ulceration appears and delaying diagnosis Continuing warfarin, which aggravates the disease, when an alternative anticoagulant may be appropriate Aggressive debridement or biopsy that can extend non-healing wounds if not carefully weighed Failing to address the underlying calcium-phosphate and parathyroid derangement Calciphylaxis is driven by progressive calcification of the media of small dermal and subcutaneous arterioles, accompanied by intimal fibrosis and microthrombosis, which occludes the vessels and causes ischaemic necrosis of skin and fat. In the uraemic form, chronic kidney disease with a deranged calcium-phosphate product, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and reduced levels of circulating calcification inhibitors allow vascular smooth-muscle cells to transform into an osteoblast-like, calcifying phenotype. Underestimating airway malacia as a cause of respiratory failure Overlooking hearing loss and cervical instability in survivors Campomelic dysplasia arises from haploinsufficiency of SOX9, a transcription factor essential both for chondrocyte differentiation and cartilage matrix gene expression and for testis determination. Disrupted SOX9 function impairs endochondral ossification, producing bowed and hypoplastic bones and a small thorax, while defective testicular development in genetically male fetuses causes the frequent gonadal sex reversal. Airway cartilage deficiency and a narrow chest contribute to the respiratory insufficiency that dominates the neonatal course. The classic form is frequently lethal in the neonatal period owing to respiratory failure, though a milder acampomelic variant and rare longer-term survivors exist. Survivors face significant respiratory, orthopaedic, and developmental morbidity and require multidisciplinary care.

Camurati-Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, TGFB1) — progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, Engelmann disease, TGFB1-related diaphyseal dysplasia, CED Other craniotubular hyperostoses such as sclerosteosis and Van Buchem disease Osteopetrosis Ribbing disease (a related but more localised diaphyseal sclerosis) Hyperostosis from chronic osteomyelitis Paget disease of bone Primary inflammatory myopathy given the muscle weakness Plain radiographs demonstrating symmetrical fusiform diaphyseal cortical thickening Skeletal survey or bone scintigraphy to assess extent and activity Genetic testing for TGFB1 mutations Bone turnover markers and inflammatory markers Cranial imaging when skull-base involvement or cranial neuropathy is suspected Assessment of muscle strength and, where needed, tests to exclude primary myopathy An autosomal dominant sclerosing bone dysplasia caused by activating mutations in TGFB1 Presents in childhood or adolescence with limb pain, a waddling gait, muscle weakness and wasting, and easy fatigability Radiographs show symmetrical fusiform cortical thickening of the diaphyses of the long bones, sparing the epiphyses and metaphyses The skull base may thicken and narrow foramina, occasionally producing cranial neuropathies, headache, and hearing or visual disturbance The proximal myopathy and slender body habitus with reduced muscle bulk can dominate the clinical picture and mimic a primary muscle disorder Bone turnover markers may be raised, and disease activity can wax and wane over time Management is symptomatic; glucocorticoids can relieve bone pain and improve strength in many patients, and physical rehabilitation is important Progressive cranial neuropathy with visual loss, deafness, or facial weakness from skull-base narrowing Features of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus Severe intractable bone pain limiting mobility Rapidly worsening weakness suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Misdiagnosing the proximal myopathy as a primary muscle disease and overlooking the bone dysplasia Attributing headaches and hearing loss to unrelated causes rather than skull-base hyperostosis Failing to recognise the symmetrical diaphyseal pattern that distinguishes it from focal lesions Not offering a trial of glucocorticoids for disabling bone pain when appropriate Camurati-Engelmann disease results from gain-of-function mutations in the gene encoding transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1). The mutations increase TGF-beta signalling, which enhances osteoblast activity and bone formation at the periosteal and endosteal surfaces of the diaphyses. The excessive but disorganised cortical apposition produces symmetrical diaphyseal hyperostosis with narrowing of the medullary canal. Involvement of the skull base can encroach on cranial nerve foramina, and altered marrow space and cytokine signalling may contribute to the anaemia and systemic features seen in some patients. The course is variable and often chronic; many patients have significant bone pain and weakness but a normal lifespan, and symptoms may improve in adulthood or with glucocorticoid therapy, though skull-base disease can cause lasting neurological deficits.

gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis Brain MRI showing diffuse symmetric white matter change MR spectroscopy demonstrating an elevated N-acetylaspartate peak Carrier screening and genetic counselling for at-risk families Developmental and feeding assessments for supportive care An autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by mutations in the ASPA gene resulting in deficiency of aspartoacylase Enzyme deficiency leads to accumulation of N-acetylaspartate, which is measurably elevated in urine and can be detected as a raised NAA peak on MR spectroscopy Classic infantile disease presents in the first months with hypotonia, poor head control, macrocephaly, and progressive developmental failure As disease progresses, hypotonia often gives way to spasticity, with seizures, feeding difficulties, and optic atrophy It is one of the leukodystrophies with increased carrier frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population, making carrier screening relevant in that group MRI shows diffuse, symmetric white matter disease, and elevated N-acetylaspartate on spectroscopy strongly supports the diagnosis Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating elevated urinary N-acetylaspartate and by ASPA gene testing Macrocephaly in an infant with developmental regression should raise suspicion and prompt appropriate metabolic and imaging workup Progressive loss of milestones with seizures in an infant Feeding and swallowing failure risking aspiration and malnutrition Rapidly enlarging head circumference Respiratory compromise in advanced disease Attributing macrocephaly to benign causes without considering a leukodystrophy Overlooking the diagnostic value of urinary N-acetylaspartate and MR spectroscopy Failing to offer carrier screening and counselling in high-risk populations Delaying supportive measures for feeding and seizures Canavan disease arises from biallelic ASPA mutations causing deficiency of aspartoacylase, the enzyme that hydrolyses N-acetylaspartate in the brain. The resulting accumulation of N-acetylaspartate is thought to disturb myelin maintenance and fluid balance, producing spongy vacuolar degeneration of white matter. The intramyelinic oedema and dysmyelination give the characteristic diffuse leukodystrophy and clinical picture of progressive neurological failure with macrocephaly. Classic infantile Canavan disease is progressive with limited life expectancy and no curative therapy, so care is supportive; milder variants with later onset follow a more variable and slower course.

Cancer cachexia — cachexia, cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome, tumour cachexia, wasting syndrome Simple starvation or undernutrition from inadequate intake Sarcopenia of ageing without underlying malignancy Malabsorption or gastrointestinal obstruction Depression causing anorexia and weight loss Hyperthyroidism or other hypermetabolic states Adrenal insufficiency Documentation of weight trajectory and body-mass index over time Assessment of muscle mass and function where available Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and albumin as prognostic indicators Nutritional assessment including intake and symptoms limiting eating Screening for reversible contributors such as nausea, constipation, oral problems, and depression Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome of ongoing loss of skeletal muscle, with or without fat loss, that cannot be fully reversed by conventional nutritional support It is driven by both reduced intake (anorexia) and metabolic derangement, so simply increasing calories does not restore muscle mass A consensus framework stages it as pre-cachexia, cachexia, and refractory cachexia, which guides how aggressively to intervene Diagnostic pointers include weight loss over roughly five percent in six months, or lesser weight loss in the setting of low body-mass index or sarcopenia Systemic inflammation, reflected in raised C-reactive protein and other markers, is central and correlates with worse outcomes Management is multimodal: nutritional support, resistance exercise where feasible, symptom control of nausea and early satiety, and treatment of the underlying cancer when possible In refractory cachexia near the end of life the emphasis shifts from reversing weight loss to comfort, and aggressive artificial feeding usually offers little benefit Family distress about reduced eating is common and benefits from explanation that appetite loss is part of the illness, not a failure of care Rapid, accelerating weight and muscle loss suggesting progressive or refractory disease Profound weakness with inability to maintain basic function Evidence of impending gastrointestinal obstruction limiting intake Severe deconditioning increasing risk of falls, pressure injury, and infection Assuming increased calorie provision alone will reverse muscle loss Pursuing burdensome artificial nutrition in refractory, end-stage disease with no meaningful benefit Overlooking treatable symptoms that limit intake, such as nausea, constipation, and oral candidiasis Failing to address family anxiety about the patient not eating Missing depression as a contributor to anorexia and weight loss Cancer cachexia results from tumour- and host-derived pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-1) and tumour-specific catabolic factors that drive a hypermetabolic, catabolic state. These mediators increase resting energy expenditure, promote skeletal muscle proteolysis and lipolysis, induce insulin resistance, and act centrally to suppress appetite. The net effect is a negative energy and protein balance dominated by muscle wasting that persists despite feeding, distinguishing cachexia from simple starvation in which muscle is relatively spared. Cachexia is a marker of advanced disease and independently predicts reduced tolerance of anticancer treatment, poorer quality of life, and shorter survival. Refractory cachexia, typically in the setting of advanced, treatment-unresponsive cancer with a short prognosis, is not reversible, and care goals appropriately shift toward comfort.

Cancer pain management — malignant pain, cancer-related pain, palliative pain control, oncological pain Pain from a non-malignant comorbidity such as osteoarthritis or neuropathy Treatment-related pain (post-surgical, post-radiation, chemotherapy-induced neuropathy) Pathological fracture through a bony metastasis Infection-related pain Oncological emergency such as spinal cord compression or bowel obstruction presenting with pain Structured pain assessment characterising site, severity, quality, temporal pattern, and impact on function Distinction of nociceptive versus neuropathic Breakthrough or incident pain is managed with short-acting rescue analgesia layered on top of the baseline regimen Opioid rotation, switching from one opioid to another, can improve the balance of analgesia and side effects when a patient has poor response or troublesome toxicity Anticipate and prevent predictable opioid effects, especially constipation, which requires prophylactic laxatives, while nausea and sedation often ease with time In older adults, reduced renal function and heightened sensitivity mean starting low, titrating slowly, and being cautious with renally cleared opioids and their metabolites Non-pharmacological measures, disease-directed treatment such as palliative radiotherapy for bone pain, and interventional techniques including nerve blocks complement drug therapy Total pain acknowledges that physical, psychological, social, and spiritual distress interact, so addressing suffering broadly improves pain control Signs of opioid toxicity such as excessive sedation, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, or slowed respiration requiring urgent dose review New back pain with neurological signs suggesting malignant spinal cord compression Sudden severe pain suggesting pathological fracture or visceral perforation Rapidly escalating opioid requirement indicating disease progression or an emergent complication Failing to prescribe prophylactic laxatives when starting an opioid Under-dosing because of undue fear of addiction or respiratory depression in appropriate palliative use Relying on opioids alone for neuropathic pain that needs adjuvants Ignoring reduced renal clearance in older adults, risking accumulation and toxicity Treating physical pain while neglecting the psychological and spiritual dimensions of suffering Cancer pain may be nociceptive (somatic pain from bone or soft-tissue involvement, or visceral pain from organ infiltration and stretch) or neuropathic (from tumour compression or infiltration of nerves, or from treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation). Persistent nociceptive input sensitises peripheral nociceptors and central pathways, producing hyperalgesia and allodynia. Opioids act at central and peripheral opioid receptors to modulate pain transmission, while adjuvants target neuropathic mechanisms, inflammation, or specific complications, and the multiplicity of mechanisms underpins the use of combination therapy. Most cancer pain can be well controlled with systematic assessment and stepwise pharmacological management, allowing meaningful quality of life. Poorly controlled or neuropathic pain, or pain complicating advanced disease, may be more difficult and often requires specialist palliative input and multimodal or interventional approaches.

mould infection in the neutropenic host Non-infective causes of persistent fever in the critically ill Contaminant growth in blood cultures (rare with Candida and should not be assumed) Drug fever or endophthalmitis Echocardiography and imaging for deep-seated foci when candidemia is persistent Culture of the catheter tip after removal and assessment of other potential sources The presence of Candida species in the bloodstream and a leading cause of healthcare-associated bloodstream infection in critically ill and immunocompromised patients Major risk factors include central venous catheters, broad-spectrum antibiotics, total parenteral nutrition, abdominal surgery, neutropenia, and prolonged ICU stay Candida albicans remains common, but non-albicans species with variable azole susceptibility, including the multidrug-resistant Candida auris, are increasingly important Any positive blood culture for Candida should be regarded as significant and never dismissed as a contaminant Echinocandins are generally favoured as initial therapy in unstable or seriously ill patients, with de-escalation to an azole guided by species and susceptibility Prompt removal or exchange of infected intravascular catheters is a key part of source control Dilated fundoscopic examination is advised to detect ocular involvement (chorioretinitis or endophthalmitis) that can affect treatment duration Follow-up blood cultures to confirm clearance, and evaluation for endocarditis or deep-seated foci in persistent candidemia, are recommended Septic shock or haemodynamic instability from candidemia requiring urgent resuscitation and source control Persistent positive cultures despite therapy suggesting endocarditis, a retained infected catheter, or another deep focus Ocular involvement threatening vision Isolation of Candida auris or other resistant species with implications for treatment and infection control Dismissing a positive Candida blood culture as a contaminant Delaying effective antifungal therapy while awaiting species identification Leaving an infected central catheter in place Omitting fundoscopy and follow-up cultures, missing ocular disease or persistent infection Candida species are common commensals of the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and mucosa. Disruption of these barriers, by mucosal breakdown, surgery, or indwelling devices, together with impaired host defences from neutropenia, immunosuppression, or broad-spectrum antibiotics that eliminate competing bacterial flora, allows Candida to translocate into the bloodstream or seed from a catheter biofilm. Once in the circulation, the organism can disseminate haematogenously to the eyes, heart valves, bones, and deep organs, producing metastatic foci that are difficult to eradicate without prolonged therapy and source control. Candidemia carries high attributable mortality, especially with delayed effective antifungal therapy, failure to remove infected catheters, persistent fungaemia, or severe underlying illness; earlier appropriate treatment and source control improve survival.

Candidiasis — Candida infection, invasive candidiasis, candidemia Dermatophytosis (tinea) on glabrous skin (Chap. 60, p.432) Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor due to Malassezia furfur (Chap. 60, p.432) Lichen planus / oral leukoplakia for oral white lesions Other invasive fungal infections in neutropenia: invasive aspergillosis and other molds (Chap. 79, p.578) Invasive aspergillosis and other molds (necrotic nodules) in immunocompromised hosts (Chap. 79, p.578; rash chapter) Disseminated cryptococcosis (molluscum-like nodular lesions) (rash chapter) Mucormycosis (rash chapter) Bacterial/septic endophthalmitis, including from endocarditis (Roth's spots also in leukemia, diabetes) (Chap. 34, p.269) KOH preparation of skin/mucosal scrapings demonstrating yeast and pseudohyphae for mucocutaneous candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.433) Culture of lesional material (Chap. 60, p.433) Blood cultures for candidemia (note insensitivity; see pitfalls) (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79) Dilated funduscopic examination to detect candidal endophthalmitis in candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269) Erythema nodosum (tender lower-extremity nodules) for nodular eruptions (rash chapter) Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) (rash chapter) Psoriasis / eczema in intertriginous areas Candidiasis spans a spectrum: mucocutaneous disease (oral thrush, esophageal, vulvovaginal, intertriginous, paronychia/onycholysis) that is usually localized, versus rare systemic, life-threatening invasive disease such as candidemia and disseminated candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.432-433). The usual causative organism is Candida albicans; these yeasts are normal saprophytic inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract that overgrow and cause disease when host defenses are altered (Chap. 60, p.432-433). Oral candidiasis (thrush) appears as white plaques on the tongue or buccal mucosa; angular fissured macerated lesions at the mouth corners (perleche) are seen with poorly fitting dentures and may be candidal (Chap. 60, p.432-433). Intertriginous candidal lesions are characteristically edematous, erythematous, and scaly with scattered 'satellite pustules'; in males the penis, scrotum, and inner thighs are often involved (Chap. 60, p.432-433). In contrast to dermatophyte infections, candidal infections are frequently painful and accompanied by a marked inflammatory response (Chap. 60, p.432-433). Disseminated candidiasis (often due to Candida tropicalis) may present with a triad of fever, myalgias, and eruptive nodules; hematogenous cutaneous disease shows multiple raised papules with systemic signs (rash chapter, p.190; Chap. 79, p.621). Candidemia and chronic disseminated candidiasis are recognized complications in neutropenic patients because Candida species are endogenous gastrointestinal flora (Chap. 79, p.578). Candidemia is a recognized cause of endogenous endophthalmitis from hematogenous seeding; Roth's spots and retinal hemorrhages were illustrated in a liver transplant patient with candidemia from immunosuppression (Chap. 34, p.269). Candidemia or suspected disseminated candidiasis in a neutropenic or immunosuppressed host (Chap. 79, p.578) Visual loss, ocular pain, or floaters in a patient with candidemia or indwelling IV catheters (endophthalmitis) (Chap. 34, p.269) Fever, myalgias, and eruptive cutaneous nodules suggesting disseminated candidiasis (rash chapter, p.190) Presence of an indwelling intravascular catheter or central line in a patient with candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79) Systemic therapy is usually reserved for immunosuppressed patients or those with chronic/recurrent disease who fail topical therapy, NOT routine mucocutaneous cases (Chap. 60, p.433). Oral nystatin is effective ONLY for candidiasis of the gastrointestinal tract, not for systemic disease (Chap. 60, p.433). Failure to remove predisposing factors (broad-spectrum antibiotics, chronic moisture/maceration) leads to treatment failure (Chap. 60, p.433). In endogenous endophthalmitis, visual loss may sometimes be the ONLY symptom even without prominent ocular pain or injection (Chap. 34, p.269). Candida species (most often C. albicans) are normal saprophytic commensals of the gastrointestinal tract and skin. They overgrow and become pathogenic when local or systemic host defenses are disrupted, e.g., by broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, diabetes mellitus, or immunosuppression. Mucocutaneous disease results from overgrowth at moist, macerated surfaces; invasive disease arises when the organism gains bloodstream access, frequently via intravascular catheters or the gut in neutropenic hosts (endogenous flora), producing candidemia and hematogenous (disseminated) seeding to organs, skin, and the eye (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578). Mucocutaneous candidiasis is generally benign and responds to removal of predisposing factors plus topical or, when needed, systemic antifungal therapy. Systemic involvement is rare but life-threatening; candidemia and chronic disseminated candidiasis are serious complications in neutropenic and immunosuppressed patients (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578). Harrison frames candidiasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading scale: localized mucocutaneous disease (oral, esophageal, vulvovaginal, intertriginous, cutaneous) versus rare systemic/invasive disease (candidemia, chronic disseminated/hepatosplenic candidiasis). Invasive disease risk rises with prolonged profound neutropenia (ANC <500/uL) (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578).

Cannabis and Cannabis Use Disorder — Marijuana use disorder, CUD, Cannabis dependence, Marijuana abuse Primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) versus cannabis-induced psychosis Other substance use disorders (alcohol, nicotine, opioids, stimulants) often co-occurring Primary anxiety, depressive, or panic disorder versus cannabis-induced symptoms Cyclic vomiting syndrome versus cannabis hyperemesis syndrome Other causes of impaired cognition, low IQ, or poor school performance in adolescents Urine immunoassay/confirmatory testing for 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), the inactive long-lived metabolite DSM-5 criteria-based clinical assessment for cannabis use disorder severity Screening for comorbid substance use (alcohol, nicotine, opioids, stimulants) and for psychiatric comorbidity (psychosis, depression, suicidality) In pregnancy: assessment of fetal growth given association with lower birth weight and preterm delivery Cyclic vomiting syndrome (mimics cannabis hyperemesis syndrome) Primary schizophrenia or other psychotic disorder (mimics cannabis-induced psychosis) Primary anxiety/panic disorder (mimics acute high-dose cannabis intoxication) EVALI (e-cigarette/vaping product use-associated lung injury) linked to vitamin E acetate diluent in black-market THC e-liquids Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive substances; surveys cited estimate tens of millions of monthly users in the U.S., including a substantial number of adolescents and young adults aged 12-25. Marijuana is legally distinguished from hemp by Delta-9-THC content: material exceeding 0.3% Delta-9-THC by dry weight is marijuana, while 0.3% or less is hemp; the principal euphoric and medicinal effects are mediated by Delta-9-THC acting on type 1 cannabinoid receptors (CB1R). Product potency has risen sharply: flower can contain 20-30% Delta-9-THC, vape concentrates are advertised up to ~75%, and solid extracts ('shatter') up to ~95%, though many high claims appear exaggerated; higher potency is linked to greater addiction and psychosis risk. Inhalation (smoking, vaping, 'dabbing') gives rapid, highly bioavailable absorption with quick onset, conditions associated with increased addiction risk; edibles have slower, less predictable onset and carry a higher risk of accidental overdose, particularly in children and inexperienced users. Following smoking, plasma Delta-9-THC peaks within 5-10 minutes, but a hysteresis exists because brain levels keep rising during the early distribution (alpha) phase (t1/2 ~6 min) even as plasma falls; subjective peak effects occur at 20-30 minutes and total effect lasts roughly 4-8 hours. Urine drug testing detects the inactive metabolite 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), whose terminal half-life is ~20 to 35+ hours, so cannabis remains detectable for days in occasional users and weeks in frequent users with saturated fat stores. Regular use produces tolerance, so a given plasma Delta-9-THC level does not reliably predict impairment, which has hampered regulation of cannabis-impaired driving; Delta-9-THC nonetheless impairs judgment, motor coordination, and reaction time, increasing crash risk. Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is a DSM-5 diagnosis defined by a problematic pattern of use causing clinically significant impairment or distress; criteria include craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to meet role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking. The withdrawal syndrome peaks within 1-3 days of stopping and manifests as anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, depression, and reduced appetite; most symptoms resolve within about 2 weeks, but insomnia often persists longer and may drive relapse. Chronic high-dose use can cause cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, presenting as recurrent cycles of severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and is a growing reason for ED visits and hospitalization. High-potency cannabis (>10% THC) can trigger acute psychotic episodes even on first exposure; these are usually transient but may become chronic with continued use and can trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals. Synthetic Delta-9-THC (dronabinol) is approved for chemotherapy-induced nausea and appetite stimulation, and a Delta-9-THC:CBD formulation is approved in some countries for chronic pain and MS-related spasticity (efficacy in MS largely based on patient report); there are currently no FDA-approved medications specifically for CUD. Acute psychosis, severe anxiety, paranoia, or panic after high-potency or high-dose exposure Tachycardia with acute cannabis toxicity, especially in children or naive users who accidentally ingest edibles Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome with intractable vomiting, dehydration, and abdominal pain Depression and suicidality, particularly with adolescent onset of use Respiratory symptoms suggesting EVALI in vaping users Use in pregnancy given fetal growth and neurodevelopmental concerns Assuming a plasma Delta-9-THC level reliably reflects impairment; tolerance breaks this correlation and complicates impaired-driving assessment. Underestimating edible dosing: delayed and variable onset (amplified by fatty meals increasing bioavailability 200-400%) leads naive users to redose and overdose. Overstating the clinical role of minor cannabinoids (e.g., CBD) or terpenes at the concentrations found in marijuana, where evidence of relevance is limited and largely unproven. Trusting product potency labels, which testing has shown to be frequently inflated. Perceiving intoxicating hemp-derived products (e.g., Delta-8-THC and others) as safe or 'legal'; some such products can be considerably more potent than Delta-9-THC. Overlooking EVALI risk historically tied to vitamin E acetate diluent rather than cannabis itself. Delta-9-THC is mainly a partial agonist at G protein-coupled cannabinoid receptors CB1R and CB2R, with euphorigenic effects mediated through CB1Rs on excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic interneurons and glial cells in brain regions processing stress, mood, and reward. These receptors are effectors of the endocannabinoid system (ECS), physiologically driven by endogenous ligands 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG, a full agonist) and anandamide (a partial agonist) that are synthesized and degraded on demand to give temporally and regionally precise modulation. Exogenous cannabinoids, defined by dose and duration rather than this 'just-in-time' synaptic signaling, disrupt ECS neuroregulation. Reward is thought to be mediated by modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic activity in the ventral tegmental area, from which dopaminergic neurons project to the nucleus accumbens where rewarding experiences are reinforced; anxiolytic effects are mediated via the amygdala. Regular use is associated with broad but reversible reduction in cannabinoid receptor density (recovering by ~28 days of abstinence). Perturbation of ECS signaling during early fetal development can affect neuronal development, migration, and connectivity. Most acute psychotic episodes are transient, but regular use can render them chronic, and cannabis may trigger or worsen schizophrenia in vulnerable individuals; adolescent and higher-frequency, higher-potency use carries the strongest associations with later psychotic disorder. Receptor downregulation is largely reversible, recovering toward control levels within about 28 days of abstinence. Withdrawal generally resolves within roughly 2 weeks, although insomnia may persist and promote relapse. Earlier age of initiation, higher use frequency, and higher-THC products increase the risk of developing CUD and of progression to other substance use disorders. Adolescent use has been associated with lower grades, lower IQ, and higher school dropout, though causation is not established. Cannabis use disorder is diagnosed and graded by DSM-5 criteria (problematic use pattern causing clinically significant impairment or distress), with features including craving, tolerance, a withdrawal syndrome, and failure to fulfill role obligations from recurrent use and drug seeking.

with cyclical vomiting The disorder is a problematic pattern of cannabis use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress, graded by severity according to features such as impaired control, craving, tolerance, and continued use despite harm Intoxication features include conjunctival injection, increased appetite, dry mouth, tachycardia, and impaired coordination, judgement, and short-term memory A recognised withdrawal syndrome occurs, with irritability, anxiety, sleep disturbance, vivid dreams, reduced appetite, and restlessness that can drive continued use Heavy or early-onset use is associated with increased risk of psychotic disorders, particularly in genetically vulnerable individuals, and can worsen anxiety and mood High-potency products and concentrates increase the likelihood of adverse effects and of developing a use disorder Management is predominantly psychosocial, including motivational interviewing, cognitive behavioural therapy, and contingency management, as no specific pharmacotherapy is firmly established Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, with cyclical vomiting relieved by hot bathing, is an increasingly recognised complication of chronic heavy use Assess and address comorbid mental illness, since cannabis is frequently used to self-medicate anxiety, insomnia, or low mood Emergence of psychotic symptoms, particularly in adolescents or those with a family history Suicidal ideation, especially with comorbid depression Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from cannabinoid hyperemesis Escalating use with functional decline in education, work, or relationships Dismissing cannabis use as harmless and missing a genuine use disorder Overlooking cannabis as a contributor to anxiety, low mood, or psychosis Missing cannabinoid hyperemesis and attributing vomiting to other causes Neglecting the recognised withdrawal syndrome that maintains use Failing to address comorbid psychiatric illness driving self-medication Cannabis use disorder involves the endocannabinoid system, with delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol acting as a partial agonist at CB1 receptors and modulating dopaminergic reward signalling in the mesolimbic pathway. Chronic exposure produces receptor downregulation and neuroadaptation underlying tolerance and withdrawal, and heavy adolescent use during neurodevelopment may have lasting effects on cognition and psychosis risk, modulated by genetic and environmental vulnerability. Cannabis use disorder often follows a chronic course, particularly with early-onset heavy use, but many people reduce or stop use with psychosocial treatment and maturation. Prognosis is better with later onset, lower potency use, strong social support, and treatment of comorbid disorders, and worse with adolescent onset, high-potency use, and untreated psychiatric comorbidity.

hypertensive small-vessel disease Multiple sclerosis and demyelinating leukoencephalopathy Mitochondrial cytopathies Other hereditary leukoencephalopathies Cerebral amyloid angiopathy Brain MRI to demonstrate diffuse white-matter change and lacunar infarcts HTRA1 genetic testing as the confirmatory investigation Spinal imaging documenting early and severe degenerative disc and spondylotic disease Detailed family history to identify recessive inheritance and consanguinity Exclusion of conventional vascular and demyelinating causes Autosomal recessive small-vessel arteriopathy caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HTRA1 gene Distinguished from CADASIL by the non-neurological triad of premature alopecia and disabling spondylosis or disc disease Presents in early adulthood with subcortical strokes, progressive gait disturbance, and cognitive decline Early-onset baldness and low back pain from lumbar spondylosis often precede the neurological events MRI shows diffuse leukoencephalopathy and lacunar infarcts similar to other hereditary small-vessel disease Confirmed by HTRA1 genetic testing, with a recessive inheritance pattern distinguishing it from CADASIL No disease-specific treatment exists, so care focuses on symptom control and vascular risk management Young-onset stroke with premature alopecia and severe spinal degeneration Progressive gait failure and cognitive decline New focal neurological deficits Family history suggesting recessive inheritance Overlooking the diagnostic clues of early alopecia and spondylosis in a young stroke patient Confusing it with CADASIL and missing the recessive inheritance pattern Attributing the leukoencephalopathy to demyelination and giving inappropriate therapy Failing to counsel families about the recessive genetic risk CARASIL is caused by biallelic mutations in HTRA1, a serine protease that normally represses transforming growth factor-beta signalling. Loss of HTRA1 function dysregulates this pathway and impairs extracellular matrix homeostasis in the walls of small cerebral arteries, leading to intimal thickening, loss of smooth muscle cells, and hyaline arteriosclerosis. The resulting non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy causes chronic ischaemia and a diffuse leukoencephalopathy, while the same signalling disturbance contributes to the associated alopecia and degenerative spondylosis. CARASIL is relentlessly progressive, with accumulating motor and cognitive disability from early adulthood and shortened life expectancy; there is no treatment that alters the underlying arteriopathy.

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency — CPS1 deficiency, carbamyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency, CPSD, hyperammonaemia due to CPS1 deficiency N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency (near-identical biochemistry, carglumic acid responsive) Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (raised orotic acid, X-linked) Citrullinaemia type 1 and argininosuccinic aciduria Organic acidaemias causing secondary hyperammonaemia Fatty acid oxidation disorders with hyperammonaemia Transient hyperammonaemia of the newborn Neonatal sepsis or hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Urgent plasma ammonia during suspected crises Plasma amino acids (low citrulline and arginine, raised glutamine) Urine orotic acid (characteristically low) Blood gas showing respiratory alkalosis with hyperammonaemia CPS1 gene sequencing for confirmation Carglumic acid trial to help distinguish from NAGS deficiency Plasma acylcarnitines/organic acids to exclude secondary hyperammonaemia Urea cycle disorder caused by biallelic CPS1 variants affecting the first, rate-limiting mitochondrial step of ureagenesis Severe neonatal form presents with rapidly progressive hyperammonaemic encephalopathy: poor feeding, vomiting, tachypnoea, hypotonia, seizures and coma Biochemistry shows marked hyperammonaemia with low/normal citrulline, low arginine, raised glutamine and characteristically low urine orotic acid Low orotic aciduria distinguishes it (and NAGS deficiency) from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, in which orotic acid is high Milder, later-onset presentations feature episodic hyperammonaemia, protein intolerance and neurocognitive problems Biochemically indistinguishable from NAGS deficiency, so a carglumic acid trial and gene testing are used to separate the two Confirm with CPS1 sequencing; enzyme assay requires liver tissue and is now rarely needed Acute management is emergency ammonia removal (haemodialysis/haemofiltration if severe), nitrogen scavengers, arginine and protein restriction; liver transplantation is definitive for severe disease Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency dialysis Cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure from severe hyperammonaemia Rapidly rising ammonia with deteriorating consciousness at any age Decompensation during catabolic illness, high protein intake or surgery Failure of ammonia to fall despite scavenger and dietary measures Delaying ammonia measurement and dialysis in an encephalopathic neonate Confusing CPS1 with OTC deficiency by not checking orotic acid Not separating CPS1 from NAGS deficiency, missing the carglumic-acid-responsive disorder Under-dialysing when ammonia is dangerously high and scavengers alone are inadequate Failing to establish an emergency regimen and long-term dietary/scavenger plan Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 is the mitochondrial enzyme that initiates the urea cycle by condensing ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, a reaction that absolutely requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator. When CPS1 activity is deficient, waste nitrogen cannot enter the urea cycle, so ammonia accumulates to toxic levels while downstream urea cycle intermediates (citrulline, arginine) are low. Because carbamoyl phosphate is not overproduced, it is not shunted into the pyrimidine pathway, so orotic acid excretion remains low, a key feature shared with NAGS deficiency and distinguishing both from the more distal OTC deficiency. Hyperammonaemia is directly neurotoxic, causing cerebral oedema and encephalopathy, particularly in the neonate. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The severe neonatal form carries a high risk of death or permanent neurological disability related to the depth and duration of hyperammonaemia, whereas milder late-onset disease can be managed medically; liver transplantation corrects the hepatic enzyme defect and can prevent further crises.

Carbon monoxide poisoning — CO poisoning, carbon monoxide toxicity, carboxyhaemoglobinaemia Viral illness or gastroenteritis Migraine or tension headache Cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation) Diabetic or other metabolic coma Acute coronary syndrome Blood carboxyhaemoglobin level by co-oximetry (venous or arterial) Arterial blood gas with metabolic acidosis and lactate ECG and cardiac biomarkers to detect myocardial ischaemia Neuroimaging in severe cases (basal ganglia changes) Pregnancy test in women of childbearing age given fetal risk Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and causing profound tissue hypoxia despite a normal arterial oxygen tension Symptoms are non-specific (headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion) and are frequently misdiagnosed as viral illness or food poisoning, especially when several household members are affected Standard pulse oximetry is misleading because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin; a co-oximeter or blood carboxyhaemoglobin level is required The classic cherry-red skin appearance is uncommon and unreliable, and its absence does not exclude poisoning The cornerstone of treatment is high-flow 100 percent oxygen, which greatly shortens the elimination half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is considered for severe poisoning (loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac involvement, pregnancy, or very high levels) to reduce delayed neurological sequelae Delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome (cognitive impairment, movement disorders, personality change) can develop days to weeks after apparent recovery Suspect concurrent cyanide poisoning in victims of smoke inhalation from enclosed-space fires Any loss of consciousness, seizure, or focal neurological deficit Chest pain, arrhythmia, or ECG evidence of ischaemia Metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate indicating severe tissue hypoxia Pregnancy, as the fetus is disproportionately affected Multiple people from the same environment falling ill simultaneously Trusting a normal pulse oximeter reading and normal arterial oxygen tension to exclude poisoning Attributing symptoms to a viral illness and discharging the patient back to the source Relying on the cherry-red sign, which is usually absent Overlooking coexisting cyanide toxicity in fire victims Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion. It binds haemoglobin with roughly 200-250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, which both reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve leftward, impairing oxygen release to tissues. CO also binds myoglobin and inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and oxidative stress. The brain and heart, with high oxygen demand, are most vulnerable, and a lipid peroxidation and inflammatory cascade underlies the delayed neurological injury. Mild poisoning usually resolves fully with oxygen, but severe exposure can cause death or lasting neurological and cardiac damage; delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae may appear after seemingly complete recovery, and early high-flow or hyperbaric oxygen reduces this risk.

while significant valve disease may require surgical valve replacement Progressive right heart failure with ascites and oedema Carcinoid crisis with flushing, haemodynamic instability, and bronchospasm, especially around procedures Severe symptomatic valve dysfunction requiring surgical evaluation Rapidly rising cardiac biomarkers indicating advancing cardiac disease Attributing right heart failure to more common causes and missing an underlying neuroendocrine tumour Not screening for cardiac involvement in patients with established carcinoid syndrome Failing to prevent and treat carcinoid crisis around surgery and interventions Delaying valve surgery until right ventricular function is irreversibly impaired Metastatic neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours, typically of midgut origin with hepatic metastases, secrete serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation. These substances stimulate fibroblast proliferation and deposition of fibrous tissue on the endocardium and valve leaflets, predominantly on the right side of the heart. The resulting plaque-like fibrosis retracts and immobilises the tricuspid and pulmonary valves, causing regurgitation and stenosis that lead to volume overload and right ventricular failure. Pulmonary inactivation of serotonin largely protects the left heart. Cardiac involvement is a major determinant of survival in carcinoid syndrome and historically indicated advanced disease with a poor outlook, but somatostatin analogue therapy, tumour-directed treatment, and timely valve surgery have improved outcomes.

Carcinoma of Unknown Primary — CUP, Cancer of Unknown Primary, Occult primary malignancy, Metastatic carcinoma of unknown origin Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (commonly misdiagnosed as liver-presenting CUP) (Harrison 22e p.731) Extragonadal germ cell tumor in men with poorly/undifferentiated midline adenopathy (Harrison 22e pp.732, 735) Occult breast carcinoma in women with isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e pp.732, 735) Primary peritoneal papillary serous carcinoma versus colon or pancreaticobiliary cancer in women with peritoneal carcinomatosis (Harrison 22e p.735) Prostate carcinoma in men with blastic bone-only metastases and elevated PSA (Harrison 22e p.735) Lung or head-and-neck primary in older smokers presenting with mediastinal adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.735) Contrast CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the standard baseline workup in all CUP patients absent contraindication (Harrison 22e p.732) Thorough history (risk factors, prior surgeries, family history) and physical exam including digital rectal exam in men and breast/pelvic exam in women (Harrison 22e p.731) Mammography (and breast MRI if mammogram/ultrasound negative) in women with metastatic adenocarcinoma, especially isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.732) For cervical squamous CUP: CT/MRI plus laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, upper endoscopy, and consideration of staging tonsillectomy (Harrison 22e p.732) 18-FDG-PET, most useful in squamous cervical CUP (identifies a head/neck primary in about 21-30%) and in solitary metastasis or bone-metastasis candidates for aggressive multimodality therapy (Harrison 22e p.732) Serum PSA in men with adenocarcinoma and osteoblastic metastasis; beta-hCG and AFP for suspected extragonadal germ cell tumor (Harrison 22e pp.731-732) Detailed pathology with hematoxylin-eosin and a tiered IHC panel (e.g., CK7/CK20, TTF-1, CDX-2, GCDFP-15/GATA3, PSA, thyroglobulin) plus molecular/tissue-of-origin profiling and next-generation sequencing (Harrison 22e pp.732-734) Endoscopy/colonoscopy/bronchoscopy reserved for symptomatic patients or those with findings suggesting high diagnostic yield (Harrison 22e p.732) Lymphoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic sarcoma (excluded from CUP because they have specific histology/staging) (Harrison 22e p.731) Peritoneal mesothelioma mislabeled as peritoneal carcinomatosis (calretinin/D2-40 positive; BerEp4/MOC-31 negative) (Harrison 22e p.735) CUP is a biopsy-proven malignancy whose anatomic site of origin stays unidentified despite a standardized, detailed diagnostic workup; it ranks among the 10 most frequently diagnosed cancers worldwide and accounts for roughly 3-5% of all malignancies (Harrison 22e p.731). Most authorities restrict the CUP label to epithelial or undifferentiated cancers and exclude lymphoma, metastatic melanoma, and metastatic sarcoma, since those have distinct histology and stage-based management even without an identified primary (Harrison 22e p.731). On light microscopy about 60-65% of CUP is adenocarcinoma and roughly 5% is squamous cell carcinoma, with the remaining 30-35% being poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma/carcinoma or poorly differentiated neoplasm; neuroendocrine tumors make up about 2% (Harrison 22e p.732). Most serum tumor markers (CEA, CA-125, CA 19-9, CA 15-3) are nonspecific and do not localize the primary; in contrast, PSA tissue/serum staining and thyroglobulin are among the most specific markers but have low yield because prostate and thyroid cancers rarely present as CUP (Harrison 22e pp.731-732). CK7 and CK20 cytokeratin patterns help narrow the putative primary: CK7 marks lung, ovary, endometrium, breast, and upper GI/pancreaticobiliary tumors, while CK20 is expressed in GI epithelium, urothelium, and Merkel cells (Harrison 22e p.733). TTF-1 nuclear staining is positive in about 68% of lung adenocarcinomas and roughly 25% of squamous lung cancers and helps distinguish a lung primary from metastatic adenocarcinoma in pleural, mediastinal, or parenchymal sites (Harrison 22e p.733). Comprehensive genomic profiling shows about 85% of CUP samples carry at least one clinically relevant genomic alteration, averaging about 4.2 alterations per tumor; the most common are TP53 (about 55%), KRAS (about 20%), CDKN2A (about 19%), and ARID1A (about 11%) (Harrison 22e pp.733-734). Tissue-agnostic biomarkers matter in a minority of CUP cases: MSI-high / mismatch-repair-deficient tumors and high tumor mutational burden tumors, as well as NTRK fusion-positive tumors, identify candidates for established histology-agnostic therapy (Harrison 22e p.734). Adequate tissue acquisition (preferably excisional or core needle biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration alone) is critical, both for histology/IHC and for molecular profiling that can suggest a primary and actionable biomarkers (Harrison 22e p.732). Liver is a common site of CUP presentation, so intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is frequently misdiagnosed as CUP; cholangiocarcinoma incidence is rising while CUP incidence is declining, partly due to improved molecular diagnostics and clinician awareness (Harrison 22e p.731). DNA methylation profiling predicted a primary in about 87% of 216 CUP patients in one study, and tissue-of-origin classifier assays suggest a plausible primary in roughly 70-80% of patients, though accuracy cannot be fully verified because the true primary is by definition unconfirmed (Harrison 22e pp.733-734). Latent primary cancers (a new primary emerging after months to years) are uncommon with modern imaging, occurring in 5% or fewer of CUP patients, typically in indolent presentations or highly treatment-responsive disease (Harrison 22e p.732). Liver, brain, or adrenal metastatic involvement, which carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.735) Disseminated disease with two or more involved sites (Harrison 22e pp.734-735) Poor performance status and elevated serum LDH, which are adverse prognostic factors (Harrison 22e p.734) Peritoneal carcinomatosis from metastatic adenocarcinoma, raising concern for gastric, appendiceal, colon, or pancreaticobiliary primaries (Harrison 22e p.735) No IHC stain is 100% sensitive or specific; under- or overinterpretation should be avoided, and poor differentiation reduces sensitivity even of hallmark markers (Harrison 22e p.732). CDX-2 positivity, while used for GI adenocarcinomas, can also occur in tumors with enteric/mucinous differentiation from other sites such as mucinous ovarian cancer (Harrison 22e p.733). Tissue antigenicity and IHC interpretation are affected by antigen retrieval, fixation/processing, observer variability, antibody performance, and tissue heterogeneity or inadequacy from small biopsies (Harrison 22e p.733). Pathologic features should not always override clinical or radiologic findings when deciding to test for therapeutic biomarkers such as EGFR, ALK, or HER2 (Harrison 22e p.733). More IHC stains are not necessarily better; staining must be interpreted alongside clinical presentation and imaging, with close clinician-pathologist communication (Harrison 22e p.732). Not all peritoneal carcinomatosis in women is primary peritoneal serous carcinoma; careful pathology can reveal a colon or pancreaticobiliary profile or mislabeled mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.735). Two randomized trials of gene-expression-directed site-specific therapy versus empiric chemotherapy failed to show a significant survival benefit, so molecular classifier results must be interpreted cautiously (Harrison 22e pp.733-734). The reasons cancers present without an identifiable primary remain unclear. One hypothesis is that the primary tumor regresses after seeding metastases or stays too small to detect, possibly contained or eliminated by host defenses including the immune system. Alternatively, CUP may reflect a distinct malignant event producing increased metastatic spread or survival relative to the primary; whether CUP metastases represent a genetically and phenotypically unique clone is unresolved. Searches for a unique CUP signature have been unrevealing: aneuploidy occurs in about 70% of metastatic adenocarcinoma/undifferentiated CUP, and overexpression of RAS, BCL2 (about 40%), HER2 (about 11%), and P53 (about 26-53%) is seen but is shared with many other malignancies. Adenocarcinoma CUP is more often driven by RTK/Ras/MAPK pathway alterations than non-adenocarcinoma CUP. No distinct molecular signature has been established (Harrison 22e pp.731-734). Median survival for most patients with disseminated CUP is about 6-10 months, and the prognosis for advanced disease remains poor with early resistance to available cytotoxic therapy. Prognosis is heterogeneous: favorable subsets (e.g., women with isolated axillary adenopathy treated as breast cancer, women with primary peritoneal serous carcinoma treated as ovarian cancer, men with midline poorly differentiated carcinoma resembling germ cell tumor, squamous cervical adenopathy, solitary metastatic sites, low-grade neuroendocrine tumors, and men with blastic bone metastases and elevated PSA) can achieve prolonged survival and occasionally cure. Recognized prognostic factors include performance status, site and number of metastases, response to therapy, and serum LDH; prognostic models (Culine using performance status and LDH; Raghav nomogram using gender, ECOG performance status, histology, number of metastatic sites, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) stratify outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.734-735). No single formal staging system; risk stratification distinguishes favorable prognostic subsets (treatable as a specific putative primary, with potential for prolonged survival/cure) from unfavorable disseminated disease. Prognostic models include the Culine model (performance status plus serum LDH, dividing patients into two outcome subgroups) and the Raghav nomogram (gender, ECOG performance status, histology, number of metastatic sites, and neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) (Harrison 22e pp.734-735).

hypertrophic disease and missing the diagnosis Interpreting bone-avid scintigraphy as diagnostic of ATTR without excluding a monoclonal protein Using standard heart-failure agents that provoke hypotension in restrictive physiology Delaying haematology referral in suspected AL disease Cardiac amyloidosis results from extracellular deposition of misfolded protein as insoluble amyloid fibrils Prognosis depends on subtype and stage; untreated AL cardiac amyloidosis has a particularly poor outlook, whereas earlier diagnosis and modern ATTR therapies can slow progression and improve survival.
