cause (the four Hs and four Ts) Prolonged interruptions in chest compressions degrading perfusion Tension pneumothorax, tamponade, or major haemorrhage as an immediately treatable cause in traumatic arrest Post-resuscitation hypoxia, hypotension, or hyperthermia worsening neurological outcome Interrupting chest compressions excessively for rhythm checks, intubation, or vascular access Delaying defibrillation of a shockable rhythm Focusing on drugs and airway while neglecting the search for reversible causes Applying standard medical algorithms to traumatic arrest without treating haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, and tamponade Neglecting structured post-resuscitation care after return of spontaneous circulation Cardiac arrest is the sudden cessation of effective cardiac output. Shockable rhythms arise from disorganised (ventricular fibrillation) or excessively rapid (pulseless ventricular tachycardia) electrical activity that prevents coordinated contraction, most often on a background of ischaemic heart disease. Non-shockable arrest reflects either absent electrical activity (asystole) or organised electrical activity without a pulse (pulseless electrical activity), commonly due to a profound reversible insult. Regardless of mechanism, cessation of circulation causes global ischaemia; the brain tolerates only minutes before injury begins, so restoration of perfusion by chest compressions and treatment of the cause is time-critical. Outcome depends on the initial rhythm, the promptness of high-quality resuscitation and defibrillation, and whether a reversible cause is corrected. Witnessed shockable arrests with early bystander CPR and defibrillation have the best prognosis, whereas unwitnessed asystolic arrest and prolonged downtime carry poor survival and higher risk of neurological injury.

Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation — Heart transplantation, Orthotopic heart transplant, Left ventricular assist device therapy, LVAS, LVAD, Mechanical circulatory support, Total artificial heart Other causes of advanced/refractory heart failure warranting evaluation: restrictive and infiltrative cardiomyopathy (e.g., amyloidosis), congenital heart disease, and chronic-infection-associated cardiomyopathy (Chagas disease, viral hepatitis-related, tuberculosis) Allograft dysfunction differential after transplant: acute cellular rejection vs antibody-mediated rejection vs cardiac allograft vasculopathy vs primary graft dysfunction Surveillance endomyocardial biopsy to grade and monitor rejection Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulin deposition and complement fixation, plus circulating donor-specific antibody testing, when AMR is suspected Cardiopulmonary exercise testing for peak VO2 to assess transplant/LVAS candidacy Invasive hemodynamic assessment of pulmonary vascular resistance and transpulmonary gradient (PVR >3 Wood units or transpulmonary gradient >15 are relative transplant contraindications unless reactive) Intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography (more sensitive than angiography) and noninvasive coronary flow reserve for CAV detection and prognosis Prospective or virtual cross-match in allosensitized recipients with preformed antibodies Doppler-derived mean arterial pressure measurement in continuous-flow LVAS patients Lactate dehydrogenase as a hemolysis biomarker to screen for pump thrombosis Advanced heart failure is a distinct syndrome marked by refractoriness to conventional therapy, intolerance of guideline-dose neurohormonal antagonists, worsening renal function, poor cardiopulmonary reserve, and a low-output state with elevated pulmonary pressures; therapeutic goals shift toward surgical support of the failing heart (Harrison 22e p.2028). Transplant candidacy generally requires refractory heart failure with a peak VO2 below ~14 mL/kg per min (below 12 if on beta blockers) or percent-predicted VO2 under 50%, combined with intolerance of disease-modifying therapy, cardiorenal syndrome, inotrope dependence, or need for an LVAS (Harrison 22e p.2028). Age is not an absolute contraindication, but frailty is a relative one; BMI above 35 should prompt weight loss, eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 is a relative contraindication possibly requiring combined kidney transplant, and tobacco use in any form must cease for at least 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2028). The transplanted heart is surgically denervated and unresponsive to sympathetic or parasympathetic stimuli; early postoperatively high-dose catecholamines are needed, and allograft bradycardia does NOT respond to atropine, so isoproterenol or temporary pacing is used (Harrison 22e p.2029). Donor ischemia (out-of-body) time is typically limited to about 4 hours unless novel ex situ normothermic perfusion transport techniques are used; allocation considers urgency, waiting-list time, distance, and ABO blood group, while HLA matching is usually impractical given time constraints (Harrison 22e p.2029). Acute cellular rejection (ACR) is a T cell-mediated process with myocardial lymphocytic infiltrates that occurs early and declines after about 6 months, whereas antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) is a noncellular, donor-specific antibody-driven process with complement fixation, endothelial swelling, and arteriolar vasculitis that carries worse allograft survival and predisposes to vasculopathy (Harrison 22e p.2029-2030). Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is an accelerated, diffuse coronary intimal proliferation that is commonly clinically silent; intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography is more sensitive than routine angiography for detection (Harrison 22e p.2030). Angiographic CAV is present in roughly 30% of patients by 5 years and about 50% by 10 years after transplant; retransplantation is the only definitive therapy for advanced CAV (Harrison 22e p.2030). Continuous-flow LVAS generate forward flow dependent on the pressure gradient between the LV cavity and aorta, so flow is critically sensitive to systemic blood pressure; because pulse is often undetectable, blood pressure is measured by Doppler (mean/opening pressure) and the target mean arterial pressure is at or below 90 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2032). LVAS-related shear stress can cause low-grade hemolysis and acquired von Willebrand disease (loss of high-molecular-weight vWF multimers), predisposing to gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal arteriovenous malformations and to iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.2032). Lactate dehydrogenase is an excellent though nonspecific biomarker of hemolysis and can herald pump thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2032). Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders are usually Epstein-Barr virus driven and are the most frequent malignancy; solid cancers most often manifest as basal- and squamous-cell skin malignancies, so routine sunscreen is advised (Harrison 22e p.2030). Hemodynamic compromise during acute cellular rejection signals severe rejection and warrants rescue polyclonal antibody therapy with corticosteroids Suspected LVAD thrombosis carries a high mortality if pump exchange or transplant is not performed; rising LDH may herald it Neurologic events (ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke) are major hemocompatibility-related complications of LVAS Driveline infection (occurs in 20-50% of LVAS patients by 5 years) predisposes to thrombosis and neurologic complications Gastrointestinal bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease and intestinal arteriovenous malformations Progressive right ventricular failure and congestion after LVAS implantation Treating allograft bradycardia with atropine, which is ineffective because the transplanted heart is denervated (use isoproterenol or pacing instead) Relying on routine coronary angiography alone, which underdiagnoses early cardiac allograft vasculopathy compared with intravascular ultrasound or OCT Attempting to palpate or auscultate a peripheral pulse for blood pressure in continuous-flow LVAS patients, who often have no detectable pulse; Doppler must be used Overlooking acquired von Willebrand disease as the cause of GI bleeding in LVAS patients Continuing aspirin in HeartMate 3 patients, which increases nonsurgical bleeding; its elimination (with a vitamin K antagonist targeting INR 2-3) reduces bleeding-related hospitalizations Failing to anticipate right ventricular failure after LV unloading by an LVAS In advanced (stage D) heart failure the myocardium can no longer maintain adequate output despite maximal medical therapy, producing a low cardiac output state with elevated filling and pulmonary pressures, intolerance of neurohormonal antagonists, and progressive cardiorenal dysfunction. Cardiac transplantation replaces the failing heart with an allograft that is surgically denervated, so it depends initially on circulating catecholamines and cannot mount reflex heart-rate responses. Allograft rejection follows two mechanisms: ACR, a T cell-mediated lymphocytic assault on donor myocardium (perivenular in mild disease, diffuse interstitial with myocyte necrosis and hemorrhage in severe disease), and AMR, an antibody/complement-mediated injury with immunoglobulin deposition, endothelial swelling, interstitial edema, and arteriolar vasculitis. Over the long term, immunologic insults (brain death, ischemia-reperfusion, alloimmunity) combined with nonimmunologic metabolic factors (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, dysglycemia from chronic immunosuppression) drive cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse fibrotic intimal proliferation narrowing the coronary tree. For mechanical support, continuous-flow LVAS divert blood from the LV apex to the aorta via a pump whose output depends on the LV-to-aorta pressure gradient; the non-physiologic flow path imposes shear stress that degrades von Willebrand factor multimers and causes hemolysis. LV unloading lowers right-sided afterload, but increased device flow raises RV preload and the displaced septum reduces RV contractile efficiency, promoting RV dilatation and maladaptation. More than 150,000 patients have undergone cardiac transplantation worldwide, with 1-year survival above 80%, median survival of ~12.5 years, and conditional survival of ~14.8 years for those surviving the first year. With the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 LVAS, median survival exceeds 5 years (about 60% survival at 5 years), and in younger patients (under 50) without comorbidity and an uncomplicated course the 5-year survival can rival transplantation (~75%). Without such support, patients with severe refractory systolic heart failure (peak VO2 <12 mL/kg per min or inotrope dependence) often have a median survival under 1 year. CAV grade correlates with prognosis and remains a leading limit on late allograft survival. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is graded by the ISHLT 2010 scheme as CAV0 (absent), CAV1 (mild), CAV2 (moderate), and CAV3 (severe), based on extent of angiographic disease and presence of allograft dysfunction by echocardiography or restrictive physiology. Transplant allocation urgency is tiered, with the highest status for critically ill patients on ECMO or temporary biventricular mechanical support, then those needing daily invasive hemodynamic monitoring plus IV inotropes or with durable LVAD complications, and lower status for ambulatory patients stable at home.

Cardiac Trauma — Blunt cardiac injury, BCI, Myocardial contusion, Penetrating cardiac injury, Commotio cordis Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (traumatic coronary dissection or thrombosis can produce STEMI) Aortic dissection (traumatic aortic rupture can mimic its presentation) Acute pericarditis Cardiac tamponade from other causes Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy following emotional or physical trauma Musculoskeletal chest wall pain from rib or sternal injury 12-lead ECG in all patients with chest trauma (repeat as needed for evolving conduction disturbance/arrhythmia) Serial cardiac troponin (I or T); normal serial levels make cardiac injury very unlikely Transthoracic echocardiography in all suspected BCI and all penetrating chest injuries to assess wall motion, effusion, valves, and shunts Transesophageal echocardiography when adequate TTE images cannot be obtained Chest x-ray (mediastinal widening suggests aortic injury) Cardiac catheterization to confirm a suspected mechanical complication (shunt/valvular lesion) Non-traumatic acute myocardial infarction Non-traumatic aortic dissection Idiopathic or other-cause acute pericarditis Takotsubo cardiomyopathy Cardiac injury is broadly divided into penetrating trauma (most often gunshot or knife wounds, where the entry site is usually obvious) and nonpenetrating, or blunt cardiac injury (BCI). BCI most commonly follows motor vehicle collisions (rapid deceleration or chest impact) but can also result from falls, crush and blast injuries, assault, or vigorous contact in sports; significant cardiac injury may occur even when there are no external signs of thoracic trauma. There is no single sign, symptom, or test that confirms BCI, and clinical, laboratory, and radiographic findings are frequently nonspecific in the setting of major trauma, so a high index of suspicion is essential. An ECG should be obtained in every patient presenting with chest trauma; abnormalities can resemble those of infarction or pericarditis and include sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, and atrial or ventricular arrhythmias. Cardiac troponin is more specific than CK-MB for myocardial damage; a normal troponin combined with a normal ECG at 6-8 hours after chest trauma essentially excludes BCI. Echocardiography is the most useful modality for detecting the structural and functional sequelae of BCI, including regional wall motion abnormalities, pericardial effusion, valvular dysfunction, and ventricular or septal rupture; the RV, interventricular septum, and LV apex are most commonly involved. Commotio cordis is ventricular fibrillation triggered by a blunt, often innocent-appearing chest impact in the absence of structural injury, occurring most often in adolescents during sports when the blow lands during the vulnerable phase of repolarization (just before the T-wave peak); survival depends on prompt defibrillation. Sudden emotional or physical stress, even without direct cardiac trauma, may precipitate a transient catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy (takotsubo / apical ballooning syndrome). Because of its anterior position in the chest, the right ventricle is the most frequently injured chamber in penetrating trauma, followed by the left ventricle; isolated atrial injury is uncommon. Iatrogenic cardiac perforation can complicate central/intracardiac catheter placement, pacemaker or defibrillator lead insertion, RV endomyocardial biopsy, and intracoronary stent deployment. Post-cardiac injury syndrome (an inflammatory process resembling the postpericardiotomy syndrome) can develop weeks to months after blunt chest trauma, presenting with pericarditis and/or pericardial effusion. Survivors of penetrating cardiac injury may present days to weeks later with a new murmur or heart failure from an occult or evolving valvular regurgitation or intracardiac shunt, so trauma patients should be re-examined several weeks after injury. Hemodynamic instability or collapse at presentation (penetrating injury mortality approaches 90% in those in hemodynamic collapse) New loud murmur with rapidly progressive heart failure (traumatic valvular rupture) Signs of pericardial tamponade (pericardial rub, distant heart sounds, hypotension) ST-segment elevation suggesting coronary dissection/occlusion Mediastinal widening on chest x-ray with upper-extremity hypertension and diminished lower-extremity pulses (aortic rupture) Sudden collapse during chest impact in an athlete (commotio cordis requiring immediate defibrillation) Even a small pericardial effusion on echo in a penetrating chest injury (suggests occult cardiac perforation) Overlooking cardiac injury because attention is focused on more obvious external injuries. Relying on sternal or rib fractures to gauge cardiac risk; there is no proven association, and significant cardiac injury can occur with a normal-appearing chest wall. Using CK-MB to confirm BCI; it is elevated in only ~20% of blunt chest trauma and is falsely raised by massive skeletal muscle injury. Attributing post-traumatic chest pain solely to musculoskeletal causes when it may reflect myocardial ischemia or pericardial injury. Assuming a hemodynamically stable penetrating chest injury excludes cardiac involvement; up to ~20% harbor occult cardiac trauma. Missing delayed complications (post-cardiac injury syndrome, late valvular regurgitation, intracardiac shunt) by not re-examining the patient weeks after injury. Blunt forces (rapid deceleration, direct chest impact, crush, or blast) and penetrating objects damage the myocardium, valves, coronary arteries, pericardium, and great vessels. Myocardial contusion produces injury pathologically similar to infarction, with necrosis arising either directly or from traumatic coronary laceration, dissection, or thrombosis, predisposing to arrhythmias and conduction block. More severe injury causes free wall rupture (hemopericardium and tamponade) or ventricular septal rupture (intracardiac shunting). Valvular apparatus rupture (most often tricuspid or aortic) causes acute incompetence. Aortic rupture or transection, typically just above the aortic valve or at the ligamentum arteriosum tethering point, is the most common vascular deceleration injury. Commotio cordis represents a purely electrical mechanism: a chest blow during the susceptible repolarization window induces ventricular fibrillation without structural damage. Outcome depends on injury mechanism, chambers involved, and clinical condition at presentation. Although myocardial rupture is generally fatal, up to ~40% of patients reach a specialized trauma center alive. In penetrating injury, gunshot wounds carry higher mortality than stab wounds (about 20% of shooting victims survive versus up to ~65% of stabbing victims), partly because ballistic injuries more often involve multiple chambers; multichamber involvement carries a worse prognosis than single-chamber injury, and RV injury may carry a better prognosis than LV injury. Patients in hemodynamic collapse on arrival have a mortality near 90%, whereas roughly 75% of those stable enough to reach the operating room survive. Iatrogenic penetrating injuries generally have a better prognosis owing to more limited injury and prompt corrective therapy. Blunt cardiac abnormalities span a spectrum: ECG changes (sinus tachycardia, RBBB, heart block, ST-T changes, arrhythmias), elevated biomarkers (troponin most specific), focal wall motion abnormality or hematoma (RV free wall, LV apex, septum), valvular insufficiency (most often mitral/tricuspid, occasionally aortic), myocardial rupture (VSD or free wall), coronary artery injury (often LAD, presenting as STEMI), and pericardial effusion/tamponade. Risk stratification: stable patients with a normal ECG and normal serial troponins are low risk; an abnormal ECG and/or elevated troponin with a normal echo warrants telemetry monitoring; mechanical complications and hemodynamic instability constitute the highest-acuity group.

ectodermal disorder Cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome is a RASopathy caused by germline activating variants in components of the RAS-MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) signalling cascade, principally BRAF and the downstream kinases MEK1 and MEK2, with a minority in KRAS. This pathway transduces growth-factor signals to control cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. Constitutive over-activation dysregulates these processes during development, producing the characteristic craniofacial, cardiac, ectodermal and neurodevelopmental abnormalities shared, with variation, across the RASopathy spectrum. Prognosis depends heavily on the cardiac phenotype, particularly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and on the severity of feeding and neurological problems; many individuals have moderate to severe intellectual disability. With multidisciplinary care most survive into adulthood, though medical needs remain substantial.

Objective parameters (cardiac index, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) help confirm a cardiac cause but are not mandatory for the diagnosis (p.2324). Compensatory rise in systemic vascular resistance is typical; left-ventricular processes elevate PCWP whereas right-ventricular processes elevate CVP (p.2311). Occasionally BP is maintained by very high SVR despite established shock, so normotension does not exclude cardiogenic shock (p.2326). Only about 10% of patients present with shock on admission; roughly 90% develop it during hospitalisation, so serial reassessment is essential (p.2123, p.2325). Shock complicating a first inferior MI should prompt a search for a mechanical complication or right-ventricular involvement (p.2325). A new systolic murmur after MI should trigger urgent echocardiography to look for VSR, papillary muscle rupture or free-wall rupture; a murmur may be absent in up to 50% of acute MR cases (p.334, p.1894). Pericardial thrombus on imaging after MI strongly suggests myocardial rupture and is a surgical emergency (p.1894). Patients who develop shock typically have severe multivessel disease with 'piecemeal' necrosis extending beyond the original infarct zone (p.2123). Lactate >8 mmol/L (places patient in SCAI stage E) (p.2326) Cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR and/or ECMO (extremis stage) (p.2326) Rising hepatic transaminases from liver hypoperfusion (~20%; high-mortality marker) (p.2326) New systolic murmur, thrill or sudden deterioration suggesting mechanical complication (VSR, papillary rupture, free-wall rupture) (p.334, p.1894) Progressive oliguria/anuria and altered mental status indicating worsening hypoperfusion (p.2326) Failure to respond to initial interventions (SCAI stage D, 'deteriorating') (p.2326) Assuming normotension excludes shock — BP may be preserved by markedly elevated SVR (p.2326). Missing a mechanical complication: a murmur is absent in up to 50% of acute papillary-muscle-rupture MR (p.334). Overlooking RV infarction in inferior MI, where fluid management differs (volume to maintain RV preload) (p.2123). Treating presumed cardiogenic shock as hypovolaemia — filling pressures (PCWP/CVP) are elevated, not low (p.2311). Failing to recognise mixed shock (e.g. sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy superimposed on distributive shock) (p.2311). A profound fall in myocardial contractility initiates a self-perpetuating spiral: reduced cardiac output and stroke volume lower blood pressure and coronary perfusion, worsening ischaemia and further depressing contractility, which left untreated leads to death. Ineffective stroke volume is the inciting event, but inadequate circulatory compensation also contributes. Early peripheral vasoconstriction may transiently improve coronary and peripheral perfusion but raises afterload and can worsen ischaemia. Over time, systemic inflammation from acute cardiac injury induces pathologic vasodilatation; inflammatory cytokines and inducible/endothelial nitric oxide synthase increase NO and its by-product peroxynitrite, which are negatively inotropic and cardiotoxic. Lactic acidosis and hypoxaemia compound the cycle because severe acidosis blunts the efficacy of endogenous and exogenous catecholamines. Bleeding and transfusion during ICU care can further trigger inflammation. Left-ventricular failure accounts for roughly 80% of cardiogenic shock complicating acute MI, with acute severe mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal rupture, predominant RV failure, and free-wall rupture/tamponade making up the remainder (p.2325). In-hospital mortality ranges from roughly 40-60% depending on shock severity and underlying cause; cardiogenic and septic shock carry the highest mortality among shock types (90-day mortality around 52% for cardiogenic shock in one ED cohort). Higher lactate, elevated admission glucose, hepatic hypoperfusion and progressive renal impairment are adverse markers. Untreated shock progresses through compensated (preshock), decompensated, and finally irreversible stages with permanent organ dysfunction and multi-organ failure. Reperfusion and modern care have reduced the incidence of shock complicating acute MI to about 5-10% (p.2311, p.2325). SCAI shock classification (2019, updated): Stage A 'at risk' — no current signs/symptoms; Stage B 'beginning'/preshock — relative hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion; Stage C 'classic' — manifest hypoperfusion requiring intervention (inotropes, vasopressors or MCS, excluding ECMO) beyond volume; Stage D 'deteriorating' — like C but worsening and failing initial therapy; Stage E 'extremis' — cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR and/or ECMO. The updated definition adds a three-axis model: (1) shock severity, (2) phenotype/aetiology, (3) risk modifiers such as cardiac arrest. Lactate >8 mmol/L marks stage E (p.2325-2326).

tamponade Severe hyperkalemia causing sinusoidal arrest Opioid or other drug overdose Hypothermia Seizure with transient unresponsiveness Harrison distinguishes three overlapping terms: cardiovascular collapse is sudden loss of effective circulation that may revert spontaneously (e.g., neurocardiogenic syncope) or require intervention; cardiac arrest is abrupt cessation of cardiac function with loss of circulation potentially reversible by prompt intervention; and sudden cardiac death is unexpected death from cardiac arrest occurring within roughly 1 hour of symptom onset (p.2332-2333). Sudden cardiac death accounts for about 15% of all deaths and roughly half of all cardiac deaths; in the United States the text cites an estimated 350,000 EMS-attended out-of-hospital arrests and 210,000 sudden cardiac deaths in adults yearly (p.2332). Up to two-thirds of sudden cardiac deaths occur as the first clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed heart disease, limiting the ability to predict and prevent events at the population level (p.2332). Coronary heart disease underlies the majority of sudden cardiac deaths, but the proportion attributable to coronary disease varies markedly by demographics: roughly 70% in white men versus 40-50% in women and black individuals, and under 40% in Asian populations (p.2333-2334). The text emphasizes the chain of survival for out-of-hospital arrest, and that survival is strongly time-dependent: neurologic recovery falls rapidly and is under 30% by 5 minutes from collapse to return of spontaneous circulation when no bystander CPR is given (p.2335-2338). Gasping (agonal) respirations and brief seizure-like activity are common during arrest and may be misinterpreted as breathing or responsiveness, leading to delayed resuscitation; a pulse check by a trained provider should take no longer than 10 seconds (p.2335-2336). The initial recorded rhythm carries prognostic and etiologic weight: ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (shockable rhythms) have the best outcomes, while pulseless electrical activity and asystole carry a poor prognosis (p.2335-2336). The proportion of arrests found in ventricular fibrillation has fallen from over half in the 1970s to only 20-25% in recent series, with pulseless electrical activity and asystole now most common; because arrhythmias are unstable after collapse, the rhythm at EMS arrival may not reflect the initiating rhythm (p.2334). Inherited arrhythmia syndromes without structural heart disease (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, early repolarization, idiopathic VF) are a more important cause of sudden death in the young and in Asian populations, accounting for around 10% of cases in Asia versus 1-2% in Western countries (p.2334). Depressed left ventricular function is the best-validated risk marker in structural heart disease; after myocardial infarction, SCD risk rises gradually as LVEF falls toward 40% and then increases exponentially below that (p.2338-2339). Following an MI, the risk of sudden death rises up to roughly 10-fold, with the highest absolute rates in the first 30 days; early deaths are more often non-arrhythmic (myocardial rupture, reinfarction) while later deaths are predominantly scar-related ventricular arrhythmias (p.2334-2335). Commotio cordis - ventricular fibrillation triggered by blunt, non-penetrating precordial impact - is a rare cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy individuals, especially after a chest blow during the vulnerable repolarization window (p.2335). while still under sedation/hypothermia or before the recommended 72 hours of normothermia Implanting an ICD for arrhythmia driven by a transient reversible cause (e.g., hyperkalemia, drug-induced torsades, or VF within 48 h of acute MI), where it is generally not indicated Withholding consideration that arrhythmia may signal end-stage heart disease, in which an ICD will not change the course absent transplant or assist-device candidacy Overlooking treatable PEA/asystole causes such as pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, hypoxia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, toxins, and massive MI Attributing sudden death in the young to coronary disease, when HCM, coronary anomalies, myocarditis, ARVC, and channelopathies are more often responsible Most sudden cardiac death stems from a lethal ventricular tachyarrhythmia (polymorphic VT degenerating to ventricular fibrillation) arising on a vulnerable myocardial substrate, though bradyarrhythmia, asystole, and pulseless electrical activity are increasingly common terminal rhythms. Coronary artery disease is the predominant substrate, acting through acute ischemia/infarction or through reentry around scar from a healed infarct. Nonischemic processes - dilated, hypertrophic, infiltrative, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies, valvular disease, congenital surgical scars, and myocarditis - produce replacement fibrosis, hypertrophy, ventricular stretch, electrical heterogeneity, altered ion-channel function, and abnormal calcium handling that lower the threshold for sustained arrhythmia. In structurally normal hearts, inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, CPVT), pre-excited atrial fibrillation in Wolff-Parkinson-White, and QT-prolonging drug toxicity cause primary electrical arrest. Pulseless electrical activity reflects mechanical or metabolic catastrophe - massive MI, pulmonary embolism, exsanguination, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, profound hypoxia or acidosis. Heightened autonomic (sympathetic) tone is the common thread linking precipitants such as vigorous exertion, emotional and environmental stress to arrhythmogenesis. After return of circulation, global ischemia-reperfusion brain injury becomes the dominant determinant of outcome. Outcomes are dominated by time to resuscitation and the presenting rhythm. Survival to hospital discharge for out-of-hospital arrest has improved but remains low - the chapter states about 90% of patients do not survive to discharge, and roughly 20% of survivors are left with severe neurologic or physical disability. Shockable rhythms (VT/VF) carry the best prognosis, with survival approaching 30% in some regions, whereas PEA and asystole carry poor outcomes. Success of resuscitation declines sharply after 5 minutes from collapse. Ischemia-reperfusion brain injury accounts for over two-thirds of post-arrest deaths; reliable neurologic prognostication is generally deferred at least 72 hours after return to normothermia (typically 4-5 days post-arrest). Features predicting poor neurologic outcome include absent pupillary light reflex, status myoclonus, absent EEG reactivity, and persistent burst suppression. Harrison frames the spectrum by terminology and reversibility: cardiovascular collapse (may revert spontaneously, includes syncope) -> cardiac arrest (rarely reverts spontaneously; reversibility depends on mechanism, setting, and speed of intervention) -> sudden cardiac death (death within ~1 hour of symptom onset). Acute risk and outcome stratify by presenting rhythm - shockable (VT/VF, better) versus non-shockable (PEA/asystole, worse). Chronic SCD risk in structural heart disease is graded chiefly by LVEF and presence of heart failure, with risk rising gradually as LVEF falls to 40% and exponentially below it.

PRKAR1A, which encodes the type 1-alpha regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. This subunit normally restrains the catalytic activity of protein kinase A; its loss leads to unregulated cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase A signalling. Overactive protein kinase A signalling promotes proliferation in hormonally responsive and other susceptible tissues, explaining the endocrine tumours, myxomas, pigmented skin lesions and schwannomas. Tumour development follows a tumour-suppressor mechanism with a somatic second hit. A minority of cases involve other loci, and some show genetic heterogeneity. Cardiac myxomas are the leading cause of mortality through embolic events, obstruction and surgical risk, and can recur, so lifelong cardiac surveillance is essential. With regular monitoring and timely surgery for tumours, overall outlook is improved, though endocrine and other tumours require ongoing management.

during a procedure in an unblocked patient Confusing the syndrome with the non-hereditary Carney triad and missing the germline SDHx cause Expecting a succinate dehydrogenase-deficient GIST to respond presents with a wild-type gastric GIST The syndrome results from germline loss-of-function variants in genes encoding subunits of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, a mitochondrial enzyme shared by the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the electron transport chain. Inactivation of the complex causes succinate to accumulate, which inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, producing a pseudohypoxic, pro-angiogenic state and widespread epigenetic changes. These effects promote the development of succinate dehydrogenase-deficient gastrointestinal stromal tumours and paragangliomas that characterise the condition. Succinate dehydrogenase-deficient GISTs tend to be indolent but can metastasise, notably to lymph nodes and liver, and respond poorly to standard targeted therapy, so surgery is central to management. Paragangliomas vary in behaviour, and with lifelong surveillance and appropriate perioperative preparation overall outcomes are often reasonable.

intravenous glucose to suppress lipolysis, avoids fasting, and supports cardiac and hepatic function Chronic care uses long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, frequent feeds and a strict emergency regimen Neonatal cardiac arrhythmia or conduction block with haemodynamic instability Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy and hyperammonaemia Cardiomyopathy with rapid deterioration Recurrent life-threatening decompensation during intercurrent illness Mistaking the biochemistry for CPT2 deficiency without confirmatory genetics Under-treating catabolism, allowing lipolysis to drive cardiac toxicity Overlooking arrhythmia as the presenting feature of metabolic collapse Permitting any fasting in a diagnosed infant The carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase is the inner mitochondrial membrane antiporter that imports long-chain acylcarnitine into the matrix in exchange for free carnitine, an essential step of the carnitine cycle linking CPT1 and CPT2. When the carrier is deficient, long-chain fatty acids cannot reach the matrix for beta-oxidation, so heart, muscle and liver are deprived of fatty-acid-derived energy during fasting or stress and ketogenesis fails. Accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines is arrhythmogenic and cardiotoxic, accounting for the prominent cardiac features, and impaired acetyl-CoA generation contributes to hyperammonaemia. The neonatal-onset severe form carries high mortality despite intensive treatment, whereas individuals with residual carrier activity and milder disease can survive with careful metabolic management; early diagnosis and aggressive prevention of catabolism are critical.

free-carnitine level, which also flags affected mothers Acute hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy during fasting or illness Decompensated cardiomyopathy with heart failure or arrhythmia Sudden cardiac events in an at-risk individual Newborn screen showing very low carnitine, which may indicate an affected and vulnerable mother Failing to distinguish primary transporter deficiency from the much commoner secondary forms Overlooking the diagnosis in unexplained childhood cardiomyopathy that could respond to carnitine Missing an affected mother identified through her infant's abnormal newborn screen Not investigating for an underlying fatty acid oxidation defect or organic acidaemia when carnitine is low Carnitine is essential for transporting long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. In primary carnitine deficiency, loss-of-function of the OCTN2 plasma-membrane transporter prevents carnitine entry into cardiac and skeletal muscle and impairs its reabsorption in the renal tubule, causing systemic depletion and urinary carnitine wasting. Without adequate carnitine, long-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidised, so energy production fails during fasting and fatty acid-dependent tissues such as heart and muscle are especially vulnerable, producing cardiomyopathy, myopathy and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Secondary deficiency occurs when carnitine is consumed conjugating accumulated acyl groups or is lost through the kidney. Primary carnitine deficiency generally has an excellent prognosis with carnitine supplementation, as cardiomyopathy and myopathy often reverse and metabolic crises are preventable; untreated disease, however, can cause sudden death or progressive cardiac failure. Prognosis of secondary deficiency depends on the underlying disorder.

arrested remodelling of the embryonic ductal plate affecting the larger intrahepatic bile ducts, leaving them congenitally and permanently dilated in a saccular or fusiform pattern that communicates with the biliary tree. The abnormal ducts promote stasis of bile, which encourages the formation of pigment stones and repeated ascending bacterial infection, producing recurrent cholangitis and sometimes hepatic abscesses. When the same ductal plate malformation also involves the smallest ducts it produces the periportal fibrosis of congenital hepatic fibrosis, giving rise to Caroli syndrome with additional portal hypertension. The shared ciliopathy mechanism, often linked to PKHD1, accounts for the frequent association with renal cystic disease, and chronic biliary inflammation underlies the raised risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Prognosis depends on the extent of ductal involvement and the frequency of infective complications; localised disease may be cured by resection, whereas diffuse disease carries recurrent cholangitis, stone disease, and an elevated cholangiocarcinoma risk, with transplantation considered for advanced or complicated cases.

MRI) to identify infarction in symptomatic patients Cardiac evaluation including ECG and echocardiography to exclude a cardioembolic source Vascular risk-factor profiling including lipids and glucose Most lesions occur at the carotid bifurcation and proximal internal carotid artery, where atherosclerotic plaque and turbulence predispose to thromboembolism Symptomatic disease typically presents as ipsilateral transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax, or hemispheric stroke rather than global symptoms A cervical bruit is neither sensitive nor specific and its absence does not exclude stratification hinges on whether the lesion is symptomatic and on the percentage stenosis, as benefit from intervention is greatest in recently symptomatic high-grade lesions Best medical therapy with antiplatelet agents, lipid lowering, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation is fundamental for all patients regardless of intervention Carotid endarterectomy and carotid artery stenting are the two revascularisation options, with choice guided by anatomy, age, comorbidity, and operative risk Intervention for symptomatic disease is most effective when performed early after the index neurological event Recent transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax, or stroke with high-grade ipsilateral stenosis, indicating high early stroke risk and need for urgent assessment Crescendo TIAs or stroke-in-evolution suggesting an unstable plaque Acute focal neurological deficit requiring emergency stroke pathway activation Contralateral occlusion or near-occlusion increasing haemodynamic vulnerability Relying on a bruit or its absence to gauge stenosis severity Delaying revascularisation in recently symptomatic patients, forfeiting the greatest window of benefit Overestimating benefit of intervention in asymptomatic patients with limited life expectancy Neglecting global vascular risk-factor modification while focusing only on the carotid lesion Carotid artery stenosis is usually caused by atherosclerotic plaque forming at the carotid bifurcation, a site of low and oscillating wall shear stress. Progressive plaque growth narrows the lumen, but the dominant mechanism of stroke is artery-to-artery thromboembolism from an unstable, ulcerated, or haemorrhagic plaque rather than simple flow limitation. Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic material, generating platelet-fibrin and cholesterol emboli that lodge in the ophthalmic or middle cerebral territory. In severe stenosis or occlusion, cerebral perfusion may also become haemodynamically compromised, particularly when collateral supply through the circle of Willis is inadequate. Recently symptomatic high-grade stenosis carries a substantial short-term risk of recurrent stroke that is markedly reduced by timely revascularisation combined with medical therapy. Asymptomatic disease has a lower annual stroke risk, and modern medical therapy has narrowed the margin of benefit from intervention.

Carotid body tumour — carotid body paraganglioma, chemodectoma, carotid body tumor, cervical paraganglioma Cervical lymphadenopathy (reactive or malignant) Branchial cleft cyst Vagal or other head and neck paraganglioma Carotid artery aneurysm Salivary gland tumour Metastatic neck node or nerve sheath tumour Duplex ultrasound and CT or MR angiography demonstrating a vascular mass splaying the carotid bifurcation Catheter angiography where detailed vascular mapping or embolisation is planned Functional and biochemical testing for catecholamine secretion when a secretory tumour is suspected Genetic testing (including succinate dehydrogenase genes) and screening for multifocal or bilateral disease Cross-sectional imaging to assess local extent and identify additional paragangliomas A paraganglioma arising from the chemoreceptor tissue of the carotid body at the carotid bifurcation Typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, pulsatile neck mass at the angle of the jaw The mass is classically mobile from side to side but not vertically because it is tethered to the bifurcation (Fontaine sign) Most are benign and non-functional, but a minority secrete catecholamines or behave malignantly with nodal or distant spread A significant proportion are familial and linked to succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations, warranting genetic assessment and screening for multiple or bilateral tumours Imaging shows a highly vascular mass splaying the internal and external carotid arteries, producing the characteristic lyre sign on angiography Biopsy is generally avoided because of the vascularity and bleeding risk; diagnosis relies on characteristic imaging Surgical resection is the mainstay for suitable lesions, with radiotherapy considered for high-risk or unresectable disease, and preoperative embolisation used in selected large tumours Features suggesting malignant paraganglioma with regional or distant spread Catecholamine excess with paroxysmal hypertension or arrhythmia requiring assessment before intervention Rapid growth or new cranial nerve deficits indicating local invasion Bilateral or familial disease prompting genetic evaluation and family screening Performing biopsy of a highly vascular mass and precipitating significant haemorrhage Failing to test for catecholamine secretion before surgery in a functional tumour Overlooking hereditary disease and the need for genetic testing and screening for additional paragangliomas Underestimating the risk of cranial nerve injury with resection of large tumours The carotid body is a small chemoreceptor organ at the carotid bifurcation that senses arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH. A carotid body tumour is a paraganglioma arising from its neural crest-derived chief cells. Chronic hypoxic stimulation, such as living at high altitude, can promote hyperplasia and tumour development, and hereditary forms result from germline mutations in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes. The tumour is intensely vascular and grows within the crotch of the bifurcation, progressively splaying and encasing the internal and external carotid arteries and potentially involving adjacent cranial nerves. Most are non-functional, but some secrete catecholamines. Most carotid body tumours are benign and slow-growing, and complete resection offers an excellent outcome, though larger lesions carry greater risk of cranial nerve injury and vascular complications. A minority are malignant, and prognosis then depends on the extent of spread and completeness of treatment.

Carpal tunnel syndrome — median nerve compression at the wrist, CTS, median neuropathy at the carpal tunnel Cervical radiculopathy (particularly C6/C7) Proximal median nerve entrapment (e.g. pronator syndrome) Peripheral polyneuropathy (e.g. diabetic) Thoracic outlet syndrome Other nerve entrapments (ulnar neuropathy) Thenar osteoarthritis (first carpometacarpal joint) Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm and grade median nerve compression Clinical provocative tests (Tinel's and Phalen's) and thenar strength assessment Blood tests for associated conditions (glucose/HbA1c, thyroid function) where indicated Wrist radiographs if there is a history of fracture, deformity, or arthritis Ultrasound of the nerve in selected or atypical cases The commonest peripheral nerve entrapment, caused by compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum at the wrist Typically presents with numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, characteristically worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand Symptoms may radiate up the forearm; in advanced cases there is weakness and wasting of the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis) Often idiopathic but associated with pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, and repetitive wrist use Provocative signs include Tinel's (tapping over the nerve) and Phalen's (sustained wrist flexion) tests, though their sensitivity is limited Nerve conduction studies confirm the diagnosis and grade severity, and are useful before surgery or in atypical cases Mild or intermittent disease often responds to nocturnal wrist splinting, activity modification, and treatment of any underlying condition; corticosteroid injection can give temporary relief Surgical division of the flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel release) is indicated for persistent symptoms, failure of conservative treatment, or established motor deficit and sensory loss Progressive thenar muscle wasting and weakness indicating advanced nerve damage warranting timely decompression Persistent dense sensory loss that may not fully recover Acute severe symptoms after a wrist fracture suggesting acute median nerve compression Bilateral or rapidly progressive neuropathy suggesting a systemic cause needing investigation Attributing hand symptoms to carpal tunnel syndrome when the cause is cervical radiculopathy or a more proximal lesion Delaying surgery until irreversible thenar wasting and sensory loss develop Overlooking a treatable underlying condition such as hypothyroidism or diabetes Relying solely on provocative clinical tests, which can be falsely negative The carpal tunnel is a rigid osseofibrous canal bounded by the carpal bones and roofed by the flexor retinaculum, through which the median nerve passes alongside the flexor tendons. Any increase in the contents or reduction in the capacity of this fixed space raises pressure on the median nerve. Compression impairs the nerve's microcirculation and, if sustained, causes segmental demyelination and eventually axonal loss. Conditions that increase tissue volume (fluid retention in pregnancy, synovial thickening in rheumatoid arthritis, tenosynovitis from overuse) or reduce tunnel size (wrist fractures, deformity) precipitate symptoms. Sensory fibres are usually affected first, with motor weakness and thenar wasting appearing later. Most patients with mild to moderate disease improve with conservative measures or gain lasting relief from surgical release; however, longstanding severe compression with thenar wasting and marked axonal loss may leave incomplete recovery of strength and sensation despite decompression.

compromise Raised intracranial pressure from multisuture or cloverleaf skull fusion Airway or feeding difficulty in the neonatal period Laterality or situs anomalies in the MEGF8-related form Confusing it with an FGFR-related syndrome and missing the recessive inheritance and recurrence risk Failing to screen for congenital heart disease at presentation Overlooking the diagnostic clue of combined polydactyly and syndactyly Not arranging developmental support because intellectual outcome varies Carpenter syndrome is a ciliopathy caused by loss of function of RAB23, a small GTPase that participates in vesicular trafficking and in the regulation of hedgehog signalling at the primary cilium. Disrupted hedgehog signalling during development perturbs cranial suture patterning, causing premature multisuture fusion, and disturbs limb patterning, producing the combination of polydactyly and syndactyly. The wide role of this pathway explains the associated cardiac, growth and genital anomalies; MEGF8 mutations affect a related pathway and add laterality defects. Prognosis depends heavily on the severity of the craniosynostosis and any associated cardiac disease; with surgical correction and multidisciplinary support many children do well, though intellectual outcome is variable and some have significant learning difficulty.

This complex participates in ribosomal RNA processing, cell-cycle-related messenger RNA cleavage and mitochondrial RNA processing. Impaired function disturbs chondrocyte proliferation (metaphyseal dysplasia and short stature), hair follicle growth, lymphocyte proliferation (immunodeficiency) and erythropoiesis, and contributes to the increased predisposition to malignancy. Prognosis depends largely on the severity of the immunodeficiency and the lifelong increased risk of malignancy; those with severe combined immune impairment have a poorer outlook and may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, whereas milder cases can have near-normal survival with surveillance and infection prevention.

psychiatric rather than encephalopathic Assuming central and peripheral features cannot coexist in one disorder Antibodies bind contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2), a cell-adhesion protein Bartonellosis (incl. Cat-Scratch Disease) — Bartonella infection, cat-scratch disease Pyogenic (bacterial) lymphadenitis Mycobacterial infection (incl. tuberculous lymphadenitis) Brucellosis Syphilis Tularemia Plague Toxoplasmosis Sporotrichosis Histoplasmosis Serology (immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay) is the most commonly used diagnostic, but has variable sensitivity/specificity; CSD serodiagnosis is often based on IgG alone (in the absence of IgM) and seroconversion may take a few weeks, complicating interpretation (p.1352). PCR of pus aspirated from a lymph node or the primary inoculation lesion is highly sensitive and specific and is particularly useful for definitive, rapid diagnosis in seronegative patients; PCR of a lymph node biopsy specimen may be less sensitive (possibly due to sampling error) (p.1352). Histopathology shows early lymphoid hyperplasia, later stellate granulomata with necrosis, coalescing microabscesses and occasional multinucleated giant cells (nonspecific but may narrow the differential) (p.1352). For endocarditis: blood cultures (even with lysis-centrifugation or EDTA tubes) are positive in only ~25% of cases (mostly B. quintana, rarely B. henselae) and require prolonged incubation up to 6 weeks; high-titer (>=1:800) IgG serology supports the diagnosis but cross-reacts between B. quintana and B. henselae and with C. burnetii and Chlamydia; species-level identification usually requires PCR and DNA sequencing of valve tissue (p.1353). For bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: diagnosis is by histologic examination; Warthin-Starry silver staining of lesions reveals clusters of bacilli; cultures are usually negative though blood cultures may be positive (p.1355). Lymphoma / malignancy (weight loss and night sweats of CSD, and CSD-associated FUO, can mimic malignancy) Kaposi's sarcoma (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis) Pyogenic granuloma (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis) Subcutaneous tumors (differential for cutaneous bacillary angiomatosis) Bartonella are fastidious, facultative intracellular, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria; clinical presentation depends on both the infecting species and the host's immune status. Of the >40 species/subspecies, B. bacilliformis, B. quintana and B. henselae are most commonly identified human pathogens (p.1350). B. henselae is the principal etiologic agent of cat-scratch disease (CSD); rare cases are associated with Afipia felis and other Bartonella species. Apparently healthy bacteremic cats (especially kittens) are the major reservoir; person-to-person transmission does not occur and intrafamilial clustering is rare (p.1351). Typical CSD (85-90% of cases) is a usually self-limited subacute regional lymphadenopathy; a small (0.3-1 cm) painless erythematous papule/pustule appears at the inoculation site within days to 2 weeks in about one-third to two-thirds of patients, with nodes enlarging 1-3 weeks (or longer) after cat contact (p.1351-1352). Affected nodes are usually painful and suppurate in ~10% of cases; axillary/epitrochlear nodes are most commonly involved, then head/neck, then inguinal/femoral. About 50% have fever, malaise and anorexia; weight loss and night sweats can mimic lymphoma (p.1351-1352). Atypical (extranodal) CSD occurs in 10-15% and includes Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis (often unilateral visual deterioration), hepatosplenic disease, encephalitis/seizures/myelitis/cranial-nerve palsies, FUO, pneumonitis, debilitating myalgia, arthritis/arthralgia (mostly women >20 yr), osteomyelitis (incl. multifocal) and erythema nodosum (p.1353). CSD-associated FUO is a unique, sometimes severe and debilitating syndrome that often mimics malignancy and may involve multiple organs (hepatosplenic space-occupying lesions, abdominal/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, ocular disease, multifocal osteomyelitis); fever may be continuous or relapsing (p.1353). In elderly patients (>60 yr), lymphadenopathy is more often absent, whereas encephalitis and FUO are more common than in younger patients (p.1353). Coxiella burnetii and Bartonella species are the most common causes of culture-negative endocarditis; in one French series Bartonella accounted for 28% of 348 culture-negative endocarditis cases. B. quintana and B. henselae are the species most often implicated (p.1353). Bartonella endocarditis often presents as a prolonged, minimally febrile or even afebrile indolent illness lasting weeks to months; initial echocardiography may not show vegetations and acute aggressive disease is rare. Most cases are native-valve, ~60% aortic; B. henselae usually infects preexisting valvulopathy while B. quintana often infects normal valves (p.1353). Bacillary angiomatosis (caused by B. henselae or B. quintana) is a neovascular proliferative disease of severely immunocompromised patients, presenting as non-painful tan/red/purple cutaneous lesions, tender subcutaneous nodules, ulcerated plaques or verrucous growths; nodular forms resemble fungal or mycobacterial infection (p.1354-1355). Bacillary peliosis is a related angioproliferative disorder caused by B. henselae involving primarily the liver (peliosis hepatis) and also spleen and lymph nodes, with blood-filled cystic structures (microscopic to several mm). In advanced immunodeficiency, B. henselae and B. quintana are important causes of FUO (p.1355). Trench fever (5-day/quintan fever) is caused by B. quintana, transmitted by the human body louse; it has reemerged as chronic bacteremia in homeless people (urban/contemporary trench fever), with alcoholism and louse infestation as risk factors (p.1354). Persistent constitutional symptoms with failure of spontaneous regression of node size, and negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera (10-20% of CSD patients) — malignancy must be ruled out (p.1352). Seronegative CSD with lymphadenopathy and severe complications (encephalitis or neuroretinitis) — early biopsy is important to establish a specific diagnosis (p.1352). Unilateral visual deterioration (neuroretinitis) in suspected CSD — ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally cause moderate to severe vision loss (p.1353). Culture-negative endocarditis, especially in a homeless/alcoholic patient with body louse infestation (B. quintana) or significant cat exposure (B. henselae) (p.1353). Bartonella is a key but easily missed cause of culture-negative endocarditis; routine blood cultures are positive in only ~25% of cases and serology cross-reacts with C. burnetii and Chlamydia, so a high titer to one organism may reflect cross-reactivity rather than the true pathogen (p.1353). CSD is a frequently overlooked cause of FUO; CSD-associated FUO can mimic malignancy with multiorgan space-occupying lesions, leading to unnecessary investigation for cancer (p.1353). Negative serology does not exclude CSD: 10-20% of patients have negative acute- and convalescent-phase sera, and seroconversion may take weeks; PCR of aspirated pus is preferred in seronegative patients (p.1352). Suppurative nodes should be drained by large-bore needle aspiration, NOT by incision and drainage, to avoid chronic draining tracts (p.1353). In elderly patients, lymphadenopathy is more often absent, so CSD may be missed when it presents instead as encephalitis or FUO (p.1353). Bartonella adapt to specific domestic/wild mammalian hosts where prolonged intraerythrocytic and endothelial-cell infection creates an immune-protected reservoir, producing chronic bacteremia that may persist even after prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Adhesion and entry to endothelial cells and erythrocytes is facilitated by Bartonella adhesin A or variably expressed outer-membrane proteins; the organism evades host immunity by modifying virulence factors (lipopolysaccharide, flagella) and attenuating the immune response. Humans are incidental hosts for most species except B. quintana and B. bacilliformis (which are not zoonotic). In CSD, the cat-to-human transmission mode is undetermined: B. henselae-infected cat saliva spreads to claws by self-licking and contaminated flea feces can be inoculated by a scratch or bite (mucous-membrane/conjunctival inoculation also possible). Lymphatic drainage to regional nodes in immunocompetent hosts triggers a TH1 response producing necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis, with dendritic cells and chemokines driving granuloma formation. In bacillary angiomatosis, Bartonella angiogenic factor A (a proangiogenic autotransporter in B. henselae) activates the host vascular endothelial growth factor pathway to drive angiogenesis (p.1350-1355). In immunocompetent individuals, CSD (whether typical or atypical) usually resolves without treatment and without sequelae; resolution is slow, requiring weeks for fever/pain and months for node shrinkage, and lifelong immunity is the rule. Some ophthalmologic manifestations may occasionally result in moderate to severe vision loss. Bartonella endocarditis is often diagnosed late, and the proportion of patients requiring valvular surgery (~60%) is high, probably as a consequence of delayed diagnosis (p.1352-1353). Cat-scratch disease is described along clinical lines rather than a formal grading scale: (1) Typical CSD (85-90%) — subacute regional lymphadenopathy, usually self-limited; (2) Atypical/extranodal CSD (10-15%) — extranodal manifestations (Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, hepatosplenic disease, neurologic disease, FUO, osteomyelitis, etc.). Severe/disseminated Bartonella disease (bacillary angiomatosis and peliosis) occurs primarily in HIV-infected persons with CD4+ T-cell counts <100/uL and in other immunosuppressed patients; Bartonella endocarditis is a separate severe culture-negative-endocarditis presentation (p.1351-1355).

Cataract — lens opacity, senile cataract, age-related cataract, nuclear sclerosis, cortical cataract, posterior subcapsular cataract Refractive error Age-related macular degeneration Diabetic retinopathy or macular oedema Open-angle glaucoma Corneal opacity or dystrophy Vitreous opacities Visual acuity and refraction Slit-lamp examination to grade and localise the opacity Assessment of the red reflex Dilated fundus examination to exclude co-existing macular or retinal disease Biometry (keratometry and axial length) for intraocular lens power calculation before surgery Presents with gradual painless blurring of vision, glare and haloes around lights, and reduced contrast, often worse in bright sunlight or oncoming headlights Nuclear sclerotic cataract can cause a temporary myopic shift ('second sight') allowing reading without glasses before vision deteriorates Posterior subcapsular cataract disproportionately impairs near vision and glare and is associated with steroid use and diabetes The red reflex is reduced or shows dark opacities against the glow on ophthalmoscopy Age is the commonest cause; other associations include diabetes, trauma, chronic steroid use, uveitis, and congenital or metabolic causes in children Surgery (phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implant) is offered when the cataract limits daily function, not merely on its presence In children a white pupil (leukocoria) demands urgent assessment to exclude congenital cataract and retinoblastoma Leukocoria in an infant or child — exclude congenital cataract and retinoblastoma urgently Sudden rather than gradual visual loss, suggesting an alternative diagnosis A mature or hypermature (intumescent) lens that may precipitate secondary (phacomorphic or phacolytic) glaucoma Associated pain or redness pointing to lens-induced inflammation Attributing all of a patient's visual loss to cataract while missing co-existing macular degeneration or glaucoma Delaying assessment of childhood leukocoria and missing retinoblastoma Overlooking a myopic shift as an early sign of nuclear cataract Recommending surgery on lens appearance alone rather than functional impairment A cataract is any opacification of the normally transparent crystalline lens. With age, lens proteins (crystallins) undergo aggregation, oxidation, and cross-linking, while accumulation of pigment and changes in hydration reduce lens transparency and scatter incoming light. Depending on where these changes concentrate, opacity develops in the nucleus, cortex, or beneath the posterior capsule, each producing a distinct visual disturbance. Metabolic, traumatic, inflammatory, and toxic insults accelerate similar biochemical changes. Cataract surgery is one of the most effective and successful operations, restoring good vision in the great majority provided the retina and optic nerve are healthy.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia — CPVT, RYR2-related CPVT, CASQ2-related CPVT, familial polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia Long QT syndrome (especially exercise-triggered LQT1) Andersen-Tawil syndrome with bidirectional ectopy Digoxin toxicity causing bidirectional ventricular tachycardia Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy Vasovagal or neurocardiogenic syncope Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation Exercise treadmill or bicycle stress testing to provoke reproducible ectopy and bidirectional VT Ambulatory (Holter) monitoring to capture exertional arrhythmia burden 12-lead resting ECG (usually normal, helps exclude QT prolongation and other channelopathies) Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to confirm structurally normal heart and exclude cardiomyopathy Targeted genetic testing for RYR2 and CASQ2 variants Cascade genetic and clinical screening of first-degree relatives Presents in childhood or adolescence with syncope, seizures, or cardiac arrest triggered by exercise or intense emotion, in a structurally normal heart The resting ECG is typically normal, so a high index of suspicion and provocative testing are essential Exercise or catecholamine stress testing reproducibly elicits ventricular ectopy that progresses to bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia as heart rate rises Most cases follow autosomal dominant inheritance through cardiac ryanodine receptor (RYR2) variants; a rarer autosomal recessive form is caused by calsequestrin (CASQ2) variants Beta-blockers, particularly non-selective agents such as nadolol, are the cornerstone of therapy and reduce arrhythmic events Flecainide is a useful adjunct that suppresses calcium-driven ectopy, and left cardiac sympathetic denervation is an option for refractory disease An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is reserved for survivors of cardiac arrest or those with breakthrough events despite optimal medical therapy Family cascade genetic screening and counselling are important because relatives may carry the variant while appearing clinically normal Exertional or emotion-triggered syncope or seizure in a young person Aborted cardiac arrest or documented polymorphic ventricular tachycardia Family history of sudden death, drowning, or unexplained syncope in youth Recurrent arrhythmic events despite beta-blocker therapy Dismissing exertional syncope as vasovagal because the resting ECG and echocardiogram are normal Relying on a single resting ECG rather than provocative exercise testing to make the diagnosis Under-dosing beta-blockade or accepting poor adherence, leaving breakthrough arrhythmia Placing an ICD as sole therapy, since painful shocks can trigger an adrenergic surge and further arrhythmia Overlooking the need to screen and counsel apparently healthy relatives CPVT arises from dysregulated calcium handling in cardiac myocytes. Variants in the ryanodine receptor (RYR2) or calsequestrin (CASQ2) genes destabilise the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release channel complex, so that during adrenergic stimulation calcium leaks into the cytosol during diastole. This calcium overload drives delayed afterdepolarisations and triggered activity, which under the influence of circulating catecholamines generate the characteristic exercise- or emotion-induced bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia despite an anatomically normal heart. Sustained runs may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. With early diagnosis, adherence to beta-blockade with or without flecainide, and activity modification, arrhythmic events can be substantially reduced; however, untreated or poorly controlled CPVT carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death from adolescence onward.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection — CRBSI, CLABSI, central line-associated bloodstream infection, line infection Bloodstream infection from another source (urinary, respiratory, abdominal) contamination with coagulase-negative staphylococci Drug fever or transfusion reaction Thrombophlebitis without infection Post-operative or malignancy-associated fever Paired peripheral and catheter-drawn blood cultures for differential time to positivity Culture of the catheter tip after removal Echocardiography when S. aureus, candidal, or persistent bacteraemia is present Repeat blood cultures to document clearance after starting treatment Imaging to seek metastatic foci if bacteraemia persists A bloodstream infection attributable to an intravascular catheter, most often a central venous line, in a patient with no other apparent source Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, enterococci, Gram-negative bacilli, and Candida species are the usual culprits Diagnosis is supported by paired blood cultures drawn simultaneously from the catheter and a peripheral vein, with a shorter time to positivity from the catheter (differential time to positivity) Purulence or erythema at the exit site, or clinical improvement after line removal, supports the diagnosis but is not always present Management principles centre on removing or exchanging the catheter, particularly for S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, or complicated infection, alongside targeted antibiotics Antibiotic lock therapy may allow catheter salvage in selected long-term lines infected with less virulent organisms S. aureus and candidal line infections mandate a search for metastatic complications such as endocarditis, and echocardiography should be considered Prevention relies on strict insertion and maintenance bundles, hand hygiene, and prompt removal of unnecessary lines Severe sepsis or septic shock arising from the line infection requiring urgent resuscitation and line removal Persistent bacteraemia despite appropriate therapy suggesting endocarditis, septic thrombophlebitis, or a retained infected device S. aureus or Candida bloodstream infection with risk of metastatic seeding Signs of tunnel or pocket infection or septic thrombosis of the cannulated vein Continuing to use an infected catheter, especially with S. aureus or Candida, instead of removing it Misinterpreting a single coagulase-negative staphylococcal culture as contamination or as true infection without corroboration Failing to seek endocarditis or metastatic foci in S. aureus or candidal bacteraemia Not confirming clearance of bacteraemia with repeat cultures Intravascular catheters can become infected by several routes: migration of skin flora along the external catheter surface to the tip, contamination of the catheter hub and lumen during handling, haematogenous seeding from a distant focus, or, rarely, contaminated infusate. Microorganisms adhere to the catheter and form a biofilm within a matrix that shields them from host defences and antibiotics, allowing persistent shedding of organisms into the bloodstream. This biofilm explains why eradication frequently requires removing the device rather than antibiotics alone. Prognosis depends on the organism and host; uncomplicated coagulase-negative staphylococcal infection often resolves with line removal, whereas S. aureus, Candida, or complicated infections carry higher morbidity, mortality, and risk of metastatic complications.

recovery New urinary retention, overflow incontinence, or loss of bladder/bowel control demanding emergency imaging and surgical decompression Saddle anaesthesia and reduced anal sphincter tone Bilateral leg pain, weakness, or numbness with sphincter disturbance Fever and severe back pain suggesting an epidural abscess requiring urgent intervention Dismissing back pain with subtle urinary or perineal symptoms and missing the diagnosis until retention is established Delaying MRI or specialist referral, forfeiting the window for effective decompression Failing to examine perineal sensation and anal tone Assuming normal voiding excludes the syndrome without checking post-void residual volume Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots within the spinal canal below the termination of the spinal cord. Because these are peripheral nerve roots, compression produces lower motor neuron deficits, radicular pain, and disruption of the sacral parasympathetic and somatic supply to the bladder, bowel, and perineum. Sustained compression causes ischaemia and mechanical injury to the roots, and delayed relief risks irreversible loss of sphincter and sexual function. Outcome depends heavily on the speed of diagnosis and decompression. Surgery performed before the onset of established urinary retention gives the best functional results, whereas delayed treatment is associated with persistent bladder, bowel, sexual, and motor deficits. Some residual dysfunction is common even after timely surgery in severe cases.
