hypermotor-tonic-spasms sequence within a single seizure has been described Development is severely impaired with profound intellectual disability, absent speech, hand stereotypies and cortical visual impairment There is clinical overlap with Rett syndrome, but classic MECP2-related regression is not the typical pattern Seizures are usually drug-resistant despite an early honeymoon period in some children Comprehensive genetic testing establishes the diagnosis and distinguishes it from related encephalopathies Refractory early-infantile seizures including epileptic spasms Developmental stagnation with acquired microcephaly Feeding difficulties, recurrent aspiration or respiratory compromise Emergence of the characteristic hypermotor-tonic-spasms seizure sequence Assuming Rett syndrome without genetic confirmation despite overlapping features Interpreting an early normal EEG or MRI as excluding the disorder Missing cortical visual impairment and its impact on development Persisting with escalating polytherapy without acknowledging drug resistance CDKL5 deficiency disorder results from loss-of-function variants in the X-linked CDKL5 gene, which encodes a serine-threonine kinase important for neuronal maturation, dendritic and synaptic development, and regulation of excitatory and inhibitory signalling. Deficient kinase activity disrupts synaptic function and network connectivity in the developing brain, producing early-onset refractory seizures and a severe developmental encephalopathy. X-linkage and patterns of X-inactivation account for the marked female predominance and phenotypic variability. Most affected individuals have lifelong drug-resistant epilepsy and severe intellectual and motor disability with limited independent function. Life expectancy can be reduced by complications including respiratory illness and SUDEP, though many survive into adulthood with supportive care.

Central core disease — CCD, RYR1-related myopathy, central core myopathy, RYR1 Nemaline myopathy Centronuclear/myotubular myopathy Congenital muscular dystrophy Spinal muscular atrophy Multiminicore disease (RYR1/SEPN1 related) Congenital myasthenic syndrome Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme histochemistry to demonstrate central cores in type 1 fibres Targeted or panel genetic testing including RYR1 sequencing and copy-number analysis Serum creatine kinase, usually normal or mildly elevated Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to exclude neurogenic and other myopathic causes Baseline and serial respiratory function testing and orthopaedic assessment for scoliosis and hip dysplasia Contracture/in-vitro contracture testing or genetic counselling regarding malignant hyperthermia susceptibility Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with hypotonia, delayed motor milestones and predominantly proximal, often static or slowly progressive weakness Caused most often by variants in the ryanodine receptor gene RYR1, usually inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern although recessive forms occur Muscle biopsy hallmark is central, well-demarcated cores running along the length of type 1 fibres that lack oxidative enzyme staining on NADH, SDH and cytochrome oxidase reactions There is a strong and clinically critical association with susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia, so anaesthetic history is essential Orthopaedic complications such as congenital hip dislocation, scoliosis and foot deformity are common and may dominate the picture Bulbar and respiratory involvement is usually milder than in other congenital myopathies but should still be monitored Creatine kinase is typically normal or only mildly raised, which helps distinguish it from dystrophies History of anaesthetic complications or family history of malignant hyperthermia Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising ventilation Feeding or swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk in infants Administering triggering anaesthetic agents without recognising malignant hyperthermia susceptibility Assuming a normal creatine kinase excludes a significant myopathy Overlooking cores because oxidative enzyme stains were not performed on biopsy Attributing static weakness purely to an orthopaedic problem and missing the underlying myopathy Central core disease is a congenital myopathy most commonly resulting from variants in RYR1, which encodes the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Abnormal channel function disturbs excitation-contraction coupling and calcium handling, and over time regions of affected fibres lose mitochondria and oxidative enzyme activity, producing the characteristic amorphous central cores. The same channel dysfunction underlies the linked risk of malignant hyperthermia, in which volatile anaesthetics and depolarising muscle relaxants trigger uncontrolled calcium release, hypermetabolism and rhabdomyolysis. Predominant involvement of type 1 fibres accounts for the proximal, often relatively non-progressive weakness. Weakness is often static or only slowly progressive and many affected individuals achieve independent ambulation, though orthopaedic and, less commonly, respiratory complications may require ongoing management. The dominant lifelong risk is malignant hyperthermia during anaesthesia, which is preventable with appropriate precautions.

Central retinal artery occlusion — CRAO, retinal artery occlusion, retinal stroke, central retinal arterial occlusion Central retinal vein occlusion Ischaemic (arteritic or non-arteritic) optic neuropathy Vitreous haemorrhage Retinal detachment Acute optic neuritis Ophthalmic artery occlusion Dilated fundoscopy for retinal pallor and cherry-red spot Assessment for a relative afferent pupillary defect ESR, CRP, and platelets to screen for giant cell arteritis, with temporal artery biopsy if suspected Carotid Doppler ultrasound to identify an embolic source Cardiac evaluation including ECG and echocardiography Blood pressure, glucose, and lipid assessment; OCT and fluorescein angiography as adjuncts Presents as sudden, painless, profound loss of vision in one eye, often to counting fingers or worse A relative afferent pupillary defect is present in the affected eye Fundoscopy shows a pale, oedematous retina with a classic cherry-red spot at the fovea and attenuated, segmented ('cattle-trucking') arterioles It is effectively a stroke of the eye — treat as a time-critical emergency and investigate the same as an acute cerebral ischaemic event Always exclude giant cell arteritis in older patients by asking about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache and checking inflammatory markers Immediate measures aim to dislodge or reperfuse (ocular massage, lowering intraocular pressure), though evidence for benefit is limited once the window has passed Urgent referral for stroke workup (carotid imaging, cardiac source, vascular risk factors) is essential to prevent a subsequent cerebral stroke Time-critical emergency — inner retinal infarction becomes irreversible within a short window, so treat and refer immediately Suspected giant cell arteritis threatens the fellow eye and requires urgent systemic treatment without waiting for biopsy It is a warning of systemic embolic disease with high risk of subsequent cerebral stroke Bilateral or ophthalmic artery involvement suggesting a major vascular or arteritic process Failing to consider and treat giant cell arteritis in an older patient, risking loss of the second eye Treating it as an isolated eye problem rather than initiating urgent stroke and vascular workup Dilating or delaying assessment and missing the narrow reperfusion window Confusing it with vein occlusion, which shows haemorrhages rather than retinal pallor Central retinal artery occlusion results from acute interruption of blood flow in the central retinal artery, most often from an embolus (carotid or cardiac) or from thrombosis, arteritis, or vasospasm. The inner retina, supplied by this artery, is exquisitely sensitive to ischaemia; sudden occlusion causes rapid infarction and oedema of the inner retinal layers. The fovea, supplied by the underlying choroid, retains its colour and stands out as a cherry-red spot against the surrounding pale, opaque ischaemic retina. Irreversible neuronal damage occurs within a short ischaemic window. Visual prognosis is generally poor, with permanent severe visual loss common; the main priority becomes preventing a devastating cerebral stroke and protecting the fellow eye.

Central retinal vein occlusion — CRVO, central retinal venous occlusion, retinal vein thrombosis Central retinal artery occlusion Ocular ischaemic syndrome Diabetic retinopathy with widespread haemorrhage Hypertensive retinopathy Hyperviscosity retinopathy (e.g. myeloma, Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia) Papilloedema or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy Dilated fundus examination to assess haemorrhage distribution, ischaemia, and disc swelling Optical coherence tomography to detect and quantify macular oedema Fluorescein angiography to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic disease and map capillary non-perfusion Intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy to detect angle neovascularisation Blood pressure, blood glucose, and lipid assessment; thrombophilia and inflammatory screen in younger patients Typically presents as sudden, painless, unilateral loss or blurring of vision, most often in older patients with vascular risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes, or hyperviscosity Fundus shows the classic 'blood and thunder' picture: widespread retinal haemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots, and optic disc swelling Clinically divided into non-ischaemic (perfused) and ischaemic (non-perfused) types, with the ischaemic form carrying much higher risk of neovascular complications A relative afferent pupillary defect and poor initial visual acuity are markers of an ischaemic occlusion The most feared complication is neovascular ('90-day') glaucoma from rubeosis iridis; the eye must be monitored for iris and angle new vessels Macular oedema is the main cause of reduced central vision and is managed with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or intravitreal steroid Ischaemic retina and neovascularisation are treated with pan-retinal photocoagulation to reduce the angiogenic drive A younger patient with CRVO warrants evaluation for thrombophilia, inflammatory, and hyperviscosity causes New iris or angle vessels (rubeosis) or a rising intraocular pressure heralding neovascular glaucoma Relative afferent pupillary defect with poor acuity indicating an ischaemic occlusion Rapidly worsening vision or pain suggesting progression to neovascular glaucoma Bilateral or young-patient presentation suggesting a systemic hyperviscosity or thrombophilic disorder Assuming a good early prognosis without follow-up, missing conversion from non-ischaemic to ischaemic disease Failing to examine the iris and angle for neovascularisation at each review Overlooking treatable systemic risk factors such as uncontrolled hypertension Not considering a hyperviscosity or thrombophilic cause in younger or bilateral cases Central retinal vein occlusion results from thrombosis of the central retinal vein at or posterior to the lamina cribrosa, where the central retinal artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath; arteriosclerotic thickening of the artery compresses the vein and promotes turbulent flow and thrombus formation. The resulting rise in venous and capillary pressure causes widespread retinal haemorrhage, oedema, and, when perfusion fails, capillary non-perfusion and retinal ischaemia. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor, driving macular oedema and neovascularisation of the retina, optic disc, and iris, which can lead to neovascular glaucoma. Non-ischaemic CRVO often has a reasonable visual outcome, though some cases convert to the ischaemic form over time. Ischaemic CRVO carries a poor visual prognosis and a high risk of neovascular glaucoma; timely anti-VEGF therapy for macular oedema and laser for ischaemia improve outcomes but vision is frequently limited.

Central sleep apnoea — CSA, central sleep apnea, central apnoea, Cheyne-Stokes breathing Obstructive sleep apnoea Mixed (complex) sleep apnoea Obesity hypoventilation syndrome Nocturnal breathlessness from decompensated heart failure Periodic breathing at high altitude Neuromuscular or chest-wall hypoventilation disorders Attended polysomnography to characterise and quantify central versus obstructive events Echocardiography and cardiac assessment when heart failure is suspected Daytime arterial or capillary blood gas to identify chronic hypercapnia Brain and brainstem imaging if a central neurological cause is suspected Review of opioid and sedative medication as a reversible contributor Central sleep apnoea reflects a transient loss of respiratory drive, so airflow and respiratory effort stop together, distinguishing it from obstructive events where effort continues against a closed airway Unlike the loud habitual snoring of obstructive disease, patients may present chiefly with fragmented sleep, frequent awakenings, nocturnal breathlessness, or witnessed pauses without much snoring A Cheyne-Stokes crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern is characteristic and points strongly towards underlying heart failure The disorder clusters into hypercapnic forms (blunted drive, as in brainstem disease or opioid use) and non-hypercapnic forms driven by an unstable, oversensitive ventilatory control loop Polysomnography is required to confirm the diagnosis and to separate central from obstructive and mixed events Treatment is directed at the underlying cause; optimising heart failure therapy often reduces central events, and supplemental oxygen or adaptive ventilatory support may be considered in selected patients Long-term opioid therapy is an increasingly common and reversible contributor that should be actively sought in the history Adaptive servo-ventilation should be used cautiously and is contraindicated in patients with symptomatic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction Cheyne-Stokes breathing indicating underlying heart failure requiring cardiac evaluation and optimisation New central apnoea with focal neurology suggesting a brainstem lesion or stroke Central events emerging or worsening on chronic opioid therapy Daytime hypercapnia, cor pulmonale, or morning headache signalling chronic ventilatory failure Assuming all sleep apnoea is obstructive and missing the absent respiratory effort that defines central events Prescribing adaptive servo-ventilation to patients with symptomatic reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure, in whom it may be harmful Overlooking chronic opioid use as a treatable cause Failing to investigate and treat underlying heart failure or brainstem pathology Central sleep apnoea arises from intermittent failure of the brainstem respiratory rhythm generator to signal the respiratory muscles, so both airflow and inspiratory effort cease simultaneously. In non-hypercapnic (high loop gain) forms, ventilatory control is unstable: an oversensitive chemoreceptor response drives arterial CO2 below the apnoeic threshold, breathing stops until CO2 rises again, and overshoot perpetuates a cyclical pattern. Prolonged circulation time in heart failure delays chemoreceptor feedback and produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes cycling. In hypercapnic forms, reduced central drive or neuromuscular capacity (brainstem lesions, opioids, chronic hypoventilation) causes sustained underventilation with superimposed central pauses. Recurrent apnoeas generate cyclical hypoxaemia, arousals, and sympathetic surges. Prognosis is largely determined by the underlying disorder; central sleep apnoea complicating advanced heart failure is a marker of poorer outcome, whereas apnoea from reversible causes such as opioids or high altitude often improves once the trigger is addressed.

hypotonia, weakness, respiratory failure and often a history of polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movements Autosomal dominant (DNM2) and recessive (BIN1) centronuclear forms are generally milder with later onset and slower progression Ophthalmoplegia and ptosis are common and are a useful clinical clue, alongside a long face and proximal weakness Muscle biopsy hallmark is centrally placed nuclei in a high proportion of fibres, often with a central zone of oxidative enzyme activity surrounded by a pale halo, resembling fetal myotubes Male infants with the X-linked form frequently have macrosomia, long digits and elongated face Creatine kinase is usually normal or mildly elevated Carrier females for MTM1 variants may occasionally show mild or asymmetric weakness Neonatal respiratory failure requiring immediate ventilatory support Recurrent aspiration from bulbar weakness Signs of hepatic peliosis or bleeding described in severe X-linked disease Progressive hypoventilation in older children with dominant or recessive forms Failing to arrange urgent respiratory support in a hypotonic newborn with the X-linked form Overlooking ptosis and ophthalmoplegia that point toward centronuclear myopathy Assuming a female carrier is unaffected when mild manifestations can occur Interpreting central nuclei as regenerating fibres rather than the primary pathology Centronuclear myopathies are congenital myopathies characterised by centrally located nuclei in muscle fibres. The severe X-linked form is caused by loss-of-function variants in MTM1, which encodes myotubularin, a phosphoinositide phosphatase important for membrane trafficking and the organisation of the triad and T-tubule system. Autosomal dominant disease is usually caused by DNM2 (dynamin 2) variants and recessive disease by BIN1 (amphiphysin 2) variants; all converge on disturbed membrane remodelling and excitation-contraction coupling. The resulting maldevelopment of the sarcotubular system impairs contractile function and, in severe cases, arrests fibres at a myotube-like stage. The severe X-linked form carries high early mortality from respiratory failure, though intensive respiratory support has improved survival in some cases. Autosomal dominant and recessive centronuclear forms are typically slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival, with disability determined mainly by limb and respiratory muscle involvement.

and normal pressure hydrocephalus Intoxication (alcohol, anticonvulsants, other drugs) Functional gait disorder Weakness or extrapyramidal disorders mimicking incoordination MRI of the brain focusing prompting evaluation for hereditary, degenerative, and metabolic causes Acute cerebellar signs with headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness suggesting cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can cause brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus requiring emergency neurosurgical assessment Rapidly progressive ataxia suggesting a paraneoplastic, inflammatory, or toxic cause Associated cranial nerve or long-tract signs indicating brainstem involvement New ataxia in a patient on potentially toxic drug levels such as anticonvulsants Failing to distinguish cerebellar from sensory or vestibular ataxia, leading to the wrong workup Missing a cerebellar stroke or haemorrhage that can rapidly deteriorate into brainstem compression Overlooking reversible causes such as drug toxicity, vitamin deficiency, or hypothyroidism Not pursuing a paraneoplastic cause in subacute progressive cerebellar degeneration Cerebellar ataxia reflects impaired function of the cerebellum or its afferent and efferent connections, which normally coordinate the timing, force, and accuracy of movement and maintain balance and posture. Damage to the cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, or connecting peduncles disrupts these predictive and error-correcting mechanisms, producing dysmetria, tremor, and incoordination. The underlying pathology may be vascular, inflammatory, neoplastic, toxic, metabolic, degenerative, or genetic. Prognosis depends entirely on the underlying cause. Some causes, such as drug toxicity, vitamin deficiency, or an inflammatory process, are reversible with treatment, whereas hereditary and neurodegenerative ataxias are typically progressive. Acute cerebellar strokes can be life-threatening but may recover substantially with timely intervention.

Cerebral aneurysm — intracranial aneurysm, berry aneurysm, saccular aneurysm Other causes of thunderclap headache (reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome) Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal haemorrhage Arteriovenous malformation Intracerebral haemorrhage from hypertension Bacterial meningitis Migraine or primary headache Non-contrast CT head to detect subarachnoid blood Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia when CT is negative but suspicion persists CT angiography or digital subtraction angiography to define aneurysm location and morphology MRI/MR angiography for detection and follow-up of unruptured aneurysms Monitoring of sodium, and transcranial Doppler or imaging for vasospasm after haemorrhage Most intracranial aneurysms are saccular (berry) lesions arising at branch points of the circle of Willis, and many are asymptomatic until they rupture Rupture causes aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, classically a sudden thunderclap headache described as the worst ever, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, and reduced consciousness A non-contrast CT performed early is highly sensitive for subarachnoid blood; if negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia is used An enlarging unruptured aneurysm can cause warning signs such as a painful third nerve palsy from a posterior communicating artery lesion Risk factors include hypertension, smoking, family history, polycystic kidney disease, and connective tissue disorders After rupture, priorities are securing the aneurysm by endovascular coiling or surgical clipping to prevent rebleeding, alongside management of complications Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, and seizures are important complications after subarachnoid haemorrhage Management of unruptured aneurysms weighs rupture risk (influenced by size, site, and morphology) against the risks of treatment, and small stable lesions may be monitored Sudden thunderclap headache suggesting aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage requiring emergency imaging Reduced or fluctuating consciousness and focal deficit indicating a large bleed or rebleeding New painful third nerve palsy as a warning sign of an enlarging or symptomatic aneurysm Acute hydrocephalus or deterioration from delayed cerebral ischaemia after haemorrhage Dismissing a sudden severe headache as migraine and missing subarachnoid haemorrhage Relying on a late CT alone, when sensitivity falls and lumbar puncture may be needed Failing to secure a ruptured aneurysm promptly, risking early rebleeding Overlooking delayed complications such as vasospasm, hyponatraemia, and hydrocephalus A cerebral aneurysm is a focal outpouching of an intracranial artery wall, typically forming at bifurcations where haemodynamic stress is greatest and the muscular and elastic layers are relatively deficient. Over time, wall degeneration and turbulent flow allow the sac to enlarge. Rupture releases arterial blood into the subarachnoid space, abruptly raising intracranial pressure and irritating the meninges. Subsequent breakdown products can trigger arterial vasospasm days later, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia, while blood interfering with cerebrospinal fluid circulation can produce acute or communicating hydrocephalus. Unruptured aneurysms may remain quiescent, but rupture carries substantial mortality and morbidity, with many deaths occurring before or soon after hospital arrival; early securing of the aneurysm and management of vasospasm and hydrocephalus improve outcomes for survivors.

Cerebral Palsy — CP, spastic diplegia, static encephalopathy Progressive neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders Spinal muscular atrophy and other neuromuscular disorders Dopa-responsive dystonia Hereditary spastic paraplegia Structural spinal cord lesions Global developmental delay without a motor disorder MRI of the brain to identify structural or ischaemic lesions EEG when seizures are suspected Metabolic or genetic testing if the presentation is atypical or progressive Assessment of vision and hearing Hip surveillance imaging to detect subluxation Evaluation of feeding, swallowing, and nutrition A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive injury or malformation of the developing brain, though the clinical picture can change as the child grows. It is the most common cause of chronic motor disability beginning in childhood. Classified by motor type (spastic, dyskinetic, ataxic, or mixed) and by topography (hemiplegia, diplegia, quadriplegia). Spastic forms are most common; early signs include abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, delayed motor milestones, and early hand preference before one year. Preterm birth, low birth weight, intrauterine growth restriction, perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic injury, infection, kernicterus, and brain malformations are recognised risk factors. Frequent comorbidities include intellectual disability, epilepsy, visual and hearing impairment, feeding and swallowing difficulties, communication problems, and orthopaedic complications such as hip subluxation and contractures. Diagnosis is largely clinical; MRI often identifies the underlying lesion and helps establish aetiology. Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, aiming to maximise function and participation with therapy, orthotics, spasticity treatment, and orthopaedic care rather than cure. Because the disorder is static, clear progression or regression of neurological signs should prompt a search for an alternative, evolving diagnosis. Loss of previously acquired skills or clear neurological progression (suggests an alternative diagnosis) New or worsening seizures Signs of aspiration or faltering growth from feeding difficulty Progressive scoliosis or hip dislocation Rapidly increasing spasticity or dystonia causing pain or care difficulty Labelling a child with cerebral palsy when the course is actually progressive (missing a treatable metabolic or genetic disorder) Focusing only on motor impairment and overlooking epilepsy, sensory, or feeding comorbidities Neglecting hip surveillance, allowing silent dislocation Underestimating cognition in non-verbal children with good comprehension Delaying nutritional and communication support Cerebral palsy results from injury or maldevelopment of the immature brain from any of a range of prenatal, perinatal, or early postnatal insults. In preterm infants, periventricular white-matter injury (periventricular leukomalacia) commonly affects descending motor tracts, producing spastic diplegia; in term infants, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, malformations, stroke, or kernicterus may be responsible. The primary lesion is non-progressive, but secondary musculoskeletal changes such as contractures and bony deformity evolve over time. The motor impairment itself is non-progressive, and life expectancy is often near normal in milder forms; outcome depends on severity, mobility level, and comorbidities, with severe quadriplegia, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and feeding problems associated with greater disability and shorter survival.

Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis — CTX, sterol 27-hydroxylase deficiency, CYP27A1 deficiency, cholestanolosis Familial hypercholesterolaemia with tendon xanthomata Sitosterolaemia (xanthomata with a plant-sterol defect) Other hereditary spastic paraplegias and cerebellar ataxias Multiple sclerosis or other progressive neuroinflammatory disease Early-onset dementia or leukodystrophy of other cause Neonatal cholestasis from other bile acid synthesis defects Plasma cholestanol concentration (characteristically raised) Urinary bile alcohol analysis Molecular genetic testing of the CYP27A1 gene Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, which may show cerebellar and dentate nucleus changes Slit-lamp examination for juvenile cataract and clinical assessment of tendon xanthomata Lipid profile, noting cholesterol may be normal or low despite xanthomata Autosomal recessive defect of bile acid synthesis caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1) The block impairs bile acid production and diverts cholesterol to cholestanol, which accumulates in the brain, tendons and other tissues A highly treatable but frequently missed cause of progressive neurological decline; early diagnosis is critical to prevent irreversible damage The classic triad comprises tendon xanthomata (especially the Achilles tendon), early-onset (juvenile) bilateral cataracts and progressive neuropsychiatric and cerebellar dysfunction Early clues in childhood include neonatal cholestasis, intractable or chronic diarrhoea and learning difficulty, preceding the neurological syndrome The biochemical hallmark is raised plasma cholestanol with normal or low cholesterol and increased urinary bile alcohols Treatment is replacement with chenodeoxycholic acid, which suppresses abnormal synthesis and can halt or improve disease if started early; a statin may be added Progressive cognitive, psychiatric or cerebellar decline in a young person with tendon xanthomata Early-onset bilateral cataracts in a child or young adult Neonatal cholestasis or intractable childhood diarrhoea of unknown cause Delay in starting bile acid replacement, risking irreversible neurological damage Assuming tendon xanthomata always indicate familial hypercholesterolaemia, since cholesterol is often normal here Missing the diagnosis during the early non-neurological phase (cholestasis, diarrhoea, cataract) Overlooking juvenile cataract as an early diagnostic clue Delaying treatment while awaiting genetic confirmation, forfeiting a treatable window Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives given the recessive inheritance Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is caused by deficiency of sterol 27-hydroxylase, an enzyme in the mitochondrial pathway of bile acid synthesis from cholesterol. Loss of this step reduces production of the primary bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid, removing the normal negative feedback on the rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis and driving overproduction of bile acid intermediates. These intermediates are shunted into cholestanol and bile alcohols, which accumulate in tissues. Deposition of cholestanol and cholesterol in the central nervous system, tendons and lens produces the characteristic xanthomata, cataracts and progressive neurodegeneration. Replacing the deficient bile acid restores feedback inhibition and reduces the toxic accumulation. If chenodeoxycholic acid replacement is started before significant neurological damage, progression can be halted and some deficits improve, giving a good outlook; late diagnosis after established neurodegeneration carries a poorer prognosis with irreversible disability.

may be treated with surgery (radical hysterectomy or fertility-sparing trachelectomy in selected women) while locally advanced disease is managed with concurrent chemoradiation Organised cytology and HPV-based screening programmes with prophylactic HPV vaccination markedly reduce incidence and mortality Advanced disease may present with pelvic or leg pain, lymphoedema, ureteric obstruction, or fistula formation into the bladder or rectum Heavy or uncontrolled vaginal haemorrhage from a friable tumour Features of ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis and renal impairment Development of vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistula Signs of pelvic sidewall involvement with leg swelling and neuropathic pain Evidence of distant metastatic spread requiring urgent oncology referral Relying on cytology alone and failing to biopsy a visibly abnormal or friable cervix Missing endocervical adenocarcinoma that lies above the reach of routine sampling Attributing postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding to benign causes without adequate assessment Underestimating local extent without appropriate cross-sectional imaging Overlooking renal impairment from silent ureteric obstruction in advanced disease Oncogenic HPV integrates into the host genome of cervical epithelial cells, and its E6 and E7 oncoproteins inactivate the tumour suppressor proteins p53 and retinoblastoma protein, deregulating the cell cycle and permitting accumulation of genetic damage. Most infections clear spontaneously, but persistent infection produces cervical intraepithelial neoplasia that may progress over years to invasive carcinoma. Invasion typically begins at the transformation zone and extends locally into the cervical stroma, vagina, and parametrium, then to pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes and distant sites. Prognosis depends strongly on stage at diagnosis: disease confined to the cervix carries high cure rates, whereas parametrial extension, nodal involvement, and distant spread substantially reduce survival. Tumour size, histological subtype, and depth of invasion further influence outcome, and screening plus vaccination continue to shift diagnosis toward earlier, more curable stages.

Cervical Incompetence — cervical incompetence, cervical insufficiency, incompetent cervix, cervical insufficiency of pregnancy Preterm labour with contractions Chorioamnionitis or intra-amniotic infection Placental abruption Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes Uterine anomaly causing recurrent loss Antiphospholipid syndrome and other causes of recurrent mid-trimester loss Serial transvaginal ultrasound cervical length measurement with assessment for funnelling Speculum examination to assess dilatation and detect bulging or ruptured membranes Screening for infection including genital and urinary cultures where relevant Review of obstetric and surgical history for prior losses and cervical procedures Assessment for alternative causes of recurrent loss such as thrombophilia or uterine anomaly where indicated Cervical incompetence is painless progressive cervical dilatation in the second trimester leading to mid-trimester pregnancy loss or spontaneous preterm birth in the absence of contractions or labour The hallmark history is recurrent second-trimester losses that are painless, often with rupture of membranes or bulging membranes and rapid, non-laborious delivery Risk factors include previous cervical surgery (cone biopsy, large loop excision), cervical trauma from dilatation, congenital collagen or Mullerian abnormalities, and prior mechanical dilatation Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length is the key surveillance tool, with progressive shortening and funnelling of the internal os indicating risk Cervical cerclage, a stitch placed to reinforce the cervix, is offered based on history, ultrasound findings, or examination findings depending on the clinical scenario Vaginal progesterone is used to reduce preterm birth risk in women with a short cervix, and can complement or substitute for cerclage in selected cases History-indicated cerclage is typically placed electively in early second trimester, whereas ultrasound- or examination-indicated (rescue) cerclage is placed when shortening or dilatation is detected Emergency rescue cerclage on a dilated cervix with exposed membranes carries higher risks of membrane rupture and infection and requires careful case selection The diagnosis is clinical and somewhat retrospective, as no single definitive test confirms it, so it must be distinguished from preterm labour and infection Painless cervical dilatation with bulging or exposed fetal membranes in the second trimester Rupture of membranes at previable or early gestation Signs of intra-amniotic infection (fever, uterine tenderness, offensive discharge, maternal or fetal tachycardia) Rapidly progressive cervical shortening on surveillance scanning Onset of contractions or bleeding suggesting labour or abruption rather than pure insufficiency Attributing painless mid-trimester loss to bad luck and not investigating for insufficiency Placing a rescue cerclage without recognising established infection or advanced labour Overlooking infection as either a cause or a contraindication to intervention Relying on a single cervical length measurement rather than trends Failing to plan surveillance or cerclage early in a subsequent at-risk pregnancy The cervix normally remains firm and closed under load until term, maintained by its collagen-rich connective tissue. In cervical insufficiency, structural or functional weakness of this tissue, whether congenital, from collagen disorders, or acquired through surgical or traumatic disruption, means the cervix cannot withstand the increasing mechanical stress of the growing pregnancy. It shortens, effaces, and dilates painlessly. As the cervix opens, the fetal membranes prolapse into the vagina, becoming exposed to ascending flora; membrane rupture and mid-trimester loss or preterm delivery follow, often without the coordinated contractions of true labour. With recognition and appropriate intervention, whether cerclage, progesterone, or close surveillance, many women achieve substantially prolonged gestation and improved neonatal outcomes in subsequent pregnancies. Prognosis is poorer when membranes are already prolapsed or ruptured, or when infection supervenes. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is significant, warranting proactive planning.

Cervical spondylosis — cervical degenerative disc disease, cervical osteoarthritis, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, cervical radiculopathy Cervical disc prolapse Peripheral nerve entrapment (e.g. carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome) Brachial plexopathy or thoracic outlet syndrome Motor neuron disease and other neurodegenerative conditions Multiple sclerosis or intramedullary cord lesion Shoulder pathology (rotator cuff disease) referring pain to the arm Spinal tumour or infection MRI of the cervical spine to assess cord and root compression Plain cervical radiographs (including flexion/extension views) for alignment and degenerative change Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to distinguish radiculopathy from peripheral entrapment CT for detailed bony anatomy when MRI is contraindicated or surgery is planned Neurological examination for upper and lower limb signs of myelopathy Age-related degeneration of the cervical discs and facet joints causing neck pain, stiffness, and sometimes referred occipital headache; it is extremely common and often asymptomatic on imaging Nerve-root compression by osteophytes or disc material produces radiculopathy with dermatomal arm pain, sensory change, weakness, and reflex loss, most often at C5/6 and C6/7 Cord compression from a narrowed canal produces cervical spondylotic myelopathy, the most important complication, which can develop insidiously Myelopathy is suggested by gait disturbance, clumsy hands, loss of dexterity, and upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, Hoffmann's sign, extensor plantars, sometimes bladder involvement) Most patients with axial neck pain or radiculopathy improve with conservative measures such as analgesia, activity modification, and physiotherapy MRI is the investigation of choice to demonstrate cord and root compression when myelopathy or persistent radiculopathy is suspected Progressive myelopathy is an indication for surgical decompression to halt deterioration, since established cord damage recovers poorly Radiographic degenerative change correlates poorly with symptoms, so imaging findings must be interpreted alongside the clinical picture Signs of cervical myelopathy (gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, sphincter dysfunction) requiring urgent specialist assessment Rapidly progressive neurological deficit Features suggesting infection or malignancy (fever, weight loss, night pain, cancer history) Acute deterioration after neck trauma in a spondylotic, stenotic spine Missing early myelopathy by attributing gait or hand-function changes to age or arthritis Over-relying on degenerative radiographic findings that are common and often asymptomatic Delaying decompression in progressive myelopathy until irreversible cord damage occurs Aggressive manipulation of a stenotic, myelopathic cervical spine With ageing the cervical intervertebral discs lose height and hydration, transferring load to the facet and uncovertebral joints, which develop osteophytes. These bony spurs, together with disc bulging, ligamentum flavum thickening, and reduced canal diameter, encroach on the neural foramina and spinal canal. Foraminal narrowing compresses nerve roots to cause radiculopathy, while central canal stenosis compresses the spinal cord, producing myelopathy through direct pressure and impaired vascular supply. Dynamic factors during neck movement can aggravate cord compression. The degenerative process is gradual, and neurological compromise may accumulate slowly before becoming clinically apparent. Axial neck pain and radiculopathy usually follow a fluctuating but generally benign course with conservative care; cervical spondylotic myelopathy tends to progress in a stepwise manner, and while surgery can arrest decline, neurological recovery of established deficits is often incomplete, making timely intervention important.

Cestode (Tapeworm) Infections — neurocysticercosis, Taenia, echinococcosis, hydatid disease Intestinal taeniasis presenting only with passage of proglottids or vague abdominal symptoms (T. saginata, T. asiatica, T. solium, D. latus, D. caninum) Megaloblastic / pernicious-type anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency in D. latus fish tapeworm infection Seizure disorder / epilepsy of other cause in regions where neurocysticercosis is endemic Obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus from ventricular or subarachnoid cysticerci Sparganosis presenting as a migrating subcutaneous, periorbital or CNS mass (Spirometra plerocercoid) Coenurosis presenting as a CNS or subcutaneous space-occupying cystic lesion (T. multiceps, T. serialis) Tuberculoma / CNS tuberculosis (major cause of focal CNS mass lesions in India and East Asia) Toxoplasma encephalitis (ring-enhancing CNS lesions, especially in immunocompromised/HIV) Pyogenic brain abscess Other tissue helminths producing CNS or hepatic cysts (e.g., schistosomiasis, sparganosis) Stool microscopy for eggs/proglottids; perianal cellophane-tape swab when taeniasis suspected (eggs of the three Taenia species are morphologically indistinguishable) Examination of mature proglottids or scolex, or molecular testing, to distinguish T. solium from T. saginata/T. asiatica Neuroimaging (MRI and CT) for neurocysticercosis, including FIESTA/3D-CISS for ventricular/subarachnoid cysts and susceptibility-weighted imaging for calcifications Enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) on serum for cysticercosis antibody CSF analysis (lymphocytic, neutrophilic or eosinophilic pleocytosis; protein may be raised; glucose usually normal but occasionally markedly reduced) Funduscopic / dilated ophthalmologic exam in all patients with suspected neurocysticercosis Ultrasound, CT or MRI with WHO ultrasound staging (CL, CE1-CE5) for hepatic cystic echinococcosis; chest x-ray/CT for pulmonary cysts ELISA/immunoblot serology for echinococcosis (cannot exclude disease if negative) PET to follow disease activity in alveolar echinococcosis Primary or metastatic brain tumor (parenchymal neurocysticercosis or spinal cysticercus can mimic intraspinal tumor) CNS lymphoma Hepatic neoplasm or simple/biliary hepatic cyst (alveolar echinococcosis mimics a slow-growing liver tumor; cystic hydatid mimics benign liver cyst) Cholelithiasis (biliary leakage/compression by a hepatic hydatid cyst) Cestodes (tapeworms) cause two clinically distinct patterns: intestinal infection by adult worms (taeniasis) and somatic/larval-tissue infection (e.g., cysticercosis, hydatid disease) (Harrison 22e p.1832). Neurocysticercosis is the most common parasitic disease of the CNS worldwide; humans acquire it by ingesting food contaminated with Taenia solium eggs, not by eating cysticerci-containing pork (which instead causes intestinal taeniasis) (Harrison 22e p.1833, p.1138). Seizures are the most frequent manifestation of neurocysticercosis and are associated with inflammation of brain parenchyma around the cysticercus; new-onset partial seizures with or without secondary generalization are the classic presentation (Harrison 22e p.1833, p.1138). On neuroimaging a cystic lesion with a mural nodule representing the scolex ('dot-in-hole') is diagnostic of neurocysticercosis; lesions evolve through vesicular, colloidal, granulonodular and nodular-calcified stages (Harrison 22e p.1833-1834, p.1138). CT is more sensitive for calcified lesions, whereas MRI is more sensitive for small cystic lesions, scolices and enhancement; FIESTA/3D-CISS sequences best detect ventricular and subarachnoid cysts (Harrison 22e p.1834). The enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) using lentil-lectin-purified glycoproteins is >99% specific/sensitive in patients with multiple cysts, but patients with a single intracranial lesion or only calcifications may be seronegative; serum is more sensitive than CSF (Harrison 22e p.1834). Crude-antigen ELISA antibody tests have high false-positive and false-negative rates and should be avoided for neurocysticercosis (Harrison 22e p.1834). In endemic-area patients with a single enhancing 5-20 mm round CT lesion, seizures, a normal exam and no systemic disease (no fever, adenopathy or chest abnormality), the lesion is almost always neurocysticercosis (validated in India) (Harrison 22e p.1834). Antiparasitic treatment of neurocysticercosis is never an emergency; initial management focuses on controlling seizures and hydrocephalus and on excluding intraocular disease before any cysticidal therapy (Harrison 22e p.1834). High-dose glucocorticoids should always accompany antiparasitic therapy of neurocysticercosis, since dying parasites provoke an inflammatory response that can worsen seizures or hydrocephalus (Harrison 22e p.1834). Bruns' syndrome is intermittent acute hydrocephalus triggered by positional change, caused by a ventricular cysticercus acting as a ball valve (Harrison 22e p.1833). In Latin America and immigrants from Latin America, T. solium (neurocysticercosis) is the most common cause of brain abscess / focal CNS mass lesion (Harrison 22e p.1136). Echinococcosis (hydatid disease) is larval Echinococcus infection: E. granulosus sensu lato causes unilocular cystic hydatid disease; E. multilocularis causes locally invasive, tumor-like alveolar disease (Harrison 22e p.1835-1836). In cystic echinococcosis the liver is involved in about two-thirds and the lungs in about 20% of cases; alveolar echinococcosis involves the liver in nearly all cases (Harrison 22e p.1836). Echinococcal cysts often remain asymptomatic for years and are frequently found incidentally on x-ray or ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.1836). Identification of daughter cysts within a larger cyst, or eggshell/mural calcification on CT, is diagnostic of cystic echinococcosis; 'hydatid sand' is visible protoscolices/brood capsules within cyst fluid (Harrison 22e p.1837). ELISA/immunoblot serology is positive in about 90% of hepatic hydatid disease but only about 50% of pulmonary cysts, and a negative test cannot exclude echinococcosis (Harrison 22e p.1837). The fish tapeworm Dibothriocephalus latus (formerly Diphyllobothrium latum) is the longest human tapeworm (up to 25 m) and its avid vitamin B12 receptors can cause B12 deficiency with megaloblastic/pernicious-type anemia and neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1838-1839). Rodentolepis nana (dwarf tapeworm, formerly Hymenolepis nana) is the most common human cestode infection and the only one not requiring an intermediate host, perpetuated by intestinal autoinfection (Harrison 22e p.1838). New-onset seizures or focal neurologic deficit in a patient from a cysticercosis-endemic area (e.g., Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, China, India, Southeast Asia) Signs of raised intracranial pressure or obstructive hydrocephalus (headache, vomiting, papilledema, altered mental status) from intraventricular/subarachnoid cysticerci Bruns' syndrome: intermittent acute hydrocephalus precipitated by head position change Subarachnoid/basal cysticerci causing chronic meningitis, arachnoiditis, vasculitis, infarction or hemorrhage Sudden pruritus, urticaria, eosinophilia or anaphylaxis from rupture/leakage of a hydatid cyst Pulmonary hydatid rupture into the bronchial tree (sudden expectoration of cyst fluid/membranes) or pleura (hydatid empyema) Do not aspirate or rupture a hydatid cyst carelessly: spillage of protoscolices can disseminate infection and provoke anaphylaxis; aspiration/PAIR should only be done by experienced operators with albendazole cover and through solid tissue. Never start antiparasitic drugs in neurocysticercosis with elevated intracranial pressure, and avoid them in diffuse cerebral edema from multiple inflamed lesions (glucocorticoids are the mainstay there). Always give high-dose glucocorticoid cover when treating neurocysticercosis, because dying cysticerci can worsen seizures and hydrocephalus. Treating T. solium intestinal taeniasis with praziquantel may occasionally trigger a CNS inflammatory response if occult (cryptic) cysticercosis is present. Avoid antiparasitic drugs before neurosurgical removal of ventricular cysticerci: they make the cyst friable and harder to extract. Crude-antigen ELISA antibody tests for cysticercosis are unreliable (high false-positive/false-negative rates) and should not be used. A negative echinococcosis serology cannot exclude the diagnosis, and sensitivity is especially low (~50%) for pulmonary cysts. Eggs/proglottids are shed intermittently, so single stool examination may miss intestinal taeniasis; Taenia species eggs are morphologically indistinguishable. For ocular and spinal cysticercosis, drug-induced inflammation may cause irreversible damage; intraocular disease should be managed surgically. Infusion of scolicidal agents during surgery is no longer recommended because of hypernatremia, intoxication and sclerosing cholangitis. Cestodes are segmented flatworms (Platyhelminthes, subphylum Cestoda) whose adult worms live in the gut of the definitive host while larval cystic forms inhabit tissues of the intermediate host. The adult tapeworm attaches to intestinal mucosa by suckers or hooks on a scolex; proglottids bud from the neck to form the ribbon-like strobila and shed eggs. In intestinal taeniasis humans are definitive hosts (T. saginata, T. asiatica, T. solium, D. latus, D. caninum). In somatic disease, ingested eggs release oncospheres that penetrate the gut wall, disseminate via blood, and encyst as a cysticercus (single scolex), coenurus (multiple scolices) or hydatid (cyst with daughter cysts and protoscolices). Cysticercosis follows ingestion of T. solium eggs (fecal-oral, including autoinfection in tapeworm carriers); lodged cysticerci initially provoke little inflammation, but as the cyst degenerates an inflammatory response develops, producing seizures, and accompanying arachnoiditis or ventricular obstruction can cause hydrocephalus. In echinococcosis ingested eggs of canine tapeworms release oncospheres that seed liver, lung and other organs; E. granulosus forms slowly enlarging unilocular hydatid cysts containing brood capsules and protoscolices, while E. multilocularis grows by invasive peripheral budding of the germinal layer like a malignancy. (Harrison 22e p.1832-1837) Intestinal tapeworm infections (taeniasis, R. nana, diphyllobothriasis, dipylidiasis) are usually mild or asymptomatic and respond to a single course of treatment. In neurocysticercosis, single enhancing lesions often resolve and seizure medication can frequently be tapered after about 6 months; calcified lesions carry a higher risk of recurrent seizures, particularly with perilesional edema, and subarachnoid/ventricular (extraparenchymal) disease is more difficult to treat and requires prolonged therapy. Cystic echinococcosis is often curable with stage-appropriate medical therapy, PAIR or surgery, with relapse rates after skilled PAIR comparable to surgery; inactive CE4/CE5 cysts need only periodic surveillance. Alveolar echinococcosis behaves like a malignancy: most cases are diagnosed too late for complete resection and require indefinite antiparasitic therapy, since even after liver transplantation immunosuppression promotes parasite recurrence. (Harrison 22e p.1834-1838) Cystic echinococcosis of the liver is staged by the WHO Informal Working Group ultrasound classification, reflecting cyst viability: active cysts (CL = cystic lesion with no visible wall, CE1 = visible wall with internal echoes/snowflake sign, CE2 = visible wall with internal septation), transitional cysts (CE3a = detached laminar membranes, CE3b = partially collapsed), and inactive cysts (CE4 = nonhomogeneous mass, CE5 = thick calcified wall). Neurocysticercosis is categorized by parasite location and viability and by lesion stage on imaging (vesicular, colloidal, granulonodular, nodular-calcified); diagnosis uses the Del Brutto revised criteria (absolute, neuroimaging [major/confirmative/minor], and clinical/exposure criteria). (Harrison 22e p.1834-1837)

most sensitive is miniature anion-exchange centrifugation, ~90%), skin biopsy, or CSF; thin/thick Giemsa smears and concentration for T. b. rhodesiense (p.1795) HAT staging: lumbar puncture with CSF examination (leukocyte count, trypanosomes after centrifugation) (p.1795) Supportive HAT labs (nonspecific): anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein and IgM (p.1794) Achalasia (Chagas megaesophagus) (p.1789) Hirschsprung's disease (Chagas megacolon) (p.1789) Dilated/ischemic cardiomyopathy (Chagas cardiomyopathy) (p.1790) Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (HAT systemic features, but endocrine tests normal) (p.1794) Primary psychiatric illness (HAT neuropsychiatric features) (p.1794) Three trypanosome species cause human disease: T. cruzi causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis); T. brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense cause human African trypanosomiasis (HAT, 'sleeping sickness'). Both are vector-borne neglected tropical diseases (p.1788). Chagas is transmitted mainly by intradomiciliary triatomine ('reduviid') bugs whose feces, deposited during a nighttime blood meal, carry the infective metacyclic form that enters through skin breaks, mucosae, or conjunctivae; nonvectorial routes include congenital, blood transfusion, organ/tissue transplant, and oral (contaminated food/drink) transmission (p.1788). Acute Chagas is asymptomatic or a mild febrile illness in >90% of cases; characteristic local swelling at the inoculation site is the Romaña sign (eyelid) or chagoma (skin) (p.1789-1790). After acute infection T. cruzi persists for life in most patients; 60-70% remain in the indeterminate form (no apparent tissue damage), while 30-40% progress over decades to determinate disease - cardiac (20-30%), digestive (5-20%), or mixed (5-10%) (p.1789). Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy produces a dilated cardiomyopathy with fibrosis, segmental contractility loss, left ventricular apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction system disease; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies including ischemic disease (p.1789-1790). Digestive Chagas (megaviscera) results from destruction of intramural autonomic ganglion cells: esophageal involvement mimics achalasia and colonic involvement mimics Hirschsprung's disease, with severe constipation, fecaloma, and risk of volvulus and toxic dilation; megacolon is diagnosed when sigmoid/descending colon diameter is >=6.5 cm (p.1789, 1791). Chagas diagnosis is stage-dependent: detect circulating parasites by blood microscopy after concentration (Strout, microhematocrit) or PCR during acute phase/reactivation; rely on serology (anti-T. cruzi IgG) once parasitemia is subpatent in the chronic phase - two positive tests using different techniques and antigens confirm chronic infection (p.1790). 12-lead ECG (with 30-s strip) is a good screening test for Chagas cardiomyopathy; common abnormalities are right bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block, ventricular premature beats, repolarization disorders, Q waves, and low QRS voltage (p.1791). HAT is restricted to sub-Saharan Africa, matching the range of its tsetse fly (Glossina) vector; T. b. gambiense (western/central Africa, humans are main reservoir, slow chronic course) differs from T. b. rhodesiense (eastern/southeastern Africa, zoonotic animal reservoirs, acute course) (p.1792-1793). T. b. gambiense HAT is a slowly evolving illness with a long incubation (months to years); T. b. rhodesiense HAT is an acute febrile illness with a short (<3-week) incubation and a shorter (weeks to months) course (p.1794). A trypanosomal chancre may develop at the tsetse bite site (more common in travelers and in T. b. rhodesiense); it is nonpurulent, painful, itchy, and resolves spontaneously in 1-3 weeks (p.1794-1795). Enlarged cervical lymph nodes are a classic HAT sign (38-85% of patients); posterior cervical involvement is the Winterbottom sign - cervical palpation is essential in suspected HAT (p.1794). HAT is called 'sleeping sickness' because of CNS (second-stage) sleep disturbances - daytime somnolence, nocturnal insomnia, dysregulated sleep/wake cycle and fragmented sleep - plus neuropsychiatric features (mood/behavioral change, psychosis, motor/extrapyramidal/cerebellar syndromes) that may mimic primary psychiatric illness (p.1794). HAT staging is by CSF examination: second-stage (CNS) disease is defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; T. b. gambiense screening uses serology (card agglutination test, CATT, or lateral flow tests) and confirmation by microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph, blood, skin, or CSF (p.1795). T. b. rhodesiense diagnosis is usually simpler because parasites are more numerous in blood; wet mounts, thin/thick Giemsa smears, and concentration techniques serve for both screening and confirmation, and parasites may be seen in chancre aspirate (p.1795). T. cruzi evades immunity to persist as low-grade amastigote replication; immunosuppression (HIV, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy) can cause reactivation with increased parasitemia and CNS/cardiac/skin lesions - clinically manifest reactivation is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection (~20% risk in untreated HIV when CD4 <100/uL) (p.1789). Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy with high risk of sudden death - bundle branch block is often the first sign and may be asymptomatic for years before serious conduction disease, arrhythmias, and LV dysfunction; 5-year mortality 2-63% depending on cardiac damage, leading causes cardiac failure and sudden death, then stroke (p.1790) Chagas digestive determinate disease: dysphagia, regurgitation, severe constipation, fecaloma, volvulus, and toxic colonic dilation (p.1790) Intramural thrombus or LV apical aneurysm in Chagas cardiomyopathy - risk of cardioembolic stroke (p.1790-1791) Chagas reactivation in immunosuppression (HIV with CD4 <100/uL, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy): myocarditis, Toxoplasma-like focal brain lesion, meningoencephalitis - AIDS-defining when clinically manifest (p.1789-1790) Untreated HAT is usually lethal - early diagnosis is crucial; second-stage (CNS) disease with decreased consciousness, dementia, epilepsy progressing to coma and death (p.1794) T. b. rhodesiense terminal sepsis-like illness with disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure, plus more rapid evolution to coma and death than gambiense (p.1794) Severe second-stage HAT signs warranting non-fexinidazole staging/treatment: mental confusion, abnormal behavior, logorrhea, anxiety, ataxia, tremor, motor weakness, speech impairment, abnormal gait/movements, or seizures (p.1795) More than 90% of Chagas infections go undiagnosed and are often identified late once chronic complications develop; the majority of infected individuals are asymptomatic (indeterminate form) (p.1790) International tourists visiting endemic areas are at very low risk of Chagas and travel-related cases are rare - the at-risk group is migrants from endemic regions, not casual travelers (p.1789) There is no evidence that bedbugs transmit T. cruzi to humans despite laboratory potential (p.1788) There is no predictor of which chronic-phase Chagas patients will progress to clinical disease (p.1790) Chronic-phase Chagas PCR has limited sensitivity (50-80%): a negative result cannot be interpreted, so patients with negative PCR but persistent positive serology should still be considered potentially infective (p.1790, 1792) Early congenital Chagas PCR may be falsely positive (maternal T. cruzi DNA fragments); testing after 4 weeks of age is most accurate (p.1790) In adults with chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, benznidazole has no impact on disease progression or mortality, and neither benznidazole nor nifurtimox is effective against digestive complications (KNOWLEDGE only - no dosing) (p.1791-1792) HAT clinical/biologic features (anemia, thrombocytopenia, raised CRP and IgM) are not specific enough to treat on suspicion - diagnostic confirmation is required in all patients (p.1794) Absence of fever does not rule out T. b. gambiense HAT (fever is more frequent in travelers than natives) (p.1794) HAT systemic features may mimic hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency but thyroid/adrenal tests are normal; mental disorder may be misdiagnosed as primary psychiatric illness (p.1794) Trypanids (HAT rashes) are almost impossible to detect on dark skin and have been reported only in Caucasians (p.1794) HIV co-infection does not appear to increase HAT risk, and the virus's effect on HAT presentation is unknown (p.1794) Eflornithine is ineffective against T. b. rhodesiense, so melarsoprol remains in use for second-stage rhodesiense disease (KNOWLEDGE only) (p.1796) Chagas (T. cruzi): trypomastigotes inoculated via triatomine feces enter the bloodstream, infect nucleated cells (notably cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle) and differentiate into amastigotes. An innate response to parasite mucins/DNA drives a predominantly Th1 response with proinflammatory cytokines and CD8+ T-cell activation that reduces parasitemia to subpatent levels in 4-8 weeks (end of acute phase). Immune evasion permits lifelong low-intensity amastigote proliferation. Chronic damage is thought to arise from parasite persistence plus a dysregulated host immune response (Th1/Th2 imbalance, excess proinflammatory cytokines), with secondary microcirculatory abnormalities and dysautonomia; the role of autoimmune mechanisms remains unresolved. In myocardium, chronic inflammation causes cellular destruction and fibrosis, segmental loss of contractility, chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction-system scarring, plus autonomic (vagal/sympathetic) denervation. In the gut, a direct toxic effect on intramural autonomic ganglion cells causes loss of neural cells, motility disorders, and organ dilation (megaviscera). African trypanosomiasis (T. b. gambiense/rhodesiense): these subspecies infect humans because they resist human serum lytic factor apolipoprotein L-1 (T. b. rhodesiense via serum resistance-associated protein; T. b. gambiense via TgsGP glycoprotein and other mechanisms). After tsetse bite and local inflammation (chancre), parasites disseminate through the hematolymphatic system, multiply in blood (with cyclic density fluctuation due to variant surface glycoprotein antigenic switching - a repertoire of ~1000 VSGs) and extravascular tissues (skin, muscle, serous membranes, heart). CNS invasion (second stage) follows weeks-to-months (rhodesiense) or months-to-years (gambiense), with predominantly white-matter perivascular astrocyte/microglial proliferation and Mott (morular) cells containing IgM; the cortex and neurons are spared until terminal stages, and inflammatory lesions are largely reversible so neuropsychiatric features may resolve with treatment (p.1789-1790, 1793-1794). Chagas: 5-10% of acute (early) infections resolve spontaneously without treatment; most become chronic, of whom 60-70% never develop tissue damage (indeterminate form) and 30-40% progress over decades to cardiac, digestive, or mixed disease. Acute-phase mortality is low (0.1-5% with oral transmission or myocarditis/encephalitis). Determinate chronic disease 5-year mortality is 2-63% depending on extent of cardiac damage, with cardiac failure, sudden death, and stroke the leading causes; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies. African trypanosomiasis: untreated HAT is usually fatal. With properly followed guidelines, >95% of first- and second-stage T. b. gambiense HAT patients are definitively cured (fexinidazole, pentamidine, nifurtimox-eflornithine), overall case-fatality <1% except in very advanced cases; relapses can occur long after treatment, so follow-up every 6 months for at least 2 years is advised. Second-stage T. b. rhodesiense HAT carries a 5-10% risk of death during/after melarsoprol treatment, though relapses are very rare (p.1790, 1796). Chagas (T. cruzi infection stages, Table 234-1): Acute phase (including congenital, vector-borne, oral, transfusion, transplant) lasting 2-8 weeks, mostly asymptomatic; Chronic indeterminate form (normal exam and ECG, no attributable mortality, lifelong or until determinate phase); Chronic determinate form (cardiac, digestive, or mixed organ damage years to decades after infection); Acute reactivation in severe immunosuppression. Diagnostic procedure of choice by stage: microscopy after concentration / PCR for acute, early congenital, and reactivation; serology (two positive tests) for chronic indeterminate and determinate. HAT staging: First stage (hemolymphatic, no CNS involvement) vs Second stage (CNS/meningoencephalitic), defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; nonsevere second stage = 6-99 leukocytes/uL CSF, severe second stage = >=100 leukocytes/uL CSF (p.1790, 1795).

Chalazion — meibomian cyst, tarsal cyst, meibomian granuloma Internal or external hordeolum (stye) Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid Basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma of the lid Preseptal cellulitis (if acutely inflamed) Pyogenic granuloma Epidermal inclusion cyst Clinical slit-lamp examination and eversion of the eyelid to assess the tarsal conjunctival surface Refraction and assessment for induced astigmatism in large lesions Histopathological examination of excised or curetted tissue in recurrent or atypical cases to exclude malignancy A chalazion is a chronic, sterile lipogranulomatous swelling of a blocked meibomian gland, presenting as a firm, painless nodule within the tarsal plate Unlike a stye (hordeolum), it is typically non-tender once the acute phase has passed and points towards the conjunctival rather than skin surface It is strongly associated with blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, and rosacea, and recurrences are common in these patients A large chalazion can press on the cornea and induce astigmatism with blurred vision Many small lesions resolve spontaneously or with conservative treatment using warm compresses and lid massage over several weeks Persistent lesions are treated with incision and curettage through a conjunctival approach, or with intralesional steroid injection A recurrent chalazion at the same site, or one with atypical features, should be biopsied to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma It should be distinguished from an internal hordeolum, which is an acute infective abscess of a meibomian gland Recurrence at the same site or failure to resolve, raising suspicion of sebaceous gland carcinoma Associated madarosis (lash loss), lid margin distortion, or induration suggesting malignancy Rapid growth or ulceration of the overlying skin Signs of secondary infection with spreading cellulitis Assuming any recurrent lid nodule is benign and not sending atypical or recurrent lesions for histology Confusing a sterile chalazion with an infective hordeolum and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics Overlooking underlying blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction that drive recurrence Missing chalazion-induced astigmatism as a cause of blurred vision A chalazion forms when a meibomian gland orifice becomes obstructed and retained sebaceous secretions leak into the surrounding tarsal tissue. This lipid material provokes a chronic granulomatous (lipogranulomatous) inflammatory reaction rather than an infection, producing a firm nodule within the tarsal plate. Predisposing factors include meibomian gland dysfunction, blepharitis, and rosacea, all of which alter meibomian secretions and promote gland blockage. The prognosis is excellent; most chalazia resolve with conservative measures or minor surgery, though recurrences are common in patients with underlying meibomian gland disease. Rarely, a persistent or atypical lesion proves to be a malignancy, which is why histology is important in suspicious cases.

Chancroid — soft chancre, Haemophilus ducreyi infection, ulcus molle Primary syphilis (painless indurated chancre) Genital herpes simplex ulceration Lymphogranuloma venereum Granuloma inguinale (donovanosis) Traumatic or fixed drug eruption ulcer Syphilitic chancre Herpes simplex virus genital ulcers Lymphogranuloma venereum with inguinal buboes Donovanosis with beefy granulomatous ulcers Dark-field microscopy and syphilis serology to exclude primary syphilis HSV PCR or culture from the ulcer to exclude herpes Nucleic acid amplification or PCR for Haemophilus ducreyi where available Gram stain and special culture media (low sensitivity) if molecular testing unavailable HIV testing at presentation and on follow-up A sexually transmitted cause of genital ulceration produced by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi, now uncommon but still important in the differential of genital ulcer disease The ulcer is typically painful, non-indurated (soft) with a ragged undermined edge and a purulent base, contrasting with the painless firm ulcer of primary syphilis Tender, often unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that may become fluctuant and suppurate into a bubo is characteristic The combination of one or more painful genital ulcers with suppurative inguinal nodes strongly suggests chancroid Culture requires special enriched media and is insensitive, so diagnosis is often clinical after excluding syphilis and herpes; molecular testing is most reliable where available Because genital ulcer disease facilitates HIV transmission, testing for HIV and syphilis is essential, with follow-up serology as needed Treatment uses recommended antibiotics such as a macrolide, ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone, and fluctuant buboes may require needle aspiration or incision Rapidly enlarging or fluctuant bubo threatening rupture and needing drainage Coexisting HIV infection, which impairs healing and alters treatment response Failure of ulcers to heal after appropriate therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Extensive tissue destruction or secondary bacterial superinfection Assuming a painful ulcer excludes syphilis or coinfection, when mixed infections occur Incising a bubo when aspiration through healthy skin is preferred to avoid sinus formation Relying on insensitive culture and missing the diagnosis Neglecting partner notification and HIV screening Haemophilus ducreyi enters through breaks in genital epithelium during sexual contact. It secretes a cytolethal distending toxin and other virulence factors that cause keratinocyte and epithelial cell damage, producing a necrotic, ulcerative lesion with a neutrophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate. The organism resists phagocytic killing and provokes a suppurative regional lymphadenitis. The disrupted mucocutaneous barrier and inflammatory milieu markedly enhance the risk of HIV acquisition and shedding, linking chancroid epidemiologically to HIV spread. With appropriate antibiotic therapy ulcers heal over one to two weeks and buboes resolve, though large nodes may need aspiration and healing is slower in people with HIV; untreated disease causes progressive ulceration and scarring.

orthoses, foot care and surgery, and avoidance of neurotoxic drugs that can worsen neuropathy Rapid or asymmetric progression suggesting an acquired inflammatory neuropathy such as CIDP Prominent sensory ataxia or systemic features pointing to an alternative diagnosis Respiratory or bulbar involvement, which is unusual and warrants reassessment Sudden deterioration after exposure to a neurotoxic medication Missing a treatable acquired neuropathy such as CIDP by assuming a hereditary cause Prescribing potentially neurotoxic drugs without considering their effect on the neuropathy Relying on gene sequencing while overlooking the need for PMP22 dosage analysis Neglecting foot care and orthotic input that preserve mobility Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease encompasses hereditary neuropathies in which mutations disrupt proteins essential to either the myelin sheath or the axon of peripheral nerves. In demyelinating subtypes such as CMT1A, PMP22 overexpression impairs Schwann cell myelination, causing slowed conduction and secondary axonal loss; in axonal subtypes the primary defect lies in axonal structure or transport. Because the pathology is length-dependent, the longest nerves to the feet and lower legs are affected first, producing the characteristic distal, symmetric motor and sensory deficits. Most forms progress slowly and do not shorten life expectancy, though they cause increasing distal disability, foot deformity, and reliance on orthoses; severity varies considerably by subtype, with some early-onset forms being more disabling.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A is a hereditary demyelinating (type 1) motor and sensory neuropathy caused in most cases by a 1.5 Mb duplication on chromosome 17 that includes PMP22, resulting in overexpression of peripheral myelin protein 22. The gene-dosage excess disrupts the normal formation and maintenance of compact myelin by Schwann cells, leading to repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination and the formation of concentric onion-bulb structures. Slowed and inefficient saltatory conduction, together with secondary axonal loss over time, produces the length-dependent distal weakness, wasting and sensory loss. The reciprocal deletion of the same region causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies. The disorder progresses slowly over decades and life expectancy is normal; most affected individuals remain ambulant, though many require orthoses, foot surgery or walking aids and experience meaningful disability from deformity and balance impairment.
