optic atrophy Assuming preserved reflexes exclude a hereditary neuropathy Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2 is a hereditary axonal (type 2) motor and sensory neuropathy in which the primary defect is degeneration of peripheral nerve axons rather than the myelin sheath. It is genetically heterogeneous, with the most common cause being variants in MFN2, which encodes a mitochondrial outer-membrane GTPase essential for mitochondrial fusion and axonal mitochondrial transport. Impaired mitochondrial dynamics and energy delivery preferentially affect the longest axons, producing a length-dependent, distal-predominant loss of motor and sensory function. Because myelin is relatively spared, conduction velocities remain near normal while response amplitudes fall as axons are lost. Progression is generally slow and life expectancy is normal, though disability from distal weakness, deformity and sensory loss accumulates over time; phenotype severity varies with the specific causative gene and variant.

Chediak-Higashi syndrome — CHS, Chediak-Higashi disease Griscelli syndrome Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome Other causes of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (familial HLH, EBV-driven HLH) Leukocyte adhesion deficiency and other neutrophil disorders Oculocutaneous albinism without immunodeficiency Peripheral blood film and bone marrow to identify giant granules in leucocytes LYST genetic testing Neutrophil function testing (chemotaxis and bactericidal activity) Natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell function assays Markers of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (ferritin, soluble IL-2 receptor, triglycerides, fibrinogen) when the accelerated phase is suspected Neurological assessment including nerve conduction studies Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of lysosomal trafficking caused by mutations in the LYST gene The diagnostic morphological clue is giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils and other leucocytes seen on the blood film Patients have partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair and photophobia, reflecting abnormal melanosome function Recurrent pyogenic infections, especially with Staphylococcus aureus and other bacteria, arise from impaired neutrophil chemotaxis, degranulation, and killing Natural killer cell and cytotoxic T-cell function is defective, contributing to both infection risk and the tendency to develop an accelerated inflammatory phase The dreaded 'accelerated phase' is a haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and lymphohistiocytic infiltration, often triggered by viral infection such as EBV A progressive neurological syndrome (peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, cognitive decline) may emerge in those who survive childhood Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct the immune and haematological disease but does not reverse the neurological degeneration; supportive care includes infection prophylaxis and treatment of the accelerated phase Features of the accelerated phase (fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperferritinaemia) requiring urgent HLH-directed treatment Recurrent or severe pyogenic infection requiring prompt immunological evaluation Live vaccines should be avoided given the cytotoxic immune defect Irradiated, leucodepleted blood products are advisable, particularly around transplantation Progressive neurological deterioration signalling advanced disease Missing the giant leucocyte granules on the blood film and delaying diagnosis Failing to recognise and aggressively treat the accelerated phase as an HLH-like emergency Assuming transplantation will halt the neurodegeneration Overlooking the albinism and hair colour clues that point to the diagnosis Not screening for EBV or other viral triggers that can precipitate the accelerated phase Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in LYST, which encodes a protein regulating the size and trafficking of lysosomes and related organelles. Defective vesicle fusion produces the characteristic giant granules and disrupts the function of cells that depend on regulated secretory lysosomes, including neutrophils (impaired chemotaxis and delayed bacterial killing), cytotoxic lymphocytes and natural killer cells (defective granule-mediated cytotoxicity), melanocytes (partial albinism), and neurons. The failure of cytotoxic cells to control activated immune cells underlies the life-threatening accelerated phase resembling haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, while accumulation of abnormal lysosomal material contributes to the progressive neurodegeneration. The prognosis is guarded: most patients enter the accelerated phase in childhood, which is frequently fatal without treatment, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, if performed before this phase, can restore immune and haematological function but does not prevent the later progressive neurological decline.

Without haematopoietic stem cell transplantation most children die in the first decade, usually during the accelerated phase or from infection. Transplantation restores immune and haematological function and prevents the accelerated phase but does not halt the later progressive neurological disease.

Chemical burns — caustic burns, corrosive injury, chemical injury Thermal burns Electrical injury Severe irritant contact dermatitis Toxic epidermal necrolysis and other blistering conditions Radiation skin injury Identification of the chemical agent and consultation of safety data sheets or a poisons service pH testing of the affected surface, particularly the eye, to confirm adequate irrigation Serum calcium, magnesium, potassium and ECG monitoring after hydrofluoric acid exposure Assessment of burn depth and surface area Screening for systemic toxicity with agents known to be absorbed Chemical burns result from corrosive substances contacting skin, eyes or mucous membranes, commonly in industrial, cleaning and laboratory settings Immediate and copious irrigation with water for a prolonged period is the priority first aid for most chemical skin and eye exposures, and should not be delayed while identifying the agent Alkalis typically cause deeper, progressive liquefactive injury that penetrates over time, whereas acids tend to produce coagulative injury with a more defined eschar; hydrofluoric acid is a special case Hydrofluoric acid causes deep tissue penetration and dangerous systemic effects including hypocalcaemia and cardiac dysrhythmia, and is treated specifically with calcium The apparent surface appearance can underestimate the true depth, which may only declare itself over hours to days Eye exposure is a sight-threatening emergency requiring immediate, prolonged irrigation and urgent ophthalmology assessment, with pH checking to guide adequacy of rinsing Some agents (for example phenol, hydrofluoric acid and cyanide-releasing compounds) are absorbed and cause systemic toxicity, so treat the whole patient, not just the wound Rescuer safety, removal of contaminated clothing and correct decontamination are essential to prevent further and secondary injury MEDICAL EMERGENCY: extensive or deep burns, airway or inhalational involvement, or eye exposure threatening sight Hydrofluoric acid exposure with hypocalcaemia and cardiac dysrhythmia Signs of systemic toxicity from absorbed agents such as phenol Circumferential burns risking compartment syndrome or airway compromise Delaying irrigation while trying to identify the chemical or find a specific antidote Underestimating burn depth from the initial surface appearance, especially with alkalis Failing to recognise and specifically treat hydrofluoric acid injury and its hypocalcaemia Neglecting systemic absorption and toxicity while focusing only on the wound Inadequate rescuer protection and decontamination leading to secondary injury Corrosive chemicals damage tissue by disrupting cell membranes and denaturing or dissolving proteins and lipids. Acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to limit their own penetration, whereas alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that allows continued deep spread. Some agents also produce heat or are absorbed to cause systemic metabolic disturbance, such as the calcium and magnesium binding and consequent hypocalcaemia seen with hydrofluoric acid. Prompt, thorough irrigation and appropriate specific treatment greatly improve outcome; however, deep or extensive burns, delayed decontamination, ocular involvement and systemic toxicity from certain agents can cause scarring, visual loss or death.

Chemical eye injury — chemical burn of the eye, ocular chemical injury, alkali burn, acid burn, caustic eye injury Thermal burn of the ocular surface Ultraviolet or radiation keratitis (e.g. welder's flash) Severe infective keratitis or corneal ulcer Toxic keratoconjunctivitis from other agents Corneal foreign body or abrasion Measurement of ocular surface pH before and after irrigation to guide continued irrigation Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein to assess epithelial defect size and corneal clarity Assessment and grading of limbal and conjunctival ischaemia Intraocular pressure measurement, as burns can cause acute and chronic pressure rise Eyelid eversion and fornix inspection for retained particulate chemical A true ocular emergency in which immediate, copious irrigation takes priority over history-taking and detailed examination Alkali burns are generally more damaging than acid burns because alkalis penetrate tissues rapidly by liquefactive necrosis, whereas acids cause coagulative necrosis that tends to limit deeper penetration Irrigation should continue until the tear film pH returns to neutral, and the fornices must be swept and everted to remove any retained particulate matter (e.g. lime or cement) The degree of limbal ischaemia (blanching) and corneal clarity are the key prognostic signs, forming the basis of grading systems such as Roper-Hall and Dua A deceptively white, non-injected eye after an alkali burn can indicate severe limbal ischaemia rather than a mild injury Later management principles aim to promote epithelial healing, control inflammation with topical steroids, prevent infection, support the ocular surface, and control intraocular pressure Severe burns can be complicated by limbal stem cell deficiency, symblepharon, corneal melting and perforation, glaucoma, and eventual scarring Bilateral injury and workplace or assault-related exposures require attention to both eyes and appropriate safeguarding and occupational follow-up Any chemical exposure requires immediate copious irrigation before other assessment, as delay worsens outcome Extensive limbal blanching/ischaemia and a hazy or opaque cornea indicating a severe, sight-threatening burn A deceptively white, quiet eye masking severe ischaemic damage after alkali injury Rising intraocular pressure, corneal melting, or threatened perforation requiring urgent specialist care Delaying irrigation to complete history or examination first Stopping irrigation before the pH has normalised or failing to check pH Not everting the lids and sweeping the fornices, leaving retained caustic particles Underestimating a white, non-inflamed eye that actually reflects severe limbal ischaemia Chemical injury damages the ocular surface through direct chemical action on cells and the extracellular matrix. Alkalis dissolve cell membrane lipids and penetrate deeply by liquefactive necrosis, reaching the anterior chamber and damaging the limbal stem cells, corneal stroma, trabecular meshwork, and intraocular structures. Acids denature and precipitate proteins, producing coagulative necrosis that can form a barrier limiting deeper spread, though strong acids still cause severe injury. Destruction of limbal stem cells impairs corneal epithelial regeneration, leading to persistent epithelial defects, conjunctivalisation, and scarring, while ischaemia and inflammation predispose to stromal melting and perforation. Prognosis correlates closely with the initial extent of limbal ischaemia and corneal opacification; mild burns with minimal limbal involvement usually heal well, whereas severe burns with extensive limbal stem cell loss risk chronic surface failure, scarring, and permanent visual loss despite intensive treatment. Prompt and thorough irrigation is the single most important factor improving outcome.

Chiari malformation — Arnold-Chiari malformation, Chiari I malformation, Chiari II malformation, cerebellar tonsillar ectopia Primary headache disorders (migraine, tension-type) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Posterior fossa tumour Multiple sclerosis or other myelopathy Craniocervical junction anomalies (e.g. basilar invagination) MRI brain and whole spine to measure tonsillar descent and identify a syrinx Cine or CSF flow MRI at the craniocervical junction in selected cases Assessment for hydrocephalus and, in type II, for an associated neural tube defect Dynamic craniocervical imaging when bony instability or basilar invagination is suspected Chiari malformation describes downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils (and, in some types, the brainstem and fourth ventricle) through the foramen magnum The type I form often presents in adolescence or adulthood with a suboccipital headache classically worsened by coughing, straining, or Valsalva Associated features can include neck pain, dizziness, imbalance, and lower cranial nerve or brainstem symptoms such as swallowing difficulty A frequent and important association is syringomyelia, a fluid-filled cavity in the cord that can cause a dissociated (cape-like) sensory loss and hand wasting The type II form is closely linked with myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus and typically presents in infancy or early childhood MRI of the brain and whole spine is the key investigation, quantifying tonsillar descent and detecting an associated syrinx Asymptomatic incidental tonsillar ectopia is often simply monitored, whereas symptomatic cases or those with a progressive syrinx may need posterior fossa decompression Surgical decompression aims to restore cerebrospinal fluid flow at the craniocervical junction and can stabilise or improve symptoms and an associated syrinx Progressive brainstem or lower cranial nerve dysfunction, including swallowing or breathing problems Rapidly enlarging syrinx with advancing weakness or sensory loss Signs of raised intracranial pressure or associated obstructive hydrocephalus Acute deterioration in an infant with type II malformation and myelomeningocele Attributing coughing-related occipital headache to migraine without considering the malformation Failing to image the whole spine and missing an associated syringomyelia Over-treating small, asymptomatic incidental tonsillar ectopia Overlooking coexisting hydrocephalus or craniocervical instability Chiari malformations involve herniation of hindbrain structures below the foramen magnum. In the type I form the cerebellar tonsils descend into the upper cervical canal, often with a small or crowded posterior fossa, obstructing normal cerebrospinal fluid movement across the craniocervical junction. This altered CSF dynamics is thought to drive syrinx formation within the spinal cord. The type II form is a more complex hindbrain anomaly with caudal displacement of the brainstem and fourth ventricle, strongly associated with open neural tube defects and hydrocephalus. Symptoms arise from direct compression of neural structures and from disturbed CSF flow. Many patients with mild or incidental type I malformation remain stable; symptomatic patients often improve or stabilise after decompression, though an established syrinx and any fixed neurological deficits may only partially recover. Type II outcomes depend heavily on the severity of associated anomalies.

Childhood Obesity — paediatric obesity, childhood overweight, obesity in children and adolescents Exogenous (lifestyle-related) obesity Hypothyroidism Cushing syndrome Growth hormone deficiency Monogenic obesity (e.g. leptin or MC4R pathway defects) Syndromic obesity (e.g. Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl syndromes) Hypothalamic obesity (e.g. after CNS tumour or its treatment) BMI plotted on age- and sex-specific percentile charts, with blood pressure measurement Fasting glucose and/or HbA1c and fasting lipid profile Liver function tests and assessment for fatty liver disease Thyroid function testing where clinically indicated Evaluation for obstructive sleep apnoea when symptoms suggest it Genetic or endocrine work-up for early-onset severe or syndromic obesity In children and adolescents obesity is defined using body mass index relative to age- and sex-specific percentiles rather than fixed adult cut-offs, with obesity typically at or above the 95th percentile. The vast majority of cases are related to lifestyle and energy balance; a monogenic or endocrine cause is uncommon but should be considered in specific circumstances. A tall child growing well who is obese is usually exogenously obese, whereas an obese child who is short or growing poorly raises suspicion of an endocrine or syndromic cause. Ask about diet, physical activity, screen time, sleep, family history, and psychosocial factors, as these shape both cause and management. Screen for comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnoea. Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical clue to insulin resistance and increased type 2 diabetes risk. Management centres on sustainable family-based lifestyle change addressing nutrition, activity, sleep, and behaviour rather than short-term restrictive dieting. Early-onset severe obesity, particularly with hyperphagia, may suggest a monogenic cause and warrants specialist evaluation. Obesity combined with poor linear growth or short stature suggesting an endocrine cause Symptoms of type 2 diabetes such as polyuria, polydipsia, or an incidental very high glucose Signs of obstructive sleep apnoea including loud snoring, apnoeic pauses, or daytime somnolence Features of Cushing syndrome (central obesity, striae, hypertension, growth deceleration) Early-onset severe obesity with extreme hyperphagia suggesting a monogenic disorder Hip or knee pain suggesting a slipped capital femoral epiphysis Assuming all obesity is lifestyle-related and missing an endocrine, syndromic, or monogenic cause when growth is impaired Failing to screen for comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and sleep apnoea Focusing on the child alone rather than engaging the whole family in change Overlooking psychosocial factors, stigma, and mental health in management Childhood obesity results from a chronic positive energy balance in which caloric intake exceeds expenditure, leading to excess adipose tissue. This arises from a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, dietary patterns, physical inactivity, sleep, and environmental and socioeconomic influences. Expanded and dysfunctional adipose tissue drives insulin resistance, low-grade inflammation, and altered adipokine signalling, which underlie the associated metabolic, hepatic, cardiovascular, and endocrine complications. Rare monogenic and syndromic disorders disrupt central appetite regulation (notably the leptin-melanocortin pathway). Childhood obesity frequently persists into adulthood and raises the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other complications; early sustained family-based lifestyle intervention can improve trajectory and reduce comorbidity.

Chlamydial Infections — Chlamydia trachomatis, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, trachoma, LGV Neisseria gonorrhoeae urethritis/cervicitis/proctitis (clinically indistinguishable; frequent co-infection) Mycoplasma genitalium (now a leading cause of Chlamydia-negative and persistent NGU) Trichomonas vaginalis and herpes simplex virus as causes of NGU Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical pneumonia pathogens (for C. pneumoniae) Crohn's disease of the rectum (mimicked by LGV proctocolitis on sigmoidoscopy and histology) Adenovirus or HSV follicular conjunctivitis (mimics adult inclusion/oculogenital conjunctivitis) Neisseria gonorrhoeae (urethritis, cervicitis, PID, proctitis, ophthalmia neonatorum) Mycoplasma genitalium urethritis/cervicitis Trichomonas vaginalis urethritis Herpes simplex virus (urethritis, proctitis, ulcerative conjunctivitis) Haemophilus influenzae or Streptococcus pneumoniae neonatal conjunctivitis Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical CAP agents (for C. pneumoniae pneumonia) Adenovirus follicular conjunctivitis Haemophilus ducreyi and other genital-ulcer pathogens (for LGV primary lesion) NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on urine, vaginal/cervical, urethral, rectal, pharyngeal or conjunctival specimens - diagnostic assay of choice First-void urine or vaginal swab self-collection for screening programs and outreach Microscopy for leukocytes (Gram stain of urethral exudate or cervical mucus; first-void urine pyuria; leukocyte esterase) to support presumptive diagnosis of urethritis/cervicitis Giemsa-stained smears for intracytoplasmic inclusions (conjunctival scrapings, neonatal specimens; less sensitive than NAAT/culture) Microimmunofluorescence (MIF) serology - test of choice for LGV and neonatal pneumonia and the serologic gold standard, though labor-intensive and largely research-only Complement fixation (CF) serology (genus-level only via LPS; fourfold titer rise supports psittacosis) PCR of respiratory secretions for C. pneumoniae (preferred) and respiratory NAAT for C. psittaci Cell culture (former gold standard) - now performed only in specialized laboratories Sigmoidoscopy with rectal biopsy for proctitis/LGV (granulomas, crypt abscesses) Laparoscopy / endometrial biopsy (plasma-cell endometritis) in suspected salpingitis/PID and perihepatitis Serovar/molecular genotyping when LGV is suspected (longer treatment duration required) Crohn's disease of the rectum (resembles LGV/serovar proctocolitis: granulomas, giant cells, crypt abscesses) Testicular torsion or testicular tumor (mimic chlamydial epididymitis; torsion must be excluded promptly) Intrauterine contraceptive device-induced cervical inflammation Functional urinary symptoms / non-infectious dysuria (acute urethral syndrome in women) Reactive arthritis / spondyloarthropathy in the differential of HLA-B27-associated joint disease C. trachomatis genital infection is the most prevalent bacterial STI worldwide and is reported more than any other infectious disease in the United States; case counts are heavily dependent on screening coverage (Harrison 22e p.1469). Most genital infections are silent: up to 80-90% of women and >50% of men with C. trachomatis genital infection lack symptoms, and pharyngeal/rectal infection is typically asymptomatic and may persist for years, sustaining a large transmission reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1469). C. trachomatis is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and postgonococcal urethritis (PGU), implicated in 30-50% of NGU cases (Harrison 22e p.1469-1470). NAATs are the CDC-recommended diagnostic assay of choice; less-invasive specimens (urine for both sexes, vaginal swabs for women) are acceptable, and self-collected or clinician-collected vaginal swabs are slightly more sensitive than urine in women (Harrison 22e p.1472-1473). Because of frequent co-infection, testing for or treating chlamydia should be considered in patients diagnosed with N. gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1474). Trachoma (serovars A, B, Ba, C) remains a leading cause of preventable infectious blindness worldwide; the WHO SAFE-era programs target elimination as a public health problem by 2030 (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475). LGV (serovars L1, L2, L3) is an invasive STI presenting classically as a transient painless genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with bubo formation, or as hemorrhagic proctocolitis in MSM (Harrison 22e p.1469, 1472). C. pneumoniae causes atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia, bronchitis, pharyngitis and sinusitis, accounting for as many as 10% of CAP cases though more typically 1-2%; PCR of respiratory secretions is the preferred diagnostic method (Harrison 22e p.1476). Psittacosis (C. psittaci) is a zoonosis acquired from birds (psittacines, poultry) presenting as atypical pneumonia or systemic febrile illness; person-to-person transmission has never been demonstrated (Harrison 22e p.1475). Neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery causes inclusion conjunctivitis (in ~20-30% of exposed infants) and, in 10-15%, pneumonia at 2 weeks to 4 months of age; standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent chlamydial conjunctivitis (Harrison 22e p.1471-1472). Acute unilateral testicular pain - exclude testicular torsion promptly by imaging or surgical exploration before attributing to epididymitis Failure of unilateral intrascrotal pain/swelling to respond to antimicrobials - exclude testicular tumor or chronic infection such as tuberculosis Hemorrhagic proctocolitis with severe anorectal pain in MSM - consider invasive LGV serovars (often with HIV co-infection) Right-upper-quadrant pain/fever/nausea in a sexually active woman - suspect perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis), associated with extensive tubal scarring Trichiasis and entropion in trachoma - lashes abrade the cornea leading to ulceration and blindness if untreated Severe psittacosis pneumonia - can be fatal in up to 10% of untreated cases and may require ICU care, with hepatitis, endocarditis or myocarditis Untreated maternal infection - risk of neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis and infant pneumonia NAATs detect nucleic acid, not viable organisms - residual DNA may yield a positive result for up to 3 weeks after effective therapy, so NAATs should not be used as a test of cure before 3 weeks; routine test of cure is not recommended except in pregnancy. Single-dose penicillins or cephalosporins used for gonorrhea lack activity against chlamydiae - hence postgonococcal urethritis and the need to co-treat or exclude chlamydia. Standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; the most effective prevention is antenatal screening and treatment. Chlamydial and gonococcal conjunctivitis cannot be distinguished from other neonatal conjunctivitis on clinical grounds - laboratory diagnosis is required. CF and LPS-based serologic tests identify chlamydiae only to the genus level (cross-reactive across all chlamydiae) and must be interpreted cautiously. Serology (including a single high IgG titer) over-attributes C. pneumoniae to atypical pneumonia; cross-reactivity limits specificity, and PCR is preferred. Serology is never recommended for diagnosis of uncomplicated genital cervical/urethral/lower-tract infection or for asymptomatic screening. Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy; beta-lactams and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are not active against C. pneumoniae. Most genital infections are asymptomatic, so clinical recognition of cervicitis requires a high index of suspicion - no genital symptom is specific for chlamydial cervical infection. C. psittaci is a biohazard category B biothreat agent associated with laboratory-acquired infections. Chlamydiae are nonmotile, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria that lack peptidoglycan (structural integrity depends on disulfide cross-linking of outer-membrane proteins) and are energy parasites using host-cell ATP. They have a unique biphasic growth cycle alternating between the infectious, extracellular-adapted elementary body (0.25-0.35 um) and the metabolically active, non-infectious intracellular reticulate body (0.5-1 um), which divides by binary fission within a membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion while preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion; the cycle lasts ~48-72 h, giving a long clinical incubation (generally 1-3 weeks). C. trachomatis has two biovars (trachoma and LGV) and 18 serovars (trachoma A/B/Ba/C; oculogenital D-K; LGV L1-L3); the trachoma biovar parasitizes squamocolumnar epithelium whereas the more invasive LGV biovar involves lymphoid cells. Disease is driven largely by immunopathology rather than direct cytotoxicity: the chlamydial heat-shock protein shares epitopes with human and other bacterial proteins and, with repeated/persistent infection, drives fibrosis and mucosal scarring leading to tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain (genital) or cicatricial trichiasis and blindness (ocular). Antigenic variation in the major outer-membrane protein (omp1) permits reinfection because immunity to one serovar is not protective against others (Harrison 22e p.1467-1469). Uncomplicated genital chlamydial infection responds well to recommended antibiotics, and clinically significant drug resistance has not been observed in C. trachomatis; apparent treatment failure usually reflects non-adherence or reinfection. However, untreated or recurrent genital infection causes substantial long-term morbidity through mucosal scarring - PID with tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain - and women bear the greatest burden of sequelae. Reactive arthritis episodes typically last 2-6 months. Untreated ocular disease progresses to blinding trachoma; the WHO estimates ~6 million people have been blinded and ~1.3 million remain blind from trachoma. Untreated psittacosis pneumonia can be fatal in up to 10% of cases. Previous chlamydial infection raises the risk of reinfection, prompting rescreening at 3 months (Harrison 22e p.1469-1475). No formal grading scale. Genital C. trachomatis infections are categorized as uncomplicated (lower genital tract) versus complicated (e.g., PID, epididymitis) requiring longer therapy; LGV is treated as invasive disease with extended therapy. Trachoma is described by phase - active trachoma (follicular conjunctivitis) versus cicatricial disease (conjunctival scarring, trichiasis, entropion) - underpinning the WHO clinical signs used for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475).

Cholangiocarcinoma — bile duct cancer, CCA, cholangiocarcinoma, Klatskin tumour Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma causing distal biliary obstruction Gallbladder carcinoma extending into the biliary tree Hepatocellular carcinoma for intrahepatic mass lesions Benign biliary stricture, including primary sclerosing cholangitis without malignancy Choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice Metastatic adenocarcinoma to the liver or porta hepatis MRI with MRCP to map biliary anatomy and assess vascular and parenchymal involvement Contrast-enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for local staging and distant metastases ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography with brush cytology or biopsy for tissue diagnosis and drainage Serum CA 19-9 and CEA as supportive and monitoring markers Molecular and genomic profiling of tumour tissue for FGFR2 fusions, IDH1 mutations, and other actionable targets Classified by anatomical site as intrahepatic, perihilar (Klatskin), or distal, and location strongly influences presentation, surgical approach, and outcome Perihilar and distal tumours typically present with painless obstructive jaundice, pruritus, pale stools, and dark urine, whereas intrahepatic tumours often present later as a liver mass with vague abdominal pain or weight loss Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a major predisposing condition, along with chronic biliary inflammation, liver fluke infestation in endemic regions, biliary tract stones, and choledochal cysts CA 19-9 is a useful supportive marker but is neither sensitive nor specific and can be elevated by biliary obstruction or cholangitis alone Tissue diagnosis and biliary anatomy are best defined with MRCP and, where needed, ERCP with brushings or cholangioscopy, taking care to avoid seeding and cholangitis Only a minority of patients are candidates for curative resection, which may require major liver resection with biliary reconstruction depending on tumour location For unresectable or metastatic disease, gemcitabine plus platinum chemotherapy is the systemic backbone, and molecular profiling for targetable alterations such as FGFR2 fusions and IDH1 mutations can guide targeted therapy Relieving biliary obstruction with stenting is central to palliation and to controlling cholangitis and pruritus Progressive painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss Cholangitis with fever and rigors on a background of biliary stricture New dominant biliary stricture in a patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis Rapidly enlarging intrahepatic mass with vascular involvement on imaging Assuming obstructive jaundice is benign and delaying malignancy workup Relying on a normal or mildly raised CA 19-9 to exclude cancer Aggressive biliary instrumentation causing cholangitis before definitive staging Missing a dominant malignant stricture within primary sclerosing cholangitis Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the epithelial cells lining the intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts, most often adenocarcinoma. Chronic inflammation and cholestasis, as seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic infection, or biliary stones, produce repeated epithelial injury and repair that promotes dysplasia and malignant transformation. The tumours are frequently desmoplastic and grow along the bile ducts, causing obstruction; perihilar lesions readily invade the portal structures and liver, while intrahepatic tumours behave as mass-forming liver cancers with early lymphatic and vascular spread. Prognosis is generally poor because most patients present with unresectable disease; complete resection with negative margins offers the best survival, while advanced disease treated with systemic therapy has limited long-term survival though molecularly targeted agents can extend it in selected patients.

Choledochal cyst — bile duct cyst, congenital biliary dilatation, choledochal malformation Biliary atresia (in the neonate) Obstruction from a biliary or gallstone Pancreatic pseudocyst Hepatic or mesenteric cyst Caroli disease (intrahepatic ductal dilatation) Abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging test Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to delineate biliary and pancreaticobiliary anatomy Liver function tests and inflammatory markers to assess cholestasis and cholangitis Serum amylase/lipase if pancreatitis is suspected Intraoperative cholangiography when needed to clarify ductal anatomy A congenital cystic dilatation of the biliary tree, most often affecting the extrahepatic common bile duct, and more common in females and in East Asian populations The classic triad of abdominal pain, jaundice, and a palpable right upper quadrant mass is present in only a minority; most children show one or two of these features Infants often present with obstructive jaundice and an abdominal mass, whereas older children more often have intermittent pain and cholangitis The Todani classification describes the anatomical types, with type I (fusiform extrahepatic dilatation) being the most frequent An anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction allowing reflux of pancreatic enzymes into the bile duct is thought to contribute to many cases Ultrasound is the usual first-line study, with MRCP providing detailed mapping of the biliary anatomy before surgery Treatment is complete excision of the cyst with reconstruction by hepaticojejunostomy, because the abnormal epithelium carries a lifelong risk of malignancy Even after excision, long-term surveillance is needed for anastomotic stricture, recurrent cholangitis, and biliary malignancy Ascending cholangitis with fever, pain, and jaundice requiring prompt treatment Cyst rupture causing biliary peritonitis, a surgical emergency Features suggesting malignant transformation, especially in longstanding or previously untreated cysts Progressive obstructive jaundice with signs of biliary sepsis Performing simple internal drainage rather than complete cyst excision, leaving malignancy risk Confusing neonatal presentation with biliary atresia and delaying appropriate imaging Failing to identify and address an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction Neglecting long-term surveillance for late strictures, cholangitis, and biliary cancer Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of part of the biliary tree. A widely accepted mechanism is an anomalous union of the pancreatic and bile ducts outside the duodenal wall, creating a long common channel that allows pancreatic secretions to reflux into the biliary system. Enzymatic damage weakens and dilates the duct wall, and chronic inflammation predisposes the abnormal biliary epithelium to stricturing, stone formation, cholangitis, and, over time, malignant change (cholangiocarcinoma). Complete surgical excision with biliary reconstruction gives good long-term results in most children and reduces but does not abolish the malignancy risk. Internal drainage procedures that leave the cyst in place are inadequate because they carry ongoing risks of cholangitis, stones, and cancer, so lifelong follow-up remains important.

head or cholangiocarcinoma) Benign biliary stricture Ascending cholangitis Gallstone pancreatitis Hepatocellular causes of jaundice (e.g. hepatitis) Liver function tests demonstrating a cholestatic cholangitis is suspected Choledocholithiasis is the presence of gallstones in the common bile duct, usually having migrated from the gallbladder, and may be silent or cause obstruction Typical features are right upper quadrant or epigastric pain with obstructive jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine, and it is a leading cause of extrahepatic biliary obstruction Liver function tests show a cholestatic (obstructive) pattern with raised bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-GT, and a duct dilated above the stone may be seen on ultrasound It is an important cause of gallstone pancreatitis when a stone obstructs at the ampulla and of ascending cholangitis when the obstructed duct becomes infected MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are accurate for confirming ductal stones when ultrasound is inconclusive but clinical suspicion is moderate to high ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is both diagnostic and therapeutic, while stones can also be cleared surgically at cholecystectomy via the cystic duct or the common bile duct Because the gallbladder remains the source of stones, cholecystectomy is generally advised after ductal clearance to prevent recurrence Ascending cholangitis with Charcot triad (fever with rigors, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain), or Reynolds pentad with hypotension and confusion indicating biliary sepsis requiring urgent decompression Severe or worsening gallstone pancreatitis Progressive obstructive jaundice with coagulopathy Septic shock or organ dysfunction from an obstructed, infected biliary tree Overlooking ductal stones in a patient with only mildly abnormal liver tests or a non-dilated duct on early ultrasound Delaying biliary decompression in cholangitis while pursuing further imaging Performing cholecystectomy without clearing the duct, leaving retained stones Failing to recognise a stone impacted at the ampulla as the cause of gallstone pancreatitis Attributing obstructive jaundice to stones and missing an underlying malignant stricture Common bile duct stones are usually cholesterol or mixed stones that form in the gallbladder and pass through the cystic duct into the common bile duct; primary duct stones (typically pigment stones) form within the duct, favoured by biliary stasis, stricture, or infection. A stone obstructing the duct raises biliary pressure and causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and cholestasis. Obstruction at the ampulla can block pancreatic outflow and trigger acute pancreatitis. Stagnant, obstructed bile readily becomes infected, and rising ductal pressure allows bacteria and endotoxin to translocate into the circulation, producing ascending cholangitis and potentially biliary sepsis. With timely stone clearance and, where appropriate, cholecystectomy the outlook is excellent and complications are prevented. Prognosis is worse when choledocholithiasis is complicated by severe cholangitis or pancreatitis, especially with delayed biliary decompression, but urgent drainage markedly improves survival in cholangitis.

Cholera — Vibrio cholerae infection Other secretory/toxigenic watery diarrhoeas: enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (produces a heat-labile toxin like cholera toxin), and other dehydrating secretory diarrhoeal illnesses to which the term cholera has historically and loosely been applied (p.1325) Diarrhoea due to non-O1/O139 (noncholera) V. cholerae, which generally do not produce cholera toxin and do not cause large epidemics (p.1330) Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (heat-labile enterotoxin resembling cholera toxin causing secretory diarrhoea) (p.1325-1326) Other Vibrio gastroenteritis, e.g. Vibrio parahaemolyticus and non-O1/O139 V. cholerae (p.1330) Stool culture on a selective medium such as taurocholate-tellurite-gelatin (TTG) agar or thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose (TCBS) agar; the organism must be specifically sought (p.1328) Direct dark-field microscopy of a wet mount of fresh stool, with serotype discernible by immobilisation with specific antisera (p.1328) Point-of-care antigen-detection cholera dipstick (rapid diagnostic test) for field use or where laboratory facilities are lacking (p.1328) Cary-Blair transport medium and/or alkaline-peptone water-enrichment medium if sample processing will be delayed (p.1328) Vibrios are oxidase-positive; standard Enterobacteriaceae biochemical testing suffices for identification (p.1328) Supportive labs in dehydrated patients: elevated haematocrit (haemoconcentration) in non-anaemic patients, mild neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (prerenal azotaemia), normal sodium/potassium/chloride, markedly reduced bicarbonate (<15 mmol/L), elevated anion gap and low arterial pH (~7.2) (p.1328) Severely dehydrating secretory diarrhoea of non-infectious aetiology, to which the term cholera has at times been loosely applied (p.1325) Cholera is an acute toxin-mediated diarrhoeal disease caused by Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 or O139 (the serogroups with epidemic potential) that can progress to profound, rapidly progressive dehydration and death within hours (p.1325-1326). After a 24-48 h incubation in a non-immune individual, illness begins with the sudden onset of painless watery diarrhoea that can rapidly become voluminous; vomiting is common and fever is usually absent (p.1327). The characteristic stool is non-bilious, gray, slightly cloudy fluid flecked with mucus, containing no blood, with a fishy, inoffensive odour, described as rice-water stool because it resembles water in which rice has been washed (p.1327). In severe cases (cholera gravis) volume loss can exceed 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h, and muscle cramps from electrolyte disturbance are common (p.1327). Symptoms parallel the degree of volume contraction: thirst at <5% body-weight loss; postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia and decreased skin turgor at 5-10%; and oliguria, weak or absent pulses, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), wrinkled washerwoman skin, somnolence and coma at >10% (p.1327-1328). If fluids and electrolytes are replaced adequately, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving in a few days (p.1328). Profound, rapidly progressive dehydration developing within hours (p.1325) Signs of severe dehydration: unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of body weight (p.1328) Voluminous ongoing stool losses (volume loss exceeding 250 mL/kg in the first 24 h in severe cases) (p.1327) Features of hypovolaemic shock, oliguria, somnolence and coma (p.1327-1328) Acute watery diarrhoea or death from acute watery diarrhoea in a patient >=5 years, even where cholera is not known to be present (p.1328) The organism is not recovered on routine media; V. cholerae must be specifically sought using selective medium, or the diagnosis will be missed (p.1328). Diagnosis is often syndromic and many endemic countries under-report to the WHO, so the true burden and distribution are unknown and cases may be unrecognised (p.1326). Cholera should still be suspected in severe acute watery diarrhoea or death even in areas not known to have cholera (p.1328). Fever is usually absent, so its absence should not dissuade from the diagnosis (p.1327). Immunity to V. cholerae O1 is not protective against O139 (and vice versa), so prior infection does not guarantee protection against the other serogroup (p.1327). Cholera is fundamentally a toxin-mediated disease. After ingestion (most often via faecally contaminated water, though contaminated food and human-to-human transmission also contribute), V. cholerae colonises the small intestine, a process dependent on the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), with cholera toxin, TCP and other virulence factors coordinately regulated by ToxR and by quorum sensing. The organism elaborates cholera toxin, a protein enterotoxin made of a monomeric enzymatic A subunit and a pentameric B-subunit binding moiety. The B pentamer binds GM1 ganglioside on the epithelial cell surface, delivering the A subunit, whose activated form (A1) irreversibly ADP-ribosylates the GTP-binding regulatory component of adenylate cyclase. This upregulates adenylate cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic AMP, which inhibits absorptive sodium transport in villus cells and activates secretory chloride transport in crypt cells, driving accumulation of sodium chloride in the lumen; water follows passively to maintain osmolality, producing isotonic fluid that exceeds the gut's reabsorptive capacity and results in watery diarrhoea. Cholera toxin also enhances secretion via prostaglandins and/or neural histamine receptors. Unless lost fluid and electrolytes are replaced, profound dehydration leads to hypovolaemic shock and bicarbonate loss leads to acidosis. The cholera toxin genes (ctxAB) are carried on the bacteriophage CTX-phi, which uses TCP as its receptor, allowing horizontal transfer to generate new toxigenic strains (p.1326-1327). Death from cholera is due to hypovolaemic shock. Historically the disease carried high mortality, but prompt aggressive fluid repletion and supportive care can obviate this. With adequate fluid and electrolyte replacement, complications are averted and the illness is self-limited, resolving over a few days. Complications derive exclusively from volume and electrolyte depletion and include renal failure due to acute tubular necrosis. Untreated cholera carries very high case-fatality (historically >50% in untreated severe cases), which falls dramatically with rehydration (p.1326, p.1328). Harrison stratifies dehydration in cholera into: (1) None or mild (diarrhoea present) - thirst in some cases, <5% loss of total body weight; (2) Moderate - thirst, postural hypotension, weakness, tachycardia, decreased skin turgor, dry mouth/tongue, no tears, 5-10% loss of total body weight; and (3) Severe - unconsciousness, lethargy or floppiness, weak or absent pulse, inability to drink, sunken eyes (sunken fontanelles in infants), >10% loss of total body weight. This dehydration assessment guides the intensity of rehydration (p.1328).

Cholesteatoma — keratoma, epidermosis of middle ear, unsafe chronic otitis media Tubotympanic (safe) chronic suppurative otitis media Keratosis obturans of the external canal Aural polyp or granulation from other causes Middle ear or external canal malignancy Glomus tumour of the middle ear Foreign body with surrounding inflammation Otoscopy and microscopy to identify retraction pockets, keratin debris and granulations High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to define extent and bony erosion Diffusion-weighted MRI to detect residual or recurrent cholesteatoma Pure tone audiometry to document conductive or mixed hearing loss Culture of discharge to guide treatment of secondary infection Fistula test if erosion into the labyrinth is suspected Cholesteatoma is a collection of keratinising squamous epithelium in the middle ear cleft; despite the name it contains neither cholesterol nor a tumour It is characteristically associated with attic or posterosuperior marginal perforations, which is why this is called the unsafe or atticoantral type of chronic otitis media Typical symptoms are scanty, foul-smelling ear discharge with progressive conductive hearing loss Otoscopy may reveal a retraction pocket, whitish debris or granulations and a crust in the attic; a polyp or aural granulation should raise suspicion It is locally destructive because the matrix and surrounding inflammation erode bone, threatening the ossicles, facial nerve, labyrinth and dura Congenital cholesteatoma can occur behind an intact drum with no history of infection Imaging with high-resolution CT maps disease extent and bony erosion, and MRI (including diffusion-weighted sequences) helps detect or confirm residual or recurrent disease The mainstay of treatment is surgical eradication by mastoidectomy and tympanoplasty, since medical therapy alone cannot cure it Vertigo or a positive fistula sign suggesting labyrinthine erosion Facial nerve weakness indicating involvement of the facial canal Severe headache, fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting intracranial complication (an emergency) Sudden worsening of hearing or new sensorineural loss Postauricular swelling or abscess signalling spread beyond the mastoid Dismissing scanty foul discharge as trivial and missing an unsafe ear Failing to inspect the attic and posterosuperior quadrant where retraction pockets hide Relying on medical treatment alone when surgery is needed for cure Not recognising an aural polyp as a possible marker of underlying cholesteatoma Neglecting long-term surveillance for residual or recurrent disease Cholesteatoma consists of a sac of keratinising stratified squamous epithelium (matrix) that sheds keratin into the middle ear and mastoid, where it accumulates and cannot escape. Acquired disease most often follows persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction that produces a retraction pocket in the pars flaccida or posterosuperior pars tensa; trapped desquamated epithelium enlarges the pocket, or squamous epithelium migrates through a marginal perforation. The expanding mass and its associated chronic inflammation release enzymes and mediators that resorb surrounding bone, progressively destroying the ossicular chain and eroding toward the facial nerve, semicircular canals and intracranial cavity. Superimposed infection produces the characteristic foul discharge and accelerates the destructive process. With complete surgical removal the disease can be controlled and complications prevented, but cholesteatoma has a tendency to recur or leave residual matrix, so long-term follow-up is essential; neglected disease leads to serious intratemporal and intracranial complications.

presentation Lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides delivered to the lysosome via receptor-mediated lipoprotein uptake. Partial deficiency in cholesteryl ester storage disease leads to lysosomal accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides, predominantly in hepatocytes, Kupffer cells, intestinal mucosa and the arterial wall. Reduced release of free cholesterol from the lysosome disturbs cellular cholesterol homeostasis, upregulating endogenous cholesterol synthesis and LDL receptor pathways, which produces the atherogenic dyslipidaemia; progressive hepatic lipid storage causes steatosis, fibrosis and, over time, cirrhosis. The course is variable and slower than Wolman disease, but untreated disease can progress to cirrhosis and accelerated atherosclerosis; enzyme replacement therapy and lipid-lowering treatment can improve hepatic and lipid parameters and alter the natural history.

Epidural-associated maternal pyrexia without infection Placental abruption causing uterine tenderness Preterm labour without infection Viral illness in pregnancy Appendicitis or other intra-abdominal confirm the diagnosis Screening for group B streptococcus and other genital pathogens Chorioamnionitis is inflammation or infection of the fetal membranes and amniotic fluid, most often from ascending organisms from the lower genital tract It is strongly associated with prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, repeated vaginal examinations, and preterm labour Clinical diagnosis is suggested by maternal fever combined with features such as maternal or fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid Infection is typically polymicrobial, involving genital tract flora including anaerobes, group B streptococcus, and enteric organisms Management centres on prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics and expediting delivery, as the infection will not resolve while the pregnancy continues It is an important cause of maternal sepsis and can lead to postpartum endometritis, wound infection, and, rarely, septic shock For the neonate it raises the risk of early-onset sepsis, pneumonia, and, particularly in preterm infants, neurological injury and cerebral palsy Delivery does not preclude ongoing infection, so mother and baby require continued observation and treatment after birth Features of maternal sepsis such as high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, or confusion requiring urgent resuscitation and delivery Non-reassuring or abnormal fetal heart rate patterns indicating fetal compromise Foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid with significant uterine tenderness Failure to improve despite antibiotics, suggesting the need to expedite delivery Signs of neonatal sepsis after birth requiring immediate paediatric assessment Attributing maternal fever solely to an epidural and missing intra-amniotic infection Delaying delivery while attempting to treat the infection conservatively Underestimating the risk of maternal sepsis and uterine atony after delivery Failing to alert the neonatal team to the risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis Overlooking anaerobic and polymicrobial cover in the choice of antibiotics Chorioamnionitis most commonly results from ascent of bacteria from the vagina and cervix into the normally sterile amniotic cavity, particularly once the membranes are ruptured or the cervix is dilated. The organisms provoke a maternal and fetal inflammatory response with release of cytokines and prostaglandins that can precipitate or accelerate labour. Inflammation of the membranes, cord, and placenta may compromise the fetus directly through infection and indirectly through the fetal inflammatory response syndrome, which is implicated in preterm birth and neurological injury. Less commonly infection reaches the cavity haematogenously or via invasive procedures. With prompt antibiotics and timely delivery most mothers recover fully, though the condition carries risks of postpartum infection, haemorrhage from uterine atony, and rarely septic shock. Neonatal outcome depends on gestation and the severity of the fetal inflammatory response; term infants generally do well with treatment, whereas preterm infants exposed to intrauterine infection face higher risks of sepsis and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

type, extraocular extension, and cytogenetic markers such as monosomy 3 A malignant intraocular tumour with potential to metastasise, particularly to the liver, requiring urgent oncology referral Extraocular or optic nerve extension indicating advanced disease Rapid growth or documented enlargement of a previously stable pigmented lesion Signs of hepatic metastasis such as deranged liver function or a liver mass Dismissing a small pigmented lesion as a benign naevus without documenting risk features and arranging follow-up Overlooking an amelanotic melanoma and mistaking it for a benign or inflammatory mass Failing to arrange systemic staging and long-term surveillance for liver metastasis Assuming successful local treatment eliminates the risk of later distant spread Choroidal melanoma arises from malignant transformation of melanocytes within the choroidal stroma. Growth breaches Bruch membrane in many tumours, producing the characteristic mushroom shape and disrupting the overlying retinal pigment epithelium and retina, which leads to serous detachment and lipofuscin deposition. Chromosomal changes, notably loss of one copy of chromosome 3 and gains of chromosome 8q, correlate with an aggressive metastatic phenotype. Spread is almost exclusively haematogenous with a strong hepatic tropism, sometimes appearing years after successful local treatment. Prognosis is determined mainly by tumour size, cell type, extraocular extension, and cytogenetics; small tumours with disomy 3 have a favourable survival outlook, whereas large tumours with monosomy 3 or chromosome 8q gain carry a high risk of fatal hepatic metastasis, and local eye-preserving radiotherapy controls the tumour without necessarily altering metastatic risk.

atrophy on the central macular island threatening acuity Development of macular oedema or complications compromising residual vision Atypical features suggesting an alternative chorioretinal dystrophy Misdiagnosing it as retinitis pigmentosa and missing the specific X-linked genetic basis and therapeutic implications Overlooking the carrier fundus in the mother, which supports the diagnosis and guides counselling Assuming poor central vision early, when the central island is usually retained until late Failing to consider eligibility for gene-therapy trials in suitable patients Choroideremia is caused by loss of function of REP1, a protein that escorts Rab GTPases for prenylation, a lipid modification essential for intracellular vesicular trafficking. Although a related protein partly compensates elsewhere, the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptors, and choroid are particularly dependent on REP1, so deficiency impairs their vesicle transport and membrane function. This leads to progressive degeneration of the photoreceptor-retinal pigment epithelium-choriocapillaris complex, beginning in the periphery and advancing centrally, with characteristic loss of the choroid exposing bare sclera. The X-linked pattern reflects the gene's location, with mosaic expression producing the milder carrier fundus. It is a slowly progressive disorder in which night blindness and peripheral field loss advance over decades, with central acuity often preserved until middle age before eventual severe visual impairment; gene therapy trials aim to slow or halt degeneration.

to prolonged antifungal therapy indicating a resistant or extensive disease Underestimating the duration of therapy required, leading to premature discontinuation and relapse Missing malignant change in a chronic lesion by not rebiopsying Confusing it with mycetoma, which has grains and sinuses rather than muriform bodies Neglecting management of lymphoedema and secondary infection Pigmented soil fungi are introduced into subcutaneous tissue through minor trauma. Within tissue they transform into thick-walled, melanised muriform (sclerotic) bodies that divide by septation and resist killing, partly because melanin scavenges free radicals and impairs phagocyte function. The host mounts a chronic mixed suppurative and granulomatous response with pseudoepitheliomatous epidermal hyperplasia, producing the characteristic verrucous surface. Slow local spread occurs through the skin and lymphatics, but systemic dissemination is rare; chronicity reflects the organism's resistance and limited effective immune clearance. Small early lesions may be cured with prolonged antifungal therapy or excision, but extensive long-standing disease is often refractory, prone to relapse, and can lead to disabling fibrosis, lymphoedema and, rarely, malignant transformation.

angiography if arteritis/stroke suspected Systemic workup: tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, chest radiograph or chest CT/MRI and sputum exam, urinalysis, CBC, renal/liver function, alkaline phosphatase, ESR, ANA, anti-Ro/anti-La, rheumatoid factor, serum IgG4 FDG-PET to locate a systemic biopsy site in suspected carcinomatous meningitis or sarcoidosis; genetic testing for monogenic autoinflammatory disorders Meningeal biopsy targeting contrast-enhancing regions when CSF is non-diagnostic and the patient is severely disabled, needs ventricular decompression, or is deteriorating rapidly Subarachnoid hemorrhage in the preceding week presenting with xanthochromia and pleocytosis IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome and Behcet's syndrome (recurrent forms) Multiple sclerosis and Sjogren's syndrome Chronic meningitis is defined by a characteristic neurologic syndrome persisting beyond 4 weeks together with a sustained CSF inflammatory response (white cell count >5/uL); appropriate treatment hinges entirely on identifying the underlying cause. Five disease categories account for most cases: meningeal infections, malignancy, autoimmune inflammatory disorders, chemical meningitis, and parameningeal infections; some recurrent cases reflect monogenic autoinflammatory disorders. Cardinal manifestations are persistent nonfocal headache, signs of hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies, radiculopathies, and cognitive or personality change; classic meningeal signs (Kernig/Brudzinski) are actually uncommon in the chronic form. Basal meningitis, where exudate collects at the skull base, presents as multiple cranial neuropathies; lower cranial nerves are involved more often because the inflammatory exudate gravitates to the base of the brain. Spinal involvement produces multiple radiculopathies (radicular pain, sensory loss, weakness, sphincter dysfunction) and may progress to arachnoiditis with clumping of lower nerve roots, again because cells settle at the bottom of the intrathecal space. Two clinical forms exist: a chronic persistent form and a recurrent form in which all clinical and CSF abnormalities resolve completely between discrete episodes (e.g., Mollaret's meningitis from HSV-2, chemical leak from epidermoid tumor, autoimmune conditions, drug hypersensitivity). Worldwide, M. tuberculosis is the most common infectious cause, followed by Cryptococcus neoformans; in immunosuppressed patients these may present with little or no headache, fever, or meningeal signs and even a pauci-cellular CSF. In most chronic (non-recurrent) meningitides mononuclear cells predominate; a neutrophilic CSF after 3 weeks points to Nocardia, Actinomyces, Brucella, certain fungi (Blastomyces, Candida, Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Pseudallescheria, Cladophialophora), or noninfectious causes (SLE, chemical meningitis). An eosinophilic CSF response suggests parasitic disease (Angiostrongylus, Gnathostoma, Baylisascaris, Toxocara, cysticercosis, schistosomiasis, echinococcosis, toxoplasmosis), coccidioidal fungal meningitis (6-20% eosinophils with lymphocytic pleocytosis), neoplasia, or sarcoidosis. Meningeal enhancement patterns localize the process: leptomeningeal enhancement follows gyri and basal cisterns (typical of infection), whereas pachymeningeal enhancement is thick, linear or nodular along dura/falx/tentorium (e.g., lymphoma, IgG4-related disease). In about one-third of cases the cause remains undiagnosed despite thorough evaluation; many causative organisms require weeks of culture, so diagnostic patience is balanced against the risk of progressive neurologic deterioration. Repeated large-volume lumbar CSF samples (three or more), and if needed cervical cisternal sampling near the basal meninges, raise the yield for fungal and malignant causes; ventricular fluid may appear sterile despite active lower lumbar infection. Signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, drowsiness, papilledema, visual loss, impaired upgaze, sixth-nerve palsy) warranting imaging before lumbar puncture Rapidly progressive neurologic deterioration requiring urgent treatment rather than awaiting culture results Multiple progressive cranial neuropathies or evolving radiculopathy/myelopathy indicating widespread CSF dissemination Focal cerebral signs suggesting brain abscess, parameningeal infection, or infarction Immunosuppression or untreated HIV, where meningeal signs are attenuated and any persistent headache or mental status change mandates CSF examination Low CSF glucose with lymphocytic pleocytosis, prompting empiric coverage for tuberculosis given the potential for devastation within weeks Performing lumbar puncture before imaging when raised ICP from a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus exists risks brain herniation Assuming a normal or pauci-cellular CSF excludes meningitis in immunosuppressed or HIV patients, in whom signs are attenuated Relying on a single small-volume CSF sample; fungal and malignant causes often require repeated large-volume sampling, and some organisms take weeks to grow in culture Interpreting a transient response to empiric glucocorticoids as confirmation of a noninfectious cause, since tuberculosis, cysticercosis, and lymphoma may also respond temporarily Overlooking false-negative cryptococcal antigen or CSF VDRL results due to the prozone effect at high antibody/antigen titers Attributing dural enhancement to disease when it can be a benign post-LP, post-neurosurgical, post-concussion, or post-CSF-leak finding Failing to recognize that ventricular CSF can appear sterile while active infection persists in the lower lumbar space Chronic inflammation of the meninges (pia, arachnoid, dura) generates neurologic deficits whose pattern is determined by the anatomic site of inflammation and its consequences. CSF, produced by the choroid plexus and circulating from the ventricles through the basal cisterns over the convexities to arachnoid villi, provides a conduit for rapid spread of infectious or infiltrative processes over the brain, cord, and nerve roots; organisms may also track along perivascular (Virchow-Robin) spaces into brain parenchyma. Intracranial inflammation stimulates meningeal nociceptive fibers (headache, neck/back pain) and may obstruct CSF flow at the cerebral aqueduct or arachnoid villi, causing hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Inflammatory exudate seeded around the brainstem and cranial nerves at the skull base produces basal meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies, while spinal exudate injures nerve roots and may encircle the cord to cause myelopathy. Vasculitis of subarachnoid vessels can lead to infarction and cognitive/behavioral decline. A recently identified dural lymphatic system drains the dura, but its role in chronic meningitis is not yet established. Outcome depends on the underlying etiology and the speed of diagnosis and treatment; many causes are effectively treatable, but untreated disease produces progressive, potentially fatal damage to the CNS, cranial nerves, and roots. Even with treatment, tuberculous meningitis carries high rates of morbidity. Fatal levels of raised intracranial pressure can occur (notably in cryptococcal meningitis) even without ventricular enlargement, and repetitive or continuous CSF drainage may be needed to prevent abrupt deterioration and death. Some recurrent forms (e.g., chronic benign lymphocytic meningitis) resolve over 2-6 months. No formal grading scale is given; severity is gauged clinically by the rate of neurologic progression, the presence of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus, and the degree of disability, which together determine whether to await culture results or proceed to meningeal biopsy and empiric therapy.

In slow-transit constipation, reduced colonic propulsive activity, often linked to abnormalities of enteric neurons and interstitial cells of Cajal, delays stool passage. In defecatory disorders, impaired coordination of the pelvic floor and anal sphincter (dyssynergia) or structural pelvic floor abnormalities prevent effective evacuation. Normal-transit constipation, the most common type, involves normal stool movement with perceived difficulty, often overlapping with irritable bowel syndrome. Secondary causes act through metabolic, endocrine, neurological, or pharmacological effects on gut motility. Chronic constipation is generally benign but frequently persistent and can significantly reduce quality of life; most patients improve with lifestyle measures and laxatives, and biofeedback is effective for defecatory disorders, though a minority remain refractory.

by mutations in any of the subunits of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex (gp91phox, p22phox, p47phox, p67phox, p40phox). This enzyme normally generates superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species that drive the microbicidal respiratory burst within the phagosome. Without a functional oxidase, phagocytes engulf organisms but fail to kill catalase-positive microbes that can neutralise their own hydrogen peroxide. Persistence of viable organisms and impaired resolution of inflammation lead to chronic granuloma formation and tissue damage. The most common form is X-linked (CYBB), with autosomal recessive forms accounting for the remainder. Prophylactic antibacterial and antifungal therapy with interferon-gamma has substantially improved survival, though serious infections and inflammatory complications still occur. Invasive fungal disease remains a leading cause of death. Haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can be curative, especially with well-matched donors performed before major organ damage.

Classification rests on three axes: (1) cause, (2) histologic activity or grade (necroinflammatory activity), and (3) degree of progression based on fibrosis or stage; neither clinical features alone nor histology alone are sufficient to characterize disease (p.2673). Grade reflects necroinflammatory activity (periportal/piecemeal necrosis or interface hepatitis, bridging necrosis, focal lobular necrosis, portal inflammation) and is scored by the histologic activity index (HAI, used in the U.S.) or METAVIR (used in Europe); chronic hepatitis is graded mild, moderate, or severe (p.2673-2674). Stage reflects fibrosis on a numerical scale (0-6 HAI or 0-4 METAVIR); when fibrous septa surround parenchymal nodules and alter normal lobular architecture, the lesion is defined as cirrhosis (p.2674). Hyperglobulinemia and circulating autoantibodies are distinctly ABSENT in chronic hepatitis B, in contrast to autoimmune hepatitis; this helps distinguish viral from autoimmune disease (p.2674). Autoimmune hepatitis has a strong female predominance (~75% of cases) with a bimodal age distribution (one peak age <30, a second often >60); fatigue is the most common symptom (~85%) and ~25% are diagnosed when asymptomatic on abnormal liver tests (p.2694-2695). Type I AIH (classic, North America/northern Europe, young women) is associated with ANA in a homogeneous pattern and anti-smooth-muscle antibody (ASMA); type II AIH (often children, Mediterranean) is associated with anti-LKM1 (directed against cytochrome P450 2D6) rather than ANA (p.2695). Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (>2.5 g/dL) is common in AIH; smooth-muscle antibodies are detected in 63% of cases and, combined with a positive ANA, have high specificity (p.2695). Anti-LKM1 (against cytochrome P450 2D6) seen in type II AIH is the same antibody found in some patients with chronic hepatitis C; rarely AIH patients with hyperglobulinemia give false-positive anti-HCV immunoassays (p.2685-2695). Cirrhosis from any cause of chronic hepatitis carries a risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; in cirrhotic hepatitis C the annual HCC rate is 1-4%, occurring primarily after 30 or more years of infection, warranting HCC surveillance (p.2685). Liver biopsy is imperative to diagnose AIH; classic features include interface hepatitis extending beyond portal tracts, plasma cells in the infiltrate, central vein perivenulitis, hepatocellular rosette formation, and frequent septal/bridging fibrosis and cirrhosis (p.2695). Complications of cirrhosis: ascites, edema, bleeding gastroesophageal varices, hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, hypersplenism Intermittent deepening of jaundice with worsening malaise/anorexia/fatigue, often coinciding with virologic reactivation, which may cause hepatic decompensation when superimposed on cirrhosis Severe AIH: aminotransferases >10x normal, marked hyperglobulinemia, multilobular collapse or bridging necrosis on histology (6-month untreated mortality up to ~40%) Failure of serum bilirubin to improve after 2 weeks of therapy in AIH (poor prognostic sign) Multilobular collapse at initial presentation in AIH (poor prognostic sign) Development of hepatocellular carcinoma in established cirrhosis Histopathologic-only classification (chronic persistent/lobular vs chronic active hepatitis) has been replaced because its presumed prognostic implications were not corroborated; classification now combines cause, grade, and stage (p.2673). Laboratory features of chronic hepatitis B do not reliably distinguish histologically mild from severe disease (p.2674). Low-titer ANA or ASMA occurs in other liver diseases including MASLD (~20% ANA-positive, ~14% ASMA-positive in one series) and viral hepatitis, so positive autoantibodies are not specific for AIH (p.2695). Rarely AIH patients with hyperglobulinemia have false-positive anti-HCV; conversely some confirmed chronic hepatitis C patients have circulating anti-LKM1, blurring the distinction between viral and autoimmune disease (p.2685-2695). ICI hepatitis resembles AIH but lacks female preponderance and is less likely to have ANA (low-titer if present) or plasma cell infiltrates (p.2695). Overlapping types of hepatitis (e.g., viral plus steatotic, alcohol plus nonalcohol steatotic) are encountered not infrequently given the high prevalence of steatotic liver disease (p.2673). Chronic hepatitis comprises liver disorders of varying cause in which hepatic inflammation and necrosis persist for at least 6 months. Broad categories include chronic viral hepatitis (B, B plus D, C), drug- or toxin-induced chronic hepatitis, alcohol-associated liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-related (steatotic) liver disease, and autoimmune chronic hepatitis; idiopathic/cryptogenic cases are also believed largely autoimmune. In chronic hepatitis B, all forms can be progressive but progression occurs primarily in patients with active HBV replication, and HCC risk is highest with continued high-level replication. In autoimmune hepatitis, progressive injury results from a cell-mediated immunologic attack on hepatocytes in the setting of lost/failed tolerance for self-liver antigens; predisposition is inherited (HLA-B8, DR3, DR4, DRB1*0301/*0401) while liver specificity is triggered by environmental factors (chemicals, drugs such as minocycline, viruses, and reported triggers including COVID-19 and COVID-19 vaccination); molecular mimicry activates infiltrating CD4+ T cells and impaired regulatory CD4+CD25+ T-cell control contributes (p.2673, 2693-2694). Outcome depends on grade and stage. In untreated chronic hepatitis B, 5-year survival was 97% for mild, 86% for moderate-to-severe, and 55% for those with cirrhosis (15-year survival 77%, 66%, 40% respectively); all forms can progress, primarily with active HBV replication. In chronic hepatitis C, liver histology is the best prognostic indicator; mild disease has an excellent prognosis, while moderate-to-severe necroinflammation or bridging fibrosis makes cirrhosis highly likely over 10-20 years. In compensated HCV cirrhosis, 10-year survival is ~80%, with mortality 2-6%/year, decompensation 4-5%/year, and HCC 1-4%/year. In autoimmune hepatitis, 10-year survival is 80-98% for treated versus 67% for untreated patients; severe symptomatic disease carries up to ~40% 6-month mortality without therapy; in a Dutch cohort, mortality exceeded the general population only in patients with cirrhosis (p.2674, 2685-2686, 2694-2695). Graded by necroinflammatory activity as mild, moderate, or severe using the histologic activity index (HAI, 0-18) or METAVIR (A0-A3). Staged by fibrosis: HAI 0-6 or METAVIR F0-F4, with cirrhosis defined when fibrous septa surround parenchymal nodules and alter lobular architecture (Table 352-2, p.2674).

femoropopliteal, or tibial arteries, reducing perfusion to the lower limb. In claudication, resting flow is adequate but cannot meet the increased metabolic demand of exercising muscle, producing reversible ischaemic pain. As stenoses progress and collateral capacity is exceeded, resting perfusion falls below tissue requirements, causing rest pain, ulceration, and tissue loss. Diabetes and renal disease accelerate distal and calcified disease, and the combination of impaired inflow and microvascular dysfunction underlies poor wound healing. Most patients with claudication remain stable and only a minority progress to limb-threatening ischaemia, but overall mortality is high because of concurrent coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia carries a substantial risk of amputation and death without timely revascularisation and wound care.
