it is a disease of older adults (median age at diagnosis 71) (p.849). Most commonly diagnosed incidentally on routine blood work showing an elevated lymphocyte count in an asymptomatic individual; the natural history is heterogeneous, with some patients never requiring therapy (p.849, p.853). On the peripheral blood smear, the small lymphocytes are increased and many rupture during smear preparation, leaving nuclear material without surrounding cytoplasm — smudge cells, which are rare in the absence of chronic lymphoid leukemia (p.443). Diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry on peripheral blood; the typical immunophenotype is CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD23+, CD200+, the T-cell marker CD5+, and dim surface immunoglobulin (kappa or lambda). A clonal B-cell count ≥5 × 10⁹/L needs no further workup to confirm CLL (p.852). Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the tissue-based counterpart of CLL (lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly with a small clonal blood population); genetic and molecular features are identical and SLL is managed identically to CLL (p.852). Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is a precursor: clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without nodal/organ involvement or cytopenias; high-count MBL progresses to overt CLL at ~1–2% per year, whereas low-count MBL has a negligible progression rate (p.849, p.852). IGHV mutational status is a key prognostic factor: ~60% have IGHV ≥2% mutated from germline (more indolent course), while ~40% are IGHV-unmutated (more rapid progression, shorter survival before BCR-targeted therapy) (p.850). B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling is central to CLL pathogenesis, characterized by low-level IgM expression and tonic activation of antiapoptotic pathways promoting tumor survival (p.850). FISH (with or without karyotype) should be checked before every line of therapy because cytogenetics can evolve even without treatment, mainly to detect acquisition of del(17)(p13.1) (p.851). Bone marrow biopsy is not undertaken until therapy is initiated, except in cases of unexplained cytopenias; CT imaging is usually unnecessary at diagnosis (p.854). A watchful-waiting strategy is used for most patients, with therapy reserved for symptomatic disease, as multiple trials show no survival advantage to earlier therapy (p.854). Hypogammaglobulinemia affects all immunoglobulin subclasses and occurs in ~85% of patients at some point; low IgG and IgA correlate with infection risk, but isolated IgM reduction does not seem to confer excess infection risk (p.852). Richter's transformation — transformation to an aggressive lymphoma (most commonly DLBCL; Hodgkin lymphoma is a recognized variant). Suspect with rapid progression of adenopathy (often localized), constitutional symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, fever, weight loss), and usually high LDH (p.853-854) del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 loss or mutation — poorest prognosis, rapid progression, poor response to DNA-damaging therapy (p.850-851) Complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) — adverse impact on time to treatment and overall survival, worsening with increasing complexity (p.851) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia — death from uncontrolled AIHA can occur without appropriate supportive care; immediate therapy is almost always necessary (p.853) Symptoms indicating need for therapy: progressive marrow failure, massive/progressive/symptomatic splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, lymphocyte doubling time <6 months, autoimmune cytopenia unresponsive to standard therapy, or constitutional symptoms (p.854) When anemia or thrombocytopenia appear, distinguish autoimmune cytopenia from marrow replacement — the therapeutic approaches differ, and autoimmune cytopenias often respond without treating the underlying CLL (p.853) AIHA can be Coombs-negative, so a negative direct antiglobulin test does not exclude it (p.853) ITP can be hard to distinguish from disease progression because no lab test directly identifies the platelet-destruction mechanism; isolated thrombocytopenia and rapid platelet decline without alternative cause point to ITP (p.853) del(13)(q14.3) seen on banded karyotype (rather than only on FISH) indicates a larger deletion involving the retinoblastoma gene, which negates the favorable prognosis usually associated with this marker (p.850) Live vaccines should be avoided in CLL because of the small risk of viral reactivation in an immunocompromised host (p.853) Fine-needle aspiration should be discouraged for diagnosing suspected Richter's transformation; excisional biopsy is preferred (p.854) Cytogenetics can change without therapy, so prior FISH results may be outdated — recheck before each line of treatment (p.851) CLL is a monoclonal expansion of mature B lymphocytes; the definitive cell of origin is not established (mature/memory B cell, stepwise transformation, or hematopoietic stem cell are all proposed). Distinct BCR signaling — low-level IgM, tonic antiapoptotic pathway activation — drives tumor survival, with upregulation of BCR-pathway genes in lymph nodes and marrow versus blood. The CLL genome is relatively simple (~20 nonsynonymous and ~5 structural changes) with no unifying driver; recurrent mutations include SF3B1, NOTCH1, MYD88, ATM, and TP53 (mostly enriched in IGHV-unmutated disease, except MYD88 which favors IGHV-mutated/indolent disease). Key cytogenetic lesions: del(13)(q14.3) (sole, indolent; causes loss of the miR15/16 cluster that normally suppresses BCL2 and other antiapoptotic genes), trisomy 12 (intermediate), del(11)(q22.3)/ATM (bulky disease, aggressive), and del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 (poorest prognosis). Immune dysregulation pervades the disease: innate defects (reduced complement, neutrophil and NK cell defects), adaptive defects (CD4+ T-cell exhaustion, Th1-to-Th2 shift, expanded T regulatory cells), nurse-like tumor-associated macrophages, and humoral hypogammaglobulinemia (p.849-852). Heterogeneous: many patients are asymptomatic and never require therapy while others need multiple lines and die of disease. Overall survival has improved markedly (5-year OS 70% in 1980, 92% in 2015, likely higher today), and only a small minority now die of CLL itself. Infections cause ~30–50% of CLL-related deaths. Favorable markers: IGHV-mutated disease, sole del(13)(q14.3), MYD88 mutation. Adverse markers: IGHV-unmutated disease, del(17p)/TP53, del(11q)/ATM, NOTCH1, complex karyotype, and high β2-microglobulin/LDH. The CLL International Prognostic Index stratifies 5-year survival from ~93% (low risk) to ~23% (very high risk) in training-set data, though it has not been validated in the era of novel targeted therapies. Richter's transformation carries a poor prognosis, with median survival of 6–16 months for clonally related DLBCL versus ~5 years for clonally unrelated lymphomas (p.849, p.851, p.853-854). Two staging systems, both based on physical exam and labs (no imaging or marrow required). Rai system (more common in the US): low risk (stage 0) = lymphocytosis only; intermediate risk (stage I/II) = lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy, with or without splenomegaly/hepatomegaly; high risk (stage III/IV) = lymphocytosis with anemia or thrombocytopenia from marrow involvement. Binet system (more common in Europe): A = <3 areas of lymphadenopathy; B = ≥3 areas of lymphadenopathy; C = hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL and/or platelets <100,000/μL. The CLL International Prognostic Index refines outcome prediction using TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854).

Chronic mesenteric ischaemia — chronic mesenteric ischemia, intestinal angina, abdominal angina Peptic ulcer disease and other upper GI causes of postprandial pain Chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic malignancy Biliary colic Gastrointestinal malignancy causing weight loss Median arcuate ligament syndrome (coeliac axis compression) Functional dyspepsia or gastroparesis CT or MR angiography of the mesenteric vessels to demonstrate stenoses Mesenteric duplex ultrasound as a non-invasive screening test Catheter angiography when revascularisation is planned Nutritional assessment given chronic weight loss Exclusion of gastrointestinal malignancy and other causes of weight loss by endoscopy and imaging Almost always caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries, so patients typically have widespread vascular disease and risk factors such as smoking The hallmark is postprandial abdominal pain (intestinal angina) beginning shortly after eating, leading to fear of food, reduced intake, and progressive weight loss Because of the rich collateral circulation between the coeliac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries, symptoms usually require significant stenosis in more than one of the three main vessels It is frequently underdiagnosed, and unexplained weight loss with food aversion in an arteriopath should prompt consideration of the diagnosis CT or MR angiography, and duplex ultrasound, are used to demonstrate the arterial stenoses Revascularisation, most often by endovascular angioplasty and stenting or by surgical bypass, relieves symptoms and prevents progression to acute intestinal infarction Untreated disease can progress to acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction, a surgical emergency Nutritional support and cardiovascular risk-factor modification are important adjuncts to revascularisation Sudden, severe, constant abdominal pain out of proportion to examination signalling acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia and bowel infarction Rising lactate, acidosis, peritonism, or shock requiring emergency surgical evaluation Rapid, marked weight loss with intractable food aversion Progression of symptoms despite conservative measures indicating imminent vascular compromise Attributing chronic postprandial pain and weight loss to malignancy or functional disease and missing a vascular cause Failing to recognise that significant multi-vessel disease is usually needed to cause symptoms, leading to under-treatment of critical single-vessel lesions Delaying revascularisation until acute infarction supervenes Neglecting cardiovascular risk-factor management after treating the mesenteric lesions Chronic mesenteric ischaemia develops when atherosclerotic stenosis of the splanchnic arteries limits the increase in blood flow required to meet the metabolic demand of the gut after meals. The resulting mismatch produces postprandial ischaemic pain. Because of extensive collateral pathways among the three main mesenteric arteries, symptomatic disease typically requires high-grade stenosis or occlusion of at least two vessels, or a critical single-vessel lesion where collaterals are inadequate. Chronic hypoperfusion impairs absorption and causes food avoidance and weight loss. Acute thrombosis superimposed on a stenosed vessel can precipitate acute mesenteric ischaemia with bowel infarction. With timely revascularisation, symptoms usually resolve, weight is regained, and the risk of catastrophic bowel infarction falls. Untreated disease carries a substantial risk of progression to acute mesenteric ischaemia, which has high mortality. Overall outlook is also influenced by the patient's generalised atherosclerotic burden.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) — CML Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis) - distinguished from CML by a high/normal leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (CML has a LOW LAP) and absence of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837) Atypical CML (BCR::ABL1-negative) - lacks the Ph chromosome/BCR::ABL1, does not respond to TKI therapy, associated with SETBP1 (about 25%) and some CSF3R mutations, poor prognosis with median survival ~2-3 years (Harrison 22e p.835) Chronic neutrophilic leukemia - frequently CSF3R-mutated (about 80%); may respond to ruxolitinib (Harrison 22e p.835) Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (Harrison 22e p.835) Myelodysplastic syndrome/myeloproliferative neoplasms, including MDS/MPN-RS-T (SF3B1-mutated) (Harrison 22e p.835) Essential thrombocythemia and other Ph-negative MPNs presenting with thrombocytosis - when JAK2 V617F is absent, cytogenetics/FISH for BCR::ABL1 are required to exclude CML (Harrison 22e p.832-833) Bone marrow aspiration with routine G-banding cytogenetics - required to confirm the Ph chromosome, detect additional chromosomal abnormalities (which FISH will not detect), and quantify marrow blasts and basophils; a diagnosis of CML must always rely on marrow analysis with cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837) FISH analysis for BCR::ABL1 on peripheral blood - quantifies percentage of Ph-positive cells; preferred when a Ph cytogenetic study is negative or for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.837) Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts on the International Scale - baseline transcript typing at diagnosis (to avoid spurious 'undetectable' results on follow-up with atypical transcripts) and serial molecular monitoring of response (Harrison 22e p.837-838) ABL1 kinase domain mutation analysis - assessed when resistance/loss of response is suspected (e.g., to detect T315I) (Harrison 22e p.836-837) Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score - characteristically LOW in CML, helping distinguish it from a leukemoid reaction (Harrison 22e p.837) Supportive biochemistry - high vitamin B12, uric acid, lactate dehydrogenase, and lysozyme are commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.837) Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis from infection, inflammation, or other stress) - mimics the leukocytosis with left shift of CML but lacks BCR::ABL1 and shows a high/normal (not low) leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (Harrison 22e p.837) Other myeloproliferative neoplasms and MDS/MPN overlap syndromes that can produce leukocytosis, basophilia, or splenomegaly without the Philadelphia chromosome (Harrison 22e p.835) CML is a clonal hematopoietic myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm driven by the BCR::ABL1 chimeric gene, which encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase (Harrison 22e p.834). BCR::ABL1 results from a balanced reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), known as the Philadelphia chromosome (Ph); the t(9;22) is present in >90% of classical CML cases (Harrison 22e p.834-835). The most common transcript in CML encodes the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein; p190BCR::ABL1 is present in two-thirds of Ph-positive ALL but rare in CML, and p230BCR::ABL1 is rare and associated with a more indolent course (Harrison 22e p.835). Untreated, CML is typically biphasic or triphasic: an early indolent chronic phase, often followed by an accelerated phase, and a terminal blastic phase (Harrison 22e p.834). Most patients (about 90%) present in chronic phase; in developed countries 50-60% are diagnosed on routine blood tests with minimal symptoms such as fatigue (Harrison 22e p.836). Common symptoms, when present, are manifestations of anemia and splenomegaly: fatigue, malaise, weight loss, early satiety, and left upper quadrant pain or mass (Harrison 22e p.836). Splenomegaly is the most common physical finding (20-70% depending on screening frequency); hepatomegaly (5-10%) and lymphadenopathy (5%) are less common (Harrison 22e p.836-837). Untreated CML shows leukocytosis (10-500 x 10^9/L) with left-shifted myeloid hematopoiesis: neutrophils plus bands, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes, and blasts (usually <=5%); basophils and/or eosinophils are frequently increased (Harrison 22e p.837). Thrombocytosis is common; thrombocytopenia is rare and, when present, suggests worse prognosis, disease acceleration, or an unrelated etiology. Anemia is present in one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.837). Diagnosis depends on documenting t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), identified by G-banding in 90% of cases; FISH and PCR aid diagnosis and estimate disease burden, and can be done on peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.837). TKIs have revolutionized CML: the estimated 10-year survival with imatinib now exceeds 85% and approaches that of a normal age-matched population; allogeneic HSCT (curative but riskier) is offered as later-line therapy after TKI failure (Harrison 22e p.834). Molecular monitoring on the International Scale (IS) guides therapy: complete cytogenetic response (0% Ph) is roughly equivalent to BCR::ABL1 <=1% (MR2); major molecular response (MMR/MR3) is BCR::ABL1 <=0.1%; deep molecular response MR4 is <=0.01% and MR4.5 is <=0.0032% (Harrison 22e p.837-838). The T315I 'gatekeeper' kinase-domain mutation prevents binding of, and causes resistance to, imatinib and the second-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib); third-generation agents (e.g., ponatinib, asciminib) retain activity against it (Harrison 22e p.836). Unexplained, sustained leukocytosis (with or without splenomegaly) should prompt marrow examination and cytogenetic analysis (Harrison 22e p.837) Increasing/therapy-resistant leukocytosis, worsening anemia, fever and constitutional symptoms, and rising blasts and basophils signal disease progression (Harrison 22e p.838) New thrombocytopenia (<100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy) suggests worse prognosis or disease acceleration (Harrison 22e p.837-838) Extramedullary disease (skin/subcutaneous lesions, soft tissue, or lytic bone lesions) with biopsy showing blast predominance indicates transformation (Harrison 22e p.837-838) Hyperleukocytosis/hyperviscosity or marked thrombocytosis with thrombotic events (priapism, MI, venous thrombosis, visual disturbance, CVA) or bleeding diathesis (Harrison 22e p.836) PITFALL: Mistaking a reactive leukemoid reaction for CML - the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score is LOW in CML but high/normal in a leukemoid reaction, and CML requires demonstration of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837). Atypical transcripts (e13a3, e14a3, e19a2, etc.) not detected at diagnosis can produce falsely 'negative/undetectable' BCR::ABL1 on follow-up PCR, giving a false impression of complete molecular response; transcript type must be documented at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.835, 837). FISH does NOT detect additional chromosomal abnormalities, so a marrow cytogenetic analysis is still required at diagnosis; relying on FISH/PCR alone can miss clonal evolution (Harrison 22e p.837). Both FISH and PCR can be falsely positive at low levels or falsely negative for technical reasons, so diagnosis must always rely on marrow analysis with routine cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837). In about 10% of patients marrow blasts and basophils are significantly higher than in peripheral blood, conferring poorer prognosis or representing transformation that peripheral counts alone would miss (Harrison 22e p.837). Failure to achieve MMR or DMR should NOT automatically be considered 'failure' of a given TKI or an indication to switch TKI or proceed to allogeneic HSCT (Harrison 22e p.838). CML is a clonal myeloproliferative stem cell neoplasm caused by the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene arising from the reciprocal balanced translocation t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2) (the Philadelphia chromosome). DNA from the ABL1 proto-oncogene on chromosome 9 is juxtaposed to the breakpoint cluster region (BCR) gene on chromosome 22, generating a hybrid oncogene whose product (most commonly the p210BCR::ABL1 oncoprotein from e13a2 or e14a2 transcripts) has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity. This drives increased proliferation and reduced apoptosis, giving CML cells a growth advantage and progressively suppressing normal hematopoiesis. Constitutive BCR::ABL1 activation triggers autophosphorylation and downstream signaling via RAS, MAP kinases, STAT, PI3K, MYC and others, mediated by adapter proteins (GRB-2, CRK, CRK-L, SHC). Most TKIs bind the ATP-binding domain to inhibit kinase activity; asciminib (a STAMP inhibitor) instead binds the ABL1 myristoyl pocket. BCR::ABL1 induces genetic instability favoring acquisition of additional defects (e.g., double Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17/17p loss of TP53, 3q26 abnormalities, mutations in TP53, RB1, RUNX1, p16) that drive transformation from chronic to accelerated to blastic phase. Notably, the BCR::ABL1 rearrangement is detectable in the blood of up to 25% of normal adults and 5% of infants but is not sufficient to cause overt CML in the overwhelming majority. (Harrison 22e p.834-836) TKIs have transformed CML prognosis. Before the TKI era median survival was 3-7 years with annual mortality of 10% in the first 2 years and 15-20% thereafter. With imatinib, annual mortality has fallen to about 1-2%, the 10-year survival rate is about 85% (CML-specific survival ~90%), and the 10-year incidence of blastic transformation is only 5-6%; more than half of deaths are now from non-CML causes. Treatment-related response milestones are the dominant modern prognostic factors: achievement of complete cytogenetic response (MR2) is the major endpoint associated with improved survival, while durable deep molecular response (MR4/MR4.5) may permit treatment-free remission (TFR rate about 50% after 2+ years of durable DMR and 80%+ after 5+ years). Historical pretreatment models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) and adverse features (age, splenomegaly, anemia, high blasts/basophils, marrow fibrosis, additional chromosomal abnormalities) have lost much of their prognostic weight in the TKI era. Accelerated phase (historical median survival <2 years) and blastic phase carry the worst outcomes; de novo accelerated phase on TKI now has an estimated 8-year survival of 60-70%, and lymphoid blastic phase responds to ALL-type chemotherapy plus TKIs (complete response ~70%, median survival ~3 years). (Harrison 22e p.834, 838-839) CML is staged by clinical phase. Chronic phase: indolent, marrow blasts typically <=5%, where ~90% of patients present. Accelerated phase (historically median survival <2 years): >=15% peripheral blasts, >=30% peripheral blasts plus promyelocytes, >=20% peripheral basophils, cytogenetic clonal evolution (additional chromosomal abnormalities beyond Ph), or thrombocytopenia <100 x 10^9/L unrelated to therapy. Blastic phase: >=30% peripheral or marrow blasts, or sheets of blasts in extramedullary disease (commonly myeloid in ~60%, lymphoid in ~25%). The newest WHO classification suggests eliminating accelerated phase and reclassifying such patients as high-risk CML, but the text argues the accelerated-phase definition should be maintained because their survival is significantly worse than high-risk CML. Risk models (Sokal, Hasford, EUTOS) were used historically. (Harrison 22e p.838)

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease — COPD, Emphysema, Chronic bronchitis, Chronic obstructive lung disease Asthma (substantial overlap in older patients; both feature airway hyperresponsiveness and may share genetic/environmental factors) Bronchiectasis Interstitial lung disease Congestive heart failure Chronic thromboembolic disease / pulmonary hypertension Lung cancer (especially when new clubbing appears) Tuberculosis-associated chronic airflow limitation (important in absence of tobacco history) Pneumonia (frequently found on imaging during presumed exacerbation) Acute bronchitis Tuberculosis (can produce chronic airflow limitation with emphysematous and fibrotic change and airway remodeling) HIV-associated emphysema/COPD (increased risk with lower CD4 counts; often underdiagnosed) Post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC) for diagnosis and severity grading (GOLD vs ATS/ERS Z-scores) Lung volumes (TLC, FRC, RV, RV/TLC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO) - DLCO reduced in emphysema Arterial blood gas and oximetry for resting/exertional hypoxemia, alveolar ventilation and acid-base status (key in exacerbation assessment) Complete blood count with differential (blood eosinophil count; hematocrit for chronic hypoxemia) Chest CT (definitive for emphysema pattern/distribution, airway disease, coexisting ILD/bronchiectasis; annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in eligible smokers) Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level with PI-type determination (isoelectric focusing, mass spectrometry/genotyping, or DNA sequencing) when low 6-minute walk distance for exercise capacity and BODE index C-reactive protein (incorporated into proposed objective criteria for staging exacerbation severity) Congestive heart failure Pulmonary embolism (incidence increased during exacerbations; should be considered) Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings can mimic an exacerbation) Large airway obstruction COPD is defined by persistent respiratory symptoms with airflow obstruction, and the umbrella term spans emphysema (alveolar destruction with air-space enlargement), chronic bronchitis (chronic cough and phlegm), and small airway disease (narrowing and loss of small bronchioles); these coexist in varying proportions between patients. Fixed airflow obstruction is the spirometric hallmark: a chronically reduced FEV1/FVC ratio that does not normalize after bronchodilator. The classic threshold is FEV1/FVC <0.7 (GOLD), with the ATS/ERS alternative using Z-scores of FEV1 below the lower limit of normal. The three cardinal symptoms are cough, sputum production, and exertional dyspnea; many patients have symptoms for months to years before presenting, and a careful history often reveals respiratory symptoms preceding an apparent acute onset. Activities involving arm work at or above shoulder level are particularly poorly tolerated, whereas activities that let the patient brace the arms and recruit accessory muscles (pushing a shopping cart, treadmill) are better tolerated. Early disease typically has a normal physical exam; advanced disease shows prolonged expiration, wheeze, barrel chest, poor diaphragmatic excursion, accessory muscle use, the tripod posture, and cyanosis of lips/nail beds. Digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD; its appearance should trigger a search for another cause, most commonly lung cancer in this population. The blood eosinophil count (on CBC with differential) is used to guide therapy aimed at reducing exacerbation risk; an elevated hematocrit suggests chronic hypoxemia. Chest CT is the definitive test for establishing presence, pattern, and distribution of emphysema and for medium/large airway disease; chest x-ray may be consistent with COPD (hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, bullae, hyperlucency) but cannot reliably make the diagnosis. Guidelines recommend testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in ALL patients with COPD or with asthma plus chronic airflow obstruction; serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is the initial test, with PI-type determination for confirmation when levels are low. Approximately only 1% of COPD patients have severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, yet it is the proven monogenic risk factor and demonstrates the powerful role of genetics in susceptibility; PiZ individuals often develop early-onset COPD, accelerated by smoking. The strongest single predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the single greatest risk factor for hospitalization with an exacerbation is a history of previous hospitalization. The BODE index (Body mass index, airflow Obstruction, Dyspnea, Exercise capacity by 6-minute walk) predicts mortality better than FEV1 alone. New digital clubbing - investigate for lung cancer, not attributable to COPD Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) signaling acute ventilatory failure New or worsening hypoxemia Mental status changes (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in full sentences, paradoxical abdominal wall motion Tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, perioral/peripheral cyanosis Cachexia with significant weight loss (independent poor prognostic factor) Signs of cor pulmonale / right heart failure (lower extremity edema, persistent activity limitation) Chest x-ray cannot reliably diagnose COPD or establish chronicity; do not rely on it to confirm emphysema. Pulmonary function testing during an exacerbation has not been shown helpful in diagnosis or management (unlike in asthma exacerbations). Smokers with normal spirometry are not necessarily spared - many have reduced quality of life, reduced exercise capacity, emphysema/airway disease on CT, and may have exacerbations (pre-COPD). Attributing new clubbing to COPD itself - it is not a feature and warrants a cancer workup. Failing to test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in COPD patients, missing a treatable genetic cause; only a small minority of the ~1 in 3000 with severe deficiency in the US have been identified. Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax during a presumed exacerbation (about 25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal). Underestimating viral causes of exacerbations - PCR studies show viruses may cause >50% of exacerbations. Race-specific reference equations for pulmonary function may be inappropriate; race-neutral interpretation may be preferable. Chronic inhaled exposures (most commonly cigarette smoke, also biomass fuels, and increasingly vaping/inhaled cannabis) in genetically susceptible individuals trigger inflammatory and immune cell recruitment in large and small airways and terminal air spaces. Large-airway changes (mucus gland enlargement, goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia) produce cough and sputum and define chronic bronchitis. Small airways (<=2 mm) are the major site of increased airflow resistance, narrowed by goblet cell metaplasia replacing surfactant-secreting club cells, smooth-muscle hypertrophy, fibrosis, mucus, edema, and cellular infiltration; small-airway narrowing and drop-out precede emphysematous destruction. Emphysema results from a four-step paradigm: inflammatory/immune recruitment; proteinase release damaging extracellular matrix; oxidant-induced structural cell death, cellular senescence and proteolytic loss of cell-matrix attachments; and disordered repair of elastin. The elastase:antielastase imbalance (epitomized by alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency permitting unopposed neutrophil elastase) plus matrix metalloproteinases (notably MMP12) degrade elastin and collagen, generating chemotactic fragments that fuel a positive-feedback inflammatory loop. Oxidative stress (with NRF2 and SOD3 implicated, and oxidant inactivation of HDAC2 unleashing NF-kB-driven transcription of MMPs, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and impaired macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and bacteria contribute. Physiologically, airflow obstruction with air trapping causes hyperinflation (raised residual volume, RV/TLC, and total lung capacity); a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically inefficient. Ventilation-perfusion mismatch accounts for essentially all of the reduction in PaO2 (shunt is minimal), explaining why modest supplemental oxygen corrects hypoxemia. Inflammation can persist even after smoking cessation in susceptible individuals. Risk of death from COPD is closely tied to reduced FEV1 and the presence of emphysema. Mortality is predicted better by the multidimensional BODE index than by FEV1 alone. The absolute annual loss of FEV1 is highest in mild COPD and lowest in very severe disease. Cachexia/wasting is an independent poor prognostic factor. Smoking cessation slows the rate of FEV1 decline (greatest benefit when earlier) and improves survival. Among survival-improving interventions are smoking cessation, long-term oxygen in chronically hypoxemic patients, and lung volume reduction surgery in selected emphysema patients. Patients with PRISm (preserved ratio-impaired spirometry) physiology carry increased risk of mortality and respiratory and cardiovascular events. Exacerbations are episodic acute worsenings (usually <14 days) that increase in frequency as obstruction worsens (severe obstruction with FEV1 <50% predicted averages 1-3 episodes per year) and account for most COPD-related health-care costs; there is currently no cure except lung transplantation. Spirometric severity of airflow obstruction (GOLD, post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7): Mild FEV1 >=80% predicted; Moderate FEV1 50 to <80%; Severe FEV1 30 to <50%; Very severe FEV1 <30% predicted. ATS/ERS alternative uses FEV1/FVC < lower limit of normal with FEV1 Z-scores (borderline zFEV1 > -1.645; mild -1.65 to -2.5; moderate -2.51 to -4; severe < -4.1). The GOLD ABE assessment additionally incorporates respiratory symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or COPD Assessment Test) and annual exacerbation frequency to guide therapy. Multidimensional BODE index (BMI, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise capacity) is used for prognosis. Ventilatory failure is defined as PaCO2 >45 mmHg, classified as acute (with acidemia) or chronic by arterial pH.

Chronic pain management — chronic pain, persistent pain, chronic pain syndrome Progressive or undiagnosed structural disease (e.g. malignancy) Inflammatory or autoimmune conditions Neuropathic pain from a specific nerve lesion Fibromyalgia and other nociplastic pain conditions Depression and anxiety contributing to pain and disability Medication-related problems including opioid-induced hyperalgesia Comprehensive biopsychosocial assessment including function, mood, and sleep Validated pain and disability questionnaires to track outcomes Targeted imaging or nerve conduction studies only when a specific treatable cause is suspected Screening for depression, anxiety, and substance use Medication review including opioid risk assessment Chronic pain persists beyond normal tissue healing, commonly defined as lasting more than about three months, and often becomes a condition in its own right rather than a symptom It is best understood through a biopsychosocial model, since biological, psychological, and social factors all influence the pain experience and disability Assessment should characterise the pain (nociceptive, neuropathic, or mixed and nociplastic), functional impact, mood, sleep, and the patient's goals Management is multidisciplinary and multimodal, combining physical rehabilitation, psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural approaches, and carefully selected medications Neuropathic pain often responds better to agents such as certain antidepressants and anticonvulsants than to conventional analgesics Interventional options, including nerve blocks, radiofrequency procedures, and neuromodulation, may help selected patients within a broader plan Long-term opioid therapy has limited benefit for most chronic non-cancer pain and carries risks of tolerance, dependence, hyperalgesia, and harm, so it requires careful selection, review, and often deprescribing Realistic goals emphasising improved function and quality of life, rather than complete pain elimination, guide effective long-term care New or changing pain with features suggesting malignancy, infection, or fracture Progressive neurological deficit or signs of cord or cauda equina compression Systemic features such as weight loss, fever, or night pain Signs of opioid misuse, escalating use, or overdose risk Managing chronic pain with escalating opioids despite limited benefit and rising harm Neglecting psychological and social contributors within a biomedical-only approach Failing to identify neuropathic pain that needs different medication Missing red-flag features that indicate serious underlying pathology Setting unrealistic goals of complete pain elimination rather than improved function Chronic pain involves persistent changes in the peripheral and central nervous systems. Ongoing nociceptor activity and inflammation can sensitise peripheral nerves, while repeated input drives central sensitisation with amplified spinal and cortical responses, reduced descending inhibition, and reorganisation of pain-processing networks. Neuropathic pain follows damage or disease of the somatosensory system, producing ectopic firing and maladaptive plasticity. In nociplastic pain, altered central processing generates pain without clear tissue damage. Psychological and social factors modulate these pathways, and this neuroplasticity explains why chronic pain often persists independently of the original injury. Chronic pain is frequently a long-term condition; while cure is often not achievable, multidisciplinary management can substantially improve function, mood, and quality of life, whereas reliance on escalating opioids tends to worsen outcomes.

Chronic Pancreatitis — Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (must be excluded on imaging) Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 AIP / IgG4-related disease; type 2 / idiopathic duct-centric) Pancreatic pseudocyst Fecal elastase-1 (random level on a formed stool specimen) to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency Abdominal CT (initial imaging modality of choice) to show calcifications, dilated pancreatic/biliary ducts, atrophy, and to exclude pseudocyst and cancer MRI/MRCP, secretin-enhanced MRCP Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS); five or more of nine endosonographic features considered diagnostic, though not specific for early disease EUS with endoscopic pancreatic function testing (EUS-ePFT) Direct pancreatic function test using secretin (best sensitivity; becomes abnormal when >=60% of exocrine function is lost) Plain abdominal film for diffuse calcifications Serum amylase/lipase (usually not strikingly elevated), serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (may indicate cholestasis from biliary stricture) Serum IgG4 (supportive of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis) Pancreatic cancer (a poor response to glucocorticoids in suspected autoimmune pancreatitis should raise suspicion of pancreatic cancer) Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 can mimic primary sclerosing cholangitis via IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis) Patients typically present with abdominal pain or symptoms of maldigestion; pain is variable in location, severity, and frequency, may be constant or intermittent, and can be exacerbated by eating, leading to fear of eating and weight loss (p.2752). There is often a disparity between the reported severity of abdominal pain and the physical findings, which mainly consist of nonfocal abdominal tenderness (p.2752). In contrast to acute pancreatitis, serum amylase and lipase are usually NOT strikingly elevated in chronic pancreatitis; low serum pancreatic enzyme levels are moderately specific but have poor sensitivity (p.2752). Cumulative prevalence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency exceeds 80%; overt steatorrhea in a patient with chronic pancreatitis is highly suggestive of this complication (p.2752). A random fecal elastase-1 level on a formed stool specimen can help confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in patients with milder symptoms (p.2752). Diffuse calcifications on a plain abdominal film usually indicate significant pancreatic damage and are pathognomonic for chronic pancreatitis; tropical pancreatitis (often SPINK1-associated) characteristically shows bulky calcifications (p.2752). Lifetime prevalence of chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes exceeds 80%; most develop hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency due to islet cell loss, but diabetic ketoacidosis, diabetic coma, and end-organ damage (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy) are uncommon (p.2752). Cigarette smoking is an independent, dose-dependent risk factor for chronic pancreatitis and recurrent acute pancreatitis; continued alcohol and smoking exposure are associated with disease progression including fibrosis and calcifications (p.2750). Metabolic bone disease is highly prevalent, with about 65% of patients having osteopenia or osteoporosis (p.2752). Increased risk of pancreatic cancer: cumulative risk is 4% at 20 years after diagnosis of chronic calcific pancreatitis; hereditary PRSS1 and tropical pancreatitis carry an even higher risk than other forms. Jaundice, cholestasis, and biliary cirrhosis from chronic inflammation around the intrapancreatic common bile duct. Gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulceration, gastritis, a pseudocyst eroding into the duodenum, arterial bleeding into the pancreatic duct (hemosuccus pancreaticus), or ruptured varices from splenic vein thrombosis. Diagnosis of early or mild chronic pancreatitis is challenging because there is no accurate biomarker, and serum amylase/lipase are usually not strikingly elevated (unlike acute pancreatitis) (p.2752). EUS is not specific enough to diagnose early chronic pancreatitis alone and may show positive features in patients with diabetes, a smoking history, or even normal aging individuals (p.2752). Elevated serum IgG4 has a low positive predictive value for autoimmune pancreatitis when used in isolation from other clinical findings (p.2751). Complete correction of steatorrhea with pancreatic enzyme replacement is uncommon, even though enzyme therapy usually controls diarrhea and improves fat absorption (p.2753). Meta-analyses show no consistent benefit of enzyme therapy at reducing pain; any pain relief may reflect improvement of dyspepsia from maldigestion (p.2753). Chronic pancreatitis is characterized by irreversible damage to the pancreas (in contrast to the reversible changes of acute pancreatitis), defined by histologic abnormalities including chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and progressive destruction (atrophy) of both exocrine and endocrine tissue. Irrespective of the mechanism of injury, pancreatic stellate cell activation leads to cytokine expression and production of extracellular matrix proteins contributing to inflammation and collagen deposition. Proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) and oxidants induce stellate cell activity with new collagen synthesis; TGF-beta-mediated autocrine self-activation pathways may explain disease progression even after removal of noxious stimuli. Etiologies are framed by the TIGAR-O classification (Toxic-metabolic, Idiopathic, Genetic, Autoimmune, Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis, Obstructive). Heavy alcohol use is the most common clinically apparent cause in U.S. adults, though additional factors are required for disease development (not all heavy drinkers develop disease). Genetic predisposition (e.g., PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen mutations preventing destruction of prematurely activated trypsin; CFTR and SPINK1 disease modifiers) accounts for up to 15% of previously idiopathic cases. Cardinal manifestations are abdominal pain, steatorrhea, weight loss, diabetes mellitus, and, less commonly, pancreatic cancer (p.2750-2752). Chronic pancreatitis is an irreversible disease; there are currently no therapies to reverse or delay disease progression, so management is focused on screening for and treating complications. Patients have impaired quality of life and significant morbidity with frequent health encounters. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (cumulative prevalence >80%) and chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes (lifetime prevalence >80%) commonly develop. The 20-year cumulative risk of pancreatic cancer in chronic calcific pancreatitis is 4%, higher in hereditary PRSS1 and tropical forms (p.2752-2754). Etiologic classification follows the TIGAR-O system: Toxic-metabolic (alcohol, tobacco smoking, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia/hypertriglyceridemia, chronic renal failure), Idiopathic (early onset, late onset, tropical), Genetic (PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen, CFTR, CASR, CTRC, SPINK1), Autoimmune (type 1 IgG4-related; type 2 idiopathic duct-centric), Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis (postnecrotic, recurrent acute), and Obstructive (pancreas divisum, duct obstruction by tumor, preampullary duodenal wall cysts, posttraumatic duct strictures). Some genetic conditions are disease modifiers requiring additional factors to cause disease (p.2750).

Chronic pelvic pain — CPP, chronic pelvic pain syndrome, CPPS Endometriosis or adenomyosis Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome Irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease Pudendal neuralgia or other nerve entrapment Pelvic floor myofascial dysfunction Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men Pelvic congestion syndrome or adhesions Thorough pelvic and musculoskeletal examination including assessment of pelvic floor tone and trigger points Urinalysis and targeted urological evaluation for bladder pain syndrome Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, MRI to assess gynaecological and structural causes Diagnostic laparoscopy in selected cases where endometriosis or adhesions are suspected Assessment for coexisting mood disorder, sleep disturbance, and central sensitisation Chronic pelvic pain is persistent, non-cyclical pain perceived in the pelvis lasting at least several months and often without a single identifiable structural cause It frequently reflects overlapping contributions from gynaecological, urological, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neurological, and psychological systems, so evaluation must be broad Pelvic floor muscle dysfunction with hypertonicity and myofascial trigger points is a common and treatable contributor that is easily overlooked Central sensitisation is often present and helps explain pain that is disproportionate to examination findings and associated with other chronic pain conditions A careful history should screen for endometriosis, interstitial cystitis or bladder pain syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, pudendal neuralgia, and a history of physical or sexual trauma Pelvic floor physical therapy is a cornerstone of management, alongside neuropathic pain agents, treatment of identified contributors, and psychological therapies A multidisciplinary, biopsychosocial approach with realistic functional goals is more effective than repeated searches for a single surgical cause Trigger-point injection and, in selected cases, nerve blocks such as pudendal blocks may be used within a broader programme Abnormal vaginal or rectal bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding, or a pelvic mass suggesting malignancy Unexplained weight loss, fever, or night sweats Acute severe pain with peritonism suggesting a surgical emergency Haematuria or new bowel symptoms warranting urgent investigation New neurological deficit in the pelvic or lower limb distribution Repeated surgery or invasive procedures in pursuit of a single structural cause when pain is centrally mediated Overlooking pelvic floor muscle dysfunction as a treatable contributor Ignoring psychological factors and a history of trauma that maintain the pain Long-term opioid use, which is generally unhelpful and harmful in this setting Failing to screen for red-flag features of malignancy or a surgical emergency Chronic pelvic pain typically arises from the interaction of peripheral visceral and somatic nociceptive input with central pain processing changes. Viscero-somatic and viscero-visceral convergence in the spinal cord means input from one pelvic organ can amplify and refer pain to others. Persistent nociception promotes peripheral and central sensitisation, with reduced descending inhibition, so pain becomes self-sustaining and disproportionate to any ongoing tissue damage. Pelvic floor muscle overactivity, myofascial trigger points, and psychological factors including anxiety, depression, and prior trauma further modulate and maintain the pain. Chronic pelvic pain often follows a fluctuating long-term course, but many patients achieve meaningful improvement in pain and function with a coordinated multidisciplinary programme that addresses physical, neurological, and psychological contributors. Outcomes are poorer when treatment focuses narrowly on a single organ and ignores central and musculoskeletal factors.
