deficiency or ciliary dysfunction in recalcitrant disease Chronic rhinosinusitis is symptomatic inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses persisting for at least twelve weeks Diagnosis requires two or more cardinal symptoms, at least one being nasal blockage or nasal discharge, alongside facial pressure/pain or reduction in sense of smell It is broadly classified into disease with nasal polyps and disease without polyps, which differ in inflammatory pattern and treatment response Objective evidence of inflammation on nasal endoscopy or CT is needed to confirm the diagnosis, as symptoms alone are non-specific Obstruction of the osteomeatal complex impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary clearance is central to the disease Contributing factors include allergy, asthma, aspirin sensitivity, structural abnormalities, biofilms and, in some cases, fungal disease and immune deficiency First-line treatment is medical, centred on saline irrigation and topical intranasal corticosteroids, with other measures directed at the underlying driver Functional endoscopic sinus surgery is reserved for disease that fails maximal medical therapy or where complications or specific anatomy demand it Strictly unilateral symptoms or bloody discharge suggesting neoplasm Periorbital swelling, proptosis, visual disturbance or ophthalmoplegia indicating orbital complication (an emergency) Severe headache, high fever, neck stiffness or neurological signs suggesting intracranial spread Clear watery rhinorrhoea after trauma or surgery suggesting a cerebrospinal fluid leak Rapidly progressive symptoms with facial numbness or palatal changes in an immunocompromised patient (invasive fungal disease) Diagnosing chronic rhinosinusitis on symptoms alone without objective endoscopic or CT confirmation Overlooking a unilateral lesion that could be a tumour Treating repeatedly with antibiotics rather than addressing the underlying inflammatory driver Missing orbital or intracranial complications during an acute exacerbation Failing to consider allergy, asthma or immune deficiency in recurrent disease Chronic rhinosinusitis reflects a persistent inflammatory process of the sinonasal mucosa rather than simple ongoing infection. Anatomical narrowing or mucosal swelling at the osteomeatal complex obstructs sinus outflow, disrupting ventilation and mucociliary clearance so that secretions stagnate and mucosal inflammation is perpetuated. Host factors (allergy, asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, immune dysfunction, ciliary disorders) and environmental factors (microbial biofilms, fungi, irritants) drive different inflammatory endotypes; polypoid disease is often eosinophilic and type 2 driven, whereas non-polypoid disease tends to be more neutrophilic. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema, polyp formation and epithelial remodelling that further obstruct drainage, creating a self-sustaining cycle. Most patients achieve good symptom control with appropriate medical therapy and, where needed, surgery, but the condition is often chronic and relapsing, particularly the polypoid, eosinophilic and aspirin-sensitive forms, which frequently recur and may require long-term treatment including biologics.

Chronic subdural haematoma — cSDH, chronic SDH, subdural haematoma (chronic) Acute or subacute subdural haematoma Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack Intracranial neoplasm or metastasis Normal pressure hydrocephalus Neurodegenerative dementia Subdural empyema or hygroma Non-contrast CT head to identify the crescentic collection, its density, and midline shift MRI brain when the diagnosis or age of blood is uncertain or isodense collections are suspected Full blood count, coagulation profile, and platelet function assessment Review of antiplatelet and anticoagulant medication and relevant drug levels or reversal targets Typically affects older adults, often with only trivial or forgotten head trauma weeks earlier, and is more common in those on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy Presentation is usually insidious over days to weeks, with headache, confusion, gait disturbance, focal weakness, or a fluctuating conscious level that can mimic dementia or stroke Brain atrophy in the elderly and in chronic alcohol use increases the subdural space and stretches bridging veins, predisposing to slow venous bleeding On CT the collection is classically crescent-shaped over the convexity and hypodense or mixed density relative to acute blood; layering or membranes suggest recurrent bleeding of differing ages Symptomatic collections causing mass effect are commonly managed with surgical drainage (burr-hole or craniotomy), while small asymptomatic collections may be observed Correction of coagulopathy and careful review of anticoagulation are central to management and to reducing recurrence Recurrence after drainage is relatively frequent, and subdural drains plus adequate brain re-expansion help lower this risk Bilateral collections can mask midline shift, so symmetry on imaging should not be taken as reassurance Rapid deterioration in conscious level or new pupillary asymmetry suggesting acute rebleeding or herniation Large collection with significant midline shift and effacement of basal cisterns New or worsening focal deficit or seizures Bilateral collections with clinical deterioration despite symmetric imaging Attributing gradual cognitive or gait decline to dementia and overlooking a treatable collection Missing an isodense collection on CT, especially when bilateral and symmetric Resuming anticoagulation without weighing rebleeding risk against thrombotic risk Assuming complete resolution immediately after drainage when residual or recurrent collections are common A chronic subdural haematoma is a slowly accumulating collection of blood and its breakdown products in the subdural space, between the dura and arachnoid. It often begins with minor tearing of bridging cortical veins, particularly where cerebral atrophy has enlarged the subdural space. An encapsulating membrane forms with fragile, leaky neovessels, and repeated micro-haemorrhages together with osmotic and inflammatory factors allow the collection to expand over weeks. Gradual enlargement produces mass effect on the underlying cortex, causing progressive or fluctuating neurological signs. Many patients recover well after drainage of a symptomatic collection, but outcome is worse in the frail elderly and those with marked preoperative neurological impairment; recurrence and the need for repeat surgery are recognised problems.

Chronic suppurative otitis media — CSOM, chronic otitis media, chronic middle ear infection Otitis externa with discharge Otitis media with effusion Tuberculous otitis media Middle ear or external canal malignancy Granulomatous disease of the ear Retained foreign body with secondary infection Otoscopy and otomicroscopy to define perforation type and detect cholesteatoma Pure tone audiometry to characterise conductive or mixed hearing loss Culture and sensitivity of ear discharge High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to map cholesteatoma extent and bony erosion MRI where intracranial complications or residual cholesteatoma are suspected Defined by a persistent or recurrent ear discharge through a chronic tympanic membrane perforation with associated hearing loss Traditionally divided into a tubotympanic (mucosal, safe) type and an atticoantral (squamous, unsafe) type associated with cholesteatoma The tubotympanic type typically causes intermittent painless mucoid discharge and a central perforation, with a comparatively low complication risk The atticoantral type is dangerous because cholesteatoma erodes bone and predisposes to serious intratemporal and intracranial complications Foul-smelling scanty discharge, an attic or marginal perforation, or visible keratin debris should raise suspicion of cholesteatoma Management principles include aural toileting, topical and systemic antibiotics for active disease, and surgery to eradicate disease and reconstruct hearing Cholesteatoma is essentially a surgical disease requiring mastoid exploration to remove the sac and prevent complications Audiometry usually shows conductive loss, but a sensorineural component suggests inner ear involvement Foul discharge with an attic or marginal perforation suggesting cholesteatoma Vertigo or a positive fistula sign indicating labyrinthine erosion Facial nerve palsy from facial canal involvement Severe headache, fever, neck stiffness or altered consciousness suggesting intracranial extension Treating a discharging ear as simple otitis externa and missing an underlying cholesteatoma Failing to recognise attic or marginal perforations as high-risk Overlooking early complications such as vertigo or facial weakness Relying on medical therapy alone when surgical clearance of cholesteatoma is required Chronic suppurative otitis media is long-standing inflammation of the middle ear cleft with a non-intact tympanic membrane. In the tubotympanic type, persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction and recurrent infection maintain mucosal inflammation and a central perforation, with reversible mucosal changes. In the atticoantral type, retraction pockets or migration of squamous epithelium form a cholesteatoma, an expanding keratinising sac whose enzymatic and pressure effects erode ossicles and surrounding bone. This bony destruction can breach the facial canal, labyrinth, or dural plates, opening routes for intracranial spread. The mucosal (tubotympanic) type generally does well with medical treatment and reconstructive surgery, while the atticoantral type with cholesteatoma carries a higher risk of serious complications and requires surgical eradication with ongoing follow-up for recurrence.

Chronic Venous Disease & Lymphedema — venous insufficiency, varicose veins, lymphedema Congestive heart failure (bilateral leg swelling) Hypoalbuminemia from nephrotic syndrome or severe hepatic disease Myxedema from hypothyroidism, or pretibial myxedema with Graves' disease Drug-induced edema (dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, thiazolidinediones) Lipedema (adipose accumulation thigh-to-ankle sparing the feet, usually in women) Ruptured leg muscle, hematoma from trauma, popliteal (Baker's) cyst (unilateral swelling) Acute deep-vein thrombosis Cellulitis (erythema and swelling of the affected limb) Bacterial lymphangitis Venous duplex ultrasonography - principal test; detects obstruction (no flow, echogenic thrombus, non-compressible vein) and reflux (prolonged flow reversal on Valsalva or cuff release) Air/strain-gauge plethysmography to quantify venous reflux and calf-muscle-pump efficiency MR, CT, or conventional venography for suspected IVC/iliofemoral obstruction, IVC filter occlusion, extrinsic compression, or May-Thurner syndrome Bedside Brodie-Trendelenburg test (deep vs superficial reflux) and Perthes test (deep-venous obstruction) - now used infrequently For lymphedema: abdominal/pelvic ultrasound and CT for obstructing neoplasm; MRI of the limb (honeycomb epifascial pattern; distinguishes lipedema) Lymphoscintigraphy and lymphangiography (rarely needed) to confirm and distinguish primary from secondary lymphedema Near-infrared fluorescence optical imaging for quantitative superficial lymph-flow assessment, useful operatively Lymphedema vs chronic venous insufficiency (venous edema is softer with stasis dermatitis, hyperpigmentation, and superficial varicosities) Lipedema (spares the feet; differentiated by MRI) Myxedema Leg ulcers from severe peripheral artery disease / chronic limb-threatening ischemia, diabetic neuropathy, skin cancer, vasculitis, or rarely hydroxyurea (distinct from venous ulcers by location and characteristics) Chronic venous disease spans a spectrum: telangiectasias and reticular veins, to varicose veins, to chronic venous insufficiency with edema, skin changes, and ulceration (p.2179). Chronic venous insufficiency arises from incompetent veins with venous hypertension and extravasation of fluid and blood elements into the limb; it may occur with superficial venous disease, but more advanced manifestations are usually caused by deep-vein disease (p.2180). Secondary deep-venous insufficiency most often follows deep-vein thrombosis (post-thrombotic syndrome): valve leaflets become thickened and contracted, losing the ability to prevent retrograde flow, and the vein wall becomes rigid and thick-walled (p.2180). Lipodermatosclerosis is the combination of induration, hemosiderin deposition, and inflammation, typically in the lower leg just above the ankle (the gaiter area) (p.2180). Atrophie blanche is a white patch of scar tissue, often with focal telangiectasias and a hyperpigmented border, usually developing near the medial malleolus (p.2180). A venous ulcer is typically shallow with an irregular border, a base of granulation tissue, and exudate, and occurs near the medial and lateral malleoli (p.2180). Venous edema is usually pitting early on, but over time may become less pitting and more indurated, particularly with secondary development of lymphatic dysfunction (phlebolymphedema) (p.2180). Lymphedema is generally a painless condition; it initially involves the foot and progresses up the leg, with early soft pitting edema that later becomes nonpitting with a woody, indurated, fibrotic texture (p.2183-2184). Stemmer's sign (inability to tent the skin at the base of the toes) and peau d'orange (orange-peel dimpling), along with squaring of the toes, are characteristic skin findings of lymphedema (p.2184). Worldwide, the most common cause of secondary lymphedema is lymphatic filariasis; in developed countries it is surgical excision or irradiation of axillary/inguinal lymph nodes for cancer (p.2183). Recurrent bacterial lymphangitis, usually streptococcal, is a very common cause of lymphedema, and lymphedema in turn predisposes to recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis - a vicious cycle (p.2183-2184). Acute unilateral leg swelling raising concern for deep-vein thrombosis (duration of edema helps distinguish DVT from chronic venous insufficiency) Suspected proximal venous obstruction (IVC/iliofemoral) warranting intervention Infected or rapidly worsening venous ulcer Lymphangiosarcoma - a rare but highly lethal complication of long-standing uncontrolled lymphedema Recurrent cellulitis/lymphangitis in a lymphedematous limb Lymphedema is often confused with chronic venous insufficiency, and the two can coexist as phlebolymphedema when venous insufficiency impairs lymphatic function - do not assume a single cause (p.2180). Distinguish bilateral venous edema and lymphedema from systemic causes (heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, myxedema, drug-induced edema) before attributing swelling to venous disease (p.2180). Distinguish unilateral leg swelling of chronic venous insufficiency/lymphedema from acute deep-vein thrombosis - the duration of edema helps differentiate them (p.2180, 2183). Compression garments improve symptoms and aid ulcer healing but are NOT curative and do NOT prevent progression of varicose veins (p.2181). Antibiotics are NOT indicated for a venous ulcer unless it is infected (p.2181). Diuretics are contraindicated in lymphedema - they may cause intravascular volume depletion and metabolic abnormalities (p.2184). No drugs are FDA-approved for chronic venous insufficiency, and there is insufficient evidence to recommend general use of venoactive herbal supplements (p.2182). In chronic venous disease, incompetent (refluxing) or obstructed veins produce sustained venous hypertension with extravasation of fluid and blood elements into limb tissues. Primary varicose veins arise from defective saphenous valves, intrinsic vein-wall weakness, and high intraluminal pressure; secondary varicosities and chronic venous insufficiency result from deep-venous obstruction or valvular incompetence, classically post-thrombotic (valve leaflets thicken and contract after DVT, the vein becomes rigid, and distal valves become incompetent as high pressure distends the vein). Other secondary causes include May-Thurner syndrome, extrinsic compression by tumor/retroperitoneal fibrosis, arteriovenous fistulas, deep-vein agenesis, and venous malformations. Lymphedema results from impaired lymph transport: deficiency, reflux, or obstruction of lymph vessels causes an imbalance between lymph production and absorption (governed by Starling forces), so protein-rich fluid accumulates in the interstitium and raises tissue osmotic load. Persistent lymphedema triggers inflammatory/immune responses with infiltration of mononuclear cells, fibroblasts, and adipocytes, leading to adipose and collagen deposition in skin and subcutaneous tissues (p.2180, 2182-2183). Approximately 20% of patients with chronic venous insufficiency develop venous ulcers. Recurrent varicose veins occur in up to 50% of patients by 5 years after ligation and stripping. Endovenous thermal ablation achieves 1- and 5-year occlusion rates exceeding ~90%; sclerotherapy averages ~81% and ~74% at 1 and 5 years. Iliac venous stenting has technical success >85% with long-term patency ~75%; venous bypass long-term patency generally exceeds 60%. Lymphedema is a chronic, generally progressive condition; failure to control limb edema may lead to recurrent infections, progressive trophic skin changes, and rarely the highly lethal complication of lymphangiosarcoma (p.2179, 2182-2184). CEAP (Clinical, Etiologic, Anatomic, Pathophysiologic) classification of chronic venous disease. Clinical: C0 no signs; C1 telangiectasias/reticular veins; C2 varicose veins (C2r recurrent); C3 edema; C4 skin/subcutaneous changes (C4a pigmentation or eczema, C4b lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche, C4c corona phlebectatica); C5 healed venous ulcer; C6 active venous ulcer (C6r recurrent). Etiologic: Ep primary, Es secondary (Esi intravenous, Ese extravenous), Ec congenital, En none identified. Anatomic: As superficial, Ap perforator, Ad deep, An none. Pathophysiologic: Pr reflux, Po obstruction, Pr,o both, Pn none. Lymphedema is staged by the International Society of Lymphology: Stage 0/Ia latent/subclinical; Stage I early protein-rich edema reduced by elevation, may pit; Stage II elevation rarely reduces swelling, pitting manifest then later non-pitting as fat/fibrosis supervene; Stage III lymphostatic elephantiasis with trophic skin changes, acanthosis, fat/fibrosis, warty overgrowths (p.2181, 2184).

Chylomicron retention disease — SAR1B, Anderson disease, CMRD, chylomicron retention disorder Abetalipoproteinaemia (MTTP deficiency) Homozygous hypobetalipoproteinaemia Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive enteropathies Cholestatic liver disease with fat malabsorption Other congenital enteropathies causing failure to thrive Fasting lipid profile showing low total and LDL cholesterol with reduced apolipoprotein B Fat-soluble vitamin levels, particularly vitamin E Small-bowel biopsy demonstrating chylomicron-laden enterocytes Molecular genetic testing for SAR1B variants Neurological and ophthalmological assessment and coagulation studies for vitamin K status Autosomal recessive fat-malabsorption disorder caused by SAR1B variants, also known as Anderson disease Presents in infancy with chronic steatorrhoea, failure to thrive and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency The defect blocks secretion of intestinal chylomicrons while hepatic VLDL export is relatively preserved Lipid studies show low total and LDL cholesterol with reduced but detectable apolipoprotein B, and low fat-soluble vitamin levels including vitamin E Small-bowel biopsy demonstrates fat-laden enterocytes engorged with chylomicron-sized lipid droplets Neurological and retinal complications are generally milder and later than in abetalipoproteinaemia but still relate to vitamin E deficiency Treatment is a low-long-chain-fat diet with fat-soluble vitamin and vitamin E supplementation Marked failure to thrive from ongoing fat malabsorption in infancy Emerging neuromuscular or ophthalmological signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency Coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency Evidence of hepatic steatosis or transaminase elevation on follow-up Failing to distinguish it from abetalipoproteinaemia, which has absent apolipoprotein B and acanthocytosis Under-supplementing vitamin E and allowing preventable neurological injury Attributing steatorrhoea to pancreatic disease without lipid and biopsy evaluation Neglecting long-term surveillance for hepatic steatosis Chylomicron retention disease is caused by variants in SAR1B, which encodes a small GTPase essential for COPII vesicle formation and the intracellular transport of prechylomicron particles from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi. When SAR1B is defective, newly formed chylomicrons cannot be trafficked and secreted from enterocytes, so dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins are trapped within the cells. This produces fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K, with characteristic lipid-laden enterocytes. Because the defect is selective for the intestinal chylomicron pathway, hepatic VLDL secretion is comparatively spared and plasma apolipoprotein B is reduced rather than absent. With early dietary fat restriction and lifelong fat-soluble vitamin, especially vitamin E, supplementation, growth improves and the usually milder neurological and retinal complications can be limited. Long-term monitoring for vitamin deficiency and hepatic changes is needed.

Chylothorax — chylothorax, chylous effusion, chylous pleural effusion Empyema (which can also appear turbid) Pseudochylothorax (cholesterol effusion in chronic effusions) Malignant pleural effusion without chyle Parapneumonic effusion Transudative effusion from heart failure or cirrhosis Pleural fluid triglyceride measurement and, if equivocal, lipoprotein analysis for chylomicrons Cross-sectional imaging to identify malignancy or thoracic duct obstruction Lymphangiography or lymphoscintigraphy to localise the site of leak in selected cases Assessment of nutritional status and lymphocyte count with prolonged drainage Investigation for underlying causes such as lymphoma or lymphangioleiomyomatosis Chylothorax is the accumulation of lymphatic fluid (chyle) in the pleural space due to disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct The aspirated fluid is classically milky and opalescent, though it may appear serous when the patient is fasting or malnourished The diagnosis is confirmed by an elevated pleural fluid triglyceride level and, when uncertain, the demonstration of chylomicrons Common causes are malignancy (especially lymphoma) obstructing lymphatic flow and trauma or surgery injuring the thoracic duct Non-traumatic causes also include lymphangioleiomyomatosis, cirrhosis, and central venous thrombosis Persistent drainage of chyle leads to loss of protein, fat, fat-soluble vitamins, and lymphocytes, causing malnutrition and immunosuppression Initial management often includes drainage and a low-fat or medium-chain-triglyceride diet, or bowel rest, to reduce chyle flow Refractory or high-output leaks may require thoracic duct ligation, embolisation, pleurodesis, or shunting High-output chyle leak causing rapid nutritional and immune depletion Signs of malnutrition, hypovolaemia, or lymphopenia-related infection Underlying malignancy such as lymphoma requiring urgent evaluation Respiratory compromise from a large or rapidly reaccumulating effusion Assuming turbid pleural fluid is empyema without measuring triglycerides Overlooking a false-negative milky appearance in a fasting patient Allowing prolonged high-volume drainage without addressing nutritional and immune depletion Failing to investigate for an underlying malignancy in non-traumatic cases The thoracic duct conveys chyle, rich in triglycerides absorbed from the gut, from the abdomen to the systemic venous circulation. When the duct is disrupted by surgery or trauma, or obstructed by tumour or fibrosis, chyle leaks into or backs up into the pleural space. Because chyle contains chylomicrons and high triglyceride content, the effusion has a characteristic milky appearance and high triglyceride level. Ongoing leakage depletes the body of nutrients, immunoglobulins, and lymphocytes, and the volume loss can cause hypovolaemia and metabolic disturbance. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and leak volume; traumatic and postsurgical chylothoraces often settle with conservative measures, whereas malignant or high-output leaks are more difficult to control and prolonged chyle loss risks serious malnutrition and immunosuppression if not addressed.

Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder — CRSWD, circadian rhythm sleep disorder, delayed sleep phase syndrome, shift work disorder, jet lag disorder Psychophysiological (behavioural) insomnia Primary hypersomnia disorders Depression or other mood disorder affecting sleep timing Poor sleep hygiene Substance or medication effects on sleep-wake timing Neurodegenerative disease with irregular sleep-wake rhythm Detailed sleep-wake history with a prospective sleep diary over one to two weeks Actigraphy to objectively document sleep-wake timing patterns Assessment of light exposure, work schedule, and travel history Where available, markers of circadian phase such as dim-light melatonin onset Screening for coexisting mood disorder or other sleep pathology Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders arise from a mismatch between the internal biological clock and the desired or socially required sleep-wake schedule, so total sleep is often normal if the patient sleeps at their preferred times Common subtypes include delayed and advanced sleep phase disorders, non-24-hour rhythm, irregular sleep-wake rhythm, and the externally imposed shift work and jet lag disorders Delayed sleep phase disorder is typical of adolescents and young adults, who cannot fall asleep or wake at conventional times and are mislabelled as insomniacs Advanced sleep phase disorder, with early evening sleepiness and early morning waking, is more common in older adults Non-24-hour rhythm disorder is characteristic of totally blind people who lack light entrainment of the clock A sleep diary, often supplemented by actigraphy, is central to demonstrating the timing pattern and confirming the diagnosis Timed bright light exposure and appropriately scheduled melatonin, applied according to circadian principles, are the mainstays of realigning the clock Shift work and jet lag disorders are managed with strategic light, scheduled sleep, and planned adaptation, since the environmental demand usually cannot be removed Sleepiness during shift work causing accidents or dangerous errors Irregular sleep-wake rhythm emerging with cognitive decline, suggesting neurodegenerative disease Severe social, educational, or occupational impairment from persistent misalignment Coexisting depression with the circadian disturbance Misdiagnosing delayed sleep phase disorder as primary insomnia and prescribing hypnotics Giving light or melatonin at the wrong circadian time and worsening the misalignment Overlooking blindness as the cause of a free-running non-24-hour rhythm Ignoring the occupational safety consequences of shift work sleepiness The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus generates an intrinsic rhythm slightly longer than twenty-four hours that is entrained to the environment chiefly by light detected through retinal photoreceptors, with melatonin secretion providing an internal darkness signal. Circadian rhythm disorders occur when this clock is misaligned with the external day. Intrinsic disorders reflect altered clock timing or entrainment: a long intrinsic period or reduced morning light sensitivity delays the phase, an advanced phase shortens it, absent light input (blindness) causes free-running non-24-hour rhythms, and weakened clock output produces an irregular rhythm as seen in neurodegenerative disease. Extrinsic disorders (shift work, jet lag) arise when behaviour and light exposure are acutely forced out of step with the still-entrained internal clock, producing sleepiness, insomnia, and impaired performance until re-entrainment occurs. Intrinsic disorders such as delayed sleep phase can usually be improved with disciplined light and melatonin timing, though relapse is common if the regimen lapses; shift work and jet lag disorders resolve with adaptation or cessation of the schedule, and outcomes are poorer when the environmental demand cannot be altered.

Cirrhosis and Its Complications — Chronic liver disease with fibrosis, Hepatic cirrhosis, Decompensated cirrhosis, Alcohol-associated cirrhosis, Posthepatitic cirrhosis Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (prehepatic portal/splenic vein thrombosis, presinusoidal schistosomiasis or congenital hepatic fibrosis) Budd-Chiari syndrome and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome as posthepatic outflow causes Congestive hepatopathy from right-sided heart failure (cardiac cirrhosis) Cryptogenic cirrhosis later reclassified as burned-out MASH Infiltrative or malignant liver disease and peritoneal carcinomatosis as alternative causes of ascites Schistosomiasis causing presinusoidal portal hypertension that mimics cirrhotic portal hypertension Chronic viral hepatitis B or C as an underlying driver where the inflammatory/fibrotic picture overlaps with other cirrhosis etiologies Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic total protein, albumin (for SAAG), cell count with differential, and cultures (inject into blood-culture bottles); amylase and cytology when indicated Upper GI endoscopy to screen for and characterize gastroesophageal varices and portal hypertensive gastropathy Etiology workup: HCV RNA and genotype; HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBe and HBV DNA; autoimmune markers (ANA, ASMA); iron studies with transferrin saturation/ferritin and HFE testing; ceruloplasmin and 24-h urinary copper; alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to show nodular liver and portosystemic collaterals; noninvasive fibrosis tests and, when needed, liver biopsy to confirm cirrhosis HVPG measurement in selected cases; MRCP (and ERCP if needed) for suspected primary sclerosing cholangitis DEXA for osteoporosis in cholestatic disease; bubble echocardiography and right-heart catheterization for hepatopulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension Cardiac cirrhosis / congestive hepatopathy from chronic right heart failure Budd-Chiari syndrome (extravasation of red cells on biopsy helps distinguish from cardiac hepatopathy) Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (venoocclusive disease) after marrow transplant conditioning or pyrrolizidine alkaloid ingestion Malignant or cardiac ascites distinguished from cirrhotic ascites by SAAG and ascitic protein Cirrhosis is the end stage of many chronic liver injuries: progressive fibrosis disrupts normal architecture and replaces hepatocytes with regenerative nodules; the main etiologic groups are alcohol-associated, chronic viral hepatitis B/C, biliary, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH, formerly NASH), and miscellaneous (cardiac, cryptogenic) (p.2708). Alcohol-associated cirrhosis is classically micronodular (nodules <3 mm); with abstinence larger nodules may form, giving a mixed micronodular/macronodular pattern (p.2708). In alcohol-related liver disease the AST is typically higher than the ALT, usually in roughly a 2:1 ratio, and aminotransferases are generally <400 IU/mL (p.2708-2709). Stigmata of chronic liver disease include scleral icterus, palmar erythema, spider angiomas, parotid enlargement, digital clubbing, muscle wasting, and in men decreased body hair, gynecomastia and testicular atrophy; these are often reversible with abstinence (p.2710). Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; clinically significant portal hypertension is an HVPG >=10 mmHg, carrying substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy) (p.2713). A serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >=1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites; cardiac ascites also shows SAAG >=1.1 g/dL but with ascitic protein >2.5 g/dL, whereas SAAG <1.1 g/dL points to infectious or malignant causes (p.2715). Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed when the ascitic absolute neutrophil count is >250/uL; ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL marks patients at higher risk for SBP (p.2715-2716). Most common SBP organisms are Escherichia coli and other gut flora; growth of more than two organisms should raise suspicion for secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus (p.2716). Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure without renal histopathology; HRS-AKI (old type 1) is rapidly progressive while HRS-CKD (old type 2) is more stable with a better prognosis (p.2716). In hepatic encephalopathy ammonia is usually elevated, but its level correlates poorly with disease severity, so most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to diagnose or follow the condition; asterixis (liver flap) is a key bedside sign (p.2716-2717). Standard PT/INR do not reliably measure clotting capacity in cirrhosis because both pro- and anticoagulant factor synthesis fall (rebalanced hemostasis); adequate thrombin generation occurs at platelet counts above ~50,000-60,000/L (p.2717). Acute-on-chronic liver failure is acute decompensation of cirrhosis with failure of one or more organ systems, behaves like a sepsis-type systemic inflammatory syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of roughly 20-70% rising with the number of organ failures (p.2717). Variceal hemorrhage - immediately life-threatening, with about 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, especially with violent agitation or progressive obtundation Rapidly rising creatinine in a patient with tense ascites suggesting HRS-AKI Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status or new AKI in a patient with ascites suggesting SBP Acute-on-chronic liver failure with multiorgan failure Refractory ascites failing maximal diuretics Relying on PT/INR (or routinely correcting it before procedures) to gauge bleeding risk in cirrhosis - hemostasis is rebalanced and these tests are unreliable Trusting ammonia levels to diagnose or grade hepatic encephalopathy despite poor correlation with severity Restricting dietary protein for encephalopathy, which worsens malnutrition and is strongly discouraged Missing SBP because classic signs may be absent - a high index of suspicion and paracentesis are needed in hospitalized ascitic patients Using nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) or unmonitored ACE inhibitors/ARBs in patients with ascites, precipitating renal failure Forgetting albumin replacement after large-volume paracentesis (>=5 L) to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction Overlooking sarcopenia masked by obesity or edema in decompensated cirrhosis Chronic, repeated hepatocellular injury (toxic, viral, immune, metabolic, cholestatic, or congestive) drives Kupffer cell activation and release of profibrogenic cytokines that activate hepatic stellate cells, producing excess collagen and extracellular matrix. Connective tissue links portal triads to central veins, hepatocytes are lost, and regenerative nodules form, so the liver contracts and loses normal architecture - a process taking years to decades. The resulting distorted vasculature raises intrahepatic resistance, which together with splanchnic arterial vasodilation (driven by mediators such as nitric oxide) produces portal hypertension. Splanchnic vasodilation causes effective arterial underfilling, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic systems, leading to renal sodium and water retention, plasma volume expansion, and a hyperdynamic circulation; combined with low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia, this generates ascites and edema. Portosystemic shunting plus reduced hepatic mass allows gut-derived neurotoxins (ammonia, false neurotransmitters, mercaptans) to reach the brain and cause encephalopathy (p.2708, p.2713-2717). Severity and bleeding risk are stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score. Once clinically significant portal hypertension leads to decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. Less than half of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Patients with complicated cirrhosis who keep drinking have under 50% 5-year survival, whereas abstinence markedly improves outlook. Development of encephalopathy is a poor prognostic sign, and HRS (AKI or CKD type) carries a poor prognosis without transplantation. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from roughly 20-70%, rising with the number of failing organs. Liver transplantation is the definitive option for end-stage disease and can reverse HRS (p.2709, p.2713, p.2715-2717). Compensated cirrhosis (HVPG 5-10 mmHg) may be asymptomatic for >=10 years; clinically significant portal hypertension is HVPG >=10 mmHg. Decompensation is marked by variceal bleeding, ascites, or encephalopathy. Overall severity is graded by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, which also predict variceal bleeding risk and guide transplant prioritization. Acute kidney injury is defined as a creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL over 48 h or a 50% rise from baseline; SBP is defined by ascitic neutrophils >250/uL (p.2713, p.2715-2716).

abnormal threonine/serine) Liver function tests and coagulation in cholestatic infants Plasma and urine galactose/galactitol in NICCD Serum pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor where available SLC25A13 gene sequencing for confirmation Fasting lipid profile and glucose tolerance assessment Brain imaging in adults with encephalopathy to exclude other causes Caused by biallelic SLC25A13 variants affecting citrin, the mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier, not a urea cycle enzyme itself Age-dependent phenotypes: neonatal cholestasis (NICCD), a childhood failure-to-thrive/dyslipidaemic stage, and adult-onset citrullinaemia (CTLN2) NICCD presents with intrahepatic cholestasis, galactosuria, hypoproteinaemia and often self-limited jaundice in infancy Adult CTLN2 causes recurrent hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with neuropsychiatric symptoms, often precipitated by alcohol, medication or carbohydrate load A striking clue is a self-selected diet rich in protein and fat with an aversion to carbohydrates and sweets Biochemistry shows raised citrulline and ammonia with an elevated arginine and abnormal threonine-to-serine ratio; pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor (PSTI) may be raised Confirmed by SLC25A13 sequencing; the disorder is especially prevalent in East Asian populations High-carbohydrate treatment is harmful; management favours a low-carbohydrate, higher-protein/fat diet, avoidance of glycerol/high-glucose infusions, arginine and nitrogen scavengers, with liver transplantation for severe CTLN2 Adult hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with rapid neurological decline Cerebral oedema during a CTLN2 crisis Precipitation of coma by high-carbohydrate/glucose infusion or glycerol Progressive cholestatic liver failure in an affected infant Recurrent unexplained neuropsychiatric episodes with hyperammonaemia Giving high-glucose or glycerol-containing infusions, which can precipitate or worsen a crisis Applying a standard high-carbohydrate, protein-restricted urea-cycle diet, which is counterproductive here Misattributing adult encephalopathy to alcohol or psychiatric disease and missing citrin deficiency Overlooking NICCD as a cause of neonatal cholestasis Ignoring the diagnostic clue of carbohydrate aversion and protein/fat preference Citrullinaemia type 2 is caused by deficiency of citrin, the liver-type mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier encoded by SLC25A13, a component of the malate-aspartate shuttle. Citrin exports aspartate from mitochondria to the cytosol, where aspartate is required by argininosuccinate synthetase to combine with citrulline in the urea cycle and for the shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents (NADH) into mitochondria. Loss of citrin therefore both limits cytosolic aspartate for ureagenesis, causing citrulline accumulation and hyperammonaemia, and impairs the malate-aspartate shuttle, raising the cytosolic NADH:NAD ratio and disturbing carbohydrate/lipid metabolism. This explains the characteristic carbohydrate intolerance, the harm from glucose loading, and the preference for protein- and fat-rich foods. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. NICCD usually resolves with supportive care and appropriate feeding, but adult CTLN2 can be life-threatening with recurrent hyperammonaemic crises and may require liver transplantation; dietary management markedly influences outcome.

prior creatinine values establish chronicity (p.2395) Acute-on-chronic kidney failure from a superimposed reversible insult: ECFV depletion (GI losses, over-diuresis), urinary tract infection, new obstructive uropathy, nephrotoxin/contrast/NSAID exposure, or flare of the primary disease (e.g., lupus, vasculitis) (p.2389, 2395-2396) Progression risk in CKD tracks three things together: the current GFR, the trajectory of GFR over time, and the degree of albuminuria - not GFR alone (p.2385). Once nephron mass is reduced, surviving nephrons undergo compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy; these short-term adaptations become maladaptive, driving glomerulosclerosis and ongoing GFR loss even after the original insult has resolved (p.2385-2386, 2396). A normal serum creatinine can mask substantial GFR loss in older patients and women (lower muscle mass); an elderly woman with a 'normal' creatinine may have a GFR under 50 mL/min/1.73 m2 (p.2387). Loss of urinary concentrating ability gives an obligate output of ~2 L/day and nocturia; paradoxically, resolution of nocturia may feel like improvement but can actually signal worsening oliguria (p.2362). Cardiac troponin is frequently chronically elevated in CKD without acute ischemia - serial trending over hours is more informative than a single value, and persistently elevated levels independently predict adverse cardiovascular events (p.2392). Most CKD patients die of cardiovascular disease before ever reaching stage 5; cardiovascular risk is increased roughly 10- to 200-fold versus age/sex-matched controls depending on stage (p.2391). In advanced CKD a malnutrition-inflammation state can paradoxically reverse classic risk factors (lowering blood pressure and lipids) and is itself a marker of poor prognosis - so 'improving' numbers can be ominous (p.2392). A drop in GFR of up to ~30% after starting an ACEi/ARB is often a benign reflection of relieved intraglomerular hyperfiltration; if stable it can be tolerated, but a progressive rise in creatinine suggests underlying renovascular disease (p.2392, 2396). A normal-sized kidney does not exclude CKD: diabetic nephropathy (early), amyloidosis, and HIV nephropathy can show normal or enlarged kidneys despite advanced disease; polycystic kidneys are typically enlarged (p.2394-2395). Hyperkalemia disproportionate to the GFR decline points to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism (e.g., diabetes) or distal-nephron disease such as obstructive uropathy or sickle cell nephropathy (p.2389). PTH is itself a uremic toxin - high levels are associated with muscle weakness, cardiac fibrosis, ESA-resistant anemia (via marrow fibrosis), and constitutional symptoms (p.2390). Erythrocytosis rather than anemia can occur in some CKD-associated conditions: urinary tract obstruction, polycystic kidney disease, renovascular disease, and renal cell carcinoma (p.2362). Uremic pericarditis (pleuritic chest pain with friction rub; ECG with PR depression and diffuse ST elevation) - absolute indication for urgent dialysis; risk of hemorrhagic effusion and tamponade, so dialyze without heparin (p.2392) Asterixis, myoclonus, seizures, or coma in advanced untreated kidney failure - uremic encephalopathy (p.2393) Peripheral neuropathy without another cause is an indication to start renal replacement therapy (p.2393) Calciphylaxis - painful livedo reticularis and subcutaneous nodules progressing to ischemic skin necrosis/ulceration (legs, thighs, abdomen, breasts); warfarin is a risk factor and should be stopped (p.2390-2391) Diuretic-resistant intractable edema and hypertension, refractory hyperkalemia, or refractory pulmonary edema in advanced CKD - indications to initiate dialysis (p.2389, 2392) Accelerating rate of GFR decline - prompts search for a reversible superimposed acute/subacute process (p.2396) Acute systemic features (fever, polyarthritis, rash) with renal impairment suggest an acute systemic illness rather than chronic CKD (p.2395) Treating an elevated creatinine as chronic without checking prior values - missing a reversible acute or acute-on-chronic process (p.2395). Assuming normal kidney size excludes CKD (diabetic nephropathy early, amyloid, HIV nephropathy retain normal/large kidneys) (p.2394-2395). Stopping ACEi/ARB for a modest (<30%) non-progressive GFR fall - discontinuation in CKD is associated with increased death/cardiovascular events; the small drop usually reflects relieved hyperfiltration (p.2392). Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB - greater incidence of AKI and adverse cardiac events; avoid dual blockade (p.2396). Overlooking occult potassium sources (dietary salt substitutes) and potassium-retaining drugs (RAS inhibitors, MRAs, potassium-sparing diuretics) as causes of hyperkalemia (p.2389). Gadolinium MRI contrast in advanced CKD - risk of nephrogenic systemic/fibrosing dermopathy; minimize in stage 3 and avoid in stages 4-5 unless essential (older agents) (p.2394). Iodinated radiographic contrast - contrast-induced nephropathy, especially in diabetic nephropathy; avoid where possible (p.2395). Pruritus and skin pigmentation often persist despite dialysis; first rule out unrelated causes (e.g., scabies) and treat hyperphosphatemia (p.2394). Metformin and sulfonylureas are contraindicated below ~half-normal GFR; insulin requirements fall as renal degradation of insulin declines (p.2394). CKD results from two overlapping processes: (1) initiating mechanisms specific to the underlying cause (developmental/genetic, immune-complex, inflammatory, metabolic, microvascular, or toxic injury to vascular, glomerular, or tubulointerstitial compartments), and (2) a nonspecific final common pathway in which loss of nephron mass triggers compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy of remaining nephrons. Intrarenal renin-angiotensin activation with blunted tubuloglomerular feedback raises intraglomerular pressure; this adaptation becomes maladaptive, distorting glomerular architecture, impairing podocyte function and the filtration barrier, and producing progressive sclerosis and nephron dropout. The uremic syndrome arises from three spheres of dysfunction: accumulation of retained solutes (urea and creatinine are only readily-measured but incomplete surrogates for many retained toxins), loss of non-excretory kidney functions (fluid/electrolyte homeostasis, hormone production/regulation - EPO, calcitriol, with altered PTH, FGF-23, insulin), and progressive systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, falling albumin/fetuin) feeding a malnutrition-inflammation-atherosclerosis/calcification syndrome (p.2385-2389). Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality at every stage, and most patients die of it before reaching stage 5; only 30-45% of those who reach stage 5 have advanced cardiovascular complications at that point. Left ventricular hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy are among the strongest predictors of cardiovascular death. Hyperphosphatemia, high FGF-23, and persistently elevated troponin independently predict worse cardiovascular outcomes. A superimposed malnutrition-inflammation-calcification state in advanced disease carries a poor prognosis. Nephrotic-range proteinuria and heavy persistent proteinuria predict faster progression and worse outcomes. Survivors of dialysis-requiring AKI are at high risk of progressive CKD, with up to ~10% developing ESKD (p.2384, 2391-2392, 2362). KDIGO classification stratifies CKD by GFR category and albuminuria, both predicting all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and progression. GFR categories: G1 >=90, G2 60-89, G3a 45-59, G3b 30-44, G4 15-29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73 m2. Albuminuria (UACR) categories: A1 <30, A2 30-299, A3 >=300 mg/g. Harrison Table 319-3 stages (abnormality >3 months): Stage 1 (>60 with abnormal urinalysis/imaging), Stage 2 (>60, mild progression risk), Stage 3a (45-60), Stage 3b (30-45), Stage 4 (15-30, prepare for RRT), Stage 5 (<15, highest RRT need). Stages 1-2 are usually asymptomatic; complications emerge in stages 3-4; the full uremic syndrome appears at stage 5 (GFR <15) (p.2385-2388, 2362, Table 319-3).

respiratory pathogen panel in acute respiratory syndromes Endomyocardial biopsy (with electron microscopy sample) when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected Coronary angiography/catheterization in patients with evidence of ischemia or infarction who are candidates for intervention Athlete's heart (mimics HCM and can show LV noncompaction) Severe chronic hypertension (mimics HCM) Aortic stenosis (mimics HCM and should be excluded) Cardiac amyloidosis (causes RCM and can produce asymmetric septal thickening mimicking HCM, especially in older patients) Storage diseases mimicking HCM morphology: GLA/Anderson-Fabry, PRKAG2, and LAMP2/Danon disease Cardiac sarcoidosis (often DCM-pattern or regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias, rather than classic restrictive morphology) Coronary artery disease/prior infarction and primary valve disease as structural causes mimicking DCM Radiation, scleroderma-type connective tissue disease, and drugs such as doxorubicin causing an RCM phenotype PVC-related cardiomyopathy versus genetic ACM in patients with frequent PVCs or nonsustained VT Cardiomyopathy denotes primary disease of the heart muscle itself; strictly it excludes myocardial dysfunction secondary to other cardiovascular disease, though common usage also folds in ischemic, valvular, and hypertensive cardiomyopathy. The traditional morphologic scheme recognizes three major phenotypes: hypertrophic (HCM), dilated (DCM), and restrictive (RCM) cardiomyopathy. HCM is characterized by increased left ventricular wall thickness (roughly 13-15 mm depending on context) with a normal or high ejection fraction; LV chamber volume is normal or smaller, and EF is usually above 0.60. DCM is defined when LVEF is at or below 0.50, although most patients present clinically with LVEF at or below 0.40; an LVEF persistently at or below 0.30-0.35 is the threshold considered for primary-prevention ICD. RCM is the least common phenotype and is defined more by physiology (moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated cardiac filling pressures) than by morphology; wall thickness is often increased but may appear normal, EF is usually only mildly reduced, and marked atrial enlargement with predominant right heart failure is typical. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC, originally arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia) is a fourth, predominantly genetic phenotype marked by life-threatening arrhythmias and abnormal RV structure/function with variable LV involvement. Evolving genotype-driven terminology reframes arrhythmogenic disease as ACM-RV (RV-predominant, formerly ARVC), ACM-LV (LV-predominant), and biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy; in ACM-LV ventricular arrhythmias can dominate before LVEF is severely reduced, so primary-prevention ICD may be considered even with LVEF above 0.35. Phenotypes overlap and shift over time: DCM can undergo reverse remodeling toward higher EF and smaller ventricles with recommended therapy, and about 5% of HCM evolves to a reduced-EF, more restrictive state (HCM-rEF). Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) commonly represents a transition state, either deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission. Clinical expression frequently follows a two-hit model in which an inherited predisposition is triggered by an acquired insult such as infection, toxic exposure, pregnancy, or tachycardia. Echocardiography is the initial imaging modality; cardiac MRI adds tissue characterization, with late gadolinium enhancement mapping fibrosis and T1/T2 mapping identifying focal and diffuse inflammation. Left ventricular noncompaction is a trait (often assessed by a noncompacted-to-compacted myocardium ratio above 2.3) that can accompany HCM, DCM, dystrophies, and syndromes, but can also appear in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and more often in athletes. Ventricular tachyarrhythmias or nonsustained VT, which may dominate before EF is severely reduced in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy Family history of sudden death, cardiomyopathy, conduction disorders, or skeletal myopathy Embolic events from atrial fibrillation or apical ventricular thrombus as a presentation of unrecognized cardiomyopathy Progressive exertional breathlessness, fatigue, orthopnea, edema, and abdominal symptoms indicating the congestion syndrome Marked wall thickening suggesting amyloidosis, inherited storage disease, or inborn metabolic disease Treating 'congestive heart failure' as a diagnosis or etiology; it is a nonspecific congestion syndrome common to many cardiac conditions (including congenital heart disease, primary pulmonary hypertension, and valve disease) and requires full etiologic evaluation. Over-relying on morphologic phenotype, since phenotypes overlap and shift over time and many entities (sarcomeric variants, storage diseases) can present as either HCM or RCM. Missing amyloidosis in older patients, where it can both cause RCM and mimic the asymmetric septal thickening of HCM. Misclassifying sarcoidosis as restrictive when it more often produces DCM-pattern, regional wall-motion abnormalities, or RV involvement with arrhythmias. Failing to distinguish PVC-related cardiomyopathy from a genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy that itself causes both the arrhythmias and the muscle disease. Interpreting LV noncompaction as inherently pathologic, since it can occur in normal hearts, in pregnancy, and in athletes. Cardiomyopathy reflects intrinsic disease of the myocardium producing characteristic structural and functional abnormalities. In HCM, abnormal myocyte/sarcomere biology drives increased wall thickness with preserved or supranormal systolic function but impaired filling. In DCM, the ventricle dilates with depressed systolic function (low LVEF). In RCM, the dominant abnormality is impaired ventricular filling from a stiff myocardium causing markedly elevated filling pressures and atrial enlargement, often with relatively preserved EF. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty or fibrotic remodeling that creates a substrate for ventricular arrhythmias with variable RV and/or LV structural change. An expanding catalog of pathogenic genetic variants underlies heritable cardiomyopathy, and inherited differences in immune-response pathways contribute to infectious and noninfectious inflammation that can manifest as myocarditis and cardiomyopathy. Clinical disease often requires a second acquired insult superimposed on a genetic predisposition. Prognosis depends on the specific phenotype and underlying cause rather than on classification alone. DCM may improve substantially with reverse remodeling on guideline-directed therapy, whereas about 5% of HCM deteriorates to a reduced-EF, restrictive state. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy carries a risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias that can precede heart failure. Persistent severe LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF at or below 0.30-0.35) identifies patients considered for primary-prevention ICD. Morphologic/functional classification: Hypertrophic (HCM) - septal thickness >=15 mm in men, >=13 mm in women (13-14 mm may suffice in relatives of a proband or with a positive genetic test), LVEF normal or high (usually >0.60), normal/small LV volume. Dilated (DCM) - early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV end-diastolic volume >112% of normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95th percentile; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditionally recommended heart-failure therapy; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Restrictive (RCM) - functional diagnosis based on moderate-to-severe diastolic dysfunction and/or elevated filling pressures, usually mildly reduced LVEF, with marked atrial enlargement. Mid-range LVEF (0.40-0.50) represents a transition zone. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy - ACM-LV (usually DCM morphology), ACM-RV/ARVC (2010 modified task force criteria combining major and minor criteria), and biventricular forms. LV noncompaction trait assessed by noncompacted/compacted ratio >2.3.

impair speech development Timing palate repair without balancing speech benefit against effects on midface growth Orofacial clefting results from failure of fusion of the embryonic facial processes. Cleft lip arises from incomplete fusion of the medial nasal and maxillary processes, which normally unite to form the primary palate, during early facial development. Cleft palate results from failure of the palatal shelves to elevate, meet, and fuse in the midline to form the secondary palate. The aetiology is multifactorial, involving genetic susceptibility and environmental influences such as maternal smoking, alcohol, folate deficiency, and certain medications, and clefts can also occur as part of recognised syndromes. With coordinated multidisciplinary care most children achieve good functional and aesthetic outcomes, normal feeding, and intelligible speech, though some require secondary speech surgery, alveolar bone grafting, orthodontics, and orthognathic surgery into adolescence. Outcomes are influenced by cleft severity, associated syndromes, and access to specialist team care.

persistent calvarial defects in young children Cleidocranial dysplasia is caused by haploinsufficiency of RUNX2, the principal transcription factor governing osteoblast differentiation and both intramembranous and endochondral bone formation. Reduced RUNX2 activity impairs ossification of bones that depend heavily on membranous ossification, especially the clavicles and cranial vault, and disrupts the tooth-forming programme. The result is clavicular hypoplasia, delayed cranial and dental maturation, and a range of skeletal ossification defects, with relative preservation of overall growth. Prognosis is excellent with a normal lifespan and intelligence. Morbidity is mainly dental and orthodontic, together with a modest increase in fracture risk and reduced bone density; multidisciplinary dental care is central to management.

CLIPPERS — chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids, CLIPPERS syndrome Central nervous system lymphoma Neurosarcoidosis Primary or secondary central nervous system vasculitis Multiple sclerosis or other demyelination Infective rhombencephalitis Histiocytic disorders Paraneoplastic brainstem encephalitis MRI of the brain with contrast to demonstrate the characteristic punctate pontine and cerebellar enhancement Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including cytology and flow cytometry to exclude lymphoma Serum and CSF markers for sarcoidosis, vasculitis, and infection Whole-body imaging to search for occult lymphoma or systemic inflammatory disease Brain biopsy in atypical, tumefactive, or steroid-unresponsive cases Serial MRI to monitor response and detect emerging lymphoma A chronic inflammatory disorder centred on the pons and hindbrain, presenting with subacute ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, and sensory disturbance The hallmark MRI finding is punctate and curvilinear ('salt-and-pepper' or peppering) gadolinium enhancement concentrated in the pons and cerebellum Pathology shows perivascular lymphocytic (predominantly T-cell) infiltration without a defined alternative cause By definition the disorder is markedly and rapidly responsive to corticosteroids, and relapse on withdrawal is characteristic It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful search for lymphoma, vasculitis, sarcoidosis, and infection Large or tumefactive enhancement, necrosis, or atypical features should prompt biopsy and reconsideration of the diagnosis Long-term steroid-sparing immunosuppression is usually required to prevent relapse and progressive disability Large, tumefactive, or necrotic lesions atypical for CLIPPERS Poor or incomplete response to corticosteroids Progressive brainstem dysfunction with bulbar or respiratory compromise Emergence of features suggesting lymphoma on follow-up Diagnosing CLIPPERS without adequately excluding lymphoma and other mimics Withdrawing corticosteroids without steroid-sparing cover and precipitating relapse Ignoring atypical imaging features that warrant biopsy Failing to arrange long-term radiological surveillance CLIPPERS is characterised by a chronic, predominantly T-lymphocytic perivascular inflammatory infiltrate concentrated in the pons, brainstem, and cerebellum, with variable extension along white-matter tracts. The inflammation surrounds small vessels and correlates with the punctate perivascular contrast enhancement seen on MRI. No specific antigen or antibody has been identified, and the disorder is defined clinically, radiologically, and pathologically together with its striking corticosteroid responsiveness. Because similar perivascular inflammation can herald lymphoma or other conditions, CLIPPERS is regarded as a syndrome requiring exclusion of mimics and ongoing surveillance. With corticosteroids and maintenance immunosuppression most patients improve and stabilise, but delayed treatment or repeated relapses can lead to pontine atrophy and fixed disability; vigilance for evolving lymphoma is essential.

Clonorchiasis — Clonorchis sinensis, Chinese liver fluke infection, Oriental liver fluke Opisthorchiasis (Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus), clinically and morphologically very similar Fascioliasis and other liver flukes Ascending bacterial cholangitis from other causes Choledocholithiasis and biliary strictures Cholangiocarcinoma arising de novo Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis of other aetiology Stool microscopy (with concentration) for the characteristic small operculated eggs Duodenal or bile aspirate examination when stool is negative but suspicion is high Full blood count for eosinophilia Liver function tests to assess cholestasis Abdominal ultrasound, CT or MRCP to show ductal dilatation, flukes, stones or a mass Serological or antigen testing where available as an adjunct Caused by the trematode Clonorchis sinensis and endemic in East Asia, including China, Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and eastern Russia, where freshwater fish is a dietary staple Acquired by eating raw, undercooked, pickled or smoked freshwater fish containing infective metacercariae The adult flukes reside in the intrahepatic bile ducts; light infections are often asymptomatic while heavy or chronic infections cause biliary symptoms Chronic infection causes cholangitis, biliary obstruction, stone formation and periductal fibrosis, and is a recognised risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma Diagnosis rests on identifying the small operculated eggs in stool or in bile/duodenal aspirate; serology and imaging are adjuncts Eosinophilia is common, and imaging may show dilated peripheral intrahepatic ducts with intraductal flukes or debris Praziquantel is the mainstay of anthelmintic treatment for clonorchiasis, with attention to relieving biliary obstruction and treating secondary bacterial cholangitis Features of ascending cholangitis with fever, jaundice and abdominal pain Progressive obstructive jaundice or a biliary mass suggesting cholangiocarcinoma Recurrent pyogenic cholangitis with intrahepatic stones Weight loss and constitutional symptoms in a chronically infected patient Attributing biliary symptoms solely to stones or bacterial cholangitis and missing the underlying fluke Relying on a single stool sample, which may miss light infections Confusing Clonorchis eggs with those of Opisthorchis or small intestinal flukes Failing to consider cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in long-standing heavy infection Neglecting dietary counselling, allowing reinfection from continued raw fish consumption Humans are infected by ingesting metacercariae in raw or inadequately processed freshwater fish. The larvae excyst in the duodenum, migrate up the ampulla into the biliary tree, and mature into adult flukes that live in the intrahepatic bile ducts for years. Mechanical irritation, secretions and immune-mediated inflammation produce biliary epithelial hyperplasia, periductal fibrosis and ductal dilatation. Chronic stasis predisposes to intrahepatic stone formation and recurrent pyogenic (bacterial) cholangitis, and long-standing epithelial injury with hyperplasia underlies the increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Light infections carry an excellent prognosis and respond well to anthelmintic therapy, but heavy chronic infection can lead to irreversible biliary fibrosis, recurrent cholangitis and a significantly increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma.
