PIK3CA-related overgrowth phenotypes Proteus syndrome (AKT1 mosaicism) Megalencephaly-capillary malformation syndrome Parkes Weber syndrome Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome and PTEN-related overgrowth Isolated lymphatic or venous malformations Deep or high-sensitivity sequencing of affected (lesional) tissue for mosaic PIK3CA variants MRI of affected regions and the spine to map lipomatous overgrowth and vascular malformations Vascular imaging to characterise capillary, venous, lymphatic, and arteriovenous components Assessment for spinal and skeletal anomalies including scoliosis Coagulation studies where extensive venous or lymphatic malformation raises thrombotic risk Renal and abdominal imaging given the reported association with Wilms tumour in PROS The acronym captures the core features: congenital lipomatous overgrowth, vascular malformations, epidermal naevi, and spinal/skeletal or scoliosis anomalies Characteristic truncal lipomatous masses are present from birth, often with overlying vascular staining and a wide sandal gap or large fatty overgrowth of the trunk Combined capillary, venous, lymphatic, and sometimes arteriovenous malformations distinguish it from simpler overgrowth conditions Part of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS) caused by post-zygotic (mosaic) activating variants in PIK3CA Because the variant is mosaic and post-zygotic it is not inherited and overgrowth is typically segmental and asymmetric, with severity depending on the tissues involved Molecular diagnosis usually requires deep sequencing of affected tissue rather than blood, since the mosaic variant may be undetectable in leucocytes Targeted PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway inhibition has emerged as a therapeutic option for severe PROS, alongside multidisciplinary supportive and surgical care Signs of high-flow arteriovenous malformation or thromboembolism from extensive vascular lesions Rapidly progressive spinal or paraspinal overgrowth causing cord compression New abdominal mass or haematuria prompting evaluation for Wilms tumour Localised intravascular coagulopathy with bleeding or clotting complications Testing blood rather than affected tissue and wrongly excluding a mosaic PIK3CA variant Confusing CLOVES with Klippel-Trenaunay or Proteus syndrome despite differing genetics and complications Underestimating thrombotic risk in extensive vascular malformations Neglecting spinal surveillance for scoliosis or cord compromise CLOVES syndrome results from somatic mosaic gain-of-function variants in PIK3CA, which encodes the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase. Constitutive activation of PIK3CA drives the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, promoting unregulated cell growth, proliferation, and survival in the tissues carrying the variant. Because the mutation arises after fertilisation, only a subset of cells is affected, producing the segmental, asymmetric overgrowth of fat, vessels, skin, and bone that defines the phenotype; the distribution and burden of mutant cells determine clinical severity. The course is highly variable and depends on the extent and location of overgrowth and vascular involvement; some individuals have limited disease while others face progressive functional and orthopaedic complications. Emerging targeted pathway inhibitors and multidisciplinary care have improved management of severe disease.

Clubfoot — congenital talipes equinovarus, CTEV, talipes, congenital clubfoot Postural (positional) talipes that corrects fully with manipulation Metatarsus adductus Congenital vertical talus Neuromuscular clubfoot (e.g. secondary to spina bifida or arthrogryposis) Syndromic foot deformity Tibial or fibular deficiency Clinical examination to assess rigidity and classify severity Full musculoskeletal and neurological examination to detect associated conditions Examination and, if indicated, imaging of the hips for developmental dysplasia Antenatal ultrasound detection and postnatal confirmation Spinal imaging or specialist assessment where a neuromuscular cause is suspected A congenital deformity present at birth in which the foot is held in equinus, hindfoot varus, midfoot cavus, and forefoot adductus (remembered as the components of talipes equinovarus) The key clinical distinction is between a rigid, structural clubfoot and a flexible 'postural' foot that corrects with gentle manipulation It is often idiopathic but may be associated with neuromuscular conditions (e.g. spina bifida), syndromes, or oligohydramnios, so a general and neurological examination is important Diagnosis is clinical; the deformity is frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound, and examination should exclude associated abnormalities such as developmental dysplasia of the hip The Ponseti method of serial casting is the mainstay of treatment, gradually correcting the deformity, usually followed by a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy to address residual equinus Maintenance with a foot-abduction (boots-and-bar) orthosis is essential to prevent relapse, and poor brace compliance is the commonest cause of recurrence Treatment should begin early in the neonatal period when the tissues are most amenable to correction Surgery is reserved for resistant, relapsed, or neglected deformities not corrected by casting Associated neuromuscular disorder or spinal dysraphism requiring broader assessment Failure to progress with casting, or early relapse, indicating a resistant or syndromic foot Neglected or late-presenting rigid deformity limiting non-surgical correction Signs of an alternative diagnosis such as congenital vertical talus Mistaking a rigid structural clubfoot for a flexible postural foot and delaying treatment Under-emphasising brace compliance, the leading cause of relapse Overlooking an associated neuromuscular or syndromic condition, or concurrent hip dysplasia Attempting forceful correction or premature surgery instead of graduated casting Congenital talipes equinovarus arises from abnormal development and positioning of the bones, joints, muscles, and soft tissues of the foot and ankle, with contracture of the medial and posterior soft tissues (including the tendo Achillis, tibialis posterior, and plantar structures) and abnormal alignment of the talus, calcaneus, and navicular. The exact cause is multifactorial, with genetic predisposition and intrauterine factors implicated; in syndromic or neuromuscular cases an underlying disorder disturbs the muscle balance across the developing foot. The result is a fixed deformity combining hindfoot equinus and varus with midfoot cavus and forefoot adduction, which becomes increasingly rigid and structurally established if untreated. With early Ponseti treatment and disciplined brace use, most idiopathic clubfeet achieve a functional, plantigrade, pain-free foot, though a minority relapse and need repeat casting or surgery; syndromic and neuromuscular clubfeet are stiffer, more prone to recurrence, and have a less predictable outcome.

Cluster headache — trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, histamine headache, suicide headache Migraine, particularly unilateral migraine Paroxysmal hemicrania (indomethacin-responsive) SUNCT/SUNA syndromes Trigeminal neuralgia Acute angle-closure glaucoma Secondary headache from a pituitary or posterior fossa lesion or carotid dissection MRI of the brain with attention to the pituitary and cavernous sinus to exclude secondary causes MR or CT angiography when a vascular cause such as dissection or aneurysm is suspected Pituitary hormone screen if imaging suggests a sellar lesion ECG before starting verapamil and monitoring during dose changes Characterised by attacks of severe, strictly unilateral pain centred on the orbit or temple, usually lasting between 15 minutes and 3 hours Attacks are accompanied by ipsilateral cranial autonomic features such as lacrimation, conjunctival redness, nasal congestion or rhinorrhoea, and sometimes a partial Horner syndrome Unlike migraine sufferers who prefer to lie still, patients are typically restless and agitated during an attack, often pacing or rocking Attacks cluster into bouts lasting weeks to months separated by remission periods, and there is a striking circadian and seasonal rhythm with nocturnal attacks common Alcohol and other vasodilators can reliably provoke attacks during an active cluster period but not during remission High-flow oxygen and fast-acting triptan therapy are the mainstays of acute abortive treatment, while verapamil is a common preventive principle The condition shows a male predominance and is strongly linked with tobacco use Neuroimaging is warranted at presentation to exclude a structural or pituitary lesion mimicking the syndrome First or worst attack, or a change in established attack pattern, suggesting a secondary cause Persistent Horner syndrome or other fixed neurological deficit between attacks Features suggesting carotid dissection such as neck pain with Horner syndrome Papilloedema or other signs of raised intracranial pressure Misdiagnosing the attacks as migraine or sinusitis and delaying effective treatment Overlooking paroxysmal hemicrania, which is exquisitely responsive to indomethacin, in short frequent attacks Failing to obtain neuroimaging to exclude a secondary or pituitary cause Starting verapamil without baseline and follow-up ECG monitoring for conduction effects Cluster headache is the most common trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia. The pain reflects activation of the trigeminovascular system, while the accompanying autonomic signs arise from cranial parasympathetic outflow and sympathetic dysfunction. The pronounced circadian and seasonal periodicity implicates the posterior hypothalamus, which shows activation on functional imaging during attacks and is thought to act as the disorder's generator or pacemaker. Episodic cluster headache typically follows a relapsing course with prolonged remissions, whereas a minority develop chronic cluster headache with little or no remission. Preventive therapy substantially reduces attack frequency in most patients, but the disorder can be highly disabling during active bouts.

Coagulation Disorders — hemophilia, von Willebrand disease, bleeding disorders Hemophilia A versus hemophilia B (clinically indistinguishable; require factor assays to differentiate) (Harrison 22e p.930) Von Willebrand disease with low FVIII versus hemophilia A (VWD must be excluded in a patient with prolonged aPTT and low FVIII and no known hemophilia history) (Harrison 22e p.930) Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) and other rare inherited factor deficiencies (FII, FV, FVII, FX, FXIII, fibrinogen) (Harrison 22e p.928, 931-932) Qualitative platelet function disorders (e.g., Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, storage pool disorder) as a cause of mucocutaneous bleeding with normal coagulation factor levels (Harrison 22e p.926) PT and aPTT as first-line screens for clotting factor deficiency (Harrison 22e p.928) Mixing study (correction with normal plasma indicates factor deficiency; failure to correct indicates an inhibitor or anticoagulant) (Harrison 22e p.928) Individual factor activity assays to identify the specific deficient factor (Harrison 22e p.928) Bethesda assay to define inhibitor specificity and titer (expressed in Bethesda units; classifies low- vs high-responder patients) with annual aPTT/mixing-study screening at hemophilia centers (Harrison 22e p.930-931) VWD laboratory panel: aPTT, VWF antigen, VWF activity, FVIII activity, and multimer analysis to classify type 1, 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N, and 3 (Harrison 22e p.926-927) Chromogenic FVIII activity assay using bovine substrates when emicizumab is present (routine aPTT and FVIII activity are inaccurate) (Harrison 22e p.931) Molecular/genetic testing for F8 or F9 mutations to enable precise carrier diagnosis in affected families (Harrison 22e p.930) Acquired von Willebrand syndrome from lymphoproliferative disorders / MGUS / multiple myeloma / Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (suspect with new-onset severe mucosal bleeding, especially in the elderly) (Harrison 22e p.927) Acquired VWD due to high shear: cardiac valvular disease and Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis with GI bleeding from angiodysplasia; shear unfolds VWF causing loss of large multimers, reversed by valve replacement) (Harrison 22e p.927) Acquired VWD in myeloproliferative disorders with markedly elevated platelet counts (>1.5 million) due to platelet-VWF binding and clearance (Harrison 22e p.926) Acquired inhibitors (autoantibodies) to clotting factors in patients without genetic deficiency: postpartum, autoimmune or neoplastic disease, idiopathic, or rarely after topical bovine thrombin exposure in complex surgery (Harrison 22e p.928) Liver disease, DIC, and vitamin K deficiency as acquired multifactor coagulopathies (Harrison 22e p.928) The most common inherited factor deficiencies are the hemophilias, X-linked recessive diseases due to deficiency of factor VIII (hemophilia A, ~80% of cases) or factor IX (hemophilia B); hemophilia A and B are clinically indistinguishable (Harrison 22e p.928, 930). Disease phenotype correlates with factor activity level: severe (<1%), moderate (1-5%), mild (6-30%). Severe and moderate disease cause bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis), soft tissues, and muscles after minor trauma or spontaneously; mild disease bleeds infrequently and usually only after trauma (Harrison 22e p.930). Recurrent hemarthroses (knees, elbows, ankles, shoulders, hips) damage a joint to create a chronically affected 'target joint' with synovitis and progressive deformity; deep-muscle hematomas can cause compartment syndrome by compressing arteries, veins, or nerves (Harrison 22e p.930). Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (symptomatic prevalence ~1 in 1000 to 1 in 10,000); VWF tethers platelets to subendothelium and is the carrier protein that prolongs the FVIII half-life (Harrison 22e p.927). Most VWD symptoms are 'platelet-like' (mucocutaneous: bruising, epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding); type 1 (parallel reduction in VWF protein, function, and FVIII) is most common (>=80% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.926-927). Type 2N VWD ('autosomal hemophilia') is caused by VWF variants that impair FVIII binding, markedly shortening the FVIII half-life and lowering FVIII levels (Harrison 22e p.927). Screening hemostasis tests: an isolated prolonged PT suggests FVII deficiency; a prolonged aPTT indicates an intrinsic-pathway deficiency, most commonly FVIII, FIX, or FXI; prolongation of both PT and aPTT suggests deficiency of FV, FX, FII, or a fibrinogen abnormality (Harrison 22e p.928). Mixing study principle: adding normal pooled plasma corrects a prolonged PT/aPTT due to a factor deficiency but fails to correct when an inhibitor (antibody) is present; if it corrects, individual factor activity assays identify the deficient factor (Harrison 22e p.928). Inhibitor (alloantibody) formation is the major complication of hemophilia treatment, with prevalence ~30% in severe hemophilia A, ~10% in nonsevere hemophilia A, and only 3-5% in hemophilia B; inhibitors increase morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.930-931). Acquired coagulation factor deficiencies are more frequent than congenital disorders; the most common are the hemorrhagic diathesis of liver disease, DIC, and vitamin K deficiency, each typically involving more than one clotting factor (Harrison 22e p.928). Bleeding into the oropharyngeal spaces, central nervous system, or retroperitoneum is life-threatening and requires immediate therapy (Harrison 22e p.930) Retroperitoneal hemorrhage may form a calcified inflammatory mass (pseudotumor syndrome) and damage the femoral nerve; pseudotumors can also form in long bones (Harrison 22e p.930) Deep-muscle hematomas of the distal limbs can cause compartment syndrome from external compression of arteries, veins, or nerves (Harrison 22e p.930) Failure to respond to factor replacement at therapeutic doses suggests an inhibitor; early detection is critical (Harrison 22e p.930) In carriers/women, postpartum hemorrhage risk rises after delivery as the pregnancy-induced rise in clotting factor levels falls rapidly (Harrison 22e p.931) FXII (Hageman factor), high-molecular-weight kininogen, and prekallikrein deficiencies markedly prolong the aPTT but do NOT cause bleeding (no bleeding phenotype; treatment is not indicated) — do not treat the lab abnormality (Harrison 22e p.928). Not all patients with low VWF levels bleed; mildly decreased VWF should be diagnosed as VWD only with bleeding symptoms and/or a family history, and type O blood physiologically lowers VWF (overlapping the diagnostic range) (Harrison 22e p.926-927). Bleeding phenotype does not always correlate with factor activity in FXI deficiency, and a negative bleeding history with prior procedures does NOT exclude increased hemorrhage risk (Harrison 22e p.931-932). Family history of hemophilia is absent in ~30% of cases (de novo mutations), so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.930). Antifibrinolytic drugs are NOT indicated for hematuria because of the risk of an occlusive clot obstructing the genitourinary tract (Harrison 22e p.931). Plasma coagulation factor deficiencies impair secondary hemostasis (the coagulation cascade). Inherited hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive disorders from mutations in F8 and F9 respectively; affected males bleed while carrier women are generally asymptomatic, although a wide range of factor activity from random X-inactivation (lyonization) can produce bleeding in some carriers. FVIII has a very short intrinsic circulating half-life (~25-30 min) that is extended to roughly 12 h when complexed with von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWD reflects quantitative or qualitative defects of VWF, which serves both as the adhesion molecule tethering platelets to exposed subendothelium (function dependent on large VWF multimers) and as the FVIII carrier; loss of high-molecular-weight multimers (e.g., via excessive ADAMTS13 cleavage in type 2A/2B, or shear-induced unfolding) impairs platelet adhesion. Acquired deficiencies (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency) usually involve multiple factors and perturb both primary (platelet/vessel wall) and secondary (coagulation) hemostasis. (Harrison 22e p.926-930) Without treatment severe hemophilia may limit life expectancy; with modern recombinant factor concentrates, prophylaxis, and viral-inactivated products, life expectancy of severe hemophilia is now only ~10 years shorter than the general male population and near normal in mild/moderate disease. Since 1998 no new viral hepatitis or HIV infections have been reported in hemophilia patients, though aging patients carry burdens of arthropathy, chronic pain, and prior HCV/HIV infection (hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common cause of death in HIV-negative patients). TTP-related microangiopathy and inhibitors worsen prognosis when present. (Harrison 22e p.930-932) Hemophilia A/B by factor VIII or IX activity: severe (<1%), moderate (1-5%), mild (6-30%); patients with baseline activity >25% may be detected only after major trauma or as an isolated prolonged aPTT. VWD classified into types 1, 2 (subtypes 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N), and 3 (severe, with virtually absent VWF and FVIII usually <10%) using VWF antigen, VWF activity, FVIII activity, and multimer pattern. Inhibitor patients classified as low responders (<5 Bethesda units) or high responders (>5 BU or anamnestic rise). (Harrison 22e p.926-931)

Coarctation of the Aorta — CoA, aortic coarctation, coarctation Interrupted aortic arch Hypoplastic left heart syndrome Critical aortic stenosis Other duct-dependent systemic circulation lesions Essential hypertension in an older child Peripheral vascular disease Four-limb blood pressure measurement and simultaneous upper- and lower-limb pulse assessment Echocardiography to define coarctation site, severity, and associated lesions such as bicuspid valve Chest radiograph for rib notching and aortic contour in older children CT or MR angiography for detailed arch anatomy Assessment for acidosis and end-organ perfusion in the collapsing neonate A narrowing of the aorta, most often just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ductal region, obstructing flow to the lower body. The hallmark examination finding is diminished, delayed, or absent femoral pulses compared with the upper limbs, with a blood pressure gradient higher in the arms than the legs. Severe coarctation may be duct-dependent in the neonate: as the ductus arteriosus closes, lower-body perfusion falls, producing shock, acidosis, and heart failure. A prostaglandin infusion is used to reopen or maintain ductal patency and restore lower-body perfusion while stabilising a critically ill neonate before repair. Older children may be asymptomatic and present with an incidentally found murmur, upper-limb hypertension, headaches, or leg claudication. Coarctation is commonly associated with a bicuspid aortic valve and may occur with other left-sided obstructive lesions and Turner syndrome. Chest radiograph in older children can show rib notching from collateral vessels and a figure-3 aortic contour. Echocardiography defines the site and severity of narrowing and associated lesions; CT or MR angiography is useful for detailed anatomy. Repair by surgery or catheter intervention relieves the obstruction, but lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation and persistent hypertension. Neonatal circulatory collapse with shock and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus closes in duct-dependent coarctation Absent or markedly weak femoral pulses with an upper-to-lower limb blood pressure gradient Signs of heart failure and poor lower-body perfusion in an infant Severe upper-limb hypertension with headaches or hypertensive complications Evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion such as oliguria or feeding intolerance Failing to palpate femoral pulses and compare limb blood pressures in an unwell neonate or hypertensive child Missing a duct-dependent coarctation until the neonate collapses as the ductus closes Attributing upper-limb hypertension in a child to essential hypertension without checking for a gradient Overlooking associated bicuspid aortic valve and other left-sided lesions Assuming successful repair eliminates the need for ongoing hypertension and recoarctation surveillance A discrete or long-segment narrowing of the aortic lumen creates a mechanical obstruction to systemic outflow. Proximal to the obstruction, pressure rises, producing upper-body hypertension and left ventricular pressure overload; distal to it, perfusion pressure falls, causing weak lower-body pulses. In severe neonatal coarctation, lower-body perfusion depends on right-to-left flow through the ductus arteriosus, so ductal closure precipitates hypoperfusion, metabolic acidosis, and circulatory collapse. In slowly progressive disease, collateral arterial channels develop to bypass the obstruction. Early repair of significant coarctation gives a good outlook, but patients need lifelong surveillance for recoarctation, residual or late hypertension, aneurysm formation, and associated valve disease. Unrecognised severe neonatal coarctation can be rapidly fatal.

Cobalamin C deficiency (cblC) — cblC disease, MMACHC deficiency, combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria type cblC, methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria cblC type Isolated methylmalonic acidaemia (mutase or other cobalamin defects) Classic homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) Other remethylation defects (MTHFR deficiency, cblE/cblG) Nutritional vitamin B12 deficiency Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy Other causes of infantile encephalopathy with retinopathy Transcobalamin deficiency Plasma and urine methylmalonic acid Plasma total homocysteine and methionine Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised C3 propionylcarnitine) Full blood count and film for megaloblastic/haemolytic changes MMACHC gene sequencing and complementation studies where needed Ophthalmological assessment for maculopathy/pigmentary retinopathy Renal function and markers of thrombotic microangiopathy Most common inborn error of intracellular cobalamin (vitamin B12) metabolism, caused by biallelic MMACHC variants Impaired processing of cobalamin blocks synthesis of both adenosylcobalamin and methylcobalamin, so both dependent pathways fail Biochemical signature is combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria with low-to-normal methionine Early-onset (infantile) disease brings failure to thrive, feeding problems, hypotonia, encephalopathy, seizures and a pigmentary retinopathy Haematological clue is megaloblastic anaemia, sometimes with a thrombotic microangiopathy (haemolytic-uraemic-like picture) Late-onset disease can present with cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, myelopathy or thromboembolism Confirmed by plasma/urine metabolites (raised methylmalonic acid and total homocysteine) plus MMACHC sequencing Treatment centres on parenteral hydroxocobalamin, with betaine, folinic acid and sometimes carnitine; oral B12 is inadequate Encephalopathy with seizures and rapid neurological deterioration in infancy Thrombotic microangiopathy with renal impairment (HUS-like presentation) Severe metabolic acidosis with feeding failure Thromboembolic events in older patients Progressive visual loss from maculopathy Treating with oral cyanocobalamin instead of parenteral hydroxocobalamin, which is far less effective Diagnosing isolated methylmalonic acidaemia without measuring homocysteine and missing the combined defect Overlooking the retinopathy, which can progress despite metabolic control Mistaking the thrombotic microangiopathy for primary atypical HUS Failing to recognise late-onset presentations with psychiatric or myelopathic features Cobalamin C disease results from deficiency of the MMACHC protein, which performs an early cytosolic step in intracellular processing of dietary cobalamin, dealkylating/decyanating incoming cobalamin so it can be converted into its two active cofactor forms. Loss of function prevents generation of both adenosylcobalamin, the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and methylcobalamin, the cofactor for methionine synthase. Consequently methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be isomerised, causing methylmalonic acid accumulation, and homocysteine cannot be remethylated to methionine, causing hyperhomocysteinaemia with low methionine. The combined metabolic block produces neurological injury, endothelial damage with thrombotic microangiopathy, megaloblastic haematopoiesis and retinopathy. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Early-onset disease often has a guarded prognosis with persistent neurological and visual impairment even when treated, whereas late-onset disease responds better to early hydroxocobalamin-based therapy; outcome depends strongly on age at diagnosis and treatment.

Cocaine, Other Psychostimulants, and Hallucinogens — Cocaine intoxication, Methamphetamine use disorder, Stimulant use disorder, MDMA (ecstasy/Molly), Cathinone / bath salts, Hallucinogen use disorder, LSD / PCP / psilocybin / ketamine Sympathomimetic toxidrome from other agents (e.g., synthetic cathinones/bath salts, prescription stimulant misuse) Anticholinergic toxidrome Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome / malignant hyperthermia (hyperthermia, rigidity) Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma / catecholamine excess Primary psychiatric psychosis or mania Alcohol or sedative withdrawal Sepsis with hyperthermia and tachycardia CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) presenting with agitation, fever, altered mental status Electrocardiogram for chest pain or arrhythmia evaluation Chest radiograph in cocaine-associated chest pain Cardiac biomarkers to exclude myocardial infarction Core body temperature monitoring (hyperthermia) Note that emerging substances/NPS are often NOT detected on standard ED drug screens or postmortem toxicology Hyperthyroidism / thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Primary psychotic or manic episode Hypoglycemia or hypoxemia (must be excluded before treating agitation) Cocaine blocks reuptake at the dopamine transporter, raising synaptic dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin in both CNS and PNS; this monoaminergic excess underlies its euphoric and sympathomimetic effects. Smoked or vaporized cocaine (freebase/crack) reaches the brain almost as fast as the IV route because of the large pulmonary vasculature, producing a rapid, intense, transient high that increases addictive potential. Acute psychostimulant intoxication produces a uniform syndrome regardless of agent: euphoria, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, decreased appetite, heightened alertness, increased libido, plus peripheral tremor, diaphoresis, hypertonia, tachypnea, hyperreflexia, and hyperthermia. Many psychostimulant effects are biphasic: low doses improve psychomotor performance and increase vagal tone (lowering heart rate), whereas high doses cause tremor/convulsions and raise heart rate and blood pressure. Combining cocaine with alcohol generates the metabolite cocaethylene, whose cardiovascular toxicity is additive to cocaine's, intensifying pathophysiologic harm. Methamphetamine is more potent than amphetamine, producing higher synaptic dopamine and greater nerve-terminal toxicity; the dextrorotatory (d-) enantiomer has 3-5 times the CNS activity of the l-form, and smoked bioavailability (~90%) far exceeds oral (~67%). MDMA acts mainly on serotonin transporters, increasing release of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; animal data show moderate-to-high doses can cause loss of serotonergic nerve endings and permanent damage. Classic (serotonergic) hallucinogens such as LSD, psilocybin, mescaline/peyote, DMT, and ayahuasca disrupt serotonin and glutamate signaling; oral onset is ~20-90 min with duration up to 6-12 h (salvia ~30 min). Dissociative agents (PCP, ketamine, high-dose dextromethorphan, salvia) distort perception of time, motion, color, sound, and self and can cause respiratory depression, heart-rate abnormalities, and a withdrawal syndrome with craving, confusion, headache, and sweating. Psychostimulant withdrawal features hypersomnia, increased appetite, and depressed mood; acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days but residual symptoms may persist for months. Conditioned (cue-triggered) craving, not physical withdrawal, is considered the primary driver of ongoing use. Stimulant use disorder is diagnosed by DSM-5 when at least 2 of 11 criteria occur within 12 months; for hallucinogen use disorder only the first 10 criteria apply because the withdrawal criterion does not apply (use is typically not chronic). Adulterants are a major and underappreciated hazard: cocaine/methamphetamine are increasingly cut with fentanyl-related opioids (overdose deaths), levamisole (agranulocytosis, leukoencephalopathy, cutaneous vasculitis with skin necrosis), clenbuterol (tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia), and xylazine (sedation, necrotic soft-tissue lesions). Severe psychomotor agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, headache, and mydriasis indicating sympathetic overactivity / overdose Hyperthermia (goal to cool to core temperature <39 C within 30 min) Seizures, coma, or focal neurologic signs Intracranial hemorrhage or cerebral infarction Chest pain, cardiac ischemia/arrhythmia, left ventricular dysfunction, aortic dissection/rupture Respiratory failure, airway burns or bronchospasm from inhaled crack ('crack lung') Rhabdomyolysis with metabolic acidosis / renal infarction Concurrent opioid co-ingestion (e.g., fentanyl-adulterated cocaine) precipitating fatal overdose 'Bad trip' with panic, paranoia, or psychosis (hallucinogens), which may persist up to 24 h Beta blockers should generally be avoided in cocaine users because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation from beta blockade may cause coronary vasoconstriction, ischemia, and infarction; if essential, mixed alpha/beta agents (e.g., labetalol, carvedilol) are preferred over nonselective beta blockers. Succinylcholine is relatively contraindicated for rapid-sequence intubation in cocaine use; a nondepolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) is the alternative. Before treating psychomotor agitation, hypoglycemia and hypoxemia must be ruled out first. Drugs sold as 'Molly'/MDMA frequently contain methylone, ethylone, or other synthetic cathinones rather than MDMA, so the reported drug may not match the actual exposure. Emerging/new psychoactive substances are often missed on standard drug tests, so a negative screen does not exclude intoxication. Fentanyl, xylazine, levamisole, and other adulterants can produce effects (and overdose) not anticipated from the intended drug. MDMA, LSD, and psilocybin remain Schedule I in the United States despite FDA breakthrough-therapy designations; investigational use does not equal approved therapy. Psychostimulants increase synaptic monoamines. Cocaine binds the dopamine transporter and blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, raising their levels centrally and peripherally; repeated exposure induces long-term neuronal changes including adaptations in glutamate-releasing neurons. Methamphetamine, a cationic lipophilic molecule structurally similar to monoamine transporters, reverses transporter function to dump newly synthesized catecholamines from storage vesicles into the synapse and also inhibits monoamine oxidase, attenuating monoamine metabolism; it is more potent than amphetamine with greater nerve-terminal toxicity. MDMA acts predominantly on serotonin transporters to release serotonin (and norepinephrine/dopamine) and can damage serotonergic nerve endings. Cathinone (from khat) increases dopamine release and reduces its reuptake. Classic hallucinogens disrupt serotonin (affecting mood, perception, sleep, appetite, temperature, sexual behavior, muscle control) and glutamate (affecting pain perception, environmental responses, emotion, learning/memory). The sympathomimetic surge drives the cardiovascular, neurologic, pulmonary, renal, and hyperthermic complications. Acute overdose is a medical emergency that can be fatal through cerebral hemorrhage/infarction, cardiac arrhythmia or ischemia, respiratory failure, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis, and management is largely supportive in an ICU/telemetry setting. Co-ingestion of other drugs (especially opioids) markedly increases morbidity and mortality, and overdose deaths involving cocaine and psychostimulants have risen sharply (cocaine-related overdose deaths more than quintupled from 2011 to 2022; psychostimulant-involved deaths reached ~36,000 in 2023). Early abstinence is frequently complicated by depression, guilt, insomnia, and anorexia that can be as severe as a major affective disorder and may persist for months to years. Contingency management has robust evidence of efficacy for stimulant use disorder with benefit lasting up to 2 years after treatment ends; no FDA-approved pharmacotherapy exists for stimulant or hallucinogen addiction. Chronic hallucinogen/dissociative use can leave persistent psychosis, memory loss, anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and flashbacks lasting a year or more. No single graded severity scale; DSM-5 stimulant use disorder severity is rated mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5), or severe (>=6) of 11 criteria over 12 months. Acute clinical severity ranges from intoxication to life-threatening overdose marked by sympathetic overactivity (agitation, hypertension, tachycardia), hyperthermia, seizures, intracranial or cardiac events, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Complications of psychostimulant use are catalogued in Table 468-1 across cardiovascular, CNS/PNS, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, renal, endocrine, and other organ systems.

Coccidioidomycosis — Valley fever, Coccidioides Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is often misdiagnosed as this) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Pulmonary malignancy (coccidioidal nodules are difficult to distinguish radiographically and, like malignancies, may enhance on PET) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Histoplasmosis (can cause false-positive coccidioidal antigen results) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Blastomycosis (can cause false-positive coccidioidal antigen results) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Tuberculosis / other chronic granulomatous pulmonary infections (upper lobe infiltrate, cavities, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy mimic) (Harrison 22e p.1697) EIA for IgM and IgG antibodies (recommended for initial diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Confirmatory immunodiffusion (IDTP/IDCF) or traditional tube-precipitin and complement-fixation assays with CF titer (CF titer is an important prognostic tool) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Culture of sputum/respiratory fluids and tissue (grows within 3-7 days at 37 degrees C on artificial media including blood agar) (Harrison 22e p.1698) Direct microscopy of respiratory specimens (Papanicolaou, Gomori methenamine silver, or calcofluor white) or fixed tissue (H&E or GMS) for spherules (Harrison 22e p.1698) Coccidioidal antigen test (antigenuria/antigenemia), including CSF assay in suspected meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698) CSF examination in suspected meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, profound hypoglycorrhachia, elevated protein, occasional CSF eosinophilia; CF antibody in CSF) (Harrison 22e p.1697) MRI with gadolinium in meningitis (frequently shows basilar meningeal enhancement; dilated ventricles indicate hydrocephalus) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Chest imaging/CT for nodules and cavities (multiple nodules and microsatellite lesions favor coccidioidomycosis over malignancy) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Pulmonary malignancy (solitary or multiple nodules, PET-avid, may require biopsy to distinguish) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Caused by dimorphic soil-dwelling fungi of the genus Coccidioides (C. immitis and C. posadasii), which are clinically indistinguishable; infection follows inhalation of airborne arthroconidia (Harrison 22e p.1696). Endemic to the Western Hemisphere between 40 degrees N and 40 degrees S; areas of high endemicity in the US include the southern San Joaquin Valley of California (hence 'Valley fever') and south-central Arizona, with other foci across the southwestern US, northern Mexico, Central America, and parts of South America (Harrison 22e p.1696). In endemic areas most human cases occur without obvious soil or dust exposure; periods of aridity following rainy seasons are associated with increases in symptomatic infections (Harrison 22e p.1696). After infection, 60% of individuals are completely asymptomatic; the other 40% have symptoms related primarily to pulmonary infection (fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain) appearing several days to up to 3 weeks after inhalation, with risk of symptomatic illness increasing with age (Harrison 22e p.1697). Immunologic manifestations of primary pulmonary disease include cutaneous reactions: a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash ('toxic erythema'), erythema nodosum (typically over the lower extremities), erythema multiforme (often in a necklace distribution), and Sweet syndrome lesions; cutaneous manifestations are especially common in women (Harrison 22e p.1697). Symmetrical arthralgias ('desert rheumatism'), often involving the ankles, knees, and hips, may occur with or without cutaneous manifestations (Harrison 22e p.1697). Serology is the most common diagnostic method; EIA for IgM and IgG is recommended for initial diagnosis, with positive results confirmed by immunodiffusion (IDTP/IDCF) or traditional tube-precipitin and complement-fixation assays (Harrison 22e p.1697). Rising complement-fixation (CF) titers reflect fungal growth and correlate with clinical progression; high CF titers (e.g., 1:32 or greater) suggest unrestrained fungal growth and the possibility of extrathoracic dissemination, while CF antibody in CSF is indicative of coccidioidal meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698). Spherules (up to 200 microns) are unique to Coccidioides and can be demonstrated in respiratory specimens after Papanicolaou, Gomori methenamine silver, or calcofluor white staining, or in fixed tissue with hematoxylin-eosin or Gomori methenamine silver (Harrison 22e p.1698). A commercial coccidioidal antigen test (antigenuria/antigenemia) is useful in immunosuppressed patients with severe or disseminated disease and when assaying CSF in suspected meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioidal meningitis is the most dire disseminated syndrome and is uniformly fatal if untreated; patients present with a persistent dull headache often with lethargy and confusion, and nuchal rigidity, if present, is not severe (Harrison 22e p.1697). Disseminated disease (occurs in approximately 1% of infections; defined as fungus found outside the thoracic cavity), more likely in male patients, those of African and perhaps Filipino ancestry, and persons with depressed cellular immunity (Harrison 22e p.1697) Coccidioidal meningitis: persistent dull headache, lethargy, confusion; uniformly fatal if untreated, may progress to communicating hydrocephalus with declining mental status and gait disturbance (Harrison 22e p.1697) Immunocompromised hosts at risk for dissemination: HIV-1 infection with CD4 count <250/microL, chronic glucocorticoid therapy, allogeneic solid-organ transplant recipients, and patients on TNF-alpha antagonists or other biological response modifiers (Harrison 22e p.1697) New coccidioidal infection acquired during the second or third trimester of pregnancy or postpartum (significant risk for disseminated disease) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Diffuse reticulonodular pneumonia with dyspnea and fever in intense exposure or profoundly suppressed cellular immunity (e.g., untreated HIV with markedly low CD4), associated with unrestrained fungal growth and frequent fungemia (Harrison 22e p.1697) High serum CF titer (e.g., 1:32 or greater) predicting disease activity and possible extrathoracic dissemination (Harrison 22e p.1698) Pulmonary cavity rupture into the pleural space causing pyopneumothorax (acute dyspnea, collapsed lung with pleural air-fluid level) (Harrison 22e p.1697) Primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is often misdiagnosed as community-acquired bacterial pneumonia; rash, symmetrical arthralgias, night sweats, marked fatigue, peripheral-blood eosinophilia, failure to improve with antibacterial therapy, or upper lobe infiltrate / hilar or mediastinal adenopathy should suggest the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1697). Coccidioides poses a significant laboratory hazard if inadvertently inhaled; the clinical laboratory should always be alerted to the possibility of this diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioidal pulmonary nodules can be difficult to distinguish radiographically from malignancy and, like malignancies, often enhance on PET; biopsy may be required (Harrison 22e p.1697). The IgM EIA in particular is occasionally falsely positive; results should be interpreted cautiously when screening asymptomatic individuals (Harrison 22e p.1698). The EIA IgG optical density does not correlate with the IDCF/traditional CF titer and should not be used as a surrogate for a titer (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioidal antigen testing may yield false-positive results in histoplasmosis or blastomycosis (Harrison 22e p.1698). The fungus is isolated from CSF in fewer than one-third of meningitis cases, so a negative CSF culture does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1697). Potassium hydroxide preparation of sputum is rarely fruitful for identifying Coccidioides (Harrison 22e p.1698). PCR genomic detection does not appear to be more sensitive than culture, though it can be more rapid (Harrison 22e p.1698). Coccidioides exists as filamentous mold (mycelia) in the environment, producing barrel-shaped airborne spores (arthroconidia, ~2 x 5 microns) that, when inhaled, are small enough to evade mucosal defenses and reach deep into the bronchial tree to initiate infection. Within the host, arthroconidia enlarge into spherules (up to 200 microns, unique to Coccidioides) containing endospores; spherules rupture and release endospores that form new spherules, propagating infection locally. A robust cellular immune response is critical to host control: resolved pulmonary infection shows necrotizing granulomas containing spherules, whereas uncontrolled disseminated disease shows poorly formed or absent granulomas and a polymorphonuclear leukocyte response. In persons with protective cellular immunity, spherules may persist in the lungs for prolonged periods (possibly lifelong) in a latent state, conferring protective immunity but creating a risk of recurrent active disease if that immunity wanes (Harrison 22e p.1696-1697). In most patients, primary pulmonary coccidioidomycosis resolves without sequelae over several weeks. Clinical dissemination occurs in approximately 1% of infected individuals and, when it occurs, is usually evident within the first 6 months after primary infection. Coccidioidal meningitis is uniformly fatal if untreated; even with treatment, relapse is common after stopping therapy. Antibodies disappear over time in persons whose illness resolves, but the presence of coccidioidal antibodies in serum does not indicate immunity or control of infection (Harrison 22e p.1696-1698). Clinical presentations and their approximate frequencies (Table 219-1, Harrison 22e p.1698): asymptomatic infection (60%); primary focal pneumonia (40%); diffuse pneumonia (<1%); pulmonary sequelae (~5%: nodule, cavity, chronic pneumonia); and disseminated disease (1% or less, including skin/bone/joint/soft tissue disease and meningitis). High CF titers (e.g., 1:32 or greater) and features such as night sweats >3 weeks, weight loss >10%, CF titer >1:16, and extensive pulmonary involvement indicate greater severity.

Care is supportive and multidisciplinary, with sun protection to limit photosensitivity.

diagnosis is clinical after excluding infective causes such as syphilis Prompt systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay for hearing preservation, with immunosuppressive or biologic agents in refractory or systemic disease Rapidly progressive sensorineural hearing loss threatening permanent deafness Signs of aortitis or new aortic regurgitation indicating systemic vasculitis Neurological features suggesting central nervous system involvement or an alternative diagnosis Systemic vasculitic manifestations requiring urgent immunosuppression Delaying corticosteroids and losing the window to preserve hearing Attributing audiovestibular symptoms to Meniere disease and missing the ocular link Failing to exclude syphilis before diagnosing autoimmune interstitial keratitis Not screening for systemic and aortic vasculitic complications Managing eye and ear disease in isolation without recognising the unifying diagnosis Cogan syndrome is regarded as an autoimmune vasculitis, possibly triggered by preceding infection, in which the immune response cross-reacts with shared antigens in the cornea and inner ear. Autoantibodies directed against inner ear and endothelial antigens have been described. Immune-mediated inflammation of the corneal stroma produces interstitial keratitis, while inflammation and damage to the cochlea and vestibular apparatus cause hearing loss and vertigo. In some patients the process extends to a systemic vasculitis affecting large vessels, leading to aortitis and aortic regurgitation. With prompt corticosteroid therapy ocular inflammation usually settles, but hearing loss is frequently permanent and may progress to bilateral deafness; associated large-vessel vasculitis and aortic valve disease carry additional morbidity and mortality.

Osteoporosis lowers the threshold for injury, explaining its predominance in postmenopausal women and older adults. The distal fragment tilts and displaces dorsally and radially and impacts proximally, shortening the radius and disrupting the normal volar tilt and radial inclination of the articular surface. Associated soft-tissue swelling or bony displacement may compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, and disruption of the distal radioulnar joint or triangular fibrocartilage can affect forearm rotation. Most stable distal radial fractures unite and recover good function with appropriate reduction and rehabilitation, but malunion with residual dorsal tilt and radial shortening can leave weakness, reduced grip, and cosmetic deformity, and intra-articular incongruity predisposes to post-traumatic arthritis.

disc or macular involvement threatening central vision Feeding, breathing or growth difficulties suggesting CHARGE syndrome Treating coloboma as purely a cosmetic iris finding and not examining the posterior segment Failing to evaluate for CHARGE syndrome and associated hearing loss Overlooking the raised retinal detachment risk and not counselling on warning symptoms Attributing all visual loss to the coloboma without excluding amblyopia or detachment Ocular coloboma results from incomplete closure of the optic (choroidal) fissure during early eye development, normally completed in the sixth week of gestation. Persistence of this fissure leaves a defect in the affected layers of the eye, characteristically in the inferonasal quadrant, and the retina and choroid overlying the gap are absent or malformed. In CHARGE syndrome, mutations in the chromatin-remodelling gene CHD7 disrupt development of multiple neural-crest and placode-derived structures during the same embryonic window, so coloboma coexists with cardiac, choanal, growth, genital and ear or hearing anomalies. The malformed retina at the coloboma margin is structurally weak, accounting for the raised risk of retinal detachment. Visual prognosis depends on which structures are involved, being good for isolated iris coloboma but guarded when the optic nerve, macula or a large chorioretinal area is affected, and further limited by the lifelong risk of retinal detachment; in CHARGE syndrome overall outcome is shaped by the systemic anomalies.
