SLC26A3 (DRA) chloride/bicarbonate exchanger in the ileum and colon. Failure of this exchanger prevents chloride absorption and bicarbonate secretion, so chloride is retained in the lumen and osmotically drives water loss, producing a secretory watery diarrhoea rich in chloride. Impaired bicarbonate loss into the gut and secondary activation of sodium- and potassium-conserving pathways lead to systemic hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Chronic volume depletion can cause secondary hyperaldosteronism and renal complications if replacement is inadequate. With early diagnosis and consistent chloride, sodium and potassium replacement, growth, development and renal function are usually preserved. Inadequate substitution predisposes to growth failure, renal damage and electrolyte crises.

Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection — cCMV, congenital CMV, congenital cytomegalovirus Other congenital infections in the TORCH group (toxoplasmosis, rubella, syphilis, herpes simplex, Zika) Neonatal sepsis or bacterial infection Congenital toxoplasmosis (also causes intracranial calcification) Haemolytic disease of the newborn Inherited metabolic or genetic disorders causing microcephaly Neonatal haematological disorders causing thrombocytopenia CMV detection by PCR from urine or saliva within the first three weeks of life Newborn and serial audiological (hearing) assessment Cranial imaging (ultrasound and/or MRI) for calcification and brain abnormalities Ophthalmological examination for chorioretinitis Full blood count, platelets, and liver function tests Dried blood spot testing when late confirmation is needed The most common congenital viral infection and a leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental disability in children. Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth, yet a proportion of these still go on to develop late-onset hearing loss. Symptomatic disease may include small size for gestational age, microcephaly, petechiae, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, and low platelets. Neurological features can include intracranial calcifications (often periventricular), chorioretinitis, and seizures. Both primary maternal infection and non-primary (reactivation or reinfection) during pregnancy can transmit to the fetus, with primary infection carrying higher risk. Diagnosis must be confirmed within the first three weeks of life to distinguish congenital from perinatally acquired infection, using viral detection from urine or saliva. Because of the risk of progressive hearing loss, confirmed cases need structured audiological surveillance over time, not just a single newborn screen. Antiviral therapy is considered for symptomatic infants, particularly those with central nervous system involvement, to improve hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Microcephaly or abnormal neuroimaging indicating central nervous system involvement Confirmed or progressive sensorineural hearing loss Symptomatic disease with thrombocytopenia, hepatitis, or petechiae Chorioretinitis threatening vision Seizures in the neonatal period Failure to confirm the diagnosis within three weeks, losing the ability to prove congenital infection Missing the diagnostic window by testing after three weeks of age and being unable to distinguish congenital from acquired infection Assuming a normal newborn hearing screen excludes future hearing loss Overlooking asymptomatic infection, which still carries a risk of late sequelae Attributing intracranial calcification solely to toxoplasmosis without confirming CMV Failing to arrange long-term audiological and developmental surveillance Cytomegalovirus, a herpesvirus, crosses the placenta following maternal infection and disseminates in the fetus, where it replicates in multiple organs. The developing central nervous system is particularly vulnerable: infection disrupts neuronal migration and brain development and causes an inflammatory response that produces calcifications, microcephaly, and migrational abnormalities. Involvement of the inner ear leads to progressive sensorineural hearing loss, while infection of the liver, bone marrow, and reticuloendothelial system accounts for hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and jaundice. Asymptomatic infants generally do well but remain at risk of late-onset hearing loss, warranting ongoing audiological follow-up; symptomatic infants, especially those with neurological involvement, have a higher risk of hearing loss, developmental delay, and other long-term deficits, though early antiviral therapy can improve outcomes in selected cases.

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia — CDH, Bochdalek hernia, diaphragmatic hernia Congenital pulmonary airway malformation Congenital lobar emphysema Pulmonary sequestration Pneumothorax or large pleural effusion Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn of other cause Eventration of the diaphragm Antenatal ultrasound and, where available, fetal MRI with lung volume estimation Chest and abdominal radiograph showing thoracic bowel loops and mediastinal shift Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and exclude associated cardiac lesions Blood gas and pre- and post-ductal oxygen saturations to gauge shunting Evaluation for associated anomalies and genetic conditions A defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax during fetal development, impairing lung growth; the posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect, more often left-sided, is most common. The principal problems are pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension rather than the anatomical defect itself. Many cases are detected on antenatal ultrasound, allowing delivery at a centre with neonatal surgical and intensive care support. A typical presentation is respiratory distress soon after birth with a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen and a shifted apex or heart sounds, and reduced breath sounds on the affected side. Bowel sounds may be audible in the chest, and the chest radiograph shows bowel loops in the thorax with mediastinal shift. Bag-mask ventilation should be avoided because it distends the herniated bowel and worsens lung compression; early endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression are preferred. Initial management focuses on gentle, lung-protective ventilation, cardiorespiratory stabilisation, and treatment of pulmonary hypertension before surgery. Surgical reduction and repair of the defect is undertaken after the infant is physiologically stabilised, not as an emergency. Severe cases may need advanced support such as inhaled pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Severe respiratory distress and hypoxaemia at or shortly after birth Persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting refractory to therapy Deterioration after bag-mask ventilation distends intrathoracic bowel Signs of inadequate oxygenation and rising acidosis Associated major cardiac or other anomalies worsening the outlook Using bag-mask ventilation and inflating herniated bowel, worsening lung compression Rushing to surgery before stabilising pulmonary hypertension and gas exchange Attributing neonatal distress to primary lung disease and missing the diagnosis on examination and radiograph Using aggressive high-pressure ventilation that risks barotrauma to hypoplastic lungs Overlooking associated cardiac and genetic anomalies that affect management and prognosis Failure of the diaphragm to close completely during embryogenesis permits abdominal organs to occupy the thoracic cavity while the lungs are developing. The space-occupying viscera restrict growth of the ipsilateral (and to a lesser extent contralateral) lung, producing pulmonary hypoplasia with fewer alveoli and abnormal, muscularised pulmonary arterioles. After birth these abnormal vessels fail to relax normally, causing persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting, hypoxaemia, and acidosis. The combination of reduced functional lung tissue and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance drives the respiratory failure that dominates the clinical course. Outcome depends chiefly on the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension and on associated anomalies. With optimal perinatal care many infants survive, though survivors may have chronic lung disease, feeding and growth problems, and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Severe hypoplasia and refractory pulmonary hypertension carry a poor prognosis.

Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia — CDA, CDA type I, CDA type II, HEMPAS, CDAN1-related anaemia, SEC23B-related anaemia, KLF1/KIF23-related dyserythropoiesis Thalassaemia syndromes Myelodysplastic syndrome with dyserythropoiesis Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency Congenital haemolytic anaemias such as hereditary spherocytosis Sideroblastic anaemias Erythropoietic porphyrias with dyserythropoiesis Bone marrow aspirate examining erythroblast multinuclearity and chromatin bridges Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film to characterise the anaemia Haemolysis markers including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and haptoglobin Iron studies (ferritin, transferrin saturation) and hepatic iron quantification by MRI Targeted genetic testing (CDAN1, C15orf41, SEC23B, KLF1, KIF23) Electron microscopy of erythroblasts in selected cases to define subtype A group of inherited anaemias characterised by ineffective erythropoiesis and morphologically abnormal, often multinucleated, erythroblasts in the marrow Type I (CDAN1 or C15orf41) shows megaloblastoid erythroblasts with internuclear chromatin bridges; type II (SEC23B), the commonest, shows binucleate late erythroblasts Type II is also known as HEMPAS, in which red cells lyse in a proportion of acidified normal sera and show characteristic membrane glycoprotein abnormalities The anaemia is typically macrocytic or normocytic with inappropriately low reticulocytes for the degree of anaemia Iron overload is common and progresses even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin Splenomegaly and jaundice from haemolysis of the abnormal cells are frequent, and gallstones may develop Diagnosis rests on marrow morphology plus genetic testing, distinguishing CDA from thalassaemia and myelodysplasia Signs of iron overload affecting heart, liver, or endocrine organs even without transfusion Severe anaemia in infancy requiring frequent transfusion Hydrops or profound anaemia detected antenatally in severe variants Progressive cytopenias or dysplasia raising concern for an alternative marrow disorder Mislabelling the marrow appearances as myelodysplasia and pursuing inappropriate therapy Failing to monitor and treat iron overload in non-transfused patients Confusing the macrocytosis with B12 or folate deficiency and missing the congenital cause Overlooking the diagnosis in a family member with milder compensated disease Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias are disorders of terminal erythroid maturation in which erythroblasts undergo abnormal nuclear division and cytokinesis, generating characteristic multinucleate and internuclear-bridged forms. The underlying genes govern nuclear envelope integrity and chromatin organisation (CDAN1 in type I), endoplasmic reticulum vesicle transport and glycoprotein processing (SEC23B in type II), and erythroid transcription or cytokinesis machinery in rarer subtypes. Defective maturation leads to apoptosis of erythroid precursors within the marrow, producing ineffective erythropoiesis with a low reticulocyte response relative to the anaemia. As with other ineffective erythropoieses, expanded but futile erythroid activity suppresses hepcidin and drives excess intestinal iron absorption, so tissue iron overload accumulates independently of transfusion. Many patients have a moderate, compatible-with-life anaemia, but long-term morbidity is dominated by iron overload and its organ complications, making iron monitoring and chelation central to care regardless of transfusion status.

Congenital erythropoietic porphyria — CEP, Gunther disease, uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency, UROS deficiency Erythropoietic protoporphyria (painful but usually non-blistering photosensitivity) Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (severe biallelic UROD deficiency) Severe porphyria cutanea tarda Xeroderma pigmentosum and other inherited photosensitivity disorders Epidermolysis bullosa in the neonate Hereditary haemolytic anaemias when anaemia dominates Quantitative urinary porphyrins showing predominant uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I Erythrocyte and plasma porphyrin measurement Examination of urine and teeth for characteristic red fluorescence under ultraviolet light (Wood's lamp) Full blood count and haemolysis screen to detect anaemia and reticulocytosis Molecular genetic testing of the UROS gene for confirmation and family counselling Assessment of spleen size and iron status in chronic haemolysis Rare autosomal recessive deficiency of uroporphyrinogen III synthase, the fourth enzyme of haem biosynthesis, causing one of the most severe cutaneous porphyrias Typically presents in infancy with pink to red-brown discoloration of the urine staining the nappy and extreme photosensitivity Severe bullous photodermatosis leads to blistering, scarring, mutilating deformity of the face and digits, and loss of features such as the ears and nose over time Erythrodontia (red-brown fluorescent teeth) and hypertrichosis are characteristic, and haemolytic anaemia with splenomegaly is common The block diverts haem synthesis toward non-physiological type I porphyrin isomers, so urine shows greatly raised uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I This is a non-acute, purely photocutaneous porphyria; there are no neurovisceral attacks Management is largely supportive with rigorous lifelong sunlight avoidance and photoprotection; severe cases may be considered for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation Severe transfusion-dependent haemolytic anaemia Progressive mutilating scarring with functional loss of digits or facial structures Secondary infection of ulcerated photodamaged skin Presentation in a neonate with red-staining urine and blistering requiring urgent photoprotection Missing the diagnosis in an infant with staining of the nappy dismissed as dietary or infective Inadequate lifelong photoprotection allowing progressive irreversible damage Confusing it with erythropoietic protoporphyria, which causes pain without blistering Underestimating the burden of chronic haemolysis and splenomegaly Failing to offer genetic counselling given the recessive inheritance Congenital erythropoietic porphyria results from markedly deficient uroporphyrinogen III synthase, the fourth enzyme of the haem pathway, which converts hydroxymethylbilane to uroporphyrinogen III. When this step fails, hydroxymethylbilane cyclises non-enzymatically to the type I isomer, which cannot be used for haem and accumulates as uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I. These photoreactive type I porphyrins accumulate massively in erythrocytes, plasma, urine, bone and teeth. Deposition in the skin causes light-induced generation of reactive oxygen species and severe phototoxic damage, while porphyrin-laden erythrocytes undergo haemolysis, producing the anaemia and splenomegaly. Prognosis depends on disease severity; many patients have progressive disfigurement and chronic haemolysis with a substantially affected quality of life, though rigorous photoprotection and, in selected severe cases, stem cell transplantation can improve outcomes.

Adult Congenital Heart Disease — ASD, VSD, tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger Atrial septal defect (secundum, primum, sinus venosus, coronary sinus types) — most common cause of right heart dilation from a shunt Patent foramen ovale (distinct from ASD; not associated with right heart dilation) Ventricular septal defect (membranous/perimembranous, muscular, AV-canal/inlet, subpulmonary/conal types) Patent ductus arteriosus Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve Tetralogy of Fallot (most common cyanotic CHD) Transposition of the great arteries (D-loop and congenitally corrected L-loop) Coarctation of the aorta (with associated bicuspid aortic valve) Single ventricle physiology (tricuspid atresia, double inlet LV, hypoplastic left heart) post-Fontan Eisenmenger syndrome (any unrepaired left-to-right shunt that has reversed) Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline (bubble) contrast — needed to diagnose PFO and non-secundum ASDs; color flow Doppler for VSDs and shunt-ratio estimation Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging — routine surveillance of RV size, function, and mass in repaired tetralogy of Fallot and other complex CHD; cross-sectional imaging detects PAPVR Surface ECG — incomplete right bundle branch block in ASD; QRS duration >=180 ms in repaired TOF flags risk of ventricular tachycardia/sudden death; ventricular pre-excitation (WPW) in up to 20% of Ebstein anomaly Cardiac catheterization — shunt quantification and hemodynamic assessment, particularly when pulmonary hypertension is suspected Genetic evaluation — testing for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) in conotruncal defects (clues: right aortic arch, aberrant subclavian artery); recognition of trisomy 21, Noonan (PTPN11), Williams (7q11.23), and Turner syndromes Fetal echocardiogram between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation for pregnant patients with CHD Atrial septal defect may be mistaken for mitral stenosis; features favoring ASD over MS include a pulmonary mid-to-upper left sternal border flow murmur, and large left-to-right shunts can produce findings overlapping with MS (Harrison 22e p.2065 / Chap. on MS). Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy and Uhl's anomaly are non-shunt myocardial causes of right heart dilation that can mimic the dilated right heart of an ASD. At least 1.4 million U.S. adults are living with congenital heart disease (CHD); the majority were diagnosed in childhood, but a substantial percentage have CHD first recognized in adulthood, so lifelong follow-up with ACHD expertise is recommended (Harrison 22e p.2067). ASD physiology is predominantly a left-to-right shunt; the degree of shunting (and thus right heart volume loading) depends on defect size and the diastolic properties of the heart. As patients age, diabetes, hypertension, and atherosclerosis reduce left-heart compliance and may increase left-to-right shunting and symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2070). The classic ASD physical finding is a wide, FIXED splitting of the second heart sound, due to prolonged RV ejection and increased pulmonary artery capacitance delaying pulmonary valve closure; the ECG commonly shows incomplete right bundle branch block (Harrison 22e p.2070). Secundum ASD (defect in the region of the fossa ovalis) is the most common type and can often be closed percutaneously with an occluder device; a patent foramen ovale (PFO) is distinct, is NOT associated with right-sided dilation, and persists in up to 25% of adults (Harrison 22e p.2070). Surgical closure (not percutaneous) is required for primum ASDs, sinus venosus defects, and coronary sinus septal defects; a sinus venosus defect is not actually a defect of the atrial septum but a communication near the SVC- or IVC-atrial junction with right pulmonary veins (Harrison 22e p.2070-2071). VSDs are the most common congenital anomaly recognized at birth but account for only ~10% of adult CHD, owing to the high rate of spontaneous closure of small VSDs in early life; the most common location is the membranous (perimembranous/outlet) septum (Harrison 22e p.2071-2072). Outcome for adults with small VSDs WITHOUT ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension is generally excellent; small muscular defects persisting into adulthood are often pressure- and flow-restricted with no significant hemodynamic consequence (Harrison 22e p.2072). Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common form of cyanotic CHD (~0.5 per 1000 live births) and comprises anterior conal-septal deviation causing RV outflow tract obstruction, a VSD, RV hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta (Harrison 22e p.2073). In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary regurgitation is common and is usually associated with RV dilation; accurate quantification of RV size, function, and mass is particularly important because RV dilation, dysfunction, and hypertrophy are associated with adverse outcomes, and cardiac MRI is routinely used for surveillance (Harrison 22e p.2073-2074). Eisenmenger syndrome is the consequence of a long-standing high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunt: excessive pulmonary blood flow leads to severely increased pulmonary vascular resistance that eventually REVERSES the shunt, creating bidirectional or right-to-left flow and cyanosis; it can complicate any CHD with an initial left-to-right shunt (Harrison 22e p.2078). Selective pulmonary vasodilators such as bosentan or sildenafil are efficacious in Eisenmenger syndrome; select patients may be candidates for combined heart-lung transplantation, or preferably lung transplantation with concomitant repair of the intracardiac defect when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2078). Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures is advised in high-risk CHD lesions: unrepaired cyanotic CHD (including palliative shunts/conduits), completely repaired defects during the first 6 months after repair, and repaired CHD with residual defects adjacent to prosthetic material (Harrison 22e p.745, Table 133-9). Reversal of a left-to-right shunt to right-to-left flow with cyanosis = Eisenmenger syndrome; develops from severely elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and is a multi-organ condition Right heart dilation in an unrepaired ASD without other cause signals risk of progression to symptomatic right heart failure, atrial arrhythmias, and pulmonary arterial hypertension QRS duration >=180 ms on resting ECG in repaired tetralogy of Fallot — associated with increased risk of ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death Systemic RV dysfunction after atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) for D-loop TGA — the most worrisome long-term complication, with no proven effective medical therapy Pregnancy in a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated due to high risk of maternal mortality; pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe systemic ventricular dysfunction are WHO class IV (extremely high maternal risk) New exercise-capacity decline in ACHD may be unrecognized by the patient; by the time symptoms appear, irreversible physiologic changes may already have occurred Confusing a PFO (flap-valve patency, present in up to 25% of adults, no right heart dilation) with a true secundum ASD. Assuming all ASDs are amenable to percutaneous closure — large defects, inadequate tissue rims, and anomalous draining pulmonary veins make device closure unfavorable, and primum/sinus venosus/coronary sinus defects require surgery. Overlooking that a sinus venosus defect is not in the atrial septum itself, so it may be missed without dedicated imaging. Routine phlebotomy in an asymptomatic adult with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated; elevated hematocrit appropriate to the degree of cyanosis should not be lowered reflexively, and iron deficiency should be corrected because it impairs quality of life and function. Using teratogenic medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct oral anticoagulants, endothelin receptor blockers) in CHD patients of childbearing potential; estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided in Eisenmenger syndrome due to thrombogenicity. Failing to test adults with conotruncal defects for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) — many were never tested, and unrecognized cognitive/psychiatric disability may go untreated. Treating an ACHD patient's seemingly minor lesion without recognizing limited hemodynamic reserve and subclinical multi-organ dysfunction before noncardiac surgery. The normal heart is analyzed segmentally (atria, ventricles, great arteries joined by the atrioventricular canal and conus), with attention to alignment (what drains into what) and connection (how segments are physically linked). The heart forms from the third week of gestation and is nearly complete by 8 weeks; cardiac neural crest cells migrating in weeks 5-6 are essential for outflow septation, semilunar valve formation, and aortic arch patterning, so disturbance of these processes underlies conotruncal defects. Shunt lesions are defined by the relative compliance, pressure, and outflow resistance of the connected chambers/vessels and the defect size. Left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA) move oxygenated blood toward the deoxygenated (right) side, volume-loading the pulmonary circulation: ASD/PAPVR (proximal to the tricuspid valve) cause right heart dilation, whereas VSD/PDA (below the tricuspid valve) cause left heart dilation. Sustained high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunting can raise pulmonary vascular resistance to the point that the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger physiology, right-to-left, cyanosis). Tetralogy of Fallot produces a right-to-left shunt across the VSD because RV outflow obstruction raises right-sided systolic pressure, mixing deoxygenated blood into the LV and causing systemic arterial cyanosis. In transposition of the great arteries the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, creating parallel rather than series circulations that are incompatible with life unless mixing exists (ASD, VSD, or PDA). Outcomes vary widely by lesion. Adults with small VSDs without ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension generally have an excellent prognosis. Repaired coarctation patients generally do well but remain at risk for systemic hypertension, premature atherosclerosis, LV failure, and aortic aneurysm/dissection and recoarctation. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, one prospective cohort of 144 adults showed 72% survival at 40 years but only 25% cumulative event-free survival (events: reintervention, most commonly pulmonary valve replacement; symptomatic arrhythmia; heart failure); LV dysfunction is present in at least 20%. The arterial switch operation for D-loop TGA has produced substantial long-term survival, whereas atrial switch leaves a systemic RV prone to dysfunction. Adults with Eisenmenger syndrome have significant morbidity but generally survive longer than patients with other forms of pulmonary arterial hypertension. In aggregate, adults with CHD have quality-of-life-limiting comorbidities and premature mortality far exceeding age-matched controls, and nearly all can be classified as stage A heart failure or greater; care within a center that has an ACHD specialty program is associated with improved overall survival. The chapter applies the modified World Health Organization (mWHO) classification of maternal risk in heart disease during pregnancy, graded mWHO I (no detectable increased mortality risk, e.g., small/mild lesions) through mWHO IV (extremely high maternal mortality risk; pregnancy generally contraindicated). Examples by class: mWHO II includes unoperated ASD/VSD and repaired tetralogy of Fallot; mWHO III includes mechanical valve, systemic RV, and Fontan circulation; mWHO IV includes pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <30% or NYHA III-IV), severe aortic dilatation, and Fontan with any complication. The CARPREG II weighted-risk score is also described (highest 3-point factors: prior cardiac event/arrhythmia, NYHA >=III, mechanical valve), stratifying predicted cardiac-event risk from 5% (<=1 point) to 41% (>4 points). For repaired tetralogy of Fallot, potential sequelae are catalogued in Table 280-3 and long-term sequelae of D-loop TGA surgery in Table 280-4.

occur when there is associated biliary ductal dilatation Management targets complications, including variceal bleeding, cholangitis, and associated renal disease, with liver or combined liver-kidney transplantation in selected cases Haematemesis or melaena from variceal bleeding Fever with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain indicating cholangitis Progressive renal impairment from associated kidney disease Rapidly enlarging spleen with worsening cytopenias from hypersplenism Mistaking preserved liver enzymes for absence of significant disease despite marked portal hypertension Overlooking the associated renal cystic disease that may dominate the long-term prognosis Failing to distinguish presinusoidal portal hypertension from true cirrhosis Not screening for and managing oesophageal varices before a first bleed Missing coexisting Caroli disease and the associated cholangitis and stone risk During normal development the embryonic ductal plate remodels to form the intrahepatic bile ducts. In congenital hepatic fibrosis this remodelling is arrested, leaving a ductal plate malformation in which persistent, irregularly shaped and ectatic bile ductules are embedded in broad bands of dense portal fibrosis. This fibrosis expands the portal tracts and compresses the portal vein branches, producing presinusoidal portal hypertension while sparing the hepatocytes, so synthetic function is largely maintained. The same ciliopathy mechanism, frequently due to PKHD1 mutations affecting fibrocystin, links the liver lesion to renal cystic disease and to overlapping conditions such as Caroli disease. Because hepatocellular function is usually preserved, the outlook depends chiefly on control of portal hypertensive complications, recurrent cholangitis, and the severity of associated renal disease; many patients do well for years, and transplantation is reserved for refractory complications.

threatening brain injury Very high glucose infusion requirements that cannot maintain normoglycaemia Failure to respond to diazoxide, indicating likely KATP channel disease needing escalation Signs of an underlying overgrowth or metabolic syndrome requiring broader evaluation Failing to obtain a critical blood sample during hypoglycaemia, losing the key diagnostic biochemistry Tolerating borderline glucose levels and underestimating the risk of permanent neurological damage Assuming diazoxide will work in KATP channel disease and delaying escalation or surgery Proceeding to extensive surgery without imaging to distinguish focal from diffuse disease Insulin secretion is normally gated by the beta-cell KATP channel, which closes as ATP rises to trigger release. In congenital hyperinsulinism, inactivating mutations in the channel genes ABCC8 or KCNJ11, or defects in other regulators of insulin secretion, cause the channel to remain closed, so insulin is released regardless of the prevailing glucose. Unregulated insulin drives profound hypoglycaemia and simultaneously suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis, depriving the brain of alternative fuels and creating a high risk of neurological injury. Focal disease reflects a localised somatic event superimposed on a paternally inherited mutation. Outcome depends on prompt prevention of hypoglycaemia to protect the brain; focal disease can be cured by targeted resection, whereas diffuse KATP channel disease is often medically resistant and may require near-total pancreatectomy with later risk of diabetes.

Congenital hypothyroidism — CH, neonatal hypothyroidism, cretinism, congenital thyroid deficiency Transient neonatal hypothyroidism (e.g. maternal antithyroid drugs, iodine exposure, maternal antibodies) Central (secondary/tertiary) hypothyroidism Other causes of prolonged neonatal jaundice Down syndrome and other conditions with hypotonia and feeding difficulty Constitutional causes of poor feeding and lethargy Newborn screening TSH and/or T4 on heel-prick blood Confirmatory serum free T4 and TSH Thyroid imaging (ultrasound and/or radionuclide scan) to define aetiology Maternal thyroid history and antibody status where relevant Knee radiograph for bone age in some cases to assess in utero severity One of the most common preventable causes of intellectual disability, resulting from inadequate thyroid hormone at birth or in early infancy. Most affected newborns appear normal at birth because of transplacental maternal thyroid hormone, so clinical detection is unreliable and newborn screening is essential. The commonest cause worldwide is thyroid dysgenesis (aplasia, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland); dyshormonogenesis and, in some regions, iodine deficiency also contribute. Later clinical features include prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, lethargy, constipation, a large fontanelle, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and hoarse cry. Screening measures TSH and/or T4 on a heel-prick sample; a raised TSH with low T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. Treatment is early thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, and the key to normal neurodevelopment is starting therapy as early as possible. Regular monitoring of growth, development, and thyroid function is needed to keep levels in the target range during infancy. Delay in starting treatment is associated with irreversible loss of cognitive potential, making prompt recognition critical. Positive newborn screen requiring urgent confirmation and treatment Signs of significant hypothyroidism (marked lethargy, poor feeding, hypothermia) Prolonged unexplained neonatal jaundice Delayed diagnosis beyond the early weeks of life, risking neurodevelopmental harm Relying on clinical signs, which are usually absent or subtle in the newborn period Delaying treatment while awaiting further tests once screening is clearly abnormal Under- or over-treating due to infrequent monitoring during infancy Missing central hypothyroidism when screening is TSH-based only Thyroid hormone is essential for normal brain growth and myelination, particularly in the first years of life. In congenital hypothyroidism, deficient hormone production results from failure of thyroid gland development, an enzymatic defect in hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis), inadequate iodine substrate, or, less commonly, hypothalamic-pituitary (central) dysfunction. In primary disease, low circulating thyroid hormone removes negative feedback on the pituitary, raising TSH. Because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta, the fetus is partly protected in utero, but after birth the untreated infant becomes progressively hypothyroid, and prolonged deficiency during the critical window of brain development produces permanent neurological injury. With early diagnosis through screening and prompt, adequately dosed replacement, neurodevelopmental outcome is typically normal; delayed or inadequate treatment risks permanent intellectual impairment.

biallelic variants in LCT, the gene encoding the brush-border enzyme lactase-phlorizin hydrolase. Without functional lactase, dietary lactose cannot be hydrolysed to glucose and galactose in the small intestine. The unabsorbed disaccharide is osmotically active, drawing water into the lumen and passing to the colon where bacterial fermentation generates gas and short-chain acids. This produces acidic, watery, gassy diarrhoea from the earliest milk feeds, with a structurally normal mucosa distinguishing it from secondary lactase deficiency due to mucosal damage. Prognosis is excellent with a strict lactose-free diet, and growth and development proceed normally. The enzyme deficiency is permanent, so dietary avoidance is lifelong.

newborn has a 46,XX karyotype without confirmation Confusing lipoid CAH with milder forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia Neglecting stress-dose glucocorticoid cover during illness or surgery The steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR) transports cholesterol into mitochondria, the essential first committed step for synthesising all steroid hormones. When StAR function is lost, cholesterol cannot be delivered for conversion, so production of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids fails across the adrenal cortex and gonads. Cholesterol and its esters accumulate within steroidogenic cells, causing the swollen lipid-laden glands and progressive cellular damage that further impairs any residual steroidogenesis. Because androgen synthesis fails, 46,XY fetuses do not virilise and are born with female-appearing genitalia. Survival depends on prompt recognition and lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement with stress dosing during illness; gonadal steroid replacement is needed at puberty, and fertility is generally severely impaired.

a child remains ambulant Not distinguishing subtypes, which is essential for prognosis, counselling, and surveillance Missing the associated eye and brain anomalies of the dystroglycanopathies Attributing neonatal hypotonia to a central cause without considering a muscle disorder The congenital muscular dystrophies result from variants in genes encoding proteins of the muscle-fibre basement membrane, extracellular matrix, or the glycosylation machinery that modifies alpha-dystroglycan. Loss of laminin alpha-2 (merosin) or collagen VI weakens the link between the muscle fibre and its surrounding matrix, while defective glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan impairs its binding to matrix ligands and, in the brain, disrupts neuronal migration. These defects cause early muscle-fibre injury and dystrophic change and, in the dystroglycanopathies, associated structural brain and eye malformations. The particular protein affected determines whether disease is confined to muscle or extends to the central nervous system. Prognosis varies enormously by subtype, from severe neonatal forms such as Walker-Warburg syndrome with early mortality to milder collagen VI-related disease compatible with prolonged survival. Respiratory involvement is often the principal determinant of outcome, so early respiratory surveillance and support are critical.

family history Episodic apnoea or respiratory crises, particularly during febrile illness in infants Rapidly worsening bulbar weakness with aspiration Deterioration after starting an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, suggesting a subtype that it worsens Feeding difficulty with failure to thrive Misdiagnosing a congenital myasthenic syndrome as seronegative autoimmune myasthenia and giving immunotherapy Prescribing acetylcholinesterase inhibitors empirically in subtypes where they are harmful Overlooking episodic apnoea syndromes that require an emergency respiratory plan Assuming absent antibodies means no neuromuscular junction disorder Congenital myasthenic syndromes arise from inherited defects in proteins essential for neuromuscular transmission, classified by the location of the defect as presynaptic, synaptic (basal lamina) or postsynaptic. Postsynaptic forms are the most common, including acetylcholine receptor deficiency (often CHRNE), kinetic abnormalities of the receptor channel (slow- and fast-channel syndromes), and defects in receptor clustering proteins such as rapsyn and the agrin-MuSK-DOK7 pathway. Each defect reduces the safety factor for transmission, so that acetylcholine release, receptor function or endplate architecture is insufficient to reliably generate a muscle action potential, producing fatigable weakness. Because the process is structural or kinetic rather than immune-mediated, there is no autoantibody and responses to specific therapies depend on the underlying mechanism. Prognosis varies widely by subtype: many forms are compatible with long, functional lives especially once correctly treated, while some cause significant disability or life-threatening apnoeic episodes. Accurate genetic diagnosis substantially improves outcomes by guiding targeted therapy.

from the hypercoagulable state Severe refractory oedema with respiratory or feeding compromise Progressive decline toward end-stage kidney disease requiring renal replacement Trialling corticosteroids or immunosuppression, which are ineffective in this genetic barrier defect Overlooking secondary hypothyroidism from urinary loss of thyroxine-binding globulin Underestimating infection and thrombosis risk from urinary loss of immunoglobulins and anticoagulant proteins Delaying genetic diagnosis, which is essential for prognosis and family counselling Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in NPHS1, encoding nephrin, a transmembrane protein that forms the structural backbone of the glomerular slit diaphragm between podocyte foot processes. Loss of functional nephrin disrupts this size- and charge-selective filtration barrier, so plasma proteins, chiefly albumin, leak massively into the urine from before birth. The resulting hypoalbuminaemia produces severe oedema, while urinary loss of immunoglobulins, anticoagulant and hormone-binding proteins predisposes to infection, thrombosis and endocrine disturbance, and ongoing podocyte injury leads to progressive glomerulosclerosis and kidney failure. Without intensive supportive care the outlook in infancy is poor, but with modern management of protein losses, nutrition and infection, and progression to dialysis and transplantation, long-term survival is achievable in specialist centres.

Congenital Pneumonia — neonatal pneumonia, intrauterine pneumonia, early-onset neonatal pneumonia Respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency) Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Meconium aspiration syndrome Early-onset sepsis without pneumonia Congenital heart disease Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Chest radiograph Blood culture and full blood count with differential Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein Pulse oximetry and blood gas Lumbar puncture when sepsis or meningitis is suspected Maternal history and cultures (group B streptococcus status, chorioamnionitis) Pneumonia acquired before or during birth typically presents as respiratory distress in the first hours to days of life and often forms part of early-onset neonatal sepsis. Infection may be acquired transplacentally, by ascending spread from the genital tract (especially with prolonged rupture of membranes or chorioamnionitis), or during passage through the birth canal. Group B streptococcus and Escherichia coli are leading bacterial causes; other organisms include Listeria, and congenital infections such as certain viruses can also involve the lungs. Clinical features overlap with other causes of neonatal respiratory distress, so it is often difficult to distinguish pneumonia from surfactant deficiency or transient tachypnoea on presentation. Maternal and perinatal risk factors, particularly chorioamnionitis, prolonged membrane rupture, and maternal group B streptococcus colonisation, raise the likelihood and guide management. Chest radiographs may show diffuse or patchy opacities, but findings can mimic respiratory distress syndrome, so imaging is supportive rather than definitive. Because differentiating infection from non-infectious causes is difficult, empirical antibiotics covering likely organisms are usually started while cultures and the clinical course are followed. Supportive care to maintain oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, and perfusion is essential alongside antimicrobial therapy. Severe or worsening respiratory distress and rising oxygen requirement Signs of septic shock or poor perfusion Apnoea Persistent pulmonary hypertension with labile oxygenation Deterioration despite initial supportive measures Attributing respiratory distress solely to surfactant deficiency and delaying antibiotics in an at-risk infant Underweighting maternal risk factors such as chorioamnionitis or prolonged membrane rupture Relying on chest radiograph appearance to exclude infection given its overlap with other conditions Failing to evaluate for accompanying bacteraemia or meningitis Organisms reach the fetal or newborn lung by several routes: transplacental spread during maternal bloodstream infection, ascending colonisation of amniotic fluid after membrane rupture or with chorioamnionitis, and aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or genital secretions around delivery. Once in the alveoli, pathogens trigger an inflammatory response with exudate, impaired gas exchange, and interference with surfactant function. In early-onset disease this frequently coexists with bacteraemia and systemic sepsis, so lung involvement is often one component of a generalised infection in the vulnerable newborn. With prompt recognition and appropriate antibiotics and supportive care many infants recover well, but outcome depends on the organism, gestational age, and severity; fulminant early-onset sepsis with pneumonia, particularly from group B streptococcus, can be life-threatening.

Congenital sideroblastic anaemia — hereditary sideroblastic anaemia, X-linked sideroblastic anaemia, ALAS2-related sideroblastic anaemia, SLC25A38 sideroblastic anaemia, XLSA, congenital sideroblastic anemia Acquired clonal sideroblastic anaemia (myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts) Iron deficiency and other microcytic anaemias Thalassaemia syndromes Lead poisoning impairing haem synthesis Copper deficiency or zinc excess causing sideroblastic change Alcohol- or drug-induced (for example isoniazid) reversible sideroblastic anaemia Bone marrow aspirate with Perls (Prussian blue) iron stain to demonstrate ring sideroblasts Full blood count and blood film assessing red cell indices and dimorphism Iron studies including ferritin and transferrin saturation to gauge overload Targeted next-generation sequencing panel (ALAS2, SLC25A38, and syndromic genes) A supervised pyridoxine trial where ALAS2 disease is likely Screening for syndromic features such as diabetes, deafness, or exocrine pancreatic dysfunction A group of inherited anaemias defined by ring sideroblasts in the marrow, reflecting iron-laden mitochondria encircling the erythroblast nucleus The commonest form is X-linked, caused by ALAS2 mutations affecting the first enzyme of haem synthesis, and characteristically responds to pyridoxine Autosomal recessive SLC25A38 disease is the next most frequent and tends to be more severe and pyridoxine-unresponsive Syndromic variants exist, including mitochondrial DNA deletion in Pearson syndrome and SLC19A2-related thiamine-responsive anaemia with diabetes and deafness The blood film typically shows a dimorphic or hypochromic microcytic anaemia, though the mean cell volume can be normal or raised in some forms Systemic iron overload develops even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin and enhances iron absorption Diagnosis combines iron-stained marrow showing ring sideroblasts with targeted gene panels; a pyridoxine trial is warranted where ALAS2 disease is suspected Evidence of iron overload with cardiac, hepatic, or endocrine dysfunction despite few or no transfusions Severe transfusion-dependent anaemia presenting in infancy Syndromic features suggesting mitochondrial disease such as lactic acidosis or multiorgan failure Progressive cytopenias raising concern for clonal or marrow-failure evolution Assuming a microcytic anaemia is iron deficiency and giving iron, which worsens overload Missing the pyridoxine-responsive ALAS2 phenotype and failing to trial the vitamin Confusing congenital disease with acquired myelodysplasia, which requires different management Neglecting iron chelation because the patient is not transfusion dependent Congenital sideroblastic anaemias result from defects that impair mitochondrial haem biosynthesis, iron-sulphur cluster assembly, or mitochondrial protein handling within developing erythroblasts. When haem synthesis stalls, iron that has been imported into the mitochondrion cannot be incorporated into protoporphyrin and instead accumulates as insoluble deposits in perinuclear mitochondria, producing the pathognomonic ring sideroblast. ALAS2 mutations cripple delta-aminolaevulinate synthase, the pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent first committed step of the pathway; SLC25A38 disrupts the mitochondrial glycine transporter that supplies substrate. The failure of effective haemoglobinisation causes ineffective erythropoiesis, and the accompanying suppression of hepcidin drives excess dietary iron absorption and progressive parenchymal iron loading. Outcome depends on subtype: pyridoxine-responsive ALAS2 disease can be well controlled, whereas SLC25A38 and syndromic forms are more severe, and long-term morbidity is dominated by iron overload requiring vigilant monitoring and chelation.

acidosis requiring correction Associated congenital anomalies indicating the syndromic form Growth failure from inadequate sodium replacement Confusing the acidotic, high-sodium picture with congenital chloride diarrhoea Underestimating ongoing sodium losses and under-replacing, causing chronic depletion and poor growth Overlooking the diagnosis in a neonate with diarrhoea attributed to feed intolerance Failing to look for associated anomalies that suggest the SPINT2-related syndrome Congenital sodium diarrhoea reflects failure of electroneutral sodium absorption across the intestinal epithelium. Loss-of-function variants in SLC9A3, which encodes the apical sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE3, impair sodium and fluid reabsorption. Activating variants in GUCY2C (guanylate cyclase 2C) raise intracellular cyclic GMP, inhibiting NHE3 and promoting chloride and fluid secretion, mimicking an enterotoxin-driven state. In both routes luminal sodium and water are retained, producing a secretory diarrhoea with high faecal sodium, systemic sodium depletion, and metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. The SPINT2-associated syndromic form combines the enteropathy with developmental anomalies. Adequate and sustained sodium, fluid and bicarbonate replacement generally permits satisfactory growth, and some children reduce supplementation over time with intestinal adaptation. Syndromic disease carries added morbidity from associated anomalies.

Conjunctivitis — pink eye, red eye, bacterial conjunctivitis, viral conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis Acute anterior uveitis Acute angle-closure glaucoma Bacterial keratitis or corneal ulcer Scleritis and episcleritis Subconjunctival haemorrhage Dry eye and blepharitis Clinical examination assessing discharge type, follicles/papillae, and preauricular nodes Visual acuity and fluorescein staining to exclude corneal involvement Conjunctival swabs for culture in severe, hyperacute, neonatal, or non-resolving cases Testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in suspected sexually transmitted or neonatal conjunctivitis Slit-lamp examination to exclude keratitis, uveitis, and angle closure Presents with a red, gritty, or irritable eye with discharge, but crucially with normal vision, a clear cornea, normal pupil, and no significant pain — features that distinguish it from serious causes of the red eye Bacterial conjunctivitis produces purulent, sticky discharge with lids stuck together in the morning; it is usually self-limiting Viral (often adenoviral) conjunctivitis gives watery discharge, follicles, a preauricular node, and is highly contagious, frequently following an upper respiratory infection Allergic conjunctivitis is bilateral and itchy with watery discharge, chemosis, and papillae, often with a personal history of atopy Redness is diffuse and superficial, sparing the circumcorneal zone seen in keratitis and uveitis Most cases are managed supportively with hygiene measures; topical antibiotics are used for bacterial cases and antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops for allergic disease Hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge suggests gonococcal infection and is an emergency because it can rapidly perforate the cornea Reduced vision, significant pain, or photophobia — points away from simple conjunctivitis to a sight-threatening cause Circumcorneal injection, a hazy cornea, or an abnormal pupil suggesting keratitis, uveitis, or angle closure Hyperacute profuse purulent discharge (possible gonococcal infection) risking rapid corneal perforation Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), which requires urgent evaluation for chlamydia and gonococcus Labelling any red eye as conjunctivitis and missing keratitis, uveitis, or angle-closure glaucoma Prescribing topical steroids inappropriately and worsening an undiagnosed herpetic keratitis Overlooking contact lens wear, which raises the risk of sight-threatening keratitis Failing to recognise hyperacute gonococcal or neonatal conjunctivitis as emergencies Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the mucous membrane lining the eyelids and covering the sclera. It arises from infection (bacterial or viral), allergy, or irritation. Inflammatory mediators dilate conjunctival vessels (causing redness) and increase vascular permeability (causing chemosis and discharge), while the cellular response produces follicles in viral and chlamydial disease or papillae in bacterial and allergic disease. Because the process is confined to the conjunctiva and spares the cornea, anterior chamber, and intraocular structures, vision and pupil responses remain normal in uncomplicated cases. Most bacterial, viral, and allergic conjunctivitis is self-limiting or responds readily to treatment with an excellent visual prognosis; serious outcomes occur mainly with gonococcal, chlamydial, or misdiagnosed sight-threatening mimics.

often asymmetric or sectorial, are a common and important association The stippled epiphyses tend to disappear after infancy, so early imaging is more informative A key differential is a phenocopy confirmed by EBP testing Dense or progressive cataracts threatening vision in infancy Rapidly progressive scoliosis requiring orthopaedic intervention Severe neonatal skin involvement with barrier compromise An affected male, prompting evaluation for mosaicism and a guarded prognosis Missing a warfarin-exposure phenocopy through inadequate medication history Delaying radiographs so that transient stippled epiphyses are no longer visible Overlooking asymmetric cataracts that need timely ophthalmic treatment Assuming autosomal recessive rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata and mismanaging counselling Conradi-Hunermann syndrome is caused by mutations in EBP, encoding emopamil-binding protein, an enzyme (sterol delta-8, delta-7 isomerase) acting late in cholesterol biosynthesis. Loss of enzyme activity leads to accumulation of abnormal sterol precursors and a relative deficiency of cholesterol in developing tissues, disturbing sterol-dependent developmental signalling and cartilage and skin development. Because the gene is X-linked and the trait behaves as dominant, random X-inactivation in females produces the mosaic, Blaschko-line pattern of skin and skeletal involvement, while non-mosaic affected males usually do not survive. Affected females usually survive with variable orthopaedic, ophthalmological and dermatological problems and generally normal cognition, whereas the non-mosaic male phenotype is typically severe or lethal; long-term care focuses on scoliosis, cataracts and skin.

Contact dermatitis — contact eczema, allergic contact dermatitis, irritant contact dermatitis Atopic dermatitis Seborrhoeic dermatitis Nummular (discoid) eczema Tinea (dermatophyte infection) Psoriasis on the hands or feet Cellulitis when acute unilateral limb involvement mimics infection Patch testing to identify causative allergens in suspected allergic contact dermatitis Detailed occupational, cosmetic, and hobby exposure history Skin swabs if secondary bacterial infection is suspected Skin scrapings or mycology to exclude dermatophyte infection Skin biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases Distinguish irritant contact dermatitis (direct chemical or physical damage, no prior sensitisation, often stinging or burning) from allergic contact dermatitis (a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is typically itchy) The distribution of the rash is the key clue to the culprit; sharply demarcated eruptions localised to sites of contact point to an external cause Common irritants include water, soaps, detergents, and solvents, while frequent allergens include nickel, fragrances, preservatives, rubber accelerators, and topical medicaments Acute lesions are erythematous, oedematous, and vesicular; chronic exposure produces dryness, scaling, fissuring, and lichenification Patch testing is the definitive method to identify a contact allergen, whereas irritant dermatitis is largely a clinical diagnosis Cornerstone management is identification and avoidance of the offending agent alongside barrier restoration with emollients and, for flares, topical corticosteroids Occupational exposure is a common driver (e.g. hairdressers, healthcare and construction workers), so take a detailed work and hobby history Widespread or erythrodermic involvement with systemic upset Rapidly spreading eruption with fever suggesting secondary infection or an alternative diagnosis Airborne or facial involvement with eyelid swelling affecting vision Occupational disease threatening ability to work and requiring formal assessment Failing to perform patch testing and thus missing a treatable allergen Overlooking a relevant occupational or cosmetic exposure in the history Assuming persistent hand eczema is purely irritant when a superimposed allergy exists Applying a topical product that itself contains a sensitising allergen and perpetuates the dermatitis Contact dermatitis has two principal mechanisms. Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct, non-immunological damage to the epidermal barrier by chemical or physical agents, triggering innate inflammation; severity relates to the concentration and duration of exposure. Allergic contact dermatitis is a type IV, T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity reaction: after an initial sensitisation phase in which small-molecule haptens bind skin proteins and prime allergen-specific T cells, re-exposure elicits an inflammatory eczematous response over one to several days. Repeated insult impairs the barrier further, perpetuating inflammation and, over time, chronic lichenified changes. Prognosis is excellent when the causative agent is identified and avoided; persistent exposure, especially occupational, leads to chronic relapsing dermatitis and may necessitate a change of work.
