latex Contact urticaria is an immediate wheal-and-flare reaction appearing within minutes of skin contact with a triggering substance, unlike the delayed pattern of allergic contact dermatitis It is divided into non-immunological reactions (direct release of mediators, for example from certain foods, plants or chemicals) and immunological IgE-mediated reactions in sensitised individuals Natural rubber latex is a classic occupational cause, notably in healthcare and among workers using latex gloves Food handlers, bakers, farmers, hairdressers and healthcare staff are commonly affected occupational groups Immunological contact urticaria can progress to generalised urticaria, angioedema, respiratory symptoms and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis The hands are the usual site of occupational reactions, and symptoms typically settle when contact ends Diagnosis is supported by the history and by cautious skin testing or specific IgE, with provocation testing done carefully because of the anaphylaxis risk Management centres on identifying and avoiding the trigger, using substitutes such as non-latex gloves, and having a plan for systemic reactions Progression to angioedema, wheeze or anaphylaxis requiring emergency treatment Widespread reaction beyond the site of contact History of previous severe systemic reaction on re-exposure Respiratory symptoms accompanying skin reactions Confusing immediate contact urticaria with delayed allergic contact dermatitis and choosing the wrong test Performing provocation testing without resuscitation facilities in a potentially anaphylactic patient Failing to recognise latex as a cause and continuing latex glove use Overlooking associated respiratory allergy Not providing an emergency plan for those at risk of systemic reactions In the immunological form, prior sensitisation leads to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells; re-exposure cross-links IgE and triggers rapid mast cell degranulation with histamine release, producing the immediate wheal and flare and, if extensive, systemic effects. In the non-immunological form, substances act directly to release vasoactive mediators without prior sensitisation, generally causing localised reactions. Symptoms usually resolve once the causative contact is avoided, and the outlook is good with effective avoidance; however, sensitised individuals remain at risk of severe reactions on re-exposure, and latex allergy in particular can have systemic consequences.

Contrast-induced nephropathy — CIN, contrast-associated acute kidney injury, CA-AKI, contrast nephropathy Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis from hypotension or the underlying illness Atheroembolic (cholesterol embolisation) renal disease after arterial procedures Prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion Other nephrotoxic drug injury Obstructive uropathy Progression of underlying chronic kidney disease Baseline and serial serum creatinine with estimated GFR before and after contrast exposure Urinalysis and urine microscopy to help distinguish tubular injury from other causes Assessment of volume status and review of the medication list for other nephrotoxins Consideration of atheroembolic disease (eosinophilia, skin changes) after arterial catheterisation Renal ultrasound if obstruction or another structural cause is suspected Contrast-induced nephropathy is an acute, usually reversible decline in renal function occurring within a few days of intravascular iodinated contrast, once other causes have been excluded The rise in creatinine typically begins within one to three days and peaks around three to five days, with recovery over one to two weeks in most cases Pre-existing chronic kidney disease is the strongest risk factor, and the risk rises steeply when diabetic nephropathy is also present Volume depletion, heart failure, higher contrast volumes, and concurrent nephrotoxins compound the risk The most effective preventive measure is adequate intravenous volume expansion with isotonic fluid before and after contrast exposure Non-essential nephrotoxic drugs should be withheld around the time of the study and the smallest necessary volume of contrast used The true incidence of contrast-related injury after intravenous contrast in modern practice is lower than once believed, and the need for imaging should be weighed against a frequently modest risk Progressive or non-recovering renal function suggesting an alternative or additional cause Oliguria or features of established acute kidney injury requiring supportive care Signs of atheroembolism such as livedo, digital ischaemia, and eosinophilia after arterial procedures Hyperkalaemia, acidosis, or fluid overload indicating a need for closer monitoring or dialysis Withholding a clinically necessary contrast study out of exaggerated fear of nephropathy in a low-risk patient Failing to provide adequate periprocedural volume expansion in high-risk patients Attributing all post-contrast creatinine rises to contrast without considering atheroembolism or ischaemic injury Overlooking continued exposure to other nephrotoxic drugs during the vulnerable period Contrast-induced nephropathy is thought to arise from a combination of renal medullary ischaemia and direct tubular toxicity. Iodinated contrast alters intrarenal haemodynamics, causing vasoconstriction and reduced medullary blood flow, which is particularly damaging to the metabolically active outer medulla. Contrast media also generate reactive oxygen species and exert direct toxic effects on tubular epithelial cells, and their osmotic and viscosity properties can impair tubular flow. The result is a predominantly acute tubular injury pattern. Patients with reduced baseline renal reserve, impaired autoregulation, or reduced effective circulating volume are least able to compensate for these insults, which explains the clustering of risk in chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and volume depletion. Most episodes are mild and self-limiting, with renal function returning toward baseline within one to two weeks. However, an episode is associated with longer hospital stay, higher risk of needing dialysis in susceptible patients, and worse long-term cardiovascular and renal outcomes, so prevention in high-risk individuals remains important.

COPD exacerbation (non-infective) — ABG CXR to exclude pneumonia/pneumothorax Distinguish infective trigger — may need antibiotics Pneumonia (a common abnormal finding on chest imaging during a presumed exacerbation) (p.2258) Congestive heart failure / decompensated heart failure (a frequent imaging finding and recognized comorbidity that can mimic or coexist with exacerbation) (p.2258) Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings or large-airway obstruction can mimic an exacerbation) (p.2258) Pulmonary embolism, whose incidence is increased in the setting of COPD exacerbation and should be actively considered (p.2258, p.2259) Pneumonia identified on chest x-ray or CT in a patient presenting as an exacerbation (~25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal, most often pneumonia) (p.2258) Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as Pco2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2258) Use of arterial pH alongside Pco2 to classify ventilatory failure (Pco2 >45 mmHg) as acute (acidemic) versus chronic, since pH changes ~0.08/10 mmHg acutely versus ~0.03/10 mmHg chronically (p.2255) Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal findings, to detect pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax (p.2258) Consideration of investigation for pulmonary embolism given its increased incidence in exacerbations (p.2259) Complete blood count with differential for blood eosinophil count to guide exacerbation-risk management (p.2255) An expert-consensus objective scheme using dyspnea, vital signs, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity (more applicable in the emergency department than outpatient setting) (p.2259) Congestive heart failure (frequent abnormal imaging finding mimicking exacerbation) (p.2258) Pneumothorax (may produce chest asymmetry mimicking an exacerbation) (p.2258) Pulmonary embolism (increased incidence during COPD exacerbations) (p.2259) An exacerbation is an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or change in sputum amount or character), typically evolving over less than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2258). COPD exacerbation is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis; spirometry/pulmonary function testing has not been shown to help diagnose or manage an exacerbation, in contrast to its role in asthma (p.2259). The single strongest predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the greatest single risk factor for hospitalization is a previous hospitalization for exacerbation (p.2258). Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens; patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average about 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients exacerbate infrequently (p.2258). Assess both the severity of the current exacerbation and the severity of the underlying COPD, because the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission (p.2258). Examination should focus on degree of distress, tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, ability to speak in full sentences, mental status, and paradoxical abdominal wall motion (p.2258). Blood eosinophil count (from CBC differential) is used to stratify exacerbation risk and to guide whether inhaled corticosteroids are added; counts below 100 cells/microliter derive no benefit while benefit rises above 100 and is favored above 300 (p.2255, p.2256). Non-infective precipitants are well recognized: air pollution (including extreme-heat days), allergens, pulmonary embolism, and medication nonadherence; in a notable minority no precipitant is identified (p.2253, p.2258). Environmental exposure and Aspergillus sensitization can drive some COPD exacerbations, relevant to the eosinophilic/allergic exacerbation phenotype (p.1756). Cor pulmonale (overt right heart failure) is now relatively uncommon since supplemental oxygen became standard, but pulmonary hypertension should be considered in patients with persistent activity limitation or lower-extremity edema; it typically arises with FEV1 <25% predicted and chronic hypoxemia (Pao2 <55 mmHg), though some develop it from vascular destruction independent of obstruction severity (p.2252, p.2254). Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (Paco2 >45 mmHg and pH <=7.35) indicating acute respiratory failure and a need for ventilatory support (p.2255, p.2259) New or worsening hypoxemia (p.2259) Mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in complete sentences, or impaired cooperation (p.2258, p.2259) Paradoxical abdominal wall motion, marked accessory muscle use, and central cyanosis signaling impending respiratory failure (p.2258) Significant comorbidity such as heart failure, or an unsafe living situation, favoring inpatient management (p.2259) New digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD itself and should prompt a search for another cause such as lung cancer (p.2254) Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention: oxygen targeted to SpO2 88-92% is appropriate, and although it may modestly raise arterial Pco2 in some hypercarbic patients by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships, this should not deter correction of hypoxemia (p.2259). Relying on spirometry to diagnose or manage an acute exacerbation, which is not supported by evidence (unlike in asthma) (p.2259). Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia, or heart failure, since each can mimic or accompany an exacerbation (p.2258, p.2259). Attributing all exacerbations to bacterial infection: PCR-based studies show viral respiratory infections may cause more than 50% of exacerbations, and in a notable minority no specific precipitant is identifiable (p.2258). A range of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation and worsening respiratory symptoms. The underlying COPD substrate is fixed airflow obstruction (chronically reduced, non-normalizing FEV1/FVC) compounded by hyperinflation and air trapping; a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically disadvantaged, raising the work of breathing during any acute decompensation. Gas exchange is impaired chiefly by ventilation-perfusion mismatching (shunt is minimal), which explains why modest supplemental oxygen usually corrects COPD hypoxemia. Hypoxemia tends not to appear until FEV1 falls below ~50% predicted, and CO2 retention is not expected until FEV1 is below ~25% predicted. Acutely, worsening obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation can precipitate alveolar hypoventilation with rising arterial CO2 and respiratory acidosis (p.2251-2252, p.2255, p.2258). Mechanical ventilatory support for a COPD exacerbation carries a hospital mortality of roughly 17-49%. After a hospitalization for COPD, about 20% of patients are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, with mortality around 20% in the year following discharge. Exacerbations are also associated with greater longitudinal loss of lung function (notably in those with better baseline function) and account for the majority of COPD-related health-care expenditure (p.2253, p.2259). Underlying COPD severity is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 plus FEV1 % predicted: GOLD 1 (mild) >=80%, GOLD 2 (moderate) 50-79%, GOLD 3 (severe) 30-49%, GOLD 4 (very severe) <30%. The GOLD ABE assessment further classifies patients using symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or CAT score) and annual exacerbation history: groups A and B for those with 0-1 moderate exacerbations not leading to hospitalization (A = mMRC 0-1/CAT <10, B = mMRC >=2/CAT >=10), and group E for those with >=2 moderate exacerbations or >=1 leading to hospitalization. The ATS/ERS alternative grades obstruction by FEV1 z-scores rather than percent predicted. For an acute exacerbation, severity itself is a clinical determination; an expert-consensus scheme stages it using dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases (p.2255, p.2256, p.2259).

Cor pulmonale — cor pulmonale, pulmonary heart disease, right heart failure from lung disease Left ventricular failure causing pulmonary congestion Primary (idiopathic) pulmonary arterial hypertension Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension Valvular heart disease Constrictive pericarditis Right heart failure from congenital heart disease Echocardiography to assess right ventricular size and function and estimate pulmonary pressures Arterial blood gas analysis to detect hypoxaemia and hypercapnia Electrocardiography for signs of right ventricular strain and right axis deviation Chest imaging and pulmonary function testing to characterise the underlying lung disease Right heart catheterisation to confirm and quantify pulmonary hypertension when indicated Cor pulmonale is right ventricular enlargement and eventual failure caused by disorders of the lungs, pulmonary vasculature, or ventilation, excluding left heart disease and congenital defects Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the most common underlying cause, with pulmonary hypertension the central intermediary Symptoms include exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and, as it progresses, ankle swelling and abdominal distension Signs of right heart failure include raised jugular venous pressure, a left parasternal heave, a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, hepatomegaly, and peripheral oedema Echocardiography helps assess right ventricular size and function and estimate pulmonary artery pressure, while right heart catheterisation confirms pulmonary hypertension Treatment is directed primarily at the underlying lung disease and at correcting hypoxaemia, since chronic hypoxia drives pulmonary vasoconstriction Long-term oxygen therapy in chronically hypoxaemic patients can reduce pulmonary vascular resistance and improve survival Diuretics can relieve congestion but require caution to avoid reducing preload excessively or worsening metabolic alkalosis Rapidly worsening right heart failure with hypotension or syncope Severe hypoxaemia or hypercapnic respiratory failure Signs suggesting acute or chronic pulmonary embolism as a cause Refractory fluid overload despite therapy Attributing right heart failure to lung disease without excluding left heart disease or thromboembolism Failing to correct hypoxaemia, a key reversible driver of pulmonary hypertension Over-diuresis reducing right ventricular preload and cardiac output Overlooking treatable causes such as chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension Chronic lung disease or pulmonary vascular disease raises pulmonary vascular resistance through several mechanisms: alveolar hypoxia causes pulmonary arteriolar vasoconstriction, destruction or remodelling of the pulmonary vascular bed reduces its cross-sectional area, and acidosis and polycythaemia further increase resistance. The right ventricle, facing sustained pressure overload, initially hypertrophies to maintain output but ultimately dilates and fails. Rising right-sided filling pressures produce systemic venous congestion, hepatic congestion, and peripheral oedema. Prognosis is largely determined by the severity and reversibility of the underlying pulmonary disorder; the onset of overt right heart failure generally marks advanced disease and portends a poorer outlook, though correcting hypoxaemia and optimising the underlying condition can improve symptoms and survival.

Spinal cord compression — Urgent whole-spine MRI Neurosurgical / oncology review Time-critical for neurological recovery; high-dose steroids if malignant Intradural extramedullary tumours (meningioma, neurofibroma/schwannoma) - usually slow-growing and benign; long symptom duration favours an intradural origin (p.3606) Intramedullary lesions (ependymoma, haemangioblastoma, low-grade astrocytoma, rarely metastasis) - present with poorly localised burning pain and SACRAL SPARING rather than radicular pain (p.3604, 3606) Cervical spondylotic / degenerative cervical myelopathy - osteophytes, ossified posterior longitudinal ligament/ligamentum flavum, disk degeneration; insidious, stepwise; early signs are subtle (paraesthesia, loss of hand dexterity, 'clumsiness') (p.173) Acute spondylytic myelopathy from hyperextension injury on a pre-existing stenotic canal, sometimes producing a central cord syndrome (p.3606) Conus medullaris syndrome - saddle anaesthesia (S3-S5), early prominent bladder/bowel dysfunction with lax anal tone, preserved leg strength (p.3604) Spinal epidural abscess - midline spinal/neck pain, fever and progressive limb weakness; mostly Staphylococcus aureus (consider MRSA), with gram-negative bacilli, streptococci, anaerobes and fungi less commonly; risk factors include diabetes, IV drug use, alcoholism, renal failure, malignancy, HIV and recent spinal surgery/anaesthesia/trauma (pp.3606-3607) Vertebral osteomyelitis / diskitis - neurological deficit in about a third of cases, mostly mediated by epidural abscess; fever may be absent, especially in cervical disease (pp.131, 1105) Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) with epidural extension - an important cause in the developing world (p.3607) Infectious noncompressive myelitis to consider once compression excluded (VZV, HSV, CMV, HIV, HTLV-1, Borrelia, Listeria, syphilis, Mycoplasma) (p.3603) MRI with gadolinium centred on the suspected level is the initial procedure; imaging the entire spine is important because up to ~40% with compression at one level have asymptomatic epidural metastases elsewhere (and multiple epidural deposits are present in ~25%) (pp.632, 3605) CT myelography reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI promptly or have non-diagnostic MRI (pp.632, 768) ESR and CRP are valuable for excluding spinal infection (raised in ~98-100% of vertebral osteomyelitis) (p.1105) Blood cultures (positive in over half of epidural abscess cases); image-guided or open biopsy/aspiration when cultures are negative (pp.1105, 3607) If cord compression suspected but only radicular symptoms without myelopathy, imaging may safely be deferred 24-48 h - but suspected myelopathic compression is imaged immediately (p.3605) In compression from an unknown primary, a simple workup (chest imaging, mammography, PSA, abdominal CT) often reveals the malignancy (p.632) Osteoporotic vertebral collapse (p.631) Spinal epidural haematoma - acute focal/radicular pain then cord or conus signs; predisposed by anticoagulation, trauma, tumour or blood dyscrasias, occasionally post-LP or epidural anaesthesia (p.3607) Hematomyelia - acute painful transverse myelopathy from intramedullary haemorrhage (trauma, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) (p.3607) Spinal cord infarction / anterior spinal artery syndrome - sudden myelopathy without antecedent pain, with preserved vibration/position sense (pp.3604-3605) Radiation myelopathy, neoplastic leptomeningitis and spinal lipomatosis (p.631) Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency), copper deficiency (p.3602) Inflammatory/demyelinating myelopathy - multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica, sarcoidosis (p.3602) A horizontally demarcated sensory level (identified by moving a pinprick or cold stimulus up the trunk) below which sensory, motor and autonomic function is impaired is the hallmark of a cord lesion; for the spinothalamic tract the true level may sit one to two segments above the clinically detected level (p.3603). The upper border of sensory loss often lies one or two vertebrae BELOW the actual site of compression, so the radiographic target may be higher than the clinical level suggests (p.631). Pain is usually the first symptom of metastatic compression and can precede neurological signs by days to months; it characteristically worsens when supine/recumbent and at night, helping distinguish it from degenerative disk pain which is often relieved by lying down (pp.631, 768, 3605). Lhermitte's sign (an electric tingling shooting down the back and limbs on neck flexion/extension) can be an EARLY clue to cervical cord compression (p.631). Loss of bowel/bladder control is usually a LATE feature; motor and sensory loss typically precede sphincter disturbance (p.631). Useful trunk sensory landmarks for localising a thoracic level are the nipples (T4) and umbilicus (T10) (p.3604). Spinal column infection (osteomyelitis/abscess) characteristically crosses the disk space to involve the adjacent vertebral body, whereas tumour tends to respect the disk space - a distinguishing imaging feature (p.3605). Vertebral collapse is not a reliable marker of malignancy - about 20% of collapses, especially in older and postmenopausal patients, are due to osteoporosis rather than tumour (p.632). Pedicle erosion (the 'winking owl' sign) is the earliest plain-film sign of vertebral tumour, but plain films are insensitive and a normal film does not exclude malignancy (p.632). Established motor deficit (paraplegia/quadriplegia) present >12 h rarely improves, and beyond 48 h the prognosis for meaningful motor recovery is poor - urgency is measured in hours (p.3606) Autonomic dysfunction (decreased anal tone, reduced perineal sensation, distended bladder, absent anal wink or bulbocavernosus reflex) signals cord involvement and is an unfavourable prognostic sign (p.631) Once weakness appears in spinal epidural abscess, progression can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606) Recent-onset persistent thoracic back pain in a cancer patient is suspicious for vertebral metastasis (the thoracic spine is rarely involved by spondylosis) (p.3605) Pain crescendo pattern, pain aggravated by cough/Valsalva/recumbency, and Lhermitte's sign warrant urgent imaging (p.632) Mistaking a myelopathy for polyneuropathy or Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending paraesthesias suggest neuropathy, but a sharply demarcated sensory level plus bladder disturbance points to a cord origin (pp.213, 3605). Acute severe transverse lesions cause initial FLACCID weakness and areflexia ('spinal shock') that can be misread as anterior horn cell disease or acute polyneuropathy before hyperreflexia supervenes over days to weeks (p.3604). Cauda equina syndrome (low back/radicular pain, saddle/perineal sensory loss, asymmetric leg weakness, sphincter and sexual dysfunction, lost ankle/bulbocavernosus/anal reflexes) reflects nerve-root rather than cord compression and must be distinguished from conus and cord syndromes - mass lesions low in the canal often produce a mixed picture (pp.132, 632, 3604). Gadolinium enhancement can deceptively 'normalise' vertebral metastases by raising their signal to that of normal marrow on MRI (p.3605). Cervical osteomyelitis/epidural abscess may present without fever, delaying recognition - keep it in mind for neck pain with IV drug use, immunosuppression or diabetes (p.131). Because the cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-section, even a small compressive mass causes disproportionately severe, often reversible-if-treated-early, deficits (p.3559). In neoplastic compression, metastases lodge in the vertebral body or pedicle (the axial skeleton is rich in marrow); the enlarging deposit compresses the underlying dura, or a paravertebral mass (lymphoma, myeloma, paediatric tumours) extends through the intervertebral foramen into the canal. Expanding extradural tumour injures axons and myelin mechanically and compromises blood flow, producing ischaemia and infarction (pp.589, 3563). In spinal epidural abscess, as the collection expands it causes additional cord damage through venous congestion and thrombosis, so that once weakness appears deterioration can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606). The thoracic spine is the commonest site of metastatic compression (~70%), followed by lumbosacral (~20%) and cervical (~10%) (p.631). Outcome is strongly time- and function-dependent: treatment is most successful in patients who are still ambulatory and have intact sphincter control when therapy begins, and a good response is expected in those ambulatory at presentation - treatment usually prevents new weakness and up to a third regain some motor function (pp.632, 3606). Motor deficits fixed for more than 12 h seldom improve, and beyond 48 h substantial recovery is unlikely (p.3606). For spinal epidural abscess, prompt diagnosis and treatment allow significant recovery in up to two-thirds, but surgery is unlikely to reverse deficits fixed for more than a few days (p.3607). Recovery from paraparesis is better after surgery than radiotherapy alone, though survival may be short with widespread metastatic disease (p.768). Harrison frames management decisions for malignant compression using the NOMS framework (Memorial Sloan Kettering): Neurologic status (degree of epidural compression, myelopathy, functional radiculopathy), Oncologic status (tumour radiosensitivity), Mechanical stability of the spine, and Systemic factors; high-grade epidural compression from a radioresistant tumour favours separation surgery followed by stereotactic body radiotherapy (pp.589-590). Clinically, prognosis is best stratified by ambulatory and sphincter status at presentation and by duration of any motor deficit (p.3606).

Umbilical Cord Prolapse — cord prolapse, umbilical cord prolapse, prolapsed cord, overt cord prolapse, occult cord prolapse Vasa praevia with fetal vessel rupture Placental abruption causing acute fetal compromise Uterine rupture Cord compression from oligohydramnios (nuchal or true knot) without frank prolapse Maternal supine hypotension causing transient fetal heart rate changes Continuous electronic fetal heart rate monitoring to detect bradycardia or variable decelerations Vaginal examination to confirm a palpable pulsating cord and assess cervical dilatation and presenting part Rapid bedside assessment of fetal viability Ultrasound where time allows to confirm presentation and fetal heart activity Preparation for theatre including maternal bloods and cross-match as part of emergency delivery Cord prolapse is descent of the umbilical cord below the presenting part after membrane rupture (overt) or alongside it with intact membranes (occult), threatening the fetal blood supply It is an acute obstetric emergency because compression of the cord and reflex vasospasm rapidly cause fetal hypoxia and can lead to stillbirth if delivery is delayed Predisposing factors include a high or poorly applied presenting part, malpresentation (breech, transverse, oblique), polyhydramnios, prematurity, multiple pregnancy, and long cord Iatrogenic rupture of membranes when the presenting part is not engaged is a recognised trigger, so artificial rupture should be avoided with an unengaged head The classic sign is an abrupt, severe fetal heart rate deceleration or bradycardia immediately after membrane rupture; a loop of cord may be palpable or visible at the introitus Immediate management aims to relieve cord compression: elevate the presenting part manually or by filling the bladder, position the mother knee-chest or in steep head-down tilt, and minimise handling of an exposed cord to prevent vasospasm Definitive treatment is the fastest safe delivery, usually emergency caesarean section, unless vaginal delivery is imminent and quicker Tocolysis may buy time by reducing contractions while preparations for delivery are made Outcome depends chiefly on the interval from diagnosis to delivery and on the setting, with the best results when it occurs in hospital with rapid theatre access OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: sudden fetal bradycardia or profound decelerations after membrane rupture demanding immediate delivery Visible or palpable pulsating cord at or beyond the introitus Loss of cord pulsation suggesting critical fetal compromise Malpresentation or unengaged presenting part with ruptured membranes Any delay in achieving delivery once prolapse is confirmed Performing artificial rupture of membranes with a high or unengaged presenting part Excessive handling or attempts to replace an exposed cord, provoking vasospasm Delaying transfer to theatre while arranging investigations Failing to relieve cord compression by positioning or bladder filling while awaiting delivery Not maintaining manual elevation of the presenting part during preparation for caesarean When the umbilical cord slips past the presenting part, it becomes trapped between the fetus and the maternal pelvis or lower uterine segment. Mechanical compression occludes the umbilical vessels, and exposure of the cord to cold air or handling induces vasospasm of the umbilical arteries. Both mechanisms interrupt oxygenated blood flow from the placenta to the fetus, producing acute fetal hypoxaemia, acidosis, and, if unrelieved, hypoxic-ischaemic injury or death. A poorly fitting presenting part leaves space for the cord to descend, which explains the association with malpresentation, prematurity, and polyhydramnios. When cord prolapse is recognised promptly and delivery is expedited, particularly in a hospital setting, perinatal survival is good and long-term neurological outcomes are usually favourable. Prognosis worsens markedly with longer diagnosis-to-delivery intervals, out-of-hospital events, and prematurity, where hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and perinatal death become more likely.

results from deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme, which normally works with phosphorylase to fully degrade glycogen at its branch points. Loss of debranching activity halts glycogenolysis once the outer glucose chains are removed, leaving an abnormal glycogen molecule with short outer branches (limit dextrin) that accumulates in liver and, in type IIIa, in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Because gluconeogenesis remains functional, patients can still generate glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors, so fasting hypoglycaemia is generally milder than in type I and is accompanied by ketosis rather than lactic acidosis. Chronic glycogen and metabolic stress produce hepatomegaly and transaminitis, and in muscle-involving disease lead to progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy. Hepatic and hypoglycaemic manifestations often improve after puberty and overall prognosis is better than type I; however, in type IIIa progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy can dominate the long-term course and determine outcome.

treatment is supportive with lubrication and topical antibiotic prophylaxis Contact lens-related abrasions and those from vegetable or organic matter carry higher infection risk and warrant closer follow-up Patching is generally avoided, particularly in contact lens wearers, as it may promote infection A white corneal infiltrate, mucopurulent discharge, or anterior chamber reaction suggesting microbial keratitis Contact lens wearers with pain out of proportion, indicating possible Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba infection Failure to heal within expected time or worsening pain and redness Suspicion of penetrating injury or high-velocity foreign body Sending patients home with topical anaesthetic, which delays healing and can cause severe corneal damage Failing to evert the lid and missing a retained foreign body Patching a contact lens wearer and precipitating infection Assuming all painful epithelial defects are simple abrasions and missing herpetic or microbial keratitis A corneal abrasion is a defect in the corneal epithelium, most often from mechanical trauma. Loss of the epithelial barrier exposes richly innervated subepithelial nerve endings, producing intense pain and reflex tearing and blepharospasm. The epithelium normally regenerates rapidly by sliding and mitosis of surrounding cells. Contamination, retained foreign material, or contact lens wear can convert a simple abrasion into a microbial keratitis, and repeated or poorly healing defects may reflect an underlying epithelial basement membrane dystrophy causing recurrent erosions. Simple abrasions heal quickly with no lasting visual effect, but infection, deep central lesions, or recurrent erosions can cause scarring and reduced vision.

dystrophies are genetically determined disorders in which abnormal material accumulates within, or normal cells are progressively lost from, a specific corneal layer. Many stromal dystrophies (lattice, granular, and the related TGFBI group) result from mutations causing deposition of amyloid or hyaline material that scatters light. Macular dystrophy reflects a defect in keratan sulphate metabolism with mucopolysaccharide deposition. In Fuchs endothelial dystrophy the endothelial pump fails as cells are lost and guttata form, so the stroma imbibes fluid and swells, producing oedema and, in advanced cases, epithelial bullae. Anterior dystrophies disrupt epithelial adhesion, predisposing to recurrent erosions. Most dystrophies progress slowly over years; anterior disease is often controlled with conservative measures, while advanced stromal opacity or endothelial decompensation may require keratoplasty, which restores useful vision in many cases although some stromal dystrophies can recur in the graft.

regulators, which normally hold sister chromatids together and also regulate transcription and chromatin architecture. Loss-of-function or missense variants in NIPBL (the commonest) or in the structural and regulatory subunits SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and HDAC8 disturb the expression of developmental gene networks. This dysregulation during embryogenesis produces the multisystem pattern of growth failure, limb reduction, craniofacial malformation and neurodevelopmental impairment. Somatic mosaicism is well recognised and can lead to false-negative blood testing. Prognosis varies widely with genotype and severity; individuals with classic NIPBL-related disease often have significant intellectual disability and medical comorbidity, whereas milder variants permit better cognitive and functional outcomes. Life expectancy is largely determined by cardiac, gastrointestinal and respiratory complications.

Strong alkalis (e.g. lye, drain cleaner) cause liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fats and dissolving proteins, allowing deep penetration and full-thickness oesophageal injury with risk of perforation and mediastinitis. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation that can limit depth of penetration but tends to pool in and damage the stomach, risking gastric perforation and peritonitis. Injury severity depends on the agent, concentration, volume, and contact time. Healing of deep circumferential burns leads to fibrosis and stricture, and chronic injury raises long-term malignancy risk. Minor mucosal injury usually heals well, but deep circumferential burns commonly progress to strictures needing repeated dilatation or surgery, and full-thickness injury with perforation carries high mortality; survivors have a lifelong increased risk of oesophageal cancer.

that may be intermittent Attributing infantile feeding failure to reflux alone and delaying tube feeding Costello syndrome is caused by germline activating variants in HRAS, a small GTPase that is a Intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate, and affected individuals often have a sociable, engaging personality.

COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) — SARS-CoV-2, coronavirus disease 2019 Influenza and other viral lower respiratory tract infections (RSV, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza, rhinovirus) Other coronaviruses: SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and common-cold coronaviruses HCoV-OC43 and HCoV-HKU1 Community-acquired or health care-associated bacterial pneumonia Any respiratory symptom occurring where SARS-CoV-2 is circulating should be considered a potential manifestation of COVID-19 Influenza Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection Human metapneumovirus and parainfluenza virus infections Rhinovirus / common cold (including HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1 coronaviruses) SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV infections Bacterial community-acquired pneumonia Molecular nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), usually RT-PCR on nasopharyngeal swab or saliva - most sensitive; cannot be done at home and is processed in a reference laboratory Antigen tests (rapid / at-home) detecting SARS-CoV-2 proteins - reliable but less accurate than molecular tests, especially in exposed asymptomatic persons CBC: lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia Inflammatory markers: elevated IL-6, TNF-alpha, ferritin, C-reactive protein Elevated liver enzymes and lactate dehydrogenase Elevated markers of acute kidney injury Elevated D-dimer and prothrombin time (coagulopathy) Elevated troponin and creatine phosphokinase (cardiac/muscle injury) Chest radiograph: bilateral consolidation and ground-glass opacities, especially in lower lung regions (may be normal despite respiratory compromise) Chest CT: ground-glass opacification +/- consolidation, pleural thickening, interlobular septal thickening, air bronchograms - interpretable as typical, indeterminate, or atypical; more sensitive than radiograph but should be used for management, not as a primary diagnostic tool Lung ultrasound to detect lung abnormalities SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped, positive-sense RNA betacoronavirus; its trimeric spike (S) protein is primed by the host protease TMPRSS2 and attaches via a receptor-binding domain to the human ACE2 receptor (p.1539). Disease course varies widely: asymptomatic infection, mild disease, moderate disease, or severe disease needing hospitalization, oxygen, intensive care, and mechanical ventilation. Possibly about a third of those infected are asymptomatic yet can still transmit the virus (p.1540). Onset of disease typically manifests within 4-5 days after exposure and nearly always within 14 days; common symptoms are cough, fever, myalgia, headache, dyspnea, sore throat, and GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) (p.1541). Sudden-onset dysgeusia and anosmia (loss of taste and smell) occur in a substantial number of cases and often resolve over weeks to months (p.1541). Spread is primarily via respiratory droplets between persons in close proximity; airborne transmission by small particles may occur but airborne transmission over long distances is unlikely. Fomite (contaminated-surface) transmission occurs, so hand washing is advised (p.1540). The basic reproduction number (R0) of SARS-CoV-2 has been estimated to peak around 6, substantially higher than seasonal influenza (typically 1-2); densely populated settings (prisons, cruise ships, nursing homes, airplanes, large indoor gatherings) facilitate high transmission, while outdoor transmission is less common (p.1540). RNA-dependent RNA polymerases are error-prone, so variants arise frequently; the WHO classifies variants under monitoring (VUMs), of interest (VOIs), and of concern (VOCs). Rapid variant evolution affecting transmission, severity, antigenicity, therapy effectiveness, and diagnostic accuracy is a distinguishing feature of the pandemic (p.1540). An excessive proinflammatory host response to infection likely contributes directly to pulmonary pathology and disease severity; later in the clinical course pathogenesis is driven more by tissue and systemic inflammation than by direct viral cytopathic effect (p.1541-1542). Children have lower rates of severe disease than adults, and schools have not been considered a primary driver of population transmission (p.1540). Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C / PMIS) is associated with COVID-19: persistent fever, multi-organ involvement (GI, dermatologic, cardiac, renal, hematologic, neurologic), and elevated inflammatory markers; highest US risk is in Black and Latino children aged 3-12 years. A similar adult syndrome (MIS-A) may rarely occur (p.1540). Long COVID is a chronic condition occurring after infection, present for at least 3 months, with a wide range of symptoms (respiratory, metabolic, neuropsychiatric, pain) that may improve, worsen, or be ongoing; affected people may have increased suicidal ideation and suicide risk (p.1541). Vaccination's principal goal is preventing severe COVID-19 (critical illness, death, hospitalization, emergency/urgent-care visits); preliminary data also suggest vaccinated persons with COVID are less likely than unvaccinated persons to develop long COVID (p.1543). Oxygen saturation <=94% on room air Respiratory rate >30 breaths/min PaO2/FiO2 <300 mmHg Lung infiltrates occupying >50% of lung fields on chest radiograph Moderate to severe dyspnea or cyanosis Change in mental status (confusion, delirium) or new-onset mental status changes Chest pain Reduced urine output or anuria Acute respiratory distress syndrome / respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation Multiorgan failure or shock Persistent fever with multiorgan disease and elevated inflammatory markers (excessive inflammatory response - high risk of fatal outcome) Thromboembolic events (VTE/PE/DVT, arterial thrombosis, acute stroke, limb ischemia) Antibiotics are NOT generally indicated, as bacterial infection is an uncommon complication of COVID-19; reserve empiric antibiotics for diagnostic uncertainty or proven secondary infection, and deescalate or stop if no evidence of bacterial infection. Chest CT should NOT be used as a primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19; it is principally for medical management of respiratory disease. COVID-19-specific therapy is NOT recommended for individuals with asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection. Antigen (rapid/at-home) tests are less accurate than molecular tests, especially when testing exposed persons without symptoms. Chest radiographs may be normal despite respiratory compromise, so a normal film does not exclude significant disease. Possible association between NSAID use and worse outcomes has been raised; acetaminophen is the preferred antipyretic where possible (knowledge point - doses omitted). Antibody-based therapies and EUAs are repeatedly revoked as new variants escape their activity, so confirm current authorization status before relying on a monoclonal antibody or long-acting antibody product. Effectiveness of masking in community or health settings has been difficult to assess (most studies observational and confounded), so evidence is uncertain rather than absent. SARS-CoV-2 (genus Betacoronavirus) is an enveloped positive-sense RNA virus with a ~30,000-nucleotide genome encoding four structural proteins (S spike, E envelope, M membrane, N nucleocapsid) plus a large polyprotein cleaved into 16 nonstructural proteins. The trimeric S protein is a type-1 fusion machine primed by the host transmembrane protease TMPRSS2 and mediates attachment via a receptor-binding domain (RBD) to the human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) receptor, allowing viral entry into respiratory epithelium. Infection spreads chiefly by respiratory droplets, with possible short-range airborne and fomite spread. Disease results from direct viral pathogenesis in tissues and the associated immune response. An excessive proinflammatory host response contributes directly to pulmonary pathology; early in infection viral load (peak titer) correlates with severity, whereas later disease is increasingly driven by tissue and systemic inflammatory responses (cytokine storm) rather than direct viral cytopathic effect. The hyperinflammatory and hypercoagulable state drives severe multi-organ complications. Symptomatic infection is usually an acute syndrome that resolves within about 2 weeks in roughly 80% of persons, especially after mild or moderate disease. Severe disease often needs several months for recovery. Advanced age is the principal risk factor for severe illness: >95% of deaths occur in persons older than 45 years and >80% in those older than 65; male sex carries higher risk (odds ratio ~1.8), and most who die have preexisting comorbidities. Risk rises markedly with elevated BMI (overweight, obesity, severe obesity). As of September 2024 the virus had caused >700 million cases and >7 million deaths worldwide. A subset progress to recurring or persisting symptoms (long COVID); those with severe acute pulmonary or cardiac injury may have persisting respiratory or cardiac impairment, and adverse long-term mental-health consequences are common. Spectrum: asymptomatic infection; mild disease (symptomatic, no pneumonia - most symptomatic cases); moderate disease; severe disease (pneumonia with dyspnea, radiographic involvement of more than half the lung, and/or hypoxia with oxygen saturation <=94%, typically requiring hospitalization and oxygen); critical disease (respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, multiorgan failure, or shock - requires intensive care).

that should prompt PTEN testing Failing to start thyroid surveillance in childhood when indicated Attributing gastrointestinal polyps or skin lesions to unrelated common conditions Not extending cancer surveillance and genetic testing to at-risk relatives Cowden syndrome is caused by germline inactivating variants in PTEN, a tumour-suppressor gene encoding a phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3 and thereby restrains the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mTOR signalling axis. The syndrome sits within the broader PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome spectrum, which also includes Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome and related phenotypes. With adherence to intensified surveillance many cancers can be detected early, but the substantial cumulative lifetime risk of breast, thyroid and endometrial malignancy means long-term outcome depends on sustained monitoring. Benign hamartomas contribute to symptom burden but are rarely life-threatening.

Cow's Milk Protein Allergy — CMPA, cow's milk protein intolerance, milk allergy in infants Lactose intolerance Infantile colic Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Infectious gastroenteritis Other food protein-induced enteropathies or proctocolitis Eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders Trial of dietary elimination and planned reintroduction Specific IgE or skin prick testing (for IgE-mediated disease) Supervised oral food challenge Stool examination for blood if allergic proctocolitis suspected Growth monitoring and, if needed, nutritional assessment This is an immune-mediated reaction to cow's milk proteins, distinct from lactose intolerance, which is a non-immune enzyme deficiency. Reactions are broadly divided into IgE-mediated (rapid onset urticaria, angioedema, vomiting, wheeze, and rarely anaphylaxis) and non-IgE-mediated (delayed gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stool, and colic-like distress). It is one of the most common food allergies in infancy and can occur in both formula-fed and exclusively breastfed infants exposed to milk protein through maternal diet. Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a compatible history, a trial of milk protein elimination, and improvement followed by recurrence on reintroduction. For IgE-mediated disease, specific IgE testing or skin prick testing can support the diagnosis, whereas these tests are unhelpful in non-IgE-mediated presentations. Management centres on strict avoidance of cow's milk protein, using an appropriate hypoallergenic formula in formula-fed infants and maternal dietary exclusion in breastfed infants. A supervised oral food challenge is the most reliable way to confirm or refute the diagnosis and to assess whether tolerance has developed. Most children outgrow cow's milk protein allergy during early childhood, so periodic reassessment for acquired tolerance is important to avoid unnecessary long-term restriction. Anaphylaxis or significant respiratory compromise after milk exposure Significant gastrointestinal bleeding or severe enteropathy Faltering growth or failure to thrive Severe dehydration or shock (as in food protein-induced enterocolitis reactions) Signs suggesting an alternative serious diagnosis Confusing cow's milk protein allergy with lactose intolerance and giving inappropriate dietary advice Relying on IgE tests to diagnose non-IgE-mediated disease Maintaining prolonged, unnecessary dietary restriction without reassessing for tolerance Using inadequately hypoallergenic substitutes or overlooking nutritional adequacy of exclusion diets The disorder results from an abnormal immune response to proteins in cow's milk, principally caseins and whey proteins. In IgE-mediated allergy, sensitisation leads to specific IgE that, on re-exposure, triggers mast cell and basophil degranulation with rapid release of histamine and other mediators, producing immediate symptoms. In non-IgE-mediated allergy, cell-mediated and mixed immune mechanisms cause a more delayed inflammatory response in the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in mucosal inflammation, altered motility, and enteropathy. Because the offending proteins can pass into breast milk, exclusively breastfed infants can react to maternal dietary intake. The prognosis is generally favourable, with the majority of children achieving tolerance during the preschool years; IgE-mediated allergy, particularly with high specific IgE levels, may persist longer than non-IgE-mediated disease.

creatine kinase between attacks excludes the disorder Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 is located on the inner face of the inner mitochondrial membrane and reconverts long-chain acylcarnitines, When the enzyme is deficient, long-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidised despite entering the mitochondrion, so tissues dependent on fatty-acid energy fail during fasting, exertion or catabolic stress. In the myopathic form, energy shortfall and accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines during sustained exercise damage muscle fibres, causing rhabdomyolysis; severe neonatal and infantile forms reflect near-complete loss of activity with multi-organ involvement. The adult myopathic form is compatible with a normal lifespan when rhabdomyolysis triggers are avoided, whereas the infantile and neonatal forms carry high morbidity and mortality despite treatment.

Craniometaphyseal dysplasia — CMD, ANKH-related craniometaphyseal dysplasia, GJA1-related craniometaphyseal dysplasia Craniodiaphyseal dysplasia (more severe, diaphyseal) Osteopetrosis (generalised increased bone density) Pyle disease (metaphyseal dysplasia with mild skull change) Frontometaphyseal dysplasia (otopalatodigital spectrum) Van Buchem disease and sclerosteosis (SOST-related sclerosis) Fibrous dysplasia of the craniofacial bones Molecular testing of ANKH (and GJA1 for suspected recessive disease) Skull and facial radiographs or CT to document hyperostosis and foraminal narrowing Long-bone radiographs to demonstrate metaphyseal flaring Audiological assessment for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss Cranial nerve examination and imaging of the skull base foramina Ophthalmological and nasal airway assessment where symptoms suggest compression A sclerosing bone dysplasia combining progressive craniofacial hyperostosis with abnormal metaphyseal modelling of the long bones The autosomal dominant form is caused by mutations in ANKH; a rarer autosomal recessive form is linked to GJA1 Facial features include a broad nasal bridge, paranasal bossing and hypertelorism that progress with age Cranial nerve compression from thickened skull base bone can cause facial palsy, hearing loss and, less often, visual impairment Nasal airway obstruction and choanal narrowing may occur from hyperostosis of the facial bones Radiographs show a widened, club-shaped or 'Erlenmeyer flask' metaphyseal deformity of the long bones alongside diffuse cranial sclerosis It must be distinguished from craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, which is far more severe with predominantly diaphyseal involvement Management is largely supportive with surgical decompression of foramina considered for symptomatic cranial nerve compression Progressive facial nerve palsy or hearing loss from foraminal narrowing Visual deterioration suggesting optic nerve compression Significant nasal airway obstruction from facial hyperostosis Rapid clinical progression raising concern for craniodiaphyseal dysplasia Confusing it with the much more severe craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, altering prognosis Attributing hearing loss solely to middle-ear disease and missing bony foraminal compression Delaying decompression until cranial nerve deficits become irreversible Overlooking the metaphyseal long-bone changes that support the diagnosis Craniometaphyseal dysplasia is a disorder of bone modelling. The dominant form results from mutations in ANKH, a transmembrane protein that transports inorganic pyrophosphate, a key inhibitor of mineralisation, out of cells; disturbed pyrophosphate handling alters the balance of bone deposition and resorption. The consequence is excessive, poorly remodelled bone in the skull and face (hyperostosis and sclerosis) together with defective tubulation of the long-bone metaphyses. The recessive form involves the gap-junction protein connexin 43 encoded by GJA1. Progressive skull-base thickening narrows the neural foramina and causes the cranial neuropathies. Life expectancy is usually normal, but the craniofacial changes are progressive and cranial nerve compression can cause lasting facial weakness, hearing loss or visual problems, so long-term surveillance and timely surgical decompression are important.

Craniosynostosis — premature suture fusion, scaphocephaly, plagiocephaly (synostotic), syndromic craniosynostosis Positional (deformational) plagiocephaly Microcephaly with a small but normally shaped producing a characteristic head shape Sagittal suture fusion gives a long, narrow head (scaphocephaly) and is the most common single-suture form The head-shape abnormality is typically present at or soon after birth and progresses, unlike positional plagiocephaly which usually improves with repositioning A palpable ridge along the affected suture and an abnormal skull contour are important clinical clues Most single-suture cases are non-syndromic and isolated, but multi-suture or syndromic forms (such as Apert, Crouzon, or Pfeiffer) carry higher risks and associated anomalies Multi-suture involvement can raise intracranial pressure and threaten vision and neurodevelopment, so fundoscopy and developmental monitoring are important Cranial CT with three-dimensional reconstruction confirms the diagnosis and defines the sutures involved when clinical assessment is uncertain Treatment is usually surgical remodelling to correct the deformity and allow normal brain growth, with timing and approach tailored to the sutures affected and the child's age Multi-suture fusion with signs of raised intracranial pressure such as papilloedema Progressive skull deformity with developmental delay or visual compromise Features of a craniofacial syndrome with airway or midface concerns Rapidly abnormal head growth or a bulging appearance suggesting elevated pressure Confusing positional plagiocephaly, which improves with repositioning, with true synostosis Missing raised intracranial pressure in multi-suture disease by omitting fundoscopy Underestimating associated anomalies and genetic implications in syndromic cases Delaying referral so that the optimal surgical window is missed Craniosynostosis arises when one or more cranial sutures fuse prematurely, before the underlying brain has finished its rapid early growth. Because bone cannot expand across the fused suture, compensatory growth occurs at the remaining open sutures, distorting the skull into a predictable shape determined by which suture is involved. When several sutures fuse, the overall cranial volume may become inadequate for the growing brain, leading to raised intracranial pressure. Syndromic forms are often driven by identifiable genetic mutations affecting fibroblast growth factor signalling and are associated with midface and limb anomalies. Isolated single-suture craniosynostosis generally has an excellent outcome after timely surgical correction; multi-suture and syndromic forms are more complex, carry a greater risk of raised intracranial pressure and neurodevelopmental problems, and often require staged, multidisciplinary management.

intellectual disability by not requesting spectroscopy or guanidinoacetate testing Assuming all creatine deficiency syndromes respond to supplementation, when the transporter defect does not Missing raised guanidinoacetate as a marker of the treatable GAMT form Delaying treatment in synthesis defects, when early therapy is most effective Creatine and its phosphorylated form provide a rapid energy buffer for tissues with high and fluctuating energy demands, notably brain and muscle. Creatine is synthesised in two steps: AGAT (encoded by GATM) forms guanidinoacetate, which GAMT then methylates to creatine; creatine is delivered to the brain and taken up by cells via the SLC6A8 transporter. Loss of any step causes cerebral creatine depletion and impaired energy homeostasis, producing neurodevelopmental impairment. In GAMT deficiency, guanidinoacetate additionally accumulates and is neurotoxic, contributing to seizures and movement disturbance. In the transporter defect, creatine is made normally but cannot enter the brain. Outcomes in the treatable synthesis defects (AGAT and GAMT) are substantially improved by early creatine supplementation, and pre-symptomatic treatment can prevent much of the neurological damage. The X-linked creatine transporter defect has a less favourable prognosis because supplementation does not restore brain creatine.

Cri-du-chat syndrome — cat cry syndrome, 5p deletion syndrome, 5p minus syndrome, Lejeune syndrome, monosomy 5p Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome Other subtelomeric deletion syndromes Trisomy 21 Cornelia de Lange syndrome Prader-Willi syndrome in the hypotonic neonate Non-specific syndromic intellectual disability Chromosomal microarray to define the deletion and its size Karyotype to detect an underlying translocation, with parental karyotypes for recurrence risk FISH targeting the 5p critical region where confirmation is needed Echocardiography for congenital heart disease Feeding and swallowing assessment in infancy Hearing and vision testing to support developmental progress The high-pitched, monotone, cat-like cry in infancy gives the syndrome its name and reflects abnormal laryngeal and neurological development; it often diminishes with age Caused by a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, with phenotype severity broadly correlating with deletion size and specific critical regions Facial features include microcephaly, a rounded face, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, down-slanting palpebral fissures and low-set ears, with the face lengthening over time Prenatal-onset growth restriction, marked feeding difficulty and hypotonia are common in infancy Most deletions are de novo, but a minority arise from an unbalanced parental translocation, so parental karyotyping is essential for recurrence-risk counselling Severe intellectual disability with markedly limited expressive language is typical, though receptive skills are relatively better Behavioural features can include hyperactivity, self-injury and stereotypies Failure to thrive from severe feeding difficulty and recurrent aspiration Unrecognised congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise Stridor or airway obstruction related to laryngeal abnormality Self-injurious behaviour requiring safeguarding and specialist input Assuming a normal standard karyotype excludes the diagnosis when small deletions require microarray or FISH Omitting parental karyotyping and mis-stating recurrence risk when a translocation is present Attributing feeding failure to behaviour rather than oromotor dysfunction Underestimating relatively preserved receptive language and social ability Cri-du-chat syndrome arises from a terminal or interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p), producing haploinsufficiency for genes in this region. Loss of specific critical intervals correlates with the characteristic cry and with the degree of intellectual disability, and candidate genes such as those influencing telomerase regulation and neuronal cytoskeletal proteins have been implicated. The reduced dosage of these developmentally important genes disrupts laryngeal, craniofacial and central nervous system formation. Deletions are commonly de novo and paternal in origin, but can result from malsegregation of a balanced parental rearrangement. Most individuals have severe intellectual disability but can achieve some self-care and communication skills with early intervention; survival into adulthood is usual. Outcome depends largely on associated malformations, especially cardiac and respiratory, and on deletion size.

residual activity, with milder jaundice that characteristically falls in response to enzyme-inducing therapy A reduction in bilirubin after an enzyme-inducer challenge helps distinguish type 2 from distinguished from the milder, common Gilbert syndrome, which also involves reduced UGT1A1 activity but does not cause dangerous bilirubin levels Rising unconjugated bilirubin with lethargy, hypotonia, or abnormal tone signalling impending kernicterus Failure of bilirubin to respond to intensive phototherapy Intercurrent illness, fasting, or drugs precipitating a sharp rise in bilirubin Progressive loss of phototherapy efficacy as skin surface area increases with growth Confusing severe Crigler-Najjar with benign Gilbert syndrome and underestimating kernicterus risk Failing to appreciate that phototherapy becomes progressively less effective with age and growth Prescribing drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin or that are conjugated by the same pathway Delaying liver transplantation assessment in type 1 disease Overlooking precipitants such as fasting, infection, or stress that acutely worsen jaundice Bilirubin produced from haem breakdown must be conjugated with glucuronic acid by the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 before it can be excreted in bile. In Crigler-Najjar syndrome, biallelic mutations in UGT1A1 abolish (type 1) or severely reduce (type 2) this enzyme activity, so unconjugated bilirubin cannot be efficiently processed and accumulates in the blood. Because unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble it can cross the blood-brain barrier, and at high concentrations it deposits in the basal ganglia and brainstem, causing bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus). The liver is otherwise structurally normal with no cholestasis or hepatocellular injury. Type 2 disease is generally compatible with a normal life expectancy and low neurological risk when managed appropriately, whereas untreated type 1 carries a high risk of kernicterus and death; sustained phototherapy delays complications, and liver transplantation offers definitive correction of the enzyme defect.

Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever — CCHF, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, viral haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), VHF Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, Lassa, hantavirus, Kyasanur Forest disease) Severe dengue with haemorrhage Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) Meningococcaemia and other bacterial sepsis with DIC Severe malaria Rickettsial disease with haemorrhage Dengue haemorrhagic fever Leptospirosis Meningococcal sepsis Severe malaria Other viral haemorrhagic fevers RT-PCR for CCHF viral RNA in early illness, performed in an appropriately biosafe laboratory CCHF-specific IgM and IgG serology later in the course Full blood count, coagulation profile, liver and renal function to gauge severity Careful exclusion of dengue, malaria, and leptospirosis given overlapping presentations All sampling and testing conducted under enhanced biosafety with prior laboratory notification A tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever caused by an orthonairovirus, transmitted mainly by Hyalomma ticks and by contact with blood or tissues of infected livestock In India it is a recognised emerging threat, with documented outbreaks in Gujarat and neighbouring regions and cases among livestock handlers and healthcare workers Onset is abrupt with fever, severe headache, myalgia, and prostration, progressing over days to a haemorrhagic phase with petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, and multi-organ involvement Nosocomial and slaughterhouse transmission is well described, so a history of tick exposure, animal contact, or care of a bleeding patient is a critical clue Laboratory features include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and rising transaminases, with deranged coagulation heralding severe disease This is a medical emergency requiring strict infection-control and barrier precautions, patient isolation, and safe handling of body fluids and laboratory specimens Management is chiefly supportive with careful correction of coagulopathy and organ support; suspected and confirmed cases must be promptly notified to public health authorities Spontaneous mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding, extensive ecchymoses, or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Rapidly falling platelet count with rising transaminases and deteriorating coagulation Hypotension, shock, or signs of multi-organ failure Any suspected case demands immediate isolation, barrier nursing, and public health notification because of nosocomial transmission risk Failing to institute isolation and barrier precautions early, exposing staff and other patients to a highly transmissible pathogen Anchoring on dengue or malaria and overlooking CCHF in someone with relevant tick or livestock exposure Performing invasive procedures or unprotected phlebotomy that increase bleeding and transmission risk Not notifying public health authorities and the receiving laboratory before sending specimens CCHF virus is an enveloped RNA virus that, following tick bite or exposure to infected blood or tissues, replicates and disseminates widely. It infects endothelial cells and cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system, and a dysregulated inflammatory and cytokine response together with direct endothelial injury leads to increased vascular permeability, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and haemorrhage. Hepatic involvement and marrow suppression contribute to the coagulopathy and cytopenias, and severe cases progress to shock and multi-organ failure. Case fatality is high, especially with delayed recognition and severe coagulopathy or multi-organ failure; early supportive care and meticulous infection control improve outcomes, and survivors who pass the acute haemorrhagic phase generally recover.

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) — laryngotracheobronchitis, laryngotracheitis, viral croup, acute laryngotracheobronchitis Epiglottitis Bacterial tracheitis Foreign body aspiration Retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscess Anaphylaxis / angioedema Spasmodic (recurrent) croup Clinical severity assessment (e.g. presence of stridor at rest and recession) Pulse oximetry Anteroposterior neck radiograph only if diagnosis is uncertain (steeple sign) Avoid interventions that distress the child until the airway is secured in severe cases A common viral illness of young children, typically 6 months to 3 years, most often caused by parainfluenza viruses, producing upper airway obstruction at the subglottis. Characterised by a barking (seal-like) cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness, usually preceded by coryza and worse at night. Diagnosis is clinical; a frontal neck radiograph may show subglottic narrowing (the steeple sign) but is not required. Corticosteroids are the mainstay and benefit essentially all severities, reducing symptoms and the need for further intervention. Nebulised adrenaline (epinephrine) provides rapid, temporary relief in moderate to severe cases and mandates a period of observation for rebound. Keeping the child calm and comfortable is important, as agitation and crying worsen airway obstruction. Stridor at rest, marked recession, or hypoxaemia indicates significant obstruction requiring active treatment. Consider alternative diagnoses when the presentation is atypical: sudden toxic appearance suggests epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis, and drooling with dysphagia is a warning sign. Stridor at rest with marked chest wall recession Cyanosis, hypoxaemia, or altered mental status / lethargy Drooling, dysphagia, or a toxic-appearing child suggesting epiglottitis Rapidly worsening obstruction or exhaustion despite treatment Biphasic stridor indicating severe fixed obstruction Distressing the child with unnecessary examination or procedures, worsening obstruction Withholding corticosteroids in mild cases where they still provide benefit Discharging a child after nebulised adrenaline without an adequate observation period for rebound Failing to recognise epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis presenting with a croup-like picture Viral infection produces inflammation and oedema of the larynx, trachea, and subglottic tissues. Because the subglottis is the narrowest part of a child's airway and is encircled by rigid cricoid cartilage, even modest mucosal swelling markedly narrows the lumen, dramatically increasing airway resistance and producing turbulent airflow heard as inspiratory stridor and the characteristic barking cough. Increased work of breathing follows, and severe obstruction can cause hypoxaemia and fatigue. Most children have mild, self-limiting illness that resolves within a few days; severe airway compromise is uncommon and the need for intubation is rare with appropriate treatment.

Crouzon syndrome — craniofacial dysostosis, FGFR2-related craniosynostosis, Crouzon craniofacial dysostosis Apert syndrome (adds complex symmetrical syndactyly) Pfeiffer syndrome (broad thumbs and great toes) Muenke syndrome (FGFR3 coronal synostosis) Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (TWIST1, ptosis, ear anomalies) Antley-Bixler syndrome (synostosis with radiohumeral fusion) Non-syndromic bicoronal craniosynostosis FGFR2 molecular testing (with FGFR3 analysis if acanthosis nigricans is present) Three-dimensional cranial CT to define fused sutures and orbital depth MRI of the brain and craniocervical junction to assess ventricles and hindbrain herniation Ophthalmology assessment for proptosis, corneal exposure and papilloedema Sleep study and airway evaluation for obstructive sleep apnoea Audiology assessment because conductive hearing loss is common Caused by gain-of-function mutations in FGFR2 and inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable expressivity The cardinal feature is craniosynostosis (commonly bicoronal) with midface hypoplasia, shallow orbits and marked proptosis, but crucially the hands and feet are normal Normal digits are the key point distinguishing Crouzon from Apert and Pfeiffer syndromes Shallow orbits cause exorbitism that can threaten the globe, and strabismus and exposure keratopathy are common Midface retrusion produces a relatively prominent lower jaw appearance, dental crowding, and airway narrowing with sleep-disordered breathing A distinct allelic variant with acanthosis nigricans is caused by a specific FGFR3 mutation (Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis nigricans) Raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus and Chiari-type hindbrain herniation may develop and warrant surveillance Care is delivered by a craniofacial team using staged vault expansion and midface advancement, with orbital protection as a priority Globe subluxation or corneal ulceration from severe exorbitism Papilloedema or other signs of raised intracranial pressure Progressive hydrocephalus or symptomatic Chiari malformation Severe obstructive sleep apnoea causing hypoxia Overlooking the diagnosis because intelligence and limbs are normal Failing to protect the exposed globe in a child with marked proptosis Missing evolving hydrocephalus or hindbrain herniation on follow-up Not screening for hearing loss and treating it, which can compound developmental delay Crouzon syndrome arises from activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) that heighten receptor signalling in cranial suture mesenchyme. Overactive signalling accelerates osteoblast differentiation and premature ossification, so the calvarial sutures and cranial base synchondroses fuse early. This restricts the growth of the skull and, importantly, the midface, producing shallow orbits, proptosis and maxillary retrusion, while limb development is spared. An allelic form linked to an FGFR3 mutation additionally shows acanthosis nigricans. Cognition is usually normal, and with timely craniofacial and neurosurgical management most children do well, but ongoing surveillance for raised intracranial pressure, visual and airway complications is essential throughout growth.

fluid resuscitation early, ideally before release of the crushed part, to protect the kidneys and dilute the metabolic load Myoglobin released from damaged muscle causes pigment-induced acute kidney develop compartment syndrome, so examine repeatedly for tense swelling and disproportionate pain Correct hypovolaemia, acidosis, and electrolyte disturbance in parallel while maintaining a good urine output Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes threatening fatal arrhythmia around the time of extrication Progressive acute kidney injury with falling urine output and dark urine Signs of compartment syndrome in the crushed limb requiring urgent assessment Metabolic acidosis and haemodynamic instability on reperfusion Sudden cardiovascular collapse immediately after release of the crushed part Delaying fluid resuscitation until after the limb is freed, when the potassium surge is already underway Overlooking hyperkalaemia and failing to monitor the electrocardiogram during extrication Missing evolving compartment syndrome in the injured limb Under-resuscitating and allowing pigment nephropathy to progress Attributing dark urine to visible blood rather than myoglobin Prolonged compression of muscle causes ischaemic and pressure necrosis (rhabdomyolysis). While compressed, the injury is largely contained, but on release reperfusion washes the accumulated intracellular contents into the systemic circulation. Potassium, myoglobin, phosphate, and organic acids surge, producing hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypocalcaemia. Myoglobin precipitates in the renal tubules, and combined with hypovolaemia from fluid sequestration into damaged muscle, causes acute kidney injury. Massive fluid shifts and the release of vasoactive and inflammatory mediators can cause shock, while swelling within fascial compartments produces compartment syndrome. Early and aggressive fluid resuscitation with prevention and treatment of hyperkalaemia and pigment nephropathy improves outcome. Untreated crush syndrome carries high mortality from arrhythmia and renal failure, though renal function often recovers with timely supportive care and dialysis where needed.

rising creatinine Widespread skin necrosis or digital ischaemia suggesting severe or hyperviscosity-related disease Progressive motor neuropathy or foot drop Features of hyperviscosity such as visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, and confusion in type I disease Gut or cardiac involvement indicating severe systemic vasculitis False-negative cryoglobulin results from allowing the sample to cool before separation Failing to test for hepatitis C in every patient with mixed cryoglobulinaemia Misreading a low C4 with normal C3 as insignificant rather than a supportive clue Treating with immunosuppression alone when an underlying infection or clonal disorder needs directed therapy Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that reversibly precipitate at temperatures below core body temperature and redissolve on warming. In mixed cryoglobulinaemia a polyclonal or monoclonal immunoglobulin with rheumatoid-factor activity binds polyclonal IgG, forming immune complexes that deposit in small and medium vessels, activate complement, and trigger a leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Chronic hepatitis C virus infection is the dominant driver, providing sustained antigenic stimulation that expands rheumatoid-factor-producing B-cell clones. Vascular deposition produces cutaneous purpura, immune-complex glomerulonephritis (often membranoproliferative), and vasa nervorum involvement causing neuropathy. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and organ involvement; hepatitis-C-related disease often improves markedly with viral eradication, whereas severe renal disease, extensive neuropathy, and underlying lymphoproliferative disorders worsen prognosis.
