sensorineural hearing loss Features of central nervous system involvement such as chronic headache, raised intracranial pressure or developmental regression in neonatal-onset disease Proteinuria signalling AA amyloidosis Visual compromise from papilloedema or uveitis Mislabelling the recurrent rash as ordinary allergic urticaria and giving antihistamines Missing the diagnosis when standard NLRP3 sequencing is negative because of somatic mosaicism Delaying interleukin-1 blockade until irreversible hearing or neurological damage has occurred Neglecting audiological and renal surveillance Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes are driven by gain-of-function mutations in NLRP3, which encodes cryopyrin, a sensor protein of the innate immune system. Cryopyrin nucleates the NLRP3 inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that activates caspase-1. The mutations lower the threshold for or constitutively enhance inflammasome assembly, leading to excessive caspase-1-mediated cleavage of pro-interleukin-1 beta into its active form. The resulting overproduction of interleukin-1 beta produces systemic and organ-specific inflammation, and the severity of the phenotype broadly tracks the degree of inflammasome dysregulation. Chronic interleukin-1-driven inflammation underlies the sensorineural deafness, central nervous system disease, and predisposition to AA amyloidosis. Milder cold-induced disease has a favourable outlook, but untreated Muckle-Wells syndrome and NOMID cause progressive deafness, neurological damage and amyloidosis; early and sustained interleukin-1 inhibition can halt organ damage and greatly improve prognosis.

Cryptococcosis — Cryptococcus neoformans infection, cryptococcal meningitis Tuberculous (chronic) meningitis Other fungal meningitides (e.g., Coccidioides, Histoplasma) Subacute dementia or depression (indolent CNS cryptococcosis mimic) Carcinomatous meningitis Pulmonary malignancy or other causes of lung nodules/masses (pulmonary cryptococcosis found incidentally on chest radiograph) Tuberculosis (chronic meningitis and pulmonary disease) Molluscum contagiosum (cutaneous cryptococcosis in highly immunosuppressed patients resembles its lesions) Other disseminated/endemic fungal infections (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis) CSF examination: opening pressure, protein, glucose, cell count, Gram stain, cultures India ink stain of CSF for encapsulated yeast Cryptococcal antigen (CRAg) assay in CSF and blood; point-of-care lateral flow assay Fungal cultures of CSF and blood (blood cultures often positive) Serum CRAg screening in HIV with low CD4+ counts PCR (confirm positive or negative results with independent methods such as CRAg and culture) Chest imaging for pulmonary disease (nodules, infiltrates, masses) Biopsy for CNS cryptococcoma or to distinguish inadequately treated infection from immune reconstitution syndrome Carcinomatous (neoplastic) meningitis Subacute dementia Depression Pulmonary malignancy (cryptococcoma/nodule mimicking neoplasm) Caused by Cryptococcus, a genus of yeast-like fungi; WHO declared C. neoformans a critical priority pathogen in 2022 (p.1703). C. neoformans and C. gattii are now regarded as species complexes; for clinical purposes both cause indistinguishable disease termed cryptococcosis (p.1703-1704). High-risk hosts for C. neoformans: hematologic malignancy, solid-organ transplant, advanced liver disease, diabetes, glucocorticoid therapy, and advanced HIV with CD4+ counts <200/uL (p.1704). C. gattii disease is NOT generally associated with specific immune deficits and often occurs in immunocompetent individuals; associated with autoantibodies to GM-CSF (p.1704). Disease usually presents as pulmonary disease and/or chronic meningoencephalitis, but cryptococcosis can affect any tissue or organ (p.1704-1705). Cryptococcal meningitis differs from bacterial meningitis: many patients present with symptoms of several weeks' duration and classic meningismus may be absent; indolent cases can present as subacute dementia or depression (p.1705). In AIDS patients, cryptococcal meningitis is the initial AIDS-defining illness in ~2% and generally occurs with CD4+ counts <100/uL; about one-third also have pulmonary disease (p.1606). Diagnosis requires demonstration of cryptococcal cells or antigen in normally sterile tissue; India ink of CSF shows encapsulated yeast and CRAg (serum/CSF) is both sensitive and specific with rapid point-of-care lateral flow assays (p.1705). Increased intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is managed by repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures and shunt placement; mannitol and acetazolamide are NOT effective (p.1706). Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) can occur after starting ART in HIV; recommended to start ART 4-6 weeks after initiating antifungal therapy (p.1706). Serum CRAg screening is recommended for asymptomatic people with HIV and CD4+ counts <100-200/uL to identify those at high risk of cryptococcal disease (p.1705-1706). Raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningoencephalitis requiring serial therapeutic lumbar puncture drainage (and possible shunt placement) Sudden catastrophic vision loss from meningeal cryptococcosis Cranial nerve paresis, vision and hearing loss Altered mental status, headache, and blurred vision as clues to elevated ICP Refractory cryptococcosis despite antifungal therapy (prompt susceptibility testing) India ink and Gram stain may be falsely negative with low fungal burden or misread as positive by inexperienced operators (p.1705). CRAg is often negative in pulmonary cryptococcosis, so it is less useful for diagnosing pulmonary disease and of only limited use in monitoring response to therapy (p.1705). Cryptococcal cells with negative cultures on CSF staining and persistently elevated CSF/blood cryptococcal antigen long after culture clearance do NOT indicate treatment failure (p.1705). Categorizing cryptococcosis as 'extrapulmonary without CNS involvement' should be made only after CSF evaluation reveals no evidence of cryptococcal infection (p.1705). Prophylactic dexamethasone in HIV-associated cryptococcosis is NOT recommended (associated with reduced fungal clearance and increased mortality); glucocorticoids are not helpful for raised ICP unless from a mass lesion with edema (p.1706). Echinocandins are NOT effective against Cryptococcus species (p.1706). IRIS can be difficult to distinguish from relapsing/refractory infection (p.1706). Cryptococcal infection is almost always acquired by inhalation of aerosolized particles (small desiccated yeast cells or basidiospores); occasionally by direct skin inoculation. C. neoformans is found in soils contaminated with avian (pigeon) excreta, whereas C. gattii inhabits arboreal species such as eucalyptus and is not found in bird feces. Infection is acquired in childhood and is common, but disease is rare in the absence of impaired immunity, indicating that intact pulmonary defenses effectively contain the fungus. Some infections lead to latency with viable organisms harbored in granulomas. Extrapulmonary dissemination to the CNS may occur via direct fungal migration across endothelium and via macrophage 'Trojan horse' carriage. Virulence factors include the antiphagocytic polysaccharide capsule, melanin production, and enzymes (phospholipase, urease). Copious release of capsular polysaccharide into tissues interferes with local immune responses, and infection may elicit little or no inflammatory response; capsular polysaccharide is the antigen measured diagnostically (p.1704). Even with antifungal therapy, cryptococcosis carries high morbidity and mortality. The most important prognostic factors are the extent and duration of the underlying immunologic deficit. Disease is often curable in those with no apparent immune dysfunction, but in irreversible immunosuppression the goal is remission maintained by lifelong suppressive therapy. Before ART, median survival for AIDS patients with cryptococcosis was <1 year. Cryptococcosis with underlying neoplastic disease has a particularly poor prognosis. Poor prognostic markers for CNS disease: positive India ink on initial CSF exam (heavy fungal burden), high CSF pressure, low CSF glucose, low CSF pleocytosis (<2/uL), recovery of yeast from extraneural sites, absence of antibody to capsular polysaccharide, CSF or serum cryptococcal antigen level >=1:32, and concomitant glucocorticoid therapy or hematologic malignancy. Relapse is common even with relatively intact immunity (p.1706). Nonsevere disease limited to the lungs or other non-CNS sites is distinguished from severe disease or CNS involvement; severe/CNS cryptococcosis is treated with induction, consolidation, and maintenance phases (p.1705).

Cryptosporidiosis — Cryptosporidium infection, crypto, cryptosporidial diarrhoea Other protozoal enteritides (giardiasis, cyclosporiasis, microsporidiosis) Bacterial and viral gastroenteritis Other opportunistic enteric infections in HIV Inflammatory bowel disease Non-infective malabsorption syndromes Other opportunistic causes of chronic diarrhoea in advanced HIV Small bowel malabsorption of non-infective cause Secretory diarrhoea from other pathogens Modified acid-fast (Kinyoun) staining of stool for oocysts Stool antigen detection or PCR for sensitive diagnosis HIV testing and CD4 count assessment when severe or chronic Evaluation of hydration and electrolyte status Imaging or biliary studies if cholangiopathy is suspected in the immunocompromised A protozoal infection caused by Cryptosporidium species, transmitted faecal-orally through contaminated water, food or contact, with a very low infectious dose In immunocompetent hosts it causes a self-limiting watery diarrhoea, but in the immunocompromised, especially advanced HIV, it can cause severe, chronic and life-threatening diarrhoea A recognised cause of waterborne outbreaks because the oocysts are highly resistant to routine chlorination An important contributor to childhood diarrhoea and to malnutrition and growth faltering in Indian children In profound immunosuppression infection may extend beyond the gut to the biliary tract, causing sclerosing cholangitis, and to the respiratory tract Restoration of immune function, particularly antiretroviral therapy in HIV, is central to control in immunocompromised patients Diagnosis requires specific tests: modified acid-fast staining of stool, antigen detection or PCR, as the oocysts are missed on routine microscopy Management emphasises rehydration; antiprotozoal drug options are limited and work best when immunity is restored Severe or high-volume dehydrating diarrhoea, especially in infants or the immunocompromised Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss in a patient with advanced HIV/AIDS Right upper quadrant pain and cholestasis suggesting biliary involvement Failure of diarrhoea to settle, signalling underlying immunodeficiency Failing to request specific staining, antigen or PCR tests, so oocysts are missed on routine stool microscopy Not testing for HIV in a patient with severe or persistent cryptosporidial diarrhoea Relying on antiprotozoal drugs alone in the immunocompromised without addressing the underlying immune deficit Underestimating waterborne outbreak potential given oocyst resistance to chlorination Ingested Cryptosporidium oocysts release sporozoites that invade the apical surface of intestinal epithelial cells, residing in an intracellular but extracytoplasmic compartment. Infection blunts villi, impairs absorption and increases secretion, producing a watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. In immunocompetent people a robust cellular immune response clears the parasite, but when T-cell immunity is deficient the organism proliferates unchecked, causing high-volume chronic diarrhoea, malabsorption and spread to biliary and respiratory epithelium. In immunocompetent individuals the illness resolves spontaneously over one to two weeks. In severely immunocompromised patients it can be chronic, debilitating and fatal unless immune function is restored, and outcome is closely tied to recovery of cellular immunity.

Crystal arthritis (gout / pseudogout) — Joint aspiration + polarised microscopy Serum urate (off-attack) Septic arthritis must be excluded by aspiration Palindromic rheumatism (Harrison 22e p.2958) Psoriatic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958) Osteoarthritis - CPPD pseudo-osteoarthritis variant mimics progressive OA, often in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) (Harrison 22e p.2960-2961) Rheumatoid arthritis - chronic symmetric CPP synovitis can clinically resemble RA (Harrison 22e p.2961) Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy - severe destructive CPPD may radiographically mimic it (Harrison 22e p.2961) Cellulitis - acute gout flare with warm, red, swollen periarticular tissue may mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958) Septic arthritis - crystal arthritis closely mimics it; aspiration with Gram stain and culture is essential, especially as bacterial infection can coexist with crystals in synovial fluid (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961) Polarized light microscopy of synovial fluid - MSU: needle/rod-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent; CPP: rhomboid/rod-shaped, weakly positively or non-birefringent; apatite: non-birefringent (requires alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy); calcium oxalate: bipyramidal, variable/strong birefringence, alizarin red S positive (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962) Synovial fluid Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting septic arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961) Synovial fluid leukocyte count - gout flare typically 5000-75,000/uL; acute CPPD ~24,000/uL (range several thousand to 100,000); apatite and calcium oxalate usually <2000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961-2962) Arthrocentesis of an unaffected first MTP joint or knee between flares can still demonstrate MSU crystals (Harrison 22e p.2959) Plain radiographs - advanced gout: well-defined erosions with sclerotic/overhanging margins, soft tissue tophi; CPPD: punctate/linear chondrocalcinosis in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961) Musculoskeletal ultrasound - double-contour sign over articular cartilage indicating MSU deposition; can also reveal chondrocalcinosis in CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2959, p.2961) Dual-energy CT - identifies MSU crystals by chemical composition (Harrison 22e p.2959) Baseline labs to assess comorbidities and treatment safety: serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, lipids (Harrison 22e p.2959) In CPPD patients under 50, evaluate for metabolic/familial causes: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, transferrin (Harrison 22e p.2960) HLA-B*5801 screening before allopurinol in high-prevalence populations (Southeast Asian, Pacific Islander/Native Hawaiian, Black patients) to reduce risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (knowledge point) (Harrison 22e p.2960) Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) mimics acute gout flares (Harrison 22e p.2960) Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) deposition disease (Harrison 22e p.2961) Calcium oxalate arthropathy - acute presentation may be indistinguishable from MSU, CPP, or apatite crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2962) Osteoarthritis (pseudo-osteoarthritis pattern of CPPD) (Harrison 22e p.2961) Initial gout flares are usually monoarticular; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases, followed by tarsal joints, ankles, and knees. Oligo- and polyarticular flares emerge over time (Harrison 22e p.2958). Gout flares often begin at night to early morning, are among the most painful conditions humans experience, and the affected joint becomes warm, red, tender, and very swollen, frequently mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.2958). Untreated flares usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intervals (intercritical gout) until the next episode (Harrison 22e p.2958). Serum urate can be normal or low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower urate by about 2 mg/dL; seek historical or post-flare urate values instead (Harrison 22e p.2959). In CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) the knee is most commonly affected, followed by the wrist; the first MTP joint (podagra) is rarely involved, a useful distinguishing clue from gout (Harrison 22e p.2960). Initial acute CPPD attacks tend to last longer than typical gout flares, sometimes weeks to months (Harrison 22e p.2960). Acute CPPD can be precipitated by trauma, severe medical illness, or surgery (especially parathyroidectomy, which rapidly lowers serum calcium and magnesium and sheds crystals) (Harrison 22e p.2960). Women account for only about 5-20% of gout patients; most are postmenopausal, elderly, and often on diuretics with coexisting osteoarthritis, hypertension, or mild renal insufficiency. Premenopausal gout is rare (Harrison 22e p.2958). Hyperuricemia in a prepubertal boy should prompt consideration of inherited enzyme defects such as HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum) or PRPP synthetase superactivity (Harrison 22e p.2958). Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) arthropathy can cause an extremely destructive arthropathy of the elderly, classically the shoulder (Milwaukee shoulder), with low synovial fluid leukocyte counts despite dramatic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2961). Hyperuricemia and gout are part of the insulin-resistance syndrome and associate with cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities: obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, CKD, and urate nephrolithiasis (Harrison 22e p.2956). Crystal-proven arthritis does not exclude concurrent septic arthritis - bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid; always Gram stain and culture (Harrison 22e p.2958, p.2961) Acute CPPD can produce systemic features (fever, chills, raised acute-phase reactants), with low-grade fever in up to 50% and temperatures occasionally as high as 40C - mandates microbial culture to exclude infection (Harrison 22e p.2960, p.2961) CPPD onset before age 50 warrants workup for underlying metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) or hereditary CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2960) Relying on a normal serum urate during an acute flare to exclude gout - urate is often normal or low at flare onset (Harrison 22e p.2959). Attributing a destructive 'osteoarthritis' in atypical joints (MCP, wrist, elbow, shoulder, ankle) to primary OA rather than recognizing pseudo-osteoarthritis from CPPD (Harrison 22e p.2961). Assuming chondrocalcinosis on imaging is always CPPD - calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure is an exception (Harrison 22e p.2961). Missing apatite arthropathy because individual apatite crystals are not visible on routine polarized light microscopy and need alizarin red S staining or electron microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2961). Overlooking inherited enzyme defects when hyperuricemia/gout presents in a young patient, particularly a prepubertal boy (Harrison 22e p.2958). Gout arises from an increased body urate pool due to chronic hyperuricemia, leading to supersaturation and crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within joints and connective tissue. Hyperuricemia is predominantly due to impaired renal urate excretion (~90%) and less often urate overproduction (~10%); a minority (~10%) of cases reflect inherited metabolic disorders (PRPP synthetase superactivity, HPRT deficiency). Crystal shedding from inert synovial deposits, triggered by metabolic factors, diuresis, rapid urate changes (including urate-lowering therapy initiation), local trauma, or medical illness, activates resident synovial phagocytes (monocytes/macrophages, mast cells) and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta and other proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by neutrophils with a respiratory burst amplifies the acute inflammatory response. Persistent MSU deposition produces tophi (granulomatous inflammation around crystals) and chronic erosive gouty arthritis. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals; their release similarly drives inflammasome-mediated inflammation, analogous to hyperuricemia in gout. Apatite and calcium oxalate crystals can likewise stimulate synovial cell proliferation and release of proteases, collagenases, and prostaglandin E2, contributing to joint destruction (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962). Untreated gout flares typically resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, but recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, joint deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Controlling the underlying chronic hyperuricemia (urate-lowering therapy to a subsaturation target) can prevent recurrent flares and dissolve tophi, generally requiring lifelong therapy. For chronic CPPD there is no means to remove established CPP crystal deposits from cartilage and synovium (unlike urate lowering in gout), and progressive destructive large-joint disease may require joint replacement. Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) progresses indolently and may also lead to joint replacement (Harrison 22e p.2958-2962).

Cushing syndrome — hypercortisolism, Cushing's syndrome, cortisol excess, Cushing disease (pituitary-dependent) Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid effect Pseudo-Cushing states from severe obesity, depression, or heavy alcohol use Metabolic syndrome with central obesity Polycystic ovary syndrome Poorly controlled diabetes with weight gain Ectopic ACTH from neuroendocrine malignancy Late-night salivary cortisol to detect loss of the normal evening nadir 24-hour urinary free cortisol, ideally on more than one collection Low-dose (overnight or 48-hour) dexamethasone suppression testing Plasma ACTH to separate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease Pituitary MRI, adrenal CT, or cross-sectional imaging for ectopic sources as directed by biochemistry Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise ACTH-dependent disease when imaging is equivocal Typical features include central weight gain, a rounded plethoric face, a dorsocervical fat pad, thin skin, and easy bruising Wide purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, and unexplained osteoporosis are among the more discriminating clinical signs Exogenous glucocorticoid use is by far the most common cause and should be excluded by careful drug history before pursuing endogenous disease Diagnosis proceeds in two stages: first confirm cortisol excess, then determine whether it is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent Screening rests on demonstrating loss of normal cortisol regulation using late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test A suppressed ACTH points to an adrenal source, whereas a normal or elevated ACTH indicates a pituitary tumour or an ectopic source Pituitary-dependent disease (Cushing disease) accounts for most endogenous ACTH-dependent cases, while ectopic ACTH is often from neuroendocrine tumours Associated metabolic consequences include hypertension, glucose intolerance or diabetes, dyslipidaemia, and increased thrombotic and infection risk Definitive management is directed at the underlying cause, most often surgical removal of the responsible tumour Rapid onset with marked hypokalaemia and pigmentation suggesting aggressive ectopic ACTH secretion New severe hypertension, hyperglycaemia, or thromboembolism from florid hypercortisolism Features of adrenal carcinoma such as very high androgen or cortisol levels with a large adrenal mass Severe proximal weakness, fractures, or psychosis reflecting advanced disease Overlooking exogenous steroid exposure, including inhaled, topical, or injected preparations Interpreting a single borderline test as diagnostic rather than repeating and combining screening tests Confusing pseudo-Cushing states with true disease during acute illness, depression, or alcohol excess Assuming a pituitary microadenoma on imaging proves the source without confirmatory biochemistry Cushing syndrome results from chronic exposure to excess glucocorticoid. This may be exogenous, from prescribed or surreptitious steroid use, or endogenous. Endogenous disease is divided into ACTH-dependent forms, in which a pituitary corticotroph adenoma or an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumour drives adrenal cortisol output, and ACTH-independent forms, in which an adrenal adenoma, carcinoma, or bilateral hyperplasia autonomously produces cortisol. Sustained cortisol excess disrupts the normal negative-feedback of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, abolishes the circadian rhythm of cortisol, and produces widespread catabolic, metabolic, immunosuppressive, and mineralocorticoid effects on multiple tissues. With successful treatment of the underlying cause many features regress over months, though hypertension, bone loss, and psychological effects may persist; untreated hypercortisolism carries substantial cardiovascular, metabolic, infective, and thrombotic mortality, and ectopic ACTH from malignancy has a poor outlook.

Cutaneous Larva Migrans — CLM, creeping eruption, sandworm disease, hookworm-related cutaneous larva migrans Larva currens due to Strongyloides (faster-moving track, often perianal) Scabies Contact dermatitis Tinea (especially of the feet) Erythema migrans of Lyme disease Loiasis or other migratory parasitic eruptions in the appropriate exposure setting Diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic migrating track and exposure history Dermoscopy may help visualise the larval track Blood eosinophilia is variable and non-specific Biopsy is usually unhelpful because the larva lies ahead of the visible track and is rarely captured Assessment for secondary bacterial infection when the site is inflamed or purulent The hallmark is an intensely itchy, serpiginous (snake-like), slightly raised erythematous track that advances a short distance each day It commonly affects the feet, buttocks, and other skin that contacts contaminated sand or soil, reflecting exposure during beach holidays or barefoot activity in warm climates Take a travel and exposure history, as most cases in temperate regions are imported from tropical and subtropical areas The larva itself lies just ahead of the visible track, so the leading edge marks its current position It is a self-limiting zoonotic infestation because the human is a dead-end host in which the animal hookworm larva cannot complete its life cycle Antihelminthic therapy shortens symptoms and is warranted for troublesome disease; the itch responds as the larva dies and the track resolves Secondary bacterial infection from scratching and, less often, a localised allergic reaction can complicate the picture Preventive advice includes wearing footwear and using barriers on contaminated sand or soil Extensive involvement or numerous tracks suggesting heavy exposure or an immunocompromised host Rapidly moving perianal tracks or features suggesting Strongyloides, which can disseminate and requires different management Signs of secondary bacterial infection such as spreading erythema, pain, or pus Systemic symptoms or respiratory features prompting reconsideration of a diagnosis with visceral involvement Failing to elicit a travel or sand-exposure history and missing the diagnosis Confusing it with the faster-moving larva currens of Strongyloides, which carries a risk of dissemination Performing an unhelpful biopsy at the visible track rather than treating clinically Overlooking secondary bacterial infection driven by scratching Cutaneous larva migrans is caused by the larvae of animal hookworms, most often Ancylostoma species from dogs and cats, whose eggs are shed in animal faeces and hatch into infective larvae in warm, moist sand or soil. On contact these larvae penetrate intact human skin but lack the enzymes to cross the basement membrane, so they remain trapped in the epidermis. As the larva migrates it provokes a local eosinophilic inflammatory and hypersensitivity response that produces the itchy, advancing serpiginous track. Because humans are accidental dead-end hosts, the parasite cannot mature or disseminate and eventually dies, giving the self-limiting course. The condition is benign and self-limiting, as the larva dies within weeks to a few months even without treatment; antihelminthic therapy shortens the intensely itchy course and speeds resolution, and lasting sequelae are uncommon apart from transient post-inflammatory change.

Cutis laxa — dermatochalasis (generalised), elastolysis, ELN-related cutis laxa, ATP6V0A2-related cutis laxa Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Pseudoxanthoma elasticum De Barsy syndrome Geroderma osteodysplasticum Wrinkly skin syndrome Age-related or actinic skin laxity Skin biopsy with elastic-tissue staining to assess elastic-fibre number and structure Molecular genetic testing with a cutis laxa gene panel to define the subtype Echocardiography and vascular imaging for aneurysm and arterial tortuosity Pulmonary function testing and chest imaging for emphysema Developmental and growth assessment in children Investigation for an underlying cause when an acquired form is suspected A heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by loose, inelastic, sagging skin that hangs in redundant folds and does not recoil when stretched It may be inherited or acquired; inherited forms include autosomal dominant (often ELN), autosomal recessive, and X-linked (occipital horn) types with differing systemic risks Unlike Ehlers-Danlos syndrome the skin is lax rather than hyperextensible, and joint hypermobility is not the dominant feature Systemic elastic-tissue involvement can cause emphysema, aortic and arterial aneurysm or tortuosity, and hollow-viscus diverticula depending on subtype Autosomal recessive and some syndromic forms may include developmental delay, growth restriction, and skeletal anomalies Acquired cutis laxa can follow inflammatory skin disease, drug reactions, or systemic conditions and may be a marker of underlying disease Diagnosis combines the clinical appearance, skin biopsy showing sparse or fragmented elastic fibres, and molecular genetic testing to define the subtype Management is supportive, with cardiorespiratory and vascular surveillance in at-risk subtypes and plastic-surgical options for the skin Acute chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting arterial aneurysm rupture or dissection Progressive breathlessness from emphysema or spontaneous pneumothorax Signs of bowel or bladder diverticular complications New neurological signs suggesting cerebrovascular involvement Rapidly progressive acquired skin laxity indicating serious underlying disease Confusing lax, non-recoiling skin with the hyperextensible skin of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Treating it purely as a cosmetic problem and missing systemic elastic-tissue disease Failing to arrange cardiovascular and pulmonary surveillance in high-risk subtypes Overlooking an underlying systemic trigger in acquired cutis laxa Not defining the subtype, which is essential for prognosis and counselling Cutis laxa reflects a defect in the formation, cross-linking, or maintenance of elastic fibres in connective tissue. Inherited forms disrupt elastin itself (for example ELN variants) or proteins and enzymes required for elastic-fibre assembly, copper-dependent cross-linking, or intracellular trafficking, leaving elastic fibres sparse, fragmented, or disorganised. Loss of functional elastic tissue removes the normal recoil of the skin and can weaken the walls of the lungs, arteries, and hollow organs, explaining the sagging skin together with emphysema, arterial aneurysm and tortuosity, and diverticula in the more severe systemic subtypes. Acquired forms arise from elastic-fibre destruction driven by inflammation or other secondary insults. Prognosis varies widely by subtype: isolated cutaneous disease is mainly a cosmetic and functional concern with a normal lifespan, whereas forms with pulmonary, cardiovascular, or multisystem involvement can significantly reduce life expectancy. Surveillance of at-risk systems guides outcome.

gingivitis and ulceration An autosomal dominant disorder caused by ELANE mutations in which neutrophil counts oscillate, typically with a regular cycle of about three weeks During the nadir, patients develop recurrent fever, mouth ulcers, gingivitis, cervical adenopathy, and skin or respiratory infections The characteristic periodicity distinguishes it from severe congenital neutropenia, which is persistent rather than oscillating Diagnosis requires serial blood counts two or three times weekly for six to eight weeks to capture the cyclical pattern Unlike severe congenital neutropenia, cyclic neutropenia carries little or no increased risk of leukaemic transformation G-CSF shortens and shallows the neutrophil nadir and reduces infection during vulnerable periods Monocytes and other cell lines often oscillate reciprocally, and symptoms tend to lessen with age Serious deep-seated infection or sepsis during a neutrophil nadir Clostridial or necrotising soft-tissue infection, a recognised hazard during severe nadirs Failure of counts to recover between cycles, prompting reconsideration of severe congenital neutropenia Persistent oral or perianal infection despite treatment Making the diagnosis from a single blood count rather than serial sampling across a cycle Confusing it with severe congenital neutropenia and overstating the leukaemia risk Underestimating the danger of clostridial or necrotising infection during a deep nadir Attributing recurrent mouth ulcers to an unrelated cause and missing the periodicity Cyclic neutropenia is caused by heterozygous mutations in ELANE, the gene for neutrophil elastase, which produce a misfolded protein that stresses developing myeloid precursors and periodically curtails granulopoiesis. The oscillation reflects a disturbance in the feedback regulation of the haematopoietic stem and progenitor compartment, so neutrophil production rises and falls in a regular rhythm of roughly three weeks. During each production trough the circulating neutrophil count falls to very low levels, leaving the patient transiently susceptible to bacterial infection and mucosal ulceration, before recovering as the next wave of granulopoiesis emerges. Although the same gene is implicated in severe congenital neutropenia, the mutational spectrum and cellular consequences differ, which is thought to explain why cyclic disease does not share the marked predisposition to myeloid malignancy. Cyclic neutropenia generally has a good long-term outlook, symptoms often attenuate with age, and it lacks the marked leukaemic risk of severe congenital neutropenia, though infections during nadirs can occasionally be life-threatening.

Cystic Fibrosis — CF, CFTR disease Non-CF bronchiectasis (CF carrier status predisposes; heterozygous CFTR mutations implicated) (p.2247) Chronic rhinosinusitis (associated with relative CFTR deficiency) (p.2247) Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens as an isolated forme fruste of CFTR mutation (p.2247) Idiopathic/recurrent pancreatitis associated with CFTR mutation in at least one allele (p.2247) Sweat chloride after pilocarpine iontophoresis (chloride >=60 mEq/L supports diagnosis; highly specific) (p.2246-2247) CFTR mutation analysis / panels of several hundred variants, or complete CFTR sequencing with splice-junction analysis (p.2246-2247) Immunoreactive trypsinogen (newborn screening) (p.2246) Fecal elastase-1 (low in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency) (p.2246) Sputum culture surveillance for resistant pathogens (Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, atypical mycobacteria, MRSA) (p.2248) FEV1 (% predicted) for monitoring and transplant referral thresholds (p.2248) Annual diabetes mellitus testing in adults; monitor liver function and CYP3A drug interactions on modulator therapy (p.2248) Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive exocrinopathy affecting multiple epithelial tissues; the gene product CFTR is an apical anion (chloride and bicarbonate) channel that regulates the volume and composition of exocrine secretion (p.2245). Major morbidity and mortality arise from pulmonary disease: copious hyperviscous adherent secretions obstruct small and medium airways, and a complex flora including Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is routinely cultured from CF sputum (p.2245). P. aeruginosa shows stereotypic pathogenesis: an early sentinel colonization often becomes lifelong infection by the same strain, and over years evolves a mucoid (alginate-producing) phenotype that confers selective advantage and poor host prognosis (p.2245). Radiographic sinusitis occurs in most patients with CF; the sinuses may act as a reservoir for bacterial seeding of the lower airways (p.2245). Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes chronic malabsorption, poor growth, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; high blood immunoreactive trypsinogen (used in newborn screening) and low fecal elastase-1 are characteristic (p.2245-2246). CF-related diabetes mellitus occurs in >30% of adults and is multifactorial (endocrine pancreatic destruction plus, in some, insulin resistance); annual diabetes testing is recommended for adults with CF (p.2246, p.2248). Men typically show complete involution of the vas deferens despite functioning spermatogenesis, and ~99% of males with CF are infertile (unable to conceive without in vitro fertilization) (p.2246). Diagnosis is confirmed by disease-causing variants on both CFTR alleles and/or sweat chloride >=60 mEq/L together with characteristic exocrine manifestations; sweat electrolyte testing follows pilocarpine iontophoresis (p.2246-2247). Several severe defects (F508del, G551D, nonsense alleles) predict pancreatic insufficiency, present in ~80% of patients; F508del alone accounts for ~85% of defective CFTR alleles in the United States (p.2247). CFTR modulators (ivacaftor potentiator; lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor correctors) are highly effective modulator therapy (HEMT); triple combination therapy is projected to benefit >90% of patients and improves FEV1, reduces exacerbations, and lowers sweat chloride (p.2247-2248). Pulmonary exacerbation poor-prognosis pathogens that are rigorously monitored include Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, and atypical mycobacteria; MRSA may also signal worse outcomes (p.2248). Infection commonly persists despite modulator therapy, so chronic respiratory infection and inflammation continue even after substantial clinical improvement on HEMT (p.2248). Hemoptysis requiring hospitalization (p.2248) Pneumothorax requiring hospitalization (p.2248) Sputum culture growing Burkholderia cepacia complex, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Achromobacter, mucoid P. aeruginosa, or atypical mycobacteria (poor prognostic indicators) (p.2248) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (~5% of patients) suggested by failure to respond to aggressive inpatient antibiotics (p.2248) FEV1 <30% predicted (threshold for lung transplant referral) (p.2248) Hyperviscosity of eccrine sweat is NOT a feature of CF; the sweat test reflects defective ductal chloride reabsorption, not thick sweat (p.2247). Anion flux through CFTR does NOT involve active transport against a concentration gradient (p.2245-2246). Genotype does NOT reliably predict respiratory prognosis or longevity, even though some severe alleles predict pancreatic insufficiency (p.2247). A subset of patients with F508del respond poorly to triple combination therapy, so modulator benefit is not universal (p.2248). HEMT may reduce sputum bacterial density but does NOT eradicate infection; chronic respiratory infection and inflammation persist (p.2248). CF has been underdiagnosed outside historically white populations (Eastern Europe, Latin America, Asia, India, and US minorities), often due to rare/poorly characterized variants and limited access to DNA/sweat testing (p.2249). Mutation of CFTR, an apical epithelial anion channel that conducts chloride and bicarbonate (~1480 amino acids, gated by ATP hydrolysis without active transport against gradient), impairs hydration and clearance of exocrine secretions. In the airway, loss of CFTR-dependent anion secretion depletes the periciliary fluid layer, causing ciliary collapse and failure to clear overlying mucus; mucoobstruction with chronic infection drives an aggressive, unrelenting neutrophilic inflammatory response with proteases and oxidants, leading to airway remodeling and bronchiectasis. Low airway-surface-fluid pH may impair bacterial killing. Similar mechanisms affect pancreatic acini/ducts (fibrotic destruction, cyst formation, exocrine and eventually endocrine insufficiency), hepatobiliary tissue (biliary obstruction, focal/multilobular cirrhosis, portal hypertension), and intestine (meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstructive syndrome). Over 2000 CFTR allelic variants are described and grouped into classes I-VI by molecular mechanism (e.g., F508del is a class II protein-maturation/folding defect degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum; G551D is a class III gating defect). Modulator and other therapies have transformed CF from a disease that historically led to death in early childhood to one with frequent survival well into the fifth decade and beyond; US median survival now exceeds 60 years. Genotype is of limited value for predicting respiratory rate of decline or longevity. End-stage pulmonary failure may be treated with lung transplantation (median survival >9 years among adults). Marked geographic disparity exists: median survival is <30 years in much of Latin America versus >60 years in the United States (p.2248-2249). CFTR mutations are categorized by molecular mechanism into classes I-VI: class I, absent synthesis (e.g., nonsense mutations G542X, R553X, W1282X); class II, defective protein maturation and premature degradation (e.g., F508del, ~85% of US alleles, the most common); class III, disordered gating/regulation (e.g., G551D, ~4% of patients); class IV, defective conductance through the channel pore; class V, reduced transcript number from promoter/splicing abnormality; class VI, accelerated turnover from the cell surface. Severity is not formally graded by stage; FEV1 <30% predicted is used as a lung-transplant referral threshold (p.2246, p.2248).

Cystic Fibrosis (Paediatric) — CF, cystic fibrosis, mucoviscidosis, paediatric cystic fibrosis Primary ciliary dyskinesia Immunodeficiency with recurrent infections Asthma with recurrent chest infections Protracted bacterial bronchitis Coeliac disease or other causes of malabsorption and failure to thrive Shwachman-Diamond syndrome Newborn screening (immunoreactive trypsinogen) with confirmatory testing Sweat chloride testing CFTR genetic analysis Assessment of pancreatic function (e.g. faecal elastase) Respiratory cultures to identify airway pathogens Chest imaging and, in older children, lung function testing Nutritional assessment and fat-soluble vitamin levels An autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, the most common of which is F508del. It is a genetic disease, not an infection, though recurrent respiratory infections dominate its course and morbidity. Suspect it in a child with chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections, failure to thrive, and greasy, bulky, foul-smelling stools from fat malabsorption. Meconium ileus in a newborn is highly suggestive and is often the earliest presentation. Many countries diagnose it through newborn screening, but a positive screen must be confirmed, classically with an elevated sweat chloride test. Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency is common and requires enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, with attention to overall nutrition. Chronic airway infection, notably with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, drives progressive bronchiectasis and lung function decline. Care is delivered by a specialist multidisciplinary team, and CFTR modulator therapies have transformed outcomes for eligible genotypes. Failure to thrive or faltering growth reflecting malabsorption and increased energy demands New or persistent Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection requiring eradication Acute pulmonary exacerbation with increased cough, sputum, breathlessness, or falling lung function Haemoptysis or pneumothorax Distal intestinal obstruction syndrome or meconium ileus in the newborn Signs of CF-related diabetes or liver disease emerging over time Attributing recurrent chest infections and loose stools to common childhood illness and missing the diagnosis Assuming a negative newborn screen fully excludes CF, since screening can miss some cases Underestimating nutritional needs and failing to optimise pancreatic enzyme and vitamin replacement Delaying treatment of new Pseudomonas infection when early eradication is most effective Overlooking emerging complications such as CF-related diabetes and liver disease Mutations in the CFTR gene impair the CFTR chloride and bicarbonate channel at epithelial surfaces. Defective ion transport produces thick, dehydrated secretions across multiple organs. In the airways, viscous mucus impairs mucociliary clearance, promoting chronic infection, neutrophilic inflammation, and progressive bronchiectasis. In the pancreas, ductal obstruction leads to exocrine insufficiency and malabsorption; similar mechanisms affect the intestine, biliary tree, sweat glands (hence high sweat chloride), and reproductive tract. Survival has improved dramatically with multidisciplinary care, aggressive infection and nutrition management, and CFTR modulator therapy, with many people now living well into adulthood; prognosis is largely determined by the rate of progressive lung disease and nutritional status.

Cystic hygroma — lymphatic malformation, lymphangioma, macrocystic lymphatic malformation Branchial cleft cyst Haemangioma or other vascular malformation Thyroglossal cyst (if midline) Lipoma or other soft-tissue mass Cervical abscess or lymphadenitis Neck and soft-tissue ultrasound to confirm the cystic nature and transillumination correlate MRI to map the full extent and involvement of adjacent structures Antenatal ultrasound and karyotyping when detected in the fetus Airway assessment (including nasendoscopy or cross-sectional imaging) for large cervical lesions Assessment for associated syndromes when clinically indicated A congenital lymphatic malformation that most often presents as a soft, compressible, painless swelling in the posterior triangle of the neck or the axilla The lesion characteristically transilluminates brightly because it is filled with clear lymphatic fluid Many are detected antenatally or in early infancy; fetal nuchal cystic hygroma is associated with chromosomal abnormalities such as Turner and Down syndromes The swelling may enlarge suddenly following intracystic bleeding or with an upper respiratory infection Large cervical lesions can extend toward the floor of the mouth or mediastinum and threaten the airway or swallowing Ultrasound and MRI define the extent and whether the lesion is macrocystic or microcystic, guiding treatment choice Management options include sclerotherapy (often effective for macrocystic lesions) and surgical excision, though complete removal can be difficult when the malformation infiltrates vital structures Because the malformation crosses tissue planes and encases nerves and vessels, incomplete excision and recurrence are common Airway compromise from a large or rapidly enlarging cervical or oral lesion, which may be life-threatening Sudden painful swelling due to intracystic haemorrhage Signs of infection within the malformation causing rapid expansion Feeding or swallowing difficulty from mass effect on the pharynx Attempting aggressive complete excision at the cost of damaging encased nerves and vessels Underestimating airway risk in large cervical lesions before intervention Assuming the lesion will spontaneously resolve, unlike infantile haemangiomas Overlooking associated chromosomal or cardiac anomalies in antenatally detected cases Cystic hygroma is a malformation of the lymphatic system in which sequestered lymphatic channels fail to connect normally with the venous drainage, producing dilated, fluid-filled cystic spaces. These may be macrocystic (large cysts) or microcystic and tend to infiltrate along tissue planes rather than respect anatomical boundaries. Accumulated lymph distends the cysts, and intralesional haemorrhage or infection can cause rapid, sometimes dangerous, enlargement. The malformation grows with the child and does not spontaneously regress in most cases. Small, well-localised macrocystic lesions often respond well to sclerotherapy or excision. Extensive, infiltrative, or microcystic malformations are harder to eradicate, recur frequently, and may require repeated interventions. Fetal cystic hygromas associated with chromosomal or cardiac anomalies carry a guarded prognosis.

this is distinct from intestinal tapeworm infection acquired by eating undercooked pork Faecal-oral spread of eggs from a tapeworm carrier means infection can occur even in people who do not eat pork, including through contaminated food and poor sanitation Cysts lodge preferentially in muscle, subcutaneous tissue, the eyes and the central nervous system; neurological involvement is the most important form Subcutaneous and muscular cysts may be palpable as painless nodules and can calcify, sometimes visible on imaging Ocular cysticercosis can threaten vision and requires careful assessment before any antiparasitic therapy It is a major public-health problem in India and other regions where pigs are raised with poor sanitation Serology (antibody detection) supports the diagnosis, but imaging is central to defining cyst location and burden Antiparasitic therapy is used with adjunctive corticosteroids to control the inflammation provoked by dying cysts, and treatment decisions depend heavily on the site and stage of cysts New-onset seizures or focal neurological deficits indicating central nervous system involvement Features of raised intracranial pressure requiring urgent evaluation Visual disturbance suggesting an ocular cyst that could be harmed by antiparasitic-induced inflammation Rapid neurological deterioration during or after starting antiparasitic therapy Starting antiparasitic drugs without first excluding ocular cysts, risking sight-threatening inflammation Overlooking a coexisting intestinal tapeworm that perpetuates transmission Attributing all soft-tissue nodules to benign causes without imaging in endemic areas Failing to give adjunctive anti-inflammatory cover when treating heavy or CNS cyst burdens When humans ingest Taenia solium eggs, oncospheres hatch in the intestine, penetrate the mucosa and disseminate through the bloodstream to tissues, where they mature into fluid-filled cysticerci. Living cysts often provoke little inflammation, but as they degenerate they release antigens that trigger a host inflammatory and immune response. This inflammation, together with mass effect and eventual calcification, produces most of the clinical manifestations, especially when cysts lie within the brain or eye. Isolated subcutaneous or muscular cysticercosis is generally benign and often asymptomatic. Prognosis is largely determined by neurological and ocular involvement, where outcome depends on cyst location, number, and the inflammatory response to treatment; many patients do well but some suffer chronic epilepsy or visual loss.

Cystinosis — cystinosin deficiency, CTNS-related cystinosis, nephropathic cystinosis Other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome such as Lowe syndrome or mitochondrial disease Other inherited tubulopathies Rickets from other metabolic causes Other lysosomal storage disorders Dent disease and other proximal tubular disorders Measurement of leukocyte cystine content, the key diagnostic and monitoring test CTNS molecular genetic testing Slit-lamp examination for corneal cystine crystals Renal function, electrolytes, and urinalysis to characterise Fanconi syndrome Assessment of growth, thyroid function, and other endocrine and organ involvement An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by defective function of cystinosin, the lysosomal membrane transporter that exports cystine, encoded by the CTNS gene Rather than an enzyme deficiency, it is a transporter defect, so cystine accumulates and crystallises within lysosomes throughout the body The classic infantile nephropathic form presents in the first year with renal Fanconi syndrome, causing polyuria, dehydration, electrolyte loss, rickets, and failure to thrive Corneal cystine crystals are a characteristic finding on slit-lamp examination and cause photophobia over time Without treatment, progressive kidney disease advances to end-stage renal failure in childhood Later extrarenal complications include hypothyroidism, growth failure, myopathy, diabetes, and central nervous system involvement Intermediate (juvenile) and non-nephropathic (ocular) forms have milder or predominantly ophthalmological features Cystine-depleting therapy with cysteamine slows systemic damage, and topical cysteamine addresses corneal crystals, alongside supportive management of Fanconi losses Progressive decline in renal function toward end-stage disease Severe electrolyte disturbance or dehydration from tubular losses Growth failure and rickets Emerging endocrine, muscular, or neurological complications Overlooking cystinosis as a cause of Fanconi syndrome and rickets in a young child Failing to examine for corneal crystals that support the diagnosis Underestimating the importance of adherence to cystine-depleting therapy and electrolyte replacement Assuming renal transplantation cures the disorder, when extrarenal cystine accumulation continues Cystinosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in CTNS, which encodes cystinosin, the transporter that moves cystine out of the lysosome. Impaired transport leads to intralysosomal cystine accumulation and crystal formation in cells across many tissues, including the kidney, cornea, thyroid, muscle, pancreas, and brain. In the kidney, damage to the proximal tubule produces a generalised reabsorptive defect (Fanconi syndrome) and, over time, progressive glomerular and interstitial injury leading to renal failure. Continued crystal accumulation elsewhere accounts for the later multisystem complications. Untreated nephropathic cystinosis progresses to end-stage renal failure in childhood with multisystem complications. Early and sustained cystine-depleting therapy with supportive care substantially delays renal deterioration and reduces extrarenal complications, improving long-term survival, though adherence is critical and complications may still accrue over time.

across the apical membrane of proximal renal tubular cells and intestinal epithelium. Biallelic mutations in SLC3A1 (encoding the rBAT subunit) or SLC7A9 (encoding the b0,+AT subunit) impair reabsorption, so large amounts of cystine reach the urine. Because cystine is relatively insoluble at normal urinary pH, it precipitates and aggregates into recurrent calculi, with solubility improving as pH rises. Stone burden and obstruction can produce recurrent colic, infection and, over time, chronic kidney damage. With lifelong high fluid intake, urinary alkalinisation and monitoring, stone recurrence can be markedly reduced, but adherence is demanding and recurrent stones or interventions may lead to chronic kidney disease over decades.

systemic or inflammatory disorder New oedema with signs of active uveitis needing evaluation for infective or immune causes Coexisting neovascularisation threatening haemorrhage or detachment Missing analogue glaucoma drop as a contributing factor Failing to treat the underlying vascular or inflammatory cause and treating only the fluid Cystoid macular oedema results from breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier, allowing fluid to accumulate in cystic spaces of the macula. Inflammatory mediators, particularly prostaglandins and vascular endothelial growth factor, increase perifoveal capillary permeability. After cataract surgery the trigger is a self-limiting inflammatory response, whereas in diabetes and vein occlusion it reflects chronic vascular incompetence and ischaemia. Post-surgical cystoid macular oedema often resolves with anti-inflammatory treatment and a good visual outcome, but oedema secondary to diabetes, vein occlusion, or chronic uveitis tends to recur and can cause lasting central visual impairment if fluid persists.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Infection — CMV Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infectious mononucleosis (heterophile-positive, with prominent exudative pharyngitis and cervical adenopathy) versus CMV mononucleosis (heterophile-negative) Congenital cytomegalic inclusion disease must be distinguished from congenital syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, Zika, herpes simplex virus, and bacterial sepsis (p.1513) CMV pneumonitis differential includes Pneumocystis, other viral/bacterial/fungal pneumonias, pulmonary hemorrhage, and irradiation or cytotoxic drug injury (p.1514) CMV retinopathy must be distinguished from toxoplasmosis, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus retinitis (p.1514) Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis Toxoplasmosis Congenital rubella, Zika, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis (in neonates) Pneumocystis pneumonia Herpes simplex virus and Candida retinitis/esophagitis Quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) for CMV DNA by PCR in blood or other specimens (preferred; same assay should be used for serial comparison) CMV pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay on peripheral-blood leukocytes CMV DNA PCR in cerebrospinal fluid for suspected encephalitis or polyradiculopathy Viral culture on human fibroblast monolayers, including the rapid overnight shell vial assay with monoclonal antibody to immediate-early antigen Serology: CMV IgG (may take up to 4 weeks to rise after primary infection) and CMV IgM (false positives possible with rheumatoid factor); serology mainly stratifies transplant risk and is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients Histopathology/biopsy demonstrating 'owl's eye' cytomegalic inclusions for tissue-invasive disease Pulmonary hemorrhage and radiation- or cytotoxic-drug-induced lung injury (mimicking CMV pneumonitis) Allograft rejection (overlapping with CMV syndrome in transplant recipients) CMV is a beta-herpesvirus carried for life after infection; the infection is usually silent, and reactivation syndromes emerge predominantly when T-lymphocyte-mediated immunity is compromised (organ transplantation, lymphoid neoplasms, HIV, or critical illness in the ICU) (p.1512). In immunocompetent hosts beyond the neonatal period, the most common manifestation is a heterophile-antibody-negative mononucleosis syndrome; unlike EBV mononucleosis, exudative pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy are rare, though splenomegaly, prolonged high fever, fatigue and malaise are common (p.1513-1514). The characteristic laboratory finding in CMV mononucleosis is relative lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes (predominantly activated CD8+ T cells); heterophile antibodies are absent (p.1514). Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection; most congenital infections are clinically inapparent at birth, yet 7-11% of asymptomatically infected infants develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years (p.1512-1513). Clinical disease in the fetus/newborn is related largely to PRIMARY maternal infection rather than reactivation; primary first-trimester infection carries up to 40-50% risk of sensorineural complications (p.1513). Preferred diagnosis is detection of virus/antigen/DNA, most commonly quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) by PCR; the pp65 antigenemia immunofluorescence assay is an alternative, and CMV DNA in CSF aids diagnosis of CMV encephalitis or polyradiculopathy (p.1515). In persons with HIV, end-organ CMV disease (especially retinitis) occurs particularly when CD4+ counts fall below 50/uL; flares of CMV retinitis can occur shortly after starting antiretroviral therapy as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) (p.1514). An immune-complex glomerulopathy has been observed in some CMV-infected patients after renal transplantation, and CMV mononucleosis can produce transient autoantibodies (cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factors, cold agglutinins, antinuclear antibodies) via polyclonal B-cell activation (p.1512-1514). Pathology shows enlarged 'cytomegalic' cells (2-4x normal) with an eccentric intranuclear inclusion surrounded by a clear halo producing the classic 'owl's eye' appearance (p.1513). Retinitis in an immunocompromised host (especially HIV with CD4+ <50/uL) - threat to vision Colitis or gastrointestinal ulceration with risk of bleeding or perforation Pneumonitis (tachypnea, hypoxemia, nonproductive cough with bilateral interstitial/reticulonodular infiltrates) Encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis or subacute progressive polyradiculopathy Persistent viremia with multi-organ involvement, pancytopenia and hypotension (associated with fatal disease) Symptomatic congenital infection (petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly with cerebral calcifications, intrauterine growth retardation) Tissue-invasive CMV disease (e.g., gastrointestinal) may be present despite NEGATIVE blood CMV antigenemia and viral-load testing - diagnosis may require endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, not blood viremia alone (p.1514). Isolation of CMV from urine, stool, or saliva does NOT by itself prove acute infection, since excretion may persist for months to years; detection of viremia by QNAT or antigenemia is a better predictor (p.1515). Serology is NOT recommended to diagnose acute disease in immunocompromised patients; IgG may not rise for up to 4 weeks and rheumatoid factor can cause false-positive IgM (p.1515). CMV detection in blood does not equate to end-organ disease; clinical and tissue correlation is required. Universal ganciclovir/valganciclovir prophylaxis is bone-marrow suppressive, favoring preemptive strategies in HSCT recipients (p.1515). CMV is a beta-herpesvirus with double-stranded DNA, icosahedral symmetry and a lipoprotein envelope; it replicates in the cell nucleus and can establish either lytic/productive or latent infection. After primary infection the virus persists indefinitely in multiple cell types and organs (silent latency). Primary infection in late childhood/adulthood elicits a vigorous CD8+ T-lymphocyte response producing atypical lymphocytes and a mononucleosis-like illness, with polyclonal B-cell activation generating autoantibodies. When host T-cell responses are compromised by disease or iatrogenic immunosuppression, latent virus reactivates; chronic antigenic stimulation under immunosuppression (e.g., post-transplant) is an ideal setting for CMV disease, and potent T-cell suppressants (antithymocyte globulin, alemtuzumab) markedly raise CMV syndrome rates. CMV itself further depresses T-lymphocyte responsiveness, predisposing to superinfection by other opportunists. Congenital disease arises chiefly from primary maternal infection; transmission to transplant/transfusion recipients reflects silent infection in donor tissues (p.1512-1513). Immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis is almost always self-limited (illness lasting 2-6 weeks); most patients recover without sequelae, though postviral asthenia may persist for months and fatal infection is rare. Severely affected congenitally infected infants have a poor prognosis with a mortality of about 5% and few survivors escaping intellectual or hearing impairment; 7-11% of asymptomatically infected neonates still develop sensorineural hearing loss over 5 years. In immunocompromised hosts, untreated CMV may progress to severe end-organ disease; CMV disease is an independent risk factor for both graft loss and death after organ transplantation, and high blood viral loads in HIV predict severe disease and death (p.1513-1514). Harrison frames CMV by host and syndrome rather than a formal grading scale: (1) congenital CMV - subclinical to severe disseminated cytomegalic inclusion disease; (2) perinatal CMV - usually asymptomatic; (3) immunocompetent CMV mononucleosis - heterophile-negative, self-limited; (4) CMV in the immunocompromised host - asymptomatic infection/viremia, 'CMV syndrome' (febrile leukopenia), and tissue-invasive end-organ disease (pneumonitis, colitis/GI disease, hepatitis, esophagitis, retinitis, encephalitis/polyradiculopathy), stratified by population in Table 200-1 (fetus/neonate, organ transplant recipient, HSCT recipient, person with HIV) (p.1513).

management is with systemic antibiotics and warm compresses in the acute phase Incision and drainage may be needed for a pointing abscess, but definitive treatment of the underlying obstruction is dacryocystorhinostomy once inflammation settles Congenital dacryocystitis in infants relates to a persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner and may need probing if it does not resolve Acute dacryocystitis can be complicated by preseptal or orbital cellulitis and rarely by fistula formation Spread to preseptal or orbital cellulitis with proptosis, restricted eye movements, or reduced vision A firm, irregular, or bloody lacrimal sac mass suggesting a lacrimal sac tumour rather than simple infection Systemic features of sepsis in an unwell patient Neonatal dacryocystitis, which can progress rapidly and needs prompt treatment Attempting probing or surgery during acute inflammation rather than treating the infection first Mislabelling the medial canthal swelling as preseptal cellulitis and missing the underlying sac infection Failing to recognise a lacrimal sac tumour presenting as atypical dacryocystitis Not addressing the underlying duct obstruction, leading to repeated infections Dacryocystitis is inflammation of the lacrimal sac, almost always resulting from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. Obstruction leads to retention and stagnation of tears and mucus within the sac, providing a medium for bacterial overgrowth. Acute infection produces a tense, inflamed sac that may progress to abscess formation, while chronic obstruction causes a mucocele with recurrent low-grade infection and persistent watering. In infants, incomplete canalisation of the duct at the valve of Hasner is the usual cause. Acute dacryocystitis usually responds well to antibiotics, but recurrence is common until the underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction is corrected surgically; dacryocystorhinostomy is highly effective at relieving obstruction and preventing further episodes.

by variants in LAMP2, which encodes lysosome-associated membrane protein 2, a protein essential for autophagy and lysosomal function. Its deficiency impairs the fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes, so autophagic vacuoles and glycogen accumulate within cardiac and skeletal muscle and other tissues. that reduces flares Darier disease results from loss-of-function variants in ATP2A2, encoding the SERCA2 pump that transports calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum of keratinocytes. Impaired intracellular calcium regulation disrupts the calcium-dependent assembly and function of desmosomal adhesion complexes. The consequence is loss of cohesion between keratinocytes (acantholysis) together with abnormal keratinisation of individual cells (dyskeratosis), giving the histological hallmarks of suprabasal acantholysis with corps ronds and grains. It is a chronic, relapsing condition that persists lifelong with seasonal flares, but most patients maintain reasonable control with skin care, avoidance of triggers, and oral retinoids in severe cases; it does not shorten life expectancy.

Systemically, raised nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF cause splanchnic arterial vasodilation, pooling blood and reducing effective circulating volume; the kidneys sense this as hypovolemia and activate ADH, the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, producing free-water and sodium retention (ascites/edema). Encephalopathy results from gut-derived neurotoxins bypassing the liver via portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatic mass. (p.370, p.2756, p.2759) Decompensation defines a poor-prognosis state: with clinically significant portal hypertension that decompensates, median survival is under 2 years, and fewer than 50% of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. PELD is the pediatric equivalent. Clinically significant portal hypertension is defined by HVPG ≥10 mmHg. (p.2675-2676, p.2756, p.2754)

require immediate high-flow oxygen and urgent recompression Rapid deterioration or evolving spinal cord signs such as leg weakness or urinary retention Sudden collapse or stroke-like presentation suggesting arterial gas embolism Cardiorespiratory compromise ('the chokes') Dismissing joint pain or vague symptoms after diving as musculoskeletal and missing early DCS Delaying recompression while arranging non-essential investigations Failing to give continuous high-flow oxygen during transfer Overlooking the risk of flying or altitude exposure soon after diving Assuming that a symptom-free interval excludes serious disease During exposure to raised pressure, inert gas (usually nitrogen) dissolves into body tissues in proportion to the pressure and time. If pressure is reduced faster than the gas can be safely eliminated through the lungs, it comes out of solution and forms bubbles within tissues and blood. These bubbles cause mechanical obstruction of vessels, mechanical tissue distortion, and secondary inflammatory and coagulation responses, producing the musculoskeletal, neurological, pulmonary and other manifestations. Prompt recompression and oxygen therapy give a good chance of full recovery, especially in milder disease; delay in treatment, severe neurological involvement or arterial gas embolism carry a higher risk of permanent deficit.

symptoms and signs are nonspecific, and unexplained breathlessness is its most common symptom. Failure to improve despite standard therapy for concurrent heart failure or pneumonia is a clue to coexisting PE. The most common DVT symptom is a persistent, intensifying calf cramp or 'charley horse'; physical findings may be limited to mild lower-calf tenderness, although massive DVT can produce marked thigh swelling, tenderness, and erythema. A diffusely edematous leg makes ordinary DVT unlikely, with the important exception of phlegmasia cerulea dolens, the most severe form of DVT. Recurrent left thigh edema, especially in young women, should raise suspicion for May-Thurner syndrome (right common iliac artery compressing the left iliac vein), which may be associated with DVT. Wells point scores estimate clinical likelihood of DVT/PE and are validated in ambulatory but not hospitalized patients; low-likelihood DVT or low-to-moderate-likelihood PE can be evaluated with d-dimer alone, while high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and go straight to imaging. Age-adjusted d-dimer (age x 10 ng/mL as the upper limit for patients over 50 with low/intermediate PE probability) reduces unnecessary CT pulmonary angiograms, but it does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT. Venous ultrasound diagnoses DVT chiefly through loss of vein compressibility; a normal vein collapses with gentle transducer pressure (the 'wink'), whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and non-compressible. CT pulmonary angiography is the principal imaging test for PE; an RV-to-LV diameter ratio greater than 1 (RV enlargement) on CT predicts increased 30-day mortality. ECG S1Q3T3 is relatively specific but insensitive for PE; the most common ECG abnormalities are sinus tachycardia and T-wave inversion in leads V1-V4 from RV strain/ischemia. McConnell's sign on echocardiography (RV free-wall hypokinesis with preserved or hyperkinetic RV apex) is a recognized indirect sign of PE, but most PE patients have a normal echocardiogram, so echo is not a reliable rule-out test. Many patients with PE have no demonstrable DVT because the leg thrombus has already embolized; paradoxical embolism to the arterial circulation can occur through a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect. Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired (not inherited) thrombophilia predisposing to both venous and arterial thrombosis, and patients often warrant lifetime anticoagulation even when the index VTE was provoked. Systemic arterial hypotension with extensive thrombosis - massive (high-risk) PE, accounting for 5-10% of cases, presenting with dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, cyanosis, and possible cardiogenic shock and multisystem organ failure RV dysfunction on echocardiography or RV enlargement on CT despite normal systemic pressure - submassive (intermediate-risk) PE Combination of right heart failure with elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin), indicating high risk of clinical deterioration Phlegmasia cerulea dolens - the most serious form of DVT with diffuse leg edema Hemodynamic instability portending high risk of adverse outcomes despite anticoagulation Relying on d-dimer in hospitalized patients - levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness, so d-dimer rarely has a useful role in inpatients. Applying the age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff to suspected acute DVT - it is validated only for ruling out PE in patients over 50 with low/intermediate probability. Using echocardiography as a rule-out test for PE - most PE patients have normal echocardiograms; echo is better for detecting mimics like MI, tamponade, and aortic dissection. Assuming absence of DVT excludes PE - the leg thrombus may have already fully embolized. Treating antiphospholipid syndrome with DOACs - warfarin, not DOACs, is the standard for APS. Mistaking a diffusely edematous leg for routine DVT and overlooking phlegmasia cerulea dolens; conversely attributing all calf pain to DVT (consider ruptured Baker's cyst) and all dyspnea to PE. Confusing cellulitis (fever, chills) with DVT. Overlooking nonthrombotic embolism (fat, tumor, bone marrow, air, amniotic fluid, cement, talc/hair in IV drug users) as a cause of PE. VTE arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release microparticles bearing proinflammatory mediators that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps; the contained histones drive platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation, and thrombi flourish in conditions of stasis, low oxygen tension, and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Inherited prothrombotic states include factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation; deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S are associated with VTE but rare. Lower-extremity DVT usually begins in the calf and may propagate to the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins; when thrombi detach they embolize through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries. PE impairs gas exchange, causing arterial hypoxemia and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient, increased anatomic and physiologic dead space, increased pulmonary vascular resistance (from mechanical obstruction and vasoconstrictors such as serotonin), reflex hyperventilation, increased airway resistance, and reduced pulmonary compliance. Rising pulmonary artery pressure increases RV wall tension, causing RV dilation and dysfunction with BNP release; the interventricular septum bows into and compresses the left ventricle, impairing LV filling; elevated RV wall tension also compresses the right coronary artery, producing RV ischemia/microinfarction with troponin release, and LV underfilling can culminate in falling cardiac output, hypotension, circulatory collapse, and death. Prognosis depends on PE severity and RV function. Low-risk PE (about 65-75% of cases) carries an excellent prognosis. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE (20-25%) with RV dysfunction and biomarker elevation has a high risk of clinical deterioration, and massive (high-risk) PE (5-10%) can cause cardiogenic shock, multisystem organ failure, and death. US PE-related mortality fell from 6 to about 4.5 per 100,000 between 2000 and 2017 but is rising among young and middle-aged adults, with the median age at PE death dropping from 73 (2000) to 68 (2018) and roughly 50% higher mortality in African Americans than Caucasians; mortality is consistently higher in socioeconomically disadvantaged communities. The 30-day all-cause readmission rate after PE hospitalization is about 11% and the 90-day rate about 15%, with recurrent PE the most common readmission cause. Long-term, roughly half of PE patients report persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity and about a quarter have persistent RV dysfunction - the post-PE syndrome; chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in about 2% of acute PE patients. DVT can lead to postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) with calf/ankle swelling, leg aching, and, in severe cases, deep skin ulceration. Pulmonary embolism is stratified into three categories: Massive (high-risk) PE - 5-10% of cases, systemic arterial hypotension with thrombosis involving at least half the pulmonary vasculature, presenting with dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, and cyanosis and capable of causing cardiogenic shock and death. Submassive (intermediate-risk) PE - 20-25% of cases, RV dysfunction despite normal systemic arterial pressure; right heart failure with biomarker (troponin) release marks high risk of deterioration. Low-risk PE - about 65-75% of cases, excellent prognosis. (Wells clinical decision rules in Table 290-2 stratify pretest probability of DVT and PE rather than anatomic severity.)
