neurological deficit in a child or young adult Intracranial haemorrhage, particularly if antithrombotic therapy is being considered Progressive cytopenias or bone marrow failure Severe systemic vasculitis with organ ischaemia Treating recurrent strokes with antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents, which increase the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage in DADA2 Diagnosing idiopathic polyarteritis nodosa in a young patient without testing ADA2 Overlooking the immunodeficiency and cytopenia phenotype that can present without prominent vasculitis Delaying tumour necrosis factor inhibition, which is the key stroke-preventing therapy DADA2 is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ADA2 gene, which encodes the secreted enzyme adenosine deaminase 2. Unlike the intracellular ADA1 enzyme whose deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, ADA2 is released chiefly by cells of the myeloid lineage and acts as a growth factor influencing endothelial integrity and the differentiation of monocytes and macrophages. Loss of ADA2 skews macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype, impairs endothelial stability, and produces a vasculopathy affecting small and medium vessels, together with excess tumour necrosis factor-driven inflammation. The endothelial and vascular damage underlies the strokes and vasculitis, while effects on haematopoiesis and lymphocytes account for the immunodeficiency and cytopenias. Untreated DADA2 carries a high burden of recurrent stroke and cumulative neurological disability, but tumour-necrosis-factor inhibition markedly reduces stroke recurrence and controls vasculitis; severe haematological or immune disease may require transplantation, and early diagnosis substantially improves outcome.

cure Marked hypotonia and respiratory difficulty in infancy Rapid loss of motor function or bulbar involvement Features suggesting a treatable inflammatory neuropathy Severe skeletal deformity compromising function or respiration Overlooking a steroid-responsive inflammatory neuropathy that can mimic the severe demyelinating picture Assuming a single gene and not testing the range of relevant myelin genes Underestimating the value of early rehabilitation and orthopaedic care Failing to provide genetic counselling given de novo and recessive inheritance patterns Dejerine-Sottas disease is a hypertrophic demyelinating neuropathy caused by mutations affecting proteins critical for peripheral myelin formation and maintenance. Severe or biallelic mutations in genes such as PMP22, MPZ, and EGR2 produce profound failure of Schwann cell myelination beginning early in life, with repeated cycles of demyelination and attempted remyelination generating the onion-bulb hypertrophy that can enlarge nerves. The severe, diffuse demyelination markedly slows conduction and causes early, disabling motor and sensory deficits. The disorder is generally more severe and disabling than typical Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, often with early and significant motor impairment, though the course varies with the underlying mutation; management remains supportive.

features raising suspicion of Turner syndrome Evidence of a chronic systemic illness or eating disorder underlying the delay Labelling all delay as constitutional and missing a treatable or serious underlying cause Overlooking anosmia, which would point to Kallmann syndrome Failing to consider chronic illness, undernutrition, or an eating disorder as functional causes Not arranging a karyotype gonadal steroid production and gametogenesis. Delayed puberty results from any interruption of this axis. In constitutional delay the axis is intrinsically normal but activates late, with a correspondingly delayed bone age. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism arises from functional suppression (chronic disease, malnutrition, intense athletic training, eating disorders, hyperprolactinaemia) or permanent central defects (Kallmann syndrome with anosmia, other congenital GnRH deficiencies, pituitary tumours or infiltration). Constitutional delay carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous progression through normal puberty and attainment of adult height and fertility; outcomes in pathological causes depend on the specific disorder and on timely diagnosis and hormone replacement.

Delirium — acute confusional state, acute brain syndrome, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy (psychiatric framing) Dementia and other major neurocognitive disorders Depression, especially where hypoactive delirium mimics low mood Acute psychosis or mania Non-convulsive status epilepticus Wernicke encephalopathy Alcohol or sedative withdrawal states Focal neurological events such as stroke Bedside attention testing and validated delirium screening instruments Search for precipitants: infection screen, oxygenation, glucose, electrolytes, renal and liver function Medication review for deliriogenic drugs Neuroimaging when a structural cause is suspected EEG if non-convulsive seizures are considered An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness accompanied by additional cognitive changes such as disorientation, memory deficit, or perceptual disturbance Onset is acute (hours to days) and the course typically fluctuates over the day, often with worsening in the evening and at night (sundowning) It is a direct physiological consequence of a medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, or multiple causes, and is best regarded as acute brain failure Recognised as hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed; the hypoactive form is easily missed and carries a worse prognosis The essential intervention is identifying and treating the underlying cause and reviewing offending medications, together with supportive care Non-pharmacological measures are first-line: reorientation, sensory aids, sleep-wake regulation, mobilisation, hydration, and a calm familiar environment Antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation or distress that threatens safety, at the lowest effective level, while benzodiazepines are generally avoided except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal Distinguish from dementia (chronic, stable, with preserved alertness early) and from primary psychiatric illness; delirium can be superimposed on dementia Underlying life-threatening cause such as sepsis, hypoxia, or hypoglycaemia Sudden focal neurological signs suggesting stroke or intracranial pathology Delirium tremens or severe withdrawal states Profound hypoactive delirium with reduced consciousness and aspiration risk Missing hypoactive delirium and mislabelling it as depression or fatigue Attributing acute confusion to dementia and failing to seek a reversible cause Using benzodiazepines routinely and worsening confusion (outside alcohol or sedative withdrawal) Sedating agitation without identifying and treating the underlying medical trigger Overlooking medication and polypharmacy as precipitants Delirium reflects diffuse, usually reversible cerebral dysfunction arising from systemic insults. Proposed mechanisms include neurotransmitter imbalance (notably cholinergic deficiency and dopaminergic excess), neuroinflammation, impaired oxidative metabolism, and disruption of neuronal networks supporting attention and arousal. Common precipitants include infection, hypoxia, metabolic and electrolyte derangements, drug effects and withdrawal, and the disorder is often multifactorial in vulnerable individuals such as the elderly. Delirium often resolves once the precipitant is treated, but it is associated with prolonged hospital stay, functional decline, increased risk of subsequent dementia, and higher mortality, particularly in older and hypoactive cases. Recovery can be incomplete and protracted in vulnerable patients.

Postoperative delirium — POD, postoperative confusion, acute postoperative brain dysfunction Dementia or pre-existing cognitive impairment Depression or acute psychiatric illness Non-convulsive seizure activity Stroke or other acute neurological event Drug or alcohol withdrawal Residual anaesthetic or sedative effect Delirium screening with a validated tool such as the Confusion Assessment Method Screening for infection, hypoxia, and metabolic or electrolyte disturbance Medication review for deliriogenic drugs Assessment for urinary retention, constipation, and pain Neuroimaging or EEG only if a focal neurological cause or seizures are suspected An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness developing after surgery, often within the first few postoperative days It may be hyperactive with agitation, hypoactive with withdrawal and drowsiness (frequently missed), or mixed, and the hypoactive form carries a worse prognosis Key predisposing factors include older age, pre-existing cognitive impairment or dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, and multiple comorbidities Common precipitants include pain, infection, metabolic and electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation, and deliriogenic medications Prevention through multicomponent non-pharmacological measures (reorientation, early mobilisation, sleep hygiene, sensory aids, hydration, and pain control) is the most effective strategy Screening tools such as the Confusion Assessment Method aid recognition, and diagnosis requires distinguishing delirium from dementia and depression Management focuses on identifying and treating underlying causes and using supportive measures; antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation posing a safety risk Benzodiazepines and anticholinergic drugs generally worsen delirium and should be minimised except for specific indications such as alcohol withdrawal Sudden confusion with focal neurological signs suggesting a stroke Delirium accompanied by hypoxia, sepsis, or severe metabolic derangement Features suggesting alcohol or sedative withdrawal with autonomic instability Severe agitation posing a risk of harm to the patient or others Missing hypoactive delirium because the patient is quiet rather than agitated Mislabelling delirium as dementia and failing to seek reversible causes Using benzodiazepines or anticholinergics that worsen confusion Reaching for antipsychotics before addressing underlying precipitants Neglecting non-pharmacological preventive measures in high-risk patients Postoperative delirium reflects acute global brain dysfunction arising from the interaction of a vulnerable brain and perioperative stressors. Proposed mechanisms include neuroinflammation from the surgical stress response, neurotransmitter imbalance (notably cholinergic deficiency and dopamine excess), impaired cerebral oxygen delivery, disrupted sleep-wake regulation, and the effects of sedative and analgesic drugs. Patients with reduced cognitive reserve are more susceptible, so relatively minor insults can precipitate delirium. The condition is typically multifactorial, and cumulative contributions from pain, infection, metabolic derangement, and medications drive the acute confusional state. Delirium is often reversible when precipitants are treated, but it is associated with longer hospital stay, functional decline, increased risk of long-term cognitive impairment, and higher mortality, particularly in the hypoactive form.

Dementia with Lewy Bodies — DLB, Lewy body disease, Lewy body dementia Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) Alzheimer's disease (and DLB with co-existing AD pathology) Multiple system atrophy (MSA) Vascular parkinsonism / vascular cognitive impairment Delirium from drugs, infection, or metabolic disturbance Brain MRI to exclude vascular parkinsonism or subdural hematoma and to look for the MSA 'hot-cross buns' pontine sign Polysomnography demonstrating REM sleep behavior disorder without atonia Seed amplification assays (e.g., RT-QuIC) detecting alpha-synuclein in CSF Skin biopsy showing cutaneous alpha-synuclein deposition I-123 MIBG cardiac scintigraphy showing postganglionic sympathetic denervation Dopamine transporter imaging by SPECT or PET showing reduced striatal (particularly putaminal) dopamine transporter FDG-PET showing occipital hypometabolism with relative posterior cingulate sparing (cingulate island sign) CSF or blood phospho-tau217/phospho-tau181 when concurrent Alzheimer pathology is suspected Multiple system atrophy, in which autonomic disturbance occurs earlier and is more severe and cognition is relatively preserved (anosmia favors LBD over MSA) Alzheimer's disease, suggested by prominent early episodic memory and semantic naming impairment Vascular parkinsonism or subdural hematoma identifiable on MRI Drug-induced, infectious, or metabolic encephalopathy producing reversible cognitive change DLB and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) are viewed as points along a single spectrum of Lewy body disease (LBD); LBD is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia after Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3491). The timing between parkinsonism and dementia distinguishes the two: when dementia and neuropsychiatric symptoms precede or emerge alongside parkinsonism, the diagnosis is DLB; when dementia appears in a patient with long-standing PD, it is PDD (Harrison 22e p.3492). Core diagnostic features of DLB are early psychosis with well-formed visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and parkinsonism (Harrison 22e p.3491). The cognitive profile shows severe executive, attentional, and visuospatial deficits with relatively preserved episodic memory; prominent early episodic memory impairment instead suggests comorbid Alzheimer pathology (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492). Fluctuations in attention and concentration can be marked, with short episodes of confusion or severe lethargy that may resolve rapidly (Harrison 22e p.3492). Patients are highly sensitive to infectious and metabolic disturbances, and delirium precipitated by infection, a new medication, or systemic illness can be the first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.3492). RBD, in which dream enactment occurs because normal dreaming muscle atonia is lost (sometimes causing injury to patient or bed partner), is a characteristic and often prodromal feature that may precede the syndrome by years (Harrison 22e p.3492). A sense of a presence behind the person may precede well-formed hallucinations; delusions are less frequent and usually involve misidentification, infidelity, theft, or persecution (Harrison 22e p.3491-3492). Autonomic and nonmotor features such as anosmia, constipation, depression, anxiety, orthostatic hypotension, and erectile dysfunction may appear early (Harrison 22e p.3492). Incidence of DLB is roughly 7 per 100,000 person-years; prevalence of both DLB and PDD rises with age and both are more common in men (Harrison 22e p.3491). About 10% of PD patients develop PDD per year, with most eventually progressing to dementia over time (Harrison 22e p.3491). A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus involvement underlies the fluctuations, inattention, and visual hallucinations (Harrison 22e p.3492). New-onset delirium precipitated by infection, a new medicine, or systemic illness as the presenting feature Severe sensitivity to dopaminergic medications and to typical neuroleptics, the latter risking neuroleptic malignant syndrome and death Recurrent falls from early postural instability and orthostatic hypotension causing syncope Violent dream enactment in RBD causing injury to patient or bed partner Misclassifying DLB as Alzheimer's disease because frequent AD co-pathology makes prediction of underlying disease challenging; prominent early episodic memory loss points to comorbid AD Confusing DLB with MSA when autonomic features appear early; MSA autonomic dysfunction is earlier and more severe with relatively preserved cognition Exposing patients to typical neuroleptics, anticholinergics, or dopamine agonists, which can trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome or worsen symptoms Overlooking that scattered Lewy body pathology in substantia nigra, amygdala, or olfactory bulb can be an incidental finding in healthy older individuals Attributing fluctuating confusion solely to delirium and missing the underlying DLB diagnosis DLB is a synucleinopathy: the defining neuropathologic lesions are Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites distributed through specific brainstem nuclei, the substantia nigra, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and ultimately the neocortex. Lewy bodies are intraneuronal cytoplasmic inclusions composed of straight 7-20 nm neurofilaments with surrounding amorphous material; they stain with PAS and ubiquitin and are now identified by antibodies to the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein. Accumulation of alpha-synuclein aggregates in neurons and glia classifies DLB and PDD molecularly as synucleinopathies, though neuronal and synaptic loss (rather than Lewy pathology itself) best predicts clinical deficits. Pathology progresses through three stages: brainstem-predominant, transitional limbic, and diffuse neocortical. Disease is thought to propagate via a prion-like mechanism in which misfolded alpha-synuclein spreads transneuronally along connection pathways; PD often begins in the enteric nervous system and ascends via the vagus nerve, and/or in the olfactory bulb. A profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain and pedunculopontine nucleus loss drives fluctuations, inattention, and hallucinations, while locus coeruleus adrenergic deficits impair arousal and alerting. Both genetic and environmental factors contribute; alpha-synuclein gene duplications/triplications and GBA (glucocerebrosidase) mutations are linked to PDD/DLB presentations, supporting a double-hit hypothesis of toxins acting on a susceptible genetic background (Harrison 22e p.3492). DLB is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with no currently available disease-modifying therapy; only symptomatic management exists. Severity of behavioral, sleep, and autonomic symptoms correlates with substantial caregiver burden, depression, and reduced caregiver quality of life (Harrison 22e p.3492-3493). Neuropathologic staging recognizes three stages of LBD progression: (1) brainstem-predominant, (2) transitional limbic, and (3) diffuse neocortical. Both DLB and PDD have a prodromal mild cognitive impairment (MCI) phase; prodromal MCI-Lewy body (MCI-LB) is distinguished from prodromal MCI-AD by clinical and biomarker features (Harrison 22e p.3492).

Dengue haemorrhagic fever — DHF, severe dengue, dengue shock syndrome, DSS Other viral haemorrhagic fevers Chikungunya and Zika co-circulating arboviral illness Severe malaria Leptospirosis Enteric fever Rickettsial infection (e.g. scrub typhus) Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation Acute leukaemia or other causes of thrombocytopenia with bleeding Immune thrombocytopenia Hantavirus or other capillary-leak syndromes NS1 antigen in early illness and dengue IgM/IgG serology or RT-PCR Serial full blood counts monitoring haematocrit and platelet trends Coagulation profile and liver enzymes to assess severity Ultrasound to detect plasma leakage (ascites, pleural effusion, gallbladder wall oedema) Blood grouping and cross-match if significant bleeding occurs A severe form of dengue, a mosquito-borne flaviviral infection spread by Aedes aegypti, with recurrent large outbreaks across India The defining features are plasma leakage (haemoconcentration, effusions, ascites), bleeding tendency and thrombocytopenia, which can progress to dengue shock syndrome The critical, most dangerous period begins around the time of defervescence, when capillary leak peaks, so patients can deteriorate just as fever settles WHO warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, fluid accumulation and a rising haematocrit with falling platelets) flag patients at risk of severe disease Secondary infection with a different dengue serotype increases the risk of severe disease through antibody-dependent enhancement Management is meticulous fluid balance guided by haematocrit and clinical status; there is no specific antiviral, and both under- and over-resuscitation are harmful Platelet transfusion is not indicated purely for a low count and should be reserved for significant bleeding Diagnosis uses NS1 antigen early and IgM/IgG serology or PCR, with serial full blood counts to track haematocrit and platelets WHO warning signs: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, restlessness or lethargy, and clinical fluid accumulation Rising haematocrit with a rapidly falling platelet count indicating intensifying plasma leak Signs of shock (narrow pulse pressure, cold clammy peripheries, tachycardia, hypotension) marking dengue shock syndrome Deterioration around defervescence, the classic timing of the critical phase Assuming a patient is improving when fever settles, missing the onset of the critical plasma-leak phase Over-transfusing platelets based on the count alone rather than for clinical bleeding Excessive intravenous fluids causing fluid overload and respiratory compromise, or inadequate fluids allowing shock Giving NSAIDs or other agents that worsen bleeding and gastric irritation Following an infective Aedes bite, dengue virus replicates and causes a systemic febrile illness. In severe dengue an intense host immune and cytokine response transiently increases vascular permeability, allowing plasma to leak from the intravascular compartment; this manifests as haemoconcentration, serous effusions and, if severe, hypovolaemic shock. Concurrent thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, coagulopathy and vascular fragility produce the bleeding diathesis. Pre-existing heterotypic antibodies from a prior infection can enhance viral uptake into cells (antibody-dependent enhancement), heightening the risk of severe disease on secondary infection. With early recognition and careful fluid management the great majority recover fully. Untreated or poorly managed severe dengue with prolonged shock or major haemorrhage carries significant mortality, but timely, judicious supportive care dramatically reduces death rates.

measurement of kidney function to monitor progression An X-linked proximal tubulopathy affecting mainly males, caused by variants in CLCN5 (Dent disease 1) or OCRL (Dent disease 2) The defining feature is low-molecular-weight proteinuria, which is often the earliest and most consistent abnormality Hypercalciuria is characteristic and drives nephrocalcinosis and recurrent nephrolithiasis Additional proximal tubular dysfunction may include phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, glycosuria and impaired urinary acidification, at times amounting to a partial Fanconi syndrome Progressive chronic kidney disease develops in many affected males, sometimes reaching kidney failure in adulthood Dent disease 2 (OCRL) can show mild extrarenal features overlapping with Lowe syndrome, such as subclinical cataract or mild cognitive involvement Female carriers may have milder manifestations such as low-molecular-weight proteinuria or hypercalciuria Rapidly declining kidney function Recurrent obstructing renal stones or symptomatic nephrocalcinosis Growth failure in a child suggesting significant tubular or renal impairment Features suggesting evolving extrarenal disease in OCRL-related cases Overlooking the diagnosis because dipstick testing detects albumin poorly and misses low-molecular-weight proteinuria Attributing recurrent stones to idiopathic hypercalciuria without checking for tubular proteinuria Failing to distinguish Dent disease 2 from Lowe syndrome when OCRL is involved Assuming female relatives are entirely unaffected Dent disease is an inherited disorder of the renal proximal tubule caused by loss of function of the endosomal chloride/proton exchanger encoded by CLCN5, or of the phosphatase encoded by OCRL. Both proteins are required for normal acidification and trafficking within the endocytic machinery that reabsorbs filtered low-molecular-weight proteins via the megalin-cubilin receptor system. Defective endosomal function impairs receptor-mediated endocytosis, so filtered proteins escape into the urine, producing the hallmark low-molecular-weight proteinuria. Associated disturbances of calcium and phosphate handling generate hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis and stones, and cumulative tubular and interstitial damage leads to progressive decline in kidney function. Dent disease is slowly progressive; many affected males develop chronic kidney disease and a proportion reach kidney failure between the third and fifth decades, while proteinuria and hypercalciuria are usually present from childhood. Progression rate varies and extrarenal disease is generally mild.

Dental caries — tooth decay, cavities, carious lesion Dental erosion from intrinsic or extrinsic acids Enamel hypoplasia or developmental defects Dentine hypersensitivity from gingival recession Fluorosis or intrinsic staining mimicking lesions Cracked tooth or fracture line Visual-tactile examination with good lighting and drying of surfaces Bitewing and periapical radiographs for interproximal and root lesions Caries risk assessment including diet and salivary evaluation Pulp sensibility testing when pulpal involvement is suspected Adjunctive detection methods (transillumination, laser fluorescence) where available Caries is a chronic, biofilm-mediated disease driven by repeated acid production from fermentable carbohydrates, not a simple one-off infection Early lesions appear as chalky white spots that represent subsurface demineralisation and can still remineralise before cavitation occurs Pit-and-fissure surfaces, interproximal contacts, and exposed root surfaces in older patients are the sites most prone to decay Symptoms often lag behind disease; sensitivity to sweet, cold, or hot stimuli suggests progression toward the pulp Bitewing radiographs are key for detecting interproximal lesions that are hidden on visual examination Management balances remineralisation strategies (fluoride, diet control, oral hygiene) for early lesions against operative restoration once cavitation is established High caries risk should prompt assessment of salivary flow, diet, fluoride exposure, and plaque control rather than only drilling and filling Untreated caries is the usual precursor to pulpitis, periapical infection, and eventual tooth loss Spreading facial swelling, fever, or trismus indicating odontogenic infection extending beyond the tooth Rampant or early childhood caries suggesting major dietary or salivary dysfunction Signs of pulpal necrosis or periapical involvement requiring urgent endodontic assessment Restoring cavities without addressing underlying diet and hygiene, leading to recurrent decay Overlooking interproximal or hidden root-surface lesions on clinical inspection alone Mistaking arrested or remineralised lesions for active disease and over-treating Ignoring salivary hypofunction as a driver of rapid caries progression Dental caries results from an ecological shift in the dental plaque biofilm favouring acidogenic and aciduric bacteria such as mutans streptococci and lactobacilli. Frequent intake of fermentable sugars fuels bacterial acid production, lowering plaque pH below the critical threshold and driving demineralisation of enamel hydroxyapatite. When acid attacks outpace the buffering and remineralising capacity of saliva and fluoride, subsurface mineral loss progresses to surface cavitation. The lesion then advances through dentine, where tubular structure allows faster spread, ultimately reaching and infecting the pulp if untreated. Early non-cavitated lesions can be arrested or reversed with preventive measures, while cavitated lesions require restoration but carry a good prognosis when risk factors are controlled; neglected disease progresses to pulpitis, abscess, and tooth loss.

or jaw fractures or non-accidental injury Dental trauma results from a direct or indirect force exceeding the resistance of the tooth and its supporting structures. Depending on the vector and magnitude, energy is dissipated as enamel or dentine fracture, pulp exposure, displacement of the tooth within or out of its socket (luxation or avulsion), or fracture of the alveolar bone. Injury to the neurovascular supply at the apex can lead to reversible or irreversible pulpal damage and later necrosis, while disruption of the periodontal ligament and its cells governs the likelihood of successful healing after repositioning or reimplantation. Extra-oral drying and delay compromise ligament cell viability and predispose to replacement resorption. Outcome depends on injury type, maturity of the tooth, and speed of appropriate care; minor fractures and promptly managed luxations often do well, whereas avulsions with prolonged dry time and mature apices frequently develop pulp necrosis or root resorption.

Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy — DRPLA, Naito-Oyanagi disease Huntington disease Spinocerebellar ataxias Progressive myoclonus epilepsies (for juvenile-onset cases) Other inherited and acquired cerebellar ataxias Friedreich ataxia ATN1 CAG repeat analysis as the confirmatory test Brain MRI to assess cerebellar, brainstem, and white matter changes EEG in patients with seizures and myoclonus Detailed pedigree analysis to identify anticipation and inheritance pattern Neurocognitive and psychiatric assessment An autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the ATN1 gene, making it a polyglutamine disease It is comparatively common in Japanese populations and rarer elsewhere, so ethnic background and family history aid recognition The phenotype depends strongly on age at onset: juvenile-onset disease resembles a progressive myoclonus epilepsy with seizures, myoclonus, and cognitive decline Adult-onset disease is dominated by cerebellar ataxia, choreoathetosis, dementia, and psychiatric features Marked anticipation occurs, with larger repeat expansions transmitted particularly through the paternal line producing earlier and more severe disease in offspring The clinical overlap with other ataxias and with Huntington disease means genetic testing is important for accurate diagnosis MRI typically shows atrophy of the cerebellum and brainstem, and white matter changes may be present, especially in older patients Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the pathological CAG repeat expansion in ATN1, and management is supportive including seizure control Refractory seizures or status in juvenile-onset disease Rapid cognitive and functional decline Severe ataxia with falls and injury Prominent psychiatric disturbance requiring urgent management Misdiagnosing it as Huntington disease or another spinocerebellar ataxia without genetic confirmation Overlooking DRPLA in the differential of progressive myoclonus epilepsy in children Failing to counsel families about anticipation and paternal transmission risk Attributing white matter changes to an unrelated process Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy is a polyglutamine disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in ATN1, which encodes atrophin-1. The elongated polyglutamine tract leads to protein misfolding and nuclear accumulation that is toxic to neurons, with degeneration concentrated in the dentatorubral and pallidoluysian systems as the name indicates. Longer repeat expansions produce earlier onset and more severe disease, and paternal transmission tends to increase repeat size, explaining the pronounced anticipation and the shift toward the juvenile epileptic phenotype in successive generations. The disorder is progressive with no curative therapy; juvenile-onset disease tends to progress more rapidly and severely, whereas adult-onset disease advances more slowly, and overall survival is shortened with care remaining supportive.

Denys-Drash syndrome — DDS, WT1-related disorder, diffuse mesangial sclerosis with Wilms tumour, WT1 Frasier syndrome (WT1 intronic splice variants) Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type (NPHS1) Other genetic (NPHS2/podocin and related) steroid-resistant nephrotic syndromes WAGR syndrome (WT1 deletion with aniridia) Isolated diffuse mesangial sclerosis Other disorders of sex development Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria; assessment for nephrotic syndrome Renal function monitoring and kidney biopsy where indicated (diffuse mesangial sclerosis) Karyotype and molecular WT1 gene analysis Endocrine and imaging evaluation of gonadal and genital development Regular renal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour Gonadal imaging and assessment of malignancy risk Denys-Drash syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the Wilms tumour suppressor gene WT1, typically missense variants affecting the zinc-finger DNA-binding domain It is classically defined by a triad of early-onset nephrotic syndrome from diffuse mesangial sclerosis, disorders of sex development, and a high risk of Wilms tumour The nephropathy usually presents in infancy and progresses rapidly to end-stage kidney disease Genital abnormalities and gonadal dysgenesis are common in genotypic males, and dysgenetic gonads carry a risk of malignancy Because of the marked Wilms tumour risk, close renal imaging surveillance is essential and risk-reducing nephrectomy may be considered The condition overlaps with Frasier syndrome, which is also WT1-related but has a distinct renal lesion and different tumour profile Management is multidisciplinary, coordinating nephrology, oncology, endocrinology and surgery, with kidney replacement therapy for renal failure Rapidly progressive nephrotic syndrome in infancy A renal mass suggesting Wilms tumour Progression to end-stage kidney disease Signs of gonadal malignancy Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment Failing to test WT1 in an infant with early diffuse mesangial sclerosis and a disorder of sex development Neglecting tumour surveillance and missing a Wilms tumour Overlooking gonadal malignancy risk in dysgenetic gonads Confusing it with Frasier syndrome, which has a different renal lesion and tumour profile Treating the nephrotic syndrome as immune-mediated and giving prolonged ineffective immunosuppression Denys-Drash syndrome arises from constitutional pathogenic variants in WT1, a transcription factor essential for normal development of the kidney and gonads. Missense variants, characteristically in the zinc-finger domains that bind DNA, act in a dominant-negative manner and disrupt the transcriptional programmes that govern podocyte and glomerular development, producing diffuse mesangial sclerosis and progressive proteinuric renal failure. Because WT1 also directs gonadal differentiation, the same variants cause disorders of sex development and gonadal dysgenesis, and the dysgenetic gonadal tissue is prone to malignant change. Loss of WT1 tumour-suppressor function in nephrogenic rests underlies the strong predisposition to Wilms tumour of the developing kidney. The renal prognosis is poor, with early progression to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis and transplantation, though the nephropathy does not recur in the allograft; overall outcome depends heavily on timely detection and management of Wilms tumour and gonadal malignancy risk.

Dermatitis Herpetiformis — DH, Duhring's disease, cutaneous coeliac disease Bullous pemphigoid Linear IgA bullous dermatosis Scabies (intensely itchy, but with burrows and different distribution) Atopic or other eczematous dermatitis Papular urticaria or insect-bite reactions Excoriated prurigo Skin biopsy of perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence showing granular papillary IgA (the diagnostic standard) Coeliac serology including anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial IgA antibodies Total IgA level to interpret serology correctly Consideration of small-bowel evaluation in conjunction with gastroenterology Screening for enzyme deficiency before starting sulphone therapy and for associated autoimmune disease, such as thyroid function Presents with intensely itchy, grouped (herpetiform) vesicles and papules symmetrically distributed over the extensor surfaces such as elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp The itch and burning are often so severe that intact blisters are rarely seen, replaced by excoriations and crusts from scratching It is the cutaneous expression of gluten sensitivity and is strongly associated with coeliac disease, although many patients have few or no bowel symptoms Diagnosis rests on skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence, which shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae of perilesional skin Supportive serology includes anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies, reflecting the shared autoimmunity with coeliac disease A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the cornerstone of management and addresses both the skin and the associated enteropathy A sulphone-class agent can rapidly control itch and blistering while the diet takes effect, but requires screening for enzyme deficiency and monitoring for haemolysis Screen for associated conditions including autoimmune thyroid disease and be aware of a small increased long-term risk of small-bowel lymphoma, which dietary control reduces New abdominal symptoms, weight loss, or anaemia raising concern for complications of coeliac disease including small-bowel lymphoma Signs of haemolysis or methaemoglobinaemia in a patient on sulphone therapy Widespread blistering with systemic upset prompting reconsideration of an alternative autoimmune bullous disease Features of malabsorption or nutritional deficiency requiring investigation Taking the biopsy for immunofluorescence from lesional rather than perilesional skin and obtaining a false-negative result Relying on the diet alone while overlooking the need to screen for and manage associated coeliac and autoimmune disease Starting sulphone therapy without checking for enzyme deficiency and monitoring blood counts Attributing the intense itch to eczema or scabies and missing the diagnosis Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering disease driven by gluten sensitivity in genetically predisposed individuals carrying HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Dietary gluten triggers production of IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase and, in the skin, cross-reactivity with epidermal transglutaminase. IgA immune complexes deposit in the dermal papillae, recruiting neutrophils that form the characteristic papillary microabscesses and cause subepidermal separation with vesicle formation. The same gluten-driven autoimmunity produces the small-bowel villous atrophy of coeliac disease, so skin and gut manifestations share a common mechanism and both respond to gluten withdrawal. Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic condition, but a strict gluten-free diet usually controls the skin disease, allows medication to be reduced or stopped over time, heals the associated enteropathy, and lowers the long-term lymphoma risk; lapses in the diet typically provoke relapse.

Dermatomyositis — DM, idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, amyopathic dermatomyositis Polymyositis and immune-mediated necrotising myopathy Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases with rash Cutaneous drug eruptions and photosensitive dermatoses Psoriasis or contact dermatitis (for Gottron/knuckle lesions) Inclusion body myositis Thyroid and other metabolic myopathies Serum creatine kinase and myositis antibody panel (anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-MDA5, antisynthetase) Electromyography and muscle MRI to localise and characterise inflammation Muscle and/or skin biopsy demonstrating characteristic histology High-resolution CT chest and pulmonary function tests for interstitial lung disease Age- and risk-appropriate malignancy screening at diagnosis and during follow-up Combines symmetric proximal muscle weakness with distinctive skin findings, though skin disease can precede, follow, or occur without myositis Characteristic rashes include the heliotrope discolouration of the eyelids, Gottron papules over the knuckles, the shawl and V-signs, and periungual telangiectasia An amyopathic (clinically hypomyopathic) form has typical skin changes with little or no measurable muscle weakness Elevated creatine kinase, myopathic EMG, and muscle MRI support the diagnosis; biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy and perivascular inflammation There is a well-recognised association with occult malignancy, so age-appropriate cancer screening is essential, particularly around diagnosis Interstitial lung disease is common and may be rapidly progressive, especially with anti-MDA5 antibodies, which also carry a characteristic cutaneous ulcerating phenotype Myositis-specific antibodies (e.g. anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-MDA5, antisynthetase) predict distinct patterns of skin, lung, and malignancy risk Treatment uses corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants, photoprotection and topical therapy for skin, and prompt management of lung involvement Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease, particularly with anti-MDA5 antibodies, which can be life-threatening Clinical features pointing to an underlying malignancy (weight loss, new mass, cytopenias) Dysphagia and respiratory muscle weakness with aspiration or ventilatory risk Cutaneous ulceration and severe vasculopathy associated with anti-MDA5 disease Cardiac involvement with arrhythmia or heart failure Failing to perform malignancy screening in newly diagnosed adults Overlooking amyopathic disease when weakness is absent despite classic skin findings Missing or underestimating rapidly progressive lung disease, especially with anti-MDA5 antibodies Undertreating skin disease and neglecting photoprotection Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes active or amyopathic disease Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterised by humorally mediated, complement-dependent microangiopathy. Immune complex deposition and complement activation (membrane attack complex) on endomysial capillaries cause capillary loss, ischaemia, and the perifascicular atrophy typical of muscle biopsy. A strong type I interferon signature is present in muscle and skin. The same immune-mediated vasculopathy affects skin and other organs, and paraneoplastic mechanisms link it to underlying malignancy in a substantial proportion of adults. Prognosis depends heavily on associated interstitial lung disease, malignancy, and cardiac involvement rather than the myositis itself. Skin and muscle disease often respond to immunosuppression, but rapidly progressive lung disease and paraneoplastic cases carry significant mortality.

candidal intertrigo in flexural disease Skin scrapings, hair, or nail clippings for direct microscopy with potassium hydroxide and fungal culture Wood's lamp examination, which fluoresces in certain Microsporum scalp infections Nail sampling for onychomycosis before starting prolonged systemic therapy Consideration of underlying diabetes or immunosuppression in extensive or recurrent disease Skin biopsy with fungal stains in diagnostically difficult cases A superficial fungal infection of keratinised tissue named by body site: tinea corporis (body), cruris (groin), pedis (feet), capitis (scalp), unguium (nails), and faciei (face) The classic lesion is an annular, scaly plaque with a raised, advancing, more inflamed edge and relative central clearing Confirm the diagnosis before treatment with skin scrapings, hair, or nail clippings for microscopy and culture, as morphology alone can mislead Prior use of topical corticosteroids alters the appearance (tinea incognito), masking scale and the active edge and delaying diagnosis Localised skin infection responds to topical antifungals, whereas tinea capitis and onychomycosis require systemic antifungal therapy because topical agents cannot penetrate hair and nail adequately Tinea capitis is largely a disease of children and can cause a boggy inflamed mass (kerion) with a risk of scarring alopecia if treatment is delayed Address sources and reservoirs: treat tinea pedis to prevent recurrent groin and body infection, and consider animal contacts for zoophilic species Consider underlying immunosuppression or diabetes in extensive, recurrent, or unusually severe infection Kerion or severe inflammatory tinea capitis risking permanent scarring alopecia Extensive, widespread, or rapidly progressive infection suggesting immunosuppression Secondary bacterial infection of macerated or fissured lesions Deep or invasive fungal infection in an immunocompromised patient Treating with topical corticosteroids and producing tinea incognito that obscures the diagnosis Failing to confirm the diagnosis mycologically before long courses of systemic antifungals Using topical-only therapy for scalp or nail infection, which will not eradicate it Neglecting reservoirs such as untreated tinea pedis or animal contacts, leading to recurrence Dermatophytosis is caused by dermatophyte fungi of the genera Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton, which possess keratinases enabling them to invade and digest keratin in the stratum corneum, hair, and nails. Infection is acquired from other people (anthropophilic), animals (zoophilic), or soil (geophilic), with zoophilic species often producing more inflammatory reactions. The fungus spreads centrifugally through the stratum corneum, producing the characteristic annular lesion with an active advancing scaly margin. The host inflammatory response accounts for erythema and, in strongly inflammatory infections such as kerion, pustulation and potential scarring. Warmth, moisture, occlusion, and impaired immunity favour infection. Prognosis is excellent with correct diagnosis and appropriate topical or systemic antifungal therapy; nail infections require prolonged treatment and relapse is common, while delayed treatment of inflammatory scalp disease can leave permanent scarring alopecia.

Desensitization — Drug desensitization, Rapid drug desensitization, Temporary drug tolerance induction Type I IgE-mediated drug allergy IgE-independent mast cell activation (complement-mediated, COX-1 inhibition, MRGPRX2-mediated) Cytokine release reaction (IL-6 driven) Mixed reaction (combined type I and CRR features) Delayed type IV maculopapular eruption Hereditary alpha tryptasemia Infusion reaction (non-allergic) Serum tryptase within 30 min to 4 h of reaction (and baseline tryptase) Baseline tryptase with TPSAB1 genotyping if elevated (hereditary alpha tryptasemia) Serum IL-6 (elevated in CRR and mixed reactions) Skin testing (epicutaneous/intradermal) for IgE-mediated reactions Basophil activation test (in vitro evidence of IgE sensitization) Drug-specific serum IgE (e.g., penicillin, platins; low sensitivity) Skin patch testing for delayed type IV reactions (high specificity, low sensitivity) Lymphocyte transformation test for SCARS-causing drugs HLA genotyping for SCARS risk (abacavir, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, vancomycin) Non-allergic infusion reaction Anxiety/vasovagal episode during infusion Kounis syndrome (allergic coronary vasospasm) Takotsubo cardiomyopathy from drug-induced anaphylaxis Drug desensitization (DD) is a temporary immunotherapy that delivers sequential, incremental small doses of a culprit drug over hours to safely reach the full therapeutic dose, taking advantage of mast cell/basophil inhibitory pathways rather than producing lasting tolerance. Tolerance achieved by DD is transient: it does not produce sustained tolerance and must be repeated for each new course, or when the interval between doses equals two or more drug half-lives; continued exposure (e.g., ongoing antibiotics or aspirin/COX-1 inhibitors) can maintain the desensitized state. Roughly 10-20% of the health-care-engaged population claims a penicillin allergy, but most labels are unconfirmed; low-risk patients can be delabeled, and single-dose oral challenges have been shown safe in low-risk children and adults. Serum tryptase is the specific biomarker of anaphylaxis: a level above the normal range (11.4 ng/mL) or above a patient's baseline (a 1.6-fold rise), measured within 30 min to 4 h of symptom onset, supports type I or mixed reactions. A baseline tryptase of 7.5 ng/mL or higher may signal hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HαT) from TPSAB1 gene duplication on chromosome 16, an autosomal dominant trait in 4-6% of Caucasians that can worsen anaphylaxis severity. Cytokine release reactions (CRRs) present with fever, chills, and back/chest/pelvic pain and headache with a transient IL-6 rise; mixed reactions combine type I and CRR features with both tryptase and IL-6 elevations. The most widely used standardized protocol uses three bags (1/100, 1/10, and undiluted target concentration) with 12 doubling steps every 15 min, reaching target dose in about 5.7 h, adaptable to IV, oral, SC, IM, intraperitoneal, intraocular, and intrathecal routes. Breakthrough reactions occur in roughly 10-30% of protocols, are usually mild and resemble the initial reaction, and do not prevent completion of DD in about 99% of cases; no deaths from DD have been reported. Corticosteroids do NOT protect against anaphylaxis during desensitization; omalizumab (anti-IgE) has been used as an adjuvant in highly sensitized patients with severe IgE-mediated reactions. Skin testing reliability falls with greater time since the index reaction and after severe anaphylaxis (mediator depletion can cause false negatives); anaphylaxis to penicillin or carboplatin has not been reported in skin-test-negative patients. Platinum-drug IgE sensitization usually requires six or more exposures (fewer in BRCA-mutation carriers); skin testing is positive in over 85% of patients with recent reactions, and reexposure of skin-test-positive patients carries high anaphylaxis risk. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP) - contraindication to desensitization, avoid the drug Type II cytotoxic, type III immune-complex, vasculitis, and single-organ toxic reactions - contraindications to DD Hypotension with cardiovascular collapse, throat tightening, oxygen desaturation (grade 3 anaphylaxis) Kounis syndrome or takotsubo cardiomyopathy from drug-induced anaphylaxis - contraindications to DD Oxaliplatin-induced immune-mediated thrombocytopenia with bleeding - precludes further DD Markedly elevated tryptase well above baseline indicating severe mast cell activation Assuming corticosteroid premedication prevents anaphylaxis during DD - it does not. Treating SCARS or other contraindicated phenotypes with DD, where even minute drug amounts can trigger severe reactions. Expecting durable tolerance - DD is temporary and must be repeated each course or after a gap of two or more half-lives. Relying on a negative skin test performed long after the index reaction or after severe anaphylaxis (false negatives from mediator depletion or time elapsed). Maintaining unconfirmed penicillin allergy labels, leading to use of less effective, costlier second-line antibiotics. Overusing one-bag protocols in highly sensitized type I patients, associated with more epinephrine use and failure to complete treatment. Missing phenotype switching in oxaliplatin DD (type I converting to CRR/mixed reactions). Drug hypersensitivity reactions are classified by timing, mechanism (endotype), and biomarkers. Type I reactions arise from mast cell and basophil activation, either IgE-dependent (requiring prior repeated sensitizing exposures, as with antibiotics, chemotherapy, and some biologics) or IgE-independent (first-exposure reactions via complement activation, COX-1 inhibition, or MRGPRX2 receptor activation by quinolones, vancomycin, icatibant, basic compounds, and certain THIQ-motif general anesthetics). Cytokine release reactions reflect T-cell and other immune-cell activation with transient IL-6 elevation. Delayed type IV reactions are T-cell mediated. Desensitization works because rapid, stepwise delivery of incremental antigen doses recruits inhibitory phosphatases to the IgE receptor, blocking signal transduction and mediator release so that the target dose can be reached without anaphylaxis; desensitized patients show transient conversion of skin tests from positive to negative. Mechanisms for non-IgE phenotypes are less well understood. Rapid multistep desensitization is highly effective and safe across thousands of patients with infections, chronic inflammatory diseases, and malignancies. Protocols are completed in roughly 95-100% of cases (taxane series completed 95-100%), breakthrough reactions occur in about 10-30% and are usually mild, and no deaths attributable to DD have been reported. Drug delivery via DD achieves efficacy equal to standard administration (expected clearance of infection, reduced inflammation, comparable cancer responses); survival of platinum-desensitized cancer patients is noninferior to that of nonallergic patients, and ovarian cancer patients undergoing carboplatin DD have shown a 5-year life-expectancy advantage in one large series. Hypersensitivity reactions are graded by organ involvement and vital signs: grade 1 (mild, one organ), grade 2 (moderate, two or more organs), grade 3 (severe, with changes in vital signs/cardiovascular collapse). Reactions are also categorized by timing as acute/immediate (during or within 1-6 h of exposure) versus delayed (6 h to days or weeks), and by endotype (type I IgE/non-IgE, cytokine release, mixed, and type II-IV delayed reactions).

Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip — DDH, congenital dislocation of the hip, hip dysplasia Benign hip clicks Septic arthritis of the hip Transient synovitis Neuromuscular hip dysplasia (e.g. in cerebral palsy or spina bifida) Proximal focal femoral deficiency or other congenital femoral anomalies Leg-length discrepancy from other causes Hip ultrasound in the first months of life Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph after the femoral head ossifies Careful serial clinical examination including Barlow, Ortolani, and Galeazzi tests Targeted imaging for high-risk infants (breech, family history) A spectrum of abnormal development of the hip ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to frank dislocation, present at or developing after birth. Major risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, oligohydramnios, first-born status, and a positive family history. Newborn screening uses the Barlow manoeuvre (to dislocate a reducible hip) and the Ortolani manoeuvre (to relocate a dislocated hip). In older infants, signs include limited hip abduction, asymmetric thigh or gluteal skin creases, and apparent limb-length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign). Ultrasound is the imaging test of choice in early infancy before the femoral head ossifies; plain radiographs become useful after a few months of age. Early treatment of a reducible hip with an abduction device such as the Pavlik harness is usually successful and avoids surgery. The later the diagnosis, the more likely that closed or open reduction and casting, or surgical procedures, will be needed. Untreated or late-treated dysplasia leads to a limp, gait abnormality, and premature degenerative hip arthritis in adulthood. Persistent clicks alone are usually benign, whereas a palpable 'clunk' of dislocation or relocation is significant. A frankly dislocated or non-reducible hip on examination Progressive limitation of abduction Delayed diagnosis presenting as a limp or abnormal gait in a walking child Bilateral dislocation, which can be harder to detect due to symmetry Failure of a hip to stabilise despite bracing Missing dysplasia in bilateral cases where symmetry masks the abnormality Over-relying on benign hip clicks or reassurance from a single normal newborn examination Not imaging or closely following high-risk infants (breech, family history) with a normal exam Applying an abduction device too tightly, risking femoral head avascular necrosis Failing to recognise late-presenting DDH in a child with a limp or waddling gait Laxity of the hip capsule and abnormal relationship between the femoral head and acetabulum, influenced by maternal hormones, intrauterine packing (as in breech position and oligohydramnios), and genetic factors, allow the femoral head to sit incompletely within or outside a shallow acetabulum. Without a well-seated femoral head, the acetabulum fails to develop its normal depth and shape, perpetuating instability and, over time, leading to secondary degenerative change. When detected and treated in early infancy, most hips develop normally with excellent long-term function; delayed diagnosis increases the need for surgery and the risk of residual dysplasia, avascular necrosis, and early osteoarthritis.

Deviated nasal septum — DNS, nasal septal deviation, septal deviation Inferior turbinate hypertrophy Nasal polyps Chronic rhinosinusitis Allergic or non-allergic rhinitis with mucosal congestion Nasal valve collapse Adenoid hypertrophy (particularly in children) Intranasal mass or tumour causing unilateral obstruction Anterior rhinoscopy after decongestion to assess the septum and turbinates Nasal endoscopy for a full view of the posterior septum and osteomeatal complex CT of the paranasal sinuses when sinus disease or surgery is planned Assessment of nasal airflow and, where indicated, allergy testing to identify a mucosal component Photographic and functional assessment if external nasal deformity coexists A deviated septum is a displacement of the bony or cartilaginous nasal septum from the midline and is extremely common, often asymptomatic It may be developmental (from differential growth of the septum and palate) or acquired following nasal trauma, sometimes at birth The dominant symptom is nasal obstruction, which may be unilateral or, with an S-shaped deviation, affect both sides Deviations take various forms including a spur, a C- or S-shaped bend, or dislocation of the caudal septum into the vestibule A prominent spur can press on the lateral wall and trigger headache or referred facial pain, and can contribute to recurrent epistaxis over the exposed area Septal deviation predisposes to sinus drainage problems and recurrent sinusitis and can worsen snoring and obstructive symptoms Diagnosis rests on anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy, decongesting the mucosa to distinguish a structural deviation from turbinate hypertrophy Symptomatic deviation is corrected surgically by septoplasty (or submucous resection), often with turbinate reduction, while asymptomatic deviation needs no treatment Strictly unilateral obstruction with blood-stained discharge suggesting a tumour rather than simple deviation A septal swelling after trauma suggesting a septal haematoma or abscess needing urgent drainage Progressive external deformity, crusting or perforation raising concern for granulomatous or destructive disease Persistent facial pain or visual symptoms suggesting significant sinus complication Attributing all nasal obstruction to the septum while overlooking turbinate hypertrophy, polyps or allergy Operating on an asymptomatic deviation found incidentally Missing a septal haematoma after trauma, risking cartilage necrosis and saddle deformity Failing to examine after decongestion, which distinguishes structural from mucosal obstruction The nasal septum is formed by the septal cartilage, the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer, meeting the maxillary and palatine crests. Deviation arises when these components grow at differing rates or are displaced by trauma, so the septum buckles or angulates away from the midline. The deviation narrows the airway on the concave side and may obstruct the osteomeatal complex, impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary drainage. Compensatory hypertrophy of the turbinate on the wider side can paradoxically cause obstruction there as well. Mucosa stretched over a spur becomes dry and prone to bleeding, and contact between the deviated septum and the lateral nasal wall can generate pressure-referred headache. Septoplasty relieves obstruction and associated symptoms in most patients with good long-term results, though some residual deviation or persistent turbinate-related congestion may remain; untreated symptomatic deviation can perpetuate sinus problems and sleep-disordered breathing.

Diabetes insipidus — DI, arginine vasopressin deficiency, AVP deficiency (central DI), AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI) Primary (psychogenic or dipsogenic) polydipsia Osmotic diuresis from uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (hyperglycaemia) Diuretic use Hypercalcaemia or hypokalaemia causing acquired nephrogenic DI Chronic kidney disease with impaired concentrating ability Post-obstructive or recovery-phase polyuria Paired serum and urine osmolality with serum sodium 24-hour urine volume to confirm true polyuria Water deprivation test followed by desmopressin challenge Plasma copeptin, ideally with hypertonic saline or arginine stimulation Serum glucose, calcium, and potassium to exclude secondary causes Pituitary and hypothalamic MRI when central DI is confirmed to seek a structural or infiltrative lesion Presents with persistent polyuria and polydipsia, typically with large volumes of dilute (hypotonic) urine and a strong thirst that drives high fluid intake The key distinction is between central DI, from deficient vasopressin secretion, and nephrogenic DI, from renal resistance to vasopressin Primary polydipsia, in which excessive drinking suppresses vasopressin, must be separated from true DI as management differs completely Serum sodium is often high-normal or elevated in true DI, whereas primary polydipsia tends toward low-normal sodium A water deprivation test with subsequent desmopressin assesses urinary concentrating ability and response to exogenous hormone Copeptin measurement, particularly after hypertonic saline stimulation, is increasingly used as a more reliable discriminator Central DI usually responds to desmopressin, whereas nephrogenic DI is managed by treating the underlying cause and supportive measures Where thirst perception is intact and access to water is preserved, patients can defend their sodium; the danger is when thirst or water access is impaired Rapidly rising sodium with altered consciousness from unreplaced free water losses DI arising after pituitary surgery or head injury, which may fluctuate through a triphasic pattern Absent or impaired thirst (adipsic DI) predisposing to dangerous hypernatraemia Loss of a previously present suprasellar lesion signal or new mass suggesting infiltrative or neoplastic disease Confusing osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia with true DI Giving desmopressin to a patient with primary polydipsia and precipitating water intoxication Restricting fluids in a patient who cannot concentrate urine, causing hypernatraemic dehydration Overlooking lithium or hypercalcaemia as reversible causes of nephrogenic DI Diabetes insipidus reflects an inability to concentrate urine appropriately. In central (cranial) DI there is deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone) due to disease of the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary, such as tumours, infiltrative disease, trauma, or surgery. In nephrogenic DI the kidney fails to respond to circulating vasopressin, from inherited receptor or aquaporin defects, drugs such as lithium, hypercalcaemia, or hypokalaemia. In both, the collecting duct cannot reabsorb enough free water, producing large volumes of dilute urine; if water intake cannot keep pace, plasma osmolality and sodium rise. Primary polydipsia is a separate entity in which excessive fluid intake physiologically suppresses vasopressin. Central DI is generally well controlled with vasopressin replacement and normal life expectancy when thirst and water access are intact; nephrogenic DI depends on reversibility of the underlying cause, and adipsic forms carry ongoing risk of severe sodium disturbances.
