includes ketosis-prone diabetes) and latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (5-10% of phenotypic type 2 have GAD/ICA) (p.3196, 3204) Pancreatogenic (type 3c) DM from pancreatitis, pancreatectomy, cystic fibrosis (CF-related diabetes prevalence ~50%), hemochromatosis (p.3203) Endocrinopathy-related hyperglycemia: acromegaly, Cushing's syndrome, glucagonoma, pheochromocytoma, somatostatinoma, hyperthyroidism (p.3196) Drug/chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoids, calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors, pentamidine, nicotinic acid, statins, HIV/protease-inhibitor therapy, thiazides, second-generation antipsychotics, immune checkpoint inhibitors (p.3196, 3203) Neonatal diabetes (onset <6 months; ATP-sensitive K+ channel subunit mutations may respond to sulfonylureas) (p.3196, 3203) HbA1c (lab method NGSP-aligned to DCCT reference) for diagnosis and monitoring; affected by hemoglobinopathies and ancestry (p.3196-3197) Fasting plasma glucose and 75-g OGTT (OGTT mainly for pregnancy/GDM and CF-related diabetes screening) (p.3197) Islet cell autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin) to classify type 1 vs type 2 and identify presymptomatic type 1 DM (p.3200-3201, 3204) C-peptide as a marker of endogenous insulin secretion (distinguishes endogenous vs exogenous insulin) (p.3198) Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR annually for nephropathy (screen 5 y after type 1 onset and at type 2 diagnosis); albuminuria = UACR >30 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g (p.3224) Annual dilated retinal exam (or retinal photography) - nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate (p.3224) Annual foot exam with 10-g monofilament, 128-Hz vibration, ankle reflexes, pedal pulses; annual DSPN screening for LOPS (p.3204, 3226) In DKA/HHS: serum/plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over nitroprusside which detects acetoacetate), glucose, electrolytes with corrected sodium, anion gap, bicarbonate, BUN/creatinine (p.3216) Stress/illness-related transient hyperglycemia from counterregulatory hormone excess (surgery, infection, critical illness) - hyperglycemia in a hospitalized patient need not indicate established DM (p.3217) Other causes of increased anion-gap acidosis when DKA is suspected: starvation ketosis and alcoholic ketoacidosis (bicarbonate usually >15 meq/L) (p.3216) DM is a group of metabolic disorders sharing the phenotype of hyperglycemia; it is defined as the level of glycemia at which a diabetes-specific complication (e.g., retinopathy) occurs, not as a deviation from a population mean (p.3195, 3197). Diagnostic criteria (any one, confirmed by repeat testing on a different day unless unequivocal hyperglycemia/acute metabolic decompensation): HbA1c >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol); fasting plasma glucose (FPG) >=7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL, fasting = no calories >=8 h); 2-h plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) on a 75-g OGTT; or a random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) PLUS classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) (p.3197). Prediabetes (each identifies different individuals via different biologic mechanisms): HbA1c 5.7-6.4%; impaired fasting glucose (IFG) FPG 5.6-6.9 mmol/L (100-125 mg/dL) per ADA; impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) 2-h glucose 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL). WHO defines IFG as FPG >6.1 mmol/L (110 mg/dL). All three confer increased risk of type 2 DM and cardiovascular disease (p.3197). Type 1 DM = autoimmune beta cell destruction with insulin deficiency; 25-50% present with DKA; ~40% of new type 1 DM now has onset after age 30 and is often initially misdiagnosed as type 2. Islet cell autoantibodies (ICAs: insulin, GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) are present in >85% at new onset and define a 3-stage model: stage 1 = >=2 autoantibodies + normoglycemia, stage 2 = autoimmunity + dysglycemia, stage 3 = overt hyperglycemia (p.3199-3201). Type 2 DM = heterogeneous: insulin resistance + impaired insulin secretion + increased hepatic glucose production; >=80% of patients are obese (central/visceral). Insulin resistance usually precedes the secretory defect, but diabetes appears only once secretion becomes inadequate for the degree of resistance (p.3195, 3201-3202). Type 2 DM may be asymptomatic for up to a decade before diagnosis, so some patients already have diabetes-specific complications at the time of diagnosis (p.3198, 3221). HbA1c can be misleading with hemoglobinopathies and varies by ancestry; OGTT is reserved mainly for pregnancy/GDM and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes screening, not routine care (p.3197). Symptoms of hyperglycemia: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, weakness, blurred vision (lens water-content change, resolves with control), recurrent superficial infections (vaginitis, fungal skin infections), slow wound healing (p.3203). Microvascular complications usually do not appear until the second decade of hyperglycemia; macrovascular (ASCVD) risk, driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, may develop before hyperglycemia is established (p.3221). Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common diabetic neuropathy and occurs in ~50% of long-standing DM; up to 50% are asymptomatic, so annual screening for loss of protective sensation (LOPS) is required - LOPS is a major risk factor for foot ulceration and amputation (p.3226). Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): hyperglycemia (glucose >13.9 mmol/L [250 mg/dL]; may be near-normal = euglycemic DKA, especially on SGLT-2 inhibitors), ketosis, anion-gap metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L); nausea/vomiting, severe abdominal pain (may mimic acute pancreatitis), Kussmaul respirations, fruity breath, volume depletion, lethargy progressing to coma; cerebral edema is a serious complication mainly in children (p.3216) Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS): older patient, more pronounced dehydration, marked hyperglycemia (often 33.3-66.6 mmol/L [600-1200 mg/dL]) with mental status changes; mortality up to 15% (higher than DKA) (p.3217) Hypoglycemia (<3.0 mmol/L, <54 mg/dL); hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy raises risk of severe events and can prolong QTc - sudden death has been attributed to cardiac autonomic neuropathy (p.3203, 3226) New blindness risk: proliferative retinopathy with neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage; clinically significant macular edema (p.3222-3223) Loss of protective sensation / foot ulceration predisposing to lower-extremity amputation (p.3226) Silent (painless) myocardial ischemia is common - absence of chest pain does not exclude coronary disease; consider cardiac evaluation before major surgery (p.3228) Do not over-rely on classic features (age of onset, obesity, insulin need) to classify DM - many adult-onset type 1 cases are misdiagnosed as type 2, and many new type 1 patients are now overweight/obese; measure ICAs when type 1 features are present (p.3199, 3204). Euglycemic DKA can occur (notably with SGLT-2 inhibitors) - a near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA; check ketones and acid-base (p.3216). In DKA, hyperamylasemia is usually salivary in origin and does NOT diagnose pancreatitis; obtain serum lipase if pancreatitis is suspected (p.3216). Measured serum sodium is falsely lowered by hyperglycemia (correct ~1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] glucose rise); a normal sodium in DKA signals a profound water deficit (p.3216). Serum potassium may be normal or high at DKA presentation despite a large total-body potassium deficit (acidosis/volume depletion shift) (p.3216). Nitroprusside ketone tests detect acetoacetate, not the predominant beta-hydroxybutyrate, and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid - prefer serum beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.3216). Glycemic control may transiently worsen established retinopathy in the first 6-12 months of improvement, and GLP-1 receptor agonists with marked glycemic improvement have been associated with worsening retinopathy (p.3224). CKD without retinopathy in type 1 DM should prompt a search for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of kidney disease (p.3224). Very strict glycemic control in acutely/critically ill patients (NICE-SUGAR) increased mortality and severe hypoglycemia - avoid overly tight targets in hospital (p.3217). Hyperglycemia results from reduced insulin secretion, decreased peripheral glucose utilization, and/or increased hepatic glucose production, with the relative contribution depending on the DM type. Insulin is produced by pancreatic beta cells (from preproinsulin -> proinsulin -> insulin + C-peptide); glucose is the key secretagogue: it enters the beta cell via GLUT transporters, glucokinase phosphorylation is rate-limiting, glycolysis generates ATP that closes the ATP-sensitive K+ channel (target of sulfonylureas/meglitinides), causing depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release; incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify glucose-stimulated secretion only when glucose is above fasting. Type 1 DM arises from interacting genetic (HLA region accounts for ~50% of risk; DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 predisposing), environmental, and immunologic factors leading to CD8+ T cell-mediated beta cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency; alpha-cell dysfunction adds fasting/postprandial hyperglucagonemia with impaired glucagon response to hypoglycemia. Type 2 DM combines impaired insulin secretion, insulin resistance (post-receptor defects in skeletal muscle, liver, fat; lipid intermediate accumulation; low-grade metabolic inflammation), excessive hepatic glucose production (failure to suppress gluconeogenesis), abnormal fat metabolism (increased free fatty acids, altered adipokines, reduced adiponectin), giving the characteristic dyslipidemia (high triglycerides, low HDL, small dense LDL); beta cell function is reduced ~50% at onset and declines progressively. Complications stem from chronic hyperglycemia driving advanced glycosylation end products (AGEs), increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, epigenetic changes ("metabolic memory"), and growth factors such as VEGF-A in proliferative retinopathy. DM is a major cause of mortality (8th leading cause of death in the US, 2021; likely underreported) and was responsible for ~6.7 million deaths worldwide in 2021 (12.2% of global all-cause mortality in adults 20-79); about one-third of diabetes-related deaths occur before age 60. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of morbidity and mortality, with ASCVD events and mortality 2-4 times greater in type 2 DM. In the US, DM is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease, nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation, and adult blindness; ~20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy. Intensive glycemic control has durable benefit ("metabolic memory"/legacy effect lasting >=10 years): DCCT/EDIC showed reductions in retinopathy (47%), albuminuria (39%), clinical nephropathy (54%), neuropathy (60%), later a 57% reduction in cardiovascular events and 33% reduction in mortality; UKPDS showed each 1% HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by 35%, and blood pressure control reduced complications even more than glycemic control. Diagnosis at younger age worsens prognosis (~3-4 years of reduced life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis). Glucose homeostasis is a spectrum: normal -> impaired (IFG/IGT/HbA1c 5.7-6.4%, i.e., prediabetes) -> diabetes mellitus. DKA severity by ADA: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mental status), moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mental status), severe (pH <7.0). Diabetic retinopathy: nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots) vs proliferative (neovascularization) +/- clinically significant macular edema. Albuminuria: moderately increased UACR 30-299 mg/g vs severely increased >300 mg/g creatinine. Neuropathy categories: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, and radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy.

Diabetes Mellitus: Complications — Diabetic complications, Microvascular and macrovascular complications of diabetes, Diabetic retinopathy, Diabetic nephropathy, Diabetic neuropathy, Diabetic foot Diabetic neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion - confirm only after excluding other neuropathy causes (e.g., B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, other metabolic/toxic neuropathies) Chronic kidney disease without retinopathy in type 1 diabetes should prompt investigation for an alternative (non-diabetic) cause of renal disease Type IV renal tubular acidosis (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism) as a cause of hyperkalemia/acidemia in diabetic patients Renovascular hypertension when blood pressure is not readily controlled in type 2 diabetes Celiac disease in type 1 diabetes presenting with diarrhea/constipation (associated anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies) Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease, possibly autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome) in type 1 diabetes with orthostatic hypotension Gas gangrene appearance in a diabetic foot may develop in the absence of clostridial infection Superficial culture of any foot ulcer yields multiple bacterial species of uncertain significance - infected ulcer is a clinical diagnosis, not a culture diagnosis Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with diabetic cystopathy and generally does not require treatment Dilated retinal examination by optometrist/ophthalmologist or retinal photography with remote reading (nondilated primary-care exams are inadequate); fluorescein angiography and optical coherence tomography to detect macular edema Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) plus estimated GFR, screening annually (start 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, at diagnosis for type 2) Annual neuropathy screening with 10-g monofilament and vibration testing to detect loss of protective sensation; begin 5 years after type 1 diagnosis and at diagnosis of type 2 Gastric scintigraphy after a radiolabeled meal to document delayed gastric emptying (may not correlate with symptoms) in suspected gastroparesis Ankle-brachial index for screening asymptomatic PAD in diabetic patients over 50 with risk factors Foot ulcer workup: probe-to-bone testing with a blunt sterile instrument, plain radiographs for osteomyelitis in chronic non-healing ulcers, MRI (most specific) with nuclear/labeled-WBC studies as alternatives; cultures from debrided ulcer base or purulent aspirate Cardiac stress testing in diabetic patients with symptoms (even atypical) suggestive of ischemia (routine screening of asymptomatic patients is not recommended) Transient worsening of established retinopathy during the first 6-12 months of improved glycemic control (and with GLP-1 receptor agonist-associated rapid glycemic improvement) can mimic disease progression but is temporary UACR can be falsely elevated by strenuous exercise, fever, infection, congestive heart failure, marked hyperglycemia, marked hypertension, or prostate disease - confirm on 2-3 occasions over 3-6 months Acute painful diabetic neuropathy may be treatment-related, triggered by improved glycemic control Diabetes-related complications are split into vascular (microvascular: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy; macrovascular: coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) and nonvascular (infections, dermatologic changes, cheiroarthropathy, hearing loss, cataracts, glaucoma, fractures, cognitive impairment); patterns are similar in type 1 and type 2 disease. Microvascular complications generally do not become evident until the second decade of hyperglycemia, whereas atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk (driven by insulin resistance and dyslipidemia) may precede frank hyperglycemia, so type 2 patients often have complications already present at diagnosis. Landmark trials established that chronic hyperglycemia is causative for microvascular disease: in the DCCT, intensive control (HbA1c 7.3% vs 9.1%) reduced retinopathy ~47%, albuminuria ~39%, clinical nephropathy ~54%, and neuropathy ~60%; the UKPDS showed each 1-percentage-point HbA1c reduction lowered microvascular complications by about 35%. A 'metabolic memory' / legacy effect exists: a period of improved glycemic control yields reduced cardiovascular events and mortality more than a decade later even after glycemic separation between groups disappears (DCCT/EDIC showed ~57% fewer cardiovascular events and ~33% lower mortality long term). Diabetic retinopathy is staged as nonproliferative (microaneurysms, blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous caliber change, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities) and proliferative (neovascularization from retinal hypoxemia, risking vitreous hemorrhage and traction retinal detachment); neovascularization is the hallmark of the proliferative stage. Macular edema can occur at either retinopathy stage and is a key cause of moderate vision loss; duration of diabetes and degree of glycemic control are the strongest predictors of retinopathy, with hypertension, nephropathy, and dyslipidemia as additional risk factors. Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and stage 5 CKD; screening combines a spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and estimated GFR because some patients lose GFR without albuminuria. Albuminuria is a persistently increased UACR >30 mg/g (moderate 30-299 mg/g, severe >300 mg/g). Diabetic neuropathy affects roughly half of long-standing patients and includes distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN), autonomic neuropathy, and mononeuropathy/radiculopathy; up to 50% of those with DSPN are asymptomatic, so screening for loss of protective sensation (10-g monofilament, vibration) is essential. Cardiovascular disease (CHD, PAD, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure) is the major cause of death in diabetes; heart failure is about twice as common (HFpEF, HFmrEF, or HFrEF) and 'silent ischemia' with absent chest pain is frequent, warranting a cardiac evaluation before major surgery. Diabetes is the leading cause of nontraumatic lower-extremity amputation; foot ulcers arise from the interaction of neuropathy, abnormal biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and poor wound healing, and a wound that probes to bone is highly likely to harbor osteomyelitis. Patients have greater frequency and severity of infections; certain severe infections occur almost exclusively in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, emphysematous cholecystitis/pyelonephritis/cystitis, and malignant (invasive) otitis externa (usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa). Characteristic dermatologic findings include xerosis/pruritus, diabetic dermopathy (pigmented pretibial papules), bullosis diabeticorum, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum (predominantly young women), acanthosis nigricans (severe insulin resistance), and vitiligo/alopecia areata in type 1 disease. Neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or traction involving the macula - urgent panretinal laser photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF; surgical vitrectomy for severe proliferative disease with vitreous hemorrhage Foot wound that probes to bone (high likelihood of osteomyelitis) or rapidly spreading cellulitis/severe infection requiring IV broad-spectrum coverage and possible surgical debridement Severe infections seen largely in diabetes: rhinocerebral mucormycosis, malignant (invasive) otitis externa progressing to osteomyelitis/meningitis, emphysematous pyelonephritis/cystitis/cholecystitis - consider especially with severe hyperglycemia Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy with resting tachycardia, reduced heart-rate variability, orthostatic hypotension, and QTc prolongation - associated with silent ischemia and reports of sudden death Hypoglycemia unawareness from autonomic neuropathy/reduced counterregulation, increasing the risk of severe hypoglycemia Hyperkalemia/acidemia from type IV RTA, potentially exacerbated by ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists Risk of radiocontrast-induced nephrotoxicity (preexisting nephropathy, volume depletion) Routine urinalysis does not detect low-level albuminuria - use UACR; and some patients lose GFR without albuminuria, so always assess both eGFR and UACR Nondilated eye exams by primary providers miss diabetic eye disease - a dilated/photographic retinal exam is required Once advanced retinopathy or moderate albuminuria is established, improving glycemic control provides less benefit - early detection is critical Diagnosing diabetic neuropathy without excluding other etiologies; metformin can lower vitamin B12 and pernicious anemia is more common in type 1 disease Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria unnecessarily; basing diabetic foot infection diagnosis on superficial swab cultures rather than clinical judgment and deep cultures Failure to hold metformin around iodinated contrast and to monitor creatinine 24-48 h afterward; failing to reassess glucose-lowering drug choice/dose as GFR falls (sulfonylureas and metformin contraindicated in advanced renal insufficiency; SGLT-2 inhibitors ineffective below eGFR 20) Overlooking silent ischemia given frequent absence of chest pain, and failing to evaluate before major surgery Chronic hyperglycemia is the principal etiologic driver of microvascular complications, though the precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined and are likely multifactorial. Proposed pathways include hyperglycemia-induced epigenetic changes altering gene expression, formation of advanced glycosylation end products (e.g., pentosidine, glucosepane, carboxymethyllysine) that cross-link proteins and bind cell-surface receptors causing endothelial and glomerular dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis, local growth-factor effects (VEGF-A drives proliferative retinopathy), and a unifying hypothesis that hyperglycemia raises mitochondrial reactive oxygen species/superoxide that activate downstream injury pathways. In nephropathy, soluble mediators (angiotensin II, endothelin, AGEs), hemodynamic alterations (glomerular hyperfiltration, increased capillary pressure), and structural changes (basement-membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, fibrosis) lead from early hyperfiltration/renal hypertrophy to irreversible albuminuria and GFR decline. Macrovascular disease additionally reflects insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation, with insulin failing to suppress adipose lipolysis and causing ectopic lipid accumulation (triglycerides, diacylglycerol, ceramides). In neuropathy both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers are lost; foot ulceration arises from sensory loss removing protective mechanisms, autonomic anhidrosis causing dry/fissured skin, motor changes producing deformity, and PAD impairing healing. Complications account for most diabetes-related morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis at a younger age increases lifetime complication burden (one estimate: 3-4 fewer years of life expectancy per decade of earlier diagnosis). Intensive glycemic control substantially improves outcomes: DCCT projections estimated several additional years free of vision loss, end-stage renal disease, and amputation, with overall added life expectancy, and 30-year follow-up showed durable reductions in retinopathy, nephropathy, and cardiovascular events (legacy/metabolic-memory effect). About 20-40% of patients develop diabetic nephropathy, and CKD on dialysis carries a poor prognosis. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death and outcomes after CHD are worse than in nondiabetic patients; CHD tends to involve multiple vessels and revascularization (PCI/CABG) is less durable, though CABG plus optimal medical therapy generally outperforms PCI. Diabetic polyradiculopathies (including amyotrophy) are usually self-limited, resolving over 6-12 months. Foot ulcers carry a substantial amputation risk (about 14-24% with that or subsequent ulceration). Some patients never develop retinopathy or nephropathy despite long-standing disease, suggesting genetic protection. Retinopathy: nonproliferative (mild to severe, with microaneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA) versus proliferative (neovascularization), with clinically significant macular edema as a separate sight-threatening category. Albuminuria/CKD: UACR normal (<30 mg/g), moderately increased (30-299 mg/g), severely increased (>300 mg/g), staged alongside eGFR; nephrology referral when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2, UACR >300 mg/g, or atypical features (hematuria, rapid decline). Diabetic neuropathy categorized as diffuse (distal symmetric polyneuropathy and/or autonomic), focal mononeuropathy, or radiculopathy/polyradiculopathy. Foot infection severity stratified clinically from mild/non-limb-threatening (oral antibiotics) to severe (IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, offloading, debridement).

symptoms usually resolve once plasma glucose is below ~200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), so therapy mainly targets complication prevention. (Harrison 22e p.3205) HbA1c reflects average glycemia over the prior 2-3 months because erythrocytes live ~120 days, with the most recent month contributing roughly half the value; it does not capture short-term variability or recent intercurrent illness the way continuous (CGM) or fingerstick (BGM) monitoring does. (Harrison 22e p.3207-3208) Continuous glucose monitoring measures interstitial glucose, which is in equilibrium with blood glucose but can lag when glucose changes rapidly or during exercise; an ambulatory glucose profile summarizes time-in-range, time above/below target, the glucose management indicator (correlating with HbA1c), and glucose variability. (Harrison 22e p.3207) The general HbA1c goal is below 7% (or <=6.5% for selected patients), but a more lenient target of <7.5-8% is appropriate for those with cognitive impairment, hypoglycemia unawareness, or limited life expectancy; about one in four people over 65 has diabetes, so elderly targets must be individualized. (Harrison 22e p.3208) A consensus CGM time-in-range goal for most patients with type 1 or type 2 DM is >70% of time within 70-180 mg/dL (3.9-10.0 mmol/L), with <4% below 70 mg/dL and <1% below 54 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3208) Ketones (preferably blood beta-hydroxybutyrate rather than urine nitroprusside assays, which detect only acetoacetate and acetone) should be checked in type 1 DM whenever plasma glucose persistently exceeds 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) or during intercurrent illness with nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. (Harrison 22e p.3216) DKA arises mostly in type 1 DM and HHS mostly in type 2 DM, but the two exist along a continuum of hyperglycemia and up to one-third of patients show features of both. (Harrison 22e p.3216) Ketosis-prone diabetes can present with DKA at diagnosis in obese young adults of Hispanic or African descent who later recover insulin secretory capacity and can discontinue insulin after weeks to months. (Harrison 22e p.3216) SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy can precipitate euglycemic DKA in type 2 DM, where glucose is normal or only mildly elevated because of glucosuria, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis; resolution should be tracked by bicarbonate correction rather than by glucose. (Harrison 22e p.3216-3217) In DKA the measured serum sodium is artifactually low; the correction adds ~1.6 mmol/L of sodium for each 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) rise in glucose, and a normal measured sodium in DKA signals a profound free-water deficit. (Harrison 22e p.3217) Inpatient hyperglycemia predicts worse outcomes, yet very strict glycemic control in the critically ill worsens outcomes; the NICE-SUGAR trial showed higher mortality and more severe hypoglycemia with a target of 81-108 mg/dL versus a moderate goal of <180 mg/dL, supporting a hospital target of roughly 140-180 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3219) Sliding-scale insulin alone (reactive treatment only when glucose is already high) is inadequate for inpatient management; scheduled basal plus prandial and corrective dosing is preferred, and CGM/automated insulin delivery are not FDA approved for ICU use. euglycemic DKA occurs with SGLT-2 inhibitors and resolution must be judged by bicarbonate, not glucose Relying on urine nitroprusside ketone tests, which miss beta-hydroxybutyrate (the dominant ketone) and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid Interpreting hyperamylasemia in DKA as pancreatitis when it is usually salivary in origin; obtain lipase Failing to correct serum sodium for hyperglycemia, masking a true free-water deficit Misreading the early/at-presentation serum potassium as adequate; total-body potassium is depleted despite a normal or high initial level, and hypokalemia develops during insulin/fluid therapy Trusting HbA1c in conditions that alter red-cell turnover (hemoglobinopathy, anemia, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, dialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy) Using sliding-scale insulin alone for inpatients, which is inadequate Applying overly strict inpatient glucose targets, which increases severe hypoglycemia and can worsen outcomes (NICE-SUGAR) Substances interfering with glucose sensors/meters (e.g., acetaminophen, ascorbic acid, hydroxyurea, mannitol/sorbitol for CGM; uric acid, galactose, xylose, L-DOPA for BGM) Hyperglycemia in diabetes reflects relative or absolute insulin deficiency with impaired glucose utilization and unrestrained hepatic glucose production. In acute decompensation, severe hyperglycemia drives osmotic diuresis with volume depletion. DKA results from relative or absolute insulin deficiency combined with excess counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone); the low insulin-to-glucagon ratio promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and ketone body formation, while increased lipolysis releases free fatty acids that are shifted toward ketogenesis, producing ketonemia and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both DKA and HHS. HHS is caused by relative (less severe) insulin deficiency plus inadequate fluid intake; insulin deficiency raises hepatic glucose output and impairs muscle uptake, and osmotic diuresis with poor fluid replacement produces extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration. The absence of significant ketosis in HHS is incompletely understood but is attributed to only partial insulin deficiency, lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels, and an insulin/glucagon balance that does not favor ketogenesis. During exercise or acute illness, surges in counterregulatory hormones and cytokines cause transient insulin resistance and can tip toward hyperglycemia or, with relative hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia. With appropriate therapy, DKA mortality is low (<1%) and relates more to the underlying or precipitating event (infection/pneumonia, COVID-19, pregnancy, end-stage renal disease, myocardial infarction) than to the metabolic derangement itself; venous thrombosis, upper GI bleeding, ARDS, and cerebral edema (chiefly in children, during resolution) can complicate the course. Even a single DKA episode carries a substantially increased 1-year mortality, and recurrent DKA may signal underlying mental health issues or barriers to care such as insulin cost. HHS carries a substantially higher mortality (up to ~15% in some series) because patients are typically older with serious precipitating illness and comorbidities. Improved glycemic control reduces microvascular complications regardless of baseline level, and early intensive control in type 1 DM (DCCT/EDIC) lowered later cardiovascular events nearly two decades on. DKA severity is graded by pH, serum bicarbonate, and mental status: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mentation); moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mentation); severe (pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10-15 meq/L, reduced mental status or coma). Representative presenting laboratory ranges: DKA glucose ~250-600 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 meq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0 mmol/L, and elevated anion gap; HHS glucose ~600-1200 mg/dL (may exceed 1000) with osmolality >300, bicarbonate >18, pH >7.3, and absent/minimal ketones; euglycemic DKA glucose ~100-250 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 and beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0.

osteomyelitis and treating for too short a duration Neglecting offloading and debridement while relying on antibiotics alone Diabetic foot infection develops when skin integrity is breached, usually over a pressure point, in a foot compromised by sensory neuropathy (loss of protective sensation), motor and autonomic dysfunction (deformity and dry, fissured skin), and often peripheral arterial disease. Impaired neutrophil function and microvascular disease blunt the immune response and reduce tissue perfusion, allowing colonising skin flora to invade soft tissue, tendon sheaths, and bone. Infection can spread rapidly along fascial and tendon planes, producing deep abscesses and osteomyelitis. Outcomes depend on infection severity, adequacy of perfusion, and glycaemic control; mild soft-tissue infection often resolves, whereas deep infection with ischaemia or osteomyelitis carries a substantial risk of amputation and is associated with reduced long-term survival.

Diabetic kidney disease — DKD, diabetic nephropathy, diabetic glomerulosclerosis Hypertensive nephrosclerosis Primary or secondary glomerulonephritis Ischaemic nephropathy from renovascular disease Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and exclude obstruction Consideration of biopsy when the clinical picture is atypical for diabetic disease Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease worldwide and develops in a substantial proportion of people with long-standing type 1 or type 2 diabetes The classic course progresses from glomerular hyperfiltration through rising albuminuria to declining glomerular filtration, though not every patient follows this sequence Persistent albuminuria is both an early marker of kidney involvement and an independent predictor of cardiovascular risk Coexisting diabetic retinopathy supports the diagnosis, and its absence in type 1 diabetes should prompt consideration of a non-diabetic cause Features that argue against pure diabetic disease include an active urinary sediment, rapid loss of function, heavy proteinuria without retinopathy, or a short duration of diabetes Control of blood pressure, glycaemia, and albuminuria, together with blockade of the renin-angiotensin system, are the mainstays of slowing progression Newer agents that reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria have been shown to slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events, changing modern management principles Regular screening with albuminuria measurement and estimated GFR allows early intervention before irreversible damage accumulates Rapid decline in renal function suggesting a superimposed or alternative process Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema Active urinary sediment or haematuria pointing to glomerulonephritis Refractory hypertension or hyperkalaemia complicating renin-angiotensin blockade Assuming all kidney disease in a diabetic patient is diabetic nephropathy and missing a treatable alternative Neglecting albuminuria screening so that intervention starts only after significant function is lost Failing to intensify renin-angiotensin blockade and other kidney-protective therapy in albuminuric patients Overlooking the high cardiovascular risk that accompanies diabetic kidney disease Diabetic kidney disease develops from chronic hyperglycaemia acting through several interlinked pathways. Excess glucose drives formation of advanced glycation end products, activation of protein kinase C, and oxidative stress, which damage the glomerular filtration barrier. Early on, altered afferent and efferent arteriolar tone produces glomerular hypertension and hyperfiltration, increasing shear stress on the capillary wall. Over time the glomerular basement membrane thickens, the mesangium expands with accumulation of matrix, and podocytes are lost, culminating in the nodular and diffuse glomerulosclerosis characteristic of the disease. These changes progressively increase albumin leakage and reduce filtration surface area. Systemic and intraglomerular hypertension, along with tubulointerstitial fibrosis, accelerates the decline toward end-stage kidney disease. Without intervention, diabetic kidney disease tends to progress steadily to end-stage kidney disease, and it markedly increases cardiovascular mortality. Intensive control of glycaemia and blood pressure, renin-angiotensin blockade, reduction of albuminuria, and modern kidney-protective therapies can substantially slow decline and reduce cardiovascular events, so early detection and comprehensive risk-factor management materially improve outcomes.

Involvement of autonomic fibres disrupts cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary regulation, while focal ischaemia or entrapment can cause mononeuropathies and radiculopathies. Neuropathy tends to progress with duration and poor control of diabetes, and established nerve damage is largely irreversible, so the emphasis is on prevention of ulceration and amputation and on symptom control; autonomic neuropathy carries an adverse cardiovascular prognosis.

With timely screening, good systemic control, and prompt laser or anti-VEGF treatment, most severe visual loss is preventable; neglected proliferative disease and macular oedema carry a high risk of blindness.

Diamond-Blackfan anaemia — DBA, congenital hypoplastic anaemia, RPS19, pure red cell aplasia of infancy Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood Parvovirus B19-associated red cell aplasia Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome Fanconi anaemia and other inherited marrow-failure syndromes Acquired pure red cell aplasia Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias Full blood count and reticulocyte count showing macrocytic anaemia with reticulocytopenia Bone marrow examination demonstrating erythroid hypoplasia Erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity Fetal haemoglobin measurement Molecular genetic testing of ribosomal protein genes Assessment for congenital anomalies with echocardiography, renal imaging and limb radiographs Inherited ribosomopathy causing a congenital pure red cell aplasia, frequently caused by variants in ribosomal protein genes such as RPS19 Typically presents in the first year of life with severe macrocytic anaemia, reticulocytopenia and a normal white cell and platelet count Bone marrow shows a selective paucity of erythroid precursors with otherwise normal cellularity Around half of patients have congenital anomalies, including craniofacial (Cathie facies), thumb (triphalangeal or duplicated), cardiac and genitourinary defects, and short stature Raised erythrocyte adenosine deaminase activity and elevated fetal haemoglobin support the diagnosis Corticosteroids induce a response in many patients; others become dependent on long-term red cell transfusion with attendant iron overload There is an increased risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute leukaemia and solid tumours over a lifetime Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can cure the haematological disease and is used for transfusion dependence or clonal progression Evolving neutropenia or thrombocytopenia suggesting progression to marrow failure or myelodysplasia Clonal cytogenetic change or blasts indicating malignant transformation Symptomatic iron overload from chronic transfusion Severe anaemia with cardiovascular compromise at presentation Confusing it with transient erythroblastopenia of childhood, which recovers spontaneously Overlooking parvovirus B19 as a cause of acute red cell aplasia Failing to monitor and treat transfusional iron overload Neglecting long-term malignancy surveillance Diamond-Blackfan anaemia is caused by haploinsufficiency of genes encoding ribosomal proteins, impairing ribosome biogenesis. Disrupted assembly of the ribosomal subunits activates stabilisation of p53 and stress pathways to which erythroid progenitors are especially sensitive, producing selective failure of red cell production. The same ribosomal stress and secondary genomic instability contribute to the congenital malformations and the heightened risk of malignancy. Many patients achieve stable disease with corticosteroids or transfusion support, and some undergo spontaneous remission; long-term outcome is influenced by transfusional iron overload and the lifelong increased risk of myelodysplasia, leukaemia and solid tumours. Transplantation is curative for the haematological disease.

and severe progressive scoliosis Caused by biallelic variants in SLC26A2, a sulphate transporter needed for proper sulphation of cartilage proteoglycans The hitch-hiker thumb, produced by a proximally Neurological deterioration from spinal deformity Missing cervical kyphosis and precipitating cord injury during airway management Overlooking the hitch-hiker thumb and ear findings that point to the diagnosis Underestimating the rate of scoliosis progression Confusing it with arthrogryposis without appropriate radiographic and genetic assessment Diastrophic dysplasia results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC26A2, a transporter that supplies sulphate for the sulphation of proteoglycans in cartilage matrix. Undersulphated proteoglycans produce structurally abnormal cartilage, impairing endochondral ossification and the integrity of articular and physeal cartilage. This underlies the short limbs, epiphyseal abnormalities, joint contractures and dislocations, spinal deformity, and the distinctive ear and hand features. Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal, but disability is often considerable owing to severe scoliosis, contractures, hip and knee deformity, and premature joint degeneration. Early cervical spine complications and respiratory compromise from spinal deformity are the main threats.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation — PT/APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer Blood film Treat the underlying trigger Often secondary to sepsis/malignancy — treat the cause Severe liver disease (thrombocytopenia from sequestration/portal hypertension/hypersplenism, decreased factor and natural-anticoagulant synthesis, elevated d-dimer) — distinguished because liver-disease parameters do not change rapidly, unlike DIC (p.977). Immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) — acute thrombocytopenia, red cell fragmentation, multiorgan failure, but identified by ADAMTS13 inhibitor (p.977). Vitamin K deficiency (isolated PT prolongation as earliest finding) (p.977-978). Gram-negative bacterial systemic infection (DIC is most commonly seen here) (p.974). COVID-19-associated coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia (p.974). ISTH overt-DIC score using platelet count, d-dimer, PT prolongation, and fibrinogen (p.977). Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes (red cell fragmentation) (p.977). Serial/repeated PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, d-dimer measurements (every 6-8 h in critically ill; daily if overt DIC) to assess trajectory and distinguish from liver disease (p.977). Fibrin degradation products (FDP) (p.976-977). ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor when TTP is in the differential (p.977). Severe/fulminant liver disease and cirrhosis (coexisting chronic or acute DIC can also occur) (p.977-978). Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS) (p.977). Dysfibrinogenemia of liver disease (p.978). DIC is an acquired syndrome of intravascular activation of coagulation with loss of localization, which can damage the microvasculature and, if severe enough, cause organ dysfunction (ISTH 2001 definition) (p.976). The central event is uncontrolled thrombin generation, compounded by disruption of physiologic anticoagulant mechanisms and abnormal fibrinolysis, producing systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels (p.976). Fibrin deposition can compromise blood supply to lung, kidney, liver and brain, causing organ failure; pulmonary microvascular thrombosis is a component of ARDS (p.976). Most common causes: bacterial sepsis (also viral and fungal), trauma, obstetric events (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism), and malignancy (especially mucin-producing adenocarcinomas and acute promyelocytic leukemia) (p.976). Sepsis-driven DIC reflects thrombo-inflammation: increased tissue factor expression, neutrophil/monocyte activation with cytokine release, neutrophil extracellular traps, and polyphosphate release driving thrombin generation (p.976). Bleeding manifestations dominate clinically: petechiae, ecchymoses, oozing from venipuncture sites, and severe hemorrhage from GI tract, lung, or CNS; thrombosis of large vessels and cerebral embolism can also occur (p.977). Chronic (low-grade, compensated) DIC is seen with giant hemangioma, metastatic carcinoma, and late-gestation fetal demise; bleeding is discrete and limited to skin/mucosa, with elevated FDP/d-dimer but PT/aPTT/fibrinogen often normal or high and only mild thrombocytopenia (p.977). In critically ill patients, coagulation parameters should be repeated over 6-8 h because patients can deteriorate rapidly; an overt-DIC score should be rechecked daily (p.977). Hemodynamic instability and shock are common in acute DIC; mortality ranges from 30% to over 80% (p.977). Purpura fulminans — extensive skin thrombosis, especially in children post-infection or with protein C pathway deficiency (p.976). Bleeding into the CNS, lung, or GI tract (p.977). Rapidly deteriorating coagulation parameters in a critically ill patient (p.977). Distinguishing DIC from severe liver disease is challenging and requires serial laboratory measurements — both share thrombocytopenia, reduced factor synthesis, and elevated d-dimer, but liver-disease values do not change rapidly (p.977). The ISTH overt-DIC scoring tool is not validated for pregnant patients; a separate tool exists for pregnancy (p.977). d-Dimer assays are not standardized and have differing normal ranges; degree of increase must be interpreted against the local laboratory range (p.977). A single low score does not exclude evolving DIC — a non-overt score (<5) should be repeated every 1-2 days (p.977). DIC arises from uncontrolled thrombin generation triggered by multiple mechanisms, with simultaneous disruption of physiologic anticoagulant pathways and abnormal fibrinolysis. In sepsis and trauma, activation of inflammatory pathways increases tissue factor expression, activates neutrophils and monocytes with cytokine release and neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and releases polyphosphates that cross-talk with the coagulation system (thrombo-inflammation); endothelial damage causes loss of native antithrombotic properties. The result is systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels causing microvascular occlusion, ischemic organ damage, and red cell fragmentation/hemolysis. Sustained activation consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing systemic bleeding that is aggravated by secondary hyperfibrinolysis in late stages. Purpura fulminans is a severe form of DIC with extensive cutaneous thrombosis, predominantly in young children after viral or bacterial infection, especially with inherited or acquired protein C pathway deficiency (p.976). Morbidity and mortality in DIC are primarily driven by the underlying disease; acute DIC carries mortality ranging from 30% to greater than 80%. Many patients with overt DIC are critically ill and require intensive care (p.977). ISTH overt-DIC score: Platelets >100x10^9/L = 0, 50-100 = 1, <50 = 2; d-dimer normal = 0, moderate increase = 2, severe increase = 3; PT prolongation <3 s = 0, 3-6 s = 1, >6 s = 2; fibrinogen >1 g/L = 0, <1 g/L = 1. Total <5 = non-overt/low-grade DIC (repeat in 1-2 days); >5 = overt DIC (repeat labs daily). Not for use in pregnant patients (p.977).

predisposition Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum with embryonal tumours Li-Fraumeni syndrome Sporadic Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour or cystic nephroma Familial non-medullary thyroid cancer Rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome (SMARCB1/SMARCA4) Germline DICER1 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis Chest imaging in early childhood to detect lung cysts and pleuropulmonary blastoma Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound for renal and ovarian tumours Thyroid ultrasound surveillance and clinical examination for goitre Tumour testing for the characteristic RNase IIIb hotspot mutation to support the diagnosis Neuroimaging where pineoblastoma or intracranial disease is suspected Caused by germline pathogenic variants in DICER1, a gene central to microRNA processing, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable, often incomplete penetrance The hallmark tumour is pleuropulmonary blastoma of early childhood, frequently preceded by lung cysts that may be mistaken for congenital malformations The broad spectrum also includes ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumour, cystic nephroma, multinodular goitre and differentiated thyroid cancer, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and pineoblastoma Many carriers remain unaffected, and manifestations cluster in childhood and adolescence, so age-appropriate surveillance matters Multinodular goitre and thyroid cancer risk are increased, particularly after chemotherapy or radiotherapy for another DICER1 tumour Tumours characteristically show a second somatic hotspot mutation in the DICER1 RNase IIIb domain in addition to the germline loss-of-function allele Surveillance focuses on chest imaging in early childhood, pelvic and abdominal assessment, and thyroid monitoring Respiratory distress or a cystic or solid lung lesion in a young child A pelvic or abdominal mass suggesting ovarian or renal tumour A rapidly enlarging or suspicious thyroid nodule Neurological signs raising concern for pineoblastoma or other intracranial tumour Dismissing childhood lung cysts as benign congenital lesions and missing early pleuropulmonary blastoma Overlooking the diagnosis because of incomplete penetrance and an unremarkable family history Failing to monitor the thyroid, especially after chemotherapy or radiotherapy Not offering cascade testing and paediatric surveillance to at-risk relatives DICER1 encodes an endoribonuclease that cleaves precursor microRNAs into mature microRNAs, which fine-tune the expression of many genes controlling growth and differentiation. In this syndrome a germline loss-of-function variant is combined with a characteristic somatic missense mutation in the RNase IIIb catalytic domain of the other allele, a distinctive two-hit mechanism that selectively impairs processing of one class of microRNAs. The resulting imbalance in microRNA regulation disrupts developmental control of susceptible tissues, giving rise to the diverse embryonal and mesenchymal tumours that define the condition. Penetrance is variable and many carriers stay healthy, but pleuropulmonary blastoma can be aggressive, so early detection through surveillance improves outcomes. Most other tumours are treatable when identified early, and long-term thyroid monitoring is warranted given the increased malignancy risk, particularly after cancer therapy.

Difficult airway — difficult intubation, difficult mask ventilation, CICO, can't intubate can't oxygenate Laryngospasm Bronchospasm or anaphylaxis limiting ventilation Airway foreign body or obstructing tumour Airway oedema from angioedema or infection Oesophageal intubation mistaken for a difficult airway Equipment failure or circuit disconnection Bedside airway assessment scores and examination of relevant pathology Nasendoscopy or flexible airway endoscopy to evaluate obstructing lesions Imaging (radiograph, CT) to characterise airway anatomy and masses when indicated Capnography to confirm tracheal placement and ventilation Review of previous anaesthetic records and airway alerts A difficult airway describes difficulty with mask ventilation, supraglottic device placement, laryngoscopy, intubation, or surgical airway access, and may be anticipated or unexpected Preoperative assessment combines several predictors (mouth opening, Mallampati class, thyromental distance, neck mobility, prognathism, prior difficulty, and pathology) since no single test is reliable A structured plan with pre-formulated backup steps and clear failure criteria is essential, and progression through a difficult-airway algorithm should be deliberate and time-limited Preoxygenation and apnoeic oxygenation extend safe apnoea time and are central to preventing hypoxic injury When intubation fails, the priority shifts from securing the tube to maintaining oxygenation using face mask or supraglottic devices A can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate situation is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate front-of-neck access (cricothyroidotomy) without delay For a known or predicted difficult airway, an awake technique with a flexible bronchoscope preserves spontaneous ventilation and airway reflexes Limiting repeated laryngoscopy attempts reduces trauma, bleeding, and oedema that can convert a difficult airway into an impossible one; documentation and patient alerting are vital afterwards Can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate scenario requiring immediate front-of-neck access Progressive desaturation despite optimal mask and supraglottic ventilation Rapidly worsening airway obstruction from oedema, bleeding, or an expanding mass Repeated failed attempts causing trauma, bleeding, and deteriorating airway conditions Persisting with repeated intubation attempts instead of prioritising oxygenation Failing to declare and act on a can't-intubate-can't-oxygenate emergency in time Inadequate preoxygenation before induction Not preparing backup equipment and a clear stepwise plan in advance Failing to document the difficulty and alert the patient for future anaesthetics Airway difficulty arises from anatomical or pathological factors that impair alignment of the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes or obstruct airflow. Congenital syndromes, obesity, limited neck extension, restricted mouth opening, tumours, infection, trauma, previous surgery, radiation, and airway oedema all contribute. Under anaesthesia, loss of muscle tone can collapse the pharynx and worsen obstruction. When ventilation and oxygenation fail, progressive hypoxaemia leads within minutes to bradycardia, hypoxic brain injury, cardiac arrest, and death, so oxygenation rather than intubation is the overriding physiological goal. Most anticipated difficult airways are managed safely with planning and appropriate techniques; unanticipated failure with delayed rescue oxygenation can cause hypoxic brain injury or death within minutes.

vaccines to a severely immunodeficient infant Assuming normal cognition and missing learning and psychiatric needs Failing to consider the diagnosis in an isolated conotruncal cardiac lesion DiGeorge syndrome is most often caused by a recurrent hemizygous microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2, encompassing the TBX1 gene among others. TBX1 is critical for development of the pharyngeal arches and pouches, and its haploinsufficiency disrupts formation of the thymus, parathyroid glands, and cardiac outflow tract, producing immunodeficiency, hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia, and conotruncal heart defects. The deletion typically arises de novo from misalignment of flanking low-copy repeats, though it can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Similar phenotypes rarely result from other causes such as maternal diabetes or teratogen exposure. Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of cardiac disease and immunodeficiency; most children with milder immune involvement do well, while those with complete thymic aplasia face life-threatening infection unless treated with thymic or immune reconstitution.

factors Presents with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion, and characteristic visual disturbances such as blurred or yellow-green tinted vision (xanthopsia) Digoxin can cause almost any arrhythmia; the combination of increased automaticity with atrioventricular block (for example atrial tachycardia with block, or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia) is highly suggestive Chronic toxicity is often precipitated by renal impairment, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia, and interacting drugs, and occurs at lower levels than acute overdose In acute overdose, hyperkalaemia results from poisoning of the sodium-potassium pump and is an important marker of severity and prognosis Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin immune Fab) are the definitive antidote and are indicated for life-threatening arrhythmia, significant hyperkalaemia in acute poisoning, or haemodynamic instability In acute toxicity, treat hyperkalaemia cautiously and avoid intravenous calcium, which is traditionally cautioned against for fear of worsening myocardial contracture Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia in chronic toxicity, as these potentiate glycoside effects and provoke arrhythmias Bradyarrhythmias may respond to atropine and temporary pacing, but definitive treatment of serious toxicity is the specific antibody Life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia or bidirectional ventricular tachycardia High-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradycardia Significant hyperkalaemia in acute poisoning Haemodynamic instability Suggestive arrhythmia combining enhanced automaticity with conduction block Overlooking chronic toxicity because the digoxin level is only modestly raised Failing to correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia that perpetuate arrhythmia in chronic toxicity Giving intravenous calcium for hyperkalaemia in acute digoxin poisoning, traditionally avoided Delaying digoxin-specific antibody in a patient with life-threatening arrhythmia or severe hyperkalaemia Digoxin inhibits the myocardial sodium-potassium ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and, through sodium-calcium exchange, intracellular calcium, which increases contractility but also enhances automaticity and the tendency to arrhythmia. It also augments vagal tone, slowing sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction. In acute overdose, widespread inhibition of the pump drives potassium out of cells, producing hyperkalaemia that reflects the degree of poisoning. Electrolyte disturbances (low potassium or magnesium, high calcium) and renal impairment increase myocardial sensitivity and reduce clearance, precipitating chronic toxicity at therapeutic or near-therapeutic levels. With timely recognition, correction of electrolytes, and use of digoxin-specific antibody fragments for severe cases, most patients recover; untreated life-threatening arrhythmias and marked hyperkalaemia in acute overdose carry high mortality.

rate-limiting enzyme degrading uracil and thymine The most clinically important consequence is severe, sometimes fatal, toxicity from fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil and its prodrug capecitabine) Because DPD normally clears the great majority of administered fluorouracil, deficient patients accumulate active drug and suffer profound myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhoea, and neurotoxicity Constitutional (non-drug) presentations range from asymptomatic carriers to a paediatric encephalopathic phenotype with developmental delay, seizures and hypotonia The biochemical signature is raised uracil and thymine in urine, plasma and cerebrospinal fluid Pre-treatment DPYD genotyping and/or measurement of the uracil-to-dihydrouracil ratio identifies at-risk patients before fluoropyrimidine exposure In deficient patients fluoropyrimidines should be avoided or given at substantially reduced exposure with close monitoring; uridine triacetate is the rescue therapy for established overdose or severe early toxicity Rapid, severe myelosuppression, mucositis or diarrhoea early in a fluoropyrimidine course Neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy or cerebellar signs during chemotherapy Planned fluoropyrimidine treatment in a patient not yet tested for DPD deficiency Progressive neurological deterioration in an affected child Giving standard-dose fluoropyrimidines without checking DPD status Assuming a normal genotype excludes deficiency, as phenotype testing may add information Attributing severe early chemotherapy toxicity to chance rather than to enzyme deficiency Failing to use the specific antidote promptly when severe toxicity occurs Overlooking that heterozygous partial deficiency can still cause serious toxicity Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase catalyses the rate-limiting first step in the degradation of the pyrimidine bases uracil and thymine. Deficiency causes accumulation of these bases and their precursors in body fluids. Clinically, the disorder has two faces. As an inborn error it can cause a variable neurological phenotype, thought to relate to accumulated metabolites and, in some, associated abnormalities of the neurotransmitter pool. More importantly for adult medicine, fluoropyrimidine drugs are analogues of uracil that are normally inactivated by this enzyme; when it is deficient, the active drug and its cytotoxic metabolites persist, producing severe dose-related toxicity even at standard doses. Constitutional cases range from entirely asymptomatic to significant neurodevelopmental impairment; the critical determinant of outcome is recognition before fluoropyrimidine exposure, since unrecognised deficiency can cause life-threatening or fatal drug toxicity.

Dilated Cardiomyopathy — DCM, cardiomyopathy Ischaemic cardiomyopathy / coronary artery disease or prior infarction (structural heart disease that can mimic or cause DCM, p.2002) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), including the ~5% that evolve to reduced EF with restrictive physiology (HCM-rEF) (p.2001-2002) Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) - functional diagnosis based on diastolic dysfunction/elevated filling pressures; some sarcomeric variants and storage diseases overlap (p.2002) Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM-LV / ACM-RV/ARVC) where ventricular arrhythmias dominate before severely reduced LVEF (p.2002) Primary valvular disease Takotsubo (stress-induced) cardiomyopathy - distinct acute presentation with apical ballooning, often resolving (p.2019) Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) - overlaps with proposed obesity and diabetic cardiomyopathy (p.2018) Viral myocarditis (coxsackie, adenovirus, COVID-19, influenza, HIV) progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy (p.2015-2016) Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) and other parasitic infection (toxoplasmosis, trypanosomiasis) (p.2016) Bacterial (diphtheria), spirochetal (Lyme disease - Borrelia burgdorferi), rickettsial (Q fever), and fungal myocarditis (p.2016) Echocardiography (initial imaging modality to define morphology and function) (p.2002) Cardiac MRI for myocardial tissue characterization, late gadolinium enhancement patterns of fibrosis, and T1/T2 mapping for focal/diffuse inflammation (note: avoid gadolinium in pregnancy) (p.2002, 2018) Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph (p.2003) Chemistry including sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, glucose/glycohemoglobin, renal and liver function, lipids, thyroid-stimulating hormone, serum iron and transferrin saturation, urinalysis, creatine kinase isoforms, cardiac troponin (p.2003) Hematology including CBC with differential, eosinophil count, ESR (p.2003) Genetic counseling and multigene cardiomyopathy panel (p.2003) Targeted infectious work-up when suspected (HIV, Chagas', Lyme, toxoplasmosis, trichinosis); rheumatologic serologies (p.2003) Endomyocardial biopsy (including electron microscopy) when a specific diagnosis with therapeutic implications is suspected (p.2003) Coronary angiography in patients with evidence of ischemia/infarction who are candidates for intervention (p.2003) Granulomatous inflammatory disease - sarcoidosis (often regional wall-motion abnormality, DCM phenotype, or RV involvement) and giant cell myocarditis (p.2002, 2016) Eosinophilic myocarditis / Loeffler endocarditis (can progress to restrictive physiology) (p.2015-2016) Collagen vascular / connective tissue disease, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2015-2016) Immune checkpoint-inhibitor myocarditis (most dramatic noninfectious inflammatory myocarditis) (p.2016) Hemochromatosis / iron overload (variably classified as metabolic or restrictive but often presents as DCM) (p.2018-2019) Endocrinopathy - thyroid disease, pheochromocytoma; very-high-renin states (renal artery stenosis) (p.2017-2018) Nutritional deficiency - thiamine (beriberi), selenium (Keshan's disease), carnitine, calcium, phosphate (p.2018) DCM is defined by decreased left ventricular systolic function, typically with increased LV dimensions, although dilation may be minimal in some cases (p.2015). Quantitatively, DCM is defined when LVEF is <=0.50, but most clinical presentations occur with LVEF <=0.40; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD (p.2001-2002). Despite multiple etiologies and variable initial presentations, DCM often progresses into a convergent clinical phenotype similar to that following acute myocardial infarction, with myocyte death, apoptosis, compensatory hypertrophy, and neurohormonal activation (p.2015). Mitral regurgitation commonly develops as the ventricle dilates and the valvular apparatus is distorted, and is commonly moderate to severe by the time heart failure is advanced (p.2015). Right ventricular dilation and dysfunction may result directly from the initial injury but more often develop later from elevated afterload due to secondary pulmonary hypertension and mechanical interaction with the failing LV (p.2015). Alcohol is the most common toxin implicated in chronic DCM, but alcoholic cardiomyopathy is relatively rare and remains a diagnosis of exclusion; atrial fibrillation occurs commonly both early ('holiday heart') and in advanced stages (p.2016). Truncating variants in TTN and other DCM disease genes can be found in about 10% of patients with presumed alcohol cardiomyopathy and about 15% of peripartum cardiomyopathy, indicating that environmental triggers can unmask genetic predisposition (p.2016-2017). Chemotherapy agents are the most common drugs implicated in toxic cardiomyopathy; doxorubicin cardiotoxicity generally does NOT cause marked LV dilation, so stroke volume and perfusion can be low with only a modest fall in ejection fraction (p.2016). Tests of thyroid function are part of the routine evaluation of cardiomyopathy because clinical signs of thyroid disease may be masked; hyperthyroidism should always be considered with new-onset atrial fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia (p.2017). Heritability is present in at least 30% of DCM without other clear etiology, and expanded genetic testing reveals pathogenic variants sufficient to cause cardiomyopathy in 20-40% of DCM patients (p.2003, 2013). Sudden cardiac death risk: ventricular arrhythmias may be presenting events; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD (p.2001-2002, 2002) Embolic events from atrial fibrillation or apical LV thrombi can be the first presentation (p.2002) Peripartum cardiomyopathy with LVEF <0.35 carries higher risk of life-threatening arrhythmias at presentation and early after discharge, and marked dilation/LVEF <0.35 raises LV thrombus and embolic risk (p.2017-2018) Acute cardiac presentation (elevated troponin, conduction blocks, bizarre arrhythmias) in a patient on immune checkpoint inhibitors warrants immediate coronary-care-unit admission and high-dose glucocorticoids without delay for biopsy (p.2016) Hyperthyroidism combined with heart failure is a dangerous combination that may decompensate precipitously and fatally during titration of antithyroid therapy (p.2017) 'Congestive heart failure' should NOT be considered a diagnosis or an etiology of cardiomyopathy - it is a nonspecific syndrome of congestion common to many cardiac diagnoses and requires thorough etiologic evaluation (p.2002). Phenotypes overlap and evolve over time (DCM can reverse-remodel to higher EF; HCM can evolve to reduced EF), so reliance on a single morphologic phenotype is diminishing (p.2001-2002). Alcoholic cardiomyopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion, and many patients are fully functional without apparent stigmata of alcoholism (p.2016). Anthracycline cardiotoxicity can produce low stroke volume/perfusion with only modestly reduced EF because marked LV dilation is usually absent (p.2016). In peripartum cardiomyopathy, edema and dyspnea may be mistakenly attributed to pregnancy itself; renin-angiotensin system inhibitors should NOT be given before delivery due to adverse fetal effects, and gadolinium should NOT be used on MRI during pregnancy (p.2017-2018). Detection of anticardiac antibodies and viral genome fragments in chronic cardiomyopathy is of uncertain significance (possible cause vs neutral bystander) and is not in routine clinical use (p.2013). Immunosuppression for nonspecific chronic lymphocytic myocarditis has not demonstrated convincing benefit (p.2013). DCM is characterized by decreased LV systolic function, typically with LV chamber dilation (LVEF <=0.50, usually <=0.40 at presentation). Multiple causes (idiopathic, familial/genetic, prior myocarditis, ischaemic, toxic/alcohol, chemotherapy, peripartum, tachycardia-mediated, metabolic/endocrine) converge on a common phenotype resembling post-infarct injury: early myocyte death, later apoptosis, and compensatory hypertrophy of remaining myocytes in response to increased wall stress. Local and circulating neurohormonal factors drive deleterious secondary remodeling; dynamic remodeling of the interstitial scaffold affects diastolic function and the degree of dilation. As the ventricle dilates, the mitral valve apparatus is distorted, producing functional mitral regurgitation. RV dilation/dysfunction develops directly from injury or, more often, secondarily from pulmonary hypertension and ventricular interaction. Chronic inflammation contributes to progression even when not initially implicated, and many 'acute' presentations have progressed silently over months to years (Harrison 22e p.2015). DCM secondary responses are often modifiable or reversible. Almost a third of patients with recent-onset cardiomyopathy without coronary artery disease show substantial spontaneous recovery to normal ejection fraction, and partial recovery to LVEF >0.40 ('heart failure with improved ejection fraction') is common with guideline-directed neurohormonal therapy, CRT for LBBB, and diuretics. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy can improve markedly within 3-6 months of abstinence but has a grim prognosis if heavy drinking continues. In peripartum cardiomyopathy, LVEF improves to >=0.50 in 50-80% of cases (often within 6 months); recovery is less likely with LVEF <0.30, LV end-diastolic dimension >=0.60, black race, and presentation >6 weeks postpartum; U.S. 1-year mortality ranged 4-11% and up to twofold higher in Africa. Takotsubo syndrome has a generally good long-term prognosis (lowest mortality with emotional rather than physical triggers) but in-hospital complications/mortality resemble acute MI, with ~10% recurrence (Harrison 22e p.2002, 2016-2019). Classification of cardiomyopathies: DCM phenotype - Early: LVEF <=0.50 and/or LVEDV >112% normal for age/sex or LVEDD >95% predicted for sex/height; LVEF <=0.40 is the threshold for traditional heart-failure therapies for low LVEF; persistent LVEF <=0.30-0.35 is the threshold for primary-prevention ICD. Mid-range LVEF 0.40-0.50 is often a transitional state (deterioration from early DCM or improvement into DCM remission). DCM is distinguished from HCM (increased wall thickness, septal >=15 mm men / >=13 mm women, LVEF >=normal usually >0.60), RCM (functional diagnosis from diastolic dysfunction/elevated filling pressures, often marked atrial enlargement), and arrhythmogenic CM (ACM-LV/ACM-RV/ARVC, ventricular arrhythmias dominating). (Harrison 22e p.2001-2002).

Diphtheria — Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (exudative, but its exudate is not tightly adherent unlike the diphtheritic pseudomembrane) (p.1223) Group C streptococcal pharyngitis (p.1223) Respiratory virus pharyngitis (rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, coronavirus, adenovirus) (p.1223) Herpes simplex virus and Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis) pharyngitis (p.1223) Atypical bacterial pharyngitis (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae) (p.1223) Acute HIV infection, gonococcal pharyngitis, and fusobacterial infection / Lemierre's syndrome (p.1223) Candida (thrush) pharyngitis (p.1223) Corynebacterium ulcerans / C. pseudotuberculosis, which express the same toxin and cause diphtheria-like disease (p.1222) Culture of pseudomembrane fragments or submembranous swabs on selective medium (Loffler's or Tinsdale's, tellurite/colistin/nalidixic-acid based) plus nonselective medium such as blood agar (p.1223-1224) Histopathologic demonstration of compatible gram-positive organisms / characteristic local lesions (p.1223-1224) Notify the laboratory that diphtheria is being considered so special selective medium and biochemical differentiation from commensal corynebacteria are performed (p.1224) Toxigenicity testing; report all toxigenic C. diphtheriae isolates to the state health department (reportable disease) (p.1224) Nasopharyngeal culture in patients with cutaneous diphtheria (p.1224) Repeat throat culture ~2 weeks after completing antimicrobial therapy to document eradication (p.1224) Cardiac workup to assess for myocarditis (p.1225) Antitoxin (antibody) titer measurement after recovery, performed 6 months after antitoxin administration (p.1224) Respiratory diphtheria is clinically diagnosed by the constellation of sore throat, adherent tonsillar/pharyngeal/nasal pseudomembranous lesions, and low-grade fever (p.1223). The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is gray or whitish and sharply demarcated; unlike the exudate of streptococcal pharyngitis it is tightly adherent to underlying tissue, and attempts to dislodge it may cause bleeding (p.1223). A few patients develop 'bull-neck' diphtheria from edema of the submandibular and paratracheal region, with massive tonsillar swelling, foul breath, thick speech, and stridorous breathing (p.1223). Diphtheria should be considered in any patient with severe pharyngitis, especially with difficulty swallowing, respiratory compromise, or signs of systemic disease (myocarditis, generalized weakness); a pharyngeal pseudomembrane or extensive exudate should prompt consideration (p.1222-1223). Toxigenic strains most often cause pharyngeal disease, while nontoxigenic strains commonly cause cutaneous disease; in tropical latitudes cutaneous diphtheria is more common than respiratory diphtheria (p.1221-1222). Once a clinical diagnosis is made, diphtheria antitoxin should be obtained and administered as rapidly as possible because antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin (p.1224). Hoarseness suggests laryngeal diphtheria, in which laryngoscopy may be diagnostically helpful (p.1223). Antibiotics in diphtheria are used primarily to prevent transmission to contacts and to halt further toxin production; they are not a substitute for antitoxin (p.1224). Patients who recover should be vaccinated, since natural infection does not reliably confer protective immunity; antitoxin levels should be measured (6 months after antitoxin administration) (p.1224). Neck (submandibular/paratracheal) edema and difficulty breathing in advanced cases carry a poor prognosis (p.1223) Airway obstruction is a major early risk and accounts for 60-65% of deaths, usually in the first 1-2 weeks; sloughing pseudomembranes may obstruct the airway or extend to larynx/tracheobronchial tree (children especially prone) (p.1224) Toxic cardiomyopathy/myocarditis (cardiac arrhythmias or congestive heart failure), a late manifestation arising >=1 week after respiratory symptoms, accounting for 20-25% of deaths (p.1223-1224) Bull-neck diphtheria, ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or complete heart block (p.1224) Polyneuropathy 3-5 weeks after onset: cranial nerve involvement (lingual/facial numbness, dysphonia, dysphagia), then weakness of respiratory and abdominal muscles, limb paresis, sensory ataxia, and autonomic dysfunction with hypotension (~15% of deaths) (p.1224) Large or extensive pseudomembranes and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement indicate severe disease and poor prognosis (p.1223-1224) Antitoxin cannot neutralize cell-bound toxin, so delay in administration worsens outcome; do not wait for laboratory confirmation once diphtheria is clinically suspected (p.1224). Antibiotics are not a substitute for antitoxin; they mainly prevent transmission and further toxin production (p.1224). Glucocorticoids have NOT been shown to reduce the risk of myocarditis or polyneuropathy (p.1225). Cutaneous diphtheria lesions are not characteristic and are indistinguishable from other dermatoses, so diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation; the punched-out appearance is only occasional, not consistent (p.1224). Corynebacterium pseudodiphtheriticum is a nontoxigenic normal throat commensal and does not pose significant risk; it must be differentiated from C. diphtheriae (p.1224). Drug-resistant and multidrug-resistant C. diphtheriae strains exist and are increasing; consider resistance when eradication efforts fail (p.1224). Natural infection does not reliably confer immunity, so survivors must be vaccinated (p.1224). Disease is driven by diphtheria toxin produced by toxigenic (tox+) strains of C. diphtheriae. The tox structural gene is carried by lysogenic corynebacteriophage beta, and nontoxigenic strains can be converted to the toxigenic phenotype; iron-limiting conditions optimize toxin expression. The toxin is a single-chain 535-amino-acid protein produced in the pharyngeal pseudomembranous lesion, taken up into the bloodstream and distributed to all organs. After binding its receptor (a heparin-binding EGF-like precursor) it is internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis; the A fragment enters the cytosol and irreversibly inhibits protein synthesis via NAD+-dependent ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2, causing cell death. Pseudomembranes consist of an inner fibrin band and a luminal neutrophil band overlying toxin-induced mucosal ulcers with edema, hyperemia, and vascular congestion; initially white and firmly adherent, they turn gray/green/black as necrosis advances and may extend into bronchial airways (p.1221-1223). A systematic review of >20 outbreaks found a case-fatality ratio of 29% among unvaccinated, untreated individuals, with children under 5 at 1.5-fold higher mortality risk. Fatal pseudomembranous diphtheria typically occurs in unimmunized patients or those with nonprotective antibody titers. Risk factors for death include bull-neck diphtheria; myocarditis with ventricular tachycardia; atrial fibrillation; complete heart block; age >60 or <6 months; alcoholism; extensive pseudomembrane elongation; and laryngeal/tracheal/bronchial involvement. A key predictor of fatal outcome is the interval between onset of local disease and administration of antitoxin. Cutaneous diphtheria has a low mortality rate and is rarely associated with myocarditis or peripheral neuropathy. Polyneuropathy is typically reversible in patients who survive the acute phase (p.1224-1225). CDC case definitions: confirmed respiratory diphtheria (laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked to a culture-confirmed case) vs probable respiratory diphtheria (clinically compatible but not laboratory proven or epidemiologically linked). Carriers are individuals with positive C. diphtheriae cultures who are asymptomatic or symptomatic but lack pseudomembranes (p.1223).
