Non-healing, ulcerated, or enlarging chronic plaque (particularly on the lip) suggesting squamous cell carcinoma Emergence of systemic symptoms (arthralgia, renal, haematological, or constitutional features) indicating progression to systemic lupus Rapidly progressive scalp involvement threatening permanent scarring alopecia Features suggesting overlap with other connective tissue disease Significant disfigurement causing psychological distress that needs support Failing to counsel on photoprotection and smoking cessation, both of which strongly influence outcome Attributing scarring alopecia to other causes and delaying treatment until hair loss is irreversible Not screening for systemic lupus or overlooking its later emergence Missing malignant transformation within a chronic plaque Underestimating the cosmetic and psychological burden of facial scarring Discoid lupus erythematosus is a chronic autoimmune interface dermatitis in which ultraviolet light and other triggers provoke keratinocyte injury and expose nuclear antigens. A cytotoxic lymphocytic response targets the basal epidermis, producing vacuolar degeneration at the dermo-epidermal junction, follicular plugging, basement-membrane thickening, and a perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate. Immune complex and complement deposition at the junction can be demonstrated on direct immunofluorescence. Sustained inflammation destroys adnexal structures, leading to the scarring, atrophy, and permanent alopecia characteristic of established lesions. Genetic predisposition, ultraviolet exposure, and smoking all contribute. Skin-limited discoid lupus often follows a chronic relapsing course; with photoprotection and treatment many lesions become inactive, but scarring, dyspigmentation, and alopecia may be permanent, and a minority of patients evolve towards systemic lupus, warranting periodic review.

with serotyping and Shiga toxin testing to identify O157 STEC Scombroid (fish) poisoning, in which Proteus-mediated histamine generation in spoiled fish produces a histamine-toxicity syndrome rather than infection Adherent-invasive E. coli associated with Crohn disease (causal role unproven; does not produce acute diarrheal illness) The enteric gram-negative bacilli (GNB) that most often cause extraintestinal infection belong to the order Enterobacterales and include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, Serratia, Citrobacter, Morganella, Providencia, Cronobacter, and Edwardsiella; Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia are covered separately as mainly enteric pathogens. Isolation of a GNB from a normally sterile site almost always signifies true infection, whereas recovery from nonsterile sites (open wounds, respiratory tract, catheterized urine) needs clinical correlation because it may represent only colonization. E. coli and, to a lesser extent, Klebsiella are the most virulent of this group and can cause severe disease even in previously healthy ambulatory people; the other genera behave mainly as opportunists in long-term-care and hospitalized patients. The urinary tract is the single most common extraintestinal site infected by extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC), and E. coli is the leading uropathogen across essentially all UTI syndromes and host groups. The urinary tract is also the most common source of E. coli bacteremia (roughly one-half to two-thirds of episodes); the abdomen is the second most common source (about one-quarter), and some abdominal sources such as abscesses can be clinically silent and require imaging. E. coli and group B Streptococcus are leading causes of neonatal meningitis; most neonatal E. coli meningitis strains carry the K1 capsular antigen, and ventriculomegaly is a common complication. Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp), first recognized in Taiwan in 1986, classically presents as community-acquired monomicrobial pyogenic liver abscess in patients without prior hepatobiliary disease, often diabetic, with a striking tendency to spread metastatically (e.g., endophthalmitis, brain/splenic/prostatic abscess, meningitis, necrotizing fasciitis). Proteus produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea to ammonia and alkalinizes the urine; this promotes struvite and carbonate-apatite crystals, catheter biofilms, and staghorn calculi, and the organism typically cannot be cleared without removing the stone or catheter. Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are classified by CDC and WHO as an urgent, critical-priority threat and were estimated to cause more than 100,000 deaths globally in 2019, with the heaviest burden in low- and middle-income regions such as the Indian subcontinent. Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock arising from any GNB focus are especially dangerous, carrying reported mortality rates of about 20 to 60 percent. Serratia marcescens is notable for environmental and outbreak associations (contaminated infusates, prefilled syringes, soaps, even chlorhexidine); some strains produce red pigment that can cause distinctive findings such as pink breast milk, pink hypopyon, or pseudohemoptysis. In children with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC) infection, antibiotics should be avoided because they may increase the risk of hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS), and adequate volume expansion may help protect the kidneys. foreign bodies), without which antimicrobial therapy often fails Empirical reliance on fluoroquinolones in critically ill patients, which is now unreliable given widespread GNB resistance often linked to ESBL production Enteric GNB are predominantly extracellular pathogens that normally reside in the colonic microbiota and environmental niches. Their outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide and capsule) is central both to virulence and to antimicrobial resistance via permeability barriers and efflux pumps. Disease requires accessory virulence genes: multiple adhesins (e.g., type 1, S, and F1C fimbriae and P pili in E. coli) for attachment; iron-acquisition systems (siderophores) and other nutrient-scavenging tools; capsule and O-antigen to resist complement and phagocytosis in the absence of antibody; and toxins (e.g., E. coli hemolysin) that cause tissue damage facilitating spread. The lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide acts as a PAMP that, through pattern-recognition receptors, can trigger an exuberant proinflammatory cascade leading to septic shock, with DAMPs such as HMGB1 propagating injury. Extensive antigenic variation (E. coli alone has more than 150 O, ~80 K, and ~53 H antigens) permits immune evasion and repeated infection and has hampered vaccine development. Host defenses are innate (intact skin/mucosa, complement, antimicrobial peptides, phagocytes, nutrient withholding) and humoral; impairment of these increases both susceptibility and severity. Intestinal pathogenic E. coli use distinct, pathotype-specific mechanisms (Shiga toxin, heat-stable/labile enterotoxins, attaching-and-effacing lesions, epithelial invasion, aggregative adherence). Outcomes correlate with severity of illness, underlying host status, and the resistance profile of the infecting organism, which can lead to suboptimal therapy. Pneumonia, sepsis, and septic shock from any GNB focus carry mortality rates of roughly 20 to 60 percent; ExPEC pneumonia specifically has high crude (20-60%) and attributable (10-20%) mortality. Uncomplicated cystitis is largely self-limited and rarely progresses, whereas pyelonephritis can take 5-7 days for fever to resolve even with effective therapy and only uncommonly causes renal parenchymal loss (mainly with obstruction). hvKp infections can be life- and organ-threatening even in young healthy hosts, with survivors often left with catastrophic sequelae such as vision loss or major neurologic deficits. Pandrug-resistant strains exist, and extensive resistance can leave few or no ideal therapeutic options. Disease is stratified clinically rather than by a single formal score: localized/uncomplicated infection (e.g., uncomplicated cystitis with dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain) versus systemic/severe infection (febrile or systemic UTI/urosepsis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis syndrome defined as dysfunction of at least one organ/system, and septic shock). Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pandrug-resistant; resistance mechanisms range from broad-spectrum beta-lactamases through ESBLs and AmpC enzymes to carbapenemases (Ambler class A serine [KPC], class B metallo-beta-lactamases [NDM, VIM, IMP], and class D [OXA-48]).

the clinical history is central to evaluation (Harrison 22e p.2503). Dysphagia for both liquids and solids suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia, whereas dysphagia for solids alone suggests a structural lesion (stricture, web, ring, or tumor) (Harrison 22e p.2504). Patient localization of where food 'hangs up' is notoriously imprecise; about 30% of distal esophageal obstructions are perceived as cervical (neck) dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.2504). Intermittent solid-food dysphagia that is unchanged or slowly progressive over years points to a benign process (Schatzki ring or eosinophilic esophagitis), whereas dysphagia progressing over weeks to months raises concern for neoplasia (Harrison 22e p.295). Odynophagia is uncommon with reflux esophagitis; its presence should raise suspicion of an alternative etiology, particularly pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.2505, p.2513). Achalasia is diagnosed by barium swallow and/or esophageal manometry; the barium study shows a dilated esophagus with poor emptying, an air-fluid level, and a tapered 'beak-like' narrowing at the LES (Harrison 22e p.2507). Manometric hallmarks of achalasia are impaired (incomplete) deglutitive LES relaxation plus absent peristalsis; manometry is the most sensitive test as it detects disease before esophageal dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508). Endoscopy is a necessary part of the achalasia evaluation to exclude pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration at the cardia/distal esophagus, which accounts for up to 5% of suspected cases (Harrison 22e p.2507). The GERD injury spectrum progresses from esophagitis to stricture to Barrett metaplasia to adenocarcinoma; esophageal adenocarcinoma incidence is rising in parallel with GERD (Harrison 22e p.2509). Erosive esophagitis at the esophagogastric junction is the endoscopic hallmark of GERD but is found in only about one-third of GERD patients (Harrison 22e p.2510). Eosinophilic esophagitis should be strongly considered in children and adults presenting with dysphagia and food impaction, especially with an atopic history (Harrison 22e p.2511). EoE is confirmed histologically by esophageal mucosal eosinophilia with a peak density of 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, in the setting of esophageal symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2512). Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss - classic presentation of esophageal cancer; warrants prompt endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2507). Odynophagia (painful swallowing) - usually indicates ulceration; raises suspicion of pill-induced or infectious esophagitis (Harrison 22e p.295, p.2513). Iron-deficiency anemia / chronic occult GI bleeding accompanying esophageal symptoms. Hoarseness developing after dysphagia - may indicate recurrent laryngeal nerve compromise by malignancy (Harrison 22e p.295). Abrupt onset of symptoms (<1 year), advanced age, and weight loss in apparent achalasia - suggests pseudoachalasia from malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2507). Food impaction with inability to pass a bolus even with liquids - typical of structural dysphagia (Harrison 22e p.295). Severe cough with swallowing - may signal tracheoesophageal fistula. Finding of high-grade dysplasia in Barrett esophagus - high rate of progression to and coexisting prevalence of adenocarcinoma; mandates intervention (Harrison 22e p.2511). Treating presumed GERD empirically without recognizing that persistent dysphagia or chest pain may instead reflect eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic stricture, motility disorder, esophageal cancer, or coronary artery disease (Harrison 22e p.2510). Attributing 'heartburn' to GERD when the term is misused for indigestion or other sensations - clarify the patient's meaning (Harrison 22e p.2503). Assuming neck-localized dysphagia is oropharyngeal - about 30% of distal esophageal lesions refer pain proximally (Harrison 22e p.2504). Mistaking pseudoachalasia (tumor infiltration, up to 5% of cases) for primary achalasia - omit endoscopy at peril (Harrison 22e p.2507). Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm before excluding the more common peptic and infectious esophagitis and, above all, cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2509). Aggressive esophageal dilation in EoE - the stiff-walled esophagus risks deep mural laceration or perforation (Harrison 22e p.2512). Relying on peripheral blood eosinophilia (present in only 25-50%) or allergy testing (poor sensitivity/specificity) to diagnose EoE or identify trigger foods (Harrison 22e p.2512). Over-interpreting nonspecific minor manometric findings (hypertensive/hypotensive peristalsis) as a defined motility disorder; reflux and anxiety/depression are common in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2509). The esophagus is a muscular tube with a sphincter at each end (UES, LES) that transports food and otherwise remains empty. Disease manifests as impaired function (swallowing disorders, excessive gastroesophageal reflux) or pain. Dysphagia is subclassified by mechanism: structural/mechanical narrowing (lumen <13 mm reliably causes solid-food dysphagia) versus propulsive/motor disorders of peristalsis and deglutitive inhibition. In achalasia, autoimmune-mediated loss of myenteric plexus ganglion cells (involving both excitatory cholinergic and inhibitory nitric-oxide neurons), linked to latent HSV-1 infection plus genetic susceptibility, produces impaired deglutitive LES relaxation and absent peristalsis. GERD results from excessive reflux of gastric acid and pepsin causing a cytokine-mediated (rather than directly caustic) inflammatory mucosal injury; pathologic reflux follows progressive distortion of esophagogastric junction architecture (hiatus widening, loss of intraabdominal esophageal segment/flap valve, axial hiatal hernia, increased junction compliance) compounded by impaired acid clearance from disrupted peristalsis or reduced salivation. Eosinophilic esophagitis is an immunologic disorder driven by antigen (chiefly food allergen) sensitization in susceptible individuals, with eosinophil-predominant inflammation. (Harrison 22e p.2503, p.2506-2510, p.2511) Esophageal cancer carries poor survival even when small because abundant esophageal lymphatics permit early regional nodal metastasis. Barrett metaplasia progresses to adenocarcinoma at an estimated 0.1-0.3% per year through low- and high-grade dysplasia, with greatest risk in obese white males in the sixth decade. Untreated achalasia predisposes to stasis esophagitis and increases squamous cell cancer risk roughly 17-fold; durable therapies (pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, POEM) achieve symptom relief in about 80-90% of patients, though peristalsis does not recover and chest pain responds less well than dysphagia. EoE is chronic with nearly universal recurrence on stopping therapy, requiring maintenance treatment. Erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become increasingly rare in the era of potent acid suppression. (Harrison 22e p.2507-2508, p.2510-2512) GERD esophageal injury spectrum: esophagitis -> stricture -> Barrett metaplasia -> adenocarcinoma; reflux testing defines GERD as esophageal pH <4 for >6% of the day. Barrett progression staged histologically as no dysplasia -> low-grade dysplasia -> high-grade dysplasia -> adenocarcinoma. High-resolution manometry differentiates three achalasia subtypes: type I classic (minimal esophageal-body pressurization), type II with esophageal compression/pressurization, and type III spastic achalasia. EoE histologic threshold: peak >=15 eosinophils per high-power field. (Harrison 22e p.2508-2511)

screening tool) Blood cultures (frequently positive in mycotic aneurysm and infective aortitis) ESR and C-reactive protein (elevated in active Takayasu and other aortitides) Genetic testing in ascending thoracic aortic disease with features of Marfan/Loeys-Dietz/vascular Ehlers-Danlos or presentation under age 60 Takayasu arteritis (large-vessel vasculitis, 'pulseless disease') Giant cell arteritis with aortic involvement IgG4-related aortitis with retroperitoneal fibrosis Isolated aortitis Rheumatic aortitis (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and other HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, relapsing polychondritis, IBD-associated) Behcet syndrome and Cogan syndrome Connective-tissue aortopathies (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos) and fibromuscular dysplasia The aorta is uniquely prone to aneurysm and rupture because, per Laplace's law, wall tension rises with the product of pressure and radius, so dilation begets further dilation; normal adult diameters are roughly 3.5 cm at origin/ascending, 2.5 cm in descending thoracic, and 1.8-2.0 cm in the abdomen. True aneurysms involve all three wall layers; pseudoaneurysms have disrupted intima and media, with the dilated segment contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Aneurysms are described as fusiform (whole circumference) or saccular (focal outpouching). A contemporary threshold for an aneurysm of the aortic root/ascending aorta is diameter >=4.5 cm, while 4.0-4.4 cm is termed aortic dilation; descending thoracic and abdominal aneurysms are defined when dilated >=50% beyond the adjacent normal segment. Medial degeneration (loss of medial smooth muscle and breakdown of collagen/elastin with mucoid/proteoglycan clefts) preferentially affects the proximal aorta and underlies ascending aneurysms in Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve, Turner, and familial thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes; atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of descending thoracic and abdominal aneurysms. Thoracic aortic aneurysms grow on average about 0.1-0.2 cm/year and are usually asymptomatic; symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hoarseness, dysphagia) arise from compression/erosion, and ascending dilation can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure. Aortic dissection classically presents with sudden, severe, tearing chest or interscapular pain with diaphoresis that migrates as the dissection propagates; complications include syncope, pulse deficits, acute aortic regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and end-organ ischemia (stroke, paraplegia, bowel/renal/myocardial ischemia). Stanford type A dissection involves the ascending aorta; type B is limited to arch and/or descending aorta. The type A/B scheme is more practical for management than the DeBakey I/II/III classification because DeBakey I and II are managed similarly. Acute aortic regurgitation complicates more than 50% of proximal (type A) dissections, producing bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, and a diastolic murmur along the right sternal border; retrograde type A dissection can cause hemopericardium and tamponade. Intramural hematoma (rupture of the vasa vasorum, no intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer are dissection variants, mostly in the descending thoracic aorta, and either can progress to dissection, false aneurysm, or rupture. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are more common in men, increase with age, and at least 90% of those >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic and infrarenal; they are usually silent and found as a pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass, while new aneurysmal pain is a harbinger of impending rupture. An ECG without ischemic changes helps distinguish aortic dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain; rarely the dissection involves a coronary ostium (usually right) and causes acute MI. Acute occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta is an emergency threatening limb viability, usually from a cardiac-origin saddle embolus, presenting with rest pain, coolness, pallor, and bilaterally absent distal pulses. Aortic occlusive disease from atherosclerosis is typically infrarenal and, when extending to the iliacs, can cause Leriche syndrome (buttock/thigh/calf claudication with impotence in men) and absent femoral pulses with an abdominal bruit. Sudden severe tearing/migrating chest or interscapular pain with diaphoresis (acute dissection) Acute hypotension or shock suggesting rupture or tamponade New aortic regurgitation murmur, pulse deficits, or blood-pressure differential between limbs Neurologic deficits (hemiplegia, paraplegia) indicating carotid or spinal cord ischemia New or worsening aneurysmal pain (back, flank, scrotum) as a harbinger of AAA rupture Acute limb ischemia with bilaterally absent distal pulses (acute aortic occlusion) Fever, sepsis, and aortic/back pain with positive blood cultures (mycotic aneurysm/infective aortitis) A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and reactive, NOT necessarily a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and falling hematocrit. About 25% of abdominal aortic aneurysms are not calcified and cannot be seen on plain x-ray, so a normal radiograph does not exclude an AAA. Mural thrombus can reduce the luminal diameter, so contrast aortography may underestimate true aneurysm size. Isolated direct vasodilators such as hydralazine are contraindicated in acute dissection because they raise hydraulic shear and heart rate and can propagate the dissection. Transthoracic and even transesophageal echocardiography are relatively poor at imaging the aortic arch, a potential blind spot for dissection. Serum IgG4 levels may be elevated but are not diagnostic of IgG4-related aortitis. With adequate collateral flow, complete abdominal aortic occlusion can occur without ischemic symptoms, masking the severity of occlusive disease. Genetic/heritable aortopathies warrant lower size thresholds for intervention; applying standard atherosclerotic thresholds risks under-treatment. The aortic wall comprises a thin endothelial intima, a thick smooth muscle/elastin/collagen tunica media, and a connective-tissue adventitia carrying the vasa vasorum. Continuous high pulsatile pressure and shear stress predispose it to injury. Aneurysms result from degradation or abnormal production of structural elastin and collagen; degenerative (most common, atherosclerosis-associated) aneurysms involve inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis (B/T lymphocytes, macrophages, cytokines, matrix metalloproteinases) and biomechanical stress, with histology showing elastin/collagen destruction, reduced smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation. Heritable aneurysms reflect medial degeneration: fibrillin-1 deficiency (FBN1 mutation in Marfan) impairs elastic-fiber microfibrils and increases TGF-beta signaling, while Loeys-Dietz arises from mutations in TGF-beta isoforms/receptors and SMAD3; vascular Ehlers-Danlos involves COL3A1 (type III procollagen) mutations. Dissection begins with an intimal tear (often the right lateral ascending aorta or just below the ligamentum arteriosum) or medial hemorrhage, with pulsatile flow splitting the elastic lamellae to create a false lumen that usually propagates distally. Aortitis is inflammation of the wall (vasculitic, rheumatic, or infective) that may produce aneurysmal dilation, aortic regurgitation, or branch occlusion. Rupture risk rises with aneurysm size and symptoms: thoracic aneurysms carry roughly 2-3%/year rupture risk below 4.0 cm rising to about 7%/year above 6 cm; for abdominal aneurysms the 5-year rupture risk is about 1-2% under 5 cm versus 20-40% above 5 cm. Marfan and certain Loeys-Dietz/nonsyndromic familial aortopathies dissect at smaller diameters and expand faster. Elective AAA surgery with careful evaluation carries about 1-2% operative mortality, whereas emergent repair after rupture carries roughly 45-50% mortality. For dissection, in-hospital mortality is about 15-25% after type A surgery and around 12% for medically managed type B; with careful follow-up the 10-year survival after treated dissection is approximately 60%, though Marfan patients remain at high risk for post-dissection complications. Aortic dissection: Stanford type A (involves ascending aorta, proximal) vs type B (arch and/or descending only, distal); DeBakey type I (ascending with propagation to arch/descending/abdominal), type II (limited to ascending), type III (descending with distal propagation). Type A/B is preferred for management decisions. Acute aortic syndromes encompass aortic rupture, dissection, intramural hematoma, and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer.

thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy (risk of epidural hematoma) or through tissue overlying an epidural abscess (risk of seeding meningitis) -- a high cervical tap may be safer Overlooking copper deficiency (with normal B12) as a cause of a subacute-combined-degeneration-like myelopathy, particularly after bariatric surgery or with excess zinc intake The spinal cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-sectional area, so focal lesions produce disproportionately severe deficits (quadriplegia, paraplegia, sensory loss). Peripherally located white matter tracts carry ascending sensory (posterior columns for position/vibration, spinothalamic for pain/temperature) and descending motor (corticospinal) pathways, while gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies. The crossing pattern of the spinothalamic tract (decussating anterior to the central canal one to two segments above entry) and the same-side course of the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts generate the characteristic clinical syndromes. The cord is supplied by a single anterior spinal artery (anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries (posterior columns); a watershed zone in the upper thoracic cord makes T3-T4 vulnerable to infarction during hypotension or aortic cross-clamping. Disease mechanisms are grouped into compressive (tumor, abscess, hematoma, disk, spondylosis), vascular/ischemic, inflammatory/immune (MS, NMO, sarcoid, systemic autoimmune), infectious/postinfectious, metabolic/nutritional (B12, copper deficiency), developmental (syringomyelia, tethered cord), and degenerative/genetic categories. Many spinal cord diseases are reversible if recognized and treated early, making them among the most critical neurologic emergencies. For neoplastic compression, ambulatory status at presentation predicts a good outcome; motor deficits established for more than 12 hours rarely improve, and beyond 48 hours the prognosis for substantial motor recovery is poor. With prompt diagnosis and treatment of spinal epidural abscess, up to two-thirds of patients achieve significant recovery, but fixed deficits more than several days old are unlikely to reverse. After cord infarction, severe motor weakness and persistent areflexia predict poor recovery, though more than half of patients in one series regained some ambulation. The prospects for recovery from an acute destructive lesion fade after about 6 months, and there are currently no effective means to repair injured cord tissue. Even complete high cervical lesions can be compatible with a productive life; ultimate disability is determined chiefly by lesion level and whether the deficit is complete or incomplete. Functional outcome after complete cord lesions is stratified by level (Harrison Table 453-4): high quadriplegia (C1-C4) -- dependent on others, requires respiratory support, motorized wheelchair; low quadriplegia (C5-C8) -- partially independent with adaptive equipment, may use a manual wheelchair and drive with adaptations; paraplegia (below T1) -- independent in self-care and transfers, ambulates short distances with aids. Lesions are also characterized clinically as complete versus incomplete, and intramedullary versus extramedullary (and extradural versus intradural, the former generally malignant and the latter benign).

Staphylococcus/Streptococcus) Complete blood count (assess hemorrhage, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia) Blood type and cross-match Renal and hepatic function panels Coagulation studies: prothrombin time and fibrinogen level; fibrin degradation products / D-dimer Creatine kinase for suspected rhabdomyolysis; urine for blood/myoglobin 20-minute whole-blood clotting test where laboratory access is limited Serial limb circumference measurements at three points every 15 min until local effects stabilize ECG and chest radiography in severe envenomation or significant comorbidity Intracompartmental pressure measurement if compartment syndrome suspected (threshold 30-40 mmHg) Imaging (soft-tissue radiography, ultrasound, or MRI) to locate retained marine spines/foreign bodies Repeat coagulation and CBC monitoring for recurrent coagulopathy after discharge Anaphylaxis to venom or to antivenom itself Compartment syndrome from other causes of limb swelling/trauma Primary cardiac dysrhythmia or shock from non-toxic causes Acute neuromuscular paralysis from other etiologies (e.g., botulism, Guillain-Barre) when neurotoxic envenomation presents with descending weakness Medically important venomous snakes fall into Viperidae (Old World vipers and New World/Asian pit vipers), Elapidae (cobras, kraits, coral snakes, sea snakes, Australian elapids), the burrowing asps (Atractaspidinae), and a few colubrids; snake envenomation is described as the world's deadliest neglected tropical disease, with roughly 63,000 deaths globally in 2019. A large fraction of bites are 'dry' (no venom injected) - about 20-25% of pit viper bites and up to 75% of sea snake bites - so the presence of fang marks alone does not equal envenomation. Viperid/cytotoxic patterns produce progressive local pain, soft-tissue swelling, ecchymosis, and hemorrhagic or serum-filled blisters, while neurotoxic elapids (kraits, some cobras, Australian elapids) and certain vipers cause cranial nerve dysfunction (ptosis, dysphagia) progressing to descending paralysis and respiratory failure. Onset and tempo of symptoms vary with species, bite location, and venom dose; coral snakes, sea snakes, and some non-North American vipers (e.g., hump-nosed pit viper) can have systemic effects delayed by several hours, mandating prolonged observation. In resource-limited settings the bedside 20-minute whole-blood clotting test detects venom-induced coagulopathy: 1-2 mL venous blood left undisturbed in a clean dry glass tube that fails to clot at 20 minutes indicates coagulopathy. Antivenom binds and neutralizes circulating (unbound) venom; it is largely ineffective at reversing damage already established (e.g., fixed paralysis, established renal failure) and offers little cross-protection outside the species it was raised against, so species-appropriate selection is essential. Compartment syndrome is uncommon after snakebite (fasciotomy needed in under 1% of cases); in North American crotalid bites fasciotomy lacks supporting evidence and may increase morbidity, since effective antivenom lowers compartment pressure. Recurrent or delayed coagulopathy can appear during the first 2-3 weeks after a bite because venom antigens may outlast antivenom, so patients are warned to avoid elective surgery/high-trauma activity and to have repeat coagulation testing. Long-term sequelae include permanent limb functional loss from muscle/nerve/vascular injury or scar contracture, and pituitary insufficiency described after Russell's viper (Daboia russelii) envenomation. Among marine animals, jellyfish/box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri), Portuguese man-of-war (Physalia), and the Irukandji jellyfish (Carukia barnesi) cause the most dangerous cnidarian stings; Irukandji syndrome is a catecholamine-excess state with hypertension, tachycardia, severe pain, and risk of pulmonary edema and cardiomyopathy. Blue-ringed octopus (Hapalochlaena) and pufferfish (order Tetraodontiformes, e.g., fugu) both cause tetrodotoxin toxicity - a sodium-channel blocker producing rapid flaccid paralysis with preserved mentation; consciousness is typically intact even during complete paralysis, so analgesia/sedation matter. Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning mimics an allergic reaction (flushing, urticaria, headache, palpitations) and arises when bacteria decarboxylate histidine to histamine in poorly refrigerated fish; the toxin is heat-stable and reactions are more severe in patients on isoniazid (histaminase blockade). Ciguatera, caused by heat-stable ciguatoxins (Gambierdiscus toxicus) bioaccumulated in large reef fish, classically produces GI symptoms plus neurologic features including reversal of hot/cold temperature sensation and a sensation of 'loose teeth'; neurologic symptoms can persist for weeks. Bite to the face or neck (risk of rapid airway-threatening swelling) Cranial nerve signs such as ptosis or difficulty swallowing (herald impending respiratory compromise in neurotoxic envenomation) Rapidly progressing swelling involving more than half the bitten limb, extensive blistering/bruising, or severe pain Spontaneous systemic bleeding, hemolysis, or laboratory evidence of coagulopathy Hypotension or shock unresponsive to fluids Rhabdomyolysis with falling urine output / acute renal failure Irukandji syndrome features: severe hypertension, chest/abdominal pain, then risk of pulmonary edema and cardiomyopathy Tetrodotoxin exposure (blue-ringed octopus, pufferfish): oral/facial numbness progressing to flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure Treating fang marks alone as proof of envenomation - many bites are dry and antivenom in such cases is useless and potentially harmful. Relying on color pattern, head shape, or pupil shape to judge whether a snake is venomous - nonvenomous species frequently mimic these features. Discharging a patient too early: significant toxicity from an apparently 'dry' viperid bite can develop after several hours, and elapid/sea snake/some viper systemic effects are characteristically delayed. Using outdated first aid (incision, suction, tourniquets/venom-sequestration devices) - these worsen local damage and increase infection risk; pressure-immobilization is reserved for reliably identified primarily neurotoxic species, not viperids. Relying on antivenom skin testing for hypersensitivity - it is neither sensitive nor specific; prophylactic antihistamines/glucocorticoids have not proven beneficial. Performing fasciotomy reflexively for limb swelling in North American crotalid bites - evidence does not support it and it may increase morbidity. Giving blood products before adequate antivenom - this can fuel ongoing consumptive coagulopathy. In marine cnidarian stings, applying vinegar indiscriminately - it relieves pain for Indo-Pacific species (C. fleckeri, C. barnesi) but can increase nematocyst discharge in Physalia physalis and Chrysaora quinquecirrha; rubbing the area also worsens stinging. Mislabeling scombroid poisoning as a seafood allergy, leading to unnecessary lifelong fish avoidance. Using beta-blockers in Irukandji syndrome hypertension - risks worsening hypertension via unopposed alpha effects. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of enzymes, polypeptides, and glycoproteins whose composition varies by species, age, diet, geography, and even within a species. They produce harm through several mechanisms: direct local tissue necrosis, disruption of the coagulation cascade at multiple steps (consumptive coagulopathy, defibrination, thrombocytopenia), organ dysfunction (notably renal), and action at the neuromuscular junction causing paralysis. Early hypotension is partly mediated by bradykinin-potentiating factors causing vasodilation and pooling, compounded by systemic bleeding, hemolysis, and third-spacing of intravascular volume. Renal injury is usually acute tubular necrosis (often reversible), but bilateral cortical necrosis carries a poorer prognosis. Marine envenomations operate by distinct toxins: cnidarian nematocysts inject venom containing phospholipases, metalloproteases, pore-forming toxins, neurotoxins, and bioactive amines (histamine, serotonin); cone snail conotoxins block acetylcholine receptors and ion channels; blue-ringed octopus and pufferfish deliver tetrodotoxin, a potent peripheral sodium-channel blocker. Marine seafood poisonings are ingestion toxidromes: scombroid from bacterial conversion of histidine to histamine in spoiled fish, and ciguatera from ciguatoxins that activate neuronal sodium channels and antagonize voltage-gated potassium channels. In settings with rapid access to care and appropriate antivenom, mortality is low - under 1% in the United States among victims who receive antivenom. Eastern and western diamondback rattlesnakes account for most U.S. snakebite deaths; globally, major killers include cobras, saw-scaled/carpet vipers (Echis), Russell's vipers, large African vipers (Bitis), lanceheads (Bothrops), and tropical rattlesnakes (Crotalus durissus). Morbidity from permanent limb functional loss is substantial and can be devastating in the developing world; in the U.S. it is more common and severe after rattlesnake bites than after copperhead or water moccasin bites. Renal failure from acute tubular necrosis is frequently reversible, whereas bilateral cortical necrosis carries a worse renal prognosis. For tetrodotoxin/blue-ringed octopus envenomation, recovery usually occurs within 24-48 h and long-term sequelae are uncommon unless hypoxia/hypoperfusion supervened. Most scombroid cases are mild and self-limited (resolving in 8-12 h), and ciguatera GI symptoms typically settle in 24-48 h though neurologic symptoms may persist for days to weeks (and a delayed 'second-phase' syndrome can last 2-6 weeks after parrotfish exposure). Harrison grades pit viper envenomation severity (U.S./Canada framework) as: None - fang marks only ('dry' bite); Mild - local findings only (pain, ecchymosis, nonprogressive swelling); Moderate - clearly progressing swelling, systemic symptoms/signs, and/or laboratory abnormalities; Severe - neurologic dysfunction, respiratory distress, and/or cardiovascular instability/shock.

SIBO and bile-acid malabsorption occur in IBS-D) (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2546) Microscopic colitis (Harrison 22e p.2546) Intestinal lymphoma, including enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.2546) Crohn's disease (Harrison 22e p.2542) Hyperthyroidism causing rapid-transit diarrhea/malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2542) Long-standing diabetes mellitus with enteric autonomic neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.2542) Scleroderma and other connective-tissue/motility disorders (Harrison 22e p.2542) Menetrier's disease (hypertrophic gastropathy) as a cause of protein-losing enteropathy (Harrison 22e p.2549) Steatorrhea (fecal fat excretion >7% of dietary fat) is a common manifestation of malabsorption, producing large, bulky, malodorous stools; malabsorptive diarrhea is typically precipitated by eating and lessens or resolves with fasting, which helps distinguish it from secretory (e.g., enterotoxigenic) diarrhea that persists during fasting (Harrison 22e p.2540-2541). Celiac disease (celiac sprue / gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is a small-intestinal enteropathy from an immune response to gluten (wheat, rye, barley, some oats), characterized by autoantibodies to tissue transglutaminase; it primarily affects the proximal small bowel, so duodenal-limited disease may present as isolated iron-deficiency anemia while diffuse jejunal disease causes severe diarrhea, weight loss, and multinutrient malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2545). Tissue transglutaminase IgA (TTG-IgA) is the celiac screening test of choice; serum IgA should be measured concurrently because IgA deficiency causes false-negative TTG-IgA, in which case IgG-based testing (TTG-IgG or anti-deamidated gliadin peptide DGP-IgG) is used (Harrison 22e p.2545). In adults with positive celiac serology, diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy with small-intestinal biopsy showing villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; the Marsh classification grades severity (Harrison 22e p.2545). PITFALL: celiac serologic and histologic testing must be performed while the patient is consuming gluten, since self-discontinuation of gluten before testing produces false-negative results; HLA-DQ2/DQ8 testing is then useful because a negative result rules out celiac disease (negative predictive value >99%) (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545). HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are necessary but not sufficient for celiac disease and are present in 25-35% of the general population, so their detection is NOT useful for diagnosis; their value lies in the very high negative predictive value when absent (Harrison 22e p.2544). Dermatitis herpetiformis, a vesicular rash mediated by IgA skin deposits, is highly associated with celiac disease; celiac disease also carries increased risk of other autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease) and is more frequent in Down and Turner syndromes (Harrison 22e p.2545). The mainstay of celiac treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with rigorous dietitian instruction; the most common cause of persistent symptoms or residual disease activity is dietary nonadherence or inadvertent gluten exposure (Harrison 22e p.2545-2546). Tropical sprue presents with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies of BOTH folate and vitamin B12; malabsorption of two unrelated substances is required for diagnosis, and it is associated with residence in or travel to specific tropical regions (southern India, Pakistan, Philippines, Puerto Rico, Haiti, Cuba) (Harrison 22e p.2546-2547). In India, tropical sprue is regarded by some as a postinfectious complication occurring in 8-20% of people after an attack of infectious gastroenteritis, with southern Indian patients often reporting acute enteritis preceding steatorrhea; tropical sprue is rarely seen in Africa, Jamaica, or Southeast Asia, and its overall incidence has declined (Harrison 22e p.2546-2547). Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei, a PAS-positive non-acid-fast rod) most often affects middle-aged men; arthralgias/arthritis precede GI symptoms by an average of ~6 years (joint disease in >80%), and CNS and cardiac involvement occur later; diagnosis uses biopsy with PCR and PAS-positive macrophages (Harrison 22e p.2546). Small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth arises from stasis (scleroderma, pseudo-obstruction, blind loops, strictures, diverticulosis) and from hypochlorhydria (chronic PPI use); it causes B12 deficiency (macrocytic anemia, peripheral neuropathy) from bacterial B12 metabolism, yet serum folate may be ELEVATED due to bacterial folate synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2543). In ileal disease/resection, <100 cm involvement causes bile-acid spillage into the colon and secretory (cholerheic) diarrhea responsive to bile-acid sequestrants, whereas >100 cm exceeds hepatic synthetic capacity to replace lost bile acids, making fat malabsorption (steatorrhea) the dominant mechanism (Harrison 22e p.2542-2543). Chronic pancreatitis and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency cause voluminous steatorrhea with deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (most commonly D and K), and stool elastase is helpful for diagnosing pancreatic insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2542, 2549). In short-bowel/lipid malabsorption with an intact colon in continuity, luminal fatty acids saponify calcium, freeing oxalate for colonic absorption and increasing the risk of calcium-oxalate renal stones (hyperoxaluria) (Harrison 22e p.2548). Persistent diarrhea, weight loss, and villus atrophy after >=1 year of a strict gluten-free diet with negative serology, indicating refractory celiac disease (Harrison 22e p.2546) Type 2 refractory celiac disease (clonal CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gamma-chain rearrangement), which progresses to enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in 33-50% within 5 years (Harrison 22e p.2546) New or worsening malabsorption with abdominal mass/imaging lymphadenopathy suggesting small-bowel adenocarcinoma or intestinal lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.2546) Hypoproteinemia with peripheral edema, diarrhea, and lymphopenia (protein-losing enteropathy) requiring exclusion of cardiac and lymphatic causes (Harrison 22e p.2548) Severe vitamin K deficiency causing coagulopathy (elevated PT/INR) and significant B12-related peripheral neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.2549) Whipple's disease relapse, frequently heralding first CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.2546) Testing for celiac disease (serology and biopsy) only after the patient has already self-removed gluten gives false-negative results; testing must be done ON a gluten-containing diet, or use HLA-DQ2/DQ8 to exclude disease (Harrison 22e p.2544-2545). Interpreting HLA-DQ2/DQ8 positivity as diagnostic of celiac disease is wrong, as 25-35% of the general population carry these alleles without disease; only a negative result is clinically useful (rules out) (Harrison 22e p.2544). Missing IgA deficiency when only TTG-IgA is ordered will produce false-negative celiac screening; order total serum IgA and use IgG-based tests if deficient (Harrison 22e p.2545). Diagnosing tropical sprue before excluding enteric infection: it should NOT be entertained until cysts and trophozoites are excluded in three stool samples, and a gluten-free diet does NOT improve tropical sprue (unlike celiac disease) (Harrison 22e p.2547). Breath hydrogen testing for lactose intolerance or SIBO can be inaccurate with abnormal gastric emptying or transit, and SIBO can itself produce false-positive/abnormal breath tests and mimic lactose intolerance (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2545). In SIBO, expecting low folate is a trap; serum folate may be ELEVATED from bacterial synthesis while B12 is low (Harrison 22e p.2543). In protein-losing enteropathy, isolated low albumin with normal globulins suggests renal/hepatic disease rather than GI loss; alpha-1 antitrypsin cannot assess gastric protein loss because it is degraded in acid (Harrison 22e p.2548-2549). Treating the hypoproteinemia of protein-losing enteropathy directly rather than the underlying disease is misdirected; therapy should target the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.2549). Malabsorption results from disruption of one or more of the three phases of nutrient assimilation. (1) Luminal/digestive phase: intraluminal hydrolysis by gastric and pancreatic enzymes and solubilization of fat in bile-salt mixed micelles; impaired by postgastrectomy rapid transit, pancreatic insufficiency, hepatobiliary disease, ileal disease interrupting the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids, and small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth (which deconjugates bile acids causing luminal bile-acid deficiency). (2) Mucosal/absorptive phase: brush-border enzymatic digestion (disaccharidases, peptidases, enterokinase) and enterocyte uptake; impaired by isolated brush-border defects (lactase deficiency, glucose-galactose malabsorption, sucrase-isomaltase deficiency) or by diffuse enteropathies (celiac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple's disease, Crohn's, infections). In celiac disease, tissue transglutaminase deamidates gluten-derived peptides, promoting their presentation by antigen-presenting cells in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 individuals, producing proximal villus atrophy with crypt hyperplasia; steatorrhea arises from mucosal malabsorption plus a secretory component from crypt hyperplasia/hypersecretion, and secondary lactase deficiency may develop. (3) Postmucosal/delivery phase: re-esterification of long-chain fatty acids into chylomicrons exiting via lymphatics; impaired by abetalipoproteinemia (failed chylomicron formation) and by lymphatic obstruction/dysfunction (lymphangiectasia, lymphoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis) or circulatory causes (Fontan physiology, constrictive pericarditis, CHF), which also cause protein-losing enteropathy. Specific nutrient deficiencies localize disease: duodenal/proximal disease causes iron and folate deficiency; ileal disease/resection causes B12 deficiency and bile-acid malabsorption; steatorrhea causes fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2540-2549). Most patients with celiac disease respond fully to a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with mucosal healing and symptom resolution; about 10% of those with persistent active disease develop refractory celiac disease, and type 2 refractory disease carries a poor prognosis with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma in 33-50% of cases at 5 years (requiring intensive chemotherapy and sometimes stem cell transplantation). Tropical sprue is most often curative with broad-spectrum antibiotics plus folic acid, especially if the patient leaves the tropical area and does not return. Whipple's disease requires prolonged antibiotics, but relapses are common. In short-bowel syndrome the intestine adapts over up to 2 years (with reports of continued improvement at 3-5 years); prognosis and parenteral-nutrition dependence relate to the extent of resection, presence of colon in continuity, and retention of the ileocecal valve, with intestinal failure defined by persistent parenteral-nutrition dependence (Harrison 22e p.2542-2548). There is no single unified severity scale for malabsorption; severity is assessed by the degree of nutrient deficiency and steatorrhea and by disease-specific schemes. Celiac mucosal injury is graded by the Marsh classification of biopsy lesions (intraepithelial lymphocytosis, crypt hyperplasia, and degrees of villus atrophy). Celiac complications are stratified into refractory celiac disease type 1 (normal intraepithelial lymphocyte population, better prognosis) versus type 2 (clonal CD3+ intraepithelial lymphocytes with monoclonal T-cell receptor gamma rearrangement, worse prognosis with high lymphoma risk). Bile-acid versus fatty-acid diarrhea are distinguished by extent of ileal disease (<100 cm vs >100 cm), degree of steatorrhea, and response to cholestyramine versus a low-fat diet. Short-bowel syndrome is defined as <200 cm of remaining small bowel, and intestinal failure as persistent parenteral-nutrition dependence (generally <100 cm of small bowel with no colon in continuity) (Harrison 22e p.2543, 2545-2548).

Classical orthostatic hypotension is a sustained fall of systolic BP >=20 mmHg or diastolic BP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt >=60 degrees; in hypertensive patients the threshold is >=30/15 mmHg. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is suggested by a blunted compensatory heart-rate rise (<15 beats/min); a heart-rate-rise/systolic-BP-fall ratio below 0.5 beats/min/mmHg after 3 minutes more accurately indicates neurogenic OH and reflects impaired cardiac baroreflex gain. POTS is defined as chronic (>3 months) orthostatic intolerance WITHOUT sustained orthostatic hypotension, with a heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (>=40 if under age 19) or a rate above 120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing; it is a sinus-rhythm disorder, four to five times more common in women aged 15-45. About half of POTS cases follow a viral illness (notably EBV, coronavirus, enteroviruses); it is the leading manifestation of long COVID, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome predisposes in up to 25% of patients. Heart-rate variation to deep breathing tests the vagal (parasympathetic) baroreflex arm; the Valsalva maneuver assesses both parasympathetic (Valsalva ratio) and sympathetic (adrenergic index, BP recovery) arms; both are diminished in most autonomic failure, diabetes, and alpha-synuclein disorders. Sudomotor localization: a postganglionic lesion shows absent sweating on BOTH QSART and thermoregulatory sweat test (TST), whereas a preganglionic lesion preserves QSART but shows anhidrosis on TST. Multiple system atrophy (Shy-Drager) combines autonomic failure with parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar features (MSA-C); the parkinsonism responds poorly/transiently to levodopa and rest tremor is not prominent. Cardiac sympathetic innervation imaging (MIBG scintigraphy or fluorodopamine PET) is typically PRESERVED in MSA but reduced in Parkinson disease, Lewy body disease, and pure autonomic failure, aiding differentiation. Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy is a treatable cause associated with high-titer antibodies to the alpha-3 ganglionic acetylcholine nicotinic receptor; it may be paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer, thymoma, lymphoma), so malignancy screening is prudent. Autonomic dysreflexia is a dramatic BP surge triggered by bladder, bowel, or skin irritation in spinal cord lesions above T6; lesions below T6 permit splanchnic vasodilation and rarely cause it. significant psychiatric disorder rates are no higher than in the general population The autonomic nervous system operates as an integrated reflex circuit linking sensory feedback from organs with central processing (insular and prefrontal cortex, limbic system, hypothalamus; brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius, dorsal motor vagal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus) and the spinal intermediolateral cell columns, then to peripheral ganglia and target organs. Dysfunction may arise from decreased activity, overactivity, or dysregulation at the afferent limb, central processor, or efferent limb. In orthostatic hypotension, standing shifts roughly 500-700 mL of blood to the lower limbs and splanchnic bed; the normal compensatory baroreflex (slight tachycardia, veno- and arteriolar constriction) maintains pressure, and neurogenic OH results from inadequate peripheral norepinephrine release with loss of vascular tone. The synucleinopathies (MSA, Parkinson disease with autonomic failure, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure) share aggregation of misfolded, phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in central and peripheral autonomic structures; MSA characteristically shows glial cytoplasmic inclusions in oligodendrocytes (versus neuronal Lewy bodies in PD/LBD), with possible prion-like cell-to-cell transfer. Peripheral autonomic neuropathies damage small myelinated and unmyelinated sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers. POTS pathophysiology is heterogeneous, including distal sympathetic denervation with preserved cardiac sympathetic function (neuropathic POTS), venous pooling, hypovolemia, deconditioning, altered baroreflex regulation, and sympathetic overactivity. Prognosis depends on etiology. Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension carries high mortality, approaching 44% over 30 months and exceeding 60% over 10 years in some series, and OH overall raises risk of falls, coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, and death. MSA progresses relentlessly to death typically 7-10 years after onset, though some survive beyond 10 years; early autonomic and bladder dysfunction, female sex, and rapid disability progression imply worse prognosis. Pure autonomic failure may evolve into a central synucleinopathy (PD, DLB, or MSA) after 5-10 years. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy increases diabetic mortality up to threefold. POTS is often chronic and self-perpetuating through deconditioning, but psychiatric comorbidity rates do not exceed the general population; graded exercise typically needs at least 6 months for benefit. Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy is important because it is treatable; about one-third of untreated seronegative cases improve spontaneously. Orthostatic hypotension can be graded into four functional classes: class I, asymptomatic (may still have syncope/falls); class II, weekly-to-monthly symptoms with mild-to-moderate limitation of daily living; class III, more severe and frequent symptoms markedly limiting daily activities; class IV, daily severe symptoms causing significant disability. OH is further distinguished as nonneurogenic (compensatory HR rise >15 beats/min) versus neurogenic (HR rise <15 beats/min, or HR-rise/SBP-fall ratio <0.5 beats/min/mmHg), and by timing as initial, classical, delayed, and postprandial variants.

The female reproductive axis is a tightly regulated hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian system. Pulsatile GnRH from roughly 7000 hypothalamic neurons, coordinated by pulsatile kisspeptin secretion (modulated by stimulatory neurokinin B and inhibitory dynorphin in KNDy neurons), drives pituitary FSH and LH release. FSH recruits secondary follicles from the resting pool (cyclic recruitment), restrained by AMH from small growing follicles. A single dominant follicle is selected within the first week of the cycle through high FSH-receptor density, high aromatase activity, and rising estradiol and inhibin A, which suppress FSH and the growth of competing follicles. Estradiol is produced by the cooperative two-cell mechanism (LH-driven theca androgen synthesis, FSH-driven granulosa aromatization). The mid-cycle estradiol-induced LH surge triggers resumption of oocyte meiosis, induction of COX-2, prostaglandins, and the progesterone receptor, and ovulation, followed by luteinization of theca and granulosa cells to form the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum. Disorders arise from defects at any level: genetic or anatomic GnRH-neuron migration defects, functional hypothalamic suppression from energy deficit, pituitary lesions, ovarian failure (gonadal dysgenesis, premature ovarian insufficiency, mutations in over 50 genes), or outflow-tract obstruction. Over 50 genes have been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency, reflecting the genetic complexity of follicle endowment and survival (Harrison 22e p.3125-p.3132). Many disorders are highly treatable when the level of the defect is identified. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from energy deficit is often reversible with restoration of energy balance. Outflow-tract obstruction has a good outcome with timely surgery, but delay increases the risk of endometriosis from retrograde menstruation. Premature ovarian insufficiency and gonadal dysgenesis carry permanent loss of fertility and require attention to long-term estrogen-deficiency consequences for bone and other tissues. Amenorrhea is classified as primary (menses never occurred without hormonal treatment) versus secondary (cessation for 3-6 months). Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) replaces the older term dysfunctional uterine bleeding and is categorized etiologically by the PALM-COEIN system into structural causes (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) and nonstructural causes (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). Precocious puberty is divided into central (GnRH-dependent) and peripheral (GnRH-independent) forms, and delayed puberty into hypergonadotropic (ovarian) and hypogonadotropic (central) forms (Harrison 22e p.3131, p.3133).

Localizing a mediastinal mass to one of the three compartments is the essential first diagnostic step, since each compartment harbors a distinct set of typical lesions. The anterior compartment is the source of thymomas, germ cell tumors (including teratomas), lymphomas, and thyroid goiter; thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal neoplasm and is closely linked to paraneoplastic syndromes, most notably myasthenia gravis. Teratomas are the most common germ cell tumor and appear as multilobulated cystic lesions containing fat, soft tissue, and calcium; elevated alpha-fetoprotein and beta-hCG distinguish nonseminomatous from seminomatous germ cell tumors. Most middle mediastinal masses are benign and developmental in origin, including bronchogenic cysts (abnormal ventral foregut budding), duplication cysts (persistent dorsal foregut diverticulum), and pericardial cysts (abnormal pericardial recess fusion). Neurogenic tumors are the most common cause of posterior mediastinal masses and are frequently benign, arising from peripheral, autonomic, or paraganglionic nervous tissue. Barium gastrointestinal studies are useful in many posterior mediastinal lesions because hernias, diverticula, and achalasia are readily identified this way. Disorders of the mediastinum arise from the anatomical structures of its three compartments. Anterior compartment lesions stem from the thymus, lymph nodes, germinal/thyroid tissue, and mammary vessels, giving rise to thymomas, germ cell tumors, lymphomas, and goiter. Middle compartment disease typically reflects embryologic developmental abnormalities producing foregut-derived cysts (bronchogenic, duplication, pericardial), or malignant lymphadenopathy and vascular masses; because central vasculature resides here, compression of structures such as the SVC can produce acute life-threatening physiology. Posterior compartment lesions are predominantly neurogenic, with contributions from diaphragmatic hernia, meningocele, esophageal diverticula, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. Acute mediastinitis is an inflammatory/infectious process driven by esophageal breach, post-sternotomy wound contamination, or descending cervicofacial infection. Chronic and fibrosing mediastinitis represents a spectrum from granulomatous lymph node inflammation to dense fibrosis, usually following granulomatous infection, with progressive encasement and obstruction of mediastinal structures (SVC, large airways, pulmonary vessels, phrenic/recurrent laryngeal nerves). Pneumomediastinum results from alveolar rupture with air dissection into the mediastinum, perforation/rupture of esophagus or airway, or dissection of air from the neck or abdomen. Prognosis depends on the underlying disorder. Most middle mediastinal masses and posterior neurogenic tumors are benign. Anterior mediastinal neoplasms vary widely, and disease severity across mediastinal masses spans a broad spectrum; clinical symptoms, patient age, and tumor location guide assessment of malignancy and need for intervention. Acute post-sternotomy mediastinitis carries a mortality rate exceeding 20% despite treatment. Fibrosing mediastinitis can be devastating in severe cases owing to obstruction/encasement of vital structures. Pneumomediastinum usually requires no treatment and resolves with absorption of air. No formal grading system; mediastinal disorders are stratified anatomically into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments, and severity is judged by clinical symptoms, patient age, lesion location, likelihood of malignancy, and presence of acute complications such as SVC obstruction or airway compromise.

neurohypophysis releases arginine vasopressin (AVP/ADH) and oxytocin from axons whose cell bodies sit in the hypothalamic paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei; AVP conserves water by concentrating urine, while oxytocin drives milk letdown and socioemotional behaviors (Harrison 22e p.3014). AVP secretion is governed mainly by an osmotic set point in anteromedial hypothalamic osmoreceptors, with the average threshold near a plasma osmolality of ~275 mosmol/L and sodium ~135 meq/L; only a 2-4% rise above this drives maximum antidiuresis (Harrison 22e p.3015). Nausea/emetic stimuli are extremely potent AVP releasers, producing 50- to 100-fold increases even without vomiting, far exceeding osmotic stimulation; AVP is also released by a >10-20% fall in blood pressure or volume, hypoglycemia, glucocorticoid deficiency, and smoking (Harrison 22e p.3015). AVP acts on V2 receptors of collecting-duct principal cells to insert aquaporin-2 water channels, enabling water reabsorption; maximum antidiuresis (urine osmolality up to ~1200 mosmol/L) occurs at plasma AVP of roughly 1-3 pg/mL (Harrison 22e p.3016). The thirst osmostat is set about 3% higher than the AVP osmostat, so antidiuresis is the first-line defense and thirst/polydipsia only engage once AVP's capacity is exceeded (Harrison 22e p.3016). Polyuria-polydipsia is defined practically by a 24-h urine volume exceeding ~40-50 mL/kg and/or >3 L/d on unrestricted intake; dehydration and hypernatremia are uncommon in diabetes insipidus unless thirst or access to water is also impaired (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017). Serum sodium at presentation is a key discriminator: a low sodium (<135 mmol/L) points toward primary polydipsia (patients can drink into hyponatremia), whereas a high sodium suggests AVP deficiency or resistance (Harrison 22e p.3017). Copeptin, the stable C-terminal fragment of the AVP prohormone, has largely replaced direct AVP assays: a baseline copeptin >21.4 pmol/L without prior water deprivation identifies AVP resistance, and a copeptin >4.9 pmol/L at plasma sodium >=150 mmol/L after hypertonic saline distinguishes AVP deficiency from primary polydipsia with ~96.5% accuracy (Harrison 22e p.3017-3018). The MRI posterior pituitary bright spot reflects AVP-containing neurosecretory vesicles and is often absent in AVP deficiency, but its absence is not diagnostic since it can persist early or be absent in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.3018). In pregnancy, placental N-terminal aminopeptidase (vasopressinase) accelerates AVP clearance three- to fourfold, producing gestational AVP deficiency that typically remits weeks after delivery; the synthetic analogue DDAVP resists this peptidase (Harrison 22e p.3016-3017). In SIAD, persistent water retention modestly expands total body water and triggers compensatory urinary sodium loss, so edema does not develop; the harm comes from intracellular (notably cerebral) swelling proportional to the speed and degree of the sodium fall (Harrison 22e p.3019). Disorders of the neurohypophysis arise from deficient or excessive AVP secretion/action. In AVP deficiency (formerly central/neurogenic diabetes insipidus) and AVP resistance (formerly nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), impaired urine concentration increases free-water excretion, causing a small (1-2%) reduction in body water and a rise in plasma osmolality/sodium that stimulates thirst and compensatory drinking; severity ranges from near-complete deficiency unresponsive to maximal stimuli to partial defects in which mild stimuli can still partially concentrate urine, though prior lack of AVP transiently blunts renal concentrating capacity. Central deficiency reflects destruction or dysfunction of AVP-producing neurons (trauma, tumors, vascular, granulomatous, infectious, autoimmune/IgG4 hypophysitis, or genetic AVP-neurophysin II mutations); resistance reflects reduced renal V2-receptor/aquaporin-2 responsiveness from drugs (lithium), hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, infiltrative or vascular disease, or AVPR2/AQP2 mutations. Primary polydipsia is the mirror image: excess intake lowers plasma osmolality, physiologically suppresses AVP, and produces a dilute compensatory diuresis. Hypodipsic/adipsic hypernatremia results from anterior hypothalamic osmoreceptor damage impairing osmotic thirst (occasionally from anti-subfornical-organ autoantibodies), so obligatory renal/insensible losses go unreplaced. In SIAD, AVP is inappropriately elevated when it should be osmotically suppressed, causing water retention, slight volume expansion with renal sodium loss (no edema), and dilutional hypoosmolality with cellular swelling (Harrison 22e p.3014-3019). Uncomplicated AVP deficiency is generally well managed with vasopressin replacement, restoring normal water balance. Hyponatremia is the most common complication of replacement and ranges from mild to severe. AVP resistance is difficult to treat and may respond only partially. Adipsic/hypodipsic hypernatremia carries higher risk because the absent thirst sensation predisposes to recurrent hypertonic dehydration and complications such as rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, and thromboembolism; long-term structured fluid-balance management is needed to prevent recurrence. In SIAD, even mild chronic hyponatremia is associated with increased falls, fractures, neurocognitive and neuromuscular symptoms, and increased morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.3017-3019). Diabetes insipidus is graded as complete versus partial AVP deficiency, and complete versus partial AVP resistance, distinguished by copeptin response, desmopressin response, and the magnitude of urine osmolality change. Hyponatremia severity is gauged by plasma sodium and tempo: severe/acute hyponatremia with neurologic symptoms warrants urgent treatment, whereas gradual or mild hyponatremia may be paucisymptomatic; replacement-related hyponatremia is categorized as mild (sodium 131-134 mmol/L) or more severe (<130 mmol/L). Hypernatremia severity in adipsic patients varies widely and correlates with hypovolemic complications (Harrison 22e p.3017-3019).

exudative effusion and pleuritic pain Malignant effusion (including mesothelioma) mimicking empyema or chronic infection Rheumatoid or lupus pleuritis mimicking infectious exudate (low glucose in rheumatoid disease) Pleural effusion ex vacuo / trapped lung mimicking persistent active disease The pleural space normally holds only a thin film of fluid acting as a coupling system, kept at roughly -3 to -5 cmH2O by the balance between lung elastic recoil (visceral pleura) and chest-wall outward expansion (parietal pleura). The first diagnostic step in any pleural effusion is distinguishing transudate from exudate via thoracentesis; this dictates whether further work-up is needed, since exudates require investigation to define their cause. Light's criteria define an exudate when at least one is met: pleural fluid/serum protein >0.5, pleural fluid/serum LDH >0.6, or pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper normal serum limit; transudates meet none. Light's criteria misclassify about 25% of transudates as exudates ('pseudoexudates'), often in a diuresed transudate; a serum-to-pleural-fluid protein gradient >3.1 g/dL or albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL helps reclassify these (high sensitivity in heart failure and hepatothorax). Left ventricular failure is the single most common cause of pleural effusion (a transudate from raised hydrostatic pressure); cirrhosis is the next leading transudative cause in the United States. Parapneumonic effusions occur in up to 50% of community-acquired pneumonias and are generally the most common exudative effusion in the U.S.; about 10% become complicated or progress to empyema (fibrinopurulent or grossly purulent fluid). Malignant pleural effusions are the second most common exudate; lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, and lymphoma together cause roughly 75% of cases, and dyspnea is often out of proportion to effusion size. Pulmonary embolism is the diagnosis most commonly overlooked in an undiagnosed exudative effusion; the fluid is almost always exudative and dyspnea is the predominant symptom. Tuberculous pleuritis arises largely as a hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculous protein in the pleural space and yields a lymphocyte-predominant exudate; pleural biopsy culture yield exceeds that of pleural fluid. Chylothorax produces milky fluid with a triglyceride level exceeding 110 mg/dL (1.2 mmol/L); prolonged chest-tube drainage should be avoided because chyle loss causes malnutrition and immunologic incompetence. Hemothorax is defined when pleural fluid hematocrit exceeds half the peripheral blood hematocrit; most are traumatic. About half of patients with an initial primary spontaneous pneumothorax (from rupture of apical subpleural blebs) will have a recurrence. Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency: positive intrapleural pressure throughout the respiratory cycle impairs ventilation and reduces venous return, lowering cardiac output. Tension pneumothorax: enlarged hemithorax with absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, contralateral mediastinal shift, and hypotension; treat as an emergency with immediate needle decompression (large-bore needle in the second anterior intercostal space). Difficulty ventilating or high peak inspiratory pressures during mechanical ventilation/resuscitation strongly suggest tension pneumothorax. Complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema markers indicating need for drainage: loculated fluid, pleural fluid pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL (<3.3 mmol/L), positive Gram stain or culture, gross pus, and elevated pleural fluid LDH (>900 IU/L). Hemothorax with ongoing pleural hemorrhage exceeding 200 mL/h warrants angiographic embolization, thoracoscopy, or thoracotomy. Secondary pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease can be more life-threatening because of reduced pulmonary reserve. Relying on Light's criteria alone can misclassify roughly 25% of transudates as exudates; failing to apply protein/albumin gradients in a clinically transudative setting leads to unnecessary work-up. Overlooking pulmonary embolism as the cause of an otherwise undiagnosed exudative effusion. Being overly aggressive in pursuing a diagnosis in a clinically improving patient whose effusion is likely viral and self-limited. Failing to recognize trapped lung: a thick pleural rind, air on imaging after thoracentesis (pneumothorax ex vacuo), and rapid re-accumulation indicate a lung that will not re-expand without decortication. Prolonged tube thoracostomy drainage of a chylothorax, which can cause malnutrition and immunologic incompetence. Not performing diagnostic thoracentesis in a presumed heart-failure effusion that is unilateral, asymmetric, febrile, or pleuritic, or that persists despite therapy. Pleural fluid normally enters from parietal pleural capillaries and is cleared by parietal pleural lymphatics, which can absorb up to 20 times the normal rate of fluid formation; fluid can also enter from lung interstitium via the visceral pleura or from the peritoneal cavity through diaphragmatic openings. An effusion forms when the hydrostatic-oncotic balance is disturbed and fluid production overwhelms lymphatic removal. Transudates result from altered systemic factors (e.g., elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure in heart failure raising hydrostatic pressure, or low oncotic pressure), whereas exudates result from altered local factors such as inflammation, infection, or malignancy increasing capillary permeability or impairing lymphatic drainage. Parapneumonic effusions begin as a sterile reactive exudate and can progress through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases. Hepatic hydrothorax reflects direct movement of ascitic fluid through small diaphragmatic defects into the pleural space. Pneumothorax results from gas entering the pleural space, abolishing the negative pressure that couples lung to chest wall; in tension pneumothorax a one-way mechanism produces sustained positive pleural pressure. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Transudative effusions from heart failure or cirrhosis improve when the primary condition is treated, and undiagnosed viral effusions usually resolve spontaneously without long-term residua. A malignant pleural effusion usually portends a poor prognosis (often less than 6-month survival) and reflects disseminated disease that is generally not curable with chemotherapy. Untreated complicated parapneumonic effusions can organize into a restrictive pleural peel (trapped lung). Tension pneumothorax is rapidly fatal from inadequate cardiac output or marked hypoxemia if not relieved. Surgical pleurodesis prevents pneumothorax recurrence in nearly 100% of cases. Parapneumonic effusions are staged along a continuum from simple (free-flowing, reactive) to complicated (loculated, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, positive Gram stain/culture) to empyema (frank pus), with progression through exudative, fibrinopurulent, and organizing (pleural peel) phases guiding the need for escalating intervention. Pneumothorax is categorized as primary spontaneous, secondary, traumatic (including iatrogenic), and tension.

Disorders of the Testes and Male Reproductive System — Male hypogonadism, Testicular failure, Testosterone deficiency syndrome, Androgen deficiency in men Erectile dysfunction without testosterone deficiency (the two are distinct disorders that may coexist) Self-limited (constitutional) delayed puberty versus congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in adolescents Hyperprolactinemia / prolactinoma causing secondary hypogonadism Hemochromatosis (pituitary and/or testicular iron deposition) Sellar mass lesions / pituitary adenoma impairing gonadotropin secretion Functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from systemic illness, malnutrition, eating disorders, or opioid use Androgen insensitivity / 5-alpha-reductase deficiency / aromatase (CYP19) deficiency Mumps orchitis (and orchitis from echovirus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, group B arboviruses) causing acquired primary testicular failure HIV infection associated with low testosterone (primary or central) Lepromatous leprosy causing testicular atrophy through direct mycobacterial invasion Fasting early-morning total testosterone (LC-MS/MS preferred, CDC HoST-certified); repeat if borderline (200-400 ng/dL) and add free testosterone Free testosterone by equilibrium dialysis when SHBG is altered (aging, obesity, chronic illness) LH and FSH to separate primary (high LH/FSH) from secondary (low/inappropriately normal LH) hypogonadism Karyotype in men with low testosterone, elevated LH, and small testes to diagnose Klinefelter syndrome Serum prolactin and ferritin/transferrin saturation; pituitary MRI when secondary hypogonadism is found Inhibin B (Sertoli cell product) to assess seminiferous tubule integrity Semen analysis and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing (AZFa/AZFb/AZFc) in oligo-/azoospermia For gynecomastia: testosterone, estradiol, estrone, androstenedione, LH, hCG (beta), TSH; testicular ultrasound and adrenal/chest imaging if an estrogen- or hCG-secreting tumor is suspected Lipomastia (excess adipose) mimicking glandular gynecomastia Retractile testis mimicking cryptorchidism Age-related decline in testosterone overlapping with symptomatic hypogonadism Obesity-related lowering of total testosterone (with often normal free testosterone) due to reduced SHBG A low serum testosterone with an elevated LH localizes the defect to the testis (primary/hypergonadotropic hypogonadism), whereas a low or inappropriately normal LH points to a hypothalamic-pituitary defect (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) (p.3107, p.3118). Acquired androgen-deficient men commonly report decreased libido, fewer sexual thoughts and acts, low energy, low mood, and (less often) hot flushes; eunuchoid body proportions (arm span >2 cm greater than height) indicate that deficiency predated epiphyseal fusion (p.3110). Klinefelter syndrome (classically 47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal cause of testicular dysfunction and male infertility, occurring in about 1 in 600 live-born males, with markedly small testes (often 1-2 mL), azoospermia, low testosterone, raised estradiol, undervirilization, and gynecomastia (p.3110, p.3114). True glandular gynecomastia (palpable firm, cord-like tissue >4 cm, often tender) reflects an increased estrogen-to-androgen ratio and must be distinguished from excess adipose (lipomastia); recent rapid onset, tenderness, or occurrence in a lean man warrants workup (p.3115). Testicular volume is a useful clinical index: normal adult testes are 3.5-5.5 cm long (about 12-25 mL by Prader orchidometer), and very small testes in a hypogonadal man should prompt a karyotype to exclude Klinefelter syndrome (p.3110, p.3119). Mumps is the classic cause of viral orchitis; orchitis develops in up to one-fourth of affected adult men, is unilateral in about two-thirds, and semen analysis normalizes in three-fourths after unilateral but only one-third after bilateral involvement (p.3114). Total testosterone can mislead when SHBG is altered (low in obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome; high in aging, hyperthyroidism, estrogen, HIV/hepatitis B and C, some anticonvulsants); measure free testosterone (ideally by equilibrium dialysis) in these settings (p.3106, p.3108).
