Cryptorchidism, even when corrected before puberty, carries increased risk of malignancy, infertility, inguinal hernia, and torsion, and is considered part of the testicular dysgenesis syndrome along with hypospadias, impaired spermatogenesis, and testicular cancer (p.3114). Selective elevation of FSH (with relatively normal LH) suggests seminiferous tubule/Sertoli cell damage, because reduced inhibin B removes the negative feedback restraining FSH (p.3104, p.3107). Up to two-thirds of pubertal boys and about half of hospitalized men have benign palpable breast tissue, so not all gynecomastia requires extensive investigation (p.3116). Kallmann syndrome is the anosmic form of congenital GnRH-deficient hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, arising from defective olfactory bulb morphogenesis and failed migration of GnRH neurons; micropenis and a history of cryptorchidism favor a congenital central defect over self-limited delayed puberty (p.3112, p.3110). Recent-onset, rapidly growing, or tender gynecomastia in a lean man, or breast tissue fixed to underlying tissue (evaluate for tumor/malignancy) Markedly elevated estradiol with suppressed LH, suggesting a testicular or adrenal estrogen-secreting tumor Elevated hCG (beta) prompting search for an hCG-producing germ cell or other tumor Very small testes with low testosterone and high LH (consider Klinefelter syndrome and its associated breast cancer risk) Diabetes insipidus accompanying hypogonadism, suggesting craniopharyngioma or infiltrative hypothalamic lesion Hyperprolactinemia with visual field defects suggesting a pituitary mass Relying on a single random or afternoon testosterone level — values are pulsatile, diurnal, lower in the late afternoon and after meals, and depressed by acute illness, so confirm with a fasting early-morning sample (p.3108, p.3118). Interpreting total testosterone without accounting for SHBG changes, leading to over- or under-diagnosis in obesity, aging, thyroid disease, or chronic illness (p.3106, p.3108). Mislabeling the normal aging decline as 'andropause' — there is no discrete andropause and population screening of all older men is not recommended (p.3117). Subjecting every man with gynecomastia to extensive workup, when most pubertal and many hospitalized men have benign glandular tissue (p.3116). Confusing retractile testis (no treatment needed) with true cryptorchidism (p.3114). Assuming corrected unilateral cryptorchidism guarantees normal fertility — sperm counts can remain reduced (p.3114). Overlooking drug, alcohol, opioid, marijuana, or anabolic-androgenic steroid use as reversible causes of suppressed testosterone (p.3114, p.3119). The hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis governs androgen production and spermatogenesis. Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH (regulated by kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin in KNDy neurons) drives pituitary LH and FSH roughly every 1-3 h. LH stimulates Leydig cell testosterone synthesis (rate-limited by StAR-mediated cholesterol transport into mitochondria and CYP11A1 side-chain cleavage); FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis and inhibin B production, the latter selectively suppressing FSH. Testosterone is converted by 5-alpha-reductase (SRD5A2) to the more potent DHT (required for external genital virilization and prostate growth) and aromatized by CYP19 to estradiol (mediating effects on bone, epiphyseal closure, libido). Disorders arise from gonadotropin deficiency (secondary/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, congenital such as GnRH-deficient/Kallmann syndrome or acquired from sellar masses, hyperprolactinemia, hemochromatosis, illness, drugs, obesity) or primary testicular failure (hypergonadotropic), e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, orchitis, chemo/radiation, torsion. Resistance syndromes (androgen receptor mutations, 5-alpha-reductase or aromatase deficiency) impair androgen action or conversion. Gynecomastia results from a relative excess of estrogen action on breast tissue (p.3102-3116). Outcomes depend on the underlying disorder. Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism is highly amenable to fertility restoration with pulsatile GnRH or gonadotropins, and 10-20% of congenital GnRH-deficient men may have spontaneous reversal in adulthood. In Klinefelter syndrome azoospermia is the rule, though sperm can sometimes be retrieved surgically (including in some non-mosaic men) for ICSI. After mumps orchitis the testis may recover or atrophy. Radiation effects on spermatogenesis are dose-dependent (transient decline below 1 Gy, temporary azoospermia at 1-2 Gy, usually permanent azoospermia above 2 Gy), while Leydig cells are relatively radioresistant (dysfunction generally only above 20 Gy). The age-related testosterone decline is gradual and progressive without a discrete abrupt fall (p.3107, p.3114-3115, p.3117). Diagnostic stratification of male testosterone deficiency (Harrison Fig. 403-8): early-morning total testosterone >350-400 ng/dL makes androgen deficiency unlikely; borderline values 200-350 ng/dL should be repeated with free testosterone; consistently low levels (notably <200 ng/dL) in association with symptoms confirm deficiency. Localization: high LH/FSH = primary (hypergonadotropic) testicular failure; low/inappropriately normal LH = secondary (hypogonadotropic). Harmonized normal total testosterone reference range in healthy young men is 264-916 ng/dL (p.3108, p.3117-3118).

Disorders of Ventilation — Alveolar hypoventilation, Hypoventilation syndromes, Chronic hyperventilation, Obesity hypoventilation syndrome, Central hypoventilation syndrome, Ondine's curse Parenchymal lung disease (obstructive such as COPD; restrictive such as interstitial lung disease; atelectasis; pulmonary embolus) Chest wall disorders (kyphoscoliosis, obesity, abdominal distention/ascites) Neuromuscular disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, phrenic nerve injury, spinal cord lesion, myopathy, muscular dystrophy) Depressed respiratory drive (narcotic/sedative use, brainstem stroke, hypothyroidism, primary alveolar hypoventilation) Brainstem structural lesions of the pons or medulla (stroke, tumor) Recurrent pneumonia from ineffective cough in neuromuscular disease can mimic or precipitate acute respiratory deterioration Arterial blood gas (the diagnostic hallmark): Paco2 >=45 mmHg defines hypoventilation; venous blood gas is an alternative, recognizing venous Pco2 runs a few points higher than arterial Serum bicarbonate (total CO2) as a sensitive but nonspecific screen: a level <27 mmol/L with normal renal function makes hypoventilation very unlikely, while >=27 mmol/L should prompt Paco2 measurement Chest x-ray and/or CT to identify lung/chest wall disease Pulmonary function testing including seated-versus-supine FVC (a 15-25% supine drop suggests diaphragmatic weakness) plus maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures Polysomnography to demonstrate nocturnal hypercapnia, central versus obstructive apneas/hypopneas, and to screen for OSA Brain CT or MRI to detect pontine/medullary structural lesions OSA screening tools (Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Berlin Questionnaire, STOP-Bang) recognizing their limited sensitivity/specificity Genetic testing for PHOX2b abnormalities in suspected congenital central hypoventilation syndrome Anxiety disorders and panic attacks (overlap with but are not equivalent to chronic hyperventilation) Mild asthma producing respiratory alkalosis (must be excluded before diagnosing chronic hyperventilation) Diabetic ketoacidosis presenting as acute hyperventilation Normal arterial CO2 (Paco2) sits between roughly 37 and 43 mmHg at sea level; all ventilatory disorders manifest as an abnormal Paco2 (Harrison 22e p.2273). Because Paco2 is governed by Paco2 = k(VCO2)/VA, every disturbance reflects altered CO2 production, minute ventilation, or dead-space fraction; a patient can breathe rapidly with a high minute ventilation yet still hypoventilate at the alveolar level if dead space is increased (Harrison 22e p.2273). Respiratory rhythm is generated in the brainstem (dorsal respiratory group and ventral respiratory column); the pre-Botzinger complex within the VRC is critical for inspiration, and its lesioning abolishes breathing entirely (Harrison 22e p.2273). Normal sleep brings an attenuated response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia, producing mild nocturnal hypoventilation that corrects on awakening (Harrison 22e p.2273). New-onset orthopnea is one of the earliest signs of reduced diaphragmatic force generation; 'paradoxical breathing' (abdomen moving inward on deep inspiration while supine) signals significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis (Harrison 22e p.2274). Chronic hypoventilation follows a characteristic sequence: an asymptomatic stage with normal daytime gases, then nocturnal hypoventilation appearing first in REM then non-REM sleep, then falling vital capacity, and finally daytime hypercapnia (Harrison 22e p.2274). The shared hallmark of all alveolar hypoventilation syndromes is a rise in alveolar and arterial Pco2 with a compensatory increase in plasma bicarbonate; the rising Paco2 displaces alveolar oxygen and commonly causes hypoxemia (Harrison 22e p.2274). Chronic hypoxemia from hypoventilation can drive secondary erythrocytosis, and the combination of chronic hypoxemia and hypercapnia can cause pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right heart failure (Harrison 22e p.2274). Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus chronic daytime hypoventilation (Paco2 >=45 mmHg) with no other explanation; obstructive sleep apnea coexists in nearly 90% of cases, with about 70% having severe OSA (Harrison 22e p.2275). In OHS, the depressed ventilatory responsiveness appears to be a consequence rather than a primary cause, since central drive often improves once sleep-disordered breathing is treated without weight change (Harrison 22e p.2276). Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine's curse, CCHS) is linked to PHOX2b gene abnormalities; affected patients lack ventilatory responses to hypoxia/hypercapnia, have mild waking hypercapnia, markedly elevated Paco2 in non-REM sleep, yet can paradoxically normalize Paco2 during exercise and REM sleep (Harrison 22e p.2276). In chronic hyperventilation, anxiety/panic are not synonymous with the condition; sustaining hypocapnia needs only about a 10% increase in alveolar ventilation, achievable through subtle pattern changes such as occasional sigh breaths or frequent yawning (Harrison 22e p.2277). Paradoxical (abdominal) breathing while supine indicating significant diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis New-onset orthopnea heralding reduced respiratory muscle force in neuromuscular disease Progressive 15-25% supine fall in FVC signaling impending chronic respiratory failure Daytime hypercapnia developing on top of established nocturnal hypoventilation Signs of secondary erythrocytosis, pulmonary hypertension, or right heart failure from chronic hypoxemia/hypercapnia Equating high minute ventilation with adequate alveolar ventilation: increased dead space can produce alveolar hypoventilation despite rapid breathing (Harrison 22e p.2273). Diagnosing primary respiratory drive disorder without excluding far more common secondary causes such as sedatives, chronic narcotics, and significant hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.2275). Misattributing chronic hyperventilation symptoms to cardiopulmonary disease and failing to exclude acute causes (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis, mild asthma) before labeling it chronic (Harrison 22e p.2276-2277). Overlooking that supplemental oxygen, even at low concentrations, can worsen hypercapnia in some hypoventilating patients (Harrison 22e p.2276). Failing to recognize that a serum bicarbonate elevated out of proportion to chronic respiratory acidosis (excess metabolic alkalosis) can itself aggravate hypoventilation (Harrison 22e p.2276). Adequate ventilation depends on a balance between respiratory drive and neuromuscular strength on one side and the elastic plus resistive loads of the respiratory system on the other. Reduced drive, impaired neuromuscular competence, or a markedly increased load lowers effective minute ventilation and produces hypercapnia; conversely, normal muscle strength combined with excessive drive yields hyperventilation and hypocapnia. Diseases reducing minute ventilation or increasing dead space fall into four broad categories: parenchymal lung/chest wall disease, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease, and respiratory drive disorders. 'Pump failure' encompasses disorders of drive, neural pathways, the neuromuscular junction, and muscle. In OHS the mechanism is multifactorial, combining OSA, increased work of breathing, respiratory muscle impairment against an excess-adiposity load, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and blunted central responsiveness to hypoxemia and hypercapnia. Chronic hyperventilation is conceptualized as having initiating and sustaining factors, with an initial event dropping Paco2 toward ~20 mmHg and resultant symptoms perpetuating overbreathing (Harrison 22e p.2273-2277). Chronic hypercapnia in COPD marks more advanced disease and carries worse survival than in equally severe normocapnic patients. Documented daytime hypercapnia treated with nocturnal noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation is associated with improved daytime gas exchange, prolonged survival, and better health-related quality of life. In OHS with severe OSA, both CPAP and NIPPV improve long-term Paco2/bicarbonate and reduce cardiovascular and overall mortality. Progressive neuromuscular disease tends to advance from sleep-only to round-the-clock ventilatory support need, though modern home ventilation can delay tracheostomy and institutionalization (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276). Diagnostic thresholds rather than a formal grading scale: hypoventilation is defined by Paco2 >=45 mmHg; OHS requires BMI >=30 kg/m2 plus Paco2 >=45 mmHg without another cause; severe OSA is an apnea-hypopnea index >30 events/h; stable chronic hypercapnic COPD considered for home high-intensity ventilation typically has Paco2 >52 mmHg with normal pH (Harrison 22e p.2275-2276).

Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, hereditary — type 1 RTA, classic distal RTA, SLC4A1, ATP6V0A4, ATP6V1B1 Proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis and Fanconi syndrome Type 4 (hyperkalaemic) renal tubular acidosis from hypoaldosteronism Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss from chronic diarrhoea Acquired distal RTA from Sjogren syndrome or other autoimmune disease Medullary sponge kidney with nephrocalcinosis Toxin- or drug-induced distal tubular dysfunction Serum electrolytes, bicarbonate and calculation of a normal serum anion gap Simultaneous urine pH and assessment of urinary anion gap or ammonium excretion Ammonium chloride or furosemide-fludrocortisone acidification testing where diagnosis is unclear Renal ultrasound or CT for nephrocalcinosis and stones Audiometry to detect associated sensorineural hearing loss Targeted genetic testing of SLC4A1, ATP6V1B1 and ATP6V0A4 Hereditary distal RTA reflects a failure of the distal nephron to secrete hydrogen ions, producing a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis The hallmark biochemical clue is an inappropriately alkaline urine (pH persistently high) despite systemic acidosis Hypokalaemia is characteristic and can cause muscle weakness, and profound hypokalaemia may precipitate paralysis or arrhythmia Chronic acidosis mobilises bone buffer, causing hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia and consequent nephrocalcinosis and stone formation Autosomal recessive forms (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4) are often associated with sensorineural hearing loss and present early; autosomal dominant SLC4A1 disease is generally milder Children may present with failure to thrive, rickets and polyuria, whereas adults may present with stones, osteomalacia or unexplained hypokalaemia Alkali replacement (for example potassium citrate or bicarbonate) corrects the acidosis, replaces potassium and raises citrate to limit nephrocalcinosis Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle paralysis or cardiac arrhythmia Failure to thrive or rickets in an infant or young child Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining renal function Obstructing stone with infection requiring urgent intervention Missing the diagnosis by not measuring urine pH during systemic acidosis, when it should be inappropriately high Overlooking associated hearing loss in recessive forms Attributing the hypokalaemia to diuretics or diarrhoea rather than tubular loss Correcting acidosis with sodium bicarbonate alone and worsening hypokalaemia by not replacing potassium Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis arises from impaired hydrogen ion secretion by the alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct. Inherited forms result from mutations affecting the apical H+-ATPase (ATP6V1B1, ATP6V0A4) or the basolateral chloride-bicarbonate exchanger AE1 (SLC4A1). Because the distal nephron cannot generate a steep enough pH gradient, net acid excretion falls and a hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis develops with inappropriately alkaline urine. Persistent acidosis drives calcium out of bone, raises urinary calcium and lowers citrate, promoting nephrocalcinosis and stones, while potassium wasting produces hypokalaemia. With sustained alkali and potassium replacement, growth, bone health and biochemistry usually improve and stone or nephrocalcinosis progression slows, though established nephrocalcinosis and chronic kidney impairment may persist.

Disturbances of Respiratory Function — Respiratory dysfunction, Disorders of lung ventilation and gas exchange, Pulmonary physiology disturbances Restrictive pattern from increased lung elastic recoil (e.g., idiopathic/interstitial pulmonary fibrosis) Restrictive pattern from chest-wall abnormality (e.g., obesity, kyphoscoliosis) Restrictive pattern from respiratory muscle weakness (e.g., myasthenia gravis, diaphragmatic paralysis, neuromuscular disease) Obstructive pattern from airway narrowing (e.g., asthma, chronic bronchitis) Obstructive pattern from loss of elastic recoil (e.g., emphysema) Pulmonary vascular disease (suggested by isolated low DLCO with otherwise preserved volumes) Upper/central airway obstruction (e.g., tracheal adenoma, post-tracheostomy stricture, tracheomalacia) Pneumonia or other alveolar-filling processes reduce respiratory system compliance and increase work of breathing, mimicking other causes of restrictive dyspnea Spirometry (FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, flow-volume loop) to characterize obstructive vs restrictive physiology and localize airway obstruction Absolute lung volumes by inert-gas (helium/neon) dilution or body plethysmography (plethysmography preferred in airflow obstruction, as dilution underestimates trapped gas) Single-breath diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) Arterial blood gas with calculation of the alveolar-arterial oxygen tension difference (A-a)DO2 and the alveolar gas equation Pulse oximetry for noninvasive hemoglobin saturation; capnography (end-tidal CO2) for noninvasive ventilation assessment Maximal inspiratory/expiratory mouth pressures and supine-vs-upright FVC to detect respiratory muscle / diaphragmatic weakness Chest imaging: ultrasound, plain radiograph (PA and lateral), CT (with contrast and/or PET when indicated) Further studies as guided by suspicion: bronchoscopy with lavage/biopsy, hypercoagulable and serologic testing, sputum analysis, echocardiography, surgical lung biopsy Pulmonary edema (alveolar filling reducing compliance) Anemia (lowers DLCO and oxygen content, mimicking a gas-transfer defect) Polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage (can elevate DLCO) Obstructive sleep apnea with associated pulmonary arterial hypertension lowering DLCO in an obese patient Cardiac causes of dyspnea (enlarged heart functioning as part of the chest-wall load) The respiratory system can be conceptualized as three functionally independent components: the lung (with its airways), the neuromuscular system (the force generated by respiratory muscles), and the chest wall (everything else, including the muscle mass itself, an obese abdomen, and an enlarged heart). Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the passive resting volume where outward recoil of the chest wall is exactly balanced by inward recoil of the lung; at FRC, negative intrapleural pressure offsets positive intrapulmonary pressure giving an airway pressure of 0. The combined respiratory system pressure-volume relationship is sigmoid: stiffness at high lung volumes is imparted by the lung, stiffness at low volumes by the chest wall (or airway closure), with compliance greatest in the mid-range where normal tidal breathing occurs. Expiratory airflow limitation is a normal lung property arising from collapsible (not rigid) bronchial airways: as gas accelerates toward the mouth the Bernoulli effect lowers intraluminal and transmural pressure, narrowing the airway, so harder effort yields no net increase in flow. Inspiratory airflow limitation is rarely caused by diffuse intrathoracic airway disease because more negative pleural pressure during inspiration increases airway transmural pressure and expands airways; instead, inspiratory flow limitation points toward extrathoracic/upper-airway narrowing (e.g., tracheal lesion, post-tracheostomy stricture). Adequacy of alveolar ventilation is reflected in PaCO2: alveolar and arterial CO2 tensions are equal, the controller normally targets ~40 mmHg, so PaCO2 below 40 indicates hyperventilation and above 40 indicates hypoventilation, with ventilatory failure being extreme hypoventilation. Only the tidal volume that exceeds the anatomic dead space delivers fresh gas to alveoli; dead space is increased functionally when ventilated lung receives no perfusion (e.g., distal to a large pulmonary embolus), 'wasting' that ventilation. Oxygen uptake in normal lung is perfusion-limited rather than diffusion-limited: hemoglobin is typically fully saturated by the time blood traverses only about one-third of the alveolar capillary. Hypoxemia from true shunt (perfusion of nonventilated lung) is refractory to supplemental oxygen, whereas hypoxemia from ventilation/perfusion heterogeneity (low V/Q regions) typically improves with oxygen therapy — a key bedside discriminator. DLCO interpretation: it falls in diseases that thicken or destroy alveolar membrane (pulmonary fibrosis, emphysema), curtail the pulmonary vasculature (pulmonary hypertension), or reduce capillary hemoglobin (anemia); it can be elevated in asthma, polycythemia, and pulmonary hemorrhage. In severe airflow obstruction, slowed expiratory flow prevents complete exhalation, raising operating FRC (dynamic hyperinflation / auto-PEEP); at these high volumes the system is less compliant, so the patient senses difficulty INHALING even though the root problem is EXPIRATORY obstruction. A normal FEV1/FVC ratio does not exclude airflow obstruction: obstruction can raise residual volume and lower FVC, rendering the ratio 'artifactually normal' — lung volumes should scale together (~85-115% predicted) in health, so disproportion is a clue. Hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen, suggesting true shunt physiology rather than simple V/Q mismatch Rising PaCO2 above 40 mmHg indicating alveolar hypoventilation, with extreme elevation signaling impending ventilatory failure Inspiratory flow plateau on the flow-volume loop, indicating extrathoracic/upper-airway obstruction Precipitous fall in PaO2 on exertion in emphysema, reflecting inability to raise cardiac output across a destroyed pulmonary vascular bed Supine FVC decrement greater than about 10-25% (versus the normal 3-8%) indicating significant diaphragmatic/neuromuscular weakness Isolated reduction in DLCO with preserved spirometry and volumes, prompting evaluation for pulmonary vascular disease Interpreting a normal FEV1/FVC ratio as excluding obstruction when raised RV has lowered FVC and made the ratio artifactually normal Relying on single-breath inert-gas dilution in airflow obstruction, which underestimates true lung volumes because poorly ventilated regions do not receive the inert gas Assuming alveolar hypoventilation alone explains severe hypoxemia at sea level breathing air — the alveolar gas equation shows this is uncommon unless barometric pressure is reduced (altitude) Forgetting that a normal chest radiograph does not exclude respiratory disease, especially airway and pulmonary vascular disorders Attributing a low DLCO to parenchymal disease without considering anemia, while overlooking that DLCO may be elevated in polycythemia or pulmonary hemorrhage Misreading dyspnea on inhalation in severe obstruction as a primary inspiratory problem when it stems from dynamic hyperinflation due to expiratory flow limitation Effective respiration requires tidal ventilation to freshen alveolar gas, perfusion of each alveolus proportional to its ventilation, and adequate diffusion of O2 and CO2 across the thin alveolar membrane (roughly 70 m2 of surface in about 7 L of thorax via multigenerational airway and vascular branching). Ventilation depends on the volume-related (elastic/static) and flow-related (dynamic) mechanical properties of lung, neuromuscular system, and chest wall; lung recoil rises with inflation while the passive chest wall stiffens at low volume. Disease deranges these properties in a limited number of ways: increased lung elastic recoil restricts volumes (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis lowers TLC/FRC/RV/FVC and DLCO but raises flow relative to volume); chest-wall abnormality (e.g., moderate obesity) blunts outward chest recoil and lowers FRC; reduced muscle strength (e.g., myasthenia gravis) lowers TLC and raises RV, reducing FVC/FEV1 as bystanders; decreased airway diameter (e.g., acute asthma) raises resistance and scoops the flow-volume loop; and decreased elastic recoil (e.g., severe emphysema) causes hyperinflation with very elevated TLC/FRC/RV and reduced DLCO. Gas-exchange failure (hypoxemia) results from low inspired oxygen tension, severe alveolar hypoventilation, perfusion of low-V/Q or unventilated (shunt) units, and, rarely, diffusion limitation; shunt blood disproportionately lowers arterial PaO2 because of the nonlinear oxyhemoglobin relationship. Hypercarbia accompanies disorders of ventilation, including severe obstruction and progressive restriction. Prognosis is determined by the underlying disorder rather than the physiologic pattern itself; the same abnormalities may arise from very different diseases, so pulmonary function testing alone often cannot discriminate among conditions. Many functional disturbances are reversible (e.g., bronchodilator-responsive airflow obstruction in acute asthma), whereas others reflect fixed structural loss (e.g., capillary and alveolar destruction in emphysema or fibrosis) that progressively impairs gas exchange and exercise capacity. No single formal severity grade applies; physiologic severity is judged by the degree of deviation from predicted values. Most lung-function measures are normal at 85-115% of predicted, and in health volumes scale together. Examples of marked derangement cited include severe emphysema (TLC ~130%, RV ~310%, FEV1 ~35% predicted, low DLCO ~40%) versus pulmonary fibrosis (TLC/FVC/FRC/RV ~60%, low DLCO). Airway resistance (Raw) is normally <2 cmH2O/L/s, and maximal mouth pressures >±60 cmH2O at FRC make significant muscle weakness unlikely.

Diverticular Disease — diverticulitis, diverticulosis Colorectal cancer (parallel epidemiology and overlapping presentation; must exclude with colonoscopy after an episode) Irritable bowel syndrome (SCAD can mimic it) Crohn's disease (diverticulitis can be confused with CD clinically and radiographically) Appendicitis Ischemic colitis Twisted ovarian cyst / gynecologic pathology Acute appendicitis Infectious colitis Pelvic inflammatory disease / tubo-ovarian abscess Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT (diagnostic modality of choice for diverticulitis) Multiplanar CT angiography for active diverticular bleeding localization Nuclear medicine tagged red-cell scan for bleeding localization Mesenteric angiography (allows superselective coil embolization if active bleeding is localized) Colonoscopy ~6 weeks after resolution to exclude malignancy (avoid during the acute attack) CRP and WBC count to gauge inflammation/disease progression risk Colorectal cancer Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis) Irritable bowel syndrome Ischemic colitis Giant sigmoid diverticulum (air-fluid level in LLQ on plain film) Diverticulosis is the most common cause of hematochezia (brisk lower-GI bleed) in patients >60 years; bleeding is abrupt in onset, usually painless, sometimes massive, and often from the right colon. Chronic or occult bleeding is NOT characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579). Only ~20% of patients with diverticulosis will ever have GI bleeding; most bleeds are self-limited and stop spontaneously with bowel rest (colonic diverticula stop bleeding spontaneously in >=90% of patients). Lifetime risk of rebleeding is ~25% (Harrison 22e p.2496, 2579). Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis characteristically presents with fever, anorexia, left lower quadrant abdominal pain, and obstipation (Harrison 22e p.2579). Diagnosis of diverticulitis is best made on a contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT showing sigmoid diverticula, thickened colonic wall >4 mm, and pericolic fat inflammation WITHOUT extravasation of contrast or fluid (Harrison 22e p.2579). Diverticula commonly affect the left and sigmoid colon and the rectum is always spared; however in Asian populations 70% of diverticula are in the right colon and cecum (Harrison 22e p.2579). The pseudodiverticulum (protrusion of mucosa and submucosa only, through the muscularis propria) is the most common type seen in the colon; a true diverticulum is herniation of the entire bowel wall (Harrison 22e p.2578). Perforated diverticular disease is staged using the Hinchey classification (I: confined paracolic abscess; II: distant/pelvic abscess after spontaneous closure; III: noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis; IV: free perforation with fecal peritonitis); modified to add stage Ia for phlegmon/early abscess (Harrison 22e p.2580). Pneumaturia or passage of stool/air through the vagina or skin signals a fistula (colovesical, colovaginal, or colocutaneous); colovaginal fistulas are more common in women who have undergone hysterectomy (Harrison 22e p.2579). Colonoscopy should be considered ~6 weeks AFTER resolution of a first episode, because colon cancer prevalence is low overall (<2%) but higher after complicated diverticulitis (6-8%) (Harrison 22e p.2580). Routine antibiotics do NOT shorten time to symptom resolution or reduce complications/recurrence in immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticular disease (AVOD and DIABOLO trials, plus meta-analysis) (Harrison 22e p.2580). Diverticulosis affects about half the population aged >60 years and the majority remain asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease (Harrison 22e p.2578). Signs of peritonitis indicating diverticular perforation Abscess formation (~16% of complicated disease) with abdominal distention and localized peritonitis Free perforation with fecal peritonitis (Hinchey IV) Fistula (colovesical with pneumaturia, colovaginal, colocutaneous) Obstruction/stricture Air-fluid level in LLQ on plain film suggesting giant sigmoid diverticulum (impending perforation) Massive or refractory lower-GI hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, or large-volume transfusion requirement Immunocompromise, chronic renal failure, or collagen-vascular disease (fivefold greater perforation risk on recurrent attacks) Do NOT perform colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis (risk of perforation); defer it ~6 weeks until the attack resolves. Do not reflexively give antibiotics for uncomplicated diverticulitis in immunocompetent patients - trials show no benefit. The historical advice to avoid nuts, corn, and popcorn rests on anecdotal data only and is not evidence-based; higher intake was actually associated with lower recurrence risk. Mesalazine appears to help symptoms in SUDD but shows no benefit once objective inflammation (CRP, imaging) is considered. A systematic review found no benefit to probiotics used alone. Right-sided diverticula predominate in Asian populations, so a right-colon source should not be dismissed. Diverticula form where the nutrient artery (vasa recta) penetrates the muscularis propria, creating a point of weakness in the colonic wall; most arise in the sigmoid colon, likely reflecting its high-pressure zone where higher-amplitude contractions and firm/constipated stool act on a weak segment. Pathogenesis is now viewed as multifactorial rather than simply low-fiber diet: gut dysbiosis, chronic low-grade inflammation driving neuronal degeneration with resulting dysmotility and high intraluminal pressure, and abnormal collagen cross-linking causing loss of compliance all contribute. Genome-wide association studies (Iceland, Denmark, UK biobanks) link LAMB4 (extracellular-matrix laminin family) and TNFSF15 (TNF family, inflammation) variants to early-onset severe disease. Complications occur when the vasa recta is compressed or eroded (bleeding) or a diverticulum perforates (Harrison 22e p.2578-2579). Most patients with diverticulosis stay asymptomatic; only ~5% develop acute diverticular disease, and 10-25% of those with diverticular disease have recurrent symptoms with up to 10% requiring surgery. Diverticular bleeds are largely self-limited (spontaneous cessation in >=90%), with lifetime rebleeding risk ~25%. After complicated diverticulitis the risk of underlying colon cancer rises to 6-8% (vs <2% overall). Elective surgical resection for recurrent SUDD improved quality of life and was more cost-effective at 5 years (DIRECT trial) (Harrison 22e p.2578-2581). Hinchey classification of perforated diverticulitis: Stage I - perforation with confined paracolic abscess (modified stage Ia = phlegmon/early abscess); Stage II - perforation that closed spontaneously with distant (pelvic) abscess; Stage III - noncommunicating perforation with purulent peritonitis (diverticular neck closed off); Stage IV - free perforation communicating with the peritoneum producing fecal peritonitis. Clinically, disease is divided into uncomplicated (~75%) and complicated (~25%: abscess 16%, perforation 10%, stricture 5%, fistula 2%) (Harrison 22e p.2579-2580).

Diabetic ketoacidosis — Venous gas Blood & urine ketones Glucose, electrolytes Search for precipitant (infection) DKA protocol; look for precipitating infection Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high-anion-gap acidosis (predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate) without hyperglycaemia, usually with preserved renal function, in chronic alcohol use with vomiting and poor intake (p.413). Starvation ketoacidosis — ketoacidosis with normal or low glucose (p.413). Other high-anion-gap acidoses: lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions (e.g. salicylates), and renal failure/uraemia (p.413). Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measured directly (more reliable than urine nitroprusside ketones) (p.413). Anion gap calculation, including assessment for a mixed non-anion-gap / high-anion-gap acidosis when the change in bicarbonate exceeds the change in anion gap (p.413). Acute pancreatitis can mimic DKA (and vice versa), with overlapping abdominal pain; DKA may itself be accompanied by amylase elevation, complicating the distinction (p.2788). An acetone-like fruity odour on the breath is a classic bedside clue to ketoacidosis (p.93). Urine dipstick (nitroprusside reaction) detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate the true degree of ketosis; measure plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate directly (p.413). As the circulation is restored with fluids, beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, so the nitroprusside ketone reading may paradoxically become more positive during treatment rather than reflecting worsening disease (p.413). Glucose may be normal or only mildly raised in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2-inhibitor associated) and in starvation ketoacidosis, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis (p.413). Excretion of ketoacids obligates loss of cations (sodium, potassium), worsening volume depletion and promoting chloride retention (p.413). Mucormycosis risk: DKA patients are at high risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis; acidosis frees iron from carrier proteins and beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates fungal adherence/penetration receptors — consider in a DKA patient with sinus/orbital/facial signs (p.1761). Severe acidaemia (pH <7.00) or shock identifies the small subset where bicarbonate may be considered; cerebral oedema risk limits its use (p.413). Hyperchloraemic (non-anion-gap) acidosis and volume overload can be precipitated by aggressive isotonic saline during treatment (p.413). Relying on urine ketone dipstick, which misses beta-hydroxybutyrate and underestimates ketosis (p.413). Interpreting a rising nitroprusside ketone result during fluid resuscitation as deterioration, when it reflects the beta-hydroxybutyrate-to-acetoacetate shift (p.413). Assuming a normal/near-normal glucose excludes DKA, missing euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors (p.413). Over-resuscitation with isotonic saline causing volume overload and/or hyperchloraemic acidosis (p.413). DKA results from increased fatty acid metabolism with accumulation of the ketoacids acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. It typically occurs in insulin-dependent diabetes when insulin is stopped or when an intercurrent illness (e.g. infection, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction) acutely raises insulin requirements. In euglycaemic DKA caused by SGLT2 inhibitors, glycosuria drives an osmotic diuresis and volume depletion while plasma glucose stays in the normal range despite the ketoacidosis (p.413).

Donovanosis — Granuloma inguinale, Granuloma venereum Primary syphilitic chancre (Harrison 22e p.1357) Secondary syphilis with condylomata lata (Harrison 22e p.1357) Chancroid (Harrison 22e p.1357) Lymphogranuloma venereum (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital herpes (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital neoplasm / carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1357) Amebiasis (Harrison 22e p.1357) Rhinoscleroma on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Leishmaniasis on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Histoplasmosis on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Tissue smear for Donovan bodies stained with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357) Crush preparation of granulation tissue spread between two slides (Harrison 22e p.1357) Histologic biopsy showing chronic inflammation, microabscesses, and rete ridge elongation (Harrison 22e p.1357) phoE gene PCR with colorimetric detection to differentiate K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species (Harrison 22e p.1357) Multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis (Harrison 22e p.1357) Cervical carcinoma (cervical lesions may mimic it) (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.1357) Chronic, progressive bacterial infection that predominantly involves the genital region and is regarded as a sexually transmitted infection of low infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1356). Caused by Klebsiella granulomatis comb nov; the older name Calymmatobacterium granulomatis is still favored by some authorities based on 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis (Harrison 22e p.1356). Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies (about 1.5 x 0.7 micrometers) within large mononuclear Pund cells, where they appear as gram-negative cysts with a characteristic safety-pin appearance (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357). When donovanosis is suspected clinically, the smear for Donovan bodies should be obtained before swabs for other genital ulcer pathogens so adequate material is collected; smears can be read at the bedside with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357). An experienced clinician's diagnosis based on lesion appearance has a high positive predictive value, and donovanosis is probably the most readily recognizable cause of genital ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358). Four lesion types are described: classic beefy-red ulcerogranulomatous ulcer that bleeds easily on touch, hypertrophic/verrucous ulcer with a raised irregular edge, necrotic foul-smelling destructive ulcer, and sclerotic/cicatricial fibrous lesion (Harrison 22e p.1357). Genitalia are affected in about 90% of patients and the inguinal region in about 10%; lymphadenitis is uncommon, in contrast to other ulcerative STIs (Harrison 22e p.1357). Cervical lesions can mimic cervical carcinoma, and in men lesions are associated with lack of circumcision (Harrison 22e p.1357). Extragenital lesions occur in about 6% of cases and may involve the lip, gums, cheek, palate, pharynx, larynx, and chest; hematogenous spread to liver and bone has been reported (Harrison 22e p.1357). Donovanosis is a recognized risk factor for HIV infection, and its global decline likely reflects more effective management of genital ulcers given their role in HIV transmission (Harrison 22e p.1357). The estimated incubation period is approximately 50 days based on experimental human infection, though it remains uncertain (Harrison 22e p.1357). A diagnostic PCR exploits two unique base changes in the phoE gene that eliminate Hae111 restriction sites, distinguishing K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species; a multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis exists (Harrison 22e p.1357). Late presentation with extensive ulceration (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358) Cervical lesion mimicking carcinoma requiring exclusion of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1357) Neoplastic change developing within chronic lesions (Harrison 22e p.1357) Stenosis of the urethra, vagina, or anus (Harrison 22e p.1357) Pseudoelephantiasis from lymphatic involvement (Harrison 22e p.1357) Lesions in newborns (may present as ear infection) or children, prompting evaluation for source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1357) Collecting other genital-ulcer swabs before the Donovan body smear can leave insufficient material for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357). Serologic tests are only poorly specific and are not currently used, so they should not be relied upon (Harrison 22e p.1357). Mixed infections with other genital ulcer pathogens are common and may obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357). Lymphadenitis is uncommon, so its absence should not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1357). Cervical lesions can be mistaken for cervical carcinoma and vice versa (Harrison 22e p.1357). During pregnancy lesions develop more quickly and respond more slowly, so closer monitoring is needed (Harrison 22e p.1357). Donovanosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the intracellular gram-negative organism Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). The lesion begins as a papule or subcutaneous nodule that ulcerates, often after trauma. The organism resides within macrophages and the stratum malpighii as intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies inside large mononuclear (Pund) cells; these cysts rupture and release infective organisms. Histology shows chronic inflammation with infiltration by plasma cells and neutrophils, and epithelial changes including ulceration, microabscesses, and elongation of the rete ridges. The organism resisted reproducible culture until the mid-1990s, when isolation in peripheral-blood monocytes and human epithelial cell lines was achieved (Harrison 22e p.1356-1357). Donovanosis is a treatable condition, and reassurance is an important part of care given the embarrassment and low self-esteem many patients experience. It is now confined to a few specific geographic locations, has been almost entirely eliminated in Australia and is close to elimination in South Africa, and its global eradication is considered a distinct possibility. Surgery may be required for very advanced lesions, and patients treated for shorter courses require monitoring until lesions heal completely (Harrison 22e p.1357-1358). No formal severity grading is given. Lesions are categorized morphologically into four types: classic ulcerogranulomatous, hypertrophic/verrucous, necrotic/destructive, and sclerotic/cicatricial (Harrison 22e p.1357).

Dopa-responsive dystonia — DRD, Segawa disease, GCH1, GTP cyclohydrolase 1 deficiency, hereditary progressive dystonia with diurnal fluctuation, DYT5 Cerebral palsy (spastic diplegia) Hereditary spastic paraplegia Young-onset Parkinson disease and other genetic parkinsonism DYT1 and other early-onset primary dystonias Juvenile Huntington disease Other inborn errors of neurotransmitter metabolism A carefully monitored therapeutic levodopa trial to demonstrate the characteristic sustained response Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter and pterin (biopterin/neopterin) analysis Phenylalanine loading test to assess tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism Molecular genetic testing of GCH1 and, where indicated, tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase genes Brain MRI, typically normal, to exclude structural and neurodegenerative causes Most often caused by autosomal dominant variants in GCH1 (GTP cyclohydrolase 1), with reduced penetrance and a female predominance; recessive forms involve tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase Classic presentation is childhood-onset lower-limb dystonia causing gait disturbance, often with a striking diurnal fluctuation (symptoms mild in the morning and worsening through the day) The defining feature is a dramatic and sustained response to low-dose levodopa, with near-complete and durable symptom control and without the motor fluctuations seen in Parkinson disease Because the levodopa response is so characteristic and life-changing, a therapeutic levodopa trial is essential in any child or young person with unexplained dystonia or an atypical spastic-diplegia-like picture Some patients are misdiagnosed with cerebral palsy or hereditary spastic paraplegia for years before a levodopa trial reveals the diagnosis Later-onset presentations can mimic parkinsonism, and features may include brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response, adding to diagnostic confusion Diagnosis is supported by cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter and pterin analysis and by phenylalanine loading, and confirmed by molecular genetic testing Unlike most dystonias the disorder is eminently treatable, so recognition carries a high clinical payoff Diurnally fluctuating dystonia in a child that has been labelled cerebral palsy without a levodopa trial Progressive dystonia with developmental regression suggesting a broader neurotransmitter disorder Severe generalised dystonia impairing gait, feeding, or respiration Failure to respond to an adequate levodopa trial, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Failing to undertake a levodopa trial in young-onset dystonia and thereby missing an eminently treatable disorder Accepting a longstanding label of cerebral palsy or spastic paraplegia without questioning atypical features such as diurnal fluctuation Attributing a partial or absent response to inadequate trial duration rather than reassessing the diagnosis Overlooking the recessive tyrosine hydroxylase and sepiapterin reductase forms, which may have a more complex phenotype Dopa-responsive dystonia is a disorder of dopamine biosynthesis. In the common autosomal dominant form, variants in GCH1 reduce GTP cyclohydrolase 1 activity, the first and rate-limiting step in producing tetrahydrobiopterin, the essential cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase. Reduced cofactor availability lowers dopamine synthesis in nigrostriatal neurons without causing their degeneration, so the deficit is biochemical rather than structural. Because the neurons remain intact, replacing the downstream product with levodopa restores near-normal dopaminergic signalling, explaining the sustained and complete response and the absence of levodopa-related motor complications. With levodopa treatment the prognosis is excellent: most patients achieve near-complete, durable symptom control and normal or near-normal function, and the benefit is sustained for decades without the motor complications typical of Parkinson disease. Untreated, symptoms progress and cause significant disability.

Down Syndrome — trisomy 21, Down's syndrome, trisomy 21 syndrome Other trisomies (trisomy 18, trisomy 13) Congenital hypothyroidism (overlapping hypotonia and coarse features) Zellweger and other syndromes with hypotonia Other syndromic causes of intellectual disability Non-syndromic congenital heart disease Karyotype to confirm trisomy 21 and identify translocation or mosaicism Echocardiography to detect congenital heart disease Thyroid function testing at birth and on a scheduled basis Hearing and vision assessments Full blood count to screen for transient myeloproliferative disorder and later leukaemia Cervical spine assessment when symptoms suggest atlantoaxial instability The most common autosomal chromosomal disorder and a leading genetic cause of intellectual disability, resulting from an extra copy of chromosome 21. Most cases are due to meiotic nondisjunction, with incidence rising markedly with advancing maternal age; a minority result from translocation or mosaicism. Recognisable features include hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, small ears, a single transverse palmar crease, and a sandal gap between the toes. Congenital heart disease is common, particularly atrioventricular septal defects, so early echocardiography is recommended. Gastrointestinal anomalies such as duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease occur more frequently. There is increased risk of hypothyroidism, hearing and visual impairment, obstructive sleep apnoea, and atlantoaxial instability, warranting scheduled surveillance. Children have a higher risk of transient myeloproliferative disorder in the newborn period and of leukaemia in childhood. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, which also identifies translocations relevant to recurrence risk and family counselling. Early developmental support and coordinated multidisciplinary care improve developmental and health outcomes. Signs of significant congenital heart disease or heart failure Bilious vomiting or abdominal signs suggesting intestinal obstruction Neurological signs of cervical cord compression from atlantoaxial instability Persistent pallor, bruising, or abnormal blood counts suggesting leukaemia Severe obstructive sleep apnoea Assuming a normal heart without echocardiographic screening Overlooking hypothyroidism, which can mimic or worsen developmental delay Missing atlantoaxial instability before activities or anaesthesia in symptomatic children Failing to follow structured health surveillance recommendations The presence of a third copy of chromosome 21 leads to over-expression of the genes it carries, disrupting normal development across multiple organ systems in a dosage-dependent manner. This gene-dosage imbalance affects neurodevelopment, cardiac and gastrointestinal morphogenesis, immune function, and haematopoiesis. Most trisomy 21 arises from failure of chromosomal separation during meiosis (nondisjunction), while translocation and mosaic forms produce the extra genetic material through other mechanisms. Life expectancy has improved substantially with modern medical and surgical care and now commonly extends into adulthood; outcomes depend largely on cardiac disease and other complications, and most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability with early-onset Alzheimer-type changes in later life.

Dracunculiasis (Guinea worm disease) — Guinea worm disease, Dracunculus medinensis infection, dracontiasis, Medina worm, guinea worm infection Cutaneous larva migrans and other migratory helminth infections Bacterial skin abscess or cellulitis Tropical (phagedenic) ulcer Myiasis Foreign body granuloma or retained foreign material Cutaneous larva currens (strongyloidiasis) Clinical identification of the emerging adult worm at the skin ulcer Microscopy of fluid expressed from the lesion for larvae after water contact Wound assessment for secondary bacterial infection Plain radiography, which may reveal a calcified dead worm in chronic cases Review of tetanus immunisation status Assessment of drinking-water source and exposure history for public health action Caused by the nematode Dracunculus medinensis, acquired by drinking stagnant water containing infected copepods (water fleas, Cyclops) The target of an international eradication programme, so cases are now rare and geographically restricted, but recognition remains important After a prolonged incubation of about a year, the gravid female worm migrates to the skin, most often of the lower leg or foot, forming a painful blister that ulcerates Contact of the lesion with water triggers the worm to discharge larvae, producing intense local burning that patients relieve by immersing the limb in water, perpetuating transmission Diagnosis is clinical, based on the visible emerging worm; larvae may be seen when the ulcer contacts water There is no reliable curative drug; management is by slow, careful extraction of the worm over days by winding it onto a stick, with wound care and prevention of secondary bacterial infection Prevention centres on safe drinking water (filtering or treating), health education, and containment of cases to interrupt the life cycle Secondary bacterial infection with spreading cellulitis, abscess, or sepsis Features suggesting tetanus from a contaminated wound Septic arthritis or contracture if a worm ruptures near a joint Severe systemic hypersensitivity if the worm breaks during extraction Pulling the worm out too quickly and rupturing it, provoking severe inflammation Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and secondary bacterial infection of the ulcer Missing the diagnosis outside classically endemic areas as eradication progresses Failing to counsel patients to avoid water contact, which perpetuates transmission Dracunculiasis results from ingesting water containing copepods infected with Dracunculus medinensis larvae. Gastric acid frees the larvae, which penetrate the intestinal wall and migrate into the abdominal and retroperitoneal tissues where they mature and mate. Over roughly a year the fertilised female worm grows to great length and migrates through subcutaneous tissue, usually to a distal limb. There it induces a painful blister; on contact with water the worm ruptures the skin and expels motile larvae, which are ingested by copepods to complete the cycle. Most symptoms arise from the migrating and emerging worm and the intense local inflammatory and allergic response, with pain, blistering, and ulceration. Secondary bacterial infection, cellulitis, abscess, tetanus, or joint involvement can complicate the emergence, and a retained or broken worm can provoke severe inflammation. The infection is rarely fatal and the worm is ultimately expelled or extracted, but the process is protracted and disabling; prognosis is good with careful wound care, though secondary infection or joint involvement can cause lasting morbidity.

Dravet syndrome — SCN1A, severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy, SMEI, polymorphic epilepsy of infancy Simple or complex febrile seizures Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) PCDH19-related epilepsy Other early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. KCNQ2, SCN2A) Mitochondrial or metabolic epilepsies Structural focal epilepsy on neuroimaging Targeted or panel gene testing for SCN1A and related epilepsy genes Prolonged or video EEG, which may be normal early and later shows generalised or multifocal epileptiform discharges Brain MRI, typically normal early but useful to exclude structural causes Metabolic screening where an inborn error of metabolism is considered Assessment of development and cognition to document the encephalopathic trajectory Presents in a previously healthy infant, typically in the first year of life, with prolonged febrile and afebrile hemiclonic or generalised seizures often triggered by fever, illness or vaccination The great majority of cases are caused by loss-of-function variants in the SCN1A gene encoding a voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit Seizures are characteristically sensitive to temperature elevation and can be precipitated by hot baths, exertion or environmental heat Multiple seizure types emerge over the second year, including myoclonic, atypical absence, focal and atonic seizures, with a tendency to status epilepticus Development is usually normal at onset but slows or regresses from the second year, with later intellectual disability, ataxia and behavioural difficulties Sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medications should generally be avoided because they typically aggravate seizures in this channelopathy There is a heightened risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), so seizure control and safety counselling are priorities Prolonged or repeated febrile seizures progressing to convulsive status epilepticus Developmental slowing or regression in the second year of life Seizure aggravation after introduction of a sodium-channel-blocking agent Features suggesting elevated SUDEP risk such as frequent nocturnal convulsions Dismissing early prolonged febrile seizures as simple febrile convulsions and delaying genetic testing Prescribing sodium-channel blockers, which commonly worsen seizures in this condition Assuming a normal early EEG or MRI excludes the diagnosis Overlooking fever, illness and heat as consistent seizure triggers requiring aggressive fever management Dravet syndrome is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused in most patients by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SCN1A, which encodes the Nav1.1 voltage-gated sodium channel. Nav1.1 is expressed preferentially in inhibitory GABAergic interneurons, so reduced channel function impairs interneuron firing and disinhibits cortical and hippocampal networks, producing hyperexcitability and a low threshold for seizures, particularly with rises in body temperature. The same interneuron dysfunction is thought to underlie the associated cognitive, motor and behavioural impairments that define the encephalopathy. Seizures typically persist into adulthood and are often drug-resistant, with associated intellectual disability, gait disturbance and behavioural problems. Mortality is elevated, largely from SUDEP and status epilepticus, so long-term multidisciplinary care and safety planning are essential.

Drowning — submersion injury, near-drowning, immersion injury Primary cardiac arrest with secondary immersion Seizure or syncope precipitating submersion Cervical spinal cord injury from diving Intoxication (alcohol or drugs) as a contributing factor Acute coronary syndrome or arrhythmia Arterial blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia and acidosis Chest imaging to assess for aspiration and pulmonary oedema Core temperature measurement for hypothermia ECG and cardiac monitoring Capillary glucose, electrolytes, and cervical spine imaging where trauma is suspected Drowning is the process of respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid; outdated terms such as near-drowning, wet, dry, and secondary drowning are no longer recommended The central injury is hypoxaemia; the historical distinction between fresh and salt water has little practical bearing on resuscitation Correcting hypoxia takes priority - rescue breathing and early effective ventilation are the most important interventions, and resuscitation should begin with airway and breathing rather than the usual circulation-first approach Aspirated water washes out surfactant and injures the alveolar-capillary membrane, and pulmonary oedema or acute respiratory distress syndrome may evolve over the following hours Symptomatic survivors need a period of observation, as respiratory deterioration can be delayed; a completely asymptomatic patient with normal oxygenation after several hours is at low risk Suspect and manage hypothermia, which frequently accompanies submersion and can be protective of the brain, so resuscitation should continue until the patient is rewarmed Consider precipitating and associated conditions, including cervical spine injury (in diving), seizures, arrhythmia, intoxication, and hypoglycaemia Prophylactic antibiotics and routine corticosteroids are not recommended; antibiotics are reserved for established infection or grossly contaminated water Hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, or need for ventilatory support Reduced conscious level or coma indicating hypoxic brain injury Cardiac arrest or significant arrhythmia Severe hypothermia requiring continued resuscitation during rewarming Delayed worsening of oxygenation over the observation period Prioritising chest compressions over ventilation in a hypoxia-driven arrest Discharging a symptomatic patient too early and missing delayed respiratory deterioration Terminating resuscitation before adequately rewarming a hypothermic patient Overlooking a precipitating cause such as seizure, arrhythmia, cervical injury, or intoxication Submersion triggers breath-holding, then involuntary aspiration of water or laryngospasm, leading to progressive hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis. Aspirated fluid disrupts and washes out pulmonary surfactant and damages the alveolar-capillary membrane, causing atelectasis, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, and potentially acute respiratory distress syndrome. Sustained hypoxia causes global tissue injury, with the brain most vulnerable to hypoxic-ischaemic damage. Cardiac arrhythmias and arrest follow severe hypoxia and acidosis, and coexisting hypothermia alters both the injury and the resuscitation. Outcome is largely determined by the duration of submersion and hypoxia and the neurological status at the scene and on arrival; prolonged submersion and persistent coma predict poor neurological recovery, whereas patients who are alert with normal oxygenation generally do well, and hypothermia can occasionally allow good recovery after prolonged arrest.

Drug allergy — drug hypersensitivity, medication allergy, adverse drug reaction (immune-mediated) Non-immune (pharmacologic) intolerance and dose-related toxicity Viral exanthem coinciding with drug therapy Direct mast-cell activation (e.g. by opioids, vancomycin infusion reaction) NSAID- or ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema through non-IgE mechanisms Underlying autoimmune or infectious disease producing rash or organ dysfunction Chronic spontaneous urticaria unrelated to the drug Skin prick and intradermal testing where validated (penicillins, perioperative agents) Serum drug-specific IgE where available and serum tryptase during acute reactions Supervised graded drug challenge to confirm or exclude allergy Delayed-reading intradermal or patch testing for suspected type IV reactions HLA genotyping before selected high-risk drugs where guidelines recommend it Blood count, eosinophils, liver and renal function in suspected DRESS or systemic involvement True drug allergy is an immune-mediated subset of adverse drug reactions and must be distinguished from predictable dose-related side effects and non-immune intolerance The Gell and Coombs framework is useful: immediate IgE-mediated reactions (type I) cause urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis, while delayed T-cell-mediated reactions (type IV) cause most drug-induced rashes The tempo matters: immediate reactions arise within minutes to an hour of exposure, whereas delayed maculopapular eruptions and severe cutaneous reactions typically appear days into a course Beta-lactam antibiotics are the commonest cause of drug-induced anaphylaxis, but a reported penicillin allergy is frequently inaccurate and unnecessarily drives use of broader, more toxic alternatives Severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and DRESS are potentially fatal and are suggested by mucosal involvement, skin pain, blistering, fever, facial oedema, and organ dysfunction Skin testing is validated mainly for penicillins and perioperative agents; specific IgE and in-vitro tests are limited, so the supervised graded challenge remains the definitive test for many drugs Management principles are immediate cessation of the culprit drug, treatment of the reaction, clear documentation and patient warning, and selection of a structurally unrelated alternative Desensitisation can allow temporary tolerance when a culprit drug is essential and no alternative exists, but it is contraindicated in severe cutaneous reactions such as SJS/TEN and DRESS Careful de-labelling of unverified penicillin allergy through history and, where appropriate, challenge is an important antimicrobial-stewardship intervention Anaphylaxis with hypotension or airway compromise requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline Mucosal erosions, skin blistering or pain, or positive Nikolsky sign suggesting SJS/TEN Fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and organ involvement suggesting DRESS Any severe cutaneous adverse reaction, in which re-exposure or desensitisation is contraindicated Accepting an unverified allergy label and defaulting to broader, more toxic alternatives Attempting desensitisation or re-challenge after a severe cutaneous reaction Mistaking a viral rash or predictable side effect for true allergy, or vice versa Failing to document the reaction clearly and counsel the patient about cross-reacting agents Immune-mediated drug reactions occur when a drug or its reactive metabolite, often after binding host protein as a hapten, is recognised by the adaptive immune system. Type I reactions involve drug-specific IgE on mast cells and basophils, producing immediate mediator release. Type II reactions are antibody-mediated cytotoxicity against drug-coated cells (e.g. immune haemolysis, thrombocytopenia), and type III reactions involve immune-complex deposition (serum sickness, vasculitis). Type IV delayed reactions are T-cell-driven and range from benign exanthems to severe cutaneous reactions; the p-i concept describes direct, non-covalent drug interaction with immune receptors, and specific HLA alleles predispose to particular severe reactions. Most benign exanthems and immediate reactions resolve fully once the drug is withdrawn and future exposure avoided. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions carry significant morbidity and mortality, particularly toxic epidermal necrolysis, and require urgent specialist and supportive care.

Drug intoxication / poisoning — Toxidrome assessment Paracetamol/salicylate levels ABG, osmolar gap Specific antidotes where available Characterise overall physiologic state and toxidrome from vital signs and neuromuscular exam (p.3704) Anion gap (raised AGMA in methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, or any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures or shock; low anion gap with bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, magnesium) (p.3705) Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as an alcohol or glycol) (p.3705) Serum lactate (low relative to anion gap in alcohol/glycol intoxication, high and near the anion gap in hypoperfusion) (p.3705) Glucose, electrolytes, ketones (hypo-/hyperglycaemia and hypo-/hyperkalaemia patterns can implicate specific agents) (p.3705) ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias suggest specific agent classes) (p.3706) Abdominal/chest radiograph (radiopaque densities suggest heavy metals, drug packets, iron, enteric-coated or salicylate tablets; CXR for pulmonary edema/aspiration) (p.3706) Quantitative serum levels (acetaminophen, alcohols incl. ethylene glycol/methanol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) guide management (p.3706) Coagulation (PT/INR) for warfarin/rodenticide risk stratification, though unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose (p.3705) Psychogenic illness / anxiety reaction (mass hysteria, fear of poisoning) producing symptoms inconsistent with the exposure history (p.3705) Structural CNS lesion - focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt evaluation for a structural cause (p.3703) Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first classify the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a recognizable toxidrome (p.3704). Core temperature is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant (e.g. cocaine) poisoning or in drug/alcohol/GHB withdrawal, so it must be measured even in difficult or combative patients (p.3704). Mydriasis is common to all stimulant states but is most marked with anticholinergics (muscarinic loss of pupil reactivity); cocaine and other sympathomimetics enlarge pupils yet retain some light reactivity (p.3704). The anticholinergic toxidrome is distinguished from other stimulant states by hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds and urinary retention, whereas sympathomimetic states cause diaphoresis and increased bowel activity (p.3704). Miosis points to a depressed state from opioids or cholinergic agents; muscarinic/nicotinic features separate cholinergic poisoning from opioid poisoning (p.3704-3705). In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangements are secondary to CNS depression and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression); marked cardiovascular depression with preserved consciousness instead suggests a peripherally acting sympatholytic (p.3705). Rotatory nystagmus among stimulated patients is essentially specific to phencyclidine and ketamine (p.3704). A near-normal exam may reflect a nontoxic exposure, psychogenic illness, or a 'toxic time-bomb' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism); once-daily reformulations have made these increasingly common (p.3705). Rapid response of altered mental status to IV dextrose, naloxone or flumazenil is virtually diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively (p.3706). Most patients who are or become asymptomatic by 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and may be discharged, but longer observation is required after 'toxic time-bomb' ingestions (p.3707). Temperature elevation (grade 4 stimulation) - most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning and withdrawal (p.3704) Coma, seizures or cardiovascular collapse (grade 4 physiologic stimulation or depression) (p.3705) Focal neurologic findings - uncommon in poisoning and suggest a structural CNS lesion (p.3703) Suspicion of 'body packing'/'body stuffing' in patients ill after foreign travel or arrest (p.3703) High blood levels of agents with more toxic metabolites (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) signalling need for antidote or dialysis (p.3707) Rapid hospital urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only, cannot confirm the exact substance, and are not diagnostic or forensic; false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones triggering false-positive opiate screens) and false negatives are common (p.3706). A negative drug screen does not exclude poisoning - the agent may be undetectable by the assay (e.g. synthetic cannabinoids/spice, cathinones/bath salts, kratom) or present below the limit of detection at the time of sampling; repeat testing later may turn positive (p.3706). Qualitative drug screens are not clinically useful or cost-effective when the patient is asymptomatic or the picture fits the reported history; reserve them for severe or unexplained toxicity (coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms) (p.3706). Blood levels obtained during absorption/distribution may exceed tissue levels and may not correlate with toxicity (p.3707). In polydrug overdose a clear toxidrome may be obscured when different drug classes counteract each other's physiologic effects (p.3704). Physostigmine fully reverses anticholinergic poisoning but can also produce some arousal in CNS depression of any cause, so arousal alone is not specific (p.3706). Overdose effects begin sooner, peak later and last longer than therapeutic-dose effects, and an agent's published (therapeutic) pharmacokinetics differ from its toxicokinetics in overdose (p.3707). Poisoning is a dose-related adverse effect from exposure to a chemical, drug or other xenobiotic. Responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphism, enzyme induction or inhibition by co-ingestants, and acquired tolerance. Toxicity may be local or systemic depending on route, the agent's physicochemical properties and mechanism, and its severity/reversibility depends on the functional reserve of the patient or target organ (influenced by age and pre-existing disease) (p.3703). Overall mortality is low (<1% of all poison exposures) but rises to 1-2% among hospitalised patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications of drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. About 20-25% of exposures need bedside professional evaluation and ~5% need hospitalisation. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning, while carbon monoxide is the leading overall cause of poisoning death (often fatal before discovery). Most patients asymptomatic at 6 h are unlikely to deteriorate (p.3703, p.3707). Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression in poisoning/withdrawal: Stimulation - grade 1 anxious/tremulous with normal vital signs; grade 2 agitated, mildly-moderately raised vitals but can follow commands; grade 3 delirious with motor hyperactivity and markedly raised vitals, possible tachyarrhythmias; grade 4 coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression - grade 1 lethargic but arousable to voice/touch; grade 2 responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, reduced tone/respiration/temperature; grade 4 flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, depressed cardiovascular signs (p.3705).

Dry eye disease — keratoconjunctivitis sicca, dry eye syndrome, ocular surface disease, DED Allergic conjunctivitis Blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction Chronic conjunctivitis (infective or toxic) Corneal epithelial disease or recurrent erosion Neurotrophic keratopathy Medication-induced ocular surface toxicity Tear film break-up time to assess tear stability Ocular surface staining with fluorescein and lissamine green Schirmer test to quantify aqueous production Tear osmolarity measurement where available Meibomian gland assessment and expression Autoantibody and systemic testing when Sjogren syndrome is suspected Presents with grittiness, burning, foreign body sensation, fluctuating vision, and paradoxical reflex tearing Broadly divided into aqueous-deficient (reduced tear production) and evaporative (mostly meibomian gland dysfunction) types, though many patients have mixed disease Symptoms often exceed clinical signs, and vision that clears on blinking is characteristic Useful clinical tests include tear film break-up time, ocular surface staining with fluorescein or lissamine green, and the Schirmer test Aqueous-deficient dry eye may signal Sjogren syndrome, so ask about dry mouth and joint symptoms A stepwise management approach begins with lubricants, lid hygiene, and environmental measures, escalating to anti-inflammatory therapy, punctal occlusion, and secretagogues Meibomian gland dysfunction is managed with warm compresses, lid hygiene, and treatment of associated blepharitis and rosacea Untreated severe disease can cause filamentary keratitis, persistent epithelial defects, and, rarely, corneal melting or perforation Persistent epithelial defect, corneal thinning, or melt indicating severe surface breakdown Features of Sjogren syndrome or other systemic autoimmune disease requiring investigation Marked reduction in corneal sensation suggesting neurotrophic keratopathy Rapidly worsening pain, photophobia, or infiltrate suggesting secondary infection Focusing on aqueous supplementation while neglecting meibomian gland dysfunction and lid disease Overlooking underlying Sjogren syndrome in aqueous-deficient patients Attributing all irritation to dryness and missing allergy, infection, or medication toxicity Long-term use of preserved drops aggravating ocular surface toxicity Dry eye disease is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterised by loss of tear film homeostasis. Reduced aqueous production (as in Sjogren and non-Sjogren lacrimal dysfunction) or excessive evaporation (chiefly from meibomian gland dysfunction with an unstable lipid layer) leads to tear hyperosmolarity. Hyperosmolarity triggers a self-perpetuating cycle of ocular surface inflammation, epithelial damage, and neurosensory dysfunction, which further destabilises the tear film. Goblet cell loss and reduced mucin worsen wetting, sustaining the inflammatory cascade. Dry eye disease is usually chronic and requires ongoing management; most patients achieve good symptom control, but severe or autoimmune-associated disease can cause persistent surface damage and visual impairment.

Dry socket — alveolar osteitis, localised osteitis, fibrinolytic alveolitis, post-extraction alveolitis Post-extraction infection with suppuration Retained root fragment or foreign body Osteomyelitis of the jaw Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw Referred or neuropathic post-surgical pain Clinical examination of the socket for an absent clot and exposed bone Assessment for systemic signs to distinguish from spreading infection Radiography if a retained root, foreign body, or bony pathology is suspected Review of risk factors including smoking and medication history Consideration of osteonecrosis risk in patients on antiresorptive therapy Dry socket is a painful complication of tooth extraction caused by disintegration or loss of the protective blood clot, exposing alveolar bone Severe throbbing pain characteristically begins two to four days after extraction, later than the pain of the surgery itself The socket appears empty with exposed bone and often malodour, but there is usually no purulent discharge or significant systemic upset It is most common after mandibular molar extractions, particularly lower third molars Recognised risk factors include smoking, oral contraceptive use, traumatic or difficult extractions, and poor oral hygiene It is primarily an inflammatory and fibrinolytic process rather than a true infection, so antibiotics are usually not indicated Management is supportive: irrigation, gentle debridement, and placement of a sedative dressing to relieve pain and protect the bone Preventive measures include atraumatic technique, avoiding smoking, and good postoperative care Spreading swelling, fever, trismus, or purulent discharge suggesting true infection rather than simple dry socket Failure to heal or exposed necrotic bone in a patient on antiresorptive or antiangiogenic drugs raising concern for osteonecrosis Persistent numbness or worsening pain suggesting nerve injury or osteomyelitis Prescribing antibiotics for
