uncomplicated dry socket, which is not an infection Mistaking spreading infection or osteomyelitis for simple alveolar osteitis Overlooking a retained root fragment as the cause of persistent socket pain Failing to consider medication-related osteonecrosis in at-risk patients with non-healing sockets Dry socket, or alveolar osteitis, develops when the blood clot that normally fills and protects an extraction socket is lost prematurely, often through excessive local fibrinolysis. Breakdown of the clot exposes the alveolar bone and nerve endings to the oral environment, producing intense pain. Contributing factors such as smoking, bacterial contamination, trauma during extraction, and elevated fibrinolytic activity impair clot stability and delay the normal organisation and healing of the socket. The condition is characterised by inflammation of the exposed bone rather than an established suppurative infection. Dry socket is self-limiting and typically resolves over one to two weeks with supportive care and adequate analgesia, without long-term sequelae in most patients.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome — ABCC2, MRP2 deficiency, chronic idiopathic jaundice, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pigmented liver Rotor syndrome Cholestatic and obstructive liver disease Viral and drug-induced hepatitis Primary biliary cholangitis and other cholestatic disorders Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis Cholestasis of pregnancy Fractionated bilirubin confirming a conjugated predominance Normal liver enzymes and synthetic function to exclude hepatocellular or obstructive disease Urinary coproporphyrin analysis showing a raised proportion of coproporphyrin I Liver biopsy demonstrating characteristic dark hepatocellular pigment Hepatobiliary scintigraphy and gallbladder imaging showing the typical excretory pattern ABCC2 molecular genetic testing where confirmation is required A benign autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in ABCC2, encoding the canalicular multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP2) It produces chronic, predominantly conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal liver enzymes and synthetic function The liver has a characteristic grossly black pigmentation and shows dark granular melanin-like pigment within hepatocytes on biopsy Total urinary coproporphyrin is normal but the proportion of the coproporphyrin I isomer is markedly increased, a useful biochemical fingerprint Oral cholecystography typically fails to visualise the gallbladder, and biliary scintigraphy shows delayed hepatic clearance Jaundice may be precipitated or worsened by pregnancy, oral contraceptives, or intercurrent illness No specific treatment is required beyond reassurance, as the condition is benign with a normal life expectancy Abnormal transaminases or synthetic dysfunction, which point away from this benign diagnosis Pruritus, pale stools, or dark urine suggesting true biliary obstruction Systemic symptoms or weight loss prompting exclusion of hepatobiliary malignancy Marked worsening of jaundice with pregnancy warranting exclusion of other cholestatic disease Mistaking benign conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia for obstructive or hepatocellular disease and pursuing invasive workup Overlooking the distinguishing coproporphyrin isomer pattern that separates it from Rotor syndrome Attributing the abnormal liver pigment to malignancy on biopsy Failing to reassure patients, leading to unnecessary anxiety and investigation Assuming imaging non-visualisation of the gallbladder implies pathological obstruction MRP2, encoded by ABCC2, is the canalicular transporter responsible for secreting conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions from the hepatocyte into bile. In Dubin-Johnson syndrome, biallelic loss-of-function mutations impair this export step, so conjugated bilirubin that has been normally taken up and glucuronidated cannot be efficiently excreted and refluxes back into the blood, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. A parallel disturbance of organic anion handling shifts urinary coproporphyrin excretion toward the isomer I fraction. The retained dark pigment, thought to derive from adrenaline metabolites, accumulates in lysosomes and gives the liver its distinctive black appearance, but hepatocyte function and architecture remain otherwise normal. Dubin-Johnson syndrome is benign with a normal life expectancy and does not progress to cirrhosis; jaundice may fluctuate with hormonal or physiological stress but requires no specific therapy.

Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy — DMD, Duchenne dystrophy, pseudohypertrophic muscular dystrophy Becker muscular dystrophy (milder allelic disorder) Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies Spinal muscular atrophy Congenital myopathies Inflammatory myopathy Metabolic myopathy Serum creatine kinase (markedly elevated) Genetic testing for DMD gene deletions, duplications, and point mutations Muscle biopsy with dystrophin immunostaining when genetics are inconclusive Electrocardiogram and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy surveillance Pulmonary function testing to monitor respiratory muscle strength The most common and most severe childhood muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder that therefore affects boys, caused by absence of functional dystrophin. Symptoms usually appear in early childhood with delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty running and climbing stairs, and a waddling gait. Gower sign - using the hands to 'climb up' the legs when rising from the floor - reflects proximal, especially pelvic girdle, weakness. Calf pseudohypertrophy from fatty and fibrous replacement of muscle is a characteristic finding. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated, often into the thousands, even before overt weakness. Weakness is progressive; most boys lose independent ambulation by around the early teens without disease-modifying therapy. Cardiomyopathy and respiratory muscle weakness are the main causes of morbidity and death, so cardiac and pulmonary surveillance is essential. Glucocorticoids slow progression and prolong ambulation and are a mainstay of care; multidisciplinary management improves outcomes. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for dystrophin gene mutations, with muscle biopsy reserved for uncertain cases; learning and behavioural difficulties are more common than in the general population. Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation Symptoms or signs of cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia Rapid loss of motor milestones or ambulation Recurrent chest infections with weak cough Perioperative risk, including reactions to certain anaesthetic agents Attributing early motor delay and clumsiness to normal variation and delaying creatine kinase testing Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy presenting with isolated raised transaminases (from muscle, not liver) Neglecting cardiac and respiratory surveillance in an ambulant child Using certain anaesthetic agents that can trigger dangerous reactions Failing to offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to the family Mutations in the DMD gene abolish functional dystrophin, a cytoskeletal protein that links the muscle fibre cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix through the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex. Without it the sarcolemma is unstable and is damaged by contraction, leading to repeated cycles of muscle fibre degeneration and regeneration, calcium influx, inflammation, and eventual replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue. Dystrophin deficiency in cardiac muscle produces cardiomyopathy. Without disease-modifying treatment, progressive weakness leads to loss of ambulation in the early teens, with respiratory and cardiac complications limiting survival; corticosteroids, cardiac and respiratory support, and multidisciplinary care have substantially improved life expectancy.

Deep vein thrombosis — Compression ultrasound (Doppler) D-dimer Wells score Anticoagulate; assess for PE Ruptured Baker's cyst (sudden severe calf discomfort) (Harrison 22e p.2159) Muscle strain or injury (Harrison 22e p.2159) Acute postthrombotic syndrome / chronic venous insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2159) May-Thurner syndrome (iliac vein compression) presenting as recurrent leg edema (Harrison 22e p.2159) Cellulitis - fever and chills more often herald cellulitis than DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159) Loss of vein compressibility is the primary ultrasound criterion for DVT; a normal vein collapses (a 'wink') under gentle transducer pressure, whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and may show central, homogeneous, low-echogenicity thrombus (Harrison 22e p.2160). Doppler interrogation adds flow data: calf compression normally augments flow, and loss of respiratory variation suggests an obstructing DVT or a pelvic obstructive process (Harrison 22e p.2160). Contrast (gadolinium) MR venography is an excellent option when pelvic or leg ultrasound is equivocal or technically nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2160-2161). Contrast phlebography is now reserved mainly for when an interventional procedure is planned (Harrison 22e p.2161). An age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff (age x 10 ng/mL in patients >50 years) is endorsed for ruling out PE but does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159-2160). d-Dimer rarely helps in hospitalized patients because levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness (MI, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, postoperative state, pregnancy) (Harrison 22e p.2159). Ruptured Baker's cyst (Harrison 22e p.2159) Muscle strain or injury (Harrison 22e p.2159) Chronic venous insufficiency / postthrombotic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2156, 2159) The classic DVT symptom is a calf cramp or 'charley horse' that persists and worsens over several days, rather than a sudden event (Harrison 22e p.2159). A diffusely edematous (whole-leg) limb actually makes ordinary DVT less likely, with the important exception of phlegmasia cerulea dolens, the most severe form of DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159). Recurrent left thigh edema, especially in a young woman, should raise suspicion of May-Thurner syndrome, in which the right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein and may precipitate DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159). Upper extremity DVT may show only subtle asymmetry of the supraclavicular fossa or upper-arm circumference; it is increasingly linked to PICC lines and rises with larger catheter diameter and more lumens (Harrison 22e p.2158-2159, 2161). Superficial vein thrombosis presents with erythema, tenderness and a palpable cord and carries a risk of extension into the deep venous system (Harrison 22e p.2158). An idiopathic (no clear precipitant) VTE is the strongest predictor of recurrence in patients without malignancy (Harrison 22e p.473). Testing for inherited thrombophilia in adults should be reserved for the rare situation where the result would actually change management (Harrison 22e p.473-474). Phlegmasia cerulea dolens - massive proximal DVT with a diffusely swollen, painful, cyanotic limb, the most serious form of DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159). Signs of pulmonary embolism (unexplained breathlessness, syncope, hypotension, cyanosis) since DVT can embolize; many PE patients have no detectable residual DVT because the leg clot has already embolized (Harrison 22e p.2158-2159). Active malignancy as the underlying driver - up to ~15% of patients who develop DVT have cancer, and unprovoked VTE may be its first manifestation (Harrison 22e p.~705). Not all leg pain is DVT - sudden severe calf pain may be a ruptured Baker's cyst, and fever/chills point more to cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.2159). Wells point-score rules are validated in ambulatory but NOT in hospitalized patients (Harrison 22e p.2159). Using d-dimer to rule out DVT in hospitalized or systemically ill patients is futile because it is frequently elevated by non-thrombotic illness (Harrison 22e p.2159). The age-adjusted d-dimer threshold validated for PE does not extend to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2160). In cancer patients, elevated d-dimer is far less predictive of DVT than in patients without cancer (Harrison 22e p.~705). IVC filters can paradoxically increase the DVT rate by acting as a nidus for clot, and may still let small-to-medium clots pass via collateral veins (Harrison 22e p.2163). Warfarin (not a DOAC) is the standard anticoagulant for antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2163). DVT arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury, now understood to be typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release proinflammatory microparticles that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); these histone-rich, web-like networks promote platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation. Thrombi form and propagate in an environment of stasis, low oxygen tension and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Lower-extremity thrombi usually begin in the calf veins and can propagate proximally to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; detached thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart into the pulmonary circulation, and rarely cross a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to cause paradoxical (arterial) embolism. VTE shares inflammation, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury with arterial atherothrombosis, so VTE patients have more than double the risk of future MI or stroke and vice versa. Common genetic prothrombotic states are factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation (raised prothrombin level); deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S also predispose but are rare; antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia causing both venous and arterial thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2156-2158). Postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) is the main long-term morbidity: damaged venous valves cause ankle/calf swelling and leg aching after prolonged standing, and in its most severe form deep skin ulceration near the medial malleolus. Notably, graduated compression stockings prescribed for asymptomatic newly diagnosed acute DVT do NOT prevent postthrombotic syndrome (they are used only for symptomatic swelling relief). Recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation is stratified (ESC 2019) as low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma), intermediate (3-8%/yr, e.g., minor surgery, hospitalization for acute illness, pregnancy/estrogen, long-haul flight, IBD, autoimmune disease, or no identifiable risk factor) and high (>8%/yr, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome). Harrison de-emphasizes the 'provoked vs unprovoked' dichotomy because many provoked VTEs recur at rates similar to unprovoked ones, and enduring risk factors (heart failure, chronic lung disease, IBD) raise recurrence risk. The Post-VTE Functional Status scale (grades 0-4) can track functional recovery (Harrison 22e p.2156-2157, 2163). Wells clinical prediction rule for DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159): low likelihood if score <=0, moderate if 1-2, high if >=3. Points: active cancer +1; paralysis/paresis or recent cast +1; bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 weeks +1; tenderness along distribution of deep veins +1; entire-leg swelling +1; unilateral calf swelling >3 cm +1; pitting edema +1; collateral superficial nonvaricose veins +1; alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT -2. Pretest-probability strategy: patients with low DVT likelihood undergo d-dimer first and need no imaging if it is normal, whereas high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and proceed straight to compression ultrasound imaging.

Dyskeratosis congenita — DKC1, TERT, TERC, telomere biology disorder, Zinsser-Cole-Engman syndrome Fanconi anaemia and other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes Acquired aplastic anaemia Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis of other cause Poikiloderma syndromes (e.g. Rothmund-Thomson) Graft-versus-host disease (mucocutaneous mimicry) Pachyonychia congenita (nail and oral involvement) Telomere length measurement by flow-FISH in leucocyte subsets Molecular genetic testing of telomere biology disorder genes Full blood count and bone marrow examination for cytopenias and marrow failure Pulmonary function tests and imaging for interstitial lung disease Liver function and imaging for hepatic involvement Surveillance examination of oral and mucosal surfaces for premalignant change A telomere biology disorder caused by variants in telomere maintenance genes (e.g. DKC1, TERT, TERC, TINF2), with X-linked, autosomal dominant, and recessive forms Classic mucocutaneous triad: reticulate skin hyperpigmentation, nail dystrophy, and oral leukoplakia Bone marrow failure is the leading cause of early mortality and may present as cytopenias or aplastic anaemia Markedly increased risk of myelodysplasia, leukaemia, and mucosal squamous cell carcinomas Pulmonary fibrosis and hepatic disease are important non-haematological complications The severe infantile variant Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome adds cerebellar hypoplasia and immunodeficiency Very short telomeres for age (measured by flow-FISH) strongly support the diagnosis alongside gene testing Progressive pancytopenia or evolving bone marrow failure Features of myelodysplasia or acute leukaemia Non-healing or indurated oral leukoplakia suggesting squamous carcinoma Progressive dyspnoea from pulmonary fibrosis Treating apparent acquired aplastic anaemia without recognising an underlying telomere disorder, which alters transplant conditioning Using standard-intensity chemotherapy or radiotherapy that is poorly tolerated in these patients Overlooking pulmonary and hepatic complications by focusing only on skin and marrow Failing to screen at-risk relatives given variable inheritance and anticipation Dyskeratosis congenita is caused by defects in the telomere maintenance machinery, including the telomerase enzyme complex and shelterin proteins that protect chromosome ends. Inadequate telomere maintenance leads to accelerated telomere shortening, so highly proliferative tissues such as bone marrow, skin, mucosa, and lung exhaust their replicative capacity prematurely. Cells undergo senescence or apoptosis, producing the progressive stem-cell failure that underlies bone marrow failure, mucocutaneous changes, and organ fibrosis. Genomic instability from dysfunctional telomeres also explains the heightened predisposition to haematological and epithelial malignancies. Prognosis is guarded and shortened, dominated by bone marrow failure, malignancy, and pulmonary or hepatic fibrosis; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can address marrow failure but does not remove the ongoing cancer and organ-fibrosis risks, so lifelong surveillance is essential.

Dyslipidemia — hyperlipidemia, hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia Fasting lipid profile: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides (Harrison 22e p.2046). Lipoprotein(a) measurement, given its role as an independent cardiovascular risk predictor (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046). Apolipoprotein B as a marker of atherogenic particle burden (Harrison 22e p.3237). Screening for secondary contributors: glucose/HbA1c and urinalysis for diabetes and renal disease, and thyroid function testing when indicated (Harrison 22e p.2046). High-sensitivity C-reactive protein may be considered as an independent cardiovascular risk marker informing therapeutic decisions (Harrison 22e p.2046). Elevated plasma LDL cholesterol is a major modifiable driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; globally high LDL is estimated to contribute to ~41% of ischemic heart disease deaths and ~9% of stroke deaths (Harrison 22e p.2017). Lipoprotein(a) appears to be an independent predictor of cardiovascular risk beyond total or LDL cholesterol, and is elevated in roughly 20% of the global population; levels are reported higher in those of African descent and intermediate in East and South Asians (Harrison 22e p.2017). Tendon xanthomas (e.g., Achilles and extensor finger tendons), xanthelasma, and plane/tuberous xanthomas reflect hypercholesterolemia (hyperlipoproteinemia types II and III); eruptive xanthomas are most commonly associated with hypertriglyceridemia (types I, IV, V) (Harrison 22e p.234, p.1860). Palmar (palmar crease) xanthomas are specific for type III hyperlipoproteinemia, and severe hypertriglyceridemia can produce eruptive xanthomatosis and lipemia retinalis (Harrison 22e p.1860). Loss-of-function PCSK9 variants are associated with lower LDL cholesterol and reduced coronary artery disease, which led to development of PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies; rare gain-of-function PCSK9 variants are a cause of familial hypercholesterolemia (Harrison 22e p.260). Tendon xanthomas with premature coronary artery disease, suggesting familial hypercholesterolemia (Harrison 22e p.234, p.260). Severe hypertriglyceridemia, which can precipitate acute pancreatitis and may manifest with eruptive xanthomatosis and lipemia retinalis (Harrison 22e p.1860). Attributing dyslipidemia solely to primary lipid disorders while overlooking secondary causes such as diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, and excess alcohol intake (Harrison 22e p.2046). Underrecognizing familial hypercholesterolemia in patients with tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease (Harrison 22e p.234, p.260). Atherogenic lipoproteins, principally LDL, deposit cholesterol within the arterial wall and disturb normal endothelial functions (control of vascular tone, maintenance of an antithrombotic surface, and regulation of inflammatory cell adhesion and diapedesis), promoting atherosclerosis; LDL, cigarette smoking, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus vary in their relative impact on these endothelial functions. Lipoprotein(a) is thought to add risk through increased cellular lipid accumulation, endothelial dysfunction, and effects on coagulation. Severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicron/VLDL accumulation) can precipitate acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046). LDL-driven dyslipidemia is a leading contributor to atherosclerotic cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, including ischemic heart disease and stroke; lowering LDL (e.g., a 50% or greater reduction with high-intensity statin therapy in patients with established atherosclerotic disease) reduces the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and death (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2056).

Dysmenorrhoea — dysmenorrhea, painful periods, menstrual cramps, period pain Endometriosis Adenomyosis Uterine fibroids Pelvic inflammatory disease Ovarian cyst Cervical stenosis or outflow obstruction Focused history and pelvic examination to distinguish primary from secondary causes Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to assess for fibroids, adenomyosis, and adnexal pathology Screening for sexually transmitted infection where pelvic inflammatory disease is suspected Diagnostic laparoscopy when endometriosis is suspected and symptoms persist Pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy-related pain Primary dysmenorrhoea is painful menstruation without underlying pelvic pathology and typically begins within a year or two of menarche once ovulatory cycles are established Secondary dysmenorrhoea arises from identifiable pelvic disease, most often endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, or pelvic inflammatory disease, and tends to begin later or change in character The pain of primary dysmenorrhoea is cramping and suprapubic, often radiating to the back and thighs, and coincides with the onset of menstrual flow Prostaglandin-driven myometrial contractions and uterine ischaemia underlie primary dysmenorrhoea, which explains the effectiveness of prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors First-line management combines non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with hormonal suppression of ovulation such as combined hormonal contraception Features suggesting secondary causes include pain that starts before bleeding or persists after it, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, or poor response to standard treatment A careful history and examination, with pelvic ultrasound and consideration of laparoscopy, help identify secondary pathology when suspected Symptoms of primary dysmenorrhoea often improve with age and after childbirth Pain beginning well after menarche or changing markedly in character, suggesting secondary pathology Associated abnormal or heavy uterine bleeding Deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, or cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms suggesting endometriosis Fever, abnormal discharge, or pelvic tenderness suggesting infection Failure to respond to first-line therapy, warranting further evaluation Assuming all menstrual pain is primary and missing endometriosis or adenomyosis Failing to reassess when standard treatment does not work Overlooking pelvic inflammatory disease as a treatable secondary cause Not offering hormonal suppression alongside anti-inflammatory therapy Attributing new-onset severe pain in an older woman to simple period pain In primary dysmenorrhoea, the fall in progesterone at the end of the luteal phase triggers release of arachidonic acid and increased endometrial production of prostaglandins, particularly PGF2-alpha. These stimulate intense, poorly coordinated myometrial contractions that raise intrauterine pressure and reduce uterine blood flow, producing ischaemic pain analogous to angina; leukotrienes and vasopressin contribute. In secondary dysmenorrhoea the pain results instead from a structural or inflammatory disorder such as ectopic endometrial tissue, myometrial invasion by endometrium, leiomyomas, or infection. Primary dysmenorrhoea is benign and commonly improves over time and after childbirth, with most women achieving good symptom control from anti-inflammatory and hormonal treatment. The prognosis of secondary dysmenorrhoea depends on the underlying condition, and outcomes improve when that cause is correctly identified and managed.

Dyspareunia — painful intercourse, coital pain, genito-pelvic pain Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (vaginal atrophy) Vulvodynia or provoked vestibulodynia Endometriosis Pelvic inflammatory disease or pelvic adhesions Vaginismus with secondary pain Vulvovaginal infection or dermatological condition Detailed history localising pain as superficial or deep and defining its timing and triggers Careful genital and pelvic examination attempting to reproduce and localise the pain Assessment for infection, atrophy, and vulval skin disease Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, laparoscopy to evaluate deep pelvic causes such as endometriosis Assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone and psychosexual contributors Dyspareunia is persistent or recurrent genital pain associated with sexual intercourse and is a common but frequently underreported complaint A key clinical step is to localise the pain as superficial (at the entrance) or deep (with deep penetration), since this narrows the likely causes Superficial pain often reflects vulvovaginal conditions such as atrophy, vestibulodynia, dermatoses, infection, or inadequate lubrication Deep pain suggests pelvic pathology including endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, adhesions, fibroids, or ovarian pathology Postmenopausal dyspareunia is commonly due to genitourinary syndrome of menopause from oestrogen deficiency and responds well to local oestrogen and lubrication Dyspareunia and vaginismus frequently coexist and reinforce each other, and both fall within genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder A careful history and a gentle, systematic examination to reproduce and localise the pain are central to diagnosis Management is directed at the identified cause and often combines physical treatment with attention to the anxiety and relationship consequences of chronic sexual pain Postcoital bleeding or an abnormal pelvic mass suggesting significant gynaecological pathology Features of endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease requiring directed investigation History of sexual trauma needing sensitive, specialised support Chronic pain driving significant psychological distress or relationship breakdown Failing to distinguish superficial from deep pain, leading to misdirected investigation Overlooking easily treatable atrophic changes in postmenopausal women Missing endometriosis or other pelvic pathology as a cause of deep dyspareunia Neglecting the secondary pelvic floor tension and anxiety that perpetuate the pain Dyspareunia is a symptom with diverse underlying mechanisms rather than a single disease. Superficial (entry) pain arises from disorders of the vulva and introitus: oestrogen-deficient atrophy thinning and drying the tissue, provoked vestibulodynia with localised hypersensitivity, inflammatory or infective vulvovaginitis, dermatoses, or insufficient arousal and lubrication. Deep (pelvic) pain results from structures reached during deep penetration, so endometriosis, chronic pelvic inflammatory disease, adhesions, fibroids, and ovarian or uterine pathology can generate pain when moved or compressed. Persistent pain from any of these causes commonly triggers protective pelvic floor muscle tension and anticipatory anxiety, so a peripheral organic problem can evolve into a mixed pain syndrome with secondary vaginismus, blurring the line between physical and psychological contributors. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; menopausal atrophic dyspareunia responds very well to local oestrogen, infective and inflammatory causes resolve with treatment, and even complex or chronic pain often improves with a combined physical and psychosexual approach, though deep pain from conditions such as endometriosis may require longer-term management.

Dysphagia — swallowing difficulty, oropharyngeal dysphagia, esophageal dysphagia, impaired swallow Stroke and other neurological disease causing oropharyngeal dysphagia Oesophageal carcinoma or peptic stricture Oesophageal motility disorder such as achalasia Eosinophilic oesophagitis Extrinsic compression, for example by a goitre or mediastinal mass Xerostomia or medication-related swallowing difficulty Globus sensation without true dysphagia Bedside swallow screening and formal speech and language therapy swallowing assessment Videofluoroscopic swallow study or fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy when an oesophageal or structural cause is suspected Nutritional assessment and monitoring of weight and hydration Evaluation for the underlying neurological or structural cause including relevant imaging Dysphagia is broadly divided into oropharyngeal difficulty initiating a swallow and oesophageal difficulty with food passing lower down, and the history usually distinguishes the two Oropharyngeal dysphagia commonly follows stroke and neurodegenerative disease and presents with coughing or choking on swallowing, nasal regurgitation, and a wet or gurgly voice Silent aspiration, in which material enters the airway without an overt cough, is a particular danger in older and neurologically impaired patients A bedside swallow screen helps identify at-risk patients, and speech and language therapy assessment guides diet texture and swallowing strategies Instrumental evaluation with videofluoroscopy or fibreoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing characterises the mechanism and directs safe management Progressive dysphagia for solids that later involves liquids, with weight loss, raises concern for oesophageal malignancy or stricture and warrants prompt endoscopy Management includes texture-modified diets and thickened fluids, positioning and swallowing techniques, oral hygiene to reduce aspiration pneumonia risk, and treating the underlying cause Decisions about feeding tubes should be individualised; in advanced dementia they do not reliably prevent aspiration or prolong life, so careful goals-of-care discussion is essential Aspiration with coughing, choking, or recurrent chest infections, and the risk of aspiration pneumonia Silent aspiration in a neurologically impaired patient Progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggesting oesophageal malignancy Complete inability to swallow secretions or acute food bolus obstruction Rapidly worsening dysphagia with new neurological signs Assuming an intact cough reflex excludes aspiration and thereby missing silent aspiration Neglecting oral hygiene, which strongly influences aspiration pneumonia risk Delaying endoscopy in progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss Defaulting to tube feeding in advanced dementia without a goals-of-care discussion Overlooking medications and dry mouth as contributors to swallowing difficulty Normal swallowing requires precise coordination of oral, pharyngeal, and oesophageal phases under neural control, with timely airway protection by laryngeal elevation and epiglottic closure. Oropharyngeal dysphagia arises from neuromuscular disorders (stroke, Parkinson disease, motor neuron disease, dementia) or local structural lesions that disrupt this coordination, impairing bolus transfer and airway protection so that material may enter the larynx and lungs. Oesophageal dysphagia results from mechanical obstruction (stricture, tumour, ring) or motility disorders that impede transit through the oesophagus. Age-related changes in muscle strength and sensation lower reserve and predispose to aspiration. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. Post-stroke dysphagia often improves over weeks with rehabilitation, whereas dysphagia from progressive neurodegenerative disease tends to worsen and, in advanced dementia, signals a poor overall prognosis. Untreated dysphagia leads to aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, dehydration, and reduced quality of life; timely assessment and tailored management reduce these complications.

Dystonia — dystonic syndrome, torsion dystonia, focal dystonia Spasticity and other causes of abnormal posturing Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism with dystonic features Tardive and acute drug-induced dystonia Wilson disease Functional (psychogenic) dystonia Stiff person syndrome and orthopaedic causes of fixed posture MRI of the brain, particularly for hemidystonia or when a secondary structural cause is suspected A trial of levodopa in young-onset generalised dystonia to identify dopa-responsive dystonia Serum copper and ceruloplasmin and slit-lamp examination to exclude Wilson disease in younger patients Genetic testing for hereditary dystonias where indicated Medication review for dopamine-blocking and other offending drugs Defined by sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions producing abnormal, often twisting or patterned postures and repetitive movements Movements are typically patterned and directional, may be action-specific (such as writer's cramp), and often worsen with fatigue or stress and lessen with rest or sleep A characteristic feature is the sensory trick (geste antagoniste), where a light touch to the affected region temporarily reduces the dystonic posture Classified by body distribution (focal, segmental, multifocal, hemidystonia, or generalised) and by age of onset and cause Focal forms such as cervical dystonia (torticollis), blepharospasm, and laryngeal dystonia are the most common adult presentations Botulinum toxin injection is a mainstay for focal and segmental dystonia, while oral agents and deep brain stimulation are options for more widespread disease Young-onset generalised dystonia may be genetic (for example DYT1) and warrants a therapeutic trial of levodopa to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia Secondary dystonia should be considered when there are additional neurological signs, a fixed posture, or hemidystonia pointing to a structural lesion Acute severe dystonic reaction, especially involving the larynx or airway, requiring urgent treatment Hemidystonia or fixed dystonia with other focal signs suggesting a structural lesion needing imaging Young onset with hepatic or psychiatric features suggesting Wilson disease Status dystonicus with continuous severe spasms causing rhabdomyolysis or respiratory compromise Failing to trial levodopa in young-onset dystonia and missing highly treatable dopa-responsive dystonia Overlooking Wilson disease, a treatable cause, in a young patient Not recognising drug-induced dystonia and continuing the offending dopamine-blocking agent Mislabelling dystonia as functional, or vice versa, without adequate assessment Dystonia arises from dysfunction of motor networks centred on the basal ganglia and their connections with the cerebellum, thalamus, and cortex, leading to loss of inhibition, abnormal sensorimotor integration, and maladaptive plasticity. Co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles with overflow to adjacent muscles produces the abnormal postures. Causes range from inherited (isolated or combined genetic forms) and idiopathic disease to acquired lesions, drugs, and neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders. Prognosis varies with cause and distribution. Focal dystonias are usually chronic but not life-threatening and often respond well to botulinum toxin. Dopa-responsive dystonia can improve dramatically with treatment. Young-onset genetic generalised dystonia tends to spread and be more disabling, though deep brain stimulation can help selected patients.

Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa — DEB, COL7A1, type VII collagen deficiency, recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, RDEB, dominant dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, DDEB Epidermolysis bullosa simplex Junctional epidermolysis bullosa Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (autoimmune, also targeting type VII collagen) Porphyria cutanea tarda and other blistering photodermatoses Bullous pemphigoid and other autoimmune blistering diseases Chronic wound conditions with scarring Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence antigen mapping localising the split below the lamina densa Transmission electron microscopy assessing anchoring fibrils Molecular genetic testing of COL7A1 Nutritional assessment with monitoring for anaemia and micronutrient deficiency Contrast swallow or endoscopy to evaluate oesophageal strictures Regular skin surveillance and biopsy of suspicious non-healing lesions for squamous cell carcinoma Caused by mutations in COL7A1, which encodes type VII collagen, the main component of the anchoring fibrils that secure the epidermis to the dermis Blistering occurs below the lamina densa (sublamina densa) in the superficial dermis, so healing characteristically produces scarring and milia It occurs in dominant (usually milder) and recessive (often severe) forms, with the severe generalised recessive type causing the most disabling disease Repeated blistering and scarring of the hands and feet leads to fusion of the digits and a mitten (pseudosyndactyly) deformity in severe recessive disease Mucosal involvement causes oesophageal strictures, dysphagia, and malnutrition, and dental and ocular complications are common Chronic non-healing wounds in severe recessive disease carry a high risk of aggressive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, a leading cause of death in adulthood Management is multidisciplinary and supportive, with meticulous wound care, nutritional support, contracture prevention, and vigilant skin cancer surveillance A new, enlarging, or non-healing indurated lesion suspicious for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma Progressive dysphagia and weight loss from oesophageal strictures Severe anaemia and failure to thrive from chronic wounds and poor intake Progressive pseudosyndactyly and contractures impairing function Failing to institute skin cancer surveillance in severe recessive disease Overlooking oesophageal strictures as a cause of malnutrition Not preventing hand and foot contractures and pseudosyndactyly with early therapy and dressings Confusing dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa with the autoimmune condition epidermolysis bullosa acquisita Underestimating the multidisciplinary nutritional, dental, and psychological support required Type VII collagen, encoded by COL7A1, forms the anchoring fibrils that tether the lamina densa of the basement membrane to the underlying papillary dermis. In dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, mutations reduce or abolish functional type VII collagen so anchoring fibrils are deficient or absent, and the skin separates beneath the lamina densa in the superficial dermis in response to minor trauma. Because the split lies within the dermis, repair occurs with fibrosis, producing scarring, milia, and progressive contractures rather than clean healing. Dominant mutations typically retain more residual collagen function and cause milder disease, whereas recessive loss-of-function mutations produce severe generalised disease with extensive scarring, mucosal strictures, and the chronic wounds that predispose to squamous cell carcinoma. The dominant forms are generally compatible with a near-normal life expectancy, whereas severe generalised recessive disease is disabling, with progressive contractures, strictures, and a markedly increased risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma that is the leading cause of premature death.

THAP1-related dystonia) Wilson disease Secondary dystonia from perinatal injury or structural lesions Juvenile Huntington disease and other combined dystonia syndromes Psychogenic (functional) dystonia Targeted TOR1A genetic testing for the recurrent GAG deletion A therapeutic levodopa trial to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia Serum copper and caeruloplasmin (and slit-lamp examination) to exclude Wilson disease Brain MRI, expected to be normal, to exclude structural and neurodegenerative causes Broader dystonia gene panel where TOR1A testing is negative but the phenotype fits an isolated dystonia Caused by a specific in-frame GAG deletion in TOR1A (encoding torsinA), inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with markedly reduced penetrance (only around a third of carriers develop symptoms) Most common cause of early-onset isolated (primary) generalised dystonia, with higher frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population Typically begins in childhood or adolescence in a limb, often a leg or foot, and tends to spread to become generalised while sparing the cranial and cervical regions in many patients It is an isolated dystonia, meaning there is no cognitive decline, ataxia, or other neurological deficit, and imaging is structurally normal A levodopa trial is important to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia, which can look identical at onset but is dramatically treatable Symptomatic options include oral anticholinergic and other centrally acting agents and botulinum toxin for focal problems Deep brain stimulation of the internal globus pallidus is notably effective for medically refractory DYT1 dystonia Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted TOR1A genetic testing for the recurrent GAG deletion Rapid generalisation of dystonia threatening ambulation or respiration Status dystonicus with severe, unremitting muscle contractions Features atypical for isolated dystonia (cognitive decline, ataxia, weakness) suggesting an alternative diagnosis Bulbar involvement compromising swallowing or airway Omitting a levodopa trial and missing coexisting or mimicking dopa-responsive dystonia Interpreting reduced penetrance incorrectly, for example reassuring a carrier that they cannot be affected or over-predicting risk Attributing childhood limb dystonia to a functional cause without genetic evaluation Delaying referral for deep brain stimulation in medically refractory generalised disease DYT1 dystonia is caused by a recurrent in-frame trinucleotide (GAG) deletion in TOR1A, which removes a glutamic acid residue from torsinA, an ATPase of the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope. The abnormal protein disturbs nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum function and impairs neuronal development and connectivity within motor circuits, particularly the basal ganglia-thalamocortical and cerebellar pathways. The result is abnormal sensorimotor integration and defective inhibition producing sustained co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, without neurodegeneration, which is why brain structure appears normal. The dystonia is usually static or slowly progressive after an initial spreading phase and does not shorten life or cause cognitive decline; disability depends on the extent of generalisation. Many refractory cases achieve substantial, durable benefit from pallidal deep brain stimulation.

burst-suppression, often accentuated in sleep Comprehensive metabolic screen including plasma and CSF amino acids and glycine Trials of vitamin-responsive treatments such as pyridoxine Epilepsy and metabolic gene panels or exome sequencing Brain MRI to exclude structural pathology Onset is in the neonatal period or first weeks of life with erratic, fragmentary myoclonus that migrates over different body parts, often followed by focal seizures and later tonic spasms The EEG shows a burst-suppression pattern that is frequently more pronounced during sleep Inborn errors of metabolism, especially non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia and other neurotransmitter or organic acid disorders, are characteristic underlying causes Development is profoundly impaired from onset and seizures are typically refractory It is distinguished from Ohtahara syndrome mainly by the predominant erratic myoclonus and the metabolic rather than structural aetiology A systematic metabolic and genetic workup is essential to identify a potentially treatable cause Vitamin-responsive epilepsies should be excluded early with therapeutic trials Refractory neonatal myoclonus with burst-suppression suggesting a metabolic encephalopathy Elevated CSF glycine indicating non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia Failure of vitamin-responsive trials Rapid clinical deterioration pointing to a progressive metabolic disorder Failing to send CSF and plasma glycine to detect non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia Not trialling vitamin-responsive therapies before concluding refractoriness Confusing erratic myoclonus with benign neonatal sleep myoclonus Attributing seizures to structural causes without a full metabolic workup Early myoclonic encephalopathy is a neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy strongly linked to inborn errors of metabolism, particularly non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia. Accumulation of neurotoxic metabolites and disturbance of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission in the immature brain produce marked cortical and subcortical hyperexcitability. This generates erratic fragmentary myoclonus and the burst-suppression pattern, while the underlying metabolic derangement causes the severe and early developmental impairment. The prognosis is generally very poor with high early mortality and profound neurodevelopmental disability in survivors, largely determined by the underlying metabolic disorder. Seizures are usually refractory to antiseizure medication.
