hypoproteinaemic oedema as a clue to protein maldigestion Failing to perform the enteropeptidase activation test on duodenal fluid Attributing the picture to a protein-losing enteropathy without assessing digestion Enterokinase deficiency arises from loss-of-function variants in TMPRSS15, which encodes the duodenal brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase. Enteropeptidase is the physiological activator of trypsinogen, cleaving it to active trypsin, which then activates the remaining pancreatic zymogens including chymotrypsinogen and proelastase. Without enteropeptidase this activation cascade fails, so dietary protein is poorly digested despite normal pancreatic secretion of enzyme precursors. The resulting protein maldigestion causes chronic diarrhoea, hypoproteinaemia with oedema and impaired growth, while fat and carbohydrate digestion remain comparatively intact. Prognosis is excellent once recognised, as pancreatic enzyme substitution restores protein digestion, reverses oedema and hypoproteinaemia and allows normal growth. Some tolerance of protein may improve with age.

Enterovirus, Parechovirus, and Reovirus Infections — Nonpolio enterovirus infection, Coxsackievirus infection, Echovirus infection, Poliovirus infection / poliomyelitis, Human parechovirus (HPeV) infection, Reovirus infection, Summer grippe, Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, Herpangina, Bornholm disease (pleurodynia) Bacterial sepsis (especially in neonatal generalized enteroviral disease) Partially treated bacterial meningitis (can be hard to exclude from enteroviral meningitis) Mumps meningitis (distinguished by low CSF glucose, vs normal in enterovirus) Rubella (enteroviral rubelliform rash lacks lymphadenopathy and occurs in summer) Measles (enteroviral enanthems may mimic Koplik's spots) Herpetic stomatitis (vs herpangina, which lacks gingivitis) Adenoviral or Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis (vs acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis) Bacterial sepsis of the newborn Bacterial (including partially treated) meningitis Mumps virus meningitis Herpes simplex stomatitis / encephalitis Adenovirus and Chlamydia trachomatis ocular infection Other respiratory viruses causing cold/pneumonia PCR is now the primary diagnostic method; pan-enterovirus reverse-transcription PCR detects all human enteroviruses (CSF PCR ~70-100% sensitive, over 80% specific, faster than culture) but does NOT detect parechoviruses. CSF PCR is less likely positive if presentation is 3 or more days after meningitis onset or with EV71; in those cases throat or rectal swab PCR (less specific) should be considered. Serum PCR is highly sensitive/specific for disseminated disease and useful for diagnosis/monitoring in immunodeficient patients on immunoglobulin whose cultures may be negative; antigen detection is less sensitive than PCR. Viral culture of CSF, serum, body-cavity fluid, or tissue is positive less often but a positive result is diagnostic; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool because shedding is shorter; coxsackievirus A may need special cell lines or suckling-mouse inoculation. For suspected poliomyelitis: obtain two or more fecal and throat swabs at least 1 day apart for culture; a positive stool culture within the first 2 weeks confirms diagnosis when CSF culture is negative, and any poliovirus isolate must be sent to CDC to distinguish wild-type from vaccine virus. Serotype identification is mainly for epidemiology; serologic diagnosis (paired acute and ~4-week convalescent neutralizing titers, the most accurate method) is limited by the many serotypes and absence of a common antigen. Dedicated parechovirus PCR (performed by CDC and research labs; often unavailable commercially) when HPeV is suspected. In acute flaccid myelitis: spinal-cord MRI may show gray-matter changes; CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein; EV-D68 antibodies are most often found in CSF though the virus itself is rarely detected there. Guillain-Barre syndrome (also associated with enterovirus but a key paralytic mimic) Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (as a sequela/overlap of enteroviral myocarditis) Erythema multiforme and other drug or immune exanthems Type 1 diabetes mellitus (epidemiologically associated with prolonged enteroviral shedding) Idiopathic dermatomyositis (chronic enteroviral infection in agammaglobulinemia mimics it) Enteroviruses are Picornaviridae with single-stranded RNA and a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid; being non-enveloped they are acid-stable (survive the stomach), resist alcohol and detergent disinfectants, persist for days at room temperature, but are susceptible to chlorine-containing cleansers. More than 50% of nonpolio enterovirus infections and over 90% of poliovirus infections are subclinical; when symptomatic, the most common picture is a nonspecific febrile illness ('summer grippe'), and in temperate climates disease clusters in summer and fall. In children and young adults enteroviruses account for up to 90% of aseptic meningitis cases with an identifiable agent; CSF shows pleocytosis that shifts from neutrophil to lymphocyte predominance within a day, total cell count usually under 1000/uL, normal glucose, and normal-to-slightly-elevated protein. A normal CSF glucose in enteroviral meningitis helps distinguish it from mumps meningitis, in which CSF glucose is low; enteroviral meningitis tends to be more severe in adults than children but neurologic sequelae are rare. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (most often coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71) is highly infectious with attack rates near 100% in young children; coxsackievirus A6 causes a more extensive atypical form, and a B16/EV71 epidemic in Taiwan (1998) and yearly EV71 epidemics in China since 2008 produced brainstem encephalitis, pulmonary edema/hemorrhage, and deaths, mostly in children 5 years or younger. Herpangina (usually coxsackievirus A) produces grayish-white papulovesicular ulcerating lesions concentrated in the posterior mouth (soft palate, anterior tonsillar pillars, uvula) and, unlike herpetic stomatitis, is NOT associated with gingivitis. Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), usually coxsackievirus B, causes paroxysms of knifelike pleuritic chest or upper-abdominal pain lasting 15-30 minutes with tender muscles and possible pleural rub; WBC and chest x-ray are typically normal. Enteroviruses cause up to one-third of acute myocarditis cases; patients (over two-thirds male, often neonates/adolescents/young adults) present after a respiratory prodrome with chest pain, arrhythmia, ST/T-wave changes and elevated cardiac enzymes; up to 10% progress to dilated cardiomyopathy. Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (enterovirus 70, coxsackievirus A24) presents with sudden severe eye pain, subconjunctival hemorrhage, chemosis, and preauricular adenopathy; its abrupt onset and short course (recovery in ~10 days) distinguish it from adenoviral or chlamydial eye disease, and EV70 cases have been linked to paralysis during epidemics. Humoral immunity is critical: patients with agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemia can develop chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (often echovirus 11) with a dermatomyositis-like syndrome and chronic hepatitis, and may relapse even while on immunoglobulin; hypogammaglobulinemic patients can shed poliovirus for more than 20 years. Human parechoviruses (HPeV, also Picornaviridae) mimic enteroviral disease (neonatal generalized disease, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, seizures, hepatitis, rash) but pan-enterovirus PCR does NOT detect HPeV, so a dedicated PCR is required; infant deaths have been associated with HPeV-1, HPeV-3, and HPeV-6. Reoviruses are double-stranded RNA viruses; most childhood infection is asymptomatic or causes mild upper respiratory symptoms, and reovirus is only a rare cause of mild gastroenteritis or meningitis, with speculative (unproven) links of reovirus type 3 to neonatal hepatitis and biliary atresia. Neonatal enteroviral illness resembling sepsis with myocarditis/hypotension, fulminant hepatitis with DIC, meningoencephalitis, or pneumonia (serious disease most often in the first week of life, up to 3 months). Rapid onset of flaccid limb paralysis after fever/respiratory symptoms (acute flaccid myelitis or paralytic enteroviral disease). Brainstem encephalitis with myoclonus, tremor/ataxia, plus pulmonary edema or hemorrhage in young children (severe enterovirus 71 disease). Bulbar involvement causing dysphagia, dysphonia, or respiratory insufficiency/circulatory collapse in poliomyelitis. Chest pain, arrhythmia, ST-segment changes, and elevated cardiac enzymes after a respiratory prodrome (enteroviral myocarditis, risk of dilated cardiomyopathy). Chronic meningoencephalitis or dermatomyositis-like syndrome in an agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemic patient. Glucocorticoids are contraindicated in enterovirus infections. A positive enterovirus culture from stool, nasopharynx, or throat does NOT prove disease causation, since these sites are colonized for weeks during subclinical infection; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool. Pan-enterovirus PCR does not detect human parechoviruses, so HPeV can be missed unless a dedicated assay is used. CSF PCR may be falsely negative if obtained 3 or more days into meningitis or in EV71 infection. Neonatal enteroviral disease can be indistinguishable from bacterial sepsis; a recent viral illness in the mother is a useful clue. Cultures may be falsely negative due to neutralizing antibody, unsuitable cell lines, or improper specimen handling. Oral poliovirus vaccine can revert to neurovirulence (vaccine-associated/vaccine-derived poliomyelitis), with risk roughly 2000-fold higher in immunodeficient persons; tonsillectomy predisposes to bulbar polio and IM injections increase paralysis risk in the involved limb. Enteroviruses multiply in the gastrointestinal tract. Based largely on poliovirus studies, after ingestion the virus infects mucosal epithelium and replicates in submucosal lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer's patches), spreads to regional lymph nodes and into a viremic phase with replication in reticuloendothelial organs; a secondary viremia may seed other tissues and cause symptomatic disease. CNS entry is thought to occur via the bloodstream (viremia precedes neurologic disease), but evidence also supports direct neural spread: the poliovirus receptor is an immunoglobulin-superfamily member expressed at the neuromuscular end-plate, and animal/transgenic-mouse studies show that cutting the sciatic nerve prevents spinal-cord involvement after IM virus injection, implying axonal transport from muscle to anterior horn cells. Poliovirus is culturable from blood 3-5 days after infection (before neutralizing antibody); it is shed from the oropharynx up to ~3 weeks and from the GI tract up to ~12 weeks (over 20 years in hypogammaglobulinemia), and attenuated oral vaccine virus can revert toward neurovirulence during GI replication. Capsid protein VP1 is the main neutralizing-antibody target, conferring lifelong serotype-specific protection that does not prevent reinfection or shedding; IgM persists under ~6 months and IgG for life. Mucosal/secretory IgA limits GI replication and shedding, and breast-milk IgA is protective. Acute flaccid myelitis and poliomyelitis both target anterior horn cells of the spinal cord. Most enterovirus infections are mild and self-limited, resolving within about a week. Enteroviral aseptic meningitis carries an excellent prognosis with rare neurologic sequelae (though CSF abnormalities can persist weeks); immunocompetent encephalitis patients generally do well. Pleurodynia resolves in days with rare recurrence; acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis usually recovers completely in ~10 days. Myocarditis in older children and adults usually resolves fully, but neonates often have severe disease and up to 10% progress to chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, with chronic constrictive pericarditis a possible sequela. In paralytic poliomyelitis most patients regain some function over weeks to months but about two-thirds have residual neurologic sequelae; postpolio syndrome has a generally good prognosis with slow progression and plateaus of 1-10 years. Acute flaccid myelitis usually leaves persistent neurologic deficits. EV71 CNS disease can leave lasting dysphagia, cranial-nerve palsies, hypoventilation, limb weakness/atrophy, and impaired cognition. HPeV infection is usually mild (HPeV-1) but has caused infant deaths. Poliovirus infection severity spectrum: asymptomatic (most) -> minor/abortive poliomyelitis (~5%: fever, malaise, sore throat, myalgia, headache, resolving in ~3 days) -> nonparalytic poliomyelitis/aseptic meningitis (~1%) -> paralytic poliomyelitis (least common; asymmetric, proximal-predominant weakness, may be bulbar/respiratory). Paralytic disease is more frequent in older individuals, pregnant women, and those exercising or experiencing trauma at symptom onset. Postpolio syndrome occurs 20-40 years after initial paralytic disease. Vaccine-associated paralytic risk is about 1 per 2.5 million OPV doses.

mucormycosis instead Extensive disfiguring disease unresponsive to therapy Relapse after treatment Confusing indolent entomophthoromycosis with aggressive angioinvasive mucormycosis and mismanaging accordingly Stopping prolonged therapy prematurely, leading to relapse Missing gastrointestinal basidiobolomycosis, which mimics malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease Failing to obtain adequate tissue for histology and culture Underestimating the disfigurement and functional impact of rhinofacial disease The Entomophthorales are environmental saprophytes of soil and decaying vegetation and are also found in the gut of amphibians and reptiles. Infection follows implantation into subcutaneous tissue through minor trauma or insect contact, or, for Conidiobolus, inhalation of spores into the nasal mucosa. The fungi grow slowly within subcutaneous or submucosal tissue, eliciting a chronic granulomatous and eosinophilic inflammatory response rather than invading blood vessels, which distinguishes them clinically from the acute mucormycoses. Subcutaneous basidiobolomycosis of the limbs often responds well to prolonged medical therapy, whereas rhinofacial conidiobolomycosis frequently leaves permanent facial disfigurement despite treatment; gastrointestinal disease carries higher morbidity and can be serious if diagnosed late.

laxity Cicatricial entropion follows conjunctival scarring from conditions such as trachoma, chemical burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and ocular cicatricial pemphigoid Chronic lash-cornea contact risks epithelial breakdown, secondary microbial keratitis, and corneal scarring Temporary measures include lubrication, taping the lid outward, and botulinum toxin, while lid-everting sutures give short-term relief Definitive management is surgical correction tailored to the underlying mechanism Distinguish from trichiasis, where lashes are misdirected but the lid margin itself is correctly positioned Corneal epithelial defect or infiltrate indicating secondary keratitis and threatened vision Progressive conjunctival scarring suggesting cicatrising disease such as pemphigoid requiring systemic workup Persistent lash-cornea contact despite temporising measures Treating symptoms with lubricants alone while ongoing lash contact damages the cornea Failing to identify a cicatricial cause requiring different surgical planning and systemic evaluation Confusing entropion with trichiasis and choosing the wrong intervention Overlooking recurrence after involutional repair due to unaddressed lid laxity Entropion is inward rotation of the eyelid margin. Involutional entropion arises from age-related horizontal lid laxity, attenuation or disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, and overriding of the preseptal orbicularis, which together destabilise the lid and allow it to rotate inward. Cicatricial entropion results from contracture of scarred tarsoconjunctiva pulling the margin toward the globe. Spastic entropion is triggered by orbicularis spasm from ocular irritation, and congenital entropion reflects a structural lid defect. In all forms the inturned lashes abrade the ocular surface, causing chronic irritation and potential corneal damage. Surgical correction is generally effective with good long-term results, though cicatricial cases may recur and require repeated intervention; untreated chronic disease can cause corneal scarring and visual loss.

Eosinophilia — peripheral blood eosinophilia, hypereosinophilia, eosinophilic disorders Helminth and other parasitic infections Atopic disease: asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis Drug hypersensitivity, including DRESS Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and eosinophilic lung diseases Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and reactive eosinophilia in solid tumours or lymphoma Adrenal insufficiency and, rarely, HIV infection Repeat full blood count to confirm and quantify the absolute eosinophil count Stool microscopy and relevant parasite serology, with Strongyloides testing before immunosuppression Serum tryptase, vitamin B12, and IgE with review of medications Molecular testing for FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other tyrosine-kinase fusions, plus marrow examination and cytogenetics when clonal disease is suspected Troponin and echocardiography (and cardiac MRI if indicated) to assess cardiac involvement Targeted imaging and biopsy of affected organs Eosinophilia is defined by an absolute eosinophil count above the normal range, with hypereosinophilia denoting persistently very high counts; the degree and persistence guide the urgency of evaluation A practical framework separates causes into reactive/secondary (allergy, parasites, drugs, malignancy) and primary/clonal (myeloid or lymphoid neoplasms) plus idiopathic disease Worldwide, helminth infection is the leading cause, so travel and exposure history and stool and serologic studies are essential, especially before immunosuppression that could disseminate strongyloidiasis In high-income settings, atopic disease and drug reactions are common causes, and a careful medication review can reveal the culprit Hypereosinophilic syndrome is diagnosed when marked eosinophilia persists with evidence of eosinophil-mediated organ damage and no identifiable secondary cause Cardiac involvement (endomyocardial fibrosis and thrombosis) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, so troponin and echocardiography are important in significant hypereosinophilia The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion defines an imatinib-responsive myeloid variant, making molecular testing pivotal because it changes treatment entirely Corticosteroids are the mainstay for symptomatic reactive and idiopathic hypereosinophilia, but empiric anti-parasitic cover for Strongyloides is prudent before starting them where exposure is possible Peripheral counts do not always reflect tissue eosinophilia, so organ-specific disease can occur with only modestly raised or normal blood counts Cardiac involvement with troponin rise, heart failure, or intracardiac thrombus Neurologic deficits, thromboembolism, or rapidly progressive organ dysfunction Very high, persistent counts (hypereosinophilia) with systemic symptoms suggesting evolving organ damage Features of an underlying haematologic malignancy such as splenomegaly, cytopenias, or blasts Starting corticosteroids without excluding Strongyloides, risking fatal hyperinfection Attributing eosinophilia to allergy without considering clonal or parasitic causes Relying on blood counts alone and missing tissue eosinophilic organ damage Overlooking treatable molecular subtypes by not sending fusion-gene testing Eosinophil production and survival are driven principally by interleukin-5, along with IL-3 and GM-CSF. In reactive eosinophilia these cytokines are overproduced by activated T cells or tumour cells in response to allergens, parasites, drugs, or malignancy. In clonal (primary) eosinophilia, a genetic lesion in the myeloid lineage-most classically the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, or rearrangements of PDGFRB, FGFR1, and JAK2-produces autonomous eosinophil proliferation. A lymphocytic variant arises from an aberrant T-cell population secreting eosinophilopoietic cytokines. Tissue injury results from release of eosinophil granule proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein), reactive oxygen species, and prothrombotic and profibrotic mediators, damaging heart, lungs, skin, gut, and nervous system. Reactive eosinophilia usually resolves once the trigger is removed or treated. Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome outcome depends on organ involvement and treatment response; the FIP1L1-PDGFRA variant generally responds very well to targeted tyrosine-kinase inhibition, whereas untreated cardiac disease carries a poor prognosis.

response to corticosteroids raising concern for an alternative fibrosing disorder Aplastic anaemia or myeloproliferative features in association with the fasciitis Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing the sparing of digits and absence of Raynaud phenomenon Taking too superficial a biopsy that fails to sample the fascia and yields a non-diagnostic result Assuming a normal eosinophil cases Eosinophilic fasciitis is an uncommon fibrosing disorder characterised by inflammation and thickening of the deep fascia. The trigger is unknown but strenuous physical exertion frequently precedes onset. An immune-mediated process recruits eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells into the fascia, with release of profibrotic mediators driving collagen deposition and fascial fibrosis. The resulting induration tethers overlying skin and can cause joint contractures. Peripheral eosinophilia and hypergammaglobulinaemia reflect the underlying inflammatory activation, and an association with clonal haematological disease is recognised. Many patients achieve substantial improvement or remission with prompt corticosteroid therapy, though residual induration or contractures may persist, and relapse can occur on tapering. An associated haematological disorder worsens the outlook.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis — EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome, Churg-Strauss, allergic granulomatosis and angiitis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis Hypereosinophilic syndrome (including clonal/myeloproliferative variants) Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis Parasitic infection with eosinophilia Drug reaction with eosinophilia (DRESS) Polyarteritis nodosa and other systemic vasculitides Full blood count documenting peripheral eosinophilia and inflammatory markers ANCA testing with anti-MPO and anti-PR3 specificities Chest imaging for pulmonary infiltrates and sinus assessment Cardiac evaluation with ECG, troponin, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI as indicated Nerve conduction studies for suspected mononeuritis multiplex Urinalysis and renal function for glomerulonephritis, with tissue biopsy of an affected organ where feasible EGPA is an eosinophil-rich, often ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that almost always arises on a background of adult-onset, frequently difficult-to-control asthma The illness classically evolves through phases: an allergic phase with asthma and rhinosinusitis, an eosinophilic phase with blood and tissue eosinophilia, and a vasculitic phase with systemic involvement Peripheral blood eosinophilia is a hallmark, and its degree helps distinguish EGPA from other ANCA-associated vasculitides Neurologic involvement, especially mononeuritis multiplex causing asymmetric sensorimotor deficits, is a characteristic and clinically important feature Cardiac involvement-myocarditis, heart failure, and coronary or pericardial disease-is a leading cause of death and mandates cardiac assessment even when asymptomatic ANCA (usually anti-MPO/p-ANCA) is positive in a minority; ANCA-positive disease tends toward vasculitic manifestations such as neuropathy and glomerulonephritis, while ANCA-negative disease more often shows cardiac and lung involvement Diagnosis integrates the clinical picture with eosinophilia and, where feasible, biopsy showing eosinophilic tissue infiltration, extravascular granulomas, and necrotising vasculitis Corticosteroids are the foundation of treatment, with additional immunosuppression for organ-threatening disease and anti-IL-5 (eosinophil-directed) biologic therapy used to control eosinophilic disease and spare steroids A recognised though debated association exists between leukotriene-receptor antagonists and unmasking of EGPA, often linked to reduction of background corticosteroids Cardiac involvement with myocarditis, heart failure, or arrhythmia, the principal cause of mortality Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine Mononeuritis multiplex or other acute neurologic deficit indicating active vasculitis Gastrointestinal ischaemia, alveolar haemorrhage, or other organ-threatening manifestations requiring urgent immunosuppression Attributing worsening asthma and eosinophilia to poorly controlled asthma alone and missing evolving vasculitis Failing to assess the heart in apparently stable patients, given the high mortality of cardiac disease Overlooking mononeuritis multiplex as a marker of active organ-threatening vasculitis Confusing EGPA with hypereosinophilic syndrome or other eosinophilic lung disease without appropriate ANCA testing and biopsy EGPA is a systemic disorder combining marked eosinophilia with small- and medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis and extravascular eosinophilic granulomas. Th2-driven immune responses with elevated interleukin-5 promote eosinophil production, survival, and tissue infiltration; eosinophil granule proteins cause direct tissue and endothelial damage, particularly in the heart, lungs, nerves, skin, and gut. In a subset, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (typically anti-myeloperoxidase) contribute to a neutrophil-mediated necrotising vasculitis, giving rise to glomerulonephritis, purpura, and peripheral neuropathy. The two mechanisms-eosinophilic tissue infiltration and ANCA-associated vasculitis-broadly correspond to the different clinical phenotypes. With corticosteroids and, when needed, additional immunosuppression and eosinophil-directed biologics, remission is achievable in most patients, though relapse is common and asthma often persists. Prognosis is worst when there is cardiac, severe gastrointestinal, or renal involvement, which are the main determinants of mortality.

wrist drop Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage causing hypoxaemia and haemoptysis Gut ischaemia from mesenteric vasculitis presenting as severe abdominal pain Assuming a negative ANCA excludes EGPA when eosinophilia and asthma are present Overlooking silent cardiac involvement, which carries the worst prognosis Attributing worsening respiratory symptoms solely to asthma and missing evolving vasculitis Failing to consider that leukotriene-receptor antagonists or steroid tapering can unmask disease rather than cause it EGPA is a small-to-medium vessel necrotising vasculitis characterised by eosinophil-rich granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract alongside tissue and blood eosinophilia. It is considered one of the ANCA-associated vasculitides, though ANCA is detectable in only a subset. Dysregulated T-helper-2 immunity drives eosinophil recruitment and activation through interleukin-5 and related cytokines; eosinophil degranulation releases cytotoxic granule proteins that injure tissue, particularly heart, nerve, and lung. In ANCA-positive disease, autoantibody-mediated neutrophil activation contributes a more classic pauci-immune vasculitic and glomerular phenotype, whereas ANCA-negative disease is dominated by eosinophilic tissue infiltration. With glucocorticoids and modern immunosuppression most patients achieve remission, but relapses are common and steroid dependence for residual asthma is frequent. Cardiac involvement remains the principal determinant of mortality.

Epidermolysis Bullosa — EB, inherited epidermolysis bullosa, mechanobullous disease Bullous impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Neonatal herpes simplex infection Autoimmune blistering diseases (e.g. pemphigoid gestationis affecting the neonate, linear IgA disease) Incontinentia pigmenti in its vesicular stage Bullous mastocytosis Aplasia cutis and mechanobullous mimics Skin biopsy for immunofluorescence antigen mapping to identify the level of cleavage Transmission electron microscopy in specialised centres Molecular genetic testing to confirm subtype and enable counselling Nutritional, growth, and haematological monitoring (including for anaemia) in severe disease Surveillance for oesophageal strictures, dental disease, and, in dystrophic EB, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited disorders in which minor friction or trauma causes blistering and skin fragility, usually presenting at or soon after birth It is classified by the level of skin cleavage: simplex (within the epidermis), junctional (at the basement membrane zone), dystrophic (below the basement membrane), and Kindler EB (mixed levels) The plane of splitting predicts scarring: intra-epidermal simplex forms tend to heal without scarring, whereas dystrophic forms scar and can cause fusion of digits (mitten deformity) Extracutaneous involvement is common in severe subtypes, including oral, oesophageal, ocular, and genitourinary mucosae, leading to feeding difficulty, strictures, and malnutrition Care is multidisciplinary and centres on meticulous wound care, non-adherent dressings, infection control, pain management, nutrition, and prevention of trauma Handle affected neonates and children gently, avoiding shearing forces, adhesive tapes, and friction that can strip the skin Junctional EB includes a severe generalised form with high infant mortality, while severe recessive dystrophic EB carries a substantial lifetime risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma Accurate subtyping through skin biopsy with mapping and genetic testing guides prognosis, genetic counselling, and emerging targeted therapies Extensive blistering and skin loss in a neonate with fluid, electrolyte, and thermoregulatory compromise and high infection risk Sepsis arising from chronically open wounds New, non-healing, or indurated ulcer in severe dystrophic EB suggesting aggressive squamous cell carcinoma Oesophageal stricturing causing dysphagia, malnutrition, and failure to thrive Airway or ocular involvement compromising breathing or vision Assuming all EB is mild and underestimating the severity of junctional or dystrophic subtypes Using adhesive dressings or tapes that strip fragile skin Neglecting nutrition, pain, and psychological support in chronic disease Failing to arrange skin cancer surveillance in severe dystrophic EB Delaying accurate subtyping and genetic counselling that guide management and family planning Epidermolysis bullosa results from mutations in genes encoding structural proteins that anchor the layers of skin together. Defects in keratins (such as KRT5 and KRT14) weaken the basal keratinocyte cytoskeleton in simplex forms; defects in laminin-332 and other hemidesmosomal components disrupt adhesion at the basement membrane in junctional forms; and defects in type VII collagen, the main component of anchoring fibrils, undermine attachment of the epidermis to the dermis in dystrophic forms. The specific protein deficiency determines the level at which the skin separates under mechanical stress, the tendency to scar, and the pattern of extracutaneous complications. Repeated blistering, wound healing, and chronic inflammation drive fibrosis and, in severe dystrophic disease, malignant transformation. Outcome varies enormously by subtype: localised simplex forms are compatible with a near-normal lifespan, whereas severe junctional disease can be fatal in infancy and severe recessive dystrophic disease causes progressive disability, contractures, malnutrition, and a high risk of fatal squamous cell carcinoma in adulthood.

when secondary infection is suspected Family history assessment and genetic counselling Assessment for extracutaneous involvement in severe subtypes The commonest and generally mildest form of inherited epidermolysis bullosa, most often autosomal dominant and caused by mutations in the basal keratins KRT5 and KRT14 Blistering occurs within the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis, so the cleavage plane is intraepidermal (above the basement membrane) Because the split is superficial, blisters tend to heal without scarring or milia, unlike the dystrophic form Trauma and friction, especially on the hands and feet, provoke blistering, and symptoms are often worse in warm weather A localised variant affecting mainly the palms and soles and more widespread generalised variants are recognised, with severe forms showing clustered (herpetiform) blistering Diagnosis is confirmed by immunofluorescence antigen mapping and electron microscopy locating the cleavage plane, with molecular genetic testing Management is supportive, centred on protecting skin from friction and trauma, wound care, avoidance of overheating, and prevention of secondary infection Extensive blistering or erosions with signs of secondary infection or sepsis Severe generalised involvement in a neonate, prompting reassessment of the subtype Failure to thrive or feeding difficulty if mucosal involvement occurs in severe variants Rapidly spreading skin loss suggesting an alternative severe blistering diagnosis Assuming all epidermolysis bullosa scars, when the simplex form typically heals without scarring Failing to distinguish it from junctional and dystrophic forms, which have a worse prognosis and deeper cleavage plane Mistaking neonatal blistering for infection such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Neglecting measures to reduce friction and overheating that precipitate blistering Overlooking secondary bacterial infection of eroded skin Epidermolysis bullosa simplex is a disorder of the mechanical integrity of the basal layer of the epidermis. Keratins 5 and 14 assemble into the intermediate filament network that gives basal keratinocytes their structural resilience; pathogenic mutations, usually dominant-negative, produce a defective keratin cytoskeleton that cannot withstand mechanical stress. As a result, minor friction or trauma causes the basal cells to rupture and split, so blister formation occurs within the epidermis above the dermo-epidermal junction. Because the basement membrane and dermis remain intact, healing generally proceeds without the scarring characteristic of deeper cleavage-plane disease. Most forms, particularly the localised variant, are compatible with a normal life expectancy and improve after childhood, though severe generalised subtypes cause more troublesome blistering; because the cleavage plane is superficial, healing is usually without scarring.

coliform urinary pathogens in older men and those with urinary tract abnormalities Prehn's sign (relief of pain on elevating the testis) and a present cremasteric reflex favour epididymo-orchitis over erythema Management principles are empirical antibiotics guided by the likely organism and patient age, supportive measures such as scrotal support, rest, and analgesia, and treatment plus screening of sexual partners in STI-related cases Mumps orchitis should be considered in unvaccinated patients, typically following parotitis, and is usually managed supportively Failure to improve or a fluctuant swelling raises concern for abscess formation requiring imaging and possible drainage In older men or recurrent cases, evaluate for underlying urinary tract obstruction, instrumentation, or structural abnormality Inability to confidently exclude testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency Progression to scrotal or testicular abscess, or testicular infarction Systemic sepsis, particularly in immunocompromised or diabetic patients (Fournier's gangrene must be considered with rapidly spreading pain and necrosis) Failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics, suggesting resistant organism, abscess, or alternative diagnosis Misdiagnosing torsion as epididymo-orchitis and delaying surgical exploration Choosing antibiotics that do not cover the likely organism for the patient's age and risk profile Neglecting partner treatment and STI screening in younger men Missing an evolving abscess in a patient not responding to therapy Failing to investigate underlying urinary tract pathology in older or recurrent cases Epididymo-orchitis is inflammation of the epididymis, frequently extending to the adjacent testis, usually caused by retrograde ascent of organisms from the urethra or bladder along the vas deferens. In younger men sexually transmitted pathogens predominate, whereas in older men Gram-negative urinary organisms associated with obstruction, catheterisation, or instrumentation are more common. The resulting inflammatory oedema, hyperaemia, and swelling can progress to suppuration, abscess, or testicular infarction from compromised blood supply. Viral causes such as mumps produce orchitis through haematogenous spread. Most cases resolve with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care, though swelling and discomfort can take weeks to settle; complications include abscess, chronic epididymitis, testicular atrophy, and, particularly with mumps or bilateral disease, impaired fertility.

Spinal epidural abscess — SEA, spinal epidural abscess, epidural empyema, extradural abscess Vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis without abscess Transverse myelitis Spinal cord tumour or metastasis Acute disc herniation with cord compression Guillain-Barre syndrome in the setting of ascending weakness Metastatic epidural cord compression from malignancy Epidural haematoma Demyelinating myelopathy Mechanical radiculopathy from disc prolapse Urgent MRI of the whole spine with contrast to localise the abscess and assess cord compression Blood cultures and inflammatory markers Culture of aspirated or surgically drained pus to guide antibiotics Screening for a primary source such as endocarditis or vertebral osteomyelitis Assessment for skip lesions, since abscesses may involve multiple non-contiguous levels A collection of pus in the spinal epidural space that is a neurosurgical emergency because of the risk of irreversible cord compression The classic triad of back pain, fever, and neurological deficit is present in only a minority, so a high index of suspicion is essential Symptoms often progress through localised back pain, then radicular pain, then motor or sensory deficit and sphincter dysfunction, and finally paralysis Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and infection may spread haematogenously or contiguously from vertebral osteomyelitis or paraspinal infection Risk factors include injecting drug use, diabetes, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters, spinal instrumentation, and recent epidural procedures Urgent MRI with contrast is the investigation of choice and should not be delayed once the diagnosis is considered Management principles combine emergency surgical decompression and drainage for neurological compromise with prolonged targeted antibiotics; selected stable patients without deficit may be managed medically with close monitoring Once a significant neurological deficit is established, the window for functional recovery is short, making speed of intervention critical Any new or progressing motor weakness, sensory level, or bladder or bowel dysfunction indicating cord or cauda equina compression requiring emergency decompression Rapid neurological deterioration signalling a closing window for recovery Back pain with fever in an injecting drug user or immunocompromised patient Sepsis complicating the abscess Waiting for the full triad of back pain, fever, and deficit before considering the diagnosis Delaying MRI or surgical referral once suspicion is raised Failing to image the entire spine and missing non-contiguous abscesses Underestimating how quickly a mild deficit can progress to permanent paralysis A spinal epidural abscess forms when bacteria reach the epidural space by haematogenous seeding, contiguous spread from vertebral osteomyelitis or a paraspinal focus, or direct inoculation during a spinal procedure. Accumulating pus causes neurological injury through two mechanisms: direct mechanical compression of the spinal cord or cauda equina and vascular compromise, with septic thrombophlebitis and arterial disruption producing cord ischaemia and infarction. This combination explains why deficits can progress rapidly and become irreversible if decompression is delayed. Outcome hinges on neurological status at the time of intervention; patients treated before a major deficit develops usually do well, whereas established paralysis, especially if present for more than a day or two before decompression, often does not recover fully.

Episcleritis — simple episcleritis, nodular episcleritis Scleritis Conjunctivitis Anterior uveitis Inflamed pterygium or pinguecula Subconjunctival haemorrhage Foreign body or localised irritation Slit-lamp examination and topical phenylephrine test to confirm superficial vessel involvement Assessment of visual acuity to confirm it is preserved Limited systemic workup only in recurrent, nodular, or atypical cases (e.g. inflammatory markers, autoimmune screen, urate) A common, benign, usually self-limiting inflammation of the episclera presenting with acute redness and mild discomfort or grittiness rather than severe pain Redness may be sectoral or diffuse with a bright red appearance, and visual acuity is preserved The superficial episcleral vessels blanch with topical phenylephrine, unlike the deeper vessels of scleritis Classified as simple (diffuse) or nodular; in nodular disease a mobile, tender nodule is seen over the sclera Most cases are idiopathic, though a minority are linked to systemic inflammatory conditions such as gout, rosacea, or connective-tissue disease It is distinguished from scleritis by the absence of deep boring pain, vessel blanching with phenylephrine, and a benign course Management is largely reassurance with lubricants; topical or short courses of oral NSAIDs and, occasionally, mild topical steroids help troublesome or nodular cases Severe boring pain, deep violaceous vessels, or failure to blanch with phenylephrine suggesting scleritis instead Reduced visual acuity, which should not occur in simple episcleritis Frequently recurrent disease suggesting an underlying systemic inflammatory condition Confusing episcleritis with scleritis and over-investigating or over-treating a benign condition Conversely, dismissing genuine scleritis as episcleritis and missing sight-threatening disease Prolonged unnecessary topical steroid use with its attendant risks of raised intraocular pressure Overlooking an associated systemic disease in recurrent cases Episcleritis is inflammation confined to the episclera, the thin vascular layer of connective tissue between the conjunctiva and the sclera. The process is typically a localised, non-granulomatous inflammatory response affecting the superficial episcleral vascular plexus, producing vasodilatation and mild oedema without the deep scleral destruction of true scleritis. It is usually idiopathic and self-limiting, though recurrent or nodular episodes can occasionally be associated with systemic inflammatory disease. Episcleritis is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving within one to two weeks without lasting visual consequences, although recurrences are common.

Epistaxis — nosebleed, nasal haemorrhage Bleeding from a nasal or sinonasal tumour Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia Coagulopathy or anticoagulant-related bleeding Haemoptysis or upper gastrointestinal bleeding mimicking nasal bleeding Trauma including base of skull fracture with CSF or blood Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to localise the bleeding point Blood pressure measurement and assessment of haemodynamic status Full blood count, coagulation profile and group and save or crossmatch in significant bleeds Review of anticoagulant and antiplatelet medication Imaging (CT or MRI) and referral where a sinonasal tumour or vascular lesion is suspected Bleeding is broadly classified as anterior or posterior, which differ in likely source, severity and management Most bleeds are anterior and arise from Little's area on the nasal septum, where several vessels anastomose (Kiesselbach's plexus) Posterior bleeds tend to occur in older patients, are more profuse, and are harder to control, with a higher risk of airway soiling and significant blood loss Causes are grouped into local (trauma, digital picking, foreign body, infection, tumour) and general (hypertension, coagulopathy, anticoagulants, hereditary telangiectasia) First aid principles are sitting upright, leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose, with attention to airway and circulation Stepwise management progresses from cautery of an identified bleeding point to anterior packing and then posterior packing or balloon devices Refractory bleeding may require endoscopic or surgical arterial ligation or embolisation of the offending vessel Unilateral persistent or recurrent bleeding, especially with nasal obstruction, warrants evaluation for a tumour such as juvenile angiofibroma in adolescent males Profuse or posterior bleeding with hypovolaemia or haemodynamic instability requiring resuscitation Airway compromise from blood aspiration in heavy or bilateral bleeding Bleeding uncontrolled by packing needing arterial ligation or embolisation Recurrent unilateral bleeding with a mass suggesting malignancy or angiofibroma Failing to assess and resuscitate the patient while focusing only on the nose Overlooking a posterior source when anterior examination appears clear Missing an underlying tumour in recurrent unilateral bleeding Neglecting to review anticoagulation and correct coagulopathy Epistaxis is bleeding from the nasal mucosa, whose rich, superficial vascular supply from branches of both the internal and external carotid systems makes it prone to haemorrhage. Anterior bleeding usually comes from the low-pressure anastomotic vessels of Little's area, provoked by drying, trauma or minor mucosal injury. Posterior bleeding tends to arise from larger branches such as the sphenopalatine artery and is aggravated by hypertension and vascular fragility in older patients. Systemic factors such as bleeding disorders, anticoagulation and platelet dysfunction impair haemostasis and prolong or worsen bleeding. Most anterior nosebleeds settle with simple first aid or cautery, whereas posterior and recurrent bleeds, particularly in patients with hypertension or coagulopathy, can be severe or life-threatening and may need aggressive intervention.

Erdheim-Chester disease — ECD, non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, polyostotic sclerosing histiocytosis Langerhans cell histiocytosis Rosai-Dorfman disease IgG4-related disease and retroperitoneal fibrosis Metastatic malignancy with osteosclerosis Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis Sarcoidosis Biopsy of an affected site showing foamy CD68-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with Touton giant cells Molecular testing for BRAF-V600E and other MAPK pathway mutations Plain radiographs and technetium bone scan showing symmetrical long-bone osteosclerosis CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for perirenal 'hairy kidney' and periaortic 'coated aorta' MRI of brain and cardiac imaging to assess neurological and cardiac infiltration PET imaging to map disease extent and monitor treatment response A rare non-Langerhans histiocytosis, now recognised as a clonal myeloid neoplasm, usually presenting in middle-aged and older adults Bilateral symmetrical osteosclerosis of the long bones (particularly around the knees) with bone pain is the most consistent finding Perirenal infiltration produces the characteristic 'hairy kidney' appearance and periaortic encasement the 'coated aorta' on cross-sectional imaging Central nervous system, retro-orbital, cardiac (periaortic and right atrial pseudotumour), and pituitary involvement (diabetes insipidus) are common and drive morbidity A large majority carry activating BRAF-V600E or other MAPK pathway mutations, which are both diagnostic and therapeutic targets Histology shows foamy (lipid-laden) CD68-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with Touton giant cells and surrounding fibrosis Targeted BRAF and MEK inhibition has transformed treatment of mutation-positive disease; interferon has historically been used Cardiac infiltration or pericardial involvement threatening haemodynamic compromise Central nervous system involvement with neurological deterioration Diabetes insipidus and other hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction Renal impairment from perirenal and periureteric encasement Mistaking foamy histiocytes for Langerhans cell histiocytosis without immunostaining (CD1a) and molecular testing Attributing bone pain to degenerative disease and missing the symmetrical osteosclerosis Overlooking cardiac and central nervous system involvement that determine prognosis Failing to test for BRAF-V600E, which guides targeted therapy Confusing periaortic and perirenal disease with retroperitoneal fibrosis alone Erdheim-Chester disease is a clonal histiocytic neoplasm arising from myeloid precursors, driven in most cases by activating mutations of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, most commonly BRAF-V600E. Constitutive pathway activation leads to accumulation and tissue infiltration by foamy, lipid-laden non-Langerhans histiocytes accompanied by fibrosis and an inflammatory milieu. This produces the characteristic bilateral long-bone osteosclerosis, perirenal and periaortic sheathing, and infiltration of the central nervous system, orbit, heart, and hypothalamic-pituitary axis, the last causing diabetes insipidus. Prognosis depends on the extent and site of involvement; central nervous system and cardiac disease historically carried high mortality, but targeted BRAF/MEK inhibition has markedly improved outcomes in mutation-positive patients.

Erectile dysfunction — ED, impotence, erectile failure Psychogenic erectile dysfunction Vascular (arteriogenic or veno-occlusive) dysfunction Neurogenic causes (diabetic neuropathy, pelvic surgery, spinal cord disease) Endocrine causes (hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease) Drug-induced erectile dysfunction Peyronie's disease Reduced libido or relationship factors Fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipid profile to assess cardiovascular and metabolic risk Morning serum testosterone, with prolactin and other hormones if deficiency is suspected Blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment Validated questionnaires such as the International Index of Erectile Function Penile Doppler ultrasound and specialist vascular studies in selected complex or younger patients Erectile dysfunction is the persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual activity, and it is common with increasing age Causes are broadly organic (vascular, neurogenic, hormonal, anatomical, drug-induced) or psychogenic, and the two frequently coexist Vascular disease is the leading organic cause, so ED often shares risk factors with, and can be an early warning sign of, cardiovascular disease and diabetes A history distinguishing gradual organic onset from sudden situational psychogenic ED is key; preserved spontaneous nocturnal or early-morning erections point toward a psychogenic cause Assessment should review medications (antihypertensives, antidepressants, antiandrogens), lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, obesity), and endocrine and psychological status First-line pharmacological management is with phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, alongside optimisation of cardiovascular risk factors and lifestyle modification PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrate therapy because of the risk of profound hypotension Second-line options include intracavernosal or intraurethral vasoactive agents and vacuum devices, with penile prosthesis implantation reserved for refractory cases ED as a sentinel marker of undiagnosed cardiovascular disease or diabetes Erectile dysfunction with neurological signs suggesting spinal cord or cauda equina pathology Concurrent nitrate use, which contraindicates PDE5 inhibitors Features suggesting a pituitary lesion (hyperprolactinaemia, visual field changes) requiring endocrine evaluation Prescribing PDE5 inhibitors to a patient taking nitrates Treating ED symptomatically without addressing underlying cardiovascular or metabolic disease Overlooking hypogonadism or hyperprolactinaemia as reversible causes Failing to consider medication side effects as a contributor Neglecting the psychological and relationship dimensions of the problem Penile erection depends on neurally mediated relaxation of cavernosal smooth muscle, increased arterial inflow, and veno-occlusion that traps blood within the corpora cavernosa; nitric oxide and the cyclic GMP pathway are central to this process. Erectile dysfunction arises when any of these mechanisms fails: arterial insufficiency from atherosclerosis reduces inflow, veno-occlusive dysfunction allows leak, neuropathy (for example from diabetes or pelvic surgery) impairs signalling, and hormonal deficiency (notably hypogonadism) reduces desire and erectile capacity. Psychogenic factors act through central inhibition of the erectile response. Many patients have a mixed, multifactorial aetiology. Erectile dysfunction is highly treatable in most men, with many responding to PDE5 inhibitors and risk-factor modification; prognosis depends on the underlying cause, and it should prompt evaluation and management of associated cardiovascular risk.
