risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops fetalis, warranting fetal surveillance after maternal exposure Sudden severe anaemia with a low reticulocyte count in a patient with an underlying haemolytic disorder (aplastic crisis) Persistent anaemia or marrow suppression in an immunocompromised patient Maternal infection in pregnancy with signs of fetal hydrops or anaemia Profound pancytopenia suggesting a broader marrow process Isolating the child once the rash appears, when infectivity has usually already passed Missing an evolving aplastic crisis in a patient with sickle cell disease or other haemolytic anaemia Overlooking recent parvovirus exposure as a cause of new symmetrical polyarthropathy in an adult Failing to arrange fetal monitoring after documented maternal infection in pregnancy Parvovirus B19 is transmitted mainly by respiratory droplets and binds the P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitor cells, halting red cell production. In healthy hosts this transient arrest is clinically silent, and the exanthem and arthropathy that follow are largely immune-complex mediated, appearing as antibody develops. In people who depend on high red cell turnover the production arrest causes an acute aplastic crisis, while persistent infection in immunocompromised patients produces chronic anaemia. Transplacental infection can cause severe fetal anaemia and hydrops. In immunocompetent children and adults the illness is self-limiting with an excellent outcome, though adult arthropathy may linger for weeks to months; the serious outcomes are aplastic crisis in haemolytic disease, chronic anaemia in the immunocompromised, and fetal loss or hydrops in pregnancy.

Erythema multiforme — EM, erythema multiforme minor, erythema multiforme major Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis Urticaria and urticarial vasculitis Fixed drug eruption Bullous or autoimmune blistering disease Viral exanthem Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic target lesions and distribution Testing for herpes simplex virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae when a trigger is sought Skin biopsy in atypical cases to distinguish from other reactions Review of recent medications to help differentiate from drug-induced severe reactions Assessment of mucosal and ocular involvement, with ophthalmology input where indicated An acute, usually self-limiting hypersensitivity reaction characterised by target (iris) lesions with three concentric zones Lesions are typically symmetrical and acral, favouring the extensor surfaces of the hands, forearms, feet, and often the palms and soles Herpes simplex virus is the commonest trigger, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an important cause, particularly in children Erythema multiforme major involves significant mucosal disease (oral, ocular, or genital) in addition to skin lesions, whereas the minor form has little or no mucosal involvement It is now regarded as distinct from Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which have different triggers (mainly drugs), morphology, and far greater skin detachment and mortality Management is largely supportive with removal or treatment of the trigger; recurrent herpes-associated disease may warrant suppressive antiviral therapy Recurrent or persistent disease should prompt a search for an underlying herpes infection or other trigger Extensive skin detachment or a positive Nikolsky sign suggesting Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis Severe mucosal involvement impairing oral intake, vision, or urination Systemic upset with fever and mucosal disease requiring urgent assessment Ocular involvement threatening long-term visual complications Confusing erythema multiforme with Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis and mismanaging severity Overlooking an underlying herpes simplex or Mycoplasma trigger, especially in recurrent disease Failing to assess and manage mucosal and ocular involvement Attributing a target-like drug eruption to infection and missing a culprit medication Erythema multiforme is a cell-mediated immune reaction, most often provoked by infection, in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes target keratinocytes expressing antigens derived from the trigger. In herpes-associated disease, viral DNA fragments are transported to the skin and drive a T-cell response with interferon-gamma-mediated inflammation at the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic target lesions with central epidermal damage. This immunopathology and its infective triggers distinguish it from the drug-driven, tumour-necrosis-factor and granulysin-mediated widespread keratinocyte apoptosis of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Erythema multiforme minor is generally self-limiting and resolves over a few weeks without scarring; the herpes-associated form is prone to recurrence, and prognosis is far better than for the more severe drug-induced blistering syndromes it must be distinguished from.

Erythroderma — exfoliative dermatitis, generalised exfoliative dermatitis, red man syndrome (dermatological) Erythrodermic psoriasis Atopic or other eczema progressing to erythroderma Drug reaction, including DRESS Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma / Sezary syndrome Pityriasis rubra pilaris Inherited ichthyoses and pemphigus foliaceus in specific settings Skin biopsy, often repeated, to help identify the underlying dermatosis Peripheral blood film and flow cytometry to look for circulating atypical (Sezary) cells Bloods assessing fluid, electrolyte, albumin, and infection status Drug history review and consideration of eosinophilia and organ involvement suggesting DRESS Cultures if secondary infection or sepsis is suspected Erythroderma is defined as erythema and scaling affecting more than about 90 per cent of the body surface, and is a clinical syndrome rather than a single disease The most frequent underlying causes are pre-existing dermatoses (psoriasis, atopic and other eczemas), drug reactions, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with a proportion remaining idiopathic Always take a careful history of prior skin disease and recent drug exposures, as these often reveal the trigger Look for diagnostic clues within the redness: nail and scalp changes suggesting psoriasis, lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma, or an eruption temporally linked to a new medication Widespread skin failure impairs thermoregulation, fluid balance, and the barrier against infection, so treat these patients as systemically unwell Management centres on supportive care (warmth, fluids, emollients, nutrition) alongside identification and treatment of the underlying cause and withdrawal of any culprit drug Repeated skin biopsies over time may be needed because early histology is frequently non-specific and the cause can declare itself later Beware secondary infection and consider it in any patient who deteriorates or develops systemic upset Dermatological emergency: extensive skin failure causes impaired thermoregulation and a high-output cardiac state requiring urgent supportive management Fluid, electrolyte, and protein loss leading to dehydration, hypotension, and metabolic derangement Secondary bacterial infection or sepsis complicating the compromised barrier Features suggesting DRESS or an evolving lymphoma requiring specialist input Frail, elderly, or comorbid patients in whom cardiovascular decompensation is more likely Focusing on the skin alone and neglecting fluid balance, temperature, and nutritional support Assuming a single early biopsy excludes lymphoma or a specific dermatosis Failing to identify and stop a causative drug Underestimating the cardiovascular strain of high cutaneous blood flow in older patients Missing secondary infection as a cause of clinical deterioration Erythroderma reflects a massive inflammatory response in the skin, whatever the trigger, with markedly increased epidermal turnover and a dense dermal inflammatory infiltrate producing generalised erythema and scaling. Loss of the intact cutaneous barrier over almost the entire surface leads to substantial transepidermal water loss, protein and heat loss, and high cutaneous blood flow. The resulting physiological derangements include impaired temperature regulation, fluid and electrolyte disturbance, hypoalbuminaemia, and high-output cardiac demand. The specific microscopic pattern depends on the underlying disease, which is why histology and clinical correlation are both required. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and the patient's comorbidities; many drug-related and dermatosis-related cases resolve with treatment, but lymphoma-associated and idiopathic erythroderma may run a protracted or relapsing course, and severe cases carry meaningful morbidity and mortality.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria — EPP, ferrochelatase deficiency, FECH deficiency, protoporphyria, X-linked protoporphyria (ALAS2 variant) Polymorphic light eruption and solar urticaria Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (blistering photosensitivity) Porphyria cutanea tarda and other bullous porphyrias Contact or phototoxic dermatitis Hydroa vacciniforme Secondary protoporphyrinaemia from lead poisoning or iron deficiency Erythrocyte protoporphyrin measurement, distinguishing free (metal-free) from zinc-bound protoporphyrin Plasma fluorescence scanning with a characteristic emission peak Molecular genetic testing of the FECH gene (and ALAS2 for the X-linked form) Liver function tests and monitoring for protoporphyric hepatopathy Iron studies, as iron status can influence the phenotype Abdominal imaging where gallstones or hepatic involvement are suspected Caused by deficient ferrochelatase, the final enzyme of haem biosynthesis; a phenotypically similar X-linked form results from gain-of-function ALAS2 mutations Typically presents in early childhood with immediate painful, burning photosensitivity on sun exposure, often without prominent visible skin lesions Acute reactions cause intense stinging or burning pain, erythema and oedema; chronic changes include waxy thickening and shallow scars over the knuckles and nose The characteristic pain without blistering distinguishes it from the bullous cutaneous porphyrias and often leads to years of diagnostic delay The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised free (metal-free) erythrocyte protoporphyrin, with normal urinary porphyrins because protoporphyrin is not water-soluble A minority develop protoporphyric hepatopathy, as excess protoporphyrin is excreted in bile and can precipitate as gallstones or cause cholestatic liver failure Management centres on strict sunlight and visible-light avoidance and photoprotection; afamelanotide is an approved treatment to increase light tolerance Signs of protoporphyric liver disease such as jaundice, rising bilirubin or hepatic failure Rapidly worsening photosensitivity suggesting deteriorating liver function Severe, disabling phototoxic pain limiting daily activity Gallstone-related biliary obstruction Long diagnostic delay because painful photosensitivity without blistering is not recognised as porphyria Relying on urinary porphyrins, which are normal, and missing the diagnosis Overlooking progressive liver disease until it is advanced Failing to protect the skin and eyes from visible as well as ultraviolet light Not screening relatives, as inheritance and the low-expression FECH allele complicate risk assessment Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from reduced activity of ferrochelatase, the last enzyme of haem biosynthesis, which inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form haem; in the X-linked variant, increased ALAS2 activity overproduces protoporphyrin. Either mechanism causes accumulation of lipophilic, photoreactive protoporphyrin, chiefly in erythrocytes. On exposure to visible light of the appropriate wavelength, protoporphyrin in dermal blood vessels generates reactive oxygen species that cause an acute, painful phototoxic reaction. Because protoporphyrin is water-insoluble it is cleared in bile rather than urine, and biliary overload can lead to gallstones and, in a minority, progressive cholestatic liver disease. Most patients have a normal lifespan with a chronic burden of painful photosensitivity; the main serious risk is the small proportion who develop rapidly progressive protoporphyric liver failure requiring specialist and sometimes transplant management.

Essential thrombocythaemia — ET, essential thrombocythemia, essential thrombocytosis, primary thrombocythaemia Reactive (secondary) thrombocytosis from iron deficiency, infection, or inflammation Chronic myeloid leukaemia Polycythaemia vera Primary myelofibrosis (prefibrotic stage) Myelodysplastic syndrome with thrombocytosis Post-splenectomy thrombocytosis Full blood count and blood film to confirm sustained thrombocytosis and assess morphology Molecular testing for JAK2 V617F, and if negative, CALR and MPL mutations BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing enlarged, clustered megakaryocytes Iron studies, inflammatory markers, and screening for occult malignancy to exclude reactive causes Assessment for acquired von Willebrand syndrome when counts are very high or bleeding occurs A myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by a sustained rise in platelet count from clonal overproduction of megakaryocytes Many patients are asymptomatic and detected on a routine blood count, while others present with vasomotor symptoms such as headache, erythromelalgia (burning red extremities), and visual disturbance Both arterial and venous thrombosis and, paradoxically, bleeding can occur; bleeding risk rises with very high platelet counts due to acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency Most cases carry a driver mutation in JAK2, CALR, or MPL, which supports clonality and helps distinguish ET from reactive thrombocytosis Reactive causes of a high platelet count (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, post-splenectomy) must be excluded before diagnosing ET Treatment intensity is guided by thrombotic risk, factoring in age, prior thrombosis, and JAK2 status; low-dose aspirin is used for microvascular symptoms and thrombosis prevention Cytoreduction (for example with hydroxyurea) is reserved for higher-risk patients to lower the platelet count and reduce thrombotic events Long-term risks include transformation to myelofibrosis or, less commonly, acute leukaemia Acute arterial or venous thrombosis, including stroke, myocardial infarction, or splanchnic vein thrombosis Significant haemorrhage, particularly with extreme thrombocytosis and acquired von Willebrand deficiency Transient neurological or visual symptoms indicating microvascular ischaemia Features of transformation to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia such as worsening cytopenias or new blasts Diagnosing ET without excluding reactive thrombocytosis and chronic myeloid leukaemia Prescribing aspirin at very high platelet counts without recognising acquired von Willebrand syndrome and bleeding risk Underestimating thrombotic risk in JAK2-positive or older patients Attributing microvascular symptoms to unrelated causes and missing the underlying disorder Failing to reassess for transformation when the blood picture changes ET is a clonal disorder of the haematopoietic stem cell in which constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, most often through JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL mutations, drives excessive megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production independent of normal regulatory signals. The expanded platelet mass and qualitatively abnormal platelets promote thrombosis in the microcirculation and larger vessels. At very high counts, platelets adsorb and clear large von Willebrand factor multimers, producing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome and a paradoxical bleeding tendency. Over years the clone may evolve towards marrow fibrosis or acute leukaemia. Life expectancy in ET is close to that of the general population for many patients, with the principal threats being thrombosis and haemorrhage; a minority progress over years to myelofibrosis or acute leukaemia, which markedly worsens outlook.

Essential tremor — ET, benign essential tremor, familial tremor Parkinson disease (resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity) Enhanced physiological tremor (e.g. anxiety, caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, drugs) Dystonic tremor Cerebellar (intention) tremor Drug-induced or withdrawal tremor Wilson disease in younger patients Clinical assessment to distinguish action tremor from resting and cerebellar tremor Thyroid function tests to exclude thyrotoxicosis as a cause of enhanced tremor Serum copper and ceruloplasmin in younger patients to exclude Wilson disease Review of medications and stimulant intake that may produce or amplify tremor DaTscan or specialist assessment when distinguishing from Parkinson disease is difficult The hallmark is a bilateral, largely symmetric postural and kinetic (action) tremor of the upper limbs, in contrast to the resting tremor of Parkinson disease The head, voice, and jaw are often involved, and a titubating head tremor or quavering voice can be prominent The tremor characteristically worsens with sustained posture and goal-directed movement and is absent at complete rest A family history is common, and inheritance frequently appears autosomal dominant Many patients report transient improvement of tremor after alcohol, a useful diagnostic clue First-line pharmacological principles include a non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol or the anticonvulsant primidone Deep brain stimulation of the ventral intermediate thalamic nucleus can help severe, medication-refractory cases Onset spans a wide age range, and prevalence and severity tend to increase with age Strictly unilateral tremor, a resting component, or associated bradykinesia and rigidity suggesting Parkinson disease Abrupt onset or rapid progression suggesting a structural, toxic, or metabolic cause Young age of onset with Kayser-Fleischer rings or hepatic dysfunction suggesting Wilson disease Accompanying cerebellar signs, ataxia, or other focal neurological deficits Confusing essential tremor with early Parkinson disease, which delays appropriate management Overlooking a reversible cause such as thyrotoxicosis, medication, or excess caffeine Missing Wilson disease in a young patient with tremor Assuming the disorder is trivial and underestimating its impact on daily function and quality of life Essential tremor is a common movement disorder thought to arise from abnormal oscillatory activity within cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits, with the inferior olive and cerebellum implicated as key nodes of a central oscillator. It is often familial with autosomal dominant inheritance and variable penetrance, though the precise genetic and neurodegenerative substrate remains incompletely defined, and some evidence points to cerebellar pathology. Essential tremor is typically slowly progressive over years. Although often labelled benign, it can become functionally and socially disabling, impairing writing, eating, and drinking; many patients gain useful relief from medication or, in refractory cases, from surgical neuromodulation.

Ethylene glycol poisoning — antifreeze poisoning, ethylene glycol toxicity, glycol poisoning Methanol poisoning Diabetic ketoacidosis Lactic acidosis from other causes Salicylate poisoning Uraemia and other high anion-gap acidoses Serum ethylene glycol level where available Arterial blood gas with calculated anion gap Serum osmolality with calculated osmolal gap Serum calcium, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine Urine microscopy for calcium oxalate crystals and ECG for QT interval Ethylene glycol, found in antifreeze and coolants, is itself relatively harmless but is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids that cause severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and organ injury The course classically evolves in stages: an early neurological phase resembling alcohol intoxication, then a cardiopulmonary phase, and finally a renal phase with acute kidney injury Precipitation of calcium oxalate crystals causes renal tubular damage and produces hypocalcaemia, which may manifest as tetany or QT prolongation Suspect it in unexplained high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with a raised osmolal gap; calcium oxalate crystals may be seen on urine microscopy Fomepizole is the antidote of choice, inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase to prevent formation of toxic acids; ethanol is an alternative where fomepizole is not available Cofactor therapy with thiamine and pyridoxine is given to divert metabolism toward non-toxic products Haemodialysis removes the parent compound and its metabolites and corrects acidosis, and is indicated for severe acidosis, renal failure, or high levels Urinary fluorescence under Wood's lamp (from fluorescein added to some antifreeze) is unreliable and should not be used to confirm or exclude the diagnosis Severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis Acute kidney injury with oliguria Hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures, or QT prolongation Reduced consciousness or coma Rising anion gap with a falling osmolal gap indicating ongoing metabolism to toxic acids False reassurance during the early intoxication-like phase before acidosis and renal injury develop Delaying antidote to await a confirmatory ethylene glycol level in a suggestive presentation Relying on urine fluorescence to make or exclude the diagnosis Missing life-threatening hypocalcaemia and its cardiac effects Ethylene glycol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycoaldehyde, then to glycolic acid and finally oxalic acid. Glycolic acid is the main contributor to the profound high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, while oxalic acid combines with calcium to form insoluble calcium oxalate crystals that deposit in renal tubules, causing acute kidney injury, and lower serum calcium. Accumulating toxic metabolites also impair oxidative metabolism, producing lactic acidosis. The parent alcohol raises serum osmolality, giving an early osmolal gap that later falls as the anion gap widens. Prompt antidote and, when needed, dialysis before significant metabolite accumulation usually allow full recovery; delayed treatment can lead to permanent renal failure, neurological injury, and death.

Ethylmalonic encephalopathy — EE, ETHE1 deficiency, ethylmalonic aciduria with encephalopathy, persulphide dioxygenase deficiency Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (also raises ethylmalonic acid) Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders including Leigh syndrome Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type II) Other causes of infantile lactic acidosis Vasculitic or coagulopathic causes of petechiae and acrocyanosis Organic acidaemias with encephalopathy Urine organic acids demonstrating persistent ethylmalonic aciduria Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised C4 butyryl and C5 species) Blood and CSF lactate Brain MRI for symmetrical basal ganglia and white-matter changes ETHE1 gene sequencing for confirmation Thiosulphate measurement as a marker of sulphide accumulation where available Assessment of coagulation and platelet function given vascular lesions Rare severe disorder caused by biallelic ETHE1 variants affecting mitochondrial sulphide detoxification Presents in early infancy with developmental regression, progressive encephalopathy and pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs Classic triad of associated features: relapsing petechiae/acrocyanosis (orthostatic), chronic diarrhoea, and recurrent vascular/haemorrhagic skin lesions Biochemical hallmark is persistently elevated ethylmalonic acid in urine, with raised C4 and C5 acylcarnitines and lactic acidaemia Brain MRI typically shows symmetrical basal ganglia signal change and patchy white-matter lesions Underlying mechanism is accumulation of hydrogen sulphide, which poisons cytochrome c oxidase and damages the vascular endothelium and gut mucosa Confirmed by ETHE1 gene sequencing; the metabolic and vascular picture together is highly suggestive Management is supportive; combined metronidazole (to reduce sulphide-producing gut flora) and N-acetylcysteine has shown some benefit Rapidly progressive encephalopathy with developmental regression Recurrent haemorrhagic/petechial skin lesions and acrocyanosis Severe lactic acidosis during intercurrent illness Refractory chronic diarrhoea with failure to thrive Neurological deterioration with new basal ganglia lesions Attributing ethylmalonic aciduria solely to short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency and missing ETHE1 disease Interpreting the petechiae as a primary bleeding or vasculitic disorder Overlooking the diagnostic value of combining the metabolic and vascular/gastrointestinal features Delaying targeted therapy while pursuing an extensive alternative workup Assuming a purely mitochondrial cocktail will help without addressing sulphide toxicity Ethylmalonic encephalopathy is caused by loss of function of ETHE1, a mitochondrial matrix sulphur dioxygenase (persulphide dioxygenase) that is essential for the detoxification of hydrogen sulphide generated by gut bacteria and endogenous metabolism. When ETHE1 activity is lost, hydrogen sulphide accumulates in tissues where it inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) of the respiratory chain and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. This produces a mitochondrial energy-failure state with lactic acidosis, accumulation of ethylmalonic acid and short-chain acylcarnitines, and toxic injury to the highly perfused brain, gastrointestinal mucosa and vascular endothelium, accounting for the encephalopathy, chronic diarrhoea and relapsing petechial/vascular skin lesions. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The disorder is typically severe and progressive with early death in classic cases, although combined metronidazole and N-acetylcysteine therapy may slow progression in some patients; overall prognosis remains guarded.

Evaluation and Management of Obesity — Obesity evaluation, Overweight and obesity assessment, Adiposity-based chronic disease Polycystic ovarian syndrome Hypothyroidism Cushing's syndrome Hypothalamic disease Monogenic/syndromic obesity (e.g., Bardet-Biedl syndrome, POMC, PCSK1, or leptin receptor deficiency) Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides) Glycated hemoglobin and chemistry panel for diabetes and metabolic screening Blood pressure measurement Waist circumference / waist-to-hip ratio for visceral adiposity Targeted endocrine workup (thyroid, cortisol/Cushing evaluation) when secondary obesity is suspected Sleep evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea when symptoms or risk factors present Drug-induced weight gain (diabetes agents such as insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones; steroid hormones; antipsychotics such as clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone; lithium; tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, paroxetine, mirtazapine; antiepileptics such as valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine) Peripheral edema mimicking fat gain (NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers do not increase body fat) More than 70% of U.S. adults are overweight or have obesity, and prevalence is rising in most industrialized nations, with accelerating rates in children and adolescents. BMI (weight in kg divided by height in m squared, or weight in lb divided by height in in squared times 703) is used to classify weight status: healthy weight 18.5-24.9, overweight 25.0-29.9, obesity class I 30.0-34.9, class II 35.0-39.9, and extreme/class III obesity 40 or greater. BMI only reflects body size; it does not capture body composition, fat distribution, or individual health, so it functions as a screening and population tool rather than a direct measure of adiposity. Waist circumference is a surrogate for visceral adipose tissue and independently predicts metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; it should be measured in the horizontal plane above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI is 35 or below. Ethnic-specific waist cutpoints differ: for Europeans, greater than 94 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women; for South Asians and Chinese, greater than 90 cm in men and greater than 80 cm in women. Lower BMI thresholds for overweight and obesity have been proposed for the Asia-Pacific population because metabolic risk appears at lower body weights. The obesity-focused history is best approached using neutral language (weight, excess weight, BMI, unhealthy weight) because terms like obesity, morbid obesity, or fatness are perceived as stigmatizing. Recommended baseline workup for all patients includes a fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides), a chemistry panel, glycated hemoglobin, and blood pressure measurement. Physical fitness and sedentary behavior are independent predictors of all-cause mortality regardless of BMI or body composition, underscoring the importance of an activity history. Staging tools such as the AACE/ACE complication-based system (stage 0 with no complications, stages 1-2 with mild-moderate or severe complications) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (graded 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) help identify high-risk patients beyond BMI alone. As BMI rises by 5 kg/m2, cancer mortality is estimated to increase by about 10%, and obesity has reportedly overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer in some countries. Not every patient meeting a BMI obesity threshold requires treatment, but those with obesity-related complications and comorbidities should be managed proactively. Features suggesting a secondary cause (e.g., signs of Cushing's syndrome, hypothyroidism, hypothalamic disease) warranting further evaluation Severe hypertriglyceridemia sufficient to risk pancreatitis Symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea or hypoventilation (heavy snoring, daytime somnolence, dyspnea) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension presentation in a patient with obesity Rapidly progressive metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease/NASH with signs of fibrosis or cirrhosis Relying on BMI alone, which does not measure body composition or fat distribution and can misclassify individual risk. Using stigmatizing language (obesity, morbid obesity, fatness) that leaves patients feeling judged and can undermine engagement. Overlooking secondary or drug-induced causes of weight gain before attributing obesity solely to lifestyle. Initiating lifestyle change when the patient is not ready, which can cause frustration and hamper future efforts. Assuming all patients with a BMI in the obesity range require treatment, when BMI is an imperfect measure of disease. Neglecting waist circumference, which adds independent risk information about visceral adiposity. Obesity arises from a chronic imbalance in which energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, leading to expansion of adipose depots. It is a highly heterogeneous condition strongly influenced by underlying genetic variation, with environmental factors ubiquitous in developed and developing countries; in some individuals it is attributable entirely to genetic causes. Insulin resistance is one of the earliest complications: muscle (glucose disposal) and liver (glucose production) become less responsive to insulin, prompting compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Two main hypotheses link adiposity to insulin resistance—macrophage- and inflammatory-cell products in obese adipose tissue disturbing insulin action, and the limited storage capacity of adipose tissue causing ectopic lipid deposition in muscle and liver (human data are stronger for the ectopic-fat mechanism). The metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular consequences may stem from chronic overnutrition and ectopic fat rather than fat mass per se, whereas certain complications (osteoarthritis, reflux esophagitis, obstructive sleep apnea) relate more directly to mass and volume effects. Obesity is a serious chronic disease associated with increased morbidity and mortality through multiple complications—type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, atherothrombotic cardiovascular disease, stroke, heart failure (often diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation, obstructive sleep apnea, fatty liver disease that can progress to NASH and cirrhosis, several cancers, osteoarthritis, and gout. Risk generally rises with increasing levels of obesity and with central (visceral) fat distribution. Obesity also worsens outcomes from some infections (notably COVID-19) and raises susceptibility to wound infection and postoperative sepsis. Realistic initial treatment goals (around 8-10% weight loss over 6 months) can meaningfully improve obesity-related complications and quality of life. WHO/BMI classification: underweight under 18.5; healthy weight 18.5-24.9; overweight 25.0-29.9 (increased disease risk); obesity class I 30.0-34.9 (high risk); class II 35.0-39.9 (very high risk); class III/extreme obesity 40 or greater (extremely high risk). Complication-based staging (AACE/ACE): stage 0 no complications, stage 1 one or more mild-moderate complications, stage 2 at least one severe complication. The Edmonton Obesity Staging System grades 0-4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains independent of BMI.

Evaluation of Liver Function — Liver function tests, LFTs, Liver biochemical tests, Hepatic panel Hepatocellular pattern (predominant aminotransferase elevation): viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic hepatitis, drug- or toxin-induced injury, autoimmune hepatitis, nonalcoholic/metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease Cholestatic pattern (predominant alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin elevation): bile duct obstruction by stone, stricture, or tumor; primary biliary cholangitis; sclerosing cholangitis; drug-induced cholestasis Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: hemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome Isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia without other test abnormalities: Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation: infiltrative liver disease, Paget's bone disease, Hodgkin's disease, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, congestive heart failure, amyloidosis AIDS cholangiopathy due to cytomegalovirus or cryptosporidial infection causing marked alkaline phosphatase elevation Hepatic tuberculosis with biliary involvement Sepsis producing an intrahepatic cholestatic pattern Battery of bilirubin (with fractionation), AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR; repeat over days to weeks for a diagnostic pattern Fractionation of alkaline phosphatase, or 5'-nucleotidase or GGT, to confirm hepatic versus bone origin of an isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation Serum globulin isotypes: IgG in autoimmune hepatitis, IgM in primary biliary cholangitis, IgA in alcoholic liver disease Etiologic workup for chronically abnormal tests: hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen, iron studies/ferritin, ANA and serum protein electrophoresis, ceruloplasmin if under 40, antimitochondrial antibody, and ultrasound for fatty liver Blood ammonia (limited value; poor correlation with encephalopathy severity, though arterial levels correlate with outcome in fulminant failure) Liver biopsy (percutaneous with ultrasound guidance, or transjugular when ascites or prolonged INR present) for unexplained hepatocellular disease, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, indeterminate lesions, fever of unknown origin, or lymphoma staging Noninvasive fibrosis assessment: FibroTest/FibroSure, Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test, FIB-4 index, transient elastography (FibroScan), and magnetic resonance elastography Ultrasonography (first-line for suspected cholestasis or Budd-Chiari), with CT, MRCP, or ERCP as directed Hypoalbuminemia from protein malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy, or nephrotic syndrome mimicking the low albumin of chronic liver disease Vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy prolonging the prothrombin time independent of hepatic synthetic failure Bone-origin alkaline phosphatase elevation (Paget's disease, growing children, late pregnancy from placental isoenzyme) mimicking hepatic cholestasis Postprandial intestinal alkaline phosphatase rise in blood group O and B individuals Serum biochemical tests labeled 'liver function tests' are useful to detect liver disease, distinguish disorder types, gauge severity, and follow treatment response, but most do not actually measure synthetic liver function; aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase instead detect hepatocyte damage or impaired bile flow (Harrison 22e p.2633). Tests should be used as a battery rather than singly; when more than one is abnormal, or abnormalities persist on serial testing, the probability of liver disease is high, whereas normal results make occult disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2633). Total bilirubin normally runs about 1-1.5 mg/dL (95% of normals 0.2-0.9 mg/dL); if the direct fraction is under 15% of total, the bilirubin is considered essentially all indirect (unconjugated) (Harrison 22e p.2634). Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia points to hemolysis or genetic conditions such as Gilbert's or Crigler-Najjar syndromes; in an otherwise healthy person without hemolysis it can be attributed to Gilbert's syndrome with no further workup needed (Harrison 22e p.2634). Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia almost always implies hepatobiliary disease; because the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport rather than conjugation, the conjugated fraction can rise in any liver disease, including fulminant failure (Harrison 22e p.2634). Aminotransferase elevations above 1000 IU/L occur almost exclusively with extensive hepatocellular injury: viral hepatitis, ischemic/hypoxic injury, or drug/toxin injury; levels up to ~300 IU/L are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635). The absolute aminotransferase level does not correlate with degree of liver cell damage and has no prognostic significance in acute hepatocellular disease; necrosis is not required for enzyme release, only increased membrane permeability (Harrison 22e p.2635). An AST:ALT ratio over 2:1 suggests, and over 3:1 strongly suggests, alcohol-related liver disease; AST is rarely above 300 IU/L in alcoholic liver disease and ALT is often normal/low because of pyridoxal phosphate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.2635). Alkaline phosphatase elevation greater than ~4x normal points to cholestatic disorders, infiltrative diseases (tumor, amyloidosis), or high-turnover bone disease such as Paget's; less than 3x elevation is nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.2635). Because clotting factors (except factor VIII, made by endothelium) are made only in hepatocytes and turn over rapidly (factor VII half-life ~6 h), the prothrombin time/INR is the single best acute marker of hepatic synthetic function (Harrison 22e p.2636). Any bilirubin in the urine is conjugated, since unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered; bilirubinuria implies liver disease or obstructive jaundice and clears before serum bilirubin during recovery (Harrison 22e p.2634). Ultrasonography is the first test when cholestasis is suspected (to assess for dilated ducts or gallstones) and is also the first study ordered when Budd-Chiari syndrome is suspected, using Doppler to assess vessel patency and flow direction (Harrison 22e p.2636). Aminotransferases above 1000 IU/L indicating extensive hepatocellular injury (viral, ischemic, or toxin/drug) Prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and uncorrected by parenteral vitamin K, a poor prognostic sign in acute viral and other liver disease Albumin below 3 g/dL in apparent hepatitis raising concern for underlying chronic liver disease Elevated total bilirubin in drug-induced liver injury signaling more severe injury Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which nearly always implies hepatobiliary disease and can occur even in fulminant liver failure Liver tests lack sensitivity and specificity; results can be normal in serious liver disease and abnormal in non-hepatic disease, and rarely indicate a specific diagnosis on their own (Harrison 22e p.2633). Relying on the absolute aminotransferase value for prognosis is an error, since it does not correlate with the degree of damage in acute hepatocellular disease (Harrison 22e p.2635). Except with isolated hyperbilirubinemia, fractionating bilirubin rarely identifies the cause of jaundice (Harrison 22e p.2634). Alkaline phosphatase level does not distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic cholestasis (Harrison 22e p.2635). Albumin is insensitive to acute or mild hepatic dysfunction owing to its long half-life and is not specific for liver disease; it should not be ordered to screen patients without suspected liver disease (Harrison 22e p.2636). Liver biopsy should not be the first procedure for cholestasis; the biliary tree must first be evaluated for obstruction, and biopsy is subject to sampling error in focal disease (Harrison 22e p.2636). Blood ammonia correlates poorly with both presence and severity of encephalopathy and with hepatic function, and can be elevated from portal shunting despite near-normal liver function (Harrison 22e p.2636). Serum liver tests reflect distinct mechanisms rather than overall hepatic function. Aminotransferases (AST, ALT) leak from hepatocytes when cell-membrane permeability increases; ALT is comparatively liver-specific while AST is also present in cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney, brain, pancreas, lung, leukocytes, and red cells. Cholestasis-associated enzymes (alkaline phosphatase, 5'-nucleotidase, GGT) rise with impaired bile flow; alkaline phosphatase and 5'-nucleotidase localize near the canalicular membrane, whereas GGT, found in endoplasmic reticulum and bile-duct epithelium, is more diffuse and less specific. Bilirubin, the end product of heme catabolism, circulates unconjugated and albumin-bound until hepatocellular uptake, intracellular binding, glucuronide conjugation, and canalicular secretion render it water-soluble and excretable; the rate-limiting step is canalicular transport of conjugated bilirubin. Biosynthetic capacity is reflected by albumin (hepatocyte-synthesized, half-life 18-20 days, so insensitive to acute injury) and the clotting factors (rapid turnover, making PT/INR a sensitive acute marker). Gamma globulins rise in chronic liver disease because the cirrhotic liver fails to clear gut-derived bacterial antigens, increasing antibody synthesis (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636). Individual tests carry prognostic weight: in viral hepatitis a higher serum bilirubin reflects greater hepatocellular damage, total bilirubin correlates with poor outcome in alcoholic hepatitis and with prognosis in primary biliary cholangitis, and an elevated bilirubin signals more severe drug-induced injury. A prothrombin time prolonged more than 5 seconds above control and not corrected by parenteral vitamin K is a poor prognostic indicator in acute viral and other liver diseases, and elevated arterial ammonia correlates with outcome in fulminant hepatic failure. Bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, and sodium are integrated into the MELD 3.0 score used to gauge hepatic decompensation and prioritize transplant allocation (Harrison 22e p.2634-2636). Liver test patterns are categorized by pattern recognition (Harrison Table 348-1): hemolysis/Gilbert's (isolated indirect bilirubin, no bilirubinuria, otherwise normal); acute hepatocellular necrosis (aminotransferases often above 500 IU/L with ALT exceeding AST, bilirubinuria, PT prognostic); chronic hepatocellular disorders (aminotransferases usually below 300 IU/L, often low albumin and prolonged PT not corrected by vitamin K); alcoholic hepatitis/cirrhosis (AST:ALT above 2); and intra/extrahepatic cholestasis or infiltrative disease (alkaline phosphatase often above 4x normal). Disease severity in chronic liver disease/cirrhosis is graded by the Child-Pugh classification and, for transplant prioritization, the MELD 3.0 score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, albumin, sodium) (Harrison 22e p.2636-2637).

head-injured patient with a skull fracture without adequate observation An extradural haematoma is a collection of blood between the inner table of the skull and the dura mater. It most often arises when a skull fracture lacerates a meningeal artery, characteristically the middle meningeal artery in the temporal region, producing brisk arterial bleeding that strips the dura from the bone. Because the dura is tightly adherent at sutures, the clot forms a biconvex shape confined by these attachments. Rapid expansion raises intracranial pressure and displaces brain tissue, culminating in transtentorial (uncal) herniation with brainstem compression if not relieved. Outcome is often excellent when a significant clot is evacuated before herniation, since the underlying brain may be relatively undamaged; however, delay to surgery after signs of herniation markedly worsens survival and neurological recovery.

function and quality of life Dismissing childhood limb pain as growing pains and delaying diagnosis for years Relying on enzyme activity alone to exclude the disease in females, in whom levels can be normal Overlooking cornea verticillata that could prompt earlier recognition Failing to screen and counsel at-risk relatives given X-linked inheritance Fabry disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the GLA gene on the X chromosome, which encodes lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A. Deficient enzyme activity prevents cleavage of terminal galactose from globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), causing progressive glycosphingolipid accumulation within lysosomes, most notably in vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, renal podocytes and tubular cells, cardiomyocytes, and neurons. This storage triggers endothelial dysfunction, a prothrombotic and pro-inflammatory state, and progressive fibrosis of the kidney, heart, and brain vasculature, producing the multisystem adult phenotype. Untreated classic disease progresses to end-stage renal disease, cardiac complications, and premature stroke, shortening life expectancy. Early initiation of enzyme replacement or chaperone therapy, together with organ-directed supportive care, can slow progression and improve outcomes, though established fibrosis is not reversible.

haemorrhage, which can cause preventable blindness The facial skeleton is organised into vertical and horizontal buttresses that transmit and dissipate forces of mastication and absorb trauma. Fractures occur when applied force exceeds bone strength, and the pattern reflects the direction and energy of impact and the relative weakness of certain regions such as the orbital floor and the Le Fort lines. High-energy injuries can separate the midface from the skull base along these predictable planes. Associated soft tissue swelling, haemorrhage, and displaced bone fragments can compromise the airway, the orbit and globe, cranial nerves, and the lacrimal and paranasal sinus systems, and disruption near the cribriform plate can breach the dura and cause CSF leak. With accurate reduction and fixation most facial fractures heal with good functional and aesthetic results and restored occlusion. Outcomes are less favourable with delayed treatment, comminution, or associated orbital and skull base injury, where diplopia, enophthalmos, malunion, sensory disturbance, and asymmetry may persist and require secondary correction.

Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy arises from failure to silence the DUX4 gene within the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat region on chromosome 4q35. In the common type, contraction of the repeat array reduces the normal epigenetic repression of this region, and in the rarer type variants in chromatin-modifying genes have a similar effect. Inappropriate expression of DUX4, a transcription factor normally silent in mature muscle, is toxic to muscle fibres and triggers a cascade of gene activation leading to muscle degeneration. The distinctive facial, scapular, and often asymmetrical pattern of weakness reflects the selective vulnerability of these muscle groups. Progression is usually slow, most patients have a normal lifespan, and a minority eventually require wheelchair support. Severe early-onset disease is associated with a greater burden of weakness and extramuscular complications such as hearing and retinal involvement.

Activated protein C normally inactivates factor Va at this site to dampen coagulation; the mutation removes this cleavage site, so factor Va persists and continues to support thrombin generation. Because the defect is a gain of prothrombotic function rather than loss of an anticoagulant protein, its per-copy thrombotic risk is lower than for antithrombin, protein C, or protein S deficiency, but its high population frequency makes it the commonest inherited contributor to venous thrombosis. Most heterozygous carriers remain asymptomatic throughout life; overall prognosis is favourable, though thrombotic risk increases with homozygosity, additional thrombophilic defects, and transient provoking factors such as hormonal therapy or surgery.

crisis Severe or disabling movement disorder Features suggesting a treatable metabolic cause such as symptomatic hypocalcaemia Diagnosing primary (genetic) disease without first excluding secondary metabolic causes, particularly parathyroid disorders Relying on MRI, which can under-detect calcification, rather than CT Interpreting minor age-related pallidal calcification as pathological ganglia and other deep brain structures in the absence of a metabolic cause. The recognised genes converge on the neurovascular unit and phosphate homeostasis: SLC20A2 and XPR1 regulate inorganic phosphate transport, while PDGFB and PDGFRB maintain pericyte function and blood-brain barrier integrity. Disruption of phosphate handling and of the barrier is thought to promote mineral deposition within and around small vessel walls, leading to the calcification that underlies the movement, cognitive, and psychiatric manifestations. The course is variable: some gene carriers remain asymptomatic while others develop progressive movement disorder, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disease, and there is no treatment that halts the calcification. Prognosis depends on the extent and rate of neurological involvement.

Failure to Thrive — faltering growth, growth faltering, weight faltering Constitutional growth patterns and familial short stature (not true failure to thrive) Malabsorption (e.g., coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis) Chronic cardiac, respiratory, renal, or gastrointestinal disease Endocrine disorders Chronic or recurrent infection Neglect or psychosocial deprivation Detailed dietary and feeding assessment with observation of a feed Plotting of serial weight, length/height, and head circumference Targeted first-line tests (full blood count, electrolytes, urinalysis) guided by findings Coeliac serology and stool studies when malabsorption is suspected Further specific testing directed by history and examination Failure to thrive describes inadequate physical growth in a young child, most often identified as weight gain that is poor for age or crosses downward through growth chart percentiles over time. A single low measurement is less meaningful than the trajectory of serial measurements plotted on an appropriate growth chart. The traditional split into organic and non-organic causes is artificial; many children have mixed contributors, and inadequate caloric intake is the final common pathway in most cases. The three broad mechanisms are insufficient intake, inadequate absorption or increased losses, and increased energy requirements, and the history usually distinguishes among them. A careful feeding, dietary, developmental, social, and psychosocial history plus observation of a feed often yields more than extensive laboratory testing. Investigations should be guided by clues from the history and examination rather than performed as an indiscriminate panel. Management prioritises adequate catch-up nutrition while addressing any medical, developmental, feeding, and psychosocial factors, often through a multidisciplinary approach. Signs of neglect, abuse, or a threatening environment must be considered, but most children with faltering growth are not victims of maltreatment. Severe or rapidly progressive weight loss or wasting Signs of dehydration or micronutrient deficiency Developmental regression or neurological signs Features suggesting abuse or neglect Symptoms or signs pointing to serious underlying organic disease Diagnosing failure to thrive from a single measurement rather than the growth trend Ordering broad laboratory panels instead of history-directed testing Assuming an organic cause and overlooking feeding technique, caloric adequacy, or psychosocial factors Mislabelling normal constitutional or genetically small children as failing to thrive Growth requires that energy and nutrient intake exceed the demands of maintenance and activity. Faltering growth arises when this balance is disturbed: intake may be insufficient because of feeding difficulties, poor appetite, incorrect feed preparation, or limited food availability; nutrients may be inadequately absorbed or lost through malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea, or vomiting; or requirements may be raised by chronic illness such as cardiac, respiratory, renal, or inflammatory disease. Prolonged deficits deplete energy stores and, if sustained, can impair linear growth and, in severe or early cases, brain development. Psychosocial and caregiving factors frequently interact with these physiological mechanisms. With timely recognition and adequate nutritional rehabilitation most children achieve catch-up growth and do well, but prolonged or severe undernutrition, especially in infancy, can be associated with lasting effects on growth and neurodevelopment.

Falls in the elderly — geriatric falls, recurrent falls, fall risk, falls syndrome Syncope from cardiac arrhythmia, structural heart disease, or vasovagal cause Orthostatic hypotension Transient ischaemic attack or stroke Seizure Vertigo from vestibular disease including benign paroxysmal positional vertigo Mechanical or purely accidental trips related to environment Multifactorial falls assessment including gait, balance, and lower-limb strength testing Orthostatic blood pressure measurement (lying and standing) Medication review focused on psychoactive and hypotensive agents Vision assessment and cognitive screening Cardiac evaluation (ECG and further testing) when syncope is suspected Bone health assessment including fracture risk and consideration of DXA Falls in older adults are usually multifactorial, and each additional risk factor further increases the likelihood of falling A single fall warrants a gait and balance assessment, while recurrent falls or a fall with injury warrant a full multifactorial evaluation Key contributors include muscle weakness, gait and balance disorders, visual impairment, cognitive impairment, environmental hazards, and culprit medications Psychoactive drugs, antihypertensives, and drugs causing orthostatic hypotension are among the most modifiable medication-related risks Always ask about loss of consciousness; syncopal falls point toward cardiac or neurological causes and require separate evaluation Fear of falling is common after a fall and can itself cause activity restriction, deconditioning, and further falls Multicomponent interventions, particularly progressive strength and balance exercise, are the most effective evidence-based prevention strategy Vitamin D repletion in deficient individuals, home hazard modification, and correcting visual and footwear problems reduce fall risk Screen for and manage osteoporosis, since the clinical consequence of falls is largely determined by fracture risk Fall with head injury, especially on anticoagulants, raising concern for intracranial haemorrhage Fall causing fracture or significant soft-tissue injury Fall associated with loss of consciousness or suspected cardiac syncope Long lie on the floor after a fall, with risk of rhabdomyolysis, pressure injury, hypothermia, and dehydration New focal neurological signs suggesting stroke Treating a fall as a simple mechanical accident and not searching for contributing medical causes Overlooking orthostatic hypotension and culprit medications Failing to distinguish a syncopal fall from a mechanical one Ignoring bone health so that fracture risk is left unaddressed Neglecting fear of falling and the resulting deconditioning spiral Safe mobility depends on the integration of sensory input (vision, vestibular function, proprioception), central processing, and effector musculoskeletal responses. Ageing degrades each of these: sensory acuity declines, reaction times lengthen, postural reflexes slow, and sarcopenia reduces the strength needed for recovery. Superimposed disease (neurodegenerative disorders, arthritis, cardiovascular instability), medications, and environmental hazards further erode the margin of safety, so that balance perturbations that a younger person would correct instead result in a fall. Falls are a leading cause of injury, disability, and loss of independence in older people. A fall with fracture, particularly hip fracture, carries substantial morbidity and elevated one-year mortality. Recurrent falls predict functional decline and institutionalisation, but structured multifactorial intervention meaningfully reduces future falls in many patients.

Familial Mediterranean Fever and Other Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases — FMF, Hereditary recurrent fever syndromes, Autoinflammatory diseases, Periodic fever syndromes Other hereditary recurrent fever syndromes (TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, FCAS, MWS, NOMID) PFAPA syndrome Systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis / adult Still's disease Porphyria Hereditary angioedema Inflammatory bowel disease Gynecologic disorders (in women presenting with recurrent abdominal pain) MEFV genetic testing (severe mutations cluster in exon 10; ~70% of clinically typical FMF have two mutations in trans; expert-curated mutation databases such as Infevers aid interpretation) Acute-phase markers during attacks: elevated ESR, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis (in children), and raised C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, and serum immunoglobulins Urinalysis (transient albuminuria/hematuria during attacks; persistent proteinuria between attacks should raise concern for amyloidosis) Renal or rectal biopsy to confirm suspected AA amyloidosis Genotype-specific testing for other syndromes: TNFRSF1A (TRAPS), MVK with markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks (HIDS/MKD), NLRP3 (cryopyrinopathies, including testing for somatic mosaicism) Imaging during attacks: chest radiograph (atelectasis/effusion in pleural attacks), upright abdominal radiograph or CT (air-fluid levels, small amount of free fluid) Systemic-onset juvenile rheumatoid arthritis / adult Still's disease Porphyria Hereditary angioedema Inflammatory bowel disease Other monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes FMF is the prototype hereditary autoinflammatory disease: recurrent self-limited fever with serosal, synovial, or cutaneous inflammation, distinguished from autoimmune disease by the relative absence of high-titer autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells and a predominant role of the innate immune system (Harrison 22e p.2934). Roughly 90% of patients have their first attack by age 20; typical episodes last about 24-72 hours, with arthritic attacks tending to run longer (Harrison 22e p.2934). Over 90% of FMF patients have abdominal (peritoneal) attacks; laparotomy reveals a sterile neutrophil-rich peritoneal exudate, and ascites is rare (Harrison 22e p.2934). Erysipelas-like erythema, a raised erythematous rash typically on the dorsum of the foot, ankle, or lower leg, is the most characteristic skin finding and occurs most often in M694V homozygotes (Harrison 22e p.2934). FMF arthritis is usually monoarticular (knee, ankle, hip) with large sterile neutrophil-rich effusions and little erythema or warmth; radiographic changes are rare even after repeated attacks (Harrison 22e p.2934). The MEFV gene encodes pyrin (~95 kDa); its N-terminal PYRIN domain nucleates the pyrin inflammasome that activates caspase-1, driving IL-1beta and IL-18 secretion and gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis (Harrison 22e p.2934). FMF-associated MEFV mutations are gain-of-function, lowering the threshold for pyrin inflammasome activation; severe disease-associated mutations cluster in exon 10, and M694V homozygosity predicts earlier onset and more arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2935-2936). The principal hereditary recurrent fever syndromes are differentiated by attack length, ethnicity, and features: TRAPS (TNFRSF1A, dominant, attacks often >7 days, migratory myalgia with overlying erythema, periorbital edema/conjunctivitis), HIDS/MKD (MVK, recessive, painful cervical adenopathy and oral ulcers), and the NLRP3-associated cryopyrinopathies FCAS, MWS, and NOMID (Harrison 22e p.2935-2937). Cryopyrinopathies form a spectrum: FCAS (cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fever, arthralgia, conjunctivitis), MWS (urticarial rash not cold-induced, progressive sensorineural hearing loss), and NOMID/neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (chronic aseptic meningitis, characteristic arthropathy, rash) (Harrison 22e p.2937). About one-third of clinically typical NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations but are mosaic for somatic NLRP3 mutations; somatic NLRP3 mosaicism has rarely been reported in Schnitzler's syndrome (middle-age recurrent fever, urticaria, monoclonal IgM gammopathy, abnormal bone remodeling) (Harrison 22e p.2936-2937). PFAPA (periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, cervical adenitis) is the most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, notable for clock-like regularity, familial but non-Mendelian clustering, and a tendency to resolve by early adulthood (Harrison 22e p.2937). Over 60 monogenic autoinflammatory diseases are now recognized, grouped mechanistically into inflammasomopathies (FMF, HIDS, CAPS, PAPA, NLRC4-related), type I interferonopathies (STING-associated vasculopathy, COPA syndrome, Aicardi-Goutieres, CANDLE), and relopathies affecting NF-kB / TNF-induced cell death (Harrison 22e p.2937). Persistent proteinuria between attacks, suggesting developing AA amyloidosis Severe hyperpyrexia or febrile seizures in infants Protracted febrile myalgia lasting several weeks In cryopyrinopathies, sensorineural hearing loss (MWS) or chronic aseptic meningitis and progressive visual/CNS involvement (NOMID) Features of secondary vasculitis (IgA vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa) occurring at increased frequency in FMF Adult-onset relapsing polychondritis, Sweet's syndrome, vasculitis, or myelodysplasia in older men suggesting VEXAS syndrome A positive family history can be elicited in only about half of cases (especially where families are small), so its absence does not exclude FMF; FMF can also occur without known Mediterranean ancestry. Only about 70% of clinically typical FMF patients carry two identifiable MEFV mutations in trans, and many clinical cases have only a single demonstrable mutation, so genetic testing cannot rule out the diagnosis. Certain variants are functional polymorphisms rather than disease-causing: E148Q (common in some Asian populations) often affects overall inflammation more than causing clinical FMF, and TNFRSF1A R92Q and P46L may behave as polymorphisms in TRAPS. Serum IgD elevation is neither sensitive nor specific for HIDS/MKD: disease activity does not track IgD levels, some FMF/TRAPS patients have modestly raised IgD, and some MVK-mutation patients have normal IgD (markedly elevated urinary mevalonate during attacks is more reliable). About one-third of NOMID patients lack germline NLRP3 mutations and require testing for somatic mosaicism, which can be missed on standard germline sequencing. These disorders reflect dysregulated innate immunity rather than adaptive autoimmunity. In FMF, gain-of-function MEFV mutations lower the activation threshold of the pyrin inflammasome; pyrin (via its PYRIN domain and an adaptor) assembles a macromolecular complex that activates caspase-1, producing IL-1beta and IL-18 and triggering gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis. Pyrin normally senses bacterial toxins that inactivate RhoA GTPase as part of host defense. The other syndromes map to specific innate pathways: TRAPS arises from misfolding, aggregation, and retention of mutant TNFR1 with ligand-independent kinase activation, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and proinflammatory cytokine release; HIDS/MKD results from mevalonate kinase deficiency that impairs isoprenoid (geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate) synthesis, mislocalizing and inactivating RhoA and thereby activating the pyrin inflammasome; FCAS/MWS/NOMID arise from NLRP3 (cryopyrin) mutations forming an overactive NLRP3 inflammasome with excess IL-1beta and IL-18. Broader categories include interferonopathies driven by aberrant intracellular nucleic-acid sensing (excess type I interferon) and relopathies that dysregulate NF-kB activation or TNF-induced cell death. Untreated chronic inflammation can lead to systemic AA amyloidosis from deposition of a serum amyloid A fragment. FMF attacks are self-limited and recur with variable frequency over a lifetime; episodes may even be associated with remission during pregnancy. The major determinant of long-term outcome is systemic AA amyloidosis, historically a common and serious complication. Amyloidosis risk is increased by the M694V homozygous genotype, positive family history, the SAA1 genotype, male gender, non-adherence to therapy, and national origin (paralleling infant mortality rate). Among the related syndromes, untreated TRAPS leads to amyloidosis in about 15% of cases, MWS in roughly 25%, while amyloidosis is uncommon in FCAS and is a late complication in NOMID. PFAPA generally has a benign course with resolution by early adulthood. NOMID is the most severe cryopyrinopathy. No formal numeric severity scale is given; the hereditary recurrent fevers are clinically stratified by syndrome (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS/MKD, and the NLRP3-associated spectrum of FCAS [mildest] -> MWS -> NOMID [most severe]) and by attack length, organ involvement, and genotype. In FMF, M694V homozygosity marks more severe disease (earlier onset; higher frequency of arthritis, rash, and amyloidosis). Development of systemic AA amyloidosis defines the severe end of the disease spectrum.
