clonal evolution Regular head and neck and gynaecological examination for early squamous malignancy Renal and skeletal imaging and endocrine assessment for associated anomalies A genetically heterogeneous DNA-repair disorder, usually autosomal recessive (with rare X-linked and dominant forms), caused by variants in one of many FANC pathway genes that repair DNA interstrand crosslinks Progressive bone marrow failure typically emerges in the first decade, presenting with cytopenias and often preceded by macrocytosis and thrombocytopenia Congenital anomalies are common but variable, including short stature, radial-ray and thumb defects, cafe-au-lait macules, renal anomalies and microphthalmia There is a very high risk of myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia, and of solid tumours, notably head and neck and gynaecological squamous cell carcinomas at young ages The diagnostic test is a chromosomal breakage study showing excessive chromosomal breakage after exposure to DNA crosslinking agents such as diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C Somatic mosaicism from reversion in haematopoietic cells can cause false-negative blood breakage tests, so fibroblast testing may be needed Extreme sensitivity to radiation and crosslinking chemotherapy demands markedly modified conditioning and treatment protocols Rapidly falling blood counts or new blasts suggesting evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukaemia A new head and neck or anogenital mucosal lesion raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma Severe unexpected toxicity from standard-dose radiotherapy or chemotherapy Signs of severe marrow failure such as life-threatening bleeding or infection Accepting a normal blood breakage test in a suspicious case without pursuing fibroblast testing for mosaicism Administering standard conditioning or chemotherapy doses, causing severe toxicity from the underlying repair defect Attributing isolated congenital anomalies to another syndrome and delaying diagnosis Relaxing cancer surveillance after transplantation despite the continuing solid-tumour risk Fanconi anaemia results from biallelic (or, in the X-linked form, hemizygous) variants in any of numerous genes that cooperate in the Fanconi anaemia/BRCA DNA-repair pathway, which recognises and repairs DNA interstrand crosslinks and helps maintain genomic stability during replication. Failure of this pathway leaves cells unable to resolve crosslink damage, producing chromosomal breakage and instability that drives progressive haematopoietic stem cell attrition (bone marrow failure) and a strong predisposition to leukaemia and squamous carcinomas. The same defect underlies the hypersensitivity of cells to crosslinking agents, which is exploited in the diagnostic breakage assay. Prognosis is guarded and dominated by progressive bone marrow failure and a lifelong, cumulative risk of leukaemia and early-onset solid cancers. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can address marrow failure but does not remove and may increase the risk of later solid tumours, so cancer surveillance must continue lifelong.

Fanconi-Bickel syndrome — FBS, glycogen storage disease type XI, GLUT2 deficiency, SLC2A2 Cystinosis and other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome Other glycogen storage disorders with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia Galactosaemia and hereditary fructose intolerance Lowe syndrome and Dent disease Tyrosinaemia type 1 Mitochondrial hepatorenal disease Fasting and postprandial blood glucose to demonstrate the paradoxical pattern Assessment of proximal tubular function including glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarbonate and low-molecular-weight proteinuria Liver imaging and function tests to assess hepatomegaly and glycogen accumulation Skeletal assessment for rickets with measurement of phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D metabolites Genetic testing of SLC2A2 Monitoring of growth and acid-base and electrolyte status A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC2A2, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT2 expressed in liver, pancreatic beta cells, intestine and the renal proximal tubule It combines hepatorenal glycogen accumulation with a generalised proximal (Fanconi-type) renal tubulopathy Typical features are hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, a doll-like face and rickets from renal phosphate and bicarbonate wasting A characteristic paradoxical glucose profile is seen: fasting hypoglycaemia together with postprandial hyperglycaemia and glucosuria The proximal tubulopathy produces glycosuria, generalised aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate wasting with proximal renal tubular acidosis and low-molecular-weight proteinuria Growth retardation and rickets often dominate the clinical picture and require attention to phosphate, alkali and vitamin D Massive glucosuria persists despite hypoglycaemia because impaired GLUT2 blocks tubular glucose exit into the blood Symptomatic fasting hypoglycaemia Severe metabolic acidosis or electrolyte disturbance from tubular losses Progressive rickets with skeletal deformity or fracture Significant failure to thrive or dehydration during intercurrent illness Being confused by the paradoxical fasting hypoglycaemia with postprandial hyperglycaemia and misclassifying the glucose disorder Failing to correct phosphate, alkali and vitamin D, leaving rickets undertreated Overlooking the generalised tubulopathy when hepatomegaly dominates the presentation Attributing persistent glucosuria to diabetes rather than proximal tubular glucose loss Fanconi-Bickel syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC2A2, encoding the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT2. GLUT2 mediates the movement of glucose across the basolateral membrane of hepatocytes, pancreatic beta cells, enterocytes and proximal tubular cells. Its deficiency traps glucose within these cells, causing glycogen accumulation in liver and kidney and disturbing glucose sensing and homeostasis, which manifests as fasting hypoglycaemia with postprandial hyperglycaemia. In the proximal tubule, failure of basolateral glucose exit, together with the intracellular glycogen burden, impairs reabsorptive function broadly, producing a generalised Fanconi syndrome with glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia and bicarbonate wasting, and the consequent phosphate loss and acidosis drive rickets and growth failure. With supportive management of hypoglycaemia, electrolyte and phosphate losses, acidosis and rickets, growth and metabolic control can improve and many patients do reasonably well, although short stature and osteopenia may persist; kidney function is often relatively preserved compared with other proximal tubulopathies.

Fanconi syndrome — renal Fanconi syndrome, proximal tubular dysfunction syndrome, De Toni-Debre-Fanconi syndrome Isolated proximal renal tubular acidosis without full Fanconi features Diabetes mellitus with glycosuria from hyperglycaemia Primary hypophosphataemic rickets Multiple myeloma or other plasma cell dyscrasia Heavy metal or drug-induced tubular toxicity Chronic interstitial nephritis Paired urine and blood glucose to demonstrate glycosuria despite normal glycaemia Serum and urine phosphate, potassium, bicarbonate, and uric acid to document tubular wasting Urine amino acid screen and low-molecular-weight (tubular) protein measurement Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains to exclude a plasma cell disorder in adults Assessment for underlying causes such as cystinosis, Wilson disease, or nephrotoxic drug exposure Bone imaging or biochemistry when rickets or osteomalacia is suspected Fanconi syndrome is a generalised defect of proximal tubular reabsorption, so multiple solutes normally reclaimed there are lost into the urine at once The hallmark laboratory picture combines glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia with hypophosphataemia, aminoaciduria, uricosuria, and a proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis Phosphate and vitamin D handling are disturbed, producing metabolic bone disease that presents as rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults In children the commonest cause is inherited cystinosis, whereas in adults acquired causes such as drugs, heavy metals, and monoclonal light chains predominate Bicarbonate wasting causes a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, and potassium wasting frequently leads to hypokalaemia Recognising the full constellation is important because finding one abnormality (e.g. isolated glycosuria) should prompt a search for the others Treatment is directed at the underlying cause where possible, together with replacement of the wasted solutes: alkali, phosphate, potassium, and active vitamin D as needed Severe hypophosphataemia causing muscle weakness or respiratory compromise Progressive metabolic bone disease with fractures or deformity Evidence of an underlying plasma cell dyscrasia in an adult Declining glomerular filtration suggesting progression of the causative disease Dismissing glycosuria as diabetes without checking blood glucose or looking for other tubular losses Missing an underlying paraproteinaemia in an adult presenting with proximal tubular dysfunction Undertreating the bone disease by giving phosphate without adequate active vitamin D Failing to review the medication list for a reversible tubulotoxic drug Fanconi syndrome results from global dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule, the segment responsible for reabsorbing the bulk of filtered glucose, amino acids, phosphate, uric acid, bicarbonate, and low-molecular-weight proteins. When proximal transport fails, all of these are wasted in the urine, giving the characteristic combination of glycosuria with euglycaemia, generalised aminoaciduria, hypophosphataemia, hypouricaemia, proximal renal tubular acidosis from bicarbonate loss, and tubular proteinuria. Impaired proximal conversion of vitamin D and phosphate depletion drive the bone disease. Underlying mechanisms include inherited defects of tubular transporters or metabolism (such as cystinosis or Wilson disease), toxic injury from drugs and heavy metals, and deposition of filtered monoclonal light chains, all of which impair the energy-dependent transport machinery of the proximal tubule. Outlook depends on the cause: reversible drug- or toxin-induced Fanconi syndrome may resolve when the offending agent is removed, while inherited forms such as cystinosis and light-chain-related disease can progress to chronic kidney failure. Early replacement therapy prevents or lessens the associated bone disease and growth impairment.

Farber disease — Farber lipogranulomatosis, acid ceramidase deficiency, ASAH1 deficiency, ceramidase deficiency Juvenile idiopathic arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis and other histiocytic disorders Rheumatoid nodulosis or subcutaneous granuloma annulare Other lysosomal storage disorders with skeletal or visceral involvement Fibromatosis or hyaline fibromatosis syndromes SMA-PME as an allelic ASAH1 phenotype Acid ceramidase enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or fibroblasts ASAH1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule showing lipogranuloma with lipid-laden macrophages Laryngoscopy and airway assessment for nodular infiltration Brain MRI and neurodevelopmental evaluation in suspected neurovisceral disease Storage/biomarker analysis of ceramide where available Rare autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder from ASAH1 variants causing acid ceramidase deficiency and ceramide accumulation Classic triad is painful, swollen joints with contractures; subcutaneous nodules (lipogranulomas) over joints and pressure points; and a hoarse or weak cry from laryngeal involvement Symptoms typically begin in early infancy and can be mistaken for juvenile idiopathic arthritis Nodular infiltration of larynx and airway causes progressive hoarseness and respiratory difficulty Severity ranges from a severe neurovisceral form with neurological regression to milder forms with predominantly joint and nodule disease Allelic to spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME), a distinct ASAH1-related phenotype Diagnosis rests on demonstrating deficient acid ceramidase activity and ASAH1 genetic testing; management is largely supportive, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered in selected non-neurological cases Progressive hoarseness with stridor or airway compromise Neurological regression indicating a severe neurovisceral phenotype Feeding and respiratory difficulty from laryngeal and pulmonary involvement Rapidly progressive joint contractures with severe pain Misdiagnosing early joint disease as juvenile idiopathic arthritis and delaying metabolic evaluation Overlooking hoarseness as a diagnostic clue to laryngeal storage Not recognising the allelic relationship with SMA-PME Assuming a uniform prognosis across the clinical spectrum Acid ceramidase normally hydrolyses ceramide into sphingosine and free fatty acid within the lysosome. Deficiency of the enzyme leads to lysosomal accumulation of ceramide in many tissues, particularly around joints, subcutaneous tissue, larynx and, in severe forms, the nervous system and viscera. The stored lipid provokes a granulomatous inflammatory response (lipogranulomas) and tissue infiltration that produces the characteristic joint, nodular and laryngeal manifestations, while central nervous system involvement in severe phenotypes drives neurological deterioration. Severe neurovisceral forms are progressive and often fatal in early childhood, whereas milder forms with predominantly joint and nodular disease may survive longer; outcome depends heavily on the degree of neurological and airway involvement.

Fascioliasis — Fasciola hepatica, Fasciola gigantica, sheep liver fluke infection, liver rot, fasciolosis Other liver flukes (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) in the chronic phase Viral or other hepatitis (acute phase) Pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess Biliary stones and other causes of obstructive jaundice or cholangitis Hypereosinophilic syndromes and other tissue-migrating helminths (e.g. toxocariasis) Hepatic malignancy Serology (antibody detection) as the key test in the acute pre-patent phase Stool microscopy for characteristic large operculated eggs in the chronic phase (with concentration) Bile or duodenal aspirate examination for eggs when stool is negative Full blood count for eosinophilia Liver function tests to assess cholestasis Abdominal ultrasound, CT or MRI showing migratory tracks (acute) or biliary flukes and dilatation (chronic) Fascioliasis is caused by the liver flukes Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, primarily parasites of sheep and cattle that also infect humans worldwide, with high-burden foci in the Andes, Nile valley and parts of Asia Humans are infected by eating aquatic plants such as watercress, or drinking water, contaminated with encysted metacercariae The acute (hepatic/migratory) phase reflects larval migration through the liver parenchyma and causes fever, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly and marked eosinophilia The chronic (biliary) phase occurs once adult flukes reside in the bile ducts, causing biliary colic, obstruction, cholangitis and sometimes obstructive jaundice During the acute phase stool ova are absent because the flukes are not yet egg-laying, so serology is the diagnostic test of choice; eggs appear in stool or bile only in the chronic phase Imaging in the acute phase may show hypodense migratory tracks or nodules in the liver, and eosinophilia is a key clue Triclabendazole is the preferred agent for fascioliasis, and notably praziquantel is ineffective against Fasciola, unlike most other trematode infections Acute cholangitis with fever, jaundice and abdominal pain Obstructive jaundice from adult flukes in the bile ducts Severe acute-phase illness with high fever and marked systemic symptoms Ectopic migration causing lesions outside the hepatobiliary system Failure to respond, given regional triclabendazole resistance concerns Relying on stool microscopy during the acute phase, when eggs are not yet produced, and missing the diagnosis Using praziquantel, which is ineffective against Fasciola, instead of triclabendazole Overlooking dietary exposure such as wild watercress ingestion Mistaking acute-phase hepatic lesions for abscess or malignancy on imaging Not considering treatment failure due to regional drug resistance Ingested metacercariae excyst in the duodenum and the immature flukes penetrate the intestinal wall, cross the peritoneal cavity and burrow through the liver capsule and parenchyma over several weeks, producing necrotic migratory tracks and an intense eosinophilic inflammatory response that underlies the acute phase. The flukes then enter the bile ducts and mature into adults, where they cause chronic mechanical and inflammatory biliary injury, ductal hyperplasia, fibrosis and obstruction. Egg production begins only after maturation, explaining the diagnostic gap in the acute phase. Ectopic migration can rarely deposit flukes in other tissues. Most infections respond well to appropriate anthelmintic therapy with full recovery, but heavy or long-standing chronic infection can cause biliary fibrosis and recurrent cholangitis, and emerging triclabendazole resistance is a growing concern in some regions.

Fat embolism syndrome — FES, fat embolism Pulmonary thromboembolism Aspiration pneumonia or hospital-acquired pneumonia Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Evolving traumatic brain syndrome in a patient who develops respiratory distress, neurological change, and a petechial rash one to three days after long-bone or pelvic fractures The classic triad is hypoxaemia, neurological dysfunction, and a petechial rash, though not all three are always present The petechial rash is characteristically distributed over the upper trunk, axillae, neck, and conjunctivae and is a helpful clue when present It is largely a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, since no single test is confirmatory Management is supportive, centred on maintaining oxygenation and ventilation and treating respiratory failure Early fracture immobilisation and timely fixation reduce the risk of developing the syndrome Consider alternative causes of the same picture, particularly pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, and evolving brain injury Rapidly worsening hypoxaemia progressing towards acute respiratory distress syndrome Deteriorating conscious level from cerebral involvement New petechial rash with respiratory and neurological change after long-bone fracture Haemodynamic instability suggesting massive embolic load Failure to improve prompting reconsideration of pulmonary embolism or sepsis Attributing early hypoxaemia solely to the injury and missing the evolving syndrome Assuming the absence of a rash excludes the diagnosis Failing to exclude pulmonary embolism, which requires different treatment Delaying fracture stabilisation, which increases risk Over-investigating for a confirmatory test rather than supporting the patient Fat embolism syndrome typically follows fractures of long bones or the pelvis, or orthopaedic instrumentation, when marrow fat enters the venous circulation. A mechanical component arises as fat globules occlude pulmonary and systemic capillaries, while a biochemical component follows as circulating free fatty acids are released and produce a toxic inflammatory injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium. The result is impaired gas exchange resembling acute lung injury, cerebral microembolism causing confusion and reduced consciousness, and dermal capillary involvement producing the characteristic petechiae. Symptoms characteristically appear after a latent interval of roughly one to three days. Most cases are self-limiting with supportive care and resolve over days, but severe presentations with marked respiratory failure or cerebral involvement carry higher morbidity and can be fatal.

Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction — FNHTR, febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, febrile nonhemolytic reaction Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction Bacterial contamination of the component with septic reaction Transfusion-related acute lung injury in its early febrile phase Underlying infection unrelated to transfusion Allergic or anaphylactic reaction with fever Clerical check of patient and unit identity Direct antiglobulin test and inspection of plasma and urine for haemolysis Repeat crossmatch and blood group verification Cultures of patient and implicated unit if sepsis is suspected Full blood count and haemolysis markers to exclude significant red cell destruction One of the most common transfusion reactions, defined by a temperature rise, often with chills or rigors, during or soon after transfusion without haemolysis It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so acute haemolytic reaction and bacterial contamination must be ruled out before attributing fever to a benign febrile reaction Caused either by recipient antibodies reacting with donor leukocytes or by cytokines that accumulate in cellular components during storage Pre-storage leukoreduction of components has markedly reduced its incidence Management is to stop the transfusion, exclude serious causes, and treat symptoms with antipyretics; meperidine may be used for severe rigors A history of prior febrile reactions raises the likelihood of recurrence and may prompt leukoreduced components Because fever can be the first sign of a dangerous reaction, initial evaluation should treat every febrile episode seriously rather than assuming it is benign A temperature rise accompanied by hypotension, back or flank pain, or dark urine suggesting acute haemolysis Rigors with rapid cardiovascular deterioration pointing to bacterial contamination and sepsis Respiratory distress raising concern for TRALI High or persistent fever that does not settle after stopping the transfusion Prematurely labelling fever as benign without excluding haemolysis and sepsis Continuing the transfusion through a febrile episode before serious causes are excluded Routinely premedicating all patients rather than reserving prophylaxis and leukoreduction for those with recurrent reactions Failing to report the reaction, losing the chance to arrange leukoreduced components Febrile non-haemolytic reactions arise through two main mechanisms. In the first, recipient antibodies formed from previous transfusions or pregnancies bind donor leukocytes, triggering complement activation and release of pyrogenic cytokines. In the second, cytokines such as interleukins and tumour necrosis factor accumulate within cellular components, particularly platelets, during storage and are passively infused, producing fever independent of any antibody. Both pathways generate an inflammatory febrile response without red cell destruction, which is why leukoreduction reduces the frequency of these reactions. The reaction itself is self-limiting and benign, resolving with supportive care, but its importance lies in not overlooking a serious reaction that presents identically at onset.

Febrile seizure — febrile convulsion, fever fit, simple febrile seizure, complex febrile seizure Meningitis or encephalitis Epilepsy with a coincidental febrile illness Rigors or shivering mistaken for a seizure Metabolic disturbance (e.g. hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia) Breath-holding spell Intracranial pathology Assessment to identify and treat the source of fever Blood glucose in any child who is drowsy or slow to recover Lumbar puncture when CNS infection is suspected or the child is very young Electrolytes only when clinically indicated (e.g. dehydration, atypical features) EEG and neuroimaging reserved for complex or recurrent focal features or an abnormal neurological exam A seizure occurring with fever in children roughly 6 months to 5 years of age, without central nervous system infection or a metabolic cause, and not in a child with prior afebrile seizures. Simple febrile seizures are generalised, last under 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex seizures are focal, prolonged, or recur within a day. The diagnosis is clinical, and the main task is to exclude meningitis, encephalitis, and other acute causes of the fever. Routine blood tests, neuroimaging, and EEG are not indicated for simple febrile seizures in an otherwise well child. Lumbar puncture is considered when meningeal signs are present, in very young or incompletely immunised infants, or when the picture is atypical. Most febrile seizures are brief and self-terminating; management centres on reassurance, identifying the febrile illness, and safety advice for parents. Prolonged seizures are treated as status epilepticus with benzodiazepine-based abortive therapy and airway support. Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reliably prevent recurrence, and daily prophylactic anticonvulsants are generally not recommended for simple febrile seizures. Signs of meningitis or encephalitis (neck stiffness, altered consciousness, bulging fontanelle) Prolonged seizure or febrile status epilepticus Focal features, or focal neurological deficit after the seizure Failure to return to baseline alertness within a reasonable period Seizure outside the typical age range or in an unwell, toxic-appearing child Assuming fever excludes meningitis and skipping evaluation in a young or unwell infant Over-investigating a well child after a simple febrile seizure Reassuring families that antipyretics prevent recurrence Starting long-term anticonvulsants for simple febrile seizures unnecessarily Febrile seizures reflect the heightened seizure susceptibility of the developing brain when exposed to fever, likely mediated by fever-associated cytokines (such as interleukin-1 beta), the effect of raised temperature on neuronal excitability, and a genetic predisposition, as demonstrated by strong familial clustering. The rate of temperature rise and the immaturity of the young brain contribute, and in most children the tendency resolves with neurological maturation. The outlook is excellent: most children have normal development and neurological outcome, though about a third experience a recurrence, and the increase in later epilepsy risk is small for simple febrile seizures.

Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children — febrile UTI, paediatric pyelonephritis, upper urinary tract infection in children Other sources of occult fever (e.g., bacteraemia, pneumonia) Viral illness with incidental contaminated urine sample Vulvovaginitis or balanitis Appendicitis or other intra-abdominal infection Contaminated specimen giving a false-positive culture Urinalysis or dipstick (leucocyte esterase, nitrites) and microscopy for pyuria Urine culture from an appropriately collected specimen Inflammatory markers and blood culture when systemically unwell Renal and bladder ultrasound Voiding cystourethrography or renal scintigraphy in selected or recurrent cases Fever with a urinary tract infection in a young child usually indicates upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) and should be taken seriously because of the risk of renal scarring. In infants and preverbal children, features are non-specific, so urinary tract infection must be considered in any young child with unexplained fever. A properly collected urine specimen is essential; contamination from bag or non-clean-catch samples is a frequent source of misleading results. Diagnosis rests on the combination of pyuria and a significant growth of a single uropathogen on culture from an appropriately obtained specimen. Escherichia coli is the predominant pathogen, and prompt appropriate antibiotic treatment reduces the likelihood of renal injury. Imaging, typically renal and bladder ultrasound, is used to detect structural abnormalities, with further studies such as voiding cystourethrography reserved for selected children. Vesicoureteral reflux and other urinary tract abnormalities predispose to recurrent infection and scarring and should be considered, especially after atypical or recurrent infections. Recurrent febrile infections and any resulting renal scarring can contribute to later hypertension and reduced renal function, so follow-up matters. Toxic appearance, signs of sepsis, or haemodynamic instability Very young infant with fever Inability to tolerate oral fluids or oral antibiotics Failure to improve on appropriate treatment Known or suspected urinary tract abnormality or recurrent febrile infections Diagnosing infection from a contaminated bag specimen instead of a properly collected sample Failing to consider urinary tract infection in an infant with unexplained fever Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria as if it were true infection Neglecting follow-up imaging or evaluation after atypical or recurrent febrile infections Most urinary tract infections are ascending: bowel-derived uropathogens, chiefly Escherichia coli, colonise the perineum, ascend the urethra, and multiply in the bladder. When bacteria and inflammation reach the kidney, pyelonephritis develops with fever and systemic signs. Bacterial virulence factors and host factors, including urinary stasis, incomplete bladder emptying, and vesicoureteral reflux that carries infected urine toward the kidney, promote upper tract infection. The inflammatory response within the renal parenchyma can injure tissue and, particularly with delayed treatment or recurrent episodes, lead to permanent scarring. Most children with a promptly treated first febrile urinary tract infection recover fully, but recurrent infections, significant vesicoureteral reflux, or renal scarring carry a risk of long-term complications including hypertension and impaired renal function.

Female infertility — female factor infertility, female subfertility, impaired female fertility Polycystic ovary syndrome with anovulation Hypothalamic amenorrhoea from weight, stress, or exercise Premature ovarian insufficiency Tubal factor from previous pelvic inflammatory disease or surgery Endometriosis Uterine fibroids, polyps, or intrauterine adhesions Confirmation of ovulation using cycle history and mid-luteal progesterone Assessment of ovarian reserve with relevant hormonal markers and antral follicle count Tubal patency evaluation by hysterosalpingography or laparoscopy Pelvic ultrasound and, where indicated, hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity Thyroid function and prolactin measurement, plus partner semen analysis Infertility is conventionally defined as failure to conceive after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse, with earlier evaluation warranted for women over thirty-five or with known risk factors Female causes fall into ovulatory, tubal/pelvic, and uterine/cervical categories, and both partners should always be assessed together Ovulatory dysfunction is a leading cause, with polycystic ovary syndrome the commonest example, alongside hypothalamic, pituitary, and premature ovarian insufficiency causes Ovarian reserve declines with age, and this age-related fall in oocyte quantity and quality is the single most important prognostic factor Confirming ovulation, assessing tubal patency, and evaluating the uterine cavity form the core diagnostic framework Tubal damage from prior pelvic infection, endometriosis, or surgery is an important and sometimes silent cause Reversible lifestyle contributors such as extremes of body weight, smoking, and excess alcohol should be identified and addressed Management ranges from ovulation induction and correction of anatomical problems to assisted reproductive techniques, chosen according to the underlying cause and ovarian reserve Amenorrhoea with elevated gonadotrophins in a young woman indicating premature ovarian insufficiency Symptoms or signs of a pituitary tumour with hyperprolactinaemia Severe pelvic pain or an adnexal mass requiring urgent gynaecological assessment Advancing maternal age prompting timely rather than delayed investigation Delaying investigation in older women where declining ovarian reserve makes time critical Assessing only the female partner and omitting semen analysis Overlooking silent tubal disease from past infection or endometriosis Failing to address modifiable factors such as weight, smoking, and alcohol before intervention Female fertility requires cyclical hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian function producing a mature oocyte, patent fallopian tubes to allow fertilisation and transport, and a receptive endometrial cavity for implantation. Ovulatory disorders arise from disrupted gonadotrophin secretion: hypothalamic causes (stress, low body weight, excessive exercise, hyperprolactinaemia), polycystic ovary syndrome with anovulation, or premature ovarian insufficiency with follicular depletion. Tubal and peritoneal factors result from scarring and adhesions after pelvic inflammatory disease, endometriosis, or surgery, impairing gamete transport. Uterine factors include fibroids distorting the cavity, intrauterine adhesions, and congenital anomalies that impair implantation. Advancing maternal age reduces both the number and chromosomal quality of remaining oocytes, lowering fecundity and raising miscarriage risk. Prognosis depends heavily on the cause and on ovarian reserve; ovulatory disorders often respond well to induction of ovulation, whereas outcomes decline with maternal age and reduced reserve, and assisted reproduction can help many but not all couples.

Femoral hernia — crural hernia, femoral canal hernia Inguinal hernia Saphena varix Enlarged inguinal or femoral lymph node Lipoma of the groin Femoral artery aneurysm Psoas abscess or bursa Ectopic diagnosis is unclear Bloods including lactate if strangulation is suspected Presents as a groin lump located below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, in contrast to an inguinal hernia which lies above and medial to it More common in women than men, particularly in older and multiparous women, though inguinal hernia remains the commonest groin hernia overall in both sexes The femoral canal has a narrow, rigid neck bounded by the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, and femoral vein, which makes strangulation far more likely than with inguinal hernias A high proportion of femoral hernias present as an emergency with incarceration or strangulation rather than as an elective referral A Richter's hernia, where only part of the bowel wall is trapped, can strangulate while the lumen stays patent, so bowel obstruction may be absent despite ischaemia Because of the high strangulation risk, femoral hernias should generally be repaired promptly rather than managed conservatively Repair may be performed by low (crural), high (McEvedy), or laparoscopic approaches, closing the femoral canal A small, deep femoral hernia can be easily missed on examination, especially in obese patients Irreducible tender groin lump below the inguinal ligament indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency) Signs of small bowel obstruction with a femoral lump Localised ischaemia despite absent obstruction in a Richter's-type hernia Systemic sepsis or peritonism suggesting perforation of strangulated bowel Confusing a femoral hernia with an inguinal hernia and adopting a conservative approach Missing a small femoral hernia in an obese patient presenting with unexplained bowel obstruction Overlooking a Richter's hernia because bowel obstruction is absent despite strangulation Delaying repair given the disproportionately high strangulation risk A femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral canal, the medial-most compartment of the femoral sheath, below the inguinal ligament. The canal normally contains fat and a lymph node (node of Cloquet) and has an unyielding boundary. Raised intra-abdominal pressure forces peritoneum and abdominal contents through the femoral ring into this confined space. The rigidity and narrowness of the neck predispose trapped contents to incarceration and rapid compromise of blood supply, causing strangulation and bowel ischaemia. The sac may turn upward over the inguinal ligament, mimicking an inguinal hernia. Prompt elective or urgent repair has a good outcome, but the high emergency presentation rate and frequent need for bowel resection mean femoral hernias carry greater morbidity and mortality than inguinal hernias, especially in elderly patients.

Fibrocystic Breast Change — fibrocystic breast change, fibrocystic breast disease, fibrocystic changes, benign breast change, cystic mastopathy Fibroadenoma Simple or complex breast cyst Breast carcinoma Breast abscess or mastitis Fat necrosis Phyllodes tumour Duct ectasia Clinical breast examination as part of triple assessment Breast ultrasound, preferred in younger women, to characterise cysts and solid lesions Mammography in older women or where malignancy is a concern Fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy of dominant, solid, or suspicious lesions Cyst aspiration for symptomatic relief and cytology of bloodstained fluid Histological assessment to identify proliferative change with atypia where relevant to risk Fibrocystic change is the commonest benign breast condition, presenting with lumpy, nodular, often tender breasts that vary with the menstrual cycle, typically in women of reproductive age Symptoms characteristically worsen in the luteal (premenstrual) phase and improve after menstruation, reflecting hormonal influence on breast tissue Examination often reveals diffuse nodularity or discrete cysts, most prominent in the upper outer quadrants, sometimes with cyclical mastalgia It is better regarded as a physiological change than a disease, and most forms carry no increased breast cancer risk; only certain proliferative changes with atypia elevate risk Assessment follows triple assessment principles, combining clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound in younger women, mammography in older), and needle sampling of any dominant or suspicious lump A simple cyst confirmed on ultrasound is benign; aspiration is done for symptomatic relief or if the cyst is complex or the fluid is bloodstained Bloodstained cyst aspirate, a residual mass after aspiration, or a rapidly recurring cyst should prompt further evaluation to exclude malignancy Management of cyclical breast pain is largely reassurance and supportive measures such as a well-fitting supportive bra and simple analgesia, with reserved use of specific pharmacological agents for severe refractory pain A new discrete, hard, or fixed lump, or one that does not fluctuate with the cycle, must be investigated rather than attributed to fibrocystic change A new hard, fixed, or irregular lump, or one that persists after aspiration Bloodstained cyst aspirate or spontaneous bloody nipple discharge Rapidly recurring cyst at the same site Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or overlying skin change Axillary lymphadenopathy or a lump that does not vary with the menstrual cycle Proliferative change with atypia on biopsy indicating elevated cancer risk Attributing a new discrete or suspicious lump to fibrocystic change without triple assessment Ignoring bloodstained aspirate or a residual mass after cyst aspiration Falsely reassuring a patient by labelling all breast lumpiness as benign disease Overlooking proliferative atypical changes that do raise cancer risk Failing to reassess a symptom that does not fluctuate with the menstrual cycle Fibrocystic change reflects an exaggerated but benign response of breast stroma and epithelium to cyclical ovarian hormones. Fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone drive proliferation and involution of the terminal duct-lobular units, producing a spectrum of histological changes including cyst formation, fibrosis (stromal overgrowth), adenosis, and varying degrees of epithelial hyperplasia. Obstruction and dilatation of ducts and lobules generate fluid-filled cysts, while fibrosis produces the palpable nodularity. The hormonal cyclicity explains the premenstrual worsening of pain and swelling and improvement after menstruation. Fibrocystic change is benign and does not, in its common forms, increase breast cancer risk; symptoms often improve with reassurance and simple measures and tend to settle after the menopause. Cysts may recur but are readily managed. Only the minority with proliferative epithelial change and atypia carry an increased future cancer risk and warrant closer surveillance.

carefully around dental and anaesthetic procedures Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is caused by an activating variant in ACVR1, a receptor in the bone morphogenetic protein signalling pathway. The mutant receptor becomes inappropriately responsive, including to activin, and drives excessive signalling that converts connective-tissue progenitor cells into cartilage and then bone through endochondral ossification. Inflammatory flare-ups, often after tissue injury, seed episodes of heterotopic ossification in muscle, tendon, ligament, and fascia. The accumulating extraskeletal bone bridges joints and restricts the chest wall, producing progressive immobility and life-limiting thoracic insufficiency. The condition is relentlessly progressive, with cumulative loss of mobility and joint ankylosis; median survival is reduced, and thoracic insufficiency from chest-wall ossification is the usual cause of death. Avoiding iatrogenic triggers is central to limiting progression.

Fibromyalgia — FM, fibromyalgia syndrome Polymyalgia rheumatica Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritides) Connective tissue disease (systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjogren's syndrome) Degenerative joint/spine/disk disease Myofascial pain syndromes Bursitis, tendinitis, repetitive strain injuries Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism Hyperparathyroidism Multiple sclerosis and neuropathic pain syndromes Major depressive disorder Drug-induced myalgia (statins, aromatase inhibitors) Hepatitis C HIV infection Lyme disease Parvovirus B19 infection Epstein-Barr virus infection Routine screen: ESR or CRP, complete blood count, and thyroid-stimulating hormone (results are normal in uncomplicated FM) Guided by history/exam: complete metabolic panel, ANA, anti-SSA/anti-SSB, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, creatine phosphokinase Viral (e.g., hepatitis C, HIV) and bacterial (e.g., Lyme) serologies when clinically indicated Radiographs used sparingly and only when inflammatory arthritis is suspected; spine MRI reserved for features of inflammatory spine disease or neurologic symptoms Repeat testing is discouraged unless the symptom complex changes Polymyalgia rheumatica Rheumatoid arthritis and spondyloarthritides Systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren's syndrome Hypo- or hyperthyroidism and hyperparathyroidism Degenerative joint/spine/disk disease and myofascial pain syndromes Neuropathic pain syndromes and multiple sclerosis Major depressive disorder Statin- or aromatase-inhibitor-induced myalgia Defined by chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain and tenderness, with pain present most of the day on most days for at least 3 months and distributed both above and below the waist, on both sides, and involving the axial skeleton (Harrison 22e p.2963). Beyond pain, patients commonly report fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive dysfunction ("fibro fog"), anxiety, and depression, which may affect function and quality of life as much as or more than the pain itself (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964). Elevated evoked pain sensitivity may be detected clinically by pain on blood-pressure cuff inflation or skin-roll tenderness; a formal tender-point exam applies ~4 kg/m2 of thumbnail pressure (enough to blanch the nail bed) at defined musculotendinous sites (Harrison 22e p.2963). Older ACR criteria required 11 of 18 tender points; newer 2016 criteria abandon tender-point counting and instead use a Widespread Pain Index plus Symptom Severity Score (e.g., WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 regions for >=3 months) (Harrison 22e p.2963-2964). Tenderness is a continuous variable; strict application of a categorical threshold is not required for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2963). Peripheral pain generators such as arthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, neuropathies, joint hypermobility, and scoliosis can trigger and perpetuate the centrally maintained widespread pain of FM (Harrison 22e p.2963). FM is one of the chronic overlapping pain conditions and frequently coexists with myalgic encephalitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, temporomandibular disorder, chronic headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, and interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome, likely sharing central mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2963). The lifetime prevalence of mood disorders in FM approaches 80%; depression is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis, but screening for depressed mood and anhedonia is important (Harrison 22e p.2964). Symptom onset and flares often cluster around periods of perceived stress, and there is a high prevalence of prior interpersonal or other violence exposure; consider posttraumatic stress disorder where relevant (Harrison 22e p.2964). Some patients meeting FM criteria have a small-fiber neuropathy, and early reports suggest possible autoimmune changes in the peripheral nervous system in subsets of patients (Harrison 22e p.2964). Functional assessment across physical, mental, and social domains is central, since improved function (rather than complete pain elimination) is the principal measure of management success (Harrison 22e p.2964). Pain extending beyond what a known triggering or inflammatory condition could reasonably explain, signaling emergence of central FM-type pain requiring a different management focus Objective inflammatory, neurologic, or systemic findings (abnormal ESR/CRP, focal neurologic deficits) that point toward an alternative or comorbid diagnosis rather than FM Screen-positive major depression with anhedonia, and history suggestive of posttraumatic stress disorder, given high comorbidity and impact on outcome Failing to consider FM, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis since musculoskeletal pain is so common (Harrison 22e p.2964). Over-investigating with repeated laboratory tests or, especially, spine MRI in the absence of inflammatory or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.2964). Continuing to treat only peripheral or inflammatory pain generators when central FM pain has emerged, instead of addressing central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964). Setting complete pain elimination, rather than improved function and quality of life, as the treatment goal (Harrison 22e p.2965). FM is regarded as a disorder in which the central nervous system maintains pain and the other core symptoms. Psychophysical testing shows altered afferent pain processing and impaired descending noxious inhibitory control, producing hyperalgesia and allodynia, and functional MRI demonstrates activation of pain-experiencing brain regions in response to stimuli that are innocuous in unaffected individuals. Pain perception is modulated by emotional and cognitive factors such as catastrophizing and perceived control. Genetic susceptibility appears polygenic, involving pathways that control pain and stress responses, including genes for metabolism, transport, and receptors of serotonin and other monoamines, with some genetic underpinnings shared across chronic pain conditions and overlapping with mood disorders. Peripheral pain generators (e.g., arthritis, bursitis, neuropathy, hypermobility) can serve as triggers that alter central pain processing (Harrison 22e p.2964). FM is a chronic condition with substantial adverse effects on physical and social functioning and on health-related quality of life. Outcomes are best when there is prompt diagnosis, assessment of pain, function, and psychosocial context, patient education, and a partnership-based strategy directed at improving function rather than eliminating pain; illness behaviors such as frequent physician visits are to be discouraged while function-promoting behaviors are encouraged (Harrison 22e p.2964-2965). Severity is captured by the 2016 diagnostic instrument combining the Widespread Pain Index (WPI, range 0-19) and the Symptom Severity Score (SSS, range 0-12, grading fatigue, unrefreshing waking, and cognitive symptoms plus selected somatic items). Diagnosis requires WPI >=7 and SSS >=5, or WPI 4-6 and SSS >=9, with generalized pain in at least 4 of 5 body regions, sustained for at least 3 months; higher WPI and SSS values reflect greater symptom burden (Harrison 22e p.2964).

Fibrous dysplasia arises from somatic gain-of-function mutations in the GNAS gene encoding the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein, leading to constitutive activation of adenylate cyclase and elevated cyclic AMP in affected cells. Because the mutation occurs after fertilisation, the resulting mosaicism explains the variable and patchy distribution of disease. In bone, the mutation impairs osteoblast differentiation so that normal bone marrow is replaced by disorganised fibrous stroma with immature woven bone. The same signalling defect in endocrine tissue drives autonomous hormone secretion, and lesional cells can produce excess FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting. Monostotic disease is often mild and stable, whereas extensive polyostotic disease and McCune-Albright syndrome can cause progressive deformity, recurrent fractures, and endocrine morbidity; malignant transformation is rare but serious.

Filariasis — lymphatic filariasis, elephantiasis, Wuchereria bancrofti, onchocerciasis Acute adenolymphangitis (ADL) vs thrombophlebitis, bacterial infection, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1821) Filarial lymphangitis vs ascending bacterial lymphangitis (distinguished by retrograde evolution) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Chronic filarial lymphedema vs lymphedema of malignancy, postoperative scarring, trauma, chronic edematous states, and congenital lymphatic abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.1821) DLA frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820) TPE vs asthma, Loffler's syndrome, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), other systemic vasculitides (notably periarteritis nodosa), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, and hypereosinophilic syndromes (Harrison 22e p.1822) Ascending bacterial lymphangitis (mimics filarial ADL) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Bacterial cellulitis (DLA is often diagnosed as cellulitis) (Harrison 22e p.1820) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (TPE differential) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Microscopy of blood, hydrocele fluid, or other body fluids for microfilariae, with concentration by polycarbonate membrane filtration (3 um pore) or Knott's formalin centrifugation technique; collection timed to microfilarial periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1821) Circulating filarial antigen assays for W. bancrofti (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow); no antigen test available for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821) PCR for W. bancrofti and B. malayi DNA in blood (sensitivity equal to or greater than parasitologic methods) (Harrison 22e p.1821) High-frequency ultrasound with Doppler of scrotum/lymph nodes/breast to visualize motile adult worms ('filarial dance sign') (Harrison 22e p.1821) Radionuclide lymphoscintigraphy (mainly a research/lymphedema-assessment tool) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Eosinophilia, elevated serum IgE, and elevated antifilarial antibody (supportive, with extensive helminth cross-reactivity; W. bancrofti- and B. malayi-specific antigen serology has specificity >98%) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Skin snip (incubated in saline/medium; microfilariae emerge in 2-4 h or overnight) or excised nodule for onchocerciasis; Onchocerca-specific antibody assays (Harrison 22e p.1823) Chest x-ray/CT and pulmonary function tests in TPE (restrictive in most, obstructive in half) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Detection of L. loa microfilariae in blood, removal of adult worm from eye/subcutaneous biopsy, or PCR/recombinant-antigen serology for loiasis (Harrison 22e p.1823) Lymphedema of malignancy, postoperative scarring, trauma, chronic edematous states, congenital lymphatic abnormalities (mimic chronic filarial lymphedema) (Harrison 22e p.1821) Asthma and Loffler's syndrome (mimic TPE) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), other systemic vasculitides including periarteritis nodosa, chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, hypereosinophilic syndromes (mimic TPE) (Harrison 22e p.1822) Eight filarial species infect humans, but four cause most symptomatic disease: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Onchocerca volvulus, and Loa loa (Harrison 22e p.1819). Filarial disease is characteristically more acute and intense in newly exposed travelers/transmigrants than in lifelong natives of endemic areas; infection usually requires repeated, prolonged exposure to infective larvae (Harrison 22e p.1819). Lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti, B. malayi, B. timori) is widely distributed; W. bancrofti affects ~51 million people and B. malayi occurs primarily in eastern India, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines; humans are the only definitive host for W. bancrofti (Harrison 22e p.1819-1820). Most W. bancrofti is nocturnally periodic (microfilariae scarce by day, increasing at night); blood for microfilaria detection must be timed to the regional periodicity (Harrison 22e p.1819-1821). Common presentations of lymphatic filariasis are asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema/elephantiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1820). Genital lymphatic involvement (funiculitis, epididymitis, hydrocele, scrotal elephantiasis) occurs almost exclusively with W. bancrofti, not Brugia (Harrison 22e p.1820). ADL lymphangitis is retrograde (spreads peripherally from the draining node), a feature that distinguishes filarial lymphangitis from ascending bacterial lymphangitis (Harrison 22e p.1820-1821). Dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA) presents with fever, chills, myalgias, demarcated edematous plaques, and entry lesions (often interdigital) and is frequently misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820). Obstruction of retroperitoneal lymphatics can rupture renal lymphatics and produce intermittent chyluria, typically most prominent in the morning (Harrison 22e p.1820). On high-frequency ultrasound, live adult worms in dilated lymphatics show a distinctive motion called the 'filarial dance sign'; worms are seen in the spermatic cord in up to 80% of W. bancrofti-infected men (Harrison 22e p.1821). Circulating antigen assays (ELISA and rapid lateral-flow) for W. bancrofti have sensitivities of 93-100% and specificity approaching 100% and detect both microfilaremic and cryptic amicrofilaremic infection; there is currently NO circulating-antigen test for brugian filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821). Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) presents with nocturnal paroxysmal cough/wheeze, weight loss, low-grade fever, marked blood eosinophilia (>3000/uL), and very high IgE and antifilarial antibody; microfilariae are cleared from blood by the lungs and are typically NOT found in peripheral blood (Harrison 22e p.1821-1822). Onchocerciasis ('river blindness'), caused by O. volvulus, primarily affects skin, eyes, and lymph nodes; pruritus and a generalized papular rash are most common, and visual impairment is the most serious complication (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823). Sclerosing keratitis (in 1-5% of infected persons) is the leading cause of onchocercal blindness; 'snowflake' punctate keratitis around dying microfilariae is common in younger patients and usually resolves (Harrison 22e p.1823). Onchocercal lymphadenopathy can produce 'hanging groin'; rarely Nakalanga dwarfism and an association with epilepsy/nodding syndrome are seen; blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.1823). Loiasis (Loa loa, the African eye worm) is suggested by transient subconjunctival worm migration and episodic Calabar swellings (evanescent angioedema); microfilariae have a diurnal periodicity peaking ~10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. (Harrison 22e p.1823). Wolbachia, an intracellular bacterial endosymbiont present in Brugia, Wuchereria, Mansonella, and Onchocerca, is a target for antifilarial (anti-Wolbachia) therapy (Harrison 22e p.1819, 1824). Sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, chorioretinal lesions, or optic atrophy in onchocerciasis (impending/established blindness) (Harrison 22e p.1823) High Loa loa microfilaremia (>30,000 microfilariae/mL): risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy with ivermectin or DEC (Harrison 22e p.1822-1823) Loiasis with CNS involvement during treatment of heavy microfilaremia (coma, encephalitis) (Harrison 22e p.1823) Chyluria from retroperitoneal lymphatic obstruction in lymphatic filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1820) Progressive interstitial pulmonary fibrosis in untreated TPE (Harrison 22e p.1822) Seropositivity (antifilarial antibody) cannot be equated with active infection; endemic residents can become sensitized via mosquito exposure without patent infection (Harrison 22e p.1821). Antifilarial antibody/antigen serology has extensive cross-reactivity with other helminths; W. bancrofti antigen tests can be falsely positive in Loa loa infection (Harrison 22e p.1821). Many infected individuals are amicrofilaremic, and travelers are often amicrofilaremic, so a negative blood smear does not exclude filariasis (Harrison 22e p.1821, 1823). Timing of blood collection to the local microfilarial periodicity is critical; mistimed samples miss nocturnally or diurnally periodic microfilariae (Harrison 22e p.1821). DLA is often misdiagnosed as cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1820). Eosinophilia and elevated IgE are nonspecific (common to many parasitic infections) and are not diagnostic by themselves (Harrison 22e p.1823). For every palpable onchocercal nodule there are an estimated four deeper nonpalpable ones (Harrison 22e p.1823). Filariae are tissue-dwelling nematodes transmitted by mosquitoes or other arthropods; insect-borne infective larvae mature into adult worms that reside in lymphatics (W. bancrofti, Brugia) or subcutaneous tissue (Loa loa, O. volvulus). Adults release microfilariae that circulate in blood or migrate through skin; adults live many years while microfilariae survive 3-36 months. In lymphatic filariasis, pathology results mainly from inflammatory damage caused by ADULT worms (not microfilariae) in afferent lymphatics, with plasma-cell/eosinophil/macrophage infiltration, lymphatic dilation, valve incompetence, and progressive granulomatous reaction and fibrosis (worsened by worm death) leading to obstruction, lymphedema, and elephantiasis; injury is due both to the worm and to host inflammatory response. In contrast, onchocerciasis pathology is elicited by MICROFILARIAE (not adults), causing chronic dermal inflammation/atrophy/fibrosis, fibrous subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomata) around adults, and corneal neovascularization/scarring and intraocular inflammation leading to blindness. In TPE, microfilariae are trapped and cleared by the lungs, provoking allergic/eosinophilic intra-alveolar inflammation that can progress to interstitial fibrosis. Calabar swellings of loiasis are thought to be a hypersensitivity reaction to adult-worm antigens. The Wolbachia endosymbiont contributes to inflammatory reactions (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823). Filarial infections are chronic with potential long-term debilitating effects; adult worms live for many years (W. bancrofti/Brugia >2 decades; O. volvulus up to ~18 years, average ~9). Most microfilaremic persons remain clinically asymptomatic for years, and only a minority progress to acute or chronic disease, but lymphatic damage can become permanent (elephantiasis, hydrocele). In onchocerciasis, visual loss is the most serious outcome and blind adults have a 3- to 4-fold increased mortality. Loiasis, historically considered relatively benign in endemic populations, is now linked to chronic morbidity and increased mortality. TPE responds to therapy but relapses in ~12-25% of cases (sometimes years later); untreated TPE can progress to pulmonary fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.1819-1823). Harrison describes lymphatic filariasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading: asymptomatic/subclinical microfilaremia, hydrocele, acute adenolymphangitis (ADL)/dermatolymphangioadenitis (DLA), and chronic lymphatic disease (lymphedema progressing to elephantiasis). Onchocerciasis severity is gauged by infection burden (skin/eye involvement increasing with moderate-to-heavy microfilarial load). Loa loa microfilaremia is stratified by treatment risk, with >30,000 microfilariae/mL marking high risk of severe post-treatment encephalopathy (Harrison 22e p.1820-1823).

Neglecting cardiac and respiratory monitoring in an ambulant patient with the milder phenotype Mistaking calf hypertrophy and high creatine kinase for a dystrophinopathy without genetic confirmation Assuming normal cognition and vision exclude the diagnosis, since these are only affected at the severe end Not recognising the wide phenotypic range attributable to the same gene FKRP-related dystroglycanopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in FKRP, encoding fukutin-related protein, an enzyme involved in the glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Alpha-dystroglycan is a central component of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex, and its sugar chains bind extracellular-matrix ligands such as laminin to link the muscle-fibre cytoskeleton to the basement membrane. Defective glycosylation weakens this linkage, so the sarcolemma is mechanically vulnerable and undergoes repeated injury and degeneration, producing a dystrophic phenotype. The severity depends on how profoundly glycosylation is impaired, ranging from a relatively mild limb-girdle dystrophy to a severe congenital form in which deficient dystroglycan function also disrupts neuronal migration and eye development. Outcome depends on where on the spectrum a patient sits, from a relatively slowly progressive limb-girdle dystrophy compatible with prolonged ambulation and near-normal lifespan to a severe congenital form with early respiratory and neurological compromise; cardiac and respiratory surveillance materially improves outcomes across the range.

monitoring Assessment for associated pneumothorax or haemothorax Serial evaluation as pulmonary contusion typically worsens over the first days Flail chest is defined by a segment of chest wall that has lost bony continuity, typically from multiple ribs each fractured in two or more places The hallmark is paradoxical movement, where the flail segment moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration, opposite to the rest of the chest The main threat to oxygenation is the underlying lung contusion rather than the chest wall movement itself It is identified during the breathing step of the primary survey and demands close monitoring for respiratory deterioration Adequate analgesia is central to management, allowing the patient to breathe deeply, cough, and clear secretions Deterioration in gas exchange may require escalating respiratory support, including positive-pressure ventilation Watch for associated injuries such as pneumothorax, haemothorax, and injury to underlying structures Progressive hypoxaemia from evolving pulmonary contusion requiring escalation of respiratory support Increasing respiratory distress and fatigue signalling impending failure Associated tension pneumothorax or large haemothorax Inadequately controlled pain preventing effective breathing and coughing Signs of underlying great-vessel or cardiac injury Focusing on the chest wall movement while underestimating the underlying lung contusion Providing inadequate analgesia, leading to poor ventilation and secretion retention Missing an associated pneumothorax or haemothorax Assuming a stable early gas exchange will remain stable as contusion evolves Excessive fluid administration worsening the pulmonary contusion When several adjacent ribs are each fractured in two or more places, an isolated segment of chest wall loses its bony connection to the rest of the thoracic cage. This segment then moves according to intrapleural pressure rather than muscular effort, producing paradoxical motion that reduces the efficiency of ventilation. More importantly, the force required to cause the injury bruises the lung beneath, and this pulmonary contusion impairs gas exchange, worsening over the first day or two. Pain from the fractures limits chest expansion and coughing, promoting atelectasis and retained secretions, all of which combine to cause hypoxaemia and, in severe cases, respiratory failure. Outcome is largely determined by the severity of the underlying lung contusion and associated injuries. With good analgesia, chest physiotherapy, and respiratory support many patients recover, but extensive contusion and respiratory failure increase morbidity and mortality.

Flexor tendon injury — flexor tendon laceration, flexor tendon repair, zone II flexor injury, digital flexor tendon injury Extensor tendon injury or combined flexor-extensor injury Digital nerve injury without tendon division Closed flexor tendon avulsion (jersey finger) Trigger finger or stenosing tenosynovitis Musculotendinous junction or forearm-level injury Retained foreign body limiting movement Careful clinical testing of profundus and superficialis function in each digit Assessment of digital nerve sensation and vascular status Plain radiographs to detect fractures, foreign bodies, or bony avulsion Ultrasound or MRI to localise a retracted tendon end or characterise closed or partial injuries Surgical exploration, which remains definitive for confirming and treating suspected injury Flexor tendon injuries are described by anatomical zones, and zone II (within the fibro-osseous flexor sheath, historically 'no man's land') is the most technically challenging because both flexor tendons run within a tight sheath Examination should test flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis separately, as one may be intact while the other is divided The resting cascade of the fingers is disrupted when a tendon is cut, and loss of the normal flexion posture on inspection is an important clue Associated digital nerve and vessel injuries are common because of their proximity to the tendons and should be actively sought Partial lacerations may retain some active movement but can still catch, rupture, or trigger, so they require careful assessment Repair aims for a strong core suture with an epitendinous suture to allow early controlled motion, and preservation of key pulleys (particularly A2 and A4) prevents bowstringing Structured early rehabilitation with a hand therapist is critical, balancing tendon glide against the risk of rupture, using controlled active or passive motion protocols The main complications are adhesions causing stiffness, repair rupture, and joint contracture, and delayed presentation may require staged grafting or tendon reconstruction Associated neurovascular injury threatening digital viability requiring urgent exploration Signs of flexor sheath infection following an open injury (a surgical emergency) Complete loss of active flexion with a retracted tendon needing timely repair before further retraction Devascularised or grossly contaminated wound requiring prompt surgical management Failing to test profundus and superficialis separately and missing a partial or isolated tendon division Overlooking associated digital nerve or vessel injury Damaging or dividing critical pulleys (A2, A4), leading to bowstringing Immobilising rather than starting an appropriate early motion protocol, causing dense adhesions Being too aggressive with rehabilitation and precipitating repair rupture Delaying repair so that tendon retraction complicates later reconstruction Flexor tendons transmit force from forearm muscles to flex the digits and glide within synovial sheaths and beneath a series of annular and cruciate pulleys that hold them close to bone. Laceration divides the tendon and causes proximal retraction of the cut end, particularly when the muscle is contracting at the time of injury. Healing occurs through both intrinsic mechanisms, from tenocytes and synovial nutrition, and extrinsic mechanisms, through ingrowth of surrounding tissue that forms adhesions. Excessive extrinsic healing produces adhesions that restrict glide, while inadequate healing or excessive load risks gap formation and rupture. Within the confined zone II sheath, even small amounts of scarring markedly impair function. Outcome depends on the zone of injury, associated damage, quality of repair, and adherence to rehabilitation. Zone II injuries carry the highest risk of adhesions and stiffness. With sound repair and supervised early motion, many patients regain good function, but adhesions, rupture, and contracture can necessitate tenolysis or staged reconstruction and may leave lasting deficits.

Focal Atrial Tachycardia — Focal AT, Atrial tachycardia, AT Sinus tachycardia (especially when the focus lies high on the crista terminalis near the sinus node, producing a near-sinus P-wave morphology; abrupt onset/offset favors AT) Inappropriate sinus tachycardia AV nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT) AV reentry tachycardia using an accessory pathway (AVRT) Atrial flutter / macroreentrant atrial tachycardia (continuous flutter waves, no isoelectric baseline) Multifocal atrial tachycardia (multiple distinct P-wave morphologies) Junctional tachycardia 12-lead ECG to characterize P-wave morphology and the R-P / P-R relationship and to localize the focus Ambulatory/Holter ECG monitoring (nonsustained AT is commonly detected and its prevalence rises with age) Maneuvers to induce AV block (carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, adenosine) to expose buried P waves and to demonstrate that the atrial tachycardia persists despite AV block Assessment for digitalis toxicity and other precipitating illness/drug toxicity when AT with AV block is seen Echocardiography to evaluate for structural heart disease and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy Electrophysiology study with electroanatomic mapping to identify the earliest activation (focal) site, typically prior to catheter ablation Sinus tachycardia (physiologic or inappropriate) Atrial flutter and macroreentrant atrial tachycardia AV-nodal-dependent SVTs (AVNRT, AVRT) Focal AT arises from a discrete atrial site and is driven by one of three mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or microreentry within diseased atrial tissue; the term 'focal' distinguishes it from typical and atypical (macroreentrant) atrial flutter and does not by itself specify the underlying mechanism (p.1937). It accounts for roughly 10% of paroxysmal SVTs in patients referred for catheter ablation, and may be sustained, nonsustained, paroxysmal, or incessant (p.1937). Because focal AT is not dependent on AV nodal conduction, it does NOT terminate when AV block is induced and the atrial rate is unaffected by AV-nodal blockade — a key feature separating it from AV-nodal-dependent SVTs such as AVNRT and AVRT (p.1937). P waves are typically discrete with an intervening isoelectric baseline (because atrial activation from a single focus occupies only a small part of the cycle), in contrast to the continuous undulating activation of atrial flutter / macroreentrant AT (p.1937). A 'warm-up' phase (gradual acceleration of atrial rate after onset) or a 'cool-down' phase (gradual slowing before termination) favors focal AT with enhanced automaticity over AV-nodal-dependent SVT (p.1937). Foci tend to cluster in areas of complex atrial anatomy — the crista terminalis, valve annuli, atrial septum, and atrial muscle sleeves extending into the thoracic veins (superior vena cava, coronary sinus, pulmonary veins) — and the focus location can often be approximated from P-wave morphology (p.1937). P-wave localization clues: septal foci give a narrower P than sinus; left atrial foci give a monophasic positive P in V1 with negative P in I and aVL; superior foci (SVC, superior pulmonary veins) are positive in II, III, aVF; inferior foci (e.g., coronary sinus ostium) are negative in II, III, aVF (p.1937). Atrial tachycardia WITH AV block is the characteristic arrhythmia of digitalis toxicity, so emergence of AT should prompt consideration of drug toxicity or another underlying illness; sympathetic stimulation promotes AT (p.1937). Incessant focal AT can cause tachycardia-induced (tachycardia-mediated) cardiomyopathy, which is an important reversible cause of LV dysfunction (p.1937). Asymptomatic nonsustained AT seen on monitoring is frequently mislabeled 'SVT' on monitor reports; treatment is NOT recommended for asymptomatic nonsustained AT identified on ECG monitoring (p.1937). Frequent atrial ectopy and nonsustained AT are often precursors to more significant arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (p.1937). Vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, or AV-nodal-blocking agents (e.g., adenosine) are used diagnostically to create transient AV block and unmask P waves when they are buried in the T wave or QRS (p.1937-1938). Incessant AT — risk of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy Hemodynamic instability with the tachycardia AT with AV block — suggests digitalis toxicity or other underlying illness/drug toxicity Rapid ventricular response causing angina, hypotension, pulmonary edema, or syncope AT as a harbinger of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter Mislabeling asymptomatic nonsustained AT on a monitor as actionable 'SVT' and over-treating it — treatment is not recommended in this setting (p.1937). Confusing focal AT with sinus tachycardia when the focus is near the sinus node; rely on abrupt onset/offset and subtle P-wave morphology differences (p.1937). Expecting AV-nodal blockade (adenosine, vagal maneuvers) to terminate the tachycardia — it usually only increases AV block while the atrial rhythm continues, since AT is independent of the AV node (p.1937-1938). Overlooking digitalis toxicity or another precipitant when AT presents with AV block (p.1937). Missing reversible tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy as the cause of new LV dysfunction in a patient with incessant AT (p.1937). Focal AT originates from a single discrete atrial site and is caused by abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, or a small reentry circuit in diseased atrial tissue. It may occur in structurally normal hearts or in association with any condition causing atrial fibrosis, including atrial tissue scarred by prior catheter ablation. Zones of fibrosis serve as a nidus for abnormal automaticity arising from injured but partially viable cells, or for microreentry within and at the border of regions of slow conduction. Sympathetic stimulation is a facilitating factor, and the appearance of AT may signal underlying illness or drug toxicity (digitalis being characteristic). The arrhythmia activates the atria from a focal source through only a small portion of the cycle, producing discrete P waves with isoelectric intervals (p.1937). Symptoms vary widely and parallel those of other SVTs. Many nonsustained, asymptomatic episodes require no treatment. The principal adverse outcome is tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy from incessant AT, which is typically reversible once rhythm is controlled. Focal AT is frequently a precursor to atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter; however, the stroke risk and the indications for long-term anticoagulation are not considered equivalent to those of AF/flutter and remain unclear. Catheter ablation targeting the focus is successful in more than 80% of patients (p.1937-1938). No formal grading scale; clinical stratification is by hemodynamic tolerance (stable vs unstable), by burden/pattern (nonsustained vs sustained, paroxysmal vs incessant), and by symptom status (asymptomatic vs symptomatic), since incessant disease carries the risk of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1937).
