with pollens and is usually mild because the allergens are heat-labile Cornerstones of management are strict avoidance of the culprit food, patient education on label reading and hidden exposures, and a written emergency action plan with a self-injectable adrenaline device Adrenaline given intramuscularly is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only and must never delay adrenaline Cofactors such as exercise, alcohol, NSAIDs, and intercurrent infection can lower the reaction threshold, as in food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis Early rather than delayed introduction of allergenic foods such as peanut in infancy reduces the risk of developing allergy in high-risk children Anaphylaxis with airway compromise, stridor, wheeze, hypotension, or collapse requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline Rapidly progressive symptoms after a known trigger, especially in patients with asthma who are at higher risk of fatal reactions Biphasic reaction recurring hours after apparent recovery Repeated accidental exposures or reactions despite avoidance suggesting inadequate education or hidden allergens Diagnosing allergy from a positive test alone without a supporting history, leading to unnecessary and potentially harmful dietary elimination Relying on antihistamines or steroids for anaphylaxis instead of giving adrenaline promptly Failing to prescribe, or not teaching correct use of, a self-injectable adrenaline device Overlooking cofactors and hidden or cross-contaminating allergens in processed foods and restaurant meals IgE-mediated food allergy arises when sensitisation to dietary protein leads to allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure the allergen cross-links surface IgE, triggering degranulation with release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and other mediators that cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, smooth-muscle contraction, and mucus secretion. Non-IgE and mixed mechanisms (e.g. eosinophil- and T-cell-driven) underlie disorders such as eosinophilic oesophagitis and food protein-induced enterocolitis, which produce more delayed, predominantly gastrointestinal disease. Loss of oral tolerance, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and cutaneous sensitisation (notably through eczematous skin) are contributing factors. Milk, egg, wheat, and soy allergy commonly resolve during childhood, whereas peanut, tree nut, fish, and shellfish allergy usually persist for life. With reliable avoidance and prompt access to adrenaline, most patients do well, but unrecognised or undertreated anaphylaxis can be fatal.

Foreign Body Aspiration — airway foreign body, aspirated foreign body, inhaled foreign body Croup or other infectious airway obstruction Asthma or viral wheeze Pneumonia Anaphylaxis with airway compromise Retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscess Structural airway lesion Chest radiograph including inspiratory and expiratory (or lateral decubitus) views Assessment for asymmetric air entry or localised findings on examination Rigid bronchoscopy for diagnosis and removal Neck radiographs if a laryngotracheal object is suspected Further imaging when diagnosis remains uncertain despite strong suspicion Aspiration of a foreign body is most common in toddlers, who explore with their mouths and have immature airway protective reflexes; food items such as nuts and seeds are frequent culprits. The classic history is a sudden episode of choking, coughing, or gagging in a previously well young child, often while eating or playing with small objects. Clinical presentation varies with the site and degree of obstruction; a lodged object may produce unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, or persistent cough. A witnessed choking event is a strong clue, but the initial episode can be unwitnessed or followed by a symptom-free interval that leads to delayed diagnosis. Chest radiographs may be normal because most aspirated objects are radiolucent; indirect signs include localised air trapping or hyperinflation, atelectasis, or a persistent infiltrate. Rigid bronchoscopy is the definitive procedure for both confirming and removing an airway foreign body. Complete upper airway obstruction is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate basic choking manoeuvres appropriate to the child's age. Delayed or missed diagnosis can lead to recurrent or persistent pneumonia, bronchiectasis, or chronic lung damage, so a high index of suspicion is important. Complete airway obstruction with inability to cough, speak, or breathe Cyanosis or rapidly progressive respiratory distress Stridor with severe distress suggesting a laryngotracheal foreign body Persistent or recurrent focal pneumonia Altered consciousness from hypoxia Excluding aspiration because the chest radiograph is normal Being falsely reassured by a symptom-free interval after the initial choking event Attributing persistent focal respiratory symptoms to recurrent infection or asthma rather than a retained foreign body Performing blind finger sweeps or inappropriate manoeuvres that may push an object further When a small object is inhaled it may lodge anywhere from the larynx to the distal bronchi, with the site determining the clinical picture. A large object at the larynx or trachea can cause complete or near-complete obstruction and rapid asphyxia. More commonly the object passes into a bronchus, producing partial obstruction: air may move past on inspiration but be trapped on expiration, causing distal hyperinflation, or the airway may become fully blocked, leading to distal atelectasis. Retained material provokes inflammation and, over time, granulation tissue, mucus retention, and secondary infection, which underlie the chronic complications seen with delayed removal. With timely recognition and bronchoscopic removal the outlook is generally excellent, whereas complete obstruction can be rapidly fatal and delayed diagnosis may result in chronic pulmonary complications such as bronchiectasis.

Fournier's gangrene — Fournier gangrene, necrotising fasciitis of the perineum, perineal necrotising soft-tissue infection, scrotal gangrene Perianal or ischiorectal abscess without necrosis Scrotal or epididymo-orchitis Simple cellulitis of the perineum Strangulated inguinoscrotal hernia Cutaneous or Bartholin abscess Testicular torsion presenting with acute scrotal pain Severe contact or irritant dermatitis of the groin Pyoderma gangrenosum of the perineum Extensive hidradenitis suppurativa flare Blood cultures and cultures of operative tissue and any discharge Full blood count, renal and liver function, glucose, lactate and coagulation to gauge sepsis severity CT or plain imaging to define the extent of gas and tissue involvement when it will not delay surgery Surgical exploration for definitive diagnosis and debridement Glycaemic assessment and screening for underlying immunosuppression A fulminant necrotising fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal region that constitutes a surgical emergency Usually polymicrobial, mixing aerobic and anaerobic organisms from the gut and skin flora, producing synergistic tissue destruction Diabetes mellitus, obesity, alcohol excess, immunosuppression, and local trauma or anorectal or urogenital infection are major predisposing factors Severe pain, systemic toxicity, and rapidly spreading swelling with skin discolouration, crepitus, or foul-smelling discharge should raise immediate suspicion Diagnosis is clinical and surgical; imaging may show subcutaneous gas but must never delay operative exploration Treatment principles are immediate wide surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, and anaerobes, and haemodynamic resuscitation Repeat debridement is commonly required, and diversion of urine or faeces may be needed to protect the wound Delay in surgery is the strongest driver of mortality, so early recognition and theatre are paramount Rapidly spreading perineal swelling with crepitus or skin necrosis demanding immediate surgical debridement Pain out of proportion to visible findings suggesting deep fascial necrosis Systemic signs of septic shock requiring urgent resuscitation and critical care Subcutaneous gas on examination or imaging indicating gas-forming necrotising infection Mistaking early disease for a simple abscess or cellulitis and delaying theatre Waiting for imaging before surgical exploration in a deteriorating patient Underestimating the extent of necrosis and performing inadequate initial debridement Neglecting planned re-exploration to remove ongoing necrotic tissue Fournier's gangrene is a necrotising infection of the fascial planes of the genitalia, perineum, and perianal area. Mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms act synergistically, generating enzymes and toxins that thrombose subcutaneous vessels and cause progressive ischaemic necrosis of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and fascia. Bacterial gas production leads to crepitus, and infection tracks rapidly along fascial planes, often outpacing the overlying skin changes, culminating in systemic sepsis and multi-organ failure. Mortality is significant and rises steeply with delayed surgery, extensive disease, advanced age, and multi-organ dysfunction; timely aggressive debridement and organ support improve survival, though survivors often need multiple operations and reconstructive procedures.

prominent forehead and jaw, large protruding ears, and macro-orchidism that becomes evident around puberty Behavioural profile often includes hyperactivity, attention problems, anxiety, hand-flapping, poor eye contact, and tactile defensiveness Connective tissue laxity may produce joint hypermobility, flat feet, and mitral valve prolapse Caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene leading to loss of the FMRP protein needed for normal synaptic function Repeat number distinguishes normal, intermediate, premutation, and full-mutation alleles, with premutations carrying separate adult risks Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted DNA testing (repeat sizing and methylation analysis) rather than routine karyotype Female premutation carriers face increased risk of primary ovarian insufficiency and reduced fertility Older premutation carriers, particularly men, may develop fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome Recurrence risk in the family is high, making prompt genetic counselling important Emerging seizures or marked behavioural deterioration warrant neurological review Assuming a normal karyotype excludes the diagnosis when specific FMR1 repeat testing is required Overlooking milder or subtle presentations in female carriers Failing to recognise premutation-related adult conditions in relatives Neglecting genetic counselling and cascade screening after diagnosis Fragile X syndrome results from an unstable expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. When the repeat expands beyond the full-mutation threshold, the gene becomes hypermethylated and transcriptionally silenced, so little or no fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) is produced. FMRP normally regulates translation of numerous messenger RNAs at synapses, and its absence disrupts synaptic maturation and pruning, producing intellectual disability and the behavioural phenotype. Premutation-length repeats are not silenced but generate excess, potentially toxic FMR1 messenger RNA, which underlies the distinct premutation-associated disorders. The repeat tends to expand across generations, particularly through the maternal line, explaining anticipation. Life expectancy is generally normal, but intellectual disability persists lifelong; early behavioural, educational, and speech interventions improve functional outcomes, and severity is typically greater in males than in females.

Frailty syndrome — frailty, frail elderly, physical frailty phenotype, frailty phenotype Depression presenting with fatigue, withdrawal, and weight loss Occult malignancy causing cachexia and functional decline Hypothyroidism or other endocrine disorders Undernutrition from social, dental, or gastrointestinal causes Chronic heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease limiting activity Anaemia contributing to fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance Comprehensive geriatric assessment across functional, cognitive, psychological, and social domains Objective performance measures such as gait speed, timed up-and-go, and grip strength Nutritional assessment and screening for unintentional weight loss Basic laboratory panel to exclude reversible contributors (anaemia, thyroid dysfunction, renal impairment, vitamin D and B12 status) Medication review to identify drugs contributing to weakness, sedation, or hypotension Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve across multiple systems, leaving the patient vulnerable to disproportionate decline after seemingly minor stressors such as an infection, a new drug, or a hospital admission The Fried phenotype describes frailty through five markers: unintentional weight loss, self-reported exhaustion, weakness (low grip strength), slow walking speed, and low physical activity, with three or more indicating frailty The cumulative deficit model quantifies frailty as a frailty index, the proportion of accumulated health deficits, and complements the phenotype approach Frailty is distinct from, though overlapping with, both multimorbidity and disability; a person can be frail without a single dominant diagnosis Simple bedside screens such as gait speed, the timed up-and-go test, and grip strength help identify frailty and predict adverse outcomes Comprehensive geriatric assessment addressing medical, functional, cognitive, psychological, and social domains is the cornerstone of managing frail patients Structured, progressive resistance and balance exercise combined with adequate protein and energy intake can improve or partly reverse frailty Recognising frailty should prompt medication review, attention to nutrition, and realistic, goal-concordant care planning rather than reflex intervention Rapid functional decline or acute loss of independence suggesting an intercurrent illness such as infection or delirium Recurrent falls, especially those causing injury Accelerating unintentional weight loss raising concern for malignancy or severe undernutrition New confusion or fluctuating cognition indicating delirium in a frail patient Equating frailty with chronological age alone and overlooking fit older adults or frail younger ones Missing reversible contributors such as depression, undernutrition, anaemia, or polypharmacy Subjecting frail patients to aggressive investigation or treatment that offers little benefit and risks harm Failing to plan proactively for goals of care before a crisis forces decisions Frailty arises from age-related dysregulation across multiple interacting systems, including chronic low-grade inflammation (raised inflammatory cytokines), sarcopenia and neuromuscular decline, endocrine changes (reduced anabolic hormones and altered cortisol rhythm), and impaired energy metabolism. These changes lower the reserve available to respond to stress, so that a modest insult produces a large, often cascading loss of function. Once physiological reserve falls below a threshold, small perturbations can precipitate falls, delirium, immobility, and dependency, and recovery to baseline becomes slower and less complete. Frailty is a strong independent predictor of falls, hospitalisation, delirium, disability, institutionalisation, and death. Trajectories vary: mild frailty may be stabilised or improved with exercise and nutritional and medical optimisation, while advanced frailty carries high short-term mortality and often signals the need for a palliative, goal-focused approach.

coordinated endocrine and psychological support around the disorder of sex development Frasier syndrome results from constitutional WT1 splice-site variants, classically in intron 9, that disturb the normal ratio of WT1 isoforms distinguished by the presence or absence of a short lysine-threonine-serine (KTS) tripeptide. Because these isoforms have distinct roles in gene regulation during kidney and gonadal development, the altered ratio impairs podocyte function and gonadal differentiation. In the kidney this produces focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with progressive proteinuria and gradual renal decline, and in the gonads it causes complete gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads in 46,XY individuals. The dysgenetic gonadal tissue carries a high risk of gonadoblastoma, distinguishing the tumour spectrum from the Wilms tumour predisposition seen with the missense WT1 variants of Denys-Drash syndrome. Renal disease progresses to end-stage kidney disease more slowly than in Denys-Drash syndrome, and importantly the glomerulosclerosis does not recur after transplantation; long-term outcome depends on timely gonadectomy to avert gonadoblastoma and on coordinated endocrine and psychological support.

heart failure, syncope or significant arrhythmia Rapidly progressive cardiac dysfunction on surveillance imaging New hyperglycaemia or diabetic decompensation Respiratory compromise from severe progressive scoliosis Neglecting cardiac surveillance, given that cardiomyopathy is a major cause of mortality Being misled by the combination of absent reflexes with extensor plantar responses and missing the diagnosis Failing to screen for and manage diabetes Attributing scoliosis and foot deformity to orthopaedic causes alone Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused most often by a large homozygous GAA repeat expansion in the first intron of FXN, which silences transcription and reduces levels of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis and iron handling. Frataxin deficiency impairs mitochondrial energy metabolism and leads to intramitochondrial iron accumulation and oxidative stress. The consequent degeneration affects dorsal root ganglia, dorsal columns, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts and the cerebellar dentate nucleus, producing the mixed sensory ataxic and pyramidal syndrome, while mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiac and pancreatic tissue accounts for the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes. Friedreich ataxia is progressive, with most affected individuals losing independent ambulation within one to two decades of onset; cardiomyopathy and its complications are the principal determinants of reduced life expectancy, though there is considerable variability related to repeat length.

Frontotemporal Dementia — FTD, behavioral variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia Alzheimer's disease (FTD has relatively preserved memory and parietal function early; a small percentage of FTD syndromes show Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487) Progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) - within the FTD spectrum; falls, vertical supranuclear ophthalmoparesis, axial rigidity (Harrison 22e p.3487) Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) - asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus, apraxia, alien limb phenomena (Harrison 22e p.3488) Idiopathic Parkinson's disease - PSP is often confused with PD, but PD does not produce downgaze paresis (Harrison 22e p.3488) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease (FTD-MND overlap) (Harrison 22e p.3486) Structural neuroimaging (MRI) to demonstrate focal frontal/insular/temporal atrophy patterns characteristic of each syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3486) Genetic testing for C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT mutations in suspected familial cases (Harrison 22e p.3486) Molecular (tau) PET imaging shows promise but to date binds robustly only to Alzheimer's-related misfolded tau; amyloid PET may help when negative (Harrison 22e p.3487) Psychiatric disease - depression, idiopathic mania, or acting out: the abulia/blandness of frontal degeneration may be misinterpreted as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD can begin with schizophrenia-like features leading to misdiagnosis of a psychiatric condition (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209) Other focal frontal lobe causes: head trauma, ruptured aneurysms, hydrocephalus, tumors (metastases, glioblastoma, meningioma) (Harrison 22e p.208) FTD is a group of clinical syndromes united by underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) pathology; like other major neurodegenerative diseases it is considered a disorder of abnormal protein aggregation, with either tau or TDP-43 (transactive response DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa) implicated in most cases (Harrison 22e p.3485). Younger onset than typical Alzheimer's: FTD most often begins in the fifth to seventh decades of life and is nearly as prevalent as Alzheimer's disease in this age group (Harrison 22e p.3485). Three core clinical syndromes are described: the behavioral variant (bvFTD, the most common) and two forms of primary progressive aphasia (PPA) - the semantic and nonfluent/agrammatic variants (Harrison 22e p.3485-3486). bvFTD manifests as social and emotional dysfunction - apathy, disinhibition, compulsivity, loss of empathy, and overeating - often but not always accompanied by deficits in executive control (Harrison 22e p.3486). In semantic variant PPA patients slowly lose the ability to decode word, object, person-specific, and emotion meaning; in nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA patients develop profound inability to produce words, often with prominent motor speech impairment (Harrison 22e p.3486). Parietal functions such as visuospatial processing and arithmetic calculation are typically unaffected even late in the FTD syndromes, helping distinguish it from Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486). Any of the three syndromes, most often bvFTD, may be accompanied by motor neuron disease (MND), in which case the term FTD-MND is applied; corticobasal syndrome (CBS) and progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) are also considered part of the FTD clinical spectrum (Harrison 22e p.3486). In contrast to Alzheimer's disease, the cholinergic system is relatively spared in FTD, which accounts for the poor efficacy of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in this group (Harrison 22e p.3486). Treatment is symptomatic only; there are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms, and no disease-modifying treatments have shown efficacy to date (Harrison 22e p.3487). New-onset disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsivity, or altered dietary preference in a middle-aged adult (Harrison 22e p.3486) Progressive language breakdown - loss of word/object meaning or inability to produce words (Harrison 22e p.3486) Emergence of motor neuron disease features in a patient with behavioral or language decline (FTD-MND) (Harrison 22e p.3486) Behavioral variant FTD is frequently mistaken for a primary psychiatric disease - the apathy/blandness can be misread as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD may even begin with schizophrenia-like features and be misdiagnosed as a psychiatric condition. Later age of onset, significant cognitive deficits, or abnormal neuroimaging point to a degenerative process (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209). Clinical features do not allow reliable prediction of the underlying FTLD molecular subtype (tau vs TDP-43 vs FET) for all syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3487). Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are largely ineffective in FTD because the cholinergic system is relatively spared, unlike Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486). Antipsychotics must be used with caution because FTD is often accompanied by parkinsonism, which they can exacerbate (Harrison 22e p.3487). FTD is linked to frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), characterized by focal atrophy of frontal, insular, and/or temporal cortex; atrophy often begins focally in one hemisphere before spreading to anatomically interconnected cortical and subcortical regions. bvFTD shows medial/orbital frontal cortex and anterior insula degeneration, semantic variant PPA the anterior temporal region, and nonfluent/agrammatic PPA the opercular frontal and precentral gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. Microscopically there is gliosis, microvacuolation, and neuronal loss; the disease is subtyped by the protein composition of neuronal and glial inclusions, which contain either tau or TDP-43 in roughly 90% of patients, with the remaining ~10% showing inclusions containing the FET family of proteins (FUS, Ewing sarcoma protein, TAF-15). Loss of cortical serotonergic innervation is common while the cholinergic system is relatively spared. Misfolded proteins are increasingly recognized to have prion-like/corruptive templating properties that may drive network-rooted patterns of disease spread. Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen in only 10-20% of cases, with mutations in C9orf72 (the most common genetic cause, a noncoding GGGGCC hexanucleotide expansion, presenting as bvFTD with or without MND and overlapping with ALS), GRN/progranulin, and MAPT/tau (Harrison 22e p.3485-3487). Caregivers carry a heavy burden, especially as the illness disrupts core emotional and personality functions. There are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms; treatment is symptomatic. For the related PSP-RS within the FTD spectrum, death occurs within 5-10 years of onset (Harrison 22e p.3487). No formal severity grading is given; FTD is categorized by core clinical syndrome - behavioral variant (bvFTD), semantic variant PPA, and nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA - and by underlying FTLD molecular class (FTLD-tau, FTLD-TDP, FTLD-FET) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487).

rewarming until definitively out of the cold Rewarming when refreezing is still possible, which greatly worsens injury Using dry or excessive heat, or rubbing the tissue, causing further damage Performing early debridement or amputation before nonviable tissue has demarcated Treating the local injury while overlooking life-threatening systemic hypothermia Underestimating eventual tissue loss based on the early appearance Neglecting analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, and prevention of recurrence Frostbite results from tissue freezing when heat loss exceeds the body's ability to maintain local warmth. Extracellular and then intracellular ice crystals form, causing direct mechanical cell damage and osmotic shifts. Vasoconstriction and increased blood viscosity reduce perfusion, and on rewarming there is a reperfusion phase with endothelial damage, inflammatory mediator release, microvascular thrombosis, and progressive dermal ischaemia. This secondary vascular injury and thrombosis, rather than the initial freezing alone, is responsible for much of the eventual tissue loss, which is why final demarcation takes time to declare. Superficial frostbite and frostnip usually recover fully, though long-term cold sensitivity, numbness, and neuropathic symptoms are common. Deep frostbite frequently leads to tissue loss and amputation, but because early appearance overstates the damage, delaying surgery until demarcation improves the extent of salvage. Overall outcome depends on depth, duration of exposure, refreezing, and timeliness of correct rewarming.

Frozen shoulder — adhesive capsulitis, shoulder contracture, periarthritis of the shoulder Rotator cuff tear or tendinopathy Glenohumeral or acromioclavicular osteoarthritis Calcific tendinitis Posterior shoulder dislocation (locked) Subacromial impingement or bursitis Referred pain from the cervical spine Septic arthritis (if acute, hot, and systemically unwell) Clinical assessment demonstrating global restriction with markedly reduced passive external rotation Plain shoulder radiographs to exclude arthritis, dislocation, or bony lesions Blood glucose or HbA1c given the association with diabetes MRI or ultrasound if a rotator cuff tear or other structural lesion is suspected Thyroid function tests where clinically indicated Characterised by painful, progressive global restriction of shoulder movement with the hallmark loss of passive external rotation, distinguishing it from rotator cuff disease The condition typically evolves through overlapping phases: a painful freezing phase, a stiff frozen phase, and a gradual thawing phase of recovery It most often affects middle-aged patients and is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, which also predicts a more resistant course May be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to trauma, immobilisation, or shoulder surgery Diagnosis is clinical; radiographs are typically normal and mainly serve to exclude other causes such as arthritis or a locked posterior dislocation Management is largely supportive: analgesia, maintaining movement, physiotherapy, and reassurance about eventual improvement Intra-articular corticosteroid injection can help pain and stiffness, particularly in the early painful phase Refractory cases may be treated with capsular hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia, or arthroscopic capsular release Constitutional symptoms or a mass suggesting tumour rather than capsulitis Hot, swollen, systemically unwell shoulder raising concern for septic arthritis History of significant trauma with fixed internal rotation suggesting a missed posterior dislocation Rapidly progressive neurological symptoms pointing to an alternative diagnosis Confusing it with a rotator cuff tear by not testing passive external rotation Forcing painful manipulation during the acute inflammatory phase, worsening symptoms Missing an underlying posterior dislocation or arthritis by omitting radiographs Overlooking undiagnosed diabetes in a patient presenting with adhesive capsulitis Frozen shoulder involves inflammation and progressive fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint capsule, particularly the rotator interval and coracohumeral ligament. Fibroblastic proliferation and contracture thicken and tighten the capsule, reducing the intra-articular volume and mechanically limiting movement, with external rotation lost first and most severely. The initial inflammatory, hypervascular stage is painful; as the capsule matures into dense fibrous tissue the pain lessens but stiffness dominates; finally the capsule gradually remodels and mobility returns. The strong association with diabetes and certain endocrine and metabolic states points to a systemic predisposition to abnormal fibrosis. Frozen shoulder is usually self-limiting, with most patients recovering good function over one to three years, though some, particularly those with diabetes, are left with residual stiffness; interventions can shorten symptoms and relieve pain but recovery is generally slow.

failure to thrive Cardiac involvement in more advanced disease Confusing the angiokeratomas with Fabry disease without appropriate enzyme testing Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the oligosaccharide pattern Assuming a uniform severe course despite the wide clinical spectrum Overlooking dysautonomia as part of the disorder Fucosidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FUCA1, encoding the lysosomal enzyme alpha-L-fucosidase. This enzyme cleaves terminal fucose residues from fucose-containing glycoproteins, glycolipids, and oligosaccharides during their lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency causes accumulation of these fucosylated substrates in tissues throughout the body, including the nervous system, skin, and viscera, with excretion of fucosylated oligosaccharides in the urine. Storage in the central nervous system drives the progressive neurodegeneration, while systemic accumulation produces the coarse features, skeletal changes, and cutaneous angiokeratomas. Residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with the range from severe infantile to attenuated later-onset disease. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Prognosis depends on the phenotype; severe infantile disease progresses rapidly with early mortality, while attenuated forms allow survival into later childhood or adulthood with progressive disability. Management is largely supportive, though haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been attempted in selected cases.

suspected Targeted biliary or pancreatic imaging when the history suggests these Functional dyspepsia is chronic epigastric pain, burning, postprandial fullness, or early satiety without an identifiable structural cause on evaluation It is subdivided into postprandial distress syndrome, dominated by meal-related fullness and early satiety, and epigastric pain syndrome Diagnosis rests on modulate symptoms Unintentional weight loss Gastrointestinal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia Progressive dysphagia or odynophagia Persistent vomiting or a palpable epigastric mass New dyspepsia in an older patient Failing to recognise and evaluate alarm features before labelling symptoms as functional Repeated normal investigations without addressing the gut-brain nature of the disorder Overlooking Helicobacter pylori as a treatable contributor Escalating acid suppression indefinitely without considering neuromodulators or psychological factors Functional dyspepsia is a disorder of gut-brain interaction without structural disease. Contributing mechanisms include delayed gastric emptying, impaired fundic accommodation to a meal, visceral hypersensitivity to gastric distension and acid, low-grade duodenal inflammation and increased mucosal permeability, and altered central processing of visceral signals. Prior infection, Helicobacter pylori, psychological stress, and genetic predisposition can all contribute, producing symptoms disproportionate to any measurable physiological abnormality. Functional dyspepsia is a benign but often chronic and relapsing condition that can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms fluctuate over time and respond variably to treatment, but there is no increase in serious organic disease.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase Deficiency — G6PD deficiency, favism, G6PD Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia Hereditary spherocytosis Other red cell enzyme defects (e.g. pyruvate kinase deficiency) Unstable haemoglobin disorders Drug- or toxin-induced haemolysis from other causes Neonatal jaundice of other aetiology (ABO/Rh incompatibility, sepsis) Quantitative G6PD enzyme activity assay (repeat after recovery if measured during crisis) Full blood count and reticulocyte count Peripheral blood film for bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz body preparation Markers of haemolysis: bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin Urinalysis for haemoglobinuria Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test to help exclude immune haemolysis The most common human enzyme defect, inherited in an X-linked pattern so that males are predominantly affected while heterozygous females show variable expression. Most individuals are asymptomatic between episodes and present only with acute haemolysis triggered by oxidative stress. Common triggers include certain infections, fava (broad) beans, and oxidant drugs such as some antimalarials, sulphonamides, and nitrofurantoin. Acute haemolysis produces sudden pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue, typically 1-3 days after exposure to a trigger. It is an important cause of neonatal jaundice, which can be severe and lead to kernicterus if unrecognised. The blood film during a crisis may show bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies, with a rise in reticulocytes. Enzyme activity assay is diagnostic but can be falsely normal during an acute crisis because young reticulocytes have higher enzyme levels, so retesting after recovery is advised. Management centres on avoiding known triggers; acute severe haemolysis may require transfusion, and neonatal jaundice is managed with phototherapy or exchange transfusion as needed. Rapidly falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic compromise Massive haemolysis with haemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia risking kernicterus Marked jaundice with lethargy or poor feeding in a neonate Ongoing exposure to an unrecognised oxidative trigger Interpreting a normal enzyme level during acute haemolysis as excluding the diagnosis Failing to counsel families about drug, food, and infection triggers Underestimating the risk of severe neonatal jaundice and kernicterus Prescribing oxidant medications without checking G6PD status in at-risk populations Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway and generates NADPH, which maintains reduced glutathione in red cells. Deficiency impairs this antioxidant defence, so under oxidative stress haemoglobin is oxidised and denatured, precipitating as Heinz bodies within red cells. These damaged cells are removed by splenic macrophages (producing bite cells) and undergo intravascular haemolysis, resulting in episodic anaemia, jaundice, and haemoglobinuria. Most affected individuals lead normal lives with trigger avoidance; haemolytic episodes are usually self-limiting once the trigger is removed, though neonatal jaundice and rare severe crises can cause serious harm if not promptly managed.

The disorder is frequently paraneoplastic, with an immune response cross-reacting with receptor expressed by an underlying tumour, most commonly small-cell lung carcinoma; identification and treatment of that tumour is central to management. Seizures and cognition often improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but outcome is heavily influenced by the underlying malignancy, and paraneoplastic cases carry a more guarded prognosis.

Galactosemia — classic galactosemia, galactosaemia, GALT deficiency Neonatal sepsis of other cause Other causes of neonatal cholestasis and liver failure Tyrosinemia and other hepatorenal metabolic disorders Hereditary fructose intolerance Neonatal hemochromatosis Urea cycle disorders presenting with encephalopathy Newborn screening result and confirmatory GALT enzyme activity assay Quantitative galactose-1-phosphate and molecular genetic testing Liver function tests and coagulation studies Urine for reducing substances (a supportive, non-specific finding) Blood cultures and sepsis evaluation given the risk of E. coli infection Ophthalmological examination for cataracts An autosomal recessive disorder of galactose metabolism; the classic and most severe form results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Symptoms typically begin in the first days to weeks of life once milk feeding (which contains lactose, a source of galactose) is established. Presenting features include poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and lethargy, often progressing to liver dysfunction and coagulopathy. Affected neonates are at markedly increased risk of Escherichia coli sepsis, which may be the presenting or dominant feature. Cataracts can develop early owing to accumulation of galactitol in the lens. Diagnosis is supported by newborn screening and confirmed by demonstrating reduced GALT enzyme activity and characteristic metabolite abnormalities; a reducing substance may be found in the urine. The cornerstone of management is strict, lifelong elimination of galactose and lactose from the diet, which reverses the acute toxicity. Despite early dietary treatment, long-term complications such as speech and cognitive difficulties, ataxia, and ovarian insufficiency in females may still occur. Milder variant forms (for example some Duarte variants) may have residual enzyme activity and a more benign course. Signs of Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative sepsis in a jaundiced neonate Acute liver failure with coagulopathy and bleeding Progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and encephalopathy Severe hypoglycaemia or metabolic decompensation Continued galactose exposure delaying recognition and worsening toxicity Treating neonatal sepsis without considering an underlying metabolic disorder such as galactosemia Delaying dietary galactose elimination while awaiting confirmatory results in a decompensating infant Assuming that early dietary treatment fully prevents all long-term complications Overlooking milder variants that may still need dietary attention Failing to arrange ophthalmological and developmental follow-up Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase blocks the conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose in the Leloir pathway. Ingested galactose, mainly from lactose in milk, cannot be normally metabolised, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in tissues including the liver, kidney, and brain and exerts toxic effects. Excess galactose is also shunted to alternative pathways, generating galactitol, which accumulates in the lens and causes cataract, and galactonate. The metabolite toxicity produces hepatocellular injury, renal tubular dysfunction, and central nervous system effects, and impairs host defences, predisposing to Gram-negative sepsis. Early diagnosis and strict dietary galactose restriction reverse the life-threatening acute manifestations. However, even with good control, a substantial proportion of children experience long-term neurodevelopmental, speech, and motor difficulties, and most affected females develop primary ovarian insufficiency. Variant forms are generally milder.

coagulopathy, renal tubular dysfunction and a characteristic oil-droplet cataract Newborn screening and early institution of a galactose-free diet prevent the acute neonatal illness Despite good dietary control, long-term complications including speech and cognitive difficulties, movement disorder and premature ovarian insufficiency in females still occur Reducing substances in the urine with a normal blood glucose is a classic clue, but diagnosis rests on enzyme assay and GALT genotyping Neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly and poor feeding after milk introduction Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative sepsis in a young infant Progressive liver failure with coagulopathy Encephalopathy or bleeding suggesting decompensation Waiting for newborn screening results before treating a clinically unwell infant Missing associated Gram-negative sepsis, which requires urgent antibiotic treatment Assuming strict dietary control prevents all long-term complications Overlooking the diagnosis when urine glucose oxidase dipstick is negative despite positive reducing substances In the Leloir pathway, dietary galactose is phosphorylated to galactose-1-phosphate, which galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase then converts to glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose. In classic galactosaemia the enzyme is deficient, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and, together with galactose and its reduced product galactitol, damages tissues. Galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to hepatocytes and renal tubular cells and interferes with several metabolic processes, while galactitol accumulation in the lens draws in water and produces cataract. The mechanisms of the long-term neurological and ovarian complications remain incompletely understood and are not fully prevented by dietary treatment. A galactose-free diet started early prevents the life-threatening neonatal illness and reverses the acute hepatic, renal and cataract manifestations. However, long-term outcomes remain guarded, with a substantial proportion developing cognitive, speech and motor difficulties, and most females experiencing premature ovarian insufficiency despite adherence.

Gallbladder cancer — gallbladder carcinoma, GBC, carcinoma of the gallbladder Cholelithiasis with chronic cholecystitis Benign gallbladder polyp or adenomyomatosis Cholangiocarcinoma involving the biliary tree Hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatic metastases involving the gallbladder fossa Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis mimicking malignancy Pancreatic head carcinoma causing biliary obstruction Abdominal ultrasound as initial imaging for wall thickening, mass, or suspicious polyp Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI with MRCP to assess local invasion, biliary involvement, and nodal or distant spread Serum tumour markers such as CA 19-9 and CEA to support diagnosis and monitoring Histopathological review of the resected gallbladder specimen with attention to depth of wall invasion and margins Staging cross-sectional imaging and, where indicated, diagnostic laparoscopy to exclude peritoneal disease Most cases are adenocarcinomas and are often silent until advanced, so many are found incidentally during or after cholecystectomy performed for presumed benign gallstone disease Chronic gallstones, a large stone burden, and long-standing inflammation are the dominant risk factors; a heavily calcified (porcelain) gallbladder and large gallbladder polyps also raise concern Symptoms when present tend to mimic biliary colic or cholecystitis, or reflect advanced disease with weight loss, jaundice, and a right upper quadrant mass Because early spread to the liver bed and regional nodes is common, tumour depth of invasion into the gallbladder wall strongly determines the extent of surgery needed An unexpected malignancy found on histology after a routine cholecystectomy usually requires re-staging and consideration of a more extensive re-resection Complete surgical resection with adequate margins, often including a wedge of adjacent liver and regional lymphadenectomy, offers the only realistic chance of cure For unresectable or metastatic disease, systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine-based platinum regimens is the standard backbone, and biliary drainage is used to palliate obstructive jaundice Anatomical association with pancreaticobiliary maljunction and geographic clustering point to both anatomical and environmental contributions to risk Painless jaundice or a palpable right upper quadrant mass suggesting advanced disease Gallbladder wall thickening or a fixed mass on imaging in a patient with weight loss Incidental carcinoma reported after cholecystectomy, mandating urgent re-staging Large or growing gallbladder polyp, particularly over one centimetre Attributing chronic right upper quadrant symptoms solely to benign gallstone disease and missing an underlying tumour Failing to send or carefully review the gallbladder specimen after routine cholecystectomy Not offering re-resection when incidental invasive cancer is identified in an otherwise fit patient Overlooking a suspicious polyp or porcelain gallbladder that warrants prophylactic or definitive surgery Gallbladder cancer usually arises from the mucosal epithelium, most commonly as adenocarcinoma, through a sequence of chronic inflammation, metaplasia, dysplasia, and invasive carcinoma. Prolonged mechanical and inflammatory irritation from gallstones and chronic cholecystitis is thought to drive this progression. The thin gallbladder wall and its lack of a serosa on the hepatic surface allow early direct extension into the adjacent liver and rapid access to lymphatics and the peritoneum, explaining the tendency for early regional nodal and hepatic spread. Outcome depends heavily on stage; tumours confined to the mucosa and found incidentally can have a good prognosis after adequate resection, whereas transmural or node-positive and metastatic disease carries a poor outlook with low long-term survival.

Gallbladder & Biliary Tract Disease — cholelithiasis, gallstones, choledocholithiasis, PSC, PBC Acalculous cholecystitis (5-14% of acute cholecystitis; associated with prolonged fasting, severe trauma/burns, postpartum, major nonbiliary surgery, TPN) (p.2733) Acalculous cholecystopathy / biliary dyskinesia (gallbladder ejection fraction <40% on CCK cholescintigraphy reproducing pain) (p.2733) Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (stenosis or dyskinesia) (p.2734) Choledochal cysts and Caroli's disease / congenital biliary ectasia (recurrent cholangitis, increased cholangiocarcinoma risk) (p.2735) Benign bile duct strictures (post-surgical, ~1 in 500 cholecystectomies) (p.2737) Extrinsic bile duct compression (most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas) (p.2737) IgG4-associated cholangitis (mimics PSC; elevated serum IgG4; steroid-responsive) (p.2737) Hyperplastic cholecystoses (adenomyomatosis, cholesterolosis/'strawberry gallbladder') (p.2737) Postcholecystectomy syndrome (overlooked reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, IBS, retained stones, bile-salt diarrhea) (p.2734) Acute (ascending) cholangitis from bacterial superinfection of obstructed bile (p.2735) Hepatobiliary parasitism (Clonorchis sinensis, Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus, Fasciola hepatica, Ascaris, Echinococcus) causing recurrent pyogenic cholangitis (p.2737) Emphysematous cholecystitis from gas-producing organisms (Clostridium welchii/perfringens, E. coli) in elderly/diabetic patients (p.2733) AIDS cholangiopathy (Cryptosporidium, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, CMV, Microsporidia, Isospora) mimicking sclerosing cholangitis (p.2737) Ultrasound - procedure of choice for gallstone detection (>95%), gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, dilated ducts (p.2730, 2733) MRCP - first choice for choledocholithiasis and the cholangiographic technique of choice in suspected PSC (beaded ducts) (p.2736-2737) ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy - diagnostic and therapeutic for CBD stones and bacterial cholangitis (p.2735-2736) Cholescintigraphy (HIDA/DISIDA) - confirms cystic duct obstruction / acute cholecystitis; CCK-stimulated for ejection fraction in acalculous cholecystopathy (p.2730, 2733) Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) - most sensitive for ampullary stones and head-of-pancreas pathology; detects microlithiasis (p.2736) Plain abdominal film - calcified stones, porcelain gallbladder, limey bile, emphysematous cholecystitis, gallstone ileus (pneumobilia) (p.2730) Serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase - elevation suggests common duct stone; ALP rise often precedes jaundice (p.2731, 2736) AMA (and sp100/gp210 if AMA-negative) for PBC; IgM elevation; serum IgG4 to exclude IgG4 cholangitis; pANCA in PSC; CA 19-9 for cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in PSC (ch.355 p.2711, ch.357 p.2737, ch.87 p.667) Endoscopic brushing of biliary strictures (more accurate than bile cytology alone) in suspected neoplastic stricture, especially in PSC (p.2737) Malignant biliary obstruction (pancreatic head carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary tumor) - Courvoisier's law: a palpably enlarged gallbladder suggests malignancy rather than stones (p.2736) Functional/vague dyspepsia, eructation, flatulence after fatty meals - common with or without gallstones but not specific for biliary calculi (p.2731) Other postcholecystectomy nonbiliary disorders (reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, irritable bowel syndrome) (p.2734) Two gallstone types: cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries, contain >50% cholesterol monohydrate) and pigment stones (mainly calcium bilirubinate, <20% cholesterol, split into 'black' and 'brown' types) (p.2728-2729). Cholesterol gallstones arise from three defects: (1) bile supersaturation with cholesterol, (2) accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals, and (3) gallbladder hypomotility/stasis (p.2729). Black pigment stones associate with chronic hemolysis, alcohol-related cirrhosis, Gilbert's syndrome, cystic fibrosis, and ileal disease/resection/bypass; brown pigment stones form secondary to chronic biliary infection/parasitism with deconjugation of bilirubin (p.2729). Biliary colic is the most specific symptom: a steady (not intermittent) severe ache or fullness in the epigastrium/RUQ radiating to the interscapular area, right scapula, or shoulder, lasting 30 min to 5 h; the word 'colic' is a misnomer (p.2730-2731). 60-80% of asymptomatic gallstones remain asymptomatic over up to 25 years; symptom development is ~2-4% per year (falling to 1-2% later) and yearly complication rate is ~0.1-0.3%, so prophylactic cholecystectomy is not warranted (p.2731). Ultrasound is the procedure of choice for detecting gallstones (>95% accuracy) and can identify stones as small as 1.5 mm using acoustic shadowing criteria (p.2730). Biliary sludge (lecithin-cholesterol liquid crystals, cholesterol monohydrate crystals, calcium bilirubinate, mucin) shifts with posture but does NOT cast an acoustic shadow, distinguishing it from stones; it can be a gallstone precursor (p.2730). Acute cholecystitis usually follows cystic duct obstruction by a stone; Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation) is characteristic, and the triad of sudden RUQ tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis is highly suggestive (p.2732-2733). Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers with chills) characterizes acute cholangitis; suppurative cholangitis with a completely obstructed duct under pressure causes mental confusion, bacteremia, and septic shock (Reynolds' pentad features) (p.2735). Choledocholithiasis (CBD stones) occurs in ~10-15% of patients with cholelithiasis; incidence rises with age (up to 25% of elderly at cholecystectomy); most are cholesterol stones that migrated from the gallbladder (p.2735). MRCP is the first choice to assess for choledocholithiasis (comparable sensitivity/specificity to ERCP); ERCP is the cholangiogram of choice when intervention is needed and ERCP with sphincterotomy is preferred for both diagnosis and therapy of bacterial cholangitis (p.2736, 2735). PBC: female-predominant (~50 yr median age) autoimmune disease with portal inflammation and necrosis of cholangiocytes in small/medium bile ducts; antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) present in ~95%; key symptoms are fatigue and pruritus (Harrison 22e ch.355 p.2711). PSC is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease (60-80%, predominantly ulcerative colitis); cholangiography shows multifocal strictures with intervening normal/dilated segments producing a 'beaded' appearance; pANCA positive in ~65% (ch.357 p.2737; ch.355 p.2712). Cholangiocarcinoma is classified as intrahepatic (~20-30%), perihilar (~50-60%), and distal (~20-30%); PSC is a clear risk factor for iCCA and pCCA with a 5-10% lifetime incidence, and is a relative contraindication to liver transplantation (ch.87 p.667; ch.355 p.2712). Gallbladder cancer: cholelithiasis is the major risk factor but <1% of patients with gallstones develop it; polyps >=10 mm are at risk of transformation; early cases are found incidentally at cholecystectomy and symptoms (jaundice, pain, weight loss) indicate advanced disease (ch.87 p.670). Biliary pain persisting beyond 5 h - raises suspicion of acute cholecystitis (p.2731) Fever or chills (rigors) with biliary pain - implies a complication (cholecystitis, pancreatitis, or cholangitis) (p.2731) Charcot's triad (biliary pain, jaundice, spiking fevers/chills) - acute cholangitis (p.2735) Mental confusion, bacteremia, septic shock (suppurative cholangitis) - mortality approaches 100% without prompt drainage (p.2735) Serum bilirubin >=342 micromol/L (20 mg/dL) - suggests neoplastic rather than calculous obstruction (p.2736) Painless jaundice and/or a palpably enlarged gallbladder (Courvoisier) - points to malignancy (p.2736) Sudden transient relief of RUQ pain followed by generalized peritonitis - free gallbladder perforation (~30% mortality) (p.2733) Pruritus preceding jaundice in PBC - indicates severe disease and poor prognosis (ch.355 p.2711) New/rising bilirubin or dominant stricture in PSC - concern for cholangiocarcinoma (ch.355 p.2712; ch.87 p.667) 'Biliary colic' is a misnomer - the pain is steady, not intermittent (p.2731) Vague postprandial dyspepsia, eructation, and flatulence are not specific for gallstones and should not be confused with biliary pain (p.2731) Pigment stones do NOT respond to UDCA dissolution therapy, and stones >10 mm rarely dissolve - only ~10% of symptomatic patients are dissolution candidates with 30-50% recurrence over 3-5 years (p.2731-2732) Jaundice is unusual early in acute cholecystitis; its presence (or bilirubin >5 mg/dL) should prompt suspicion of a CBD stone (p.2732, 2736) Missing Mirizzi's syndrome preoperatively risks CBD injury at surgery (p.2733) AMA is negative in 5-10% of PBC - liver biopsy and sp100/gp210 are needed, and PSC should be excluded by cholangiography (ch.355 p.2711) Every patient diagnosed with sclerosing cholangitis should have serum IgG4 checked to exclude IgG4-associated (secondary) cholangitis, especially without IBD (p.2737) Routine prophylactic cholecystectomy in asymptomatic stones (including young patients and diabetics) is not warranted (p.2731) The carcinoma risk of porcelain gallbladder has been challenged; cholecystectomy is no longer absolute and surveillance is acceptable (p.2734) Bile flow depends on sphincter of Oddi tone and cholecystokinin (CCK)-mediated gallbladder contraction after fatty/amino-acid meals. Gallstones form from abnormal bile composition. Cholesterol stones (>90% in Western countries) require three converging defects: hepatic hypersecretion of cholesterol producing lithogenic/supersaturated bile (driven by obesity, metabolic syndrome, estrogens, rapid weight loss, age, CYP7A1 or MDR3/ABCB4 gene defects, ABCG5/G8 variants), accelerated nucleation of cholesterol monohydrate crystals (excess pronucleating mucin/immunoglobulins vs deficient antinucleating apolipoproteins), and gallbladder hypomotility with stasis (fasting, TPN, pregnancy, octreotide). Pigment stones contain calcium bilirubinate: black stones from chronic hemolysis, cirrhosis, Gilbert's, cystic fibrosis, or ileal disease (enterohepatic bilirubin recycling); brown stones from deconjugation of bilirubin by bacterial beta-glucuronidase in chronically infected/parasitized bile. Symptoms arise when stones obstruct the cystic duct (cholecystitis) or migrate into the CBD (choledocholithiasis) causing biliary obstruction, cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis as they pass through the ampulla of Vater. PBC and PSC are chronic cholestatic syndromes from immune-mediated destruction of bile ducts (small/medium ducts in PBC; entire biliary tree in PSC) progressing to biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Most asymptomatic gallstones stay silent (60-80% over up to 25 years); cumulative death risk on expectant management is small. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the gold standard with complications ~4%, conversion ~5%, death rate <0.1%, and bile duct injury 0.2-0.6%; it relieves preoperative symptoms in 75-90%. Acute cholecystitis: ~75% remit medically within 2-7 days but ~25% recur within 1 year and 60% within 6 years; free perforation carries ~30% mortality and suppurative cholangitis approaches 100% mortality without drainage. PSC is progressive with a median survival of 12-18 years regardless of therapy and is a common indication for liver transplantation; small-duct PSC has a significantly better prognosis. PBC: UDCA slows but does not reverse disease; transplantation for decompensated cirrhosis. Cholangiocarcinoma has a 5-year survival of ~10%; gallbladder cancer is curable (5-yr survival 60-90%) only when local and resected (~20% of patients), with median survival 10-12 months in advanced disease (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711-2712; ch.87 p.667-670). Stone-based spectrum: asymptomatic gallstones -> biliary colic (cystic duct/CBD obstruction) -> acute cholecystitis -> complications (empyema, hydrops/mucocele, gangrene, perforation, fistula with gallstone ileus, emphysematous cholecystitis, Mirizzi's syndrome). CBD stone (choledocholithiasis) complications: cholangitis (nonsuppurative vs suppurative), obstructive jaundice, gallstone pancreatitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis. Cholangitis severity by Charcot's triad (pain + jaundice + fever/chills) advancing to suppurative cholangitis (adds confusion + septic shock). PBC has four histologic stages from chronic nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis to cirrhosis. PSC: small-duct (better prognosis) vs classic (large-duct) disease. Cholangiocarcinoma classified anatomically as intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal; gallbladder cancer staged as local vs advanced (ch.357 p.2731-2737; ch.355 p.2711; ch.87 p.667-670).

Gallstone ileus — gallstone bowel obstruction, biliary ileus, mechanical obstruction from gallstone Adhesional small bowel obstruction Obstructing small bowel or caecal tumour Incarcerated or strangulated hernia Intussusception Crohn stricture Bezoar-related obstruction Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen (investigation of choice) to show obstruction, ectopic stone, and pneumobilia Abdominal radiograph for signs of obstruction and pneumobilia Full blood count, electrolytes, and renal function to assess dehydration and sepsis Ultrasound to assess the gallbladder and biliary tree where CT is unavailable Serial imaging or examination if the stone is migrating with intermittent symptoms Despite its name, gallstone ileus is a mechanical small bowel obstruction caused by a large gallstone impacting in the gut lumen, not a true paralytic ileus It follows the formation of a cholecystoenteric fistula, usually between an inflamed gallbladder and the duodenum, through which a stone passes into the bowel The stone most often impacts at the narrowest point, the terminal ileum, producing distal small bowel obstruction It characteristically affects older patients, often with comorbidity, and symptoms may be intermittent as the stone tumbles distally before final impaction The classic Rigler triad on imaging is pneumobilia, a mechanical small bowel obstruction, and an ectopic (aberrantly located) gallstone, best appreciated on CT Treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction by enterolithotomy to remove the stone, with the diseased gallbladder and fistula either dealt with at the same operation or later depending on fitness A stone impacting in the duodenum causing gastric outlet obstruction is termed Bouveret syndrome Established small bowel obstruction with distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation requiring urgent surgery Features of bowel ischaemia or perforation (peritonism, systemic sepsis, free gas) Gastric outlet obstruction from a duodenal stone (Bouveret syndrome) Progressive dehydration, electrolyte derangement, and haemodynamic instability in a frail patient Failing to recognise pneumobilia and the ectopic stone on imaging, delaying diagnosis Attempting concurrent cholecystectomy and fistula repair in an unstable or high-risk patient rather than a limited enterolithotomy Not palpating the whole bowel for a second obstructing stone at operation, risking early recurrence Attributing intermittent symptoms to a resolving obstruction and discharging before impaction Underestimating fluid and electrolyte deficits in these often elderly patients Chronic cholelithiasis and recurrent cholecystitis cause dense adhesions between the gallbladder and an adjacent hollow viscus, most often the duodenum. Ongoing inflammation and pressure necrosis create a fistulous communication, allowing a large gallstone to erode directly into the gut. Small stones pass uneventfully, but a stone large enough (typically over about 2.5 cm) can lodge in the bowel and obstruct it, usually at the ileocaecal region where the lumen is narrowest. Air refluxes through the fistula into the biliary tree, producing pneumobilia. The obstruction leads to proximal bowel distension, fluid sequestration, and, if unrelieved, ischaemia and perforation. Mortality is higher than for other causes of small bowel obstruction, largely because patients are elderly with comorbidity and diagnosis is often delayed. Prompt relief of the obstruction gives good results; recurrence from further stones is uncommon, and the need to definitively address the gallbladder and fistula is balanced against operative risk.

Ganglion cyst — ganglion, synovial cyst, dorsal wrist ganglion, Bible cyst Giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath Lipoma or other benign soft-tissue tumour Extensor tenosynovitis or synovial swelling Carpal boss (osteoarthritic osteophyte) Aneurysm at the volar wrist (near the radial artery) Rarely, a soft-tissue sarcoma Usually diagnosed clinically, aided by transillumination Ultrasound to confirm a cystic lesion, identify an occult ganglion, and assess its relation to vessels and tendons MRI for occult, deep, or atypical swellings and to exclude other soft-tissue lesions Consider vascular imaging for a pulsatile volar wrist mass before any intervention Histology after excision to confirm the diagnosis A ganglion is the commonest soft-tissue swelling of the hand and wrist, presenting as a smooth, firm, rounded lump that may fluctuate in size The most frequent sites are the dorsal wrist (arising from the scapholunate region), the volar wrist, and the flexor tendon sheath of the fingers The cyst contains a viscous, gelatinous mucin and typically transilluminates, which helps distinguish it from a solid mass It arises from a joint capsule or tendon sheath and communicates with the joint through a valve-like stalk, so it is not a true cyst with an epithelial lining Many are painless and diagnosed on appearance alone; discomfort, if present, relates to size, position, or pressure on adjacent structures A small occult dorsal ganglion can cause wrist pain before it becomes visible and may only be found on imaging Reassurance and observation are appropriate for most, as a significant proportion resolve spontaneously Aspiration can relieve symptoms but recurrence is common, and the old practice of striking the cyst is not recommended Surgical excision including the stalk and capsular origin gives the lowest recurrence rate but still carries a risk of recurrence and of scar or stiffness A rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed, or irregular mass suggesting a soft-tissue tumour A pulsatile volar wrist swelling raising the possibility of an aneurysm Neurological symptoms from compression of an adjacent nerve Signs of infection or unexpected features prompting further imaging or biopsy Assuming any wrist lump is a ganglion and missing a tumour or aneurysm Aspirating a volar wrist mass without first excluding a vascular lesion Underestimating recurrence after aspiration or incomplete excision Overlooking an occult dorsal ganglion as a cause of unexplained wrist pain A ganglion forms from mucoid degeneration of the connective tissue of a joint capsule or tendon sheath. Mucin accumulates to form a cyst that connects to the underlying joint via a tortuous, valve-like duct, allowing one-way flow of fluid that fills the cyst. It lacks a true synovial or epithelial lining. Local irritation or minor trauma may contribute, and the fluctuation in size reflects communication with the joint. Ganglia are benign, and a large proportion resolve without treatment; aspiration has a high recurrence rate, and surgical excision reduces but does not eliminate recurrence.

Gas Gangrene (Clostridial Myonecrosis) — clostridial myonecrosis Necrotizing fasciitis (including type I polymicrobial and C. perfringens necrotizing fasciitis); distinction from clostridial myonecrosis is made by muscle biopsy (p.1218/1241) Other histotoxic clostridial necrotizing soft tissue infections (C. histolyticum, C. septicum, C. novyi, C. sordellii) (p.1241) Synergistic necrotizing cellulitis / crepitant (crepitus) cellulitis due to mixed anaerobic and aerobic flora (p.gas-forming soft-tissue infections) Fournier's gangrene (C. perfringens with mixed aerobic/anaerobic microbes can cause aggressive type I necrotizing fasciitis or Fournier's gangrene) (p.1239) Clostridial sepsis / bacteremia with myonecrosis (grave prognosis when bacteremia accompanies myonecrosis) (p.1240) Gram stain of a smear of involved tissue (direct examination is of major importance): large gram-positive/gram-variable rods with paucity of leukocytes (p.1242) Surgical exploration with histopathologic examination (widespread tissue destruction, paucity of leukocytes in infected tissue with accumulation of leukocytes in adjacent vessels, gram-positive rods with or without spores) (p.1242) Blood cultures (anaerobic) - obtain when spontaneous gas gangrene is suspected, as bacteremia usually precedes cutaneous manifestations by several hours (p.1242) CT and MRI to define localized vs fascial-plane spread (adjunct only; must not delay surgery) (p.1242) Needle aspiration or punch biopsy may provide an etiologic diagnosis in at least 20% of cases (p.1242) In survivors of C. septicum bacteremia/spontaneous gangrene: aggressive diagnostic workup to rule out gastrointestinal pathology (e.g., colonic malignancy) (p.1241) Gas tracking/dissecting tissue planes from non-clostridial gas-forming processes; note gas gangrene may develop in the ABSENCE of clostridial infection (other gas-producing organisms) (p.crepitus/gas-forming infections) C. perfringens myonecrosis (gas gangrene) is one of the most fulminant gram-positive bacterial infections of humans; it is a true emergency requiring immediate surgical debridement and is invariably fatal if untreated (p.1241). Traumatic gas gangrene presents with sudden onset of excruciating pain at the affected site and rapid development of a foul-smelling wound with thin serosanguineous discharge and gas bubbles; brawny edema and induration give way to cutaneous blisters with bluish to maroon-colored fluid (p.1241). The patient's pain and toxic appearance are characteristically out of proportion to physical findings; the patient may be febrile, apathetic, tachycardic, tachypneic, and may express a feeling of impending doom (p.1218, cross-ref Chap.159). The margin between healthy and necrotic tissue often advances several inches per hour despite appropriate antibiotic therapy; radical amputation remains the single best life-saving intervention (p.1241). Incubation period for traumatic gas gangrene can be as short as 6 h and is usually <4 days (p.1241). Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene arises by hematogenous seeding of normal muscle, principally with C. septicum (aerotolerant), C. perfringens, and C. novyi, from a gastrointestinal portal of entry (p.1241). First symptom of spontaneous gas gangrene may be confusion followed by abrupt onset of excruciating pain in the absence of trauma; with fever, these findings should heighten suspicion (p.1242). Gram staining of drainage or tissue biopsy is usually definitive in traumatic disease, showing large gram-positive (or gram-variable) rods, an ABSENCE of inflammatory cells, and widespread soft tissue necrosis (p.1241). CT and MRI help determine whether infection is localized or spreading along fascial planes, but must NOT replace surgical exploration, Gram's staining, and histopathologic examination (p.1242). Emergent thorough surgical debridement with wide resection back to healthy viable muscle and skin is of extreme importance; closure of traumatic wounds or compound fractures should be delayed 5-6 days until sites are certain to be free of infection (p.1242). Pain out of proportion to physical findings - excruciating pain at the affected site (p.1241/1218) Crepitus and gas in the tissues / gas on imaging with rapidly progressive necrosis (p.1241-1242) Tissue margin advancing several inches per hour despite antibiotics (p.1241) Systemic toxaemia: shock, hypotension, multiorgan failure, bacteremia, intravascular hemolysis (p.1241-1242) Foul-smelling serosanguineous wound discharge with bluish/maroon hemorrhagic bullae and brawny induration (p.1241) Spontaneous excruciating pain with confusion and fever and NO obvious portal of entry - suggests spontaneous gas gangrene (correct diagnosis frequently delayed or missed) (p.1242) Feeling of impending doom with apathy, tachycardia, tachypnea (p.1218) Diagnosis depends on clinical signs and symptoms, not solely on bacteriologic findings - 30-80% of open traumatic wounds are contaminated with clostridia and clostridia are isolated equally from suppurative and well-healing wounds (p.1239). In spontaneous gas gangrene the lack of an obvious portal of entry means the correct diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed (p.1242). Adjunctive procedures (CT, MRI) or transport to hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) units must NOT delay emergent surgical debridement (p.1243). The value of HBO remains controversial; HBO inhibits C. perfringens but not the more aerotolerant C. septicum, and blood/macerated muscle inhibit its bactericidal potential in vitro - HBO provides benefit only if surgery and antibiotics precede it (p.1243). Avoid prolonged tourniquet application and surgical closure of contaminated traumatic wounds; patients with compound fractures are at significant risk if the wound is closed surgically (p.1243). C. perfringens remains largely penicillin-susceptible but clindamycin resistance has been reported and is increasing in some regions; C. tertium is resistant to penicillin, cephalosporins, and clindamycin - good anaerobic susceptibility testing matters (p.1242-1243). Development requires an anaerobic environment and wound contamination with clostridial spores or vegetative organisms. Devitalized tissue, foreign bodies, and ischemia lower local oxygen and favor outgrowth. For C. perfringens and C. novyi, trauma must be sufficient to interrupt the blood supply to establish the anaerobic niche; the more aerotolerant C. septicum and C. tertium can seed normal tissue from GI lesions without this. Once established, organisms proliferate and elaborate exotoxins. The major C. perfringens toxins in gas gangrene are alpha toxin (a lethal hemolysin with phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activity; the major virulence factor) and theta toxin (perfringolysin, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin). Severe pain, rapid progression, marked tissue destruction, and the characteristic paucity of neutrophils in tissue are largely attributable to alpha-toxin-induced vascular occlusion by heterotypic platelet/neutrophil aggregates (via activation of platelet gpIIb/IIIa). Late cardiovascular collapse reflects theta toxin causing reduced systemic vascular resistance with increased cardiac output ('warm shock') and alpha toxin directly suppressing myocardial contractility, producing profound hypotension (p.1242). Invariably fatal if untreated. When patients become bacteremic the mortality rate exceeds 50%. Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene mortality ranges from 67-100% in adults and 59% in children (most childhood deaths within 24 h of onset). Prognosis is more favorable when an extremity is involved (easier debridement) than the trunk or visceral organs. Disease is most likely to progress to shock and death in patients with associated bacteremia and intravascular hemolysis; mortality is highest for patients in shock at diagnosis. Gas gangrene associated with bacteremia represents a later stage with the worst outcomes. Survivors may undergo multiple debridements and face prolonged hospitalization and rehabilitation (p.1242-1243).
