paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia without volvulus Myocardial infarction (given epigastric pain) Acute pancreatitis Small bowel or colonic obstruction Chest and erect abdominal radiographs showing an abnormally sited, distended stomach or intrathoracic gastric bubble CT of the chest and abdomen to confirm rotation, define the axis, and identify a diaphragmatic defect Contrast study demonstrating the site and level of obstruction where the patient is stable Upper GI endoscopy in selected non-emergency cases (with caution) Bloods including lactate and inflammatory markers to detect ischaemia Gastric volvulus is an abnormal rotation of the stomach, classified as organoaxial (around its long axis, more common and often associated with diaphragmatic defects) or mesenteroaxial (around the short axis) The classic Borchardt triad of acute presentation is severe epigastric pain and distension, retching with an inability to vomit, and difficulty passing a nasogastric tube It is frequently associated with a large paraoesophageal or hiatus hernia, diaphragmatic defects, and lax gastric ligaments, and occurs across all ages including infants Acute volvulus is a surgical emergency because rotation can obstruct and strangulate the stomach, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation Chest and abdominal radiographs may show an abnormally positioned, distended gas-filled stomach, and CT confirms the rotation and any associated hernia Initial management of acute presentation is resuscitation and attempted nasogastric decompression, followed by urgent surgery to reduce the volvulus, assess viability, and repair the predisposing defect Chronic or intermittent volvulus causes recurrent postprandial pain, bloating, and early satiety and is easily overlooked Acute presentation with the Borchardt triad indicating a surgical emergency Features of strangulation or ischaemia (severe unremitting pain, haemodynamic instability, rising lactate) Inability to pass a nasogastric tube with progressive distension Signs of gastric perforation with peritonitis and sepsis Mistaking acute volvulus for simple gastric dilatation and delaying surgery Persisting with attempts to pass a nasogastric tube instead of recognising the emergency Failing to assess gastric viability and repair the predisposing hernia or defect at operation Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient with a known large hiatus hernia and vague chronic symptoms Underestimating the severity in elderly patients with atypical or referred pain The stomach is normally anchored by the gastrohepatic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, and gastrophrenic ligaments and by its fixation at the oesophagogastric junction and pylorus. Laxity, elongation, or absence of these attachments, or a diaphragmatic defect such as a large paraoesophageal hernia, allows the stomach to rotate abnormally. Rotation of more than around 180 degrees produces a closed-loop obstruction at both the gastro-oesophageal junction and the pylorus. Progressive gaseous and fluid distension raises intragastric pressure and, together with twisting of the mesentery, compromises the blood supply. Unrelieved, this leads to venous congestion, ischaemia, full-thickness necrosis, and perforation with catastrophic sepsis. Prompt reduction and repair of acute volvulus before ischaemia develops carries a good outcome, but delayed diagnosis with strangulation and necrosis is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Chronic volvulus generally does well after elective repair of the underlying defect, with low recurrence when fixation and hernia repair are adequate.

Gastrointestinal Endoscopy — GI endoscopy, EGD, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, ERCP, endoscopic ultrasound, EUS Melena: distinguish proximal upper-GI bleeding from slow right-colon or small-bowel sources, especially in older patients with slow colonic transit Hematochezia: colonic source vs brisk upper-GI bleed with rapid transit Dyspepsia: gastroesophageal reflux vs peptic ulcer disease vs nonulcer (functional) dyspepsia vs uncommon gastric/esophageal malignancy Colonic dilatation: mechanical obstruction (e.g., malignancy, sigmoid volvulus) vs acute colonic pseudoobstruction Diverticular hematochezia: exclude vascular ectasias, colitis, and colon cancer before attributing bleeding to a diverticulum 24-hour ambulatory pH and impedance monitoring as the most sensitive test for GERD, capturing nonerosive reflux disease that endoscopy may miss MRCP and EUS for bile duct stones (>90% accurate), reserving ERCP for cases needing therapy or high pretest probability Noninvasive H. pylori testing (serology for past/current infection; urea breath test and stool antigen for current infection) before or in lieu of endoscopy in younger patients without alarm features Capsule endoscopy as the typical next test after negative upper and lower endoscopy in suspected small-bowel bleeding (diagnostic yield ~55%), with a patency capsule beforehand if stricture risk exists Plain abdominal radiography (and water-soluble contrast enema or CT) to assess colonic dilatation and differentiate obstruction from pseudoobstruction; neck/chest radiographs before endoscopy for esophageal obstruction with fever, >=24-h impaction, or sharp object Flexible endoscopes generate an electronic video image from a CCD or CMOS chip at the tip, with operator tip-deflection controls, light delivery, and working channels for washing, suction, and accessory passage (Harrison 22e p.2465). Upper endoscopy (EGD) is the best method for examining the upper GI mucosa and is superior to a barium upper-GI series for detecting gastric ulcers and flat lesions such as Barrett's esophagus, while also permitting directed biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465). Colonoscopy is the gold standard for imaging the colonic mucosa, reaching the cecum in over 95% of cases, with greater sensitivity than barium enema for colitis, polyps, and cancer; CT colonography rivals it for many polyps and cancers but is less sensitive for flat serrated lesions (Harrison 22e p.2465). For obscure small-bowel bleeding, capsule endoscopy visualizes mucosa beyond the reach of a conventional endoscope but is purely diagnostic; push and balloon-assisted enteroscopy allow deeper intubation with biopsy and therapy (Harrison 22e p.2465-2466). EUS provides the most accurate preoperative local staging of esophageal, pancreatic, and rectal malignancies but does not detect distant metastases beyond its imaging range; it also enables fine-needle aspiration/biopsy and a growing range of therapeutic drainage procedures (Harrison 22e p.2468). Endoscopic stigmata of a peptic ulcer carry prognostic value: a clean-based ulcer has a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, flat pigmented spots ~10%, adherent clot ~20%, a visible vessel ~40%, and active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479). Over 90% of patients with melena bleed proximal to the ligament of Treitz and ~85% with hematochezia bleed from the colon, but massive hematochezia can reflect a brisk upper-GI source with rapid transit, warranting urgent upper endoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2476). Severity of the initial hemorrhage is the most important indicator for urgent endoscopy; falling hematocrit and hemoglobin lag behind the clinical course and are unreliable gauges of acute blood loss (Harrison 22e p.2476). Acute esophageal obstruction from food impaction or a foreign body is an endoscopic emergency; untreated it can lead to esophageal ulceration, ischemia, and perforation, and an underlying web, ring, or stricture is often present (Harrison 22e p.2484-2485). In acute colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie's), the risk of cecal perforation rises when cecal diameter exceeds 12 cm, prompting decompression with intravenous neostigmine or colonoscopy (Harrison 22e p.2487). Charcot's triad (jaundice, abdominal pain, fever) is present in ~70% of ascending cholangitis; the addition of shock and confusion (Reynolds's pentad) signals high mortality and warrants urgent biliary drainage, typically by ERCP (Harrison 22e p.2489). Long-standing GERD confers a roughly sixfold increased risk of Barrett's esophagus versus reflux of under one year; screening EGD should be considered after a chronic (>=10-year) GERD history even when symptoms are mild (Harrison 22e p.2490-2491). Resting hypotension, orthostatic vital-sign change, repeated hematemesis, bloody nasogastric aspirate not clearing with lavage, or transfusion requirement — consider urgent endoscopy within 12-24 h Dyspepsia or reflux with alarm features (weight loss, obstructive symptoms, dysphagia, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia) — perform endoscopy at the outset Esophageal food/foreign-body impaction with hypersalivation and inability to swallow water — endoscopic emergency Reynolds's pentad (Charcot's triad plus shock and confusion) in ascending cholangitis — urgent biliary drainage Cecal diameter exceeding 12 cm in colonic pseudoobstruction — impending perforation Age >70, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, or respiratory/renal failure with GI bleeding — higher rebleeding risk warranting prompt evaluation Relying on hematocrit/hemoglobin to gauge acute bleeding — these lag behind the clinical course Assuming melena always means an upper-GI source or hematochezia always a colonic source — exceptions occur with transit-dependent presentations Performing ERCP indiscriminately in gallstone pancreatitis — only ~20% retain an ampullary/common-bile-duct stone, and initial MRCP/EUS reduces unnecessary ERCP and its adverse events Using endoscopy to diagnose nonerosive reflux disease — it will miss symptomatic reflux without esophagitis Treating a Mallory-Weiss tear bearing a nonbleeding sentinel clot like a peptic ulcer — unlike ulcers, such tears rarely rebleed and need no endoscopic therapy Relying on epinephrine injection alone for ulcer hemostasis — it slows bleeding but is not definitive monotherapy Obtaining radiographic contrast studies before endoscopy in suspected esophageal obstruction — contrast interferes with the subsequent endoscopic procedure Proceeding to endoscopy in marked coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia without correction — hemostatic techniques are limited and correction may itself resolve bleeding Gastrointestinal endoscopy is a diagnostic and therapeutic modality rather than a disease; it directly visualizes mucosal and luminal pathology and adjacent structures (via EUS) and provides access for tissue sampling and intervention. Many of the conditions it manages share a vascular or mechanical basis: peptic ulcers bleed when erosion exposes a submucosal vessel; a Dieulafoy's lesion is an abnormally large-caliber persistent artery running just beneath the epithelium that bleeds through a focal mucosal defect; a Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal rent at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching/vomiting that can disrupt a submucosal arteriole; colonic diverticular bleeding arises from the nutrient artery at the base of a diverticulum; and vascular ectasias are flat mucosal vascular anomalies (e.g., GAVE/watermelon stomach) that cause slow blood loss. Variceal bleeding reflects portal hypertension. Obstructive syndromes (esophageal food impaction, gastric outlet obstruction, colonic obstruction/pseudoobstruction, biliary obstruction by stone) produce luminal blockage that endoscopy can relieve. Barrett's esophagus represents columnar metaplasia of distal esophageal squamous mucosa driven by chronic acid reflux and is a precursor to adenocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491). Outcomes depend on the underlying condition and endoscopic findings. Most GI bleeding stops spontaneously. Endoscopic therapy of high-risk peptic ulcer stigmata lowers rebleeding to about 5-10%. Endoscopic variceal ligation controls acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage in up to 90% of patients, though chronic eradication therapy prevents long-term rebleeding in only ~50%. A clean-based ulcer carries a low (3-5%) rebleeding risk, permitting early discharge of suitable patients. Post-ERCP pancreatitis is usually mild and self-limited but can be severe. Delayed biliary drainage in ascending cholangitis increases morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2464-2491). Peptic ulcer rebleeding risk by endoscopic stigmata: clean base 3-5%; flat pigmented spots ~10%; adherent clot ~20%; nonbleeding visible vessel ~40%; active spurting ~90% (Harrison 22e p.2478-2479). Procedural adverse-event risk: bleeding/perforation under 1:1000 for diagnostic EGD, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and colonoscopy, rising to 0.5-5% with therapeutic maneuvers; ERCP carries ~5% pancreatitis risk (up to ~25% in young, anicteric patients with normal ducts) and ~1% post-sphincterotomy bleeding; PEG placement has a 10-15% adverse-event rate (Harrison 22e p.2473-2474).

Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumors — GI NETs, Carcinoid tumors, Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, GEP-NETs, Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, Islet cell tumors Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and other nonneuroendocrine pancreatic cancers Irritable bowel syndrome (small-bowel NETs are frequently misattributed to IBS for months to years) Psychiatric illness (insulinoma hypoglycemic symptoms may be mistaken for psychiatric disease) Mixed neuroendocrine-adenocarcinoma tumors (adenocarcinoids) of the appendix Somatostatin-receptor imaging: gallium-68 dotatate (or DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) PET, highly sensitive for primaries and metastases Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI; endoscopic ultrasound especially for small pancreatic primaries such as insulinomas FDG-PET (often negative in low-grade well-differentiated NETs but positive in higher-grade tumors) Fasting insulin with proinsulin and C-peptide (elevated in insulinoma; proinsulin/C-peptide normal with exogenous insulin) and serum/plasma sulfonylurea levels Fasting serum gastrin (interpret with awareness of PPI and achlorhydria effects) Plasma glucagon (glucagonoma generally >1000 pg/mL), plasma somatostatin, plasma VIP 24-hour urinary or plasma 5-HIAA for carcinoid syndrome (suggestive, not diagnostic; serotonin-rich foods such as salmon and eggs cause false positives) Chromogranin A (neither sensitive nor specific; falsely elevated in renal impairment and with PPI use) Histologic grading with mitotic count and Ki-67 plus chromogranin/synaptophysin immunostaining; vitamin B12 and antiparietal evaluation in type 1 gastric NET with atrophic gastritis Systemic mastocytosis (symptoms can be easily confused with carcinoid syndrome) Other causes of fasting hypoglycemia: severe liver disease, alcoholism, poor nutrition, post-gastric-bypass postprandial hypoglycemia, surreptitious insulin or sulfonylurea use (mimicking insulinoma) Causes of secretory diarrhea mimicking VIPoma: inflammatory bowel disease, short-bowel after small-bowel resection, radiation enteritis, surreptitious laxative/diuretic use Causes of hypergastrinemia other than gastrinoma: proton pump inhibitor use and achlorhydria from chronic atrophic gastritis (mimicking gastrinoma) Drug-induced valvulopathy mimicking carcinoid heart disease: fenfluramine and ergot-containing dopamine agonists (both act via 5-HT2B receptors) GI NETs are broadly grouped by origin into extrapancreatic NETs (historically called carcinoid tumors) and pancreatic NETs; they typically follow a more indolent course than most malignancies but can synthesize peptides, growth factors, and bioactive amines that are ectopically secreted (Harrison 22e p.676). Tumors are classified by differentiation (well vs poorly differentiated) and grade 1-3, which closely correlates with mitotic count and Ki-67 index: grade 1 is <2 mitoses/10 HPF and Ki-67 <3%, grade 2 is 2-20/10 HPF and 3-20%, grade 3 is >20/10 HPF and >20%; poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas are the most aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677). Only about 20% of pancreatic NETs are functional (hormone-secreting); the majority are nonfunctional and present incidentally or with mass-related symptoms such as abdominal pain and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.677). The most common functional pancreatic NET is insulinoma, followed by glucagonoma and gastrinoma; somatostatinoma, VIPoma, ACTHoma and others are uncommon (Harrison 22e p.677). Most gastrinomas actually arise in the gastrinoma triangle (bounded by duodenum, pancreas, and confluence of cystic and common bile ducts) rather than the pancreas, and 50-90% of sporadic gastrinomas arise in the duodenum, where they are often small and hard to localize (Harrison 22e p.678). Glucagonoma classically presents with necrolytic migratory erythema (often intertriginous, waxing and waning), glucose intolerance and weight loss; a hypercoagulable state is reported in up to one-third of patients (Harrison 22e p.679). Gastric NETs fall into three types: type 1 (chronic atrophic gastritis, most common, generally benign), type 2 (associated with gastrinoma/ZES), and type 3 (sporadic, normal gastrin, potentially far more aggressive) (Harrison 22e p.680). Small-bowel NETs (most often terminal ileum) arise within the muscularis/submucosa and are notoriously hard to diagnose early; mesenteric fibrosis from serotonin-driven fibroblast proliferation produces a classic calcified spoke-and-wheel mesenteric mass on CT and can cause intermittent obstruction and bowel ischemia (Harrison 22e p.680). Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, watery diarrhea, right-sided valvular heart disease, mesenteric fibrosis) is most associated with small intestine or appendiceal primaries and usually develops only after hepatic metastases or retroperitoneal lesions allow serotonin and vasoactive substances to enter systemic circulation (Harrison 22e p.681). More than 90% of NETs express somatostatin receptors, making somatostatin-analogue PET tracers (gallium-68 dotatate, DOTATOC, copper-64 dotatate) highly sensitive for detecting primaries and metastases (Harrison 22e p.681). Carcinoid heart disease occurs in roughly two-thirds of patients with carcinoid syndrome and is characterized by plaque-like fibrous endocardial thickening classically on the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation (nearly universal) plus possible tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary regurgitation, and pulmonary stenosis (Harrison 22e p.683). A minority of NETs arise within inherited syndromes; MEN 1 (menin gene, 11q13) is the most common, and gastrinoma should prompt a family history and assessment for hyperparathyroidism since up to 25% of ZES patients have MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.676, 678). Carcinoid crisis: life-threatening profound hypotension or hypertension triggered by tumor manipulation during surgery, hepatic artery embolization, radionuclide therapy, exogenous epinephrine, or anesthesia induction Right-sided heart failure from carcinoid heart disease, a major source of morbidity and mortality Severe refractory hypoglycemia from insulinoma causing confusion, coma Mesenteric fibrosis causing intermittent small-bowel obstruction or bowel ischemia Profound watery diarrhea with hypokalemia and dehydration in VIPoma (Verner-Morrison/WDHA syndrome) PPIs and achlorhydria can both raise serum gastrin and confound the diagnosis of gastrinoma Chromogranin A is frequently falsely elevated (renal impairment, PPI use) and is neither sensitive nor specific; assay variability complicates interpretation Elevated 5-HIAA is suggestive but not diagnostic of carcinoid syndrome, with false positives from serotonin-rich foods Somatostatin-receptor PET can be falsely positive (physiologic uptake in the pancreatic uncinate process, sarcoidosis, meningiomas, thyroid goiter/thyroiditis) and falsely negative in higher-grade tumors with lower receptor expression Insulinomas are less reliably avid on somatostatin scintigraphy and are usually small (<2 cm), making EUS the preferred localization tool Insulinoma may be misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness; surreptitious insulin/hypoglycemic-agent use can mimic it Small-bowel NETs are easily missed at colonoscopy due to submucosal location beyond the ileocecal valve and may be misattributed to IBS for years Reduction of serotonin levels does not reverse established carcinoid valvular lesions GI NETs arise from neuroendocrine cells and contain electron-dense neurosecretory granules holding peptides and bioactive amines that can be ectopically secreted. Sporadic pancreatic NETs most frequently harbor MEN1 mutations (about 44%), with frequent mutations in the DAXX/ATRX chromatin-remodeling complex (about 43%) and mTOR-pathway genes (about 15%); recurrent mutations in extrapancreatic NETs are rare, though small-bowel NETs commonly show loss of chromosome 18 and CDKN1B mutations in a minority. In carcinoid syndrome the principal mediator is serotonin (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase; up to 50% of dietary tryptophan can be diverted into this pathway, which can deplete niacin and produce pellagra-like lesions. Histamine and tachykinins such as substance P also contribute. Serotonin stimulates intestinal secretion and motility and drives fibroblast growth, accounting for mesenteric fibrosis and for valvular fibrosis via activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart-valve fibroblasts. Right-sided cardiac predominance reflects venous delivery of serotonin from hepatic/retroperitoneal deposits to the right heart, with pulmonary metabolism sparing the left heart. Inherited syndromes (MEN 1, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, tuberous sclerosis) underlie a minority of cases (Harrison 22e p.676-683). NETs are typically more indolent than other malignancies, and both incidence and survival have risen over recent decades (US incidence rose about 6.4-fold from 1973 to 2012; prevalence exceeded 170,000). Prognosis depends strongly on primary site and histologic grade. Median survival for advanced pancreatic NETs rose from roughly 2 years in early SEER analyses to about 4 years more recently, and median survival for well-differentiated advanced small-intestine NETs exceeds 5 years. Appendiceal NETs that are well differentiated and <2 cm have extremely low metastatic risk and excellent prognosis, while metastatic risk rises to about 20-30% for 2-3 cm tumors and is even higher beyond 3 cm. Most rectal NETs are small (<1 cm), well differentiated and rarely metastasize, but up to one-third of 1-2 cm rectal NETs metastasize and >2 cm rectal NETs metastasize in over 70%. Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas carry markedly worse prognosis. The natural history is ultimately progressive (Harrison 22e p.677-682). WHO-type histologic classification used in Harrison: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor grade 1 (low grade, <2 mitoses/10 HPF, Ki-67 <3%); grade 2 (intermediate, 2-20/10 HPF, Ki-67 3-20%); grade 3 (well-differentiated high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%); and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma (high grade, >20/10 HPF, Ki-67 >20%), the most clinically aggressive category (Harrison 22e p.677).

Gastroparesis — delayed gastric emptying, gastric stasis, diabetic gastroparesis, gastroparetic syndrome Mechanical gastric outlet obstruction Functional dyspepsia Cyclic vomiting syndrome or cannabinoid hyperemesis Rumination syndrome Small bowel dysmotility or pseudo-obstruction Peptic ulcer disease or malignancy Upper endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction Scintigraphic solid-meal gastric emptying study Wireless motility capsule or breath test as alternatives Blood glucose and HbA1c assessment in diabetic patients Review of medications affecting gastric motility Nutritional and electrolyte assessment in severe or chronic disease Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction, presenting with nausea, vomiting, early satiety, bloating, and postprandial fullness The commonest identifiable causes are diabetes mellitus and prior gastric or vagal surgery, but many cases are idiopathic and some follow a viral illness Mechanical obstruction must be excluded, typically by endoscopy, before the diagnosis is made A scintigraphic gastric emptying study of a solid meal is the standard confirmatory test, with wireless motility capsule and breath tests as alternatives Medications that slow gastric emptying, especially opioids and GLP-1 receptor agonists, can cause or worsen symptoms and should be reviewed Management combines dietary modification toward small, low-fat, low-fibre meals with prokinetic and antiemetic therapy Refractory disease may require enteral feeding beyond the stomach, gastric electrical stimulation, or endoscopic pyloric procedures Intractable vomiting with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Significant weight loss or malnutrition Features suggesting mechanical obstruction or malignancy Marked or unstable glycaemic control complicating diabetic gastroparesis Diagnosing gastroparesis without first excluding mechanical obstruction Overlooking opioids or GLP-1 receptor agonists as reversible contributors Ignoring hyperglycaemia, which acutely delays emptying and undermines treatment Missing alternative diagnoses such as rumination or cyclic vomiting that mimic gastroparesis Gastroparesis arises from impaired neuromuscular coordination of gastric emptying. Injury to the vagus nerve, abnormalities of the interstitial cells of Cajal that pace gastric contractions, smooth muscle dysfunction, and autonomic neuropathy disrupt fundic accommodation, antral contractility, and pyloric relaxation. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycaemia and autonomic neuropathy impair motility, and acute hyperglycaemia itself further slows emptying. The result is retained gastric contents, which produce nausea, vomiting, and impaired nutrient and drug absorption. Gastroparesis is often a chronic, fluctuating condition; many patients achieve reasonable symptom control with diet and medication, but a subset have refractory, disabling symptoms with recurrent hospitalisation and nutritional compromise.

Gastroschisis — abdominal wall defect, paraumbilical wall defect Omphalocele (exomphalos) with intact sac Ruptured omphalocele Umbilical cord hernia Body stalk anomaly / limb-body wall complex Bladder or cloacal exstrophy Antenatal ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis and monitor bowel appearance Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, typically elevated Postnatal assessment of bowel viability and search for associated atresia Serial electrolytes and fluid balance monitoring given large insensible losses Echocardiography if any additional anomaly is suspected A full-thickness abdominal wall defect, almost always to the right of the umbilical cord, through which bowel eviscerates without any covering membrane Because the exposed bowel has no protective sac, it is vulnerable to fluid and heat loss and to inflammatory damage from amniotic fluid, so immediate protection is essential Associated anomalies are uncommon apart from intestinal problems such as atresia, in contrast to omphalocele where The infant should be nursed to avoid kinking of the mesentery, since the narrow defect can compromise blood flow to the herniated bowel Closure may be achieved primarily if the defect and bowel volume allow, or staged using a silo to gradually reduce the bowel before fascial closure Prolonged ileus and delayed feeding tolerance are expected postoperatively because of the intrauterine inflammatory thickening (peel) on the bowel Most cases are detected antenatally on ultrasound and by a raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, allowing planned delivery at a surgical centre Exposed uncovered bowel requiring immediate protection to prevent catastrophic heat, fluid, and evaporative losses Dusky, ischaemic, or constricted bowel at the defect indicating threatened viability and need for urgent intervention Signs of hypovolaemia or hypothermia from inadequate resuscitation Evidence of associated intestinal atresia or perforation requiring surgical planning Delaying protection of the exposed bowel, leading to hypothermia and severe fluid loss Positioning the infant so the mesentery kinks and the bowel becomes ischaemic Forcing primary closure under excessive tension and causing abdominal compartment syndrome Underestimating the duration of postoperative ileus and stopping nutritional support too early Gastroschisis is a defect in the anterior abdominal wall adjacent to the umbilicus, thought to result from a vascular or developmental disruption of the wall, allowing loops of bowel and occasionally other viscera to herniate freely into the amniotic cavity. Unlike omphalocele there is no covering sac, so the exposed intestine is bathed in amniotic fluid, becoming oedematous, foreshortened, and matted with an inflammatory peel. The small mesenteric opening also predisposes the herniated segment to ischaemia and to associated intestinal atresia. Survival is generally high with modern neonatal and surgical care. Recovery is often prolonged by intestinal dysmotility and delayed feeding, and outcome is worse when there is complex disease with atresia, perforation, or extensive bowel loss leading to short bowel syndrome.

Gaucher disease — glucocerebrosidase deficiency, acid beta-glucosidase deficiency, glucosylceramide lipidosis Niemann-Pick disease Other lysosomal storage disorders with hepatosplenomegaly Haematological malignancy such as leukaemia or lymphoma Myelofibrosis or other causes of splenomegaly with cytopenia Chronic liver disease with portal hypertension Assay of glucocerebrosidase enzyme activity in leukocytes or cultured fibroblasts GBA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling Full blood count to detect anaemia and thrombocytopenia Plasma biomarkers such as chitotriosidase or glucosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb1) to support diagnosis and monitor disease Skeletal imaging including MRI to assess marrow infiltration and bone complications The most common lysosomal storage disorder, caused by deficient activity of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase) and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner Undegraded glucocerebroside accumulates within macrophages, producing the characteristic lipid-laden 'Gaucher cells' seen in marrow and other tissues Type 1 is non-neuronopathic and dominates in adults and older children, with hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone involvement but sparing of the central nervous system Type 2 is the acute neuronopathic form of infancy with rapid neurological deterioration and a poor outlook, while type 3 shows slower, chronic neurological disease Bone manifestations include marrow infiltration, painful crises, avascular necrosis, and the classic Erlenmeyer-flask deformity of the distal femur Splenomegaly with thrombocytopenia and anaemia is a frequent presenting picture and can mimic a haematological malignancy Enzyme replacement therapy is effective for the visceral and haematological features of type 1, and oral substrate reduction therapy is an alternative in selected patients Disease-modifying therapy does not correct neurological disease because infused enzyme does not cross the blood-brain barrier Increased susceptibility to Parkinsonism is recognised in patients and carriers with glucocerebrosidase gene variants Rapid neurological regression in infancy suggesting acute neuronopathic (type 2) disease Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding or profound anaemia Acute bone pain crisis or evidence of avascular necrosis Massive splenomegaly with risk of rupture or hypersplenism Misdiagnosing splenomegaly with cytopenia as a primary haematological malignancy and pursuing unnecessary invasive workup Assuming enzyme replacement therapy will halt neurological progression in neuronopathic forms Overlooking bone disease, which can progress even when visceral parameters improve Failing to offer genetic counselling and carrier testing to at-risk relatives Gaucher disease results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the GBA gene encoding lysosomal glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase). Reduced enzyme activity impairs breakdown of glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide), which accumulates predominantly within the lysosomes of macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. These engorged macrophages (Gaucher cells) infiltrate the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and, in neuronopathic forms, the nervous system, driving organomegaly, marrow replacement with cytopenias, and skeletal disease. The pattern and severity of residual enzyme activity, influenced by genotype, largely determine whether the phenotype is non-neuronopathic (type 1) or neuronopathic (types 2 and 3). Type 1 disease generally has a good outlook, especially with enzyme replacement or substrate reduction therapy, which reverses much of the visceral and haematological burden. Type 2 carries a poor prognosis with early death, whereas type 3 has an intermediate course with progressive neurological involvement despite treatment of systemic features.

Guillain-Barré syndrome — Nerve conduction studies CSF (albuminocytologic dissociation) Serial vital capacity / NIF Respiratory failure & autonomic instability — monitor FVC, may need ventilation Acute myelopathies, especially with prolonged back pain and sphincter disturbance (p.3620) Diphtheria with early oropharyngeal disturbance (p.3620) Porphyria (clues: abdominal pain, seizures, psychosis) (p.3620) Vasculitic neuropathy (check ESR) (p.3620) Critical illness neuropathy or myopathy (p.3620) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) in patients with late or recurrent relapses (p.3622) Poliomyelitis and acute flaccid myelitis (wild-type poliovirus, West Nile virus, enterovirus D68, enterovirus A71, Japanese encephalitis virus) (p.3620) Lyme polyradiculitis and other tick-borne paralyses (p.3620) CMV polyradiculitis in immunocompromised patients (p.3620) Botulism (a neuromuscular junction disorder; pupillary reactivity lost early) (p.3620) CSF protein may be normal when symptoms have been present <=48 h and usually rises only by the end of the first week, so a normal early CSF does not exclude GBS (p.3619). A sustained CSF pleocytosis (or counts above the GBS range) should prompt a search for an alternative or concurrent diagnosis such as viral myelitis, HIV, leukemia/lymphoma infiltrating nerves, or neurosarcoidosis (p.3619). Electrodiagnostic abnormalities are mild or absent early and lag behind the clinical course; earliest AIDP findings are prolonged F-wave and distal latencies and reduced CMAP amplitudes (p.3619). Antiganglioside antibodies (e.g., anti-GM1 in AMAN/AMSAN, anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher) can support specific subtypes (p.3618-3619). Test for HIV in patients with risk factors or CSF pleocytosis (p.3620). Myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorder) (p.3620) Poisoning with organophosphates, thallium, or arsenic (p.3620) Paralytic shellfish poisoning (p.3620) Severe hypophosphatemia (rare) (p.3620) About 70% of cases follow an acute infection (usually respiratory or GI) by 1-3 weeks; roughly 20-30% are preceded by Campylobacter jejuni, with a similar share after herpesvirus infection (often CMV or EBV) (p.3617). Weakness usually evolves over hours to a few days and is classically ascending (legs more than arms), often first noticed as 'rubbery legs', with tingling dysesthesias in the extremities (p.3617). Facial diparesis occurs in ~50% of patients and lower cranial nerve/bulbar involvement is common; bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions can initially be mistaken for brainstem ischemia (p.3617). Pain (neck, shoulder, back, or diffuse spinal pain) is common early, in ~50% of patients, and deep aching muscle pain plus dysesthetic limb pain also occur (p.3617). Large-fiber functions (deep tendon reflexes, proprioception) are affected more severely than cutaneous pain/temperature sensation (p.3617). AMAN and AMSAN are axonal variants associated with anti-GD1a/anti-GM1 antibodies and preceding C. jejuni; AMAN can occur in seasonal outbreaks (e.g., rural China) and is prevalent in China and Mexico (p.3617-3619). Miller Fisher syndrome (~5% of cases) presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia without limb weakness and carries anti-GQ1b antibodies in >90% (p.3617, p.3619). If diagnosis is strongly suspected, treatment should not wait for the characteristic CSF or electrodiagnostic findings to evolve (p.3620). Rapid tempo of progression and severe weakness on admission, plus facial and/or bulbar weakness in the first week, predict the need for mechanical ventilation (up to ~30% of patients require ventilatory support) (p.3617). Bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions threatens the airway (p.3617). Autonomic instability — wide blood pressure swings, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias — can be fatal and may occur even when limb weakness is otherwise mild (p.3617). Presence of fever or constitutional symptoms at onset casts doubt on the diagnosis and should prompt reconsideration (p.3617). Prominent or early bladder dysfunction, or a sensory level, should raise suspicion for spinal cord disease rather than GBS (p.3617). Corticosteroids have NOT been found effective in GBS and should not be relied on as treatment (p.3621). Treatment timing matters: each day counts, and by ~2 weeks after the first motor symptoms it is unknown whether immunotherapy is still effective; if a patient has reached the plateau, treatment is probably no longer indicated unless severe weakness suggests ongoing immune attack (p.3620). Lack of improvement after a course of IVIg or plasmapheresis is NOT an indication to switch to the other modality, and combining the two is not significantly better than either alone (p.3621). Early CSF and electrodiagnostic studies can be normal/minimal; relying on them to confirm before treating can cause harmful delay (p.3619-3620). Acute flaccid myelitis can closely mimic GBS because sphincter disturbances may be absent (p.3620). GBS is an acute, often fulminant autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy thought to arise from immune responses to non-self antigens (infections, vaccines) that cross-react with peripheral nerve via molecular mimicry, with gangliosides (glycosphingolipids concentrated at sites such as nodes of Ranvier) as likely targets. In AIDP, the demyelinating and most common form, both cellular and humoral mechanisms operate: complement deposits on the outer Schwann cell surface, triggering membrane-attack-complex formation, vesicular myelin disintegration, and macrophage-mediated removal of myelin. The resulting conduction block (with axons left intact) explains the flaccid paralysis and the potential for rapid recovery once remyelination occurs; secondary axonal degeneration in severe cases slows recovery and worsens residual deficit. In the axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN), IgG and complement deposit at the nodes of Ranvier of motor axons, with anti-GD1a antibodies preferentially targeting motor over sensory roots; low CMAP amplitudes often reflect reversible nodal/paranodal conduction block rather than true axon loss, though severe cases show axonal degeneration (p.3617-3620). About 85% of patients reach full functional recovery within several months to a year, though minor signs (e.g., persistent areflexia) and complaints such as fatigue may remain. Mortality is <5% in optimal settings, usually from secondary pulmonary complications. The outlook is worst with severe proximal motor and sensory axonal damage; other adverse factors are advanced age, a fulminant or severe attack, and delayed treatment. Elevated serum neurofilament light chains and high anti-GM1 titers both correlate with greater axonal involvement and poorer recovery. Between 5 and 10% of typical GBS patients have one or more late relapses, many later reclassified as CIDP (p.3621-3622). Brighton Collaboration case definitions (2011) grade diagnostic certainty in three levels. Level 1 (highest certainty) requires bilateral flaccid limb weakness, decreased/absent reflexes in weak limbs, a monophasic course with onset-to-nadir of 12 h to 28 days followed by plateau, electrophysiology consistent with GBS, cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with CSF white cell count <50/microL), and no alternative diagnosis. Lower levels relax the laboratory/electrophysiologic requirements. Parallel criteria exist for Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia without limb weakness) (p.3620-3621).

not used to diagnose HCM but can exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease) Enzyme activity assay and/or GLA sequencing when Fabry's disease suspected Ambulatory ECG monitoring and exercise testing for nonsustained ventricular tachycardia and outflow gradient provocation Athlete's heart (physiologic hypertrophy that regresses with detraining, with supernormal VO2max >50 mL/kg/min, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function) Hypertensive or aortic valve disease causing secondary LV hypertrophy Infiltrative/storage disease mimicking HCM via pseudohypertrophy (often with short PR interval) Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-variant amyloid causing restrictive physiology Each traditional morphologic form of cardiomyopathy (hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive) can be caused or modified by underlying genetic factors; heritability is well recognized in HCM and present in at least 30% of dilated cardiomyopathy without another clear etiology (p.2003-2004). Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant, with occasional autosomal recessive, matrilineal (mitochondrial), and X-linked inheritance; missense and truncating variants are the commonest abnormalities (p.2003). Genetic cardiomyopathy shows age-dependent and incomplete penetrance: the phenotype is rarely present at birth and in some carriers may never manifest; relatives carrying the same variant can differ markedly in severity and progression (p.2004). Penetrance and clinical severity tend to be greater in men for most cardiomyopathies; current therapy is based on phenotype rather than the genetic defect (p.2004). The greatest current utility of genetic testing is to focus and inform family evaluations; it can also provide risk stratification and occasionally identify a treatable disorder such as Fabry's or Gaucher's disease (p.2004). A sarcomere gene variant is found in roughly 40-50% of HCM patients, more often with familial disease and asymmetric septal hypertrophy; about 80% of these involve MYH7 or MYBPC3 encoding the thick myofilament (p.2005). HCM is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy developing without a causative hemodynamic factor (e.g., hypertension, aortic valve disease) or infiltrative/storage disease; prevalence is about 1:500 (p.2005). Outflow tract obstruction is present at rest in about 30% of HCM patients and provoked by exercise in another ~30%; systolic anterior motion of an enlarged anterior mitral leaflet against the hypertrophied septum produces obstruction and posteriorly directed mitral regurgitation (p.2006). Truncating variants in TTN (titin) are the commonest genetic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy, accounting for up to 25% of familial DCM; men with TTN truncating variants typically develop disease about a decade before women (p.2008-2009). DCM is considered present when LVEF is <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension exceeds the 95th percentile predicted for age and sex; some patients have reduced LVEF with minimal dilation (nondilated/minimally dilated cardiomyopathy) (p.2008). Inherited metabolic and storage disorders can mimic HCM by thickening the myocardium with abnormal products ('pseudohypertrophy'), classically with a short PR interval; most are diagnosed in childhood (p.2010). Fabry's disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency from GLA variants) can affect female carriers; endomyocardial biopsy shows diagnostic concentric lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy, and diagnosis matters because enzyme replacement can reduce deposits (p.2010). Most identified variants are 'private' to individual families, complicating interpretation; growing recognition that multiple intermediate-effect alleles and polygenic risk influence penetrance and expression. Athlete's heart can mimic mild HCM; distinguishing features include regression with detraining, supernormal exercise capacity, mild dilation, and normal diastolic function. Late gadolinium enhancement on MRI, once attributed to prior viral myocarditis, is now recognized as common in genetic cardiomyopathy. Cardiac glycosides should be avoided in HCM with obstruction because they increase contractility and worsen obstruction. The positive predictive value of most HCM sudden-death risk factors is low, so many patients receiving a defibrillator never receive appropriate device therapy. Endomyocardial biopsy is not used to diagnose HCM itself but may exclude infiltrative/metabolic disease. Many distinct genes are implicated (locus heterogeneity), each with numerous pathogenic variants (allelic heterogeneity). Mutant proteins can interfere with the normal allele via a dominant-negative mechanism, while nonsense/frameshift variants may yield truncated or unstable proteins whose absence causes disease through haploinsufficiency; some genetic DCM combines both effects. Functional gene groups include sarcomeric proteins, Z-disk/cytoskeletal proteins, nuclear membrane proteins, excitation-contraction coupling proteins, metabolic enzymes, mitochondrial DNA, sarcolemmal membrane proteins, and desmosomal proteins. In HCM, sarcomere variants enhance calcium sensitivity, maximal force generation, and ATPase activity, producing abnormal energetics and impaired relaxation; myofibril and myocyte misalignment/disarray occurs, with interstitial fibrosis appearing before overt hypertrophy and focal replacement fibrosis providing arrhythmic substrate, plus microvascular ischemia from thickened intramural vessels. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, cytoskeletal, sarcolemmal (dystrophin), nuclear membrane (lamin A/C, emerin), and desmosomal protein defects impair force transmission, mechanical/electrical coupling, and cell survival; desmosomal disruption activates Wnt/beta-catenin and proinflammatory signaling with replacement of myocytes by fat and fibrous tissue, creating arrhythmogenic, sometimes aneurysmal regions. HCM prognosis is better than in early referral-population studies but mortality remains higher than in age-matched individuals without cardiomyopathy; sudden death risk is under 1% per year (about 0.5% per year baseline). Up to 1 in 20 HCM patients progress to overt systolic dysfunction (EF <50%) with or without dilation ('burned out'/end-stage HCM), with increased risk of death from progressive heart failure and sudden death unless transplanted. In DCM and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, prognosis is driven by disease stage and sudden-death risk, which is higher for variants in DES, DSP, DSC2, FLNC, LMNA, PKP2, PLN, RBM20, SCN5A, and TMEM43; progression rate is also gene-dependent, and patients with TTN truncating variants frequently recover with medical therapy. HCM sudden-death risk stratification uses major risk factors (prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT, exertional/nonvagal syncope, family history of sudden cardiac death, LV apical aneurysm, maximal wall thickness >30 mm, LVEF <50%) plus modifying factors (late gadolinium enhancement burden, spontaneous nonsustained VT). The externally validated European Society of Cardiology HCM Risk-SCD calculator integrates age, LV outflow tract gradient, left atrial diameter, maximal wall thickness, syncope, family history, and nonsustained VT to estimate 5-year cardiac-arrest risk: ICD generally advised at >=6%, considered at 4-6%, and not advised at <4%. DCM is defined by LVEF <=0.50 and/or LV diastolic dimension >95th percentile for age and sex.

Features that favour an oesophageal rather than cardiac source include pain that is nonexertional, prolonged, meal-related, relieved by antacids, accompanied by heartburn/dysphagia/regurgitation, and that interrupts sleep - but every one of these overlaps with cardiac pain, which must remain the primary consideration (p.2509). Heartburn (pyrosis) is the most common oesophageal symptom and its link to GERD is strong enough that empirical acid-suppression has become accepted management; chest pain and persistent dysphagia are the key exceptions that warrant evaluation rather than empirical treatment (p.2503, p.2510). Gastrointestinal disorders are the single most common cause of nontraumatic chest discomfort, yet fewer than 15% of ED chest-pain presentations turn out to be ACS (p.104). A burning quality suggests acid reflux but can also occur with myocardial ischaemia; conversely oesophageal spasm can produce a severe squeezing pain identical to angina - quality alone never establishes a diagnosis (p.105). Both reflux relief and ischaemia relief overlap with nitroglycerin: oesophageal spasm may be relieved promptly by nitroglycerin just as angina can be, so a nitroglycerin response does not confirm cardiac origin (p.106). Chest wall tenderness on palpation does NOT exclude myocardial ischaemia, and a normal physical exam is not reassuring in unstable ischaemic heart disease (p.106-107). Some patients with acid reflux on pH testing report epigastric/abdominal pain or nausea instead of classic heartburn (atypical GERD) (p.301, ch.48). Visceral hypersensitivity is increasingly recognised as a cofactor in GERD symptom generation, beyond simple mucosal erosion and afferent nerve activation (p.2510). Dysphagia (concerning for oesophageal obstruction - stricture, EoE, or cancer) Odynophagia (suggests infectious or pill esophagitis, or extensive ulceration) Unexplained weight loss Recurrent vomiting Occult or gross gastrointestinal bleeding / anaemia Jaundice Palpable mass or lymphadenopathy Family history of gastro-oesophageal malignancy Nocturnal symptoms Heartburn >5 years' duration, especially age >50, or new dyspepsia age >60 (screen for Barrett's / malignancy by endoscopy) Failure to respond to acid suppression (up to one-third of presumed GERD) Any diagnostic doubt about a cardiac cause - acute exertional/pressure pain, radiation to both arms, diaphoresis, dyspnoea, syncope, hypotension/tachycardia Attributing chest pain to GERD before excluding a cardiac cause - coronary artery disease must be given early consideration because of its potentially lethal implications, and oesophageal pain closely mimics angina. Relying on pain quality, nitroglycerin response, or chest-wall tenderness to distinguish cardiac from oesophageal pain - all overlap and none is reliable; a normal exam and even a normal resting ECG do not exclude ischaemia. Treating a normal endoscopy as ruling out GERD - erosive esophagitis is seen in only about one-third of GERD patients. Overlooking that up to one-third of presumed-GERD patients fail to respond to acid suppression and may have an alternative diagnosis (functional, hypersensitivity, motility, nonacid reflux). Diagnosing distal esophageal spasm or nonspecific manometric abnormalities prematurely - these are made only after GERD, peptic and infectious esophagitis, and cardiac disease are excluded; minor manometric findings are of unclear significance and often coexist with anxiety/depression and IBS. Missing alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, bleeding/anaemia) that mandate endoscopy rather than continued empirical therapy. Forgetting that nausea/vomiting and epigastric pain can accompany MI (especially inferior MI via vagal/Bezold-Jarisch reflex) and need not indicate a GI cause. Pathologic reflux arises from anatomic and physiologic failure of the oesophagogastric junction valve - widening of the diaphragmatic hiatus with diminished crural diaphragm function, loss of the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment disabling the flap valve, axial (sliding) hiatus hernia causing LES hypotension, and increased junctional compliance allowing liquid to escape during transient LES relaxations (the belch reflex). Some reflux is physiologic and intertwined with belching, but esophagitis follows excessive reflux plus impaired acid clearance, which depends on peristalsis returning fluid to the stomach and bicarbonate in swallowed saliva neutralising residual acid; impaired peristalsis and reduced salivation therefore prolong acid contact. Mucosal injury is driven by a cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathway rather than purely direct caustic injury. Gastric acid hypersecretion is usually NOT the dominant factor (exceptions: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe esophagitis in ~50%); chronic H. pylori gastritis may even be protective by inducing hypoacidity. Pepsin, bile, and pancreatic enzymes also injure the epithelium, and bile persists in refluxate despite acid suppression and is implicated as a cofactor in Barrett's metaplasia and adenocarcinoma. Exacerbating factors include abdominal obesity, pregnancy, gastric hypersecretory states, delayed gastric emptying, disrupted peristalsis, and overeating. Esophageal chest pain itself reflects a shared nerve plexus with the heart and poor discriminative ability of oesophageal afferents (p.2503-2504, p.2509-2510). Most patients in whom an acute cardiopulmonary cause is excluded have a favourable prognosis; in low-risk patients the 30-day major cardiovascular event rate is about 2.5%. However, historically 2-6% of presumed-nonischaemic chest pain patients discharged from the ED were later found to have had a missed myocardial infarction, underscoring the cost of misclassification. For GERD itself, erosive esophagitis and peptic strictures have become rare with potent acid suppression, but Barrett's metaplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma have increased; progression of Barrett's to adenocarcinoma is estimated at roughly 0.1-0.5% per year, with obese white men in their sixth decade at greatest risk. High-grade dysplasia in Barrett's carries a high rate of progression and a high prevalence of coexisting unrecognised cancer (p.104, p.2510-2511, ch.85 p.92). GERD spans a spectrum of oesophageal injury: nonerosive reflux disease, erosive esophagitis (graded by antisecretory-responsive severity), peptic stricture, Barrett's metaplasia, and adenocarcinoma. Barrett's dysplasia is staged as low-grade vs high-grade, the latter mandating intervention. For the chest-pain presentation itself, Harrison frames risk by clinical decision pathways categorising patients as low, intermediate, or high probability of ACS using symptoms, age, risk factors, ECG, and serial high-sensitivity troponin (HEART/EDACS scores) (p.107-109, p.2510-2511).

glycaemic control suggesting undiagnosed overt diabetes Coexisting hypertension or pre-eclampsia Reduced fetal movements or non-reassuring fetal surveillance Missing overt pre-existing diabetes by not testing high-risk women in early pregnancy Relying on symptoms, which are usually absent, rather than screening Assuming a normal-sized fetus excludes risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia Failing to arrange postpartum glucose reassessment and long-term follow-up Neglecting neonatal glucose monitoring after delivery Pregnancy is a progressively insulin-resistant state driven by placental hormones such as human placental lactogen, progesterone, and cortisol. Gestational diabetes develops when maternal pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion cannot compensate for this physiological resistance, leading to maternal hyperglycaemia. Glucose crosses the placenta freely and stimulates fetal insulin secretion; the resulting fetal hyperinsulinaemia acts as a growth factor causing macrosomia and, after cord clamping removes the maternal glucose supply, predisposes the neonate to hypoglycaemia. Well-controlled gestational diabetes has an excellent outcome, approaching that of the non-diabetic population. Poor control raises risks of macrosomia, operative delivery, birth trauma, and neonatal metabolic problems. Long term, affected women have a markedly increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and their offspring have higher rates of obesity and glucose intolerance.

trophoblastic disease is a spectrum of proliferative disorders of placental trophoblast ranging from benign hydatidiform mole to malignant gestational trophoblastic neoplasia including choriocarcinoma A complete mole usually arises from fertilisation of an ovum lacking maternal genetic material and contains no fetal tissue, whereas a partial mole is typically triploid with some fetal parts Classic presentation includes irregular vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, a uterus large for dates, markedly elevated hCG, and sometimes early or severe hyperemesis or pre-eclampsia before twenty weeks Ultrasound may show a vesicular or snowstorm appearance with absent or abnormal fetal development, and diagnosis is confirmed histologically Uterine evacuation by suction curettage is the treatment for molar pregnancy, followed by structured monitoring of serial hCG to detect persistent disease Persistently elevated or rising hCG after evacuation indicates gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly chemosensitive and generally curable even when metastatic Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance is essential because a new pregnancy would obscure the marker used to detect persistent disease Choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy, including normal or ectopic, and may present with metastatic symptoms such as haemoptysis or neurological signs Rising or plateauing hCG after evacuation signalling gestational trophoblastic neoplasia requiring urgent oncology referral Heavy vaginal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise Respiratory symptoms or haemoptysis suggesting pulmonary metastases Neurological signs suggesting cerebral metastatic choriocarcinoma Pre-eclampsia, thyrotoxic features, or hyperemesis occurring unusually early in pregnancy Failing to arrange structured hCG follow-up after evacuation Allowing pregnancy during surveillance, which masks persistent disease Missing early or atypical pre-eclampsia and hyperthyroid features as clues to molar pregnancy Not considering choriocarcinoma in a woman with metastatic disease and any recent pregnancy Assuming a benign miscarriage without histological examination of tissue Gestational trophoblastic disease results from abnormal fertilisation and proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. A complete mole typically arises when an anucleate ovum is fertilised and the paternal chromosomes duplicate, giving a diploid androgenetic genome with swollen avascular chorionic villi and no fetus, while a partial mole usually results from dispermic fertilisation producing a triploid conceptus with focal villous change and a nonviable fetus. Excessive trophoblast produces very high hCG. In gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, trophoblast invades the myometrium and vasculature, and choriocarcinoma disseminates haematogenously, favouring the lungs, brain, and liver. Most hydatidiform moles are cured by evacuation alone, and even when gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops it is one of the most curable malignancies, with excellent survival when managed in specialist centres using chemotherapy guided by prognostic scoring. Outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, adherence to hCG surveillance, and risk stratification, with high-risk and heavily metastatic disease requiring more intensive multi-agent treatment.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumour — GIST, gastrointestinal stromal tumor, GI stromal tumour Leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma of the gut Gastrointestinal schwannoma Neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour Gastric or small-bowel adenocarcinoma or lymphoma Extrinsic compression from an adjacent mass Pancreatic or splenic lesion mimicking a gastric submucosal mass Endoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound to characterise the submucosal lesion and guide sampling Contrast-enhanced CT for staging, size assessment, and detection of liver or peritoneal metastases Immunohistochemistry for KIT (CD117) and DOG1 to confirm the diagnosis Mutational analysis of KIT and PDGFRA to guide targeted therapy and predict response Mitotic count and tumour size assessment for risk stratification The most common mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal tract, thought to arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, most often in the stomach and next most often in the small intestine Most are driven by activating mutations in the KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinases, and KIT immunostaining is the diagnostic hallmark Presentation ranges from an incidental finding to vague abdominal discomfort, a palpable mass, or gastrointestinal bleeding from mucosal ulceration On endoscopy they typically appear as a smooth submucosal bulge with normal overlying mucosa, sometimes with central umbilication Malignant potential is estimated mainly from tumour size and mitotic rate together with anatomical site, rather than being simply benign or malignant Surgical resection with negative margins is the mainstay of treatment for localised disease, and routine lymph node dissection is generally unnecessary because nodal spread is rare Tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting KIT/PDGFRA have transformed management of advanced, metastatic, or high-risk disease and are used in adjuvant and neoadjuvant settings Biopsy should be approached cautiously because of bleeding and rupture risk; endoscopic ultrasound-guided sampling is often preferred when tissue is needed The liver and peritoneum are the usual sites of metastatic spread Large tumour with high mitotic rate indicating high malignant potential and need for oncological management Significant or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding from an ulcerated tumour Tumour rupture (spontaneous or during biopsy) causing peritoneal dissemination and haemoperitoneum New liver or peritoneal lesions signalling metastatic progression Assuming a submucosal lesion is benign without adequate risk stratification by size and mitotic rate Performing incautious biopsy of a friable tumour and precipitating bleeding or rupture Omitting mutational testing, which can predict poor response to standard targeted therapy Confusing a GIST with other spindle-cell tumours when immunohistochemistry is not performed GISTs originate from or resemble the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells of the gut. Gain-of-function mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene, or less commonly in PDGFRA, produce constitutive receptor tyrosine kinase signalling that drives uncontrolled proliferation. A minority are wild-type for these genes and involve alternative pathways such as succinate dehydrogenase deficiency, which is more common in younger patients and in syndromic disease. Tumours grow as submucosal or intramural masses; larger and more mitotically active lesions have greater potential for haematogenous spread, particularly to the liver and peritoneal surfaces. Small, low-mitotic-rate, completely resected tumours have an excellent outlook, whereas large or mitotically active lesions carry a substantial risk of recurrence and metastasis. Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival in advanced disease, though resistance can develop over time.

Giardiasis — Giardia lamblia infection, Giardia intestinalis infection, Giardia duodenalis infection, beaver fever Other causes of chronic or malabsorptive diarrhoea (coeliac disease, tropical sprue) Cryptosporidiosis and other protozoal enteritides Bacterial enteritis Lactose intolerance Irritable bowel syndrome Coeliac disease Tropical sprue Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth Inflammatory bowel disease Repeated stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites Stool antigen detection (ELISA) or PCR for greater sensitivity Duodenal aspirate or biopsy in difficult cases Assessment for malabsorption and nutritional status in chronic disease Evaluation for immunoglobulin deficiency in recurrent or refractory infection A protozoal infection of the small intestine caused by Giardia, acquired by faecal-oral spread of cysts through contaminated water or food, or person to person Highly endemic in India, contributing to childhood diarrhoea, malabsorption and faltering growth Typical illness is prolonged, with foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps and weight loss rather than blood or fever Many infections are asymptomatic, and cyst passage can continue in the absence of symptoms, sustaining transmission Chronic infection can cause fat and lactose malabsorption and, in children, nutritional deficiencies and stunting Diagnosis traditionally relies on detecting cysts or trophozoites on repeated stool examination, with stool antigen and PCR tests being more sensitive Because cyst excretion is intermittent, a single negative stool sample does not exclude infection Treatment is with antiprotozoal agents; attention to safe water and hygiene prevents reinfection and outbreaks Severe dehydration or significant weight loss, particularly in young children Malabsorption with nutritional deficiency and growth faltering Persistent or relapsing infection suggesting underlying immunodeficiency Failure to respond to standard therapy, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Excluding giardiasis on the basis of a single negative stool sample despite intermittent cyst shedding Overlooking it as a treatable cause of chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption Missing underlying immunodeficiency in recurrent or refractory cases Neglecting water and hygiene measures, leading to reinfection or household spread Ingested Giardia cysts excyst in the small intestine and release trophozoites that attach to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa via a ventral adhesive disc. Colonisation causes villous shortening, disruption of the brush-border enzymes and a mucosal inflammatory response, impairing absorption of fats, carbohydrates and other nutrients. This produces the characteristic malabsorptive, non-inflammatory diarrhoea. Trophozoites encyst as they pass down the gut, and the environmentally hardy cysts are excreted to continue the cycle. Most cases respond well to antiprotozoal therapy with full recovery. Untreated or recurrent infection, especially in children, can cause lasting malabsorption and growth impairment, and reinfection is common where sanitation is poor.

Gilbert syndrome — Gilbert's syndrome, constitutional hepatic dysfunction, familial nonhaemolytic jaundice Haemolytic anaemia Crigler-Najjar syndrome (types I and II) Ineffective erythropoiesis Resolving or physiological neonatal jaundice Drug-induced impairment of bilirubin conjugation or uptake Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes (conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia) Fractionated serum bilirubin showing a predominantly unconjugated (indirect) elevation Normal liver enzymes and synthetic function tests Full blood count, reticulocyte count, and blood film to exclude haemolysis Repeat testing to demonstrate fluctuating mild hyperbilirubinaemia, sometimes accentuated by fasting UGT1A1 genotyping in selected or atypical cases A common, benign inherited disorder of bilirubin conjugation causing mild, fluctuating unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia Due to reduced activity of the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), most often from a promoter polymorphism inherited in a recessive pattern Jaundice is typically intermittent and provoked by fasting, intercurrent illness, dehydration, physical stress, or alcohol Liver enzymes, liver synthetic function, and the blood film are normal, and there is no haemolysis, which helps distinguish it from other causes of raised bilirubin The diagnosis is essentially clinical, based on isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal tests and no evidence of haemolysis or liver disease No treatment is needed; reassurance is the mainstay because the condition is harmless and does not progress to liver damage Reduced UGT1A1 activity can impair metabolism of certain drugs (for example irinotecan), which is a clinically relevant consideration It should not be confused with the far more serious Crigler-Najjar syndromes, which cause severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia or abnormal liver enzymes, which point away from Gilbert syndrome to genuine liver or biliary disease Anaemia or a raised reticulocyte count suggesting haemolysis rather than a benign conjugation defect Very high bilirubin levels, especially from infancy, raising concern for Crigler-Najjar syndrome Bilirubin rising with systemic symptoms indicating an alternative serious diagnosis Over-investigating or mislabelling harmless isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia as liver disease Failing to exclude haemolysis, which can also cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia Not fractionating bilirubin and therefore missing a conjugated (and more concerning) pattern Overlooking altered metabolism of drugs such as irinotecan in affected patients Gilbert syndrome results from partially reduced activity of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1, the enzyme that conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble for biliary excretion. The commonest genetic basis is an expanded TA repeat in the UGT1A1 gene promoter, which lowers enzyme expression. The consequent modest reduction in conjugating capacity produces mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, accentuated when bilirubin load or physiological stress increases, such as during fasting or illness. There is no structural liver disease and no haemolysis, and bilirubin levels usually remain modestly elevated. Excellent. Gilbert syndrome is a lifelong but entirely benign condition that does not cause liver damage or reduce life expectancy, and no specific treatment is required.

Gingivitis — gum inflammation, plaque-induced gingivitis, marginal gingivitis Early periodontitis with attachment loss Necrotising ulcerative gingivitis Drug-influenced gingival enlargement
