absence of attachment loss Review of medications and hormonal or systemic factors Radiographs when needed to exclude bone loss Blood investigations if systemic disease is suspected Gingivitis is reversible inflammation confined to the gingiva without loss of periodontal attachment or bone The cardinal sign is bleeding on gentle probing or brushing, alongside redness, swelling, and loss of the normal stippled contour It is overwhelmingly plaque-induced, so improved oral hygiene and professional cleaning usually reverse it within days to weeks Hormonal changes in pregnancy and puberty, and certain medications, can exaggerate the gingival response to plaque Unlike periodontitis, probing depths remain shallow and there is no true pocketing or attachment loss Untreated gingivitis is a risk state that may progress to periodontitis in susceptible individuals Necrotising gingivitis is a distinct painful form with ulcerated, punched-out interdental papillae and characteristic malodour Persistent gingival inflammation despite good hygiene should prompt consideration of systemic or drug-related causes Spontaneous gingival bleeding or florid enlargement suggesting leukaemia or a bleeding disorder Painful necrotising gingivitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients Gingival changes that fail to resolve with good hygiene, indicating an underlying systemic cause Assuming all gingival inflammation is simple plaque-induced gingivitis and missing early periodontitis Overlooking systemic, hormonal, or drug-related contributors to gingival changes Attributing spontaneous bleeding to local causes when a haematological disorder is present Failing to reinforce oral hygiene, leading to recurrence Plaque-induced gingivitis develops when microbial biofilm accumulates at the gingival margin and triggers a localised host inflammatory response. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability cause the classic erythema, oedema, and bleeding tendency, while the junctional epithelium remains intact and attachment is preserved, making the condition reversible. If the biofilm persists, the chronic inflammatory infiltrate can, in susceptible hosts and under modifying influences such as hormonal changes, systemic disease, or medications, evolve toward the attachment and bone loss that define periodontitis. Plaque-induced gingivitis is fully reversible with effective plaque control, but if neglected it can act as a precursor to irreversible periodontitis in susceptible people.

Gitelman syndrome — Gitelman's syndrome, familial hypokalaemia-hypomagnesaemia, thiazide-like tubulopathy Bartter syndrome Surreptitious thiazide diuretic use Chronic vomiting Laxative abuse Primary hypomagnesaemia from other causes Primary hyperaldosteronism (distinguished by hypertension) Serum potassium, magnesium, and bicarbonate to define the hypokalaemic, hypomagnesaemic alkalosis Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating hypocalciuria Plasma renin and aldosterone, usually elevated Urine electrolytes and screening for covert diuretic use Genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and for family counselling ECG when significant hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia is present Gitelman syndrome is an inherited tubulopathy that mimics chronic thiazide diuretic use because the defect is in sodium chloride transport in the distal convoluted tubule The distinguishing electrolyte signature is hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis together with hypomagnesaemia and low urinary calcium excretion It usually presents later than Bartter syndrome, often in adolescence or adulthood, with mild symptoms such as cramps, fatigue, tetany, and salt craving Hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia are the key features separating it from Bartter syndrome, which typically shows normal or high calcium excretion Blood pressure is normal or low, and renin and aldosterone are elevated as a compensatory response to salt wasting Chondrocalcinosis and joint symptoms can occur, related to chronic magnesium depletion Management principles are generous replacement of potassium and magnesium, liberal salt intake, and sometimes potassium-sparing agents, with magnesium repletion being essential for correcting the hypokalaemia Symptomatic hypomagnesaemia with tetany or seizures Severe hypokalaemia with arrhythmia risk or marked weakness Prolonged QT interval predisposing to dangerous arrhythmia Persistent symptoms despite apparent replacement, suggesting inadequate magnesium correction Attempting to correct hypokalaemia without also replacing magnesium, so the potassium remains refractory Confusing Gitelman with Bartter syndrome by not measuring urinary calcium and serum magnesium Missing surreptitious thiazide use as a mimic of the syndrome Overlooking the diagnosis in a normotensive adult with chronic unexplained hypokalaemic alkalosis Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule. Impaired sodium chloride reabsorption at this site leads to renal salt wasting and mild volume contraction, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Increased distal sodium delivery combined with secondary hyperaldosteronism promotes potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The defect enhances calcium reabsorption downstream, giving the characteristic hypocalciuria, while magnesium wasting from altered distal tubular handling causes hypomagnesaemia. The overall picture closely resembles the effect of long-term thiazide therapy. The long-term outlook is generally good, with preserved renal function in most patients, though lifelong electrolyte replacement is required and symptoms can affect quality of life. Correcting magnesium is often the key to stabilising potassium and preventing arrhythmia.

Gitelman-spectrum salt-losing tubulopathy — Gitelman syndrome, SLC12A3, NCCT defect, familial hypokalaemia-hypomagnesaemia Bartter syndrome Surreptitious diuretic use or misuse Chronic vomiting or laxative abuse Primary or secondary hyperaldosteronism Other causes of hypomagnesaemia (e.g. drug-induced, gastrointestinal loss) Familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria (contrasting phenotype) Serum electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, bicarbonate and calcium Blood gas or bicarbonate to confirm metabolic alkalosis Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating hypocalciuria Urinary electrolytes and, where needed, a urinary diuretic screen to exclude surreptitious diuretic use Plasma renin and aldosterone showing activation of the axis Genetic testing of SLC12A3 (and related tubulopathy genes) to confirm the diagnosis An autosomal recessive salt-losing tubulopathy caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC12A3, which encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule The biochemical signature is hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesaemia and, characteristically, low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria) It effectively mimics the biochemical effect of chronic thiazide diuretic use, so surreptitious diuretic misuse must be excluded Presentation is often in adolescence or adulthood with fatigue, muscle cramps and weakness, tetany, carpopedal spasm and salt craving, and it is generally milder than Bartter syndrome Blood pressure tends to be low or low-normal and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is activated The combination of hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria helps distinguish it from Bartter syndrome, which typically shows normal or high urinary calcium Chondrocalcinosis and QT prolongation can complicate longstanding electrolyte disturbance Severe hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia with cardiac arrhythmia or marked QT prolongation Tetany or seizures from profound electrolyte depletion Severe muscle weakness or rhabdomyolysis Acute decompensation during intercurrent illness with vomiting or diarrhoea Failing to exclude surreptitious diuretic use, which produces an identical biochemical picture Confusing it with Bartter syndrome by not checking urinary calcium and magnesium Neglecting magnesium repletion, without which potassium is difficult to correct Underestimating arrhythmia risk from combined hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia Gitelman-spectrum tubulopathy results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC12A3, which encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCCT) in the apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule. Impaired sodium and chloride reabsorption at this site causes mild renal salt wasting and volume contraction, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; the resulting increased distal sodium delivery and aldosterone drive potassium and hydrogen secretion, producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Associated downregulation and remodelling of the distal tubule impair magnesium reabsorption and enhance passive calcium reabsorption, generating the characteristic hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria. The phenotype thus recapitulates chronic thiazide exposure. Gitelman syndrome generally has a good long-term prognosis with appropriate electrolyte supplementation and normal life expectancy in most patients, although chronic symptoms and occasional severe electrolyte disturbances can affect quality of life. Kidney function is usually preserved.

Glanzmann thrombasthenia (ITGA2B/ITGB3) — GT, ITGA2B, ITGB3, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa deficiency, integrin alphaIIbbeta3 deficiency Bernard-Soulier syndrome Von Willebrand disease Storage pool and other platelet secretion defects Immune thrombocytopenia (distinguished by low platelet count) Acquired antiplatelet drug effect Mild inherited platelet function disorders Full blood count and blood film confirming normal platelet number and morphology Light-transmission platelet aggregometry showing absent response to physiological agonists with preserved ristocetin response Flow cytometry for platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa expression Von Willebrand studies to exclude von Willebrand disease Coagulation screen to confirm normal clotting factor pathways ITGA2B and ITGB3 genetic testing for confirmation and counselling An autosomal recessive platelet function disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet integrin alphaIIbbeta3 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa), encoded by ITGA2B and ITGB3 Bleeding is of the mucocutaneous (platelet-type) pattern: epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental work The platelet count and platelet morphology are normal, which helps distinguish it from thrombocytopenic disorders The characteristic laboratory hallmark is absent or markedly reduced platelet aggregation to all physiological agonists (ADP, collagen, adrenaline, thrombin) but a preserved response to ristocetin The preserved ristocetin response, which depends on the glycoprotein Ib-von Willebrand factor axis, contrasts with the absent aggregation and points away from Bernard-Soulier syndrome Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating reduced glycoprotein IIb/IIIa by flow cytometry and, where needed, ITGA2B/ITGB3 genetic testing Management centres on local haemostatic measures, antifibrinolytics, and platelet transfusion for major bleeding, with alloimmunisation and, in selected cases, recombinant activated factor VII considered Major or life-threatening haemorrhage such as gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding Severe menorrhagia causing haemodynamic compromise Uncontrolled bleeding around surgery or childbirth Platelet refractoriness from alloimmunisation limiting transfusion response Mislabelling the disorder as immune thrombocytopenia despite a normal platelet count Transfusing platelets for minor bleeds and hastening alloimmunisation that impairs future responses Overlooking the diagnosis when aggregometry is not performed because routine coagulation tests are normal Failing to plan peri-procedural haemostatic cover before surgery or delivery Glanzmann thrombasthenia results from biallelic mutations in ITGA2B or ITGB3, which encode the two subunits of the platelet integrin alphaIIbbeta3 (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa). This integrin is the fibrinogen receptor that mediates platelet-to-platelet bridging during aggregation. When it is quantitatively deficient or functionally defective, activated platelets can adhere and change shape but cannot cross-link through fibrinogen to form a stable aggregate, so primary haemostasis fails despite normal platelet numbers and normal von Willebrand-dependent adhesion. The result is a lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding tendency of variable severity that does not correlate closely with the residual receptor level. With modern supportive care most patients have a normal life expectancy, though bleeding episodes can be serious and platelet alloimmunisation may complicate the response to transfusion over time.

Glioblastoma — GBM, glioblastoma multiforme, grade 4 astrocytoma, high-grade glioma Brain metastasis Primary CNS lymphoma Cerebral abscess Lower-grade glioma Tumefactive demyelination Subacute infarct with mass effect MRI brain with contrast, including advanced sequences (perfusion, spectroscopy) to characterise the lesion Histopathological and molecular analysis of biopsy or resection tissue (including IDH and MGMT status) Staging or systemic imaging when metastasis is a differential Assessment of performance status and comorbidity to guide treatment intensity Glioblastoma is the most common and most aggressive primary malignant brain tumour in adults, classified as a grade 4 glioma Presentation is usually subacute over weeks, with progressive headache, focal deficits, cognitive or personality change, and seizures Headaches suggesting raised intracranial pressure, worse in the morning or with Valsalva, and new focal neurology should prompt urgent imaging On MRI it typically appears as an irregularly enhancing mass with central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic oedema, often crossing the corpus callosum as a butterfly lesion Definitive diagnosis and molecular characterisation require tissue from biopsy or resection, with markers such as IDH status and MGMT promoter methylation guiding prognosis and therapy Corticosteroids are used to control symptomatic peritumoural oedema and mass effect while treatment is planned Standard management combines maximal safe surgical resection with subsequent radiotherapy and chemotherapy, individualised to patient fitness and molecular profile Despite multimodal treatment the tumour almost always recurs, so realistic goal-setting and supportive care are integral Rapidly progressive neurological deficit or declining consciousness from mass effect Symptoms and signs of raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation New-onset seizures, including status epilepticus Acute deterioration from intratumoural haemorrhage or worsening oedema Assuming a solitary enhancing lesion is glioblastoma without considering metastasis, lymphoma, or abscess Starting high-dose steroids before biopsy when lymphoma is a possibility, as this can obscure the diagnosis Underestimating infiltration beyond the enhancing margin when planning treatment Neglecting seizure control, symptom management, and early supportive care discussions Glioblastoma is a highly malignant, infiltrative tumour arising from glial (astrocytic-lineage) cells. It is characterised histologically by marked cellular atypia, brisk mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation, and regions of necrosis. The tumour cells invade diffusely along white matter tracts well beyond the enhancing margin seen on imaging, which underlies the difficulty of complete removal and the near-inevitable recurrence. Aberrant angiogenesis produces leaky vessels that generate surrounding vasogenic oedema and contribute to mass effect and raised intracranial pressure. Distinct molecular alterations define subgroups with differing behaviour and treatment response. Glioblastoma carries a poor prognosis with median survival typically measured in months to a couple of years even with optimal multimodal therapy; younger age, good performance status, greater extent of resection, and favourable molecular markers such as MGMT methylation are associated with better outcomes.

Glomerular Diseases (Spectrum) — glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy, FSGS, membranous nephropathy, minimal change disease Acute nephritic syndrome: poststreptococcal GN, subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated GN, lupus nephritis, anti-GBM disease, IgA nephropathy, ANCA small-vessel vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA), IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), cryoglobulinemia, MPGN, C3 glomerulopathy, mesangioproliferative GN (Harrison 22e p.2414-2415). Nephrotic syndrome: minimal change disease, FSGS, membranous glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, AL/AA amyloidosis, light-chain deposition disease, fibrillary-immunotactoid disease, Fabry's disease (Harrison 22e p.2415). Pulmonary-renal syndromes: Goodpasture's/anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.2414-2415). Basement membrane syndromes: anti-GBM disease, Alport's syndrome, thin basement membrane disease, nail-patella syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2415). Glomerular vascular syndromes: atherosclerotic and hypertensive nephropathy, cholesterol emboli, sickle cell disease, thrombotic microangiopathies, antiphospholipid syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2415). Microscopic hematuria with minimal proteinuria can also reflect non-glomerular causes: urinary tract malignancy (especially older men), BPH, interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis, hypercalciuria, kidney stones, cystic kidney disease, or renal vascular injury (Harrison 22e p.2414). Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis after nephritogenic streptococcal pharyngitis (1-3 weeks) or skin infection (2-6 weeks) (Harrison 22e p.2417-2418). Subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated and other persistent-infection (shunt, abscess, infected prosthesis; often Staphylococcus) glomerulonephritis, which can mimic or coexist with ANCA vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2417). Hepatitis B and C (membranous, MPGN, cryoglobulinemic patterns), HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing FSGS), syphilis, leprosy, malaria, and schistosomiasis - globally, malaria and schistosomiasis may be the most common causes of glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2416, 2459). IgA-dominant Staphylococcus-associated infectious glomerulonephritis can mimic primary IgA nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.2419). Urinalysis with microscopy for dysmorphic red cells, red blood cell casts, pyuria; quantify proteinuria by spot urine albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR >30 mg/g abnormal) or 24-h collection; distinguish selective (albumin-predominant, childhood MCD) from nonselective proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414). Serologies: ASO/anti-DNase/antihyaluronidase and streptozyme; ANA and anti-dsDNA; complement C3 and C4 (low C3 with normal C4 in poststreptococcal GN and C3 glomerulopathy; hypocomplementemia in active lupus nephritis); ANCA (anti-PR3, anti-MPO); anti-GBM antibody to the alpha3 NC1 domain specifically; cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor; antiphospholipid antibodies; HIV and hepatitis B/C serologies (Harrison 22e p.2416). Target-antigen antibodies in nephrotic disease: anti-PLA2R and anti-THSD7A (membranous nephropathy); DNAJB9 (fibrillary GN) (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417, 2422-2423). Kidney ultrasound to assess kidney size (small kidneys suggest chronicity) and exclude obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2416). Kidney biopsy with light microscopy (H&E, PAS, Jones silver, Congo red, Masson trichrome), immunofluorescence (IgG/IgM/IgA, C3/C4, PLA2R/THSD7A/DNAJB9), and electron microscopy to localize deposits and assess the GBM (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417). C3 nephritic factor, factor H, soluble C5b-9, paraprotein screening, and CFHR genetic testing (with family screening) when C3 glomerulopathy is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2420). Diabetic nephropathy and amyloidosis both thicken the GBM and can mimic membranous nephropathy on light microscopy (Harrison 22e p.2422-2423). Secondary FSGS (adaptive hyperfiltration/obesity, reflux, hypertension, drugs such as heroin/interferon/bisphosphonates, viruses) and genetic/familial podocytopathies must be excluded before diagnosing primary FSGS, as immunosuppression is not indicated in secondary/genetic forms (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422). Secondary membranous nephropathy from malignancy (breast, lung, colon), infection, lupus or other autoimmune disease, IgG4 disease, or drugs (gold, penicillamine, NSAIDs) (Harrison 22e p.2422). Membranous lupus nephritis (subendothelial deposits/tubuloreticular inclusions) may precede extrarenal lupus and mimic primary MGN (Harrison 22e p.2423). C3 glomerulopathy can be morphologically indistinguishable from resolving postinfectious glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2420). Mesangioproliferative pattern is shared by IgA nephropathy, P. falciparum malaria, resolving postinfectious GN, and lupus class II (Harrison 22e p.2421). Glomerular disease is grouped into six clinical syndromes that overlap and are not mutually exclusive: acute nephritic, pulmonary-renal, nephrotic, basement membrane, glomerular-vascular, and infectious disease-associated (Harrison 22e p.2414-2416). Nephritic syndrome = inflammatory pattern: hematuria with red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, pyuria, hypertension, fluid retention, only mild-to-moderate (1-2 g/24 h) proteinuria, and a falling GFR (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2416). Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria (>3.0-3.5 g/24 h) with hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, edema/anasarca, hypertension, and only minimal/microscopic hematuria; isolated heavy proteinuria without these features is termed nephrotic-range proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2420). Red blood cell casts or dysmorphic red cells in the sediment make glomerulonephritis likely; as few as 3-5 red cells in spun first-morning urine is suspicious (Harrison 22e p.2414). Gross hematuria is rare in glomerular disease except in IgA nephropathy and sickle cell disease; most glomerular hematuria is asymptomatic and microscopic (Harrison 22e p.2414). Kidney biopsy is the key diagnostic step in most glomerulonephritis; it identifies the lesion and often directs treatment, but is reserved for clinically stable patients with adequate clotting who can receive therapy (Harrison 22e p.2416-2417). Minimal change disease (MCD) causes 70-90% of childhood nephrotic syndrome but only 10-15% in adults; light microscopy is normal, immunofluorescence negative (or scant mesangial IgM), and electron microscopy shows foot-process effacement; childhood proteinuria is selective (mostly albumin) (Harrison 22e p.2420-2421). FSGS is the most common cause of primary glomerular disease leading to ESKD in the US; lesions are focal and segmental and concentrated at the corticomedullary junction, so a superficial biopsy can miss them and be misread as MCD (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422). Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) accounts for ~25% of adult nephrotic syndrome; 70-80% of primary cases have circulating IgG4 anti-PLA2R antibodies, and biopsy may no longer be required when anti-PLA2R is positive with normal creatinine and no secondary cause (Harrison 22e p.2422-2423). IgA nephropathy is defined by dominant/codominant mesangial IgA deposits and is one of the most common glomerulonephritides worldwide; the two classic presentations are persistent asymptomatic microscopic hematuria and recurrent gross hematuria during/just after an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic) (Harrison 22e p.2419). Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN) is now viewed as a pattern of injury (mesangial/subendothelial immune complexes, complement, or monoclonal deposits) producing GBM double contours ('tram-tracking'), rather than a single disease; classify by underlying immune-complex, complement, or monoclonal cause (Harrison 22e p.2420-2421). C3 glomerulopathy (dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis) shows sole/dominant glomerular C3 with little or no immunoglobulin and is driven by alternative-complement-pathway dysregulation (e.g., CFHR mutations, C3 nephritic factor) (Harrison 22e p.2420). RPGN is the clinical picture of acute nephritis with serum creatinine rising over days; crescentic glomerulonephritis is its pathologic equivalent and warrants urgent biopsy and treatment (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2419). When RPGN presents with lung hemorrhage it is a pulmonary-renal syndrome; consider anti-GBM/Goodpasture disease, ANCA small-vessel vasculitis, lupus, and cryoglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2418). ANCA small-vessel vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA, renal-limited) causes a pauci-immune (little/no immune-complex deposition) segmental necrotizing/crescentic glomerulonephritis; anti-PR3 is more common in GPA and anti-MPO in MPA/EGPA (Harrison 22e p.2419-2420). Anti-GBM disease targets the alpha3 NC1 domain of type IV collagen; biopsy shows linear IgG staining along the GBM (versus the granular 'lumpy-bumpy' deposits of immune-complex disease); 10-15% also have anti-MPO ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2418-2419). Poststreptococcal GN classically shows subepithelial 'humps' on electron microscopy, low C3/CH50 with normal C4 in the first week, and a positive streptozyme test; it rarely requires biopsy and has a good prognosis in children (Harrison 22e p.2417-2418). Lupus nephritis is classified ISN/RPS class I-VI; proliferative class III/IV lesions (and class IV with crescents) carry the worst prognosis, while mesangial class I/II need little therapy and class V is a membranous pattern (Harrison 22e p.2418). Kidney failure in glomerulonephritis correlates histologically with the degree of tubulointerstitial nephritis and interstitial fibrosis rather than with the specific glomerular lesion; interstitial fibrosis is an ominous sign of irreversibility (Harrison 22e p.2413-2414, 2416). On biopsy, <50% glomerular involvement is focal and >50% diffuse; injury within a tuft is segmental (part) or global (most); endocapillary proliferation is within the tuft and extracapillary proliferation (crescents) extends into Bowman's space (Harrison 22e p.2417). RPGN / crescentic glomerulonephritis - serum creatinine rising over days is a nephrologic emergency requiring urgent biopsy and immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2419). Pulmonary-renal syndrome (glomerulonephritis with lung hemorrhage/hemoptysis and falling hemoglobin) - consider anti-GBM/Goodpasture, ANCA vasculitis, lupus, cryoglobulinemia; lung hemorrhage responds to plasmapheresis (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2418-2419). Anti-GBM disease with oliguria, serum creatinine >5-6 mg/dL, need for acute dialysis, or >50% crescents on biopsy - markers of a poor prognosis requiring prompt treatment (Harrison 22e p.2419). ANCA small-vessel vasculitis - high mortality without treatment; virtually all patients need urgent induction therapy (Harrison 22e p.2419). Malignant hypertension can rapidly complicate glomerulosclerosis with fibrinoid arteriolar necrosis, thrombotic microangiopathy, and acute kidney failure (Harrison 22e p.2412). Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state - membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and deep-vein thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2423). A superficial kidney biopsy that fails to sample deeper corticomedullary glomeruli can miss the focal/segmental lesions of FSGS and be misdiagnosed as minimal change disease - suspect FSGS in steroid-resistant 'MCD' (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422). Test serum specifically against the alpha3 NC1 domain of collagen IV: non-nephritic anti-alpha1 NC1 antibodies in paraneoplastic syndromes cannot be distinguished by assays using whole basement-membrane fragments (Harrison 22e p.2419). ANCA-associated vasculitis can accompany or be confused with subacute bacterial endocarditis-associated GN; it must be ruled out because the treatments differ (Harrison 22e p.2417). There is no role for immunosuppression in poststreptococcal GN even when crescents are present, nor in secondary or genetic FSGS (Harrison 22e p.2418, 2422). Glomerular hematuria is usually microscopic and asymptomatic, so the diagnosis is often delayed; isolated microscopic hematuria in older men still requires exclusion of urinary tract malignancy (Harrison 22e p.2414). Nephrotic-range proteinuria without edema or hypoalbuminemia is not necessarily full nephrotic syndrome, and transient/orthostatic proteinuria (fever, exercise, obesity, CHF, upright posture) must be distinguished from sustained pathologic proteinuria (Harrison 22e p.2414, 2420). Each kidney holds ~0.9 million glomerular tufts whose fenestrated endothelium, GBM, and podocyte foot processes with slit-pore membranes form a size- and charge-selective filtration barrier; glomerular injury allows gram quantities of protein (mainly albumin) to escape (Harrison 22e p.2411-2412). Disease arises through genetic mutations (e.g., NPHS1/nephrin, NPHS2/podocin, TRPC6, APOL1 risk variants for FSGS; type IV collagen alpha3/4/5 in Alport's; complement-pathway/CFHR mutations in MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy/aHUS), infection, toxins, autoimmunity, hypertension/atherosclerosis, thrombosis/emboli, and diabetes; many cases remain idiopathic (Harrison 22e p.2411-2412). Inflammation of glomerular capillaries (glomerulonephritis) is typically immune-mediated: preformed circulating immune complexes deposit on the subendothelial side or mesangium, while in-situ formation produces subepithelial deposits; anti-GBM antibodies bind linearly to the GBM. Deposits and Toll-like receptor activation recruit neutrophils, macrophages, and T cells, activate complement to C5-9 membrane-attack complexes, and release proteases and oxidants that damage the mesangium, capillaries, and GBM and efface podocytes; early CD4/CD8 T-cell activation is important. Depending on antigen location and host genetics, injury produces endocapillary or extracapillary (crescentic) proliferation. Progression to chronic kidney failure tracks with downstream tubulointerstitial nephritis and fibrosis, driven by proteinuria-laden filtrate, inflammatory mediators carried from inflamed glomeruli, and fibroblast/myofibroblast expansion (TGF-beta, FGF-2, HIF-1alpha, PDGF) laying down collagen (Harrison 22e p.2412-2414). Prognosis is lesion-specific and tracks with the degree of tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Poststreptococcal GN resolves in most children within 3-6 weeks with rare progression to ESKD, but is worse in the elderly (up to 60% azotemia) (Harrison 22e p.2418). Minimal change disease responds to steroids in 90-95% of children and 80-90% of adults though relapse is common (70-75% of children) (Harrison 22e p.2421). Primary FSGS with nephrotic-range proteinuria reaches ESKD in ~50% by 10 years and rarely remits spontaneously, but treatment-induced remission improves outcome (Harrison 22e p.2421-2422). In membranous nephropathy roughly one-third remit spontaneously, one-third have relapsing nephrotic syndrome with preserved function, and one-third progress to kidney failure or die of complications (Harrison 22e p.2423). IgA nephropathy progresses to ESKD in only 25-30% over 20-25 years; persistent proteinuria >=6 months is the strongest adverse predictor (Harrison 22e p.2419). Dense deposit disease progresses to ESKD in ~50%. Untreated RPGN/crescentic disease and ANCA vasculitis carry high mortality, but ANCA vasculitis achieves remission in 75-90% with treatment (relapse 25-50%) (Harrison 22e p.2419-2420). Glomerular disease is organized into six clinical syndromes (acute nephritic, pulmonary-renal, nephrotic, basement membrane, glomerular-vascular, infectious disease-associated) graded semiquantitatively by proteinuria, hematuria, and vascular injury (Table 326-2, Harrison 22e p.2414-2416). Biopsy descriptors: focal (<50% of glomeruli) vs diffuse (>50%); segmental (part of a tuft) vs global; endocapillary vs extracapillary (crescentic) proliferation (Harrison 22e p.2417). Lupus nephritis uses the ISN/RPS class I-VI scheme (I minimal mesangial, II mesangial proliferative, III focal, IV diffuse, V membranous, VI sclerotic) (Table 326-3, Harrison 22e p.2418). IgA nephropathy uses the Oxford MEST-C score (mesangial/endocapillary hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, tubular fibrosis, crescents) (Harrison 22e p.2419). Albuminuria is staged normal (8-10 mg/24 h), microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/24 h), and frank proteinuria (>300 mg/24 h) (Table 326-1, Harrison 22e p.2414).

defines pattern, prognosis, and treatment (p.341-343, p.2355) Renal microvasculature disease — hemolytic-uremic syndrome and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (MAHA with schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, thrombocytopenia, end-organ injury) (p.341, p.2353) Malignant hypertension (p.341) Renal vein thrombosis (heavy proteinuria and hematuria) and renal artery thrombosis (p.341) Isolated hematuria from stones, neoplasm, tuberculosis, trauma, prostatitis (postrenal/non-glomerular) (p.342-343) The nephritic urinalysis is the foundation of diagnosis: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, pyuria, and proteinuria; always examine a freshly spun sediment to confirm active GN (p.2353-2354). Dysmorphic ('acanthocyte') RBCs on phase-contrast microscopy point to a glomerular bleeding source; RBC casts are highly specific but very insensitive for GN, so their absence does not exclude glomerular disease (p.341-342). The triad of dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and proteinuria >500 mg/day is essentially diagnostic of glomerulonephritis and warrants serologic workup plus biopsy even when creatinine is still normal (p.343). RPGN is a clinical diagnosis: any nephritic picture with rapidly rising creatinine should be treated as crescentic GN until proven otherwise (p.2355). At least three immunologic studies (ANCA, anti-GBM, complement) should be sent early to triage the three RPGN categories before immunosuppression (p.2355). Gross/cola-coloured glomerular hematuria with concurrent pharyngitis (synpharyngitic, day 1-3) suggests IgA nephropathy rather than post-streptococcal GN, which classically follows infection by 10 days to 3 weeks (p.2354). Both PIGN and IgA nephropathy deposit C3 in the glomerulus, but only PIGN lowers serum complement; a normal serum C3 with mesangial IgA favours IgA nephropathy/IgA vasculitis (p.2354-2356). Infection-associated GN occurring during an ongoing infection (e.g., MRSA abscess, osteomyelitis, empyema) is characteristically associated with glomerular IgA deposition and differs from classic post-infectious GN (p.2355). Rapidly rising creatinine with a nephritic sediment = crescentic RPGN, a nephrology emergency requiring urgent immunology and biopsy (p.2355) Hemoptysis, pulmonary infiltrates, or alveolar hemorrhage with renal failure = pulmonary-renal syndrome (anti-GBM/Goodpasture, ANCA vasculitis, SLE, cryoglobulinemia) — potentially fatal pulmonary hemorrhage (p.2355-2356) Upper-airway symptoms (sinusitis, nasal congestion, epistaxis) with GN suggest ANCA-associated vasculitis (p.2355) Anuria in acute GN indicates severe RPGN among the catastrophic anuric causes (p.342) Anti-GBM disease typically presents as a single fulminant episode demanding rapid diagnosis and prompt plasma exchange to preserve kidney function (p.2355) Relying on dipstick alone: it detects only albumin and can be falsely positive at pH >7 or with concentrated/blood-contaminated urine, and falsely negative in dilute urine or with non-albumin (light-chain) proteinuria (p.341). False-positive dipstick hematuria when myoglobinuria/rhabdomyolysis is present with no RBCs on microscopy (p.342-343). Assuming absence of RBC casts excludes GN — casts are highly specific but very insensitive (p.341). Mislabeling synpharyngitic gross hematuria as post-streptococcal GN; it is usually IgA nephropathy and PIGN instead follows infection by 10 days-3 weeks (p.2354). Expecting low serum complement in IgA nephropathy/IgA vasculitis — serum C3 is normal despite glomerular C3 deposition (p.2356). Withholding biopsy in azotemia-free patients with the diagnostic nephritic triad — they still warrant serologic workup and biopsy (p.343). Both anti-GBM and ANCA can be co-positive with pauci-immune pathology; such cases are managed as ANCA disease (p.2355). GN reflects glomerular inflammation producing hypertension, volume expansion (edema, sometimes ascites), and an abnormal (nephritic) urinalysis; intense cellular proliferation reduces filtering surface area, causing oliguria/anuria, sodium and water retention, and concentrated low-sodium urine. Three mechanistic categories underlie RPGN: (1) ANCA-associated pauci-immune vasculitis (anti-proteinase-3/cANCA, anti-myeloperoxidase/pANCA) where autoantibodies recruit complement and drive inflammatory vasculitis of kidney and peripheral vessels; (2) anti-GBM disease, where circulating IgG directed at an epitope in the alpha-3 chain of the non-collagenous domain of type IV collagen binds in situ with C3; and (3) immune-complex disease with low circulating C3 from subendothelial deposits (post-infectious/PIGN, endocarditis, SLE, cryoglobulinemia, hepatitis B/C, syphilis). In PIGN, antibody-bacterial antigen complexes form ~10 days-3 weeks after pharyngeal or skin (impetigo) infection by nephritogenic group A strep, activate complement causing hypocomplementemia and subendothelial deposits, with later subepithelial 'humps'. Pathologically, RPGN shows parietal epithelial and inflammatory cell proliferation forming cellular crescents that compress capillaries; crescents progress to fibrosis and global glomerulosclerosis. IgA nephropathy results from mesangial deposition of C3 binding galactose-deficient IgA-1. (p.2354-2356) Outcome depends on acuity vs chronicity: early reversible inflammatory/proliferative/necrotizing lesions can respond to prompt treatment, whereas sclerotic and atrophic biopsy findings indicate chronicity. Untreated RPGN capillaritis leads to complete, irreversible loss of kidney function; crescents that become fibrotic and atrophic cause global glomerulosclerosis, and when >50% of glomeruli are involved (diffuse) the process usually progresses to global glomerulosclerosis. Anti-GBM disease is usually a single acute fulminant event, while ANCA vasculitides may relapse (even subclinically) over time. IgA nephropathy can show rapid GFR decline to end-stage disease, especially in those of African ancestry with high-risk APOL1 alleles. Early diagnosis is critical. (p.2354-2356) RPGN crescent burden on biopsy stratifies severity: focal and segmental necrotizing GN when <50% of glomeruli are acutely and only segmentally involved (better preserved), versus diffuse involvement when >50% of glomeruli are affected, which usually progresses to global glomerulosclerosis. Healed focal segmental lesions yield secondary FSGS, distinct from primary podocytopathic FSGS. RPGN is mechanistically triaged into three serologic categories: ANCA-associated (pauci-immune), anti-GBM, and low-C3 immune-complex disease. (p.2355-2356)

paraganglioma Glomus tympanicum is a paraganglioma derived from paraganglion cells associated with the tympanic branches of the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves along the cochlear promontory. These tumours are highly vascular, composed of nests of chief cells in a rich capillary network, and grow slowly to fill the middle-ear cleft, impairing ossicular movement and producing conductive hearing loss and pulsatile tinnitus. Although almost always benign and non-secretory, a minority of paragangliomas produce catecholamines or occur within hereditary syndromes such as those linked to succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations, and multicentric tumours can occur. As a benign, slow-growing tumour, a glomus tympanicum confined to the middle ear has an excellent outlook with complete surgical excision, which is usually curative; larger or jugulare lesions are more challenging and carry greater risk to hearing and cranial nerves.

deficiencies that perpetuate the rash A glucagonoma is a functioning neuroendocrine tumour of pancreatic alpha cells that oversecretes glucagon. Glucagon is a catabolic, counter-regulatory hormone that promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing hyperglycaemia, and stimulates lipolysis and amino acid catabolism, leading to weight loss and depletion of circulating amino acids. The resulting hypoaminoacidaemia, together with deficiencies of zinc and essential fatty acids, is thought to underlie necrolytic migratory erythema. Glucagon excess also promotes a prothrombotic state. Because symptoms are non-specific and evolve slowly, diagnosis is often delayed until the tumour is large or metastatic, most commonly to the liver. Complete resection of localised disease can be curative and reverses the syndrome, but many patients present with metastatic disease; even then, these tumours are often relatively indolent and symptoms can be controlled for prolonged periods with somatostatin analogues and other systemic therapy.

diarrhoea caused by defective apical monosaccharide uptake. Variants in SLC5A1 impair the sodium/glucose cotransporter SGLT1, which normally drives coupled absorption of glucose, galactose and sodium across the enterocyte brush border. When this transporter fails, glucose and galactose accumulate in the lumen along with sodium and water, producing a profuse osmotic diarrhoea. Because dietary lactose and sucrose are digested to these monosaccharides, all glucose- and galactose-containing feeds cause symptoms, whereas fructose, absorbed via GLUT5, is well tolerated. With a strict fructose-based diet free of glucose and galactose the prognosis is excellent and growth is normal; tolerance to small carbohydrate loads may improve modestly with age. Lifelong dietary vigilance is required.

fasting-dependent fluctuation of symptoms Failing to consider the ketogenic diet as specific, effective treatment GLUT1 deficiency syndrome results from variants in SLC2A1 encoding the GLUT1 transporter responsible for facilitated glucose entry across the blood-brain barrier and into astrocytes. Reduced transporter function causes a chronic shortfall of glucose in the brain despite normal blood glucose, so cerebral energy supply becomes inadequate, particularly at times of increased demand such as fasting or exertion. This energy deficit produces seizures, movement disorder and impaired brain development, and it is bypassed therapeutically by providing ketone bodies through the ketogenic diet as an alternative fuel. With early institution of the ketogenic diet, seizure control and movement symptoms often improve substantially, though some cognitive and motor impairment may persist. Delayed diagnosis and treatment are associated with worse neurodevelopmental outcomes.

during fever, vomiting or poor intake Misinterpreting subdural collections and macrocephaly as non-accidental injury Missing low-excretor patients whose urine organic acids appear near normal Failing to provide aggressive emergency treatment during minor illnesses in the vulnerable age window Assuming absence of severe acidosis excludes an organic acid disorder Glutaric aciduria type 1 is an autosomal recessive deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme in the degradation pathway of lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan. Deficiency leads to accumulation of glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and glutarylcarnitine. These metabolites, particularly 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, are neurotoxic and, during periods of catabolic stress, cause selective injury to the striatum, producing a dystonic-dyskinetic movement disorder. Chronic accumulation is also associated with characteristic structural brain changes and a predisposition to subdural haemorrhage. Unlike the classic organic acidaemias, severe systemic metabolic acidosis is not the dominant feature; the main threat is acute neurological injury. Outcome is largely determined by whether the child suffers a striatal metabolic crisis; presymptomatic detection through newborn screening with dietary treatment and emergency management can prevent the dystonic movement disorder, whereas an established crisis causes permanent and often disabling neurological injury.

not always elevated in late-onset Pompe) Blood ketones during fasting/illness for liver GSDs Molecular/genetic testing (e.g., AGL, GBE1, PYGL, PHKA2/PHKB/PHKG2, GAA, PYGM, PFKM, GALT, aldolase B genes) now preferred over biopsy Enzyme assays (e.g., acid alpha-glucosidase in blood/fibroblasts/muscle for Pompe; CRIM status determination) Nonischemic forearm exercise test for suspected muscle GSD (abnormal lactate response); ischemic test largely abandoned ECG (high-voltage QRS and short PR in infantile Pompe; WPW pattern in Danon/PRKAG2), echocardiography, and cardiac/muscle MRI or ultrasound Liver biopsy/histology and abdominal imaging (CT/MRI surveillance for hepatocellular adenoma and carcinoma in liver GSDs) Newborn screening (Pompe on the U.S. RUSP; galactosemia screening programs) Idiopathic or familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (mimicked by Pompe, Danon, PRKAG2 syndrome) Polymyositis (McArdle disease may produce inflammatory-appearing EMG) Statin-induced myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (patients with GSD V and VII are at increased risk and may be confused with primary statin myopathy) Polycystic ovarian syndrome features (hirsutism, irregular menses) reported in GSD I and GSD III Glycogen storage diseases (GSDs) are inherited defects of glycogen metabolism producing glycogen that is abnormal in structure and/or quantity; collectively their prevalence is estimated at roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 25,000 live births, with most being autosomal recessive and a minority X-linked or autosomal dominant. GSDs are grouped by the predominant organ affected (liver vs muscle). The most common childhood forms are glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (GSD I), acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency (GSD II/Pompe), debrancher deficiency (GSD III), and liver phosphorylase kinase deficiency (GSD IX); the most common adult form is myophosphorylase deficiency (GSD V/McArdle). GSD I (von Gierke) classically presents around 3-4 months with hepatomegaly, doll-like facies with round cheeks, thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen; lab hallmarks are fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated LDL with low HDL producing milky/cloudy serum. A key distinction of GSD III from GSD I is that lactate and uric acid are normal in GSD III, whereas aminotransferases and urine glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4) are markedly elevated early then decline with age; GSD III hypoglycemia is typically ketotic and gluconeogenesis remains intact (unlike GSD I, which impairs both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis). GSD I type Ib differs from Ia by additional neutropenia and impaired neutrophil function, causing recurrent bacterial infections, mucosal ulceration, inflammatory-bowel-disease-like findings, and periodontal disease. Pompe disease (GSD II) is unique in storing glycogen primarily within lysosomes rather than cytoplasm; classic infantile-onset disease presents with hypotonia, generalized weakness, macroglossia, and rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with death usually before age 2 if untreated, whereas late-onset disease is defined by absence of cardiomyopathy in the first year and slowly progressive proximal/respiratory (diaphragm) weakness. McArdle disease (GSD V) is a prototypical muscle-energy disorder with exercise-induced cramps, myalgia, weakness, and myoglobinuria; the characteristic 'second wind' phenomenon (continuing exercise pain-free after a brief rest, as fatty-acid oxidation takes over) is unique to GSD V and there is no rise in blood lactate with exercise. Tarui disease (GSD VII, phosphofructokinase-M deficiency) mimics GSD V but shows an 'out of wind' phenomenon worsened by carbohydrate-rich meals and exercise, no spontaneous second wind, plus compensated hemolysis and hyperuricemia; giving IV dextrose or pre-exercise simple carbohydrates is detrimental in GSD VII (opposite to GSD V). In a young male with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) pattern on ECG strongly suggests Danon disease (X-linked LAMP2), where the WPW prevalence is about five times that in idiopathic/familial HCM. Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) presents after milk feeding with vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, hepatomegaly, aminoaciduria, and a notable susceptibility to gram-negative (especially E. coli) sepsis that may precede diagnosis; even with early dietary galactose elimination, long-term outcomes remain poor (speech/learning disorders, cataracts, primary ovarian insufficiency in females). Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) patients are asymptomatic until fructose/sucrose/sorbitol is ingested, then develop postprandial hypoglycemia, jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions; affected children characteristically develop an aversion to sweets. Genetic/molecular testing has largely replaced invasive tissue biopsy for diagnosis and subtyping of many GSDs; Pompe disease is now on the U.S. recommended uniform newborn screening panel. Neonatal/infant hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis (GSD I) or with sepsis-like presentation Rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure in infancy (infantile Pompe; congenital PRKAG2; massive myocardial glycogen deposition) WPW pattern with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a young male (Danon disease) Burgundy/dark urine with myoglobinuria after strenuous exercise (rhabdomyolysis) risking acute renal failure and acute compartment syndrome in muscle GSDs Respiratory insufficiency/failure as a presenting or progressive feature of late-onset Pompe disease Easy bruising, epistaxis, and prolonged bleeding time from platelet dysfunction/acquired von Willebrand-like disease in GSD I Hepatocellular adenoma with hemorrhage or malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma in liver GSDs (I, III, IV, VI, IX) Risk of malignant hyperthermia with halogenated anesthetics/muscle relaxants in GSD V and VII Normal serum creatine kinase does not exclude muscle involvement, including in late-onset Pompe disease, and normal muscle histology or EMG can occur due to disease heterogeneity. GSD VI and hepatic GSD IX were historically considered benign but show clinical heterogeneity, with reported fibrosis, cirrhosis, HCA, and HCC, including in the X-linked form. Giving IV dextrose or pre-exercise simple carbohydrates worsens GSD VII (Tarui), the opposite of the beneficial effect of pre-exercise carbohydrate in GSD V (McArdle). PRKAG2 syndrome can be misdiagnosed as infantile-onset Pompe disease due to phenotypic similarity of severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Diagnosing galactokinase (type II) deficiency is often missed because many newborn screening programs measure GALT activity rather than galactose directly, so it requires excluding GALT deficiency. Complete galactose elimination is NOT recommended in GALE deficiency (type III), because galactose is needed for nervous-system structural proteins and these patients cannot synthesize UDP-galactose from glucose; dietary restriction rather than elimination is used. The traditional discrete hepatic versus neuromuscular subtyping of GSD IV is now viewed as an oversimplification; it is better conceptualized as a multidimensional clinical continuum. McArdle disease may mimic inflammatory myopathy/polymyositis on EMG, risking misdiagnosis. Glycogen is the branched storage polymer of glucose, formed from alpha-1,4 chains branched by alpha-1,6 linkages. Inherited enzyme defects along glycogen synthesis, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and the linked galactose/fructose pathways disrupt glucose homeostasis. In GSD I, deficient glucose-6-phosphatase (Ia) or its translocase (Ib) blocks the final conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to glucose, impairing both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and causing fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and secondary hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia. In disorders of glycogenolysis with intact gluconeogenesis (GSD III debrancher, GSD VI liver phosphorylase, GSD IX phosphorylase kinase), incomplete glycogen breakdown causes hepatomegaly and milder, often ketotic hypoglycemia. GSD IV (brancher deficiency) produces poorly soluble abnormal glycogen (polyglucosan) injuring liver, heart, muscle, and nervous system. Pompe disease (GSD II) results from lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Muscle-energy GSDs (V/McArdle myophosphorylase, VII/Tarui phosphofructokinase, and rarer defects of phosphoglycerate mutase, LDH-A, aldolase A, beta-enolase) limit ATP generation from glycogenolysis/glycolysis, producing exercise intolerance, cramps, and rhabdomyolysis. In galactosemia, deficiency along the Leloir pathway (most commonly GALT) leads to accumulation of toxic galactose-1-phosphate injuring liver, kidney, brain, lens, and ovary. In hereditary fructose intolerance, aldolase B deficiency causes fructose-1-phosphate accumulation and ATP depletion that inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Prognosis varies widely by disorder and treatment. GSD I requires lifelong fasting avoidance; survivors face long-term gout, osteopenia/osteoporosis, hepatocellular adenoma with potential HCC, progressive renal disease/proteinuria advancing to end-stage renal disease, and increased pancreatitis and cardiovascular risk. GSD III liver disease often appears to improve in childhood but can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and HCC, while GSD IIIa muscle and cardiac disease may worsen after the third-fourth decade with risk of sudden death from arrhythmia. Classic infantile Pompe disease is fatal within about 2 years untreated, but enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved survival in both infantile and late-onset forms; CRIM-negative patients fare worse without immunomodulation. McArdle disease has a generally good prognosis with lifestyle measures, and physically active patients do better than inactive ones. Andersen disease (GSD IV) classic hepatic form is often fatal before age 5 without liver transplantation. Danon disease carries a poor prognosis with progressive end-stage heart failure in early adulthood. Classic galactosemia has poor long-term neurodevelopmental and ovarian outcomes despite early diet, whereas clinical-variant galactosemia and well-treated hereditary fructose intolerance generally have good prognoses; benign fructosuria and biochemical-variant (Duarte) galactosemia are essentially benign. Several GSDs are stratified by clinical severity and onset. Pompe disease (GSD II): classic infantile-onset (cardiomyopathy at/near birth, fatal within ~2 years untreated, GAA typically <1%), nonclassic infantile-onset (less severe cardiomyopathy, slower progression), and late-onset (no cardiomyopathy in first year, slowly progressive proximal/respiratory weakness, GAA ~2-35%); CRIM-positive versus CRIM-negative status further guides immunomodulation. GSD III is subclassified IIIa (~85%, liver plus cardiac/skeletal muscle) versus IIIb (~15%, liver only). GSD I is divided into Ia (~80%) and Ib (~20%, with neutropenia/neutrophil dysfunction). GSD IV/Andersen spans a continuum from lethal perinatal/congenital neuromuscular forms through classic progressive and nonprogressive hepatic forms to adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD). Galactosemia type I is graded as classic (absent/barely detectable GALT, severe), clinical variant (residual activity, milder, common in African Americans), and biochemical/Duarte variant (asymptomatic).

regression in an infant with organomegaly Emerging seizures or feeding and swallowing difficulty Progressive dystonia in juvenile or adult presentations Cardiac involvement in more severe phenotypes Confusing it with a mucopolysaccharidosis because of the shared skeletal and facial features Not distinguishing it from the GM2 gangliosidoses without enzyme testing Overlooking the milder adult dystonic form Failing to provide genetic counselling to at-risk relatives GM1 gangliosidosis results from biallelic pathogenic variants in GLB1, encoding lysosomal beta-galactosidase. Deficient enzyme activity impairs removal of terminal galactose residues, causing accumulation of GM1 ganglioside within neurons and of galactose-containing oligosaccharides and keratan sulfate in visceral and skeletal tissues. Neuronal ganglioside storage drives progressive neurodegeneration, while systemic substrate accumulation produces the organomegaly and dysostosis that overlap with the mucopolysaccharidoses. The severity and phenotype depend on residual enzyme activity, spanning severe infantile disease to milder adult-onset forms. The infantile form is severe and progressive, typically fatal in early childhood. Late-infantile and juvenile forms progress more slowly, and the adult form has a protracted course often dominated by movement disorder. No disease-modifying therapy is currently established, so care is supportive.

GM2 activator deficiency — AB variant of GM2 gangliosidosis, GM2 gangliosidosis AB variant, GM2A deficiency, GM2 activator protein deficiency Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency, HEXA) Sandhoff disease (hexosaminidase A and B deficiency, HEXB) Other infantile neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses Mitochondrial encephalopathies of infancy Other causes of a macular cherry-red spot (e.g. sialidosis, Niemann-Pick) Hexosaminidase A and B enzyme assay (characteristically normal, excluding classic Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff) GM2A molecular genetic testing to confirm activator deficiency Ophthalmological examination for a macular cherry-red spot Brain MRI to characterise the neurodegenerative process Specialised functional studies of GM2 degradation using natural substrate Developmental and neurophysiological assessment to document progression Rarest form of GM2 gangliosidosis, caused by biallelic GM2A variants abolishing the GM2 activator protein rather than the hexosaminidase enzyme itself The activator is an essential cofactor that presents GM2 ganglioside to hexosaminidase A; without it, degradation fails despite normal enzyme activity Clinically mimics infantile Tay-Sachs disease with early developmental arrest, hypotonia, progressive neurodegeneration and an exaggerated startle response A cherry-red spot at the macula is a characteristic ophthalmological finding Standard hexosaminidase A and B enzyme assays are normal, so the diagnosis is missed unless the activator defect is specifically considered Diagnosis relies on molecular testing of GM2A or specialised substrate/activator functional studies rather than routine enzyme assays No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is supportive with a multidisciplinary neurodegenerative approach Progressive loss of acquired developmental milestones in infancy Exaggerated startle response with a cherry-red macular spot Feeding difficulty, aspiration and respiratory compromise as disease advances Refractory seizures and neurological deterioration Excluding GM2 gangliosidosis on the basis of normal hexosaminidase assays Overlooking the activator defect as a cause of a cherry-red spot with neurodegeneration Delaying molecular testing when enzyme results are unexpectedly normal Not offering genetic counselling and carrier testing to the family The GM2 activator protein is a small lysosomal lipid-transfer cofactor that extracts GM2 ganglioside from the membrane and presents it to beta-hexosaminidase A for hydrolysis. In the AB variant the activator is deficient while hexosaminidase activity measured against artificial substrates is normal, so GM2 ganglioside cannot be catabolised and accumulates progressively within neuronal lysosomes. Neuronal storage drives the relentless central nervous system degeneration that clinically resembles the other GM2 gangliosidoses. The infantile presentation is progressive and fatal in early childhood, mirroring classic Tay-Sachs disease; management is palliative and supportive as no curative treatment is available.

Gnathostomiasis — Gnathostoma spinigerum infection, larva migrans profundus, Yangtze oedema, wandering swelling Cutaneous larva migrans Loiasis (Calabar swellings) Angioedema or urticaria Sparganosis and other migrating tissue helminths Fascioliasis in its migratory phase Other causes of eosinophilic meningitis such as angiostrongyliasis Bacterial or inflammatory panniculitis Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia Gnathostoma-specific serology Detailed dietary and travel history Cerebrospinal fluid examination (often eosinophilic, sometimes xanthochromic) if neurological involvement is suspected MRI of the brain or spinal cord in neurological disease Histology or identification of a larva if surgically retrieved A food-borne tissue nematode infection caused chiefly by Gnathostoma spinigerum, acquired by eating undercooked freshwater fish, eels, frogs, poultry or snakes Endemic in Southeast Asia, notably Thailand, and increasingly reported from Latin America and among returning travellers The hallmark is intermittent, migratory subcutaneous swellings that move over days, often with overlying erythema, itch or pain Peripheral eosinophilia is common and supports the diagnosis in the right exposure context The larva cannot mature in humans and wanders through tissues, so the most feared complication is invasion of the central nervous system causing eosinophilic meningitis, radiculomyelitis or haemorrhage Serology helps confirm the diagnosis, as recovering the larva is uncommon Treatment uses anthelmintics such as albendazole or ivermectin, sometimes with corticosteroids for the inflammatory reaction; surgical removal is possible if a migrating larva is accessible A dietary history of raw or undercooked freshwater animal flesh is a key diagnostic clue Headache, radicular pain, limb weakness or altered consciousness suggesting central nervous system invasion Signs of intracranial or spinal haemorrhage Ocular involvement threatening vision Rapidly progressive neurological deficit Not eliciting a history of eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish or other flesh Attributing migratory swellings to allergy or angioedema Failing to consider neurognathostomiasis in eosinophilic meningitis from an endemic area Assuming a single course of anthelmintic guarantees cure, as relapse can occur Overlooking the diagnosis in a returning traveller with eosinophilia Human gnathostomiasis follows ingestion of third-stage Gnathostoma larvae in undercooked or raw intermediate hosts such as freshwater fish and other flesh. Humans are accidental hosts in which the larva cannot develop into an adult worm. Instead it penetrates the gut wall and migrates through the liver and other tissues, then wanders through the subcutaneous tissues and, less often, deeper structures. This migration provokes eosinophil-rich inflammation and produces the characteristic shifting swellings. Aberrant migration into the central nervous system causes tracking damage and haemorrhage, giving rise to eosinophilic meningitis and myeloradiculopathy that account for the most serious morbidity. Cutaneous disease is generally benign though it may relapse over months to years, whereas central nervous system gnathostomiasis carries a serious prognosis with a risk of permanent neurological deficit or death.

Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an inflammatory rather than genetic myopathy Prominent inflammation on biopsy that would favour sporadic inclusion body myositis Respiratory muscle involvement in advanced disease Loss of ambulation requiring mobility and falls assessment Misdiagnosing it as sporadic inclusion body myositis and treating with immunotherapy, which is ineffective Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase and dismissing a genetic myopathy Attributing the foot drop to a peripheral neuropathy without recognising the myopathic pattern Overlooking the characteristic quadriceps sparing that points to the diagnosis GNE myopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in GNE, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase that catalyses the rate-limiting steps of sialic acid biosynthesis. Reduced enzyme activity leads to hyposialylation of muscle glycoproteins and glycolipids, which is thought to impair muscle-cell function and promote the accumulation of autophagic and protein aggregates seen histologically as rimmed vacuoles and inclusions. The resulting slow degeneration of muscle fibres produces the characteristic distal-onset, quadriceps-sparing pattern of weakness, although the precise link between hyposialylation and fibre loss is incompletely understood. GNE myopathy is slowly progressive, with many patients losing independent ambulation roughly one to two decades after onset, but life expectancy is usually preserved as respiratory and cardiac involvement are uncommon and generally late.

a progressive eccentric flexor-pronator strengthening programme Steroid injection carries the added risk of ulnar nerve injury and offers only short-term benefit, so it is used cautiously Consider valgus overload and medial collateral ligament pathology in throwing athletes with medial elbow pain Progressive ulnar nerve symptoms with weakness or intrinsic hand muscle wasting Night pain, systemic features, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour Significant trauma or instability raising concern for ligament rupture Persistent symptoms despite appropriate rehabilitation prompting diagnostic review Missing associated ulnar nerve entrapment, which can dominate the clinical picture Injecting corticosteroid without regard to the closely applied ulnar nerve Failing to recognise medial collateral ligament injury in throwing athletes Treating as inflammatory with rest rather than addressing the tendinopathy with loading Golfer's elbow is an overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor-pronator origin at the medial epicondyle, particularly involving pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis. Repetitive flexion, pronation, and valgus loading cause microtrauma and a failed healing response, producing mucoid degeneration and disorganised collagen. Proximity to the ulnar nerve means concurrent nerve irritation is common. Most patients improve with load management and progressive strengthening, though recovery may take months; coexisting ulnar neuropathy or valgus instability tends to worsen outcomes and may need specific treatment.

Gonorrhea — gonococcal infection, Neisseria gonorrhoeae Nongonococcal urethritis (C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, HSV) - clinically often impossible to distinguish from gonococcal urethritis (p.1255-1256) Bacterial cystitis/urinary tract infection versus the urethral syndrome in women presenting with dysuria (p.1256) For the bacteremic stage of DGI: reactive arthritis, acute rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, erythema nodosum, drug-induced arthritis, and viral infections including hepatitis B and acute HIV infection (p.1257) Suppurative gonococcal arthritis in the absence of symptomatic genital infection cannot be distinguished from septic arthritis caused by other pathogens (p.1257) Meningococcemia, which can produce a dermatitis-arthritis syndrome, purulent monoarthritis, and reactive polyarthritis similar to DGI (p.1058) Acute HIV infection and hepatitis B (viral causes mimicking the bacteremic arthritis-dermatitis stage of DGI) (p.1257) Gram stain of urethral discharge for gram-negative intracellular monococci/diplococci - highly sensitive in symptomatic men, only ~50% sensitive for cervicitis (p.1255, 1257) NAAT (e.g., Aptima Combo 2, Xpert CT/NG, BD ProbeTec, COBAS) on urine, urethral, cervical or self-collected vaginal swabs - more sensitive than culture and co-detects C. trachomatis; point-of-care NAAT with ~30-minute turnaround available (p.1257) Culture on modified Thayer-Martin/selective medium with prompt processing (gonococci do not tolerate drying); single endocervical culture ~80-90% sensitive (p.1257) In MSM, screen rectum and pharynx in addition to urine, since urine alone will miss the majority of cases (p.1257) Blood cultures (Isolator tubes may improve yield; positivity falls after 48 h of illness) and synovial fluid (inoculate into blood culture broth and chocolate agar) in suspected DGI; organisms are seldom recovered from blood and synovial fluid in the same patient (p.1257) Standardized culture is the preferred legal-evidence method in children for suspected sexual abuse; two NAATs targeting different sequences may substitute (p.1257) Total hemolytic complement activity assay in anyone with more than one episode of DGI (p.1255, 1260) Reactive arthritis (joint distribution differs from DGI; skin and genital manifestations also differ) (p.1257) Acute rheumatoid arthritis (p.1257) Sarcoidosis (p.1257) Erythema nodosum (p.1257) Drug-induced arthritis (p.1257) Gonorrhea is a sexually transmitted infection of the epithelium that commonly presents as cervicitis, urethritis, proctitis, or conjunctivitis; if untreated it can cause local complications including endometritis, salpingitis, tuboovarian abscess, bartholinitis, peritonitis, and perihepatitis in women, and periurethritis and epididymitis in men (p.1253). In men, acute urethritis is the most common manifestation, typically after a 2-7 day incubation, with discharge that is initially scant and mucoid but becomes profuse and purulent within a day or two; however, a reservoir of infected men remains asymptomatic (p.1255). About half of women infected with N. gonorrhoeae develop symptoms; many have only minor symptoms (scant cervical discharge, dysuria) and may delay care, so the asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic reservoir is key to ongoing transmission (p.1256). Gram stain of urethral exudate showing gram-negative intracellular monococci and diplococci is highly specific and sensitive in symptomatic men, but is only about 50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis, so women should be diagnosed by culture or a nonculture (NAAT) method (p.1257). Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are now widely used, are more sensitive than culture for both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, allow urine and self-collected vaginal swab testing, and simultaneously detect chlamydial co-infection (p.1257). Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) results from gonococcal bacteremia and most commonly presents as an arthritis-dermatitis syndrome with fever, chills, tenosynovitis, polyarthralgias, and characteristic skin lesions (papules/pustules with a hemorrhagic component, ~5-40, on the extremities) seen in about 75% of patients (p.1257). Menstruation is a risk factor for dissemination and roughly two-thirds of DGI cases occur in women; in about half of affected women symptoms begin within 7 days of onset of menses (p.1257). Persons deficient in terminal complement components (C5-C9) and those receiving the C5-blocking monoclonal antibody eculizumab are predisposed to recurrent neisserial bacteremia; anyone with more than one episode of DGI should be screened for complement deficiency (p.1255, 1260). Ceftriaxone is the recommended first-line agent for uncomplicated gonococcal infection, now at twice the previously recommended dose because mean inhibitory concentrations of current strains have doubled relative to 20 years ago (p.1259). Quinolone-containing regimens and cefixime are no longer recommended as first-line treatment in the United States because of widespread quinolone resistance and rising cefixime MICs (p.1259). Because co-infection with C. trachomatis occurs frequently, concurrent treatment for chlamydia (doxycycline) is recommended whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded (p.1259). Disseminated gonococcal infection with the joint-localized suppurative arthritis stage - hospitalization indicated, may need joint aspiration and higher/longer therapy (p.1259) Gonococcal meningitis - rare complication of DGI requiring high-dose IV ceftriaxone for 10-14 days (p.1257, 1260) Gonococcal endocarditis - rare today but historically accounted for about one-quarter of endocarditis cases; requires at least 4 weeks of IV therapy (p.1257, 1260) Ophthalmia neonatorum and adult ocular gonorrhea - prompt recognition and treatment essential, as corneal ulceration may progress to perforation, panophthalmitis and blindness (p.1256-1257) Pelvic inflammatory disease should be considered when cervical infection extends to cause dyspareunia or lower abdominal/back pain (p.1256) Because co-infection with C. trachomatis is frequent, treatment of gonorrhea must include concurrent therapy for chlamydia (doxycycline) whenever chlamydial infection cannot be excluded - omitting this is a key pitfall (p.1259). Azithromycin is no longer recommended as part of the first-line regimen because U.S. gonococcal resistance to azithromycin rose more than sevenfold to 4.7% in 2021 (p.1259). A presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea cannot be made from gram-negative diplococci on a pharyngeal Gram stain, because commensal Neisseria species are normal pharyngeal flora (p.1257). Gram stain is only ~50% sensitive for gonococcal cervicitis; relying on it in women risks missed diagnoses, so culture or NAAT is required (p.1257). DGI strains often do not incite a local genital inflammatory response and may not cause genital symptoms, so disseminated disease can occur without an obvious mucosal source (p.1254, 1257). Quinolones and cefixime are no longer first-line in the United States due to resistance and rising MICs - using them empirically risks treatment failure (p.1259). Persistent symptoms after a recommended regimen should prompt evaluation for reinfection, a drug-resistant strain, or an alternative diagnosis rather than simple re-treatment; culture and susceptibility testing should be performed (p.1259). Because of high reinfection rates within 6-12 months, persons treated for gonorrhea should be retested at 3 months (p.1259). N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative, nonmotile, non-spore-forming, oxidase-positive diplococcus and an exclusively human pathogen; it carries on average three genome copies per coccal unit, and this polyploidy supports a high level of antigenic variation that aids host survival. Pili (fimbriae) mediate initial adherence to nonciliated columnar epithelial cells and enable invasion, transcytosis, genetic competence and transformation; pilus expression is switched off on subculture as a basis for antigenic variation. Opacity-associated protein (Opa) mediates intergonococcal and epithelial adhesion and binds CEACAM receptors, promoting invasion, suppressing CD4+ T-cell activation, and enabling nonopsonic neutrophil phagocytosis. Porin (the most abundant surface protein) forms the basis of serotyping; PorB.1A strains are associated with disseminated infection, resist normal human serum killing, bind complement-inhibitory molecules and may not cause local symptoms, whereas PorB.1B strains usually cause local genital infection. Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) has marked endotoxic activity; sialylation of LOS inhibits classical and alternative complement pathways and reduces neutrophil killing. Iron/zinc scavenging proteins (transferrin-, lactoferrin-, hemoglobin-binding proteins) and IgA1 protease promote survival. Host entry into nonphagocytic cells involves phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activation with ceramide-mediated apoptosis, and inflammation is driven by LOS and peptidoglycan-induced cytokine release (p.1254-1255). A single recommended ceftriaxone regimen almost always cures uncomplicated urethral, cervical, rectal, or pharyngeal infection, and true treatment failure with a recommended regimen is rare. Symptomatic pharyngeal gonorrhea is harder to eradicate than genital infection. In the preantibiotic era untreated urethritis persisted about 8 weeks. DGI incidence has fallen (from ~0.5-3% of untreated mucosal infections in the 1970s) likely due to a decline in disseminating strains. A dramatic alleviation of arthritis-dermatitis symptoms within 12-24 h of appropriate antibiotics supports a clinical diagnosis of DGI even when cultures are negative. Rising worldwide resistance, including reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility, threatens future treatment efficacy (p.1257-1260). Clinical manifestations span uncomplicated mucosal infection (urethritis, cervicitis, proctitis, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis) versus complicated/disseminated disease. DGI has historically been described in two overlapping stages: a bacteremic stage (higher fever, chills, polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and skin lesions) and a joint-localized stage with suppurative (septic) arthritis, though a clear-cut progression is usually not evident (p.1257).
