proliferation, radiotherapy, and surgical stabilisation Dyspnoea and a chylous pleural effusion indicating thoracic duct or rib involvement Rapidly progressive osteolysis threatening the spine with instability or cord compromise Pathological fracture in a weight-bearing or load-critical bone Skull-base involvement with neurological deficit or cerebrospinal fluid leak Labelling the osteolysis as malignancy or infection without appropriate biopsy Underestimating the risk of chylothorax when ribs, spine, or thorax are affected Assuming stabilisation is permanent and stopping surveillance too early Attempting isolated surgery without addressing the underlying vascular-lymphatic process, risking recurrence Gorham-Stout disease is characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of vascular and lymphatic endothelial channels within bone that progressively replace and destroy the osseous matrix. The abnormal vessels and associated osteoclastic activity dissolve bone in a relentless, often locally aggressive fashion, though the process does not metastasise. The trigger is not fully understood, but dysregulated lymphangiogenesis and angiogenesis, with increased osteoclast sensitivity to humoral factors, are thought central. When the disease reaches the thoracic cavity or thoracic duct, abnormal lymphatic channels can leak, producing chylous effusions that carry significant morbidity and mortality. The course is unpredictable; disease may stabilise spontaneously or progress relentlessly, and prognosis is generally good when confined to an extremity but markedly worse with thoracic involvement and chylothorax.

Gorlin syndrome — naevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, NBCCS, basal cell naevus syndrome, PTCH1, Gorlin-Goltz syndrome Sporadic multiple basal cell carcinomas from chronic sun exposure Bazex-Dupre-Christol syndrome Rombo syndrome Trichoepitheliomas of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome Xeroderma pigmentosum with early skin cancers Isolated odontogenic keratocysts Germline molecular genetic testing of PTCH1 and SUFU including deletion/duplication analysis Orthopantomogram or jaw imaging for odontogenic keratocysts Skull and skeletal radiographs for falx calcification and rib or vertebral anomalies Dermatological mapping and biopsy of suspicious skin lesions Baseline and clinically guided brain MRI in young children for medulloblastoma surveillance, favouring non-ionising imaging Cardiac and ovarian ultrasound where fibromas are suspected Autosomal dominant syndrome most often caused by germline loss-of-function variants in PTCH1, a negative regulator of the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway; SUFU variants are a less common cause Multiple basal cell carcinomas develop from a young age, often on sun-exposed and non-exposed skin, and may number in the many across a lifetime Odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw are an early and characteristic feature, frequently causing swelling or being found incidentally on dental imaging Palmar and plantar pits are a useful clinical clue on close skin examination Skeletal anomalies include bifid or splayed ribs, and calcification of the falx cerebri is commonly seen on skull imaging There is markedly increased radiosensitivity, so diagnostic and therapeutic radiation should be minimised to avoid inducing new basal cell carcinomas in the treatment field Childhood medulloblastoma (desmoplastic subtype) occurs in a minority and is an important early risk, particularly with SUFU variants New neurological signs in a young child raising concern for medulloblastoma Rapidly enlarging or aggressive basal cell carcinoma, particularly around the eyes, nose or ears Expanding jaw swelling or pathological fracture from an odontogenic keratocyst Extensive prior therapeutic radiotherapy given before the diagnosis was recognised Using radiotherapy for basal cell carcinomas and thereby inducing numerous new tumours in the irradiated field Dismissing multiple early-onset basal cell carcinomas as ordinary sun damage Missing palmar and plantar pits and jaw cysts that would prompt the diagnosis Failing to counsel on sun protection and to arrange paediatric medulloblastoma awareness Gorlin syndrome arises from germline inactivating variants in PTCH1 (or less often SUFU), key components of the Sonic hedgehog signalling pathway. PTCH1 normally inhibits the transmembrane protein Smoothened; loss of PTCH1 function releases this inhibition, leading to constitutive hedgehog pathway activation and unchecked proliferation in susceptible tissues. As a tumour-suppressor mechanism, tumour formation follows a somatic second hit. Aberrant hedgehog signalling explains the developmental anomalies and the predisposition to basal cell carcinomas, odontogenic keratocysts and medulloblastoma. The same pathway dependence underlies the therapeutic use of hedgehog pathway inhibitors in advanced disease. Life expectancy is usually near normal, but lifelong burden from recurrent basal cell carcinomas and jaw cysts is considerable and requires ongoing surveillance and treatment. Medulloblastoma in early childhood is the most serious potential complication and drives paediatric monitoring.

Gout and Other Crystal-Associated Arthropathies — Gout, Podagra, Crystal-induced arthritis, Pseudogout, Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, CPPD, Chondrocalcinosis, Basic calcium phosphate disease, Apatite arthropathy, Calcium oxalate arthropathy Septic (bacterial) arthritis Other crystal-associated arthropathies (CPPD/pseudogout, apatite, calcium oxalate) Palindromic rheumatism Psoriatic arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis (especially chronic tophaceous gout or pseudo-rheumatoid CPPD) Osteoarthritis (pseudoosteoarthritis pattern of CPPD) Cellulitis (pseudocellulitis appearance of an acute flare) Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy (mimicked by severe destructive CPPD) Acute septic arthritis can closely resemble an acute crystal flare, and bacterial infection can coexist with MSU or CPP crystals in synovial fluid, so joint fluid should be Gram-stained and cultured Acute flares with overlying erythema, warmth, and swelling can mimic cellulitis (pseudocellulitis) Synovial fluid aspiration with polarized light microscopy to identify and distinguish crystal type (MSU vs CPP); apatite is not identifiable by polarized light alone Synovial fluid leukocyte count and microbial Gram stain and culture to exclude coexisting infection Serum urate (interpreting with awareness it may be transiently normal during a flare) Alizarin red S staining for calcium-containing (apatite, CaOx) crystals; electron microscopy with energy-dispersive analysis, x-ray diffraction, infrared or Raman spectroscopy for definitive apatite identification Plain radiography (erosions with overhanging margins in gout; chondrocalcinosis in CPPD; periarticular calcification in apatite disease) Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign) and dual-energy CT for MSU detection In CPPD patients under 50: serum calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase, magnesium, iron, and transferrin, plus screening for familial aggregation and metabolic disease (hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) Serum creatinine, liver function tests, hemoglobin, WBC count, HbA1c, and lipids at baseline to assess comorbidities and treatment risk Osteoarthritis (pseudoosteoarthritis form of CPPD) Rheumatoid arthritis (chronic tophaceous gout; chronic symmetric synovitis pattern of CPPD) Neuropathic arthropathy (severe destructive CPPD) Erosive osteoarthritis of the fingers (apatite-associated) Spinal stenosis or crowned dens syndrome (CPPD spinal involvement) Gout is a hyperuricemic metabolic disorder in which chronic hyperuricemia leads to supersaturation and deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and connective tissue; it typically presents with episodic, intensely painful inflammatory arthritis in middle-aged-to-elderly men and postmenopausal women (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957). The first metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases; other early targets are tarsal joints, ankles, and knees, while finger, wrist, and elbow involvement is more typical of elderly patients or advanced disease (Harrison 22e p.2958). Flares often begin at night or in the early morning and are among the most painful conditions humans experience; affected joints rapidly become warm, red, tender, and swollen, sometimes mimicking cellulitis (pseudocellulitis), and usually subside spontaneously within 1-2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2958). Definitive diagnosis rests on demonstrating needle-shaped MSU crystals (intracellular and extracellular) showing strong negative birefringence under compensated polarized light; synovial fluid is cloudy with leukocyte counts roughly 5000-75,000/uL (Harrison 22e p.2958-2959). Serum urate may be normal or even low during an acute flare because inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 are uricosuric and can lower it by about 2 mg/dL, so a normal level during a flare does not exclude gout; historical or postflare values are more diagnostically useful (Harrison 22e p.2959). Musculoskeletal ultrasound (double-contour sign over articular cartilage) and dual-energy CT (chemical identification of MSU) aid early diagnosis; plain radiographs in advanced tophaceous gout show well-defined erosions with sclerotic, overhanging margins and soft-tissue masses, though these are absent early (Harrison 22e p.2959). Hyperuricemia is most often due to impaired renal urate excretion (about 90%) rather than overproduction (about 10%); roughly two-thirds of daily uric acid is eliminated renally and one-third through the gut (intestinal uricolysis by gut bacteria) (Harrison 22e p.2957). Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) is strongly age-related, with prevalence in articular tissues roughly doubling each decade after 60 and reaching nearly 50% in those over 85; most deposition is asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2960). Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout) most often affects the knee, then the wrist, and rarely the first MTP joint; episodes tend to last longer than gout flares (weeks to months) and may be accompanied by fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2960). Chondrocalcinosis (punctate/linear radiodense deposits in fibrocartilage or hyaline cartilage) supports CPPD; definitive diagnosis requires rhomboid or rod-shaped weakly positively birefringent or nonbirefringent crystals in synovial fluid or tissue (Harrison 22e p.2961). Apatite (basic calcium phosphate) crystals are extremely small and individually visible only by electron microscopy; clumps appear as nonbirefringent globules staining bright red with alizarin red S, and apatite underlies the destructive 'Milwaukee shoulder' of the elderly (Harrison 22e p.2961). Calcium oxalate (CaOx) arthropathy is largely a disease of patients on long-term dialysis, especially with ascorbic acid supplementation, since ascorbate is metabolized to oxalate that is poorly cleared in uremia; the readily recognized crystals are bipyramidal with strong birefringence (Harrison 22e p.2962). Acutely hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis cannot be excluded clinically, mandating synovial fluid Gram stain and culture Fever, chills, and elevated acute-phase reactants during a crystal flare (seen in up to 50% of acute CPPD episodes, occasionally to 40 C), which overlap with infection Hyperuricemia in prepubertal boys, which should prompt evaluation for inherited enzyme defects (HPRT deficiency, PRPP synthetase superactivity) CPPD arthritis in patients under 50, raising concern for an underlying metabolic disorder (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypophosphatasia, hypomagnesemia) Progressive destructive large-joint disease (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) signaling severe apatite-associated joint destruction Assuming a normal serum urate during an acute attack excludes gout; cytokine-mediated uricosuria (e.g., IL-6) can lower it by about 2 mg/dL during flares Failing to exclude infection: bacterial sepsis can coexist with crystals, and crystals do not rule out a septic joint Relying on polarized light microscopy to detect apatite, whose individual crystals require electron microscopy and special stains/techniques Overlooking a secondary metabolic cause when CPPD presents before age 50 Confusing intra-/periarticular apatite calcifications with the linear calcifications of CPPD on radiographs Diagnosing chondrocalcinosis as CPPD without considering calcium oxalate deposition in chronic renal failure as an alternative Chronic hyperuricemia is a prerequisite for gout but not sufficient alone, since only a minority of hyperuricemic individuals ever develop disease. Humans uniquely develop gout spontaneously because of an evolutionary species-wide loss of uricase, the enzyme that converts urate to highly soluble allantoin; at physiologic pH uric acid (pKa about 5.8) exists mainly as ionized urate. An increased urate body pool leads to MSU supersaturation (favored above roughly 6.85 mg/dL) and crystal formation/deposition in joints and connective tissue, modulated by temperature, pH, intra-articular dehydration, cation concentration, and matrix proteoglycans/collagen. Hyperuricemia stems predominantly from impaired renal excretion (about 90%) and less often overproduction (about 10%); overproduction relates to increased cell turnover (hematologic malignancy, psoriasis), chemotherapy, tissue hypoxia, or inherited defects such as PRPP synthetase superactivity or HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan spectrum). Renal handling involves sodium-dependent apical reabsorption via URAT1/OAT10, basolateral GLUT9 efflux, and intestinal excretion via ABCG2. Acute flares are triggered when MSU crystals are shed from inert deposits and activate resident synovial macrophages, mast cells, and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-alpha; neutrophil phagocytosis of crystals amplifies inflammation via a respiratory burst. Untreated, growing tophaceous MSU deposits with granulomatous inflammation produce chronic gouty arthritis with erosive deformity. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals that, like MSU, activate phagocytes and the inflammasome. Apatite deposition occurs in tissue damage (dystrophic), hypercalcemic/hyperparathyroid states (metastatic), connective tissue disease (calcinosis), and chronic renal failure (tumoral calcinosis, calciphylaxis). CaOx deposits accumulate in cartilage, synovium, bone, and viscera in chronic renal failure and primary oxalosis (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962). Typical acute gout flares are self-limited, resolving spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, with symptom-free intercritical intervals; however, untreated recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Gout is associated with multiple cardiometabolic-kidney comorbidities (obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, stroke, chronic kidney disease, urate nephrolithiasis). Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) tends to progress indolently but can cause severe pain, instability, and disability requiring joint replacement, and CaOx and chronic CPP arthropathies may progressively destroy joints (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962). Gout is described as a clinical continuum rather than by a formal grading scale: asymptomatic hyperuricemia; acute (episodic) gout flares with intercritical symptom-free intervals; and chronic (tophaceous) gouty arthritis with persistent synovitis, tophi, deformity, and bony destruction. Crystal-induced disease is categorized by pattern as acute (episodic) mono-, oligo-, or polyarthritis; periarticular inflammation (bursitis, tendinitis, enthesitis); tophaceous deposits; chronic destructive or chronic inflammatory arthropathy; a peculiar osteoarthritis-like form; spinal arthritis; and carpal tunnel syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2956-2957).

generalised disease Confusing subcutaneous GA with rheumatoid nodules and pursuing unnecessary rheumatological work-up Granuloma annulare is characterised histologically by focal degeneration of dermal collagen (necrobiosis) surrounded by a palisaded or interstitial histiocytic and lymphocytic infiltrate, with mucin deposition in the altered dermis. The process is thought to represent a cell-mediated, delayed-type hypersensitivity or macrophage-driven reaction to an as-yet undefined trigger, with cytokine-mediated matrix degradation. Precipitants proposed in individual cases include trauma, infection, insect bites, drugs, and immune dysregulation, and there are reported associations with metabolic and, less commonly, malignant or infective conditions in certain subtypes. Localised granuloma annulare is benign and frequently resolves on its own without scarring, though recurrence is common; the generalised form tends to be more chronic and less responsive to treatment, but it remains a benign condition.

ANCA activate primed neutrophils, causing degranulation, release of reactive oxygen species and proteases, and endothelial injury, producing pauci-immune (minimal immune complex) inflammation. The disease combines this small-vessel vasculitis with granuloma formation in the respiratory tract. Injury to alveolar capillaries causes diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, and glomerular capillary damage produces crescentic, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Once almost uniformly fatal, the disease now has good remission rates with modern induction therapy, but relapse is common and requires ongoing surveillance. Prognosis is worse with severe renal impairment at presentation and with alveolar haemorrhage; long-term morbidity includes chronic kidney disease and treatment-related complications.

haemorrhage requiring intervention Rapidly falling platelet count that could reflect marrow failure Bleeding during pregnancy or delivery in an affected woman Misdiagnosing it as immune thrombocytopenia and using immunosuppression or splenectomy Overlooking the characteristic grey agranular platelets on the film Attributing the marrow fibrosis to a primary myeloproliferative disorder Failing to counsel about the progressive nature of the fibrosis and splenomegaly Gray platelet syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in NBEAL2, a gene required for the biogenesis and retention of alpha-granules in megakaryocytes and platelets. Alpha-granules normally store a large array of proteins involved in haemostasis, wound healing, and inflammation, including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, platelet factor 4, and growth factors. Without functional NBEAL2 these granules fail to form or retain their cargo, so platelets are released large and agranular, appearing grey on staining, and function poorly. Premature release of granule proteins such as platelet-derived growth factor and transforming growth factor beta into the marrow microenvironment is thought to drive the progressive myelofibrosis that characterises the disorder, while ineffective thrombopoiesis contributes to the thrombocytopenia. The bleeding tendency is usually mild to moderate and manageable, but the outlook is influenced by progressive myelofibrosis and splenomegaly, which can worsen cytopenias over time.

MYO5A (type 1) encodes a motor protein required in melanocytes and neurons; RAB27A (type 2) is essential for both melanosome transfer and the exocytosis of cytotoxic granules by lymphocytes and natural killer cells; MLPH (type 3) links the two in melanocytes only. Consequently, all types share defective pigment distribution, while RAB27A loss additionally impairs cytotoxic granule release, predisposing to haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Type 2 is fatal without treatment of the accelerated phase and definitive haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can be curative for the immune disease. Type 1 carries a poor neurological prognosis, whereas type 3 has a benign course limited to pigmentary change.

ovarian cancers are split into indolent type 1 (low-grade, KRAS/BRAF/PTEN/PIK3CA mutations) and aggressive type 2 high-grade serous cancers, the latter driven by TP53 loss (about 95%) and BRCA1/2 dysfunction, with growing evidence that many high-grade serous cancers actually originate in the fallopian tube epithelium. Germline BRCA1/2 testing is recommended for all incident epithelial ovarian cancers; lifetime ovarian cancer risk is roughly 39 to 63 percent for BRCA1 and 16.5 to 27 percent for BRCA2, and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing (ideally before age 40) is highly protective and also lowers subsequent breast cancer risk by about 50 percent. About 70 percent of ovarian cancer patients present at stage III; a markedly elevated serum CA-125 (shed MUC16) is characteristic but not specific, and PET is generally not required for evaluation. Bilateral ovarian masses from metastatic mucin-secreting gastrointestinal cancers are termed Krukenberg tumors; metastatic disease to the ovary also arises from colon, appendix, stomach, and breast primaries, so other malignancies must be considered in the workup. High-risk HPV infection (especially types 16 and 18, also 31, 33, 35, 52, 58) is the primary initiating event in the vast majority of invasive cervical cancers; viral E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and RB respectively, but full transformation requires additional acquired mutations over years. Cervical cancer staging is fundamentally clinical: stage I confined to cervix, stage II into upper vagina/paracervical tissue, stage III to lower vagina or pelvic sidewall, stage IV invading bladder/rectum or distant; MRI better estimates uterine and paracervical soft-tissue extension while CT detects hydronephrosis indicating sidewall disease. Endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma is the most common gynecologic malignancy in the United States; unopposed estrogen exposure is the principal risk factor, so obesity, postmenopausal estrogen therapy, estrogen-producing tumors, and tamoxifen (weakly estrogenic in uterine epithelium) all increase risk while progestins are protective. Most women with uterine corpus cancer present with postmenopausal bleeding (or atypical intermenstrual bleeding premenopausally), leading to early-stage detection and high cure rates; about 75 percent are stage I. Routine microsatellite instability (MSI) testing of all endometrial cancers is now standard, because MSI/mismatch-repair-deficient tumors that recur or present advanced are likely to respond to PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint therapy. Gestational trophoblastic disease spans benign hydatidiform mole to choriocarcinoma; complete moles are diploid with entirely paternal genetic material (uniparental disomy, no fetal development), while partial moles are triploid (egg fertilized by two sperm) and may show early fetal development. Trophoblastic disease is exquisitely chemosensitive and monitored by serial serum beta-hCG; even very advanced disease is almost uniformly curable when managed by an expert. Gardasil-9 protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; vaccination before sexual activity dramatically lowers high-risk infection and dysplasia, but vaccinated women remain at residual risk and still need Pap screening. high-grade (type 2) serous cancers begin in fallopian tube epithelium with BRCA1/2 loss and TP53 mutation producing intraepithelial cancer, then shed and disseminate across the peritoneum aided by MUC16 expression and mesothelin binding, whereas indolent type 1 cancers carry KRAS/BRAF/PTEN/PIK3CA mutations. Cervical cancer follows persistent high-risk HPV infection near the cervical transformation zone, where viral E6/E7 inactivate p53 and RB to immortalize epithelium; HPV genome integration plus APOBEC-pattern mutagenesis and further hits drive progression from dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma. Endometrial type 1 (endometrioid) cancers are driven by relative estrogen excess unopposed by progesterone, with secondary PI3K mutation or PTEN loss; type 2 (serous, clear cell) cancers show TP53 loss and behave like high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia results from outgrowth/persistence of placental trophoblast, with complete moles being androgenetic diploid tumors and partial moles triploid. Ovarian epithelial cancer 5-year survival correlates strongly with stage: roughly 90 to 95 percent stage I, 70 to 80 percent stage II, 25 to 40 percent stage III, and 10 to 15 percent stage IV; prognosis improves with lower histologic grade and BRCA1/2 germline mutation, and complete (R0) cytoreduction yields median survival beyond 60 months versus 28 to 42 months with macroscopic residual disease. Endometrial cancer is usually localized (about 75 percent stage I) with high cure; cervical cancer 5-year survival declines from about 85 percent (stage I) to roughly 7 percent (stage IV). Borderline (low malignant potential) ovarian tumors and ovarian germ cell tumors (including dysgerminoma) are highly curable. Gestational trophoblastic disease is almost uniformly curable, with single-agent therapy curing about 90 percent of low-risk cases. Staging per Table 94-1: Ovarian - I confined to ovary (88-95%), II confined to pelvic organs (70-80%), III intra-abdominal spread to omentum/diaphragm/nodes (20-40%), IV spread outside abdominal cavity/parenchymal/pleural (10-20%); most present as stage IIIC (bulky intraperitoneal or positive nodes). Endometrial - I confined to corpus (>90%), II corpus and cervix (~75%), III outside uterus but within true pelvis (45-60%), IV beyond true pelvis or bladder/rectum (~20%). Cervix - 0 carcinoma in situ (100%), I confined to uterus (85%), II beyond uterus not to pelvic wall (65%), III to pelvic wall and/or lower third vagina or hydronephrosis (35%), IV invading bladder/rectal mucosa or beyond true pelvis (7%). Gestational trophoblastic disease is risk-stratified (low/intermediate/high) by scoring algorithms guiding single- versus multiagent therapy.

liver, kidney, or thyroid disease Mistaking fatty pseudogynaecomastia for true glandular tissue and over-investigating Failing to examine the testes and missing a hormone-secreting tumour Overlooking an offending drug as the simplest reversible cause Dismissing a suspicious unilateral mass rather than excluding male breast cancer Gynaecomastia is benign proliferation of the glandular component of the male breast driven by an imbalance between stimulatory oestrogen and inhibitory androgen effects on breast epithelium. This imbalance can arise from decreased androgen production or action (hypogonadism, androgen resistance), increased oestrogen production (testicular or adrenal tumours, hCG-secreting tumours, aromatisation in obesity), or altered clearance and binding of hormones (liver disease, drugs affecting SHBG or steroid metabolism). Physiological forms in the neonate, at puberty, and with ageing reflect transient shifts in this hormonal balance. Over time, early ductal proliferation gives way to fibrosis, which is less responsive to medical treatment. Physiological and drug-related gynaecomastia often resolves once the trigger is removed or with time, particularly in early stages; long-standing fibrotic tissue tends to persist and may require surgical treatment, and prognosis in secondary cases depends on the underlying disorder.

the OAT gene encoding ornithine aminotransferase, a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that converts ornithine to glutamate semialdehyde. Enzyme deficiency causes ornithine to accumulate in plasma and tissues. Chronically raised ornithine is thought to be toxic to the retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris, producing progressive atrophy of the choroid and outer retina. The metabolic block also disturbs the urea cycle and creatine synthesis pathways. The characteristic well-circumscribed peripheral chorioretinal lesions enlarge and merge, ultimately encroaching on the macula and destroying central vision. The condition is progressive, and most patients experience severe visual impairment or blindness by middle age; dietary control of ornithine and pyridoxine supplementation in responsive individuals may slow but not fully arrest the decline.

Haemophilia — haemophilia A, haemophilia B, factor VIII deficiency, factor IX deficiency, Christmas disease, hemophilia Von Willebrand disease Other clotting factor deficiencies (e.g. factor XI) Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease Disseminated intravascular coagulation Platelet function disorders or thrombocytopenia Non-accidental injury when bruising pattern is unexplained aPTT, prothrombin time, and platelet count as initial screen Specific factor VIII and factor IX activity assays Mixing study to demonstrate factor deficiency versus inhibitor Inhibitor (Bethesda) assay when replacement therapy is failing Von Willebrand factor studies to exclude von Willebrand disease Genetic testing for carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis An X-linked recessive bleeding disorder affecting mainly males; haemophilia A results from factor VIII deficiency and haemophilia B from factor IX deficiency. The two types are clinically indistinguishable and are separated by specific factor assays. Disease severity correlates with residual factor activity: severe disease often presents with spontaneous bleeding, while milder forms bleed mainly after trauma or surgery. Hallmark manifestations are deep bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) and muscles rather than mucocutaneous bleeding. Screening typically shows a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal prothrombin time and platelet count. Recurrent joint bleeds lead to chronic synovitis and progressive haemophilic arthropathy if not prevented. Management centres on replacing the deficient clotting factor, with prophylactic regimens preventing bleeds in severe disease and on-demand treatment for acute bleeds. Development of inhibitory antibodies against the replaced factor is a major complication that reduces treatment efficacy. Intracranial haemorrhage is a life-threatening event that warrants immediate factor replacement, and newer therapies such as non-factor agents and gene therapy are changing management. Suspected intracranial haemorrhage (headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, focal signs) Bleeding into the neck, throat, or retroperitoneum threatening the airway or causing large occult loss Compartment syndrome from muscle bleeding Poor response to factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor Significant bleeding after trauma or before surgery without prophylaxis Delaying factor replacement while awaiting imaging in suspected serious bleeding Attributing bleeding solely to trauma and missing an underlying disorder Using aspirin or NSAIDs and intramuscular injections that increase bleeding risk Overlooking inhibitor development when a previously effective factor dose stops working Deficiency of factor VIII or factor IX impairs the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade, reducing generation of activated factor X and thereby the thrombin burst required for a stable fibrin clot. Primary haemostasis (platelet plug formation) is intact, so initial bleeding may stop, but the fibrin clot is inadequate and delayed or recurrent bleeding follows, characteristically into joints and muscles. Repeated haemarthroses cause iron deposition, synovial hypertrophy, and cartilage destruction leading to chronic arthropathy. With modern factor replacement and prophylaxis, life expectancy and quality of life approach normal; outcomes worsen with inhibitor development, chronic arthropathy, and delayed treatment of major bleeds.

Haemophilus and Moraxella Infections — Haemophilus influenzae infection, Hib disease, Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), Moraxella catarrhalis infection Pneumococcal pneumonia and other bacterial pneumonias (clinically indistinguishable from H. influenzae pneumonia) Bacterial meningitis due to other pathogens Acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae or M. catarrhalis For chancroid: primary syphilis, secondary syphilis (condyloma latum), genital herpes, donovanosis, lymphogranuloma venereum, and folliculitis For H. ducreyi cutaneous ulcers: yaws (Treponema pallidum subsp. pertenue) Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis) Moraxella catarrhalis vs commensal Neisseria species on respiratory culture Haemophilus haemolyticus, a respiratory commensal with identical growth requirements that can be mistaken for H. influenzae Herpes simplex virus and Treponema pallidum in genital ulcer disease Culture from a normally sterile site (blood, CSF, joint, pleural, pericardial fluid, or subdural effusion) is the most reliable means of diagnosing invasive H. influenzae and is needed for susceptibility testing Gram stain of CSF showing gram-negative coccobacilli supports Hib meningitis; predominant gram-negative coccobacilli among abundant neutrophils in sputum suggests nontypeable H. influenzae pneumonia PCR and other DNA-based detection methods, now common in clinical labs Genotypic markers (16S rRNA, superoxide dismutase, outer-membrane protein P6, protein D, fuculose kinase) and whole-genome sequencing to distinguish H. influenzae from H. haemolyticus Pneumatic otoscopy detects middle-ear fluid; tympanocentesis with culture gives etiologic diagnosis of otitis media but is not routine For chancroid: culture of H. ducreyi (requires selective/supplemented media) from the lesion or node aspirate, and PCR; dark-field exam and syphilis serology to exclude T. pallidum and HSV testing of exudate H. influenzae is a small, pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus that often stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum, so it is easily overlooked on Gram stain. Aerobic growth of H. influenzae requires both hemin (X factor) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (V factor) and needs preheated blood, so it grows on chocolate agar but not on ordinary (unheated) blood agar. Six capsular serotypes (a-f) exist plus unencapsulated nontypeable strains; type b (Hib) and nontypeable strains are the most clinically important, with Hib being invasive (hematogenous spread) and nontypeable being primarily mucosal pathogens. Maternally acquired anticapsular (anti-PRP) antibody declines from birth to about 6 months; the antibody nadir corresponds to the peak age of type b disease, and systemic Hib disease is unusual after age 6 owing to acquired protective antibody. Hib meningitis primarily affects children under 2 years; subdural effusion is the most common complication and should be suspected when seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation follow 2-3 days of appropriate therapy. Hib epiglottitis is a life-threatening cellulitis of the epiglottis and supraglottic tissues occurring in an older age group (2-7 years) than other Hib infections; in countries with childhood Hib vaccination it now occurs mainly in adults. Nontypeable H. influenzae is the most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations and, in recent years, has caused community-acquired pneumonia more frequently than S. pneumoniae. Nontypeable H. influenzae is one of the three most common causes of childhood otitis media (with S. pneumoniae and M. catarrhalis); clinical clues include recurrent episodes, treatment failure, concomitant conjunctivitis, and bilateral disease. Invasive nontypeable strains causing neonatal/puerperal sepsis after colonizing the female genital tract have been provisionally named Haemophilus quentini (related to but distinct from H. haemolyticus). Moraxella catarrhalis is an unencapsulated gram-negative diplococcus of the respiratory tract; its colonies can be slid intact across the agar surface (the hockey puck sign) and turn pink after 48 h, distinguishing them from commensal Neisseria. M. catarrhalis is the second most common bacterial cause of COPD exacerbations after H. influenzae and accounts for roughly 15-20 percent of acute otitis media cases by middle-ear culture (30-50 percent by molecular detection). Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer disease; prior chancroid does not confer protection, and H. ducreyi is also an important cause of non-sexually transmitted cutaneous ulcers in children in the South Pacific and Africa. Sore throat and fever rapidly progressing to dysphagia, drooling, and airway obstruction (epiglottitis) - a medical emergency requiring airway maintenance Fever with altered CNS function and nuchal rigidity (which may be absent) in a young child suggesting Hib meningitis Seizures, hemiparesis, or persistent obtundation after 2-3 days of appropriate antibiotics, suggesting subdural effusion Underlying immunosuppression, HIV, cardiopulmonary disease, alcoholism, or cancer in a patient with H. influenzae bacteremia H. influenzae may be missed on Gram stain because it stains only faintly with safranin in CSF and sputum. Ordinary (unheated) blood agar fails to grow H. influenzae, which can lead to false-negative cultures if chocolate agar is not used. Distinguishing H. influenzae from the commensal H. haemolyticus is difficult because they share growth requirements and many H. haemolyticus isolates are now nonhemolytic. M. catarrhalis has historically been overlooked as a pathogen because its colonies resemble those of commensal Neisseria species on respiratory cultures. Approximately 30-40 percent of nontypeable H. influenzae produce beta-lactamase (conferring ampicillin/amoxicillin resistance), and a second mechanism, altered penicillin-binding proteins (beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant strains), is increasing in Europe and common in Japan. Over 90 percent of M. catarrhalis strains now produce beta-lactamase and are resistant to amoxicillin; macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance is emerging, notably in Asia. Clinical diagnosis of chancroid is often inaccurate, so laboratory confirmation should be attempted; in HIV-positive patients apparent treatment failure may reflect HSV co-infection. Isolation of M. catarrhalis from expectorated sputum during an exacerbation is suggestive but not diagnostic of it as the cause. Hib strains produce systemic disease by invading the respiratory mucosa and spreading hematogenously to distant sites such as meninges, bones, and joints; the type b polysaccharide capsule (ribosyl-ribitol phosphate) is a key virulence factor that resists opsonization. Nontypeable strains lack a capsule and cause disease by local mucosal invasion (e.g., otitis media via the eustachian tube, lower respiratory infection in COPD), persisting in airways both extracellularly and intracellularly and forming biofilms in the middle ear that resist host clearance and antibiotics; they vary expression of virulence genes by slipped-strand mispairing and phase-variable DNA methylases. M. catarrhalis colonizes the upper airway and infects by contiguous spread, often following a viral upper respiratory infection (e.g., rhinovirus promotes adhesion); it uses multiple adhesins, invades several cell types with an intracellular lymphoid reservoir, and sheds outer-membrane vesicles that deliver beta-lactamase and induce inflammation, potentially protecting co-pathogens such as group A streptococci and H. influenzae. H. ducreyi infects through an epithelial break during sexual contact, producing ulcers with predominantly T-cell infiltrate. The overall mortality of Hib meningitis is about 5 percent with a high morbidity rate; about 6 percent of survivors have permanent sensorineural hearing loss, roughly one-fourth have a significant disability, and up to half have some neurologic sequela such as partial hearing loss or delayed language development when sought carefully. Hib epiglottitis is life-threatening due to risk of acute upper-airway obstruction. Glucocorticoids reduce the incidence of neurologic sequelae in Hib meningitis. Nontypeable strains tend to cause recurrent otitis media and recurrent COPD exacerbations because immunity is strain-specific. M. catarrhalis otitis media and exacerbations are clinically milder (less fever, less red bulging tympanic membrane) than pneumococcal disease, and invasive M. catarrhalis infection is rare. Repeated H. ducreyi infections can occur because infection confers no protection; in HIV-positive patients chancroid healing may be slow and require longer therapy.

Hailey-Hailey disease — ATP2C1, benign familial pemphigus, familial benign chronic pemphigus, HHD Darier disease Intertrigo (candidal or bacterial) Inverse psoriasis Pemphigus vegetans Contact dermatitis of the flexures Extramammary Paget disease (persistent unilateral plaque) Skin biopsy showing extensive suprabasal acantholysis ('dilapidated brick wall') Direct immunofluorescence (negative, to exclude pemphigus) ATP2C1 molecular genetic testing Bacterial, fungal, and viral swabs during flares to identify superinfection Family history assessment for dominant inheritance Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP2C1, encoding a Golgi calcium/manganese pump (SPCA1) Presents in early adulthood with recurrent flaccid vesicles, erosions, and macerated fissured plaques in the flexures (axillae, groin, neck, inframammary folds) Lesions have a characteristic macerated appearance with painful longitudinal 'ripped-fabric' fissures Friction, sweating, heat, and secondary infection are major aggravating factors Unlike pemphigus it is not autoimmune; direct immunofluorescence is negative Histology shows widespread suprabasal acantholysis giving a 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance Secondary bacterial, candidal, or herpetic infection frequently drives flares and malodour Sudden painful vesicular flare suggesting herpes simplex superinfection Spreading cellulitis or systemic features from bacterial superinfection A persistent, non-healing, or indurated plaque raising concern for squamous carcinoma within chronic lesions Diagnosing recurrent intertrigo or candidiasis and missing the underlying genodermatosis Failing to look for and treat secondary herpetic or bacterial infection during flares Confusing it with autoimmune pemphigus and initiating inappropriate immunosuppression Overlooking rare squamous change in longstanding lesions Hailey-Hailey disease is caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP2C1, encoding SPCA1, a pump that transports calcium and manganese into the Golgi apparatus of keratinocytes. Disturbed intracellular calcium homeostasis impairs the processing and trafficking of proteins needed for desmosomal adhesion, weakening keratinocyte cohesion. The resulting acantholysis is most pronounced in flexural skin subjected to heat, sweat, and friction, which further stress the fragile epidermis. The defect is partial and mosaic in effect, which is why lesions are localised to intertriginous sites rather than generalised. It is a chronic relapsing condition with a benign course that does not affect life expectancy, but recurrent flexural erosions can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms often improve in later life and some patients respond well to measures reducing friction and infection.

antibiotics have no role Poor oral intake from painful mouth ulcers is the commonest reason for medical attention and can lead to dehydration in small children Diagnosis is usually clinical, with PCR or viral culture reserved for severe or atypical cases Good hand hygiene and exclusion of unwell children help limit institutional spread Lethargy, persistent vomiting, ataxia or myoclonic jerks suggesting Enterovirus 71 neurological involvement Signs of severe dehydration from inability to drink Respiratory distress or circulatory collapse indicating brainstem/cardiopulmonary complications Seizures or rapidly declining consciousness Prescribing antibiotics for what is a self-limiting viral illness Underestimating dehydration risk from painful oral ulcers in toddlers Missing early neurological warning signs of Enterovirus 71 disease Confusing severe or atypical rashes with drug reactions or varicella Non-polio enteroviruses (notably Coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71) enter via the gastrointestinal or respiratory tract, replicate in lymphoid tissue of the pharynx and gut, and produce a viraemia that seeds the skin and oral mucosa, giving the characteristic vesicular enanthem and exanthem. Enterovirus 71 has neurotropic potential and can invade the central nervous system, particularly the brainstem, producing the severe neurological syndromes and, rarely, neurogenic pulmonary oedema and cardiorespiratory collapse. The overwhelming majority of cases resolve within a week to ten days without sequelae. A small subset, particularly Enterovirus 71 infections in young children, develop serious neurological or cardiopulmonary complications that can be fatal or leave lasting deficits.

systemic sepsis suggesting necrotising infection Deep palmar space abscess or infection tracking proximally along fascial planes Signs of tissue necrosis or compartment involvement Underestimating a fight bite and closing or under-treating a wound that has penetrated the joint Incising a herpetic whitlow, which worsens the viral infection Delaying surgical drainage of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis while relying on antibiotics alone Missing a retained foreign body as the source of persistent infection Failing to elevate and splint, leading to persistent oedema and stiffness Overlooking gout or crystal arthropathy masquerading as infection Hand infections usually follow inoculation of bacteria through a break in the skin from trauma, bites, splinters, or nail-care injury. The hand's compartmentalised anatomy - closed pulp spaces, synovial flexor sheaths, web spaces, and deep palmar spaces - confines infection under pressure and allows it to track along defined planes. Rising pressure within closed spaces impairs perfusion and can cause tissue and tendon necrosis. In pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, pus within the closed synovial sheath compromises the gliding surface and blood supply of the flexor tendon, leading to adhesions and stiffness if not decompressed. Bite wounds introduce mixed oral flora deep into tissues and joints. Superficial infections such as early paronychia treated promptly usually resolve fully. Deep and closed-space infections carry a higher risk of stiffness, contracture, and functional loss, and outcome is closely tied to how quickly drainage and appropriate antibiotics are provided. Untreated flexor sheath and deep space infections can lead to tendon necrosis, amputation, or long-term disability.

Hantavirus infection — hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, HPS, haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, HFRS, VHF Leptospirosis Severe dengue Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (CCHF, Lassa) Bacterial sepsis with ARDS Severe atypical or community-acquired pneumonia Acute glomerulonephritis or other causes of acute kidney injury (for HFRS) Leptospirosis Severe dengue Bacterial sepsis / ARDS Other viral haemorrhagic fevers Hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG serology, which is usually positive by the time of severe illness RT-PCR for viral RNA in early disease and for genotyping Full blood count (looking for haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, immunoblasts) and renal function Chest imaging showing bilateral infiltrates and pulmonary oedema in the pulmonary syndrome Exclusion of leptospirosis, dengue, and bacterial sepsis given overlap Rodent-borne viruses acquired mainly by inhaling aerosolised excreta (urine, droppings, saliva) of infected rodents, with exposure often occurring in rural, agricultural, or rodent-infested settings Two main clinical syndromes exist: hantavirus pulmonary (cardiopulmonary) syndrome, seen chiefly in the Americas, and haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, seen across Eurasia The pulmonary syndrome begins with a febrile prodrome of fever and myalgia, then progresses rapidly to a cardiopulmonary phase with capillary leak, pulmonary oedema, and shock Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome evolves through febrile, hypotensive, oliguric, and later polyuric phases, with bleeding tendency and acute kidney injury Haemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, and the presence of immunoblasts on the blood film are helpful early clues to the pulmonary syndrome Because these are viral haemorrhagic fevers, suspected cases warrant infection-control caution, isolation, and safe specimen handling, though person-to-person spread is limited for most strains Care is supportive with meticulous fluid and haemodynamic management and organ support; there is no widely available specific antiviral, so early recognition and referral to intensive care are vital Rapid onset of dyspnoea, hypoxia, and pulmonary oedema signalling the cardiopulmonary phase Hypotension or shock with rising haematocrit from capillary leak Oliguria, rising creatinine, and bleeding indicating severe renal syndrome Any suspected viral haemorrhagic fever requires isolation, barrier precautions, and public health notification Aggressive fluid resuscitation worsening pulmonary oedema in the cardiopulmonary phase Missing rodent-exposure history in an acutely breathless or febrile patient Confusing the illness with community-acquired pneumonia and delaying intensive supportive care Underestimating the polyuric recovery phase and precipitating dehydration or electrolyte disturbance in HFRS Hantaviruses are enveloped RNA viruses that infect vascular endothelial cells, particularly in the lungs and kidneys, without causing marked direct cell destruction. Instead, the host immune and cytokine response increases capillary permeability. In the pulmonary syndrome this produces non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and cardiovascular collapse, whereas in haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome the leaky vasculature and renal microvascular injury drive haemorrhage, hypotension, and acute kidney injury with the characteristic sequence of oliguric and polyuric phases. Outcome depends on syndrome and speed of supportive care: the cardiopulmonary syndrome can be rapidly fatal despite intensive care, whereas most patients with haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome recover renal function, though severe strains carry appreciable mortality.

variants in ABCA12, a lipid transporter essential for lamellar granule function Neonates are encased in thick, plate-like armoured scale separated by deep erythematous fissures Severe ectropion, eclabium, flattened ears, and constricting bands on digits are characteristic The rigid encasing membrane restricts chest expansion and feeding and predisposes to constriction ischaemia of extremities Barrier failure causes profound transepidermal water loss, hypernatraemic dehydration, temperature instability, and high infection risk Early systemic retinoid therapy has substantially improved survival when combined with intensive neonatal supportive care Survivors typically transition to a severe erythrodermic ichthyosis phenotype resembling congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma Respiratory compromise from restricted chest wall movement Hypernatraemic dehydration and thermoregulatory collapse Digital or limb ischaemia from constricting bands Overwhelming neonatal sepsis Delaying transfer to neonatal intensive care and delaying consideration of systemic retinoids Underestimating fluid and electrolyte losses through the defective barrier Missing digital constriction bands that threaten limb viability Neglecting corneal protection in the presence of severe ectropion Harlequin ichthyosis is caused by loss of function of ABCA12, an ATP-binding cassette transporter that loads lipids into lamellar granules within keratinocytes. Without functional ABCA12, lipids cannot be delivered to the extracellular space of the stratum corneum, so the lamellar lipid bilayers that normally provide the epidermal permeability barrier fail to form. The result is grossly abnormal cornification with massive hyperkeratosis, a rigid non-pliable scale, and a catastrophically leaky barrier. This produces extreme transepidermal water loss and impaired thermoregulation and defence against infection from birth. Historically usually fatal in the neonatal period, but with modern neonatal intensive care and early systemic retinoid therapy a majority of infants now survive, transitioning to a chronic severe ichthyosis with lifelong skin and ocular problems.

Head and Neck Cancer — head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, HNSCC Carcinoma of unknown primary presenting as cervical adenopathy without an identifiable mucosal lesion Lymphoma presenting as cervical adenopathy Salivary gland tumors (mucoepidermoid, adenoid cystic carcinoma, adenocarcinoma) Sarcoma, including radiation therapy-induced sarcoma after prior radiotherapy Metastasis to supraclavicular nodes from a primary site in the chest or abdomen Thorough otolaryngologic examination including inspection of all visible mucosal surfaces and palpation of the floor of mouth, tongue, and neck CT or MRI of the head and neck to define disease extent (comparably accurate, 65-90%, for cervical nodal metastases) CT of chest and upper abdomen for patients with lymph node involvement to screen for distant metastases; chest CT also screens for second lung primary in heavy smokers PET scan to identify or exclude distant metastases and assess treatment response Endoscopic examination under anesthesia (panendoscopy) with multiple biopsies Fine-needle aspiration or excisional lymph node biopsy when no primary is visible HPV testing of oropharyngeal tumors at diagnosis; EBV antibody titers / plasma EBV DNA for nasopharyngeal cancer screening TNM staging per AJCC (varies by anatomic subsite) Premalignant mucosal lesions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) representing hyperplasia, dysplasia, or carcinoma in situ Most head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the mucosal surfaces of the paranasal sinuses, oral cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx (Harrison 22e p.610). Alcohol and tobacco are the most significant environmental risk factors and act synergistically when used together; smokeless tobacco is an etiologic agent for oral cancers (Harrison 22e p.610). In Western countries, HPV (predominantly HPV-16) causes over 50% of oropharyngeal cancers (tonsillar bed and base of tongue); these occur in younger patients and carry a better prognosis, especially in nonsmokers (Harrison 22e p.610-611). EBV infection is frequently associated with nasopharyngeal cancer, especially in endemic areas (East Asia, some Mediterranean countries); EBV antibody titers can be used to screen high-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.610). HPV testing should be performed at diagnosis for all patients with oropharyngeal tumors; HPV-related disease has a more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging (advanced nodal stage can still be equivalent to overall early stage) (Harrison 22e p.611-613). Panendoscopy under anesthesia (laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy) with multiple directed biopsies is the definitive staging procedure to establish diagnosis, define extent, and identify second primaries (Harrison 22e p.611). When a head and neck lesion treated initially with antibiotics does not resolve in a short period, further workup is indicated; simply continuing antibiotics may lose the chance for early diagnosis of a malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611). For an enlarged cervical node with no visible primary, diagnose by fine-needle aspiration or lymph node excision; if squamous cell carcinoma, perform panendoscopy with directed biopsies of nasopharynx, tonsil, tongue base, and pyriform sinus (Harrison 22e p.611-612). Most parotid tumors are benign, but about half of submandibular and sublingual tumors and most minor salivary gland tumors are malignant; adenoid cystic carcinoma tends to recur along nerve tracks and metastasize as late as 10-20 years (Harrison 22e p.610-611, 613). Persistent hoarseness requiring referral for indirect laryngoscopy and/or radiographic studies (possible early laryngeal cancer) Non-healing ulcer of the oral cavity Persistent neck mass / cervical lymphadenopathy, especially a solitary, hard, nontender node in an older chronic tobacco user Dysphagia, odynophagia, or decreased tongue mobility Sore throat and/or otalgia, or a head/neck lesion that does not resolve after antibiotics Unilateral serous otitis media, nasal obstruction, or epistaxis (nasopharyngeal cancer); cranial neuropathies from skull base involvement Head and neck symptoms persisting longer than 2-4 weeks Continuing antibiotic treatment for a non-resolving head and neck lesion rather than pursuing workup may delay diagnosis of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611). Fine-needle aspiration should not be the first diagnostic procedure for a suspicious cervical node when a head and neck primary is suspected; perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first (Harrison 22e p.4012-type cross-reference, p.611). EGFR overexpression does not reliably predict response to EGFR inhibitors (active in only ~10-15% as single agents); substituting cetuximab for cisplatin in HPV-related cancers has shown inferior survival (Harrison 22e p.611, 613). Retinoid supplements (e.g., cis-retinoic acid) have not been shown to prevent head and neck (or lung) cancer and may increase risk in active smokers (Harrison 22e p.610). About 50% of patients develop hypothyroidism after treatment; thyroid function should be monitored (Harrison 22e p.613). Squamous cell carcinomas arise from the mucosal surfaces of the upper aerodigestive tract. The entire pharyngeal mucosa is exposed to alcohol- and tobacco-related carcinogens, producing field cancerization with risk of premalignant lesions (erythroplakia, leukoplakia) progressing through hyperplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ to invasive carcinoma. In HPV-negative tumors, p53 mutations are frequent along with mitotic-signaling and Notch pathway alterations and dysregulated cell-cycle control. HPV oncogenes drive carcinogenesis by directly inhibiting the p53 and RB tumor-suppressor genes; HPV-positive tumors carry a distinct mutational signature with frequent PI3K pathway alteration. EGFR is frequently overexpressed and correlates with poor prognosis. EBV is associated with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (lymphoepithelioma) (Harrison 22e p.610-611). Poorly differentiated tumors have a worse prognosis than well-differentiated tumors. Overt distant metastases are present in <10% at diagnosis. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers consistently carry a better prognosis (reflected in a separate, more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging system), especially in nonsmokers. For localized disease (about one-third of patients), overall 5-year survival is 60-90%, with most recurrences occurring within the first 2 years and usually local. For locally/regionally advanced disease (>50% of patients at presentation), 5-year survival exceeds 50% in many trials (partly due to the increasing fraction of HPV-related tumors); advanced nasopharyngeal cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by concomitant chemoradiotherapy has achieved 5-year survival exceeding 80% in a Southeast Asian study. Patients cured of early-stage tobacco/alcohol-related disease are at greater risk of dying from a second malignancy than from recurrence of the primary (Harrison 22e p.611-613). Clinically categorized into three groups: (1) localized disease (T1-T2 / stage I-II without nodal or distant spread), (2) locally or regionally advanced disease (large primary and/or cervical nodal metastases, lymph-node positive), and (3) recurrent and/or metastatic disease below the neck. Staged by the AJCC TNM system, which varies by anatomic subsite: primary tumors T1-T3 by increasing size with T4 representing invasion of adjacent structures (bone, muscle, root of tongue), and nodes staged by size, number, and laterality. A separate, more favorable staging system applies to HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer in the AJCC 8th edition (Harrison 22e p.611-613).

Acute heart failure / pulmonary edema — CXR BNP/NT-proBNP ECG, troponin Echocardiogram Address precipitant; not an infection Chronic lung disease (orthopnoea and nocturnal dyspnoea can mimic HF; relieved by coughing/expectoration rather than sitting upright) (p.1986) Pulmonary arterial hypertension (p.1986) Neuromuscular disease causing dyspnoea (p.1986) Anaemia / iron-deficiency anaemia (p.1986) Venous insufficiency, lymphoedema or obesity as non-cardiac causes of leg oedema (p.1986) Nephrotic syndrome and deep vein thrombosis (causes of oedema) (p.1986) Hepatic cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis, malignant carcinomatosis (causes of ascites) (p.1986) Constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion or superior vena cava syndrome (causes of jugular venous distension) (p.1986) Low-grade fever from cytokine activation may occur in severe HF and resolves once compensation is restored, mimicking infection (p.1983) Congestive hepatomegaly with raised transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin can be misread as biliary tract disease (p.1983) Chronic lower-limb oedema in HF may become weeping or progress to cellulitis (p.1984) Comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood count, coagulation studies and urinalysis as baseline; targeted testing for diabetes, lipids and thyroid function (p.1984) Serum sodium and potassium (hyponatraemia is an adverse prognostic marker; hypo-/hyperkalaemia predispose to arrhythmia) (p.1984) Renal function (urea/creatinine, consider cystatin C which is less affected by muscle mass) (p.1984-1986) Iron studies/ferritin to detect iron deficiency (with or without anaemia) (p.1985) Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging for tissue characterisation and aetiology (ischaemic, myocarditis, amyloidosis, haemochromatosis) (p.1985) Cardiac CT / coronary CT angiography to exclude pericardial disease, apical thrombus or obstructive CAD when CMR not feasible (p.1985) Cardiac PET for ischaemia/viability and to assess cardiac sarcoid inflammation (p.1985) Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope) for prognosis and transplant/MCS evaluation (p.1985) Transoesophageal echocardiography or contrast cardiac CT to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion (p.1985) Right-heart catheterisation / pulmonary artery catheter to distinguish cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and guide therapy in severe HF (p.1985) Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases (suspected myocarditis - lymphocytic, eosinophilic, sarcoid or giant cell - amyloidosis, or allograft rejection) (p.1985) Newer biomarkers galectin-3 and soluble ST2 are approved for prognosis but not widely used (p.1985) Acute respiratory distress syndrome and other non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (p.1986) Acute or chronic kidney disease causing salt/water retention with normal cardiac structure and function (p.1986) Restrictive cardiomyopathy versus constrictive pericarditis (distinguished by simultaneous right- and left-heart filling pressures) (p.1985) Reactive airways disease/bronchial asthma versus cardiac asthma (cardiac asthma more often shows diaphoresis and cyanosis) (p.1986) HF is a clinical syndrome, not a single disease; it is the common final pathway for most chronic cardiovascular conditions, especially hypertension, coronary artery disease and valvular disease (p.1975). About half of patients with HF have a reduced ejection fraction and half have a near-normal/preserved EF, so a normal LVEF does not exclude HF (p.1977). The signs and symptoms of HF are neither specific nor sensitive, so a high index of suspicion is needed in higher-risk patients (older, with hypertension, diabetes or CKD) (p.1984). NYHA functional class correlates poorly with objective measures such as LV size, EF or peak oxygen consumption (p.1982). An S3 gallop usually accompanies volume overload and tachycardia, suggests significant haemodynamic compromise and carries adverse prognostic weight; an S4 is non-specific and may be heard in HFpEF from hypertension (p.1984). Bendopnea (breathlessness on bending forward, e.g. tying shoes) reflects raised filling pressure, particularly with low cardiac output (p.1982). Holosystolic murmurs of mitral/tricuspid regurgitation often appear in advanced HF even when the valves are structurally normal (functional/secondary regurgitation) (p.1984). In acute or younger chronic HF patients, leg oedema may be absent despite marked systemic venous hypertension (p.1984). A very low BNP/NT-proBNP can help exclude HF as the cause of dyspnoea in non-obese patients (p.1985-1986). The obesity paradox: obese HF patients tend to have a more favourable prognosis than those with low or normal BMI (p.1986). Acute pulmonary oedema with pink frothy sputum reflects marked elevation of pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (p.1982) Hypotension with narrow pulse pressure and a rapid, thready pulse indicates severe HF; pulsus alternans signals severely depressed LV function (p.1983) Cool extremities, peripheral cyanosis, mental dullness/confusion and oliguria suggest low-output/advanced-stage HF (p.1982-1983) Marked elevation of transaminases and lactic acid suggests cardiogenic shock with severe low output (p.1984) Cardiac cachexia (unintentional oedema-free weight loss >5% over 12 months) marks longstanding severe HF (p.1983) An S3 gallop carries negative prognostic significance (p.1984) Cheyne-Stokes/periodic breathing and central sleep apnoea are features of advanced HF (p.1983) Abandon the old terms systolic and diastolic HF: most HF patients, regardless of EF, have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities (p.1977) BNP/NT-proBNP may be falsely low in obesity and falsely elevated by age, female sex, CKD, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism and pulmonary hypertension, so interpret in context (p.1985-1986) Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, uric acid) are non-specific and do not establish the diagnosis of HF (p.1984) Congestive hepatopathy and gut-wall oedema can be mistaken for primary biliary or bowel disease (p.1983) Distinguishing cardiac from pulmonary dyspnoea may be impossible when both coexist (common in older smokers); post-diuresis pulmonary function tests or cardiopulmonary exercise testing can help (p.1986) Failure to identify and correct a precipitant can leave HF persistent despite adequate treatment; a precipitant is identifiable in 50-90% of admissions (p.1983) Nonpitting oedema unresponsive to escalating diuretics may be lymphoedema, not HF (p.1984) High-output HF (anaemia, thyrotoxicosis, AV shunt, cirrhosis, severe obesity, beriberi) will be missed if not actively considered in predisposed patients (p.1978, p.1982) HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index injury (e.g. acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months-to-years of structural and functional cardiovascular remodelling; patients may stay asymptomatic for long periods because compensatory mechanisms are activated that ultimately drive further deterioration. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric (dilated) hypertrophy, accompanied by myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, apoptosis and re-expression of fetal genes. Sustained activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but becomes maladaptive, causing excessive vasoconstriction, sodium/water retention, electrolyte and renal disturbance, direct myocardial toxicity and arrhythmias; counter-regulatory natriuretic peptides, prostaglandins, bradykinin and nitric oxide are upregulated but inadequate. Therapies that antagonise RAAS and the sympathetic system (RAAS inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, beta blockers) attenuate or reverse remodelling and improve outcomes. Secondary mitral regurgitation arises from ventricular dilatation, sphericity and annular changes, perpetuating a vicious cycle. HFpEF reflects multiple mechanisms beyond diastolic dysfunction (impaired calcium reuptake, vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, inflammation related to adiposity, oxidative/nitrosative stress, insulin resistance). The cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by low forward flow but importantly by systemic venous congestion and raised intra-abdominal/splanchnic pressure, so relief of congestion improves renal function (p.1977-1982). Overall 5-year survival after a HF diagnosis is roughly 50%, and in severe HF 1-year mortality may reach 40%; one in eight U.S. deaths lists HF on the certificate, most dying of progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. After a HF admission, mortality runs from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, CKD, CAD, advanced NYHA class, a third heart sound or raised JVP, reduced LV (or RV) EF, secondary mitral/tricuspid regurgitation, raised wedge pressure, pulmonary hypertension, low peak VO2, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, worsening renal function, raised troponin/natriuretic peptides and neurohormones, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmia. HFrecEF (recovered EF) generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF, but withdrawing therapy can cause relapse in up to half within 6 months (p.1976-1977). HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF phenotype by EF: reduced EF (HFrEF) <=40%, mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) 41-49%, preserved EF (HFpEF) >=50%; LVEF >=50% is considered normal systolic function (p.1977-1978, p.1984). NYHA functional class I-IV grades symptoms by the activity that provokes them: class I none with ordinary activity, class II mild symptoms on ordinary exertion, class III symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity, class IV symptoms (or angina) at rest worsening with any activity (p.1982). ACC/AHA stages describe disease progression: stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction, stage C symptomatic HF, stage D advanced/refractory HF with high mortality where transplant or mechanical circulatory support may be considered (p.1987). Killip classification (originally for acute MI) grades pump failure: class I no congestion; class II basal rales, S3 or right-heart congestion; class III pulmonary oedema; class IV cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg with peripheral vasoconstriction, cyanosis, confusion, oliguria) - historically rising mortality from class I to IV (p.2247).

levels may be falsely low in obesity and raised by age, female sex, CKD, atrial fibrillation, PE, and pulmonary hypertension Cardiac MRI for ventricular mass/volumes/function and tissue characterization (ischemic cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, amyloidosis, hemochromatosis) Cardiac CT / coronary CT angiography to exclude obstructive coronary disease or evaluate pericardium and apical thrombus Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope) for prognosis and transplant/MCS evaluation Coronary angiography to exclude reversible ischemic cause; right heart catheterization/pulmonary artery catheter for filling pressures and cardiac output in unstable patients Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases (giant cell, eosinophilic, lymphocytic or sarcoid myocarditis, amyloidosis, allograft rejection) Comprehensive metabolic panel, CBC, coagulation, urinalysis, thyroid function; iron studies for iron deficiency with or without anemia Bronchial asthma or COPD (cardiac asthma can mimic reactive airways disease) Biliary tract disease (right HF with hepatic congestion causes RUQ pain and abnormal liver function tests) Cellulitis arising from chronic dependent edema versus primary skin/soft-tissue infection Cardiac cirrhosis with ascites mimicking primary liver failure Management is driven by clinical phenotype and by left ventricular ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%); the older terms systolic and diastolic heart failure have been abandoned because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.1987, 1978). The disease is staged along the ACC/AHA framework: stage A (at risk), stage B (asymptomatic structural/ventricular dysfunction), stage C (symptomatic HF), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF); approach to therapy escalates across these stages (Harrison 22e p.1987). Stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction is treated to facilitate ventricular recovery and prevent progression to clinical HF, whereas stage D carries a high risk of death from sudden death or end-stage pump failure and may prompt consideration of transplant, mechanical circulatory support, or palliative care (Harrison 22e p.1987). The robust randomized-trial evidence base supporting disease-modifying therapy applies to HFrEF (LVEF <=40%); historically HFmrEF and HFpEF management was symptom-focused owing to lack of outcome-improving therapies (Harrison 22e p.1987). Even with effective therapy, patients across all EF categories remain at risk for clinical deterioration, typically from progressive sodium and fluid retention that drives congestive symptoms and acute decompensated HF (Harrison 22e p.1987). Trials of agents that improve outcomes in HFrEF (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, digoxin, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) have generally been unsuccessful when exported to HFpEF, with several large trials showing reduced HF hospitalizations but no all-cause mortality benefit (Harrison 22e p.1987-1988). Management of HFpEF has centered on lifestyle modification, control of congestion, rhythm stabilization (especially atrial fibrillation), blood pressure control to guideline targets, and treatment of comorbidities such as obesity, obstructive lung disease, sleep apnea, diabetes/insulin resistance, anemia, iron deficiency, and chronic kidney disease (Harrison 22e p.1987). A favorable signal for spironolactone in HFpEF emerged mainly from the subgroup randomized in the Americas in the TOPCAT trial, supporting only a weak guideline recommendation in selected patients at low risk for hyperkalemia and worsening renal function (Harrison 22e p.1988). The microvascular endothelial inflammation paradigm proposes that comorbidity-driven inflammation impairs nitric oxide signaling and increases myocardial stiffness in HFpEF; trials enhancing NO bioavailability (sildenafil in RELAX, nitrates in NEAT-HFpEF, inorganic nitrite in INDIE-HFpEF) failed to improve functional capacity or quality of life (Harrison 22e p.1988-1989). Approximately one-half of patients with HF have reduced EF and one-half have preserved or mildly reduced EF; classifying by EF matters because of differences in demographics, comorbidities, and treatment response (Harrison 22e p.1978). Acute heart failure (formerly acute decompensated HF) refers to rapid onset or worsening of symptoms; most episodes are decompensations of chronic HF, but roughly 20% are new-onset, occurring with acute coronary syndrome, acute valvular dysfunction, hypertensive urgency, or postcardiotomy syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1976). HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF) is a subgroup whose EF normalizes on therapy; predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of disease-modifying therapy can cause recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1977). Right HF with hepatic congestion can elevate transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin and be misdiagnosed as biliary tract disease (Harrison 22e p.1984).
