NYHA functional class correlates poorly with objective measures of cardiac structure (LV size, EF) and function (peak VO2) (Harrison 22e p.1982). Natriuretic peptide levels may be falsely low in obesity and elevated by noncardiac factors (age, female sex, CKD) and other cardiac conditions, limiting interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1985). Lower extremity edema may be absent in acute HF or in younger adults despite marked systemic venous hypertension; unilateral edema suggests DVT, prior trauma, or vein harvest rather than HF (Harrison 22e p.1984). Drugs causing salt/water retention (NSAIDs) or negative inotropy (calcium channel blockers) can precipitate decompensation and should be recognized as provider-related triggers (Harrison 22e p.1983). Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, RAAS inhibitors, and potassium supplements can cause hyperkalemia, particularly with reduced GFR, requiring monitoring (Harrison 22e p.1984-1985). HFrEF is a progressive disorder in which an index event (acute myocardial infarction, chronic pressure or volume overload, inherited or congenital disease) is followed by months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Concentric hypertrophy reduces wall stress in pressure overload, while eccentric hypertrophy (chamber dilation) occurs in volume overload; remodeling involves myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium handling, fetal gene reexpression, necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy. Maladaptive activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but ultimately produces excessive vasoconstriction, volume retention, electrolyte and renal abnormalities, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, and arrhythmias, with antagonism of these systems shown to attenuate or reverse remodeling and reduce mortality. Counterregulatory vasodilatory hormones (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated; neprilysin inactivates natriuretic peptides and bradykinin, the rationale for angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling, and the cardiorenal syndrome reflects both reduced forward flow and systemic venous/abdominal congestion. HFpEF pathophysiology is less defined and involves diastolic dysfunction together with vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, comorbidity-driven microvascular inflammation, and impaired nitric oxide/cGMP/protein kinase G signaling causing myocardial stiffening (Harrison 22e p.1978-1982, 1989). Overall 5-year survival after a primary-care diagnosis of HF is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. After an HF admission, mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission rates of 20-25% at 60 days approaching 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive pump failure or sudden cardiac death. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, presence of an S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV ejection fraction, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index, reduced peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, raised neurohormones, tachycardia, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular ectopy. Black patients have higher case-fatality rates and there is regional variation (highest in the US Midwest and rural areas). HFrecEF generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with guideline-directed therapy and risk-factor control (Harrison 22e p.1976-1977). Two complementary frameworks are used. The NYHA functional classification grades symptom-limiting activity: class I (no limitation), class II (mild; symptoms with ordinary activity), class III (moderate; symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity), and class IV (severe; symptoms at rest worsening with any activity). The ACC/AHA staging is progressive and irreversible: stage A (at risk, no structural disease or symptoms), stage B (structural disease/asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction without symptoms), stage C (structural disease with current or prior symptoms), and stage D (advanced/refractory HF requiring specialized interventions). Patients are additionally phenotyped by ejection fraction: HFrEF (LVEF <=40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), and HFpEF (>=50%) (Harrison 22e p.1982-1983, 1987).

speckle-tracking strain imaging for prognosis Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) for diagnosis, severity, and prognosis Cardiac MRI for etiology and tissue characterization; cardiac CT/coronary CT angiography when MRI contraindicated; combined right/left heart catheterization to distinguish restriction from constriction) Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases (myocarditis, amyloidosis, chemotherapy/immunotherapy injury, transplant rejection) Targeted etiologic screening: hemochromatosis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis; serum free light chains/SPEP, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, ANA, RF, hepatitis C, HIV; three-generation family history and genetic testing for inherited cardiomyopathy Pulmonary embolism (precipitant and elevates BNP) Pulmonary arterial hypertension and right HF Lymphedema (nonpitting edema unresponsive to diuretics) Deep venous thrombosis (unilateral leg edema) Cirrhosis or primary liver failure (ascites) Cardiac amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis (infiltrative mimics) Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs arising from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection; it is the common final pathway for most chronic cardiovascular diseases including hypertension, coronary artery disease, and valvular disease (p.1975). Roughly half of patients with HF have reduced ejection fraction (EF less than or equal to 40%, HFrEF) and about half have preserved (greater than or equal to 50%, HFpEF) or mildly reduced (41-49%, HFmrEF) EF; because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities, the older terms 'systolic' and 'diastolic' heart failure have been abandoned (p.1977). An EF that recovers to normal on guideline-directed therapy defines HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF); predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of therapy can cause symptom and EF recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (p.1977). Dyspnea progresses in severity as exertional dyspnea, then orthopnea, then paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, then dyspnea at rest; bendopnea (breathlessness when bending forward) reflects elevated filling pressure, especially with low cardiac output (p.1982). Orthopnea typically occurs within 1-2 minutes of lying down, whereas paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occurs after prolonged recumbency and may require 30 minutes or more upright for relief; cardiac asthma (wheezing) can mimic primary lung disease (p.1982). An S3 gallop indicates volume overload, suggests severe hemodynamic compromise, and carries negative prognostic significance, whereas an S4 is nonspecific and often reflects hypertensive HFpEF (p.1984). Pulmonary rales may be ABSENT in longstanding HF despite chronically elevated wedge pressures because increased lymphatic drainage prevents alveolar spillage, so a clear chest does not exclude congestion (p.1983, p.1985). Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) rise with wall stress and aid diagnosis when uncertain, but levels are falsely LOW in obesity and falsely elevated by age, female sex, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (p.1985). Cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by reduced forward cardiac output but importantly by systemic and abdominal venous congestion; relieving congestion (diuretics or ultrafiltration) often improves renal function (p.1981). High-output HF is rare and usually requires underlying structural heart disease; consider it with severe anemia (often hemoglobin less than or equal to 8 g/dL), arteriovenous fistula, severe obesity, cirrhosis, thyrotoxicosis, end-stage renal disease, or beriberi (p.1982). Iron deficiency (with or without anemia) is common in chronic HF; IV iron (not oral) improves symptoms, exercise capacity, and reduces hospitalizations, though survival benefit is uncertain (p.1985). Q waves with reduced QRS voltage (pseudo-infarct pattern) suggest infiltrative or restrictive cardiomyopathy such as amyloid, and conduction system disease should raise suspicion for cardiac sarcoid or Chagas in the right setting (p.1985). Acute pulmonary edema with severe dyspnea and pink frothy sputum (marked wedge pressure elevation) Hypotension with narrow pulse pressure and rapid thready pulse, cool extremities, peripheral cyanosis (low-output/cardiogenic shock) Pulsus alternans (severely reduced LV contraction) Kussmaul's sign (inspiratory rise in JVP) signaling severe biventricular HF and poor outcome Oliguria from severely reduced renal blood flow (advanced-stage HF) Cheyne-Stokes/periodic breathing in advanced HF Marked elevation of transaminases and lactic acid suggesting cardiogenic shock Cardiac cachexia (unintentional edema-free weight loss greater than 5% over 12 months) with muscle wasting and frailty Hyponatremia at hospitalization (negative prognostic marker) New S3 gallop Relying on signs and symptoms alone, which are neither sensitive nor specific for HF; maintain a high index of suspicion in high-risk patients (older, hypertension, diabetes, CKD). Excluding HF because the lung exam is clear; rales can be absent in chronic HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures. Misreading right-HF hepatic congestion (elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) as biliary tract disease. Misdiagnosing cardiac asthma/bronchial congestion as primary asthma or COPD and treating inappropriately. Over- or under-interpreting natriuretic peptides without accounting for obesity (falsely low) and for age, female sex, CKD, AF, PE, and PAH (falsely elevated). Equating NYHA functional class with objective cardiac structure or function; it correlates poorly with EF and peak VO2. Attributing diuretic-refractory nonpitting edema to HF when it represents lymphedema needing different workup. Failing to seek precipitating factors (identifiable in 50-90% of admissions), such as nonadherence, excess salt/fluid, NSAIDs, negative inotropes, ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, anemia, thyroid disease, or sleep apnea. HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index event (acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric hypertrophy; both involve myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium-handling and cytoskeletal proteins, reexpression of fetal genes, and myocyte necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy, completing a vicious cycle of pump dysfunction and rising wall stress. Compensatory neurohormonal activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports output but becomes maladaptive, causing vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, arrhythmia, and adverse remodeling of heart, vessels, and kidneys. Counterregulatory vasodilators (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated and act via guanylate cyclase to promote vasodilation and natriuresis; bradykinin and natriuretic peptides are degraded by neprilysin. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling. HFpEF mechanisms are less defined but extend beyond diastolic dysfunction to vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, adiposity-related inflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and insulin resistance. Electrical dyssynchrony (LBBB/IVCD), secondary mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, cardiorenal and splanchnic/hepatic congestion, gut microbiome alterations with endotoxemia, and high-output states further drive progression. Overall 5-year survival after HF diagnosis in primary care is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. Post-admission mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. Black patients have higher case-fatality, men higher age-adjusted mortality than women. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV EF, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index and peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, elevated neurohormones, widened QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular arrhythmias. HFrecEF carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with risk-factor treatment and guideline-directed therapies. New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification: Class I, no limitation, ordinary activity causes no undue symptoms; Class II, mild limitation, comfortable at rest but ordinary activity (e.g., carrying heavy packages) causes fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations, or angina; Class III, moderate limitation, comfortable at rest but less-than-ordinary activity (e.g., getting dressed) provokes symptoms; Class IV, severe, symptoms of HF or angina at rest, worsening with any activity. EF-based phenotypes: HFrEF (EF less than or equal to 40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), HFpEF (greater than or equal to 50%). The chapter notes NYHA class correlates poorly with objective measures such as LV size, EF, and peak oxygen consumption.

Heat-Related Illnesses — Heatstroke, Heat exhaustion, Heat cramps, Heat syncope, Heat edema, Hyperthermia (environmental) Malignant hyperthermia (e.g., after general anesthesia) Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Serotonin syndrome Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Diabetic ketoacidosis Drug/toxin toxidromes (amphetamines, cocaine, sympathomimetics, salicylates, anticholinergics, strychnine, dietary supplements, hallucinogens) Withdrawal syndromes (ethanol, hypnotics) Stroke / cerebral hemorrhage and other CNS causes of altered thermoregulation Cardiovascular, neurologic, and metabolic causes of syncope (for heat syncope) Sepsis syndrome / SIRS of infectious origin Meningitis Encephalitis Cerebral abscess Malaria Typhoid Tetanus Core (central) temperature monitoring; peripheral temperature is unreliable Serum electrolytes (sodium, chloride, potassium) - hyponatremia/hypochloremia in salt-depletion states Hepatic aminotransferases (AST, ALT) - markedly elevated in heatstroke, mildly elevated in heat exhaustion Coagulation studies (platelets, fibrinogen, prothrombin) - decreased; assess for DIC Creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase - elevated, suggesting EHS/rhabdomyolysis Renal function and calcium/phosphate - evaluate for rhabdomyolysis complications (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia) Urinalysis - microscopic hematuria, myoglobinuria, granular or red cell casts Blood glucose - hypoglycemia is frequent Lactate - mild acidosis in CHS, marked lactic acidosis in EHS Cardiac biomarkers and ECG - tachyarrhythmias, nonspecific ST-T changes, heat-related ischemia/infarction Toxicologic screening, cranial CT, and CSF analysis if mental status does not improve with cooling Malignant hyperthermia Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Serotonin syndrome Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Diabetic ketoacidosis Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (noninfectious) Toxicologic causes of hyperthermia (sympathomimetics, anticholinergic toxidrome, salicylates) Heat-related illnesses span a spectrum from minor syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat, heat syncope, heat cramps) through heat exhaustion to heatstroke, a true medical emergency. Heatstroke is distinguished by the historical/physical triad of heat-stress exposure, CNS dysfunction, and a core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F); some patients with impending heatstroke may initially appear lucid. In contrast to heatstroke, fever reflects intact thermoregulation, whereas heatstroke represents total loss of thermoregulatory control. Heat exhaustion is characterized by preserved thermoregulatory control and CNS function with core temperature usually below 40.5C (105F); more profound CNS impairment should raise concern for heatstroke or another cause. Two clinical forms of heatstroke exist: classic (epidemic) heatstroke (CHS) in older or chronically ill, often medicated, sedentary patients during heat waves (skin frequently hot and dry from ceased sweating), and exertional heatstroke (EHS) in young healthy exercising individuals who are often profusely diaphoretic despite dehydration. Evaporation of skin moisture is the single most efficient mechanism of heat loss but becomes progressively ineffective once relative humidity exceeds 70%; conduction and convection fail once ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature. Many patients are unaware that their medications impair heat tolerance: anticholinergics, phenothiazines, and heterocyclic antidepressants blunt sweating and central thermoregulation, while beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and various stimulants reduce cutaneous perfusion or increase heat production. Hepatocytes are highly heat sensitive: AST is routinely elevated on presentation in heatstroke, and both AST and ALT can eventually rise to over 100 times normal values. Core-temperature elevation duration directly drives morbidity and mortality; peripheral (non-core) temperature measurement is unreliable, and continuous core monitoring is needed. Heatstroke commonly produces a thermal cardiomyopathy with potentially elevated CVP despite dehydration, plus deceptive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and basilar rales in a hypovolemic patient. The wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) is a superior environmental heat-load index to the simple heat index because it incorporates radiant heat and wind speed in addition to air temperature and humidity. Acclimatization to heat develops over one to several weeks (lowered sweat threshold, increased sweat volume with lower salt content, plasma volume expansion, lower heart rate with higher stroke volume) and dissipates rapidly within weeks after leaving the hot environment. Core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F) with CNS dysfunction in the setting of heat stress (heatstroke) Persistent or worsening altered mental status, seizures, or failure to improve with cooling Hot, dry, anhidrotic skin in a dehydrated patient (classic heatstroke) Hypotension with widened pulse pressure, tachypnea, and tachyarrhythmia Evidence of rhabdomyolysis (markedly elevated CK, myoglobinuria, oliguria) Coagulopathy / disseminated intravascular coagulation Markedly elevated transaminases indicating hepatic injury Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, aspiration Heat exhaustion that progresses to heatstroke even after removal from heat stress Treating heat edema with diuretics, which are ineffective and predispose to volume depletion and more serious heat illness. Failing to recognize that heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke after the patient is removed from heat stress. Relying on peripheral temperature measurements, which are unreliable in heatstroke. Mistaking cold-induced tonic-clonic muscular rigidity during cooling for seizure activity. Misinterpreting an elevated CVP as adequate volume status, since thermal cardiomyopathy and a hyperdynamic circulation can elevate CVP despite significant dehydration. Assuming hemoconcentration is always present in heat exhaustion (it is not), and overlooking that most cases reflect mixed sodium and water depletion. Correcting free water deficits too rapidly, risking an excessive fall in serum osmolality. Overlooking medication and substance contributions (anticholinergics, antipsychotics, stimulants) to impaired thermoregulation. Pursuing the broad infectious/toxic/endocrine differential without simultaneously initiating rapid cooling in suspected heatstroke. The central thermostat in the preoptic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus orchestrates heat dissipation via autonomic-driven cutaneous vasodilation and diaphoresis. Heat is lost through evaporation, radiation, conduction, and convection; skin blood flow can rise 25-30 fold with compensatory splanchnic and renal vasoconstriction. When heat load overwhelms dissipation, illness results. Heat cramps reflect relative intracellular deficiency of sodium, potassium, and fluid, compounded by copious hypotonic fluid replacement that produces hyponatremia and hypochloremia. Heat exhaustion arises from water depletion, sodium depletion, or both. Heatstroke begins when maintaining perfusion forces peripheral vasoconstriction, which halts cutaneous heat radiation and causes core temperature to rise sharply. Above 42C (107.6F) direct cellular injury occurs: thermosensitive enzymes fail, oxidative phosphorylation uncouples irreversibly, heat-shock proteins and cytokines drive a systemic inflammatory response, and endothelial damage activates the coagulation cascade. Splanchnic shunting causes gut ischemia with endotoxin release that further impairs thermoregulation, potentially progressing to hepatic dysfunction, renal failure, DIC, and fulminant multisystem organ failure. Minor heat syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat, heat syncope, hyperventilation tetany, heat cramps) and heat exhaustion generally resolve favorably with removal from heat, cooling, and fluid/electrolyte repletion; younger, previously healthy heat-exhaustion patients without major laboratory abnormalities often do well, while older patients with comorbidities frequently require inpatient management. Heatstroke prognosis is closely tied to the duration of core-temperature elevation: delayed cooling can lead to severe hepatic dysfunction, permanent renal failure, DIC, and fulminant multisystem organ failure. Heat-related cardiac biomarker elevations and thermal cardiomyopathy may be reversible. Heat waves substantially increase mortality, especially among the elderly and malnourished, and secondary vascular events (strokes, myocardial infarctions) occur at least ten times more often during extreme heat. Severity ladder of heat-related illness: minor heat-emergency syndromes (heat edema, prickly heat/miliaria rubra, heat syncope, hyperventilation tetany) and heat cramps are mild and self-limited; heat exhaustion is intermediate with core temperature usually below 40.5C (105F) and preserved CNS function; heatstroke is the most severe with core temperature above 40.5C (104.9F), CNS dysfunction, and loss of thermoregulation. Heatstroke is further classified as classic (epidemic) heatstroke (CHS - older/chronically ill, sedentary, anhidrotic, milder coagulopathy and lactic acidosis, mild CK rise) versus exertional heatstroke (EHS - younger/healthy, exercising, diaphoretic, with rhabdomyolysis, marked lactic acidosis, acute renal failure, DIC, hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia).

Heavy Metal Poisoning — Toxic metal poisoning, Arsenic poisoning, Lead poisoning, Mercury poisoning, Cadmium poisoning Other causes of acute gastroenteritis with hemodynamic collapse (arsenic, mercuric salt, or cadmium ingestion) Acquired peripheral polyneuropathy from other toxic/metabolic causes (arsenic, thallium, lead) Parkinsonism from other causes (manganese-induced parkinsonism vs idiopathic Parkinson disease) Microcytic/normocytic anemia from other causes (lead-related anemia with basophilic stippling; cadmium-related microcytic hypochromic anemia unresponsive to iron) Encephalopathy of other etiology (lead encephalopathy; aluminum-related dialysis encephalopathy) Fanconi syndrome / proximal tubulopathy from other nephrotoxins Bacterial or viral gastroenteritis (mimicked by acute arsenic, mercuric salt, or cadmium ingestion) Pneumonia (mimicked by acute cadmium or mercury vapor inhalation causing pneumonitis/noncardiogenic pulmonary edema) 24-h urinary arsenic (toxic >67 umol/d or 50 ug/d, after 24 h without seafood); serum arsenic >0.9 umol/L (7 ug/dL) if recent; arsenic in hair/nails Whole-blood lead level (not serum); blood protoporphyrin (free erythrocyte or zinc); peripheral smear for basophilic stippling; nerve conduction studies; long-bone x-ray for epiphyseal 'lead lines' KXRF (in vivo x-ray fluorescence) bone lead measurement to assess cumulative lead exposure Serum cadmium >500 nmol/L (5 ug/dL) if recent; urinary cadmium >100 nmol/L (10 ug/g creatinine); urinary beta-2-microglobulin >750 ug/g creatinine Blood mercury (recent) or hair mercury (chronic organic exposure); urine mercury; provocation: >20-ug rise in 24-h urine mercury after a 2-g succimer dose for remote exposure ECG (arsenic: QRS broadening, QT prolongation, ST depression, T-wave flattening); abdominal x-ray for radiopaque arsenic or thallium Idiopathic Parkinson disease (manganese parkinsonism) Alzheimer disease / other neurodegeneration (aluminum association) Iron-deficiency anemia (cadmium-induced anemia unresponsive to iron) Pyelonephritis and other renal disease causing elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin (overlaps with cadmium nephropathy marker) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and hearing loss (associations described with lead) The U.S. ATSDR ranks arsenic, lead, mercury, and cadmium as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 7th most hazardous substances at toxic waste sites; the WHO lists all four among the 10 chemicals of greatest public-health concern globally (Harrison 22e p.3699). Lead and mercury are xenobiotic metals with no clear safe threshold, whereas copper and selenium are essential trace elements that become toxic only at high exposure (Harrison 22e p.3699). Acute arsenic poisoning produces hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with intestinal mucosal necrosis, fluid loss and hypotension, plus delayed cardiomyopathy, acute tubular necrosis, and hemolysis; chronic exposure causes peripheral neuropathy, hyperkeratosis/hyperpigmentation, and cancers of skin, lung, liver (angiosarcoma), bladder, and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3700). Classic arsenic signs include a garlicky breath odor and Mees' lines (transverse white striae on the fingernails); arsenic is radiopaque and may be visible on abdominal x-ray (Harrison 22e p.3700). Cadmium has a biologic half-life of 10-30 years; severe food/water contamination in Japan caused itai-itai (ouch-ouch) disease with painful bone fractures from cadmium-induced bone toxicity (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700). Lead in blood is 95-99% sequestered in red cells, so lead must be measured in whole blood rather than serum; about 15% of an absorbed dose is stored in bone with a half-life >20 years, making bone (KXRF) levels a marker of cumulative exposure (Harrison 22e p.3700). Impairment of childhood IQ from lead occurs with no measurable threshold down to the assay limit of detection (~1 ug/dL); the CDC recommends screening children at about 6 months and intervening if blood lead exceeds 3.5 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700). Chronic metallic mercury vapor exposure produces an intention tremor and mercurial erethism (excitability, memory loss, insomnia, timidity, delirium) -- the historical 'mad as a hatter' picture (Harrison 22e p.3701). Children exposed to mercury in any form may develop acrodynia ('pink disease'): flushing, itching, swelling, tachycardia, hypertension, excessive salivation/perspiration, irritability, weakness, and desquamation of palms and soles (Harrison 22e p.3701). Dimethylmercury is 'supertoxic' -- a few drops absorbed through skin or inhaled can cause fatal cerebellar degeneration (Harrison 22e p.3701). Manganese overexposure (miners, welders, dry-battery workers) causes a parkinsonian syndrome within 1-2 years that, unlike idiopathic Parkinson disease, is nonresponsive to L-dopa (Harrison 22e p.3702). The single most important treatment is recognizing and stopping the exposure; activated charcoal does not bind metals and is of limited value in acute metal ingestion (Harrison 22e p.3699). Acute encephalopathy with convulsions and coma at very high blood lead (>80-120 ug/dL) -- risk of death Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema after acute cadmium or mercury-vapor inhalation Hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with hypotension and delayed cardiomyopathy in acute arsenic poisoning Cardiovascular collapse after acute ingestion of inorganic mercury (lethal dose 10-42 mg/kg) Garlicky breath, Mees' lines, or a gingival 'lead line' indicating significant metal exposure Skin or inhalational exposure to dimethylmercury (supertoxic; minute amounts fatal) Pregnancy exposure to mercury or high maternal bone lead -- risk of severe fetal neurodevelopmental injury Measuring lead in serum instead of whole blood (95-99% of lead is in red cells) (Harrison 22e p.3700). Relying on activated charcoal for metal ingestion -- charcoal does not bind metals (Harrison 22e p.3699); however thallium is an exception, where charcoal interrupts enterohepatic circulation (Harrison 22e p.3702). Attributing high urinary beta-2-microglobulin solely to cadmium -- it also rises in other renal diseases such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.3700). Misreading elevated total arsenic from recent seafood (nontoxic organic arsenobetaine/arsenocholine) as toxic inorganic arsenic -- test after 24 h without seafood (Harrison 22e p.3700). Attempting chelation for cadmium poisoning -- chelation is not useful and dimercaprol can worsen cadmium nephrotoxicity (Harrison 22e p.3700). Expecting chelation to improve outcomes in asymptomatic childhood lead exposure -- a large randomized trial showed no benefit on intelligence at BPb 20-40 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700). Mistaking manganese parkinsonism for idiopathic Parkinson disease and expecting an L-dopa response (Harrison 22e p.3702). Metals enter the body chiefly by inhalation of dusts/fumes, ingestion of contaminated food or water (especially via hand-to-mouth activity in children), and sometimes vapor (e.g., mercury) or dermal absorption (organic lead, thallium). Gastrointestinal absorption varies markedly with the chemical form of the metal and host nutritional status. Once absorbed, metals are transported in blood and sequestered in organs such as bone, liver, and kidney, sometimes for years, then excreted mainly by renal and gastrointestinal routes (with minor losses via sweat, saliva, breath, milk, skin, hair, and nails). Toxicity arises from enzyme inhibition, damage to subcellular organelles and DNA, covalent protein modification, generation of reactive oxygen species, and displacement of essential metals from metal-dependent proteins; metals also alter DNA methylation and other epigenetic marks, dysregulating gene and microRNA expression. Many metals bind sulfhydryl (thiol) groups; cadmium and mercury both bind cellular sulfhydryls, cadmium competing with zinc and calcium, and lead interferes with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, ATPases, and calcium-dependent messengers while enhancing oxidation and apoptosis. Genetic polymorphisms affecting metal binding/transport and nutritional/comorbid factors modify individual susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700). Outcome depends on the metal, dose, acuity, and promptness of exposure termination. Acute high-dose poisoning can be fatal (e.g., lead encephalopathy at BPb >120 ug/dL; inorganic mercury ingestion at 10-42 mg/kg; cadmium or mercury-vapor pulmonary edema; dimethylmercury exposure). Many effects of chronic exposure are irreversible or only partly reversible, including peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, manganese parkinsonism (L-dopa nonresponsive), itai-itai bone disease, and cadmium-related chronic renal failure for which no effective chelation exists. Cumulative lead burden is an established risk factor for chronic disease, including hypertension, cardiovascular morbidity/mortality, and chronic kidney disease, and prenatal exposure carries lasting offspring neurodevelopmental risk (Harrison 22e p.3699-3702). No single unified grading; severity is metal- and level-specific. Lead: subclinical childhood effects at BPb ~25-60 ug/dL, with IQ impairment down to ~1 ug/dL; clinically apparent neurodevelopmental delay at BPb 40-80 ug/dL; acute impaired neurotransmission/neuronal death at BPb >60-80 ug/dL; acute encephalopathy with convulsions/coma at BPb >80-120 ug/dL. Adult occupational removal at BPb >40 ug/dL (proposed newer target <10 ug/dL, removal if >20 ug/dL). Arsenic lethal dose 120-200 mg in adults, 2 mg/kg in children. Inorganic mercury ingestion lethal at 10-42 mg/kg; organic mercury CNS lesions at >1.7 mg/kg. Thallium severe poisoning after single dose >1 g or >8 mg/kg (Harrison 22e p.3700-3702).

Helicobacter pylori Infection — H. pylori Urea breath test (noninvasive) for active infection and for confirming eradication. Stool (fecal) antigen test (noninvasive) for active infection and eradication confirmation. Endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, including for gastric lymphoma staging. PCR or FISH for the t(11;18) translocation in gastric MALT lymphoma to predict responsiveness to eradication therapy (p.649). H. pylori has a proven etiologic role in peptic ulcer disease; together with NSAID use it is one of the two most common causes of gastroduodenal ulcers (p.302). In dyspeptic patients under 60 with no alarm features, test-and-treat is the recommended initial strategy: assess H. pylori status by fecal (stool) antigen or urea breath testing, and treat those who are positive (p.303). Eradication of H. pylori in patients with bleeding ulcers lowers rebleeding rates to under 5% (p.272). H. pylori is a known driver of gastric cancer; the intestinal subtype of gastric adenocarcinoma is associated with H. pylori infection and atrophic/atopic gastritis (p.646, p.647). Although H. pylori is extremely common (present in roughly half of all humans), gastric cancer develops in only a small subset of those infected, so infection alone is not sufficient (p.646). Treating H. pylori reduces future gastric cancer risk: eradication lowered gastric cancer incidence in people with a first-degree relative who had gastric cancer, and reduced second cancers in patients with prior early-stage gastric cancer (p.646). All patients with gastric lymphoma should have H. pylori status evaluated; if histopathology is negative, confirm with a stool antigen test or urea breath test (p.649). For gastric MALT lymphoma, antibiotic eradication of H. pylori alone is highly effective and is the initial therapy when H. pylori is positive and the t(11;18) translocation assay is negative, producing high response and complete-remission rates (p.649-650). Dyspepsia with alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding/anemia, jaundice, palpable mass or adenopathy, family history of gastroesophageal malignancy) or age over 60 warrants upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy rather than test-and-treat alone (p.302-303). Failure to respond to eradication, or recurrent/refractory symptoms, should prompt further evaluation. PITFALL: PPIs and other acid-suppressing drugs can cause false-negative urea breath and stool antigen tests; acid suppression must be stopped before testing for active H. pylori infection. Confirmation of eradication should be performed 4-6 weeks after completing therapy, not immediately (p.303). Do not rely on a single negative histopathology result in gastric lymphoma; confirm with noninvasive stool antigen or urea breath testing (p.649). NEGATION: Even H. pylori-negative MALT tumors may respond to anti-H. pylori therapy, so a negative test does not preclude a trial of eradication; the t(11;18) translocation identifies a subgroup less likely to respond (p.649-650). NEGATION: H. pylori eradication does NOT worsen GERD symptoms, despite H. pylori infection being associated with a reduced prevalence of GERD (p.302). H. pylori is a flagellated gastric bacterium whose colonization triggers chronic mucosal inflammation. The flagellum lets the organism access the gastric epithelium and is essential for virulence; H. pylori evades innate immunity by producing a flagellin epitope that does not bind TLR5 and tetra-acylated LPS that does not activate TLR4 (p.1009-1010). Adhesion and gastric tropism are mediated by bacterial outer-membrane proteins BabA and SabA interacting with epithelial GM1 ganglioside (p.1009). Chronic H. pylori inflammation, partly via generation of carcinogenic nitrites from dietary nitrates, drives the gastritis-to-cancer sequence and is a recognized cause of peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal subtype), and gastric MALT lymphoma; certain higher-virulence strains carry greater cancer risk (p.646). Eradication markedly improves ulcer outcomes (rebleeding falls below 5%). In gastric MALT lymphoma, H. pylori eradication yields high response rates with complete remission in the majority, though time to remission can be prolonged (averaging ~15-16 months in some studies), requiring patient monitoring before declaring non-response (p.272, p.650). Benefit in functional dyspepsia is limited but statistically significant (about a 9% risk reduction vs placebo) (p.302).

Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation — HCT, Bone marrow transplantation, Stem cell transplantation, Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, HSCT Acute GVHD versus conditioning regimen toxicity, drug eruption, or infection as a cause of post-transplant rash, diarrhea, and hepatic dysfunction (biopsy of skin, liver, or gut often needed for confirmation) (Harrison 22e p.917) Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome versus other causes of tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, and fluid retention early after transplant (Harrison 22e p.916) Transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy versus other microangiopathic processes (schistocytes, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury) (Harrison 22e p.916-917) Idiopathic/diffuse interstitial pneumonia from conditioning toxicity can mimic infectious pneumonia early post-transplant (Harrison 22e p.916) Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia and bronchiolitis obliterans (late, often GVHD-associated) can mimic chronic respiratory infection (Harrison 22e p.916) HLA typing of HLA-A, -B, -C, and -D (and DRB1) to assess donor-recipient matching; AML/ALL candidates should be HLA-typed soon after diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.915, 919) Screening recipients for donor-directed anti-HLA antibodies before transplant, since their presence predicts poor engraftment (Harrison 22e p.917) Chimerism/engraftment documentation by fluorescence in situ hybridization of sex chromosomes (sex-mismatched pairs) or short tandem repeat polymorphism analysis after DNA amplification (Harrison 22e p.916) CD34 antigen quantification or colony-forming unit assays to gauge stem cell dose adequacy (Harrison 22e p.915) PCR monitoring of blood for CMV (and other viral) DNA to guide preemptive therapy (Harrison 22e p.918) Minimal residual disease assessment by multidimensional flow cytometry or molecular methods to refine transplant candidacy in acute leukemia (Harrison 22e p.919) GVHD severity biomarkers including ST2, REG3a, and TNF R1 (Harrison 22e p.917) Many noninfectious conditions can mimic acute GVHD, so histologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.917) Post-transplant autoimmune phenomena (autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenia) in 3-5% can mimic relapse-related or drug-induced cytopenias (Harrison 22e p.918) Hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is the umbrella term that has replaced 'bone marrow transplantation,' reflecting that hematopoietic stem cells can be sourced from marrow, growth-factor-mobilized peripheral blood, or umbilical cord blood (Harrison 22e p.914). It is used both to replace a defective but non-malignant lympho-hematopoietic system with a normal donor system and to treat malignancy, the latter by permitting higher myelosuppressive doses and, in allogeneic transplant, by adding an immunologic graft-versus-tumor effect (Harrison 22e p.914). Transplant categories are syngeneic (identical twin, ~1% of cases, no GVHD and no tumor contamination), allogeneic (genetically non-identical donor, risk of GVHD and graft rejection), and autologous (patient's own stored cells, no GVHD/rejection but lacks a graft-versus-tumor effect and may carry contaminating tumor cells) (Harrison 22e p.914-915). The chance any one full sibling is HLA-matched is 1 in 4; the probability a patient has an HLA-identical sibling is 1 - (0.75)^n where n is the number of siblings (Harrison 22e p.915). With registries exceeding 40 million volunteer donors, an HLA-matched unrelated donor can be found for about 60% of patients, with higher rates in Caucasians and lower rates in minorities and people of mixed ancestry; a search and scheduling typically takes 3-4 months (Harrison 22e p.915). Autologous engraftment is reliable when more than 2.5 x 10^6 CD34+ cells/kg are infused; the 5-10% of patients who mobilize poorly with growth factor alone may benefit from plerixafor, a CXCR4 antagonist that releases stem cells from the marrow niche (Harrison 22e p.915). Stem cell homing depends on P- and E-selectin/integrin (e.g., VLA-4) interactions and on niche-derived CXCL12 binding CXCR4 on the stem cell; human HSCs tolerate cryopreservation, enabling autologous storage (Harrison 22e p.914-915). After marrow grafting, granulocytes recover to ~100/uL by about day 16 and ~500/uL by day 22; mobilized peripheral blood speeds recovery by ~1 week while cord blood delays it by ~1 week (Harrison 22e p.916). Innate immunity recovers quickly, but adaptive (T- and B-cell) immunity may take 1-2 years; early T-cell recovery is dominated by infused donor CD8+ T cells with a limited repertoire, with diverse de novo CD4+/CD8+ cells emerging months later (Harrison 22e p.916). Reduced-intensity and nonmyeloablative conditioning rely heavily on the graft-versus-tumor effect; they carry higher relapse but lower transplant-related mortality, favoring older patients and those with comorbidities, whereas high-dose conditioning is preferred when measurable disease is present and the patient can tolerate it (Harrison 22e p.915-916). Evidence for the graft-versus-tumor effect: relapse is lowest in patients who develop acute and chronic GVHD, higher without GVHD, and highest after T-cell-depleted allogeneic or syngeneic grafts; donor lymphocyte infusions can induce remission in post-transplant relapse (Harrison 22e p.916). Worldwide more than 100,000 transplants were performed in 2022, with frequency closely tracking gross national income per capita (Harrison 22e p.914). Tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, and fluid retention within the first month (peak ~day 16) suggest sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, which carries ~30% mortality and can progress to fatal hepatorenal syndrome (Harrison 22e p.916) Erythematous maculopapular rash, persistent anorexia or diarrhea, and rising bilirubin/transaminases/alkaline phosphatase in the first 3 months point to acute GVHD; grades II-IV require aggressive therapy (Harrison 22e p.917) Schistocytes, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury about a month post-transplant indicate transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (Harrison 22e p.916-917) Diffuse fluffy pulmonary infiltrates with alveolar hemorrhage on lavage suggest conditioning-related diffuse alveolar damage rather than infection (Harrison 22e p.916) Failure of marrow function to return, or loss after initial engraftment, signals graft failure/rejection; persistence of host-origin lymphocytes indicates immunologic rejection (Harrison 22e p.917) Fever once the granulocyte count falls below 500/uL prompts broad-spectrum empiric antibacterial therapy because infection risk is so high (Harrison 22e p.918) Community respiratory viruses (RSV, parainfluenza, influenza, metapneumovirus) can be life-threatening or fatal in transplant recipients (Harrison 22e p.918) Premedication is not a reliable solution: in transfusion-related GVHD analogies aside, here the key pitfall is assuming infectious causes for early rash/diarrhea/hepatic dysfunction; acute GVHD typically needs biopsy because many conditions mimic it (Harrison 22e p.917) Grade I acute GVHD is clinically minor, does not affect survival, and does not require treatment; over-treating it adds unnecessary immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.917) Mobilized peripheral blood gives faster engraftment but, in matched-unrelated-donor transplant, increases chronic GVHD without a compensatory survival advantage (Harrison 22e p.916) No prospective randomized trial has shown that purging autologous grafts of tumor cells reduces relapse or improves survival (Harrison 22e p.915) Standard high-dose conditioning is poorly tolerated if given within 100 days of a first transplant due to cumulative toxicity; reduced-intensity regimens may be needed for graft failure salvage (Harrison 22e p.917) Patients with Fanconi anemia are abnormally sensitive to alkylating agents, so less intensive conditioning must be used (Harrison 22e p.918) Vaccine-preventable antibody titers wane after transplant unless recipients are revaccinated; live vaccines (MMR/MMR-V) are generally avoided until 2 years post-transplant (Harrison 22e p.918) Reinfusing donor stem cells into a patient with immunologic graft rejection is usually futile unless preceded by a second immunosuppressive conditioning regimen (Harrison 22e p.917) A single hematopoietic stem cell can regenerate the entire lympho-hematopoietic system, including red cells, granulocytes, B and T lymphocytes, platelets, and fixed-tissue macrophages (Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, osteoclasts, Langerhans cells). Infused cells home to the marrow via selectin/integrin adhesion and CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling. In allogeneic transplant, the central immunologic axis is HLA matching: HLA molecules present antigenic peptides to T cells, so mismatched 'major antigens' provoke strong T-cell reactions while even HLA-matched pairs can react against 'minor' endogenous antigens. Donor T cells reacting against host tissue cause graft-versus-host disease, whereas residual immunocompetent host cells can mediate graft rejection if conditioning is insufficiently immunosuppressive. The same alloreactivity underlies the beneficial graft-versus-tumor effect. Conditioning regimens combine antineoplastic activity, myelosuppression, and (for allogeneic) immunosuppression to eradicate disease and prevent rejection (Harrison 22e p.914-916). Outcomes are highly disease- and stage-dependent (CIBMTR estimates, transplants 2010-2020). Reported approximate 3-year survival: severe combined immunodeficiency ~95% allogeneic; aplastic anemia ~98% allogeneic; thalassemia ~95% allogeneic; AML 57% (first remission) and 53% (second remission); ALL 64% (first remission) and 45% (second remission); CML 71% (chronic phase), 67% (accelerated), 28% (blast crisis); CLL ~64%; myelodysplasia ~50%; multiple myeloma ~80% autologous as initial therapy; non-Hodgkin lymphoma 45% allogeneic / 55% autologous (first relapse/second remission); Hodgkin disease 68% allogeneic / 89% autologous (first relapse/second remission). Matched-unrelated-donor survival now essentially equals matched-sibling survival. Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome carries ~30% mortality; chronic GVHD mortality averages ~15% (range 5-50% by severity). HLA-matched sibling allogeneic transplant carries roughly a 1-3% graft rejection risk and ~15% risk of severe acute GVHD (Harrison 22e p.915-920). Acute GVHD is staged per organ and combined into an overall grade (Harrison 22e p.917). Skin stage 1-4 (rash <25% body surface up to generalized desquamation/bullae); liver stage by bilirubin from 34-51 umol/L [2-3 mg/dL] up to >257 umol/L [>15 mg/dL]; gut stage by diarrhea volume from 500-1000 mL/d up to ileus. Overall grade I (skin 1-2 only) is clinically insignificant; grades II-IV reflect progressively greater organ involvement, worse survival, and need for aggressive therapy. Myelodysplasia transplant timing uses the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS), with transplant generally reserved for Int-2 or higher (or selected Int-1 with poor features) (Harrison 22e p.919).

Hematopoietic Stem Cells — HSC, blood stem cells, hematopoiesis Deep/next-generation sequencing to detect somatic mutations and clonal hematopoiesis (e.g., DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1 variant allele fractions) Surface immunophenotyping of stem/progenitor markers (CD34, CD90/Thy-1, CD117/c-Kit, CD133, CD164, CD110/c-Mpl) as described in murine-based studies Every blood cell type and certain tissue-resident cells (e.g., microglia, some macrophages) arise from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs); catastrophic loss of HSC function leaves a person able to survive only about 2-4 weeks without extraordinary support. The HSC pool is estimated at only about 20,000-200,000 cells, yet it generates hundreds of billions of mature blood cells daily and sustains this output over decades. Stem cells are defined by two cardinal properties: self-renewal (dividing while staying undifferentiated) and differentiation into mature effector cells; loss of either leads to pool exhaustion or to organ failure/neoplasia. A dividing HSC can yield two stem cells, two differentiating cells (symmetric division), or one of each (asymmetric division); this asymmetry lets a small pool produce roughly seven orders of magnitude more mature cells daily. Mature blood cell lifespans vary widely, from hours for neutrophils to a few months for red cells to years for memory lymphocytes, but the durable source is the persistent stem cell pool. HSCs circulate in blood throughout life, but free-circulating time is brief (minutes in the mouse); circulating HSCs remain functional and usable for transplantation. The bone marrow niche (notably perivascular regions near trabecular bone) is both nurturing and constraining: mesenchymal and endothelial cells supply kit ligand and CXCL12, and the niche limits how many stem cells are produced. CXCR4/CXCL12 (SDF1) signaling retains HSCs in marrow; disrupting it (via CXCR4 blockade, CXCL12 cleavage, or receptor downregulation) mobilizes stem cells into blood, enabling collection by leukapheresis rather than operative marrow harvest. Differentiation proceeds along a branching hierarchy (stem cell to multipotent progenitor to lineage-committed precursor to mature cell), with progressive loss of plasticity and, in most lineages, loss of proliferative capacity. Maturation of progenitors into mature cells takes roughly 10-14 days in humans, clinically reflected in the lag between cytotoxic chemotherapy and blood count recovery. HSCs are heterogeneous: individual stem cells can be biased toward particular lineages and differ in proliferation and death responses, so the population behaves as an aggregate. Clonal hematopoiesis: HSCs accumulate roughly 17 somatic mutations per year of life; variant alleles contributing to over 1% of blood cells become nearly universal by age 70, with an inactivating TET2 mutation able to worsen outcomes of some chronic inflammatory conditions. Genetically modifying long-lived HSCs underlies curative cell therapies for cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy and the hemoglobinopathies, including a CRISPR gene-edited approach that suppresses BCL11A to reactivate fetal hemoglobin in beta thalassemia and sickle cell anemia. Complete failure of HSC function (e.g., after a nuclear/radiation accident) predicts survival of only about 2-4 weeks without extraordinary support Expansion of clones carrying 'driver' mutations seen in myelodysplasia and myeloid leukemias, with low-frequency progression to overt neoplastic disease Acquired self-renewal via oncogenic mutation in stem or more mature populations, providing a substrate for leukemia Regulators of mature/progenitor cells do not predict HSC behavior: erythropoietin and G-CSF drive precursor proliferation but do not directly cycle stem cells (G-CSF instead mobilizes HSCs by altering CXCL12 tethering). Deep HSC quiescence and resistance to cytokines make robust in vitro expansion of human HSCs difficult. Assuming leukemia must arise only from normal stem cells is an oversimplification, since less self-renewing mature populations can also be transformed and self-renewal can be acquired by mutation. The classic differentiation hierarchy diagram is a simplification; lineage-biased and intermediate cell states are increasingly recognized. Progenitor (transient amplifying) cells are short-lived and largely lack durable self-renewal, so gene-modifying progenitors rather than true stem cells fails to give lasting benefit. Hematopoiesis originates from a small self-renewing HSC pool. During development, blood production shifts sequentially from the yolk sac (embryonic-hemoglobin red cells and tissue-resident macrophages) to the placenta and intraembryonic sites near the aorta-gonad-mesonephros region, then to fetal liver, and in the second trimester to bone marrow and spleen; HSCs reach marrow via bloodborne transit from fetal liver after long-bone calcification, and proliferation falls sharply soon after birth. HSCs reside in a specialized perivascular/endosteal marrow niche where mesenchymal, endothelial, neural, and other cells provide regulatory signals (kit ligand, CXCL12) governing survival, expansion, and constraint. Trafficking depends on selectins binding CD162/CD44, integrin-mediated firm adhesion (VCAM-1/VLA-4), and CXCL12-CXCR4 plus calcium-sensing receptor signaling. Most HSCs are deeply quiescent and cytokine-resistant, dividing on the order of months to years; quiescence is enforced by high cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (e.g., p57/CDKN1c blocking the G1-S transition) and niche signals such as angiogenin, IL-18, and angiopoietin 1. Self-renewal preserves any acquired mutation in the durable stem pool, whereas progenitor mutations are largely lost through terminal differentiation; epigenetic regulators (DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1) are critical for pool homeostasis and for restraining outgrowth of potentially pathogenic clones. In the absence of disease the HSC pool is essentially inexhaustible: serial murine transplants can reconstitute several animals in succession and allogeneic transplant recipients never run out of blood cells over decades, indicating even limiting stem cell numbers suffice. With aging, clonal diversity declines as a small number of expanded clones (estimated 10-20 clones supplying 30-60% of blood cells by age 70) dominate; most such clones are benign, but some carry driver mutations with a low risk of progression to myeloid malignancy.

Hemifacial spasm — HFS, facial hemispasm Blepharospasm and other focal dystonias Facial myokymia Facial tics and functional facial movements Post-facial-palsy synkinesis Partial motor seizures involving the face Brain MRI with attention to the facial nerve root and vascular structures Electrophysiological testing showing lateral spread response where diagnosis is uncertain Evaluation for secondary structural or demyelinating causes when features are atypical Clinical assessment to differentiate from blepharospasm and synkinesis A movement disorder of involuntary, unilateral, irregular twitching of muscles innervated by the facial nerve, usually beginning around the eye and spreading over time to the lower face It is typically unilateral and, unlike many other facial movement disorders, can persist during sleep The most common cause is vascular compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone from the brainstem, often by an ectatic or aberrant artery Secondary causes include tumours, vascular malformations, and demyelinating or other lesions affecting the facial nerve pathway, which imaging helps exclude Contraction of the frontalis and platysma together, or elevation of the eyebrow with eye closure (the 'other Babinski' sign), supports the diagnosis It should be distinguished from blepharospasm, which is bilateral and involves only eye closure, and from facial myokymia and tics MRI, often with vascular sequences, is used to evaluate for a compressive vessel or structural lesion along the nerve Treatment principles include botulinum toxin injections as first-line symptomatic therapy and microvascular decompression surgery for suitable candidates seeking a durable cure Additional cranial nerve deficits or other neurological signs suggesting a structural posterior fossa lesion Rapid progression or bilateral involvement warranting reassessment Facial weakness or sensory change accompanying the spasm Features suggesting a tumour or vascular malformation on imaging Confusing it with bilateral blepharospasm and choosing the wrong treatment approach Failing to image for a compressive vessel or secondary lesion Overlooking the diagnostic clue that spasms may persist during sleep Not recognising post-palsy synkinesis, which can mimic hemifacial spasm Hemifacial spasm is usually caused by pulsatile compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone from the brainstem, most often by an aberrant or ectatic blood vessel. Chronic compression is thought to cause focal demyelination and ephaptic (cross) transmission between nerve fibres, together with hyperexcitability of the facial motor nucleus, generating spontaneous and spreading involuntary contractions. Secondary cases result from any lesion irritating the nerve along its course, and the pathophysiological common pathway is abnormal facial nerve excitability. Hemifacial spasm is typically chronic and does not resolve spontaneously, but it is not life-threatening; symptoms are well controlled with repeated botulinum toxin injections, and microvascular decompression offers a lasting cure in appropriately selected patients.

Hemochromatosis — iron overload, HFE hemochromatosis Secondary (acquired) iron overload from chronic transfusion in hemoglobinopathies/thalassemia (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.821) Other metabolic causes of skin hyperpigmentation: porphyria cutanea tarda, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, pellagra, malabsorption/Whipple's disease (Harrison 22e p.443) Transferrin saturation (serum iron / total iron-binding capacity) as a key screening test for iron overload (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805) Serum ferritin to assess body iron stores (Harrison 22e p.805) MRI quantitation of hepatic and cardiac iron stores (Harrison 22e p.2062) Genetic testing for HFE mutations (the gene underlying the common autosomal recessive form) (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702) Endomyocardial biopsy with Prussian blue iron stain (reserved; not usually needed when MRI is available) (Harrison 22e p.2062) Other causes of restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy; hemochromatosis is listed among restrictive cardiomyopathies but often presents clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy (Harrison 22e p.2062) Other chronic liver diseases progressing to cirrhosis (alcohol, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) (Harrison 22e p.702) Hemochromatosis is variably classified as a metabolic or storage disease; the common autosomal recessive form is related to the HFE gene (Harrison 22e p.2062). Up to 10% of the population is heterozygous for one HFE mutation, so clinical prevalence might be as high as 1 in 500, though observed rates are lower because of limited (incomplete) penetrance (Harrison 22e p.2062). Increased iron in the skin in types 1 and 2 hemochromatosis stimulates melanin pigment production and leads to the classic bronze color (Harrison 22e p.443). Systemic iron overload is diagnosed from serum iron and transferrin saturation, with thresholds noted around >60% in men and >45-50% in women; ferritin and transferrin saturation are the main usable laboratory biomarkers of iron status (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.805). MRI is used to quantitate iron stores in the liver and heart; for cardiac iron overload the diagnosis is made principally by MRI, and endomyocardial biopsy (Prussian blue stain) is not usually needed (Harrison 22e p.2062). When diagnosed early, hemochromatosis can often be managed by repeated phlebotomy to remove iron (Harrison 22e p.2062). Hepcidin-regulating proteins HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin, whose mutations cause different forms of hemochromatosis, normally contribute to hepcidin upregulation; impaired hepcidin signaling allows excess iron entry into plasma (Harrison 22e p.805). There is no regulated mechanism for iron excretion; physiologic iron loss occurs only through cell desquamation and menses, which is why unregulated absorption produces progressive overload (Harrison 22e p.805). Hemochromatosis (HFE germline mutations) is a recognized risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, typically via cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.702) Progression to cirrhosis from hepatic iron loading (Harrison 22e p.2062) Cardiomyopathy from cardiac siderosis, which may cause heart failure or arrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2062) Markedly increased susceptibility to Vibrio vulnificus sepsis (primary sepsis develops most often in patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis) (Harrison 22e p.1373) Increased susceptibility to Yersinia (Y. enterocolitica / Y. pseudotuberculosis) septicemia, with iron overload providing accessible iron; iron chelators such as desferrioxamine can precipitate Yersinia infection (Harrison 22e p.1392) Incomplete penetrance: many HFE mutation carriers never develop clinical iron-overload disease, so genotype does not equal phenotype, and additional genetic and environmental factors (e.g., alcohol) modify expression (Harrison 22e p.2062). Hemochromatosis may present clinically as a dilated cardiomyopathy even though it is categorized among restrictive cardiomyopathies (Harrison 22e p.2062). Iron chelation therapy itself (e.g., desferrioxamine) can supply accessible iron to Yersinia and impair neutrophil function, precipitating Yersinia septicemia in iron-overloaded patients (Harrison 22e p.1392). Systemic iron homeostasis is controlled by hepcidin, a hepatocyte-derived peptide that blocks the iron exporter ferroportin, limiting iron flux from duodenal enterocytes, recycling macrophages, and storing hepatocytes. High plasma/liver iron normally raises hepcidin via the BMP-SMAD pathway, with HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin contributing to hepcidin upregulation. Mutations in these genes (most commonly HFE) lead to inappropriately low hepcidin, increased iron absorption, and rising transferrin saturation. Because no regulated route of iron excretion exists, iron accumulates progressively. When transferrin saturation exceeds ~60%, non-transferrin-bound iron (NTBI) appears in the circulation and is taken up by liver, pancreas, and heart, driving parenchymal injury. In the heart, excess iron deposits in the perinuclear compartment of cardiomyocytes, disrupting intracellular architecture and mitochondrial function (Harrison 22e p.805, p.2062). If diagnosed early, iron overload can often be removed by repeated phlebotomy, and cardiac function can improve with iron removal provided myocyte loss and replacement fibrosis are not too severe. Late disease carries the burden of established cirrhosis (with hepatocellular carcinoma risk) and irreversible cardiac and endocrine damage (Harrison 22e p.2062, p.702).

Hemolytic Anemia — haemolytic anaemia Inherited intracorpuscular defects: hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemia; Chap. 103), enzymopathies (G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency), membrane-cytoskeleton defects (hereditary spherocytosis) (p.791-792, Table 105-1) Acquired extracorpuscular causes: autoimmune (warm AIHA, cold agglutinin disease, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria), microangiopathic/mechanical (prosthetic valve, march hemoglobinuria), paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, toxic/drug-induced, infectious (p.792, 801-804, Table 105-1) Familial (atypical) hemolytic-uremic syndrome from inherited dysregulation permitting excessive complement activation (p.799-800) Malaria - the most frequent infectious cause of HA in endemic areas (p.801) Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 causing HUS, more common in children (p.801) Clostridium perfringens sepsis - life-threatening intravascular hemolysis from lecithinase toxin (open wounds, septic abortion, contaminated blood unit) (p.801, Table 105-7) Babesia, and Mycoplasma infection (associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria); viral triggers (EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19, HIV, HCV) of secondary autoimmune HA (p.801-802, Table 105-8) Reticulocyte count - corrected percentage and absolute count (often neglected in initial anemia workup) (p.791) Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, AST, LDH, haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2) Urine for hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria and stool/urine urobilinogen when intravascular hemolysis suspected (p.791) Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes (microangiopathy/fragmentation), spherocytes (AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis), bite cells (G6PD), basophilic stippling (lead/P5N deficiency) (p.799-804) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test - broad-spectrum then specific anti-Ig/anti-C reagents (p.801) Quantitative G6PD assay (screening tests can miss deficiency soon after a hemolytic attack because young high-G6PD reticulocytes mask it); DNA testing and point-of-care tests available (p.799-800) Flow cytometry for CD59-negative red cell population in PNH (p.801, Table 105-7) Donath-Landsteiner antibody for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria; blood cultures for clostridial septicemia (p.801, Table 105-7) Red cell survival study (51Cr or nonradioactive 15N) as the gold standard for shortened life span; bone marrow (if done) shows erythroid hyperplasia, usually not required (p.791-792) Compensated hemolysis presenting without anemia, mimicking a non-hemolytic state until it decompensates (p.792) Reticulocytosis-driven macrocytosis that can be mistaken for a megaloblastic process (p.791) Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis causing a precipitous hemoglobin fall in a chronic hemolytic patient, mimicking acute worsening of hemolysis (p.792) Coombs-negative AIHA, which can still be severe when a high-affinity antibody opsonizes red cells with few molecules (p.802) Hemolytic anemia (HA) is anemia from increased red-cell destruction with a normal (usually increased) marrow supply; unlike acute blood loss, cells are destroyed within the body rather than physically lost (p.791). Classify by primary etiology (inherited vs acquired), tempo (acute vs chronic), severity, site of hemolysis (intravascular vs extravascular), and mechanism (intracorpuscular vs extracorpuscular defects) (p.791, Table 105-1). Inherited HA generally reflects intracorpuscular defects (hemoglobinopathies, enzymopathies such as G6PD, membrane-cytoskeleton defects); acquired HA generally reflects extracorpuscular factors (autoimmune, microangiopathic/mechanical, toxins, drugs, infection). Exceptions: PNH (inherited-like somatic mutation but acquired) and familial/atypical HUS (p.791-792, Table 105-1). Core clinical sign is jaundice; patients may report dark urine; splenomegaly is common as a preferential site of hemolysis, the liver may enlarge, and pigment gallstones are common with chronic hemolysis (p.791). Laboratory hallmarks: increased reticulocytes (both percentage and the more definitive absolute count), raised MCV with macrocytes/polychromasia on smear, increased unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin and AST, raised LDH, and reduced-to-absent haptoglobin (p.791, Table 105-2). Extravascular hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen; intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria (often with hemosiderinuria), free plasma hemoglobin, markedly raised LDH (up to ~10x), and low haptoglobin, with bilirubin only mildly elevated (p.791, Table 105-2). A positive broad-spectrum direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is on its own almost diagnostic of autoimmune HA; the broad reagent detects bound immunoglobulin and/or complement (C3 fragments) on red cells (p.801). Warm AIHA (mostly IgG, optimal 37C) causes predominantly extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes; cold agglutinin disease (mostly IgM anti-I, optimal 4-30C) activates complement causing intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria plus Kupffer-cell extravascular destruction in the liver (p.801-803, Fig. 105-9, Table 105-8). Compensated hemolysis: a brisk EPO-driven erythropoietic response can fully offset red-cell destruction so an inherited hemolytic condition may present without anemia; it can decompensate in pregnancy, folate deficiency, or renal failure (p.792). Schistocytes (fragmented/helmet cells) on smear indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) - consider TTP, HUS, and DIC; an emergency requiring urgent evaluation (p.799, 801, Table 105-7) Abrupt severe drop in hemoglobin (to as low as 4 g/dL within days) in warm AIHA with jaundice and splenomegaly - a medical emergency (p.801) Acute renal failure - the most serious threat from acute hemolytic attacks in adults (e.g., G6PD-related), and a predictor of poor AIHA outcome (p.799, 801) Hemoglobinuria signalling intravascular hemolysis (mismatched transfusion, PNH, clostridial sepsis, march hemoglobinuria, favism) (p.801, Table 105-7) Evans syndrome (AIHA plus autoimmune thrombocytopenia) signals high-risk disease and may indicate underlying immune deficiency (p.801) Mismatched (usually ABO-incompatible) blood transfusion causing abrupt intravascular hemolysis (p.801, Table 105-7) Clostridium perfringens sepsis causing life-threatening intravascular hemolysis (p.801) Neglecting the reticulocyte count, a key early clue to a hemolytic mechanism (p.791) Screening (semiquantitative) G6PD tests give falsely normal results immediately after a hemolytic attack because the oldest deficient cells are destroyed and young reticulocytes have higher G6PD - use a quantitative assay; female heterozygotes may also be missed (p.799-800) Dismissing Coombs-negative AIHA as not serious - high-affinity antibody can cause severe disease with few bound molecules; false-positive Coombs can follow transfusion, organ transplant, or Ig/anti-lymphocyte products (p.801-802) Assuming an inherited hemolytic disorder always causes anemia - compensated hemolysis can be normo-hemoglobinemic until decompensation (p.792) In cold agglutinin disease, prednisone and splenectomy are ineffective (unlike warm AIHA), and transfused (I-positive) red cells survive no longer than the patient's; the blood bag and patient extremities must be kept warm (p.803) Misattributing favism to fava bean pollen inhalation (it does not cause favism) or to other beans (which are safe) (p.799) The mature red cell loses mitochondria and ribosomes, leaving anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) as the sole source of ATP and the hexose-monophosphate shunt (via G6PD-generated NADPH and reduced glutathione) as defense against oxidant stress; damaged proteins cannot be replaced, so any metabolic failure ultimately damages the membrane or the cation pump and shortens the ~120-day life span. Senescent or damaged red cells expose band-3 neoantigens, become opsonized, and are phagocytosed by splenic, hepatic, and other macrophages (extravascular hemolysis); this senescence process is accelerated in many HAs. The essential common feature is increased red-cell turnover; when destruction outpaces marrow production, anemia results. Chronic intravascular hemolysis causes iron loss via hemoglobinuria, whereas chronic extravascular hemolysis (especially if transfused) tends toward iron overload and, untreated, secondary hemochromatosis (p.791-792). Transient hemolysis usually has no long-term consequences beyond increased erythropoietic (folate) requirement; recurrent or persistent hemolysis predisposes to pigment gallstones, splenomegaly with hypersplenism (neutropenia/thrombocytopenia), and, with chronic extravascular hemolysis or repeated transfusion, iron overload progressing to secondary hemochromatosis affecting liver and heart. Warm AIHA carries ~5-10% mortality even with appropriate management; predictors of worse outcome/relapse include Evans syndrome, hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and high-affinity antibody. G6PD-related acute hemolysis generally resolves fully once the trigger is removed and in the absence of comorbidity, with full recovery from renal failure the rule when there is no prior kidney disease (p.792, 799, 801). No single formal grading. Severity is gauged clinically by the hemoglobin level and tempo (mild compensated hemolysis without anemia through to abrupt severe drops to ~4 g/dL in AIHA) and by the site of hemolysis: intravascular hemolysis is signalled by hemoglobinuria, free plasma hemoglobin, LDH up to ~10x normal, and absent haptoglobin, whereas extravascular hemolysis chiefly raises unconjugated bilirubin and urobilinogen. High-risk markers in AIHA include hemoglobin <6 g/dL, acute renal failure, infection, and Evans syndrome (p.791-792, 801, Tables 105-2, 105-7).

Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn — HDN, hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, HDFN, erythroblastosis fetalis Non-immune hydrops fetalis Hereditary red cell membrane or enzyme defects (e.g. spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency) Sepsis-associated haemolysis or jaundice Cephalohaematoma or extravascular blood breakdown causing jaundice Physiological or breast-milk jaundice Twin-to-twin transfusion and other causes of neonatal anaemia Maternal and infant blood group and antibody screening Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the newborn Serial total and unconjugated bilirubin measurements Full blood count with reticulocyte count and blood film Fetal middle cerebral artery Doppler to assess for fetal anaemia antenatally Follow-up haemoglobin to detect late anaemia Immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal or neonatal red cells caused by maternal antibodies crossing the placenta and targeting fetal red cell antigens inherited from the father. Rhesus (anti-D) disease was historically the most severe form; ABO incompatibility is now a more common but generally milder cause, and other minor blood-group antibodies can also be responsible. Rh disease typically requires prior maternal sensitisation, so it usually spares the first pregnancy and worsens with subsequent affected pregnancies, whereas ABO disease can affect a first-born. Severe fetal anaemia can cause hydrops fetalis with generalised oedema, effusions, hepatosplenomegaly, and heart failure. In the newborn the dominant problem is rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin from ongoing haemolysis, which can appear within the first day of life. A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test on the infant supports immune haemolysis, along with anaemia, reticulocytosis, and a rising bilirubin. Rh disease is largely preventable by giving anti-D immunoglobulin to at-risk Rh-negative mothers to prevent sensitisation. Management ranges from monitoring and phototherapy for hyperbilirubinaemia to exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly rising bilirubin, and intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia. Late anaemia can develop over the following weeks as haemolysis and marrow suppression continue, so follow-up haemoglobin monitoring is important. Hydrops fetalis with severe anaemia and heart failure Rapidly rising or very high unconjugated bilirubin threatening bilirubin encephalopathy Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor feeding, hypertonia, abnormal cry) Severe or late anaemia requiring transfusion Underestimating ABO disease because it can affect a first-born and cause significant jaundice Failing to monitor bilirubin closely and intervene before it reaches neurotoxic levels Overlooking late anaemia in the weeks after birth once early jaundice has settled Missing an opportunity for anti-D prophylaxis in an at-risk mother Attributing early jaundice to physiological causes when haemolysis is occurring When fetal red cells carrying a paternally inherited antigen absent in the mother enter the maternal circulation, the mother may form IgG alloantibodies. These IgG antibodies cross the placenta, bind fetal red cells, and cause their destruction, chiefly in the fetal spleen. The resulting anaemia stimulates extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, causes high-output cardiac failure, hepatic dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia, and hydrops. After birth, loss of placental clearance means the newborn must conjugate the large bilirubin load from continuing haemolysis with an immature liver, producing rapidly rising unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that risks bilirubin neurotoxicity. With antenatal surveillance, intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia, and neonatal phototherapy or exchange transfusion, outcomes are generally good. Prophylactic anti-D has dramatically reduced severe Rh disease. Prognosis worsens if severe hyperbilirubinaemia progresses to kernicterus or if profound fetal anaemia and hydrops are untreated.

features and severe ADAMTS13 deficiency predominate Measuring ADAMTS13 activity helps separate TTP (severely reduced) from HUS (usually normal or only modestly reduced), which is critical because treatments differ Shiga-toxin-associated HUS is largely managed with meticulous supportive care and dialysis when needed, and antibiotics are generally avoided as they may worsen toxin release Complement-mediated atypical HUS responds to terminal complement blockade, which has substantially improved renal and overall outcomes Rapidly progressive acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria requiring urgent dialysis Severe thrombocytopenia with active bleeding Neurological deterioration raising concern for overlapping TTP or CNS involvement Hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, or refractory hypertension as life-threatening complications of renal failure Confusing HUS with TTP and delaying the correct treatment; ADAMTS13 testing helps distinguish them Giving antibiotics in Shiga-toxin-associated HUS, which may increase toxin release and worsen disease Attributing thrombocytopenia and anaemia to sepsis or DIC without examining the film for schistocytes Failing to consider atypical HUS in relapsing or familial disease and missing the opportunity for complement inhibition Transfusing platelets reflexively, which can aggravate microvascular thrombosis HUS is a thrombotic microangiopathy in which endothelial injury triggers platelet-rich microthrombi in small vessels, especially the renal microvasculature. In Shiga-toxin-associated disease, toxin absorbed from the gut binds glomerular and endothelial cells, causing injury, platelet activation, and microvascular thrombosis. In atypical HUS, uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, from inherited or acquired defects in complement regulatory proteins, drives endothelial damage. The resulting microthrombi mechanically shear passing red cells (producing schistocytes and haemolysis), consume platelets (causing thrombocytopenia), and obstruct renal perfusion (causing acute kidney injury). Shiga-toxin-associated HUS in children often recovers with supportive care, though a minority sustain chronic kidney damage; atypical, complement-mediated HUS historically carried a high risk of end-stage renal disease and death, but outcomes have improved markedly with complement-blocking therapy.
