factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor Missing von Willebrand disease as the reason for a low factor VIII level Overlooking an inhibitor when bleeding fails to respond to appropriate replacement Giving intramuscular injections or arterial punctures that provoke deep bleeding Delaying treatment of a suspected head bleed to await imaging or laboratory confirmation Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in F8 on the X chromosome that reduce the activity of coagulation factor VIII, a cofactor that greatly accelerates factor IXa-mediated activation of factor X within the intrinsic tenase complex. Without adequate factor VIII the propagation phase of coagulation is impaired, so thrombin generation on the platelet surface is markedly reduced and the fibrin clot forms slowly and is unstable. Because the initial platelet plug still forms, bleeding is typically delayed and occurs into joints and deep tissues; repeated haemarthroses cause synovial inflammation and progressive destructive arthropathy. With prophylactic replacement or modern non-factor therapies most patients achieve near-normal life expectancy and greatly reduced joint damage, but inhibitor development and established arthropathy remain important sources of morbidity.

Activated factor IX, with factor VIII as cofactor, forms the intrinsic tenase complex that activates factor X on the platelet surface. Deficiency of factor IX therefore impairs the same propagation step of coagulation as factor VIII deficiency, reducing thrombin generation and producing a slow, unstable clot. As in haemophilia A the initial platelet plug forms normally, so bleeding is delayed and occurs into joints and deep tissues, and recurrent haemarthroses drive progressive arthropathy. With prophylaxis using factor IX or modern non-factor therapy, most patients have near-normal life expectancy and much reduced joint damage, though inhibitors, when they occur, can be complicated by allergic reactions and are harder to manage.

confirms the diagnosis Management is largely tailored to the bleeding history and procedure, using antifibrinolytics, factor XI replacement or plasma products, with individualised peri-operative planning Excessive bleeding after surgery or trauma at fibrinolytic-rich sites (oral, nasal, genitourinary) Unexpected postpartum haemorrhage Bleeding disproportionate to the measured factor level Rare inhibitor development, particularly in severely deficient patients after replacement Predicting bleeding risk from the factor XI level, which correlates poorly with clinical bleeding Confusing an isolated prolonged aPTT with a non-bleeding contact-factor deficiency or a lupus anticoagulant Over-transfusing plasma products and risking volume overload or unnecessary exposure Failing to plan haemostatic cover before high-risk procedures at fibrinolytic sites Haemophilia C results from mutations in F11 that reduce the activity of coagulation factor XI, a component of the intrinsic pathway that, once activated, amplifies thrombin generation partly through activation of factor IX. Its role is chiefly in reinforcing and sustaining the clot rather than initiating haemostasis, which explains why bleeding is usually milder and less consistent than with factor VIII or IX deficiency. Because factor XI contributes to protecting clots against fibrinolysis, bleeding is particularly prone to occur at sites rich in local fibrinolytic activity, and the poor correlation between factor level and bleeding suggests additional modifying haemostatic factors. Prognosis is generally good, with many patients only bleeding in response to surgery or trauma, and careful individualised peri-procedural management usually prevents serious bleeding.

bleeding Aggressive banding or surgery in patients with portal hypertension or coagulopathy Overlooking thrombosis or strangulation as the cause of acute severe pain Haemorrhoids result from abnormal engorgement and downward displacement of the normal anal cushions, which are vascular submucosal structures that contribute to continence. Chronic straining, constipation, and raised intra-abdominal pressure disrupt the supporting connective tissue, allowing the cushions to enlarge, congest, and prolapse. The classical sites are the left lateral, right anterior, and right posterior positions. Bleeding is arteriovenous in origin, giving the characteristic bright red colour. Thrombosis of external components or prolapsed internal haemorrhoids produces acute pain, and long-standing prolapse can cause mucous discharge and pruritus. Most haemorrhoids respond to conservative measures or office procedures with good symptom control, though recurrence is possible. Surgical treatment of advanced disease is effective but may cause post-operative pain and, rarely, incontinence or stenosis.

exploration Using crystalloid alone rather than blood products in significant haemorrhage Overlooking a great-vessel injury as the source Haemothorax is accumulation of blood in the pleural space, usually from injury to the chest wall vessels (such as intercostal or internal mammary arteries), the lung, or the great vessels. The pleural cavity can hold a large proportion of the circulating blood volume, so bleeding into it causes hypovolaemic shock. At the same time, the collected blood compresses the ipsilateral lung and can shift the mediastinum, impairing ventilation and, when large, venous return. Thus a massive haemothorax produces the dual insult of haemorrhage and respiratory compromise, and the blood must be evacuated while the circulation is restored. Prognosis depends on the rate and source of bleeding and associated injuries. Prompt drainage with adequate transfusion allows recovery in many cases, while massive or ongoing haemorrhage that is not controlled surgically carries high mortality.

Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) — HSP, IgA vasculitis, anaphylactoid purpura, Henoch-Schonlein syndrome Meningococcaemia / sepsis with purpura Immune thrombocytopenia and other bleeding disorders Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Acute abdomen from other causes (e.g. appendicitis) Other systemic vasculitides Systemic lupus erythematosus Urinalysis for haematuria and proteinuria (repeated over follow-up) Blood pressure measurement Full blood count and coagulation studies to confirm normal platelets and exclude bleeding disorders Renal function and serum albumin Abdominal ultrasound if intussusception or significant gut involvement is suspected Skin or renal biopsy showing IgA deposition in atypical or severe cases The most common small-vessel vasculitis of childhood, typically affecting children 3-10 years, often following an upper respiratory infection. The classic tetrad is palpable purpura (predominantly on the buttocks and lower limbs), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. The rash is non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura, distinguishing it from bleeding disorders; platelet count and coagulation are normal. Gastrointestinal involvement causes colicky abdominal pain and can be complicated by intussusception, which is typically ileo-ileal. Renal involvement ranges from isolated microscopic haematuria to nephritis; it is the main determinant of long-term prognosis. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by palpable purpura plus at least one of abdominal pain, arthritis, or renal involvement; biopsy shows IgA deposition when needed. Most cases are self-limiting; management is largely supportive with analgesia and hydration, and corticosteroids are considered for severe abdominal or other significant organ involvement. Prolonged urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring are needed after recovery to detect delayed or progressive nephritis. Severe abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, or signs of intussusception or bowel ischaemia Gastrointestinal bleeding Hypertension, oliguria, heavy proteinuria, or rising creatinine indicating significant nephritis Scrotal pain or swelling (testicular involvement mimicking torsion) Purpura in an unwell, febrile, toxic child raising concern for meningococcaemia Confusing the purpura with a bleeding disorder and missing that platelets are normal Failing to monitor urinalysis and blood pressure after the acute illness, missing delayed nephritis Overlooking intussusception as a cause of worsening abdominal pain Attributing all abdominal pain to HSP and missing a surgical abdomen Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterised by deposition of IgA1-containing immune complexes in the walls of small vessels of the skin, gut, joints, and kidney. This triggers a leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration and vessel wall inflammation, producing the palpable purpura and visceral manifestations. In the kidney, mesangial IgA deposition causes a glomerulonephritis histologically similar to IgA nephropathy. A preceding infection or other antigenic trigger is thought to initiate the abnormal IgA response in susceptible children. Most children recover completely within weeks, though relapses can occur; long-term outcome is dictated by renal involvement, with a small proportion developing chronic kidney disease, so renal follow-up is essential.

are avoided unless there is serious bleeding New arterial or venous thrombosis accompanying a heparin-associated fall in platelet count, which is a medical emergency Limb ischaemia, skin necrosis at injection sites, or acute systemic reactions after heparin exposure Continued heparin exposure once HIT is suspected Introduction of a vitamin K antagonist before platelet recovery, risking venous limb gangrene Attributing thrombocytopenia to other causes and continuing heparin Merely stopping heparin without starting an alternative anticoagulant, leaving the patient prothrombotic Relying on a positive immunoassay alone without considering pretest probability or functional confirmation Giving prophylactic platelet transfusions or starting a vitamin K antagonist prematurely Heparin binds platelet factor 4 released from platelets, forming complexes that can be recognised by IgG antibodies in susceptible patients. The resulting immune complexes engage platelet Fc-gamma-RIIa receptors, driving platelet activation, aggregation, and consumption, which lowers the platelet count. Activated platelets shed procoagulant microparticles and the antibodies also activate monocytes and endothelium to express tissue factor, generating a strongly prothrombotic state. This explains the characteristic combination of falling platelets with new arterial or venous thrombosis rather than bleeding. With prompt withdrawal of heparin and prompt anticoagulation using a non-heparin agent, outcomes improve substantially, but delayed recognition carries a high risk of thrombosis, limb loss, and death.

Hepatic encephalopathy — Ammonia, LFT, coagulation Identify precipitant (SBP, GI bleed) Look for precipitating infection (e.g. SBP) Other causes of altered mental status must always be considered, since the diagnosis is clinical (Harrison 22e p.2716) Sedative/narcotic intoxication (Harrison 22e p.2629) Renal failure / uremic encephalopathy (Harrison 22e p.2629) Respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.2629) Electrolyte imbalance as a primary cause of confusion (Harrison 22e p.2629) Careful mental status examination is the central assessment (Harrison 22e p.2629) Trail-making (connect-the-dots / number-connection) test: normal 15-30 s, markedly prolonged in early HE (Harrison 22e p.2629) Bedside cognitive tasks such as drawing abstract objects or comparing the patient's signature with prior examples (Harrison 22e p.2629) Diagnostic paracentesis of ascites to exclude infection as a precipitant (Harrison 22e p.2716) Evaluate for GI bleeding (Harrison 22e p.2716) Serum electrolytes (Harrison 22e p.2716) EEG and visual evoked potentials can detect mild forms but are rarely clinically useful (Harrison 22e p.2629) Metabolic encephalopathy from other causes (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperosmolar states, hypercapnia, hypercalcemia, renal failure) — asterixis and multifocal myoclonus are nonspecific and indicate a metabolic or toxic process generally, not HE specifically (Harrison 22e p.230, p.225) Drug intoxication, which likewise can produce asterixis in a drowsy, confused patient (Harrison 22e p.231) Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol withdrawal in patients with alcohol-associated liver disease (Harrison 22e p.2674) Hepatic encephalopathy is far more common in chronic liver disease than in acute liver injury; in severe acute liver injury its presence is itself a defining criterion for acute liver failure (Harrison 22e p.2716). Asterixis (the 'liver flap') is typically present and is elicited by having the patient extend the arms and dorsiflex the wrists, looking for a sudden forward jerk of the wrist; it requires a cooperative patient (Harrison 22e p.2716). Earliest manifestations are subtle and nonspecific: altered sleep pattern, personality change, irritability, and mental dullness, progressing to confusion, disorientation, stupor and coma (Harrison 22e p.2629). Patients may be agitated, violent and hard to manage, or alternatively very sleepy and difficult to rouse (Harrison 22e p.2716). In acute liver failure, presentation may include excitability or mania rather than depressed consciousness (Harrison 22e p.2629). Fetor hepaticus, a sweetish ammoniacal breath odor, can accompany liver failure, especially with portosystemic shunting of blood (Harrison 22e p.2629). After a first episode, patients and caregivers often learn to recognize recurrences early and can self-medicate to prevent worsening (Harrison 22e p.2717). Gut-derived neurotoxins that bypass the liver because of vascular shunting and reduced hepatic mass reach the brain and produce the syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2716). Encephalopathy appearing during acute hepatitis is the major criterion for acute liver failure and indicates a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2629) In acute liver failure, severe encephalopathy with cerebral edema can progress to cerebral herniation (Harrison 22e p.2716) Other presenting features of poor prognosis in acute hepatitis: ascites, peripheral edema, prolonged PT, hypoalbuminemia, hypoglycemia, very high bilirubin (Harrison 22e p.2672) HE may herald acute-on-chronic liver failure (brain is one of the failing organ systems), which carries 28-day mortality of 20-70% rising with the number of organ failures (Harrison 22e p.2717) Ammonia levels are typically elevated but correlate poorly with severity of liver disease; most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to make the diagnosis or to follow clinical progress (Harrison 22e p.2716). Always identify and treat a precipitant — in cirrhosis, encephalopathy is usually triggered by volume depletion/dehydration, GI bleeding, infection, constipation, hyponatremia, overdiuresis, uremia, electrolyte imbalance, or sedatives/narcotic analgesics; correcting hydration and electrolytes alone is sometimes sufficient (Harrison 22e p.2629, p.2716). Asterixis is nonspecific — it also occurs in other metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, so it does not by itself establish HE (Harrison 22e p.230-231). The diagnosis is clinical and requires an experienced clinician to integrate the various features; there is no single confirmatory test (Harrison 22e p.2716). Hepatic encephalopathy is an alteration of mental status and cognition resulting from liver failure, in which gut-derived neurotoxins are not cleared because of portosystemic vascular shunting and decreased functional hepatic mass and thus reach the brain. Ammonia is the principal candidate toxin: high ammonia concentrations are thought to drive increased synthesis of glutamine within astrocytes, causing osmotic astrocyte swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, and generation of reactive nitrogen and oxygen species, together with increased levels of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and synthesis of putative 'false' neurotransmitters. No single one of these mechanisms fully explains the confusion and stupor, and which is mainly responsible for hepatic coma is not known. Other contributing compounds include certain false neurotransmitters and mercaptans. Chronic HE is characteristically accompanied by diffuse astrocytosis. In acute liver failure (but not chronic liver disease) cerebral edema with gray-matter swelling can occur and carries a risk of cerebral herniation (Harrison 22e p.230-231, p.2716). Development of hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is a poor prognostic sign, although the complication can be managed in the vast majority of patients. Hepatic encephalopathy grade is one of the five Child-Pugh variables (with bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time, and ascites severity) used to stratify cirrhosis into classes A-C of predicted survival. In acute hepatitis, the appearance of encephalopathy defines acute liver failure and indicates poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2717, p.2629). Severity is graded clinically along a continuum from the earliest covert/subtle changes (altered sleep, personality change, irritability, mental dullness — detectable mainly by mental-status testing such as the trail-making test) through confusion and disorientation to stupor and coma. Encephalopathy grade is incorporated as one component of the Child-Pugh classification of cirrhosis severity. (Note: Harrison 22e describes this graded clinical spectrum and 'grade' in the Child-Pugh score but the supplied text does not lay out the explicit numbered West Haven criteria; Harrison 22e p.2629, p.2716, p.2715/HCC staging.)

ACE inhibitors and oestrogen-containing agents should be avoided as they worsen disease Laryngeal or tongue swelling, voice change, stridor, or difficulty swallowing indicating life-threatening airway obstruction requiring urgent bradykinin-targeted therapy and airway management Severe abdominal attacks risking misdiagnosis as an acute surgical abdomen Swelling unresponsive to adrenaline, antihistamines, and corticosteroids Rapid progression of facial or oropharyngeal oedema, particularly after dental or surgical procedures Treating attacks as allergic and relying on antihistamines, steroids, or adrenaline, which are ineffective Failing to recognise abdominal attacks and proceeding to unnecessary surgery Prescribing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing contraceptives, which precipitate attacks Omitting short-term prophylaxis before dental, surgical, or airway procedures Hereditary angioedema most often results from autosomal dominant deficiency or dysfunction of C1 inhibitor (SERPING1 mutations). C1 inhibitor normally restrains the contact (kallikrein-kinin), complement, and fibrinolytic systems. Its deficiency permits unchecked activation of plasma kallikrein, which cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to generate excess bradykinin. Bradykinin acting on B2 receptors increases vascular permeability, producing the characteristic submucosal and subcutaneous oedema. A minority of patients have HAE with normal C1 inhibitor caused by mutations that enhance contact-system activation (e.g. factor XII, plasminogen, angiopoietin-1). Because the mechanism is kinin- rather than histamine-driven, mast-cell-directed therapies are ineffective. With modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy targeting the bradykinin pathway, most patients achieve good disease control and near-normal life expectancy. Untreated or unrecognised laryngeal attacks, however, carry a substantial risk of death from asphyxiation.

Weakening of these vertical linkages allows portions of the lipid bilayer to be lost, so the cell reduces its surface-area-to-volume ratio and becomes spherical rather than biconcave. These spherocytes are poorly deformable and cannot easily traverse the narrow cords of the splenic red pulp, where they are retained and prematurely destroyed by macrophages. The resulting extravascular haemolysis produces anaemia, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with jaundice, splenomegaly, and a compensatory reticulocytosis. With supportive care and, where indicated, splenectomy, most patients have a good long-term outlook and near-normal life expectancy; the main hazards are aplastic and haemolytic crises, gallstone complications, and, after splenectomy, serious infection.

In the common dehydrated variant, gain-of-function mutations in the mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1, or in the Gardos potassium channel KCNN4, lead to net cation and water loss, so cells become dehydrated and rigid (xerocytes), shortening their survival. In the rarer overhydrated form, cation influx exceeds efflux and cells become overhydrated and swollen. The altered hydration and deformability cause a variably compensated haemolytic anaemia and the characteristic stomatocyte morphology. As in other chronic haemolytic states, ineffective regulation of iron balance and enhanced absorption predispose to iron overload, and the disorders carry a notable thrombotic tendency that is greatly amplified by splenectomy. Many patients have a mild, well-compensated haemolytic anaemia with a good outlook, but long-term morbidity is driven by iron overload and by thrombotic risk that is markedly increased if the spleen is removed.

allopurinol is ineffective and inappropriate Obstructing xanthine stones causing acute kidney injury Recurrent urinary tract infection with obstructing calculi Progressive renal impairment from recurrent stone disease Myopathy with rising creatine kinase from tissue xanthine deposition Prescribing a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, which cannot work and worsens xanthine load Overlooking radiolucent xanthine stones on plain imaging Dismissing marked hypouricaemia as laboratory error rather than investigating it Failing to distinguish type I from type II, which has implications for associated aldehyde oxidase deficiency Not advising adequate fluid intake to prevent stone formation Hereditary xanthinuria is an inborn error of the terminal steps of purine degradation. Xanthine oxidase/dehydrogenase normally oxidises hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid; when it is deficient (type I) or when the molybdenum cofactor sulfurase needed for its activity is lacking (type II, which also disables aldehyde oxidase), these purines cannot be converted to uric acid. Consequently uric acid levels are strikingly low while xanthine and hypoxanthine accumulate and are excreted in excess. Because xanthine is far less soluble than uric acid, it may crystallise in the urinary tract to form calculi and can deposit in tissues such as muscle. Many patients remain asymptomatic with a normal life expectancy; in those who form stones, adequate hydration and dietary measures usually limit complications, though recurrent obstructive calculi can occasionally threaten renal function.

Heritable Disorders of Connective Tissue — Osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Chondrodysplasias, Heritable thoracic aortic aneurysm disease (HTAD) Postmenopausal or secondary osteoporosis (can mimic mild adult-onset OI) Battered child syndrome / non-accidental injury (versus OI fractures in infants) Nutritional deficiencies (e.g., rickets) and hypophosphatasia Other chondrodysplasias and skeletal dysplasias presenting with short stature Homocystinuria (marfanoid habitus with ectopia lentis - lens dislocation typically downward) Mucopolysaccharidoses and other lysosomal storage disorders Acquired/secondary causes of joint hypermobility distinct from hereditary EDS Targeted candidate-gene sequencing, multigene skeletal/EDS/HTAD panels, or whole-exome sequencing for molecular diagnosis Skin fibroblast culture biochemistry for collagen synthesis/structure in selected cases DXA bone densitometry (note it underestimates true mineral in OI; quantitative backscattered electron imaging or 3D CT reveals hypermineralization) Skeletal radiographs (Wormian skull bones, popcorn metaphyses, beaded ribs, undertubulated long bones in OI) Echocardiography for aortic root and valve assessment (MFS, LDS, and adults with OI) Slit-lamp ophthalmologic examination for ectopia lentis in suspected MFS Plasma amino acid analysis to exclude homocystinuria in marfanoid patients Spirometry/pulmonary function testing in moderate-to-severe OI Bone histomorphometry in selected diagnostically difficult OI cases Osteoporosis and osteopenia of other cause Acromegaly (paw-like hand/foot enlargement of primary hypertrophic osteopathy can mimic it) Secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy from pulmonary disease Osteoarthritis (mild adult chondrodysplasia can resemble primary generalized OA) Homocystinuria mimicking Marfan syndrome Non-syndromic familial thoracic aortic aneurysm versus syndromic HTAD This is an umbrella group of several hundred genetic disorders affecting bone, cartilage, skin, tendons and other connective tissues; mutations in over 550 genes underlie 771 defined skeletal disorders, so classification by either clinical phenotype or causative gene remains a continuing challenge. Connective tissue strength comes from fibrillar collagens (types I, II, III) whose alpha chains have a repeating Gly-X-Y sequence; glycine, the smallest amino acid, must occupy every third position, so substitution of glycine by a bulkier residue is a frequent disease-causing mechanism. Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is dominated by bone fragility, deformity and growth deficiency; ~80-85% of cases stem from heterozygous COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations, and secondary features include blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, basilar invagination and cardiac-valve abnormalities. OI bone is paradoxically hypermineralized: DXA returns a reduced density value, yet quantitative backscattered electron imaging and 3D CT show the bone is over-mineralized, making it both weak and brittle so that it snaps like chalk. Null COL1A1 mutations (about half-normal but structurally normal collagen) produce mild type I OI, whereas structural glycine-substitution defects produce the more severe types II-IV; type II causes in-utero fractures and perinatal death. The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) share soft hyperextensible skin, abnormal wound healing with atrophic/papyraceous scarring, easy bruising and joint hypermobility; the current classification recognizes 13 clinical types across roughly 20 genes. Vascular EDS (COL3A1, type III collagen) is the dangerous form: medium- and large-vessel arterial rupture, sigmoid colon perforation without prior colon disease, and uterine rupture in the third trimester can occur, often in skin that is thin and translucent rather than velvety hyperextensible. Classic EDS is most often due to COL5A1/COL5A2 (type V collagen) mutations in ~90% of patients; hypermobile EDS has no identified gene, so it remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Marfan syndrome (MFS) classically combines a tall marfanoid habitus with arachnodactyly, ectopia lentis (lens dislocation, ~60%), and aortic root dilation at the sinuses of Valsalva; ~95% of cases are due to fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutations. FBN1 defects impair not only microfibril structure but also TGF-beta bioavailability; reduced/altered fibrillin-1 releases sequestered TGF-beta in the aortic wall, driving remodeling, excess MMP-2/MMP-9, and the aneurysmal phenotype. Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/2, TGFB2/3, SMAD2/3) overlaps with MFS but is distinguished by arterial tortuosity and aneurysms beyond the aortic root, hypertelorism, and cleft palate or bifid uvula; ectopia lentis is typically absent. Achondroplasia, the common short-limb dwarfism, is caused by a gain-of-function FGFR3 mutation; most cases are sporadic, and the homozygous form is more severe and may be lethal in the neonate. Acute severe chest, back or abdominal pain in MFS/LDS or vascular EDS - possible aortic dissection or arterial rupture Rapidly enlarging aortic root or sinus of Valsalva dilation on echocardiography Spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation or organ rupture in vascular EDS Uterine rupture in the third trimester (vascular EDS) and obstetric complications Recurrent or in-utero fractures with progressive deformity (severe/lethal OI) Progressive basilar invagination/impression with neurologic compromise in severe OI Declining pulmonary function or recurrent pneumonia in severe OI (leading cause of death) DXA underestimates true bone mineral in OI - a low DXA value coexists with actual hypermineralization, so bone is brittle despite the reading. Marfan-like presentation may actually be homocystinuria; always check plasma amino acids before settling on MFS. Hypermobile EDS has no confirmed gene; it is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be confirmed by genetic testing. Same clinical OI subtype may be assigned different type labels over a patient's lifetime or among family members under clinical (versus genetic) classification. Blue sclerae are not specific to OI - they occur in EDS, MFS and even healthy individuals; conversely severe neonatal OI with white sclerae suggests recessive prolyl 3-hydroxylation defects. In infants, OI fractures may be mistaken for non-accidental injury (battered child syndrome). Tissues in MFS/LDS and EDS are friable, complicating surgical repair. Connective tissues (skin, bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon, vessel wall) are built from an extracellular matrix of fibrillar collagens, proteoglycans, elastin/fibrillin microfibrils and noncollagenous glycoproteins. Fibrillar collagen monomers are triple helices of alpha chains with a repeating Gly-X-Y motif; glycine at every third position is sterically required, and proline/hydroxyproline confer rigidity. Procollagen undergoes extensive post-translational processing (prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation requiring ascorbate, glycosylation, triple-helix folding aided by chaperones, secretion, N- and C-propeptide cleavage, then self-assembly into fibrils stabilized by lysyl-oxidase cross-links). Mutations may be quantitative (null alleles giving reduced normal collagen, generally milder) or structural (glycine substitutions, splice defects, charged/branched residue substitutions in X/Y positions) that disrupt folding, fibril assembly and mineralization. OI arises mainly from dominant type I collagen defects, plus rarer recessive defects in collagen modification, processing, folding/cross-linking and osteoblast differentiation. EDS reflects defects in collagen types I/III/V, in processing enzymes (ADAMTS2), cross-linking (PLOD1/lysyl hydroxylase 1), glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, or matrix glycoproteins (tenascin X). Marfan/HTAD reflects fibrillin-1 microfibril dysfunction with secondary dysregulation of TGF-beta signaling; Loeys-Dietz reflects primary mutations in the TGF-beta pathway. Chondrodysplasias reflect intrinsic cartilage/growth-plate abnormalities (e.g., FGFR3 gain-of-function in achondroplasia, COL2A1 in type II collagenopathies). Highly variable, even within a single disorder type and among family members carrying the same mutation. In OI, type I is mild and fractures often decline after puberty, while type II is lethal in the perinatal period; pulmonary disease is the leading cause of death in OI. In Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, cardiovascular disease (aortic dilation, dissection, rupture; mitral valve disease) is the major source of morbidity and mortality, and dilation rate is unpredictable and accelerated by exertion, emotional stress and pregnancy. Vascular EDS carries serious risk from arterial, intestinal and uterine rupture. Milder phenotypes across these disorders may go undiagnosed and have near-normal life expectancy. Osteogenesis imperfecta is classified by the Sillence system (clinical/radiologic types I-IV: type I mildest with normal-quality but reduced collagen; type II perinatal lethal; type III progressively deforming; type IV mild-to-moderate) extended to genetic types V-XXII grouped by causative gene and mechanism. Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are classified into 13 clinical types (e.g., classic, vascular, hypermobile, arthrochalasia, dermatosparaxis, kyphoscoliotic) by clinical features, inheritance and molecular defect. Marfan syndrome diagnosis uses the revised Ghent nosology, emphasizing aortic root dilation/dissection and ectopia lentis as cardinal features plus a systemic score. Heritable thoracic aortic disease is divided into syndromic and nonsyndromic (familial thoracic aortic aneurysm) forms.

bleeding, particularly around surgery or childbirth Recurrent severe infection in immunodeficiency-associated subtypes Refractory colitis with weight loss and systemic upset Attributing the bleeding dental procedures Mislabelling the granulomatous colitis as classic inflammatory bowel disease Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome results from biallelic variants in genes encoding subunits of protein complexes (including AP-3 and the biogenesis of lysosome-related organelle complexes, BLOC) that direct cargo to lysosome-related organelles. Defective biogenesis impairs melanosomes (albinism), platelet dense granules (bleeding) and other specialised organelles. Progressive accumulation of ceroid lipofuscin and dysregulated lysosomal function in the lung and gut contribute to pulmonary fibrosis and granulomatous colitis in susceptible subtypes. Prognosis depends on subtype: pigmentary and bleeding features are lifelong but manageable, whereas subtypes prone to pulmonary fibrosis (notably HPS1 and HPS4) have a substantially reduced life expectancy from progressive respiratory failure.

Herpes Simplex Virus Infection — HSV, HSV-1, HSV-2 Varicella-zoster virus (chickenpox/shingles) for vesicular eruptions Coxsackievirus A16 (hand-foot-and-mouth disease) Aphthous ulcers (recurrent oral ulceration) Other causes of genital ulcer disease (e.g., syphilis, chancroid) in genital HSV Varicella-zoster virus infection (vesicular lesions are individually similar to HSV; Tzanck smear cannot distinguish them) Reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) due to Mycoplasma/other respiratory infections, which mimics mucositis seen with HSV-associated erythema multiforme Disseminated VZV versus disseminated HSV (individual lesions similar for VZV and HSV) PCR of CSF for HSV in suspected encephalitis (diagnostic test of choice; may be falsely negative early in the course of disease) (Harrison p.747) Tzanck smear of an early unroofed vesicle (Giemsa/Wright stain): multinucleated epithelial giant cells suggest HSV or VZV, but cannot identify the specific virus (Harrison p.~480) Viral culture, immunofluorescence microscopy, or genetic/PCR testing to identify the specific virus type (Harrison p.~480) In FUO with headache, CSF microbiologic examination including HSV (especially type 2) (Harrison p.~149) Erythema multiforme major / Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (HSV is itself a common trigger of EM, but drug-induced SJS/TEN must be distinguished) Pemphigus vulgaris (blistering eruption with mucositis) Aphthous stomatitis Primary HSV infection produces erythema followed by hallmark painful grouped vesicles that may evolve into pustules and ulcerate, especially on mucosal surfaces; lesions appear at the site of inoculation (Harrison p.~1010, App. A1). HSV-1 classically causes orolabial disease (cold sores, herpes labialis) and HSV-2 causes genital lesions, but either type can infect either site (Harrison p.1050). Non-genital cutaneous presentations include herpes gladiatorum (head and neck of young wrestlers) and herpetic whitlow (digits of health care workers) (Harrison p.1050). Primary acute herpetic gingivostomatitis (usually HSV-1) presents with labial vesicles that rupture and crust plus intraoral vesicles that quickly ulcerate; it is extremely painful, with acute gingivitis, fever, malaise, foul odor, and cervical lymphadenopathy, occurring primarily in infants, children, and young adults (Harrison p.~325, Table 38-1). Recurrent disease is milder than primary infection, and there is typically no fever in recurrent infection; herpes labialis recurrences typically do not involve the oral mucosa (Harrison App. A1). Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide, and there is a documented positive-feedback loop between HSV and HIV transmission (Harrison p.1096). Although the HSV–HIV epidemiologic link is consistent, randomized trials of antiviral suppression of HSV showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison p.1096). Fever with decreased level of consciousness and unilateral temporal-lobe involvement on imaging suggests HSV encephalitis - start empiric aciclovir promptly because CSF PCR may be falsely negative early (Harrison p.747) Disseminated/visceral HSV in immunocompromised or neonatal patients; HSV can disseminate viscerally even with only localized mucocutaneous disease Eczema herpeticum (HSV dissemination in eczematous skin) Neonatal HSV disease (skin lesions are diagnostically helpful when present but may be absent) CSF HSV PCR may be falsely negative early in the course of encephalitis, so a negative early result does not exclude the diagnosis and should not delay empiric aciclovir (Harrison p.747) Tzanck smear cannot distinguish HSV from VZV; type-specific identification requires culture, immunofluorescence, or genetic testing (Harrison p.~480) HSV visceral dissemination can occur with only localized mucocutaneous disease, so absence of widespread skin lesions does not exclude serious systemic infection (Harrison App. A1) Oral lesions lasting more than 3 weeks should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis rather than primary HSV (Harrison Table 38-1) HSV-1 and HSV-2 are neurotropic DNA herpesviruses that establish lifelong latency in sensory ganglia after primary mucocutaneous infection; periodic reactivation produces recurrent localized disease (e.g., recurrent herpes labialis with HSV-1 and herpes genitalis with HSV-2). Virus enters and replicates within the epidermis at the site of inoculation. In HSV encephalitis there is characteristic unilateral temporal-lobe involvement. The virus can disseminate, particularly in the setting of disrupted skin (eczema herpeticum) or impaired cell-mediated immunity; visceral dissemination may occur even with only localized mucocutaneous disease (Harrison pp.1050, 1010 App. A1, p.747). Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis heals spontaneously in 10-14 days; lesions persisting beyond 3 weeks (unless secondarily infected) are not due to primary HSV infection. Recurrent disease is generally milder than primary infection. Approximately 25% of patients with herpes simplex encephalitis subsequently develop an autoimmune (anti-NMDAR) encephalitis weeks after the viral infection resolves - in children often with choreoathetosis and in adults with cognitive/psychiatric symptoms (Harrison pp.325, 821).

Herpes simplex keratitis — HSV keratitis, herpetic keratitis, dendritic keratitis, HSK Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with pseudodendrites Acanthamoeba keratitis (especially in contact lens wearers) Bacterial or fungal keratitis Recurrent corneal erosion Healing epithelial defect with a pseudodendrite Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein and rose bengal or lissamine green staining Testing of corneal sensation before instilling anaesthetic Corneal scrape for viral PCR or culture in atypical or unclear cases Assessment of stromal involvement, endothelial oedema, and intraocular pressure Consideration of immune status in severe or bilateral disease Presents with a red, painful, watery eye, photophobia, and blurred vision, often preceded by mild irritation The classic sign is a branching dendritic epithelial ulcer with terminal end-bulbs that stains with fluorescein, with the ulcer bed highlighted by rose bengal or lissamine green Reduced corneal sensation is a valuable clue to a herpetic cause Disease may be epithelial (active viral replication), stromal (immune-mediated, with the risk of scarring and neovascularisation), or endothelial (disciform keratitis) Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in active epithelial (dendritic) disease as they promote unchecked viral replication and can enlarge the ulcer into a geographic form Epithelial disease is treated with topical or oral antiviral therapy; stromal and endothelial immune disease requires cautious steroids under antiviral cover and specialist supervision Recurrences are common because the virus remains latent in the trigeminal ganglion; repeated episodes cause cumulative scarring and neurotrophic changes Long-term oral antiviral prophylaxis reduces recurrence in patients with frequent episodes A dendritic (or geographic) ulcer, which mandates avoidance of topical steroids in active epithelial disease Worsening or enlarging ulcer after steroid exposure suggesting steroid-driven progression Stromal necrosis, thinning, or a neurotrophic non-healing defect threatening perforation Deep central scarring or dense keratitis causing significant visual loss Signs of secondary microbial superinfection Prescribing topical steroids for an undiagnosed red eye and worsening a dendritic ulcer Mistaking a herpetic dendrite for a healing abrasion or zoster pseudodendrite Overlooking reduced corneal sensation as a diagnostic clue Failing to consider prophylaxis in patients with frequent recurrences Herpes simplex keratitis is caused by herpes simplex virus, usually type 1, which after primary infection establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation, precipitated by stress, illness, ultraviolet light, or immunosuppression, sends the virus along sensory nerves to the cornea. Active viral replication in the epithelium produces the dendritic ulcer. Persisting viral antigen and the host immune response drive stromal inflammation (immune stromal keratitis) and endothelial disease (disciform keratitis), which can cause oedema, scarring, neovascularisation, and thinning. Repeated episodes and antiviral toxicity contribute to reduced corneal sensation and a neurotrophic cornea. Isolated epithelial disease usually heals with antiviral treatment, but recurrent stromal disease can cause progressive scarring, neovascularisation, and neurotrophic complications with permanent visual loss; prophylaxis improves long-term outcomes.
