replacement to halt neurological decline Hunter syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the IDS gene on the X chromosome, which encodes iduronate-2-sulfatase. Deficient activity blocks degradation of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, leading to their progressive lysosomal accumulation in connective tissue, bone, viscera, heart valves, airways, and, in the severe form, the central nervous system. This storage produces the multisystem somatic phenotype and, when neuronal involvement is present, progressive neurodegeneration. Because inheritance is X-linked, affected individuals are usually male. The severe neuronopathic form progresses to significant disability and death in childhood or adolescence, whereas the attenuated form is compatible with survival into adulthood with preserved cognition. Enzyme replacement therapy improves somatic outcomes and quality of life but does not address the central nervous system disease with standard delivery.

Huntington disease — HD, Huntington's chorea, chronic progressive hereditary chorea Other genetic choreas including Huntington disease-like syndromes and neuroacanthocytosis Sydenham chorea and other autoimmune/post-infectious choreas Drug-induced chorea or tardive dyskinesia Wilson disease Systemic causes of chorea such as thyrotoxicosis, polycythaemia, and antiphospholipid syndrome Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy Genetic testing for the CAG repeat expansion in HTT, with appropriate counselling MRI of the brain to assess striatal atrophy Screening for reversible or secondary causes of chorea when the diagnosis is uncertain (thyroid function, copper studies, autoimmune and antiphospholipid screen, blood film for acanthocytes) Psychiatric assessment including screening for depression and suicide risk Neuropsychological evaluation to characterise cognitive impairment An autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder classically presenting in mid-adult life with the triad of a movement disorder, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbance The characteristic movement disorder is chorea, though rigidity and bradykinesia predominate in juvenile and late-stage disease Caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, and genetic testing confirms the diagnosis The disease shows anticipation, with larger repeat expansions producing earlier onset, particularly with paternal transmission Psychiatric features including depression, irritability, apathy, and a raised suicide risk often precede overt motor signs Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary; agents that deplete or block dopamine can reduce disabling chorea while psychiatric symptoms are treated on their own merits Predictive genetic testing requires careful pre- and post-test counselling because of profound psychological and familial implications MRI typically shows atrophy of the caudate and putamen with enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles Emergent depression, hopelessness, or expressed suicidal ideation requiring urgent psychiatric intervention Rapid functional decline, dysphagia, and aspiration risk in advanced disease Juvenile-onset (Westphal) variant presenting with rigidity, seizures, and rapid progression Psychosis or severe behavioural disturbance placing the patient or others at risk Attributing early psychiatric or behavioural changes to a primary psychiatric illness and missing the underlying diagnosis Performing predictive genetic testing without adequate counselling and consideration of familial impact Failing to recognise and treat depression and suicide risk, which are major sources of morbidity Overlooking the rigid, non-choreic presentation of juvenile-onset or advanced disease Huntington disease results from an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene encoding a polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein. The mutant protein exerts a toxic gain of function, causing progressive neuronal loss most marked in the medium spiny neurons of the striatum (caudate and putamen), with later cortical involvement. Disruption of basal ganglia circuitry underlies the chorea and other movement abnormalities, while cortical and striatal degeneration drives cognitive and psychiatric decline. Huntington disease is relentlessly progressive over one to two decades from motor onset, leading to severe motor, cognitive, and functional decline. Death commonly results from complications such as aspiration pneumonia; treatment remains symptomatic without proven disease-modifying therapy in routine practice.

Hurler-Scheie syndrome results from biallelic IDUA variants that leave an intermediate level of residual alpha-L-iduronidase activity, producing a phenotype between the severe and attenuated poles of mucopolysaccharidosis type I. Deficient enzyme activity impairs the stepwise degradation of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate, causing lysosomal accumulation of these glycosaminoglycans throughout connective tissue, cartilage, cornea, heart valves, meninges, and viscera. Progressive substrate storage produces the characteristic multisystem somatic disease, while the greater residual activity compared with Hurler syndrome largely spares the central nervous system. Excess glycosaminoglycan is excreted in the urine. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Survival into adulthood is common, but progressive cardiorespiratory, skeletal, and ocular disease causes significant disability. Enzyme replacement therapy can improve somatic manifestations, though it does not cross the blood-brain barrier or reverse established corneal and skeletal changes.

Early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can preserve neurocognitive function and prolong survival, and enzyme replacement therapy improves somatic disease, although skeletal and corneal changes respond less well.

Hydatid liver cyst — hepatic hydatid disease, hepatic echinococcosis, liver hydatid cyst, cystic echinococcosis of the liver Simple hepatic cyst Pyogenic or amoebic liver abscess Polycystic liver disease Cystic liver neoplasm (cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma) Choledochal cyst Caroli disease Abdominal ultrasound to characterise and stage the cyst CT or MRI for anatomical detail, biliary communication, and surgical planning Echinococcal serology (with awareness of false negatives) Full blood count for eosinophilia MRCP or ERCP when biliary communication or obstruction is suspected Chest imaging to exclude concurrent pulmonary hydatid disease Hepatic hydatid disease is caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, with dogs as definitive hosts and humans as accidental intermediate hosts, and is endemic in sheep- and cattle-rearing regions The liver is the commonest organ affected, and cysts are frequently asymptomatic for years, presenting as a slowly enlarging right upper quadrant mass or dull ache Ultrasound and CT show a characteristic cyst with a wall, internal daughter cysts, and detached membranes; the Gharbi/WHO classification helps stage activity Serology supports the diagnosis, though false negatives occur, and eosinophilia may be present Diagnostic aspiration is traditionally avoided because of the risk of spillage causing anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding, although image-guided PAIR is used in selected cases under cover Management options include the PAIR technique (puncture, aspiration, injection of a scolicidal agent, and re-aspiration), surgery, and anthelmintic therapy, chosen by cyst stage, size, and complications Perioperative and periprocedural anthelmintic cover and meticulous protection of the field with scolicidal precautions reduce recurrence and spillage Cyst rupture provoking anaphylaxis or anaphylactic shock, a life-threatening emergency Rupture or communication into the biliary tree causing cholangitis and obstructive jaundice Secondary bacterial infection of the cyst with sepsis Rupture into the peritoneum or thorax with widespread secondary seeding Aspirating or biopsying an undiagnosed cyst and precipitating spillage, seeding, or anaphylaxis Omitting perioperative anthelmintic cover and scolicidal precautions, increasing recurrence Injecting a scolicidal agent when there is biliary communication, risking sclerosing cholangitis Missing associated pulmonary hydatid disease Mistaking a hydatid cyst for a simple cyst or abscess and managing it inappropriately Humans acquire infection by ingesting Echinococcus eggs shed in canine faeces. Embryos penetrate the intestinal wall and travel via the portal circulation, with the liver acting as the first filter and commonest site of lodgement. There the larva develops into a fluid-filled hydatid cyst with three layers: an outer host-derived fibrous pericyst, a middle acellular laminated membrane, and an inner germinal layer that produces protoscolices and daughter cysts. The cyst enlarges slowly and can compress adjacent liver, bile ducts, and vessels. Cyst fluid is highly antigenic, so rupture, whether spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic, can release protoscolices that seed new cysts and trigger a severe allergic or anaphylactic reaction. Communication with the biliary tree can cause cholangitis and obstructive jaundice. The outlook is generally good for uncomplicated cysts treated appropriately, with high cure rates after surgery or PAIR combined with anthelmintic therapy. Recurrence can occur from spillage of viable protoscolices, and prognosis is worse with complications such as anaphylaxis, biliary rupture, or secondary infection.

Hydranencephaly — hydranencephalus, cystic degeneration of the cerebral hemispheres, in-utero cerebral infarction Severe hydrocephalus with a thin preserved cortical mantle Alobar holoprosencephaly with a monoventricle and fused midline structures Bilateral open-lip schizencephaly Large bilateral porencephaly Massive bilateral subdural collections Severe destructive encephalopathy from congenital infection Brain imaging with ultrasound, CT, or MRI to demonstrate absent hemispheres with a present falx and preserved posterior fossa Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected Electroencephalography to characterise seizures A severe destructive disorder in which the cerebral hemispheres are largely absent and replaced by cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sacs, while the falx, brainstem, and cerebellum are relatively preserved It is generally a disruption rather than a primary malformation, usually attributed to bilateral internal carotid territory infarction or a destructive insult after the brain has begun to form The relatively intact brainstem means neonates may initially appear deceptively normal, with preserved brainstem reflexes, sucking, and spontaneous movements Head size may be normal, small, or progressively enlarged, and transillumination of the skull is characteristically strikingly positive It must be distinguished from severe hydrocephalus, in which a rim of compressed cortex persists, and from alobar holoprosencephaly, in which midline structures are fused Later features include developmental failure, irritability, seizures, spasticity, temperature instability, and feeding difficulty Diagnosis is by imaging, with ultrasound, CT, or MRI showing absent hemispheres, a present falx, and preserved posterior fossa structures Progressive macrocephaly with raised intracranial pressure Refractory seizures Temperature instability and autonomic dysfunction Recurrent aspiration and feeding failure Being reassured by an apparently normal early neonatal examination because of preserved brainstem function Mistaking hydranencephaly for severe hydrocephalus and pursuing inappropriate expectations from shunting Confusing it with alobar holoprosencephaly, which has fused midline structures and an absent falx Overlooking hypothalamic dysfunction such as temperature instability and endocrine disturbance Hydranencephaly is thought to result from a destructive vascular event, typically bilateral occlusion or infarction in the internal carotid artery territories, occurring after the cerebral hemispheres have begun to develop. The cortex supplied by these vessels undergoes necrosis and resorption, leaving cerebrospinal-fluid-filled sacs bounded by leptomeninges where the hemispheres should be. Because the posterior circulation is spared, the brainstem, cerebellum, and often the thalami and basal structures are relatively preserved, and the falx cerebri, which forms early, usually remains. Other proposed mechanisms include severe intrauterine infection and profound hypoxic-ischaemic injury. Hydranencephaly carries a very poor prognosis, with most affected infants having profound neurological impairment; many die in infancy, although some survive longer with intensive supportive care. Management is supportive, with shunting sometimes needed for progressive head enlargement.

Hydrocele — hydrocoele, scrotal hydrocele, processus vaginalis fluid collection Inguinoscrotal hernia Testicular tumour with reactive hydrocele Epididymal cyst or spermatocele Varicocele Haematocele (post-traumatic) Epididymo-orchitis with reactive effusion Transillumination of the scrotal swelling Scrotal ultrasound when the testis is impalpable or a secondary cause is suspected Assessment for underlying infection, trauma, or torsion as clinically indicated Tumour markers if testicular malignancy is a concern on imaging A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis, presenting as a painless, fluctuant scrotal swelling that transilluminates brightly A key examination finding is the ability to get above the swelling, distinguishing it from an inguinoscrotal hernia, and the testis is often impalpable within a large tension hydrocele In infants, communicating hydroceles arise from a patent processus vaginalis and commonly resolve spontaneously within the first year or two of life Adult hydroceles are usually idiopathic (primary) but may be secondary to underlying pathology such as tumour, infection, trauma, or torsion, so the testis must be assessed Ultrasound is indicated when the testis cannot be palpated or when a secondary cause is suspected, to exclude an underlying testicular tumour A rapidly developing or blood-stained hydrocele after trauma or in a young man should prompt evaluation for testicular malignancy or haematocele Treatment principles include observation for asymptomatic cases, with surgical repair (hydrocelectomy) preferred for large or symptomatic adult hydroceles and aspiration reserved for those unfit for surgery due to high recurrence In children, persistent or symptomatic hydroceles beyond infancy are managed by ligation of the patent processus via an inguinal approach An impalpable testis within the hydrocele, mandating ultrasound to exclude tumour Rapidly enlarging, tense, or blood-stained (haematocele) swelling following trauma A reactive hydrocele masking an underlying testicular malignancy Signs of associated infection or torsion requiring urgent evaluation Assuming a scrotal swelling is a simple hydrocele without confirming a normal underlying testis Aspirating an adult hydrocele as definitive treatment, given the high recurrence and risk of missing tumour Failing to recognise a reactive hydrocele overlying a testicular tumour Confusing a hydrocele with an inguinoscrotal hernia when unable to get above the swelling Operating on infantile hydroceles prematurely before allowing spontaneous resolution A hydrocele results from an imbalance between secretion and absorption of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Congenital (communicating) hydroceles occur when the processus vaginalis fails to obliterate, allowing peritoneal fluid to track into the scrotum. Non-communicating hydroceles arise from excess fluid production or impaired reabsorption by the tunica. Secondary hydroceles develop as a reactive effusion in response to underlying testicular or epididymal disease such as tumour, infection, torsion, or trauma. Chronic large hydroceles may occasionally impair testicular perfusion or spermatogenesis. Infantile communicating hydroceles usually resolve spontaneously; primary adult hydroceles are benign and surgery is generally curative, whereas the outlook of secondary hydroceles depends on the underlying cause.

Hydrocephalus — obstructive hydrocephalus, communicating hydrocephalus, normal pressure hydrocephalus, NPH Cerebral atrophy with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly Intracranial mass causing focal obstruction Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Neurodegenerative dementia (in suspected NPH) Shunt malfunction in a previously treated patient CT or MRI brain to assess ventricular size, the level of obstruction, and periventricular changes MRI with CSF flow studies when aqueductal or outflow obstruction is suspected Head circumference monitoring and cranial ultrasound in infants with an open fontanelle Large-volume lumbar puncture or external drainage trial to predict shunt response in suspected NPH Shunt series and imaging to evaluate suspected shunt malfunction Hydrocephalus reflects an imbalance between cerebrospinal fluid production and absorption or a blockage to its flow, producing ventricular enlargement It is broadly divided into obstructive (non-communicating), where flow is blocked within the ventricular system, and communicating, where absorption at the arachnoid granulations is impaired Acute obstructive hydrocephalus is a neurosurgical emergency presenting with headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, and papilloedema from rapidly rising intracranial pressure In infants, before fusion of the sutures, features include an enlarging head circumference, bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, and the sunsetting sign of downward-deviated eyes Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically presents in older adults with the triad of gait apraxia, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence, and gait often improves after CSF drainage Treatment principles include relieving the obstruction where possible and diverting CSF, commonly by ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy for suitable obstructive cases Shunt complications such as infection, blockage, over-drainage, and disconnection are common and should be considered in any shunted patient who deteriorates Imaging helps distinguish true hydrocephalus with raised pressure from ex vacuo ventricular enlargement due to brain atrophy Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with falling conscious level, severe headache, and vomiting requiring emergency CSF diversion Signs of impending herniation from rapidly rising intracranial pressure Rapidly enlarging head with bulging fontanelle and sunsetting eyes in an infant Shunt malfunction or shunt infection presenting with headache, drowsiness, or fever in a shunted patient Mistaking ex vacuo ventriculomegaly from atrophy for treatable hydrocephalus Delaying CSF diversion in acute obstructive hydrocephalus while awaiting further tests Overlooking shunt malfunction as a cause of deterioration in a shunted patient Attributing the NPH triad solely to ageing or dementia and missing a reversible component Hydrocephalus is an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricular system, usually resulting in ventricular dilatation and, when acute, raised intracranial pressure. CSF is produced largely by the choroid plexus, circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid space, and is absorbed at the arachnoid granulations. Obstruction along this pathway (for example at the aqueduct, fourth ventricular outflow, or by a mass or blood clot) causes non-communicating hydrocephalus, while impaired absorption after haemorrhage, infection, or inflammation causes communicating hydrocephalus. Rising pressure and ventricular expansion compress adjacent white matter and, if unrelieved, can lead to herniation. Prognosis depends on the cause, speed of onset, and timeliness of treatment; well-selected patients do well after CSF diversion, but outcomes are limited by the underlying pathology and by recurrent shunt complications, and untreated acute obstruction can be rapidly fatal.

Hydronephrosis — hydronephrosis, pelvicalyceal dilatation, renal pelvis dilatation, obstructive uropathy, hydroureteronephrosis Ureteric or renal calculus Pelviureteric junction obstruction Vesicoureteric reflux (non-obstructive dilatation) Ureteric stricture or malignancy Extrinsic compression by pelvic or retroperitoneal masses, or retroperitoneal fibrosis Bladder outlet obstruction (e.g. prostatic enlargement) Physiological dilatation of pregnancy Extrarenal pelvis or parapelvic cyst mimicking dilatation Renal tract ultrasound as first-line to confirm and grade dilatation CT urography or non-contrast CT to identify stones, level, and cause of obstruction Diuretic renography (e.g. MAG3) to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive dilatation and assess differential function Serum creatinine and electrolytes to assess renal function Urinalysis and culture to detect infection Micturating cystourethrogram in children where reflux is suspected Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces, most often due to obstruction of urinary outflow but sometimes non-obstructive, and it is a radiological finding rather than a diagnosis in itself The clinical priority is to determine whether true obstruction is present, since obstruction threatens renal function, whereas dilatation without obstruction may need only surveillance Causes are classified by level: intraluminal (stones, clots, tumour), mural (pelviureteric junction obstruction, strictures), and extrinsic (pelvic masses, retroperitoneal fibrosis, pregnancy) Acute unilateral obstruction typically causes severe colicky loin-to-groin pain, whereas chronic or bilateral obstruction may be insidious with vague symptoms or present with renal impairment Obstruction combined with infection above the blockage produces an infected, obstructed system (pyonephrosis), a urological emergency requiring urgent drainage and antibiotics Bilateral hydronephrosis or hydronephrosis of a solitary kidney can cause acute kidney injury and post-obstructive changes, and demands prompt relief Antenatally detected hydronephrosis is common and often transient, but significant or persistent dilatation needs postnatal assessment for underlying uropathy and reflux Ultrasound is the first-line investigation, with CT and functional renography used to define the cause, level, and the affected kidney's function and drainage Relief of obstruction is achieved by drainage (ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) followed by treatment directed at the underlying cause Infected obstructed system (pyonephrosis) with fever, loin pain, and sepsis requiring emergency drainage Bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney causing acute kidney injury Anuria or rapidly rising creatinine indicating significant obstructive nephropathy Severe uncontrolled pain or haemodynamic instability Post-obstructive diuresis after relief, risking fluid and electrolyte disturbance Assuming all dilatation means obstruction and intervening unnecessarily Failing to recognise and urgently drain an infected obstructed system Overlooking bladder outlet obstruction as a cause of bilateral upper tract dilatation Not anticipating and managing post-obstructive diuresis after relieving obstruction Delaying functional imaging so that salvageable renal function is lost When urine outflow is obstructed, pressure builds up proximal to the blockage and is transmitted back to the renal pelvis and calyces, causing them to dilate. Persistently raised intrapelvic and intratubular pressure impairs glomerular filtration and, over time, produces progressive tubular and parenchymal damage with cortical thinning and loss of function. Superimposed infection in a stagnant, obstructed system allows rapid bacterial proliferation and pus accumulation. Non-obstructive hydronephrosis arises where the collecting system is dilated without a pressure gradient, for example vesicoureteric reflux, high urine flow, or a capacious but unobstructed system, and these generally do not damage the kidney. Outcome depends on the cause, the duration and completeness of obstruction, and whether infection intervenes. Prompt relief of acute obstruction usually allows recovery of renal function, but prolonged or severe obstruction leads to irreversible parenchymal loss. Non-obstructive dilatation and much antenatally detected hydronephrosis resolve or remain stable without harm. Infected obstruction is life-threatening if drainage is delayed but recovers well with timely intervention.

Hyper-IgE syndrome — HIES, hyperimmunoglobulin E syndrome, Job syndrome (autosomal dominant form) Severe atopic dermatitis with recurrent skin infection DOCK8 deficiency and other combined immunodeficiencies Chronic granulomatous disease Cystic fibrosis (recurrent pneumonia with structural lung change) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome Omenn syndrome and other conditions with eosinophilia and high IgE Serum IgE level and eosinophil count Genetic testing for STAT3, DOCK8, and related genes Lymphocyte subset analysis and Th17 cell enumeration where available Clinical scoring (for example an NIH-type score) to gauge probability of the STAT3 form Chest imaging to detect pneumatoceles, bronchiectasis, and fungal colonisation Skeletal and dental assessment for fractures, scoliosis, and retained teeth Hyper-IgE syndrome is a group of primary immunodeficiencies characterised by markedly elevated serum IgE, recurrent skin and lung infections, and often connective tissue or skeletal abnormalities The classic autosomal dominant form results from dominant-negative STAT3 mutations, while autosomal recessive forms (for example DOCK8 deficiency) show overlapping but distinct features The infection pattern is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses that may be surprisingly non-inflamed ('cold' abscesses) and recurrent pneumonias that can leave pneumatoceles Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and other fungal infections are common, reflecting impaired Th17-mediated immunity in the STAT3 form DOCK8 deficiency is distinguished by severe cutaneous viral infections, food allergies, eosinophilia, and a high risk of malignancy Non-immune features of the STAT3 form include a characteristic coarse facial appearance, retained primary teeth, hyperextensible joints, scoliosis, and a tendency to bone fractures Serum IgE is often very high but does not correlate tightly with disease activity, and eosinophilia is frequent Management centres on long-term antistaphylococcal and antifungal prophylaxis, aggressive treatment of infections, and skin care; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct the recessive DOCK8 form Recurrent or severe deep-seated infections, including 'cold' abscesses and pneumonia with cavitation, warranting urgent immunological workup Aspergillus or other fungal infection colonising pneumatoceles, risking invasive disease or haemorrhage Severe disseminated viral skin infection in suspected DOCK8 deficiency New or accelerating malignancy, particularly in the recessive form Vascular aneurysms in the STAT3 form Attributing recurrent staphylococcal abscesses to simple atopic dermatitis and missing the underlying immunodeficiency Assuming a very high IgE alone confirms the diagnosis, since it is neither fully sensitive nor specific Overlooking the skeletal, dental, and vascular features that distinguish the STAT3 form Failing to recognise DOCK8 deficiency as a transplantable condition with a different management path Not monitoring pneumatoceles for secondary fungal infection Hyper-IgE syndromes arise from defects in signalling pathways that govern T-helper cell differentiation and epithelial immunity. In the autosomal dominant form, dominant-negative mutations in STAT3 impair the development of Th17 cells and the response to several cytokines, reducing antimicrobial peptide production at skin and mucosal surfaces and blunting the acute inflammatory response, which explains the 'cold' abscesses. STAT3 also influences tissue remodelling and skeletal biology, accounting for the connective tissue, dental, and bony features. Autosomal recessive forms such as DOCK8 deficiency disrupt cytoskeletal function and lymphocyte survival, producing profound susceptibility to cutaneous viruses and severe allergic disease. Dysregulated IgE production and eosinophilia are shared consequences of the altered T-cell cytokine milieu. With sustained prophylaxis and prompt treatment of infections, many patients with the autosomal dominant STAT3 form reach adulthood, though pulmonary complications and vascular aneurysms remain important causes of morbidity. The autosomal recessive DOCK8 form carries a poorer outlook because of severe viral infections and malignancy, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the best chance of cure.

neutropenia with oral ulceration and sepsis risk Failure to thrive with recurrent invasive infection Labelling the condition as a pure antibody deficiency and missing the combined immunodeficiency behaviour of the CD40L/CD40 subtypes Failing to institute Pneumocystis prophylaxis in the CD40 pathway forms Overlooking Cryptosporidium as a cause of chronic diarrhoea and biliary disease Attributing raised IgM to infection alone and not pursuing class-switch defect testing Hyper-IgM syndromes arise from defects in the molecular machinery that allows activated B cells to switch from producing IgM to producing IgG, IgA and IgE and to undergo affinity maturation. In the X-linked form, mutations in the gene encoding CD40 ligand on activated T cells prevent effective engagement of CD40 on B cells and other antigen-presenting cells, disrupting both antibody class-switching and cell-mediated immune signalling. The result is a failure to generate mature isotype antibody responses, leaving normal or elevated IgM but deficient protective immunoglobulin. Outcome depends on subtype: the autosomal recessive humoral forms generally do well on immunoglobulin replacement, whereas untreated CD40 ligand or CD40 deficiency carries high morbidity from opportunistic infection, liver disease and malignancy, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the prospect of cure when performed early.

Pneumocystis prophylaxis Overlooking Cryptosporidium as a cause of chronic diarrhoea and liver disease Missing associated neutropenia Failing to distinguish the combined X-linked form from the milder B-cell-intrinsic recessive forms, which affects prognosis and transplant decisions Hyper-IgM syndromes disrupt immunoglobulin class-switch recombination. In the X-linked form, mutations in the gene for CD40 ligand deprive B cells and antigen-presenting cells of the CD40 signal that activated T cells normally deliver, preventing class switching, germinal centre development, and effective T-cell-dependent activation of macrophages and dendritic cells. This dual impairment of humoral and cell-mediated immunity explains both the pyogenic infections and the opportunistic infections. Autosomal recessive forms caused by intrinsic B-cell defects, such as deficiency of activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AICDA) or uracil-DNA glycosylase, block the enzymatic machinery of switching within the B cell itself, producing a purely humoral phenotype with prominent lymphoid hyperplasia. The X-linked CD40L-deficient form has a serious prognosis because of opportunistic infections, liver disease from cryptosporidiosis, and an increased risk of malignancy, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is often recommended; the B-cell-intrinsic recessive forms generally have a better outlook managed with immunoglobulin replacement.

Hyperbaric and Diving Medicine — HBO2T, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, decompression sickness, the bends, DCS, cerebral arterial gas embolism, CAGE, diving barotrauma, dysbarism Stroke or transient ischemic attack (can mimic or be mimicked by cerebral arterial gas embolism) Inner ear barotrauma versus vestibulocochlear decompression sickness (both cause sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo) Middle ear barotrauma (should never be invoked to explain post-dive sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo) Acute coronary syndrome or musculoskeletal injury versus DCS limb pain Other causes of post-dive neurologic symptoms not explained by an alternative mechanism Transcutaneous oximetry (transcutaneous Po2 mapping) around a wound on air and on oxygen at pressure to assess HBO2T suitability Ankle-brachial index and skin perfusion pressure as alternative wound perfusion assessments Carboxyhemoglobin level in suspected CO poisoning (confirms exposure but does not gauge severity or prognosis) Arterial blood-gas analysis for metabolic acidosis in CO poisoning (a marker of poor prognosis) Audiometry / otologic evaluation for suspected inner ear barotrauma Dive profile review combined with clinical examination (there are no useful confirmatory diagnostic tests for DCS) Ischemic stroke / TIA mimicking CAGE Migraine or other transient neurologic events after diving Decompression sickness mimicking CAGE and vice versa (clinically the distinction is unimportant because first aid and definitive management are identical) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO2T) means breathing physician-prescribed medical-grade oxygen while the whole body is enclosed in a chamber pressurized to at least 2.0 ATA; most regimens use 2-2.8 ATA for roughly 90-120 minutes per session. At 2.8 ATA, arterial Po2 can theoretically rise above ~2025 mmHg and dissolved plasma oxygen to ~60 mL/L, enough to sustain life without hemoglobin in animal studies, which sharply improves oxygen diffusion through tissues. Even a single HBO2T exposure produces durable cell-signaling effects (on fibroblasts, leukocytes, angiogenesis, antioxidant defenses) that persist for hours after oxygen levels return to baseline, mediated by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. The UHMS recognizes 15 accepted indications, including air/gas embolism, carbon monoxide poisoning, gas gangrene, crush injury, decompression sickness, problem wounds, intracranial abscess, necrotizing soft tissue infection, refractory osteomyelitis, delayed radiation injury, and sudden sensorineural hearing loss. For chronic problem wounds, candidate selection is often guided by transcutaneous oximetry around the wound while breathing air and oxygen at pressure; in diabetic patients a transcutaneous Po2 threshold of <50 mmHg may be more appropriate than the usual <40 mmHg cutoff. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with more than 200 times the affinity of oxygen and shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve leftward; HBO2T shortens the COHb half-life to about 21 min at 2.0 ATA versus roughly 5.5 h breathing air at sea level. Admission carboxyhemoglobin levels confirm CO exposure but do NOT reliably predict severity or prognosis; delayed neuropsychological sequelae can appear after days to months of apparent recovery. Ambient pressure increases by 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa) for every 10.1 m of seawater, so a diver at 20 m experiences about 3 ATA. In diving, the maximum acceptable inspired Po2 is generally considered 1.6 ATA (lower than therapeutic HBO2T pressures) because immersion and exercise raise the risk of oxygen-toxic seizures; helium replaces nitrogen at depth to cut narcosis and gas density. Cerebral arterial gas embolism (CAGE) from pulmonary barotrauma presents within minutes of surfacing with loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance, and can be mistaken for stroke or TIA by clinicians unfamiliar with diving. Decompression sickness occurs in roughly 1 in 5000-10,000 recreational dives; most cases are mild (limb pain, fatigue, patchy paresthesias), and serious DCS usually appears within 60 min of surfacing. Symptoms beginning more than 24 h after a dive are very unlikely to be DCS unless the diver was subsequently exposed to reduced ambient pressure such as air travel or higher-altitude surface travel. About 25% of adults have a patent foramen ovale; right-to-left shunting (PFO, atrial septal defect, intrapulmonary shunt) lets venous bubbles 'arterialize' and raises the risk of cerebral, spinal cord, inner ear, and skin DCS manifestations. Neurologic symptoms after diving (loss of consciousness, confusion, hemiplegia, visual or speech disturbance) suggesting CAGE or serious DCS — discuss with a diving medicine specialist and consider recompression Spinal cord involvement in DCS (weakness, paralysis, bladder/sphincter dysfunction) which frequently causes permanent disability Pulmonary and cardiovascular DCS manifestations (cough, dyspnea, hypotension, hemoconcentration, coagulopathy) which can be life-threatening Sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo with nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, ataxia after diving (inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear DCS) Untreated pneumothorax before any hyperbaric exposure (intrapleural gas can expand and tension on decompression) Tonic-clonic seizure during HBO2T or diving from cerebral oxygen toxicity, sometimes preceded by facial twitching, anxiety, and agitation Moderate-to-severe CO poisoning, especially age over 35, prolonged exposure, acidosis, or loss of consciousness Attributing post-dive sensorineural hearing loss or true vertigo to middle ear barotrauma — these point instead to inner ear barotrauma or vestibulocochlear DCS. Misdiagnosing CAGE as a typical stroke or TIA when the clinician is unfamiliar with diving medicine. Relying on admission carboxyhemoglobin level to judge severity or prognosis of CO poisoning. Assuming there is a confirmatory diagnostic test for DCS — diagnosis rests on dive profile, symptom timing, and examination. Treating CAGE/DCS distinction as clinically critical — first aid and definitive management are the same for both. Compressing a patient with an untreated pneumothorax or with gas-trapping lesions such as bullae without careful risk assessment and, for pneumothorax, a patent chest drain. Overstating the risk of pulmonary oxygen toxicity from remote bleomycin exposure; published experience suggests the relationship may have been exaggerated, though recent bleomycin or mitomycin C with pneumonitis warrants careful evaluation. Promoting HBO2T (sometimes with air) as a panacea for unproven indications, general well-being, or anti-aging — practice should be confined to accepted, periodically updated indications. Hyperbaric oxygen exerts effects through both physical mechanisms and biochemical cell signaling. Physically, raising ambient pressure shrinks gas bubbles per Boyle's law and steepens inert-gas diffusion gradients from bubble to tissue to blood and lungs, the basis for treating decompression sickness and arterial gas embolism. The markedly elevated arterial Po2 fully saturates hemoglobin and greatly increases dissolved plasma oxygen, improving diffusion into hypoxic and irradiated tissue. Beyond simple oxygen delivery, intermittent hyperoxia generates reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide) and reactive nitrogen species (nitric oxide) that drive cytokine and angiogenic growth-factor production, stimulate fibroblast activity, enhance macrophage bacterial killing, mobilize vasculogenic progenitor cells from marrow, and paradoxically produce anti-inflammatory effects such as reduced leukocyte beta-2 integrin adhesion. Hyperoxia also causes vasoconstriction and an osmotic gradient that reduce tissue edema and is directly toxic or bacteriostatic to anaerobes. In late radiation tissue injury, irradiation produces fibrosis and obliterative endarteritis leaving hypovascular hypoxic tissue (an alternative model emphasizes cytokine-driven fibrosis from oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction); HBO2T's most important benefit is promoting angiogenesis and increasing microvascular density. In carbon monoxide poisoning, CO impairs oxygen carriage, acts as an anesthetic, disrupts cellular oxidative processes, binds heme proteins including cytochrome a/a3, and peroxidizes brain lipids, with brain and heart most vulnerable. In diving, breathing gas at elevated ambient pressure loads inert gas (usually nitrogen) into tissues; if washout during ascent lags the falling ambient pressure, tissues become supersaturated and bubbles form, causing mechanical distortion of tissues and, in the venous circulation, inflammatory and coagulation cascades, endothelial injury, capillary leak, hemoconcentration, and pulmonary vascular obstruction. Barotrauma arises when noncompliant gas-filled spaces fail to equalize with changing ambient pressure. Most HBO2T adverse events are mild and self-limiting, and the therapy is generally safe. For late radiation tissue injury pooled data suggest improved tissue healing and reduced wound dehiscence in jaw osteoradionecrosis. About 70% of indolent problem ulcers are substantially improved or healed 6 months after a course, and meta-analyses report increased complete healing and reduced amputation of diabetic foot ulcers. In CO poisoning the most rigorous trial showed fewer cognitive sequelae at 6 weeks (25% vs 46%) and 12 months (18% vs 32%) with HBO2T, though a Cochrane review found overall evidence insufficient. Survivors of CO poisoning may develop delayed neuropsychological sequelae; risk factors for poor outcome are age over 35, exposure beyond 24 h, acidosis, and loss of consciousness. In diving, CAGE often shows substantial or complete early resolution as bubbles involute, but secondary deterioration or re-embolization can occur. Most DCS cases are mild, but spinal cord DCS frequently causes permanent disability and pulmonary/cardiovascular forms can be fatal. Decompression sickness manifestations (Harrison Table 476-2) are grouped by organ system: musculoskeletal (limb pain); neurologic cerebral (confusion, visual and speech disturbances), spinal (weakness, paralysis, upper motor neuron signs, bladder/sphincter dysfunction, dermatomal sensory disturbance, abdominal/girdle pain), vestibulocochlear (hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia, nausea/vomiting), and peripheral (patchy nondermatomal sensory disturbance); pulmonary (cough, dyspnea); cardiovascular (hemoconcentration, coagulopathy, hypotension); cutaneous (rash, itch); lymphatic (localized soft tissue edema); and constitutional (fatigue, malaise). Most cases are mild; serious DCS usually manifests within 60 min of surfacing.

>0.02 fractional excretion supports pHPT) (p.363) Genetic testing (CASR, GNA11, AP2S1) if FHH suspected and urine studies inconclusive (p.363) ECG — may show shortened QTc/ST segments, bradyarrhythmias, AV block, QRS widening, bundle branch block (p.364, 738) Primary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism — PTH-driven hypercalcaemia mimicking malignant hypercalcaemia (p.362-364) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia — benign mimic where surgery is ineffective (p.363) Sarcoidosis and other non-infectious granulomatous/foreign-body reactions (p.362-363) Pseudohypercalcaemia (e.g. calcium-binding IgM in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia, or spuriously high reading from altered albumin binding) (p.362-363) Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to ~20% of cancer patients; the typical picture is a patient with known malignancy found hypercalcaemic on routine labs, though occasionally hypercalcaemia is the presenting feature of an undiagnosed cancer (p.737). Most malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia runs a relatively acute course, in contrast to the chronic, fluctuating high-normal pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism or occasionally myeloma (p.363). An elevated PTHrP level confirms HHM and is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcaemic cancer patients; PTH should be suppressed in true HHM (p.738). Features favouring HHM over primary hyperparathyroidism: known malignancy, recent onset, and very high serum calcium levels (p.738). PTHrP shares homology with the first ~13 amino acids of PTH and binds the PTH receptor, explaining the PTH-like biochemical effects on bone and kidney (p.363, 737). Serum free light chains should be checked when myeloma is suspected, since ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (p.364). Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is one of the few clinical settings where measuring serum 1,25(OH)2D is genuinely useful — it is elevated or inappropriately normal in lymphoma- and granulomatous-mediated hypercalcaemia (p.364). Always confirm true hypercalcaemia first by correcting for albumin (add ~0.8 mg/dL to total calcium per 1.0 g/dL fall in albumin below 4.0 g/dL) to exclude pseudohypercalcaemia (p.363). Markedly elevated calcium (>14 mg/dL / >3.5 mmol/L) with progressive lethargy, stupor or coma (p.363-364, 737) Severe GI involvement — nausea, vomiting, anorexia, peptic ulcer or pancreatitis (p.364) Acute renal failure and volume depletion from hypercalcaemia-induced nephrogenic concentrating defect and polyuria (p.364) Cardiac conduction abnormalities — bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc (p.364) Failing to correct calcium for albumin can produce pseudohypercalcaemia or pseudohypocalcaemia and a false diagnosis (p.363). FHH may present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcaemia and be mistaken for primary hyperparathyroidism — parathyroid surgery is ineffective in FHH and must be excluded (p.363). Mild hypercalcaemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is often asymptomatic or causes only vague neuropsychiatric or constitutional symptoms, so it may be overlooked (p.363). Ionised calcium measurement is easily distorted by collection technique (e.g. prolonged tourniquet); corrected total calcium is generally preferable (p.363). Up to ~3% of myeloma is undetected by serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — check free light chains (p.364). In immobilisation-related hypercalcaemia, an unrecognised underlying driver (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may coexist and should be sought, especially in older patients (p.363). Calcium balance is governed by PTH and the vitamin D metabolites 1,25(OH)2D and 25(OH)D acting across parathyroid, kidney, intestine and bone. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy arises mainly through three mechanisms. (1) PTHrP overproduction by solid tumours (squamous head/neck, lung, skin; breast; genitourinary; gastrointestinal) — PTHrP mimics PTH at the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. (2) Local osteolysis from skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma), where metastatic deposits secrete PTHrP and chemokines driving bone breakdown. (3) Excess 1,25(OH)2D production, notably by lymphomas (and granulomatous disease) via macrophage CYP27B1 converting 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. PTHrP induction is linked to PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli signalling, TGF-beta, oncogene activation (e.g. Ras) and p53 loss. In all these malignant mechanisms, the high serum calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR and appropriately suppresses endogenous PTH (p.363, 737). By total serum calcium: mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (often asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor or coma, prominent GI symptoms and acute renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.363-364).

Hyperemesis gravidarum — HG, severe pregnancy sickness, intractable vomiting of pregnancy Molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease) Gastroenteritis or other gastrointestinal infection assessment of hydration Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine Full blood count and liver function tests Thyroid function tests where clinically indicated Pelvic ultrasound to confirm viability and exclude multiple or molar pregnancy Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe, persistent nausea and vomiting of early pregnancy causing dehydration, weight loss (often more than 5 percent of pre-pregnancy weight), and electrolyte disturbance It typically begins in the first trimester and is a diagnosis reached after excluding other causes of vomiting Ketonuria, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, and a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid are characteristic Association with high levels of human chorionic gonadotrophin means it is more common in multiple and molar pregnancies Management is supportive: rehydration with intravenous fluids and electrolyte correction, antiemetics, and thiamine to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy Thiamine supplementation before giving glucose-containing fluids is essential to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy A stepwise antiemetic approach is used, escalating therapy for refractory cases, with nutritional support if intake remains inadequate Transient biochemical hyperthyroidism can occur due to the thyroid-stimulating activity of hCG and usually needs no antithyroid treatment Severe dehydration, oliguria, or haemodynamic instability Confusion, ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia suggesting Wernicke encephalopathy Refractory vomiting with significant weight loss and inability to maintain any oral intake Severe electrolyte derangement or acid-base disturbance Haematemesis from Mallory-Weiss tears or signs of an alternative serious diagnosis Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine and precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy Attributing all vomiting to pregnancy without excluding molar pregnancy, infection, or metabolic causes Undertreating dehydration and electrolyte loss Overtreating the transient hCG-mediated hyperthyroidism with antithyroid drugs Overlooking the substantial psychological impact and risk of inadequate nutrition The cause is multifactorial. Rising human chorionic gonadotrophin and oestrogen are strongly implicated, explaining the peak in the first trimester and the higher frequency in molar and multiple pregnancies where hCG is elevated. Genetic factors, including variants affecting the appetite-regulating hormone GDF15, and altered gut motility contribute. Protracted vomiting leads to loss of fluid, hydrogen, chloride, and potassium ions, producing dehydration, hypokalaemia, and a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, while starvation drives ketosis and depletes thiamine stores. Most cases settle by the second trimester and, with adequate rehydration and antiemetic therapy, have a good outcome for mother and baby. Severe untreated disease can cause serious maternal complications including Wernicke encephalopathy, and recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common.

and between attacks Genetic testing of MVK Full blood count to document attack-related leucocytosis and exclude cyclical neutropenia Mevalonate kinase enzyme activity assay where available An autosomal recessive autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in MVK, encoding mevalonate kinase, that spans milder hyper-IgD syndrome to severe mevalonic aciduria Recurrent fevers usually begin in the first year of life and last several days, often provoked by vaccination, infection or stress Attacks characteristically feature tender cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain with vomiting or diarrhoea, arthralgia, aphthous ulcers and a variable rash A raised serum IgD, and often IgA, is supportive but neither sensitive nor specific and may be normal, especially in young children Elevated Management targets the interleukin-1 pathway, with interleukin-1 inhibition the mainstay for frequent or severe attacks Developmental delay, ataxia or failure to thrive suggesting the severe mevalonic aciduria phenotype Signs of AA amyloidosis such as new proteinuria in long-standing disease Severe dehydration from recurrent vomiting and diarrhoea during attacks Attacks that are increasing in frequency or severity despite treatment Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgD is normal, which is common in young children Missing the diagnostic window by not collecting urine for mevalonic acid during a febrile attack Confusing frequent early-childhood attacks with recurrent infections and treating with repeated antibiotics Failing to recognise the more severe mevalonic aciduria phenotype in an infant with neurological features Hyper-IgD syndrome lies on the mevalonate kinase deficiency spectrum, caused by biallelic MVK mutations that reduce activity of mevalonate kinase, an enzyme early in the mevalonate (isoprenoid/cholesterol) biosynthetic pathway. Reduced enzyme activity impairs production of downstream non-sterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, which is required for prenylation of small regulatory GTPases. Deficient protein prenylation destabilises inhibitory signals on the innate immune system and enhances NLRP3 inflammasome activation with excess interleukin-1 beta release, producing recurrent inflammatory attacks. Enzyme activity worsens transiently with fever, creating a self-amplifying inflammatory cycle, and profound deficiency produces the severe multisystem phenotype of mevalonic aciduria. Attack frequency in the hyper-IgD end of the spectrum often lessens with age and responds to interleukin-1 blockade, giving a reasonable outlook, whereas severe mevalonic aciduria carries significant neurodevelopmental morbidity and higher mortality, and AA amyloidosis remains a long-term risk in poorly controlled disease.

cytomegalovirus; tuberculosis; disseminated fungal infection) presenting with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia (p.402) Serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, serum osmolality, Mg2+ and Ca2+, complete blood count (p.403) Urinary pH, osmolality, creatinine and electrolytes (urine Na+ <20 mM indicates distal Na+ delivery limits K+ excretion) (p.403) Transtubular K+ gradient (TTKG) as a bedside index of urinary K+ excretion — expected >7-8 in hyperkalaemia; values <8 suggest tubular resistance/low aldosterone (interpret cautiously) (p.403) Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, with 9-alpha-fludrocortisone response, to characterise hypoaldosteronism (p.403) Pseudohyperkalaemia (factitious hyperkalaemia) — artefactual K+ release during/after venepuncture from fist clenching, marked thrombocytosis/leukocytosis/erythrocytosis with in vitro efflux, cold storage of the sample, or hereditary red-cell membrane transport defects (e.g. SLC4A1/AE1 mutations) (p.401-402) Acute anxiety at venepuncture with respiratory alkalosis causing redistributive (true but transient) hyperkalaemia (p.402) Hyperkalaemia (plasma K+ ≥5.5 mM) occurs in up to 10% of hospitalised patients; severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) in ~1% and carries significantly increased mortality (p.401). Reduced renal K+ excretion is the single most common underlying cause; transcellular shift and reduced tissue uptake act mainly as acute contributors (p.401). Excess dietary intake alone is a rare cause because the kidney can normally upregulate secretion — but small intake increments can provoke severe hyperkalaemia in susceptible patients (e.g. diabetics with hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism and CKD); occult sources include K+-containing salt substitutes (p.401-402). The ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are notoriously INSENSITIVE, particularly in CKD/ESRD patients — a normal ECG does NOT exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia (p.403). Hyperkalaemia per se impairs renal acid excretion (K+ competes with NH4+ for TALH reabsorption), so it can itself contribute to metabolic acidosis; restoring normokalaemia often corrects this hyperkalaemic acidosis (p.403). Hyperkalaemia can produce a type I Brugada ECG pattern (pseudo-RBBB with coved ST elevation in precordial leads); the hyperkalaemic Brugada sign is distinguished from genetic Brugada syndrome by absent P waves, marked QRS widening and an abnormal QRS axis (p.403). A urine Na+ concentration <20 mM signals that low distal Na+ delivery is limiting K+ excretion, suggesting volume repletion or a loop diuretic may help lower K+ (p.403). Hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency because of its cardiac effects — arrhythmias include sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, slow idioventricular rhythms, VT, VF and asystole (p.402-403). ECG progression as a severity cue: tall peaked T waves (5.5-6.5 mM) -> loss of P waves (6.5-7.5 mM) -> widened QRS (7.0-8.0 mM) -> sine-wave pattern (>8.0 mM), heralding impending VF/asystole (p.403). ECG manifestations mandate urgent treatment; but K+ ≥6.5 mM WITHOUT ECG changes should still be managed aggressively, because ECG findings are an unreliable predictor of cardiac toxicity (p.403-404). Management principle (knowledge): a three-stage sequence — (1) immediately antagonise cardiac effects (IV calcium stabilises the myocardium by raising the action-potential threshold), (2) shift K+ into cells, (3) remove K+ from the body (p.403-404). Secondary hyperkalaemic paralysis — ascending paralysis that can include diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory failure (p.403). Treating a falsely high K+: failing to exclude pseudohyperkalaemia before intervening (haemolysed sample, fist clenching, extreme thrombo/leuko/erythrocytosis, cold storage) (p.401-402). Relying on a normal/near-normal ECG to exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia — ECG changes are notoriously insensitive, especially in CKD/ESRD (p.403). Forgetting drug and dietary causes: ACEi/ARB/renin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid-receptor blockers (spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone) — additive in combination; K+-sparing diuretics and the structurally similar antibiotics trimethoprim and pentamidine block ENaC; NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors and beta-blockers cause hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism; heparin/LMWH inhibit aldosterone synthesis (p.402). Drugs blocking the RAA axis also blunt the adrenal aldosterone response to a rising K+, compounding the effect (p.402). Anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis) do NOT shift K+ out by the acidosis mechanism, unlike non-anion-gap and respiratory acidoses — so attributing hyperkalaemia to acidosis in these settings can mislead (p.402). Plasma K+ rises when efflux of intracellular K+ outpaces clearance or when renal excretion falls. Acidaemia drives K+ out of cells via effective K+-H+ exchange to buffer extracellular pH — but this shift is seen mainly with non-anion-gap (mineral) and respiratory acidoses; it does NOT occur with the organic anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). Hyperosmolality (mannitol, hypertonic saline, IVIG, hypertonic glucose without insulin in diabetics) shifts K+ out by solvent drag. Cationic amino acids (lysine, arginine, epsilon-aminocaproic acid) and Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitors (digoxin and related cardiac glycosides from yellow oleander, foxglove, cane-toad bufadienolide; fluoride) cause efflux. Succinylcholine depolarises muscle via upregulated acetylcholine receptors (contraindicated after burns, neuromuscular injury, disuse atrophy, prolonged immobilisation). Impaired excretion arises from blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, reduced distal Na+/flow delivery, hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, mineralocorticoid resistance, and reduced functioning nephron mass. Cardiotoxicity reflects altered cardiac membrane excitability: mild rises alter repolarisation (T-wave changes), higher levels depress intracardiac conduction (PR/QRS prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, sine wave). (p.401-403) Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) is associated with a significantly increased risk of mortality. Cardiac toxicity can progress rapidly to fatal arrhythmia, but is reversible with prompt treatment; hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis frequently corrects once normokalaemia is restored. weakness Measuring potassium too late, when a transiently elevated level has already returned to normal Failing to recognise coexisting myotonia that would point away from the hypokalaemic form Attributing hyperkalaemia to primary renal or adrenal disease and missing the channelopathy Overlooking that potassium supplementation or potassium-rich diets can precipitate rather than relieve attacks Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis is caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, the gene for the alpha subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutant channels fail to inactivate completely, producing a persistent inward sodium current that keeps the sarcolemma partially depolarised. A modest rise in extracellular potassium further depolarises the membrane, and when depolarisation is sufficient the sodium channels become inactivated and the fibre inexcitable, causing flaccid paralysis. When depolarisation is milder it instead produces repetitive firing experienced as myotonia, explaining the frequent overlap of weakness and stiffness in affected individuals. Attacks tend to be brief and frequent in childhood and often become milder in adult life, and most patients have a normal life expectancy, although some develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy over time.

Hypernatraemia — hypernatremia, hypertonic dehydration, elevated serum sodium Central diabetes insipidus Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Osmotic diuresis (hyperglycaemia, high protein feeds, mannitol) Extrarenal water loss from gastrointestinal or insensible routes Inadequate water intake in dependent patients Sodium overload from hypertonic fluids or salt ingestion Serum sodium and plasma osmolality with assessment of volume status Urine osmolality and urine volume to characterise water handling Water deprivation testing and response to desmopressin when diabetes insipidus is suspected Blood glucose and review of osmotic loads or hypertonic fluids Assessment of renal function and other electrolytes Neuroimaging or pituitary evaluation when central diabetes insipidus is considered Hypernatraemia reflects a deficit of water relative to sodium and almost always signifies a problem with water intake or excessive water loss rather than sodium excess Because thirst is a powerful defence, sustained hypernatraemia usually occurs in those who cannot access or request water, such as infants, the elderly, and patients with impaired consciousness The main causes are pure or hypotonic water loss (renal or extrarenal), including diabetes insipidus, and less commonly a gain of sodium Assessment of urine osmolality helps localise the problem: dilute urine in the face of hypernatraemia points to a renal concentrating defect such as diabetes insipidus Clinical features are predominantly neurological, ranging from lethargy and irritability to seizures and coma, reflecting brain cell shrinkage Management principles are to restore water gradually, address ongoing losses, and treat the underlying cause, while calculating and replacing the water deficit Correction of chronic hypernatraemia must be slow because the brain accumulates osmoles to adapt, and rapid rehydration risks cerebral oedema Diabetes insipidus is distinguished into central and nephrogenic forms by the response to desmopressin, which guides treatment Depressed consciousness, seizures, or coma indicating severe hypernatraemia Rapidly rising sodium or profound water deficit Signs of severe volume depletion with haemodynamic compromise Overly rapid correction risking cerebral oedema Correcting chronic hypernatraemia too rapidly and causing cerebral oedema Failing to account for ongoing water losses when calculating replacement Overlooking diabetes insipidus in a patient passing large volumes of dilute urine Assuming hypernatraemia means too much sodium rather than too little water Hypernatraemia results from a relative water deficit that raises plasma osmolality. Normally, a rise in osmolality stimulates thirst and antidiuretic hormone release, restoring water balance; hypernatraemia therefore develops when water is unavailable or the thirst mechanism is impaired, or when water losses overwhelm intake. Losses may be extrarenal (through the gut, skin, or lungs) or renal, the latter including osmotic diuresis and the failure to concentrate urine in diabetes insipidus. Central diabetes insipidus reflects deficient antidiuretic hormone production, whereas the nephrogenic form reflects renal resistance to the hormone. Less commonly, administration or ingestion of excess sodium produces hypernatraemia with volume expansion. The rise in extracellular osmolality draws water out of cells; shrinkage of brain cells produces the neurological manifestations, and the brain's compensatory accumulation of intracellular solutes over time is what makes rapid correction hazardous. Outcome depends heavily on the severity, rate of onset, and underlying condition. Acute severe hypernatraemia and hypernatraemia in critically ill or elderly patients carry significant mortality, largely reflecting the underlying illness. With appropriate identification of the cause and carefully paced water replacement, milder cases generally recover fully, while cautious correction avoids the danger of cerebral oedema.
