in HP the lung bases are frequently spared Nonspecific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP) Sarcoidosis - distinguished by prominent hilar adenopathy, extrapulmonary involvement and well-formed noncaseating granulomas Organic toxic dust syndrome (OTDS) - neither requires prior sensitization nor shows specific IgG antibodies Acute lung injury / ARDS (mimicked by acute eosinophilic pneumonia) Hypereosinophilic syndromes (HES) and EGPA when nonrespiratory features accompany an eosinophilic pneumonia Respiratory infection (nonfibrotic HP can be mistaken for it) Loffler syndrome from Ascaris or hookworm larvae Strongyloides stercoralis (chronic infection and, in immunocompromised/steroid-treated hosts, fatal hyperinfection) Paragonimiasis, filariasis (tropical eosinophilia from Wuchereria), visceral larval migrans Nonparasitic infections: coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, basidiobolomycosis, tuberculosis Careful occupational/home/avocational exposure history (cornerstone of HP diagnosis), possibly with site visit HRCT: ground-glass opacities and centrilobular nodules in nonfibrotic HP, expiratory air trapping; reticular changes/traction bronchiectasis and basal-sparing honeycombing in fibrotic HP Pulmonary function tests (restrictive OR obstructive; not diagnostic but track impairment and response; DLCO may be markedly reduced in fibrotic HP) Serum precipitins / specific IgG to suspected antigens (presence alone insufficient; limited panels give false negatives) Bronchoscopy with BAL (lymphocytosis, CD4/CD8 <1 in most) Lung biopsy (transbronchial, cryobiopsy, or surgical) for noncaseating granulomas - not absolutely required For eosinophilic syndromes: blood eosinophil count, BAL eosinophil percentage (>25% in AEP; ~60% mean in CEP), ESR/CRP/IgE, ANCA (anti-MPO in EGPA), and as needed echocardiogram, electromyogram, bone marrow biopsy ABPA: total IgE (>500, often >1000 IU/mL), Aspergillus skin test/specific IgE, Aspergillus precipitins/specific IgG, chest imaging for central bronchiectasis and mucus impaction Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis Sarcoidosis Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia Pulmonary Langerhans cell granulomatosis Drug/toxin reaction (NSAIDs, systemic antibiotics, particulate metals, inhalational drugs of abuse, post-radiation pneumonitis) Malignancy-associated eosinophilia (leukemia, lymphoma, lung cancer, adenocarcinoma/squamous cell carcinoma) Systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren syndrome) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP, extrinsic allergic alveolitis) results from inhalational exposure to a wide range of antigens, producing an inflammatory response of the alveoli and small airways; systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue can accompany the respiratory complaints (p.2228). Sensitization to an inhaled antigen (specific circulating IgG) is necessary but NOT sufficient to define HP, because many sensitized individuals never develop disease (p.2228-2229). There is an as-yet-unexplained DECREASED risk of developing HP in smokers (p.2229). US risk groups include farmers (farmer's lung: thermophilic actinomycetes/Aspergillus from grain, moldy hay, silage), bird owners (bird fancier's lung: feather, dropping and serum-protein antigens), industrial workers (chemical worker's lung: diphenylmethane and toluene diisocyanate), and hot tub users; mycobacteria can cause HP rather than frank infection in hot tub lung and metalworking-fluid HP (p.2229). Recent guidelines advocate ABANDONING the acute/subacute/chronic terminology in favor of categorizing HP as either nonfibrotic or fibrotic; cluster analysis splits patients into a recurrent-systemic-symptom group and a more-severe-respiratory group (p.2229). Antigen avoidance generally results in resolution of symptoms; acute symptoms may resolve within hours to days, while a more subacute course resolves over weeks to months (p.2229). Chronic/fibrotic HP can present insidiously with progressive dyspnea, cough, fatigue, weight loss and digital clubbing, and—unlike other forms—can have an irreversible respiratory component NOT responsive to antigen removal; bird-antigen exposure tends toward a fibrotic phenotype while farmer's lung may show an emphysematous phenotype (p.2229). Diagnosis depends foremost on a history of exposure to an offending antigen that correlates with symptoms; a careful occupational and home exposure history is essential and may be supplemented by a clinician visit to the work or home environment, with reexposure sometimes used to confirm the diagnosis (p.2229). BAL lymphocytosis is characteristic of HP though not specific; most cases have a CD4+/CD8+ ratio <1, but a lower lymphocyte threshold should be applied in active smokers (p.2230). Characteristic HP histology is loose, poorly defined NONcaseating granulomas near small airways—contrasting with the well-formed granulomas of sarcoidosis—plus a patchy lymphocyte-predominant interstitial infiltrate and bronchiolitis with organizing exudate (p.2230). HP Study Group clinical prediction rule: six significant predictors, the strongest being exposure to a known HP antigen; others are serum precipitins, recurrent symptoms, symptoms 4-8 h after exposure, inspiratory crackles, and weight loss (p.2230). Pulmonary eosinophilic syndromes share pulmonary infiltrates plus increased eosinophils in tissue, sputum and/or BAL; the first classifying step is distinguishing PRIMARY disorders from eosinophilia SECONDARY to a drug, infection, malignancy, or another pulmonary condition such as asthma (p.2231). Acute eosinophilic pneumonia (AEP): acute febrile illness <1 month with hypoxemic respiratory failure (often needing ventilation), diffuse infiltrates and BAL eosinophilia >25%; typically affects men aged 20-40 with NO asthma history and is often linked to recent tobacco initiation, vaping, or dust from indoor renovation (p.2231). AEP is often initially mistaken for acute lung injury/ARDS until BAL reveals >25% eosinophils; peripheral eosinophilia is often ABSENT at presentation but appears 7-30 days later; it is distinguished by absence of organ failure beyond the lungs, high corticosteroid responsiveness, excellent prognosis, and recovery without relapse (p.2231-2232). Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP): indolent illness, mostly female nonsmokers (mean age 45), many with asthma; the 'photographic negative of pulmonary edema' (peripheral/pleural-based opacities) is pathognomonic but seen in <25% of patients; ~90% have peripheral eosinophilia and >50% relapse, often needing prolonged corticosteroids (p.2232). EGPA (formerly Churg-Strauss): eosinophilic vasculitis with asthma and multi-organ involvement (lung, heart, skin, GI, nerve, kidney); peripheral eosinophilia >1000/uL (or >10% WBC) and ANCA (perinuclear/anti-MPO) in about one-third of patients; cardiac, GI and renal involvement portend a poorer prognosis (p.2232-2233). ABPA is an eosinophilic disorder from allergic sensitization to Aspergillus, presenting asthmatically with brownish mucus plugs; it features prominent peripheral eosinophilia, IgE >500 (often >1000) IU/mL, and Aspergillus sensitivity—central bronchiectasis is a classic finding but is NOT required for diagnosis; consider ABPA in refractory asthma and as a complication of cystic fibrosis (p.2233-2234). Loffler syndrome is transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia from helminthic larvae passing through the lung, most commonly Ascaris (also hookworm); symptoms are generally self-limited (p.2234). Hypoxemic respiratory failure with diffuse infiltrates in a previously healthy young man - consider acute eosinophilic pneumonia Progressive dyspnea, weight loss and digital clubbing with honeycombing - chronic/fibrotic HP that may be irreversible and IPF-like Asthma with neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), purpura, cardiac or renal involvement and eosinophilia - EGPA; cardiac involvement portends worse prognosis and up to 50% of untreated EGPA die within 3 months Refractory asthma with brownish mucus plugs and very high IgE - evaluate for ABPA Eosinophilia in an immunocompromised or steroid-treated patient - risk of fatal Strongyloides hyperinfection Failing to obtain a detailed exposure history - the single most important step, as the strongest HP predictor is exposure to a known antigen Relying on specific IgG/precipitins alone: asymptomatic exposed individuals (farmers, pigeon breeders) can be IgG positive, and limited antigen panels often yield false negatives Expecting a particular PFT pattern - HP can be restrictive OR obstructive, so PFTs do not establish the diagnosis Misdiagnosing AEP as ARDS/acute lung injury because peripheral eosinophilia is often absent at presentation (BAL eosinophilia is the key) Treating EGPA-prone severe asthma with corticosteroids can mask systemic eosinophilia and vasculitis and delay the EGPA diagnosis Confusing fibrotic HP with IPF/NSIP even on biopsy (basal sparing favors HP) HP is an immune-mediated reaction to inhaled antigens small enough to deposit in distal airways and alveoli, characterized by dysregulated TH1 and TH17 responses. Precipitating IgG antibodies indicate adaptive immunity, but innate mechanisms also contribute, with Toll-like receptors and downstream MyD88 signaling driving neutrophil recruitment. No clear genetic basis is established, though polymorphisms in antigen-processing genes (TAP1, MHC class II) occur in some cohorts. In chronic HP, bone marrow-derived fibrocytes may contribute to inflammation and fibrosis, and chronic HP shares the MUC5B promoter polymorphism with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. In the pulmonary eosinophilic syndromes, the eosinophil is central; pathology shows tissue eosinophil infiltration, and in EGPA extravascular granulomas and necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis/thrombosis may involve lung, heart, skin, muscle, liver, spleen and kidney. These syndromes are thought to arise from dysregulated eosinophilopoiesis or autoimmunity (elevated IgE, IgG4, rheumatoid factor; heightened T-cell immunity); IL-5 is hypothesized to be etiologic, and ANCAs binding vascular walls likely contribute to vascular injury in EGPA (p.2229, 2231). HP that has not progressed to chronic lung disease has a favorable outcome with likely resolution if antigen avoidance is achieved; chronic HP with lung fibrosis has a poorer prognosis, with chronic pigeon breeder's lung showing mortality similar to IPF. Acute eosinophilic pneumonia has an excellent prognosis with near-complete recovery and no recurrence. Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia responds rapidly to corticosteroids but >50% of patients relapse. In EGPA, up to 50% of untreated patients die within 3 months of diagnosis whereas treated patients have >70% six-year survival; clinical remission is achievable in >90% with ~25% relapsing, and myocardial, GI and renal involvement portend a poor prognosis. HES respond less reliably to corticosteroids (<50% first-line responders) (p.2229, 2232, 2233). Current guidance categorizes HP as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic scheme). Acute eosinophilic pneumonia diagnostic criteria: acute febrile respiratory illness <1 month, hypoxemic respiratory failure, diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray, BAL eosinophilia >25%, absence of parasitic/fungal/other infection, absence of drugs known to cause pulmonary eosinophilia, quick corticosteroid response, and failure to relapse after stopping corticosteroids.

Hypersomnia — hypersomnolence, excessive daytime sleepiness, idiopathic hypersomnia, central disorders of hypersomnolence Chronic insufficient sleep syndrome Obstructive sleep apnoea Narcolepsy type 1 and type 2 Idiopathic hypersomnia Medication or substance-related sleepiness Depression and other psychiatric or medical illness Detailed sleep history and sleep diary, sometimes with actigraphy, to exclude insufficient sleep Epworth Sleepiness Scale to quantify subjective daytime sleepiness Overnight polysomnography to exclude sleep apnoea and other fragmenting disorders Multiple sleep latency test to measure objective sleepiness and detect early REM onsets Selected testing such as CSF orexin or HLA typing when narcolepsy is suspected Hypersomnia denotes excessive daytime sleepiness or an excessive need for sleep that is not explained by insufficient sleep opportunity, and it should be distinguished from fatigue and low motivation The most common cause overall is chronic insufficient sleep, and this behavioural cause must be excluded before pursuing primary hypersomnia disorders Secondary hypersomnia from obstructive sleep apnoea, medication or substance effects, depression, and other medical conditions is far more common than the central disorders of hypersomnolence Narcolepsy, especially type 1 with cataplexy, is the prototypical central hypersomnia and is linked to loss of hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) signalling Idiopathic hypersomnia produces prolonged, non-refreshing sleep with severe sleep inertia and is a diagnosis of exclusion The Epworth Sleepiness Scale quantifies subjective sleepiness, while objective assessment relies on polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test Documenting short sleep latency and early transitions into REM sleep on testing supports a diagnosis of narcolepsy Management combines good sleep hygiene, treatment of any underlying cause, scheduled naps, and, on principle, wake-promoting pharmacotherapy where required Cataplexy, indicating narcolepsy type 1 and warranting confirmatory evaluation Sudden severe sleepiness following a central nervous system insult or with new neurological signs Sleepiness causing motor vehicle or occupational accidents, a safety priority Hypersomnia masking underlying depression with suicide risk Failing to exclude chronic insufficient sleep before diagnosing a primary hypersomnia Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as a treatable cause of daytime sleepiness Missing cataplexy in the history and thereby delaying a narcolepsy diagnosis Neglecting the road-safety and occupational implications of severe daytime sleepiness Normal daytime alertness depends on adequate prior sleep and on wake-promoting neuronal systems, prominently the hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) network. In narcolepsy type 1, selective loss of orexin-producing neurons, thought to be autoimmune and associated with specific HLA types, destabilises the boundaries between wake, non-REM, and REM sleep, producing sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations as REM phenomena intrude into wakefulness. Idiopathic hypersomnia has a less well-defined mechanism, possibly involving enhanced GABAergic sedation or altered sleep homeostasis. Secondary hypersomnias arise when sleep is fragmented (as in sleep apnoea or periodic limb movements), curtailed (insufficient sleep), or suppressed in quality by drugs, depression, or systemic illness, reducing restorative sleep and driving daytime sleepiness. Secondary hypersomnia often improves substantially when the underlying cause is treated; narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia are typically lifelong but manageable, with most patients achieving meaningful symptom control through combined behavioural and pharmacological measures.

avoids radioactivity (p.3034) Unbound (free) T3 - to detect T3 toxicosis (2-5% of patients have only elevated T3) (p.3034) TPO and thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies; serum Tg increased in all thyrotoxicosis EXCEPT factitia (low in factitia, high in thyroiditis) (p.3033-3034, 3037) Pituitary MRI/CT and alpha-subunit if TSH inappropriately non-suppressed (suspect TSH-secreting adenoma) (p.3034, 3037) Panic / anxiety attacks (p.3034) Mania (p.3034) Phaeochromocytoma (p.3034) Malignancy-associated weight loss (p.3034) Depression (especially apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly) (p.3033) Thyrotoxicosis (state of thyroid hormone excess) is NOT synonymous with hyperthyroidism (excessive thyroid gland function); destructive thyroiditis and ingestion of exogenous hormone cause thyrotoxicosis without true hyperthyroidism (p.3032). Graves' disease accounts for 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis; affects up to 2% of women, ~10x less common in men, typically ages 20-50 (p.3032). In the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss ('apathetic thyrotoxicosis'), and may be mistaken for depression (p.3033). Weight loss occurs despite increased appetite due to raised metabolic rate, but ~5% of patients GAIN weight due to increased food intake (p.3033). Atrial fibrillation is more common in patients >50 years; treating the thyrotoxic state alone reverts AF to sinus rhythm in up to 75% of those without underlying cardiac disease (p.3033). Symptoms in descending frequency: hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance/sweating, palpitations, fatigue/weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhoea, polyuria, oligomenorrhoea/loss of libido (p.3033 Table 396-2). Signs: tachycardia (AF in elderly), fine tremor, goitre, warm moist skin, proximal myopathy, lid retraction/lag (p.3033 Table 396-2). Fine tremor is best elicited by having the patient stretch out the fingers while feeling the fingertips with the palm (p.3033). Lid retraction (staring appearance) results from sympathetic overactivity and occurs in ANY form of thyrotoxicosis; it is distinct from the specific eye signs of Graves' ophthalmopathy (p.3033). Graves' ophthalmopathy specific signs (proptosis, periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, diplopia) occur in ~one-third of Graves' patients clinically; ~10% of ophthalmopathy is unilateral (p.3033-3034). Graves' ophthalmopathy can occur in the absence of hyperthyroidism in ~10% (euthyroid ophthalmopathy); onset is within a year before/after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (p.3034). A diffuse, firm (non-nodular) goitre with a thrill or bruit at the inferolateral margins points to Graves' disease (p.3033). Thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is a recognised association, particularly common in Asian males (p.3033). Mild hypercalcaemia occurs in up to 20% of patients (hypercalciuria more common) from thyroid-hormone-driven bone resorption; long-standing disease causes osteopenia and a small increased fracture rate (p.3033). Optic nerve compression at the orbital apex -> papilloedema, peripheral field defects and permanent vision loss; sight-threatening ophthalmopathy is an emergency (p.3034, 3036) Corneal exposure/ulceration when lids fail to close during severe proptosis (p.3034) Atrial fibrillation or worsening angina/heart failure, especially in elderly or pre-existing cardiac disease - high cardiac output can precipitate high-output failure (p.3033) Features suggesting thyroid storm: fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice (p.3036) Do NOT assume thyrotoxicosis means hyperthyroidism - low radionuclide uptake indicates destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess or factitia rather than gland overactivity, which changes management (p.3032, 3037). T3 toxicosis: 2-5% have suppressed TSH with elevated T3 but normal T4, so a normal T4 does not exclude thyrotoxicosis; conversely iodine-induced T4 toxicosis can show elevated T4 with normal T3 (p.3034). Diagnostic confusion: thyrotoxicosis can elevate bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, and cause microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia (p.3034). Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis (<1%) is idiosyncratic and abrupt - routine prospective blood-count monitoring is NOT useful; instead warn patients to stop the drug and obtain an urgent FBC for sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers (p.3036). Suppressed TSH may persist for several months after starting antithyroid drugs, so TSH is not a reliable early index of response - titrate on unbound T4; euthyroidism is usually not reached until 6-8 weeks (p.3035). Thyroid acropachy/clubbing without coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy in a Graves' patient should prompt a search for an alternative cause of clubbing (p.3034). A normal TSH with normal unbound T4/T3 excludes thyrotoxicosis and excludes Graves' as the cause of a diffuse goitre (p.3034). Graves' hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs, detected as TSH-receptor antibodies/TRAb) that activate the TSH receptor. Susceptibility involves genetic (HLA-DR, CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, TSH-R gene) and environmental factors; concordance is 20-30% in monozygotic vs <5% in dizygotic twins. Triggers/risk factors include stress, smoking (moderate for Graves', major for ophthalmopathy), sudden iodine intake increases, the postpartum period (threefold rise), and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors. Coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis and TPO/Tg antibodies (up to 80%) mean there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy is driven by cytokine-mediated (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) infiltration of extraocular muscles by activated T cells, fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan deposition trapping water, and aberrant IGF-1R signalling; the TSH-R is expressed in orbital tissue (p.3032-3033). Untreated, clinical features generally worsen; historical mortality was 10-30% before effective therapy. Mild Graves' may show spontaneous relapses and remissions, and rarely fluctuates between hypo- and hyperthyroidism with changing TRAb activity. About 15% of treated patients in remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from the destructive autoimmune process. Ophthalmopathy runs an independent course: typically worsens over 3-6 months, plateaus over 12-18 months, then partially improves (soft-tissue changes especially); fulminant in up to 5% requiring acute intervention. Thyrotoxic crisis carries 4-17% mortality even with treatment (p.3034-3036). Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH with normal free T3 and free T4; treatment is increasingly recommended in the elderly to reduce atrial fibrillation and bone-loss risk (p.3034, 3041). Graves' ophthalmopathy severity is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs e.g. lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), though activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring/treatment decisions (p.3034).

the major hyperthyroid causes are Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and toxic adenoma (Harrison 22e p.3032). Graves' disease accounts for roughly 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis, occurs in up to 2% of women (about one-tenth as frequent in men), and typically presents between 20 and 50 years of age (Harrison 22e p.3032). Graves' hyperthyroidism is driven by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins acting on the TSH receptor; TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) can be measured and, because they cross the placenta, are useful for monitoring pregnant Graves' patients for neonatal thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3033). Symptoms in descending frequency include hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance with sweating, palpitations, fatigue and weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, and diarrhea; signs include tachycardia (atrial fibrillation in the elderly), tremor, goiter, warm moist skin, and proximal myopathy (Harrison 22e p.3033). Apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly may present mainly with fatigue and weight loss and can be mistaken for depression; features may be subtle or masked in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3033). Treating the thyrotoxic state alone converts atrial fibrillation to normal sinus rhythm in up to about 75% of patients without underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3033). Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease) is specific to Graves'; about one-third of patients have clinical eye disease, it can occur without hyperthyroidism in ~10%, and onset is within the year before or after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (Harrison 22e p.3033). Destructive (subacute or silent) thyroiditis causes a transient thyrotoxic phase from release of preformed hormone with characteristically LOW radionuclide uptake and elevated thyroglobulin; true hyperthyroidism is absent (Harrison 22e p.3035). Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis classically evolves through three phases over about 6 months: thyrotoxic, then hypothyroid, then recovery; it is supported by a high ESR and a tender goiter, and the T4/T3 ratio is higher (T3 less disproportionately elevated) than in Graves' or thyroid autonomy (Harrison 22e p.3038). Toxic multinodular goiter typically affects elderly patients with subclinical or mild overt hyperthyroidism, often presenting with atrial fibrillation; iodine exposure (e.g., contrast dye) can precipitate thyrotoxicosis, and the scan shows heterogeneous patchy uptake (Harrison 22e p.3042). A toxic (hyperfunctioning) adenoma usually causes only mild thyrotoxicosis, generally detectable when the nodule exceeds about 3 cm, and over 90% harbor activating somatic mutations in the TSH receptor or GSalpha (Harrison 22e p.3043). Mild hypercalcemia occurs in up to 20% of thyrotoxic patients (hypercalciuria is more common), and longstanding thyrotoxicosis causes osteopenia with a small increase in fracture rate due to direct stimulation of bone resorption (Harrison 22e p.3033). Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm): fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhea, and jaundice with a high mortality (about 4-17% even with treatment) New or worsening atrial fibrillation or high-output heart failure, particularly in the elderly or those with preexisting cardiac disease Sight-threatening ophthalmopathy from optic nerve compression (papilledema, peripheral field defects, loss of vision) or corneal ulceration/exposure Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis (notably in Asian males) Diplopia or severe proptosis with corneal exposure during sleep Equating thyrotoxicosis with hyperthyroidism: destructive thyroiditis, factitia, and iodine excess cause hormone excess without true gland hyperfunction (low uptake) Missing apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly, where it can present as fatigue/weight loss or be mistaken for depression or malignancy Overlooking that there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels because coexisting thyroiditis affects function Interpreting thyroid function tests during acute severe illness (sick euthyroid/nonthyroidal illness) as true thyroid disease; routine testing in acutely ill patients should be avoided, though an undetectable TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) makes primary thyroid disease more likely Failing to recognize that radioiodine therapy can worsen ophthalmopathy in a small proportion of patients, especially smokers Attributing clubbing to thyroid acropachy in a Graves' patient who lacks coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy, where another cause should be sought Graves' disease results from a combination of genetic susceptibility (HLA-DR and immunoregulatory genes such as CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, plus the TSH-R gene) and environmental triggers (smoking, stress, sudden iodine excess, the postpartum period, and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors). Hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins that bind and stimulate the TSH receptor; coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis (TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies in up to 80%) means there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy reflects activated T-cell infiltration of extraocular muscles with cytokine-driven (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan accumulation that traps water and causes muscle swelling, increased orbital fat, and late irreversible fibrosis; the TSH-R is an orbital autoantigen and aberrant IGF-1 receptor signaling on orbital fibroblasts contributes. In destructive thyroiditis, follicular disruption releases preformed hormone (low radionuclide uptake). Toxic multinodular goiter reflects acquired functional autonomy of nodules, while toxic adenoma reflects constitutive cyclic AMP signaling from activating TSH-R or GSalpha mutations. Untreated, clinical features generally worsen and mortality was historically 10-30% before effective therapy. Some patients with mild Graves' disease have spontaneous relapses and remissions, and about 15% of those who enter remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from ongoing autoimmune destruction. Ophthalmopathy follows an independent course, typically worsening over 3-6 months, plateauing over the next 12-18 months, then partially improving, though up to ~5% have a fulminant course. Subacute thyroiditis usually resolves completely, with late permanent hypothyroidism in about 15%. Thyrotoxic crisis carries a high mortality (about 4-17%) even with treatment, due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia, or hyperthermia. Toxic multinodular goiter and toxic adenoma do not remit spontaneously and require definitive therapy. Graves' ophthalmopathy is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs such as lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement/periorbital edema; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), although activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring and treatment decisions. Thyrotoxicosis itself ranges from subclinical (low TSH, normal free T4/T3) to overt disease and may escalate to thyrotoxic crisis/thyroid storm.

to heart failure Using preload- or afterload-reducing agents that can worsen dynamic outflow obstruction Misclassifying HCM as physiological athlete's heart or hypertensive hypertrophy Missing an infiltrative mimic such as cardiac amyloidosis Neglecting sudden death risk assessment and family screening HCM is most often caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance. The result is myocyte hypertrophy and disarray with interstitial fibrosis, producing a thickened, stiff, non-compliant left ventricle and diastolic dysfunction. Asymmetric septal hypertrophy, together with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, can create dynamic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract and associated mitral regurgitation. Myocardial fibrosis and disarray provide a substrate for ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, while microvascular dysfunction contributes to ischaemia despite normal epicardial arteries. Many patients have a near-normal life expectancy, but HCM carries risks of sudden cardiac death, atrial fibrillation with embolism, and progression to heart failure; risk stratification and defibrillator therapy in high-risk individuals substantially reduce sudden death, and outcomes are worse with extensive fibrosis or progression to a dilated, hypokinetic end stage.

malignancy rather than a simple scar Progressive contracture across a joint causing functional loss Signs of secondary infection within the scar or wound Confusing a hypertrophic scar with a keloid, leading to inappropriate treatment expectations Performing surgical revision alone without adjuncts, resulting in recurrence Delaying preventive measures such as pressure garments in burn scars Repeated or excessive corticosteroid injection causing skin atrophy, telangiectasia, or hypopigmentation Overlooking functional contracture while focusing only on cosmetic appearance Hypertrophic scarring reflects a dysregulated wound-healing response in which the proliferative phase is prolonged and remodelling is impaired. Excessive and persistent inflammation drives fibroblast proliferation and overproduction of collagen, with an imbalance between collagen synthesis and breakdown. The collagen is deposited in comparatively organised bundles aligned parallel to the skin surface, distinguishing it histologically from the thick, disorganised collagen of keloids. Mechanical tension across the wound and prolonged inflammation from infection or delayed healing promote this fibrotic response, and myofibroblast activity contributes to scar contraction. Hypertrophic scars often mature and flatten over one to two years and generally respond better to conservative therapy than keloids, with a lower recurrence rate after appropriately combined treatment. Outcomes are less favourable for burn-related scars and scars under tension or across joints, which may require ongoing management to prevent contracture.

avoiding antiplatelet and anticoagulant agents where possible Corneal blood staining and glaucoma are the main sight-threatening complications requiring surgical washout if uncontrolled All patients of African, Mediterranean, or Middle Eastern descent should be screened for sickle cell status Uncontrolled raised intraocular pressure threatening the optic nerve, especially in sickle cell disease Rebleeding with a larger, darker hyphema Early corneal blood staining indicating endothelial compromise Signs of globe rupture or associated posterior segment injury Spontaneous hyphema in a child raising concern for retinoblastoma Failing to screen for sickle cell disease, in which tolerable pressures for others become sight-threatening Missing associated injuries such as angle recession, lens dislocation, or globe rupture Underestimating rebleeding risk and permitting excessive activity Overlooking a spontaneous hyphema as a marker of neovascular disease or tumour Hyphema results from disruption of iris or ciliary body vessels, most often by blunt trauma that causes rapid globe compression and a sudden shift of intraocular structures, tearing vessels at the iris root or angle. Red cells settle inferiorly under gravity. Clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis create a window of rebleeding risk. Blood and inflammatory debris obstruct the trabecular meshwork, raising intraocular pressure; in sickle cell disease, red cells sickle in the low-oxygen, acidotic aqueous, further impairing outflow and increasing susceptibility to optic nerve damage. Prolonged high pressure with an intact endothelial insult leads to corneal blood staining. Small hyphemas usually clear without sequelae, but larger bleeds, rebleeding, sickle cell disease, and sustained pressure elevation carry a higher risk of glaucoma, corneal staining, and permanent visual loss.

Hypoglycemia complicating severe malaria carries a poor prognosis, especially in children and pregnant women, and the usual warning signs may be absent (p.1807) Recurrent hypoglycemia blunts counterregulation, causing hypoglycemia unawareness — loss of the warning symptoms that normally prompt correction (p.204) Coma or seizures from neuroglycopenia indicate severe, potentially irreversible CNS compromise (p.721, p.782) Repeated hypoglycemia produces hypoglycemia unawareness by impairing the counterregulatory response, so the absence of adrenergic warning symptoms does not exclude dangerous hypoglycemia (p.204). In severe malaria the clinical signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are typically absent and its neurologic effects mimic the underlying disease, so it is easily missed without glucose measurement (p.1807). Failing to measure C-peptide/proinsulin can miss surreptitious exogenous insulin use, which mimics insulinoma (p.721). Circulating IGF-II may not be overtly elevated in tumor-induced hypoglycemia, so a normal IGF-II level does not exclude it; the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio is more informative (p.635-636, p.782). A markedly raised leukocyte count can cause artifactual low glucose (pseudohypoglycemia) if the sample is not processed promptly (p.635-636). Falling glucose triggers counterregulatory autonomic activation (catecholamines) producing adrenergic warning symptoms, while inadequate glucose supply to the brain produces neuroglycopenia. Non-islet-cell tumors can cause hypoglycemia chiefly through secretion of incompletely processed IGF-II ('big' IGF-II), which weakly activates insulin receptors and more strongly IGF-I receptors; reduced IGFBP-3 and acid-labile subunit increase IGF-II bioavailability to target tissues, and large tumors may also impair hepatic gluconeogenesis or consume glucose. In severe malaria, hypoglycemia arises from failed hepatic gluconeogenesis combined with increased host (and to a lesser extent parasite) glucose consumption, and may be worsened by quinine-induced insulin secretion (p.204, p.635-636, p.721, p.782, p.1807). Hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible with glucose, but in severe malaria it independently signals a poor prognosis, particularly in children and pregnant women (p.1807).

bone loss Diagnosing hypogonadism from a single non-fasting or afternoon testosterone sample Ignoring SHBG effects so that total testosterone misrepresents androgen status Starting testosterone in a man wishing to conceive, thereby suppressing sperm production Overlooking a treatable central cause such as prolactinoma or iron overload Male hypogonadism is deficient testicular function affecting testosterone production, sperm production, or both. Primary hypogonadism arises from disease of the testes themselves, such as Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, orchitis, trauma, chemotherapy, or radiation, and is characterised by low testosterone with compensatory elevation of LH and FSH. Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism arises from impaired hypothalamic or pituitary signalling, from congenital GnRH deficiency, pituitary tumours or infiltration, hyperprolactinaemia, haemochromatosis, or suppression by systemic illness and drugs, and shows low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal gonadotrophins. Testosterone deficiency reduces libido and sexual function, impairs spermatogenesis, and, if prolonged, decreases muscle mass, bone density, and erythropoiesis. Outcomes depend on cause and reversibility; central hypogonadism from a treatable pituitary lesion or hyperprolactinaemia may recover, whereas primary testicular failure is usually permanent, and appropriate testosterone replacement improves symptoms, body composition, and bone health when fertility is not the immediate goal.

severe generalised paralysis during an attack Cardiac arrhythmia or marked electrocardiographic disturbance during potassium shifts Rebound hyperkalaemia following overzealous potassium replacement Progressive fixed proximal weakness suggesting an established vacuolar myopathy Assuming a true potassium deficit and over-replacing, which can precipitate dangerous rebound hyperkalaemia Overlooking thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, a treatable acquired mimic Relying on interictal potassium and creatine kinase, which are frequently normal between attacks Missing the association with certain general anaesthetic and glucose-loading situations that can provoke attacks Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis arises from mutations in genes encoding skeletal-muscle voltage-gated ion channels, most commonly the dihydropyridine receptor calcium channel (CACNA1S) and less often the sodium channel (SCN4A). Many disease-causing variants affect arginine residues in the voltage-sensing domains, creating an aberrant gating-pore current that leaks cations through the sensor. During provocation, an insulin- or catecholamine-driven shift of potassium into muscle cells combines with this abnormal leak to paradoxically depolarise and then inactivate the sarcolemma, rendering the fibre inexcitable and producing flaccid weakness. The transient low serum potassium reflects redistribution rather than depletion, and repeated depolarisation over years may contribute to the vacuolar myopathy seen in some patients. Attack frequency often lessens with age and with effective prophylaxis, and most patients have a normal lifespan, but a proportion develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy that can cause lasting disability independent of the acute episodes.

Symptomatic hyponatraemia / SIADH — Serum & urine osmolality, urine Na⁺ Volume status assessment Correct slowly (osmotic demyelination risk) Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390). Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391). Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391). Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391). Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391). Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391). Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392). SIAD causes: malignancy (especially small-cell lung carcinoma — 75% of malignancy-associated SIAD; ~10% present with Na+ <130 mM), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, abscess, pleural effusion), CNS disease (tumour, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus), drugs, and transient causes (pain, nausea, stress, endurance exercise, general anaesthesia) (p.391-392). Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393). Serum osmolality, converted to effective osmolality/tonicity by subtracting urea (in mg/dL divided by 2.8) — true hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; this also excludes pseudohyponatraemia (p.393). Serum K+, BUN/creatinine — hyperkalaemia suggests adrenal insufficiency/hypoaldosteronism; raised urea/creatinine suggests renal cause (p.393). Urine osmolality — <100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia; >400 mOsm/kg indicates dominant AVP excess; intermediate values suggest multifactorial physiology (p.393). Urine Na+ — <20-30 mM suggests hypovolaemia; >30 mM suggests SIAD, but values overlap, especially in the elderly (p.393). Urine K+ — to calculate the urine-to-plasma electrolyte ratio, useful for predicting response to fluid restriction (p.393). Demonstration that plasma Na+ corrects after isotonic saline hydration is the diagnostic gold standard for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (p.393). Pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia: measured Na+ is low but plasma tonicity is normal or high; exclude by measuring serum osmolality (p.393). Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia: a translocational, true hyponatraemia driven by glucose-induced water efflux that corrects once glucose is lowered (p.393). Hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ <135 mM) is very common, affecting up to ~22% of hospitalised patients (p.390). The absolute plasma Na+ concentration says nothing about a patient's volume status, which must be assessed separately for both diagnosis and management (p.390). Hyponatraemia is almost always driven by excess circulating AVP and/or increased renal sensitivity to AVP combined with free-water intake; the main exception is hyponatraemia from low solute intake (p.390). Diagnostically subdivide by ECF volume into hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, and hypervolaemic groups based on clinical history and volume status (p.390). In hypovolaemic patients, a urine Na+ <20 mM predicts a brisk rise in plasma Na+ with isotonic saline, because AVP falls and a water diuresis ensues (p.391). Serum uric acid helps discriminate: SIAD is typically associated with low uric acid (<4 mg/dL), whereas hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is often hyperuricaemic (p.391, p.393). Thiazides can mimic SIAD and do not impair urinary concentrating ability, so AVP retains full effect; defer diagnosing SIAD until 1-2 weeks after stopping the thiazide (p.391, p.393). The 48-hour mark distinguishes acute from chronic hyponatraemia and is decisive for how aggressively/cautiously sodium may be corrected (p.392). Cerebral salt wasting (a rare hypovolaemic cause linked to intracranial disease) responds to aggressive salt-and-water repletion, so distinguishing it from SIAD is critical because their management diverges (p.391). Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia is a medical emergency: nausea/headache/vomiting can rapidly progress to seizures, brainstem herniation, coma and death (p.392). Acute hyponatraemia can cause normocapnoeic or hypercapnoeic respiratory failure, typically from non-cardiogenic 'neurogenic' pulmonary oedema with normal wedge pressure; resulting hypoxia amplifies neurological injury (p.392). Premenopausal women are far more likely than men to develop encephalopathy and severe neurological sequelae (p.392). Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or >18 mM in 48 h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically central pontine myelinolysis — presenting days later with para-/quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, 'locked-in' syndrome, or reduced consciousness (p.393). ODS can occur even with appropriately slow correction in high-risk patients: alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, and liver transplantation (p.393). Plasma Na+ <125 mM is the threshold at which chronic hyponatraemia commonly becomes overtly symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures) (p.392). Iatrogenic settings for acute hyponatraemia: postoperative premenopausal women given hypotonic fluids, glycine irrigation (TURP/uterine surgery), colonoscopy prep, recent thiazide initiation (Table 56-2, p.392). MDMA ('Ecstasy'/'Molly') causes potent thirst and AVP induction leading to severe acute hyponatraemia; exercise-associated (endurance/marathon) hyponatraemia is another acute setting (p.392). Hypovolaemic patients may appear clinically euvolaemic, with only a low urine Na+ to reveal the cause (p.390). Hyponatraemia is frequently multifactorial, especially when severe — evaluate every source of excess AVP (volume status, drugs, nausea, pain) rather than settling on one (p.393). Failing to exclude pseudohyponatraemia/hyperglycaemia before correcting; check serum osmolality and glucose first (p.393). The 93%-water assumption used by ion-sensitive electrodes makes plasma Na+ falsely low in extreme hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia (p.393). Urine Na+ values overlap substantially between SIAD and hypovolaemia (particularly in the elderly); the saline-challenge response is the definitive discriminator (p.393). Diagnosing SIAD in a patient on thiazides — defer the SIAD label until 1-2 weeks after stopping the drug (p.393). Distinguishing cerebral salt wasting from SIAD is critical because management differs (salt repletion vs fluid restriction) (p.391). Hyponatraemia reflects a relative excess of body water to sodium, almost always from increased circulating AVP (or heightened renal AVP sensitivity) together with free-water intake. Volume status modulates AVP release: hypovolaemia raises AVP at any given osmolality, and 'hypervolaemic' arterial underfilling (heart failure, cirrhosis) triggers neurohumoral activation that likewise elevates AVP, causing water retention. In hypovolaemia, AVP-mediated V2-receptor water reabsorption plus free-water intake lowers Na+. In hypervolaemic oedematous states (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total-body Na+ rises but water rises proportionally more; reduced arterial filling drives the AVP response. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIAD is the commonest cause: free-water intake persists at osmolalities below the normal thirst threshold, with patients subclinically volume-expanded (so-called 'AVP escape' limits distal tubular transport, preserving a modestly hypervolaemic steady state). Four AVP-secretion patterns occur in SIAD: erratic unregulated secretion (~1/3 of patients), failure to suppress at low osmolality, a 'reset osmostat', and a subset with undetectable AVP (gain-of-function V2-receptor mutations causing 'nephrogenic' SIAD). At the brain level, hyponatraemia causes water to move down the osmotic gradient from hypotonic ECF into cells, producing cellular swelling and cerebral oedema within the rigid skull; acute encephalopathy results when volume-regulatory mechanisms (CSF shunting, efflux of Na+/K+/Cl-) are overwhelmed. In chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells extrude organic osmolytes (creatine, betaine, glutamate, myoinositol, taurine), a process largely complete within 48 h, which mitigates but does not abolish symptoms (p.390-392). Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia carries high risk of severe neurological injury and death; encephalopathy is more severe in premenopausal women. The degree of hyponatraemia is an important prognostic indicator in hypervolaemic states, reflecting the intensity of neurohumoral activation. Chronic hyponatraemia, even when judged 'asymptomatic', is associated with subtle gait and cognitive deficits (reversible with correction), increased risk of falls, and an increased fracture risk due to neurological dysfunction and reduced bone density — so safe correction is warranted even without overt symptoms. Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection can produce permanent disabling neurological deficits (p.392-393). By volume status: hypovolaemic (total body water down, total body Na+ down more), euvolaemic/no oedema (total body water up, Na+ near-normal), and hypervolaemic (total body water up markedly, Na+ up) — Fig. 56-5, p.391. By chronicity: acute hyponatraemia is <48 h (osmolyte extrusion incomplete, higher cerebral-oedema risk) and chronic is >48 h (osmolytes largely extruded, lower acute symptom risk but higher ODS risk on correction), p.392. By tonicity: true hypotonic hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, distinct from pseudohyponatraemia (normal/high tonicity) and hyperglycaemic translocational hyponatraemia, p.393. Symptomatic threshold for chronic disease is generally plasma Na+ <125 mM (p.392). SIAD diagnostic features include euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality typically >400 mOsm/kg / not maximally dilute), urine Na+ >30 mM, low serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL), and absence of thyroid/adrenal dysfunction, diuretics, hypovolaemia or hypervolaemia (p.391, p.393).

underlying malignancy, pulmonary, or central nervous system disease when SIADH is suspected Hyponatraemia is the most common electrolyte disturbance in hospitalised patients and reflects a relative excess of water compared with sodium, usually driven by impaired water excretion The diagnostic approach begins by confirming true hypotonic hyponatraemia, then assessing volume status and measuring urine osmolality and urine sodium SIADH is a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine, elevated urine sodium, and normal thyroid and adrenal function, diagnosed after excluding other causes Common triggers of SIADH include malignancy, pulmonary disease, central nervous system disorders, and numerous drugs The severity of symptoms depends more on how quickly sodium falls than on the absolute value, ranging from mild confusion to seizures and cerebral oedema in acute severe cases The cornerstone of management in SIADH is fluid restriction, with the underlying cause treated wherever possible Correction must be gradual in chronic hyponatraemia because overly rapid rises in sodium risk osmotic demyelination, whereas acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with severe neurological signs warrants prompt but controlled correction with hypertonic saline Exclude pseudohyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia-related dilution before attributing a low sodium to a water-handling disorder Seizures, marked confusion, or reduced consciousness indicating severe or acute hyponatraemia Rapid onset of symptoms suggesting acute cerebral oedema Signs of raised intracranial pressure Overly rapid correction risking osmotic demyelination Correcting chronic hyponatraemia too quickly and precipitating osmotic demyelination Diagnosing SIADH without excluding hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and volume depletion Giving isotonic saline in SIADH, which can paradoxically worsen the sodium Overlooking a drug or occult malignancy as the driver of persistent SIADH Hyponatraemia develops when water intake exceeds the kidney's ability to excrete free water, diluting plasma sodium. Antidiuretic hormone is central: when its release is appropriate (as in volume depletion or reduced effective circulating volume in heart failure and cirrhosis) or inappropriate (as in SIADH), water is retained and urine remains concentrated. In SIADH, ADH is secreted or acts independently of osmotic and volume signals, so the kidney retains water despite plasma hypotonicity; patients are clinically euvolaemic because the retained water distributes across body compartments and mild volume expansion promotes natriuresis. The fall in plasma osmolality drives water into brain cells, and the resulting cerebral oedema accounts for the neurological features. In chronic hyponatraemia the brain adapts by extruding solutes, which is why rapid correction can dehydrate neurons and cause osmotic demyelination. Mild chronic hyponatraemia is often well tolerated but is associated with falls, cognitive impairment, and worse outcomes in the underlying illness. Acute severe hyponatraemia can be life-threatening from cerebral oedema, while inappropriately rapid correction can cause devastating osmotic demyelination. With cause-directed treatment and appropriately paced correction most patients recover, and SIADH prognosis largely follows that of its underlying cause.

acute hypocalcaemia is a medical emergency requiring intravenous calcium and cardiac monitoring Long-term management uses calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol) analogues, aiming to relieve symptoms while avoiding hypercalciuria and renal complications Autoimmune, genetic, and magnesium-related causes should be considered when there is no surgical history, as hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and action Tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, or carpopedal spasm Prolonged QT interval or cardiac arrhythmia from acute hypocalcaemia Rapidly falling calcium in the early postoperative period after neck surgery Altered mental status or stridor accompanying severe hypocalcaemia Overlooking coexisting hypomagnesaemia, which must be corrected before hypocalcaemia will respond Interpreting calcium without correcting for albumin or measuring the ionised fraction Aiming for fully normal serum calcium and inducing hypercalciuria and renal damage Failing to anticipate and monitor for hypocalcaemia after thyroid or parathyroid surgery Hypoparathyroidism results from deficient secretion or action of parathyroid hormone, most often after surgical injury to the glands but also from autoimmune destruction, genetic syndromes, infiltration, or severe magnesium disturbance. Lack of PTH reduces renal calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion, decreases bone resorption, and impairs conversion of vitamin D to its active form, together producing hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia. Low ionised calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, causing the characteristic clinical features. With appropriate calcium and active vitamin D therapy most patients maintain adequate calcium and lead normal lives, though lifelong treatment and monitoring are needed and chronic therapy carries risks of hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and renal impairment.

inherited recessively and milder forms sometimes dominant The biochemical hallmark is a persistently low serum alkaline phosphatase with raised natural substrates, namely inorganic pyrophosphate, pyridoxal-5-phosphate (vitamin B6) and urinary phosphoethanolamine A low alkaline phosphatase is the diagnostic clue and is the opposite of most other rickets and metabolic bone diseases, so it must not be dismissed as unimportant Clinical severity spans a wide spectrum from lethal perinatal disease with almost unmineralised bone to mild adult disease with fractures and early tooth loss Premature
