pyrophosphate analogues and may worsen the condition Perinatal or infantile respiratory failure from an unmineralised, poorly compliant chest Vitamin B6-responsive seizures in an infant with a low alkaline phosphatase Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment Craniosynostosis with raised intracranial pressure in infantile disease Ignoring a low alkaline phosphatase as a laboratory artefact rather than a diagnostic clue Giving bisphosphonates, which can aggravate the mineralisation defect Supplementing with high-dose vitamin D reflexively, risking worsening hypercalcaemia Misclassifying severe perinatal disease as osteogenesis imperfecta Hypophosphatasia results from deficient activity of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme that normally hydrolyses inorganic pyrophosphate at the mineralising surface of bone and teeth. Because inorganic pyrophosphate is a potent inhibitor of hydroxyapatite crystal formation, its accumulation blocks normal mineralisation, producing rickets and osteomalacia despite adequate calcium and phosphate. Accumulation of pyridoxal-5-phosphate impairs vitamin B6 delivery to the brain and can cause seizures in severe forms, while phosphoethanolamine accumulates and is excreted in the urine. The perinatal and infantile forms were historically often lethal, but enzyme replacement therapy has markedly improved survival and skeletal outcome; milder childhood and adult forms have a good prognosis with attention to fractures, dental health and pain.

Hypopituitarism — panhypopituitarism, Sheehan syndrome Pituitary adenoma (mass on MRI may be indistinguishable from lymphocytic hypophysitis) Craniopharyngioma, Rathke's cyst, meningioma, germinoma, glioma, ependymoma Pituitary metastases (breast, lung, colon) and lymphoma/leukemia Empty sella syndrome Primary (target-organ) endocrine failure as opposed to central deficiency Tuberculosis involving the pituitary/hypothalamus Fungal infection (histoplasmosis) and opportunistic fungal infection in AIDS Parasitic infection (toxoplasmosis) Pneumocystis jirovecii Tertiary syphilis Low target-organ hormone with low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone (e.g., low free thyroxine with low/inappropriately normal TSH = secondary hypothyroidism; low testosterone without elevated gonadotropins = hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) Dynamic/provocative testing of pituitary reserve GH reserve: insulin-induced hypoglycemia, arginine, glucagon, l-dopa, GHRH, or macimorelin; AGHD defined by peak GH response to hypoglycemia <3 ug/L ACTH/cortisol reserve: most reliably assessed during insulin-induced hypoglycemia; CRH stimulation and cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) testing also used Pituitary MRI or CT to identify mass, hemorrhage, stalk deviation, or empty sella; age-matched IGF-1 as an index of GH therapeutic response Lymphocytic and granulomatous hypophysitis Sarcoidosis Hemochromatosis Histiocytosis X (Langerhans cell histiocytosis) Amyloidosis Checkpoint-inhibitor immunotherapy hypophysitis Deficient production of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones produces the clinical features of hypopituitarism; most adult cases are acquired (Harrison 22e p.2992). With pituitary compression or destruction, trophic hormone failure usually occurs sequentially: GH first, then FSH, LH, TSH, and ACTH last; in children growth retardation is often the presenting feature, in adults hypogonadism is the earliest symptom (Harrison 22e p.2992). Clinical manifestations depend on which hormones are lost and the degree of deficiency: GH deficiency causes growth disorders in children and abnormal body composition in adults; gonadotropin deficiency causes menstrual disorders/infertility/loss of secondary sexual characteristics; TSH deficiency causes hypothyroidism; ACTH deficiency causes secondary adrenal insufficiency; PRL deficiency causes failure of lactation (Harrison 22e p.2996). Secondary adrenal insufficiency from ACTH deficiency causes hypocortisolism with relative preservation of mineralocorticoid production (unlike primary adrenal failure) (Harrison 22e p.2996). Pituitary apoplexy is an endocrine emergency: acute intrapituitary hemorrhage/infarction presenting with severe headache, meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, ophthalmoplegia, and in severe cases cardiovascular collapse and loss of consciousness (Harrison 22e p.2993). Lymphocytic hypophysitis occurs most often in postpartum women, presents with hyperprolactinemia and an MRI mass resembling an adenoma, and may be transient or permanent; it should be considered before unnecessary surgery in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass (Harrison 22e p.2993). Up to 20% of patients receiving CTLA-4 inhibitor immunotherapy (e.g., ipilimumab) develop hypophysitis; PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) can also cause it, sometimes with delayed presentation (Harrison 22e p.2993). Patients on glucocorticoid replacement require careful dose escalation (stress dosing) during acute illness, dental procedures, trauma, and hospitalization (Harrison 22e p.2996). Pituitary apoplexy: an endocrine emergency that may cause severe hypoglycemia, hypotension/shock, CNS hemorrhage, and death; severe ophthalmoplegia or progressive visual loss indicates need for urgent surgical decompression Secondary adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis: hypocortisolism that can precipitate life-threatening shock, especially during stress, illness, surgery, or trauma Acute severe headache with meningeal signs, bilateral visual changes, or loss of consciousness in a patient with known/suspected pituitary mass Critical sequencing pitfall: in suspected combined deficiency, glucocorticoid replacement must be started BEFORE thyroid hormone, because giving thyroxine first can accelerate cortisol clearance and precipitate an adrenal crisis in a patient with unrecognized secondary adrenal insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.3133). Insulin-induced hypoglycemia testing must be performed cautiously in suspected adrenal insufficiency (enhanced susceptibility to hypoglycemia/hypotension) and is contraindicated in active coronary artery disease or known seizure disorders (Harrison 22e p.2996). Lymphocytic hypophysitis may be radiologically indistinguishable from a pituitary adenoma and should be considered in a postpartum woman with a new pituitary mass before surgery is undertaken (Harrison 22e p.2993). Radiation-induced and brain-injury-related hypopituitarism develops insidiously over 5-15 years (and in 25-40% after brain injury), so long-term periodic endocrine follow-up is required even after apparently successful treatment (Harrison 22e p.2993). Empty sella patients usually have normal pituitary function, but hypopituitarism may develop insidiously (Harrison 22e p.2994). Impaired synthesis or secretion of one or more anterior pituitary trophic hormones (GH, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, PRL), and sometimes posterior pituitary AVP. Causes are developmental/genetic (transcription factor mutations such as PROP1, PIT-1, TPIT, midline defects) or, more commonly in adults, acquired from compressive mass effect of tumors or from local pituitary/hypothalamic traumatic, autoimmune, inflammatory, infiltrative, or vascular damage. The same processes may impair hypothalamic hormone production with secondary pituitary failure. With progressive compression/destruction, hormone loss is typically sequential (GH > FSH > LH > TSH > ACTH) (Harrison 22e p.2992). Hormone replacement is usually safe and effective at maintaining homeostasis when it mimics physiologic secretion. However, long-standing pituitary damage carries an increased mortality rate, primarily from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease; adult hypopituitarism is associated with an approximately threefold increase in cardiovascular mortality versus age- and sex-matched controls. Prior head/neck irradiation is an additional determinant of increased mortality, especially from cerebrovascular disease. Lymphocytic hypophysitis may resolve with recovery of pituitary function after glucocorticoid treatment depending on extent of damage; hypopituitarism is common after apoplexy (Harrison 22e p.2996).

Hypothermia and Peripheral Cold Injuries — Accidental hypothermia, Primary accidental hypothermia, Secondary hypothermia, Frostbite, Peripheral cold injury, Chilblain, Pernio, Trench foot, Immersion foot, Nonfreezing cold injury Hypoglycemia Hypothyroidism / myxedema coma Adrenal insufficiency and hypopituitarism Sepsis (hypothermia is a poor prognostic sign) Drug or ethanol intoxication / overdose Diabetic ketoacidosis and other metabolic acidoses Uremia CNS injury (cerebrovascular accident, subarachnoid hemorrhage, hypothalamic lesion, spinal cord injury) Shapiro syndrome (agenesis of corpus callosum with episodic hypothermia) Continuous core temperature monitoring, ideally esophageal (lower third); rectal/bladder as ancillary ECG (look for J/Osborn wave, bradydysrhythmias, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias) Arterial blood gas read uncorrected for temperature Serum potassium (prognostic in arrest), glucose, electrolytes, renal function Coagulation studies, fibrinogen, and platelet count (interpret with caution) Hematocrit (artificially elevated by cold) and white-cell count Bedside echocardiography and end-tidal CO2 to confirm perfusion status For frostbite: angiography, fluorescence microangiography, technetium-99 / pyrophosphate bone scan, or MR angiography to assess tissue viability and demarcation Cold-induced ileus with rectus abdominis spasm mimicking an acute abdomen Areflexia attributed to hypothermia masking a spinal cord lesion J (Osborn) waves misinterpreted as an injury current / ischemia Trench/immersion foot bullae indistinguishable from frostbite Shaking rigors of infection mistaken for shivering Accidental hypothermia is defined as an unintentional fall in core temperature below 35C (95F); at this threshold the compensatory mechanisms that conserve heat begin to fail. Primary hypothermia follows direct cold exposure of a previously healthy person, while secondary hypothermia complicates a systemic illness or injury and carries a much higher mortality. Core temperature cannot be reliably predicted from the clinical picture, so confirmation requires direct measurement; a probe in the lower third of the esophagus with continuous monitoring is preferred because rectal and bladder readings lag behind true core changes. Severity grading by core temperature: mild 35C to 32.2C (initial tachycardia then bradycardia, shivering, apathy, dysarthria, impaired judgment, cold diuresis); moderate 32.2C to 28C (declining consciousness, pupillary dilation, paradoxical undressing, atrial/ventricular arrhythmias, J-wave changes, loss of protective airway reflexes); severe below 28C (coma, loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole, apnea, poikilothermia). Vital signs are difficult to interpret without the core temperature: respiratory rate should be low because CO2 production declines, so persistent hyperventilation suggests a CNS lesion or organic acidosis, and tachycardia out of proportion to temperature suggests secondary causes such as hypoglycemia, hypovolemia, or toxin overdose. Paradoxical undressing (inappropriate removal of clothing in response to cold stress) is a classic maladaptive behavior; cold-induced ileus and rectus abdominis spasm can mimic or mask an acute abdomen, and confusion or combativeness resolves faster with rewarming than with chemical or physical restraint. The J (Osborn) wave at the QRS-ST junction supports the diagnosis and is frequently misread by automated ECG software as an injury current. Laboratory values are systematically distorted by cold: hematocrit rises about 2% per 1C drop (masking anemia), white-cell sequestration and marrow suppression can mask infection, and coagulation tests run at 37C appear deceptively normal despite a genuine in-vivo coagulopathy, so platelet and fresh-frozen-plasma transfusion is ineffective for the cold-induced coagulopathy. Arterial blood gases should NOT be temperature-corrected; an uncorrected pH of 7.42 and PCO2 of 40 mmHg reflect appropriate ventilation and acid-base balance at any core temperature, and overzealous hyperventilation is a common error given depressed CO2 production. Frostbite occurs when tissue temperature falls below 0C (32F): ice-crystal formation distorts cellular architecture, endothelial damage produces microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing there is progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, edema, and superficial necrosis, with mummification and demarcation taking weeks to months. Frostbite always produces a sensory deficit (light touch, pain, or temperature); superficial frostbite causes anesthesia and erythema without tissue loss, whereas vesiculation with surrounding edema/erythema indicates deeper injury and hemorrhagic vesicles signal severe microvascular damage that may lead to amputation. Chilblain (pernio) is a nonfreezing injury from repetitive damp-cold exposure above freezing, most common in young women with a history of Raynaud phenomenon, producing erythema, edema, pruritus, then plaques, blue nodules, and ulcerations on the dorsa of hands and feet. Trench foot / immersion foot results from repetitive wet-cold exposure above freezing; feet are initially cyanotic, cold, and edematous, with bullae progressing to ulceration and liquefaction gangrene, and survivors may have hyperhidrosis, cold sensitivity, and painful ambulation for years. Core temperature below 28C (severe): coma, maximal risk of ventricular fibrillation and asystole Potassium >12 mmol/L during resuscitation indicates widespread cell lysis and grave prognosis Core temperature <10-12C, pH <6.5, or fibrinogen <0.5 g/L may preclude continued resuscitation Hypothermia complicating sepsis is a poor prognostic sign Asphyxia preceding cooling (e.g., avalanche burial) is the strongest negative predictor of survival Hemorrhagic vesicles or persistent cyanosis after rewarming in frostbite (risk of amputation, compartment syndrome) Frostbite with rhabdomyolysis and completely frozen extremities Correcting arterial blood gases for temperature; the uncorrected values guide management Overzealous hyperventilation despite depressed CO2 production, dangerously raising pH Applying direct heat to extremities in chronic severe hypothermia, which causes peripheral vasodilation and core 'afterdrop' Transfusing platelets or fresh-frozen plasma for the cold coagulopathy (ineffective, as the defect is temperature-dependent enzyme inhibition) Deep insertion of central venous catheters or pulmonary artery catheters into the cold heart, which can precipitate refractory arrhythmias or perforation Trusting coagulation tests or hematocrit at face value (assays run at 37C; hematocrit falsely elevated) Premature termination of frostbite thawing because reperfusion is intensely painful Repeated dosing of drugs (e.g., digoxin, insulin) that are ineffective while cold but become toxic during rewarming Heat is lost by radiation (55-65%), conduction (10-15%, markedly increased in cold water), convection (increased with wind), respiration, and evaporation. The preoptic anterior hypothalamus orchestrates thermoregulation: the immediate autonomic defense releases norepinephrine, raises muscle tone, and triggers shivering to increase the basal metabolic rate, while cutaneous cold reception drives reflex vasoconstriction; prolonged cold also stimulates the thyroid axis. When these defenses are overwhelmed, hypothermia first stimulates and then progressively depresses every organ system. In peripheral freezing injury, tissue freezing causes ice-crystal formation that destroys cellular architecture; endothelial damage leads to stasis and microvascular thrombosis, and after thawing progressive dermal ischemia, arteriovenous shunting, rising tissue pressures, edema, and necrosis develop. Nonfreezing injuries (chilblain, trench/immersion foot) arise from neuronal and endothelial damage caused by repetitive cold exposure above the freezing point. Outcome depends heavily on whether hypothermia is primary or secondary, the precipitating cause, and the presence of asphyxia. Secondary hypothermia complicating systemic illness carries much higher mortality, and hypothermia with sepsis is a poor prognostic sign. Because cold itself is protective, survival has been reported after cardiac arrest times exceeding 7 hours, and intact neurologic recovery has occurred at extremely low core temperatures; the patient is not dead until warm and dead. Markers of a grave prognosis during resuscitation include potassium >12 mmol/L (cell lysis), pH <6.5, fibrinogen <0.5 g/L, and core temperature <10-12C, while preceding asphyxia (avalanche) is the most important negative predictor. The HOPE score uses six covariates to predict which arrested hypothermic patients may benefit from extracorporeal life support. Frostbite sequelae often persist as paresthesia, thermal misperception, and hyperhidrosis, with delayed nail deformities, cutaneous carcinomas, and epiphyseal damage in children. Hypothermia is graded by core temperature: Mild = 35C (95F) to 32.2C (90F); Moderate = below 32.2C (90F) to 28C (82.4F); Severe = below 28C (82.4F). Frostbite is classified as superficial (anesthesia and erythema, no tissue loss) versus deep (vesiculation, hemorrhagic vesicles, possible amputation); an alternative scheme grades by the proximal extent of presenting cyanosis: grade 1 none, grade 2 distal phalanx, grade 3 to the metacarpophalangeal joint, grade 4 proximal to the MP joint.

Hypothyroidism — Hashimoto thyroiditis, underactive thyroid Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis (opposite end of thyroid dysfunction; thyroiditis can pass through both phases) Sick euthyroid (nonthyroidal illness) syndrome Secondary (central) hypothyroidism from hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disease Multinodular goiter or thyroid carcinoma (asymmetric Hashimoto goiter may mimic these) Primary thyroid lymphoma (rare, strongly associated with pre-existing autoimmune thyroiditis) Depression and dementia (overlapping fatigue, poor concentration, slowing) Serum TSH as the primary screening test (most sensitive for primary disease) Free/unbound T4 to confirm clinical hypothyroidism when TSH is elevated (T3 measurement is not indicated) TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies to establish autoimmune etiology Lipid panel (cholesterol, triglycerides), creatine phosphokinase, and full blood count for associated abnormalities Anterior pituitary function testing when central hypothyroidism is suspected (after excluding drug effect and sick euthyroid syndrome) Thyroid ultrasound to distinguish heterogeneous Hashimoto echotexture from true nodules warranting FNA Depression Dementia Nephrotic syndrome (edema, hyperlipidemia) Chronic fatigue states Anemia of other cause In iodine-sufficient regions the most common causes are autoimmune disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) and iatrogenic injury (treatment of hyperthyroidism); iodine deficiency remains a leading cause worldwide (p.3027). Biochemical hallmark of primary hypothyroidism is an elevated TSH with a low unbound (free) T4; a normal TSH excludes primary, but not secondary/central, disease (p.3030-3031). Subclinical hypothyroidism is biochemical thyroid hormone deficiency (raised TSH, usually still-normal free T4) with few or no symptoms; overt hypothyroidism typically corresponds to TSH >10 mIU/L with a low free T4 (p.3029, p.3032). Symptoms (descending frequency) include tiredness/weakness, dry skin, cold intolerance, hair loss, poor concentration and memory, constipation, and modest weight gain with poor appetite (the weight gain is mainly fluid retention in myxedematous tissue) (p.3028-3029). Signs include dry coarse skin, cool extremities, nonpitting puffiness of face/hands/feet (myxedema), diffuse alopecia with thinning of the outer eyebrow, bradycardia, peripheral edema, and delayed relaxation of tendon reflexes (p.3028-3029). TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are present in >95% of autoimmune hypothyroidism and confirm the etiology once hypothyroidism is established (p.3030). Onset is usually insidious, so patients may only recognize symptoms once euthyroidism is restored; Hashimoto's patients may present with goiter (irregular, firm) rather than hypothyroid symptoms (p.3029-3030). Associated laboratory abnormalities include raised creatine phosphokinase, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, and a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, which generally resolve with thyroxine replacement (p.3030). Autoimmune hypothyroidism clusters with other autoimmune disorders, particularly vitiligo, pernicious anemia, Addison's disease (Schmidt's syndrome), type 1 diabetes, and the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes (p.3030). Myxedema coma — the severe end of untreated hypothyroidism: reduced level of consciousness (sometimes seizures), hypothermia (can reach 23 C), with 20-40% mortality despite treatment; almost always in the elderly and often precipitated by infection, cold, sedatives, or acute cardiopulmonary events. Hypoventilation with hypoxia and hypercapnia, plus hypoglycemia and dilutional hyponatremia, in profound hypothyroidism. Impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism (consider co-existing adrenal insufficiency before/with thyroid replacement). Neonatal/congenital hypothyroidism — risk of permanent neurologic damage if treatment is delayed, mandating neonatal screening. Significant pericardial or other serous effusions, conductive deafness, or carpal tunnel/entrapment syndromes as manifestations of severe disease. Central (secondary) hypothyroidism is missed if TSH is used alone: in pituitary/hypothalamic disease TSH may be low, normal, or even slightly raised, so a low free T4 is needed to make the diagnosis and TSH cannot be used to monitor therapy. A normal TSH excludes primary but NOT secondary/central hypothyroidism. T4 alone is an inferior screening test because it will not detect subclinical hypothyroidism; T3 is normal in ~25% of patients and is not indicated. An elevated TSH with normal/high free T4 in a patient on adequate levothyroxine usually reflects poor adherence (taking medication only shortly before testing), not a TSH-secretion disorder. Confirm that a raised TSH is sustained over ~3 months before treating subclinical hypothyroidism. TSH should not be relied on in the months immediately after radioiodine for Graves' disease (it stays suppressed); use unbound T4 instead. External rewarming in myxedema coma can precipitate cardiovascular collapse, and hypotonic fluids can worsen hyponatremia. Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone action, most often from primary thyroid failure. In autoimmune (Hashimoto's) disease, T cell-mediated lymphocytic infiltration with germinal-center formation, follicular atrophy, oxyphil metaplasia, and fibrosis progressively destroy the gland; atrophic thyroiditis represents its fibrotic end stage. As function declines there is a compensated phase in which a rising TSH maintains hormone levels (subclinical hypothyroidism); later free T4 falls and TSH rises further, producing overt disease. Susceptibility reflects genetic factors (HLA-DR3/DR4/DR5, PTPN22, CTLA-4) and environmental factors including high iodine intake. TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are markers; up to 20% of patients have TSH-receptor-blocking antibodies that prevent TSH binding and can cause thyroid atrophy and, by transplacental passage, transient neonatal hypothyroidism. Increased dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition traps water, producing nonpitting myxedema (Harrison 22e p.3029-3030). With levothyroxine replacement and dose titration to a normal TSH, prognosis is excellent and most laboratory and clinical abnormalities resolve, though full symptomatic relief may take months and about 10-15% report persistent symptoms despite biochemical euthyroidism. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes permanent neurologic damage, and myxedema coma still carries a 20-40% mortality independent of T4 and TSH levels (Harrison 22e p.3031-3032). Spectrum from subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH, normal free T4, few/no symptoms) to overt/clinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH usually >10 mIU/L with low free T4 and symptoms); myxedema coma represents the severe, life-threatening end. Etiologically classified as primary (thyroidal), secondary/central (pituitary or hypothalamic), congenital, or transient (Harrison 22e p.3027-3032).

rectal exam may reveal GI bleeding (pp.851, 2313) Cardiogenic shock - shares cool peripheries and narrow pulse pressure (low output) but is distinguished by raised JVP, peripheral oedema, an S3/S4 gallop and pulmonary crackles, indicating high filling pressures rather than volume depletion (p.2313, pp.2336-2337) Obstructive shock - low-output state but typically with an elevated JVP; tamponade (pulsus paradoxus, raised JVP, low-voltage ECG with electrical alternans) and tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation) mimic the hypoperfusion of hypovolemia (p.2313) Distributive shock unmasked after fluid loss (e.g. adrenal insufficiency with aldosterone-deficient hypovolaemia) (pp.2310-2311) Hypovolemic shock is haemodynamically a low-output state: reduced cardiac output and oxygen delivery driven by low preload, with a compensatory rise in systemic vascular resistance and low CVP and PCWP from depleted intravascular volume (p.2311). Divide causes into haemorrhagic (external/trauma or internal, most often upper or lower GI bleeding) and non-haemorrhagic fluid loss (profuse vomiting/diarrhoea; renal losses such as osmotic diuresis in DKA or diabetes insipidus; skin losses from severe burns or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) (p.2311). On examination it presents as a cold, low-output shock: cool/clammy peripheries, narrow pulse pressure, delayed capillary refill and a reduced JVP (<8 cm) - the heart is 'empty' - in contrast to the warm peripheries and wide pulse pressure of distributive shock (pp.2312-2313, p.2335). Tachycardia and tachypnoea are early compensatory signs, but hypotension may be a late finding; younger patients in particular can compensate for an extended period before blood pressure falls (pp.2312-2313). Signs of vascular instability appear once roughly 25% of blood volume is lost; the usual sympathetic compensation (tachycardia, vasoconstriction, regional flow shift) fails beyond ~30% loss, and loss of >40% (>2 L in an average adult) produces overt shock (confusion, dyspnoea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia) (pp.850-851). Among hypovolemic causes, haemorrhage is the most common; non-haemorrhagic GI, renal and skin fluid losses are also recognised causes (p.2311). Overt features of severe blood-volume loss (>40%): confusion, dyspnoea, diaphoresis, hypotension and tachycardia indicating critical vital-organ hypoperfusion needing immediate volume replacement (pp.850-851) New altered mental status or new oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) - signs the compensatory mechanisms have been overwhelmed (decompensated shock) (p.2312) Occult bleeding sites - retroperitoneal haemorrhage, long-bone fracture haematoma, intra-abdominal/intrapleural bleeding - that may not be externally apparent (pp.851, 2315) Elevated shock index (HR/SBP >0.9) flagging critical bleeding and likely transfusion need in haemorrhagic shock (p.2313) Compensated shock can present with a normal blood pressure: relying on an absolute SBP/MAP threshold misses early shock, since young patients may maintain pressure with tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure and only a mildly raised lactate before decompensating (pp.2312-2313). Do not be falsely reassured by tachycardia without hypotension, nor exclude shock because the heart rate is normal - patients on nodal-blocking drugs or with conduction disease may have a blunted or absent tachycardic response (pp.2312-2313). A normal initial haemoglobin/haematocrit does NOT exclude significant active haemorrhage; values fall only later as haemodilution develops, and the haematocrit does not reflect the true volume lost early on (pp.2313, 850-851). Misclassifying low-output shock: an elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, gallop or crackles point to cardiogenic/obstructive rather than hypovolemic shock and warn against indiscriminate large-volume resuscitation (pp.2313, 2336-2337). Over-resuscitation is harmful - targeted, reassessed fluid therapy is the goal rather than maximal volume (pp.2336-2337). Estimates of external blood loss at a bloody scene are often overestimated, while large internal bleeds may be clinically inapparent - examine carefully for localising signs (p.851). Hypovolemic shock arises when a fall in intravascular volume reduces preload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output and therefore systemic oxygen delivery; CVP and PCWP are low and systemic vascular resistance rises as a compensatory response (p.2311). Inadequate oxygen delivery forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, so pyruvate is converted to lactate with markedly less ATP generation; failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps disrupts ionic and pH homeostasis, and calcium influx activates phospholipases/proteases causing cell swelling and death, with leaked intracellular contents driving inflammation and microvascular injury (p.2310). In acute haemorrhage, hypovolaemia dominates first and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys); the haemoglobin is initially normal and only falls over hours as fluid shifts from the extravascular to the intravascular space (haemodilution), so the haematocrit does not reflect the volume lost early on (pp.850-851). Hypovolemic shock carries a lower mortality than septic or cardiogenic shock, which have the highest death rates among shock types (p.2311). Organ dysfunction in early (compensated) shock is often reversible if perfusion and oxygen delivery are restored, but untreated shock progresses through a decompensated phase to an irreversible phase with permanent multisystem organ dysfunction and death (pp.2311-2312). Harrison frames severity along the shock continuum (compensated/pre-shock to decompensated to irreversible) (pp.2311-2312) and, for haemorrhage, by the fraction of blood volume lost rather than an ATLS Class I-IV table (not present in this source): vascular instability emerges at about 25% loss; compensation fails beyond ~30% (postural hypotension and tachycardia); and loss of >40% (>2 L in an average adult) produces overt hypovolemic shock with confusion, dyspnoea, diaphoresis, hypotension and tachycardia (pp.850-851). The shock index (HR/SBP; normal 0.5-0.7) is a bedside severity marker, with values >0.9 indicating critical bleeding and likely transfusion need (p.2313).

I-cell disease results from deficiency of the enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, encoded (alpha/beta subunits) by GNPTAB. This enzyme adds the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker that normally directs newly synthesised lysosomal hydrolases to the lysosome. Without the marker, multiple enzymes are instead secreted into the extracellular space, so lysosomes are depleted of hydrolases and undigested substrates accumulate as characteristic inclusion bodies within cells. The biochemical signature is therefore paradoxical: low intracellular lysosomal enzyme activity but high activity of the same enzymes in plasma. Widespread lysosomal dysfunction produces severe multisystem storage disease. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The disorder is severe and progressive, with cardiorespiratory complications commonly limiting survival to early childhood. Management is supportive, as no established disease-modifying therapy exists.

this distribution difference is a key way to separate the two (p.2555-2556). A first 'flare' of bloody diarrhoea may actually be an infectious colitis (e.g., Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, C. difficile, amoebic) - infection should be excluded before diagnosing IBD; Campylobacter and others can also reactivate established UC (p.2559-2560). Granulomas are frequently absent on mucosal biopsy even in Crohn's, so their absence does not rule it out (p.2556). Effective medical therapy can normalise mucosal appearance and create apparent skip areas in UC, mimicking Crohn's distribution; biopsy normal-appearing mucosa (p.2555-2556). In patients on glucocorticoids, peritoneal signs of perforation may be blunted/absent (p.2557). An impassable colonic stricture should be presumed malignant rather than benign inflammatory (p.2557). IBD is a chronic idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract regarded as a dysregulated, inappropriate immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host. Homeostasis among the gut microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells, and mucosal immune system is normally maintained by regulatory pathways (e.g., FoxP3 T-regulatory cells); environmental factors (smoking, antibiotics, enteropathogens, diet) acting on genetic susceptibility (>240 GWAS loci, ~20% of risk explained; rare single-gene defects such as IL10/IL10R in very-early-onset disease) disrupt this balance and produce sustained inflammation. UC is a mucosal/superficial-submucosal disease, while Crohn's is transmural with fissuring and fistula/stricture formation (p.2551-2556). Toxic megacolon occurs rarely; about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, but those that do not require urgent colectomy. Perforation complicating toxic megacolon carries ~15% mortality. Risk of colorectal cancer rises with duration and extent of colitis (historically ~2% at 10 yr, 8% at 20 yr, 18% at 30 yr, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; still ~1.5-2x the general population). Extensive long-standing colitis carries the highest cancer risk. Strictures occur in ~5% of UC patients. Up to one-third of IBD patients develop at least one extraintestinal manifestation (p.2557-2563, p.2570). Montreal classification of UC severity (Harrison Table 337-4, p.2557): S0 clinical remission (no symptoms); S1 mild = up to 4 stools/day +/- blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate = 4 or more stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe = 6 or more bloody stools/day plus pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5 C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, and ESR >=30 mm/h. (These severe-disease physiologic thresholds mirror the classic Truelove-Witts criteria for acute severe colitis.) Montreal extent: E1 proctitis, E2 left-sided (distal to splenic flexure), E3 extensive/pancolitis. Crohn's is categorised by the Vienna/Montreal classification (Table 337-5, p.2558) by age at diagnosis (A), location ileal/colonic/ileocolonic/upper (L), and behaviour nonstricturing-nonpenetrating/stricturing/penetrating (B) with a perianal modifier.

abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week over the prior 3 months plus at least two of being related to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form, with onset at least 6 months earlier. Rome IV is stricter than Rome III: it requires pain at least weekly and dropped 'discomfort' as a qualifying symptom; painless diarrhoea or constipation alone does NOT meet criteria. Abdominal pain is mandatory for the diagnosis; it is typically episodic and crampy, often worsened by eating or emotional stress and relieved by passing flatus or stool. Subtype by predominant stool form: IBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed) — but subtypes are unstable, with about three-quarters of patients changing subtype and ~29% switching between IBS-C and IBS-D over a year. Onset is usually before age 45 and IBS is two to three times more common in women, who make up ~80% of severe cases. Symptoms commonly overlap with other functional disorders (fibromyalgia, headache, backache, genitourinary symptoms) and with functional dyspepsia, suggesting a shared, more extensive digestive disorder. Bloating and a subjective sense of excess gas are common, but most patients actually generate a normal volume of intestinal gas and instead have impaired gas transit/tolerance and proximal reflux of gas. Malnutrition is exceedingly rare in IBS and the pain almost always occurs only during waking hours, so sleep disruption from pain is unusual. First appearance of symptoms in old age Progressive course from the time of onset Rectal bleeding Persistent diarrhoea after a 48-hour fast Nocturnal diarrhoea Steatorrhoeal stools Anaemia, elevated sedimentation rate, or leukocytes/blood in stool Stool volume >200-300 mL/day Family history of colorectal malignancy (lowers threshold for thorough evaluation) Treating IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion only and over-investigating: few tests are needed when symptoms are typical and alarm features are absent, and unnecessary investigations may be costly and even harmful. Missing organic disease in higher-risk patients: older age, rapidly progressive symptoms, or alarm features should prompt a thorough work-up to exclude IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer rather than labelling as IBS. Attributing bloating to excess gas when most patients produce a normal gas volume but have impaired gas transit. Over-interpreting an abnormal hydrogen breath test, which can be positive simply from rapid small-bowel transit and does not reliably predict treatment response. IBS is a multifactorial functional bowel disorder with no structural lesion. Proposed mechanisms include altered GI motor activity (e.g., exaggerated postprandial and distention-evoked colonic contractions, increased high-amplitude propagating contractions with rapid transit in IBS-D), visceral hypersensitivity (lower thresholds to rectal balloon distention with sparing of somatic pain pathways), and disordered brain-gut interaction with central neural dysregulation (greater activation of mid-cingulate and prefrontal cortices on functional imaging). Psychological factors (anxiety, depression, somatization, prior physical/sexual abuse) modulate pain thresholds, and genetic factors such as serotonin transporter (SERT) polymorphisms are implicated. Peripheral contributors include low-grade mucosal immune activation with mast cells, lymphocytes and proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF), upregulated TRPV1 sensory channels, increased intestinal permeability ('leaky gut', chiefly in IBS-D and post-infectious IBS), gut dysbiosis (reduced microbial diversity, fewer Bifidobacterium/Faecalibacterium, more Enterobacteriaceae), abnormal serotonin pathways with increased enterochromaffin-cell serotonin in IBS-D, and bile acid malabsorption in up to ~25% of IBS-D. Harrison classifies IBS by predominant bowel pattern under Rome IV into IBS-C (predominant constipation), IBS-D (predominant diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed constipation and diarrhoea); these subtypes are noted to be unstable over time. Overall symptom severity ranges from mild to severe with significant quality-of-life impairment, but no formal graded severity score is specified.

compared with ischaemic stroke, headache is more common, but imaging is still required to distinguish the two (p.3453). Putaminal haemorrhage damages the adjacent internal capsule, so contralateral hemiparesis is the sentinel sign, often with the eyes deviated away from the side of the weakness (p.3454). Thalamic haemorrhage produces a prominent all-modality contralateral sensory deficit and characteristic ocular signs from inferior extension into the upper midbrain (e.g. eyes deviated down-and-in 'looking at the nose', poorly reactive unequal pupils, vertical-gaze palsy) (p.3454). Pontine haemorrhage causes rapid deep coma with quadriplegia, decerebrate rigidity and reactive 'pinpoint' (~1 mm) pupils (p.3454). Cerebellar haemorrhage classically gives occipital headache, repeated vomiting and gait ataxia; in mild cases gait ataxia may be the only sign (p.3454). Lobar haemorrhage symptoms mirror the lobe involved: occipital → hemianopia, left temporal → aphasia and confusion, parietal → hemisensory loss, frontal → arm weakness (p.3454). Seizures are uncommon at presentation but occur in roughly 6-15% of patients within the first 3 days (p.3453). Lumbar puncture is generally unnecessary and should usually be avoided in ICH because focal signs and raised ICP make it potentially herniation-inducing (p.3455). ICH accounts for about 10% of all strokes, with disproportionately high incidence in Asian and Black populations (p.3453). 'Spot sign' on CTA/post-contrast CT - associated with increased haematoma expansion, higher mortality and lower likelihood of favourable outcome (p.3455) Haematoma expansion: about a third of patients (even without coagulopathy) have significant expansion within the first day; anticoagulant-related bleeds may keep enlarging for 24-48 h (p.3454) Progressive decline in consciousness with headache and vomiting signalling rising ICP; deterioration may continue over 24-96 h from perihaematoma oedema (p.3453-3454) Cerebellar haemorrhage with depressed consciousness or obstructive hydrocephalus, or radiographic hydrocephalus - high risk of rapid brainstem-compression deterioration requiring immediate neurosurgical evaluation (p.3454) Signs of herniation (stupor/coma, dilated fixed pupil, decerebrate rigidity) (p.3453-3454) Intraventricular extension of blood - substantially increases morbidity and may cause hydrocephalus (p.3454) Cerebellar haemorrhage can deteriorate precipitously from brainstem compression or obstructive hydrocephalus; immediate surgical evacuation before severe brainstem compression may be lifesaving, and hydrocephalus from a cerebellar haematoma should generally be managed by definitive evacuation rather than ventricular drainage alone (p.3454). Haemorrhage outside the typical deep hypertensive sites, or in a non-hypertensive patient, should prompt a search for other causes (amyloid angiopathy, tumour, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) rather than being assumed hypertensive (p.3454). Conflating hypertensive encephalopathy/PRES with hypertensive ICH leads to inappropriately aggressive BP lowering - hypertensive encephalopathy warrants less aggressive reduction (p.3455). ICP is often normal even with large ICHs, so it cannot be assumed; conversely induced hyperventilation can cause ischaemia and should be limited to acute resuscitation only (p.3456). Glucocorticoids are not recommended for treating ICH (p.3456). In ICH on antiplatelet drugs without thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion showed no benefit and possible harm (p.3456). Despite the presence of haemorrhage, venous sinus thrombosis is an indication for anticoagulation to relieve venous hypertension (p.3455). Hypertensive ICH usually results from spontaneous rupture of a small (~30-100 microns) penetrating artery deep in the brain, with chronic hypertension producing vascular injury preferentially at the basal ganglia (especially putamen), thalamus, cerebellum and pons. The clot may stay small or enlarge to compress adjacent tissue and cause herniation; dissection into the ventricles markedly increases morbidity and can produce hydrocephalus. Most hypertensive bleeds evolve over 30-90 minutes, whereas anticoagulant-related bleeds may keep expanding for 24-48 h. By ~48 h macrophages begin phagocytosing the haemorrhage at its surface, and over 1-6 months it resolves to a slit-like glial-scarred cavity with haemosiderin-laden macrophages. In cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriolar degeneration with amyloid deposition in cortical vessel walls causes single and recurrent lobar haemorrhages, the commonest cause of lobar bleeding in the elderly (p.3453-3454). Overall, about 35-45% of patients die within the first month, and roughly 40% with a hypertensive ICH die, though survivors can achieve good to complete recovery because peri-haematoma tissue is displaced rather than infarcted and often regains function as the clot resorbs over months. The validated ICH Score stratifies mortality and outcome but should not be used to precisely prognosticate an individual, since withholding early aggressive care risks a self-fulfilling prophecy of poor outcome. Deep pontine haemorrhage with coma usually ends in death or a locked-in state, but small bleeds are compatible with survival; in cerebellar haemorrhage, full recovery is common if the deep cerebellar nuclei are spared (p.3453-3456). ICH Score (Hemphill et al., Stroke 2001) - validated grading scale for mortality/outcome stratification, summing five factors: age >=80 (1 pt), haematoma volume >=30 cc (1 pt), intraventricular haemorrhage present (1 pt), infratentorial origin (1 pt), and Glasgow Coma Scale 13-15 (0), 5-12 (1) or 3-4 (2); total 0-6 (p.3455-3456).

and examination, including family history and age of onset, to separate inherited from acquired disease Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is unclear Targeted investigation for underlying malignancy or systemic disease when adult-onset acquired ichthyosis is suspected Biochemical or genetic testing to define specific subtypes (for example steroid sulfatase assessment in suspected X-linked disease) Neonatal monitoring of hydration, temperature, and electrolytes in severe congenital forms Ichthyosis describes a group of disorders of cornification characterised by persistent, generalised dry, scaly skin, most of which are inherited, though acquired ichthyosis also occurs Ichthyosis vulgaris is the commonest form, presenting with fine scaling that spares the flexures, associated hyperlinear palms, and a strong link to atopy and filaggrin mutations X-linked recessive ichthyosis affects males and produces larger, darker (dirty-brown) scales, and may be associated with corneal opacities and, in some, cryptorchidism Congenital ichthyoses can present dramatically at birth, including the collodion baby encased in a taut membrane and, at the severe end, the harlequin phenotype Acquired ichthyosis appearing in an adult without a childhood history should prompt a search for underlying malignancy (notably lymphoma), metabolic, autoimmune, or nutritional disease, or a drug cause Management is largely supportive, centred on regular emollients, keratolytics or humectants to reduce scale, and gentle skin care, with systemic retinoid therapy reserved for severe congenital forms under specialist care Neonates with severe congenital ichthyosis are at risk of dehydration, temperature instability, infection, and, with a constricting collodion membrane, feeding and breathing difficulty Genetic counselling and accurate classification through clinical, and where needed genetic, assessment are valuable for families Severe congenital ichthyosis in a neonate with impaired thermoregulation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and infection risk Constricting collodion or harlequin membrane restricting respiration, feeding, or limb perfusion New adult-onset acquired ichthyosis signalling possible underlying malignancy or systemic disease Signs of secondary skin infection in a compromised barrier Ectropion, eclabium, or ocular exposure requiring protective ophthalmic care in severe forms Overlooking adult-onset acquired ichthyosis as a marker of underlying malignancy or systemic disease Attributing chronic scaling simply to dry skin or eczema without considering an ichthyosis Under-treating with insufficient emollient use, allowing scale and fissuring to persist Failing to anticipate dehydration and infection risk in affected neonates Neglecting genetic counselling and accurate subtyping for affected families The ichthyoses share a defect in the formation or shedding of the stratum corneum, resulting in accumulation of scale and an impaired epidermal barrier. In ichthyosis vulgaris, loss-of-function mutations in filaggrin reduce production of the protein that aggregates keratin filaments and generates natural moisturising factors, causing retention hyperkeratosis and barrier dysfunction. X-linked ichthyosis stems from steroid sulfatase deficiency, leading to cholesterol sulfate accumulation that impairs corneocyte shedding. The congenital autosomal recessive ichthyoses involve mutations affecting lipid processing and cornified envelope formation. Across subtypes, the disrupted barrier drives increased water loss, compensatory hyperproliferation, and inflammation, with the specific molecular defect determining scale pattern and severity. Most common inherited ichthyoses, such as ichthyosis vulgaris and X-linked ichthyosis, are lifelong but manageable with regular skin care and compatible with normal life expectancy; severe congenital forms carry significant neonatal risk and lifelong burden, while acquired ichthyosis often improves when the underlying cause is treated.

IgG4-Related Disease — IgG4-RD, IgG4-related systemic disease, Type 1 (IgG4-related) autoimmune pancreatitis, Lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis, Mikulicz's disease Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (mimicked by type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis) Primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma (mimicked by IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis) Sjogren's syndrome (Mikulicz's disease presentation) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (when destructive sinus/middle-ear/nasopharyngeal lesions occur) Lymphoma and other causes of lymphadenopathy or pseudotumor Riedel's thyroiditis and fibrosing variant of Hashimoto's thyroiditis Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephropathy Orbital pseudotumor / orbital myositis from other causes Serum IgG4 concentration (commonly elevated, but normal in ~30% of histologically proven cases; usually measured by nephelometry). Awareness of the prozone effect: very high serum IgG4 can yield spuriously low/normal nephelometric values, correctable by serum dilution; failure to detect dramatic elevations misses the subset at greatest risk for multiorgan disease and end-organ injury. Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) to map multiorgan involvement and detect subclinical or incidental disease. MRI of brain/orbits for pachymeningeal thickening and enhancement or enlarged extraocular muscles in CNS/orbital disease. Tissue biopsy with immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 and IgG, quantifying IgG4+ plasma cells per high-power field and the IgG4:total IgG ratio. Complement levels (hypocomplementemia associated with renal/tubulointerstitial involvement). Serial serum IgG4 monitoring after treatment to detect rising levels signaling possible flare. Malignancy (carcinoma, lymphoma) presenting as a tumefactive mass Sarcoidosis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Sjogren's syndrome Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis and inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm A fibroinflammatory disorder whose hallmark is a tendency to form tumefactive (mass-like) lesions that frequently mimic malignancy; initial misdiagnosis as cancer is extremely common. Protean and multisystem: can affect virtually any organ, with predilection for pancreas, biliary tree, major salivary glands (submandibular, parotid), periorbital/lacrimal tissues, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, and retroperitoneum; meninges, aorta, prostate, thyroid, pericardium, and skin are also described. Regarded as a variable-vessel vasculitis because it can target arteries and veins of any size, with venous involvement (obliterative phlebitis) being a particular hallmark. Typical patient is a middle-aged to elderly man (male-to-female ratio about 2:1), contrasting with classic autoimmune diseases that favor young women; head-and-neck (orbit, lacrimal, salivary) disease has a sex ratio closer to 1:1. Usually presents subacutely; most patients lack fever or marked C-reactive protein elevation even with multiorgan disease. Substantial weight loss can occur, often from exocrine pancreatic failure. Mikulicz's disease (lacrimal, parotid, and submandibular gland enlargement), once thought to be a Sjogren's subset, is one of the most common presentations of IgG4-RD. Allergic features are common: atopy, eczema, asthma, nasal polyps, sinusitis, and modest peripheral eosinophilia. Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis classically shows a diffusely enlarged 'sausage-shaped' pancreas with loss of normal lobularity; 20-50% of patients present with acute glucose intolerance and a pancreatic mass mimicking adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis requires correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings; pathology alone is never sufficient, and biopsy is often done mainly to exclude malignancy. Renal involvement (tubulointerstitial nephritis) is strongly associated with hypocomplementemia; membranous glomerulonephropathy is a less common renal manifestation that must be distinguished from idiopathic disease. Clinical course is variable: disease may relapse and remit within a given organ, accumulate new organ involvement over time, or be found incidentally on imaging. Disease can evolve over months, years, or even decades before an organ becomes symptomatic enough to prompt medical attention. New tumefactive mass mimicking cancer in pancreas, salivary gland, orbit, lung, or other organ. Obstructive jaundice from pancreatic or biliary involvement (undiagnosed/undertreated sclerosing cholangitis can lead to hepatic failure within months). Ureteral entrapment, hydronephrosis, postobstructive uropathy, and renal atrophy from retroperitoneal fibrosis. Aortic involvement causing aneurysm or dissection. Anterior pituitary hormone deficiency and/or central diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic-pituitary involvement. Spinal cord compression, cranial nerve palsies, or radiculopathy from hypertrophic pachymeningitis. Destructive bone lesions of sinuses, head, and middle ear mimicking granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Persistently rising serum IgG4 concentrations signaling risk of clinical flare and serious organ involvement. Coronary arteritis (wall thickening, periarterial encasement, stenosis, calcification, aneurysm/ectasia) in longstanding disease with high IgG4 and biomarker levels. Treating the disease as purely IgG4-antibody-mediated; the IgG4 molecule is largely noninflammatory and may be counterregulatory rather than a primary driver. Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgG4 is normal: ~30% of histologically proven cases have normal levels, and retroperitoneal fibrosis (often advanced/fibrotic at presentation) frequently shows normal IgG4. Missing markedly elevated IgG4 because of the prozone effect on nephelometry; suspect this when results are normal despite strong clinical features and re-test with dilution. Relying on pathology alone for diagnosis; histopathology, while characteristic, is essentially never diagnostic by itself and must be interpreted with clinical, serologic, and radiologic data. Mistaking tumefactive lesions for malignancy and proceeding to major resections (e.g., Whipple procedure, thyroidectomy) before the correct diagnosis is recognized. Histologic features such as intense neutrophilic infiltration, leukocytoclasis, granulomatous inflammation, multinucleated giant cells, or fibrinoid necrosis are uncommon in IgG4-RD and argue against the diagnosis. Assuming serum IgG4 reliably tracks disease activity; correlations are imperfect, levels often do not fully normalize, and remissions can occur with persistently elevated levels. IgG4-RD is characterized by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, a distinctive storiform (woven-mat / basket-weave) pattern of fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis reflecting vascular tropism, and a mild-to-moderate tissue eosinophilia. The infiltrate combines B cells (organized in germinal centers, with IgG4+ CD19/CD138 plasma cells radiating outward) and a more diffusely distributed, predominant population of CD4+ T cells. Despite the disease's name, the IgG4 molecule itself is not thought to directly drive injury in most organs: IgG4 undergoes Fab-arm exchange, binds antigen weakly, and has low affinity for Fc receptors and C1q, making it a generally noninflammatory immunoglobulin that may even play a counterregulatory role. A unique oligoclonally expanded CD4+ cytotoxic T cell, abundant at tissue sites, secretes interferon-gamma, TGF-beta, and interleukin-1 (driving storiform fibrosis) as well as perforin, granzymes A/B, and granulysin (mediating cytotoxicity), and appears to be a major disease driver. Oligoclonal plasmablast expansions in blood, with continuous B-cell/plasmablast antigen presentation, are thought to support these profibrotic, tissue-injuring CD4+ cytotoxic T cells. Course is generally subacute but can cause major morbidity and organ failure. Aggressive disease may rapidly produce end-stage liver disease, permanent pancreatic exocrine and endocrine (diabetes) impairment, renal atrophy, aortic dissection or aneurysm, and destructive sinonasal lesions. Some manifestations (e.g., IgG4-related lymphadenopathy) can remain indolent and asymptomatic for years. Even with apparently effective immunosuppression, renal atrophy is a frequent sequel to tubulointerstitial nephritis, and end-organ fibrotic damage may be irreversible if diagnosis is delayed. Relapses are common, including in patients with persistently normal IgG4 levels. No formal numeric severity score is given. Practical stratification distinguishes vital/organ-threatening involvement (e.g., pancreas, biliary tree/liver, kidneys, aorta, sinonasal destruction, pituitary, meninges) requiring prompt treatment from indolent manifestations (e.g., asymptomatic lymphadenopathy) amenable to watchful waiting with close monitoring; classification of disease itself relies on correlation of clinical, serologic, radiologic, and pathologic findings (ACR/EULAR classification criteria are referenced).

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension — Fundoscopy (papilloedema) MRI + MR venography LP with opening pressure Progressive visual loss needs urgent treatment Optic disc drusen, which produce pseudopapilloedema and can be mistaken for true papilloedema (p.229). Obstructive sleep apnoea and poorly controlled hypertension, which also cause morning or nocturnal headache (p.117). MRI as the initial study, including MR venography, to look for a mass and to search for dural venous sinus thrombosis or an AV shunt (p.117, p.229). Lumbar puncture performed while the patient is symptomatic, measuring opening pressure in the lateral decubitus position; both the pressure and the symptomatic response to removing 20-30 mL of CSF can be assessed (p.117, p.229). Formal visual field testing, performed even when there is no overt ophthalmic involvement (p.117). B-mode ocular ultrasound to detect buried optic disc drusen (hyperechoic due to calcium) when pseudopapilloedema is suspected (p.229). Space-occupying intracranial lesion causing raised CSF pressure headache (p.117). Dural venous sinus thrombosis (p.229). Arteriovenous (dural) shunt (p.229). Headache is typically generalized, present on awakening, eases through the day, and worsens on lying down (p.117). Transient visual obscurations are a classic feature: brief (usually seconds), in one or both eyes, often triggered by a postural shift, and most frequent when headache is at its worst (p.117, p.228-229). Obscurations that are prolonged or spontaneous indicate more threatening papilloedema (p.229). The syndrome can occur without visual symptoms, especially when the fundi look normal, so it must be considered even when funduscopy is unremarkable (p.117). Persistently raised intracranial pressure can itself trigger a chronic migraine syndrome (p.117). Visual acuity is usually preserved in papilloedema unless it is severe, longstanding, or complicated by macular oedema and haemorrhage; field loss precedes acuity loss (p.229). Unilateral or bilateral abducens (6th nerve) palsy is a classic false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure and is corroborated by papilloedema on fundoscopy (p.235). Prolonged or spontaneous transient visual obscurations signal more threatening papilloedema (p.229). Insidious peripheral visual field loss with progressive optic atrophy under unremitting papilloedema; in this setting a reduction in disc swelling is an ominous sign of a dying nerve, not resolution (p.229). Fulminant papilloedema can cause rapid-onset blindness and constitutes an emergency (p.229). Inaccurate CSF opening-pressure readings at lumbar puncture are a common pitfall (p.229). Failing to exclude a dural venous sinus thrombosis before attributing raised pressure to IIH (p.229). Mistaking buried optic disc drusen (pseudopapilloedema) for true papilloedema, prompting an unnecessary work-up (p.229). Assuming a normal fundus excludes the diagnosis; IIH can occur without funduscopic changes, so formal perimetry is still warranted (p.117). Raised CSF pressure without a space-occupying lesion, occurring in the setting of obesity, female sex, and occasionally pregnancy; partial obstruction of the cerebral venous sinuses is found in a small number of cases (p.117). Stenosis at the transverse-sigmoid sinus junction is commonly present, providing the rationale for venous sinus stenting (p.229). Vitamin A excess is a recognised cause of pseudotumor cerebri (p.3379). Headache often improves within weeks of starting medical therapy (p.117). However, unremitting papilloedema leads to progressive peripheral field loss and optic atrophy, and fulminant cases can cause rapid blindness, so visual loss is the feared outcome that drives urgent intervention (p.229).

the interstitial space between epithelium and endothelium is the dominant site, but alveolar epithelium and endothelial (airway and vessel) cells also drive pathogenesis (p.2259). No single piece of data is diagnostic on its own; a confident ILD diagnosis requires the combined weight of clinical, laboratory, PFT, imaging and (when obtained) histopathologic findings, ideally reviewed in a multidisciplinary conference of pulmonologists, rheumatologists, radiologists and pathologists (pp.2259-2260). Fine end-inspiratory bibasal crackles described as sounding like Velcro being pulled apart are characteristic of fibrotic ILD such as IPF and may be one of the earliest signs (pp.2200, 2261). Egophony, whispered pectoriloquy and bronchial breath sounds suggest alveolar filling (e.g. pneumonia) rather than interstitial fibrosis (IPF); their absence helps distinguish fibrotic crackles from consolidation (p.2200). Age strongly shifts pretest probability: IPF is most common in patients over 60 and rare under 50, whereas sarcoidosis, CTD-ILD, LAM and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically present between ages 20 and 40 (p.2260). On HRCT, apical-predominant interstitial thickening favours NSIP, whereas a basal and subpleural/dependent predominance favours IPF (p.2211). A dry cough can be the most prominent symptom of IPF; some patients (even with extensive disease) report no dyspnoea at all (p.2261). HRCT is now standard of care in initial ILD evaluation and can be diagnostic for IPF in the right clinical context, sparing the patient a lung biopsy (p.2262). BAL findings can point to specific entities: eosinophilia >25% suggests chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, fat globules in macrophages suggest lipoid pneumonia, and serial bloody lavage indicates diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (p.2262). A close relative with an idiopathic interstitial pneumonia is among the strongest risk factors for IPF; up to ~20% of pulmonary fibrosis is familial, and diverse IIP subtypes (IPF, NSIP, DIP) can run in the same family (p.2261). Acute exacerbation of IPF - acute (<30 days) onset of respiratory distress and hypoxaemia in a patient with underlying fibrosis, not explained by infection or heart failure; reported mortality >85% (p.2265) Acute interstitial pneumonia (Hamman-Rich) - acute respiratory distress and hypoxaemia with >50% mortality within 6 months (p.2265) Haemoptysis suggesting diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (Goodpasture's, GPA) or LAM - warrants urgent evaluation (p.2261) Honeycombing or extensive fibrosis on HRCT indicating advanced disease and worse prognosis (p.2262) Signs of advanced disease: cyanosis, digital clubbing and cor pulmonale (p.2262) Rapidly progressive ILD in anti-Jo-1-positive inflammatory myopathy (p.2266) A declining FVC on serial testing, which signals elevated mortality risk (p.2261) Attributing all wheezing to asthma - wheeze can reflect heart failure or other airway narrowing; conversely wheeze is uncommon in ILD but does occur in sarcoidosis, HP and eosinophilic GPA (pp.2200, 2262). Forgetting that a UIP pattern on biopsy is not unique to IPF - it also occurs in CTD (e.g. RA-associated) ILD (p.2260). Misreading acute ILD presentations as pneumonia, COPD exacerbation or heart failure, since acute ILD is unusual (p.2260). Treating presumed IPF with immunosuppression - this has been shown to increase morbidity and mortality in IPF (p.2263). Relying on PFT pattern to diagnose HP - HP can be restrictive or obstructive, so the pattern is not diagnostic (p.2229). Over-relying on HP serum precipitin panels - they cover a limited antigen set and frequently give false negatives, and a positive IgG alone does not confirm HP (p.2230). Confusing HP granulomas with sarcoidosis - HP granulomas are loose/poorly formed and peribronchiolar, whereas sarcoid granulomas are well-formed; caseating granulomas should prompt a search for infection (pp.2230, 2264). Assuming CTD must be apparent - ILD can precede other CTD features by years or be the sole manifestation (pp.2261, 2265). Diagnosing IPF without excluding a treatable mimic - heart failure, infection (e.g. PCP) and malignancy must be considered first (p.2260). ILDs are characterised by remodelling of the interstitium with variable degrees of inflammation and fibrosis, but alveolar epithelial and endothelial cell injury is also central to pathogenesis. The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are the most common group. In IPF the histologic hallmark is a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural reticulation with honeycomb change and fibroblast foci (subepithelial collections of myofibroblasts and collagen) alternating with preserved normal alveolar architecture, producing temporal and spatial heterogeneity. NSIP shows more uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis with honeycombing usually absent and fibroblast foci rare. Genetic studies show that a substantial fraction of familial and even sporadic/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has a genetic basis: a MUC5B promoter variant (present in ~20% of Caucasians, 35-45% of IPF patients) confers an approximately sixfold risk, and variants in telomere-length genes (TERT, TERC, RTEL1) and surfactant protein genes (SFTPA2) are also implicated. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens small enough to reach distal airways and alveoli, driven by dysregulated TH1/TH17 responses with precipitating IgG and innate (Toll-like receptor/MyD88) signalling; chronic HP shares the MUC5B variant with IPF (pp.2259-2266; 2228-2229). Prognosis varies widely by ILD subtype and disease extent. IPF carries a poor prognosis (~50% survival at 3-5 years; pre-antifibrotic-era life expectancy 3-5 years from diagnosis). Idiopathic NSIP is comparatively favourable (>80% 5-year survival), with cellular NSIP doing better than fibrosing NSIP. Reported subtype mortality includes RB-ILD ~25% at 7 years and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD ~20-30% at 10 years; sarcoidosis mortality is generally low but state-dependent. RB-ILD usually has prolonged survival with death from progressive ILD rare. AIP has >50% 6-month mortality with frequent recurrences, though survivors can recover substantial lung function. Acute exacerbations of fibrotic ILD carry very high mortality (>85%). In CTD-ILD, a UIP pattern and more extensive fibrosis (e.g. in RA) predict reduced survival. Chronic fibrotic HP can mirror IPF in radiology and prognosis (pp.2260, 2262-2266; 2229). Harrison frames ILD pattern recognition rather than a single numeric severity score. ILDs are first split into known cause (occupational e.g. asbestosis/silicosis; drug-induced e.g. amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin; systemic/CTD-associated; granulomatous including HP) versus unknown cause (idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, plus rarer entities such as LAM, PAP, PLCH, sarcoidosis). The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are further classified (per the ATS/ERS consensus) into chronic fibrosing (IPF, idiopathic NSIP), smoking-related (RB-ILD, DIP), and acute/subacute (COP, acute interstitial pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia). The UIP pattern (subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) defines IPF, while NSIP shows more ground-glass and rare honeycombing. HP is now classified as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic terminology). Disease severity is gauged by extent of fibrosis/honeycombing on HRCT, degree of PFT (FVC/DLCO) impairment and its rate of decline, and presence of pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale (pp.2259-2266; 2229).

The disorder often requires prolonged immunosuppression and relapses are common, but many patients regain strength with treatment; anti-SRP disease tends to be more severe, and outcome worsens with cardiac or respiratory involvement or associated malignancy.

patient with diarrhoea or deranged liver function Radiation-related organ injury in previously irradiated fields Baseline and interval bloods including liver and renal function, thyroid function, and such as thyroid dysfunction and hypophysitis Management principles centre on grading severity, withholding or discontinuing the drug, and using corticosteroids for moderate to severe events, with additional immunosuppression for steroid-refractory cases Endocrine toxicities such as hypophysitis and adrenal insufficiency often require long-term hormone replacement even after the immune reaction settles Endocrinopathy is a critical mimic to recognise, because unrecognised adrenal insufficiency or hypophysitis can precipitate life-threatening adrenal crisis Toxicity from these agents differs fundamentally from cytotoxic chemotherapy side effects, and excluding infection and disease progression is essential before attributing symptoms to an immune reaction Immune-related myocarditis presenting with chest pain, arrhythmia, or heart failure, which can be rapidly fatal Severe immune colitis with profuse diarrhoea, dehydration, and risk of bowel perforation Pneumonitis with hypoxia and progressive breathlessness Adrenal crisis from unrecognised hypophysitis or adrenal insufficiency, and other severe events such as neurological or hepatic toxicity Attributing new symptoms to infection or cancer progression and missing an immune-related cause Delaying corticosteroids in severe toxicity while awaiting further tests Overlooking endocrine toxicity and failing to replace deficient hormones, risking adrenal crisis Assuming toxicity cannot occur because therapy was stopped weeks or months earlier Immune checkpoint inhibitors release the normal brakes on T-cell activation by blocking inhibitory pathways such as CTLA-4 and the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. This enhances antitumour immunity but also reduces self-tolerance, allowing activated T cells, autoantibodies, and inflammatory cytokines to attack normal tissues. The resulting immune-related adverse events reflect off-target autoimmune inflammation that can involve the skin, gut, liver, endocrine glands, lungs, heart, kidneys, nervous system, and other organs, with severity ranging from mild to fatal. Most immune-related adverse events are reversible with prompt recognition, drug interruption, and immunosuppression, but severe events such as myocarditis, colitis with perforation, or pneumonitis carry significant mortality, and some endocrine effects are permanent.

Imperforate anus — anorectal malformation, ARM, anal atresia Anal stenosis Rectal atresia with a normal-appearing anus Meconium plug syndrome Hirschsprung disease Anteriorly displaced (ectopic) anus Cross-table lateral prone radiograph (invertogram) to estimate the level of the rectal pouch Distal colostogram to delineate fistula anatomy prior to definitive surgery Renal and pelvic ultrasound to detect associated urological anomalies Echocardiography and spinal imaging as part of a VACTERL screen Sacral radiographs to assess sacral ratio, which correlates with continence potential A congenital defect in which the anal opening is absent or abnormally positioned; usually detected on the routine newborn examination or when meconium fails to pass normally Malformations are broadly grouped as low or high depending on whether the rectal pouch ends below or above the levator ani muscle complex, which guides operative approach and prognosis Most cases in both sexes involve a fistula connecting the blind rectum to the perineum, urinary tract, or genital tract, and meconium seen at an abnormal site is a useful clue The condition frequently forms part of the VACTERL group, so vertebral, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies should be actively sought Initial management is to keep the infant nil by mouth, decompress the stomach, and give intravenous fluids while assessing the level of the lesion High or complex lesions are typically managed with an initial diverting colostomy followed by definitive posterior sagittal anorectoplasty, whereas some low lesions can be corrected in one stage Long-term outcome depends heavily on the quality of the sphincter mechanism and sacral development, so continence must be followed over years A distal colostogram and cross-table lateral radiography help define the anatomy before definitive repair Signs of intestinal obstruction (abdominal distension, bilious vomiting) requiring urgent decompression and surgical review Meconium in the urine indicating a rectourinary fistula and risk of urinary contamination Associated cardiac or renal anomalies that may destabilise the neonate before surgery Failure to identify any perineal opening in a distended infant, mandating prompt surgical decompression Missing the diagnosis when a perineal fistula allows some meconium to pass, giving false reassurance Attempting a primary perineal repair on a high lesion without a protective colostomy Overlooking associated VACTERL anomalies, particularly cardiac and renal lesions Underestimating the long-term need for bowel management and continence follow-up Imperforate anus results from abnormal development of the hindgut and its separation from the urogenital sinus during early embryogenesis, so the terminal rectum fails to descend and open normally onto the perineum. The rectal pouch commonly ends blindly or communicates through a fistula with the urinary system, vagina, or perineal skin. The relationship of the pouch to the levator ani and external sphincter complex, together with the degree of sacral and spinal development, determines whether continence structures are adequate and largely predicts functional outcome. Outcomes vary with the type of malformation: low lesions with good sphincter and sacral development often achieve near-normal continence, while high or cloacal lesions carry higher rates of faecal incontinence and constipation requiring long-term bowel management. Associated anomalies significantly influence overall morbidity.

characteristic golden-yellow (honey-coloured) crusts, often around the nose and mouth Bullous impetigo produces larger flaccid blisters that leave a collarette of scale, and is driven by exfoliative systemic antibiotics for widespread, bullous, or systemically unwell cases, guided by local resistance patterns Advise on reducing transmission, including handwashing, not sharing towels, and keeping children away from school or nursery until lesions have crusted or treatment has been under way for the recommended period Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a recognised complication following certain streptococcal strains, so watch for signs such as dark urine or oedema Recurrent impetigo warrants consideration of staphylococcal carriage and decolonisation Rapidly spreading erythema, pain out of proportion, or systemic toxicity suggesting cellulitis or a deeper, necrotising infection Widespread tender blistering and skin peeling in a young child indicating staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome Features of eczema herpeticum such as punched-out erosions and systemic upset in an atopic patient Dark urine, facial oedema, or hypertension after infection suggesting post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Missing an underlying dermatosis such as scabies or eczema that will drive recurrence if untreated Failing to recognise eczema herpeticum and treating presumed impetigo with antibiotics alone Overusing topical antibiotics and promoting resistance Neglecting infection-control advice, allowing continued spread among household and school contacts Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis caused predominantly by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, alone or together. Organisms colonise and then invade skin whose barrier has been breached by minor trauma, bites, or pre-existing dermatoses. In bullous disease, staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis, causing intraepidermal separation and blister formation. The host inflammatory response and serous exudate dry to form the typical crusts. Certain nephritogenic streptococcal strains can trigger immune-complex-mediated post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Impetigo generally responds well to treatment and often heals without scarring, though it can recur, particularly with staphylococcal carriage or an untreated underlying skin condition; serious sequelae are uncommon but include post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Incisional hernia — ventral incisional hernia, post-operative hernia Divarication of the recti Recurrent primary ventral hernia at another site Seroma or haematoma at the operative site Abdominal wall
