previous abdominal wound where the fascial closure has failed, presenting as a bulge that enlarges with straining Risk factors include wound infection, obesity, poor surgical technique, emergency surgery, chronic cough, steroids, diabetes, malnutrition, and smoking The defect and sac often enlarge over time, and large long-standing hernias may develop multiple loculations and adhesions Small defects with a narrow neck carry a higher risk of incarceration and strangulation than broad-necked defects Very large hernias may result in loss of abdominal domain, where returning contents to the abdomen risks respiratory compromise and abdominal compartment syndrome Repair is usually with mesh, either open (onlay, sublay/retrorectus, or intraperitoneal) or laparoscopic, as suture-only repair of larger defects has high recurrence Optimising modifiable risk factors such as weight, glycaemic control, and smoking before elective repair improves outcomes A previous wound dehiscence or a burst abdomen strongly predisposes to later incisional herniation Irreducible, tender bulge with loss of cough impulse indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency) Bowel obstruction associated with the hernia Skin breakdown or ischaemia over a large or rapidly enlarging hernia Systemic sepsis or peritonism from strangulated bowel Performing suture-only repair of a sizeable defect and accepting a high recurrence risk Failing to optimise obesity, diabetes, and smoking before elective repair Underestimating loss of domain and precipitating abdominal compartment syndrome at repair Overlooking a small tender defect that is at high risk of strangulation An incisional hernia develops when the musculo-aponeurotic layers of a healed surgical wound fail to maintain their integrity, allowing peritoneum and abdominal contents to protrude beneath the intact skin. Impaired wound healing, whether from infection, ischaemia, raised intra-abdominal pressure, technical factors, or patient factors such as obesity, diabetes, and malnutrition, weakens the fascial repair. Over time the defect enlarges and the sac expands, sometimes housing much of the abdominal contents. Narrow-necked defects can trap and strangulate bowel, while very large defects lead to loss of domain and altered abdominal wall mechanics. Recurrence rates are higher than for primary hernias but are substantially reduced by mesh repair and by optimising risk factors. Large hernias with loss of domain require specialised techniques and carry greater perioperative risk, while emergency presentation with strangulation increases morbidity.

dystrophies presenting in adulthood Myasthenia gravis with limb and bulbar weakness Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy Hereditary inclusion body myopathies Muscle biopsy showing rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and characteristic protein aggregates Creatine kinase measurement, typically normal or only mildly elevated Electromyography showing a mixed myopathic and corticosteroids and immunosuppression Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk Recurrent falls from quadriceps failure Rapid functional decline suggesting an alternative diagnosis Marked weight loss or bulbar deterioration Misdiagnosing it as treatment-resistant polymyositis and prolonging futile immunosuppression Being reassured by a normal creatine kinase into excluding a myopathy Overlooking the diagnostic finger-flexor and quadriceps weakness pattern Failing to recognise and manage dysphagia and aspiration risk Sporadic inclusion body myositis is a slowly progressive myopathy with combined inflammatory and degenerative features. Endomysial T-cell infiltration and up-regulation of major histocompatibility complex on muscle fibres coexist with a degenerative process marked by rimmed vacuoles and intracellular accumulation of misfolded proteins, including beta-amyloid, phosphorylated tau, TDP-43, and p62. The relative contribution of autoimmunity and protein mishandling remains debated, but the degenerative component is thought to explain the characteristic treatment resistance and the selective, progressive involvement of finger flexors and quadriceps. The condition progresses slowly but relentlessly over years, leading to significant disability, dependence on mobility aids, and swallowing difficulties; life expectancy is relatively preserved but quality of life declines with functional loss.

usually lethal in males in utero, so it predominantly affects females Skin lesions evolve through four classic stages along Blaschko lines: vesicular, verrucous, hyperpigmented (whorled/swirled), and atrophic/hypopigmented The blistering first stage in a neonate can be mistaken for infection, and there is often a peripheral eosinophilia Associated dental anomalies (peg or missing teeth), alopecia, and nail dystrophy are common Ocular involvement includes a retinal vasculopathy that can cause retinal detachment and blindness if not detected Neurological complications (seizures, stroke-like episodes, developmental delay) may occur, mainly in the neonatal period Diagnosis rests on characteristic staged skin findings, Blaschkoid distribution, and IKBKG genetic testing Retinal neovascularisation or detachment threatening vision Neonatal seizures or stroke-like neurological events Extensive vesicular eruption mistaken for, or complicated by, infection Developmental regression requiring neurological evaluation Mistaking the neonatal vesicular stage for herpes or bacterial infection and delaying diagnosis Failing to arrange prompt retinal screening, risking preventable visual loss Overlooking the diagnostic significance of Blaschko-linear lesions and eosinophilia Not counselling about X-linked inheritance and male lethality for family planning Incontinentia pigmenti is caused by loss-of-function variants in IKBKG, encoding NEMO, an essential regulatory component of the NF-kappaB signalling pathway. NF-kappaB activation protects cells from apoptosis and coordinates inflammatory responses, so cells that carry the mutation on the active X chromosome are prone to death and to abnormal inflammatory signalling. Random X-inactivation produces a mosaic of affected and unaffected cells, explaining the Blaschko-linear pattern of skin lesions and the variable multisystem involvement. The histological hallmark of 'pigment incontinence', with melanin dropping from damaged basal keratinocytes into the dermis, gives the disorder its name. The skin manifestations are generally self-limiting and evolve to subtle residual changes, and most affected females have a normal lifespan; overall prognosis is determined largely by the presence and severity of ocular and neurological involvement.

Infant Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease — infant GORD, infant GERD, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in infancy Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux (normal regurgitation) Cow's milk protein allergy Pyloric stenosis (with projectile non-bilious vomiting) Overfeeding Infection (including urinary tract infection) Intestinal obstruction or malrotation (particularly with bilious vomiting) Clinical assessment with growth monitoring (usually sufficient) Trial of cow's milk protein elimination when allergy is suspected Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to assess anatomy if obstruction or malrotation is a concern Oesophageal pH or impedance monitoring in selected complex cases Endoscopy when oesophagitis or another mucosal complication is suspected It is essential to distinguish physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux, which is common and benign in healthy infants, from reflux disease, in which reflux causes troublesome symptoms or complications. Effortless regurgitation or posseting in a thriving, comfortable infant (the happy spitter) is normal and typically improves as the infant matures and begins to sit and take solids. Reflux disease is suggested by poor weight gain, feeding refusal or distress, persistent irritability, back-arching with feeds, or respiratory symptoms attributable to reflux. Diagnosis is largely clinical from the history and examination; investigations are reserved for atypical presentations, complications, or diagnostic uncertainty. First-line management uses conservative measures such as optimising feeding volume and technique, thickened feeds where appropriate, and positioning advice consistent with safe sleep guidance. A trial of cow's milk protein elimination is reasonable when allergy is suspected, since it can mimic or coexist with reflux disease. Acid-suppressing medication is not appropriate for uncomplicated physiological reflux and should be limited to infants with clear evidence of reflux disease. Warning features such as bilious or forceful vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, or onset of vomiting after six months point away from simple reflux and toward an alternative diagnosis. Bilious vomiting or haematemesis Forceful or projectile vomiting suggesting pyloric stenosis Faltering growth or feeding refusal Onset of vomiting after six months or persistence beyond infancy Systemic signs such as fever, lethargy, or a bulging fontanelle Treating benign physiological reflux with acid suppression or unnecessary investigation Missing an alternative diagnosis such as pyloric stenosis or malrotation presenting with vomiting Overlooking cow's milk protein allergy as a mimicking or coexisting cause Recommending positioning that conflicts with safe sleep advice Gastro-oesophageal reflux occurs when gastric contents pass back into the oesophagus, largely through transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Reflux is especially common in infancy because of a short oesophagus, a predominantly liquid and high-volume diet, frequent recumbency, and immaturity of the antireflux barrier. In most infants this is physiological and self-resolving. Reflux disease develops when refluxate causes oesophageal mucosal injury and pain, impairs feeding and growth, or reaches the airway to provoke respiratory symptoms. Contributing factors include delayed gastric emptying and, in some infants, cow's milk protein allergy that produces overlapping symptoms. Physiological reflux resolves in the great majority of infants during the first year to eighteen months as the infant matures; reflux disease also generally improves with time and appropriate management, though some infants with underlying conditions require more prolonged treatment.

Infantile Colic — colic, excessive infant crying, baby colic Cow's milk protein allergy Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease Infection (including urinary tract infection or otitis media) Feeding difficulties or underfeeding Incarcerated hernia, intussusception, or other acute abdominal cause Corneal abrasion, hair tourniquet, or other occult source of pain Thorough history and full physical examination (colic is clinical and one of exclusion) Growth assessment to confirm normal weight gain Targeted tests only if history or examination suggests an organic cause Trial of maternal or infant dietary modification when cow's milk protein allergy is suspected Urinalysis if infection is a concern Infantile colic describes recurrent, prolonged episodes of inconsolable crying and fussiness in an otherwise healthy, well-fed, and thriving young infant. It is often characterised by the rule of threes: crying for more than about three hours a day, on more than three days a week, for more than three weeks, though clinical judgement matters more than strict criteria. Episodes commonly cluster in the late afternoon and evening and may be accompanied by drawing up of the legs, a flushed face, and clenched fists. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, established when a careful history and thorough examination reveal no underlying organic cause and growth is normal. Typical onset is in the first few weeks of life, with peak intensity around six weeks and spontaneous resolution by around three to four months of age. The cause is not fully understood and is likely multifactorial, involving normal developmental crying, gut and feeding factors, and infant-caregiver interaction. Management centres on parental reassurance, education about the benign and self-limiting nature, soothing techniques, and support for exhausted caregivers. Because the crying is intense and distressing, clinicians should assess caregiver stress and coping and be alert to the risk of frustration-related harm such as abusive head trauma. Poor weight gain or failure to thrive Fever or signs of systemic illness Vomiting (especially bilious), blood in stool, or abdominal distension Lethargy, abnormal tone, or an unwell appearance Signs of possible non-accidental injury or a caregiver at breaking point Labelling crying as colic without excluding organic causes or confirming normal growth Missing a serious acute condition such as intussusception or infection presenting as excessive crying Overmedicalising a benign condition or making unnecessary formula changes Neglecting caregiver distress and the associated risk of abusive head trauma Infantile colic does not have a single established mechanism and is best understood as excessive crying at the upper end of the normal developmental crying curve, which peaks in early infancy. Proposed contributors include transient gastrointestinal factors such as immature motility, gas, or feeding-related discomfort, alterations in the gut microbiome, cow's milk protein sensitivity in a subset of infants, heightened infant sensitivity or difficult temperament, and stress within the infant-caregiver relationship. In most infants no pathological process is identified, and the self-limited course paralleling normal maturation supports a developmental rather than a disease-based explanation. Infantile colic is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously by around three to four months of age in most infants, with no adverse effect on long-term growth or development.

(rapidly involuting or non-involuting types) Pyogenic granuloma Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma Nasal glioma or encephalocele for midline facial lesions Dermoid cyst or other soft-tissue tumours Clinical diagnosis in most cases based on characteristic appearance and evolution Ultrasound with Doppler to characterise deep or ambiguous lesions MRI to define extent of large, segmental, or deep lesions and detect associated anomalies Abdominal imaging (liver ultrasound) when multiple cutaneous haemangiomas are present Assessment for PHACE or LUMBAR/PELVIS-type associations characteristic course: often absent or subtle at birth, they proliferate over the first months of life, then slowly involute over subsequent years Superficial lesions are bright red and lobulated (the strawberry appearance), while deeper ones appear as bluish, soft, compressible swellings with little surface change They are more frequent in premature and low-birth-weight infants and in girls, and most are uncomplicated and need only reassurance and monitoring The key management question is whether a lesion is high-risk by virtue of its site, size, number, or growth, since early treatment can prevent lasting complications Beta-blocker therapy has transformed treatment of problematic haemangiomas, with intervention prioritised during the proliferative phase when it is most effective Periocular lesions can obstruct vision and cause amblyopia, and airway involvement (suggested by a beard-distribution facial lesion with stridor) can be life-threatening Ulceration is the most frequent complication and is painful, prone to infection, and can scar, so it needs prompt wound care and pain control Multiple cutaneous haemangiomas raise the possibility of visceral (especially hepatic) involvement and warrant imaging Periocular lesions threatening the visual axis and risking amblyopia or astigmatism Beard-distribution facial haemangioma with stridor or respiratory difficulty suggesting airway involvement Large segmental facial lesions raising concern for PHACE association (cardiac, cerebrovascular, and ocular anomalies) Lumbosacral or perineal lesions suggesting underlying spinal or urogenital anomalies Painful ulceration, bleeding, or signs of infection, and multiple lesions suggesting visceral involvement Assuming a vascular birthmark is always an infantile haemangioma when a malformation or another vascular tumour is present Adopting a wait-and-see approach for a high-risk lesion and missing the proliferative window for treatment Overlooking amblyopia risk from a periocular lesion Failing to image multiple cutaneous lesions for hepatic involvement Underestimating the significance of a segmental facial or lumbosacral lesion as a marker of associated anomalies Infantile haemangiomas are proliferations of endothelial cells that uniformly express the marker GLUT1, distinguishing them from vascular malformations and other vascular tumours. During the proliferative phase there is rapid, disorganised angiogenesis with plump endothelial cells forming densely cellular masses; hypoxia-driven and angiogenic signalling pathways, including vascular endothelial growth factor mechanisms, are implicated. Over time the lesion enters an involuting phase in which the vascular channels are gradually replaced by fibrofatty tissue. The natural rise and fall in growth explains why timing of intervention matters and why many lesions ultimately regress spontaneously. The great majority of infantile haemangiomas are benign and resolve substantially over the first several years of life, often with little residual change; however, high-risk lesions can cause functional impairment, disfigurement, ulceration, or, rarely, life-threatening complications, and timely treatment improves these outcomes.

Infantile Spasms — West syndrome, epileptic spasms, salaam attacks Benign non-epileptic myoclonus of infancy Sandifer syndrome (dystonic posturing with reflux) Exaggerated startle response or hyperekplexia Infantile colic Other early-onset epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. Ohtahara syndrome) Tonic seizures of other origin Urgent EEG, ideally capturing sleep, to identify hypsarrhythmia MRI brain to detect structural or malformative causes Skin examination and evaluation for tuberous sclerosis Metabolic and genetic testing to establish an underlying aetiology Developmental assessment to document baseline and progress Fundoscopy and ophthalmological review where indicated An age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy, with onset usually in the first year of life and peaking around 4-8 months. Spasms are brief, often symmetrical contractions producing sudden flexion or extension of the trunk and limbs, typically occurring in clusters especially on waking. The full West syndrome triad comprises epileptic spasms, the EEG pattern of hypsarrhythmia, and arrest or regression of development. Developmental regression or loss of previously acquired skills, including loss of social smile or visual attention, is a crucial and sometimes early sign. Spasms are frequently mistaken for colic, startle, or normal infant movements, causing dangerous delays in diagnosis. An urgent EEG is essential; hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern that supports the diagnosis. Many cases have an identifiable underlying cause such as a structural brain abnormality, tuberous sclerosis, genetic or metabolic disease, or perinatal injury, so investigation for aetiology is important. Rapid initiation of effective treatment is critical, as prompt control of spasms and resolution of hypsarrhythmia is associated with better developmental outcomes. New clusters of spasms in an infant require urgent EEG and prompt treatment (EMERGENCY) Developmental regression or loss of acquired milestones Hypsarrhythmia on EEG Delay between symptom onset and treatment, which worsens prognosis Signs suggesting an underlying structural, metabolic, or genetic disorder Evolution to other seizure types or epileptic encephalopathy Dismissing spasms as colic, reflux, or benign startle and delaying EEG Failing to appreciate developmental regression as a warning sign Not pursuing a thorough search for an underlying cause Delaying initiation of effective therapy, which reduces the chance of good outcome Under-recognising subtle spasms occurring in clusters around sleep transitions Infantile spasms represent an age-dependent epileptic encephalopathy in which diverse insults to the developing brain converge on a common electroclinical expression. Structural, genetic, metabolic, or acquired abnormalities disrupt the maturing cortical and subcortical networks during a vulnerable developmental window, producing the hypersynchronous discharges seen as hypsarrhythmia and the characteristic spasms. The ongoing epileptic activity itself further disrupts normal brain development, contributing to the associated cognitive and developmental regression. Prognosis is variable and strongly influenced by the underlying cause and by how quickly spasms and hypsarrhythmia are controlled; delayed treatment and identifiable structural or genetic causes are associated with worse developmental outcomes, while prompt effective therapy in previously normal infants offers the best chance of favourable development.

Infections Acquired in Health Care Facilities — Nosocomial infections, Health care-associated infections, HAI, Hospital-acquired infections Community-acquired infection (onset within 48-72 h of admission) Asymptomatic bacteriuria versus true catheter-associated urinary tract infection Noninfectious causes of fever or organ dysfunction in the critically ill Drug-related or transfusion-related complications mimicking infection Asymptomatic bacteriuria mistaken for symptomatic urinary tract infection (especially in the elderly with nonspecific confusion) Colonization with multidrug-resistant organisms misread as active infection Ventilator-associated events that are noninfectious complications of mechanical ventilation Laboratory-based surveillance supplemented by clinical chart review by infection preventionists Whole genome sequencing as the gold standard for establishing clonality and detecting plasmid-borne resistance genes during outbreak investigation Molecular typing of bacterial/fungal (less commonly viral) isolates to confirm an outbreak PCR or culture screening for Candida auris in patients transferred from long-term care facilities (isolate pending results) Interferon-gamma release assay (preferred over tuberculin skin test) for preemployment tuberculosis screening of health care personnel Targeted water testing for Legionella pneumophila in facilities with prior nosocomial cases Dedicated public health laboratory testing (nasopharyngeal swabs/washes, conjunctival swabs) for strain identification when novel influenza such as H5N1 is suspected, as commercial multiplex PCR panels are insufficient Aspiration pneumonitis without bacterial infection Postoperative inflammatory fever Thrombotic or chemical phlebitis at vascular access sites Infections appearing within the first 48-72 hours of admission are generally regarded as community-acquired (or attributed to a transferring institution); those arising afterward are considered health care-associated (nosocomial). Patient-related vulnerabilities to nosocomial infection include indwelling invasive devices, immune deficiency (congenital or acquired), renal insufficiency, diabetes, and other major comorbidities. Disruption of a patient's own microbiota by antibiotics or other drugs promotes colonization with multidrug-resistant organisms; colonized patients then act as silent reservoirs for transmission to others and to the environment. Colonization pressure (the proportion of patients on a ward who are colonized) is itself a risk factor for the spread of resistant organisms. Catheter-associated bloodstream infections roughly triple the risk of in-hospital death; central lines are foreign objects in direct contact with the bloodstream and each handling is a potential contamination event. Ventilator-associated pneumonia occurs in up to 10% of mechanically ventilated patients and can prolong ventilation and ICU stay or be fatal. Clostridioides difficile infection is both the most frequent cause of health care-associated diarrhea and the most frequent hospital-acquired infection in the United States; recent antibiotic exposure is the most common precipitant. Alcohol-based hand gel and standard hospital cleaners do NOT kill C. difficile spores or inactivate norovirus, so handwashing with soap and water plus sporicidal (e.g., bleach) cleaning is required. Candida species account for the vast majority of health care-associated fungal infections; antifungal prophylaxis can select for non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata. Candida auris is a multidrug-resistant, environment-adapted pathogen that survives long periods on surfaces and is resistant to some standard disinfectants, requiring select agents and strict contact precautions. Tap water is not sterile; waterborne organisms such as Legionella pneumophila and nontuberculous mycobacteria colonize plumbing biofilm, favored by low disinfectant levels, warm temperatures, and stagnation. Apart from pregnant patients, asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients should generally not be cultured or treated; in the elderly nonspecific symptoms like confusion are often unrelated to bacteriuria, and overtreatment drives a cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance. Surveillance infection rates are expressed as standardized infection ratios (observed infections divided by predicted infections), benchmarked through the CDC National Healthcare Safety Network. New bloodstream infection in a patient with a central venous catheter (markedly elevated in-hospital mortality) Nosocomial diarrhea progressing toward toxic megacolon in C. difficile colitis A single case of nosocomial Legionnaires disease, which should trigger a full investigation Suspected active tuberculosis requiring immediate airborne precautions Identification of Candida auris, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, or other high-priority multidrug-resistant organisms requiring coordinated containment Presentation of a returning traveler with possible viral hemorrhagic fever (Ebola, Marburg) Culturing and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterized patients, then re-testing for 'clearance', fueling a cycle of escalating antimicrobial use and resistance. Relying on alcohol-based hand gel against C. difficile spores or norovirus, which it does not eliminate. Failing to remove indwelling urinary catheters and central lines promptly when no longer needed, the principal driver of these preventable device infections. Overlooking that patients already colonized with C. difficile on admission are by far the most likely to develop infection during the stay. Missing exogenous transmission of Candida auris because it resists some standard disinfectant cleaners and recontaminates surfaces rapidly. Treating commercial multiplex respiratory PCR results as adequate to exclude or identify novel influenza strains such as H5N1. Hospitalized patients are exposed to pathogens from other patients, visitors, staff, and the inanimate environment. Health care personnel carry multidrug-resistant organisms between patients on hands or shared equipment (stethoscopes, portable imaging machines); spread also occurs via contaminated plumbing, person-to-person respiratory routes, or contamination of food, water, and medications. Antibiotic exposure disrupts the host microbiota, permitting colonization with resistant organisms; colonized but immunocompromised patients, or those whose barriers are breached by surgery or invasive devices, then develop infection either from their own flora or from cross-transmitted pathogens. Invasive devices (urinary catheters, central venous catheters, endotracheal tubes) create direct portals of entry, bypassing normal defenses. Resistant organisms frequently colonize the gastrointestinal and respiratory tracts and can establish enduring environmental reservoirs, with potential horizontal transfer of resistance genes between co-colonizing strains. Health care-associated infections are a substantial source of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients, frequently caused by antimicrobial-resistant organisms that prolong hospital stays and worsen outcomes. Catheter-associated bloodstream infections triple in-hospital mortality risk, and ventilator-associated pneumonia can be fatal or prolong ICU stay. Multidrug-resistant organism infections are associated with higher morbidity, higher mortality, and added costs; globally about 1.27 million deaths were attributed to antibiotic-resistant infections in 2019. After years of decline from prevention efforts, device-related and other nosocomial infection rates rose during the COVID-19 pandemic. C. difficile colitis spans a clinical spectrum from mild diarrhea to life-threatening toxic megacolon. Pathogen transmission risk is operationally classified by route into contact, droplet, and airborne precautions (per WHO and CDC); some conditions (e.g., concurrent varicella and SARS-CoV-2) warrant combined precautions. Airborne isolation requires a negative-pressure room with at least 12 air changes per hour, exhausted outdoors or through a HEPA filter, with respirator use; protective (positive-pressure, HEPA-filtered) isolation is used for highly susceptible patients such as those with prolonged neutropenia or stem cell transplants to exclude mold spores.

Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms — Campylobacteriosis, Campylobacter jejuni enteritis, Campylobacter enteritis, Campylobacter fetus infection Salmonella gastroenteritis Shigellosis Yersinia enterocolitica enteritis Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli infection Typhoid fever (when fever is the sole early manifestation) Acute appendicitis (versus C. jejuni pseudoappendicitis) Ulcerative colitis Crohn's disease Salmonella enteritis Shigella dysentery Yersinia enterocolitica infection Enterohemorrhagic E. coli colitis Early typhoid fever Stool culture on Campylobacter-specific selective media (diagnostic gold standard) Species-specific real-time PCR (more sensitive than culture) Culture-independent diagnostic tests / antigen detection (may detect nonviable organisms and give false positives) MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for species identification Gram or Wright stain of fecal smear for vibrioid morphology; phase-contrast or dark-field microscopy for darting motility Fecal leukocyte/erythrocyte examination Peripheral leukocyte count (reflects inflammatory severity) Blood cultures (note: low metabolic activity can make Campylobacter bacteremia hard to detect) Ulcerative colitis Crohn's disease Acute appendicitis Campylobacters are motile, non-spore-forming, curved (vibrio-like) gram-negative rods that are microaerophilic, and the genus was split off from Vibrio in 1973; over 20 species now span the genera Campylobacter, Arcobacter, and Helicobacter (Harrison 22e p.1304). C. jejuni is the dominant diarrheal pathogen, accounting for roughly 80-90% of recognized illness in this group, while C. fetus is the principal cause of extraintestinal/systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.1304). Undercooked poultry is the leading source in developed countries (30-70% of cases); other routes include unpasteurized milk, untreated water, infected pets, contaminated seafood, foreign travel, and oral-anal sexual contact (Harrison 22e p.1304). Enteritis typically begins 2-4 days after exposure (range 1-7 days) and is often preceded 12-48 h by a prodrome of fever, headache, myalgia, and malaise (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305). Visibly bloody stool occurs in about 10% of adult cases; most patients presenting for care have 10 or more bowel movements on the worst day, and cramping abdominal pain may be the most prominent feature (Harrison 22e p.1305). C. jejuni can produce pseudoappendicitis, and isolated fever can be the only early sign, mimicking the onset of typhoid fever; myocarditis and pericarditis have been seen, especially in young men, and febrile young children may have convulsions (Harrison 22e p.1305). C. fetus has a tropism for vascular sites, causing endocarditis, mycotic aneurysm, and septic thrombophlebitis; its protective S-layer resists complement-mediated killing and opsonization, enabling bacteremia and antigenic variation (Harrison 22e p.1305). About 90% of bacteremic cases are due to C. jejuni and C. fetus in roughly equal numbers, despite C. jejuni being far more common overall (Harrison 22e p.1305). The two major postinfectious sequelae are reactive arthritis (up to 2.5% of cases, no HLA-B27 association, averaging about 3.2 joints, knees most often) and Guillain-Barre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1305). Sialylated lipopolysaccharide on certain C. jejuni strains drives molecular mimicry against axonal cell-surface molecules; Campylobacter is estimated to trigger 20-40% of all Guillain-Barre cases despite occurring in only ~1 per 1000-2000 infections (Harrison 22e p.1305). Diagnosis rests on culture on Campylobacter-selective fastidious media (the gold standard), with species-specific real-time PCR being more sensitive; MALDI-TOF identifies species, and Gram/Wright fecal smears or dark-field microscopy may reveal vibrioid forms with characteristic darting motility (Harrison 22e p.1305-1306). Infection with C. jejuni in low- and middle-income countries, even when asymptomatic, is associated with childhood stunting (short stature) and a distinctive microbiome signature (Harrison 22e p.1304). High fever Grossly bloody or severe diarrhea Symptoms persisting beyond one week or worsening Signs of sepsis, meningitis, or endovascular infection (suggesting C. fetus) Septic abortion or infection during pregnancy (often leads to fetal death) Septic thrombophlebitis (suggests C. fetus) Immunocompromise, diabetes, liver disease, or extremes of age (risk of severe/recurrent extraintestinal disease) Neurologic symptoms suggesting Guillain-Barre syndrome or its Miller Fisher variant following infection Labeling inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's) before excluding Campylobacter and related infections, since presentations and biopsy findings can overlap and Campylobacter enteritis is far more common in young adults (Harrison 22e p.1306). Assuming a negative stool culture excludes Campylobacter, as these fastidious organisms are missed without selective media or techniques (Harrison 22e p.1306). Over-interpreting culture-independent test positivity, which may reflect nonviable bacteria and can be falsely positive, unlike culture which usually implies active or recent infection (Harrison 22e p.1306). Treating commensal oral organisms (C. sputorum, C. concisus) as pathogens, since they rarely have pathogenic significance (Harrison 22e p.1306). Missing C. fetus bacteremia because of its low metabolic activity in standard blood culture media (Harrison 22e p.1306). Overlooking that not every patient with enteritis benefits from antimicrobials, and that antimotility agents can prolong symptoms and have been associated with toxic megacolon and death (Harrison 22e p.1306). Campylobacters survive in the gastrointestinal mucous layer of food animals and pets and reach humans mainly via undercooked/contaminated food or animal contact. In C. jejuni enteritis the jejunum, ileum, and colon are injured; biopsy shows a nonspecific acute inflammatory reaction with neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils in the lamina propria plus epithelial damage, mucus loss, glandular degeneration, and crypt abscesses. Strain motility and adherence favor disease, whereas classic entero- and cytotoxins (including cytolethal distending toxin) seem not to drive tissue injury; tissue invasion and occasional bacteremia indicate clinically significant invasion. C. fetus pathogenesis is better defined: nearly all clinical isolates bear a proteinaceous S-layer capsule-like structure conferring resistance to complement and opsonization, allowing bacteremia and seeding of extraintestinal sites, while antigenic switching of S-layer proteins contributes to chronicity and recurrence in compromised hosts. Protective immunity is incompletely understood but appears antibody-dependent and may be short-lived without continuous exposure (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305). Almost all patients recover fully from Campylobacter enteritis, spontaneously or with therapy; the rare deaths are linked largely to volume depletion. Symptoms persist beyond one week in 10-20% of patients seeking care, and clinical relapses occur in 5-10% of untreated patients. Some patients develop reactive arthritis or Guillain-Barre syndrome. Systemic C. fetus infection is far more often fatal than infection with related species, with overall reported bacteremia mortality around 12%; outcome depends on how promptly appropriate therapy begins. Otherwise healthy hosts usually survive C. fetus infection without sequelae, whereas compromised hosts often suffer recurrent and/or life-threatening disease (Harrison 22e p.1306). Three patterns of extraintestinal infection are described: (1) transient bacteremia in a normal host with enteritis, which is benign and needs no specific treatment; (2) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a normal host, arising from enteritis and responding well to antimicrobials; and (3) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a compromised host, in which enteritis may not be apparent and prompt, possibly prolonged, therapy is required (Harrison 22e p.1305).

Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms — Anaerobic bacterial infections, Mixed aerobic-anaerobic infection, Polymicrobial anaerobic infection, Bacteroides fragilis infection, Non-clostridial anaerobic infection Aerobic abscess (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus), which can also produce deep abscesses and lung abscess without an anaerobic component Chemical pneumonitis / Mendelson syndrome (acid aspiration) versus bacterial aspiration pneumonia Foreign-body aspiration with obstruction and atelectasis versus bacterial aspiration pneumonia Simple parapneumonic effusion (e.g., pneumococcal) versus anaerobic empyema Necrotizing pneumonia, bronchopleural fistula with purulent effusion, and pneumatocele in the lung-abscess differential Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis versus mixed aerobic-anaerobic (polymicrobial) necrotizing fasciitis Malignancy or granulomatous disease mimicked by cervicofacial actinomycosis ('lumpy jaw') Staphylococcus aureus abscess or lung abscess (no anaerobic component) Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis (more rapid, 1-3 day progression) Pneumococcal pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion Gram stain of pus/sputum showing a mixed bacterial population, especially when routine culture is negative or grows only streptococci or a single aerobe such as E. coli Anaerobic culture from normally sterile sites (blood, pleural/peritoneal fluid, CSF, sterile-site aspirates or biopsies); samples from mouth, nose, vagina, or feces are unacceptable due to commensal contamination Air-free syringe collection capped and placed in anaerobic transport media with rapid transport; liquid/tissue specimens preferred over swabs Pleural fluid analysis (WBC count, LDH, pH) to distinguish empyema from a simple parapneumonic effusion Imaging (chest x-ray/CT) showing dependent-segment consolidation or cavitary abscess; cross-sectional imaging for intraabdominal/pelvic abscess and for typhlitis bowel-wall thickening (>4 mm) Referral to a reference laboratory for susceptibility testing in serious, refractory, or prolonged-therapy infections (brain abscess, meningitis, joint infection, osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, endocarditis) Chemical pneumonitis from gastric acid aspiration (Mendelson syndrome) Foreign-body airway obstruction Malignancy or granulomatous disease mimicked by chronic actinomycotic 'lumpy jaw' Most clinically relevant anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella melaninogenica, Fusobacterium nucleatum) are relatively aerotolerant rather than strict obligate anaerobes; obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen at or above roughly 0.5%, whereas facultative anaerobes grow with or without oxygen (Harrison 22e p.1371). Anaerobes dominate the normal mucocutaneous microbiota, accounting for about 99.0-99.9% of cultivable organisms, with concentrations ranging from ~10^3/mL in the nose to ~10^12/mL in gingival crevices and colon; the lower GI tract is the major reservoir (anaerobe-to-aerobe ratio ~1000:1) (Harrison 22e p.1371-1372). Infections are typically polymicrobial, commonly yielding three to six species, and occasionally more than 10 species from a single suppurative site; the etiologic organisms mirror the neighboring resident microbiota (Harrison 22e p.1372-1373). Bacteroides fragilis, though only ~0.5-1% of the colonic microbiota, is the anaerobe most often isolated from intraabdominal infections and bacteremia; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A (PSA) is the principal virulence factor driving abscess formation via a TLR2-dependent cytokine/chemokine response (IL-8, IL-17, TNF-alpha) (Harrison 22e p.1373). Anaerobic gram-negative endotoxin (lipid A) is roughly 100-1000 times less biologically potent than aerobic gram-negative endotoxin, which helps explain why DIC, purpura, and septic shock are less frequent in anaerobic gram-negative bacteremia; Fusobacterium LPS is an exception and contributes to the severity of Lemierre's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1373). A putrid/foul-smelling discharge is considered suggestive of anaerobic infection but is a late finding present in only about 30-50% of cases, so its absence does not exclude anaerobes (Harrison 22e p.1374). Sterile pus paradox: an abscess that yields no growth on routine culture but shows teeming organisms on Gram stain strongly suggests anaerobes that failed to grow because of inadequate transport/culture technique (Harrison 22e p.1373-1378). Anaerobes are recovered in up to ~30% of brain abscesses, ~20% of epidural abscesses, and ~10% of subdural empyemas, but rarely cause meningitis; brain abscesses from contiguous (otogenic, odontogenic, sinus) spread are the most likely to involve anaerobes (Harrison 22e p.1375). Bacterial aspiration pneumonia evolves indolently over days to weeks, distinguishing it from chemical pneumonitis (e.g., Mendelson syndrome from acid aspiration), which develops within 4-6 hours and can produce a bilateral chest x-ray 'whiteout' within 8-24 hours (Harrison 22e p.1375). Empyema fluid characteristics (mean WBC ~55,000 cells/mL, LDH >1000 IU/L, pH <7.2, loculations, thick pleural peel) contrast sharply with a simple parapneumonic effusion (mean WBC ~5000 cells/mL, LDH >200 IU/L, pH ~7.4) (Harrison 22e p.1376). Aspiration pneumonia/lung abscess localizes to dependent segments: basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright, and posterior upper-lobe (usually right) or superior lower-lobe segments if supine (Harrison 22e p.1375-1376). Clostridium septicum bacteremia, often arising via neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis), is strongly associated with underlying malignancy, particularly colon cancer (Harrison 22e p.1376). Clostridium septicum bacteremia signaling possible occult colon malignancy B. fragilis-group bacteremia indicating underlying colonic pathology (neoplasia, diverticulitis) and carrying high untreated mortality Submitting specimens from heavily colonized sites (mouth, nose, vagina, feces) or expectorated sputum for anaerobic culture, which yields uninterpretable results from commensal contamination Dismissing an infection as 'sterile' when routine culture is negative despite a Gram stain teeming with organisms, missing inadequate anaerobic transport/culture Prior antibiotic therapy reducing the cultivability of anaerobes and masking the diagnosis Using agents with no useful anaerobic activity (aminoglycosides, monobactams, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and attributing nonresponse to other causes; failure to respond to such agents itself suggests an anaerobic etiology Treating gas in tissue or a putrid odor as pathognomonic for anaerobes; gas can be produced by aerobes and putrid odor appears in only 30-50% of cases Overlooking that right-lower-quadrant pain and tenderness are absent in nearly half of typhlitis cases (and may be absent entirely in patients on glucocorticoids) Relying on antibiotics alone without surgical debridement of devitalized tissue and drainage of large abscesses Anaerobic infection requires an anaerobic microenvironment with a lowered oxidation-reduction potential, which arises directly from tissue ischemia, trauma, surgery, or a perforated viscus, or is established and maintained by co-infecting facultative organisms that consume local oxygen. Disease typically follows breakdown of a mucosal barrier (intestinal perforation, ischemia, surgery) or direct inoculation (bite wounds, trauma), seeding normally sterile tissue with commensal organisms. The resulting infections are usually polymicrobial, with facultative and obligate anaerobes acting synergistically: facultative organisms create and sustain the reduced-oxygen environment, short-chain fatty acids and succinic acid impair phagocyte clearance, certain organisms supply growth factors to others (e.g., oral diphtheroids producing vitamin K needed by P. melaninogenica), and tissue damage promotes spread. Virulence factors include adhesins/fimbriae (P. gingivalis, B. fragilis pili, F. nucleatum as a bridging coaggregator), exoproteins such as P. gingivalis collagenase, and capsular polysaccharides. The B. fragilis capsular polysaccharide complex, particularly the zwitterionic PSA, is the most studied factor; its charged repeating-unit motif drives abscess formation by stimulating peritoneal macrophages (via TLR2) to release IL-8, IL-17, and TNF-alpha, recruiting PMNs that adhere to ICAM-1-upregulated mesothelial cells to form the abscess nidus, with T-cell IL-17/IFN-gamma also required (Harrison 22e p.1372-1373). Manifestations of severe sepsis and DIC are unusual in purely anaerobic infection, and septic shock is less common with B. fragilis than with aerobic gram-negative bacillary bacteremia. Nonetheless, isolation of a B. fragilis-group organism from blood indicates serious underlying infection with an untreated mortality rate of about 60%; case-fatality rises with advancing age (reported >66% in patients over 60), with isolation of multiple species, and with failure to surgically remove the focus. Reported relative mortality has been suggested to vary by species (B. thetaiotaomicron > P. distasonis > B. fragilis). Anaerobic endocarditis, though rare, carries significant mortality (~21-43%). Noma is highly lethal without treatment (70-90%). Recovery from empyema may take several months, particularly without surgical intervention (Harrison 22e p.1374, 1377-1378). No single formal grading scheme; severity is judged by anatomic site, extent, and systemic involvement. Localized/indolent processes (chronic sinusitis, periodontal disease, indolent anaerobic cellulitis) contrast with severe, life-threatening forms (Ludwig's angina with airway compromise, noma, Lemierre's syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis/Fournier gangrene, brain abscess, B. fragilis-group bacteremia, endocarditis). Antibiotic selection is guided empirically by infection location, severity, and local resistance patterns; reference-laboratory susceptibility testing is reserved for serious, refractory, or prolonged-therapy infections (Harrison 22e p.1374-1379).

Infections Due to Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas Species — Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, Burkholderia cepacia complex infection, Melioidosis, Glanders, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infection, Pseudomallei infection, Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas) Other gram-negative bacterial pneumonia and sepsis (clinically often indistinguishable from P. aeruginosa) Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (can also produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions) Tuberculosis (chronic cavitary melioidosis mimic) Pyogenic meningitis of other bacterial etiology (CSF profile of Pseudomonas meningitis is nonspecific) Polymicrobial osteomyelitis from trauma or decubitus ulcers Aspergillosis and mucormycosis (can produce ecthyma-gangrenosum-like lesions) Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus species causing malignant/necrotizing otitis externa Tuberculosis mimicked by chronic pulmonary melioidosis Other gram-negative enterocolitis mimicked by Pseudomonas enterocolitis / Shanghai fever Sputum Gram stain showing predominant polymorphonuclear leukocytes plus culture positive for P. aeruginosa supports acute pneumonia rather than colonization Multiplex PCR platforms on respiratory and blood samples identify P. aeruginosa earlier than classical culture Technetium-99 bone scan as the gold standard for malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa MRI and bone scan for puncture-wound foot osteomyelitis; needle aspiration usually yields the diagnosis Deep bone biopsy before treating presumed P. aeruginosa osteomyelitis in trauma or decubitus settings to confirm its causative role Blood cultures plus echocardiographic/clinical signs for endocarditis (blood cultures often negative in vertebral osteomyelitis unless endocarditis coexists) Mandatory laboratory susceptibility testing before using newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase-inhibitor agents or cefiderocol against MDR/XDR strains Fluid overload mistaken for pneumonia on CT in ventilated patients (contributes to overdiagnosis of HAP/VAP) The pseudomonads are a heterogeneous group of non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacteria now split across three medically important genera: Pseudomonas, Burkholderia, and Stenotrophomonas; most cause disease opportunistically, the exceptions being the primary pathogens B. pseudomallei and B. mallei. P. aeruginosa rarely causes infection without a breach in host defenses; disease typically requires compromised immunity, mucosal trauma, physiologic derangement, or antibiotic-mediated suppression of normal flora, so most infections cluster in intensive care units. On primary culture P. aeruginosa is identified by a yellow to dark-green or bluish pigment, a shiny gun-metal colony sheen, a characteristic fruity odor, failure to ferment lactose on MacConkey agar, and a positive oxidase reaction; cystic fibrosis isolates may appear mucoid from overproduction of alginate. Ecthyma gangrenosum is the distinctive skin lesion of P. aeruginosa bacteremia, occurring almost exclusively in markedly neutropenic patients and those with AIDS; lesions begin pink, darken to purple, then become black and necrotic, and histologically are due to vascular invasion teeming with bacteria. P. aeruginosa keratitis is a medical emergency because it can progress over roughly 48 hours to involve the entire cornea with opacification and even perforation; it is strongly associated with contact lenses, especially the extended-wear type. Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa most often occurs in elderly diabetics and can extend to cranial nerve palsies (most commonly cranial nerve VII) or cavernous sinus thrombosis; the ESR is invariably elevated, often 100 mm/h or more. Hot-tub folliculitis, toe-web infection, and the green-nail syndrome (pyocyanin diffusing into the nail bed of a Pseudomonas paronychia) are characteristic community skin manifestations; whirlpools, spas, and pools are common sources, and folliculitis is usually self-limited. Vertebral osteomyelitis and sternoclavicular septic arthritis are uncommon but characteristic complications in people who inject drugs; Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the foot typically follows a puncture wound through a sneaker, mainly in children, often with negative blood cultures. Melioidosis (B. pseudomallei) is geographically restricted chiefly to Southeast Asia and northern Australia (with cases in India and China); the organism is a facultative intracellular pathogen acquired from soil and water that can cause latent infection presenting long after exposure. Melioidosis can mimic tuberculosis with chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary upper-lobe disease, and may also present as skin ulceration with lymphangitis and regional lymphadenopathy or as high-mortality septicemia. Burkholderia cepacia complex can cause the rapidly fatal cepacia syndrome (respiratory distress plus septicemia) in cystic fibrosis; B. cenocepacia in particular is a barrier to lung transplantation, with relatively high one-year mortality. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is an opportunist whose emergence requires major disruption of host flora, classically broad-spectrum cephalosporin or carbapenem therapy; distinguishing colonization from true infection in ventilated, non-neutropenic patients is a recurring clinical dilemma. Ecthyma gangrenosum in a neutropenic or AIDS patient suggesting P. aeruginosa bacteremia Rapidly progressive corneal opacification/perforation indicating sight-threatening Pseudomonas keratitis (medical emergency) Severe lancinating ear pain with granulation tissue in a diabetic, plus cranial nerve palsy, signaling malignant otitis externa Hypothermia or shock in P. aeruginosa bacteremia (marker of severe illness) Cepacia syndrome: rapidly fatal respiratory distress with septicemia in cystic fibrosis Hemoptysis, night sweats, and cavitary disease in a patient from an endemic region suggesting melioidosis with systemic spread Overdiagnosing HAP/VAP: positive sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or PCR results may reflect tracheobronchial colonization, endotracheal-tube biofilm, or simple tracheobronchitis rather than true pneumonia; clinical judgment is essential. In trauma- or decubitus-associated osteomyelitis, infection is often polymicrobial and the causative role of P. aeruginosa can be overstated without a deep bone biopsy. Treating S. maltophilia or P. aeruginosa pulmonary cultures as infection when they may represent colonization, especially in non-neutropenic patients; unnecessary therapy promotes resistance. Assuming community sputum cultures prove community-acquired P. aeruginosa pneumonia in patients prone to airway colonization by multiple bacterial strains. Empirically relying on first-line antipseudomonal agents in settings where susceptibility is below 80%, or on the newer agents/cefiderocol without susceptibility testing given unpredictable resistance mechanisms. Failing to remove indwelling foreign bodies (urinary catheters, stents, stones, central lines) — relapse of UTI or bacteremia may be due to the retained device or ongoing obstruction rather than antibiotic resistance. Not recognizing that melioidosis can present long after travel to an endemic area due to latent intracellular infection. P. aeruginosa possesses an unusually large arsenal of putative virulence factors, yet few are individually proven to drive human disease, and there is great redundancy. Adhesins (pili, flagellin/flagellar cap binding mucins, LPS outer core binding CFTR to aid internalization, and alginate in mucoid strains) mediate colonization, with adhesion strongest to injured cell surfaces. A type III secretion system injects toxins (ExoS or ExoU, ExoT, ExoY) into host cells, allowing evasion of phagocytes; strains secreting ExoU are associated with higher mortality. A type II secretion system releases diffusible toxins including exotoxin A, multiple proteases (which degrade host cytokines and chemokines), and phospholipases. Rhamnolipids, pyocyanin, and hydrocyanic acid further injure tissue and can cause neutrophil death. Inflammatory responses to lipid A and flagellin via Toll-like receptors (principally TLR4 and TLR5) are required for defense but, when florid, contribute to sepsis and septic shock. In chronic infection (cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, diffuse panbronchiolitis) defective mucociliary clearance and mucus stasis select for P. aeruginosa, which adapts over time by losing pili and flagella, losing the O side chain of LPS (becoming complement-sensitive), and overproducing mucoid exopolysaccharide, dampening the host response and enabling decades of persistence with attenuated virulence factor production. B. pseudomallei survives within neutrophils and macrophages, aided by a polysaccharide capsule and a type III secretion system, and provokes a florid inflammatory response. B. cepacia complex organisms bind lung mucus and possess potent LPS that drives lung inflammation. S. maltophilia virulence is limited, with disease largely a host inflammatory response to LPS and flagellin; its hallmark is broad intrinsic antibiotic resistance via efflux pumps and the L1 and L2 beta-lactamases. P. aeruginosa carries high attributable mortality and is among the most feared pathogens in neutropenic patients. Historical crude bacteremia mortality exceeded 50%, with more recent attributable mortality of about 28 to 44% depending on adequacy and timing of treatment and underlying disease severity. Pneumonia mortality has been reported at 40 to 80%, though the fraction attributable to underlying disease is uncertain, and VAP outcomes are poor. Chronic airway infection (e.g., cystic fibrosis) is rarely eradicated and is the leading contributor to respiratory failure and death in CF. Pseudomonas endovascular infection in people who inject drugs is more indolent than S. aureus endocarditis and is more often curable when right-sided. Melioidosis septicemia carries high mortality, with rates as high as 44% reported in Thailand. B. cenocepacia infection has relatively high one-year mortality after lung transplantation. S. maltophilia pneumonia/bacteremia can cause septic shock, with a severe high-mortality form described in neutropenic patients. No single formal severity score is presented. Resistance is graded as multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) P. aeruginosa, with extremely high MDR rates reported from eastern/southern Europe, Latin America, India, and China, especially in ICUs. Carbapenemase production is highlighted as the most threatening resistance mechanism. The B. cepacia cepacia syndrome denotes a rapidly fatal severe phenotype. Melioidosis spans a clinical spectrum from asymptomatic infection through localized abscesses and pneumonia to high-mortality disseminated septicemic disease.

Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria — HACEK endocarditis, HACEK group infections, Fastidious gram-negative bacterial infections, Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella infections Viridans group streptococcal endocarditis (also subacute, culture-positive, common in dental-source disease) Enterococcal endocarditis Culture-negative endocarditis (Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei) when blood cultures are sterile Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis when the course is more acute Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis from Staphylococcus aureus in children (where K. kingae may have surpassed S. aureus as a leading cause) Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection when ecthyma gangrenosum-like skin lesions are present (Aeromonas) Neisseria meningitidis sepsis (K. kingae bacteremia can produce a similar petechial rash) Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (Aeromonas can cause indistinguishable ecthyma gangrenosum) Other gram-negative bacteremic pneumonias (Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia, similar high mortality) Other causes of culture-negative or slow-growing endocarditis Blood cultures with notification of the laboratory that a HACEK organism is suspected; modern automated systems (e.g., BACTEC) usually yield growth within the first week 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) of blood or cardiac valve specimens for culture-negative or fastidious cases MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry performed directly on colonies for rapid, accurate species identification Echocardiography to detect valvular vegetations (seen in up to 85% of HACEK endocarditis) Real-time PCR of blood or joint fluid for Kingella kingae; inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles to improve recovery In vitro antimicrobial susceptibility testing, including Etest, given slow growth and possible undetected beta-lactamase; susceptibility testing is essential for the miscellaneous multidrug-resistant gram-negative organisms Noninfective embolic disease and vasculitis (HACEK endocarditis frequently presents with embolic, vascular, and immunologic phenomena such as cerebrovascular accidents, mycotic aneurysms, and immune-complex glomerulonephritis that may mimic primary vasculitic or thromboembolic disorders) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (rare HUS following bloody diarrhea has been linked to Aeromonas, but HUS itself is the differential) HACEK is an acronym for a group of fastidious, slow-growing gram-negative bacteria that require a carbon-dioxide-enriched atmosphere and do not grow on routine enteric media such as MacConkey agar: Haemophilus species, Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) species, Cardiobacterium species, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae. These organisms normally colonize the oral cavity; invasive disease characteristically follows a recent dental procedure or nasopharyngeal infection in a patient with underlying valvular heart disease or prosthetic valves. A positive HACEK blood culture is strongly predictive of underlying infective endocarditis, with an overall positive predictive value around 60%, though this varies sharply by organism (e.g., 62-100% with Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans bacteremia versus only 0-6% with Eikenella bacteremia). HACEK organisms cause roughly 0.8-6% of infective endocarditis cases, most often due to Aggregatibacter species, Haemophilus species, and Cardiobacterium hominis; the aortic and mitral valves are most commonly affected. Compared with non-HACEK endocarditis, HACEK endocarditis occurs in younger patients and is more frequently associated with embolic, vascular, and immunologic manifestations; systemic embolization is common (major emboli in roughly 28-71% of cases) and vegetations are seen on echocardiography in up to 85% of patients. Kingella kingae behaves differently from the other HACEK organisms: more than half of K. kingae infections are bone and joint infections, oropharyngeal colonization peaks in the first 3 years of life and is higher in daycare-attending children, and it can be transmitted child-to-child and cause outbreaks; K. kingae bacteremia can present with a petechial rash resembling Neisseria meningitidis sepsis. Capnocytophaga canimorsus and C. cynodegmi are endogenous to the dog and cat mouth; infection often follows a dog or cat bite (or exposure without a bite), and asplenia, glucocorticoid use, and alcohol abuse predispose to severe sepsis with shock and DIC, classically with a petechial rash progressing to purpura and gangrene. Pasteurella multocida colonizes the respiratory and GI tracts of domestic animals (oropharyngeal colonization 50-90% in cats, 50-70% in dogs) and is transmitted by bites, scratches, or licking; most human infections are skin and soft tissue, and almost two-thirds are caused by cats. Aeromonas can produce ecthyma gangrenosum (hemorrhagic vesicles with a rim of erythema and central necrosis/ulceration) resembling lesions of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and is associated with water exposure, floods, and other hydrologic disasters (along with Shewanella and Chromobacterium). Diagnostic recovery of HACEK organisms is improved by alerting the microbiology laboratory; most cultures turn positive within the first week with modern systems (e.g., BACTEC), and prolonged incubation has not been shown to increase recovery of clinically significant isolates. Molecular methods aid diagnosis: 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) on blood or cardiac valve tissue and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry on colonies increase the accuracy and speed of HACEK identification; real-time PCR and inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles enhance recovery of K. kingae in culture-negative cases. Chromobacterium violaceum causes rare but often fatal soft tissue infections and metastatic abscesses, occurring especially in children with defective neutrophil function such as chronic granulomatous disease. Systemic embolization (cerebral and other major emboli are common in HACEK endocarditis) Congestive heart failure complicating endocarditis (reported in roughly 19-50% of Haemophilus HACEK cases) Mycotic aneurysm formation Petechial/purpuric rash with sepsis after a dog or cat bite in an asplenic, alcohol-abusing, or glucocorticoid-treated patient (Capnocytophaga canimorsus, may progress to shock, DIC, and gangrene) Petechial rash with bacteremia mimicking meningococcemia (Kingella kingae) Necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis after water/wound exposure (Aeromonas; very high mortality with myonecrosis) Sepsis with metastatic abscesses in a child with defective neutrophil function (Chromobacterium violaceum) Because of slow growth, antimicrobial susceptibility testing may be difficult and beta-lactamase production may go undetected; resistance is most common in Haemophilus and Aggregatibacter species. Prolonged blood-culture incubation has not been shown to improve recovery of clinically significant HACEK isolates, so relying on extended incubation alone may delay diagnosis—molecular methods may be needed. Failing to alert the microbiology laboratory that a fastidious HACEK organism is suspected can compromise recovery and identification. Eikenella corrodens is resistant to clindamycin, metronidazole, and aminoglycosides, so empirical regimens chosen for typical gram-negatives may fail. Many miscellaneous gram-negative organisms (Achromobacter, Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Chromobacterium, Aeromonas) are frequently multidrug-resistant—Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium are typically resistant to carbapenems while Aeromonas can produce carbapenemases—so therapy must be guided by susceptibility testing rather than assumptions. Capnocytophaga canimorsus infection may be missed when there is exposure without an obvious scratch or bite, and severe disease can occur in patients without an apparent wound. HACEK organisms are commensals of the human oral cavity. Disruption of the oral mucosa (dental procedures, nasopharyngeal infection, periodontal disease) allows transient bacteremia; in patients with damaged native valves or prosthetic material, the slow-growing organisms seed and form valvular vegetations, producing a typically subacute, indolent endocarditis. Their fastidious, CO2-dependent slow growth accounts for delayed culture positivity and difficulty in susceptibility testing (including underdetection of beta-lactamase). The remaining fastidious and miscellaneous gram-negative organisms in this chapter act largely as opportunists: animal-mouth flora (Pasteurella multocida, Capnocytophaga canimorsus) inoculated through bites/scratches/licking, environmental and waterborne organisms (Aeromonas, Shewanella, Chromobacterium violaceum, Achromobacter xylosoxidans) introduced through wounds or contaminated fluids, and nosocomial nonfermenters (Elizabethkingia/Chryseobacterium, Rhizobium radiobacter, Alcaligenes faecalis) associated with contaminated fluids, indwelling devices, and immunocompromised hosts. Overall prognosis in both native-valve and prosthetic-valve HACEK endocarditis is excellent and significantly better than endocarditis caused by non-HACEK pathogens; one case-control study found significantly lower 1-year mortality than viridans group streptococcal endocarditis. Mortality associated with HACEK endocarditis in older series ranged from about 28 to 71% depending on the cohort. By contrast, several miscellaneous organisms carry high mortality: Pasteurella multocida invasive disease up to ~30% despite therapy, Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia up to ~67%, Aeromonas sepsis ~25% in immunocompromised adults and >90% with myonecrosis, Chryseobacterium indologenes up to ~50%, and Elizabethkingia anophelis bloodstream infection ~18%. No formal grading system; clinical severity is stratified by site and host factors. HACEK endocarditis runs a typically subacute course (more aggressive with Kingella kingae) with severity marked by embolic, vascular, and immunologic complications, heart failure, and mycotic aneurysm. For the miscellaneous organisms, severity escalates with immunocompromise, asplenia, cirrhosis, malignancy, diabetes, neutrophil dysfunction, and extremes of age, and with deep/invasive presentations such as bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, myonecrosis, and septic shock with DIC.
