history and sleep diary over one to two weeks Screening questionnaires for sleep apnoea and other sleep disorders Assessment for comorbid depression, anxiety, and substance use Review of medications and stimulant intake Polysomnography reserved for suspected apnoea, periodic limb movements, or atypical features The disorder is dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, with difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or early morning waking, causing significant daytime distress or impairment For a chronic diagnosis the difficulty is present several nights per week over an extended period, typically at least three months, despite adequate opportunity to sleep Daytime consequences such as fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, and impaired performance are integral to the diagnosis, not merely the nocturnal complaint A thorough evaluation should exclude other sleep disorders such as obstructive sleep apnoea and restless legs, and identify medical, psychiatric, and substance-related contributors Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the recommended first-line treatment and is more durable than hypnotic medication Sleep hygiene alone is usually insufficient, but stimulus control, sleep restriction, and cognitive techniques are the effective components of behavioural treatment Hypnotic medications may help in the short term but carry risks of tolerance, dependence, daytime sedation, and rebound insomnia, so long-term use is discouraged Insomnia is bidirectionally linked with depression and anxiety, and treating it can improve mood and reduce relapse risk Excessive daytime sleepiness with witnessed apnoeas suggesting untreated sleep apnoea Suicidal ideation associated with comorbid depression Escalating hypnotic or alcohol use to induce sleep Severe sleep deprivation impairing safety, such as while driving Reaching for hypnotics as first-line rather than offering cognitive behavioural therapy Relying on sleep hygiene advice alone, which is rarely sufficient Missing obstructive sleep apnoea or restless legs as the true cause Overlooking caffeine, alcohol, and stimulant contributions Failing to recognise and treat comorbid depression or anxiety Insomnia disorder is conceptualised through a model of hyperarousal, in which heightened cognitive, emotional, and physiological arousal impairs the normal sleep process. Predisposing traits, precipitating stressors, and perpetuating behaviours and beliefs (such as excessive time in bed and worry about sleep) interact, with dysregulation of arousal and sleep-wake regulatory systems maintaining the condition over time. Insomnia disorder often becomes chronic and relapsing, particularly when perpetuating behaviours and beliefs are established, but cognitive behavioural therapy produces durable improvement in most patients. Prognosis is better with early behavioural treatment and management of comorbidities, and worse with long-term hypnotic reliance and untreated psychiatric or medical contributors.

Interferon-gamma pathway defect — MSMD, Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, IFN-gamma/IL-12 axis defect HIV/AIDS and other causes of acquired T-cell deficiency with mycobacterial disease Severe combined immunodeficiency and combined immunodeficiencies Chronic granulomatous disease Anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome (an acquired phenocopy) Disseminated tuberculosis or non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection in an immunocompetent host Genetic testing of the IL-12/interferon-gamma axis (IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1 and related genes) Functional assays of interferon-gamma production and receptor signalling Flow cytometry for interferon-gamma receptor expression Cultures and molecular identification of mycobacterial and Salmonella species Testing for anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies to exclude the acquired phenocopy Imaging to define the extent of disseminated infection Defects of the interferon-gamma/IL-12 axis cause Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD), a selective vulnerability to weakly virulent mycobacteria Affected individuals develop disseminated infection with environmental (non-tuberculous) mycobacteria and with the BCG vaccine strain, as well as an increased risk of severe tuberculosis and salmonellosis The underlying problem is failure of the cytokine circuit by which macrophages and T/NK cells communicate to control intracellular pathogens, involving genes such as IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, and STAT1 IL-12 produced by macrophages normally drives lymphocytes to secrete interferon-gamma, which in turn activates macrophages to kill intracellular organisms; breaking this loop cripples defence against mycobacteria The clinical severity depends on the specific defect, ranging from complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency with severe early disseminated disease to partial defects with milder, more localised infection Because the immune defect is narrow, patients are typically not broadly susceptible to the wide range of pathogens seen in combined immunodeficiencies Complete receptor defects respond poorly to interferon-gamma therapy, whereas partial or IL-12-axis defects may benefit from adjunctive interferon-gamma alongside prolonged antimycobacterial treatment Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered for severe complete defects, though outcomes can be challenging Disseminated mycobacterial or salmonella infection requiring urgent diagnosis and prolonged therapy Disseminated BCG infection following vaccination (BCG and other live vaccines must be avoided) Severe complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency presenting with overwhelming early infection Recurrent or unusually severe intracellular infection prompting immunological evaluation Administering BCG or other live vaccines before recognising the defect, risking disseminated vaccine-strain infection Stopping antimycobacterial therapy too early, since prolonged and sometimes lifelong treatment may be needed Assuming a broad immunodeficiency and missing the selective nature of the defect Overlooking the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome as a phenocopy in adults Expecting interferon-gamma therapy to help in complete receptor deficiency This group of disorders disrupts the interferon-gamma-dependent axis that controls intracellular pathogens. Following ingestion of mycobacteria, macrophages secrete IL-12, which acts on T cells and natural killer cells (via the IL-12 receptor) to induce production of interferon-gamma. Interferon-gamma then signals through its receptor and the JAK-STAT1 pathway to activate macrophages, enhancing their capacity to kill ingested organisms and to form protective granulomas. Mutations at any point in this circuit, in the interferon-gamma receptor chains, IL-12 or its receptor, or STAT1, impair macrophage activation and granuloma formation, leaving weakly virulent mycobacteria and Salmonella able to disseminate. The narrow, well-defined nature of the defect explains the characteristic selective infection susceptibility. Prognosis depends heavily on the molecular defect: complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency carries a poor outlook with severe, recurrent disseminated disease that responds poorly to cytokine therapy, whereas partial receptor and IL-12-axis defects often have a much better prognosis with prolonged antimycobacterial treatment and, where appropriate, adjunctive interferon-gamma.

Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome — interstitial cystitis, bladder pain syndrome, IC/BPS, painful bladder syndrome, Hunner lesion cystitis Urinary tract infection Overactive bladder Bladder carcinoma, including carcinoma in situ Bladder or ureteric calculi Endometriosis and other gynaecological pelvic pain Chronic prostatitis / chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men Radiation or chemical cystitis Urinalysis and urine culture to exclude infection Urine cytology and cystoscopy where malignancy is a concern, particularly with haematuria Bladder diary documenting frequency, voided volumes, and symptom pattern Validated symptom and pain questionnaires to assess severity and monitor response Cystoscopy, with or without hydrodistension, to identify Hunner lesions Imaging to exclude stones or other structural pathology when indicated Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome is a chronic condition of bladder or pelvic pain perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary urgency and frequency, in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause Pain characteristically worsens as the bladder fills and is relieved by voiding, a pattern that helps distinguish it from overactive bladder It is far more common in women and frequently coexists with other chronic pain and functional conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, and chronic pelvic pain Diagnosis is essentially clinical and one of exclusion, requiring that infection, malignancy, stones, and other bladder pathology be ruled out Cystoscopy may be normal or may reveal Hunner lesions, whose presence defines a distinct phenotype that responds to lesion-directed treatment Management is stepwise, beginning with education, dietary trigger avoidance, stress and pain management, and pelvic floor physical therapy Oral and intravesical therapies form later steps, and Hunner lesions are specifically treated by fulguration or resection Refractory disease may be considered for neuromodulation or, rarely, major reconstructive surgery, reserved for carefully selected severe cases New haematuria, especially in older patients or smokers, must trigger evaluation for bladder cancer rather than being ascribed to the syndrome Visible or microscopic haematuria requiring exclusion of bladder cancer New or changing symptoms in an older patient or smoker Persistent sterile pyuria warranting exclusion of tuberculosis or malignancy Abnormal urine cytology Rapidly worsening or atypical pain suggesting an alternative diagnosis Repeatedly treating for infection despite negative cultures Missing bladder cancer by attributing haematuria to the syndrome Failing to identify and treat Hunner lesions, which need specific therapy Escalating to invasive surgery before conservative and behavioural measures are exhausted Overlooking coexisting pelvic floor dysfunction and other chronic pain conditions The mechanism is incompletely understood and probably multifactorial. A leading hypothesis is a defective bladder urothelial glycosaminoglycan (GAG) layer, which normally protects the underlying tissue; increased permeability allows urinary solutes such as potassium to penetrate the urothelium and irritate sensory nerves and detrusor muscle. Mast cell activation, neurogenic inflammation, and up-regulation of sensory pathways contribute to chronic pain and central sensitisation. In the Hunner lesion subtype there is a demonstrable inflammatory bladder wall change, whereas non-lesion disease is dominated by neuropathic and functional pain mechanisms, explaining the frequent overlap with other chronic pain disorders. The condition is chronic and typically follows a relapsing and remitting course; it is rarely progressive but can significantly impair quality of life. Many patients gain meaningful symptom control with a multimodal, stepwise approach, and the Hunner lesion subtype often responds well to lesion-directed therapy. A minority with severe refractory disease may ultimately require advanced interventions.

Intestinal malrotation — malrotation, midgut malrotation, malrotation with volvulus Duodenal atresia or stenosis Jejunoileal atresia Necrotising enterocolitis Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (non-bilious vomiting) Incarcerated hernia causing obstruction Upper gastrointestinal contrast series to locate the duodenojejunal junction Abdominal ultrasound to assess superior mesenteric vessel orientation and look for a whirlpool sign Plain abdominal radiograph, which may show a paucity of distal gas or a double-bubble pattern Blood gas and lactate to detect metabolic acidosis suggesting bowel ischaemia Baseline bloods and cross-match in preparation for emergency laparotomy Arises from incomplete rotation and fixation of the midgut, leaving a narrow mesenteric base that predisposes to twisting (volvulus) The classic presentation is a previously well neonate who develops sudden bilious vomiting, which must be treated as a surgical emergency until proven otherwise Bilious vomiting in an infant should trigger urgent imaging because midgut volvulus can infarct the entire small bowel within hours The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the key investigation, showing an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction and a corkscrew or spiral appearance if volvulus is present Ultrasound may reveal an inverted relationship of the superior mesenteric artery and vein or a whirlpool sign of twisted mesentery Abnormal peritoneal (Ladd) bands can cross and obstruct the duodenum even without volvulus, producing intermittent obstructive symptoms The definitive operation is the Ladd procedure: untwisting the volvulus, dividing Ladd bands, broadening the mesenteric base, and placing the bowel in a non-rotated position, usually with appendicectomy Some children present later in life with intermittent, vague abdominal pain or feeding difficulty rather than acute obstruction Bilious vomiting in a neonate or infant, which mandates emergency evaluation for midgut volvulus Abdominal distension, tenderness, or rectal bleeding suggesting established bowel ischaemia Rapidly worsening metabolic acidosis or haemodynamic instability indicating strangulated midgut requiring immediate laparotomy Any delay in diagnosis, as the whole midgut can become necrotic within a few hours of volvulus Dismissing bilious vomiting as feed intolerance or reflux and delaying imaging Assuming a normal plain radiograph excludes malrotation or volvulus Failing to arrange emergency surgery once volvulus is suspected while awaiting further tests Overlooking older children with intermittent symptoms in whom malrotation is still possible During normal development the midgut herniates, rotates counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery, and returns to the abdomen with broad mesenteric fixation. In malrotation this process is incomplete, so the caecum sits abnormally and the mesenteric root is short and narrow. This narrow pedicle allows the midgut to twist around the superior mesenteric vessels, compromising blood supply and causing ischaemia, while abnormal fibrous bands may simultaneously compress the duodenum and produce obstruction. When volvulus is corrected before ischaemia sets in, outcomes are excellent with low recurrence after a Ladd procedure. Delayed presentation with extensive bowel infarction can necessitate massive resection, leading to short bowel syndrome and long-term nutritional dependence, and carries significant mortality.

Intestinal Nematode (Roundworm) Infections — soil-transmitted helminths, Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides Strongyloides midepigastric pain resembles peptic ulcer disease, except it is aggravated by food ingestion (p.1816) Heavy trichuriasis with bloody/mucoid diarrhea may resemble inflammatory bowel disease (p.1818) Intestinal/biliary ascariasis may present as a surgical acute abdomen mimicking acute appendicitis in endemic areas (p.1815) Strongyloides hyperinfection-associated gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis can dominate or be mistaken for primary bacterial infection (p.1817) Hookworm rhabditiform larvae in non-fresh stool must be differentiated from Strongyloides larvae (p.1816) Stool microscopy for characteristic ova and parasites: Ascaris eggs (~65 x 45 um), hookworm eggs (~40 x 60 um, species indistinguishable by light microscopy), Trichuris lemon-shaped eggs (~50 x 20 um) (p.1815-1818) Strongyloides: rhabditiform larvae (~250 um, short buccal cavity) on stool microscopy; single stool detects only ~one-third of uncomplicated cases, so serial examinations and agar plate method improve sensitivity; duodenojejunal aspirate/biopsy; ELISA serum antibody serology (sensitive for uncomplicated infection); in dissemination, filariform larvae in stool, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or surgical drainage fluid (p.1817) Enterobius: eggs are NOT found in stool - diagnose with morning cellulose acetate tape applied to the perianal region (eggs oval, ~55 x 25 um, flattened on one side) (p.1818) Ascaris lung phase: larvae detectable in sputum or gastric aspirates before eggs appear in stool; chest imaging showing transient rounded infiltrates (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815) PCR of stool worm DNA (increasing use, mostly research/some clinical) for species-level diagnosis (p.1815-1818) Abdominal imaging: plain film for masses of worms in obstruction; ultrasound and ERCP for pancreaticobiliary Ascaris (ERCP can also extract worms) (p.1815) Hookworm disease bloodwork: hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia (p.1816) Inflammatory bowel disease (heavy trichuriasis) (p.1818) Peptic ulcer disease (strongyloidiasis epigastric pain) (p.1816) Acute appendicitis / surgical acute abdomen (intestinal or biliary ascariasis) (p.1815) More than one billion people worldwide are infected with one or more intestinal nematode species; they are most common where sanitation and fecal-waste disposal are inadequate, especially resource-limited tropical and subtropical regions, but are seen with increasing frequency among immigrants and refugees to developed countries (p.1814). The major intestinal roundworms are Ascaris lumbricoides, the hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, A. ceylanicum), Strongyloides stercoralis, Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), and Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) (p.1815). Ascaris, Trichuris, and the hookworms require a soil phase for development, whereas S. stercoralis and E. vermicularis can be transmitted directly from person to person (p.1814). Because most helminths cannot fully complete their life cycle within the same human host, heavy adult-worm burdens require repeated exposure; clinical disease (versus asymptomatic/subclinical infection) generally develops only with repeated exposure and is typically related to infection intensity (p.1814). Eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE are features of many helminth infections, the latter particularly when the life cycle involves tissue migration (Ascaris, Strongyloides, hookworms) (p.1814). Ascaris larval migration through the lungs (~9-12 days after egg ingestion) can cause an irritating nonproductive cough, substernal discomfort, eosinophilia, and transient rounded pulmonary infiltrates - eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815). Heavy Ascaris infection can cause small-bowel obstruction by a bolus of entangled worms (more common in children with narrow lumens), sometimes complicated by perforation, intussusception, or volvulus; an adult worm migrating into the biliary tree can cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or rarely intrahepatic abscess (p.1815). In highly endemic areas, intestinal and biliary ascariasis can rival acute appendicitis as a cause of surgical acute abdomen (p.1815). The major consequence of chronic hookworm infection is iron deficiency; symptoms are minimal if iron stores are adequate, but undernourished individuals develop progressive iron-deficiency anemia and hypoproteinemia (fatigue, weakness, dyspnea). Hookworm disease requires the combination of heavy worm burden, prolonged duration, and inadequate iron intake (p.1816). Hookworm larvae may cause a pruritic maculopapular rash (ground itch) at the skin penetration site; hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes with eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia, is characteristic of hookworm disease (p.1816). S. stercoralis is distinguished by its ability - unique among helminths except Capillaria - to complete its life cycle and replicate within a human host (autoinfection), so infection can persist for decades without further exogenous exposure (p.1816). Larva currens, a rapidly advancing (up to ~10 cm/h) pruritic serpiginous skin eruption, is pathognomonic of strongyloidiasis; recurrent urticaria, often on the buttocks, is the most common cutaneous manifestation (p.1816). Impaired cell-mediated immunity - especially high-dose glucocorticoid therapy, and less commonly other immunosuppressants or HTLV-1 infection - can trigger Strongyloides hyperinfection with massive larval numbers, leading to colitis/enteritis/malabsorption and disseminated disease (CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys) (p.1817). Disseminated strongyloidiasis is often complicated by gram-negative bacteremia, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocating through disrupted mucosal barriers; eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severely infected patients (p.1817). Even asymptomatic strongyloidiasis must be treated because of the potential for later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination; Strongyloides serology should be performed before starting glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation in patients with prior potential exposure, especially with eosinophilia (p.1817). Most Trichuris (whipworm) infections are asymptomatic, but heavy infections may cause anemia and bloody/mucoid diarrhea resembling inflammatory bowel disease; massive infection in children can cause rectal prolapse from protracted tenesmus (p.1818). Enterobius (pinworm) is more common in temperate climates than the tropics; perianal pruritus, worse at night when gravid females emerge, is the cardinal symptom, and eosinophilia is uncommon (p.1818). Disseminated strongyloidiasis - particularly in patients with unsuspected infection who are taking glucocorticoids - has a HIGH mortality rate (p.1817) Strongyloides hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocation (p.1817) Eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severe/disseminated strongyloidiasis, removing a reassuring marker (p.1817) Complete intestinal obstruction with perforation, intussusception, or volvulus from a heavy Ascaris worm bolus (p.1815) Biliary Ascaris causing cholangitis, pancreatitis, or intrahepatic abscess (p.1815) Failing to screen for and treat asymptomatic strongyloidiasis before glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation - asymptomatic infection must still be treated because of the risk of later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination (p.1817) Relying on eosinophilia to exclude strongyloidiasis - it is often absent in severe/disseminated disease (p.1817) Using routine stool ova-and-parasite microscopy to diagnose pinworm - Enterobius eggs are not passed in feces; perianal cellulose acetate tape is required (p.1818) Single stool examination for Strongyloides detects only about one-third of uncomplicated cases (p.1817) Misidentifying hookworm rhabditiform larvae (in non-fresh stool) as Strongyloides (p.1816) Intestinal nematodes are nonsegmented roundworms ranging from ~1 mm to many centimeters. Ascaris and the hookworms have life cycles involving migration through the heart and lungs before maturing in the intestine (larvae penetrate alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and reach the small bowel). Ascaris adults live in the small-intestinal lumen and females are extraordinarily fecund (>200,000 eggs/day); eggs are highly environmentally resistant and become infective after maturation in warm, moist soil. Hookworm adults attach to the small-bowel mucosa using buccal teeth (Ancylostoma) or cutting plates (Necator), invade submucosa, and ingest blood and villous tissue, producing iron-deficiency anemia; filariform larvae penetrate skin. S. stercoralis filariform larvae penetrate skin or mucous membranes, migrate via blood to the lungs and then the small intestine, where parthenogenetic adult females embed in the mucosa; rhabditiform larvae can transform directly into filariform larvae that re-penetrate the colonic wall or perianal skin to drive ongoing autoinfection - which can amplify into hyperinfection and dissemination under immunosuppression. Trichuris adults embed their thin anterior portions in colonic/cecal mucosa with no pulmonary larval passage. Enterobius adults dwell in the cecum; gravid females migrate nocturnally to the perianal skin to deposit eggs, which become infective within hours and spread by hand-to-mouth (autoinfection from scratching) and retroinfection. (p.1814-1818) Intestinal nematode infections are not usually fatal but contribute to malnutrition, impaired physical and cognitive development, and diminished work capacity, particularly in children with marginal nutritional status. Significant protective immunity does not appear to develop in humans. The major exception is strongyloidiasis: autoinfection allows decades-long persistence, and in immunocompromised hosts hyperinfection and dissemination can be fatal (high mortality, especially with unrecognized infection on glucocorticoids). (p.1814, p.1816-1817) Harrison does not provide a formal severity classification for intestinal nematode infections; severity correlates with infection intensity (worm burden) and host factors. Disease ranges from asymptomatic/subclinical light infection to clinical disease with heavy burden (e.g., Ascaris bowel/biliary obstruction; hookworm iron-deficiency anemia/hypoproteinemia; Trichuris dysentery and rectal prolapse). For Strongyloides, the spectrum is uncomplicated strongyloidiasis vs. hyperinfection (amplified autoinfection, larvae confined largely to the normal migration route) vs. disseminated strongyloidiasis (larvae in CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys). (p.1814-1817)

Intraabdominal Infections and Abscesses — Peritonitis, Primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis, SBP, Secondary peritonitis, Intraperitoneal abscess, Pyogenic liver abscess, Splenic abscess, Perinephric abscess, Renal abscess, Psoas abscess Primary versus secondary peritonitis (single organism without source versus mixed flora with an identifiable viscus source) Pancreatitis versus its infectious complications (infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic necrosis) - fever, leukocytosis, and abdominal pain alone do not distinguish them Diverticular abscess versus simple diverticulitis Tuboovarian abscess and other female genital tract infection extending into the pelvis Perinephric/renal abscess versus uncomplicated pyelonephritis when fever persists beyond 4-5 days of therapy Hemoperitoneum (especially in trauma) mimicking infective peritonitis Tuberculous peritonitis (cross-reference Chap. 183) Amebic liver abscess (cross-reference Chap. 230) - positive amebic serology in over 95% of cases Candidal liver or renal abscess following fungemia, often unmasked when PMNs recover after neutropenia Diagnostic paracentesis of any cirrhotic with ascites and fever, with PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic of PBP) and culture of fluid in blood-culture bottles plus simultaneous blood cultures Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to exclude or identify a primary intraabdominal source (highest yield for abscess localization) Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air signaling perforation (pneumoperitoneum) and to suggest liver abscess via raised right hemidiaphragm, basilar infiltrate, or pleural effusion Ultrasonography (particularly useful for right upper quadrant, kidneys, and pelvis) and MRI for abscess characterization Indium-labeled WBC scan or gallium scan to localize occult collections (indium preferred near bowel); PET scanning for resolution and availability Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated in about 70% of liver abscess - the single most reliable laboratory finding), bilirubin (elevated in ~50%), AST (~48%); leukocytosis, normochromic normocytic anemia (~50%), hypoalbuminemia (~33%) Amebic serology and PCR to exclude amebic liver abscess In CAPD-associated peritonitis, dialysate cell count with differential (cloudy fluid with >100 WBC/uL, >50% neutrophils, or >50% PMN with shortened dwell time) and concentrated dialysate culture in blood-culture bottles Needle aspiration under CT guidance for culture in suspected infected pancreatic necrosis Acute pancreatitis without infected necrosis (sterile inflammation producing fever and leukocytosis) Chemical peritonitis from a ruptured gastric ulcer in the absence of significant bacterial load Malignant ascites or metastatic intraabdominal malignancy Congestive heart failure, systemic lupus erythematosus, and lymphedema as noncirrhotic settings reported with PBP Intraperitoneal infection follows disruption of a normal anatomic barrier (ruptured appendix, diverticulum, or ulcer; ischemic, tumor-related, or inflammatory bowel wall weakening; or leakage from adjacent pancreatitis or pelvic inflammatory disease), and evolves in two sequential stages: peritonitis first, then abscess formation if the patient survives untreated. Primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis (PBP) in adults occurs chiefly with cirrhotic ascites, develops in up to about 10% of cirrhotic patients, and is thought to arise from hematogenous spread when impaired hepatic filtration and altered portal flow allow organisms to seed and multiply in ascitic fluid. A peritoneal-fluid count of more than 250 polymorphonuclear leukocytes/uL is diagnostic of PBP; this threshold does not apply to secondary peritonitis. Normal peritoneal fluid contains under 300 WBC/uL (mainly mononuclear) and protein under 30 g/L. PBP is typically caused by a single organism (often enteric gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, but increasingly gram-positive cocci and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae); recovery of multiple organisms including anaerobes should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and a search for a secondary source. Fever is the most common manifestation of PBP (up to 80%), but abdominal pain and peritoneal signs may be absent; nonlocalizing features such as malaise, encephalopathy, jaundice, or unexplained acute kidney injury in a cirrhotic with ascites should also trigger diagnostic paracentesis. Yield of peritoneal-fluid culture is improved by inoculating about 10 mL directly into a blood-culture bottle, and simultaneous blood cultures should be drawn because bacteremia frequently accompanies PBP; samples are best obtained before antibiotics. Secondary peritonitis results from spillage from an intraabdominal viscus and yields a mixed flora dominated by facultative gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, especially with a colonic source; early death is driven by gram-negative bacillary sepsis and circulating endotoxin. The bacterial burden of a perforation depends on site: a ruptured gastric ulcer (if not achlorhydric) causes mainly low-pH chemical irritation with a low bacterial load, whereas leaked colonic contents (pH 7-8, ~10^11 anaerobes/g feces) cause intense infection from heavy bacterial load. Bacteroides fragilis, though only about 0.5% of normal colonic flora, is the anaerobe most frequently isolated from intraabdominal infections and abscesses and the most common anaerobic bloodstream isolate; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide (polysaccharide A) drives abscess localization via a CD4+ T-cell-dependent host response. Of all intraabdominal abscesses, about 74% are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal (non-visceral); most intraperitoneal abscesses arise from fecal spillage (e.g., an inflamed appendix), and diverticular abscesses are the least likely to rupture. The liver is the organ most subject to abscess; biliary tract disease is now the most common source (formerly ruptured appendicitis), and pylephlebitis (suppurative portal vein thrombosis) is another route of seeding. Half of liver-abscess patients lack hepatomegaly, right-upper-quadrant tenderness, or jaundice, so liver abscess can present as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly. Hypermucoviscous (hypervirulent) Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a distinctive community-acquired syndrome of liver abscess with bacteremia and metastatic infection of the eye(s) and lung(s), originally described in Southeast Asia and now emerging in North America and elsewhere. Splenic abscess is rare but frequently fatal if untreated and often diagnosed late (at autopsy in about 37% of one series); hematogenous spread predominates, with bacterial endocarditis the most common associated infection and streptococci then S. aureus the usual isolates. More than 75% of perinephric and renal abscesses now arise from ascending urinary tract infection rather than hematogenous seeding; concomitant obstructing nephrolithiasis is the most important risk factor (renal stones in 20-60% of perinephric abscess cases). Free air under the diaphragm on upright chest film indicating bowel perforation with peritonitis requiring urgent intervention Hemodynamic instability in suspected secondary peritonitis warranting surgery without delay for imaging Persistent fever after 4-5 days of treatment for pyelonephritis suggesting perinephric or renal abscess Polymicrobial growth in PBP-suspected peritoneal fluid signaling missed secondary peritonitis source Liver abscess presenting only as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae liver abscess with metastatic eye and lung involvement Splenic abscess with underlying endocarditis or hemoglobinopathy given high untreated fatality Failing to perform diagnostic paracentesis in a febrile cirrhotic with ascites, as PBP is often subtle and abdominal pain/peritoneal signs may be absent Misclassifying secondary peritonitis as PBP - the >250 PMN/uL threshold and single-organism rule apply only to PBP; mixed flora or anaerobes indicate a secondary source Relying on cultures from chronic drain sites, which are not reliable for defining infection etiology Attributing fever, leukocytosis, and pain in pancreatitis to the inflammation itself and overlooking an infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, or infected necrosis Most clinical treatment failures in abscesses result from failure to achieve source control (drainage), not antibiotic selection Injecting barium when perforation is suspected (contraindicated), even though barium enema may occasionally reveal a diverticular abscess Missing splenic or perinephric abscess because of nonspecific presentation and frequently delayed diagnosis Overlooking polymicrobial urine culture, known renal stones, or sterile pyuria as clues to perinephric/renal abscess Intraperitoneal infection begins when a normal anatomic barrier is breached and organisms normally contained within the bowel or another organ enter the sterile peritoneal cavity. Inflammation triggers an early influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes followed by a prolonged phase of mononuclear cell migration, with the leukocyte phenotype shaped by resident-cell chemokine synthesis. In primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis, a diseased liver with altered portal circulation impairs the normal filtration function, allowing hematogenous organisms to seed ascites; cirrhosis-related defects (low peritoneal complement, diminished PMN opsonic and phagocytic capacity, gut dysbiosis with overgrowth of Enterobacteriaceae, reduced Paneth cell defensins, decreased motility, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy) promote bacterial translocation. Secondary peritonitis follows direct viscus spillage; an early containment phase produces a fibrin- and PMN-rich exudate, and severity reflects whether spillage is chemically irritant (acidic gastric contents) or heavily bacterial (colonic contents). If overt gram-negative sepsis does not prove fatal, the host walls off persisting organisms and PMNs in a fibrous capsule to form an abscess; B. fragilis is uniquely able to induce abscesses, with its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A stimulating peritoneal macrophages (TNF-alpha, ICAM-1) and CD4+ T lymphocytes that secrete leukoattractant cytokines, while the alternative complement pathway and fibrinogen also participate. PBP carries substantial morbidity and mortality, reflecting its concentration among patients with advanced liver disease; reported in-hospital mortality was about 17.6% in a 2018 US cohort, and another series found 23% mortality at 30 days and 37% at 90 days. PBP recurs frequently, with up to 70% of patients experiencing recurrence within 1 year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within 72 h, and delayed therapy increases mortality. In secondary peritonitis, early death is attributable to gram-negative bacillary sepsis and endotoxemia, and the urgency and success of source control - rather than the choice of empiric antibiotics - drive survival odds. Pyogenic liver abscess mortality averaged about 15% despite treatment. Splenic and perinephric abscesses are frequently fatal when diagnosis is delayed, so early diagnosis is the most important determinant of outcome. No single formal severity score is given; the text frames disease along the peritonitis-to-abscess continuum and stratifies risk by setting. PBP is graded operationally by ascitic-fluid PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic) and by markers of advanced liver disease (serum creatinine, BUN, total bilirubin, Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) that identify highest-risk and worst-prognosis patients. Secondary and abscess-related infection severity is stratified clinically as community-acquired mild-to-moderate disease versus critically ill or health care-associated infection, which guides anticipated flora and management intensity.

potential, and it should be distinguished from constitutionally small but healthy fetuses It is broadly divided into placental (uteroplacental insufficiency), maternal, and fetal causes, with restriction cannot be assessed reliably without a correct gestational age Surveillance combines serial ultrasound biometry, amniotic fluid assessment, and umbilical artery Doppler to detect deterioration A progression of Doppler abnormalities, from raised umbilical artery resistance to absent or reversed end-diastolic flow and abnormal ductus venosus, reflects worsening fetal compromise Management balances the risks of prematurity against those of continued exposure to a hostile intrauterine environment, and antenatal corticosteroids are given when early delivery is anticipated end-diastolic flow indicating severe placental compromise Abnormal ductus venosus flow or a non-reassuring cardiotocograph signalling impending fetal decompensation Reduced or absent fetal movements Static or falling growth on serial scans with oligohydramnios Coexisting severe pre-eclampsia threatening both mother and fetus Confusing a constitutionally small healthy fetus with pathological growth restriction, or vice versa Relying on a single scan rather than serial measurements to judge growth Neglecting accurate early dating, which undermines all subsequent assessment Delivering too early for prematurity risk or too late with ongoing fetal hypoxia Overlooking congenital infection or aneuploidy in early symmetrical restriction The commonest pathway is uteroplacental insufficiency, in which inadequate trophoblastic remodelling of the spiral arteries produces a poorly perfused placenta with reduced capacity to deliver oxygen and nutrients. The fetus adapts by redistributing cardiac output to preserve the brain, heart, and adrenals at the expense of the abdominal viscera and peripheral tissues, producing asymmetrical growth and oligohydramnios from reduced renal perfusion. Progressive hypoxaemia and acidaemia manifest as deteriorating Doppler indices and, ultimately, cardiovascular decompensation. Other cases stem from fetal chromosomal or structural abnormalities, congenital infection, or maternal disease reducing substrate supply. Outcome depends on the underlying cause, the severity and gestation at onset, and the timeliness of surveillance and delivery. Early-onset severe placental disease carries the greatest risk of stillbirth and neonatal morbidity, whereas late-onset restriction is often milder but still increases perinatal risk. Survivors have higher rates of neurodevelopmental impairment and of adult cardiovascular and metabolic disease, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring and appropriately timed birth.

Intussusception — intestinal invagination, bowel telescoping, ileocolic intussusception Gastroenteritis Incarcerated hernia Malrotation with volvulus Appendicitis Henoch-Schonlein purpura with bowel involvement Constipation or other causes of colicky pain Abdominal ultrasound (target/doughnut sign) as first-line imaging Abdominal radiograph to look for obstruction or free air Air or contrast enema (diagnostic and therapeutic in stable children) Full blood count and electrolytes to assess dehydration Assessment for an underlying lead point in older or atypical cases The most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants and toddlers, typically between 6 months and 3 years, in which one segment of bowel telescopes into the adjacent distal segment. The classic triad is intermittent colicky abdominal pain (with drawing up of the legs), vomiting, and red currant jelly stool, but all three are present in only a minority. Between painful episodes the infant may appear well or lethargic; lethargy can be a prominent and misleading feature. A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable, often in the right upper quadrant, with an empty right lower quadrant. Most cases are ileocolic and idiopathic, sometimes following a viral illness with hypertrophied Peyer patches acting as a lead point. Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, showing a target or doughnut sign on cross-section. In a stable child without peritonitis or perforation, non-operative reduction with an air or contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Surgery is required when enema reduction fails, or when there is perforation, peritonitis, shock, or a pathological lead point. Signs of peritonitis or a rigid, tender abdomen Free air on radiograph indicating perforation Shock, marked lethargy, or haemodynamic instability Bilious vomiting and abdominal distension indicating established obstruction Fever with toxic appearance suggesting bowel ischaemia or sepsis Waiting for the full classic triad, which is often incomplete, and delaying diagnosis Attributing marked lethargy to another cause and missing intussusception Attempting enema reduction in a child with peritonitis, perforation, or shock Failing to consider a pathological lead point in older children or recurrent cases A proximal segment of bowel (the intussusceptum) invaginates into the lumen of the adjacent distal segment (the intussuscipiens), dragging its mesentery with it. This compromises venous and lymphatic drainage, producing bowel wall oedema and engorgement; the mixture of sloughed mucosa, blood, and mucus produces the characteristic red currant jelly stool. Progressive swelling obstructs the lumen and, if unrelieved, arterial compromise leads to ischaemia, necrosis, and perforation. In infants a lead point is usually hypertrophied lymphoid tissue, whereas older children more often have a pathological lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum or polyp. With early diagnosis and reduction the outlook is excellent; delay increases the risk of ischaemia, resection, and complications, and a proportion recur after non-operative reduction.

Iodine deficiency — iodine deficiency disorders, endemic goitre, endemic cretinism Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto or Graves) Sporadic non-toxic goitre and thyroid nodules Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis Goitre from goitrogen exposure Other causes of developmental delay Thyroid function tests including TSH and free thyroid hormones Urinary iodine concentration for assessing population and individual status Thyroid ultrasound to characterise goitre or nodules Neonatal thyroid screening where available Developmental and neurological assessment in affected children Iodine deficiency is the leading preventable cause of goitre and of acquired intellectual disability worldwide It occurs in regions with iodine-poor soil and water, historically including large parts of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan belt of India, and salt iodisation is the mainstay of control Deficiency in pregnancy is the most serious consequence, causing impaired fetal brain development and, in severe cases, endemic cretinism The clinical spectrum ranges from diffuse or nodular goitre to hypothyroidism, growth and developmental delay, and neurological deficits The population iodine status is assessed by median urinary iodine concentration rather than by individual blood tests Rapid correction of longstanding deficiency, or excess iodine, can occasionally provoke thyroid dysfunction, so replacement is at physiological population levels Neurological damage sustained in fetal life and infancy is largely irreversible, making prevention through adequate maternal intake essential Deficiency in pregnancy threatening fetal neurodevelopment Large goitre causing airway or oesophageal compression Overt hypothyroidism, especially in infants where it threatens development Signs of endemic cretinism requiring urgent public health and clinical action Relying on individual blood iodine levels rather than urinary iodine for status assessment Overlooking maternal iodine adequacy in pregnancy Assuming a goitre is always autoimmune and missing endemic iodine deficiency Causing iodine-induced thyroid dysfunction through excessive supplementation Iodine is an essential substrate for the synthesis of the thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodothyronine. When dietary intake is inadequate, reduced hormone production lowers feedback inhibition and raises thyroid-stimulating hormone, driving thyroid hyperplasia and goitre as a compensatory response; over time nodularity and, if compensation fails, hypothyroidism develop. Thyroid hormone is critical for normal neuronal migration and myelination in the developing brain, so maternal and early-life deficiency impairs neurodevelopment irreversibly, producing the cognitive and neurological features of iodine deficiency disorders, including cretinism in severe endemic areas. Goitre and hypothyroidism from deficiency can improve with adequate iodine intake, but neurodevelopmental damage from fetal and early-life deficiency is largely permanent, underscoring prevention.

count and haemolysis screen for autoimmune cytopenias IPEX syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by mutations in FOXP3, the master transcription factor for regulatory T cells Loss of functional regulatory T cells leads to severe, early-onset systemic autoimmunity affecting multiple organs The classic triad is severe enteropathy with intractable watery diarrhoea, early-onset endocrinopathy (especially neonatal type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis), and eczematous dermatitis It typically presents in male infants and can be rapidly life-threatening from malabsorption, failure to thrive, and metabolic derangement Additional autoimmune features include haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, nephropathy, and hepatitis Infections may occur, partly reflecting the underlying immune the only definitive cure Intractable diarrhoea with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and failure to thrive as a neonatal emergency Neonatal or early-onset diabetes with metabolic decompensation Severe autoimmune cytopenias or nephropathy Live vaccines should be avoided given the immune dysregulation and immunosuppressive therapy Overwhelming infection during intensive immunosuppression Attributing intractable infantile diarrhoea to food allergy and missing autoimmune enteropathy Overlooking a monogenic cause of neonatal diabetes in a boy with multi-organ autoimmunity Delaying genetic testing and transplant referral in a critically ill infant Giving live vaccines during immunosuppression Confusing IPEX with APECED, which is autosomal recessive, AIRE-related, and presents later IPEX syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in FOXP3 on the X chromosome, the transcription factor essential for the development and function of CD4-positive CD25-positive regulatory T cells. Without functional regulatory T cells, peripheral tolerance collapses and autoreactive effector T cells drive widespread tissue-specific autoimmunity. The resulting immune attack on the gut epithelium, endocrine organs (pancreatic islets, thyroid), skin, blood cells, and kidneys produces the characteristic multi-organ autoimmune phenotype. Because the defect is one of immune regulation rather than a simple failure of host defence, the dominant problem is aggressive autoimmunity from early infancy, though secondary infection is common. Untreated IPEX is frequently fatal in infancy or early childhood from enteropathy, metabolic complications, and infection; immunosuppression can achieve temporary control, but haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally undertaken early, provides the best prospect of long-term survival.

Iron Deficiency Anemia — IDA Anemia of inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) - the second most common anemia worldwide, due to functional iron deficiency; a diagnosis of exclusion usually occurring with an inflammatory disorder such as cancer or infection (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Thalassemia trait - microcytosis with normal-to-high ferritin and serum iron; red cells are more homogeneous in volume with a low/normal RDW (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767). Mixed forms (combined absolute and functional iron deficiency) (Harrison 22e p.767). Other nutritional anemias - vitamin B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic, macrocytic); may coexist with and mask iron deficiency in malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.765). Sideroblastic anemia (rare) as a cause of microcytic hypochromic red cells (Harrison 22e p.~). Serum ferritin (mainstay; <30 µg/L diagnostic, sensitivity 92% / specificity 98%); note ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may rise severalfold in inflammation (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC); iron-restricted erythropoiesis at <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765). Serum iron (reduced, but diurnal fluctuation prevents use as a single test) (Harrison 22e p.765). MCV and RDW from the CBC (MCV <80 fL when established; RDW often elevated reflecting anisocytosis) (Harrison 22e p.765). Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) - increased in iron deficiency; sTfR/log ferritin ratio >2 favors iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767). Reticulocyte hemoglobin content (CHr, reduced) and percentage of hypochromic red cells (%HYPO, increased >6%), reflecting iron availability days to months before testing (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767). Serum hepcidin (low/undetectable in absolute deficiency; not routinely measured, reference values not standardized) (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767). Absence of stainable iron in bone marrow remains the gold standard, although it is rarely needed and unacceptably invasive (Harrison 22e p.765). Endoscopy and/or radiographic imaging to identify the cause - essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe bleeding sources (Harrison 22e p.765, p.~). Anemia of inflammation / chronic disease (functional iron deficiency from high hepcidin: low serum iron and transferrin saturation with NORMAL-to-HIGH ferritin) (Harrison 22e p.764, p.767). Thalassemia trait (microcytic but with normal-to-high ferritin and iron, and a low/normal RDW) (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767). Classic blood picture is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia (MCV <80 fL in established disease), but microcytosis can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency or masked by liver disease or concomitant folate/B12 deficiency (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Low serum ferritin is the mainstay of absolute iron deficiency, reflecting depleted stores; ferritin <30 µg/L has high sensitivity and specificity (92% and 98%) and can be used as a single diagnostic test (Harrison 22e p.765). Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC) measures iron available for erythropoiesis; erythropoiesis becomes iron-restricted at values <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765). Anemia develops only in the LATE stage because the erythron is relatively spared compared with heart and skeletal muscle, which become iron-depleted earlier; slow progression plus compensation means anemia is often undetected, especially in the young, until hemoglobin falls below ~8 g/dL (Harrison 22e p.765). Clinical clues include pica (compulsive ingestion of nonnutritive substances such as ice, soil, or clay), nail fragility and koilonychia, hair loss, cheilosis, atrophic glossitis, and dysphagia from esophageal webs (Plummer-Vinson syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.765; Koilonychia association noted p.~). Even symptomatic isolated iron deficiency WITHOUT anemia matters: suboptimal myocyte, cardiomyocyte, and neuron function can cause fatigue, irritability, poor concentration, restless legs syndrome, and reduced exercise capacity (Harrison 22e p.765). Severe iron-deficiency anemia may be accompanied by thrombocytosis, due to prevalent megakaryocyte commitment of the common erythroid-platelet progenitor when iron is insufficient (Harrison 22e p.766). Serum hepcidin is low/undetectable in absolute iron deficiency (maximizing dietary iron absorption) but elevated in inflammation and in IRIDA (TMPRSS6 mutations) (Harrison 22e p.766). Inadequate therapeutic response (no reticulocytosis after 1 week, or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise after 2 weeks of iron therapy) should prompt a search for the cause: noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.766). Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in any adult (with the possible exception of a premenopausal, multiparous woman) MANDATES thorough endoscopic and/or radiographic visualization of the entire large bowel - right (ascending) colon cancer causes insidious blood loss and often presents as IDA (Harrison 22e p.~, colorectal cancer chapter). Imaging and endoscopy to trace the cause are essential in males and postmenopausal females to rule out malignancy or other severe causes of bleeding (Harrison 22e p.765). Hemoglobin falling below ~8 g/dL or otherwise severe anemia (Harrison 22e p.765). Myelophthisic blood smear (nucleated red cells, teardrop cells, immature white cells) suggesting marrow infiltration mandates marrow examination - a competing cause of anemia to recognize (Harrison 22e p.450). Classic microcytosis/hypochromia can be ABSENT in early iron deficiency, in elderly patients, or when masked by concomitant folate/B12 deficiency or liver disease - do not exclude IDA on a normal MCV alone (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; normal or high ferritin during inflammation can mask coexisting iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.450). Serum iron alone is unreliable as a single test due to diurnal variation (Harrison 22e p.765). Treating IDA without investigating the cause can miss occult GI malignancy; isolated symptomatic iron deficiency without anemia should not be underestimated (Harrison 22e p.764, p.765). Biomarkers other than ferritin and transferrin saturation are limited by poor standardization and accessibility (Harrison 22e p.766). Iron supply becomes inadequate for needs through excessive demand, insufficient intake, defective absorption, or blood loss; multiple causes frequently co-occur, especially in the elderly and in multimorbidity (Harrison 22e p.764). In ISOLATED iron deficiency, stores are depleted while hemoglobin is still normal; when iron remains sufficient for erythropoiesis, red cells are normochromic/normocytic with decreased ferritin (<15-30 µg/L). As transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, iron supply to erythropoiesis is insufficient and cells become hypochromic and microcytic, the classic feature of iron-deficiency anemia (Harrison 22e p.764). Iron deficiency is ABSOLUTE when stores are exhausted and FUNCTIONAL when erythropoiesis is iron-restricted but stores are adequate or even increased. Low hepcidin in iron deficiency maximizes dietary absorption; TMPRSS6 mutations cause hereditary iron-refractory IDA (IRIDA) with reduced absorption and oral-iron refractoriness. In inflammation, high hepcidin sequesters iron into stores, producing functional iron deficiency with low serum iron and transferrin saturation despite elevated ferritin; absolute and functional deficiency often coexist (IBD, CKD, aging). Beyond anemia, heart, muscle, and brain are affected; immune response may be blunted as lymphocytes require iron during the metabolic burst (Harrison 22e p.764). Iron deficiency and IDA are highly treatable with iron replacement. Oral iron usually requires at least ~3 months of therapy to restore hemoglobin and replenish stores and prevent early recurrence; inadequate response (no reticulocytosis at 1 week or <1 g/dL hemoglobin rise at 2 weeks) should prompt a search for noncompliance, ongoing blood loss, or malabsorption. Prognosis ultimately depends on the underlying cause (e.g., occult GI malignancy) rather than the anemia itself (Harrison 22e p.766). Harrison describes a continuum rather than a formal grading scale: (1) isolated/absolute iron deficiency with depleted stores (ferritin <15-30 µg/L) but NORMAL hemoglobin and normochromic-normocytic cells; (2) iron-restricted erythropoiesis once transferrin saturation falls <15-20%, with hypochromic microcytic cells; (3) overt iron-deficiency anemia. Severe anemia is generally taken as hemoglobin <=8 g/dL (the threshold at which anemia commonly becomes detectable and at which rapid IV correction is considered) (Harrison 22e p.764-766).

Iron poisoning — iron overdose, iron toxicity, ferrous sulfate poisoning Other corrosive or caustic ingestions Acute gastroenteritis of infective cause Other causes of high anion-gap metabolic acidosis Paracetamol or other hepatotoxic ingestion Sepsis with shock Serum iron level, ideally timed to peak absorption Abdominal radiograph for radiopaque tablets Arterial blood gas with anion gap and lactate Liver function tests and coagulation profile to track hepatic injury Full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, and glucose Toxicity relates to the amount of elemental iron ingested, not the total salt weight, so the specific preparation must be identified The classic course has recognised stages: early GI toxicity, a deceptive latent phase of apparent improvement, then shock and metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure, and finally late gastric scarring and outlet obstruction Early severe vomiting, diarrhoea, and haematemesis reflect direct corrosive injury to the gut mucosa Do not be misled by the quiescent second phase; serious systemic toxicity can still evolve after the patient seems to settle Radiopaque tablets may be visible on an abdominal radiograph and can confirm ingestion and guide decontamination Whole-bowel irrigation is the preferred decontamination method for significant ingestions, as activated charcoal does not bind iron Deferoxamine is the specific chelating antidote, indicated for systemic toxicity, shock, significant acidosis, or high serum iron levels A high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and progressive hepatic injury mark severe poisoning requiring urgent chelation and intensive support Haematemesis or melaena indicating corrosive GI injury Hypotension, shock, or lethargy signalling systemic toxicity High anion-gap metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate Evidence of hepatic injury or coagulopathy Persistent or worsening symptoms after the apparent latent phase Calculating dose from tablet weight rather than elemental iron content Discharging a patient during the deceptive latent phase before systemic toxicity manifests Giving activated charcoal, which does not adsorb iron Delaying deferoxamine in a patient with shock, acidosis, or high iron levels In overdose, free iron overwhelms the body's binding capacity (transferrin) and circulates unbound. It is directly corrosive to the gastrointestinal mucosa, causing haemorrhagic gastroenteritis and fluid loss. Absorbed free iron is a potent catalyst of free-radical formation and disrupts mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, causing cellular injury most prominently in the liver, along with a high anion-gap metabolic (lactic) acidosis. Iron-induced vasodilatation, increased capillary permeability, and myocardial depression produce shock. Healing of the corrosive gastric injury can later cause strictures and gastric outlet obstruction. Small ingestions causing only GI upset usually resolve, but severe poisoning with shock, acidosis, and hepatic failure carries significant mortality; early recognition, decontamination, and deferoxamine chelation greatly improve survival, though late gastric strictures may still occur.

Ischaemic colitis — ischemic colitis, colonic ischaemia, colonic ischemia Acute mesenteric ischaemia (small bowel) Infective (bacterial) colitis Inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn colitis Diverticular haemorrhage or diverticulitis Colorectal malignancy Pseudomembranous (Clostridioides difficile) colitis CT of the abdomen and pelvis to assess segmental wall thickening and exclude perforation Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy showing segmental mucosal injury with an abrupt transition zone Serum lactate and inflammatory markers to gauge severity and detect possible gangrene Stool studies to exclude infective causes when the picture is atypical Cardiac and vascular assessment to identify a precipitating low-flow state The commonest form of intestinal ischaemia, usually affecting older adults and typically arising from a transient, non-occlusive fall in colonic perfusion rather than a fixed arterial blockage Classic presentation is sudden mild crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed within a day by the passage of bloody or maroon stool, with only modest blood loss The watershed zones (splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction) are most vulnerable, while the rectum is usually spared because of its dual blood supply CT often shows segmental bowel-wall thickening, and colonoscopy is the key diagnostic test showing segmental oedema, haemorrhage, and mucosal ulceration with an abrupt transition to normal mucosa Most cases are non-gangrenous and settle with supportive care: bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and correction of any precipitating hypoperfusion Right-sided (isolated right colon) involvement carries a worse prognosis and should raise concern for coexisting acute mesenteric ischaemia Distinguish from infective colitis and inflammatory bowel disease; the segmental distribution and rapid resolution favour an ischaemic cause Recognised triggers include hypotension, cardiac or vascular surgery, dehydration, hypercoagulable states, and certain drugs such as vasoconstrictors Peritonism, fever, marked leucocytosis, or rising lactate suggesting gangrenous colitis and impending perforation Isolated right-sided colonic involvement, which may signal concurrent acute mesenteric ischaemia Persistent bleeding, haemodynamic instability, or failure to improve on supportive care Development of a colonic stricture with obstruction during recovery Assuming rectal sparing excludes colonic ischaemia, or mistaking segmental ischaemic changes for inflammatory bowel disease Delaying surgical review when signs of transmural necrosis are present Overlooking a precipitating hypoperfusion event that will otherwise recur Failing to recognise that isolated right colon disease may reflect small-bowel mesenteric ischaemia needing urgent vascular evaluation Ischaemic colitis results from a temporary reduction in blood flow to a colonic segment, most often a low-flow (non-occlusive) event superimposed on the marginal circulation of watershed areas. Reduced perfusion injures the mucosa first, producing oedema, submucosal haemorrhage, and superficial ulceration. In most patients reperfusion allows healing, but persistent or severe ischaemia can progress to transmural (gangrenous) necrosis with perforation or, later, to fibrotic stricture. It is usually a disease of small vessels and systemic hypoperfusion rather than a large-artery occlusion, which distinguishes it from acute mesenteric ischaemia. Non-gangrenous ischaemic colitis usually resolves within a few days with conservative management and has a good outcome. Gangrenous disease requiring surgery carries substantial mortality, and right-sided involvement predicts a worse course. A minority develop chronic segmental colitis or a stricture.

the dominant cause is atherosclerotic narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries reducing regional myocardial perfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090). Anginal discomfort is classically described as heaviness, pressure, squeezing, smothering or choking rather than frank pain, is crescendo-decrescendo, typically lasts 2-5 minutes, and may be signaled by a clenched fist over the sternum (Levine's sign) (Harrison 22e p.2092). Anginal pain may radiate to either shoulder, both arms (especially the ulnar forearm/hand), back, interscapular region, neck, jaw, teeth, or epigastrium; it is rarely localized below the umbilicus or above the mandible (Harrison 22e p.2092). Radiation to the trapezius muscles is NOT typical of myocardial ischemia and points more toward pericarditis; this is a useful discriminating feature (Harrison 22e p.2092). Anginal equivalents (dyspnea, nausea, fatigue, faintness) and atypical presentations are more common in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes mellitus, in whom angina may not relate strictly to provoking factors (Harrison 22e p.2093). A resting 12-lead ECG may be entirely normal in typical angina; ST-T and LVH changes are suggestive but nonspecific, whereas dynamic ST-T changes appearing with an anginal episode and resolving afterward are more specific (Harrison 22e p.2094). A stenosis must reduce epicardial luminal diameter by about 50% to limit flow augmentation on demand, and by roughly 80% before resting flow falls; beyond that, small further reductions cut flow dramatically (Harrison 22e p.2091). Reversible ischemic injury occurs within roughly 20 minutes of total occlusion (without collaterals); occlusion beyond 20 minutes leads to myocardial necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2091). The Canadian Cardiovascular Society class grades angina severity and the New York Heart Association class grades functional limitation (Harrison 22e p.2093). An ischemic stress-ECG response is flat or downsloping ST depression >0.1 mV lasting >0.08 s; upsloping or junctional ST changes are not diagnostic, and a test failing to reach 85% of age/sex-predicted maximal heart rate is nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2094-2095). Chest wall tenderness, pain reproduced by palpation, or pain localizable with a single fingertip makes a myocardial ischemic origin unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094). Most patients who die suddenly from IHD do so from ischemia-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.2092). Angina occurring with less exertion than before, at rest, or awakening the patient from sleep (features of an unstable syndrome) (Harrison 22e p.2093) Angina accompanied by symptoms or signs of heart failure, pulmonary edema, transient third heart sound, or mitral regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2092, 2097) Inability to exercise beyond 6 minutes / stage II of the Bruce protocol (Harrison 22e p.2097) Ischemia at low workload, >=0.2 mV ST depression, or ST depression persisting >5 minutes after exercise (Harrison 22e p.2097) A fall in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg during exercise or exercise-induced ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Harrison 22e p.2096-2097) Large or multiple perfusion defects, increased lung tracer uptake, or a fall in LV ejection fraction during stress imaging (Harrison 22e p.2097) Reduced resting LV ejection fraction (<0.40) (Harrison 22e p.2097) Sudden cardiac death may be the unheralded presenting manifestation of IHD (Harrison 22e p.2092) Relying on coronary artery calcium as the primary screening test or sole basis for therapeutic decisions; it is adjunctive only (Harrison 22e p.2092). Interpreting a stress ECG without accounting for pretest probability; false positives rise in low-probability patients (e.g., asymptomatic men <40, premenopausal women without risk factors) and in those on digitalis/antiarrhythmics, with conduction disturbances, LVH, resting ST-T abnormalities, or abnormal potassium (Harrison 22e p.2095). Assuming a negative stress ECG excludes CAD; sensitivity is only about 75%, though it makes three-vessel or left main disease unlikely (Harrison 22e p.2095). Circumflex-territory disease may yield a false-negative stress test because the posterolateral wall is poorly represented on the surface 12-lead ECG (Harrison 22e p.2095). Coronary arteriography images only the lumen and can miss severe non-luminal (remodeled, outwardly bulging) atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2097). Missing atypical/anginal-equivalent presentations in women, the elderly, and patients with diabetes (Harrison 22e p.2093). Overlooking that about 25% of acute MI survivors never come to medical attention yet share the same adverse prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2092-2093). Myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2) is governed by heart rate, contractility, and wall tension, while supply depends on oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and coronary blood flow (predominantly diastolic). Coronary resistance resides mainly in prearteriolar (R2) and arteriolar/capillary (R3) microvascular beds, which normally dilate to match demand (metabolic regulation and autoregulation). Atherosclerosis of epicardial arteries, driven by endothelial dysfunction from high LDL, smoking, hypertension, and diabetes, produces subintimal plaques; plaque rupture or erosion exposes contents to blood, triggering platelet activation/aggregation and the coagulation cascade with fibrin deposition and thrombus formation. As proximal stenoses worsen, distal resistance vessels dilate maximally and flow becomes pressure-dependent, so increased demand (exertion, emotion, tachycardia) precipitates ischemia. Ischemia causes regional contractile dysfunction (hypokinesis to dyskinesis), impaired relaxation, a metabolic shift to anaerobic lactate production with falling intracellular pH and high-energy phosphate depletion, membrane dysfunction with potassium leak and cytosolic calcium rise, characteristic ECG repolarization changes, and electrical instability. The subendocardium is most vulnerable to underperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2090-2092). Principal prognostic determinants are age, left ventricular function, the location and severity of coronary stenoses, and the severity/activity of ischemia. Recent-onset or unstable angina, early post-MI angina, angina poorly responsive to therapy, and angina with heart failure all carry increased risk. Elevated LV end-diastolic pressure/volume and reduced ejection fraction signal poor prognosis. Left main (>50% diameter) or proximal LAD obstruction carries greater risk than right or circumflex lesions because more myocardium is jeopardized. With any obstructive disease, mortality rises sharply when LV function is impaired; the larger the established necrosis, the poorer the prognosis. Conversely, patients with chest discomfort but normal LV function and normal coronary arteries have an excellent prognosis, as do those completing stage III of the Bruce protocol with a normal perfusion scan or negative stress echo. Greater number/severity of risk factors (advanced age >75, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, morbid obesity, peripheral/cerebrovascular disease, prior MI), elevated CRP, extensive coronary calcification, and increased carotid intimal thickening all worsen prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2097). Angina severity is graded by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) functional classification (Class I: angina only with strenuous/rapid/prolonged exertion; Class II: slight limitation of ordinary activity; Class III: marked limitation with ordinary activity such as walking 1-2 blocks; Class IV: inability to perform any physical activity without discomfort, angina may be present at rest). Functional impact is described by the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification (Classes I-IV) (Harrison 22e p.2093).

sensory/motor deficits migrate slowly over minutes and may cross vascular territories Metabolic encephalopathy (fluctuating mental status, typically without focal signs) Hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia (check finger-stick glucose before thrombolysis) Intracranial tumour Stroke is a clinical diagnosis: abrupt-onset focal neurologic deficit from a vascular cause; imaging is used to support it and to separate ischemia from hemorrhage (p.3427). Time-is-brain: with complete arterial occlusion, neurons die within roughly 4-10 minutes; flow <16-18 mL/100 g/min infarcts within an hour, while 18-20 mL/100 g/min causes reversible ischemia unless prolonged (p.3439). The ischemic penumbra is reversibly dysfunctional tissue around the infarct core; it is the target of reperfusion and can be visualized as a perfusion-diffusion (or CT-perfusion) mismatch (p.3439). A useful triage rule of thumb is that a deficit maximal at onset (or one that remits) favors ischemia, whereas a depressed conscious level, very high initial blood pressure, or progressive worsening favors hemorrhage - though no clinical feature reliably separates them, so CT is required (p.3440). The public FAST acronym (Facial weakness, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time) captures common stroke features and emphasizes time-sensitivity; about 85% of ischemic stroke patients have hemiparesis (p.3428). Stroke onset is timed from when the patient was last seen well, not when found; wake-up strokes default to bedtime, though advanced imaging may still allow treatment selection (p.3441). Cerebellar infarction can masquerade as labyrinthitis with vertigo and vomiting; accompanying head/neck pain should prompt suspicion of vertebral dissection, and even small cerebellar edema can obstruct CSF and compress the brainstem (p.3440). Roughly 30% of ischemic strokes remain cryptogenic despite thorough evaluation (p.3443). Painful neck or head pain preceding stroke in a young patient (under ~60) suggests arterial dissection (p.3445). Disabling deficit (NIHSS >5) - candidate for thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy; act fast Suspected large-vessel occlusion (ICA terminus, M1/M2, basilar) - candidate for mechanical thrombectomy Cerebellar infarct with declining consciousness or new brainstem signs - impending herniation/hydrocephalus needing emergency decompression Large hemispheric (malignant MCA) infarct - 5-10% develop space-occupying edema peaking on day 2-3, may need hemicraniectomy Painful neck/Horner's or recent neck trauma/manipulation - suspect arterial dissection Multifocal deficits with fever - suspect septic emboli from endocarditis Treating a stroke mimic as stroke: a postictal (Todd's) paralysis, acephalgic migraine, or hypoglycaemia can convincingly imitate acute stroke - always confirm glucose and seek an observer history of convulsive onset. Mislabelling cerebellar stroke as benign labyrinthitis and missing life-threatening brainstem compression / hydrocephalus. Omitting the embolic-source workup (carotid, heart) after a lacunar-appearing infarct, since a large-vessel source can present as a small-vessel syndrome. A normal early CT does not exclude infarction; CT may be only subtly abnormal acutely and the hyperdense MCA sign is specific but seen in only ~20% of MCA occlusions (DWI-MRI is far more sensitive). Over-attributing stroke to a patent foramen ovale, which is present in ~15% of the general population and is often incidental. Aggressively lowering blood pressure acutely can reduce pressure-dependent collateral flow and worsen the penumbra; permissive hypertension is generally allowed early. Distinguish benign reperfusion petechial haemorrhage within an infarct from frank haemorrhagic transformation with mass effect. Acute occlusion of an intracranial artery reduces regional cerebral blood flow; the resulting deficit depends on collateral supply, occlusion site, and systemic pressure. Energy failure from loss of glucose and oxygen halts ATP-dependent ion pumps, causing depolarization, sodium and calcium influx, excess synaptic glutamate, and excitotoxicity with reactive oxygen species that damage membranes and DNA, followed by an innate inflammatory response. Fever and hyperglycaemia (glucose >200 mg/dL) worsen the injury. Mechanistically, ischemic stroke arises by three routes (the basis of TOAST-style classification): (1) embolic occlusion of a large intracranial vessel - either cardioembolic (e.g., atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, valvular disease) or artery-to-artery from carotid/aortic-arch plaque; (2) in-situ thrombosis of small penetrating arteries from lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, producing lacunar (small-vessel) infarcts; and (3) hypoperfusion from flow-limiting stenosis of a major extracranial or intracranial vessel, producing watershed/border-zone ischemia. Cardioembolism causes ~20%, large-artery/carotid atherosclerosis ~10%, and small-vessel disease ~20% of ischemic strokes (p.3439, p.3443-3446). Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide; outcome hinges on time to reperfusion ('time-is-brain'). For large-vessel occlusion, the chance of a good outcome falls steeply with delay - the odds of a good result exceed 3 if groin puncture for thrombectomy is within 2 h but fall to about 2 by 8 h, and over 80% do well if the vessel opens within 1 h of arrival versus about one-third at 6 h. In pooled thrombectomy trials ~46% achieved functional independence (modified Rankin 0-2) versus ~26.5% with medical care, with a mortality benefit. Small-vessel (lacunar) strokes generally recover more rapidly and completely than large-vessel strokes, though some stutter or leave severe disability. Without secondary prevention the annual risk of a further stroke after atherothrombotic stroke/TIA is about 8-10%; symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis and untreated symptomatic carotid stenosis each carry ~15% per year. Care in a dedicated stroke unit followed by rehabilitation improves neurologic outcome and reduces mortality (p.3427, p.3441-3442, p.3445-3446). Severity is graded clinically by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS). A disabling deficit (NIHSS >5) flags potential eligibility for thrombolysis/endovascular therapy, whereas minor non-disabling stroke (NIHSS 0-5) may be managed with aspirin or short-term dual antiplatelet therapy. Mechanism-based (TOAST-style) classification - cardioembolic, large-artery atherosclerosis (carotid/intracranial), small-vessel/lacunar, other defined cause, and cryptogenic (~30%) - drives secondary prevention. Carotid disease is further classed as symptomatic vs asymptomatic and by degree of stenosis, with risk rising with stenosis severity except for near-occlusions, which carry lower risk (p.3440-3441, p.3443, p.3445).
