enhances detoxification Under-treating catabolic stress during intercurrent illness Overlooking neutropenia and infection risk during acute crises Isovaleric acidemia is an autosomal recessive defect of isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, an enzyme of the leucine degradation pathway. Deficiency causes isovaleryl-CoA and its derivatives (isovaleric acid, isovalerylglycine, isovalerylcarnitine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid) to accumulate. Isovaleric acid is responsible for the characteristic odour and, together with the other metabolites, produces metabolic acidosis and is toxic to the central nervous system and bone marrow. Accumulated organic acids also secondarily impair the urea cycle, contributing to hyperammonaemia. Conjugation of isovaleryl-CoA with glycine and carnitine forms non-toxic, readily excreted products, which is exploited therapeutically. With newborn screening and early treatment many patients have a favourable outcome and normal development; the chronic intermittent form is often milder, but untreated acute neonatal disease can be fatal or cause neurological damage, and outcome depends on preventing and promptly treating decompensations.

In children ITP is usually acute, often follows an infection, and is self-limited; in adults it tends to be chronic, though some adults remit spontaneously within months of diagnosis (p.924). It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion: characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding and a low (often very low) platelet count with otherwise normal peripheral blood cells and smear (p.924). Presentation is either with ecchymoses/petechiae or with thrombocytopenia found incidentally on a routine CBC (p.924). Mucocutaneous bleeding may include oral mucosal, gastrointestinal, or heavy menstrual bleeding; rarely life-threatening (including CNS) bleeding occurs (p.924). Wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) and retinal hemorrhages may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924, p.922). Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages that signal decreased platelet number rather than platelet dysfunction, and first appear in dependent areas of increased venous pressure (ankles/feet in an ambulatory patient) (p.922). Serologic (antiplatelet antibody) testing is generally not helpful because of low sensitivity and specificity of current tests (p.924). The peripheral smear may show large platelets with otherwise normal morphology, reflecting young/rapidly turned-over platelets (p.924, p.916). Failing to take a careful drug/herbal/OTC history, since drugs are the most common cause of thrombocytopenia (p.922). ITP results from immune-mediated destruction of antibody-coated platelets by the reticuloendothelial system, and possibly impaired platelet release from megakaryocytes. Primary ITP has no identifiable cause; secondary ITP is associated with an underlying disorder such as autoimmune disease (notably SLE) or infection (HIV, hepatitis C). Childhood ITP commonly follows a viral infection through immune mechanisms and usually resolves spontaneously (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924). Childhood ITP is usually acute and almost always resolves spontaneously. Adult ITP is more often chronic, though some adults remit spontaneously within months. Patients with platelet counts >30,000/uL appear not to have increased mortality related to the thrombocytopenia, so diagnosis does not mandate treatment (Harrison 22e p.924). Harrison does not give a formal grading scale. Practical thresholds noted: platelet counts >30,000/uL are not associated with increased mortality; ~5000-10,000/uL is the level needed to maintain microvascular integrity; severe thrombocytopenia is cited as <5000/uL for treatment-decision purposes (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924).

Humans are incidental dead-end hosts. Following a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing a viraemia that may seed the central nervous system across the blood-brain barrier. Neuronal infection and the accompanying inflammatory response cause neuronal death particularly in the thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem and cerebral cortex, accounting for the movement disorders and depressed consciousness seen clinically. Symptomatic encephalitis carries substantial mortality, and a large proportion of survivors are left with lasting neurological or psychiatric sequelae including motor deficits, movement disorders, cognitive impairment and epilepsy. Outcome is worse at the extremes of age and with delayed presentation.

inheritance is autosomal recessive The same channel is needed for endolymph production in the inner ear and for cardiac repolarisation, explaining the combined phenotype Presents with syncope, seizures or sudden collapse triggered by exertion, emotion or startle, reflecting torsades de pointes Any deaf child with unexplained syncope, seizures or a family history of sudden death must have an ECG to look for QT prolongation Heterozygous carriers may have isolated long QT (Romano-Ward pattern) without deafness Cardiac risk is high and untreated patients face a substantial risk of sudden cardiac death, so cardiology referral is urgent Syncope, seizures or cardiac arrest, particularly during exertion, emotion or sudden noise Family history of sudden unexplained death or long QT syndrome Documented torsades de pointes or very prolonged corrected QT interval Exposure to QT-prolonging medications that could precipitate arrhythmia Not performing an ECG in a deaf child with syncope or seizures and missing the cardiac diagnosis Misdiagnosing arrhythmic collapse as epilepsy and delaying cardiac treatment Prescribing QT-prolonging medications, which can precipitate fatal arrhythmia Overlooking the recessive inheritance and failing to screen at-risk relatives Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in KCNQ1 or KCNE1, subunits forming the slow delayed-rectifier potassium current channel. In the stria vascularis of the inner ear this current is essential for secreting potassium-rich endolymph; its loss disrupts the endocochlear potential and causes profound congenital sensorineural deafness. In cardiac myocytes the same current contributes to repolarisation, so its loss prolongs the action potential and the QT interval, predisposing to torsades de pointes ventricular arrhythmia, syncope and sudden death. The recessive combined phenotype requires two defective alleles, whereas single-allele defects tend to cause isolated long QT syndrome. Untreated the syndrome carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death from malignant arrhythmia, but prognosis improves substantially with beta-blockade, avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs, and consideration of an implantable defibrillator, alongside hearing rehabilitation for the profound deafness.

Because the primary cilium is essential for hedgehog and other signalling that governs skeletal patterning and growth-plate function, its disruption impairs endochondral ossification, producing a constricted thoracic cage and short limbs. The same ciliary dysfunction in the kidney, liver, and retina accounts for the progressive extraskeletal disease seen in longer-term survivors. Prognosis depends heavily on the severity of thoracic constriction: severe cases are frequently fatal in infancy from respiratory failure, whereas those surviving early childhood may have relative thoracic growth but face progressive renal and other organ complications.

Confusing it with the recessive DOCK8 form, which has a different infection profile and management Job syndrome results from heterozygous dominant-negative mutations in STAT3, a transcription factor central to signalling downstream of numerous cytokines. Defective STAT3 signalling impairs the differentiation of Th17 cells and reduces the production of antimicrobial peptides at epithelial surfaces, which underlies the susceptibility to Staphylococcus aureus and Candida and the failure to mount a brisk inflammatory response (the 'cold' abscess phenomenon). Because STAT3 also regulates connective tissue, bone, dental, and vascular biology, patients develop the characteristic facial, skeletal, and dental abnormalities and are prone to aneurysm formation. IgE production is markedly increased and eosinophilia is common, reflecting the skewed cytokine environment. Many patients survive into adulthood with consistent prophylaxis and prompt treatment of infections, but chronic lung damage, fungal superinfection of pneumatoceles, and vascular aneurysms are important sources of long-term morbidity and can be life-threatening.

Joubert syndrome — Joubert syndrome and related disorders, JSRD, molar tooth sign syndrome, AHI1, CEP290, NPHP1, TMEM67, CC2D2A Dandy-Walker malformation and other posterior fossa cystic malformations Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia from other causes such as congenital disorders of glycosylation Rhombencephalosynapsis Pontocerebellar hypoplasia Other ciliopathies such as Meckel-Gruber and Bardet-Biedl syndrome Isolated nephronophthisis or Senior-Loken syndrome Brain MRI to demonstrate the molar tooth sign and characterise vermian and brainstem anatomy Molecular genetic testing, typically a ciliopathy gene panel or exome sequencing Renal ultrasound and renal function testing to screen for nephronophthisis or cystic disease Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for retinal dystrophy and oculomotor evaluation Liver ultrasound and liver function tests to detect hepatic fibrosis Developmental and neuropsychological assessment to guide support A ciliopathy defined neuroradiologically by the molar tooth sign, produced by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia or aplasia together with thickened, horizontally oriented and elongated superior cerebellar peduncles and a deepened interpeduncular fossa Classic neonatal picture combines episodic tachypnoea alternating with apnoea, abnormal eye movements including oculomotor apraxia and nystagmus, hypotonia evolving into ataxia, and developmental delay Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive with marked genetic heterogeneity; more than thirty causative genes encode proteins of the primary cilium and basal body Because it is a ciliopathy, extra-neurological involvement is common and defines subtypes, including retinal dystrophy, nephronophthisis or cystic renal disease, hepatic fibrosis, and polydactyly The CEP290 and NPHP1 genotypes carry higher risk of renal disease, while TMEM67 is associated with hepatic fibrosis, guiding organ-directed surveillance Cognitive outcome is variable and many children have moderate impairment, so early developmental support and multidisciplinary follow-up are important Prenatal suspicion may arise from vermian abnormality on foetal imaging, and diagnosis is confirmed by the molar tooth sign on postnatal MRI plus molecular testing Neonatal apnoea and irregular breathing requiring respiratory monitoring Progressive renal impairment from nephronophthisis leading to end-stage kidney disease Deteriorating vision from retinal dystrophy Signs of portal hypertension or hepatic decompensation from fibrosis Attributing neonatal apnoea and hypotonia to birth asphyxia and missing the underlying malformation Failing to recognise the molar tooth sign on suboptimal or non-dedicated posterior fossa imaging Not screening for renal, hepatic, and retinal disease that may present years after the neurological diagnosis Assuming a uniform prognosis despite wide genotype and phenotype variability Joubert syndrome is a disorder of the primary cilium and basal body (a ciliopathy). Pathogenic variants in genes encoding ciliary transition-zone and axonemal proteins disrupt ciliary signalling that guides mid-hindbrain patterning and axonal decussation. The resulting failure of cerebellar vermis development and abnormal crossing of superior cerebellar peduncle and corticospinal fibres produce the characteristic mid-hindbrain malformation seen as the molar tooth sign. The same ciliary dysfunction in the retina, renal tubule, and biliary tract accounts for the frequently associated multi-organ features. Prognosis depends on the degree of neurological impairment and the extent of renal, hepatic, and retinal involvement. Many individuals survive into adulthood with variable cognitive and motor disability, but progressive kidney or liver disease can substantially affect life expectancy.

management is supportive with wound care and nutritional support Airway involvement with stridor or respiratory compromise from laryngeal granulation tissue Extensive skin loss with sepsis, fluid, and electrolyte disturbance in a neonate Failure to thrive and severe anaemia from chronic wounds and poor intake Rapid deterioration in the severe generalised subtype, which carries high infant mortality Failing to identify the severe generalised subtype early, delaying appropriate supportive and palliative planning Overlooking airway involvement heralded by perioral and perinasal granulation tissue Neglecting nutritional support, dental care, and anaemia management Mistaking neonatal junctional disease for infection Assuming a uniform prognosis rather than recognising the wide spectrum of severity The dermo-epidermal junction is held together by hemidesmosomes and their associated anchoring filaments, which span the lamina lucida of the basement membrane and connect basal keratinocytes to the underlying lamina densa. Laminin-332 and collagen XVII (the bullous pemphigoid antigen 180) are key structural components of this adhesion complex. In junctional epidermolysis bullosa, biallelic mutations reduce or abolish these proteins, weakening adhesion so that the skin separates within the lamina lucida under minimal mechanical stress. The same proteins are important in mucosal epithelia and in tooth enamel formation, which explains the mucosal involvement and enamel defects. The most severe subtypes cause extensive skin and mucosal loss with a high risk of infection, fluid loss, and airway compromise in infancy. Outlook varies markedly by subtype: the severe generalised form carries high mortality in infancy from sepsis, respiratory involvement, and failure to thrive, whereas milder junctional variants are compatible with survival into adulthood with chronic blistering and extracutaneous complications.

Juvenile Dermatomyositis — JDM, juvenile dermatomyositis Muscular dystrophy Systemic lupus erythematosus / overlap connective tissue disease Viral or post-viral myositis Polymyositis Hypothyroid or metabolic myopathy Spinal muscular atrophy or other neuromuscular disorders Serum muscle enzymes (creatine kinase, aldolase, LDH, transaminases) MRI of muscle to identify inflammation and guide biopsy site Nailfold capillaroscopy Myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibodies Muscle biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain Electromyography in selected cases The most common inflammatory myopathy of childhood, characterised by proximal muscle weakness together with distinctive skin changes. Look for the heliotrope rash (violaceous discolouration of the upper eyelids) and Gottron papules over the knuckles, elbows, and knees. Weakness is typically symmetrical and proximal, so children struggle to climb stairs, rise from the floor, or lift their arms overhead. Nailfold capillary changes (dilated, dropout, or tortuous loops) are a useful bedside clue and correlate with disease activity. Calcinosis of skin and soft tissues is a late complication, more likely when treatment is delayed or inadequate. Unlike adult dermatomyositis, an underlying malignancy is rarely associated in children. A small vessel vasculopathy can affect the gastrointestinal tract, potentially causing ulceration, bleeding, or perforation. Early diagnosis and adequate immunosuppression improve outcomes and reduce the risk of chronic disability and calcinosis. Severe dysphagia or nasal regurgitation indicating pharyngeal muscle involvement with aspiration risk Respiratory muscle weakness or interstitial lung disease causing hypoventilation Gastrointestinal vasculopathy with abdominal pain, bleeding, or perforation Rapidly progressive weakness or inability to protect the airway Extensive skin ulceration reflecting severe vasculopathy Attributing subtle proximal weakness to clumsiness or normal fatigue and delaying diagnosis Assuming normal muscle enzymes exclude the disease, as they can be near-normal in some children Under-treating early disease and thereby increasing the risk of calcinosis Overlooking dysphagia and aspiration risk when pharyngeal muscles are involved Juvenile dermatomyositis is an immune-mediated systemic vasculopathy affecting small vessels of skeletal muscle, skin, and other organs. Complement-mediated injury to the capillary endothelium leads to capillary dropout, ischaemia, and perifascicular muscle fibre atrophy. Interferon-driven inflammation and immune complex deposition contribute to ongoing muscle and skin damage, producing the characteristic weakness and rash. With prompt, adequate immunosuppression many children achieve remission and regain function; delayed or insufficient treatment increases the risk of chronic disease, calcinosis, and long-term disability. A monocyclic course carries the best prognosis.

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis — JIA, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile chronic arthritis Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis Reactive and post-infectious arthritis (including acute rheumatic fever) Leukaemia and other malignancy presenting with bone or joint pain Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases Inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthritis Non-inflammatory causes such as trauma, hypermobility, and benign limb pains Full blood count, ESR, and C-reactive protein Antinuclear antibody (informs uveitis risk) and rheumatoid factor HLA-B27 in suspected enthesitis-related arthritis Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination for uveitis screening Joint imaging (ultrasound or MRI) to assess synovitis and effusion Ferritin, triglycerides, and fibrinogen if macrophage activation syndrome is suspected The most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood, defined by arthritis beginning before 16 years of age and persisting for at least 6 weeks, with other causes excluded. It is a heterogeneous group of subtypes, including oligoarticular, polyarticular, systemic, enthesitis-related, and psoriatic forms, each with distinct features and prognosis. Arthritis presents with joint swelling, morning stiffness or gelling, and limited movement, often with less pain than expected; young children may present with limp or refusal to use a limb. Oligoarticular JIA is the most common subtype, typically affecting large joints in young girls and carrying a significant risk of chronic anterior uveitis. Uveitis is frequently asymptomatic, so regular ophthalmological slit-lamp screening is essential to prevent visual loss, particularly in young ANA-positive children. Systemic JIA features prominent extra-articular disease with quotidian high fever, an evanescent salmon-coloured rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis. The diagnosis is clinical and one of exclusion; laboratory tests support rather than confirm it, and inflammatory markers may be normal in oligoarticular disease. A serious complication of systemic JIA is macrophage activation syndrome, a form of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis that can be rapidly fatal. Management principles combine anti-inflammatory therapy, disease-modifying agents, and increasingly biologic therapy, alongside physiotherapy to preserve joint function and growth. Features of macrophage activation syndrome (persistent fever, falling cell counts, very high ferritin, hepatic dysfunction) Findings suggesting malignancy such as severe night pain, cytopenias, or systemic decline A hot, acutely swollen joint with fever suggesting septic arthritis Visual symptoms or complications of uveitis Systemic features such as high spiking fever with serositis Missing asymptomatic uveitis by omitting scheduled slit-lamp screening Overlooking leukaemia in a child with bone pain and abnormal counts before starting steroids Failing to recognise early macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA Attributing a single hot joint to JIA and missing septic arthritis JIA results from immune dysregulation leading to chronic inflammation of the synovium. In most subtypes, an aberrant adaptive immune response with T-cell activation and autoantibody production drives synovial proliferation (pannus), which can erode cartilage and bone and disturb the growth of nearby physes. Systemic JIA is instead an autoinflammatory condition driven predominantly by the innate immune system and proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, accounting for its prominent systemic features and its predisposition to macrophage activation syndrome. Outcome varies by subtype; many children with oligoarticular disease do well, while polyarticular and systemic forms may follow a more persistent course, and modern therapy has substantially improved remission rates and reduced long-term joint damage. Uveitis and macrophage activation syndrome remain important causes of morbidity.

Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy — JME, Janz syndrome Other idiopathic generalised epilepsies (childhood or juvenile absence epilepsy) Progressive myoclonic epilepsies Focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation Benign physiological (hypnagogic) myoclonus Non-epileptic movements or tics Psychogenic non-epileptic events EEG, ideally including a recording after sleep deprivation and on awakening Photic stimulation during EEG to elicit a photoparoxysmal response MRI brain, mainly to exclude structural or progressive causes in atypical cases Detailed history focusing on early-morning jerks and provoking factors Metabolic or genetic testing when a progressive myoclonic epilepsy is suspected A common idiopathic (genetic) generalised epilepsy syndrome, usually beginning in adolescence. The defining seizure type is myoclonic jerks, typically of the arms and shoulders, occurring soon after waking. Most patients also have generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and a subset have absence seizures. Early morning clumsiness, such as dropping objects like a toothbrush or cup, is a classic historical clue that is often overlooked. Seizures are strongly provoked by sleep deprivation, alcohol, and sometimes photic stimulation. The interictal EEG characteristically shows generalised polyspike-and-wave discharges, and a photoparoxysmal response may be seen. Development and intelligence are typically normal, and neuroimaging is usually unremarkable. Seizures are generally well controlled with appropriate broad-spectrum treatment, but the condition usually requires long-term therapy as relapse on withdrawal is common; certain narrow-spectrum antiseizure medicines can worsen it. Progressive cognitive decline or neurological deterioration suggesting a progressive myoclonic epilepsy Focal neurological signs or focal features on EEG or imaging Seizures worsening after starting treatment (possible inappropriate narrow-spectrum drug) Frequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures or status epilepticus Recurrent seizures driven by unrecognised sleep deprivation or non-adherence Missing the diagnosis by not asking specifically about early-morning myoclonic jerks Misclassifying generalised seizures as focal and selecting a drug that aggravates myoclonus and absences Underestimating the impact of sleep deprivation, alcohol, and poor adherence on seizure control Attempting early withdrawal of treatment and precipitating relapse Overlooking coexisting absence seizures JME is a genetically determined generalised epilepsy involving abnormal thalamocortical network excitability and synchronisation rather than a focal structural lesion. Inherited susceptibility, likely polygenic in most cases, produces a lowered threshold for generalised epileptiform discharges. The characteristic myoclonus and generalised seizures arise from these hyperexcitable cortico-thalamic circuits, and the strong link with the sleep-wake transition reflects state-dependent changes in cortical excitability. Prognosis for seizure control is favourable with suitable therapy and lifestyle measures, and cognition is preserved, but JME is generally a lifelong tendency; most patients relapse if medication is stopped, so long-term or indefinite treatment is often needed.

nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a histologically benign tumour composed of a fibrous stroma interspersed with numerous thin-walled vascular channels that frequently lack a complete muscular coat, which It typically originates around the sphenopalatine foramen and pterygopalatine fossa and grows submucosally along natural pathways, expanding into the nasopharynx and nasal cavity and eroding bone to reach the orbit, infratemporal fossa, and skull base. Although histologically benign, the tumour is locally aggressive and prone to recurrence when incompletely excised; complete removal, aided by preoperative embolisation, gives good long-term control, while extensive skull-base or intracranial disease is more difficult to eradicate and may require radiotherapy.

Overlooking early hearing loss that warrants audiological follow-up Attributing the very high alkaline phosphatase to liver disease rather than bone turnover Delaying antiresorptive treatment that can alter the disease trajectory Juvenile Paget disease is caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in TNFRSF11B, which encodes osteoprotegerin, a decoy receptor that normally binds RANKL and prevents it from activating RANK on osteoclast precursors. Without functional osteoprotegerin, RANKL signalling is unopposed, leading to greatly increased osteoclast formation and activity. Coupled to this is a compensatory surge in osteoblastic bone formation, so the skeleton undergoes extremely rapid but disorganised remodelling. that presents insidiously Overlooking neonatal or later hypoglycaemia from hyperinsulinism Failing to recognise the diagnosis when facial features are subtle in infancy Kabuki syndrome is a disorder Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) — visceral leishmaniasis, VL, black fever, Leishmania donovani infection Malaria Enteric (typhoid) fever Miliary or disseminated tuberculosis Haematological malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma) Chronic myeloproliferative disorders causing massive splenomegaly Infective endocarditis or other causes of prolonged fever with organomegaly Lymphoma or leukaemia with organomegaly and cytopenias Tropical splenomegaly syndrome Disseminated histoplasmosis Chronic malaria (hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly) rK39 rapid serological test for L. donovani Demonstration of amastigotes in bone marrow, splenic or lymph node aspirates Full blood count showing pancytopenia and protein electrophoresis showing hypergammaglobulinaemia HIV testing given the impact of co-infection on treatment and relapse PCR-based parasite detection where available A systemic protozoal infection caused by Leishmania donovani, transmitted by the bite of female phlebotomine sandflies In India it is concentrated in Bihar and adjoining eastern states and is the target of a national elimination programme, with humans the main reservoir for the Indian form Classic presentation is prolonged fever with progressive splenomegaly (often massive), hepatomegaly, weight loss, and darkening of the skin that gives the disease its name Laboratory hallmarks are pancytopenia and a marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia Untreated visceral leishmaniasis is almost uniformly fatal, and secondary bacterial infections and bleeding are common causes of death Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis can appear after apparent cure and acts as a human reservoir, so its recognition is important for elimination efforts Diagnosis combines serology (e.g. rK39 rapid test) with demonstration of amastigotes in splenic, bone marrow or other aspirates Effective antileishmanial therapy exists, with liposomal amphotericin B favoured in India; HIV co-infection worsens response and relapse risk Prolonged fever with massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia requiring urgent diagnosis and treatment Severe anaemia, bleeding or intercurrent bacterial infection from marrow suppression, which can be fatal Failure to respond to therapy or relapse, especially with HIV co-infection Emergence of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, signalling a transmission reservoir Attributing prolonged fever with splenomegaly to malaria or typhoid and missing visceral leishmaniasis in endemic areas Overlooking HIV co-infection, which alters treatment response and relapse risk Failing to recognise post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis as a source of ongoing transmission Delaying treatment while awaiting invasive confirmation when serology and clinical picture are diagnostic Sandfly bites inoculate Leishmania promastigotes, which are taken up by macrophages and transform into amastigotes that multiply within the mononuclear phagocyte system. The parasite disseminates to the spleen, liver and bone marrow, driving reticuloendothelial hyperplasia that produces organomegaly and, through hypersplenism and marrow infiltration, the characteristic pancytopenia. A vigorous but non-protective humoral response causes hypergammaglobulinaemia, while impaired cell-mediated immunity permits unchecked parasite proliferation and progressive, potentially fatal systemic disease. With prompt, effective antileishmanial therapy most patients recover fully, and liposomal amphotericin B has markedly improved outcomes in India. Untreated disease is nearly always fatal, and prognosis is poorer in the very young, malnourished, and those with HIV co-infection or advanced disease.

During development, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons originate in the olfactory placode and migrate along the olfactory nerve fibres to reach the hypothalamus. In Kallmann syndrome, mutations affecting the genes that guide this migration disrupt both the olfactory pathway and the arrival of GnRH neurons in the hypothalamus. The resulting deficiency of hypothalamic GnRH leads to reduced pituitary secretion of luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormones and consequent hypogonadism, while the shared developmental defect explains the coexisting impairment of smell. With appropriate hormone replacement, secondary sexual characteristics and bone health can be maintained, and fertility is frequently achievable with gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy; a minority experience reversal of the hypogonadism.

Immune dysfunction, whether from HIV infection or iatrogenic immunosuppression, permits viral reactivation and tumour development, which is why the disease is strongly linked to immunocompromise and often regresses when immunity is restored. Prognosis depends on the clinical form and immune status: classic Kaposi sarcoma is usually indolent, and iatrogenic and epidemic disease often regress when immune function is restored, whereas disseminated or visceral disease, particularly pulmonary involvement, carries significant morbidity and can be fatal without effective treatment.

Failure of mucociliary clearance leads to chronic retention of secretions with recurrent sinopulmonary infection and progressive bronchiectasis. Because embryonic nodal cilia also fail to establish normal left-right asymmetry, laterality is randomised and roughly half of affected individuals develop complete situs inversus, defining the Kartagener phenotype. With early diagnosis and consistent airway clearance many patients maintain reasonable lung function, but chronic infection can cause progressive bronchiectasis; the situs inversus itself is usually of little functional consequence unless accompanied by cardiac anomalies.

Kawasaki Disease Shock Syndrome — KDSS, Kawasaki shock syndrome, Kawasaki disease with shock Toxic shock syndrome (staphylococcal or streptococcal) Septic shock Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis with macrophage activation Severe adenoviral or other viral infection Drug reaction with systemic involvement Echocardiography to assess coronary arteries and ventricular function Inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) Full blood count with attention to platelets and anaemia Serum albumin, sodium, and liver function tests Cardiac biomarkers (troponin, natriuretic peptides) Blood cultures and infection screen to exclude sepsis and toxic shock Coagulation studies A severe presentation of Kawasaki disease in which children develop haemodynamic instability and hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation or inotropic support. It should be considered in a child with features of Kawasaki disease (prolonged fever, mucocutaneous changes, conjunctival injection, extremity changes, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy) who also appears shocked. Compared with classic Kawasaki disease, shock syndrome is more often associated with incomplete presentations, greater systemic inflammation, and a higher risk of coronary artery involvement. Laboratory markers tend to show more intense inflammation, lower platelet counts, and evidence of consumptive or capillary-leak processes. These children are more likely to be initially resistant to intravenous immunoglobulin and may need additional immunomodulatory therapy. The overlap with toxic shock syndrome and septic shock frequently leads to diagnostic delay, so a high index of suspicion is essential. Prompt echocardiography is important because of the elevated risk of coronary artery aneurysms and myocardial dysfunction. Timely treatment of the underlying vasculitis, in addition to circulatory support, is key to reducing coronary complications. Hypotension or shock requiring fluids or inotropes (EMERGENCY) Signs of myocardial dysfunction or heart failure Evidence of coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiography Resistance to first-line immunoglobulin therapy Rapidly rising inflammatory markers with falling platelets Multi-organ hypoperfusion or deteriorating conscious level Mislabelling the presentation as septic or toxic shock and delaying Kawasaki-directed treatment Missing incomplete or atypical Kawasaki features in a shocked child Aggressive fluid loading without recognising myocardial dysfunction Assuming a single dose of immunoglobulin has controlled the disease without monitoring for resistance Neglecting early and repeat echocardiography for coronary surveillance Kawasaki disease is a self-limited medium-vessel vasculitis of childhood driven by intense systemic immune activation. In the shock variant, an exaggerated inflammatory response with high circulating cytokine levels produces vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, and increased vascular permeability with capillary leak. The combination of impaired cardiac contractility and fluid shifts out of the intravascular space results in hypotension and organ hypoperfusion, superimposed on the vasculitic damage that threatens the coronary arteries. With early recognition and treatment most children recover, but the shock variant carries a higher rate of coronary artery abnormalities, myocardial dysfunction, and immunoglobulin resistance than classic disease, so outcomes depend on prompt immunomodulation and cardiac follow-up.

KCNQ2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — KCNQ2, KCNQ2 encephalopathy, Kv7.2 encephalopathy, neonatal epileptic encephalopathy KCNQ2 Benign familial neonatal epilepsy (KCNQ2/KCNQ3) Ohtahara Kv7.2 combines with Kv7.3 to generate the M-current, a slow potassium current that stabilises the resting membrane potential and limits repetitive firing. Disruption of this current increases neuronal excitability in the neonatal brain, producing early tonic seizures and a severe epileptic encephalopathy, in contrast to the milder self-limited phenotype seen with less disruptive variants. Outcome varies with the underlying variant: many children with the encephalopathy form have intellectual disability and persistent epilepsy, though seizures may improve over the first years. Early recognition and use of sodium-channel-blocking therapy can improve seizure control in responsive cases.

or bulbar deterioration Progressive respiratory muscle weakness Failing to institute cardiac surveillance and offer timely pacing for conduction block Mistaking the ophthalmoplegia for myasthenia The deletion removes genes encoding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation chain and mitochondrial transfer RNAs, impairing energy production. Heteroplasmic distribution of deleted genomes across tissues, with a bias toward post-mitotic high-energy-demand organs such as extraocular muscle, retina, cardiac conduction tissue, brain and endocrine glands, explains the characteristic multisystem phenotype. The condition is progressive and multisystem; prognosis is largely determined by cardiac conduction disease, which can cause sudden death and is mitigated by surveillance and pacing. Life expectancy is reduced, with care focused on supportive and organ-specific management.

Keloid — keloid scar, keloidal scar Hypertrophic scar (raised but confined to the wound edges and tends to regress) Dermatofibroma Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Foreign-body granuloma Cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis in a scar Nodular presentation of acne keloidalis nuchae on the occipital scalp Diagnosis is clinical based on history and morphology Skin biopsy only when an alternative or malignant process is suspected, recognising that biopsy itself may stimulate keloid growth Photographic documentation to monitor size and response to treatment A keloid is firm, rubbery, and shiny, and crucially extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, distinguishing it from a hypertrophic scar that stays within the wound margins Lesions often itch or feel tender and may continue to enlarge over months to years rather than regressing Predilection sites include the earlobes, presternal chest, shoulders, upper back, and jawline Risk is higher in people with darker skin phototypes, in younger patients, and where there is a family history Even minor triggers such as ear piercing, acne, vaccination, or surgery can precipitate lesions in predisposed individuals Prevention matters: minimise tension on wounds, avoid unnecessary elective procedures in prone sites, and counsel high-risk patients before piercings or cosmetic surgery Treatment is often multimodal and includes intralesional anti-inflammatory injection, pressure or silicone therapy, and carefully planned surgery combined with adjuvant measures to reduce recurrence Surgical excision alone carries a high recurrence rate and can produce a larger keloid, so it should be paired with adjuvant therapy Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, or fixation suggesting a fibrosarcomatous tumour rather than a keloid Recurrent or aggressive lesions in a scar raising the possibility of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans Functional impairment or contracture over a joint or the ear requiring specialist input Excising a keloid without adjuvant therapy, which commonly produces a larger recurrence Failing to distinguish a keloid from a self-limiting hypertrophic scar and over-treating Performing elective cosmetic procedures or piercings in high-risk patients without counselling Overlooking the symptom burden of itch and pain and treating only for appearance Keloids arise from dysregulated wound healing in which the normal resolution of the proliferative phase fails and fibroblasts remain persistently activated. Overexpression of profibrotic mediators, notably transforming growth factor-beta, drives excessive and disorganised deposition of thick, hyalinised collagen bundles that extend into surrounding normal dermis. Reduced apoptosis of fibroblasts, altered mechanotransduction from wound tension, and a genetic predisposition all contribute. Unlike hypertrophic scars, keloids do not remodel and regress over time, reflecting a sustained imbalance between collagen synthesis and breakdown. Keloids are chronic and prone to recurrence; some stabilise with combined therapy, but complete and permanent resolution is difficult, and lesions frequently recur after excision unless adjuvant treatment is used. They do not spontaneously involute in the way hypertrophic scars often do.

an alternative or superimposed diagnosis Emergence of upper motor neuron signs prompting reconsideration of ALS Misdiagnosing it as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and giving an unduly poor prognosis carrier daughters Kennedy disease is a polyglutamine disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. The elongated polyglutamine tract renders the mutant, ligand-bound androgen receptor prone to misfolding and nuclear accumulation, which is toxic to lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord and to dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons. The androgen-dependent toxicity explains why the phenotype is expressed in males and why partial androgen insensitivity features accompany the neuronopathy. The disorder progresses slowly over many years, and life expectancy is often near normal, though bulbar weakness can lead to aspiration and disability; mobility and swallowing decline gradually and management is supportive.

progression, and keratoplasty for advanced scarring or intolerance to lenses Acute corneal hydrops causes sudden pain, redness, and reduced vision from a break in Descemet membrane allowing aqueous into the stroma Sudden pain, marked visual loss, and corneal oedema suggesting acute hydrops Rapidly progressive steepening in young patients requiring urgent cross-linking assessment Corneal scarring or lens intolerance indicating need for keratoplasty referral Repeatedly changing spectacle prescriptions instead of recognising an underlying ectasia Overlooking eye rubbing as a modifiable driver of progression Delaying cross-linking in demonstrable progression, allowing avoidable visual loss Mistaking acute hydrops for infective keratitis Keratoconus is a progressive, non-inflammatory ectasia in which the cornea thins and steepens into a conical shape, producing irregular astigmatism and myopia. The stromal thinning reflects disorganisation of collagen lamellae and altered enzyme activity with increased degradation of the corneal matrix. Mechanical stress from chronic eye rubbing and an association with atopy and certain systemic syndromes are recognised contributors. As the cone advances, the apex scars and Descemet membrane may rupture, precipitating acute hydrops with corneal oedema. Progression is most rapid in younger patients and often stabilises with age; timely cross-linking can halt deterioration, and most patients achieve good functional vision with lenses, though a minority need corneal transplantation.

Kernicterus — bilirubin encephalopathy, chronic bilirubin encephalopathy, acute bilirubin encephalopathy Neonatal sepsis or meningitis Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Inborn errors of metabolism causing encephalopathy Neonatal seizures of other cause Hypoglycaemic or electrolyte-related encephalopathy Other causes of neonatal hypertonia or abnormal movements Serial total and unconjugated bilirubin, interpreted against age-in-hours nomograms Albumin level and bilirubin-to-albumin ratio to gauge binding reserve Haemolysis workup (blood group, direct antiglobulin test, blood film, reticulocytes) Auditory brainstem response testing for auditory neuropathy MRI showing characteristic basal ganglia signal changes in established disease Evaluation for contributing factors such as sepsis, acidosis, and prematurity Kernicterus refers to the neurological injury caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, classically in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei. It is a preventable complication of severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and represents the chronic, permanent form of bilirubin neurotoxicity. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy evolves through phases: early lethargy, hypotonia, and poor feeding, followed by hypertonia with backward arching (retrocollis and opisthotonus), high-pitched cry, and fever, and later apnoea, seizures, and coma. The classic chronic tetrad includes choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (or auditory neuropathy), impaired upward gaze, and dental enamel dysplasia. Only unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin that is not bound to albumin can cross the blood-brain barrier, so free bilirubin and factors lowering albumin binding increase risk. Prematurity, haemolysis, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, and certain drugs that displace bilirubin heighten vulnerability at any given bilirubin level. Prevention rests on identifying and monitoring at-risk newborns, timely phototherapy, and exchange transfusion when bilirubin approaches neurotoxic thresholds. Once established, chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is largely irreversible, underscoring the importance of early recognition and treatment of hyperbilirubinaemia. Structured predischarge risk assessment and follow-up of jaundiced newborns reduce the incidence of this now-rare but devastating condition. Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy or hypertonia, retrocollis/opisthotonus, high-pitched cry, poor feeding Bilirubin approaching or exceeding exchange transfusion thresholds for the infant's age and risk Apnoea, seizures, or coma in a severely jaundiced newborn Rapidly rising bilirubin, especially with haemolysis, sepsis, or acidosis Jaundice in a preterm or unwell infant where binding reserve is reduced Interpreting bilirubin values without reference to the infant's age in hours and risk factors Underestimating neurotoxic risk in preterm, acidotic, hypoalbuminaemic, or septic infants at lower bilirubin levels Delaying phototherapy or exchange transfusion while bilirubin rises Missing early, subtle neurological signs of acute encephalopathy Discharging a jaundiced newborn without adequate follow-up and risk assessment Unconjugated bilirubin is normally tightly bound to albumin and does not enter the brain. When the bilirubin load overwhelms albumin binding capacity, or binding is reduced by acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia, prematurity, or competing substances, free unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is neurotoxic, being preferentially deposited in and damaging the basal ganglia (notably the globus pallidus and subthalamic nuclei), the brainstem auditory and oculomotor nuclei, hippocampus, and cerebellum. Bilirubin impairs mitochondrial function and neuronal signalling, causing acute dysfunction and, if sustained, permanent neuronal loss and gliosis with the characteristic clinical sequelae. Acute bilirubin encephalopathy may be partly reversible if bilirubin is lowered promptly, but progression to chronic kernicterus produces permanent, often severe disability including movement disorder, hearing loss, and gaze abnormalities. Because the condition is largely preventable, prognosis hinges on timely detection and treatment of severe hyperbilirubinaemia.

corticosteroids are reserved for severe or recurrent disease Persistent or progressive lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma Development of features of systemic lupus erythematosus Prolonged high fever or systemic deterioration Rare aseptic meningitis or other extranodal involvement Misdiagnosing it as lymphoma on histology and initiating unnecessary treatment Failing to consider or later screen for systemic lupus erythematosus Relying on fine-needle aspiration, which is often non-diagnostic, rather than excisional biopsy Mistaking the necrosis for tuberculous lymphadenitis Prescribing antibiotics for a non-infective, self-limiting condition Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a self-limiting histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis of uncertain cause, thought to represent an exuberant T-cell and histiocyte-mediated immune response, possibly triggered by a viral or other infectious agent in a genetically predisposed individual. Affected lymph nodes show paracortical zones of coagulative necrosis populated by proliferating histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and CD8-positive T lymphocytes, with prominent karyorrhectic (apoptotic) debris and a striking paucity of neutrophils and plasma cells. The same mechanisms of immune dysregulation link it to systemic lupus erythematosus. The condition is benign and usually resolves spontaneously over several weeks to a few months; recurrence occurs in a minority, and patients warrant follow-up for the possible later emergence of systemic lupus erythematosus.

corticosteroids and other systemic immunosuppression are used for extensive or recurrent disease Nephrotic-range proteinuria indicating renal involvement Rapidly enlarging or systemic lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma Constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss requiring exclusion of malignancy Airway compromise from large head and neck masses Confusing it with angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia, a distinct entity Failing to check for renal involvement and missing associated nephrotic syndrome Attributing the mass to malignancy without histological confirmation, or vice versa Assuming surgical excision is curative when relapse is common Overlooking the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained eosinophilia and raised IgE Kimura disease is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory condition of unknown cause, possibly reflecting an aberrant T-helper-2 driven allergic or autoimmune response. There is exuberant reactive lymphoid proliferation with well-formed germinal centres accompanied by heavy eosinophil recruitment, elevated IgE, and proliferation of small blood vessels within affected soft tissue and lymph nodes. Cytokines such as interleukin-4 and interleukin-5 are thought to promote the eosinophilia and IgE production. The immune dysregulation may also injure the glomerulus, accounting for the associated nephrotic syndrome. Kimura disease is benign and does not undergo malignant transformation, but it is characterised by a chronic, relapsing course with frequent recurrence after excision; associated nephrotic syndrome influences long-term outcome.

requiring evaluation Significant congenital heart disease needing cardiology management Recurrent or severe infection prompting immune assessment Mistaking the facial features and hypotonia for Down syndrome and not pursuing microarray Assuming a normal microarray excludes the diagnosis when an intragenic EHMT1 variant may be responsible Failing to anticipate and monitor for adolescent or adult Reduced EHMT1 activity, whether from a 9q34.3 deletion or an intragenic variant, dysregulates transcriptional programmes controlling neuronal development and function, producing intellectual disability, hypotonia, speech impairment, and behavioural features.
