Intellectual disability and speech impairment are lifelong and most individuals require ongoing support, with the additional long-term concern of possible regression or psychiatric deterioration in later life. Systemic complications are managed as they arise, and multidisciplinary care optimises function and wellbeing.

Klinefelter syndrome — 47,XXY, XXY syndrome, seminiferous tubule dysgenesis Other causes of primary hypogonadism Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Marfan syndrome (for tall stature) Fragile X syndrome (for learning difficulties) Constitutional tall stature Karyotype to confirm the diagnosis and define any mosaicism or higher-grade aneuploidy Testosterone with luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone measurement Semen analysis when fertility is a concern Bone density assessment given osteoporosis risk Metabolic screening for glucose intolerance and dyslipidaemia Most common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males, caused by one or more extra X chromosomes, typically a 47,XXY karyotype Often unrecognised until adolescence or adulthood, when hypogonadism and infertility prompt evaluation Characteristic features include tall stature with long legs, small firm testes, reduced facial and body hair, and gynaecomastia Testicular failure produces low testosterone with elevated gonadotrophins and, usually, azoospermia Learning difficulties, particularly with language and executive function, are common though intelligence is usually within the normal range Testosterone replacement supports pubertal development, bone health, and wellbeing but does not restore fertility Sperm retrieval techniques can occasionally allow biological fatherhood in selected men Associated with an increased risk of osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome, venous thromboembolism, and certain tumours Untreated hypogonadism leading to osteoporosis and fragility fractures Increased risk of venous thromboembolism Mediastinal germ cell tumours and a raised risk of male breast cancer Significant psychosocial and educational difficulties requiring support Delaying diagnosis by attributing tall stature and learning issues to other causes Overlooking hypogonadism and its long-term skeletal and metabolic consequences Assuming complete infertility without offering fertility counselling and sperm retrieval options Not screening for associated metabolic and thromboembolic risks Klinefelter syndrome results from the presence of one or more supernumerary X chromosomes in a phenotypic male, most commonly a single extra X producing a 47,XXY karyotype, arising from meiotic nondisjunction in either parent. The additional X chromosome material leads to progressive seminiferous tubule fibrosis and hyalinisation, causing primary testicular failure with impaired spermatogenesis and reduced testosterone production, while Leydig cell dysfunction raises luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone levels. Extra X-linked gene dosage, including genes escaping X-inactivation, is thought to underlie the tall stature, cognitive profile, and other systemic features. Higher-grade aneuploidies produce more severe phenotypes. Life expectancy is close to normal, and with testosterone replacement and multidisciplinary support most men lead full lives, though infertility is usual and comorbidity risk is increased.

Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome — KTS, Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome, angio-osteohypertrophy syndrome, PIK3CA-related overgrowth Parkes-Weber syndrome (high-flow arteriovenous malformations with overgrowth) CLOVES syndrome and other PIK3CA-related overgrowth phenotypes Proteus syndrome (AKT1 mosaic overgrowth) Sturge-Weber syndrome with facial capillary malformation Isolated venous or lymphatic malformation Maffucci syndrome with vascular malformations and enchondromas Targeted molecular testing for a mosaic PIK3CA variant on affected tissue where available Duplex ultrasound to map venous anatomy and detect deep venous anomalies or thrombosis MRI/MR venography to delineate the extent of vascular malformation and soft-tissue overgrowth Serial limb-length and orthopaedic assessment through childhood Coagulation studies (including D-dimer and fibrinogen) to assess localised intravascular coagulopathy Lymphoscintigraphy where lymphatic malformation is prominent A combined vascular malformation and overgrowth disorder, most often caused by a postzygotic mosaic activating variant in PIK3CA and placed within the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum Classic triad comprises a capillary malformation (port-wine stain), venous and/or lymphatic malformation, and limb overgrowth, usually affecting one lower limb Persistent embryonic lateral (marginal) veins and deep venous anomalies predispose to venous insufficiency and thromboembolism Limb-length and girth discrepancy can cause gait disturbance, scoliosis and orthopaedic complications requiring monitoring through growth Lymphatic malformations may cause recurrent cellulitis, lymphatic vesicles and leakage The presence of significant arteriovenous fistulae suggests Parkes-Weber syndrome, a related but distinct high-flow entity with different management Care is multidisciplinary, with compression, orthopaedic and interventional radiology input, and targeted mTOR/PI3K pathway inhibitors used in selected severe cases Signs of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism arising from venous anomalies Evidence of arteriovenous fistulae or high-output cardiac features suggesting Parkes-Weber syndrome Severe or recurrent bleeding from vascular malformations or gastrointestinal/pelvic involvement Recurrent cellulitis or rapidly worsening limb function and deformity Failing to distinguish Klippel-Trenaunay (low-flow) from Parkes-Weber (high-flow) disease, which changes management Overlooking localised intravascular coagulopathy and thromboembolic risk before procedures Neglecting orthopaedic surveillance for progressive limb-length discrepancy and scoliosis Intervening on anomalous superficial veins without confirming adequate deep venous drainage Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is largely driven by somatic mosaic activating variants in PIK3CA, which encodes the catalytic subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase. Because the variant arises after fertilisation, only a proportion of cells are affected, producing the segmental and asymmetric pattern of disease. Constitutive activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway promotes tissue growth and abnormal vascular development, giving rise to the combined capillary, venous and lymphatic malformations and the overgrowth of soft tissue and bone. Anomalous and persistent embryonic veins contribute to venous hypertension and thrombotic risk. The disorder is sporadic and not inherited. Most affected individuals have a normal life expectancy, but chronic pain, venous insufficiency, orthopaedic problems and recurrent infections cause significant long-term morbidity. Thromboembolic complications and, in some, extensive malformations are the principal serious risks, and targeted pathway inhibitors offer benefit in severe disease.

Krabbe disease — globoid cell leukodystrophy, galactosylceramidase deficiency, galactocerebrosidase deficiency, GALC deficiency Metachromatic leukodystrophy Other leukodystrophies including X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy GM1 and GM2 gangliosidoses Non-accidental injury or other causes of infantile irritability and hypertonia Acquired encephalopathies of infancy Assay of galactocerebrosidase enzyme activity, including newborn screening in some programmes GALC molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Psychosine measurement to support diagnosis and assess severity Brain MRI to characterise white matter involvement Nerve conduction studies and cerebrospinal fluid protein assessment An autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by deficiency of the enzyme galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramidase), leading to demyelination and formation of characteristic multinucleated globoid cells The classic early-infantile form presents in the first months with irritability, feeding difficulty, stiffness, and hyperirritability, followed by rapid neurodegeneration Marked irritability, hypertonicity, and exaggerated startle to stimuli are prominent early features Accumulation of the toxic metabolite psychosine (galactosylsphingosine) is central to the destruction of myelin-forming cells Peripheral neuropathy with slowed nerve conduction and raised cerebrospinal fluid protein commonly accompany the central disease Later-onset (late-infantile, juvenile, and adult) forms present with more insidious motor, visual, and cognitive decline MRI shows white matter change, and globoid cells are a defining pathological hallmark Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in presymptomatic infants can alter the course, while symptomatic infantile disease responds poorly Extreme irritability with hypertonia and feeding failure in early infancy Rapid neurodevelopmental regression Emerging seizures or loss of vision Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk Mistaking early extreme irritability and stiffness for colic, reflux, or a behavioural problem Confusing it with metachromatic leukodystrophy without appropriate enzyme testing Missing the narrow presymptomatic window for transplantation Overlooking peripheral neuropathy as a supportive diagnostic clue Krabbe disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GALC, encoding the lysosomal enzyme galactocerebrosidase. Deficient activity impairs degradation of galactolipids found in myelin, notably galactosylceramide, and leads to accumulation of the cytotoxic metabolite psychosine (galactosylsphingosine). Psychosine is toxic to oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, causing widespread loss of myelin-forming cells and demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous system. The pathological response includes infiltration by characteristic multinucleated macrophages (globoid cells), giving the alternative name globoid cell leukodystrophy. The early-infantile form is rapidly progressive and usually fatal within the first few years of life. Later-onset forms progress more slowly and variably. Stem cell transplantation offers benefit mainly when performed in presymptomatic infants, and once symptoms are established the outlook remains poor.

Kwashiorkor — oedematous malnutrition, protein-energy malnutrition (oedematous), protein malnutrition Marasmus and marasmic-kwashiorkor Nephrotic syndrome causing oedema and hypoalbuminaemia Protein-losing enteropathy Chronic liver disease with ascites and oedema Congestive cardiac failure Anthropometry with weight-for-height and mid-upper-arm circumference, and assessment for oedema Blood glucose to detect hypoglycaemia and temperature to detect hypothermia Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate Screening for infection, which is often occult Assessment for micronutrient deficiencies and anaemia The defining feature is bilateral pitting oedema, which can mask underlying wasting and lead to underestimation of the severity of malnutrition Other signs include a distended abdomen with fatty liver, sparse depigmented hair, flaky-paint dermatosis, apathy, and irritability It typically affects young children after weaning onto a starchy, protein-poor diet, often precipitated by an intercurrent infection It remains relevant in parts of India and other low-income settings, particularly in food-insecure and displaced populations Affected children are immunodeficient, so infection is common, frequently without fever, and is a leading cause of death Feeding must follow a cautious, staged protocol because rapid refeeding risks fatal metabolic and cardiac complications Hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbance must be actively sought and corrected Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, which are life-threatening in severe malnutrition Signs of sepsis, which may present without fever Circulatory or cardiac failure and danger of fluid overload with rehydration Refeeding-related electrolyte shifts during early nutritional rehabilitation Underestimating malnutrition because oedema masks wasting Refeeding too aggressively and precipitating cardiac failure or refeeding syndrome Overzealous intravenous rehydration causing fluid overload Missing occult infection because the usual signs of fever and inflammation are blunted Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition in which protein deficiency is relatively greater than energy deficiency. Reduced hepatic synthesis of albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, and this, together with increased capillary permeability, sodium retention, and oxidative stress, produces the characteristic oedema. Fatty infiltration of the liver reflects impaired lipoprotein export. Loss of immune competence, gut mucosal atrophy, and micronutrient deficiencies compound the picture, and metabolic adaptation to starvation makes the child vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, and dangerous fluid and electrolyte shifts during treatment. With careful staged nutritional rehabilitation and treatment of infection, recovery is possible, but mortality is high when complications such as sepsis, hypoglycaemia, or refeeding are not anticipated and managed.

Kyasanur Forest disease — KFD, monkey fever, Kyasanur forest disease virus infection Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever Severe dengue Leptospirosis Severe malaria Scrub typhus and other rickettsial infections Other viral encephalitides (for the neurological phase) Dengue haemorrhagic fever Leptospirosis Scrub typhus Severe malaria Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever RT-PCR for KFD viral RNA during the early viraemic phase KFD-specific IgM and IgG serology in the later course Full blood count, liver function, and coagulation studies to assess severity CSF examination and neuroimaging if the neurological second phase is suspected Exclusion of dengue, malaria, leptospirosis, and scrub typhus given the endemic overlap in India A tick-borne flaviviral haemorrhagic fever endemic to India, first recognised in the Kyasanur forest of Karnataka and now reported across several Western Ghats states Transmitted mainly by Haemaphysalis ticks, with monkeys serving as amplifying hosts, so the disease clusters among forest workers, farmers, and people with rural forest exposure Illness typically begins abruptly with high fever, severe headache, myalgia, and prostration, often with conjunctival injection and gastrointestinal symptoms A haemorrhagic phase with bleeding from gums, nose, or gut and thrombocytopenia may develop, and a subset of patients experience a biphasic course with a later neurological phase The second phase, after an afebrile interval, can bring meningoencephalitic features such as headache, tremor, and altered mentation Laboratory clues include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and raised transaminases; diagnosis is confirmed by RT-PCR early and serology later, handled with appropriate biosafety Management is supportive; a vaccine has been used in endemic districts of Karnataka, and tick-bite avoidance is central to prevention Mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding with progressive thrombocytopenia Return of fever with neurological features such as altered mentation, tremor, or meningism marking the second phase Hypotension, dehydration, or signs of multi-organ involvement Severe hepatic derangement or coagulopathy indicating a complicated course Attributing a forest-exposed febrile patient's illness to dengue or malaria and missing KFD in an endemic Western Ghats setting Interpreting the afebrile interval as recovery and discharging before the neurological second phase declares itself Neglecting biosafety precautions when handling blood and specimens from a suspected haemorrhagic fever Overlooking occupational and vaccination history in patients from endemic districts Kyasanur Forest disease virus is an RNA flavivirus transmitted to humans through the bite of infected hard ticks, with monkeys acting as amplifying hosts during epizootics. After inoculation the virus disseminates and infects multiple organs, producing viraemia with a systemic inflammatory response, increased vascular permeability, and haemorrhagic manifestations together with cytopenias and hepatic involvement. In some patients the virus involves the central nervous system during a second phase, producing meningoencephalitis. Most patients recover with supportive care, though the illness can be severe with haemorrhagic and neurological complications and a meaningful case-fatality rate; the biphasic form with encephalitis tends to have a more protracted recovery.

Lactational Mastitis — lactational mastitis, puerperal mastitis, breastfeeding mastitis, postpartum mastitis Breast abscess Blocked (plugged) duct without infection Engorgement Inflammatory breast carcinoma (especially if non-lactating or non-resolving) Candidal nipple or ductal infection causing pain Galactocele Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient; investigations are reserved for atypical or non-resolving cases Breast milk culture and sensitivity where infection is severe, recurrent, hospital-associated, or unresponsive to first-line antibiotics Breast ultrasound to identify or exclude an abscess when a fluctuant or non-resolving mass is present Needle aspiration of a suspected abscess for both diagnosis and drainage with culture of the aspirate Consideration of biopsy and specialist referral if inflammatory changes fail to resolve, to exclude malignancy Lactational mastitis is an inflammatory, usually infective, condition of the breast in a breastfeeding woman, presenting with a tender, hot, erythematous, wedge-shaped area often accompanied by fever and flu-like malaise It typically begins with milk stasis from ineffective or infrequent drainage, which then becomes secondarily infected, most often by Staphylococcus aureus entering through a cracked or damaged nipple Continued effective milk removal is the cornerstone of treatment; breastfeeding from the affected side should continue and is safe for the infant Supportive measures include frequent feeding or expression, correcting attachment and positioning, warmth before feeds and cold after for comfort, adequate hydration, rest, and simple analgesia Antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus are indicated when symptoms are severe, systemic, or fail to improve within a short period of conservative management, or when a nipple fissure is infected A localised fluctuant, non-resolving mass suggests a breast abscess, which requires drainage by needle aspiration or incision alongside antibiotics Failure to improve with appropriate treatment should prompt consideration of an abscess or, in a non-lactating or persistent case, inflammatory breast cancer Prevention centres on good breastfeeding technique, ensuring full drainage, avoiding abrupt weaning, and prompt attention to nipple trauma Recurrent mastitis warrants review of feeding technique and evaluation for a persistent focus or underlying breast pathology A fluctuant or non-resolving mass indicating breast abscess requiring drainage Systemic sepsis with high fever, rigors, tachycardia, or hypotension Failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics and milk drainage within a few days Persistent inflammatory changes, skin thickening, or peau d'orange raising concern for inflammatory breast cancer Overlying skin breakdown or rapidly spreading erythema Advising cessation of breastfeeding, which worsens stasis and prolongs the illness Failing to recognise and drain a breast abscess, treating with antibiotics alone Overlooking inflammatory breast cancer in non-lactating or persistent presentations Not addressing the underlying poor attachment or drainage, leading to recurrence Delaying antibiotics when systemic or severe features are present Inadequate or infrequent milk drainage leads to milk stasis and rising intraductal pressure, causing milk to leak into the surrounding stroma and provoke a local inflammatory response. Nipple trauma, commonly from poor latch, provides a portal of entry for skin flora, predominantly Staphylococcus aureus, so the stagnant milk becomes a culture medium and infection is established. If untreated, the localised infection can organise into a walled-off collection of pus, forming a breast abscess. The wedge-shaped distribution reflects involvement of a segment of the ductal-lobular system. Most cases resolve quickly with effective milk removal and, when needed, appropriate antibiotics, and breastfeeding can continue throughout. Delayed or inadequate treatment increases the risk of abscess formation, which then requires drainage. Recurrence is uncommon when feeding technique is optimised, and the majority of women recover fully without lasting effect on lactation.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — LEMS, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, myasthenic syndrome of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenia gravis Inflammatory or metabolic myopathy Motor neuron disease Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy Botulism (also a presynaptic disorder) Guillain-Barre syndrome Serum antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels Repetitive nerve stimulation at low and high frequency and post-exercise testing CT of the chest and, if negative, FDG-PET to search for small-cell lung cancer Interval tumour surveillance imaging when initial screening is negative but risk is high SOX1 antibodies as a marker supporting an underlying small-cell lung cancer Single-fibre electromyography in equivocal neuromuscular transmission cases A presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission caused by antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels that reduce acetylcholine release Presents with proximal limb weakness, especially the legs, together with autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation, and erectile dysfunction Strength may transiently improve with sustained or repeated effort (post-exercise facilitation), and depressed reflexes can augment after exercise Ocular and bulbar symptoms are usually milder than in myasthenia gravis, though some overlap occurs About half of cases are paraneoplastic, most often linked to small-cell lung cancer, and may precede the tumour diagnosis Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a low baseline compound muscle action potential with decrement at low frequency and marked increment at high frequency or after exercise Treatment addresses any underlying tumour and enhances acetylcholine release; immunotherapy is used for symptom control A validated screening score helps stratify the likelihood of underlying small-cell lung cancer and guides surveillance Any new diagnosis should trigger a directed search for occult malignancy, especially small-cell lung cancer Weight loss, haemoptysis, or a smoking history increasing suspicion of underlying tumour Progressive bulbar or respiratory weakness requiring monitoring of airway and ventilation Severe autonomic failure causing symptomatic hypotension or gastrointestinal stasis Misdiagnosing LEMS as myasthenia gravis and missing the search for lung cancer Stopping tumour surveillance too early after an initially negative chest scan Overlooking autonomic symptoms that are an important diagnostic clue Failing to appreciate post-exercise facilitation on examination and electrophysiology Attributing proximal weakness to a primary myopathy without neuromuscular junction testing In LEMS, IgG autoantibodies target P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic motor nerve terminal. Reduced calcium influx during depolarisation diminishes the quantal release of acetylcholine, so the endplate potential often fails to reach threshold at rest, causing weakness. Repeated activity allows calcium to accumulate in the terminal, temporarily augmenting release and improving strength, which explains facilitation. The same antibodies act on autonomic ganglia and terminals, producing cholinergic autonomic failure. In paraneoplastic cases the tumour expresses calcium channels that trigger the cross-reactive immune response. Symptoms often improve with treatment of any underlying cancer and with therapies that enhance acetylcholine release; the overall outlook is dominated by the associated malignancy when present, whereas non-paraneoplastic disease tends to follow a more indolent, manageable course.

Lamellar ichthyosis — TGM1, transglutaminase-1 deficiency, autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, LI Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma Harlequin ichthyosis (severe end of spectrum) X-linked ichthyosis Netherton syndrome Ichthyosis vulgaris Acquired ichthyosis from systemic disease Molecular genetic testing including TGM1 and other congenital ichthyosis genes Skin biopsy showing marked orthohyperkeratosis with a normal or thickened granular layer In vitro transglutaminase-1 activity assay where available Ophthalmology assessment for ectropion and corneal exposure Assessment of thermoregulation and hydration, particularly in neonates Prenatal or carrier genetic testing for at-risk families A form of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis, most often caused by variants in TGM1 encoding transglutaminase-1, with several other causative genes Typically presents at birth as a collodion baby encased in a taut, shiny membrane that sheds over the first weeks Evolves into large, plate-like, dark brown adherent scales with relatively little underlying erythema, contrasting with the erythrodermic phenotype Ectropion and eclabium are common and cause chronic ocular exposure problems Scalp scarring alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, and reduced sweating with heat intolerance are frequent Sits on a clinical spectrum with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma; some patients show overlapping features Management centres on topical emollients and keratolytics, with oral retinoids for severe disease Neonatal dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and temperature instability in the collodion phase Corneal exposure and ulceration from severe ectropion Heat intolerance and hyperthermia from impaired sweating Secondary skin infection of fissured skin Assuming all collodion babies have lamellar ichthyosis when the membrane can precede several distinct disorders Overlooking heat intolerance from anhidrosis, risking hyperthermia in warm environments or exercise Neglecting ophthalmic monitoring for ectropion-related corneal damage Failing to counsel on the recessive inheritance and recurrence risk Lamellar ichthyosis most commonly arises from deficiency of transglutaminase-1, an enzyme that cross-links structural proteins to form the cornified cell envelope and covalently attaches lipids to the envelope surface. Loss of enzyme activity prevents formation of a normal cornified envelope and disrupts the lipid scaffold of the stratum corneum, impairing the permeability barrier and desquamation. Compensatory hyperproliferation and retention of corneocytes produce the characteristic thick, plate-like scaling. Other causative genes (including those for lipid transport and processing) can produce overlapping phenotypes within the autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis spectrum. It is a lifelong disorder; after the vulnerable collodion period most patients stabilise into chronic generalised scaling that requires continuous skin care, with visual and thermoregulatory complications influencing overall morbidity.

Landau-Kleffner syndrome — LKS, acquired epileptic aphasia, acquired aphasia with epilepsy Autism spectrum disorder with language regression Acquired hearing loss or auditory processing disorder Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep (broader spectrum) Other causes of acquired childhood aphasia (structural or inflammatory) Selective mutism and psychiatric causes of language loss Neurodegenerative or metabolic regression Sleep EEG or prolonged/overnight EEG to demonstrate electrical status epilepticus in slow-wave sleep Formal audiological assessment to exclude deafness Language, developmental and neuropsychological evaluation Brain MRI to exclude a structural or inflammatory cause Genetic and, where indicated, metabolic or autoimmune investigations An acquired epileptic aphasia in which a previously normally developing child loses language, typically between three and eight years of age The hallmark is acquired verbal auditory agnosia, so children may appear not to understand speech and can be mistaken for deaf The EEG shows marked activation of epileptiform discharges during sleep, often reaching electrical status epilepticus in slow-wave sleep Clinical seizures may be infrequent or absent, so the language regression and EEG findings are central to diagnosis Behavioural disturbance and features overlapping with autism spectrum disorder commonly accompany the language loss It lies on a continuum with the broader condition of epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep Treatment aims to suppress the sleep-activated discharges, using antiseizure medication and corticosteroid or immunomodulatory therapy in resistant cases Progressive loss of language and comprehension in a previously typical child Electrical status epilepticus in slow-wave sleep on EEG Marked behavioural or autistic regression accompanying language loss Failure of language to recover despite apparent seizure control Misdiagnosing the child as deaf or as having primary autism and missing the EEG diagnosis Relying on a routine awake EEG, which may miss the sleep-activated discharges Judging treatment success by seizure control alone rather than language recovery Delaying immunomodulatory or steroid therapy in resistant cases with ongoing regression Landau-Kleffner syndrome is an epileptic encephalopathy in which intense epileptiform activity, markedly activated during non-REM sleep, disrupts the function of language-related cortical networks, particularly perisylvian regions. Continuous or near-continuous spike-wave discharges through slow-wave sleep are thought to interfere with the sleep-dependent consolidation and maturation of language and other higher functions, producing acquired aphasia and cognitive-behavioural regression even when overt seizures are few. The underlying cause is often unknown, with genetic and immune contributions implicated in some cases. Seizures, when present, usually remit by adolescence, but language and cognitive outcomes are variable and a significant proportion of children have persistent language or learning difficulties. Earlier recognition and effective suppression of the sleep-activated discharges are associated with better language recovery.

Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis — LCH, histiocytosis X, eosinophilic granuloma, Hand-Schuller-Christian disease, Letterer-Siwe disease Osteomyelitis or Ewing sarcoma (for bone lesions) Leukaemia or lymphoma Neuroblastoma with bony metastases Seborrhoeic or atopic dermatitis (for skin lesions) Other histiocytic disorders (e.g. haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma) Chronic infection (e.g. tuberculosis) Biopsy with immunohistochemistry for CD1a and CD207 (langerin) BRAF V600E and broader MAPK pathway mutation testing Skeletal imaging survey (radiographs and/or PET) to map bone lesions Assessment of risk organs: liver and spleen imaging, full blood count, liver function Endocrine evaluation and MRI of the pituitary/hypothalamus if diabetes insipidus is suspected Baseline evaluation for pulmonary and CNS involvement when indicated A clonal proliferative disorder of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can range from a single isolated lesion to widespread multisystem disease. Bone is the most commonly involved site, often presenting as a painful lytic lesion, classically in the skull but also in other flat and long bones. Skin involvement can mimic seborrhoeic dermatitis or a persistent scaly, petechial rash, particularly in infants. Diabetes insipidus from pituitary or hypothalamic involvement is a characteristic endocrine manifestation and may be the presenting feature. Risk organ involvement (liver, spleen, and bone marrow) identifies higher-risk multisystem disease with greater mortality. Diagnosis rests on biopsy showing characteristic cells expressing CD1a and CD207 (langerin); Birbeck granules may be seen on electron microscopy. Many cases harbour activating mutations in the MAPK pathway, most commonly BRAF V600E, which has therapeutic implications. Treatment ranges from observation or local therapy for single-system disease to systemic chemotherapy for multisystem or risk-organ disease. Risk-organ (liver, spleen, marrow) involvement indicating high-risk multisystem disease Cytopenias suggesting marrow infiltration Polyuria and polydipsia indicating diabetes insipidus from CNS/pituitary disease Rapidly progressive multisystem disease in an infant Neurodegenerative CNS involvement causing progressive neurological decline Mistaking the infantile skin rash for simple seborrhoeic dermatitis and delaying diagnosis Overlooking diabetes insipidus as an early or isolated manifestation Assuming a solitary lytic bone lesion is infection or a benign cyst without biopsy Failing to assess for risk-organ involvement, which changes treatment intensity and prognosis Langerhans cell histiocytosis is now understood as a myeloid neoplasm driven by activating mutations of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, most often BRAF V600E, in dendritic cell precursors. Constitutive pathway activation causes accumulation of pathological CD1a-positive, langerin-positive histiocytes that, together with eosinophils and other inflammatory cells, form granulomatous infiltrates. These lesions destroy local tissue (such as lytic bone lesions) and, when disseminated, impair function of organs including the liver, spleen, marrow, and pituitary. Single-system disease, especially isolated bone lesions, often has an excellent prognosis and may even regress; multisystem disease with risk-organ involvement carries higher mortality. Survivors are at risk of long-term sequelae such as diabetes insipidus, other endocrinopathies, orthopaedic problems, and neurodegeneration.

Larsen syndrome — FLNB, filamin B disorder Atelosteogenesis (also FLNB-related) Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita Ehlers-Danlos syndromes with joint instability Desbuquois dysplasia Otopalatodigital spectrum disorders Recessive Larsen-like syndromes Skeletal survey documenting joint dislocations, accessory carpal ossification, and spinal anomalies Cervical spine imaging including flexion-extension views to assess kyphosis and instability FLNB molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Airway and respiratory assessment for tracheomalacia before anaesthesia Echocardiography where cardiac involvement is suspected Audiological assessment for hearing loss Characterised by congenital dislocations of large joints, notably bilateral knee dislocations, together with hip and elbow dislocations and severe talipes The dominant form is caused by variants in FLNB encoding filamin B, a cytoskeletal protein regulating chondrocyte function; rarer recessive Larsen-like phenotypes have distinct causes A characteristic flat facial appearance with a depressed nasal bridge, prominent forehead, and widely spaced eyes aids recognition Hand findings include cylindrical, spatulate fingers and, radiographically, an accessory carpal ossification centre Cervical spine abnormalities with kyphosis and instability are a critical hazard that can cause myelopathy and complicate airway management Additional features may include cleft palate, hearing loss, and, in some, cardiac and respiratory (tracheomalacia) involvement Diagnosis integrates the pattern of congenital joint dislocations and facial features with FLNB molecular testing Cervical kyphosis or instability with myelopathy, particularly around anaesthesia Airway compromise from tracheomalacia or cervical involvement Neurological deterioration from spinal cord compression Respiratory distress in infancy Overlooking cervical kyphosis and instability, risking cord injury during airway management Reducing knee or hip dislocations without recognising the underlying syndrome and its spinal risks Failing to assess for tracheomalacia before anaesthesia Confusing it with arthrogryposis without appropriate radiographic and genetic evaluation Larsen syndrome most often results from dominant variants in FLNB, which encodes filamin B, a cytoskeletal protein that cross-links actin and regulates signalling and mechanical responses in chondrocytes. Disturbed filamin B function alters chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation and the development of joints, ligaments, and the vertebral column. This produces the hallmark congenital large-joint dislocations, ligamentous laxity, cervical spine anomalies, and characteristic craniofacial and hand features. FLNB variants underlie a spectrum of skeletal disorders ranging from Larsen syndrome to more severe atelosteogenesis phenotypes. With careful orthopaedic and spinal management, intelligence and lifespan are generally normal, but untreated cervical instability can cause devastating neurological injury, and joint dislocations and foot deformity require staged surgical and physiotherapy management.

Laryngeal cancer — larynx cancer, laryngeal carcinoma, cancer of the voice box Benign vocal cord lesions such as nodules, polyps, or cysts Chronic laryngitis or reflux-related laryngeal irritation Vocal cord palsy from other causes Laryngeal papillomatosis Hypopharyngeal or thyroid carcinoma involving the larynx Granulomatous or infective laryngitis (e.g. tuberculosis) Flexible or rigid laryngoscopy to inspect the larynx and vocal cord mobility Direct laryngoscopy with biopsy under anaesthesia for tissue diagnosis and mapping CT or MRI of the neck to assess local invasion, cartilage involvement, and nodal spread CT chest and PET-CT for distant staging and synchronous second primaries Assessment of voice, swallowing, and airway to guide organ-preservation decisions The vast majority are squamous cell carcinomas, and tobacco and alcohol use are the dominant, synergistic risk factors, with HPV playing a lesser role than in oropharyngeal cancer Persistent hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks is the classic early symptom of glottic tumours and warrants prompt laryngoscopic assessment Supraglottic and subglottic tumours often present later with sore throat, referred otalgia, dysphagia, a neck mass, or airway symptoms because they cause voice change only when advanced Anatomical subsite matters: glottic cancers tend to present early with hoarseness and have relatively sparse lymphatics, while supraglottic cancers spread earlier to cervical nodes Diagnosis requires visualisation of the larynx with flexible or rigid endoscopy and biopsy, together with imaging to define tumour extent and nodal disease Early-stage disease can be treated with either radiotherapy or conservation surgery, including transoral laser microsurgery, with excellent voice-preservation outcomes Advanced disease is managed with organ-preservation chemoradiotherapy or total laryngectomy, balancing cure against loss of natural voice and swallowing function Stridor or rapidly worsening airway obstruction is an emergency that may require urgent airway intervention before definitive treatment Hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks, especially in a smoker Stridor or progressive airway obstruction requiring urgent airway management A firm cervical lymph node with throat symptoms Dysphagia, odynophagia, or referred ear pain with weight loss Attributing persistent hoarseness to benign causes without laryngoscopy Missing advanced supraglottic tumours that present without early voice change Underestimating impending airway compromise in a patient with stridor Neglecting the functional impact of treatment on voice and swallowing when counselling patients Laryngeal carcinoma arises from the squamous epithelium lining the supraglottis, glottis, or subglottis. Chronic carcinogen exposure from tobacco smoke and alcohol produces field change with progressive dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Behaviour depends on subsite anatomy: the true vocal cords have limited lymphatic drainage so glottic tumours cause early hoarseness but spread to nodes late, whereas the richly lymphatic supraglottis allows earlier cervical nodal metastasis. Local extension can involve cartilage, paraglottic and pre-epiglottic spaces, and adjacent hypopharynx. Early glottic cancers have high cure and voice-preservation rates, whereas advanced or node-positive supraglottic and subglottic tumours carry poorer prognosis; overall outcome depends on stage, subsite, and treatment response.

Laryngeal papillomatosis — recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, RRP, juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis, laryngeal papilloma Vocal cord nodules or polyps Laryngeal keratosis or leukoplakia Laryngeal in a juvenile form, typically multiple and more aggressive, and an adult form that is often more localised The usual presentation is progressive hoarseness or a weak or abnormal cry in a child, and atypical lesions warrant biopsy Progressive stridor and airway obstruction from bulky laryngeal disease requiring urgent airway management Distal spread into the trachea and bronchi indicating aggressive disease Features suggesting malignant transformation such as a firm, ulcerated, or rapidly enlarging lesion Rapid recurrence needing frequent surgical intervention Aggressive surgery that damages the vocal cords and causes scarring or web formation Performing a tracheostomy that may encourage distal tracheobronchial spread Assuming benignity and not biopsying atypical or persistent lesions Overlooking airway compromise in a child presenting only with a hoarse cry Laryngeal papillomatosis results from infection of the respiratory epithelium by human papillomavirus, most often types 6 and 11, which drives proliferation of squamous epithelium into finger-like papillary fronds supported by fibrovascular cores. Lesions favour the transition zones between squamous and ciliary epithelium, so the vocal cords are commonly affected. In children the virus is usually acquired at birth from an infected maternal genital tract, and the immature or immunologically naive host tends to develop multiple, recurrent lesions. Latent virus in adjacent normal-looking mucosa underlies the persistent recurrence after removal, and lesions may seed distally in the airway. The course is unpredictable and marked by recurrence; juvenile disease may require many procedures over years before eventual regression around puberty in some children, while adult disease is often more limited, and although malignant change is rare it is an important long-term consideration.

difficulty, especially in a child, suggesting airway compromise or epiglottitis Hoarseness persisting beyond a few weeks in a smoker raising concern for laryngeal cancer Associated dysphagia, weight loss, haemoptysis or a neck mass Rapidly worsening symptoms with drooling and toxaemia Attributing persistent hoarseness to simple laryngitis and delaying laryngoscopy in a smoker Overlooking laryngopharyngeal reflux as a driver of chronic symptoms Underestimating airway risk in a child with laryngeal inflammation Failing to address vocal misuse and continued irritant exposure Laryngitis is inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa, especially the vocal folds. In acute laryngitis, viral (or sometimes bacterial) infection produces mucosal hyperaemia and oedema that increase the mass and stiffness of the vocal folds, disturbing their vibratory pattern and causing hoarseness. In chronic laryngitis, sustained irritation from voice overuse, tobacco smoke, gastric reflux or persistent infection leads to ongoing mucosal changes such as oedema, thickening and keratosis. In children, the narrow subglottis means that inflammatory swelling can significantly compromise the airway. Acute laryngitis usually resolves within days to a couple of weeks with conservative measures, whereas chronic laryngitis requires removal of the underlying irritant for improvement; persistent hoarseness always warrants exclusion of a serious cause.

Laryngomalacia — floppy larynx, congenital laryngeal stridor, soft larynx Vocal cord paralysis Subglottic stenosis Vascular ring or other extrinsic airway compression Laryngeal web, cyst, or haemangioma Tracheomalacia Acquired causes of stridor such as croup or foreign body Flexible awake laryngoscopy Assessment of feeding and growth Pulse oximetry or sleep study if obstruction or apnoea is suspected Bronchoscopy or airway endoscopy to exclude synchronous lesions in severe or atypical cases Evaluation for gastro-oesophageal reflux when contributory Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of chronic stridor in infants and results from collapse of soft, immature supraglottic structures during inspiration. The typical presentation is inspiratory stridor that begins in the first weeks of life, worsens with feeding, crying, agitation, or lying supine, and improves when the infant is calm or prone. In most infants the condition is mild and self-limiting, with symptoms peaking in the early months and resolving as the airway matures, usually within the first one to two years. Flexible laryngoscopy in the awake infant is the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating the characteristic dynamic supraglottic collapse. Gastro-oesophageal reflux commonly coexists and can aggravate symptoms, so it is often addressed as part of management. Feeding difficulty, choking or coughing with feeds, and poor weight gain indicate more significant disease and warrant closer evaluation. Severe disease with significant obstruction, apnoea, or failure to thrive may require surgical intervention such as supraglottoplasty. Persistent or atypical stridor should prompt evaluation for additional or synchronous airway lesions. Cyanosis, apnoea, or significant desaturation Marked work of breathing or worsening obstruction Feeding difficulty with choking, aspiration, or failure to thrive Stridor that is severe, progressive, or atypical for laryngomalacia Life-threatening obstructive episodes Assuming all infant stridor is laryngomalacia and missing another airway lesion Underestimating severity by not assessing feeding, growth, and oxygenation Overlooking a synchronous second airway abnormality Failing to recognise and manage contributing gastro-oesophageal reflux In laryngomalacia the supraglottic tissues, including the epiglottis and aryepiglottic folds, are excessively soft and poorly supported, and there is often associated neuromuscular immaturity affecting airway tone and coordination. During inspiration the negative airway pressure draws these floppy structures inward, causing dynamic collapse over the laryngeal inlet and producing turbulent airflow and inspiratory stridor. The obstruction is worse when airflow demand or negative pressure increases, such as with crying, feeding, or agitation, and lessens with maturation as the tissues become firmer and neuromuscular control improves. Coexisting reflux can worsen supraglottic oedema and symptoms. The outlook is excellent for the majority, in whom mild laryngomalacia resolves spontaneously as the airway matures; a minority with severe disease require surgery, which is generally effective.

Lassa fever — Lassa virus infection, Lassa haemorrhagic fever, VHF Severe malaria Typhoid (enteric) fever Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola, CCHF) Severe bacterial sepsis Leptospirosis Severe dengue Severe malaria Typhoid fever Ebola virus disease Bacterial sepsis RT-PCR for Lassa virus RNA in early illness, performed under strict biosafety Lassa-specific IgM and IgG serology and antigen detection where available Full blood count, liver and renal function, and coagulation studies to gauge severity Exclusion of malaria and typhoid, which are common and treatable co-considerations in endemic regions All sampling coordinated with the laboratory and public health authorities under enhanced biosafety A viral haemorrhagic fever endemic to West Africa, caused by an arenavirus, with the multimammate rat as the natural reservoir; humans are infected through contact with rodent excreta or contaminated food Onset is typically gradual with fever, malaise, headache, sore throat, and retrosternal or muscular pain, which makes early distinction from other febrile illnesses difficult Many infections are mild or subclinical, but severe cases progress to bleeding, facial and neck oedema, pleural and pericardial effusions, encephalopathy, and shock Sensorineural hearing loss is a characteristic and often permanent complication, sometimes occurring during recovery Person-to-person and nosocomial transmission through body fluids is well recognised, so isolation, barrier precautions, and safe specimen handling are essential It is especially severe in pregnancy, with high maternal and fetal mortality, particularly in the third trimester This is a medical emergency and a notifiable disease; ribavirin is used and is most effective when started early, alongside intensive supportive care Mucosal bleeding, facial or neck oedema, or effusions indicating severe disease Encephalopathy, seizures, or rapidly rising transaminases Hypotension, shock, or signs of multi-organ failure Any suspected case requires immediate isolation, barrier nursing, and notification because of high nosocomial transmission risk, with pregnancy signalling especially high risk Delaying isolation and barrier precautions, exposing staff and other patients to nosocomial spread Attributing the gradual febrile onset solely to malaria or typhoid and missing Lassa in an endemic or travel context Starting antiviral therapy too late, when its benefit is greatest early in the illness Overlooking evolving hearing loss and failing to counsel about this recognised sequela Lassa virus is an enveloped RNA arenavirus that, after exposure to rodent excreta or infected body fluids, replicates in multiple organs and suppresses innate immune responses. Widespread infection of endothelial cells and immune dysregulation lead to impaired vascular integrity and platelet dysfunction rather than large-scale tissue necrosis, producing capillary leak, oedema, and haemorrhage. Hepatic, adrenal, and endothelial involvement, together with a poorly controlled inflammatory response, drive progression to shock and multi-organ failure in severe cases. Most infections are mild, but hospitalised severe cases carry a high case-fatality rate, worse with delayed treatment, bleeding, and organ failure; survivors may be left with permanent sensorineural hearing loss, and pregnancy is associated with markedly poorer maternal and fetal outcomes.

Unexplained weight loss suggesting advancing insulin deficiency Coexisting autoimmune disorders such as adrenal or thyroid disease Assuming all adult-onset diabetes is type 2 and missing the autoimmune nature Delaying insulin when oral agents are clearly failing Not testing autoantibodies in a leaner adult with atypical type 2 diabetes Overlooking associated autoimmune endocrine disease Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults is an autoimmune diabetes in which immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells proceeds more slowly than in classic childhood type 1 diabetes. Circulating islet autoantibodies, most often against glutamic acid decarboxylase, reflect this ongoing autoimmune process. Because residual beta-cell function persists at diagnosis, patients initially maintain some endogenous insulin secretion and may be controlled without insulin, but progressive loss of beta-cell mass leads to eventual insulin dependence. The disorder shares genetic and immunological features with type 1 diabetes while its adult onset and initial non-insulin-requiring course cause frequent misclassification as type 2 diabetes. Patients generally progress to insulin dependence over months to years as beta-cell function declines; with timely recognition and appropriate transition to insulin, glycaemic control and complication risk can be managed similarly to other forms of diabetes, and monitoring for associated autoimmune conditions is advisable.

Latent tuberculosis infection — LTBI, latent TB, TB infection Active pulmonary tuberculosis (must be excluded) Prior BCG vaccination causing tuberculin reactivity Non-tuberculous mycobacterial sensitisation Old healed tuberculosis on imaging without active disease Subclinical active tuberculosis Non-tuberculous mycobacterial exposure causing test cross-reactivity BCG-related tuberculin positivity Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay to detect infection Symptom screening and chest radiography to exclude active tuberculosis HIV testing given its major impact on reactivation risk Assessment for other risk factors such as diabetes, immunosuppressive therapy and silicosis Sputum evaluation if any features suggest active disease Latent tuberculosis infection is a state of persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis without clinical, radiological or bacteriological evidence of active disease People with LTBI are asymptomatic and non-infectious, but carry a lifetime risk of reactivation into active tuberculosis, greatest in the first two years after infection Diagnosis relies on the tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assays, both of which detect immune sensitisation but cannot distinguish latent from active disease Active tuberculosis must always be excluded, by symptom screening and chest imaging, before treating someone for latent infection Reactivation risk is markedly increased by HIV, anti-TNF therapy, organ transplantation, silicosis, diabetes, malnutrition and other immunosuppressive states TB preventive treatment substantially reduces the risk of progression, using rifamycin- or isoniazid-based short-course regimens without specifying doses India's NTEP prioritises TB preventive treatment for household contacts of pulmonary TB, people living with HIV and other high-risk groups as part of the End TB strategy Any symptoms or imaging findings suggesting active tuberculosis, which changes management entirely Recent close contact with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis, especially in children under five Planned immunosuppression such as anti-TNF therapy or transplantation Coexisting HIV infection markedly raising reactivation risk Starting preventive treatment without first excluding active tuberculosis, risking monotherapy of active disease and resistance Interpreting a positive test as active disease when it only indicates infection Overlooking preventive treatment in eligible high-risk contacts and people living with HIV Ignoring the reduced sensitivity of immune-based tests in severe immunosuppression After inhalation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most immunocompetent individuals mount a cell-mediated immune response that contains the organism within granulomas, where bacilli persist in a dormant, metabolically quiescent state. This equilibrium between host immunity and bacillary persistence defines latency, and there is likely a spectrum from complete eradication to subclinical infection. When immunity wanes or is suppressed, dormant bacilli can resume replication, breaching the granuloma and producing active, potentially transmissible disease. The tuberculin and interferon-gamma tests measure the memory T-cell response to mycobacterial antigens rather than the presence of live bacilli. Most people with latent infection never develop active disease, but progression risk is highest soon after infection and in the immunocompromised; TB preventive treatment substantially lowers this risk and is central to India's elimination goals.

Latex allergy — natural rubber latex allergy, latex hypersensitivity, NRL allergy Irritant contact dermatitis from gloves or hand hygiene Type IV allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerator chemicals Anaphylaxis from perioperative drugs, antiseptics (chlorhexidine), or antibiotics Food-related latex-fruit cross-reactive allergy Idiopathic urticaria or angioedema Serum latex-specific IgE testing Skin prick testing with a standardised latex extract where available Patch testing for suspected delayed contact dermatitis to rubber chemicals Serum tryptase during a suspected acute systemic reaction Supervised glove-use or challenge testing in specialist settings when the diagnosis is uncertain IgE-mediated (type I) reactions to natural rubber latex proteins range from contact urticaria to rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma, and anaphylaxis, and are distinct from irritant or allergic contact dermatitis from rubber-processing chemicals Healthcare workers, patients with spina bifida or urogenital anomalies, and those with repeated surgical or catheter exposure are at highest risk owing to frequent mucosal and cutaneous contact Powdered gloves historically amplified sensitisation because latex allergen adsorbed to cornstarch became airborne, so a shift to powder-free low-protein or non-latex gloves has markedly reduced new cases The latex-fruit syndrome reflects cross-reactivity between latex proteins and plant allergens, so patients may also react to banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut Diagnosis combines a compatible history with skin testing and serum latex-specific IgE; a validated skin test extract may not be uniformly available, making the history and in-vitro testing important Reactions can occur through skin, mucosal, inhalational, or parenteral routes, and intraoperative anaphylaxis may be the presenting event when latex is contacted internally Cornerstones of care are strict avoidance, a latex-safe environment for procedures, medical-alert identification, and a self-injectable adrenaline device for those with systemic reactions Type IV allergic contact dermatitis from rubber accelerators (e.g. thiurams, carbamates) presents as delayed eczema and is confirmed by patch testing, not by IgE tests Intraoperative or procedural anaphylaxis with hypotension or bronchospasm requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline and removal of all latex sources Progressive airway or respiratory symptoms after mucosal or inhalational latex exposure Systemic reaction in a high-risk patient (spina bifida, multiple surgeries) not previously identified as latex-allergic Recurrent reactions despite avoidance suggesting unrecognised hidden latex exposure Confusing delayed contact dermatitis from rubber chemicals with true IgE-mediated latex allergy Failing to arrange a latex-safe environment for surgery or dental and radiological procedures Overlooking cross-reactive foods in the latex-fruit syndrome Not counselling the patient to carry medical-alert identification and an adrenaline device Type I latex allergy results from IgE sensitisation to water-soluble proteins in natural rubber harvested from Hevea brasiliensis. Repeated cutaneous, mucosal, or airborne exposure drives production of latex-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils; re-exposure cross-links this IgE and triggers mediator release causing urticaria, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis. Airborne allergen bound to glove powder facilitates respiratory sensitisation. Structural homology between latex proteins (e.g. hevein-related and profilin allergens) and plant proteins accounts for cross-reactivity in the latex-fruit syndrome. A separate delayed, T-cell-mediated contact dermatitis is caused not by latex protein but by rubber-manufacturing chemicals. With reliable avoidance and a latex-safe healthcare environment, most patients avoid further reactions and occupational sensitisation often improves after exposure ceases. Unrecognised sensitisation, however, can lead to severe or fatal perioperative anaphylaxis.

Long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency — LCHAD deficiency, LCHADD, HADHA deficiency, mitochondrial trifunctional protein alpha-subunit deficiency, long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency Generalised mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency (alpha and beta subunit involvement) Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II and translocase deficiencies Other causes of infantile cardiomyopathy or hepatopathy Inherited retinal dystrophies and peripheral neuropathies of other cause Sepsis or metabolic acidosis in a decompensating infant Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing raised long-chain hydroxyacylcarnitines (e.g. C16-OH, C18:1-OH) Urine organic acids seeking 3-hydroxydicarboxylic aciduria Blood glucose, ketones, ammonia, lactate and liver function during illness Ophthalmological assessment and electroretinography for retinopathy, and nerve conduction studies for neuropathy HADHA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Echocardiography and creatine kinase during acute decompensation Caused by HADHA variants affecting the alpha subunit of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein, which carries the long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity; the common c.1528G>C variant is characteristic Distinctive complications not seen in most other oxidation defects are progressive pigmentary retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy Carrying an affected fetus is strongly associated with maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome Newborn screening shows elevated long-chain hydroxyacylcarnitines, notably 3-hydroxytetradecanoylcarnitine (C16-OH) and related hydroxy species Acute presentations include hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, hepatic dysfunction and rhabdomyolysis, overlapping with generalised trifunctional protein deficiency Management combines long-chain fat restriction with medium-chain triglyceride substitution, avoidance of fasting and an emergency regimen during illness Regular ophthalmological surveillance is needed because retinopathy can progress despite metabolic control Maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome prompting testing of the infant Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy or cardiomyopathy Rhabdomyolysis with pigmenturia and acute kidney injury risk Progressive visual loss or neuropathic symptoms indicating chronic complications Not testing the neonate after maternal acute fatty liver of pregnancy or HELLP syndrome Overlooking retinopathy or neuropathy because acute metabolic control appears adequate Using unrestricted long-chain fat instead of medium-chain triglyceride substitution Permitting fasting for procedures without a glucose-containing infusion The mitochondrial trifunctional protein is a membrane-bound complex that catalyses three sequential steps of long-chain fatty-acid beta-oxidation; isolated LCHAD deficiency reflects selective loss of the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity of its alpha subunit. Blocked long-chain oxidation impairs energy supply to heart, muscle and liver during fasting and stress and prevents hepatic ketogenesis, while accumulation of long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl metabolites is thought to be toxic and to underlie the retinopathy and neuropathy. Transplacental passage of these hydroxy intermediates from an affected fetus is implicated in the maternal liver disease of pregnancy. Early screen-detected diagnosis and dietary management improve survival and reduce acute crises, but retinopathy and neuropathy may progress over time, so long-term morbidity remains a concern even with good metabolic control.

hyperopia A group of severe inherited retinal dystrophies presenting in infancy with profound visual impairment, usually autosomal recessive Caused by variants in many genes, including RPE65, CEP290, disc pallor RPE65-associated disease is treatable with an approved subretinal gene therapy, making genetic diagnosis clinically actionable Certain genotypes have systemic associations (e.g. CEP290 with ciliopathy features), so systemic evaluation may be warranted Systemic features suggesting an associated ciliopathy (renal impairment, neurological or developmental signs) Rapidly progressive visual loss or atypical course prompting reassessment Failure to consider a treatable genotype (e.g. RPE65) that has an approved therapy Attributing infantile nystagmus and poor vision to cortical visual impairment without electrophysiology Failing to obtain genetic testing and missing a treatable RPE65 genotype Overlooking systemic ciliopathy associations that require renal or neurological monitoring Not correcting the frequently high hyperopic refractive error Leber congenital amaurosis encompasses genetically heterogeneous defects that disrupt photoreceptor development or function and the visual (retinoid) cycle. In RPE65-related disease, for example, the retinal pigment epithelium cannot regenerate the chromophore needed to restore light sensitivity to photoreceptors, so phototransduction fails and photoreceptors degenerate. Other causative genes impair photoreceptor ciliary transport, guanylate cyclase signalling, or outer-segment structure. The common consequence is early and severe loss of rod and cone function, reflected in a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram and progressive retinal degeneration. Vision is severely impaired from infancy and most genotypes are progressive, though some are relatively stable; the prognosis is being transformed for RPE65-related disease by gene therapy, and genotype-specific trials are altering outlook for other subtypes.

sequential involvement of the second eye Atypical features (pain, response to steroids, or optic disc leakage) suggesting an alternative diagnosis Systemic or neurological signs indicating a 'LHON-plus' phenotype Continued smoking or alcohol exposure accelerating visual loss Misdiagnosing it as atypical optic neuritis and giving prolonged unhelpful immunosuppression Failing to counsel on maternal inheritance and the risk to relatives Overlooking modifiable triggers such as smoking and alcohol in carriers Not recognising the disc appearance can mimic true papilloedema early on Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is caused by pathogenic point mutations in mitochondrial DNA that impair complex I of the respiratory chain, reducing ATP production and increasing oxidative stress. Retinal ganglion cells, particularly the small fibres of the papillomacular bundle, are exquisitely dependent on mitochondrial energy and are preferentially vulnerable. Energy failure and oxidative damage trigger dysfunction and then apoptotic loss of these ganglion cells, producing the characteristic central visual loss and subsequent optic atrophy. Incomplete penetrance and the male bias reflect the influence of mitochondrial heteroplasmy, nuclear modifiers, hormonal factors, and environmental triggers. Most patients suffer severe and permanent bilateral central visual loss, although a minority recover useful vision, most commonly those with the m.14484 mutation and younger patients; avoidance of smoking and excess alcohol and emerging gene and pharmacological therapies may modify outcomes.
