Continued exposure to mitochondrial toxins during acute visual decline Assuming carriers will inevitably lose vision, ignoring the marked incomplete penetrance and sex bias Overlooking dystonia and basal ganglia lesions that distinguish LHON-plus from isolated LHON Failing to counsel about maternal inheritance and avoidance of tobacco and alcohol Misattributing subacute visual loss to optic neuritis and delaying mitochondrial testing Leber hereditary optic neuropathy results from maternally inherited point mutations in mitochondrial DNA that encode subunits of respiratory-chain complex I, impairing electron transport, reducing ATP synthesis and increasing reactive oxygen species. Retinal ganglion cells, whose small unmyelinated axons in the papillomacular bundle have high energy demand, are selectively vulnerable, leading to their degeneration and central visual loss. In LHON-plus the same energy failure and oxidative stress extend to other high-demand neurons, particularly in the basal ganglia, producing dystonia and additional neurological features; the reasons some carriers develop the extended phenotype relate to mutant load, nuclear and mitochondrial genetic background, hormonal factors and environmental exposures. Visual prognosis is generally poor with most affected individuals reaching legal blindness, though the m.14484T>C mutation carries a better chance of partial recovery; when dystonia and other extraocular features are present the neurological disability tends to persist and may progress.

Left ventricular non-compaction cardiomyopathy — LVNC, left ventricular non-compaction, spongy myocardium, non-compaction cardiomyopathy, hypertrabeculation Dilated cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Prominent normal trabeculation or physiological hypertrabeculation in athletes and pregnancy Endomyocardial fibrosis Apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Cardiac masses or apical thrombus Transthoracic echocardiography with assessment of the non-compacted to compacted layer ratio Cardiac MRI for tissue characterisation, late gadolinium enhancement and trabecular quantification 12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia Assessment of left ventricular systolic function and volumes Genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives Evaluation for associated neuromuscular disease when clinically suggested Characterised by prominent left ventricular trabeculations with deep intertrabecular recesses and a two-layered myocardium of thin compacted and thick non-compacted layers The clinical triad of concern is heart failure, arrhythmia (including sudden death) and systemic thromboembolism May present in neonates and children or be discovered incidentally in adults; presentation ranges from asymptomatic to severe cardiomyopathy Frequently familial with heterogeneous genetics, including sarcomeric gene variants that overlap with hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy Cardiac MRI is more sensitive than echocardiography for quantifying the non-compacted to compacted myocardial ratio and detecting fibrosis Anticoagulation is considered when ventricular function is impaired, atrial fibrillation is present, or thrombus is identified, given the risk of embolism from deep recesses Management otherwise follows standard heart failure and arrhythmia principles, with defibrillator therapy for those at high arrhythmic risk It can occur in isolation or in association with neuromuscular disorders and congenital heart disease New or worsening heart failure symptoms Syncope or documented sustained ventricular arrhythmia Systemic embolic event such as stroke Family history of cardiomyopathy or premature sudden death Overdiagnosing the condition from prominent trabeculation in athletes or pregnancy on echocardiography alone Failing to consider anticoagulation in patients with impaired function or atrial fibrillation Assuming an incidental finding is benign without assessing arrhythmic and thromboembolic risk Neglecting family screening given the frequently inherited nature Overlooking associated neuromuscular or congenital conditions Left ventricular non-compaction is thought to reflect arrest of the normal compaction of the trabeculated embryonic myocardium during development, though acquired remodelling may also contribute. The result is a distinctive two-layered ventricular wall with a thin compacted epicardial layer and a thick, heavily trabeculated non-compacted endocardial layer containing deep recesses that communicate with the cavity. This architecture impairs contractile function, promotes microvascular dysfunction and fibrosis, provides a substrate for ventricular arrhythmia, and creates areas of stasis within the recesses that favour thrombus formation and systemic embolism. The genetics overlap with other inherited cardiomyopathies, particularly sarcomeric protein variants. Outcome depends chiefly on ventricular function and arrhythmic burden; incidentally detected cases with preserved function may remain stable, whereas those with impaired systolic function face risks of progressive heart failure, arrhythmia and thromboembolism.

Legionellosis (Legionnaires' Disease) — Legionnaires disease, Pontiac fever Other atypical-pneumonia pathogens, notably Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae (Harrison 22e p.1272) In immunocompromised patients, Legionella can present as pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation that mimic fungal infection, or as lung abscesses (Harrison 22e p.1273) Lower-respiratory culture (sputum, BAL fluid, lung tissue, or extrapulmonary sites) on cysteine-supplemented buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar is the gold standard and is essential for epidemiologic typing; growth is slow (typically 3-5 days, longer for non-pneumophila species) (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274) Polymerase chain reaction / nucleic acid amplification (including LAMP and multiplex respiratory panels) on lower-tract specimens is more sensitive than culture and remains useful during antibiotic therapy, but does not provide serotype information and most assays target only L. pneumophila (Harrison 22e p.1274-1275) Bronchoscopy when urinary antigen is negative and the patient cannot produce adequate sputum, or in severe disease requiring ICU care (Harrison 22e p.1273) Serology (paired acute/convalescent titers; fourfold rise to L. pneumophila serogroup 1 confirms) has limited acute sensitivity but aids outbreak investigation (Harrison 22e p.1274) Direct fluorescent antibody testing of sputum has low and variable sensitivity (~20-70%) and is not recommended for low-risk screening due to false positives (Harrison 22e p.1274) Legionella species cause two distinct illnesses collectively termed legionellosis: Legionella pneumonia (Legionnaires' disease) and Pontiac fever; most clinical disease is driven by L. pneumophila, predominantly serotype 1 (Harrison 22e p.1269). Almost all cases trace to waterborne exposure; aerosolizing or aspiration sources include cooling towers, fountains, water misters, HVAC systems, hot tubs/spas, ice machines, and showerheads/sinks in large premise-plumbing systems (Harrison 22e p.1270-1271). Legionella pneumonia presents as an 'atypical pneumonia' with nonspecific onset of fever, myalgias, headache, breathlessness, and dry or productive cough; accompanying neurologic or gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion) raise the likelihood of legionellosis (Harrison 22e p.1272). A characteristic laboratory cluster supports the diagnosis: hyponatremia and/or renal dysfunction are frequent, with elevated liver enzymes, and leukocytosis or leukopenia plus thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.1272). Per CDC, a single confirmed Legionella case in a patient who did not leave a health care facility/campus for the 10 days before onset should trigger an outbreak investigation, because nosocomial cases may signal water-system contamination (Harrison 22e p.1270-1273). Pontiac fever is a milder, self-limited influenza-like illness defined by the ABSENCE of pneumonia, with fever, headache, myalgias, chills, vertigo, nausea/vomiting and diarrhea; antibiotics are not required (Harrison 22e p.1273). Severe pneumonia with acute respiratory failure or a sepsis-like presentation warrants testing for Legionella (Harrison 22e p.1272) Pneumonia developing during hospitalization, after recent travel, or during a known or possible outbreak should prompt Legionella testing (Harrison 22e p.1272) Immunosuppressed patients may lack typical features such as fever and may show radiographic progression during early therapy (Harrison 22e p.1272-1273) Urinary antigen testing detects ONLY L. pneumophila serotype 1; it gives false-negative results in most cases caused by non-serotype 1 L. pneumophila and non-pneumophila species, so a negative result does not exclude legionellosis (sensitivity for serotype 1 is ~70%, though specificity is high) (Harrison 22e p.1274). Urinary antigen can be falsely negative very early in disease yet remain positive for months after infection (especially in immunosuppressed patients), and it cannot be used in anuric patients (Harrison 22e p.1274). Because community-acquired pneumonia guidelines recommend empirical coverage active against Legionella, specific testing is often skipped and cultures are frequently collected only after antibiotics, reducing yield (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274). Diagnosis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinical-prediction tools (e.g., Winthrop-University Hospital Criteria, Legionella Score) are more useful for their negative than their positive predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1272). Routine testing is less common in children, so pediatric cases may be underreported; immunosuppressed patients may present without fever or pulmonary exam findings (Harrison 22e p.1271-1272). Legionellae are aerobic gram-negative bacteria ubiquitous in aquatic environments, damp soil, and compost. Their natural hosts are amoebae and other free-living protozoa, within which they replicate intracellularly; humans are accidental hosts. They have a biphasic life cycle (a nutrient-rich replicative phase and a transmissive phase under resource scarcity) and persist in biofilms within natural and engineered water systems, including building premise plumbing where temperature and nutrients support protozoal hosts. After inhalation or aspiration of small aerosol particles, the organisms are phagocytized by alveolar macrophages and monocytes; pathogenic species evade intracellular defenses (forming Legionella-containing vacuoles, downregulating cytokine receptors, inhibiting host protein synthesis, and avoiding lysosomal degradation) and replicate. Innate pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like and NOD-like receptors) together with adaptive CD4 and CD8 T-cell responses drive interferon-gamma, TNF, and neutrophil recruitment, which can clear the pathogen but may also produce immunopathology. L. pneumophila is more cytopathogenic than most non-pneumophila species, which may underlie its association with severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1269). Legionella pneumonia carries significant morbidity and mortality, with most patients hospitalized and many requiring ICU admission. The reported case-fatality rate is about 10%, rising to roughly 25% in health care-associated L. pneumophila pneumonia and to approximately 30-50% in immunocompromised hosts. Delayed antibiotic treatment is associated with about a threefold higher mortality. More than a quarter of survivors of severe disease have lasting complications, including recurrent hospitalizations, acute renal failure, respiratory sequelae, and recurrent pneumonias. By contrast, Pontiac fever is self-limited, usually resolving within 3-5 days, with hospitalization, complications, and death extremely rare (Harrison 22e p.1275). Treatment is stratified by severity: Pontiac fever requires no antibiotics (supportive care only), whereas Legionella pneumonia is managed as mild versus moderate/severe disease. All immunosuppressed patients are considered to have moderate or severe disease and should receive IV therapy where possible; all patients needing inpatient care should receive IV therapy until improving before switching to an oral agent. CDC distinguishes health care-associated cases as presumptive (Legionella pneumonia after >=10 days continuous stay in a health care facility during the 14 days before symptom onset) versus possible (some health care exposure in that window but insufficient to meet presumptive criteria) (Harrison 22e p.1272-1275).

Leigh syndrome — Subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy, Leigh disease, SURF1, MT-ATP6 Other mitochondrial encephalopathies including MELAS and MERRF Biotinidase or biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease Wilson disease and other basal ganglia metabolic disorders Kernicterus or hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury Organic acidaemias such as glutaric aciduria Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate and pyruvate with calculation of the lactate/pyruvate ratio Brain MRI with spectroscopy demonstrating symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions and a lactate peak Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids to exclude mimicking metabolic disorders Molecular genetic testing including mitochondrial DNA analysis and nuclear gene panels (e.g. SURF1) Skeletal muscle biopsy for respiratory-chain enzyme assays where genetics are inconclusive Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex enzyme activity when a PDH defect is suspected Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, feeding and swallowing difficulty, and often follows an intercurrent illness The radiological signature is bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia and brainstem, frequently with elevated lactate on MR spectroscopy It is genetically heterogeneous: causative defects lie in either mitochondrial DNA (for example MT-ATP6, giving maternal inheritance) or numerous nuclear genes such as SURF1 (autosomal recessive) The common final pathway is impaired oxidative phosphorylation, most often affecting complex I, complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) or pyruvate metabolism Brainstem involvement can produce respiratory irregularity, abnormal eye movements, nystagmus and central apnoea Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate are commonly raised, and the CSF-to-blood lactate ratio can be informative Management is supportive with attention to nutrition, intercurrent illness and generic cofactor supplementation, avoiding respiratory-chain toxins and, where a pyruvate dehydrogenase defect is confirmed, considering a generically high-fat ketogenic dietary approach under specialist supervision Brainstem dysfunction with central hypoventilation or apnoea Rapid neurological regression triggered by intercurrent infection or fasting Progressive bulbar weakness with aspiration risk Decompensating lactic acidosis Assuming a single gene: Leigh syndrome requires both mitochondrial DNA and nuclear testing because it is highly heterogeneous Overlooking treatable phenocopies such as biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease or a pyruvate dehydrogenase defect Missing brainstem respiratory involvement that can cause sudden deterioration Exposing patients to mitochondrial toxins or prolonged fasting that precipitate crises Leigh syndrome is a genetically diverse but phenotypically convergent disorder of mitochondrial energy metabolism. Whatever the underlying gene, the result is deficient ATP production, most often from defects of respiratory-chain complex I or IV, ATP synthase, or the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. When the defect resides in mitochondrial DNA the disorder is maternally inherited and heteroplasmic with a threshold effect, whereas nuclear-encoded forms follow Mendelian, usually autosomal recessive, patterns. Chronically energy-starved neurons in the basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem and cerebellum undergo the characteristic focal, bilaterally symmetrical necrosis with capillary proliferation, gliosis and demyelination that gives the disorder its descriptive name. Leigh syndrome is generally progressive with a guarded outlook; classic infantile forms often follow a stepwise decline with intercurrent illnesses and reduced survival, though later-onset and some nuclear-gene forms can run a more indolent course.

Leishmaniasis — kala-azar, visceral leishmaniasis Malaria (VL is easily mistaken for it) Typhoid (enteric) fever Tuberculosis Brucellosis Schistosomiasis Histoplasmosis Splenomegaly from portal hypertension Chronic myeloid leukemia Tropical splenomegaly syndrome (hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly) For CL: cutaneous tuberculosis, fungal infections, leprosy, sarcoidosis, and malignant ulcers Malaria Typhoid fever Tuberculosis Brucellosis Schistosomiasis Histoplasmosis Splenic aspirate smear (highest sensitivity >95%, but invasive and potentially dangerous) Bone marrow aspirate smear (sensitivity 60-85%) Lymph node aspirate smear (sensitivity ~50%) Culture of tissue aspirates (increases sensitivity) rK39 rapid immunochromatographic antibody test (fingerprick blood/serum, result in ~15 min) ELISA and indirect immunofluorescent antibody test (IFAT) Qualitative and quantitative (real-time) PCR for leishmanial nucleic acid (allows species identification) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) of nucleic acids (point-of-care for VL and PKDL) Slit skin smears, lesion aspirates/biopsies for CL; tissue biopsy plus PCR for ML Splenomegaly from portal hypertension Chronic myeloid leukemia Tropical splenomegaly syndrome Malignant ulcers (for cutaneous disease) Sarcoidosis (for cutaneous disease) Caused by obligate intracellular protozoa of the genus Leishmania (~20 species), transmitted by phlebotomine sandflies (Phlebotomus in the Old World, Lutzomyia in the New World); syndromes fall into three categories: visceral (VL), cutaneous (CL), and mucosal (ML) (p.1781). Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar, Hindi for 'black fever') is caused by the L. donovani complex (L. donovani, L. infantum); classic presentation is abrupt moderate-to-high fever with rigors, progressive massive splenomegaly, moderate hepatomegaly, weight loss/wasting, and skin hyperpigmentation (p.1782-1783). Lymphadenopathy is common in most VL-endemic regions but is rare on the Indian subcontinent (p.1783). VL causes pancytopenia from bone marrow dysfunction and reticuloendothelial infiltration: leukopenia and anemia appear early, followed by thrombocytopenia; there is a marked polyclonal increase in serum immunoglobulins (hypergammaglobulinemia) (p.1782-1783). Fever with neutropenia or pancytopenia in a patient from an endemic region strongly suggests VL; hypergammaglobulinemia in long-standing illness strengthens the diagnosis (p.1784). Demonstration of amastigotes in tissue aspirate smears is the gold standard for VL: splenic smear sensitivity is >95%, bone marrow 60-85%, lymph node aspirate ~50% (p.1783). The rK39 rapid immunochromatographic antibody test is used worldwide for VL field diagnosis (sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~90% in immunocompetent individuals; both lower in East Africa) (p.1783). Cutaneous leishmaniasis: a sandfly bite is followed days-to-weeks later by a papule that becomes a nodule and ulcerates over weeks-to-months, with raised, indurated margins and a usually painless base; most lesions heal spontaneously over 2-15 months, leaving a scar (p.1786). Mucosal leishmaniasis (espundia) is typically caused by L. (Viannia) braziliensis and is almost entirely confined to the Americas; it presents with nasal stuffiness and bleeding followed by destruction of nasal cartilage, septal perforation, and collapse of the nasal bridge (p.1787-1788). Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) develops in 2-50% of patients during or after cure of VL on the Indian subcontinent and in East Africa, presenting as hypopigmented macules, papules, nodules, or diffuse skin infiltration (p.1785). Visceral leishmaniasis is a recognized cause of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH); Leishmania is the most common parasite associated with HLH (p.1369-1370). Massive (hugely enlarged) splenomegaly with fever and pancytopenia in a patient from or returning from an endemic region Severe anemia, which may cause congestive heart failure Bleeding (epistaxis, retinal hemorrhages, gastrointestinal bleeding) from thrombocytopenia Hypoalbuminemia with pedal edema and ascites in advanced illness HIV co-infection (untreated VL is fatal in 100% of HIV-co-infected patients) Secondary infections (pneumonia, tuberculosis, dysentery, gastroenteritis) In ML: destruction of nasal cartilage/septal perforation; aspiration pneumonia may be fatal VL is easily mistaken for malaria and other tropical febrile illnesses; a careful travel history is essential in nonendemic countries. Antibody detection tests (rK39, ELISA, IFAT) remain positive for years after cure, so they cannot be used to assess cure or detect relapse, and positive serology does not help diagnose PKDL. In HIV/VL co-infection serodiagnostic tests may be negative in up to 50% of patients, and parasites may be found in unusual sites (e.g., bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, buffy coat). Splenic aspiration, though most sensitive, is invasive and may be dangerous in untrained hands. In PKDL, parasites are scanty and skin smear sensitivity is low, especially in hypopigmented macules (parasites are more readily found in nodular lesions). Patients with active VL and IL-10-mediated suppression do not have a positive leishmanin (Montenegro) skin test. In ML the strongly positive DTH response fails to distinguish past from present infection. Sandflies inoculate flagellate promastigotes into the skin; neutrophils first take up the organisms, then macrophages and dendritic cells engulf them, and parasites multiply as nonflagellate amastigotes within macrophages, rupturing cells and invading new macrophages. Acquired resistance depends on a T helper 1 (TH1) response driven by IL-12, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha; most infected individuals control infection and never develop symptomatic disease. In active VL there is markedly elevated IL-10, which conditions macrophages for parasite survival, downregulates TNF-alpha and nitric oxide, and suppresses antigen presentation, so patients lack a positive leishmanin (Montenegro) skin test. In VL the reticuloendothelial organs (spleen, liver, lymph nodes, tonsils, intestinal submucosa) are heavily parasitized, and bone marrow dysfunction produces pancytopenia. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis reflects an absent cell-mediated/DTH response with high IL-10, TGF-beta, and IL-4, allowing unchecked parasite multiplication (p.1781-1786). Untreated visceral leishmaniasis is fatal in most patients, including 100% of those with HIV co-infection. With effective treatment, recovery is quick: defervescence, regression of splenomegaly, weight gain, and hematologic recovery occur within a week, and continued improvement over 12 months suggests cure; a small percentage relapse (usually within 6-12 months) but respond to retreatment. Cutaneous lesions heal spontaneously in most cases (2-15 months), leaving a scar, but may cause permanent scarring and social stigma. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis does not heal spontaneously and is difficult to treat. Mucosal leishmaniasis does not heal spontaneously despite strong TH1/DTH immunity; the more extensive the disease, the worse the prognosis (p.1782-1788). Harrison does not give a formal grading system; leishmaniasis is classified clinically by syndrome: visceral leishmaniasis (VL/kala-azar), cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL, with Old World and New World forms, plus leishmaniasis recidivans and diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis [DCL]), and mucosal leishmaniasis (ML). Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a sequel of VL.

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome — LGS, childhood epileptic encephalopathy with diffuse slow spike-wave West syndrome (from which LGS may evolve) Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome) Dravet syndrome Atypical benign focal epilepsy of childhood (pseudo-Lennox) Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep Structural focal epilepsy with secondary generalisation Prolonged or video EEG demonstrating slow spike-wave and sleep-activated paroxysmal fast activity Brain MRI to identify structural or malformative causes Genetic and metabolic testing when no structural cause is found Developmental and neuropsychological assessment Evaluation for surgical or neuromodulation options in refractory disease Defined by a triad of multiple drug-resistant seizure types, a characteristic EEG, and intellectual impairment, usually beginning between one and eight years of age Tonic seizures, especially in sleep, are the hallmark, alongside atonic (drop) attacks, atypical absences and frequent episodes of non-convulsive status epilepticus The EEG shows diffuse slow spike-wave complexes when awake and paroxysmal fast activity during sleep It is aetiologically heterogeneous, arising from structural, genetic, metabolic or perinatal causes, and may evolve from earlier encephalopathies such as West syndrome Drop attacks cause frequent injury, so protective measures and helmets are often needed Management usually requires broad-spectrum antiseizure medications and combination therapy, with dietary therapy, callosotomy or vagus nerve stimulation considered for refractory drop seizures Cognitive and behavioural problems tend to worsen with ongoing seizures and are core to the encephalopathy Frequent drop attacks causing recurrent head and facial injury Prolonged non-convulsive status epilepticus with obtundation Progressive cognitive regression accompanying uncontrolled seizures Evolution from an earlier infantile encephalopathy signalling a severe course Labelling any child with mixed seizures and learning difficulty as LGS without the characteristic EEG features Failing to investigate for a treatable structural or metabolic cause Aggressive polytherapy causing sedation that worsens function without reducing seizures Underestimating injury risk from drop attacks and omitting protective measures Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy representing a shared final pathway of diffuse cortical network dysfunction from many underlying causes. Widespread abnormal thalamocortical synchronisation and impaired inhibition generate the characteristic generalised tonic seizures and slow spike-wave activity. Because the epileptic activity itself contributes to cognitive stagnation and regression, ongoing seizures and interictal discharges drive the intellectual and behavioural deterioration that characterises the syndrome. The outlook is generally poor, with lifelong drug-resistant seizures and significant intellectual disability in most patients. Seizure freedom is uncommon, and there is increased mortality including from injury and SUDEP, though seizure burden and quality of life can be improved with tailored therapy.

Leprosy (Hansen's Disease) — Hansen's disease Hypopigmented macules: pityriasis alba, vitiligo, progressive macular hypomelanosis, pityriasis versicolor, pityriasis rosea, postinflammatory hypopigmentation, sarcoidosis, post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, morphea (p.1410) Plaque/nodular lesions: granuloma annulare, cutaneous sarcoidosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, nodular histiocytosis, lupus erythematosus, cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (especially mycosis fungoides), secondary syphilis (p.1410) ENL (type 2 reaction) lesions: erythema nodosum of other etiologies, nodular vasculitis, cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (p.1410) Mononeuropathy: diabetes, amyloidosis, myxedema (p.1410) Acute-onset polyneuropathy: Guillain-Barre syndrome, toxic polyneuropathy (p.1410) Cutaneous leishmaniasis (p.1410) Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (p.1410) Secondary syphilis (p.1410) Pityriasis versicolor (p.1410) Slit-skin smear from standard sites (right earlobe, forehead, chin, and left buttock/upper thigh), Ziehl-Neelsen stained, graded by bacteriologic index (0-6) and microbiologic index (p.1410) Skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis, classify disease, support diagnosis of reactions, and assess cure; immunochemical staining for M. leprae antigens aids detection of early lesions (p.1410) PCR / gene amplification (conventional, RT-PCR, multiplex targeting RLEP, 16S rRNA, SodA, antigen genes) - useful in bacteriologic-index-negative cases and for subclinical infection in contacts (p.1410) PGL-1 antibody testing (ELISA, ML flow lateral-flow assay, UPC-LFA) - more often positive in multibacillary than paucibacillary disease (p.1410) Lepromin (Mitsuda) skin test - measures cellular immunity; negative in LL/BL leprosy (p.1410) Nerve function assessment: Semmes-Weinstein monofilament (or WHO-recommended ballpoint pen) touch testing, voluntary muscle testing, nerve conduction studies, and ultrasound of peripheral nerves (p.1410-1411) Vitiligo (p.1410) Sarcoidosis / cutaneous sarcoidosis (p.1410) Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, especially mycosis fungoides (p.1410) Lupus erythematosus (p.1410) Granuloma annulare (p.1410) Diabetic, amyloid, or myxedema-related mononeuropathy (p.1410) Leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae, with manifestations largely confined to skin, peripheral nerves, eyes, and the upper respiratory tract; M. leprae has a predilection for peripheral nerves (p.1404). Diagnosis rests on three cardinal signs, of which at least one establishes the diagnosis: (1) a hypopigmented or erythematous skin lesion with definite loss/impairment of sensation, (2) involvement of peripheral nerves shown by definite thickening with sensory impairment, and (3) a positive result for acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy, or a positive biopsy PCR (p.1409-1410). The differing immune responses to M. leprae produce a clinical spectrum; immunologic resistance is strong at the tuberculoid end and weakest at the lepromatous end (p.1404, p.1406). Skin surfaces in tuberculoid lesions are dry, hairless, and anaesthetic owing to destruction of underlying cutaneous nerves, plus autonomic damage causing loss of sweating (p.1407). Slit-skin smear bacteriologic index runs from negative (tuberculoid) up to 4+ to 6+ with globi (lepromatous), and falls an average of ~1 log unit per year on multidrug therapy (p.1404, p.1407-1408). Leprosy is the principal treatable cause of peripheral neuropathy worldwide in some settings; nerve enlargement is often palpable (e.g., greater auricular, ulnar, median, radial, lateral popliteal, posterior tibial, sural, superficial peroneal) (p.1409-1410). Treatment principle: WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (a combination of rifampin, dapsone, and clofazimine) is the standard of care and cures the disease; paucibacillary disease uses two drugs and multibacillary disease uses three, with the cure rate ~99% (no doses given here) (p.1410, p.1412). M. leprae has never been grown in artificial media; it is propagated only in animal models (mouse footpad, armadillo), which underlies the difficulty of culture-based diagnosis (p.1404). Type 1 (reversal) reaction: delayed-hypersensitivity reaction with sudden upgrading of CMI; acute swelling and redness of existing lesions, painful/tender nerves with neuritis; can cause silent neuritis and irreversible sensory/motor nerve damage - a medical urgency to prevent disability (p.1407, p.1408-1409) Type 2 reaction / erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL): immune-complex-mediated syndrome with crops of painful red nodules, fever, malaise, and possible neuritis, iridocyclitis, orchitis, nephritis/renal failure, and (late) amyloidosis (p.1408-1409) Neuritis with nerve function impairment, including 'silent neuritis' (progressive sensory/motor loss without pain or tenderness) - requires prompt treatment to avoid permanent disability and blindness (p.1409, p.1410-1411) Lucio's phenomenon in diffuse leprosy of Lucio and Latapi: vasculitis and thrombosis causing hemorrhagic skin infarction and necrotic ulcers (p.1409) Eye involvement (corneal anaesthesia, iridocyclitis, lagophthalmos, corneal ulceration) threatening sight (p.1408) Leprosy is frequently diagnosed late - in non-endemic countries it is often misdiagnosed simply because it is not considered - increasing the risk of irreversible nerve damage and disability (p.1404, p.1410) On the face, sensory impairment may be difficult to demonstrate because of generous bilateral sensory innervation, which can compensate for damage to certain nerve branches and obscure the indeterminate stage (p.1407, p.1409) 'Silent neuritis' / 'quiet nerve paralysis': nerve function can be lost progressively without pain, paresthesia, tenderness, or other signs of reaction - regular nerve function assessment is needed during and after therapy (p.1409, p.1411) Distinguishing relapse from a type 1 reaction in paucibacillary disease can be difficult; a therapeutic glucocorticoid trial helps - improvement within 4 weeks favors T1R, lack of response favors relapse (p.1412) Patients often equate cure with absence of symptoms, but in leprosy bacteriologic cure does not eliminate established nerve-impairment sequelae - this must be explained at completion of therapy (p.1412-1413) Multidrug therapy for clinical leprosy has apparently not interrupted transmission, and subclinical/undiagnosed multibacillary cases are likely a main source of ongoing spread (p.1405) Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular, acid-fast, rod-shaped bacterium with a preferred growth temperature of 27-30 degrees C, explaining its predilection for cooler surface tissues (skin, peripheral nerves, testes, upper airways) and relative sparing of inner viscera. After entry (assumed mainly via the respiratory tract, sometimes through damaged skin), the pathogenic process usually begins in peripheral nerves once bacilli are engulfed by Schwann cells. The histopathologic outcome - and thus the type of leprosy - depends on the host cell-mediated immune (CMI) response. The Ridley-Jopling spectrum (TT, BT, BB, BL, LL, with indeterminate IL as an early form) reflects this: at the tuberculoid pole, strong CMI produces epithelioid/giant-cell granulomas that destroy nerves (causing anaesthesia and muscle weakness) but contain few bacilli; toward the lepromatous pole, weak CMI permits unrestricted multiplication of bacilli within macrophages (lepra cells) as clumps/globi, with widespread dissemination and high bacterial load. Tissue damage is largely due to delayed hypersensitivity. M. leprae carries the species-specific phenolic glycolipid PGL-1, used in serodiagnosis. M. lepromatosis is a related species associated with diffuse leprosy of Lucio and Latapi. Leprosy can be cured effectively: the cure rate with multidrug therapy is ~99% and treatment-failure rates are very low when therapy is completed. Relapse rates are well below 1% except in patients with a very high baseline bacillary load (bacteriologic index >=4), and relapses usually occur within 5 years of finishing therapy; antimicrobial resistance is rare, so relapsed multibacillary patients can be re-treated with the same regimen. The major determinant of long-term outcome is nerve damage and resulting disability, which drives stigma and social exclusion. Highest risk of (additional) nerve damage is in multibacillary patients with nerve impairment already present at diagnosis (up to ~65%); intermediate risk (~16%) in multibacillary patients without impairment or paucibacillary patients with impairment at diagnosis; and lowest (~3%) in paucibacillary patients without impairment. Leprosy reactions and new nerve damage can occur even after completing therapy, up to 3 years afterward. Cure (cessation of bacterial activity) must be distinguished from sequelae (nerve impairment, reactions, disabilities such as claw hand or neuropathic foot) that may persist and require chronic care. Ridley-Jopling classification (1962) defines five overlapping categories along the immunologic spectrum: tuberculoid (TT), borderline tuberculoid (BT), mid-borderline (BB), borderline lepromatous (BL), and lepromatous (LL), with indeterminate leprosy (IL) as an early form; immunologic resistance is strongest at TT and weakest at LL, with TT and LL relatively stable and BT/BB/BL unstable. For operational/treatment purposes the WHO simplified classification is used: paucibacillary disease = negative slit-skin smears at all sites (or, on clinical criteria, one to five skin lesions and no/only one involved nerve), and multibacillary disease = positive smear at any site (or six or more lesions and/or more than one involved nerve). The WHO disability grading system scores eyes, hands, and feet (grades 0-2), summed into the Eye-Hand-Foot (EHF) score as an overall impairment indicator (p.1405-1406).

type) Other causes of childhood dystonia and choreoathetosis Primary or secondary hyperuricaemia and juvenile gout Neuroacanthocytosis and other self-mutilation syndromes Autism spectrum disorder with variants in HPRT1, encoding hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, so it almost exclusively affects males Loss of purine salvage drives overproduction of uric acid, causing hyperuricaemia, hyperuricosuria, gout and urate nephrolithiasis The complete deficiency (classic Lesch-Nyhan syndrome) produces a triad of hyperuricaemia, a dystonic-choreoathetoid movement disorder and compulsive and delayed motor development with evolving dystonia Partial HPRT deficiency (Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome) causes hyperuricaemia and gout with little or no neurological involvement Urate-lowering Evolving dystonia with developmental delay in a young boy Compulsive self-injurious behaviour, particularly self-biting Urate crystals or stones with renal impairment Acute urate nephropathy or obstructive uropathy Assuming that urate-lowering therapy will improve neurological or behavioural symptoms Misdiagnosing the movement disorder as dyskinetic cerebral palsy Overlooking hyperuricaemia as a diagnostic clue in a boy with dystonia and self-injury Failing to implement protective measures against self-mutilation Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase catalyses the salvage of the purine bases hypoxanthine and guanine back into nucleotides. When the enzyme is deficient, salvage fails and the purine bases are instead degraded to uric acid, while de novo purine synthesis is disinhibited; the combined effect is marked uric acid overproduction with hyperuricaemia and its complications. The neurological and behavioural phenotype is less well understood but is linked to dysfunction of dopaminergic pathways in the basal ganglia, which correlates with the dystonia, choreoathetosis and compulsive self-injury. The severity of the phenotype tracks closely with the amount of residual enzyme activity. Systemic urate complications can be controlled with urate-lowering therapy, preventing gout and nephropathy, but the neurological and behavioural features of the complete syndrome are not reversible and cause lifelong disability. Life expectancy is reduced, with renal failure and complications of the movement and behavioural disorder contributing to mortality.

Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies — Rare lymphoid malignancies, Rare myeloid malignancies, Unusual hematologic neoplasms Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (distinguished from splenic marginal zone lymphoma by CD5 positivity) Mantle cell lymphoma (overlaps with B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia via CD5 and t(11;14)) Nodular sclerosing Hodgkin's disease (versus mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma; the latter is CD45 positive, lacks lacunar Reed-Sternberg variants) Anaplastic large T-cell lymphoma with t(2;5) (versus primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoma, which lacks t(2;5)) Chronic myeloid leukemia, BCR::ABL1 positive (versus atypical CML and chronic neutrophilic leukemia) Reactive neutrophilia from infection or inflammation (mimics chronic neutrophilic leukemia) Reactive monocytosis from tuberculosis, fungal infection, subacute bacterial endocarditis, viral or protozoal infection (mimics chronic myelomonocytic leukemia) Hypereosinophilia from tissue-invasive helminths and other parasitic infection (mimics primary/clonal eosinophilic disorders) Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow morphology with immunophenotyping/flow cytometry for lineage markers Cytogenetics and molecular testing: CSF3R (CNL), KIT D816V (mastocytosis), GATA1 (transient myeloproliferative disorder), SETBP1, RAS-pathway mutations (JMML) FISH or RT-PCR screening for PDGFRA and PDGFRB rearrangements in hypereosinophilia Serum tryptase (mast cell disease; elevation also prompts FIP1L1-PDGFRA testing) and soluble CD25 as a hairy cell leukemia activity marker T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies and T-cell immunophenotyping in hypereosinophilia to detect lymphocytic-variant disease Echocardiogram and serum troponin to screen for cardiac involvement in hypereosinophilic syndrome (apical thrombus, endocardial thickening, valve abnormality) Electron microscopy/immunostaining for Birbeck granules, CD1a, S100, and langerin in Langerhans cell histiocytosis Plasma cell neoplasms and metastatic solid tumors producing secondary neutrophilia (mimic chronic neutrophilic leukemia) Connective tissue disease, sarcoidosis, lipid storage disorders, postsplenectomy state, and marrow regeneration after chemotherapy (mimic CMML monocytosis) Allergic/vasculitic disease and drug reactions (mimic primary hypereosinophilia) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (raises serum tryptase, confounding mastocytosis criteria) This chapter covers the uncommon hematologic neoplasms, each individually accounting for under 1% of hematologic malignancies; the rare lymphoid tumors are all mature B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell neoplasms (Harrison 22e p.871). Splenic marginal zone lymphoma cells express surface immunoglobulin and CD20 but are negative for CD5, CD10, CD43, and CD103; absence of CD5 separates it from CLL and absence of CD103 separates it from hairy cell leukemia, and circulating cells are villous lymphocytes (Harrison 22e p.872). Hairy cell leukemia is a frequent cause of a 'dry tap' on marrow aspiration because of increased reticulin fibers; it shows profound monocytopenia (predisposing to atypical mycobacterial infection), strong CD22/CD25/CD103 expression, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity, and the activating BRAF V600E mutation in most cases (Harrison 22e p.872-873). Mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma typically remains confined to the mediastinum, affects women more than men (ratio about 1:2-3) at a median age of 35-40 years, is CD20 positive and CD45 positive (unlike classical Hodgkin's), and may lack surface immunoglobulin and HLA class I/II expression (Harrison 22e p.873). Primary effusion lymphoma presents with effusions usually without a tumor mass, is caused by HHV-8/KSHV (often EBV co-infected), occurs mainly in immunodeficiency such as AIDS, and follows a rapidly fatal course (Harrison 22e p.873). T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is aggressive with very high WBC counts often exceeding 100,000/uL, hepatosplenomegaly, and adenopathy; chromosome 14 inversion between q11 and q32 occurs in about 80% of patients (Harrison 22e p.874). T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia is dominated by severe neutropenia and is frequently associated with systemic autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis; pure red cell aplasia occurs in 15-20% and the course is generally indolent (Harrison 22e p.874). Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, is an EBV-related angiocentric/angiodestructive CD56-positive lesion prevalent in Asia, Mexico, and Central/South America; historic names include lethal midline granuloma and polymorphic reticulosis (Harrison 22e p.874). Enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma is a rare complication of longstanding celiac disease, usually arising in jejunum or ileum, with most patients carrying the celiac-associated HLA DQA1*0501 or DQB1*0201 genotype (Harrison 22e p.874). Chronic neutrophilic leukemia is a clonal proliferation of mature neutrophils molecularly defined by activating CSF3R mutations (most commonly the membrane-proximal T618I, found in about 90% of cases); diagnosis requires excluding reactive neutrophilia and other myeloid neoplasms (Harrison 22e p.875-876). Systemic mastocytosis diagnosis rests on a major criterion (multifocal aggregates of >=15 mast cells) or three minor criteria including >25% atypical mast cells, aberrant mast cell expression of CD25/CD2/CD30, KIT D816V or other activating KIT mutation, and serum tryptase >20 ng/mL (Harrison 22e p.881). Transient myeloproliferative disorder occurs in about 10% of infants with Down syndrome, carries somatic GATA1 mutations, and either regresses spontaneously (about 75%) or progresses to acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (about 25%) (Harrison 22e p.879). Aggressive NK cell leukemia presenting with fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, hemophagocytosis, coagulopathy, or multiorgan failure Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with small-vessel occlusion, neurologic symptoms, and thrombus formation, often diagnosed only late or at autopsy Hemophagocytic syndrome complicating extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma or subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (can drive a fulminant downhill course) Cardiac involvement in hypereosinophilic syndrome (cardiomyopathy, ventricular apical thrombus, elevated troponin) Mast cell organopathy C findings: cytopenias, hepatomegaly with portal hypertension/ascites, splenomegaly with hypersplenism, GI infiltration with malabsorption and weight loss, large osteolytic lesions with pathologic fractures True mast cell leukemia, regarded as an oncologic emergency requiring expedited diagnosis Bowel perforation from tumor response in treated enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma Misclassifying nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma as classical Hodgkin's; the L&H 'popcorn' cell is a clonal B cell expressing CD45/CD79a/CD20/CD19/BCL2 and lacking CD30/CD15, behaving more like indolent B-cell NHL Confusing B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia with leukemic mantle cell lymphoma, since both can express CD5 and t(11;14) and no reliable distinguishing criteria have emerged Overlooking that a dry tap on marrow aspiration may signal hairy cell leukemia, myelofibrosis, metastatic carcinoma, CML, or acute leukemia rather than a technical failure Mistaking lymphomatoid granulomatosis for extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, since both are angiodestructive and EBV-related Attributing the presence of t(2;5) in a cutaneous CD30+ lesion to primary cutaneous disease; its presence should prompt evaluation for systemic anaplastic T-cell lymphoma Failing to exclude reactive causes of neutrophilia, monocytosis, or eosinophilia before diagnosing CNL, CMML, or a primary eosinophilic disorder Diagnosing systemic mastocytosis without accounting for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia when interpreting elevated serum tryptase These entities are individually rare clonal neoplasms of the lymphoid or myeloid lineages. Rare lymphoid tumors are mature B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell neoplasms; several B-cell variants of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma have distinctive biology, such as intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (confined to vessel lumens, postulated to reflect defective adhesion molecule and homing function with absent beta-1 integrin and ICAM-1), primary effusion lymphoma (HHV-8/KSHV-driven, frequently EBV co-infected), and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (an angiodestructive EBV-infected monoclonal B-cell proliferation outnumbered by reactive T cells). Many T/NK entities are EBV-associated and angiocentric. On the myeloid side, distinct molecular drivers define the entities: activating CSF3R mutations in chronic neutrophilic leukemia, GM-CSF hypersensitivity from dysregulated RAS/MAPK signaling (mutually exclusive RAS, PTPN11, NF1 mutations) in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, somatic GATA1 mutations in transient myeloproliferative disorder of Down syndrome, and constitutively active tyrosine kinase gene fusions (involving PDGFRA such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, ABL1, JAK2, FLT3) in eosinophilic myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Mastocytosis reflects neoplastic mast cell proliferation typically driven by KIT D816V. Dendritic/histiocytic neoplasms arise from antigen-presenting or antigen-processing cell lineages; Langerhans cell histiocytosis cells are S100+/CD1a+ with Birbeck granules and about 55% carry BRAF V600E. Outcomes vary widely by entity. Indolent disorders include splenic marginal zone lymphoma (median survival over 10 years), T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoma (5-year survival over 90%). Aggressive entities carry poor outcomes: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (median survival about 12 months), enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma (median 7-11 months), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (median about 2 years), primary effusion lymphoma (death typically within 6 months), and intravascular large B-cell lymphoma. Mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma is potentially curable with good multi-year survival. In extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, survival tracks with the number of risk factors (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, regional node involvement), with 5-year survival ranging from 81% (zero risk factors) down to 7% (three to four factors). Chronic neutrophilic leukemia has a median survival of about 2 years, atypical CML around 10-25 months, and CMML survival ranges by Mayo Molecular Model risk from about 16 to 97 months. Histiocytic sarcoma has a poor prognosis with median survival measured in months to about 2 years. Several entities have formal staging/risk schemes. Myeloid neoplasms are classified by the ICC and WHO systems using blood counts, smear, marrow morphology, and cytogenetic/molecular tests. CMML is graded as CMML-1 (<10% marrow and <5% blood blasts) and CMML-2 (10-19% marrow or 5-19% blood blasts), with the Mayo Molecular Model assigning low to high risk by truncating ASXL1 mutation, absolute monocytes >10 x10^9/L, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, platelets <100 x10^9/L, and circulating immature myeloid cells. Systemic mastocytosis is subclassified into indolent, smoldering (requires two or more B findings), aggressive, SM with associated myeloid/hematologic neoplasm, and mast cell leukemia (>=20% mast cells in marrow aspirate); advanced SM is defined by an associated neoplasm or organopathy (C findings). Hypereosinophilia is defined as absolute eosinophil count >=1500 x10^9/L, with hypereosinophilic syndrome requiring eosinophil-mediated organ damage. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma nasal type uses a four-factor risk model (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, regional node involvement).

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency — LAD, LAD-1, leucocyte adhesion deficiency Chronic granulomatous disease Congenital or cyclic neutropenia Chediak-Higashi syndrome Other neutrophil functional disorders Glanzmann thrombasthenia (for the bleeding seen in LAD-3) Flow cytometry for CD18 and CD11 expression on neutrophils (reduced or absent in LAD-1) Full blood count demonstrating marked neutrophil leucocytosis Genetic testing (ITGB2 for LAD-1, SLC35C1 for LAD-2, FERMT3 for LAD-3) Neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis functional assays Assessment of sialyl-Lewis X expression and blood group testing where LAD-2 is suspected Platelet aggregation studies when LAD-3 is considered Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is a group of autosomal recessive disorders in which neutrophils cannot adhere to and migrate across the vascular endothelium to reach sites of infection The most common form, LAD-1, results from defects in the beta-2 integrin common chain (CD18), impairing firm adhesion of leucocytes A cardinal clinical clue is delayed separation of the umbilical cord accompanied by omphalitis in the newborn period Recurrent bacterial and fungal soft-tissue infections occur characteristically without pus formation, because neutrophils fail to enter the tissues A persistently high blood neutrophil count (marked leucocytosis) is typical, since neutrophils remain in the circulation rather than migrating out Severe gingivitis, periodontitis, and poor wound healing are frequent features LAD-2 involves defective fucosylation of selectin ligands and is associated with the Bombay blood group and developmental abnormalities, while LAD-3 combines adhesion failure with a bleeding tendency due to impaired integrin activation in platelets Management includes aggressive treatment of infections and antimicrobial prophylaxis, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering cure in severe LAD-1 Delayed umbilical cord separation with omphalitis in a neonate requiring urgent evaluation Severe soft-tissue or invasive infection without pus formation requiring prompt antimicrobial therapy Life-threatening sepsis given the severe impairment of neutrophil migration Live vaccines and non-irradiated blood products should be approached cautiously, especially peri-transplant Bleeding episodes in suspected LAD-3 Interpreting the high neutrophil count as ongoing bacterial infection rather than a diagnostic clue to impaired migration Expecting pus and abscess formation and being falsely reassured by its absence Missing the neonatal sign of delayed cord separation Failing to distinguish the LAD subtypes, which differ in associated features and management Delaying transplant referral in severe LAD-1 Leukocyte adhesion deficiency arises from defects in the adhesion cascade that normally allows leucocytes to roll along, firmly adhere to, and transmigrate across activated endothelium. In LAD-1, mutations in ITGB2 reduce or abolish the shared CD18 subunit of the beta-2 integrins, so neutrophils cannot form the firm adhesion needed to exit the bloodstream, leaving tissues undefended despite abundant circulating neutrophils. LAD-2 results from a defect in GDP-fucose transport that impairs synthesis of sialyl-Lewis X, the selectin ligand required for rolling, and also causes the rare Bombay phenotype and neurodevelopmental problems. LAD-3 stems from defective inside-out signalling (kindlin-3/FERMT3) that prevents activation of integrins on both leucocytes and platelets, combining infection susceptibility with a Glanzmann-like bleeding disorder. Severe LAD-1 with very low CD18 expression carries a high risk of early fatal infection unless corrected by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, whereas moderate phenotypes with partial expression can survive longer with vigilant infection control; LAD-2 tends to have a milder infectious course dominated by developmental issues, and LAD-3 combines infection and bleeding risks.

LGI1 limbic encephalitis — anti-LGI1 encephalitis, leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 antibody encephalitis, VGKC-complex (LGI1) limbic encephalitis Herpes simplex and other infective limbic dementia including Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease Wernicke encephalopathy Serum and cerebrospinal fluid testing for LGI1 antibodies, with serum often more sensitive for this antigen MRI of the brain showing medial temporal and sometimes basal ganglia signal change Electroencephalography to characterise temporal seizures and subclinical activity Serum sodium measurement to detect hyponatraemia Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for inflammation and to exclude infection Targeted tumour screening given the small paraneoplastic association Faciobrachial dystonic seizures — brief, frequent unilateral contractions of the face and arm — are highly characteristic and often precede the cognitive syndrome The limbic phase brings subacute short-term memory loss, confusion, temporal-lobe seizures, and disturbed sleep or behaviour Hyponatraemia is common and helps raise suspicion of the diagnosis Antibodies target LGI1, a secreted neuronal protein once grouped within the voltage-gated potassium channel complex Most cases are non-paraneoplastic, but tumour screening remains appropriate as a minority harbour an underlying neoplasm Recognising and treating faciobrachial dystonic seizures early with immunotherapy may prevent progression to fixed cognitive impairment First-line immunotherapy is corticosteroids with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab in refractory disease Frequent faciobrachial dystonic seizures signalling active, treatable disease before cognitive decline Rapidly progressive memory loss or confusion Severe hyponatraemia risking seizures and reduced consciousness Status epilepticus or evolving encephalopathy Mistaking faciobrachial dystonic seizures for tics, myoclonus, or psychogenic movements and delaying treatment Relying on antiseizure drugs alone rather than starting immunotherapy Overlooking hyponatraemia as a diagnostic clue Assuming the disorder is always non-paraneoplastic and omitting tumour screening Antibodies are directed against leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1), a protein secreted by neurons that bridges presynaptic ADAM23 and postsynaptic ADAM22 to regulate synaptic excitability and AMPA-receptor clustering. Antibody-mediated disruption of this signalling increases neuronal excitability within the temporal lobes and basal ganglia, producing seizures, and impairs limbic circuits underlying memory. Inflammation concentrates in the medial temporal structures, and associated hypothalamic involvement is thought to contribute to the frequent hyponatraemia. The response is usually not tumour-driven but is strongly linked to specific HLA types. Prompt immunotherapy often improves seizures and cognition, but delayed treatment is associated with persistent memory impairment and medial temporal atrophy. Relapses can occur, so ongoing monitoring is warranted.

Li-Fraumeni syndrome — TP53, LFS, sarcoma, breast, leukaemia and adrenal gland (SBLA) syndrome, germline TP53 mutation Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (BRCA1/BRCA2) Constitutional mismatch-repair deficiency syndrome Neurofibromatosis type 1 with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours Sporadic early-onset breast cancer without an identifiable germline cause Familial adenomatous polyposis presenting with childhood brain tumours Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum with embryonal tumours Germline TP53 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, ideally within a multigene cancer panel adrenal screening in children Detailed multigenerational pedigree assessment against classic and Chompret criteria Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the TP53 tumour-suppressor gene, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with very high lifetime cancer risk The core tumour spectrum comprises soft-tissue and osteosarcomas, premenopausal breast cancer, brain tumours, adrenocortical carcinoma and leukaemia, often with childhood or early-adult onset Suspect the syndrome when there are multiple primary tumours in one individual, cancers at unusually young ages, or clustering of the characteristic tumours across generations Paediatric adrenocortical carcinoma and choroid plexus carcinoma are near-pathognomonic and warrant TP53 testing regardless of family history Intensive whole-body MRI surveillance (Toronto protocol) with breast MRI, brain imaging and biochemical monitoring is the cornerstone of early detection Therapeutic radiotherapy is used cautiously because of the risk of radiation-induced second malignancies in TP53 carriers Classic and Chompret criteria guide who should be offered germline testing, but many carriers fall outside strict clinical criteria Multiple primary malignancies in a single individual, especially with early onset Childhood adrenocortical carcinoma or choroid plexus tumour A new mass or persistent symptom in a known carrier suggesting a further primary cancer Radiation-field second malignancy after prior therapeutic irradiation Excluding the diagnosis because family history is limited, since de novo variants and incomplete pedigrees are frequent Using therapeutic radiotherapy without weighing the heightened risk of radiation-induced tumours Overlooking a second primary by attributing new symptoms solely to a prior cancer Failing to offer cascade testing and paediatric surveillance to at-risk relatives The syndrome results from a heterozygous germline loss-of-function variant in TP53, the gene encoding the p53 protein that acts as a master regulator of the cellular response to DNA damage. Normally p53 arrests the cell cycle to permit repair or triggers apoptosis when damage is irreparable, so its impairment allows cells carrying genomic damage to survive and proliferate. Loss or mutation of the remaining wild-type allele in somatic tissue removes this checkpoint entirely, producing genomic instability and driving the diverse, early-onset tumours characteristic of the condition. Carriers face a very high cumulative lifetime cancer risk, frequently developing more than one primary tumour, and childhood-onset disease is common. Structured surveillance improves early detection and survival, but the diversity and aggressiveness of tumours mean prognosis remains guarded and lifelong monitoring is required.

Lichen planus — LP, lichen planus (cutaneous) Lichenoid drug eruption Psoriasis Discoid lupus erythematosus (for scalp and mucosal disease) Secondary syphilis Leukoplakia or candidiasis for oral white lesions Chronic graft-versus-host disease Skin biopsy showing a lichenoid interface dermatitis in uncertain cases Direct immunofluorescence to help distinguish from lupus or immunobullous disease when needed Hepatitis C testing where epidemiologically appropriate Review of medication history to identify a lichenoid drug trigger Biopsy of persistent erosive or indurated oral or genital lesions to exclude dysplasia or malignancy Remember the classic six P's: pruritic, purple (violaceous), polygonal, planar (flat-topped) papules and plaques Lesions favour the flexor wrists, forearms, and ankles, and fine white lacy lines on the surface (Wickham striae) are a helpful diagnostic clue New lesions can appear along lines of trauma or scratching (Koebner phenomenon) Oral lichen planus commonly presents as a white reticular lacy pattern on the buccal mucosa; erosive oral or genital disease is painful and warrants monitoring Nail involvement can cause ridging and, if severe, scarring with pterygium formation, while scalp disease (lichen planopilaris) causes scarring alopecia Consider a lichenoid drug eruption when a similar rash follows introduction of a new medication, and screen for hepatitis C where locally relevant Treatment centres on topical corticosteroids for cutaneous and localised mucosal disease, with phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators for widespread or resistant cases Long-standing erosive oral or genital lichen planus carries a small risk of malignant transformation and should be followed up Erosive oral or genital disease with non-healing or indurated areas suggesting malignant change Scarring alopecia or nail destruction indicating a need for prompt treatment to limit permanent damage Rapidly extensive eruption suggesting a drug cause requiring medication review Severe painful mucosal disease impairing eating or causing significant morbidity Overlooking a lichenoid drug reaction and continuing the causative medication Failing to examine the mouth, genitalia, nails, and scalp for additional sites of involvement Not monitoring erosive oral or genital disease for malignant change Attributing scarring alopecia to non-scarring causes and delaying treatment Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder in which cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes target basal keratinocytes, apparently in response to an altered self-antigen. The resulting band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction produces the characteristic histological features of basal cell degeneration, a saw-tooth epidermal profile, hypergranulosis, and apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies). Pigment released from damaged basal cells accounts for the post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation often seen, particularly in darker skin. Triggers can include certain drugs (lichenoid reactions) and, in some populations, hepatitis C infection. Cutaneous lichen planus is often self-limiting, frequently resolving within one to two years but leaving post-inflammatory pigmentation; mucosal, nail, and scalp forms tend to be chronic, and erosive mucosal disease requires long-term surveillance for malignant transformation.

tight, non-retractile foreskin (phimosis) and meatal narrowing Extragenital lesions appear as white atrophic patches, classically on the trunk, and are usually asymptomatic Long-term topical anti-inflammatory therapy and regular emollient use are the mainstays, aiming to control symptoms and reduce scarring and malignant risk There is a recognised, though modest, increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma at affected genital sites, so persistent, thickened, ulcerated, or non-healing areas need biopsy Arrange long-term follow-up to monitor for scarring, functional problems, and malignant change, and address sexual and urinary dysfunction sympathetically Persistent thickened, warty, ulcerated, or non-healing areas suggesting squamous cell carcinoma and requiring biopsy Progressive scarring causing urinary obstruction or inability to retract the foreskin Significant introital stenosis interfering with micturition or intercourse New fixed nodule or enlarging lesion at a chronically affected site Symptoms unresponsive to adequate treatment, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Dismissing genital symptoms as thrush or non-specific irritation and delaying diagnosis Under-treating with only intermittent or weak topical therapy, allowing progressive scarring Failing to biopsy persistent or changing lesions and missing early malignancy Overlooking the condition in men and children, in whom presentation differs Neglecting the psychological and sexual impact of chronic genital disease Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis thought to have an autoimmune basis, with associations to other autoimmune conditions and to specific autoantibodies in some patients. The characteristic histology shows epidermal atrophy, hyperkeratosis, a homogenised (hyalinised) upper dermis with loss of normal elastic fibres, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate beneath this zone. Genetic predisposition, hormonal influences, local trauma or the Koebner phenomenon, and possibly infective triggers have all been implicated. Chronic inflammation and scarring drive the architectural distortion, and sustained epithelial disturbance underlies the small risk of malignant transformation. Lichen sclerosus is typically a chronic relapsing condition; symptoms and inflammation can be well controlled with maintenance therapy, but architectural scarring is often permanent and lifelong surveillance is advised because of the small risk of genital squamous cell carcinoma.

Liddle syndrome — pseudoaldosteronism, ENaC gain-of-function, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, epithelial sodium channel disorder Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) Apparent mineralocorticoid excess (HSD11B2 deficiency) Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (familial hyperaldosteronism type 1) Cushing syndrome with mineralocorticoid effect Renovascular or other secondary hypertension Licorice ingestion or exogenous mineralocorticoid effect Plasma renin activity and aldosterone (both suppressed) Serum potassium and bicarbonate to document hypokalaemic alkalosis Aldosterone-to-renin ratio to exclude primary hyperaldosteronism Assessment of therapeutic response to ENaC blockade versus aldosterone antagonism Screening for licorice and exogenous mineralocorticoids Molecular genetic testing of SCNN1B and SCNN1G Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant cause of early-onset, low-renin hypertension caused by gain-of-function variants in the beta or gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel (SCNN1B, SCNN1G) The variants disrupt channel removal from the collecting-duct membrane, so ENaC remains constitutively active regardless of aldosterone The typical picture is hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, and characteristically both renin and aldosterone are suppressed It behaves like a mineralocorticoid excess state but there is no excess hormone, hence the older term pseudoaldosteronism Because the defect is at the sodium channel itself, an ENaC-blocking potassium-sparing diuretic (amiloride or triamterene) is effective, whereas an aldosterone-receptor antagonist is not Dietary salt restriction complements pharmacological ENaC blockade Consider it in young patients with resistant hypertension, hypokalaemia and a suppressed renin and aldosterone, especially with a supportive family history Severe or resistant hypertension in a young person Profound hypokalaemia with muscle weakness or arrhythmia End-organ damage from long-standing untreated hypertension Strong family history of early hypertension or premature stroke Treating with an aldosterone-receptor antagonist, which is ineffective because the defect is downstream of the receptor at the channel Misdiagnosing it as primary hyperaldosteronism despite the suppressed aldosterone Overlooking the diagnosis in young hypertensive patients without checking renin and aldosterone Failing to screen and counsel first-degree relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance Liddle syndrome is driven by activating variants in the SCNN1B or SCNN1G genes that encode the beta and gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel in the distal nephron. These variants typically delete or alter a cytoplasmic motif that is normally recognised by the ubiquitin ligase machinery, so the channel is not internalised and degraded and instead accumulates at the apical membrane. The result is excessive, aldosterone-independent sodium reabsorption with parallel renal loss of potassium and hydrogen ion, generating volume expansion, hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The expanded volume and raised pressure suppress renin release and therefore aldosterone secretion, giving the paradoxical combination of a mineralocorticoid-excess phenotype with low aldosterone. With ENaC-blocking therapy and salt restriction, blood pressure and potassium usually normalise and long-term outlook is good; untreated disease carries the cardiovascular and renal risks of chronic hypertension.

Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy — LGMD, sarcoglycanopathy, calpainopathy, dysferlinopathy Becker and Duchenne muscular dystrophies Inflammatory myopathies Metabolic and mitochondrial myopathies Spinal muscular atrophy Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy Congenital and myofibrillar myopathies Serum creatine kinase measurement Next-generation sequencing gene panel for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for specific structural proteins Muscle MRI to characterise the pattern of muscle involvement Electrocardiography and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy Pulmonary function testing for respiratory muscle weakness A genetically diverse group of muscular dystrophies unified by predominantly proximal weakness of the shoulder and pelvic girdles, with both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms Autosomal recessive subtypes are generally more common and include calpainopathy, dysferlinopathy, and the sarcoglycanopathies Onset ranges from childhood to adulthood, typically with difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, and lifting the arms Serum creatine kinase is usually elevated, sometimes markedly, especially in the recessive subtypes Some subtypes carry a significant risk of cardiomyopathy or respiratory muscle involvement, which guides surveillance Dysferlinopathy characteristically presents with distal calf involvement and very high creatine kinase in young adults Diagnosis increasingly relies on next-generation sequencing panels, complemented by muscle biopsy with protein immunostaining and imaging Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with physiotherapy, aids to mobility, and cardiac and respiratory monitoring targeted to the subtype Symptoms of cardiomyopathy or conduction disturbance in cardiac-associated subtypes Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an inflammatory or alternative cause Dysphagia or aspiration risk Acute rhabdomyolysis with very high creatine kinase and dark urine Grouping all cases together and missing subtype-specific cardiac or respiratory risks Overlooking a treatable inflammatory myopathy that can mimic the phenotype Failing to pursue genetic confirmation, which is essential for prognosis and counselling Attributing a very high creatine kinase solely to exercise in dysferlinopathy Neglecting cardiac surveillance in subtypes with known cardiomyopathy risk The limb-girdle muscular dystrophies result from variants in a wide range of genes encoding proteins essential to muscle-fibre structure and function, including components of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (such as the sarcoglycans), membrane-repair proteins (dysferlin), enzymes (calpain-3), and nuclear and glycosylation-related proteins. Loss of these proteins impairs sarcolemmal stability, membrane repair, or muscle-fibre maintenance, leading to repeated fibre injury, necrosis, and progressive replacement of muscle by fat and connective tissue. The predominant involvement of proximal girdle muscles produces the characteristic pattern of weakness, while the specific protein defect determines any associated cardiac or respiratory involvement. Prognosis varies widely by subtype, from slowly progressive forms compatible with a near-normal lifespan to more severe childhood-onset disease with early loss of ambulation. Cardiac and respiratory involvement in certain subtypes are the principal determinants of survival, underscoring the value of precise genetic diagnosis.
