standard blood counts may give clues (cytopenias) Fibromyalgia Chronic fatigue syndrome Allergic reaction to tick saliva Peripheral spondyloarthropathy / juvenile idiopathic arthritis (for the arthritis presentation) Caused by spirochetes of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato group (also called Borreliella spp.), transmitted by Ixodes ricinus complex ticks; B. burgdorferi sensu stricto is the predominant cause in the United States, while B. afzelii, B. garinii, and B. bavariensis also occur in Europe and Asia. (p.1448-1449) Staged illness: stage 1 (early localized) presents with erythema migrans (EM); stage 2 (early disseminated) may follow with secondary skin lesions, neurologic involvement (meningitis, cranial neuritis, radiculoneuritis), carditis with atrioventricular block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain; stage 3 (late/persistent) typically manifests as intermittent arthritis and, rarely, chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis. (p.1448-1449) EM begins after an incubation period of roughly 3-32 days as a red macule or papule at the bite site that expands into a large annular lesion, often with a bright red outer border and partial central clearing; common sites include the thigh, groin, and axilla, and the lesion is warm but usually not painful. (p.1451) Approximately 20% of patients do NOT develop the characteristic EM skin lesion, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. (p.1451) Cardiac involvement occurs in about 8% of patients within weeks of onset; the most common abnormality is fluctuating atrioventricular block (first-degree, Wenckebach, or complete heart block), and most cardiac involvement lasts only a few weeks. (p.1451) About 15% of untreated patients develop frank neurologic abnormalities after weeks to months; the typical U.S. pattern is fluctuating meningitis with facial palsy (cranial neuritis, often the facial nerve, sometimes bilateral) and peripheral radiculoneuropathy. CSF in U.S. neuroborreliosis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (~100 cells/uL) with elevated protein and normal or slightly low glucose. (p.1451) In Europe and Asia the characteristic first neurologic sign is radicular pain followed by CSF pleocytosis (meningopolyneuritis or Bannwarth's syndrome), often without meningeal or encephalitic signs. (p.1451) Lyme arthritis (stage 3) develops in about 60% of untreated U.S. patients months after onset; the typical pattern is intermittent oligoarticular attacks in large joints, especially the knees. Joint fluid white cell counts range widely (500-110,000/uL, average ~25,000/uL), mostly neutrophils, and rheumatoid factor and ANA tests are usually negative. (p.1451) Most patients experience early symptoms during summer, reflecting transmission by nymphal Ixodes ticks; the tick must usually remain attached for at least about 24 hours for transmission of B. burgdorferi. (p.1449-1450) Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne infection in the United States and Europe; in the U.S. more than 30,000 cases are reported annually but true cases are estimated at about 476,000 per year. (p.1450) Posttreatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) affects roughly 10% of treated patients (reported figures vary widely) with persistent subjective pain, neurocognitive symptoms, or fatigue; there is NO evidence these symptoms reflect active infection, and randomized trials show repeated antibiotic courses do not help and are not recommended. (p.1451-1453) Reinfection can occur after EM treated with antibiotics because the immune response after early infection is not protective; however, patients who develop an expanded immune response over months (e.g., those with Lyme arthritis) have protective immunity for years and rarely become reinfected. (p.1454) Maternal-fetal transmission of B. burgdorferi appears to occur rarely if at all; standard therapy is recommended for pregnant women. (p.1453) No Lyme disease vaccine is currently commercially available; the previously marketed vaccine was discontinued by its manufacturer. (p.1454) High-degree (third-degree) atrioventricular block or PR interval >0.3 s in carditis, warranting IV therapy and cardiac monitoring Severe objective neurologic abnormalities (e.g., meningitis, encephalitis, severe neuroborreliosis) Optic nerve involvement in children from inflammation or raised intracranial pressure, which may lead to blindness Borrelial encephalomyelitis/leukoencephalitis (rare, mainly B. garinii in Europe) with spastic paraparesis and bladder dysfunction Rare fatal pancarditis or cardiomegaly Suspected tick-borne co-infection (e.g., babesiosis, anaplasmosis, Powassan virus), which can cause severe or fatal illness, especially in the very young or elderly Assuming a negative serologic test excludes acute Lyme disease - serology may be negative during the first several weeks (early seronegativity), so diagnosis of early Lyme disease is clinical Missing the diagnosis because of atypical EM morphology or because ~20% of patients never develop EM Relying on a positive IgM result alone in illness lasting more than 2 months - such an isolated IgM is likely false-positive and should not support the diagnosis Misusing or misinterpreting IgM Western blots, a recognized cause of incorrect Lyme diagnoses in patients with other illnesses Using serology as a screening test in patients with nonspecific pain or fatigue (low pretest probability), where a false-positive result is more likely than a true-positive Interpreting persisting seropositivity (including VlsE C6 and IgM responses, which can persist for years after therapy) as evidence of active, recent, or recurrent infection Treating persistent subjective symptoms as active infection - 'chronic Lyme disease' equated with chronic B. burgdorferi infection is a misnomer, and repeated/prolonged antibiotic courses lack benefit and carry documented harm Using PCR positivity in joint fluid to judge active infection or adequacy of therapy, since DNA may persist for weeks after spirochetal killing B. burgdorferi is a fastidious microaerophilic spirochete with an unusually small genome and more than 100 predicted lipoproteins, mostly plasmid-encoded and displayed on the outer membrane to interact with host and tick. It expresses outer-surface protein A (OspA) in the tick midgut and upregulates OspC during migration to the salivary gland, where OspC binds the tick salivary protein Salp15 (required for mammalian infection). After injection into skin the organism downregulates OspC and upregulates the antigenically variable VlsE lipoprotein, then may migrate outward to produce EM and spread hematogenously or via lymphatics to skin, nervous system, heart, and joints. Its only known virulence factors are surface proteins that attach to host proteins, integrins, glycosaminoglycans, or glycoproteins (e.g., plasminogen binding aids tissue spread; complement regulators such as Factor H protect against lysis; decorin-binding proteins bind collagen-associated decorin, possibly explaining alignment with collagen fibrils). The host mounts innate and adaptive responses producing proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IFN-gamma) and opsonizing antibodies; immune mechanisms eventually control disseminated infection even without antibiotics, though spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. Postinfectious (antibiotic-refractory) Lyme arthritis is not due to persistent infection (culture and PCR of synovium are uniformly negative after antibiotics) but to a dysregulated, excessive proinflammatory response with very high IFN-gamma, host genetic factors (HLA-DRB1*0401, TLR1 1805GG polymorphism), and autoimmune responses to vascular and extracellular matrix autoantigens. Response to treatment is best when given early in the disease; later treatment remains effective but the convalescent period may be longer. Eventually most patients recover with minimal or no residual deficits. Even without antibiotics, innate and adaptive immunity usually control disseminated infection within weeks to months, though untreated spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. A small percentage develop persistent postinfectious arthritis or, rarely, chronic encephalopathy or polyneuropathy, and about 10% have PTLDS, which usually improves over months but may last years. Staged clinical classification per Harrison: Stage 1 - early localized infection (erythema migrans at the bite site). Stage 2 - early disseminated infection (secondary annular skin lesions, neurologic involvement such as meningitis/cranial neuritis/radiculoneuritis/peripheral neuritis, carditis with atrioventricular nodal block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain). Stage 3 - late/persistent infection (intermittent or persistent arthritis, and rarely chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans). For diagnostic/testing purposes, the American College of Physicians algorithm stratifies by pretest probability: high (EM - treat empirically without serology), intermediate (e.g., oligoarticular arthritis - test and treat if positive), and low (nonspecific symptoms - neither test nor treat).

Lymphoedema — lymphedema, lymphatic oedema, primary lymphoedema, secondary lymphoedema Chronic venous insufficiency and venous oedema Deep vein thrombosis Systemic causes of oedema (cardiac, renal, hepatic, hypoalbuminaemia) Lipoedema Dependent or immobility-related oedema Myxoedema Clinical assessment including Stemmer sign and limb circumference or volume measurement Lymphoscintigraphy to confirm lymphatic dysfunction when the diagnosis is unclear Duplex ultrasound to exclude venous disease or thrombosis Cross-sectional imaging to identify malignancy or nodal obstruction in secondary cases Evaluation for filariasis in endemic regions Results from impaired lymphatic drainage causing accumulation of protein-rich interstitial fluid and progressive limb swelling Primary forms arise from congenital or inherited lymphatic maldevelopment, while secondary forms follow damage from surgery, radiotherapy, malignancy, infection, or trauma Worldwide, filarial infection is the leading cause of secondary lymphoedema, whereas in high-income settings cancer treatment predominates Early swelling is soft and pitting but becomes non-pitting and fibrotic over time, with skin thickening and a positive Stemmer sign at the base of the toes The distribution characteristically includes the dorsum of the foot and toes, helping distinguish it from other causes of limb swelling Diagnosis is largely clinical; lymphoscintigraphy can confirm lymphatic dysfunction when the cause is uncertain Cornerstone management is complete decongestive therapy with skin care, manual lymphatic drainage, compression, and exercise Meticulous skin hygiene reduces recurrent cellulitis, which itself further damages lymphatics and worsens the oedema Features of cellulitis (spreading erythema, warmth, fever) requiring prompt treatment Rapidly progressive or unilateral swelling raising concern for underlying malignancy New or changing cutaneous lesions suggesting lymphangiosarcoma in longstanding lymphoedema Sudden painful swelling that could indicate concurrent deep vein thrombosis Confusing lymphoedema with venous oedema or lipoedema and applying inappropriate treatment Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial disease Overlooking an underlying malignancy in new unilateral limb swelling Neglecting skin care, allowing recurrent cellulitis that accelerates progression Lymphoedema develops when lymphatic transport capacity is exceeded by the lymphatic load, leading to accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitium. In primary disease the lymphatic vessels or nodes are congenitally hypoplastic, aplastic, or dysfunctional. In secondary disease, previously normal lymphatics are obstructed or destroyed by surgery, radiotherapy, tumour infiltration, recurrent infection (notably filariasis), or trauma. Stagnant protein draws further fluid osmotically and incites chronic inflammation, fibrosis, adipose deposition, and skin changes, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Impaired local immune surveillance predisposes to recurrent cellulitis. Lymphoedema is generally a chronic, progressive condition without cure, but sustained decongestive therapy and compression can control swelling, preserve function, and reduce complications. Poor adherence, recurrent infection, and untreated underlying causes worsen the outlook, and rarely longstanding disease can undergo malignant change.

tumours in one individual Postmenopausal or unexplained abnormal uterine bleeding in a carrier suggesting endometrial cancer Painless haematuria in a carrier raising concern for urothelial malignancy Labelling a microsatellite-unstable tumour as Lynch syndrome without excluding MLH1 promoter methylation Relying solely on family history criteria and missing carriers who do not meet Amsterdam or Bethesda thresholds Overlooking endometrial and other extracolonic risks by focusing only on the colon Failing to arrange cascade testing of relatives once a germline variant is confirmed The syndrome stems from a germline defect in the DNA mismatch-repair system, which normally corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that arise during replication. When the remaining functional allele is lost in a somatic cell, repair fails and errors accumulate, most conspicuously in repetitive microsatellite sequences, producing the microsatellite instability that characterises these tumours. The resulting hypermutable state generates numerous mutations in growth-regulatory genes, accelerating carcinogenesis and also creating neoantigens that make the tumours responsive to immune checkpoint blockade. Cancer risk is high but gene-dependent, being greatest for MLH1 and MSH2 and lower for MSH6 and PMS2. Colonoscopic surveillance markedly reduces colorectal cancer mortality, and mismatch-repair-deficient tumours often respond well to immune checkpoint inhibitors, so outcomes are frequently favourable when the diagnosis is recognised.

early infancy Adrenal calcification with signs of adrenal insufficiency Progression to hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis or portal hypertension Premature cardiovascular disease from severe dyslipidaemia Missing the diagnosis in infants by not measuring enzyme activity in unexplained hepatosplenomegaly and failure to thrive Mislabelling later-onset disease as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease or familial hypercholesterolaemia Overlooking adrenal insufficiency in the infantile form Delaying enzyme replacement therapy in rapidly progressive infantile disease Lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides taken up by cells through lipoprotein endocytosis, releasing free cholesterol and fatty acids for cellular use. Complete or near-complete deficiency causes massive lysosomal accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in liver, spleen, intestine, adrenal glands and macrophages, producing the fulminant multi-organ infantile Wolman phenotype; partial deficiency causes the slower cholesteryl ester storage disease phenotype. Impaired liberation of free cholesterol disrupts cholesterol homeostasis, driving compensatory synthesis and the characteristic dyslipidaemia, while progressive tissue storage leads to hepatic failure or, in milder disease, fibrosis and premature atherosclerosis. Untreated infantile Wolman disease is almost uniformly fatal within the first months of life, whereas the later-onset form is more indolent; enzyme replacement therapy substantially improves survival and hepatic and metabolic outcomes across the spectrum.

Lysosomal Storage Diseases — Lysosomal system diseases, LSDs, Tay-Sachs disease, Fabry disease, Gaucher disease, Niemann-Pick disease, Mucopolysaccharidoses, Pompe disease, Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, LALD, Krabbe disease, CLN2 Batten disease, Alpha-mannosidosis Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (mimicked by late-onset Pompe disease) Idiopathic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (about 1-3% have Fabry disease) Idiopathic stroke at 35-50 years (about 2-5% carry GLA mutations) Idiopathic renal failure in males (about 5% have GLA mutations) Cryptogenic cirrhosis / nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (childhood/adult-onset LALD) Familial hyperlipidemia (LALD) Parkinson disease (associated with GBA1 carriage) Acute appendicitis or renal colic (Fabry abdominal pain can mimic these) Enzyme assay in nucleated cells, serum/plasma, or leukocytes specific to the suspected disorder Molecular/genetic testing: whole GBA1 sequencing is the standard for Gaucher (enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for heterozygote detection) Slit-lamp examination for corneal and lenticular lesions to support a Fabry diagnosis Decreased acid beta-glucosidase activity (0-20% of normal) in nucleated cells establishes Gaucher disease; the enzyme is normally absent from bodily fluids Markedly reduced acid sphingomyelinase activity (1-10% of normal) in nucleated cells confirms Niemann-Pick A/B Confirmation of specific enzyme deficiency in Morquio (GALNS vs acid beta-galactosidase) before therapy Gene sequencing to confirm CLN2 given overlap among the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses Newborn screening (now includes MPS I and, in many states, Pompe disease) Bone imaging / nuclear scan in Gaucher bone crises (localized absent uptake of pyrophosphate agents indicates acute bone infarction) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Fabry cardiac variant) Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (late-onset Pompe) Cryptogenic/idiopathic cirrhosis (childhood/adult-onset LALD) Other neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (significant clinical overlap with CLN2) Lysosomes are subcellular organelles holding specific hydrolases that process or degrade proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids; there are more than 50 distinct lysosomal storage diseases (now also called lysosomal system diseases), grouped by the predominant accumulated material. Consider an LSD in the differential when a patient has unexplained neurologic, renal or muscular degeneration, or unexplained hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, cardiomyopathy, or skeletal dysplasias/deformities; physical findings are disease-specific and diagnosis is confirmed by enzyme assay or genetic testing. Nearly all LSDs are autosomal recessive, with notable exceptions: Hunter disease (MPS II), Danon disease and Fabry disease are X-linked, and two autosomal dominant conditions exist (Parry-type CLN from DNAJC5 mutations, and frontotemporal dementia/CLN11 from GRN/progranulin mutations). Tay-Sachs disease (total hexosaminidase A deficiency) is carried by roughly 1 in 30 Ashkenazi Jews; the infantile form features macrocephaly, loss of motor skills, an exaggerated startle reaction and a macular cherry-red spot, with carrier screening recommended in this population. Fabry disease (X-linked, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) presents with angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, corneal and lenticular opacities, debilitating episodic burning pain of the hands and feet (acroparesthesia), and progressive renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease; angiokeratomas are punctate, dark red to blue-black, do not blanch and cluster in the 'bathing suit area' between umbilicus and knees. Gaucher disease (acid beta-glucosidase deficiency, GBA1) is classified by CNS involvement: type 1 is nonneuronopathic with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease, type 2 is a severe progressive CNS disease causing death by about 2 years, and type 3 has variable CNS and visceral disease; early CNS signs in type 3 may be limited to supranuclear lateral gaze palsy. GBA1 mutations, whether heterozygous or homozygous, substantially raise the lifetime risk of Parkinson disease. Niemann-Pick types A and B reflect acid sphingomyelinase deficiency: type A has early onset with rapid CNS deterioration, while type B is later/variable with hepatosplenomegaly, cirrhosis, and lethal progressive pulmonary disease (foam cells in alveoli, lymphatics and pulmonary arteries); Niemann-Pick C is a separate disorder from NPC1/NPC2 defects in cholesterol/sphingolipid transport. Pompe disease (acid alpha-glucosidase/acid maltase deficiency, GAA) is the only LSD causing primary glycogen storage; the classic infantile form has hypotonia, cardiomyopathy and hepatosplenomegaly with near-total enzyme deficiency, whereas late-onset forms resemble a limb-girdle myopathy and may not have cardiomyopathy. Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LIPA mutations) spans infantile Wolman syndrome (failure to thrive, vomiting, hepatosplenomegaly; median death about 3.7 months) and childhood/adult-onset cholesterol ester storage disease (elevated liver enzymes, microvesicular fatty liver, cryptogenic cirrhosis); neither variant causes primary CNS disease and statins do not halt the underlying tissue pathology. CLN2 (neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2, TPP1/tripeptidyl peptidase 1 deficiency) usually begins at age 2-4 years with seizures, ataxia, myoclonus and vision loss, progressing to severe disability and death around age 12; it is the only NCL with a specific approved treatment. Alpha-mannosidosis (MAN2B1 biallelic loss of function) accumulates mannose-rich oligosaccharides and causes intellectual disability, incapacitating skeletal changes, immunodeficiency, ataxia, hearing loss, neurodegeneration and psychosis. Macular cherry-red spot with macrocephaly and exaggerated startle in an infant (infantile Tay-Sachs) Splenic infarction in Gaucher disease that can present as an acute abdomen Gaucher 'bone crisis' with excruciating localized pain, sometimes erythema, fever and leukocytosis, representing acute bone infarction Pulmonary hypertension or alveolar Gaucher cell accumulation (uncommon but life-threatening, more common in splenectomized females) Vertebral collapse and avascular necrosis (femoral head) with potential spinal cord involvement in Gaucher disease Infantile-onset LALD presenting as a medical emergency with severe failure to thrive, vomiting and hepatosplenomegaly Fetal hydrops in severe MPS VII (Sly), which can cause stillbirth or perinatal demise Progressive pulmonary disease with dyspnea and hypoxemia in Niemann-Pick type B Respiratory insufficiency requiring ventilation in late-onset Pompe disease Treating the disease nosology as fixed discrete entities is misleading: each LSD is heuristic and clinically expresses a continuous spectrum from severe to attenuated forms. Angiokeratomas of Fabry disease can be easily overlooked and also occur in several other rare LSDs, so they are not specific. Fabry abdominal pain may be mistaken for appendicitis or renal colic, delaying diagnosis. Enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for Gaucher heterozygote detection; molecular GBA1 sequencing is required. In Niemann-Pick, hepatic or bone marrow transplantation has produced more complications than expected (recurrent hepatic disease from ASM-deficient myeloid repopulation after liver transplant, or failure to clear hepatocyte sphingomyelin after BMT/HSCT). Enzyme replacement therapy does not cross the blood-brain barrier and does not directly treat CNS disease (e.g., MPS I, MPS II); HSCT has not succeeded against CNS disease in MPS II. Statins lower hypercholesterolemia in LALD but do not alter the underlying progressive tissue (e.g., liver) pathology. Late cardiac and respiratory complications of MPS I (obstructive breathing, cardiomyopathy, valve disease) can emerge even after successful HSCT, so lifelong follow-up is required. Morquio variants A and B require confirmation of the specific enzyme deficiency because approved enzyme therapy (elosulfase alfa) applies only to MPS IVA. Lysosomal biogenesis requires ongoing synthesis of lysosomal hydrolases, membrane proteins and new membranes; lysosomes form by fusion of trans-Golgi network vesicles with late endosomes, and progressive acidification creates a pH gradient that drives pH-dependent dissociation of receptors from ligands and activates the hydrolases. Lysosomes are part of the lysosome/autophagy/mitophagy system regulated by mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of transcription factors TFEB/TFE3, which balances anabolic and catabolic pathways; this regulation is disrupted to varying degrees in tissues affected by specific LSDs. Defects at any biosynthetic step can impair enzyme function: oligosaccharide remodeling in the Golgi (including the mannose-6-phosphate lysosomal targeting ligand), membrane sorting signals, phosphorylation, sulfation, additional proteolysis and heteromer assembly are all critical, and abnormalities in these shared processes can produce multiple simultaneous enzyme/protein deficiencies. The final common pathway is accumulation of specific macromolecules within tissues and cells that normally carry a high flux of those substrates; most deficiencies arise from point mutations or rearrangements at a single hydrolase/subunit locus, though some mutations affecting targeting, active sites, macromolecular assembly or trafficking impair several hydrolases at once. Substrate buildup distorts lysosomes and may exert pharmacologic effects, notably activation of innate immune responses. Some substrates are made within the tissue of pathology, while others are delivered exogenously (LDL receptor-mediated uptake in Fabry and LALD; phagocytosis in Gaucher type 1). The threshold hypothesis holds that disease emerges below a certain level of residual enzyme activity, and that activity can be challenged by changes in substrate flux from genetic background, cell turnover, recycling or metabolic demand, so a given residual level may suffice in some tissues but not others. Prognosis varies enormously across and within disorders, each spanning a spectrum from severe to attenuated forms. Infantile Tay-Sachs is fatal in infancy; juvenile-onset Tay-Sachs causes death by 10-15 years. In Fabry disease, death results from cardiovascular, renal or cerebrovascular disease; renal insufficiency, cardiac fibrosis and stroke are irreversible, so early therapy offers the best chance to slow life-threatening complications, and heart disease is the most common life-threatening manifestation in females while renal then cardiovascular disease predominates in males. Gaucher type 2 leads to death by about 2 years, while type 1 and type 3 are highly variable. Niemann-Pick type B can progress to death in adolescence or early adulthood from hepatic or pulmonary disease. Infantile Pompe is rapidly progressive with death typically in the first year without treatment. Infantile-onset LALD is fatal by about 1 year (median 3.7 months) untreated, and untreated childhood/adult-onset LALD progresses to early cirrhosis (mean about age 13) and early-adulthood atherosclerosis. Early infantile Krabbe presents around 4 months and progresses rapidly to death at a mean of about 18 months. CLN2 progresses to severe disability with most children wheelchair-bound in late childhood, death at a mean of about 12 years, and survival beyond adolescence rare. Within individual diseases, severity is typically stratified by age of onset and CNS involvement. Examples: Tay-Sachs is divided into infantile, juvenile-onset and adult-onset forms. MPS I is graded as Hurler (MPS I H, severe with neurodegeneration), Hurler-Scheie (MPS I H/S, intermediate, severe somatic disease without major neurologic decline), and Scheie (MPS I S, later-onset without neurologic involvement). Gaucher disease is classed as type 1 (nonneuronopathic), type 2 (acute severe CNS), and type 3 (variable subacute/chronic CNS). Niemann-Pick distinguishes type A (early-onset, progressive CNS), type B (later, variable, with an A/B variant having slowly progressive CNS involvement), and the separate type C. LALD ranges from infantile-onset (Wolman) to childhood/adult-onset (cholesterol ester storage disease). Pompe and Krabbe are divided into early/infantile and later-onset variants.

Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) — SCA3, spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, Machado-Joseph disease, ATXN3-related ataxia, ataxin-3 CAG repeat expansion Other dominant spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA1, SCA2, SCA6, SCA7) Multiple system atrophy Parkinson disease or dystonia syndromes when extrapyramidal features dominate Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis when amyotrophy is prominent Friedreich ataxia Acquired cerebellar degenerations Targeted molecular genetic testing for ATXN3 CAG repeat expansion Brain MRI showing cerebellar, brainstem, and sometimes basal ganglia atrophy Nerve conduction studies for associated peripheral neuropathy Detailed oculomotor examination for ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus Assessment for dystonia, spasticity, and parkinsonism Swallowing and speech assessment as bulbar involvement progresses The most common autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia worldwide, caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the ATXN3 gene encoding a polyglutamine tract in ataxin-3 Presents with progressive cerebellar ataxia combined with variable pyramidal, extrapyramidal, and peripheral features, giving a broad clinical spectrum Characteristic signs include prominent, bulging eyes with lid retraction, gaze-evoked nystagmus, and progressive external ophthalmoplegia Faciolingual fasciculations and myokymia, dystonia, spasticity, and a peripheral neuropathy with amyotrophy are recognised features Recognised clinical subtypes range from early-onset spastic-dystonic forms to later-onset predominantly ataxic or peripheral-neuropathy phenotypes depending on repeat length and age Demonstrates anticipation, with earlier onset and greater severity as the repeat expands across generations Confirmed by molecular testing for the ATXN3 CAG expansion; treatment is symptomatic and multidisciplinary Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk Severe spasticity or dystonia impairing mobility and safety Respiratory or bulbar decline in advanced disease Attributing the diverse features to separate diagnoses rather than recognising the SCA3 spectrum Assuming a subtype without gene-specific confirmation Missing the characteristic bulging eyes and faciolingual fasciculations as diagnostic clues Neglecting anticipation and genetic counselling for at-risk relatives Machado-Joseph disease (SCA3) is a polyglutamine disorder caused by expansion of the CAG repeat in the ATXN3 gene. Ataxin-3 normally functions as a deubiquitinating enzyme involved in protein quality control; the expanded polyglutamine tract confers a toxic gain of function, promoting misfolding, aggregation, and formation of neuronal intranuclear inclusions that impair the ubiquitin-proteasome system and cellular homeostasis. Neurodegeneration affects the cerebellum and its connections, brainstem and cranial nerve nuclei, basal ganglia, spinal motor and sensory pathways, and peripheral nerves, accounting for the wide phenotypic range. Repeat length correlates inversely with age at onset, underlying anticipation. The disease is progressive over one to several decades with steadily accumulating disability; life expectancy is reduced, usually as a consequence of bulbar dysfunction and respiratory complications, although progression rate varies with subtype.

Macrophage Activation Syndrome — MAS, secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, secondary HLH Primary (familial) haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis Sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation Flare of the underlying rheumatic disease Systemic infection (EBV and other viruses, intracellular pathogens) Malignancy, particularly lymphoma or leukaemia Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) Serum ferritin (very high levels are characteristic and trended for response) Full blood count to detect evolving cytopenias Fibrinogen, D-dimer, and full coagulation profile Fasting triglycerides Liver function tests and lactate dehydrogenase Soluble interleukin-2 receptor (soluble CD25) and natural killer cell function where available Bone marrow aspirate to look for haemophagocytosis when the diagnosis is uncertain A life-threatening hyperinflammatory state, considered a form of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, characterised by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and T cells. It most commonly complicates rheumatic conditions, especially systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, but can be triggered by infection or malignancy. Suspect it when a child with an underlying inflammatory disease develops persistent high fever, worsening general condition, and hepatosplenomegaly. A characteristic and counterintuitive clue is falling blood counts (cytopenias) and a paradoxically falling or normalising ESR despite active inflammation. Markedly elevated ferritin is a hallmark laboratory feature and useful for both suspicion and monitoring. Other typical findings include high triglycerides, low fibrinogen, deranged liver function, and coagulopathy, sometimes with overt bleeding. Bone marrow examination may show haemophagocytosis, but a normal marrow does not exclude the diagnosis and treatment should not be delayed for it. This is a medical emergency requiring rapid immunosuppression to interrupt the cytokine storm before multi-organ failure develops. Rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction from cytokine storm (EMERGENCY) Persistent high fever with deteriorating clinical state Falling cell counts across multiple lineages Falling fibrinogen with rising ferritin and clinical bleeding Neurological involvement: seizures, altered consciousness Progression toward disseminated intravascular coagulation or shock Being falsely reassured by a falling or normal ESR, which can accompany the low fibrinogen of MAS Interpreting the picture solely as a disease flare or sepsis and delaying specific treatment Waiting for bone marrow confirmation of haemophagocytosis before starting therapy Underappreciating how quickly the condition can progress to coagulopathy and organ failure Not monitoring ferritin and blood counts closely to track response MAS results from defective downregulation of the immune response, with impaired cytotoxic function of natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. This allows persistent activation and proliferation of T cells and well-differentiated macrophages (histiocytes), which phagocytose blood cells and release a flood of pro-inflammatory cytokines. This cytokine storm produces sustained fever, cytopenias from marrow phagocytosis and suppression, hepatic dysfunction, coagulopathy resembling disseminated intravascular coagulation, and progressive multi-organ damage. MAS carries significant mortality if unrecognised, but early aggressive immunosuppression can be life-saving and many children recover; outcome depends on prompt diagnosis, control of the trigger, and reversal of organ dysfunction before it becomes irreversible.

risk to the only good eye Traumatic hole with other posterior segment injury Confusing a pseudohole or lamellar hole with a full-thickness hole without OCT confirmation Delaying referral so that a small, highly repairable hole enlarges and chronifies Overlooking a coexisting retinal detachment in a myopic eye Setting unrealistic expectations for visual recovery in long-standing holes An idiopathic full-thickness macular hole develops when tangential and anteroposterior traction from the perifoveal vitreous acts on the fovea during posterior vitreous detachment. This traction elevates and then dehisces the foveal tissue, creating a full-thickness defect with surrounding cuff of subretinal fluid and cystic change. Progressive stages run from foveal detachment and pseudocyst through to an established round hole. Secondary holes may follow blunt trauma or the mechanical stresses of high myopia, where posterior staphyloma adds traction. Modern vitrectomy with membrane peeling closes the large majority of idiopathic holes, and visual improvement is best when the hole is small and of short duration; large, chronic, or myopic holes have lower closure rates and more limited recovery.

depressed mood Grief and bereavement reactions Hypothyroidism and other endocrine or metabolic disorders Substance-induced or medication-induced mood disorder Depression in the context of a neurocognitive disorder (pseudodementia) Structured suicide risk assessment Standardised symptom rating scales to gauge severity and track response Thyroid function testing Full blood count and metabolic panel to exclude anaemia and other medical contributors Vitamin B12 and folate where clinically indicated Substance use screening Diagnosis requires a sustained period (at least around two weeks) of either persistently low mood or loss of interest/pleasure, together with several additional symptoms causing significant distress or functional impairment Associated features commonly include disturbed sleep, appetite or weight change, fatigue, poor concentration, psychomotor slowing or agitation, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, and recurrent thoughts of death Always screen actively for suicidal ideation, intent, and plan, and ask about prior attempts and access to means Screen for a past manic or hypomanic episode before starting an antidepressant, because an unrecognised bipolar diathesis can be destabilised Exclude medical and substance-related contributors such as hypothyroidism, anaemia, and medication effects before attributing symptoms solely to a primary mood disorder Management principles combine evidence-based psychotherapy (such as cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy) with antidepressant pharmacotherapy, typically first-line SSRIs, chosen by side-effect profile and comorbidity Antidepressant benefit is often delayed by several weeks, adherence should be reinforced, and treatment is generally continued well beyond symptom remission to reduce relapse Severe, psychotic, treatment-resistant, or high-suicide-risk presentations may warrant combination pharmacotherapy, augmentation, or electroconvulsive therapy Active suicidal ideation with plan, intent, or access to means Psychotic features such as mood-congruent delusions or hallucinations Profound self-neglect, refusal of food or fluids, or catatonia Rapid deterioration or emerging manic symptoms after starting an antidepressant Starting an antidepressant without screening for a prior manic or hypomanic episode Underestimating suicide risk or failing to reassess it during treatment Stopping antidepressants too early once mood improves, increasing relapse risk Attributing symptoms to depression while missing an underlying medical cause such as hypothyroidism Judging non-response before an adequate dose and duration of treatment Major depressive disorder is understood as a multifactorial condition arising from interactions among genetic vulnerability, dysregulation of monoamine neurotransmission (serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine), and disturbance of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis stress responses. Contemporary models also emphasise impaired neuroplasticity and neurotrophic signalling, altered function in limbic and prefrontal circuits, and the role of chronic stress and adverse life events acting on a predisposed individual. Major depressive disorder is frequently recurrent; many patients respond to treatment but relapse risk rises with each subsequent episode and with residual symptoms. Prognosis is generally better with early treatment, good adherence, and psychosocial support, and worse with comorbid substance use, chronic medical illness, and untreated recurrent episodes.

Male infertility — male factor infertility, male subfertility, impaired male fertility Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (pituitary or hypothalamic) Primary testicular failure including Klinefelter syndrome Varicocele Obstructive azoospermia including congenital absence of the vas deferens Retrograde or failed ejaculation Exogenous androgen or anabolic steroid use suppressing spermatogenesis Repeated semen analysis performed to standard laboratory criteria Hormonal profile including FSH, LH, testosterone, and prolactin Scrotal examination and ultrasound to detect varicocele or obstruction Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion analysis in severe cases Post-ejaculatory urinalysis when retrograde ejaculation is suspected A male factor contributes to roughly half of couples presenting with infertility, so both partners should be evaluated in parallel from the outset Semen analysis is the cornerstone investigation and should be repeated because of considerable biological variability before conclusions are drawn Abnormalities are described in terms of sperm concentration, motility, and morphology, with azoospermia, oligozoospermia, and asthenozoospermia denoting the main patterns Causes are grouped into pre-testicular (hypothalamic-pituitary and hormonal), testicular (primary spermatogenic failure), and post-testicular (obstruction or ejaculatory disorders) Endocrine evaluation with gonadotrophins and testosterone helps localise the problem; low gonadotrophins suggest a central cause whereas high FSH indicates primary testicular failure Varicocele is a common and potentially correctable cause, and reversible contributors such as heat, smoking, alcohol, obesity, and certain drugs should be sought Azoospermia should be characterised as obstructive or non-obstructive, since surgical sperm retrieval with assisted reproduction can achieve fatherhood in many cases Genetic evaluation, including karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing, is indicated in severe oligozoospermia or non-obstructive azoospermia Azoospermia requiring prompt distinction between obstructive and non-obstructive causes Signs of a pituitary mass such as visual field loss or headache with low gonadotrophins Bilateral testicular atrophy or gynaecomastia suggesting significant endocrine or genetic disease A testicular mass discovered during fertility evaluation, raising concern for malignancy Investigating and treating only the female partner while overlooking male factor contribution Drawing conclusions from a single abnormal semen analysis without repeat testing Missing exogenous androgen or anabolic steroid use as a reversible cause of azoospermia Failing to offer genetic counselling before assisted reproduction in men with genetic causes Male fertility depends on the integrity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, on spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubules driven by FSH and intratesticular testosterone, and on an unobstructed ductal system allowing sperm transport and ejaculation. Pre-testicular disease reflects deficient gonadotrophin stimulation (hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism from pituitary or hypothalamic disorders, hyperprolactinaemia, or exogenous androgen use). Testicular causes include genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, prior orchitis, chemotherapy or radiation, and varicocele-related impairment of the testicular thermal and vascular environment. Post-testicular causes include congenital absence or acquired obstruction of the vas deferens, ejaculatory duct obstruction, retrograde ejaculation, and antisperm antibodies. The final common pathway is a reduction in the number or function of sperm reaching the oocyte. Outcome depends on the cause; hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and obstruction are often correctable, varicocele repair may improve parameters in selected men, and even severe spermatogenic failure can frequently be overcome by surgical sperm retrieval combined with assisted reproductive techniques.

Malignancy (B-symptoms) — Imaging directed to site Biopsy/histology LDH, blood film Persistent unexplained B-symptoms warrant urgent workup Hodgkin lymphoma (classical) - nontender cervical/supraclavicular/axillary nodes, frequent mediastinal involvement (Harrison 22e p.869) Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860) Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476) Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897) Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477) Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477) Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317) Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476) Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477) Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477) Toxoplasmosis - generalised reactive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476) HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903) Excisional biopsy of the largest abnormal node is preferred; fine-needle aspiration should NOT be the first procedure as it usually yields insufficient tissue and delays diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.478) Serum protein electrophoresis to detect a monoclonal paraprotein (Harrison 22e p.903) Serum beta2-microglobulin and LDH - independent prognostic markers in NHL (Harrison 22e p.903) CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic/liver panel, uric acid and calcium (Harrison 22e p.317, p.904) ESR and CRP as part of the constitutional-symptom / weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869) Contrast CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; FDG-PET/CT preferred for aggressive lymphomas and Hodgkin lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.904) Bone marrow biopsy where indicated; lumbar puncture if CNS-risk histology or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.903-904) HIV and hepatitis B and C serology - risk factors for NHL and relevant to hepatitis B reactivation risk (Harrison 22e p.904) Cervical node ultrasound long-to-short axis ratio (<2.0 favours malignancy) where head/neck cancer is suspected (Harrison 22e p.478) Age/sex/risk-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. faecal occult blood, colonoscopy, mammography) and abdominal ultrasound in occult-malignancy weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.318) Sarcoidosis - mediastinal/hilar adenopathy and constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.477) Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease - generalised adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476) Drug-induced (phenytoin/diphenylhydantoin and others) lymphadenopathy, including DRESS/DIHS with eosinophilia and extensive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193, p.476) Castleman disease, Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, IgG4-related disease (Harrison 22e p.476) B symptoms are formally defined for lymphoma staging (the Ann Arbor 'B' suffix) as unexplained fever (>38C), drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869). The tempo of symptoms helps separate aggressive from indolent lymphoma: rapid symptomatic progression and the presence of B symptoms suggest a more aggressive process (Harrison 22e p.903). Among malignancies, lymphoma is by far the commonest cause of malignancy-related fever of unknown origin, and the fever can precede any palpable lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193). About one-third of patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma present with B symptoms; Hodgkin disease can even present as a fever of unknown origin, more often in older patients with abdominal mixed-cellularity disease (Harrison 22e p.869). Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever lasting days to weeks alternating with afebrile intervals) is a rare but classic Hodgkin lymphoma presentation (Harrison 22e p.869). Node character matters: lymphomatous nodes tend to be large, firm, rubbery, mobile, symmetric and non-tender, whereas metastatic carcinoma nodes are typically hard, non-tender and fixed to surrounding tissue (Harrison 22e p.477). Supraclavicular and scalene node enlargement is always abnormal and warrants prompt evaluation; a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) classically reflects a gastrointestinal primary, but lung, breast, testis and ovarian cancers also seed these nodes (Harrison 22e p.477). Examination in suspected lymphoma should systematically cover all peripheral nodal sites plus Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen size, effusions/ascites, and testicular, breast or skin involvement, since any of these can change staging and management (Harrison 22e p.903). Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes are usually malignant (lymphoma, or germ-cell tumour in young men), in contrast to the largely benign causes of cervical adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.477). Half of all cancer patients lose some weight and up to 20% of cancer deaths are attributable directly to cachexia; malignancy that declares itself through marked weight loss generally carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.317). Supraclavicular or scalene adenopathy - always abnormal, biopsy promptly (Harrison 22e p.477-478) Solitary hard non-tender cervical node in an older tobacco user - prompt biopsy after ENT mucosal assessment (Harrison 22e p.478) Node size >2 cm with an abnormal chest x-ray in younger patients - predicts malignant/granulomatous biopsy yield (Harrison 22e p.521) Hard fixed nodes, or firm mobile generalised adenopathy suggestive of lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.478) Airway, oesophageal or SVC compression from thoracic adenopathy (cough/wheeze, hoarseness, dysphagia, facial/arm/neck swelling) (Harrison 22e p.520) Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes (usually malignant) (Harrison 22e p.477) Involuntary weight loss >=5% over 6 months prompting structured malignancy workup (Harrison 22e p.358) Do NOT give glucocorticoids for undiagnosed lymphadenopathy - their lympholytic effect can obscure lymphoma, leukaemia and Castleman disease and delay/disrupt diagnosis (the rare exception is life-threatening pharyngeal obstruction from Waldeyer-ring tissue in mononucleosis) (Harrison 22e p.521). Fine-needle aspiration is inadequate for an initial lymphoma diagnosis - obtain an excisional/core biopsy; FNA is reserved for thyroid nodules and confirming relapse of a known cancer (Harrison 22e p.478). Antibiotics are NOT indicated for lymphadenopathy unless there is strong evidence of bacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.521). Localized-versus-generalized adenopathy has limited discriminatory value because many causes produce either pattern; do not over-rely on it (Harrison 22e p.476). In primary care most lymphadenopathy is benign (>two-thirds nonspecific/URI, <1% malignant) and needs only short-interval follow-up - but persistent or enlarging nodes must be re-evaluated and biopsied (Harrison 22e p.476, p.521). If a head-and-neck primary is suspected behind a solitary cervical node, perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first before excising the node (Harrison 22e p.478). B symptoms in lymphoma are cytokine-mediated systemic effects of the tumour rather than direct mass effects. In classical Hodgkin lymphoma the malignant Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells are rare within a tumour mass that is largely a polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate reacting to tumour-derived cytokines; this inflammatory milieu drives constitutional symptoms and contributes to the generalised immune suppression seen in these patients. Involuntary weight loss in malignancy reflects a combination of anorexia, sarcopenia and a cytokine-driven cachexia syndrome. (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869) Lymphoma prognosis is stage- and biology-dependent. For NHL the International Prognostic Index uses five factors (age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site); for DLBCL treated with R-CHOP, 0 factors gives ~94% 4-year survival versus ~53% with 3-5 factors. Across lymphomas, decreased outcome is associated with B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH and bulky disease (e.g. lymph-node mass >7 cm). In occult solid malignancy, presentation through significant involuntary weight loss generally carries a very poor prognosis, whereas when no cause is found after thorough workup the prognosis is comparatively favourable. (Harrison 22e p.317, p.861, NHL prognosis section) Ann Arbor staging (stages I-IV) with suffix A (no systemic symptoms) or B (presence of B symptoms: fever >38C, drenching night sweats, or weight loss >10% body weight over preceding 6 months); suffix E for localized extralymphatic extension. B-symptom status (the A/B designation) and stage drive prognosis and therapy. (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869)

Malignant hyperthermia — MH, malignant hyperpyrexia, anaesthetic-induced hypermetabolic crisis Inadequate anaesthesia or analgesia with sympathetic response Sepsis or systemic inflammatory response Thyroid storm or phaeochromocytoma crisis Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome Equipment-related rebreathing or exhausted carbon dioxide absorbent Environmental or iatrogenic hyperthermia Continuous capnography and core temperature monitoring to detect the crisis early Arterial blood gas showing combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis Serial potassium, creatine kinase, and myoglobin to track rhabdomyolysis Coagulation studies to detect disseminated intravascular coagulation Later in-vitro contracture testing and RYR1 genetic analysis for confirmation A pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile anaesthetics and depolarising neuromuscular blockers in susceptible individuals The earliest and most sensitive sign is an unexplained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide despite increased ventilation, often with tachycardia and mixed acidosis Masseter or generalised muscle rigidity, rapidly rising temperature, and dark urine from myoglobin are later features; hyperthermia is frequently a late rather than early sign Immediate management is to stop triggering agents, call for help and the emergency supply of dantrolene, hyperventilate with high-flow oxygen, and switch to a non-triggering technique Dantrolene is the specific antidote and should be given without delay and repeated until the hypermetabolic state resolves Supportive care includes active cooling, treating hyperkalaemia and arrhythmias, correcting acidosis, and maintaining urine output to protect against myoglobinuric renal injury Susceptibility is largely inherited (commonly RYR1 gene variants) and is linked to certain myopathies; a family or personal history should prompt a trigger-free anaesthetic Confirmatory testing uses the in-vitro contracture (caffeine-halothane) test with genetic testing, and survivors should be counselled and referred to an MH unit Rapidly rising end-tidal carbon dioxide with tachycardia and rigidity indicating an evolving MH crisis Severe hyperthermia with mixed acidosis and hyperkalaemia threatening arrhythmia and arrest Cardiac arrhythmia or arrest during or after a triggering anaesthetic Dark urine and rising creatine kinase signalling rhabdomyolysis and renal risk Attributing rising carbon dioxide or tachycardia to light anaesthesia and delaying diagnosis Failing to have dantrolene immediately available or delaying its administration Confusing an isolated masseter spasm with a full crisis or, conversely, dismissing it entirely Neglecting active cooling and management of hyperkalaemia and myoglobinuria Not counselling the patient and family or arranging specialist referral after recovery Malignant hyperthermia results from abnormal regulation of skeletal muscle calcium, most often due to mutations affecting the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) that controls calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. On exposure to volatile agents or succinylcholine, uncontrolled calcium release produces sustained muscle contraction and a massive increase in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism. This drives rapid carbon dioxide and heat generation, oxygen consumption, lactic acidosis, ATP depletion, and eventually muscle breakdown with hyperkalaemia, myoglobinaemia, and rhabdomyolysis. Dantrolene reduces calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and interrupts the cycle. Mortality has fallen dramatically with early recognition and prompt dantrolene, but delayed treatment can lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation, renal failure, and death; survivors and relatives require testing and lifelong trigger avoidance.

spasm), hyperthermia that is often a late sign, and metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and rhabdomyolysis Most susceptibility is autosomal dominant and linked to mutations in RYR1, encoding the ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel, with a minority linked to CACNA1S Emergency management is immediate withdrawal of triggering agents, dantrolene, and aggressive supportive cooling and correction of acidosis and hyperkalaemia, alongside a switch to a trigger-free anaesthetic technique The in-vitro (caffeine-halothane) contracture test on freshly biopsied muscle remains the diagnostic reference standard, complemented by genetic testing Susceptibility overlaps with certain RYR1-related myopathies such as central core disease, and a personal or family history of investigation Unexplained rising end-tidal carbon dioxide with tachycardia and rigidity under anaesthesia Masseter spasm after succinylcholine Rapidly rising core temperature with metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia or dark myoglobinuric urine Family history of anaesthetic death or unexplained perioperative crisis Waiting for hyperthermia, which is frequently a late sign, before acting on rising carbon dioxide and rigidity Confusing a crisis with neuroleptic malignant or serotonin syndrome and delaying dantrolene Assuming a previously uneventful anaesthetic excludes susceptibility, since crises can occur on later exposures Failing to refer the patient and family for contracture and genetic testing and to document trigger-agent avoidance Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility most often results from mutations in RYR1, the gene encoding the ryanodine receptor that releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during excitation-contraction coupling, and less often from mutations in the CACNA1S calcium channel that triggers it. The abnormal channel is hypersensitive, so on exposure to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine it releases uncontrolled calcium into the myoplasm. Sustained high calcium drives continuous muscle contraction and a runaway increase in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism, generating heat, carbon dioxide and lactate, depleting adenosine triphosphate, and causing membrane breakdown with rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Without prompt treatment this hypermetabolic cascade progresses to multi-organ failure. With early recognition, prompt dantrolene and modern supportive care the mortality of an acute crisis is now low, and susceptible individuals can undergo safe anaesthesia using trigger-free agents, but an unrecognised or untreated crisis remains rapidly fatal.

Malnutrition and Nutritional Assessment — Protein-calorie malnutrition, Protein-energy malnutrition, Undernutrition Sarcopenia (progressive generalized loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength; screened with SARC-F) Sarcopenic obesity Cachexia of chronic disease (malignancy, organ failure) Frailty syndrome Dehydration / fluid shifts mimicking weight change Micronutrient deficiency states Validated risk-screening tools: Malnutrition Screening Tool, Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), Nutritional Risk Screening 2002, Mini Nutritional Assessment, Subjective Global Assessment Anthropometrics: serial body weight (without shoes/heavy garments), BMI, calf circumference, mid-upper arm circumference; height estimated by arm span or knee-height caliper when needed Body composition: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA, portable), dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), air displacement plethysmography, and opportunistic CT/MRI muscle measurement Laboratory: complete blood count with differential (screen for iron, B12, folate, vitamin C deficiencies), C-reactive protein for inflammation, specific micronutrient levels Indirect calorimetry for resting energy expenditure; 24-h urine urea nitrogen and nitrogen balance to gauge catabolism and protein adequacy (normal renal/hepatic function required) Functional tests: handgrip strength, Sit-to-Stand test, 6-Meter Walk Test, Clinical Frailty Scale, SARC-F Nutrition-focused physical examination for edema, subcutaneous fat and muscle loss; diet history including oral supplements, enteral and parenteral intake Edema or fluid overload masking true weight loss (dry weight estimation may be needed) Hypoalbuminemia from systemic inflammation, hepatic or renal insufficiency, protein-losing enteropathy, or corticosteroid use rather than nutrition itself Low BUN/creatinine from renal or hepatic disease falsely suggesting reduced muscle mass Hypocholesterolemia related to acute illness rather than malnutrition per se Malnutrition affects roughly 30-50% of hospitalized patients, with the exact prevalence varying by clinical setting, underlying diagnosis, and the diagnostic criteria applied (Harrison 22e p.2615). The 2019 GLIM (Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition) consensus requires at least one phenotypic criterion (nonvolitional weight loss, low BMI, or reduced muscle mass) PLUS at least one etiologic criterion (reduced food intake/assimilation, or disease burden/inflammation) to diagnose malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2616). Severity grading in GLIM is determined by the phenotypic criterion: moderate (stage 1) malnutrition is 5-10% weight loss within 6 months (or 10-20% beyond 6 months), and severe (stage 2) is >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond) (Harrison 22e p.2616). Patients at any BMI can be malnourished; overweight or obese individuals may have sarcopenic obesity from muscle loss, and conversely being underweight does not by itself equal malnutrition (Harrison 22e p.2617). Handgrip strength is among the more clinically useful functional measures because it is easy to perform and helps identify which patients are most likely to benefit from individualized nutritional support (Harrison 22e p.2617). Patients with apparently adequate oral intake may still be at risk of malnutrition when chronic gastrointestinal disease compromises nutrient assimilation or absorption (Harrison 22e p.2617). A 5-10% loss of body weight over 6 months is clinically relevant, while >10% loss over the same period is considered severe (Harrison 22e p.2617). Albumin and prealbumin are negative acute-phase reactants and fall with injury, disease, or inflammation; they have poor sensitivity and specificity for malnutrition, though they retain value for predicting clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618). C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase reactant useful for confirming inflammation, with the chapter noting supportive thresholds of mild 3.0-9.9 mg/L, moderate 10-50 mg/L, and severe >50 mg/L (Harrison 22e p.2616). Calf circumference is a practical, valid estimate of skeletal muscle mass that requires less training than mid-upper arm circumference, with ethnicity-specific reference ranges that should be adjusted for BMI extremes (Harrison 22e p.2618). When inflammation is severe, nutrition care tends to be supportive only; at low-to-moderate inflammation, nutrition care may be therapeutic and improve clinical outcomes (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2616). Calf circumference, BMI, and other GLIM parameters make malnutrition diagnosis feasible even in the outpatient/ambulatory setting where dietitian access may be limited (Harrison 22e p.2617). Nonvolitional weight loss >10% within 6 months (or >20% beyond 6 months) indicating severe malnutrition BMI <18.5 kg/m2 in adults <70 years (or <20 if >=70 years) indicating severe malnutrition by GLIM Severe acute inflammatory state with negative nitrogen balance and elevated resting energy expenditure Low handgrip strength predicting poorer clinical outcomes Hypocholesterolemia (<120 mg/dL) developing during hospitalization, linked to worse outcomes Reduced food intake/assimilation (<=50% of energy requirement for >1 week, any reduction >2 weeks, or chronic GI condition impairing absorption) Relying on albumin or prealbumin to diagnose malnutrition or judge response to nutrition therapy; they reflect inflammation, hepatic/renal status, hydration, and other factors and have poor specificity (Harrison 22e pp.2617-2618). Assuming a normal or high BMI excludes malnutrition; sarcopenic obesity and muscle loss can occur at any BMI (Harrison 22e p.2617). Overlooking edema, which can mask true weight loss unless dry weight is estimated (Harrison 22e p.2617). Using BUN/creatinine, total lymphocyte count, cholesterol, creatinine-height index, cytokines, ECG, recall-antigen skin testing, or urine 3-methylhistidine as malnutrition indicators; the chapter lists these as NOT recommended for diagnosis (Harrison 22e pp.2618-2619). Comparing malnutrition prevalence across studies without accounting for differences between diagnostic tools, which yield incomparable rates (Harrison 22e p.2616). Failing to recognize prolonged pre-admission decreases in intake when an acute event is superimposed on chronic disease (Harrison 22e p.2617). Malnutrition arises from an imbalance between nutrient intake/assimilation and metabolic demand, and acute or chronic inflammation is now recognized as central to its pathophysiology. Inflammatory mediators raise resting energy expenditure, promote anabolic resistance and muscle catabolism, and cause anorexia that further reduces intake. Severe acute inflammation (e.g., critical illness, sepsis, burns, trauma, closed head injury) may be superimposed on a mild-to-moderate chronic inflammatory state (e.g., malignancy, COPD, congestive heart failure, chronic renal disease, chronic GI disease). The resulting deficits impair wound healing, immune function, and organ function. Because albumin and prealbumin behave as negative acute-phase reactants, the inflammatory milieu also distorts these traditional nutrition biomarkers (Harrison 22e pp.2615-2617). Malnutrition is associated with poor wound healing, compromised immunity, and impaired organ function, leading to longer hospital stays, more readmissions, higher mortality, and increased health care costs. Severe inflammation may limit nutritional interventions to a supportive rather than therapeutic role, and the associated malnutrition can diminish the effectiveness of medical therapies. Robust evidence indicates that a multipronged approach to malnutrition intervention reduces mortality and holds promise for improving quality of life, so timely diagnosis and treatment are important (Harrison 22e pp.2615, 2618). GLIM severity grading by phenotypic criteria. Stage 1 (moderate): weight loss 5-10% within 6 months or 10-20% beyond 6 months; BMI <20 (<70 years) or <22 (>=70 years); mild-to-moderate muscle mass deficit. Stage 2 (severe): weight loss >10% within 6 months or >20% beyond 6 months; BMI <18.5 (<70 years) or <20 (>=70 years); severe muscle mass deficit. WHO/NIH BMI categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 desirable, 25.0-29.9 overweight, >=30 obese (Harrison 22e pp.2616-2617).

radiograph (orthopantomogram) as an initial survey of the mandible CT for detailed assessment of condyle, displacement, and comminution Careful occlusal and dental examination to detect malocclusion and tooth injury Inferior alveolar nerve sensory testing of the lower lip and chin Assessment for a second fracture given the ring anatomy of the mandible The mandible commonly fractures at more than one site because of its arch shape, so a fracture at one point should prompt a search for a second, often contralateral, fracture such as the condyle Malocclusion, a change in the patient's usual bite, is a sensitive sign of mandibular fracture and must be specifically asked about and examined Other clinical signs include pain on jaw movement, trismus, a step in the dental arch, sublingual haematoma, and numbness of the lower lip from inferior alveolar nerve injury Panoramic radiography and CT are used to define fracture site, displacement, and the relationship to tooth roots and the inferior alveolar nerve Fractures involving tooth-bearing bone communicate with the mouth and are effectively open, requiring antibiotics and timely management to reduce infection risk Restoring the pre-injury occlusion is the central goal, achieved with maxillomandibular fixation and/or open reduction with internal fixation depending on the pattern Many condylar fractures, particularly in children and minimally displaced cases, can be managed conservatively with a short period of fixation and early mobilisation to avoid ankylosis Bilateral anterior (parasymphyseal) fractures can allow the tongue and anterior segment to fall backward and threaten the airway Airway compromise from bilateral parasymphyseal fractures with posterior displacement of the tongue (emergency) Displaced open fracture through tooth-bearing bone with infection risk Signs of associated cervical spine or head injury in high-energy trauma Progressive infection or abscess from an untreated open mandibular fracture Missing a second (often condylar) fracture after identifying the first Failing to recognise malocclusion as a key diagnostic sign Underestimating infection risk in fractures communicating with the oral cavity Overlooking airway risk in bilateral anterior fractures Prolonged rigid immobilisation of condylar fractures leading to stiffness or ankylosis Neglecting to document inferior alveolar nerve deficit before intervention The mandible is a mobile, U-shaped bone whose weaker regions - the condylar neck, angle (often at an unerupted third molar), and parasymphysis - are prone to fracture. Because it forms a ring-like structure articulating at both temporomandibular joints, force at one point is frequently transmitted to produce a second fracture elsewhere. Displacement is influenced by the pull of the muscles of mastication, which can distract or override fracture segments depending on their orientation (favourable versus unfavourable patterns). Fractures through tooth-bearing segments breach the oral mucosa, creating a contaminated, effectively open injury, and disruption of the inferior alveolar nerve within the canal causes lower lip and chin numbness. Most mandibular fractures heal well with restored occlusion and function when reduction and fixation are appropriate, and many condylar fractures do well with conservative management. Poorer outcomes - malunion, malocclusion, nonunion, infection, temporomandibular joint stiffness or ankylosis, and persistent nerve numbness - are associated with delayed treatment, inadequate reduction, open contaminated fractures, or prolonged immobilisation.
