affecting the posterior (parieto-occipital) cortex The great majority of cases carry the maternally inherited m.3243A>G point mutation in the MT-TL1 gene encoding the mitochondrial transfer RNA for leucine Expression is governed by heteroplasmy and a tissue threshold effect, so the mutant load, clinical severity and age of onset vary widely within a maternal lineage Elevated blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate, worsening with exertion, is typical, and MR spectroscopy often shows a lactate doublet within affected cortex Common systemic features include short stature, sensorineural hearing loss, migraine-like headaches, seizures, diabetes and cardiomyopathy Muscle biopsy classically shows ragged-red fibres on modified Gomori trichrome staining and strong succinate dehydrogenase but cytochrome c oxidase deficiency in a subset of fibres Management is supportive, favouring aerobic activity as tolerated, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins, and generic use of cofactor and antioxidant supplements while avoiding agents that impair respiratory-chain function Acute stroke-like episode with encephalopathy, seizures or status epilepticus requiring urgent neurological support New or decompensating cardiomyopathy or cardiac conduction block Rapidly rising lactic acidosis with metabolic decompensation Exposure to mitochondrial toxins that may precipitate deterioration Misdiagnosing stroke-like episodes as conventional ischaemic stroke and overlooking the underlying mitochondrial disease Testing only blood, where the m.3243A>G mutation may be undetectable or at low level; urine or muscle sampling improves yield Using agents that impair mitochondrial function, which can trigger decompensation Attributing hearing loss, diabetes or short stature to unrelated causes rather than recognising a unifying maternal disorder MELAS results from a defect of oxidative phosphorylation, most often the m.3243A>G substitution in the mitochondrial transfer RNA(Leu) gene, which impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and reduces the activity of respiratory-chain complexes. Because mitochondrial DNA is maternally transmitted and present in many copies per cell, a mixture of mutant and normal genomes (heteroplasmy) exists, and disease appears only once the mutant proportion exceeds a tissue-specific threshold. Energy-demanding tissues such as brain, muscle and the endocrine pancreas are preferentially affected. The stroke-like episodes are thought to reflect a combination of neuronal hyperexcitability, an angiopathy of small cerebral vessels with dysfunctional mitochondria in endothelium and smooth muscle, and a mismatch between metabolic demand and impaired energy supply rather than true thromboembolic occlusion. MELAS is a progressive multisystem disorder; recurrent stroke-like episodes tend to accumulate neurological disability, dementia and, in many patients, a shortened lifespan, though the course is highly variable and depends on mutant load and organ involvement.

Melasma — chloasma, mask of pregnancy, melasma faciei Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation following acne or dermatitis Solar lentigines and other photo-induced pigmentation Drug-induced pigmentation Ochronosis (which can be exogenous, from overuse of hydroquinone) Riehl's melanosis / pigmented contact dermatitis Naevus of Ota or acquired dermal melanocytosis Primarily a clinical diagnosis supported by dermoscopy Wood's lamp examination to help assess pigment depth Skin biopsy only in atypical or treatment-resistant cases Review of hormonal and drug history as part of assessment Presents as symmetrical, poorly defined brown to grey-brown patches on sun-exposed facial skin, typically the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, and chin It is far more common in women and in people with darker skin phototypes, and often follows pregnancy or hormonal exposure Recognised patterns are centrofacial, malar, and mandibular; a similar eruption can also occur on the forearms Wood's lamp examination can help gauge the depth of pigment, with epidermal pigment enhanced and dermal pigment less so, which influences treatment expectations Ultraviolet and visible light, including screen and heat exposure, are major drivers, so broad-spectrum photoprotection with a tinted (iron-oxide-containing) product is the cornerstone of care Combination topical lightening agents and gentle chemical peels can help, but aggressive procedures risk post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin Review and, where feasible, stop contributory hormonal exposures such as combined oral contraception Set realistic expectations: recurrence is common and lifelong sun protection and maintenance are usually needed Asymmetric, irregular, or evolving pigmented lesions raising concern for melanoma rather than melasma Rapidly darkening or nodular change within a pigmented area Paradoxical darkening or blue-black discolouration suggesting exogenous ochronosis from prolonged skin-lightening use Neglecting visible-light protection and relying only on conventional UV sunscreen Provoking post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation with overly aggressive peels or lasers in darker skin Causing exogenous ochronosis through prolonged, unsupervised use of skin-lightening agents Promising a permanent cure rather than emphasising control and maintenance Melasma reflects an acquired disorder of localised hyperpigmentation in which functionally hyperactive melanocytes deposit excess melanin in the epidermis, dermis, or both. Ultraviolet and visible light, hormonal influences (pregnancy, oestrogen), and a genetic predisposition upregulate melanogenic signalling, while an altered dermal environment with solar elastosis, increased vascularity, and a disrupted basement membrane allows pigment to drop into the dermis. This basement-membrane damage helps explain the chronic, relapsing nature and the resistance of dermal pigment to topical therapy. Melasma is typically chronic and relapsing; pregnancy-related disease may fade after delivery, but many patients experience persistence or recurrence, and long-term photoprotection with maintenance therapy is usually required to sustain improvement.

hyperostosis appears to flow along the length of a bone The radiographic hallmark is irregular, wavy cortical thickening likened to dripping candle wax down one side of a long bone Lesions frequently discrepancy or deformity, often beginning in adulthood Overlying soft-tissue changes such as fibrosis, contractures, oedema, and skin thickening can accompany the bony disease Somatic mosaic mutations, notably in MAP2K1 and related pathway genes, have been implicated in the endosteal and soft-tissue components Management is symptomatic, addressing pain and function, with orthopaedic surgery reserved for disabling deformity or contracture New rapidly enlarging mass or pain raising concern for a surface osteosarcoma Progressive contracture or neurovascular compromise of a limb Significant limb-length discrepancy or deformity in a growing child Severe intractable pain limiting function Mistaking the flowing hyperostosis for an aggressive surface bone tumour and vice versa Assuming the condition is purely osseous and overlooking disabling soft-tissue fibrosis and contracture Expecting a hereditary pattern when the disorder is typically sporadic and mosaic Undertaking extensive surgery that may be complicated by recurrence and poor soft-tissue healing Melorheostosis is characterised by localised, progressive hyperostosis affecting the cortex of long bones and adjacent soft tissues. It is generally sporadic and non-hereditary, and recent work has identified somatic mosaic mutations, including activating changes in MAP2K1 within the MAP-kinase pathway, in affected lesional tissue, with other genetic changes reported in the endosteal component. Enhanced local signalling drives excess bone formation confined to affected regions, often distributed along a sclerotome, producing the characteristic asymmetrical flowing cortical thickening. Associated fibrosis and contracture of surrounding soft tissue contribute to the pain and functional limitation. The condition is benign and slowly progressive with a normal lifespan, but it can cause chronic pain, joint contracture, and functional impairment; outcomes depend on lesion location and the degree of soft-tissue involvement.

endolymph volume within the membranous labyrinth Management principles include dietary salt restriction, diuretics and vestibular sedatives for acute attacks, with lifestyle measures to reduce triggers Escalating options for intractable disease range from intratympanic therapy to surgical procedures such as endolymphatic sac decompression or labyrinthine ablation Sudden drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) can cause falls without warning and pose an injury risk Progressive unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus raising concern for vestibular schwannoma Neurological signs suggesting a central cause Sudden severe sensorineural hearing loss requiring urgent assessment Recurrent drop attacks causing injury Diagnosing Meniere's without excluding a retrocochlear lesion such as acoustic neuroma Confusing it with vestibular migraine, which can present similarly Overusing vestibular sedatives beyond acute attacks and impairing compensation Underestimating the psychosocial and safety impact of unpredictable attacks Meniere's disease is attributed to endolymphatic hydrops, an abnormal accumulation of endolymph that distends the membranous labyrinth. Impaired production, circulation or absorption of endolymph, potentially involving the endolymphatic sac, raises pressure within the scala media. Episodic rupture or dysfunction of the membranes allows mixing of endolymph and perilymph, disturbing the ionic environment of the sensory hair cells and producing acute vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Repeated insults cause progressive damage to cochlear and vestibular structures, leading to permanent hearing loss and vestibular hypofunction. The course is variable and unpredictable, with clustered attacks and remissions; vertigo often diminishes over years as vestibular function declines, but hearing loss tends to be progressive and permanent.

Meningioma — meningeal tumour, dural-based tumour Dural metastasis Solitary fibrous tumour / haemangiopericytoma Schwannoma (at skull base sites) Dural-based lymphoma or granulomatous disease Extra-axial abscess or empyema MRI brain or spine with contrast to characterise the extra-axial dural-based mass and dural tail CT to assess associated hyperostosis, calcification, or bony erosion Serial imaging to monitor growth of incidental or conservatively managed lesions Histopathology and grading after biopsy or resection Vascular imaging when preoperative embolisation of a highly vascular tumour is considered Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumours and are usually slow-growing and benign, arising from the meningeal covering of the brain and spinal cord Many are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons When symptomatic, features depend on location and result from gradual compression, producing focal deficits, seizures, or symptoms of raised intracranial pressure They are more common in women and their growth can be influenced by hormonal factors; some carry hormone receptors On imaging they are typically well-defined, extra-axial, dural-based, avidly and homogeneously enhancing masses, often with a dural tail and sometimes adjacent bony change Small asymptomatic meningiomas are frequently managed by surveillance imaging, reserving intervention for growth or symptoms Symptomatic or enlarging tumours are usually treated by surgical resection, with radiotherapy or radiosurgery for residual, recurrent, higher-grade, or surgically inaccessible lesions Although most are low grade, a minority are atypical or malignant with a greater tendency to recur, so histological grading guides follow-up Rapid growth or atypical imaging features suggesting a higher-grade tumour Progressive neurological deficit, new seizures, or cranial nerve compromise Signs of raised intracranial pressure from a large lesion with oedema and mass effect Acute deterioration from peritumoural oedema or, rarely, haemorrhage Assuming every dural-based enhancing mass is a benign meningioma without considering metastasis or other lesions Over-treating small, stable, asymptomatic incidental tumours Underestimating the recurrence risk of atypical or malignant subtypes Overlooking peritumoural oedema as a treatable cause of symptoms Meningiomas arise from meningothelial (arachnoid cap) cells of the meninges and are therefore extra-axial, growing outside the brain parenchyma and compressing it from the surface. They are typically slow-growing and attached to the dura, and their growth can distort adjacent brain, cranial nerves, and vessels, provoke surrounding oedema, and erode or hyperostose overlying bone. Symptoms arise from mass effect at the specific location rather than infiltration. Most are histologically low grade, but atypical and anaplastic variants show more aggressive behaviour and higher recurrence rates. Prior cranial irradiation and certain genetic conditions increase risk. Most meningiomas are benign and, when completely resected, have an excellent prognosis with low recurrence; incompletely removed, atypical, or malignant tumours recur more often and may need adjuvant radiotherapy and closer surveillance.

Meningococcal Disease — meningococcemia, Neisseria meningitidis infection Other causes of bacterial meningitis (presentation of meningococcal meningitis is indistinguishable unless an associated petechial/purpuric rash or gram-negative diplococci are present) (p.1248-1249) Differential of chronic meningococcemia: bacterial endocarditis, acute rheumatic fever, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, infectious mononucleosis, disseminated gonococcal infection, immune-mediated vasculitis (p.1248-1249) Viral infections (enteroviruses, influenza and other respiratory viruses, measles, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus) - most patients presenting with a petechial/purpuric rash have a viral infection (p.1248) Pneumococcal, streptococcal, staphylococcal, or other gram-negative bacterial sepsis (p.1248) Blood culture for confirmation and public health investigation (positive in up to ~75% of cases); avoid media containing sodium polyanethol sulfonate, which may inhibit meningococcal growth, and avoid delay in transport (p.1249) Real-time PCR of whole blood increases diagnostic yield by more than 40% and may remain positive for several days after antibiotics (p.1249) Lumbar puncture for CSF in suspected meningitis (unless contraindicated); CSF Gram stain is up to ~80% sensitive, CSF culture sensitivity ~90%, plus PCR where available; CSF latex agglutination antigen testing is insensitive and should be replaced by molecular diagnosis (p.1249) Inflammatory markers (WBC count, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR) may support the diagnosis but can be normal or low in rapidly progressive disease and do not exclude it (p.1249) Severe septicemia laboratory findings: hypoglycemia, acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, anemia, coagulopathy (p.1249) Measure total hemolytic complement activity to assess for complement deficiency in patients with recurrent disease, particularly non-B capsular groups (p.1247) Protein C or S deficiency (including post-varicella protein S deficiency) (p.1248) Platelet disorders (e.g., idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, drug effects, bone marrow infiltration) (p.1248) Henoch-Schonlein purpura, connective tissue disorders, and trauma (including nonaccidental injury in children) (p.1248) Neisseria meningitidis most commonly causes asymptomatic nasopharyngeal colonization; invasive disease is rare and usually presents as either bacterial meningitis or meningococcal septicemia (p.1244). A nonblanching petechial or purpuric rash develops in over 80% of cases, but it is often absent early in the illness and may begin as a blanching maculopapular or urticarial eruption indistinguishable from common viral rashes before becoming petechial/purpuric over hours; some patients, including those with overwhelming sepsis, have no rash at all (p.1248). In the most severe cases large purpuric lesions develop (purpura fulminans) with signs of peripheral ischemia (p.1248). Roughly 30-50% present with a meningitis syndrome alone, up to 40% of meningitis patients also have features of septicemia, and meningococcal septicemia alone accounts for up to 20% of cases (p.1248). In fulminant disease death may occur within hours of the first symptoms; early septicemic symptoms are nonspecific and influenza-like (fever, headache, myalgia, vomiting, abdominal pain) (p.1248). In children, hypotension is a late sign; they more commonly present with compensated shock (tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, normal blood pressure) (p.1248). Terminal complement component (C5-9), properdin or factor D deficiency, and treatment with complement inhibitors such as eculizumab, increase the risk of meningococcal disease (up to ~600-fold) and may cause recurrent attacks (p.1247). Chronic meningococcemia is rarely recognized and presents as recurrent episodes of petechial rash with fever, joint pain/arthritis, and splenomegaly, with bacteremia that characteristically clears without treatment then recurs (p.1248-1249). Tobacco smoking (and passive smoke exposure) is an important risk factor that damages the nasopharyngeal epithelium and increases both carriage and invasive disease (p.1247). Immunization is regarded as the only rational approach to prevention at a population level; chemoprophylaxis of close contacts aims to eradicate carriage of the invasive strain (p.1250-1253). A nonblanching (petechial or purpuric) rash in a febrile patient should be treated as a medical emergency suggestive of meningococcal disease (p.1248) Purpura fulminans / large purpuric lesions with peripheral ischemia (p.1248) Signs of shock: tachycardia, poor peripheral perfusion, tachypnea, oliguria, cold mottled extremities, limb pain (hypotension is a late sign in children) (p.1248) Reduced level of consciousness, agitation, or confusion (decreased cerebral perfusion or raised intracranial pressure) (p.1248) Features of raised intracranial pressure: reduced consciousness, relative bradycardia and hypertension, focal neurologic signs, abnormal posturing, unequal/dilated/poorly reactive pupils (p.1248) Rapid progression - death may occur within hours of first symptoms in fulminant cases (p.1248) A normal or low WBC count and inflammatory markers do not exclude meningococcal disease and may occur in rapidly progressive disease (p.1249) The rash may be absent early or absent altogether (including in overwhelming sepsis), and may initially appear blanching/viral before becoming petechial or purpuric (p.1248) Most patients with a petechial/purpuric rash and fever do NOT have meningococcal disease - fewer than 10% of children (and in some settings under 1%) with this presentation are found to have it, so most have a viral cause (p.1248) Lumbar puncture should generally be avoided in meningococcal septicemia because positioning may critically compromise circulation in hypovolemic shock; it is also contraindicated with raised intracranial pressure, uncorrected shock, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, respiratory insufficiency, local infection, or ongoing convulsions (p.1249) A normal CT brain scan does not exclude raised intracranial pressure in meningococcal meningitis (p.1249) CSF latex agglutination antigen testing and urinary antigen testing are insensitive; throat-swab identification has limited diagnostic value because N. meningitidis is normal nasopharyngeal flora (p.1249) Postmeningococcal reactive (immune-complex) disease arising ~4-10 days after onset (rash, arthritis, iritis, pericarditis/polyserositis with fever) can be mistaken for relapse and lead to unnecessarily prolonged antibiotics; it resolves spontaneously (p.1249) Aggressive fluid resuscitation with unbuffered electrolyte solutions was found to increase mortality in febrile African children (p.1249-1250) N. meningitidis colonizes the human nasopharynx, then in a susceptible individual may invade the mucosa into the bloodstream, usually within a few days of acquisition. The polysaccharide capsule is a key virulence factor providing resistance to phagocytosis; acapsular strains rarely cause invasive disease. During growth meningococci shed outer-membrane blebs containing lipopolysaccharide (LPS, endotoxin), which binds CD14/TLR4 to trigger an inflammatory cascade (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, PAI-1 and others). Disease severity relates to both endotoxin levels and the magnitude of the inflammatory response. Endothelial injury is central to meningococcemia, causing increased vascular permeability (capillary leak with hypovolemia, tissue and pulmonary edema), altered vascular tone, loss of thromboresistance, intravascular coagulation, and myocardial dysfunction. Procoagulant activation with tissue factor upregulation, downregulation of anticoagulant pathways (loss of thrombomodulin/protein C receptors; reduced antithrombin III, protein C, protein S, tissue factor pathway inhibitor) and impaired thrombolysis from high PAI-1 produce purpura fulminans and skin/limb infarction. Shock results from hypovolemia plus myocardial depression (hypoxia, metabolic derangements such as hypocalcemia, cytokines). Bacteria reaching the meninges provoke a local cytokine-driven inflammatory response that can cause cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure (p.1247-1248). About 10% of patients with meningococcal disease die despite antimicrobial therapy and intensive care. Fulminant meningococcemia is more likely to cause death or ischemic skin loss than meningitis alone. Factors associated with poorer prognosis include shock; extremes of age (infancy and old age) and adolescence; coma; purpura fulminans; disseminated intravascular coagulation; thrombocytopenia; leukopenia; absence of meningitis; metabolic acidosis; low antithrombin and protein S/C levels; high PAI-1; and a low ESR or C-reactive protein. The Glasgow Meningococcal Septicaemia Prognostic Score (GMSPS) performs well for severity assessment, though scoring systems do not direct specific interventions; the management priority remains recognition and urgent treatment of compromised airway, breathing, or circulation. Most patients improve rapidly with appropriate antibiotics and supportive care. Complications include scarring after purpuric skin necrosis (~10%, sometimes requiring skin grafting), amputation in 1-2% of survivors after peripheral ischemia or compartment syndrome, hearing loss (~5%), neurologic complications (~7%), chronic pain, and psychological/psychosocial sequelae (p.1249-1250). Clinical spectrum spans asymptomatic nasopharyngeal carriage, occult bacteremia, localized/focal infection (pneumonia, arthritis, osteomyelitis, pericarditis, conjunctivitis), meningitis, and meningococcal septicemia, with chronic meningococcemia as a relapsing form. The Glasgow Meningococcal Septicaemia Prognostic Score (GMSPS) is used for severity assessment. Fulminant meningococcemia with purpura fulminans and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (overwhelming meningococcal sepsis) represents the most severe end of the spectrum (p.1244, p.1248-1249).

Meniscal injury — meniscal tear, torn meniscus, cartilage tear of the knee, bucket-handle tear Anterior cruciate ligament tear Collateral ligament injury Osteochondral injury or loose body Patellofemoral pain or patellar instability Osteoarthritis of the knee Plica syndrome Osteochondritis dissecans MRI of the knee to characterise the tear and assess associated ligament and cartilage injury Clinical joint-line palpation and provocative tests (e.g. McMurray's, Apley's grind) Plain radiographs to assess for degenerative change or loose bodies and to exclude fracture Diagnostic arthroscopy in selected cases where imaging is equivocal and intervention is planned In younger patients tears usually follow a twisting injury on a loaded, flexed knee; in older patients they are often degenerative and may occur with minimal trauma Typical symptoms are joint-line pain, an effusion developing over a day or so, and mechanical features such as clicking, catching, or locking A knee locked in flexion that cannot be fully extended suggests a displaced bucket-handle tear and warrants prompt treatment Joint-line tenderness and provocative rotation tests (e.g. McMurray's) support the diagnosis, and MRI is the investigation of choice The peripheral (outer) third of the meniscus is vascular and can heal, favouring repair, whereas the avascular inner portion has poor healing potential Repair is preferred where feasible, especially in younger patients with peripheral tears, to preserve meniscal function; partial meniscectomy is reserved for irreparable tears Meniscus preservation is important because meniscectomy increases contact stress and the long-term risk of osteoarthritis Degenerative tears in older knees with early arthritis often respond as well to conservative management and rehabilitation as to arthroscopic surgery A truly locked knee unable to fully extend, suggesting a displaced bucket-handle tear needing prompt surgery Acute tense haemarthrosis suggesting a significant associated injury such as an ACL rupture Hot, swollen, systemically unwell knee raising concern for septic arthritis Signs of associated ligamentous instability or fracture Performing meniscectomy on a degenerative tear in an arthritic knee that would do as well with rehabilitation Removing repairable peripheral tissue rather than attempting repair, accelerating arthritis Missing a locked knee from a displaced bucket-handle tear Overlooking a concurrent ACL injury that leaves the meniscal repair at risk of re-tear The menisci are fibrocartilaginous, wedge-shaped structures that deepen the tibial articular surface, distribute load, absorb shock, and contribute to joint stability and lubrication. A twisting force on a weight-bearing flexed knee shears the meniscus between the femoral and tibial condyles, producing longitudinal, radial, horizontal, or complex tears; a longitudinal tear whose free fragment displaces into the notch forms a bucket-handle lesion that can block extension. With age the meniscal tissue degenerates and tears more readily under low loads. Only the peripheral third has a blood supply capable of healing, so the location of a tear largely determines whether repair or excision is appropriate. Loss of meniscal tissue raises articular contact pressures and predisposes to degenerative change. Peripheral tears repaired successfully can restore durable meniscal function, while small stable tears may settle with conservative care; extensive meniscectomy relieves mechanical symptoms but increases the long-term likelihood of osteoarthritis, and degenerative tears in already arthritic knees have a more limited response to surgery.

and subdural collections) Other neonatal-onset epileptic encephalopathies Mitochondrial disorders with early neurodegeneration Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other connective tissue disorders Nutritional copper deficiency Trichothiodystrophy and other hair-shaft disorders Serum copper and caeruloplasmin (characteristically low, interpreted cautiously in neonates) Plasma and cerebrospinal fluid catecholamine ratios reflecting dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency Light microscopy of hair demonstrating pili torti Molecular genetic testing of ATP7A to confirm the diagnosis and enable carrier testing Neuroimaging showing atrophy, subdural collections and tortuous intracranial vessels Skeletal survey for metaphyseal changes and wormian bones X-linked recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in ATP7A, encoding a copper-transporting P-type ATPase, so affected infants are almost always male The defect impairs intestinal copper absorption and delivery of copper to cuproenzymes, producing low serum copper and low caeruloplasmin Presents in early infancy with progressive neurodegeneration, hypotonia, seizures and failure to thrive after an initially unremarkable neonatal period The characteristic sparse, depigmented, brittle hair shows pili torti (twisted shafts) on microscopy, giving the 'kinky hair' appearance Connective tissue and vascular abnormalities arise from deficient lysyl oxidase activity, causing tortuous cerebral and systemic vessels, bladder diverticula and joint laxity Parenteral copper-histidine may help if started very early, but neurological outcome remains poor once degeneration is established Occipital horn syndrome is an allelic, milder ATP7A phenotype dominated by connective tissue features Neonatal screening pitfalls exist because serum copper and caeruloplasmin are physiologically low in healthy newborns Progressive seizures and developmental regression in a young male infant Unexplained fractures or subdural haemorrhage that may mimic non-accidental injury Vascular tortuosity with risk of aneurysm or haemorrhage Rapid neurological deterioration signalling advanced disease Interpreting low neonatal serum copper and caeruloplasmin as normal and delaying diagnosis Attributing fractures and subdural collections solely to non-accidental injury Starting copper replacement too late, after irreversible neurodegeneration Overlooking the diagnosis because early neonatal development can appear normal Menkes disease results from loss of function of the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7A, which normally moves copper across the enterocyte basolateral membrane and delivers it within cells to copper-dependent enzymes. The defect traps dietary copper in intestinal and renal cells while depriving other tissues, so despite total-body copper accumulation in some sites, functional copper deficiency dominates. Reduced activity of cuproenzymes explains the phenotype: deficient lysyl oxidase impairs collagen and elastin cross-linking (vascular tortuosity, connective tissue laxity), deficient dopamine beta-hydroxylase disturbs catecholamine metabolism, and reduced cytochrome c oxidase and other enzymes contribute to the neurodegeneration and hair changes. The classic form is progressive and usually fatal in early childhood, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment. Very early parenteral copper replacement, particularly with certain ATP7A variants retaining residual function, may improve survival and neurological outcome, but many children remain profoundly affected.

Menopause and Postmenopausal Hormone Therapy — Menopause, Perimenopause, Postmenopausal hormone therapy, Climacteric, Menopausal transition Pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea in perimenopausal women (unintentional pregnancy rate in the forties rivals that of adolescents) Premature ovarian insufficiency / primary ovarian insufficiency when ovarian failure occurs well before the usual age Thyroid dysfunction or other endocrine causes of menstrual irregularity and vasomotor-like symptoms Uterine structural lesions (leiomyomata, endometrial polyps, hyperplasia or carcinoma) presenting as abnormal/heavy bleeding Other age-related conditions causing midlife mood, sleep, cognitive, or sexual complaints not attributable to ovarian senescence Menstrual cycle history as the principal STRAW+10 criterion for staging reproductive aging, with biomarkers as supportive criteria FSH measurement: random level >25 IU/L is characteristic of the late menopausal transition; day-3 levels <20, 20 to <30, and >=30 IU/L indicate good, fair, and poor pregnancy likelihood respectively Estradiol levels, recognizing that FSH and estradiol are imperfect diagnostic indicators in still-menstruating perimenopausal women due to marked intraindividual variability Anti-mullerian hormone and inhibin B as additional markers of reproductive aging Transvaginal ultrasound (with saline enhancement) to detect leiomyomata or polyps when bleeding is abnormal Endometrial aspiration/biopsy to identify hyperplastic or premalignant changes when menorrhagia or abnormal bleeding occurs Bone mineral density assessment and FRAX 10-year fracture risk estimation to guide osteoporosis decisions; 25-hydroxyvitamin D level >=50 nmol/L considered sufficient for bone maintenance Thyroid disease producing vasomotor-like flushing and menstrual change Anxiety or panic disorder mimicking hot flashes Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma presenting as abnormal bleeding rather than physiologic transition Medication effects or other causes of secondary amenorrhea Menopause is the permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function and is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhea; the average age in U.S. women is about 51 years. Perimenopause is the transition preceding menopause when fertility wanes and cycles become irregular, typically beginning 2-8 years before the final menses (mean duration about 4 years); smoking advances the transition by roughly 2 years. Perimenopause is marked by 'irregularly irregular' hormone levels rather than the consistently high FSH and low estradiol of established menopause; intermenstrual intervals often shorten (by about 3 days) due to an accelerated follicular phase. FSH rises before LH during the transition, attributed to loss of inhibin and estrogen feedback; after menopause estradiol falls markedly while estrone is relatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens. Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, night sweats), irregular bleeding, and vaginal dryness are strongly attributable to the transition; sleep disturbance has moderate supporting evidence, while mood swings, memory/concentration changes, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction are not clearly caused by ovarian aging alone. Nearly 60% of women in one U.S. study reported hot flashes in the 2 years before their final menses; symptom intensity, frequency, duration, and quality-of-life impact are highly variable. Estrogen therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms; randomized trial data suggest hormone therapy reduces menopausal symptoms by roughly 65-90%. The 'timing hypothesis' holds that estrogen may slow early atherosclerosis but adversely affect advanced lesions, so women initiating hormone therapy early after menopause may differ in cardiovascular outcome from those starting many years later. Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease should NOT be considered an expected benefit of hormone therapy; an increased stroke risk and a small early increase in coronary risk should be weighed. A 1-year absence of spontaneous menses reliably indicates ovulation has ceased, but natural menstrual pattern cannot be assessed while a woman is taking oral contraceptives. Estrogen reduces bone turnover and resorption; postmenopausal estrogen (with or without a progestogen) increases spine bone density by about 4-6% and hip density by about 2-3%, with WHI showing roughly a 33% reduction in hip fractures. Unopposed estrogen markedly raises endometrial cancer risk; adding a progestogen opposes this effect and can even reduce endometrial cancer risk, which is why estrogen-only therapy is reserved for women without a uterus. Unexplained or undiagnosed vaginal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma before attributing it to the transition An acute coronary event or stroke while on hormone therapy mandates immediate discontinuation of therapy New or worsening vasomotor symptoms accompanied by features suggesting thromboembolism, given the increased VTE risk with oral estrogen Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) in perimenopause warrants evaluation for uterine disorders rather than assumption of benign cause Symptoms or signs of estrogen-dependent malignancy in a woman considering or using hormone therapy Observational studies overstated cardiovascular benefit because women choosing hormone therapy tend to be healthier and more health-conscious (healthy-user confounding); randomized trials did not confirm the benefit. Relying on a single FSH or estradiol value to diagnose perimenopause in a menstruating woman is unreliable given extreme intraindividual variability. Prescribing unopposed estrogen to a woman with an intact uterus markedly raises endometrial cancer and atypical hyperplasia risk; a progestogen is needed for endometrial protection. Attributing midlife mood, cognitive, urinary, or sexual complaints to menopause when evidence does not support ovarian aging as the principal cause. Counseling should emphasize absolute rather than relative risk measures, since absolute risks rise with age even when relative risks are similar. Apparent excess breast cancer detection in early hormone therapy users may partly reflect more frequent screening mammography rather than a true biologic effect. Assuming the cardiovascular and other effects of one formulation/route apply to all, since transdermal estrogen may carry lower thrombotic and gallbladder risk than oral estrogen. Ovarian mass and fertility decline sharply after age 35 and more steeply during perimenopause as the pool of primary follicles, depleting since before birth, runs down. Altered folliculogenesis and reduced inhibin secretion cause FSH to rise; the propensity for anovulatory cycles produces a relatively hyperestrogenic, hypoprogestagenic milieu that may underlie the increased perimenopausal incidence of endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma, uterine polyps, and leiomyomata. With transition into menopause, estradiol falls markedly while estrone is comparatively preserved through peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androgens; FSH rises more than LH owing to loss of inhibin plus estrogen feedback. Exogenous estrogen lowers LDL and raises HDL cholesterol by about 10-15% and favorably affects lipoprotein(a), LDL oxidation, and endothelial function, but it also raises triglycerides, promotes coagulation (factor VII, prothrombin fragments, fibrinopeptide A), and elevates C-reactive protein, providing a mechanistic basis for both potential benefits and thrombotic/inflammatory harms. Most peri- and postmenopausal symptoms are self-limited though variable in duration and intensity. In the WHI, many risks and benefits of hormone therapy dissipated within 5-7 years after stopping, though some persisted: with estrogen-progestin an elevated breast cancer risk continued over long follow-up and a reduced hip fracture risk and reduced endometrial cancer risk persisted; with estrogen alone the breast cancer risk reduction became significant on extended follow-up. Estrogen-progestin carried an overall unfavorable global benefit-risk profile that did not vary by 10-year age group, whereas estrogen-only therapy had a roughly neutral profile overall with a more favorable balance in younger women (relative risks for the global index of about 0.84, 0.99, and 1.17 in ages 50-59, 60-69, and 70-79). Over extended follow-up estrogen alone was associated with reduced all-cause mortality in women aged 50-59 (notably those with bilateral oophorectomy), while estrogen-progestin showed elevated breast cancer risk and a suggestion of increased breast cancer mortality. The Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop +10 (STRAW+10) system stages reproductive aging using menstrual cycle characteristics as principal criteria (e.g., persistent >=7-day differences in consecutive cycle length in the early transition; an interval of amenorrhea of >=60 days in the late transition) with endocrine markers (FSH, AMH, inhibin B, antral follicle count) as supportive criteria, spanning reproductive, menopausal transition (perimenopause), and postmenopause stages around the final menstrual period.

Menstrual Disorders and Pelvic Pain — Amenorrhea, Abnormal uterine bleeding, Dysfunctional uterine bleeding, Oligomenorrhea, Dysmenorrhea, Pelvic pain Pregnancy (must be excluded first in amenorrhea and in any reproductive-age woman with pelvic pain or bleeding) Outflow-tract obstruction: transverse vaginal septum, imperforate hymen Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome; WNT4 mutations) Androgen insensitivity syndrome (about 10% of primary amenorrhea; 46,XY karyotype, female external genitalia, absent pubic/axillary hair, male-range testosterone) 5-alpha reductase type 2 deficiency Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions, usually post-curettage; serial/repeat sampling in suspected POI Prolactin in all patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Estradiol, testosterone and androgen assessment for hyperandrogenism; AMH (low in POI, may be elevated in PCOS) Karyotype in primary amenorrhea with suspected chromosomal cause and in all POI patients POI work-up: anti-cortical and 21-hydroxylase antibodies (specific but not sensitive for future adrenal insufficiency), thyroid function and thyroid peroxidase antibodies, FMR1 premutation screening, and bone mineral density (ovarian biopsy is NOT indicated) Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal) as first-line imaging for amenorrhea work-up, pelvic pain, ovarian cysts, torsion (with Doppler for ovarian blood flow), endometrioma, and fibroids MRI of the pelvis for better delineation of reproductive-tract anomalies before surgery and for higher sensitivity/specificity in endometriosis Cranial MRI when history is atypical, with headache, other hypothalamic dysfunction, or hyperprolactinemia Wet-mount of vaginal discharge plus nucleic acid amplification testing for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in suspected PID CA-125 may be elevated in endometriosis but has low negative predictive value; diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard for endometriosis when empiric treatment fails Ectopic pregnancy Threatened abortion Ruptured or hemorrhagic ovarian cyst Ovarian (or rarely tubal) torsion Mittelschmerz (ovulation pain) Endometriosis and endometrioma Uterine fibroids (including acutely degenerating leiomyoma) and adenomyosis Pelvic adhesions Pelvic congestion syndrome Vulvodynia Pelvic malignancy Amenorrhea is the absence of menses: primary when bleeding has never occurred without hormonal treatment, secondary when established cycles stop for 3-6 months; primary amenorrhea is rare (<1% of women), whereas roughly 3-5% of women have at least 3 months of secondary amenorrhea in a given year. Pregnancy is the single most common cause of amenorrhea and must be excluded in every case with a beta-hCG, regardless of the history offered. A normal cycle recurs every 21-35 days, lasts 4-7 days, and involves up to about 80 mL of blood loss; the term abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) has replaced dysfunctional uterine bleeding and is categorized by the PALM-COEIN scheme (structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not yet classified). Evaluation of ovulatory disorders rests on three initial tests: a pregnancy test, an FSH level (to localize the problem to the ovary versus a central cause), and assessment for hyperandrogenism. FSH is a better marker of ovarian failure than LH because it reflects loss of negative feedback from both estradiol and the inhibins and is less variable; anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) is also low in primary ovarian insufficiency. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is a diagnosis of exclusion, typically driven by a mismatch between energy expenditure and intake and/or significant stress, with suppressed GnRH, low gonadotropins, and normal prolactin; eating disorders, excessive exercise, and chronic disease must be specifically ruled out. Isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH) is three times more common in men; about half of affected women have anosmia (Kallmann syndrome), and roughly half have an identifiable genetic cause. Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) - the preferred term over premature menopause/ovarian failure - denotes ovarian failure before age 40, accounts for about 10% of secondary amenorrhea, and can wax and wane so serial measurements may be needed. Roughly up to one-third of women between menarche and menopause experience abnormal uterine bleeding at some point. Up to 60% of pelvic pain is attributable to gastrointestinal causes (appendicitis, cholecystitis, infection, obstruction, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease); urinary and musculoskeletal disorders are also common, so pelvic pain is frequently not gynecologic in origin. Beta-hCG normally roughly doubles every 48 h in the early first trimester, and 99% of viable intrauterine pregnancies show at least a 53% rise over 2 days; the discriminatory zone (about 1500-3000 IU/mL) is the level above which a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on ultrasound. Dysmenorrhea begins with menstrual flow and eases over 12-72 h; primary dysmenorrhea is largely prostaglandin-mediated, while secondary dysmenorrhea reflects underlying pelvic pathology such as endometriosis or adenomyosis. Shock or peritoneal signs in a woman with pelvic pain - identify life-threatening conditions first as they may need emergent surgery Reproductive-age woman with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding - maintain high suspicion for ectopic pregnancy regardless of contraceptive use; tubal rupture is a life-threatening emergency Severe pain with fever and peritoneal signs in PID suggests tubo-ovarian abscess or peritonitis Right upper quadrant pain in PID suggests perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome) Acute unilateral intermittent pain raising concern for ovarian torsion (confirm by absent Doppler flow) Atypical amenorrhea history with headache, signs of hypothalamic dysfunction, short stature, diabetes insipidus, or galactorrhea - evaluate for a neuroanatomic lesion Heavy or prolonged bleeding warrants prompt attention, but infrequent or absent bleeding is often under-reported and should be actively elicited Failing to exclude pregnancy before pursuing an amenorrhea or pelvic-pain work-up. Overlooking infrequent or absent menses because the patient does not volunteer it - a focused menstrual history is needed at every encounter. Attributing pelvic pain to the reproductive tract when up to 60% of cases are gastrointestinal and urinary/musculoskeletal causes are common. Waiting for positive microbiology before treating suspected PID - a presumptive clinical diagnosis is sufficient to begin treatment, and negative tests do not exclude it. Confusing androgen insensitivity syndrome with mullerian agenesis - absent pubic/axillary hair and a male-range testosterone distinguish AIS. Diagnosing PCOS without excluding mimics (hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, adrenal hyperandrogenism); it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and in adolescents one should wait at least 3 years after menarche and not rely on ultrasound/AMH criteria. Performing ovarian biopsy in POI - it is not indicated; routine genetic testing beyond FMR1 is also not currently recommended. Assuming endometriosis severity at laparoscopy correlates with pain - it does not always; a normal CA-125 does not exclude endometriosis. Delaying surgery for outflow-tract obstruction - early correction reduces the risk of endometriosis from retrograde menstruation. Menstrual function depends on coordinated signaling among four compartments - hypothalamus, pituitary, ovary, and uterus/outflow tract - linked by feedback loops involving GnRH, the gonadotropins FSH and LH, and the ovarian products estradiol, progesterone, and the inhibins (inhibin A and B). Disorders divide into outflow-tract/uterine problems and ovulatory disorders. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism arises when anatomic, genetic, or functional disturbances impair hypothalamic GnRH output or pituitary responsiveness, producing low estrogen with normal or low LH/FSH; in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea, energy deficit and stress raise CRH, suppress GnRH, and lower TRH input, with leptin and hypothalamic kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin signaling transducing metabolic and stress cues to the GnRH pulse generator. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (ovarian insufficiency) removes negative feedback, raising FSH and LH. In PCOS, abnormal GnRH pulsatility elevates LH and drives ovarian androgen output, and insulin resistance in muscle and fat further augments insulin-stimulated ovarian androgen production; frequent anovulation yields irregular menses and unopposed estrogen effect on the endometrium. Pelvic pain shares mechanisms with abdominal pain - parietal peritoneal inflammation, hollow-viscus obstruction, vascular compromise (e.g., ovarian torsion), and abdominal-wall pain - and may be referred from extrapelvic sources. Primary dysmenorrhea is mediated chiefly by prostaglandin pathways causing intense uterine contractions, reduced blood flow, and peripheral nerve hypersensitivity, with PG-independent mediators such as platelet-activating factor also contributing. Endometriosis reflects ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus that respond to hormonal stimulation. Outcome depends on cause. Many causes of functional hypothalamic amenorrhea are reversible with restoration of energy balance, though bone density may not fully recover with hormone replacement alone. Amenorrhea of any cause is usually associated with chronically low estrogen, carrying risk to bone and cardiovascular health if untreated. PID untreated risks infertility and ectopic pregnancy, and subclinical PID remains a major worldwide cause of these complications. PCOS carries elevated long-term risk of metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, steatotic liver disease, and a two- to sixfold increase in endometrial hyperplasia/cancer from chronic anovulation; symptoms often improve with age, with most women regaining regular menses and normal androgens by the fourth decade. POI is associated with additional health problems and infertility, though oocyte donation has high success. Ectopic pregnancy with tubal rupture can be fatal. Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized etiologically by the PALM-COEIN system (structural causes: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia; non-structural: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified). PCOS is diagnosed by the updated Rotterdam criteria (2023 international guidelines): two of three among irregular menses (fewer than 8 per year), clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (>=20 antral follicles or ovarian volume >=10 cm3 in one ovary) or elevated AMH, yielding hyperandrogenic and non-hyperandrogenic phenotypes. Pelvic pain is classified as acute versus chronic and cyclic versus noncyclic to guide evaluation. Endometriosis is staged by laparoscopy.

of other cause Acute corrosive ingestion of other agents Acute kidney injury from other nephrotoxins Blood mercury (more useful for recent organic exposure) and urinary mercury (for elemental and inorganic exposure) Renal function and urinalysis to detect tubular injury Neurological and neuropsychological assessment Chest imaging in acute vapour inhalation for pneumonitis Exposure history covering occupation, dental amalgam handling, and dietary fish intake The clinical picture depends on the chemical form: elemental mercury vapour, inorganic mercury salts, and organic mercury (such as methylmercury) each cause distinct patterns Inhaled elemental mercury vapour, seen in industries such as chloralkali and instrument work, chiefly affects the central nervous system and can cause an acute chemical pneumonitis at high concentrations Chronic elemental and inorganic exposure produces the classic triad of tremor, gingivostomatitis and neuropsychiatric changes ('erethism') with irritability, shyness and memory impairment Ingested inorganic mercury salts are corrosive, causing gastrointestinal burning and haemorrhage and acute kidney injury Organic methylmercury, the cause of environmental epidemics from contaminated fish, targets the nervous system with sensory disturbance, ataxia, visual field constriction and hearing loss, and crosses the placenta to harm the developing fetus Diagnosis uses blood and urine mercury levels, with the appropriate specimen depending on the form of exposure, interpreted with the exposure history Management centres on removing exposure and supportive care, with a chelating agent used in significant inorganic or elemental poisoning under specialist advice, while chelation is less effective for organic mercury Acrodynia (pink disease) is a distinctive reaction to mercury seen particularly in children, with painful pink extremities, irritability and desquamation MEDICAL EMERGENCY: acute high-level vapour inhalation causing respiratory distress and chemical pneumonitis Corrosive ingestion of inorganic salts with gastrointestinal haemorrhage and shock Acute kidney injury Pregnancy with organic mercury exposure given the risk of fetal neurological harm Using the wrong specimen (for example relying on blood levels for chronic elemental exposure) Expecting chelation to reverse established organic mercury neurotoxicity Attributing neuropsychiatric change to primary psychiatric illness without an exposure history Overlooking dietary fish as a source of methylmercury Missing the risk to the fetus in exposed pregnant women Mercury binds avidly to sulfhydryl groups, disrupting numerous enzymes and cellular proteins. Lipophilic elemental vapour and organic mercury readily cross the blood-brain barrier (and placenta), producing neuronal injury and the neurological and neuropsychiatric features, while inorganic salts concentrate in and damage the renal tubules and are locally corrosive to the gut. Oxidative stress and immune-mediated renal effects contribute to the tissue damage. Removal from exposure often allows gradual improvement of inorganic and elemental effects, but severe neurological injury, especially from organic methylmercury, may be permanent, and prenatal exposure can cause lasting developmental impairment.

MERRF syndrome — Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres, m.8344A>G, MT-TK, MERRF Other progressive myoclonic epilepsies such as Unverricht-Lundborg and Lafora disease MELAS and overlap mitochondrial syndromes Sialidosis and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis Spinocerebellar ataxias with myoclonus Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy Coeliac-associated or paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia Resting and post-exercise blood lactate and pyruvate Electroencephalography to characterise generalised epileptiform and photosensitive discharges Brain MRI, which may show cerebellar and brainstem atrophy or basal ganglia calcification Targeted molecular testing for m.8344A>G with heteroplasmy quantification in appropriate tissue Skeletal muscle biopsy for ragged-red fibres and respiratory-chain enzymology Audiometry and nerve conduction studies for associated deafness and neuropathy The defining tetrad is myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia and a myopathy with ragged-red fibres on muscle biopsy Most cases are due to the maternally inherited m.8344A>G point mutation in the MT-TK gene encoding the mitochondrial transfer RNA for lysine As with other mitochondrial tRNA disorders, heteroplasmy and a threshold effect explain the variable severity and age of onset across a maternal lineage Additional features may include sensorineural deafness, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, dementia and multiple symmetrical lipomatosis of the neck and trunk Elevated resting or exercise-induced lactate supports the diagnosis but is neither universal nor specific Myoclonus is frequently stimulus-sensitive and can be difficult to control; some anticonvulsants worsen mitochondrial function and are best avoided Muscle histochemistry shows ragged-red fibres that are typically cytochrome c oxidase deficient, reflecting the tRNA translation defect Poorly controlled myoclonic seizures or status epilepticus Rapid neurological deterioration or new cardiorespiratory compromise Cardiac conduction abnormality or cardiomyopathy on surveillance Metabolic decompensation with rising lactic acidosis Labelling the disorder an idiopathic progressive myoclonic epilepsy without pursuing mitochondrial testing Relying on blood alone for genetic testing, since low-level heteroplasmy may be missed Prescribing anticonvulsants that impair respiratory-chain or mitochondrial function Overlooking cardiac and audiological involvement that warrants surveillance MERRF is caused by a mitochondrial tRNA mutation, usually m.8344A>G in MT-TK, that impairs mitochondrial translation and thereby the synthesis of respiratory-chain subunits, reducing oxidative phosphorylation capacity. The mutation is maternally inherited and heteroplasmic, so clinical expression depends on the proportion of mutant genomes and the energy threshold of each tissue. Neurons of the cerebellum, brainstem and cerebral cortex, together with skeletal muscle, are especially vulnerable to the resulting energy deficit, producing the characteristic myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and myopathy. Accumulation of abnormal mitochondria beneath the sarcolemma gives the ragged-red appearance on trichrome staining. MERRF is slowly progressive with a broad spectrum of severity; many patients have a normal early childhood before symptoms emerge, but accumulating myoclonus, ataxia and dementia can be disabling, and lifespan may be reduced in severely affected individuals.

Acute mesenteric ischemia — CT angiography (mesenteric) Lactate Urgent surgical/vascular review Pain out of proportion to exam — time-critical Chronic mesenteric ischaemia / intestinal angina (postprandial pain, weight loss, fear of eating) Ischaemic colitis (notably after elective or emergent aortic repair) Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in chronic presentations) Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (duodenal compression after weight loss/immobilisation) Median arcuate ligament syndrome (celiac artery compression) Thin-cut (1 mm or thinner) CT angiography is the gold standard for detecting mesenteric arterial occlusive (embolic/thrombotic) disease and for assessing bowel; venous-phase imaging detects mesenteric venous thrombosis with diffuse bowel-wall thickening and splanchnic thrombus (p.2588-2589). Mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a sensitive/specific screening tool; a high SMA peak flow velocity carries ~80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex virtually excludes mesenteric ischaemia (test must be done fasting) (p.2588). Leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis and lactic acidosis support advanced ischaemia but may be absent in reversible ischaemia and cannot reliably distinguish reversible ischaemia from frank necrosis (p.2589). ECG and echocardiogram may help identify an embolic cardiac source but must not delay surgical therapy (p.2588). Hypercoagulability workup in suspected mesenteric venous thrombosis (e.g. factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome) (p.2587, 2589). Colonoscopy if ischaemic colitis is suspected, to grade mucosal injury (p.2589). Acute intestinal obstruction (mechanical or strangulated bowel) Other noninflammatory causes of abdominal pain such as biliary colic and neoplasia Inflammatory abdominal conditions: pancreatitis, cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease Severe, acute, non-remitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical findings is the most common complaint in arterial acute mesenteric ischaemia, present in about 95% of cases; pain precedes signs because ischaemia begins in the mucosa and progresses outward to the serosa (p.2588). About half of acute mesenteric ischaemia cases are embolic, lodging in the mid-to-distal SMA just past the middle colic artery origin; emboli commonly arise from atrial fibrillation, recent MI, soft atherosclerotic plaque, infective endocarditis, valvular heart disease, or recent cardiac/vascular catheterisation (p.2587). Acute-on-chronic thrombotic ischaemia (about 25-30% of cases) occurs at sites of severe atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA or celiac artery, typically in patients with pre-existing mesenteric atherosclerosis who may have had prior chronic mesenteric ischaemia (p.2587, 2588). Embolic disease is suggested by older patients with a predisposing cardiac source (AF, prior embolic event, recent infective endocarditis), whereas thrombotic disease suggests underlying atherosclerosis with possible prior intestinal angina (p.2588). Chronic mesenteric ischaemia classically presents as recurrent dull, crampy, postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina') with fear of eating and weight loss; chronic diarrhoea may occur and symptoms typically last 6-12 months before diagnosis (p.2587-2588). Mesenteric venous thrombosis tends to present more vaguely and subacutely with non-specific abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, distension, mild-to-moderate tenderness and dehydration, making it easy to under-recognise (p.2589). The decision to operate in suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is often based on a high index of suspicion from history and examination despite normal laboratory results (p.2588). Pain out of proportion to examination with a high-risk cardiac source (AF, recent MI, endocarditis) — embolic acute mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise Later signs of peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse indicate established transmural infarction Blood per rectum, marked distension or obtundation in a critically ill/shocked patient (suggests non-occlusive ischaemia) Rising lactate / metabolic acidosis is a late marker and its absence does not exclude ischaemia Treating pain out of proportion to examination as benign — early ischaemia produces severe pain with deceptively unremarkable abdominal signs because injury starts in the mucosa (p.2588). Waiting for abnormal labs before acting — lactate and acidosis are late and may be normal in reversible ischaemia or even necrosis; the operative decision is often made on clinical suspicion despite normal results (p.2588-2589). Overlooking non-occlusive ischaemia in obtunded/critically ill patients where examination findings are absent or obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589). Missing the vaguer, subacute presentation of mesenteric venous thrombosis (non-specific pain, nausea, distension) (p.2589). Failing to perform mesenteric duplex while fasting — bowel gas obscures flow and the post-prandial vasodilatory response (p.2588). Intestinal ischaemia occurs when splanchnic perfusion fails to meet the bowel's metabolic demand, producing ischaemic tissue injury. The gut is supplied by the celiac artery, SMA and IMA with extensive collateralisation between major trunks and mesenteric arcades; protective responses include this collateral network, autoregulation of flow and the ability to increase oxygen extraction. Watershed colonic zones with inherently lower flow are Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (descending/sigmoid colon), the commonest sites of colonic ischaemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to 30% of cardiac output. Occlusive ischaemia results from an embolus or progressive thrombosis in a major mesenteric artery (over 75% of emboli are cardiac in origin and lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic artery). Chronic intestinal angina generally requires progressive stenosis of two of the three major vessels. Non-occlusive ischaemia is driven by disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiological stress such as shock; untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis is usually precipitated by a hypercoagulable state. (p.2587-2588) Acute mesenteric ischaemia carries a high mortality, roughly 50-80% at presentation (with the acute arterial form quoted at over 50%); it is one of the most challenging diagnoses, and the single most important determinant of survival is the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment. Endovascular stenting for chronic mesenteric ischaemia has about an 80% long-term success rate. (p.2587-2588) Harrison classifies intestinal ischaemia into chronic mesenteric ischaemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI). Acute mesenteric vascular insufficiency is subdivided into (1) arterio-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia — further split into arterial embolus (~50%) and arterial thrombosis (~25-30%, often acute-on-chronic), (2) non-occlusive/vasospastic mesenteric ischaemia (~20%, vasospasm or hypoperfusion), and (3) mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10%). Ischaemic colitis mucosal injury is graded as mild (minimal erythema), moderate (pale ulceration extending into muscularis), or severe (black/green discoloration with full-thickness necrosis). (p.2587-2589)

Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency — Intestinal ischemia, Mesenteric ischemia, Chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI), Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), Intestinal angina, Nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI), Mesenteric venous thrombosis, Ischemic colitis Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in CMI before intervention) Peptic ulcer disease and other causes of epigastric/postprandial pain Biliary colic / biliary tract disease Acute pancreatitis Inflammatory bowel disease (ischemic colitis is commonly confused with IBD) Acute intestinal obstruction (especially strangulated obstruction with vascular insufficiency) Infectious colitis Infectious gastroenteritis CT angiography with thin (1-mm or finer) cuts, including venous phase for venous thrombosis (gold standard) Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound (screening; SMA peak velocity) Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy (to exclude malignancy in CMI and assess colonic mucosa in ischemic colitis) Abdominal CT and abdominal ultrasound Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram (to identify embolic source such as atrial fibrillation; should not delay surgery) Laboratory markers: leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, lactic acidosis (support advanced ischemia but do not reliably distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis) Hypercoagulability workup in mesenteric venous thrombosis Inflammatory bowel disease Diverticular disease / diverticulitis Colonic neoplasm Peptic ulcer disease Biliary tract disease Intestinal ischemia arises when splanchnic perfusion cannot meet the metabolic demands of the gut; it is broadly divided into chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI), with the latter carrying a high mortality (~50-80%) and depending critically on early diagnosis and prompt intervention (p.2586). AMI is mechanistically categorized into three patterns: arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), and mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587). Roughly half of AMI cases are embolic, with emboli typically lodging in the mid-to-distal superior mesenteric artery (SMA) just beyond the origin of the middle colic artery; about 25-30% are acute-on-chronic thrombosis on preexisting mesenteric atherosclerosis (p.2586-2587). The hallmark of acute arterial mesenteric ischemia is severe, abrupt, nonremitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical examination findings, present in roughly 95% of cases (p.2588). Pain is disproportionate to exam because ischemia begins in the mucosal layer and advances outward toward the serosa, so peritoneal signs and cardiovascular collapse are late developments (p.2588). CMI classically presents with insidious, recurrent dull crampy postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina'), fear of eating, and consequent weight loss, often over 6-12 months, in a malnourished patient with other signs of atherosclerosis (p.2587). CT angiography with 1-mm or thinner cuts is the gold-standard diagnostic test for both acute and chronic mesenteric arterial occlusive disease; a venous-phase study aids detection of mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587-2588). Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a useful screening tool: a high SMA peak flow velocity carries about an 80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex study virtually excludes mesenteric ischemia (p.2587). In suspected AMI the decision to operate is frequently driven by a high index of suspicion from history and exam despite normal laboratory values, and surgical consultation should not be delayed (p.2588). Mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10% of cases) tends to be associated with hypercoagulable states; documented inherited thrombophilia warrants long-term anticoagulation (p.2587, p.2588-2589). Severity of ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy from mild (minimal erythema) to moderate (pale ulcerations extending into muscularis) to severe (black/green discoloration indicating full-thickness necrosis) (p.2589). Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings Blood per rectum / bloody stools Peritonitis and cardiovascular collapse (late findings indicating advanced ischemia) Leukocytosis with metabolic/lactic acidosis suggesting advanced ischemia or necrosis Black or green colonic mucosal discoloration on colonoscopy indicating full-thickness necrosis Atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or infective endocarditis in a patient with acute abdominal pain (embolic source) Anchoring on a benign cause and underestimating severity because abdominal pain is markedly out of proportion to a relatively unremarkable exam (p.2588). Waiting for abnormal laboratory values before acting; lactate, leukocytosis, and acidosis may be normal early or fail to distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis (p.2588-2589). Performing mesenteric duplex without fasting, since bowel gas obscures flow and the postprandial vasodilation response (p.2587). Mistaking ischemic colitis for inflammatory bowel disease (p.2589). Overlooking nonocclusive ischemia in obtunded, critically ill patients in whom physical findings are obscured by the underlying illness (p.2589). Failing to recognize that the proximal jejunum may be spared in SMA embolism while the rest of the small bowel to the transverse colon becomes ischemic, leading to incomplete bowel assessment (p.2589). The intestine is perfused by the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), with extensive collateralization through the mesenteric arcades; small-bowel collaterals converge at the duodenum and pancreatic bed, while colonic collaterals meet at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and the descending/sigmoid colon (Sudeck's point), the watershed zones most prone to colonic ischemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to ~30% of cardiac output, and protective mechanisms include abundant collaterals, autoregulation of flow, and the capacity to increase oxygen extraction. Occlusive ischemia results from embolic or thrombotic interruption of a major mesenteric artery (emboli, originating from the heart in >75% of cases, preferentially lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic origin); development of chronic intestinal angina generally requires significant stenosis of two of the three major vessels, with SMA involvement most concerning. CMI reflects failure to mount the normal postprandial hyperemic increase in intestinal blood flow, analogous to cardiac angina, due to atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA and/or celiac origins. Nonocclusive ischemia represents disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiologic stress such as shock; if untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis arises from inherited or acquired hypercoagulable states (p.2587). Acute mesenteric ischemia carries a mortality rate exceeding 50% and is among the most challenging diagnoses; the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment is the single most important determinant of survival. Chronic mesenteric ischemia managed with revascularization has favorable long-term outcomes, with endovascular stenting associated with about an 80% long-term success rate. Outcomes hinge on early recognition before progression to full-thickness bowel necrosis and peritonitis (p.2587-2588). Ischemic colonic mucosal injury is graded by colonoscopy: mild = minimal mucosal erythema; moderate = pale mucosal ulcerations with extension into the muscular layer; severe = severe ulcerations with black or green mucosal discoloration consistent with full-thickness bowel-wall necrosis. Mechanically, mesenteric ischemia is classified as chronic (CMI) versus acute (AMI), and AMI is subclassified as arterio-occlusive (embolic or thrombotic), nonocclusive (vasospastic/hypoperfusion), or mesenteric venous thrombosis (p.2587, p.2589).

involvement Attributing subacute nonspecific abdominal pain to benign causes and delaying imaging Failing to obtain venous-phase CT and missing the venous thrombus Delaying anticoagulation in the absence of infarction Not investigating for an underlying thrombophilia or malignancy after the acute event Mesenteric venous thrombosis occurs when thrombus obstructs venous outflow from the bowel, most commonly in the superior mesenteric vein. Impaired venous drainage raises intestinal capillary and interstitial pressure, producing bowel wall oedema, arterial inflow compromise, and progressive congestion. If flow is not restored, transmural ischaemia and infarction ensue, with translocation of bacteria, peritonitis, and sepsis. It is usually driven by hypercoagulable states (primary thrombophilia, malignancy) or local factors such as portal hypertension, abdominal sepsis or inflammation, and recent surgery. The extent of collateral drainage and the speed of thrombus propagation determine whether ischaemia remains reversible. When diagnosed before infarction and treated promptly with anticoagulation, mesenteric venous thrombosis has a better prognosis than acute arterial mesenteric ischaemia. Delayed diagnosis with established bowel necrosis carries high morbidity and mortality, and recurrence risk depends on the underlying prothrombotic cause and duration of anticoagulation.

Mesothelioma — malignant mesothelioma, malignant pleural mesothelioma, MPM Metastatic adenocarcinoma to the pleura Primary lung carcinoma with pleural involvement Benign asbestos-related pleural disease and pleural plaques Reactive pleuritis or empyema Pleural lymphoma or other rare pleural tumours Peritoneal carcinomatosis for peritoneal presentations Chest radiograph and contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to assess pleural thickening and effusion Pleural fluid aspiration for cytology, recognising its limited sensitivity Thoracoscopic or image-guided pleural biopsy with immunohistochemistry for definitive diagnosis MRI or PET-CT to define local extent and staging in surgical candidates Detailed documentation of asbestos exposure history for clinical and medicolegal purposes Asbestos exposure is the dominant cause, with a characteristically long latency of several decades between exposure and disease onset The pleura is the most common site, presenting with breathlessness and chest pain, often accompanied by a unilateral pleural effusion; the peritoneum is a less common site A detailed occupational and environmental exposure history is essential, since exposure may have been remote, indirect, or through household contact Pleural fluid cytology alone is often insufficient, and definitive diagnosis usually requires tissue biopsy, best obtained by thoracoscopy with immunohistochemical confirmation The epithelioid subtype carries a better prognosis than the sarcomatoid or biphasic subtypes, which are more aggressive The disease tends to spread by local extension over the pleural surfaces and encases the lung rather than forming discrete masses, making complete surgical clearance difficult Management is usually multimodal and largely palliative, combining platinum-based chemotherapy, increasingly with immunotherapy, alongside radiotherapy and surgery in selected fit patients Effusion control with pleurodesis or an indwelling catheter and good symptom management are central to care, and cases often carry medicolegal and compensation implications Progressive breathlessness with a large or recurrent unilateral pleural effusion Persistent chest wall pain suggesting local tumour invasion Rapid clinical deterioration or weight loss indicating aggressive disease Superior vena cava obstruction or extensive chest wall involvement Relying on pleural fluid cytology alone and delaying tissue biopsy Failing to elicit a remote or indirect asbestos exposure history Overlooking the medicolegal and compensation dimensions of the diagnosis Offering aggressive surgery to patients unlikely to benefit given subtype or stage Malignant mesothelioma arises from the mesothelial cells lining the pleural, peritoneal, or, rarely, pericardial cavities. Inhaled asbestos fibres, particularly amphibole types, are retained in tissues and provoke chronic inflammation, oxidative injury, and DNA damage over many years, leading to malignant transformation. The tumour characteristically grows as a diffuse rind along serosal surfaces, encasing the lung and invading the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum. Histological subtypes range from epithelioid through biphasic to the more aggressive sarcomatoid form. Prognosis is generally poor with limited long-term survival; the epithelioid subtype, early stage, and good performance status favour longer survival, while sarcomatoid histology and advanced disease predict rapid progression.
