vomiting, diuretic, or laxative use Metabolic alkalosis is a primary rise in serum bicarbonate with a compensatory increase in carbon dioxide from reduced ventilation Understanding it requires separating the process that generates the alkalosis from the factors that allow the kidney to maintain it Urine chloride is the single most useful test for classification, dividing cases into chloride-responsive (low urine chloride) and chloride-resistant (high urine chloride) forms Chloride-responsive alkalosis, from vomiting, nasogastric suction, or diuretics, is accompanied by volume and chloride depletion and corrects with saline and potassium repletion Chloride-resistant alkalosis reflects mineralocorticoid excess or severe potassium depletion and does not respond to saline, so the underlying disorder must be treated Hypokalaemia both contributes to and is worsened by alkalosis, and the two often need correcting together Maintenance of the alkalosis depends on factors such as volume contraction, chloride depletion, potassium depletion, and mineralocorticoid activity that impair renal bicarbonate excretion Severe alkalaemia can cause neuromuscular irritability, arrhythmias, and reduced tissue oxygen delivery, and may need more aggressive correction Severe alkalaemia causing tetany, seizures, or cardiac arrhythmia Profound hypokalaemia with muscle weakness or arrhythmia risk Marked volume depletion with haemodynamic compromise Hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis suggesting mineralocorticoid excess Giving saline to a chloride-resistant alkalosis that will not respond Failing to measure urine chloride and thereby misclassifying the disorder Neglecting concurrent potassium and magnesium deficits that perpetuate the alkalosis Overlooking surreptitious vomiting or diuretic use as the underlying cause Metabolic alkalosis arises when there is a net gain of bicarbonate or a loss of hydrogen ions, but its persistence depends on the kidney's inability to excrete the excess bicarbonate. Normally the kidney can excrete a large bicarbonate load rapidly, so an alkalosis is only sustained when a maintenance factor is present. Generation occurs through loss of acid from the upper gastrointestinal tract or the kidney, or from a gain of alkali. Maintenance results from conditions that increase renal bicarbonate reabsorption, including reduced effective circulating volume, chloride depletion, potassium depletion, and excess mineralocorticoid activity, all of which enhance sodium and bicarbonate reabsorption and hydrogen secretion. In chloride-responsive states, volume and chloride depletion drive the maintenance and are corrected by saline; in chloride-resistant states, ongoing mineralocorticoid excess or profound potassium loss sustains the alkalosis despite adequate volume. Most cases resolve readily once the generating cause is removed and the maintenance factors (volume, chloride, and potassium depletion) are corrected. Chloride-resistant forms require treatment of the underlying disorder and may persist otherwise. Severe alkalaemia is dangerous but usually reversible with appropriate management, and overall outcome is governed by the underlying condition.

Metabolic encephalopathy — Electrolytes, glucose, calcium Renal & liver panel, ammonia ABG Reversible — correct the derangement Dementia and pre-existing cognitive impairment - the major predisposing condition; at least two-thirds of delirium occurs in patients with underlying dementia, and the two coexist and overlap (p.183). Dementia with Lewy bodies - fluctuating course, prominent visual hallucinations and parkinsonism can closely mimic hyperactive delirium (p.183). Nonconvulsive status epilepticus and recurrent seizures with prolonged postictal confusion (p.185). Focal stroke or haemorrhage in nondominant (right) parietal lobe or medial dorsal thalamus - rare structural cause of an acute confusional state (p.184-185). Hypertensive encephalopathy / posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and eclampsia (p.184, p.190). Diffuse neoplastic disease - multiple brain metastases, diffuse glioma, CNS lymphoma, carcinomatous meningitis (p.184). Postoperative encephalopathy from a shower of microemboli, particularly after cardiac/cardiopulmonary bypass surgery (p.2348). Acute primary psychiatric disturbance, depression and catatonia - must be distinguished, particularly from the quiet hypoactive subtype (p.184). Systemic infections - urinary tract infection, pneumonia and other respiratory infections, skin/soft tissue infection and frank sepsis; a UTI precipitating acute confusion in an elderly patient with baseline dementia is a classic scenario (p.184). CNS infections - bacterial meningitis, encephalitis (including herpes simplex) and brain abscess; less common causes but high morbidity/mortality if missed (p.184). Sepsis-associated ('septic') encephalopathy - diffuse cytokine-mediated brain dysfunction occurring in the majority of patients with sepsis and multiorgan failure (p.184, p.2348-2349). Severe systemic infections causing coma - septicaemia, typhoid fever, malaria (including cerebral malaria), Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (p.190). Complete blood count and full electrolyte panel including magnesium and phosphorus (p.185). Serum/urine toxicology screen - performed earlier in younger patients (p.185). TSH and free T4, and serum cortisol for suspected endocrinopathy (p.185). Vitamin levels - B12, folate, thiamine (p.185). EEG - essential when seizures are suspected or when no cause is found after initial workup; shows nonspecific diffuse symmetric slowing in encephalopathy, frontal high-voltage slow or triphasic waves in metabolic (e.g., hepatic) coma, and can reveal nonconvulsive status epilepticus (p.184-185, p.190). Brain imaging - MRI with diffusion and gadolinium is the preferred study (CT often used first for speed/availability) to exclude structural causes; note imaging is frequently unrevealing in pure metabolic delirium (p.185, p.189-190). Lumbar puncture (after neuroimaging) when CNS infection, autoimmune, inflammatory or neoplastic disease is suspected, or in any delirium with a negative workup (p.185, p.190). Inflammatory and autoimmune serologies - ESR, ANA, complement, p-/c-ANCA, and paraneoplastic/autoimmune encephalitis panels in serum and CSF when indicated (p.185). ECG and infectious serologies (RPR, HIV; fungal/viral if high suspicion) as second-tier tests (p.185). Anticholinergic, opioid, sedative-hypnotic and other prescription drug toxicity, and drugs of abuse (alcohol, opiates, MDMA/ecstasy, GHB, ketamine/PCP, cocaine, 'bath salts', synthetic cannabinoids) (p.184). Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal - to be considered in all delirium including the elderly, since even modest daily drinkers can withdraw on admission (p.184). Poison/toxin exposure - carbon monoxide, ethylene glycol, inhalants, pesticides (p.184). Endocrinopathies - hyper- or hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency / Addisonian crisis (p.184, p.190). Hypothermia and hyperthermia (p.184, p.190). Global cerebral hypoperfusion from hypotension - heart failure, septic shock, severe dehydration or anaemia (p.184-185). Autoimmune and paraneoplastic disorders - CNS vasculitis, cerebral lupus, autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis shows a characteristic 'extreme delta brush' EEG) (p.184, p.190). Sedative drug overdose mimicking structural brainstem disease or even brain death (e.g., barbiturates) - toxic causes must be excluded before diagnosing brain death (p.189). Delirium is an acute, relatively rapid decline in cognition (hours to days) that characteristically fluctuates; the cardinal neuropsychological deficit is inattention, though memory, executive function, visuospatial skills and language are variably affected (p.181-182). It is a purely clinical bedside diagnosis. The validated Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) requires (1) acute onset with fluctuating course and (2) inattention, plus either (3) disorganized thinking or (4) altered level of consciousness (p.184). Recognize two ends of a spectrum: a hyperactive subtype (classic example: delirium tremens, with agitation, hallucinations, tremor, autonomic instability) and a hypoactive subtype (e.g., benzodiazepine intoxication, with apathy and psychomotor slowing); hypoactive cases are frequently overlooked, especially on wards and in the ICU (p.182). Bilateral asterixis and multifocal myoclonus on motor exam are non-focal signs that, while nonspecific, usually point to a metabolic or toxic encephalopathy / drug intoxication rather than a structural lesion (p.184, p.190). A simple bedside test of attention is forward digit span: healthy adults manage 5-7 digits, while a span of 4 or fewer suggests an attentional deficit; many delirious patients can repeat only 3 or fewer (p.184). Worsening in the evening (sundowning) is typical but not required; because the course fluctuates, a single morning assessment can be falsely reassuring and serial examinations are needed (p.184). About one-third of delirium cases are drug-related, especially agents with anticholinergic or sedative properties, narcotics and benzodiazepines; nearly any drug can precipitate delirium in a predisposed patient (p.184). Delirium can act as a 'stress test for the brain' - a minor insult (UTI, elective surgery, hospitalization) that unmasks delirium in a previously well person should prompt later outpatient screening for an unrecognized underlying neurodegenerative or cerebrovascular disorder (p.183). The MMSE is unreliable in delirium because tasks such as spelling 'world' backward and serial subtraction are corrupted by the underlying attentional deficit (p.184). New focal neurologic deficit, meningismus, fever or papilloedema - point away from a simple metabolic cause toward a structural, infectious or raised-ICP process needing urgent imaging/LP (p.184, p.189-190). Suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus - if suspicion is high, EEG should be obtained immediately as it is treatable and easily missed in a fluctuating patient (p.185). Sodium <125 mmol/L (especially if acute) causing confusion, and <119 mmol/L acutely associated with coma and convulsions (p.188-189). In-hospital delirium carries a 25-33% mortality (comparable to sepsis) and a roughly fivefold higher mortality in following months - it signals serious underlying illness, not a benign transient state (p.182). Delirium in the ICU should be regarded as organ dysfunction on a par with liver, kidney or heart failure, and is associated with worse outcomes (p.182, p.2348). Treating the symptoms of delirium pharmacologically while neglecting the underlying cause merely prolongs the confused state and can mask important diagnostic clues (p.185). Missing nonconvulsive status epilepticus - its fluctuating presentation mimics ordinary delirium, and only EEG will reveal it (p.185). Diagnosing delirium without knowledge of the patient's cognitive baseline, so that dementia or long-standing depression is mistaken for an acute confusional state - collateral history is essential (p.184). Overlooking the quiet hypoactive subtype, which is commonly missed and may be wrongly attributed to depression or sedation (p.182, p.2348). Attributing coma to incidental imaging findings (small subdural, old stroke) when the true cause is intoxication; a normal CT does not exclude an anatomic lesion, and most coma/confusion is metabolic or toxic in origin (p.190). Forgetting that the severity of metabolic encephalopathy depends on how rapidly the derangement developed, so a 'mildly' abnormal value reached acutely can produce marked impairment (p.188-189). Diagnosing brain death without first excluding sedative/toxic causes (e.g., barbiturates) that can mimic its findings (p.189). Delirium reflects diffuse rather than focal brain dysfunction; the attentional deficit localizes broadly to brainstem, thalamus, prefrontal cortex and parietal lobes, and most cases arise from widespread cortical and subcortical disturbance rather than a single lesion. Acetylcholine deficiency is thought to be central (explaining the potency of anticholinergic drugs), with additional roles for excess dopamine, proinflammatory mediators and individual susceptibility. The concept is that of an insult acting on a vulnerable, low-reserve brain. For most metabolic causes (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperosmolarity, hypercapnia, hypercalcaemia, hepatic and renal failure) the brain shows little or no structural damage and the effects are largely reversible, attributed to impaired energy supply, altered ion fluxes across neuronal membranes and neurotransmitter abnormalities. In hepatic encephalopathy, raised ammonia is proposed to drive astrocytic glutamine synthesis and osmotic swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, reactive nitrogen/oxygen species, increased inhibitory GABA tone and 'false' neurotransmitters, with chronic disease producing diffuse astrocytosis. Uraemic encephalopathy is multifactorial (urea itself is not the cause): accumulated neurotoxins, catecholamine depletion, altered glutamate/GABA tone, raised brain calcium and blood-brain-barrier disruption. Importantly, the degree of neurologic change in metabolic encephalopathies depends heavily on the rapidity with which the serum derangement develops, not just its absolute level. In sepsis-associated encephalopathy, circulating inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) appear to cause diffuse cerebral dysfunction that is not simply explained by the metabolic derangements of organ failure (p.183, p.188-189, p.2348-2349). Once viewed as benign and transient, delirium is now recognized as a marker of serious illness with substantial morbidity and mortality: in-hospital mortality is roughly 25-33% (similar to sepsis), and delirious patients have about a fivefold higher mortality in the ensuing months versus matched non-delirious inpatients, plus longer stays, more nursing-home discharge, higher readmission and recurrent episodes. Most metabolic and toxic encephalopathies are reversible with no or minimal structural brain damage, and drug/toxin-induced coma typically resolves fully provided hypoxia or severe hypotension has not occurred. However, some episodes persist for weeks to months or longer, delirium can cause lasting cognitive decline, and lingering effects (ranging from amnesia for the episode to PTSD-like re-experiencing) are common. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy severe enough to cause coma carries a mortality approaching 50%, though this mainly reflects severity of the underlying critical illness rather than the encephalopathy itself (p.182, p.188-189, p.2349). No formal grading scale is described; severity is gauged clinically by the level of consciousness (a continuum from hyperarousal through lethargy to coma) and by the depth of the attentional deficit (e.g., forward digit span). The EEG correlates with severity, showing progressive generalized background slowing as the encephalopathy deepens (p.184, p.190).

well toddler Combined central and peripheral neurological signs Rapid cognitive or psychiatric deterioration in older patients Feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk Being misled by pseudodeficiency alleles that lower measured enzyme activity without causing disease Attributing early behavioural or psychiatric changes in adults to a primary psychiatric disorder Missing the peripheral neuropathy that helps distinguish it from other leukodystrophies Delaying assessment for disease-modifying therapy until symptoms are advanced Metachromatic leukodystrophy results from biallelic pathogenic variants in ARSA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase A, which desulfates sulfatide (cerebroside sulfate). Deficient activity causes sulfatides to accumulate within lysosomes of myelin-forming cells (oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells) and other tissues. The accumulated sulfatide is toxic to myelin-producing cells, driving progressive demyelination of the central and peripheral nervous system and the resulting motor, cognitive, and neuropathic decline. Stored material stains metachromatically, giving the disease its name. The late-infantile form progresses rapidly to severe disability and death within a few years of onset. Juvenile and adult forms progress more slowly and variably. Presymptomatic or very early treatment with stem cell transplantation or gene therapy offers the best chance of altering the course, but symptomatic disease responds poorly.

acquired skills Progressive bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk New-onset seizures or status epilepticus Airway compromise from combined storage-related upper-airway and skeletal changes Testing only arylsulfatase A and diagnosing isolated metachromatic leukodystrophy while missing the combined deficiency Overlooking the somatic and dermatological clues (coarse features, ichthyosis, dysostosis) that point away from an isolated leukodystrophy Attributing the neuropathy solely to a central process and not testing nerve conduction Failing to recognise the multisystem nature when planning surveillance and supportive care In multiple sulfatase deficiency, biallelic variants in SUMF1 impair the formylglycine-generating enzyme that performs a post-translational modification essential for the catalytic activity of every sulfatase. As a result all sulfatases are simultaneously deficient, so sulfated substrates accumulate across multiple pathways: sulfatides build up in myelin (as in metachromatic leukodystrophy), glycosaminoglycans accumulate (as in mucopolysaccharidoses), and cholesterol sulfate accumulates in skin (as in X-linked ichthyosis). The combined storage produces central and peripheral demyelination alongside the somatic, skeletal, and dermatological features of the overlapping disorders. The disorder is progressive with a poor prognosis, especially in neonatal and late-infantile presentations, which typically lead to severe disability and early death; later-onset forms progress more slowly but remain relentless. No disease-modifying treatment is currently available.

toxicity comes from hepatic metabolism to formaldehyde and then formic acid, which produces severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and target-organ injury There is a characteristic latent period of hours (longer if ethanol is co-ingested) before symptoms appear, so early presentation can look deceptively mild Visual symptoms are a hallmark - blurred vision, photophobia, a snowfield or blizzard-like whiteout, and potentially permanent blindness from optic nerve injury Look for a wide anion-gap metabolic acidosis together with a raised osmolal gap; the osmolal gap falls as methanol is metabolised while the anion gap rises Fomepizole is the preferred antidote as it inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and blocks formation of toxic metabolites; ethanol is an alternative competitive substrate where fomepizole is unavailable Folinic acid (or folic acid) is given to accelerate metabolism of formic acid to carbon dioxide and water Haemodialysis removes methanol and formate and corrects acidosis, and is indicated in severe acidosis, visual impairment, renal failure, or high methanol levels Consider methanol in any unexplained high anion-gap acidosis with visual complaints, particularly after consumption of illicit or adulterated spirits Visual disturbance or reduced acuity signalling optic nerve toxicity and impending blindness Severe high anion-gap metabolic acidosis Reduced consciousness, seizures, or coma Rising anion gap with a narrowing osmolal gap indicating ongoing conversion to toxic metabolites Consumption of illicit or home-distilled alcohol in a cluster of patients Being falsely reassured by the asymptomatic latent period, especially with co-ingested ethanol Waiting for a confirmatory methanol level before starting antidote in a strongly suggestive case Overlooking the diagnosis when the osmolal gap has already normalised late in the course Failing to arrange haemodialysis for severe acidosis or visual symptoms Methanol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, which is rapidly converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid. Formic acid is the principal toxin: it inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing cellular hypoxia and lactate accumulation, and produces a profound high anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Formate is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve, causing oedema and demyelination that can lead to irreversible blindness, and can injure the basal ganglia (putaminal necrosis). Because the parent alcohol elevates serum osmolality, an early osmolal gap precedes the later anion-gap acidosis. Outcome depends on the interval to treatment and the depth of acidosis at presentation; early antidote and dialysis can be curative, but delayed treatment risks permanent blindness, neurological deficits, and death.

glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, risking haemolysis and worsening Failing to identify and stop the causative oxidant exposure Haemoglobin normally keeps its iron in the reduced ferrous state, which binds oxygen; a small fraction is continually oxidised to the ferric methaemoglobin form and reduced again, mainly by the cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH-dependent) system. Methaemoglobinaemia develops when oxidative stress from drugs or chemicals overwhelms this reducing capacity, or when the reductase enzyme or the globin chain is congenitally abnormal. Ferric haem cannot carry oxygen, and its presence increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining ferrous haem, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. The NADPH-dependent methaemoglobin reductase pathway becomes relevant therapeutically because methylene blue acts through it, which is why it fails when glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is deficient. Acquired disease usually resolves well once the offending agent is removed and, where needed, methylene blue is given; congenital reductase deficiency is generally compatible with normal life, whereas very high acute levels can be fatal without prompt treatment.

depletion Allowing prolonged perioperative or illness-related fasting without an emergency plan 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses a step in the Deficiency, from defects in either the alpha (MCCC1) or beta (MCCC2) subunit, blocks leucine catabolism so that 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA is diverted to 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, which accumulate and are excreted. The conjugation of these metabolites with carnitine and glycine can deplete free carnitine. Although the biochemical defect is consistent, clinical expression is highly variable and often benign, so it is regarded as a condition of low and unpredictable penetrance. During catabolic stress a minority develop a Reye-like metabolic crisis with acidosis and hyperammonaemia. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The great majority of individuals identified are asymptomatic with a normal outlook; a minority experience metabolic crises, and with fasting avoidance and carnitine supplementation the prognosis is generally good.

illness, fasting or increased protein catabolism Progressive renal impairment or acute basal ganglia injury with a new movement disorder Attributing an acidotic, unwell neonate to sepsis and delaying metabolic investigation Failing to trial and document vitamin B12 responsiveness Overlooking evolving chronic kidney disease during long-term follow-up Under-treating catabolism during intercurrent illness, allowing preventable decompensation Methylmalonic acidemia results from a block in the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, a step catalysed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase using adenosylcobalamin. This reaction lies on the final common pathway for catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids isoleucine and valine, methionine, threonine, odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol side chains. Enzyme deficiency or impaired cofactor synthesis causes methylmalonic acid and related organic acids to accumulate, producing severe metabolic acidosis. These metabolites inhibit ureagenesis (causing secondary hyperammonaemia) and mitochondrial energy metabolism, are toxic to bone marrow and renal tubules, and injure the basal ganglia during decompensation. Prognosis varies by subtype; cobalamin-responsive forms generally do better, whereas mutase-deficient disease carries significant risk of recurrent metabolic crises, chronic kidney disease and neurological injury, and severe cases may require kidney or combined liver-kidney transplantation. Early screening detection and meticulous metabolic control improve outcomes.

because serum IgD is normal Missing the raised urinary mevalonic acid by sampling only between attacks Overlooking the risk of secondary amyloidosis with chronic inflammation Failing to distinguish of the isoprenoid biosynthetic pathway downstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Impaired production of non-sterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, disrupts prenylation of small GTPases and activates the inflammasome, driving excess interleukin-1 beta release. The milder periodic fever form tends to improve with age but can be complicated by secondary amyloidosis if inflammation is poorly controlled. Mevalonic aciduria carries a poor prognosis with significant neurodevelopmental disability and early mortality; IL-1 blockade can substantially reduce flare frequency.

Microphthalmia and anophthalmia — MAC spectrum, microphthalmia-anophthalmia-coloboma, SOX2, OTX2, clinical anophthalmia Isolated coloboma at the milder end of the MAC spectrum Cryptophthalmos and other eyelid or orbital malformations Congenital cystic eye or orbital cyst Phthisis bulbi from an acquired process mimicking a small eye Nanophthalmos and posterior microphthalmos with a normal external appearance Syndromic associations such as CHARGE syndrome Detailed ophthalmic examination and measurement of axial length by ocular biometry Orbital and cranial imaging (ultrasound, CT or MRI) to confirm the presence and size of ocular tissue Systemic and neurodevelopmental assessment, including for pituitary and brain anomalies Chromosomal and molecular genetic testing including SOX2 and OTX2 Assessment of the fellow eye and orbit to guide prosthetic and reconstructive planning Microphthalmia is an abnormally small, disorganised eye, whereas anophthalmia is the complete absence of ocular tissue; the two lie on a continuous spectrum Both often coexist with coloboma as part of the microphthalmia-anophthalmia-coloboma (MAC) spectrum Presentation ranges from an obviously small or absent eye to a clinically normal-looking eye with reduced axial length (nanophthalmos or posterior microphthalmos) Frequently syndromic, with SOX2 and OTX2 among the most important causative genes, and association with chromosomal and multisystem disorders Can be caused by genetic, chromosomal or environmental (including gestational infective and teratogenic) factors, so a broad aetiological workup is needed True clinical anophthalmia is confirmed only when imaging shows no ocular tissue, as a rudimentary globe may be hidden Early involvement of ocularists and orbital specialists supports socket and facial growth in severe cases Bilateral severe microphthalmia or anophthalmia implying profound visual impairment Associated neurological, endocrine or systemic anomalies requiring urgent evaluation Progressive orbital or facial asymmetry from impaired socket growth Family history indicating a heritable cause needing genetic counselling Diagnosing anophthalmia clinically without imaging to exclude hidden rudimentary ocular tissue Overlooking associated brain, pituitary or systemic anomalies Delaying socket expansion and prosthetic management, impairing orbital and facial development Assuming a normal-appearing eye excludes posterior microphthalmos without biometry Microphthalmia and anophthalmia arise from disturbance of early eye morphogenesis. Normal eye formation depends on outgrowth of the optic vesicle from the developing forebrain and its invagination to form the optic cup, guided by a network of transcription factors including SOX2 and OTX2. Mutations in these developmental genes, chromosomal abnormalities, or environmental insults during embryogenesis can halt or distort this process, so the eye fails to grow to normal size (microphthalmia) or fails to develop at all (anophthalmia). Because the same signalling controls closure of the optic fissure, coloboma frequently coexists, and because these genes act in other tissues, associated brain, pituitary and systemic anomalies are common. Visual prognosis depends on the severity and laterality of the malformation, ranging from useful vision in mild unilateral microphthalmia to no vision in bilateral anophthalmia; in severe cases the focus shifts to promoting orbital and facial growth with expanders and prostheses, and overall outcome is strongly influenced by associated systemic conditions.

pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitis within the ANCA-associated spectrum. Circulating anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies prime and activate neutrophils, which adhere to and degranulate against endothelium, releasing reactive oxygen species and proteolytic enzymes that produce necrotising inflammation of capillaries, venules, and arterioles. In the kidney this yields a focal segmental necrotising and crescentic glomerulonephritis with minimal immunoglobulin deposition, and in the lung it can cause alveolar capillaritis with haemorrhage. Unlike granulomatosis with polyangiitis, granuloma formation is characteristically absent. Prompt immunosuppression induces remission in most patients, but many are left with chronic kidney disease and some progress to end-stage renal failure. enterocyte. Loss-of-function variants in MYO5B (and less often STX3 or STXBP2) disrupt the myosin Vb-mediated recycling of apical membrane and transporter proteins to the brush border. The result is failure to assemble a normal apical microvillus surface, with brush-border components mislocalised into cytoplasmic vesicles and microvillus inclusions. Because functional transporters and the absorptive surface are lost, the intestine cannot reabsorb fluid and electrolytes, producing a severe secretory diarrhoea that continues even when enteral feeds are withheld. Milder late-onset phenotypes may be managed with prolonged nutritional support.

Migraine — Clinical diagnosis (POUND criteria) Neuroimaging only if red flags New focal deficit, thunderclap onset, or fever → exclude secondary cause Tension-type headache - the main differential; distinguished by being completely featureless (no nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing or aggravation with movement), whereas migraine has one or more of these (p.3471). Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (p.3462). Acephalgic migraine / typical aura without headache - recurrent neurologic symptoms with little or no headache (p.3464). Vestibular migraine - common, underdiagnosed cause of episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, sometimes without headache (p.3464). Migraine with brainstem aura (formerly basilar/basilar-type migraine) (p.3464). Medication-overuse headache complicating an underlying migraine tendency (p.115-116). Bacterial/viral meningitis - acute severe headache with stiff neck and fever; can be mistaken for migraine because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting are shared cardinal features, and there is often striking accentuation of pain on eye movement; lumbar puncture is mandatory (p.113-114). Migraine is a clinical diagnosis in patients with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause for headache (Table 441-3, p.3466). A headache diary aids diagnosis and quantifies disability and attack frequency (p.3462). The Migraine Disability Assessment Score (MIDAS) is a validated tool to grade disability (p.3465). CT or MRI of the brain (equally sensitive as initial screen for intracranial pathology) is indicated for an abnormal neurologic examination or recent-onset headache; lumbar puncture may additionally be required when a benign cause cannot otherwise be established (p.113). General acute-headache workup may include palpation of cranial arteries, assessment of the cervical spine, blood pressure and urine examination, and funduscopy with intraocular pressure measurement (p.113). Subarachnoid hemorrhage / ruptured aneurysm, AVM or intraparenchymal hemorrhage - thunderclap headache maximal in under 5 min lasting over 5 min, stiff neck without fever; CT may rarely be normal so LP may be needed (p.114). Brain tumor - intermittent deep dull aching, may worsen with exertion or position change and cause nausea/vomiting; vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumors (p.114). Temporal (giant cell) arteritis - dull/boring headache with superimposed stabbing pains, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, polymyalgia, fever, weight loss in patients over ~50; migraineurs may report relief with prednisone, confounding interpretation of treatment response (p.114-115). Acute angle-closure glaucoma - prostrating headache with nausea/vomiting beginning with severe eye pain; red eye with a fixed, mid-dilated pupil (p.115). Transient ischemic attack / vertebrobasilar insufficiency - acute homonymous visual symptoms with fogging/graying and positive phenomena that can mimic migraine aura (p.230). Ischemic stroke - migraine can mimic stroke even without prior migraine history, especially acephalgic migraine (p.3429). Migraine is the second most common cause of headache and the leading neurologic cause of disability worldwide; over a 1-year period it affects roughly 15% of women and 6% of men (p.3462). An attack classically evolves through three phases - premonitory (prodrome), headache, and postdrome - and only about 20-25% of patients also experience an aura phase (p.3462). Premonitory symptoms (yawning, sleepiness, fatigue, cognitive 'fog', mood change, neck discomfort, polyuria/polydipsia, food cravings) can begin hours to days before the pain; some apparent 'triggers' such as light sensitivity may actually be part of this early phase rather than true precipitants (p.3462). Postdromal tiredness, poor concentration and mild neck discomfort can persist for hours and occasionally up to a day after the pain settles (p.3462). Simplified diagnostic criteria require repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 h with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause, plus at least 2 of (unilateral, throbbing, aggravated by movement, moderate/severe) and at least 1 of (nausea/vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia) (Table 441-3, p.3466). Cranial autonomic symptoms (lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, periorbital swelling, ptosis) can occur in migraine - even in children - and may be mistaken for sinus disease, leading to overdiagnosis of sinusitis and inappropriate treatment (p.114). Migraine is a brain disorder, not a 'vascular headache'; vascular changes when present are secondary, driven by cranial parasympathetic activation, and treatment response cannot be predicted by vascular effects (p.114). The vast majority of patients presenting with severe headache have a benign cause, most often migraine; brain tumor is a rare cause of isolated headache and an even rarer cause of severe pain (p.114). Migraineurs do not encounter more stress than headache-free people; the problem is overresponsiveness to changes in stress, and they are characteristically sensitive to environmental/sensory stimuli, failing to habituate easily (p.3462, p.3508). Vertigo can be a prominent migraine feature - about one-third of patients referred for vertigo/dizziness have a primary diagnosis of migraine (vestibular migraine) (p.3464). Sudden-onset (thunderclap) headache or first/worst-ever severe headache (p.114). Vomiting that precedes the headache (p.114). Subacute worsening over days or weeks (p.114). Pain induced by bending, lifting or cough (p.114). Pain that disturbs sleep or is present immediately on awakening (p.114). New headache in a patient with a known systemic illness (e.g., malignancy) (p.114). Onset after age 55 (p.114). Fever or unexplained systemic signs (p.114). Abnormal neurologic examination (p.114). Pain with local tenderness, e.g., over the temporal artery (p.114). Mistaking migraine-related cranial autonomic symptoms for sinusitis, leading to overdiagnosis and inappropriate sinus treatment (p.114). Misdiagnosing meningitis as migraine (or vice versa) because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting overlap - hence LP is mandatory when fever and stiff neck are present (p.113-114). Attributing a steroid-responsive headache in an elderly patient to giant cell arteritis when migraine (far more prevalent in the elderly) also improves with prednisone (p.115). Treating headache from a reawakened migraine syndrome (e.g., after otologic or endodontic procedures) without first addressing the primary problem - the headache stays refractory until the cause is treated (p.113). Failing to recognize acephalgic migraine, which can present de novo even after age 65 and is easily confused with stroke; the sensory/motor deficit migrates slowly across a limb over minutes (versus seconds in stroke) (p.3429). Continuing acute analgesics while starting a preventive - a common cause of treatment failure and of medication-overuse headache (p.115-116). Migraine is understood as a brain disorder of sensory processing rather than a primary vascular disease. The characteristic sensory sensitivity is attributed to dysfunction of monoaminergic and other sensory-control systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus. The key nociceptive pathway is the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal innervation of large intracranial vessels and dura, with terminals that, when activated, release vasoactive neuropeptides - notably calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) - at vascular terminals and within the trigeminal nucleus. Second-order neurons of the trigeminocervical complex (caudal trigeminal nucleus extending into the upper cervical dorsal horns, receiving C1-C2 input) decussate and project via the quintothalamic tract to ventrobasal and posterior thalamic nuclei, with additional projections to periaqueductal gray and hypothalamus that exert descending antinociceptive modulation; the dorsal raphe nucleus, locus coeruleus, parabrachial nucleus and rostroventromedial medulla are implicated in this modulation. Serotonin (5-HT) is involved - triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists (some also 5-HT1F) and ditans are selective 5-HT1F agonists - and dopamine contributes, with dopamine-receptor hypersensitivity in migraineurs. Functional imaging shows hypothalamic activation in the premonitory phase and persistent dorsolateral pontine (including locus coeruleus) activation during attacks and in chronic migraine, with lateralization correlating with the side of head pain. Genetic study of familial hemiplegic migraine implicates ion channels (CACNA1A/Cav2.1 P/Q calcium channel in FHM1 ~50%; ATP1A2 Na-K ATPase in FHM2 ~20%; SCN1A sodium channel in FHM3), suggesting altered membrane excitability predisposes to aura. The slowly advancing visual scotoma with luminous (fortification) edges is recognized as a marker of spreading cortical depression associated with migraine (p.3462-3464, p.3379). Patients should understand that migraine is an inherited tendency to headache that can be modified and controlled by lifestyle measures and medication but not eradicated. Except on some occasions in women taking oral estrogens or contraceptives, migraine is not associated with serious or life-threatening illness (p.3464). Migraine is nonetheless the most common neurologic cause of disability worldwide (p.3462). Recognized complications (ICHD-3) include status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, and migraine aura-triggered seizure; migraine may also progress to chronic migraine (Table 441-1, p.3463). Overuse of acute analgesics can transform episodic migraine into refractory medication-overuse headache; many patients improve after withdrawal, though residual headache often persists reflecting the underlying primary disorder (p.115-116). ICHD-3 (IHS 2018) classifies migraine into migraine without aura, migraine with aura (typical aura with/without headache, migraine with brainstem aura, hemiplegic migraine including FHM1-3 and sporadic, retinal migraine), chronic migraine, complications of migraine (status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, migraine aura-triggered seizure), probable migraine, and episodic syndromes that may be associated with migraine (cyclical vomiting, abdominal migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo/torticollis, infantile colic, vestibular migraine). Chronic migraine is defined as migraine on 8 or more days per month with at least 15 total headache days per month (Table 441-1, p.3463; p.3462). Disability is graded by MIDAS: Grade I 0-5, Grade II 6-10, Grade III 11-20, Grade IV over 20 (Fig. 441-4, p.3466).

Miliaria — heat rash, prickly heat, sweat rash, miliaria rubra, miliaria crystallina Folliculitis Acute eczema or contact dermatitis Candidal intertrigo in flexures Viral exanthem or drug eruption Neonatal erythema toxicum or transient neonatal pustular melanosis Grover's disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) in adults Diagnosis is clinical, based on morphology and a history of heat, occlusion, or fever Skin swab if secondary bacterial infection (pustular miliaria) is suspected Investigations are seldom required, and biopsy is reserved for atypical or persistent cases Assessment of the environment and clothing or dressing practices, especially in infants and bedridden patients Miliaria arises from blockage of eccrine sweat ducts, so it favours hot, humid conditions, febrile illness, occlusion, and overdressing, and is common in neonates and in the newly bedridden The subtype reflects the depth of duct obstruction: crystallina shows tiny clear, easily ruptured superficial vesicles; rubra produces itchy or prickly erythematous papulovesicles; and the deeper profunda presents as firm, skin-coloured papules Typical sites are areas of occlusion and friction such as the trunk, flexures, and skin under clothing or dressings In infants it commonly affects the neck, groin, and axillae and is easily provoked by warm environments and heavy wrapping The cornerstone of management is cooling and reducing sweating: a cooler environment, loose breathable clothing, and avoiding occlusion, which allow the ducts to reopen It is generally self-limiting once the provoking heat and occlusion are removed, and specific drug treatment is rarely needed Widespread deep miliaria can impair sweating and predispose to heat intolerance and, in extreme heat, heat exhaustion Secondary bacterial infection (miliaria pustulosa) can complicate the picture if lesions are scratched or persist Extensive deep (profunda) involvement impairing sweating with symptoms of heat intolerance or heat exhaustion Signs of secondary bacterial infection such as pustules, increasing pain, or spreading erythema Systemic upset or fever suggesting an alternative or complicating diagnosis Failure to settle after removing heat and occlusion, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Treating with occlusive creams or heavy dressings that worsen duct blockage Overwrapping or overdressing infants and perpetuating the rash Mistaking pustular miliaria with secondary infection for a primary bacterial folliculitis or vice versa Overlooking impaired thermoregulation in extensive deep disease during hot conditions Miliaria results from obstruction of the eccrine sweat ducts, which causes sweat to leak into the surrounding skin rather than reach the surface. Keratin plugging of the duct, often aggravated by an overgrowth of skin flora producing occlusive material, blocks flow at varying levels. The level of the block determines the clinical form: obstruction within the stratum corneum causes the superficial vesicles of crystallina, blockage within the epidermis produces the inflammatory papulovesicles of rubra, and obstruction at the dermo-epidermal junction gives the deeper papules of profunda. The extravasated sweat provokes local inflammation and the sensation of prickling, while widespread duct blockage can compromise thermoregulation. Miliaria is benign and typically resolves quickly once overheating and occlusion are addressed; recurrence is common with repeated heat exposure, and only extensive deep disease or secondary infection causes significant problems.

preceding respiratory or gastrointestinal infection Regarded as a variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome and part of the anti-GQ1b antibody spectrum Serum anti-GQ1b antibodies are positive in the great majority of cases and strongly support the diagnosis Consciousness is preserved, distinguishing it from Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis, which shares the anti-GQ1b mechanism but adds encephalopathy diagnosis when early cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal Overlooking the encephalopathy that would reclassify the case as Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis Miller Fisher syndrome is an acute immune-mediated neuropathy triggered by infection, in which antibodies against the GQ1b ganglioside are generated through molecular mimicry with microbial (often Campylobacter jejuni)
