GQ1b is densely expressed in the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nerves and in muscle-spindle afferents, so antibody binding there produces ophthalmoplegia and sensory ataxia, while impaired large-fibre afferent function causes areflexia. The peripheral, largely nodal-paranodal site of injury and the self-limiting immune response underlie the generally favourable outcome. The prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients recovering fully over weeks to months, though those with overlapping Guillain-Barre features may have a more prolonged course.

Minimal Change Nephrotic Syndrome (Child) — minimal change disease, MCNS, idiopathic nephrotic syndrome of childhood, steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Membranous nephropathy Post-infectious or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Congenital nephrotic syndrome (in infants) Secondary nephrotic syndrome (e.g. Henoch-Schonlein, infection-related) Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein) Serum albumin, lipid profile, and renal function Serum complement (C3, C4) Autoimmune serology when secondary causes are suspected Assessment for infection and, in selected cases, screening for thrombosis Renal biopsy in atypical presentations or steroid resistance Minimal change disease accounts for the large majority of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, most commonly presenting between about 1 and 6 years of age. The defining features are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. Oedema is typically dependent and periorbital and can progress to generalised swelling with ascites and pleural effusions. Most children are steroid-responsive, and a favourable response to corticosteroids is both diagnostic and therapeutic in the typical age group. Renal biopsy is generally reserved for atypical features such as age under 1 or over 10 years, persistent hypertension, gross haematuria, low complement, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance. Children are at increased risk of infection, particularly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from encapsulated organisms, because of urinary immunoglobulin losses. A hypercoagulable state develops from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, increasing the risk of venous and arterial thrombosis. Relapses are common, and some children become frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent, requiring steroid-sparing agents. Signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain, tenderness) Features of venous or arterial thrombosis, including limb swelling, respiratory compromise, or neurological signs Hypovolaemic shock during aggressive diuresis Severe respiratory distress from large pleural effusions or ascites Steroid resistance or deteriorating renal function suggesting a more aggressive lesion Missing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis because ascitic signs can be subtle in an oedematous child Overlooking thrombosis risk during periods of heavy proteinuria and diuresis Assuming all childhood nephrotic syndrome is minimal change and delaying biopsy in atypical cases Over-diuresing and precipitating hypovolaemia in a child with low intravascular volume A poorly understood immune dysregulation, involving circulating permeability factors and T-cell mediated signalling, injures the glomerular podocytes. On light microscopy the glomeruli appear normal, but electron microscopy reveals diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Loss of the size- and charge-selective filtration barrier permits massive albumin leakage into the urine, producing hypoalbuminaemia, reduced oncotic pressure, oedema, and compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidaemia. Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have an excellent long-term renal prognosis, though many experience relapses over several years before remitting; steroid-resistant disease, often reflecting focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.

Mitochondrial disease — mitochondrial cytopathy, mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, oxidative phosphorylation disorder, respiratory chain disorder, MELAS/MERRF/Leigh syndrome (subtypes) Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency and other primary lactic acidoses Organic acidaemias and fatty acid oxidation defects Inflammatory or infectious encephalopathy and stroke (for stroke-like episodes) Muscular dystrophies and inflammatory myopathies Neurodegenerative and demyelinating disorders Acquired causes of raised lactate (hypoperfusion, sepsis) Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate with lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Plasma amino acids (alanine) and urine organic acids Neuroimaging (MRI and MR spectroscopy showing a lactate peak; symmetrical basal ganglia or brainstem lesions in Leigh syndrome) Muscle biopsy with histochemistry (ragged-red and COX-deficient fibres) and respiratory chain enzyme assays Molecular testing of mitochondrial DNA and nuclear gene panels Organ-specific assessment (echocardiography, audiometry, endocrine and ophthalmological review) A heterogeneous group of disorders of oxidative phosphorylation caused by mutations in either mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes affecting the respiratory chain Should be suspected when unexplained multisystem disease affects high-energy organs such as brain, muscle, heart, eye, endocrine glands, liver and kidney in unusual combinations Mitochondrial DNA disorders are maternally inherited and show heteroplasmy, so severity and tissue involvement vary with the proportion of mutant genomes (threshold effect) Recognisable syndromes include MELAS (stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis), MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres), Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotising encephalopathy), Kearns-Sayre and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy Elevated lactate in blood or CSF, and a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, support the diagnosis but are neither fully sensitive nor specific Muscle biopsy may show ragged-red fibres and cytochrome-c-oxidase-deficient fibres, and definitive diagnosis increasingly relies on genetic testing of mitochondrial and nuclear genomes There is no curative therapy; management is largely supportive with cofactor and antioxidant cocktails, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins, and treatment of organ-specific complications Certain metabolic markers may appear on newborn screening, but most mitochondrial disorders are not reliably detected by standard screening Stroke-like episodes with encephalopathy, seizures and lactic acidosis (as in MELAS) Acute metabolic decompensation with severe lactic acidosis Rapidly progressive encephalopathy, respiratory failure or brainstem dysfunction in Leigh syndrome Cardiac conduction block (e.g. in Kearns-Sayre) with risk of sudden death, and status epilepticus Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal blood lactate, which can be intermittent Using medications toxic to mitochondria (e.g. valproate in some contexts, certain antivirals) without caution Failing to screen for treatable organ complications such as cardiac conduction disease and endocrinopathy Overlooking maternal inheritance and the implications of heteroplasmy for family counselling Mitochondrial diseases arise from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, the process by which the electron transport chain generates ATP. Because mitochondria contain their own DNA encoding some respiratory chain subunits, while most subunits and assembly factors are nuclear-encoded, disease can follow maternal, autosomal or X-linked inheritance. Mutations reduce ATP production and may increase reactive oxygen species and lactate. Tissues with high energy demand are preferentially affected, and in mitochondrial DNA disorders the mixture of normal and mutant genomes within cells (heteroplasmy) and a threshold of mutant load determine which tissues manifest disease and how severely, explaining the marked clinical variability. Prognosis is highly variable, ranging from severe fatal infantile encephalopathy to slowly progressive or relatively stable adult disease, depending on the genetic defect, mutant load and organs involved; most forms are progressive with no cure, and management aims to preserve function and prevent decompensation.

Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes — MDS, MDDS, mtDNA depletion syndrome, TK2, DGUOK, MPV17, SUCLA2, RRM2B Primary mitochondrial DNA point mutation or deletion syndromes Spinal muscular atrophy and congenital myopathies (for myopathic forms) Neonatal haemochromatosis and other infantile liver failure syndromes Glycogen storage and fatty acid oxidation disorders Leigh syndrome Congenital disorders of glycosylation Quantification of mitochondrial DNA copy number in muscle or liver Nuclear gene panel or exome sequencing covering TK2, DGUOK, MPV17, SUCLA2, RRM2B, POLG and related genes Respiratory-chain enzyme assays in affected tissue showing combined complex deficiencies Liver function and coagulation studies in hepatocerebral presentations Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids (for example methylmalonic aciduria in SUCLA2/SUCLG1 defects) This is a group of autosomal recessive nuclear disorders in which the amount, rather than the sequence, of mitochondrial DNA is reduced in affected tissues They are broadly grouped by phenotype into myopathic (for example TK2), encephalomyopathic (for example SUCLA2, RRM2B), hepatocerebral (for example DGUOK, MPV17, POLG) and neurogastrointestinal forms Causative genes maintain the mitochondrial nucleotide pool or replicate mitochondrial DNA, so their failure starves post-mitotic tissues of intact mitochondrial genomes Because inheritance is Mendelian and nuclear, recurrence risk follows autosomal recessive expectations rather than the maternal transmission seen with primary mitochondrial DNA mutations Hepatocerebral forms present in infancy with liver failure and neurological features, while myopathic forms present with progressive weakness and hypotonia Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number in affected tissue alongside targeted or panel nuclear gene testing Sodium valproate is avoided where POLG or a hepatocerebral depletion disorder is suspected because of hepatotoxicity risk, and care is otherwise supportive Infantile hepatic failure with coagulopathy Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory muscle involvement Encephalopathy or refractory seizures Metabolic decompensation with severe lactic acidosis Confusing these nuclear, Mendelian disorders with maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA diseases when counselling families Failing to sample the clinically affected tissue, so depletion is missed in blood Administering valproate in POLG or hepatocerebral forms and precipitating liver failure Not recognising specific biochemical clues such as mild methylmalonic aciduria pointing to SUCLA2 or SUCLG1 defects Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes are caused by recessive mutations in nuclear genes that either supply the deoxyribonucleotide building blocks for mitochondrial DNA (such as TK2, DGUOK, SUCLA2, SUCLG1 and RRM2B), maintain the mitochondrial environment (such as MPV17), or replicate the genome directly (POLG, TWNK). Impairment of any of these functions reduces the number of intact mitochondrial genomes per cell, and because mitochondrial DNA encodes essential respiratory-chain subunits, oxidative phosphorylation fails in a tissue-specific pattern that reflects each gene's expression and each tissue's energy demand. Post-mitotic, energy-hungry tissues such as muscle, brain and liver are most vulnerable, giving the myopathic, encephalomyopathic and hepatocerebral phenotypes. Prognosis varies by subtype and gene: severe infantile hepatocerebral and encephalomyopathic forms often carry a poor outlook with early mortality, whereas some myopathic forms are more slowly progressive, and outcome depends heavily on the specific genetic defect and organ involvement.

Mitral Regurgitation — MR Aortic stenosis (basally-radiating MR murmur from posterior leaflet prolapse/flail can be confused with AS) (p.2054) Mitral stenosis (a brief early-diastolic LA-LV gradient with rapid filling sound and mid-diastolic rumble in pure severe MR can masquerade as MS) (p.2053-2054) Ventricular septal defect and other causes of a holosystolic murmur Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) with Doppler to define mechanism and severity (jet width/area, regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction, effective regurgitant orifice area, LV volumes/EF, LA/LV size, chordal integrity, annular calcification) (p.2053) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) for greater anatomic detail (p.2053-2054) Estimation of pulmonary artery systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity (p.2053) Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess exercise capacity and dynamic change in MR severity, PA pressures, and biventricular function when clinical and resting findings disagree (p.2053) Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for quantitative regurgitant measures when TTE is discordant or insufficient (noted as not widely available) (p.2052-2053) ECG (LA enlargement, possible RA enlargement with pulmonary hypertension, AF, eccentric LVH) (p.2053) Chest X-ray (LA/LV enlargement, pulmonary venous congestion, Kerley B lines, mitral/annular calcification; asymmetric pulmonary edema possible in acute MR) (p.2053-2054) Left and right heart catheterization with contrast ventriculography and coronary angiography when noninvasive findings are discrepant or to identify coronary disease before surgery (p.2053, p.2056) Distinguish primary (degenerative) MR, where the leaflets and/or chordae are themselves abnormal, from secondary (functional) MR, where leaflets and chordae are usually normal and regurgitation is driven by LV/LA remodeling, annular dilation, papillary muscle displacement, dyssynchrony, or leaflet tethering; assessment, treatment, and prognosis differ significantly between the two (p.2052). The characteristic murmur of chronic severe MR is a holosystolic, plateau-configuration systolic murmur of at least grade III/VI, most prominent at the apex and radiating to the axilla (p.2053-2054). Murmur radiation reflects jet direction: with posterior leaflet prolapse/flail the eccentric anteriorly-directed jet strikes the LA wall near the aortic root and the murmur radiates to the base (can mimic aortic stenosis), whereas anterior leaflet prolapse/flail directs the jet and murmur toward the axilla (p.2054). Ruptured chordae tendineae may give the systolic murmur a cooing or 'seagull' quality; a flail leaflet may produce a musical murmur (p.2054). The murmur of chronic MR not due to MVP is intensified by isometric handgrip and reduced during the strain phase of Valsalva (decreased LV preload) (p.2054). In acute severe MR the murmur is early in timing and decrescendo, ending well before S2, reflecting the rapidly rising LA pressure and diminishing LV-LA gradient — in contrast to the holosystolic plateau murmur of chronic MR (p.2053-2054). Because EF rises in severe MR when LV function is normal, even a modest fall in EF (below 60%) reflects significant contractile dysfunction (p.2052-2053). Atrial fibrillation is almost invariably present once the LA dilates significantly in chronic severe MR; LA enlargement and AF support the diagnosis on ECG (p.2053). 'MR begets MR': LA enlargement tensions the posterior leaflet pulling it away from the orifice, and LV dilation increases regurgitation, enlarging LA and LV further in a vicious cycle (p.2052). With post-MI papillary muscle rupture the posteromedial papillary muscle is involved far more often than the anterolateral muscle because of its single blood supply (p.2052). Acute severe MR is a surgical emergency: papillary muscle rupture post-MI or leaflet destruction/perforation in infective endocarditis can cause sudden pulmonary edema and hemodynamic collapse, requiring urgent stabilization and emergent surgery (p.2052, p.2055-2056) Acute pulmonary edema, hypotension with narrow pulse pressure, and prominent signs of pulmonary congestion with a non-displaced apex point to acute severe MR (p.2053) Onset of palpitations or atrial fibrillation in chronic severe MR (p.2053) Late-onset right heart failure with hepatic congestion, ankle edema, distended neck veins, ascites, and secondary tricuspid regurgitation, indicating pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension (p.2053) Falling LVEF (to 60% or below) or rising LV end-systolic dimension (40 mm or more), even when asymptomatic, signals contractile dysfunction warranting surgical referral (p.2053, p.2056) In secondary MR the severity can be underappreciated by echocardiographic/Doppler techniques, and lesser degrees of regurgitation may carry relatively greater prognostic weight (p.2053). An S3 in MR may reflect rapid LV filling, but in ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy an S3 may instead signify ventricular dysfunction (p.2054). Because EF is artifactually elevated in severe MR with normal myocardium, a 'low-normal' EF may already represent meaningful contractile dysfunction (p.2052-2053). Routine surgical valve repair for significant secondary MR due to dilated cardiomyopathy has NOT been shown to improve long-term survival versus optimal guideline-directed medical therapy, especially in the era of quadruple HFrEF therapy (p.2056). Direct oral anticoagulants should NOT be used if moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis coexists, and are NOT approved for mechanical prosthetic valves (p.2055). A presystolic murmur is not ordinarily heard with isolated MR (p.2054). MR can arise from disease of any of the five components of the mitral apparatus: leaflets, annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and subjacent myocardium (p.2052). MR reduces resistance to LV emptying (lowers afterload); the LV decompresses into the LA during ejection, so initial compensation is more complete LV emptying. Over time LV volume rises as regurgitation worsens and contractile function deteriorates, and forward cardiac output falls; LV compliance is often increased so LV diastolic pressure does not rise until late (p.2052-2053). The regurgitant volume varies directly with LV systolic pressure and the size of the regurgitant orifice (influenced by LV and annular dilation and leaflet morphology). LA compliance governs the clinical picture: in acute severe MR the regurgitant volume enters a normal-sized, noncompliant LA so LA and pulmonary venous pressures rise sharply with a prominent v wave and pulmonary edema is common; in chronic severe MR the LA enlarges and becomes more compliant, buffering pressure so pulmonary congestion is initially less prominent and fatigue from low forward output predominates (p.2053). Chronic secondary MR results from annular dilation, ventricular remodeling, papillary muscle displacement, and leaflet tethering (e.g., after MI, in dilated cardiomyopathy once LV end-diastolic dimension reaches ~6 cm, or atrial functional MR from chronic AF with annular dilation) (p.2052). Chronic mild-to-moderate isolated MR is well tolerated and usually asymptomatic. Chronic severe MR tends to be progressive ('MR begets MR') and, when secondary, severity correlates inversely with prognosis, with adverse outcome tied to the degree of LV remodeling and myocardial dysfunction (p.2052-2053). With surgery, repair carries substantially lower risk than replacement; a 2023 STS database analysis reported mean perioperative mortality of about 1.16% (under 0.5% in patients younger than 65) for repair of primary MR, durable repair is feasible in up to 95% of degenerative cases at high-volume centers, and reoperation runs about 1% per year over the first 10 years. In ischemic MR with severely impaired LV function (EF below 30%), surgical risk is higher, recovery of LV performance is incomplete, and long-term survival is reduced (p.2055-2056). Chronic severe MR (Doppler/CMR quantitative criteria) is defined by a regurgitant volume of at least 60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction of at least 50%, and effective regurgitant orifice area of at least 0.40 cm2 (p.2053). ACC/AHA disease staging (Stages B, C1, C2, D) is applied: Stage C is asymptomatic severe MR (C1 normal LV systolic function with LVEF above 60% and ESD below 40 mm; C2 LV systolic dysfunction with LVEF at or below 60% or ESD at or above 40 mm) and Stage D is symptomatic severe MR (p.2054-2055).

Mitral Stenosis — MS Mitral regurgitation (may have an apical diastolic flow murmur, but it begins slightly later, S1 is soft or absent, and there is no opening snap; LV enlargement is common) (p.2049) Severe aortic regurgitation with an Austin Flint murmur (apical mid-diastolic murmur not intensified in presystole and softened by amyl nitrite/arterial vasodilators) (p.2049) Tricuspid stenosis (rare without MS; its diastolic murmur increases with inspiration and the jugular venous y descent is delayed) (p.2049-2050) Atrial septal defect (RV enlargement and increased pulmonary vascularity, but no LA enlargement or Kerley B lines, with fixed splitting of S2) (p.2050) Left atrial myxoma (obstructs LA emptying causing a positional diastolic murmur; often with systemic features such as weight loss, fever, anemia, emboli, elevated IgG/IL-6) (p.2050) Infective endocarditis with large vegetations is itself a recognized (uncommon) cause of left ventricular inflow obstruction mimicking MS (p.2048) Transthoracic echocardiography with color flow and spectral Doppler for mitral inflow velocities, peak/mean gradients, mitral orifice area, leaflet calcification and restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (p.2049) Transesophageal echocardiography when TTE is inadequate, and specifically to exclude left atrial thrombus before commissurotomy (p.2049) Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess mean mitral diastolic gradient, PA pressures, and RV function when clinical and resting hemodynamic findings are discrepant (p.2049) ECG showing left atrial enlargement (P-wave changes), and right axis deviation/RV hypertrophy when severe pulmonary hypertension supervenes (p.2049) Chest X-ray showing straightening of the left cardiac border, prominent main PAs, upper-lobe pulmonary venous dilation, an enlarged LA, and Kerley B lines when mean LA pressure exceeds about 20 mmHg (p.2049) Left and right heart catheterization when clinical and noninvasive findings are discrepant; CT coronary angiography to screen for coronary disease before valve surgery (p.2050) Congenital mitral valve stenosis (parachute valve, cor triatriatum) (p.2048) Severe mitral annular calcification with extension onto the leaflets (p.2048) Systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis involving the valve (p.2048) Left atrial myxoma (p.2048) Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis; pure or predominant MS occurs in roughly 40% of patients with rheumatic heart disease and a history of rheumatic fever (p.2048). Although declining in temperate, middle- to high-income climates, MS remains a major problem in low-income countries, especially sub-Saharan Africa, India, Southeast Asia, and Oceania (p.2048). Auscultation classically reveals an accentuated first heart sound (S1), an opening snap (OS) of the mitral valve heard best in expiration at or just medial to the apex, followed by a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur heard best at the apex in the left lateral recumbent position (p.2049). The A2-to-opening-snap interval varies inversely with severity of MS: a shorter interval indicates more severe stenosis (p.2049). In patients in sinus rhythm, the diastolic murmur often reappears or becomes louder during atrial systole (presystolic accentuation) (p.2049). Development of persistent atrial fibrillation often marks a turning point in the patient's course and is associated with acceleration of symptom progression (p.2048). Echocardiography (TTE with Doppler) provides mitral orifice area, transvalvular gradients, leaflet calcification/restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy; TEE is especially indicated to exclude LA thrombus before intervention (p.2049). Mitral valve area 1-1.5 cm2 denotes severe MS; an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg is needed to maintain normal cardiac output when the orifice falls below 1.5 cm2 (p.2048-2049). Atrial fibrillation, which accelerates symptom progression and markedly increases thromboembolic risk (p.2048) Systemic embolization (incidence 10-20%), more frequent with AF, age over 65, and reduced cardiac output; may be the presenting feature even in mild MS (p.2049) Hemoptysis from rupture of pulmonary-bronchial venous connections due to pulmonary venous hypertension (p.2048) Pulmonary hypertension and right-sided heart failure (hepatomegaly, ankle edema, ascites, pleural effusion) (p.2048-2049) Recurrent pulmonary emboli, sometimes with infarction, an important late cause of morbidity and mortality (p.2048) Decompensation precipitated by tachycardia, fever, severe anemia, paroxysmal AF, thyrotoxicosis, exertion, or pregnancy (p.2048) In pregnancy, increased blood volume, cardiac output, and tachycardia can raise the transmitral gradient and cause pulmonary edema or tachyarrhythmias, with the immediate postpartum period a time of particular concern due to rapid volume shifts (p.3900) When cardiac output is markedly reduced, the typical auscultatory findings including the diastolic rumble may be undetectable (silent MS) and may reappear only as compensation is restored (p.2049) Systemic embolization may be the presenting feature in otherwise asymptomatic patients with only mild MS (p.2049) The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation can be indistinguishable from aortic regurgitation, though it may increase with inspiration and is accompanied by a loud, often palpable P2 (p.2049) A history of rheumatic carditis is increasingly rare and often cannot be elicited (p.2048) In normal adults the mitral valve orifice area is 4-6 cm2. Significant obstruction occurs when the orifice is reduced to less than about 2 cm2, so blood can only flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle if propelled by an abnormally elevated left atrioventricular pressure gradient, the hemodynamic hallmark of MS. When the orifice is below 1.5 cm2 (severe MS), an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg is required to maintain normal cardiac output. Elevated pulmonary venous and PA wedge pressures reduce pulmonary compliance and cause exertional dyspnea. Because tachycardia shortens diastole proportionately more than systole, an increased heart rate (including rapid AF) augments the transvalvular gradient and further elevates LA pressure. Chronic LA pressure elevation leads to LA enlargement, predisposing to AF and to thrombus formation (particularly in the LA appendage) with risk of systemic embolization. Pulmonary hypertension develops from passive backward transmission of elevated LA pressure, reactive pulmonary arteriolar constriction (the so-called second stenosis), interstitial edema of small pulmonary vessels, and, at end stage, obliterative pulmonary vascular changes; severe pulmonary hypertension produces RV enlargement, secondary tricuspid and pulmonic regurgitation, and right-sided heart failure (p.2048-2049). In temperate climates the latent period between the initial attack of rheumatic carditis and symptomatic MS is generally about two decades, with disability typically beginning in the fourth decade. Historical studies before surgical valvotomy showed that once a patient became seriously symptomatic, the disease progressed inexorably to death within 2-5 years. Onset of persistent AF generally marks acceleration of symptom progression (p.2048). Severity is graded by mitral valve area. The normal orifice is 4-6 cm2; significant obstruction begins below about 2 cm2. A valve area below 1.5 cm2 is termed severe MS (with an LA pressure of about 25 mmHg required to maintain normal cardiac output), and an area below 1 cm2 is very severe, at which cardiac output is subnormal at rest. Echocardiographic measurement of mitral orifice area and transvalvular gradient is the basis for grading; commissurotomy is generally indicated for symptomatic patients with valve area below about 1 cm2/m2 body surface area or below 1.5 cm2 in normal-sized adults (p.2048-2051).

Mitral Valve Prolapse — MVP, Systolic click-murmur syndrome, Barlow's syndrome, Floppy-valve syndrome, Billowing mitral leaflet syndrome Other causes of primary mitral regurgitation Rheumatic mitral valve disease (chordae thickened but not fused in MVP, unlike rheumatic disease) Innocent or functional systolic murmurs Angina pectoris (when atypical chest pain is present) ECG (often normal; may show biphasic or inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF and supraventricular or ventricular premature beats) Transthoracic echocardiography to identify abnormal leaflet position and prolapse and define the >=2 mm displacement criterion Color flow and continuous-wave Doppler to assess associated MR and estimate severity Three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MRI for more precise LV volumes and detection of papillary muscle fibrosis/late gadolinium enhancement Transesophageal echocardiography when detailed anatomy is needed and for intraoperative or transcatheter procedural guidance Exercise testing (often with rest and immediate poststress TTE) to assess functional capacity, LV/RV function, dynamic MR, and pulmonary pressures Left ventriculography during catheterization (rarely necessary) MVP is a clinically variable syndrome arising from diverse pathologic mechanisms affecting the mitral valve apparatus, commonly excessive or redundant leaflet tissue associated with myxomatous degeneration and increased glycosaminoglycan concentrations (p.2057). It is the most common abnormality leading to primary mitral regurgitation and to mitral valve repair surgery, and in North America is now the most common cause of isolated severe MR requiring surgery (p.2057-2058). MVP is more common in women than men and typically presents between ages 15 and 30 with a generally benign course; in older patients (>50 years, often men) MR tends to be more severe because of chordal rupture (p.2058). The posterior leaflet is usually more affected than the anterior, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae tendineae frequently cause or contribute to regurgitation (p.2058). The hallmark auscultatory finding is a mid- or late nonejection systolic click occurring 0.14 s or more after S1, often followed by a high-pitched mid-late systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur best heard at the apex, sometimes described as whooping or honking (p.2058). Dynamic auscultation aids diagnosis: standing, the strain phase of Valsalva, and any maneuver decreasing LV volume make the click and murmur occur earlier, whereas squatting and isometric exercise (increasing LV volume) delay the click-murmur complex and may make it disappear (p.2058). Murmur radiation depends on the leaflet involved: posterior leaflet prolapse directs the jet anteriorly with radiation toward the base, while anterior leaflet involvement directs the jet posteriorly with radiation to the axilla and back (p.2058). A useful echocardiographic definition is systolic displacement of the belly of the mitral leaflets by at least 2 mm into the left atrium above the plane of the mitral annulus in the parasternal long-axis view (p.2058). Chest pain in MVP is often substernal, prolonged, and unrelated to exertion, and only rarely resembles angina pectoris (p.2058). Most patients are asymptomatic and remain so for life; the disease may progress slowly over years to decades or worsen abruptly from chordal rupture or endocarditis (p.2058). MVP can occur as a rare sequel to acute rheumatic fever, in ischemic heart disease, in various cardiomyopathies, and in about 20% of patients with ostium secundum atrial septal defect (p.2058). Severe MR with depressed LV systolic function (highest risk for sudden death) Flail leaflet, which carries an excess risk of sudden death and usually accompanies severe MR High-grade ventricular ectopy with inferior-apical T-wave abnormalities, high-density premature ventricular complexes at rest, mitral annular disjunction, and papillary muscle fibrosis on cardiac MRI Syncope or light-headedness from arrhythmias Transient ischemic attacks from emboli due to endothelial disruption on the valve Features suggesting infective endocarditis in patients with MR and/or leaflet thickening Relying on a static exam can miss MVP; the click and murmur are dynamic and shift with maneuvers that alter LV volume (Valsalva/standing exaggerate, squatting/isometrics diminish them). Presentations vary: some patients have a mid-systolic click without a murmur, others a murmur without a click, and still others both at different times. The eccentric MR jet typical of MVP makes effective regurgitant orifice area and regurgitant volume difficult to assess with standard techniques. Atypical, prolonged, non-exertional chest pain may be misattributed to coronary disease and is often difficult to evaluate. Sudden death and significant arrhythmias can occur even in patients with normal LV size and function, so apparently low-risk patients are not entirely without risk. MVP results from myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve apparatus with excessive or redundant leaflet tissue and markedly increased glycosaminoglycan content. In many cases the cause is unknown, but some forms are genetically determined; reduced type III collagen production has been implicated, and electron microscopy shows fragmentation of collagen fibrils. Genome-wide association work has identified multiple genetic loci (candidate genes include LMCD1, SPTBN1, LTBP2, TGFB2, NMB, and ALPK3), and associations with LMNA, FLNC, and FLNA that are often expressed as cardiomyopathies. The posterior leaflet is typically more affected, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured chordae contribute to regurgitation. Prolapse may impose excessive stress on the papillary muscles, producing localized ischemia, infarction, and replacement fibrosis that can serve as a nidus for ventricular arrhythmias (visible as late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI even without coronary disease). Chordal rupture along with progressive annular dilation and calcification worsen regurgitation, placing further stress on the diseased apparatus in a self-perpetuating cycle (p.2057-2058). The clinical course is most often benign, and the majority of patients remain asymptomatic for their entire lives. In many the condition progresses gradually over years to decades, while in others it worsens rapidly from chordal rupture or endocarditis. Sudden death is a very rare complication, occurring most often with severe MR and depressed LV systolic function but possible even with normal LV size and function; a small high-risk subset has high-grade ventricular ectopy with characteristic imaging features, and patients with a flail leaflet carry an excess sudden-death risk (p.2058). Severity is anchored on the associated mitral regurgitation, ranging from a benign isolated systolic click with mild posterior-leaflet prolapse to severe MR from chordal rupture and leaflet flail. Echocardiographic prolapse is defined as >=2 mm systolic displacement of the leaflet belly into the left atrium above the annular plane (parasternal long-axis), with Doppler used to grade MR severity (p.2058).

disease-modifying strategies that lower toxic nucleosides are handled in specialist centres Intestinal pseudo-obstruction or perforation from diverticular disease Severe malnutrition and cachexia requiring nutritional rescue Aspiration from dysphagia and gastroparesis Rapidly progressive neuropathy causing loss of ambulation Misdiagnosing the cachexia and gastrointestinal symptoms as an eating disorder or functional gut disorder Overlooking the diagnosis because the leukoencephalopathy is often clinically silent Attributing ophthalmoplegia to an isolated ocular myopathy rather than the systemic disease Not measuring plasma nucleosides, the most accessible and specific biochemical clue MNGIE is caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in TYMP, the gene encoding cytosolic thymidine phosphorylase. Without this enzyme, the pyrimidine nucleosides thymidine and deoxyuridine accumulate in blood and tissues. The resulting imbalance of the mitochondrial deoxyribonucleotide pool disturbs mitochondrial DNA replication, causing depletion, multiple deletions and point mutations and thereby a secondary failure of oxidative phosphorylation. The smooth muscle of the gut, peripheral nerves, extraocular muscles and cerebral white matter are particularly affected, producing the visceral myopathy and dysmotility, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and leukoencephalopathy that define the disorder. MNGIE is a progressive, life-limiting disorder; the relentless gastrointestinal dysmotility and cachexia are major contributors to morbidity and premature death, typically in early to mid adulthood without disease-modifying therapy.

the young comprises several monogenic disorders in which a mutation in a single gene critical to pancreatic beta-cell development or function impairs insulin secretion. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so an affected parent transmits the condition to roughly half of offspring, producing diabetes across successive generations at a young age. Unlike type 1 diabetes, there is no autoimmune beta-cell destruction, and unlike type 2 diabetes, obesity and insulin resistance are not central. deficiency by checking uric acid Molybdenum cofactor is a pterin-based cofactor synthesised through a multistep pathway (involving MOCS1, MOCS2 and gephyrin) that is essential for the activity of the molybdoenzymes sulphite oxidase, xanthine oxidase/dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase. When cofactor synthesis fails, all three enzymes are inactive. The most damaging consequence is loss of sulphite oxidase, which normally converts sulphite to sulphate in cysteine catabolism; sulphite accumulates and is directly neurotoxic, while S-sulphocysteine builds up and may act as an excitotoxin. Xanthine oxidase deficiency additionally causes low uric acid and elevated hypoxanthine and xanthine. The combined effect is severe, progressive neonatal brain injury with cystic encephalomalacia. The classic neonatal form is usually devastating, with profound neurodevelopmental impairment and early death. Type A (MOCS1) disease may respond to early substrate replacement therapy, so prognosis can improve markedly when treatment is started before irreversible brain injury; type B and other genetic forms currently lack specific treatment.

Multiplex assays combining NVO- and MPXV-specific targets, and clade-specific testing (U.S. Government and Public Health Laboratories), are available (Harrison 22e p.1519). Viral culture: orthopoxviruses grow well in standard clinical tissue culture; parapoxviruses are difficult to isolate (primary cells best); MCV cannot be cultured (Harrison 22e p.1519). Electron microscopy: characteristic large brick-shaped particles on negative stain for orthopoxvirus, yatapoxvirus, or MCV; parapoxviruses show an ovoid structure with crisscross spicules (Harrison 22e p.1519). Histopathology of biopsy: MCV shows classic Henderson-Patterson bodies (Harrison 22e p.1519). Serology can demonstrate orthopoxvirus reactivity but most assays cannot distinguish between orthopoxvirus species due to broad antigenic similarity (Harrison 22e p.1519). Classic mpox/smallpox prodrome: fever first, followed days later by rash; other prodromal features include malaise, sore throat, and headache (Harrison 22e p.1519). Lymphadenopathy is a key historical feature distinguishing mpox (present) from smallpox (absent) in endemic countries (Harrison 22e p.1519). Classic systemic orthopoxvirus rash evolves through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular phases (the pustular stage with central umbilication), each stage lasting 2-3 days, with lesions in the same anatomic location typically at the same stage of development (Harrison 22e p.1519). Classic distribution is diffuse, well-circumscribed, and centrifugal: lesions more prominent on face and extremities (including palms and soles) than on the trunk; lesions are painful as they emerge and become pruritic in later stages (Harrison 22e p.1519). In the 2022 clade IIb outbreak, transmission was primarily through close, intimate (e.g., sexual) contact and predominantly affected gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (MSM) (Harrison 22e p.1518). Clade IIb mpox often departed from the classic picture: rash was frequently the first or only sign (prodrome absent or concurrent), lesions were often localized to the anogenital region, smaller, fewer (often <10), and could be at different stages at the same anatomic site (Harrison 22e p.1519). Up to 50% of those diagnosed during the 2022 outbreak in the U.S. context were also living with HIV (Harrison 22e p.1518). Molluscum contagiosum (MCV) has a classic pearly appearance that may umbilicate as it matures, with little surrounding inflammation and painless lesions that persist for months but gradually regress over 6-12 months (Harrison 22e p.1519). The infectious period for orthopoxvirus infections lasts from symptom onset until all lesions have crusted, the crusts have separated, and fresh healthy skin has formed underneath; lesion scabs contain viable virus (Harrison 22e p.1518). Two distinct MPXV clades exist: Clade I (formerly Congo Basin, Central Africa) causes a higher proportion of severe disease than Clade II (formerly West African); Clade II subdivides into IIa (endemic West Africa) and IIb (spread worldwide in 2022) (Harrison 22e p.1517). Severe immunocompromise (advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, especially <50; organ transplantation) predisposes to severe, disseminated, prolonged mpox with numerous large coalescing or necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement (GI tract, liver, lungs, brain) (Harrison 22e p.1519). Ocular involvement: eye pain, redness, vision changes/loss, periorbital swelling, blepharitis, conjunctivitis, keratitis - can result in vision loss (Harrison 22e p.1519). Neurologic complications: encephalitis, myelitis - severe headache, neck pain, altered mentation, focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.1519). Myopericarditis: dyspnea or palpitations with elevated cardiac biomarkers and ECG changes (Harrison 22e p.1519). Mucosal complications affecting alimentation, urination, or defecation due to painful or obstructive lesions; may lead to strictures, edema, and severe lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1519). Most deaths have occurred predominantly among people with advanced HIV and CD4 <50 cells/mm3 (Harrison 22e p.1519). Do not assume a classic systemic presentation: during the 2022 clade IIb outbreak rash was often the first/only sign with prodrome absent, lesions localized to the anogenital area, smaller, fewer (<10), and could be at different stages at the same site - contrary to the classic rule that lesions in the same location are at the same stage (Harrison 22e p.1519). Anogenital mpox lesions can be mistaken for common STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis); up to 10% of mpox patients may be coinfected with an STI, so a positive STI test does not exclude mpox (Harrison 22e p.1519). Characteristic lesions plus exposure history narrow the differential, but laboratory testing is required to confirm the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1519). Distinguish mpox from varicella (VZV), herpes simplex, and syphilis - overlapping vesiculopustular/anogenital presentations are a recognized diagnostic trap (Harrison 22e p.1519). MCV cannot be cultured, so reliance on culture for diagnosis of molluscum is futile; biopsy (Henderson-Patterson bodies) or clinical/EM findings are needed (Harrison 22e p.1519). Poxviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that replicate entirely in the cytoplasm. Orthopoxvirus infection (variola, MPXV) is thought to involve systemic spread from the inoculation site to local lymph nodes, seeding of lymphoreticular tissue, and then symptomatic (febrile) viremia with viral skin tropism; disease severity reflects how well innate immune and interferon responses control early infection. Immunocompetent hosts develop lesions (often at the exposure site) about 1 week after exposure, progressing through staged phases over 7-14 days with scabbing and resolution by 14-21 days after rash onset. In severe immunocompromise (e.g., advanced HIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm3, organ transplantation), MPXV spread/growth goes unchecked, producing wide dissemination with large confluent lesions persisting for months and additional organ involvement. Most other poxvirus infections (e.g., parapoxviruses, MCV) involve only local viral growth at the inoculation site; yatapoxvirus (tanapox) pathogenesis is poorly understood (Harrison 22e p.1518). In immunocompetent hosts most poxvirus infections are self-limited, resolving in weeks (or months for molluscum contagiosum). Exceptions are the generalized orthopoxvirus infections caused by MPXV and variola, which carry higher case-fatality. In unvaccinated individuals smallpox mortality is up to 30%; MPXV mortality is approximately 1.4-10% (clade I), ~1% (clade IIa), and <1% (clade IIb). Immunocompromised hosts may have more severe orthopoxvirus and parapoxvirus disease (severe mpox, progressive vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum, severe borealpox) with higher mortality, or atypical presentations (e.g., giant orf). In advanced HIV, effective antiretroviral therapy is essential to favorable outcomes. MCV can be diffuse in the immunocompromised, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) has been associated with recrudescence of MCV. Poxvirus reinfections are seldom reported (Harrison 22e p.1521). Mpox ranges from typical self-limited disease (immunocompetent, including HIV with CD4 >200 cells/mm3, generally without increased severity) to severe mpox. Severe manifestations include ocular infection, neurologic complications (encephalitis, myelitis), myopericarditis, obstructive mucosal disease, and uncontrolled viral replication with disseminated/necrotic lesions and multi-organ involvement, occurring chiefly in severely immunocompromised patients (advanced HIV, organ transplantation). Clade I causes a higher proportion of severe disease than clade II (Harrison 22e p.1519).

settings Mononeuritis multiplex arises from multifocal damage to individual peripheral nerves, most classically through occlusion or inflammation of the vasa nervorum (nerve ischaemia) in systemic or non-systemic vasculitis. Ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles produces predominantly axonal loss in the territories supplied by affected vessels, explaining the patchy, asymmetric deficits. Other mechanisms include direct infiltration, compression at multiple sites, immune-mediated demyelination, and metabolic injury as in diabetes. The random distribution reflects the scattered nature of the underlying microvascular or infiltrative lesions. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and the speed of treatment; vasculitic cases can recover substantially if immunosuppression is started before extensive axonal infarction, but delayed treatment or severe systemic disease leaves persistent deficits.

options range from topical and phototherapy approaches to systemic immunomodulation in extensive or deep disease Physiotherapy and monitoring for joint contractures are important in linear and deep subtypes Distinguish morphea from systemic sclerosis clinically and, if needed, serologically, to avoid unnecessary alarm and inappropriate investigation Craniofacial linear morphea (en coup de sabre / Parry-Romberg) with neurological symptoms, seizures, or eye involvement Rapidly extending or deep lesions crossing joints and threatening contractures Growth disturbance or limb length discrepancy in affected children Extensive generalised disease causing functional impairment Diagnostic uncertainty where systemic sclerosis cannot be confidently excluded Confusing morphea with systemic sclerosis and triggering unnecessary anxiety or investigation Missing the active inflammatory (lilac ring) phase when treatment is most effective Underappreciating growth and contracture risk in paediatric linear disease Failing to screen for neurological and ocular involvement in craniofacial disease Assuming established sclerosis will respond to anti-inflammatory therapy Morphea is an immune-mediated fibrosing process in which an initial inflammatory phase, characterised by a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and endothelial activation, is followed by excessive deposition of collagen in the dermis and, in deeper subtypes, the subcutis and fascia. Dysregulated production of pro-fibrotic cytokines and growth factors drives fibroblasts to lay down dense, thickened collagen bundles, with loss of adnexal structures and normal fat. Vascular changes and, in some cases, autoimmune associations contribute. The result is progressive induration and, later, atrophy; when fibrosis extends across joints or affects growing tissues in children, functional and cosmetic sequelae follow. Many plaque-type lesions eventually become inactive over several years, leaving pigmentary change and atrophy, whereas linear and deep subtypes, particularly in children, carry a higher risk of lasting functional and cosmetic sequelae; early treatment of the inflammatory phase improves outcomes.

Morquio syndrome is caused by deficiency of enzymes needed to degrade keratan sulfate. In type A, biallelic GALNS variants cause deficiency of N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase; in type B, GLB1 variants cause deficiency of beta-galactosidase. The resulting block in keratan sulfate (and, in type A, also chondroitin-6-sulfate) degradation leads to lysosomal accumulation, which disproportionately affects cartilage and bone and produces the distinctive spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. Because keratan sulfate is concentrated in cartilage and cornea rather than the brain, intelligence is characteristically normal. Excess keratan sulfate is excreted in the urine, though levels can normalise with age. Both subtypes are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Intelligence is preserved and survival into adulthood is usual, but skeletal complications, especially cervical instability and restrictive respiratory disease, cause significant morbidity and can be life-threatening if unrecognised. Enzyme replacement therapy is available for type A and may improve endurance and some somatic features.

Morvan syndrome is an autoimmune disorder in which antibodies against the voltage-gated potassium channel complex, most often the CASPR2 protein, disrupt neuronal excitability. CASPR2 is expressed at juxtaparanodal regions of peripheral nerves and within limbic and thalamic circuits, so loss of its function produces both continuous peripheral motor nerve firing and central nervous system dysfunction. The result is peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with neuromyotonia, autonomic overactivity, and an encephalopathy dominated by intractable insomnia and fluctuating cognition. A subset is paraneoplastic, driven by thymoma, which sustains the aberrant immune response. With immunotherapy and removal of any associated tumour many patients improve substantially, but relapses occur and paraneoplastic cases carry the prognosis of the underlying malignancy. Autonomic instability can be life-threatening during the acute phase.

young patient with chorea, dystonia, parkinsonism or tremor) Drug-induced movements from dopamine-receptor blockers (tardive dyskinesia, acute dystonia) Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Hyperthyroidism (fine tremor; chorea rare) Movement disorders are classified as hypokinetic (poverty of movement, e.g. parkinsonism with rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia) versus hyperkinetic (excess movement, e.g. chorea, dystonia, tremor); the rest tremor and cogwheel rigidity of Parkinson's disease are extrapyramidal signs distinct from the action tremor of essential tremor (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. p.197 ch.31). Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor; a key pitfall is mislabeling it as Parkinson's disease, but Parkinson tremor is characteristically a rest tremor accompanied by cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia, whereas essential tremor lacks these and worsens with sustained posture or movement (Harrison 22e p.3508). Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant degenerative disorder producing the triad of chorea, psychiatric/behavioral disturbance (mood, anxiety, psychosis), and progressive dementia; the unpredictable choreic movements give the gait a characteristic dancing quality (Harrison 22e p.3508; gait described p.~3535 ch.32; HD as autosomal-dominant dementia p.198 ch.31). Dystonia is defined as sustained muscle contractions producing repetitive twisting movements and abnormal posture; it often has a genetic basis, but new asymmetric dystonia—particularly involving gait—in a younger adult may be an early sign of Parkinson's disease (Harrison 22e p.3508; cf. gait chapter p.~3535). Sydenham's chorea (a manifestation of acute rheumatic fever after group A streptococcal infection) is the prototypical post-infectious chorea: it occurs mainly in females after a prolonged latent period, affects especially the head (darting tongue movements) and upper limbs, may be generalized or hemichoreic, and is frequently accompanied by emotional lability or obsessive-compulsive traits; >50% of patients presenting with chorea have carditis, so echocardiography is warranted (Harrison 22e p.3508; ch. on rheumatic fever p.~2992). Tardive dyskinesia is a drug-induced hyperkinetic disorder seen with chronic exposure to antipsychotics and other agents that block the D2 dopamine receptor, and is a common cause of stereotypic movement and gait disturbances (Harrison 22e p.3508). New chorea, dystonia, tremor or parkinsonism in an adolescent or young adult — exclude Wilson's disease (treatable; look for Kayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper) before manifestations become irreversible Chorea with autosomal dominant family history plus psychiatric change and cognitive decline — consider Huntington's disease Acute chorea (especially in a young female) — evaluate for acute rheumatic fever and carditis with echocardiography Abnormal movements in a patient on long-term antipsychotics/D2 blockers — recognize tardive dyskinesia and acute dystonic reactions Misdiagnosing essential (action) tremor as Parkinson's disease, or vice versa — Parkinson tremor is a rest tremor with cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia Failing to test for Wilson's disease in a young patient with new movement disorder; Wilson's may present with chronic hepatitis long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear Overlooking carditis in a patient presenting with chorea (Sydenham's), since chorea may be the sole or delayed manifestation of rheumatic fever Not recognizing drug-induced/tardive movements from D2-blocking medications Movement disorders arise predominantly from dysfunction of the basal ganglia (striatum = caudate plus putamen) and their cortical and thalamic connections, which modulate motor output rather than directly generating it; disruption of these circuits yields either hypokinetic syndromes (parkinsonism) or hyperkinetic syndromes (chorea, dystonia, tremor). Huntington's disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat (autosomal dominant) with degeneration of the striatum. Wilson's disease results from impaired copper excretion with copper accumulation in liver and brain. Tardive dyskinesia reflects chronic blockade of striatal D2 dopamine receptors (Harrison 22e p.3508; basal ganglia/striatum anatomy p.~199-200 ch.31). Prognosis is disorder-specific. Essential tremor is typically slowly progressive and non-degenerative. Huntington's disease is relentlessly progressive and degenerative. Wilson's disease can improve substantially with prompt diagnosis and copper-chelating treatment before end-stage manifestations become irreversible. Sydenham's chorea is usually self-limited, with choreiform movements resolving within about 6 weeks, occasionally up to 6 months, though associated obsessive-compulsive or emotional symptoms may persist longer (Harrison 22e p.3508; Wilson p.~2713 ch.355; chorea p.~2992). No single unified severity scale spans all movement disorders; assessment is disorder-specific and functional. Chorea, for example, ranges from movements evident only on careful examination in mild cases to inability to perform activities of daily living in severe cases (Harrison 22e p.3508).

as hypospadias Failing to consider ZEB2 testing when the facial gestalt is present without overt bowel disease Mowat-Wilson syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of ZEB2, a transcription factor (also called SIP1) that represses target genes and is essential for the development and migration of neural crest cells and for central nervous system patterning. Loss-of-function point variants and whole-gene deletions reduce ZEB2 activity, disrupting neural crest derivatives, which explains the enteric nervous system defect underlying Hirschsprung disease as well as the craniofacial, cardiac and genitourinary malformations, together with the neurodevelopmental impairment from disturbed brain development. Individuals typically have severe intellectual disability with lifelong dependency but a characteristically cheerful temperament; survival into adulthood is common with appropriate management of bowel, cardiac and neurological complications. Enterocolitis and cardiac disease are the main threats to life.

completed strokes Ischaemic symptoms provoked by hyperventilation, especially in children Rapid clinical or angiographic progression Mistaking the arteriopathy for atherosclerosis and withholding revascularisation assessment Aggressive blood pressure lowering that compromises collateral-dependent perfusion Overlooking secondary causes when labelling the pattern as idiopathic disease Failing to protect against hypocapnia during anaesthesia, which can precipitate ischaemia Moyamoya disease is a chronic, progressive, non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory steno-occlusive arteriopathy of the distal internal carotid arteries and their proximal branches. Intimal thickening from smooth muscle cell proliferation and luminal narrowing reduce anterior circulation flow, prompting the growth of fragile lenticulostriate and leptomeningeal collateral networks that give the smoky angiographic appearance. These collaterals are prone to ischaemic failure and, being thin-walled and under haemodynamic stress, to rupture and haemorrhage. Genetic susceptibility, notably RNF213 variants, underlies many idiopathic cases. Untreated moyamoya tends to progress with recurrent ischaemic or haemorrhagic events and cumulative neurological deficit; surgical revascularisation can reduce stroke risk and stabilise the disease, though outcome depends on the stage at diagnosis.

disorder Not trialling mannose supplementation because the transferrin screen looks like PMM2-CDG Overlooking combined bleeding and thrombotic risk when planning procedures Attributing chronic diarrhoea and hypoalbuminaemia to a primary gut disease alone Missing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia as a treatable complication MPI-CDG is caused by deficiency of phosphomannose isomerase, which interconverts fructose-6-phosphate and mannose-6-phosphate. Because mannose-6-phosphate is the precursor for GDP-mannose and the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide used in N-glycosylation, enzyme deficiency limits mannose supply and impairs assembly of the lipid-linked glycan precursor, producing hypoglycosylation of serum and membrane glycoproteins similar to PMM2-CDG. The block lies upstream of the point where free mannose enters the pathway, so providing exogenous mannose (phosphorylated directly to mannose-6-phosphate by hexokinase) restores substrate and largely corrects glycosylation, explaining the disorder's responsiveness to dietary mannose. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the phenotype centres on the gut, liver and coagulation rather than the brain. With early recognition and dietary mannose supplementation the gastrointestinal and coagulation abnormalities often improve substantially and neurodevelopment is typically preserved, although hepatic fibrosis may progress and thrombotic risk persists.
