cord atrophy correlates more strongly) (p.3583) T1 imaging for 'black holes' (markers of irreversible demyelination and axonal loss) (p.3583) Visual, somatosensory, brainstem-auditory, and motor evoked potentials (p.3583-3584) Workup to exclude mimics in suspected MS: ESR, serum B12, antinuclear antibodies, and treponemal antibody (p.3585) NMOSD (anti-AQP4) and MOGAD - consider with bilateral/severe optic neuritis or severe transverse myelitis (p.3584) ADEM - consider with hyperacute or postinfectious presentation (p.3584) Tumefactive demyelination mimicking a primary or metastatic brain tumor (p.3584, 3589) Sarcoidosis, Sjogren's syndrome, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, vasculitis (p.3584-3585) Vitamin B12 deficiency, hereditary leukodystrophies, CADASIL, MELAS (p.3585) MS is defined by lesions disseminated in both time and space: plaques arise at different times and in anatomically separate CNS sites (p.3577). Typical onset is age 20-40 (slightly later in men); women are affected roughly three times as often as men (p.3577). The most common presenting symptoms are sensory loss (~37%) and optic neuritis (~36%), followed by limb weakness (~35%) and paresthesias (p.3577). Optic neuritis usually causes monocular reduced acuity, dimness, and color desaturation, with periorbital pain worsened by eye movement and an afferent pupillary defect; uveitis is uncommon and should prompt thought of sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577). A bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion) is particularly suggestive of MS; related gaze findings include horizontal gaze palsy and the 'one-and-a-half' syndrome (p.3578). Lhermitte's symptom is a neck-flexion-induced electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine/legs; it is not specific to MS and can occur with other cervical cord disease such as spondylosis (p.3578). Uhthoff's symptom (heat sensitivity) is transient worsening of neurologic symptoms with elevated core temperature (hot shower, exercise, fever) and reflects temperature-dependent conduction block rather than a true new lesion (p.3578). Exercise-induced weakness is characteristic; weakness is of upper-motor-neuron type with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, though a tendon reflex can occasionally be lost if a plaque disrupts the afferent reflex arc (p.3578). Paroxysmal symptoms (tonic spasms, paroxysmal dysarthria/ataxia, sensory bursts) are brief (10 s-2 min), frequent (5-40/day), without altered consciousness, and self-limited; they arise from spontaneous discharges at the edges of demyelinated plaques (p.3578). Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, or glossopharyngeal neuralgia in a young patient, or with bilateral/atypical features or objective sensory loss, should raise suspicion of MS involving the cranial nerve root entry zone (p.3578). Fatigue is experienced by most patients and is the leading cause of work-related disability in MS; depression affects about half of patients (p.3578). On MRI, MS plaques are oriented perpendicular to the ventricular surface (Dawson's fingers) reflecting perivenous demyelination; lesions >6 mm in the corpus callosum, periventricular white matter, brainstem, cerebellum, or cord are especially helpful diagnostically (p.3583). A central vein sign within plaques on susceptibility-weighted (T2*) imaging supports an MS diagnosis (p.3583). Two or more discrete CSF oligoclonal bands not present in paired serum are found in >90% of MS patients; bands may be absent at onset and increase over time (p.3583). Evoked potential abnormalities occur in 80-90% of MS patients; a marked latency delay (rather than reduced amplitude or distorted waveform) is what suggests demyelination, and EPs are most informative when testing a clinically uninvolved pathway (p.3583-3584). Most MRI-visible lesions and most early disease activity in MS are clinically silent—bursts of focal inflammation on serial MRI far exceed the relapse rate (p.3583). Even relapse-free RRMS patients undergo subtle 'silent progression,' and disability accumulation is now attributed mainly to progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) rather than incomplete recovery from relapses (RAW), across RRMS, SPMS, and PPMS (p.3578-3580). A radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) is incidental MRI evidence of MS in an asymptomatic person; clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is a first demyelinating event at high risk for MS (p.3577-3580). Distinguish a true relapse from a pseudoexacerbation driven by raised ambient temperature, fever, or infection - glucocorticoids are inappropriate for a pseudoexacerbation (p.3585). Features atypical for MS that should prompt an alternative diagnosis: symptoms confined to posterior fossa/craniocervical junction/spinal cord; onset <15 or >60 years; progressive course from onset; never any visual, sensory, or bladder symptoms; or atypical MRI/CSF/EP findings (p.3584). Symptoms rare/uncommon in MS that favor another diagnosis: aphasia, parkinsonism, chorea, isolated dementia, severe muscle atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, episodic loss of consciousness, fever, headache, seizures, or coma (p.3584). Bilateral and/or severe optic neuritis or severe transverse myelitis should raise NMOSD, MOGAD, or GFAP autoimmunity rather than MS (p.3584). Uveitis is uncommon in MS and should suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577). Intense inflammatory swelling can produce a mass lesion mimicking tumor (tumefactive MS), sometimes requiring brain biopsy (p.3584, 3589). Do not over-diagnose MS from a single isolated event or from MRI white-matter lesions alone - the diagnosis requires dissemination in space and time (clinical, MRI, or CSF evidence) per the McDonald criteria, and there is no single confirmatory test (p.3582-3583). A pseudoexacerbation from heat/fever/infection (Uhthoff phenomenon) can mimic a relapse but reflects transient conduction block, not a new lesion; treating it as a relapse with steroids is inappropriate (p.3578, 3585). Failing to distinguish NMOSD, MOGAD, and GFAP autoimmunity from MS - clues are bilateral/severe optic neuritis, severe longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 vertebral segments), brain MRI lesions that are non-destructive/cloud-like and can fully resolve, and CSF pleocytosis greater than in MS with neutrophils/eosinophils and oligoclonal bands in <20% (p.3584, 3590). ADEM should be considered for hyperacute or postinfectious demyelinating presentations rather than assuming a first MS attack (p.3584). MS-associated genetic variants (including HLA-DRB1*1501) lack the sensitivity and specificity to be used for diagnosis (p.3581). Highly restricted CNS oligoclonal antibodies are characteristic of MS but their specific antigenic targets differ between patients and their pathogenic role is uncertain - they aid diagnosis, not mechanistic certainty (p.3581). Lhermitte's symptom and trigeminal neuralgia are not specific to MS and occur with other cervical cord/cranial nerve pathology (p.3578). MS is an autoimmune CNS disease producing chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (sclerotic plaques) and neuronal/axonal loss (p.3577). New lesions begin with perivenular cuffing by T cells and macrophages and blood-brain-barrier (BBB) disruption with a preserved vessel wall (unlike vasculitis); cytotoxic CD8 cells line the leading edge, B cells infiltrate, myelin-specific autoantibodies coat degenerating myelin, and complement is activated (p.3581). Sharply demarcated demyelination is the hallmark; axons are relatively spared early but can be destroyed in highly inflammatory lesions, and partial remyelination produces 'shadow plaques' (p.3581). Cumulative axonal/neuronal loss drives irreversible disability (up to ~70% of corticospinal axons lost in MS paraplegia) via demyelination-related loss of trophic support, ion-channel redistribution, and dying-back axonopathy (p.3581). Progressive MS features more diffuse microglial activation, chronic active (slowly expanding) plaques with microglia at a leading edge behind an intact BBB, cortical/subpial plaques poorly seen on MRI, and meningeal ectopic lymphoid follicles linked to subpial cortical demyelination (p.3581-3582). Physiologically, demyelination causes conduction block (hyperpolarization from exposed potassium channels) and conduction slowing; temperature and metabolic changes worsen block, explaining heat- and fever-related fluctuations (p.3582-3583). Susceptibility is polygenic with the strongest signal at HLA-DRB1*1501 (~10% of risk), and EBV seroconversion appears a near-universal prerequisite, plausibly via molecular mimicry between EBV peptides and myelin autoantigens (p.3580-3581). The clinical course is highly variable. RRMS accounts for ~90% of cases with attacks evolving over days to weeks and substantial early recovery; PPMS (~10%) declines steadily from onset, begins later (mean ~40 years), has a more even sex ratio, and accrues disability faster (p.3578-3580). In the pretreatment era, by 15 years after onset only ~20% had no functional limitation and one-third to one-half of relapsing patients had progressed to SPMS needing ambulatory assistance, with ~80% reaching that level by 25 years; the prior RRMS-to-SPMS conversion rate of ~3%/year has fallen to <1%/year in the high-efficacy-therapy era (p.3579, 3588). Favorable prognostic features (pretreatment data): optic neuritis or sensory onset, fewer than two relapses in the first year, and minimal impairment at 5 years; adverse predictors: older onset age, male sex, greater disability, and motor signs in the first year. About <10% have a benign variant that never produces disability even untreated (p.3588). Pregnancy: fewer attacks during gestation (especially the third trimester) but more in the first 3 months postpartum, with the overall pregnancy-year course unchanged (p.3588). Course-based subtypes: relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS, ~90%), secondary progressive MS (SPMS, always evolves from RRMS), and primary progressive MS (PPMS, ~10%); 'relapsing MS (RMS)' covers all relapsing patients and 'active progressive MS' denotes SPMS/PPMS with ongoing relapses or new MRI lesions (p.3578-3579). Neurologic impairment is graded with the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), 0 (normal) to 10 (death), built from Functional Status (FS) subscores; EDSS <3.5 generally indicates normal walking and little disability, whereas EDSS >4.0 indicates gait-impaired progressive (SPMS/PPMS) disease. An EDSS >=4 plus a motor FS score >=2 supports an SPMS diagnosis (p.3579-3580, 3585). Fulminant clinical variants include Marburg's (acute fulminant) MS, tumefactive MS, and Balo's concentric sclerosis (p.3589).

Mucopolysaccharidosis — MPS, mucopolysaccharidoses, glycosaminoglycan storage disorders Other lysosomal storage disorders such as the oligosaccharidoses and mucolipidoses GM1 gangliosidosis with coarse features and skeletal changes Skeletal dysplasias from other causes Congenital hypothyroidism with coarse features Multiple sulfatase deficiency Urinary glycosaminoglycan quantification and electrophoresis as a screening step Specific lysosomal enzyme assays to identify the subtype Molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and guide counselling Skeletal survey to demonstrate dysostosis multiplex and assess spine stability Echocardiography, audiology, ophthalmology, and airway assessment for multisystem involvement A group of lysosomal storage disorders caused by deficiency of specific enzymes needed to degrade glycosaminoglycans (mucopolysaccharides), leading to their accumulation in tissues and excretion in urine Most subtypes are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner; the notable exception is MPS II (Hunter syndrome), which is X-linked recessive Shared features across many subtypes include coarse facial features, short stature, joint stiffness or contractures, hepatosplenomegaly, and dysostosis multiplex on radiographs Corneal clouding is prominent in several subtypes (for example MPS I and MPS VI) but characteristically absent in MPS II and in the neuronopathic MPS III Neurocognitive decline is a major feature of severe MPS I, MPS II, and especially MPS III (Sanfilippo), whereas MPS IV (Morquio) primarily affects the skeleton with preserved intellect Cardiac valve disease, airway narrowing, hearing loss, and carpal tunnel syndrome are common and progressive complications Cervical spine instability and cord compression are important risks, particularly in Morquio syndrome Enzyme replacement therapy exists for several subtypes, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can benefit selected patients, most notably severe MPS I when performed early Signs of cervical spine instability or spinal cord compression Progressive airway obstruction or obstructive sleep apnoea Cardiac valve disease or heart failure Rapid neurocognitive regression in neuronopathic subtypes Missing early disease because features can be subtle in infancy and evolve over time Overlooking cervical spine risk before anaesthesia or intubation Assuming enzyme replacement will reverse neurological or advanced skeletal disease Not recognising the X-linked inheritance of MPS II when counselling families The mucopolysaccharidoses arise from deficiency of one of the lysosomal enzymes required for the stepwise degradation of glycosaminoglycans such as dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, keratan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate. Incomplete breakdown leads to progressive accumulation of partially degraded glycosaminoglycans within lysosomes across many tissues, including connective tissue, cartilage, bone, cornea, heart valves, airways, and the central nervous system. This storage produces the progressive, multisystem, and often neurodegenerative phenotypes. The specific enzyme deficiency and the glycosaminoglycans that accumulate determine the clinical subtype. Prognosis varies widely by subtype and severity. Severe neuronopathic forms progress to early disability and death, while attenuated forms are compatible with longer survival. Enzyme replacement and, for selected patients, stem cell transplantation can slow somatic disease, but established skeletal and neurological damage is often irreversible and does not fully respond to enzyme therapy.

Mucormycosis — zygomycosis, rhinocerebral mucormycosis Aspergillosis Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium species) Fusariosis (Fusarium species) Dematiaceous (brown-pigmented) mold infections Entomophthoromycosis (Basidiobolus and Conidiobolus) Bacterial orbital cellulitis / cavernous sinus thrombosis (Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, gram-negative species) Rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) Tolosa-Hunt syndrome Aspergillosis (septate mold, may co-infect with Mucorales) Scedosporiosis Fusariosis Dematiaceous mold infection Entomophthoromycosis (Basidiobolus, Conidiobolus) Bacterial orbital cellulitis / cavernous sinus thrombosis (S. aureus, streptococci, gram-negatives) Rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) Biopsy with histopathologic examination (most sensitive/specific; PAS or H&E staining) Culture from a sterile site (needle aspirate, tissue biopsy, pleural fluid) for definitive species identification; tissue sectioned NOT homogenized, incubated at both room temperature and 37C CT of the chest (best method to define extent of pulmonary disease; may detect infection before chest x-ray) MRI of head/sinuses (more sensitive ~80% than CT for orbital and CNS extension) Endoscopy and/or surgical exploration with biopsy of suspected areas; blind biopsy of normal-appearing sinus tissue when suspicion is high Mucorales-specific PCR (useful but no FDA-approved assay) Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (painful ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, headache, cavernous sinus inflammation; lacks progression) Mucormycosis is a group of life-threatening infections caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (subphylum Mucoromycotina); it is highly invasive and relentlessly progressive, with morbidity/mortality higher than many other infections (Harrison 22e p.1717). Rhizopus oryzae and R. delemar (family Mucoraceae) are by far the most common causes in the Western Hemisphere; Apophysomyces elegans is a notable cause in India and Mucor irregularis in China (Harrison 22e p.1718). Five well-defined clinical syndromes: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, and disseminated; specific host defects predispose to specific syndromes (diabetes/DKA to rhino-orbital-cerebral; leukemia/HSCT to pulmonary) (Harrison 22e p.1718). Rhino-orbital-cerebral disease is the most common form worldwide; early symptoms are nonspecific (eye/facial pain, facial numbness) progressing to conjunctival suffusion, blurry vision, proptosis, and chemosis (Harrison 22e p.1718-1719). Biopsy with histopathology is the most sensitive and specific modality: wide (>=6-30 microm), thick-walled, ribbon-like, ASEPTATE hyphae branching at RIGHT angles, in contrast to thinner, septate, acute-angle-branching Aspergillus/Fusarium/Scedosporium (Harrison 22e p.1719). Mucorales are best visualized with periodic acid-Schiff or H&E; methenamine silver may NOT stain them optimally (Harrison 22e p.1719). Tissue for culture should be cut into sections and placed in the center of culture media, NOT homogenized, because homogenization kills the long filamentous hyphae and lowers culture yield; the lab should be alerted when mucormycosis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1720). It is important to distinguish mucormycosis from aspergillosis because treatments differ: polyenes for Mucorales versus expanded-spectrum triazoles for most septate molds; voriconazole is the first-line treatment for aspergillosis but EXACERBATES mucormycosis in animal models (Harrison 22e p.1719-1720). Rhino-orbital-cerebral involvement with a black necrotic eschar and/or painful necrotic ulceration of the hard palate (late finding indicating extensive, well-established angioinvasive infection) is a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement. Bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and ophthalmoplegia (contralateral eye involvement) suggest cavernous sinus thrombosis and are ominous. Hyperglycemia or DKA with sinusitis and possible orbital extension, even without a known diabetes history, should raise high suspicion (presentation may be the first recognition of diabetes, often unmasked by recent glucocorticoids). Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous mucormycosis (mortality approaching 80%) and necrotic skin lesions from hematogenous dissemination. Disseminated disease (most lethal form), seen with antifungal prophylaxis breakthrough and in highly immunocompromised patients. Misperception that mucormycosis is always rapidly progressive; rate of progression is in fact highly variable (days to a year or more). Cultures are positive in fewer than half of cases, and up to half of cases are diagnosed only at autopsy; a negative culture does NOT exclude the diagnosis. Standard tissue homogenization for culture kills the filamentous Mucorales and lowers yield; tissue must be sectioned and not homogenized, and the lab alerted. Imaging underestimates disease: sinus CT may look like ordinary bacterial sinusitis, and bony erosion into the orbit is rarely seen on CT even when clinically present. Treating with voriconazole (first-line for aspergillosis) can exacerbate mucormycosis; distinguish the two molds because preferred treatments differ, and consider dual infection in highly compromised patients. Delaying treatment of the underlying malignancy until mucormycosis is 'cured' is a common error; antifungals provide only a holding action until near-normal immunity is restored, and untreated underlying disease is the typical primary driver of death. Iron administration and liberal blood transfusion (free iron from hemolysis) should be avoided as iron exacerbates infection. Therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic confirmation: when suspicion is reasonable, empirical lipid polyene therapy should be started early because earlier polyene therapy improves survival. Mucorales are ubiquitous environmental fungi to which humans are constantly exposed; they cause invasive, angioinvasive infection primarily in hosts with uncontrolled diabetes, phagocytic defects (neutropenia or high-dose corticosteroids), and/or elevated free iron, which supports fungal growth in serum and tissue. Iron-overloaded end-stage renal failure patients treated with the iron chelator deferoxamine had high risk of rapidly fatal disseminated disease, because deferoxamine acts as a fungal xenosiderophore that delivers iron directly to the Mucorales. In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), acidosis dissociates iron from sequestering proteins (enhancing fungal survival/virulence) and the ketoacid beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates host and fungal receptors that increase fungal adherence and tissue penetration; however the majority of diabetic patients with mucormycosis are NOT acidotic on presentation. Even without acidosis, hyperglycemia raises risk via hyperglycation of iron-sequestering proteins, upregulation of the host receptor GRP78 (which binds Mucorales and enables tissue penetration), poorly characterized phagocytic defects, and enhanced expression of the Mucorales-specific invasin CotH (which binds GRP78). Blood vessel thrombosis and tissue necrosis impair antifungal penetration to the site of infection. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1718) Overall mortality remains high though it has declined with earlier initiation of effective antifungal therapy; outcome is often driven by progression of the underlying predisposing condition. Necrotizing fasciitis from cutaneous disease carries mortality approaching 80%, gastrointestinal disease progressing to perforation has extremely high mortality, and widely disseminated disease exceeds 90% mortality. In contrast, isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous mucormycosis treated with prompt aggressive surgical debridement has a favorable prognosis and low mortality. Rate of progression is highly variable (days to a year or more), not invariably rapid. (Harrison 22e p.1717-1720) Harrison classifies mucormycosis by clinical syndrome rather than a numeric severity score: rhino-orbital-cerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous (ranging from isolated nonnecrotizing cutaneous disease with favorable prognosis to necrotizing fasciitis), gastrointestinal, and disseminated/miscellaneous disease, with mortality rising steeply from localized cutaneous disease to disseminated disease (>90%). (Harrison 22e p.1718-1720)

antibodies are negative Failing to search adequately for conduction block outside common entrapment sites Multifocal motor neuropathy is an immune-mediated disorder of motor axons in which antibodies, frequently against the GM1 ganglioside enriched at the node of Ranvier, disrupt nodal sodium-channel clusters and paranodal architecture. This produces persistent focal conduction block along motor fibres while sensory fibres are spared, generating the pattern of weakness confined to individual nerve territories without sensory loss. Over time some axonal degeneration occurs, but the primary and treatment-responsive abnormality is the focal motor conduction block, which explains both the clinical picture and the benefit from immunoglobulin therapy. Many patients maintain function with regular intravenous immunoglobulin, though the disorder is usually chronic and requires ongoing treatment; progressive axonal loss can cause slowly accumulating disability over years.

a dominant or suspicious nodule should be sampled by fine-needle aspiration to exclude malignancy Thyroid function tests and, where autonomy is suspected, a radionuclide uptake scan help distinguish hot (autonomous) from cold nodules Surgical management is usually total or near-total thyroidectomy for compressive symptoms, cosmetic concern, suspected malignancy, or toxicity not controlled medically Sudden painful enlargement of a single nodule often represents haemorrhage into a cyst rather than malignant change Stridor, orthopnoea, or acute airway compromise from tracheal compression Rapid enlargement, fixation, hoarseness, or cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting malignancy Symptoms of severe thyrotoxicosis or impending thyroid storm in a toxic goitre Superior vena cava obstruction features from a large retrosternal goitre Assuming all nodular goitres are benign and omitting cytology of a dominant or suspicious nodule Overlooking retrosternal extension and airway narrowing before anaesthesia Failing to render a toxic goitre biochemically controlled before surgery, risking perioperative thyrotoxic crisis Not documenting preoperative vocal cord status, obscuring the cause of any postoperative hoarseness Missing postoperative hypocalcaemia or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after total thyroidectomy A multinodular goitre develops through cycles of thyroid follicular hyperplasia and involution, driven by relative iodine deficiency, fluctuating TSH stimulation, and heterogeneous growth responses among follicular cells. Over time the gland becomes structurally heterogeneous, with colloid nodules, cystic degeneration, haemorrhage, fibrosis, and calcification. Some clones of cells acquire autonomous function independent of TSH, which can lead to subclinical or overt hyperthyroidism (toxic multinodular goitre). Progressive enlargement, particularly with retrosternal growth, can compress the trachea and oesophagus and displace or narrow the airway. The outlook is generally good; benign euthyroid goitres often remain stable or are cured by thyroidectomy, and toxic goitres respond to definitive treatment. Recurrence can occur after subtotal resection, and lifelong thyroid hormone replacement is expected after total thyroidectomy.

treatment also includes fasting avoidance, glucose during crises and carnitine Neonatal hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with severe acidosis and cardiomyopathy Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy during an acute crisis Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and risk of renal failure Cardiac arrhythmia or heart failure from lipid accumulation Rapid decompensation with fasting or intercurrent illness Mistaking the multiple acylcarnitine elevations for an isolated fatty acid oxidation defect Not trialling riboflavin in a myopathic or ETFDH-related case Allowing fasting for procedures or illness without a glucose-based emergency plan Overlooking cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia in the acute setting Failing to monitor for rhabdomyolysis and renal compromise in late-onset disease MADD results from deficiency of electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF) or ETF-ubiquinone oxidoreductase (ETF dehydrogenase), which shuttle electrons from numerous mitochondrial flavin-adenine-dinucleotide-dependent dehydrogenases into the respiratory chain. Because these carriers serve the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of fatty acid beta-oxidation as well as several dehydrogenases of amino acid catabolism, a single defect simultaneously impairs oxidation of fatty acids of all chain lengths, and of glutaryl-, isovaleryl- and sarcosine-related substrates. The consequence during fasting or catabolic stress is failure of fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and energy deficiency, with accumulation of glutaric and dicarboxylic acids and secondary hyperammonaemia. ETFDH variants that destabilise the flavoprotein can be stabilised by riboflavin (the FAD precursor), which underlies the riboflavin-responsive phenotype. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The severe neonatal form, especially with congenital anomalies, carries a poor prognosis with high early mortality; late-onset disease is often milder and many riboflavin-responsive patients improve markedly, though relapses can occur with catabolic stress.

Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease — Multivalvular heart disease, Mixed valve disease, Combined valvular heart disease Patent ductus arteriosus (continuous murmur mimicking combined AS and AR systolic-diastolic murmurs) Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (continuous murmur, often after acute chest pain) Isolated single-valve lesion with falsely overestimated or underestimated severity due to a masked second lesion Pulmonary hypertension or right-sided valve disease underlying ECG signs of right heart abnormality in a left-sided valve lesion Transthoracic echocardiography as the principal modality, assessing valve morphology and function, calcification, chamber size, wall thickness, biventricular function, estimated PA systolic pressure, and great-vessel dimensions Transesophageal echocardiography for more accurate valve (especially mitral) assessment and when infective endocarditis is suspected Exercise testing with or without echocardiography when symptoms exceed resting TTE findings Cardiac MR for additional anatomic and physiologic data when echocardiography is suboptimal (less suited to valve morphology) Cardiac CT for intracardiac structures in complicated IE and for planning transcatheter valve implantation; coronary CT angiography as a noninvasive coronary assessment Right and left heart catheterization to characterize individual lesion contributions, measure PA pressures, and calculate pulmonary vascular resistance, strongly recommended when clinical and noninvasive findings are discrepant in a symptomatic patient ECG for ventricular hypertrophy/atrial enlargement and right-sided signs; chest x-ray for chamber enlargement, valve/annular calcification, pulmonary vascular changes (Kerley B lines, enlarged azygos vein indicating RA hypertension) Patent ductus arteriosus Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm Multiple acquired and congenital lesions can produce stenosis and/or regurgitation across one or more valves; rheumatic disease classically affects mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves alone or in combination. In multivalvular disease, derangements from the more proximal valve lesion can mask the full hemodynamic expression of a more distal lesion. Reduced cardiac output from mitral valve disease lowers transaortic flow and can lead to underestimation of the severity of a coexisting aortic lesion. Functional tricuspid regurgitation accompanying significant mitral valve disease is one of the most common forms of multivalve disease; the tricuspid leaflets are morphologically normal and TR arises from right ventricular and annular dilation. Onset of atrial fibrillation can be especially deleterious in rheumatic mitral plus aortic disease: loss of atrial systole can critically reduce cardiac output and raise left atrial and LV diastolic pressures. When AR or MR is the dominant lesion in mixed aortic or mitral disease, the LV is dilated; when AS or MS predominates, LV chamber size is normal or small. Secondary (functional) MR complicating severe AS reflects altered LV geometry and systolic leaflet tethering with normal leaflets and chordae; it may improve after relief of afterload with valve replacement. Persistent significant secondary MR after aortic valve replacement is associated with impaired functional outcomes and reduced survival. Severe mitral annular calcification can cause both regurgitation (reduced systolic annular shortening) and mild-to-moderate stenosis (calcium extending onto the leaflets restricting opening). An early ejection click, typical of bicuspid aortic valve in young adults, is often absent in congenital mixed AS and AR. Patients with multiple or mixed valve disease may become symptomatic earlier than those with isolated single-valve lesions, sometimes even with only moderate individual lesions. Palpitations suggesting AF can flag clinically unsuspected mitral valve disease as an important component of the presentation. Abrupt development of acute aortic regurgitation (e.g., from IE or paravalvular leak after AVR/TAVI) in a noncompliant, nondilated, hypertrophied LV, causing rapid rise in diastolic pressure and severe heart failure New atrial fibrillation in moderate mitral disease precipitating heart failure when severe aortic disease coexists Significant paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter AVR (risk factor for short- to intermediate-term death) Symptoms of right heart failure (abdominal fullness/bloating, edema, ascites) signaling advanced disease ECG or chest x-ray signs of pulmonary hypertension or RA hypertension in a patient with left-sided valve disease The Gorlin formula is inaccurate in mixed aortic valve disease because augmented transvalvular flow from AR inflates the gradient relative to true orifice size. Doppler-derived LV-aortic gradients and systolic murmur intensity overestimate true valve orifice severity in mixed AS/AR with preserved LV function. A high mitral E-wave velocity in severe MR may be misread as indicating significant MS contribution to LA hypertension. Low cardiac output from a proximal lesion (or AF) can mask the true severity of a more distal aortic or tricuspid lesion, leading to underestimation. A mid-systolic outflow murmur is common in significant AR even without valve sclerosis/stenosis, so other signs of AS must be sought rather than assuming combined disease. Combined aortic and mitral valve replacement carries significantly higher perioperative mortality than single-valve surgery, so the decision must be made carefully. In multivalvular heart disease the hemodynamic effects of a proximal valve lesion can mask those of a more distal lesion. With combined rheumatic mitral and aortic disease, the reduced cardiac output imposed by mitral disease lessens the apparent severity of the aortic lesion, while AF arising during mitral stenosis can abruptly worsen previously silent aortic disease. Reactive pulmonary vascular disease acts as a secondary obstructive lesion in series, and as cardiac output falls with progressive tricuspid disease, associated mitral or aortic disease may be underestimated. Functional TR follows right ventricular and annular dilation with morphologically normal leaflets, producing large systolic c-v waves in the RA pressure pulse whose height depends on RA compliance and regurgitant volume; advanced chronic severe TR ventricularizes the RA waveform. In MS with concomitant AR, enhanced LV filling raises diastolic pressure depending on chamber compliance. Secondary MR in severe AS arises from LV remodeling and leaflet tethering under high systolic pressures. In mixed AS/AR, augmented transvalvular systolic velocities inflate the Doppler gradient and murmur intensity relative to true orifice size, and the Gorlin formula is inaccurate. In mixed mitral disease, the elevated mitral E-wave velocity in severe MR may not reflect any contribution of associated MS to LA hypertension. Noncompliant, nondilated, concentrically hypertrophied ventricles (as in significant AS, radiation heart disease, cardiac amyloid, or obesity/diabetes cardiomyopathy) tolerate acute volume loads poorly, so sudden AR causes rapid rise in LV diastolic pressure and severe heart failure. Natural history is usually driven by the dominant valve lesion; for moderate mixed AS/AR in which stenosis dominates, the course tends to parallel isolated severe AS. Patients with multiple or mixed disease may develop limiting symptoms or physiologic impairment even with only moderate lesions. Persistent significant secondary MR after AVR carries worse functional outcomes and survival, and significant paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter AVR is a notable risk factor for short- to intermediate-term death. No discrete severity grading scheme for combined disease; severity is determined by an integrated clinical and noninvasive assessment that identifies the dominant lesion, whose grading and management recommendations are then applied, with attention to lesion severity, ventricular remodeling, functional capacity, and PA pressures.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) — MEN1, MEN2, MEN syndromes Germline RET mutation testing in all patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma, with cascade screening of relatives (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). MEN1 (menin) gene testing in patients with the parathyroid/pancreatic-islet/pituitary tumor pattern or relevant family history (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.376). Biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism in RET-mutation carriers identified as at risk for MEN2 (Harrison 22e p.3079). Other familial pituitary tumor / endocrine neoplasia syndromes: MEN 4 (CDKN1B mutation; hyperparathyroidism and pituitary adenomas), Carney complex (PRKAR1A; spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, endocrine tumors), McCune-Albright syndrome, and familial isolated pituitary adenomas (AIP) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392). Other inherited predispositions to pheochromocytoma that overlap with MEN2: von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis, and hereditary paraganglioma syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.247). MEN1 is characterized primarily by the triad of parathyroid, pancreatic islet, and pituitary tumors (the '3 Ps'); it is an autosomal dominant syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.388). MEN2 predisposes to medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3079). There are three familial forms of MTC: MEN 2A, MEN 2B, and familial MTC without other features of MEN; MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than in MEN 2A, and familial MTC is more aggressive than sporadic MTC (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). MEN1 is caused by inactivating germline mutations of the MEN1 (menin) tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13; about half of affected patients develop prolactinomas, while acromegaly and Cushing's disease are less common (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392). MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations of the RET protooncogene (a receptor tyrosine kinase) in a single allele, in contrast to the tumor-suppressor loss-of-function mechanism of MEN1 (Harrison 22e p.3079). Early genetic screening for RET mutations identifies individuals at risk for MEN2 who may benefit from prophylactic thyroidectomy and biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3079). All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations, because genetic counseling and cascade testing of family members can then be offered to those who test positive (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). Exclude pheochromocytoma BEFORE any surgery: prior to surgery, pheochromocytoma should be excluded in all patients with a RET mutation (failure to do so risks an intraoperative hypertensive crisis) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). MTC in the context of MEN 2B carries a more aggressive course than MEN 2A and warrants early/prophylactic intervention (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). Proceeding to surgery (e.g., thyroidectomy or parathyroid surgery) without first excluding an unsuspected pheochromocytoma in a RET-mutation carrier (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). Failing to perform RET testing in all MTC patients and thereby missing cascade screening opportunities for at-risk family members (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). MEN1 follows the two-hit tumor-suppressor paradigm: the affected individual inherits a mutant copy of the MEN1 gene (menin, chromosome 11q13), and tumorigenesis follows a somatic 'second hit' (deletion or point mutation) that inactivates the remaining normal allele. In contrast, MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations in a single allele of the RET protooncogene, encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase; constitutive RET activity leads to thyroid C-cell hyperplasia in childhood that precedes the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.388/ch.397). Prognosis is driven by the component tumors and genotype. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than in MEN 2A, and familial MTC is more aggressive than sporadic MTC; early genetic identification permits prophylactic thyroidectomy before malignant transformation, improving outcome (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397).

nuclear protein acting as a tumour suppressor involved in transcriptional regulation and genome stability. Affected individuals inherit one defective allele, and tumours arise when the remaining functional allele is lost within an endocrine cell, consistent with a two-hit mechanism. Loss of menin function removes a brake on proliferation in susceptible endocrine tissues, giving rise to hyperplasia and multiple, often synchronous or metachronous, neoplasms across the parathyroids, pancreatic islets and pituitary. The multiglandular and recurrent nature of disease reflects this germline predisposition throughout the endocrine system. Prognosis depends largely on pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, which are the leading disease-related cause of death, so structured lifelong surveillance and timely intervention are central to improving long-term outcomes.

buccal swab is the best specimen Viral culture Mumps-specific IgM serology (note: often undetectable, transient, or delayed in vaccinated patients, and can give false positives from cross-reactions) Paired acute- and convalescent-phase IgG for a fourfold rise (IgG testing generally not recommended, as titers may already be elevated in vaccinated/previously infected patients) Serum amylase and lipase (both elevated suggests pancreatitis in addition to parotitis) Sarcoidosis Sjogren's syndrome Mikulicz's syndrome Parinaud's oculoglandular syndrome Uremia Diabetes mellitus Malnutrition / laundry starch ingestion / cirrhosis Drug-induced parotid swelling Salivary ductal obstruction, cysts, or tumors Testicular torsion (mimicking orchitis) Acute, self-limited systemic viral illness typically characterized by parotitis or other salivary gland swelling; suspect in any patient with parotitis or mumps complications regardless of age, vaccination status, or travel history (p.1646). Parotitis is generally bilateral but may not be synchronous on both sides; unilateral involvement occurs in about one-third of cases, with tenderness and obliteration of the space between the earlobe and angle of the mandible (p.1647). Parotitis is often preceded by a several-day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, and anorexia; it typically lasts ~5 days (range 3-7) with most cases resolving within 10 days (p.1647). Infection is asymptomatic in ~20% of unvaccinated patients; it can also present as nonspecific respiratory symptoms (p.1647). Fully vaccinated persons can still contract mumps, but are at lower risk for mumps and for mumps complications (p.1647). Buccal swabs are the best specimens for virus detection; the parotid gland should be massaged for 30 s before collection, and specimens collected as close to parotitis onset as possible (maximal shedding within 5 days of symptom onset) (p.1649). Complications can occur in the absence of parotitis and are more common in adults than children and in males than females (largely due to orchitis) (p.1648). Orchitis (most common complication; up to 30% of unvaccinated and 6% of vaccinated postpubertal males) with possible testicular atrophy and temporary subfertility Aseptic meningitis (up to 10% of unvaccinated, <=1% of vaccinated patients) Encephalitis (<=1% of patients; high fever, altered consciousness, seizures, focal neurologic signs; mortality ~1.5%) Sensorineural hearing loss / deafness (usually sudden, unilateral, transient; bilateral and permanent loss are rare) Oophoritis (~7% unvaccinated, <=1% vaccinated postpubertal women) Pancreatitis (~4% unvaccinated, <1% vaccinated) Supraglottic edema (rare, life-threatening) from obstructed lymphatic drainage Other CNS complications: cerebellar ataxia, facial palsy, transverse myelitis, hydrocephalus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, flaccid paralysis Myocarditis and endocardial fibroelastosis (rare but potentially severe) A negative virologic or serologic result does NOT rule out mumps in a person with clinical signs, especially in vaccinated patients (p.1649). Failure to detect mumps IgM is very common in vaccinated patients (IgM response often undetectable, transient, or delayed); IgM can also yield false positives from cross-reactions (p.1649). Presence of parotitis, orchitis, or oophoritis supports a mumps diagnosis but their absence does NOT exclude it; complications can occur without parotitis (p.1648). A positive IgG titer indicates only prior exposure (vaccination or natural infection) and does NOT predict protection; IgG titers should NOT be used to infer immunity in close contacts since they may instead reflect acute infection (p.1649). Elevated serum amylase can arise from parotitis OR pancreatitis; lipase is needed to distinguish (p.1648). Mumps reinfection and recurrent infection can occur and may be more common than previously thought (p.1648). MMR vaccine has NOT been shown to prevent illness or alter severity in persons already infected and is NOT recommended as postexposure prophylaxis; mumps immune globulin is also NOT recommended for postexposure prophylaxis or treatment (p.1649). Caused by mumps virus, a single-stranded negative-sense enveloped RNA paramyxovirus (Rubulavirus genus, Paramyxoviridae); there is only one serotype (p.1646). Humans are the only known natural reservoir; transmission is via direct contact with respiratory droplets or saliva of an infected person. Incubation averages 16-18 days (range 12-25). A person is most infectious from 2 days before until 5 days after onset of parotitis (virus detected in saliva as early as 7 days before to as late as 9 days after onset) (p.1647). Primary replication likely occurs in the nasal/upper respiratory mucosal epithelium, with spread to regional lymph nodes and infection of mononuclear cells facilitating viremia lasting ~3-5 days. Viremia produces acute inflammatory reactions most commonly in the salivary glands (parotitis) and testes (orchitis), with dissemination also to kidneys, CNS, pancreas, heart, ovaries, mammary glands, cochlear perilymph, and (in pregnancy) the fetus. Mumps encephalitis in many cases appears to be a para- or postinfectious demyelinating process rather than direct viral cytotoxicity, though rare primary encephalitis with viral isolation from brain tissue does occur (p.1647-1648). Generally a benign, self-resolving illness; death due to mumps is exceedingly rare (p.1648). Aseptic meningitis is self-limited without significant risk of death or long-term sequelae. Encephalitis carries a mortality of ~1.5%, may leave permanent sequelae, and has poorer outcomes in adults than children. Orchitis can cause testicular atrophy in ~30-50% of affected testicles and temporary sterility/subfertility, but no studies have assessed the risk of permanent infertility. Mumps-related hearing loss is usually transient; bilateral permanent loss is rare. Mumps in pregnancy is generally benign and no more severe than in non-pregnant women, and evidence for an association with increased spontaneous abortion or fetal death is inconclusive (p.1648). No formal severity classification in the source. Spectrum ranges from asymptomatic infection (~20% of unvaccinated) through classic self-limited parotitis to complicated disease (orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis); subclinical CNS involvement (CSF pleocytosis) occurs in up to 55% of patients.

autoantibody panels (including anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, anti-GAD for stiff-person syndrome) Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy mimicking limb-girdle dystrophy clinically and histopathologically (screen for anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP antibodies) Sarcoid granulomatous infiltration or amyloid deposition producing muscle enlargement Focal myositis or fasciitis Hepatic disease wrongly inferred from muscle-derived transaminase/aldolase/LDH elevations Thyrotoxic hyperreflexia with fasciculations mimicking amyotrophic lateral sclerosis Diabetic muscle infarction presenting as acute painful indurated thigh/calf swelling Most myopathies cause persistent, symmetric, proximal (limb-girdle) weakness with preserved reflexes and intact sensation; associated sensory loss instead points toward a peripheral neuropathy or CNS (myelopathy) process rather than primary muscle disease. The pattern of muscle involvement is the single most useful clue for narrowing the differential: facial weakness with scapular winging suggests FSHD, facial/distal weakness with grip myotonia is virtually diagnostic of myotonic dystrophy type 1, ptosis/ophthalmoparesis suggests oculopharyngeal dystrophy or mitochondrial myopathy, and asymmetric flexor-forearm plus quadriceps weakness suggests inclusion body myositis. Creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive marker of muscle damage; the MM isoenzyme predominates in skeletal muscle while CK-MB marks cardiac muscle. CK can be elevated in healthy people after strenuous activity, trauma, prolonged cramp, or seizure. Elevated AST, ALT, aldolase, and LDH can originate from muscle and be misattributed to liver disease; a normal gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) helps confirm a muscle (rather than hepatic) source because GGT is not present in muscle. The Gower sign (using the arms to climb up the legs to rise from the floor) and a waddling or hyperlordotic toe-walking gait reflect proximal hip, thigh, and trunk weakness. Calf enlargement in many limb-girdle dystrophies represents true muscle hypertrophy that stays strong late in the disease, so the term 'pseudohypertrophy' is best avoided; by contrast, early medial gastrocnemius atrophy characterizes Miyoshi myopathy (dysferlin/anoctamin-5). Cardiac and ventilatory muscle involvement are the leading causes of mortality across the dystrophies, so cardiology follow-up, ECG monitoring, and surveillance for respiratory insufficiency are central to care. Genetic testing is the gold standard for hereditary myopathies, but next-generation panels can miss large deletions/duplications and intronic mutations and frequently return variants of uncertain significance; muscle imaging (MRI/ultrasound) can support a specific diagnosis by showing characteristic involvement patterns. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is multisystem: hatchet facies, frontal balding, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction block, insulin resistance, gonadal atrophy, hypersomnia, and cognitive impairment; congenital DM1 occurs almost exclusively in infants of affected mothers. Episodic weakness beginning after age 25 is almost never due to a periodic paralysis, with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis being the notable exception (favoring men of Asian descent despite higher thyrotoxicosis rates in women). In McArdle disease, a slow warm-up or brief rest produces a 'second-wind' phenomenon as the muscle shifts to fatty acid utilization; the forearm exercise test shows a blunted venous lactate rise with a normal ammonia rise. Ragged red fibers and cytochrome-oxidase (COX)-negative fibers on muscle biopsy, often with elevated serum lactate, FGF-21, and GDF-15, point toward a mitochondrial myopathy. Cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular/complete heart block, atrial standstill) in EDMD and myotonic dystrophy carrying risk of sudden death Dilated cardiomyopathy or heart failure in DMD/BMD, LGMD, and myofibrillar myopathies Ventilatory/diaphragmatic muscle weakness causing respiratory insufficiency (may be the presenting feature in adult Pompe disease and LGMD) Myoglobinuria with CK rising to over 100 times normal, signaling rhabdomyolysis Life-threatening hypokalemia-related arrhythmias during hypokalemic periodic paralysis attacks; potentially serious long-QT and ventricular arrhythmias in Andersen-Tawil syndrome Dysphagia with aspiration risk in oculopharyngeal dystrophy/OPDM and myotonic dystrophy Complete heart block and cardiac arrest in Kearns-Sayre syndrome; stroke-like episodes in MELAS Attributing isolated fatigue to primary muscle disease: fatigue without abnormal clinical or laboratory findings almost never indicates a myopathy, and asthenia must be distinguished from true pathologic fatigability. Misreading muscle-derived transaminase/aldolase/LDH elevations as liver disease; checking GGT clarifies the source. Diagnosing myositis in FSHD when biopsy shows an inflammatory infiltrate, leading to incorrect immunosuppressive treatment. Overlooking immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (a treatable autoimmune cause) in apparent LGMD without an identified pathogenic mutation; antibody screening is warranted. Calling calf enlargement 'pseudohypertrophy' when it is true hypertrophy in many LGMDs. Assuming hyperkalemia in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis; patients are often normokalemic during attacks, and the disorder is defined by precipitation with potassium loading. Misattributing exertional cramps: cramps follow short intense bursts in glycolytic defects, whereas CPT2-deficiency pain appears only after prolonged exercise once muscle breakdown has begun. Preferring muscle biopsy over imaging in suspected diabetic muscle infarction, where hemorrhage into the biopsy site can occur. Relying solely on next-generation sequencing panels, which can miss large deletions/duplications and intronic mutations and may yield variants of uncertain significance. Myopathies reflect structural or functional impairment intrinsic to muscle, distinguishing them from anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, and neuromuscular junction disorders. In the dystrophies, the molecular defect lies in proteins linking the sarcolemma to the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix: dystrophin (DMD/BMD) connects the actin cytoskeleton through the dystroglycan complex to the matrix, and mutations in sarcoglycans, dysferlin, calpain-3, anoctamin-5, glycosylation enzymes of alpha-dystroglycan, and sarcomeric/Z-disk and nuclear-envelope proteins underlie the limb-girdle, distal, and Emery-Dreifuss phenotypes. Nuclear-membrane protein defects (emerin, lamin A/C, nesprin-1/2, LUMA) destabilize the inner nuclear envelope and cause EDMD with prominent contractures and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Myotonic dystrophies arise from non-coding repeat expansions (CTG in DMPK for DM1, CCTG in CNBP for DM2) acting through a toxic RNA gain of function: mutant RNA forms nuclear inclusions that sequester splicing regulators, causing widespread aberrant splicing and the multisystem phenotype, with anticipation as repeat length grows across generations. FSHD results from hypomethylation at 4q35 (contracted D4Z4 repeats in FSHD1; SMCHD1/DNMT3B/LRIF1 mutations in FSHD2) that permits toxic expression of the DUX4 transcription factor. Energy-metabolism disorders impair glycolysis (e.g., myophosphorylase/McArdle), glycogen handling (acid maltase/Pompe), or fatty-acid transport into mitochondria via carnitine palmitoyltransferase, producing either exertional cramping with rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria or progressive weakness. Mitochondrial myopathies stem from maternally inherited mtDNA point mutations or deletions, or nuclear-gene defects of mtDNA maintenance/replication, impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Channelopathies of the sarcolemma (calcium CACNA1S, sodium SCN4A, potassium Kir2.1, chloride CLCN1) disturb membrane excitability to produce periodic paralysis and/or myotonia. Endocrine and toxic myopathies act through hormonal or pharmacologic injury, often producing fiber atrophy rather than destruction. The dystrophies generally follow a slowly progressive course, though severity varies between and within subtypes. Life expectancy is reduced in DMD and BMD, with most BMD patients surviving into the fourth or fifth decade; death is often attributable to associated cardiomyopathy. FSHD usually spares the heart, but about 20% of patients progress to pelvic-girdle involvement and possible wheelchair dependence. In Kearns-Sayre syndrome, death from heart block occurs in roughly 20% of patients, underscoring the value of cardiac surveillance and prophylactic pacing for conduction defects. MELAS in full expression can lead to dementia, a bedridden state, and a fatal outcome. Most endocrine myopathies respond to treatment of the underlying disorder. For many hereditary myopathies no specific disease-modifying therapy exists, and care centers on preserving function and managing cardiac and respiratory complications. No single unifying grading system; severity is assessed disease-specifically. Functional milestones (Gower sign, gait pattern, ambulatory status, wheelchair dependence) and manual muscle testing (e.g., biopsy is best taken from a muscle around grade 4/5) gauge weakness. Mortality risk is stratified by cardiac (conduction disease, cardiomyopathy) and respiratory (ventilatory insufficiency) involvement. In rhabdomyolysis, CK over 100 times normal accompanies myoglobinuria, and for statin myotoxicity, marked CK elevation (more than 3 to 5 times baseline) with severe myalgia, weakness, or myoglobinuria is an indication to stop the drug.

gastrointestinal surveillance for duodenal disease MUTYH encodes a DNA glycosylase that is part of the base-excision-repair system responsible for correcting the mutagenic effects of oxidative DNA damage. When both alleles carry loss-of-function variants, the enzyme can no longer remove adenines misincorporated opposite the oxidised guanine lesion 8-oxoguanine, so characteristic G-to-T transversions accumulate. These mutations preferentially strike growth-regulatory genes such as APC and KRAS, driving adenoma formation through the same adenoma-carcinoma sequence seen in other colorectal polyposis syndromes. With regular colonoscopic surveillance and polypectomy the colorectal cancer risk can be substantially reduced, and prognosis is favourable when disease is detected early. Because risk persists lifelong and extends to the duodenum, ongoing surveillance and, where required, surgical management remain important.

Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/ Chronic Fatigue Syndrome — ME/CFS, Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, Myalgic Encephalomyelitis, CFS, ME Broad differential of fatigue (medical and psychiatric causes evaluated per chronic fatigue workup) Thyroid dysfunction (e.g., hypothyroidism) Anemia / iron deficiency or iron overload Celiac disease Depression and anxiety disorders Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and other dysautonomia Idiopathic chronic fatigue (unexplained chronic fatigue not meeting full ME/CFS criteria) Postinfectious fatiguing illness following Epstein-Barr virus Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) postinfectious fatigue Ross River virus infection Post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (Long COVID) with prolonged fatiguing illness Giardia-associated postinfectious fatigue Complete blood count Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein Electrolytes, fasting glucose, calcium, phosphate Renal function tests (blood urea nitrogen, glomerular filtration rate) Liver function panel (bilirubin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, total protein, albumin/globulin ratio) Thyroid function tests (TSH, free thyroxine) Iron studies to assess both deficiency and overload (serum iron, transferrin saturation, ferritin) Celiac disease screening tests Urinalysis Lean/standing (orthostatic) test for POTS Mental health assessment screening for depression and anxiety Fibromyalgia Hypothyroidism and other endocrine disorders Depression and other psychiatric conditions presenting with fatigue Anemia Celiac disease Sjogren's syndrome ME/CFS is a chronic, complex, multisystem illness whose functional impact on daily functioning has been compared to that of multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and congestive heart failure. The defining feature is persistent, unexplained fatigue causing substantial functional impairment, together with postexertional malaise (PEM) - worsening of symptoms after physical, mental, or emotional exertion that would not have been a problem before the illness. PEM relapses last longer than a day and can persist for weeks; the relationship between a relapse and the preceding activity is often not apparent to the patient, so PEM may go unrecognized. Common accompanying symptoms include pain, cognitive dysfunction (patient-described 'brain fog'), unrefreshing sleep, headache, sore throat, tender lymph nodes, muscle and joint aches, feverishness, and orthostatic intolerance. There is no diagnostic test; diagnosis rests on a characteristic profile of patient-reported symptoms, requiring evaluation by an experienced clinician. The 2015 Institute of Medicine criteria require substantial activity reduction with profound new-onset fatigue not relieved by rest, plus PEM, plus unrefreshing sleep, plus either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance. Routine laboratory tests are typically within normal limits in ME/CFS; their value lies in identifying alternative or contributing illnesses rather than confirming the diagnosis. Roughly 10% of patients remain ill for 6 months or more after a variety of infections (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus, Ross River virus, Q fever, Ebola, SARS-CoV-1, Giardia); recovery is otherwise the rule. Recognition of ME/CFS as a diagnosable component of Long COVID has increased clinical awareness, but patients still encounter stigma and misunderstanding from clinicians. An estimated 80% or more of people who meet ME/CFS criteria have never been diagnosed by a health care provider. Patients are reported to be more medication-sensitive than the general population, so any drug should begin at lower-than-usual doses and be increased slowly. Patients may appear well during an office visit and then relapse afterward from the exertion of attending the consultation. Continued decline in function (should prompt evaluation for another illness rather than being attributed to ME/CFS) New, worsening, or unusual symptoms warranting further workup for a new illness Serious depression and increased suicide risk associated with social isolation and loss of hope Severe disease leaving the patient essentially homebound Trivializing the illness or dismissing patients, contributing to stigma and underdiagnosis (most who meet criteria are never diagnosed). Failing to recognize PEM because patients do not connect relapses to preceding exertion, and may appear well in clinic only to crash afterward. Attributing a continued functional decline to ME/CFS rather than investigating an alternative diagnosis. Standard-dose medication initiation in patients who are unusually drug-sensitive, increasing toxicity risk. Encouraging overexertion on 'good days' that leads to the 'push and crash' cycle and negates functional gains. Relying on laboratory tests for diagnosis - results are usually normal and serve only to exclude other conditions. ME/CFS is understood as a complex disorder involving alterations across multiple interrelated homeostatic systems rather than a single mechanism. A wide range of infectious agents (viral and nonviral) can trigger a postinfectious fatiguing illness resembling ME/CFS, and noninfectious stressors - toxins, physical trauma, adverse life events, and cumulative allostatic load ('wear and tear') - are also associated. Twin and family studies suggest contributions from shared environment and genetic factors. Evidence for immunologic dysfunction is inconsistent and not established in most patients; reported findings include modest antinuclear antibody elevations, reduced immunoglobulin subclasses, impaired mitogen-driven lymphocyte proliferation, decreased natural killer cell activity, altered cytokine production, and altered T-cell metabolism. A hypothesis that excess cytokines such as interleukin-1 or interferon-alpha drive the fatigue and flulike symptoms lacks compelling supporting data. Other inconsistent and nondiagnostic findings include nonspecific regional brain MRI changes, autonomic nervous system dysfunction, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis abnormalities, altered metabolism, and gut microbiome dysbiosis. Unifying multisystem models integrate infection, immune, central and autonomic nervous system, metabolic, genetic, lifestyle, and stress factors. Severity ranges from mild or moderate (retaining varying degrees of pre-illness function) to severe (essentially homebound). Most patients experience some improvement and stabilize, but a return to the prior level of function is unusual. A continued functional decline is atypical and should trigger evaluation for other illnesses. Because of social isolation and loss of hope, serious depression and an increased risk of suicide are reported, warranting active screening and referral. Severity is described clinically as mild/moderate (patients retain varying degrees of pre-illness function) versus severe (patients essentially homebound). Diagnostically, the 2015 IOM criteria require substantial activity reduction lasting more than 6 months with profound new-onset fatigue not relieved by rest, plus postexertional malaise, plus unrefreshing sleep, plus either cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance, with symptoms present at least half the time and of at least moderate intensity.

Ocular and eyelid muscles are commonly involved early; diplopia and ptosis are frequent initial symptoms, and facial weakness can produce a 'snarling' expression on attempted smiling (Harrison 22e p.3626). Bulbar involvement causes nasal/dysarthric 'mushy' speech, dysphagia with nasal regurgitation or aspiration, and chewing weakness; neck extensor weakness can cause head drop (Harrison 22e p.3626). If weakness stays confined to ocular muscles for 3 years, later generalization is unlikely (ocular MG), though rare patients generalize beyond 5 years (Harrison 22e p.3626). Bulbar, neck, and ventilatory weakness can be especially prominent in MuSK antibody-positive MG (Harrison 22e p.3626). Ice-pack test: applying ice over a ptotic eye for 2 min produces a lid rise of 2 mm or more (positive) when ptosis is due to an NMJ defect; it is a quick, very sensitive bedside test (Harrison 22e p.3626-3627). Approximately 10-15% of MG patients have a thymoma, so chest CT or MRI to evaluate the thymus is performed at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3628). Myasthenic crisis: ventilatory weakness requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation, managed in intensive care (treat respiratory infection, attend to fluids); requires rescue therapy with IVIg or plasmapheresis (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3628-3629). Dysphagia with nasal regurgitation or aspiration of liquids/food (bulbar involvement) (Harrison 22e p.3626). Enlargement of the thymus in a patient older than 40 years is highly suspicious for thymoma (Harrison 22e p.3628). Infection or tapering of MG therapy can precipitate myasthenic exacerbation or crisis (Harrison 22e p.3626). ICI-related MG with concurrent myocarditis carries a high fatality rate in fulminant disease (Harrison 22e p.3627). A negative anti-AChR antibody test does not exclude MG, and the antibody level does not correlate well with disease severity (Harrison 22e p.3627). Distinguish LEMS from MG: LEMS is presynaptic (P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies), preferentially affects proximal lower-limb muscles, typically spares prominent ocular/bulbar onset, and shows depressed/absent reflexes plus autonomic features (dry mouth, orthostasis, impotence); unlike MG, strength and CMAP amplitude increase (incremental response) after brief exercise or high-rate (20-50 Hz) stimulation. In older adults LEMS is associated with malignancy, most commonly small-cell lung cancer (Harrison 22e p.3628). Anti-striated muscle (titin) antibodies are not pathogenic and do not confirm MG or a thymoma (Harrison 22e p.3627). Aminoglycoside, quinolone, and macrolide antibiotics, IV magnesium, procainamide, and penicillamine can exacerbate myasthenic weakness; botulinum toxin injections should be avoided in MG patients (Harrison 22e p.3627). Anti-MuSK MG generally responds less to anticholinesterase agents (and may worsen) and does not respond to complement inhibition because MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and do not activate complement (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3628-3629). Diagnosis must be confirmed definitively before treatment because other treatable conditions mimic MG and treatment carries surgical/drug risks (Harrison 22e p.3626). MG is an autoimmune NMJ disorder in which the number of available postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) is reduced and the postsynaptic folds are flattened ('simplified'), decreasing the efficiency of neuromuscular transmission so that normally released ACh produces small end-plate potentials that may fail to trigger muscle action potentials. Anti-AChR antibodies (IgG, T-cell dependent) act by three mechanisms: accelerated AChR turnover via cross-linking and endocytosis, complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, and blockade of the ACh-binding site. Anti-MuSK antibodies (IgG4, do not activate complement) impair MuSK-LRP4 interaction and AChR clustering; anti-LRP4 antibodies (IgG1) cause complement-mediated destruction. The normal decline in ACh release on repeated activity (presynaptic rundown) combined with reduced transmission efficiency produces myasthenic fatigue and the decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation. The thymus is abnormal in ~75% of AChR antibody-positive patients (~65% hyperplastic, ~10% thymoma) (Harrison 22e p.3624-3626). Prognosis has improved strikingly with modern treatment, and nearly all myasthenic patients can be returned to full productive lives with proper therapy. The course is variable, with exacerbations and remissions, particularly in the first 1-3 years; in ~85% of patients weakness becomes generalized. A cure remains elusive (Harrison 22e p.3625-3628). Weakness is classified as ocular versus generalized (the latter affecting facial, bulbar, axial, or limb muscles in ~85% of patients). Worsening requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation defines myasthenic crisis; all other worsening is termed exacerbation. Standardized measures referenced include the Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MGADL) and Quantitative MG (QMG) scores (Harrison 22e p.3626, p.3631).

Thyroid function tests, antinuclear antibodies, and rheumatoid factor to detect associated/exacerbating conditions; testing for tuberculosis, fasting glucose/HbA1c, and bone densitometry before immunotherapy (p.3630). MRI of the brain/orbits to exclude intracranial lesions in ocular or cranial presentations (p.3627-3628). Cholinergic crisis from excessive anticholinesterase medication can mimic worsening MG; it is considered in the differential but is unlikely now because very high cholinesterase-inhibitor doses are rarely used (p.3632). ICI-associated myositis can clinically resemble MG (prominent or exclusive ocular weakness) but lacks a decrementing response on repetitive nerve stimulation (p.3633). Myasthenic crisis is an exacerbation of weakness severe enough to endanger life, typically with ventilatory failure from diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle weakness; by definition, ventilatory weakness requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation constitutes crisis, whereas lesser worsening is termed exacerbation (p.3625, 3632). Weakness is characteristically fatigable: it worsens with repeated use and late in the day and improves with rest or sleep, and strength can improve with serial effort (contrast with LEMS) (p.3625). Cranial muscles are often involved early, with diplopia and ptosis common initial symptoms; facial weakness gives a 'snarling' expression on attempted smile, and bulbar involvement causes nasal/'mushy' dysarthria, hoarseness, and dysphagia with risk of nasal regurgitation or aspiration (p.3625). Bulbar, neck, and ventilatory weakness can be especially prominent in MuSK antibody-positive MG; neck extensor weakness can cause head drop (p.3625). Deep tendon reflexes are typically preserved and sensory symptoms, sensory loss, and pain are absent in MG (p.3625). Anti-AChR antibodies are present in ~85% of generalized MG and ~50% of ocular MG; a positive test is virtually diagnostic, but a negative test does not exclude MG, and antibody level does not correlate well with severity (p.3627). About 10% of MG patients (~40% of AChR-negative generalized MG) have anti-MuSK antibodies, and 1-3% have anti-LRP4; ~10% of generalized MG is double-seronegative (p.3625, 3627). The ice-pack test (ice over a ptotic lid for 2 min, positive if lid rises >=2 mm) is a quick, very sensitive bedside test for an NMJ cause of ptosis (p.3627). Edrophonium (anticholinesterase) testing was historically used for diagnosis but is no longer used due to side effects and lack of availability (p.3627). Thymic abnormality occurs in ~75% of AChR-positive patients; thymoma is present in ~10-15% of MG patients, so chest CT/MRI is performed at diagnosis (thymic enlargement in a patient >40 years is highly suspicious for thymoma) (p.3625, 3630). Ventilatory failure from diaphragmatic/intercostal weakness is the life-threatening feature defining crisis; need for intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation marks the transition from exacerbation to crisis (p.3625, 3632). Intercurrent infection is the most common cause of crisis and must be treated immediately, as the patient's mechanical and immunologic defenses are compromised; fever with early infection should be managed as in an immunocompromised patient (p.3632). Exposure to drugs that exacerbate weakness (e.g., aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers, magnesium, procainamide, quinine derivatives, neuromuscular blocking agents) can precipitate or worsen crisis (p.3633). Tapering of MG therapies, unrelated infections, systemic disorders, or surgery can precipitate exacerbation or crisis; some exacerbations have no identifiable precipitant (p.3625). Prominent bulbar/neck weakness (notably in MuSK-positive MG) signals aspiration and airway risk (p.3625). Failing to distinguish myasthenic crisis from cholinergic crisis (deterioration due to excessive anticholinesterase medication); the latter is now unlikely because very high cholinesterase-inhibitor doses are rarely used but should still be considered (p.3632). Treating before the diagnosis is confirmed: confirmation is essential because other treatable conditions closely resemble MG and treatment involves surgery and long-term drugs with side effects (p.3625). Interpreting a negative anti-AChR antibody test as excluding MG, or using antibody level to gauge severity (it correlates poorly) (p.3627). Overlooking that anti-MuSK MG generally responds poorly to anticholinesterase agents and may actually worsen with them (p.3629). Ordering anti-striated muscle (titin) antibodies expecting them to confirm MG or thymoma: they are non-pathogenic and do not confirm either (p.3627). MG is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder in which the number of available postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) is reduced and postsynaptic folds are flattened/simplified, decreasing the efficiency of neuromuscular transmission; ACh is released normally but produces small end-plate potentials that may fail to trigger muscle action potentials. The normal decline in ACh release on repeated activity (presynaptic rundown) combined with reduced transmission efficiency activates fewer fibers with successive impulses, producing fatigable weakness (myasthenic fatigue) and the decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation. Anti-AChR antibodies (IgG, T-cell dependent) reduce receptors by three mechanisms: accelerated AChR turnover via cross-linking/endocytosis, complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, and blockade of the ACh-binding site. Anti-MuSK antibodies (IgG4, non-complement-activating) impair MuSK-LRP4 binding and AChR clustering, so MuSK-positive MG does not respond to complement inhibition; anti-LRP4 antibodies (IgG1) cause complement-mediated destruction. Thymic abnormality (hyperplasia in ~65%, thymoma in ~10%) and dysfunction of regulatory T cells contribute to the autoimmune process (p.3624-3626). Mortality from MG has fallen dramatically over the last century (from ~70% a century ago to ~2-30% by the 1950s) to contemporary estimates of ~1-5%. About 20% of patients achieve sustained remission and can be tapered off immunotherapy, with no clear correlation between disease severity and likelihood of remission. Anti-MuSK MG was historically harder to treat, but rituximab has improved its prognosis. Most patients can be returned to full productive lives with proper therapy (p.3629, 3633). Harrison distinguishes ocular MG (weakness confined to ocular muscles; if restricted for 3 years, generalization is unlikely) from generalized MG (facial, bulbar, axial, or limb involvement, occurring in ~85%). Worsening is graded as exacerbation (any deterioration short of needing ventilatory support) versus myasthenic crisis (life-threatening weakness, usually with ventilatory failure requiring intubation or noninvasive ventilation to avoid intubation) (p.3625, 3632).
