Following traumatic inoculation of soil-dwelling fungi or aerobic actinomycetes, the organisms aggregate into grains (microcolonies) within subcutaneous tissue. The host mounts a suppurative and granulomatous response, forming abscesses and sinus tracts that discharge grains to the surface. Chronic inflammation and progressive spread involve fascia, muscle and bone, producing swelling, fibrosis, deformity and osteolysis. The grain structure and, in eumycetoma, a surrounding cement substance protect organisms from host defences and antimicrobials, accounting for the chronicity and treatment difficulty. Actinomycetoma generally responds well to prolonged combination antibacterial therapy, whereas eumycetoma is often refractory, requires prolonged antifungals with surgery and has a higher relapse rate; late presentation with bone disease may necessitate amputation.

Mycoplasma Infection — Mycoplasma pneumoniae, atypical pneumonia, walking pneumonia Chlamydia (Chlamydophila) pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia Legionella species pneumonia Streptococcus pneumoniae and other bacterial community-acquired pneumonia Viral respiratory tract infection / pneumonia Chlamydophila pneumoniae pneumonia Legionella pneumonia Viral atypical pneumonia Respiratory PCR for M. pneumoniae (sensitivity 65-90%, specificity 90-100%) - allows rapid early diagnosis Paired acute- and convalescent-phase serology (IgM and IgG) by enzyme-linked immunoassay; a single acute sample is inadequate because antibodies may not develop until ~2 weeks Respiratory culture on special media (sensitivity <=60%, specificity 100%) - not recommended for routine diagnosis as it may take weeks Chest radiography Cerebrospinal fluid PCR for extrapulmonary (CNS) infection Macrolide-resistance testing by culture and/or PCR when resistance is suspected Asthma / reactive airway disease (wheezing overlap) Drug-induced or herpes-associated erythema multiforme major (overlapping with Mycoplasma-associated SJS/MIRM) M. pneumoniae pneumonia is also called Eaton agent pneumonia, primary atypical pneumonia, and 'walking' pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465). Onset of pneumonia is usually gradual over several days; the most common presenting symptom is cough, which is typically nonproductive, though headache, malaise, chills, and fever are noted in the majority of patients (Harrison 22e p.1465). Pneumonia develops in only 3-13% of infected individuals; upper respiratory illness is far more common, with an estimated incidence up to 20 times that of pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465). Wheezes or rales are detected in about 80% of patients with M. pneumoniae pneumonia, but in many patients pneumonia can be diagnosed only by chest radiography (Harrison 22e p.1465). The most common radiographic pattern is peribronchial pneumonia with thickened bronchial markings, streaks of interstitial infiltration, and subsegmental atelectasis; segmental or lobar consolidation is not uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1465). Clinical presentation does not reliably distinguish M. pneumoniae pneumonia from other causes of community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1465). Many patients with extrapulmonary M. pneumoniae disease do not have respiratory disease (Harrison 22e p.1465). Hematologic manifestations include hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, cold agglutinins, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and hypercoagulopathy; when anemia occurs it generally develops in the second or third week of illness (Harrison 22e p.1466). Erythema multiforme major (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) is the most clinically significant skin eruption associated with M. pneumoniae and appears to occur more commonly with M. pneumoniae than with other infectious agents; in M. pneumoniae-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM)/reactive infectious mucocutaneous eruption (RIME) there may be minimal cutaneous involvement with prominent mucosal disease (Harrison 22e p.1466, p.591). M. pneumoniae has been implicated as a likely etiologic agent in 5-7% of cases of encephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1465). Diagnosis is most sensitively and rapidly made by combining PCR of respiratory tract secretions with serologic testing of paired acute- and convalescent-phase samples (Harrison 22e p.1466). M. pneumoniae is the most frequently detected 'atypical' organism in adult community-acquired pneumonia; older pooled data gave a prevalence of about 22.7%, and more recent (2002-2015) analyses gave about 7.2% (Harrison 22e p.1465). Neurologic manifestations: meningoencephalitis, encephalitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, cerebrovascular thromboembolic events, acute psychosis, cerebellar ataxia, cranial neuropathy Severe mucocutaneous disease: erythema multiforme major / Stevens-Johnson syndrome / MIRM Hemolytic anemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hypercoagulopathy Disseminated infection (septic arthritis, meningitis, osteomyelitis), especially in hypogammaglobulinemic / humorally immunodeficient patients Community-acquired pneumonia failing to respond to a penicillin or cephalosporin Because mycoplasmas lack a cell wall, beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) are ineffective; consider M. pneumoniae particularly when community-acquired pneumonia fails to respond to these agents (Harrison 22e p.1464-1465). M. pneumoniae lacks a cell wall and is therefore not visible on Gram stain (Harrison 22e p.1466). Measurement of cold agglutinin titers is no longer recommended for diagnosis because the findings are nonspecific and specific M. pneumoniae assays are now available (Harrison 22e p.1466). A single acute-phase serum sample is not adequate for diagnosis, and IgM antibody can persist for up to 1 year, so its presence may indicate recent rather than acute infection - paired samples are needed (Harrison 22e p.1466). Little evidence supports the commonly held belief that M. pneumoniae is an important cause of otitis media, with or without bullous myringitis (Harrison 22e p.1465). A test of cure for eradication is not suggested, because appropriate antibiotics do not appear to shorten the duration of detection by culture or PCR (Harrison 22e p.1466). Ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin are not recommended for M. pneumoniae owing to high MICs and poor experimental performance, in contrast to respiratory fluoroquinolones (Harrison 22e p.1466). Mycoplasmas are prokaryotes of the class Mollicutes, the smallest organisms capable of independent replication; they lack a cell wall and are bound only by a cell membrane, which explains the inactivity of beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins and cephalosporins) against them. M. pneumoniae is generally an extracellular pathogen that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelial cells via a complex terminal organelle using interactive adhesins and accessory proteins. Tissue injury is thought to be mediated by production of hydrogen peroxide and an ADP-ribosylating and vacuolating cytotoxin similar to pertussis toxin. Lacking a cell wall, mycoplasmas lack cell-wall-derived innate immune stimulators (lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan), but membrane lipoproteins act through Toll-like receptors (primarily TLR2). Innate immunity provides most lung defense, cellular immunity may be immunopathogenic, and humoral immunity protects against dissemination; patients with humoral immunodeficiency are prone to disseminated disease (arthritis, meningitis, osteomyelitis). Extrapulmonary manifestations may arise from disseminated infection, postinfectious autoimmune phenomena (e.g., Guillain-Barre syndrome), or possibly an ADP-ribosylating toxin (Harrison 22e p.1464-1466). M. pneumoniae pneumonia is generally self-limited, with symptoms usually resolving within 2-3 weeks of onset even without treatment; appropriate antimicrobial therapy significantly shortens the duration of clinical illness. Infection uncommonly results in critical illness and only rarely in death. Long-term recurrent wheezing or reactive airway disease may follow resolution of acute pneumonia, and a possible link to asthma is under investigation. Immunity following severe infection is more protective and longer-lasting than after mild infection, and genuine second attacks of pneumonia are reported infrequently (Harrison 22e p.1465). No formal severity classification is given for Mycoplasma infection; M. pneumoniae illness is generally graded clinically from mild self-limited upper respiratory illness through pneumonia to severe/refractory or critical disease, with macrolide resistance and extrapulmonary involvement marking more severe courses (Harrison 22e p.1464-1466).

Mycosis Fungoides — MF, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, CTCL Chronic eczema or atopic dermatitis Psoriasis and parapsoriasis Drug eruptions and chronic contact dermatitis Tinea corporis and other superficial dermatoses Erythroderma of other causes (for the erythrodermic variant) Other cutaneous lymphomas and lymphomatoid conditions Skin biopsy, often repeated, with immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement (clonality) studies Peripheral blood examination including flow cytometry for circulating atypical (Sezary) cells Full staging with lymph node assessment and imaging (such as CT or PET-CT) in advanced disease Lactate dehydrogenase and other bloods to help gauge tumour burden Lymph node biopsy where nodal involvement is suspected Mycosis fungoides is the commonest form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and usually runs an indolent course over years, evolving classically through patch, plaque, and tumour stages Early patches are erythematous, finely scaly, and often persistent in sun-protected sites such as the buttocks and trunk (the bathing-trunk distribution), frequently mimicking eczema or psoriasis for years before diagnosis A high index of suspicion is warranted for atypical, treatment-resistant, or variably shaped chronic dermatitis in an adult, particularly with poikilodermatous change Diagnosis often requires multiple biopsies over time, since early histology can be subtle and non-specific; T-cell clonality studies and immunophenotyping support the diagnosis Staging assesses skin (patch/plaque/tumour or erythroderma), lymph nodes, blood, and viscera, and drives both prognosis and treatment intensity Skin-directed therapies (topical agents, phototherapy, radiotherapy) are used for early-stage disease, while advanced or transformed disease requires systemic and specialist haemato-oncological management Sezary syndrome is the leukaemic, erythrodermic variant, characterised by widespread redness, circulating atypical (Sezary) cells, and lymphadenopathy, and carries a poorer prognosis Large-cell transformation, tumour-stage disease, and extracutaneous spread mark a more aggressive course and warrant prompt reassessment Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is a malignancy: persistent, atypical, or treatment-resistant chronic dermatitis in an adult should prompt biopsy and specialist referral Development of tumours, ulceration, or rapid progression suggesting large-cell transformation Erythroderma with circulating atypical cells indicating Sezary syndrome Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or systemic symptoms suggesting extracutaneous spread Signs of secondary infection or sepsis in extensively involved or eroded skin Labelling persistent atypical dermatitis as eczema or psoriasis for years and delaying biopsy Relying on a single non-diagnostic biopsy to exclude the diagnosis Overlooking Sezary syndrome as a cause of adult erythroderma Undertreating early disease or, conversely, overtreating indolent disease with aggressive therapy Missing large-cell transformation or extracutaneous progression during follow-up Mycosis fungoides is a malignant proliferation of skin-homing mature memory T-helper lymphocytes, typically expressing a CD4-positive phenotype with characteristic loss of certain T-cell surface antigens. The neoplastic cells display epidermotropism, migrating into the epidermis and forming intraepidermal collections (Pautrier microabscesses), a histological hallmark. A clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement can often be demonstrated. Over time, accumulating genetic and epigenetic alterations, altered cytokine signalling, and impaired antitumour immunity allow progression from patches and plaques to tumours, large-cell transformation, and dissemination to blood, nodes, and organs, as seen in advanced disease and Sezary syndrome. Early patch- and plaque-stage mycosis fungoides is often indolent with a life expectancy close to normal, but prognosis worsens markedly with tumour-stage disease, large-cell transformation, nodal or visceral involvement, and Sezary syndrome; ongoing surveillance is needed because progression can occur after years of stable disease.

Myelodysplastic syndrome — MDS, myelodysplasia, myelodysplastic syndromes, preleukaemia Aplastic anaemia (especially hypoplastic MDS) Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency causing megaloblastic dysplasia Acute myeloid leukaemia Myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative overlap syndromes (e.g. CMML) Reactive dysplasia from alcohol, copper deficiency, or drugs Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Full blood count, reticulocytes, and careful blood film review for dysplastic changes Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with blast count and assessment of dysplasia and ring sideroblasts Cytogenetic analysis and targeted molecular/next-generation sequencing panels Serum erythropoietin level to predict response to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents B12, folate, and copper levels to exclude reversible mimics Flow cytometry and PNH clone testing when the picture overlaps with marrow failure A group of clonal stem cell disorders defined by ineffective haematopoiesis, producing peripheral cytopenias despite a marrow that is usually normocellular or hypercellular Typically affects older adults, often presenting with symptomatic anaemia; neutropenia and thrombocytopenia may also occur, sometimes with recurrent infection or bleeding The paradox of low blood counts with a busy marrow reflects intramedullary apoptosis of dysplastic precursors Diagnosis rests on morphological dysplasia in one or more lineages, blast percentage, and cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities; ring sideroblasts and specific mutations (e.g. SF3B1) carry prognostic meaning Risk stratification with scoring systems that weight blast count, cytogenetics, and depth of cytopenias guides both prognosis and treatment intensity Lower-risk disease is managed supportively with transfusions, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, and iron chelation when transfusion burden is high; an isolated 5q deletion responds well to lenalidomide Higher-risk disease is treated with hypomethylating agents, and allogeneic stem cell transplant offers the only potential cure for suitable patients Progression to acute myeloid leukaemia is a defining risk, greatest in high-risk categories with excess blasts and adverse cytogenetics Rising blast percentage or new adverse cytogenetics signalling transformation to acute leukaemia Severe neutropenia with fever requiring urgent treatment for sepsis Profound thrombocytopenia with clinically significant bleeding Rapidly worsening pancytopenia demanding urgent haematology review and transplant assessment Diagnosing MDS without excluding reversible causes of dysplasia such as B12 or folate deficiency, copper deficiency, alcohol, or recent chemotherapy Failing to obtain cytogenetics and molecular testing, which are central to risk stratification Undertreating iron overload in chronically transfused patients Overlooking an isolated 5q deletion that has a favourable, targeted treatment Missing the transition to acute leukaemia by not repeating marrow assessment when counts deteriorate MDS arises from an acquired mutation in a haematopoietic stem cell that gains a clonal growth advantage. Accumulating mutations in genes governing RNA splicing, epigenetic regulation, transcription, and signalling produce disordered maturation. Precursors are produced abundantly but undergo excessive apoptosis within the marrow, so mature cells are released ineffectively, giving cytopenias in the face of a cellular marrow. Over time the clone may acquire further mutations and expand, with rising blast counts marking transformation towards acute myeloid leukaemia. Prior chemotherapy or radiotherapy can cause therapy-related MDS, which typically carries adverse cytogenetics. Outcomes vary widely by risk category: lower-risk patients may live many years with supportive care, whereas high-risk disease carries short survival and a substantial chance of progression to acute myeloid leukaemia. Allogeneic transplant is the only curative option but is limited by age and comorbidity.

myeloma must be specifically excluded with serum free light chains as ~3% are missed by serum/urine electrophoresis (Ch.57, p.349-350 region) Other causes of marrow-infiltrative normocytic anemia in the elderly (p.886) MGUS or smoldering myeloma misclassified as active disease without myeloma-defining events (p.887) Bone pain is the most common presenting symptom, affecting nearly 70% of patients; lesions are purely lytic (osteoblast suppression by DKK-1), so a radioisotope bone scan is LESS useful than plain radiography (p.886-887). Serum alkaline phosphatase is typically NORMAL despite extensive bony disease because osteoblastic activity is suppressed (p.889). Myeloma bone lesions are classically 'punched-out' lytic lesions (e.g. skull); diffuse osteopenia may also occur (p.887-889). A reduced or negative anion gap may be a clue: the cationic M protein causes chloride retention; an associated pseudohyponatremia reflects reduced serum water from the high protein load (p.887). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is characteristically elevated (p.889). Urine dipstick is unreliable for light chains and the heat test for Bence Jones protein is falsely negative in ~50% of light-chain myeloma; a 24-h urine and serum free light chains are needed (p.888-889). About 20% of myelomas secrete only light chains; <1% are truly non-secretory (M protein undetectable even by serum free light chain assay) (p.884, p.888-889). Median age at diagnosis is ~69 years; uncommon under age 40; nearly twice the incidence in Black versus White populations; male predominance (p.885). Susceptibility to infection is driven by hypogammaglobulinemia (of the non-M-component immunoglobulins), impaired antibody responses to polysaccharide antigens, and granulocyte/complement/T-cell dysfunction (p.886). Most common infections are pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae) and pyelonephritis/UTI (E. coli and other gram-negatives) (p.886). Renal light-chain cast nephropathy, light chain deposition disease, and AL amyloidosis are at least partially reversible with effective antimyeloma therapy (p.887). Patients are prone to acute kidney injury when dehydrated or after iodinated contrast; NSAIDs and hypercalcemia further worsen renal function (p.887). Plasma cell leukemia (>2000 circulating plasma cells/microL) is rare (~1%) but disproportionately frequent in IgD (12%) and IgE (25%) myeloma (p.889). Spinal cord compression from vertebral collapse or plasmacytoma - radicular pain, loss of bowel/bladder control (oncologic emergency) (p.887) Symptomatic hypercalcemia - lethargy, weakness, confusion, AKI (p.886-887) Acute kidney injury, especially with dehydration, contrast, NSAIDs, or hypercalcemia (p.887) Hyperviscosity syndrome - headache, visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding, somnolence, heart failure, retinopathy; symptoms above ~4 cP, most common with IgM > IgG3 > IgA (p.887) Sepsis / serious bacterial infection (recurrent infection is the presenting feature in ~25%) (p.886) Pathologic fracture (p.887) Relying on urine dipstick (detects albumin, not light chains) or the Bence Jones heat test (false-negative ~50%) to exclude light-chain myeloma - use 24-h urine immunofixation and serum free light chains (p.888-889). Excluding myeloma in hypercalcemia of malignancy without serum free light chains - ~3% of myeloma is missed by serum/urine electrophoresis with immunofixation. Ordering a radionuclide bone scan instead of skeletal radiography/CT/PET-CT - lytic lesions lack osteoblastic activity and may be missed (p.887). Misreading a normal alkaline phosphatase as evidence against bone disease (p.889). Interpreting hyponatremia at face value - it is often pseudohyponatremia from high serum protein (p.887). Labeling all monoclonal proteins as myeloma - M components occur in many neoplastic, autoimmune, and reactive conditions and require myeloma-defining events for the diagnosis (p.883, p.887). Failing to distinguish MGUS/smoldering myeloma from active myeloma; active disease requires marrow clonal plasmacytosis (and/or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event (CRAB or a malignancy biomarker). Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of a single plasma-cell clone. Myeloma cells adhere to bone marrow stromal cells and extracellular matrix, triggering cytokine loops (IL-6, IGF-1, VEGF) and signaling (Ras/Raf/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, PKC) that drive growth, survival, drug resistance, and migration. Osteoclast-activating factors (RANK ligand, MIP-1alpha, IL-1, lymphotoxin, TNF, VEGF) increase bone resorption while DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts, producing purely lytic bone disease, hypercalcemia, fractures, and cord compression. The immune microenvironment is remodeled (expansion of MDSCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TH17; suppression of effective antimyeloma T/B/NKT responses). Recurrent cytogenetic events include hyperdiploidy (trisomies) in ~half, and 14q32 IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)] in the rest, plus del13q, 1q amplification/1p deletion, and del17p; KRAS/NRAS are the most frequently mutated genes (~20% each), with TP53, DIS3, FAM46C, BRAF in 5-10%. No single unifying mutation exists; subclonal heterogeneity present at diagnosis drives genomic evolution. All myeloma is preceded by MGUS (p.883-885). Serum beta-2-microglobulin is the single most powerful survival predictor; combined with albumin it defines the 3-stage International Staging System (ISS): Stage I (b2M <3.5 mg/L, albumin >=3.5 g/dL) median survival ~62 months; Stage II ~44 months; Stage III (b2M >5.5 mg/L) ~29 months. High LDH, circulating plasma cells, high labeling index, and poor performance status indicate worse outcome. Cytogenetic risk: high-risk = del(17p) (>=20% clonality)/TP53 mutation, t(4;14)/t(14;16)/t(14;20) with 1q gain or 1p deletion, biallelic/del1p with 1q gain, and high b2M with normal creatinine (~20-25% of patients, expected survival 3-4 years); standard-risk includes t(11;14), del(13), hyperdiploidy (~75-80%, survival 8-10+ years). del(13q) and t(11;14) are NOT high-risk markers. MGUS progresses ~1%/yr; SMM higher (high-risk SMM ~76% at 5 years). Solitary plasmacytomas carry median survival >=10 years. The Durie-Salmon system is no longer used (p.888-889). Diagnosis (IMWG, Table 116-1): clonal marrow plasma cells (or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma) PLUS >=1 myeloma-defining event. CRAB end-organ damage: hyperCalcemia (>2.75 mmol/L or >0.25 mmol/L above ULN); Renal insufficiency (CrCl <40 mL/min or creatinine >177 micromol/L [>2 mg/dL]); Anemia (Hb <100 g/L or >20 g/L below LLN); Bone lesions (>=1 lytic lesion on radiograph/CT/PET-CT). SLiM biomarkers of malignancy (any one): clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%; involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100; >1 focal lesion (>=5 mm) on MRI. Staging severity: International Staging System (ISS) I-III by serum beta-2-microglobulin and albumin; cytogenetic high-risk vs standard-risk further stratifies (R-ISS combines ISS with high-risk cytogenetics and LDH). MGUS = M protein <30 g/L, marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events; smoldering myeloma = M protein >=30 g/L (or urine >=500 mg/24h) and/or marrow plasma cells 10-60%, no myeloma-defining events (p.887-889).

monitor sensorineural hearing loss Urinalysis and renal function tests to screen for nephropathy Ophthalmological assessment for cataract An autosomal dominant disorder caused by MYH9 mutations affecting non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA, presenting with macrothrombocytopenia The blood film shows large or giant platelets together with pale blue Dohle-like cytoplasmic inclusions in neutrophils The historical eponyms (May-Hegglin, Sebastian, Fechtner, Epstein) are now recognised as one disease spectrum defined by the MYH9 gene Extra-haematological features may include progressive sensorineural deafness, presenile cataract, and nephropathy that can advance to renal failure The thrombocytopenia is often mild and the bleeding tendency modest, so the low platelet count is frequently discovered incidentally Automated counters may undercount the giant platelets and overstate the severity, so film review is essential Diagnosis combines macrothrombocytopenia with leucocyte inclusions on immunofluorescence for myosin IIA and MYH9 sequencing Progressive proteinuria or declining renal function heralding nephropathy Rapidly progressive hearing loss requiring audiological intervention Significant bleeding disproportionate to the platelet count, prompting review of the diagnosis Unnecessary immunosuppression or splenectomy after misdiagnosis as immune thrombocytopenia Misdiagnosing the condition as immune thrombocytopenia and giving steroids, immunoglobulin, or splenectomy Relying on automated platelet counts that miss giant platelets Failing to screen for and monitor renal, auditory, and ocular involvement Overtreating a mild, incidentally found thrombocytopenia MYH9-related disorder results from mutations in MYH9, which encodes the heavy chain of non-muscle myosin IIA, a cytoskeletal motor protein expressed in platelets, leucocytes, cochlea, lens, and kidney. In megakaryocytes, defective myosin IIA disrupts the cytoskeletal remodelling required for orderly proplatelet formation, so platelets are released as fewer, abnormally large cells, producing macrothrombocytopenia. In neutrophils, the mutant protein aggregates into cytoplasmic inclusions visible as Dohle-like bodies. The same protein is essential in other tissues, so its dysfunction can cause sensorineural hearing loss, cataract, and a glomerular nephropathy, with the pattern and severity of extra-haematological involvement varying by the specific mutation. The haematological course is usually benign with only a modest bleeding tendency, but long-term prognosis is shaped by extra-haematological complications, particularly progressive nephropathy and hearing loss in susceptible genotypes.

Myiasis — fly larval infestation, maggot infestation, Dermatobia hominis (human botfly), Cordylobia anthropophaga (tumbu fly), Cochliomyia hominivorax (screwworm) Bacterial furuncle or abscess Tungiasis Infected epidermoid cyst Cutaneous larva migrans (for migratory forms) Retained foreign body with granuloma Cellulitis of other cause Clinical examination with travel/exposure history and inspection of the central punctum Occlusion test to observe the larval breathing movements Dermoscopy or ultrasound to visualise the embedded larva in furuncular myiasis Identification of the extracted larva to species where relevant Wound swab and culture if secondary bacterial infection is suspected Assessment of tetanus immunisation status Myiasis is infestation of living tissue by dipterous (fly) larvae; clinical patterns include furuncular (boil-like), wound (traumatic), migratory (creeping), and cavity/body-orifice forms Furuncular myiasis is classically caused by the human botfly (Dermatobia hominis) in the Americas and the tumbu fly (Cordylobia anthropophaga) in sub-Saharan Africa Dermatobia eggs are carried to skin by biting insects (phoresis), whereas tumbu fly eggs are laid on soil or drying laundry and larvae penetrate contact skin The typical furuncular lesion is a painful nodule with a central punctum that intermittently discharges serosanguineous fluid; patients often describe movement or a sensation of crawling A central breathing pore that bubbles, and sometimes a visible larval tip, help confirm the diagnosis; occlusion can bring the larva to the surface Wound and cavity myiasis (e.g. screwworm) can be aggressively tissue-destructive and occurs in neglected wounds, orifices or debilitated patients Treatment is removal of the larva (occlusion and extraction or minor surgical removal), wound care, and tetanus/antibiotic cover for secondary infection where indicated Aggressive wound or cavity (e.g. nasal, orbital, aural) myiasis with rapid tissue destruction Screwworm infestation requiring prompt eradication and public health notification Secondary cellulitis, abscess or signs of systemic sepsis Involvement of the eye, sinuses or central structures threatening deep spread Infestation in a neglected, debilitated or cognitively impaired patient Rupturing or fragmenting the larva during extraction, leaving parts that provoke a foreign-body reaction Misdiagnosing furuncular myiasis as a simple boil and incising without recognising the larva Underestimating aggressive wound or cavity myiasis and its capacity for deep destruction Neglecting tetanus prophylaxis and secondary infection management Failing to notify authorities for obligate parasites such as screwworm where reportable Fly larvae invade host tissue by species-specific routes: some deposit larvae directly, some lay eggs transferred by biting arthropods, and others deposit eggs on soil or clothing from which larvae penetrate intact or broken skin. The larva develops within the dermis or a wound, feeding on tissue and exudate while maintaining a respiratory opening at the skin surface. Local host inflammation produces a furuncle-like nodule in obligate skin-dwelling species, whereas facultative or obligate wound feeders such as screwworm can burrow and destroy tissue extensively. Secondary bacterial infection frequently complicates the lesion. Furuncular myiasis is generally benign and resolves completely once the larva is removed, whereas wound and cavity myiasis, especially screwworm, can cause serious tissue destruction and requires urgent intervention; secondary infection is the main complication.

essential, epileptic, and symptomatic (secondary) forms, the last being the most common in clinical practice A crucial step is to identify secondary causes, particularly metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, since these are often reversible Asterixis (negative myoclonus) is a classic sign of hepatic, renal, and other metabolic encephalopathies Neurophysiological localisation into cortical, subcortical, spinal, or peripheral origin helps guide investigation and treatment Post-hypoxic action myoclonus (Lance-Adams syndrome) can follow cardiac arrest and cerebral hypoxia Treatment principles combine correcting any underlying cause with symptomatic antimyoclonic agents chosen according to the presumed generator Myoclonus with declining consciousness suggesting a serious metabolic, toxic, or hypoxic encephalopathy Rapidly progressive myoclonus with cognitive decline raising concern for prion disease or an autoimmune encephalitis Myoclonus following cardiac arrest, which may indicate severe hypoxic brain injury Myoclonus as part of a status myoclonicus or in the context of status epilepticus requiring urgent treatment Failing to search for and correct a reversible metabolic or drug-induced cause Misclassifying myoclonus as tremor, tics, or seizures and mismanaging it Overlooking a serious progressive cause such as prion disease or autoimmune encephalitis Not localising the myoclonus neurophysiologically, leading to poorly targeted therapy Myoclonus results from abnormal, excessive neuronal discharge that can arise at several levels of the nervous system. Cortical myoclonus reflects hyperexcitability of the sensorimotor cortex and often coexists with epilepsy; subcortical and brainstem forms arise from deeper generators; and spinal and peripheral forms originate in the cord or nerve. Loss of normal inhibitory control, frequently involving impaired GABAergic and serotonergic mechanisms, allows brief synchronous muscle discharges. Underlying processes include metabolic derangement, drugs and toxins, neurodegeneration, hypoxia, and epilepsy. Prognosis is dictated by the underlying cause. Myoclonus due to reversible metabolic or drug causes typically resolves once the trigger is corrected, whereas myoclonus from neurodegenerative, prion, or severe hypoxic injury carries a poor outlook. Symptomatic treatment can meaningfully reduce disability in many chronic cases even when the cause cannot be cured.

Myoclonus-dystonia — myoclonus-dystonia syndrome, DYT11, SGCE, epsilon-sarcoglycan deficiency, M-D, alcohol-responsive myoclonic dystonia Essential tremor and other tremor syndromes Primary (isolated) dystonias such as DYT1 Progressive myoclonic epilepsies and other myoclonus syndromes Tic disorders including Tourette syndrome Functional (psychogenic) jerks Cortical myoclonus from other neurological disease SGCE molecular genetic testing, interpreted with attention to maternal imprinting Neurophysiological studies (EMG with back-averaging) to characterise the myoclonus as subcortical EEG to distinguish myoclonic epilepsy Brain MRI, expected to be normal, to exclude structural or degenerative causes Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease when the picture is atypical Most commonly caused by variants in SGCE (epsilon-sarcoglycan), inherited autosomal dominantly with maternal imprinting, so penetrance depends on parent of origin (usually manifest only when inherited from the father) Core phenotype combines lightning-like myoclonic jerks, predominantly of the upper body and arms, with milder dystonia (often cervical dystonia or writer's cramp) Onset is typically in childhood or adolescence, and the myoclonus is usually the more disabling feature A characteristic and well-recognised feature is marked, if temporary, improvement of myoclonus with alcohol, which can lead to alcohol misuse Psychiatric comorbidity is common, including anxiety, obsessive-compulsive features, and depression The disorder is non-degenerative with normal cognition and structural imaging, and course is generally benign and non-progressive Symptomatic treatment may target myoclonus and dystonia; deep brain stimulation is an option in severely affected, refractory cases Diagnosis is supported by the clinical picture and family history and confirmed by SGCE molecular testing, keeping imprinting in mind when interpreting inheritance Development of alcohol dependence driven by self-medication of myoclonus Severe psychiatric symptoms including suicidal ideation Atypical progression, cognitive decline, or additional neurological signs suggesting another diagnosis Disabling myoclonus or dystonia refractory to medical therapy Misinterpreting the inheritance by ignoring maternal imprinting and wrongly excluding the diagnosis in an unaffected carrier parent Overlooking or inadvertently reinforcing alcohol misuse arising from symptom self-treatment Labelling the jerks as tics or a functional disorder without neurophysiology or genetic testing Failing to address the frequently associated psychiatric comorbidity Myoclonus-dystonia is most often caused by loss-of-function variants in SGCE, encoding epsilon-sarcoglycan, a transmembrane protein widely expressed in neurons including cerebellar Purkinje cells and monoaminergic neurons. SGCE is maternally imprinted, so only the paternally inherited allele is normally expressed, which explains why the disorder typically manifests when the variant is inherited from the father. Deficiency of epsilon-sarcoglycan is thought to disrupt cerebellothalamocortical and striatal network function, producing subcortical myoclonus and dystonia without neurodegeneration, consistent with the normal cognition and imaging. The condition is generally benign and non-progressive, compatible with a normal lifespan and preserved cognition, though myoclonus and dystonia can cause functional and social disability and psychiatric comorbidity may be significant. Selected refractory patients benefit from deep brain stimulation.

Myofascial pain syndrome — MPS, myofascial trigger point pain, muscular trigger point syndrome Fibromyalgia Radiculopathy or peripheral nerve entrapment Cervical or lumbar facet joint pain Bursitis or tendinopathy Inflammatory or crystal arthropathy Referred visceral pain Polymyalgia rheumatica Clinical examination to locate taut bands, trigger points, and reproducible referred pain Assessment of posture, ergonomics, and mechanical perpetuating factors Investigations to exclude mimics, such as imaging or nerve conduction studies when a structural or neurological cause is suspected Screening for contributing conditions including thyroid dysfunction, vitamin deficiency, and sleep disturbance Blood tests such as inflammatory markers where inflammatory or systemic disease is considered Myofascial pain syndrome is a regional pain disorder characterised by myofascial trigger points, which are hyperirritable spots within a palpable taut band of skeletal muscle Pressing a trigger point reproduces the patient's familiar pain and refers it in a characteristic, reproducible pattern that does not follow dermatomal boundaries A local twitch response, elicited by snapping palpation or needling of the taut band, supports the diagnosis, which is fundamentally clinical It is distinguished from fibromyalgia, which is a widespread pain disorder with diffuse tender points rather than regional referring trigger points Perpetuating factors such as poor posture, ergonomic strain, muscle overload, and underlying structural or psychological stressors should be identified and corrected Core treatment is manual and physical therapy including trigger-point release, stretching, spray-and-stretch techniques, and posture and activity correction Trigger-point injection or dry needling can deactivate stubborn points, and botulinum toxin injection is used for selected refractory cases Addressing sleep, mood, and contributing chronic conditions improves durability of the response, and long-term management emphasises self-directed exercise Constitutional features such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats suggesting infection or malignancy Progressive neurological deficit indicating a radicular or cord lesion rather than muscular pain Sudden severe pain or a mass suggesting an alternative acute pathology Pain unresponsive to appropriate myofascial treatment prompting review of the diagnosis Mislabelling widespread fibromyalgia as regional myofascial pain, or vice versa Treating trigger points while ignoring the posture, ergonomic, or structural factors that perpetuate them Relying on passive treatments and medication without an active exercise programme Overlooking sleep disturbance, mood, and stress that maintain chronic muscle pain Repeated needling of trigger points without addressing the underlying cause Myofascial trigger points are thought to develop where sustained or repetitive muscle overload leads to localised areas of contracted sarcomeres and a taut band. A widely cited model proposes excessive acetylcholine release at dysfunctional motor endplates, producing sustained contraction, local ischaemia and energy crisis, and accumulation of sensitising biochemical mediators. This lowers the local pain threshold, sensitises peripheral nociceptors, and, through convergence in the dorsal horn, generates referred pain and contributes to central sensitisation when the process becomes chronic. Acute myofascial pain from an identifiable overload often resolves well when the trigger points are treated and perpetuating factors corrected. Chronic cases with central sensitisation and unaddressed contributing factors can be persistent, but most patients improve with an active, multimodal rehabilitation approach.

proteins, with desmin (DES) and alpha-B-crystallin (CRYAB) among the classic causes, alongside myotilin, ZASP, filamin C and others Respiratory muscle weakness and peripheral neuropathy may accompany the myopathy Muscle biopsy shows Z-disc streaming, rimmed vacuoles and aggregates of desmin and other proteins on immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy Because cardiac and respiratory complications drive morbidity, systematic cardiac and respiratory surveillance is central to management Cardiac conduction block, arrhythmia or heart failure, which can be life-threatening and may precede weakness Respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation Rapid functional decline suggesting an aggressive subtype Sudden cardiac events in the patient or affected relatives Focusing on the skeletal weakness and failing to screen for the potentially fatal cardiac disease Mislabelling it as a limb-girdle dystrophy and missing the diagnostic aggregate pathology Overlooking coexisting peripheral neuropathy or respiratory involvement Assuming a single gene, when the group is genetically heterogeneous and needs broad testing Myofibrillar myopathies are caused by mutations in genes encoding proteins of the sarcomeric Z-disc and its associated cytoskeletal network, including desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, myotilin, ZASP and filamin C. These proteins maintain the structural integrity and mechanical linkage of the myofibrils and the intermediate-filament scaffold that connects sarcomeres to the sarcolemma and organelles. When they are defective, the Z-disc disintegrates and misfolded proteins, particularly desmin, accumulate as insoluble aggregates that disrupt myofibrillar architecture, mitochondrial positioning and protein-quality-control pathways. The resulting mechanical and metabolic failure of the fibre produces progressive weakness, and because several of these proteins are also essential in cardiac muscle, cardiomyopathy and conduction disease are frequent. Prognosis varies with the causative gene, but progression is usually slow for the skeletal weakness while cardiac and respiratory complications are the main determinants of morbidity and mortality, so outcomes are substantially improved by early detection and treatment of heart and respiratory involvement.

at the bedside, and eyelid myotonia may follow sustained forced closure Cold can accentuate stiffness but, unlike paramyotonia congenita, myotonia congenita characteristically improves rather than worsens with continued activity Symptomatic relief is achieved with sodium-channel-blocking antimyotonic agents when stiffness is disabling Cardiac conduction disturbance or systemic features suggesting myotonic dystrophy rather than a pure channelopathy Progressive fixed weakness, which is not expected and points to an alternative diagnosis Severe stiffness compromising airway, swallowing or safe mobility Adverse response to depolarising neuromuscular blockade during anaesthesia Mistaking it for myotonic dystrophy and missing the systemic surveillance the latter requires, or vice versa Confusing the warm-up phenomenon of myotonia congenita with the paradoxical cold-worsened myotonia of paramyotonia congenita Overlooking the transient exercise-induced weakness of Becker myotonia and labelling it a fixed myopathy Not warning about depolarising muscle relaxants and other anaesthetic triggers of severe myotonia Myotonia congenita results from loss-of-function mutations in CLCN1, the gene encoding the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated chloride channel ClC-1. This channel carries most of the resting membrane conductance and normally stabilises the sarcolemma after an action potential. When chloride conductance is reduced, potassium that accumulates in the transverse tubules during activity depolarises the membrane more readily, producing runs of repetitive after-discharges experienced as delayed muscle relaxation, or myotonia. The autosomal dominant form reflects a dominant-negative effect on the dimeric channel, whereas the recessive form arises when both alleles are severely impaired, and the transient warm-up improvement reflects redistribution of ions with repeated activity. Myotonia congenita is a non-progressive, non-dystrophic disorder compatible with a normal lifespan, and although stiffness can be functionally limiting it often stabilises or improves in adulthood and usually responds to antimyotonic therapy.

the clinical picture, demonstration of myotonia (clinically or on electromyography), and targeted repeat-expansion genetic testing Syncope, palpitations, or a high-grade conduction block indicating risk of sudden cardiac death Respiratory failure, especially in the congenital form or during anaesthesia Neonatal hypotonia and respiratory distress suggesting congenital DM1 Excessive daytime sleepiness with signs of hypoventilation Heightened sensitivity to anaesthetic and sedative agents Focusing on skeletal weakness and neglecting the potentially fatal cardiac conduction disease Giving standard doses of anaesthetic or sedative agents to which patients are unusually sensitive Not recognising anticipation and its implications for family counselling Missing the diagnosis in a mildly affected parent of a floppy neonate Overlooking treatable comorbidities such as cataracts, diabetes, and sleep-disordered breathing Myotonic dystrophy is caused by expanded non-coding repeats (CTG in DMPK for DM1 and CCTG in CNBP for DM2) that are transcribed into RNA containing long repeat tracts. These toxic RNA transcripts accumulate in the nucleus and sequester RNA-binding proteins, particularly muscleblind-like proteins, disrupting the normal alternative splicing of many downstream genes. The resulting misregulated splicing of ion-channel, insulin-receptor, and other transcripts produces myotonia, progressive muscle degeneration, and the wide-ranging systemic features. Prognosis depends on the type and severity: DM1 tends to be more severe than DM2, and the congenital form carries high neonatal morbidity and mortality. Cardiac conduction disease and respiratory failure are the leading causes of premature death, so lifelong cardiac and respiratory surveillance is central to care.

Myxoedema coma — TFTs, cortisol ECG, electrolytes (Na↓) IV thyroxine + hydrocortisone; treat precipitant Sick euthyroid syndrome confounding thyroid function tests in a critically ill or hypothermic patient (p.3769). Adrenal insufficiency / hypopituitarism, which independently increase susceptibility to hypothermia and may coexist (p.3768). Hashimoto's encephalopathy - a steroid-responsive syndrome with TPO antibodies, myoclonus and EEG slow-wave activity (relationship to hypothyroidism not established) (p.3030). Sepsis should be actively suspected as a precipitant; hypothermia obscures fever and leukocytosis, and infectious rigors may be mistaken for shivering (p.3032, p.3769). Pneumonia as a respiration-impairing precipitant (p.3032). Arterial blood gas to detect hypoxia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation (p.3032). Glucose to detect contributing hypoglycemia (p.3032). Septic screen / cultures, since infection is a common precipitant and is masked by hypothermia (p.3032, p.3769). Core temperature measurement (may be very low, down to ~23 degrees C) (p.3032). Environmental / accidental hypothermia from cold exposure, drugs (ethanol, sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants), or malnutrition (p.3768). Hypoglycemia from insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, which itself causes hypothermia via neuroglycopenic hypothalamic effects (p.3768). Myxedema coma carries a 20-40% mortality despite intensive care, and outcome does not correlate with the degree of T4 or TSH abnormality (p.3032). It occurs almost exclusively in the elderly, often in winter, and may arise either in a known hypothyroid patient with poor treatment adherence or in someone not previously diagnosed (p.3032). Hypothermia in myxedema can be profound, reaching as low as 23 degrees C (74 degrees F) (p.3032). Reduced consciousness is the hallmark and may be accompanied by seizures, alongside the usual signs of hypothyroidism (p.3032). A distinguishing examination clue in hypothyroidism is a deep tendon reflex (e.g., Achilles) whose relaxation phase is prolonged out of proportion to the contraction phase (p.3769). Hypothyroidism, especially extreme as in myxedema coma, is a recognised endocrine cause of hypothermia by reducing metabolic rate and impairing thermogenesis and behavioural responses (p.3768). Bradycardia, reduced myocardial contractility and stroke volume, and pericardial effusion (up to ~30% of hypothyroid patients) reflect the cardiac depression that underlies the haemodynamic picture (p.3030). Carotene accumulation can give the skin a yellow tinge, and nonpitting (myxedematous) tissue swelling distinguishes the oedema from pitting fluid overload (p.3029-3030). Reduced level of consciousness with seizures in a hypothyroid patient (p.3032). Profound hypothermia (toward 23 degrees C) (p.3032). Hypoventilation with hypoxia/hypercapnia signalling impending respiratory failure (p.3032). Severe dilutional hyponatremia and hypoglycemia (p.3032). An identifiable precipitant such as infection, MI, CHF, GI bleeding, cerebrovascular accident, or respiratory-depressant drugs (p.3032). Sedatives, anesthetics, and antidepressants can precipitate or worsen myxedema coma, and impaired drug metabolism means standard doses may accumulate (p.3032). Hypothermia masks fever and leukocytosis, so infection can be missed; rigors may be misread as shivering (p.3769). Giving parenteral levothyroxine to a euthyroid hypothermic patient is potentially hazardous, so clinical/historical evidence of hypothyroidism should be sought first (p.3769). Sick euthyroid syndrome can confound thyroid function tests in the acutely ill patient (p.3769). Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism, and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (p.3032; p.3768). Mortality remains 20-40% even with intensive treatment, and prognosis is independent of the measured T4 and TSH levels. Hypothermia associated with concurrent sepsis is a poor prognostic sign (p.3032, p.3769).

(biochemically near-identical) Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (raised orotic acid, X-linked) Citrullinaemia type 1 and argininosuccinic aciduria Organic acidaemias causing secondary hyperammonaemia Fatty acid oxidation disorders with hyperammonaemia Transient hyperammonaemia of the newborn Neonatal sepsis Urgent plasma ammonia during suspected crises Plasma amino acids (low/normal citrulline, low arginine, raised glutamine) Urine orotic acid (characteristically low, separating from OTC deficiency) Blood gas showing respiratory alkalosis of hyperammonaemia NAGS gene sequencing for confirmation Documented biochemical response to a carglumic acid trial Plasma acylcarnitines/organic acids to exclude secondary hyperammonaemia Rarest of the urea cycle disorders, caused by biallelic NAGS variants NAGS makes N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, so its loss shuts down the first committed step of ureagenesis Biochemically resembles CPS1 deficiency: hyperammonaemia with low/normal citrulline, low arginine and a characteristically low urine orotic acid Presents as neonatal hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, or later with episodic hyperammonaemia and neurocognitive symptoms The key distinguishing feature is its responsiveness to carglumic acid, a synthetic N-acetylglutamate analogue that restores CPS1 activity Low or absent orotic aciduria helps separate proximal urea cycle defects (NAGS, CPS1) from OTC deficiency Confirm with NAGS gene sequencing and by demonstrating a therapeutic response to carglumic acid Acute management is emergency ammonia lowering (dialysis if needed) with carglumic acid, nitrogen scavengers, arginine and protein restriction Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency ammonia removal Cerebral oedema from severe hyperammonaemia Rapidly rising ammonia with encephalopathy at any age Decompensation triggered by catabolic illness, high protein load or surgery Failure of ammonia to fall despite standard scavenger therapy (prompting carglumic acid) Not distinguishing NAGS from CPS1 deficiency and thereby missing a treatable disorder Failing to trial carglumic acid, which is specifically effective in NAGS deficiency Overlooking the low orotic acid clue that points to a proximal urea cycle defect Delaying emergency ammonia lowering while awaiting confirmatory genetics Assuming carglumic acid is equally effective in all urea cycle disorders N-acetylglutamate synthase catalyses formation of N-acetylglutamate from glutamate and acetyl-CoA. N-acetylglutamate is the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), the enzyme that initiates the urea cycle by incorporating ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate. In NAGS deficiency the activator is not produced, so CPS1 remains inactive and the urea cycle cannot begin, leading to accumulation of ammonia. Because the block is at the very first step, downstream intermediates such as citrulline and arginine are low, and carbamoyl phosphate is not diverted into pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid excretion stays low (mirroring CPS1 deficiency and contrasting with OTC deficiency). Uniquely, the missing activator can be replaced pharmacologically by carglumic acid, which reactivates CPS1. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. NAGS deficiency is one of the few urea cycle disorders with a specific pharmacological treatment; with early diagnosis and carglumic acid therapy long-term metabolic control and outcome can be excellent, whereas delayed treatment of severe neonatal hyperammonaemia risks permanent neurological injury.

MASLD / NAFLD (Fatty Liver Disease) — NAFLD, NASH, MASLD, MASH, fatty liver Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) and the intermediate MetALD category (metabolic dysfunction with social alcohol use, 20-50 g/d women, 30-60 g/d men) Hepatitis C, particularly genotype 3 Autoimmune hepatitis Wilson disease Hemochromatosis / iron overload Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Inborn errors of metabolism (abetalipoproteinemia, cholesterol ester storage disease, galactosemia, glycogen storage disease, hereditary fructose intolerance, homocystinuria, systemic carnitine deficiency, tyrosinemia) Weber-Christian syndrome Chronic hepatitis C (genotype 3 causes hepatic steatosis) Chronic hepatitis B Serum aminotransferases (ALT/AST) - true normal ALT is ~29-33 U/L (men) and ~19-25 U/L (women); normal liver enzymes do NOT exclude MASLD FIB-4 score (age, AST, ALT, platelet count) - first-line noninvasive fibrosis risk score Vibration-controlled transient elastography / liver stiffness measurement (VCTE <8 kPa low, >12 kPa high; LSM >12 kPa associated with cirrhosis) Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) blood test (ELF >=9.8 increased risk; >11.8 suspect cirrhosis) Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) and cT1 for refined risk stratification Abdominal ultrasound / cross-sectional imaging for steatosis Workup to exclude other causes: viral hepatitis serologies, autoimmune markers, iron/copper studies, alpha-1 antitrypsin Screening for T2DM; assessment of metabolic syndrome components Liver biopsy - historical gold standard for staging, reserved for indeterminate/discordant NITs, diagnostic uncertainty, or suspected concurrent chronic hepatitis (limited by sampling and observer variability) Alcohol-associated liver disease (histologically can be indistinguishable; alcohol intake must be excluded) Autoimmune hepatitis (note ~20% of steatotic liver disease patients have a positive ANA) Medication/drug-associated steatosis or steatohepatitis Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is the most common cause of chronic liver disease in the US and worldwide; metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and steatohepatitis (MASH) now replace the older terms NAFLD and NASH, with ~98% population overlap (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701). Diagnosis of MASLD requires hepatic steatosis plus little/no alcohol intake (<20 g/d women, <30 g/d men) and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance/T2DM) (Harrison 22e p.2700, 2703). Most patients are asymptomatic; MASLD is typically detected incidentally via raised ALT or steatosis on imaging done for other reasons (Harrison 22e p.2702-2703). Disease spans a dynamic, potentially reversible spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis/HCC; chronic steatohepatitis is the primary driver of fibrosis, and fibrosis severity is the chief predictor of liver-related morbidity/mortality (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701, 2704). FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) is the recommended first-line noninvasive score with excellent negative predictive value: FIB-4 <1.3 = low risk (manage in primary care), >=2.67 = moderate/high risk warranting a secondary test (elastography or ELF) (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705). T2DM is the strongest risk factor for MASLD acquisition, fibrosis progression, and HCC; the MASLD-T2DM relationship is bidirectional, so patients with MASLD should be screened for T2DM (Harrison 22e p.2703). Foundational treatment is lifestyle modification with weight loss: ~5% weight loss improves steatosis, while >10% improves MASH and can reverse fibrosis; cardiovascular risk reduction and treatment of metabolic comorbidities apply to all patients (Harrison 22e p.2706). Statins are safe across the MASLD spectrum and indicated for dyslipidemia given high cardiovascular risk; reluctance to use them is not supported by evidence of liver harm (Harrison 22e p.2707). FIB-4 >=2.67 (moderate/high risk for advanced fibrosis - needs secondary testing/specialist referral) Fibrosis stage >=F2 = 'at-risk MASH' with increased risk of further progression and adverse liver outcomes Persistently elevated AST and ALT Stigmata of advanced disease: spider angiomata, palmar erythema, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, clubbing, ascites, encephalopathy Features of decompensation/end-stage disease: jaundice, ascites, variceal hemorrhage Clinical/radiologic suspicion of cirrhosis or ELF >11.8 Failing to exclude significant alcohol intake and other chronic liver diseases (viral, autoimmune, iron/copper overload, alpha-1 antitrypsin) before attributing steatosis to MASLD. Assuming normal liver enzymes exclude MASLD - they do not; normal ALT 'reference ranges' are inflated by including people with undiagnosed liver disease. Relying on liver tests for staging - aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, and PT may all be completely normal even with significant disease. MASLD can occur in lean individuals (BMI <25, or <23 in Asians), especially with truncal/visceral adiposity, so a normal BMI does not exclude it. FIB-4 has reduced accuracy in patients >65 and <35 years and is a less robust predictor in T2DM, so a secondary noninvasive test is needed in these groups. Liver biopsy is limited by sampling error, inter/intraobserver variability (worse with cores <2 cm), and gives only a static snapshot of disease activity. MASLD arises from imbalance between energy intake and expenditure: excess caloric intake, reduced physical activity, and limited peripheral adipose expansion drive visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and metabolic dysfunction. Hepatocyte triglyceride accumulates from increased free fatty acid delivery (dietary uptake, adipose lipolysis, de novo lipogenesis), impaired fatty acid disposal, or impaired triglyceride export; triglyceride storage itself is relatively safe, so steatosis per se does not damage the liver but is a biomarker of metabolic dysfunction. When adaptive mechanisms are overwhelmed, lipotoxicity from dysfunctional lipid handling injures and kills hepatocytes, producing steatohepatitis (MASH) with inflammation and ballooned hepatocytes. Repeated/protracted MASH triggers regenerative responses that become maladaptive, promoting progressive fibrosis (replacement of functional parenchyma by scar) and primary liver cancer; cirrhosis represents futile repair. Heritable factors (e.g., PNPLA3, TM6SF2, MBOAT7 variants), epigenetic influences, gut microbiota alterations, and environmental factors (high-fat/high-sugar diets) modify susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.2701-2702). Variable and stage-dependent. The 10-year probability of liver-related morbidity/mortality is negligible with steatosis alone, so this group is managed conservatively. Fibrosis severity is the primary predictor of outcome: average fibrosis progression is roughly one stage every 14 years in steatosis versus one stage every 7 years in MASH; once at stage >=F2 ('at-risk MASH') the risk of further progression and bad outcomes rises. Once MASLD-related cirrhosis develops, progression to decompensation runs 3-20% per year and annual primary liver cancer incidence can reach 1-2% per year, prompting biannual HCC surveillance and variceal screening. Cirrhosis can regress, and MASLD outcomes after liver transplantation are generally good in well-selected patients, though comorbid diabetes, obesity, and CVD limit candidacy and disease may recur post-transplant. MASLD is also a premalignant condition increasing risk of primary and extrahepatic malignancy even in noncirrhotic livers (Harrison 22e p.2701, 2704, 2708). Histopathologic/fibrosis staging spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis. Fibrosis stages F0 (none), F1 (minimal), F2 (significant), F3 (advanced/bridging), F4 (cirrhosis, further stratified into compensated and decompensated). 'At-risk MASH' = MASH with fibrosis stage >=F2. Noninvasive risk stratification: FIB-4 <1.3 low risk, >=1.3 intermediate, >=2.67 moderate/high; secondary tests VCTE <8 kPa low / 8-12 intermediate / >12 high, ELF <7.7 low / 7.7-9.8 intermediate / >9.8 high (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705).

driving or operating machinery Status cataplecticus with prolonged, near-continuous cataplexy Abrupt withdrawal of anticataplectic therapy precipitating rebound cataplexy Attributing chronic sleepiness to lifestyle or depression and delaying diagnosis for years Missing cataplexy because patients do not volunteer it or it is mistaken for syncope or seizures Failing to screen for and address driving and occupational safety risks Overlooking a secondary hypothalamic cause in atypical or late-onset presentations Narcolepsy type 1 results from selective loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, most likely through an autoimmune process in genetically susceptible individuals carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02. Hypocretin normally stabilises wakefulness and suppresses inappropriate REM sleep; its deficiency destabilises the sleep-wake switch, producing daytime sleepiness and the intrusion of REM features such as cataplexy into wakefulness. Type 2 has preserved hypocretin levels and a less well-defined mechanism. Narcolepsy is a lifelong disorder, but symptoms can usually be controlled well enough with treatment and behavioural measures to allow good function. It carries important safety implications for driving and work, and untreated disease significantly impairs quality of life, mood, and daytime performance.

phenotype New seizures or encephalopathy Progressive visual loss impairing safety and function Cardiorespiratory compromise during metabolic stress Excluding a mitochondrial disorder because lactate is normal, which is common in NARP Failing to recognise the NARP-Leigh continuum and its dependence on heteroplasmy level Attributing retinitis pigmentosa to an isolated retinal dystrophy and missing the systemic mitochondrial cause Not counselling about maternal inheritance and variable transmission of mutant load to offspring NARP arises from point mutations in MT-ATP6, which encodes a subunit of ATP synthase (respiratory-chain complex V). The mutations impair proton flux through the enzyme and reduce ATP generation while altering mitochondrial membrane potential. Because the gene is mitochondrial, inheritance is maternal and the mutation is heteroplasmic, so the phenotype depends on the mutant load within energy-dependent tissues. Neurons of the peripheral nerves, cerebellum and retina, which have high and sustained energy requirements, are preferentially affected, producing the neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa. At very high mutant proportions the same defect causes the more severe maternally inherited Leigh phenotype. NARP tends to run a slowly progressive course with episodic worsening during metabolic stress; visual, sensory and cerebellar disability accumulate over time, and prognosis is worse at high mutant loads where a Leigh-type picture may supervene.

Nasal fracture — fractured nose, broken nose, nasal bone fracture Naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture Septal haematoma or septal fracture without nasal bone fracture Nasal soft tissue contusion without fracture Associated midface (Le Fort) or orbital fracture Pre-existing nasal deformity mistaken for acute injury Frontal sinus or skull base fracture with CSF leak Clinical examination for external deformity, mobility, and airflow Internal nasal examination with a speculum to exclude septal haematoma Pre-injury photographs to assess the original nasal shape CT when naso-orbito-ethmoid, midface, clinical, based on deformity, swelling, epistaxis, tenderness, and mobility or crepitus of the nasal bridge Plain radiographs add little to management, so imaging is reserved for suspicion of associated injuries such as naso-orbito-ethmoid or midface fractures The nose should be examined internally with a speculum to exclude a septal haematoma, which is the key finding not to miss A septal haematoma requires prompt drainage because untreated it can cause septal cartilage necrosis, perforation, and a saddle-nose deformity It is important to establish the pre-injury shape of the nose, often with a photograph, to judge post-traumatic deformity accurately Reduction, when needed, is best performed either within the first few hours before swelling develops or after several days once swelling subsides but before the fracture sets, generally within about two weeks Persistent deformity or nasal obstruction after healing may need later formal septorhinoplasty rather than early manipulation Clear rhinorrhoea after nasal trauma should raise concern for a CSF leak from an associated skull base or cribriform injury Septal haematoma requiring urgent drainage to prevent cartilage necrosis Clear rhinorrhoea suggesting a CSF leak from skull base or cribriform injury Telecanthus, medial canthal disruption, or features of a naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture Uncontrolled epistaxis or signs of a more extensive midface fracture Failing to examine the septum and missing a septal haematoma Relying on plain radiographs, which rarely change management Attempting reduction during peak swelling, giving an inaccurate result Delaying reduction beyond the window in which the fracture can be manipulated Overlooking an associated naso-orbito-ethmoid or skull base injury Not documenting the pre-injury appearance, leading to unrealistic expectations The prominent, relatively thin nasal bones and the cartilaginous septum are readily displaced by frontal or lateral trauma. Lateral forces tend to displace the nasal bones to one side, while frontal impact can flatten and splay the bones and buckle the septum. Bleeding into the subperichondrial space of the septum forms a septal haematoma, which strips the perichondrium from the cartilage and deprives it of its blood supply; the resulting ischaemia and any superimposed infection can destroy the cartilage, leading to septal perforation and loss of dorsal support (saddle deformity). Higher-energy injuries may extend into the naso-orbito-ethmoid region or the skull base. Most isolated nasal fractures heal well, and timely closed reduction gives good cosmetic and functional results in many patients. A proportion are left with residual deformity or nasal obstruction that may require later septorhinoplasty. The main preventable adverse outcome is the saddle-nose deformity and septal perforation that follow an undrained septal haematoma.

malignancy or other lesions Unilateral polyp with bleeding or an atypical firm appearance suggesting malignancy or angiofibroma Orbital signs such as proptosis, diplopia or visual disturbance indicating spread A polypoidal mass in a child that could be an encephalocoele, warranting caution before biopsy Rapid growth, facial pain or cranial nerve involvement Assuming all nasal masses are benign polyps and missing a tumour or angiofibroma Biopsying a suspected polyp in a child without first excluding an encephalocoele Relying on surgery alone without ongoing medical control of underlying inflammation Overlooking associated asthma and aspirin sensitivity Nasal polyps are pedunculated masses of oedematous, chronically inflamed sinonasal mucosa, most often stemming from persistent inflammation in the ethmoid region. Ongoing mucosal inflammation, frequently eosinophil-rich, causes fluid accumulation within the lamina propria, and gravity together with impaired lymphatic drainage encourages the mucosa to prolapse into the nasal cavity as polyps. Contributing factors include chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin sensitivity and, in children, cystic fibrosis. The antrochoanal polyp arises from maxillary sinus mucosa, passes through its ostium and enlarges into the choana and nasopharynx. Nasal polyps are benign but tend to be chronic and recurrent, particularly in association with asthma and aspirin sensitivity; symptoms are usually controllable with combined medical and surgical management, though repeated treatment is often needed.

otitis media in an adult, which mandates nasopharyngeal examination to exclude this tumour A persistent painless neck mass, especially in the upper deep cervical chain Blood-stained nasal or postnasal simple Eustachian tube dysfunction without examining the nasopharynx Attributing a neck node to benign causes and delaying evaluation of the primary Taking an inadequate or superficial biopsy of a submucosal tumour Underestimating skull base and perineural spread by relying on CT alone rather than MRI Overlooking cranial nerve findings as unrelated Nasopharyngeal carcinoma develops in the epithelial lining of the nasopharynx, typically in the recess of the fossa of Rosenmuller near the Eustachian tube opening. Malignant transformation is closely linked to latent Epstein-Barr virus infection, together with genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures such as diets rich in preserved salted foods and nitrosamines. The tumour tends to spread submucosally and infiltrate early, obstructing the Eustachian tube to cause middle ear effusion, and eroding through the skull base foramina to involve cranial nerves and the cavernous sinus. Its rich lymphatic drainage leads to early and often bilateral cervical lymph node metastasis, and distant spread to bone, lung and liver can occur. Outcome depends heavily on stage at presentation; early disease treated with radiotherapy has a favourable prognosis, whereas advanced disease with skull base invasion or distant metastasis carries a poorer outlook, and the frequently late presentation makes vigilance for early signs important.

before symptoms appear Confusing it with dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and overlooking recessive inheritance and family risk Permitting intense exercise, which accelerates the cardiomyopathy Not distinguishing it from the desmoplakin-related Carvajal syndrome Naxos disease is caused by recessive variants in JUP, which encodes plakoglobin, a component of the desmosomes and adherens junctions that mechanically couple cells. Because plakoglobin is expressed in both cardiac muscle and the epidermis, its dysfunction weakens cell-cell adhesion in both tissues. In the heart, impaired desmosomal integrity under mechanical stress leads to myocyte death and fibrofatty replacement, creating an arrhythmogenic substrate akin to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. In the skin and hair follicles, defective adhesion produces the woolly hair and palmoplantar keratoderma that characterise the syndrome. The cutaneous features are benign, but the associated arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is progressive and carries a significant risk of ventricular arrhythmia, heart failure and sudden death; early recognition through the skin phenotype allows timely cardiac surveillance and risk reduction.

Necrotizing Enterocolitis — NEC, necrotising enterocolitis Neonatal sepsis with ileus Spontaneous intestinal perforation Malrotation with midgut volvulus Hirschsprung enterocolitis Infectious gastroenteritis Milk protein intolerance / allergic colitis Supine and lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral abdominal radiographs for pneumatosis, portal gas, or free air Full blood count (looking for neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) and inflammatory markers Blood culture and blood gas with lactate Serum electrolytes and glucose, coagulation studies Abdominal ultrasound to assess bowel wall perfusion and free fluid The most common acquired gastrointestinal emergency of the newborn, occurring mainly in preterm, low-birth-weight infants and usually within the first weeks after birth. Presentation ranges from feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, and bloody stools to systemic signs such as lethargy, temperature instability, apnoea, and shock. The pathognomonic radiographic sign is pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas); portal venous gas and free intraperitoneal air are more ominous findings. Prematurity is the dominant risk factor; enteral feeding, particularly with formula, and intestinal dysbiosis are contributory, while human milk is protective. Initial management is medical: stop enteral feeds, decompress the bowel with a nasogastric tube, give intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and provide supportive care. Serial abdominal radiographs and clinical review guide progression; free air on imaging indicates perforation and the need for surgery. Surgical options include peritoneal drainage or laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel, sometimes with a stoma. The Bell staging system grades severity from suspected to advanced disease with perforation and is used to guide management. Extensive resection can leave short bowel syndrome with long-term dependence on parenteral nutrition. Free intraperitoneal air indicating perforation Portal venous gas Persistent metabolic acidosis or rising lactate Thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, or evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation Abdominal wall erythema, fixed mass, or clinical deterioration despite medical therapy Attributing early nonspecific signs to feeding intolerance and delaying evaluation Advancing enteral feeds too rapidly in vulnerable preterm infants Missing a subtle pneumoperitoneum on a single supine film Underestimating rapid clinical deterioration and delaying surgical consultation Overlooking strictures that can develop weeks after apparent recovery Necrotizing enterocolitis reflects a multifactorial injury to the immature intestine. An excessive inflammatory response of the immature gut mucosa, altered microbial colonisation, ischaemia or impaired mucosal perfusion, and enteral substrate combine to cause mucosal injury, bacterial translocation, and gas production within the bowel wall. Progression leads to full-thickness necrosis, perforation, peritonitis, and systemic inflammatory response with sepsis and shock. Outcome depends on gestational age and severity; mild disease often resolves with medical management, but advanced disease requiring surgery carries substantial mortality and long-term morbidity including strictures, short bowel syndrome, and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.

with a neuromuscular junction disorder Assuming a normal creatine kinase excludes a congenital myopathy Nemaline myopathy is a congenital myopathy caused by variants in genes encoding thin-filament and Z-disc-associated proteins of the skeletal muscle sarcomere, including nebulin, skeletal alpha-actin, and the tropomyosin and troponin genes. Disruption of thin-filament assembly and regulation impairs force generation and leads to the aggregation of Z-disc material into the characteristic rod-like inclusions. The resulting contractile dysfunction produces predominantly proximal, facial and bulbar weakness with notable respiratory muscle involvement.
