Outcome depends strongly on subtype: the severe neonatal form carries a high risk of early respiratory failure, whereas typical congenital and milder forms are often static or slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival and useful function. Respiratory surveillance is the key determinant of long-term outcome.

Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome — NAS, neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, NOWS Neonatal sepsis or infection Hypoglycaemia Hypocalcaemia or other electrolyte disturbance Hyperthyroidism (neonatal thyrotoxicosis) Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Central nervous system haemorrhage or injury Serial standardised withdrawal scoring (e.g. modified Finnegan) or function-based assessment Maternal history of substance use and prescribed medications Toxicology testing of infant urine, meconium, or other matrices where appropriate Blood glucose monitoring Electrolytes and calcium if clinically indicated Sepsis screen when infection cannot be excluded A constellation of withdrawal signs in a newborn following intrauterine exposure to substances, most commonly opioids, that the infant is no longer receiving after birth. Signs typically involve central nervous system irritability, autonomic disturbance, and gastrointestinal dysfunction. Common features include tremors, high-pitched crying, poor sleep, irritability, hypertonia, sweating, sneezing, nasal stuffiness, feeding difficulty, vomiting, and loose stools. The timing of onset depends on the substance and its half-life; short-acting opioids produce earlier withdrawal, while longer-acting agents may delay onset for days. Standardised scoring tools are used to assess severity and guide whether pharmacological treatment is needed. First-line care emphasises supportive, non-pharmacological measures such as a low-stimulation environment, swaddling, gentle handling, and rooming-in with the mother. The Eat, Sleep, Console approach focuses on the infant's function rather than symptom counts alone. When supportive care is insufficient, opioid-based pharmacological treatment is used with gradual weaning; polysubstance exposure and breastfeeding considerations should also be addressed. Seizures attributable to withdrawal Severe feeding intolerance with dehydration or poor weight gain Excessive weight loss or failure to thrive Marked autonomic instability or persistent high scores despite supportive care Signs suggesting an alternative serious diagnosis such as sepsis or hypoglycaemia Difficulty consoling with escalating pharmacological requirements Relying on medication before optimising non-pharmacological, function-focused care Excessive handling and stimulation that worsen the infant's symptoms Overlooking polysubstance exposure, which alters the withdrawal course Missing concurrent problems such as sepsis or hypoglycaemia Inconsistent scoring between assessors leading to inappropriate treatment decisions Neglecting maternal support, breastfeeding counselling, and social care coordination During pregnancy, drugs that cross the placenta reach the fetus and lead to physiological dependence, particularly with opioids acting on central opioid receptors. After delivery the sudden loss of transplacental drug supply removes this stimulation, producing a hyperexcitable state affecting the central and autonomic nervous systems and the gastrointestinal tract. The resulting neurotransmitter imbalance manifests as the characteristic irritability, autonomic instability, and feeding disturbance; the pattern and timing vary with the specific agent, dose, and its pharmacokinetics. Acute withdrawal is usually self-limited and manageable, and most infants recover well with appropriate supportive and, when needed, pharmacological care; longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes are influenced more by the broader social and environmental context, so coordinated family support and follow-up are important.

Neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy belongs to the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, in which recessive mutations in PEX genes prevent the normal assembly of functional peroxisomes. Because the organelle itself is defective, the many enzymatic functions it houses are lost together: beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids fails so these accumulate, alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid is impaired, bile acid synthesis is incomplete, and plasmalogen biosynthesis is deficient. The combined biochemical disturbance disrupts membrane and myelin formation and produces toxic lipid accumulation, leading to the progressive leukodystrophy, adrenocortical dysfunction, hepatic disease and multisystem involvement that characterise the disorder. Neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy is progressive with a poor prognosis; although milder than classic Zellweger syndrome, most affected children have severe neurodevelopmental impairment and shortened survival, with outcome depending on residual peroxisomal function.

rising ATP normally closes the channel, depolarising the cell and triggering secretion. Activating mutations in KCNJ11 or ABCC8 hold the channel open, preventing depolarisation and impairing insulin release, yet high-affinity sulfonylureas can close the channel independently of ATP and restore secretion. INS mutations instead cause misfolding of proinsulin and beta-cell stress, while chromosome 6q24 abnormalities perturb imprinted growth-regulating genes and typically produce transient disease. Prognosis varies by genotype: many KATP channel cases achieve excellent control on sulfonylureas with potential neurodevelopmental benefit, transient forms may remit though relapse is common, while syndromic and INS-related forms carry a more guarded outlook.

recurrence risk and the opportunity for maternal treatment in future pregnancies Delaying alloimmune-directed therapy while awaiting confirmatory tests in a deteriorating neonate In gestational alloimmune liver disease, maternal immunoglobulin G antibodies directed against a fetal hepatocyte antigen cross the placenta and activate the complement cascade on fetal liver cells, causing widespread hepatocyte injury and necrosis in utero. The resulting fetal liver failure disturbs the regulation of iron transport across the placenta, leading to excessive iron loading of fetal tissues. Iron therefore accumulates in the liver and in extrahepatic parenchymal sites such as the pancreas, heart, and salivary and other glands, characteristically sparing the reticuloendothelial system. The severe hepatic dysfunction present at birth reflects damage that began during gestation, and the same maternal alloimmunity tends to recur in later pregnancies. Untreated the condition carries a very high mortality from neonatal liver failure, but alloimmune-directed therapy and, when needed, liver transplantation have improved survival; recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is common and can be mitigated by maternal treatment during gestation.

Neonatal Hypoglycaemia — low blood sugar in newborn, hypoglycaemia of the newborn, neonatal low glucose Sepsis Neonatal seizures from other causes Hypocalcaemia or other electrolyte disturbance Congenital hyperinsulinism Panhypopituitarism or cortisol deficiency Inborn errors of metabolism Confirmatory laboratory plasma glucose Critical sample during hypoglycaemia (insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, free fatty acids) when persistent Serum electrolytes and calcium Sepsis screen if clinically indicated Metabolic screen (ammonia, lactate, acylcarnitine profile) in recurrent or refractory cases Low blood glucose is common in the transitional period after birth as the newborn adapts from continuous placental glucose supply to intermittent feeding. Infants at highest risk include those of diabetic mothers, large- or small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm infants, and any newborn who is stressed, cold, or septic. Signs are often subtle and non-specific: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, temperature instability, apnoea, or seizures; many affected infants appear asymptomatic. At-risk and symptomatic infants should be screened with bedside glucose testing, with low values confirmed on a laboratory sample given the imprecision of point-of-care meters. Early and frequent feeding is the first-line measure; infants who cannot maintain adequate glucose or who are symptomatic require intravenous dextrose. Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with a documented low glucose that resolves when glucose is normalised (Whipple triad) warrants investigation and treatment. Persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the first days of life suggests an underlying disorder such as hyperinsulinism, endocrine deficiency, or an inborn error of metabolism. The clinical concern is that prolonged or severe low glucose can injure the developing brain, so prevention and prompt correction are priorities. Seizures, apnoea, or coma Persistent hypoglycaemia despite feeding and initial glucose infusion High glucose infusion requirement suggesting hyperinsulinism Recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the transitional period Associated hypotonia, poor feeding, or encephalopathy Treating an isolated low bedside meter reading without confirming on a laboratory sample or clinical context Assuming all at-risk infants are symptomatic, or dismissing subtle signs as normal newborn behaviour Failing to investigate hypoglycaemia that persists or recurs beyond the first days of life Overlooking hyperinsulinism when a high rate of glucose infusion is needed to keep glucose normal After the cord is cut, the newborn loses its steady maternal glucose supply and must mobilise hepatic glycogen, activate gluconeogenesis, and use alternative fuels such as ketones and lactate, processes driven by a surge in counter-regulatory hormones and a fall in insulin. When glycogen stores are limited (prematurity, growth restriction), glucose demand is high (stress, sepsis, hypothermia), or insulin secretion is excessive (infant of a diabetic mother, hyperinsulinism), this adaptation fails and blood glucose falls. Because the neonatal brain depends heavily on glucose, inadequate supply combined with immature ketogenesis in some infants places the brain at risk. Brief, promptly treated transitional hypoglycaemia in an otherwise well infant usually has an excellent outcome, whereas severe, prolonged, symptomatic, or recurrent hypoglycaemia carries a risk of long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

Physiological jaundice appears after the first 24 hours, peaks around days 3-5 in term infants, and resolves without harm; it reflects normal neonatal bilirubin handling. Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological and demands urgent evaluation, commonly for haemolysis. Key pathological causes include blood-group incompatibility (Rh, ABO), G6PD deficiency, sepsis, and other haemolytic conditions. Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia is never physiological and requires investigation for cholestasis, notably biliary atresia, which needs early surgery. Breastfeeding-associated (early, from inadequate intake) and breast-milk (later, prolonged) jaundice are common benign patterns once other causes are excluded. Management depends on bilirubin level plotted against age in hours and risk factors; phototherapy is first-line and exchange transfusion is reserved for dangerously high or rapidly rising levels. The feared complication is bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction (acute encephalopathy progressing to kernicterus), which is preventable with timely treatment. Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life Rapidly rising bilirubin or a level near the exchange-transfusion threshold Signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia progressing to hypertonia, high-pitched cry, arching Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pale stools, and dark urine suggesting biliary atresia Prolonged jaundice beyond two weeks (term) or three weeks (preterm) requiring evaluation Dismissing jaundice in the first 24 hours as physiological Failing to fractionate bilirubin and missing cholestasis / biliary atresia Assessing jaundice by clinical appearance alone rather than measured bilirubin against age-specific thresholds Overlooking dehydration from inadequate feeding as a contributor in early breastfeeding jaundice Not investigating jaundice that persists beyond the expected period Newborns have increased bilirubin production from a high red cell mass with shorter red cell lifespan, combined with immature hepatic conjugation (low UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity) and enhanced enterohepatic recirculation of bilirubin. These factors produce transient physiological unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Pathological jaundice arises when production is excessive (haemolysis, extravasated blood), conjugation or uptake is impaired, or excretion is obstructed (cholestasis). Unbound unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and can cross the blood-brain barrier, depositing in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei to cause neurotoxicity. Most neonatal jaundice is benign and resolves without sequelae; with appropriate monitoring and treatment, kernicterus is largely preventable, but untreated severe hyperbilirubinaemia can cause permanent neurological injury.

Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome — hyaline membrane disease, RDS, surfactant deficiency disease, respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Neonatal pneumonia or early-onset sepsis (especially group B streptococcus) Meconium aspiration syndrome Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Congenital heart disease Air-leak syndromes (pneumothorax) Chest radiograph to assess the reticulogranular pattern and lung volumes Arterial or capillary blood gas to quantify hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis Pulse oximetry and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring Blood culture and inflammatory markers when sepsis cannot be excluded Blood glucose and electrolyte monitoring Echocardiography if congenital heart disease or pulmonary hypertension is suspected A disease of surfactant deficiency affecting mainly preterm infants; incidence rises steeply as gestational age falls, being greatest below about 28 weeks. Distress typically begins at or soon after birth with tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal recession, and cyanosis that worsen over the first hours to days. Chest radiograph classically shows a diffuse fine reticulogranular (ground-glass) pattern with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Antenatal maternal corticosteroids given before anticipated preterm delivery accelerate lung maturation and markedly reduce incidence and severity. Exogenous surfactant replacement, delivered into the airway, is a cornerstone of treatment and improves oxygenation and survival. Early nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) helps maintain functional residual capacity and can reduce the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation. Maternal diabetes, male sex, second-born twins, caesarean delivery without labour, and perinatal asphyxia increase risk, whereas chronic intrauterine stress and prolonged rupture of membranes may reduce it. Untreated disease tends to worsen for about 2-3 days before recovery begins, often heralded by a spontaneous diuresis. This causes progressive diffuse atelectasis, reduced lung compliance, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia with acidosis follow, and pulmonary vascular resistance may remain elevated with right-to-left shunting. Epithelial injury and protein-rich exudate form the hyaline membranes that give the disease its historical name, further impairing gas exchange. With antenatal steroids, surfactant, and modern respiratory support, survival is high, particularly in more mature preterm infants; outcome worsens with decreasing gestational age and with complications such as air leak, intraventricular haemorrhage, and progression to bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Neonatal Seizures — seizures in the newborn, neonatal convulsions, newborn fits Jitteriness or benign neonatal sleep myoclonus Apnoea of other cause Hypoglycaemia or electrolyte disturbance Meningitis or encephalitis Intracranial haemorrhage or perinatal stroke Inborn errors of metabolism and vitamin-responsive epilepsies EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG monitoring Blood glucose, electrolytes, calcium, and magnesium Cranial imaging (ultrasound and MRI) Lumbar puncture and sepsis evaluation when infection is possible Metabolic and genetic testing in unexplained or refractory cases Seizures in the newborn period are usually a symptom of an acute underlying brain insult rather than a chronic epilepsy, so the priority is to find and treat the cause. Presentations are often subtle: repetitive eye deviation or blinking, lip-smacking or chewing, cycling or boxing limb movements, and apnoea, in addition to clonic or tonic activity. Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is the most common cause; other important causes include stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, infection, metabolic disturbances, and inborn errors of metabolism. Because clinical signs are unreliable and electroclinical dissociation is common, EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG monitoring is central to accurate diagnosis. Immediate workup should exclude readily treatable causes such as hypoglycaemia and electrolyte abnormalities, correcting these before escalating anticonvulsant therapy. Non-epileptic movements like jitteriness can mimic seizures but are stimulus-sensitive, suppressible by gentle restraint, and lack autonomic or ocular features. Neuroimaging and, where appropriate, lumbar puncture and metabolic or genetic testing help establish aetiology and guide prognosis. Pyridoxine-dependent and other vitamin-responsive epilepsies should be considered when seizures are refractory to standard agents. Status epilepticus or very frequent recurrent seizures Seizures refractory to first-line therapy Encephalopathy with depressed consciousness and abnormal tone Signs of meningitis or sepsis Focal neurological deficits suggesting stroke or a structural lesion Relying on clinical observation alone and missing electrographic-only seizures Mistaking jitteriness or benign myoclonus for seizures and over-treating Escalating anticonvulsants before correcting hypoglycaemia or electrolyte abnormalities Failing to consider vitamin-responsive epilepsies in seizures resistant to standard drugs The immature neonatal brain is intrinsically more excitable because excitatory glutamatergic circuits mature earlier than inhibitory GABAergic systems, and GABA can be depolarising early in development. An acute insult, most often hypoxia-ischaemia, disrupts energy metabolism and ion gradients, leading to neuronal depolarisation and synchronised, excessive electrical discharges. Metabolic derangements, structural lesions, infection, or genetic and metabolic disorders lower the seizure threshold further. Frequent dissociation between electrical seizures and visible clinical signs reflects this immaturity and underlies the need for electrographic monitoring. Outcome depends largely on the underlying cause and the severity of any brain injury; seizures due to transient metabolic disturbances often resolve well, whereas those from severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury, major structural lesions, or certain genetic-metabolic disorders carry a higher risk of epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment.

Neonatal sepsis — sepsis neonatorum, newborn sepsis, early-onset neonatal sepsis, late-onset neonatal sepsis, EOS, LOS Transient tachypnoea of the newborn Respiratory distress syndrome Congenital heart disease with poor perfusion Inborn errors of metabolism Neonatal encephalopathy / birth asphyxia Congenital viral infection (e.g. herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus) Blood culture before starting antibiotics Complete blood count with differential and immature-to-total neutrophil ratio C-reactive protein and/or procalcitonin, ideally serially Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose and culture Urine culture (more relevant in late-onset disease) Chest radiograph if respiratory signs are present Blood glucose, electrolytes and blood gas to assess metabolic status A systemic bacterial (occasionally fungal or viral) infection in the first 28 days of life, conventionally split into early-onset (within roughly the first 72 hours, often maternally acquired) and late-onset (after 72 hours, frequently nosocomial or community-acquired). Signs are notoriously nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or hypothermia), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, respiratory distress, apnoea, tachycardia, and abdominal distension. Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli dominate early-onset disease; coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Gram-negative organisms are common in late-onset disease, especially in preterm infants with indwelling lines. Maternal risk factors include prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, maternal fever, and GBS colonisation without adequate intrapartum prophylaxis. Blood culture is the diagnostic gold standard; a lumbar puncture should be considered because meningitis frequently coexists and may be missed. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started promptly after cultures because deterioration can be rapid; the regimen is later narrowed to culture results. Supportive care (thermoregulation, respiratory and haemodynamic support, glucose management) is as important as antimicrobials. A low threshold for treatment is appropriate given nonspecific signs, but antibiotics are stopped early when cultures remain negative and the infant is well. Septic shock: poor perfusion, hypotension, prolonged capillary refill Apnoea or worsening respiratory failure requiring support Bulging fontanelle, seizures, or other signs suggesting meningitis Petechiae, purpura, or bleeding suggesting disseminated intravascular coagulation Persistent hypoglycaemia or profound metabolic acidosis Attributing nonspecific signs to prematurity or feeding issues and delaying evaluation Omitting a lumbar puncture and missing coexisting meningitis Relying on a single normal inflammatory marker to exclude sepsis early in the illness Failing to remove or consider infected central venous catheters in late-onset disease Neonates are relatively immunocompromised, with immature innate and adaptive defences, low immunoglobulin levels, and impaired neutrophil function. Organisms reach the infant by ascending or intrapartum transmission from the maternal genital tract in early-onset disease, or from the postnatal environment and invasive devices in late-onset disease. Once bloodstream invasion occurs, bacterial products trigger a systemic inflammatory response with cytokine release, endothelial injury, capillary leak, and impaired perfusion that can progress to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multi-organ dysfunction. The immature blood-brain barrier and limited containment of infection predispose to meningitis. Outcome depends on gestational age, organism, and speed of treatment; prompt therapy usually leads to recovery, but meningitis, shock, and prematurity carry higher mortality and risk of neurodevelopmental sequelae.

neuroendocrine markers (CD56/NCAM, synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) for SCLC Thoracentesis with cell block for suspected malignant pleural effusion (repeat if first sample negative) Spinal CT/MRI for suspected cord compression; brain/spine MRI plus lumbar puncture for suspected leptomeningeal disease Physiologic evaluation: spirometry (FEV1), DLCO, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (VO2max) before surgical resection Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disorders Benign pulmonary nodules (hamartoma, hamartochondroma) Pulmonary metastases from non-lung primaries Mesothelioma Paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes mimicking primary neurologic disease Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in the United States; over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease at diagnosis. Tobacco smoking accounts for roughly two-thirds of lung cancer deaths globally, but about 65% of new U.S. diagnoses are now in former smokers or never-smokers; one in five women and one in twelve men diagnosed have never smoked. The WHO divides epithelial lung cancers into four major types: small-cell carcinoma (SCLC) and three non-small-cell types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large-cell). Together these account for about 90% of epithelial lung cancers; adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype. Separating SCLC from NSCLC and, within NSCLC, squamous from nonsquamous histology is essential because natural history and management differ markedly; a generic diagnosis of 'non-small-cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified' is no longer acceptable. A chronic cough with or without hemoptysis in a current or former smoker with COPD aged 40 or older warrants thorough evaluation for lung cancer even with a normal chest x-ray; a persistent pneumonia unresponsive to repeated antibiotics also requires workup. Tissue sampling is required to confirm diagnosis in all suspected cases; a core biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration to provide adequate material for molecular and PD-L1 testing. Central, endobronchial lesions (squamous cell, small-cell, carcinoid) are more readily reached by bronchoscopy, whereas peripheral lesions (adenocarcinoma, large-cell) are more amenable to transthoracic biopsy. Driver oncogenes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, RET, NTRK, BRAF, MET, HER2, KRAS) are enriched in nonsquamous NSCLC and define distinct molecular cohorts; nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations. Paraneoplastic syndromes are common, especially with SCLC, and may be the presenting feature or first sign of recurrence; they can mimic metastatic disease and lead to inappropriately palliative rather than curative management. Hypercalcemia from ectopic PTH-related peptide is the most common life-threatening metabolic complication of malignancy and occurs primarily with squamous cell carcinoma. On FDG PET, a standardized uptake value (SUV) above 2.5 is highly suspicious for malignancy, but PET must never be used alone to diagnose cancer, nodal involvement, or metastasis because of false positives (infection, granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis) and false negatives (lesions under 8 mm, slow-growing tumors, diabetes). Adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (solitary lesions 3 cm or less with pure or predominant lepidic growth and 5 mm or less invasion) achieve near 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection. Hemoptysis in a smoker over 40 with chronic cough Hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) or superior vena cava syndrome Pancoast/superior sulcus presentation: shoulder pain radiating in ulnar distribution with destruction of first/second ribs, often with Horner syndrome Signs of cord compression: pain, weakness, paralysis, urinary retention Weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight (poor prognostic sign) Hypercalcemia with nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, altered mental status Symptomatic brain metastases (headache, nausea/vomiting, seizures, focal deficits) or pathologic fractures/bone pain A normal chest x-ray does not exclude lung cancer in a high-risk symptomatic smoker. Negative TTF-1 does not exclude a pulmonary primary; TTF-1 is also positive in neuroendocrine and thyroid tumors. PET-CT cannot establish a tissue diagnosis: false positives occur with tuberculosis/granulomatous and infectious disease and false negatives with sub-8 mm, slow-growing, or carcinoid/well-differentiated tumors. Paraneoplastic syndromes may be mistaken for metastatic disease, risking inappropriate palliative rather than curative treatment. A single negative thoracentesis does not exclude a malignant effusion; repeat sampling is essential. Diagnosing on small biopsy/cytology specimens may blur squamous-versus-nonsquamous distinction; repeat biopsy is advised in advanced disease for adequate molecular and PD-L1 testing. Low-dose CT screening carries a high false-positive rate (false-positive rate about 96% among positive screens in NLST), with attendant risks of overdiagnosis, unnecessary procedures, and radiation exposure. Inhaled environmental carcinogens, principally those in tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells to a malignant phenotype. Susceptibility is modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolizing genes (e.g., CYP1A1) and by genetic loci affecting nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and telomerase (5p15, 6p21, 15q25). Tumorigenesis reflects accumulation of gain-of-function mutations in oncogenes and loss-of-function mutations in tumor-suppressor genes, with the sequence differing by histologic type. Adenocarcinomas frequently harbor targetable driver alterations: activating receptor tyrosine kinase mutations (EGFR, HER2/ERBB2, MET), intracellular signaling mutations (KRAS, BRAF), and chromosomal rearrangements activating ALK, ROS1, RET, and NTRK. Squamous tumors may show FGFR1 amplification, DDR2 mutations, PIK3CA mutations/PTEN loss, and BRAF/MET alterations. Inactivated tumor suppressors include TP53, RB1, RASSF1A, CDKN2A/B, LKB1 (STK11), and FHIT; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. Clinical manifestations arise from central/endobronchial growth (cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, postobstructive pneumonia), peripheral growth (pleural/chest-wall pain, dyspnea, cavitation), regional intrathoracic spread (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness, phrenic nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, Pancoast syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome, pericardial/lymphatic involvement), distant metastasis, or paraneoplastic mechanisms. Outcome is strongly stage-dependent. For NSCLC by the eighth-edition TNM system, 5-year overall survival ranges from roughly 90% for the earliest (stage IA1) disease down to about 10% for stage IVB; SEER data report a 5-year survival of about 63% for localized NSCLC. Lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma has a favorable prognosis, acinar and papillary intermediate, and solid-predominant and micropapillary patterns poor. SCLC is more aggressive: 60-70% present with extensive-stage disease, and even in limited-stage SCLC median survival is roughly 12-20 months historically. Weight loss over 10% of body weight and thrombotic complications of malignancy are poor prognostic signs. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in over 50% of squamous, about 80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and over 95% of SCLC cases. NSCLC is staged with the eighth-edition (2018) TNM system: T1 (3 cm or less; subdivided T1a 1 cm or less, T1b over 1 to 2 cm, T1c over 2 to 3 cm), T2 (over 3 to 5 cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus involvement/atelectasis; T2a over 3 to 4 cm, T2b over 4 to 5 cm), T3 (over 5 to 7 cm or invasion of chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve or satellite nodule in same lobe), T4 (over 7 cm or invasion of mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, recurrent laryngeal nerve, esophagus, vertebra, carina, or separate nodule in a different ipsilateral lobe). Nodes: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or scalene/supraclavicular. Metastasis: M1a contralateral nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single extrathoracic metastasis, M1c multiple extrathoracic metastases. SCLC is commonly classified by the two-stage Veterans Administration system: limited-stage (confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port) versus extensive-stage (overt metastatic disease). Physiologic operability thresholds: FEV1 over 2 L or over 80% predicted suggests tolerance of pneumonectomy; FEV1 over 1.5 L suggests adequate reserve for lobectomy; VO2max under 15 mL/kg/min predicts higher postoperative risk; contraindications to thoracic surgery include FEV1 under 1 L, resting PCO2 over 45 mmHg, DLCO under 40%, severe pulmonary hypertension, and recent myocardial infarction.

X-linked disease results from loss-of-function mutations in AVPR2, the gene for the V2 vasopressin receptor, so hormone binding cannot trigger the intracellular signalling that normally inserts water channels into the apical membrane. Autosomal forms result from mutations in AQP2, the aquaporin-2 water channel itself, impairing its trafficking or function. Either defect prevents water reabsorption, producing large volumes of inappropriately dilute urine, a tendency to hypernatraemia and dehydration, and compensatory polydipsia. With early diagnosis, reliable access to water and volume-reducing measures, growth and development are usually preserved, but repeated episodes of severe hypernatraemic dehydration in infancy can cause lasting neurological injury.

Nephrolithiasis — Kidney stone disease, Renal calculi, Urolithiasis, Renal stones Acute cholecystitis (right ureteropelvic-junction stone) Acute appendicitis (stone at right pelvic brim) Acute diverticulitis (stone at left pelvic brim) Bacterial cystitis (ureterovesical-junction stone causing urgency/frequency) Acute pyelonephritis (obstructing stone with proximal infection) Musculoskeletal pain Herpes zoster Duodenal ulcer Abdominal aortic aneurysm Gynecologic conditions Ureteral stricture Ureteral obstruction by blood clot or sloughed papilla Extraluminal ureteral compression (typically gradual onset, not true colic) Acute pyelonephritis (an obstructing stone with proximal infection can present this way) Bacterial cystitis (ureterovesical stone causes urgency/frequency with red and white cells in urine but a negative urine culture) Noncontrast helical CT (gold standard; detects stones as small as 1 mm and uric acid stones) Renal ultrasound (avoids radiation, shows hydronephrosis, but insensitive for ureteral stones) Plain abdominal radiograph (KUB) (may miss ureteral/renal stones and gives no obstruction information) Urinalysis with sediment examination for red/white cells and crystals (calcium oxalate dihydrate = bipyramidal; cystine = hexagonal) Urine culture if infection is suspected Serum electrolytes (for hypokalemia/RTA), creatinine, calcium, phosphorus, uric acid PTH and 25-hydroxy vitamin D when serum/urine calcium is elevated or high/low-normal At least two 24-h urine collections on usual diet (volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, creatinine; supersaturation when available) Stone composition analysis of any passed or retrieved stone Acute cholecystitis Acute appendicitis Acute diverticulitis Abdominal aortic aneurysm Duodenal ulcer Herpes zoster Gynecologic conditions Musculoskeletal pain Calcium oxalate stones are by far the most common type (~75%), followed by calcium phosphate (~15%), uric acid (~8%), struvite (~1%), and cystine (<1%); many stones are mixtures and contain protein matrix (Harrison 22e p.2448). Identifying the stone type is clinically important because it informs prognosis and the choice of preventive strategy; patients should be encouraged to retrieve and submit passed stones for composition analysis (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452). The two classic acute presentations are renal colic and painless gross hematuria; symptom onset reflects a stone moving into the ureter and gives no clue as to when the stone actually formed, since stone growth is typically clinically silent over weeks to years (Harrison 22e p.2450). Pain radiation depends on stone location: an upper ureteral stone may radiate anteriorly, while a lower ureteral stone may radiate to the ipsilateral testicle (men) or labium (women); a ureterovesical-junction stone can cause urinary urgency and frequency (Harrison 22e p.2450). Absence of hematuria does not exclude a stone, particularly when urine flow is completely obstructed (Harrison 22e p.2450). Noncontrast helical CT is the gold-standard imaging test: it detects stones as small as 1 mm and visualizes uric acid stones that are traditionally considered radiolucent on plain films (Harrison 22e p.2450). Urine pH governs solubility of several stone types: uric acid stones form at pH consistently <=5.5, calcium phosphate stones are favored at pH >=6.5, and cystine is more soluble at higher pH; calcium oxalate stone risk is not influenced by urine pH (Harrison 22e p.2450). Urine citrate is the most clinically important natural inhibitor of calcium-containing stones; metabolic acidosis (including from high animal-flesh intake) lowers citrate excretion by enhancing its tubular reabsorption (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2449). Dietary calcium restriction is counterproductive: higher dietary calcium intake lowers stone risk by binding intestinal oxalate and reducing urinary oxalate, whereas low calcium intake increases stone risk and may lower bone density (Harrison 22e p.2449). Two 24-h urine collections on the patient's usual diet are the cornerstone of preventive evaluation, measuring volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, pH, and creatinine; two collections are needed because of substantial day-to-day variability (Harrison 22e p.2451-2452). Urinary risk factors (calcium, oxalate, citrate) are continuous variables with no valid normal/abnormal cutoff; dichotomizing them is misleading and arbitrary thresholds should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.2449, 2452). Pure uric acid stones can be recognized by their low Hounsfield units on CT, helping distinguish stone composition non-invasively (Harrison 22e p.2452). UTI in the setting of an obstructing stone is a urologic emergency ('pus under pressure') requiring urgent restoration of drainage via ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy Complete urinary obstruction by a stone (hematuria may be absent) Stone measuring >=6 mm or anatomic abnormality (low probability of spontaneous passage) Intractable pain unresponsive to analgesia Staghorn or multiple bilateral stones (suggest cystinuria or struvite/infection stones) Infection (struvite) stones, which if untreated can lead to end-stage renal disease Assuming a normal urinalysis (no hematuria) rules out a stone, which is false especially with complete obstruction Recommending low dietary calcium, which actually increases stone risk and harms bone density Using arbitrary normal/abnormal thresholds for urine calcium, oxalate, or citrate when risk is continuous Basing the preventive regimen on a single 24-h urine collection despite large day-to-day variability Mistaking a preexisting residual stone for a new stone when baseline imaging was suboptimal, leading to unnecessary changes in therapy Misattributing flank/abdominal pain to a stone and missing cholecystitis, appendicitis, diverticulitis, AAA, or an occlusive vascular event Failing to recognize that symptom onset does not indicate when the stone formed Stones form when urine becomes supersaturated with lithogenic solutes, i.e., when the concentration product exceeds the solubility product. Most people's urine is supersaturated for one or more crystal types, but crystallization inhibitors (notably urine citrate) prevent continuous stone formation. Recent biopsy data have shifted the paradigm for stone initiation: calcium phosphate deposits in the renal interstitium, hypothesized to begin at the thin limb of the loop of Henle, then extends to and erodes through the papillary epithelium, forming Randall's plaque on which most calcium oxalate stones grow. Tubular plugs of calcium phosphate may initiate calcium phosphate stones. Thus stone formation can begin years before a stone is clinically detectable. Higher urine calcium (from greater GI absorption and/or bone turnover) and higher urine oxalate (largely dietary, with higher dietary calcium reducing GI oxalate absorption) raise calcium oxalate/phosphate risk, while low urine citrate removes a key inhibitor (Harrison 22e p.2448-2450). Although renal colic is reported as among the worst pain patients experience, nephrolithiasis is rarely fatal. More than half of first-time stone formers have a recurrence within 10 years, but recurrence of most or all stone types can be prevented with careful evaluation and targeted, often lifelong, intervention. Untreated infection (struvite) stones can have devastating consequences and progress to end-stage renal disease, and repeated obstruction and instrumentation (e.g., in cystinuria) can reduce GFR. Primary hyperoxaluria can cause intraparenchymal calcium oxalate deposition leading to renal failure (Harrison 22e p.2448, 2450, 2451). No formal grading; clinical risk stratification rests on likelihood of spontaneous passage (stone size and location, e.g., >=6 mm or anatomic abnormality favoring intervention) and on presence of emergency features such as obstruction with superimposed infection.

Early features reflect impaired urinary concentration: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia and secondary enuresis, often with salt wasting Growth retardation and anaemia can be disproportionate to the distinguishing it from polycystic kidney disease with its large kidneys Extrarenal ciliopathy features may coexist, including retinal degeneration (Senior-Loken syndrome), cerebellar vermis hypoplasia (Joubert syndrome), liver fibrosis and skeletal changes Blood pressure is often normal until late, unlike many other progressive nephropathies Progressive decline toward kidney failure requiring planning for kidney replacement therapy Marked polyuria with dehydration and electrolyte disturbance Visual symptoms suggesting associated retinal degeneration Neurological signs suggesting a syndromic ciliopathy such as Joubert syndrome Expecting enlarged kidneys and dismissing the diagnosis when ultrasound shows normal-sized echogenic kidneys Missing the diagnosis in a child with unexplained polyuria, anaemia and growth failure Failing to screen for retinal and neurological extrarenal manifestations Attributing early salt wasting and polyuria to a primary concentrating defect without considering nephronophthisis Nephronophthisis is an inherited ciliopathy in which variants in NPHP genes disrupt proteins (nephrocystins) that localise to the primary cilium, basal body and cell junctions of renal tubular epithelial cells. Impaired ciliary signalling and planar cell polarity disturb tubular development, cell adhesion and repair, leading to a chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular basement membrane disruption, interstitial fibrosis and small corticomedullary cysts. Because the concentrating mechanism is affected early, the disease presents with polyuria and salt wasting before progressing to fibrosis and kidney failure. The same ciliary dysfunction in other organs accounts for the associated retinal, cerebellar, hepatic and skeletal syndromes. Nephronophthisis is progressive and typically leads to kidney failure, with the age of onset varying by subtype (infantile, juvenile and adolescent forms); the juvenile form commonly reaches kidney failure in the teenage years. Outcome after transplantation is generally good as the disease does not recur in the graft.

Periorbital, facial and eyelid swelling (worst on waking) helps distinguish nephrotic oedema from the dependent oedema/orthopnoea of heart failure; penile and scrotal oedema may be severe enough to obstruct urinary flow in men (p.324, p.2358). Relying on dipstick alone — it misses light chains, so myeloma-associated overflow proteinuria can be overlooked; total protein:creatinine ratio is not specific for albumin (p.385, p.2357). Equating subnephrotic albuminuria with absence of significant glomerular disease — focal disease causes lower albuminuria yet can be significant (p.2357). Misreading biopsy-proven FSGS as a single entity — primary podocytopathic FSGS, secondary/adaptive FSGS, and post-GN healing scars are distinct (p.2356, p.2398). Nephrotic syndrome reflects increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins. Minimal change disease causes diffuse fusion (effacement) of podocyte foot processes producing predominantly 'selective' albumin loss, whereas immune-complex disruption of the basement membrane and slit diaphragms yields 'nonselective' loss of albumin and larger proteins. Hypoalbuminaemia results from urinary loss plus increased proximal-tubule catabolism of filtered albumin, exceeding hepatic synthesis (a hypercatabolic, negative-nitrogen-balance state). Oedema arises from renal sodium retention and reduced plasma oncotic pressure; perceived reduction in effective intravascular volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, AVP and the sympathetic nervous system, and filtered proteases can directly activate the epithelial Na channel (ENaC) in principal cells, promoting further salt/water retention. Hyperlipidaemia/hypercholesterolaemia reflect increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Notably, hypertension is uncommon in primary kidney diseases causing nephrotic syndrome (p.385). Hereditary nephrotic syndrome can result from podocyte slit-diaphragm gene mutations (nephrin NPHS1, podocin NPHS2); APOL1 risk variants predispose to FSGS, with disease expression triggered by a 'second hit' of infection/inflammation damaging podocytes and glomerular endothelium (p.2357-2358). Glomerular proteinuria in diabetes typically appears after years of small-vessel disease (hence frequent coexistent retinopathy) and predicts progression to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure; the rate of progression is faster with hypertension, obesity and poor glucose control. Diffuse glomerular involvement (most glomeruli) makes nephrotic syndrome likely, whereas focal disease (<50% of glomeruli) tends to give subnephrotic albuminuria. In membranous nephropathy, ~70% of primary cases are anti-PLA2R associated. Collapsing glomerulopathy (HIVAN) is a severe, treatment-resistant FSGS variant. Quartan malarial nephropathy responds poorly to therapy (p.2356-2358). Albuminuria categories (Ch.55 Fig.55-3): moderately increased 30-300 mg/d or mg/g (formerly microalbuminuria); severely increased 300-3500 mg/d or mg/g (formerly macroalbuminuria); nephrotic range >3500 mg/d or mg/g. Full nephrotic syndrome defined by the triad of oedema, hypoalbuminaemia (<3.5 g/dL) and proteinuria >3.5 g/d, usually with lipid abnormalities (high LDL, low HDL, lipiduria) (p.385, p.2357).

Nephrotic syndrome (paediatric) — childhood nephrotic syndrome, idiopathic nephrotic syndrome, minimal change disease, paediatric nephrotic syndrome Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome) Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Membranous nephropathy (uncommon in children) Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis Systemic lupus erythematosus nephritis Congenital nephrotic syndrome in infants Oedema from cardiac, hepatic, or nutritional causes Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or timed collection) Serum albumin, total protein, and lipid profile Renal function and electrolytes Full blood count Complement levels and autoimmune serology when nephritic features are present Renal biopsy in atypical or steroid-resistant cases Defined by the tetrad of heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. In children it is most often idiopathic, and minimal change disease is the predominant histology, especially in preschool children. Oedema is the usual presenting feature, typically starting periorbitally and becoming generalised with dependent swelling and sometimes ascites. Most childhood cases are steroid-responsive, so an empirical corticosteroid trial is standard first-line therapy without initial biopsy in the typical age group. Renal biopsy is reserved for atypical features: older or very young age, gross haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance. Children are at increased risk of infection (notably pneumococcal peritonitis) from urinary immunoglobulin loss, and of thromboembolism from a hypercoagulable state. Supportive care includes sensible salt restriction, careful management of oedema, and attention to nutrition and infection prevention including vaccination. Relapses are common; the pattern of response guides classification into steroid-sensitive, frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant disease. Fever with abdominal pain suggesting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Signs of thromboembolism (limb swelling, respiratory distress, neurological signs) Hypertension, gross haematuria, or reduced renal function suggesting a nephritic process Severe hypovolaemia from rapid fluid shifts, or tense ascites and respiratory compromise Steroid resistance prompting reassessment and biopsy Attributing oedema to another cause and missing proteinuria on urinalysis Overlooking infection or thrombosis, the major acute complications Missing atypical features that warrant biopsy rather than empirical steroids Aggressive diuresis precipitating hypovolaemia and thrombosis in an intravascularly depleted child Injury to the glomerular filtration barrier, particularly the podocytes and their slit diaphragms, increases permeability to plasma proteins, producing heavy albuminuria. In minimal change disease, light microscopy is near-normal and electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement, implicating a circulating permeability factor and immune dysregulation. Urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and, together with secondary sodium retention, causing oedema. The liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low oncotic pressure, producing hyperlipidaemia. Loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors predisposes to infection, and loss of anticoagulant proteins with raised procoagulants predisposes to thrombosis. Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have a good long-term renal outcome despite frequent relapses; steroid resistance, often from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.

toxicology screen in unexplained encephalopathy Somatosensory evoked potentials (N20) and neuron-specific enolase for post-arrest prognostication Carboxyhemoglobin measurement for suspected carbon monoxide poisoning Bubble study (agitated saline echocardiography) to evaluate right-to-left shunt after embolic infarction in transplant patients Sedative/analgesic or polypharmacy-induced delirium misattributed to depression Postcardiac bypass microembolic encephalopathy Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) neurotoxicity / PRES, possible even at normal drug levels Checkpoint inhibitor immune encephalitis and CAR-T neurotoxicity Posthypoxic myoclonus / myoclonic status epilepticus after cardiac arrest Korsakoff amnestic state evolving from Wernicke's disease Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) equals mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus intracranial pressure (ICP); the general targets in neurocritical care are ICP below 20 mmHg and CPP at or above 60 mmHg (Harrison 22e p.2345). Cerebral autoregulation normally keeps cerebral blood flow constant across a wide MAP range, but in severe brain injury it can be lost, making flow directly pressure-dependent so that hypotension causes ischemia and hypertension causes hyperperfusion (Harrison 22e p.2343-2344). Cerebral blood flow rises with hypercapnia/acidosis and falls with hypocapnia/alkalosis, which is the basis for short-term hyperventilation to lower ICP; the effect is short-lived (hours) due to interstitial buffering, and abrupt discontinuation can cause rebound ICP elevation (Harrison 22e p.2344, p.2345). In altered consciousness, the first task is to separate a diffuse/metabolic process from a focal/structural one; prominent focal signs such as pupillary asymmetry, hemiparesis, gaze palsy, or visual field deficit suggest a structural lesion and mandate urgent neuroimaging (Harrison 22e p.2344). After cardiac arrest, poor-prognosis indicators include absent pupillary light reflex or extensor/absent motor response to pain at days 5-7, bilateral absence of the N20 somatosensory evoked potential component, a burst-suppression or nonreactive EEG, and a markedly elevated neuron-specific enolase (NSE), but sedation, metabolic derangements, and hypothermia confound these signs (Harrison 22e p.2346). Osmotic demyelination syndrome (formerly central pontine myelinolysis) is typically precipitated by rapid correction of hyponatremia or hyperosmolar states, presenting days later with quadriplegia and pseudobulbar palsy; corrective sodium changes should be limited to roughly 8 mmol/L per 24 h and 15 mmol/L per 48 h (Harrison 22e p.2348-2349). Wernicke's disease is a thiamine-deficiency emergency; only about one-third of patients show the classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and global confusion, and IV glucose can precipitate or worsen it, so thiamine must precede glucose in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.2349). Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) reflects hyperperfusion/vasogenic edema favoring posterior (occipital) regions; the rate of blood pressure rise rather than the absolute value is the key risk factor, and the syndrome is not always reversible or strictly posterior (Harrison 22e p.2349-2350). Sepsis-associated encephalopathy is a diffuse brain dysfunction without focal findings, occurs in the majority of patients with sepsis and multiorgan failure, and is not simply explained by metabolic derangements; cytokines such as TNF and interleukins are implicated (Harrison 22e p.2348). Critical illness polyneuropathy is the most common PNS complication of prolonged critical illness and sepsis; it is a distal axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and should be suspected when a patient fails to wean from the ventilator despite resolving sepsis (Harrison 22e p.2351). Persistent neuromuscular junction weakness in the ICU is almost always drug-related, most often from nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium, cisatracurium) and potentiated by aminoglycosides; recovery is full once the drug is cleared (Harrison 22e p.2351-2352). In PNS weakness, intubation should be considered when maximal inspiratory force falls below -25 cmH2O or vital capacity is under 1 L, and the decision should be clinical rather than waiting for oxygen desaturation or CO2 retention (Harrison 22e p.2351). antibiotics for suspected bacterial meningitis while awaiting diagnostic studies Attributing the hypoactive confusional state of microembolic encephalopathy after cardiac surgery to depression or sedative delirium Giving IV glucose before thiamine in malnourished/alcoholic patients, precipitating or worsening Wernicke's disease Correcting hyponatremia too rapidly and triggering osmotic demyelination syndrome Assuming normal serum calcineurin inhibitor levels exclude drug-induced PRES or neurotoxicity Prolonged or unmonitored use of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers leading to persistent blockade or thick-filament myopathy (use lowest effective dose with peripheral nerve stimulator monitoring) Using glucocorticoids for ICP in head trauma or ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke, where they are not indicated (reserved for vasogenic edema from tumor or abscess) Sustained or aggressive hyperventilation, which can worsen cerebral ischemia and cause rebound ICP on discontinuation Life-threatening neurologic illness in the critically ill arises from primary lesions anywhere along the neuraxis or as a consequence of systemic disorders (hepatic failure, multiorgan failure, cardiac arrest). The unifying goal is preventing secondary brain injury from ischemia, hemorrhage, edema, herniation, and elevated ICP. Brain edema is vasogenic (fluid crossing an incompetent blood-brain barrier) and/or cytotoxic (cellular swelling and death); clinically significant edema usually combines both and can raise ICP and cause tissue shifts. Inadequate oxygen/glucose delivery triggers the ischemic cascade: excitatory amino acid (glutamate) release, calcium and sodium influx, protease/lipase activation, lipid peroxidation, free-radical membrane injury, cytotoxic edema, and necrotic cell death; an alternative apoptotic pathway occurs without edema and is often not seen on imaging. Penumbra denotes still-salvageable ischemic tissue. Secondary insults (hypotension, hypoxia, fever, seizures, hyperglycemia) worsen the cascade. The skull tolerates little added volume, so once intracranial compliance is exhausted, small volume increases sharply raise ICP, lower CPP, and provoke ischemia; ischemia-driven autoregulatory vasodilation can paradoxically further raise blood volume and ICP, creating a vicious cycle. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying disorder and on prevention of secondary injury. After hypoxia-ischemia, recovery may be full if circulation is restored within 3-5 minutes, while longer insults often cause permanent damage; the brain tolerates pure hypoxia better than combined hypoxia-ischemia. Reliable post-arrest prognostication requires sufficient observation time, and hypothermia/sedation delay when predictors become valid; some patients awaken after a week or longer, so premature withdrawal risks a self-fulfilling prophecy. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy carries roughly 50% mortality when severe enough to cause coma, though this mainly reflects underlying illness severity; the encephalopathy usually improves substantially with successful treatment, but long-term cognitive dysfunction is increasingly recognized, especially in older survivors. Critical illness polyneuropathy and thick-filament critical illness myopathy generally recover spontaneously if the patient survives, though recovery may take weeks to months and some residual weakness can persist. Prolonged neuromuscular blockade causes no permanent damage and resolves once the agent clears. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8 or less defines severe traumatic brain injury and is a key criterion for ICP monitoring (Harrison 22e p.2345). Operational neurocritical care targets include ICP below 20 mmHg and CPP at or above 60 mmHg, with stepwise escalation of therapy for sustained ICP above 20-25 mmHg; CAR-T cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity severity track with degree of fever, CRP, and ferritin elevation.

SPINK5 genetic testing supported by absent LEKTI staining on immunohistochemistry Neonatal hypernatraemic dehydration and thermoregulatory instability from barrier failure Sepsis or recurrent severe skin and systemic infections Failure to thrive and growth faltering Signs of systemic toxicity from absorbed topical agents (particularly calcineurin inhibitors) Misdiagnosing it as recalcitrant atopic dermatitis and delaying genetic evaluation Applying topical calcineurin inhibitors over large areas of impaired barrier, risking systemic absorption and toxicity Sampling only scalp hair and missing the diagnostic shaft defect best seen in eyebrows Underestimating fluid, electrolyte, and infection risk in the erythrodermic neonate Netherton syndrome results from loss of function of the LEKTI protein, a multidomain serine protease inhibitor expressed in the granular and uppermost spinous layers of the epidermis. Without LEKTI, kallikrein-related peptidases (notably KLK5 and KLK7) are unrestrained, leading to premature and excessive degradation of corneodesmosomes and detachment of the stratum corneum. The result is a profoundly defective epidermal barrier with abnormal desquamation. Unchecked protease activity also drives proinflammatory and pro-allergic signalling, producing the severe atopic phenotype, elevated IgE, and susceptibility to cutaneous infection. It is a lifelong condition; the neonatal period carries the highest mortality risk from dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and infection, after which the phenotype tends to stabilise into ichthyosis linearis circumflexa with persistent atopy, though quality of life and growth remain affected.

Neuroblastoma — neuroblastic tumour Wilms tumour Rhabdomyosarcoma Lymphoma or leukaemic infiltration Phaeochromocytoma Ewing sarcoma / other small round blue cell tumours Hepatoblastoma or other abdominal masses Urinary catecholamine metabolites (HVA and VMA) Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the primary site MIBG scintigraphy for functional imaging and metastasis detection Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for marrow involvement Tumour biopsy for histology and biology including MYCN status Full blood count, renal and liver function, lactate dehydrogenase and ferritin The most common extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the most common malignancy of infancy, arising from primitive sympathetic neural crest cells. It can occur anywhere along the sympathetic chain; the adrenal medulla and paraspinal abdomen are the most frequent primary sites. An abdominal primary often presents as a firm, irregular mass that crosses the midline, distinguishing it from Wilms tumour. Presentation is highly variable and may include systemic upset, bone pain, proptosis with periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') from orbital metastases, or a paraspinal mass causing cord compression. Distinctive paraneoplastic features include opsoclonus-myoclonus (dancing eyes, dancing feet) and secretory diarrhoea from vasoactive intestinal peptide. Most tumours secrete catecholamines, so urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) are useful markers. Behaviour spans a remarkable spectrum, from spontaneous regression in infants (including stage MS/4S disease) to aggressive, widely metastatic disease. MYCN amplification is a key adverse biological marker that upstages risk and intensifies therapy. Risk stratification integrating age, stage, histology, and genetics guides treatment ranging from observation or surgery to intensive multimodal therapy. Signs of spinal cord compression from a paraspinal (dumbbell) tumour Rapidly progressive or widely metastatic disease Periorbital bruising and proptosis suggesting orbital metastases Severe secretory diarrhoea from a VIP-secreting tumour Systemic deterioration with bone pain and marrow failure Confusing it with Wilms tumour when it presents as an abdominal mass Missing spinal cord compression from a paraspinal component Overlooking opsoclonus-myoclonus as a paraneoplastic clue to occult tumour Failing to obtain MYCN status, which changes management Assuming all disease is aggressive and over-treating low-risk or regressing tumours Neuroblastoma develops from neural crest-derived precursors of the sympathetic nervous system, giving rise to a spectrum from undifferentiated neuroblastoma to more mature ganglioneuroblastoma and benign ganglioneuroma. Tumour behaviour is strongly governed by biology: MYCN amplification, segmental chromosomal changes, and DNA ploidy correlate with aggressiveness, while some infant tumours undergo differentiation or apoptosis and regress spontaneously. Outcome is extremely variable: low-risk and infant disease (including 4S/MS) often has excellent survival and may regress, whereas high-risk disease with MYCN amplification or widespread metastases has a much poorer prognosis despite intensive therapy.

Neurocysticercosis — NCC, CNS cysticercosis, cerebral cysticercosis Tuberculoma Cerebral toxoplasmosis Pyogenic or fungal brain abscess Primary or metastatic brain tumour Other parasitic CNS lesions (e.g. hydatid cyst) CNS tuberculosis Toxoplasma encephalitis in immunocompromised patients Primary CNS neoplasm Vasculitic or demyelinating lesions MRI brain to characterise cyst stage, detect a scolex and assess perilesional oedema CT to identify calcified lesions Serological antibody testing (e.g. EITB) as supportive evidence Ophthalmological examination to exclude ocular cysts before therapy CSF studies and assessment for hydrocephalus in suspected extraparenchymal disease Central nervous system infection by larval Taenia solium and one of the leading causes of acquired epilepsy in India and other endemic regions Seizures are the most frequent presentation, typically from a single or few degenerating parenchymal cysts Clinical features depend on cyst number, location and stage, ranging from asymptomatic calcified lesions to disabling neurological disease Extraparenchymal disease (intraventricular, subarachnoid or racemose forms) can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus, and behaves more aggressively MRI and CT are central to diagnosis; the finding of a cyst with a visible scolex is highly characteristic, and calcified lesions indicate old, dead cysts Antiparasitic therapy is combined with corticosteroids to blunt the inflammatory reaction to dying cysts, with antiseizure medication for those presenting with seizures Treatment must be individualised: viable parenchymal cysts, calcified lesions and intraventricular cysts are managed differently, and some forms need neurosurgical intervention Fundoscopy or ophthalmic assessment is advised before antiparasitic treatment to exclude ocular cysts New-onset or breakthrough seizures, including status epilepticus, requiring urgent management Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus from intraventricular disease, a neurosurgical emergency Rapid neurological deterioration precipitated by inflammation when antiparasitic therapy is started Focal deficits, altered consciousness or signs of stroke from subarachnoid vasculitis Giving antiparasitic drugs without corticosteroid cover, risking severe inflammatory worsening and seizures Treating without first excluding ocular or intraventricular cysts, where drug-induced inflammation is dangerous Assuming all ring-enhancing brain lesions are neurocysticercosis and missing tuberculoma or tumour Overlooking hydrocephalus as a cause of deterioration in extraparenchymal disease Ingested Taenia solium eggs release oncospheres that reach the brain and develop into cysticerci. Viable cysts in the parenchyma may remain quiescent, but immune-mediated degeneration releases antigens that provoke perilesional inflammation and oedema, generating seizures and focal deficits. As cysts die they may calcify, and these calcified foci can remain epileptogenic. In the ventricles and subarachnoid space, cysts and the associated inflammation can block cerebrospinal fluid pathways, producing raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, while subarachnoid (racemose) disease may cause arachnoiditis and vasculitis. Solitary parenchymal cysts often resolve with good seizure control and a favourable outcome, though some patients develop chronic epilepsy from residual calcified lesions. Extraparenchymal, subarachnoid and heavy-burden disease carries a worse prognosis with risk of hydrocephalus, recurrent complications and higher mortality.

causes of chronic diarrhoea Hepatic metastases from other primary malignancies Histological grading with Ki-67 index and mitotic count to determine differentiation Serum chromogranin A and, for
