evaluation for hereditary syndromes such as MEN when indicated Neuroendocrine tumours are a heterogeneous group arising most commonly in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, and lungs, ranging from indolent well-differentiated tumours to highly aggressive neuroendocrine carcinomas Tumour grade, based on proliferative markers such as mitotic count and Ki-67 index, is central to classifying behaviour and guiding treatment Many are non-functioning and present late with mass effect or metastasis, while functioning tumours cause distinctive hormonal syndromes The carcinoid syndrome, with flushing, diarrhoea, and wheeze, typically appears only once a midgut tumour has metastasised to the liver, allowing vasoactive mediators to bypass hepatic clearance Chromogranin A is a widely used circulating marker, and urinary 5-HIAA supports the diagnosis of serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumours Somatostatin receptor imaging, such as gallium-labelled PET, is valuable for localisation and staging and predicts response to somatostatin receptor-targeted therapy Somatostatin analogues control hormonal symptoms and can slow tumour growth, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy is an option for receptor-positive progressive disease Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas behave like aggressive high-grade cancers and are treated with platinum-based chemotherapy, in contrast to the more indolent management of well-differentiated tumours Carcinoid crisis with severe flushing, haemodynamic instability, and bronchospasm, particularly around procedures Rapidly progressive high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma with widespread metastases Severe hormonal effects such as refractory hypoglycaemia from an insulinoma Carcinoid heart disease with right-sided valve involvement in metastatic midgut tumours Assuming a normal-appearing indolent tumour is benign and underestimating metastatic potential Failing to prevent carcinoid crisis with somatostatin analogue cover before surgery or interventions Managing high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma as if it were an indolent tumour Overlooking an associated hereditary syndrome that alters surveillance and family screening Neuroendocrine tumours originate from cells of the diffuse neuroendocrine system distributed throughout the body, which share the capacity to synthesise and secrete peptide hormones and biogenic amines. Well-differentiated tumours retain hormone production and receptor expression, including somatostatin receptors that are exploited for imaging and therapy, and generally grow slowly. Functioning tumours produce clinical syndromes through hormone excess, such as serotonin in carcinoid syndrome or insulin, gastrin, and other peptides from pancreatic tumours. Poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas lose these features and behave aggressively with rapid proliferation and early metastasis. Some tumours occur within hereditary syndromes such as multiple endocrine neoplasia. Prognosis varies widely by grade, differentiation, site, and stage; well-differentiated low-grade tumours can be compatible with prolonged survival even with metastases, whereas poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas have an aggressive course and poor outcome.

Neuroferritinopathy — FTL, ferritin light chain disease, hereditary ferritinopathy, NBIA-related ferritin disorder, adult-onset basal ganglia disease Huntington disease Other NBIA subtypes (PKAN, aceruloplasminaemia) Wilson disease Idiopathic torsion dystonia and other adult-onset dystonias Young-onset Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism Benign hereditary chorea and other choreiform syndromes Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences to demonstrate basal ganglia and dentate iron and any putaminal/pallidal cavitation FTL molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Serum ferritin, which may be low, along with iron studies Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease and aceruloplasminaemia Detailed family history and consideration of testing at-risk relatives given dominant inheritance Autosomal dominant NBIA subtype caused by variants (typically insertions) in FTL, encoding the ferritin light chain One of the few dominantly inherited NBIA disorders, usually presenting in adulthood Phenotype is dominated by an extrapyramidal movement disorder: chorea, dystonia (often orofacial or action-specific), and parkinsonism, frequently asymmetrical at onset Characteristic orolingual and facial dystonia may cause dysarthria and can resemble Huntington disease Cognition is relatively preserved until late, in contrast to many other neurodegenerative movement disorders Serum ferritin may be low or low-normal, particularly in affected males, providing a useful clue MRI with iron-sensitive sequences shows iron in the basal ganglia and dentate nuclei and may reveal cystic cavitation of the putamen and globus pallidus in advanced disease Diagnosis is confirmed by FTL molecular testing in the context of the imaging and family history; management is symptomatic Severe or disabling generalised chorea or dystonia Bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia and aspiration risk Status dystonicus in advanced disease Rapid functional decline or new significant cognitive or psychiatric change Diagnosing Huntington disease on clinical grounds without pursuing NBIA imaging and FTL testing when the huntingtin expansion is negative Overlooking a low serum ferritin as a diagnostic clue Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI sequences that reveal the deep grey-matter iron and cavitation Not recognising the dominant inheritance and missing the opportunity for family counselling Neuroferritinopathy is caused by dominant variants in FTL, the gene for the ferritin light chain, most commonly small insertions that disrupt the carboxy-terminus of the protein. The abnormal ferritin has impaired capacity to sequester iron safely, so iron and abnormal ferritin aggregates accumulate within neurons and glia, particularly in the basal ganglia and cerebellar dentate nuclei. The resulting iron-mediated oxidative stress and inclusion formation drive progressive neurodegeneration, and advanced disease may lead to tissue cavitation within the affected deep grey-matter structures. The disorder is slowly progressive over years to decades, with worsening movement disorder and eventual loss of independence, although cognition is often comparatively spared. Prognosis and rate of progression vary between affected individuals and families.

Neurofibromatosis — NF1, NF2, von Recklinghausen disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2 Legius syndrome (cafe-au-lait macules without neurofibromas) McCune-Albright syndrome Schwannomatosis Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency Multiple lipomatosis Clinical assessment against established diagnostic criteria, supported by NF1 or NF2 molecular testing when needed Ophthalmological examination including slit-lamp for Lisch nodules and optic pathway assessment Magnetic resonance imaging for suspected central or peripheral nervous system tumours Blood pressure monitoring for hypertension including phaeochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis Audiological evaluation and brain imaging for suspected NF2 Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically using criteria that include multiple cafe-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, characteristic bony lesions, and an affected first-degree relative Cafe-au-lait macules and axillary or inguinal freckling are usually the earliest features in NF1 Optic pathway gliomas are a recognised childhood complication and warrant ophthalmological and imaging surveillance Plexiform neurofibromas can be disfiguring and carry a risk of malignant transformation Neurofibromatosis type 2 is distinct, typically presenting with bilateral vestibular schwannomas causing hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance problems NF1 is caused by mutations in the NF1 gene encoding neurofibromin, a tumour suppressor regulating RAS signalling; NF2 involves the NF2 gene encoding merlin Both are autosomal dominant with high penetrance, variable expressivity, and a high de novo mutation rate Learning difficulties, hypertension, and skeletal complications such as scoliosis are common in NF1 New or rapidly enlarging, painful, or firm masses suggesting malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and needing urgent evaluation Visual changes indicating optic pathway glioma progression Hypertension that may reflect phaeochromocytoma or renovascular disease Progressive hearing loss or neurological signs from vestibular schwannomas or other tumours in NF2 Attributing multiple cafe-au-lait macules alone to NF1 without considering mimics such as Legius syndrome Failing to institute malignancy surveillance for changing plexiform neurofibromas Overlooking hypertension and its treatable secondary causes Missing NF2 in a young adult with unilateral or bilateral hearing loss Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein that downregulates RAS signalling; loss of neurofibromin increases RAS-pathway activity and predisposes to tumour formation in neural crest-derived tissues. Neurofibromatosis type 2 results from mutations in the NF2 gene encoding merlin (schwannomin), another tumour suppressor, leading characteristically to schwannomas and meningiomas. Both disorders are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner but frequently arise de novo, and tumour development typically follows a second somatic hit inactivating the remaining normal allele, consistent with the two-hit tumour suppressor model. Most people with NF1 have a good quality of life, but morbidity and reduced life expectancy relate to tumour complications, particularly malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours and vascular disease; NF2 prognosis depends on the burden and location of nervous system tumours.

Neurogenic bladder — neuropathic bladder, neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, NLUTD Detrusor overactivity from non-neurogenic causes (idiopathic overactive bladder) Bladder outlet obstruction (BPH, stricture) Diabetic cystopathy Cauda equina syndrome Multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating disease Spinal cord injury or compression Pelvic surgery-related denervation Video-urodynamic studies to assess detrusor pressure, compliance, and sphincter coordination Renal function tests and upper tract imaging (ultrasound) to monitor for hydronephrosis Post-void residual measurement Urinalysis and culture for infection surveillance Neurological evaluation and imaging directed at the underlying condition Periodic surveillance for bladder stones and, where relevant, malignancy in long-term catheterised patients Neurogenic bladder describes bladder dysfunction due to disease or injury of the nervous system, with the pattern depending on the level of the neurological lesion Suprapontine and suprasacral (upper motor neuron) lesions typically cause a spastic, overactive detrusor, often with detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, whereas sacral or peripheral (lower motor neuron) lesions cause a flaccid, areflexic, poorly emptying bladder Common causes include spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida, diabetes mellitus, Parkinson's disease, stroke, and cauda equina lesions The paramount goal of management is protection of the upper urinary tracts, because high storage pressures and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia can cause hydronephrosis and renal failure Video-urodynamics is central to characterising bladder behaviour, storage pressures, and sphincter coordination to guide safe management Clean intermittent catheterisation is a cornerstone for bladders that do not empty adequately, reducing residual urine and infection risk while preserving the upper tracts Management principles combine measures to lower storage pressure and improve emptying, such as antimuscarinics, intradetrusor botulinum toxin, catheterisation regimens, and, in selected cases, augmentation or diversion surgery Patients are at risk of recurrent urinary infection, stones, and, in high spinal cord injuries, autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension High detrusor storage pressures or detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia threatening the upper tracts and renal function New or progressive hydronephrosis and rising creatinine Autonomic dysreflexia in high spinal cord injury, a potentially life-threatening emergency triggered by bladder overdistension Urosepsis in an obstructed or poorly draining neurogenic bladder Acute cauda equina syndrome presenting with retention and neurological deficit Focusing on continence while neglecting upper tract protection and storage pressures Failing to recognise and treat detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia Not anticipating autonomic dysreflexia during bladder distension or instrumentation in high spinal injuries Inadequate surveillance for renal deterioration, stones, and infection Treating overactivity with antimuscarinics without ensuring adequate emptying Normal micturition depends on coordinated control between the pontine micturition centre, spinal pathways, and sacral (S2-S4) reflexes governing the detrusor and urethral sphincter. Neurological lesions disrupt this coordination in patterns determined by lesion level. Upper motor neuron lesions above the sacral cord release the sacral reflex from higher inhibition, producing detrusor overactivity and often detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, in which the sphincter contracts against a contracting bladder, generating dangerously high pressures. Lower motor neuron or peripheral lesions abolish the reflex arc, producing an acontractile, flaccid bladder with retention and overflow. Sustained high intravesical pressure and incomplete emptying threaten the upper tracts and predispose to infection and stones. With structured management focused on low-pressure storage, adequate emptying, and regular upper tract surveillance, many patients maintain renal function and continence; neglected high-pressure bladders carry a significant risk of progressive renal impairment and recurrent complications.

Neuroimaging in Neurologic Disorders — Neuroimaging, CT and MRI in neurology, Brain and spine imaging Ring-enhancing lesion: cerebral abscess versus high-grade glioma or metastasis (restricted central diffusion favors abscess) Restricted diffusion in medial temporal lobe: herpes simplex encephalitis versus acute infarction versus other limbic inflammatory processes Multiple low-signal SWI foci: cerebral amyloid angiopathy versus chronic hypertensive microbleeds versus hemorrhagic metastases versus diffuse axonal injury Focal arterial narrowing/wall enhancement: atherosclerosis versus primary CNS vasculitis versus reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Noncontrast CT for acute hemorrhage, trauma, and acute mental-status change MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for suspected ischemia, encephalitis, or abscess CT angiography or gadolinium-enhanced/time-of-flight MR angiography for vascular assessment Vessel wall MR imaging to characterize arteriopathies and vasculitis Perfusion CT or perfusion MRI/ASL to assess core versus penumbra and tumor vascularity CT myelography for failed-back syndrome, CSF fistula localization, and meningeal/arachnoid cysts FDG-PET and amyloid/tau PET ligands for oncologic staging and neurodegenerative evaluation Estimated GFR before contrast in at-risk patients MRI is generally more sensitive than CT for lesions of the central and peripheral nervous system, whereas CT is faster and the pragmatic first choice for uncooperative patients and for suspected acute stroke, hemorrhage, or acute intracranial/spinal trauma (Harrison 22e p.3383). Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the single most sensitive technique for detecting acute cerebral or spinal cord ischemia, with restricted diffusion (high DWI signal) appearing in infarction of less than about 7 days; it also lights up encephalitis, abscess, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Harrison 22e p.3383, 3389). CT is superior to MRI for fine osseous detail and is preferred for the initial workup of conductive hearing loss and skull/spine bone lesions, while MRI better detects bone-marrow infiltrative processes that CT may miss (Harrison 22e p.3383). On unenhanced CT, denser structures such as bone or acute blood appear bright (high attenuation), whereas water, air, and soft tissue appear dark; this is why acute hemorrhage and bone are well seen on noncontrast CT (Harrison 22e p.3383-3384). Iodinated contrast highlights vascular structures and blood-brain barrier defects; in the normal CNS only vessels and structures lacking a blood-brain barrier (pituitary, choroid plexus, dura) enhance (Harrison 22e p.3384). Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is highly sensitive to blood, calcium, and air and is the sequence of choice for microhemorrhages seen in amyloid angiopathy, hypertension, hemorrhagic metastases, traumatic brain injury, and thrombotic states (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388). FLAIR suppresses the bright CSF signal of T2 imaging, improving detection of edematous/water-containing lesions adjacent to CSF spaces such as periventricular plaques and cortical lesions (Harrison 22e p.3387). Gadolinium-based contrast does not cause contrast-induced nephropathy, but linear (group 1/3) agents can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with severe renal impairment; macrocyclic (group 2) agents are far safer and preferred in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.3388-3389). Perfusion imaging that shows a region of prolonged mean transit time with preserved cerebral blood volume identifies tissue at risk (ischemic penumbra) that may be salvageable, distinct from infarcted core where blood volume and flow are reduced (Harrison 22e p.3390). CTA and gadolinium-enhanced MRA have largely replaced catheter angiography, which is now reserved for cases needing fine small-vessel detail or planned interventional therapy (Harrison 22e p.3383). Vessel wall MR imaging is a high-resolution technique that interrogates the arterial wall itself and helps distinguish atherosclerosis, primary CNS vasculitis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3390). Amyloid PET can be positive in up to about 25% of cognitively normal older adults, so a positive scan does not by itself diagnose Alzheimer disease; tau PET appears more specific (Harrison 22e p.3392). Acute change in mental status, new focal deficit, or head/spine trauma warranting urgent noncontrast CT Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (CT then CTA, with lumbar puncture if CT negative) Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2) or dialysis raising concern for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with linear gadolinium agents Prior severe contrast (anaphylactoid) reaction, with eightfold higher recurrence risk for gadolinium Ferromagnetic implants (some aneurysm clips, non-conditional pacemakers/defibrillators) or ocular metallic foreign body before MRI Suspected spinal block or elevated intracranial pressure before myelography/lumbar puncture Reliance on shellfish or iodine allergy to predict contrast reactions is unreliable; the strongest predictor is a prior contrast reaction (about fivefold risk), plus atopy/asthma and other drug/food allergies (Harrison 22e p.3385). Premedication regimens shorter than 4-5 hours have no demonstrated efficacy and do not guarantee prevention of contrast reactions (Harrison 22e p.3387). Bicarbonate and acetylcysteine have not shown protection over normal saline against contrast-associated AKI in recent meta-analyses (Harrison 22e p.3385). MRA has lower spatial resolution than catheter angiography, is insensitive to slow flow, and may not distinguish near-complete from complete occlusion or detect small-vessel vasculitis/distal vasospasm (Harrison 22e p.3390). Brain gadolinium deposition (dentate nuclei, globus pallidus) occurs even with normal renal/hepatic function, is dose-dependent and greater with linear agents, but to date has no proven neurotoxic histologic correlate (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388). The MR magnet is always on; ferromagnetic missile injuries and torqued implants can be fatal, so rigorous screening of patients and staff is mandatory (Harrison 22e p.3389). Patient motion degrades MRI; uncooperative patients should be sedated or imaged with CT, and children under ~8 years often require monitored anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.3389). Iodinated contrast should be avoided before planned radioactive iodine thyroid therapy because it reduces radioisotope uptake (Harrison 22e p.3387). Neuroimaging techniques exploit differing physical tissue properties. CT reconstructs a cross-sectional map of x-ray attenuation: dense tissue (bone, acute clot) attenuates heavily and appears bright, while water and air appear dark. MRI maps the distribution and relaxation behavior of (mainly hydrogen) protons placed in a strong static magnetic field and excited by radiofrequency pulses; T1 relaxation is the time for ~63% of protons to return toward equilibrium and T2 the time for ~63% to dephase. Manipulating pulse timing (TR and TE) yields T1-weighted images (fat and subacute hemorrhage bright; CSF/edema dark) or T2-weighted images (CSF/edema/demyelination/infarct bright). Gray matter contains roughly 10-15% more water than white matter, providing intrinsic contrast. Pathology such as infarction, abscess, and dense tumor restricts microscopic water motion, producing high DWI signal. Iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents reveal blood-brain barrier breakdown by tumor, infarct, or infection. Flow phenomena underlie MR angiography, and regional changes in oxy/deoxyhemoglobin underlie the BOLD signal of functional MRI (Harrison 22e p.3383-3392). As a diagnostic modality, neuroimaging itself is generally safe. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury from iodinated contrast is rare, usually transient with creatinine returning toward baseline within 1-2 weeks, and most strongly associated with preexisting severe renal insufficiency; gadolinium does not cause it. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis from linear gadolinium agents in severe renal failure is rare (reported incidence ~0.19-4% in GFR <30) but can be severely disabling with multiorgan fibrosis. Severe allergic reactions are uncommon (~0.04% with nonionic iodinated agents; gadolinium severe reactions exceedingly rare). Radiation-induced malignancy from diagnostic CT is felt to be minimal but is dose-dependent (Harrison 22e p.3384-3389). Contrast-associated acute kidney injury is defined per KDIGO criteria within 48 h of contrast: absolute serum creatinine rise >=0.3 mg/dL (>26.4 micromol/L), a >=50% (>=1.5-fold) increase over baseline, or urine output <=0.5 mL/kg per h for at least 6 h. Renal-risk stratification for contrast uses eGFR, with <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2 carrying the greatest evidence for risk (normal >=90 mL/min per 1.73 m2) (Harrison 22e p.3384-3386).

Neuromyelitis Optica — NMO, NMOSD, Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, Devic's disease, Devic disease Multiple sclerosis (especially opticospinal MS subtype in Asian/African ancestry, which can itself be AQP4-seropositive and represent NMOSD) MOG antibody-associated disease (AQP4-negative cases) Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Idiopathic or postinfectious transverse myelitis Neurosarcoidosis Systemic autoimmune myelopathy (SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, Behcet's disease) Spinal cord infarction (longitudinally extensive anterior cord syndrome) Viral myelitis (e.g., herpes simplex virus type 2 causing recurrent myelitis) Tuberculous CNS involvement HIV-associated myelopathy Serum AQP4-IgG testing using a cell-based assay (strongly recommended detection method) MOG-IgG testing in AQP4-seronegative patients Spinal cord MRI to demonstrate longitudinally extensive (>=3 segment) gray matter-centered lesions Brain MRI to detect area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, or cloud-like hemispheric lesions Optic nerve MRI (T2/gadolinium-enhancing lesion over >half optic nerve length or chiasm) Lumbar puncture for CSF pleocytosis, cell differential, and oligoclonal bands Screening for coexisting systemic autoimmune disease Multiple sclerosis MOG antibody-associated disease Neurosarcoidosis Systemic lupus erythematosus / Sjögren's-associated myelopathy Paraneoplastic optic neuropathy/myelopathy Spinal cord infarction NMO is an aggressive antibody-mediated inflammatory CNS disorder defined by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis; the broader term NMOSD captures partial forms and cases with additional CNS involvement (Harrison p.3590). Strongly female-predominant (women:men roughly 9:1), with a mean onset around age 40 but possible at any age (Harrison p.3590). Optic neuritis in NMO can be bilateral and cause severe vision loss, a pattern uncommon in MS; myelitis is often severe, transverse, and longitudinally extensive spanning three or more contiguous vertebral segments (Harrison p.3590). Unlike MS, NMO rarely follows a progressive course; accumulated disability results from attack-related injury rather than progression (Harrison p.3590). Brain MRI is not invariably normal: lesions may involve the area postrema (intractable hiccups or vomiting), hypothalamus (sleep disorder or endocrinopathy), or cerebral hemispheres; large hemispheric lesions can be asymptomatic, show a 'cloud-like' appearance, be non-destructive, and resolve completely (Harrison p.3590). Spinal cord lesions are focal enhancing areas of swelling and tissue destruction over three or more segments and are centered on the gray matter on axial imaging (Harrison p.3590). CSF typically shows greater pleocytosis than MS, sometimes with neutrophils and eosinophils in acute cases, while oligoclonal bands are uncommon (present in fewer than 20% of patients) (Harrison p.3590-3591). A highly specific serum autoantibody against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) is present in about 90% of patients and is diagnostic when paired with a typical clinical presentation (Harrison p.3590). In a subset of AQP4-negative cases, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) are found (Harrison p.3591). Up to 40% of NMO patients have a coexisting systemic autoimmune disorder (e.g., SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, p-ANCA vasculitis, myasthenia gravis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, mixed connective tissue disease) - a feature distinguishing it from MS (Harrison p.3591). Symptomatic onset may follow acute infection with varicella-zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, or tuberculosis; rare cases are paraneoplastic (breast, lung, or other cancers) (Harrison p.3592). Asian and African ancestry populations are disproportionately affected, with the highest reported prevalence in Martinique; among white populations MS is far more common than NMO (Harrison p.3591). Bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis with severe vision loss Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments Intractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting (area postrema syndrome) Cervical myelitis threatening respiratory failure Acute brainstem or diencephalic syndrome (e.g., symptomatic narcolepsy, hypothalamic dysfunction) Recurrent attacks, since more than half of untreated AQP4-seropositive patients relapse within 1 year Assuming a normal brain MRI excludes NMO - characteristic area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, and cloud-like hemispheric lesions can be present (Harrison p.3590). Conflating NMO with MS: bilateral severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, marked CSF pleocytosis, and frequent absence of oligoclonal bands favor NMO (Harrison p.3590). Relying on oligoclonal bands, which are present in fewer than 20% of NMO patients (Harrison p.3590-3591). Overlooking that NMO frequently coexists with systemic autoimmune disease, unlike MS (Harrison p.3591). Failing to recognize AQP4-negative disease, where MOG antibodies may be present and where seronegative NMOSD requires both optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis to meet criteria (Harrison p.3591-3592). NMO is an autoimmune astrocytopathy driven by autoantibodies against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which is concentrated on astrocyte foot processes apposed to endothelium and at paranodal regions near nodes of Ranvier. Pathology shows loss of AQP4 staining with antibody and complement deposition, astrocyte cytolysis, thickened vessel walls, demyelination, and inflammation. AQP4 antibodies are likely pathogenic, since passive transfer reproduces disease features in animals; both complement fixation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity contribute to astrocyte injury, and TH17 proinflammatory T cells recognizing an immunodominant AQP4 epitope may also participate. A thymic B-cell population that constitutively expresses AQP4 normally interacts with AQP4-specific T cells to maintain tolerance, and impairment of this interaction may contribute. During acute myelitis attacks, CSF levels of IL-6 and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) are markedly elevated, reflecting active inflammation and astrocyte injury (Harrison p.3590-3591). NMO is typically a relapsing disease; a monophasic course occurs in fewer than 10% of patients and is somewhat more likely in AQP4-antibody-negative individuals. Untreated disease is severely disabling: historically about one-third of patients developed respiratory failure from cervical myelitis, and by 8 years roughly 60% were blind and more than half had permanent limb paralysis. AQP4-seropositive patients carry a high relapse risk (more than half relapse within 1 year if untreated). Long-term outcomes have substantially improved with the advent of attack and relapse therapies, with reported 5-year survival rising from about 68-75% around 1999 to 91-98% by 2017 (Harrison p.3590-3591). No formal severity grading; diagnosis follows the 2015 International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for NMOSD, which stratify by AQP4-IgG status. AQP4-IgG-positive disease requires at least one core clinical characteristic, a positive AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. AQP4-IgG-negative or unknown-status disease requires at least two core characteristics (one of which must be optic neuritis, acute myelitis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, or area postrema syndrome), dissemination in space, fulfillment of additional MRI requirements, a negative or unavailable AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. Core clinical characteristics: optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/acute diencephalic syndrome with typical MRI lesions, and symptomatic cerebral syndrome with typical brain lesions (Harrison p.3591, Table 456-1).

Neuropathic pain — nerve pain, neurogenic pain, neuralgia Nociceptive musculoskeletal pain Inflammatory or ischaemic pain Complex regional pain syndrome Fibromyalgia and centralised pain states Myofascial pain syndrome Vascular claudication mimicking limb pain Detailed sensory examination mapping the distribution and testing for allodynia and hyperalgesia Nerve conduction studies and electromyography where a peripheral nerve or root lesion is suspected Screening questionnaires such as DN4 or painDETECT to support recognition Targeted investigation of the underlying cause, for example glycaemic testing, imaging of the spine, or metabolic screening Quantitative sensory testing or skin biopsy for small-fibre assessment in selected cases Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system and is distinct from nociceptive pain caused by ongoing tissue damage Typical descriptors are burning, shooting, electric-shock, or stabbing pain, often with numbness, and it characteristically maps to a recognisable neuroanatomical distribution Hallmark abnormal sensory findings include allodynia, where a normally non-painful stimulus causes pain, and hyperalgesia, an exaggerated response to a painful stimulus Common causes span diabetic and other polyneuropathies, postherpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, radiculopathy, post-stroke central pain, spinal cord injury, and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy Screening tools such as the DN4 or painDETECT can support recognition, but diagnosis rests on history, distribution, and confirmatory sensory examination First-line pharmacological principles favour gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, with topical agents for localised pain and opioids generally avoided as first choice A multimodal, multidisciplinary approach combining medication, physical therapy, psychological strategies, and treatment of the underlying cause gives the best results Interventional options such as nerve blocks and neuromodulation may help selected patients with refractory pain Realistic goals centre on partial pain reduction and improved function and sleep rather than complete pain relief Progressive motor weakness, sphincter disturbance, or saddle anaesthesia suggesting cord or cauda equina compression Rapidly worsening deficit implying an evolving compressive or inflammatory lesion Systemic features such as weight loss or night pain raising concern for malignancy or infection New severe pain with fever suggesting an infective or inflammatory neurological process Treating neuropathic pain with conventional analgesics or NSAIDs alone, which are usually ineffective Escalating opioids for a pain type that responds poorly to them and carries dependence risk Missing a serious underlying cause such as cord compression or malignancy Setting an expectation of complete pain relief rather than functional improvement Neglecting the psychological and sleep dimensions that amplify chronic neuropathic pain Neuropathic pain results from maladaptive changes throughout the nervous system after nerve injury or disease. Damaged neurons develop ectopic and spontaneous discharge and altered ion-channel expression, producing peripheral sensitisation. In the dorsal horn, increased excitability, loss of inhibitory interneuron function, and glial activation drive central sensitisation and wind-up. Structural and functional reorganisation extends to the brain, and descending modulatory pathways may shift toward facilitation of pain. These changes together explain the spontaneous pain, allodynia, and hyperalgesia that persist beyond any ongoing tissue injury. Neuropathic pain is often chronic and only partially responsive to treatment, but many patients achieve meaningful reductions in pain intensity and improved function with a structured multimodal approach. Prognosis is better when a reversible underlying cause is identified and treated early.

Neurosarcoidosis — neurological sarcoidosis, CNS sarcoidosis, sarcoid neuropathy Tuberculous or fungal meningitis CNS lymphoma or leptomeningeal carcinomatosis Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating disease IgG4-related disease and other granulomatous vasculitides Idiopathic hypertrophic pachymeningitis Neuro-Behcet and neurosyphilis Contrast-enhanced brain and spinal MRI to map meningeal and parenchymal involvement Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, and exclusion of infection and malignancy Serum and CSF angiotensin-converting enzyme with awareness of limited sensitivity and specificity Whole-body imaging such as CT chest and FDG-PET to find accessible extraneural biopsy sites Tissue biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas with special stains and cultures to exclude infection Cranial neuropathy is the commonest presentation, with facial nerve palsy the classic finding, often bilateral Basal meningeal involvement favours the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, causing diabetes insipidus and other endocrine deficits Presentations are protean and include aseptic meningitis, myelopathy, seizures, hydrocephalus, and peripheral neuropathy Only a minority have isolated neurological disease; most have systemic sarcoidosis providing an accessible biopsy target Contrast MRI often shows leptomeningeal enhancement, dural masses, or parenchymal and spinal cord lesions Diagnosis rests on demonstrating non-caseating granulomas while rigorously excluding infection and lymphoma Corticosteroids are first-line, with steroid-sparing immunosuppression and anti-TNF agents for refractory disease Acute hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure from meningeal disease Hypothalamic-pituitary failure with hyponatraemia or adrenal insufficiency Rapidly progressive myelopathy with sphincter involvement Diagnostic uncertainty where lymphoma or infection has not been excluded Diagnosing neurosarcoidosis on imaging alone without histological or robust supportive evidence Missing coexisting infection because granulomas can occur in tuberculosis and fungal disease Under-treating and allowing relapse when corticosteroids are tapered too quickly Overlooking neuroendocrine dysfunction in basal meningeal involvement Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder in which an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response leads to non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. When the nervous system is affected, granulomatous inflammation tends to concentrate around the basal meninges and perivascular spaces, spreading along Virchow-Robin spaces into brain parenchyma, cranial nerves, the hypothalamic-pituitary region, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. The inflammatory infiltrate and secondary vasculopathy produce the diverse neurological syndromes seen, and chronic meningeal involvement can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow to cause hydrocephalus. Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but the course is often chronic or relapsing and some develop fixed neurological deficits; parenchymal and spinal disease and hydrocephalus carry a less favourable outlook.

Nicotine Addiction — Tobacco dependence, Tobacco use disorder, Nicotine dependence, Cigarette addiction Other substance use disorders (alcohol use disorder, stimulant use) Caffeine use/dependence Primary mood or anxiety disorders presenting with cravings or restlessness Cannabis use via vaping devices (refillable pods may aerosolize marijuana oils) Structured history of total daily frequency of all nicotine products used (cigarettes, cigars, roll-your-own, vaping, oral pouches/snuff) Duration of regular use, prior quit experiences, and current interest in quitting Markers of addiction intensity: episodes per day, spacing through the day, and use within 30 minutes of waking Biomarkers of smoke-toxicant exposure (markedly lower in exclusive e-cigarette users than in cigarette smokers) Withdrawal-related irritability and restlessness mimicking primary anxiety or depressive disorders Chronic cough from smoking-related mucous hyperplasia mimicking other causes of chronic productive cough Addiction is established when nicotine in any form (combusted or heated tobacco, oral pouches, or vaped nicotine/nicotine salt) is used with sufficient intensity for a sufficient duration; addicted users self-titrate the frequency and intensity of use to achieve psychoactive effects and avoid withdrawal. The diagnosis is clinical and hinges on loss of control over the next use of a nicotine product, evidenced by daily use, high number of episodes per day, use shortly after waking, craving during abstinence, and prior failed quit attempts. The clinically important metric is the cumulative frequency of any nicotine dosing across all products used, not the specific product source, because it is dosing frequency that creates and sustains addiction. Nicotine itself causes relatively little disease (notably pregnancy complications); the majority of disease burden comes from repetitive exposure to the carcinogens and toxicants carried with nicotine in various products, which addiction drives by compelling multiple daily exposures. Withdrawal symptoms intensify with longer abstinence as blood nicotine falls and detaches from receptors, and these symptoms can persist for roughly 4-6 weeks. Acidic aerosols (cigarettes and nicotine salt vaping devices) reduce airway irritation, permit deep inhalation, and produce rapid arterial nicotine rises reaching the brain, making them more addictive than products with slower delivery. Cancer risk rises linearly with the number of cigarettes per day and logarithmically with duration of smoking; relative risk of lung cancer in current smokers ranges roughly 13-28 across age groups. Cigarette smoking accounts for about 80% of COPD, about 90% of peripheral vascular disease in nondiabetics, about 50% of aortic aneurysms, about 24% of coronary artery disease, and about 11% of strokes. Smoking induces the cytochrome P450 system, which can lower serum levels of drugs such as warfarin; conversely, levels may rise during hospitalization when a patient stops smoking, an important consideration for narrow-therapeutic-index agents. About 40% of cigarette smokers die prematurely from smoking unless they quit; the population still smoking has shifted toward socially disadvantaged groups, and prevalence has declined more slowly in those over 40 who are most likely to develop disease. 'Lower tar/nicotine' filtered cigarettes do not reduce real exposure because smokers compensate by altering puffing behavior or number smoked; ventilation-hole designs lower only machine-measured yields, not delivered toxicants. Several genes are associated with nicotine addiction (some reducing nicotine clearance, others increasing dependence likelihood or depression risk), but the large declines in smoking since the mid-1950s indicate non-genetic factors dominate population trends. Continued smoking during chemotherapy or radiation, associated with poorer outcomes and reduced survival Smoking in pregnancy: premature rupture of membranes, abruptio placentae, placenta previa, preterm delivery, small-for-gestational-age, increased perinatal mortality and sudden infant death syndrome Dual use of e-cigarettes and combusted cigarettes, which negates toxicant-reduction benefits High-frequency use of noncombusted inhaled nicotine products in patients who never used combusted tobacco Multiplicative cardiac risk when smoking is combined with hypertension or elevated lipids Higher vascular graft occlusion rates in smokers after bypass surgery Assuming cigars or pipe tobacco are lower-risk: most cigars are now made like cigarettes and most pipe tobacco is used for roll-your-own, so risks are similar; clinicians should ask about and not recommend them. Treating 'low tar/nicotine' cigarettes as safer; compensatory smoking negates any benefit and design changes have raised adenocarcinoma rates. Focusing only on cigarettes and missing cumulative nicotine intake from vaping, oral pouches, and other products when assessing addiction intensity. Overlooking smoking-induced cytochrome P450 changes when adjusting drug doses around hospitalization or discharge. Dismissing patients not currently interested in quitting; many still attempt cessation in the subsequent year and benefit from a clear personalized message. Equating exclusive e-cigarette use (lower toxicant exposure) with cessation of addiction, since persistent nicotine dependence and relapse risk remain. Nicotine reaching the brain reversibly binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that are highly active in networks mediating mood, reward, joy, and excitement. With sustained high exposure, nicotinic receptors are upregulated on brain cells, so that for most people daily use is required to maintain the addicted state. As blood nicotine falls between doses, nicotine detaches from receptors and addicted individuals no longer feel 'normal,' producing a compulsive drive for the next dose. The strength and speed of addiction depend on dosing frequency and on the arterial nicotine concentration reaching the brain, which varies by product. Unprotonated (freebase) nicotine, favored at alkaline pH, is absorbed readily across mucosa but is airway-irritating at high concentration; addictive products use mildly acidic aerosols in the mouth to limit irritation and permit deep inhalation, after which alveolar pH shifts toward blood pH (~7.4), rapidly liberating absorbable unprotonated nicotine and driving fast arterial rises to the brain. Cessation produces substantial reversible benefit: risk of a second coronary event falls within 6-12 months, and first myocardial infarction and coronary death rates decline within 2-4 years; after about 15 years of abstinence cardiovascular risk approaches that of never-smokers. Cancer risk declines relative to continued smoking after about 4 years, but a roughly three- to fourfold excess lung cancer risk persists even 20 years after quitting. Small-airway changes in young smokers reverse after 1-2 years of abstinence; in established airflow obstruction cessation mainly slows further decline rather than restoring lung function. Quitting is typically cyclical with multiple attempts: about 70-80% of smokers want to quit and over half try in a given year, but only about 6% remain abstinent at 6 months and about 3% at 2 years; systemwide tracking and assistance can raise 12-month abstinence to as high as 25%. No formal grading is presented; addiction intensity is gauged clinically by cumulative daily dosing frequency across all products, spacing of use through the day, use within 30 minutes of waking, craving during abstinence, and history of failed quit attempts.

Niemann-Pick disease — acid sphingomyelinase deficiency, sphingomyelin lipidosis, NPD, NPC Gaucher disease GM1 gangliosidosis Other lysosomal storage disorders with hepatosplenomegaly Haematological malignancy causing organomegaly Other causes of neurodegeneration with visceromegaly in infancy Acid sphingomyelinase enzyme activity in leukocytes for types A and B Molecular genetic testing of SMPD1, or NPC1/NPC2 for type C Bone marrow examination showing foamy storage cells when performed Specialised biomarkers and cell-based cholesterol studies for type C Ophthalmological examination for cherry-red spot and imaging for organomegaly and lung disease An autosomal recessive group of storage disorders; types A and B result from deficiency of the enzyme acid sphingomyelinase, while type C is a distinct defect of intracellular cholesterol trafficking Type A is a severe infantile neurovisceral form with hepatosplenomegaly, failure to thrive, and rapid neurodegeneration, often fatal in early childhood Type B is a chronic, largely non-neurological visceral form with organomegaly and pulmonary involvement that is compatible with survival into adulthood A cherry-red macular spot may be seen, particularly in the acute infantile (type A) form Type C arises from defects in the NPC1 or NPC2 proteins, causing impaired cholesterol handling and a variable neurological course Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is a characteristic clinical clue to type C disease Lipid-laden foamy macrophages (Niemann-Pick cells) infiltrate the marrow, spleen, and liver Enzyme replacement therapy is available for the non-neurological manifestations of acid sphingomyelinase deficiency, and substrate reduction therapy is used to modify neurological progression in type C Rapid neurodevelopmental regression in an infant with hepatosplenomegaly Progressive respiratory compromise from pulmonary infiltration in type B New vertical gaze palsy or ataxia suggesting type C Severe hypersplenism with cytopenias or risk of splenic rupture Confusing the acid sphingomyelinase forms with type C, which requires different diagnostic tests and therapies Attributing organomegaly solely to a haematological cause and missing a storage disorder Overlooking vertical supranuclear gaze palsy as a specific pointer to type C Assuming enzyme replacement will address the neurological features In Niemann-Pick types A and B, pathogenic variants in SMPD1 reduce acid sphingomyelinase activity, so sphingomyelin cannot be hydrolysed and accumulates within lysosomes of macrophages and other cells, producing visceral organomegaly and, when severe, progressive neurodegeneration. Niemann-Pick type C is mechanistically distinct: variants in NPC1 or NPC2 disrupt the intracellular transport of unesterified cholesterol and other lipids out of the late endosomal/lysosomal compartment, leading to lipid accumulation, neuronal dysfunction, and secondary sphingomyelin storage. All forms are inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Type A is uniformly severe with death typically in early childhood. Type B has a more favourable course with survival into adulthood, though pulmonary and hepatic disease may limit outcomes. Type C is progressive and variable, with age of onset strongly influencing survival; disease-modifying and supportive therapies can slow but not cure neurological decline.

imaging Autosomal recessive chromosomal-instability disorder caused by biallelic variants in NBN, encoding nibrin, a component of the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex involved in DNA double-strand break repair Progressive microcephaly is present from birth or infancy and is a cardinal feature, accompanied by a characteristic bird-like facial appearance Combined immunodeficiency causes recurrent respiratory and other infections, with low immunoglobulins and reduced lymphocyte subsets There is a very high risk of malignancy in childhood, predominantly lymphomas and leukaemias, but also solid tumours Growth restriction and, in females, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with ovarian failure are common Cells show increased chromosomal breakage and characteristic rearrangements involving chromosomes 7 and 14, with radiosensitivity There is a founder variant common in Slavic populations, and marked radiosensitivity means ionising radiation should be avoided wherever possible New lymphadenopathy, organomegaly or cytopenias suggesting lymphoma or leukaemia Severe or recurrent infections indicating significant immunodeficiency Unexpected severe toxicity after exposure to ionising radiation Rapid neurological or developmental deterioration Exposing patients to avoidable ionising radiation for imaging or radiotherapy given their radiosensitivity Ascribing microcephaly to a non-genetic cause and missing the diagnosis Underestimating the degree of immunodeficiency and infection risk Delaying investigation of possible lymphoma because symptoms overlap with infection Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in NBN, encoding nibrin, a subunit of the MRE11-RAD50-NBN (MRN) complex that senses and initiates repair of DNA double-strand breaks and coordinates cell-cycle checkpoint signalling through the ATM pathway. Impaired nibrin function leaves cells unable to repair double-strand breaks efficiently, producing chromosomal instability, characteristic rearrangements and hypersensitivity to ionising radiation. This defect underlies the immunodeficiency (from impaired lymphocyte development requiring efficient DNA recombination), the microcephaly and the strong predisposition to lymphoid and other malignancies. Prognosis is poor, driven principally by the very high childhood risk of lymphoid and other cancers and by complications of immunodeficiency. Radiosensitivity constrains both diagnostic imaging and cancer treatment, and management is largely supportive with infection prophylaxis and vigilant, radiation-sparing cancer monitoring.

Nipah virus infection — NiV, Nipah encephalitis, Nipah virus disease Japanese encephalitis and other viral encephalitides Herpes simplex encephalitis Cerebral malaria Bacterial or tuberculous meningoencephalitis Scrub typhus with CNS involvement Leptospirosis with meningoencephalitis Autoimmune encephalitis Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Severe sepsis with encephalopathy RT-PCR of throat/nasal swabs, CSF, urine and blood in a biosafe reference laboratory Nipah-specific IgM and IgG serology by ELISA MRI brain, which may show disseminated small cortical and subcortical lesions CSF examination when safe, typically showing lymphocytic pleocytosis Chest imaging if respiratory involvement is suspected A highly lethal zoonotic paramyxovirus (henipavirus) whose natural reservoir is fruit bats (Pteropus species) In India transmission has been linked to consumption of date-palm sap contaminated by bat secretions and to close contact with infected patients, with documented person-to-person and nosocomial spread Presents as rapidly progressive encephalitis with fever, headache, altered mental status and often prominent brainstem signs; respiratory involvement may also occur Case fatality is very high, and survivors may suffer residual neurological deficits or relapsing/late-onset encephalitis No licensed antiviral or vaccine is established; management is supportive with rigorous infection control Strict barrier precautions, patient isolation and contact tracing are essential because human-to-human transmission drives outbreaks It is classified as a priority pathogen of pandemic potential requiring immediate public-health notification Diagnosis uses RT-PCR on respiratory secretions, CSF, urine or blood, and serology (IgM/IgG ELISA), performed in high-containment laboratories Rapidly deteriorating consciousness or brainstem dysfunction signalling life-threatening encephalitis Any respiratory distress raising concern for airborne/droplet transmissibility and severe disease Cluster of cases or contact with a confirmed case, mandating immediate isolation and outbreak response Autonomic instability or seizures requiring critical-care support Failing to institute isolation and barrier precautions early, allowing nosocomial and family transmission Delaying notification to public-health authorities during a suspected cluster Attributing the illness to more common encephalitides and not sending appropriate high-containment testing Underestimating the risk to healthcare workers during aerosol-generating procedures Nipah virus is an enveloped RNA henipavirus that infects endothelium and neurons. After spillover from fruit bats (directly, via contaminated food, or from intermediate hosts such as pigs), the virus causes a systemic vasculitis with endothelial infection, syncytium formation, thrombosis and microinfarction, particularly in the central nervous system. This vasculitic and direct neuronal injury produces the severe encephalitis, while pulmonary endothelial and epithelial infection can cause acute respiratory distress. The capacity of the virus to persist may underlie relapsing or delayed-onset encephalitis in some survivors. Nipah virus disease is one of the most lethal human encephalitides, with case fatality frequently exceeding half of symptomatic cases. Survivors may be left with persistent neurological impairment, and a minority develop relapsing or late-onset encephalitis months to years later.

Severe, disseminated, or recurrent herpesvirus infection requiring urgent antiviral therapy and immunological workup Progressive cytopenias or evolving myeloid malignancy in GATA2-associated disease Live vaccines should be approached with caution given impaired antiviral immunity Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in functional cytotoxicity defects Attributing severe herpesvirus infections to bad luck rather than investigating NK cell function Relying on NK cell numbers alone and missing a functional deficiency with normal counts Failing to recognise GATA2 deficiency as a cause with wider haematological consequences Not excluding secondary causes of reduced NK cells before diagnosing a primary deficiency Overlooking the need for antiviral prophylaxis Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that provide early defence against virally infected and transformed cells through cytotoxic granule release and cytokine production, and they are particularly important in controlling herpesviruses. In classical NK cell deficiency, mutations disrupt the development or survival of the NK lineage, so few or no NK cells are present; in functional deficiency, NK cells develop but cannot kill their targets because of defects in cytotoxic machinery or activating signals. The loss of this early antiviral surveillance leaves patients unable to contain herpesvirus infections, which can become severe or disseminated. Some causative genes, such as GATA2, also affect broader haematopoiesis, producing additional cytopenias and predisposition to myeloid malignancy. Outcome varies with the specific defect and the severity of viral disease; isolated functional deficiencies may be managed with antiviral strategies, whereas broader defects such as GATA2 deficiency carry risks of bone marrow failure and malignancy and may require haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Nocardiosis — Nocardia infection, Actinomycetoma (Nocardia) Lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) presentation overlaps with Sporothrix schenckii and Mycobacterium marinum infection (p.1360). Mycetoma differential: actinomycetoma (filamentous bacteria, e.g., Nocardia), eumycetoma (fungal), and botryomycosis (cocci/bacilli, often Staphylococcus aureus) are difficult to separate clinically and require granule microscopy, culture, or biopsy (p.1361). Ocular nocardiosis (keratitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis) cannot be distinguished from other ocular infections by signs and symptoms alone (p.1360). Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichosis) for lymphocutaneous disease Mycobacterium marinum for lymphocutaneous disease Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) for actinomycetoma Botryomycosis (often Staphylococcus aureus) for actinomycetoma Other causes of pulmonary nodules/cavitation and ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., fungi, mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis as discussed in brain abscess context) Sputum or pus microscopy for branching beaded Gram-positive filaments plus modified (weak-acid) acid-fast staining; organisms may also take up silver stains (p.1360-1361). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or lung biopsy when sputum smears are negative, as they frequently are in pulmonary nocardiosis (p.1361). Selective media (colistin-nalidixic acid agar, modified Thayer-Martin agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar) for mixed-flora specimens; avoid mycobacterial decontamination procedures, which can kill nocardiae; alert the laboratory to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (up to 2-4 weeks) (p.1361). Species/complex identification by MALDI-TOF or genomic sequencing (16S rRNA, secA1, hsp65, or gyrB), with antimicrobial susceptibility testing (ideally CLSI broth dilution); susceptibility testing requires experience because nocardiae grow slowly and clump (p.1361). Granule examination in mycetoma: wash suspect particles in saline, examine microscopically, and culture; culture is the most reliable way to identify the causative organism (p.1361). Contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred, with IV gadolinium more sensitive than CT) in all patients with non-cutaneous/non-ocular nocardiosis to detect occult brain abscess (p.1360-1362). Testing for underlying immunodeficiency in patients lacking typical risk factors, including HIV testing; test for chronic granulomatous disease in children and adults with nocardiosis who have no major risk factor (p.1359, p.1362). Pulmonary or cerebral malignancy/metastases presenting as nodules, masses, or ring-enhancing lesions Nocardiosis is usually an opportunistic infection occurring primarily in hosts with impaired defenses, especially defects in cell-mediated immunity and specific phagocyte function; typical risk factors include solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, systemic corticosteroids or Cushing syndrome, other immunosuppressive therapy, and HIV infection (p.1358-1359). Pulmonary disease is the usual portal after inhalation of fragmented mycelia; onset is typically subacute over days to weeks (more acute in the severely immunocompromised), with prominent cough producing thick non-malodorous purulent sputum, fever, anorexia, and malaise (p.1359). Typical chest imaging shows infiltrates, nodules, and masses in one or more lobes, and nodules frequently cavitate; pleural effusion or empyema occurs in about one-third of cases, occasionally without lung involvement (p.1359). Dissemination occurs in up to one-third of patients with pneumonia, most often to the CNS and to skin/subcutaneous tissues; virtually any organ can be involved (p.1359-1360). CNS involvement occurs in up to two-thirds of disseminated cases; brain imaging classically shows one or more ring-enhancing, multilobulated lesions, and multiple abscesses are seen in two-thirds of patients (p.1360). Diagnosis starts with examining sputum or pus for branching, beaded, Gram-positive filaments (~1 um wide, up to 50 um long) that fragment into apparent cocci/coccobacilli; most nocardiae are modified (weak) acid-fast (e.g., modified Kinyoun, modified Ziehl-Neelsen, Fite-Faraco) (p.1360-1361). Primary cutaneous nocardiosis follows transcutaneous inoculation (often thorn/gardening injury) and takes three forms: cellulitis, lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) syndrome, or actinomycetoma; N. brasiliensis is the usual cause of skin-limited and lymphocutaneous disease and of actinomycetoma (p.1358, p.1360). Nocardiosis tends to remit and relapse; without definitive treatment, pulmonary disease characteristically follows a course of remissions and exacerbations over weeks to months, and prolonged therapy (months) is required (p.1359, p.1362-Table 179-1). CNS dissemination: brain abscess may be clinically silent, so absence of neurologic symptoms does not exclude it - one-third of patients with CNS involvement have no CNS symptoms and one-fourth have no apparent pulmonary disease at presentation (p.1360). Disseminated nocardiosis carries a higher mortality than localized pulmonary disease, especially with CNS involvement (p.1362). Nocardiosis in a patient without a major risk factor should prompt evaluation for an undiagnosed immunologic defect, including HIV and chronic granulomatous disease (p.1359, p.1362). Failing to image the brain: because brain abscess may be asymptomatic, all patients with pulmonary or systemic nocardiosis should have contrast-enhanced CNS imaging (MRI preferred) regardless of neurologic symptoms (p.1360, p.1362). Missing the diagnosis on smear: sputum smears are frequently negative in pulmonary nocardiosis, and the modified (weak) acid-fast technique must be used or organisms may be overlooked; standard mycobacterial decontamination can kill nocardiae (p.1360-1361). Cultures lost to short incubation: nocardiae grow slowly (colonies up to 2 weeks, characteristic appearance up to 4 weeks), so the laboratory must be informed to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (p.1361). Overcalling colonization or contamination: Nocardia can colonize the respiratory tract in bronchiectasis/structural lung disease, and isolation from a respiratory specimen does not always indicate infection; blood culture isolates may be contaminants in low-risk patients without clinical disease (p.1361). Adjunctive topical corticosteroids should NOT be given to patients with nocardial keratitis (p.1362). Nocardia species are saprophytic, filamentous, aerobic Gram-positive bacteria ubiquitous in soil, water, and decaying organic matter; their cell walls contain mycolic acids and trehalose (Mycobacteriales order), and they are weakly (modified) acid-fast and catalase positive. Pulmonary and systemic disease follow inhalation of fragmented bacterial mycelia, while primary cutaneous and ocular disease follow direct inoculation. Most immunocompetent people clear inhaled nocardiae without disease; invasive infection is favored by impaired host defenses. Innate and adaptive responses, with neutrophils and macrophages central to antinocardial defense (underscored by the frequency of nocardiosis in chronic granulomatous disease), normally control the organism. Nocardiae have evolved mechanisms to survive within phagocytes, including neutralization of oxidants and prevention of phagosome-lysosome fusion and phagosome acidification; neutrophils limit but do not efficiently kill them. The characteristic pathology is an abscess with neutrophilic infiltration and prominent necrosis, with little fibrosis/encapsulation, whereas actinomycetoma shows granulomatous inflammation with sinus tract formation. (p.1358-1359) With appropriate treatment, mortality for localized pulmonary nocardiosis is less than 10%. Disseminated disease carries a higher mortality, especially with CNS involvement. Primary cutaneous and ocular disease often respond to therapy. Mortality from actinomycetoma is exceedingly low, but patients often suffer substantial morbidity, disfigurement, disability, and/or stigmatization. Prolonged therapy is required and disease tends to relapse, so secondary prophylaxis is considered by some experts for patients who remain at high risk after completing antimicrobial therapy. (p.1362) Disease is categorized clinically and by host status to guide therapy duration: pulmonary/systemic disease in hosts with intact defenses versus deficient defenses, CNS disease, primary cutaneous disease (cellulitis, lymphocutaneous), osteomyelitis/arthritis/laryngitis/sinusitis, actinomycetoma, and keratitis - longer courses for immunocompromised and CNS disease, with indefinite therapy considered in some AIDS patients with CD4 below 200/uL or chronic granulomatous disease (p.1362). [Durations noted as classification context only; not dosing guidance.]

Nocturnal Enuresis — bedwetting, nighttime wetting, sleep enuresis Urinary tract infection Constipation with secondary bladder dysfunction Diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus Overactive bladder or other daytime voiding dysfunction Obstructive sleep apnoea Psychosocial stressors (particularly in secondary enuresis) Urinalysis to screen for infection and glucosuria Assessment of bowel habits for constipation Bladder diary of daytime symptoms and voiding pattern Blood glucose if polyuria or other features suggest diabetes Renal or bladder imaging only when structural or neurological pathology is suspected Nocturnal enuresis is involuntary voiding during sleep in a child old enough to be expected to have night-time bladder control, generally around five years and older. It is classified as primary when the child has never achieved a sustained period of night-time dryness and secondary when wetting returns after at least six months of dryness. Monosymptomatic enuresis involves night-time wetting alone, whereas non-monosymptomatic enuresis is accompanied by daytime lower urinary tract symptoms such as urgency, frequency, or daytime wetting. Common contributing factors include a family history, delayed maturation of arousal and bladder control, reduced overnight bladder capacity, and relative overnight excess of urine production. Most primary monosymptomatic enuresis is not caused by serious disease, and evaluation is mainly history, examination, and urinalysis to exclude infection and glycosuria. Secondary enuresis or associated daytime symptoms warrant closer evaluation for causes such as urinary tract infection, constipation, diabetes, or psychosocial stress. First-line management emphasises reassurance, education, and behavioural measures, with the enuresis alarm being the most effective long-term intervention for motivated families. Constipation frequently coexists and, when treated, wetting often improves, so bowel habits should always be assessed. New-onset (secondary) enuresis with weight loss, polyuria, or polydipsia Daytime incontinence, straining, or a poor urinary stream Recurrent urinary tract infections Neurological signs or spinal abnormalities Significant behavioural change or evidence of psychosocial distress or abuse Treating the child punitively or blaming the child for an involuntary problem Overlooking coexisting constipation as a contributor Failing to distinguish monosymptomatic from non-monosymptomatic enuresis before choosing therapy Missing an underlying cause of secondary enuresis such as infection or diabetes Night-time continence depends on the balance between overnight urine production, bladder storage capacity, and the ability to either suppress bladder contractions during sleep or wake in response to a full bladder. Enuresis arises when this balance fails: some children produce a relatively large volume of urine at night, some have a smaller functional bladder capacity or overactive bladder, and many have a high arousal threshold so a full or contracting bladder does not wake them. These factors, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition and developmental maturation, often coexist. Constipation can reduce functional bladder capacity and provoke bladder overactivity, and secondary enuresis may reflect an acquired medical or psychosocial trigger. Primary monosymptomatic enuresis has a high rate of spontaneous resolution with age, and treatment can accelerate dryness; the outlook is generally excellent, though relapses can occur and cases with daytime symptoms may need more prolonged management.
