enforce hearing protection and noise control at source Excessive acoustic energy causes mechanical and metabolic injury to the outer hair cells of the cochlea, initially at the basal turn that encodes higher frequencies around 3 to 6 kHz. Repeated exposure produces oxidative stress and progressive, irreversible hair cell loss, giving a sensorineural deficit that begins as the characteristic high-frequency notch and widens with continued exposure. Established noise-induced loss does not recover and there is no curative treatment; however, further deterioration can be halted by removing or controlling exposure, and communication is aided by hearing devices, making prevention the decisive factor.

Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma — NHL Hodgkin's lymphoma (distinguished by Reed-Sternberg cells) Reactive follicular hyperplasia (major differential for follicular lymphoma on biopsy) Lymphoid leukemias (CLL/SLL, ALL), plasma cell disorders (multiple myeloma) Other causes of lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or B-symptom-like constitutional illness Infectious mononucleosis / EBV infection and other viral lymphadenopathies Reactive lymphadenopathy from systemic infection Multicentric Castleman's disease (HHV-8), which causes diffuse lymphadenopathy with fever, malaise, and weight loss mimicking lymphoma B symptoms Adequate tissue biopsy reviewed by an expert hematopathologist (follicular lymphoma and Burkitt's lymphoma can be diagnosed on morphology; immunophenotyping required) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863) Complete blood count, routine chemistries, liver function tests, uric acid, calcium Serum protein electrophoresis (to detect monoclonal paraproteins) Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin (prognostic) (Harrison 22e p.860) CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (essential for staging, especially indolent lymphomas) (Harrison 22e p.861) FDG-PET (preferred for aggressive lymphomas such as DLBCL and Burkitt's, and to assess suspected transformation of indolent disease) (Harrison 22e p.861) Bone marrow biopsy Lumbar puncture in lymphoblastic, Burkitt's, and DLBCL with positive marrow biopsy or CNS-risk presentations (Harrison 22e p.861) Screening for HIV and hepatitis B and C at diagnosis (risk factors and risk of HBV reactivation with therapy) (Harrison 22e p.861) Autoimmune disease with lymphadenopathy (e.g., Sjögren's syndrome, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis) Reactive follicular hyperplasia Sarcoidosis and other causes of constitutional symptoms with adenopathy NHLs are cancers of mature B, T, and NK cells; ~90% are of B-cell origin. They are distinguished from Hodgkin's lymphoma by the absence of the Reed-Sternberg cell and differ from HL in biology, natural history, and the more variable prognosis (Harrison 22e p.857). Clinically, NHL is grouped by behavior: indolent/slow-growing (e.g., follicular lymphoma, the most common indolent NHL), aggressive (DLBCL, the most common subtype overall, ~one-third of cases), and highly aggressive/most rapidly growing (Burkitt's lymphoma, doubling time <24 h). Mantle cell lymphoma is intermediate-grade (Harrison 22e p.857, 862). The duration and pace of symptoms help distinguish aggressive from indolent disease, as does the presence or absence of 'B' symptoms — fevers, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss (>10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.860-861). Most common presentation of follicular lymphoma is new, painless lymphadenopathy at multiple sites; most patients lack elevated LDH or B symptoms. Asymptomatic indolent disease should be observed, as treating asymptomatic patients does not improve survival (Harrison 22e p.863-864). Serum LDH and serum beta-2-microglobulin are important independent prognostic factors in NHL and should be measured at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.860). Aggressive lymphomas (DLBCL, Burkitt's) are potentially curable with combination chemotherapy, whereas most indolent lymphomas are very responsive to therapy but not ultimately curable in the vast majority of cases except in localized early-stage disease (Harrison 22e p.862-863). Burkitt's lymphoma is highly aggressive (doubling time <24 h) — treatment must be initiated quickly and the tumor carries a high risk of tumor lysis syndrome; TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.862, 1014) Rapid growth of lymph nodes with new B symptoms in known indolent (follicular) lymphoma suggests histologic transformation to DLBCL (~3% per year) (Harrison 22e p.864) Disease involving paranasal sinuses, testes, breast, kidneys, adrenal glands, or epidural space — and highly aggressive histologies like Burkitt's — carries increased risk of CNS dissemination (Harrison 22e p.861) Concerning neurologic signs/symptoms warrant lumbar puncture for CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.860) 'Double-hit' high-grade B-cell lymphoma (concurrent MYC and BCL2 rearrangements) has an extremely poor prognosis (median OS ~12-18 months) (Harrison 22e p.862-863) Diagnosis requires an adequate tissue sample interpreted by an expert hematopathologist; an inadequate or unrepresentative specimen risks misclassification (e.g., missing coexisting DLBCL within follicular lymphoma or confusing lymphoma with reactive follicular hyperplasia) (Harrison 22e p.860, 863). The Ann Arbor anatomic staging system is less useful in NHL than in Hodgkin's lymphoma because NHL disseminates widely rather than in an ordered stepwise fashion; histology and the IPI matter more than stage (Harrison 22e p.861). Treating asymptomatic indolent (follicular) lymphoma does not improve survival — appropriate patients should be observed rather than treated immediately (Harrison 22e p.864). Failing to anticipate and prevent tumor lysis syndrome before treating rapidly proliferating Burkitt's lymphoma can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.862). A residual mass on CT after therapy may represent treated fibrosis rather than active disease; PET can help distinguish, but end-of-treatment PET should be delayed (preferably 6-8 weeks after chemotherapy) to avoid false positives (Harrison 22e p.861). NHLs arise from mature B, T, or NK lymphocytes, with ~90% being B-cell neoplasms; transformation typically requires several genetic events. Characteristic chromosomal translocations create fusion or deregulated oncogenes: t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression in follicular lymphoma (>85% of cases, necessary but not sufficient for transformation); MYC rearrangement at 8q24 in >95% of Burkitt's lymphoma (most often t(8;14) fusing MYC to IgH); and t(11;18) (API2-MLT) in MALT lymphoma. Gene-expression profiling subdivides DLBCL into germinal-center B-cell (GCB)-like and activated-B-cell (ABC)-like subtypes with differing prognoses. Several NHLs are linked to chronic antigenic stimulation or infection-driven immune dysregulation, and immunodeficiency states strongly predispose to (often EBV-associated) lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.857-863). Prognosis is highly variable and driven more by histology and clinical parameters than by anatomic stage. Overall 5-year survival for NHL is ~74%. The International Prognostic Index (IPI; age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site) is the best predictor for aggressive NHL: 5-year overall survival ~73%, 51%, 43%, and 26% for 0-1, 2, 3, and 4-5 risk factors. With R-CHOP, ~65-70% of DLBCL patients are cured. The FLIPI predicts follicular lymphoma outcome; most FL patients live 15-20 years but the disease is generally not curable (except localized early-stage), and Burkitt's lymphoma is curable in ~80-90% when treated promptly and correctly (Harrison 22e p.857, 861-862). WHO (WHO-HAEM5) classification of lymphoid malignancies categorizes NHL by cell of origin (mature B-cell vs mature T/NK-cell neoplasms) and entity. Anatomic extent is described by the Ann Arbor staging system (Stage I-IV, with suffix A/B for absence/presence of B symptoms). Prognostic stratification uses the International Prognostic Index (IPI) for aggressive NHL and the FLIPI for follicular lymphoma; follicular lymphoma is also graded I-III by centroblasts per high-power field (Harrison 22e p.857-862).

Nonketotic hyperglycinaemia (glycine encephalopathy) — glycine encephalopathy, NKH, glycine cleavage system deficiency, GLDC deficiency, AMT deficiency Ketotic hyperglycinaemia from organic acidaemias (propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric) Pyridoxine- or pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent epilepsy Neonatal hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Sepsis or meningitis with neonatal encephalopathy Sulphite oxidase/molybdenum cofactor deficiency Mitochondrial encephalopathies presenting in the neonate Transient neonatal hyperglycinaemia (self-limiting) Paired CSF and plasma glycine to calculate the CSF:plasma ratio Plasma and urine amino acids and urine organic acids (to exclude ketotic causes) EEG looking for burst-suppression or hypsarrhythmia Brain MRI including diffusion imaging and corpus callosum assessment Molecular analysis of GLDC, AMT and GCSH Blood gas and ketone/lactate measurement to confirm the nonketotic state Liver enzyme (glycine cleavage) assay when genetics are inconclusive Caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system, most often from GLDC or AMT variants Classic neonatal form presents with lethargy, profound hypotonia, hiccups, apnoea, myoclonic jerks and intractable seizures within the first days of life A characteristic EEG finding is a burst-suppression pattern evolving to hypsarrhythmia The biochemical hallmark is a raised cerebrospinal fluid to plasma glycine ratio, more discriminating than plasma glycine alone Crucially it is nonketotic: unlike organic acidaemias there is no ketosis or acidosis to explain the glycine elevation Distinguish from ketotic hyperglycinaemia, which reflects secondary glycine rise in propionic/methylmalonic/isovaleric acidaemia Confirm with molecular testing of GLDC/AMT (and rarely GCSH) and, where needed, enzyme assay in liver Treatment is supportive with glycine reduction using sodium benzoate and NMDA-receptor antagonism (e.g. dextromethorphan); outcome is often poor Central apnoea requiring ventilatory support in the neonate Intractable seizures and burst-suppression progressing to status Rapidly deteriorating consciousness with profound hypotonia Progressive microcephaly and developmental arrest Family history of unexplained neonatal deaths Interpreting a raised plasma glycine without a paired CSF sample and missing the diagnostic ratio Mistaking secondary (ketotic) hyperglycinaemia of an organic acidaemia for true NKH Blood contamination of CSF invalidating the CSF glycine measurement Assuming valproate is safe, when it can worsen hyperglycinaemia and should be avoided Overlooking transient neonatal hyperglycinaemia, which resolves and does not need lifelong therapy Nonketotic hyperglycinaemia arises from impaired activity of the glycine cleavage system, a mitochondrial multienzyme complex (comprising the P-protein/GLDC, T-protein/AMT, H-protein/GCSH and a lipoamide dehydrogenase) that degrades glycine. Loss of function causes glycine to accumulate in body fluids and especially the central nervous system. Excess glycine acts both as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brainstem and spinal cord, causing apnoea and hypotonia, and as a co-agonist at excitatory NMDA glutamate receptors in the forebrain, driving seizures and neuronal injury. The elevated CSF glycine relative to plasma reflects central overproduction/accumulation and is the diagnostic signature. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The severe neonatal form carries a poor prognosis with high early mortality and profound intellectual disability, intractable epilepsy and spasticity in survivors; attenuated forms have a milder course, and genotype and residual enzyme activity are the main determinants.

isolated intrathoracic NTM mistaken for cancer) Bronchiectasis exacerbation / underlying structural lung disease Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (predisposes to NTM and Nocardia) Sporotrichosis (sporotrichoid spread mimicked by M. marinum) M. tuberculosis (clinical, radiographic, and AFB-smear overlap) Nocardia (gram-positive beaded filamentous rods; alveolar proteinosis predisposes to both) Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichoid ascending nodules akin to M. marinum) Acid-fast or fluorochrome smears of sputum or body fluids (organisms may appear as beaded gram-positive rods at high burden, but this is unreliable) Mycobacterial culture using separate processing and dedicated blood culture media; differentiate rapidly growing (<7 days) from slowly growing (>=7 days) species; some labs hold cultures 6 weeks Liquid culture media for faster isolation; lower incubation temperature (30C) for M. marinum, M. haemophilum, M. ulcerans; special additives (iron/blood for M. haemophilum, mycobactin J for M. genavense) Species-level identification by biochemical tests, nucleic acid probes/sequencing, HPLC or mass spectrometry; molecular detection for noncultivable species (e.g., M. tilburgii) Chest CT (tree-in-bud bronchiolar pattern, lingular and right-middle-lobe involvement, bronchiectasis, cavitation) IGRA (note M. marinum, M. kansasii, M. szulgai carry ESAT6/CFP10 and may cause false-positive IGRA; IGRA is indeterminate with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies) Genetic evaluation of the IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway and screening for anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies in disseminated disease without iatrogenic cause; GATA2 evaluation when myelodysplasia coexists Malignancy presenting as painless cervical or intrathoracic adenopathy Hot-tub lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis-type reaction to NTM rather than invasive infection) NTM (also termed atypical, environmental, or mycobacteria other than tuberculosis) are ubiquitous in soil and water and refer to mycobacteria other than M. tuberculosis and its close relatives and M. leprae; over 199 species are recognized (p.1414). Most NTM cause human disease only when host defense is impaired (e.g., bronchiectasis) or breached by inoculation (liposuction, trauma, cardiac surgery); human-to-human transmission is rare and occurs almost exclusively in cystic fibrosis (p.1414). Pulmonary disease is by far the most common form in North America and is highly associated with pulmonary epithelial defects but NOT with systemic immunodeficiency; disseminated disease instead denotes significant immune dysfunction such as advanced HIV (p.1414, 1416). Pulmonary MAC most commonly presents in the 6th-7th decade in women with months to years of nagging intermittent cough and fatigue; pulmonary NTM in a tall, thin woman with chest-wall abnormalities is termed 'Lady Windermere syndrome' (p.1416). Pulmonary MAC affects older nonsmoking white women more than men (onset ~60 years); such patients tend to be taller and thinner with high rates of scoliosis, mitral valve prolapse, and pectus anomalies (p.1416). Male smokers with upper-lobe cavitary disease tend to carry the same single MAC strain indefinitely, whereas nonsmoking women with nodular bronchiectasis carry several MAC strains simultaneously that change over the disease course (p.1416). M. kansasii can produce a clinical syndrome strongly resembling tuberculosis with hemoptysis, chest pain, and cavitary lung disease (p.1416). Disseminated MAC (or M. kansasii) in advanced HIV is now uncommon in North America owing to effective prophylaxis and improved HIV treatment; when common, the portal of entry was the bowel with spread to bone marrow and bloodstream (p.1415). Disseminated NTM is often indolent and progressive over weeks to months with malaise, fever, weight loss, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and anemia; blood cultures may be negative even though involved organs carry heavy organism burdens, sometimes with grossly impaired granulomatous response (p.1415). Isolated cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common form of NTM infection in young children in North America (usually MAC); the swelling is firm and relatively painless with few systemic signs and is often diagnosed inadvertently at biopsy for suspected malignancy (p.1416). Children with isolated cervical or intrathoracic NTM infection do NOT commonly have underlying immune defects and usually do NOT go on to develop other opportunistic infections (p.1416). Cutaneous NTM usually requires a break in the skin; rapidly growing NTM (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum, M. chelonae) cause outbreaks via contaminated surgical instruments/injections, with painful erythematous draining subcutaneous nodules typically WITHOUT fever or systemic symptoms (p.1416). M. marinum (fish tanks, pools, fish handling) causes 'fish-tank granuloma' and can spread up the arm in a sporotrichoid pattern; M. ulcerans causes painless Buruli ulcer via the toxin mycolactone (p.1416). 'Hot-tub lung' is a pulmonary hypersensitivity reaction to NTM (most often MAC) growing in underchlorinated water, distinct from true pulmonary or disseminated infection (p.1415). For susceptibility testing, only MAC testing for clarithromycin and M. kansasii testing for rifampin is indicated; few data support other in vitro susceptibility tests, and MAC isolates not previously exposed to macrolides are almost always susceptible (p.1417). Disseminated involvement of two or more organs without an iatrogenic cause (prompts IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway genetic investigation) Disseminated NTM with bacterial/viral infections plus conical/peg/missing teeth or abnormal hair pattern in males (suggests NEMO/IKBKG NF-kB defect, possibly with immunoglobulin defects) Mycobacterial disease with myelodysplasia (investigate GATA2 deficiency) Disseminated MAC and rapidly growing NTM with other opportunistic infections (e.g., Talaromyces), especially in East Asian women (anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies) Infected indwelling IV catheters/lines (M. abscessus, M. fortuitum from contaminated water) requiring catheter removal Not all NTM isolations, especially from the lung, reflect disease or require treatment; distinguishing colonization/contamination from true infection requires an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting (nodules, bronchiectasis, cavities) plus repeated isolation per American Thoracic Society criteria (p.1417). The single most critical and sensitive step in diagnosis is simply to suspect NTM and request the correct, separately processed mycobacterial smears, cultures, and dedicated blood culture media; many cases go undiagnosed because the appropriate test was never ordered (p.1416-1417). M. gordonae is frequently recovered from respiratory samples but is almost never a pathogen (p.1417). PPD does not differentiate NTM from M. tuberculosis well; intermediate (~10 mm) reactions overlap, BCG cross-reacts, but large reactions (>15 mm) most commonly signify TB (p.1416-1417). Slow-growing NTM typically do NOT proliferate in routine blood culture media, so suspicion and correct bottles are essential; biopsy isolation is strong evidence but laboratory contamination does occur (confirm with organisms on stained sections) (p.1417). NTM are ubiquitous environmental organisms (soil and water) with specific niches (e.g., M. simiae in aquifers, M. fortuitum in pedicure baths, M. immunogenum in metalworking fluids). Because exposure is essentially universal yet disease is rare, normal host defenses are strong and significant disease implies a specific susceptibility. Mycobacteria are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release IL-12; IL-12 activates T and NK cells (via STAT4) to secrete IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages/neutrophils (via STAT1) and upregulates TNF-alpha, forming a positive IFN-gamma/IL-12 feedback loop critical for mycobacterial control. Disseminated NTM correlates with declining CD4+ T cells (advanced HIV, idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia), TNF-alpha inhibitors (which impair granuloma formation), Mendelian mutations in the IFN-gamma/IL-12 pathway (IFNG, IFNGR1, IFNGR2, STAT1, GATA2, ISG15, IRF8, IL-12A, IL-12RB1, IL-12RB2, CYBB, IKBKG/NEMO and others), or neutralizing anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies. Only ~70% of non-HIV disseminated cases have a genetic diagnosis. In contrast, the best-recognized substrate for pulmonary NTM is bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, STAT3 hyper-IgE/Job's syndrome, idiopathic), but the mechanism by which bronchiectasis predisposes to locally destructive yet non-systemic disease is unknown (p.1414-1415). NTM cause chronic infections evolving slowly over weeks to years, so emergent therapy before diagnosis and speciation is rarely needed. Treatment is complex, often poorly tolerated, and potentially toxic; inadequate single-drug therapy is almost always associated with emergence of resistance and relapse. Pulmonary MAC therapy is prolonged, generally continued for 12 months after culture conversion (typically at least 18 months total). The typical lag between symptom onset and diagnosis is about 5 years in older women (p.1416-1418). American Thoracic Society criteria for pulmonary NTM diagnosis: growth of NTM from two of three sputum samples (regardless of smear), OR a positive bronchoalveolar lavage sample (regardless of smear), OR a lung parenchymal biopsy with granulomatous inflammation or mycobacteria on section plus NTM on culture, in an appropriate clinical and radiographic setting. Isolation of NTM from blood or organ biopsy in a compatible clinical setting is considered diagnostic. NTM are categorized as rapidly growing (<7 days) versus slowly growing (>=7 days) (p.1417).

Turner syndrome without genetic testing Not monitoring for evolving hypertrophic cardiomyopathy over time Noonan syndrome is one of the RASopathies, a family of disorders caused by germline mutations that increase signalling through the RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase (RAS-MAPK) pathway, which governs cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. The most frequent gene involved is PTPN11, with additional cases attributed to SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS, and others. Excess pathway activity during development produces the cardiac defects, characteristic facial and skeletal features, growth restriction, and haematological abnormalities. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, and many cases arise de novo. Most individuals have a good long-term outlook with normal or near-normal cognition, though prognosis is influenced by the severity of cardiac disease, particularly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

normal development of the retinal and inner-ear vasculature. Visual prognosis is very poor, with most affected males blind from birth or early infancy and little response to surgical intervention; sensorineural hearing loss tends to progress over time, and prognosis for hearing and development varies, so long-term multidisciplinary support is needed.

shock, or acute heart failure Sustained ventricular arrhythmia or high-grade conduction block New mechanical complications such as acute mitral regurgitation Interpreting any raised troponin as type 1 infarction without considering type 2 injury or non-ischaemic causes Mislabelling an NSTEMI as STEMI or vice versa and applying the wrong reperfusion pathway Relying on a single early troponin or ECG to exclude infarction Delaying dual antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy while awaiting angiography in eligible patients NSTEMI most commonly arises from rupture or erosion of a coronary plaque with partially occlusive thrombus, or from severe fixed stenosis with superimposed thrombosis, producing prolonged ischaemia sufficient to cause myocyte necrosis. Because flow is reduced rather than completely and persistently interrupted, injury is often subendocardial and the ECG lacks persistent ST elevation. Outcomes depend on infarct size, coronary anatomy, left ventricular function, and comorbidities; timely risk-based invasive management and secondary prevention improve survival, though NSTEMI carries meaningful medium- and long-term mortality, sometimes exceeding STEMI over the longer term because of older age and comorbidity burden.

Nutritional Rickets — rickets, vitamin D deficiency rickets, calcipenic rickets Hypophosphataemic (vitamin D-resistant) rickets Vitamin D-dependent rickets (types 1 and 2) Renal osteodystrophy from chronic kidney disease Hypophosphatasia Osteogenesis imperfecta Skeletal dysplasias and physiologic bowing Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase 25-hydroxyvitamin D level Parathyroid hormone Renal function and, where indicated, urine calcium and phosphate Wrist or knee radiographs for metaphyseal changes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in atypical or treatment-resistant cases A disorder of defective mineralisation of growing bone, most commonly due to deficiency of vitamin D and/or dietary calcium. Risk factors include exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, darker skin pigmentation, limited sun exposure, and prematurity. Skeletal signs include widening of the wrists and ankles, a rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, and bowing of the legs once weight-bearing begins. Non-skeletal features can include delayed motor milestones, hypotonia, growth faltering, and increased susceptibility to fractures. Severe hypocalcaemia may present with tetany, carpopedal spasm, or seizures, especially in infants. Biochemistry classically shows low or low-normal calcium and phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase, raised parathyroid hormone, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Radiographs of the wrist or knee reveal metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widening of the growth plate. Treatment replaces vitamin D and ensures adequate dietary calcium, with biochemical and radiological healing confirming response. Prevention through routine vitamin D supplementation in infancy is highly effective, and failure to respond should prompt evaluation for inherited or renal forms. Hypocalcaemic seizures, tetany, or laryngospasm Cardiomyopathy associated with severe hypocalcaemia or vitamin D deficiency Pathological fractures Failure to respond to appropriate vitamin D and calcium therapy Progressive deformity or signs suggesting an inherited or renal cause Attributing bowed legs solely to physiologic causes and missing biochemical rickets Overlooking dietary calcium deficiency as a cause even when vitamin D is adequate Failing to investigate inherited or renal rickets when there is no response to treatment Not providing routine vitamin D supplementation to exclusively breastfed infants Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, lowering their availability for bone mineralisation. The falling calcium stimulates parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which mobilises calcium from bone and promotes renal phosphate wasting. The combination of low calcium-phosphate product and PTH-driven bone resorption leaves the expanding cartilage of the growth plate and newly formed osteoid unmineralised, producing the soft, deformable bones and characteristic metaphyseal changes of rickets. With adequate treatment, biochemical recovery occurs within weeks and radiographic healing over months; most deformities remodel in young children, though severe or late-treated cases may leave residual bowing.

Obesity — overweight Hypothyroidism — may cause weight gain but is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity; check TSH (and free thyroxine for rare secondary hypothyroidism) in any patient presenting with obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188) Cushing's syndrome / endogenous hypercortisolism — suggested by spontaneous bruising, livid striae, myopathy and marked centripetal fat distribution; confirmed via 24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression (Harrison 22e p.3185) Hypothalamic obesity — from tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma), inflammatory masses, or severe head injury disrupting hypothalamic energy-balance centres, often with anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction and short history of hyperphagia (Harrison 22e p.3185) Insulinoma — weight gain driven by frequent eating to avoid hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.3185) Polycystic ovarian syndrome — secondary cause/association meriting evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3188) Monogenic / syndromic obesity — leptin or leptin-receptor deficiency, POMC, PCSK1, MC4R, SIM1, BDNF/TrkB, SH2B1 mutations; syndromes such as Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl, Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy/pseudohypoparathyroidism, Cohen's, Carpenter's, Alström's, Tubby (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185) Drug-induced weight gain — insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, glucocorticoids, antipsychotics (clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone), lithium, antidepressants (tricyclics, MAOIs, paroxetine, mirtazapine), antiepileptics (valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine) (Harrison 22e p.3188) BMI calculation plus waist circumference (surrogate for visceral fat; measure horizontally above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI ≤35) and/or waist-to-hip ratio (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187) Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides), chemistry panel, glycated haemoglobin, and blood pressure in all patients (Harrison 22e p.3187) TSH ± free thyroxine to evaluate for hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188) 24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression test when Cushing's syndrome is suspected (Harrison 22e p.3185) Genetic testing in severe early-onset obesity (up to ~20% of children with severe obesity have chromosomal abnormalities or highly penetrant mutations) (Harrison 22e p.3183) Very muscular body habitus — BMI may overestimate body fat (Harrison 22e p.3181) Peripheral edema from NSAIDs or calcium channel blockers — increases weight without increasing body fat (Harrison 22e p.3188) Obesity is defined as a state of excess adipose tissue mass that adversely affects health; because direct measurement of fat mass is impractical in routine clinical practice, the body mass index (BMI = weight/height² in kg/m²) is used as a proxy (Harrison 22e p.3181). WHO BMI classes: underweight <18.5; normal 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obesity ≥30 kg/m². AACE/ACE management staging further subdivides obesity into class I (30.0–34.9), class II (35.0–39.9), and class III / extreme obesity (≥40) with correspondingly higher disease risk (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). BMI-based cutoffs were derived largely from white Western populations; adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, so lower thresholds and ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints (e.g., South Asians/Chinese, Japanese) are recommended (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). Fat distribution matters independent of overall BMI: a waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 in women and >1.0 in men, and excess abdominal (visceral) adiposity, are independently associated with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). Energy balance is under homeostatic control by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose-derived hormone leptin (rises with fat stores, falls fast with caloric restriction) with gut signals — GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin — plus pancreatic insulin and amylin (Harrison 22e p.3181–3182). Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia is one of the earliest and most prominent biochemical abnormalities of obesity, is worse with central adiposity, and underlies/precedes many adverse cardiometabolic consequences (Harrison 22e p.3186). Two leading (not mutually exclusive) hypotheses link obesity to insulin resistance: adipose-tissue inflammation (macrophage accumulation around dying adipocytes), and ectopic lipid deposition once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded — with stronger human data supporting the ectopic-fat / limited-storage mechanism (Harrison 22e p.3186). Obesity care begins with sensitive, non-stigmatizing language and an obesity-focused history covering diet, physical activity, sleep, stress, contributing factors, complications, and the patient's readiness/motivation to change (Harrison 22e p.3187–3188). Short history of hyperphagia and rapid weight gain with signs of anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction — suggests hypothalamic damage from tumor, inflammation, or head injury (Harrison 22e p.3185) Spontaneous bruising, livid striae, proximal myopathy, marked centripetal fat — suggests Cushing's syndrome rather than common obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185) Severe early-onset obesity in childhood with intense hyperphagia/food-seeking — prompts screening for monogenic/syndromic causes (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185) Severe hypertriglyceridemia secondary to insulin resistance — risk of pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.3186) Treating BMI alone: BMI only reflects body size, not body composition, fat distribution, health, or quality of life — not all patients with a high BMI need treatment, and BMI overestimates fat in very muscular individuals (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187, 3190). Applying white-Western-derived BMI cutoffs uniformly: adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, and ethnic-specific (e.g., Asia-Pacific) thresholds should be used (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187). Overlooking that severe hypothyroidism is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity, yet thyroid function should still always be checked (Harrison 22e p.3185). Mistaking the lower GH response to provocative testing in common obesity for a structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (Harrison 22e p.3186). Assuming a specific macronutrient ratio is key: weight loss depends primarily on total caloric reduction and adherence, not on the proportion of carbohydrate, fat, or protein (Harrison 22e p.3190). Using stigmatizing language ('obesity', 'morbid obesity', 'fatness') rather than neutral terms ('weight', 'excess weight', 'unhealthy weight'), which leaves patients feeling judged (Harrison 22e p.3188). Initiating lifestyle change before assessing readiness, which leads to frustration and may hamper future efforts (Harrison 22e p.3188). Adipose tissue evolved to store excess calories as triglyceride in unilocular lipid droplets and release free fatty acids and glycerol when needed. In an obesogenic environment (abundant energy-dense palatable food, larger portions, reduced physical activity), chronic energy intake exceeding expenditure — even by as little as ~7 kcal/day sustained over years — produces a cumulative excess of adipose triglyceride. Genetic factors strongly determine individual susceptibility (twin studies show adiposity tracks with biological, not adoptive, family), acting largely through the brain's control of food intake. Body weight is homeostatically defended by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose hormone leptin (whose fall below an individual's habitual level is a powerful drive to eat) with gut hormones (GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin) and pancreatic insulin/amylin. Within the arcuate nucleus, leptin stimulates POMC neurons (whose products α-/β-MSH act via MC4R in the paraventricular nucleus to reduce intake and raise energy expenditure) and inhibits orexigenic AGRP/NPY/GABA neurons. Leptin defends strongly against fat loss but responds weakly to fat excess ("leptin resistance"), explaining why rising leptin does not prevent obesity. As obesity develops, the earliest abnormality is insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, worse with central fat; this arises from adipose-tissue inflammation and/or ectopic lipid deposition in liver and muscle once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded (the human data favouring the ectopic-fat mechanism, as illustrated by lipodystrophy). Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia then predisposes to the metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular complications of obesity (Harrison 22e p.3181–3186). Obesity is a serious, highly heterogeneous chronic disease that increases morbidity and mortality across many organ systems. The number and severity of complications generally rise with increasing BMI, and excess abdominal/visceral fat confers added cardiometabolic risk. As BMI rises by 5 kg/m², cancer mortality increases by ~10%; in some countries obesity has overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer. People with obesity have increased morbidity and mortality from atherothrombotic vascular disease (coronary artery disease, stroke) even without diabetes, and are at increased risk of heart failure (especially diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation. Modest, sustained weight loss (an initial goal of ~8–10% over 6 months) improves obesity-related complications and quality of life; some complications, including type 2 diabetes (e.g., the DiRECT trial showed remission in nearly half of participants with intensive low-energy dietary intervention), can substantially improve or remit with weight loss (Harrison 22e p.3186–3187, 3190). BMI-based (kg/m²): underweight <18.5; healthy/normal weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25.0–29.9; obesity class I 30.0–34.9 (high disease risk); obesity class II 35.0–39.9 (very high risk); extreme/class III obesity ≥40 (extremely high risk). Risk is refined by excess abdominal fat (ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints; waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 women / >1.0 men). Disease-staging systems augment BMI: the AACE/ACE staging (stage 0 = no complications; stage 1 = mild-moderate complications; stage 2 = at least one severe complication) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS, grades 0–4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187–3188).

sedative drugs Severe hypoxaemia or respiratory acidosis requiring urgent ventilatory support Attributing hypercapnia to obstructive sleep apnoea alone and missing the hypoventilation syndrome Giving uncontrolled high-flow oxygen and worsening carbon dioxide retention Using sedatives that further depress ventilation Overlooking a raised bicarbonate as an early clue to chronic hypercapnia Severe obesity increases the mechanical load on the respiratory system through chest wall and abdominal fat, reducing lung volumes and respiratory compliance and increasing the work of breathing. Combined with blunted central ventilatory responsiveness to carbon dioxide and, in most patients, coexisting upper airway obstruction during sleep, this leads to chronic alveolar hypoventilation. Sustained carbon dioxide retention drives renal bicarbonate retention, which further blunts the ventilatory drive. Chronic hypoxaemia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and, over time, pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure. Positive airway pressure therapy and weight reduction improve gas exchange, symptoms, and survival; untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from respiratory failure and cor pulmonale.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder — OCD, obsessive compulsive disorder Generalized anxiety disorder Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder Body dysmorphic disorder Hoarding disorder Tic disorders and Tourette syndrome Illness anxiety disorder Psychotic disorder when insight is absent Standardised OCD severity rating scales to quantify symptoms and monitor treatment Screening for comorbid depression, anxiety, and tic disorders Assessment of insight and degree of functional impairment Consideration of post-streptococcal aetiology in abrupt paediatric onset Characterised by obsessions (intrusive, unwanted, distressing thoughts, images, or urges) and/or compulsions (repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to reduce anxiety or prevent a feared outcome) Symptoms are time-consuming or cause marked distress and functional impairment; patients often recognise them as excessive, though insight varies Common themes include contamination with washing, doubt with checking, symmetry with ordering, and taboo intrusive thoughts First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, which is highly effective Pharmacotherapy principles favour SSRIs, often needing higher doses and longer trials than in depression before judging response Clomipramine is an effective alternative, and augmentation strategies are considered in resistant cases Distinguish from obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, which involves ego-syntonic perfectionism and rigidity rather than distressing intrusive symptoms Assess for comorbid depression, tic disorders, and hoarding, and ask about suicidal ideation Suicidal ideation, particularly with comorbid depression Severe functional incapacity from time-consuming rituals Complete loss of insight suggesting a psychotic process Self-harm from compulsions such as excessive washing causing skin breakdown Confusing OCD with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder Judging SSRI non-response before an adequately high dose and prolonged trial Providing reassurance that inadvertently reinforces compulsive checking Overlooking comorbid depression and suicide risk Failing to offer or refer for exposure and response prevention, the most effective psychotherapy Obsessive-compulsive disorder is associated with dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, particularly hyperactivity involving the orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, and basal ganglia, together with serotonergic and glutamatergic dysregulation. Genetic factors contribute, and in some children symptom onset has been linked to post-streptococcal autoimmune processes. Obsessive-compulsive disorder is typically chronic with waxing and waning severity, but many patients achieve substantial improvement with exposure and response prevention and adequate pharmacotherapy. Early onset, poor insight, and comorbidity are associated with a more persistent course.
