intrinsic liver disease Gallstone disease or biliary obstruction Serum bile acid measurement, ideally with serial monitoring of peak levels Liver function tests including transaminases and bilirubin Coagulation studies where cholestasis is prolonged or severe Viral hepatitis screen and liver autoantibodies to exclude other liver disease Liver ultrasound to exclude biliary obstruction Fetal surveillance, recognising that routine monitoring poorly predicts sudden stillbirth Obstetric cholestasis is a pregnancy-specific liver disorder characterised by pruritus and raised bile acids, typically presenting in the second half of pregnancy The hallmark symptom is generalised itching, often severe and worse at night, classically involving the palms and soles, in the absence of a primary skin rash Diagnosis rests on elevated serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases once other causes of itch and abnormal liver function are excluded The main concern is fetal rather than maternal, as high bile acid concentrations are associated with an increased risk of stillbirth, preterm birth, and meconium-stained liquor The risk of stillbirth rises with the degree of bile acid elevation, so severity is graded on peak bile acid levels and guides timing of delivery Ursodeoxycholic acid is commonly used to relieve maternal itching, though its effect on fetal outcome is limited, and vitamin K may be considered if there is prolonged clotting from fat malabsorption Symptoms and biochemistry resolve after delivery, but the condition recurs in a high proportion of future pregnancies and with oestrogen-containing contraception Persistent abnormal liver function after delivery should prompt investigation for underlying hepatobiliary disease Markedly elevated bile acids indicating higher stillbirth risk and need for planned delivery Coexisting features of pre-eclampsia or HELLP suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or systemic upset suggesting significant hepatic pathology Reduced fetal movements or other signs of fetal compromise Prolonged clotting from vitamin K deficiency increasing bleeding risk Dismissing severe pruritus in pregnancy without checking bile acids and liver function Failing to exclude pre-eclampsia, HELLP, and acute fatty liver in a woman with abnormal liver tests Over-reliance on cardiotocography to predict a sudden stillbirth it cannot reliably foresee Not grading severity by bile acid level to guide timing of delivery Overlooking persistent postpartum liver dysfunction that signals underlying disease Obstetric cholestasis reflects impaired hepatocellular secretion and enterohepatic circulation of bile acids in genetically susceptible women, in whom the high oestrogen and progesterone levels of pregnancy reduce the function of bile acid transport proteins. This leads to accumulation of bile acids in the maternal circulation, causing pruritus, and their transfer across the placenta is thought to underlie the fetal risks, with high concentrations having arrhythmogenic and vasoconstrictive effects that may contribute to sudden fetal death. Cholestasis can also impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin K. For the mother the condition is usually self-limiting and resolves promptly after birth, though it recurs frequently in later pregnancies and with oestrogen exposure. The principal concern is the fetus, and careful monitoring of bile acid levels with timely delivery reduces perinatal risk; failure of liver function to normalise postpartum should prompt further hepatological assessment.

Obstructive sleep apnoea — OSA, OSAS, obstructive sleep apnoea-hypopnoea syndrome, sleep-disordered breathing Central sleep apnoea Obesity hypoventilation syndrome Narcolepsy and other primary hypersomnias Insufficient sleep or poor sleep hygiene Hypothyroidism-related somnolence Depression-related fatigue In-laboratory polysomnography to confirm diagnosis and grade severity Home sleep apnoea testing in appropriately selected patients without significant comorbidity Overnight or nocturnal oximetry as a screening adjunct Validated questionnaires and sleepiness scales to assess pretest probability and symptom burden Assessment for associated conditions including hypertension, thyroid dysfunction, and metabolic disease Characterised by repetitive collapse of the upper airway during sleep, producing apnoeas and hypopnoeas with recurrent oxygen desaturations and arousals Typical features include loud habitual snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, choking or gasping at night, and unrefreshing sleep Excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headache, poor concentration, and mood disturbance are common daytime consequences Obesity, increased neck circumference, male sex, retrognathia, and enlarged tonsils are important predisposing factors Polysomnography is the diagnostic standard, with severity graded by the apnoea-hypopnoea index; home sleep testing can be used in selected patients Continuous positive airway pressure is the mainstay of therapy for moderate-to-severe disease, splinting the airway open during sleep Weight reduction, avoidance of alcohol and sedatives, positional therapy, and treatment of nasal obstruction are useful adjuncts Untreated OSA is linked to hypertension, arrhythmias, ischaemic heart disease, stroke, insulin resistance, and increased motor-vehicle accident risk Severe daytime sleepiness in occupational drivers or machine operators posing safety risk Signs of daytime hypoventilation or right heart failure suggesting overlap with hypoventilation syndromes Resistant hypertension or nocturnal arrhythmias Rapidly progressive symptoms or marked nocturnal desaturation Attributing daytime sleepiness solely to lifestyle and missing significant OSA Overlooking OSA as a driver of resistant hypertension or atrial fibrillation Assuming all patients are obese; OSA can occur with normal body habitus due to craniofacial anatomy Failing to address poor CPAP adherence, which undermines treatment benefit During sleep, reduced tone of the pharyngeal dilator muscles allows the anatomically narrowed or collapsible upper airway to close, producing partial (hypopnoea) or complete (apnoea) obstruction despite continued respiratory effort. The resulting hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, and rising respiratory effort trigger brief cortical arousals that restore airway patency but fragment sleep. Recurrent cycles of desaturation-reoxygenation and arousal drive sympathetic activation, surges in blood pressure, oxidative stress, and systemic inflammation, which over time contribute to cardiovascular and metabolic disease. With consistent adherence to positive airway pressure and weight management, symptoms and quality of life usually improve markedly and cardiovascular risk is reduced; poorly controlled or untreated disease carries substantial long-term cardiovascular, metabolic, and accident-related morbidity.

Occupational asthma — work-related asthma, OA, sensitiser-induced asthma, irritant-induced asthma Non-occupational (constitutional) asthma coincidentally worsened by workplace conditions Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) Vocal cord dysfunction Rhinitis with post-nasal symptoms mimicking lower airway disease Hyperventilation or anxiety-related breathlessness Serial peak expiratory flow diaries covering periods at work and away from work Spirometry with reversibility testing Non-specific bronchial challenge testing to document hyper-responsiveness Specific IgE or skin prick testing to suspected occupational allergens where available Specific inhalation (bronchial provocation) challenge in specialist centres when diagnosis is uncertain Detailed occupational history including materials, processes and temporal pattern of symptoms Suspect a work cause when asthma symptoms improve on days away from work, during holidays, and worsen on returning to the workplace Two broad forms exist: sensitiser-induced disease, which follows a latency period of exposure, and irritant-induced disease that can follow a single high-level exposure (reactive airways dysfunction syndrome) Common high-molecular-weight sensitisers include flour, animal proteins, latex and enzymes; frequent low-molecular-weight agents include isocyanates, colophony solder flux and certain wood dusts Serial peak flow monitoring recorded several times a day at and away from work is a practical and valuable tool for confirming a work relationship Early diagnosis matters because prolonged continued exposure after symptoms begin predicts persistent asthma even after removal Complete removal from the causative agent, rather than simply reducing exposure, gives the best chance of recovery A confident diagnosis has major implications for the worker's livelihood, so objective confirmation should be sought before advising job change Consider workplace surveillance and review of coworkers, since others exposed to the same agent may also be affected Acute severe bronchospasm following a major irritant exposure or spill Progressive symptoms despite continued exposure indicating risk of fixed airflow obstruction Nocturnal attacks or falling peak flows suggesting poorly controlled disease Features of anaphylaxis with certain protein allergens such as latex Attributing symptoms to ordinary asthma and failing to take an occupational history Advising reduced rather than complete removal from a sensitising agent Relying on symptoms alone without objective serial lung function data Delaying diagnosis so that airway changes become irreversible Overlooking coexisting occupational rhinitis, which often precedes asthma Sensitiser-induced occupational asthma develops through immunological sensitisation to an inhaled workplace agent, often IgE-mediated for high-molecular-weight proteins, leading to airway inflammation, bronchial hyper-responsiveness and reversible airflow obstruction on re-exposure. Irritant-induced asthma arises from direct toxic injury to the airway epithelium after intense exposure to a respiratory irritant, provoking inflammation and lasting hyper-responsiveness without a prior latency period. Outcome depends heavily on how quickly the diagnosis is made and exposure stopped; early cessation gives a good chance of improvement, whereas prolonged exposure before removal is associated with persistent asthma and airway hyper-responsiveness that may not fully resolve.

Occupational and Environmental Lung Disease — pneumoconiosis, silicosis, asbestosis Asbestosis vs other causes of diffuse interstitial fibrosis (IPF/UIP) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Chronic beryllium disease vs sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Silicosis (complicated/PMF) vs coal worker's pneumoconiosis and progressive massive fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute silicosis vs pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) vs influenza or community-acquired pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234) Occupational asthma / RADS vs nonoccupational asthma and COPD (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis from thermophilic actinomycete spores) presenting 4-8 h after exposure with fever, chills, malaise, cough, and dyspnea can mimic influenza or pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute silicosis with profuse miliary infiltration may radiographically resemble miliary infectious processes (Harrison 22e p.2234) Pre- and post-shift spirometry (change in FEV1) to detect acute bronchoconstriction (Harrison 22e p.2234) Chest radiograph graded by the ILO International Classification of Radiographs of Pneumoconioses (Harrison 22e p.2234) CT and high-resolution CT (HRCT) - more sensitive than radiograph for lung opacities, pleural thickening, and interstitial change (Harrison 22e p.2234) Pulmonary function testing (restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes and diffusing capacity in fibrosing disease) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Skin prick testing or specific IgE for immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., flour antigens in bakers) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Specific IgG precipitating antibody titers for hypersensitivity pneumonitis agents (e.g., pigeon antigen in bird handlers) (Harrison 22e p.2234) Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) for beryllium sensitization (Harrison 22e p.2234) Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with transbronchial lung biopsy (e.g., to diagnose chronic beryllium disease); occasionally video-assisted thoracoscopic surgical biopsy for definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Chronic beryllium disease closely mimics sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Aluminum and titanium dioxide exposure can produce a sarcoid-like reaction in lung tissue (Harrison 22e p.2234) Asbestosis mimics idiopathic and other diffuse interstitial fibroses (Harrison 22e p.2234) Hard-metal (tungsten carbide/cobalt) exposure can cause giant cell interstitial pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.2234) A detailed occupational and environmental exposure history is the single most important step; include hobbies, home characteristics, secondhand smoke, and proximity to traffic/industry, plus short- and long-term exposures in the distant past (Harrison 22e p.2234). Inorganic/organic dust exposure characteristically causes interstitial lung disease with a restrictive pattern and reduced diffusing capacity, whereas dusts/chemicals causing occupational asthma or COPD produce airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2234). A drop in FEV1 measured before vs after a work shift can detect an acute occupational bronchoconstrictive response (Harrison 22e p.2234). Radiographic pattern hints at etiology: small rounded opacities suggest silicosis or coal worker's pneumoconiosis, while small linear/irregular opacities suggest asbestosis (Harrison 22e p.2234). Asbestos exposure causes a spectrum of disease: pleural plaques and benign effusions (marking exposure only), asbestosis (interstitial fibrosis), bronchogenic lung cancer, and pleural/peritoneal mesothelioma (Harrison 22e p.2234). Pleural plaques indicate past asbestos exposure but, by themselves, imply only exposure and not pulmonary impairment (Harrison 22e p.2234). Smoking and asbestos exposure interact more than additively, producing lung cancer risk greater than the sum of each factor; mesothelioma risk is NOT associated with smoking (Harrison 22e p.2234). Silicosis raises the risk of mycobacterial (including M. tuberculosis), atypical mycobacterial, and fungal infection because silica impairs alveolar macrophage function; treatment of latent TB is given for a longer duration in these patients (Harrison 22e p.2234). Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes (seen in up to ~20% of cases) is a characteristic radiographic clue to silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234). Acute (accelerated) silicosis from very heavy exposure (e.g., sandblasting in confined spaces, denim sandblasting, artificial-stone countertop fabrication) can resemble pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with a 'crazy paving' HRCT pattern and may progress despite stopping exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234). Chronic beryllium disease mimics sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the distinguishing feature is a beryllium-specific cell-mediated (delayed hypersensitivity) immune response demonstrated by the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) (Harrison 22e p.2234). Caplan syndrome is the combination of pneumoconiotic nodules and seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, first described in coal miners and later in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234). Documented mesothelioma in a patient with occupational/environmental asbestos exposure may be compensable, as >80% of mesotheliomas are associated with asbestos exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234). Mesothelioma may follow relatively short asbestos exposures (<=1-2 years) with latency up to ~40 years - a thorough exposure history is essential (Harrison 22e p.2234) Lung cancer after asbestos exposure has a minimum latency of ~15-19 years from first exposure (Harrison 22e p.2234) Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), occurring in complicated silicosis and CWP, causes severe lung function deficits and is associated with premature mortality; PMF is rising at an alarming rate in the Appalachian coal belt (Harrison 22e p.2234) Active tuberculosis risk is increased in silicosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) Acute silicosis can be severe and progressive even after exposure ceases (Harrison 22e p.2234) Failing to take an occupational/environmental exposure history is the cardinal pitfall - the etiologic link to occupation is missed unless specifically sought, e.g., asking about beryllium exposure in a patient labeled as having sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2234) The ILO radiographic classification, though useful for screening populations, is problematic for the individual worker: rounded-opacity disease may look extensive on film with minimal functional impairment, whereas linear/irregular opacities (asbestosis) may lead to underestimation of impairment until late (Harrison 22e p.2234) In early chronic beryllium disease both chest imaging and pulmonary function tests may be normal (Harrison 22e p.2234) Attributing dust-related chronic bronchitis/COPD solely to occupation without accounting for cigarette smoking, whose effect is generally additive (Harrison 22e p.2234) Overlooking that talc and vermiculite may be contaminated with asbestos, conferring fibrosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma risk (Harrison 22e p.2234) Combat-related embedded metal fragments (shrapnel) in veterans may contain beryllium and serve as an unrecognized exposure source (Harrison 22e p.2234) Disease depends on the chemical/physical properties of the inhaled agent, which determine dose and site of deposition: water-soluble gases (ammonia, SO2) are absorbed in proximal airways causing irritation/bronchoconstriction, while less-soluble gases (NO2, phosgene) reach bronchioles/alveoli causing chemical pneumonitis. Particles >10-15 micrometres deposit in the nose/throat; particles <10 micrometres reach below the larynx, with coarse-mode (~2.5-10 micrometres, crustal elements like silica) depositing high in the tracheobronchial tree, fine-mode (<2.5 micrometres, from combustion/high-temperature processes) dominating surface area for toxin delivery to lower airways, and ultrafine (<0.1 micrometres, nanoparticles) potentially entering the circulation. Asbestos fibers induce fibrosis through oxidative injury from reactive oxygen species generated by surface transition metals and by phagocytosing cells. Silica causes alveolar macrophage dysfunction (predisposing to infection) and has immunoadjuvant properties (predisposing to autoimmune connective tissue disease). Beryllium drives a CD4+ T-cell-mediated granulomatous inflammation, with susceptibility strongly linked to HLA-DP alleles bearing glutamic acid at position 69 of the beta chain. (Harrison 22e p.2234) Outcome varies by exposure and disease. Pleural plaques alone do not imply impairment. Simple silicosis and simple CWP are often present without significant functional impairment, but nodular fibrosis can progress even after exposure ceases, coalescing into complicated disease and PMF, which carries severe functional deficits and premature mortality. Acute silicosis may be severe and progressive despite stopping exposure. No specific therapy exists for asbestosis (supportive care as for any diffuse interstitial fibrosis); newly diagnosed cases usually reflect exposures from many years earlier. Asbestos exposure carries excess lung cancer risk (latency ~15-19 years) and mesothelioma risk (latency up to ~40 years). (Harrison 22e p.2234) Silicosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis are categorized as simple (small rounded opacities, usually without functional impairment) versus complicated (nodules >=1 cm) which can progress to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF, conglomerate masses >1 cm with restrictive and obstructive impairment). Acute (accelerated) silicosis is distinguished from chronic silicosis by very heavy short-duration exposure and an alveolar-proteinosis-like presentation. Occupational asthma is divided into immunologic (high- vs low-molecular-weight stimuli, with a latency period) and irritative (reactive airway dysfunction syndrome, RADS) forms. (Harrison 22e p.2234)

Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy — OPMD, PABPN1-related dystrophy Myasthenia gravis Mitochondrial disease with chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia Myotonic dystrophy Oculopharyngodistal myopathy Thyroid eye disease causing ptosis or ophthalmoplegia Motor neurone disease with bulbar involvement Targeted repeat-expansion genetic testing of PABPN1 Videofluoroscopic or instrumental swallowing assessment Electromyography showing a myopathic pattern Serum creatine kinase, which is normal or mildly elevated Muscle biopsy with characteristic intranuclear inclusions in selected cases Nutritional assessment and monitoring of weight Late-onset muscular dystrophy, usually autosomal dominant, caused by a short GCN trinucleotide repeat expansion in PABPN1 encoding poly(A)-binding protein nuclear 1 Typically presents in mid-to-late adulthood with progressive ptosis and dysphagia as the cardinal features Ptosis is usually bilateral and slowly progressive, and patients often adopt a head-tilt-back posture to see beneath the drooping lids Dysphagia progresses over time and predisposes to aspiration, weight loss, and malnutrition, which are the main sources of morbidity Proximal limb-girdle weakness, particularly of the pelvic girdle, develops later in the disease course External ophthalmoplegia may occur but is usually mild and rarely causes troublesome diplopia Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted repeat-expansion testing of PABPN1, supported by the characteristic clinical picture Management is supportive, with swallowing assessment and dietary modification, aspiration precautions, and surgical options such as ptosis correction and cricopharyngeal intervention for selected patients Recurrent aspiration or aspiration pneumonia from progressive dysphagia Significant weight loss or malnutrition Choking episodes indicating unsafe swallowing Ptosis obscuring vision and impairing safe mobility Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis Mistaking the ptosis and ophthalmoplegia for myasthenia gravis and giving inappropriate treatment Underestimating the aspiration risk from progressive dysphagia Overlooking the family history given the autosomal dominant late-onset pattern Neglecting nutritional assessment as swallowing deteriorates Failing to consider the diagnosis in older adults presenting with isolated ptosis Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy is caused by a modest expansion of a GCN repeat in PABPN1, which lengthens the polyalanine tract of the poly(A)-binding protein nuclear 1. The mutant protein misfolds and aggregates into intranuclear inclusions within muscle-fibre nuclei, disturbing RNA processing and polyadenylation. The selective vulnerability of the levator palpebrae, pharyngeal, and later proximal limb muscles produces the characteristic combination of progressive ptosis, dysphagia, and eventual limb-girdle weakness. Aggregate accumulation over decades accounts for the late onset and slow progression. Progression is slow and life expectancy is often near normal, but dysphagia-related complications such as aspiration and malnutrition are the principal threats to health. Proactive swallowing management and timely surgical intervention improve quality of life and reduce aspiration risk.

Odontogenic sinusitis — dental sinusitis, maxillary sinusitis of dental origin, odontogenic maxillary sinusitis Rhinogenic (non-dental) bacterial or viral sinusitis Allergic rhinosinusitis Fungal sinusitis Sinonasal tumour Oroantral fistula without active sinusitis Cone-beam or conventional CT to localise the dental source and sinus disease Thorough dental examination with pulp testing of upper posterior teeth Assessment for oroantral communication after recent extraction Nasal endoscopy and ENT assessment where indicated Culture of purulent discharge in resistant or severe cases Odontogenic sinusitis is maxillary sinus inflammation arising from a dental source and accounts for a significant minority of maxillary sinus infections It should be suspected in unilateral maxillary sinusitis, particularly when symptoms are refractory to standard rhinological treatment A foul smell or taste and unilateral purulent discharge are characteristic clues pointing to a dental origin Common causes include periapical infection of upper posterior teeth, periodontal disease, oroantral communication after extraction, and displaced roots or implants The close relationship between the roots of maxillary premolars and molars and the sinus floor explains the spread of infection Cone-beam CT is valuable for identifying the culprit tooth and the extent of sinus involvement Effective treatment must address the dental cause, since sinus-directed therapy alone often fails Management may combine dental treatment or extraction, closure of any oroantral communication, and sinus care in collaboration with ENT Spread beyond the sinus with orbital swelling, visual changes, or signs of intracranial extension Features suggesting invasive fungal sinusitis in immunocompromised or diabetic patients Persistent unilateral disease or a mass raising suspicion of malignancy Systemic sepsis from an odontogenic infection extending into deep spaces Treating recurrent unilateral maxillary sinusitis medically while missing the dental cause Overlooking an oroantral communication after upper molar extraction Failing to test the vitality of upper posterior teeth adjacent to the sinus Neglecting displaced roots or implants within the sinus as a persistent nidus Odontogenic sinusitis develops when the integrity of the barrier between the maxillary posterior teeth and the sinus floor is breached, allowing bacteria and inflammatory products to enter the sinus. This may follow periapical or periodontal infection extending through thin or dehiscent bone, an oroantral communication created during extraction, or displacement of roots, foreign material, or implants into the sinus. The resulting mixed, often anaerobic, infection disrupts mucociliary clearance and can obstruct the ostiomeatal complex, perpetuating sinus inflammation. Because the driver is dental, the process persists until the source is eliminated. Prognosis is good when the dental cause is identified and treated, with resolution of sinus symptoms; failure to address the source leads to persistent or recurrent sinusitis and occasional serious complications.

Ohtahara syndrome — early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, EIEE, early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with burst-suppression, STXBP1 Early myoclonic encephalopathy West syndrome (infantile spasms) Neonatal seizures from hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Pyridoxine-dependent and other vitamin-responsive epilepsies Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with neonatal seizures Malformations of cortical development EEG demonstrating burst-suppression in both wakefulness and sleep Brain MRI to detect malformations of cortical development and structural lesions Epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing (e.g. STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A, ARX) Metabolic workup including trials of vitamin-responsive causes such as pyridoxine CSF studies where a metabolic or neurotransmitter disorder is suspected Onset is very early, usually within the first weeks to three months of life, with frequent tonic spasms occurring both awake and asleep The defining EEG hallmark is a burst-suppression pattern present in both wakefulness and sleep Causes are heterogeneous, including structural brain malformations and pathogenic variants in genes such as STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A and ARX Development is severely impaired from onset, and seizures are typically drug-resistant It may evolve into West syndrome and later into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome as the child grows Structural imaging is essential because malformations of cortical development are a frequent underlying cause Distinguishing it from early myoclonic encephalopathy rests on the predominant seizure type and the state-dependence of the EEG pattern Refractory tonic spasms with persistent burst-suppression in early infancy Failure to respond to pyridoxine trial when a vitamin-responsive cause is possible Evidence of a progressive metabolic disorder Rapid developmental arrest from birth Failing to trial vitamin-responsive treatments before concluding refractoriness Overlooking a subtle malformation of cortical development on early imaging Confusing it with early myoclonic encephalopathy by not characterising the predominant seizure type Not pursuing genetic testing, which increasingly identifies a specific cause Ohtahara syndrome is an early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in which severe disruption of neuronal networks in the immature brain produces continuous epileptic activity. The underlying causes, whether structural malformations of cortical development or pathogenic variants affecting synaptic transmission and ion channels, converge on profound cortical hyperexcitability and impaired inhibition. This generates the persistent burst-suppression pattern and frequent tonic spasms, while the same widespread dysfunction arrests brain development from the outset. The prognosis is generally very poor, with high early mortality, severe intellectual and motor disability in survivors, and frequent evolution to West and then Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Outcome is strongly influenced by the underlying cause.

Omenn syndrome — OS, RAG1, RAG2, leaky severe combined immunodeficiency Classic severe combined immunodeficiency without the Omenn phenotype Maternal T-cell engraftment in severe combined immunodeficiency Neonatal or infantile graft-versus-host disease Atopic dermatitis or other neonatal erythrodermas Netherton syndrome Langerhans cell histiocytosis Full blood count with differential showing eosinophilia Immunoglobulin levels demonstrating raised IgE with low IgG, IgA and IgM Lymphocyte subset analysis and T-cell receptor repertoire (clonality) studies Molecular genetic testing of RAG1, RAG2 and other combined immunodeficiency genes Newborn screening T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) assay where available Skin biopsy and infection screen for opportunistic pathogens A form of leaky combined immunodeficiency, most often caused by hypomorphic variants in RAG1 or RAG2 that permit limited, oligoclonal T-cell development Presents in early infancy with an erythrodermic, often exfoliative rash, alopecia and loss of eyebrows and eyelashes Generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly accompany failure to thrive and chronic diarrhoea Characteristic laboratory picture is an elevated eosinophil count and markedly raised IgE with low or absent other immunoglobulins T cells are present but restricted (oligoclonal) and activated, whereas B cells are typically absent or very low The autologous activated T cells infiltrate skin, gut and other organs, producing a picture that can mimic graft-versus-host disease Susceptibility to opportunistic and severe infection is high and the condition is fatal without treatment Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment, with immunosuppression to control the inflammatory phenotype beforehand Severe or opportunistic infection in an infant with erythroderma Rapidly worsening exfoliative rash with fluid and protein loss Signs of end-organ infiltration or systemic inflammatory decompensation Failure to thrive with intractable diarrhoea Misdiagnosing the erythroderma as atopic dermatitis and delaying immunological evaluation Overlooking the diagnosis because T cells are present, unlike classic severe combined immunodeficiency Failing to consider maternal engraftment or graft-versus-host disease in the differential Administering live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products before the immune defect is recognised Omenn syndrome arises when residual (hypomorphic) activity of the V(D)J recombination machinery, most commonly RAG1 or RAG2, allows a small number of autoreactive T-cell clones to develop rather than complete arrest of lymphocyte maturation. Defective central and peripheral tolerance, thymic dysfunction and reduced regulatory T cells permit these oligoclonal, activated, T-helper-2-skewed T cells to expand and infiltrate the skin and gut, generating the erythroderma, eosinophilia and raised IgE. B-cell development fails, causing agammaglobulinaemia and profound infection susceptibility. Omenn syndrome is uniformly fatal in infancy without treatment. Timely haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally after control of the inflammatory phenotype, offers the prospect of immune reconstitution and long-term survival.

Omphalocele — exomphalos, umbilical eventration Gastroschisis Umbilical cord hernia Umbilical hernia Pentalogy of Cantrell Cloacal or bladder exstrophy Antenatal ultrasound and karyotyping given the high rate of chromosomal anomalies Fetal and postnatal echocardiography to detect cardiac defects Blood glucose monitoring, particularly if Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is suspected Assessment of respiratory status for possible pulmonary hypoplasia in giant defects Renal and cranial imaging as part of anomaly screening A central abdominal wall defect at the umbilicus in which abdominal contents herniate into a sac formed by peritoneum and amniotic membrane, with the cord inserting onto the sac The covering sac distinguishes it from gastroschisis and offers some protection, but it can rupture during delivery or handling Strongly associated with other anomalies, including chromosomal disorders, cardiac defects, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, so a thorough workup is essential Large or giant defects may contain the liver, complicating reduction and closure and raising the risk of respiratory compromise Initial management protects the sac, keeps it moist and covered, maintains temperature and fluids, and decompresses the stomach Small defects can often be closed primarily, whereas giant omphaloceles may be managed with staged reduction or a delayed approach allowing the sac to epithelialise Associated pulmonary hypoplasia and hypoglycaemia (in Beckwith-Wiedemann) must be anticipated and monitored Antenatal detection allows delivery planning, genetic counselling, and fetal echocardiography Rupture of the sac exposing viscera, converting it to an emergency similar to gastroschisis with major fluid and heat loss Respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia or from raised intra-abdominal pressure after reduction Severe hypoglycaemia in the context of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome Haemodynamic instability from a major associated cardiac anomaly Allowing the sac to dry out or become damaged through poor handling Failing to search for and manage associated cardiac and chromosomal anomalies Forcing rapid reduction of a giant defect and precipitating abdominal compartment syndrome or respiratory failure Overlooking hypoglycaemia in infants with features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome Omphalocele results from failure of the midgut to return fully to the abdominal cavity and complete the normal closure of the abdominal wall at the umbilical ring during early gestation. The herniated viscera remain covered by a membranous sac of peritoneum and amnion with Wharton's jelly between them. Because the defect reflects a broader disturbance of ventral body wall folding, it is frequently accompanied by chromosomal, cardiac, and syndromic abnormalities, and large defects are associated with a small, underdeveloped abdominal cavity and pulmonary hypoplasia. Prognosis is driven largely by associated anomalies rather than the defect itself; isolated small omphaloceles do well, whereas giant defects and those with chromosomal, cardiac, or pulmonary problems carry higher morbidity and mortality. Staged management of giant lesions can yield good long-term results.

Onchocerciasis (river blindness) — river blindness, Onchocerca volvulus infection, onchocerciasis, Robles disease, Mazzotti reaction Loiasis and lymphatic filariasis Scabies and other causes of chronic pruritic dermatitis Cutaneous leishmaniasis Leprosy (for skin and nerve changes) Other causes of chorioretinitis or anterior uveitis Streptocerciasis (Mansonella streptocerca) Skin snips examined microscopically for emerging microfilariae Palpation and examination or excision of subcutaneous nodules for adult worms Slit-lamp examination for microfilariae and ocular inflammatory changes Serological (Ov-16) antibody or antigen testing PCR assays on skin snips for species confirmation Assessment for Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic areas before treatment Caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by the bite of Simulium blackflies that breed in fast-flowing rivers, hence 'river blindness' Chronic infection produces intensely itchy dermatitis, altered skin pigmentation ('leopard skin'), skin atrophy, and firm subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) housing adult worms Microfilariae migrating to the eye cause keratitis, iritis, chorioretinitis, and optic atrophy, leading to progressive and potentially irreversible blindness The endosymbiotic bacterium Wolbachia within the worm drives much of the inflammatory response, making doxycycline for Wolbachia a useful adjunct that also sterilises adult female worms Diagnosis is classically by skin snips examined for emerging microfilariae, supported by nodule examination and antigen/antibody or PCR testing Ivermectin is the mainstay microfilaricidal treatment and the basis of mass drug administration control programmes, given repeatedly as it does not reliably kill adult worms Ivermectin can precipitate a severe reaction in patients heavily co-infected with Loa loa, so loiasis must be considered in co-endemic areas before treatment Ocular involvement threatening progressive or irreversible visual loss Severe Mazzotti reaction after microfilaricidal treatment Risk of severe reaction if ivermectin is given with high Loa loa co-infection Extensive sight-threatening keratitis or optic atrophy Giving ivermectin without excluding heavy Loa loa co-infection in co-endemic regions Expecting a single course of ivermectin to cure infection despite persistence of adult worms Underestimating the sight-threatening potential of ocular microfilariae Failing to anticipate and manage the Mazzotti reaction after treatment Onchocerciasis results from infection with Onchocerca volvulus. Infective larvae are introduced by biting Simulium blackflies and mature into adult worms that reside coiled within fibrous subcutaneous nodules. Adult females release large numbers of microfilariae that migrate through the skin, connective tissue, and eye. Most disease is driven not by the live microfilariae but by the inflammatory reaction to dying microfilariae and to their endosymbiotic Wolbachia bacteria, which provoke dermal and ocular inflammation. In the eye, repeated microfilarial death causes punctate then sclerosing keratitis, anterior uveitis, and posterior segment damage, culminating in blindness. In the skin, chronic inflammation produces pruritus, depigmentation, and atrophy. Killing microfilariae abruptly, as with treatment, can intensify this inflammatory response (the Mazzotti reaction). With repeated ivermectin therapy and vector control, transmission and morbidity can be greatly reduced; however, established ocular damage and optic atrophy are irreversible, and untreated chronic infection remains a leading infective cause of blindness.

Oncologic Emergencies — tumor lysis syndrome, superior vena cava syndrome SVCS in a young man with a mediastinal mass: lymphoma versus primary mediastinal germ cell tumor (Harrison 22e p.585) Cauda equina syndrome: low back pain, saddle sensory loss, rectal/bladder dysfunction, sexual impotence and absent reflexes from compression of nerve roots forming the cauda equina (Harrison 22e p.589) Abrupt stroke-like onset of headache, nausea, vomiting and focal deficit in brain metastasis usually indicates hemorrhage into the metastasis (melanoma, germ cell and renal cell tumors bleed readily) (Harrison 22e p.590) Pyogenic epidural abscess or vertebral tuberculosis can mimic malignant spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.589) SVCS: chest radiograph (superior mediastinal widening, usually right-sided), CT thorax (most reliable mediastinal view; 'hot quadrate' hepatic hotspot sign suggests SVC obstruction), MRI (100% sensitivity/specificity but supine positioning may be difficult in dyspneic patients) (Harrison 22e p.586) Spinal cord compression: neurologic exam and plain spine films first (earliest finding is the 'winking owl' sign of pedicle erosion; plain films are insensitive), then full-length spinal MRI (procedure of choice); myelography reserved for poor or unobtainable MRI (Harrison 22e p.589) Brain metastases/raised ICP: gadolinium-enhanced MRI is superior to CT and more sensitive for meningeal involvement and small posterior-fossa lesions (Harrison 22e p.590) TLS pretreatment evaluation in at-risk patients: complete blood count, serum chemistry (electrolytes, creatinine, calcium, phosphate, uric acid) and urinalysis; follow plasma rather than serum potassium when pseudohyperkalemia is suspected; sonography/CT of kidneys and retroperitoneum if baseline renal function is abnormal (Harrison 22e p.593) A urinary uric acid to urinary creatinine ratio >1 supports acute hyperuricemic nephropathy; <1 suggests renal failure of other cause (Harrison 22e p.593) Spinal cord compression mimics: osteoporotic vertebral collapse, disk disease, radiation myelopathy, neoplastic leptomeningitis, benign tumors, epidural hematoma and spinal lipomatosis (Harrison 22e p.589) About 20% of vertebral collapse (especially in older patients and postmenopausal women) is due to osteoporosis rather than cancer (Harrison 22e p.589) Benign causes of SVCS: aortic aneurysm, thyromegaly, thrombosis, and fibrosing mediastinitis from prior irradiation, histoplasmosis or Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.585) Pseudohyperkalemia from high leukocyte/platelet counts (cell lysis after blood draw) can falsely elevate potassium in TLS; no ECG abnormalities are present (Harrison 22e p.593) Pseudohypoglycemia from glucose consumption in the test tube with hyperleukocytosis, myeloproliferative disease or CSF treatment (Harrison 22e p.593) Emergencies in cancer fall into three groups: pressure/obstruction from a space-occupying lesion (structural-obstructive), metabolic or hormonal problems (paraneoplastic), and treatment-related complications (Harrison 22e p.585). Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) reflects SVC obstruction with severe reduction of venous return from head, neck and upper extremities; lung cancer (especially small-cell and squamous) accounts for ~85% of malignant cases, and in young adults lymphoma is a leading cause (Harrison 22e p.585). Benign causes of SVCS are increasing with intravascular device use (central catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads) and now account for at least 40% of cases (Harrison 22e p.585). SVCS typically presents with neck and facial swelling (especially periorbital), dyspnea, cough, dilated neck veins, collateral chest-wall veins, cyanosis and facial plethora that worsens when supine; bending forward or lying down aggravates symptoms (Harrison 22e p.585). The diagnosis of SVCS is clinical; the most significant chest radiograph finding is widening of the superior mediastinum (most often right-sided), and CT provides the most reliable mediastinal anatomy (Harrison 22e p.586). Malignant spinal cord compression (MSCC) is compression of cord and/or cauda equina by an extradural tumor mass; spinal cord compression occurs in 5-10% of cancer patients and is the first manifestation of malignancy in ~10% (Harrison 22e p.588). Localized back pain and tenderness is the most common initial symptom of spinal cord compression, often present for days to months before neurologic findings; it characteristically worsens when supine, unlike disk-disease pain (Harrison 22e p.588-589). The thoracic spine is the most common site of cord compression (70%), followed by lumbosacral (20%) and cervical (10%); lung, breast and prostate cancers are the most frequent offenders (Harrison 22e p.588). Treatment of spinal cord compression is more often successful in patients still ambulatory and with sphincter control at initiation; patients whose exam suggests compression should receive dexamethasone immediately and undergo MRI (Harrison 22e p.589). Full-length spinal MRI is the imaging procedure of choice for cord compression and is as good as or better than myelography plus post-myelogram CT (Harrison 22e p.589). About 25% of cancer patients die with intracranial metastases; lung and breast cancer and melanoma metastasize to brain most often, and brain metastases present features of an expanding intracranial lesion: headache, nausea, vomiting, behavioral change, seizures and focal progressive deficits (Harrison 22e p.589-590). Dexamethasone is the best initial treatment for all symptomatic patients with brain metastases and raised intracranial pressure (Harrison 22e p.590). Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome, and SIADH is the most common cause of hyponatremia among cancer patients (both detailed in Chaps. 98 and 422/393) (Harrison 22e p.592). Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is characterized by hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia from destruction of large numbers of rapidly proliferating cells; acidosis may develop and acute renal failure occurs frequently (Harrison 22e p.593). TLS is most often associated with treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma, ALL, AML and other rapidly proliferating lymphomas, and usually occurs during or shortly (1-5 days) after chemotherapy; risk correlates with tumor burden and high LDH (>1500 U/L) (Harrison 22e p.593). Recognition of risk and prevention are the most important steps in TLS management; the standard preventive approach is allopurinol plus aggressive hydration (Harrison 22e p.593). Febrile neutropenia is the clinical presentation of fever with <1500 granulocytes/uL; it is a key treatment-related emergency in cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.575). SVCS with cerebral and/or laryngeal edema, proptosis, glossal/laryngeal edema, obtundation or postural hypotension carries poorer prognosis and requires urgent evaluation and early stenting (Harrison 22e p.585-586) Tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass is the one potentially life-threatening complication of SVCS and demands emergent therapy; cardiac arrest or respiratory failure can occur, particularly with sedatives or general anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.585-586) Cancer patient with back pain plus a crescendo pain pattern, Lhermitte's sign, or pain aggravated by cough/Valsalva/recumbency should be evaluated for cord compression as quickly as possible (Harrison 22e p.589) Loss of bowel or bladder control, autonomic dysfunction (decreased anal tone, distended bladder, absent anal wink/bulbocavernosus reflex) signals significant cord involvement and is an unfavorable prognostic feature (Harrison 22e p.588) Hyperkalemia in TLS with renal failure can rapidly become life-threatening, causing ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death (Harrison 22e p.593) Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) is potentially lethal and may be masked by nonspecific symptoms attributed to cancer or therapy (Harrison 22e p.593) Febrile neutropenia (fever with <1500 granulocytes/uL) is a treatment-related emergency requiring prompt management (Harrison 22e p.575) A normal chest radiograph is still compatible with the diagnosis of SVCS if other characteristic findings are present (Harrison 22e p.586) A normal appearance of plain spine films does not exclude cancer; plain films are insensitive for cord compression (Harrison 22e p.589) Vertebral collapse is not a reliable indicator of tumor since ~20% of collapses are osteoporotic (Harrison 22e p.589) After SVC stenting, the prompt increase in venous return may precipitate heart failure and pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.586) Urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate is no longer recommended in TLS: although it increases uric acid solubility, a high pH decreases solubility of xanthine, hypoxanthine and calcium phosphate, potentially increasing intratubular crystallization (Harrison 22e p.593) Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and it causes ex vivo degradation of uric acid in the test tube giving spuriously low levels unless samples are cooled immediately (Harrison 22e p.594) Pseudohyperkalemia in TLS shows no ECG abnormalities; plasma rather than serum potassium should be followed (Harrison 22e p.593) Arterial blood gas oxygen tension can be spuriously low in hyperleukocytosis due to oxygen consumption by white cells; pulse oximetry is the most accurate measure of oxygenation (Harrison 22e p.591) Oncologic emergencies arise by three mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.585). Structural-obstructive emergencies result from a space-occupying lesion: in SVCS, malignant tumor or thrombosis obstructs the superior vena cava, reducing venous return from head, neck and upper limbs; in malignant spinal cord compression, an expanding extradural tumor (usually metastasis to vertebral body or pedicle, or paravertebral extension through the intervertebral foramen) mechanically injures axons and myelin and compromises blood flow, causing ischemia/infarction; raised intracranial pressure results from brain metastases and surrounding edema, sometimes with hemorrhage or CSF obstruction causing hydrocephalus and herniation (Harrison 22e p.585-590). Metabolic/hormonal (paraneoplastic) emergencies include hypercalcemia, SIADH-related hyponatremia, lactic acidosis and hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.592-593). Treatment-related TLS occurs when cytotoxic killing of a large rapidly proliferating tumor releases intracellular contents: nucleic acid turnover raises uric acid which precipitates in the acidic renal tubules; released phosphate causes hyperphosphatemia with reciprocal hypocalcemia and calcium-phosphate nephrocalcinosis; and massive cell destruction releases potassium causing hyperkalemia, which in renal failure can cause fatal ventricular arrhythmias (Harrison 22e p.593). In SVCS, mortality relates to the underlying cause rather than to caval obstruction itself, and clinical improvement occurs in most patients (sometimes via collateral circulation); SVCS recurs in 10-30% (Harrison 22e p.586). For spinal cord compression, tumor histology is an important determinant of recovery and survival, and rapid onset/progression of signs and symptoms are poor prognostic features; treatment is more often successful in ambulatory patients who retain sphincter control (Harrison 22e p.589). Brain metastases frequently cause major symptoms, disability and early death (Harrison 22e p.590). Lactic acidosis in cancer carries a poor prognosis regardless of treatment, and cancer patients with malignant cells on pericardial cytology have very poor survival (Harrison 22e p.587, 592). Despite aggressive prophylaxis, TLS with oliguric/anuric renal failure may still occur and often requires renal replacement therapy (Harrison 22e p.594). Spinal cord compression management uses the NOMS framework (Memorial Sloan Kettering): Neurologic assessment (degree of epidural compression, myelopathy, functional radiculopathy), Oncologic assessment (tumor radiosensitivity), Mechanical assessment (spinal stability), and Systemic factors (extent of disease and comorbidities determining tolerance of therapy) (Harrison 22e p.589-590). TLS risk is stratified by tumor burden, renal function, hyperuricemia and high LDH (>1500 U/L); a high-risk management algorithm escalates from hydration and allopurinol to recombinant urate oxidase/rasburicase and hemodialysis based on serum uric acid, creatinine, potassium, phosphate and symptomatic hypocalcemia thresholds (Harrison 22e p.593-594).

Opioid overdose — Clinical (pinpoint pupils, ↓RR) Trial of naloxone Respiratory depression — naloxone + airway support Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning — also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748) Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) — depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748) Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747) Other causes of coma including hypoglycemia (reversed by dextrose) (p.3748) Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690) ECG to detect QT prolongation (e.g. methadone), which can cause sudden death (p.3733) Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749) In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733) Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748) Benzodiazepine intoxication (responds to flumazenil) (p.3748) The classic overdose picture is shallow/slow respirations, miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; toxicology can confirm but immediate management is clinical (p.3690). Pinpoint pupils are characteristic, BUT mydriasis (dilated pupils) appears once significant cerebral anoxia supervenes — dilated pupils do not exclude opioid toxicity in a deteriorating patient (p.3690). Hypoxia, not the drug itself, is what kills: in opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign changes are secondary to CNS depression or consequent hypoxemia and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression) (p.3748). Aspiration pneumonia is common in overdose because of loss of the gag reflex (p.3733). Opioids generally do NOT cause seizures, except in polydrug use, with meperidine, with high-dose tramadol, or in the newborn (p.3690). Fentanyl and its derivatives may require severalfold higher reversal doses than other opioids, and adulteration of illicit fentanyl with xylazine markedly worsens respiratory suppression (p.3689, p.3733). Prompt reversal of altered mental status and vital signs within minutes of IV naloxone is virtually diagnostic of opioid poisoning (alongside dextrose for hypoglycemia and flumazenil for benzodiazepine intoxication) (p.3748). Fluoroquinolones commonly cause false-positive opiate urine screens; rapid urine drug screens are screening-only, prone to false results, and miss agents such as kratom (p.3748). When naloxone has only a limited effect, suspect a co-ingested sedative — most commonly a benzodiazepine, which has caused fatal overdoses in combination with buprenorphine (p.3691). Dilated pupils in a suspected opioid overdose suggest cerebral anoxia has already occurred (p.3690) Re-sedation: naloxone lasts only a few hours while most opioids (especially methadone, sustained-release/'toxic time-bomb' formulations) last far longer (p.3691, p.3747) Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3749) Methadone-associated QT prolongation and sudden death (p.3733) Necrosis and limb-loss risk with fentanyl-xylazine injection (p.3733) Do not assume normal-sized or dilated pupils exclude opioids — mydriasis does NOT occur until significant brain anoxia supervenes (p.3690). Significant vital-sign abnormalities do NOT occur in opioid poisoning until there is a marked decrease in level of consciousness, so early near-normal vitals are falsely reassuring (p.3748). A negative urine drug screen does NOT rule out opioid toxicity (concentration too low, or agent such as kratom not detected); opiate screens also give false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones) (p.3748). Primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible because it is a partial agonist with increasing antagonist activity at higher doses; failure to respond to naloxone should prompt search for a co-ingested sedative (p.3690-3691). Be sure a patient is not also withdrawing from alcohol or sedatives, which may be more dangerous to manage than opioid withdrawal (p.3733). Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690). Potentially lethal but rapidly reversible if respiratory depression is recognized and supported; untreated overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Opioid use disorder is chronic and relapsing, and most patients relapse during or after detoxification (p.3690, p.3691). Some opioid intoxications can leave delayed diffuse white-matter injury producing a persistent coma syndrome (p.232). Harrison frames poisoning severity by physiologic state (Tables 470-1/470-2): opioids produce a 'depressed' physiologic state (decreased pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, neuromuscular activity, with miosis). Severity is graded by depth of CNS/physiologic depression (grades 1-4); marked vital-sign abnormalities indicate grade 3-4 depression (p.3747-3748). Note: opioid WITHDRAWAL is a separate 'stimulated' syndrome — onset 8-10 h after the last dose with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning and sweating, progressing to gooseflesh, nausea/vomiting, myalgia, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, hypertension, mydriasis over a 7-10 day acute course (p.3690).

Opioid-Related Disorders — Opioid use disorder, Opioid addiction, Opioid dependence, Opioid intoxication, Opioid withdrawal, Opioid overdose Concurrent sedative-hypnotic (benzodiazepine) overdose or withdrawal, which may coexist and be more dangerous to manage Alcohol intoxication or withdrawal in a polydrug user Stimulant co-intoxication (cocaine/methamphetamine), including combined 'speedball' use Other causes of coma with respiratory depression (CNS structural lesion, metabolic encephalopathy) before miosis-based diagnosis is confirmed Blood or urine toxicology to confirm a suspected opioid diagnosis (management must not wait for results) ECG for QT-interval monitoring, particularly with methadone or in overdose Arterial/clinical assessment of respiratory status and gag reflex (aspiration pneumonia risk in overdose) Liver function tests when considering opioid-antagonist relapse-prevention therapy (most providers avoid it if LFTs exceed about three times normal) Screening for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV) in people who inject Toxic megacolon from severe opioid-induced constipation mimicking primary abdominal catastrophe MPTP-induced parkinsonism from contaminated illicitly synthesized meperidine, mimicking idiopathic Parkinson disease Orthostatic hypotension from opioid-related histamine release mimicking other causes of hypotension DSM-5 (2022) replaced the older terms dependence and addiction with opioid use disorder, opioid intoxication, and opioid withdrawal; the disorder is defined as repeated use over a 12-month period causing problems in two or more domains (tolerance, withdrawal, using larger amounts than intended, craving, and continued use despite adverse consequences) (Harrison 22e p.3688). The mu receptor is the receptor most clinically relevant to opioid effects; mu actions include analgesia, euphoric reinforcement, cough and appetite suppression, decreased respiration, decreased GI motility, sedation, and hormonal changes, while kappa activation tends to produce dysphoria and psychotic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3689). An opioid 'high' occurs only when the rate of rise in dopamine is fast, so rapid routes such as smoking and intravenous injection produce a 'rush' whereas oral and transdermal routes give analgesia/sedation without the euphoric high (Harrison 22e p.3689). Opioid overdose is recognized clinically by shallow, slow respirations, pupillary miosis (mydriasis appears only after significant brain anoxia), bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; immediate management is based on clinical criteria rather than waiting for toxicology (Harrison 22e p.3690). Fentanyl overdose may require roughly twice the reversal-agent dose needed for other opioids, and reversal antagonists are short-acting relative to most opioids, so re-sedation can occur after an initial response (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3690). Adding xylazine (a nonopioid veterinary sedative) to illicit fentanyl markedly worsens respiratory suppression and is associated with tissue necrosis and increased risk of limb amputation in people who inject (Harrison 22e p.3690). Opioids generally do not cause seizures except in unusual situations: polydrug use with meperidine, high-dose tramadol, or the newborn (Harrison 22e p.3690). Withdrawal risk has a strong genetic component (up to ~50% related to functional polymorphisms), including a mu-opioid receptor variant conferring threefold higher affinity for opioids and beta-endorphin; epigenetic methylation may compensate by reducing mu-receptor numbers (Harrison 22e p.3689). Methadone can prolong the QT interval (rates reported as high as ~16% above non-methadone injecting patients) and has caused sudden death; QT monitoring is relevant during overdose and maintenance (Harrison 22e pp.3690, 3691). Heroin users are frequently polydrug users (alcohol, sedatives, cannabinoids, stimulants); none substitute for opioids but they have additive effects, so concurrent alcohol or sedative withdrawal (which can be more dangerous) must be excluded before managing opioid withdrawal (Harrison 22e p.3690). Buprenorphine's partial agonism means escalating doses shift toward antagonist activity, so primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible, but high doses can precipitate withdrawal in patients on full agonists such as morphine or methadone (Harrison 22e pp.3690-3691). Most opioid-using individuals meet more than three diagnostic criteria, so reducing the DSM threshold from three to two problem areas did not change measured disease rates (Harrison 22e p.3688). Shallow/slow respirations with pinpoint miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma indicating life-threatening overdose Mydriasis in a suspected overdose suggesting significant brain anoxia has supervened Limited or absent response to standard reversal dosing, prompting suspicion of fentanyl, high antagonist requirement, or concurrent benzodiazepine overdose Loss of gag reflex with aspiration pneumonia risk Skin necrosis or limb compromise suggesting xylazine-adulterated fentanyl use Septic complications of injection use such as meningitis, osteomyelitis, or organ abscesses Administering so much antagonist that opioid withdrawal is precipitated, rather than targeting reversal of respiratory depression Assuming a single antagonist dose is sufficient, since antagonists last only a few hours while most opioids persist longer, risking re-sedation (close monitoring/continuous antagonism often needed) Overlooking concurrent benzodiazepine or alcohol/sedative involvement when reversal has only limited effect Misjudging dose in naive or infrequent users because actual ingested potency is hard to estimate, especially with fentanyl derivatives Forgetting that buprenorphine and methadone themselves can be misused and that buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal in fentanyl- or high-dose-methadone-dependent patients Opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin) are G protein-linked and coupled to the cyclic AMP (cAMP) second-messenger system and to G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs); receptor binding increases potassium permeability, hyperpolarizes neurons, and inhibits action potentials, producing analgesia, sedation, and reinforcement. Reinforcing euphoria is mediated through the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, where opioids indirectly raise dopamine by inhibiting GABAergic interneurons; the subjective high requires a fast rate of dopamine change. Tolerance and withdrawal arise from adaptive upregulation of the cAMP-PKA-CREB cascade in locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons after chronic mu-receptor inhibition: sustained inhibition triggers compensatory increases in cyclic AMP enzyme activity, so abrupt opioid cessation produces unopposed noradrenergic overactivity and withdrawal symptoms; this model underlies the use of alpha2-agonists to suppress that activation. PKA-driven phosphorylation of CREB also induces genes such as tyrosine hydroxylase and BDNF, the latter implicated in long-term neuroplastic changes (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690). Opioid use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition; most patients tend to relapse during or after detoxification, and stopping use is far easier than preventing relapse. Long-term relapse prevention requires combined pharmacologic and psychosocial approaches. Medication-free inpatient/outpatient programs have poor 1- to 5-year outcomes compared with pharmacotherapy, except for residential programs lasting roughly 6-18 months. Untreated potentially lethal overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Globally the World Drug Report attributes the greatest burden of drug-related morbidity and mortality to opioid misuse; in 2022 over 76,000 US overdose deaths involved opioids, with rates accelerating due to high-potency fentanyl derivatives and stimulant co-use (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3691-3692). Withdrawal time course (heroin): symptoms begin ~8-10 h after the last dose, with early lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, and sweating; later stages bring restless sleep, weakness, chills, piloerection ('cold turkey'), nausea/vomiting, muscle aches, involuntary movements, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, and hypertension. Acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days, followed by a protracted abstinence phase of ~26-30 weeks (hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, mydriasis, blunted respiratory CO2 responsiveness). Tolerance/withdrawal can develop within ~6-8 weeks of chronic daily use. Plasma half-lives vary widely: ~2.5-3 h for morphine, >22 h for methadone, minutes for fentanyl-related opioids, and longest for buprenorphine/metabolites (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690).

Non-opioid causes of altered consciousness such as hypoglycaemia or head injury Sepsis or other acute medical illness in an injecting drug user Comorbid depression or anxiety driving misuse Urine whether of prescribed analgesics or illicit opioids such as heroin, leading to clinically significant impairment or distress with impaired control, craving, and continued use despite harm Intoxication
