evidence-based cornerstone of treatment and substantially reduces mortality and illicit use Antagonist treatment is an option for motivated, detoxified patients, while overdose reversal with an opioid antagonist is a life-saving emergency intervention Take-home overdose-reversal medication and harm-reduction measures should be offered to patients and, where appropriate, their families Injecting use carries risks of blood-borne virus transmission, endocarditis, and skin and soft-tissue infection, so screening and preventive care are essential Comorbid mental illness, chronic pain, and social instability are common and should be addressed within an integrated treatment plan Respiratory depression or reduced consciousness indicating overdose requiring immediate reversal Features of endocarditis, sepsis, or deep soft-tissue infection in injecting users High overdose risk following loss of tolerance, such as after detoxification or release from custody Suicidal ideation or intent Abrupt discontinuation of opioids or detoxification without maintenance planning, which raises overdose risk Failing to offer take-home overdose-reversal medication Undertreating pain or comorbid mental illness, perpetuating illicit use Overlooking the sharply increased overdose risk after periods of abstinence Stigmatising attitudes that deter engagement with treatment Opioid use disorder results from repeated stimulation of mu-opioid receptors, producing potent dopaminergic reward signalling and rapid neuroadaptation in reward, stress, and executive-control circuits. Tolerance and physical dependence develop through receptor and second-messenger adaptations, and withdrawal reflects rebound noradrenergic overactivity, particularly from the locus coeruleus, while genetic, psychiatric, and environmental factors modulate vulnerability and relapse. Opioid use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition with substantial mortality, largely from overdose, but agonist maintenance treatment markedly improves survival, retention in care, and function. Prognosis is better with sustained maintenance treatment, psychosocial support, and social stability, and worse with continued injecting, polysubstance use, and disengagement from care.

Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome — opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, OMS, dancing eyes-dancing feet syndrome, Kinsbourne syndrome Cerebellar ataxia of infective, toxic, or metabolic cause Other paraneoplastic cerebellar or brainstem syndromes Drug or toxin-induced ocular flutter and myoclonus Brainstem encephalitis Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis to search for neuroblastoma or other tumour Metabolic tumour imaging and urinary catecholamine metabolites in children Paraneoplastic antibody panel in serum and cerebrospinal fluid MRI of the brain to exclude structural and inflammatory lesions Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for inflammation Whole-body tumour screening in adults, including for small-cell lung and breast carcinoma Characterised by opsoclonus (chaotic, involuntary, multidirectional saccades), myoclonus, and cerebellar ataxia Behavioural disturbance, irritability, and sleep disruption are common, especially in children In children it is strongly associated with neuroblastoma, so cross-sectional and metabolic tumour imaging is mandatory In adults it may be parainfectious or paraneoplastic, notably with small-cell lung and breast carcinoma Opsoclonus persists during eye closure and sleep, helping distinguish it from other abnormal eye movements First-line immunotherapy uses corticosteroids or corticotropin with intravenous immunoglobulin, escalating to rituximab or other agents in refractory disease In paraneoplastic cases, removal or treatment of the underlying tumour is central to management Failure to identify an occult neuroblastoma or other tumour on initial screening Severe ataxia or myoclonus impairing safety and function Progressive encephalopathy or developmental regression in children Relapse after apparent recovery suggesting undertreated disease or occult tumour Failing to search repeatedly for an occult tumour when initial imaging is negative Mistaking opsoclonus for nystagmus or a functional disorder Under-treating, as inadequate immunotherapy is linked to relapse and long-term sequelae Overlooking behavioural and developmental effects that require broader support Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome is an immune-mediated disorder affecting brainstem and cerebellar circuits that control eye movements and coordination. Loss of inhibitory control over the saccadic burst neurons, thought to involve dysfunction of omnipause and fastigial-cerebellar pathways, produces the chaotic saccades of opsoclonus, while cerebellar involvement generates myoclonus and ataxia. The immune response is frequently triggered by an occult tumour, classically neuroblastoma in children through cross-reacting antineural immunity, or by preceding infection; a defined single antibody is often not identified. Many patients, especially children, improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but relapses and residual cognitive, behavioural, or motor deficits are common, and outcome in paraneoplastic adult cases depends on the underlying malignancy.

Optic neuritis — ON, retrobulbar neuritis, papillitis, optic nerve inflammation, demyelinating optic neuritis Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (arteritic and non-arteritic) Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder MOG-antibody-associated optic neuritis Compressive optic neuropathy from tumour or aneurysm Toxic, nutritional, or hereditary (Leber) optic neuropathy Central retinal artery occlusion and other causes of acute visual loss Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, and relative afferent pupillary defect Visual field testing (commonly shows a central scotoma) Contrast MRI of the brain and orbits to assess the nerve and demyelinating lesions Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibody testing in atypical or severe cases OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to monitor atrophy; bloods/lumbar puncture where an infective or inflammatory cause is suspected Typically presents in a young adult (more often female) with subacute unilateral visual loss developing over hours to days, accompanied by pain worse on eye movement A relative afferent pupillary defect is present, and colour vision (especially red desaturation) is impaired out of proportion to acuity In retrobulbar neuritis the optic disc looks normal at onset ('the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing'), whereas papillitis shows a swollen disc It is commonly the presenting or an associated feature of multiple sclerosis, so demyelination should be considered MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast assesses the optic nerve and detects demyelinating white-matter lesions that predict multiple sclerosis risk Vision usually recovers spontaneously over weeks; intravenous corticosteroids speed recovery but do not change final visual outcome Atypical features (bilateral, no pain, poor recovery, severe disc swelling) should prompt consideration of neuromyelitis optica, MOG-associated disease, or an infective/compressive cause Bilateral simultaneous, severe, or poorly recovering visual loss suggesting neuromyelitis optica or a non-demyelinating cause Absence of pain or a progressive course pointing to a compressive or ischaemic optic neuropathy Systemic features suggesting infection, sarcoidosis, or vasculitis Older patient with headache and jaw claudication — exclude giant cell arteritis as a cause of ischaemic optic neuropathy Attributing every acute optic neuropathy to demyelination and missing arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy in older patients Assuming steroids improve the final visual outcome rather than just the speed of recovery Overlooking neuromyelitis optica or MOG disease in atypical or severe cases that need different management Failing to counsel on and investigate the associated risk of multiple sclerosis Optic neuritis is inflammation and demyelination of the optic nerve, most commonly immune-mediated and associated with multiple sclerosis. An inflammatory, often T-cell-driven process attacks the myelin sheath of optic nerve axons, disrupting conduction and causing loss of visual acuity, colour vision, and contrast. Because conduction rather than the axon itself is initially affected, remyelination allows substantial recovery, though repeated or severe attacks cause axonal loss and permanent deficits with optic atrophy. Antibody-mediated variants (aquaporin-4 in neuromyelitis optica, MOG antibody disease) and infective or granulomatous causes produce similar inflammation through different mechanisms. Most patients with typical demyelinating optic neuritis recover good vision over several weeks regardless of steroid use, though some residual colour and contrast deficits and a risk of future multiple sclerosis remain.

Oral cancer — oral cavity cancer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, mouth cancer Traumatic ulcer from dentures or a sharp tooth Aphthous ulceration or other benign oral ulcers Oral leukoplakia or erythroplakia without invasion Oral lichen planus Infective causes such as fungal or specific granulomatous lesions Salivary gland or other non-squamous oral tumours Thorough inspection and palpation of the oral cavity and neck with biopsy of the lesion CT or MRI to assess local extent, bony invasion, and nodal disease Chest imaging and PET-CT for distant staging and second primaries Examination under anaesthesia and panendoscopy where indicated to map extent and exclude synchronous tumours Dental assessment and nutritional evaluation before treatment Most oral cavity cancers are squamous cell carcinomas driven by tobacco in all its forms, betel or areca nut chewing, and heavy alcohol use, which act synergistically It typically presents as a persistent ulcer, red or white patch, lump, or non-healing sore in the mouth, often with pain, bleeding, or loose teeth as disease advances Any oral lesion that fails to heal within a few weeks should be biopsied rather than treated repeatedly as trauma or infection Premalignant lesions such as leukoplakia, erythroplakia, and oral submucous fibrosis carry malignant potential and warrant monitoring and biopsy Cervical lymph node metastasis is common and significantly worsens prognosis, so neck examination and imaging are integral to staging Surgical resection with adequate margins is the mainstay for most tumours, often combined with neck dissection and reconstruction depending on extent Radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, is used adjuvantly for adverse features or as definitive treatment in selected cases Treatment can markedly affect speech, swallowing, and appearance, so multidisciplinary rehabilitation and dental assessment before radiotherapy are important A mouth ulcer or lesion that fails to heal within a few weeks A firm, fixed, or enlarging cervical lymph node Unexplained loosening of teeth, numbness, or difficulty moving the tongue Persistent oral bleeding, pain, or difficulty swallowing with weight loss Repeatedly treating a persistent oral ulcer as trauma or infection without biopsy Neglecting to examine and image the cervical lymph nodes Overlooking premalignant lesions that require surveillance Failing to arrange dental and rehabilitation input before and after treatment Oral squamous cell carcinoma arises from the mucosal lining of the oral cavity through cumulative genetic damage caused by carcinogens in tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol. This produces field cancerisation with premalignant changes such as leukoplakia and erythroplakia that can progress through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. The tumour invades local structures including muscle, bone, and nerves, and spreads readily to regional cervical lymph nodes; distant metastasis occurs later. Chronic mucosal irritation and conditions such as oral submucous fibrosis further predispose to malignant change. Prognosis depends on stage, tumour thickness, and nodal status; early localised tumours have good cure rates, whereas nodal metastasis, deep invasion, and advanced stage substantially reduce survival and increase recurrence.

Oral candidiasis — oral thrush, oral candidosis, candidal stomatitis, moniliasis Oral leukoplakia and other keratotic white lesions Lichen planus and lichenoid reactions Geographic tongue for the atrophic form Chemical or thermal mucosal burns Mucosal manifestations of anaemia or nutritional deficiency Oral swab, smear, or oral rinse for microscopy and culture Biopsy for adherent white patches to assess hyperplastic candidiasis and dysplasia Blood glucose and screening for diabetes Haematinics (iron, folate, B12) where atrophic or recurrent disease Evaluation for immunodeficiency, including HIV, in unexplained or severe cases Oral candidiasis is usually an opportunistic infection by Candida species, most often Candida albicans, and typically signals a local or systemic predisposing factor The pseudomembranous form (thrush) shows white curd-like plaques that wipe off to reveal an erythematous, sometimes bleeding, base Erythematous (atrophic) candidiasis presents as a red, sore mucosa or a depapillated tongue, and is common under dentures or after antibiotics Angular cheilitis at the mouth corners frequently coexists and reflects candidal and bacterial colonisation with local moisture Denture stomatitis appears as erythema confined to the denture-bearing palatal mucosa and relates to poor denture hygiene and continuous wear Common predisposing factors include inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, xerostomia, diabetes, and immunosuppression Management combines antifungal therapy with correction of the underlying cause, including denture hygiene and control of dry mouth Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis presents as an adherent white patch that will not rub off and carries a small malignant potential warranting biopsy Unexplained or severe oral candidiasis in a previously healthy adult raising suspicion of undiagnosed HIV or other immunodeficiency Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis with dysplasia and potential for malignant transformation Extension into the oesophagus with dysphagia suggesting significant immunosuppression Treating recurrent candidiasis without seeking and correcting the underlying predisposing factor Assuming an adherent white patch is thrush when it is hyperplastic candidiasis or leukoplakia needing biopsy Overlooking denture hygiene and continuous wear as the driver of denture stomatitis Missing an immunocompromising condition in unexplained or florid infection Candida species are common oral commensals kept in check by intact mucosal defences, salivary factors, and the resident microbiota. Disruption of this balance allows overgrowth and conversion to an invasive hyphal form that adheres to and penetrates the epithelium. Local factors such as denture coverage, dry mouth, and topical steroids, together with systemic factors such as antibiotics, immunosuppression, diabetes, and nutritional deficiency, create the conditions for opportunistic infection. The clinical pattern (pseudomembranous, erythematous, or hyperplastic) reflects the host state and chronicity rather than different organisms. Most acute candidiasis responds well to antifungal treatment when predisposing factors are corrected, but recurrence is common if the underlying cause persists, and chronic hyperplastic lesions require monitoring for dysplasia.

Oral-facial-digital syndrome — orofaciodigital syndrome, OFD syndrome, OFD1, OFD type I (Papillon-Leage-Psaume) Joubert syndrome and related disorders Pallister-Hall syndrome Ellis-van Creveld syndrome Meckel-Gruber syndrome Mohr syndrome (OFD type II) versus other OFD subtypes Isolated cleft palate with limb anomaly Detailed dysmorphology and oral examination to document tongue, frenula, and palatal anomalies Radiographs of the hands and feet to characterise digital malformations Brain MRI for callosal, cerebellar, and posterior fossa anomalies including the molar tooth sign Renal of ciliopathies defined by malformations of the oral cavity, face, and digits, with several distinct subtypes differing in inheritance and associated features Oral findings include lobulated or bifid tongue with hamartomas, multiple frenula, cleft palate or lip, and dental anomalies Facial features may include hypertelorism, a broad or bifid nasal tip, and micrognathia, while digital anomalies include brachydactyly, syndactyly, clinodactyly, and polydactyly Type I is X-linked dominant, caused by OFD1 variants and typically lethal in males, and is frequently associated with polycystic kidney disease and central nervous system malformation Central nervous system involvement can include agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebellar and posterior fossa anomalies including the molar tooth sign, and intracerebral cysts As a ciliopathy it overlaps with Joubert syndrome and other disorders, and the OFD1 gene product localises to the centriole and basal body of the primary cilium Diagnosis integrates the oral-facial-digital pattern with imaging of brain and kidneys and molecular confirmation for subtype classification and counselling Progressive polycystic kidney disease leading to renal failure Significant central nervous system malformation with neurological impairment or seizures Airway or feeding compromise from severe oral and palatal malformation Male fetal or neonatal loss suggesting an X-linked dominant lethal genotype Classifying an affected child into the wrong OFD subtype and giving inaccurate prognostic and recurrence advice Overlooking the ciliopathy association with progressive renal cystic disease requiring long-term surveillance Missing subtle central nervous system malformation without dedicated brain imaging Attributing oral hamartomas or extra frenula to isolated dental problems Oral-facial-digital syndromes are ciliopathies in which defective primary cilium and basal body function disrupts developmental signalling that patterns midline craniofacial structures, the palate and tongue, and the limbs. The prototypic type I results from variants in OFD1, encoding a centriolar and basal body protein; because the gene is X-linked, hemizygous males are usually not viable while heterozygous females show variable manifestations owing to X-inactivation. Impaired ciliary signalling in the kidney predisposes to cystic renal disease, and in the developing brain it contributes to callosal, cerebellar, and other midline malformations. Prognosis varies by subtype and organ involvement. Many females with type I have a normal or near-normal lifespan but may develop progressive polycystic kidney disease, while central nervous system malformation and severe systemic involvement worsen the outlook in some subtypes.

Oral leukoplakia — leukoplakia, oral white patch, potentially malignant white lesion Frictional or traumatic keratosis Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis Oral lichen planus Leukoedema White sponge naevus Established oral squamous cell carcinoma Incisional or excisional biopsy for histological grading of dysplasia Careful documentation of site, size, and clinical pattern Removal of local irritants and reassessment to exclude frictional keratosis Fungal investigation where hyperplastic candidiasis is suspected Adjunctive imaging or referral when carcinoma is suspected Leukoplakia is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion: a white patch that cannot be wiped off and cannot be attributed to any other definable lesion It is regarded as an oral potentially malignant disorder, meaning it carries an increased risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma Tobacco use, including smokeless forms, areca nut, and alcohol are the principal risk factors Homogeneous, uniformly white, flat lesions carry lower risk than non-homogeneous, nodular, or speckled (erythroleukoplakia) lesions Speckled lesions with a red component and lesions on the floor of mouth or ventrolateral tongue have a higher malignant potential Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is a distinct, multifocal, treatment-resistant form with high transformation risk Biopsy is essential to assess for and grade epithelial dysplasia, which is the key predictor of malignant change Management combines removal of risk factors, treatment or surveillance of the lesion, and long-term monitoring for recurrence or transformation Non-homogeneous, speckled, or verrucous lesions and any red component, indicating higher malignant potential Ulceration, induration, or a developing mass suggesting transformation to carcinoma High-risk sites such as the floor of mouth and ventrolateral tongue Presence of moderate to severe epithelial dysplasia on biopsy Labelling a white patch as benign without biopsy or follow-up Assuming absence of symptoms means absence of risk Sampling only a homogeneous area and missing dysplasia in a red or nodular component Failing to address tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol use that perpetuate the lesion Leukoplakia reflects an alteration in the oral epithelium in which increased keratin production and epithelial thickening scatter light to produce a white appearance that does not rub off. Chronic exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco and areca nut drives genetic and epigenetic changes in basal keratinocytes, which may manifest histologically as hyperkeratosis with or without epithelial dysplasia. Dysplastic change represents disordered maturation and cellular atypia that can accumulate over time, and lesions with higher grades of dysplasia carry a greater likelihood of progressing to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Many lesions remain stable or regress after risk factors are removed, but a proportion undergo malignant transformation, and the risk rises with non-homogeneous appearance, high-risk sites, and higher grades of dysplasia, making long-term surveillance important.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma — oral cancer, oral SCC, mouth cancer, squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity Traumatic ulcer Recurrent aphthous ulceration Oral leukoplakia or erythroplakia without invasion Chronic infective ulcers such as tuberculosis or syphilis Erosive lichen planus Salivary gland or other oral malignancy Incisional biopsy of the lesion for histological diagnosis and grading Examination and imaging of the neck for lymph node involvement Cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI) to assess local extent and staging Assessment for distant metastasis and synchronous primaries Multidisciplinary evaluation for treatment planning Oral squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the oral cavity and often presents as a non-healing ulcer, lump, or persistent red or white patch Classic worrying features are an indurated ulcer with rolled margins, fixation to underlying tissue, and failure to heal beyond two to three weeks Tobacco in all forms, areca nut, and alcohol are the dominant risk factors and act synergistically The lateral and ventral tongue and the floor of mouth are high-risk sites, though any oral surface can be affected Early lesions may be painless, so any persistent oral abnormality warrants a high index of suspicion and referral Cervical lymphadenopathy, especially firm or fixed nodes, may indicate regional metastatic spread Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy, and staging guides treatment involving surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy as appropriate Prognosis depends heavily on stage at diagnosis, underscoring the value of early detection and opportunistic screening Any oral ulcer or lesion persisting beyond two to three weeks requires urgent specialist referral to exclude cancer Induration, fixation, rolled margins, or spontaneous bleeding of a lesion Unexplained firm or fixed cervical lymphadenopathy Persistent unexplained pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, or difficulty swallowing Attributing a persistent ulcer to trauma or denture irritation and delaying biopsy Reassurance because a lesion is painless, since early cancers are often symptomless Failing to examine and palpate the neck for nodal disease Overlooking the risk of second primaries in a field-changed mucosa Oral squamous cell carcinoma develops through the accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations in oral keratinocytes, typically driven by chronic exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol. Many tumours arise within or adjacent to potentially malignant disorders such as leukoplakia or erythroplakia, progressing through increasing grades of epithelial dysplasia to carcinoma in situ and then invasive disease when malignant cells breach the basement membrane. The invasive tumour infiltrates local tissue, can destroy bone, and spreads via lymphatics to cervical nodes, with distant metastasis in advanced disease. Field change means the whole mucosa is at risk of further primaries. Outcome is strongly stage-dependent, with early localised disease carrying a favourable prognosis, whereas advanced tumours with nodal involvement have substantially poorer survival and higher morbidity from treatment.

Orbital cellulitis — postseptal cellulitis, post-septal cellulitis, orbital infection Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis Idiopathic orbital inflammation (orbital pseudotumour) Thyroid eye disease Cavernous sinus thrombosis Orbital tumour or rhabdomyosarcoma in children Allergic or traumatic periorbital oedema Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbit, sinuses, and brain to detect abscess and sinus disease Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, pupil reactions, and eye movements Blood cultures and inflammatory markers Swabs/cultures of any discharge or drained material Ophthalmology and ENT review; consider MRI if intracranial extension is suspected A sight- and life-threatening infection of the orbital tissues behind the orbital septum, most often spreading from adjacent (especially ethmoid) sinusitis Key features distinguishing it from preseptal cellulitis are painful or restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), proptosis, and pain on eye movement Systemic signs of fever and malaise accompany a red, swollen, tender lid; a relative afferent pupillary defect signals optic nerve compromise Reduced visual acuity, colour vision loss, or an afferent pupillary defect indicate optic nerve threat and demand emergency intervention Commonest in children and frequently caused by Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Haemophilus species, sometimes anaerobes Urgent contrast CT of the orbit and sinuses identifies subperiosteal or orbital abscess and sinus involvement Requires admission and prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, with surgical drainage of abscesses or sinuses when needed Emergency — threatens vision (optic nerve compression) and life (cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess) Reduced acuity, impaired colour vision, or a relative afferent pupillary defect indicate imminent optic nerve damage Restricted or painful eye movements and proptosis distinguishing it from benign preseptal cellulitis Bilateral involvement, drowsiness, or cranial nerve palsies suggesting cavernous sinus or intracranial spread Mistaking sight-threatening orbital cellulitis for benign preseptal cellulitis and failing to assess eye movements and optic nerve function Delaying CT imaging and abscess drainage Treating as an outpatient rather than admitting for intravenous therapy Overlooking the underlying sinusitis that needs concurrent treatment Orbital cellulitis is infection of the soft tissues posterior to the orbital septum. Infection most commonly extends directly from the paranasal sinuses (particularly the ethmoid, separated from the orbit only by the thin lamina papyracea), but can also arise from trauma, dacryocystitis, dental infection, or haematogenous spread. Inflammation and oedema within the confined bony orbit raise pressure, displace the globe forward (proptosis), impair extraocular muscle function, and can compress or ischaemically injure the optic nerve. Spread posteriorly risks cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, and intracranial abscess. With prompt intravenous antibiotics and timely drainage the outlook is good, but delay can lead to permanent visual loss, intracranial complications, and death.

Organophosphate / cholinergic poisoning — Clinical cholinergic toxidrome Plasma/RBC cholinesterase Atropine + pralidoxime; airway/secretion control Carbamate insecticide poisoning (aldicarb, carbaryl, propoxur) — same cholinergic mechanism (p.3712) Other acetylcholinesterase inhibitors: medicinal agents neostigmine, physostigmine, tacrine (p.3712) Muscarinic agonists: bethanechol, pilocarpine, and muscarine-containing mushrooms (Boletus, Clitocybe, Inocybe spp.) (p.3712) Nicotine / tobacco and lobeline (nicotinic agonists) (p.3712) Opioid poisoning (also causes miosis and physiologic depression) (p.3705) Cholinesterase activity in plasma and red cells is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning (p.3712) ECG — may show bradycardia and atrioventricular block (p.3706) EMG/nerve conduction studies in delayed neuropathy — early repetitive firing of CMAPs and decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation; later, axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (p.3610) Guillain-Barré syndrome / acute flaccid paralysis — organophosphate, thallium and arsenic poisonings are listed in the GBS differential (p.3620) Botulism and myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorders in the acute paralysis differential) (p.3620) Paralytic shellfish poisoning, ciguatera, type E botulism and tetrodotoxin poisoning — organophosphate poisoning is in their shared differential (ciguatera chapter) Belongs to the depressed physiologic state / cholinergic toxidrome; miosis is common and is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning, distinguished from other depressant syndromes by muscarinic and nicotinic signs (p.3705). Muscarinic features: seizures, excessive secretions (lacrimation, salivation, bronchorrhoea and wheezing, diaphoresis), and increased bowel/bladder activity with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and incontinence of faeces and urine (p.3712). Nicotinic features: hypertension, tachycardia, muscle cramps, fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis — note these oppose the muscarinic picture, so vital signs can be mixed (p.3712). Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Organophosphates and carbamates can produce bradycardia and atrioventricular block on ECG (p.3706). Organophosphate (and amanita/mushroom) poisoning can present as acute, often systemic-compromising diarrhoea (p.46/Acute Diarrhea chapter). Organophosphates can cause a delayed organophosphate-induced neuropathy: early generalised weakness from neuromuscular blockade, then an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy ensues (p.3610). Bronchorrhoea, wheezing and excessive secretions with progression to respiratory failure — the usual cause of death (p.3712) Nicotinic weakness, fasciculations and paralysis (p.3712) Seizures (p.3712) Bradycardia / atrioventricular block (p.3706) Vital signs may be discordant: muscarinic effects cause bradycardia while nicotinic stimulation can cause hypertension and tachycardia, so a 'normal' or mixed heart rate does not exclude poisoning (p.3712). Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' requiring metabolic activation, so a patient may be initially well or minimally symptomatic and deteriorate later (p.3704). Cholinesterase activity is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning — a key confirmatory threshold not to overlook (p.3712). Organophosphate (and carbamate) insecticides, and nerve agents such as sarin, soman, tabun and VX, inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of synaptic acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptor sites; the resulting overstimulation produces the combined muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS toxidrome. Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' in that they may require metabolic activation, so onset of toxicity can be delayed. Separately, organophosphates bind and inhibit neuropathy target esterase, with axonal degeneration of the gracile fasciculus and corticospinal tracts producing a delayed sensorimotor polyneuropathy. (p.3610, p.3712, p.3704) Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Outcome and reversibility of any poisoning depend on the functional reserve of the individual or target organ, influenced by age and preexisting disease (p.3704). Harrison grades poisoning by degree of physiologic depression rather than by a disease-specific scale: grade 1 — arousable by voice/touch, can converse and follow commands; grade 2 — responds to pain but not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 — unresponsive to pain, brainstem reflexes depressed, decreased respirations and temperature; grade 4 — flaccid paralysis with absent brainstem reflexes and respirations and decreased cardiovascular vital signs (p.3705).

Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency — OTC deficiency, OTCD, ornithine carbamoyltransferase deficiency, X-linked urea cycle disorder Other urea cycle disorders (CPS1, NAGS, citrullinemia, argininosuccinic aciduria) Organic acidaemias with secondary hyperammonaemia Fatty acid oxidation disorders Neonatal sepsis Reye-like syndrome and other causes of acute encephalopathy Postpartum or valproate-associated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy in carrier females Urgent plasma ammonia and arterial blood gas (respiratory alkalosis) Plasma amino acids (low citrulline, low arginine) and urine orotic acid (elevated) Allopurinol loading or protein challenge to unmask carriers, used cautiously in specialist settings Molecular testing of the OTC gene and enzyme assay on liver tissue where needed Family screening and genetic counselling given X-linked inheritance Neuroimaging in severe or prolonged hyperammonaemia The most common urea cycle disorder and the only one that is X-linked, so severe disease predominantly affects hemizygous males Affected male neonates classically appear well then develop lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting and encephalopathy with severe hyperammonaemia in the first days of life Heterozygous females have a variable phenotype depending on X-inactivation and may present later with episodic hyperammonaemic crises, protein intolerance, migraine-like symptoms or psychiatric disturbance The biochemical signature is hyperammonaemia with low or normal citrulline, elevated urine orotic acid, and typically a respiratory alkalosis without metabolic acidosis Elevated orotic acid distinguishes OTC deficiency from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 and N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiencies, in which orotic acid is not raised Acute crises can be precipitated by infection, fasting, high protein load, surgery, or the postpartum period Acute management follows urea cycle disorder principles: halt protein, reverse catabolism with glucose and lipid, give nitrogen scavengers and arginine, and use haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia Because inheritance is X-linked rather than reflected by a single metabolite, standard newborn screening may miss cases, so a high index of suspicion and family testing are important Severe hyperammonaemic encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency mandating immediate ammonia lowering and often dialysis Deteriorating consciousness, seizures or signs of cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure A previously well neonatal boy collapsing after the first feeds, easily mistaken for sepsis Carrier female with unexplained encephalopathy postpartum, after surgery, or on valproate Assuming females who are carriers are unaffected and overlooking symptomatic heterozygotes Missing the diagnosis because newborn screening is insensitive for OTC deficiency Delaying ammonia measurement in an encephalopathic patient and attributing illness to sepsis Giving valproate or a high protein load to an undiagnosed carrier and precipitating a crisis Ornithine transcarbamylase is a mitochondrial enzyme that combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline, the second step of the urea cycle. Its deficiency, caused by mutations in the X-linked OTC gene, blocks ureagenesis and causes waste nitrogen to accumulate as ammonia. Because the block is proximal, carbamoyl phosphate builds up and is diverted into the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, generating excess orotic acid excreted in urine. Ammonia is neurotoxic, producing glutamine accumulation, astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema. Females show a spectrum of severity determined by the pattern of X-chromosome inactivation in hepatocytes. Neonatal-onset disease in boys is severe and, without rapid control of hyperammonaemia, carries a high risk of death or lasting neurodevelopmental impairment; later-onset and carrier presentations vary widely, and outcome depends on prompt recognition and management of crises, with liver transplantation offering definitive correction in selected patients.

Orthostatic hypotension — postural hypotension, orthostatic intolerance, postural drop, OH Vasovagal syncope Cardiac arrhythmia or structural heart disease causing syncope Dehydration or acute blood loss Post-prandial hypotension Vertigo or other non-cardiovascular dizziness Adrenal insufficiency Lying and standing blood pressure measurements at one and three minutes Medication review to identify contributing agents Assessment of hydration status and relevant bloods including electrolytes and haemoglobin ECG and cardiac evaluation when arrhythmia or structural disease is suspected Evaluation for autonomic neuropathy or neurodegenerative disease when a neurogenic cause is likely Orthostatic hypotension is conventionally defined as a sustained fall in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg, or diastolic of at least 10 mmHg, within three minutes of standing Symptoms include light-headedness, dizziness, visual dimming, weakness, and falls on standing, but many older adults are asymptomatic Measure blood pressure supine and then after standing, ideally at one and three minutes, to detect both early and delayed drops Medications are among the commonest and most reversible causes, including antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-blockers, and drugs with anticholinergic or vasodilating effects Volume depletion from dehydration, bleeding, or diuretics should always be considered and corrected Neurogenic causes include diabetic and other autonomic neuropathies and neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson disease and related synucleinopathies Non-drug management comes first: gradual position change, adequate fluid and salt intake where appropriate, compression garments, avoiding large meals and alcohol, and reviewing culprit drugs A large post-prandial blood pressure fall is a related phenomenon in older adults and can also precipitate falls and syncope Syncope resulting in injury or occurring without warning Orthostatic drop accompanied by chest pain, palpitations, or signs of cardiac disease Evidence of significant volume loss such as gastrointestinal bleeding Recurrent falls attributable to postural drops Severe, treatment-resistant orthostatic hypotension suggesting advanced autonomic failure Measuring standing blood pressure only once and missing delayed orthostatic drops Overlooking medications as the reversible cause Failing to consider volume depletion or occult bleeding Aggressively treating supine hypertension in ways that worsen orthostatic symptoms Not recognising post-prandial hypotension as a distinct contributor to falls On standing, gravity shifts blood to the lower body, and normally baroreceptor-mediated reflex increases in heart rate and vascular tone maintain cerebral perfusion. Ageing blunts baroreflex sensitivity and reduces cardiac and vascular compensatory responses. Orthostatic hypotension develops when these mechanisms fail, either because of impaired autonomic reflexes (neurogenic causes) or because of reduced circulating volume or vasodilating and blood-pressure-lowering drugs (non-neurogenic causes). The resulting transient cerebral hypoperfusion produces symptoms and predisposes to falls and syncope. Orthostatic hypotension is common in older adults and is associated with falls, syncope, reduced quality of life, and higher cardiovascular and overall mortality. Many cases improve substantially once contributing medications are withdrawn, volume is restored, and non-pharmacological measures are applied, though neurogenic forms can be chronic and challenging.

Osteoarthritis — OA, degenerative joint disease Inflammatory arthritis (suggested by prolonged morning stiffness and involvement of many joints) Bursitis (anserine bursitis medial/distal to the knee; trochanteric bursitis lateral to the hip) Iliotibial band syndrome Internal derangement of the knee (anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal tear), especially after acute injury Septic arthritis (consider when synovial fluid white count is elevated/inflammatory) No blood tests are routinely indicated unless symptoms or signs suggest inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2953). Synovial fluid examination is often more helpful diagnostically than x-ray; a white count >1000/uL suggests inflammatory arthritis, gout, or pseudogout, the latter two confirmed by crystals (Harrison 22e p.2953). Radiographs are not routinely indicated; order only when pain and findings are atypical of OA or when pain persists after effective treatment. Imaging findings correlate poorly with pain, and x-rays may be normal in early disease (insensitive to cartilage loss) (Harrison 22e p.2953). MRI is not indicated in the diagnostic workup; meniscal tears and cartilage/bone lesions are common both in OA and in older persons without joint pain, and MRI findings rarely warrant a change in therapy (Harrison 22e p.2953). Gout and pseudogout (crystal arthritis; suggested by synovial fluid white count >1000/uL with identifiable crystals) Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides Fibromyalgia (noninflammatory pain amplification) OA is the most common type of arthritis and a leading cause of disability in the elderly; prevalence rises strikingly with age, being uncommon before 40 and highly prevalent after 60 (Harrison 22e p.2949). Joint involvement is characteristic: hips, knees, first MTP joint, cervical/lumbosacral spine, and in the hands the DIP, PIP, and thumb base; the wrist, elbow, and ankle are usually spared (Harrison 22e p.2949). Joint pain is primarily activity-related early on, coming on during or just after use and resolving with rest; as disease progresses pain becomes continuous and may be bothersome at night (Harrison 22e p.2952). Morning stiffness, when present, is usually brief (<30 min), in contrast to the prolonged stiffness (hours) of inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2952). Hand OA produces bony enlargement of the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes) (Harrison 22e p.2949). On hip examination, OA can be detected by loss of internal rotation on passive movement (Harrison 22e p.2953). Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) are common in knee OA and need further evaluation for internal derangement only when they follow an acute knee injury (Harrison 22e p.2952). Osteophytes are an important radiographic hallmark of OA, along with joint-space narrowing reflecting cartilage loss (Harrison 22e pp.2952-2953). Prominent nocturnal pain in the absence of end-stage OA merits a distinct workup (Harrison 22e p.2953). Prolonged morning stiffness with many joints affected suggests inflammatory arthritis rather than OA (Harrison 22e p.2952). Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) developing after an acute knee injury warrant evaluation for internal derangement (Harrison 22e p.2952). Distinguish OA from rheumatoid (and other inflammatory) arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout/pseudogout), and septic arthritis; prolonged morning stiffness, systemic features, and an inflammatory synovial fluid white count point away from OA. Do not rely on radiographs to gauge symptom severity: x-ray changes correlate poorly with pain, and films may be normal in early disease. Many persons with x-ray or MRI evidence of OA have no joint symptoms, so structural findings alone do not establish symptomatic OA. Back pain and neck pain are not tied to x-ray findings of spinal OA and are evaluated separately. OA is joint failure in which all joint structures undergo pathologic change. The pathologic hallmark is focal, initially nonuniform loss of hyaline articular cartilage, accompanied by thickening and sclerosis of the subchondral bony plate, marginal osteophyte outgrowth, stretching of the articular capsule, variable synovitis, and weakness of muscles bridging the joint (meniscal degeneration occurs in knees). Disease begins with joint injury when protective mechanisms (joint capsule/ligaments, bridging muscle, sensory afferents, underlying bone, and synovial-fluid lubrication via hyaluronic acid and lubricin) fail. Cartilage shows depletion of aggrecan and loss/unfurling of type 2 collagen, losing compressive stiffness; chondrocytes shift toward catabolism, producing matrix-degrading enzymes (MMPs, ADAMTS-5). Local inflammation (including mechanoinflammation), with cytokines, alarmins/DAMPs, and growth factors (BMP-2, TGF-beta drive osteophytes; VEGF drives vascular invasion), accelerates progression. Risk reflects the balance between joint vulnerability (age, female sex, genetics such as GDF5, prior damage, malalignment, bridging-muscle weakness, high bone density) and joint loading (obesity, occupational/repetitive use, major injury) (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952). OA is a chronic, generally progressive disorder of the elderly whose high prevalence and impact on physical function make it a leading cause of disability. Severely malaligned knees may be destined to progress regardless of other risk factors, whereas weight loss greater than 10% of body weight reduces cartilage loss and, in most affected persons, alleviates pain (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952). Harrison's chapter 383 does not present a single formal grading scale; OA is characterized clinically along a spectrum from early, episodic activity-related pain with brief morning stiffness to advanced/end-stage disease with continuous and nocturnal pain. The chapter references the WOMAC index as a patient-reported outcome measure of pain, stiffness, and function (Harrison 22e p.2952).

Osteogenesis imperfecta — OI, brittle bone disease, COL1A1, COL1A2, Sillence types I-IV Non-accidental injury (inflicted skeletal trauma) Idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis Hypophosphatasia Bruck syndrome (OI with congenital contractures) Cole-Carpenter and other osteoporosis-fracture syndromes Menkes disease and other collagen or copper metabolism disorders Skeletal survey to characterise fracture pattern, bowing, wormian bones, and vertebral changes Molecular genetic testing of COL1A1/COL1A2 and, if negative, an extended skeletal dysplasia/recessive OI gene panel Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to quantify bone mineral density Audiological assessment for conductive or mixed hearing loss Dental review for dentinogenesis imperfecta Craniocervical imaging in severe disease to detect basilar invagination Classically presents with bone fragility and recurrent fractures from little or no trauma, often prompting consideration of non-accidental injury which must be excluded Most cases result from dominant pathogenic variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2 affecting type I collagen quantity or structure, though recessive forms involving collagen-processing genes exist Extraskeletal features frequently include blue or grey sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, ligamentous laxity, and progressive conductive or mixed hearing loss The Sillence classification (types I-IV, with expanded modern subtypes) ranges from mild (type I) through perinatally lethal (type II) to progressively deforming (type III) Radiographs show generalised osteopenia, thin cortices, gracile or bowed long bones, wormian bones in the skull, and vertebral compression Bisphosphonates are used to reduce fracture frequency and bone pain, alongside physiotherapy, orthopaedic fracture and deformity management, and audiology surveillance Basilar invagination is an important late craniocervical complication in severe deforming disease Multiple fractures at different healing stages requiring careful differentiation from non-accidental injury Progressive spinal deformity with restrictive respiratory compromise Neurological signs suggesting basilar invagination or brainstem compression Perinatal presentation with a small deformed thorax and multiple in-utero fractures suggesting a lethal form Attributing fractures solely to abuse, or conversely dismissing genuine inflicted injury as OI, without appropriate multidisciplinary assessment Relying on sclerae colour alone, as blue sclerae are non-specific and may be absent in some types Overlooking hearing loss and dental disease, which need proactive surveillance Failing to monitor for basilar invagination in progressively deforming disease Osteogenesis imperfecta is a heritable disorder of connective tissue in which abnormal type I collagen, the principal protein of bone matrix, leads to reduced bone mass and mechanical fragility. Most patients carry dominant variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2; null variants reduce the amount of otherwise normal collagen and cause milder disease, whereas variants that distort the collagen triple helix produce a more severe dominant-negative effect. Rarer recessive forms disrupt genes involved in collagen folding, post-translational modification, or bone mineralisation. The resulting defective matrix impairs bone strength and also affects other collagen-rich tissues such as sclera, dentine, and the middle ear ossicles. Prognosis spans from a near-normal lifespan and function in mild type I disease to perinatal lethality in type II. Severe deforming forms carry lifelong mobility limitation, and outcome is strongly influenced by respiratory reserve and craniocervical complications.

CT to guide biopsy and assess sequestra; plain radiography useful mainly in subacute/chronic disease 18F-FDG PET when MRI contraindicated or multifocal/implant disease suspected (sensitive but not specific; useful to exclude PJI) SPECT/CT with labeled leukocytes or antigranulocyte antibodies for osteomyelitis of >1 year duration; three-phase bone scan limited within ~1 year of surgery due to ongoing bone remodeling Synovial fluid leukocyte count and alpha-defensin, multiple intraoperative tissue cultures/histology, and sonication of explanted hardware for biofilm organisms in suspected PJI Seronegative spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, reactive, enteropathic arthritis), including Andersson erosive diskovertebral lesions Spinal stenosis Gouty spondylodiskitis Septic/aseptic bone necrosis Osteoporotic fracture and bone metastases on imaging Three mechanisms underlie osteomyelitis: hematogenous spread, contiguous spread after surgery or trauma, and secondary infection due to vascular insufficiency or neuropathy; in adults hematogenous disease most often involves the vertebral column, whereas in children long bones are seeded (Harrison 22e p.1061). The clinically decisive distinction is not a fixed duration but the presence or absence of bone necrosis (sequestra): acute osteomyelitis without necrosis can generally be cured with antimicrobials alone, while chronic osteomyelitis with sequestra requires combined surgical debridement (Harrison 22e p.1062). Back pain is the leading symptom of vertebral osteomyelitis (>85%), and the location maps to the level of infection (lumbar ~60%, thoracic ~30%, cervical ~10%); only about half of patients are febrile, partly because of analgesic use (Harrison 22e p.1062). ESR and CRP are markedly more useful than the leukocyte count for screening: CRP is elevated in essentially all and ESR in ~98% of vertebral osteomyelitis cases, whereas leukocytosis and neutrophilia have sensitivities of only ~65% and ~40% (Harrison 22e p.1062). In patients without sepsis syndrome, antibiotics should be withheld until a pathogen is documented (by blood culture, bone biopsy, or aspirated pus), because pretreatment markedly lowers culture yield and an established microbiologic diagnosis guides therapy (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063). MRI is the diagnostic gold standard for vertebral osteomyelitis and should be obtained urgently when neurologic impairment is present to detect epidural abscess or exclude disk herniation; 18F-FDG PET is the alternative when MRI is contraindicated or implants/multifocal disease are suspected (Harrison 22e p.1062). A primary focus is found in only about half of hematogenous cases; common sources are the urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, intravascular catheters, and the endocardium, and endocarditis is identified in roughly 10% overall (and in ~50% of viridans streptococcal cases) (Harrison 22e p.1061-1062). Implanted foreign material creates a zone of local immunodeficiency and a host-protein-coated surface that promotes staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation, so device-related bone and joint infection generally cannot be cured by antimicrobials alone (Harrison 22e p.1062, 1066). Brodie's abscess is a subacute form occurring mainly in young males, presenting with pain (~98%) and swelling (~53%) in the tibia or femur, with a median diagnostic delay of about 3 months; localized unexplained tibial/femoral pain in a young patient warrants imaging (Harrison 22e p.1064). Subacute or chronic vertebral disease is typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Brucella in endemic regions, and by low-virulence organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes) in implant-associated infection; tuberculous spondylitis preferentially involves the thoracic spine (about two-thirds of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1062). Synovial fluid analysis is central to diagnosing periprosthetic joint infection: leukocyte thresholds of ~1700/uL (knee) and ~4200/uL (hip) are about 90% sensitive and specific, and alpha-defensin is highly specific but limited by cost and sensitivity, so it should confirm rather than screen (Harrison 22e p.1066). Chronic osteomyelitis can reactivate decades later; recurrence after a symptom-free interval exceeding 70 years has been described, most often in elderly patients with S. aureus disease acquired in the preantibiotic era (Harrison 22e p.1063-1064). New or progressive neurologic deficit (radiculopathy, weakness, sensory loss, bowel/bladder dysfunction, paralysis) suggesting spinal epidural abscess, present in about one-third of vertebral cases Cervical or thoracic spinal involvement and S. aureus etiology, identified risk factors for severe neurologic deficit Persistent or rising CRP, persistent pain, or sepsis syndrome indicating undrained abscess or treatment failure Persistent pain after CRP normalization, suggesting mechanical complication such as severe osteonecrosis or spinal instability requiring orthopedic evaluation Sinus tract, wound-healing impairment, or implant loosening signaling deep device-related infection Starting empiric antibiotics before obtaining cultures in a non-septic patient, which markedly lowers culture yield and obscures the microbiologic diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063). Relying on plain radiographs or the leukocyte count in acute disease, both of which have low sensitivity; normal radiographs do not exclude acute osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1062). Using follow-up MRI to judge treatment response in uncomplicated cases, since radiologic improvement correlates poorly with clinical healing; imaging follow-up is reserved for pyogenic complications (Harrison 22e p.1063). Misinterpreting a three-phase bone scan or 18F-FDG PET within ~1 year of surgery, when ongoing bone remodeling produces nonspecific uptake (Harrison 22e p.1064, 1066). Assuming antimicrobials alone will cure device-associated osteomyelitis or PJI; without appropriate surgery such therapy is generally only suppressive (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1067). Dismissing coagulase-negative staphylococci or Cutibacterium acnes as contaminants, when in the setting of an implant or prolonged bacteremia they may be the true low-virulence pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1062). Failing to consider tuberculous or brucellar disease in patients from or traveling to endemic regions, where subacute/chronic vertebral osteomyelitis predominates (Harrison 22e p.1063-1065). Osteomyelitis is infection of bone reached by microorganisms via one of three routes. In hematogenous disease, circulating organisms seed the metaphyses of long bones in children and the vertebral column in adults; because the adult intervertebral disk is avascular, organisms enter through the segmental arteries supplying the adjacent endplates and then spread into the disk, producing the characteristic involvement of two contiguous vertebrae and the intervening disk. Alternative routes include retrograde seeding through the prevertebral venous plexus and direct inoculation during spinal surgery, epidural procedures, or trauma. Contiguous-focus disease follows bone trauma or surgery, with wound infection after sternotomy, open-fracture repair, or prosthetic-joint placement. Vascular-insufficiency/neuropathic disease, most often in poorly controlled diabetes, arises from progressively deep foot infection driven by ischemia of skin, soft tissue, and bone combined with motor, sensory, and autonomic neuropathy. Foreign material is highly vulnerable: host proteins such as fibronectin coat the device, favoring staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation that resists phagocytosis and antibiotics. Failure of timely or adequate therapy leads to bone necrosis (sequestra) and progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue destruction (Harrison 22e p.1061-1066). Prognosis depends on early diagnosis, presence of bone necrosis, and whether an implant is involved. Acute hematogenous vertebral and long-bone osteomyelitis without sequestra or hardware can usually be cured with antimicrobials alone; a randomized trial in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis reported ~91% cure at one year with no difference between 6- and 12-week regimens. Failure of adequate treatment, open fractures, and unaddressed implant infection drive progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue damage. In fracture-related infection, implant-retention success falls with chronicity (about 86-100% in early, 82-89% in delayed, and ~67% in late infection). In periprosthetic joint infection, implant retention offers >80% infection-free survival only when the infection is acute, the implant is stable, the pathogen is susceptible to a biofilm-active agent, and the soft tissues are intact; in patients with severe comorbidity, lifelong suppressive therapy may be the chosen goal rather than cure (Harrison 22e p.1063-1067). No single accepted comprehensive scheme exists. Osteomyelitis is categorized by pathogenesis (hematogenous, contiguous, vascular insufficiency/neuropathic), by course (acute versus subacute/chronic, with the presence or absence of sequestra being the decisive feature), and by location (long bone, vertebral, periarticular). The Cierny-Mader staging system classifies long-bone disease by anatomic extent, host physiologic class (systemic and local compromise of immunity, metabolism, and vascularity), and radiographic findings, and is used mainly to guide surgical management. Implant-associated disease is further classified by timing relative to surgery (e.g., early/acute, delayed, late), and periprosthetic joint infection is grouped for therapeutic decisions as acute hematogenous, early postinterventional, or chronic (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1066).

decompression consideration Marrow failure with severe anaemia, thrombocytopenia, or recurrent serious infection Osteomyelitis, particularly of the mandible Hypocalcaemic complications in the infantile form Assuming dense bone is strong and underestimating fracture risk Delaying transplantation assessment in severe infantile disease Missing progressive cranial nerve compression, especially optic nerve involvement Failing to distinguish osteoclast-intrinsic from osteoclast-poor forms, which affects transplant suitability Osteopetrosis results from failure of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, most often due to defects in the machinery that acidifies the resorption lacuna, such as the proton pump subunit encoded by TCIRG1 or the chloride channel encoded by CLCN7. Without effective resorption, bone remodelling is disrupted and immature, poorly organised, densely mineralised bone accumulates. This encroaches on the marrow cavity, causing cytopenias and extramedullary haematopoiesis, narrows cranial foramina to compress nerves, and produces bone that is dense yet mechanically brittle. Some forms reflect defective osteoclast differentiation rather than function, which influences whether transplantation is likely to help. Untreated severe infantile osteopetrosis is often fatal in early childhood from marrow failure and infection, whereas transplantation can be curative in suitable osteoclast-intrinsic forms. The dominant adult form is compatible with a normal lifespan but carries fracture, osteomyelitis, and nerve-compression morbidity.

osteopenia (low bone density) is a T-score of -1.0 to -2.5 and is a risk factor for developing osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291). A fragility fracture (hip or vertebral) by definition establishes osteoporosis and warrants treatment, regardless of the T-score; patients presenting with hip or spine fractures by definition have osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298). Osteoporosis is most common among postmenopausal women, but ~30% of fragility fractures occur in men; secondary osteoporosis arises from other underlying diseases (Harrison 22e p.3291). >50% of fractures, including hip fractures, among postmenopausal women occur in individuals with osteopenia rather than densitometric osteoporosis, because that population is much larger - hence the shift toward absolute fracture-risk assessment (Harrison 22e p.3291). FRAX and the Garvan Fracture Risk Calculator estimate 10-year probability of hip or major osteoporotic fracture by combining age, sex, and clinical risk factors with or without BMD, and inform country-specific intervention thresholds distinct from diagnostic thresholds (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3298). Glucocorticoids are the most common cause of medication-induced osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3296). Any fracture (excluding fingers, toes, face, skull) in a woman aged >50 or a man aged >60 should trigger investigation for osteoporosis (Harrison 22e p.3293). Vertebral fracture (even asymptomatic) is a major sign of skeletal fragility and markedly increases risk of subsequent fracture, especially within the first 12-24 months (imminent fracture risk) Significant height loss (>4 cm) suggesting occult vertebral fracture Hip fracture - high mortality (20-25% die within the year) and major loss of independence More chronic severe pain after vertebral fracture should raise suspicion of multiple myeloma or other underlying bone condition Failing to exclude secondary causes of osteoporosis (e.g. myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, Cushing's, malabsorption/celiac, hypogonadism, mastocytosis) before attributing low bone mass to primary disease, particularly in patients with fractures or unexpectedly low Z-scores. Excluding a patient from osteoporosis evaluation simply because a fracture was traumatic - patients with osteoporosis are also more likely to sustain traumatic fractures, and any fracture warrants skeletal assessment. Relying solely on BMD, which can underestimate fragility (microarchitectural deterioration not captured) and is falsely elevated in the spine by osteoarthritic bone spurs/spondylosis; small slim people show falsely low DXA values. Fewer than 20% of fracture patients are investigated or treated for osteoporosis within 6 months; postfracture care remains fragmented. Drug holidays are appropriate to consider for oral/IV bisphosphonates but should be avoided for denosumab and anabolic agents because of more rapid offset. Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength leading to skeletal fragility and fractures; BMD alone underestimates fragility because microarchitectural deterioration and component misalignment also contribute. A low peak bone mass (genetic, hormonal, nutritional) may underlie disease, with superimposed age-related and extrinsic changes in bone remodeling. In adults remodeling (not modeling) predominates and serves to repair microdamage and supply calcium. Estrogen deficiency drives bone loss by (1) activating new remodeling sites and (2) creating an imbalance favoring resorption over formation: loss of estrogen increases RANKL and reduces osteoprotegerin, increasing osteoclast formation/recruitment, while shortening osteoblast life span and prolonging osteoclast longevity/activity. Trabecular bone (80% of surface area) is preferentially affected, so vertebral fractures are the earliest skeletal consequence. Estrogen also regulates remodeling in men. Heritability of BMD is ~50-80%; LRP5 activating mutations cause high bone mass and inactivating mutations cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3293-3295). Lifetime osteoporotic fracture risk for a 50-year-old Caucasian woman is ~50% and ~25% for a man; lifetime hip fracture probability ~14% (women) and ~5% (men), roughly half for African Americans. Hip fractures carry high morbidity and mortality with 20-25% of patients dying within the year (higher among men and African Americans), and ~30% of survivors requiring long-term care, many never regaining prior independence. A first fracture exponentially increases risk of further fracture, especially in the first year; almost 20% of women sustain a second fracture within 2 years (Harrison 22e p.3291-3293). WHO densitometric categories: normal (T-score >= -1.0), osteopenia/low bone density (T-score -1.0 to -2.5), osteoporosis (T-score <= -2.5 at lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip). Presence of a fragility fracture (notably hip or vertebral) defines established/clinical osteoporosis regardless of T-score. Absolute fracture risk (FRAX/Garvan 10-year hip and major osteoporotic fracture probability) is increasingly used alongside or instead of T-score for treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.3291, p.3297-3298).

second peak occurs in older adults, often secondary to Paget's disease or previous irradiation Persistent or night-time bone pain with swelling in a child, adolescent, or young adult requiring urgent specialist referral Pathological fracture through a destructive bone lesion A biopsy performed outside the treating centre risking tumour contamination and jeopardising limb salvage Rapidly enlarging soft-tissue mass over bone Dismissing persistent bone pain in a young person as growing pains or a sports injury, delaying diagnosis Performing an ill-planned biopsy that contaminates tissue planes and precludes limb salvage Confusing osteosarcoma with osteomyelitis and vice versa without adequate imaging and histology Failing to stage the chest and missing pulmonary metastases Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour of mesenchymal cells that produce osteoid or immature bone. It typically arises in the metaphysis of rapidly growing long bones, explaining its predilection for the knee region in adolescence during the growth spurt. The tumour destroys normal bone while laying down disorganised neoplastic osteoid, lifts and stimulates the periosteum, and breaks through the cortex to form a soft-tissue mass. It spreads haematogenously, with a strong tendency to metastasise to the lungs, and micrometastases are often present at diagnosis even when not radiologically evident. Predisposing factors include prior radiation, Paget's disease of bone, and genetic conditions such as hereditary retinoblastoma and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Prognosis depends principally on the presence of metastases at diagnosis and the tumour's response to chemotherapy; with modern combined chemotherapy and surgery many patients with localised, chemosensitive disease achieve long-term survival, whereas metastatic or chemoresistant disease carries a substantially worse outlook.

of the skin lining the external auditory canal. Breakdown of the canal's protective barrier, through excess moisture, mechanical trauma, cerumen removal, or altered pH, allows bacterial or fungal overgrowth. The resulting inflammation causes oedema, discharge and narrowing of the canal, producing pain and conductive hearing loss when the lumen is occluded. In malignant otitis externa, infection (typically Pseudomonas) spreads from the soft tissue into the temporal bone and skull base, causing progressive osteomyelitis and potential cranial nerve involvement. Uncomplicated otitis externa usually resolves with topical treatment and ear care, but malignant otitis externa is potentially life-threatening and requires prolonged systemic therapy and close monitoring.

Extension of foci into the cochlear endosteum can damage the neural elements and cause sensorineural loss. The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance, and hormonal factors appear to modulate its activity. The disease is progressive but stapes surgery closes the conductive gap and restores useful hearing in most suitably selected patients, while hearing aids remain an effective non-surgical option; established cochlear involvement, however, is not reversible.

tests Coagulation profile given the prothrombotic state Pelvic and abdominal ultrasound to document ovarian size and ascites Serum or urine hCG to confirm pregnancy contributing to late OHSS Chest imaging or echocardiography where pleural effusion or respiratory compromise is suspected Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is an iatrogenic complication of controlled ovarian stimulation for assisted reproduction, characterised by enlarged ovaries and a fluid shift out of the intravascular space It is classified by severity from mild (abdominal distension and discomfort) through moderate (ascites on imaging, nausea, vomiting) to severe and critical (tense ascites, haemoconcentration, oliguria, thromboembolism, and organ dysfunction) Early OHSS occurs within days of the ovulation trigger and relates to the trigger itself, whereas late OHSS occurs later and is driven by endogenous hCG from an established pregnancy, tending to be more severe Key risk factors are young age, low body weight, polycystic ovary syndrome, high antral follicle count or anti-Mullerian hormone, and a strong ovarian response with many follicles and high oestradiol Prevention strategies include individualised stimulation, use of a GnRH antagonist protocol with a GnRH agonist trigger, freezing all embryos to avoid pregnancy-related hCG, and cabergoline Management of significant disease is largely supportive: symptom control, careful fluid balance, and thromboprophylaxis because of the prothrombotic haemoconcentrated state Tense, symptomatic ascites can be relieved by paracentesis, which improves comfort, respiratory function, and urine output Because of the venous thromboembolism risk, thromboprophylaxis and a low threshold for imaging unusual or persistent symptoms are important, including for atypical thrombosis Pelvic pain with an enlarged ovary should also raise suspicion of ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency that can complicate OHSS Tense ascites with breathlessness or respiratory compromise Features of venous thromboembolism, including atypical sites such as upper limb or cerebral veins Haemoconcentration with oliguria, hypotension, or evidence of renal impairment Severe abdominal pain suggesting ovarian torsion or cyst rupture Rapid clinical deterioration or signs of organ dysfunction requiring hospital admission Aggressive intravenous crystalloid loading that worsens third-space fluid shift rather than judicious fluid management Omitting thromboprophylaxis and missing atypical-site thrombosis Failing to consider ovarian torsion in a woman with an enlarged ovary and acute pain Not recognising that pregnancy-driven late OHSS may be more severe and prolonged Overlooking the option of freezing all embryos or agonist trigger to prevent the syndrome in high responders Exogenous gonadotrophin stimulation, followed by an hCG or agonist trigger, produces multiple corpora lutea that secrete large amounts of vasoactive mediators, principally vascular endothelial growth factor. hCG amplifies this response, which is why an established pregnancy prolongs and worsens the syndrome. VEGF-driven increases in vascular permeability allow protein-rich fluid to shift from the intravascular compartment into the peritoneal, and sometimes pleural, spaces. This produces ascites, intravascular volume depletion, haemoconcentration, and a hypercoagulable state, which in severe cases lead to oliguria, electrolyte disturbance, thromboembolism, and multi-organ compromise. Most cases are mild and self-limiting, resolving as hCG levels fall, typically within one to two weeks unless pregnancy sustains the process. Severe and critical OHSS, though uncommon, can be life-threatening from thromboembolism, renal failure, or respiratory compromise, but with prompt supportive care and thromboprophylaxis outcomes are generally good. Preventive strategies have markedly reduced the incidence of severe disease.

Ovarian Torsion — adnexal torsion, torsion of the ovary, ovarian and tubal torsion, twisted ovarian cyst Ruptured or haemorrhagic ovarian cyst Ectopic pregnancy Acute appendicitis Pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess Ureteric colic Degenerating or torting pedunculated fibroid Transvaginal or transabdominal pelvic ultrasound with Doppler to assess ovarian size, mass, and blood flow Urine or serum beta-hCG to exclude pregnancy and ectopic Full blood count and inflammatory markers to help exclude infective or appendiceal causes Diagnostic laparoscopy, which is both confirmatory and therapeutic when suspicion is high Pelvic MRI in selected non-acute or pregnant cases when ultrasound is inconclusive Torsion is a gynaecological emergency in which the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, twists on its pedicle and compromises its blood supply, threatening ovarian viability It classically presents with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, often colicky and associated with nausea and vomiting, sometimes provoked by exertion or a change in position An enlarged ovary or an ovarian mass, particularly cysts around five centimetres or larger, predisposes to torsion, so it is uncommon in a normal-sized ovary Doppler ultrasound may show reduced or absent flow, but preserved arterial flow does not exclude torsion because dual blood supply and intermittent twisting can maintain signals Torsion can occur in pregnancy, especially after ovulation induction with enlarged ovaries, and in premenarchal girls in whom the diagnosis is easily missed Prompt surgical intervention, usually laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary, is preferred over oophorectomy even when the ovary looks dusky, as tissue often recovers The classic error is delay: repeated observation while awaiting imaging or normalisation of pain risks irreversible ischaemic loss of the ovary Intermittent torsion produces recurrent self-limiting episodes of pain and warrants evaluation before a definitive infarction occurs Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an adnexal mass, mandating urgent assessment to preserve the ovary Persistent pain with peritonism suggesting ischaemia or necrosis Haemodynamic instability raising concern for haemorrhage or a ruptured ectopic Signs of sepsis suggesting necrotic or infected adnexa Recurrent episodic pain indicating intermittent torsion needing prompt surgical evaluation Excluding torsion because Doppler shows preserved arterial flow Delaying surgery for repeated imaging or observation while ischaemia progresses Performing oophorectomy on a dusky ovary that would recover after simple detorsion Failing to consider torsion in premenarchal girls and pregnant women Missing intermittent torsion by attributing recurrent pain to functional cysts When the ovary or adnexa rotates about the infundibulopelvic and utero-ovarian ligaments, the lower-pressure venous and lymphatic drainage is occluded first, producing congestion and marked ovarian oedema and enlargement. Continued or tightening rotation eventually compromises arterial inflow, leading to ischaemia, haemorrhagic infarction, and necrosis. Because arterial flow may persist longer than venous outflow owing to the thicker arterial wall and dual blood supply, viability can be maintained for a variable period, defining a window in which detorsion can salvage the ovary. When detorsion is performed promptly the ovary usually recovers function even if it appeared ischaemic at surgery, and future fertility is generally preserved. Delayed diagnosis leads to infarction requiring oophorectomy and loss of that ovary's function; recurrence can occur, and oophoropexy may be considered in selected cases such as recurrent torsion or a normal ovary in a child.

neonatal teeth occur with KRT17-related disease Genotype influences phenotype, so keratin gene testing helps classify and counsel patients Severe plantar pain limiting mobility and function Secondary bacterial or fungal infection of fissured keratoderma Laryngeal involvement causing hoarseness or airway symptoms in early-onset severe disease Persistent oral white plaque needing evaluation to exclude other pathology Repeatedly treating nails for presumed onychomycosis without recognising the genetic disorder Mistaking oral leukokeratosis for candidiasis or premalignant leukoplakia
