variants in genes encoding the keratins K6a, K6b, K16, and K17, which pair to form the intermediate filament cytoskeleton of specialised epithelia such as palmoplantar skin, nail bed, oral mucosa, and pilosebaceous structures. Mutant keratins disrupt filament assembly and weaken the mechanical resilience of these cells, so they cannot withstand normal physical stress. This provokes reactive hyperproliferation and hyperkeratosis in weight-bearing skin and nails and produces the painful plantar keratoderma, nail thickening, and mucosal and follicular manifestations that characterise the disorder. It is a lifelong condition without effect on life expectancy, but the painful plantar keratoderma often causes chronic disability and reduced mobility; management is supportive, focused on mechanical offloading, keratolysis, and pain control.

Paget's Disease of Bone — osteitis deformans Osteosarcoma or other sarcoma arising in long-standing pagetic bone (new pain in a long-standing lesion) Osteoclast-rich benign giant cell tumor arising adjacent to pagetic bone (responds to glucocorticoids) Metastatic disease in bone (assessed by MRI; definitive diagnosis of malignancy often requires bone biopsy) Other causes of an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase Plain radiographs (typical findings: bone enlargement/expansion, cortical thickening, coarsened trabeculae, lytic and sclerotic changes; skull 'cotton wool'/osteoporosis circumscripta; 'picture frame' or 'ivory' vertebra; pelvic 'brim sign' and protrusio acetabuli; long-bone bowing) Radionuclide 99mTc bone scan (more sensitive but less specific than radiographs for active lesions) Serum total alkaline phosphatase (ALP) - first-line for diagnosis and monitoring; bone-specific ALP may be raised when total ALP is normal in single-site disease Bone formation marker P1NP (reflects disease activity; can be used instead of total ALP) Bone resorption markers (serum/urine N-telopeptide or C-telopeptide) Serum calcium and phosphate (normal in Paget's disease) CT for assessment of possible fracture; MRI to assess possible sarcoma, giant cell tumor, or metastatic disease Bone biopsy for definitive diagnosis of suspected malignancy Note: serum osteocalcin is NOT always elevated and is NOT recommended for diagnosis or management Familial bone disorders that clinically and radiographically resemble Paget's disease with more severe, earlier-onset presentation: juvenile Paget's disease (familial idiopathic hyperphosphatasia, TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin deletion), familial expansile osteolysis, expansile skeletal hyperphosphatasia, and early-onset Paget's disease (TNFRSF11A/RANK mutations) Inclusion body myopathy with Paget's disease and frontotemporal dementia (IBMPFD; valosin-containing protein mutation) Sarcoma, giant cell tumor, or metastatic disease producing focal changes in or near pagetic bone A localized bone-remodeling disorder affecting widespread, noncontiguous areas of the skeleton; initiated by overactive osteoclastic resorption followed by compensatory osteoblastic new bone formation, producing a disorganized mosaic of woven and lamellar bone (p.3311). Most patients are asymptomatic; diagnosis is often made incidentally from an elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) on routine blood chemistry or an abnormal skeletal radiograph obtained for another indication (p.3311, p.3312-3313). Serum calcium and phosphate levels are normal in Paget's disease; isolated/raised ALP with normal calcium is the characteristic biochemical picture (p.3314). Sites most commonly involved are the pelvis, vertebral bodies, skull, femur, and tibia; familial early-onset cases often have numerous active sites (p.3313). The most common presenting symptom is pain, which may arise from increased bony vascularity, expanding lytic lesions, fractures, bowing, or deformity; long-bone bowing causes gait abnormalities and secondary osteoarthritis of hip or knee (p.3313). Skull involvement may cause headaches, frontal bossing, increased head size, and narrowing of cranial foramina leading to hearing loss (cochlear nerve damage from temporal bone involvement), cranial nerve palsies, and platybasia with risk of brainstem compression (p.3313). For most patients, serum total ALP remains the test of choice for both diagnosis and assessing response to therapy; bone resorption markers (N-telopeptide, C-telopeptide) fall more rapidly with treatment than ALP (p.3313). Radionuclide 99mTc bone scans are less specific but more sensitive than standard radiographs for identifying sites of active skeletal lesions (p.3313). New pain in a long-standing pagetic lesion - suggests sarcomatous (most often osteosarcoma) transformation, although neoplasms arising from pagetic bone are rare (<0.5%) High-output cardiac state and cardiac enlargement from extensive arteriovenous shunting when large portions (15-35%) of the skeleton are involved with high disease activity (e.g., ALP four times above normal); overt high-output heart failure is relatively rare and usually requires concomitant cardiac pathology Platybasia (softening of the skull base) with risk of brainstem compression; spinal cord compression from bone enlargement or vascular steal syndrome Fractures, typically in long bones at areas of active or advancing lytic lesions (common at femoral shaft and subtrochanteric regions) Discovery of hypercalcemia (even with immobilization) should prompt a search for another cause of hypercalcemia Assuming an isolated raised ALP is benign - it can be the only clue to asymptomatic Paget's disease and warrants workup (radiograph plus bone scan). A symptomatic patient with progression at a single site may have a normal total ALP but an increased bone-specific ALP. Using serum osteocalcin to diagnose or monitor disease - it is not always elevated and is not recommended. Attributing hypercalcemia to Paget's disease/immobilization - normal calcium and phosphate are expected, so hypercalcemia should prompt a search for another cause. Starting bisphosphonate therapy without ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake first - very active bone formation with rapid resorption suppression can precipitate hypocalcemia or mild secondary hyperparathyroidism. The principal abnormality is increased number and activity of osteoclasts, which are large, increased 10- to 100-fold in number, and contain many nuclei (up to 100 vs 3-5 in normal osteoclasts), creating a sevenfold rise in resorptive surfaces. Contributing mechanisms include osteoclast precursor hypersensitivity to 1,25(OH)2D3, hyperresponsiveness to RANK ligand (RANKL), increased RANKL expression by marrow stromal cells, increased IL-6 (raising precursor recruitment), increased c-fos expression, and overexpression of the antiapoptotic oncogene Bcl-2. Osteoblasts are recruited to resorption sites and lay down large amounts of new bone matrix, so turnover is high and bone mass is normal or increased (not reduced) unless there is concomitant calcium/vitamin D deficiency. The process passes through an initial osteolytic phase (prominent resorption and hypervascularization, seen radiographically as an advancing lytic wedge or 'blade of grass' lesion), an active mixed phase replacing lamellar bone with haphazard woven bone (marrow may be replaced by fibrous tissue), and a final sclerotic ('burned-out') phase of hard, dense, less vascular mosaic bone; all three phases may coexist at different sites. Etiology remains unknown but evidence supports both genetic (family history in 15-25%; familial syndromes linked to TNFRSF11B/osteoprotegerin, TNFRSF11A/RANK, profilin 1, valosin-containing protein, and the common SQSTM1/p62 mutation) and viral (paramyxovirus-like inclusions and viral mRNA in osteoclasts) contributions (p.3311-3313). Most patients are asymptomatic and have a benign course; for unclear reasons the prevalence and severity are decreasing and the age of diagnosis is increasing. Effective potent antiresorptive (bisphosphonate) therapy can normalize bone turnover and is associated with an apparently decreasing incidence of sarcoma. Serious complications - fractures, deformity, secondary osteoarthritis, neurologic compromise (hearing loss, cranial nerve palsies, cord/brainstem compression), high-output cardiac state, and rare (<0.5%) malignant transformation (usually osteosarcoma) - drive morbidity. Whether early therapy prevents late complications remains to be determined; deformities may take many years to manifest (p.3312-3314). Harrison does not give a formal staging system. Disease activity is gauged by the extent of skeletal involvement and the degree of bone-turnover marker elevation (notably total ALP, with ALP roughly four times above normal cited as marking high activity and cardiovascular risk when 15-35% of the skeleton is involved). Pathologically the disease evolves through three phases that may coexist: an osteolytic phase, an active mixed (woven-bone) phase, and a final sclerotic 'burned-out' phase (p.3313-3314).

analysis or microarray on skin fibroblasts or buccal cells rather than blood, to detect the mosaic isochromosome FISH for 12p to confirm tetrasomy and estimate the mosaic fraction Prenatal detection via amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling when suspected antenatally Echocardiography for congenital heart disease Imaging to detect diaphragmatic hernia and other structural anomalies Electroencephalography and neuroimaging for seizures Caused by mosaic tetrasomy of the short arm of chromosome 12, usually from a supernumerary isochromosome 12p present in only a proportion of cells A characteristic pattern of pigmentary skin anomalies (streaks of hyper- and hypopigmentation) and localised areas of alopecia, along with a coarse face, may develop over time Facial features include a high forehead with frontotemporal balding, sparse eyebrows and eyelashes, hypertelorism, a short nose with anteverted nares and a long philtrum Profound hypotonia, severe intellectual disability and epilepsy are typical Diaphragmatic hernia, congenital heart disease and other malformations are recognised associations Because the isochromosome is often absent from blood lymphocytes with age, skin fibroblast analysis or buccal sampling is the preferred diagnostic tissue Recurrence risk is generally low as the abnormality is sporadic and mosaic Respiratory distress at birth from congenital diaphragmatic hernia Undiagnosed congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise Refractory seizures Severe feeding difficulty with aspiration and failure to thrive Excluding the diagnosis on a normal blood karyotype because the isochromosome is lost from lymphocytes Failing to test fibroblasts or buccal cells, the tissues most likely to reveal the mosaic Attributing the pigmentary changes to an unrelated skin disorder Underestimating the risk of associated diaphragmatic hernia and cardiac anomalies Pallister-Killian syndrome results from mosaic tetrasomy 12p, most often due to a supernumerary isochromosome composed of two copies of the short arm of chromosome 12, giving four copies of 12p in affected cells. The extra genetic material causes an imbalance of dosage-sensitive genes during development. Because the isochromosome is unstable and tends to be lost from rapidly dividing tissues such as blood, the mosaicism is often confined to fibroblasts and other tissues, which accounts for the diagnostic difficulty and the tissue-dependent detection. Outcome is variable and correlates with the tissue distribution of the mosaicism; many affected children have profound intellectual disability and significant medical needs, and severe cases with diaphragmatic hernia have high early mortality. Those surviving infancy generally live into childhood or beyond with major disability.

Pancreatic Cancer — pancreatic adenocarcinoma Chronic pancreatitis Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Acinar cell carcinoma Colloid carcinoma Medullary carcinoma Adenosquamous carcinoma Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) Mucinous cystic neoplasm Metastasis to the pancreas (renal, breast, lung, urothelial carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma) Dual-phase contrast-enhanced CT using a pancreas-cancer protocol (arterial and portal venous phases) to assess tumor-vessel relationships, resectability, and staging Abdominal ultrasonography (often first imaging in the jaundiced patient) MRI 18F-glucose PET to detect occult metastatic disease Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with EUS-guided core needle biopsy of pancreatic lesions Tru-Cut core needle biopsy (preferred over fine-needle aspiration) for histologic diagnosis; percutaneous biopsy for liver/lymph node lesions Next-generation sequencing for genomic alterations (including KRAS) and microsatellite status Serum CA19-9 (drawn after bilirubin normalizes), CEA, and CA125 Staging laparoscopy (selectively, before or at definitive surgery) Chronic pancreatitis (can be difficult to distinguish from adenocarcinoma and is itself a risk factor) Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Mucinous cystic neoplasm and IPMN Metastatic disease to the pancreas from other primaries The classic presentation of cancer arising in the head of the pancreas is 'painless' jaundice; jaundice is visually detectable once bilirubin exceeds ~2 mg/dL and may be accompanied by pruritus from bile salt skin deposition (p.672). Pain, when present, is typically mid-epigastric and 'boring' with radiation to the back (from retroperitoneal invasion of the splanchnic nerve plexus) and may be worsened by eating or lying flat (p.672). A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in the setting of biliary obstruction is Courvoisier's sign (p.672). Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and combined deep venous plus arterial thromboses (Trousseau's syndrome) can occur; metastatic disease is frequently associated with a hypercoagulable state requiring anticoagulation (p.672-674). New-onset diabetes (especially with concomitant weight loss) or unexplained worsening of type 2/type 3c diabetes, or rising HbA1c/hyperglycemia in the preceding 1-2 years, may signal underlying pancreatic cancer (p.671-672). CA19-9 is best drawn after the bilirubin has normalized because biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9; CA125 can help in the 8-15% of Lewis-antigen non-secretors who have undetectable CA19-9 (p.674). Cigarette smoking is the greatest environmental risk factor, accounting for an estimated 25-30% of cases, with risk persisting at least 10 years after cessation (p.671). Histologic/cytologic tissue diagnosis is essential and also enables molecular testing (next-generation sequencing for KRAS and other alterations) and microsatellite status determination, which increasingly guide therapy (p.674). Signs of late-stage disease include a left supraclavicular Virchow's node and a periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule indicating peritoneal metastases (p.672-673). Painless obstructive jaundice (classic for head-of-pancreas tumor) Palpable non-tender gallbladder with obstruction (Courvoisier's sign) Unintentional weight loss with loss of muscle mass New-onset diabetes, especially with concomitant weight loss Mid-epigastric boring pain radiating to the back Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis / venous or arterial thrombosis (Trousseau's syndrome) Left supraclavicular Virchow's node or periumbilical Sister Mary Joseph's nodule (late disease) Light/clay-colored stools and steatorrhea Drawing CA19-9 while bilirubin is elevated falsely raises the level, since biliary obstruction itself elevates CA19-9 (p.674). 8-15% of patients are Lewis-antigen non-secretors with undetectable CA19-9, so a normal CA19-9 does not exclude disease; CA125 may help in this group (p.674). Even high-grade PanIN precursor lesions are not detectable by current imaging, limiting early detection (p.672). For average-risk individuals with no predisposing factors there is currently no recommended screening (p.671). Whether diabetes causes or is caused by pancreatic cancer is not clearly established (p.671). Fine-needle aspiration cytology is acceptable but less preferred than core (Tru-Cut) biopsy, which yields adequate tissue for molecular testing (p.674). Biliary stenting is not necessarily warranted if upfront surgery is planned, but is required (where medically indicated) before neoadjuvant systemic therapy (p.674). Ductal adenocarcinoma is the most common and most lethal exocrine pancreatic neoplasm, characterized by infiltrating desmoplastic stromal reaction and arising in the head, body, or tail. Most cancers arise from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN, graded 1-3 in a progression model), with genetic alterations accumulating as PanIN grade increases; some arise from noninvasive cystic precursors (e.g., IPMN). The mutational landscape is dominated by four commonly altered genes: KRAS (mutated in 90-95%, primarily codon 12), p16/CDKN2A (inactivated in >90% of invasive tumors), TP53 (~75%), and DPC4/SMAD4 (~50%); BRCA2 is mutated in 3.5-10%. A 'KRAS wildtype' subset (more common in patients under 55) may harbor actionable BRAF mutations, oncogenic fusions (NRG-1, NTRK1-3), or microsatellite instability (p.672). Pancreatic cancer is the most lethal human cancer, with an overall 5-year survival of about 13% (up from 3% in 1975). SEER estimates 5-year survival of ~44% for localized disease, ~16% for regional disease, and ~3.2% for metastatic disease. Late presentation is common, only about 10-20% of tumors are resectable, and the disease is the third leading cause of cancer mortality in the U.S. and projected to become the second by 2030 (p.671-672). Staged by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system. Clinically also categorized by extent of disease and therapeutic approach: resectable (~10-20%), borderline resectable/locally advanced, and metastatic (p.674).

Pancreatic pseudocyst — pseudocyst of the pancreas, pancreatic fluid collection, post-pancreatitis pseudocyst Cystic pancreatic neoplasm (serous or mucinous cystadenoma, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm) Acute peripancreatic fluid collection or walled-off necrosis Pancreatic abscess Mesenteric or omental cyst Duplication cyst or choledochal cyst Pancreatic pseudoaneurysm Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to characterise the collection and its wall Endoscopic ultrasound with fluid aspiration for amylase, CEA, and cytology to exclude a neoplasm Serum amylase and lipase and liver function tests MRCP or ERP to assess pancreatic ductal anatomy and communication before drainage Ultrasound for follow-up of size in conservatively managed cysts A pancreatic pseudocyst is a persistent, encapsulated collection of pancreatic fluid that develops weeks after acute or chronic pancreatitis, or after pancreatic trauma Unlike a true cyst it lacks an epithelial lining and is bounded by a wall of fibrous and granulation tissue, requiring around four weeks to mature Common presentations include persistent or recurrent upper abdominal pain, a palpable epigastric mass, early satiety, nausea, and failure to recover after an episode of pancreatitis A raised serum amylase and high amylase within aspirated fluid support the diagnosis and help distinguish it from a cystic neoplasm Contrast CT and endoscopic ultrasound define the collection, its relation to the stomach and duodenum, and any ductal communication Many small, asymptomatic pseudocysts resolve spontaneously and can be observed, whereas large, symptomatic, enlarging, or complicated collections need drainage Drainage is increasingly endoscopic (transmural cystgastrostomy or cystduodenostomy), with surgical internal drainage or percutaneous approaches reserved for selected cases In older patients or those without a clear pancreatitis history, a cystic pancreatic neoplasm must be excluded before assuming a pseudocyst Sudden severe pain, expanding mass, or gastrointestinal bleeding suggesting pseudoaneurysm erosion or rupture Fever, rigors, and systemic sepsis indicating an infected pseudocyst Progressive gastric outlet or biliary obstruction from a large cyst Rapid clinical deterioration suggesting free rupture into the peritoneal cavity Mistaking a cystic pancreatic neoplasm for a pseudocyst and draining rather than resecting it Draining a collection before the wall has matured, increasing the risk of leakage and failure Overlooking an associated pseudoaneurysm, so that drainage precipitates torrential bleeding Ignoring underlying pancreatic ductal obstruction, leading to recurrence after drainage Delaying treatment of an infected pseudocyst presenting with sepsis Pancreatic pseudocysts arise when pancreatic ductal disruption, from acute inflammation, chronic pancreatitis, or trauma, allows enzyme-rich secretions to leak and collect in or around the pancreas. The surrounding tissue reacts, and over several weeks an inflammatory capsule of fibrous and granulation tissue forms, producing a mature pseudocyst without a true epithelial lining. Persistent communication with the pancreatic duct maintains the collection. Enlargement can compress adjacent structures, and complications develop when the cyst becomes infected, erodes into a vessel to form a pseudoaneurysm or bleed, or ruptures into the peritoneum or an adjacent viscus. Small uncomplicated pseudocysts frequently resolve without intervention, and drainage of symptomatic collections has good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with complications such as haemorrhage from a pseudoaneurysm, infection, or rupture, and recurrence is more likely when underlying ductal disease or chronic pancreatitis is not addressed.
