ALT - ALT >3x ULN supports gallstone aetiology (Harrison 22e p.2745) Serum triglycerides - to detect hypertriglyceridaemic cause (levels usually >1000 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.2744, p.2748) Serum calcium - to detect hypercalcaemic cause and to monitor for hypocalcaemia (~25% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745) Hematocrit - hemoconcentration >44% is a severity marker (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746) Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at admission and 48 h - rising BUN predicts mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745, p.2748) White cell count - leukocytosis 15,000-20,000/uL is common (Harrison 22e p.2745) MRI/MRCP - more sensitive than CT for mild pancreatitis, necrosis, choledocholithiasis and ductal abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.2739) EUS - useful for occult microlithiasis/biliary cause and choledocholithiasis; best performed ~4 weeks after resolution to find predisposing lesions (Harrison 22e p.2741) Contrast-enhanced CT - to assess necrosis and local complications when not improving, ideally at 3-5 days (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746) C-reactive protein - severity marker during hospitalization (thresholds >100 mg/L reported) (Harrison 22e p.2748) Diabetic ketoacidosis - abdominal pain with raised TOTAL amylase mimics pancreatitis, but lipase is often NOT elevated and pancreatic imaging is normal (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746) Perforated peptic ulcer - can raise serum/ascitic amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745) Acute cholecystitis / biliary colic - amylase may be raised; pain is more right-sided/epigastric and ileus is usually absent (Harrison 22e p.2745) Mesenteric ischemia/infarction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745) Intestinal obstruction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase; differentiated by crescendo-decrescendo pain and obstruction pattern on CT (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745) Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase/amylase >=3x ULN, or characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (Harrison 22e p.2745). Lipase is more pancreas-specific than amylase and is the single best enzyme to measure; it stays elevated longer (7-14 days) whereas amylase often normalises by 3-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745). Gallstones and alcohol together account for ~80-90% of cases; gallstones are the single most common cause (30-60%), alcohol the second (15-30%) (Harrison 22e p.2744). ALT >3x ULN strongly points to a gallstone aetiology in acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745). Abdominal ultrasound is the recommended initial imaging study, chiefly to assess for gallstones and bile-duct dilation; contrast CT is best deferred to ~3-5 days if the patient is not improving and is usually not needed in the first 48-72 h (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746). Persistent organ failure (>48 h) is the most important determinant of severity; if SIRS has resolved by 24 h, organ failure or necrosis is unlikely to develop (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748). Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and a rising BUN are early warning signs of more severe disease and higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748). Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank discoloration) are rare but signal severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic disease (Harrison 22e p.2745). Persistent organ failure >48 h (respiratory, cardiovascular or renal) - hallmark of severe disease (Harrison 22e p.2746) Modified Marshall organ-failure signs: systolic BP <90 mmHg, HR >130/min, PaO2 <60 mmHg, or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL (Harrison 22e p.2748) BISAP score >=3 - increased in-hospital mortality (Harrison 22e p.2748) APACHE II >=8 at 24 h (Harrison 22e p.2748) Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and rising/admission BUN - predict severe disease and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748) Persistent SIRS at 24 h - predisposes to organ failure and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748) Pancreatic necrosis on CT - greatest mortality risk (3-10% with single-organ failure, ~50% with multiorgan failure) (Harrison 22e p.2747) Hypoxemia (PaO2 <=60 mmHg) - may herald ARDS (Harrison 22e p.2745) Cullen's sign / Grey Turner's sign - severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745) Ascending cholangitis (sepsis + biliary obstruction) complicating gallstone pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2748) Enzyme magnitude does NOT track severity - degree or serial trend of lipase/amylase does not correlate with how severe the pancreatitis is (Harrison 22e p.2745). Serum amylase can be falsely normal or low in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, masking the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745). Amylase is non-specific - raised in salivary, tubo-ovarian, pulmonary, malignant and other conditions, and spuriously high in acidemia/DKA (arterial pH <=7.32) without true pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745). Lipase can be mildly elevated in renal failure, and >3x ULN can occur in hepatobiliary/GI malignancy, sepsis, cirrhosis, SLE, head injury, chronic alcoholism, diabetes and post-ERCP without pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740). Routine/early CT (within 72 h) is overused and usually unnecessary, especially in mild disease; necrosis may not be visible until several days in (Harrison 22e p.2746-2747). Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended, even in severe or necrotizing pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2749). Enzyme levels may be normal if blood is drawn 2-5 days after onset or if the underlying problem is chronic rather than acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740). Acute pancreatitis is thought to begin with autodigestion: intracellular premature activation of trypsin (via lysosomal cathepsin B colocalising with digestive zymogens) within acinar cells, which then activates other proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, phospholipase A2). A second phase recruits and sequesters leukocytes/macrophages, amplifying intrapancreatic inflammation, and a third phase results from activated enzymes and cytokines acting on distant organs, producing edema, hemorrhage, vascular damage, fat necrosis and coagulation/cellular necrosis. Release of bradykinin, vasoactive substances and histamine drives vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and edema, and can culminate in SIRS, ARDS and multiorgan failure. Pathologically the spectrum runs from interstitial (perfusion preserved, self-limited) to necrotizing pancreatitis (perfusion interrupted). Genetic susceptibility/modifier variants include PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen), SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC, CASR and CLDN2, all converging on control of intrapancreatic trypsin activity (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745). Overall mortality is low (~1%) and median hospital stay ~4 days; most cases are mild and self-limited within 3-7 days. Interstitial pancreatitis (90-95% of admissions) carries low mortality, whereas necrotizing pancreatitis (5-10%) drives most deaths. In necrotizing disease the median prevalence of organ failure exceeds 50% (slightly higher with infected vs sterile necrosis); mortality is 3-10% with single-organ failure but approaches 50% with multiorgan failure. Patients with only extrapancreatic necrosis fare better than those with pancreatic parenchymal necrosis. About 25% of patients have a recurrence, most commonly from alcohol or gallstones (Harrison 22e p.2747, p.2749). Revised Atlanta classification (Banks et al., Gut 2013). PHASES: early (<2 weeks; severity judged clinically, not by morphology) and late (>2 weeks; imaging for local complications). SEVERITY: (1) Mild - no local complications and no organ failure (most interstitial cases; self-limited 3-7 days); (2) Moderately severe - transient organ failure (resolves <48 h) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure; (3) Severe - persistent organ failure >48 h in >=1 organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal; defined by modified Marshall score >=2). MORPHOLOGY: two types - interstitial (parenchymal enhancement, no necrosis) vs necrotizing (lack of parenchymal enhancement and/or peripancreatic necrosis); local collections - acute pancreatic fluid collection and pseudocyst (interstitial, pseudocyst usually >4 wk) vs acute necrotic collection (ANC) and walled-off necrosis (WON, usually >4 wk, encapsulated). SEVERITY SCORES/MARKERS: BISAP >=3 (BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status/GCS<15, SIRS >=2/4, Age >60, Pleural effusion); APACHE II >=8 at 24 h; SIRS >=2 of 4 (temp <36 or >38C, HR >90, RR >20 or PCO2 <32, WCC >12,000 or <4000 or >10% bands); hematocrit >44%; admission BUN >20 mg/dL; persistent organ failure >=48 h, and pancreatic/extrapancreatic necrosis as in-hospital markers. Ranson criteria are a traditional severity index (referenced contextually).

Panic attack / anxiety — Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out ACS/PE first ECG normal Do not anchor on anxiety until cardiac/pulmonary emergencies excluded Hyperventilation syndrome (respiratory alkalosis) — itself a diagnosis of exclusion (p.376) Generalized anxiety disorder and somatization presenting with palpitations or pseudo-syncope (p.161, p.291) Vasovagal syncope precipitated by fear/stress/anxiety (distinguished by accompanying hypotension +/- bradycardia, unlike psychogenic pseudo-syncope) (p.161) Cataplexy / narcolepsy as a cause of episodic collapse (consciousness preserved) (p.161) Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) and chronic subjective dizziness, in which anxiety disorders are common comorbidities (p.165) Resting 12-lead ECG, with serial tracings, to exclude arrhythmia and ischemia in palpitations/chest discomfort (p.291); note hyperventilation in panic can itself produce nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities (p.107) Ambulatory rhythm monitoring (Holter, event/loop recorder, implantable loop recorder, or mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry) for infrequent recurrent palpitations (p.291) Arterial blood-gas analysis when hyperventilation suspected: shows respiratory alkalosis with hypocapnia (Paco2 ~15-30 mmHg) but no hypoxemia (p.376) Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial ischemia (aching, heavy, squeezing retrosternal discomfort) (p.103) Pulmonary embolism (chest discomfort, sinus tachycardia, ECG axis shift/S1Q3T3) (p.107) Supraventricular or ventricular tachyarrhythmia and atrial fibrillation (palpitations) (p.291) Thyrotoxicosis / hyperthyroidism (palpitations, hyperdynamic state) (p.291, p.376) Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-driven palpitations, hyperdynamic cardiovascular state) (p.291) Hypoglycemia (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias from autonomic activation) (p.161) Systemic mastocytosis; stimulant/drug effects (caffeine, cocaine, amphetamines, cannabis, ethanol); post-COVID syndrome — as causes of palpitations (p.291) Up to ~10% of patients presenting to emergency departments with acute chest discomfort have an underlying panic disorder or a related condition (p.104). Psychiatric/emotional chest discomfort is variable in duration (fleeting to prolonged), often felt as chest tightness and breathlessness with a sense of panic or impending doom, and may be retrosternal; situational triggers and a prior history of panic attacks or depression support the diagnosis (p.103). A psychiatric cause for palpitations is favoured when the sensation is reported as lasting longer (>15 min) and is accompanied by additional symptoms, in contrast to most arrhythmic causes (p.291). Panic attacks can arise out of sleep and must be distinguished from parasomnias and other nocturnal events (p.215). Apparent (psychogenic) loss of consciousness can occur in panic disorder and related conditions; suspect it in patients who faint frequently without prodrome, are rarely injured despite repeated falls, and have no concurrent hemodynamic change (no hypotension/bradycardia) during the event (p.161). Normocapnia together with hypoxemia in a hyperventilating patient is a warning sign that may herald impending respiratory failure — do not assume benign anxiety (p.376) High-risk syncope features that argue against a psychogenic cause: new chest discomfort, dyspnea, exertional or supine syncope, palpitations preceding syncope, structural/coronary heart disease (p.161) Chest discomfort with features of an acute cardiopulmonary catastrophe (ACS, acute aortic syndrome, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, pericarditis with tamponade) must be excluded first (p.105) Anchoring on anxiety/panic prematurely: because attacks mimic ACS, PE, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, pheochromocytoma and hypoglycemia, organic emergencies must be excluded — panic disorder and the hyperventilation syndrome are diagnoses of exclusion (p.105, p.376). Misreading hyperventilation-related nonspecific ST-segment/T-wave changes as evidence of ischemia (or vice versa) (p.107). When ruling in a hyperventilation/psychiatric cause, still exclude pulmonary embolism, coronary artery disease and hyperthyroidism (p.376). Acute attacks are commonly accompanied by hyperventilation; the resulting hypocapnia (Paco2 often 15-30 mmHg) produces an acute respiratory alkalosis without hypoxemia, which underlies many of the somatic symptoms (paresthesia, circumoral numbness, chest-wall tightness, dizziness, air hunger, and rarely tetany) and can perpetuate the disorder. Catecholaminergic/hyperadrenergic activation contributes to palpitations and the hyperdynamic sensation (Harrison 22e p.376, p.291).

Panic disorder — panic attacks disorder, episodic paroxysmal anxiety Cardiac arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome Hyperthyroidism and other endocrine disturbances Phaeochromocytoma Hypoglycaemia Substance intoxication or withdrawal, including caffeine, stimulants, and alcohol Other anxiety disorders such as generalised anxiety disorder or social anxiety disorder Vestibular or respiratory disorders presenting with dizziness or breathlessness Electrocardiogram to exclude arrhythmia in appropriate presentations Thyroid function testing Blood glucose measurement during symptomatic episodes Substance and caffeine use screening Standardised anxiety rating scales to gauge severity and monitor response The core feature is recurrent, unexpected surges of intense fear or discomfort that peak within minutes, accompanied by prominent physical symptoms such as palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, sweating, trembling, dizziness, and a sense of impending doom Diagnosis also requires persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour to avoid them, distinguishing the disorder from isolated panic attacks Many patients present first to emergency or cardiology services convinced they are having a heart attack, so a compassionate explanation of the mind-body link is central to engagement Exclude medical mimics before settling on the diagnosis, including arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma, asthma, and caffeine or stimulant effects Agoraphobic avoidance frequently develops as patients begin to avoid places or situations from which escape might feel difficult during an attack First-line management combines cognitive behavioural therapy, including interoceptive exposure and breathing retraining, with SSRIs or SNRIs as pharmacological options Benzodiazepines may give rapid relief but carry dependence and rebound risks, so they are generally reserved for short-term or adjunctive use rather than maintenance Reassurance, psychoeducation about the self-limiting nature of attacks, and reduction of stimulants can markedly reduce anticipatory anxiety Syncope, sustained chest pain, or objective signs suggesting a primary cardiac event Emerging suicidal ideation, particularly with comorbid depression Escalating benzodiazepine or alcohol use to self-manage symptoms Severe agoraphobic avoidance causing housebound behaviour and functional collapse Repeated extensive medical investigations that reinforce illness beliefs rather than addressing the anxiety Relying on long-term benzodiazepines and creating dependence Missing comorbid depression and its associated suicide risk Underdosing or prematurely stopping SSRIs before an adequate therapeutic trial Overlooking caffeine, stimulants, or withdrawal states as drivers of attacks Panic disorder is thought to arise from dysregulation of fear-processing circuits, particularly hypersensitivity of the amygdala and brainstem structures involved in the alarm and respiratory response, with contributions from serotonergic, noradrenergic, and GABAergic dysfunction. A heritable predisposition interacts with heightened sensitivity to internal bodily cues (interoceptive conditioning) and catastrophic misinterpretation of benign somatic sensations, which perpetuates the cycle of fear and physiological arousal. Panic disorder tends to run a chronic, fluctuating course, but a substantial proportion of patients achieve marked improvement or remission with adequate treatment. Prognosis is better with early intervention and engagement in cognitive behavioural therapy, and worse when agoraphobia, depression, or substance misuse is comorbid or when treatment is delayed.

Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration — PKAN, PANK2, NBIA type 1, Hallervorden-Spatz syndrome, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1 Other NBIA subtypes (PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration, BPAN, aceruloplasminaemia, neuroferritinopathy) Wilson disease Juvenile Huntington disease Dopa-responsive dystonia and other early-onset dystonias Mitochondrial disorders with basal ganglia involvement Secondary pallidal injury from hypoxia or manganese exposure Brain MRI including iron-sensitive sequences to demonstrate the eye-of-the-tiger sign and pallidal iron PANK2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Ophthalmological assessment including electroretinography for pigmentary retinopathy Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease Serum ferritin and caeruloplasmin to help distinguish other NBIA subtypes Most common form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA), inherited autosomal recessively through biallelic PANK2 variants Classic early-onset form presents in childhood with gait disturbance, dystonia, rigidity, and pigmentary retinopathy, progressing over years Atypical later-onset form has slower progression with prominent speech and neuropsychiatric features and less retinopathy Oromandibular and limb dystonia can be severe and may lead to status dystonicus, a neurological emergency The pathognomonic MRI finding is the eye-of-the-tiger sign: a central region of T2 hyperintensity within surrounding hypointensity in the globus pallidus, reflecting focal gliosis amid iron deposition Iron-sensitive MRI sequences (T2*/gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted imaging) accentuate the pallidal iron and support the NBIA diagnosis Management is symptomatic, targeting dystonia and spasticity with oral agents, botulinum toxin, and in selected refractory cases deep brain stimulation Diagnosis is confirmed by PANK2 molecular testing in the setting of the characteristic clinical and imaging picture Status dystonicus with unremitting severe dystonia causing pain, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis Acute swallowing failure with aspiration risk Rapid loss of ambulation or new bulbar dysfunction Self-injury from severe oromandibular dystonia Mistaking the eye-of-the-tiger appearance for another basal ganglia lesion or dismissing subtle pallidal iron on standard sequences Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI sequences that reveal the diagnostic iron deposition Overlooking status dystonicus as an emergency requiring prompt escalation Not screening for Wilson disease, a treatable mimic, before settling on an NBIA diagnosis Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PANK2, encoding a mitochondrial pantothenate kinase that catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of coenzyme A biosynthesis from vitamin B5. Impaired coenzyme A synthesis is thought to disrupt lipid and energy metabolism and to allow accumulation of cysteine-containing substrates that chelate iron, driving oxidative damage. The net effect is progressive iron deposition and neurodegeneration concentrated in the globus pallidus, producing the extrapyramidal features and the characteristic pallidal imaging changes. The classic childhood-onset form is progressive, with most patients losing independent ambulation within years of onset, whereas the atypical form advances more slowly over decades. Life expectancy is reduced, largely from complications of severe dystonia and immobility.

Papilloedema — papilledema, optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure Optic neuritis (usually unilateral, with pain and reduced acuity) Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy Malignant hypertension with hypertensive retinopathy Pseudopapilloedema from optic disc drusen or a crowded hypermetropic disc Central retinal vein occlusion Infiltrative or inflammatory optic disc swelling Urgent neuroimaging (MRI or CT with venography) to exclude a mass lesion or venous sinus thrombosis Lumbar puncture with opening pressure and cerebrospinal fluid analysis once imaging excludes a mass Visual field testing to detect an enlarged blind spot and peripheral loss Blood pressure measurement to exclude malignant hypertension Optical coherence tomography and fundus photography to grade and monitor disc swelling Assessment of colour vision and pupils to help distinguish from optic neuropathies The term papilloedema refers specifically to optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure, and is characteristically bilateral Central vision is often preserved early, while an enlarged blind spot and transient visual obscurations lasting seconds are typical Accompanying symptoms of raised intracranial pressure include headache worse on waking or with Valsalva, nausea, vomiting, and pulsatile tinnitus, and a sixth nerve palsy may be a false localising sign Fundus signs include blurred disc margins, hyperaemia, loss of the physiological cup, obscuration of vessels crossing the disc, and loss of spontaneous venous pulsation, with haemorrhages and cotton wool spots in more advanced cases Idiopathic intracranial hypertension classically affects young women who are overweight, but a space-occupying lesion or venous sinus thrombosis must be excluded first It must be distinguished from other causes of a swollen disc, such as optic neuritis, anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, and pseudopapilloedema from optic disc drusen Chronic untreated papilloedema leads to progressive optic atrophy and irreversible visual field loss Bilateral disc swelling mandating urgent workup for raised intracranial pressure, including neuroimaging to exclude a tumour or venous sinus thrombosis Progressive visual field loss or declining acuity indicating threatened optic nerve function New focal neurological signs or a sixth nerve palsy Very high intracranial or blood pressure requiring emergency management Mistaking pseudopapilloedema from disc drusen for true papilloedema and initiating unnecessary invasive workup Diagnosing idiopathic intracranial hypertension before excluding a mass lesion or venous thrombosis Reassuring the patient because central acuity is normal while field loss progresses Overlooking malignant hypertension as a cause of disc swelling Papilloedema is passive swelling of the optic nerve head produced by raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve. The elevated pressure impedes axoplasmic flow within the retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic disc, causing them to become distended, along with venous congestion and leakage that produce the characteristic disc appearance. Because the mechanism is mechanical rather than primarily ischaemic or inflammatory, central acuity is often spared until late. Persistently raised pressure eventually causes axonal loss and secondary optic atrophy. Vision can be preserved if the underlying cause of raised intracranial pressure is treated promptly, but delayed or chronic papilloedema leads to optic atrophy and permanent visual field loss.

Paracoccidioidomycosis — Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Paracoccidioides lutzii, South American blastomycosis, Lutz-Splendore-Almeida disease, PCM Pulmonary tuberculosis (frequently co-exists and mimics the chronic form) Histoplasmosis and other endemic dimorphic mycoses Oral or laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma Leishmaniasis (mucocutaneous) Lymphoma or other causes of generalised lymphadenopathy in the juvenile form Sarcoidosis Direct microscopy of sputum, mucosal scrapings or aspirated pus with potassium hydroxide preparation for multiple-budding yeasts Fungal culture on appropriate media (slow-growing) with demonstration of dimorphism Histopathology of biopsy material with special fungal stains showing the pilot's-wheel yeast Serology by immunodiffusion or complement fixation for diagnosis and follow-up Chest imaging to characterise the pulmonary infiltrates and fibrosis Screening for co-existing tuberculosis and for HIV in atypical or severe presentations Endemic to humid rural areas of Central and South America, especially Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela and Argentina, and typically affects male agricultural workers exposed to soil Caused by the thermally dimorphic fungi Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and P. lutzii, acquired by inhalation of conidia; the acute/subacute (juvenile) form and the chronic (adult) form behave very differently The chronic adult form is dominated by pulmonary disease with mucocutaneous lesions of the mouth, gums and oropharynx, often with a characteristic mulberry-like haemorrhagic stippling The acute juvenile form presents with prominent reticuloendothelial involvement: generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and marrow involvement, and is more aggressive Microscopy of pus, sputum or tissue classically shows the multiple-budding 'pilot's wheel' or 'Mickey Mouse' yeast form, which is diagnostic Serology (immunodiffusion, complement fixation) supports diagnosis and helps monitor treatment response and relapse Prolonged therapy with azole antifungals is standard for most cases, with amphotericin-based therapy reserved for severe or disseminated disease and long consolidation required to prevent relapse Progressive dyspnoea and respiratory compromise from advanced pulmonary fibrosis Laryngeal or tracheal involvement threatening the airway Disseminated juvenile-type disease with marrow failure or extensive lymphadenopathy Central nervous system or adrenal involvement Relapse or deterioration on treatment suggesting inadequate duration or immunosuppression Misdiagnosing the chronic form as tuberculosis or cancer and delaying antifungal therapy Stopping treatment when symptoms resolve rather than continuing prolonged consolidation, leading to relapse Overlooking co-existing tuberculosis, which can worsen if only one condition is treated Failing to recognise adrenal insufficiency arising from adrenal involvement Not screening for underlying immunosuppression in unusually severe disease Paracoccidioidomycosis follows inhalation of airborne conidia of Paracoccidioides species from contaminated soil in endemic zones. At body temperature the fungus converts to its pathogenic multiply-budding yeast form and establishes a primary pulmonary focus, which may remain latent for years or decades before reactivating, often when cell-mediated immunity wanes. A vigorous granulomatous response tends to contain infection in the chronic adult form, whereas an inadequate Th1 response permits lymphohaematogenous dissemination in the acute juvenile form. Chronic pulmonary involvement produces progressive fibrosis, and mucosal seeding gives rise to the destructive oral and laryngeal lesions. With prolonged antifungal therapy most patients improve, but chronic pulmonary fibrosis and mucosal scarring can leave permanent disability; the acute juvenile and disseminated forms carry higher mortality, and relapse is common if treatment is stopped early.

Paragonimiasis — Paragonimus westermani, lung fluke infection, oriental lung fluke, pulmonary distomiasis, endemic haemoptysis Pulmonary tuberculosis (closely mimicked and often co-endemic) Bronchiectasis or chronic bacterial lung infection Lung abscess or necrotising pneumonia Bronchogenic carcinoma Other causes of haemoptysis and pleural effusion Neurocysticercosis or other space-occupying lesions (for cerebral disease) Microscopy of sputum for characteristic operculated eggs (repeated samples improve yield) Stool microscopy for swallowed eggs when sputum is negative Serology (antibody detection), useful especially in ectopic disease and light infection Full blood count for eosinophilia Chest imaging (radiograph/CT) for cysts, ring shadows, infiltrates or pleural effusion Brain imaging when cerebral involvement is suspected Paragonimiasis is caused by lung flukes of the genus Paragonimus, chiefly P. westermani, endemic in East and Southeast Asia, with other species in Africa and the Americas Infection follows eating raw, undercooked or pickled freshwater crabs or crayfish, or in some regions raw meat of paratenic hosts, containing infective metacercariae After ingestion the larvae penetrate the gut and diaphragm and produce migratory subcutaneous swellings before settling in the lungs to form parasitic cysts The pulmonary syndrome mimics tuberculosis: chronic cough, chest pain and haemoptysis with rusty-brown or blood-streaked sputum, often in an otherwise well patient Ectopic (extrapulmonary) disease is important, particularly cerebral paragonimiasis, which can cause seizures, focal deficits and space-occupying lesions Diagnosis rests on finding the characteristic operculated eggs in sputum or stool, supported by serology, eosinophilia and imaging showing cysts, ring shadows or pleural effusion Praziquantel is the treatment of choice for paragonimiasis, with corticosteroid cover considered in cerebral disease to limit inflammatory reaction Neurological features (seizures, focal deficit, raised intracranial pressure) suggesting cerebral paragonimiasis Massive or persistent haemoptysis Large pleural effusion or empyema causing respiratory compromise Diagnostic confusion with tuberculosis leading to inappropriate anti-TB therapy Extensive or multiorgan ectopic disease Treating the patient as smear-negative tuberculosis and overlooking lung fluke eggs in sputum Relying on a single sputum sample, which may miss eggs Not considering cerebral paragonimiasis in an endemic patient with seizures Neglecting dietary counselling, allowing reinfection from raw crab or crayfish Omitting corticosteroid cover in cerebral disease where an inflammatory reaction to dying flukes is a concern Ingested metacercariae excyst in the small intestine, penetrate the intestinal wall into the peritoneal cavity, and migrate through the diaphragm into the pleural space and lungs, where paired adult flukes become enclosed in fibrous cysts that communicate with bronchioles. Eggs are coughed up and either expectorated or swallowed and passed in stool. Local inflammation, cyst formation and rupture into airways produce the chronic cough and haemoptysis, while pleural involvement causes effusion. Aberrant migration of larvae to the brain, subcutaneous tissue, abdomen or other sites produces ectopic disease, with cerebral involvement being the most serious. Pulmonary paragonimiasis usually responds well to anthelmintic therapy with a good outlook, but cerebral and other ectopic disease can leave lasting neurological deficits, and misdiagnosis as tuberculosis often delays effective treatment.

Paramyotonia congenita — PMC, paramyotonia congenita of von Eulenburg, SCN4A, sodium channelopathy of muscle, cold-induced paradoxical myotonia Myotonia congenita Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis Potassium-aggravated myotonias Myotonic dystrophy types 1 and 2 Andersen-Tawil syndrome Schwartz-Jampel syndrome Electromyography with myotonic discharges, including recordings before and after muscle cooling Short exercise electromyography protocol with cooling, showing the characteristic decrement pattern Serum creatine kinase and interictal potassium Targeted SCN4A genetic testing Assessment to exclude myotonic dystrophy and its systemic features Muscle biopsy only where diagnostic uncertainty persists Distinguished by paradoxical myotonia, in which stiffness worsens rather than improves with repeated activity, the opposite of the warm-up seen in myotonia congenita Symptoms are markedly precipitated or aggravated by cold exposure, classically affecting the face, eyelids, tongue and hands Cold-induced stiffness can be followed by a period of flaccid weakness that may persist for some time after rewarming Caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A skeletal-muscle sodium channel gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern It sits on a clinical continuum with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis and the potassium-aggravated myotonias, all allelic SCN4A disorders Management combines avoidance of cold and other triggers with sodium-channel-blocking antimyotonic agents when symptoms are troublesome Bedside cooling of a hand, or asking the patient to repeatedly forcefully close the eyes, can reproduce the paradoxical worsening Prolonged or severe cold-induced weakness impairing safe function Respiratory or bulbar involvement during a severe episode Susceptibility to anaesthetic complications with depolarising muscle relaxants and hypothermia Emergence of a fixed myopathy, which would prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis Confusing the paradoxical cold-worsened myotonia with the warm-up improvement of myotonia congenita Failing to test after cooling, so mild or intermittent myotonia is missed on standard examination or electromyography Not recognising the overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis when weakness dominates Overlooking anaesthetic risks from cold theatres and depolarising neuromuscular blockade Paramyotonia congenita is caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, encoding the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutant channels show impaired or slowed inactivation, and this defect is temperature sensitive so that cooling exaggerates the persistent sodium current. Incomplete inactivation produces sustained membrane depolarisation, which at moderate levels causes repetitive firing perceived as myotonia and, when depolarisation becomes severe, inactivates the remaining channels to render the fibre inexcitable and weak. Because the abnormality worsens with sustained activity and with cold, patients experience the characteristic paradoxical, cold-sensitive myotonia followed by weakness rather than the warm-up improvement of chloride channelopathies. Paramyotonia congenita is a non-progressive disorder compatible with a normal lifespan, and although cold-triggered stiffness and weakness can be disabling in cold climates or occupations, symptoms are usually manageable with trigger avoidance and antimyotonic therapy.

Paraneoplastic Syndromes: Endocrinologic/Hematologic — Ectopic hormone syndromes, Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, Tumor-associated SIADH, Ectopic ACTH syndrome, Trousseau's syndrome Primary hyperparathyroidism (vs HHM) Non-malignant causes of SIADH: CNS trauma, infection, pulmonary disease, medications including many chemotherapeutic agents Pituitary (Cushing's disease), adrenal adenoma, and iatrogenic/exogenous glucocorticoid causes of Cushing's syndrome Granulomatous disorders producing 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D Polycythemia vera and hemoglobinopathies with increased O2 affinity (vs paraneoplastic erythrocytosis) Myeloproliferative disorders causing primary granulocytosis/thrombocytosis/eosinophilia Renal, adrenal, or thyroid insufficiency as causes of hyponatremia Granulocytosis from infection or tumor necrosis mimicking paraneoplastic granulocytosis Eosinophilia with pulmonary infiltrates resembling infectious or hypersensitivity pneumonitis Serum calcium with PTH (suppressed in HHM) and PTHrP level; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in suspected lymphoma Serum sodium and osmolality with paired urine osmolality and urine sodium for SIADH Plasma ACTH, urine-free cortisol, high-dose (8 mg) dexamethasone suppression test, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation (>3:1 central:peripheral ACTH ratio suggests pituitary source) Serum glucose with insulin, IGF-II, and IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1 suggestive) for tumor hypoglycemia Serum phosphorus, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D for oncogenic osteomalacia; octreotide scan to localize tumor Hematocrit, red cell mass, and serum erythropoietin for erythrocytosis Compression ultrasonography/impedance plethysmography (venography if equivocal) for DVT; ventilation-perfusion scan, chest radiograph, ECG, and ABG for suspected pulmonary embolism Functional imaging (CT, MRI, PET, octreotide scintigraphy) to localize hormone-producing tumors, particularly when endocrine features precede cancer diagnosis Hypercalcemia of primary hyperparathyroidism Exogenous glucocorticoid (iatrogenic) Cushing's syndrome Drug-induced or volume-depletion hyponatremia Insulinoma or factitious hypoglycemia (vs IGF-II tumor hypoglycemia) Paraneoplastic syndromes are disorders accompanying benign or malignant tumors that are NOT due to direct mass effect, invasion, or metastasis; neuroendocrine tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) and carcinoids are especially common sources, and these syndromes are more common than generally appreciated (Harrison 22e p.736). Hormones may be eutopic (from normal tissue of origin) or ectopic (atypical source); ectopic expression is often quantitative rather than absolute and is characterized by defective feedback regulation (e.g., ectopic ACTH) and release of large, unprocessed precursor peptides such as POMC (Harrison 22e p.736). The three most common paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes are hypercalcemia from PTHrP overproduction, hyponatremia from excess vasopressin (SIADH), and Cushing's syndrome from ectopic ACTH (Harrison 22e p.737). Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) occurs in up to 20% of cancer patients, is most often caused by PTHrP, and favoring features over primary hyperparathyroidism are known malignancy, recent onset, and very high calcium; PTH is suppressed and an elevated PTHrP is raised in roughly 80% of hypercalcemic cancer patients (Harrison 22e p.737-738). HHM produces hypercalciuria and hypophosphatemia like hyperparathyroidism, but is typically accompanied by metabolic alkalosis rather than the hyperchloremic acidosis of hyperparathyroidism; lymphomas can cause hypercalcemia via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rather than PTHrP (Harrison 22e p.737-738). Ectopic vasopressin causes SIADH in at least half of SCLC patients; hyponatremia with low serum osmolality occurs alongside an inappropriately normal or high urine osmolality, and intake of free water (oral or IV) can rapidly worsen the hyponatremia (Harrison 22e p.738). Ectopic ACTH accounts for 10-20% of Cushing's syndrome; SCLC is the leading cause, followed by bronchial and thymic carcinoids; plasma ACTH is usually >22 pmol/L (>100 pg/mL) and urine-free cortisol is typically more than 2-4 times normal (Harrison 22e p.738-739). Ectopic ACTH Cushing's differs from pituitary disease: less weight gain/centripetal fat (brief exposure plus cachexia), but prominent fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, glucose intolerance, and hyperpigmentation from MSH within the POMC precursor (Harrison 22e p.739). Most ectopic ACTH sources fail to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone (8 mg suppresses ~80% of pituitary adenomas but fails in ~90% of ectopic cases), though bronchial and other carcinoids are notable exceptions that may show pituitary-like feedback (Harrison 22e p.739). Non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia is driven by IGF-II precursor; serum IGF-II may not be markedly elevated, but an IGF-II/IGF-I ratio greater than 10:1 is suggestive, and the responsible tumor is usually large (>10 cm) and clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.739-740). Oncogenic (tumor-induced) osteomalacia from FGF23 (phosphatonin) presents with low serum phosphorus, renal phosphate wasting, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, but NORMAL serum calcium and PTH; it is usually caused by benign mesenchymal tumors and reverses with tumor resection (Harrison 22e p.739-741). Among paraneoplastic hematologic syndromes (erythrocytosis, granulocytosis, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia), red/white/platelet elevations are usually self-limited and asymptomatic; by far the most consequential hematologic abnormality in cancer patients is hypercoagulability (Harrison 22e p.740). Migratory or recurrent thrombophlebitis can be the initial manifestation of cancer; peripheral venous thrombosis coexisting with visceral carcinoma, especially pancreatic cancer, is termed Trousseau's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.741). Markedly elevated calcium (>3.5 mmol/L [>14 mg/dL]) with fatigue, altered mentation, polyuria, dehydration, or arrhythmias (short ST/QT, bundle branch block, bradyarrhythmia) Severe hyponatremia (Na <115 meq/L) or any hyponatremia with confusion, depressed mental status, or seizures Profound hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis and hypertension in ectopic ACTH; opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, mycoses) are a frequent cause of death Increased venous thromboembolism risk in ectopic ACTH and in cancer generally; migratory/recurrent thrombophlebitis or clot in an unusual site New atypical clinical or metabolic findings in a known cancer patient should prompt consideration of a paraneoplastic syndrome Markedly elevated eosinophils (>5000/uL) causing dyspnea, wheezing, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates Attributing atypical metabolic or neurologic findings to the malignancy or its treatment and overlooking a paraneoplastic syndrome Confusing HHM with primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH should be suppressed and acid-base pattern differs (alkalosis in HHM vs hyperchloremic acidosis in hyperparathyroidism) Rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, which can precipitate central pontine myelinolysis; correction should be gradual (about 0.5-1 meq/L per hour) Excluding ectopic ACTH on the basis of high-dose dexamethasone suppression alone, since bronchial/thymic carcinoids can suppress like pituitary adenomas; conversely a suppressed ACTH indicates an ACTH-independent cause Relying on serum IGF-II levels, which may be normal in tumor hypoglycemia because assays may miss IGF-II precursors (use the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio) Over-relying on D-dimer in cancer patients, where it is less predictive of DVT and rises with age without thrombosis Pursuing extensive cancer work-up after a first unprovoked thrombophlebitis or PE in a patient without cancer; targeted evaluation is reserved for refractory, unusual-site, or migratory/recurrent clots Neoplastic cells, particularly those of neuroendocrine origin (SCLC, carcinoids), secrete peptide hormones, cytokines, and growth factors or induce antibody production, altering endocrine, hematologic, and other systems independently of tumor bulk. Most ectopic hormone production reflects cellular dedifferentiation with derepression of developmental gene programs (epigenetic changes, altered microRNA expression); genetic rearrangements bringing a hormone gene under aberrant regulatory control are a rare alternative mechanism. HHM arises chiefly from tumor PTHrP, which binds the PTH receptor to mimic hyperparathyroidism (driven by PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli, TGF-beta, Ras activation, p53 loss); lymphomas may instead convert 25-OH vitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. SIADH results from ectopic vasopressin (often with co-expressed oxytocin) causing water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Ectopic ACTH comes from unregulated POMC expression, with release of large biologically inactive fragments plus small amounts of active ACTH; very high cortisol overwhelms renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type II, allowing cortisol to act at mineralocorticoid receptors and produce severe hypokalemia. IGF-II precursor (from loss of 11p15 imprinting) causes hypoglycemia by acting on insulin/IGF-I receptors and suppressing GH and insulin. FGF23 forms a ternary complex with klotho and renal FGF receptors to reduce phosphate reabsorption and inhibit 1-alpha-hydroxylation. Hematologic syndromes are mediated by ectopic erythropoietin (erythrocytosis); G-CSF, GM-CSF, IL-6 (granulocytosis); IL-6/thrombopoietin (thrombocytosis); IL-5 (eosinophilia); and poorly defined procoagulants/cytokines (hypercoagulability). Endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes can cause substantial morbidity and may be the presenting clue to an occult malignancy; treatment of the underlying tumor is the mainstay but rarely alters overall survival or cancer progression. Hematologic cell-count syndromes are generally self-limited and asymptomatic, but thrombocytosis can mark advanced-stage disease and poorer prognosis. Hypercoagulability is the most consequential hematologic complication, and oncogenic osteomalacia and several endocrinopathies can reverse with successful tumor resection; checkpoint-inhibitor-associated endocrinopathies are generally irreversible and require lifelong hormone replacement. No single formal severity scale; severity is gauged by the magnitude and acuity of the biochemical derangement (e.g., calcium level and rate of rise, sodium level [Na <115 meq/L denotes severe hyponatremia], eosinophil count >5000/uL). For venous thromboembolism risk during chemotherapy, the Khorana risk score (Harrison Table 98-3) stratifies patients using cancer type, therapy, blood counts, and body mass index.

Paraquat poisoning — paraquat toxicity, herbicide poisoning, gramoxone poisoning Corrosive ingestion from other agents Other lethal pesticide ingestions (organophosphate, aluminium phosphide) Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Acute interstitial pneumonitis Caustic oesophageal injury Plasma or urine paraquat level and the urine dithionite qualitative test Serial renal and liver function tests Arterial blood gas and serial chest imaging to track evolving lung injury Full blood count and electrolytes Prognostic assessment using plasma concentration versus time since ingestion A highly lethal herbicide with no effective antidote; even small deliberate ingestions of concentrated solution are frequently fatal It concentrates in and selectively destroys the lungs, causing progressive pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage, and then relentless fibrosis over days to weeks Early features include painful corrosive burns to the mouth, throat, and oesophagus, vomiting, and abdominal pain Oxygen supplementation should generally be avoided or minimised, as high oxygen tension accelerates free-radical lung injury; supplemental oxygen is reserved for severe, refractory hypoxaemia Immediate gastrointestinal decontamination with an adsorbent such as activated charcoal or Fuller's earth is a priority if the patient presents very early Enhanced elimination (haemoperfusion or haemodialysis) and immunosuppression with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide have been tried, but none reliably alters the poor outcome Acute kidney injury and hepatic injury commonly precede the delayed, usually fatal, pulmonary fibrosis Plasma paraquat concentration plotted against time since ingestion helps estimate prognosis and guide the intensity of intervention Ingestion of concentrated solution or any large deliberate ingestion Early acute kidney injury, which predicts high toxin burden and poor outcome Progressive hypoxaemia and radiographic lung changes Extensive oropharyngeal and oesophageal corrosive burns Rising plasma paraquat level for the time since ingestion indicating a lethal exposure Giving liberal supplemental oxygen, which accelerates oxidative lung injury Delaying adsorbent decontamination in an early presentation Offering false reassurance during the deceptively stable early period before lung failure Underestimating lethality and under-treating the psychosocial and palliative needs of the patient Paraquat undergoes cyclical reduction and oxidation (redox cycling), generating large amounts of superoxide and other reactive oxygen species that deplete NADPH and cause lipid peroxidation and cell death. It is actively taken up and concentrated by alveolar epithelial (type I and II) cells, making the lung the primary target: an early destructive phase of alveolitis and haemorrhagic oedema is followed by an obliterative pulmonary fibrosis. The kidneys and liver, which also accumulate the compound, sustain acute injury, and high oxygen tensions worsen the oxidative damage. Prognosis is generally poor and dose-dependent; ingestion of concentrated formulation is usually fatal, with death from multi-organ failure early or from progressive pulmonary fibrosis over subsequent days to weeks, and no treatment has been shown to reliably improve survival.

Parasomnia — parasomnias, NREM parasomnia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, RBD, sleepwalking, night terrors Nocturnal (frontal-lobe) epilepsy Obstructive sleep apnoea with confusional arousals Nocturnal panic attacks Periodic limb movement disorder Dissociative or psychogenic nocturnal episodes Nocturnal delirium in the elderly Detailed history from patient and bed partner, including timing within the night and degree of recall Video polysomnography with expanded EEG montage to capture events and exclude seizures Neurological assessment and, where indicated, dopaminergic imaging when REM sleep behaviour disorder is suspected Screening for coexisting sleep apnoea as a trigger for arousals Review of medications and substances that can provoke parasomnias Parasomnias are undesirable physical or experiential events that intrude on sleep and are broadly divided by the sleep stage from which they arise into non-REM (NREM) and REM types NREM disorders of arousal (confusional arousals, sleepwalking, night terrors) typically occur in the first third of the night during deep slow-wave sleep, with the person appearing awake but confused and having little or no recall REM sleep behaviour disorder involves loss of the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep, so patients physically act out vivid, often violent dreams and can injure themselves or a bed partner REM sleep behaviour disorder is strongly associated with, and may precede by years, neurodegenerative alpha-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies NREM parasomnias are common and usually benign in children, tending to resolve with age, whereas new-onset events in adults warrant more careful evaluation Triggers that deepen or fragment sleep, including sleep deprivation, alcohol, fever, stress, and certain medications, can precipitate NREM events Management prioritises sleep hygiene, safety-proofing the bedroom, and removal of precipitants; pharmacological treatment is reserved for frequent, dangerous, or distressing episodes Nocturnal frontal-lobe seizures can mimic parasomnias and should be considered when events are stereotyped, very frequent, or occur repeatedly within a single night Dream enactment with violent behaviour suggesting REM sleep behaviour disorder and possible underlying neurodegeneration New-onset complex nocturnal behaviour in an adult without childhood history Stereotyped, repetitive episodes clustering within one night raising suspicion of nocturnal seizures Episodes causing injury to the patient or bed partner Mislabelling nocturnal seizures as benign parasomnia and delaying appropriate neurological workup Failing to counsel patients with REM sleep behaviour disorder about future neurodegenerative risk and bedroom safety Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea as the arousal trigger driving NREM events Attempting to forcibly wake a sleepwalker, which may increase agitation and injury risk Parasomnias reflect incomplete or dysregulated transitions between wakefulness and sleep states rather than a single disease. In NREM disorders of arousal, partial awakening from slow-wave sleep leaves motor and autonomic systems active while consciousness and memory circuits remain asleep, producing complex behaviours without awareness; a genetic predisposition and any factor that increases slow-wave sleep or arousal frequency raises the risk. REM sleep behaviour disorder results from failure of the brainstem circuits that normally impose skeletal muscle atonia during REM sleep, allowing dream enactment; the underlying neuronal dysfunction is closely linked to synucleinopathy neurodegeneration. Other parasomnias, such as sleep-related eating or nightmare disorder, arise from analogous state-boundary instability. Most childhood NREM parasomnias are benign and remit spontaneously; adult NREM events can often be controlled by addressing precipitants, while REM sleep behaviour disorder tends to persist and carries an appreciable long-term risk of evolving neurodegenerative disease.

Parathyroid adenoma — primary hyperparathyroidism, PHPT, solitary parathyroid adenoma, hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenoma Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide or bony metastases) Parathyroid hyperplasia (four-gland disease) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease Vitamin D intoxication or granulomatous disease (e.g. sarcoidosis) Parathyroid carcinoma Serum calcium (corrected or ionised), phosphate, and intact PTH 24-hour urinary calcium to help exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Vitamin D level and renal function assessment Neck ultrasound and technetium-99m sestamibi scintigraphy for localisation 4D-CT or selective venous sampling in reoperative or non-localising cases Bone density (DXA) scan and renal imaging for end-organ effects The commonest cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a single hyperfunctioning adenoma, with hyperplasia and, rarely, carcinoma accounting for the remainder Many patients are asymptomatic and detected on incidental hypercalcaemia; classical symptoms are summarised as bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans The biochemical hallmark is hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately non-suppressed or elevated parathyroid hormone level Chronic disease can cause nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis or osteitis fibrosa cystica, peptic ulceration, and pancreatitis Localisation before surgery combines neck ultrasound with sestamibi scintigraphy, and 4D-CT is useful when these are discordant or negative Minimally invasive (focused) parathyroidectomy is favoured when a single adenoma is confidently localised, often guided by intraoperative parathyroid hormone measurement Consider familial and syndromic disease (MEN 1, MEN 2A, familial hyperparathyroidism) in young patients or those with multigland involvement Severe hypercalcaemia with confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia, or hypercalcaemic crisis requiring urgent treatment Very high calcium with a palpable neck mass or markedly elevated PTH raising suspicion of parathyroid carcinoma Renal impairment or obstructing calculi from longstanding disease Pathological fractures from advanced skeletal involvement Attributing hypercalcaemia to an adenoma without excluding familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, in whom surgery is inappropriate Relying on a single localising study and missing an ectopic (mediastinal or intrathyroidal) gland Overlooking four-gland hyperplasia and performing an inadequate focused exploration Failing to recognise MEN syndromes, leading to incomplete treatment and missed associated tumours Not monitoring for postoperative hypocalcaemia, including hungry bone syndrome after severe disease A parathyroid adenoma is a benign clonal proliferation of chief cells that secretes parathyroid hormone autonomously, independent of the normal negative feedback from serum calcium. Excess PTH increases osteoclastic bone resorption, enhances renal tubular calcium reabsorption while promoting phosphate excretion, and stimulates renal activation of vitamin D, which raises intestinal calcium absorption. The net result is hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Sustained bone resorption reduces bone density, and the filtered calcium load promotes renal stone formation and, over time, renal impairment. Surgical removal of a solitary adenoma is curative in the great majority, with normalisation of calcium and PTH and improvement in bone density and stone risk over time. Outcomes are excellent when a single gland is correctly identified; multigland disease or missed ectopic glands increases the risk of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism.

Parathyroid & Calcium Disorders — hyperparathyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, hypocalcemia Primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH-dependent hypercalcemia) - parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma Hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTH-suppressed) - PTHrP overproduction or lytic skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) - inactivating CASR/GNA11/AP2S1 mutations Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (long-standing renal insufficiency) Granulomatous disease- or lymphoma-associated hypercalcemia (extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D) Vitamin D intoxication Hypercalcemia of immobilization, thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, milk-alkali syndrome Multiple myeloma Postsurgical (post-thyroidectomy / post-parathyroidectomy) hypoparathyroidism Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism (including APS-1) Vitamin D deficiency / chronic renal insufficiency causing secondary hyperparathyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PTH resistance) Hypomagnesemia (or severe hypermagnesemia) impairing PTH Autosomal dominant hypocalcemia (activating CaSR/GNA11 mutations) Tuberculosis - granulomatous extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production causing hypercalcemia Leprosy and fungal infections - granulomatous causes of 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia COVID-19 - reported transient hypoparathyroidism (and even spontaneous resolution of pHPT) via unknown mechanisms Total serum calcium with serum albumin to calculate corrected calcium (add 0.8 mg/dL per 1.0 g/dL albumin below 4.0; subtract when albumin is high) Intact PTH by two-site assay - the key second test that separates PTH-dependent from PTH-independent disorders Serum phosphorus (low/low-normal in pHPT; elevated in some hypocalcemic states) Serum magnesium (hypo- or severe hypermagnesemia impairs PTH) Serum creatinine / renal function Serum 25(OH)D - useful in both hyper- and hypocalcemia to assess vitamin D stores Serum 1,25(OH)2D - useful in hypercalcemia (increased/inappropriately normal in granulomatous disease or lymphoma) and suspected vitamin D resistance PTHrP level when hypercalcemia of malignancy is suspected with suppressed PTH Serum free light chains / SPEP-UPEP with immunofixation to exclude multiple myeloma Calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01 suggests FHH); 24-hour urinary fractional calcium excretion (>0.02 supports pHPT) Genetic sequencing of CASR, GNA11, AP2S1 for definitive FHH diagnosis when urine studies are inconclusive; genetic testing for syndromic/hereditary pHPT (MEN, CDC73) ECG (hypercalcemia: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc; hypocalcemia: QTc prolongation) Pseudohypercalcemia (e.g., calcium-binding IgM in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia) and pseudohypocalcemia (low albumin from malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis; gadoversetamide MRI contrast) - artifactual values requiring albumin correction before workup Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease - 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcemia Lymphoma (B cell, cutaneous T cell/Sezary) - extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D Thyrotoxicosis, Paget's disease, immobilization - increased bone resorption mimicking parathyroid hypercalcemia Thiazides, lithium, vitamin A, foscarnet, teriparatide, aromatase inhibitors - drug-induced hypercalcemia Acute pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, burns - hypocalcemia from tissue injury / hyperphosphatemia Respiratory or metabolic alkalosis - hypocalcemia from increased calcium binding to albumin Primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT) and malignancy are the two most common causes of hypercalcemia; the diagnostic split hinges on the PTH level (Harrison 22e p.3271). pHPT is almost always a benign neoplastic disorder of the parathyroids (adenoma or hyperplasia) producing PTH that is not appropriately suppressed by the elevated calcium; parathyroid carcinoma is a rare cause (Harrison 22e p.3271). In hypercalcemia, an elevated or 'inappropriately normal' PTH with elevated calcium and low/low-normal phosphorus is almost always pHPT; because of PTH's phosphaturic action, pHPT hypercalcemia is often accompanied by low/frankly low serum phosphate (Harrison 22e p.3271). A suppressed PTH in the face of hypercalcemia means the process is independent of the parathyroid glands and is most often malignancy; many solid tumors secrete PTHrP, which mimics PTH at its receptor on bone and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hypercalcemia from lymphoma or granulomatous disease (e.g., sarcoidosis, tuberculosis) is driven by extrarenal macrophage CYP27B1 conversion of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D; in such cases 1,25(OH)2D is increased or inappropriately normal (Harrison 22e p.3271). Classic chronic hypercalcemia (months to years, fluctuating between high-normal and just above normal) is most often pHPT or FHH, occasionally multiple myeloma; malignancy-associated hypercalcemia usually has a more acute course (Harrison 22e p.3271). Mild hypercalcemia (10.5-11.9 mg/dL) is largely asymptomatic; symptoms ('stones, bones, groans') include nephrolithiasis, reduced bone density / bone pain or pathologic fractures with long-standing hyperparathyroidism, constipation/nausea/vomiting/anorexia/peptic ulcer/pancreatitis, plus fatigue, proximal weakness, hyporeflexia, and neuropsychiatric changes (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hypocalcemia is differentiated by whether PTH is low (hypoparathyroidism) or high (secondary hyperparathyroidism); a low or 'inappropriately low' PTH with hypocalcemia establishes hypoparathyroidism, whereas an elevated PTH points to the vitamin D axis or primary small-bowel calcium malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.3271). In adults, hypoparathyroidism most commonly results from inadvertent damage to all four parathyroid glands during thyroid or parathyroid surgery; autoimmune endocrinopathy accounts for about a quarter of cases (Harrison 22e p.3271). Neuromuscular irritability of hypocalcemia is detected by Chvostek's sign (perioral twitch on tapping the facial nerve) and the more specific Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic for 3 min); paresthesias of fingers, toes, and circumoral region are typical (Harrison 22e p.3271). Because PTH is the main minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism can produce profound, life-threatening hypocalcemia, whereas vitamin D deficiency causes less severe hypocalcemia since the parathyroids mount a compensatory PTH rise (at the expense of bone) (Harrison 22e p.3271). Impaired PTH secretion may be secondary to magnesium deficiency (via intracellular effects); hypomagnesemic hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is repleted (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy is a recognized cause of post-operative hypocalcemia with high PTH (Harrison 22e p.3271). Moderate-to-severe hypercalcemia (>=12-14 mg/dL) with progressive lethargy, stupor, or coma Hypercalcemia with acute renal failure and volume depletion from polyuria Hypercalcemic ECG changes: bradycardia, AV block, QRS widening, short QTc Severe hypocalcemia causing seizures, carpopedal spasm, bronchospasm, or laryngospasm Hypocalcemic QTc prolongation with risk of ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Torsade) and sudden death Tetany (positive Trousseau's sign / carpal spasm) signaling impending neuromuscular crisis New severe hypocalcemia after thyroid or parathyroid neck surgery (damage to all four glands), especially in patients with prior malabsorption Syndromic pHPT with a jaw tumor (CDC73 mutation) carrying ~30% lifetime risk of parathyroid carcinoma Failing to correct calcium for albumin before launching a workup - low albumin can mask true hypercalcemia and falsely suggest hypocalcemia (Harrison 22e p.3271). Mistaking FHH for pHPT: FHH can present with mildly elevated PTH and hypercalcemia, but parathyroid surgery is ineffective; a calcium/creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 and family history of mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia or repeated failed neck surgeries should prompt CASR/GNA11/AP2S1 testing (Harrison 22e p.3271). Overlooking lithium therapy, which raises the CaSR set point and can cause hyperparathyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3271). Not repleting magnesium in hypocalcemia: hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and the hypocalcemia will not correct until magnesium is restored (Harrison 22e p.3271). Chvostek's sign is nonspecific - present in ~10% of normal individuals; Trousseau's sign is the more definitive marker of neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271). Attributing hypercalcemia of immobilization solely to bed rest - an unrecognized resorptive process (pHPT, Paget's, myeloma) may be the real driver, especially in older patients (Harrison 22e p.3271). When tetany accompanies alkalosis, a second cause of impaired calcium homeostasis is usually present (Harrison 22e p.3271). Ectopic PTH secretion, unlike pHPT, does not fluctuate with correction of calcium because it is not under CaSR control (Harrison 22e p.3271). Extracellular calcium is held in a narrow range (~8.5-10.5 mg/dL) by feedback among the parathyroids, kidney, bone, and intestine. A fall in ECF calcium is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on parathyroid chief cells, triggering PTH release; PTH increases bone calcium resorption, distal-tubule reabsorption of filtered calcium, and renal proximal-tubule 1,25(OH)2D production, and 1,25(OH)2D in turn raises intestinal calcium absorption. Hypercalcemia arises from derangements of this loop: PTH-dependent overproduction (pHPT due to adenoma/hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma; tertiary hyperparathyroidism; ectopic PTH; FHH and CaSR-altering states such as lithium), or PTH-independent mechanisms (PTHrP-secreting tumors, lytic skeletal metastases, extrarenal 1,25(OH)2D production in granulomatous disease/lymphoma, vitamin D intoxication, increased bone resorption from thyrotoxicosis/Paget's/immobilization, and calcium overload e.g. milk-alkali). Hypocalcemia results from low PTH (hypoparathyroidism: surgical, autoimmune, infiltrative, genetic, CaSR-activating, or magnesium-related) or high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, intestinal malabsorption, or PTH resistance/pseudohypoparathyroidism). Low calcium increases neuromuscular irritability (Harrison 22e p.3271). Mild, asymptomatic hypercalcemia (commonly pHPT detected incidentally in settings with routine calcium screening) carries a benign short-term course, whereas advanced pHPT can cause severe skeletal disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica). Hypoparathyroidism, because PTH is the chief minute-by-minute defense against hypocalcemia, can be profound, debilitating, and life-threatening, while vitamin D-deficiency hypocalcemia is typically milder owing to compensatory PTH secretion (at the expense of bone). Severe hypercalcemia (coma, renal failure, arrhythmia) and severe hypocalcemia (seizures, laryngospasm, Torsade) are medical emergencies (Harrison 22e p.3271). Hypercalcemia severity (Harrison 22e p.3271): mild 10.5-11.9 mg/dL (largely asymptomatic); moderate >=12-14 mg/dL; severe >=14 mg/dL (progressive lethargy, stupor, coma, prominent GI symptoms, acute renal failure). Hypocalcemia severity ranges from asymptomatic (mild/chronic) to moderate-severe with paresthesias, positive Chvostek's/Trousseau's signs, through severe with seizures, carpopedal spasm, broncho-/laryngospasm, and QTc prolongation with arrhythmia risk.

new-onset PD has been reported following SARS-CoV-2 infection, which can also worsen existing PD features Dopamine-system imaging with PET or SPECT (reduced, asymmetric striatal/posterior-putamen uptake); not routinely required Metabolic basal ganglia/thalamus imaging (18F-deoxyglucose) - may help distinguish atypical parkinsonism (decreased GPi with increased thalamic activity, the reverse of PD) MRI - to evaluate for vascular/structural causes and atypical features (e.g., midbrain 'hummingbird sign' in PSP, putaminal rim change or pontine 'hot cross bun' sign in MSA); transcranial sonography or special MRI protocols may detect increased SNc iron Alpha-synuclein seeding amplification assay (SAA) on CSF or skin - high sensitivity and specificity, can distinguish PD from other parkinsonisms (currently mainly research use) Genetic testing - selective use for strong family history, early onset (<40 years), or particular ethnic backgrounds (GBA1, LRRK2, SNCA, etc.); monogenic forms account for ~5% of cases (~15% including GBA1 variants) Serum/urinary copper studies to exclude Wilson's disease, which is treatable with copper chelators Drug-induced parkinsonism - most commonly dopamine-blocking neuroleptics, and also metoclopramide (a neuroleptic agent used for GI problems), tetrabenazine, calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), amiodarone, and lithium Vascular parkinsonism (stroke affecting the SNc may closely resemble PD) Toxin-induced parkinsonism (carbon monoxide or manganese damaging the globus pallidus resemble atypical parkinsonism with poor levodopa response) Tumor and normal-pressure hydrocephalus Atypical parkinsonism (MSA, PSP, CBS) Essential tremor Dopa-responsive dystonia PD is the second most common age-related neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer's; mean age of onset ~60 years, lifetime risk ~3% in men and ~2% in women, though cases can occur in the twenties or younger, particularly with a pathogenic gene mutation (p.3493). Cardinal motor features are bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and gait dysfunction with postural instability; additional motor features include freezing of gait, micrographia, masked facies (hypomimia), reduced eye blinking, drooling, soft voice (hypophonia), and dysphagia (p.3493-3494). Parkinsonism (bradykinesia with rigidity and/or tremor) combined with rest tremor, asymmetry of motor impairment, and a good levodopa response is much more likely to predict the correct pathologic diagnosis; with these U.K. Brain Bank Criteria, PD can be confirmed pathologically in >90% of patients (p.3495). Levodopa is the gold standard symptomatic therapy; almost all PD patients improve, and failure to respond to an adequate trial of levodopa should cause the diagnosis to be questioned (p.3501). Dopamine-system imaging (PET/SPECT) typically shows reduced, asymmetric striatal uptake, most pronounced in the posterior putamen with relative sparing of the caudate; it is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain but is not routinely required (p.3495-3496). Among forms of parkinsonism, PD is the most common (~75% of cases) (p.3495). Early speech and gait impairment with early falls, lack of rest tremor, and lack of motor asymmetry - suggests atypical parkinsonism Poor or no response to an adequate trial of levodopa - suggests atypical or secondary parkinsonism Exposure to neuroleptics - suggests drug-induced parkinsonism Onset before age 40 years - consider a genetic form of PD, Wilson's disease, or dopa-responsive dystonia Liver disease - consider Wilson's disease or non-Wilsonian hepatolenticular degeneration Hallucinations and dementia preceding or as the first/early feature - suggests dementia with Lewy bodies Diplopia, impaired vertical gaze, slow saccades with impaired downgaze - suggests PSP Prominent orthostatic hypotension or prominent cerebellar signs - suggests MSA Diagnosing PD on two of three cardinal features alone carries a ~24% postmortem error rate; rest tremor, motor asymmetry, and a good levodopa response markedly improve diagnostic accuracy (p.3495). Drug-induced parkinsonism is the most common secondary parkinsonism and is easily missed - remember that metoclopramide, used for GI symptoms, is a neuroleptic, and that calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), tetrabenazine, amiodarone, and lithium can also be responsible (p.3497). Wilson's disease must be actively excluded because progression can be prevented with copper chelators (p.3497). Dopamine-system imaging cannot separate PD from atypical parkinsonism, since striatal dopamine depletion occurs in both (p.3496). Some genetic forms of PD (e.g., certain LRRK2 cases) may occur without Lewy bodies, and MPTP toxicity causes parkinsonism typically without Lewy bodies (p.3496, p.3498). Pathologic hallmarks are degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), reduced striatal dopamine, and intraneuronal alpha-synuclein-staining inclusions in cell bodies and axons (Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites; collectively Lewy pathology). Lewy pathology can also affect cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, serotonergic raphe neurons, and the olfactory system, cerebral hemispheres, spinal cord, and peripheral autonomic nervous system, accounting for nonmotor features. Pathology may begin in the peripheral autonomic nervous system, GI tract, olfactory system, or dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and spread sequentially (Braak staging), giving rise to 'body-first' versus 'brain-first' concepts. In the basal-ganglia network, dopamine denervation leads to increased firing of the subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus interna (GPi), excessive inhibition of the thalamus, reduced cortical motor activation, and the emergence of parkinsonian features. Pathogenesis involves an interacting network of oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation, excitotoxicity, and inflammation; a 'double hit' of genetic susceptibility plus an environmental insult has been proposed (p.3493-3494, p.3498-3500). PD is progressive. Levodopa prolongs independence and employability, improves quality of life, and increases life span, but chronic treatment with ongoing disease progression is associated in most patients with motor complications - response fluctuations ('on'/'off', wearing-off, on-off phenomenon) and dyskinesias. As the disease advances, nondopaminergic features that respond poorly to levodopa emerge - falling, freezing, autonomic dysfunction, sleep disorders, and dementia - and these (especially falls and dementia) are the primary source of disability and the main reason for hospitalization and nursing home placement in advanced PD. Atypical parkinsonisms generally follow a more aggressive course than classic PD (p.3496-3497, p.3501). Harrison does not present a single formal severity grading; clinical diagnostic confidence is staged by the MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria into 'clinically established PD' and 'clinically probable PD', which combine core motor parkinsonism with supportive criteria, absolute exclusion criteria, and red flags. Disease evolution is commonly framed by the emergence of levodopa-related motor complications and levodopa-unresponsive nondopaminergic features in advanced PD (p.3495-3496, p.3501).

PNKD (MR-1) gene mutations Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia is provoked by sustained exertion and can be associated with GLUT1 deficiency, which has important dietary treatment implications Consciousness is preserved during attacks, which helps distinguish these disorders from epileptic seizures Kinesigenic forms are often strikingly responsive to low-dose anticonvulsant therapy, whereas
