coronal sulcus, or inner prepuce Key risk factors include phimosis, chronic inflammation, poor hygiene, smoking, and persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection, while childhood circumcision appears protective It typically presents as a persistent penile ulcer, nodule, or warty growth that fails to heal, sometimes with foul discharge, and is frequently delayed by embarrassment or misdiagnosis as infection Regional inguinal lymph nodes are the principal route of spread, so careful assessment and management of the groin nodes is central to staging and prognosis Any suspicious non-healing penile lesion requires biopsy, since treatment and prognosis depend on histological grade and depth of invasion Early and superficial tumours can be treated with organ-preserving approaches such as topical therapy, laser, local excision, or glansectomy, preserving function where oncologically safe Advanced primary tumours may require partial or total penectomy, and management of inguinal nodes ranges from surveillance to lymphadenectomy depending on risk Platinum-based chemotherapy is used for bulky nodal or metastatic disease, sometimes combined with surgery or radiotherapy in a multimodal approach A non-healing penile ulcer or nodule persisting despite treatment for presumed infection Palpable or enlarging inguinal lymph nodes Bleeding, foul discharge, or destruction of penile tissue Fixed or ulcerated groin nodes suggesting advanced regional disease Treating a persistent penile lesion repeatedly as infection without biopsy Underestimating the importance of early inguinal node evaluation and management Delaying referral due to patient embarrassment, allowing progression Choosing organ-preserving therapy for lesions that are too advanced for safe conservation Penile squamous cell carcinoma develops from the epithelium of the glans and prepuce, arising either through human papillomavirus-driven pathways or through chronic inflammatory conditions such as lichen sclerosus and long-standing phimosis. Precursor penile intraepithelial neoplasia progresses to invasive carcinoma that infiltrates the corpora and surrounding tissues. The tumour spreads in a predictable stepwise fashion first to superficial and deep inguinal nodes and then to pelvic nodes, with distant metastasis occurring late. Prognosis correlates strongly with inguinal nodal status; localised node-negative disease has high cure rates with appropriate treatment, whereas extensive nodal involvement or distant metastasis markedly reduces survival.

Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed — Upper GI endoscopy CBC, crossmatch Stop NSAIDs; start PPI infusion Haemodynamic instability → resuscitate, urgent endoscopy Functional (non-ulcer/essential) dyspepsia - the commonest cause of upper abdominal discomfort, subdivided into postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome; up to ~80% of patients evaluated for dyspepsia have a negative work-up (p.2523). Proximal gastrointestinal tumours (p.2523). Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (p.2523). Pancreaticobiliary disease - biliary colic, chronic pancreatitis (p.2523). Endoscopy is the most sensitive and specific test, allowing direct visualisation, biopsy to exclude malignancy (GU) and to test for H. pylori, and identification of a bleeding source (p.2523). Barium studies of the upper GI tract can document an ulcer but are now rarely used as a first test (p.2523). Biopsy urease tests (e.g. CLOtest, PyloriTek, Hpfast, Pronto Dry) with sensitivity/specificity >90-95% for H. pylori (p.2523). Non-invasive H. pylori tests - serology, 13C-urea breath test, and monoclonal stool antigen test; the urea breath test or monoclonal stool antigen test is preferred to document eradication, performed off antisecretory drugs for at least 7 days (serology is not useful for confirming eradication) (pp.2523, 2531). Fasting serum gastrin and gastric acid analysis, or secretin stimulation testing, in complicated or refractory ulcers to exclude Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (pp.2523, 2531-2532). Screening for surreptitious aspirin/NSAID use (blood or urine) in refractory H. pylori-negative PUD (p.2523). Multiple biopsies of any gastric ulcer at the index endoscopy, with repeat endoscopy at 8-12 weeks to document healing and re-biopsy if the ulcer persists (pp.2531-2532). Functional/non-ulcer dyspepsia closely mimics ulcer symptoms without an actual ulcer (p.2523). Drug- or toxin-induced ulceration not from NSAIDs/H. pylori - bisphosphonates, immune checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, clopidogrel, crack cocaine, glucocorticoids combined with NSAIDs, mycophenolate mofetil, potassium chloride (p.2523). Infiltrative/inflammatory mimics - Crohn's disease, sarcoidosis, eosinophilic infiltration, amyloidosis, lymphoma (pp.2523, 2532). Ischaemia and radiation-induced mucosal injury (p.2523). Idiopathic acid-hypersecretory states distinct from Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (p.2523). Around two-thirds of patients with peptic ulcer disease have no abdominal pain, and up to ~87% of those with NSAID-related mucosal injury first present with a complication (bleeding, perforation, or obstruction) without any preceding symptoms (p.2522). Classic duodenal ulcer pain comes on roughly 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating and is typically eased by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 a.m. is the most discriminating symptom and is reported by about two-thirds of duodenal ulcer patients (p.2522). Gastric ulcer pain can instead be provoked by eating, and nausea and weight loss are commoner with gastric than duodenal ulcers (p.2522). Elderly and immunosuppressed patients are less likely to have typical pain and may present directly with bleeding or perforation (pp.2522-2523). H. pylori and NSAIDs are the dominant risk factors (US odds ratios ~3.7 and ~3.3); NSAIDs are now described as the most common cause of PUD, with only ~one-quarter of duodenal and ~one-sixth of gastric ulcers now attributable to H. pylori (pp.2518, 2520). More than half of patients with ulcer-related haemorrhage bleed without any preceding warning signs or symptoms (p.2522). Endoscopy detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients investigated for dyspepsia, reflecting how poorly symptoms predict an actual ulcer (p.2522). Alarm features warranting prompt endoscopy rather than empirical test-and-treat - nausea, vomiting, weight loss, evidence of GI bleeding, or age >=60 years with new dyspepsia (pp.2523, 2531). Constant pain no longer relieved by food/antacids and radiating to the back suggests a penetrating ulcer (e.g. into the pancreas) (p.2522). Sudden severe generalised abdominal pain with a board-like, rigid abdomen (the triad of acute pain, tachycardia, and rigidity) suggests perforation (pp.2522-2523). Pain worsening with meals plus vomiting of undigested food, early satiety, weight loss, or a succussion splash suggests gastric outlet obstruction (pp.2522-2523). Tarry stools or coffee-ground emesis indicate bleeding; tachycardia and orthostasis suggest hypovolaemia from blood loss or vomiting (p.2522). Every gastric ulcer must be biopsied (multiple samples) at discovery because a GU may be malignant, and healing on therapy does not exclude cancer - about 70% of GUs ultimately found malignant show significant (usually incomplete) healing; repeat endoscopy with biopsy at 8-12 weeks is needed if the ulcer persists (pp.2519, 2531-2532). Abdominal pain has poor predictive value for an ulcer, and a normal exam or absent pain does not exclude PUD - many patients, especially the elderly or those on NSAIDs, present first with a complication (pp.2522-2523). Right-sided epigastric tenderness in about 20% of patients can mislead the examiner; epigastric tenderness overall has low predictive value (p.2522). Widespread PPI use can mask and delay the diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and increase false-positive gastrin results (p.2534). Consider gastrinoma/ZES when ulcers occur in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), are multiple, are refractory, recur after acid-reducing surgery, present with frank complications, or arise without H. pylori or NSAID use (p.2535). Peptic ulcers are mucosal breaks >5 mm extending into the submucosa, occurring in the stomach (gastric ulcer, GU) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer, DU); >95% of DUs lie in the first part of the duodenum, within about 3 cm of the pylorus. The disease reflects an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin) and mucosal defence. H. pylori and NSAIDs cause the majority of ulcers but act differently: H. pylori-associated benign GUs show antral gastritis, whereas NSAID-related GUs typically lack chronic active gastritis and instead show a chemical gastropathy (foveolar hyperplasia, lamina propria oedema). Duodenal ulcer patients tend to have increased basal and nocturnal acid secretion (with substantial overlap with controls) and reduced duodenal bicarbonate, both potentially influenced by H. pylori; gastric acid output in GU patients is usually normal or reduced, implying impaired mucosal defence. H. pylori is a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod living in the gastric mucous layer; virulence factors such as the cag pathogenicity island (delivering CagA), VacA, and urease determine the clinical outcome among colonisation, PUD, MALT lymphoma, and gastric adenocarcinoma (pp.2518-2520). More than 90% of both gastric and duodenal ulcers heal with conventional therapy; a GU not healed by 12 weeks or a DU not healed by 8 weeks is considered refractory. Eradicating H. pylori has cut duodenal ulcer recurrence by >80%. GI bleeding complicates roughly 15% of PUD with a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% (most deaths from non-bleeding causes such as multiorgan failure, pulmonary complications, and malignancy). Perforation occurs in ~6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality >20%, and penetration carries comparable mortality; gastric outlet obstruction is least common (~1-2%). Complications and mortality rise in patients over 60, partly reflecting greater NSAID use (pp.2522-2523, 2532).

biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy) H. pylori testing: rapid urease biopsy test, histology, culture (allows susceptibility testing) Noninvasive H. pylori tests: 13C-urea breath test and stool monoclonal antigen test (both >95% sensitivity/specificity); serology cannot distinguish active from prior infection Fasting serum gastrin (two occasions) when ZES is suspected Secretin stimulation test (rise >=120 pg/mL at 15 min) and gastric pH/acid analysis for gastrinoma Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, prolactin, and pancreatic polypeptide to screen for MEN 1 in gastrinoma patients Tumor localization imaging and somatostatin-receptor-based studies for gastrinoma Screening blood/urine for surreptitious aspirin/NSAID use in refractory H. pylori-negative ulcers Functional dyspepsia Drug/toxin-induced ulceration (bisphosphonates, clopidogrel, glucocorticoids combined with NSAIDs, potassium chloride, mycophenolate, chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, crack cocaine) Crohn's disease and eosinophilic gastroenteritis Sarcoidosis and other infiltrative disease Ischemia and radiation injury Menetrier's disease and gastric polyposis presenting as large gastric folds Idiopathic hypersecretory state A peptic ulcer is a break in the mucosa larger than 5 mm that extends into the submucosa; more than 90% of patients with the classic dyspepsia symptom complex have no ulcer, and many patients with true ulcers are asymptomatic (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2522). Burning/gnawing epigastric pain typically occurs 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating in duodenal ulcer and is relieved by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 A.M. is the most discriminating symptom (about two-thirds of DU patients), though it also occurs in roughly one-third with non-ulcer dyspepsia (Harrison 22e p.2522). In gastric ulcer the pain may instead be precipitated by food, and nausea and weight loss are more common than in duodenal ulcer (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523). H. pylori and NSAIDs are the two dominant risk factors (US odds ratios about 3.7 and 3.3); idiopathic and non-Hp/non-NSAID ulcers are rising as H. pylori prevalence falls (Harrison 22e p.2518, p.2522). Gastric ulcers can be malignant and must be biopsied at discovery; duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant (Harrison 22e p.2518). NSAID toxicity correlates poorly with symptoms: over 80% of patients with serious NSAID-related complications had no preceding dyspepsia, and even 75 mg/day of aspirin can cause serious ulceration, so no NSAID dose is completely safe (Harrison 22e p.2520-2521). About two-thirds of PUD patients have no abdominal pain, and up to 87% of those with NSAID-induced disease present with a complication without prior symptoms; more than 50% of ulcer hemorrhages occur without warning (Harrison 22e p.2522). Antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis predisposes to duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant gastritis predisposes to gastric ulcer, atrophy, and ultimately gastric carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.2519-2520). Endoscopy is the most sensitive and specific test; it detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients presenting with dyspepsia, allows biopsy to exclude malignancy and detect H. pylori, and barium studies are now rarely used (Harrison 22e p.2523). A fasting serum gastrin above ten times normal strongly suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, but two-thirds of ZES patients have gastrin levels that overlap with commoner causes; a secretin-stimulated rise of 120 pg/mL or more within 15 minutes is over 90% sensitive and specific (Harrison 22e p.2535-2536). Suspect gastrinoma with ulcers in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), refractory or recurrent ulcers, ulcers with complications, or ulcers without H. pylori or NSAID use; about 25% of gastrinomas arise in MEN 1 (Harrison 22e p.2534-2535). Stress-related mucosal injury (Cushing's ulcer after head injury, Curling's ulcer after burns) histologically lacks inflammation and H. pylori, so 'gastritis' is a misnomer; bleeding typically appears 48-72 h after the insult with mechanical ventilation and coagulopathy as key risk factors (Harrison 22e p.2536). Sudden severe generalized abdominal pain with a board-like, rigid abdomen suggesting perforation Tarry stools or coffee-ground emesis indicating gastrointestinal bleeding; tachycardia/orthostasis indicating hypovolemia Persistent pain no longer relieved by food/antacids and radiating to the back suggesting posterior penetration (pancreas) Early satiety, vomiting of undigested food, and a succussion splash suggesting gastric outlet obstruction Weight loss, anorexia, or new dyspepsia at age 60 or older warranting endoscopy before empiric therapy Ulcers in unusual locations, refractory/recurrent ulcers, or multiple ulcers prompting evaluation for gastrinoma Treating dyspepsia as PUD: abdominal pain has poor predictive value and most dyspeptic patients have no ulcer, so empiric assumptions can miss alternative diagnoses. Relying on symptoms to gauge NSAID risk: serious complications usually occur without preceding dyspepsia. Failing to biopsy a gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy. Misinterpreting an elevated fasting gastrin: PPIs, hypochlorhydria/achlorhydria, pernicious anemia, H. pylori, renal insufficiency, retained antrum, and G-cell hyperplasia all raise gastrin, and PPIs must be stopped (about 7 days, bridged with an H2 antagonist) before ZES testing to avoid false positives. Assuming serology proves active H. pylori infection, when it cannot distinguish current from prior infection and is unreliable for follow-up. Abruptly stopping PPIs in gastrinoma patients, which can precipitate severe acid-related complications. Calling stress-related mucosal injury 'gastritis' despite the absence of inflammation, or labeling endoscopic erythema as gastritis without histology. Ulcers result from an imbalance between mucosal aggressive factors (gastric acid secreted by parietal-cell H+,K+-ATPase, pepsin from chief cells) and mucosal defense/repair (a preepithelial mucus-bicarbonate-phospholipid layer, epithelial restitution and tight junctions, and a subepithelial microvascular bed), with prostaglandins, nitric oxide, and mucosal blood flow central to protection. H. pylori, a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod, colonizes gastric mucus, causes chronic active gastritis in nearly all infected individuals, and produces frank ulceration in only 10-15%; virulence factors include urease (generating ammonia), CagA delivered by a type IV secretion system from cag-PAI-positive strains, VacA, and adhesins. Antral-predominant gastritis raises acid and promotes duodenal ulcer, whereas corpus-predominant pangastritis lowers acid and favors gastric ulcer and carcinoma. NSAIDs injure mucosa both systemically (COX-1 inhibition depletes protective prostaglandins) and topically (weak acids that become trapped and ionized intracellularly), with neutrophil adherence to the gastric microcirculation initiating injury; H. pylori and NSAIDs act as independent and synergistic risk factors. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a neuroendocrine tumor drives acid hypersecretion, parietal-cell hyperplasia, ulceration, esophagitis, and diarrhea (Harrison 22e p.2514-2521, p.2534). Eradication of H. pylori reduces duodenal ulcer recurrence by more than 80%, and improving sanitation has steadily lowered ulcer incidence, surgery rates, and physician visits over the past decades. Complications still carry meaningful mortality: GI bleeding (the commonest, ~15% of patients) has a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% and is more frequent in those over 60; perforation occurs in about 6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality over 20%; gastric outlet obstruction is the least common (1-2%). Approximately 15,000 deaths per year in the US are attributed to complicated PUD. For gastrinoma, overall 5- and 10-year survival is about 62-75% and 47-53%; complete resection or negative laparotomy yields survival over 90%, while hepatic metastasis drops 5-year survival below 20% (Harrison 22e p.2514, p.2516, p.2522-2523, p.2536). PUD severity is framed clinically by the presence and type of complication: uncomplicated ulcer versus bleeding (commonest, ~15%, 30-day mortality ~2.5-10%), perforation/penetration (~6-7%, 30-day mortality >20%; DU penetrates posteriorly into pancreas, GU into left hepatic lobe), and gastric outlet obstruction (1-2%, may be inflammatory/reversible or fixed scar). For gastrinoma, prognosis is stratified by resectability and metastatic burden rather than a formal stage in this chapter (Harrison 22e p.2522-2523, p.2536).

Perforated peptic ulcer — peptic ulcer perforation, perforated duodenal ulcer, perforated gastric ulcer Acute pancreatitis Acute cholecystitis or biliary perforation Perforation elsewhere in the GI tract (colonic, appendiceal) Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm Myocardial infarction (inferior) Mesenteric ischaemia Ruptured ectopic pregnancy or ovarian pathology Erect chest radiograph to look for free subdiaphragmatic gas CT abdomen and pelvis as the most sensitive test for free air and to localise the perforation Bloods including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, amylase or lipase, CRP, and lactate Arterial blood gas and group and save or crossmatch for resuscitation and theatre Helicobacter pylori testing and, later, endoscopy to confirm ulcer healing and exclude malignancy in gastric ulcers Classically presents with sudden, severe, generalised abdominal pain in a patient who may have a history of dyspepsia or NSAID use Examination shows a rigid, board-like abdomen with generalised tenderness, guarding, and absent bowel sounds from peritonitis Perforation evolves through phases: initial chemical peritonitis from gastric acid, a deceptive period of apparent improvement, and then bacterial peritonitis with sepsis An erect chest radiograph often shows free air under the diaphragm, but its absence does not exclude perforation; CT is more sensitive Key risk factors are Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID and aspirin use, smoking, and physiological stress Initial management is aggressive resuscitation, analgesia, nasogastric decompression, intravenous proton pump inhibition, and broad-spectrum antibiotics while preparing for surgery The standard operation is closure of the perforation, commonly with an omental (Graham) patch, and thorough peritoneal lavage; large or malignant gastric perforations may require resection Selected patients with a sealed perforation and no generalised peritonitis may be managed non-operatively with close monitoring Sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen and generalised peritonitis (surgical emergency) Free intraperitoneal gas on imaging Sepsis, haemodynamic instability, or rising lactate indicating septic shock Deterioration after a deceptive symptom-free interval signalling established bacterial peritonitis Excluding perforation on the basis of a normal erect chest radiograph alone Being reassured by the transient improvement of the deceptive second phase Delaying resuscitation and surgery in a septic patient Failing to biopsy or follow up a perforated gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy Perforation occurs when a peptic ulcer erodes through the full thickness of the gastric or duodenal wall, allowing gastric and duodenal contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity. Mucosal breakdown is driven by an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs) and mucosal defence. Escaped acidic contents first cause a sterile chemical peritonitis, followed within hours by bacterial contamination and generalised bacterial peritonitis. The resulting inflammatory cascade produces fluid sequestration, sepsis, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure. Duodenal and pyloric ulcers most often perforate anteriorly. Outcome depends on age, comorbidity, size of perforation, and, critically, the delay before surgery; early intervention gives good recovery, whereas delayed presentation with established peritonitis and sepsis carries high morbidity and mortality.

Perianal fistula — fistula-in-ano, anal fistula, anorectal fistula, perianal fistula-in-ano Perianal or ischiorectal abscess Pilonidal sinus disease Hidradenitis suppurativa Crohn perianal disease Anal fistula secondary to tuberculosis Anorectal malignancy or fistulating carcinoma Examination under anaesthesia to define the tracks and internal opening MRI of the pelvis for complex or recurrent fistulae Endoanal ultrasound to map tracks and sphincter involvement Colonoscopy or ileocolonoscopy when Crohn disease is suspected Biopsy of atypical or non-healing tracks to exclude malignancy or tuberculosis Anorectal physiology and continence assessment when division of sphincter is contemplated A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal track lined by granulation tissue connecting the anal canal or rectum to the perianal skin, usually the sequel of a drained or spontaneously discharging anorectal abscess Typical symptoms are recurrent perianal discharge, intermittent pain and swelling that flares when the external opening blocks, and pruritus, often with a history of a previous abscess The Parks classification describes tracks in relation to the sphincters as intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, and extrasphincteric Goodsall rule helps predict the internal opening: anterior openings tend to track radially, while posterior openings tend to curve to a posterior midline internal opening MRI of the pelvis and endoanal ultrasound accurately map complex tracks, secondary extensions, and the relationship to the sphincter complex before surgery The therapeutic balance is eradicating the fistula while preserving continence; low simple tracks may be laid open, whereas tracks involving significant sphincter muscle need sphincter-preserving techniques or a seton Recurrent, multiple, or complex fistulae should raise suspicion of Crohn disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy and prompt appropriate investigation Spreading perianal sepsis, cellulitis, or features of necrotising infection (Fournier gangrene) requiring emergency surgery Systemic sepsis from an undrained abscess Suspicion of underlying malignancy in a chronic, indurated, or non-healing fistula Extensive or multiple complex tracks suggesting Crohn disease with risk to continence Dividing significant sphincter muscle and causing incontinence, particularly in anterior fistulae in women or high tracks Missing a secondary track or the true internal opening, leading to early recurrence Laying open a fistula in a patient with undiagnosed Crohn disease with poor healing Treating an abscess without recognising or planning for an underlying fistula Failing to biopsy a chronic, atypical, or non-healing track and missing malignancy Most fistulae-in-ano arise from the cryptoglandular theory: infection of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane at the level of the dentate line forms an abscess, which discharges and leaves a persistent epithelialising or granulating track between the internal opening in the anal canal and an external opening on the perianal skin. The course of the track relative to the internal and external anal sphincters determines its classification and surgical difficulty. Secondary tracks and horseshoe extensions can develop. A minority result from specific conditions such as Crohn disease, tuberculosis, pelvic sepsis, radiation, or malignancy, which alter management and prognosis. Simple low fistulae have a high cure rate after laying open with preservation of continence, whereas complex, high, or recurrent tracks carry greater risk of recurrence and incontinence and often require staged, sphincter-preserving strategies. Fistulae associated with Crohn disease are more difficult to heal and tend to recur, and outcomes depend on control of the underlying disease.

Periapical abscess — dentoalveolar abscess, apical abscess, acute periapical abscess, dental abscess Periodontal abscess arising from the gingival sulcus Irreversible pulpitis without abscess formation Periapical granuloma or radicular cyst Osteomyelitis of the jaw Odontogenic infection of adjacent teeth or sinus Pulp sensibility testing (expected non-vital response) Percussion, palpation, and mobility assessment Periapical radiography and, when needed, cone-beam CT for extent Assessment for fascial-space spread and airway compromise in swelling Culture and systemic markers if severe or spreading infection A periapical abscess is a localised collection of pus at the root apex arising from a necrotic, infected pulp Classic features are severe, well-localised pain, tenderness to percussion, and a feeling that the tooth is extruded or high on biting The affected tooth is typically non-vital, so pulp sensibility testing is negative while percussion and palpation are markedly positive Pus may drain spontaneously through a sinus tract (gum boil), which can relieve pain and produce a chronic, less symptomatic picture Early radiographs may look normal because bone changes lag behind, whereas chronic lesions show a periapical radiolucency Primary management is drainage and elimination of the source through root canal treatment or extraction; antibiotics are adjuncts reserved for spreading infection or systemic involvement Infection can track along fascial planes, so the pattern of swelling depends on tooth position relative to muscle attachments Recurrent or persistent sinus tracts indicate ongoing infection needing definitive endodontic or surgical treatment Rapidly spreading swelling of the floor of mouth or submandibular region raising concern for Ludwig angina and airway obstruction Trismus, difficulty swallowing, drooling, or voice change indicating deep-space infection Systemic sepsis, high fever, or periorbital/cavernous sinus spread from upper anterior teeth Immunocompromised or diabetic patients in whom infection can progress dangerously fast Prescribing antibiotics without draining the abscess or removing the source Being reassured by a normal early radiograph despite clear clinical signs Missing progression to a deep-space or airway-threatening infection Confusing a periodontal abscess with a periapical abscess and mistreating the cause A periapical abscess develops when pulp necrosis, usually secondary to caries or trauma, allows bacteria and their toxins to egress through the apical foramen into the periapical tissues. The host inflammatory response produces a purulent collection localised to the periradicular bone. Rising pressure causes intense pain and may resorb surrounding bone, seen later as a radiolucency. Pus follows the path of least resistance, perforating cortical bone and tracking into soft tissue, where the relationship of the perforation to muscle attachments determines whether a localised vestibular swelling, a draining sinus, or a spreading fascial-space infection results. With timely drainage and source control the prognosis is excellent, but delayed treatment risks spread to fascial spaces, osteomyelitis, airway compromise, or life-threatening sepsis.

Periarticular Disorders of the Extremities — Bursitis, Rotator cuff tendinitis, Impingement syndrome, Frozen shoulder, Adhesive capsulitis, Tennis elbow, Golfer's elbow, De Quervain's tenosynovitis, Plantar fasciitis, Iliotibial band syndrome, Calcific tendinitis Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Gout and crystal arthropathy Spondyloarthritis Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder Acromioclavicular joint pathology Intraarticular knee pathology (osteoarthritis, meniscal injury) versus periarticular knee pain Septic bursitis (e.g., olecranon or prepatellar) Infectious tenosynovitis Septic arthritis presenting as periarticular pain and swelling History and directed physical examination (often sufficient for diagnosis) Provocative maneuvers (painful abduction arc, drop-arm test, Finkelstein test, Yergason's test) Bursal aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis when infection or gout is suspected Ultrasound (for bursitis, tendinitis, rotator cuff tears, calcific deposits, plantar fascia thickening, and guided injection) Plain radiographs (may show tendon calcification or incidental heel spurs) MRI (sensitive for rotator cuff tears, tendon integrity, and plantar fasciitis when diagnosis is unclear) Gouty bursitis/tendinitis (urate deposition) Calcium pyrophosphate or apatite crystal deposition Rheumatoid or inflammatory arthritis involving periarticular structures Referred pain from intraarticular degenerative joint disease Periarticular disorders are common soft-tissue musculoskeletal problems affecting people of any age, arising from structures around (rather than within) the joint such as bursae, tendons, fascia, and connective-tissue bands. Bursitis is inflammation of a synovial-lined sac; adults have over 150 bursae that ease gliding of tendons and muscles over bony prominences, and overuse, trauma, systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, gout), or infection can trigger inflammation. Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis is the most common bursitis and frequently coexists with rotator cuff tendinitis, presenting with anterolateral shoulder pain. Acutely inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis with warmth/redness warrants aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal examination to exclude infection or gout before assuming a mechanical cause. Rotator cuff tendinitis (impingement syndrome) is the leading cause of a painful shoulder; the supraspinatus tendon is most often affected due to impingement between the humeral head and the anterior acromion/coracoacromial ligament, classically producing a painful abduction arc of 60-120 degrees. Calcific tendinitis reflects hydroxyapatite (calcium salt) deposition within a tendon, most often the supraspinatus (involved in about 63% of cases), typically after age 40, and may be asymptomatic or cause sudden severe shoulder pain. De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid; a positive Finkelstein test (thumb tucked in fist with ulnar wrist deviation) reproduces radial styloid pain. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) causes painful, globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion, usually without intrinsic joint disease, and is associated with diabetes, thyroid disease, chronic pulmonary disease, and prior myocardial infarction. Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) arises from repetitive resisted wrist extension/supination; most patients are injured by activities other than tennis such as pulling weeds, carrying briefcases, or using a screwdriver. Plantar fasciitis classically causes severe heel pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, easing with initial activity then worsening with prolonged weight-bearing; tenderness localizes to the medial calcaneal attachment of the fascia. Drug-induced tendinopathy is increasingly recognized, with quinolones, glucocorticoids, aromatase inhibitors, and statins implicated; the Achilles tendon is most often affected and rupture can be the presenting event. Yergason's test (pain on resisted forearm supination with the elbow at 90 degrees) supports bicipital tendinitis; biceps tendon rupture in older patients may be painless and recognized by a retracted bulge of the long head. Acutely warm, red, tender bursa suggesting septic bursitis or gout requiring aspiration Weakness of abduction/external rotation or a positive drop-arm test suggesting a rotator cuff tear Acute tendon rupture (e.g., Achilles in drug-induced tendinopathy, biceps in active patients) Globally restricted active and passive shoulder motion suggesting adhesive capsulitis rather than a focal tendinitis Periarticular pain in the setting of systemic disease (rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, thyroid disease) prompting evaluation of the underlying condition Anserine bursitis is a frequently overlooked periarticular cause of knee pain. Assuming inflamed olecranon or prepatellar bursitis is mechanical without excluding infection or gout by aspiration. Mislabeling globally restricted shoulder motion as simple tendinitis when it is adhesive capsulitis. Attributing heel pain to a radiographic heel spur, which is of little diagnostic significance in plantar fasciitis. Overlooking medication as a cause of tendon pain or rupture (drug-induced tendinopathy), and reintroducing the offending agent. Confusing iliopsoas bursitis pain with pain originating within the hip joint itself. These are disorders of the soft tissues surrounding joints rather than the synovial joint itself. Bursitis is synovial inflammation of a bursa from frictional overuse, trauma, systemic inflammatory/crystal disease, or infection. Tendinopathies (rotator cuff, bicipital, patellar, epicondylar, De Quervain's) result from mechanical impingement and repetitive resisted loading producing microtears, inflammation, and degeneration at tendon insertions; the supraspinatus is uniquely vulnerable to impingement beneath the acromion. Calcific tendinitis is caused by hydroxyapatite deposition within tendon substance through poorly understood phases of calcification that can incite acute inflammation. Adhesive capsulitis features a thickened shoulder capsule with mild chronic inflammatory infiltrate and fibrosis, often after a period of immobility. Plantar fasciitis arises at the fascial origin on the medial calcaneal tuberosity from cumulative loading. Drug-induced tendinopathies have an unknown mechanism but are linked to specific drug classes. Most periarticular disorders are self-limited and respond to conservative measures. Adhesive capsulitis usually improves spontaneously over 1-3 years, though many patients retain some residual loss of shoulder motion. More than 80% of plantar fasciitis cases resolve within 12 months. Calcific tendinitis is largely self-limited. Rotator cuff tears vary in outcome depending on tear size, chronicity, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis. No formal grading system; rotator cuff tears are clinically characterized as acute, subacute, or chronic and as partial- or full-thickness, with management guided by tear severity, symptom duration, pain, functional loss, and coexisting osteoarthritis.
