must be distinguished from constrictive pericarditis because the latter is surgically correctable) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Right ventricular infarction (may mimic tamponade with hypotension, elevated JVP, slow y descent, occasional paradoxical pulse) (Harrison 22e p.2082) Cor pulmonale (systemic venous hypertension and paradoxical pulse, but Kussmaul's sign is negative and advanced parenchymal lung disease is apparent) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Tricuspid stenosis (congestive hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, venous distention, but characteristic murmur present) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Hepatic cirrhosis (constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites may be mistaken for cirrhosis; inspection of distended neck veins avoids the error) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Viral pericarditis (coxsackievirus A and B, echovirus, influenza, mumps, herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, post-acute COVID, mpox) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082) Tuberculous pericarditis (effusion, constriction, or effusive-constrictive disease; suggested by high adenosine deaminase or M. tuberculosis DNA by PCR, often requiring pericardial tissue) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084) Pyogenic/purulent bacterial pericarditis (pneumococcus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Legionella, Chlamydia; from cardiothoracic surgery, lung/pleural extension, esophageal rupture, or valve-ring abscess; fever, chills, septicemia, poor prognosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Fungal pericarditis (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, aspergillosis, candidiasis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Parasitic/protozoal and syphilitic pericarditis (amebiasis, toxoplasmosis, echinococcosis, trichinosis) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Transthoracic echocardiography: most widely used, sensitive, specific, bedside-capable; localizes and estimates pericardial fluid and shows late-diastolic collapse of the RV free wall and right atrium in tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082) Doppler echocardiography: in tamponade and constriction, inspiratory increase in tricuspid/pulmonic flow velocities with decrease in pulmonary venous/mitral/aortic velocities and a leftward septal shift (respirophasic variation) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084) CT and MRI: superior for loculated effusions, pericardial thickening, pericardial masses, calcification, and detecting pericardial inflammation; more accurate than echocardiography for confirming or excluding constriction (MRI assesses myocardial involvement) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084) ECG: stage 1-4 evolution in acute pericarditis; low QRS voltage and electrical alternans with large effusion/tamponade; low voltage and diffuse T-wave changes with atrial fibrillation in constriction (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2081, p.2083) Chest radiograph: enlarged cardiac silhouette with a 'water bottle' configuration in large effusion; pericardial calcification (most common in tuberculous constriction) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2084) Pericardiocentesis with fluid analysis: cell counts, cytology for neoplastic cells, cultures, M. tuberculosis PCR and adenosine deaminase (Harrison 22e p.2082) Pericardial biopsy (e.g., via limited thoracotomy) when fluid analysis is non-diagnostic, especially for suspected tuberculous or neoplastic disease (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084) Laboratory: elevated C-reactive protein and white blood cell count in viral/idiopathic pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2082) Uremic and dialysis-associated pericarditis (renal failure; fibrinous, serosanguinous effusions, friction rub common but pain usually mild) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Neoplastic pericarditis (lung and breast carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, leukemia; metastatic invasion, primary tumors, mesothelioma) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Postcardiac injury syndrome (postpericardiotomy, posttraumatic, post-MI Dressler's syndrome; hypersensitivity/autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens 1-4 weeks after injury) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2082) Collagen vascular / autoimmune disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, ankylosing spondylitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4 disease, rheumatic fever, polyarteritis nodosa) (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Drug-induced pericarditis (procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin, isoniazid, minoxidil, anticoagulants, methysergide) (Harrison 22e p.2078) Postirradiation (mediastinal radiation) pericarditis, acute or chronic constrictive (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2083) Aortic dissection with leakage into the pericardial sac (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081) Acute myocardial infarction and metabolic causes (myxedema, cholesterol pericarditis) (Harrison 22e p.2078) Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (Harrison 22e p.2078) Acute pericarditis has four principal diagnostic features: chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, characteristic ECG changes, and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2078). Pericarditic chest pain is typically retrosternal/left precordial, often pleuritic, may radiate to the trapezius ridge, and is characteristically intensified by lying supine and relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079). A pericardial friction rub is audible at some point in approximately 85% of patients with acute pericarditis; it may have up to three components per cycle and is best heard at end expiration with the patient upright and leaning forward (Harrison 22e p.2079). The ECG of acute pericarditis classically evolves through four stages: stage 1 widespread upwardly-concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression, stage 2 normalization of ST, stage 3 T-wave inversion, and stage 4 return to normal (Harrison 22e p.2079). Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade is hypotension, soft or absent heart sounds, and jugular venous distention with a prominent x descent but an absent y descent (Harrison 22e p.2081). Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is an important clue to tamponade, but also occurs in about one-third of constrictive pericarditis cases and in hypovolemic shock, obstructive airway disease, and pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.2081-2082). In constrictive pericarditis the rigid thickened pericardium limits ventricular filling only after early diastole (unimpeded in early diastole, then abruptly reduced), whereas in tamponade filling is impeded throughout diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083). Kussmaul's sign (failure of venous pressure to decline, or a rise, during inspiration) is common in chronic constrictive pericarditis but is also seen in tricuspid stenosis, right ventricular infarction, and restrictive cardiomyopathy; it is negative in cor pulmonale (Harrison 22e p.2083-2084). A pericardial knock, an early third heart sound at the apex from abrupt cessation of ventricular filling, is often conspicuous in constrictive pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.2083). Constrictive pericarditis produces an M-shaped atrial pressure contour with prominent x and y descents; the y descent (diminished/absent in tamponade) is the most prominent deflection, and the ventricular pressure pulse shows a 'square root' sign in diastole (Harrison 22e p.2083). In developing nations a high percentage of chronic constrictive pericarditis is tuberculous, but TB is now an uncommon cause in North America and Western Europe; other causes include prior viral/idiopathic pericarditis, cardiac surgery, mediastinal irradiation, and neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.2083). Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and unexplained sudden enlargement of the cardiac silhouette; may be rapidly fatal if not recognized and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.2081) Reduced QRS amplitude with electrical alternans of P, QRS, or T waves raises suspicion of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2081) Predictors of poor prognosis warranting hospitalization in acute pericarditis: fever >38C, subacute onset, large pericardial effusion, immunosuppression, or evidence of tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080) Purulent (pyogenic) pericarditis carries a poor prognosis and requires immediate drainage and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.2083) Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease can progress to constriction; constriction should be treated surgically (Harrison 22e p.2084) Distinguishing constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy is critical because constriction is surgically correctable; their hemodynamics overlap (square-root sign and equalized diastolic pressures occur in both) and echocardiography alone cannot definitively establish or exclude constriction, so MRI/CT is needed (Harrison 22e p.2083, p.2084). Acute pericarditis is commonly mistaken for AMI and vice versa; in pericarditis the ST elevations are upwardly concave, reciprocal depression is limited to aVR/V1, and biomarker rises (from epi-myocarditis) are modest relative to AMI (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083). Pericardial calcification may occur without constriction, and constriction may occur without calcification, so calcification neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2084). Acute idiopathic pericarditis is a diagnosis of exclusion with no specific test; all other causes of fibrinous pericarditis must be considered (Harrison 22e p.2082-2083). Constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites can be misdiagnosed as hepatic cirrhosis unless the distended neck veins with characteristic waveform are recognized (Harrison 22e p.2084). Pain is often absent in slowly developing tuberculous, postirradiation, neoplastic, and uremic pericarditis, so its absence does not exclude pericardial disease (Harrison 22e p.2079). Anticoagulants should be avoided in acute pericarditis because they could cause bleeding into the pericardial cavity and tamponade (Harrison 22e p.2080). The pericardium is a double-layered sac (visceral and parietal layers) separated by 15-50 mL of plasma ultrafiltrate; it restrains sudden cardiac chamber dilation and fixes cardiac position. In acute pericarditis, inflammation produces fibrinous or effusive disease. Cardiac tamponade occurs when fluid accumulates in the pericardial space in quantity sufficient to obstruct ventricular inflow, raising intrapericardial pressure and limiting diastolic filling throughout diastole, reducing stroke volume, cardiac output, and arterial pressure. As little as 200 mL can cause tamponade when fluid develops rapidly, versus >2000 mL when it accumulates slowly and the pericardium stretches. In chronic constrictive pericarditis, healing of fibrinous/serofibrinous pericarditis or resorption of effusion produces granulation tissue that contracts into a rigid, sometimes calcified scar encasing the heart; ventricular filling is unimpeded early in diastole then abruptly halts at the pericardium's elastic limit. End-diastolic pressures in both ventricles and mean atrial, pulmonary venous, and systemic venous pressures equalize within ~5 mmHg, while resting systolic function is typically normal or only mildly impaired (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2081, p.2083). Viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis usually runs its course in a few days to 4 weeks; recurrent (relapsing) pericarditis occurs in approximately one-fourth of patients, and both tamponade and constriction are possible but infrequent complications. Most patients with acute pericarditis can be managed as outpatients with careful follow-up. Untreated cardiac tamponade may be rapidly fatal. Purulent pericarditis generally has a poor prognosis. Without treatment, tuberculous pericardial disease may progress to constriction. Pericardial resection is the only definitive treatment of constrictive pericarditis, with benefits accruing progressively over months; operative mortality is in the range of 5-10% even at experienced centers, highest in the most severe disease, especially radiation-induced (Harrison 22e p.2080, p.2082, p.2083, p.2084). Clinical classification: I. Acute pericarditis (<6 weeks) - A. Fibrinous, B. Effusive (serous or sanguineous); II. Subacute pericarditis (6 weeks to 6 months) - A. Effusive-constrictive, B. Constrictive; III. Chronic pericarditis (>6 months) - A. Constrictive, B. Adhesive (nonconstrictive). Etiologic classification: infectious, noninfectious, and presumed autoimmune. Table 281-2 distinguishes tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right ventricular myocardial infarction, and effusive-constrictive pericarditis by clinical, ECG, echocardiographic, and CT/MRI features (Harrison 22e p.2078, p.2080).

Acute pericarditis — ECG (diffuse ST elevation, PR depression) Echocardiogram Inflammatory markers Tamponade if effusion enlarges Acute myocardial ischaemia / STEMI Acute aortic syndrome (dissection) Pulmonary embolism Pleuritis / pneumonia Musculoskeletal chest wall pain (e.g. costochondritis) Gastro-oesophageal reflux / oesophageal disease Herpes zoster Acute myocarditis (often viral; chest discomfort and ST/T-wave changes can overlap) Pneumonia / pleuritis 12-lead ECG looking for diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression (p.149) Chest radiograph (pericardial calcification suggests chronic pericarditis; usually unremarkable in acute disease) (p.150) Echocardiography to detect effusion (may be normal in 34-50% of acute cases) (p.90) Measurement of pulsus paradoxus when tamponade is suspected (p.312) Acute coronary syndrome / STEMI (diffuse ST elevation of pericarditis can be mistaken for infarction) Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (ST elevation and biomarker rise mimicking MI) Aortic dissection extending into the pericardium Pulmonary embolism Diagnosis rests on the combination of characteristic chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and characteristic ECG changes; echocardiography can be normal in roughly a third to half of cases, so a normal echo does not exclude pericarditis (p.90). The pericardial pain is typically pleuritic and positional: worse supine and on inspiration/coughing, relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (p.146, p.149). Pain referred to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericardial inflammation and is not typical of angina (p.149). Most of the pericardium is insensitive to pain; the discomfort of pericarditis is thought to arise largely from accompanying pleural inflammation, explaining its pleuritic, positional quality and referral to shoulder/neck (p.147). A pericardial friction rub on auscultation reflects pericardial inflammation and is a key physical sign (p.149). Pericarditis is an uncommon final diagnosis among undifferentiated acute chest pain presentations (about 4% in one ED series), so other causes are statistically more likely (p.145). Hypotension with significant tachycardia, suggesting tamponade and haemodynamic compromise (pericarditis with tamponade is a high-risk, potentially life-threatening cause of chest pain) (p.147, p.150) Abnormal jugular venous pulse pattern consistent with pericardial tamponade (p.149) Pulsus paradoxus (points to tamponade physiology) (p.312) Tamponade is a recognised cause of obstructive shock (p.102) Diffuse (multi-lead) ST-segment elevation not confined to a single coronary territory, together with PR-segment depression, helps distinguish pericarditis from acute MI; ascribing these ECG changes to ischaemia is a key pitfall (p.149). A normal echocardiogram does not exclude pericarditis (effusion absent in 34-50%) (p.90). Chest-wall tenderness does not exclude myocardial ischaemia, and an unremarkable physical exam is not reassuring (p.149). Low-grade fever is nonspecific and can accompany MI and thromboembolism as well as pericardial inflammation (p.149). Inflammation of the pericardium from infectious or noninfectious causes. Because the visceral and most of the parietal pericardium are insensitive to pain, the discomfort is attributed mainly to associated pleural inflammation, producing pleuritic, position-dependent pain that, via overlapping phrenic and C3-C5 somatic innervation, may be referred to the shoulder, neck, and trapezius ridge (p.147, p.149).

Perinatal Hypoxic-Ischaemic Encephalopathy — HIE, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, birth asphyxia encephalopathy, neonatal encephalopathy Neonatal sepsis or meningitis Inborn errors of metabolism Neonatal (arterial or venous) stroke Intracranial haemorrhage Neonatal seizures from other causes (e.g. electrolyte disturbance) Congenital brain malformation or genetic encephalopathy Umbilical cord and early postnatal blood gas for acidosis and base deficit EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG for seizure detection and background assessment MRI of the brain (usually within the first week) for injury pattern and prognosis Assessment of multi-organ function (renal, hepatic, cardiac, coagulation, glucose, electrolytes) Evaluation to exclude infection and metabolic causes Brain injury in the newborn resulting from a perinatal event that reduces cerebral oxygen delivery and blood flow, producing an evolving encephalopathy. It is a leading cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability, including cerebral palsy. Severity is graded clinically using the Sarnat stages (mild, moderate, severe) based on level of consciousness, tone, reflexes, autonomic function, and seizures. Supportive evidence of a hypoxic-ischaemic insult includes fetal distress, low Apgar scores, the need for resuscitation, and a low umbilical cord arterial pH with metabolic acidosis. Therapeutic hypothermia, started within the first hours of life for eligible term and near-term infants with moderate to severe encephalopathy, reduces death and disability. Seizures are common and may be subtle; EEG or amplitude-integrated EEG assists detection and monitoring. The injury frequently involves other organs, causing renal, cardiac, hepatic, and haematological dysfunction that also require support. MRI in the first week helps define the pattern and extent of injury and informs prognosis. Important mimics, including infection, metabolic disorders, and stroke, should be considered rather than assuming every encephalopathy is purely hypoxic-ischaemic. Deep coma, absent brainstem reflexes, or flaccid tone Refractory or clinically evident status epilepticus Multi-organ failure Severely abnormal EEG background or extensive injury on MRI Persistent need for cardiorespiratory support Assuming all neonatal encephalopathy is hypoxic-ischaemic and missing infection, metabolic disease, or stroke Missing subtle seizures without EEG monitoring Delaying assessment for and initiation of therapeutic hypothermia within the treatment window Allowing hyperthermia, which worsens injury Overlooking coexisting multi-organ dysfunction A hypoxic-ischaemic insult around the time of birth causes an initial phase of energy failure with cellular depolarisation, excitotoxic glutamate release, and calcium influx. After partial recovery of cerebral metabolism, a delayed (secondary) phase of energy failure ensues over hours to days, driven by mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptotic and necrotic cell death. This latent window is the rationale for early therapeutic hypothermia, which slows the destructive secondary cascade. Outcome depends on severity: mild encephalopathy usually recovers well, moderate carries a variable risk of impairment, and severe disease is associated with high mortality and a high rate of cerebral palsy, epilepsy, and cognitive and sensory disability; therapeutic hypothermia improves outcomes in eligible infants.

Perinatal HIV Infection — mother-to-child HIV transmission, vertical HIV transmission, paediatric HIV Other congenital infections (e.g., cytomegalovirus, syphilis) Primary immunodeficiency disorders Failure to thrive of other cause Recurrent infections from other immune defects Tuberculosis HIV nucleic acid (virological) testing on the recommended schedule CD4 count and percentage HIV viral load Screening for co-infections (tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C, syphilis) Full blood count and growth and developmental assessment Most childhood HIV infection is acquired from the mother during pregnancy, around delivery, or through breastfeeding, and transmission is largely preventable with effective interventions. Maternal antiretroviral therapy that suppresses viral load, appropriate mode of delivery, infant antiretroviral prophylaxis, and safe infant feeding practices dramatically reduce vertical transmission. Infected infants are frequently asymptomatic at birth, so diagnosis relies on virological (nucleic acid) testing rather than antibody tests, because maternal antibodies cross the placenta and persist for months. Untreated perinatal infection can progress rapidly in infancy, with failure to thrive, recurrent or severe infections, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and developmental regression. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a serious early opportunistic infection, so prophylaxis is important in at-risk and infected infants. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy in infected infants improves survival and outcomes and is recommended as soon as diagnosis is confirmed. A definitive diagnosis of infection or its exclusion requires a defined schedule of repeat virological testing over the first months of life. Comprehensive care includes immunisations adapted to immune status, growth and developmental monitoring, and support for the whole family. Failure to thrive or growth faltering Recurrent, severe, or unusual infections Signs of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia or other opportunistic infection Developmental regression or encephalopathy Persistent hepatosplenomegaly or generalised lymphadenopathy Using antibody testing rather than virological testing to diagnose infection in young infants Interpreting a single negative early test as excluding infection without completing the testing schedule Delaying antiretroviral therapy or Pneumocystis prophylaxis in an at-risk or infected infant Overlooking co-infections such as tuberculosis or hepatitis HIV crosses to the infant transplacentally, through exposure to maternal blood and genital secretions during delivery, or via breast milk. The virus infects CD4 T lymphocytes and other immune cells, integrating into host DNA and causing progressive depletion and dysfunction of CD4 cells. In infants the immune system is immature and the initial viral burden relative to immune capacity is high, so without treatment immunodeficiency and disease progression can occur faster than in adults, predisposing to opportunistic and recurrent infections and end-organ involvement. With early diagnosis, prompt antiretroviral therapy, and prophylaxis against opportunistic infections, children can achieve viral suppression, immune recovery, and near-normal life expectancy; untreated perinatal infection carries high morbidity and mortality in early childhood.

PFAPA Syndrome (Periodic Fever, Aphthous Stomatitis, Pharyngitis, Adenitis) — PFAPA, Marshall syndrome, periodic fever syndrome Recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis or tonsillitis Cyclic neutropenia Familial Mediterranean fever and other monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes Hyper-IgD syndrome (mevalonate kinase deficiency) TNF-receptor associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) Recurrent viral infections in young children Documentation of the fever pattern with a symptom and temperature diary Full blood count during and between episodes (to exclude cyclic neutropenia) Inflammatory markers during an attack Throat swab or streptococcal testing to exclude recurrent bacterial pharyngitis Genetic testing for monogenic periodic fever syndromes when features are atypical Immunoglobulin levels where an alternative autoinflammatory diagnosis is suspected The most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, typically beginning before the age of five. The defining feature is highly regular, recurrent episodes of fever occurring at strikingly predictable intervals, often every 3-6 weeks. Episodes classically combine aphthous mouth ulcers, pharyngitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy, though not every feature is present each time. A hallmark is that the child is entirely well, thriving, and asymptomatic between episodes with normal growth and development. It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion; recurrent streptococcal infection, cyclic neutropenia, and monogenic autoinflammatory disorders should be considered. Fevers respond dramatically to a single dose of corticosteroid, which can be both therapeutic and supportive of the diagnosis, though steroids may shorten the interval between episodes. Routine antibiotics are ineffective because the condition is inflammatory rather than infective. The disorder is self-limiting, usually resolving spontaneously over several years without long-term sequelae; tonsillectomy is an option in selected cases. Poor growth or failure to thrive, which is not expected in PFAPA Persistent symptoms or inflammation between episodes Irregular, unpredictable, or evolving fever patterns suggesting another diagnosis Neutropenia coinciding with fevers (points to cyclic neutropenia) Features suggesting a monogenic autoinflammatory disorder such as serositis, rash, or a strong family history Repeatedly treating episodes with antibiotics for presumed bacterial pharyngitis Diagnosing PFAPA in a child who is unwell or failing to thrive between episodes Overlooking cyclic neutropenia by not checking blood counts during febrile episodes Assuming steroid responsiveness alone confirms the diagnosis without excluding mimics Not recognising that corticosteroids may shorten the interval to the next attack PFAPA is regarded as an autoinflammatory disorder of innate immunity rather than an infection or classic autoimmune disease. During attacks there is dysregulated activation of the innate immune system with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling (including interleukin-1 beta pathway activity), producing the stereotyped febrile episodes. Unlike the monogenic periodic fever syndromes, no single consistent genetic cause has been identified, and inflammation resolves completely between episodes. Excellent; PFAPA is benign and self-limiting, typically resolving over several years with no lasting effect on growth, development, or long-term health, and it is not associated with amyloidosis or organ damage.

Periodontitis — periodontal disease, chronic periodontitis, gum disease Gingivitis without attachment loss Necrotising periodontal disease Periodontal abscess Endodontic-periodontal combined lesions Occlusal trauma causing mobility Manifestations of systemic disease affecting the periodontium Full-mouth periodontal charting of probing depths and attachment loss Bleeding on probing and plaque indices Periapical and bitewing radiographs to assess bone loss Assessment of tooth mobility and furcation involvement Screening for diabetes and smoking status as risk modifiers Periodontitis is a biofilm-driven inflammatory disease causing irreversible destruction of the periodontal attachment and alveolar bone The hallmark distinguishing it from gingivitis is loss of clinical attachment and true periodontal pocketing, not just bleeding gums It is often painless and slowly progressive, so patients may present late with mobility, drifting teeth, or gingival recession Probing depths, attachment levels, bleeding on probing, and radiographic bone loss are the core diagnostic measurements Smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, and genetic susceptibility strongly modify disease severity and treatment response There is a bidirectional relationship with diabetes and associations with cardiovascular and other systemic conditions Treatment centres on meticulous plaque control and mechanical debridement to disrupt the subgingival biofilm, with surgery for residual defects Long-term supportive periodontal maintenance is essential because the disease tends to recur without ongoing care Rapid attachment and bone loss in a young patient suggesting aggressive disease Necrotising periodontitis with pain, ulceration, and tissue destruction, especially in immunocompromised patients Periodontal manifestations pointing to undiagnosed diabetes or immune deficiency Treating bleeding gums as simple gingivitis while missing established attachment loss Neglecting smoking cessation and glycaemic control that undermine treatment Relying on antibiotics instead of mechanical biofilm disruption Failing to arrange ongoing maintenance, allowing recurrence Periodontitis arises from a dysbiotic subgingival biofilm dominated by anaerobic and gram-negative species that provoke a chronic host immune-inflammatory response. Bacterial virulence factors and the resulting inflammatory mediators drive activation of osteoclasts and matrix-degrading enzymes, leading to breakdown of the periodontal ligament and resorption of alveolar bone. This produces apical migration of the junctional epithelium and true pocket formation. The extent of tissue destruction reflects the balance between microbial challenge and host response, which is heavily modulated by risk factors such as smoking, diabetes, and genetics, ultimately threatening tooth support. With effective plaque control and professional care, disease progression can usually be halted and teeth retained, but lost attachment and bone do not regenerate spontaneously and advanced cases carry a guarded prognosis for affected teeth.

Perioperative anaphylaxis — anaesthetic anaphylaxis, intraoperative anaphylaxis, perioperative hypersensitivity reaction Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity Primary cardiac event or arrhythmia High or total spinal anaesthesia Severe bronchospasm from asthma Pulmonary embolism or air embolism Haemorrhagic or septic shock Serial mast cell tryptase levels during the reaction and after recovery Continuous ECG, blood pressure, and oxygenation monitoring Arterial blood gas to assess oxygenation and acidosis Referral for later skin and specific IgE allergy testing to identify the trigger Review of all agents and materials administered around the time of the reaction A life-threatening acute hypersensitivity reaction during anaesthesia, often presenting abruptly with cardiovascular collapse rather than the skin signs seen in awake patients Common triggers include neuromuscular blocking agents, antibiotics, latex, and chlorhexidine, with contrast and colloids as additional causes Cardiovascular features (profound hypotension, tachycardia, and collapse) and respiratory features (bronchospasm, high airway pressures, desaturation) predominate under drapes Cutaneous signs such as flushing, urticaria, and angioedema may be absent, masked, or noticed late because the patient is covered Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first-line treatment, titrated to severity, alongside stopping the likely trigger, giving oxygen, and aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation Refractory cases may need escalating vasopressor support, and cardiac arrest is managed with standard advanced life support with prolonged effort as needed A mast cell tryptase level taken during and after the reaction supports the diagnosis, and the patient must be referred for allergy testing to identify the culprit Clear documentation and patient warning about the responsible agent are essential to prevent recurrence at future anaesthetics Sudden cardiovascular collapse or cardiac arrest during anaesthesia Severe bronchospasm with high airway pressures and difficulty ventilating Profound refractory hypotension despite fluids and vasopressors Rapidly progressive airway swelling or angioedema threatening the airway Delaying adrenaline while awaiting confirmation of the diagnosis Expecting skin signs and dismissing anaphylaxis when they are absent under drapes Failing to send timed tryptase samples or to refer for allergy testing Under-resuscitating the large fluid deficit caused by capillary leak Not documenting or warning the patient about the causative agent Perioperative anaphylaxis is usually an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, often IgE-mediated, in which prior sensitisation leads to cross-linking of IgE on mast cells and basophils upon re-exposure to an antigen. Some reactions are non-IgE-mediated or result from direct mast cell activation. Degranulation releases histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and other mediators that cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability with fluid shift, bronchoconstriction, and myocardial depression. The result is rapid loss of intravascular volume, distributive shock, and airway compromise. Adrenaline counteracts these effects through vasoconstriction, bronchodilation, and stabilisation of mast cells. With prompt recognition and early adrenaline most patients recover, but delayed treatment or severe refractory shock can be fatal or cause hypoxic organ injury; identifying and avoiding the trigger prevents recurrence.

Peripheral arterial disease — PAD, peripheral vascular disease, PVD, lower limb arterial disease Lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication Deep vein thrombosis and chronic venous insufficiency Musculoskeletal or arthritic leg pain Peripheral neuropathy Chronic compartment syndrome Nerve root compression or sciatica Ankle-brachial index measurement, with exercise testing if resting values are equivocal Duplex ultrasound to localise and grade stenoses CT or MR angiography, or invasive angiography, to plan revascularisation Assessment of cardiovascular risk factors including lipids, glucose, and smoking status Toe-brachial index or other measures when arteries are incompressible Wound and infection assessment in patients with ulcers or tissue loss PAD is atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the limbs, most often the lower extremities, and is a marker of widespread atherosclerosis with high cardiovascular risk The classic symptom is intermittent claudication, exertional muscle pain in the calf, thigh, or buttock that is relieved by rest, though many patients are asymptomatic or have atypical leg symptoms Examination may reveal diminished or absent pulses, arterial bruits, cool skin, hair loss, and delayed capillary refill The ankle-brachial index is a simple, key bedside test; a reduced value confirms obstruction, while an abnormally high or incompressible value suggests medial calcification, common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease Critical limb ischaemia, with rest pain, non-healing ulcers, or gangrene, indicates severe disease that threatens the limb and warrants urgent vascular assessment Acute limb ischaemia is a vascular emergency presenting with the classic features of a suddenly painful, pale, pulseless, cold limb with sensory and motor changes Management emphasises aggressive cardiovascular risk reduction, structured exercise, and antiplatelet and statin therapy, with revascularisation for lifestyle-limiting or limb-threatening disease Because PAD reflects systemic atherosclerosis, coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease should be actively addressed MEDICAL EMERGENCY: acute limb ischaemia with a painful, pale, pulseless, cold limb and sensory or motor deficit requiring urgent revascularisation Critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, non-healing ulceration, or gangrene threatening the limb Rapidly progressive tissue loss or signs of spreading infection in an ischaemic foot Sudden onset of severe leg symptoms suggesting embolic occlusion Relying on a normal or high ankle-brachial index in patients with incompressible calcified vessels, as in diabetes or renal disease Attributing exertional leg pain to musculoskeletal or neurogenic causes and missing PAD Focusing on the limb while neglecting the high coronary and cerebrovascular risk Failing to recognise acute limb ischaemia as an emergency requiring urgent revascularisation PAD is usually caused by atherosclerosis, in which lipid-laden plaque progressively narrows the arterial lumen and limits blood flow to the limbs. When demand rises with exertion, a flow-limiting stenosis cannot meet the increased oxygen requirement of exercising muscle, producing the ischaemic pain of claudication. As disease advances, resting perfusion becomes inadequate, causing rest pain, impaired wound healing, ulceration, and tissue loss (critical limb ischaemia). Acute limb ischaemia results from sudden occlusion by thrombosis of a diseased segment or by embolism, abruptly interrupting flow and threatening tissue viability within hours. Limb prognosis is often stable in claudication with good risk-factor control, but PAD signals a substantially elevated risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular death; critical and acute limb ischaemia carry high risks of amputation and mortality without timely intervention.

Peripheral nerve injury — PNI, peripheral nerve lesion, traumatic neuropathy, nerve injury Radiculopathy or plexopathy Entrapment neuropathy such as carpal or cubital tunnel syndrome Motor neuron disease or other central cause of weakness Generalised peripheral polyneuropathy Compartment syndrome affecting nerve and muscle Tendon rupture mimicking motor loss Detailed motor and sensory examination to localise and grade the lesion Nerve conduction studies and electromyography, timed appropriately after injury to assess severity and reinnervation Serial examination for an advancing Tinel sign as evidence of regeneration Imaging such as ultrasound or MRI to define nerve continuity and identify compression or neuroma Assessment for coexisting vascular or musculoskeletal injury in trauma Peripheral nerve injuries are graded by severity using the Seddon classification of neurapraxia, axonotmesis, and neurotmesis, and the more detailed Sunderland scheme, which together guide prognosis and management Neurapraxia is a conduction block with intact axons that usually recovers fully; axonotmesis involves axonal disruption with preserved connective tissue framework and slow recovery; neurotmesis is complete transection that generally requires surgical repair Clinical assessment maps motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits to the affected nerve and helps localise the lesion and estimate its completeness Electrodiagnostic studies are most informative after a few weeks, once Wallerian degeneration is established, and are useful for confirming the lesion, grading severity, and tracking reinnervation Rehabilitation emphasises preventing complications during recovery: maintaining joint range of motion, protective splinting, skin care in insensate areas, and preventing contracture and disuse An advancing Tinel sign along the nerve over successive examinations is a helpful bedside indicator of regenerating axons Axonal regrowth proceeds slowly at roughly a millimetre per day, so recovery of distal muscles can take many months and the muscle must remain viable for reinnervation to be useful Neuropathic pain following nerve injury is managed with neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids and antidepressants alongside therapy, and surgical exploration or nerve transfer is considered when there is no recovery within the expected window Suspected complete nerve transection or a sharp penetrating injury that may need early surgical exploration and repair Signs of compartment syndrome in an acutely painful, tense limb Rapidly progressive or multifocal deficits suggesting a systemic or inflammatory neuropathy Vascular compromise accompanying the nerve injury No sign of recovery within the expected timeframe, warranting reassessment for surgery Performing electrodiagnostic studies too early, before Wallerian degeneration makes findings interpretable Missing a transection that requires timely surgical repair Allowing contractures and joint stiffness to develop during the long recovery period Neglecting skin protection in areas rendered insensate by the injury Failing to reassess and refer for surgery when expected recovery does not occur Peripheral nerve injury disrupts axonal continuity and myelin to varying degrees depending on the mechanism, whether compression, traction, laceration, or ischaemia. In neurapraxia there is focal demyelination and conduction block without axonal loss. When axons are disrupted, the segment distal to the injury undergoes Wallerian degeneration, and regeneration then proceeds from the proximal stump along preserved endoneurial tubes, guided by Schwann cells and neurotrophic signals. The integrity of the connective tissue sheaths determines whether regrowing axons reach their correct targets; disrupted architecture leads to misdirection, neuroma formation, and incomplete recovery. Prognosis depends chiefly on the injury grade: neurapraxia typically recovers fully within weeks to months, axonotmesis recovers slowly and often incompletely, and neurotmesis requires surgical repair with outcomes limited by the distance to the target and the age of the patient. More proximal injuries and delayed treatment carry a poorer outlook because muscle may atrophy irreversibly before reinnervation occurs.

Peripheral Neuropathy — polyneuropathy, peripheral nerve disease Inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy - Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute) and CIDP (chronic/relapsing) (Pattern 1) (Harrison 22e p.3595) Cryptogenic/idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy (CSPN) - no etiology found in about half of patients despite extensive evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3595) Diabetes mellitus and other metabolic neuropathies (DSPN, autonomic, radiculoplexus/Bruns-Garland, mononeuropathies) (Harrison 22e p.3604) Hereditary neuropathies - Charcot-Marie-Tooth, HSAN, familial amyloid polyneuropathy, SORD neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3596) Vasculitic neuropathy presenting as mononeuropathy multiplex (Pattern 3) (Harrison 22e p.3596) Uremic neuropathy in renal failure (~60% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.3605) Nutritional/toxic neuropathies (B12, thiamine, alcohol, drugs, chemotherapy, heavy metals) (Harrison 22e p.3611) Sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy - paraneoplastic (anti-Hu), Sjogren's syndrome, CANVAS, cisplatin, vitamin B6 toxicity (Pattern 9) (Harrison 22e p.3596) Connective tissue/autoimmune disease - rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma, sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.3605) HIV infection - distal symmetric polyneuropathy, AIDP/CIDP, progressive polyradiculopathy, multiple mononeuropathies, sensory ganglionopathy (Harrison 22e p.3606) Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) - most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America; mononeuropathies or symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3606) Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) - facial neuropathy (bilateral in ~half, unlike idiopathic Bell's palsy), polyradiculoneuropathy, multiple mononeuropathies (Harrison 22e p.3606) Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) - toxin-mediated neuropathy 3-4 weeks after infection (Harrison 22e p.3606) Other infectious/inflammatory causes producing CSF pleocytosis in suspected GBS/CIDP - HIV, Lyme, sarcoidosis, lymphomatous/leukemic root infiltration (Harrison 22e p.3598) Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG to localize (mono- vs polyneuropathy vs radiculopathy/plexopathy) and classify as axonal vs demyelinating (Harrison 22e p.3597) Autonomic testing (heart rate response to deep breathing, Valsalva, tilt-table, quantitative sudomotor axon reflex) for pure small-fiber or autonomic neuropathy when routine NCS are normal (Harrison 22e p.3597) Baseline labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal and hepatic function, fasting glucose and HbA1c, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR, rheumatoid factor, ANA, SPEP with immunofixation, and serum/urine free light chains (Harrison 22e p.3597) Oral glucose tolerance test in painful sensory neuropathy even when fasting glucose and HbA1c are normal (abnormal in ~one-third) (Harrison 22e p.3597) Serum free light chains and kappa/lambda ratio (more sensitive than SPEP/immunofixation) and skeletal survey if amyloidosis or monoclonal gammopathy suspected; hematology referral for marrow biopsy (Harrison 22e p.3597) Vasculitis workup for mononeuropathy multiplex: ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis serology, Lyme Western blot, HIV, occasionally CMV titer (Harrison 22e p.3598) Lumbar puncture in suspected GBS/CIDP for elevated CSF protein (pleocytosis should be absent in idiopathic cases) (Harrison 22e p.3598) Antibodies to SS-A/Ro, SS-B/La, and antineuronal nuclear (anti-Hu) antibodies in sensory ataxia/ganglionopathy; nerve biopsy reserved mainly for suspected amyloid or vasculitis and only when NCS are abnormal; skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3598) Motor neuron disease (e.g., ALS) - asymmetric distal weakness without sensory loss, especially with upper motor neuron findings (Pattern 5) (Harrison 22e p.3596) Multifocal motor neuropathy - treatable mimic of motor neuron disease (Harrison 22e p.3596) Radiculopathy, plexopathy, and compressive/entrapment mononeuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3596) Neuromuscular junction disorders - myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3596) Myopathy, including isolated neck extensor myopathy (Harrison 22e p.3596) Combined system degeneration - distal sensory signs plus symmetric upper motor neuron involvement from B12, copper, or vitamin E deficiency, severe hepatic disease, or adrenomyeloneuropathy (Pattern 6) (Harrison 22e p.3597) Critical illness polyneuropathy versus critical illness myopathy in the ICU patient who cannot be weaned from the ventilator (Harrison 22e p.3606) Three goals in the patient with neuropathy: localize the lesion, identify the cause, and determine treatment; the assessment is structured around seven key questions covering systems involved, distribution of weakness, nature of sensory loss, upper motor neuron signs, temporal evolution, hereditary clues, and associated medical conditions (Harrison 22e p.3595). Pattern recognition is central: length-dependent symmetric distal sensory loss (Pattern 2) points to diabetes/metabolic, drugs, toxins, alcohol, hereditary causes; symmetric proximal AND distal weakness with sensory loss (Pattern 1) is the hallmark of acquired immune demyelinating polyneuropathy (GBS and CIDP); asymmetric/multifocal deficits (Pattern 3, mononeuropathy multiplex) suggest vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, amyloid, sarcoid, or infection (Harrison 22e p.3596). Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG distinguish axonal degeneration (low-amplitude potentials, relatively preserved distal latencies and conduction velocities, fibrillations on EMG) from segmental demyelination (slow conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, relatively preserved amplitudes, no fibrillations) (Harrison 22e p.3597). Nonuniform slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion on NCS suggests an ACQUIRED demyelinating neuropathy (GBS or CIDP), whereas uniform slowing suggests a HEREDITARY demyelinating neuropathy (e.g., CMT type 1) (Harrison 22e p.3597). Pure loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration/position sense, normal strength and reflexes, and normal NCS indicates a small-fiber neuropathy; the most commonly identified causes are diabetes mellitus or glucose intolerance, with amyloid neuropathy also to be considered (Harrison 22e p.3596). Dramatic proprioceptive/vibratory loss with normal strength, especially when non-length-dependent (arms more than legs or asymmetric), points to a sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy (Pattern 9) rather than a typical length-dependent polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3597). Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in developed countries; distal symmetric sensory/sensorimotor polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form, beginning in the toes and ascending (Harrison 22e p.3604). Diabetic third nerve palsies are characteristically pupil-sparing (Harrison 22e p.3604). Rapidly progressive symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss (Pattern 1) - acute (GBS) or chronic (CIDP) demyelinating neuropathy; GBS can require respiratory support, so identifying this treatable pattern is critical (Harrison 22e p.3596) Acute/subacute course (days to weeks) - GBS, vasculitis, diabetic or Lyme radiculopathy require prompt evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3597) Autonomic dysfunction without diabetes (orthostatic drop without compensatory tachycardia, bowel/bladder/sexual dysfunction) - should raise concern for amyloid polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3595) Mononeuropathy multiplex pattern - suggests vasculitis and warrants an urgent vasculitis workup (Harrison 22e p.3596) Severe sensory ataxia from a ganglionopathy - consider paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, often small-cell lung cancer); the neuropathy can precede detection of malignancy and should prompt a cancer search (Harrison 22e p.3598) Missing a treatable cause - acquired demyelinating neuropathy (GBS/CIDP) and multifocal motor neuropathy are treatable and should be distinguished from untreatable mimics such as ALS (Harrison 22e p.3596) Overlooking treatable systemic/metabolic causes such as B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, or a paraprotein/monoclonal gammopathy in an apparently idiopathic polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3597) B12-deficiency neuropathy can occur with only peripheral findings and without anemia or macrocytosis (lacking in up to 40%); check methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when suspicion is high (Harrison 22e p.3612) Routine antiganglioside autoantibody panels have no proven added value beyond a complete clinical exam and detailed EDx, and a heavy metal screen is not a useful blind screening test without exposure history or suggestive findings (Harrison 22e p.3598) Nerve biopsy rarely distinguishes one neuropathy from another beyond clinical exam and NCS; reserve it for suspected amyloid or vasculitis and only when NCS are abnormal (Harrison 22e p.3598) A hereditary neuropathy can be missed when patients have marked sensory signs but few sensory symptoms plus slowly progressive distal weakness and skeletal clues (high/flat arches, hammer toes, scoliosis); examining family members may be needed (Harrison 22e p.3597) Peripheral nerves contain mixed sensory, motor, and autonomic fibers grouped as large myelinated, small myelinated, and small unmyelinated classes; motor axons are usually large myelinated fast-conducting (~50 m/s) fibers, large-diameter sensory fibers carry proprioception and vibration, and small myelinated/unmyelinated fibers carry pain, temperature, and autonomic signals. Disease may target the neuronal cell body (neuronopathy/ganglionopathy), the myelin sheath (myelinopathy/demyelination), or the axon (axonopathy), each producing distinct clinical and electrophysiologic features. Most generalized polyneuropathies are length-dependent axonopathies producing distal (glove-and-stocking) deficits, whereas ganglionopathies produce non-length-dependent loss. Demyelination slows or blocks conduction; axonal loss reduces response amplitudes (Harrison 22e p.3594). Most neuropathies are insidious and slowly progressive; course may be monophasic, progressive, or relapsing (e.g., CIDP, porphyria). Despite extensive evaluation, about half of patients have no etiology identified (cryptogenic/idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy). Outcome depends heavily on cause: treatable acquired demyelinating neuropathies (GBS, CIDP) and treatable systemic causes can respond to therapy, whereas axonal degeneration tends to recover slowly and incompletely. Even with adequate cobalamin replacement, treatment of B12-deficiency neuropathy usually does not fully reverse deficits and at least 50% of patients retain some permanent neurologic deficit (Harrison 22e p.3595, p.3612). No formal numeric severity score is used; characterization is by anatomic/electrophysiologic classification rather than a grading scale - by fiber type affected (motor, sensory, autonomic, or combined; large- vs small-fiber), by distribution (mononeuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex, polyneuropathy, radiculopathy, plexopathy; ten clinical patterns in Table 457-2), by underlying pathology (axonal degeneration vs segmental demyelination on NCS/EMG, Table 457-3), and by temporal course (acute: days to 4 weeks; subacute: 4-8 weeks; chronic: >8 weeks) (Harrison 22e p.3595, p.3597).

and trismus Needle aspiration to confirm and localise pus Full blood count and inflammatory markers Contrast CT of the neck when deep neck space extension is suspected or examination is limited Airway assessment and monitoring in severe cases A collection of pus in the peritonsillar space, usually a complication of acute tonsillitis, most common in young adults Presents with severe unilateral sore throat, progressively worsening odynophagia, fever and marked malaise Classic signs include trismus, a muffled hot-potato voice, drooling and foul breath Examination shows a bulging, congested soft difficult, so vigilance for airway compromise is essential Untreated infection can spread to the parapharyngeal space and beyond, risking deep neck infection and airway obstruction Signs of airway compromise such as stridor, respiratory distress, severe trismus or drooling requiring urgent airway management Rapid spread into parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spaces indicating deep neck infection Neck swelling, torticollis or signs of vascular involvement Systemic sepsis or failure to improve after drainage and antibiotics Underestimating airway risk in a patient with severe trismus and drooling Treating with antibiotics alone when pus requires drainage Missing extension into deep neck spaces Failing to arrange follow-up and consider interval tonsillectomy in recurrent cases Peritonsillar abscess develops when infection extends beyond the tonsillar capsule into the loose peritonsillar space between the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle, typically as a progression of acute tonsillitis or from obstructed minor salivary (Weber) glands. Cellulitis in this space evolves into a localised collection of pus, most often at the upper pole. The expanding abscess pushes the tonsil and soft palate medially, irritates the pterygoid muscles to cause trismus, and can dissect into adjacent deep neck spaces, threatening the airway and vascular structures. With timely drainage and antibiotics the outlook is good, but delayed treatment can lead to airway obstruction, deep neck space infection, mediastinitis or vascular complications, which carry significant risk.

Periventricular nodular heterotopia — PVNH, periventricular heterotopia, subependymal heterotopia, FLNA (filamin A), ARFGEF2 Subependymal nodules of tuberous sclerosis, which may calcify and enhance Subependymal spread of tumour or subependymoma Subcortical band heterotopia and other heterotopia patterns Tuberous sclerosis complex more broadly Grey-matter signal artefact along the ventricle Polymicrogyria with associated heterotopia Brain MRI to identify grey-matter-signal nodules lining the ventricles and any cortical involvement Molecular genetic testing including FLNA analysis and, where indicated, ARFGEF2 Cardiac evaluation with echocardiography and aortic imaging in FLNA-related disease Assessment for bleeding tendency and connective-tissue features in FLNA variants Electroencephalography to characterise focal epilepsy Developmental and cognitive assessment A malformation of neuronal migration in which nodules of grey matter fail to migrate and remain lining the walls of the lateral ventricles On MRI the nodules follow grey-matter signal on all sequences, are typically smooth and rounded, and do not enhance, distinguishing them from subependymal tumours The classic form is X-linked, caused by FLNA (filamin A) variants, and is often bilateral and nodular; it is usually lethal in males, so most affected individuals are female FLNA-related heterotopia carries systemic associations including cardiovascular anomalies such as aortic and valvular disease, and a bleeding or connective-tissue tendency, warranting cardiac surveillance The autosomal recessive form due to ARFGEF2 is associated with microcephaly and more severe developmental impairment Many individuals present in adolescence or adulthood with focal epilepsy and otherwise normal or near-normal intellect, particularly in the FLNA form Diagnosis is by MRI recognition of grey-matter nodules along the ventricular margin combined with targeted genetic testing Aortic dilatation, valvular disease, or other cardiovascular complications in FLNA-related heterotopia Bleeding tendency associated with filamin A dysfunction Drug-resistant focal epilepsy Microcephaly with severe developmental impairment suggesting the ARFGEF2 form Mistaking heterotopic nodules for the enhancing, sometimes calcified subependymal nodules of tuberous sclerosis Failing to arrange cardiovascular surveillance in FLNA-related disease Overlooking X-linked inheritance and its implications for male fetal loss and family counselling Attributing new focal seizures in an adult to another cause without considering heterotopia on MRI Periventricular nodular heterotopia results from failure of neurons to migrate away from the germinal (ventricular) zone during cortical development, so that collections of neurons persist as nodules along the ependymal lining of the lateral ventricles. The X-linked form is caused by variants in FLNA, which encodes filamin A, an actin-binding protein required for the cytoskeletal dynamics that drive early neuronal migration and also important in vascular and connective tissue, explaining the cardiovascular associations. The autosomal recessive ARFGEF2 form disrupts vesicle trafficking needed for migration and proliferation, producing microcephaly with heterotopia. In the common FLNA-related form, many individuals have normal or near-normal cognition with focal epilepsy that is often manageable, though cardiovascular and vascular complications can affect long-term health. The ARFGEF2 form and syndromic presentations carry a poorer neurodevelopmental prognosis.

Persistent depressive disorder — dysthymia, dysthymic disorder, chronic depression, PDD Major depressive disorder, episodic type Bipolar disorder, particularly bipolar II, in a depressive phase Cyclothymic disorder Hypothyroidism and other chronic medical illness Substance-induced or medication-induced mood disorder Adjustment disorder with prolonged stressor Personality traits or disorder contributing to chronic dysphoria Structured suicide risk assessment Standardised depression rating scales to track chronic severity Thyroid function testing Full blood count and metabolic panel to exclude medical contributors Screening for hypomanic or manic episodes Substance use screening The defining feature is chronically depressed mood present more days than not for at least two years in adults, or one year in children and adolescents, with fewer symptom-free intervals Associated symptoms may include poor appetite or overeating, sleep disturbance, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and feelings of hopelessness Because symptoms are long-standing, patients often regard the low mood as part of their personality and may not recognise it as a treatable illness A major depressive episode can be superimposed on the chronic baseline, a pattern often described as double depression, which increases severity and risk Suicide risk is present and should be assessed actively despite the seemingly milder day-to-day picture Management combines evidence-based psychotherapy with antidepressant pharmacotherapy, and chronic forms may need longer treatment to achieve and maintain response Screen for a history of hypomania or mania and for medical contributors such as hypothyroidism before attributing chronic low mood solely to a primary mood disorder Functional impairment accumulates over years, so early recognition and sustained treatment can substantially improve quality of life Active suicidal ideation with plan, intent, or access to means Emergence of a superimposed major depressive episode with worsening severity Emerging manic or hypomanic symptoms after starting an antidepressant Profound self-neglect or loss of function Assuming chronic low mood is fixed personality rather than a treatable disorder Underestimating suicide risk because symptoms appear mild day to day Missing a superimposed major depressive episode (double depression) Failing to screen for bipolarity before antidepressant treatment Ending treatment too early given the chronic, relapsing nature of the condition Persistent depressive disorder shares much of the neurobiology of major depression, with contributions from genetic vulnerability, monoamine dysregulation, and altered stress-axis and neuroplastic signalling, but is characterised by chronicity. Early adversity, ongoing psychosocial stressors, temperament, and reinforced negative cognitive styles are thought to sustain the persistent low-grade mood disturbance over years. Persistent depressive disorder is by definition chronic and can be more treatment-resistant than episodic depression, with high rates of relapse and comorbidity. Prognosis improves with sustained combined treatment and psychosocial support, but is worse with early onset, superimposed major depression, and untreated comorbid conditions.

Perthes' disease — Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, coxa plana Transient synovitis (irritable hip) Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the hip Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (in older children) Developmental dysplasia of the hip Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Skeletal dysplasia or epiphyseal dysplasia (especially if bilateral) Hypothyroidism and avascular necrosis from other causes (e.g. sickle cell disease, steroids) Anteroposterior and frog-lateral radiographs of both hips to assess and stage the changes MRI for early detection before radiographic changes appear and to assess the extent of necrosis Clinical assessment of hip range of movement, particularly abduction and internal rotation Investigations to exclude infection or inflammatory arthritis when the presentation is acute Consideration of bilateral or systemic workup (e.g. thyroid function, skeletal survey) if presentation is atypical or bilateral An idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children, typically presenting between about 4 and 8 years and more common in boys Presents with a limp and hip, groin, or referred knee pain, often intermittent, with restricted abduction and internal rotation of the hip Knee pain in a child can be referred from the hip, so the hip must always be examined in a limping child Early radiographs may be normal; later changes include increased femoral head density, fragmentation, flattening, and eventual remodelling The key aims are to relieve symptoms, maintain hip movement, and keep the femoral head 'contained' within the acetabulum so it remodels into a congruent, spherical shape Younger children with more remaining growth and greater remodelling potential generally have a better prognosis than older children Treatment ranges from observation, activity restriction, and physiotherapy to containment by bracing or surgery (femoral or pelvic osteotomy) in more severe or older cases Bilateral or atypical presentations should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses such as skeletal dysplasia or hypothyroidism Fever, systemic upset, and an acutely irritable hip suggesting septic arthritis requiring urgent exclusion Bilateral or atypical disease suggesting skeletal dysplasia or an underlying systemic cause Marked loss of hip movement and femoral head extrusion indicating a head at risk of permanent deformity An older child at presentation, associated with a poorer remodelling capacity Attributing a child's knee pain to the knee and failing to examine the hip Assuming a normal early radiograph excludes the disease and missing early presentation on MRI Not distinguishing Perthes' disease from septic arthritis in the acutely painful hip Overlooking bilateral involvement that should prompt evaluation for an underlying systemic disorder Perthes' disease results from a temporary interruption of the blood supply to the immature femoral head epiphysis, causing avascular necrosis. The precise trigger is unknown but the epiphysis undergoes a sequence of ischaemic necrosis, followed by fragmentation and resorption of dead bone, then reossification and remodelling as revascularisation occurs. During the biologically 'plastic' necrotic and fragmentation phases the softened femoral head is vulnerable to deformation under load, and can flatten and enlarge (coxa magna) or become incongruent if not well contained within the acetabulum. The ultimate shape of the healed head, and hence long-term function, depends on how well sphericity and containment are preserved through this self-limiting but prolonged process. The disease is self-limiting and many younger children with limited head involvement remodel to a near-normal, congruent hip; however, older children, extensive necrosis, and a poorly contained or deformed femoral head are associated with residual incongruity and an increased risk of premature hip osteoarthritis in adulthood.

Pertussis (Whooping Cough) — whooping cough, Bordetella pertussis Bordetella parapertussis (causes a similar but typically milder illness; does not express pertussis toxin gene) (p.1276). Bordetella holmesii (found in up to 20% of patients with a pertussis-like syndrome using improved PCR) (p.1276). Mycoplasma pneumoniae (p.1280). Chlamydia pneumoniae (p.1280). Adenovirus (p.1280). Influenza virus and other respiratory viruses (p.1280). Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus -- isolated from patients with clinical pertussis but probably represent co-infection, particularly in children under 1 year (p.1280). Bordetella parapertussis infection (p.1280) Bordetella holmesii infection (p.1276) Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection (p.1280) Chlamydia pneumoniae infection (p.1280) Adenovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viral infections (p.1280) Nasopharyngeal culture (Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium) -- gold standard owing to 100% specificity; cultures become positive by day 5 of incubation (p.1279). PCR / multitarget real-time PCR -- has replaced culture in most laboratories due to greater sensitivity and faster (hours) results; differentiates B. pertussis, B. parapertussis, and B. holmesii (p.1279). Nasopharyngeal aspiration is the best specimen; B. pertussis is highly sensitive to drying so specimens must be inoculated without delay or placed in transport medium (p.1279). Complete blood count for lymphocytosis (informative in young children, not in adolescents/adults) (p.1279). Serology -- enzyme immunoassays for IgA/IgG to pertussis toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, pertactin, and fimbriae; increasingly used in adolescents, adults, and those symptomatic >4 weeks; single-specimen anti-pertussis-toxin serology is becoming standardized, especially for outbreaks and surveillance (p.1279). ACE inhibitor-induced cough (p.1280) Reactive airway disease (p.1280) Gastroesophageal reflux disease (p.1280) Acute respiratory tract infection caused by Bordetella pertussis; 'pertussis' means 'violent cough' and the inspiratory whoop at the end of a paroxysm gives the disease its common name (p.1276). Classic course runs through three stages: catarrhal phase (1-2 weeks of coryza, lacrimation, mild cough, low-grade fever, malaise, indistinguishable from a common cold), then paroxysmal phase (frequent spasmodic bursts of 5-10 coughs within a single expiration), then convalescent phase (p.1278-1279). Paroxysms may end in an audible whoop produced by rapid inspiration against a closed glottis; post-tussive vomiting is frequent and a mucous plug may be expelled (p.1279). During a coughing spasm there may be neck-vein distension, bulging eyes, tongue protrusion, and cyanosis; paroxysms can be precipitated by noise, eating, or physical contact and are often worse at night (p.1279). Between attacks the patient looks normal but shows increasing fatigue; fever is uncommon and, when present, suggests bacterial superinfection (p.1279). The convalescent phase lasts 1-3 months with gradual resolution; for 6-12 months afterward, intercurrent viral infections may trigger a recrudescence of paroxysmal cough (p.1279). Incubation period averages 7-10 days (p.1279). The whoop is variable: uncommon in infants 6 months of age or younger and frequently absent in older children and adults (p.1276). Lymphocytosis (absolute lymphocyte count >108-109/L) is common in young children and unusual with other infections, but is not a feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279). Highly communicable: attack rates of 80-100% among unimmunized household contacts; cyclical outbreaks occur every 3-5 years despite widespread immunization (p.1277). Severe morbidity and high mortality are restricted almost entirely to infants; in the US (2000-2017) infants under 2 months accounted for 84% of pertussis deaths (p.1278). Apnea in infants (occurred in 27.1% of children under 2 years hospitalized with pertussis) (p.1279). Cyanosis during coughing spasms (p.1279). Seizures and encephalopathy, thought to result from hypoxia of paroxysms/apnea (p.1278-1279). Very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension in young infants -- frequently associated with death (p.1278). Pneumonia (occurs in up to 22% of infants with pertussis) (p.1278-1279). Infants, especially those under 2-3 months, carry the highest risk of complications and death and should generally be hospitalized (p.1278, 1279). In adolescents and adults the presentation is often atypical -- frequently no paroxysmal cough or whoop -- so pertussis is a commonly missed cause of prolonged cough; B. pertussis may be the agent in 12-30% of adults whose cough does not improve within 2 weeks (p.1278). Antibiotic therapy aims to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage; it does NOT substantially alter the clinical course unless given early in the catarrhal phase (p.1279). Cough suppressants are NOT effective and have no role in management; beta-adrenergic agonists and glucocorticoids have been advocated but are NOT proven effective (p.1280). Lymphocytosis is helpful in young children but is NOT a reliable feature in adolescents and adults (p.1279). There is only a small window for culture/PCR diagnosis because much of the period of organism recovery is during the catarrhal phase when pertussis is not yet suspected (p.1279). Cross-reactivity of antigens such as filamentous hemagglutinin and pertactin among Bordetella species makes diagnosis based on seroconversion of a single antibody type unreliable (p.1279). Suspect pertussis in any patient with a cough not improving within 14 days, a paroxysmal cough of any duration, cough followed by vomiting (adolescents/adults), or respiratory symptoms after contact with a laboratory-confirmed case (p.1280). Waning vaccine-derived immunity (faster with acellular vaccines) underlies resurgent outbreaks even in fully immunized older children, adolescents, and adults (p.1278). Infection begins with attachment of B. pertussis to ciliated epithelial cells of the nasopharynx, mediated by surface adhesins (pertactin, filamentous hemagglutinin) binding integrin-family proteins, probably with pertussis toxin. The organism multiplies locally and produces toxins causing mucosal damage (tracheal cytotoxin, dermonecrotic toxin); host defense is impaired by pertussis toxin and adenylate cyclase-hemolysin toxin. There is local cellular invasion with intracellular persistence, but systemic dissemination does NOT occur; systemic manifestations such as lymphocytosis result from the toxins. The cause of the hallmark paroxysmal cough is not known; a pivotal role for pertussis toxin has been proposed but not confirmed. Neurologic events (seizures, encephalopathy) are thought to result from hypoxia due to coughing paroxysms or apnea rather than from specific bacterial products. Deaths in young infants are frequently associated with very high leukocytosis and pulmonary hypertension (p.1278). With universal childhood immunization, reported cases fell by >90% and mortality declined even more dramatically. Severe morbidity and high mortality remain almost entirely restricted to infants; WHO estimates ~40 million cases and ~400,000 deaths globally each year, mostly among infants under 3 months. Immunity after natural infection is NOT lifelong; immunity after whole-cell vaccination is short-lived (little protection after 10-12 years) and wanes even faster (within 2-4 years of the fifth or sixth dose) in those immunized with acellular vaccines (p.1277-1278).

Peters anomaly — anterior segment dysgenesis, Peters anomaly with corneal opacity, PAX6, central corneal leukoma with iridocorneal adhesions Congenital glaucoma with corneal oedema and clouding Sclerocornea and other congenital corneal opacities Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome within the anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy Birth-related corneal injury with Descemet tears Mucopolysaccharidoses and metabolic corneal clouding Examination under anaesthesia with slit-lamp assessment of the cornea and anterior segment Intraocular pressure measurement and gonioscopy to detect glaucoma and angle anomalies Anterior segment imaging or ultrasound biomicroscopy to define adhesions and lens position Systemic and dysmorphology assessment for Peters-plus features Molecular genetic testing of anterior segment dysgenesis genes where indicated A form of anterior segment dysgenesis defined by a central corneal opacity (leukoma) with a defect in the underlying corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane Iridocorneal or keratolenticular adhesions strand from the iris or lens to the back of the corneal opacity Presents in the newborn with central corneal clouding, and may be unilateral or bilateral Glaucoma is a frequent and important association, so intraocular pressure must be assessed and monitored Peters-plus syndrome adds systemic features such as short stature, developmental delay and cleft lip or palate Implicated developmental genes include PAX6, PITX2, FOXC1 and CYP1B1, reflecting overlap with other anterior segment dysgenesis disorders Dense bilateral corneal opacity threatens vision through both media opacity and deprivation amblyopia Raised intraocular pressure indicating associated glaucoma Dense bilateral corneal opacity risking irreversible deprivation amblyopia Progressive corneal decompensation or worsening opacity Systemic features suggesting Peters-plus syndrome requiring paediatric evaluation Failing to detect and treat associated glaucoma, a major cause of poor outcome Overlooking amblyopia management alongside surgical treatment of the opacity Assuming an isolated eye disorder and missing Peters-plus systemic features Underestimating the difficulty and risks of paediatric corneal transplantation Peters anomaly is a developmental defect of the anterior segment arising from abnormal migration and differentiation of neural-crest-derived tissues that form the cornea, iris and anterior chamber angle. Failure of normal separation of the lens and iris from the developing cornea leaves a central defect in the corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane, producing a central opacity, and persistent adhesions between the iris or lens and the posterior cornea. Disruption of the same developmental structures frequently affects the drainage angle, predisposing to glaucoma. Mutations in transcription-factor and related developmental genes underlie many cases and account for the overlap with the broader anterior segment dysgenesis spectrum. Prognosis depends on the density and laterality of the opacity and on glaucoma control; milder unilateral cases may retain useful vision, while dense bilateral disease has a guarded outlook even after corneal transplantation, which carries high rejection and complication rates in infants.
