abdominal pain with vomiting suggesting intussusception or small-bowel obstruction Gastrointestinal bleeding or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia from bleeding polyps New breast, pancreatic or gastrointestinal symptoms in an affected adult raising concern for malignancy Precocious puberty or gynaecomastia suggesting a hormonally active gonadal tumour Attributing periorificial pigmentation to benign freckling and missing the diagnosis, especially as macules fade in adults Underestimating small-bowel polyp burden by relying on colonoscopy and gastroscopy alone Failing to begin multi-organ cancer surveillance, including breast and pancreatic screening, at recommended ages Not testing and counselling at-risk relatives Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is caused by germline inactivating variants in STK11, which encodes a serine-threonine kinase (also called LKB1) that regulates cellular energy metabolism, polarity and growth largely through the AMP-activated protein kinase and mTOR pathways. Loss of STK11 tumour-suppressor function, typically with a somatic second hit, disrupts these regulatory signals and drives the development of hamartomatous polyps and an elevated risk of multiple epithelial malignancies. The mucocutaneous pigmentation reflects abnormal melanocyte behaviour associated with the underlying genetic defect. The syndrome carries a high cumulative lifetime risk of malignancy across several organs, so long-term prognosis depends heavily on adherence to structured surveillance and early intervention. Polyp-related complications such as intussusception contribute significant morbidity, particularly in younger patients.

Peyronie Disease — Peyronie disease, Peyronie's disease, penile fibrosis, induratio penis plastica, penile curvature disorder Congenital penile curvature (present since puberty, no plaque) Penile fracture or acute trauma Penile cancer or other penile mass Dorsal vein thrombosis of the penis Erectile dysfunction from other causes Lymphangiosclerosis of the penis Focused history and palpation of the plaque in the flaccid state Objective measurement of curvature during an induced or photographically documented erection Penile duplex ultrasound to characterise plaque, calcification, and vascular status where relevant Assessment of erectile function using validated questionnaires Evaluation for associated conditions such as diabetes and Dupuytren contracture Peyronie disease is an acquired fibrotic disorder of the tunica albuginea of the penis, producing a palpable plaque, penile curvature, and sometimes pain, deformity, and shortening It typically presents in middle-aged men and can cause difficulty with penetration and considerable psychological distress The disease has two phases: an active (acute) phase with pain and evolving deformity, and a stable (chronic) phase in which the curvature and plaque have plateaued Erectile dysfunction commonly coexists and should be assessed, as it influences both distress and treatment choice It is associated with penile trauma or microtrauma during intercourse and with other fibrosing conditions such as Dupuytren contracture, as well as with diabetes Diagnosis is largely clinical from the history and palpation of the plaque, supplemented by objective assessment of curvature, often after inducing an erection Non-surgical options during the active phase and for milder deformity include oral and injectable therapies and traction, aiming to reduce curvature and stabilise disease Surgery is reserved for stable disease with functionally significant deformity and includes plication, plaque incision or excision with grafting, or penile prosthesis when erectile dysfunction is also present Intervention decisions should await disease stability, since operating during the active phase risks recurrence and further change Rapidly enlarging or atypical penile mass raising concern for malignancy Acute severe pain with deformity suggesting penile fracture rather than Peyronie disease Deformity severe enough to prevent intercourse or urinary function Significant psychological distress or relationship impact Progressive deformity that has not stabilised, indicating ongoing active disease Operating during the active, unstable phase and risking recurrence Overlooking coexisting erectile dysfunction that alters the treatment approach Mistaking congenital curvature, which lacks a plaque, for Peyronie disease Failing to address the psychological impact on the patient and partner Assuming a penile mass is a benign plaque without excluding malignancy when features are atypical Peyronie disease is thought to begin with repetitive microtrauma to the tunica albuginea, most often during sexual activity, in a susceptible individual. The injury triggers an aberrant, exaggerated wound-healing response with local inflammation, fibroblast activation, and deposition of disorganised collagen and elastin. This forms a fibrous, sometimes calcified, plaque that is less elastic than the surrounding tunica. During erection the inelastic segment fails to expand normally, bending the penis toward the plaque and producing the characteristic curvature and deformity. Over time inflammation subsides and the plaque matures and stabilises, marking the transition to the chronic phase. The natural history is variable: a minority of men improve spontaneously, many stabilise with residual deformity, and a proportion progress. Pain from the active phase usually resolves over time. With appropriate treatment tailored to disease phase and severity, most men can achieve functional improvement, and surgery in stable disease offers reliable correction of significant curvature, though some penile shortening or altered sensation may persist.

hydrocephalus during follow-up Pfeiffer syndrome is driven by activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 or 2 that amplify FGF signalling in cranial sutures and limb buds. Excess receptor activity promotes premature suture ossification and disturbs the development of the digits, producing broad, deviated thumbs and great toes with variable soft-tissue syndactyly. The degree of receptor activation broadly tracks with clinical severity, so the more disruptive FGFR2 changes tend to cause the multisuture, cloverleaf-skull phenotypes with greater neurological compromise. Type 1 disease generally has a favourable outcome with normal cognition after craniofacial management, whereas types 2 and 3 carry high early morbidity and mortality from airway, brain and visual complications and demand intensive multidisciplinary care.

Phantom limb pain — PLP, phantom pain, post-amputation pain Residual limb (stump) pain from neuroma Prosthetic-related mechanical pain or pressure injury Residual limb infection or wound breakdown Ischaemia of the residual limb Referred pain from the spine or proximal joints Heterotopic ossification in the residual limb Clinical history and examination distinguishing phantom pain from stump pain and non-painful phantom sensation Inspection and palpation of the residual limb for neuroma, tenderness, and prosthetic fit Imaging of the residual limb where neuroma, heterotopic ossification, or bony spur is suspected Vascular assessment if ischaemia of the residual limb is a concern Assessment for infection when there are local inflammatory signs or wound problems Phantom limb pain is painful sensation perceived in a limb or body part that has been amputated, and must be distinguished from non-painful phantom sensation and from residual limb (stump) pain Most amputees experience some phantom phenomena; pain often begins within the first days to weeks after amputation and may follow a telescoping pattern where the phantom seems to shorten over time Pre-amputation limb pain and its intensity are recognised risk factors, and the phantom pain may echo the character of the pain felt before surgery Careful examination of the residual limb is essential to separate phantom pain from stump pain caused by neuroma, poor prosthetic fit, infection, or ischaemia Non-pharmacological approaches including mirror therapy, graded motor imagery, desensitisation, and early prosthetic use address the cortical reorganisation thought to drive the pain Pharmacological principles favour neuropathic agents such as gabapentinoids and certain antidepressants, with opioids reserved and used cautiously A multidisciplinary rehabilitation approach that combines prosthetic training, psychological support, and pain management gives the best functional outcomes Perioperative and preventive analgesic strategies may reduce the likelihood or severity of later phantom pain Residual limb signs of infection or wound dehiscence requiring urgent treatment Features of critical ischaemia in the residual limb Rapidly worsening or new pain pattern suggesting an alternative surgical or vascular cause Severe intractable pain with mood deterioration and suicidal ideation Confusing phantom pain with stump pain and missing a treatable neuroma or prosthetic-fit problem Neglecting early prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation, which can worsen cortical reorganisation Dismissing patient reports of pain in an absent limb as psychological Over-reliance on opioids for a fundamentally neuropathic pain problem Overlooking pre-amputation pain control that could reduce later phantom pain Phantom limb pain arises from maladaptive changes at multiple levels of the nervous system after amputation. Peripherally, injured axons form neuromas that generate ectopic and spontaneous discharge. In the spinal cord, deafferentation leads to central sensitisation and disinhibition of dorsal horn neurons. Within the brain, the somatosensory and motor cortices undergo reorganisation, with cortical territory representing the missing limb being invaded by adjacent regions; the degree of this remapping correlates with pain intensity. Psychological factors and pre-existing pain memory further modulate the experience. Phantom pain often diminishes in frequency and intensity over the months to years following amputation, and many patients cope well with a combination of therapy and prosthetic use. A subset develop persistent, treatment-resistant pain that requires ongoing multidisciplinary management.

psychiatric illness in adolescence or adulthood New seizures requiring evaluation Absent pain perception masking serious injury or intra-abdominal pathology Significant renal or cardiac anomaly identified on screening Labelling the presentation as idiopathic autism without performing microarray and SHANK3 testing Missing a parental balanced translocation and giving incorrect recurrence-risk advice Overlooking reduced pain perception, which can delay recognition of injury or illness Not anticipating and monitoring for regression and psychiatric change in later life Phelan-McDermid syndrome results from loss of functional SHANK3 at chromosome 22q13.3, either through a terminal deletion of varying size or a pathogenic sequence variant. SHANK3 encodes a scaffolding protein at the postsynaptic density of excitatory synapses that organises glutamatergic signalling, so its haploinsufficiency impairs synapse formation and function, producing hypotonia, developmental delay, absent speech, and autistic features. Larger deletions remove additional genes, contributing to more extensive systemic and dysmorphic features and greater phenotypic severity. Developmental disability and speech impairment are lifelong and most individuals need substantial support, while the risk of adolescent or adult regression and psychiatric illness adds long-term uncertainty. Larger deletions tend to correlate with greater severity, and multidisciplinary care improves quality of life.

Phenylketonuria — PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, hyperphenylalaninaemia Tetrahydrobiopterin (cofactor) deficiency disorders Transient hyperphenylalaninaemia of the newborn Other inborn errors of metabolism presenting with developmental delay Non-metabolic causes of intellectual disability and seizures Tyrosinaemia Newborn bloodspot screening for elevated phenylalanine Quantitative plasma amino acids (phenylalanine and tyrosine) Tetrahydrobiopterin loading test and pterin studies to exclude cofactor defects Dihydropteridine reductase activity measurement Genetic analysis of the PAH gene Serial blood phenylalanine monitoring to guide dietary treatment An autosomal recessive inborn error of amino acid metabolism caused most often by deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. Untreated, accumulation of phenylalanine causes progressive and irreversible intellectual disability, seizures, and behavioural problems. Affected infants are typically normal at birth, so detection relies on newborn screening rather than clinical signs. Classic untreated features can include a musty or mousy body odour, eczema, and reduced pigmentation with fair hair and skin. Early diagnosis through screening and prompt dietary treatment prevent the neurological damage almost entirely. Treatment centres on a lifelong low-phenylalanine diet with a special protein substitute, guided by regular monitoring of blood phenylalanine levels. A subset of patients respond to the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (sapropterin), and disorders of biopterin metabolism must be excluded as a separate cause of high phenylalanine. Maternal PKU with poorly controlled phenylalanine during pregnancy can damage the fetus, causing microcephaly, congenital heart disease, and developmental delay, so strict control is essential before and during pregnancy. Lifelong follow-up in a metabolic service supports adherence and long-term neurocognitive outcomes. Markedly elevated phenylalanine levels requiring urgent dietary intervention Seizures or neurological deterioration in an untreated infant Poor metabolic control during pregnancy (maternal PKU) risking fetal harm Failure of phenylalanine to fall despite dietary treatment, suggesting a cofactor defect Signs of nutritional deficiency from an overly restricted diet Assuming a normal newborn appearance excludes the diagnosis Failing to exclude tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency as a treatable alternative cause Relaxing dietary control in older children and adults, risking cognitive and neuropsychiatric effects Overlooking the need for strict preconception and pregnancy control in affected mothers Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or, less commonly, of its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor) blocks the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Phenylalanine therefore accumulates in blood and tissues and is diverted to alternative metabolites such as phenylketones. High phenylalanine levels are neurotoxic to the developing brain, interfering with amino acid transport across the blood-brain barrier, neurotransmitter synthesis, and myelination, producing the intellectual disability and neurological features of untreated disease. Reduced tyrosine availability also limits synthesis of melanin, contributing to hypopigmentation. With early diagnosis and consistent dietary control, cognitive development is normal or near-normal; delayed treatment or poor lifelong control leads to irreversible neurocognitive impairment, and maternal control critically affects offspring.

Phaeochromocytoma crisis — Plasma/urine metanephrines CT/MRI adrenals Paroxysmal severe hypertension — alpha-blockade before beta Cushing's syndrome and other secondary causes of hypertension (more common than pheochromocytoma, so the classic triad is frequently misleading) (p.2140). Thyrotoxicosis / hyperthyroidism (overlapping palpitations, sweating, tremor; an endocrine cause of palpitations) (palpitations chapter). Panic / anxiety disorder and somatization (episodic palpitations, sweating, sense of doom mimicking paroxysms) (palpitations chapter). Stimulant toxicity — cocaine, amphetamines and related catecholaminergic drugs (produce hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, microvascular ischaemia resembling pheochromocytoma) (cardiomyopathy chapter). Systemic mastocytosis / mast-cell activation (flushing, palpitations, hypotensive episodes) (mastocytosis chapter). Blood and 24-hour urinary catecholamine measurement (in addition to plasma/urine metanephrines) (p.2140). Functional/positron emission tomography (PET) imaging in addition to CT/MRI of the abdomen for localisation (p.2140). Nuclear localisation with 131-I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scanning, e.g. for extra-adrenal/cardiac paraganglioma (cardiac-tumour chapter). Genetic evaluation when a hereditary predisposition is suspected (MEN2/RET, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, hereditary paraganglioma syndromes) (p.2140). Systemic mastocytosis — flushing and palpitation attacks; urinary metanephrines help exclude pheochromocytoma when evaluating mast-cell symptoms (mastocytosis chapter). Carcinoid tumour — overlapping flushing/paroxysmal symptoms; assessed together with metanephrines in differential testing (mastocytosis chapter). Stimulant (cocaine/amphetamine) toxicity producing a catecholaminergic crisis with hypertension and arrhythmia (cardiomyopathy chapter). Takotsubo (stress / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy — catecholamine-mediated, can follow a surge resembling pheochromocytoma (cardiac trauma / cardiomyopathy chapters). The classic triad is episodic headache, palpitations and sweating (diaphoresis) occurring with paroxysmal hypertension (p.2140). Most patients present with hypertension at a relatively young age, often between 30 and 50 years (p.2140). Many patients have only non-specific symptoms; the florid paroxysmal presentation is not universal, so the diagnosis is easily missed (p.2140). Catecholamine-secreting tumours arise from chromaffin cells: roughly 80-85% are in the adrenal medulla, the remainder being extra-adrenal paraganglioma in paraganglion tissue (p.2140). Patients with pheochromocytoma frequently have postural (orthostatic) hypotension despite the hypertension, reflecting volume contraction and impaired sympathetic reflexes (cardiomyopathy chapter). Catecholamine excess can produce a hyperdynamic state and palpitations, and is one of the recognised endocrine causes alongside thyrotoxicosis and mastocytosis (palpitations chapter). Pheochromocytoma in crisis is named alongside aortic dissection and eclampsia as a hypertensive emergency demanding particularly rapid management; control blood pressure with a titratable IV agent (p.2141). Very labile blood pressure and heart rate with episodic palpitations occurring together with new heart failure should raise suspicion of pheochromocytoma (cardiomyopathy chapter). Coexisting postural hypotension with paroxysmal hypertension is a clue to catecholamine excess rather than essential hypertension (cardiomyopathy chapter). Representativeness-heuristic trap: clinicians overestimate the probability of pheochromocytoma when the classic headache-palpitations-sweating triad is present, because they neglect its low prevalence relative to common causes of hypertension; the triad also occurs in patients who do not have the tumour (clinical-reasoning chapter, p.~? — diagnostic reasoning). Conversely, non-specific or atypical presentations can lead to the diagnosis being missed entirely (clinical-reasoning chapter). Postural hypotension may be wrongly attributed to over-treatment of hypertension rather than recognised as a catecholamine-excess clue (cardiomyopathy chapter). Excess production of catecholamines, usually by a benign neuroendocrine tumour of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (80-85%) or in extra-adrenal paraganglion tissue (paraganglioma). The catecholamine surge drives paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and cardiac arrhythmias, and produces a hyperdynamic catecholaminergic state. Chronic/episodic catecholamine exposure can cause microvascular myocardial ischaemia (microinfarcts similar to those seen with stimulant toxicity) and a catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy; the same mechanism of sudden catecholamine release underlies stress (takotsubo / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy (hypertension, cardiomyopathy and cardiac-tumour chapters). A benign tumour is usual; definitive treatment is surgical extirpation (complete or partial adrenalectomy, typically minimally invasive), which is generally curative. Surgery requires prior alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade. Untreated catecholamine excess can precipitate hypertensive emergency, arrhythmia, catecholamine cardiomyopathy and heart failure (hypertension and cardiomyopathy chapters).

Pheochromocytoma — Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, PPGL, Paraganglioma, Chromaffin cell tumor Essential hypertension Anxiety/panic attacks (may be mistaken for psychiatric illness) Cocaine or amphetamine use Mastocytosis or carcinoid syndrome (usually without hypertension) Intracranial lesions Clonidine withdrawal Autonomic epilepsy Factitious crises (sympathomimetic amine use) For an asymptomatic adrenal mass: nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma, aldosteronoma, cortisol-producing adenoma (Cushing's syndrome) 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (high sensitivity for initial screening) Plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive, least stress-confounded) Contrast CT or T2-weighted MRI with gadolinium for localization (MRI somewhat better for extra-adrenal disease) Functional imaging: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT and 18F-DOPA PET/CT (very high sensitivity and specificity, >95%) 123I/131I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG PET, useful in hereditary and metastatic disease Immunohistochemistry (chromogranin, synaptophysin, S-100, SDHB) on resected tissue Universal germline genetic panel testing Postoperative documentation of catecholamine normalization and ACTH stimulation test after bilateral cortex-sparing surgery Essential hypertension with adrenergic features Panic disorder / anxiety attacks Sympathomimetic drug effect (cocaine, amphetamines) Carcinoid syndrome and systemic mastocytosis Clonidine or other antihypertensive withdrawal Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) are catecholamine-producing tumors arising from sympathetic (adrenal medulla, sympathetic trunk) or parasympathetic (carotid body, glomus tympanicum/jugulare/vagale) paraganglia; by WHO usage pheochromocytoma denotes the adrenal tumor and paraganglioma denotes tumors at all other sites. The classic triad is episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating, present in roughly one-third of patients; the combination of this triad with hypertension makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis, though tumors can remain asymptomatic for years. Hypertension is the dominant sign and may be paroxysmal (classic) or sustained (also common); paroxysms generally last under one hour. The classic 'rule of tens' states that about 10% are bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, and 10% metastatic. Diagnosis rests on two equally important pillars: biochemical documentation of catecholamine excess and imaging localization of the tumor. Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive biochemical test and are less prone to false-positive elevation from stress including venipuncture; most tumors continuously leak O-methylated metabolites even when catecholamine secretion fluctuates. Values three times the upper limit of normal make the diagnosis highly likely regardless of assay; because the tumor is rare, borderline elevations are more likely to be false positives, so drug/dietary confounders should be excluded and testing repeated. On unenhanced CT, an adrenal mass with attenuation below 10 Hounsfield units makes pheochromocytoma unlikely; about 5% of adrenal incidentalomas prove to be pheochromocytomas on endocrine evaluation. Histology classically shows a 'Zellballen' pattern of neuroendocrine chief cell nests with peripheral sustentacular cells; chief cells stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin, sustentacular cells for S-100, and loss of SDHB staining suggests an underlying germline SDH mutation. About 25-33% of patients have an inherited syndrome (MEN 2, VHL, NF1, paraganglioma syndromes, TMEM127, MAX); these patients present on average about 15 years younger than those with sporadic tumors. Universal germline panel testing is the gold standard and identifies a genetic cause in up to about 30% of cases, with higher yield in early onset, extra-adrenal, multiple, or metastatic tumors or a family history. Pheochromocytoma in pregnancy may produce adrenergic crises, possibly via hCG/LHCG-receptor-mediated stimulation of epinephrine production, and is challenging to manage. Catecholamine crisis causing heart failure, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, or intracranial hemorrhage Paroxysms precipitated by surgery, anesthesia/intubation, positional change, exercise, micturition (bladder paraganglioma), pregnancy, or drugs (tricyclics, opiates, metoclopramide) Paradoxical hypertensive response to antihypertensive drugs Beta blockade given before adequate alpha blockade (risk of worsened hypertension) Hypertensive crisis or adrenergic crisis during pregnancy Features suggesting a hereditary syndrome (early onset, bilateral/multifocal, extra-adrenal, family history, MTC, retinal/CNS/renal tumors) Borderline biochemical elevations are frequently false positives given tumor rarity; failing to exclude dietary/drug confounders (sympathomimetics, diuretics, tricyclics, alpha/beta blockers, levodopa withdrawal) and repeat testing leads to overdiagnosis. Serial catecholamine levels vary widely due to fluctuating secretion, so reliance on a single catecholamine measurement can miss the diagnosis; metanephrines are continuously leaked. Starting a beta blocker before adequate alpha blockade can precipitate severe hypertension. FNA of a presumed adrenal mass that is actually a pheochromocytoma can provoke a crisis. Standard histologic atypia, mitoses, and local invasion do not reliably establish malignancy. Symptoms can be misattributed to a primary psychiatric/panic disorder. NF1 germline mutations are essentially never found in sporadic pheochromocytoma, so NF1 testing is unnecessary without other neurofibromatosis features. Sequencing protocols may miss large single- or multi-exon deletions. PPGLs are well-vascularized neuroendocrine tumors derived from chromaffin cells of the sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglial system. They synthesize and store catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine), and tumoral release drives the clinical syndrome; the name pheochromocytoma reflects the dark staining produced by chromaffin oxidation of catecholamines. The etiology of sporadic tumors is unknown, but 25-33% carry germline mutations. Susceptibility genes fall into three pathogenetic clusters: cluster 1 (pseudohypoxia: SDHx, FH, VHL, HIF2A), cluster 2 (kinase signaling: RET, NF1, TMEM127, MAX, HRAS, KIF1B-beta, PDH), and cluster 3 (Wnt signaling: CSDE1, MAML3). Most genes act as tumor suppressors with biallelic inactivation, while RET is a protooncogene whose mutations activate receptor tyrosine kinase activity; SDH is a Krebs-cycle/mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme, and the VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin E3 ligase whose loss upregulates cell-cycle, glucose metabolism, and oxygen-sensing pathways. Complete tumor removal is potentially curative and can prevent lethal hypertensive crises. About 5-10% of PPGLs are metastatic; histologic criteria alone are insufficient to define malignancy, and the WHO now uses 'metastatic' (lymph node or distant spread, commonly to lung, bone, or liver) rather than 'malignant.' The prognosis of metastatic disease is variable with 5-year survival of roughly 30-60%. Hereditary syndromes influence risk: about one-third of PGL4 (SDHB) patients develop metastases, the highest rate among the associated syndromes, and metastatic disease also occurs notably with VHL, NF1, and PGL1. Malignancy/recurrence risk is assessed by markers including tumor size >5 cm, the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS), the Grading system for Adrenal Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma (GAPP), and SDHB status, although these remain controversial. Disease is now categorized by the WHO as localized versus metastatic (regional lymph node or distant metastasis) rather than benign versus malignant.

Phimosis — non-retractile foreskin, preputial stenosis, tight foreskin Paraphimosis Balanitis or balanoposthitis Balanitis xerotica obliterans (lichen sclerosus) Preputial adhesions (physiological) Penile carcinoma or premalignant lesion Meatal stenosis Clinical examination of the foreskin, glans, and meatus Assessment for the cicatricial white ring of lichen sclerosus Urinalysis if infection or voiding symptoms are present Histological examination of excised preputial tissue after circumcision, particularly when lichen sclerosus or malignancy is suspected Phimosis is an inability to retract the foreskin over the glans; it is physiological in most infants and young boys and usually resolves as natural preputial separation occurs with age Pathological (acquired) phimosis follows scarring from recurrent balanitis, forced retraction, or the skin condition balanitis xerotica obliterans (lichen sclerosus), producing a firm white cicatricial ring It must be distinguished from paraphimosis, in which a retracted foreskin becomes trapped behind the glans and cannot be reduced, causing painful swelling and constituting an emergency Symptoms may include ballooning of the foreskin on voiding, difficulty with hygiene, recurrent infection, painful erections, and, in severe cases, obstructive voiding Physiological phimosis is managed conservatively with reassurance, gentle hygiene, and avoidance of forcible retraction, often supplemented by topical corticosteroid application to soften the ring Balanitis xerotica obliterans is an important pathological cause that typically requires circumcision and histological confirmation, and can involve the meatus and urethra Circumcision or preputioplasty is indicated for true pathological phimosis, recurrent balanoposthitis, or troublesome symptoms not responding to conservative measures Persistent phimosis in adults, particularly with lichen sclerosus, is a risk factor for penile carcinoma and warrants careful examination of the glans Paraphimosis with a trapped, swollen, painful glans requiring emergency reduction Severe phimosis causing obstructed voiding or acute urinary retention Suspicious glans lesion or induration suggesting penile carcinoma Features of lichen sclerosus with meatal or urethral involvement Forcibly retracting a young boy's physiological phimosis, which can cause scarring and true phimosis Mislabelling normal developmental non-retractility as pathological and recommending unnecessary surgery Missing lichen sclerosus or an underlying penile malignancy in an adult with acquired phimosis Confusing phimosis with paraphimosis and delaying emergency reduction Overlooking meatal stenosis in patients with lichen sclerosus after circumcision In physiological phimosis the foreskin is non-retractile simply because natural adhesions between the inner prepuce and glans have not yet separated and the preputial opening is developmentally narrow. Pathological phimosis results from fibrosis and scarring of the preputial ring, most often due to chronic or recurrent inflammation (balanoposthitis), repeated trauma from forced retraction, or lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans), an inflammatory dermatosis that causes progressive sclerosis. The scarred, inelastic ring restricts retraction and may obstruct the urinary stream. Physiological phimosis almost always resolves with growth and conservative care; pathological phimosis is effectively cured by circumcision, but lichen sclerosus can recur or involve the meatus and carries a long-term association with penile malignancy.

as obstructive lung disease (barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing) The jugular venous pressure is the single most important bedside measurement for estimating volume status; the internal jugular vein is preferred over the external because the latter is valved and not directly in line with the superior vena cava and right atrium. Using the sternal angle (angle of Louis) as the reference point systematically underestimates central venous pressure, so it is better used to separate normal from elevated CVP than to quantify it; venous pulsations above the clavicle in the sitting position are clearly abnormal since the clavicle-to-right-atrium distance is at least 10 cm. The venous waveform is biphasic in sinus rhythm whereas the carotid pulse is monophasic; the venous pulse is not easily obliterated by palpation and changes with posture and inspiration, helping distinguish it from the arterial pulse. A cannon a wave occurs with atrioventricular dissociation when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve; in a wide-complex tachycardia, cannon a waves identify the rhythm as ventricular in origin. The a wave is absent in atrial fibrillation. Kussmaul's sign (a rise or lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration) is classically associated with constrictive pericarditis but also occurs with restrictive cardiomyopathy, massive pulmonary embolism, right ventricular infarction, and advanced left ventricular systolic heart failure, and is common after cardiac surgery. Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid pulse) suggests severe aortic stenosis, whereas a sharp rapidly collapsing carotid upstroke (Corrigan's or water-hammer pulse) points to chronic severe aortic regurgitation. Pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory fall in systolic pressure >10 mmHg) is seen in pericardial tamponade but also occurs with massive pulmonary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, severe obstructive lung disease, and tension pneumothorax; it reflects exaggerated interventricular dependence. Fixed splitting of S2 (a wide A2-P2 interval that does not vary with respiration) is characteristic of a secundum atrial septal defect, while reversed (paradoxical) splitting occurs with left bundle branch block, right ventricular pacing, severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, and acute myocardial ischemia. The mitral valve prolapse click-murmur complex moves away from S1 with maneuvers that increase preload (squatting) and closer to S1 on standing, a dynamic behavior that helps distinguish it from other systolic events. Lower extremity edema with an elevated JVP indicates volume overload (heart failure or constrictive pericarditis), whereas edema without jugular venous hypertension suggests hypoalbuminemia (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), venous insufficiency, or dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker use. Janeway lesions (nontender hemorrhagic macules on palms and soles) and Osler's nodes (tender nodules on finger/toe pads), along with splinter hemorrhages in the mid-nail bed, are peripheral signs of infective endocarditis. An ankle-brachial index (ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure) is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality; a >2% finger-to-toe oxygen saturation difference on pulse oximetry performs comparably for detecting lower extremity peripheral arterial disease. Markedly elevated JVP that does not pulsate with a dusky cyanotic head and neck, suggesting superior vena cava syndrome Pulsus paradoxus with elevated JVP and blunted y descent, suggesting pericardial tamponade An interarm systolic blood pressure difference >10 mmHg or femoral pulse delay, raising concern for aortic dissection or coarctation Differential cyanosis of the lower extremities with a large patent ductus and pulmonary hypertension (right-to-left shunting) New peripheral embolic stigmata with fever pointing toward infective endocarditis Orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia, suggesting autonomic insufficiency Using an inappropriately small blood pressure cuff overestimates pressure, while an oversized cuff underestimates it; the bladder should be about 80% of arm length and 40% of arm circumference. Examining the carotid upstrokes simultaneously, or before auscultating for a bruit, and applying heavy pressure can precipitate carotid hypersensitivity and syncope in susceptible elderly patients. A cervical bruit correlates poorly with the degree of carotid stenosis, and its absence does not exclude significant obstruction. Palpation alone is insufficiently accurate to diagnose an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and sensitivity falls with increasing body size. Homans' sign is neither sensitive nor specific for deep venous thrombosis. Arcus senilis lacks specificity as a marker of coronary heart disease risk. Physician-measured blood pressures tend to be higher than nurse- or self-recorded values, contributing to white coat hypertension; conversely masked hypertension can be missed when clinic pressures are normal despite target organ damage. Heart and pulse findings can be misleading in low cardiac output states and in stiffened arteries from aging, hypertension, or peripheral arterial disease. The cardiovascular examination derives diagnostic and prognostic information from the mechanical and hemodynamic consequences of cardiac and vascular disease. The jugular venous waveform reflects right atrial pressure dynamics: the a wave is presystolic right atrial contraction, the x descent is atrial relaxation, the c wave is the systolic bulging of the closed tricuspid valve, the v wave is atrial filling during ventricular systole, and the y descent is right atrial emptying after tricuspid opening. Reduced right ventricular compliance accentuates the a wave; tricuspid regurgitation accentuates the v wave with a rapid y descent and progressively 'ventricularizes' the waveform; obstruction to right ventricular inflow (tricuspid stenosis, tamponade) blunts or prolongs the y descent. Arterial pulse contour depends on stroke volume, ejection velocity, vascular compliance, and systemic vascular resistance, so fixed outflow obstruction blunts and delays the upstroke while wide pulse pressure states produce a bounding collapsing pulse. Heart sound intensity reflects valve leaflet excursion and mobility, ventricular contractility, and the PR interval, while the distance between the stethoscope and the cardiac event (obesity, lung disease, effusion) attenuates all sounds. Splitting of S2 depends on the relative timing of aortic and pulmonic valve closure, which is altered by conduction delays, shunts, and outflow obstruction. Bedside findings carry independent prognostic weight. In heart failure, an elevated JVP and a third heart sound predict the pulmonary artery wedge pressure and are associated with higher risk of heart failure hospitalization and death; an estimated right atrial pressure >10 mmHg predicted a wedge pressure >22 mmHg with high positive value in advanced heart failure. The ankle-brachial index is a powerful predictor of long-term cardiovascular mortality, and higher ambulatory systolic pressures independently predict cardiovascular events and all-cause death. Pulsus alternans indicates severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and when accompanied by electrocardiographic T-wave alternans the arrhythmic risk appears increased. No formal grading scale; specific findings convey severity within individual conditions (e.g., pulsus parvus et tardus and a soft A2 indicate severe aortic stenosis; the A2-opening snap interval in mitral stenosis is inversely proportional to the left atrial-left ventricular gradient; a JVP distance >4.5 cm above the sternal angle at 30 degrees, or any venous pulsation above the clavicle in the sitting position, is abnormal; orthostatic hypotension is a fall in systolic pressure >20 mmHg or diastolic >10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing).

Physiologic and Nonphysiologic Sinus Rhythm — Sinus tachycardia, Sinus arrhythmia, Sinus bradycardia, Inappropriate sinus tachycardia, IST, Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, POTS Focal atrial tachycardia arising near the sinus node (abrupt onset/offset favors AT) Premature atrial contractions causing rhythm irregularity (varying P-wave morphology) Inappropriate sinus tachycardia versus appropriate physiologic sinus tachycardia Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome Anxiety or panic disorder presenting with sinus tachycardia Fever or systemic infection driving appropriate (physiologic) sinus tachycardia Postviral autonomic dysfunction producing a POTS-like picture, including post-COVID-19 (long COVID) 12-lead ECG to confirm sinus P-wave morphology and axis Ambulatory / outpatient telemetry monitoring to distinguish gradual sinus tachycardia from paroxysmal atrial tachycardia Thyroid function testing to exclude hyperthyroidism as a reversible cause Hemoglobin / evaluation for anemia Orthostatic (supine-to-standing) heart rate and blood pressure assessment when POTS is suspected Invasive electrophysiology study in selected cases where the ECG distinction remains unclear Anemia Hyperthyroidism and other thyroid dysfunction Dehydration / volume depletion Pulmonary embolism Pheochromocytoma Decompensated heart failure or valvular disease Anxiety / panic attack Stimulant or drug effect (caffeine, sympathomimetics, cocaine, amphetamines, beta-blocker withdrawal) The sinus node sits at the lateral-superior junction of the right atrium and superior vena cava, within the upper portion of the crista terminalis where the smooth posterior wall (from the sinus venosus) meets the trabeculated anterior right atrium. Normal sinus rhythm runs between roughly 60 and 100 beats/min, with a sinus P wave that is upright in leads II, III, and aVF, negative in aVR, and initially positive/biphasic in V1, reflecting an inferiorly and leftward-directed frontal-plane axis. Sinus arrhythmia is a common, usually asymptomatic finding defined as a sinus-origin rhythm with P-P interval variation greater than 120 ms; when P-wave morphology also varies, premature atrial contractions rather than true sinus arrhythmia are the likely cause. Three patterns of sinus arrhythmia are described: respirophasic (vagal tone reflexively falls in inspiration and is restored in expiration), ventriculophasic (seen with heart block or after a PVC, where an interposed ventricular beat shortens the P-P interval), and nonphasic (P-P variation unrelated to cardiac or respiratory cycle). Sinus tachycardia (>100 beats/min) arises from sympathetic stimulation and/or vagal withdrawal; the earliest activation focus shifts more leftward toward the superior septal crista terminalis, producing taller inferior-lead P waves than in resting sinus rhythm. Sinus bradycardia is defined as a rate <60 beats/min but can be entirely normal during sleep and in physically fit individuals. A gradual rate rise with an identifiable trigger (such as exertion) favors sinus tachycardia, whereas abrupt onset and offset favor focal atrial tachycardia originating near the sinus node. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST) is an uncommon disorder of autonomic dysregulation in which the sinus rate climbs at rest or out of proportion to physiologic demand; it most often affects women in their third or fourth decade. POTS is defined by symptomatic sinus tachycardia on standing, with a rate increase of at least 30 beats/min or to >120 beats/min within 10 minutes of standing in the absence of hypotension. POTS can follow a viral illness and may resolve spontaneously over 3-12 months; a POTS-like autonomic picture has been described in prolonged post-COVID-19 (long COVID) syndromes. Distinguishing IST from POTS is clinically critical because they require fundamentally different management approaches; conflating them risks worsening symptoms. Asymptomatic sinus arrhythmia is physiologic, is not considered pathogenic, and does not warrant further cardiac evaluation. Sinus tachycardia accompanied by hypotension, impaired consciousness, angina, or heart failure, suggesting a serious underlying cause requiring urgent attention Unexplained or persistent sinus tachycardia mandating exclusion of pulmonary embolism, myocardial ischemia, and structural/functional cardiac disease before labeling it nonphysiologic Syncope or disabling palpitations accompanying tachycardia Sinus tachycardia as a possible marker of underlying systemic illness (e.g., infection, malignancy, endocrine disorder) or drug toxicity Mislabeling rhythm irregularity with varying P-wave morphology as sinus arrhythmia when it is actually premature atrial contractions. Diagnosing nonphysiologic sinus tachycardia before excluding reversible drivers such as anemia, thyroid disease, and pulmonary embolism. Failing to separate inappropriate sinus tachycardia from POTS, since blood-pressure-raising strategies appropriate for POTS are inappropriate for IST, and sinus node modification is ineffective for POTS and may worsen its nontachycardia features. Pursuing catheter-based sinus node modification for IST, which often yields poor long-term symptom control and can lead to symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, or chronotropic incompetence requiring a permanent pacemaker. Overtreating an asymptomatic, constitutionally elevated resting or exercise sinus rate with no identifiable underlying cause. Sinus rhythm originates from spontaneous depolarization of pacemaker cells in the sinus node at the right atrium-SVC junction within the crista terminalis. Heart rate is modulated by the autonomic balance between sympathetic input (which accelerates and shifts the activation focus) and parasympathetic (vagal) input (which slows the node). Sinus arrhythmia reflects normal beat-to-beat shifts in autonomic tone, classically respiratory-linked vagal modulation. Sinus tachycardia results from increased sympathetic drive and/or vagal withdrawal raising the rate of spontaneous nodal depolarization; when this is an appropriate response to exercise, stress, or illness it is physiologic. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is thought to stem from an imbalance between sympathetic and parasympathetic input to the node, altered membrane automaticity of sinus node cells, or both, though the precise mechanism remains poorly defined. POTS reflects orthostatic autonomic dysfunction, sometimes postviral. Sinus arrhythmia is benign and physiologic, requiring no treatment. Physiologic sinus tachycardia resolves with correction of the underlying condition and often needs no specific therapy. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia tends to be a chronic, often disabling condition that responds poorly to therapy and may be difficult to control long term. POTS frequently improves over time, and postviral POTS may resolve spontaneously within 3-12 months. Sinus tachycardia is rate-defined as >100 beats/min and sinus bradycardia as <60 beats/min, with normal sinus rhythm spanning 60-100 beats/min. POTS is defined diagnostically by an orthostatic heart-rate rise of >=30 beats/min (or to >120 beats/min) within 10 minutes of standing without hypotension. Sinus arrhythmia is defined by P-P interval variability >120 ms of sinus origin.

pilonidal disease Neglecting hair control and hygiene advice, allowing recurrence Failing to biopsy a chronic non-healing sinus Pilonidal disease is now regarded as an acquired condition in which loose hairs are driven into the skin of the natal cleft, provoking a foreign-body inflammatory reaction and forming midline pits. The pits become epithelialised sinuses that trap further hair and debris, leading to chronic infection, abscess formation, and secondary tracks extending laterally. Acute abscesses settle with drainage, but pilonidal disease is prone to recurrence. Definitive excisional and flap-based procedures improve healing and lower recurrence, and long-term outcome is strongly influenced by ongoing hair control and hygiene.

Pinta — Treponema carateum, carate, azul, mal del pinto Vitiligo (for late achromic lesions) Pityriasis versicolor and other superficial mycoses Other endemic treponematoses (yaws, bejel) Leprosy (hypopigmented patches) Post-inflammatory dyspigmentation Psoriasis or chronic eczema (for scaly plaques) Dark-field microscopy of scrapings from active lesions for spirochaetes Non-treponemal serology (e.g. RPR/VDRL) for activity and follow-up Treponemal serology (e.g. TPPA/TPHA) for confirmation Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain PCR of lesion material where available Assessment of close contacts in endemic communities Pinta is a chronic non-venereal treponematosis caused by Treponema carateum and is confined to the skin, occurring in remote rural areas of Central and South America Transmission is by prolonged direct skin-to-skin contact with lesion material, favoured by crowding and poor hygiene; it is not sexually transmitted Unlike the other endemic treponematoses, pinta affects only the skin and does not involve bone, viscera or the nervous system The primary lesion is an erythematous scaly papule or plaque that slowly enlarges, usually on exposed limbs Secondary lesions (pintids) are disseminated scaly patches that undergo striking colour changes, becoming blue, violet, brown then depigmented Late pinta is characterised by symmetrical achromic (depigmented) and atrophic patches that resemble vitiligo and are cosmetically disfiguring Diagnosis uses dark-field microscopy and treponemal/non-treponemal serology (indistinguishable from syphilis); treatment for the endemic treponematoses is benzathine penicillin Extensive disfiguring depigmentation causing psychosocial harm Diagnostic uncertainty with vitiligo or leprosy delaying treatment Positive syphilis serology raising confusion about venereal infection Persistence or spread of active lesions despite treatment Mistaking late depigmented lesions for vitiligo and missing a treatable infection Interpreting positive treponemal serology as venereal syphilis Expecting depigmented skin to re-pigment fully after treatment Failing to treat contacts and interrupt transmission Confusing pinta with other endemic treponematoses without regional context Treponema carateum enters through breaks in the skin during prolonged close contact. It multiplies locally to form the primary lesion and then, over months, produces disseminated secondary skin lesions (pintids) through local and lymphatic spread. The immune response and disturbance of melanocytes produce the characteristic sequence of dyschromic changes, progressing from hyperpigmentation to permanent depigmentation and skin atrophy in late disease. Because the organism does not disseminate to deep tissues, pinta remains a purely cutaneous disease throughout its course. Early and secondary pinta respond fully to penicillin, but late achromic and atrophic skin changes are often permanent and cosmetically disfiguring even after cure; the disease carries no systemic morbidity.

Hirschsprung disease Feeding difficulty with aspiration risk Mistaking the breathing episodes for primary epilepsy or a psychiatric disorder Confusing the phenotype with Angelman syndrome and stopping at negative methylation testing Overlooking severe constipation or Hirschsprung disease Attributing the sociable demeanour and hand stereotypies solely to autism without genetic testing Pitt-Hopkins syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of TCF4 (transcription factor 4), a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor essential for neuronal development and differentiation in the central nervous system. Loss-of-function point variants, intragenic deletions and larger chromosomal rearrangements reduce functional TCF4, disrupting the transcriptional programmes that govern brain development and autonomic control. This underlies the severe neurodevelopmental impairment, the distinctive breathing abnormality reflecting brainstem autonomic dysregulation, and the associated craniofacial and gastrointestinal features. Individuals have severe, lifelong intellectual disability and require continuous support, but the condition is generally compatible with survival into adulthood and is associated with a characteristically cheerful temperament. Breathing episodes, while alarming, are not usually life-limiting on their own.

emergency Haemodynamic instability and hyponatraemia from acute adrenal insufficiency requiring immediate corticosteroids Rapidly progressive or severe visual field loss needing urgent surgical decompression Declining conscious level or signs of raised intracranial pressure Withholding stress-dose steroids while awaiting hormone results in a suspected case Relying on CT alone and missing the diagnosis when MRI would reveal the lesion Mistaking the presentation for subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis and delaying endocrine treatment Failing to arrange long-term endocrine follow-up for evolving hormone deficiencies Pituitary apoplexy results from acute haemorrhage, infarction, or both within the pituitary gland, most commonly in an existing (often previously undiagnosed) adenoma. Rapid expansion of the gland within the confined sella and suprasellar space compresses adjacent structures: upward pressure on the optic chiasm impairs vision, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus affects the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens, and trigeminal branches. Sudden loss of functioning pituitary tissue precipitates hypopituitarism, with acute corticotroph failure being the immediate threat to life. Leakage of blood and necrotic material can also cause meningism. With prompt corticosteroid cover and, when indicated, timely decompression, visual and neurological recovery is often good; however, permanent hypopituitarism is common and delayed recognition of adrenal crisis can be fatal.

TRH stimulation may provoke atypical gonadotropin/subunit rise TSH-secreting adenoma: free T4, free T3, TSH, alpha-subunit (inappropriately normal/high TSH with high free T4/T3) Immunohistochemistry for hormones and cell-specific transcription factors on resected tissue for histologic confirmation Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia (antipsychotics esp. risperidone, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, estrogens, opiates, H2 blockers) Primary hypothyroidism causing reflex hyperprolactinemia Chronic renal failure and cirrhosis (reduced PRL clearance) Pregnancy, lactation, chest-wall stimulation, stress and sleep as physiologic PRL elevation Polycystic ovarian syndrome (overlap with FSH/LH-secreting tumor causing ovarian hyperstimulation) Iatrogenic/exogenous glucocorticoid excess mimicking Cushing's disease Ectopic ACTH or ectopic CRH secretion mimicking Cushing's disease Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma or adrenal hyperplasia as ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome Ectopic GHRH (bronchial/abdominal carcinoid) or rare ectopic GH causing acromegaly Pituitary adenomas are benign monoclonal neoplasms arising from one of the five anterior pituitary cell types; the secreted hormone (PRL, GH, ACTH, TSH, or LH/FSH) determines the clinical syndrome. About one-third are clinically nonfunctioning, most of these originating from gonadotrope or null cells (p.3003-3004). Hormone output does not reliably track tumor size: small secretory microadenomas can be highly symptomatic, whereas large adenomas producing little hormone may stay clinically silent until mass effects appear (p.3003). Suprasellar extension classically compresses the optic chiasm to produce bitemporal hemianopia, often worse superiorly, because crossing nasal ganglion-cell fibers in the ventral chiasm are most vulnerable; loss of red color perception can be an early sign (p.2998-2999). The 'stalk section' phenomenon: any sellar mass that compresses the pituitary stalk and portal vessels causes early hyperprolactinemia (typically 30-100 ug/L) with later loss of other anterior pituitary hormones, even when the mass itself is not a prolactinoma (p.2998-2999). Hyperprolactinemia is the most common pituitary hypersecretion syndrome; PRL levels above 200 ug/L almost always indicate a prolactin-secreting adenoma, while milder elevations are more often drug-induced, stalk-related, or due to hypothyroidism or renal failure (p.3004-3005). Microprolactinomas show a marked female predominance (~20:1) and present early with amenorrhea/galactorrhea/infertility, whereas macroprolactinomas have a near 1:1 sex ratio and men tend to present later with larger, invasive tumors and mass effects (p.3005-3006). Acromegaly is typically indolent and may go undiagnosed for a decade or more; acral and soft-tissue overgrowth (frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged hands/feet, coarse features) plus visceromegaly are characteristic, and GH excess before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism (p.3008-3009). Random single GH measurement is not diagnostic for acromegaly because of GH pulsatility; an age- and sex-matched IGF-1 is the screening test, and diagnosis is confirmed by failure of GH to suppress below threshold after an oral glucose load (p.3009). Cushing's disease (corticotrope adenoma) accounts for ~70% of endogenous Cushing's syndrome, is 5-10 times more common in women, and the tumors are usually small microadenomas, about half undetectable on MRI (p.3010-3011). Iatrogenic glucocorticoid use remains the most common overall cause of cushingoid features and must be excluded by history before pursuing an endogenous workup (p.3010). ACTH-secreting adenomas retain partial suppressibility by high-dose glucocorticoids, distinguishing them from ectopic ACTH sources; inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH (central:peripheral ratio >2 basal, >3 post-CRH) has >95% sensitivity for localizing a pituitary source (p.3011-3012). Nonfunctioning/gonadotrope adenomas are the most common adenoma type at presentation and are usually macroadenomas discovered through mass effect or as incidentalomas; mildly elevated PRL from stalk compression must not be mistaken for a true prolactinoma since these tumors do not shrink with dopamine agonists (p.3012-3013). Most pituitary glands harbor an unsuspected microadenoma at autopsy (up to one-quarter), and imaging detects clinically inapparent lesions (incidentalomas) in at least 10% of people; small nonsecretory intrasellar lesions can be safely followed with serial MRI (p.2999, p.3003). Progressive visual field loss or new bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression) Cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsy, diplopia, ptosis, or facial numbness indicating cavernous sinus invasion Severe sudden headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia suggesting pituitary apoplexy (intratumoral hemorrhage/infarction) Signs of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, papilledema, hydrocephalus Arginine vasopressin deficiency (polyuria) as a presenting feature, which suggests posterior pituitary involvement or a non-adenomatous lesion such as metastasis or germ cell tumor Rapid-onset hypercortisolism with hyperpigmentation, severe myopathy, and hypokalemic alkalosis suggesting an ectopic ACTH source Features of acute adrenal insufficiency from coexisting hypopituitarism Assuming PRL suppression by a dopamine agonist proves a prolactinoma: stalk-compression hyperprolactinemia from a nonfunctioning mass also falls with dopamine agonists even though the mass does not shrink.
