Attributing every small pituitary lesion to a secretory tumor: incidental microadenomas are very common, and ~50% of ACTH adenomas are MRI-occult, so imaging cannot reliably localize the ACTH source. Overlap in basal ACTH levels between pituitary and ectopic ACTH sources means ACTH measurement alone cannot distinguish them; dynamic testing or petrosal sampling is needed. Mistaking iatrogenic glucocorticoid excess for endogenous Cushing's syndrome. Headache severity correlates poorly with adenoma size; a small intrasellar tumor can cause significant headache while a large tumor may not. Pituitary adenomas are benign, almost always monoclonal neoplasms derived from a single anterior pituitary cell lineage, implying acquisition of somatic mutation(s) conferring a growth advantage. Hormonally active tumors secrete autonomously with reduced responsiveness to physiologic feedback. Several molecular events are implicated: about 35% of GH-secreting tumors carry activating Gs-alpha mutations that lower GTPase activity, raise cyclic AMP, and drive somatotrope proliferation; growth factors (bFGF, EGFR signaling, the latter linked to USP8 mutation in some ACTH tumors), activated oncogenes (RAS, PTTG), loss of suppressors (e.g., MEG3), and loss of negative feedback (as in primary hypothyroidism/hypogonadism) also contribute. Hypothalamic hormones GHRH and CRH can additionally stimulate mitotic activity, so ectopic GHRH/CRH-producing chest or abdominal tumors can cause somatotrope or corticotrope hyperplasia. Familial settings include MEN 1 (MENIN, 11q13), MEN 4 (CDKN1B), Carney complex (PRKAR1A), McCune-Albright (mosaic Gs-alpha), and familial acromegaly (AIP). Clinical effects arise both from hormone hyper-/hyposecretion and from local mass effect: dorsal expansion lifts the optic chiasm, stalk compression disrupts dopaminergic inhibition of lactotropes (hyperprolactinemia) and portal hormone delivery, and lateral extension into the cavernous sinus impairs cranial nerves III, IV, VI and trigeminal branches. Pituitary tumors are overwhelmingly benign and slow growing; true carcinomas with extracranial metastases are exceedingly rare. Outcomes depend on tumor type and size and require lifelong follow-up. Prolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normoprolactinemia and gonadal recovery in roughly 80% of microadenomas and tumor shrinkage in most macroadenomas; about 20% (especially men) are dopamine-resistant, and hyperprolactinemia may resolve spontaneously in up to 30% of hyperprolactinemic patients without a visible adenoma. Surgical PRL normalization reaches ~70% for microprolactinomas but only ~40% for macroadenomas, with substantial long-term recurrence (>50% for macroadenomas). In acromegaly, untreated GH excess roughly triples mortality and shortens survival by about 10 years, driven by cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory disease and increased colon cancer risk; transsphenoidal remission is ~70% for microadenomas and under 50% for macroadenomas. Cushing's disease has a microadenoma surgical remission of ~80% (<50% for macroadenomas), with ~5% biochemical recurrence and a postoperative period of ACTH deficiency. Untreated hypercortisolism carries excess mortality, chiefly cardiovascular, plus increased infection and suicide risk. Pituitary adenomas are conventionally classified by size into microadenomas (<10 mm) and macroadenomas (>=10 mm, often locally invasive with parasellar extension), and by secretory phenotype into functioning (lactotrope/PRL, somatotrope/GH, corticotrope/ACTH, thyrotrope/TSH, gonadotrope/FSH-LH, or plurihormonal) versus clinically nonfunctioning (frequently gonadotrope or null-cell). Sellar mass severity is further graded by anatomic impact in Table 392-1 (compression of pituitary, optic chiasm, hypothalamus, cavernous sinus, frontal lobe, or brain), as larger/invasive tumors carry higher surgical risk and lower cure rates.

Pityriasis Rosea — PR, pityriasis rosea of Gibert Secondary syphilis (especially with palm and sole involvement) Guttate psoriasis Tinea corporis (the herald patch can be mistaken for ringworm) Nummular eczema Drug-induced pityriasis rosea-like eruption Pityriasis lichenoides Diagnosis is clinical based on the herald patch and characteristic distribution Syphilis serology when the presentation is atypical or there are risk factors, or when palms and soles are involved Mycology to exclude tinea when a solitary herald patch is uncertain Review of medication history to identify a possible drug-induced eruption Skin biopsy reserved for persistent or diagnostically unclear cases A single larger oval plaque (the herald patch) commonly precedes the widespread eruption by days to a couple of weeks The secondary rash consists of smaller oval, salmon-coloured plaques with a fine trailing collarette of scale at the inner edge of the border Lesions align along skin cleavage lines on the trunk, producing the classic Christmas-tree pattern over the back It is often preceded or accompanied by a mild viral prodrome and is self-limiting, so reassurance is usually the mainstay of management Symptomatic itch can be eased with emollients, mild topical anti-inflammatory agents, and antihistamines; some evidence supports sunlight or phototherapy for extensive or itchy disease Because a widespread scaly eruption on the trunk can mimic secondary syphilis, palmar and plantar involvement or risk factors should prompt syphilis serology Consider a drug-induced pityriasis rosea-like reaction when the history includes a recently started medication or when features are atypical Counsel pregnant patients appropriately, as some data suggest an association between early-pregnancy disease and adverse outcomes Involvement of the palms and soles or a suggestive sexual history pointing to secondary syphilis Failure to resolve within the expected few months, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Atypical morphology or a temporal link to a new drug suggesting a drug-induced reaction Early-pregnancy disease, given a possible association with adverse pregnancy outcomes Overlooking secondary syphilis in a widespread scaly truncal eruption Mistaking the herald patch for tinea and treating with antifungals alone Failing to link an atypical eruption to a recently started drug Over-investigating or over-treating a self-limiting condition instead of reassuring the patient Pityriasis rosea is widely regarded as a self-limiting exanthem linked to reactivation of human herpesviruses 6 and 7, supported by the viral prodrome, seasonal clustering, and detection of viral markers in some patients. The eruption reflects a T-cell-mediated inflammatory response in the skin producing spongiotic dermatitis with focal parakeratosis, which accounts for the fine collarette of scale. The alignment of lesions along Langer's cleavage lines gives the distinctive distribution. A clinically indistinguishable pityriasis rosea-like eruption can be triggered by certain drugs and vaccines through a similar hypersensitivity mechanism. The condition is benign and self-limiting, typically clearing over several weeks to a few months without scarring; post-inflammatory pigment change may persist for a while, especially in darker skin, and recurrence is uncommon.

PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration — PLAN, PLA2G6, infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, INAD, NBIA type 2, atypical neuroaxonal dystrophy, PLA2G6-related dystonia-parkinsonism Other NBIA subtypes, especially PKAN and BPAN Leukodystrophies with early regression and spasticity Mitochondrial encephalopathies (including Leigh syndrome) Cerebellar ataxias of early childhood Young-onset Parkinson disease and other genetic parkinsonism (for the adult form) Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses Brain MRI to show cerebellar atrophy and, with iron-sensitive sequences, later pallidal and nigral iron PLA2G6 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Electrophysiology and nerve conduction studies reflecting axonal involvement Ophthalmological assessment and electroretinography for optic atrophy and visual pathway involvement Serum caeruloplasmin, copper, and ferritin to distinguish other NBIA subtypes and Wilson disease Autosomal recessive NBIA subtype caused by biallelic variants in PLA2G6, encoding a calcium-independent phospholipase A2 Spans a spectrum from classic infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy through atypical childhood forms to adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy presents in the first years with psychomotor regression, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and visual impairment with optic atrophy Characteristic pathology is widespread axonal spheroids (dystrophic axonal swellings) throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems Cerebellar atrophy is an early and prominent MRI feature, and brain iron accumulation in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra develops later, often not present at first imaging Iron-sensitive MRI sequences help detect the later basal ganglia iron that classifies the disorder within the NBIA group The adult-onset form can resemble idiopathic Parkinson disease with dystonia, cognitive decline, and neuropsychiatric features Diagnosis is confirmed by PLA2G6 molecular testing supported by the imaging evolution; care is symptomatic Rapid developmental regression with loss of vision and motor skills in an infant Progressive bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk New seizures or status epilepticus Acute respiratory compromise from progressive neuromuscular weakness Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal early MRI when brain iron has not yet accumulated Missing the early cerebellar atrophy that is often the first imaging clue Attributing adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism to idiopathic Parkinson disease without considering a genetic cause Overlooking the peripheral nervous system involvement when interpreting neurophysiology PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration arises from biallelic variants in PLA2G6, which encodes a calcium-independent phospholipase A2 that remodels membrane phospholipids and maintains membrane integrity. Loss of enzyme function disturbs phospholipid homeostasis and mitochondrial membrane maintenance, leading to lipid peroxidation and progressive axonal degeneration with the formation of dystrophic axonal spheroids. Over time secondary iron accumulates in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, placing the disorder within the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation spectrum, though early in the disease iron deposition may be absent. The classic infantile form is relentlessly progressive, typically leading to severe disability and death in childhood, whereas atypical and adult-onset forms progress more slowly over years to decades. No disease-modifying therapy is currently available.

Placenta Accreta Spectrum — placenta accreta, placenta increta, placenta percreta, morbidly adherent placenta, PAS, abnormally invasive placenta Simple placenta praevia without abnormal invasion Uterine atony causing postpartum haemorrhage Retained placenta without morbid adherence Placental abruption Uterine scar dehiscence or rupture Gestational trophoblastic disease Detailed obstetric ultrasound including transvaginal assessment of the lower segment and colour Doppler of the placental bed Pelvic MRI when depth of invasion, posterior placentation, or bladder/parametrial involvement is uncertain Full blood count and baseline coagulation screen Blood group, antibody screen, and cross-match with activation of a massive transfusion pathway Cystoscopy or urological assessment where bladder invasion (percreta) is suspected Anaesthetic and critical care review as part of multidisciplinary planning Placenta accreta spectrum describes abnormal trophoblastic invasion into or through the uterine wall, graded as accreta (adherent to myometrium), increta (invading myometrium), and percreta (penetrating serosa and sometimes adjacent organs such as the bladder) The dominant risk factors are a previous caesarean scar combined with a placenta praevia overlying that scar; risk rises steeply with each additional caesarean delivery Antenatal diagnosis is largely by ultrasound, with features such as loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, and disruption of the bladder-uterine interface; MRI is a useful adjunct when posterior placentation or bladder involvement is suspected Attempted separation of an adherent placenta at delivery provokes torrential, life-threatening haemorrhage, so the management principle is to avoid forced removal Planned delivery in a specialist multidisciplinary centre, typically by scheduled preterm caesarean with the placenta left in situ and caesarean hysterectomy, gives the best maternal outcomes Preparation includes large-bore venous access, cross-matched blood and a massive transfusion protocol, cell salvage where available, and involvement of urology and interventional radiology Percreta invading the bladder may require urological support for cystotomy repair or ureteric stenting, hence multidisciplinary planning is essential Conservative uterus-preserving approaches exist but carry risks of delayed haemorrhage, infection, and the need for later intervention, so they are reserved for selected cases Any woman with placenta praevia and a prior uterine scar should be actively screened for accreta rather than assumed to have simple praevia OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: catastrophic intrapartum or postpartum haemorrhage on attempted placental separation requiring immediate massive transfusion and surgical control Haemodynamic instability, tachycardia, and hypotension indicating major blood loss Placenta percreta with bladder or bowel involvement risking visceral injury and uncontrolled bleeding Coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation complicating massive transfusion Unplanned delivery outside a specialist centre without blood products or surgical backup Failing to screen for accreta in a woman with placenta praevia and a previous caesarean scar Attempting to deliver the placenta manually and precipitating uncontrolled haemorrhage Delivering in a non-specialist setting without blood products, cell salvage, or surgical support Underestimating bladder involvement in percreta and omitting urological planning Assuming a conservative uterus-preserving approach is low risk when delayed haemorrhage and sepsis can follow The disorder arises from a defect in the decidua basalis, usually within a uterine scar, so that the normal Nitabuch fibrinoid layer that limits trophoblast invasion is deficient or absent. Chorionic villi therefore anchor directly onto or into the myometrium instead of the decidua. The depth of invasion determines the grade. Scar tissue is poorly vascularised and lacks a decidual cleavage plane, so at delivery the placenta cannot separate physiologically; disruption of the abnormal placental-myometrial interface tears richly vascular tissue and causes massive obstetric haemorrhage. Neovascularisation around the invasion front contributes to the bleeding risk. With antenatal diagnosis and planned management in an experienced multidisciplinary unit, maternal survival is high and morbidity is reduced, though many women require hysterectomy and lose future fertility. Undiagnosed cases presenting acutely carry a substantially higher risk of massive haemorrhage, intensive care admission, visceral injury, and maternal death. Recurrence risk relates to the underlying scarring and future uterine surgery.

Placenta praevia — placenta previa, low-lying placenta, praevia Placental abruption Vasa praevia Local causes such as cervical ectropion, polyp, or cervical carcinoma Bloody show of labour Uterine rupture Transabdominal and confirmatory transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta relative to the os Colour Doppler or MRI to evaluate for placenta accreta spectrum, especially with prior caesarean Full blood count, group and save or cross-match according to bleeding Coagulation studies if haemorrhage is significant Cardiotocography to assess fetal wellbeing during bleeding episodes Placenta praevia is placental implantation over or very close to the internal cervical os, classically presenting as painless bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy Digital vaginal examination must be avoided when praevia is suspected because it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage; ultrasound is the diagnostic tool Many low-lying placentas identified early in pregnancy migrate upward as the lower segment develops, so diagnosis is confirmed on later transvaginal scanning Risk factors include previous caesarean section, prior praevia, multiparity, advanced maternal age, multiple pregnancy, and assisted conception Prior caesarean scars raise the risk of associated placenta accreta spectrum, which should be actively sought on imaging The fetus often lies in an abnormal (transverse or breech) presentation because the placenta occupies the lower segment Delivery is by caesarean section for significant praevia; timing and setting are planned to allow for major haemorrhage Management of bleeding episodes includes resuscitation, blood availability, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm, and anti-D for rhesus-negative women Heavy or recurrent vaginal bleeding causing maternal haemodynamic instability Signs of hypovolaemic shock requiring urgent resuscitation and delivery Imaging features of placenta accreta, increta, or percreta Non-reassuring fetal heart pattern during a bleed Bleeding with uterine contractions suggesting onset of labour with praevia Performing a digital vaginal examination before excluding praevia Labelling an early low-lying placenta as definitive praevia without rescanning later Overlooking placenta accreta spectrum in women with previous caesarean and anterior praevia Underestimating blood loss and failing to prepare adequate transfusion support Attributing painless antepartum bleeding to a benign local cause without imaging In placenta praevia the placenta implants in the lower uterine segment overlying or adjacent to the internal os. As the lower segment stretches and the cervix effaces in later pregnancy and labour, the inelastic placental attachment is disrupted from the underlying decidua, tearing maternal vessels and causing painless bleeding. Because the lower segment contracts poorly after delivery, the placental bed is prone to continued haemorrhage. Prior uterine scarring predisposes to abnormally adherent or invasive placentation (accreta spectrum). With antenatal diagnosis, planned caesarean delivery, and ready access to blood products, maternal and perinatal outcomes are generally good. Uncontrolled haemorrhage, particularly with coexisting accreta spectrum, remains a major cause of maternal morbidity, massive transfusion, and peripartum hysterectomy.

Placental abruption — abruptio placentae, placental abruptio, premature separation of the placenta Placenta praevia Uterine rupture Preterm labour Vasa praevia Local genital tract causes of bleeding Acute abdomen from a non-obstetric cause Continuous cardiotocography to detect fetal compromise and uterine hypertonicity Full blood count and serial haemoglobin Coagulation screen including fibrinogen to identify disseminated intravascular coagulation Group and cross-match for transfusion Ultrasound mainly to exclude praevia rather than to confirm abruption Kleihauer test in rhesus-negative women to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage Abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta before delivery, classically presenting with painful vaginal bleeding and a tender, firm, or hypertonic uterus Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so the degree of vaginal blood loss can badly underestimate the true haemorrhage Risk factors include hypertension and pre-eclampsia, trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, polyhydramnios with rapid decompression, and thrombophilia Fetal compromise or death can occur rapidly because the separated placenta cannot support gas exchange It is largely a clinical diagnosis; ultrasound is insensitive and a normal scan does not exclude abruption Disseminated intravascular coagulation is an important complication, particularly with large abruptions or fetal demise Management depends on maternal and fetal status: resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often by caesarean) when there is fetal distress or maternal instability Anti-D should be given to rhesus-negative women and blood products used to correct coagulopathy Maternal haemodynamic instability or shock, which may be disproportionate to visible blood loss due to concealed haemorrhage Non-reassuring or absent fetal heart activity Developing coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen and abnormal clotting A rigid, exquisitely tender uterus with frequent contractions Rapid clinical deterioration requiring emergency delivery Being falsely reassured by minimal external bleeding when concealed haemorrhage is severe Relying on ultrasound to rule out abruption Underestimating and undertreating evolving coagulopathy Delaying delivery in the face of fetal distress or maternal instability Failing to consider abruption after seemingly minor abdominal trauma in pregnancy Abruption begins with rupture of maternal decidual vessels, causing bleeding into the decidua basalis that splits the placenta from the uterine wall. The expanding retroplacental clot further separates the placenta, reducing the functional area for maternal-fetal exchange and provoking uterine irritability and contraction. Thromboplastins released from the disrupted placenta and decidua enter the maternal circulation and can trigger consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation), while extravasation of blood into the myometrium (Couvelaire uterus) impairs contractility and postpartum haemostasis. Small abruptions with a stable mother and reassuring fetus may allow expectant management with good outcomes. Large abruptions carry high risks of fetal death, maternal haemorrhage, coagulopathy, and organ injury, and abruption is a leading cause of perinatal mortality and antepartum stillbirth. Recurrence risk in future pregnancies is increased.

Plague — Yersinia pestis Acute focal lymphadenopathy of other etiologies (for bubonic plague): streptococcal or staphylococcal infection, tularemia, cat-scratch disease, tick typhus, infectious mononucleosis, lymphatic filariasis (p.1343). Tuberculosis (in differential of fever and hemoptysis in plague-endemic areas, as a small-airborne-particle-transmitted infection) (p.1347). Tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscess (resembles plague pharyngitis) (p.1344). Tularemia (Francisella tularensis) (p.1343) Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) (p.1343) Tick typhus (rickettsial) (p.1343) Infectious mononucleosis (p.1343) Lymphatic filariasis (p.1343) Streptococcal or staphylococcal lymphadenitis (p.1343) Tuberculosis (fever and hemoptysis differential) (p.1347) Bubo aspirate (bubonic), bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or sputum (pneumonic), and blood (septicemic) are the appropriate specimens; culture of postmortem organ biopsy can also be diagnostic. Transport medium such as Cary-Blair preserves viability (p.1345). Direct microscopy: Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic bipolar 'closed safety pin' appearance on Wayson or Wright-Giemsa stain; bipolar bacilli may be visible on direct blood smear in septicemic plague, indicating very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345). Culture on nutrient-rich media (sheep blood agar, brain-heart infusion broth) and selective agar (MacConkey, EMB, or Yersinia-specific CIN agar); optimal growth at <37 degC (25-29 degC). Y. pestis is oxidase-negative, catalase-positive, urease-negative, indole-negative, lactose-negative, and nonmotile (distinguishing it from other Yersinia species) (p.1345). F1 antigen detection: direct immunofluorescence and rapid immunochromatographic test strip (F1RDT), effective on bubo aspirates and sputum and widely used in endemic countries; a Pla antigen strip can detect F1-negative strains (p.1345). PCR/RT-PCR requiring positivity for at least two Y. pestis-specific targets (e.g., caf1, pla, and chromosomal genes); FDA-authorized BioFire FilmArray panels include Y. pestis (p.1346). Serology: rising hemagglutinating antibody titer to F1 antigen, or seroconversion/fourfold rise in paired sera; ELISA for IgG and IgM to F1 antigen (p.1345-1346). WHO case definitions (suspected/probable/confirmed) guide presumptive diagnosis followed by reference laboratory confirmation (p.1345). Plague is a systemic zoonosis caused by Yersinia pestis, predominantly affecting small rodents in rural areas of Africa, Asia, and the Americas and usually transmitted to humans by an arthropod (flea) vector; less often via contact with animal tissues or respiratory droplets (p.1341). Three principal clinical forms: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic. Worldwide, bubonic plague is the predominant reported form; a minority (10-20%) present as primary septicemic or pneumonic disease (p.1343). Bubonic plague: after a 2-6 day incubation, sudden onset of fever (>38 degC), malaise, myalgia, dizziness, and increasing pain from progressive regional lymphadenitis. The bubo is a tense, tender swelling with a boggy consistency and underlying hard core, usually solitary and erythematous with periganglionic edema, most commonly inguinal but may be crural, axillary, cervical, or submaxillary depending on bite site (p.1343). Children most commonly present with cervical or axillary buboes; abdominal pain from intraabdominal node involvement can occur without other visible signs (p.1343). Primary pneumonic plague follows inhalation of infectious droplets from another person or animal with plague pneumonia; short incubation (a few hours to 2-3 days, range 1-7 days) with abrupt fever, headache, myalgia, weakness, nausea, vomiting, dizziness; respiratory signs (cough, dyspnea, chest pain, sputum with hemoptysis) typically appear after 24 h (p.1344). Primary pneumonic plague is generally the least common but most fatal of the main presentations; treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% versus 98% for untreated pneumonic plague (p.1343). Primary septicemic plague (10-25% of infections) presents as gram-negative septicemia (hypotension, shock) WITHOUT preceding lymphadenopathy; occurs in all age groups but risk is elevated in persons over 40 (p.1344). WBC count is generally raised (10,000-20,000/uL) with neutrophilic leukocytosis and left shift; counts can be very high in children (>100,000/uL), but in some cases the WBC is normal or leukopenia develops. DIC occurs in a significant minority (p.1346). Appropriate treatment of bubonic plague resolves fever within 2-5 days, but buboes may remain enlarged for more than a week after initial treatment and can become fluctuant (p.1344). Pneumonic plague is transmissible person-to-person via respiratory droplets (productive cough), making it a public-health emergency requiring immediate isolation and notification (p.1344, 1347). Aerosolized Y. pestis is a recognized potential bioterrorism agent (Tier 1 select agent); an outbreak of primary pneumonic plague in a nonendemic region or urban setting should raise concern for intentional release (p.1342, 1344, 1345). Rapid progression of primary pneumonic plague from segmental pneumonitis to lobar and bilateral involvement with hemoptysis and ARDS within hours to days (p.1344). Bipolar bacilli visible on direct blood smear indicate very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345). Disseminated intravascular coagulation with shock in septicemic disease (p.1346). The term 'septicemic plague' can be confusing because most patients with buboes have detectable bacteremia at some stage, with or without systemic sepsis signs (p.1344). Automated biochemical or mass-spectrometry identification systems can misidentify Y. pestis as Y. pseudotuberculosis or other species (p.1345). Meningeal plague may be associated with suboptimal antimicrobial therapy (delayed treatment, penicillin use, or low-dose tetracycline) (p.1344). A single negative rapid antigen test is insufficient to exclude plague; WHO exclusion requires two negative F1RDT tests on specimens collected 24 h apart when confirmatory tests are unavailable (p.1345-1346). F1RDT specificity for culture-confirmed pneumonic plague was only 71%, so a positive sputum test in an endemic area identifies a probable case requiring treatment but needs additional confirmatory testing (p.1345-1346). Culture yield can be low after prehospital antimicrobial use (as observed in the 2017 Madagascar outbreak) (p.1345). Y. pestis is a gram-negative bacterium of the order Enterobacterales that recently evolved from the enteric pathogen Y. pseudotuberculosis. It has a two-stage life cycle alternating between arthropod (flea) and a wide range of mammalian hosts. In the flea, the organism multiplies and forms biofilm-embedded aggregates in the midgut; some fleas become 'blocked' at the proventriculus and regurgitate bacteria into the bite site, while early-phase unblocked transmission also occurs. In the mammalian host, dissemination from the inoculation site is initially dependent on plasminogen activator (Pla), which activates plasminogen, degrades complement, and binds laminin, and is essential for high-level virulence and bubo formation. Bacteria are rapidly transported to regional lymph nodes where Y. pestis replicates extracellularly with full expression of antiphagocytic systems (type III secretion machinery and effectors encoded by pYV plus the F1 capsule), producing a bubo (hemorrhagic/necrotic node with thrombosed vessels, replaced architecture, and abundant bacteria). LcrV targets phagocytes and exerts an anti-inflammatory effect, and modified lipopolysaccharide minimizes Toll-like receptor 4 stimulation, prolonging high-grade bacteremia. Spread via efferent lymphatics to the thoracic duct produces high-grade bacteremia and hematogenous seeding of spleen, liver, secondary buboes, lungs (secondary plague pneumonia), and meninges, with uncontrolled septicemia leading to death; the septicemic phase can occur without an obvious prior bubo (p.1342-1343). Untreated plague carries high mortality, but it is treatable with antimicrobials. Treated pneumonic plague has an estimated death rate of about 17% compared with 98% for untreated pneumonic plague. In the United States, case-fatality fell from 66% in 1900-1941 to 16% in the post-antibiotic era (1942 onward); in 2000-2018, mortality was 8% in patients receiving any antimicrobial and 4% in those receiving currently recommended high-efficacy agents. The global case-fatality rate notified to WHO for 2013-2018 was 17%. Visible bipolar bacilli on direct blood smear signal very high bacteremia and poor prognosis (p.1343, 1345). WHO case classification of plague: Suspected case (clinical presentation suggestive of plague plus an epidemiologic context of possible exposure within 10 days of onset); Probable case (suspected case plus one of: F1 antigen detected by rapid test or immunofluorescence, a single anti-F1 serology without prior infection/immunization, or direct microscopy showing bipolar-staining gram-negative coccobacilli); Confirmed case (suspected case plus one of: isolation of Y. pestis, seroconversion or fourfold anti-F1 titer change in paired sera, or species-specific PCR positivity); Not a case (suspected case with negative confirmatory testing) (p.1345).

Plantar fasciitis — plantar fasciopathy, plantar heel pain, plantar fasciosis, heel spur syndrome Calcaneal stress fracture Fat-pad atrophy or contusion Tarsal tunnel syndrome or entrapment of the nerve to abductor digiti minimi (Baxter's nerve) S1 radiculopathy referring to the heel Inflammatory enthesitis from seronegative spondyloarthropathy Insertional Achilles or retrocalcaneal pathology (posterior heel) Usually diagnosed clinically without imaging Ultrasound to demonstrate a thickened, hypoechoic proximal plantar fascia MRI in atypical or refractory cases and to exclude calcaneal stress fracture or nerve entrapment Plain radiographs to identify a calcaneal stress fracture or other bony pathology Inflammatory screen and referral if a spondyloarthropathy is suspected The hallmark is sharp inferior heel pain that is worst with the first few steps in the morning or after periods of rest, then eases with activity Tenderness is maximal at the medial calcaneal tubercle where the plantar fascia originates It is a degenerative fasciopathy from repetitive overload rather than a primarily inflammatory condition, despite the -itis suffix Risk factors include obesity, prolonged standing, reduced ankle dorsiflexion, tight calf muscles, and a sudden increase in running load Diagnosis is clinical; a windlass test reproducing pain on passive great-toe dorsiflexion supports it Heel spurs seen on radiographs are common incidental findings and do not cause the pain Management principles are calf and plantar fascia stretching, load management, supportive footwear, and orthoses or heel cushioning Most cases resolve within a year with conservative care; corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief but risks fat-pad atrophy and fascial rupture Persistent bilateral heel pain, especially in a young person with inflammatory features, should prompt consideration of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy Features suggesting inflammatory arthropathy such as young age, bilateral disease, and other enthesitis or back symptoms Focal bony tenderness or night pain raising concern for stress fracture or tumour Numbness, tingling, or a positive Tinel sign suggesting nerve entrapment Systemic symptoms or signs of infection Attributing symptoms to an incidental heel spur Overusing corticosteroid injection with risk of fat-pad atrophy or fascial rupture Missing a calcaneal stress fracture or nerve entrapment presenting as heel pain Overlooking an underlying inflammatory spondyloarthropathy in bilateral or young patients Plantar fasciitis results from repetitive traction overload at the origin of the plantar aponeurosis on the medial calcaneal tuberosity. The tissue undergoes microtearing and a degenerative response with collagen disorganisation, mucoid change, and thickening of the fascia rather than sustained acute inflammation. Impaired ankle dorsiflexion and tight gastrocsoleus increase tensile strain, and the failed healing perpetuates pain. The large majority of patients improve within six to twelve months with conservative treatment, though symptoms can be protracted; recalcitrant cases may benefit from extracorporeal shockwave therapy before considering surgery.

Plasma Cell Disorders (MGUS, Waldenström) — MGUS, monoclonal gammopathy, Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, POEMS Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) Smoldering (asymptomatic) multiple myeloma Symptomatic multiple myeloma (CRAB / myeloma-defining events) Solitary plasmacytoma of bone or soft tissue Nonsecretory myeloma Plasma cell leukemia (>2000 circulating plasma cells/uL) Waldenström's macroglobulinemia IgM myeloma (lytic lesions, CD138+ plasma cells, t(11;14)) POEMS syndrome AL (primary) amyloidosis Heavy chain diseases (gamma/Franklin's, alpha/Seligmann's and IPSID, mu) Marginal zone lymphoma and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for M-protein quantitation Serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) to confirm monoclonality and identify heavy/light chain type Urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) / 24-h urine for Bence Jones (free light chain) protein Serum free light chain assay with kappa/lambda ratio (essential to assess ratio, not just absolute level, since renal insufficiency nonspecifically raises both) Bone marrow biopsy/aspirate for clonal plasma cell percentage and CD138+ / kappa or lambda light chain restriction by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or in situ hybridization MYD88 (L265P) and CXCR4 mutation testing to discriminate WM from MZL, IgM myeloma, and CLL Skeletal survey, CT, or PET-CT for osteolytic lesions; MRI of spine/pelvis for focal lesions Serum calcium, creatinine/creatinine clearance, and hemoglobin (to assess CRAB end-organ damage) VEGF level and evaluation for Castleman's disease when POEMS is suspected Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry-based typing when amyloidosis is suspected (SPEP/UPEP alone are inadequate screens for AL) M components in other lymphoid neoplasms (CLL, B- or T-cell lymphomas) M components in nonlymphoid neoplasms (chronic myeloid leukemia, breast cancer, colon cancer) Nonneoplastic conditions: cirrhosis, sarcoidosis, parasitic diseases, Gaucher's disease, pyoderma gangrenosum Autoimmune conditions: rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, cold agglutinin disease Post organ-transplant immunosuppression (and rarely allogeneic transplant) Skin diseases with monoclonal gammopathy: lichen myxedematosus (papular mucinosis), necrobiotic xanthogranuloma (~10% progress to myeloma) Mixed cryoglobulinemia (IgM/IgA complexed with IgG) seen in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune disease, usually not associated with malignancy Plasma cell disorders are monoclonal neoplasms of late B-lymphocyte lineage; the group includes multiple myeloma (MM), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, primary (AL) amyloidosis, and the heavy chain diseases, also termed monoclonal gammopathies, paraproteinemias, plasma cell dyscrasias, or dysproteinemias (Harrison 22e p.883). MGUS is vastly more common than myeloma, occurring in ~1% of the population aged >50 and up to ~10% of those aged >75; no specific intervention is indicated and annual (or less frequent) follow-up is adequate, with closer monitoring only for higher-risk MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887-890). About ~1% of MGUS patients per year progress to myeloma, but essentially all cases of myeloma are preceded by MGUS (Harrison 22e p.887). Higher-risk MGUS features are non-IgG subtype, abnormal kappa/lambda free light chain ratio, and serum M-protein >15 g/L (1.5 g/dL); absence of all three predicts ~5% progression while presence of all three predicts ~60% progression over 20 years (Harrison 22e p.887). Diagnostic workup for a monoclonal protein uses serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for quantitation and immunoelectrophoresis/immunofixation for confirmation of a single heavy and/or light chain; serum free light chain assay and urine studies (UPEP) detect light-chain-only and Bence Jones disease (Harrison 22e p.883-884). An M component must be present at ~5 g/L (0.5 g/dL) to be accurately quantitated by electrophoresis; the serum M-protein level is a reliable measure of tumor burden but is not specific enough to screen asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.883-884). MGUS diagnostic criteria: serum monoclonal protein (non-IgM) <30 g/L, clonal bone marrow plasma cells <10%, and absence of myeloma-defining events or amyloidosis attributable to the plasma cell disorder (Harrison 22e p.888, Table 116-1). Waldenström's macroglobulinemia (WM) is a malignancy of IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytoid cells; unlike myeloma it presents with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly and its major manifestation is hyperviscosity syndrome (Harrison 22e p.893). A distinct MYD88 L265P somatic mutation is present in >90% of WM patients and the majority of IgM MGUS, and is used as a diagnostic test to discriminate WM from marginal zone lymphoma, IgM-secreting myeloma, and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation (Harrison 22e p.893). In WM the IgM may have specificity for myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG); a peripheral neuropathy may precede the neoplasm and about half of these patients are anti-MAG positive (Harrison 22e p.893). POEMS syndrome = Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M-protein, and Skin changes; patients typically have a severe progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy with sclerotic bone lesions, and polyneuropathy occurs in only ~1.4% of myelomas with POEMS being a rare subset (Harrison 22e p.893). AL (primary) amyloidosis is a plasma cell disorder most often caused by clonal bone marrow plasma cells secreting a misfolding monoclonal light chain; it can coexist with multiple myeloma, Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, or non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.896-897). Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic but uncommon signs of AL amyloidosis, each seen in only ~10% of patients (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897). Hyperviscosity syndrome in Waldenström's macroglobulinemia / IgM gammopathy: headache, visual disturbance, retinal vein segmentation and dilation, epistaxis, altered consciousness, paresis (most IgM is intravascular and responds to plasmapheresis) Myeloma-defining end-organ damage (CRAB): hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions Spinal cord compression: new lower-extremity neurologic deficit, severe localized back pain, or loss of bowel/bladder control requiring emergency MRI and radiation/decompression Acute renal failure from light chain cast nephropathy, especially with dehydration Cardiac involvement in AL amyloidosis (70-80%) is the leading cause of death; low-voltage ECG with pseudo-infarct pattern and thickened ventricles on echo MGUS with severe polyneuropathy (consider causal IgM/anti-MAG neuropathy) Do not equate a monoclonal protein with malignancy: distinguish MGUS (clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, M-protein <30 g/L, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis) from multiple myeloma, which requires marrow plasmacytosis and myeloma-defining events / CRAB end-organ damage (Harrison 22e p.887-888). SPEP/UPEP are useful in myeloma but are NOT adequate screening tests for AL amyloidosis, because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce an M-spike; use serum/urine immunofixation and free light chain assay (>90% positive) (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897). A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; when MGUS coexists with biopsy-proven amyloidosis, AL type must be ruled out and 'smoldering myeloma' patients should be screened for AL (Harrison 22e ch.117 p.897). WM does not cause bone lesions or hypercalcemia (unlike myeloma); large IgM paraprotein causes little renal excretion so renal disease is uncommon (~20% excrete light chains)—reserve the diagnosis of IgM myeloma for lytic bone lesions with CD138+ plasma cells and t(11;14) (Harrison 22e p.893). Suspected cryoglobulin: draw blood into a warm syringe and transport in warm water to avoid errors in quantitation (Harrison 22e p.893). Rituximab can produce an IgM flare in WM—use plasmapheresis first or initially withhold rituximab in patients with high IgM levels (Harrison 22e p.894). Pseudohyponatremia and a decreased anion gap can occur in myeloma because the cationic M component retains chloride and displaces serum water (Harrison 22e p.887). In normal B-cell maturation, antigen exposure drives differentiation of mature B lymphocytes into antibody-secreting plasma cells; in plasma cell disorders this control is lost, producing a monoclonal expansion that secretes a single (monoclonal) immunoglobulin or fragment (M component). Clinical manifestations arise from neoplastic cell expansion, from the secreted products (intact immunoglobulin, free light/heavy chains, lymphokines), and from the host response. In multiple myeloma, recurrent chromosomal lesions include hyperdiploidy and 14q32 translocations (e.g., t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)), with errors in immunoglobulin switch recombination implicated in early transformation. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia arises from a post-germinal-center IgM-bearing memory B cell, driven by MYD88 L265P (TLR/IL-1R IRAK and NF-kB signaling, plus BTK/HCK signaling) and frequently CXCR4 mutations. In AL amyloidosis, clonal plasma cells produce a monoclonal light chain (lambda predominates) that misfolds into insoluble amyloid fibrils deposited extracellularly in tissues (Harrison 22e p.883-884, 893; ch.117 p.896-897). MGUS carries a low malignant potential, with ~1% per year progression to myeloma (risk stratified by IgG vs non-IgG subtype, free light chain ratio, and M-protein level: ~5% at 20 years with no risk features vs ~60% with all three). Smoldering myeloma progresses to symptomatic MM in ~25% at 5 years with one risk feature and ~76% with all three high-risk features. Waldenström's macroglobulinemia is often indolent and may not require therapy; median survival is reported as ~50 months, with older age, male sex, general symptoms, and cytopenias defining a high-risk group. AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive and fatal if untreated (occurs after age 40); very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts significantly better outcome (Harrison 22e p.887-888, 893-894; ch.117 p.896-898). MGUS vs smoldering (asymptomatic) myeloma vs symptomatic multiple myeloma per IMWG criteria (Harrison Table 116-1). MGUS: non-IgM serum M-protein <30 g/L, clonal marrow plasma cells <10%, no myeloma-defining events/amyloidosis. Smoldering MM: serum M-protein (IgG/IgA) >=30 g/L or urine M-protein >=500 mg/24h and/or clonal marrow plasma cells 10-60%, without myeloma-defining events. Symptomatic MM: clonal plasma cells (or plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event—CRAB end-organ damage (hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions) or a biomarker of malignancy (clonal marrow plasma cells >=60%, involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100, or >1 focal MRI lesion). POEMS requires polyneuropathy + monoclonal plasma cell disorder + (sclerotic bone lesions / Castleman's / elevated VEGF) + an additional system feature.
