Inflammatory markers, renal function, and urinalysis (typically without active urinary sediment) Nerve conduction studies for mononeuritis multiplex and ANCA testing (expected negative) A necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries that characteristically spares the lungs and is not associated with ANCA Presents with systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, malaise) plus organ-specific ischaemic damage Peripheral nervous system involvement, especially mononeuritis multiplex, is common and an important clue Skin manifestations include livedo reticularis, tender nodules, ulcers, and digital ischaemia Renal involvement is typically renovascular ischaemia and hypertension rather than glomerulonephritis, and gut involvement can cause mesenteric ischaemia and abdominal pain A recognised association with hepatitis B infection exists, so viral serology should be checked Diagnosis rests on biopsy of affected tissue showing necrotising arteritis, or angiography demonstrating microaneurysms and stenoses in visceral vessels Treatment uses corticosteroids with additional immunosuppression for severe disease, while hepatitis B-associated cases also require antiviral therapy Acute abdomen from mesenteric ischaemia, bowel infarction, or perforation Rapidly progressive renal impairment or malignant hypertension from renal artery involvement Cardiac ischaemia or heart failure from coronary arteritis New neurological deficit including stroke or severe mononeuritis multiplex Ruptured visceral microaneurysm causing haemorrhage Confusing it with ANCA-associated vasculitis and expecting lung or glomerular disease Failing to test for hepatitis B, which alters management Missing mesenteric ischaemia in a patient with vague abdominal pain Overlooking mononeuritis multiplex as a diagnostic clue Delaying tissue or angiographic confirmation in a critically ill patient Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic necrotising vasculitis affecting medium and small muscular arteries. Transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis weakens the vessel wall, producing the microaneurysms characteristic of visceral angiography, while intimal proliferation and thrombosis cause luminal narrowing and downstream tissue infarction. Lesions are segmental and favour branch points. Unlike small-vessel vasculitides it does not typically involve capillaries, glomeruli, or the pulmonary circulation and is ANCA-negative. Immune complex mechanisms are implicated, particularly in hepatitis B-associated disease. Untreated disease has a poor outlook, but immunosuppression markedly improves survival. Prognosis is worse with significant gastrointestinal, renal, cardiac, or central nervous system involvement; hepatitis B-associated disease can respond well when the virus is also treated.

Polycystic Kidney Disease — ADPKD, PKD Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD, PKHD1) - distal/collecting-duct cysts, oligohydramnios if severe, hypertension, congenital hepatic fibrosis and Caroli disease; absence of renal cysts in either parent >40y on ultrasound helps distinguish ARPKD from ADPKD (p.2430, p.2434) ADPKD-like disease (GANAB, DNAJB11) - normal-to-smaller kidneys with fewer cysts, variable liver cysts (p.2430-2432) Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD; UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B, SEC61A1) - small fibrotic kidneys, medullary cysts, gout in adults (p.2430) Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2) - renal cysts (20-30%), angiomyolipomas, increased risk of renal cell carcinoma, facial angiofibromas, CNS hamartomas; TSC2 is adjacent to PKD1 so a contiguous gene deletion can cause both ADPKD and TS (p.2430, p.2434) Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) - renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma, retinal angiomas, CNS hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas (p.2430) Nephronophthisis and other ciliopathies (e.g., Bardet-Biedl, Meckel-Gruber, Senior-Loken) - cystic kidney phenotypes with syndromic features (p.2430) Renal cysts and diabetes syndrome (HNF1B) - kidney cysts with aberrant nephrogenesis and diabetes (p.2430) Acquired simple renal cysts (increase in frequency with age and can confound diagnostic cyst counts) (p.2432-2433) Renal ultrasonography - first-line for presymptomatic screening and donor evaluation; age-stratified cyst-count criteria for diagnosis (p.2432-2433) CT and T2-weighted MRI (with/without contrast) - more sensitive than ultrasound, detect smaller cysts (MRI with gadolinium can detect 2-3 mm cysts); useful to distinguish malignancy from a complex cyst (p.2432-2433) Magnetic resonance angiography for presymptomatic intracranial aneurysm screening in patients with a positive family history of aneurysm (p.2432) CT scan as first diagnostic test for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, with lumbar puncture to confirm (p.2432) Genetic testing by linkage and mutational analysis for ambiguous cases; PKD1 analysis is difficult and costly owing to gene size and homologous pseudogenes (paired-end next-generation sequencing may improve this) (p.2433) Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common life-threatening monogenic disease, affecting ~12 million people worldwide (estimated prevalence 1:1000 to 1:400), and is a leading cause of kidney failure; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance but variable expressivity (p.2430-2431). ADPKD is caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16p13, ~85% of cases, encodes polycystin-1) and PKD2 (chromosome 4q21-q23, ~15% of cases, encodes polycystin-2); PKD2 patients tend to have milder disease and may be underdiagnosed. Polycystins are localized on the primary cilium, and defective ciliary function places ADPKD among the ciliopathies (p.2430-2431). It is characterized by progressive bilateral formation of epithelial-lined renal cysts; cysts arise in only ~5% of tubules but their enormous growth destroys surrounding tissue. Enlarged kidneys can reach a fourfold increase in length and up to 20 times the normal weight (p.2430-2431). Back or flank pain is a frequent symptom in ~60% of patients and may result from cyst infection, hemorrhage, or nephrolithiasis; gross hematuria from cyst rupture occurs in ~40% during the disease course, often recurrently (p.2432). Hypertension is common and typically occurs before any reduction in GFR; it is a risk factor for both cardiovascular and kidney disease progression. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality in ADPKD (p.2432). Intracranial (berry) aneurysm occurs four to five times more frequently than in the general population and causes high mortality; about 20-50% of patients may have 'warning headaches' preceding subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm (p.2432). Liver (biliary epithelial) cysts are the most common extrarenal complication; massive polycystic liver disease occurs almost exclusively in women, particularly those with multiple pregnancies. Mitral valve prolapse occurs in up to 30% of patients, and colonic diverticulae and abdominal wall hernias are also increased (p.2432). Diagnosis is typically made from a positive autosomal dominant family history plus bilateral kidney cysts on ultrasonography; in at-risk subjects aged 15-29 years, two renal cysts (unilateral or bilateral) suffice (sensitivity 96%, specificity 100%), with higher cyst counts required at older ages because simple cysts increase with age (p.2432-2433). Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2-receptor (V2R) antagonist, inhibits the cAMP pathway in collecting ducts and reduces cell proliferation by lowering renal cAMP, slowing the decline of renal function; the FDA has indicated it only for patients at risk of rapidly progressing disease (p.2433). Infection is the second most common cause of death; up to half of patients have one or more renal infections, most commonly an infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis due to gram-negative bacteria, with fever and flank pain (p.2432). Sudden severe headache or 'warning headache' suggesting subarachnoid hemorrhage from ruptured intracranial (berry) aneurysm (p.2432) Positive family history of intracranial aneurysm - a risk factor for aneurysm rupture warranting presymptomatic MRA screening (p.2432) Fever and flank pain indicating infected cyst or acute pyelonephritis (with or without bacteremia); infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2432) Gross hematuria from cyst rupture (p.2432) Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the cerebral circulation predisposing to arterial dissection and stroke (p.2432) Proteinuria is usually only a MINOR feature of ADPKD, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis (p.2432). Renal cell carcinoma is NOT increased in frequency compared with the general population, but when it does occur in ADPKD it is more often bilateral, multicentric, and sarcomatoid; radiologic imaging is often unable to distinguish cyst infection from cyst hemorrhage due to their complexity (p.2432). Diagnostic cyst-count thresholds rise with age because simple renal cysts increase with age; criteria have lower sensitivity for PKD2 patients owing to late onset (p.2432-2433). No specific FDA-approved treatment prevents cyst growth or the decline of renal function; more rigorous blood pressure control does not equal greater benefit, and targeting systolic pressure to 110 mmHg in moderate/advanced disease may worsen progression by reducing renal blood flow (p.2433). Most renal cysts are not connected to glomerular filtration, so cyst infection requires lipid-soluble antibiotics that penetrate cyst walls (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones, chloramphenicol), often for 4-6 weeks (p.2433). Polycystic liver disease in ADPKD is distinct from isolated autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease (ADPLD; PRKCSH/SEC63), which does NOT progress to renal failure (p.2432). ADPKD results from mutations in PKD1 and PKD2, encoding polycystin-1 (PC1, a large 11-transmembrane G-protein-coupled-receptor-like protein) and polycystin-2 (PC2, a calcium-permeable six-transmembrane TRP-family cation channel). PC1 and PC2 bind via their C-terminal tails to form a receptor-channel complex (proposed 1:3 PC1:PC2 stoichiometry) located on the primary cilium and at cell membranes and cell-cell junctions of tubular epithelium, functioning as a mechano-/chemosensor regulating calcium and G-protein signaling. Every cell carries a germline mutant allele, but cysts develop in only a small fraction of nephrons, thought to arise from clonal growth of cells sustaining a somatic 'second hit' in the normal allele; a 'third hit' such as renal injury or an additional genetic/epigenetic event may accelerate cyst formation. Loss of ciliary PC1/PC2 function is hypothesized to cause aberrant calcium signaling, increased adenylyl cyclase and decreased phosphodiesterase activity, raising cellular cAMP; increased cAMP promotes protein kinase A activity, driving cyst growth through proliferation and chloride/aquaporin-mediated fluid secretion. Cellular defects include increased proliferation and fluid secretion, decreased differentiation, and abnormal extracellular matrix; affected signaling pathways include Wnt, mTOR, STAT3, cMET, PI3K/Akt, GPCR, EGFR, and CFTR. Rarer ADPKD-associated genes GANAB and DNAJB11 affect PC1 trafficking and cause milder cystic disease. ADPKD progression shows striking inter- and intrafamilial variability; disease can present as early as in utero, but end-stage renal disease typically occurs in late middle age. Risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size; PKD2 disease is generally milder with later onset. More than half of patients eventually require peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, or kidney transplantation. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of mortality, and renal infection is the second most common cause of death (p.2431-2433). Harrison does not provide a formal stage-based severity classification for ADPKD. Genotype broadly stratifies severity (PKD1 disease ~85% of cases is more severe with earlier onset than PKD2 disease ~15%; GANAB/DNAJB11 mutations cause milder cystic disease). Risk of rapid progression - used to select patients for tolvaptan - is estimated by combining genotypic and imaging (kidney growth rate) information; recognized clinical risk factors for progression include early diagnosis, hypertension, gross hematuria, multiple pregnancies, and large kidney size (p.2431-2433).

Polycystic ovary syndrome — PCOS, polycystic ovarian syndrome, Stein-Leventhal syndrome Thyroid dysfunction Hyperprolactinaemia Non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia Cushing syndrome Androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea Serum total and free testosterone and other androgens Luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and sex hormone-binding globulin Thyroid function and prolactin to exclude alternative causes 17-hydroxyprogesterone to screen for non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia Transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian morphology and antral follicle count Oral glucose tolerance test and lipid profile to assess metabolic risk PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria, requiring at least two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding mimics Common presentations include irregular or absent periods, hirsutism and acne, subfertility, and difficulty with weight Insulin resistance is central to the syndrome and is often present regardless of body weight, though obesity worsens it It is the leading cause of anovulatory infertility Unopposed oestrogen from chronic anovulation increases the long-term risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, so regular endometrial protection is important Lifestyle modification with weight management is the first-line intervention and can restore ovulation and improve metabolic profile Management is symptom-directed: cycle regulation and endometrial protection, treatment of hyperandrogenic features, and ovulation induction when fertility is desired Screening for and managing metabolic complications, including impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia, is an essential part of long-term care Rapid onset or severe virilisation suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour rather than PCOS Prolonged amenorrhoea with abnormal bleeding raising concern for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma Markedly elevated androgens beyond the range typical of PCOS Features of Cushing syndrome Severe metabolic derangement such as newly diagnosed diabetes Diagnosing PCOS without excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and other mimics Relying on ultrasound alone, since polycystic ovarian morphology can occur in healthy women Overlooking endometrial protection in women with prolonged amenorrhoea Focusing only on fertility and neglecting long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risk Attributing severe or rapidly progressive virilisation to PCOS PCOS reflects a complex interplay of hormonal and metabolic disturbances. Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinaemia stimulates ovarian theca cells to overproduce androgens and reduces hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin, raising free androgen levels. Altered gonadotrophin secretion, with a relatively high luteinising hormone drive, further promotes androgen production and disrupts follicular maturation, so multiple small antral follicles accumulate without a dominant follicle emerging, causing anovulation. Chronic unopposed oestrogen exposure from anovulation places the endometrium at risk of hyperplasia. PCOS is a lifelong condition whose reproductive symptoms often improve with weight management and targeted therapy, and many women conceive with or without ovulation induction. The main long-term concerns are metabolic, with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and, through chronic anovulation, endometrial cancer; proactive metabolic surveillance improves outcomes.

Polycythemia Vera and Other Myeloproliferative Neoplasms — Myeloproliferative neoplasms, MPN, PV, Primary myelofibrosis, PMF, Agnogenic myeloid metaplasia, Myelofibrosis with myeloid metaplasia, Essential thrombocytosis, Essential thrombocythemia, ET Relative (spurious/stress) erythrocytosis from plasma volume contraction (Gaisbock's syndrome) due to dehydration, diuretics, ethanol, androgens, or tobacco Hypoxic erythrocytosis (pulmonary disease, right-to-left shunt, sleep apnea, high altitude, carbon monoxide, high-oxygen-affinity hemoglobin) Tumor- or renal-disease-associated erythrocytosis (hypernephroma, hepatoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, uterine myoma, pheochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis, renal cysts, post-transplant) Congenital/familial erythrocytosis (erythropoietin receptor, VHL/Chuvash, 2,3-BPG, PHD2/EGLN1, HIF2alpha/EPAS1, LNK mutations) and recombinant erythropoietin or SGLT2-inhibitor effect Reactive thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, infection, inflammation, malignancy, hemorrhage, surgery, postsplenectomy, B12/folate-deficiency rebound) Chronic myeloid leukemia (BCR-ABL positive), myelodysplasia including 5q- syndrome and sideroblastic anemia (SF3B1) Secondary myelofibrosis (myelophthisis) from metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, hairy cell leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, and nonmalignant causes such as HIV, tuberculosis, SLE, hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency HIV infection (can cause secondary myelofibrosis) Tuberculosis (can cause secondary myelofibrosis and constitutional symptoms) Quantitative next-generation-sequencing assay for JAK2 V617F or JAK2 exon 12 mutations (now supersedes surrogate tests for PV diagnosis) Red cell mass and plasma volume determination to confirm absolute versus relative erythrocytosis when hemoglobin is below ~20 g/dL Serum erythropoietin level (elevated level favors a secondary cause; a normal level does not exclude PV) Red cell count, mean corpuscular volume, and red cell distribution width (microcytic erythrocytosis narrows differential) Mutation testing for MPL and CALR (exon 9, type 1 deletions and type 2 insertions) in JAK2-negative ET/PMF FISH for BCR-ABL to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy (megakaryocyte clustering/hyperplasia, reticulin/collagen fibrosis in PMF; absent stainable iron with hypercellularity favors PV) Cytogenetic analysis (del 20q, del 13q, trisomy 8/9, partial trisomy 1q; complex karyotype portends poor prognosis in PMF) Mutational analysis of ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 for refined PMF prognosis Ristocetin cofactor activity to detect acquired von Willebrand disease at very high platelet counts Serum lactate dehydrogenase and alkaline phosphatase (may be elevated in PMF), uric acid Reactive thrombocytosis from iron deficiency, inflammation, or malignancy mimicking ET Stress/spurious erythrocytosis (Gaisbock's syndrome) mimicking PV Chronic myeloid leukemia mimicking ET or PMF Myelodysplastic syndromes (5q- syndrome, sideroblastic anemia) presenting with thrombocytosis Metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, or systemic mastocytosis causing myelophthisic marrow fibrosis Systemic lupus erythematosus, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, and renal osteodystrophy causing nonmalignant myelofibrosis The classic chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms covered here (PV, PMF, ET) all arise from a hematopoietic stem cell and share constitutive activation of JAK2 through driver mutations in JAK2, MPL, or CALR; their natural histories are usually measured in decades, and leukemic transformation is uncommon in the absence of chemotherapy or radiation (Harrison 22e p.818). JAK2 V617F is expressed in more than 95% of PV patients and in roughly 50% of PMF and ET patients; most JAK2-negative PV patients carry a JAK2 exon 12 mutation, while a few have LNK or calreticulin mutations (Harrison 22e p.818-819). In PV the plasma volume is expanded, unlike other causes of true erythrocytosis, so an elevated red cell mass can be masked, especially in women; below a hemoglobin of about 20 g/dL (hematocrit 60%) one cannot reliably separate true erythrocytosis from plasma-volume contraction without red cell mass and plasma volume measurement (Harrison 22e p.819-820). PV should be suspected in any woman presenting with hepatic vein (Budd-Chiari) thrombosis, since this is the type of thrombosis particularly associated with JAK2 V617F; portal vein thrombosis is more common in male PV patients (Harrison 22e p.819). Aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia are the symptoms that can suggest PV over other causes of erythrocytosis; pruritus may reflect JAK2 V617F-driven mast cell activation, and Helicobacter pylori incidence is increased in PV (Harrison 22e p.819-820). Only three conditions cause microcytic erythrocytosis: beta-thalassemia trait, hypoxic erythrocytosis, and PV; the red cell distribution width is typically normal in thalassemia trait but may be elevated in hypoxic erythrocytosis or PV when iron deficiency coexists (Harrison 22e p.820). In a PV patient with massive splenomegaly, a 'normal' hematocrit or hemoglobin should be regarded as indicating an elevated red cell mass until proven otherwise, because the associated plasma volume increase masks the true red cell mass (Harrison 22e p.820). In PMF the peripheral smear shows a leukoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells, nucleated red cells, myelocytes, and promyelocytes; marrow is usually inaspirable ('dry tap') owing to fibrosis, and bone x-rays may show osteosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.821-822). PMF marrow fibroblasts are polyclonal and not part of the neoplastic clone; fibrosis is driven by overproduction of transforming growth factor beta, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases, and thrombopoietin, while osteosclerosis relates to osteoprotegerin and angiogenesis to vascular endothelial growth factor (Harrison 22e p.821). In ET the large platelet mass can cause spurious (test-tube) hyperkalemia from platelet potassium release on clotting, with no electrocardiographic correlate, and can make arterial oxygen measurements inaccurate unless blood is collected on ice (Harrison 22e p.823). Very high platelet counts (above about 1 million/microL) are associated primarily with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease due to proteolysis of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand multimers, not with thrombosis; tobacco use is the most important thrombotic risk factor in ET (Harrison 22e p.823-824). PMF and ET diagnoses are largely diagnoses of exclusion: significant splenomegaly in apparent ET suggests another MPN, and FISH for BCR-ABL is preferred to exclude CML in JAK2-negative thrombocytosis because reverse-transcriptase PCR for BCR-ABL is prone to false positives (Harrison 22e p.823-824). Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) in a young woman, or portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, as a presenting feature of PV Neurologic hyperviscosity symptoms: vertigo, tinnitus, headache, visual disturbance, transient ischemic attack Arterial or venous thrombosis in cerebral, cardiac, or mesenteric vessels Platelet count above 1 million/microL with bleeding from acquired von Willebrand disease Sudden splenic enlargement with painful splenic infarction (fever, pleuritic chest pain) Development of transfusion-dependent anemia, increasing organomegaly, or peripheral blood blasts signaling marrow failure or accelerated/blastic transformation in PMF Constitutional symptoms (night sweats, fatigue, weight loss) suggesting a myeloproliferative rather than reactive process Spinal cord compression, pericardial tamponade, or ureteral/intestinal obstruction from exuberant extramedullary hematopoiesis in PMF Treating the platelet count rather than the patient in ET: a high platelet count alone does not establish thrombotic risk, and the cause of any symptom must be confirmed to be platelet-related before therapy Assuming a high platelet count causes thrombosis when very high counts more often cause hemorrhage via acquired von Willebrand disease; aspirin can promote bleeding in this setting Interpreting a normal hematocrit/hemoglobin as excluding elevated red cell mass in a PV patient with massive splenomegaly (plasma volume expansion masks it) Relying on a low-level JAK2 V617F allele burden (VAF 5% or less) to diagnose a blood disease, since not everyone with low burden has one Assuming a normal serum erythropoietin excludes PV (it does not), or overlooking that an elevated level points to a secondary cause Diagnosing ET in a JAK2 V617F-positive patient without red cell mass/plasma volume studies, since many such patients actually have PV Misreading spurious hyperkalemia or inaccurate arterial oxygen values caused by the large platelet mass in ET Mistaking secondary myelofibrosis/myelophthisis for PMF and missing a treatable underlying disorder Using leukemogenic agents (alkylating agents, radioactive phosphorus-32) and prolonged hydroxyurea, which is itself mutagenic and antagonizes TP53, in disorders with otherwise long survival These chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms originate in a single hematopoietic stem cell and produce overabundant mature blood elements without significant dysplasia, together with a tendency toward extramedullary hematopoiesis, myelofibrosis, and eventual leukemic transformation. PV, PMF, and ET share constitutive activation of the nonreceptor tyrosine kinase JAK2, the cognate kinase and chaperone for the erythropoietin and thrombopoietin receptors. The JAK2 V617F mutation in the autoinhibitory pseudokinase domain causes ligand-independent kinase activation, explaining erythropoietin hypersensitivity, erythropoietin-independent erythroid colony growth, increased Bcl-XL expression, and apoptosis resistance in PV progenitors. Loss of heterozygosity on chromosome 9p (uniparental disomy) leads to JAK2 V617F homozygosity, common in PV, less so in PMF, and rare in ET. JAK2 V617F alone does not account for the entire phenotype and is probably not the initiating lesion: the same mutation yields different phenotypes in ET versus PMF, familial PV can occur without it, and leukemia may arise in a JAK2-negative progenitor, implying an ancestral precursor. PMF and ET may instead carry MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) or CALR (calreticulin) mutations; mutant CALR binds and activates MPL at the cell surface. In PMF, marrow fibrosis is a reactive, polyclonal fibroblast response driven by cytokines from the clone (TGF-beta, thrombopoietin), with extramedullary hematopoiesis in liver and spleen. Megakaryocyte genome reduplication is endomitotic and thrombopoietin-driven; paradoxically, MPL expression is reduced and plasma thrombopoietin is increased across these MPNs despite the expanded megakaryocyte/platelet mass. PV is generally indolent, with a clinical course measured in decades; most patients live long lives without functional impairment when red cell mass is controlled, and the incidence of acute leukemia is very low in those not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation. Myelofibrosis is part of the natural history of PV but is usually reactive and reversible without prognostic significance, although about 15% develop hematopoietic stem cell failure with extramedullary hematopoiesis and transfusion-dependent anemia. PMF has the shortest survival of the three: it follows a course of progressive marrow failure and organomegaly, can evolve to an accelerated phase, and about 10% transform spontaneously to a treatment-refractory acute leukemia. PMF survival is stratified by IPSS, DIPSS, and DIPSS-Plus risk factors (anemia, leukocytosis, peripheral blasts, constitutional symptoms, age over 65, unfavorable karyotype, thrombocytopenia, transfusion dependence); ASXL1, EZH2, SRSF2, and IDH1/2 mutations and complex cytogenetics independently predict early death or leukemic transformation, and triple-negative PMF carries the worst prognosis. ET is more benign than previously thought; survival is comparable to the general population regardless of driver mutation, and leukemic evolution is more often a consequence of therapy than of the disease. For primary myelofibrosis, prognostic risk is estimated by the IPSS (2009), DIPSS (2010), and DIPSS-Plus (2011) scoring systems. Risk factors include anemia (hemoglobin <10 g/dL), leukocytosis (>25,000/microL), peripheral blood blasts (>=1%), constitutional symptoms, and age over 65; DIPSS-Plus adds unfavorable karyotype, platelet count <100,000/microL, and transfusion dependence. In DIPSS, anemia is weighted as 2 points. Categories run Low, Intermediate-1, Intermediate-2, and High by number/weight of factors. These systems are not accurate for risk assessment of PV or ET patients who have developed secondary myelofibrosis.

Polymicrogyria — PMG, bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria, cortical dysplasia (polymicrogyria type), GPR56 (ADGRG1), TUBB2B Pachygyria and other lissencephaly-spectrum malformations Cobblestone malformation of the dystroglycanopathies Schizencephaly, which is frequently lined by polymicrogyria Focal cortical dysplasia Congenital cytomegalovirus-related cortical malformation Tubulinopathy-related cortical dysgenesis High-resolution brain MRI to define the distribution and extent of the malformation Testing for congenital cytomegalovirus infection, including stored newborn blood spot analysis where available Chromosomal microarray, including assessment for 22q11.2 deletion Gene panel or exome sequencing for cortical malformation genes Electroencephalography to characterise seizures Swallowing and speech assessment for perisylvian involvement A malformation of late cortical organisation in which the cortex forms excessive small, fused gyri with abnormal lamination, producing an irregular or bumpy cortical surface It is often bilateral and symmetric in recognised patterns, the perisylvian region being the most common site, giving the bilateral perisylvian syndrome MRI shows an irregular grey-white junction with numerous small gyri; the cortex may look deceptively thickened because the tiny folds are packed together Causes are heterogeneous and include genetic variants such as GPR56 and tubulin genes, chromosomal disorders including 22q11.2 deletion, and acquired insults, notably congenital cytomegalovirus infection and in-utero ischaemia The bilateral perisylvian form typically causes pseudobulbar palsy with oromotor dysfunction, dysarthria, feeding difficulty, epilepsy, and variable cognitive impairment Clinical severity depends on extent and location, ranging from focal, minimally symptomatic lesions to widespread malformation with severe disability Diagnosis rests on the MRI pattern combined with genetic testing and evaluation for congenital infection Severe oromotor dysfunction with aspiration and feeding failure Drug-resistant epilepsy Evidence of congenital cytomegalovirus infection with hearing loss requiring intervention Rapidly progressive neurological decline suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Misreading the packed small gyri as a thick, smooth cortex and mistaking it for pachygyria Failing to test for congenital cytomegalovirus, an important and potentially preventable acquired cause Overlooking associated 22q11.2 deletion and its systemic implications Assuming all polymicrogyria is genetic and neglecting acquired prenatal causes in counselling Polymicrogyria is a disorder of the late stages of cortical development, arising after neurons have largely completed migration, during cortical organisation and lamination. Both genetic factors, including variants in genes governing the neuronal cytoskeleton and cortical patterning, and acquired prenatal insults such as congenital cytomegalovirus infection or focal ischaemia can disrupt normal gyral formation. The cortex develops an excess of small, abnormally laminated and fused convolutions. The distribution of the malformation, often bilateral and region-specific, determines the neurological consequences such as perisylvian oromotor dysfunction and epilepsy. Outcome ranges widely with the extent and location of involvement. Small focal lesions may be asymptomatic or cause only focal epilepsy, whereas extensive bilateral malformation causes significant motor, oromotor, cognitive, and seizure disability.

Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia and Ventricular Fibrillation — Polymorphic VT, Torsades des pointes, Ventricular fibrillation, VF Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (implies a fixed structural substrate or automatic focus, unlike polymorphic VT) Acquired (drug- or electrolyte-induced) long QT with torsades des pointes Congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS-1, -2, -3) Short QT syndrome Brugada syndrome Early repolarization syndrome Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (bidirectional VT) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Genetic dilated cardiomyopathies (e.g., Lamin A/C, SCN5A) 12-lead ECG with measurement of corrected QT (QTc); congenital LQTS typically prolongs QTc to >440 ms in men and >460 ms in women (p.1969) Short QT syndrome: QTc <360 ms, usually <300 ms (p.1970) Telemetry/rhythm strip to capture pause-dependent initiation of torsades and characteristic morphologies (p.1969) Genetic testing/genotyping for family screening and diagnostic reassurance in LQTS (p.1970) Provocative sodium channel blocker testing (e.g., flecainide, ajmaline, procainamide) to unmask Brugada ST elevation (p.1970) Assessment of residual LV function/ejection fraction to guide ICD decisions (p.1969) Reference resource crediblemeds.org to check whether a medication has been reported to prolong the QT interval (p.1969) Brugada pattern ST elevation must be distinguished from LV hypertrophy, pericarditis, myocardial ischemia/MI, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, right bundle branch block, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (p.1970) Asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern versus the clinical Brugada syndrome (analogous to Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern versus syndrome) J-point elevation as a benign normal variant versus early repolarization syndrome associated with arrhythmia risk Sustained polymorphic VT shows a QRS configuration that changes continuously beat to beat, reflecting an ever-changing ventricular activation sequence; unlike monomorphic VT it does not necessarily imply a fixed structural abnormality or single automatic focus (p.1968). Sustained polymorphic VT commonly degenerates into ventricular fibrillation (p.1969). Acute myocardial infarction or ischemia is a frequent cause and should be the first consideration; roughly 10% of acute MI patients develop VT that degenerates to VF, with greatest risk in the first hour (p.1969). Polymorphic VT/VF occurring within the first 48 hours of acute MI carries higher in-hospital mortality, but survivors to discharge are not at increased risk of later arrhythmic sudden death (p.1969). Torsades des pointes is the polymorphic VT linked to QT prolongation and classically begins in a pause-dependent fashion: a PVC induces a pause, the following sinus beat has a longer QT, and a PVC interrupting that T wave starts the run (p.1969). Congenital long QT syndrome stems from ion-channel gene mutations; LQTS-1, -2, and -3 account for roughly 80-90% of cases, with LQTS-1/-2 involving potassium channels and LQTS-3 involving the sodium channel (p.1969-1970). Genotype influences triggers: LQTS-1 events tend to occur during exertion (notably swimming), LQTS-2 with sudden auditory stimuli or emotional upset, and LQTS-3 sudden death tends to occur during sleep (p.1970). Brugada syndrome causes syncope or cardiac arrest from polymorphic VT in the absence of structural heart disease; arrest may occur during sleep or be provoked by febrile illness, and males are more commonly affected (p.1970). Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT is a rare familial disorder of abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling producing arrhythmias resembling digitalis toxicity, often with bidirectional (alternating QRS morphology) VT, presenting in childhood with exertion- or emotion-induced events (p.1971). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common genetic cardiovascular disorder (about 1 in 500), is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35, typically via polymorphic VT/VF (p.1971). Ventricular fibrillation shows disordered electrical ventricular activation with no identifiable QRS complexes; spiral wave reentry and multiple circulating reentry wavefronts are proposed mechanisms (p.1971). After surviving acute MI and revascularization, poorly coupled but surviving Purkinje fibers (which tolerate ischemia owing to glycogen stores and oxygenation from the LV cavity) can trigger PVCs and ventricular fibrillation (p.1971). Near-syncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest as the presenting event (p.1969) Repeated episodes of polymorphic VT suggesting ongoing myocardial infarction/inadequate reperfusion (p.1969) QTc exceeding 500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest as markers of increased risk in LQTS (p.1970) Family history of sudden death (relevant in Brugada syndrome, early repolarization syndrome, and genetic cardiomyopathies) (p.1970-1971) Febrile illness provoking cardiac arrest in Brugada syndrome (p.1970) HCM features: young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope (within 6 months), ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1971) Assuming polymorphic VT implies a fixed structural focus as monomorphic VT does (p.1968) Overlooking ongoing ischemia/inadequate reperfusion when polymorphic VT/VF recurs after MI (p.1969) Failing to recognize numerous noncardiac QT-prolonging drugs and drug interactions that raise levels of an offending agent as precipitants of torsades (p.1969) Re-exposing a patient who had QT-prolongation-induced polymorphic VT to QT-prolonging medications; such patients should be considered susceptible and avoid all future exposure (p.1969) Misinterpreting benign J-point elevation (a common normal variant) as pathologic early repolarization syndrome (p.1971) Confusing the asymptomatic Brugada ECG pattern with true Brugada syndrome (p.1970) Polymorphic VT arises from a continually changing ventricular activation sequence. Proposed mechanisms include reentry with variable paths, spiral wave reentry, and multiple automatic foci, often near fibrotic myocardium and potentiated by damaged Purkinje cells or ventricular hypertrophy. Abnormal transmural dispersion of repolarization can drive it in the setting of channelopathies or antiarrhythmic drugs even without structural disease. In acute MI/ischemia, reentry through the infarct border zone is implicated, and surviving automatic Purkinje cells can initiate it. Torsades des pointes is associated with abnormal QT prolongation and pause-dependent initiation. Congenital LQTS reflects mutations in ion-channel genes governing repolarization (potassium channels in LQTS-1/-2, sodium channel in LQTS-3, and calcium channels in others). Short QT syndrome reflects a gain of function of the IKr potassium channel or reduced inward depolarizing currents. Brugada syndrome reflects dispersion of repolarization across the ventricular wall, with epicardial and M cells more affected than endocardial cells, localized to the right ventricular outflow tract; sodium channel mutations (SCN5A, SCN1B, SCN10A) are found in about 25% of cases. Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT results from cardiac ryanodine receptor (and less often calsequestrin 2) mutations causing abnormal sarcoplasmic calcium handling. Ventricular fibrillation represents disordered activation without organized QRS, frequently as degeneration of sustained polymorphic or monomorphic VT (p.1968-1971). Polymorphic VT/VF within the first 48 hours of acute MI is associated with greater in-hospital mortality, yet patients who survive to discharge are not at increased risk for later arrhythmic sudden death. Long-term risk after infarction is governed largely by residual LV function. In LQTS, higher risk is conferred by QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope or cardiac arrest. HCM is a prominent cause of sudden death before age 35; surgical myectomy carries a sudden death rate <1% per year, and transcoronary ethanol septal ablation has a reported annual rate of sustained VT or sudden death of roughly 1-5% (p.1969-1971). No single formal severity grade; risk is stratified by substrate. In post-MI patients, an ICD is indicated for persistent severe LV dysfunction (LV ejection fraction <35%). In LQTS, high-risk features include QTc >500 ms, female gender, and prior syncope/cardiac arrest. In HCM, high-risk markers include young age, nonsustained VT, failure of blood pressure to rise with exercise, recent syncope, and ventricular wall thickness >3 cm (p.1969-1971).

Polymyositis — PM, idiopathic inflammatory myopathy Dermatomyositis Inclusion body myositis Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (including statin-associated) Metabolic, mitochondrial, or muscular dystrophy Endocrine myopathy (hypothyroidism, Cushing) and drug-induced myopathy Motor neuron disease and myasthenia gravis Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes Myositis-specific and myositis-associated antibody panel including anti-Jo-1 Electromyography showing a myopathic pattern with irritability MRI of muscle to identify oedema and guide biopsy Muscle biopsy for endomysial inflammation; screening for interstitial lung disease with pulmonary function tests and high-resolution CT Presents with progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness affecting shoulder and hip girdles, causing difficulty rising from chairs, climbing stairs, and lifting the arms Weakness rather than pain predominates, and there is no characteristic rash (distinguishing it from dermatomyositis) Serum creatine kinase is typically markedly elevated, reflecting muscle fibre damage Myositis-specific antibodies, including the antisynthetase antibodies (e.g. anti-Jo-1), help define clinical subsets The antisynthetase syndrome combines myositis with interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and 'mechanic's hands' It is a diagnosis of exclusion; inclusion body myositis in older patients and other myopathies must be considered before labelling weakness as polymyositis Muscle biopsy classically shows endomysial CD8 T-cell infiltration surrounding and invading non-necrotic fibres Corticosteroids are the mainstay of initial treatment, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants added to control disease and limit steroid toxicity Rapidly progressive dyspnoea or hypoxia from interstitial lung disease, especially with antisynthetase antibodies Bulbar or respiratory muscle weakness causing dysphagia, aspiration, or ventilatory compromise Cardiac involvement with arrhythmia or heart failure Features suggesting an underlying occult malignancy Severe dysphagia risking aspiration pneumonia Diagnosing polymyositis without excluding inclusion body myositis and necrotising myopathy, which respond differently to therapy Overlooking interstitial lung disease, a major cause of morbidity and mortality Attributing weakness solely to steroid myopathy during treatment without reassessing disease activity Failing to screen for dysphagia and aspiration risk Missing an associated malignancy or overlap connective tissue disease Polymyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy driven by cell-mediated autoimmunity. Cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes recognise antigens expressed on muscle fibres and invade non-necrotic myofibres, causing fibre necrosis and regeneration and consequent weakness. Upregulation of MHC class I on muscle fibres is characteristic. Associations with specific autoantibodies define distinct phenotypes, and there is overlap with other connective tissue diseases and, less strongly than in dermatomyositis, with malignancy. With treatment many patients regain strength, but relapses are common and prognosis is worse in the presence of interstitial lung disease, cardiac involvement, severe dysphagia, or associated malignancy. Long-term functional outcome depends on early treatment and control of extramuscular disease.

symptoms Non-adherence causing apparent treatment failure Drug-disease interaction worsening an existing condition Delirium or cognitive decline attributable to cumulative drug burden Structured medication reconciliation including over-the-counter drugs, supplements, and herbal products Application of explicit criteria such as Beers and STOPP/START during medication review Calculation of anticholinergic burden Renal function assessment to guide dose adjustment and drug selection Review of adherence, including pill counts or pharmacy refill data where available Polypharmacy is commonly defined by the concurrent use of five or more medicines, but the clinically important question is whether each drug remains appropriate and beneficial Each additional medication increases the risk of adverse drug reactions, drug-drug and drug-disease interactions, and poor adherence Prescribing cascades occur when the side effect of one drug is misread as a new problem and treated with another drug rather than by stopping the offending agent Age-related changes in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, particularly reduced renal clearance and heightened CNS sensitivity, amplify drug risks in older adults Explicit tools such as the Beers criteria and the STOPP/START criteria help identify potentially inappropriate medications and prescribing omissions Anticholinergic burden from multiple drugs contributes to confusion, falls, constipation, and urinary retention and should be tallied and minimised Deprescribing is a structured, shared-decision process of tapering or stopping drugs whose harms outweigh benefits, aligned with the patient's goals and life expectancy Regular structured medication reconciliation and review, especially at transitions of care, is the key preventive measure New falls, confusion, or delirium temporally linked to a medication change Symptoms of drug toxicity such as bradycardia, hypotension, bleeding, or hypoglycaemia Multiple sedating or anticholinergic drugs used together Unexplained functional or cognitive decline that may be iatrogenic Adding a drug to treat the side effect of another instead of reassessing the original agent Continuing medications indefinitely without reassessing ongoing indication or benefit Failing to adjust doses for declining renal function Stopping several drugs abruptly and precipitating withdrawal effects rather than tapering Overlooking over-the-counter drugs and supplements as sources of interactions With ageing, reduced lean body mass and total body water, increased fat, declining hepatic metabolism, and especially reduced renal excretion alter drug distribution and clearance, prolonging exposure to many agents and their metabolites. Pharmacodynamic sensitivity also changes, notably increased susceptibility to central nervous system depressants, anticholinergics, and drugs affecting blood pressure. As the number of medications rises, the probability of interactions grows combinatorially, and overlapping adverse effects (sedation, hypotension, anticholinergic load) summate to produce falls, delirium, and functional decline. Inappropriate polypharmacy is associated with increased adverse drug events, hospitalisation, falls, cognitive impairment, and mortality. Thoughtful deprescribing and ongoing medication optimisation can reduce these harms and improve quality of life without compromising the treatment of important conditions.

tamponade or tension pneumothorax as the cause of shock Medical collapse (e.g. cardiac event, seizure) preceding a traumatic mechanism Toxicological or metabolic contribution to altered consciousness
