environment control Life threats identified during the primary survey are treated as they are found, before moving to the next step The most common preventable cause of early death is uncontrolled haemorrhage, so external bleeding is compressed and internal sources are sought promptly Permissive hypotension and balanced resuscitation with blood products help avoid dilutional coagulopathy in bleeding patients until definitive control is achieved The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy worsens outcomes and guides damage-control strategies A structured secondary survey (head-to-toe examination and history) is performed only once the patient is stabilised, to detect injuries missed initially Reassess frequently, as trauma physiology is dynamic and deterioration can be rapid Adjuncts such as focused ultrasound, chest and pelvic imaging, and blood gases are integrated into the primary survey Persistent or recurrent hypotension despite resuscitation, indicating ongoing haemorrhage requiring immediate surgical or interventional control Rising lactate or worsening base deficit signalling inadequate perfusion Signs of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) mandating damage-control resuscitation Deteriorating conscious level suggesting evolving brain injury or shock Mechanism or examination suggesting occult truncal or pelvic bleeding Completing the secondary survey before life threats in the primary survey are addressed Over-resuscitation with crystalloid worsening dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia Anchoring on an obvious dramatic injury while missing a silent source of shock Failing to reassess after each intervention as physiology evolves Neglecting active warming and haemostatic resuscitation in the bleeding patient Polytrauma involves injury to two or more body regions or systems, at least one of which is life-threatening. Simultaneous tissue damage triggers haemorrhage, hypovolaemic shock, and a systemic inflammatory response. Hypoperfusion causes tissue hypoxia and lactic acidosis, while ongoing bleeding and crystalloid dilution impair clotting. Hypothermia further inhibits enzymatic coagulation, and the resulting lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy establishes a self-reinforcing cycle. Later, immune activation predisposes to systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute respiratory distress, and multi-organ dysfunction. Outcome depends on injury burden, time to haemorrhage control, and physiological reserve. Early definitive control of bleeding and correction of the lethal triad improve survival, whereas prolonged shock and multi-organ dysfunction carry high mortality.

Pompe disease — acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, acid maltase deficiency, glycogen storage disease type II, GSD II Spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of infantile hypotonia Congenital muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies Other causes of infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies in later-onset presentations Other glycogen storage disorders affecting muscle Assay of acid alpha-glucosidase activity, including dried blood spot screening with confirmatory testing GAA molecular genetic testing Serum creatine kinase measurement Echocardiography and ECG to assess cardiomyopathy in infants Pulmonary function testing and muscle assessment in later-onset disease An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase), resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation; it is classified as glycogen storage disease type II It is unusual among the glycogenoses in being a lysosomal disorder rather than affecting cytoplasmic glycogen metabolism, so fasting hypoglycaemia is not a feature The classic infantile form presents in the first months with profound hypotonia, a rapidly enlarging heart (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and feeding and respiratory difficulty A markedly enlarged tongue and prominent cardiomegaly on chest imaging are useful clues in infants Late-onset (juvenile and adult) forms present with progressive proximal and respiratory muscle weakness and often lack significant cardiac involvement Diaphragmatic weakness can cause respiratory failure that is disproportionate to limb weakness Serum creatine kinase is commonly elevated, reflecting the underlying myopathy Enzyme replacement therapy has transformed the outlook, particularly in infantile disease, and newborn screening enables earlier treatment Rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in an infant Respiratory compromise from diaphragmatic weakness Severe feeding difficulty with failure to thrive Progressive respiratory decline out of proportion to limb weakness in older patients Expecting hypoglycaemia and being misled when it is absent, since this is a lysosomal rather than cytoplasmic glycogenosis Attributing infantile hypotonia to a neuromuscular cause without checking for cardiomyopathy Underestimating respiratory muscle involvement in later-onset disease Delaying treatment when early initiation most influences outcome Pompe disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the GAA gene encoding acid alpha-glucosidase, the lysosomal enzyme that degrades glycogen to glucose within the lysosome. Deficient activity leads to progressive lysosomal glycogen accumulation, most damaging in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Lysosomal engorgement and subsequent autophagic dysfunction impair muscle architecture and function, producing cardiomegaly and hypotonia in infants and progressive skeletal and respiratory muscle weakness in later-onset disease. The degree of residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with age of onset and severity. Untreated classic infantile disease is usually fatal within the first year from cardiorespiratory failure. Enzyme replacement therapy substantially improves survival and cardiac outcomes, especially when started early, though respiratory and motor sequelae may persist. Late-onset disease progresses more slowly, with respiratory function being a key determinant of long-term outcome.

Porphyria — acute intermittent porphyria, porphyria cutanea tarda Intestinal obstruction (acute abdomen) — pain of porphyria is usually difficult to distinguish because severe hyperperistalsis is prominent in both (p.3344-ch.40) Lead colic / lead intoxication (lead inhibits ALA-dehydratase, raising urinary ALA and coproporphyrin III) (p.3342, ch.40) Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (succinylacetone inhibits ALA-dehydratase, mimicking acute porphyria) (p.3342) Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute attack with ascending weakness mimics GBS) (p.3603) Chronic liver disease (can cause nonspecific increases in urinary porphyrins leading to misdiagnosis) (p.3345) Spot (single-void) urine for porphobilinogen (PBG) — first-line; always raised in acute attacks of AIP/HCP/VP and specific; 24-h collection unnecessary (p.3345-3346) Quantitative urinary ALA, PBG, and creatinine on the same spot sample (also detects ADP) (p.3345) Total urinary porphyrins (interpret cautiously — often nonspecific) (p.3345) Urinary, fecal, and plasma porphyrins to distinguish AIP from HCP and VP (fecal porphyrins normal/minimal in AIP) (p.3346) Total plasma porphyrins with fluorometric scanning of diluted plasma at neutral pH (distinguishes VP from PCT; VP emission peak ~626 nm) for cutaneous porphyrias (p.3346, 3348) Erythrocyte protoporphyrin (more sensitive for EPP/XLP; confirm EPP by predominant free, not zinc, protoporphyrin) (p.3346) Isocoproporphyrins in feces — diagnostic of hepatic URO-decarboxylase deficiency (PCT) (p.3348) Erythrocyte URO-decarboxylase activity (~50% in type 2 PCT; markedly deficient, 3-10%, in HEP) (p.3348) Molecular genetic mutation analysis of the relevant heme-pathway gene (definitive; diagnostic even when precursor levels have normalized, and for latent heterozygotes/relatives) (p.3342, 3346) Acute surgical abdomen / intestinal obstruction (acute hepatic porphyria attack mimics this) (p.3344, ch.40) Lead poisoning (lead colic and neuropathy mimic acute porphyria) (p.3342) Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending motor weakness in an acute attack) (p.3603) Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (biochemical and clinical mimic of acute porphyria) (p.3342) The porphyrias are metabolic disorders, each from deficient (or, for XLP, increased) activity of a specific enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway; inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, except porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) which is usually sporadic (p.3340). Classified as hepatic or erythropoietic (by primary site of porphyrin/precursor overproduction) and as acute or cutaneous (by clinical manifestation) (p.3340, 3344). Acute hepatic porphyrias (AIP, HCP, VP) usually present in adult life after puberty with acute attacks of neurovisceral symptoms and elevated urinary porphyrin precursors ALA and/or PBG (p.3344). Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is autosomal dominant from half-normal HMB-synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase) activity; the most common acute hepatic porphyria (~1 in 20,000 Caucasians), especially frequent in Scandinavia and Great Britain (p.3340, 3346). AIP abdominal pain is the most common symptom: poorly localized, often with cramping, ileus, distention, and decreased bowel sounds (though increased bowel sounds and diarrhea may occur) (p.3346). AIP attacks also feature nausea, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, mental symptoms, limb/head/neck/chest pain, muscle weakness, sensory loss, dysuria, and urinary retention; tachycardia, hypertension, restlessness, tremor, and sweating reflect sympathetic overactivity (p.3346). AIP peripheral neuropathy is due to axonal degeneration (not demyelination) and primarily affects motor neurons; proximal muscles (shoulders/arms) are involved first, and it may be focal or involve cranial nerves (p.3346). Mental symptoms in acute attacks include anxiety, insomnia, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, and paranoia; seizures may be neurologic or due to hyponatremia (p.3346). Diagnosis of an acute attack rests on substantial elevation of urinary PBG (and ALA); urinary PBG is always increased during acute attacks of AIP, HCP, and VP and is not substantially raised in any other condition, making a spot urine PBG both sensitive and specific (p.3345-3346). PCT is the most common porphyria overall; hepatic URO-decarboxylase is deficient in all types, and ~80% of patients have no UROD mutation (sporadic type 1) (p.3347). PCT presents with blistering, photosensitive skin lesions most commonly on the backs of the hands that rupture, crust, and scar, with skin friability, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation; neurologic features are absent (p.3347). An acute attack may begin with sharp abdominal pain, then agitation/hallucinations/seizures, with back and extremity pain followed by weakness several days later, mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome; weakness may be asymmetric, proximal or distal, and involve facial/bulbar muscles (p.3602-3603). Urine may appear brownish during an attack due to high porphyrin metabolite concentration (p.3602-3603). Acute neurovisceral attack: severe poorly-localized abdominal pain with autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating), motor neuropathy/weakness, and psychiatric disturbance — the AIP acute hepatic porphyria red-flag constellation (p.3346) Hyponatremia (from inappropriate vasopressin secretion or electrolyte depletion) and seizures during an attack (p.3346) Markedly raised urinary PBG/ALA in a patient with abdominal pain after puberty (p.3345-3346) Exposure to a porphyria-precipitating drug, low-calorie diet, alcohol, infection, or surgery preceding the attack (p.3346) Progression to respiratory and bulbar paralysis; sudden death may result from sympathetic overactivity and cardiac arrhythmia, especially with delayed diagnosis/treatment (p.3346) A great mimic of the acute abdomen: porphyric (and lead colic) pain is hard to distinguish from intestinal obstruction because of prominent hyperperistalsis — risking unnecessary surgery (p.3344, ch.40). Because symptoms are nonspecific and rarely occur before puberty, diagnosis is often delayed; a high index of suspicion is required (p.3340, 3346). Measuring urinary porphyrins alone for screening should be avoided — minimal nonspecific increases (e.g., in chronic liver disease) cause misdiagnosis; use urinary PBG (p.3345). Erythrocyte HMB-synthase assay is not a useful first-line test: activity is not decreased in all AIP patients, borderline-low values are not diagnostic, and it is not deficient in other acute porphyrias; some HMBS mutations give normal erythrocyte enzyme so genetic testing is needed (p.3345-3346). ALA/PBG levels often remain high after symptoms resolve, so diagnosing an acute attack in a biochemically proven AIP patient relies primarily on clinical features (p.3346). Most antiseizure drugs can exacerbate AIP, making seizure treatment difficult (clonazepam may be safer than phenytoin or barbiturates) (p.3346). Abdominal tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis are usually absent or mild in AIP because the process is neurologic, not inflammatory — their prominence should prompt reconsideration (p.3346). In PCT, neurologic features are absent — abdominal/neurovisceral attacks should not be attributed to it (p.3347). Each porphyria results from deficient (or, in XLP, increased) activity of one of the eight enzymes of the heme biosynthetic pathway converting glycine and succinyl-CoA to heme. In acute hepatic porphyrias, half-normal enzyme activity becomes limiting when hepatic heme synthesis is increased: induction of the rate-limiting hepatic gene ALAS1 (regulated in part by PGC-1alpha, which is induced by fasting) leads to accumulation and urinary excretion of the porphyrin precursors ALA and PBG, which underlie the acute neurovisceral attacks. Common precipitating factors include endogenous and exogenous steroids (estrogens/progestins), porphyrinogenic drugs (often P450-metabolized), alcohol, low-calorie/low-carbohydrate diets, infections, and surgery. AIP is almost always latent before puberty, suggesting adult steroid hormone levels drive expression; symptoms are commoner in women, with premenstrual (luteal-phase progesterone) attacks. Hyponatremia results from hypothalamic involvement with inappropriate vasopressin secretion or from electrolyte depletion (vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, renal sodium loss). In PCT, substantial deficiency of hepatic URO-decarboxylase (to ~20% of normal or less, via an iron- and oxidative-stress-dependent uroporphomethene inhibitor) causes accumulation of porphyrins that, on excitation by long-wave UV light in the skin, produce blistering photosensitivity (p.3340, 3345-3347). AIP can be disabling but is rarely fatal; the prognosis of individuals with HMBS mutations is generally favorable, and most heterozygotes remain latent. When an attack resolves, abdominal pain may disappear within hours and paresis begins to improve within days, sometimes continuing to improve over years; recovery from severe motor neuropathy may take months to years and depends on the degree of neuronal damage and early treatment. Long-term complications of AIP include increased risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (up to 59% develop CKD), chronic liver function abnormalities with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (warranting hepatic imaging at least every 6 months), and persistent neuropathy, fatigue, chronic pain, nausea, depression, and anxiety. Homozygous dominant AIP usually presents in infancy and most affected children die at an early age. PCT can almost always be brought into complete remission with treatment, but patients characteristically have chronic liver disease, sometimes cirrhosis, and are at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (p.3346-3348). Porphyrias are classified by primary overproduction site (hepatic vs erythropoietic) and by clinical manifestation (acute neurovisceral vs cutaneous). Acute hepatic porphyrias: AIP, HCP, VP (and the rare autosomal recessive ADP) present with acute neurovisceral attacks and raised ALA/PBG; AIP causes neurovisceral disease without photosensitivity, whereas HCP and VP can have both neurovisceral attacks and PCT-like cutaneous photosensitivity. Cutaneous: PCT (and HEP) present with chronic blistering photosensitivity. Erythropoietic porphyrias (CEP, EPP, XLP) present with cutaneous photosensitivity (EPP/XLP non-blistering, immediate and painful). Acute-attack severity ranges from mild (abdominal pain without paresis or hyponatremia, manageable with carbohydrate loading) to severe (paresis, hyponatremia, bulbar/respiratory paralysis) (p.3340, 3344, 3346-3347).

Porphyria cutanea tarda — PCT, uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, UROD deficiency, symptomatic porphyria Pseudoporphyria from drugs (e.g. NSAIDs, diuretics) or renal dialysis Variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria with skin involvement Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita Bullous pemphigoid and other subepidermal blistering disorders Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (severe biallelic UROD deficiency) Polymorphic light eruption and other photodermatoses Quantitative urinary porphyrins showing uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin excess Faecal porphyrin analysis for isocoproporphyrin, characteristic of the condition Plasma fluorescence scanning to support the porphyria diagnosis Iron studies and ferritin, with HFE genotyping where iron overload is present Hepatitis C and HIV serology, and assessment of alcohol intake and liver function UROD gene testing when a familial form is suspected The most common porphyria, resulting from deficient activity of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, the fifth enzyme of haem biosynthesis Predominantly acquired (type I) with a normal gene, occurring when hepatic enzyme activity is inhibited; a familial (type II) form has an inherited UROD mutation Presents as a chronic blistering photosensitivity with skin fragility, vesicles and bullae, milia, erosions and scarring on sun-exposed skin, especially the backs of the hands Additional features include hypertrichosis (notably on the temples and cheeks), hyperpigmentation and, in some, sclerodermoid change It is a purely cutaneous (non-acute) porphyria without neurovisceral attacks, as the accumulating porphyrins are photoreactive rather than neurotoxic precursors Key susceptibility factors include hepatic iron overload (often with HFE haemochromatosis variants), hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol excess and oestrogen exposure The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised urinary uroporphyrin and heptacarboxyl porphyrin with raised isocoproporphyrin in faeces Management combines removal of contributory factors, iron reduction by venesection and low-dose antimalarial therapy, alongside sun protection Features of advanced chronic liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma given the raised long-term risk Severe childhood-onset blistering suggesting hepatoerythropoietic porphyria Secondary infection or scarring of fragile skin lesions Unrecognised underlying hepatitis C or HIV Overlooking treatable drivers such as hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol, oestrogen use and iron overload Confusing it with pseudoporphyria, which has identical skin changes but normal porphyrins Failing to distinguish it from variegate porphyria, which can look identical on the skin Neglecting sun protection while awaiting the effect of definitive treatment Missing familial disease and the need for family assessment Porphyria cutanea tarda develops when hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity falls below a critical threshold, whether from acquired inhibition alone or on the background of an inherited mutation. The enzyme sequentially decarboxylates uroporphyrinogen, so its deficiency causes accumulation of highly carboxylated, water-soluble and photoreactive porphyrins, particularly uroporphyrin. Hepatic iron, oxidative stress and cofactors such as hepatitis C, alcohol and oestrogens generate an inhibitor of the enzyme. Circulating porphyrins deposit in the skin and, on ultraviolet and visible light exposure, generate reactive oxygen species that damage the dermo-epidermal junction, producing the characteristic fragility and blistering. Prognosis is good when contributory factors are addressed; skin lesions usually remit with iron reduction and antimalarial therapy, although there is a long-term risk of hepatic fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly with concurrent hepatitis C or alcohol excess.

Port-Wine Stain — naevus flammeus, capillary malformation, PWS Infantile haemangioma (proliferates then involutes, unlike a port-wine stain) Naevus simplex / salmon patch (transient, midline, fades) Other capillary malformations within overgrowth syndromes Angioma serpiginosum and other acquired vascular patches Early or atypical vascular tumours Reticulate vascular patterns such as cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita Clinical diagnosis based on a congenital, non-involuting, well-demarcated vascular patch Ophthalmological review for glaucoma with ophthalmic-distribution facial lesions Brain MRI to assess for leptomeningeal involvement when Sturge-Weber syndrome is suspected Assessment for limb overgrowth and, if indicated, imaging for associated vascular or overgrowth syndromes Genetic evaluation in syndromic or extensive presentations where appropriate A port-wine stain is a capillary (vascular) malformation present at birth that, unlike an infantile haemangioma, does not proliferate and does not spontaneously resolve It appears as a flat, sharply demarcated pink to red patch that often follows a segmental or dermatomal distribution and tends to darken and thicken with age Over decades some lesions develop cobblestoning, nodularity, and soft-tissue or bony overgrowth of the affected area A facial stain involving the ophthalmic (forehead and upper eyelid) distribution raises concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, with associated leptomeningeal vascular malformation and glaucoma Any child with a periocular or ophthalmic-distribution stain needs ophthalmological assessment for glaucoma and appropriate neurological evaluation Extensive limb capillary malformations can be a feature of overgrowth syndromes, so assess for limb asymmetry and hypertrophy Pulsed-dye laser is the mainstay of treatment and works best when started early, though multiple sessions are needed and complete clearance is not guaranteed The visible facial lesion carries a significant psychosocial burden, and support and camouflage advice are an important part of holistic care Ophthalmic-distribution facial stain raising concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, seizures, and developmental effects Signs of glaucoma such as a large or cloudy eye, tearing, or photophobia requiring urgent ophthalmology input Progressive soft-tissue or skeletal overgrowth of the affected region Extensive limb capillary malformation with asymmetry suggesting an overgrowth syndrome New nodularity, bleeding, or ulceration within a long-standing lesion prompting reassessment Confusing it with an infantile haemangioma and wrongly reassuring parents it will disappear Missing the association with Sturge-Weber syndrome in an ophthalmic-distribution facial lesion Failing to arrange glaucoma screening in at-risk infants Overlooking limb overgrowth syndromes in extensive capillary malformations Neglecting the psychological impact and the value of early laser referral A port-wine stain results from a developmental malformation of the superficial dermal capillaries and postcapillary venules, which are abnormally dilated and increase in ectasia over time. Many cases are associated with somatic activating mutations in genes of the GNAQ/GNA11 pathway, arising during embryogenesis and affecting a clone of vascular and surrounding cells. Because the abnormality is structural rather than proliferative, the number of vessels is essentially fixed, but progressive vascular dilatation and, in some cases, associated soft-tissue overgrowth account for the darkening and thickening seen with age. The same mosaic mutations underlie the neurological and ocular features when the malformation extends beyond the skin. A port-wine stain is a lifelong lesion that persists and typically darkens and thickens over time; the skin lesion itself is benign, but associated syndromic features determine broader outcome, and laser treatment can substantially lighten many lesions though results vary and maintenance may be required.

Portal hypertension — portal venous hypertension, raised portal pressure, portal HTN Cirrhosis of any aetiology Portal or splenic vein thrombosis (prehepatic) Hepatic schistosomiasis (presinusoidal) Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction) Right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis (posthepatic) Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension / idiopathic portal hypertension Upper GI endoscopy to grade and treat varices Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler of the portal and hepatic veins to assess flow, thrombosis, and splenomegaly Liver function tests, coagulation profile, and full blood count (for hypersplenism-related cytopenias) Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for hepatic architecture, collaterals, and vascular patency Hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement where available to quantify portal pressure Liver biopsy or elastography to assess fibrosis and clarify aetiology Portal hypertension is a sustained rise in portal venous pressure and is most often caused by cirrhosis in the developed world and by schistosomiasis or portal vein thrombosis elsewhere Clinical consequences arise from portosystemic collaterals and splanchnic congestion: gastro-oesophageal varices, splenomegaly with hypersplenism, ascites, and caput medusae Variceal haemorrhage is the most dangerous complication and presents as haematemesis or melaena, often with haemodynamic instability Causes are usefully grouped as prehepatic (e.g. portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (presinusoidal, sinusoidal as in cirrhosis, or postsinusoidal), and posthepatic (e.g. Budd-Chiari syndrome, constrictive pericarditis) Endoscopy characterises and treats varices, while non-selective beta-blockade reduces portal pressure and the risk of first or recurrent bleeding Acute variceal bleeding is managed with resuscitation, vasoactive splanchnic vasoconstrictors, endoscopic band ligation, and antibiotic prophylaxis, with balloon tamponade or TIPS as rescue Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) and, less commonly, surgical shunts decompress the portal system but can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy Active variceal haemorrhage with haematemesis, melaena, and haemodynamic instability requiring emergency resuscitation and endoscopy Encephalopathy with reduced consciousness and risk of aspiration Rapidly accumulating tense ascites or spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Signs of decompensation (jaundice, coagulopathy, hepatorenal syndrome) indicating advanced liver failure Over-transfusing during variceal bleeding, which can raise portal pressure and worsen haemorrhage Omitting antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhotic patients with gastrointestinal bleeding Aggressive correction of coagulopathy or platelet counts without regard to the rebalanced haemostasis of cirrhosis Creating a shunt without anticipating precipitation or worsening of hepatic encephalopathy Attributing all upper GI bleeding to varices and missing coexisting peptic ulceration or portal hypertensive gastropathy Portal hypertension results from increased resistance to portal blood flow combined with increased splanchnic inflow. In cirrhosis, fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort the hepatic architecture and raise sinusoidal resistance, compounded by intrahepatic vasoconstriction. Splanchnic arterial vasodilatation, mediated in part by nitric oxide, increases portal inflow and sustains the elevated pressure. As pressure rises, portosystemic collateral channels open at sites of communication between the portal and systemic circulations, producing varices at the gastro-oesophageal junction, rectum, and anterior abdominal wall. Splenic congestion causes splenomegaly and hypersplenism, and the combination of portal hypertension and hepatic dysfunction drives ascites and hepatic encephalopathy. Prognosis is dominated by the underlying liver disease and by whether decompensation has occurred; variceal bleeding carries substantial mortality, particularly in advanced cirrhosis. Effective prophylaxis, endoscopic therapy, and shunting reduce rebleeding, but long-term survival depends on hepatic reserve and, in suitable candidates, transplantation.

Postoperative nausea and vomiting — PONV, post-anaesthetic nausea and vomiting, postoperative emesis Bowel obstruction or ileus Gastric distension from mask ventilation Raised intracranial pressure or neurological cause Metabolic disturbance such as hyponatraemia or hypoglycaemia Medication or opioid effect Hypotension or hypovolaemia Clinical assessment of hydration, pain, and haemodynamics Review of anaesthetic and analgesic agents administered Electrolytes and glucose if vomiting is persistent Abdominal imaging if obstruction or ileus is suspected Neurological assessment if a central cause is possible A common and distressing complication after anaesthesia that reduces patient satisfaction, delays discharge, and occasionally causes serious complications Established patient risk factors include female sex, non-smoking status, history of PONV or motion sickness, and younger age, often summarised in simplified risk scores Anaesthetic and surgical factors include use of volatile agents and nitrous oxide, perioperative opioids, and longer or certain types of surgery A multimodal approach works best: reducing baseline risk (opioid-sparing analgesia, regional techniques, total intravenous anaesthesia) and combining antiemetics from different classes Prophylactic agents span several receptor targets, including serotonin antagonists, corticosteroids, dopamine antagonists, and antihistamines, chosen according to risk For breakthrough symptoms, an antiemetic from a class not already used for prophylaxis is preferred rather than repeating the same drug Adequate hydration, avoidance of unnecessary opioids, and treatment of pain and hypotension help reduce symptoms Persistent or severe postoperative vomiting should prompt consideration of surgical, metabolic, or intracranial causes rather than assuming simple PONV Persistent vomiting causing dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, or aspiration risk Vomiting with headache, focal neurology, or reduced consciousness suggesting an intracranial cause Bilious or feculent vomiting indicating bowel obstruction Vomiting with severe abdominal pain suggesting a surgical complication Relying on a single antiemetic in high-risk patients instead of combining agents Repeating the same drug class for breakthrough symptoms Overlooking modifiable contributors such as opioids, hypotension, and dehydration Assuming all postoperative vomiting is benign and missing a surgical or neurological cause Failing to risk-stratify and tailor prophylaxis preoperatively Nausea and vomiting are coordinated by brainstem centres receiving input from the chemoreceptor trigger zone, vestibular system, higher cortical centres, and vagal afferents from the gastrointestinal tract. Multiple neurotransmitters, including serotonin, dopamine, histamine, acetylcholine, and substance P, mediate these pathways. Anaesthetic agents, opioids, gastric distension, hypotension, and surgical stimulation activate one or more of these inputs. Because several receptor systems contribute, blocking a single pathway is often insufficient, which is why combining antiemetics acting at different receptors is more effective than escalating a single agent. PONV is usually self-limiting and responds to multimodal prophylaxis and treatment, but uncontrolled symptoms can delay recovery, cause dehydration, and rarely lead to aspiration or wound complications.

Postdural puncture headache — PDPH, post-lumbar puncture headache, low-pressure headache Migraine or tension-type headache Meningitis (infective) or chemical meningism Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis Subdural haematoma Pre-eclampsia or eclampsia in the obstetric patient Pneumocephalus or caffeine-withdrawal headache Clinical assessment focusing on the postural nature of the headache Neurological examination to exclude focal signs Brain imaging (CT or MRI) when features are atypical, worsening, or accompanied by neurological signs Investigations for pre-eclampsia in the postpartum patient when relevant Assessment for infection if fever or meningism is present A characteristically postural headache that worsens on sitting or standing and improves on lying flat, developing within a few days of dural puncture Typically frontal or occipital and may be accompanied by neck stiffness, photophobia, nausea, tinnitus, or hearing changes Risk is higher with larger-gauge and cutting (rather than pencil-point) needles, younger age, female sex, and after accidental dural puncture during epidural placement Diagnosis is largely clinical, but a headache lacking postural features or with neurological signs should prompt evaluation for other causes Initial management is conservative with rest as needed, hydration, simple analgesia, and reassurance, as many cases resolve spontaneously An epidural blood patch is the definitive treatment for severe or persistent headache and is generally highly effective Caffeine and other pharmacological measures have limited and temporary benefit compared with a blood patch Rare but serious complications of intracranial hypotension include subdural haematoma and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, so atypical or worsening features require imaging Loss of the postural component or a headache that becomes constant, suggesting an alternative or serious cause Focal neurological deficit, seizure, or reduced consciousness suggesting subdural haematoma or venous thrombosis Fever, neck stiffness, or photophobia raising concern for meningitis Sudden thunderclap onset or features suggesting subarachnoid haemorrhage Assuming every post-procedure headache is a postdural puncture headache and missing a dangerous cause Delaying an effective blood patch in severe, disabling headache Overlooking evolving neurological signs that indicate subdural haematoma or venous sinus thrombosis Failing to consider pre-eclampsia in a postpartum woman with headache Relying on caffeine or bed rest alone for persistent severe symptoms A persistent hole in the dura allows cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the epidural space faster than it is produced, lowering cerebrospinal fluid volume and pressure. In the upright position, reduced buoyant support causes traction on pain-sensitive intracranial structures such as the meninges and bridging veins, and compensatory cerebral vasodilation may contribute, producing the postural headache. Larger dural defects leak more and cause more severe symptoms. An epidural blood patch works by sealing the defect and raising epidural and cerebrospinal fluid pressure. Most postdural puncture headaches resolve within days to weeks with conservative care, and a blood patch relieves the majority of severe cases; rare progression to intracranial haemorrhage or venous thrombosis can cause serious morbidity.

Posterior urethral valves — PUV, congenital obstructing posterior urethral membrane Ureteropelvic or ureterovesical junction obstruction Prune belly (Eagle-Barrett) syndrome Bilateral high-grade vesicoureteric reflux Neurogenic bladder Urethral atresia or stricture Voiding cystourethrogram to demonstrate the valves and assess reflux and bladder morphology Renal and bladder ultrasound to evaluate hydronephrosis and bladder wall thickness Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine to assess renal function (interpreted after the first days of life) Cystoscopy for direct visualisation and treatment of the valves Isotope renography to assess differential renal function and drainage The most common cause of congenital lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants, caused by obstructing membranous folds in the posterior urethra Many cases are suspected antenatally from bilateral hydronephrosis, a thick-walled distended bladder, a dilated posterior urethra (keyhole sign), and oligohydramnios Severe early obstruction and oligohydramnios can lead to pulmonary hypoplasia, which may be the immediate life-threatening problem at birth Postnatal presentation ranges from a palpable bladder, poor urinary stream, and straining to urosepsis or failure to thrive, and older boys may present with voiding difficulty or incontinence The voiding cystourethrogram is the key diagnostic study, showing a dilated posterior urethra, bladder trabeculation, and often vesicoureteric reflux Initial management is bladder decompression with a catheter, correction of fluid and electrolyte disturbance, and treatment of infection before definitive intervention Definitive treatment is endoscopic ablation of the valves, with temporary urinary diversion (vesicostomy) reserved for selected infants Long-term follow-up is essential because bladder dysfunction and progressive renal impairment can persist or evolve even after successful valve ablation Neonatal respiratory distress from pulmonary hypoplasia secondary to oligohydramnios, which is immediately life-threatening Urosepsis in an infant with obstruction requiring urgent decompression and antibiotics Acute kidney injury with electrolyte disturbance and rising creatinine Progressive deterioration in renal function or bladder function despite valve ablation Attributing an antenatal keyhole bladder or bilateral hydronephrosis to a benign cause and delaying evaluation Interpreting neonatal creatinine in the first day or two as the baby's true renal function rather than the mother's Assuming valve ablation cures the child and neglecting long-term renal and bladder surveillance Overlooking bladder dysfunction as an ongoing cause of upper tract deterioration Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing tissue folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra of males that impede bladder emptying from early in fetal life. The resulting high-pressure obstruction causes bladder wall hypertrophy and trabeculation, vesicoureteric reflux, and back-pressure that dilates the ureters and damages the developing kidneys, producing dysplasia and impaired concentrating ability. Reduced fetal urine output causes oligohydramnios, which in turn impairs lung development and can result in pulmonary hypoplasia. The renal and bladder damage sustained in utero often determines lifelong outcome. Outcome depends largely on the degree of irreversible renal dysplasia established in utero. Many boys do well after valve ablation, but a significant proportion develop chronic kidney disease and bladder dysfunction, and some progress to end-stage renal failure requiring transplantation. Early nadir creatinine after treatment is a useful prognostic indicator.

Posterior uveitis — choroiditis, chorioretinitis, retinochoroiditis Intraocular lymphoma masquerading as chronic vitritis Central serous chorioretinopathy Retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema Endophthalmitis Age-related macular degeneration with choroidal neovascular membrane Hereditary retinal dystrophy Dilated fundus examination and vitreous haze grading to assess activity Optical coherence tomography to detect macular oedema and monitor response Fundus fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography to map retinal and choroidal inflammation Serology and targeted testing for toxoplasma, syphilis, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis Vitreous or aqueous sampling with PCR or cytology when infection or lymphoma is suspected Systemic imaging (e.g. chest imaging) when sarcoidosis or tuberculosis is considered Typically presents with painless blurred vision and floaters rather than the pain and redness seen with anterior involvement Inflammation centres on the choroid and retina, so signs are found on fundus examination as vitritis, focal or multifocal chorioretinal lesions, and vascular sheathing Vitreous haze grading gives a useful measure of activity and treatment response Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis is a leading infective cause and characteristically produces a focal lesion adjacent to an old pigmented scar Non-infective causes include sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, sympathetic ophthalmia, and the white-dot syndromes Distinguishing infective from immune-mediated aetiology is essential because immunosuppression can worsen an untreated infection Management of non-infective disease relies on corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression, whereas infective disease requires targeted antimicrobial cover first Complications that threaten sight include cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment, choroidal neovascular membranes, and optic nerve involvement Rapidly progressive retinitis suggesting viral (necrotising) infection needing urgent antiviral therapy Bilateral panuveitis after ocular injury or surgery raising concern for sympathetic ophthalmia Persistent vitritis in an older patient that may represent intraocular lymphoma Macular or optic nerve involvement with declining acuity requiring prompt treatment Starting immunosuppression before excluding an infective cause, which can allow infection to progress Overlooking cystoid macular oedema as the reason for reduced acuity in a quiet-looking eye Attributing chronic vitritis in an older patient to inflammation and missing masquerade lymphoma Failing to screen for a systemic disease that the eye findings are heralding Posterior uveitis is inflammation predominantly affecting the choroid and overlying retina, often with secondary vitreous involvement. It may arise from direct infection (for example Toxoplasma, tuberculosis, syphilis, viral retinitis) or from immune-mediated processes such as sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, or an autoimmune reaction to ocular antigens as in sympathetic ophthalmia. Inflammatory cells and mediators disrupt the outer blood-retinal barrier, causing exudation, oedema, and eventual chorioretinal scarring. Ischaemia and chronic inflammation can drive neovascularisation, and macular or optic nerve involvement determines the visual outcome. Outcome depends on the underlying cause and on whether the macula and optic nerve are spared; focal treatable infections such as toxoplasmosis often heal with scarring away from the fovea, but recurrent or immune-mediated disease can cause cumulative visual loss from macular oedema, scarring, or neovascular complications.

Postpartum depression — postnatal depression, peripartum depression, major depressive disorder with peripartum onset, PPD Postpartum blues (transient and self-limiting) Postpartum psychosis Bipolar disorder presenting or relapsing in the perinatal period Postpartum thyroiditis and other thyroid dysfunction Anaemia and other medical causes of fatigue Anxiety disorders or obsessive-compulsive disorder with perinatal onset Validated perinatal depression screening, such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale Structured suicide risk assessment and assessment of thoughts of harm to the infant Thyroid function testing Full blood count to exclude anaemia Screening for a history of bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant This is a major depressive episode with onset during pregnancy or in the weeks following delivery, presenting with persistent low mood, loss of interest, and the associated features of depression It must be distinguished from the common, transient postpartum blues, which are mild and self-limiting within about two weeks, and from the rare psychiatric emergency of postpartum psychosis Presentations often include prominent anxiety, guilt about parenting ability, and intrusive thoughts, and mothers may be reluctant to disclose symptoms for fear of judgement Actively assess suicidal ideation and any thoughts of harming the infant, as these carry serious risk and require urgent action Routine screening in the perinatal period, for example with a validated postnatal depression scale, improves detection of an often hidden condition Management combines psychotherapy and, when indicated, antidepressant pharmacotherapy, with treatment choices weighing symptom severity against breastfeeding considerations Untreated maternal depression can adversely affect mother-infant bonding and child development, so timely treatment benefits both mother and child Postpartum psychosis, with confusion, delusions, or thoughts of harming the infant, is an emergency requiring immediate assessment and usually admission Suicidal ideation with plan or intent Thoughts of harming the infant or command-type intrusive urges Features of postpartum psychosis such as confusion, delusions, or hallucinations Severe self-neglect or inability to care for the infant Dismissing significant depression as normal postpartum blues Failing to ask directly about suicidal thoughts and thoughts of harming the infant Missing an underlying bipolar disorder before prescribing an antidepressant Overlooking postpartum thyroiditis as a contributor Not recognising postpartum psychosis as an emergency requiring urgent care Postpartum depression is thought to result from the interaction of an abrupt drop in reproductive hormones after delivery with a predisposing vulnerability, superimposed on the neurobiology shared with major depression, including monoamine and stress-axis dysregulation. Sleep deprivation, psychosocial stressors, a history of mood disorder, and inadequate support further increase risk in susceptible women. Postpartum depression generally responds well to treatment, and most women recover, but there is an increased risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies and of future depressive episodes. Prognosis is better with early detection, treatment, and social support, and worse when the condition is unrecognised, when there is a bipolar diathesis, or when comorbidities and psychosocial adversity persist.

Postpartum haemorrhage — postpartum hemorrhage, PPH, obstetric haemorrhage after delivery Uterine atony Genital tract trauma including cervical or vaginal lacerations and haematomas Retained placenta or retained products of conception Placenta accreta spectrum Uterine inversion or rupture Inherited or acquired coagulopathy including disseminated intravascular coagulation Quantitative measurement of blood loss and continuous vital sign monitoring Full blood count and serial haemoglobin Coagulation screen with fibrinogen level Group and cross-match with early activation of transfusion support Examination under anaesthesia and ultrasound to identify retained tissue or genital tract trauma Postpartum haemorrhage is excessive bleeding after birth; primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours and secondary PPH from 24 hours up to about 12 weeks postpartum The causes are usefully remembered as the four Ts: tone (uterine atony), trauma (genital tract lacerations), tissue (retained placenta or products), and thrombin (coagulopathy) Uterine atony is by far the commonest cause, so uterine massage and uterotonic agents are first-line alongside resuscitation Active management of the third stage of labour with a prophylactic uterotonic reduces the incidence and severity of PPH Blood loss is frequently underestimated visually, so vital signs, quantitative assessment, and a high index of suspicion are essential A structured stepwise escalation moves from uterotonics to mechanical measures (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) and then to surgical options such as compression sutures, vessel ligation, or hysterectomy Tranexamic acid given early reduces death from bleeding and should be administered promptly Early involvement of senior obstetric, anaesthetic, and haematology teams with activation of a massive transfusion protocol improves outcomes Tachycardia, hypotension, and other signs of hypovolaemic shock Continued brisk bleeding despite uterotonics and uterine massage Clinical or laboratory evidence of coagulopathy A high uterine fundus with a boggy uterus indicating atony, or a suddenly inverted uterus Suspected placenta accreta spectrum after a difficult placental delivery Underestimating blood loss by visual assessment alone Failing to recognise ongoing bleeding masked by the physiological cardiovascular reserve of pregnancy until late collapse Not systematically excluding retained tissue and genital tract trauma when atony seems controlled but bleeding persists Delaying tranexamic acid and blood product replacement Escalating too slowly to mechanical and surgical measures when medical therapy fails Normal postpartum haemostasis depends on vigorous myometrial contraction that mechanically compresses the spiral arteries of the placental bed, supported by the clotting cascade. Postpartum haemorrhage results when one or more of these mechanisms fail: the uterus fails to contract (atony, often from overdistension, prolonged or augmented labour, infection, or retained tissue); vessels are torn by genital tract trauma; retained placental tissue or invasive placentation prevents effective contraction; or coagulation is impaired by dilution, consumption, or a pre-existing disorder. Ongoing loss can precipitate hypovolaemic shock and a self-perpetuating coagulopathy. With prompt recognition, resuscitation, and stepwise treatment most women recover fully. Delay in diagnosis or treatment can lead to shock, organ failure, need for hysterectomy with loss of fertility, and death; postpartum haemorrhage remains one of the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings.

Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis — PSGN, acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, APSGN, acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis IgA nephropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) nephritis Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease Serum complement C3 (and C4) with follow-up to document normalisation Antistreptococcal serology (ASO, anti-DNase B) or streptozyme panel Throat or skin swab and culture if active infection present Urinalysis with microscopy for red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells Serum urea, creatinine, and electrolytes to assess renal function Renal biopsy only in atypical or progressive cases A classic cause of acute nephritic syndrome in children, most often between about 5 and 12 years of age. Follows infection with specific nephritogenic strains of group A streptococcus, typically 1-2 weeks after pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks after skin infection. Presents with the nephritic picture of haematuria (often cola- or tea-coloured urine), oedema, hypertension, and variable reduction in urine output. Complement C3 is characteristically low and typically returns to normal within about 6-8 weeks; persistently low C3 beyond this window suggests another diagnosis. Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is supported by elevated or rising antistreptococcal antibodies such as ASO or anti-DNase B. Management is largely supportive, centred on salt and fluid restriction and control of hypertension and fluid overload. Antibiotics treat any active streptococcal infection but do not alter the course of the established nephritis. Renal biopsy is usually unnecessary and reserved for atypical features such as persistent low complement, progressive kidney failure, or nephrotic-range proteinuria. The prognosis in children is excellent, with the large majority recovering complete renal function. Severe or refractory hypertension, including hypertensive encephalopathy Rapidly rising creatinine suggesting rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis Pulmonary oedema or heart failure from fluid overload Marked oliguria or anuria Persistently low complement or nephrotic-range proteinuria indicating an alternative diagnosis Attributing every child with haematuria and low C3 to PSGN without follow-up complement testing Overlooking hypertensive complications by not monitoring blood pressure closely Failing to consider alternative glomerulonephritides when complement stays low beyond eight weeks Aggressive fluid administration worsening volume overload in an oliguric child Infection with nephritogenic strains of group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus triggers an immune-complex-mediated glomerular injury. Streptococcal antigens (such as nephritis-associated plasmin receptor and streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B) deposit in the glomeruli and, together with circulating and in situ immune complexes, activate the complement system, predominantly via the alternative pathway. The resulting inflammation causes endocapillary proliferation and neutrophil infiltration, reducing glomerular filtration and producing sodium and water retention, which manifests as haematuria, oedema, and hypertension. Most children recover fully; acute complications resolve over days to weeks, complement normalises within about two months, and microscopic haematuria may persist for up to a year with an excellent long-term outlook.

Prader-Willi syndrome arises from loss of function of paternally expressed, imprinted genes in the 15q11-q13 region. Because maternal copies of these genes are normally silenced by imprinting, absence of the paternal contribution leaves the region functionally inactive. This most commonly results from a de novo paternal deletion, and less commonly from maternal uniparental disomy (two maternal copies and no paternal copy) or an imprinting defect. Hypothalamic dysfunction is central to the phenotype, driving the abnormal satiety regulation and hyperphagia, growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and temperature and sleep disturbances. With rigorous dietary control, a structured food-secure environment, and growth hormone therapy, individuals can achieve improved health and function; without weight control, morbid obesity substantially shortens life expectancy.

Precocious Puberty — sexual precocity, central precocious puberty, peripheral precocious puberty, early puberty Premature thelarche (benign isolated breast development) Premature adrenarche (early pubic/axillary hair without other puberty) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Gonadal or adrenal tumour McCune-Albright syndrome CNS lesion (hamartoma, tumour, prior irradiation, or injury) Exogenous sex steroid exposure Bone age radiograph Basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH Sex steroid levels (oestradiol or testosterone) Adrenal androgens and 17-hydroxyprogesterone when a peripheral cause is suspected Pelvic ultrasound in girls to assess ovarian and uterine development MRI of the brain, particularly in boys or where a central lesion is suspected Precocious puberty is conventionally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before about 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys. It is broadly classified as central (gonadotropin-dependent, from early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis) or peripheral (gonadotropin-independent, from sex steroids produced outside the normal axis). Central precocious puberty is far more common in girls and is usually idiopathic, whereas in boys an underlying CNS lesion is more likely and must be excluded. Accelerated linear growth and advanced bone age are typical; paradoxically, premature epiphyseal fusion can compromise final adult height. A GnRH (or GnRH-agonist) stimulation test helps distinguish central from peripheral causes by assessing the gonadotropin response. Isolated premature thelarche or premature adrenarche are usually benign normal variants but should be monitored to ensure they are not the start of true precocity. Peripheral causes include congenital adrenal hyperplasia, gonadal or adrenal tumours, McCune-Albright syndrome, and exogenous sex steroid exposure. Beyond physical changes, early puberty can carry psychosocial consequences that warrant support for the child and family. Neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion Rapidly progressive virilisation or a palpable abdominal/gonadal mass suggesting a hormone-secreting tumour Precocious puberty in a boy, which more often has a serious underlying cause Very early or rapidly advancing puberty threatening severe height compromise Cafe-au-lait macules with bony abnormalities suggesting McCune-Albright syndrome Assuming precocious puberty is idiopathic in a boy without imaging to exclude a CNS lesion Confusing benign premature thelarche or adrenarche with true central precocity Overlooking the impact of advanced bone age on final adult height Neglecting the psychosocial needs of a child developing ahead of peers In central precocious puberty the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis reactivates prematurely, with pulsatile GnRH secretion stimulating pituitary gonadotropins and subsequent gonadal sex steroid production, reproducing normal but early puberty. In peripheral precocious puberty sex steroids arise independently of GnRH from the gonads, adrenals, tumours, or exogenous sources, producing secondary sexual characteristics without central axis activation. Sex steroids accelerate growth and skeletal maturation, so advanced bone age can ultimately limit final height. Idiopathic central precocious puberty generally has a good outcome, and appropriate treatment can preserve growth potential and address psychosocial concerns; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying cause, such as a CNS lesion or hormone-secreting tumour.

timing balances gestational age against maternal and fetal risk Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease and to treat eclamptic seizures, not as an antihypertensive Antihypertensive therapy aims to lower dangerously high blood pressure to reduce maternal stroke risk while preserving placental perfusion Low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy reduces incidence in women at high risk (prior pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, multiple pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome) Severe hypertension unresponsive to treatment threatening maternal stroke Neurological signs (severe headache, visual loss, hyperreflexia with clonus) heralding impending eclampsia Right upper quadrant pain with abnormal liver enzymes suggesting HELLP or hepatic haematoma/rupture Pulmonary oedema or oliguria indicating organ failure Fetal growth restriction with abnormal Dopplers or non-reassuring fetal status Excluding the diagnosis because proteinuria is absent despite organ dysfunction Underestimating severity in HELLP syndrome where blood pressure may be only mildly raised Over-aggressive blood pressure lowering compromising placental perfusion Failing to continue monitoring postpartum, when eclampsia and severe hypertension can still occur Treating magnesium sulfate as an antihypertensive rather than as seizure prophylaxis Pre-eclampsia originates in abnormal placentation: inadequate remodelling of the maternal spiral arteries by trophoblast leads to a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta. The ischaemic placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (such as soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and soluble endoglin) that antagonise vascular endothelial and placental growth factors, producing widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction. This causes vasospasm, increased vascular permeability, activation of coagulation, and multi-organ hypoperfusion, manifesting as hypertension, proteinuria, hepatic and cerebral involvement, and fetal growth restriction. With timely surveillance, blood pressure control, seizure prophylaxis, and appropriately timed delivery most women recover fully postpartum, though there is an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular and renal disease. Severe or early-onset disease carries higher maternal and perinatal morbidity, and recurrence in future pregnancies is common.

Premature ejaculation — PE, early ejaculation, rapid ejaculation Erectile dysfunction with compensatory rapid ejaculation Chronic prostatitis or pelvic pain contributing to ejaculatory symptoms Hyperthyroidism Performance anxiety and situational sexual dysfunction Relationship or psychosexual conflict Substance or medication effects Focused sexual and psychosocial history distinguishing lifelong from acquired patterns Assessment of erectile function to identify coexisting erectile dysfunction Thyroid function testing when an endocrine cause is suspected Evaluation for prostatitis or lower urinary tract symptoms where indicated Screening for depression, anxiety, and relationship stressors Premature ejaculation is the most common male sexual complaint and is defined by ejaculation occurring sooner than desired, with a perceived inability to delay it and associated distress It is classified as lifelong (present since first sexual experiences) or acquired (developing later after a period of normal control), which guides evaluation and management Diagnosis is clinical and rests on the history; the intravaginal ejaculatory latency time and degree of control, distress, and interpersonal difficulty frame the assessment Acquired cases warrant a search for contributing conditions such as erectile dysfunction, thyroid dysfunction, prostatitis, or psychological stressors Erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation frequently coexist, and treating the erectile problem first may resolve the ejaculatory complaint Behavioural techniques such as the stop-start and squeeze methods can improve ejaculatory control, often combined with partner involvement and counselling Pharmacological options work by delaying the ejaculatory reflex, and topical desensitising agents or centrally acting serotonergic medication are used according to principle rather than fixed dosing A collaborative, non-judgemental approach that addresses relationship and psychological factors improves outcomes Sudden acquired premature ejaculation with erectile dysfunction, which may signal underlying vascular or endocrine disease Associated pelvic or perineal pain suggesting prostatitis Significant psychological distress, relationship breakdown, or depression Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis accompanying new-onset ejaculatory change Treating premature ejaculation in isolation while missing coexisting erectile dysfunction Neglecting the partner and relationship dimension, which strongly influences distress and outcome Overlooking treatable contributors such as thyroid disease or prostatitis in acquired cases Framing the problem as purely psychological when a neurobiological basis is likely in lifelong disease Ejaculation is a spinal reflex coordinated by sympathetic, parasympathetic, and somatic pathways and modulated by supraspinal serotonergic centres. Serotonin (5-HT) generally raises the ejaculatory threshold, and variation in central serotonergic tone and receptor sensitivity is thought to underlie lifelong premature ejaculation, giving it a substantial neurobiological and genetic basis. Acquired premature ejaculation is more often secondary, arising from erectile dysfunction (where a man rushes before losing his erection), prostatic or thyroid disease, or psychological factors such as anxiety and performance pressure that heighten sympathetic arousal and shorten latency. Premature ejaculation responds well to a combination of behavioural therapy, pharmacological delay of the reflex, and treatment of any coexisting condition, though lifelong forms may require ongoing management to maintain control.

Premature Ventricular Contractions, Nonsustained Idioventricular Rhythm — PVCs, Ventricular premature complexes, Ventricular ectopy, Nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, NSVT, Accelerated idioventricular rhythm, AIVR Idiopathic outflow-tract or fascicular ventricular arrhythmia (benign) Papillary muscle ectopy associated with mitral valve prolapse and mitral annular disjunction Sustained monomorphic VT (must be distinguished from NSVT by duration and hemodynamic impact) Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction (wide-complex differential) Genetic arrhythmia syndromes: long QT, Brugada, short QT, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 12-lead ECG in sinus rhythm (benign idiopathic arrhythmia usually shows a completely normal ECG; any abnormality warrants further workup) Ambulatory/telemetry monitoring to quantify PVC burden and capture NSVT Transthoracic echocardiography to assess ventricular function, wall-motion abnormalities, and valvular disease Contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI to detect scar and late gadolinium enhancement suggesting underlying cardiomyopathy Exercise stress testing for effort-related symptoms or coronary risk Assessment of electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) during acute illness Family history evaluation and consideration of genetic syndromes when a family history of sudden death exists Electrolyte abnormality (especially hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) provoking ectopy Stimulant or adrenergic effect (caffeine, alcohol, sympathomimetics) Myocardial ischemia presenting as new ventricular ectopy Drug or toxic effect on conduction (e.g., sodium-channel-blocking agents producing slowed, wide QRS rhythms) Ventricular ectopy spanning PVCs, nonsustained VT (NSVT), and accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) is very common and is most often asymptomatic, detected incidentally on telemetry or prompted by palpitations. A PVC is a single ventricular beat occurring earlier than the next expected supraventricular beat; PVCs from one focus share an identical QRS morphology (unifocal), while differing morphologies indicate multifocal origin and raise suspicion for structural or myopathic disease. Two consecutive ventricular beats form a couplet; three or more consecutive beats above 100/min define VT, and VT terminating spontaneously within 30 seconds is termed nonsustained. QRS morphology localizes the focus: a dominant S wave in V1 (left bundle branch block-like) points to the right ventricle or septum, whereas a dominant R wave in V1 (right bundle branch block-like) points to the left ventricle; the frontal-plane axis distinguishes superior (inferior-wall) versus cranial origin. Most ventricular arrhythmias without structural disease have a left bundle branch block-like pattern, while a right bundle branch block configuration or multiple PVC morphologies more often signal structural heart disease. Idiopathic ectopy commonly arises from the right or left ventricular outflow tracts near the valve annuli, and also from papillary muscles and fascicular tissue; benign idiopathic NSVT is usually monomorphic with rates under 200/min. Bigeminy (every other beat a PVC) can cause pseudobradycardia because the premature beats may not generate a palpable pulse, so counted rate can read falsely low. In the peri-infarct period, PVCs and NSVT are common early manifestations of ischemia and can herald ventricular fibrillation. AIVR is defined as three or more ventricular beats at a rate slower than 100/min, usually due to enhanced automaticity; it is common during acute MI and may emerge during sinus bradycardia or sleep. Frequent ectopy can itself depress ventricular function (PVC-induced cardiomyopathy), but this rarely occurs unless PVCs account for at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours, and only a minority of such patients develop reversible cardiomyopathy. Smooth, sharp QRS deflections of a PVC suggest a focus in relatively normal myocardium, whereas broad notching and slurring suggest a diseased substrate. Recently inflammation has been recognized as contributing to PVC genesis in inflammatory and inherited cardiomyopathies. Syncope or near-syncope, especially without prodrome, during exertion, or with an abnormal ECG or structural heart disease Very rapid or polymorphic NSVT, or a 'short-coupled' first beat occurring before the peak of the T wave Family history of sudden death prompting evaluation for inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy Any abnormality on the 12-lead ECG (Q waves of prior infarction, ventricular hypertrophy, repolarization abnormalities of long QT/Brugada/ARVC) Right bundle branch block-like or multifocal PVC morphology suggesting structural disease Depressed ventricular function with frequent/repetitive ectopy Bigeminal PVCs can produce pseudobradycardia, leading to an erroneously low measured heart rate. Asymptomatic PVCs and NSVT discovered in a hospitalized or acutely ill patient generally do not require specific antiarrhythmic treatment beyond addressing the underlying illness and correcting aggravating factors. Assuming all ventricular ectopy is benign; very rapid, polymorphic, short-coupled, or multifocal patterns and any ECG/structural abnormality demand evaluation for sudden-death risk. Overlooking reversible PVC-induced cardiomyopathy in patients with very frequent ectopy and otherwise unexplained left ventricular dysfunction. Attributing a wide-complex rhythm to VT without distinguishing it from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy. PVCs arise via enhanced (abnormal) automaticity, triggered activity, or localized reentry. They are frequently sympathetically sensitive and can reflect heightened sympathetic tone, myocardial ischemia, hypoxia, electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), or underlying structural heart disease. The site of earliest ventricular activation dictates the activation sequence and therefore the QRS morphology, allowing the surface ECG to suggest the anatomic origin and the likelihood of structural disease. In the setting of ischemia or structural disease, PVCs and NSVT can be harbingers of sustained VT or VF. AIVR is typically driven by automaticity, though rare reentrant circuits in diseased myocardium can produce it. PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction is thought to act through a mechanism akin to chronic tachycardia or through ventricular dyssynchrony. PVCs, NSVT, and AIVR are most often benign when they occur in structurally normal hearts with normal ECGs, and idiopathic ectopy generally has excellent long-term arrhythmia-free outcomes (catheter ablation suppresses idiopathic PVCs in roughly 90% of patients). In contrast, the same arrhythmias carry prognostic weight in the presence of structural disease: after MI and in heart failure, frequent (typically >10 PVCs/h), repetitive PVCs, couplets, and NSVT are markers of depressed ventricular function and increased mortality, and they are likewise associated with worse outcomes in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and congenital heart disease with ventricular dysfunction. AIVR is usually well tolerated, though loss of AV synchrony may cause hemodynamic compromise in susceptible patients. Risk is stratified less by ectopy count alone than by context: (1) structurally normal heart with normal ECG and monomorphic NSVT under 200/min - benign/low risk; (2) structural heart disease (post-MI, heart failure, HCM, congenital disease) where greater frequency and complexity (couplets, NSVT) mark more severe disease and higher mortality; (3) high-risk features warranting concern - syncope, very rapid/polymorphic/short-coupled NSVT, multifocal or RBBB-like morphology, abnormal ECG, or family history of sudden death. PVC burden of at least 10-20% of total beats over 24 hours is the threshold associated with potential PVC-induced ventricular dysfunction.

Premenstrual dysphoric disorder — PMDD, severe premenstrual syndrome, premenstrual dysphoria Premenstrual exacerbation of major depressive or anxiety disorder Bipolar affective disorder Thyroid irritability, mood lability, depressed mood, anxiety, and a sense of being overwhelmed, alongside physical complaints such as bloating and breast tenderness Diagnosis should be confirmed by disorder, which persists throughout the cycle Serotonergic antidepressants are a first-line treatment and can be given continuously or restricted to the luteal phase according to principle Suppressing ovulation, for example with combined hormonal contraception, can relieve symptoms by abolishing the cyclical hormonal trigger Lifestyle measures, cognitive behavioural therapy, and attention to suicide risk during the luteal phase are important adjuncts Suicidal ideation, which may intensify during the luteal phase Symptoms persisting throughout the cycle, suggesting a primary psychiatric disorder rather than PMDD Severe functional impairment or inability to maintain work and relationships Features suggesting bipolar disorder that would alter treatment choice Diagnosing on retrospective history without prospective symptom charting Missing an underlying mood disorder that is merely worsened premenstrually Underestimating luteal-phase suicide risk Attributing all cyclical physical symptoms to PMDD without considering other causes Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is thought to arise from an abnormal central nervous system sensitivity to the normal cyclical fluctuations of ovarian steroids rather than from any abnormal hormone level. Progesterone metabolites such as allopregnanolone, which modulate GABA-A receptor function, and interactions with serotonergic neurotransmission appear central, so susceptible women experience marked mood and behavioural symptoms during the luteal phase when these hormones fluctuate. Because the trigger is ovulatory cycling, symptoms resolve when the cycle ends and can be abolished by suppressing ovulation. The rapid response to serotonergic agents, often faster than in major depression, supports a serotonergic mechanism. With accurate diagnosis and treatment, most women achieve substantial symptom control; symptoms recur if treatment stops while ovulatory cycles continue and typically resolve after the menopause or with sustained ovulation suppression.

benefit Marked asymmetry between ears suggesting a retrocochlear or other unilateral lesion Sudden or rapidly progressive hearing loss requiring urgent evaluation Unilateral tinnitus, vertigo or facial numbness raising concern for acoustic neuroma Associated neurological signs that point away from simple age-related loss Assuming all hearing loss in the elderly is presbycusis and missing wax, effusion or a tumour Overlooking asymmetry that warrants imaging Neglecting the impact of poor speech discrimination and recruitment on hearing aid success Failing to address modifiable contributors such as ongoing noise exposure and ototoxic medication Presbycusis results from cumulative degenerative changes in the auditory system with age. Several subtypes are described: sensory presbycusis from loss of hair cells in the basal (high-frequency) cochlea; neural presbycusis from loss of spiral ganglion neurons, which particularly impairs speech discrimination; strial or metabolic presbycusis from atrophy of the stria vascularis affecting the endocochlear potential across frequencies; and cochlear conductive (mechanical) presbycusis from stiffening of the basilar membrane. Central auditory pathway changes further degrade processing of speech, especially in noise. Genetic predisposition, lifelong noise exposure, vascular and metabolic disease and ototoxins accelerate these changes. Presbycusis is irreversible and slowly progressive, but most patients maintain good communication and quality of life with hearing aids and rehabilitation, and cochlear implantation can help those with severe loss and poor aided speech understanding.

exudate, and tissue type Nutritional assessment and screening for undernutrition Evaluation of perfusion, continence, and mobility as modifiable contributors Investigations for infection such as wound and systemic assessment when osteomyelitis or spreading infection is suspected Pressure injuries are localised damage to skin and underlying tissue over a bony prominence, caused by sustained pressure often combined with shear and friction Common sites include the sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters, and occiput, reflecting where soft tissue is compressed against bone Staging runs from non-blanchable erythema of intact skin, through partial- and full-thickness skin loss, to exposure of muscle or bone, with unstageable and deep-tissue-injury categories where depth is obscured Prevention is far more effective than treatment and rests on risk assessment, regular repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces, skin care, and nutritional support Validated risk tools such as the Braden or Waterlow scales help identify at-risk patients and target preventive resources Immobility, malnutrition, incontinence, poor perfusion, sensory impairment, and advanced age are the principal risk factors Management combines pressure offloading, wound cleansing, appropriate dressings for the wound bed, debridement of devitalised tissue where indicated, and optimisation of nutrition Near the end of life, skin failure can occur despite excellent care, and goals may appropriately prioritise comfort over aggressive wound healing Spreading erythema, purulent discharge, or systemic features suggesting wound infection or sepsis Deep wounds exposing bone with suspected underlying osteomyelitis Rapidly deteriorating or new deep-tissue injury indicating ongoing unrelieved pressure Signs of necrotising soft-tissue infection requiring urgent surgical assessment Focusing on dressings while failing to relieve the underlying pressure Neglecting nutrition, which is essential to wound healing Missing deep-tissue injury because early damage lies beneath intact-looking skin Overlooking heels and medical-device-related sites during skin inspection Pursuing aggressive healing goals at the end of life when comfort should take priority Sustained pressure over a bony prominence exceeds capillary closing pressure, obstructing microcirculation and causing local ischaemia. If pressure is not relieved, ischaemia progresses to tissue hypoxia, inflammation, and cell death, with damage often beginning in deeper tissues adjacent to bone before it becomes visible at the surface. Shear forces distort and occlude vessels, and friction and moisture from incontinence weaken the epidermal barrier. Impaired perfusion, undernutrition, reduced sensation, and immobility all lower tissue tolerance and accelerate breakdown. Superficial pressure injuries can heal with consistent offloading and good wound and nutritional care, whereas deep, full-thickness injuries heal slowly and may recur. Pressure injuries are markers of illness severity and are associated with pain, infection, prolonged hospitalisation, and increased mortality, particularly in frail and end-of-life patients in whom prevention and comfort are paramount.

frequently more advanced in the deeper tissues nearest the bone Prevention through repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces, skin care, moisture control, and nutrition is more effective than incontinence, and infection Deep ulcers with dead space or exposed bone may require surgical debridement and reconstruction with local flaps, and osteomyelitis should be considered when bone is
