addressing mobility, sensation, continence, and social circumstances is essential to prevent recurrence Spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or signs of necrotising infection arising from the ulcer Exposed bone with suspected osteomyelitis Rapid deterioration or deep tissue injury under intact skin Chronic non-healing ulcer with atypical features suggesting malignant transformation Underestimating the depth of tissue damage from the surface appearance alone Attempting surgical closure without first correcting pressure, nutrition, spasticity, and incontinence Failing to debride nonviable tissue and eschar before assessing wound bed Overlooking underlying osteomyelitis in deep ulcers with exposed bone Neglecting prevention and repositioning, leading to new or recurrent ulcers Missing malignant change in a long-standing chronic ulcer Pressure ulcers result from prolonged unrelieved pressure, often combined with shear and friction, that compresses soft tissue between bone and an external surface. When interface pressure exceeds capillary closing pressure, local ischaemia and impaired lymphatic drainage lead to tissue hypoxia, accumulation of metabolic waste, and cell death. Muscle is more susceptible to ischaemia than skin, so damage typically begins in deep tissue near the bony prominence and progresses outward, producing a cone-shaped area of necrosis. Contributing factors include immobility, impaired sensation, malnutrition, moisture, incontinence, vascular disease, and advanced age. Superficial pressure injuries can heal with conservative care once pressure is relieved, but deep ulcers heal slowly and often require surgery. Even after successful flap reconstruction, recurrence rates are high in patients who remain immobile or insensate, so long-term outcome depends heavily on ongoing prevention and management of underlying risk factors.

contractility, cervical ripening, and decidual-membrane activation. Recognised triggers include intrauterine infection and inflammation, uteroplacental ischaemia or haemorrhage (decidual bleeding), excessive uterine distension (as in multiple pregnancy or polyhydramnios), cervical insufficiency, and maternal or fetal stress activating the corticotrophin-releasing hormone axis. Priapism — persistent erection, ischaemic priapism, low-flow priapism, non-ischaemic priapism Ischaemic (low-flow) versus non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism distinction Stuttering (recurrent) priapism Penile trauma with fistula Drug-induced erection (intracavernosal agents, psychotropics, recreational drugs) Sickle cell disease or other haemoglobinopathy Pelvic or penile malignant infiltration Cavernosal blood gas analysis to differentiate ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism Penile colour Doppler ultrasound to assess cavernosal blood flow and identify a fistula Full blood count and film with haemoglobinopathy screen (sickle cell testing) Toxicology and medication review for causative agents Selective pudendal arteriography if embolisation of a high-flow fistula is planned Priapism is a prolonged penile erection (typically beyond four hours) unrelated to sexual stimulation, and the critical first step is to distinguish ischaemic (low-flow) from non-ischaemic (high-flow) types Ischaemic priapism is a painful, rigid erection representing a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa and is a urological emergency because prolonged ischaemia causes fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism is usually painless, semi-rigid, and follows perineal or penile trauma with an arteriolar-sinusoidal fistula; it is not an emergency and often resolves or is managed by embolisation Cavernosal blood gas analysis distinguishes the two: ischaemic blood is dark and hypoxic/acidotic, whereas high-flow blood is bright red with near-arterial values Common causes of ischaemic priapism include sickle cell disease, haematological malignancy, and drugs, notably intracavernosal vasoactive agents and certain psychotropic and recreational drugs Emergency management of ischaemic priapism proceeds stepwise from corporal aspiration and irrigation to intracavernosal sympathomimetic injection, and to surgical shunting if these fail Underlying conditions such as sickle cell disease require concurrent systemic treatment alongside local measures Stuttering (recurrent) priapism, common in sickle cell disease, warrants preventive strategies to reduce recurrent ischaemic episodes Ischaemic priapism is a urological emergency; delay leads to corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction A rigid, painful erection persisting beyond four hours Underlying sickle cell crisis or haematological malignancy requiring urgent systemic treatment Failure of aspiration and intracavernosal therapy, mandating urgent surgical shunting Failing to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism before treatment, leading to inappropriate management Delaying emergency intervention in ischaemic priapism and risking irreversible fibrosis Overlooking an underlying cause such as sickle cell disease or a causative medication Treating high-flow priapism as an emergency with aggressive corporal procedures Neglecting preventive management of recurrent stuttering priapism Priapism reflects a disturbance of the normal mechanisms that terminate erection. In ischaemic (low-flow) priapism, veno-occlusion persists so blood becomes trapped in the corpora cavernosa, producing stagnant, hypoxic, acidotic blood and a compartment-syndrome-like state; prolonged ischaemia leads to smooth muscle necrosis and corporal fibrosis. Causes include sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies, leukaemic infiltration, and pharmacological agents. Non-ischaemic (high-flow) priapism results from unregulated arterial inflow, typically through a cavernosal artery fistula created by perineal or penile trauma, so oxygenation is maintained and tissue ischaemia does not occur. Prompt relief of ischaemic priapism improves the chance of preserved erectile function, but episodes lasting many hours frequently result in fibrosis and long-term erectile dysfunction; non-ischaemic priapism has a benign course and often resolves spontaneously or after embolisation.

CT only if MRI not possible FLAIR sequences to detect non-enhancing low-grade glioma and infiltrative disease Functional MRI for presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex PET, MR perfusion, and MR spectroscopy to assess metabolic activity and help distinguish tumor progression from treatment-related necrosis Molecular/integrated histopathologic testing (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT promoter methylation, H3 status, etc.) for classification and prognosis Stereotactic biopsy for histologic diagnosis of PCNSL (withhold glucocorticoids until biopsy where possible, as they are cytolytic to lymphoma) CSF cytology and flow cytometry for leptomeningeal and primary CNS lymphoma; HIV testing and EBV DNA in immunocompromised PCNSL Whole-spine MRI (or CT myelography if MRI impossible) for suspected epidural cord compression Demyelinating lesions Sarcoidosis Radiation necrosis in a previously treated patient Cerebral infarction or hemorrhage Migraine (when tumor headache has migrainous features) Depression (apathy/social withdrawal from a frontal tumor) Epidural hematoma, epidural lipomatosis, or extramedullary hematopoiesis (mimicking epidural tumor) Arthritic/degenerative back pain (vs epidural metastasis pain) Brain tumors of any histology tend to present with a mixture of generalized features (headache, nausea/vomiting, cognitive decline, personality change, gait disturbance from raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus) and focal features (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field defect) (Harrison 22e p.716). The classic morning-predominant brain tumor headache that eases through the day is actually seen in only a minority of patients; tumor headaches may be holocephalic, ipsilateral to the lesion, or even migraine-like with throbbing pain and scotoma (Harrison 22e p.716). Seizures occur in roughly 25% of patients with brain metastases or malignant gliomas but are the presenting symptom in up to 90% of low-grade gliomas; all tumor-related seizures have a focal onset whether or not that is clinically apparent (Harrison 22e p.716). Contrast (gadolinium) MRI is the preferred diagnostic study; CT is reserved for patients who cannot undergo MRI. Neuroimaging is generally the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumor, and laboratory tests are rarely useful (Harrison 22e p.716). Malignant tumors (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, show central necrosis, and are ringed by white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen on FLAIR sequences (Harrison 22e p.716). Meningiomas are dural-based enhancing extra-axial masses with a characteristic dural tail that compress but do not invade brain; their principal differential is a dural metastasis or dural lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.716, p.722). Adult diffuse gliomas are now classified molecularly: IDH-mutant astrocytoma (1p/19q intact), IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma (1p/19q co-deleted), and IDH wild-type glioblastoma; these molecular markers carry major prognostic weight (Harrison 22e p.718-719). An unmethylated MGMT promoter predicts relative temozolomide resistance and a worse glioblastoma prognosis; MGMT promoter hypermethylation (gene silencing) predicts better response (Harrison 22e p.720). Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumor (~35%), are more common in women and with prior cranial irradiation and NF2, and many are found incidentally; small asymptomatic ones can simply be monitored with serial MRI (Harrison 22e p.721-722). Most brain metastases lodge at the gray-white junction in watershed territories; ~85% are supratentorial and ~15% in the posterior fossa, and distribution roughly mirrors regional blood flow (Harrison 22e p.723). Melanoma has the greatest propensity to seed the brain (found in ~80% at autopsy), but lung and breast carcinomas are the most common sources overall; prostate and breast cancers also favor dural metastases that can mimic meningioma (Harrison 22e p.723). In epidural spinal metastasis, back pain is the presenting symptom in virtually all patients and may precede neurologic signs by weeks to months; the pain characteristically worsens on lying down, in contrast to arthritic pain which eases with recumbency (Harrison 22e p.725). Any cancer patient with severe back pain should undergo whole-spine MRI; plain films, bone scan, or CT may show bony disease but only MRI reliably delineates epidural tumor (Harrison 22e p.725). New focal neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual-field loss) that is subacute and progressive New-onset focal seizures, especially in an adult without prior epilepsy Severe back pain in a cancer patient (suggests epidural metastasis) — warrants urgent whole-spine MRI Leg weakness, sensory level, or sphincter dysfunction suggesting evolving spinal cord compression (a neuro-oncologic emergency) New limb pain in a patient with breast, lung cancer, or melanoma (consider leptomeningeal spread) Signs of raised intracranial pressure / hydrocephalus (worsening headache, vomiting, declining consciousness) Multilevel neuraxis signs (combined cranial neuropathies plus radiculopathies) suggesting leptomeningeal carcinomatosis Assuming a tumor headache must be morning-predominant — most are not, and tumor headaches can mimic migraine. Misattributing frontal-lobe apathy and withdrawal to primary depression rather than tumor. Giving glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL — their cytolytic effect on lymphoma cells can yield non-diagnostic tissue. Relying on a single CSF cytology in suspected leptomeningeal disease — it is positive in only ~50% on first lumbar puncture and still misses ~10% after three samples; imaging is diagnostic in only ~75%. Forgetting that the smallest brain metastases can produce extensive edema while large ones cause little, and that imaging appearance is nonspecific. Overlooking that ~10% of systemic cancers can first present with a brain metastasis, sometimes requiring biopsy of the brain lesion when no accessible systemic site exists. Treating low-grade glioma as benign — most ultimately transform to higher grade. Delaying spine imaging in a cancer patient with back pain until neurologic deficits appear. Most primary brain tumors have no identified cause; established risk factors are limited to ionizing radiation exposure (meningiomas, gliomas, schwannomas) and immunosuppression (primary CNS lymphoma), while electromagnetic field/cell-phone exposure, head injury, dietary N-nitroso compounds, and occupational factors are not proven. Tumors arise through a multistep accumulation of genetic alterations: loss of tumor-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of proto-oncogenes (EGFR, PDGFR), producing uncontrolled growth; many gliomas show marked molecular heterogeneity. The 2016 and 2021 WHO classifications integrate molecular parameters (e.g., IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, H3 K27/G34 alterations) with histology. Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the gray-white junction; leptomeningeal disease reaches the subarachnoid space via arterial circulation or retrograde venous flow and may also follow resection of a cerebellar metastasis. Epidural cord compression generally results from metastases to the axial skeleton (typically breast and prostate), though lymphoma can invade through an intervertebral foramen without bone destruction (Harrison 22e p.717, p.719, p.723, p.724-725). Outcome is highly histology- and molecular-subtype-dependent. Low-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas have median survival around 10 years (most eventually transform to higher grade); oligodendrogliomas (1p/19q co-deleted) generally exceed 10 years. Glioblastoma carries a poor prognosis with median survival in the 15-18 month range with combined therapy and ~10% 5-year survival; adverse factors are older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor Karnofsky status, and unresectable tumor. H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma has a median survival of roughly 1 year regardless of grade; H3 G34-mutant hemispheric glioma about 18-22 months. Medulloblastoma achieves long-term survival in ~70% but often with neurocognitive cost, varying by molecular subgroup (WNT best; group 3 worst). Completely resected meningiomas and schwannomas can be cured. Brain metastases treated with whole-brain radiotherapy alone yield median survival of only ~4-6 months, though stereotactic radiosurgery achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure. Leptomeningeal metastasis is treated palliatively with no curative therapy. In epidural metastasis, patients fare well if treated before a severe deficit develops, but overall survival is often short owing to widespread systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.718-725). Gliomas are graded by the WHO into grades 2-4 (low- vs high-grade) integrating histology with molecular markers (IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion; CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion upgrades an IDH-mutant astrocytoma to grade 4). Meningiomas are WHO grade I (benign), II (atypical), or III (malignant). Brain tumor symptoms are categorized as generalized (raised-ICP related) versus focal/lateralizing. Nervous-system metastatic disease is grouped clinically into intraparenchymal brain metastases, leptomeningeal (carcinomatous meningitis) metastases, and epidural spinal cord compression (Harrison 22e p.716, p.719, p.722).

spares large arteries on angiography Primary angiitis of the central nervous system is an idiopathic inflammatory vasculitis restricted to vessels of the brain, spinal cord, and meninges. Segmental infiltration of small and medium arterial walls by lymphocytes, granulomas, or necrotising inflammation leads to vessel wall thickening, luminal narrowing, and thrombosis, producing progressive multifocal ischaemia and occasionally haemorrhage. Because inflammation is patchy and confined to the CNS, systemic markers are typically unremarkable and diagnosis can be difficult, with progressive rather than reversible arterial narrowing distinguishing it from vasoconstrictive syndromes. Untreated PACNS is often severely disabling or fatal, but many patients stabilise or improve with immunosuppression; relapses occur and outcome depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment.

deterioration during fasting or intercurrent illness Failing to distinguish primary transporter deficiency from secondary carnitine depletion Not testing the mother when a newborn screens with low free carnitine Interrupting carnitine supplementation, risking recurrence of cardiomyopathy Overlooking asymptomatic adults who remain at risk of sudden cardiac events OCTN2 is a high-affinity sodium-dependent carnitine transporter expressed in heart, muscle, kidney and other tissues, responsible for cellular carnitine uptake and renal tubular reabsorption. Loss of function causes urinary carnitine loss and systemic carnitine depletion, so long-chain fatty acids cannot be shuttled into mitochondria for beta-oxidation because carnitine, the obligatory carrier, is lacking. The resulting energy deficit affects the heart and skeletal muscle, producing cardiomyopathy and myopathy, and impairs hepatic ketogenesis during fasting, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia; unlike downstream oxidation defects, the block is due to substrate (carnitine) deficiency rather than a defective enzyme. Prognosis is generally excellent with early diagnosis and consistent carnitine supplementation, which reverses cardiac and muscle disease; the main risks are arrhythmia and sudden death in untreated or non-adherent individuals.

and cardiac anomalies requiring cardiology assessment in infancy Attributing lifelong wet cough to recurrent viral infection or asthma and delaying diagnosis for years Relying on a single test result, Overlooking the situs inversus clue on a chest radiograph Forgetting to counsel about fertility implications Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a mostly autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding components of the motile cilium (for example the outer and inner dynein arms and radial spokes). Defective assembly or function of these structures impairs the coordinated beating of respiratory cilia, so mucociliary clearance fails and mucus and bacteria are retained throughout the airways and sinuses. The same defect in embryonic nodal cilia disrupts left-right patterning during development, explaining the frequent situs anomalies, while shared axonemal components account for impaired sperm and fallopian tube function. With early diagnosis and structured airway clearance many patients maintain reasonable lung function into adulthood, but chronic infection can cause progressive bronchiectasis, and outcomes vary with genotype, adherence to therapy, and access to specialist multidisciplinary care.

transplantation, with newer RNA-targeted therapies now available Progressive decline in renal function toward end-stage disease Systemic oxalosis with cardiac, skeletal, retinal, or vascular involvement Recurrent obstructing stones with infection or acute kidney injury Early-onset stone disease with nephrocalcinosis suggesting a severe genotype Treating recurrent stones symptomatically without recognising an underlying inherited metabolic cause Confusing primary with enteric hyperoxaluria, which have different mechanisms and management Overlooking systemic oxalosis as renal function falls Performing isolated kidney transplantation in type 1 disease without addressing continued hepatic oxalate overproduction Primary hyperoxaluria results from autosomal recessive defects in enzymes of hepatic glyoxylate detoxification. In type 1, deficiency of the peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase allows glyoxylate to be oxidised to oxalate; types 2 and 3 involve other enzymes in the same pathway. The liver overproduces oxalate, which the kidneys excrete in high amounts, promoting calcium oxalate crystallisation, stone formation, and nephrocalcinosis. Because oxalate is poorly cleared once renal function fails, it accumulates systemically and is deposited in multiple tissues as oxalosis. The outlook varies with type and genotype; type 1 disease can progress to end-stage renal failure and life-threatening systemic oxalosis, whereas some pyridoxine-responsive and non-type-1 forms are milder, and early diagnosis with modern therapies has improved outcomes considerably.

Primary hyperparathyroidism — PHPT, primary HPT, parathyroid adenoma-related hypercalcaemia Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (PTH-related peptide or bony metastases) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease Vitamin D or vitamin A intoxication Granulomatous disease producing excess active vitamin D Thiazide diuretic or lithium effect on calcium Simultaneous serum calcium (corrected or ionised) and intact PTH Serum phosphate, magnesium, and renal function 25-hydroxyvitamin D level, as deficiency can worsen disease and confound interpretation 24-hour urinary calcium to help distinguish FHH and assess stone risk Bone mineral density including a cortical site such as the distal one-third radius Renal imaging for stones or nephrocalcinosis, and parathyroid localisation studies before surgery The leading cause of hypercalcaemia in ambulatory patients, most often detected incidentally on routine biochemistry The biochemical hallmark is hypercalcaemia with a PTH level that is elevated or inappropriately normal rather than suppressed Most cases are due to a single parathyroid adenoma; a minority reflect four-gland hyperplasia or, rarely, carcinoma Classic symptomatic disease is summarised as stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric moans, but most patients are now asymptomatic Skeletal effects include reduced bone density, particularly at cortical sites such as the distal radius, with fracture risk Renal complications include nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and impaired renal function; urine calcium helps assess risk Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is a key mimic and is distinguished by a low urinary calcium excretion Parathyroidectomy is curative and is indicated for symptomatic disease and for asymptomatic patients meeting defined criteria on calcium, bone density, renal parameters, or age Severe hypercalcaemia with dehydration, confusion, or cardiac dysrhythmia Rapidly rising calcium with a palpable neck mass suggesting parathyroid carcinoma Acute kidney injury or symptomatic nephrolithiasis Very high PTH with markedly elevated calcium out of keeping with a simple adenoma Failing to distinguish familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, leading to unnecessary neck surgery Overlooking concurrent vitamin D deficiency that masks or modifies the biochemical picture Attributing hypercalcaemia to hyperparathyroidism when PTH is actually suppressed, indicating another cause Neglecting bone density and renal assessment that determine the need for surgery in asymptomatic patients Primary hyperparathyroidism results from autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone by one or more parathyroid glands, usually a benign adenoma. Excess PTH raises serum calcium by increasing bone resorption, enhancing renal tubular calcium reabsorption, and stimulating renal conversion of vitamin D to its active form, which augments intestinal calcium absorption. PTH also promotes renal phosphate excretion, tending to lower serum phosphate. The loss of normal calcium-mediated negative feedback on the parathyroid glands sustains the hypercalcaemia. Chronic PTH excess drives cortical bone loss and contributes to hypercalciuria and stone formation. Successful parathyroidectomy cures the disease, halts bone loss with partial recovery of density, and reduces stone recurrence; asymptomatic patients managed conservatively often remain stable but require monitoring, and parathyroid carcinoma has a worse outlook with a tendency to recur.

recurrent allergic or autoimmune manifestations may also be the alerting feature (Harrison 22e p.2793). PIDs are classified by (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect; the major categories are antibody/B-cell defects (agammaglobulinaemia, CVID, hyper-IgM, IgA deficiency), T-cell/cellular defects, combined defects (SCID), and innate-immune defects of phagocytes, complement, or innate receptors/signalling (Harrison 22e p.2794). The site of infection and the causal microorganism point to the affected compartment: respiratory-tract (sinus, bronchial) infection mostly suggests defective antibody responses; invasive bacterial infection can result from complement deficiency, innate-signalling defects, asplenia, or antibody defects; viral, recurrent Candida, and opportunistic infections suggest impaired T-cell immunity; skin infections and deep abscesses primarily reflect innate (phagocyte) defects such as chronic granulomatous disease (Harrison 22e p.2794). B-lymphocyte (antibody) deficiencies are the most frequent PIDs, accounting for 60-70% of all cases; T-cell deficiencies account for ~20% and innate-immune defects for ~10% (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2796, 2797). Encapsulated/pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) and recurrent sinopulmonary infection are the hallmark of defective antibody production; untreated recurrent bronchial infection leads to bronchiectasis, cor pulmonale, and death (Harrison 22e p.2801). Invasive Neisseria infection points to deficiencies of the complement lytic phase (C5-C9) or the alternative pathway (factors D, properdin); classic-pathway and lytic-phase complement deficiencies may also predispose to autoimmune disease, notably SLE (Harrison 22e p.2797). CVID is recognised predominantly in adults, although clinical manifestations can begin earlier in life; in most cases no molecular cause is identified and the diagnosis is made only after excluding hypomorphic agammaglobulinaemia mutations and more subtle T-cell defects, especially in children (Harrison 22e p.2802). First-line laboratory work-up is guided by the clinical picture and includes blood cell counts/morphology, serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE), specific antibody responses to vaccines (tetanus toxoid, unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide), and lymphocyte subset phenotyping; more specific (genetic) tests then confirm a definitive diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2794-2795). Even with profound B-cell deficiency, infections rarely occur before 6 months of age because of transplacental maternal IgG; conversely, in SCID clinical consequences typically appear within 3-6 months of birth (Harrison 22e p.2801, 2799). Immunoglobulin replacement should be guided by the occurrence of infection, not by laboratory IgG/antibody levels alone, to avoid unjustified infusions; it is lifelong therapy (Harrison 22e p.2802). A precise molecular/genetic diagnosis has become a milestone in the care of PID patients, guiding treatment selection, genetic counselling, and prenatal diagnosis; suspected cases should be referred to experienced centres (Harrison 22e p.2804). Recurrent, unusually severe, or persistent infections, or infection by unusual/opportunistic organisms A family history of early childhood deaths (suggesting X-linked or recessive inheritance, e.g., SCID) Lymphocytopenia in an infant (strongly suggestive of SCID in >90% of cases) or absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray Failure to thrive with protracted diarrhoea, recurrent oral candidiasis, or Pneumocystis pneumonia in early infancy Complications of live vaccines (e.g., BCG dissemination, rotavirus diarrhoea) signalling a severe T-cell defect Invasive Neisseria infection (complement lytic-phase or alternative-pathway deficiency) or recurrent encapsulated-organism sepsis with asplenia Recurrent infection accompanied by autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, or lymphoma Absence of pus at sites of infection (hallmark of severe congenital neutropenia) CVID can present in adulthood and is easily missed; it is recognised predominantly in adults although manifestations may begin earlier (Harrison 22e p.2802). High variability of expression for a given PID (e.g., WAS, XLA, CTLA4 deficiency) can hamper diagnosis; modifier genes and environmental triggers such as EBV (in XLP) modulate the phenotype (Harrison 22e p.2804). Leaky BTK mutations causing mild hypogammaglobulinaemia with low but detectable B cells should not be confused with CVID (Harrison 22e p.2802). T-cell lymphopenia in SCID may be masked by maternally-engrafted T cells, so screening for maternal cells with genetic markers should be performed when needed (Harrison 22e p.2799). Somatic mutations in an affected gene can attenuate the phenotype of T-cell PIDs (described for ADA, X-linked SCID, RAG, NEMO, and most often WAS), while somatic mutations can also create PID-like disease (as in ALPS) (Harrison 22e p.2804). Cytokine-neutralising autoantibodies (to IFN-gamma, IL-6, IL-7, type I interferon) can mimic a PID (Harrison 22e p.2804). Caution with immunoglobulin replacement in patients with complete IgA deficiency and residual antibody production: anti-IgA antibodies can trigger anaphylactic shock, so IgA-free IgG preparations should be used (Harrison 22e p.2803). Ataxia-telangiectasia should be considered in young children with IgA deficiency and recurrent problematic infections, as ataxia and telangiectasia may not appear before age 3-4 years (Harrison 22e p.2799-2800). PIDs are predominantly Mendelian genetic diseases that arise whenever the expression or function of a nonredundant effector or mediator of the immune system is genetically impaired. More than 550 conditions have been described, with deleterious mutations identified in roughly 500 genes; estimated prevalence is 5-10 per 100,000 (probably an underestimate). They are increasingly grouped within the broader category of inborn errors of immunity that also includes autoinflammatory syndromes. Defects can involve any aspect of innate or adaptive immunity, cell differentiation, effector function, or immune regulation. The clinical consequence is multiple levels of vulnerability to infection, ranging from extremely broad (as in SCID, where T-cell development is blocked) to narrowly restricted to a single class of organism (as in Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, an IL-12-IFN-gamma axis defect). Antibody (B-cell) defects (agammaglobulinaemia from BTK and pre-B-cell-receptor gene defects, hyper-IgM from class-switch-recombination defects such as CD40L/CD40, IgA deficiency, and CVID) impair production or class switching of immunoglobulins, leaving patients unable to opsonise and neutralise pyogenic encapsulated bacteria. Cellular (T-cell) defects impair help for antibody production, macrophage activation, and cytotoxicity, causing susceptibility to viral, fungal (Candida), and opportunistic infections (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptosporidium). Combined defects (SCID) abolish both arms. Innate defects affect phagocyte number (severe congenital neutropenia), adhesion (LAD), or microbial killing (chronic granulomatous disease, from defective NADPH-oxidase reactive-oxygen-species production), as well as complement components and innate receptor/signalling pathways (TLR adaptors IRAK4/MYD88). Beyond infection, PIDs can drive immunopathology including allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity, and an increased risk of malignancy (notably lymphoma) (Harrison 22e p.2793-2794, 2796-2802). Prognosis varies widely with the molecule and arm of immunity affected. T-cell and combined defects generally carry a poor prognosis and require early diagnosis and intervention; SCID is fatal in infancy without treatment, but allogeneic HSCT offers a high curative potential in patients in otherwise reasonable condition, and gene therapy has succeeded in X-linked (gamma-c) SCID, ADA-SCID, and Artemis deficiency. Functional T-cell defects carry a worse HSCT prognosis than SCID because many patients are already chronically infected at diagnosis. For antibody deficiencies, lifelong immunoglobulin replacement combined with management of chronic lung disease reduces respiratory infections and prevents progression to bronchiectasis and cor pulmonale; in CVID, lymphoproliferation, granulomatous disease, autoimmunity, and lymphoma define long-term prognosis. DNA-repair disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia are progressive and carry a very high risk of lymphoma, leukaemia, and (in adulthood) carcinoma. Newborn TREC screening, by enabling treatment of uninfected SCID patients, maximises the chance of cure. Early diagnosis with referral to experienced centres is essential to optimal outcome (Harrison 22e p.2794, 2799-2800, 2802, 2804). PIDs are classified along two axes: (1) the arm of the immune system that is defective and (2) the mechanism of the defect (when known). The two main divisions are deficiencies of the innate immune system (phagocytic cells - impaired production [severe congenital neutropenia], asplenia, impaired adhesion [LAD], impaired killing [CGD]; innate-immunity receptors/signal transduction [TLR-signalling defects, MSMD]; complement deficiencies of the classical/alternative/lectin pathways and the lytic phase) and deficiencies of the adaptive immune system (T lymphocytes - SCID, DiGeorge, combined immunodeficiencies, hyper-IgE, DOCK8, CD40L, Wiskott-Aldrich, ataxia-telangiectasia and DNA-repair defects; B lymphocytes - X-linked/AR agammaglobulinaemia, hyper-IgM, CVID, IgA deficiency), together with regulatory defects (autoinflammatory syndromes, severe colitis, HLH, ALPS, autoimmunity such as IPEX and APECED). The classification is acknowledged to involve some arbitrary decisions because of overlap and incomplete data (Harrison 22e p.2794).

Primary myelofibrosis — PMF, myelofibrosis, chronic idiopathic myelofibrosis, agnogenic myeloid metaplasia Secondary (reactive) myelofibrosis from metastatic cancer or infection Post-polycythaemia vera or post-essential thrombocythaemia myelofibrosis Chronic myeloid leukaemia Myelodysplastic syndrome with fibrosis Hairy cell leukaemia and other marrow-infiltrating disorders Autoimmune myelofibrosis Full blood count and blood film for leucoerythroblastic changes and teardrop cells Bone marrow trephine biopsy with reticulin/collagen staining to grade fibrosis Molecular testing for JAK2, CALR, and MPL, plus high-molecular-risk mutation panels BCR-ABL1 testing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia Cytogenetic analysis for prognostic stratification Abdominal imaging to document splenomegaly and extramedullary disease A myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by clonal proliferation with progressive marrow fibrosis and extramedullary haematopoiesis, classically producing marked splenomegaly Typical features include fatigue and anaemia, constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever), and abdominal discomfort or early satiety from splenic enlargement The blood film shows a leucoerythroblastic picture with teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes), nucleated red cells, and immature myeloid forms Attempts to aspirate marrow often yield a dry tap because of fibrosis, so a trephine biopsy demonstrating reticulin or collagen fibrosis is essential Driver mutations in JAK2, CALR, or MPL are present in most cases and support the diagnosis; additional high-risk mutations refine prognosis Prognostic scoring incorporates age, symptoms, cytopenias, blast count, and cytogenetic/molecular features to guide management decisions JAK inhibitors reduce spleen size and constitutional symptoms and can improve quality of life, though they are not curative Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only curative therapy and is considered for suitable higher-risk patients; transformation to acute leukaemia is a feared complication Rapidly rising blast count or new cytogenetic changes indicating leukaemic transformation Severe anaemia or thrombocytopenia with bleeding requiring urgent support Massive symptomatic splenomegaly with risk of splenic infarction or rupture Portal hypertension or splanchnic vein thrombosis from extramedullary haematopoiesis and hypercoagulability Assuming a leucoerythroblastic film always indicates PMF without excluding marrow infiltration by malignancy or infection Relying on a marrow aspirate alone when fibrosis produces a dry tap and a biopsy is needed Failing to exclude chronic myeloid leukaemia with BCR-ABL1 testing Overlooking prognostic mutations that would prompt earlier transplant referral Not recognising that a JAK inhibitor controls symptoms and spleen size but does not prevent progression Primary myelofibrosis originates from a clonal haematopoietic stem cell with dysregulated JAK-STAT signalling, most often driven by JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations. The abnormal clone, particularly its megakaryocytes, secretes fibrogenic cytokines and growth factors (such as transforming growth factor-beta and platelet-derived growth factor) that stimulate marrow fibroblasts to deposit reticulin and collagen. As the marrow becomes progressively fibrotic, haematopoiesis relocates to the spleen and liver (extramedullary haematopoiesis), causing organomegaly and release of immature cells into the circulation. A chronic inflammatory cytokine state produces constitutional symptoms, and clonal evolution can culminate in acute leukaemia. Survival in primary myelofibrosis is highly variable, ranging from many years in low-risk disease to under two years in high-risk categories; adverse cytogenetics, high-risk mutations, transfusion dependence, and excess blasts predict poorer outcomes, and only allogeneic transplant offers cure.

outflow through an anatomically open trabecular meshwork is impaired, raising resistance to drainage. The resulting intraocular pressure, sometimes within the normal range, contributes to mechanical and vascular stress at the optic nerve head, causing loss of retinal ganglion cell axons. This produces characteristic cupping of the optic disc and a corresponding pattern of arcuate and peripheral visual field loss that advances slowly over years. With early detection and sustained pressure control most patients retain useful vision for life, but untreated or poorly controlled disease progresses to irreversible visual field loss and blindness.

Prion Diseases (CJD) — Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, CJD, spongiform encephalopathy Alzheimer's disease (can occasionally present as rapidly progressive dementia) Corticobasal degeneration (CBD) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD Other rapidly progressive dementias Viral encephalitides Bacterial encephalitides Other CNS infections causing rapidly progressive dementia MRI diffusion-weighted imaging - restricted diffusion in cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia (cortical ribboning); basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR EEG - periodic complexes (repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves) Lumbar puncture/CSF - to exclude CNS infection or inflammation among rapidly progressive dementia mimics MRI/neuroimaging to exclude treatable structural causes (neoplasm, subdural hematoma, NPH) Hashimoto's encephalopathy CNS vasculitis CNS lymphoma Paraneoplastic/autoimmune syndromes (autoimmune encephalitis) Prolonged focal or generalized seizures (can rarely produce a similar imaging appearance) CJD is a rapidly progressive disorder associated with dementia, focal cortical signs, rigidity, and myoclonus, causing death less than 1 year after first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526). CJD is the classic cause of a rapidly progressive dementia (RPD: progression from symptom onset to dementia within a year or less), especially when associated with myoclonus, though more often RPD is due to AD, another neurodegenerative disorder, or autoimmune encephalitis (p.237). On examination, CJD is suggested by diffuse rigidity, an akinetic-mute state, and prominent, often startle-sensitive myoclonus (p.239). MRI diffusion-weighted imaging reveals restricted diffusion within the cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia in most patients; basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity may also be seen on diffusion/FLAIR MRI (p.240, p.3526). EEG is not routinely used but can suggest CJD by showing repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves (periodic complexes) (p.241). Prion diseases such as CJD are rare (prevalence ~1 per million); the rapidity of progression distinguishes CJD from AD, though AD can occasionally present as a rapidly progressive dementia (p.3525-3526). Prion disease is one cause of subacute progressive ataxia, especially when an infectious etiology such as transmission from contaminated human growth hormone is responsible (p.3590). Rapidly progressive dementia (onset to dementia within a year or less) Dementia accompanied by myoclonus (often startle-sensitive) Diffuse rigidity and akinetic-mute state Subacute progressive ataxia Cortical ribboning / basal ganglia or thalamic hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR MRI Periodic complexes on EEG Must exclude treatable causes of rapidly progressive dementia (e.g., autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis, Hashimoto's encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, CNS infection, lymphoma) before attributing a rapidly progressive dementia to CJD. More rapid degenerative dementias with prominent movement abnormalities (CBD, DLB) are more likely to be mistaken for CJD. Rarely, prolonged focal or generalized seizures can produce an MRI appearance similar to CJD. Prion diseases are caused by prions, host-encoded proteins (the prion protein) that adopt an alternative, abnormal conformation (misfolded PrPSc) which undergoes self-propagation. PrPSc imposes its conformation on the normal precursor protein, which in turn becomes self-templating, producing faithful copies; the misfolded protein is enriched for beta-sheet and assembles into amyloid fibrils. The amyloid plaques in kuru and CJD are filled with PrPSc prions assembled into fibrils. CJD is one of the major degenerative dementias characterized by abnormal aggregation of a specific protein (misfolded prion protein, PrPSc). Familial CJD is genetically linked to mutations in the PrP gene (p.237, p.3400-3401). Uniformly fatal. CJD causes death less than 1 year after the first symptoms appear (p.3525-3526). Etiologic classification of prion diseases (all caused by PrPSc): sporadic (e.g., classic CJD), familial/genetic (linked to PrP gene mutations - includes familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease [GSS], and fatal insomnia), iatrogenic (transmission e.g. from contaminated human growth hormone), and acquired/transmissible forms (kuru). PrPSc prions also cause animal spongiform encephalopathies including scrapie, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and chronic wasting disease (p.3400-3401, p.3590).

and function Confusing preserved intelligence with other progeroid syndromes that feature cognitive impairment Underestimating cardiovascular risk in a young child and delaying cardiology involvement Attributing early features to a non-syndromic failure to thrive Overlooking the sclerodermatous skin as a diagnostic clue Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome is usually caused by a de novo point variant in LMNA that activates a cryptic splice site, producing progerin, a truncated lamin A that cannot be properly processed and remains farnesylated. Accumulation of progerin distorts the nuclear envelope, destabilises the nuclear lamina and disrupts chromatin organisation, DNA repair and mechanotransduction. This drives premature cellular senescence and, in vascular smooth muscle, accelerated atherosclerosis that dominates the clinical course. The condition is progressive and life-limiting, with death typically in the second decade, most often from myocardial infarction or stroke secondary to accelerated atherosclerosis. Multidisciplinary supportive care and cardiovascular risk management are central, and disease-modifying therapy targeting protein farnesylation has been developed.

FIC1 (ATP8B1) is an aminophospholipid flippase whose loss disrupts the canalicular membrane; BSEP (ABCB11) is the main bile salt export pump, so its failure traps bile acids inside hepatocytes; and MDR3 (ABCB4) translocates phosphatidylcholine into bile, so its deficiency yields bile that is toxic to the biliary tree. In each case impaired bile acid secretion produces intracellular accumulation of bile acids, hepatocyte injury, and progressive cholestasis that evolves to fibrosis and cirrhosis. The characteristic difference in gamma-glutamyl transferase reflects whether the underlying lesion damages the bile duct epithelium (high, as in MDR3 disease) or not (low or normal, as in FIC1 and BSEP disease). Without intervention most subtypes progress to biliary cirrhosis and liver failure during childhood, though disease-modifying therapy such as ileal bile acid transport inhibitors, surgical biliary diversion, and liver transplantation can markedly improve outcomes. BSEP disease additionally carries a lifelong risk of hepatobiliary malignancy requiring surveillance.

Mechanisms include abnormal intracellular storage material (polyglucosan bodies in Lafora disease, lipopigment in the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses), impaired lysosomal enzyme function (sialidoses), defective protein handling (Unverricht-Lundborg disease) and mitochondrial energy failure (MERRF). Most forms cause increasing disability over years, and treatment is largely symptomatic.

swallowing assessment Rapid cognitive or behavioural decline affecting safety and capacity Features suggesting an alternative treatable diagnosis such as hydrocephalus Misdiagnosing early PSP as Parkinson disease before the gaze palsy is evident Attributing frequent falls to general frailty rather than the disease Persisting with high-dose dopaminergic therapy despite a clearly poor response Overlooking dysphagia and aspiration risk until a pneumonia occurs Missing the surprised facial appearance and slowed vertical saccades as early clues PSP is a four-repeat tauopathy in which abnormal tau aggregates as neurofibrillary tangles, tufted astrocytes, and coiled bodies in the basal ganglia, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra, midbrain tegmentum, and brainstem nuclei controlling eye movements. Degeneration of the midbrain and its ocular motor circuitry produces the supranuclear gaze palsy, while nigral and striatal involvement causes the poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Damage to brainstem postural and gait pathways underlies the early instability and falls, and frontal-subcortical involvement drives the cognitive and behavioural features. PSP is relentlessly progressive with no disease-modifying therapy; mobility, communication, and swallowing decline over several years, and death is commonly related to aspiration and its complications.

Prolactinoma — prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma, lactotroph adenoma, hyperprolactinaemia (tumoural) Physiological hyperprolactinaemia of pregnancy or lactation Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia (antipsychotics, antiemetics, some antidepressants) Primary hypothyroidism raising prolactin via TRH Chronic kidney disease reducing prolactin clearance Stalk-effect hyperprolactinaemia from a non-lactotroph sellar mass Macroprolactinaemia (biologically inactive complexed prolactin) Fasting serum prolactin, repeated if borderline, with sample dilution when a hook effect is suspected Pregnancy test, thyroid function, and renal function to exclude secondary causes Review of medications that raise prolactin Pituitary MRI to characterise adenoma size and suprasellar extension Assessment of macroprolactin when clinical picture and level are discordant Visual fields and anterior pituitary hormone panel for macroadenomas The commonest hormone-secreting pituitary tumour; presentation differs by sex, with menstrual disturbance and galactorrhoea in women and reduced libido or erectile dysfunction in men Because men lack an early hormonal warning sign, they more often present late with large tumours causing mass effect Hyperprolactinaemia suppresses gonadotrophin secretion, producing hypogonadism, infertility, and reduced bone density over time Before diagnosing a prolactinoma, exclude other causes of raised prolactin such as pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, and dopamine-blocking drugs Stalk compression by any large sellar mass can modestly raise prolactin; very high levels are more specific for a true prolactinoma In large tumours with only mildly elevated prolactin, laboratory dilution may be needed to exclude the hook effect artefact Unlike most pituitary tumours, prolactinomas are usually managed medically with dopamine agonists rather than surgery as first line Dopamine agonist therapy typically lowers prolactin, restores gonadal function, and shrinks tumour volume Bitemporal visual field loss from chiasmal compression by a macroadenoma Sudden severe headache with visual or cranial nerve signs suggesting apoplexy Symptoms and signs of coexisting hypopituitarism, including adrenal insufficiency Very large invasive tumours threatening vision or requiring urgent decompression Diagnosing a prolactinoma without excluding drugs, hypothyroidism, renal failure, and pregnancy Missing the hook effect and underestimating prolactin in a large tumour, leading to inappropriate surgery Overlooking macroprolactin as a cause of asymptomatic elevation Failing to counsel on bone health and fertility implications of chronic hypogonadism A prolactinoma is a benign lactotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that autonomously secretes prolactin. Prolactin is normally under tonic inhibitory control by hypothalamic dopamine, which is why dopamine agonists are effective and dopamine-blocking drugs raise prolactin. Excess prolactin inhibits pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone secretion, reducing LH and FSH and causing hypogonadism, galactorrhoea, and infertility. Larger tumours (macroadenomas) may compress the optic chiasm and adjacent pituitary tissue, producing visual field defects and hypopituitarism. Non-tumoural hyperprolactinaemia from stalk disconnection, drugs, or systemic disease must be distinguished from a true adenoma. Most microprolactinomas respond well to dopamine agonists with normalisation of prolactin, restoration of fertility, and often no significant growth; macroadenomas also usually shrink with medical therapy, and in selected patients treatment can eventually be tapered, though relapse of hyperprolactinaemia is possible.

may dominate the picture, and hypoglycaemia and bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) frequently occur Elevated propionylcarnitine (C3) on acylcarnitine profile with characteristic urine organic acids (e.g. 3-hydroxypropionate, methylcitrate) supports the diagnosis, and MMA is not elevated (distinguishing it from methylmalonic acidemia) Long-term complications include cardiomyopathy, prolonged QT and arrhythmia, pancreatitis, movement disorder from basal ganglia injury, and developmental delay Chronic management principles include protein restriction limiting generally not cofactor-responsive, though biotin is often trialled Included in newborn screening via elevated C3 acylcarnitine, enabling early diagnosis Acute metabolic decompensation with severe acidosis and hyperammonaemia is a medical emergency Encephalopathy from hyperammonaemia during crises Cardiomyopathy or QT prolongation with risk of life-threatening arrhythmia Rapid clinical deterioration during infection, fasting or catabolic stress Confusing it with methylmalonic acidemia without checking that methylmalonic acid is not elevated Overlooking cardiac surveillance, since cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia can be fatal even with good metabolic control Attributing the acidotic neonate to sepsis and delaying specific therapy Under-recognising secondary hyperammonaemia as a driver of encephalopathy Propionic acidemia arises from deficient propionyl-CoA carboxylase, a mitochondrial biotin-dependent enzyme that converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA. This step is part of the catabolic pathway for the amino acids isoleucine, valine, methionine and threonine, as well as odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol. Enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of propionyl-CoA and its derivatives (propionic acid, 3-hydroxypropionate, methylcitrate, propionylcarnitine). These organic acids produce severe metabolic acidosis, inhibit the urea cycle to cause hyperammonaemia, impair mitochondrial energy production, and are toxic to the myocardium, bone marrow, pancreas and basal ganglia. Propionic acidemia is among the more severe organic acidaemias, with high risk of recurrent metabolic crises and long-term neurological and cardiac complications despite treatment; early detection and rigorous metabolic management improve survival, and selected patients are considered for liver transplantation.

treat symptomatic bacterial prostatitis with antibiotics before biopsy, but routine antibiotics in an asymptomatic patient with elevated PSA are discouraged) Recurrent urinary tract infection as a complication of bladder-outlet obstruction Digital rectal exam (assesses size, symmetry, consistency, nodules; NOT a validated standalone screening test due to frequent false positives and false negatives) Serum PSA (total); free/total PSA ratio; common biopsy-prompting cut point total PSA >=4 ng/mL (no PSA level carries zero cancer risk) Second-line stratifying tests after elevated PSA: 4K Score, Prostate Health Index (PHI = free PSA + total PSA + [-2]proPSA), urine ExoDx exosome test, Select-MDx mRNA test Multiparametric prostate MRI (mpMRI) with PI-RADS scoring before biopsy Image-guided needle biopsy (TRUS-, MRI-, or fusion-guided; extended 12-core pattern; MRI-guided superior to ultrasound-guided) Gleason grading and the five-tier grade group system (grade group 1 = Gleason <=6 favorable, up to grade group 5 = Gleason 9-10) TNM staging (T1c PSA-detected, T2 palpable organ-confined, T3-T4 extraprostatic); risk stratification into low/intermediate(favorable vs unfavorable)/high/very-high risk PSMA PET scan (FDA approved for intermediate/high-risk disease; more sensitive/specific than conventional imaging but cannot detect low-volume microscopic disease) For BPH: AUA Symptom Index (AUASI) / International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), uroflowmetry, bladder ultrasound for postvoid residual, pressure-flow urodynamics, cystoscopy if hematuria, upper-tract imaging if hematuria/calculi/prior tract problems BPH-related induration on DRE mimicking carcinoma Prostatic calculi causing nodularity Degenerative spine disease, spinal stenosis, or osteoporotic vertebral collapse mimicking metastatic bone pain in advanced disease (require accurate diagnosis before attributing pain to metastases) Direct invasion of the prostate by colon cancer or bladder transitional cell carcinoma (true metastases TO the prostate are rare) Both benign and malignant prostate changes rise sharply with age: autopsies of men in the eighth decade show hyperplastic changes in >90% and malignant changes in >70%, so management is risk-adapted and weighed against competing causes of morbidity and mortality (p.695). BPH arises in the periurethral transition zone surrounding the urethra, whereas most cancers arise in the peripheral zone; peripheral-zone cancers may or may not be palpable on digital rectal exam (DRE) (p.696). BPH causes lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) split into obstructive symptoms (hesitancy, straining, weak stream, terminal dribbling, prolonged voiding, incomplete emptying) and irritative symptoms (frequency, urgency, urge incontinence, small voided volumes); LUTS reflect both prostatic enlargement and age-related detrusor dysfunction, not mass effect alone (p.703). PSA (kallikrein KLK3) is prostate specific, NOT prostate cancer specific: it can rise from prostatitis, BPH, or cancer; a lower free PSA fraction is more likely associated with cancer at biopsy (p.696-697). After radical prostatectomy PSA should become undetectable within about 6 weeks (no prostate = no detectable PSA); persistence of measurable PSA after gland removal is typical of recurrent cancer (p.696-697). Only 20-25% of patients with an abnormal DRE have prostate cancer; carcinoma is characteristically hard, nodular, irregular, asymmetric, but induration can also be BPH or calculi (p.696). >95% of prostate cancers are adenocarcinomas; the remainder are squamous, transitional cell, rarely carcinosarcoma or small-cell histologies (p.697). Most men diagnosed with prostate cancer will NOT die of it; the incidence/mortality ratio is extremely high relative to other malignancies, which drives the active-surveillance vs treatment balance (p.695). Multiparametric prostate MRI (mpMRI) graded by PI-RADS is now obtained in most cases BEFORE biopsy: PI-RADS 1-2 lesions can safely avoid biopsy; PI-RADS 3-5 lesions get targeted biopsy, reducing detection of indolent Gleason 6 (grade group 1) cancers without missing clinically relevant ones (p.697). Osteoblastic bone metastases (prostate cancer characteristically produces bone-forming metastases) presenting as back/skeletal pain; bone is the dominant site of metastatic and castration-resistant progression Spinal cord compression / cord compromise or base-of-skull symptoms from metastatic disease require EMERGENCY evaluation because loss of neurologic function may be permanent if not treated quickly GnRH agonists are relatively contraindicated in patients with significant urinary obstruction, cancer-related pain, or spinal cord compromise because the initial testosterone surge can cause a disease flare (AR antagonists are added to blunt flare; GnRH antagonists and abiraterone do not cause a surge) BPH danger signs mandating evaluation/treatment regardless of gland size: inability to urinate (acute urinary retention), gross hematuria, recurrent infection, or bladder stones Rising nadir PSA >4 ng/mL at 6-8 months after starting androgen deprivation predicts markedly inferior survival Marrow infiltration (myelophthisis), coagulopathy, or thromboembolism as manifestations of widespread metastatic disease PSA screening is controversial: it generates both false positives and false negatives and can lead to diagnosis and treatment of indolent cancers that pose little risk; the decision (USPSTF: individual shared decision for men 55-69, recommended AGAINST screening at age >=70; AUA: shared decision, earlier for Black ancestry/germline mutations/strong family history) must balance benefit against overtreatment harm. PSA is prostate specific, not cancer specific - do not equate an elevated PSA with cancer; BPH and prostatitis also raise it. There is NO PSA level below which prostate cancer risk is zero (Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial); a 'normal' PSA does not exclude cancer. DRE alone is inaccurate for staging (capsular invasion, seminal-vesicle and nodal involvement) and is not a validated screening test by itself. Patients misread Gleason 6 as 'mid-scale' and assume aggressive disease; the grade group system was created because Gleason 6 (grade group 1) is actually the lowest, favorable-risk category. PSMA PET, despite high sensitivity, cannot detect low-volume microscopic nodal disease - a negative scan does not exclude micrometastasis. A negative biopsy in a patient with elevated PSA does NOT rule out a future cancer diagnosis - continue follow-up. No agent is currently approved for prostate cancer prevention (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduced mainly low-risk indolent cancers; vitamins/supplements showed no benefit). No rationale to screen asymptomatic men with short life expectancy; antiandrogen monotherapy gives inferior cancer-specific outcomes versus castration. The prostate (pelvic, adjacent to rectum, bladder, neurovascular bundles and urinary sphincter) is composed of tubuloalveolar glands in fibromuscular stroma. PSA is produced by epithelial cells; both epithelial and stromal cells express androgen receptors (AR) and depend on androgens for growth. Testosterone is converted by prostatic 5alpha-reductase to the more potent dihydrotestosterone. BPH is non-malignant proliferation of the periurethral transition zone (begins at puberty, accelerates after age 55) producing bladder-outlet obstruction; symptoms also reflect age-related detrusor dysfunction. Malignancy usually arises in the peripheral zone; the cancer continuum runs from preneoplastic/localized lesion to metastatic, symptomatic, lethal disease over years to decades. Prostate cancer is AR-signaling dependent, so androgen deprivation is the mainstay of metastatic therapy; castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) progresses despite castrate testosterone (<=50 ng/mL) because most CRPCs continue to express and signal through the AR, and androgen-resistant cells are present from diagnosis (cure is not achieved by androgen depletion alone). (p.695-696, 702-703) Most men with prostate cancer do not die from it; >70-80% of newly diagnosed cancers are now organ-confined. Nonmetastatic disease is stratified low/intermediate/high (and very-high) risk; grade group system accurately predicts prognosis with grade group 1 (Gleason <=6) being favorable. A single PSA at age 60 correlates strongly (AUC 0.90) with lifetime risk of death from prostate cancer, and ~90% of prostate-cancer deaths occur in the top PSA quartile (>2 ng/mL), though only a minority of those men develop lethal disease. Androgen deprivation produces an initial response and dormant period but is not curative; PSA normalizes in 60-70% and measurable disease regresses in >50%, with survival inversely proportional to disease extent at treatment start and to the 6-8 month nadir PSA. Castration-resistant prostate cancer is lethal for most patients; multiple agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide, docetaxel, cabazitaxel, radium-223, Lu-177 PSMA-617, PARP inhibitors for BRCA/DNA-repair mutations, checkpoint inhibitors for MSI-high/dMMR) prolong survival. (p.695, 697, 701-703) Gleason grade group system: grade group 1 (Gleason <=6), 2 (3+4=7), 3 (4+3=7), 4 (4+4=8), 5 (Gleason 9-10). TNM staging: T1c clinically inapparent PSA-detected; T2 palpable, confined within prostate; T3 extends through capsule/seminal vesicles (T3b); T4 fixed or invading adjacent structures. Nonmetastatic risk groups: low (organ-confined, PSA <10, grade group 1); intermediate (organ-confined, PSA 10-20, or grade group 2 favorable / 3 unfavorable, with >50% positive cores = unfavorable); high (extraprostatic, PSA >20, or grade group 4-5); very-high (seminal vesicle T3b or adjacent-organ T4 invasion or multiple high-grade biopsy samples). Metastatic states: noncastrate metastatic (testosterone >50 ng/dL) vs castration-resistant (CRPC, testosterone <=50 ng/mL). (p.697-698, 701-703)

its deficiency is a strong inherited thrombophilia Heterozygous deficiency causes venous thromboembolism, often beginning in young adulthood and sometimes provoked by additional risk factors Homozygous or compound heterozygous deficiency presents in the newborn period with purpura fulminans, a life-threatening microvascular thrombotic emergency Starting a vitamin K antagonist without concurrent heparin-type cover can precipitate skin necrosis, because protein C levels fall faster than the procoagulant factors Levels are lowered by acute thrombosis, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, and vitamin K antagonist therapy, so timing of testing is critical Both functional (activity) and antigenic assays are used to distinguish reduced production from a dysfunctional protein Confirmation ideally requires repeat testing away from the acute event and off vitamin K antagonists, with family studies where appropriate Neonatal purpura fulminans indicating severe homozygous deficiency and requiring emergency treatment Skin necrosis developing after initiation of a vitamin K antagonist Extensive or recurrent venous thromboembolism at a young age Widespread microvascular thrombosis suggesting an acute prothrombotic crisis Diagnosing deficiency from levels drawn during acute thrombosis or vitamin K antagonist therapy Initiating a vitamin K antagonist without overlapping parenteral anticoagulation, risking skin necrosis Confusing acquired causes such as liver disease or DIC with inherited deficiency Failing to repeat and confirm a low result before committing to lifelong conclusions Protein C circulates as an inactive precursor and is activated on the endothelial surface by the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex. Activated protein C, with its cofactor protein S, proteolytically inactivates factors Va and VIIIa, thereby limiting thrombin generation. Inherited deficiency, whether from reduced synthesis (type I) or a functionally impaired protein (type II), removes this brake and shifts haemostasis toward thrombosis. The short half-life of protein C explains the transient hypercoagulable window at the start of vitamin K antagonist therapy, when protein C is depleted before the longer-lived procoagulant factors, producing the risk of skin necrosis. Heterozygous carriers have a good prognosis with appropriate management of thrombotic events and high-risk periods, whereas homozygous deficiency presenting with neonatal purpura fulminans is life-threatening and requires urgent replacement and long-term anticoagulation.

Protein-Losing Enteropathy — PLE, intestinal protein loss, gut protein loss Nephrotic syndrome Chronic liver disease with impaired synthesis Malnutrition or inadequate protein intake Malabsorption syndromes Congestive heart failure Sepsis or capillary leak states Serum albumin and total protein Stool alpha-1-antitrypsin (clearance) Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte count Urinalysis to exclude renal protein loss Endoscopy with biopsy when mucosal disease is suspected Imaging or echocardiography to assess lymphatics and cardiac status This is a syndrome, not a single disease, in which excessive loss of plasma proteins into the gastrointestinal tract leads to hypoproteinaemia and oedema. It should be suspected in a child with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema once liver disease, kidney protein loss, and inadequate intake have been excluded. Underlying mechanisms fall into two broad groups: lymphatic obstruction or elevated lymphatic pressure, and mucosal disease with increased permeability or erosion. Lymphatic causes include intestinal lymphangiectasia and elevated central venous pressure after cardiac surgery (notably the Fontan circulation), while mucosal causes include inflammatory, allergic, infectious, and infiltrative enteropathies. Because losses are non-selective, other serum proteins such as immunoglobulins and clotting factors may also fall, sometimes causing lymphopenia and predisposing to infection. A stool alpha-1-antitrypsin measurement is a useful non-invasive marker of enteric protein loss because it is not degraded in the gut. Management is directed at the underlying cause together with nutritional support, and in lymphatic causes a low-fat diet enriched with medium-chain triglycerides can reduce lymphatic protein loss. Peripheral oedema, ascites, or effusions in a child with unexplained low albumin should prompt evaluation of the gut as a source. Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca, ascites, or effusions Signs of immunodeficiency or recurrent infection from immunoglobulin loss Evidence of underlying serious cardiac or lymphatic disease Growth failure Features of an underlying inflammatory or malignant infiltrative process Attributing hypoalbuminaemia and oedema to renal or hepatic causes without considering the gut Overlooking accompanying immunoglobulin loss and infection risk Failing to identify and treat the specific underlying disorder Neglecting nutritional support and the role of a low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet in lymphatic loss Plasma proteins normally enter the gut lumen only in small amounts. In protein-losing enteropathy this loss is markedly increased by one of two general processes. In lymphatic disorders, obstructed or high-pressure intestinal lymphatics (from congenital lymphangiectasia or raised systemic venous pressure, as after Fontan surgery) leak protein-rich lymph into the lumen. In mucosal disorders, inflammation, ulceration, or increased epithelial permeability from infectious, allergic, inflammatory, or infiltrative disease allows serum proteins to escape across the damaged barrier. Because the loss is non-selective, albumin, immunoglobulins, and other proteins are depleted, producing hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and sometimes immune compromise. Outlook depends heavily on the underlying cause; some mucosal causes resolve when the primary disease is treated, whereas lymphangiectasia and Fontan-associated protein loss can be chronic and difficult to manage.

its deficiency predisposes to venous thromboembolism Only free protein S is functionally active, because much of it circulates bound to C4b-binding protein Deficiency is classified by total antigen, free antigen, and functional activity, which distinguish the different subtypes Levels are physiologically lowered by pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, and the acute-phase response, and by vitamin K antagonists, so testing timing strongly affects interpretation As with protein C, severe homozygous deficiency can cause neonatal purpura fulminans, and vitamin K antagonist initiation without cover risks skin necrosis Free protein S measurement is generally preferred, and confirmation requires repeat testing under stable conditions off interfering drugs A result should be interpreted alongside clinical risk, since isolated low values do not by themselves dictate anticoagulation duration Neonatal purpura fulminans indicating severe homozygous deficiency Skin necrosis after starting a vitamin K antagonist Extensive or recurrent venous thromboembolism at a young age Widespread microvascular thrombosis requiring urgent intervention Interpreting low levels during pregnancy, oestrogen use, or acute illness as inherited deficiency Measuring total rather than free protein S and missing or misclassifying the defect Starting a vitamin K antagonist without overlapping parenteral anticoagulation Testing during acute thrombosis or on anticoagulation without confirmatory repeat testing Protein S acts as a non-enzymatic cofactor that accelerates the inactivation of factors Va and VIIIa by activated protein C, and it also has some direct anticoagulant activity. In plasma it exists in a free active form and a fraction bound to C4b-binding protein, which is inactive as a cofactor. Inherited deficiency reduces free active protein S and weakens the activated protein C pathway, promoting thrombin generation and thrombosis. Because C4b-binding protein is an acute-phase reactant and oestrogen and pregnancy lower free protein S, acquired reductions are common and can be mistaken for inherited deficiency. Heterozygous deficiency generally carries a good prognosis with appropriate treatment of events and prophylaxis during high-risk periods, while severe homozygous deficiency presenting with purpura fulminans is a life-threatening neonatal emergency.

with PIK3CA-related overgrowth, which has different management implications Proteus syndrome is caused by a specific activating variant in AKT1 arising after fertilisation, producing a mosaic Because only a subset of cells is affected and this expands during development, the result is progressive, patchy and disproportionate overgrowth of the involved tissues. Prognosis varies widely with the extent and location of overgrowth; progressive skeletal deformity and functional disability are common, and venous thromboembolism is a leading cause of premature mortality. Multidisciplinary management can reduce complications, but the overgrowth itself is difficult to reverse.
