electron microscopy often required in tissue Repeated stool sampling, duodenal fluid aspiration, and small-bowel biopsy when cyst/oocyst excretion is intermittent or low-level Wet-mount microscopy of vaginal or prostatic secretions for motile trichomonads (sensitivity only ~50-60%); NAATs on urine or vaginal/endocervical swabs are first-line Celiac disease / gluten-sensitive enteropathy Tropical sprue Inflammatory bowel disease (for invasive colonic balantidiasis) Functional/chronic diarrhea of uncertain cause Giardia (G. duodenalis, assemblages A and B in humans) is a non-invasive parasite confined to the proximal small bowel that does not spread hematogenously; an inoculum of as few as ~10 cysts can establish infection, and cysts resist routine chlorination but are killed by boiling or filtration. Giardiasis classically presents with upper-intestinal/small-bowel features (nausea, vomiting, bloating, belching, sulfurous flatus, abdominal pain) and non-bloody diarrhea; fever, blood, or mucus in stool point away from giardiasis toward colitis or a concomitant illness. Cryptosporidium (C. hominis, C. parvum) is self-limited (about 1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but causes chronic, profuse watery diarrhea with stool volumes ranging from 1 to 25 L/day in AIDS patients with CD4 counts below 100/uL. Cystoisospora belli is distinctive among enteric protozoa in that it can produce peripheral eosinophilia in immunocompetent hosts; in AIDS it mimics cryptosporidiosis with chronic profuse watery diarrhea. Cyclospora cayetanensis is linked to foodborne outbreaks from imported produce (basil, sweet peas, raspberries) and waterborne spread, and characteristically causes prolonged diarrhea that may persist beyond one month; absence of fecal blood and leukocytes indicates the small-bowel mucosa is not destroyed. Conventional ova-and-parasite (O+P) stool examination does NOT reliably detect Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, or microsporidia; specific tests (modified acid-fast stain, immunoassays, direct fluorescent antibody, or NAATs) must be requested explicitly. Microsporidia are obligate intracellular spore-forming organisms that are small and gram-positive; they are most often opportunistic in AIDS, where Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis cause chronic diarrhea and wasting and have been found in 10-40% of patients with chronic diarrhea. Encephalitozoon species can disseminate beyond the gut to cause keratoconjunctivitis, sinusitis, bronchiolitis/respiratory disease, cholangitis, nephritis, and cystitis, so microsporidiosis is not solely an intestinal disease. Balantidium coli is a large ciliated protozoan producing a large-bowel disease resembling amebiasis (mucosal invasion, focal necrosis, ulceration); it is zoonotic from pigs and, unlike amebiasis, only rarely disseminates hematogenously to other organs. Blastocystis hominis has uncertain pathogenicity; finding it in stool warrants a full search for other bacterial, viral, or protozoal causes of diarrhea before attributing symptoms to it. Dientamoeba fragilis is unique among intestinal protozoa in having only a trophozoite stage and no cyst stage; immediate fixation of stool improves detection of the labile trophozoites and NAATs outperform microscopy. Trichomonas vaginalis is one of the most prevalent protozoal parasites in the United States (an estimated 2-3 million infections per year); it is essentially always transmitted venereally, and most infected men are asymptomatic, serving as a reservoir for reinfection. CD4+ T-cell count below 100/uL with watery diarrhea (risk of severe, chronic, profuse cryptosporidiosis) Very high stool output (up to 25 L/day) with marked fluid and electrolyte depletion in immunocompromised cryptosporidiosis Significant weight loss, wasting, dehydration, or growth retardation in children with chronic giardiasis or cryptosporidiosis Right-upper-quadrant or mid-epigastric pain suggesting biliary tract involvement (cryptosporidiosis or microsporidiosis: papillary stenosis, sclerosing cholangitis, cholecystitis) Hypogammaglobulinemia presenting with prolonged, treatment-refractory giardiasis Fever, blood, or mucus in stool during presumed giardiasis - suggests an alternative diagnosis or coinfection Eosinophilia with enteric symptoms (suggests cystoisosporiasis among the enteric protozoa, or sarcocystosis-associated myositis) Disseminated microsporidiosis (fever, sinusitis, cholangitis, bronchiolitis, keratoconjunctivitis, encephalitis) in AIDS Relying on routine stool O+P examination, which misses Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and microsporidia - specific stains or NAATs must be ordered Stopping at a single stool exam: cyst/oocyst excretion is variable and intermittent, so repeated sampling or duodenal aspiration/biopsy may be needed Attributing symptoms to Blastocystis hominis without excluding other pathogens, given its uncertain pathogenicity Missing Dientamoeba fragilis because of delayed fixation of stool, which degrades its labile trophozoites (it has no cyst stage) Assuming routine water chlorination eliminates Giardia and Cryptosporidium - their cysts/oocysts resist standard chlorination; boiling or submicron filtration is needed Diagnosing trichomonal vaginitis by wet mount alone, given its modest (~50-60%) sensitivity Treating trichomoniasis without concurrently treating sexual partners, leading to apparent treatment failure that is actually reinfection (true high-level metronidazole resistance also occurs) Most of these protozoa are acquired by fecal-oral ingestion of environmentally resistant cysts or oocysts (Trichomonas is the exception, being venereally transmitted). Giardia trophozoites excyst in the small intestine, adhere to but do not invade the proximal small-bowel epithelium, and may cause enterocyte apoptosis, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and malabsorption/secretion; the precise mechanism of diarrhea is unknown, and consequent loss of brush-border enzyme activity produces lactose intolerance and, in some chronic cases, malabsorption with villous flattening resembling tropical sprue or celiac disease. Cryptosporidium sporozoites infect intestinal epithelial cells within an intracellular vacuole, completing asexual and sexual cycles to generate immediately infectious oocysts; the means of secretory diarrhea are uncertain, infection can be patchy in the small bowel, and biliary tract involvement may cause papillary stenosis, sclerosing cholangitis, or cholecystitis, especially in AIDS. Cystoisospora and Cyclospora similarly invade small-bowel epithelial cells (Cyclospora oocysts must mature in the environment before becoming infectious). Microsporidia inject sporoplasm into host cells via an extruded polar tubule and replicate by merogony and sporogony, releasing spores in stool, urine, respiratory secretions, or other fluids. Hypogammaglobulinemia predisposes to prolonged, severe, treatment-refractory giardiasis, indicating humoral immunity is important for control. Outcomes depend heavily on immune status. Giardiasis ranges from asymptomatic carriage to fulminant diarrhea and malabsorption; most patients are cured, though some with chronic infection have delayed symptom resolution attributed to slow brush-border enzyme regeneration, and hypogammaglobulinemic or AIDS patients may have refractory disease. Cryptosporidiosis is self-limited (1-2 weeks) in immunocompetent hosts but can be chronic and severe in AIDS, where improved immune status from antiretroviral therapy can lead to resolution. Cystoisosporiasis and cyclosporiasis can be self-limited but tend to relapse and become chronic in HIV-infected patients. Microsporidiosis can be self-limited in the immunocompetent but contributes to chronic diarrhea and wasting in AIDS, and definitive therapy is not well established. Balantidiasis ranges from asymptomatic to fulminant dysentery; sarcocystosis and most Blastocystis or Dientamoeba infections are mild or self-limited. No formal staging; severity is gauged clinically by host immune status (notably CD4 count below 100/uL marking risk of severe cryptosporidiosis), stool volume and degree of fluid/electrolyte loss (up to 25 L/day in severe cryptosporidiosis), presence of malabsorption/weight loss/wasting, dehydration, growth retardation in children, and biliary or disseminated extraintestinal involvement.

The course is slowly progressive, and many patients survive into adulthood; the main long-term burden comes from joint contractures, hip disease, and cardiac valve involvement, which can cause significant disability.

Cervical instability requires vigilance to prevent neurological injury.

Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 — PHA1, NR3C2, mineralocorticoid receptor deficiency, ENaC loss-of-function, SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, aldosterone resistance Primary adrenal insufficiency (aldosterone deficiency, e.g. salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia) Aldosterone synthase deficiency Transient pseudohypoaldosteronism secondary to urinary tract infection or obstructive uropathy in infants Cystic fibrosis (salt loss with respiratory disease, mimicking the systemic form) Renal tubular acidosis type 4 Congenital adrenal hypoplasia Serum sodium, potassium and bicarbonate to document salt-wasting hyperkalaemic acidosis Plasma renin and aldosterone (both markedly elevated) Urinary electrolytes to confirm renal sodium loss Sweat chloride testing to assess systemic involvement and exclude cystic fibrosis Renal tract imaging to exclude secondary/transient causes such as obstruction or infection Molecular genetic testing of NR3C2 and the ENaC subunit genes Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is a state of target-organ resistance to aldosterone, so despite very high aldosterone the kidney cannot retain sodium normally The autosomal dominant (renal) form is due to loss-of-function variants in NR3C2, the mineralocorticoid receptor, and tends to be milder and to improve with age The autosomal recessive (systemic) form is due to loss-of-function variants in the epithelial sodium channel subunits (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G) and is more severe and persistent The biochemical signature is salt wasting with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, alongside markedly elevated renin and aldosterone In the systemic form, sodium loss also affects sweat, salivary glands and colon, and recurrent respiratory symptoms can mimic cystic fibrosis It is effectively the mirror image of Liddle syndrome, with an underactive rather than overactive sodium channel pathway Management rests on generous sodium supplementation and control of hyperkalaemia; the recessive systemic form typically needs lifelong high-dose salt replacement Life-threatening neonatal salt-wasting crisis with severe hyperkalaemia Cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalaemia Severe dehydration and circulatory collapse Failure to thrive despite feeding Recurrent respiratory infections in the systemic form Misdiagnosing it as adrenal insufficiency and giving mineralocorticoid replacement, which is ineffective because the defect is resistance, not deficiency Failing to distinguish the transient secondary form (infection/obstruction) from inherited disease Overlooking systemic salt loss and confusing the recessive form with cystic fibrosis Underestimating the very large sodium requirements of the systemic form Not appreciating the mode of inheritance when counselling families Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is caused by failure of aldosterone signalling in the distal nephron. In the dominant renal form, loss-of-function variants in the mineralocorticoid receptor gene NR3C2 blunt the response to aldosterone; in the recessive systemic form, loss-of-function variants in the epithelial sodium channel subunits prevent sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and in other epithelia. Because sodium cannot be reabsorbed and the electrochemical gradient for potassium and hydrogen secretion is lost, the kidney wastes salt while retaining potassium and hydrogen ion, producing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis. The salt loss and hypovolaemia strongly stimulate renin and aldosterone, but the target tissues cannot respond, so the very high hormone levels coexist with continued salt wasting. The dominant renal form often attenuates with age and may need little treatment in adulthood, whereas the recessive systemic form is severe, persists lifelong, and requires continuous salt supplementation and careful management of hyperkalaemia.

hyperkalaemia to renal failure when the glomerular filtration rate is actually preserved Prescribing renin-angiotensin blockade for the hypertension, which can worsen the hyperkalaemia Missing the diagnosis by not recognising the mirror-image relationship to Gitelman syndrome Overlooking the excellent and specific response to thiazide treatment Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 results from dysregulation of the WNK kinase signalling network that controls the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Variants in WNK1 or WNK4, or in the KLHL3 and CUL3 components of the ubiquitin ligase complex that normally degrades WNK kinases, lead to excessive kinase activity and increased cotransporter abundance and function. Enhanced distal sodium-chloride reabsorption expands extracellular volume and raises blood pressure, and by consuming luminal sodium it reduces the electrochemical driving force for potassium and hydrogen secretion in the downstream nephron. The net effect is salt-dependent, low-renin hypertension with hyperkalaemia and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, which is reversed by inhibiting the cotransporter with a thiazide. Prognosis is generally excellent because low-dose thiazide therapy typically normalises blood pressure and electrolytes; untreated disease carries the usual cardiovascular risks of hypertension and the hazards of hyperkalaemia.

The resulting imbalance allows calcium and phosphate to deposit on elastic fibres in the skin, the Bruch membrane of the eye, and the arterial wall. Life expectancy is usually near normal, but progressive visual loss from retinal complications and the burden of premature vascular disease are the main sources of morbidity. Early retinal surveillance and cardiovascular risk management improve outcomes.

immunomodulators for severe or refractory disease Screen for and address associated cardiometabolic risk, obesity, and depression, as psoriasis is a systemic inflammatory condition Avoid abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids, which can precipitate a pustular or erythrodermic flare Erythroderma with widespread redness, scaling, and impaired thermoregulation requiring urgent care Generalised pustular psoriasis with fever and systemic upset Rapidly progressive joint destruction or dactylitis suggesting aggressive psoriatic arthritis Signs of secondary infection or sepsis in extensive skin breakdown Mislabelling scalp or flexural psoriasis as seborrhoeic dermatitis or fungal infection Overlooking psoriatic arthritis until irreversible joint damage has occurred Using potent topical steroids in flexures or on the face without appropriate caution Precipitating pustular or erythrodermic flares by withdrawing systemic corticosteroids Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated disorder driven by dysregulated activation of the innate and adaptive immune systems, particularly the interleukin-23/T-helper-17 axis and tumour necrosis factor signalling. Activated T cells and dendritic cells release cytokines that drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation and abnormal differentiation, dramatically shortening epidermal turnover time and producing thickened, scaly plaques. Dilated dermal vessels and a neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate account for the erythema and, in pustular variants, sterile collections of neutrophils. A strong polygenic predisposition (including PSORS1/HLA-C associations) interacts with triggers such as infection, trauma, drugs, and stress. Psoriasis is a lifelong relapsing-remitting condition; most patients achieve good control with appropriate therapy, but disease severity fluctuates and associated arthritis and cardiometabolic disease influence long-term outcomes.

skin disease usually precedes joint involvement but arthritis can appear first or without evident skin lesions Presents in several patterns including asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis resembling rheumatoid arthritis, distal interphalangeal predominant disease, spondylitis, and the destructive arthritis mutilans Dactylitis ('sausage digit') and enthesitis are hallmark features that help distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis Nail changes such as pitting and onycholysis correlate with distal interphalangeal joint involvement Usually seronegative for rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies Radiographs may show combined erosion and new bone formation, with the classic 'pencil-in-cup' deformity in advanced disease Associated comorbidities include uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk Treatment is guided by domains involved (peripheral joints, axial disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, skin, nails), using NSAIDs, conventional DMARDs, and biologic or targeted synthetic agents (TNF, IL-17, IL-23, JAK inhibitors) Rapidly progressive, deforming or mutilating arthritis with joint destruction (arthritis mutilans) Acute painful red eye indicating uveitis requiring ophthalmology review Features suggesting axial disease with neurological compromise Symptoms of undiagnosed inflammatory bowel disease Extensive or erythrodermic/pustular skin disease indicating severe systemic involvement Missing the diagnosis when arthritis precedes or occurs without obvious skin psoriasis Mislabelling it as rheumatoid arthritis and overlooking dactylitis, enthesitis, and nail disease Failing to assess and treat all involved domains rather than joints alone Neglecting cardiovascular, metabolic, and uveitis comorbidities Assuming seronegativity excludes an inflammatory arthritis Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy resulting from immune-mediated inflammation in genetically predisposed individuals. Dysregulation of the TNF and IL-23/IL-17 axes drives inflammation at synovium, entheses, and skin. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, both bone erosion and pathological new bone formation occur, producing the mixed destructive and proliferative changes seen radiographically. Enthesitis is considered a primary lesion, and there are associations with HLA-B27 (particularly axial disease) and other HLA alleles. Course ranges from mild intermittent arthritis to progressive erosive disease with joint destruction and disability. Early recognition and treat-to-target therapy improve outcomes; poor prognostic markers include polyarticular involvement, elevated inflammatory markers, early erosions, and dactylitis.

valproate level 50-125 ug/mL; carbamazepine 4-12 ug/mL In anorexia nervosa: CBC (leukopenia/relative lymphocytosis), electrolytes (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis with purging), BUN, and bone-density assessment for osteoporosis Pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, and hypoglycemia presenting as anxiety/panic Hyperthyroidism, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and cerebrovascular accidents presenting as secondary mania Hypothyroidism (including subclinical) and hyperthyroidism presenting with depressed mood and cognitive/memory impairment Frontal-lobe tumor presenting as personality change with a normal neurologic exam Depressive pseudodementia in the elderly mimicking neurodegenerative dementia Cardiovascular conditions (paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, mitral valve prolapse) detected on ECG/echocardiography in patients labeled with panic Drug- or medication-induced psychosis (parkinsonian agents, clonidine, quinacrine, procaine derivatives) mimicking schizophrenia Mental or substance use disorders affect roughly 30% of the U.S. population, yet only about one-third of those affected are currently in treatment; four of the ten leading causes of global disability are psychiatric in origin, and depression is the single largest contributor to disability worldwide. Brief validated office instruments (PRIME-MD / Patient Health Questionnaire, SDDS-PC, the four-item PC-PTSD screen) take only minutes and map patient responses onto formal DSM criteria, helping primary care clinicians make the initial diagnosis. Panic attacks reach peak intensity within about 10 minutes and usually resolve within an hour; up to ~75% of panic disorder patients eventually meet criteria for major depression, and panic is a frequent occult cause of chest pain with normal coronary angiograms and of unexplained syncope. Agoraphobia and housebound behavior are often concealed out of embarrassment, so the syndrome is missed unless the clinician asks directly; about one-third of patients presenting with anxiety have an underlying medical etiology. Major depression requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus a total of at least 5 of 9 symptoms for a minimum of 2 weeks; key distinguishing features from grief are pervasive worthlessness/self-loathing and persistent (rather than wave-like) dysphoria. Suicide risk must be probed by direct, empathic questioning: about 4-5% of depressed patients die by suicide, and most have seen a physician within the month before death; coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation raises near-term risk. Recognizing a bipolar diathesis in a patient presenting with depression is essential because antidepressant monotherapy can worsen symptoms and accelerate cycling; clues include childhood onset, antidepressant treatment failure, atypical features (hypersomnia, weight gain), and marked irritability/impulsivity. Anorexia nervosa carries the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (~5.1 per 1000 untreated); characteristic lab and exam findings include leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis, raised BUN, metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia with purging, amenorrhea, lanugo, hypotension, hypothermia, and sinus bradycardia. Bulimia nervosa usually occurs at normal or slightly above-normal weight, and physical exam is often unremarkable except for dental enamel erosion and parotid gland enlargement; medical danger stems from purging-related fluid/electrolyte disturbance and cardiac conduction abnormalities. Schizophrenia requires at least two characteristic symptoms (positive and/or negative) over a 1-month period with continuous signs for at least 6 months; about 10% of patients die by suicide, and negative symptoms predominate in roughly one-third and predict poor drug response. Personality change can be the first manifestation of serious neurologic, endocrine, or other medical disease (e.g., a frontal-lobe tumor presenting with altered motivation while the neurologic exam stays normal), so a personality disorder is a diagnosis that requires exclusion of such causes. In somatic symptom disorder the defining feature is the patient's disproportionate interpretation and preoccupation with symptoms, not the absence of a medical explanation; patients with genuine medical disease can still qualify, and repeated tests and exploratory surgery are counterproductive. Suicidal or homicidal ideation, a specific plan, or prior attempts - warrants immediate referral to a mental health specialist Psychotic symptoms, mania, or severe depression/anxiety failing first-line treatment - indications for psychiatric consultation or transfer of care Coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation in a depressed patient, which raises near-term suicide risk Critical weight loss, hypotension, hypothermia, bradycardia, or electrolyte/cardiac conduction abnormalities in eating disorders Refeeding syndrome risk when restoring weight too rapidly in anorexia nervosa (target gain ~0.5-1 lb/week) Serotonin syndrome (myoclonus, agitation, abdominal cramping, hyperpyrexia, hypertension) - a contraindication to combining MAOIs with SSRIs Hypertensive crisis from tyramine-containing foods or sympathomimetics in patients taking MAOIs New-onset psychosis requiring exclusion of a drug/medication cause before diagnosing schizophrenia Basing psychiatric referral on the mere absence of a physical explanation rather than on positive signs/symptoms of a mental disorder Failing to ask directly about agoraphobia, OCD behaviors, or suicidal ideation, all of which patients commonly conceal Subjecting somatic symptom disorder patients to repeated tests and exploratory surgery, or confronting them in a way that causes humiliation and treatment abandonment Treating an unrecognized bipolar depression with antidepressant monotherapy, risking induction of mania or cycle acceleration Prescribing benzodiazepines beyond 4-6 weeks (tolerance, abuse, dependence) and not anticipating withdrawal, which can include seizures Giving benzodiazepines or SSRIs in the immediate aftermath of trauma, and using debriefing, which does not prevent PTSD and may worsen symptoms Using TCAs in patients with serious cardiovascular risk or bundle branch block, and providing large supplies to suicidal patients (TCA overdose can be lethal, desipramine highest risk) Overlooking lithium's narrow therapeutic index and its antithyroid/renal effects during maintenance monitoring Psychiatric disorders are conceptualized as CNS disorders arising from interacting genetic, developmental, and environmental factors, with substantial heritability and considerable overlap of genetic risk variants across diagnoses (pleiotropy). Anxiety and panic involve noradrenergic discharge from the locus coeruleus and serotonergic dorsal-raphe pathways, with lactate, yohimbine, CCK-4, and CO2 capable of provoking attacks; generalized anxiety implicates the GABA-A receptor/chloride-channel complex and serotonergic modulation. PTSD is associated with excessive locus coeruleus norepinephrine release facilitating fear-memory encoding, insular threat-detection overactivity, and blunted pituitary-adrenal responses. OCD involves orbitofrontal cortex-caudate-globus pallidus circuitry. Major depression shows elevated cortisol and CRH, dexamethasone non-suppression, blunted TSH response to TRH, shortened REM latency with increased REM density and reduced slow-wave sleep, altered proinflammatory cytokines and neurotrophins, oxidative stress, telomere shortening, and possible gut-microbiome changes; delayed therapeutic action of antidepressants implicates adaptive second-messenger and neurotrophic changes. Bipolar disorder shows very high monozygotic concordance (approaching 80%) with risk genes (CACNA1C, ANK3, NCAN, ODZ4, TRANK1) shared with schizophrenia and autism, plus circadian and calcium dysregulation. Schizophrenia involves dopamine D2/D3 signaling in the ventral striatum, many small-effect GWAS loci and rare copy-number variants, and pathways of immunity, inflammation, and cell signaling. Outcomes vary widely by disorder. Panic disorder responds to treatment in 75-85% of patients, though complete remission is somewhat lower. Most depressed patients (60-70%) respond to an adequately dosed antidepressant over 6-8 weeks, and about three-quarters improve by ~2 months; the best predictor of recurrence is the number of prior episodes (50-60% of first-episode patients have at least one or two recurrences). Bipolar disorder is recurrent and requires maintenance therapy; lithium responses are 70-80% in acute mania and a sustained level >=0.8 meq/L reduces suicide risk. About 4-5% of depressed and ~10% of schizophrenic patients die by suicide. Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric condition (~5.1/1000 untreated), though most patients achieve remission within 5 years; binge-eating disorder has the most favorable prognosis among eating disorders. Schizophrenia often has a poor outcome with insidious onset, but positive symptoms tend to attenuate with age and permanent remission occasionally occurs. Diagnoses are framed by DSM-5-TR (with ICD-10-CM used more widely worldwide); alternative research frameworks include NIMH RDoC and the dimensional HiTOP taxonomy, none yet adequately validated. Severity and subtyping markers within disorders include: bipolar I (full manic episode >=1 week) vs bipolar II (hypomania >=4 days plus recurrent depression) vs cyclothymia (>=2 years of subthreshold fluctuations); rapid cycling defined as >=4 mood episodes per year; persistent depressive (dysthymic) disorder as chronic symptoms >=2 years; PTSD specifiers (with dissociative symptoms, with delayed expression >=6 months); anorexia nervosa restricting type vs binge-eating/purging type; and Munchausen's syndrome as the most severe form of factitious disorder.

Pterygium — surfer's eye, pterygia Pinguecula Pseudopterygium (from prior injury or inflammation) Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia) Conjunctival naevus or other pigmented lesion Limbal dermoid Slit-lamp examination to document size, vascularity, and encroachment onto the cornea Refraction and corneal topography to assess induced astigmatism Serial photography to monitor progression Excision biopsy with histology when ocular surface neoplasia is suspected A pterygium is a wing-shaped fibrovascular growth of conjunctival tissue that encroaches onto the cornea, most commonly on the nasal side Strongly associated with chronic exposure to ultraviolet light, wind, and dust, and therefore more common in people living in sunny, outdoor environments near the equator It is distinguished from a pinguecula, which is a similar degenerative conjunctival lesion that does not cross onto the cornea Symptoms range from a cosmetic concern and irritation or redness to visual disturbance when it induces astigmatism or approaches the visual axis A leading edge (Stocker's line of iron deposition) and a fibrovascular head advancing over the cornea are characteristic Management is conservative with lubricants and UV protection for mild lesions; surgical excision is indicated for visual axis threat, marked astigmatism, discomfort, or cosmesis Recurrence after excision is common, and adjuncts such as conjunctival autografting reduce this risk compared with bare-scleral excision Atypical or rapidly growing lesions should be evaluated to exclude ocular surface squamous neoplasia Rapid growth, marked thickening, or leukoplakic change suggesting ocular surface squamous neoplasia Encroachment onto or across the visual axis threatening vision Significant induced astigmatism degrading acuity Restricted ocular motility from a large or recurrent lesion with scarring Assuming all fleshy conjunctival lesions are benign pterygia and missing ocular surface neoplasia Operating too early on quiescent lesions given the risk of recurrence Using bare-scleral excision alone, which has a high recurrence rate compared with grafting Neglecting UV protection advice, allowing progression or recurrence A pterygium is a degenerative and proliferative condition of the bulbar conjunctiva in which chronic ultraviolet and environmental exposure causes elastotic degeneration of subepithelial collagen along with fibrovascular proliferation. The abnormal tissue invades the superficial cornea, disrupting Bowman's layer and the corneal architecture at its advancing head. Progressive growth can flatten the cornea and induce astigmatism, and encroachment onto the visual axis reduces vision. Most pterygia are benign and slowly progressive with a good prognosis; surgery is effective for symptomatic or vision-threatening lesions, though recurrence is a recognised problem, particularly with bare-scleral techniques and in younger patients.

Ptosis — blepharoptosis, drooping eyelid Aponeurotic (involutional) ptosis Third nerve palsy Horner syndrome Myasthenia gravis and other myogenic causes Mechanical ptosis from lid mass or oedema Pseudoptosis from dermatochalasis, brow ptosis, or contralateral lid retraction Measurement of margin-reflex distance, palpebral aperture, levator function, and skin crease position Pupil examination to identify Horner syndrome or third nerve palsy Assessment for fatigability and ice-pack or targeted testing when myasthenia is suspected Neuroimaging when a compressive or neurogenic cause is suspected Systemic and antibody testing for suspected myasthenia gravis Ptosis is abnormal drooping of the upper eyelid; severity is gauged by the margin-reflex distance and the effect on the visual axis Assessing levator function is central to classification and surgical planning Aponeurotic (involutional) ptosis is the commonest, showing good levator function, a high skin crease, and often thinning of the eyelid A ptosis with a small pupil and ipsilateral anhidrosis suggests Horner syndrome; a ptosis with a dilated pupil and an eye deviated down and out suggests a third nerve palsy Variable, fatigable ptosis worsening through the day points to myasthenia gravis and warrants systemic evaluation Congenital ptosis usually reflects levator dystrophy with poor function and risks amblyopia if the visual axis is occluded in a child The rare Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon links lid elevation to jaw movement Painful ptosis with a dilated pupil and ophthalmoplegia suggesting a compressive third nerve palsy (possible aneurysm) requiring urgent imaging Ptosis with anisocoria and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome), which may indicate serious underlying pathology such as an apical lung lesion or carotid dissection Fatigable or variable ptosis with diplopia or bulbar symptoms suggesting myasthenia gravis Ptosis occluding the visual axis in a child, threatening amblyopia Treating ptosis as purely cosmetic and missing a serious neurological cause such as third nerve palsy or Horner syndrome Failing to test for fatigability and overlooking myasthenia gravis Not recognising amblyopia risk in congenital ptosis Mistaking pseudoptosis from brow droop or dermatochalasis for true ptosis Ptosis results from impaired elevation of the upper lid, which is normally raised by the levator palpebrae superioris (oculomotor nerve) and Muller muscle (sympathetic). Aponeurotic ptosis is caused by dehiscence or stretching of the levator aponeurosis with age. Neurogenic ptosis follows interruption of the nerve supply, as in third nerve palsy or sympathetic denervation (Horner syndrome). Myogenic ptosis reflects muscle disease such as myasthenia gravis, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, or myotonic dystrophy. Mechanical ptosis arises from lid mass or scarring, and congenital ptosis from maldevelopment of the levator muscle. Aponeurotic and congenital ptosis generally respond well to surgery; the outlook for neurogenic and myogenic ptosis depends on the underlying cause, and childhood ptosis carries a risk of amblyopia if not managed promptly.

Post-traumatic stress disorder — PTSD, post traumatic stress disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder Acute stress disorder Adjustment disorder Major depressive disorder Panic disorder and other anxiety disorders Obsessive-compulsive disorder Substance use disorder Psychosis when flashbacks are mistaken for hallucinations Traumatic brain injury Structured trauma history and PTSD symptom rating scales Suicide risk assessment Screening for comorbid depression and substance use Assessment for traumatic brain injury where relevant Evaluation of sleep disturbance and nightmares Develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, whether directly experienced, witnessed, or learned about affecting a close other Core symptom clusters are intrusion (flashbacks, nightmares, distressing memories), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative alterations in mood and cognition, and heightened arousal and reactivity Symptoms persist beyond about one month and cause significant distress or impairment; an acute stress reaction is the label used within the first month Hyperarousal features include hypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance, and concentration problems Trauma-focused psychotherapies (such as trauma-focused CBT and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing) are first-line treatments Pharmacotherapy principles favour SSRIs or SNRIs; prazosin may help trauma-related nightmares, and benzodiazepines are generally avoided Screen for common comorbidities including depression, substance use, and suicidal ideation, and for traumatic brain injury in relevant populations Dissociative symptoms and delayed onset (months to years after the event) are recognised presentations Suicidal ideation or self-harm Severe dissociative episodes with risk to safety Escalating substance or alcohol use to cope with symptoms Aggression or risk to others during flashbacks or heightened arousal Using benzodiazepines, which do not treat core symptoms and may impair recovery Missing comorbid depression, substance use, and suicide risk Overlooking delayed-onset presentations by not taking a trauma history Mislabelling normal early stress reactions as PTSD before the required duration Failing to refer for evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy Post-traumatic stress disorder reflects dysregulated fear processing, with exaggerated amygdala responses, impaired prefrontal inhibition, and hippocampal changes affecting contextual memory, alongside altered hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and noradrenergic stress responses. These changes underpin persistent conditioned fear, impaired extinction of trauma memories, and chronic hyperarousal. Many people recover within the first year, especially with early trauma-focused treatment, but a substantial minority develop a chronic course. Prognosis is worse with severe or prolonged trauma, lack of social support, and comorbid depression or substance use.

Pulmonary fibrosis — IPF, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial lung disease, fibrosing ILD Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Pneumoconioses such as asbestosis or silicosis Drug-induced or radiation-induced lung injury Sarcoidosis with fibrosis Chronic left heart failure with interstitial oedema High-resolution CT of the chest to assess for a UIP pattern and distribution of fibrosis Full pulmonary function testing including spirometry, lung volumes, and diffusing capacity Serological screen for connective tissue disease and, where indicated, hypersensitivity precipitins Six-minute walk test with oximetry to assess functional impairment and desaturation Surgical or transbronchial lung biopsy in selected cases where imaging is non-diagnostic Presents with progressive exertional breathlessness and a persistent dry cough, often over months to years Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles (often described as Velcro-like) and finger clubbing are characteristic examination findings High-resolution CT showing a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, with subpleural and basal reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and honeycombing, is central to diagnosis Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring careful evaluation for connective tissue disease, drug toxicity, and environmental or occupational exposures Pulmonary function tests typically show a restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes and impaired gas transfer (low DLCO) Multidisciplinary discussion combining clinical, radiological, and where needed histological data improves diagnostic accuracy Antifibrotic therapy can slow the decline in lung function in IPF; supportive measures include oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, and vaccination Acute exacerbations cause rapid deterioration and carry high mortality; lung transplantation should be considered in suitable candidates Rapid worsening of dyspnoea with new diffuse ground-glass change suggesting an acute exacerbation Resting hypoxaemia or significant desaturation on exertion Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure Features suggesting an underlying treatable systemic disease that alter management Labelling fibrosis as idiopathic without excluding occupational, drug, and connective tissue causes Using corticosteroids or immunosuppression indiscriminately in IPF, where they may be harmful Missing coexisting emphysema, which can mask spirometric restriction Delaying transplant referral until the patient is too deconditioned to be a candidate Repeated microinjury to the alveolar epithelium in a susceptible (often ageing, genetically predisposed) individual triggers aberrant wound-healing rather than normal repair. Activated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts accumulate in fibroblastic foci and deposit excess extracellular matrix, progressively distorting and stiffening the lung architecture. The result is loss of functional alveolar units, honeycomb cystic change, impaired gas exchange, and reduced compliance, producing a restrictive physiology with worsening hypoxaemia. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is generally progressive with a poor prognosis and median survival of only a few years from diagnosis, though the course is variable; antifibrotic drugs slow decline and transplantation can prolong survival in eligible patients, while acute exacerbations markedly worsen outcome.

among the most common causes of PAH globally) Right heart catheterisation (RHC) - gold standard for diagnosis and severity assessment; required mPAP >20 mmHg Transthoracic echocardiography with agitated-saline (bubble) study - most important initial screening test Electrocardiography - may show right ventricular hypertrophy or strain in advanced disease Chest roentgenography - enlargement of central pulmonary arteries and obliteration of the retrosternal space Pulmonary function testing including DLCO (isolated low DLCO classic for PAH) High-resolution CT of the chest (vascular pruning, distinguishing ILD/emphysema/overlap; signs of venous congestion) Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan - primary screen for CTEPH CT pulmonary angiography and digital subtraction pulmonary angiography (definitive for CTEPH; shows webbing, stricture, tapering) 6-minute walk distance (6-MWD) for functional capacity and prognosis Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET); peak VO2 <15 mL/kg/min is prognostic but not diagnostic Nocturnal oximetry screening in all patients (nocturnal desaturation common even without sleep-disordered breathing) BNP / NT-proBNP Serology: HIV test (when indicated), antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-Scl-70; liver function and hepatitis serology; methamphetamine screening where relevant Vasoreactivity testing (idiopathic/hereditary PAH only) Asthma (overlapping nonspecific dyspnoea) Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction Physical deconditioning Obstructive sleep apnoea / obesity-hypoventilation syndrome Sarcoidosis with pulmonary vascular involvement PH is diagnosed when mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) is >20 mmHg by right heart catheterisation; this threshold was lowered from the older >=25 mmHg cut-off to emphasise earlier disease detection (p.2185, 2191). The most common causes of PH are left heart disease or primary lung disease; pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an uncommon but distinct subtype with an obliterative arteriopathy (p.2185). Most patients present with dyspnoea and/or fatigue; oedema, chest pain, presyncope and syncope are less common and signal more advanced disease (p.2188). The current WSPH classification (last revised 2018, Sixth World Symposium) defines five groups: 1 = PAH; 2 = PH due to left heart disease; 3 = PH due to chronic lung disease/hypoxia or sleep-disordered breathing; 4 = chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH); 5 = miscellaneous/multifactorial (p.2191). Echocardiography with agitated-saline (bubble) study is the most important initial screening test; estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure >35 mmHg, a notched continuous-wave Doppler waveform, or a hypertrophied/dilated right ventricle supports the diagnosis (p.2188). Hemodynamic subtypes by RHC: precapillary PH = PAWP/LVEDP <=15 mmHg with PVR >2.0 Wood units; isolated postcapillary PH = PAWP >15 mmHg with PVR <=2.0 WU; combined pre-/postcapillary PH = mPAP >20 mmHg with PAWP >15 mmHg and PVR >2.0 WU (p.2191). In PAH, an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) on pulmonary function testing is a classic finding (p.2189). BNP and NT-proBNP correlate with right ventricular dysfunction, hemodynamic severity and functional status in PAH, and NT-proBNP can serve as a biomarker of treatment response once a baseline is established (p.2191). Vasoreactivity testing (with short-acting agents such as inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled epoprostenol) is reserved for idiopathic or hereditary PAH; a positive response is a fall in mPAP by >=10 mmHg to an absolute level <=40 mmHg without a fall in cardiac output, seen in <5% of patients but carrying a particularly favourable prognosis (p.2191). CTEPH is curable in many patients by surgical pulmonary endarterectomy but is widely underdiagnosed; ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning remains the primary screening test and should be considered in any PH of unclear cause (p.2190-2191). Syncope or presyncope (signals advanced disease) Signs of right ventricular failure: elevated jugular venous pressure, lower-extremity oedema, ascites Rapid progression of symptoms with severely reduced exercise capacity Decompensated right heart failure (the major cause of mortality if untreated) Significant decline in exercise tolerance from baseline even when CPET appears reassuring (e.g. in athletes - may indicate early PAH or subacute PE) Right heart catheterisation - not echocardiography - is the diagnostic gold standard; echocardiography only screens, and an echo in which tricuspid regurgitation is simply not detected does NOT exclude PH (PH is found in one-third of such patients). PH symptoms are nonspecific, insidious and overlap with asthma, HFpEF and deconditioning, so the diagnosis is frequently missed without a reasonable index of suspicion. Do not assume that PH in patients with comorbid cardiopulmonary disease (e.g. ILD, mitral valve disease) is merely an extension of the underlying condition rather than a specific entity. Patients with left heart disease aggressively diuresed before RHC may falsely appear to have an isolated precapillary (PAH-like) profile - diuresis can mask the true hemodynamic classification. A low peak VO2 occurs across the heart-lung disease spectrum and is NOT diagnostic of PH per se. Chronic thromboembolic disease (thrombotic remodelling with reduced exercise capacity but without PH) requires consideration in patients with prior PE and dyspnoea even when echocardiography is reassuring. PAH arises from apoptosis resistance, cell proliferation, dysregulated metabolism and increased oxidant stress in pulmonary vascular cells, pericytes and adventitial fibroblasts, producing hypertrophic, fibrotic and plexogenic remodelling of distal (small) pulmonary arterioles with extracellular-matrix expansion, reduced vascular compliance and in-situ thrombosis. This raises pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP). To preserve cardiac output against the elevated right-ventricular afterload, RV work increases; sustained overload depletes myocardial energy and causes right ventricular-pulmonary arterial uncoupling, and in end-stage disease cardiac output and mPAP both fall. The most common germline driver of hereditary PAH is a BMPR2 variant (a TGF-beta superfamily receptor) with variable penetrance (as low as ~20%); other drivers include TBX4 and SOX17, and EIF2AK4 for pulmonary veno-occlusive disease. In group 2 PH the hallmark is elevated left atrial pressure causing pulmonary venous hypertension, venule sclerosis and secondary arteriolar remodelling. (p.2185-2192) If left untreated, PH carries a high mortality rate, largely owing to decompensated right heart failure. Idiopathic PAH is progressive and leads to right heart failure and early mortality; in left-sided heart failure or HFpEF even mildly elevated mPAP carries adverse outcome. Among IPAH, prevalence favours women ~3:1 but hemodynamics are more severe and prognosis less favourable in men. Hereditary BMPR2 PAH presents younger with more severe hemodynamics and greater clinical risk (conversion ~2.3%/year in carriers). Vasoreactive responders (<5%) have a particularly favourable prognosis. Scleroderma-associated PAH and HIV-PAH carry especially poor prognoses; portopulmonary hypertension is a marker of adverse post-liver-transplant outcome (up to 100% mortality reported with mPAP >=50 mmHg in one study). Peak VO2 <15 mL/kg/min is prognostic. (p.2185, 2191-2192) World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) clinical classification (revised 2018) into 5 groups: Group 1 - pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH: idiopathic, heritable, drug/toxin-associated, or associated with connective tissue disease, HIV, portal hypertension, congenital heart disease, schistosomiasis; plus PVOD/PCH and persistent PH of the newborn); Group 2 - PH associated with left heart disease (HFpEF, HFrEF, valvular, congenital/acquired postcapillary); Group 3 - PH associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia (obstructive, restrictive, mixed, hypoventilation, high-altitude hypoxia, developmental); Group 4 - PH associated with pulmonary artery obstruction (CTEPH and other obstructions); Group 5 - PH with unclear/multifactorial mechanisms (haematological, systemic, metabolic, chronic renal failure +/- haemodialysis, pulmonary tumour thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrosing mediastinitis). Hemodynamic categorisation by RHC: precapillary, isolated postcapillary, and combined pre-/postcapillary PH. (Table 294-1, p.2191)

Pulmonic Valve Disease — Pulmonary valve disease, Pulmonic stenosis, Pulmonic regurgitation, PS, PR Aortic regurgitation (the Graham Steell murmur of PR can mimic the AR murmur) Other causes of a midsystolic murmur such as aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive physiology, or an atrial septal defect with enhanced pulmonic flow Pulmonary hypertension as the dominant clinical problem rather than the valve lesion itself Infective endocarditis of the pulmonic valve (an etiology of both PS from bulky vegetations and PR) ECG: right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, and right atrial enlargement in severe PS; RVH/RA enlargement may appear in PR depending on etiology and severity Chest x-ray: poststenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery on the frontal view, retrosternal airspace filling from RV enlargement on the lateral view, and apex lifted off the left hemidiaphragm in some patients Transthoracic echocardiography (Doppler): definitive diagnosis in most cases, with jet velocity, gradient, RV function, pulmonary artery pressures (which should be low in PS), and associated lesions; RV systolic pressure estimated from the tricuspid regurgitant jet Transesophageal echocardiography: better delineation of the RV outflow tract and infundibular hypertrophy when needed Cardiac MR: greater anatomic detail and precise RV volume/function assessment, especially in repaired congenital heart disease Cardiac catheterization: not routinely required; if performed in PS, pressures are taken just below and above the valve with attention to a possible dynamic gradient Carcinoid heart disease causing mixed pulmonic valve lesions Obstructing tumors producing RV outflow obstruction that mimics valvular PS Idiopathic dilation of the pulmonary artery / annulus causing functional PR Marfan syndrome-related annular enlargement Pulmonic stenosis is overwhelmingly a congenital lesion; the valve is typically domed in isolated cases, and the pulmonic valve is only very rarely affected by the rheumatic process. Dysplastic pulmonic valves occur as a feature of Noonan syndrome (mapped to chromosome 12), with PTPN1 gene mutations identified in roughly half of Noonan cases. The pulmonic ejection sound (click) is the single right-sided acoustic event that DECREASES in intensity with inspiration, because elevated RV end-diastolic pressure pre-opens the valve. As pulmonic stenosis worsens, the ejection sound migrates toward S1 and eventually becomes inaudible, the systolic murmur peaks later and may extend past A2, and P2 becomes reduced or absent. The systolic murmur of pulmonic stenosis is mid-systolic and crescendo-decrescendo, best heard in the left second interspace, and it increases in intensity during inspiration. The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation is a high-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur along the left sternal border that can be mistaken for aortic regurgitation; it tends to grow louder with inspiration. In survivors of childhood tetralogy of Fallot or PS/pulmonary atresia repair, an RV-PA conduit lacking a valve can be freely regurgitant, producing a misleadingly low-pitched, short diastolic murmur despite significant PR and RV volume overload. Right ventricular dysfunction from afterload mismatch appears earlier and at lower peak systolic pressures in pulmonic stenosis than left ventricular failure does in aortic stenosis, because the RV tolerates pressure overload poorly. Cardiac output is maintained until late in pulmonic stenosis, so many patients with mild or even moderate disease are asymptomatic and are detected only by an incidental murmur or click. A reduction in RV ejection fraction may be an early sign of hemodynamic compromise in pulmonic regurgitation, before overt symptoms develop. Trace or mild pulmonic regurgitation of no hemodynamic significance is frequently seen on transthoracic echocardiography even when the valve is structurally normal. Carcinoid characteristically produces mixed pulmonic valve disease, combining both regurgitation and stenosis. Exertional dyspnea or early-onset fatigue indicating severe pulmonic stenosis Anginal chest pain from RV oxygen supply-demand mismatch, or syncope, with very severe obstruction Destabilizing triggers (atrial fibrillation, fever, infection, anemia, pregnancy) precipitating decompensation in severe PS Signs of right heart failure (hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema) from RV systolic dysfunction Abdominal fullness/bloating and lower-extremity swelling in progressive severe PR with RV dysfunction The Graham Steell murmur of PR is easily confused with aortic regurgitation along the left sternal border. A valveless RV-PA conduit after congenital repair can give a low-pitched, short diastolic murmur that understates the true severity of PR and RV volume overload. Doppler peak instantaneous gradient correlates only weakly with the catheterization peak-to-peak gradient; the catheter peak-to-peak value tends to track better with the Doppler MEAN gradient. Trace or mild PR seen on echocardiography is usually of no clinical or hemodynamic consequence and should not be over-interpreted. Relying on the systolic ejection sound can mislead in severe PS, where the click moves toward S1 and may become inaudible. Pulmonic stenosis is defined hemodynamically by a systolic pressure gradient between the right ventricle and the main pulmonary artery. Sustained obstruction to RV outflow drives RV hypertrophy and prolongs systolic ejection; because the RV adapts poorly to pressure overload, dysfunction from afterload mismatch develops earlier and at lower pressures than analogous left-sided changes in aortic stenosis. The right atrial a wave rises in proportion to the higher pressures needed to fill a stiff, hypertrophied RV, and a prominent RA v wave reflects functional tricuspid regurgitation from RV and annular dilation; cardiac output is preserved until late. Pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses when mild but can worsen with age in moderate disease owing to valve thickening and calcification. In pulmonic regurgitation, severe disease causes RV chamber enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy, creating a state of increased preload and afterload. The diastolic pressure gradient from pulmonary artery to RV that drives the regurgitant flow falls progressively through diastole, explaining the decrescendo murmur, and the murmur shortens as RV diastolic pressure rises. Forward output is preserved early but fails to augment normally with exercise and declines over time; advanced stages show marked RV and RA enlargement with elevated jugular venous pressure. PR arises from primary valve pathology, annular enlargement (e.g., long-standing severe pulmonary hypertension dilating the valve ring), or their combination, and may follow surgical relief of RV outflow obstruction or balloon valvotomy. Mild pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses, whereas moderate disease may worsen with age due to valve thickening and calcification. Because cardiac output is maintained until late, many patients remain asymptomatic for years; severe disease eventually brings RV dysfunction and, uncommonly and only very late, overt right heart failure. In pulmonic regurgitation, forward output is preserved early but does not rise normally with exertion and declines over time, with a falling RV ejection fraction serving as an early marker of compromise and advanced disease producing marked RV/RA enlargement and elevated jugular venous pressure. Pulmonic stenosis severity (normal systolic function and cardiac output): severe = peak systolic gradient >64 mmHg (mean gradient >35 mmHg, Doppler jet velocity >4 m/s); moderate = peak gradient 36-64 mmHg (jet velocity 3-4 m/s); mild = jet velocity <3 m/s (peak gradient <36 mmHg).

to evaluate caries depth and apical changes Bite test and transillumination for suspected cracks Selective anaesthesia to localise the source of poorly localised pain Pulpitis is inflammation of the dental pulp, most often a consequence of deep caries, cracks, or trauma allowing bacterial ingress Reversible pulpitis produces sharp, short-lived pain to stimuli such as cold that settles quickly once the stimulus is removed Irreversible pulpitis causes spontaneous, lingering, often throbbing pain that may worsen when lying down and can be poorly localised Heat that intensifies pain and cold that relieves it can indicate an irreversibly inflamed or partly necrotic pulp Pulp sensibility testing (cold, electric) helps distinguish vital from non-vital teeth and reversible from irreversible states Reversible pulpitis is managed by removing the cause and placing a protective restoration, whereas irreversible pulpitis requires root canal treatment or extraction As inflammation progresses to necrosis, pain may transiently ease before periapical infection develops Referred pain patterns mean patients frequently misidentify which tooth or arch is affected Facial swelling, fever, or trismus signalling spread of odontogenic infection Rapidly worsening pain with systemic upset suggesting progression to abscess or cellulitis Airway-threatening swelling from infection tracking into deep neck spaces Assuming pain localisation is accurate when pulpal pain is often diffuse and referred Treating irreversible pulpitis with a simple restoration and expecting resolution Missing a maxillary sinus origin for upper posterior tooth pain Interpreting a sudden reduction in pain as recovery rather than progression to necrosis Pulpitis begins when bacterial products, most commonly from advancing caries, reach the pulp through dentinal tubules or direct exposure, triggering an inflammatory response within the rigid, low-compliance confines of the pulp chamber. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability raise intrapulpal pressure, and because the pulp cannot expand, this compresses vessels and nerves, amplifying pain. In reversible disease the inflammation is limited and the pulp can recover once the irritant is removed. With continued insult the inflammation becomes irreversible, progressing to ischaemia, localised then total pulp necrosis, and eventual extension of infection through the apical foramen into the periapical tissues. Reversible pulpitis usually resolves fully after the irritant is treated, while irreversible pulpitis will not recover and needs endodontic treatment or extraction; treated teeth generally have a good outcome when infection is eliminated.

Pycnodysostosis (CTSK) — pyknodysostosis, cathepsin K deficiency, CTSK-related osteosclerosis, Toulouse-Lautrec syndrome Osteopetrosis Cleidocranial dysplasia Sclerosteosis and Van Buchem disease Idiopathic acro-osteolysis (Hajdu-Cheney syndrome) Osteogenesis imperfecta given the fracture tendency Craniometaphyseal dysplasia Plain radiographs showing generalised osteosclerosis, acro-osteolysis of distal phalanges, and open fontanelles Skull imaging for delayed suture closure, wormian bones, and obtuse mandibular angle Genetic testing for CTSK mutations Full blood count to distinguish from osteopetrosis with marrow failure Dental and orthodontic assessment Sleep study when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected An autosomal recessive osteosclerosis caused by loss-of-function mutations in CTSK, encoding the osteoclast enzyme cathepsin K Osteoclasts are present but cannot degrade bone matrix collagen, so bone becomes dense yet abnormally brittle and prone to fracture Clinical features include short stature, a large head with open or delayed-closing fontanelles, frontal and occipital bossing, and a small receding chin Acro-osteolysis of the distal phalanges produces short, stubby fingers, and the nails are often dysplastic Dental anomalies, a high-arched palate, and obstructive sleep apnoea from midface hypoplasia are common Distinguished from osteopetrosis by the brittle bone, acro-osteolysis, and typically preserved marrow function without the severe cytopenias of malignant osteopetrosis Management is supportive with fracture prevention and orthopaedic care; cathepsin K biology has informed development of antiresorptive drug targets Recurrent or non-healing fractures, particularly of the long bones and mandible Severe obstructive sleep apnoea causing hypoxaemia Basilar skull deformity or neurological compromise Signs suggesting marrow failure that would point instead to osteopetrosis Assuming dense bone is strong and underestimating the high fracture risk Confusing it with osteopetrosis and expecting marrow failure or with osteogenesis imperfecta on the basis of fractures alone Overlooking acro-osteolysis and delayed fontanelle closure as diagnostic clues Neglecting airway and dental complications during anaesthesia and routine care Pycnodysostosis results from biallelic mutations in CTSK, the gene encoding cathepsin K, a cysteine protease secreted by osteoclasts that degrades the organic collagen matrix of bone during resorption. Because the enzyme is defective, osteoclasts can demineralise but cannot properly break down the collagenous matrix, leaving behind poorly remodelled, densely mineralised but structurally weak bone. This uncoupling of mineral removal from matrix degradation explains the paradox of a sclerotic, radiodense skeleton that fractures readily. Impaired remodelling at the acral skeleton produces the characteristic acro-osteolysis, and defective skull remodelling underlies the delayed fontanelle closure and craniofacial features. Lifespan is usually normal, but patients face recurrent fragility fractures, orthopaedic deformity, dental complications, and potential airway problems that require long-term multidisciplinary management.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis — infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, IHPS, pyloric stenosis, congenital pyloric stenosis Gastro-oesophageal reflux Overfeeding Malrotation with volvulus (bilious vomiting) Gastroenteritis Cow's milk protein intolerance Metabolic disorders or raised intracranial pressure causing vomiting Adrenal insufficiency (salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia) Abdominal ultrasound to measure pyloric muscle thickness and channel length Serum electrolytes, chloride, and bicarbonate Blood gas to characterise the alkalosis Assessment of hydration status and weight Blood glucose Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction, typically presenting between 3 and 6 weeks of age and more common in firstborn males. The hallmark is progressive, forceful non-bilious (projectile) vomiting shortly after feeds, with the infant remaining hungry and eager to feed again. The classic metabolic picture is a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric acid and chloride. A palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium/right upper quadrant and visible gastric peristalsis are classic but not always present. Ultrasound is the diagnostic investigation of choice, demonstrating a thickened and elongated pyloric muscle. The vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, because the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla of Vater; bilious vomiting should prompt consideration of other diagnoses. Initial management is medical resuscitation: correcting dehydration and the electrolyte and acid-base disturbance before any operation. Definitive treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy, which is not an emergency and should follow adequate fluid and electrolyte correction. Signs of significant dehydration or shock Severe electrolyte or acid-base derangement Bilious vomiting, which points away from pyloric stenosis toward a surgical emergency such as volvulus Lethargy or reduced responsiveness from dehydration and electrolyte imbalance Rushing to surgery before correcting fluid and electrolyte abnormalities Mistaking the illness for simple reflux or overfeeding and delaying diagnosis Overlooking that vomiting is characteristically non-bilious, and failing to reconsider the diagnosis if it is bilious Underestimating the degree of dehydration and metabolic alkalosis Progressive hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular smooth muscle of the pylorus narrows and elongates the pyloric channel, obstructing gastric emptying. The exact cause is unknown but involves genetic and environmental factors. Persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to loss of hydrogen and chloride ions, producing a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; ongoing losses and renal compensation drive potassium loss and, later, paradoxical aciduria. Fluid losses cause dehydration. The obstruction is proximal to the biliary drainage, so vomitus is non-bilious. Prognosis is excellent after appropriate resuscitation and pyloromyotomy, with prompt recovery and no long-term gastrointestinal sequelae.

Skeletal muscle is normally resistant to infection, but injury allows haematogenously seeded bacteria to establish a focus that progresses from diffuse inflammation to a walled-off intramuscular abscess. Without drainage the infection can extend, cause systemic sepsis, and, if untreated, seed distant sites. With timely antibiotics and adequate drainage the outlook is generally good; delayed diagnosis, extensive or multifocal disease, and progression to septic shock worsen outcomes, and immunocompromised patients are at higher risk of complications.

step essential for gluconeogenesis, the citric acid cycle and neurotransmitter synthesis Presents with lactic acidosis, often accompanied by hypoglycaemia, and a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio The from biotinidase and holocarboxylase synthetase deficiencies Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy Recurrent hypoglycaemia with metabolic acidosis Rapid neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness Failure of acidosis to respond to conventional resuscitation Confusing it with pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, which typically shows a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Missing the diagnosis when lactic acidosis is attributed to sepsis or tissue hypoperfusion Overlooking hyperammonaemia and the urea cycle contribution Failing to prevent catabolism and fasting, which precipitate crises Pyruvate carboxylase catalyses the ATP-dependent, biotin-requiring carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate within mitochondria. This reaction replenishes citric acid cycle intermediates (anaplerosis) and provides oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis and, in the brain, for aspartate and glutamate synthesis. Enzyme deficiency blocks gluconeogenesis, causing fasting hypoglycaemia, and diverts pyruvate towards lactate, producing lactic acidosis with an elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. Depletion of oxaloacetate impairs the malate-aspartate shuttle and urea cycle function, contributing to hyperammonaemia and abnormal amino acids, while cerebral aspartate deficiency disturbs myelination and neurotransmitter metabolism. The severe neonatal form carries a very poor prognosis with early death, and even the milder infantile form is usually associated with significant developmental delay and recurrent metabolic crises. Rare attenuated cases with more residual enzyme activity have better outcomes.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency — PDH deficiency, PDHC deficiency, pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency, PDHA1 deficiency Mitochondrial respiratory chain disorders (high lactate-to-pyruvate ratio) Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency Organic acidaemias and other causes of lactic acidosis Biotinidase and multiple carboxylase deficiency Leigh syndrome of other genetic cause Hypoxic-ischaemic or septic (secondary) lactic acidosis Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Plasma amino acids (elevated alanine) Neuroimaging for corpus callosum abnormalities and Leigh-pattern lesions Enzyme assay of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in fibroblasts or leukocytes Molecular testing including the X-linked PDHA1 gene Assessment of the lactate response to a carbohydrate load A major cause of primary (congenital) lactic acidosis, resulting from deficient activity of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle The most common form is due to X-linked mutations in the E1-alpha subunit (PDHA1), so both males and females can be affected Presentations range from severe neonatal lactic acidosis to progressive neurological disease with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures and episodic ataxia A characteristic feature is that lactate rises rather than falls after carbohydrate intake, and the blood lactate-to-pyruvate ratio is typically normal (in contrast to respiratory chain defects where it is high) Structural brain abnormalities such as corpus callosum agenesis, and a Leigh syndrome pattern of basal ganglia and brainstem lesions, may be present Because glucose cannot be used efficiently, a ketogenic (high-fat, low-carbohydrate) diet is a central management principle, providing an alternative fuel that bypasses the block Thiamine (a cofactor of the complex) is supplemented and may benefit thiamine-responsive variants; dichloroacetate has been used to lower lactate Not a standard target of newborn screening, so diagnosis rests on recognising congenital lactic acidosis and neurological features and confirming enzymatically or genetically Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with encephalopathy is a metabolic emergency Acute worsening of lactic acidosis and neurological function after carbohydrate loading Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or brainstem involvement in a Leigh-syndrome presentation Intractable seizures or apnoea in the neonatal period Loading a hypotonic, acidotic infant with intravenous glucose, which can worsen lactic acidosis Confusing it with respiratory chain disease by not checking the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Overlooking treatable thiamine-responsive variants Missing affected females because the common defect is X-linked The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate, the end product of glycolysis, into acetyl-CoA, linking carbohydrate metabolism to the citric acid cycle and oxidative energy production. When the complex is deficient, pyruvate cannot enter the cycle and is instead diverted to lactate and alanine, producing lactic acidosis with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. The brain, which depends heavily on glucose oxidation for energy, is particularly affected, resulting in structural malformations, neurodegeneration and a Leigh-like phenotype. Providing fat-derived ketones and acetyl-CoA through a ketogenic diet bypasses the enzymatic block and supplies the brain with usable fuel. Prognosis is generally guarded and correlates with the severity of residual enzyme activity; severe neonatal forms often have a poor outcome, whereas milder and thiamine-responsive variants and early ketogenic dietary treatment can improve neurological outcome, though the disorder is not curable.

of lactic acidosis Assessment of response to a supervised ketogenic dietary trial and thiamine Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive cause of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex dysfunction, usually from PDP1 mutations The phosphatase normally dephosphorylates and thereby activates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, so its loss leaves the complex locked in an inactive, phosphorylated state The result is impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, with accumulation of pyruvate and lactate and a characteristically normal or low lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Presentation is with neonatal or infantile lactic acidosis, hypotonia, feeding difficulty, developmental delay and, in some, features overlapping Leigh syndrome Because the block is at the entry to the citric acid cycle, glucose loading tends to worsen lactic acidosis, whereas fat is a useful alternative fuel Thiamine is a cofactor of the complex and a trial of generic thiamine supplementation is standard, and a high-fat, low-carbohydrate ketogenic dietary approach is used under specialist supervision to bypass the block Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity that is restorable, with confirmation by PDP1 genetics Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with metabolic decompensation Refractory seizures or encephalopathy Worsening acidosis after carbohydrate loading Rapid neurological deterioration during intercurrent illness Treating lactic acidosis with glucose-rich fluids, which can worsen it when the block is at pyruvate oxidation Not distinguishing this from respiratory-chain disorders, which typically raise the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio Failing to trial thiamine and a supervised ketogenic dietary approach that can bypass the metabolic block Overlooking the enzyme assay conditions needed to reveal a phosphatase (activation) defect rather than a primary complex defect The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle by converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, and its activity is regulated by reversible phosphorylation: pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase inactivates it and pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase reactivates it. In this disorder, recessive mutations (typically in PDP1) render the phosphatase deficient, so the complex remains phosphorylated and inactive. Pyruvate cannot be efficiently oxidised, so it and lactate accumulate while acetyl-CoA supply to the citric acid cycle falls, starving the brain of energy. Because pyruvate is diverted to lactate at the level of pyruvate rather than through a redox imbalance, the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio is usually normal or low, helping to distinguish it from respiratory-chain defects. Prognosis varies with residual enzyme activity: severe neonatal presentations carry high mortality and significant neurodisability, whereas milder cases may stabilise with dietary and cofactor management, though neurological impairment often persists.

of very variable severity, from mild to transfusion-dependent Because the block is in glycolysis, upstream 2,3-diphosphoglycerate accumulates and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve, so anaemia is often better tolerated than the haemoglobin level suggests Presentation ranges from neonatal jaundice and anaemia to gallstones, splenomegaly and iron overload in later life Diagnosis relies on demonstrating reduced red-cell pyruvate kinase enzyme activity and confirmatory PKLR genetic testing, after excluding commoner causes The blood film is non-specific, and characteristic echinocytes may become prominent only after splenectomy Management includes folate support, transfusion when required, cholelithiasis surveillance, iron-overload monitoring, and splenectomy or newer targeted therapy in selected severe cases Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 with a sharp fall in haemoglobin Severe neonatal jaundice risking kernicterus Symptomatic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction Interpreting a normal-looking enzyme level without correcting for reticulocytosis, which can mask deficiency Overlooking iron overload in patients who are not regularly transfused Assuming the haemoglobin concentration reflects symptom burden despite the compensatory oxygen-delivery shift Missing gallstones as a cause of recurrent biliary symptoms Pyruvate kinase catalyses the final adenosine-triphosphate-generating step of glycolysis, the mature red cell's sole source of energy since it lacks mitochondria. Autosomal recessive PKLR mutations reduce enzyme activity, depleting cellular ATP and impairing the ion pumps and membrane maintenance that keep the red cell flexible, so cells become rigid, dehydrated and are removed prematurely, chiefly in the spleen and liver. The upstream metabolic block raises 2,3-diphosphoglycerate, which lowers haemoglobin oxygen affinity and improves tissue oxygen delivery, partly offsetting the anaemia; chronic haemolysis in turn produces jaundice, gallstones and, over time, iron loading. Prognosis is highly variable; many patients live well with intermittent support, while severely affected individuals face transfusion dependence, iron overload and gallstone complications, with splenectomy or targeted therapy able to reduce transfusion needs in selected cases.
