with high phase I antibody titres suggesting chronic infection New or changing murmur, embolic events, or heart failure indicating endocarditis Fever in a patient with a prosthetic valve or vascular graft and compatible exposure Q fever in pregnancy, which carries risks of chronic infection and adverse fetal outcomes Failing to take an occupational or animal-contact history in an atypical pneumonia or unexplained hepatitis Labelling endocarditis as culture-negative without serological testing for Coxiella Stopping therapy too early in chronic disease, risking relapse Not screening or offering prophylaxis considerations to high-risk patients with valvulopathy after exposure Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that survives as a hardy spore-like form in the environment. After inhalation it is taken up by alveolar macrophages and replicates within acidified phagolysosomes, disseminating to liver, lung, and other organs and provoking granulomatous inflammation. It undergoes antigenic phase variation, which underlies the serological distinction between acute and chronic infection. In chronic disease the organism persists at sites such as damaged or prosthetic heart valves and vascular tissue, driving endovascular infection. Acute Q fever usually resolves, often even without treatment, whereas chronic Q fever endocarditis is a serious condition requiring prolonged therapy and carries appreciable morbidity and mortality if not recognised and adequately treated.

Rabies — rabies encephalitis Herpes simplex encephalitis Arboviral encephalitis (e.g., West Nile) Anti-NMDA receptor and other autoimmune encephalitides Postinfectious (immune-mediated) encephalomyelitis (following influenza, measles, mumps, or neural-tissue rabies vaccine) Guillain-Barre syndrome (mimicked by paralytic rabies) Rabies hysteria / somatic symptom disorder (psychological response to fear of rabies) Misdiagnosis as a primary psychiatric disorder Herpes simplex encephalitis Arboviral (e.g., West Nile) encephalitis Postinfectious encephalomyelitis after influenza, measles, or mumps Rabies virus-specific serum neutralizing antibodies (diagnostic in a previously unimmunized patient; may not develop until late and some patients die without them) Rabies virus-specific neutralizing antibodies in CSF (suggest rabies encephalitis regardless of immunization status) RT-PCR for rabies virus RNA (highly sensitive/specific; saliva, skin biopsy, CSF [less sensitive], brain tissue; genetic sequencing can identify the variant/source) Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing for rabies virus antigen (skin biopsy and brain tissue; in skin, antigen detected in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles) Skin biopsy from hairy skin at the nape of the neck CSF examination (typically mild mononuclear pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein) MRI brain (variable, nonspecific brainstem/gray-matter signal abnormalities); CT usually normal; EEG nonspecific Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (especially young females; behavioral changes, autonomic instability, hypoventilation, seizures) Other antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis Guillain-Barre syndrome Rabies hysteria (somatic symptom disorder) with shorter course and eventual recovery Psychiatric disorder Rabies is a rapidly progressive acute CNS infection by rabies virus (a lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae), normally transmitted via the bite of an infected animal; it has encephalitic and paralytic forms that progress to death (p.1650). Worldwide, ~99% of human rabies is transmitted from dogs in countries with endemic canine rabies; endemic canine rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths annually, with most deaths in Asia and Africa and rural populations and children disproportionately affected (p.1650-1651). Incubation period is usually 20-90 days but in rare cases may be as short as a few days or longer than 1 year (p.1651). Earliest specific neurologic symptoms are paresthesias, pain, or pruritus near the exposure site, occurring in 50-80% of patients and strongly suggesting rabies; the wound has usually healed by this point (p.1652). Two acute neurologic forms occur: encephalitic (furious) in ~80% and paralytic (dumb) in ~20% (p.1652). Encephalitic rabies presents as atypical encephalitis with relative preservation of consciousness; episodes of hyperexcitability alternate with periods of complete lucidity that shorten as disease progresses (p.1652). Early brainstem involvement produces the classic hydrophobia (involuntary painful contraction of diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles on swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (same response to a draft of air) (p.1652). Autonomic dysfunction is common and may cause hypersalivation, gooseflesh, cardiac arrhythmia, and priapism; hypersalivation plus pharyngeal dysfunction produces the classic 'foaming at the mouth' (p.1652). Paralytic rabies features early prominent flaccid weakness often beginning in the bitten extremity, progressing to quadriparesis and facial weakness, with sphincter involvement common and sensory involvement usually mild (p.1652). The Negri body (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion in brain neurons, e.g. cerebellar Purkinje cells and hippocampal pyramidal neurons) is the most characteristic pathologic finding, but is NOT seen in all cases (p.1651-1652). Diagnosis should be considered in patients with acute atypical encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis, including those in whom Guillain-Barre syndrome is suspected; absence of an animal-bite history is common in North America due to unrecognized bat exposures (p.1653). Postexposure prophylaxis must be initiated after a recognized exposure and before any symptoms or signs develop; the emphasis for prevention is on PEP (p.1652). Near-100% fatal once symptomatic, so post-exposure prophylaxis is everything - do NOT delay PEP after a recognized exposure. Paresthesias, pain, or pruritus at a healed animal-bite site preceding neurologic illness strongly suggest rabies. Hydrophobia or aerophobia with preserved consciousness (atypical encephalitis) is essentially diagnostic of encephalitic rabies. Absence of a recalled animal bite does NOT exclude rabies - bat exposures are frequently unrecognized; consider PEP when a small child or sleeping adult shared a space with a bat and an unrecognized bite cannot be reliably excluded. Negative antemortem rabies-specific laboratory tests never exclude the diagnosis; repeat testing may be needed. Acute flaccid paralysis resembling Guillain-Barre syndrome may be paralytic rabies - fever, bladder dysfunction, normal sensory exam, and CSF pleocytosis favor rabies. Rabies is often not considered until late in the clinical course in North America even with a typical presentation. Relying on a history of animal bite to make the diagnosis - many cases (especially bat-associated) have no recalled exposure. Assuming absence of hydrophobia excludes rabies - lack of hydrophobia is not unusual. Misdiagnosing paralytic rabies as Guillain-Barre syndrome. Treating negative antemortem rabies-specific tests as exclusionary. Severe CSF pleocytosis (>1000 white cells/uL) is unusual for rabies and should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis. Delaying local wound care while awaiting the 10-day animal observation period - wound care should not be delayed. Administering passive immunization (RIG) more than 7 days after the first vaccine dose, when endogenous antibody production has begun and passive immunization may be counterproductive; rabies vaccine and RIG must never be given at the same site. Minor deviations from current PEP recommendations can lead to prophylaxis failure. Rabies virus, a single-strand negative-sense RNA lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae), is usually inoculated by an animal bite. During most of the incubation period the virus remains at or near the inoculation site; in muscle it binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. It spreads centripetally along peripheral nerves toward the spinal cord or brainstem by retrograde fast axonal transport (up to ~250 mm/d, with ~12-h delays at each synapse). Once in the CNS it disseminates rapidly along neuroanatomic connections; neurons are prominently infected while astrocyte infection is unusual. After CNS infection is established there is centrifugal spread along sensory and autonomic nerves to salivary glands, heart, adrenal glands, and skin; viral replication in salivary gland acinar cells leads to secretion in saliva (the vehicle of animal transmission). There is no well-documented evidence for hematogenous spread. CNS inflammatory changes are mild (mononuclear infiltrate, perivascular cuffing, microglial Babes nodules) with little neuronal death; clinical disease is attributed to neuronal dysfunction rather than death, with oxidative stress from mitochondrial dysfunction implicated. (p.1650-1652) Rabies is an almost uniformly fatal disease but is nearly always preventable after recognized exposures with appropriate postexposure therapy during the early incubation period. Most patients die within several days of symptom onset despite aggressive critical-care support. There is no established treatment and no antiviral has demonstrated efficacy; aggressive supportive care has yielded at least 33 documented survivors (many recently reported from India), but recent treatment failures (>60) have far outnumbered successes. All but 2 of the 33 documented survivors had received one or more doses of rabies vaccine before disease onset, and the unvaccinated survivors had neutralizing antibodies in CSF at presentation. A palliative approach may be appropriate for patients who are not candidates for aggressive management. (p.1654) Clinical stages: incubation period (20-90 days, asymptomatic); prodrome (2-10 days: fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting; paresthesias/pain/pruritus at the wound site); acute neurologic disease - encephalitic form (~80%, 2-7 days: anxiety, agitation, hyperactivity, bizarre behavior, hallucinations, autonomic dysfunction, hydrophobia) or paralytic form (~20%, 2-10 days: flaccid limb paralysis progressing to quadriparesis with facial paralysis); then coma and death (0-14 days; recovery rare). (p.1653)

superimposed infection Extensive bilateral changes extending beyond the radiation field Progression toward respiratory failure despite corticosteroid therapy Assuming symptoms represent infection and delaying appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment Missing tumour progression or pulmonary embolism by anchoring on radiation pneumonitis Tapering corticosteroids too rapidly and provoking a symptom flare Failing to consider concurrent immune-related pneumonitis in patients on checkpoint inhibitors Ionising radiation damages alveolar epithelial and vascular endothelial cells within the treated lung volume, triggering release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This produces an acute to subacute alveolitis with increased capillary permeability, protein-rich exudate, and impaired gas exchange, seen clinically as radiation pneumonitis. If inflammation and fibroblast activation persist, the process evolves into progressive collagen deposition and radiation fibrosis with permanent architectural distortion and volume loss. The severity relates to the dose delivered and the volume of normal lung exposed, modified by patient and treatment factors. Most mild to moderate cases respond well to corticosteroids and resolve, but severe pneumonitis, extensive lung involvement, or progression to fibrosis can cause lasting respiratory impairment and, uncommonly, death.

Acute radiation syndrome — ARS, radiation sickness, acute radiation syndrome Acute gastroenteritis or food poisoning Sepsis of other cause Chemotherapy or other cytotoxic drug toxicity Acute leukaemia or bone marrow failure of other cause Chemical or toxic exposure causing vomiting Serial full blood counts with attention to the rate of lymphocyte decline Estimation of absorbed dose using time to vomiting and available dosimetry Biological dosimetry such as chromosome aberration analysis where available Assessment and monitoring for radioactive contamination Baseline organ function tests and cultures to guide supportive care Acute radiation syndrome follows a high, acute whole-body or large partial-body dose of penetrating ionising radiation, as in criticality accidents or radiological incidents It classically evolves through a prodromal phase (nausea, vomiting, malaise), a latent phase, a manifest illness phase and then either recovery or death The speed of onset of vomiting is a useful early guide to dose severity, with earlier vomiting indicating higher exposure Recognised dose-dependent sub-syndromes affect the bone marrow (haematopoietic), the gastrointestinal tract, and at very high doses the cardiovascular and central nervous systems Serial lymphocyte counts over the first day or two are a practical biological indicator of the dose received and prognosis Management is supportive with infection prevention, blood product and fluid support, and treatment of the failing organ systems, ideally with specialist and haematology input Contamination with radioactive material must be distinguished from irradiation, and decontamination plus staff protection are early priorities Localised high-dose exposure can cause cutaneous radiation injury with erythema, blistering and later necrosis, sometimes appearing after a delay MEDICAL EMERGENCY: high-dose exposure with very early vomiting, rapidly falling lymphocytes, or neurological or cardiovascular signs indicates severe, potentially fatal illness Signs of gastrointestinal syndrome with intractable diarrhoea and bleeding Profound neutropenia with infection or sepsis Confusion, hypotension or seizures suggesting a very high dose Mistaking early prodromal vomiting for simple gastroenteritis Being reassured by the latent phase and underestimating impending marrow failure Confusing external irradiation with radioactive contamination and neglecting decontamination Failing to protect staff and control the scene during care Not obtaining serial lymphocyte counts for dose estimation Ionising radiation deposits energy that damages DNA and cellular structures, with the greatest harm to rapidly dividing tissues. Loss of proliferating stem cells in the bone marrow causes pancytopenia, while injury to the intestinal crypt cells breaks down the mucosal barrier, leading to fluid loss, bleeding and sepsis. Very high doses cause vascular and neurological injury. The clinical course reflects the differing turnover rates of these tissues, giving the characteristic phased illness. Outcome is strongly dose-dependent: lower doses causing mainly marrow suppression may recover with intensive support, whereas gastrointestinal and neurovascular syndromes from very high doses carry a poor to near-uniformly fatal outlook despite treatment.

Radiculopathy — nerve root compression, pinched nerve, cervical radiculopathy, lumbosacral radiculopathy Peripheral entrapment neuropathy or mononeuropathy Brachial or lumbosacral plexopathy Referred pain from shoulder, hip, or joint disease Spinal cord compression or myelopathy Peripheral polyneuropathy Infective or neoplastic root involvement (e.g. epidural abscess, metastasis, meningeal disease) MRI of the relevant spinal region to identify compressive pathology CT or CT myelography when MRI is contraindicated Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to localise the root and exclude mimics Inflammatory markers and imaging for infection or malignancy when red flags are present Plain radiographs for alignment, instability, or degenerative change in selected cases Results from dysfunction of one or more spinal nerve roots, producing pain, sensory change, and weakness in a dermatomal and myotomal distribution Pain characteristically radiates along the affected root and is often aggravated by manoeuvres that raise intraspinal pressure such as coughing or straining The commonest cause is a degenerative disc or spondylotic osteophyte compressing the root within or near the intervertebral foramen Localising signs follow the root: for example L5 causes foot-drop with weak dorsiflexion, while S1 reduces the ankle reflex and plantar flexion Provocative tests such as straight-leg raise (lumbar) or Spurling manoeuvre (cervical) support a root cause Most cases are self-limiting and improve with conservative management, so imaging is guided by red flags and by persistence or progression of deficits MRI is the preferred imaging test to correlate structural compression with the clinical level Electromyography helps confirm the affected root and distinguish radiculopathy from plexopathy or peripheral neuropathy New bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, or bilateral leg symptoms suggesting cauda equina syndrome (surgical emergency) Progressive or severe motor weakness rather than isolated pain Fever, systemic illness, or immunosuppression raising concern for spinal infection History of cancer, unexplained weight loss, or night pain suggesting malignant infiltration Missing cauda equina syndrome by not asking about sphincter and saddle symptoms Over-reliance on incidental imaging findings that do not match the clinical level Attributing radicular pain to a benign disc when infection or malignancy is the true cause Delaying surgical referral in progressive motor weakness Confusing peripheral entrapment or plexopathy with root disease without electrophysiology Radiculopathy reflects mechanical compression, inflammation, or ischaemia of a nerve root, most often where a herniated disc or degenerative spondylotic change narrows the intervertebral foramen or lateral recess. Compression and local inflammatory mediators disrupt axonal conduction and cause both ectopic pain signals and conduction failure, producing radicular pain, dermatomal sensory loss, and myotomal weakness. Chronic compression may lead to axonal loss with denervation. Non-degenerative causes include infection, malignant infiltration, and inflammatory or infiltrative processes affecting the roots. Most degenerative radiculopathies resolve or substantially improve with conservative treatment over weeks to a few months; persistent severe compression, marked motor deficit, or a serious underlying cause predicts a poorer outcome and may require surgery.

Rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism — RDP, DYT12, ATP1A3, Na+/K+-ATPase alpha-3 disorder, DYT-ATP1A3 Young-onset Parkinson disease and other genetic parkinsonism Dopa-responsive dystonia DYT1 and other early-onset dystonias Wilson disease Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder given the abrupt stress-related onset Other ATP1A3-related phenotypes (alternating hemiplegia of childhood, CAPOS syndrome) ATP1A3 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Brain MRI, expected to be unremarkable, to exclude structural causes Dopaminergic (presynaptic) imaging, typically normal, to distinguish degenerative parkinsonism A levodopa trial, which characteristically shows little benefit, helping separate it from dopa-responsive conditions Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP1A3, which encodes the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase Hallmark is abrupt or subacute onset of dystonia and parkinsonism, often over hours to days, frequently triggered by physical or emotional stress, fever, childbirth, or alcohol Symptoms characteristically follow a rostrocaudal gradient, with prominent bulbar and upper-limb involvement (dysarthria, dysphagia, arm dystonia) more than lower limbs Parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia and postural instability accompany the dystonia, but there is typically little or no tremor and a poor response to levodopa After the dramatic initial onset the deficit tends to stabilise, sometimes with a second abrupt worsening, rather than steadily progressing ATP1A3 variants cause a spectrum that also includes alternating hemiplegia of childhood and the CAPOS syndrome, which can overlap Brain imaging and dopaminergic imaging are typically unremarkable, distinguishing it from degenerative parkinsonism Diagnosis rests on the distinctive stress-triggered abrupt onset and is confirmed by ATP1A3 molecular testing; treatment is largely supportive as levodopa is generally ineffective Abrupt bulbar dysfunction with dysphagia and aspiration or airway risk Severe generalised dystonia or status dystonicus following a trigger Rapid neurological deterioration during febrile illness or physiological stress Secondary decompensation with dehydration or immobility during an acute episode Misdiagnosing the stress-triggered abrupt onset as a functional movement disorder Expecting and relying on a levodopa response, which is characteristically poor Overlooking the diagnosis because imaging is normal Not recognising the broader ATP1A3 spectrum and its overlapping phenotypes when counselling families Rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism is caused by dominant variants in ATP1A3, encoding the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase that maintains transmembrane ion gradients essential for repolarisation and neuronal excitability. The variants reduce pump function, and this reserve deficit is thought to become clinically manifest when metabolic demand rises, which is why physiological stressors such as fever, exertion, emotional stress, or childbirth precipitate the abrupt onset. Impaired ion homeostasis within cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits produces combined dystonia and parkinsonism without frank neurodegeneration, accounting for the normal structural and dopaminergic imaging. After the characteristic abrupt onset the disorder tends to plateau rather than progress steadily, though a further stepwise deterioration can occur; disability is often significant, particularly from bulbar and upper-limb involvement, and response to medication is generally limited.

Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — RPGN, crescentic glomerulonephritis, crescentic GN Acute tubular necrosis Acute interstitial nephritis Thrombotic microangiopathy Atheroembolic renal disease Severe acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis Accelerated hypertension with renal injury Urine microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts Kidney biopsy for crescent quantification and immunofluorescence pattern ANCA testing (including antigen-specific assays) and anti-GBM antibody titres Complement levels and other autoimmune serologies including antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies Chest imaging when pulmonary haemorrhage is suspected Quantification of proteinuria and serial renal function monitoring RPGN is a nephrological emergency defined by a rapid loss of renal function over days to weeks, accompanied by a nephritic urine sediment with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts The histological hallmark is crescent formation in a large proportion of glomeruli, reflecting severe glomerular injury and rupture of capillary walls It is classified into three immunopathological groups: anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, immune-complex-mediated disease, and pauci-immune (usually ANCA-associated) disease Coexisting pulmonary haemorrhage with glomerulonephritis (pulmonary-renal syndrome) suggests anti-GBM disease or ANCA-associated vasculitis and demands urgent evaluation Early kidney biopsy is central to diagnosis and to gauging the balance of active (treatable) crescents versus fibrous (irreversible) scarring Serological testing for ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, complement levels, and other markers helps categorise the disease and guide treatment Outcome depends critically on how quickly immunosuppression is started, since delay allows crescents to organise into irreversible fibrosis Management principles centre on prompt aggressive immunosuppression, with plasma exchange added in anti-GBM disease and in selected severe or dialysis-dependent vasculitis cases Pulmonary haemorrhage with haemoptysis and hypoxaemia indicating a pulmonary-renal syndrome Rapidly rising creatinine or oliguria threatening imminent dialysis dependence Severe hypertension or fluid overload Systemic vasculitic features such as mononeuritis, purpura, or ENT involvement Delaying biopsy and treatment while awaiting serology, allowing crescents to become irreversible Missing coexisting pulmonary haemorrhage that changes urgency and management Assuming a negative ANCA excludes vasculitis, since a minority are seronegative Starting heavy immunosuppression in a kidney already dominated by fibrous scarring with little chance of recovery Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis describes a clinical syndrome of accelerating renal failure caused by severe inflammatory glomerular injury, characterised pathologically by extensive crescents. Crescents form when damage to the glomerular capillary wall allows plasma proteins, fibrin, and inflammatory cells to enter Bowman space, where proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages compress the glomerular tuft. Three mechanisms underlie the syndrome: linear deposition of antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM disease), deposition of immune complexes as seen in lupus, post-infectious, and IgA-related disease, and a pauci-immune process typically associated with ANCA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. In all forms, unchecked inflammation rapidly destroys glomeruli and, without timely treatment, progresses to fibrous scarring and end-stage kidney disease. Untreated RPGN progresses to end-stage kidney disease within weeks. With early immunosuppression many patients recover useful renal function, but prognosis worsens sharply with delayed treatment, a high proportion of fibrous crescents, dialysis dependence at presentation, and anti-GBM disease with advanced injury. Relapse is common in ANCA-associated disease and requires ongoing surveillance.

Rat-bite fever — Streptobacillus moniliformis infection, Spirillum minus infection, streptobacillary rat-bite fever, Haverhill fever, sodoku Meningococcaemia and other causes of fever with petechial rash Disseminated gonococcal infection (fever, rash, arthritis) Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses Leptospirosis Secondary syphilis (rash on palms and soles) Reactive or septic arthritis of other cause Infective endocarditis from other organisms Blood cultures (prolonged incubation for the fastidious organism) and culture of joint aspirate Dark-field microscopy of blood, lesion exudate or lymph node aspirate for Spirillum minus Molecular testing (PCR/16S sequencing) for Streptobacillus moniliformis Full blood count and inflammatory markers Echocardiography if endocarditis is suspected Joint imaging or aspiration in arthritis, and lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected Rat-bite fever has two forms: streptobacillary disease (Streptobacillus moniliformis), predominant in the Americas and Europe, and spirillary disease (Spirillum minus, 'sodoku'), predominant in Asia Acquired from the bite or scratch of rats or other rodents, or by handling them; streptobacillary disease may also be foodborne (Haverhill fever) from contaminated milk or water Streptobacillary disease presents abruptly with fever, rigors, myalgia, a maculopapular or petechial rash favouring the extremities including palms and soles, and a migratory polyarthritis Spirillary disease has a longer incubation, relapsing fever, induration or ulceration at the healed bite site with regional lymphadenopathy, and a rash, but arthritis is uncommon Diagnosis of streptobacillary disease relies on culture of blood or joint fluid (fastidious organism) or molecular methods; Spirillum minus cannot be cultured and is identified by dark-field microscopy of lesion or blood material Untreated disease can lead to endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, abscesses and septic arthritis, with appreciable mortality Penicillin-class antibiotics are the treatment of choice, with alternatives for penicillin allergy and escalation for endocarditis Features of endocarditis, myocarditis or a new murmur Meningism or altered consciousness suggesting central nervous system involvement Septic arthritis or deep abscess formation Haemodynamic instability or sepsis Persistent or relapsing fever despite initial treatment Not eliciting a history of rodent exposure, which is key to considering the diagnosis Discarding blood cultures too early before the fastidious organism grows Attempting to culture Spirillum minus, which does not grow on artificial media Mistaking the rash and arthritis for meningococcaemia or disseminated gonococcal infection without pursuing exposure history Under-treating when endovascular or CNS involvement is present The causative bacteria are commensals of the rodent nasopharynx and are introduced into humans through bites, scratches, handling or ingestion of contaminated food and water. Streptobacillus moniliformis, a fastidious pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus, disseminates haematogenously to produce systemic febrile illness, immune-mediated rash and a reactive or septic polyarthritis, and can seed heart valves and other sites. Spirillum minus, a spiral organism, causes relapsing fever with characteristic reactivation of the healed inoculation site and regional lymphadenitis. Both can progress to metastatic infection and endovascular involvement if untreated. With prompt antibiotic therapy the prognosis is excellent, but untreated rat-bite fever carries substantial mortality, largely from endocarditis and other metastatic complications.

Raynaud phenomenon — Raynaud's phenomenon, Raynaud syndrome, primary Raynaud, secondary Raynaud Systemic sclerosis and other connective tissue diseases (secondary Raynaud) Thoracic outlet syndrome and other causes of arterial compression Atherosclerotic or embolic peripheral arterial disease Vibration-induced (hand-arm) vascular injury and occupational causes Drug- or toxin-induced vasospasm Acrocyanosis, chilblains, and cryoglobulinaemia Nailfold capillaroscopy to distinguish primary from secondary disease Antinuclear antibody and, if positive, connective tissue disease-specific antibodies Inflammatory markers and assessment for features of systemic autoimmune disease Vascular assessment for fixed arterial obstruction when ischaemia is asymmetric or severe Targeted investigations for occupational, drug, or haematological causes when suspected Episodic, reversible digital vasospasm provoked by cold or emotional stress, classically producing a triphasic colour change of pallor, then cyanosis, then reactive hyperaemia Primary Raynaud is common, typically begins in young women, is symmetric, and occurs without an underlying disease or tissue damage Secondary Raynaud arises from an underlying condition, most importantly connective tissue disease, and carries a greater risk of digital ischaemia and ulceration Features favouring a secondary cause include older age at onset, asymmetry, digital ulcers or pitting scars, and abnormal nailfold capillaries A positive antinuclear antibody and abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy suggest an evolving connective tissue disease, often systemic sclerosis General measures emphasise cold avoidance, keeping the whole body warm, and smoking cessation Pharmacological therapy, when needed, uses vasodilators (calcium channel blockers first-line, with other agents for refractory or ischaemic disease) Critical digital ischaemia is an emergency requiring urgent assessment and consideration of secondary causes Digital ulceration, gangrene, or critical ischaemia threatening tissue loss Asymmetric or unilateral symptoms suggesting fixed arterial obstruction or embolism New Raynaud phenomenon in an older adult indicating a likely secondary cause Accompanying features of connective tissue disease such as skin tightening, dysphagia, or breathlessness Abnormal nailfold capillaries with positive autoantibodies signalling evolving systemic sclerosis Labelling all Raynaud as benign primary disease without screening for secondary causes Missing evolving systemic sclerosis by not performing nailfold capillaroscopy and autoantibody testing Underestimating critical digital ischaemia as ordinary vasospasm Overlooking drug, occupational, or vascular contributors Neglecting non-pharmacological measures such as whole-body warming and smoking cessation Raynaud phenomenon results from exaggerated vasoconstriction of digital arteries, precapillary arterioles, and cutaneous arteriovenous shunts in response to cold or stress. In primary disease this reflects a functional imbalance of vascular tone with heightened sympathetic and local vascular reactivity and no structural vessel damage. In secondary disease, structural vasculopathy, endothelial dysfunction, and abnormal balance of vasoconstrictors (such as endothelin) and vasodilators (such as nitric oxide), often in the setting of systemic sclerosis or other connective tissue disease, produce fixed narrowing that predisposes to persistent ischaemia, ulceration, and tissue loss. Primary Raynaud phenomenon is benign, usually stable or improving over time, and rarely causes tissue damage. Secondary Raynaud has a more variable outlook determined by the underlying disease and carries a real risk of digital ulceration and loss, particularly in systemic sclerosis.

Rectal prolapse — procidentia, complete rectal prolapse, full-thickness rectal prolapse, rectal procidentia Prolapsing (third- or fourth-degree) haemorrhoids Mucosal-only rectal prolapse Internal rectal intussusception Prolapsing rectal polyp or tumour Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome Anal or perianal skin tags or condylomata Examination with the patient straining to reproduce the prolapse Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy to exclude a lead-point lesion or synchronous colorectal pathology Defecating proctography or dynamic pelvic MRI for internal intussusception and pelvic floor assessment Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound when incontinence is prominent Colonic transit studies where significant constipation coexists Full-thickness (complete) rectal prolapse is protrusion of the entire rectal wall through the anus, with concentric mucosal folds, whereas mucosal prolapse and internal intussusception are distinct, less severe entities It is most common in older women and in children, and is frequently associated with chronic straining, pelvic floor weakness, and a redundant sigmoid colon Typical symptoms are a protruding mass on defecation, mucous discharge, bleeding, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation, with faecal incontinence in a large proportion The diagnosis is often made by asking the patient to strain, ideally on a commode, to reproduce the prolapse; concentric rings distinguish it from the radial folds of prolapsing haemorrhoids Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI can demonstrate internal intussusception and associated pelvic floor abnormalities when clinical findings are equivocal Coexisting incontinence and constipation should be assessed, and colonic evaluation is prudent to exclude a lead point or synchronous pathology Definitive treatment is surgical and is broadly divided into abdominal approaches (rectopexy, with or without resection) and perineal procedures, chosen according to fitness, symptoms, and surgeon preference Irreducible, incarcerated prolapse with congestion, ulceration, or impending strangulation requiring urgent reduction or surgery Ischaemic or gangrenous prolapsed bowel Significant bleeding or a palpable mass suggesting an underlying tumour Acute large prolapse in a frail patient with obstruction Confusing full-thickness prolapse with prolapsing haemorrhoids and offering inappropriate treatment Failing to reproduce the prolapse on examination and therefore missing or underestimating it Not excluding a colorectal neoplasm acting as a lead point before elective repair Ignoring coexisting incontinence or constipation, leading to poor functional results despite anatomical success Delaying intervention in an incarcerated or ischaemic prolapse Full-thickness rectal prolapse is understood as a circumferential intussusception of the rectum that progresses until the bowel protrudes through the anal canal. Contributing factors include a deep rectovaginal or rectovesical pouch, loss of the normal posterior rectal fixation, a redundant mobile rectosigmoid, weak pelvic floor and anal sphincter musculature, and chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from straining. Repeated prolapse stretches and damages the pudendal nerves and sphincter complex, which explains the frequent association with faecal incontinence, while chronic mucosal exposure produces discharge, bleeding, and ulceration. Surgical repair relieves the prolapse in most patients with acceptable recurrence rates that vary by procedure, and continence often improves over time though it may not fully recover if pelvic floor and nerve damage is longstanding. Constipation can persist or occasionally worsen, and outcomes are best when associated functional problems are addressed alongside the anatomical repair.

Recurrent pregnancy loss — RPL, recurrent miscarriage, recurrent spontaneous abortion, habitual abortion Antiphospholipid syndrome Parental balanced chromosomal translocation Uterine anomalies, submucosal fibroids, or intrauterine adhesions Thyroid dysfunction or poorly controlled diabetes Inherited thrombophilia Unexplained recurrent loss Antiphospholipid antibody testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I) with confirmatory repeat testing Parental karyotyping and, where available, cytogenetic analysis of pregnancy tissue Pelvic imaging such as ultrasound or hysteroscopy to assess uterine anatomy Thyroid function tests and glycaemic assessment Selective thrombophilia screening where clinically indicated Recurrent pregnancy loss is generally defined as two or more consecutive clinical pregnancy losses and warrants systematic evaluation of both partners Despite thorough investigation, a large proportion of cases remain unexplained, and even then the prognosis for a future successful pregnancy is often favourable Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important treatable cause and should be specifically excluded, since it is amenable to anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy Sporadic early losses are most often due to embryonic chromosomal abnormalities, whereas recurrent loss prompts a search for maternal and parental factors Parental balanced chromosomal rearrangements are an uncommon but important cause identified by karyotyping both partners Uterine anatomical abnormalities, endocrine disorders such as thyroid disease and poorly controlled diabetes, and inherited thrombophilias should be considered Maternal age and the number of previous losses are the strongest predictors of further loss Management combines treatment of any identified cause, notably antiphospholipid syndrome, with supportive early-pregnancy care and reassurance Positive or suspected antiphospholipid syndrome requiring confirmatory testing and antithrombotic management in future pregnancy Second-trimester loss suggesting cervical insufficiency or a uterine anomaly A parental chromosomal rearrangement necessitating genetic counselling Significant psychological distress and grief requiring support Failing to test for and treat antiphospholipid syndrome, the key reversible cause Not confirming antiphospholipid antibodies with appropriately spaced repeat testing Omitting parental karyotyping when a chromosomal rearrangement is possible Neglecting the substantial psychological impact and need for supportive counselling Recurrent pregnancy loss is a heterogeneous problem in which established pregnancies fail repeatedly. Genetic causes include embryonic aneuploidy (rising sharply with maternal age) and inherited parental balanced translocations that yield unbalanced gametes. Antiphospholipid syndrome, an acquired autoimmune thrombophilia, causes loss through placental thrombosis and impaired trophoblast function driven by antibodies such as lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I. Anatomical uterine factors (congenital malformations, adhesions, submucosal fibroids, and possibly cervical insufficiency in later loss) impair implantation or placentation. Endocrine disturbances, including thyroid dysfunction and poorly controlled diabetes, disrupt the hormonal environment needed to sustain pregnancy. In many couples no cause is found, and losses are attributed to unrecognised embryonic or implantation factors. The outlook for a subsequent successful pregnancy is often good, particularly when a treatable cause such as antiphospholipid syndrome is identified and managed, and even most couples with unexplained recurrent loss eventually achieve a live birth, though the chance declines with maternal age and the number of prior losses.

Refeeding syndrome — refeeding hypophosphataemia, nutritional recovery syndrome Sepsis with metabolic derangement Primary cardiac failure or arrhythmia of other cause Other causes of hypophosphataemia such as renal loss Diabetic ketoacidosis and its treatment-related electrolyte shifts Adrenal insufficiency Baseline and frequent monitoring of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium Glucose, sodium, and fluid balance assessment during refeeding ECG monitoring for arrhythmia in high-risk patients Assessment of nutritional risk before starting feeding Renal function and, where indicated, markers of rhabdomyolysis It is a potentially fatal set of metabolic shifts triggered when nutrition, especially carbohydrate, is reintroduced to a malnourished or starved patient The hallmark biochemical abnormality is a sharp fall in serum phosphate, often with falls in potassium and magnesium and fluid retention Highest-risk groups include those with very low body mass index, prolonged fasting or minimal intake, chronic alcohol use, anorexia nervosa, and severe malnutrition Clinical consequences include cardiac arrhythmia and failure, respiratory muscle weakness, seizures, confusion, and rhabdomyolysis Prevention is key: identify at-risk patients, correct electrolytes, give thiamine before feeding, and start nutrition cautiously with slow escalation Electrolytes must be monitored frequently during early refeeding and replaced as they fall rather than waiting for symptoms It can complicate refeeding in any setting, including treatment of severe childhood malnutrition and hospital nutritional support Rapidly falling phosphate, potassium, or magnesium after feeding begins Cardiac arrhythmia or acute heart failure during refeeding Respiratory muscle weakness or respiratory failure Seizures, confusion, or reduced consciousness attributable to electrolyte shifts or thiamine deficiency Starting full-rate nutrition immediately in a severely malnourished patient Being falsely reassured by normal pre-feeding serum electrolytes despite depleted body stores Omitting thiamine before a carbohydrate load Monitoring electrolytes too infrequently to catch the early post-feeding fall During prolonged starvation the body shifts to fat and protein catabolism, depletes intracellular electrolytes and vitamins despite near-normal serum levels, and reduces insulin secretion. Reintroducing carbohydrate causes a surge of insulin that drives glucose, phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and stimulates synthesis of phosphorylated intermediates, abruptly lowering their serum concentrations. Thiamine, needed for carbohydrate metabolism, is rapidly consumed and can become critically deficient. Insulin also promotes sodium and water retention. The combination of hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, and fluid overload produces the cardiac, neurological, and neuromuscular manifestations. With early identification of at-risk patients, cautious feeding, thiamine, and proactive electrolyte replacement the syndrome is largely preventable and recoverable; unrecognised, it can cause fatal arrhythmia and multi-organ dysfunction.

Refsum disease — Classic Refsum disease, Heredopathia atactica polyneuritiformis, Phytanic acid storage disease, PHYH, PEX7 Other causes of syndromic retinitis pigmentosa such as Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy Charcot-Marie-Tooth and other hereditary neuropathies Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (PEX7-related, with high phytanic acid) Generalised peroxisome biogenesis disorders (Zellweger spectrum) Abetalipoproteinaemia and vitamin E deficiency Plasma phytanic acid level, which is markedly elevated Plasma pristanic acid and very-long-chain fatty acids to distinguish from generalised peroxisomal disorders Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing raised protein with normal cell count Ophthalmological assessment with electroretinography for pigmentary retinopathy Nerve conduction studies and audiometry PHYH and PEX7 molecular genetic testing Classic Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder of phytanic acid alpha-oxidation, usually from PHYH mutations and less often from PEX7 defects The cardinal tetrad is retinitis pigmentosa, chronic peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar ataxia and raised cerebrospinal fluid protein without pleocytosis (albuminocytological dissociation) Night blindness and progressively constricted visual fields from pigmentary retinopathy are often the earliest and most consistent feature Additional clues include anosmia, sensorineural deafness, ichthyosis, skeletal abnormalities such as a shortened fourth toe, and cardiac conduction disturbance Diagnosis rests on a markedly elevated plasma phytanic acid with normal or only mildly elevated very-long-chain fatty acids, distinguishing it from generalised peroxisomal disorders Because phytanic acid is entirely of dietary (exogenous) origin, strict dietary restriction of phytanic acid, avoiding ruminant fats, dairy and certain fish, is the mainstay of treatment Rapid weight loss and fasting mobilise phytanic acid from fat stores and can precipitate acute deterioration, so these are avoided; plasma exchange is used generically for acute severe episodes Cardiac arrhythmia or conduction block, a recognised cause of sudden death Acute worsening of weakness or ataxia after fasting, illness or rapid weight loss Rapidly progressive visual or hearing loss Severe polyneuropathy compromising mobility or respiration Permitting rapid weight loss or fasting, which mobilises stored phytanic acid and can trigger acute deterioration Failing to measure phytanic acid, so a treatable disorder is mistaken for another hereditary neuropathy or retinopathy Overlooking cardiac conduction disease that requires monitoring Not distinguishing classic Refsum disease from generalised peroxisomal disorders by checking very-long-chain fatty acids Classic Refsum disease is a peroxisomal single-enzyme disorder in which deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (encoded by PHYH), or less commonly a defect of the peroxisomal targeting receptor PEX7, blocks the alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid. Phytanic acid is a branched-chain fatty acid derived exclusively from the diet, and because its beta-methyl group prevents beta-oxidation it must first undergo alpha-oxidation. When this pathway fails, phytanic acid accumulates in blood and lipid-rich tissues, where it is incorporated into membranes and disrupts myelin, retinal and neural function, producing the neuropathy, retinopathy and ataxia. Its wholly dietary origin is what makes dietary restriction effective. With early diagnosis and sustained dietary phytanic acid restriction the neuropathy and ataxia can stabilise or partially improve and progression slows, although retinopathy, deafness and anosmia tend to persist; untreated disease progresses and carries a risk of fatal cardiac complications.

Relapsing Fever — Louse-borne relapsing fever, LBRF, Soft tick relapsing fever, STRF, Hard tick relapsing fever, HTRF, Borrelia recurrentis infection, Borrelia miyamotoi disease Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses Ehrlichiosis Anaplasmosis Tick-borne viral infection (including a viral encephalitis transmitted by Ixodes) Babesiosis Lyme disease (especially when STRF presents with Bell's palsy in co-endemic areas) Malaria Typhoid fever Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus Dengue Leptospirosis Trench fever (Bartonella quintana, also louse-transmitted) Influenza (LBRF cough plus fever and myalgia can mimic it) Undifferentiated sepsis (notably with B. miyamotoi disease) Malaria (periodic fever, co-endemic, can coexist as co-infection) Typhoid fever Epidemic louse-borne typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii) and other rickettsioses Leptospirosis Dengue Lyme disease (cross-reactive serology and shared Bell's palsy) Anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, and babesiosis Influenza Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright-stained thin blood smear examined over several oil-immersion fields (sensitive when spirochete density is >= 10^5/mL), ideally drawn at or just before the fever peak Thick blood smear treated with 0.5% acetic acid before staining, or a wet mount of citrated blood examined by phase-contrast/dark-field microscopy for motile spirochetes PCR / nucleic acid amplification testing of blood or CSF (more sensitive than thin smear, especially between febrile episodes; preferred for B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari) Culture of blood or CSF in Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly broth medium (slow, rarely offered) GlpQ-based serologic assay (specific for relapsing-fever Borrelia and negative in Lyme disease species, but often negative when smear/PCR are positive) CSF analysis in any case with signs of meningitis/meningoencephalitis (mononuclear pleocytosis and mildly-to-moderately elevated protein support CNS involvement) Complete blood count (normocytic anemia; variable leukocyte count; thrombocytopenia, sometimes <50,000/uL) C-reactive protein and procalcitonin (elevated) Liver enzymes and coagulation studies (elevated aminotransferases; PT/PTT may be moderately prolonged) ECG and chest radiography where myocarditis is suspected (prolonged QTc, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema) Relapsing fever is caused by several Borrelia spirochete species and occurs in three epidemiologic forms: louse-borne (LBRF, B. recurrentis), soft tick-borne (STRF, multiple Ornithodoros-transmitted species), and hard tick-borne (HTRF, mainly B. miyamotoi and B. lonestari) (p.1444). The hallmark is two or more febrile episodes separated by afebrile intervals of well-being; the relapsing course reflects antigenic variation of the spirochete's surface lipoproteins, with each variant cleared as specific antibody develops (p.1444-1446). In LBRF the first fever is typically unremitting for 3-6 days and is usually followed by a single milder relapse, whereas STRF produces multiple febrile periods of 1-3 days each; interfebrile intervals span roughly 4-14 days (p.1446). A 'crisis' may terminate the first fever episode (rigors, a further rise in temperature, increased pulse and blood pressure for about 15-30 min), followed by drenching sweats, falling temperature, and hypotension lasting several hours (p.1446). Soft ticks (Ornithodoros) feed briefly, often under 30 minutes and usually while the victim sleeps, then leave undetected, so the exposure may go unrecognized (p.1445). Transovarial transmission in soft ticks means infection risk can persist in a dwelling for years, and a case may be diagnosed long after the last reported local case (p.1445-1447). LBRF is acquired not from the louse bite itself but by rubbing crushed louse hemolymph into the bite site or auto-inoculating it into conjunctivae or a wound; humans are the sole reservoir of B. recurrentis (p.1445). Jaundice, epistaxis, and subconjunctival hemorrhages are common in LBRF but typically absent in STRF and HTRF; splenomegaly or splenic tenderness is common in both LBRF and STRF (p.1446). Localizing neurologic signs are more frequent in STRF than in LBRF/HTRF; B. turicatae is notably neurotropic, and unilateral or bilateral Bell's palsy (cranial neuritis) characteristically appears in the second or third febrile episode rather than the first (p.1446). B. miyamotoi disease (HTRF) is less distinctive, often presenting as acute fever with chills, headache, and myalgia 1-2 weeks after a tick bite, and has been mistaken for undifferentiated sepsis; meningoencephalitis occurs particularly in patients with impaired humoral immunity (e.g., after rituximab) (p.1446). Diagnosis of LBRF/STRF rests on direct microscopic detection of spirochetes in blood (Wright, Giemsa, or Giemsa-Wright stain), best collected at or just before the fever peak; spirochete density in B. miyamotoi/B. lonestari may be too low for smear alone (p.1447). Outbreaks of LBRF (often alongside typhus) cluster in settings of famine, war, refugee migration, homelessness, and incarceration, and can appear in migrant camps far from the country of origin (p.1445). Signs of meningitis or meningoencephalitis (warrants CSF analysis and consideration of CNS-directed therapy) Cranial neuritis, especially uni- or bilateral Bell's palsy, or visual impairment from iridocyclitis/panophthalmitis (which may be permanent) Myocarditis: gallop rhythm, prolonged QTc, cardiomegaly, and pulmonary edema Acute respiratory distress syndrome Diffuse bleeding, jaundice, and poor liver function Stupor or coma on admission Pregnancy (high risk of abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death) Concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid Abrupt clinical worsening within 1-3 h of starting antibiotics (Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction with hypotension and falling platelets), which can be fatal without monitoring Whole-cell serologic assays (including ELISA and the C6 peptide ELISA for Lyme disease) can be falsely positive in relapsing fever due to antigenic cross-reactivity among spirochetes (p.1447). Serology cannot distinguish among Borrelia species as the cause, and a positive IgG on a single specimen may reflect past infection rather than the current illness (p.1447). Specific serologic assays (e.g., GlpQ-based) are commonly negative at the very time a blood smear or PCR would be positive (p.1447). Spirochete density in B. miyamotoi or B. lonestari infection may be too low for diagnosis by blood smear alone, so PCR is preferred (p.1447). Smears drawn during afebrile intervals may miss spirochetemia; sampling at/just before the fever peak (or using NAAT) improves yield (p.1447). For B. miyamotoi HTRF, prompt removal of an embedded tick may not prevent infection because transmission occurs soon after feeding begins (p.1447). STRF presenting with Bell's palsy can be misdiagnosed as Lyme disease in co-endemic regions (p.1447). Co-infections (malaria, typhus, typhoid with relapsing fever; B. miyamotoi with Lyme disease) may obscure the diagnosis (p.1447). A Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can be provoked even by antibiotics with suboptimal antiborrelial activity (e.g., ciprofloxacin) given for an unsuspected case (p.1448). Borrelia are slender, double-membrane spirochetes that are extracellular pathogens with a limited biosynthetic genome about one-quarter the size of E. coli; their flagella lie between the two membranes. Tick-borne spirochetes enter in tick saliva at the onset of feeding, and from a small inoculum STRF organisms proliferate in blood (doubling roughly every 6 h) to 10^6-10^7/mL or more, while HTRF organisms grow more slowly to lower densities. Although they lack potent exotoxins and lack lipopolysaccharide endotoxin, abundant Borrelia lipoproteins activate Toll-like receptors, driving an endotoxemia-like proinflammatory response with elevated TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IL-8. Spirochete binding to erythrocytes causes red cell aggregation, splenic/hepatic sequestration, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia; bleeding reflects thrombocytopenia, impaired hepatic clotting-factor production, and small-vessel blockage by aggregates of spirochetes, erythrocytes, and platelets. Serotype-specific IgM appears after a few days and lyses circulating bacteria by bactericidal action or opsonization; release of bacterial products from dying organisms drives a spontaneous 'crisis,' the antibiotic-triggered counterpart of which is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Antigenic variation of surface lipoproteins produces successive bacteremic relapses, each ended by variant-specific antibody. Some species are neurotropic and enter the relatively immune-sheltered brain, and spirochetes can cross the maternal-fetal barrier to cause placental damage, intrauterine growth retardation, and congenital infection (p.1444-1447). Untreated mortality is approximately 10-70% for LBRF and 4-10% for STRF, depending heavily on coexisting conditions (e.g., malnutrition, other infection) and available medical support. With prompt antibiotic treatment, mortality falls to about 2-5% for LBRF and under 2% for STRF; no deaths from HTRF have been reported. Poor-prognosis features include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia. The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in LBRF carries roughly a 5% mortality without adequate monitoring and resuscitation. LBRF or STRF in pregnancy frequently causes abortion, stillbirth, or perinatal death, though congenital malformations have not been reported. Documented posttreatment sequelae and prolonged disability have not been established for any form, and partial immunity to reinfection appears to develop in residents of perennially high-risk areas (p.1448). No formal numeric severity score is given. Clinically, severity is stratified by relapsing-fever type and complications: LBRF carries higher untreated mortality (about 10-70%) than STRF (about 4-10%), while HTRF/B. miyamotoi disease is mildest with no reported deaths. CNS involvement (confirmed or suspected meningitis/meningoencephalitis, supported by CSF mononuclear pleocytosis and elevated protein) marks severe disease warranting parenteral therapy. Features defining a severe/poor-prognosis course include concurrent malaria, typhus, or typhoid; pregnancy; stupor or coma at admission; diffuse bleeding; poor liver function; myocarditis; and bronchopneumonia (p.1446-1448).

Relapsing Polychondritis — RP Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) - distinguished by ANCA positivity and glomerulonephritis, which are not features of RP (p.2920) Autoinflammatory diseases (p.2920) VEXAS syndrome - especially in older males with cytopenia, macrocytosis, and lymphopenia (p.2920) Rheumatoid arthritis - the small-joint pattern can mimic RA but RP arthritis is nonerosive and nondeforming (p.2919) Behcet's syndrome - overlap via MAGIC syndrome (p.2920) Adult-onset asthma - airway chondritis is frequently misattributed to asthma (p.2919) Infectious diseases of the external ear mimicking ear chondritis (p.2920) Infectious diseases mimicking nasal chondritis (p.2920) Infectious airway disease mimicking airway chondritis (p.2920) Audiometry to assess for conductive and sensorineural hearing loss in all suspected patients (p.2920) Dynamic expiratory-phase chest CT to evaluate tracheobronchomalacia (p.2920) Direct laryngoscopy to visualize upper-airway cartilage damage; bronchoscopy of the lower airway can exacerbate disease and must be used with caution (p.2920-2921) Echocardiography to assess valvular heart disease (p.2921) FDG-PET to detect inflammation in large arteries and larger airways (p.2921) Vestibular testing (finger-to-nose, Romberg, nystagmus) when dizziness is present (p.2920) Genetic testing for UBA1 and bone marrow assessment for VEXAS in older males with cytopenias (p.2920) Cartilage biopsy reserved for excluding mimics (infection, malignancy) since findings are nonspecific (p.2918, 2921) Traumatic otohematoma and red ear syndrome (ear) (p.2920) Cutaneous diseases of the external ear (p.2920) Angiocentric centrofacial lymphoma (nasal chondritis) (p.2920) Traumatic airway stenosis and congenital airway disorders (p.2920) Rare systemic disease defined by recurrent inflammation of cartilaginous structures, with the ears, nose, respiratory tract, and joints as hallmark sites; the eyes, inner ear, nervous system, skin, and cardiovascular system may also be involved (p.2917). Ear involvement is the most common manifestation, affecting roughly 80-90% of patients, and typically spares the non-cartilaginous lobule; pain may occur with minimal visible swelling or erythema (p.2918). Triggers for ear pain often include minor trauma (lying on the affected side, wearing glasses) or temperature change; 'cauliflower ear' from cartilage damage occurs only in a small subset after recurrent episodes (p.2918). Nasal disease often presents as a pressure sensation at the bridge of the nose; a saddle-nose deformity may develop but is not universal, and unlike GPA the nasal perforations in RP are usually anterior rather than septal (p.2918-2919). Airway involvement such as subglottic stenosis may be misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma; severe narrowing can cause stridor and is a medical emergency, and chronic damage can lead to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification (p.2919). Costochondral joint inflammation can produce severe bilateral chest pain that is reproducible on palpation and not movement-related, sometimes mimicking acute coronary syndrome and prompting emergency evaluation (p.2919-2920). Recurrent chondritis of the ears and nose in older male patients with severe systemic inflammation and progressive bone marrow failure should prompt evaluation for VEXAS syndrome (somatic UBA1 mutation) (p.2917, 2920). Episcleritis is the most frequent ocular manifestation; scleritis is rare but warrants urgent ophthalmologic evaluation given the risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920). Because disease activity is intermittent and patients may appear non-inflamed during a clinic visit, a longitudinal history and review of patient-provided photographs are essential to diagnosis (p.2918). MAGIC syndrome (mouth and genital ulcers with inflamed cartilage) overlaps with Behcet's syndrome features such as pathergy and GI involvement and may include large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta (p.2920). Some patients carry concurrent rheumatologic diagnoses such as Sjogren's syndrome or systemic lupus erythematosus (p.2917). Neurologic attribution to RP is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection and malignancy must be ruled out first, though encephalitis and meningitis can occur in RP (p.2920). Stridor from severe airway/subglottic narrowing - a medical emergency requiring urgent attention to avoid mortality (p.2919) Features of scleritis - urgent ophthalmology referral due to risk of vision loss, scleromalacia, or globe rupture (p.2920) Cytopenia with macrocytosis and lymphopenia in older males - suggests VEXAS and possible progressive bone marrow failure (p.2917, 2920) Severe costochondral chest pain that can mimic acute coronary syndrome (p.2919-2920) Airway involvement is commonly misdiagnosed as adult-onset asthma, delaying treatment and risking chronic large-airway damage (p.2919) Normal ESR and CRP do not exclude active RP, as acute-phase reactants are not reliably elevated (p.2918) There is no diagnostic blood or tissue biomarker; relying on a single test is a pitfall - diagnosis rests on clinical pattern recognition over time (p.2918, 2920) Cartilage biopsy yields nonspecific findings and can cause morbidity; it should not be expected to confirm RP (p.2918, 2921) Patients may appear non-inflamed at a single visit because disease activity is intermittent (p.2918) Published diagnostic criteria were derived from small cohorts, are largely expert-opinion-based, and have not been formally validated (p.2920) Assuming a saddle nose implies GPA - in RP the deformity usually lacks septal perforation (perforations are anterior) (p.2918-2919) The exact mechanisms remain unclear despite study of genetic, environmental, and immunologic factors. Limited animal-model data suggest autoimmunity against cartilage components may contribute: immunizing certain animals against type II collagen, type IX collagen, or matrilin-1 can reproduce aspects of the human phenotype. However, autoantibodies (including anti-type II collagen) are neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis, and observational data showing B-cell-depleting therapy is not particularly effective argue against a dominant antibody-mediated mechanism. Proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines linked to both innate and adaptive immunity have been associated with RP but are inconsistent. Histologically, acute cartilage shows a mixed myeloid and lymphoid inflammatory infiltrate at the cartilage interface; over time there is lacunar breakdown, loss of chondrocytes, and replacement by fibrosis (p.2918). Outcomes depend heavily on organ involvement. Airway disease can progress to tracheomalacia, bronchomalacia, or tracheal calcification, and severe subglottic narrowing carries mortality risk. Scleritis can lead to vision loss or globe rupture. VEXAS-associated disease involves progressive bone marrow failure and is potentially life-threatening, so prompt recognition is essential. Acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP) are not reliably elevated, so they cannot be used to gauge severity (p.2917-2920). No formally validated severity grading exists. Several diagnostic schemes have been proposed: McAdam's criteria require 3 of 6 features (bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, ocular inflammation, respiratory-tract chondritis, vestibular/cochlear dysfunction); the Damiani-Levine modification accepts 3 clinical features, or 1 feature plus histologic chondritis, or 2 features plus clinical response to treatment; Michet's criteria use 3 major criteria (ear, nose, or respiratory-tract inflammation) and 4 minor criteria (ocular inflammation, hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, seronegative inflammatory arthritis), requiring 2 major or 1 major plus 2 minor. All are limited by lack of precise organ-involvement definitions (p.2920).

Screening for other secondary causes of hypertension when appropriate Renal artery stenosis is a narrowing of one or both renal arteries that can cause secondary hypertension and, when bilateral or affecting a single kidney, progressive ischaemic nephropathy Atherosclerosis accounts for the great majority of cases, typically in older patients with widespread vascular disease, while fibromuscular dysplasia is the main cause in younger women Clues suggesting a renovascular cause include hypertension of abrupt onset or that is severe or resistant, an abdominal bruit, and unexplained kidney oedema without a clear cardiac cause can be a manifestation of severe bilateral stenosis Non-invasive imaging such as duplex ultrasound, CT angiography, or MR angiography is used for diagnosis, with
