fetal red cells and develops anti-D antibodies that can cross the placenta in subsequent pregnancies Sensitising events include delivery, miscarriage, termination, ectopic pregnancy, antepartum bleeding, abdominal trauma, and invasive procedures such as amniocentesis Because sensitisation usually produces no maternal symptoms, prevention and surveillance depend on routine antenatal blood grouping and antibody screening Prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin given after sensitising events and routinely in the third trimester has dramatically reduced the incidence of the disease Once a woman is sensitised, anti-D immunoglobulin is no longer protective, and management focuses on monitoring the fetus for anaemia Fetal anaemia is assessed non-invasively by Doppler measurement of the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity, which rises as anaemia develops Severe fetal anaemia can be treated by intrauterine transfusion, and timing of delivery is balanced against the severity of disease Other red cell antibodies such as anti-Kell and anti-c can also cause severe haemolytic disease, so screening is not limited to the D antigen Rising antibody titres or Doppler velocities indicating progressive fetal anaemia and risk of fetal compromise Ultrasound evidence of hydrops fetalis signalling severe disease A significant sensitising event without timely anti-D prophylaxis Reduced fetal movements or non-reassuring fetal assessment in a sensitised pregnancy Previous pregnancy affected by severe haemolytic disease, predicting earlier and more severe recurrence Omitting anti-D prophylaxis after a sensitising event or assuming it helps an already sensitised woman Focusing only on anti-D and overlooking other antibodies such as anti-Kell Relying on antibody titres alone without fetal Doppler surveillance in established sensitisation Underestimating small but sensitising fetomaternal haemorrhages Failing to quantify large fetomaternal haemorrhage so that the anti-D dose is inadequate When Rh(D)-positive fetal red cells enter the circulation of a Rh(D)-negative mother, her immune system mounts an antibody response, initially IgM and then IgG anti-D. In a later pregnancy with a Rh(D)-positive fetus, maternal IgG crosses the placenta, binds fetal red cells, and leads to their destruction in the fetal reticuloendothelial system. The resulting fetal anaemia drives extramedullary haematopoiesis and, when severe, high-output cardiac failure with generalised oedema known as hydrops fetalis, alongside accumulation of bilirubin that threatens the neonate after birth. With routine antenatal screening, effective anti-D prophylaxis, non-invasive monitoring, and intrauterine transfusion, most affected pregnancies now achieve good outcomes. Prognosis worsens with early-onset severe anaemia and hydrops, and sensitised pregnancies tend to be affected earlier and more severely in successive gestations, making specialist surveillance essential.

Rhabdomyolysis — Creatine kinase (markedly raised) Renal function, K⁺ Urine myoglobin Aggressive fluids; watch hyperkalaemia and AKI Clostridial myositis/myonecrosis — predictably precipitates acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Streptococcal (group A) myositis — also predictably causes acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Viral myositis — influenza, echovirus, coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus infections may be associated with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Legionella infection — reported association with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Urine dipstick for blood with microscopy — dipstick blood-positive but RBC-negative supports myoglobinuria rather than true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343). Urine sediment / microscopy for muddy-brown (pigmented) granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, indicating accompanying acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343). Serum phosphate and calcium — hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany acute muscle injury (Harrison 22e p.359, p.363). Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — may be <1% in early rhabdomyolysis-associated ATN, limiting its discriminatory value (Harrison 22e p.343). Myoglobinuria characteristically produces a positive urine dipstick for blood while urine microscopy shows no (or few) red cells — a key clue distinguishing pigment nephropathy from true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343). In rhabdomyolysis-associated acute tubular necrosis the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) may be paradoxically low (<1%), unlike the classic >1% of established ATN, because the injury is often early/non-oliguric (Harrison 22e p.343). Rhabdomyolysis is listed among the 'don't-miss' metabolic emergencies whose urgency can be underappreciated, alongside malignant hyperthermia and tumour lysis syndrome (Harrison 22e p.102). Heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis is a recognised, albeit rare, cause of sudden death in sickle cell trait carriers during strenuous exercise — a reason to counsel carriers before sports participation (Harrison 22e p.818). Hyperkalaemia from release of intracellular potassium during muscle necrosis — predictable and potentially life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.359). Rising creatinine with pigmented granular casts signalling evolving pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343). Interpreting a dipstick-positive 'haematuria' as bleeding from the urinary tract when no RBCs are seen on microscopy — this pattern reflects myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.343). Relying on a low FENa to exclude ATN: rhabdomyolysis-related ATN can present with FENa <1% (Harrison 22e p.343). Acute rhabdomyolysis typically causes hypocalcaemia, but the recovery phase (with renal failure) can produce rebound hypercalcaemia — calcium should not be over-corrected early (Harrison 22e p.362, p.363). Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases intracellular contents — including myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase — into the circulation. Filtered myoglobin (a heme protein) is nephrotoxic and contributes to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis; the released heme pigment also causes a false-positive dipstick reaction for blood. Concurrent volume sequestration into injured muscle produces a prerenal/hypovolaemic insult that compounds the tubular injury (Harrison 22e p.343). Rhabdomyolysis-associated acute kidney injury is frequently of the milder, non-oliguric ATN type and is potentially reversible with adequate perfusion; the recovery phase may be complicated by rebound hypercalcaemia (Harrison 22e p.343, p.362).

Rheumatic heart disease — RHD, chronic rheumatic valvular disease, post-rheumatic valve disease Degenerative (calcific) valve disease Congenital valve abnormalities such as bicuspid aortic valve Infective endocarditis affecting native valves Non-rheumatic mitral regurgitation from prolapse or ischaemia Other causes of mitral stenosis such as severe annular calcification Cardiomyopathy presenting with functional valve regurgitation Transthoracic and, when needed, transoesophageal echocardiography to define valve morphology and severity 12-lead ECG to detect atrial fibrillation and chamber enlargement Chest radiography for chamber size, pulmonary congestion, and valve calcification Evidence of prior streptococcal infection and inflammatory markers in suspected acute disease Assessment of pulmonary pressures and right heart consequences Blood cultures and endocarditis workup when infection is suspected Rheumatic heart disease is the chronic valvular sequel of acute rheumatic fever, an immune-mediated complication of group A streptococcal infection, and remains a major cause of valve disease in many parts of the world The mitral valve is most often affected, and mitral stenosis is the most characteristic lesion, though mixed mitral and aortic valve involvement is common Patients may be asymptomatic for years before developing exertional breathlessness, fatigue, palpitations from atrial fibrillation, or features of heart failure Although the valve damage itself is non-infective, these valves are prone to infective endocarditis, which must be considered when there is fever or clinical deterioration Mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation and left atrial thrombus, and to systemic embolism including stroke Echocardiography is central to assessing valve morphology, severity, and haemodynamic consequences Prevention relies on prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis and long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever Advanced disease may require balloon valvuloplasty for suitable mitral stenosis, or surgical repair or valve replacement Fever or systemic features suggesting superimposed infective endocarditis on a damaged valve New atrial fibrillation with embolic risk, or acute systemic embolism such as stroke Acute pulmonary oedema or rapidly progressive heart failure Haemoptysis or severe pulmonary hypertension in advanced mitral stenosis Overlooking superimposed infective endocarditis when a patient with known rheumatic valve disease develops fever Failing to maintain long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever Underestimating stroke risk from atrial fibrillation and left atrial thrombus in mitral stenosis Delaying valve intervention until irreversible pulmonary hypertension or ventricular dysfunction has developed Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis in susceptible individuals, in whom molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and host tissue drives a cross-reactive immune response affecting the heart, joints, skin, and nervous system. Recurrent or severe carditis produces chronic inflammation and scarring of the valves, with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening. Over years this yields stenosis, regurgitation, or mixed dysfunction, most commonly of the mitral valve. The resulting pressure and volume loading leads to atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, and eventually heart failure. Prognosis depends on the valves involved, severity, and access to secondary prophylaxis and intervention; secondary prophylaxis and timely valve intervention allow many patients to do well, but advanced disease with pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure carries significant morbidity and mortality.

Rheumatoid arthritis — RF, anti-CCP, ESR/CRP X-rays of hands/feet Septic arthritis can complicate a known RA joint Primary Sjogren's syndrome - polyarthralgia and mild synovitis can mimic RA, and ~50% are RF-positive; distinguished by predominant sicca symptoms, ANA positivity and anti-Ro/SSA in about two-thirds (Harrison 22e p.2847). Spondyloarthropathies (psoriatic arthritis, enteropathy-associated arthritis) - distinguished by sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, and presence of psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease (Harrison 22e p.2847). Polymyalgia rheumatica in elderly patients - can resemble seronegative RA; PMR centres on neck/shoulder and hip girdle, whereas RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet, especially at onset (Harrison 22e p.2847). Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) - features prominent distal-limb pitting edema (unusual in RA) and responds promptly to low-dose prednisone (Harrison 22e p.2847). Paraneoplastic syndromes - may be confused with early RA (Harrison 22e p.2847). Virus-related polyarthritis syndromes - can mimic RA and cause transient RF production, but usually resolve within 2-3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2847). Hepatitis C-related arthropathy - often involves small joints of the hands and is RF-positive in about half of cases, but generally anti-CCP negative (Harrison 22e p.2847). Subacute bacterial endocarditis and chronic hepatitis B/C - chronic infections that can produce a positive RF and confound interpretation (Harrison 22e p.2847). Anti-CCP (ACPA) antibodies - high specificity (~95%) for RA; useful diagnostically and prognostically (Harrison 22e p.2847). Synovial fluid aspiration with cell count and crystal/microbiology analysis - confirms inflammatory arthritis and excludes infection or crystal disease (Harrison 22e p.2847). MRI - greatest sensitivity for synovitis, effusions and early bone/bone-marrow changes; bone marrow edema predicts subsequent erosions (Harrison 22e p.2848). Musculoskeletal ultrasound with power Doppler - detects synovitis, increased joint vascularity and erosions, often more than plain films; portable and radiation-free (Harrison 22e p.2848). ANA and ANCA - may be positive in RA (~30% ANA, occasional p-ANCA), but anti-MPO/anti-PR3 should be negative (Harrison 22e p.2847). High-resolution chest CT - to detect and characterise interstitial lung disease (UIP vs NSIP patterns) when respiratory symptoms arise (Harrison 22e p.2840). Chronic tophaceous gout - can mimic severe RA, and tophi may be mistaken for rheumatoid nodules (Harrison 22e p.2847). Pseudogout (CPPD crystal arthritis) - inflammatory arthritis excluded via synovial fluid crystal analysis (Harrison 22e p.2847). Osteoarthritis - non-inflammatory; DIP involvement and synovial fluid under 2,000 WBC/uL favour OA over RA (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847). Early-morning joint stiffness lasting more than 1 hour that improves with activity is characteristic; the earliest joints involved are typically the small joints of the hands and feet (Harrison 22e p.2839). Wrists, MCP and PIP joints are most often affected; isolated DIP involvement usually reflects coexistent osteoarthritis rather than RA itself (Harrison 22e p.2839). Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark, producing reduced range of motion, weakened grip and trigger fingers, and can lead to tendon rupture (most commonly flexor pollicis longus) (Harrison 22e p.2839-2840). Anti-CCP (ACPA) and RF are useful both diagnostically and as prognostic biomarkers; anti-CCP carries the most value for predicting worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847). Anti-CCP has sensitivity similar to RF but much higher specificity (approaching 95%), so a positive anti-CCP in early inflammatory arthritis helps distinguish RA from other arthritides; testing both RF and anti-CCP adds incremental yield because some patients are positive for only one (Harrison 22e p.2847). About three-quarters of RA patients are seropositive (RF and/or ACPA) and one-quarter are seronegative; seronegative RA is a clinical diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2847). A fever above 38.3C (101F) at any point in the course should raise suspicion of systemic vasculitis or superimposed infection rather than being attributed to RA activity alone (Harrison 22e p.2840). Approximately 30% of RA patients are ANA-positive and some have p-ANCA, but anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are not expected and their presence points to an ANCA-associated vasculitis instead (Harrison 22e p.2847). Synovial fluid in RA is inflammatory (typically 5,000-50,000 WBC/uL, neutrophil-predominant) versus under 2,000 WBC/uL in osteoarthritis; aspiration is most useful to confirm inflammation and to exclude infection or crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2847). Fever above 38.3C (101F) during the course should prompt evaluation for systemic vasculitis or infection rather than being ascribed to RA activity (Harrison 22e p.2840). RA patients have the highest incidence of septic (most often S. aureus) arthritis due to chronically inflamed joints, glucocorticoid therapy and breakdown of nodules/vasculitic ulcers; TNF inhibitors add risk of mycobacterial and other infections (Harrison 22e Chap. 124, p.~). Atlantoaxial (C1-C2) subluxation can cause compressive myelopathy; neurologic signs may evolve slowly with progressive instability (now seen in under 10% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2840). New-onset numbness, tingling or focal weakness (mononeuritis multiplex) suggests systemic rheumatoid vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2841). Two- to fourfold increased risk of lymphoma (most often diffuse large B-cell), greatest with high disease activity or Felty's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2841). The 2010 ACR-EULAR criteria are classification (not diagnostic) criteria intended to identify early patients likely to progress; a positive RF or anti-CCP alone does not establish the diagnosis without supporting clinical features (Harrison 22e p.2847). A negative RF does not exclude RA - IgM RF is found in only ~75% of patients, and RF also occurs in other connective tissue diseases, chronic infections and 1-5% of healthy people (Harrison 22e p.2847). Accelerated growth of subcutaneous nodules can occur in up to 10% of patients on long-term methotrexate and should not automatically be read as worsening disease (Harrison 22e p.2840). Rheumatoid nodules and chronic tophaceous gout tophi can be confused with one another (Harrison 22e p.2840, p.2847). Periarticular osteopenia, the classic earliest x-ray finding, is difficult to appreciate on plain (especially digitised) films, so early radiographs may appear normal (Harrison 22e p.2848). RA is a chronic, systemic, symmetric erosive polyarthritis driven by an interaction of genetic predisposition (e.g., the HLA shared epitope) and environmental triggers such as cigarette smoking. Antigen-presenting cells activate synovial CD4+ T cells (via TCR-MHC class II and CD28-CD80/86 co-stimulation), which differentiate into TH1 and TH17 subsets. These activate B cells that mature into plasma cells producing autoantibodies (RF and anti-CCP/ACPA); immune complexes form within the joint and activate complement, amplifying inflammation. T effector cells stimulate synovial macrophages and fibroblasts to release pro-inflammatory cytokines, with TNF-alpha playing a central role by upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules and driving IL-1, IL-6 and GM-CSF production. TNF-alpha also disrupts the bone balance: it raises DKK-1 (inhibiting Wnt-driven osteoblastic bone formation) and promotes osteoclastogenesis through M-CSF and RANKL signalling, with osteoprotegerin acting as a decoy that limits bone loss. The net result is pannus formation, cartilage and bone erosion, and generalised inflammatory bone loss (Harrison 22e p.2845). Most patients show persistent, waxing-and-waning progressive disease; about 10% (particularly seronegative) remit spontaneously within 6 months, while a minority follow either a relapsing explosive course or an aggressively erosive course (now less common with modern therapy). Early disability is driven mainly by joint inflammation (potentially reversible) and later by cumulative irreversible joint damage. Overall mortality is roughly twice that of the general population, with excess deaths from respiratory illness, cardiovascular disease and infection; median life expectancy is shortened by about 7 years in men and 3 years in women. Worse survival is associated with systemic extraarticular involvement, low functional capacity, low socioeconomic status, low education and chronic prednisone use. Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2848). Seropositivity for RF and especially anti-CCP predicts worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2847). Diagnosis is supported by the 2010 ACR-EULAR classification criteria (for patients with at least one joint of definite clinical synovitis not better explained by another disease), scored 0-10 across four domains - joint involvement (0-5), serology (RF/ACPA, 0-3), acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR, 0-1), and symptom duration (0-1); a score of 6 or more fulfils requirements for definite RA. Disease activity (the main driver of treatment decisions) is tracked with composite indices: ACR 20/50/70 improvement criteria (mainly for trials) and continuous measures including DAS, SDAI, CDAI and RAPID3 used in practice. Functional disability is measured with the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) (Harrison 22e p.2847-2848).

Airway compromise from a large nasopharyngeal mass Rapid change or atypical features raising concern for coexisting malignancy Underestimating the vascularity and provoking significant bleeding during biopsy or removal Incomplete excision that leaves endospores and leads to recurrence Mistaking the mass for a simple polyp and not obtaining histology Overlooking disease at other sites in disseminated cases Rhinosporidiosis is caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, now regarded as an aquatic protistan parasite, which is thought to enter the mucosa through minor trauma after contact with contaminated stagnant water. The organism proliferates within the mucosa, maturing through trophic stages into large sporangia packed with endospores. Rupture of a sporangium releases endospores that seed adjacent tissue, driving formation of highly vascular polypoidal granulomatous masses. The rich vascularity accounts for the marked tendency to bleed, and local dissemination of endospores explains frequent recurrence after incomplete removal. Complete excision with cautery of the base usually gives a good outcome, but recurrence is common owing to local spread of endospores, and disease occasionally disseminates to other mucosal sites; the condition is chronic and can be troublesome to eradicate fully.

also impaired, so plasma phytanic acid can be elevated while very-long-chain fatty acids remain normal Radiographs show punctate epiphyseal calcification (chondrodysplasia punctata) and coronal clefts respiratory infection, seizures, orthopaedic contractures and cataracts, with generic dietary phytanic-acid restriction considered where phytanic acid is raised Recurrent aspiration or respiratory infection compromising ventilation Refractory seizures Severe feeding failure and failure to thrive Rapid clinical deterioration in the neonatal or infantile period Mistaking the punctate calcification for warfarin embryopathy or X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata without biochemical testing Checking only very-long-chain fatty acids, which are normal, and missing the low plasmalogens that establish the diagnosis Overlooking treatable contributors such as elevated phytanic acid in the PEX7 form Failing to arrange early cataract assessment and airway or feeding support Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata is a disorder of peroxisomal metabolism in which the import or activity of a small group of peroxisomal enzymes is disrupted. In the common PEX7 form, the receptor for the peroxisomal targeting signal 2 fails, so enzymes bearing that signal, including those for plasmalogen biosynthesis and phytanic acid alpha-oxidation, are not correctly delivered to the peroxisome. Types 2 and 3 involve direct deficiency of the plasmalogen synthetic enzymes encoded by GNPAT and AGPS. The shared consequence is severely deficient plasmalogen synthesis, which impairs formation of myelin and other specialised membranes; accumulation of phytanic acid contributes in the PEX7 form. These defects underlie the skeletal, ocular and neurological features. The classic form carries a poor prognosis with severe developmental impairment and reduced survival, many affected children not surviving early childhood, although milder variants with residual enzyme function can survive longer with a less severe course.

CSF analysis when meningoencephalitis is suspected Immune thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Kawasaki disease Drug hypersensitivity / drug rash Immune-complex (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis Acute abdomen prompting exploratory laparotomy when abdominal pain and tenderness dominate Rickettsiae are small, obligately intracellular, gram-negative coccobacilli/short bacilli, most spread by a tick, mite, flea, or louse; except for louse-borne typhus, humans are incidental hosts. The agents span seven genera (Rickettsia, Orientia, Ehrlichia, Anaplasma, Neorickettsia, Candidatus Neoehrlichia, and Coxiella). During the first roughly 5 days the acute presentations are largely indistinguishable: fever, headache, and myalgia, with or without nausea, vomiting, and cough; later differentiating features such as rash, eschar, pneumonitis, or meningoencephalitis emerge. Heightened clinical suspicion based on exposure history should prompt empiric antibiotics rather than waiting for confirmation (p.1454). A characteristic laboratory triad supports the diagnosis across many of these infections: thrombocytopenia, a normal or low white-cell count, mildly to moderately elevated hepatic aminotransferases, and hyponatremia (p.1454). Coxiella burnetii, R. prowazekii, and R. typhi can survive long periods outside the host and are highly infectious by inhalation (a single Coxiella organism can cause pneumonia), making several agents bioterrorism concerns (p.1454). In Rocky Mountain spotted fever the rash is progressive and unreliable: present in only about 14% on day 1 and roughly 49% by day 3, appearing on day 6 or later in ~20% and never appearing in about 10% of cases; classic palm/sole involvement tends to come late and may not occur at all (p.1456-1457). Only about 3% of RMSF patients show the classic triad of fever, rash, and tick exposure in the first 3 days, and only ~60% recall a tick bite; serology is typically negative at presentation, so treatment must not await a positive result (p.1457). An eschar (tache noire) at the bite site is a useful clue in several spotted fevers (notably African tick-bite fever ~90%, rickettsialpox, Mediterranean spotted fever ~50%) and in scrub typhus, but is absent in the typhus group (epidemic and murine typhus have no eschar) (p.1455). Ehrlichioses/anaplasmoses (Anaplasmataceae) target hematopoietic cells: E. chaffeensis (HME) and E. muris infect mononuclear phagocytes, while E. ewingii and A. phagocytophilum (HGA) infect neutrophils; intracytoplasmic morulae may be seen on blood smear but only in a minority (about 20% or less in HME, 20-75% in HGA) (p.1460-1462). Of the Rickettsiaceae, in descending case-fatality order the life-threatening species are R. rickettsii (RMSF), R. prowazekii (louse-borne typhus), Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus), R. conorii (MSF), and R. typhi (murine typhus); many spotted-fever species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never been documented to cause a fatal illness (p.1456). Of the rickettsial agents, only C. burnetii is documented to cause chronic illness, and only R. prowazekii causes a recrudescent illness (Brill-Zinsser disease) when latent infection reactivates years after the acute episode (p.1454, p.1459). Q fever is an inhalational zoonosis from sheep, goats, and cattle (organism shed heavily in parturition material); the infectious dose is extremely low (probably 1-10 organisms) and ~60% of infections are asymptomatic seroconversions. Acute disease presents geographically as either pneumonia or hepatitis (p.1462). Scrub typhus shows remarkable antigenic diversity with rapid loss of cross-protective immunity, so reinfection can occur within weeks to months; the classic eschar/rash/lymphadenopathy triad is often absent, with under half of travelers developing an eschar and under 40% a rash (p.1460). Petechial or hemorrhagic rash, especially with palm/sole involvement, in a febrile patient with possible tick exposure (advanced RMSF) Progressive worsening over days after an initial viral-seeming presentation - mandates re-evaluation, as RMSF mimics viral illness early Altered mental status, confusion, lethargy, stupor, ataxia, seizures, or coma (meningoencephalitis) Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, ARDS, or need for mechanical ventilation Hypotension, sepsis/septic-shock-like or toxic-shock-like presentation with multiorgan failure Fulminant RMSF (death within 5 days), seen most often in Black male patients with G6PD deficiency Acute kidney injury / oliguria, jaundice, gastrointestinal bleeding (hematemesis/melena) Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or a DIC-like picture in ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis Immunocompromise (diabetes, cancer, transplant, asplenia, hepatitis C, HIV, immunosuppressive drugs) markedly raises risk of severe/fatal ehrlichiosis and anaplasmosis Culture-negative endocarditis, infected aneurysm, or infected vascular prosthesis suggesting chronic Q fever Waiting for serologic confirmation before treating - serology is usually negative at acute presentation; delay worsens outcome and empiric doxycycline should not be withheld Excluding RMSF because there is no rash or no recalled tick bite (~10% never rash; only ~60% recall a bite) or because palms/soles are not involved Interpreting a single acute-phase positive titer as diagnostic in endemic areas - cross-reactive preexisting antibody (e.g., from the highly prevalent R. amblyommatis or in HGA-endemic regions) can mislead; the recent apparent RMSF surge largely reflects cross-reactive single-titer enzyme immunoassays rather than true R. rickettsii disease Relying on blood PCR for RMSF or typhus - insufficiently sensitive because organisms reside in endothelium, not blood; skin/eschar biopsy is preferable Assuming negative HME serology because E. chaffeensis tests can cross-react when the true agent is another Ehrlichia; separate specific tests are needed for HME vs HGA Overlooking chronic Q fever as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis or unexplained infected aneurysm/vascular prosthesis - median latency from primary infection is ~13 months and can exceed 9 years Mislabeling epidemic typhus as typhoid fever in tropical/resource-limited settings Attributing prolonged post-Q-fever fatigue to active infection and prescribing antibiotics - a randomized trial showed long-term doxycycline did not reduce fatigue versus placebo The spotted fever and typhus group organisms (Rickettsia and Orientia) infect vascular endothelial cells and disseminate lymphohematogenously, producing widespread small-vessel infection. The fundamental injury is increased vascular permeability rather than occlusive thrombosis or ischemic necrosis; resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia drive the clinical picture. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in roughly a third to half of RMSF cases, but overt DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; thrombin generation and fibrinolysis appear to be homeostatic responses to nonocclusive hemostatic plugs at sites of endothelial injury. Hyponatremia reflects appropriate ADH secretion in response to hypovolemia. Pathogenic rickettsiae have small, reductively evolved genomes lacking biosynthetic genes for intracellularly available molecules. Ehrlichia and Anaplasma instead parasitize vacuoles of hematopoietic cells; vasculitis and granulomas are not features of HME or HGA. Coxiella burnetii is genetically distinct from the Rickettsiaceae, survives harsh environments, escapes macrophage killing by inhibiting the final step of phagosome maturation, and adapts to the acidic phagolysosome. Outcome depends heavily on early recognition and prompt empiric therapy. RMSF mortality was 20-25% before antibiotics and is roughly 3-5% now, principally driven by diagnostic/treatment delay; confirmed-case fatality is higher (~9-10% in regions where R. rickettsii is the sole spotted-fever species), is highest in children under 10 and adults over 70, and approaches 50% in parts of Mexico and Brazil for unknown reasons. Untreated fatal RMSF typically dies 8-15 days after onset. Survivors usually recover fully, but severe disease can leave permanent neurologic deficits or gangrene requiring amputation. Mediterranean spotted fever has a severe form (~50% mortality) in patients with diabetes, alcoholism, or heart failure. Epidemic (louse-borne) typhus is fatal in 7-40% of untreated cases. Untreated classic scrub typhus has ~6% case-fatality. Acute Q fever case-fatality is ~1-2%; chronic Q fever carries high mortality (~25% in proven Dutch-outbreak cases, highest at 33% when both endocarditis and vascular infection are present). Q fever fatigue syndrome follows up to 20% of acute cases. Many SFG species (e.g., R. parkeri, R. africae, R. akari, R. felis) have never caused documented fatal illness, and African tick-bite fever is typically mild. No single unified rickettsial severity score; severity is judged by organ-system involvement and progression. Across the group, escalating clinical lines after nonspecific fever are: (1) macular/maculopapular rash; (2) eschar at the bite site; (3) vesicular rash; (4) pneumonitis with radiographic opacities/rales; (5) meningoencephalitis; and (6) progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (sepsis/toxic-shock-like). For Q fever, the Dutch consensus group classifies chronic disease as proven, probable, or possible based on PCR positivity in blood/tissue or phase I IgG IFA >=1:800/1:1024 combined with endocarditis (modified Duke criteria), proven large-vessel/prosthetic infection on imaging, or compatible clinical and histologic findings.

Robinow syndrome — fetal face syndrome, ROR2-related recessive Robinow syndrome, WNT5A/DVL-related dominant Robinow syndrome Aarskog-Scott syndrome (FGD1, facial and genital features) Omodysplasia (mesomelic limb shortening) Other mesomelic dysplasias (e.g. Langer, Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, SHOX-related) Craniofrontonasal syndrome (EFNB1, hypertelorism) Fetal alcohol spectrum (facial overlap) Disorders of sex development for the genital hypoplasia Molecular testing of ROR2 and of dominant genes (WNT5A, DVL1, DVL3) to define the form Skeletal survey to document mesomelic shortening, brachydactyly and vertebral/rib anomalies Spinal radiographs and follow-up for segmentation defects and scoliosis in the recessive form Renal and cardiac assessment where associated anomalies are suspected Endocrine and genital assessment to characterise hypoplasia and guide management Dental and orthodontic evaluation for crowding and gum overgrowth A skeletal dysplasia characterised by a distinctive 'fetal face' with frontal bossing, hypertelorism, a short upturned nose and a broad forehead The autosomal recessive form is caused by ROR2 mutations and is generally more severe; dominant forms arise from WNT5A, DVL1, DVL3 and related genes in the non-canonical WNT pathway Mesomelic limb shortening (short forearms and lower legs) is typical, with brachydactyly and short stature Genital hypoplasia is characteristic, with a micropenis in males and clitoral/labial hypoplasia in females, and may cause diagnostic confusion The recessive ROR2 form frequently includes vertebral segmentation defects with scoliosis and rib anomalies Dental crowding, gum hypertrophy and a broad mouth are common oral features Some dominant forms (notably certain DVL and WNT5A variants) are associated with osteosclerosis Diagnosis is clinical and radiographic, confirmed by molecular testing to distinguish the dominant and recessive forms for counselling Progressive scoliosis from vertebral segmentation defects in recessive disease Congenital cardiac or renal anomalies causing functional compromise Marked genital hypoplasia requiring endocrine evaluation and psychosocial support Airway or feeding difficulty in severely affected neonates Misattributing genital hypoplasia to a primary disorder of sex development and missing the syndromic diagnosis Not distinguishing dominant from recessive forms, leading to incorrect recurrence-risk counselling Overlooking vertebral segmentation anomalies and progressive scoliosis on follow-up Confusing the facial features with a fetal alcohol phenotype Robinow syndrome is a disorder of the non-canonical WNT/planar cell polarity signalling pathway, which governs skeletal patterning, limb outgrowth and craniofacial and genital development. The recessive form is caused by loss of function of ROR2, a receptor tyrosine kinase that acts as a co-receptor for WNT5A; the dominant forms result from variants in WNT5A itself or in downstream DVL genes. Disruption of this pathway impairs the coordinated growth and orientation of skeletal elements, producing the mesomelic limb shortening, vertebral anomalies, characteristic facial appearance and genital hypoplasia. Intelligence is usually normal and life expectancy is generally good, particularly in the dominant forms; the recessive ROR2 form is more severe, with skeletal and vertebral complications, but with orthopaedic, endocrine and multidisciplinary care most individuals do well.

Rosacea — acne rosacea, rhinophyma (severe phymatous form) Acne vulgaris (presence of comedones) Perioral dermatitis Seborrhoeic dermatitis Systemic lupus erythematosus (malar rash) Flushing from carcinoid syndrome or menopause Contact or photodermatitis of the face Clinical diagnosis based on morphology and distribution Ophthalmological assessment when ocular involvement is suspected Skin biopsy only in atypical cases to exclude lupus or other diagnoses Investigation for systemic causes of flushing when the history is atypical Consideration of Demodex assessment in treatment-resistant papulopustular disease A chronic facial condition centred on the convexities of the central face (cheeks, nose, chin, forehead), typically in fair-skinned middle-aged adults Cardinal features are persistent central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, and inflammatory papules and pustules The absence of comedones is a key point distinguishing rosacea from acne vulgaris Recognise clinical subtypes: erythematotelangiectatic (flushing and redness), papulopustular, phymatous (skin thickening such as rhinophyma), and ocular Ocular rosacea (grittiness, dryness, blepharitis, conjunctival injection) is common, frequently underdiagnosed, and can threaten vision if untreated Trigger avoidance is central: sun exposure, heat, hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol, and emotional stress commonly provoke flares Treatment is tailored to subtype, using topical anti-inflammatory agents, oral tetracycline-class antibacterials for their anti-inflammatory effect in papulopustular disease, and laser or light therapy for telangiectasia and erythema Daily photoprotection and gentle skin care are important adjuncts for all patients Ocular rosacea with pain, photophobia, or visual disturbance suggesting keratitis Rapidly progressive facial swelling or induration requiring reassessment Features suggesting lupus or systemic disease rather than rosacea Disfiguring phymatous change causing functional or psychological impact Misdiagnosing rosacea as acne and prescribing inappropriate comedolytic-only regimens Overlooking ocular rosacea and risking corneal complications Applying potent topical corticosteroids, which can trigger or worsen a rosacea-like eruption Neglecting trigger identification and photoprotection, leading to persistent flares Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory disorder of uncertain cause with several contributing mechanisms. Dysregulation of the innate immune system with abnormal cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide processing promotes inflammation and vascular changes. Neurovascular dysregulation drives flushing and persistent erythema, while an increased density of Demodex mites and altered cutaneous microbiome may stimulate the inflammatory response. Ultraviolet radiation, chronic inflammation, and vascular and lymphatic changes contribute to telangiectasia and, over time, the fibrous and sebaceous overgrowth of phymatous disease. Genetic predisposition and environmental triggers modulate expression. Rosacea is a chronic relapsing condition that is controllable but not curable; symptoms often persist for years with fluctuating severity, and phymatous changes, once established, tend to be permanent without procedural treatment.

for limited disease to corticosteroids, surgery, or systemic therapy for extensive or organ-threatening involvement Central nervous system or spinal involvement causing neurological deficit Airway or orbital compromise from bulky masses Vital-organ infiltration (kidney, liver, lower respiratory tract) associated with worse outcomes Features suggesting concurrent lymphoma or autoimmune disease Misinterpreting the histiocytic infiltrate as lymphoma and missing emperipolesis Failing to use S100 and CD1a staining to distinguish it from Langerhans cell histiocytosis Overtreating limited disease that would resolve spontaneously Underestimating the extent of extranodal or central nervous system involvement Not looking for associated autoimmune or lymphoproliferative conditions Rosai-Dorfman disease is a histiocytic proliferative disorder characterised by accumulation of large, activated histiocytes derived from the monocyte-macrophage lineage within lymph node sinuses and extranodal tissues. The hallmark is emperipolesis, the presence of intact inflammatory cells within histiocyte cytoplasm. Although historically considered reactive and possibly infection- or immune-triggered, a subset harbours clonal MAPK pathway mutations, placing it within the histiocytic neoplasm spectrum. The infiltrating S100-positive histiocytes expand lymph nodes and infiltrate extranodal sites, producing the clinical manifestations. Most patients, particularly those with isolated nodal disease, follow a benign self-limiting or relapsing-remitting course, but extensive extranodal disease, central nervous system involvement, or associated immune dysregulation confers a more guarded prognosis.

Roseola infantum — sixth disease, exanthem subitum, HHV-6 infection, three-day fever Measles Rubella Scarlet fever Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) Drug hypersensitivity eruption Enteroviral exanthem Measles Rubella Enteroviral rash illness Early meningococcal or other bacterial infection presenting with high fever Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient in a well child with the typical fever-then-rash sequence HHV-6 PCR or serology reserved for atypical, severe, or immunocompromised presentations Basic bloods to exclude bacterial sepsis when the febrile child appears unwell Neuroimaging and CSF studies if encephalitis or complicated seizures are suspected Classically affects infants and toddlers between roughly 6 months and 2 years, caused mainly by human herpesvirus 6 (and less often HHV-7) The hallmark pattern is several days of high fever in a child who otherwise looks relatively well, followed by defervescence and then the eruption of a rash The rash typically appears as the fever breaks: small rose-pink macules or maculopapules starting on the trunk and spreading to the neck and limbs, usually non-pruritic and fading within days Febrile seizures are a recognised complication because of the height of the fever, and can be the presenting concern Diagnosis is generally clinical; the temporal sequence of high fever resolving just before the rash is the key clue Because most cases are self-limiting, management centres on supportive care, hydration, and antipyresis rather than antiviral therapy in the immunocompetent child HHV-6 establishes lifelong latency after primary infection and can reactivate, which is clinically important in immunocompromised and transplant patients Toxic or lethargic appearance suggesting bacterial sepsis or meningitis rather than benign roseola Prolonged, complex, or focal seizures rather than a simple brief febrile convulsion Signs of encephalitis such as altered consciousness or focal neurological deficit Severe or unusual disease in an immunocompromised or transplant patient Attributing the rash to an antibiotic or antipyretic given during the febrile phase and mislabelling the child as drug-allergic Overlooking bacterial sepsis in a highly febrile infant by assuming roseola too early Failing to reassure parents that the rash appearing as fever resolves signals recovery, not deterioration Not considering HHV-6 reactivation in an unwell immunocompromised patient Primary infection with human herpesvirus 6B (and sometimes HHV-7) is acquired in early childhood, often via the saliva of asymptomatic carriers. The virus infects lymphocytes and other cells, producing a viraemia that drives the high fever. As host immunity controls the viraemia the temperature falls and the characteristic exanthem appears. Like other herpesviruses, HHV-6 then persists in a latent state and can reactivate later, particularly under immunosuppression, where it is linked to encephalitis, marrow suppression, and graft complications. In healthy infants the illness is self-limiting with full recovery and no long-term sequelae; complications such as encephalitis are rare and are seen chiefly in immunocompromised hosts.

Rotator cuff tear — rotator cuff rupture, supraspinatus tear, cuff tear, rotator cuff injury Subacromial impingement or bursitis without tear Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) Calcific tendinitis Glenohumeral or acromioclavicular osteoarthritis Cervical radiculopathy Axillary or suprascapular nerve injury Biceps tendon pathology Ultrasound of the shoulder to assess cuff integrity dynamically MRI to characterise tear size, retraction, and muscle quality (fatty atrophy) Plain radiographs to assess acromial morphology, humeral head position, and arthropathy Clinical cuff-specific strength tests (e.g. empty-can, external rotation, lift-off, drop-arm) MR arthrography where partial or labral lesions are suspected Presents with shoulder pain, weakness on elevation and abduction, and difficulty with overhead activities; supraspinatus is the most commonly torn tendon Tears may be degenerative (attritional, in older patients) or traumatic (e.g. after a fall or dislocation, especially in those over 40) A painful mid-range arc of abduction and positive cuff tests (e.g. weakness of resisted abduction or external rotation, drop-arm sign) support the diagnosis Ultrasound and MRI are the key investigations, distinguishing partial from full-thickness tears and assessing tendon retraction and muscle atrophy Many degenerative partial or small full-thickness tears are managed conservatively with physiotherapy, activity modification, and analgesia Acute traumatic tears in younger, active patients and large tears with functional loss are generally considered for surgical repair, ideally before significant retraction and fatty muscle degeneration Chronic massive, irreparable tears may lead to cuff-tear arthropathy, sometimes treated with reverse shoulder arthroplasty New weakness after shoulder dislocation in an older patient should prompt assessment for an acute cuff tear, not just presumed axillary nerve injury Acute loss of active shoulder movement after trauma or dislocation suggesting an acute repairable tear Weakness that could reflect nerve injury (axillary or suprascapular) requiring differentiation from cuff rupture Signs of infection in a hot, swollen, systemically unwell shoulder Progressive functional loss and pseudoparalysis indicating a large or massive tear Assuming all post-dislocation weakness in older patients is axillary nerve palsy and missing an acute cuff tear Delaying repair of an acute traumatic tear until retraction and fatty atrophy make it irreparable Relying on radiographs alone, which do not show the tendon Confusing frozen shoulder with a cuff tear by not distinguishing passive from active range restriction The rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis) stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid and enables elevation and rotation. Tendon integrity is compromised by age-related degeneration, hypovascularity near the supraspinatus insertion, and mechanical impingement beneath the coracoacromial arch, making tears increasingly common with age. Repetitive overhead loading and acute trauma superimpose on this degeneration. Once a tear occurs, the tendon tends to retract and the corresponding muscle undergoes atrophy and fatty infiltration over time, reducing repairability and allowing superior migration of the humeral head, which can eventually produce cuff-tear arthropathy. Many small and degenerative tears remain functionally acceptable with rehabilitation, but larger or acute traumatic tears repaired promptly generally do better than chronic retracted tears with fatty muscle degeneration; untreated massive tears can progress to cuff-tear arthropathy with persistent weakness and pain.

Rotavirus Gastroenteritis — rotavirus diarrhoea, rotavirus infection, viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus) Norovirus and other viral gastroenteritis Bacterial enteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, enterotoxigenic E. coli) Parasitic infection (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea Systemic infection presenting with diarrhoea (e.g. urinary tract infection, sepsis) Surgical abdomen (intussusception) when vomiting and lethargy predominate Stool rotavirus antigen enzyme immunoassay or PCR when confirmation is needed Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine in moderate to severe dehydration Capillary or venous blood gas to assess acid-base status in severe illness Blood glucose in a lethargic or severely dehydrated child Stool culture if bacterial infection is suspected (blood, mucus, high fever) A leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants and young children, especially between about 3 and 24 months of age. Typically presents with abrupt onset of vomiting followed by profuse watery, non-bloody stools, often with fever. Spread is faecal-oral; the virus is highly contagious and stable in the environment, so outbreaks in daycare and hospital settings are common. Assessment of hydration status guides management far more than laboratory testing, which is rarely needed for diagnosis. Oral rehydration therapy is the cornerstone of treatment for mild to moderate dehydration; intravenous fluids are reserved for severe dehydration or failed oral therapy. Early refeeding with an age-appropriate diet is encouraged once rehydration is achieved; prolonged fasting and dilute feeds are discouraged. Antibiotics and antimotility agents have no role and may be harmful; routine antiemetics are generally avoided in young children. Live oral rotavirus vaccines given in infancy substantially reduce severe disease and hospitalisation. Antigen immunoassay or PCR on stool can confirm the pathogen when confirmation is required for epidemiologic or infection-control purposes. Signs of severe dehydration or hypovolaemic shock Persistent vomiting preventing oral rehydration Altered consciousness, lethargy, or seizures Bloody stools or high fever suggesting alternative or complicating diagnosis Abdominal distension or severe pain raising concern for intussusception Underestimating fluid deficit and failing to reassess hydration during treatment Using dilute or lactose-heavy feeds and prolonged fasting instead of prompt refeeding Prescribing antibiotics or antimotility drugs that offer no benefit Missing intussusception in a child with vomiting, lethargy, and abdominal signs Rotavirus infects the mature enterocytes at the tips of the small intestinal villi, causing villous blunting and loss of absorptive surface. This produces malabsorption of nutrients and water with an osmotic diarrhoea, while the viral nonstructural protein NSP4 acts as an enterotoxin that triggers secretory diarrhoea and disrupts calcium homeostasis. The combination of impaired absorption, secretion, and reduced disaccharidase (including lactase) activity leads to voluminous watery stool and rapid fluid and electrolyte losses. Most children recover fully within about a week with appropriate rehydration; mortality is low where fluid therapy is accessible but remains significant in resource-limited settings due to severe dehydration.

Deficient RECQL4 function leads to genomic instability, which underlies the predisposition to osteosarcoma and other tumours and contributes to the poikilodermatous skin changes, growth failure and skeletal defects. A proportion of clinically diagnosed cases (type 1) lack an identified RECQL4 variant and are associated more strongly with juvenile cataract, indicating genetic heterogeneity within the phenotype. For individuals without malignancy, life expectancy may be near normal, but the elevated risk of osteosarcoma, most pronounced in RECQL4-associated disease and typically in childhood or adolescence, is the main determinant of outcome. Later skin cancers and the cumulative effects of photosensitivity add to long-term morbidity.

A portion of conjugated bilirubin normally effluxes from hepatocytes back into the sinusoids and is then re-taken up by these transporters. In Rotor syndrome, combined deficiency of both transporters abolishes this reuptake, so conjugated bilirubin accumulates in the circulation, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Because the canalicular excretory machinery and hepatocyte architecture are intact, the liver appears normal without the pigment seen in Dubin-Johnson syndrome. Rotor syndrome is benign with a normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease; recognition mainly serves to avoid unnecessary investigation and to anticipate altered disposition of OATP-dependent drugs.

Rubella (German Measles) — German measles, three-day measles, Rubivirus infection, Congenital rubella syndrome, CRS Measles (rubeola) Scarlet fever Roseola (exanthem subitum) Toxoplasmosis Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum / parvovirus B19) Zika virus infection Other febrile illnesses with suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy Measles (rubeola) Roseola Fifth disease (parvovirus B19) Toxoplasmosis Zika virus infection For CRS: other intrauterine (TORCH) infections such as cytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis producing nonspecific neonatal findings Serology: rubella IgM in an acute-phase serum specimen, or a fourfold rise in IgG titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; IgM-capture ELISA is regarded as most accurate (Harrison 22e p.1644). Timing of paired sera: acute specimen within 7-10 days of illness onset, convalescent specimen about 14-21 days later; repeat IgM testing if an early specimen (before day 5 after rash) is negative (Harrison 22e p.1644). IgG avidity testing to distinguish primary infection (low-avidity antibodies, recent infection) from reinfection (mature high-avidity IgG indicating infection at least ~2 months earlier); especially useful in pregnant women to assess CRS risk (Harrison 22e p.1644). RT-PCR for viral RNA detection (preferred from nasopharyngeal swab; throat swab or urine acceptable), collected as soon as possible after onset, ideally 1-3 days and no later than 7 days; virus isolation by culture also possible (Harrison 22e p.1644). CRS confirmation: serum IgM (normally present up to ~6 months, sometimes up to 1 year; may be absent at birth and require retesting at 1 month), and persistence of rubella IgG beyond the expected decline of passively transferred maternal antibody (titer not declining at the expected twofold-per-month rate); RT-PCR/culture of nasopharyngeal, throat, or urine specimens, most likely positive within the first 6 months (Harrison 22e p.1644). Routine prenatal screening for rubella IgG; a positive IgG indicates immunity (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645). Scarlet fever (toxin-mediated streptococcal exanthem clinically similar to rubella) Other drug or hypersensitivity maculopapular eruptions Caused by rubella virus, an enveloped single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus of the Matonaviridae family (genus Rubivirus); only a single antigenic type exists and humans are the only known reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1643). Acquired rubella typically presents as a mild generalized maculopapular rash lasting up to about 3 days, but as many as roughly half of infections are subclinical or occur without a rash (Harrison 22e p.1643). Incubation period averages 14 days (range about 12-23 days); in older children and adults a 1- to 5-day prodrome of low-grade fever, malaise, and upper respiratory symptoms may precede the rash, whereas in young children rash is often the first sign (Harrison 22e p.1643). Occipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy is characteristic and may appear during the second week after exposure (Harrison 22e p.1643). Arthralgia and arthritis are common complications in infected adults, particularly women; thrombocytopenia and encephalitis are less common (Harrison 22e p.1643). Persons with acquired rubella may shed virus from about 7 days before rash onset to roughly 5-7 days afterward, and both clinical and subclinical infections are considered contagious (Harrison 22e p.1643). The most serious consequence is congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), which results from maternal infection during pregnancy, especially the first trimester; the classic triad is cataracts, hearing impairment, and heart defects (Harrison 22e p.1644). Hearing impairment is the single most common defect of CRS, and the classic complete triad is seen in only about 10% of CRS infants (Harrison 22e p.1644). Maternal infection within the first 10 weeks of gestation carries roughly a 90% risk of delivering an infant with CRS; risk declines later in pregnancy and fetal defects are rare after about 16 weeks, though sensorineural hearing deficit can still occur with infection up to about 20 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645). Infants with CRS can shed large quantities of virus (notably from throat secretions and urine) for up to 1 year, so only rubella-immune individuals should care for them (Harrison 22e p.1643). Reinfection with rubella virus, although uncommon, is possible and may produce detectable IgM antibodies (Harrison 22e p.1644). Rubella is no longer endemic in the United States (endemic transmission interrupted by 2001), but importations and sporadic cases continue, so vigilance is warranted in adults migrating from or returning from areas without rubella control (Harrison 22e p.1643). Maternal rubella infection during the first trimester (highest risk of CRS, up to ~90% within the first 10 weeks of gestation) (Harrison 22e p.1644). A susceptible pregnant woman with exposure to or symptoms of a rubella-like illness, requiring IgM testing and low-avidity IgG confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1645). A neonate with cataracts, hearing impairment, congenital heart defects, or 'blueberry muffin' purpura suggestive of CRS (Harrison 22e p.1644). Encephalitis or significant thrombocytopenia complicating acquired rubella (Harrison 22e p.1643). An index case of CRS in a nosocomial or congregate setting, given prolonged viral shedding and outbreak potential (Harrison 22e p.1643). Relying on clinical diagnosis is unreliable because rubella mimics many rash illnesses, has varied presentations, and is frequently subclinical or mild; laboratory confirmation is the only reliable way to confirm acute disease (Harrison 22e p.1644). A negative rubella IgM drawn before day 5 after rash onset does not exclude infection and should be repeated (Harrison 22e p.1644). Rubella IgM testing is not recommended in pregnant women without a history of illness or contact with a rubella-like illness because of the risk of false-positive results (Harrison 22e p.1645). An infant with suspected CRS who tests IgM-negative shortly after birth should be retested at 1 month, since IgM may not yet be detectable (Harrison 22e p.1644). Worldwide rubella case counts are likely underestimated because disease is often mild, care may not be sought, cases may go unrecognized or unreported, and some countries detect cases only through measles surveillance (Harrison 22e p.1643). Live attenuated rubella-containing vaccine should not be given to women known to be pregnant, and pregnancy should be avoided for 28 days after vaccination; however, inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy is not ordinarily a reason to consider termination, as no CRS occurred among ~3000 such pregnancies followed (Harrison 22e p.1645). Rubella virus spreads person to person via respiratory droplets. After primary implantation and replication in the nasopharynx it spreads to regional lymph nodes, followed by viremia. In pregnant women the viremia frequently infects the placenta; placental replication can then seed fetal organs. In the infected fetus nearly all organs may be involved, and the hallmark is a chronic infection that persists throughout intrauterine development and for up to 1 year after birth. Tissue effects of rubella virus range from no obvious impact to cell destruction. The pathology of postnatal (acquired) rubella is limited because the disease is mild, whereas the pathology of CRS is well defined even though its pathogenesis remains poorly delineated (Harrison 22e p.1643). Acquired rubella is generally a mild, self-limited illness; the rash usually resolves within about 3 days, and serious complications such as encephalitis and thrombocytopenia are uncommon. The major prognostic concern is congenital infection: maternal infection in early pregnancy may lead to miscarriage, fetal death, premature delivery, or live birth with severe and often permanent defects (eyes, ears, heart, and CNS). Permanent CRS manifestations include deafness, congenital heart defects, cataracts and other eye defects, microcephaly, and neurodevelopmental sequelae, whereas manifestations such as hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura, and adenopathy are transient. Immunity following infection or a single dose of rubella-containing vaccine (seroconversion in >=95%) is considered long-term and probably lifelong (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645). No formal severity grading system is described. Clinically, infection is categorized by host and timing: subclinical/mild acquired rubella; symptomatic acquired rubella (rash with possible arthralgia/arthritis, rarely thrombocytopenia or encephalitis); congenital rubella virus infection without apparent signs; and congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) with transient versus permanent manifestations, where fetal risk is greatest with maternal infection in the first 10 weeks of gestation (~90%) and declines markedly after ~16 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1644-1645).

Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome — RTS, RSTS, broad thumb-hallux syndrome, CREBBP, EP300 Cornelia de Lange syndrome Floating-Harbor syndrome Saethre-Chotzen syndrome Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome Cohen syndrome Kabuki syndrome Sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of CREBBP and EP300 Chromosomal microarray to detect 16p13.3 microdeletions involving CREBBP Echocardiography for congenital heart disease Renal tract ultrasound for structural anomalies Ophthalmology review for refractive error, strabismus, glaucoma and lacrimal duct obstruction Hearing assessment and monitoring for recurrent otitis media Broad, often angulated thumbs and great toes are the signature finding and a key diagnostic clue The facial gestalt includes down-slanting palpebral fissures, a beaked or convex nose with the columella extending below the alae, highly arched eyebrows, and a grimacing smile Postnatal growth failure, microcephaly and intellectual disability with a friendly, sociable temperament are typical Most cases arise from de novo autosomal dominant variants in CREBBP; a minority involve EP300 and tend to be milder facially but may include maternal pre-eclampsia in pregnancy Both genes encode histone acetyltransferases, so the condition is a disorder of chromatin regulation Keloid formation, recurrent respiratory and ear infections, and feeding difficulties are common There is an increased lifetime risk of benign and malignant tumours, warranting attention to new lesions New or rapidly enlarging masses given the increased neoplasia risk Signs of raised intraocular pressure or glaucoma threatening vision Recurrent aspiration or severe apnoea related to airway and feeding problems Anaesthetic difficulty from a narrow airway and reported arrhythmia risk Missing the diagnosis when digital broadening is subtle and the facial features are mild, as in some EP300 cases Overlooking treatable glaucoma or lacrimal duct obstruction Failing to warn about keloid risk before elective surgery Inadequate preoperative airway and cardiac assessment before anaesthesia Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of transcriptional coactivators with intrinsic histone acetyltransferase activity, encoded by CREBBP and its paralogue EP300. These proteins acetylate histones and remodel chromatin to permit transcription of numerous developmental genes. Reduced acetyltransferase dosage impairs the coordinated gene expression required for skeletal, craniofacial and neuronal development, producing the characteristic broad digits, dysmorphism, growth impairment and cognitive deficit. The same chromatin-regulatory role underlies the elevated tumour predisposition. Most individuals survive into adulthood with moderate intellectual disability and require lifelong support; overall outlook is shaped by cardiac anomalies, infection burden and tumour surveillance. Life expectancy can approach normal with good multidisciplinary care.

Sacrococcygeal teratoma — SCT, presacral teratoma Myelomeningocele or other neural tube defect Anterior meningocele Lipoma or lipomeningocele Rectal duplication cyst Neuroblastoma or other pelvic tumour Antenatal and postnatal ultrasound to assess size, vascularity, and internal extent MRI of the pelvis and spine to define intrapelvic extension and exclude a spinal component Serum alpha-fetoprotein at baseline and during follow-up Fetal echocardiography and monitoring for hydrops in large vascular antenatal lesions Histological examination of the resected specimen to grade maturity and detect malignant elements The most common congenital tumour of the newborn, arising at the base of the coccyx and typically presenting as a large sacral mass, more often in females The Altman classification describes the balance of external versus internal (presacral/pelvic) tumour, which affects detectability and surgical difficulty Predominantly external tumours are usually recognised at birth, whereas mainly internal lesions may present later with pelvic mass effect, constipation, or urinary symptoms Most tumours found in the neonatal period are benign (mature or immature teratoma), but the risk of malignancy rises the later the lesion presents Serum alpha-fetoprotein is a useful marker; persistently elevated or rising levels after resection raise concern for malignant (yolk sac) elements or recurrence Large vascular tumours detected antenatally can cause high-output cardiac failure and fetal hydrops due to arteriovenous shunting Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision including the coccyx, since leaving the coccyx behind markedly increases recurrence Long-term follow-up with clinical review and tumour markers is required to detect recurrence and to monitor bowel and bladder function Antenatal high-output cardiac failure or hydrops from a large vascular tumour, which is life-threatening Rapid tumour growth or haemorrhage requiring urgent surgical planning Rising alpha-fetoprotein after resection suggesting malignant recurrence Delayed presentation of an internal tumour, which carries higher malignancy risk Failing to remove the coccyx, which greatly increases recurrence risk Missing a predominantly internal (presacral) tumour on external examination alone Neglecting postoperative alpha-fetoprotein surveillance for recurrence Overlooking associated anorectal or spinal anomalies and later functional problems Sacrococcygeal teratoma is a germ cell tumour thought to arise from pluripotent cells near the primitive streak (Hensen's node) at the caudal end of the embryo. It therefore contains tissues derived from multiple germ layers and grows at the coccygeal region, extending externally, into the pelvis, or both. Large, highly vascular tumours can act as arteriovenous shunts, causing high-output heart failure and hydrops in the fetus. Malignant transformation, usually to yolk sac tumour, becomes more likely with delayed diagnosis and with predominantly internal, poorly detected lesions. Benign lesions completely excised in the neonatal period with removal of the coccyx have an excellent prognosis. Prognosis worsens with malignant histology, incomplete excision, delayed diagnosis, and antenatal complications such as hydrops. Even after benign resection, some children have long-term bowel or bladder dysfunction.

pressure from multisuture involvement Ptosis severe enough to obscure the visual axis and risk amblyopia Developmental regression or delay suggesting a larger contiguous gene deletion Progressive facial asymmetry needing surgical planning Mislabelling the condition as Muenke syndrome without molecular testing, as the phenotypes overlap Overlooking amblyopia risk from ptosis Not performing Subarachnoid hemorrhage — Non-contrast CT head (urgent) LP for xanthochromia if CT negative CT angiography Thunderclap headache is SAH until proven otherwise — image immediately Primary thunderclap headache / reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) — many otherwise-undiagnosed thunderclap headaches are attributed to RCVS (p.3462) Cervicocephalic arterial dissection (p.3462) Cerebral venous (sinus) thrombosis (p.3462) Ruptured arteriovenous malformation — but blood is usually intraparenchymal, not deposited in the basal cisterns, and symptomatic vasospasm is rare (p.3457) Dural arteriovenous fistula (a recognised cause of SAH) (p.3457) Noncontrast CT detects >95% of cases when obtained within 72 h; sensitivity falls as time from ictus increases (p.3459) Four-vessel conventional x-ray (catheter) angiography — gold standard to localise/define aneurysm anatomy and detect additional aneurysms; ruptured aneurysm can be treated at the same sitting (p.3459) CT perfusion imaging — adjunct to identify potentially reversible ischaemic deficits in suspected delayed cerebral ischaemia (p.3459) Transcranial Doppler ultrasound — daily/alternate-day bedside monitoring detects rising flow velocities of vasospasm (p.3459) Serial (daily or twice-daily) serum electrolytes to detect early hyponatraemia (p.3459) ECG and echocardiography to detect neurogenic cardiac changes and stress (catecholamine) cardiomyopathy (p.3459-3460) Thunderclap migraine — a migraine variant that can simulate SAH; a definitive workup to exclude aneurysm/other intracranial pathology is required before attributing sudden severe headache to it (p.3458) The single most important feature of aneurysmal SAH headache is its sudden (abrupt) onset, even more than its severity; ruptures may occasionally present as only moderate headache or as a change in the patient's usual headache pattern (p.3458). Transient loss of consciousness occurs in nearly half of patients at the moment of rupture, reflecting an abrupt rise in intracranial pressure; many patients only report the headache after regaining consciousness (p.3458). A third nerve palsy with pupillary dilation and pain around/behind the eye suggests an expanding aneurysm at the posterior communicating artery-internal carotid junction; a sixth nerve palsy may indicate a cavernous-sinus aneurysm (p.3458). Quivering, jerking, or extensor posturing accompanying loss of consciousness at SAH onset is usually caused by the sharp ICP rise rather than true seizure activity (p.3461). ECG changes mimicking cardiac ischaemia (ST/T changes, long QT, peaked or deeply inverted T waves) and a reversible (catecholamine-mediated) cardiomyopathy with regional wall-motion abnormalities can occur after SAH; an asymptomatic troponin rise is common (p.3459-3460). Nimodipine improves outcomes in aneurysmal SAH, apparently by limiting ischaemic injury rather than by reducing vasospasm itself (knowledge, no dose) (p.3461). Perimesencephalic (idiopathic) SAH localised to the perimesencephalic cisterns is benign, probably venous/capillary in origin, and angiography is typically unrevealing (p.3458). Sudden unexplained headache of any location may represent a sentinel bleed (small aneurysmal leak) heralding imminent major haemorrhage and must be investigated (p.3459) Declining mental status with worsening headache 4-14 days after SAH suggests delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm (p.3459-3460) High ICP refractory to treatment is a poor prognostic sign (p.3461) A normal CT does not exclude SAH, especially as time elapses or with small or infratentorial bleeds; if CT is non-diagnostic and there is no mass lesion/obstructive hydrocephalus, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is required (p.3458-3459). Xanthochromia (yellow CSF from haemoglobin-to-bilirubin conversion) takes 6-12 h to appear, peaks at ~48 h, and persists 1-4 weeks; an LP performed too early may miss it (p.3459). Free-water restriction should NOT be used to treat SAH-associated hyponatraemia (cerebral salt wasting): the resulting hypovolaemia/hypotension can precipitate cerebral ischaemia (p.3459, p.3461). Marked hyponatraemia of several days' duration must not be corrected too rapidly because of the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (p.3461). Lumbar puncture before imaging is appropriate only when CT is unavailable at the time of suspected SAH (p.3459). Excluding trauma, the commonest cause is rupture of a saccular ('berry') aneurysm, which forms at bifurcations of large- to medium-sized intracranial arteries (about 89% in the anterior circulation, mostly on the circle of Willis). Aneurysm walls show loss of the internal elastic lamina at the neck base with medial thinning and replacement of smooth muscle by connective tissue; rupture is usually at the thin-walled dome through a tear often <=0.5 mm. Rupture deposits blood in the subarachnoid space of the basal cisterns (and sometimes adjacent parenchyma), abruptly raising ICP. Other causes include vascular malformations (AVM, dural arteriovenous fistula) and subarachnoid extension of a primary intracerebral haemorrhage. Roughly 2% of adults harbour intracranial aneurysms and about 20% of affected patients have multiple aneurysms (frequently mirror-image bilateral). Delayed cerebral ischaemia is thought to arise from clot breakdown products acting on basal arteries to cause vasospasm and vessel-wall thickening, but also from vasospasm-independent mechanisms (microthrombosis, inflammation, microvascular dysregulation, cortical spreading depolarisation). Hyponatraemia results from natriuresis with volume depletion ('cerebral salt wasting'), mediated by atrial and brain natriuretic peptides (p.3457-3461). Overall mortality of aneurysmal SAH is about 35%, with roughly a third dying before reaching hospital; over half of survivors are left with significant neurologic deficits from the initial bleed, delayed cerebral ischaemia, or hydrocephalus. Outcome worsens with increasing presentation grade: grade 1 (Hunt-Hess) patients rarely die if treated, whereas mortality for grades 4-5 may reach about 60%. In an untreated aneurysm, rebleeding risk is about 20% in the first 2 weeks, 30% in the first month, then about 3% per year; rerupture (~30% in the first month, peaking in the first 7 days) carries about 50% mortality. Delayed cerebral ischaemia occurs in about 30% and is the leading cause of delayed morbidity and death among initial survivors. Unruptured aneurysms <7 mm had ~0% 5-year rupture risk in a large study (though many ruptured aneurysms are <6 mm); giant aneurysms (>25 mm) carry ~8-10% annual rupture risk (p.3458-3460). Two presentation-based clinical grading scales are used: the Hunt-Hess scale (1 = asymptomatic/minimal headache and slight nuchal rigidity through 5 = coma with reflex posturing or flaccidity) and the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) scale based on Glasgow Coma Scale score and motor deficits (1 = GCS 15 no motor deficit through 5 = GCS 3-6). Higher grade predicts worse outcome. The modified Fisher CT grading system predicts symptomatic vasospasm by the amount and distribution of subarachnoid/intraventricular blood ('thin' <1 mm vs 'thick' >=1 mm), with risk rising from 0% (grade 0) to ~40% (grade 4, thick blood with intraventricular blood) (p.3459-3460).

Benign tumours such as pleomorphic adenoma grow slowly and are well circumscribed but can recur if incompletely excised and, rarely, undergo malignant transformation over time.
