NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited: diarrhea resolves within 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; stool cultures may remain positive for 4-5 weeks after infection (p.1320). Globally S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis are the most common serotypes causing human disease; in the United States NTS is the second most common cause of foodborne outbreaks after norovirus (p.1319). Unlike S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi (human-only reservoir), NTS is acquired from multiple animal and plant reservoirs - especially eggs, poultry, undercooked ground meat, and dairy, plus produce contaminated with animal waste and contact with animals (reptiles, amphibians, chicks, etc.) (p.1319). Up to 8% of patients with NTS gastroenteritis develop bacteremia, and of those 5-10% develop localized (metastatic) infections; bacteremia and metastatic infection are most common with S. Choleraesuis and S. Dublin and among infants, the elderly, and the immunocompromised, especially those with HIV (p.1320). Invasive NTS disease (predominantly S. Typhimurium ST313 and S. Enteritidis ST11) is a leading cause of bacteremia in children and HIV-infected adults in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia; it typically presents as a nonspecific febrile illness resembling enteric fever and uncommonly causes diarrhea (p.1319-1320). Diagnosis rests on isolating the organism from freshly passed stool or from blood or another normally sterile fluid; culture-independent molecular tests are increasingly used but positive specimens should still undergo primary isolation, and all NTS isolates should be referred to public health for serotyping (p.1320-1321). Reactive arthritis can follow NTS gastroenteritis, occurring most frequently in persons carrying the HLA-B27 antigen (p.1321). Localized NTS infections include intraabdominal (hepatic/splenic abscess, cholecystitis), CNS (meningitis - chiefly in infants 1-4 months and HIV-infected adults), pulmonary (lobar pneumonia), urinary/genital, and bone/joint disease; Salmonella osteomyelitis classically affects the femur, tibia, humerus, or lumbar vertebrae and is strongly linked to sickle cell disease and hemoglobinopathies (p.1320-1321). Invasive disease / bacteremia and endovascular seeding in the elderly, immunocompromised (including HIV), infants/neonates, and patients with sickle cell disease or other hemoglobinopathies High-grade or persistent bacteremia, particularly with preexisting valvular heart disease, atherosclerotic vascular disease, prosthetic vascular graft, or aortic aneurysm - suspect NTS endovascular infection Prolonged fever with back, chest, or abdominal pain after an episode of gastroenteritis in an elderly patient - suspect arteritis/mycotic aneurysm NTS meningitis in infants 1-4 months of age or HIV-infected adults - severe sequelae and death in up to 60% of cases Persons >50 years with known or suspected atherosclerosis (increased risk of invasive infection and endovascular seeding) Antibiotics should NOT be used routinely to treat uncomplicated NTS gastroenteritis - the illness is usually self-limited and antibiotics do not significantly shorten fever or diarrhea, while they have been associated with increased relapse rates, prolonged fecal/gastrointestinal carriage, and adverse drug reactions. Only ~1% of clinical isolates ferment lactose, so a high index of suspicion is needed to detect rare lactose-fermenting strains. Decreased-ciprofloxacin-susceptibility NTS strains may not be reliably detected by nalidixic acid susceptibility testing or standard ciprofloxacin disk diffusion, risking missed resistance and treatment failure. Neonates, the elderly, and immunosuppressed patients with NTS gastroenteritis are especially prone to dehydration and invasive infection and may need hospitalization and antibiotic therapy - they are exceptions to the no-routine-antibiotics rule. All Salmonella infections begin with ingestion of organisms, usually in contaminated food or water; the infectious dose ranges from ~200 to 10^6 CFU, and the ingested dose helps determine incubation period and severity. Conditions reducing gastric acidity (age <1 year, acid-suppression therapy, achlorhydria) or compromising intestinal integrity (inflammatory bowel disease, cytotoxic chemotherapy, prior GI surgery, antibiotic-induced microbiome alteration) increase susceptibility. In contrast to enteric fever (mononuclear infiltration of small-bowel mucosa), NTS gastroenteritis is characterized by massive polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration into both large- and small-bowel mucosa. This response depends largely on induction of interleukin 8, a strong neutrophil chemoattractant secreted by intestinal cells in response to NTS colonization and translocation of bacterial proteins and LPS into host cytoplasm with subsequent inflammasome activation; neutrophil degranulation and release of toxic substances damages the mucosa, producing inflammatory diarrhea. NTS persistence is aided by its ability to use tetrathionate (generated from thiosulfate via inflammatory reactive oxygen species) for metabolism in a microaerophilic, inflamed gut, allowing it to outcompete endogenous flora. Unlike typhoidal serotypes, NTS effectively colonizes the intestinal tract rather than evolving as a primarily systemic pathogen. NTS gastroenteritis is usually self-limited, with diarrhea resolving in 3-7 days and fever within 72 h; chronic carriage develops in <1% of cases. Outcomes worsen markedly with invasive disease: endocarditis and arteritis are rare (<1%) but carry serious, potentially fatal complications (valve perforation, endomyocardial abscess, infected mural thrombus, pericarditis, mycotic aneurysm, aneurysm rupture, aortoenteric fistula, vertebral osteomyelitis), and NTS meningitis is fatal in up to 60% of cases. In 2017 there were ~535,000 invasive NTS cases and ~77,500 deaths worldwide, ~80% in sub-Saharan Africa. Acute NTS gastroenteritis was associated with a threefold increased risk of dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome at 1 year in a Spanish study. Harrison does not provide a formal graded severity score for NTS. Disease is described along a clinical spectrum: (1) uncomplicated self-limited gastroenteritis; (2) bacteremia (low-grade defined as <50% of blood cultures positive vs high-grade >50% of three or more sets positive, the latter raising concern for endovascular infection); and (3) localized/metastatic infection (intraabdominal, CNS, pulmonary, urinary/genital, bone/joint/soft tissue) and endovascular infection (endocarditis, arteritis). Host-risk stratification for invasive disease includes neonates (up to ~3 months), persons >50 years with atherosclerosis, and those with immunosuppression, cardiac valvular/endovascular abnormalities, or significant joint disease.

malignancy/chemoimmunotherapy Lymphoma presenting with hilar/mediastinal adenopathy Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause; the lung is involved in over 90% of cases, but roughly half of patients have extrapulmonary disease and almost any organ can be affected (p.2921, p.2924). Diagnosis rests on three criteria: a compatible clinical picture, nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation on tissue, AND exclusion of other causes of granulomas — it is never made with absolute certainty, so new signs during follow-up should be re-evaluated (p.2923-2924). Löfgren syndrome (fever, erythema nodosum, ankle arthralgias, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) occurs in up to ~10% of cases and, like Heerfordt syndrome, carries an excellent prognosis with frequent spontaneous resolution (p.2923). Heerfordt syndrome = facial nerve palsy, fever, anterior uveitis, and bilateral parotid gland enlargement (p.2923, p.2928). In very compelling presentations (classic Löfgren, Heerfordt, lupus pernio, or asymptomatic symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy), biopsy may be deferred, but close clinical follow-up is still required (p.2924). A BAL CD4:CD8 lymphocyte ratio >3.5 supports the diagnosis when combined with consistent clinical/radiographic findings, but a normal ratio does NOT exclude sarcoidosis; BAL is also important to exclude infection (p.2924). Endobronchial ultrasound-guided lymph node sampling has high diagnostic yield with low procedural risk when hilar/mediastinal nodes are the prominent feature (p.2924). Sarcoidosis is upper-lobe predominant on imaging with a lymphangitic (perilymphatic/subpleural/peribronchovascular) nodular distribution; airflow obstruction can occur in up to one-third of patients despite the classically restrictive pattern (p.2924-2925). Every sarcoidosis patient should be screened for cardiac involvement (baseline ECG) because severity of lung disease does not predict cardiac sarcoidosis and sudden death can be the initial presentation (p.2925-2926). Baseline workup in every patient should include PFTs, chest imaging, an ophthalmologic exam (to detect clinically silent uveitis), an ECG, and serum creatinine/alkaline phosphatase/calcium/CBC (p.2924). Hypercalcemia from dysregulated macrophage/granuloma production of calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D) occurs despite suppressed PTH; patients should limit vitamin D intake, avoid excess sunlight, and stay hydrated (p.2927-2928). Optic neuropathy in ocular sarcoidosis is an emergency requiring immediate immunosuppression to prevent sudden permanent vision loss (p.2927). Smoking is a consistent NEGATIVE predictor of incident sarcoidosis (reduced odds), an unusual feature among lung diseases (p.2921-2922). Exclude infection (especially TB and fungi such as histoplasmosis) before starting immunosuppression — abundant necrosis on biopsy points away from sarcoidosis toward infection Acute symptomatic hypercalcemia can require hospital admission and urgent corticosteroids Optic neuropathy threatens sudden permanent vision loss and is an ophthalmologic emergency Cardiac involvement (new-onset AV block, ventricular arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy in younger patients) carries risk of sudden death and can be the first presentation Neurologic involvement (basal/cranial nerve disease, mass lesions, meningitis) can cause neurologic demise Untreated hypercalcemia leads to nephrocalcinosis and renal failure New reproductive-organ nodules/masses require exclusion of malignancy given the rarity of genital sarcoidosis A normal BAL CD4:CD8 ratio, normal PFTs, or a normal lung exam does NOT exclude sarcoidosis despite active granulomatous inflammation (p.2924). Serum ACE has low sensitivity and is not a reliable diagnostic or prognostic test; it only roughly tracks granuloma burden and is best used to monitor activity (p.2929). Scadding (CXR) stages reveal overall resolution rates but do NOT predict disease activity, lung-function progression, or extrapulmonary involvement in an individual (p.2929). Cardiac involvement is frequently subclinical and endomyocardial biopsy has poor sensitivity (patchy granulomas, basal predominance, sparing of the right ventricle), so a negative biopsy does not exclude cardiac sarcoidosis (p.2926). Failing to screen for cardiac, ocular, and neurologic disease at baseline misses life- or sight-threatening involvement because pulmonary severity does not predict it (p.2924-2926). Isolated extrapulmonary sarcoidosis (cardiac, hepatic, neurologic) can occur without lung disease and is easily overlooked (p.2926-2927). Loosely formed granulomas suggest hypersensitivity pneumonitis and abundant necrosis suggests infection — misreading these as sarcoidosis is a classic error (p.2924). Always re-evaluate alternative causes for isolated hepatic granulomas, which carry a broad differential (p.2927). Sarcoidosis is thought to arise from a heightened, antigen-driven host immune response to an undetermined (likely inhaled bioaerosol or inorganic) environmental antigen in a genetically susceptible person; the inciting antigen may differ between individuals/populations. A poorly degradable material is presented to lymphocytes by dendritic cells/macrophages via MHC, triggering an innate cytokine/chemokine cascade and recruitment of adaptive immune cells. The immunopathologic hallmark is highly polarized CD4+ TH1 lymphocytes (less so CD8+) producing IFN-gamma, with upregulation of TH1-promoting cytokines/chemokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-15, IL-18, CXCR3) that activate macrophages and drive formation of tightly organized nonnecrotizing (noncaseating) granulomas. Altered regulatory T-cell and TH17 responses are implicated in failure to resolve and in progression to fibrosis. Granulomas comprise macrophages, epithelioid cells, and multinucleated giant cells rimmed by lymphocytes/fibroblasts (CD4+ central, CD8+ and B cells peripheral). Mycobacterial proteins (mKatG, ESAT-6, superoxide dismutase A, antigen 85A, heat-shock proteins) and Cutibacterium acnes have been disproportionately implicated; the transmissibility seen with the Kveim-Siltzbach reagent and via organ transplantation supports an antigenic trigger (p.2922-2923). Disease resolves spontaneously in just over half of patients, but 30-40% develop chronic disease threatening vital organs or causing debilitating symptoms. Most patients show radiographic or spirometric improvement by 2 years (treated or untreated). Death attributable to sarcoidosis occurs in roughly 1-5%, most often from progressive respiratory insufficiency/pulmonary fibrosis (leading cause in the US/Northern Europe) or cardiac involvement (predominant cause of death in Japan). A robust acute initial immune response predicts a better outcome: Löfgren and Heerfordt syndromes remit spontaneously in up to ~80%, and immunosuppression is rarely needed. Adverse prognostic factors include lupus pernio, chronic uveitis, older age, chronic hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis, African ancestry, pulmonary hypertension, fibrotic pulmonary disease, sinus involvement, cystic bone lesions, neurosarcoidosis, and cardiac involvement. Relapses are common and associated with shorter treatment duration (p.2928-2929). Scadding chest x-ray stages describe the pulmonary pattern and correlate with spontaneous resolution rates (NOT with activity or prognosis in the individual): Stage 1 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal involvement (resolution ~55-90%); Stage 2 = bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy WITH parenchymal involvement (resolution ~40-70%); Stage 3 = parenchymal involvement without lymphadenopathy (resolution ~10-20%); Stage 4 = pulmonary fibrosis with architectural distortion and volume loss (resolution ~0%) (p.2925).

corticosteroids are reserved for significant or progressive organ involvement, with immunosuppressants as steroid-sparing options Symptoms or findings suggesting cardiac sarcoidosis such as arrhythmia, heart block, or heart failure Neurosarcoidosis with cranial nerve or central nervous system involvement Significant hypercalcaemia with renal impairment Progressive pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary hypertension Diagnosing sarcoidosis without excluding tuberculosis and other infective granulomatous disease Relying on serum ACE levels for diagnosis or disease monitoring Missing clinically silent but dangerous cardiac or neurological involvement Treating asymptomatic or mildly affected patients who may remit without therapy Sarcoidosis is thought to arise when an unknown antigen triggers an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response in a genetically susceptible host. Antigen-presenting cells activate CD4 T-helper lymphocytes that secrete Th1 cytokines, driving accumulation of macrophages and their organisation into compact non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. In the lung these granulomas cluster along lymphatics and around bronchovascular structures. Granulomas may resolve or, with persistent inflammation, be replaced by fibrosis, causing irreversible architectural distortion and functional impairment. Prognosis is generally favourable, with a substantial proportion of patients undergoing spontaneous remission, especially in acute presentations such as Loefgren syndrome; however, chronic progressive disease with pulmonary fibrosis, cardiac involvement, or neurosarcoidosis carries greater morbidity and mortality.

vitamin D, thyroid function, and inflammatory markers Sarcopenia is the progressive, generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass together with reduced muscle strength or physical performance Current definitions emphasise low muscle strength as the primary criterion, with low muscle mass confirming the diagnosis and poor performance marking severity Grip strength and gait speed are simple, validated bedside measures that flag probable sarcopenia The SARC-F questionnaire is a quick screening tool for case finding in clinical practice Sarcopenia can be primary (age-related) or secondary to disease, inactivity, or undernutrition, and it overlaps with but is distinct from frailty and cachexia It is a major contributor to falls, disability, loss of independence, and adverse surgical and hospital outcomes Progressive resistance exercise is the most effective intervention and is more powerful than nutrition alone Adequate protein and total energy intake, correction of vitamin D deficiency, and treatment of underlying conditions support muscle maintenance Rapid muscle loss suggesting underlying malignancy or cachexia rather than age-related decline Recurrent or injurious falls resulting from profound weakness Progressive functional decline threatening independence Neurological features pointing to a primary neuromuscular disorder Attributing weakness solely to old age and not screening or intervening Relying on nutritional supplementation without prescribing resistance exercise Overlooking secondary and reversible causes such as vitamin D deficiency and endocrine disorders Missing the overlap with frailty and cachexia and thereby underestimating overall risk Sarcopenia results from an imbalance between muscle protein synthesis and breakdown, driven by ageing changes including loss of motor neurons and motor units, reduced anabolic hormone levels, anabolic resistance to dietary protein, mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic low-grade inflammation, and physical inactivity. Type II (fast-twitch) fibres are preferentially lost, and fatty and fibrous infiltration of muscle further reduces quality and strength. The result is diminished force generation and impaired physical performance out of proportion to the loss of mass alone. Sarcopenia predicts falls, fractures, functional decline, hospitalisation, and mortality, and it worsens outcomes across surgery and acute illness. It is at least partly reversible: resistance training combined with adequate protein intake can improve strength and performance, and earlier intervention yields better results.

Scabies — sarcoptic itch, seven-year itch, Sarcoptes scabiei infestation Atopic dermatitis or other eczema Papular urticaria and insect bite reactions Dermatitis herpetiformis Contact dermatitis Pruritus from systemic causes (renal, hepatic, haematological) Bullous pemphigoid in older patients with intense itch Skin scraping of a burrow examined microscopically for mites, eggs, or faecal pellets Dermoscopy to visualise the mite at the end of a burrow (delta-wing sign) Clinical diagnosis supported by history of contacts with similar itch Skin biopsy occasionally in crusted or atypical disease Assessment for immunosuppression when crusted scabies is present Suspect scabies in any patient with severe, generalised itch that is characteristically worse at night The pathognomonic lesion is the burrow, a fine serpiginous track most often found in finger webs, wrists, and other warm intertriginous sites Typical distribution spares the head in adults but involves the face, scalp, palms, and soles in infants Itch results from a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, so symptoms may take weeks to appear after first infestation but recur within days on re-infestation It spreads by prolonged skin-to-skin contact, so all close contacts and household members should be treated simultaneously even if asymptomatic Treatment is with a topical scabicide applied to the whole body per protocol, with laundering of clothing and bedding; oral therapy is useful for outbreaks or when topical treatment is impractical Crusted (Norwegian) scabies presents with hyperkeratotic crusted plaques, carries an enormous mite burden, is highly contagious, and occurs in immunosuppressed or debilitated patients Warn patients that itch can persist for weeks after successful eradication (post-scabetic itch) and does not necessarily indicate treatment failure Crusted (Norwegian) scabies with widespread hyperkeratosis and high transmission risk Secondary bacterial infection with impetiginisation, and risk of post-streptococcal complications Institutional or household outbreaks requiring public health and infection-control measures Immunosuppression predisposing to severe or atypical infestation Treating the patient alone and not treating asymptomatic close contacts, leading to reinfestation Incorrect application of the scabicide, missing sites such as under nails, genitalia, or the feet Interpreting persistent post-scabetic itch as treatment failure and repeatedly re-treating Missing crusted scabies in an immunosuppressed or institutionalised patient and allowing an outbreak Scabies is caused by infestation with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. The fertilised female mite burrows into the stratum corneum, laying eggs and depositing faeces as she tunnels. The clinical eruption and intense pruritus are largely due to a delayed type IV hypersensitivity response to the mite, its eggs, and its excreta, which explains the delay in symptoms after primary infestation. In classic scabies the mite burden is low (typically a small number of adult mites), whereas in crusted scabies impaired immune control permits proliferation of thousands to millions of mites, producing thick hyperkeratotic crusts and extreme infectivity. Prognosis is excellent with correct treatment of the patient and all contacts; failures usually reflect incomplete application, missed contacts, or re-infestation rather than true drug resistance.

Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase catalyses the initial dehydrogenation of short-chain (predominantly butyryl-CoA) substrates in the final rounds of mitochondrial beta-oxidation. Reduced activity leads to accumulation of butyryl-CoA and its derivatives, detectable as raised C4 acylcarnitine and as ethylmalonic and methylsuccinic acids in urine. Because short-chain oxidation contributes relatively little to overall energy generation and the block is late in the pathway, the biochemical abnormality often occurs without a clear clinical syndrome, and many carriers of the common variants remain well. The great majority of screen-detected individuals remain healthy with a normal outlook, and current evidence does not support classifying isolated SCAD deficiency as a reliably harmful disorder; reported symptoms often reflect coincidental or alternative conditions.

In a host lacking antibody to the relevant toxin, these act as superantigens and toxins that cause the characteristic diffuse erythematous eruption and systemic features. The primary focus is usually the pharynx. Beyond the local infection, immune-mediated sequelae can follow, including acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and unchecked infection can extend to suppurative complications. With prompt antibiotic therapy the outlook is excellent and most children recover fully; the main concern with untreated or inadequately treated disease is the risk of rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis, and suppurative spread.

Diagnosis rests on demonstrating reduced alpha-L-iduronidase activity together with raised urinary dermatan and heparan sulfate Molecular confirmation of IDUA gene variants clarifies the phenotype and supports genetic counselling Progressive aortic valve regurgitation or other cardiac valve dysfunction Visual deterioration from advancing corneal clouding Median nerve compression causing hand weakness and wasting Cervical spine or airway compromise from connective tissue deposition Attributing joint stiffness to inflammatory arthritis and missing the underlying storage disorder Assuming preserved intellect excludes a mucopolysaccharidosis Overlooking silent valvular heart disease that requires surveillance Delaying enzyme replacement therapy because early features are subtle Scheie syndrome arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in the IDUA gene, which encodes the lysosomal hydrolase alpha-L-iduronidase. Residual enzyme activity is greater than in Hurler syndrome, producing a milder phenotype within the same disease continuum. Impaired breakdown of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate leads to their progressive accumulation within lysosomes of connective tissue, cornea, cartilage, heart valves, and other organs. The stored substrate is also excreted in excess in the urine. Because intellectual function is generally spared, the clinical burden is dominated by musculoskeletal, ocular, and cardiac involvement that worsens slowly over years. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Life expectancy can approach normal in many patients, though progressive cardiac valve disease, corneal clouding, and joint limitation cause substantial long-term morbidity. Enzyme replacement therapy may help systemic manifestations but does not correct established corneal or valvular changes.

Progressive developmental regression with seizures in infancy Cortical visual impairment Loss of previously acquired motor and cognitive skills New angiokeratomas prompting distinction from Fabry disease Confusing the adult angiokeratoma phenotype with Fabry disease without appropriate enzyme testing Overlooking the diagnosis in infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy without metabolic screening Relying only on glycosaminoglycan screening and missing the oligosaccharide pattern Assuming a single uniform phenotype given the wide clinical spectrum Schindler disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in NAGA, encoding lysosomal alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase. This enzyme removes terminal alpha-N-acetylgalactosamine residues from glycoproteins, glycopeptides, and glycolipids during lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency leads to accumulation of these incompletely degraded compounds and their excretion in the urine. The mechanism linking substrate storage to the severe infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy of type I remains incompletely understood, but the phenotype features widespread axonal swellings (spheroids). Type II (Kanzaki disease) presents in adulthood with cutaneous angiokeratomas and only mild neurological involvement, and intermediate presentations occur. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. The infantile type I form is severe with profound neurological deterioration and a poor outlook, whereas the adult type II form follows a much milder course compatible with long survival. No disease-modifying therapy is established.

Schistosomiasis — bilharzia, trematode infection Malaria (acute febrile illness in returning traveler/migrant) (p.1829) Salmonellosis (p.1829) Acute viral hepatitis (p.1829) Trichinosis (fever with eosinophilia) (p.1829) Strongyloidiasis (fever with eosinophilia) (p.1829) Visceral larva migrans / toxocariasis (fever with eosinophilia) (p.1829) Other causes of portal hypertension and hepatosplenomegaly, including cirrhosis (p.1829) Opisthorchis and Clonorchis (liver fluke) infections causing fever and eosinophilia (p.1829) Invasive ankylostomiasis (hookworm) (p.1829) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (p.1829) Strongyloidiasis (p.1829) Malaria (p.1829) Microscopic detection of eggs in stool (e.g., ~50 mg) or urine (filtration of ~10 mL) with quantitation (eggs per gram or per 10 mL); concentration methods (e.g., formol-ether) for low-burden travelers (p.1829) Full blood count showing eosinophilia (p.1829) Rectal biopsy for eggs (S. mansoni and S. haematobium); occasionally Pap smears and semen samples (S. haematobium) (p.1829) PCR-based detection of Schistosoma DNA in stool or urine (more sensitive than parasitology); CSF Schistosoma DNA for neuroschistosomiasis (p.1829) Serology for anti-schistosome antibodies (CDC: FAST-ELISA with S. mansoni microsomal antigen plus confirmatory species-specific immunoblot) - useful in travelers, less so in endemic populations (p.1829-1830) Circulating anodic/cathodic antigen (CAA/CCA) detection in serum or urine by ELISA or lateral flow as a marker of active infection; point-of-care urine CCA assay used in community screening (p.1830) Ultrasonography to demonstrate periportal fibrosis, portal vein dilation, and obstructive uropathy/hydronephrosis (p.1829) Cystoscopy showing 'sandy patches' of calcified eggs in chronic urogenital disease; endoscopy or ultrasound for esophageal varices (p.1829) Cirrhosis from other causes presenting with portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and variceal bleeding (p.1829) Bladder squamous cell carcinoma from non-schistosomal causes (chronic urogenital disease) (p.1829) Infection is contracted through contact with freshwater bodies harboring infected intermediate-host snails; cercariae penetrate intact human skin within a few minutes (p.1826). A travel/migration history of freshwater exposure (bathing, washing, fishing, rice-field work, swimming) in an endemic area is central to the diagnosis, especially in travelers (p.1827, p.1829). Most disease manifestations are due to immunologic granulomatous reactions to eggs retained in host tissues, not to the adult worms; about half of eggs are trapped in tissue (p.1827). Cercarial dermatitis ('swimmer's itch') is a maculopapular rash from cercarial skin penetration; a severe form follows exposure to avian schistosomes (e.g., lakes in Europe/US) that die in the skin (p.1828). Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) occurs 2 weeks to 3 months after exposure, usually in first-time-infected travelers, with fever, myalgia, malaise, headache, nonproductive cough, and abdominal symptoms (p.1828). Eosinophilia is a common finding and is often associated with schistosomiasis; transient pulmonary infiltrates may accompany Katayama fever (p.1828, p.1829). Intestinal schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): worms in mesenteric veins; eggs trapped in intestinal tissue cause granulomatous inflammation, microulceration, intermittent abdominal pain, and sometimes bloody diarrhea (p.1829). Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (S. mansoni, S. japonicum): late disease produces periportal (Symmers clay-pipestem) fibrosis with portal vein occlusion, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, esophageal varices, and hematemesis; hepatic function usually remains normal (p.1827, p.1829). Urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium): hallmark of the active stage is painless terminal hematuria, with dysuria and suprapubic discomfort; eggs in bladder mucosa cause inflammation, fibrosis, 'sandy patches', and possible ureteric obstruction with hydronephrosis (p.1829). S. haematobium is an IARC group 1 carcinogen; chronic infection is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder (p.1829). Detection of schistosome eggs in stool or urine indicates active infection and is the standard diagnostic method; S. haematobium eggs (terminal spine) are excreted in urine, other species (S. mansoni lateral spine, S. japonicum small lateral knob) in feces (p.1826, p.1829). Neuroschistosomiasis is one of the most severe forms: S. mansoni/S. haematobium can cause transverse myelitis (an acute complication in returning travelers), while S. japonicum causes cerebral granulomas with seizures and focal neurologic deficits (p.1829). Hematemesis or melena from esophageal varices in hepatosplenic disease - the most severe complication; death may result from massive blood loss (p.1829) Acute transverse myelitis or other cerebral/spinal cord manifestations - neuroschistosomiasis, even from light infections (p.1829) Severe Katayama fever with weight loss, dyspnea, diarrhea, and hepatomegaly; rarely fatal (p.1829) Painless terminal hematuria in a traveler/migrant from an endemic area (urogenital S. haematobium) (p.1829) Obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia from ureteral fibrosis (p.1829) Patients with periportal fibrosis (late hepatosplenic disease) may excrete very few or no eggs in feces, so a negative stool exam does not exclude advanced disease (p.1829). In the chronic urogenital stage, urinary egg excretion may be sparse or absent despite ongoing urogenital tract pathology (p.1829). Egg excretion may be very low in people from nonendemic areas (travelers), requiring larger samples and concentration methods (p.1829). Katayama fever is rare in people chronically exposed in S. mansoni- or S. haematobium-endemic areas, so its absence does not exclude infection in residents (p.1829). CAA/CCA antigen detection is not currently suitable for diagnosing travelers, who have low worm burdens (p.1830). Serology is less useful in people from endemic areas with ongoing transmission (p.1829-1830). Free-swimming cercariae released from infected freshwater snails penetrate intact skin within minutes, transform into schistosomula, enter veins/lymphatics, traverse the lungs and heart, and mature in the portal vein into paired adult male and female worms that migrate to the mesenteric (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) or pelvic/vesical (S. haematobium) venous plexus. The prepatent period is 5-7 weeks (up to 12 for S. haematobium). About half of the eggs produced are excreted in feces or urine; the remainder become trapped in tissue. Most morbidity results from egg-induced, TH2-driven granulomatous immune responses (lymphocytes, eosinophils, alternatively activated macrophages; IL-4/5/13). Egg antigen excess early in infection forms soluble immune complexes causing a serum sickness-like illness (Katayama fever). Hepatic egg deposition leads to periportal (Symmers) fibrosis, portal-branch occlusion, and portal hypertension; S. haematobium egg deposition in the bladder/ureters causes inflammation, fibrosis, obstructive uropathy, and predisposes to squamous bladder carcinoma (p.1826-1829). Many patients recover spontaneously from acute schistosomiasis after 2-10 weeks, though some follow a more severe course, and the acute syndrome can rarely be fatal. In hepatosplenic disease, hepatic function usually remains normal even with marked periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension; however, severe periportal (Symmers) fibrosis is often irreversible, and hematemesis from variceal bleeding may be fatal. Early inflammatory hepatosplenomegaly in children generally decreases over time as immunity develops. Ureteral fibrosis can cause irreversible obstructive uropathy progressing to uremia. The adult worm lifespan averages 3-5 years but can reach 30 years (p.1826-1829). Disease is staged clinically by duration and intensity of infection into three phases - acute (cercarial dermatitis and Katayama fever), active/established, and chronic (e.g., late hepatosplenic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension, or chronic urogenital fibrosis with sandy patches and obstructive uropathy). Severity of early hepatosplenomegaly is closely associated with infection intensity (p.1828-1829).

Schizencephaly — cleft brain, open-lip schizencephaly, closed-lip schizencephaly, EMX2-associated schizencephaly Porencephaly, which is lined by white matter or glial tissue rather than grey matter Open-lip schizencephaly versus severe hydrocephalus or hydranencephaly Septo-optic dysplasia Polymicrogyria without a full-thickness cleft Focal cortical dysplasia Arachnoid cyst communicating with the ventricle Brain MRI to confirm the grey-matter-lined transmantle cleft and its laterality and type Assessment of the septum pellucidum and optic nerves for associated septo-optic dysplasia Ophthalmological examination for optic nerve hypoplasia Endocrine evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis when midline anomalies are present Electroencephalography to characterise epilepsy Genetic evaluation including EMX2 and cortical malformation testing where indicated A malformation characterised by a full-thickness cleft extending from the pial surface to the lateral ventricle, lined throughout by grey matter, usually polymicrogyric cortex It is classified as closed-lip when the cleft walls are apposed or open-lip when they are separated by cerebrospinal fluid, and it may be unilateral or bilateral The grey-matter lining distinguishes it from an acquired porencephalic cyst, which is lined by white matter or gliotic tissue It is frequently associated with absence of the septum pellucidum and with optic nerve hypoplasia, overlapping with septo-optic dysplasia Most cases are thought to result from a destructive vascular or disruptive insult to the developing cortex, though some carry genetic contributions such as EMX2 variants Clinical features vary with size and laterality, from hemiparesis and focal epilepsy in unilateral closed-lip clefts to severe global delay, spasticity, and refractory seizures in bilateral open-lip disease Diagnosis is by MRI demonstrating the grey-matter-lined cleft, with evaluation for associated midline and optic anomalies Drug-resistant focal or generalised epilepsy Endocrine dysfunction when associated with septo-optic dysplasia Progressive macrocephaly or raised intracranial pressure in large open-lip clefts Visual impairment from optic nerve hypoplasia Mistaking schizencephaly for a porencephalic cyst by failing to identify the grey-matter lining Overlooking associated absence of the septum pellucidum and optic nerve hypoplasia Not screening for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction when septo-optic features coexist Confusing a large open-lip cleft with hydrocephalus or hydranencephaly on imaging Schizencephaly is a disorder of cortical formation in which a cleft lined by dysplastic grey matter spans the full thickness of the hemisphere from the ventricle to the cortical surface. It is thought to arise most often from a disruptive prenatal insult, such as a vascular event, that damages the germinal zone and developing cortex, sometimes combined with genetic susceptibility affecting cortical patterning. Because the injury occurs while the cortex is still developing, the cleft becomes lined by abnormal, typically polymicrogyric grey matter, and associated failure of midline structures such as the septum pellucidum and optic apparatus is common. Prognosis depends on the size, type, and laterality of the cleft. Unilateral closed-lip schizencephaly may cause only mild hemiparesis and manageable epilepsy, whereas bilateral open-lip disease is typically associated with severe motor and cognitive disability and refractory seizures.

Schizoaffective disorder — schizoaffective psychosis Schizophrenia Bipolar disorder with psychotic features Major depressive disorder with psychotic features Substance-induced psychotic disorder Psychosis due to a general medical condition Delusional disorder Schizophreniform disorder Longitudinal assessment documenting the temporal relationship of mood and psychotic symptoms Structured suicide risk assessment Urine drug screen and substance use history Baseline metabolic monitoring before and during antipsychotic treatment Neuroimaging and medical workup where an organic cause is suspected Collateral history to clarify longitudinal course The concept describes an illness in which a major mood episode (depressive or manic) coexists with psychotic symptoms that also meet criteria characteristic of schizophrenia over the same continuous period The distinguishing requirement is that delusions or hallucinations must be present for a substantial period in the absence of a prominent mood episode, separating it from mood disorder with psychotic features Two subtypes are recognised according to whether the mood disturbance is predominantly bipolar or depressive in nature Diagnosis is longitudinal and often provisional, requiring observation over time, because the relative burden of mood and psychotic symptoms determines the label Management typically combines an antipsychotic with mood stabilisation or antidepressant treatment guided by the predominant mood pattern Suicide risk is significant and should be assessed repeatedly, particularly during depressive phases and following resolution of psychosis Exclude substance-induced psychosis and general medical causes, and confirm that psychotic symptoms are not confined to mood episodes Psychosocial support, adherence promotion, and long-term follow-up are important because the course is chronic and relapsing Active suicidal or homicidal ideation with plan or intent Command hallucinations directing harm to self or others Acute manic escalation with dangerous behaviour or impaired judgement Catatonia, severe self-neglect, or refusal of food and fluids Labelling mood disorder with psychotic features as schizoaffective without evidence of psychosis outside mood episodes Underestimating suicide risk during and after psychotic phases Neglecting metabolic monitoring during antipsychotic treatment Missing substance-induced or medical causes of combined mood and psychotic symptoms Making a firm diagnosis prematurely without longitudinal observation Schizoaffective disorder is conceptualised as lying on a spectrum between schizophrenia and the mood disorders, sharing neurobiological features with both, including dopaminergic dysregulation implicated in psychosis and monoaminergic and stress-axis disturbances implicated in mood pathology. Genetic vulnerability overlapping with both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, neurodevelopmental factors, and altered corticolimbic circuitry are thought to contribute. The prognosis of schizoaffective disorder is generally intermediate between that of schizophrenia and the mood disorders, tending to be better than schizophrenia but worse than a pure mood disorder. Outcome is more favourable with predominant mood symptoms, good treatment adherence, and strong psychosocial support, and less favourable with prominent persistent psychosis and poor functioning between episodes.

Schizophrenia — schizophrenic disorder, chronic psychosis Schizoaffective disorder Bipolar disorder or major depression with psychotic features Brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder Delusional disorder Substance-induced psychosis Psychosis secondary to a medical or neurological condition Autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis presenting with psychosis Substance use screening including cannabis and stimulants Neuroimaging and, where indicated, investigation for organic or autoimmune causes in first-episode psychosis Baseline metabolic parameters (weight, glucose, lipids) and ECG before and during antipsychotic treatment Full blood count monitoring during clozapine treatment Cognitive assessment to characterise functional impairment A chronic psychotic disorder defined by a combination of positive symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech and behaviour) and negative symptoms (blunted affect, avolition, social withdrawal), with significant functional decline Diagnosis requires continuous disturbance over an extended period (on the order of six months) with an active phase of characteristic symptoms, after excluding mood and substance-related causes Onset is typically in late adolescence or early adulthood, often somewhat earlier and with poorer premorbid function in men Cognitive impairment (attention, working memory, executive function) is a core feature and a major driver of disability Antipsychotic medication is the cornerstone of treatment, described here as a principle; clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and requires haematological monitoring Comprehensive care combines pharmacotherapy with psychosocial interventions, family education, supported employment, and relapse prevention Suicide risk is elevated, particularly early in the illness and in those with insight into their deterioration Duration of untreated psychosis affects outcome, so early recognition and intervention are important Command hallucinations or suicidal ideation with risk to self Delusional beliefs that place others at risk First-episode psychosis with atypical features suggesting an organic cause Signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome such as rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability Agranulocytosis during clozapine therapy Attributing first-episode psychosis to a primary psychiatric disorder without excluding organic and substance causes Neglecting metabolic monitoring in patients on antipsychotics Delaying a clozapine trial in genuinely treatment-resistant illness Underestimating suicide risk, especially early in the course Focusing only on positive symptoms while ignoring disabling negative and cognitive symptoms Schizophrenia is a neurodevelopmental disorder with strong genetic contribution in which aberrant dopaminergic signalling (mesolimbic overactivity linked to positive symptoms and mesocortical hypofunction linked to negative and cognitive symptoms) interacts with glutamatergic and other neurotransmitter abnormalities. Structural and functional brain changes, synaptic pruning abnormalities, and gene-environment interactions such as obstetric complications and cannabis exposure contribute to the emergence of illness. Schizophrenia usually follows a chronic course with episodic exacerbations and variable residual impairment. Better outcomes are associated with acute onset, good premorbid functioning, prominent mood symptoms, and early treatment, whereas insidious onset, prominent negative symptoms, and long untreated psychosis predict poorer functional recovery.

Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (particularly adult Muckle-Wells syndrome) Adult-onset Still disease Urticarial vasculitis Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia and other lymphoproliferative neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis Acute phase reactants including C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A Bone imaging for osteosclerosis or osteolytic changes Bone marrow examination and monitoring for lymphoproliferative disease NLRP3 genetic testing to exclude a late-presenting cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome where clinically indicated An acquired, adult-onset autoinflammatory disorder defined by a chronic urticarial rash together with a monoclonal gammopathy, typically IgM kappa The urticarial lesions are usually non-pruritic or minimally itchy and, unlike ordinary urticaria, are neutrophilic on biopsy Supporting features include recurrent fever, bone pain with radiological osteosclerosis, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy and raised inflammatory markers The Strasbourg criteria combine the two obligate features (urticarial rash and monoclonal IgM or IgG) with minor clinical and laboratory criteria The clinical picture and dramatic response to interleukin-1 blockade place it firmly among the acquired autoinflammatory conditions There is a long-term risk of progression to a lymphoproliferative disorder, particularly Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia, requiring ongoing surveillance Interleukin-1 inhibition typically produces a rapid and near-complete clinical response and is the treatment of choice Rising paraprotein, new cytopenias or organomegaly suggesting transformation to a lymphoproliferative malignancy New proteinuria indicating possible AA amyloidosis Unexplained weight loss, night sweats or progressive lymphadenopathy Severe refractory bone pain with lytic lesions Treating the rash as ordinary allergic urticaria and relying on antihistamines, which are largely ineffective Failing to perform serum immunofixation and therefore missing the defining monoclonal gammopathy Not arranging long-term haematological surveillance for lymphoproliferative transformation Confusing it with a late-onset cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome without appropriate testing Schnitzler syndrome is an acquired autoinflammatory condition in which excessive activation of the innate immune system, particularly interleukin-1-driven inflammation, produces a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis and systemic inflammation. It occurs in the context of a monoclonal gammopathy, most often IgM kappa, and although the precise link between the paraprotein and the inflammatory drive is not fully defined, the disease behaves as an interleukin-1-mediated process, as evidenced by its striking response to interleukin-1 blockade. Chronic overproduction of interleukin-1 beta and downstream cytokines accounts for the fever, bone changes and acute phase response, while the underlying clonal B-cell process explains the association with, and risk of evolution to, lymphoproliferative malignancy. Inflammatory symptoms are usually well controlled with interleukin-1 inhibition and quality of life can be restored, but the disorder is chronic and carries a persistent long-term risk of evolving into a lymphoproliferative malignancy, so lifelong monitoring is required.

dystrophy Isaacs syndrome (neuromyotonia) and other peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndromes Congenital myasthenic syndromes with abnormal cholinesterase Skeletal dysplasias with contractures and reactions and difficult airway Progressive kyphoscoliosis compromising respiratory function Severe joint contractures limiting mobility and function Attributing the stiffness to a pure muscle channelopathy and missing the skeletal chondrodysplasia that defines the syndrome Overlooking the anaesthetic and airway risks in a child with facial and jaw stiffness Confusing the continuous discharges with the discharges of Isaacs syndrome or true myotonia Failing to arrange orthopaedic and ophthalmological surveillance for the skeletal and eye complications Schwartz-Jampel syndrome is caused by mutations in HSPG2, which encodes perlecan, a large heparan sulphate proteoglycan that is a major structural and signalling component of basement membranes and of cartilage extracellular matrix. Deficient or dysfunctional perlecan disrupts cartilage development, producing the chondrodysplasia, short stature and skeletal deformities. At the neuromuscular junction, perlecan anchors acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic basal lamina, and its deficiency reduces cholinesterase activity so that acetylcholine action is prolonged, contributing, together with abnormal muscle-membrane excitability, to the sustained muscle activity and stiffness that clinically resembles myotonia. Prognosis varies with severity, but many children with the classic form survive into adulthood with persistent stiffness and skeletal deformity, whereas a rarer severe neonatal presentation carries higher early morbidity; the disorder is generally non-progressive once established but causes lasting orthopaedic and functional handicap.

claudication Spondylolisthesis Piriformis syndrome or deep gluteal syndrome Peripheral neuropathy or nerve entrapment (e.g. peroneal nerve) Hip or sacroiliac joint pathology referring to the leg Vascular claudication Spinal tumour or infection compressing a nerve root Clinical diagnosis with root localisation; imaging not required for typical early sciatica without red flags MRI of the lumbar spine for severe, persistent, or progressive symptoms or when intervention is planned CT if MRI is contraindicated Nerve conduction studies and electromyography in selected cases to clarify the level or exclude peripheral neuropathy Blood tests and targeted imaging if infection or malignancy is suspected Sciatica describes radicular leg pain following a dermatomal distribution below the knee, often with associated tingling, numbness, or weakness, and typically worse than any back pain The commonest cause is compression or irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root by a prolapsed intervertebral disc, most often at L4-5 or L5-S1 In older patients, lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication is a frequent cause, with leg symptoms brought on by walking and relieved by sitting or flexion A positive straight-leg raise (and crossed straight-leg raise) suggests lower lumbar nerve root tension, while the femoral stretch test targets higher roots Examination should localise the affected root through its characteristic sensory, motor, and reflex changes Most disc-related sciatica improves over weeks to a few months with conservative care, staying active, analgesia by principle, and physiotherapy MRI is reserved for severe or persistent symptoms, progressive deficit, or when surgery or injection is being considered, not for routine early management Surgery such as discectomy is considered for persistent disabling radicular pain that fails conservative treatment, or urgently for significant or progressive neurological deficit Screen every patient for cauda equina and other red flags at presentation and again if symptoms change Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, faecal incontinence, and bilateral or progressive leg weakness requiring emergency imaging and decompression Progressive or severe motor deficit such as foot drop needing urgent assessment Features suggesting malignancy: previous cancer, unexplained weight loss, age over 50, and night pain Features suggesting infection: fever, immunosuppression, intravenous drug use, and severe unremitting pain Failing to ask about and detect cauda equina features, risking permanent deficit Ordering early MRI and over-attributing symptoms to incidental disc findings Mistaking peripheral entrapment, hip, or vascular pathology for radicular pain Delaying referral for progressive motor deficit Sciatica is caused by compression, tension, or chemical irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root, most commonly from a herniated disc whose nucleus material both mechanically compresses and inflames the root. Other causes include degenerative foraminal or central canal stenosis, spondylolisthesis, and less often tumour or infection. Nerve root inflammation and ischaemia generate the characteristic radiating pain and neurological signs in the corresponding dermatome and myotome. The majority of disc-related cases resolve within six to twelve weeks with conservative treatment, but a proportion have persistent or recurrent symptoms; surgery gives faster relief of leg pain in selected patients, and outcomes worsen if significant neurological deficit is not treated promptly.

Scleredema (of Buschke) — scleredema of Buschke, scleredema adultorum, scleredema diabeticorum, Buschke disease Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) Scleromyxoedema Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis Eosinophilic fasciitis Myxoedema of hypothyroidism Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerosis Skin biopsy showing dermal thickening, separated collagen bundles, and mucin deposition Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation for monoclonal gammopathy Fasting glucose and HbA1c to assess for diabetes Streptococcal and viral serology when a post-infectious form is suspected Thyroid function to exclude myxoedema Autoantibody screen to help exclude systemic sclerosis A deposition dermatosis with diffuse, non-pitting induration and thickening of the skin, typically over the upper back, posterior neck, and shoulders The affected skin feels woody and firm, and movement of the neck and trunk can become restricted Three recognised clinical settings: a post-infectious form after streptococcal or viral illness, an association with monoclonal gammopathy, and a form linked to long-standing diabetes (scleredema diabeticorum) Unlike systemic sclerosis it spares the fingers and lacks Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and nailfold capillary changes Histology shows thickened dermis with widely separated collagen bundles and accumulation of mucin (glycosaminoglycans) The diabetes-associated form tends to be chronic and persistent, whereas the post-infectious form may resolve over months There is no uniformly effective treatment; options explored include physiotherapy, phototherapy, and immunomodulatory approaches, alongside management of the underlying association Detection of a monoclonal protein warranting haematological evaluation for myeloma or related dyscrasia Restriction of chest wall movement or dysphagia from extensive induration Rapidly progressive or widespread skin involvement Features suggesting an alternative systemic sclerosing disease Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing that the fingers are spared without Raynaud phenomenon Failing to screen for a monoclonal gammopathy that may herald a plasma-cell disorder Overlooking poorly controlled diabetes as the underlying association Interpreting the non-pitting swelling as simple oedema Scleredema is characterised by excessive deposition of collagen and mucopolysaccharide (mucin) in the reticular dermis, which thickens the skin and produces its firm, non-pitting induration. Fibroblasts in affected skin appear to be stimulated to overproduce collagen and glycosaminoglycans. The mechanisms differ by clinical context: a post-infectious immune response is implicated after streptococcal or viral illness, non-enzymatic glycosylation and altered collagen metabolism are thought relevant in diabetes, and a paraproteinaemic form is associated with monoclonal gammopathy, sometimes progressing to a plasma-cell dyscrasia. The dermal expansion, not oedema fluid, explains why the swelling does not pit. The post-infectious form often improves spontaneously over months to a couple of years, whereas the diabetes-associated and paraproteinaemic forms tend to be chronic and refractory; overall prognosis depends on any underlying disorder.

Scleritis — anterior scleritis, posterior scleritis, necrotising scleritis, scleromalacia perforans Episcleritis Anterior uveitis Conjunctivitis Orbital cellulitis or orbital inflammatory disease (posterior scleritis) Infective (e.g. herpetic or pseudomonal) scleritis Choroidal tumour or exudative retinal detachment (posterior scleritis) Slit-lamp examination with assessment of deep vessel involvement and response to topical phenylephrine B-scan ultrasonography for posterior scleritis (scleral thickening and T-sign) Inflammatory and autoimmune workup: full blood count, ESR/CRP, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor Investigations for infective causes (including syphilis and tuberculosis) when indicated Imaging or systemic referral when an underlying vasculitis is suspected Presents with severe, deep, boring ocular pain that is often worse at night, may radiate to the face or jaw, and characteristically disturbs sleep The redness has a bluish or violaceous hue from involvement of the deep scleral vessels, unlike the bright red of episcleritis Scleral vessels do not blanch with topical phenylephrine, which helps distinguish scleritis from episcleritis Classified into anterior (diffuse, nodular, or necrotising) and posterior forms; necrotising scleritis is the most destructive and sight-threatening Scleromalacia perforans is a painless necrotising form seen in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis Roughly half of cases are associated with systemic disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis and ANCA-associated vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis Posterior scleritis can mimic other conditions with proptosis, pain on eye movement, and disc swelling, and is confirmed on ultrasound (T-sign) Management is with systemic anti-inflammatory therapy: oral NSAIDs for milder disease and systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppression for necrotising or refractory cases Necrotising scleritis with scleral thinning or threatened perforation Severe pain with reduced vision indicating posterior segment or optic nerve involvement Features of systemic vasculitis (e.g. granulomatosis with polyangiitis) requiring urgent systemic treatment Rapid progression despite therapy suggesting infective scleritis or aggressive vasculitis Mistaking scleritis for the benign, self-limiting episcleritis and undertreating it Failing to search for and treat an underlying systemic vasculitis or connective-tissue disease Missing posterior scleritis, which lacks obvious external redness and mimics orbital disease Using topical steroids alone when systemic immunosuppression is required for necrotising disease Scleritis is inflammation of the sclera, frequently immune-mediated and often a manifestation of systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disease. Immune-complex deposition and T-cell-mediated inflammation cause oedema and cellular infiltration of the sclera and episclera; in necrotising disease, occlusive vasculitis of the deep episcleral vessels leads to scleral ischaemia, necrosis, and thinning, with risk of perforation. Chronic or severe inflammation can extend to adjacent structures causing keratitis, uveitis, glaucoma, and, in posterior disease, exudative retinal detachment and optic nerve involvement. Diffuse and nodular anterior scleritis usually respond to anti-inflammatory treatment with good visual outcomes, but necrotising scleritis is associated with significant ocular morbidity and, when linked to systemic vasculitis, increased mortality if the underlying disease is untreated.

treatment, with other systemic immunomodulatory options for resistant disease Acute encephalopathy, seizures, or coma suggesting the dermato-neuro syndrome Cardiac or oesophageal involvement causing functional compromise Progression of the paraprotein towards multiple myeloma Rapidly progressive skin induration limiting mobility Mistaking it for systemic sclerosis and missing the associated paraprotein Failing to perform serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation in a patient with unexplained waxy skin induration Overlooking systemic and neurological involvement Assuming absence of myeloma excludes significant disease Tracking treatment response by paraprotein level rather than clinical activity Scleromyxoedema is a generalised form of lichen myxoedematosus characterised by deposition of mucin (glycosaminoglycans) in the dermis together with proliferation of fibroblasts and increased collagen. It is almost invariably associated with a monoclonal gammopathy, usually IgG lambda, though the paraprotein's precise pathogenic role is unclear and disease activity does not track paraprotein levels. Circulating factors are thought to stimulate dermal fibroblasts to overproduce mucin and collagen, and the process may extend to internal organs, producing systemic and, in the dermato-neuro syndrome, central neurological complications. Scleromyxoedema is a chronic, often progressive disorder; skin disease may respond to intravenous immunoglobulin and immunomodulation, but systemic and central nervous system involvement, particularly the dermato-neuro syndrome, can be life-threatening.

Sclerosteosis (SOST) — SOST-related sclerosteosis, cortical hyperostosis with syndactyly, sclerostin deficiency Van Buchem disease Camurati-Engelmann disease Osteopetrosis Pycnodysostosis Craniometaphyseal dysplasia Paget disease of the skull Plain radiographs showing generalised osteosclerosis, cortical thickening, and calvarial hyperostosis Genetic testing for SOST mutations Cross-sectional skull-base imaging to assess foraminal narrowing and cranial nerve compression Audiology and formal visual assessment Monitoring for raised intracranial pressure including fundoscopy Examination for syndactyly and nail changes An autosomal recessive sclerosing dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in SOST, which encodes sclerostin Loss of sclerostin removes a natural brake on Wnt-driven bone formation, producing progressive generalised high bone mass Characterised by a large mandible, frontal bossing, facial distortion, and tall stature with a heavy skeleton Syndactyly of the fingers, often with nail dysplasia, is a distinctive associated feature that helps separate it from Van Buchem disease Skull thickening entraps cranial nerves, so facial-nerve palsy, hearing loss, and optic compromise are characteristic complications Progressive skull-base overgrowth can raise intracranial pressure and, rarely, cause life-threatening brainstem compression Management focuses on surgical decompression of entrapped nerves and monitoring for raised intracranial pressure; bisphosphonates are not effective at reducing bone mass Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as headache, papilloedema, and vomiting Progressive facial-nerve palsy or rapidly worsening hearing or vision Brainstem or cerebellar signs suggesting posterior fossa crowding Sudden neurological deterioration requiring urgent decompression Confusing sclerosteosis with Van Buchem disease, distinguished by the presence of syndactyly and generally greater severity in sclerosteosis Attributing progressive facial palsy to idiopathic Bell palsy rather than bony entrapment Failing to monitor and treat rising intracranial pressure Expecting antiresorptive drugs to reduce the excess bone mass Sclerosteosis is caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in SOST, the gene encoding sclerostin, a protein secreted by osteocytes that normally inhibits the Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway in bone. Without functional sclerostin, Wnt signalling is unrestrained, driving markedly increased osteoblastic bone formation throughout the skeleton. The result is progressive, dense, sclerotic bone with cortical and skull thickening. Overgrowth of the calvaria and skull base narrows cranial foramina, entrapping cranial nerves and, in severe cases, elevating intracranial pressure. The same pathway biology has informed development of anti-sclerostin therapy for osteoporosis. The disorder is progressive; without intervention, cranial nerve entrapment and raised intracranial pressure can cause serious neurological disability, and severe cases may be life-limiting, though timely surgical decompression can relieve complications.

SCN2A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — SCN2A, Nav1.2 encephalopathy, SCN2A-related epilepsy Benign familial neonatal-infantile seizures KCNQ2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy Ohtahara syndrome of other cause Dravet syndrome (SCN1A) Autism spectrum disorder with or without epilepsy Other early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies SCN2A testing or an epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing with functional interpretation EEG appropriate to age and seizure type Brain MRI to exclude structural pathology Metabolic screening in neonatal presentations phenotype and treatment: early-onset (neonatal-infantile) seizures usually reflect gain-of-function, while later-onset seizures, autism or intellectual disability often reflect loss-of-function Early-onset gain-of-function cases frequently respond well to sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medications In contrast, later-onset loss-of-function cases may be worsened by sodium-channel blockers, so age at onset guides drug choice The spectrum ranges from self-limited familial neonatal-infantile seizures to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy Autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability without epilepsy are recognised presentations, particularly with loss-of-function variants Genetic testing with functional interpretation is central to management Refractory neonatal or infantile seizures with developmental arrest Seizure aggravation after starting a sodium-channel-blocking agent in a later-onset case Regression or emergent movement disorder Diagnostic uncertainty between gain- and loss-of-function phenotypes affecting drug choice Applying a single treatment strategy without regard to age at onset and channel effect Using sodium-channel blockers in later-onset loss-of-function cases and worsening seizures Overlooking SCN2A in autism or intellectual disability without prominent epilepsy Interpreting a variant of uncertain significance without functional or phenotypic context SCN2A encephalopathy is caused by variants in SCN2A encoding the Nav1.2 sodium channel, which mediates action-potential initiation and propagation in excitatory neurons, especially early in development. Gain-of-function variants increase sodium current and neuronal excitability, producing early-onset seizures that respond to sodium-channel blockade. Loss-of-function variants reduce excitatory signalling and impair network development, more often causing later-onset seizures, autism and intellectual disability, and such cases may deteriorate with sodium-channel-blocking agents. This mechanistic dichotomy makes age at onset a practical proxy for the underlying channel effect. Outcome is highly variable and correlates with variant type and age at onset, ranging from self-limited neonatal-infantile seizures with normal development to severe drug-resistant epilepsy with profound disability. Later-onset loss-of-function cases frequently have autism and intellectual disability regardless of seizure control.

Scoliosis — spinal curvature, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, lateral curvature of the spine Postural (non-structural) scoliosis that corrects on forward bending Leg-length discrepancy causing compensatory curvature Congenital vertebral anomalies Neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy) Syndromic scoliosis (e.g. neurofibromatosis, Marfan syndrome) Intraspinal pathology (syrinx, tethered cord, tumour) causing an atypical or painful curve Standing posteroanterior and lateral spinal radiographs to measure the Cobb angle and assess balance Assessment of skeletal maturity (e.g. Risser sign, hand/wrist bone age) Forward-bending (Adam's) test with a scoliometer to gauge rotation MRI of the whole spine for atypical, painful, rapidly progressive, or early-onset curves, or when there are neurological signs Pulmonary function testing for large thoracic or neuromuscular curves A three-dimensional deformity combining lateral curvature and vertebral rotation, most commonly adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in otherwise healthy children, predominantly girls It is often painless and detected as asymmetry of the shoulders, waist, or scapulae; a rib hump on the forward-bending (Adam's) test reflects the rotational component Curve magnitude is quantified by the Cobb angle on a standing radiograph, and skeletal maturity (e.g. Risser sign) helps predict the risk of progression Significant back pain, a rapidly progressive curve, an atypical (e.g. left thoracic) curve, or neurological signs should prompt a search for an underlying cause and MRI Scoliosis may be idiopathic, congenital (vertebral anomalies), or neuromuscular (e.g. cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy), and management differs accordingly Small curves are observed, moderate curves in a growing child may be braced to limit progression, and large or progressive curves are considered for surgical correction and fusion The likelihood of progression is greatest during the adolescent growth spurt, so monitoring is intensified during rapid growth Severe thoracic curves can restrict pulmonary function, an important consideration in early-onset and neuromuscular disease Neurological signs or symptoms suggesting an intraspinal cause requiring MRI Significant or persistent back pain, unusual for idiopathic scoliosis Rapid curve progression or an atypical curve pattern (e.g. left thoracic) Respiratory compromise from a severe thoracic curve Assuming all scoliosis is benign idiopathic disease and missing an underlying intraspinal or neuromuscular cause Overlooking a painful or atypical curve that warrants MRI Failing to monitor closely during the adolescent growth spurt when progression is most likely Confusing a compensatory postural curve from leg-length discrepancy with structural scoliosis Scoliosis is a structural lateral deviation of the spine accompanied by rotation of the vertebrae, which produces the characteristic rib or paravertebral prominence. In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis the cause is unknown but multifactorial, with genetic, growth-related, and neuromuscular balance factors implicated, and the deformity tends to worsen during periods of rapid skeletal growth. Congenital scoliosis results from failures of vertebral formation or segmentation present from birth, while neuromuscular scoliosis arises from asymmetrical muscle forces acting on the growing spine in conditions such as cerebral palsy. Progressive rotation and wedging of vertebrae make the curve increasingly rigid, and large thoracic curves can distort the chest and compromise lung capacity. Most mild adolescent idiopathic curves remain stable and require only monitoring, and bracing can prevent progression of moderate curves during growth; large or progressive curves may need surgical correction, and untreated severe curves can cause deformity, back pain, and in extreme thoracic cases cardiopulmonary compromise, while neuromuscular and congenital curves tend to be more progressive.

Scorpion sting — scorpion envenomation, scorpion bite, scorpionism Other venomous envenomation (snakebite, spider bite) Acute myocarditis from other causes Sympathomimetic drug toxicity Acute anaphylaxis Acute coronary syndrome with pulmonary oedema Continuous ECG monitoring for arrhythmia and ischaemic changes Echocardiography to assess left ventricular function in systemic envenomation Cardiac biomarkers (troponin) where myocardial injury is suspected Chest imaging for pulmonary oedema Blood glucose, electrolytes, and arterial blood gas in severe cases Venom is a mixture of neurotoxins that activate sodium channels and drive a massive autonomic (catecholamine) surge, producing a mixed sympathetic and parasympathetic toxidrome Local effects are often minor (intense pain, tingling, minimal swelling), so systemic severity can be underestimated from the sting site alone Early cholinergic features (vomiting, profuse sweating, salivation, priapism) are typically followed by an adrenergic phase with hypertension, tachycardia, and agitation The feared complication is myocardial dysfunction with acute pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock, particularly in children Prazosin, an alpha-blocker, is a key pharmacological measure to counter the catecholamine storm and offload the heart in significant envenomation Species-specific scorpion antivenom may be indicated for systemic envenomation where available, ideally given early Supportive care includes analgesia, close cardiorespiratory monitoring, and management of pulmonary oedema; dobutamine may help the failing heart Children and those presenting late with signs of myocarditis or shock carry the greatest risk and need intensive monitoring Acute pulmonary oedema, respiratory distress, or frothy sputum indicating myocardial involvement Signs of cardiogenic shock or cool clammy peripheries Priapism, profuse sweating, and repeated vomiting signalling significant systemic envenomation Young children with any systemic feature, who deteriorate rapidly New arrhythmia or ECG changes suggesting myocarditis Judging severity by the local reaction and missing evolving systemic toxicity Delaying prazosin or antivenom while awaiting overt pulmonary oedema Aggressive fluid loading in a patient with myocardial dysfunction, worsening pulmonary oedema Under-monitoring children, who can deteriorate abruptly Scorpion venom contains peptide neurotoxins that delay inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels and block potassium channels at nerve terminals, causing repetitive depolarisation and unregulated release of neurotransmitters. This produces an initial cholinergic outpouring followed by an overwhelming sympathetic (catecholamine) surge. The resulting effects include hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, increased systemic vascular resistance, and direct catecholamine-mediated myocardial injury. Myocarditis, transient left ventricular dysfunction, and increased capillary permeability lead to acute pulmonary oedema, which is the principal cause of death, especially in children. Most stings cause only local pain and resolve without sequelae, but systemic envenomation with myocardial dysfunction and pulmonary oedema can be fatal, particularly in children; early alpha-blockade, antivenom where indicated, and intensive supportive care markedly improve outcomes.

Scurvy — vitamin C deficiency, ascorbic acid deficiency, hypovitaminosis C Bleeding disorders and thrombocytopenia Vasculitis with purpura Gingivitis or periodontal disease from other causes Child abuse (mimicked by bone and periosteal changes in children) Other nutritional deficiencies causing anaemia Careful dietary history for prolonged lack of fruit and vegetables Plasma or leucocyte ascorbic acid level where available Full blood count and iron studies for associated anaemia Coagulation and platelet studies to exclude a primary bleeding disorder Radiographs in children showing characteristic metaphyseal and subperiosteal changes Characteristic features are swollen, spongy, bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, and easy bruising Impaired collagen formation causes poor wound healing, reopening of old scars, and painful subperiosteal or joint haemorrhages It should be suspected in people with very restricted diets, chronic alcohol use, severe mental illness, isolation, or malabsorption In infants and children it can cause painful pseudoparalysis from subperiosteal bleeding and bone changes A normocytic or, with associated deficiencies, mixed anaemia is common Symptoms respond rapidly and dramatically to restoration of dietary vitamin C, which strongly supports the diagnosis The diagnosis is largely clinical and dietary, since the vitamin is abundant in fresh fruit and vegetables and deficiency reflects their prolonged absence Significant haemorrhage, including gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding Painful pseudoparalysis in a child from subperiosteal haemorrhage Profound weakness and collapse in advanced deficiency Coexisting severe malnutrition requiring broader nutritional support Attributing bleeding gums or purpura to a primary haematological disorder and missing the dietary cause Failing to take an adequate dietary history in at-risk individuals Misinterpreting childhood bone changes as trauma or abuse Overlooking coexisting deficiencies in a globally malnourished patient Ascorbic acid is a cofactor for enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues, a step essential for stable collagen cross-linking. Deficiency yields defective, unstable collagen, weakening blood vessel walls, connective tissue, bone matrix, and wound repair, which manifests as haemorrhage, gum disease, and impaired healing. Vitamin C also acts as an antioxidant and aids intestinal iron absorption, so deficiency can contribute to anaemia. Humans cannot synthesise the vitamin and body stores are limited, so deficiency develops after weeks to months without dietary intake. Excellent with restoration of vitamin C intake; bleeding and gum changes resolve within days to weeks and full recovery is expected.
