Secondary peritonitis — acute secondary peritonitis, surgical peritonitis, generalised peritonitis Primary (spontaneous bacterial) peritonitis Acute pancreatitis Mesenteric ischaemia Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm Intra-abdominal abscess without generalised peritonitis Medical causes of acute abdomen (diabetic ketoacidosis, inferior myocardial infarction) Bloods including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, CRP, amylase or lipase, blood cultures, and lactate Arterial blood gas to assess acid-base status and organ perfusion Erect chest radiograph for free subdiaphragmatic gas CT abdomen and pelvis to identify the source and any collections Peritoneal fluid sampling and culture when the diagnosis or source is unclear Results from bacterial contamination of the peritoneal cavity following perforation, ischaemia, or inflammation of an abdominal viscus, unlike primary (spontaneous) peritonitis Presents with severe, constant abdominal pain worsened by movement, with tenderness, guarding, rigidity, and rebound, and the patient characteristically lies still Common sources include perforated peptic ulcer, perforated appendix, perforated diverticular disease, and bowel ischaemia or anastomotic leak Systemic features of sepsis develop rapidly: fever, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria, and, if untreated, septic shock and multi-organ failure The management triad is aggressive resuscitation, appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics, and prompt source control of the underlying cause Source control, achieved surgically or by radiological drainage, is the definitive step; antibiotics and resuscitation support but do not replace it Faeculent peritonitis from colonic perforation carries a particularly heavy bacterial and endotoxin load and a high mortality Peritoneal contamination is often graded (localised, diffuse, purulent, faeculent) and guides the extent of surgery and lavage Generalised peritonitis with sepsis, hypotension, or rising lactate indicating septic shock (surgical emergency) Faeculent contamination from colonic perforation with heavy sepsis burden Progressive organ dysfunction (oliguria, confusion, respiratory compromise) Failure to improve after resuscitation, indicating inadequate source control Delaying source control while awaiting response to antibiotics and fluids Under-resuscitating a patient with large third-space and septic losses Attributing peritonism to a medical cause and missing a surgical source Inadequate peritoneal lavage or failing to address ongoing contamination at surgery Secondary peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneum caused by spillage of gastrointestinal contents and micro-organisms into the peritoneal cavity following a breach of a hollow viscus or transmural necrosis. Gut flora, typically a mix of coliforms and anaerobes, provoke an intense inflammatory response with fibrinopurulent exudate, large third-space fluid losses, and paralytic ileus. Absorption of bacteria and endotoxin across the vast peritoneal surface drives systemic inflammatory response, sepsis, and septic shock. The peritoneum may localise infection into abscesses, but diffuse contamination overwhelms these defences and threatens life. Outcome hinges on early recognition, prompt resuscitation, and timely source control; delay, faeculent contamination, advanced age, and comorbidity markedly increase mortality, which remains high in established diffuse peritonitis with septic shock.

equipment, oxygen, suction, and reversal agents must be immediately available, and staff must be trained to manage airway and cardiovascular emergencies Reversal agents (such as an opioid antagonist for opioids and a benzodiazepine antagonist for benzodiazepines) can be used, but their duration may be shorter than the sedative, risking re-sedation Elderly, frail, obese, and sleep-apnoea patients, saturation Unintended progression to deep sedation or general anaesthesia without rescue capability Significant hypotension or bradycardia Aspiration during sedation in an at-risk patient Providing sedation without the skills or equipment to rescue a deeper-than-intended level Relying on oximetry alone and missing early hypoventilation that capnography would detect Underestimating the additive respiratory depression of sedative-opioid combinations Assuming a reversal agent fully solves the problem despite its shorter duration and risk of re-sedation Inadequate pre-procedure assessment of airway, comorbidity, and aspiration risk Sedative and analgesic agents depress the central nervous system in a dose-dependent way, reducing conscious level, blunting protective airway reflexes, and depressing respiratory drive and upper airway muscle tone. Loss of pharyngeal tone causes obstruction, while reduced central drive causes hypoventilation and apnoea, together producing hypoxaemia and hypercapnia. Many agents also cause vasodilation and myocardial depression, leading to hypotension, and some blunt compensatory reflexes. Because effects are additive, combinations of sedatives and opioids produce disproportionate respiratory and cardiovascular depression. Depressed reflexes also raise the risk of aspiration in patients with a full stomach. With appropriate patient selection, monitoring, and prompt rescue, procedural sedation is generally safe; unrecognised respiratory depression can cause hypoxic injury or death, and most serious events are linked to inadequate monitoring or rescue.

mandatory in all HIV-infected patients even without signs of infection (p.3417) Serum and CSF autoantibody testing when epilepsy onset is fulminant or accompanied by psychiatric/cognitive disturbance (autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis) (p.3417) MRI preferred over CT for detecting structural lesions; CT performed emergently when MRI is not immediately available or when a mass/infection is suspected (p.3417-3418) Interictal and ictal EEG, with activating procedures (hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep, sleep deprivation); a normal routine interictal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy - it is normal in 50-80% of known epileptics initially (p.3416-3417) Continuous video-EEG telemetry for poorly characterized events or seizures that are difficult to control, and to distinguish epileptic from psychogenic events (p.3417, p.3419) Genetic testing in infants/children with suspected genetic epilepsy syndromes, and selected older patients with an undiagnosed early-life epilepsy syndrome (p.3418) Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) - nonepileptic behaviors, often a conversion reaction; clues include side-to-side head turning, ictal eye closure, asynchronous large-amplitude limb shaking, four-limb twitching without loss of consciousness, pelvic thrusting, and prolonged waxing/waning episodes; surface EEG may be normal especially for frontal-lobe-like events, and PNES can coexist with true epilepsy (p.3419) Convulsive syncope - a brief (1-10 s) burst of convulsive movements at the onset of a faint, especially if the patient stays upright; postictal confusion is much less prominent than after a true seizure (p.3419) Alcoholic blackouts and delirium tremens (p.3419) Hypoglycemia and hypoxia as metabolic mimics of seizure (p.3419) Hyperventilation and panic attack (p.3419) Effects of psychoactive drugs / hallucinogens (p.3419) A seizure is a transient event from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of recurrent unprovoked seizures from a chronic underlying process. A single seizure, or seizures due to a correctable/avoidable cause, is not by itself epilepsy (p.3408). Operationally, epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures, though a single seizure with clinical or EEG features portending high recurrence risk can establish the diagnosis (p.3408-3409). Seizures are fundamentally classified as focal (network limited to one hemisphere; often structural) versus generalized (rapidly engaging both hemispheres) versus unknown onset; the older terms 'partial', 'simple/complex partial' are no longer used (p.3409). Focal seizures are subclassified by awareness (intact vs impaired) and onset (motor vs nonmotor); a focal seizure can evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (formerly 'secondary generalization') (p.3409). Distinguishing a focal seizure that evolves to generalized from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure is critical but difficult, because bystanders emphasize the dramatic convulsive phase and overlook the subtle focal onset; a careful history for a preceding aura or focal features, and EEG, are needed because evaluation and treatment differ substantially (p.3410). Status epilepticus is continuous seizures, or repetitive discrete seizures with impaired consciousness between them; for generalized convulsive status epilepticus the practical operational threshold is seizures lasting beyond 5 minutes (older definitions used 15-30 min) (p.3425). Generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) is a medical emergency: prolonged seizures cause cardiorespiratory dysfunction, hyperthermia, and metabolic derangements that can produce irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426). Treatment principle for status epilepticus is an escalating sequence beginning with a benzodiazepine, followed by an IV antiseizure drug, with anesthetic agents for refractory cases - alongside attention to airway, oxygenation, glucose, and reversible metabolic causes (no doses given here) (p.3426). After 30-45 min of uninterrupted GCSE the motor signs can become very subtle (only fine finger twitching or rapid eye movements); if a patient stops overt convulsions yet remains comatose, an EEG is required to exclude ongoing (nonconvulsive) status epilepticus (p.3426). If the sole cause of a seizure is a correctable metabolic disturbance (e.g., electrolyte or glucose abnormality), or a precipitant drug/illicit substance, treatment targets the underlying problem and chronic antiseizure drugs are usually unnecessary (p.3419). An apparently unprovoked first seizure carries a recurrence risk estimated at roughly 31-71% in the first 12 months; accepted risk factors favoring treatment are prior brain insult (stroke/trauma), epileptiform EEG, a significant imaging abnormality, or a nocturnal seizure (p.3420). A serum prolactin rise in the 30 min after most generalized and some focal seizures can support an epileptic cause, but it is unreliable because baseline levels are rarely available and some drugs elevate prolactin (p.3419). The clinical range of focal seizure behaviors is extremely broad, so caution is advised before dismissing paroxysmal stereotypic bizarre episodes as non-epileptic (p.3409). The age of the patient strongly informs the likely etiology of new seizures - e.g., febrile seizures and genetic/developmental causes in young children versus cerebrovascular disease, tumor, metabolic disturbance and degenerative disease in older adults (p.3411-3414). Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - immediate emergency due to risk of cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426) Persistent coma after overt convulsions stop - suspect ongoing nonconvulsive status epilepticus and obtain EEG (p.3426) Focal features, focal neurologic deficit, or abnormal/changing neurologic exam - points to a structural cause (mass, stroke, infection, trauma, degenerative disease) requiring imaging (p.3416) Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change - suspect autoimmune/antibody-mediated encephalitis (p.3413-3414, p.3417) First seizure in a patient with HIV - lumbar puncture is mandatory even without signs of infection (p.3417) Atonic ('drop attack') seizures - substantial risk of direct head injury from the fall (p.3410) Failing to exclude a treatable provoking cause (metabolic, toxic, structural, or infective) before labeling a patient as having epilepsy - many such seizures need only correction of the underlying problem, not chronic antiseizure drugs (p.3408, p.3419, p.3416-3417). Assuming a normal interictal EEG rules out epilepsy - the initial routine EEG is normal in 50-80% of patients with known epilepsy, and EEG has limited sensitivity (p.3417). Missing nonconvulsive status epilepticus: in altered consciousness or persistent coma without overt convulsions, NCSE can be present and is only revealed by EEG; intermittent seizures with prolonged postictal states are easily overlooked as causes of unexplained encephalopathy (p.3426). Overlooking a focal onset by focusing on the dramatic generalized convulsive phase, thereby misclassifying the seizure and choosing the wrong evaluation/treatment pathway (p.3410). Mistaking psychogenic nonepileptic seizures for epilepsy (or vice versa) on clinical grounds alone - even experienced epileptologists err; PNES and epilepsy can coexist, and video-EEG is the arbiter (p.3419). Misinterpreting convulsive syncope (brief convulsive jerks at the start of a faint) as a primary seizure (p.3419). Relying on headache or incontinence to distinguish seizure from syncope - these features are unreliable (p.3419). Forgetting that the postictal Todd's paralysis (focal weakness for minutes to hours after a focal seizure) can mimic an acute structural deficit such as stroke (p.3409). Misdiagnosing childhood absence epilepsy as attention deficit disorder or simple 'daydreaming' (p.3410). A seizure reflects a shift in the normal balance between excitation and inhibition in the CNS. At the cellular level the hallmark of focal seizure activity is the electrographic spike, generated by near-simultaneous bursting (the 'paroxysmal depolarization shift') of local excitatory neurons - a prolonged membrane depolarization driven by calcium influx that opens voltage-gated sodium channels, followed by a GABA- or potassium-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Surrounding inhibition normally limits spread; when recruitment overwhelms it (via rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation with enhanced transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects), activity propagates through local cortical and long commissural pathways (e.g., corpus callosum). Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges of absence seizures arise from thalamocortical oscillatory circuits involving GABA-B receptors, T-type calcium channels, and potassium channels. Many causes converge on three interacting factor classes: endogenous (genetic/developmental seizure-threshold) factors, epileptogenic factors (CNS injury such as severe penetrating head trauma, stroke, infection, or neurodegeneration that, over months to years, transforms a normal network into a chronically hyperexcitable one - 'epileptogenesis'), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, certain drugs, photic stimulation). Many inherited epilepsies are channelopathies due to ion-channel mutations (p.3411-3415). About half of people respond to the first antiseizure drug; roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite drug combinations (refractory epilepsy). People with epilepsy have a 2-3 times higher mortality than matched controls, mostly driven by the underlying etiology (e.g., tumor, stroke); excess deaths also arise from accidents, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), which typically affects young patients with convulsive seizures and tends to occur at night, possibly via brainstem-mediated cardiorespiratory/arousal effects. Simple febrile seizures do not raise the risk of later epilepsy, whereas complex febrile seizures carry a 2-5% risk. Severe penetrating head trauma carries up to a ~45% (penetrating/depressed fracture/hemorrhage/prolonged coma: 30-50%) risk of subsequent epilepsy, closed head injury with contusion 5-25%, and mild concussion only slightly increased risk. Favorable factors for staying seizure-free after planned drug withdrawal include 1-5 years of control, a single seizure type, normal exam/intelligence, normal EEG, and no family history (p.3411, p.3414, p.3420, p.3424, p.3426-3427). Seizures are classified (ILAE 2017) by onset: (1) Focal onset (with intact or impaired awareness; motor or nonmotor onset; may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); (2) Generalized onset - motor (tonic-clonic, or other such as atonic/myoclonic) or nonmotor (absence); (3) Unknown onset. Status epilepticus is staged by duration/refractoriness in management terms: impending/early (5-30 min), established and early-refractory (30 min to 48 h), and late refractory (>48 h), with subtypes generalized convulsive (GCSE) versus nonconvulsive (NCSE) (p.3409, p.3425-3426).

a normal routine interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy and is normal in 50-80% of known epilepsy patients on first recording Prolonged video-EEG telemetry for poorly characterized or refractory events and to distinguish psychogenic from epileptic seizures MRI (superior to CT) for structural lesions including hippocampal sclerosis and neuronal migration abnormalities; emergent CT when MRI unavailable or mass/infection suspected Routine bloods - electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, hepatic and renal function; toxicology screen of blood and urine Lumbar puncture when meningitis/encephalitis suspected, and mandatory in HIV-infected patients Serum and CSF autoantibody testing in fulminant epilepsy with psychiatric or cognitive features Genetic testing in suspected genetic epilepsy syndromes (diagnostic and may guide therapy choice and predict drug toxicity, e.g., HLA-B*1502 and severe cutaneous reactions) Functional imaging (PET, SPECT) and advanced localization (high-density EEG/ESI, magnetoencephalography/MSI) in medically refractory focal epilepsy Convulsive syncope (brief tonic-clonic-like movements during a faint, especially when kept upright) Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (side-to-side head movement, ictal eye closure, asynchronous limb shaking, pelvic thrusting, waxing-waning prolonged events) Transient ischemic attack Migraine aura Movement disorders and parasomnias A seizure is a transient event caused by abnormal excessive or hypersynchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of a chronic underlying tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, so a single or provoked seizure does not by itself constitute epilepsy (though a single seizure with high-risk clinical/EEG features may suffice). Roughly 5-10% of people experience at least one seizure in life, with peaks in early childhood and late adulthood; epilepsy prevalence is approximately 5-30 per 1000. The 2017 ILAE scheme classifies seizures by onset as focal, generalized, or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness (intact vs impaired) and motor vs nonmotor onset, replacing the older 'simple/complex partial' and 'secondary generalization' terms. Focal motor seizures may show a Jacksonian march (spread along the motor strip), and a postictal focal weakness (Todd's paralysis) lasting minutes to hours can mimic a stroke. Auras are themselves focal seizures with intact awareness; temporal-lobe auras include rising epigastric sensations, foul smells/tastes, fear, deja vu, and micropsia/macropsia. Typical absence seizures produce brief lapses of consciousness without postural loss or postictal confusion, with a 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave EEG provoked by hyperventilation; they are frequently misdiagnosed as attention-deficit disorder or daydreaming. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures begin with a tonic phase (ictal cry, apnea/cyanosis, tongue biting, sympathetic surge) evolving to a clonic phase, followed by postictal flaccidity, confusion, headache, and myalgia. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis is the most common cause of focal seizures with impaired awareness and is characteristically medically refractory but responds well to surgery. Etiology is strongly age-dependent: neonates - perinatal hypoxia-ischemia, infection, and metabolic derangements; young children - febrile seizures; adolescents/young adults - trauma, genetic syndromes, drugs, autoantibodies; older adults - cerebrovascular disease (up to ~50% of new epilepsy over 65), tumor, and degenerative disease. Distinguishing seizure from syncope: aura, cyanosis, prolonged motor activity (30-60 s), and many minutes to hours of postictal confusion favor seizure, whereas brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, pallor, and provocation by pain/standing favor syncope; headache and incontinence are unreliable discriminators. A transient serum prolactin rise in the first 30 minutes after most generalized and some focal seizures can support a true seizure over a psychogenic event, but is unreliable without a baseline and because some drugs elevate prolactin. Penetrating head injury carries up to a 45% risk of subsequent epilepsy via epileptogenesis, illustrating how an acquired structural lesion can permanently lower seizure threshold. Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - continuous or repetitive seizures (practically, GCSE lasting beyond ~5 min); a medical emergency that can cause cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury After 30-45 minutes of uninterrupted seizures the clinical signs may become subtle while damaging electrographic seizures continue, including in patients paralyzed by neuromuscular blockade Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change suggesting autoimmune (e.g., anti-potassium-channel or anti-glutamate-receptor) epilepsy New seizure in an older adult suggesting cerebrovascular disease, tumor, or degenerative disease First seizure with focal features, persistent neurologic deficit, fever, or suspected CNS infection prompting urgent imaging and possible lumbar puncture Atonic 'drop attacks' with high risk of head injury Failing to distinguish a focal seizure that secondarily generalizes from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure because bystanders emphasize the convulsive phase and overlook subtle focal onset/aura - a distinction that materially changes evaluation and treatment. Misdiagnosing absence epilepsy as attention-deficit disorder or simple daydreaming. Concluding bizarre paroxysmal stereotyped behavior is non-epileptic; focal (especially frontal-lobe) seizures can produce highly unusual behaviors. Assuming a normal interictal EEG excludes epilepsy, or that epileptiform discharges by themselves prove epilepsy. Over-relying on incontinence or headache to separate seizure from syncope, as these are unreliable. Assuming psychogenic nonepileptic seizures exclude true epilepsy - the two frequently coexist. Misreading subtle late-stage status epilepticus as resolution when damaging electrographic seizures persist. Seizures arise from a shift in the normal balance between neuronal excitation and inhibition in the CNS. Focal seizure activity begins in a discrete cortical region and can invade surrounding cortex; the hallmark is the electrographic spike produced by near-simultaneous bursting of many excitatory neurons (hypersynchronization). At the cellular level, a prolonged paroxysmal depolarization shift driven by calcium influx opens voltage-dependent sodium channels and generates repetitive action potentials, followed by a GABA- or potassium-channel-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Spread is normally limited by intact hyperpolarization and feedforward surround inhibition; recruitment of neighboring neurons occurs through rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation enhancing transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects, allowing propagation via local and commissural (corpus callosum) pathways. Epilepsy results from a dynamic interplay of endogenous (often genetic, maturational) factors, epileptogenic factors (e.g., severe head trauma, stroke, infection, neurodegeneration, developmental malformations), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, photic stimulation). Many gene mutations affecting ion channels (e.g., SCN1A, KCNQ2), neurotransmitter receptors, and metabolic transporters (e.g., SLC2A1/GLUT-1) underlie specific syndromes. Outcome varies widely by syndrome and etiology. Typical absence epilepsy and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy generally respond well to medication (though JME remission is uncommon), whereas mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and epilepsies tied to structural lesions or developmental delay are often refractory. About half of patients do not respond to the first medication, and roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite optimal drug therapy. Favorable predictors for successfully discontinuing therapy include 1-5 years of complete control, a single seizure type (generalized carrying a better prognosis than focal), normal neurologic examination and intelligence, no family history of epilepsy, and a normal EEG; a normal EEG generally implies a better prognosis. People with epilepsy have a death rate roughly 2-3 times that of matched controls, mostly attributable to the underlying cause but also to accidents, status epilepticus, and SUDEP. Seizures are classified by ILAE 2017 onset: focal (with intact or impaired awareness, motor or nonmotor), generalized (motor such as tonic-clonic, atonic, myoclonic; or nonmotor/absence), or unknown onset. Severity at the syndromic extreme is status epilepticus: continuous or repetitive seizures with impaired interictal consciousness, subdivided into generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) and nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE). Although traditionally defined as 15-30 minutes of activity, GCSE is practically treated as an emergency when convulsions last beyond about 5 minutes. Febrile seizures are graded as simple (single, brief, symmetric) versus complex (repeated, lasting over 15 minutes, or with focal features).

Selective IgA deficiency — IgA deficiency, selective immunoglobulin A deficiency, sIgAD Common variable immunodeficiency (may share features and can evolve from IgA deficiency) Transient low IgA in early childhood before immune maturation Drug-induced IgA suppression (e.g. certain anticonvulsants) IgG subclass or specific antibody deficiency presenting with recurrent infection Coeliac disease and other associated autoimmune disorders Secondary immunodeficiency from protein loss Serum IgA, IgG, and IgM to confirm isolated IgA deficiency IgG subclass levels and vaccine-specific antibody responses to assess for broader deficiency Coeliac evaluation using IgG-based serology or duodenal biopsy given unreliable IgA-based tests Screening for associated autoimmune disease when clinically indicated Testing for anti-IgA antibodies before transfusion in patients with prior reactions Periodic reassessment of immunoglobulins to detect evolution toward CVID Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and is defined by a very low or absent serum IgA with normal IgG and IgM and otherwise intact immunity The majority of affected individuals are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally, so a low IgA alone does not equate to clinical disease When symptomatic, patients tend to have recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, reflecting the loss of secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces There is a recognised association with atopy and with autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease, so unexplained IgA deficiency warrants screening for these Coeliac serology based on IgA antibodies can be falsely negative in IgA deficiency, so IgG-based testing or histology should be used instead A minority have severe anaphylactic reactions to blood products because of anti-IgA antibodies, so washed or IgA-deficient blood components may be required There is no specific replacement therapy because IgA cannot be effectively replaced; management centres on prompt treatment of infections and, where needed, prophylactic antibiotics A small proportion, particularly those with associated IgG subclass deficiency or poor vaccine responses, can progress over time toward common variable immunodeficiency and need monitoring Anaphylactic transfusion reaction from anti-IgA antibodies, requiring IgA-deficient or washed blood products Progressive fall in IgG or poor vaccine responses signalling evolution to CVID Recurrent severe or invasive infection prompting reassessment of the full antibody profile Unexplained malabsorption or systemic autoimmune features suggesting an associated disorder Interpreting an incidental low IgA as clinically significant disease in an asymptomatic person Missing coeliac disease because of falsely negative IgA-based serology Transfusing standard blood products in a patient with anti-IgA antibodies Failing to reassess immunoglobulins over time and thus missing progression to CVID Selective IgA deficiency results from a failure of terminal differentiation of IgA-committed B cells into IgA-secreting plasma cells, so that little or no IgA reaches serum and mucosal secretions. The loss of secretory IgA impairs mucosal immune exclusion of pathogens at the respiratory and gastrointestinal surfaces, though compensatory secretory IgM often limits the clinical impact. The precise molecular basis is usually unknown; it shares genetic susceptibility loci (including MHC haplotypes and TACI variants) with CVID, and the two conditions can occur within the same families and occasionally evolve into one another. Immune dysregulation underlies the associated atopic and autoimmune disease. Most individuals with selective IgA deficiency remain well and have a normal life expectancy. Symptomatic patients generally do well with treatment of infections, but a subset with additional immune defects have more infections and may progress to CVID, and rare transfusion anaphylaxis is a serious hazard.

to cardiomyopathy or myopathy Failing to consider geographic and dietary risk in endemic regions Assuming repletion will reverse advanced established cardiac damage Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins, notably the glutathione peroxidases and thioredoxin reductases that defend cells against oxidative damage, and into the deiodinases that convert thyroxine to active triiodothyronine. Deficiency reduces antioxidant defence, leaving tissues, especially cardiac and skeletal muscle, vulnerable to oxidative injury, which underlies the cardiomyopathy and myopathy. Impaired deiodinase function can also affect thyroid hormone metabolism. Repletion can halt progression and prevent deficiency-related disease, and early cardiomyopathy may improve, but established myocardial damage in Keshan disease may be irreversible.

Sengers syndrome — Cataract-hypertrophic cardiomyopathy-mitochondrial myopathy, AGK deficiency, Acylglycerol kinase deficiency, AGK Other mitochondrial cardiomyopathies and Barth syndrome Infantile Pompe disease and other metabolic cardiomyopathies Sarcomeric (genetic) hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without metabolic features Congenital cataract syndromes of other cause Congenital myopathies and myasthenic syndromes Other combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency disorders Echocardiography and ECG to detect and monitor hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia Resting and post-exercise blood lactate Ophthalmological examination for congenital or early cataract AGK molecular genetic testing Skeletal muscle biopsy for histology and respiratory-chain enzymology Creatine kinase and assessment of the myopathy The defining combination is congenital cataracts, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal (mitochondrial) myopathy and exercise intolerance with lactic acidosis It is an autosomal recessive nuclear disorder caused by mutations in AGK, encoding acylglycerol kinase, a mitochondrial protein involved in lipid metabolism and mitochondrial protein import Congenital or early cataracts are a consistent and often presenting feature that should prompt cardiac evaluation Lactate rises markedly with exertion despite normal cognition, and the myopathy causes hypotonia and fatigue The hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the principal determinant of prognosis and can cause heart failure or arrhythmia A severe neonatal form presents early with profound cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis, while a milder form allows survival into adulthood Care is supportive with cataract surgery, cardiac management and avoidance of mitochondrial toxins; intellect is typically preserved Decompensated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or heart failure Life-threatening arrhythmia Severe neonatal lactic acidosis with cardiorespiratory compromise Rapid clinical deterioration during intercurrent illness or metabolic stress Treating congenital cataracts in isolation without evaluating the heart, thereby missing the cardiomyopathy Attributing the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to a sarcomeric cause and overlooking a metabolic origin Assuming cognitive impairment, when intellect is characteristically preserved Exposing patients to mitochondrial toxins that can worsen the energy deficit Sengers syndrome is caused by recessive loss-of-function mutations in AGK, which encodes acylglycerol kinase. This mitochondrial enzyme phosphorylates monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol and also functions as a component of the TIM22 carrier import machinery that inserts certain proteins, including the adenine nucleotide translocator, into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of AGK disturbs mitochondrial membrane lipid composition and impairs import of key carriers, secondarily compromising oxidative phosphorylation and ATP export. Tissues with high and sustained energy demand, notably cardiac and skeletal muscle, and the metabolically specialised lens are preferentially affected, giving the cardiomyopathy, myopathy and cataracts. Prognosis is bimodal: the severe neonatal form usually causes death in infancy from cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis, whereas the milder form permits survival into adulthood with cataract, myopathy and manageable cardiac disease, cardiac status being the main prognostic factor.

requiring dialysis or transplantation Rapidly declining vision in an infant suggesting Leber congenital amaurosis Growth failure and anaemia signalling advanced chronic kidney disease Electrolyte disturbance from severe polyuria and salt wasting Missing the renal diagnosis in a child evaluated only for visual impairment Overlooking nephronophthisis because kidneys appear normal-sized on ultrasound Attributing polyuria and enuresis to behavioural causes rather than a renal concentrating defect Failing to test for the ciliopathy overlap that may include neurological features Senior-Loken syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in nephronophthisis-associated genes that encode proteins localising to the primary cilium, basal body, and centrosome. Defective ciliary function in renal tubular epithelium leads to progressive tubulointerstitial nephropathy with tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and cyst formation at the corticomedullary junction, the hallmark of nephronophthisis. The same proteins are essential for the connecting cilium of photoreceptors, so their loss produces photoreceptor degeneration and inherited retinal dystrophy, explaining the combined renal and retinal phenotype. The renal disease is progressive and most affected individuals reach end-stage kidney disease during childhood or adolescence, requiring renal replacement therapy. Visual prognosis depends on the retinal genotype, ranging from profound early blindness to slowly progressive visual loss.

treatment Failure to improve after aspiration and antibiotics indicating a loculated or abscessed collection needing drainage Immunocompromised host in whom infection may progress atypically or rapidly Assuming an inflamed bursa is gouty or traumatic and missing infection Confusing septic bursitis with septic arthritis, which requires more aggressive intervention Injecting corticosteroid into a bursa without excluding infection Stopping treatment prematurely and precipitating relapse A bursa is a synovial-lined sac that reduces friction over bony prominences. Superficial bursae such as the olecranon and prepatellar sit just beneath the skin and are readily seeded by direct trauma or overlying cellulitis. Introduced bacteria, usually skin flora, provoke an inflammatory exudate within the bursal cavity, producing pain, swelling, warmth, and sometimes abscess formation. Because the bursa is anatomically separate from the joint, infection tends to remain localised unless it extends into surrounding tissue. Superficial septic bursitis generally resolves well with aspiration and appropriate antibiotics; recurrence or chronicity is more likely with repeated trauma or delayed treatment, and a minority require surgical bursectomy.

Serotonin syndrome / NMS — Medication review (serotonergics/antipsychotics) CK, renal function Temperature Hyperthermia + rigidity — stop agent, cooling, supportive ICU care Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs serotonin syndrome (mutual differential; distinguish by onset speed, neuromuscular pattern and offending drug class) Lithium toxicity (tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, encephalopathy, may include hyperthermia and seizures in severe cases) Anticholinergic toxidrome Sympathomimetic toxicity (amphetamines, cocaine) Strychnine poisoning Withdrawal syndromes (ethanol, sedative-hypnotics) Meningitis Encephalitis (including brainstem encephalitis) Cerebral abscess Sepsis / systemic inflammatory response syndrome Malaria Typhoid Tetanus Core temperature measurement (most reliable prognosticator of poor outcome in stimulant/withdrawal-type toxidromes) Creatine kinase (markedly elevated in NMS; rhabdomyolysis complicates both) Lactate / arterial blood gas (lactic acidosis is a recognised complication) Coagulation studies (monitor for disseminated intravascular coagulation when hyperthermia is sustained) Toxicology screen and detailed medication review (serotonergic agents, dopamine antagonists, recent dose changes or dopaminergic withdrawal) Cranial CT and CSF analysis if mental status fails to improve, to exclude structural or infectious CNS causes Malignant hyperthermia (e.g. after general anesthesia) Heatstroke / exertional and classic heat illness Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Diabetic ketoacidosis Status epilepticus Anticholinergic toxidrome Stimulant/sympathomimetic toxicity Serotonin syndrome and NMS overlap closely (both cause fever, altered mental status, rigidity and autonomic instability), but prominent myoclonus is characteristically a feature of serotonin syndrome and helps separate it from NMS (p.3517). NMS typically evolves over days to weeks after a neuroleptic/dopamine-antagonist is started or up-titrated, i.e. a comparatively slow, subacute onset (p.3517). NMS is not only triggered by antipsychotics: it can also be precipitated by abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medication in Parkinson's disease patients (p.3517). Serotonin syndrome arises from agents with serotonin-like activity or that block serotonin reuptake (e.g. tryptophan, MDMA/'ecstasy', meperidine, SSRIs), and is rare but potentially fatal (p.3517). The serotonin-syndrome picture is attributed to hyperstimulation of brainstem 5-HT1A (and 5-HT2) receptors (p.3667). The antibiotic linezolid (and to a lesser degree tedizolid) is a monoamine-oxidase inhibitor: combined with serotonergic agents such as SSRIs it can precipitate serotonin syndrome (p.1172). Combining an MAOI with an SSRI is an absolute contraindication because of serotonin-syndrome risk; serotonergic agonists (tryptophan, fenfluramine, triptans) carry a similar hazard (p.3667). Both syndromes are toxidromes in the CNS-syndrome / 'stimulated' physiologic category, alongside lithium toxicity, extrapyramidal reactions and strychnine (p.3715). Hyperthermia — sustained core temperature elevation predicts poor outcome and can progress to irreversible cellular injury Rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine kinase Autonomic instability — labile blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis Acute renal failure Lactic acidosis Disseminated intravascular coagulation / coagulopathy Coma, seizures or multisystem organ failure Mistaking one syndrome for the other: rapid-onset hyperreflexia/myoclonus/clonus after a serotonergic drug points to serotonin syndrome, whereas slow (days-to-weeks) lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia after a dopamine-antagonist points to NMS — the offending drug class and onset tempo are the key discriminators (p.3517). Overlooking non-psychiatric culprits: the antibiotic linezolid is an MAOI and can trigger serotonin syndrome with concurrent SSRIs (p.1172). Forgetting that NMS can be precipitated by stopping dopaminergic drugs (not only by starting antipsychotics) in Parkinson's disease (p.3517). Anchoring on infection: the fever-plus-rigidity-plus-altered-mental-status picture closely mimics meningitis/encephalitis and sepsis, and structural/infectious causes should be excluded if mental status does not improve (p.3715, p.3773). Dantrolene is ineffective for hyperthermia not caused by malignant hyperthermia, so a hyperthermia mechanism must be identified rather than assumed (p.3776). Some atypical antipsychotics (e.g. chlorpromazine used for agitation) can themselves cause or worsen NMS — adding a neuroleptic to an undifferentiated hyperthermic patient can be harmful (p.3776). Serotonin syndrome results from excess CNS and peripheral serotonergic activity — promotion of serotonin release, inhibition of its reuptake, or direct stimulation of serotonin receptors (chiefly 5-HT1A and 5-HT2), occurring alone or when serotonergic drugs are combined. NMS, in contrast, is linked to dopamine-antagonist (neuroleptic) exposure or abrupt loss of dopaminergic tone, producing central hyperthermia, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction; central dopamine depletion impairs hypothalamic (preoptic/anterior) thermoregulation. Both are classified among the hypothalamic disorders of autonomic/temperature regulation (Harrison 22e p.3541, p.3517, p.3715). Both syndromes are potentially fatal; serotonin syndrome is described as rare but able to progress to death, and NMS can be lethal (e.g. typical neuroleptics in Lewy body disease can cause NMS and death). The duration of hyperthermia drives morbidity and mortality, and progression to rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, DIC and multisystem organ failure marks severe disease (Harrison 22e p.3517, p.3715, p.3773). Harrison frames severity by the physiologic toxidrome state (stimulated vs depressed vs discordant) and by the degree of physiologic derangement on serial vital signs; escalating findings — hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and multisystem organ failure — mark severe serotonin syndrome, while marked CK elevation with renal failure and labile autonomic signs marks severe NMS. No formal numeric grading scale is given in the source (Harrison 22e p.3715, p.3517).

raised colorectal cancer risk and warrant earlier and more frequent colonoscopic screening Management is regular colonoscopic surveillance with clearance of significant polyps, and surgery is reserved for uncontrollable polyp burden or malignancy The serrated pathway is frequently associated with BRAF mutation, CpG island methylation and, in some tumours, acquired mismatch-repair deficiency A large or endoscopically complex serrated lesion suspicious for malignancy A discrete mass or advanced histology on biopsy Iron-deficiency anaemia or rectal bleeding Rapidly increasing polyp burden that cannot be cleared endoscopically Missing flat, pale sessile serrated lesions in the proximal colon during suboptimal colonoscopy Dismissing hyperplastic-appearing polyps without recognising the cumulative diagnostic criteria Failing to screen first-degree relatives at increased colorectal cancer risk Assuming a germline mutation must be present and stopping surveillance when testing is negative Serrated polyposis reflects dysregulation of the serrated neoplasia pathway, a route to colorectal cancer distinct from the conventional adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Sessile serrated lesions commonly carry activating BRAF mutations and develop widespread promoter hypermethylation known as the CpG island methylator phenotype, which silences tumour-suppressor and repair genes. Epigenetic silencing of a mismatch-repair gene in some lesions leads to acquired microsatellite instability, driving progression from serrated polyp to carcinoma; while the condition clusters in families, a consistent germline determinant has not been established for most patients. With diligent colonoscopic surveillance and complete removal of significant serrated lesions, colorectal cancer risk can be well controlled and prognosis is good. Risk persists lifelong and depends on the completeness of examinations, so meticulous ongoing surveillance and family screening are important.

Serum sickness — serum sickness reaction, type III hypersensitivity reaction, serum-sickness-like reaction Serum-sickness-like reaction to antibiotics (e.g. cefaclor) Acute viral infection (e.g. hepatitis B, parvovirus) with rash and arthralgia Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective-tissue disease Urticarial vasculitis and other small-vessel vasculitides Acute drug reaction such as DRESS or an urticarial drug eruption Reactive or infectious arthritis Serum C3 and C4, which fall during the active immune-complex phase Full blood count and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) Urinalysis to detect renal involvement Assessment for circulating immune complexes or cryoglobulins where available Serologies to exclude viral and autoimmune mimics Skin biopsy in atypical cases to evaluate for vasculitis Serum sickness is the classic immune-complex (type III) hypersensitivity reaction, presenting with fever, rash, arthralgia or arthritis, and lymphadenopathy Symptoms characteristically begin about one to three weeks after first exposure to the offending agent, with a faster onset on re-exposure because the patient is already sensitised Historically it followed heterologous (animal) antiserum, and today it is most often triggered by antitoxins, antivenoms, therapeutic antibodies, and certain drugs The rash is often urticarial or a serpiginous purplish eruption at the border of the palms and soles, a helpful clinical clue During the active phase complement is consumed, so serum C3 and C4 fall and can be used to support the diagnosis and track resolution A serum-sickness-like reaction, most often attributed to antibiotics such as cefaclor, resembles serum sickness clinically but lacks the true immune-complex and hypocomplementaemic features and is generally benign The condition is usually self-limiting once the causative agent is withdrawn, with recovery over days to a couple of weeks Management principles are stopping and avoiding the trigger, symptomatic relief with antihistamines and anti-inflammatory agents, and corticosteroids for severe or systemic disease Significant renal involvement with proteinuria, haematuria, or rising creatinine Concurrent anaphylaxis or angioedema at the time of re-exposure to the antigen Neurologic involvement or severe systemic illness suggesting extensive immune-complex disease Features pointing to a severe drug reaction such as DRESS rather than simple serum sickness Failing to take a careful exposure history for antisera, antivenoms, or therapeutic antibodies given weeks earlier Confusing serum sickness with an acute IgE-mediated allergic reaction and mismanaging the tempo of illness Overlooking renal involvement by not checking urinalysis and renal function Re-administering the same heterologous protein or drug without recognising the sensitisation risk Serum sickness is mediated by circulating antigen-antibody (immune) complexes. After exposure to a foreign protein or drug-protein conjugate, the host mounts an antibody response; as antibody rises while antigen is still present, soluble immune complexes form in antigen-relative excess. These complexes deposit in small vessels of the skin, joints, kidneys, and elsewhere, where they activate complement and recruit neutrophils, producing local inflammation and tissue injury (a type III hypersensitivity reaction). Complement activation consumes C3 and C4, accounting for the transient hypocomplementaemia. Once the antigen is cleared and complexes are removed, the process resolves. Serum-sickness-like reactions produce a similar clinical picture through incompletely understood mechanisms without demonstrable immune-complex disease. Serum sickness is generally self-limiting and resolves without sequelae once the causative agent is removed, with symptoms settling over days to a couple of weeks. Recovery may be hastened by corticosteroids in severe cases; significant organ involvement is uncommon but warrants closer follow-up.

Severe acute malnutrition — SAM, severe malnutrition, marasmus, kwashiorkor, protein-energy malnutrition Oedema from nephrotic syndrome or cardiac/hepatic failure Chronic infection (including tuberculosis and HIV) Malabsorption syndromes (e.g. coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis) Chronic diarrhoeal disease Underlying malignancy or chronic illness causing wasting Weight, height/length, and mid-upper arm circumference with oedema assessment Blood glucose (to detect hypoglycaemia) Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium, and phosphate Haemoglobin and assessment for anaemia Screening for infection (including tuberculosis, HIV where relevant) and malaria in endemic areas Assessment of hydration status, which is difficult to judge clinically in SAM Defined in young children by severe wasting (weight-for-height well below the reference median, or a very low mid-upper arm circumference) and/or bilateral pitting oedema of nutritional origin. Marasmus is severe wasting from overall energy deficit; kwashiorkor is characterised by oedema, and mixed pictures occur. Kwashiorkor features include oedema, sparse depigmented hair, skin changes (flaky-paint dermatosis), an enlarged fatty liver, and apathy. Children with SAM are highly vulnerable to hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and overwhelming infection, which is often present without classic signs. Refeeding must be cautious and staged to avoid refeeding syndrome; overly rapid feeding and excess fluid or sodium can precipitate cardiac failure and death. Initial stabilisation prioritises treating and preventing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia, correcting dehydration carefully, and giving broad micronutrient support. Rehydration is preferably oral or nasogastric with a low-sodium, higher-potassium solution, because intravenous fluids readily cause fluid overload. Management follows a stabilisation phase with cautious feeding, followed by a rehabilitation phase with catch-up growth once appetite and stability return. Hypoglycaemia and hypothermia Signs of shock or severe dehydration (difficult to assess and easy to overtreat) Developing signs of heart failure during rehydration or refeeding (refeeding syndrome) Severe anaemia requiring careful transfusion Lethargy, hypothermia, or hypoglycaemia as subtle markers of serious infection Feeding too much too quickly and precipitating refeeding syndrome and heart failure Using standard intravenous rehydration and causing fluid overload Relying on usual signs of infection, which are often absent Missing hypoglycaemia and hypothermia because signs are subtle Treating oedema as fluid overload rather than recognising nutritional kwashiorkor Prolonged inadequate intake of energy, protein, and micronutrients forces the body into a state of reductive adaptation: metabolic rate falls, organ function is downregulated, and body composition shifts with loss of fat and muscle. Sodium-potassium pump activity is impaired, causing intracellular sodium retention and total-body potassium and magnesium depletion despite oedema. Hepatic and cardiac function, immune competence, and thermoregulation are all compromised. In kwashiorkor, hypoalbuminaemia and increased capillary permeability contribute to oedema. These adaptations make the child dangerously intolerant of the metabolic demands of aggressive feeding and fluid loads. With careful phased management and treatment of complications, most children recover, but case fatality is high when complications such as hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, sepsis, or refeeding syndrome are missed or when rehydration is too aggressive.

and chest imaging for thymic assessment Group of inherited disorders defined by profound impairment of T-cell development, with variable B-cell and natural killer cell involvement, causing severe combined immune failure Affected infants typically present in the first months of life with recurrent, severe, or opportunistic infections, chronic diarrhoea, and failure to thrive Persistent or excision circles enables presymptomatic detection and early treatment Definitive treatment is immune reconstitution, principally haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with gene therapy and enzyme replacement for specific subtypes Early diagnosis before infections develop markedly improves transplant outcomes This is a paediatric emergency: suspected SCID requires immediate specialist referral and protective isolation Live vaccines, including BCG and rotavirus, are contraindicated and can cause fatal disseminated infection Blood products must be irradiated, cytomegalovirus-safe, and leucodepleted to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease Any infection can rapidly become life-threatening and needs urgent aggressive management Administering live vaccines before immunodeficiency is excluded Transfusing non-irradiated blood products Delaying referral by attributing recurrent infections to ordinary childhood illness Overlooking lymphopenia on a routine full blood count Severe combined immunodeficiency comprises a genetically diverse group of disorders that share a failure of adaptive immunity due to absent or non-functional T lymphocytes, with associated defects in B-cell and sometimes natural killer cell function. Underlying defects disrupt lymphocyte development or function through varied mechanisms, such as impaired cytokine receptor signalling in common gamma-chain deficiency, toxic metabolite accumulation in adenosine deaminase deficiency, or failure of antigen-receptor gene rearrangement. Without functional T cells, the coordinated immune response to pathogens collapses, leaving infants unable to clear common and opportunistic organisms. Most forms are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with the common gamma-chain form being X-linked. Without immune reconstitution the condition is usually fatal within the first year or two of life, but early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly before infections occur, offers a high chance of long-term survival and immune recovery.

cytogenetic abnormality, rising blasts, or acquired CSF3R/RUNX1 mutation signalling leukaemic transformation Escalating G-CSF requirement with declining response Sepsis or deep-seated infection in a febrile neutropenic infant requiring urgent broad-spectrum cover Mistaking severe congenital neutropenia for autoimmune neutropenia and delaying G-CSF Failing to perform serial marrow surveillance and missing early clonal evolution Attributing a poor G-CSF response solely to under-dosing rather than considering transformation Overlooking syndromic features that point to a specific genetic diagnosis Severe congenital neutropenia is a group of inherited disorders of granulopoiesis in which neutrophil precursors fail to mature. ELANE mutations produce a misfolded neutrophil elastase that triggers the unfolded protein response and endoplasmic reticulum stress, driving apoptosis of promyelocytes; HAX1 mutations remove a protein that maintains mitochondrial membrane potential, again promoting precursor apoptosis. Other genes converge on similar pathways of accelerated myeloid progenitor death or defective intracellular trafficking. The net effect is arrest of myeloid maturation with near-absent circulating neutrophils. Chronic G-CSF stimulation of a genetically unstable myeloid compartment, together with acquisition of CSF3R and other somatic mutations, underlies the elevated risk of transformation to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia. G-CSF has transformed survival by controlling infection, but patients carry a substantial lifelong risk of transformation to myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia, so surveillance is essential and transplantation is curative for high-risk or refractory disease.
