arousal disorder Female orgasmic disorder Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (vaginismus, dyspareunia) Depression, anxiety, or relationship dysfunction Medication-induced or endocrine (menopausal) sexual dysfunction Comprehensive biopsychosocial and sexual history including relationship context Review of medications, particularly antidepressants, and chronic medical conditions Pelvic examination to identify atrophy, pain, or structural causes Targeted endocrine assessment where indicated, including menopausal status Screening for depression, anxiety, and history of sexual trauma Female sexual dysfunction spans disorders of desire, arousal, orgasm, and sexual pain, and is only a clinical diagnosis when the problem is persistent and causes personal distress The female sexual response is better understood as a circular, intimacy-driven model rather than a rigid linear sequence, so context and relationship factors are central Causes are typically multifactorial, combining biological, psychological, and interpersonal contributors that should all be explored Hormonal changes, especially the oestrogen decline of menopause, commonly reduce arousal and lubrication and contribute to genitourinary and pain symptoms Many common medications, particularly serotonergic antidepressants, and chronic illnesses such as diabetes, depression, and vascular disease impair sexual function A sensitive, open history that legitimises the concern is essential, as patients often will not raise the topic themselves Management addresses reversible contributors, optimises relationship and psychological factors, and considers psychosexual therapy alongside targeted treatments such as local oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms Persistent pain with intercourse points towards specific disorders such as vaginismus or dyspareunia that require directed assessment Sexual pain or bleeding suggesting an underlying gynaecological pathology History of sexual abuse or trauma requiring sensitive, specialised support Coexisting depression with suicidal ideation New sexual dysfunction accompanying signs of significant systemic or neurological disease Not asking about sexual health, so distressing problems go unrecognised Attributing dysfunction to a single cause when it is usually multifactorial Overlooking medication, especially antidepressants, as a reversible contributor Neglecting relationship and psychological dimensions in favour of a purely biomedical approach Female sexual function integrates neurological, vascular, hormonal, and psychological systems. Sexual arousal depends on genital vasocongestion and lubrication mediated by autonomic and nitric-oxide pathways, while desire and orgasm involve central dopaminergic, serotonergic, and hormonal modulation. Dysfunction arises when any of these are disrupted: oestrogen deficiency thins and dries the vaginal epithelium and reduces blood flow, vascular and neurological disease (as in diabetes) impairs the genital response, and medications such as SSRIs blunt desire and orgasm. Psychological factors including depression, anxiety, past trauma, body image, and relationship conflict powerfully influence desire and arousal, and pain disorders can create a self-reinforcing cycle of anticipatory anxiety and avoidance. The circular, context-dependent nature of female sexual response means these factors interact rather than act in isolation. Outcomes are generally good when contributing factors are identified and addressed; genitourinary symptoms of menopause respond well to local oestrogen, medication-related effects may improve with adjustment, and psychosexual and relationship interventions can substantially help desire and arousal disorders.

Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach — STI overview, STD overview, Sexually transmitted diseases, Venereal disease Acute epididymitis must be distinguished from testicular torsion (a surgical emergency with sudden pain, testicular elevation, and absent Doppler flow), testicular tumor, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1101) Dysuric women: STI-associated urethral syndrome (sterile pyuria, <10^2 conventional uropathogens/mL) versus bacterial cystitis (single uropathogen >=10^2/mL) versus acute pyelonephritis (costovertebral tenderness/fever) (Harrison 22e p.1100-1101) Persistent genital ulcer not resolving with syndrome-based therapy: consider donovanosis, carcinoma, and other nonvenereal dermatoses on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1108) Pelvic inflammatory disease that is not due to specific STIs (secondary to appendicitis, regional ileitis, diverticulitis, hematogenous tuberculosis or staphylococcal bacteremia, or tropical disease such as schistosomiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1104) Chronic granulomatous epididymal disease such as tuberculosis mimicking sexually acquired epididymitis when symptoms persist after therapy (Harrison 22e p.1101) Risk assessment using a structured sexual-history questionnaire (e.g., the eleven-question STD/HIV risk assessment) to guide screening and presumptive treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.1098) Urethral Gram's stain to confirm urethritis and detect gram-negative diplococci, recognizing that up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections can yield a negative Gram's stain (Harrison 22e p.1099) Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, M. genitalium, and T. vaginalis on appropriate genital/urine specimens (Harrison 22e p.1099-1100) Genital ulcer workup: dark-field examination, direct fluorescent antibody, or PCR for T. pallidum; RPR/VDRL/EIA serology for syphilis; culture, FA, ELISA, or PCR for HSV; HSV-2 type-specific serology; PCR or culture for H. ducreyi in chancroid-endemic settings (Harrison 22e p.1108-1109) Biopsy of a genital ulcer persisting beyond the expected natural history (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid or syphilis up to 6 weeks) to exclude donovanosis and malignancy (Harrison 22e p.1108) Aspiration of fluctuant inguinal nodes for culture/PCR (H. ducreyi) plus Gram's stain to exclude other pyogenic bacteria (Harrison 22e p.1108) Cervical ectopy (columnar epithelium on the ectocervix), often mislabeled 'cervical erosion,' confused with infectious endocervicitis but showing clear/cloudy mucus and intact epithelium on colposcopy (Harrison 22e p.1104) Testicular tumor or trauma presenting as scrotal pain/swelling mimicking epididymitis (Harrison 22e p.1101) Genital carcinoma or nonvenereal dermatoses presenting as a persistent genital ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1108) STIs are syndrome-driven in practice: most patients are managed initially by presenting symptoms, signs, and risk factors rather than by a confirmed microbial diagnosis, with common syndromes including male urethritis, epididymitis, mucopurulent cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital/perianal ulcers, PID, and proctitis (Harrison 22e p.1100). More than 40 microorganisms are now recognized as predominantly sexually transmitted or frequently sexually transmissible, spanning bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi, and ectoparasites (Harrison 22e p.1096). The initial rate of spread of any STI in a population is the product of three factors: the rate of sexual exposure of susceptible to infectious persons, the per-exposure transmission efficiency, and the duration of infectivity (Harrison 22e p.1096). Genital HPV is described as the most common sexually transmitted pathogen in the United States, and HPV and hepatitis B virus remain major causes of cervical and hepatocellular carcinoma respectively in the developing world (Harrison 22e p.1096-1097). Reported syphilis in the United States in 2022 (207,255 cases, all stages and congenital) was the highest since 1950, with congenital syphilis rate of 102.5 per 100,000 live births and 282 congenital syphilis-related stillbirths/infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097). All four major curable STIs (gonorrhea, chlamydial infection, syphilis, trichomoniasis) plus bacterial vaginosis have been associated with increased risk of HIV transmission or acquisition (Harrison 22e p.1097). Acute epididymitis in sexually active men under 35 is most often due to C. trachomatis (less often N. gonorrhoeae) and usually accompanies overt or subclinical urethritis, whereas in older men or after urinary instrumentation it is usually caused by urinary pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1101). Unsolicited reporting of abnormal vaginal discharge (increased amount or abnormal odor) most often denotes bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis, not cervical gonorrhea or chlamydia, which usually do not increase discharge volume or odor (Harrison 22e p.1101). Sexually transmitted HSV causes most genital ulcer disease worldwide; HSV-2 produces more frequent genital recurrences and is more infectious to partners than HSV-1, so typing has prognostic value (Harrison 22e p.1097, 1108). STI control combines reducing exposure (education, behavior change, post-exposure prophylaxis), shortening infectivity (early diagnosis and curative or suppressive treatment), and reducing per-exposure transmission (condoms, vaccines, male medical circumcision) (Harrison 22e p.1096). Despite the strong epidemiologic HSV-HIV link, randomized trials of antiviral HSV suppression showed no protective effect against HIV acquisition or transmission (Harrison 22e p.1097). Sudden severe testicular pain with testicular elevation and absent Doppler flow indicating testicular torsion, a surgical emergency (Harrison 22e p.1101) Costovertebral angle pain/tenderness or fever in a dysuric woman suggesting acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1100) Genital ulcer in a patient with HIV risk (e.g., MSM, known HIV infection): treat presumptively for syphilis rather than awaiting seroconversion given high syphilis rates (Harrison 22e p.1108) Suspected PID with peritoneal extension (pelvic or generalized peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess) (Harrison 22e p.1104) Congenital syphilis exposure in pregnancy, given the sharp recent rise including syphilis-related stillbirths and infant deaths (Harrison 22e p.1097) Treating genital symptoms without performing the microbiologic tests needed to establish a cause; self-diagnosis of vulvovaginal candidiasis is often incorrect (Harrison 22e p.1101) Relying on urethral Gram's stain alone to exclude gonorrhea, since up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections are smear-negative (Harrison 22e p.1099) Misreading cervical ectopy as infectious endocervicitis and unnecessarily cauterizing it (Harrison 22e p.1104) Assuming a positive HSV-2 serology proves current lesions are herpetic, when nearly one-fifth of the U.S. population becomes HSV-2 seropositive in early adulthood and type-specific assays are not 100% specific (Harrison 22e p.1108) Failing to evaluate and treat sexual partners with contact in the relevant window (e.g., within the prior 60 days for urethritis), allowing reinfection (Harrison 22e p.1099) Withholding presumptive syphilis treatment in a high-risk patient with a genital ulcer while awaiting seroconversion (Harrison 22e p.1108) Attributing male urethritis recurrence to treatment failure without considering reexposure to an untreated partner or M. genitalium (often resistant to doxycycline and azithromycin) (Harrison 22e p.1100, 1099) STIs are acquired through sexual exposure to a susceptible person from an infectious one, with spread amplified within highly interconnected sexual networks marked by high partner-change rates or concurrent partners (e.g., transactional sex, some MSM, drug-using populations), while infections such as chlamydia, genital HPV, and genital herpes propagate efficiently even in relatively low-risk populations. Many of these organisms colonize or invade genital, anal, oral, or systemic epithelium; ascending spread from cervix or vagina to endometrium and fallopian tubes underlies PID, with potential extension to pelvic peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or abscess. Immunopathology contributes to tissue damage in chlamydial salpingitis, where repeated exposure produces the greatest inflammation. Hormonal and anatomic factors modulate susceptibility (e.g., cervical ectopy may increase susceptibility to gonococcus, chlamydia, and HIV; oral contraceptives favor ectopy persistence; menstruation appears to facilitate ascending gonococcal/chlamydial infection). Many STIs are curable when diagnosed and treated early, and prompt treatment shortens infectivity and reduces onward transmission. Outcomes worsen with delayed care: untreated chlamydial and gonococcal infection can ascend to cause PID with risk of tubal damage and infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain, and immunopathology contributes to chlamydial tubal injury. HPV and HBV carry long-term oncogenic risk (cervical and other anogenital cancers; hepatocellular carcinoma). HSV-2 causes lifelong recurrent infection with asymptomatic shedding and ongoing transmission risk. In men, urethritis with neither chlamydiae nor gonococci detected carries a higher risk of recurrent nongonococcal urethritis, and most persistent urethritis is attributable to M. genitalium. Congenital syphilis can result in stillbirth or infant death. No single staging system applies to STIs as a group; severity is assessed by syndrome and complications. Localized lower-tract syndromes (uncomplicated urethritis, cervicitis, vulvovaginitis, genital ulcer) are distinguished from complicated or upper-tract/disseminated disease (PID with peritonitis, perihepatitis, perisplenitis, or pelvic abscess; disseminated gonococcal infection; epididymo-orchitis), and from long-term oncologic or reproductive sequelae (cervical/anogenital neoplasia, infertility). Genital ulcer evaluation also uses lesion natural-history timelines (herpes 2-3 weeks; chancroid and syphilis up to ~6 weeks) to flag atypical persistence (Harrison 22e p.1104, 1108).

Shigellosis — bacillary dysentery Salmonella infection Campylobacter jejuni infection Clostridium difficile colitis Yersinia enterocolitica infection Entamoeba histolytica (amebic dysentery) Inflammatory bowel disease (first flare of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis), particularly in industrialized countries Enteroinvasive E. coli (can cause a shigellosis-like dysentery) Salmonellosis Campylobacter jejuni enteritis Clostridium difficile colitis Yersinia enterocolitica enterocolitis Amebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica) Enteroinvasive E. coli dysentery Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) infection (predominant cause of HUS in industrialized countries) Stool culture is the gold standard; sample the bloody/mucopurulent portion directly, or use rectal swabs (highest yield in the acute phase). Because Shigella is fragile and dies during transport, use a holding medium (buffered glycerol saline or Cary-Blair) with prompt inoculation onto isolation media. Use multiple media to raise yield: nonselective (bromocresol-purple lactose), low-selectivity (MacConkey, eosin-methylene blue), and high-selectivity (Hektoen, Salmonella-Shigella, or xylose-lysine-deoxycholate agar). Microscopy of stool smears: bacterial enteroinvasive infection (including shigellosis) shows high PMN counts per field, whereas E. histolytica shows erythrophagocytic trophozoites with very few PMNs. Identify shigellae as non-lactose-fermenting colonies that are glucose-positive (usually no gas), lactose-negative, H2S-negative, and nonmotile; confirm serogroup by slide agglutination. Blood cultures are positive in fewer than 5% of cases but should be obtained when there is a clinical picture of severe sepsis. Abdominal x-ray when toxic megacolon is suspected (transverse colon dilation, thumbprinting, loss of haustra, pseudopolyps; pneumoperitoneum if perforated). In HUS: full blood count and smear (schizocytes), platelets, LDH, free hemoglobin, reticulocytes, creatinine; Coombs test (HUS is Coombs-negative). PCR for Shigella virulence genes or mass spectrometry are available but not yet standardized for global use. Inflammatory bowel disease - Crohn's disease Inflammatory bowel disease - ulcerative colitis Classic dysentery is a syndrome of fever, intestinal cramps, and frequent passage of small, bloody, mucopurulent stools; tenesmus is characteristic (p.1322). Shigella has a very low infectious dose; experimental infection of volunteers occurs with as few as ~100 CFU, accounting for high attack rates in day-care centers (33-73%) and high secondary attack rates among family members (26-33%) (p.1322). Spread is primarily fecal-oral via hand carriage; the organism survives gastric passage owing to acid resistance, and can also be transmitted sexually (p.1322-1323). Shigellosis typically evolves through four phases: incubation (usually 1-4 days, up to 8), watery diarrhea, dysentery, and a postinfectious phase (p.1323). Dysentery reflects invasion of the colonic mucosa, producing acute colitis mainly involving the distal colon and rectum, with uninterrupted small-volume bloody mucopurulent stools, tenesmus, and cramps (p.1323). Of the four species, S. flexneri predominates in least-developed areas while S. sonnei is more common in industrialized/emerging economies; S. dysenteriae type 1 (Shiga-toxin producer) drives the most severe epidemic disease (p.1322). With effective antibiotics, clinical improvement occurs within ~48 h, with fewer complications, shorter symptoms, and clearance of Shigella from stool; in the US every culture-confirmed case is recommended for treatment because of transmissibility (p.1324). Reactive arthritis (arthritis, ocular inflammation, urethritis) can develop weeks to months after infection, almost exclusively after S. flexneri and in HLA-B27-positive patients (about 3% of S. flexneri infections) (p.1323-1324). Nonbloody diarrhea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteremia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, and rectal prolapse are risk factors for death in clinically severe cases. Altered consciousness (seizures, delirium, coma), especially in children under 5, carries a poor prognosis. Abdominal distention and tenderness suggesting toxic megacolon, with or without peritonitis. Pallor, asthenia, irritability, oliguria, increasing edema, or mucosal bleeding heralding hemolytic-uremic syndrome (most often after several days of diarrhea). Fever persisting beyond 48-72 h in toxic megacolon raises the possibility of local perforation or abscess. Severe, unusual manifestations such as meningitis in the absence of serious malnutrition may indicate an inborn innate-immune defect (e.g., IRAK-4 deficiency) and warrant genetic investigation. Avoid antimotility agents in bloody diarrhea: they have been implicated in prolonged fever in shigellosis, are suspected of increasing the risk of toxic megacolon, and were implicated in HUS in children with EHEC infection. Because shigellosis often manifests only as watery diarrhea, systematic attempts to isolate Shigella are necessary - a watery presentation does not exclude the diagnosis. Shigella is fragile and commonly disappears during transport with changes in temperature and pH; failure to use a holding medium and prompt inoculation leads to false-negative cultures. Negative initial blood cultures do not exclude shigellosis (positive in fewer than 5% of cases). Predisposing factors for toxic megacolon - hypokalemia and use of opioids, anticholinergics, loperamide, psyllium seeds, and antidepressants - should be sought and addressed. In HUS, oral rehydration solutions and potassium-rich nutrition must be discontinued (water restriction is required), in contrast to routine rehydration management. Bacteriologic proof in mild adult cases often arrives only after symptoms have resolved, so empiric decisions cannot await culture in fragile patients. Pathogenicity is governed by a ~214-kb virulence plasmid encoding a type III secretion system that injects effectors into host cells. After acid-resistant passage through the stomach, bacteria invade colonic epithelium either directly at crypt openings or after crossing M cells over mucosal lymphoid follicles; they induce apoptosis of resident macrophages, drive cytoskeletal uptake, lyse the containing vacuole to reach the cytosol, then spread cell-to-cell using actin-based motility. A massive cytokine-driven influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes destabilizes the epithelial barrier and produces the acute colitis of shigellosis. Early watery diarrhea is attributed to combined enterotoxin (ShET-1) action and mucosal inflammation. In S. dysenteriae type 1, Shiga toxin (an A1-B5 toxin binding globotriaosylceramide and inhibiting protein synthesis via 28S rRNA N-glycosidase activity) is translocated into the circulation and, by acting on renal target cells, can cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome (p.1322-1323). Most episodes are self-limited and resolve without treatment within about 1 week; with appropriate therapy recovery occurs within a few days to a week, usually without sequelae. Acute life-threatening complications occur most often in children under 5 (especially the malnourished) and the elderly. In HUS, acute renal failure occurs in 55-70% of cases but renal function recovers in most (up to ~70%). S. dysenteriae type 1 epidemics historically caused high mortality. Shigellosis is a major contributor to stunted growth among children in endemic regions because of the exudative enteropathy and anorexia it causes. Harrison does not provide a formal grading scale. Severity is described as depending on infecting serotype and, more importantly, on host age, immunologic and nutritional status. The clinical course is staged in four phases (incubation, watery diarrhea, dysentery, postinfectious). Severe/complicated disease is recognized by markers of poor outcome (nonbloody diarrhea, moderate-to-severe dehydration, bacteremia, absence of fever, abdominal tenderness, rectal prolapse, altered consciousness) and by major complications: intestinal (toxic megacolon, perforation, rectal prolapse), metabolic (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, dehydration), and HUS (in S. dysenteriae type 1).

Short bowel syndrome — SBS, short gut syndrome, intestinal failure Chronic pancreatic exocrine insufficiency Coeliac disease and other mucosal malabsorptive disorders Small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth Inflammatory bowel disease with active malabsorption Chronic infective or inflammatory diarrhoea Enteric fistula causing functional bowel loss Assessment of remaining bowel anatomy and length from operative records and imaging Nutritional and electrolyte panel including magnesium, calcium, and trace elements Fat-soluble vitamin, vitamin B12, and iron status Monitoring of fluid balance and stool or stoma output Liver function monitoring in patients on parenteral nutrition and evaluation for bacterial overgrowth A malabsorptive state resulting from loss of functional small-intestinal length, usually after extensive surgical resection for conditions such as mesenteric ischaemia, Crohn disease, trauma, or radiation injury Clinical severity depends on the length and site of remaining bowel, whether the ileocaecal valve and colon are preserved, and the health of the residual intestine The main manifestations are diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, weight loss, and specific nutrient deficiencies Loss of the terminal ileum impairs absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts, and bile-salt spillage into the colon can worsen diarrhoea and predispose to gallstones An intact colon is nutritionally valuable because it salvages energy by fermenting malabsorbed carbohydrate into short-chain fatty acids Over months to years the residual bowel undergoes adaptation, increasing absorptive capacity, so nutritional needs may lessen with time Management is staged: fluid and electrolyte correction, parenteral nutrition when needed, gradual introduction of enteral feeding to drive adaptation, and dietary modification Long-term parenteral nutrition carries important complications including catheter-related bloodstream infection, venous thrombosis, and intestinal-failure-associated liver disease Enterohormonal therapy (such as GLP-2 analogues) and, in selected refractory cases, intestinal transplantation are options for those dependent on parenteral support Severe dehydration with acute kidney injury or dangerous electrolyte disturbances Catheter-related bloodstream infection or sepsis in patients on parenteral nutrition Progressive intestinal-failure-associated liver disease or cholestasis Central venous thrombosis threatening long-term access for parenteral nutrition Underestimating fluid and electrolyte losses, particularly magnesium, in high-output patients Withholding enteral nutrition entirely and thereby delaying adaptation Overlooking vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency after ileal resection Missing small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth or catheter sepsis as causes of deterioration Short bowel syndrome arises when the absorptive surface of the small intestine is reduced below the level needed to maintain nutrition and hydration, most often after massive resection. The functional consequences depend on which segment is lost: jejunal loss reduces overall absorptive surface, while ileal loss additionally impairs vitamin B12 and bile-salt reabsorption, disrupting the enterohepatic circulation and causing bile-salt diarrhoea and fat malabsorption. Loss of the ileocaecal valve accelerates transit and predisposes to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Rapid transit and reduced surface lead to fluid, electrolyte, and nutrient losses. Over time the remnant intestine adapts through mucosal hyperplasia and slowed transit, partially restoring absorptive capacity. Outlook depends on residual bowel length and anatomy and on adaptation. Many patients eventually achieve enteral autonomy, while those with very short remnants or absent colon may need lifelong parenteral nutrition, whose complications (liver disease, line sepsis, thrombosis) drive much of the long-term morbidity and mortality.

Short QT syndrome — SQTS, short QT interval syndrome, KCNH2-related short QT, familial short QT Normal QT variant or measurement error Hypercalcaemia causing QT shortening Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves Effects of digoxin on the ST segment and QT Early repolarisation syndrome Brugada syndrome (with overlapping calcium channel variants) 12-lead ECG with careful measurement of the corrected QT interval and T-wave morphology Serial or repeat ECGs to confirm a persistently short QT Ambulatory monitoring for atrial and ventricular arrhythmia Correction and reassessment after excluding electrolyte and drug causes of QT shortening Echocardiography to confirm a structurally normal heart Genetic testing for potassium and calcium channel variants with family cascade screening A rare inherited channelopathy defined by an abnormally short QT interval and a high risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death May present with palpitations, syncope, atrial fibrillation at a young age, or aborted cardiac arrest, sometimes as the first event The ECG shows a persistently short QT interval with tall, peaked, symmetrical T waves and often a short or absent ST segment Most identified variants are gain-of-function changes in potassium channel genes (such as KCNH2, KCNQ1 and KCNJ2) that shorten repolarisation; some loss-of-function calcium channel variants overlap with a Brugada phenotype Diagnosis rests on the corrected QT interval together with symptoms, family history and genetic findings, as the QT alone can overlap with normal variants An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is the mainstay for those who survive cardiac arrest or are at high risk Quinidine can prolong the QT interval and is used to reduce arrhythmic events, particularly when a defibrillator is unsuitable Family screening is important because the first manifestation may be sudden death Aborted cardiac arrest or documented ventricular fibrillation Unexplained syncope in a young person with a short QT Atrial fibrillation presenting at an unusually young age Family history of sudden cardiac death Overlooking a short QT interval because attention focuses on QT prolongation Attributing a short QT to hypercalcaemia or digoxin without reassessing after correction Relying on the QT value alone without integrating symptoms, family history and genetics Failing to screen relatives given that sudden death can be the first event Assuming a structurally normal heart excludes life-threatening arrhythmia Short QT syndrome is caused by ion channel dysfunction that accelerates cardiac repolarisation. Gain-of-function variants in potassium channel genes increase outward repolarising currents, shortening the action potential duration and thereby the QT interval; loss-of-function variants in calcium channel subunits can produce a similar phenotype. The abbreviated and heterogeneous repolarisation shortens refractory periods across the atria and ventricles, creating a substrate for re-entry that predisposes to atrial fibrillation and to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, and hence sudden death, in a structurally normal heart. The natural history is dominated by the risk of sudden arrhythmic death, which can occur across all ages including infancy; appropriate defibrillator therapy and, where used, QT-prolonging drug therapy substantially improve outcome for high-risk individuals.

Short Stature — growth failure, poor linear growth, faltering height, paediatric short stature Familial (genetic) short stature Constitutional delay of growth and puberty Growth hormone deficiency Hypothyroidism Chronic systemic disease (e.g. coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, renal or cardiac disease) Turner syndrome and other genetic/syndromic causes Skeletal dysplasia Undernutrition or psychosocial deprivation Accurate serial height and weight with growth velocity calculation Bone age radiograph Screening bloods (full blood count, renal and liver function, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology) Thyroid function and, where indicated, IGF-1 and growth hormone provocation testing Karyotype or genetic testing in girls (to exclude Turner syndrome) and where a syndrome is suspected Skeletal survey if disproportion suggests a dysplasia Short stature is generally defined as height more than about 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, but the growth velocity and trajectory matter more than a single measurement. The two most common causes are normal variants: familial (genetic) short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty. Serial, accurately measured heights plotted on a growth chart are the single most valuable assessment, since a falling growth velocity is a key warning sign. Bone age radiography helps distinguish constitutional delay (delayed bone age, preserved height potential) from familial short stature (bone age near chronological age). A low or crossing-down growth velocity with poor weight gain suggests systemic disease or malnutrition, whereas short but proportionate growth with normal velocity favours a normal variant. Endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency and hypothyroidism typically produce a child who is relatively overweight for height, in contrast to malnutrition or chronic illness. Disproportionate short stature points towards a skeletal dysplasia and warrants assessment of body segment ratios. Estimating mid-parental target height helps interpret whether a child's growth is appropriate for their genetic background. A crossing-down growth velocity or fall across major height centiles Short stature with neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion Disproportionate short stature suggesting a skeletal dysplasia Poor growth with weight loss or gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting chronic disease Dysmorphic features or other findings suggesting a genetic syndrome Relying on a single height measurement rather than growth velocity over time Labelling a child as a normal variant without excluding treatable disease when velocity is poor Missing an intracranial cause of growth hormone deficiency Failing to consider Turner syndrome in a short girl Linear growth depends on an intact growth plate responding to growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1, thyroid hormone, and sex steroids, supported by adequate nutrition and freedom from chronic illness. Short stature arises when any of these are disturbed: genetic determination of a lower height potential, temporary delay in the tempo of maturation, endocrine deficiency, chronic systemic disease, undernutrition, or intrinsic bone/cartilage disorders. The pattern of growth velocity, body proportions, and bone age reflects which mechanism predominates. Normal variants such as familial short stature and constitutional delay have an excellent prognosis with normal health, and constitutional delay usually reaches a normal adult height; outcomes for pathological causes depend on early identification and treatment of the underlying condition.

Shoulder Dystocia — shoulder dystocia, impacted shoulders, obstetric shoulder impaction Difficulty from a tight nuchal cord without true shoulder impaction Fetal anomalies causing enlarged trunk or abdomen (e.g. large abdominal mass, hydrops) Locked twins Uterine or contraction abnormality causing prolonged second stage Cephalopelvic disproportion with obstructed labour Immediate clinical recognition rather than investigation is the priority in the acute event Neonatal assessment of the arms, clavicles, and neurology for brachial plexus injury or fracture after delivery Cord blood gas analysis to document the degree of any acidosis Maternal assessment for postpartum haemorrhage and perineal or anal sphincter trauma Antenatal estimation of fetal weight and screening for diabetes in at-risk pregnancies Shoulder dystocia is failure of the shoulders to deliver after the head, caused by impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the maternal pubic symphysis, and is a time-critical obstetric emergency The warning sign is the turtle sign, where the delivered head retracts tightly against the perineum, and failure of restitution and of routine gentle traction to deliver the body Risk factors include fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, obesity, prolonged labour, and instrumental delivery, but many cases occur without identifiable risk factors so all birth attendants must be prepared Management follows a structured sequence: call for help, avoid the harmful HELPER pitfalls, and apply the McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure as first-line steps If initial measures fail, internal rotational manoeuvres (such as delivery of the posterior arm or rotational techniques) are used, and the mother should not be pushed while shoulders are impacted Fundal pressure must be avoided because it worsens impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture Excessive or downward traction on the fetal head is the main modifiable cause of brachial plexus injury and should be avoided Complications include brachial plexus palsy (Erb palsy), clavicular or humeral fracture, hypoxic injury from delay, and maternal postpartum haemorrhage and perineal trauma Accurate contemporaneous documentation of the sequence, manoeuvres, timings, and personnel is essential given the medicolegal significance OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: head delivered with turtle sign and shoulders not delivering despite routine traction, requiring immediate structured manoeuvres Prolonged head-to-body delivery interval with rising risk of hypoxic-ischaemic injury Signs of neonatal brachial plexus injury or limb fracture after delivery Maternal postpartum haemorrhage or severe perineal and anal sphincter trauma Use of fundal pressure or excessive head traction indicating unsafe technique Applying fundal pressure, which worsens impaction and can cause uterine rupture Using excessive downward traction on the head, the leading cause of brachial plexus injury Encouraging maternal pushing while the shoulder remains impacted Failing to summon senior and neonatal help early Poor documentation of manoeuvres and timings in a medicolegally significant event After the fetal head delivers, the shoulders normally rotate into the wider oblique diameter of the pelvis. In shoulder dystocia the anterior shoulder fails to rotate and becomes wedged above the pubic symphysis (or, less commonly, the posterior shoulder impacts on the sacral promontory). Because the fetus can no longer descend, the umbilical cord is compressed within the pelvis and placental gas exchange is impaired, so fetal hypoxia and acidosis progress with time. Rotational manoeuvres and delivery of the posterior arm work by reducing the shoulder-to-shoulder (bisacromial) diameter or moving it into a larger pelvic diameter, freeing the impaction. Most shoulder dystocias are relieved with recognised manoeuvres and the majority of infants have no lasting harm. Brachial plexus injuries are the commonest fetal complication and most resolve within the first year, though a minority are permanent. Prolonged impaction risks hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or death. Women who have had shoulder dystocia have an increased recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies.

With enzyme replacement and infection management many patients do well in childhood, but the lifelong risk of marrow failure, myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia dominates long-term prognosis and mandates surveillance; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used for marrow failure or malignant transformation.

neck or floor of mouth extension (an emergency) A persistent hard gland mass, facial nerve weakness or skin fixation suggesting malignancy Fluctuant swelling indicating an abscess requiring drainage Failure to resolve with appropriate treatment, prompting imaging and reassessment Bilateral gland involvement with systemic features suggesting a systemic or autoimmune cause Overlooking dehydration and reduced salivary flow as the precipitant, especially postoperatively Missing an obstructing calculus in recurrent mealtime swelling Assuming all salivary swellings are infective and overlooking a tumour Delaying drainage of an established abscess Neglecting facial nerve assessment when a hard parotid mass is present Salivary glands are normally protected from ascending infection by continuous salivary flow, which flushes the ducts, and by antibacterial constituents of saliva. When flow is reduced, by dehydration, poor oral intake, debility, medications that dry the mouth, or mechanical obstruction from a duct stone or stricture, oral bacteria ascend the duct and infect the gland, producing acute suppurative sialadenitis with parenchymal inflammation and pus. Stasis of saliva also predisposes to stone formation, and calculi in turn obstruct outflow, causing painful mealtime swelling and recurrent infection. Repeated episodes lead to chronic inflammation, ductal changes and glandular fibrosis. Viral sialadenitis such as mumps causes a non-suppurative inflammatory swelling. Acute bacterial sialadenitis usually resolves with rehydration, salivary stimulation and antibiotics, and outcomes are good when the cause is treated; recurrent obstruction from stones or strictures and chronic sialadenitis may require repeated treatment or gland surgery.

Free sialic acid storage disease — FSASD, SLC17A5 deficiency, sialin deficiency, Salla disease (milder form), infantile free sialic acid storage disease (ISSD) Sialidosis (neuraminidase deficiency) and galactosialidosis Other lysosomal storage disorders with coarse features and visceromegaly (e.g. mucopolysaccharidoses, I-cell disease) Hypomyelinating leukodystrophies including Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease Other causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis Congenital disorders of glycosylation Cerebral palsy or other static encephalopathies in milder presentations Urine free (unconjugated) sialic acid quantification (markedly elevated) SLC17A5 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis Brain MRI demonstrating hypomyelination and a thin corpus callosum Assessment for proteinuria and renal involvement in infantile disease Developmental and neurological evaluation to characterise the phenotype Skin fibroblast free sialic acid measurement where available Autosomal recessive defect of SLC17A5, which encodes sialin, the lysosomal membrane transporter that exports free sialic acid from the lysosome Spans a spectrum from severe infantile free sialic acid storage disease (ISSD) to the milder Salla disease common in Finland Salla disease presents with early hypotonia, delayed development, progressive ataxia, spasticity and intellectual disability with a relatively long survival Infantile ISSD is severe, with coarse features, hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis, nephrotic-range proteinuria and hydrops fetalis, and early death Hypomyelination on brain MRI, including a thin corpus callosum, is a characteristic radiological clue Diagnosis is supported by markedly increased free (unconjugated) sialic acid in urine and confirmed by SLC17A5 genetic testing No specific therapy exists; care is supportive with developmental, neurological and, where relevant, renal support Non-immune hydrops fetalis or severe multisystem disease in the neonate Nephrotic-range proteinuria with renal involvement Progressive neurological regression with spasticity Feeding difficulty and respiratory compromise in the infantile form Not measuring urinary free sialic acid in unexplained hypotonia with hypomyelination Confusing free sialic acid storage disease with sialidosis, where bound sialic acid metabolism differs Overlooking renal involvement in the infantile form Attributing a milder phenotype to cerebral palsy without metabolic evaluation Sialin is a proton-driven transporter in the lysosomal membrane that carries free sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) generated by glycoconjugate degradation out of the lysosome into the cytoplasm. When sialin is defective, free sialic acid accumulates within lysosomes across many tissues, which are consequently distended by storage. The nervous system is particularly affected, with disturbed myelination underlying the hypotonia, developmental impairment and progressive motor signs, while severe transporter loss produces the multisystem infantile phenotype with visceromegaly, bone changes and, in the most severe cases, hydrops. Infantile free sialic acid storage disease is severe and usually fatal in early childhood, whereas Salla disease follows a slower course with prolonged survival and predominantly neurological disability; prognosis depends on residual sialin function.

gene testing Progressive myoclonus and seizures unresponsive to standard therapy Rapid visual deterioration Hydrops fetalis or severe neonatal presentation in the congenital form Cardiorespiratory decline in type 2 disease Attributing progressive myoclonic epilepsy to an idiopathic cause and missing the cherry-red spot Failing to distinguish sialidosis from galactosialidosis by not assaying beta-galactosidase Screening only for glycosaminoglycans and missing the sialylated oligosaccharide pattern Overlooking sialidosis in the differential of non-immune hydrops fetalis Sialidosis is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in NEU1, encoding lysosomal alpha-N-acetylneuraminidase (sialidase). This enzyme removes terminal sialic acid residues from sialylated glycoconjugates during their lysosomal degradation. Its deficiency causes accumulation of sialyloligosaccharides and sialylated glycopeptides within lysosomes and their excretion in the urine. The severity spectrum reflects residual enzyme activity: type 1 causes a progressive myoclonic epilepsy with visual decline and preserved somatic appearance, while type 2 causes earlier, more generalised storage disease with dysmorphism, skeletal changes, and visceromegaly, including a congenital hydropic form. Neuraminidase normally functions in a complex with beta-galactosidase and the protective protein cathepsin A, and defects in that protective protein instead cause galactosialidosis. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Type 1 follows a slowly progressive course with disabling myoclonus and visual loss but relatively preserved somatic health, whereas type 2, especially the congenital form, is severe with high early mortality. No disease-modifying therapy is established, so care is supportive.

or ambulatory monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm Implantable loop recorder when symptoms are infrequent Review of rate-slowing medications and thyroid function testing Electrolyte assessment and evaluation for ischaemia when relevant Exercise testing to assess chronotropic competence Echocardiography to evaluate structural heart disease Sick sinus syndrome is a spectrum of sinoatrial node dysfunction producing inappropriate bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, sinoatrial exit block, and chronotropic incompetence A common variant is the tachy-brady syndrome, in which paroxysms of atrial tachyarrhythmia (often atrial fibrillation) alternate with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses, especially on termination of the tachyarrhythmia Symptoms are often intermittent and non-specific, required to correlate them with rhythm disturbances It is predominantly a disease of older adults from degenerative fibrosis of the sinus node, but drugs, ischaemia, and infiltrative disease can contribute Reversible contributors such as rate-slowing drugs, hypothyroidism, and electrolyte disturbance should be excluded before attributing symptoms to intrinsic node disease Permanent pacing is the main treatment for symptomatic bradycardia, and the tachy-brady form often needs both pacing and rhythm or rate control of the tachyarrhythmia Anticoagulation should be considered when atrial fibrillation coexists, based on thromboembolic risk Syncope or recurrent presyncope from prolonged sinus pauses or arrest Very long pauses, particularly following termination of a tachyarrhythmia in tachy-brady syndrome Haemodynamic compromise from severe bradycardia Coexisting atrial fibrillation raising thromboembolic and stroke risk Attributing symptoms to intrinsic node disease without excluding reversible drug or metabolic causes Failing to capture the arrhythmia because monitoring was too brief for paroxysmal symptoms Overlooking the need for anticoagulation when atrial fibrillation coexists Treating bradycardia with pacing while ignoring the tachyarrhythmia component of tachy-brady syndrome Sick sinus syndrome results from failure of normal impulse generation in the sinoatrial node or failure of conduction from the node to the surrounding atrium. The most common cause is idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the node and perinodal tissue with ageing. Ischaemia, infiltrative and inflammatory diseases, prior cardiac surgery, and autonomic influences also contribute, and many drugs suppress node function. In the tachy-brady syndrome, atrial remodelling supports tachyarrhythmias, while the diseased node produces prolonged pauses when the tachyarrhythmia stops because of overdrive suppression of an already impaired pacemaker. Sick sinus syndrome is rarely immediately life-threatening but causes considerable morbidity from recurrent symptoms; pacing effectively relieves bradycardic symptoms, and overall outcome is largely determined by associated atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic risk and by underlying cardiac disease.

Sigmoid volvulus — volvulus of the sigmoid colon, sigmoid colon volvulus Caecal volvulus Obstructing colorectal carcinoma Pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) Diverticular stricture with obstruction Faecal impaction with megacolon Adhesional or hernia-related large bowel obstruction Plain abdominal radiograph for the characteristic dilated sigmoid loop CT abdomen and pelvis to confirm the diagnosis, show the whirl sign, and assess for ischaemia or perforation Bloods including full blood count, electrolytes, and lactate to gauge ischaemia and fitness for intervention Endoscopic assessment of mucosal viability during attempted decompression Presents with the features of large bowel obstruction: gross abdominal distension, colicky pain, absolute constipation, and often relatively little vomiting early on Most common in elderly, institutionalised, or neuropsychiatric patients and those with chronic constipation and a long redundant sigmoid loop on a narrow mesenteric base The abdominal radiograph classically shows a hugely dilated loop arising from the pelvis, described as a coffee-bean or inverted-U sign pointing toward the right upper quadrant In the absence of peritonitis or bowel compromise, initial treatment is endoscopic decompression (flexible sigmoidoscopy or rigid scope) with insertion of a flatus tube Successful decompression relieves the acute episode but recurrence is common, so elective sigmoid resection is often advised in fit patients Signs of peritonitis, failed decompression, or suspicion of gangrenous or perforated bowel mandate emergency laparotomy At emergency operation for compromised bowel, resection (commonly a Hartmann's procedure) is performed rather than simple untwisting A CT scan confirms the diagnosis, shows the whirl sign of the twisted mesentery, and assesses for ischaemia or perforation Peritonitis, systemic sepsis, or shock suggesting ischaemic or perforated bowel (surgical emergency) Bloodstained or necrotic mucosa or dark fluid at decompression indicating gangrene Failure of endoscopic decompression Rising lactate, worsening distension, or free gas on imaging Persisting with endoscopic decompression when peritonitis or ischaemia is present Mistaking the presentation for simple constipation and delaying imaging Failing to offer elective resection to fit patients after decompression, allowing recurrence Overlooking an obstructing carcinoma as an alternative cause of distal large bowel obstruction Sigmoid volvulus occurs when a redundant, elongated sigmoid loop twists around its narrow mesenteric pedicle, producing a closed-loop large bowel obstruction. Chronic constipation and a lengthy, mobile sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric base predispose to torsion. The twist obstructs the lumen at both ends, and progressive distension raises intraluminal and intramural pressure. If the mesenteric vessels are compromised by the torsion, the loop becomes ischaemic, progressing to gangrene and perforation with faeculent peritonitis and sepsis. Massive gaseous distension of the closed loop is characteristic. Uncomplicated cases usually respond to endoscopic decompression but recur frequently unless definitive surgery is performed. Emergency surgery for gangrenous or perforated bowel in typically frail, elderly patients carries substantial morbidity and mortality.

Silicosis — silicosis, silica pneumoconiosis, quartz dust lung disease Other pneumoconioses such as coal workers' pneumoconiosis Pulmonary tuberculosis (which may coexist) Sarcoidosis Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases Metastatic or miliary nodular lung disease Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Chest radiography with attention to upper-zone nodularity and eggshell nodal calcification High-resolution CT to characterise nodules and detect progressive massive fibrosis Pulmonary function testing to quantify restrictive, obstructive, or mixed impairment Screening for tuberculosis given the heightened risk Detailed occupational exposure history including engineered-stone and sandblasting work Silicosis is a fibrotic lung disease caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust, seen in mining, quarrying, sandblasting, stone-cutting, and engineered-stone work Chronic silicosis develops after prolonged exposure and may be asymptomatic initially, later causing exertional dyspnoea and cough Accelerated and acute (silicoproteinosis) forms follow intense exposure and progress far more rapidly Chest imaging classically shows small upper-zone nodular opacities, sometimes with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes Simple nodular disease can coalesce into progressive massive fibrosis, producing large conglomerate masses and significant impairment Silica exposure substantially increases susceptibility to tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis), which should be actively sought and treated There is no treatment that reverses fibrosis; management focuses on stopping exposure, supportive care, and screening for and treating complications Silica is also associated with increased risks of lung cancer, chronic airflow obstruction, and certain autoimmune diseases New constitutional symptoms, haemoptysis, or cavitation suggesting tuberculosis or malignancy Rapidly progressive breathlessness indicating accelerated or acute silicosis Enlarging conglomerate masses consistent with progressive massive fibrosis Development of respiratory failure or cor pulmonale Failing to elicit an occupational silica exposure history, especially newer engineered-stone work Overlooking coexisting tuberculosis in a patient with silicosis Attributing all nodular change to silicosis without considering malignancy Not removing the worker from ongoing dust exposure Inhaled crystalline silica particles reaching the alveoli are taken up by macrophages. The reactive silica surface is toxic to these macrophages, triggering activation of inflammasome pathways, cell death, and release of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This provokes recruitment of further inflammatory cells and stimulation of fibroblasts, which lay down collagen to form the characteristic silicotic nodules. Continued or intense exposure sustains the cycle, with nodules enlarging and coalescing into progressive massive fibrosis, while impaired macrophage function increases vulnerability to mycobacterial infection. Chronic simple silicosis may remain stable with limited impairment, but progressive massive fibrosis, accelerated, and acute forms carry a poor prognosis with progressive respiratory failure; the lifelong increased risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer means continued surveillance is important, and outcomes improve when exposure ceases early.

uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy-number causes of growth restriction Blood glucose monitoring for fasting hypoglycaemia in infancy Growth monitoring with assessment of body asymmetry and limb-length discrepancy Endocrine evaluation including growth hormone axis assessment Nutritional and feeding assessment for failure to thrive An imprinting disorder causing severe pre- and postnatal growth restriction with relative macrocephaly (head sparing) at birth Characteristic features include a triangular face, broad forehead, body asymmetry (hemihypotrophy), and fifth-finger clinodactyly Feeding difficulties, marked failure to thrive, and fasting hypoglycaemia due to low muscle and fat mass are common in infancy Most cases are explained by loss of methylation at the IC1 (H19/IGF2) region on chromosome 11p15 or by maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 It is broadly the molecular mirror image of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, with reduced rather than increased IGF2-driven growth The Netchine-Harbison clinical scoring system guides diagnosis and directs molecular testing when features are suggestive Management centres on optimising nutrition and growth, monitoring for hypoglycaemia, and endocrine input including growth-promoting therapy where indicated Fasting hypoglycaemia risking neurological harm, especially during intercurrent illness Severe failure to thrive requiring intensive nutritional support Significant limb-length discrepancy affecting gait and posture Signs of relative intracranial disproportion or raised pressure requiring assessment Attributing severe growth restriction to placental insufficiency alone and not testing for imprinting defects Missing fasting hypoglycaemia because of the child's small size and low reserves Overlooking body asymmetry, which is a useful diagnostic clue Failing to recognise the mirror-image relationship with Beckwith-Wiedemann when interpreting 11p15 results Silver-Russell syndrome is an imprinting disorder most often caused by hypomethylation of the paternally derived IC1 domain at chromosome 11p15, which reduces expression of the growth-promoting gene IGF2, or by maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7. Reduced IGF2-driven growth signalling produces profound intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction with relative sparing of head growth. Because the affected loci are imprinted, the parental origin of the epigenetic or chromosomal change determines the phenotype, and body asymmetry reflects mosaic distribution of the molecular defect. With early nutritional optimisation, hypoglycaemia prevention, and endocrine management, growth and general health improve, though final stature is often below average. Cognition is usually normal or near normal, and adult outcomes are generally favourable with appropriate support.

congenital heart disease, diaphragmatic hernia, polydactyly, supernumerary nipples, and genitourinary anomalies Caused by loss-of-function variants or deletions in GPC3 (with GPC4 involvement in some) particularly Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma, warranting tumour surveillance in childhood Overlaps clinically with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome but is distinguished by X-linked inheritance and the neonatal period Cardiac decompensation from structural heart disease Neonatal hypoglycaemia or arrhythmia requiring urgent management Confusing the syndrome with Beckwith-Wiedemann and thereby overlooking X-linked inheritance and carrier risk to relatives Omitting embryonal tumour surveillance in a child with overgrowth and organomegaly Underestimating disease in carrier females who may show subtle features Missing a diaphragmatic hernia or cardiac lesion in the newborn assessment Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome arises from loss of function of GPC3, an X-linked gene encoding glypican-3, a cell-surface heparan sulfate proteoglycan that modulates growth factor signalling and helps restrain cell proliferation during development, in part by regulating hedgehog and IGF-related pathways. Absent or reduced glypican-3 removes this brake on tissue growth, producing generalised overgrowth, organomegaly, and a predisposition to embryonal tumours, while disturbed developmental signalling accounts for the structural malformations and characteristic facies. Prognosis depends on the severity of malformations and tumour occurrence; severe cases may present with neonatal complications, while milder cases have a favourable outlook with appropriate surveillance. Early detection of embryonal tumours through structured screening improves outcomes.

Sitosterolaemia — phytosterolaemia, ABCG5 deficiency, ABCG8 deficiency, sterolin deficiency, STSL Familial hypercholesterolaemia (xanthomata with markedly raised LDL cholesterol) Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (xanthomata with neurological features) Other causes of macrothrombocytopenia and haemolytic anaemia Secondary hyperlipidaemias Autosomal recessive hypercholesterolaemia Tangier disease and other rare lipid disorders Plasma plant sterol quantification (sitosterol and campesterol) by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry Fasting lipid profile, recognising cholesterol may be only mildly elevated Full blood count and film for haemolysis, stomatocytes and macrothrombocytopenia Molecular genetic testing of the ABCG5 and ABCG8 genes Cardiovascular assessment for premature atherosclerosis Family screening given the recessive inheritance Autosomal recessive sterol-storage disorder caused by mutations in the ABCG5 or ABCG8 sterol transporter genes The defective transporter fails to limit intestinal absorption of plant and shellfish sterols and to promote their biliary excretion, so dietary phytosterols accumulate Presents with tendon and tuberous xanthomata, often from childhood, sometimes with a normal or only modestly raised total cholesterol Carries a markedly increased risk of premature atherosclerosis and coronary disease, occasionally with sudden cardiac events in young patients Haematological features can include haemolytic anaemia with stomatocytes and abnormally large platelets (macrothrombocytopenia) The biochemical hallmark is grossly raised plasma plant sterols (sitosterol, campesterol) measured by specialised chromatography, which routine cholesterol assays miss Treatment is a diet low in plant and shellfish sterols combined with ezetimibe and/or bile-acid sequestrants; statins are relatively ineffective and this must be distinguished from familial hypercholesterolaemia Premature coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac event in a young patient Extensive xanthomata in childhood, particularly with normal or near-normal cholesterol Significant haemolytic anaemia or bleeding from macrothrombocytopenia Family history of early cardiovascular death Misdiagnosing it as familial hypercholesterolaemia and relying on statins, which are relatively ineffective Missing the diagnosis because routine cholesterol assays do not measure plant sterols Overlooking haematological clues such as haemolysis and large platelets Underestimating cardiovascular risk when cholesterol appears near normal Failing to advise dietary restriction of plant and shellfish sterols Sitosterolaemia results from loss of function of the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimeric transporter expressed on enterocytes and hepatocytes. Normally this pump exports non-cholesterol sterols back into the gut lumen and into bile, keeping absorption of dietary plant sterols very low. When it is defective, plant sterols such as sitosterol and campesterol, along with cholesterol, are absorbed in excess and poorly excreted, so they accumulate in plasma and tissues. Deposition in tendons and skin causes xanthomata and in arterial walls accelerates atherosclerosis, while incorporation of abnormal sterols into red cell and platelet membranes underlies the haemolysis and macrothrombocytopenia. With early diagnosis, sterol-restricted diet and sterol-absorption-blocking therapy, plant sterol levels fall, xanthomata regress and cardiovascular risk improves; undiagnosed disease carries a substantial risk of premature atherosclerotic events.

anticentromere (limited scleroderma–like), antimitochondrial (autoimmune cholangitis), anti-21-hydroxylase (blunted adrenal response), anti-citrullinated peptide (arthritis), anticalponin-3 (peripheral neuropathy) Complement (low C4), serum protein electrophoresis, cryoglobulins, serum IgG4, thyroid autoantibodies Testing to exclude chronic viral infection (HCV, HIV) and chest x-ray to exclude sarcoidosis FDG-PET/CT to help exclude lymphoma when suspected Sarcoidosis IgG4-related disease Amyloidosis Autoimmune thyroid disease Diabetes mellitus, hyperlipoproteinemia (types IV and V), chronic pancreatitis, hepatic cirrhosis Acromegaly and gonadal hypofunction Eosinophilic sialodochitis Drug-induced or radiation-induced gland dysfunction Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigoid, chronic conjunctivitis/blepharitis, hypovitaminosis A (dry eye) Prototype autoimmune disease defined by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands causing xerostomia and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca), together with marked B-cell hyperactivity. Strongly female-predominant (female-to-male ratio roughly 10–20:1) and chiefly affects middle-aged women, but can present at any age including childhood; prevalence is approximately 0.5–1%. Earlier age at onset tends to mark a more aggressive phenotype with more systemic manifestations and more serum autoantibodies. Can occur alone or in association with other systemic rheumatic diseases, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis, limited scleroderma, and systemic lupus erythematosus; 5–20% of patients with other autoimmune diseases can have sicca features. Principal oral symptom is dryness (xerostomia) with difficulty swallowing dry food, burning mouth, increased dental caries; examination may show dry erythematous sticky mucosa, atrophic tongue papillae, and a deeply fissured tongue. Intermittent or persistent enlargement of the parotid or other major salivary glands occurs in about two-thirds of patients. Ocular involvement classically produces a sandy or gritty sensation under the lids, with burning, stranded secretions at the inner canthi, reduced tearing, redness, and photosensitivity from corneal and conjunctival epithelial destruction (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). Extraglandular (systemic) manifestations occur in about one-third of patients and are categorized as nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma. Carries the highest risk of lymphoma among all autoimmune diseases; most are extranodal, low-grade, marginal zone (MALT) B-cell lymphomas, often found incidentally on labial minor salivary gland biopsy. Most patients (about two-thirds) have an elevated ESR, hypergammaglobulinemia, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, and anti-Ro52/Ro60 and anti-La autoantibodies. The disease course is usually slow and benign in the majority of patients; antecedent major stressful life events have been reported prior to onset. Recently described as triggerable by PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor therapy. Parotid or major salivary gland enlargement, especially persistent or with a lymph node mass >7 cm — concern for lymphoma Palpable purpura, urticarial lesions, skin ulcerations, or mononeuritis multiplex (immune complex–mediated vasculitis) Low C4 complement, monoclonal gammopathy (paraproteinemia), and cryoglobulins — lymphoma risk markers Heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates with germinal center formation on salivary biopsy — lymphoma risk B symptoms (constitutional) with lymphadenopathy Severe tongue atrophy and leukopenia in the appropriate context Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with mixed type II/III cryoglobulinemia Myelitis with anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (rare CNS involvement) Failing to take a careful medication history — diuretics, antihypertensives, anticholinergics, and antidepressants can themselves cause dryness and mimic or worsen sicca. Overlooking HIV- or HCV-associated sicca syndrome, which can closely resemble Sjögren’s but lacks anti-Ro/La and has distinct demographics and glandular infiltrate phenotype. Missing renal tubular dysfunction: interstitial nephritis may be asymptomatic, presenting only as hyposthenuria or renal tubular acidosis, and untreated acidosis can progress to nephrocalcinosis. Attributing all salivary gland enlargement to benign disease and missing an incidental MALT lymphoma on labial biopsy. Not excluding sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, IgG4-related disease, graft-versus-host disease, and prior head/neck radiation before diagnosing Sjögren’s disease. Assuming arthritis is erosive — arthritis in primary Sjögren’s disease is characteristically nonerosive (may lead to Jaccoud’s arthropathy). Activated T lymphocytes are the major infiltrating cells in affected exocrine (chiefly salivary and lacrimal) glands, with B-cell populations prevailing in heavily infiltrated labial minor salivary gland tissue; follicular, myeloid, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages are also present, the latter (with inflammasome activation) being linked to lymphoma risk. Ductal and acinar epithelial cells play an active pathogenic role: they aberrantly express costimulatory molecules and surface Ro/La autoantigens, secrete proinflammatory cytokines and lymphocyte-attracting chemokines that support ectopic germinal center formation, express innate-immunity Toll-like receptors (TLR3, 7, 9), and display immunoregulatory molecules (ICAM, CD40). Epithelial cells produce B cell–activating factor (BAFF), induced by type I and II interferons, and circulating BAFF is elevated (especially with hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibodies), exerting an antiapoptotic effect on B lymphocytes; epithelial cells themselves show increased apoptosis. Disease initiation and perpetuation reflect interplay of endogenous triggers (intracellular stress, inappropriate expression of endogenous nucleic acids) and exogenous triggers (viruses, hormonal factors, stressful life events) on a genetically hyperactive immune background. Established genetic loci include HLA-DQA1*0501, interferon/BAFF axis variants (IRF5, STAT4, BAFF), B-cell function genes (EBF1, BLK), and combined deficiencies of the classical complement pathway. The disease usually evolves slowly and follows a benign course in most patients. The dominant adverse outcome is malignant transformation: Sjögren’s disease carries the highest lymphoma risk of any autoimmune disease, with clinical (parotid enlargement, severe tongue atrophy, palpable purpura), hematologic/serologic (leukopenia, autoantibodies, low C4, monoclonal gammopathy, cryoglobulins), and histopathologic (germinal center formation, heavy focal lymphocytic infiltrates) risk factors. Survival is reduced in patients with B symptoms, lymph node mass >7 cm, and high or intermediate histologic grade. Patients also have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, paralleling rheumatoid arthritis and SLE. Diagnosis/classification per the 2016 ACR-EULAR criteria: suspect in patients with dry eyes and/or dry mouth (or systemic features such as major salivary gland enlargement, fatigue, Raynaud’s, small-joint arthralgia/arthritis, palpable purpura/urticaria, renal tubular acidosis/membranoproliferative GN, ILD/small airway disease, autoimmune cholangitis, peripheral neuropathy, or MS-like lesions), supported by objective findings: unstimulated whole saliva flow ≤0.1 mL/min, Schirmer’s test ≤5 mm/5 min, ocular staining score ≥5 (or van Bijsterveld ≥4), serum anti-Ro antibodies, and minor salivary gland biopsy focus score ≥1. Exclusions include prior head/neck radiation, active HCV, AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, graft-versus-host disease, and IgG4-related disease. Extraglandular disease severity is gauged by the categories of involvement (nonspecific, periepithelial, immune complex–mediated, and lymphoma).

Sjögren syndrome — SS, sicca syndrome, Sjogren's syndrome, autoimmune epithelitis Age-related or medication-induced sicca (anticholinergics) Sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease affecting salivary glands Chronic viral infection (hepatitis C, HIV) Radiation-induced glandular damage Other connective tissue diseases with secondary sicca Amyloidosis Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies, ANA, and rheumatoid factor Schirmer test and ocular surface staining for aqueous tear deficiency Unstimulated whole salivary flow and salivary gland ultrasound or imaging Labial minor salivary gland biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis Serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis; monitoring for lymphoma if persistent gland enlargement or new lymphadenopathy Characterised by dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) from immune-mediated destruction of lacrimal and salivary glands Predominantly affects middle-aged women and may be primary or secondary to another connective tissue disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus Systemic features include fatigue, arthralgia, Raynaud phenomenon, parotid gland swelling, and cutaneous vasculitis Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies are characteristic, along with positive antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor Objective sicca can be confirmed with Schirmer test, ocular surface staining, and unstimulated salivary flow; labial minor salivary gland biopsy shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis There is a markedly increased lifetime risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, particularly MALT lymphoma Anti-Ro antibodies in pregnancy carry a risk of neonatal lupus and congenital heart block Management centres on symptomatic relief of dryness (tear and saliva substitutes, secretagogues) with immunosuppression reserved for significant systemic involvement Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement, lymphadenopathy, or new cytopenias suggesting lymphoma transformation Signs of systemic vasculitis, mononeuritis multiplex, or interstitial lung disease Renal involvement such as renal tubular acidosis or interstitial nephritis Pregnancy with anti-Ro antibodies given the risk of fetal congenital heart block Severe corneal complications from untreated dry eye Dismissing sicca symptoms as trivial and missing systemic or lymphomatous complications Failing to consider mimics such as IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, or viral infection Not counselling and monitoring anti-Ro-positive women in pregnancy for fetal heart block Overlooking increased dental caries and ocular surface damage from chronic dryness Attributing new persistent gland swelling to disease flare rather than investigating for lymphoma Sjögren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy in which lymphocytic (mainly CD4 T-cell and B-cell) infiltration of the exocrine glands destroys secretory epithelium, sometimes termed autoimmune epithelitis. B-cell hyperactivity produces autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB) and hypergammaglobulinaemia, and sustained clonal B-cell proliferation underlies the elevated lymphoma risk. Type I interferon signalling and genetic HLA associations contribute to disease susceptibility. Extraglandular disease reflects immune complex deposition and lymphocytic infiltration of organs including skin, joints, lungs, kidneys, and nervous system. Most patients have a good prognosis with a slowly progressive course dominated by sicca symptoms, but systemic involvement and, importantly, lymphoma development can worsen outcomes. Lifelong monitoring for lymphoproliferative disease is warranted.

cleavage is superficial (subcorneal), spares mucosa DRESS / drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome - maculopapular eruption, facial edema, eosinophilia, multiorgan (especially hepatic) involvement Erythema multiforme major - target lesions with mucous-membrane involvement Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) - sterile pustules on erythema, flexural predominance Exfoliative erythroderma syndrome - diffuse erythema/scaling, may be drug-induced Autoimmune blistering disease (e.g., bullous pemphigoid, which can also be drug-induced/exacerbated) SJS/TEN is a single disease spectrum of full-thickness epidermal necrosis with blistering and mucosal/epidermal detachment, separated only by the extent of body surface area (BSA) detachment. Drugs cause roughly 80% of cases; the most frequently implicated agents are sulfonamide antibiotics, allopurinol, antiepileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), oxicam NSAIDs, beta-lactam and other antibiotics, and nevirapine. Onset is typically delayed, around 5-28 days after starting the culprit drug. Prodrome: fever >39 C (102.2 F), sore throat, and conjunctivitis precede or accompany the rash; lesions are painful, dusky, atypical and target-like. It is uncommon in children and over-represented among people with HIV, SLE, certain HLA types, and slow acetylators. Mucosal surfaces are characteristically involved, and Nikolsky's sign is positive. SJS/TEN is mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognizing a drug-HLA class I complex; granulysin released by these cells is thought to be the principal mediator of keratinocyte death. Strong, drug- and phenotype-specific HLA associations exist: HLA-B*15:02 with carbamazepine SJS/TEN (Han Chinese), HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol, HLA-B*13:01 with dapsone/sulfonamide. Frozen-section skin biopsy can aid rapid diagnosis and distinguish SJS/TEN (full-thickness epidermal necrosis) from mimics. Loss of skin barrier integrity leads to dehydration and secondary sepsis, which are major causes of death. Extensive/rapidly progressing epidermal detachment (BSA toward TEN range) - maximal-severity form Older age, malignancy, or renal insufficiency - independently associated with poor prognosis Signs of sepsis or dehydration from loss of skin barrier integrity Mucosal (ocular, oral, urogenital, respiratory) involvement - risk of acute and long-term sequelae Early SJS may be hard to distinguish from AGEP; in AGEP erosions are superficial and prominent mucosal involvement is NOT present. Drugs may be implicated even when the eruption appears shortly AFTER the drug has been discontinued (delayed-type reactions). A risk HLA allele does NOT by itself cause SJS/TEN - most carriers remain drug-tolerant; other factors (e.g., drug metabolism) are required. Designation of a single diagnosis is NOT always possible in overlap hypersensitivity syndromes; manage according to the dominant evolving clinical features. Skin biopsy helps characterize the reaction but does NOT by itself establish drug causality. A delayed, T-cell-mediated (type IVa, cytotoxic) severe cutaneous adverse reaction. A drug or metabolite-altered antigen is presented in association with a risk HLA class I allele by keratinocytes or other antigen-presenting cells; a restricted T-cell receptor on skin-enriched CD8+ T cells recognizes this drug-HLA complex, triggering activation and release of cytolytic mediators (notably granulysin) that cause full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte death and detachment. Proposed antigen-presentation models include hapten/prohapten covalent binding, the pharmacologic-interaction (p-i) noncovalent model, and the altered-peptide-repertoire model (as proven for abacavir-HLA-B*57:01). Carbamazepine SJS/TEN shows a highly restricted V-alpha/V-beta TCR repertoire shared among HLA-B*15:02 patients. A risk HLA allele alone is insufficient; non-MHC factors such as drug metabolism (e.g., CYP2C9*3 slow metabolism with phenytoin) contribute. (Harrison 22e p.417-420) Mortality is substantial and rises with the extent of epidermal detachment: at least ~10% of SJS and ~30% of TEN patients die from the disease (overall reported mortality up to ~30%). Older age, greater BSA detachment, malignancy, and renal insufficiency are independent poor-prognostic factors. Best outcomes follow early diagnosis and immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug. (Harrison 22e p.142, p.424-425) Classified by percent body surface area (BSA) of epidermal detachment: SJS = <10% BSA; SJS/TEN overlap = 10-30% BSA; TEN = >30% BSA (maximal form). (Harrison 22e p.142, p.424). SCORTEN (severity-of-illness score for TEN) is the standard prognostic tool; note the source text does not enumerate its parameters.
