incisional (shave, saucerization, or punch) biopsy of the most nodular/darkest area when excision is impractical - incisional biopsy does not facilitate melanoma spread Histopathology report should include Breslow thickness, mitotic rate, ulceration, lymphatic/vascular/neural invasion, regression, microsatellitosis, and margin status Dermoscopy (low-level magnification with polarized light or water interface) and total-body photography for surveillance in high-risk patients Genetic expression profiles (GEP, e.g. 31-gene), FISH with multiple probes, or comparative genomic hybridization to distinguish difficult melanomas from benign nevi and estimate prognosis Complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, and serum LDH (LDH is part of AJCC stage IV criteria) Sentinel lymph node biopsy for pathologic staging CT, PET, or combined CT/PET (and MRI) when symptoms, exam, or abnormal labs suggest metastatic disease Genetic testing for individuals with >=3 primary melanomas or with families having >=1 invasive melanoma plus >=2 cases of melanoma and/or pancreatic cancer, ocular melanoma, mesothelioma, or renal cell carcinoma on one side Superficial BCC mimicking nummular eczema or psoriasis SCC mistaken for a wart or callus when inflammatory response is minimal Pigmented (nodular) BCC mimicking melanoma Desmoplastic melanoma mimicking nodular basal cell carcinoma Benign nevus mimicking melanoma Apply the ABCDE rule to pigmented lesions to detect melanoma early: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variegation, Diameter >6 mm (pencil-eraser size), and Evolving (any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or new symptoms such as bleeding, itching, or crusting) (p.601). The 'ugly duckling' sign: any nevus that looks atypical and different from the rest of an individual's nevi should be considered suspicious (p.601). Melanoma is an aggressive malignancy of melanocytes and accounts for over half of all deaths from skin cancer, even though it is far less common than nonmelanoma skin cancer (p.598). Basal cell carcinoma is among the most common cancers; its natural history is a slowly enlarging, locally invasive neoplasm with low metastatic potential (~0.1% in immunocompetent patients), though the risk of recurrence or a new primary NMSC is about 40% over 5 years (p.607). Nodular BCC classically presents as a pearly nodule with tortuous telangiectatic vessels, rolled borders, and a central crust; pigmented BCC may contain melanin and be confused with melanoma (p.606-607). Squamous cell carcinoma arises from keratinizing epidermal cells on sun-exposed skin and can metastasize (0.3-5.2%), most often to regional lymph nodes; lower-lip and ear tumors metastasize in 13% and 11% respectively (p.606-607). Actinic keratoses and actinic cheilitis are premalignant forms of SCC; SCC in situ (Bowen's disease) presents as a scaling erythematous plaque, and treating premalignant/in-situ lesions reduces subsequent invasive disease (p.607). NMSCs (SCC ~80%, BCC ~18% of cases) are the most common cancers in the US, with an estimated >5.3 million cases annually (p.606). Breslow thickness (greatest tumor thickness measured from the top of the granular layer or ulcer base to the bottom of the tumor) is the best predictor of melanoma recurrence and, with ulceration, defines the T stage (p.601-602). Any pigmented lesion that has changed (size, shape, color, elevation) or that meets ABCDE criteria is a candidate for biopsy An 'ugly duckling' nevus that differs from a patient's other nevi New bleeding, itching, or crusting in a pigmented lesion Thick and/or ulcerated melanoma (key adverse T-stage features) Microsatellite lesions, in-transit metastases, nodal involvement, elevated LDH, or distant metastases to brain/liver/bone SCC on the lower lip or ear, recurrent SCC (~30% metastatic risk), or SCC in scars/chronic ulcers, genital/mucosal surfaces, or in immunosuppressed patients (aggressive behavior) Rapidly expanding lesion in an older, immunosuppressed, UV-exposed patient (MCC: AEIOU - Asymptomatic, Expanding rapidly, Immunosuppression, Older than 50, UV-exposed site) Morpheaform, infiltrative, and micronodular BCCs have indistinct borders and subtle presentation, so treatment is often delayed and tumors are more extensive than they appear clinically SCC can be mistaken for a benign wart or callus when the inflammatory response is minimal Pigmented BCC may be confused with melanoma; desmoplastic melanoma can mimic nodular BCC Melanoma frequently develops on non-sun-exposed skin (acral, mucosal); in dark-skinned, Hispanic, and East Asian populations melanoma is often non-UV-related, diagnosed at higher stage, and has worse outcomes The 31-gene GEP can estimate distant-relapse probability but has not supplanted prognostic estimates from surgical staging, and genomic pathway data are not yet incorporated into AJCC staging Standard labs and imaging rarely detect occult metastatic disease in early melanoma and should be directed by symptoms/exam findings Melanoma is a malignancy of melanocytes, neural-crest-derived pigment-producing cells; most melanomas arise in skin but can occur in mucosa, eye, meninges, and upper esophagus. UV radiation is the dominant environmental driver, and cutaneous melanomas carry one of the highest somatic mutation rates of any cancer (>10 mutations/Mb), the majority bearing a UV signature. Key driver mutations affect the MAP-kinase and PI3K/AKT proliferative pathways: BRAF (commonly V600E) in 40-50% of cutaneous melanomas, NRAS in ~20%, and loss-of-function NF1 in 10-15%; germline CDKN2A (p16/ARF, RB and p53 pathways), CDK4, MITF, BAP1, POT1, TERT, and moderate-risk MC1R variants underlie inherited susceptibility. Nonmelanoma skin cancers are also UV-driven: SCC is associated with p53 and N-RAS damage, whereas BCC is driven by hedgehog (Hh) pathway activation, usually loss of function of the tumor-suppressor PTCH1 (which normally inhibits SMO). Merkel cell carcinoma is linked to the oncogenic Merkel cell polyomavirus, present in ~80% of tumors (p.598-607). Melanoma prognosis is dominated by Breslow thickness and ulceration (T stage); favorable primary sites are the forearm and leg, unfavorable sites the scalp, hands, feet, and mucous membranes. 10-year melanoma-specific survival ranges from >99% for stage 0 (in situ) and ~98% for stage IA down to ~24-30% for stage IIID. Women with stage I/II disease and younger patients do better; older men have worse outcomes (delayed diagnosis, thicker tumors, more head/neck, acral and BRAF wild-type tumors). High mitotic rate and lymphatic/vascular invasion are additional adverse factors. Overall melanoma mortality has been falling, attributed to immunotherapy and targeted therapy. BCC rarely metastasizes (~0.1% in immunocompetent patients) but recurs frequently. Cutaneous SCC metastasizes in 0.3-5.2% of cases overall, higher for lip/ear/recurrent/immunosuppressed disease. Merkel cell carcinoma is aggressive: ~90% cure with local disease but ~52% survival with nodal and ~10% with distant disease (p.602-609). Melanoma is staged by the AJCC TNM system (T stage built primarily on Breslow thickness and ulceration; pathologic stage incorporates sentinel lymph node biopsy results), from stage 0 (in situ, Tis) through stage IV (distant metastasis); 10-year melanoma-specific survival is depicted by stage in Table 81-3. Merkel cell carcinoma has its own TNM staging incorporating tumor size (<2 cm vs >2 cm), nodal status, and distant metastases (p.602-609).

prevalence is highest among Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women; disease tends to be more severe in non-White patients (p.2827). Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so a positive serology in a symptomatic patient supports attributing nonspecific complaints to SLE (p.2827, 2829). Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; treatment goals are low disease activity (SLEDAI 0-4) or remission on ≤5 mg/day prednisone equivalent (p.2829, 2832). A proposed clinical split distinguishes type 1 lupus (classic inflammatory/organ manifestations such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis that respond to immunosuppression) from type 2 lupus (fatigue, diffuse pain, brain fog, depression, sleep disturbance that respond poorly to immunosuppression) (p.2827). Anti-dsDNA titers and C3/C4 levels track disease activity: anti-dsDNA is produced by short-lived plasmablasts that turn over quickly, and complement falls during high activity as it is consumed by immune complexes (p.2832). Rising anti-dsDNA and falling C3/C4 can serve as warning signs of impending active nephritis even in an asymptomatic patient (p.2830). Lupus arthritis is typically non-erosive (Jaccoud-like reversible deformity from ligamentous laxity); overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829). Pain out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee — especially with prior corticosteroid use — should raise concern for avascular necrosis of bone (p.2829). Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death, notably myocardial infarction and stroke in young patients without traditional risk factors, and is the leading cause of death after ~5 years of disease (p.2829, 2836). Antiphospholipid antibodies/APS coexist in about a third of SLE patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, stroke (reported in up to 19%), Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and pregnancy loss (p.2829, 2830, 2831). Rapidly declining eGFR, rising proteinuria, or active urinary sediment — class III/IV proliferative lupus nephritis; ~20% of class IV patients die or reach ESRD within 10 years (p.2830) Crescentic / rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (cellular crescents or fibrinoid necrosis) — poor prognostic features (p.2834) Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with capillaritis (p.2829) Mesenteric vasculitis — risk of intestinal perforation, bleeding, and ischemia (p.2830) Neuropsychiatric flare: seizures, acute psychosis/confusion, transverse myelitis (p.2829) Atypical HUS/TTP-like crisis: hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, microvascular thrombosis (p.2831) Severe thrombocytopenia (<20-50 x10^9/L) with bleeding risk; severe hemolytic anemia (p.2830, 2833) Stroke or arterial/venous thrombosis suggesting APS (p.2829-2830) Pulmonary arterial hypertension, prior arterial thrombosis, or severe end-organ damage — highest maternal mortality; pregnancy should strongly be reconsidered (p.2836) Distinguishing flare from infection is a central challenge: cytopenias and constitutional symptoms can stem from disease activity, medication, OR infection, and acute lupus pneumonitis can look identical to pneumonia on imaging — infection must be excluded before escalating immunosuppression (p.2829-2830). Classification criteria (2019 EULAR/ACR; 2012 SLICC) were built for trial enrollment, not diagnosis — diagnosis remains an individualized clinical judgment; relying on criteria alone can mislead, and ANA-negative or incomplete-lupus patients are excluded by EULAR/ACR (p.2827). A positive ANA or even antihistone antibody alone does not confirm SLE — many drugs induce a positive ANA in patients who never develop symptoms, and antihistone antibodies occur in most SLE cases too (p.2835). Drug-induced lupus can be hard to separate from SLE because skin biopsy and many labs overlap; presence of additional SLE-specific autoantibodies (rarely seen in DIL) and symptom resolution after stopping the drug help distinguish (p.2835). Acute psychosis/confusion may be glucocorticoid-induced rather than neuropsychiatric lupus — and infectious encephalitis must also be ruled out (p.2829). Single-joint pain out of proportion may be avascular necrosis (steroid-related), not arthritis flare (p.2829). Estrogen-containing contraceptives/HRT should be avoided in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or moderate-severe/active lupus due to thromboembolism risk (p.2836). SLE arises from overactive innate and adaptive immunity with autoantibodies directed at nuclear components (nucleic acids, nucleosomes, RNA-binding proteins). Impaired clearance of cellular debris — driven by high neutrophil turnover/NETosis and defective complement-mediated phagocytosis — overwhelms macrophages and dendritic cells. Accumulated nucleic acids engage toll-like receptors and nucleic-acid sensors in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving type 1 interferon production that primes the immune response. Autoreactive B cells (including expanded age-associated B cells) lose tolerance and, with help from T follicular/T peripheral helper cells, mature into autoantibody-secreting plasma cells, while regulatory T-cell function is defective. Resulting immune complexes deposit in tissues and cause inflammation, repair, and eventual fibrosis after recurrent flares. Strong genetic component (monozygotic twin concordance 24% vs 2% dizygotic; >150 GWAS loci, with the MHC the strongest and nearly half of loci linked to type 1 interferon; monogenic complement-pathway deficiencies — C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4 — cause severe SLE). Environmental triggers include UV light, smoking, crystalline silica, mercury/toxins, sex hormones, EBV, and gut microbiome/permeability changes (p.2827-2829). Prognosis and survival vary widely by geography, race/ethnicity, and access to care/medications. Renal disease, especially class IV nephritis, carries substantial risk of ESRD and death (~20% within 10 years), and is more severe in non-White patients. Accelerated atherosclerosis is a major cause of premature death and the leading cause after ~5 years of disease, driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, high homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoid exposure independently accrues irreversible organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at doses as low as 5 mg prednisone equivalent. Class V (membranous) nephritis has a better prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2+ years is associated with significantly less damage. Recent meta-analyses suggest an increased overall cancer risk and cancer-related mortality (p.2830, 2835-2836). Disease activity is graded for treatment using SLEDAI/SLEDAI-2K (low disease activity = SLEDAI 0-4; remission/DORIS = SLEDAI 0). EULAR severity tiers: mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6); moderate (RA-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12); severe (major organ-threatening disease e.g. cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or acute hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Lupus nephritis is graded by ISN/RPS renal biopsy classes I-V (class I mesangial deposits; II mesangial proliferative; III focal proliferative; IV diffuse proliferative; V membranous; III/IV +/- V combinations), with class III/IV (and III/IV+V) being proliferative forms warranting aggressive therapy (p.2827, 2830-2831, 2833-2834).

Sleep Apnea — obstructive sleep apnea, OSA, central sleep apnea Narcolepsy (multiple sleep latency / maintenance of wakefulness testing helps distinguish from OSA) Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea Nocturnal asthma Acid reflux with laryngospasm Insomnia (common in the general population, may coexist with OSA) Obesity-hypoventilation / hypoventilation syndromes Periodic limb movement disorder Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG) - gold standard Home sleep test (respiratory and cardiac channels) for cost-effective diagnosis Apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) and respiratory disturbance index (RDI) quantification Overnight oximetry profile (mean, nadir, time at low saturation) Multiple sleep latency test / maintenance of wakefulness test (quantify sleepiness, distinguish narcolepsy) Upper-airway imaging (cephalometry, MRI, CT) and fibreoptic endoscopy to identify anatomic risk factors (not routine; useful for surgical planning) Cardiac evaluation for systolic/diastolic dysfunction or structural abnormality Overnight blood-pressure monitoring (may show nondipping pattern) Arterial blood gas (usually normal awake; waking hypoxaemia/hypercarbia suggests cardiopulmonary disease or hypoventilation) Drug-induced sleep endoscopy (for hypoglossal-nerve stimulation candidacy) Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea Nocturnal asthma Acid reflux with laryngospasm Narcolepsy Cheyne-Stokes / central sleep apnoea of heart failure OSA diagnosis requires either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbance (snoring, snorting, gasping, breathing pauses) impairing quality of life or unexplained daytime sleepiness/fatigue, PLUS at least 5 obstructive apnoeas/hypopnoeas per hour of sleep (apnoea-hypopnoea index, AHI) on a sleep study; OSA may also be diagnosed without symptoms if AHI is at least 15 episodes/h (p.2277-2278). Each apnoea/hypopnoea is a reduction in breathing for at least 10 s, commonly causing a fall in oxygen saturation of at least 3% or a cortical arousal (p.2278). The major risk factors for OSA are obesity, male sex, and older age; roughly 40-60% of cases are attributable to excess weight, but the absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.2278). Snoring is the most common symptom, but its absence does NOT exclude OSA because pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration; the most common daytime symptom is excessive sleepiness, though women preferentially report fatigue rather than sleepiness (p.2279). Dyspnoea is unusual in OSA, and its absence generally distinguishes OSA from paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, nocturnal asthma, and acid reflux with laryngospasm (p.2279). Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for diagnosis; a negative in-lab PSG usually rules out OSA, but false-negatives can occur with night-to-night variation, insufficient REM sleep, or less supine sleep than typical (p.2279). Home sleep tests recording only respiratory and cardiac channels are a cost-effective option; when prior probability of OSA is high, a negative home study should be followed by PSG (p.2279). CPAP is the standard medical therapy with the highest level of evidence; it acts as a mechanical splint to hold the airway open during sleep, and auto-titrating (APAP) home devices have eliminated the need for titration studies in many patients (p.2281). Although CPAP reduces 24-h ambulatory blood pressure, the overall effect is modest (averaging 2-4 mmHg), with larger improvements in patients with high AHI, daytime sleepiness, or resistant hypertension (p.2280-2281). Large randomized trials have FAILED to show that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival, possibly because sleepy patients (who may have the greatest risk) were excluded and because of limited treatment adherence (p.2281). Central sleep apnoea (CSA) is less common than OSA and may occur alone or, more often, combined with obstructive events as mixed apnoeas; it is often driven by increased sensitivity to PCO2 causing unstable breathing, and a prolonged circulation delay (as in congestive heart failure) produces the crescendo-decrescendo Cheyne-Stokes pattern (p.2282). Treatment of CSA has NOT been shown to improve long-term health outcomes, so specific treatment is generally indicated only for symptomatic CSA; unlike OSA, treatment is difficult and depends on the underlying cause (p.2282). Waking hypoxaemia or hypercarbia, suggesting coexisting cardiopulmonary disease or a hypoventilation syndrome Evidence of cor pulmonale, suggesting a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition (OSA alone is NOT thought to cause right-heart failure) Resistant or uncontrolled hypertension Excessive daytime sleepiness with occupational accident or motor-vehicle-crash risk (drowsy driving) Coexisting heart failure (raises risk of both OSA and CSA) Severe nocturnal hypoxaemia with elevated haemoglobin Assuming absence of snoring excludes OSA - pharyngeal collapse can occur without tissue vibration. Assuming a normal weight excludes OSA - absence of obesity does NOT exclude the diagnosis. Underrecognising OSA in women, who have a lower arousal threshold, shorter and more REM-predominant apnoeas, and tend to report fatigue/insomnia rather than classic sleepiness. Relying on symptoms/signs to gauge severity - they do not accurately predict the severity of sleep-related breathing disturbance; objective measurement is required. Treating a single negative home sleep study as definitive when prior probability is high - follow with PSG. Attributing right-heart failure/cor pulmonale to OSA alone, which is not thought to cause it - look for a comorbid cardiopulmonary condition. Using adaptive servoventilation in patients with CSA and LVEF below 45% (FDA warning following increased mortality). Sedative-hypnotics have inconsistent effects and should be avoided in most patients with moderate-to-severe OSA; opioids worsen CSA in a dose-dependent way. In OSA the pharyngeal airway lacks fixed bony/cartilaginous support, so patency depends on pharyngeal dilator muscles. Inspiration generates increasingly negative intraluminal pressure (a suctioning force); at sleep onset neuromuscular output to these muscles declines, and in a collapsible airway this causes transient pharyngeal collapse (apnoea) or near-collapse (hypopnoea), typically terminated by an arousal that restores muscle activity. Collapse sites include the soft palate (most common), tongue base, lateral pharyngeal walls, and epiglottis. OSA is often worst in REM sleep (lowest skeletal-muscle output) and supine (gravity). A small pharyngeal lumen (soft-tissue enlargement from fat, lymphoid tissue, or genetic variation; craniofacial factors such as mandibular retroposition/micrognathia), low lung volume (reduced caudal pharyngeal traction, pronounced in obesity), and high nasal resistance all predispose to collapse. Pharyngeal muscle activation is linked to ventilatory drive: an over-sensitive ventilatory control system, a low arousal threshold (preempting CO2-mediated muscle compensation), or a high arousal threshold (prolonging apnoeas) all contribute. In OSA-related disease, sleep fragmentation, cortical arousals, and intermittent hypoxaemia/hypercapnia drive sympathetic overactivity, blood-pressure surges, a prothrombotic/proinflammatory state, insulin resistance, and large negative intrathoracic pressure swings that alter cardiac preload/afterload and promote cardiac/electrical remodelling. CSA is usually caused by increased PCO2 sensitivity producing hyperventilation alternating with apnoea, plus prolonged circulatory delay (heart failure) giving Cheyne-Stokes breathing. OSA is the most common medical cause of daytime sleepiness and reduces quality of life. It is strongly associated with cardiac, cerebrovascular and metabolic disease (coronary artery disease, heart failure with and without reduced EF, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, atherosclerosis, stroke, diabetes), premature death, and increased risk of certain cancers. Untreated OSA carries a roughly twofold risk of occupational accidents and a two- to threefold increase in motor-vehicle crashes. CPAP improves alertness, mood, quality of life, blood pressure and insulin sensitivity, but randomized trials have NOT shown that CPAP reduces cardiovascular/stroke events or prolongs survival. CSA carries increased risk for heart failure and atrial fibrillation, and its treatment has not been shown to improve long-term outcomes; adaptive servoventilation showed no cardiovascular or mortality benefit and increased mortality in patients with LVEF below 45%. OSA severity by apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI = apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep): mild OSAHS = AHI 5-14 events/h; moderate OSAHS = AHI 15-29 events/h; severe OSAHS = AHI at least 30 events/h. The respiratory disturbance index (RDI) additionally counts respiratory effort-related arousals (RERAs). Each AHI level can be further qualified by the degree of sleepiness and associated hypoxaemia (Table 308-2, p.2280).

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis — SCFE, SUFE, slipped upper femoral epiphysis, femoral head epiphysis slip Perthes' disease Transient synovitis of the hip Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis Juvenile idiopathic arthritis Femoral neck stress fracture or trauma Muscle strain or apophyseal avulsion Referred pain from other hip or spinal pathology Anteroposterior and frog-lateral pelvic radiographs of both hips (the lateral view is key for subtle slips) Assessment of Klein's line and the physeal appearance MRI or ultrasound in equivocal cases or to assess a pre-slip Endocrine and metabolic workup (e.g. thyroid function, renal function) in young, atypical, or bilateral presentations Careful hip examination for loss of internal rotation and obligatory external rotation on flexion A displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis through the growth plate, typically in overweight adolescents around the time of the pubertal growth spurt Presents with hip, groin, thigh, or referred knee pain and a limp; knee or thigh pain in an adolescent must always prompt examination of the hip A characteristic sign is obligatory external rotation of the hip when it is passively flexed, with limited internal rotation Radiographs should include a frog-lateral view, as subtle slips are best seen laterally; a line along the superior femoral neck (Klein's line) normally intersects the epiphysis Slips are classified by symptom duration (acute, chronic, acute-on-chronic) and by whether the child can weight-bear (stable versus unstable), which strongly influences the risk of avascular necrosis It is an orthopaedic urgency: once suspected the child should stop weight-bearing and be referred promptly, as further slipping worsens the outlook Treatment is surgical stabilisation, usually in-situ pinning to prevent progression, and the contralateral hip may be pinned if at high risk Consider an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder (e.g. hypothyroidism, renal disease) in atypical, young, or bilateral cases SURGICAL URGENCY: suspected SCFE requires immediate non-weight-bearing and prompt referral to prevent further slip Unstable slip (inability to weight-bear) carrying a high risk of avascular necrosis Adolescent knee or thigh pain that could be referred from an undiagnosed hip slip Bilateral or very young presentation suggesting an underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder Attributing knee or thigh pain to the knee and failing to image the hip, leading to missed or late diagnosis Allowing continued weight-bearing on a suspected slip, risking further displacement and avascular necrosis Missing a subtle slip by not obtaining a frog-lateral radiograph Overlooking an underlying endocrine cause in atypical or bilateral cases Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs when shear forces exceed the strength of the proximal femoral physis, allowing the epiphysis to displace, typically posteriorly and inferiorly, relative to the femoral neck (so the neck effectively rotates anteriorly and externally on the head). The physis is mechanically weakest during the adolescent growth spurt, and obesity increases the mechanical load, while hormonal factors influence physeal strength, explaining associations with endocrine disorders. In unstable slips the epiphyseal blood supply, which runs along the femoral neck, is at high risk of disruption, predisposing to avascular necrosis. Residual deformity from a healed slip alters femoral head-neck morphology and can cause femoroacetabular impingement and early osteoarthritis. Stable slips treated promptly with in-situ fixation generally do well, whereas unstable slips carry a substantial risk of avascular necrosis and chondrolysis; even after successful fixation, residual femoral head-neck deformity can cause impingement and predispose to premature osteoarthritis, so long-term follow-up is important.

testing where hydrops fetalis occurs Skeletal survey for dysostosis multiplex Echocardiography and developmental assessment for systemic and neurological involvement Caused by deficiency of beta-glucuronidase, impairing degradation of dermatan, heparan, and chondroitin sulfates One of the recognised metabolic causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis, which may present at birth or in utero Phenotype is broad, ranging from severe neonatal disease to attenuated forms presenting later in childhood Features overlap with other mucopolysaccharidoses: coarse facies, dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, and variable cognitive impairment Multiple glycosaminoglycans accumulate and are excreted because the deficient enzyme acts on several substrates Diagnosis rests on deficient beta-glucuronidase activity confirmed by GUSB gene testing Enzyme replacement therapy is available and may improve some systemic manifestations Non-immune hydrops fetalis or severe neonatal presentation Progressive cardiorespiratory compromise Cervical spine instability with cord compression Rapid neurodevelopmental decline in severe forms Not considering a lysosomal storage disorder in the workup of non-immune hydrops fetalis Assuming a uniform severe course given the wide phenotypic range Confusing the mixed glycosaminoglycan pattern with other mucopolysaccharidoses without enzyme testing Overlooking cervical spine and cardiac surveillance Sly syndrome is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GUSB, encoding the lysosomal enzyme beta-glucuronidase. This enzyme participates in the degradation of dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, and chondroitin-4/6-sulfate, so its deficiency causes accumulation of all these glycosaminoglycans within lysosomes across many tissues. The resulting storage produces multisystem disease affecting the skeleton, connective tissue, viscera, cardiovascular system, and, in more severe forms, the central nervous system. Severe cases can present antenatally with non-immune hydrops fetalis. Excess glycosaminoglycans are excreted in the urine. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the degree of residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with the wide clinical spectrum. Prognosis depends heavily on the phenotype; severe neonatal disease with hydrops carries high early mortality, while attenuated forms may allow survival into adulthood with variable disability. Enzyme replacement therapy can improve some somatic manifestations.

or sterol synthesis Disorders of sexual development from other causes CHARGE and other multiple congenital anomaly syndromes Syndromic autism with dysmorphism Holoprosencephaly of other aetiologies biosynthesis caused by variants in DHCR7, encoding 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase, the final enzyme of the pathway The biochemical hallmark is a raised concentration of 7-dehydrocholesterol with low or low-normal cholesterol Characteristic malformations include microcephaly, distinctive facial features, cleft palate, and cardiac and genital anomalies Syndactyly of the second and third toes (Y-shaped 2-3 toe syndactyly) is a classic and useful clinical clue Ambiguous or undervirilised genitalia in genetic males reflects impaired steroidogenesis downstream of cholesterol The clinical spectrum is wide, from mild learning and behavioural difficulties to severe multiple congenital anomalies incompatible with survival Behavioural features overlapping with autism spectrum disorder are common Dietary cholesterol supplementation is used, though its effect on neurodevelopmental outcome remains uncertain Multiple congenital anomalies with microcephaly and dysmorphism in a neonate Ambiguous genitalia requiring urgent endocrine evaluation Feeding difficulties, failure to thrive and recurrent illness Signs of adrenal insufficiency during stress Measuring only total cholesterol, which can be normal, rather than specific sterol profiling Missing adrenal insufficiency during intercurrent illness or surgery Attributing the phenotype to a chromosomal syndrome without sterol testing Assuming cholesterol supplementation reliably improves neurodevelopment 7-Dehydrocholesterol reductase catalyses the last step of cholesterol synthesis, reducing 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol. In Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome this enzyme is deficient, so cholesterol production falls and the immediate precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol and its isomer accumulate. Cholesterol is essential for cell membranes, myelin, bile acids, steroid hormones and Sonic hedgehog signalling during embryogenesis. Deficiency during development therefore disrupts morphogenesis (explaining the malformation pattern, including holoprosencephaly-spectrum features from impaired hedgehog signalling), while accumulated precursor sterols may exert additional toxic effects. Impaired steroidogenesis contributes to the genital and adrenal manifestations. Prognosis correlates with disease severity: the most severely affected infants have major malformations and high early mortality, whereas milder cases survive with variable intellectual disability and behavioural difficulties. Cholesterol supplementation may improve some physical parameters, but its benefit for cognition and behaviour is not clearly established.

Smith-Magenis syndrome — SMS, RAI1, 17p11.2 deletion syndrome, retinoic acid-induced 1 gene disorder Potocki-Lupski syndrome (reciprocal 17p11.2 duplication) Down syndrome and other chromosomal microdeletion/duplication syndromes Fragile X syndrome Autism spectrum disorder with sleep disturbance Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes Other syndromic intellectual disability with self-injurious behaviour Chromosomal microarray to detect the 17p11.2 deletion RAI1 sequencing when microarray is normal but the phenotype is suggestive Assessment of the circadian rhythm and melatonin profile where sleep disturbance is prominent Audiological and ophthalmological evaluation for associated sensory deficits Skeletal assessment for scoliosis and developmental/behavioural evaluation Neurodevelopmental disorder caused by a recurrent interstitial deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 encompassing RAI1, or by a pathogenic variant within RAI1 itself Cardinal feature is a severely disrupted circadian sleep-wake rhythm with an inverted melatonin cycle (melatonin secreted during the day rather than at night), causing daytime sleepiness and marked night-time waking Characteristic behavioural phenotype includes self-injurious behaviours (notably nail-yanking and inserting objects into body orifices) and self-hugging or hand-squeezing stereotypies Intellectual disability, developmental delay, and expressive speech difficulties are typical, alongside a generally sociable but impulsive temperament Recognisable dysmorphic features include a broad, square face, brachycephaly, midface hypoplasia, and a tented upper lip, evolving with age Associated medical issues include hearing loss, ophthalmological problems, scoliosis, and features that may mimic other neurodevelopmental syndromes Management of the sleep disturbance addresses the abnormal melatonin rhythm and sleep hygiene, and behavioural and developmental support is central to care Diagnosis is established by chromosomal microarray to detect the 17p11.2 deletion, or by RAI1 sequencing when a deletion is not found Severe self-injurious behaviour causing significant tissue damage Profound sleep deprivation affecting safety and daytime functioning New or worsening scoliosis with respiratory or neurological compromise Acute behavioural crisis posing risk to the patient or others Attributing the sleep disturbance to primary behavioural insomnia and missing the underlying inverted melatonin rhythm Overlooking the diagnosis in a child labelled with non-syndromic autism or intellectual disability Failing to recognise the characteristic self-injurious and self-hugging behaviours as diagnostic clues Not arranging chromosomal microarray, or stopping at a normal microarray without considering RAI1 sequencing Smith-Magenis syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of RAI1 (retinoic acid-induced 1), whether through the common 17p11.2 microdeletion or a point variant within the gene. RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator with widespread roles in neurodevelopment and, importantly, in the control of circadian gene expression. Reduced RAI1 dosage disrupts the molecular circadian clock, producing the hallmark inversion of the melatonin secretion rhythm and the resulting sleep-wake disturbance, while its broader transcriptional effects account for the cognitive, behavioural, craniofacial, and multisystem features of the syndrome. Smith-Magenis syndrome is a lifelong condition; intellectual disability and behavioural and sleep difficulties persist, but life expectancy is generally not markedly reduced and structured behavioural, sleep, and developmental interventions can meaningfully improve quality of life.

antiphospholipid syndrome New focal neurological deficits despite antithrombotic therapy Dismissing livedo racemosa as benign livedo reticularis and missing the underlying vasculopathy Failing to test for antiphospholipid antibodies, which alters anticoagulation decisions Taking skin biopsy from the wrong site so the occlusive lesion is missed Attributing young-onset stroke to a single episode rather than a systemic vasculopathy Sneddon syndrome is a non-inflammatory occlusive arteriopathy affecting small and medium arteries of the skin and brain. Progressive endothelial injury and subintimal proliferation lead to partial then complete occlusion of dermal and cerebral vessels, producing the characteristic livedo racemosa and recurrent cerebral ischaemia. In antiphospholipid-antibody-positive cases a prothrombotic autoimmune mechanism contributes, whereas seronegative cases appear to reflect a primary vasculopathy; both converge on chronic small-vessel occlusion and cumulative brain injury. The condition tends to be progressive, with recurrent strokes and stepwise cognitive decline leading to vascular dementia in many patients; antithrombotic therapy and risk-factor control may slow but rarely halt the course.

sedative use to cope with social situations Progressive social isolation with collapse of education, employment, or relationships Dismissing the presentation as mere shyness and missing significant impairment Overlooking comorbid alcohol misuse used as self-medication Failing to include exposure-based work, which is central to durable improvement Prescribing daily benzodiazepines and risking dependence Stopping SSRIs prematurely before an adequate response has developed Social anxiety disorder reflects an interaction between heritable temperamental traits, notably behavioural inhibition Soft Tissue & Bone Sarcoma — sarcoma, osteosarcoma, GIST, Ewing sarcoma Benign soft tissue tumor / well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumor) - lacks metastatic potential Benign bone lesions with malignant potential: enchondroma and osteochondroma (to chondrosarcoma); fibrous dysplasia, bone infarcts, Paget's disease (to UPS or osteosarcoma) Lymphoma, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and small-cell carcinoma (can be confused with the small round blue cells of Ewing's sarcoma) Osteoporosis vs metastatic spine disease in older patients (cortical bone preserved in osteoporosis; cortical destruction with metastases) Plasma cell tumors (the most common malignant tumor of bone) Core-needle (cutting needle) or small-incision biopsy of all new, persistent, or growing masses, placed so it can be encompassed in the definitive resection Plain radiographs and MRI for primary tumors of extremities or head/neck (MRI best for intramedullary and soft-tissue extension) CT for tumors of the chest, abdomen, or retroperitoneum (CT best for bone destruction and calcification pattern in osteosarcoma) Chest radiograph and chest CT to detect lung metastases Bone scan or FDG-PET to detect skeletal metastases (almost all osteosarcomas are hypervascular and PET-avid) Radionuclide bone scanning (sensitive to new bone formation) for osteoblastic lesions; plain radiography for osteolytic lesions (may not be apparent until >1 cm) Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated with prominent osteoblastic activity) and monitoring for hypercalcemia (osteolytic) or hypocalcemia (extensive osteoblastic) Osteoporotic vertebral disease mimicking spinal bone metastasis in older patients Benign enchondroma / osteochondroma mimicking low-grade chondrosarcoma (difficult to distinguish by x-ray or histology; new pain, inflammation, or progressive size increase suggests malignancy) Well-encapsulated benign-appearing lesion produced by the compressed pseudocapsule of a soft tissue sarcoma Sarcomas are rare (<1% of all malignancies) mesenchymal neoplasms arising in bone and soft tissues, usually of mesodermal origin and biologically distinct from the more common epithelial cancers (p.727). The most common presentation of a soft tissue sarcoma is an asymptomatic mass; mechanical symptoms from pressure, traction, or entrapment of nerves or muscles may also occur (p.728). Approximately 60% of soft tissue sarcomas arise in the extremities (lower limbs involved three times as often as upper), 30% in the trunk (retroperitoneum = 40% of trunk lesions), and 10% in the head and neck (p.727). The pulmonary parenchyma is the most common site of metastasis for soft tissue sarcomas; lung radiograph plus chest CT is important for detecting lung metastases (p.728). Histologic grade and primary tumor size are the most important prognostic factors; prognosis is related to AJCC stage and cure is common in the absence of metastatic disease (p.728). About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry a characteristic translocation with diagnostic/prognostic relevance (e.g., t(X;18)(p11;q11) involving SYT in ~90% of synovial sarcomas) (p.728). Most malignant GISTs carry activating c-kit mutations causing ligand-independent KIT receptor tyrosine kinase activation; ~5-10% have PDGFRA mutations, and KIT/PDGFRA wild-type GISTs may show SDH B/C/D mutations (p.728). Osteosarcoma accounts for almost 45% of bone sarcomas, is a spindle-cell neoplasm producing osteoid/bone, with predilection for metaphyses of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, proximal humerus); ~60% occur in the second decade (p.729-730). Classic osteosarcoma radiographic findings: a destructive moth-eaten lesion, spiculated periosteal reaction (sunburst appearance), and a cuff of periosteal new bone at the soft-tissue mass margin (Codman's triangle) (p.730). The most important predictive factor for long-term survival in osteosarcoma is response to chemotherapy; long-term survival in extremity osteosarcoma ranges from 60-80% (p.730). Ewing's sarcoma (~10-15% of bone sarcomas) peaks in the second decade, shows an 'onion peel' periosteal reaction with a soft-tissue mass, expresses p30/32 (MIC-2 product), and carries the t(11;22) translocation fusing fli-1 (chr 11) and ews (chr 22) (p.730). Chondrosarcoma (~20-25% of bone sarcomas) is a tumor of adulthood/old age (peak 4th-6th decades) with predilection for flat bones (shoulder, pelvic girdles); it has an indolent natural history and is mostly chemoresistant, with surgical resection the mainstay (p.730). Prostate, breast, and lung primaries account for 80% of all bone metastases; metastatic bone tumors are more common than primary bone tumors (p.730). Bone is a common metastatic site for prostate, breast, lung, kidney, bladder, and thyroid carcinomas and for lymphomas and sarcomas; in descending frequency the sites are vertebrae, proximal femur, pelvis, ribs, sternum, proximal humerus, and skull (p.730). When a patient with back pain develops neurologic signs or symptoms, emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression is indicated (p.730). An enlarging, deep, or large soft tissue mass requires biopsy - all new, persistent, or growing masses should be biopsied rather than ignored Back pain with new neurologic signs or symptoms mandates emergency evaluation for spinal cord compression New onset of pain, signs of inflammation, and progressive size increase in a cartilaginous lesion suggest malignant (chondrosarcoma) transformation Bone pain that develops gradually over weeks, is localized, and is more severe at night suggests bone metastasis Pathologic fracture, nerve root or cord compression, or myelophthisis from a destructive bony lesion Hypercalcemia symptoms in the setting of bony destruction Soft tissue sarcomas grow along fascial planes and compress surrounding tissue into a pseudocapsule, giving a deceptive well-encapsulated appearance; 'shelling out' (marginal excision / enucleation) results in a 50-90% probability of local recurrence - wide excision with a negative margin incorporating the biopsy site is standard. A biopsy of an enlarging/deep/large mass must be planned so the tract can be encompassed in the definitive resection and does not compromise a limb-sparing operation; an inappropriately placed incision compromises future limb salvage. Low-grade chondrosarcoma is difficult to distinguish from benign lesions on x-ray or histology, so diagnosis is influenced by clinical history and examination. Osteosarcoma is radioresistant - radiation therapy has no role in routine management. Forgetting non-pulmonary metastatic patterns: GISTs metastasize to liver, myxoid liposarcomas seek fatty tissue (retroperitoneum, mediastinum, subcutaneous), clear cell sarcomas may go to bone, and alveolar soft part sarcoma to CNS. In older patients (especially women), metastatic spine disease must be distinguished from osteoporosis - cortical bone is preserved in osteoporosis but destroyed by metastatic cancer. Sarcomas are mesenchymal neoplasms (mostly mesodermal, occasionally neuroectodermal) classified into ~20 groups by their pattern of differentiation toward normal tissue (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma shows skeletal-muscle cross-striations, leiomyosarcoma shows smooth-muscle spindle fascicles, liposarcoma contains adipocytes). Malignant transformation of benign soft tissue tumors is extremely rare, except that malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (neurofibrosarcoma, malignant schwannoma) can arise from neurofibromas in neurofibromatosis. Etiologic contributors include radiation (tumor arises in the irradiated field, risk rising with time), scar tissue (prior surgery, burn, fracture, foreign body), chemical carcinogens (polycyclic hydrocarbons, asbestos, dioxin), HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma - the only sarcoma virus-associated), and immunodeficiency/immunosuppression. Genetic syndromes include Li-Fraumeni (germline p53), neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1 on chr 17, encoding neurofibromin which inhibits ras), and germline RB1 mutation (chr 13q14, predisposing to osteosarcoma and radiation-unrelated soft tissue sarcomas). About one-third of soft tissue sarcomas carry characteristic translocations; most malignant GISTs have activating c-kit (KIT receptor tyrosine kinase) mutations, fewer have PDGFRA mutations. Bone metastases occur via hematogenous spread (or local invasion); tumors produce osteolytic lesions (via PTH-related peptide, vitamin D-like steroids, prostaglandins, IL-1, TNF inducing osteoclasts) and/or osteoblastic lesions (cytokines activating osteoblasts), with most lesions showing a mix. For soft tissue sarcoma, histologic grade and size are the most important prognostic factors and prognosis tracks AJCC stage; cure is common without metastatic disease, and a small number with metastases can still be cured. Metastatic soft tissue sarcomas are largely incurable, but up to 20% achieving complete response become long-term survivors. Historically most stage IV patients died within 12 months, but with multiple treatment lines, median survival in second-line and beyond is now 13-18 months and some live with stable/slowly progressive disease for years. Extremity osteosarcoma long-term survival is 60-80%, with response to chemotherapy the key predictor. Ewing's sarcoma overall cure rates approach 60-70% for localized tumors. For bone metastases, overall survival is related to the prognosis of the underlying tumor; some (lymphoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma) are curable while most are treated palliatively. Soft tissue sarcomas use the AJCC (8th edition) TNM/grade system: T1 (<=5 cm), T2 (>5-10 cm), T3 (>10-15 cm), T4 (>15 cm); N0/N1; M0/M1; with grade G1-G3 driving stage grouping (e.g., Stage IA = T1 N0 M0 G1; Stage IV = any T N1 M0, or any T any N M1). Bone sarcomas use the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society system (stage I low grade, II high grade, III nodal/distant metastases; A = intracompartmental, B = extracompartmental) and a TNM system: T1 (<=8 cm), T2 (>8 cm), T3 (discontinuous tumors in the primary bone); M1a (lung) vs M1b (other sites); grade G1-G4 (Ewing's always G4).

Somatic symptom disorder — SSD, somatization, somatisation disorder, somatoform disorder Illness anxiety disorder Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) Factitious disorder and malingering Major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders with somatic features Panic disorder Undiagnosed genuine medical illness Body dysmorphic disorder Focused, proportionate medical evaluation guided by objective findings rather than repeated broad testing Review of prior investigations to avoid duplication Screening for comorbid depression and anxiety Assessment of functional impairment and healthcare utilisation patterns Defined by one or more distressing physical symptoms accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours related to those symptoms The diagnosis rests on the disproportionate and persistent nature of the response, not on whether the symptoms are medically explained Features include disproportionate and persistent worry about the seriousness of symptoms, high health-related anxiety, and excessive time and energy devoted to symptoms or health concerns Symptoms are typically persistent (often more than six months) even if individual complaints vary over time Distinguish from illness anxiety disorder (preoccupation with having illness with few or no somatic symptoms) and from conversion disorder (neurological symptoms incompatible with recognised disease) Management principles emphasise a consistent single coordinating clinician, regular scheduled visits, limiting unnecessary tests and referrals, and validating distress while gently shifting focus toward functioning Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best-supported psychotherapy; treat comorbid depression and anxiety, where SSRIs or SNRIs may help A genuine coexisting medical illness does not exclude the diagnosis, so maintain appropriate but restrained medical vigilance New objective clinical signs suggesting an emergent genuine medical condition Suicidal ideation associated with comorbid depression Escalating analgesic or sedative use and dependence Iatrogenic harm from repeated invasive investigations or procedures Ordering repeated investigations and referrals that reinforce illness behaviour and risk iatrogenic harm Dismissing symptoms as not real, which damages the therapeutic alliance Assuming the diagnosis excludes genuine disease and missing a new medical problem Failing to identify and treat comorbid depression and anxiety Lack of a single coordinating clinician leading to fragmented, duplicated care Somatic symptom disorder is understood through a biopsychosocial model in which heightened attention to and amplification of bodily sensations, cognitive misinterpretation of benign symptoms as dangerous, and autonomic and stress responses interact. Predisposing factors include early adverse experiences, trauma, comorbid anxiety and depression, and learned illness behaviour, with reinforcement from repeated medical attention perpetuating the pattern. Somatic symptom disorder is often chronic and fluctuating, but consistent, coordinated care can reduce distress, unnecessary investigations, and healthcare costs while improving function. Prognosis is worse with prolonged illness, multiple comorbidities, and ongoing reinforcement through repeated medical intervention.

Sotos syndrome — cerebral gigantism, NSD1-related overgrowth, Sotos sequence Weaver syndrome (EZH2-related overgrowth) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome Fragile X syndrome and other macrocephaly-associated intellectual disability syndromes Malan syndrome (NFIX-related overgrowth) Marfan syndrome and other tall-stature connective tissue disorders Molecular testing for NSD1 sequence variants and 5q35 deletion by targeted analysis, microarray, or overgrowth gene panel Chromosomal microarray to detect contiguous 5q35 microdeletion and other copy-number causes Bone age radiograph, which is characteristically advanced Developmental and neuropsychological assessment for learning and behavioural needs Echocardiography and renal ultrasound to evaluate associated structural anomalies Cranial imaging where indicated to characterise ventricular or midline brain findings Classic triad of prenatal and postnatal overgrowth (tall stature and macrocephaly), a characteristic facial gestalt, and variable learning difficulty The facial pattern includes a broad prominent forehead, sparse frontotemporal hair, downslanting palpebral fissures, malar flushing, and a long narrow chin Advanced bone age and rapid early growth are typical, although final adult height is often within or near the normal range Caused by haploinsufficiency of NSD1 on chromosome 5q35, usually from a de novo point mutation or a 5q35 microdeletion Inheritance is autosomal dominant with most cases arising de novo; microdeletions are more common in some populations and tend to give more marked learning difficulty Neonatal hypotonia, feeding difficulty, jaundice, and delayed early motor and speech milestones are common, with behaviour and autistic features seen in a proportion Tumour risk is modestly increased but low overall, so intensive tumour surveillance is generally not recommended for isolated NSD1 disease Rapidly enlarging head circumference or neurological signs prompting exclusion of hydrocephalus or an intracranial lesion Seizures requiring assessment and management New mass or unexplained systemic symptoms raising concern for an embryonal tumour Feeding failure or profound neonatal hypotonia needing supportive care Attributing tall stature or macrocephaly to familial variation and missing the diagnosis Confusing Sotos with Weaver syndrome, which shares overgrowth but has distinct facial features and gene Applying intensive tumour surveillance protocols that are not warranted by the low risk Overlooking behavioural and autistic features that need targeted intervention Sotos syndrome results from loss of function of NSD1, a gene encoding a histone methyltransferase that regulates chromatin and transcription of growth and developmental pathways. Haploinsufficiency, whether from an intragenic mutation or a contiguous 5q35 microdeletion, disturbs regulation of growth-promoting genes, producing generalised pre- and postnatal overgrowth with disproportionate head growth. The same disturbance of neuronal chromatin regulation underlies the cognitive and behavioural phenotype, while the recognisable facial gestalt reflects altered craniofacial patterning. Most individuals have a good general prognosis with growth normalising through childhood and adult height often near the normal range, though learning difficulty and behavioural challenges frequently persist and require support. Overall tumour risk is low and life expectancy is generally normal.

suspected Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone with exaggerated tendon reflexes, arising as part of the upper motor neuron syndrome after brain or spinal cord injury It should be assessed for its functional impact using scales such as the Modified Ashworth Scale, since not all spasticity is harmful and some may aid standing or transfers A key first step is to identify and remove noxious triggers such as infection, pressure injury, constipation, urinary retention, ingrown nails, or poor positioning that can suddenly worsen tone Management follows a stepped approach beginning with therapy and physical measures: stretching, positioning, splinting, serial casting, and an appropriate seating and standing programme Focal spasticity affecting a few muscles is well suited to intramuscular botulinum toxin injection to reduce tone in targeted muscles and enable therapy Generalised spasticity may require oral agents such as baclofen, tizanidine, dantrolene, or benzodiazepines, weighing benefit against sedation and weakness Severe, diffuse spasticity refractory to oral treatment may be managed with intrathecal baclofen delivered by an implanted pump Treatment goals should be explicit and functional, whether to improve mobility, ease care and hygiene, relieve pain, or prevent contracture, and outcomes reassessed regularly Untreated spasticity can lead to fixed contractures, pain, pressure injury, and impaired hygiene, so proactive management is important A sudden, unexplained increase in tone that may signal infection, pressure injury, fracture, or another noxious stimulus New or rapidly progressive spasticity suggesting an evolving spinal cord or intracranial lesion such as syringomyelia Signs of intrathecal baclofen withdrawal, which can be life-threatening with high fever, rebound spasticity, and rhabdomyolysis Developing pressure injury or contracture threatening skin integrity and function Treating spasticity aggressively when it is actually providing useful functional support for standing or transfers Failing to look for and remove a noxious trigger before escalating drug therapy Over-sedating patients with oral agents, causing weakness and functional decline Missing intrathecal baclofen pump malfunction or abrupt withdrawal Neglecting stretching, positioning, and therapy while relying solely on medication Spasticity results from loss of descending inhibitory control over spinal reflex circuits following upper motor neuron lesions. Reduced supraspinal inhibition leads to hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex arc, with increased alpha motor neuron excitability, altered interneuronal modulation, and diminished presynaptic and reciprocal inhibition. Over time, secondary changes within muscle and connective tissue, including altered viscoelastic properties and contracture, add a non-neural component to the increased resistance felt on passive movement. With individualised, goal-directed treatment most patients achieve meaningful reductions in tone, pain, and care burden, though spasticity in progressive neurological disease may continue to evolve. Early and consistent management reduces the risk of irreversible contracture and secondary complications.

Specific phobia — simple phobia, isolated phobia Panic disorder with situational attacks Agoraphobia Social anxiety disorder when avoidance centres on scrutiny Post-traumatic stress disorder with stimulus and avoidance Assessment of functional impairment attributable to the phobia Screening for comorbid anxiety, mood, and substance use disorders In blood-injection-injury type, evaluation of any history of syncope The hallmark is marked, disproportionate fear or anxiety about a specific object or situation that almost always provokes an immediate response and is actively avoided or endured with intense distress Common types include animals, the natural environment such as heights or storms, blood-injection-injury, situational triggers such as flying or enclosed spaces, and other stimuli The blood-injection-injury type is distinctive because it can provoke a vasovagal response with fainting, unlike most phobias where arousal is heightened Diagnosis generally requires that the fear is persistent, typically lasting six months or more, and causes clinically significant distress or impairment Exposure-based cognitive behavioural therapy, especially graded in vivo exposure, is the treatment of choice and is often highly effective, sometimes in a single prolonged session Pharmacotherapy plays only a limited, adjunctive role, and long-term medication is usually unnecessary for isolated phobias For blood-injection-injury phobia, applied tension techniques help counter the drop in blood pressure and prevent fainting during exposure Assess how much the phobia genuinely restricts the person's life, since avoidance of rare triggers may need no treatment while others cause major impairment Phobic avoidance that prevents essential medical care, such as avoidance of injections or blood tests in a patient needing treatment Syncope with injury risk in blood-injection-injury phobia Comorbid depression with emerging suicidal ideation Avoiding exposure work in favour of reassurance, which maintains the fear Overlooking a phobia that blocks necessary medical procedures Relying on as-needed sedatives that undermine exposure learning Mislabelling situational panic or agoraphobia as an isolated phobia Failing to teach applied tension in blood-injection-injury phobia Specific phobia is understood through models of classical fear conditioning and its persistence, in which a stimulus becomes associated with danger and avoidance prevents extinction of the learned fear. Heritable predisposition, heightened amygdala-driven threat responses, evolutionary preparedness for certain stimuli, and vicarious or informational learning all contribute, while the blood-injection-injury type involves a biphasic autonomic response predisposing to vasovagal syncope. Specific phobias arising in childhood may remit spontaneously, whereas those persisting into adulthood tend to be chronic if untreated. The prognosis with exposure-based therapy is generally excellent, with many patients achieving lasting improvement, though untreated phobias affecting essential activities can cause enduring impairment.

malfunction Overlooking neurogenic bladder and the associated risk to the upper urinary tract Attributing new deficits in a growing child to the original lesion rather than a tethered cord Spina bifida results from failure of the neural tube to close completely during early embryonic development, leaving a midline defect in the vertebral arches and, in open forms, in the overlying tissues. In myelomeningocele the meninges and dysplastic spinal cord protrude through the defect, so neural function below the lesion is impaired. Disordered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics and the commonly associated Chiari II malformation predispose to hydrocephalus. In occult forms the cord may be abnormally low and tethered by a thickened filum or lipoma, and growth-related traction can produce progressive neurological, urological, or orthopaedic deterioration. Outcome varies widely with the level and severity of the lesion; occulta is usually benign, whereas myelomeningocele typically causes lasting motor, sensory, and sphincter deficits, though multidisciplinary care and timely surgery improve function and reduce complications.

motor weakness, sensory loss, or bladder/bowel dysfunction suggesting cord or cauda equina compression Severe or worsening back pain with neurological signs after neuraxial block Failing to anticipate and promptly treat sympathetic-blockade hypotension and bradycardia Not recognising an ascending high spinal early enough to support ventilation Overlooking neuraxial haematoma risk in anticoagulated patients Attributing new neurological deficits to residual block and delaying urgent imaging Missing urinary retention in the postoperative period Injection of local anaesthetic into the subarachnoid space blocks nerve roots and the spinal cord, producing sensory, motor, and autonomic blockade. Sympathetic blockade causes vasodilation and, with higher blocks, loss of cardiac accelerator fibre activity, leading to hypotension and bradycardia. Excessive cephalad spread can impair respiratory muscles and brainstem perfusion. Dural puncture allows cerebrospinal fluid leakage, lowering intracranial pressure and producing a postural headache. Mechanical trauma, mass lesions such as haematoma or abscess, or neurotoxicity can compress or injure neural tissue, causing ischaemia and potentially permanent deficit if not decompressed promptly. Common physiological effects such as hypotension resolve with treatment and most postdural puncture headaches settle, but a missed compressive haematoma or abscess can cause permanent paralysis, so outcome depends on rapid recognition and decompression.

Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease) — SBMA, Kennedy disease, Kennedy's disease, X-linked bulbospinal neuronopathy, AR CAG repeat disorder Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease Adult-onset (type 4) spinal muscular atrophy (SMN1 related) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy Myasthenia gravis with bulbar features Inclusion body myositis Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy Genetic testing for the androgen receptor CAG repeat expansion, which is diagnostic Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showing chronic neurogenic changes with reduced sensory action potentials Serum creatine kinase, often moderately elevated Endocrine assessment including testosterone, gonadotrophins and lipids/glucose given metabolic associations Swallowing assessment to quantify aspiration risk Family history and genetic counselling regarding X-linked inheritance An X-linked recessive lower motor neuron disorder affecting adult men, caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the androgen receptor gene (AR) Presents in mid-adult life with slowly progressive proximal limb weakness, cramps, and prominent bulbar involvement including dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue atrophy Perioral and chin fasciculations and a characteristic postural or action tremor are useful clinical clues Partial androgen insensitivity produces gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy and reduced fertility The disorder is a polyglutamine disease; longer CAG expansions tend to correlate with earlier onset Sensory involvement is frequently detectable on nerve conduction studies even when clinically silent, reflecting a sensory neuronopathy component It must be distinguished from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which it can mimic but from which it differs by its slower course, absence of upper motor neuron signs, and androgen features Significant dysphagia with aspiration and weight loss Recurrent aspiration pneumonia Choking episodes or nocturnal respiratory symptoms Rapid deterioration suggesting an alternative motor neuron disease Misdiagnosing the condition as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and giving an inappropriately grave prognosis Overlooking the androgen features (gynaecomastia, subfertility) that point to the diagnosis Failing to recognise the subclinical sensory neuronopathy on nerve conduction studies Not counselling about X-linked inheritance and carrier status in female relatives Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat encoding a polyglutamine tract in the androgen receptor. The expanded, ligand-activated receptor misfolds and accumulates, exerting a toxic gain of function that preferentially damages lower motor neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord, together with dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons. Because the toxicity is androgen-dependent, disease is largely confined to men, while the same receptor dysfunction produces partial androgen insensitivity with gynaecomastia and reduced fertility. Progressive motor neuron degeneration leads to bulbar and proximal limb weakness and muscle atrophy. The condition progresses slowly over decades and life expectancy may be near normal or only modestly reduced, with morbidity and mortality driven mainly by bulbar dysfunction, aspiration and falls. Most affected men remain ambulant for many years before requiring aids.

at-risk patients Relying on indwelling catheters and neglecting upper urinary tract protection Inadequate pressure relief leading to preventable pressure injuries in insensate skin Overlooking respiratory decline in high cervical injuries until failure occurs Underestimating the psychological impact and the need for coordinated long-term support Spinal cord injury involves a primary mechanical insult to the cord followed by a secondary injury cascade of ischaemia, oedema, excitotoxicity, inflammation, and free-radical damage that extends the initial neurological loss. Interruption of ascending and descending tracts produces motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below the lesion. After the initial period of spinal shock with flaccid areflexia resolves, reflex activity returns below the level of injury, giving rise to spasticity, neurogenic bladder and bowel, and, in higher lesions, disordered autonomic control including autonomic dysreflexia and orthostatic hypotension. Prognosis depends chiefly on the neurological level and completeness of injury; incomplete injuries and preserved sacral function carry a better outlook for recovery. Most neurological recovery occurs within the first months, and long-term outcomes are strongly influenced by prevention of complications such as pressure injury, urinary tract deterioration, and respiratory disease.
