genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance Stickler syndrome results from defects in the fibrillar collagens types II and XI, which are major structural components of the vitreous, cartilage, and inner ear. Variants in COL2A1 or the type XI collagen genes disrupt normal collagen fibril assembly, producing an abnormal vitreous gel that predisposes to retinal tears and detachment, cartilage that is prone to early degeneration and mild skeletal dysplasia, and inner-ear structures vulnerable to sensorineural hearing loss. The same collagen deficiency during craniofacial development underlies the midface and palatal anomalies, including the Pierre Robin sequence. Most patients have a normal lifespan, but vision is threatened by retinal detachment, which is the principal preventable cause of morbidity, and joint and hearing problems accumulate over time. Outcomes improve markedly with proactive ophthalmic surveillance and detachment prophylaxis.

Stiff-person syndrome — SPS, stiff-man syndrome, Moersch-Woltman syndrome Tetanus Neuromyotonia and other peripheral hyperexcitability syndromes Dystonia and other movement disorders Parkinsonism and progressive supranuclear palsy with axial rigidity Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Myelopathy with spasticity Anti-GAD65 antibodies, with glycine receptor and amphiphysin antibodies when indicated Electromyography demonstrating continuous motor unit activity Screening for associated autoimmune disease including diabetes and thyroid disorders Investigation for an underlying malignancy in suspected paraneoplastic cases MRI to exclude structural spinal or cerebral causes of rigidity An immune-mediated disorder of central nervous system inhibition characterised by progressive axial and proximal muscle rigidity with superimposed painful spasms Rigidity typically involves the trunk and abdominal wall, producing an exaggerated lumbar lordosis and a stiff, board-like posture Spasms are often triggered by startle, emotional stress, or sudden movement and can be severe enough to cause falls or fractures Most cases are associated with high-titre antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65); a smaller subset relate to antibodies against amphiphysin or glycine receptors It commonly coexists with other autoimmune conditions, particularly type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, and pernicious anaemia A paraneoplastic form, often linked to amphiphysin antibodies and breast or other tumours, should be considered especially with atypical or rapidly progressive disease Electromyography characteristically shows continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles that persists at rest Treatment principles combine GABA-enhancing symptomatic therapy for rigidity and spasm with immunotherapy directed at the underlying autoimmune process Spasms severe enough to impair breathing or cause fractures and falls Rapid progression or atypical features suggesting a paraneoplastic cause Autonomic instability during severe spasm episodes New systemic symptoms prompting malignancy search Mistaking the disorder for a functional or psychiatric condition given the stress-sensitive spasms Failing to check for associated autoimmune diseases and an occult malignancy Overlooking the diagnostic value of anti-GAD antibodies and characteristic EMG findings Relying on symptomatic drugs alone without considering immunotherapy Stiff-person syndrome is thought to arise from impaired GABAergic inhibition in the central nervous system, largely on an autoimmune basis. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that synthesises the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, or to other synaptic proteins such as glycine receptors and amphiphysin, are associated with reduced inhibitory tone in spinal and brainstem circuits. The loss of descending and segmental inhibition leads to continuous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, producing sustained rigidity and stimulus-sensitive spasms. The course is usually chronic and progressive but often responsive, at least partially, to symptomatic and immunomodulatory treatment; some patients stabilise or improve, while paraneoplastic cases depend on treatment of the underlying tumour and can be more refractory.

Strabismus — squint, ocular misalignment, esotropia, exotropia, heterotropia Pseudostrabismus from prominent epicanthic folds or facial asymmetry Cranial nerve palsy (third, fourth, or sixth nerve) Restrictive myopathy (e.g. thyroid eye disease, orbital fracture) Myasthenia gravis Internuclear ophthalmoplegia and other supranuclear disorders Retinoblastoma or other cause of sensory deprivation in a child Cover-uncover and alternate cover tests to detect and measure the deviation Assessment of visual acuity in each eye to detect amblyopia Cycloplegic refraction to identify a correctable refractive cause Ocular motility examination and assessment of binocular function/stereopsis Neuroimaging when an incomitant or paralytic squint suggests a neurological lesion Strabismus is a misalignment of the visual axes and is described by direction: esotropia (inward), exotropia (outward), hypertropia (upward), and hypotropia (downward) It is classified as concomitant (the deviation is similar in all directions of gaze, typical of childhood squints) or incomitant (varying with gaze, suggesting a nerve palsy or restriction) In children the main concern is amblyopia in the deviating eye, whereas new-onset strabismus in adults usually causes diplopia The cover test (cover-uncover and alternate cover) is the key clinical method for detecting and characterising a manifest or latent deviation Accommodative esotropia is linked to uncorrected hypermetropia and often improves substantially with the appropriate glasses A new incomitant squint, especially with a cranial nerve palsy pattern, warrants investigation for a neurological cause Management principles include correcting refractive error, treating any amblyopia (e.g. occlusion), and surgical realignment of the extraocular muscles when indicated Leukocoria or a sudden squint in a child requires urgent examination to exclude retinoblastoma or other serious pathology New-onset incomitant squint with features of a cranial nerve palsy suggesting intracranial pathology Leukocoria or a squint accompanying poor vision in a child, raising concern for retinoblastoma Sudden diplopia with headache or other neurological signs Painful or restricted eye movements suggesting orbital or inflammatory disease Dismissing a genuine squint as pseudostrabismus and delaying amblyopia treatment Failing to perform cycloplegic refraction and missing correctable accommodative esotropia Not investigating a new incomitant or paralytic squint for a neurological cause Overlooking a serious underlying cause such as retinoblastoma in a child presenting with a squint Strabismus arises from a failure of the normal binocular alignment maintained by coordinated extraocular muscle action and central fusional control. Causes include refractive error (notably hypermetropia driving accommodative esotropia), sensory deprivation from poor vision in one eye, abnormalities of the neuromuscular pathways (cranial nerve palsies), mechanical restriction of muscles, and disorders of central fusion. In children, misalignment during the critical period of visual development leads to suppression of the deviating eye's image and can result in amblyopia and loss of binocular single vision. Outcomes are generally favourable when strabismus and any associated amblyopia are detected and treated early in childhood, with good prospects for alignment and, in some cases, binocular vision; late detection reduces the chance of restoring binocularity, and adult acquired strabismus depends on the underlying cause.

Streptococcal Infections — group A strep, GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes, group B strep, GBS, Streptococcus agalactiae Scarlet fever differential: measles and other viral exanthems, Kawasaki disease, toxic shock syndrome, and systemic allergic/drug eruptions (p.1209) Pharyngitis differential includes group C/G streptococci, mixed anaerobes (Vincent's angina), Arcanobacterium haemolyticum, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, EBV/CMV/HIV, and other viruses (Table 153-2, p.1208) Impetigo differential: bullous impetigo due to S. aureus, and herpetic lesions (orolabial HSV, chickenpox, or zoster), distinguished by grouped discrete vesicles and positive Tzanck/PCR (p.1210) Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis/soft tissue infection mimicking streptococcal cellulitis (suspect S. aureus when cellulitis develops around a wound or ulcer) (p.1210-1211) Bullous impetigo (S. aureus) mimicking streptococcal impetigo (p.1210) Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (shares features with streptococcal TSS, but staph TSS patients are usually not bacteremic) (p.1211-1212) Herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster lesions mimicking impetigo (p.1210) Throat culture (gold standard; vigorous rubbing of both tonsillar pillars) and rapid antigen test (latex agglutination/EIA, specificity >95%, relative sensitivity 70-90%); confirm negative rapid test with culture in higher-risk individuals (p.1208) Antibody tests to streptolysin O (ASO) and DNase B for serodiagnosis of preceding streptococcal infection in suspected ARF or PSGN (p.1207) emm-typing by PCR/sequencing of the variable region of the emm gene (CDC database) for strain typing (p.1207) In streptococcal TSS, laboratory findings: marked left shift with immature granulocytes, hypocalcemia, hypoalbuminemia, and thrombocytopenia (worsening on day 2-3) (p.1211) Blood cultures (most streptococcal TSS patients are bacteremic) (p.1211-1212) Early surgical exploration of suspected necrotizing fasciitis for diagnosis (reveals fascial-plane necrosis and inflammatory fluid without muscle involvement) (p.1211) Cultures of vesicular fluid in difficult impetigo cases; culture to rule out MRSA if empirical treatment fails (p.1210) Kawasaki disease (mimics scarlet fever) (p.1209) Systemic allergic reactions / drug eruptions (mimic scarlet fever) (p.1209) Group A Streptococcus (GAS; S. pyogenes) is the only common cause of sore throat that should be treated with antibiotics; GAS accounts for 20-40% of exudative pharyngitis in children and is rare under age 3 (p.1208). Streptococcal pharyngitis cannot be reliably diagnosed on clinical grounds alone given overlap with many viral and bacterial causes; throat culture remains the diagnostic gold standard, with rapid antigen tests (specificity >95%) a useful adjunct (p.1208). Antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis is given primarily to prevent suppurative complications and acute rheumatic fever; symptoms resolve in 3-5 days and are shortened little by treatment (p.1208). Prevention of ARF depends on eradicating the organism from the pharynx (not just symptom resolution) and requires a 10-day penicillin course; a single dose or short course is inadequate (p.1208). Penicillin treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis reduces the likelihood of ARF but NOT of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (p.1209). Worldwide, GAS infections and their post-infectious sequelae (chiefly ARF and rheumatic heart disease) cause an estimated 500,000 deaths/year; incidence of GAS disease and RHD is roughly tenfold higher in resource-limited countries (p.1206-1207). Scarlet fever is streptococcal infection (usually pharyngitis) plus a rash from pyrogenic exotoxins: blanching sandpaper-textured papular rash on trunk and extremities sparing palms and soles, with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines in skin folds, followed by desquamation of palms and soles (p.1209). Impetigo is most often a superficial GAS infection (occasionally other streptococci or S. aureus) of young children; honey/amber crusted lesions on face and legs; lesions are generally NOT painful and fever is NOT a feature — if fever is present, suspect deeper infection or another diagnosis (p.1209-1210). Erysipelas is a streptococcal cellulitis of the superficial dermis: bright red, warm, shiny, edematous plaque with a sharply demarcated raised border and peau d'orange texture, typically on the face (malar) or lower extremities, with abrupt onset, fever and chills; classic cases are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci (usually GAS) (p.1210). Streptococcal cellulitis favors sites of disrupted lymphatic drainage (prior cellulitis, post-mastectomy/axillary dissection arm, prior DVT or lymphedema leg, saphenous vein harvest site); treating tinea pedis can stop recurrent leg cellulitis after vein harvest (p.1210-1211). GAS is among the few pathogens producing wound infection and surrounding cellulitis within the first 24 h after surgery, with thin exudate and rapid spread (p.1211). Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: GAS is implicated in ~60% of cases; early surgical exploration and extensive debridement are diagnostic, therapeutic, and life-saving, with antibiotics as a critical adjunct (p.1211). Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) features fever, hypotension, renal impairment, and respiratory distress; in contrast to staphylococcal TSS, most patients with streptococcal TSS are bacteremic, rash usually does NOT develop, and the most common associated infection is a soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or cellulitis) (p.1211-1212). Streptococcal TSS carries a mortality rate of >=30%, mostly from shock and respiratory failure; because of its rapidly progressive lethal course, early recognition is essential (p.1212). Group B Streptococcus (GBS; S. agalactiae) is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis and of peripartum fever; early-onset disease (first week, median 20 h) is acquired from the colonized maternal genital tract, while late-onset disease (1 week-3 months) most often presents as meningitis, frequently capsular type III (p.1212-1213). GBS infection in adults increasingly affects the elderly and those with chronic illness (e.g., diabetes, malignancy), presenting as cellulitis/soft-tissue infection including diabetic ulcers, UTI, pneumonia, endocarditis, and septic arthritis (p.1213-1214). Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: severe pain out of proportion to physical findings, with only minimal early skin erythema; progression over hours to dusky/mottled erythema and edema; tenderness evolving into anesthesia from infarction of cutaneous nerves — demands early surgical exploration and debridement (p.1211) Streptococcal TSS: rapidly progressive, lethal (mortality >=30%) with hypotension and multiorgan failure; early recognition essential (p.1211-1212) Fever in a patient with impetigo suggests extension to deeper tissues or an alternative diagnosis (p.1210) GAS bacteremia without an identified source raises the possibility of endocarditis, occult abscess, or osteomyelitis (p.1212) Unusually severe or prolonged pharyngitis, or localized pain with high fever and toxic appearance, suggests a peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess (p.1209) Diagnosing streptococcal pharyngitis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinicians over-prescribe antibiotics for sore throat (p.1208) Rapid antigen tests are less sensitive than culture (relative sensitivity 70-90%), so a negative rapid test should be confirmed by throat culture in higher-risk patients (p.1208) Improper swab technique lowers rapid-test sensitivity; both tonsillar pillars (and any exudate/ulceration) must be vigorously sampled (p.1208) In necrotizing fasciitis, early physical findings may be unimpressive despite severe pain; relying on skin appearance delays diagnosis (p.1211) Macrolide resistance is common in many countries and rising in invasive US GAS isolates (>30% since 2021); avoid macrolides where resistance exceeds 5-10% unless susceptibility is known (p.1208-1209) Clindamycin resistance occurs in >=30% of invasive GAS isolates; susceptibility should not be assumed without in vitro testing before relying on clindamycin (p.1212) Aggressive eradication of asymptomatic GAS pharyngeal carriage is usually not justified (carriers have lower risk of ARF and of transmission than symptomatic patients); exceptions arise when a carrier is a source of transmission to others (p.1209) Endocarditis due to nonenterococcal group D streptococci (S. gallolyticus/S. bovis group) is associated with occult GI neoplasm (often colon carcinoma/polyp; abnormalities in >60%) and should prompt GI evaluation (p.1214) GAS (S. pyogenes) is the single species of Lancefield group A, a beta-hemolytic, chain-forming, gram-positive facultative anaerobe. M protein (encoded by the emm gene, >200 emm types) is the major surface protein and chief virulence factor: it resists phagocytic killing partly by binding plasma fibrinogen and interfering with complement deposition, and type-specific anti-M antibody confers protection only against the same M type. A hyaluronic acid capsule (a weak immunogen owing to structural identity with mammalian connective tissue) protects against phagocytosis and aids pharyngeal colonization via CD44 binding; capsule is not essential for virulence. GAS elaborates streptolysins S and O, streptokinase, DNases, SpyCEP (cleaves IL-8 to impair neutrophil recruitment), and pyrogenic exotoxins (formerly erythrogenic toxins) that cause the scarlet fever rash and act as superantigens triggering T-cell cytokine release, implicated in severe invasive disease including necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS. The post-infectious sequelae ARF (uniquely associated with S. pyogenes) and PSGN are thought to result from immune responses to streptococcal infection. GBS is encapsulated by 1 of 10 polysaccharides; the capsule is a key virulence factor and type-specific anticapsular antibody is protective. Uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis is self-limited, with symptoms resolving in 3-5 days. Suppurative complications (peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, cervical lymphadenitis, sinusitis, otitis, meningitis, bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia) are now uncommon with antibiotics; nonsuppurative sequelae are ARF and PSGN. Necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS are rapidly progressive and life-threatening; streptococcal TSS has a mortality rate of >=30%. Globally GAS sequelae account for ~500,000 deaths/year. Neonatal GBS incidence has fallen from ~2-3 to ~0.6 per 1000 live births with prenatal screening. Recurrent invasive GBS in adults occurs in ~4% of cases. Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (CDC, 1993; updated 2010; Table 153-4): I. Isolation of GAS from (A) a normally sterile site or (B) a nonsterile site; II. Clinical signs of severity = (A) hypotension AND (B) >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, liver function impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous macular rash that may desquamate, or soft tissue necrosis (including necrotizing fasciitis or myositis) or gangrene. A DEFINITE case meets IA + IIA + IIB; a PROBABLE case meets IB + IIA + IIB if no other etiology is identified. Pharyngitis pretest risk is stratified clinically by the Centor criteria (fever history, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate/swelling).

Stress fracture — fatigue fracture, insufficiency fracture, march fracture, bone stress injury Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) Chronic exertional compartment syndrome Tendinopathy or muscle strain Nerve entrapment Osteomyelitis or bone infection Osteoid osteoma or other bone tumour Pathological fracture from metastasis or metabolic bone disease Plain radiographs, recognising they are frequently normal early and may show periosteal reaction or a fracture line later MRI as the preferred sensitive test to grade bone marrow oedema and confirm the fracture Radionuclide bone scan as an alternative sensitive investigation CT for suspected navicular or other fractures needing detailed cortical assessment Metabolic and endocrine workup, vitamin D, and bone density assessment in recurrent, atypical, or insufficiency fractures Presents as gradually worsening, activity-related localised bone pain that eases with rest, typically after a change or increase in training load Fatigue fractures occur when normal bone is subjected to repetitive abnormal load, whereas insufficiency fractures occur when normal load acts on weakened bone such as osteoporotic or pathological bone Common sites include the metatarsals (march fracture), tibia, navicular, and femoral neck, with the tibia most frequent in runners Focal bony tenderness, pain on hopping or percussion, and pain reproduced by loading the bone support the diagnosis Early plain radiographs are often normal, and MRI or bone scan is more sensitive for detecting bone stress injury Certain high-risk sites, including the tension side of the femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, and base of the fifth metatarsal, are prone to non-union or completion and need protected weight-bearing or surgical referral Management of low-risk fractures is relative rest, activity modification, and graduated return to loading once pain-free In female athletes consider the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport, with attention to energy availability, menstrual function, and bone health Recurrent or multiple stress fractures warrant assessment for metabolic bone disease, vitamin D deficiency, and endocrine causes High-risk sites such as the femoral neck (especially tension side), anterior tibia, tarsal navicular, and fifth metatarsal base that risk non-union or displacement Groin or hip pain with weight-bearing suggesting femoral neck stress fracture requiring urgent assessment Features of pathological or insufficiency fracture such as minimal trauma, older age, or known malignancy Systemic symptoms or signs suggesting infection or tumour Excluding a stress fracture on the basis of a normal early radiograph Failing to recognise high-risk sites and continuing loading with risk of completion or non-union Overlooking relative energy deficiency in sport or metabolic bone disease in recurrent cases Returning to full training too early before the bone has healed A stress fracture develops when repetitive submaximal loading causes microdamage to accumulate faster than bone can remodel and repair it. Osteoclastic resorption temporarily outpaces osteoblastic formation, weakening the cortex and, if loading continues, progressing from a stress reaction to a frank fracture line. Fatigue fractures reflect excessive load on normal bone, while insufficiency fractures reflect normal load on abnormally weak bone. Low-risk stress fractures generally heal fully within six to twelve weeks with load modification and graded return, whereas high-risk fractures may progress to non-union or complete fracture and can require prolonged protection or surgery.

Stress Urinary Incontinence — stress urinary incontinence, stress incontinence, SUI, effort urinary incontinence, exertional incontinence Urgency urinary incontinence / overactive bladder Mixed urinary incontinence Overflow incontinence from chronic retention Urinary tract infection causing transient symptoms Vesicovaginal or urethrovaginal fistula (continuous leakage) Urethral diverticulum Functional incontinence from mobility or cognitive impairment Bladder (frequency-volume) diary to characterise the pattern of leakage Cough stress test to demonstrate leakage with raised abdominal pressure Urinalysis and culture to exclude infection Post-void residual measurement to exclude incomplete emptying Pad testing to quantify leakage where useful Urodynamic studies in complex, mixed, recurrent, or pre-surgical cases Stress urinary incontinence is involuntary leakage of urine on effort or exertion, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or physical activity, when abdominal pressure rises It results from a weakened sphincter mechanism or poor support of the bladder neck and urethra, so that a rise in intra-abdominal pressure overcomes urethral closure Key risk factors include vaginal childbirth, ageing and menopause, obesity, chronic cough or straining, and previous pelvic surgery It must be distinguished from urgency incontinence (leakage with a sudden compelling desire to void); many women have a mixed picture with features of both Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by a bladder diary, cough stress test, and exclusion of infection and significant post-void residual urine First-line management is conservative: supervised pelvic floor muscle training, weight loss, treatment of chronic cough or constipation, and lifestyle measures Adjuncts include continence pessaries or devices, and duloxetine may be considered in selected cases where surgery is unsuitable or declined Surgical options for persistent bothersome stress incontinence include mid-urethral slings, colposuspension, and urethral bulking agents, chosen according to patient factors and shared decision-making Urodynamic testing is reserved for complex, mixed, or recurrent cases or before surgery where the diagnosis is uncertain, rather than being routine Visible haematuria requiring exclusion of urinary tract malignancy Continuous leakage suggesting a fistula Significant post-void residual or voiding difficulty indicating retention with overflow New neurological symptoms suggesting a neurological cause Recurrent urinary infections or pain warranting further evaluation Labelling all incontinence as stress type without identifying a mixed or urgency component Proceeding to surgery without a trial of conservative therapy or without clarifying the diagnosis Missing overflow incontinence by not checking post-void residual Overlooking a fistula in a patient with continuous leakage, especially after surgery or childbirth Attributing symptoms to stress incontinence when haematuria or infection needs investigation Continence during exertion depends on adequate urethral closure pressure and on the bladder neck and urethra being well supported so that rises in abdominal pressure are transmitted equally to the bladder and proximal urethra. Two overlapping mechanisms cause stress incontinence: urethral hypermobility, in which weakened pelvic floor and endopelvic fascial support (often after childbirth or with ageing) allows the bladder neck to descend and the pressure transmission to become unequal; and intrinsic sphincter deficiency, in which the urethral closure mechanism itself is weakened, for example after surgery, radiation, or oestrogen deficiency. In either case a cough or exertion transiently raises bladder pressure above urethral resistance and urine escapes. Stress incontinence is not life-threatening but can substantially impair quality of life. Many women improve significantly with conservative measures, particularly sustained pelvic floor muscle training and weight loss. Surgical procedures offer high rates of symptom improvement in appropriately selected patients, though some experience recurrence or complications, so treatment is individualised through shared decision-making.

and continence Dysphagia screening before oral intake is essential to reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonia, with formal swallowing assessment where concerns arise Common complications requiring reintegration and vocational return are integral to the rehabilitation programme New or worsening neurological deficit suggesting recurrent or extending stroke or haemorrhagic transformation Signs of aspiration or pneumonia in a patient with dysphagia Symptoms of pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis in an immobile patient Sudden severe headache, reduced consciousness, or new seizures Rapidly developing pressure injury or sepsis Allowing oral intake before dysphagia screening and risking aspiration Delaying rehabilitation until the patient is deemed fully stable, losing the early window for gains Neglecting shoulder positioning and support, leading to painful subluxation Overlooking post-stroke depression and cognitive impairment that limit engagement Failing to address secondary prevention and carer support alongside physical recovery Stroke causes focal brain injury through either ischaemia or haemorrhage, producing loss of function referable to the affected vascular territory. The initial deficit reflects both the infarct or haematoma core and the surrounding penumbra and oedema. Functional recovery over subsequent weeks and months depends on resolution of oedema and diaschisis together with neuroplastic reorganisation, including recruitment of perilesional and contralateral networks, synaptic remodelling, and cortical remapping. Rehabilitation harnesses these adaptive processes through repetitive, goal-directed activity, while maladaptive changes such as spasticity and learned non-use can impede recovery. Recovery is most rapid in the first weeks to months and can continue for a year or more, though the extent varies with stroke size, location, initial severity, age, and comorbidity. Early, intensive, multidisciplinary rehabilitation improves functional outcome, while persisting severe deficits, cognitive impairment, and depression predict greater long-term disability.

Strongyloidiasis — Strongyloides stercoralis infection, threadworm infection, strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome Other soil-transmitted helminth infections (hookworm, ascariasis) Peptic ulcer disease or functional dyspepsia Inflammatory bowel disease Chronic urticaria of other cause Hypereosinophilic syndromes Drug-induced eosinophilia Allergic/atopic disease with urticaria Other causes of Gram-negative sepsis in the immunosuppressed Eosinophilic gastroenteritis Serology for Strongyloides antibodies, which is more sensitive than single stool testing Repeated stool microscopy with concentration or agar-plate culture to detect larvae Full blood count looking for eosinophilia (which may be absent in dissemination) Examination of sputum, duodenal aspirate or other fluids for larvae in suspected hyperinfection Screening for HTLV-1 and assessment of immune status in severe disease A soil-transmitted intestinal nematode acquired when larvae in contaminated soil penetrate skin, endemic in warm, humid parts of India Uniquely among common helminths it can complete its life cycle within the host (autoinfection), so infection may persist silently for decades Chronic infection is often mild, with intermittent abdominal symptoms, urticaria, and a characteristic migratory serpiginous rash (larva currens); eosinophilia is a common clue The feared complication is hyperinfection/disseminated disease, precipitated by immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids and HTLV-1 co-infection Screening and treating latent infection before starting immunosuppression is a key preventive principle Disseminated strongyloidiasis often carries Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis as larvae transport gut bacteria A single stool examination is insensitive; serology and repeated or concentrated stool studies improve detection Antiparasitic therapy with ivermectin is the treatment principle, with prolonged/repeated courses needed in disseminated disease Hyperinfection or dissemination in an immunosuppressed patient, a life-threatening emergency Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis complicating heavy larval migration Planned corticosteroid or other immunosuppression in someone from an endemic area without prior screening Rapid respiratory or gastrointestinal deterioration with detectable larvae Starting corticosteroids or immunosuppression without screening at-risk patients, precipitating fatal hyperinfection Relying on a single negative stool sample to exclude infection Assuming eosinophilia will always be present, as it is often absent in dissemination Failing to give a sufficiently prolonged antiparasitic course in disseminated disease Filariform larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the circulation to the lungs, ascend the airways and are swallowed, maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Females produce eggs that hatch into rhabditiform larvae; some transform into infective filariform larvae within the gut or perianal skin and reinvade the host, sustaining autoinfection. When host cellular immunity is impaired, this autoinfective cycle accelerates uncontrollably, causing massive larval migration through multiple organs (hyperinfection and dissemination) and carrying enteric bacteria that seed the bloodstream, meninges and other sites. Chronic uncomplicated infection responds well to antiparasitic therapy and has an excellent outlook, though eradication should be confirmed given the autoinfection risk. Hyperinfection and disseminated disease, by contrast, carry very high mortality despite treatment, particularly when diagnosis is delayed.

indicated Neurocutaneous disorder characterised by a facial capillary malformation (port-wine birthmark), leptomeningeal angiomatosis, and eye involvement The facial birthmark typically follows the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and upper facial involvement raises the risk of brain and eye disease Leptomeningeal angiomatosis predisposes to seizures, which often begin in infancy and can be difficult to control Stroke-like episodes, hemiparesis, and progressive cognitive impairment may occur from impaired cortical perfusion Glaucoma is a common ocular complication and requires ongoing monitoring of intraocular pressure Caused by a somatic mosaic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene arising during early development, so it is not typically inherited Characteristic tram-track cortical calcification may be seen on imaging in affected brain regions A port-wine birthmark alone, without brain or eye involvement, does not constitute the full syndrome Poorly controlled or prolonged seizures requiring urgent treatment to limit neurological injury Stroke-like episodes with acute focal deficits Rising intraocular pressure or visual deterioration from glaucoma Progressive developmental regression signalling worsening cortical involvement Assuming any facial port-wine birthmark implies the full syndrome without assessing brain and eye involvement Failing to monitor for glaucoma, which can present at any age Undertreating early seizures with consequences for development Not recognising the mosaic somatic cause and incorrectly counselling about heritability Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene occurring in a subset of cells during early embryogenesis, producing a mosaic distribution that explains the segmental capillary malformations. The mutation dysregulates signalling in vascular and other tissues, leading to abnormal capillary-venous malformations in the skin, leptomeninges, and eye. The leptomeningeal vascular malformation impairs normal venous drainage and cortical perfusion, causing chronic ischaemia, cortical atrophy, calcification, and a lowered seizure threshold. Because the mutation is somatic and mosaic rather than germline, the condition arises sporadically and is not inherited. Outcome varies with the extent of brain and eye involvement; some individuals have well-controlled seizures and near-normal development, while extensive leptomeningeal disease can lead to refractory epilepsy, hemiparesis, and cognitive impairment.

Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord — SCD, SACD, subacute combined degeneration, B12 myelopathy Copper deficiency myelopathy (clinically near-identical picture) Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating myelopathy Compressive cervical myelopathy or spondylotic myelopathy Tabes dorsalis and other causes of sensory ataxia Hereditary spastic paraplegia HTLV-1 associated myelopathy Serum vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when B12 is borderline Full blood count and blood film for macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies to identify pernicious anaemia MRI of the spine showing high T2 signal in the dorsal columns (inverted V or dot sign) Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude copper deficiency mimicking the syndrome Nerve conduction studies if a coexisting peripheral neuropathy is suspected Caused by vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, which preferentially damages the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts of the spinal cord Typically presents with symmetrical distal paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and joint-position sense, and a progressive spastic-ataxic gait Combines upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, extensor plantars) with impaired proprioception and sometimes absent ankle reflexes, giving a mixed picture Neuropsychiatric features such as cognitive slowing, irritability, or depression may accompany or precede the myelopathy Serum B12 can be borderline or normal, so raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are more sensitive markers of tissue deficiency Common causes include pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, strict vegan diet, gastric surgery, and prolonged nitrous oxide exposure Early replacement of B12 can halt and partially reverse deficits; delayed treatment risks permanent disability Macrocytic anaemia may be absent, so neurological disease can occur without haematological changes Rapidly progressive myelopathy causing gait failure or sphincter disturbance Recent or repeated nitrous oxide use with acute neurological decline Severe anaemia or pancytopenia requiring urgent evaluation Coexisting cognitive decline suggesting advanced or long-standing deficiency Relying on a normal serum B12 and missing functional deficiency demonstrable by methylmalonic acid Assuming anaemia must be present, thereby overlooking purely neurological presentations Failing to ask about recreational or repeated medical nitrous oxide exposure Overlooking copper deficiency, which produces an indistinguishable myelopathy Attributing spastic-ataxic gait solely to spondylosis and delaying B12 assessment Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency impairs myelin synthesis and maintenance, leading to vacuolar demyelination and axonal degeneration that begins in the dorsal columns and later involves the lateral (corticospinal) columns, hence the term 'combined'. Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin and can precipitate the disorder in those with marginal stores. The pathology accounts for the combination of sensory ataxia from posterior column loss and spasticity from corticospinal tract involvement. Recovery depends on how early replacement begins; symptoms present for less than a few months often improve substantially, whereas long-standing deficits may only stabilise, leaving residual sensory ataxia or spasticity.

Subacute thyroiditis — de Quervain thyroiditis, subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, giant cell thyroiditis, painful subacute thyroiditis Graves' disease Painless (silent) thyroiditis and postpartum thyroiditis Acute suppurative thyroiditis Haemorrhage into a thyroid cyst or nodule Toxic multinodular goitre or toxic adenoma Thyroid function tests to characterise the phase of disease Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein Radioactive iodine uptake scan showing low uptake in the thyrotoxic phase Thyroid ultrasound with reduced vascularity distinguishing it from Graves' disease TSH-receptor antibody testing when Graves' disease is a serious consideration Typically follows a viral upper respiratory illness by a few weeks and presents with a painful, tender thyroid and referred pain to the jaw or ears Classically evolves through phases: an early thyrotoxic phase from follicular disruption, followed by transient hypothyroidism, and usually a return to euthyroidism In the thyrotoxic phase radioiodine uptake is characteristically low, which distinguishes it from Graves' disease where uptake is high The erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are markedly elevated, reflecting the inflammatory process Thyrotoxic symptoms arise from release of preformed hormone rather than increased synthesis, so antithyroid drugs are ineffective Management is largely symptomatic, with anti-inflammatory agents for milder disease and corticosteroids reserved for severe pain, alongside beta-blockade for adrenergic symptoms A minority of patients are left with permanent hypothyroidism, so thyroid function should be monitored during recovery Severe fever, fluctuance, or a rapidly enlarging tender gland suggesting suppurative thyroiditis needing drainage and antimicrobials Marked thyrotoxic symptoms with cardiac compromise Persistent hypothyroid symptoms indicating the need for hormone replacement Compressive symptoms or an atypical mass raising concern for malignancy Mistaking destructive thyrotoxicosis for Graves' disease and prescribing ineffective antithyroid drugs Failing to check radioiodine uptake or ultrasound vascularity to separate the two Overlooking the later hypothyroid phase and not monitoring thyroid function through recovery Attributing a painful gland to malignancy without recognising the inflammatory picture Subacute thyroiditis is thought to result from a viral infection or post-viral inflammatory response affecting the thyroid, producing granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and destruction of thyroid follicles. Disruption of follicles releases stored thyroid hormone into the circulation, causing an initial destructive thyrotoxicosis with suppressed TSH and low radioiodine uptake. As follicular stores are depleted and the gland heals, patients pass through a hypothyroid phase before glandular recovery restores normal hormone production in most cases. The illness is usually self-limiting over weeks to months with full recovery of thyroid function in most patients, though pain can be prolonged, recurrences occur occasionally, and a small proportion develop permanent hypothyroidism.

Subconjunctival haemorrhage — subconjunctival hemorrhage, hyposphagma, SCH Conjunctivitis (bacterial, viral, haemorrhagic) Ruptured globe with subconjunctival bleeding after trauma Conjunctival or Kaposi lesion mimicking haemorrhage Anterior uveitis or scleritis (painful red eye) Bleeding from orbital or retrobulbar haemorrhage Blood pressure measurement, especially in recurrent cases Review of anticoagulant and antiplatelet medication Coagulation studies and platelet count when bleeding is recurrent or spontaneous Slit-lamp examination to exclude other causes of red eye Assessment for globe rupture or orbital injury when trauma is involved Presents as a painless, flat, bright red patch of blood beneath the conjunctiva with a sharply defined border and normal vision Usually benign and self-limiting, resolving over one to two weeks as the blood is reabsorbed and changes colour Common precipitants include Valsalva-type events such as coughing, sneezing, straining, or vomiting, minor trauma, and rubbing Recurrent or bilateral haemorrhages should prompt review of hypertension, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, and bleeding disorders The absence of pain, discharge, and visual disturbance distinguishes it from more serious causes of a red eye A haemorrhage without a visible posterior margin after trauma may indicate a source from behind the orbit, raising concern for orbital fracture or ruptured globe Reassurance is the mainstay; lubricants may ease mild irritation History of significant trauma with a haemorrhage lacking a posterior border, suggesting globe rupture or orbital fracture Associated pain, reduced vision, or a relative afferent pupillary defect Recurrent or spontaneous bilateral haemorrhages indicating a systemic bleeding disorder or uncontrolled hypertension Proptosis or restricted eye movements suggesting orbital pathology Attributing a traumatic haemorrhage to a benign cause and missing an occult globe rupture Failing to check blood pressure and clotting in recurrent cases Overlooking anticoagulant overtreatment as a contributor Providing unnecessary antibiotics for a non-infective condition A subconjunctival haemorrhage is bleeding from small conjunctival or episcleral vessels into the potential space between the conjunctiva and the underlying sclera. Because blood is confined to this superficial layer, it appears as a well-demarcated red sheet without affecting the cornea or intraocular structures. Rises in venous pressure (Valsalva), fragile vessels, trauma, or impaired haemostasis predispose to rupture. The blood is gradually cleared by resorption, passing through the usual colour changes of a resolving bruise. Isolated spontaneous subconjunctival haemorrhage resolves completely without treatment and carries no visual risk; prognosis depends on any underlying systemic or traumatic cause.

Subdural haematoma — Non-contrast CT head Coagulation; reverse anticoagulation Neurosurgical review Expanding bleed — may need evacuation Epidural haematoma (lenticular/lens-shaped on CT, usually arterial from a torn middle meningeal artery, classic lucid interval, more rapid evolution) Cerebral contusion / convexity contusion (can produce focal deficits such as aphasia or mild hemiparesis) Carotid or vertebral artery dissection (can mimic focal deficits seen with subdural) Posttraumatic headache syndrome (chronic subdural may mimic this) (p.160) MRI reliably identifies both subacute and chronic subdural haematomas and is useful when CT is equivocal (p.3573) Contrast-enhanced imaging demonstrates enhancement of the vascular fibrous capsule surrounding a chronic collection (p.3573) Serial imaging for clinical observation of small chronic collections without mass effect (p.3573) Transient ischemic attack (rarely chronic subdural causes brief episodes of hemiparesis or aphasia indistinguishable from TIA) (p.3573) Dementia / Alzheimer or other neurodegenerative disease (chronic subdural is a treatable cause of dementia, often on a background of cortical atrophy) (pp.238, 3527) Stroke (subdural is considered when excluding stroke in older fallers) (p.3929) Normal-pressure hydrocephalus and other reversible dementia causes (listed alongside subdural among treatable dementias) (p.238) Direct cranial trauma may be minor and is not always required for an acute subdural bleed, particularly in the elderly and those on anticoagulants; acceleration forces alone (e.g. whiplash) can suffice (p.3572). Up to one-third of patients with acute subdural haematoma have a lucid interval of minutes to hours before coma supervenes, but most are drowsy or comatose from the moment of injury (p.3572). A unilateral headache with a slightly enlarged pupil on the side of the haematoma is frequently, though not invariably, present (p.3572). Small subdural haematomas may be asymptomatic and usually do not require evacuation unless they enlarge (p.3572). In chronic subdural haematoma, drowsiness, inattentiveness and incoherent thinking are generally more prominent than focal signs such as hemiparesis (p.3573). Chronic subdural haematoma headache typically fluctuates in severity, sometimes with changes in head position (p.3573). A history of trauma may be absent in chronic subdural haematoma; the injury may have been trivial and forgotten, especially in the elderly and those with clotting disorders (p.3572). Recurrent falls in older adults place them at risk for subdural haematoma; brain imaging is warranted when neurologic signs are present (pp.222-223, 3927, 3929). Trauma should be considered in any patient with an unexplained acute neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, stupor, confusion), particularly after a fall (p.3498). Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement indicate a larger acute haematoma (p.3572) Acutely deteriorating patient requiring emergency craniotomy (p.3572) Repetitive vomiting, nystagmus, drowsiness and unsteadiness may signal a posterior fossa subdural haematoma (p.3619) Large bleed after only minor trauma should raise concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy (p.3573) Subacute pitfall: between roughly 2 and 6 weeks after the initial bleed the clot becomes isodense relative to adjacent brain on non-contrast CT and may be inapparent/missed (p.3573). Acute subdural produces more horizontal displacement (mass effect) than expected from its thickness because of its large rostral-caudal extent, so mass effect can be underestimated from clot thickness alone (p.3572). Absence of a trauma history does not exclude chronic subdural haematoma in the elderly or anticoagulated (p.3572). Skull fractures are markers of injury site/severity, not the haematoma itself, and may be absent (p.3572). Bleeding occurs beneath the dura (subdural space). The bleeding producing larger subdural haematomas is primarily venous in origin, classically from torn bridging veins, although arterial bleeding sites are occasionally found at operation and a few large haematomas are purely arterial. Chronic subdural haematomas develop days to weeks after (often trivial) injury, favoured by age-related cerebral atrophy that stretches bridging veins; they organise into a vascular fibrous capsule, and weeks-old collections often contain a mixture of blood and serous fluid. Anticoagulant-related intracranial haemorrhages are often subdural and may continue to evolve over 24-48 h if coagulopathy is insufficiently reversed (pp.3572-3573, 3498). In contrast to epidural haematomas, acute subdural haematomas requiring surgery carry significant morbidity and mortality, partly reflecting frequently associated underlying cortical brain damage. Chronic subdural collections evacuated through burr holes are usually treated successfully when a postoperative cranial drain is used; encapsulating fibrous membranes may require craniotomy to prevent recurrent fluid accumulation (pp.3572-3573). Harrison frames subdural haematoma by acuity and imaging appearance rather than a numeric grade: ACUTE — non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense crescentic clot with an irregular brain interface; SUBACUTE (~2-6 weeks) — clot becomes isodense and easily overlooked, often with mixed blood and serous fluid; CHRONIC — hypodense crescentic collection over one or both convexities, most often frontotemporal (pp.3572-3573).

Subglottic stenosis — SGS, subglottic narrowing, laryngotracheal stenosis Laryngomalacia Vocal cord palsy Recurrent croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) Subglottic haemangioma in an infant Vascular ring or extrinsic tracheal compression Granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting the airway Flexible and rigid endoscopy of the airway to assess and grade the stenosis Sizing of the airway with endotracheal tubes to quantify the degree of narrowing Cross-sectional imaging to map the length of the stenotic segment and exclude external compression Evaluation for inflammatory or autoimmune disease when clinically suspected Assessment of reflux, which can aggravate airway inflammation Narrowing of the airway at the subglottis, the region just below the vocal cords, which is the narrowest part of the paediatric airway and bounded by the complete cricoid ring It may be congenital or acquired, and prolonged endotracheal intubation is the leading acquired cause Presents with biphasic stridor, recurrent or prolonged croup-like episodes, exertional breathlessness, and in severe cases respiratory distress In infants it can masquerade as recurrent croup or failure to extubate after ventilation Endoscopic assessment of the airway defines the site, length, and severity of narrowing, and grading systems (such as Cotton-Myer) quantify the degree of luminal loss Management depends on severity and ranges from observation and endoscopic dilatation or laser to open reconstruction such as laryngotracheal reconstruction or cricotracheal resection A tracheostomy may be needed to secure the airway in severe or complex cases before or during definitive repair Minimising intubation trauma and duration, and using appropriately sized tubes, helps prevent acquired stenosis Progressive stridor with respiratory distress indicating critical airway narrowing requiring urgent airway control Failure to extubate or recurrent severe respiratory episodes in an infant Rapidly worsening obstruction suggesting superimposed oedema or infection on a fixed stenosis Signs of an underlying systemic inflammatory disease driving the stenosis Repeatedly treating a child for croup while missing a fixed subglottic stenosis Using oversized endotracheal tubes and prolonging intubation, promoting acquired stenosis Underestimating severity by relying on symptoms alone without endoscopic grading Overlooking an inflammatory cause such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis Subglottic stenosis is a fixed reduction in the cross-sectional area of the subglottic airway. The congenital form reflects abnormal development of the cricoid cartilage producing an inherently narrow lumen. The acquired form typically follows mucosal injury, most often from a tightly fitting or prolonged endotracheal tube, which causes pressure ischaemia, ulceration, perichondritis, and healing by fibrosis with scar contracture; trauma, infection, inflammatory disease, and prior airway surgery are other causes. Because the cricoid is a complete non-expansile ring, even modest circumferential scarring or oedema markedly reduces the lumen and airflow. Mild congenital stenosis often improves as the airway grows, and mild acquired disease may respond to endoscopic measures; more severe or long-segment stenosis usually needs open reconstruction, which has good success in restoring an adequate airway, though multiple procedures and temporary tracheostomy are sometimes required.

Substance use disorder — SUD, addiction, substance dependence, substance abuse Primary mood or anxiety disorder driving or mimicking substance-related symptoms Psychotic disorder versus substance-induced psychosis Delirium or other cognitive disorder from intoxication or withdrawal Other behavioural addictions Non-adherence or physiological dependence on prescribed medication without a use disorder Underlying medical illness producing similar symptoms Validated screening instruments and a detailed substance use history Urine or serum toxicology as appropriate Liver function tests and other markers of organ damage Screening for blood-borne viruses in injecting drug use Assessment of withdrawal severity using standardised scales Screening for comorbid psychiatric disorders and suicide risk The disorder is a cluster of cognitive, behavioural, and physiological features indicating continued use of a substance despite significant harm, with severity graded from mild to severe by the number of features present Core domains include impaired control over use, social impairment, risky use in hazardous situations, and pharmacological features such as tolerance and withdrawal Tolerance and withdrawal alone in a patient taking a prescribed medication as directed do not by themselves indicate a use disorder Craving, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, and continued use despite recognised harm are central to the behavioural picture Screening should be routine and non-judgemental, using validated tools, and should cover alcohol, tobacco, prescription medicines, and illicit substances Management integrates psychosocial interventions such as motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy with substance-specific pharmacotherapy and relapse-prevention strategies Comorbid psychiatric illness is common, and integrated treatment of both the substance disorder and the mental disorder improves outcomes Withdrawal from some substances, notably alcohol and sedatives, can be life-threatening and may require medically supervised detoxification Signs of severe or complicated withdrawal such as seizures, autonomic instability, or delirium tremens Overdose or respiratory depression requiring urgent intervention Suicidal ideation or intent, which is elevated in substance use disorders Injecting practices with risk of sepsis, endocarditis, or blood-borne infection Mislabelling appropriate physiological dependence on prescribed medication as a use disorder Underestimating the danger of alcohol or sedative withdrawal Treating the substance disorder while ignoring comorbid psychiatric illness A judgemental stance that undermines engagement and honest disclosure Overlooking elevated suicide and overdose risk Substance use disorders arise from repeated activation of the mesolimbic dopaminergic reward pathway, producing neuroadaptations in reward, motivation, memory, and executive control circuits that drive compulsive use and craving. Genetic vulnerability, early exposure, psychiatric comorbidity, and environmental and social stressors interact with these neuroadaptations, while allostatic changes in stress and reward systems underlie tolerance, withdrawal, and relapse liability. Substance use disorders are chronic, relapsing conditions, but many people achieve sustained remission, particularly with sustained treatment engagement and social support. Prognosis is worse with early onset, severe dependence, polysubstance use, untreated psychiatric comorbidity, and limited social stability, and better with strong recovery support and continuity of care.

Congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency — SI, CSID, genetic sucrase-isomaltase deficiency, GSID Glucose-galactose malabsorption Congenital or adult-type hypolactasia (lactase deficiency) Coeliac disease with secondary disaccharidase deficiency Functional gastrointestinal disorders and irritable bowel syndrome Cow's milk protein or other food intolerances Giardiasis and post-infective disaccharidase deficiency Duodenal biopsy with disaccharidase enzyme assay showing reduced sucrase activity Sucrose or starch hydrogen/methane breath testing Stool pH and reducing substances after a carbohydrate challenge Molecular genetic testing for SI variants Trial of sucrose and starch elimination with symptom monitoring Autosomal recessive disaccharidase defect caused by SI variants that impair the brush-border sucrase-isomaltase enzyme Symptoms typically appear when sucrose and starch are introduced, with watery osmotic diarrhoea, bloating, abdominal pain and failure to thrive The osmotic diarrhoea abates during fasting or a sucrose-free diet, distinguishing it from secretory diarrhoeas Unabsorbed sugars are fermented by colonic bacteria, giving acidic, frothy stool with a low stool pH and reducing substances Diagnosis is supported by low sucrase activity on duodenal disaccharidase assay of biopsy tissue and by sucrose or starch breath testing Management is dietary restriction of sucrose and starch, with enzyme substitution therapy as an adjunct to broaden dietary tolerance Symptoms often become milder with age as diet and intestinal capacity adjust Significant dehydration during acute diarrhoeal episodes in infants Failure to thrive from chronic carbohydrate malabsorption Persistent symptoms despite dietary measures suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis Onset of new alarm features prompting evaluation for coeliac or other mucosal disease Attributing chronic osmotic diarrhoea to a functional disorder and not testing disaccharidase activity Overlooking hidden sucrose and starch in processed foods and medicines during dietary restriction Missing coeliac disease, which can cause a secondary reduction in disaccharidase activity Assuming a negative single breath test excludes the condition without correlating with biopsy or genetics Congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency is an osmotic malabsorption disorder of the small-intestinal brush border. Variants in SI reduce or abolish the activity of the sucrase-isomaltase complex, which normally hydrolyses sucrose and the alpha-1,6 and some alpha-1,4 bonds of starch-derived oligosaccharides. Undigested disaccharides and oligosaccharides remain in the lumen, drawing water osmotically into the bowel and passing to the colon where bacterial fermentation produces gas and short-chain acids. This yields acidic, watery, gassy diarrhoea that resolves when the offending carbohydrates are withheld. Prognosis is excellent with appropriate dietary management, and many patients tolerate increasing amounts of sucrose and starch with age. Growth and quality of life are normal once symptoms are controlled.

Sudden Infant Death Syndrome — SIDS, cot death, crib death Accidental asphyxia or unsafe sleep-related suffocation Undiagnosed infection or sepsis Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g. fatty acid oxidation defects) Cardiac channelopathy or arrhythmia (e.g. long QT syndrome) Non-accidental injury or inflicted harm Occult congenital or structural abnormality Full postmortem examination (autopsy) Detailed death scene investigation and review of circumstances Comprehensive clinical and family history review Metabolic screening including postmortem samples where indicated Genetic testing for cardiac channelopathies in selected cases Microbiology and toxicology as part of the exclusion process Defined as the sudden and unexpected death of an infant under one year that remains unexplained after a thorough death scene investigation, review of history, and complete postmortem examination. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and forms part of the broader category of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID). Incidence peaks between about 2 and 4 months of age, and most deaths occur during sleep. Prone and side sleeping positions are major modifiable risk factors; supine sleep is strongly protective. Additional risks include soft bedding, bed-sharing, overheating, maternal smoking during and after pregnancy, prematurity, and low birth weight. Protective measures include breastfeeding, immunisation, pacifier use at sleep, and room-sharing without bed-sharing. The prevailing model proposes a vulnerable infant meeting an exogenous stressor during a critical developmental period (the triple-risk hypothesis). Safe-sleep counselling for every family is a core preventive intervention, and any death requires a compassionate, thorough investigation to exclude other causes. Modifiable risk factors that mandate active safe-sleep counselling for prevention Non-supine sleep position, soft bedding, or bed-sharing Exposure to tobacco smoke before or after birth History or scene findings suggesting suffocation or non-accidental injury Recurrent unexplained infant deaths in a family, warranting careful evaluation Prematurity or low birth weight increasing baseline risk Assigning the label SIDS without a complete investigation that excludes other causes Failing to deliver safe-sleep advice at every relevant contact Overlooking an unsafe sleep environment as a contributing factor Not considering metabolic or cardiac causes in apparently unexplained deaths Neglecting sensitive support and follow-up for the bereaved family SIDS is thought to arise when an underlying vulnerability, an environmental stressor, and a critical developmental window coincide (the triple-risk model). The vulnerability is believed to involve abnormalities in brainstem regions that regulate arousal, cardiorespiratory control, and responses to hypoxia and hypercarbia, including serotonergic network dysfunction. When such an infant encounters a stressor, for example a prone position, rebreathing of expired air, or overheating during sleep, an impaired protective arousal and autonomic response may fail to correct hypoxia, leading to death. SIDS is by definition fatal; the clinical focus is prevention through consistent safe-sleep practices, which have substantially reduced incidence, and supportive bereavement care for affected families.

Sudden sensorineural hearing loss — SSNHL, sudden deafness, idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss Impacted cerumen or other conductive causes (must be excluded) Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) Meniere's disease Perilymph fistula Ototoxicity from drugs Central causes such as stroke affecting auditory pathways Otoscopy and tuning fork tests to distinguish sensorineural from conductive loss Pure tone audiometry to confirm and quantify the sensorineural loss MRI of the internal auditory meatus and posterior fossa to exclude retrocochlear pathology Blood tests for infective, inflammatory or autoimmune causes as indicated Vestibular assessment when vertigo accompanies the hearing loss Defined as a rapid-onset sensorineural hearing loss developing over hours to a few days, most often unilateral It is an otological emergency where prompt evaluation and treatment offer the best chance of hearing recovery Patients often report a blocked ear, tinnitus and sometimes vertigo, and may notice the loss on waking Tuning fork tests help confirm a sensorineural pattern: Weber lateralises to the better-hearing ear and Rinne remains positive The majority of cases are idiopathic, but identifiable causes include infection, vascular events, trauma, ototoxic drugs and, importantly, vestibular schwannoma Management principles centre on early corticosteroid therapy, given systemically or intratympanically, after excluding a conductive cause MRI of the internal auditory meatus is important to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as acoustic neuroma Delay in diagnosis and treatment reduces the likelihood of hearing recovery, so urgent referral is essential Sudden unilateral hearing loss itself, which is an emergency requiring urgent assessment and treatment Accompanying neurological signs or severe vertigo suggesting a central or serious cause Progressive or fluctuating loss with tinnitus indicating possible vestibular schwannoma Bilateral sudden loss suggesting a systemic, autoimmune or ototoxic process Dismissing sudden hearing loss as wax or a benign blocked ear and delaying treatment Failing to distinguish sensorineural from conductive loss with tuning fork tests Not arranging MRI to exclude a vestibular schwannoma Missing the narrow window in which corticosteroid therapy is most effective Sudden sensorineural hearing loss reflects acute dysfunction of the cochlea or auditory nerve. Although often idiopathic, proposed mechanisms include viral infection or inflammation of the labyrinth, microvascular compromise of the cochlear blood supply, rupture of intracochlear membranes, and autoimmune injury. These processes damage the delicate hair cells and neural elements or disturb the cochlear ionic and metabolic environment, producing abrupt hearing loss. A minority result from identifiable structural causes such as a vestibular schwannoma compressing the cochlear nerve, which is why imaging is required. Outcome is variable; a substantial proportion recover partially or fully, particularly with early treatment, but severe loss, delayed presentation, vertigo and poor initial audiometry are associated with worse recovery.

Isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency — ISOD, SUOX deficiency, sulphite oxidase deficiency, isolated sulphite oxidase deficiency Molybdenum cofactor deficiency (biochemically similar but with low uric acid) Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Neonatal epileptic encephalopathies of other causes Non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia Homocystinuria (another cause of ectopia lentis) Vitamin-responsive neonatal epilepsies Fresh urine sulphite testing and quantitation of urinary S-sulphocysteine Plasma uric acid, which is normal (distinguishing it from molybdenum cofactor deficiency) Plasma total homocysteine and cystine, which tend to be low Neuroimaging showing early oedema followed by cystic change and atrophy Molecular genetic testing of SUOX Ophthalmological assessment for lens dislocation Autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in SUOX, encoding the molybdenum-dependent enzyme sulphite oxidase The enzyme catalyses the final step of sulphur amino acid catabolism, converting sulphite to sulphate; its deficiency causes accumulation of neurotoxic sulphite and S-sulphocysteine Unlike molybdenum cofactor deficiency, xanthine oxidase is unaffected, so plasma uric acid is normal, which is the key distinguishing feature The severe neonatal form presents with intractable seizures, feeding difficulty, hypotonia evolving to spasticity and rapidly progressive encephalopathy Ectopia lentis (dislocation of the ocular lens) is a characteristic later finding A fresh-urine sulphite dipstick may be positive, and raised urinary S-sulphocysteine supports the diagnosis; plasma total homocysteine is often low Milder, later-onset phenotypes exist with developmental delay, movement disorder and a more indolent course There is no established disease-modifying treatment, and dietary restriction of sulphur amino acids has limited proven benefit Intractable neonatal seizures with rapidly evolving encephalopathy Imaging suggesting hypoxic-ischaemic injury without a perinatal history Ectopia lentis in an infant with neurological impairment Progressive spasticity and acquired microcephaly Mistaking the presentation for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy Failing to distinguish it from molybdenum cofactor deficiency by not checking uric acid Relying on stored urine for sulphite testing, as sulphite degrades quickly Overlooking milder late-onset phenotypes Sulphite oxidase is a mitochondrial molybdoenzyme that oxidises sulphite to sulphate, the terminal reaction in the degradation of the sulphur-containing amino acids cysteine and methionine. When SUOX is defective, sulphite accumulates and reacts with cystine to form S-sulphocysteine, a structural analogue of glutamate that is thought to act as an excitotoxin at NMDA receptors. Sulphite is also directly toxic and can disrupt cerebral connective tissue and lens zonules, explaining the lens dislocation. The result is severe neuronal injury, cystic white matter change and progressive cerebral atrophy in the classic neonatal form. The classic neonatal form carries a poor prognosis, with severe neurodevelopmental impairment and often early death. Later-onset, attenuated forms follow a more variable course but still cause significant neurological disability; effective disease-modifying therapy is currently lacking.

Superficial Fungal Infections — Dermatophytosis, Ringworm, Tinea, Pityriasis versicolor, Tinea versicolor, Onychomycosis, Mucocutaneous candidiasis Contact dermatitis Eczema Psoriasis (can mimic both tinea corporis and onychomycosis) Erythrasma Intertriginous candidiasis Vitiligo (for tinea versicolor; differentiated by absence of scale) Bacterial folliculitis Seborrheic dermatitis / dandruff Leukoplakia (for oral thrush) Intertriginous candidiasis (vs tinea cruris) Bacterial folliculitis (vs Malassezia folliculitis) Oral leukoplakia from other infections vs Candida thrush KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy of scrapings from the lesion edge to detect hyphae Fungal culture, indicated when an outbreak is suspected or when there is no response to therapy KOH preparation showing budding bottle-shaped yeasts with short septate hyphae for Malassezia Culture of Malassezia requires sterile olive oil added to the medium for suspected disseminated infection Skin biopsy or nail clippings with culture and microscopy for skin and nail candidiasis Biopsy of oral/esophageal tissue to distinguish invasive thrush (yeasts, pseudohyphae, and hyphae invading epithelium) from mere colonization (superficial yeast forms only) and from mimics such as leukoplakia Culture and microscopy of vaginal secretions (swab) for vulvovaginal candidiasis Psoriasis Eczema Contact dermatitis Vitiligo Seborrheic dermatitis Mucosal leukoplakia Superficial fungal infections are caused by molds and yeasts that colonize the outer skin layers, hair follicles, and nails without invading deeper tissue; they are the most common human fungal infections but rarely cause serious disease. Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) are not part of normal skin flora and confine themselves to keratinized structures; symptoms arise from inflammatory reaction to fungal antigens rather than tissue invasion, and an estimated billion people are affected worldwide. The annular, ring-shaped cutaneous lesion ('ringworm') results from centrifugal outward growth of the organism in the stratum corneum; the term tinea (Latin for worm) is preferred and is paired with the affected body site. Tinea capitis predominantly affects children aged 3 to 7 years, producing well-demarcated scaly patches with hair shafts broken off near the skin surface and possible alopecia. Tinea pedis typically begins in the toe web spaces with peeling, maceration, and pruritus, and is a recognized portal of entry for streptococci and staphylococci, predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis through interdigital fissures. Onychomycosis affects toenails more often than fingernails, is most common in those with tinea pedis, and shows thickened, discolored, crumbling nails with onycholysis; older age, vascular disease, diabetes, and nail trauma are risk factors. Malassezia yeasts (notably M. furfur, M. pachydermatis) are lipophilic commensals of sebum-rich areas (back, chest, scalp, face) and cause tinea/pityriasis versicolor, folliculitis, and seborrheic dermatitis; cutaneous IL-17 signaling normally controls them. Tinea versicolor appears as flat round scaly hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the neck, chest, or upper arms, usually asymptomatic, and can be confused with vitiligo (which is non-scaly). KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation of lesion-edge scrapings demonstrating hyphae is the key bedside diagnostic test; Malassezia shows a characteristic mix of budding bottle-shaped yeasts and short septate hyphae. Mucocutaneous candidiasis is most often caused by Candida albicans; oral thrush yields white mucosal plaques that scrape off, and antibiotic use, diabetes, and pregnancy are major risk factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis. Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant species that persistently colonizes human skin, hair follicles, healthcare environments, and devices, grows avidly in human sweat, and drives nosocomial outbreaks. Seborrheic dermatitis (a Malassezia-associated condition) can be especially severe in patients with AIDS, and Malassezia fungemia, though rare, occurs almost exclusively in premature neonates receiving parenteral lipid nutrition. Tinea pedis with interdigital fissuring predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis from streptococcal/staphylococcal entry Severe seborrheic dermatitis as a clue to AIDS / advanced immunosuppression Malassezia fungemia/disseminated infection in premature neonates on parenteral lipid nutrition Candida auris colonization as a nosocomial multidrug-resistant outbreak risk Recurrent or extensive mucocutaneous candidiasis suggesting inborn errors of immunity (e.g., STAT1 gain-of-function, IL-17 signaling defects) or AIDS Moderate-to-severe oral thrush or esophageal involvement requiring systemic evaluation Diagnosing onychomycosis clinically without confirmation, since psoriasis can mimic nail fungal disease (usually with associated skin lesions) Mistaking tinea versicolor for vitiligo; the absence of scale distinguishes vitiligo Interpreting superficial yeast forms on oral/esophageal biopsy as invasive candidiasis when they actually represent colonization only Overlooking tinea pedis as a portal for bacterial cellulitis Not pursuing culture when a patient fails to respond to empiric therapy or when an outbreak is suspected Superficial fungi inhabit only the keratinized superficial layers (stratum corneum, hair follicles, nail plate) and do not invade beneath the stratum corneum. Dermatophytes live within keratin and produce disease through host inflammatory responses to fungal antigens rather than by direct tissue invasion; nail involvement begins via the lateral or superficial nail plate then spreads, and hair-shaft invasion may be intra- or peri-shaft. Host defense is mediated by IL-17 responses, which restrict dermatophyte growth and control cutaneous Malassezia; infections are more frequent in males, and progesterone can inhibit dermatophyte growth. Malassezia organisms are lipophilic commensals of sebaceous areas that elicit little inflammation but, when IL-17 responses are excessive, can exacerbate atopic inflammation. Candida species are mucosal/cutaneous commensals; control depends on IL-17-producing lymphoid cells (TH17, gamma-delta T cells, innate lymphoid cells) at barrier sites, and defects in IL-17 signaling predispose to oral and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Superficial fungal infections rarely cause serious disease. Malassezia skin infections are benign and self-limited, though recurrences are common. Dermatophyte infections generally respond well to therapy, but onychomycosis is slow to clear and prone to relapse. The outcome of rare systemic Malassezia infection depends on the host's underlying condition, though most affected neonates do well. Clinically stratified by extent and site: localized cutaneous tinea versus extensive tinea and onychomycosis; for mucocutaneous candidiasis, mild oral thrush is distinguished from moderate/severe or esophageal disease that requires systemic management.

The elements of Virchow's triad apply: venous stasis (notably in varicose veins), endothelial injury (for example from cannulation), and hypercoagulability. Thrombus formation within the superficial vein triggers a local inflammatory response producing the characteristic tender palpable cord. Because superficial and deep systems communicate through perforators and saphenous junctions, thrombus can propagate into the deep veins, linking the condition to venous thromboembolism. Localised superficial thrombophlebitis in varicose veins is usually self-limiting with a good outcome, whereas extensive disease or thrombus near a deep junction carries a meaningful risk of progression to deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism. Recurrence is common when underlying venous disease or a prothrombotic state persists.

cardioversion in an unstable patient while attempting pharmacological control Overlooking reversible precipitants such as stimulants, thyroid disease, or electrolyte disturbance Most paroxysmal SVT is caused by reentry. In AV nodal reentrant tachycardia a functional circuit forms within or near the AV node using fast and slow pathways. In AV reentrant tachycardia the circuit incorporates an accessory pathway connecting atrium and ventricle, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White. Atrial tachycardias instead arise from an ectopic atrial focus with enhanced automaticity or microreentry. In reentrant mechanisms a premature beat finds one limb refractory and conducts down the other, then returns retrogradely, establishing a self-sustaining loop that the AV node often participates in, which is why AV nodal blockade frequently terminates the arrhythmia. Most forms of SVT are not life-threatening and carry an excellent prognosis, with catheter ablation curing the majority of reentrant cases; prognosis worsens when SVT complicates structural heart disease or occurs as pre-excited tachycardia with a risk of rapid ventricular rates.
