Sustained Ventricular Tachycardia — Sustained monomorphic VT, Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, Idiopathic VT, Belhassen's VT, Verapamil-sensitive VT, Bundle branch reentry VT, Outflow tract VT Supraventricular tachycardia with left or right bundle branch block aberrancy Supraventricular tachycardia conducted to the ventricles over an accessory pathway (pre-excited tachycardia) Rapid ventricular pacing (appropriate or inappropriate) in a patient with a pacemaker or defibrillator Telemetry noise and movement artifact simulating VT 12-lead ECG during tachycardia analyzing AV dissociation, aVR morphology, and V1-V6 concordance to differentiate VT from SVT with aberrancy Comparison of tachycardia QRS morphology with the baseline sinus-rhythm QRS (identical morphology in a known bundle branch block favors SVT but is not definitive) Echocardiography to assess ventricular function and detect segmental wall-motion abnormalities indicating scar Cardiac MRI for delayed gadolinium enhancement to identify and localize fibrosis (intramural/subepicardial in nonischemic cardiomyopathy) Nuclear imaging for wall-motion abnormalities Cardiac biomarkers (troponin, CK-MB) to evaluate myocardial injury, recognizing that acute MI rarely causes sustained monomorphic VT and modest elevations usually reflect demand ischemia during the arrhythmia rather than an acute coronary event Electrophysiologic study when noninvasive criteria leave the diagnosis uncertain SVT with aberrant conduction (bundle branch block) Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia / pre-excited SVT over an accessory pathway Pacemaker-mediated rapid ventricular pacing Sustained monomorphic VT is a wide-QRS ventricular arrhythmia lasting at least 30 seconds, or one requiring intervention (antitachycardia pacing or cardioversion) for termination; each QRS resembles the others, pointing to a single focal origin or repetitive exit from a fixed reentry circuit. In structural heart disease the usual substrate is patchy replacement fibrosis from prior infarction, fibrosis, inflammation, or previous cardiac surgery, which sets up anatomic or functional reentry; less often VT arises from reentry or automaticity in diseased Purkinje conduction tissue. Clinical tolerance depends on rate, baseline ventricular function, and autonomic response: rapid VT may cause hypotension and syncope (especially with poor LV function), while patients with normal function may have only palpitations despite fast rates. Hemodynamic stability during a wide-complex tachycardia does NOT distinguish VT from supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy; tolerance of the rhythm should never be used to exclude VT. Ventriculoatrial (AV) dissociation is a reliable marker of VT, provided the atrial rate is slower than the ventricular rate; however a P wave following every QRS does not exclude VT because 1:1 ventriculo-atrial conduction can occur. A monophasic R or Rs complex in lead aVR, or concordance (all monophasic R or all S waves) across V1 to V6, is relatively specific for VT. In a patient with known structural heart disease, a wide-QRS tachycardia is most likely VT regardless of QRS morphology; depressed LV function or evidence of structural disease makes scar-related reentry the most likely mechanism of sustained monomorphic VT. Scar is suggested by pathologic Q waves on ECG, segmental wall-motion abnormalities on echo or nuclear imaging, and areas of delayed gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI. Idiopathic VT occurs in structurally normal hearts (normal sinus ECG, normal function and no scar on imaging), is provoked by sympathetic stimulation or acute sympathetic withdrawal (e.g. immediately post-exercise), and is generally benign with low risk of sudden death. Outflow tract VT most often arises in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing a left bundle branch block pattern in V1 with an inferiorly directed axis (tall R waves in II, III, aVF); a prominent R wave in V1 or V2 suggests a left ventricular outflow tract or aortic-root origin. LV fascicular VT (Belhassen's / verapamil-sensitive VT) is the second most common idiopathic form: it shows a right bundle branch block-like configuration negative in the inferior leads and is due to a small reentry circuit near the septal ramifications of the left Purkinje system; despite being reentrant its course is typically benign. Repeated incessant bursts of nonsustained monomorphic VT (repetitive monomorphic VT) can produce a tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy with depressed ventricular function that recovers once the arrhythmia is suppressed. Hypotension, impaired consciousness, or pulmonary edema accompanying the tachycardia (hemodynamic instability) Rapid VT in a patient with significant ventricular dysfunction (high risk of syncope and degeneration to VF) VT presenting as resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest where VF was the initial recorded rhythm Sustained monomorphic VT in the setting of structural heart disease (high recurrence and sudden-death risk) Frequent recurrent or incessant VT episodes Syncope or cardiac arrest as the presenting event in inherited cardiomyopathies (ARVC, repaired tetralogy of Fallot) Using hemodynamic stability to rule out VT - tolerance of the rhythm does not exclude VT. Assuming a P wave after every QRS excludes VT, when 1:1 ventriculo-atrial conduction can mimic this. Relying on a single QRS-morphology criterion; all such criteria have limitations and are unreliable in severe heart disease, and bundle branch reentry VT can closely resemble the native sinus QRS. Interpreting troponin/CK-MB elevations during VT as proof of an acute coronary event - these usually reflect demand ischemia from hypotension and fixed coronary disease; acute MI is rarely the cause of sustained monomorphic VT. Mistaking telemetry noise or movement artifact for VT, leading to unnecessary tests and interventions. Attributing a typical outflow-tract QRS morphology automatically to benign idiopathic VT, since cardiomyopathies (notably ARVC) can produce PVCs/VT from the same region and must be excluded. Failing to recognize repetitive monomorphic (incessant nonsustained) VT as a reversible cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Sustained monomorphic VT most commonly results from reentry around a fixed substrate. In structural heart disease this substrate is an area of patchy replacement fibrosis (from infarction, inflammation, fibrosis, or surgical scar) creating anatomic or functional reentrant circuits; the uniform QRS reflects a single focal origin or repetitive exit from a stable circuit. In coronary artery disease the typical setting is a remote large myocardial infarction with a remodeled ventricle and depressed LV function, where the infarct scar provides a durable reentry substrate that is not generally dependent on ongoing acute ischemia. In nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, scar-related reentry from progressive replacement fibrosis underlies VT, with scars often intramural or subepicardial and frequently adjacent to a valve annulus; sarcoidosis, Chagas' disease, and Lamin A/C mutation cardiomyopathy are particularly associated. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy involves fibrofatty replacement chiefly of right ventricular myocardium producing a left bundle branch block-like VT. Bundle branch reentry VT (about 5% of monomorphic VT with structural disease) uses a macroreentrant circuit through the Purkinje system, usually retrograde up the left bundle and anterograde down the right bundle, generating a left bundle branch block configuration. Idiopathic VT in structurally normal hearts arises either from focal triggered automaticity (outflow tract foci near the pulmonic or aortic annuli) or from small reentry circuits in the Purkinje system (fascicular VT). Rapid or scar-associated monomorphic VT may degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Prognosis hinges on the presence and type of underlying heart disease. Scar-related monomorphic VT in structural heart disease carries a high recurrence risk; with ischemic cardiomyopathy and a prior large MI, up to 70% of patients have arrhythmia recurrence within 2 years, and even after device-based secondary prevention the depressed-ejection-fraction population remains at risk for heart failure, recurrent ischemic events, and recurrent VT, with a 5-year mortality exceeding 30%. Device shocks and antitachycardia pacing are themselves adverse events linked to higher rates of heart failure, mortality, and psychological stress. By contrast, idiopathic VT in a structurally normal heart is generally benign, sudden death is rare, and a defibrillator is not recommended; LV fascicular (Belhassen's) VT likewise follows a benign course despite being reentrant. In ARVC, clinical heart failure is rare until late stages and survival to advanced age can be expected provided the VT is controlled. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot the risk of sudden cardiac death may reach roughly 1% per year in adulthood by the fourth or fifth decade. Harrison classifies sustained ventricular arrhythmias by substrate/etiology rather than a graded severity scale: (1) idiopathic VT without structural heart disease - outflow tract (RV outflow: LBBB pattern in V1 with inferior axis and late precordial transition; LV outflow: inferior axis with early precordial transition and prominent R in V2-V3), LV fascicular VT (RBBB pattern in V1 with left axis deviation), and papillary muscle VT; (2) ischemic cardiomyopathy (monomorphic VT common after large prior MI); (3) nonischemic cardiomyopathy (fibrotic scar VT, e.g. sarcoidosis, Chagas', Lamin A/C); (4) arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy (RV-origin LBBB-pattern VT); (5) repaired tetralogy of Fallot (RV-origin VT); (6) hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; and (7) genetic arrhythmia syndromes (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, short QT/early repolarization). Practically, the most important severity distinction is between benign idiopathic VT in a structurally normal heart and scar-related VT in structural heart disease, the latter conferring substantial sudden-death risk.

Malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma, metastatic tumours) accounts for most cases, but benign causes now make up at least 40% owing to widespread use of intravascular devices (central venous catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads). Lung cancer—particularly small-cell and squamous-cell histology—causes around 85% of malignant SVCS. In a young adult/young man with a mediastinal mass and SVCS, think lymphoma versus primary mediastinal germ cell tumour. Symptoms are characteristically worse on bending forward or lying supine; facial swelling and plethora are exacerbated when supine. The clinical picture is milder when the obstruction is above the azygos vein. Symptoms may actually improve over time as collateral venous circulation develops, and most patients improve partly for this reason. Small-cell lung cancer patients with SVCS have a higher incidence of brain metastases than those without SVCS; new seizures more likely reflect brain mets than venous cerebral oedema. Tissue diagnosis (bronchoscopy, percutaneous needle biopsy, mediastinoscopy, endobronchial/oesophageal ultrasound-guided aspiration, or even thoracotomy) can generally be obtained safely without major bleeding risk despite the venous congestion. For a patient with no prior cancer history, a full evaluation is essential to exclude benign causes and define a specific diagnosis before directing therapy; in known cancer, treatment may begin after a thoracic CT. Signs/symptoms of cerebral and/or laryngeal oedema — rare but carry a poorer prognosis and demand urgent evaluation Upper airway/tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass — the one potentially life-threatening complication, demands emergent therapy Cardiorespiratory symptoms at rest, especially with positional change — indicate significant airway/vascular obstruction and limited physiologic reserve Risk of cardiac arrest or respiratory failure, particularly with sedation or general anaesthesia Proptosis, glossal and laryngeal oedema, and obtundation indicate severe disease Postural hypotension with severe symptoms Variceal (downhill oesophageal varices) bleeding as a late complication of chronic SVCS Do not assume SVCS is always malignant — benign device/catheter-related causes now account for at least 40% of cases. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude SVCS when other characteristic findings are present. Attributing seizures to venous cerebral oedema when brain metastases are the more likely cause (especially in small-cell lung cancer). Sedatives or general anaesthesia in a patient with airway/vascular obstruction may precipitate cardiac arrest or respiratory failure. In a patient without known cancer, omitting a full diagnostic workup risks missing benign causes and a treatable specific diagnosis. SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava causing a severe reduction in venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Obstruction may be due to external compression, direct tumour invasion, intraluminal thrombosis (often device-related), or fibrosis. Venous congestion produces facial/upper-body swelling, distended neck veins, and development of collateral venous channels over the chest wall. The 'hot quadrate' focal hepatic hotspot on CT reflects portosystemic shunting between the SVC and portal vein. Chronic SVCS can produce 'downhill' oesophageal varices (cephalad-to-caudad flow, opposite to portal-hypertension 'uphill' varices), which may bleed late. Clinical improvement occurs in most patients, partly attributable to the development of adequate collateral circulation. Mortality is determined by the underlying cause rather than by the caval obstruction itself. SVCS recurs in roughly 10-30% of patients. Cerebral or laryngeal oedema portends a worse prognosis. Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading scale. Severity is described clinically by features such as presence of cerebral/laryngeal oedema, proptosis, glossal/laryngeal oedema, obtundation, postural hypotension, and cardiorespiratory symptoms at rest with positional change, which together denote severe, potentially life-threatening disease; obstruction above the azygos vein produces a milder picture.

dermatosis in which activated neutrophils accumulate in the dermis, producing tender inflammatory plaques, fever, and systemic inflammation. Staging is the organizing framework: a primary chancre at the site of inoculation, then generalized secondary mucocutaneous disease, followed by latency, and in a minority of untreated patients tertiary disease (gumma, cardiovascular, late neurosyphilis) (Harrison 22e p.1428, p.1430). Primary chancre is typically a single painless papule that erodes into an indurated ulcer with a firm cartilaginous edge; it is accompanied by regional (usually inguinal) lymphadenopathy that is firm, nonsuppurative, and painless, and heals spontaneously in about 4-6 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1430). Secondary syphilis classically produces a widespread macular-to-papular, nonpruritic rash that frequently involves the palms and soles, plus generalized nontender lymphadenopathy (noted in ~85% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.1430-1431). Condylomata lata (broad, moist, highly infectious lesions in intertriginous areas, ~10% of secondary cases) and mucous patches (painless silver-gray erosions of oral/genital mucosa) are characteristic secondary lesions (Harrison 22e p.1431). Latent syphilis is defined by reactive serology with a normal CSF and no clinical manifestations; early latent is within the first year, late latent is >=1 year or of unknown duration (Harrison 22e p.1431). Two classes of serologic tests: lipoidal (nontreponemal) RPR/VDRL, which are quantitative and reflect disease activity, and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPPA, EIA/CIA); a reactive lipoidal screen must be confirmed by a treponemal test (Harrison 22e p.1433). RPR is preferred for rapid serologic diagnosis; the VDRL remains the standard for CSF examination and is superior to RPR for that purpose (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434). After treatment of early syphilis a fourfold (two-dilution) fall in VDRL/RPR titer (e.g., 1:32 to 1:8) signals adequate response; treponemal tests typically remain reactive and are not useful for monitoring therapy (Harrison 22e p.1433, p.1435). Penicillin is the drug of choice for all stages as a principle; its efficacy against T. pallidum remains undiminished after decades of use (Harrison 22e p.1434). Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, chills, myalgia, headache, tachycardia) may follow the start of therapy, thought to be a response to lipoproteins released by dying treponemes; it occurs in ~50% of primary and ~90% of secondary cases, defervesces within 12-24 h, is self-limited, and does not require steroids (Harrison 22e p.1435). Earliest manifestations of early congenital syphilis include rhinitis ('snuffles'), mucocutaneous lesions, periostitis/bone changes, and hepatosplenomegaly; classic late stigmata include Hutchinson's teeth, mulberry molars, saddle nose, and saber shins (Harrison 22e p.1432-1433). Neurosyphilis at any stage: meningeal syphilis (headache, neck stiffness, cranial nerve involvement, seizures, mental status change), meningovascular syphilis (stroke syndrome in a relatively young adult), or late parenchymatous disease (general paresis, tabes dorsalis) (Harrison 22e p.1432) Ocular syphilis (uveitis, iritis, optic neuritis, pupillary abnormalities)—permanent blindness may result without prompt diagnosis and treatment (Harrison 22e p.1431) Otic syphilis (sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus)—deafness may result if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1431) Cardiovascular syphilis: aortitis with aortic regurgitation, saccular aneurysm of the ascending aorta, or coronary ostial stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1432) Maternal syphilis in pregnancy: high risk of fetal loss, stillbirth, prematurity, neonatal death, and congenital syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1432) Serum RPR titer >=1:32 marks higher risk of neurosyphilis (Harrison 22e p.1432, p.1434) Prozone phenomenon: a high-titer specimen may give a nonreactive or only weakly reactive lipoidal test with undiluted serum that becomes reactive only on dilution—a falsely negative screen if dilution is not performed (Harrison 22e p.1433). Primary syphilis is often missed in women and in MSM because chancres on the cervix, vaginal wall, anal canal, rectum, or mouth go unseen; atypical or trivial dark-field-negative genital lesions should still prompt consideration of syphilis (Harrison 22e p.1430). Both lipoidal and treponemal tests may be nonreactive in early primary syphilis; an early primary ulcer can present with nonreactive serology, so negative serology does not exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1431-1433). Biological false-positive lipoidal tests occur (usually titer <=1:8, e.g., in autoimmune disease or injection drug use); a nonreactive treponemal test excludes syphilis in this setting (Harrison 22e p.1433-1434). Treponemal tests usually remain reactive for life after treatment and cannot distinguish active from past infection or gauge response to therapy (Harrison 22e p.1433, p.1435). CSF VDRL is highly specific but insensitive—it may be nonreactive even in symptomatic neurosyphilis—and RPR must not be substituted for VDRL on CSF (Harrison 22e p.1434). Benzathine penicillin does not achieve treponemicidal levels in CSF even at high doses, so it is inadequate for neurosyphilis and viable T. pallidum has been recovered from CSF after such treatment (Harrison 22e p.1434). Syphilis is a 'great imitator': its protean mucocutaneous and systemic features overlap with many other diseases, so it must be considered broadly (Harrison 22e p.1430-1431). Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum is a thin spiral organism with a lipid-rich outer membrane and periplasmic endoflagella that drive motility; it has severely limited metabolic capacity and depends on host amino acids, carbohydrates, and lipids. Humans are the only known natural host. After penetrating intact mucous membranes or skin abrasions, treponemes reach the lymphatics and blood within hours, producing systemic dissemination and metastatic foci well before the primary lesion appears (median incubation ~21 days, rarely >6 weeks). Tissue damage reflects the host immune response rather than a direct treponemal toxin: lesions show perivascular infiltration by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, plasma cells, and macrophages with endarteritis obliterans (obliteration of small vessels). Antigenic variation of the TprK outer-membrane protein allows immune evasion and persistence, explaining the paradoxical appearance of secondary lesions after primary lesions clear. Tertiary lesions (gumma, aortitis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, parenchymal neurosyphilis) arise from a slowly progressive inflammatory process that begins early in infection (Harrison 22e p.1428-1430, p.1432). Untreated primary and secondary lesions resolve spontaneously, but infection persists. In the preantibiotic era about one-third of untreated patients with latent infection progressed to tertiary disease; the Tuskegee Study showed untreated syphilis raised the death rate ~17%, largely from cardiovascular disease. With early treatment, prognosis is excellent and tertiary syphilis is now nearly eliminated in Western countries; the clinical response to therapy for benign tertiary (gumma) disease is usually impressive. Congenital syphilis prognosis is poor when fulminant disease is clinically apparent at birth, but adequate maternal treatment before the 16th week of pregnancy should prevent fetal damage. Response to therapy is monitored by a fourfold decline in VDRL/RPR titer (Harrison 22e p.1430, p.1432, p.1435). Disease is described by clinical stage rather than a graded severity score: primary syphilis (chancre with regional lymphadenopathy); secondary syphilis (generalized mucocutaneous rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucous patches, constitutional symptoms); latent syphilis (reactive serology, normal CSF, no clinical signs; early latent <1 year vs late latent >=1 year or unknown duration); tertiary/late syphilis (gumma, cardiovascular syphilis, late neurosyphilis). Neurosyphilis spans a continuum: early (asymptomatic meningitis, meningeal and meningovascular syphilis) and late parenchymatous disease (general paresis, tabes dorsalis). Congenital syphilis is divided into early (within first 2 years) and late (after 2 years) (Harrison 22e p.1428, p.1431-1433).

secondary syrinx Failing to recognise dissociated sensory loss and its localising value Overlooking an associated Chiari malformation or underlying tumour as the treatable cause Attributing hand wasting solely to motor neuron disease without imaging the cord Not counselling patients about protecting insensate areas from burns and injury Syringomyelia is characterised by a longitudinal cavity within the spinal cord that disrupts neural tissue from the centre outward. Altered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, often related to obstruction at the craniocervical junction as in Chiari I malformation, are thought to drive fluid accumulation and cavity expansion. The central location preferentially damages the decussating spinothalamic fibres, producing dissociated sensory loss, and progressive enlargement affects anterior horn cells, long tracts, and autonomic pathways. Syringomyelia often progresses slowly over years, with a stepwise or gradual accumulation of deficits. Treating the underlying cause, particularly decompressing a Chiari malformation, can stabilise or improve symptoms, but established neurological deficits may not fully reverse and some patients continue to deteriorate despite surgery.

peripheral smear for schistocytes and ADAMTS13 activity plus LDH if microangiopathy suspected Renal assessment: eGFR, serum creatinine, random or 24-h urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, screened quarterly Renal biopsy (ISN/RPS classification) when UPCr exceeds 0.5 or renal function declines Emerging urinary biomarkers when available (urinary IL-16, CD163, type 1 IFN, TGF-beta) Creatine kinase and aldolase with muscle biopsy if inflammatory myopathy suspected Baseline and yearly retinal examination when on hydroxychloroquine (maculopathy surveillance) Glucocorticoid-induced psychosis (mimics neuropsychiatric lupus psychosis) Migraine or tension headache (overlaps with neuropsychiatric lupus headache) Rosacea (mimics the malar/butterfly rash) Drug-induced lupus (clinically and serologically overlaps with SLE) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome (microangiopathy mimic) SLE is an autoimmune disease driven by overactive innate and adaptive immunity, with tissue injury mediated by autoantibodies and immune complexes; cutaneous, musculoskeletal, and renal systems are most often affected, followed by pulmonary, hematologic, cardiovascular, serosal, and CNS involvement (p.2827). Roughly 90% of patients are women, most of childbearing age; in the US the highest prevalence is in Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women, and non-White patients tend to have more severe disease (p.2827). Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so seropositivity helps attribute nonspecific constitutional symptoms to SLE (p.2827, p.2830). ANA at a titer of at least 1:80 is the best screening test and is present in nearly all patients; repeatedly negative immunofluorescence ANA makes the diagnosis unlikely, though about 5% of patients are ANA-negative (p.2832). Anti-dsDNA (present in ~40-60%, specificity ~75-99%) and anti-Sm (present in ~30%, highly specific) are the only ANA subtypes in the EULAR/ACR criteria; rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3/C4 signals active disease, especially impending nephritis (p.2832, p.2830). Lupus arthritis is a nonerosive polyarthritis of wrists, MCP/PIP joints, and knees; periarticular ligament damage can cause reversible Jaccoud-like deformities, and overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829). The classic malar 'butterfly' rash spares the nasolabial folds (distinguishing it from rosacea); subacute cutaneous lupus is photosensitive and linked to anti-Ro/SSA, while discoid lesions are the most common chronic cutaneous form (p.2829). Nephritis occurs in about 35% of patients, may be asymptomatic, and warrants screening every 3 months with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio; biopsy is generally prompted by UPCr >0.5 or declining renal function (p.2830, p.2833). Antiphospholipid antibodies are present in ~50% of patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, recurrent fetal loss, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and stroke (p.2830, p.2832). Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus (transient rash/lab abnormalities or, less commonly, congenital heart block); high-titer Ro warrants fetal echocardiography screening (p.2836). Avascular (osteo)necrosis should be suspected when pain is out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee, particularly with prior corticosteroid use (p.2829). Some patients are categorized as 'type 1 lupus' (classic immune-driven features such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis, generally steroid-responsive) versus 'type 2 lupus' (fatigue, diffuse pain, cognitive dysfunction/'brain fog', less responsive to immunosuppression) (p.2827-2828). Rapidly declining renal function or rising proteinuria suggesting class III/IV proliferative lupus nephritis (~20% of class IV cases die or reach ESRD within 10 years) Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage or acute pneumonitis (life-threatening pulmonary involvement) Severe neuropsychiatric disease: psychosis, seizures, transverse myelitis, stroke Severe thrombocytopenia (<20,000-50,000/uL) with bleeding risk, or life-threatening hemolytic anemia Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, high LDH) Mesenteric vasculitis (risk of intestinal perforation, bleeding, ischemia) Antiphospholipid syndrome with arterial/venous thrombosis or catastrophic APS Pulmonary arterial hypertension or prior arterial thrombosis in pregnancy (highest maternal mortality risk) New chest pain in a young patient given accelerated atherosclerosis and premature coronary disease Treating ANA positivity as diagnostic: ANA occurs at low titer in healthy people and in many other autoimmune diseases; diagnosis ultimately rests on clinical judgment, and classification criteria were designed for trial enrollment, not diagnosis. Excluding SLE because ANA is negative: about 5% of patients are ANA-negative, where anti-Ro/SSA can support the diagnosis. Missing asymptomatic lupus nephritis or cytopenias by not screening quarterly, since renal and hematologic disease can be present without symptoms. Attributing acute pulmonary infiltrates to lupus pneumonitis when infection looks identical on imaging. Ascribing psychosis or confusion to neuropsychiatric lupus without ruling out glucocorticoid-induced psychosis and infectious encephalitis. Overlooking avascular necrosis as a cause of disproportionate single-joint pain in patients on corticosteroids. Confusing drug-induced lupus (antihistone-positive, usually sparing kidney/brain, resolving after withdrawal) with idiopathic SLE. Using estrogen-containing contraceptives or HRT in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or active disease, increasing thromboembolism risk. Using direct oral anticoagulants instead of warfarin for concomitant APS, or continuing teratogenic agents (mycophenolate, methotrexate, warfarin) in pregnancy. SLE arises from multiple immunoregulatory defects in genetically predisposed individuals interacting with environmental triggers. There is a strong genetic component (24% vs 2% concordance in monozygotic vs dizygotic twins; >150 GWAS susceptibility loci), with the MHC the most common association and nearly half of loci tied to type 1 interferon production or signaling (e.g., TLR7, IRF5/7/8, STAT4); complement-cascade defects (C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, C4) impair clearance of apoptotic debris and immune complexes and underlie severe monogenic disease. Environmental contributors include UV light, crystalline silica, smoking, sex hormones, Epstein-Barr virus, and gut-microbiome-related increased intestinal permeability. Innate defects cause excess cellular debris (high neutrophil turnover and NETosis) that overwhelms macrophage/dendritic clearance, triggering nucleic-acid sensors and TLRs in plasmacytoid dendritic cells to produce type 1 interferon, which sensitizes the adaptive immune system. Loss of B- and T-cell tolerance (including expansion of age-associated B cells, T follicular/peripheral helper cell help, and defective regulatory T cells) drives production of pathogenic autoantibodies; autoantibody-nucleic acid immune complexes deposit in tissue, activate monocytes, and produce inflammation, repair, and eventually fibrosis after recurrent flares. Prognosis and survival vary widely by geographic region, race/ethnicity, and access to care and medications. Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; about 15% have relatively mild disease. Renal disease is a major determinant of outcome: roughly 20% of US patients with class IV lupus nephritis die or develop ESRD within 10 years, and non-White patients more often progress to ESRD. Accelerated atherosclerosis becomes a leading cause of death after about 5 years of disease, with elevated myocardial infarction and stroke rates driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, elevated homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoids contribute to irreversible, dose-dependent organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at low doses; class V nephritis carries a better renal prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2 or more years is associated with significantly less damage, and meta-analyses suggest an increased overall risk of cancer and cancer-related death. Lupus nephritis is graded by the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classes: I (mesangial deposits without hypercellularity), II (mesangial proliferative), III (focal proliferative glomerulonephritis), IV (diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis), and V (membranous), with III/IV +/- V combinations carrying the highest risk; class V (~20% of nephritis) more often presents with nephrotic syndrome but has a better prognosis than III/IV. Disease activity is quantified with the SLEDAI (and SLEDAI-2K), where low disease activity is a score of 0-4 and remission a score of 0 (with stable hydroxychloroquine/immunosuppressive use and prednisone equivalent 5 mg/day or less). Overall disease severity is also stratified clinically as mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6), moderate (rheumatoid-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12), and severe (major organ-threatening disease such as cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Treat-to-target endpoints include LLDAS and DORIS remission, and trials use SRI, BICLA, and CLASI instruments.

Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma) — scleroderma Localized scleroderma (morphea, linear scleroderma, coup de sabre) - generally not complicated by Raynaud's or internal organ involvement (p.2860, 2871) Mixed connective tissue disease and SSc overlap syndromes (with polymyositis, Sjogren's, SLE, polyarthritis, autoimmune liver disease) (p.2860, 2866) Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman's disease) (p.2860) Scleromyxedema (papular mucinosis) and scleredema (Buschke / diabetic) (p.2860) Chronic graft-versus-host disease (p.2860) Primary Raynaud's disease - benign, must be differentiated from early/limited SSc (p.2867, 2871) ANA and SSc-specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere, anti-topoisomerase I/Scl-70, anti-RNA polymerase III, U3-RNP/fibrillarin, Th/To, PM/Scl) for diagnosis and risk stratification (p.2864, 2871) Nailfold capillaroscopy (low-power stereomicroscope or videocapillaroscopy under immersion oil) (p.2867) High-resolution chest CT (HRCT) for ILD detection and prognostic assessment of fibrosis extent (p.2868) Pulmonary function testing including FVC and DLCO for ILD monitoring (a DLCO reduction out of proportion to lung volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease) (p.2868) Doppler echocardiography for PAH screening; right heart (cardiac) catheterization to confirm PAH and exclude venoocclusive/postcapillary causes (p.2868) NT-proBNP correlates with presence/severity of PAH and survival (not specific) (p.2868-2869, 2871) Cardiac MRI / tissue Doppler / SPECT for occult myocardial involvement (p.2871) Blood film for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, platelet count, urinalysis and creatinine in suspected renal crisis (p.2871) Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (associated with gadolinium exposure) (p.2860) Vinyl chloride-induced disease and other chemically/drug-associated scleroderma-like conditions (p.2860) Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (L-tryptophan contaminant) (p.2860) Stiff skin syndrome and pachydermoperiostosis (p.2860) Paraneoplastic scleroderma-like syndrome (p.2860) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic microangiopathy - scleroderma renal crisis is sometimes initially misdiagnosed as TTP (p.2871) Two major subsets: limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) with skin confined to fingers, distal limbs and face (trunk spared) and an indolent course; and diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) with rapidly progressive skin involvement of fingers, extremities, face and trunk (p.2859, 2866). In lcSSc, Raynaud's phenomenon typically precedes sclerodactyly and other manifestations, sometimes by years; the CREST constellation (calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is a distinct lcSSc subset (p.2859). Bilateral symmetrical skin thickening starting in the fingers and advancing distal-to-proximal is the hallmark distinguishing SSc from other connective tissue diseases (p.2867). SSc-specific autoantibodies are mutually exclusive and aid risk stratification: anti-centromere is associated with lcSSc and isolated PAH (renal crisis rare); anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) with dcSSc, extensive skin, early ILD and cardiac involvement; anti-RNA polymerase III with rapidly progressive skin, renal crisis and contemporaneous cancer (p.2864, 2871). Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are detectable in virtually all SSc patients, even in early/preclinical stages (p.2864, 2871). Nailfold capillaroscopy distinguishes primary Raynaud's disease (regular, evenly spaced parallel hairpin loops) from secondary Raynaud's/SSc (giant capillaries, dilated and distorted loops, microhemorrhages, capillary dropout) and helps establish early SSc diagnosis (p.2867, 2871). ILD and pulmonary vascular disease together account for the majority of SSc-related deaths; survival is particularly poor when both coexist (p.2868). Scleroderma renal crisis presents with accelerated hypertension plus acute kidney injury, occurs in <15% of patients almost always within 4 years of onset, and is associated with diffuse/progressive skin involvement and anti-RNA polymerase III (up to 50%); anti-centromere appears protective (p.2870-2871). Palpable tendon friction rubs are associated with increased risk of renal and cardiac complications and reduced survival, and may be a harbinger of impending renal crisis (p.2871). SSc patients should be screened for PAH at initial evaluation and annually thereafter, and screened for ILD with regular pulmonary monitoring for several years after diagnosis (p.2868, 2872). SSc sine scleroderma: characteristic Raynaud's plus typical clinical/serologic features of SSc in the absence of detectable skin thickening (~10% of patients) (p.2859, 2866, 2872). Scleroderma renal crisis: accelerated/new hypertension (generally >150/90 mmHg) with progressive oliguric renal failure - a medical emergency (note ~10% present normotensive, with poorer outcome) (p.2870-2871) Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with fragmented red cells and thrombocytopenia (hallmark of renal crisis) (p.2871) New unexplained anemia, thrombocytopenia, pericardial effusion or new tendon friction rubs as harbingers of impending renal crisis (p.2871) Pulmonary arterial hypertension: exertional dyspnea, near-syncope, loud P2, right heart failure - 3-year survival of untreated PAH <50% (p.2868) Rapidly progressive ILD with declining FVC (can fall ~30%/year), most rapid in the first 3-5 years (p.2868) Critical digital ischemia with fingertip ulceration/necrosis and acro-osteolysis (p.2867) Early dcSSc may present with only upper-extremity edema and puffy fingers and Raynaud's may be absent, leading to misdiagnosis as arthritis, SLE, myositis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease (p.2872) Scleroderma renal crisis can be misdiagnosed as TTP or other thrombotic microangiopathy; renal biopsy and von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity may help (p.2871) Glucocorticoids (especially prednisone >=10 mg/d) are associated with precipitating scleroderma renal crisis and should be used only when essential and at low dose in high-risk patients (p.2870) PFTs and conventional echocardiography are relatively insensitive for early ILD and early cardiac involvement, respectively (p.2868, 2871) Echocardiography can over- or underestimate pulmonary artery pressures, so PAH must be confirmed by cardiac catheterization (p.2868) SSc sine scleroderma can be missed because diagnostic skin induration is absent despite organ involvement (p.2872) SSc is a chronic, often progressive disease of unknown etiology defined pathologically by widespread microangiopathy (fibroproliferative vasculopathy with capillary loss and obliteration) combined with multiorgan fibrosis, on a background of autoimmunity. An initial vascular insult in a genetically predisposed individual (modest HLA class II and immune-regulatory gene associations) triggers inflammation, generation of SSc-specific autoantibodies, and sustained activation of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts driven by mediators such as TGF-beta, IL-6, CTGF, PDGF and endothelin. Maladaptive repair leads to replacement of normal tissue with rigid, avascular, acellular connective tissue affecting skin, lungs, heart, GI tract, kidneys and other organs (p.2859-2866). Highly variable; dcSSc carries a more rapidly progressive course and worse prognosis than lcSSc. SSc confers a fivefold to eightfold higher age/sex-adjusted mortality, with median survival ~11 years; 5- and 10-year survival are ~70%/55% in dcSSc and ~90%/75% in lcSSc. Major causes of death are PAH, pulmonary fibrosis, GI involvement and cardiac disease. Scleroderma renal crisis carries ~30% 3-year mortality (markedly improved by ACE inhibitors). Poor-prognosis markers include male sex, African ancestry, older age at onset, extensive truncal skin involvement, palpable tendon friction rubs, significant/progressive visceral involvement, and laboratory findings of elevated ESR, anemia, proteinuria and anti-topoisomerase I antibodies (p.2873). ACR/EULAR classification criteria are >90% specific and sensitive but are intended for research rather than clinical practice; weighted items include skin thickening proximal to MCP joints (score 9), sclerodactyly/puffy fingers, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, ILD/PAH, Raynaud's phenomenon, and SSc-specific autoantibodies (anti-centromere, Scl-70, RNA polymerase III). Clinically, patients are stratified into limited cutaneous and diffuse cutaneous subsets by extent of skin involvement (p.2860).

destruction or non-healing trophic ulcers indicating advanced sensory loss Overlooking syphilis as a cause of sensory ataxia in the modern era Confusing the picture with B12 deficiency and not sending treponemal serology Failing to test for and address concurrent HIV infection Misattributing lightning pains to a primary painful neuropathy Expecting antibiotics to reverse fixed neurological deficits and neglecting supportive care Chronic infection with Treponema pallidum leads, in the tertiary phase, to inflammatory degeneration of the posterior (dorsal) columns and the dorsal nerve roots and ganglia. Loss of large sensory fibres carrying proprioception and vibration produces sensory ataxia, areflexia, and the characteristic gait, while dorsal root involvement generates the lancinating lightning pains. The associated pupillary and autonomic findings reflect more widespread involvement of the nervous system. The condition is now rare where syphilis is treated early but persists in undertreated populations and those with HIV co-infection. Antibiotic treatment arrests further progression and treats active infection, but long-established dorsal column and root damage often persists, so residual ataxia, pain, and pupillary abnormalities are common; earlier treatment yields better outcomes.

or in large volumes without reassessment between units Confusing TACO with TRALI and withholding beneficial diuresis Overlooking cumulative volume from concurrent intravenous fluids Failing to document and report the reaction, missing prevention opportunities for future transfusions TACO results from an acute increase in intravascular volume that exceeds the recipient's cardiovascular capacity, raising pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure and causing transudation of fluid into the alveoli. Patients with reduced cardiac reserve, renal impairment, or extremes of body size are least able to accommodate the transfused volume, especially when infusion is rapid. Unlike TRALI, the alveolar fluid reflects hydrostatic pressure rather than increased capillary permeability, so the oedema is cardiogenic and responds to volume reduction. Prognosis is generally good when recognised early and treated with volume reduction, oxygen, and diuresis, but delayed recognition can lead to respiratory failure and death, particularly in frail patients with cardiac disease.

stenoses, occlusions, and aneurysms Blood pressure should be measured in the arm with the least affected artery, as readings can be falsely low with subclavian stenosis Corticosteroids are first-line, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants or biologics for relapsing disease, and revascularisation reserved for critical lesions once inflammation is controlled Cerebrovascular symptoms, visual loss, or syncope from carotid or vertebral artery involvement Severe or refractory hypertension from renal artery stenosis with risk of end-organ damage Critical limb or mesenteric ischaemia Aortic aneurysm with risk of dissection or rupture, or significant aortic regurgitation Myocardial ischaemia from coronary ostial involvement Missing the diagnosis in a young woman with nonspecific systemic symptoms before vascular signs appear Relying on a single-arm blood pressure that is falsely low due to subclavian stenosis Assuming normal inflammatory markers exclude active disease Attempting revascularisation during active inflammation with high restenosis risk Overlooking renovascular hypertension as a treatable cause of raised blood pressure Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of unknown cause. Cell-mediated immunity drives infiltration of the arterial wall by T cells, macrophages, and giant cells, beginning in the adventitia and vasa vasorum and extending through the media. Chronic inflammation produces intimal proliferation, medial destruction, and fibrosis, leading to segmental stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm formation, and thrombosis of the aorta and its principal branches. The resulting reduced or absent blood flow causes the ischaemic and 'pulseless' clinical manifestations. With early diagnosis and immunosuppression many patients do well, but relapses are common and progressive vascular damage can cause hypertension, ischaemic complications, and aneurysms. Long-term morbidity relates to arterial stenoses, aortic regurgitation, and cardiovascular events.

Talaromycosis — penicilliosis, Talaromyces marneffei infection, Penicillium marneffei infection Disseminated tuberculosis Disseminated histoplasmosis Cryptococcosis Molluscum contagiosum (for skin lesions) Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection Disseminated tuberculosis Histoplasmosis Cryptococcosis with umbilicated skin lesions Molluscum contagiosum in HIV Fungal culture of blood, skin lesion, bone marrow or lymph node aspirate Microscopy of skin scrapings or tissue for intracellular fission yeasts HIV testing and CD4 count in all suspected cases Antigen-based assays where available for earlier diagnosis Assessment for concurrent opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis An invasive mycosis caused by the dimorphic fungus Talaromyces marneffei, endemic to South-East Asia, southern China and parts of north-eastern India It occurs predominantly in people with advanced HIV and low CD4 counts, and is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection in endemic regions Typical features are fever, weight loss, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and characteristic umbilicated, molluscum-like skin papules often on the face and trunk Exposure to bamboo rats and their habitats is epidemiologically linked, though the precise mode of human acquisition is thought to be inhalational Diagnosis is confirmed by culture from blood, skin, bone marrow or lymph node, with the fungus showing characteristic fission-yeast morphology and a diffusible red pigment in culture It closely mimics disseminated tuberculosis, histoplasmosis and cryptococcosis, so a high index of suspicion is essential in HIV-positive travellers or residents from endemic areas Treatment follows an induction phase with amphotericin-based therapy followed by azole consolidation and, in HIV, secondary prophylaxis until immune reconstitution Disseminated disease with sepsis and multiorgan involvement Advanced HIV with very low CD4 count and high fungal burden Respiratory failure or haemodynamic instability Delayed diagnosis due to mimicry of tuberculosis, which markedly increases mortality Misdiagnosing it as tuberculosis and delaying antifungal therapy Stopping antifungals or secondary prophylaxis prematurely before immune reconstitution Overlooking the diagnosis in HIV patients with relevant travel or residence history Attributing umbilicated skin lesions solely to molluscum contagiosum Talaromyces marneffei is inhaled as conidia that convert to a pathogenic yeast-like form dividing by fission at body temperature. In hosts with intact cell-mediated immunity infection is usually contained, but in advanced HIV or other T-cell deficiency the organism proliferates within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. Haematogenous dissemination follows, seeding skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen and lymph nodes, producing a granulomatous, suppurative or necrotising reaction depending on immune status. Uncontrolled fungaemia leads to sepsis and multiorgan involvement. Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is almost uniformly fatal, but early antifungal induction and consolidation with antiretroviral therapy and secondary prophylaxis achieve good outcomes; mortality remains high when diagnosis is delayed or the patient presents with sepsis.

Cardiac tamponade — Urgent echocardiogram ECG (electrical alternans) Obstructive shock — urgent pericardiocentesis Constrictive pericarditis (also impairs cardiac filling via a thick, noncompliant pericardium; on the differential for dyspnea) (p.1938) Acute right ventricular dysfunction (can mimic the elevated JVP / characteristic jugular waveform pattern) (p.147) Sepsis (can produce a paradoxical-type arterial waveform) (p.1906) Pericardiocentesis under echocardiographic guidance, with pericardial fluid sent for biochemical, cytologic, and microbiologic analysis (p.630, p.1432) Pericardial fluid cytology when malignancy is suspected (diagnostic in most malignant cases; fluid may be serous, serosanguineous, or hemorrhagic) (p.630) Pericardial/epicardial biopsy and pericardioscopy to distinguish neoplastic from benign disease (p.630) Chest CT, CMR, or echocardiography to assess effusion size and pericardial thickness (p.1432, p.1938) In suspected tuberculous etiology, pericardial fluid adenosine deaminase, lysozyme, and IFN-gamma, plus culture/biopsy (fluid is exudative, lymphocyte/monocyte-rich, often hemorrhagic) (p.1432) Massive pulmonary embolism (shares hypotension/tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus) (p.147, p.1906) Tension pneumothorax (life-threatening cause of obstructive shock and pulsus paradoxus) (p.147, p.1906) Hemorrhagic shock (cause of pulsus paradoxus) (p.1906) Severe obstructive lung disease / asthma (cause of pulsus paradoxus) (p.1906) Acute MI with cardiogenic shock (hypotension + tachycardia in chest-pain patient) (p.147) Acute aortic dissection (may extend into the pericardium and itself cause tamponade) (p.147, p.1938) Tamponade is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis in an unstable patient; the textbook triad is hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with neck-vein distention, and quiet/muffled heart sounds (p.630). It is the balance between intrapericardial pressure and ventricular (especially right ventricular) filling pressure that drives compression, not the absolute volume of fluid (p.1938). Rate of accumulation matters more than total volume: slowly forming effusions (e.g. malignant) can become large without classic tamponade physiology, whereas rapid accumulation (e.g. cardiac rupture, perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) can cause tamponade with only a small effusion (p.1938). Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg and represents an exaggerated form of normal interventricular dependence (p.1906). Measure pulsus paradoxus by deflating the cuff slowly and noting the gap between the pressure where Korotkoff sounds are first heard (only in expiration) and the pressure where they are heard with every beat regardless of respiration; a difference >15 mmHg may even be palpable at the brachial or femoral pulse (p.1906). A pulsus paradoxus exceeding 12 mmHg in a patient with a large pericardial effusion is highly predictive of tamponade (reported sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~83%) (p.1910). The ECG triad of sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and total electrical alternans (beat-to-beat P-QRS-T alternation) strongly suggests pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology, though it is insensitive (p.1917). Total electrical alternans (whole-complex) is relatively specific for effusion/tamponade; in contrast, pure repolarization (ST-T/U-wave) alternans signals electrical instability and risk of ventricular arrhythmia, not tamponade (p.1917). Echocardiography is the initial test of choice for suspected effusion/tamponade and can usually be done rapidly at the bedside (p.1938). Hypotension with tachycardia in a chest-pain patient mandates rapid evaluation for tamponade as one of the immediately life-threatening causes (p.147) Life-threatening hemodynamic instability with acute tamponade requires immediate fluid drainage (p.630) Hemorrhagic tamponade from cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, or aortic dissection into the pericardium can be catastrophic at small effusion volumes (p.1938) Do not delay decompression in a hemodynamically unstable patient waiting for confirmatory tests; tamponade is a clinical/emergency diagnosis and instability requires immediate drainage (p.147, p.630). Failing to appreciate the urgency of the situation is a recognized diagnostic error for tamponade (listed among can't-miss time-critical diagnoses) (p.102). Pulsus paradoxus can be hard to measure or unreliable in tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or tachypnea (p.1906). A large slowly-accumulating effusion may lack classic tamponade signs, while a small rapidly-accumulating effusion may already be causing tamponade; judging severity by volume alone is misleading (p.1938). In malignant tamponade, relatively specific signs (paradoxical pulse, diminished heart sounds, pulsus alternans, friction rub) are LESS common than in nonmalignant disease, so their absence does not exclude tamponade (p.630). ECG and chest radiograph are abnormal in ~90% of malignant pericardial cases but about half of those abnormalities are nonspecific (p.630). Pericardial fluid accumulates between the visceral (epicardial) and parietal pericardial layers. Tamponade develops when intrapericardial pressure rises enough to exceed the filling pressures of the cardiac chambers, generally the right ventricle, impairing diastolic filling. Because the relatively non-distensible pericardial sac determines tolerance, the rate of fluid accumulation is more important than absolute volume: slow accumulation allows large effusions without compromise, while rapid accumulation (trauma, cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) causes tamponade at small volumes. Inspiratory augmentation of right-heart filling at the expense of the left, mediated by exaggerated interventricular dependence within the fixed pericardial space, produces pulsus paradoxus (p.1906, p.1938). Outcome depends heavily on cause and timeliness of drainage. Untreated tuberculous pericarditis is usually fatal and even treated TB pericarditis carries case-fatality rates up to ~40% in some series, with risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis. Cancer patients whose pericardial fluid contains malignant cells on cytology have very poor survival. After percutaneous catheter drainage of malignant effusions the recurrence rate is ~20%, and a subset develop paradoxical hemodynamic worsening after drainage (post-drainage low cardiac output syndrome) (p.630, p.1432).

Tarui disease (glycogen storage disease type VII) — glycogen storage disease type VII, GSD VII, muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency, PFK deficiency, PFKM deficiency McArdle disease (GSD V) Other distal glycolytic enzyme defects (e.g. phosphoglycerate kinase or mutase deficiency) Fatty acid oxidation disorders Mitochondrial myopathies Haemolytic anaemias from other causes Exertional rhabdomyolysis of other aetiology Forearm exercise test showing a flat lactate response Full blood count and reticulocyte count for compensated haemolysis Serum uric acid and bilirubin Creatine kinase at rest and after exertion, with urine myoglobin during episodes Molecular genetic testing of the PFKM gene Muscle biopsy with phosphofructokinase enzyme assay Autosomal recessive glycogenosis caused by deficiency of the muscle isoform of phosphofructokinase (PFKM gene), a key regulatory glycolytic enzyme Presents like McArdle disease with exercise intolerance, cramps, and exertional muscle pain, but symptoms are often worse after a carbohydrate-rich meal A carbohydrate load does not improve and may worsen exertional symptoms (the 'out of wind' effect), unlike the fuel benefit seen in some other glycogenoses Because the enzyme is also partially deficient in red cells, a compensated haemolytic anaemia with reticulocytosis and hyperuricaemia frequently coexists The forearm exercise test shows a flat lactate response, similar to McArdle disease Exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria can occur, and some patients develop gout from the associated hyperuricaemia Management is supportive with avoidance of intense exertion and, in contrast to some other glycogenoses, avoidance of high-carbohydrate pre-exercise loading Severe exertional rhabdomyolysis with pigmenturia and risk of acute kidney injury Symptomatic anaemia or marked reticulocytosis Gout or urate nephropathy from hyperuricaemia Advising carbohydrate loading before exercise, which can worsen symptoms in this glycogenosis Confusing it with McArdle disease and missing the associated haemolysis and hyperuricaemia Overlooking gout or urate nephropathy as a complication Failing to counsel about rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury risk during strenuous activity Tarui disease is caused by deficiency of the muscle subunit of phosphofructokinase, which catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, a committed and rate-limiting step of glycolysis. The block prevents muscle from using both stored glycogen and blood glucose for anaerobic energy production, so exercise capacity is limited and lactate fails to rise with exertion. Because ingested glucose cannot be utilised and instead suppresses the alternative free-fatty-acid fuel supply, a carbohydrate meal can paradoxically worsen exercise tolerance. The muscle-type PFK subunit is also expressed in erythrocytes, so its deficiency reduces red-cell glycolysis and causes a compensated haemolysis, with increased purine turnover contributing to hyperuricaemia. Most patients have a normal life expectancy with lifestyle adaptation, though exercise capacity is limited; recurrent rhabdomyolysis, complications of haemolysis, and gout are the main long-term concerns, and rare infantile-onset forms carry a poorer prognosis.

Tay-Sachs disease — hexosaminidase A deficiency, GM2 gangliosidosis type 1, beta-hexosaminidase A deficiency Sandhoff disease GM1 gangliosidosis Niemann-Pick disease Other causes of infantile neurodegeneration with cherry-red spot Leukodystrophies presenting with developmental regression Assay of hexosaminidase A activity in serum or leukocytes HEXA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and enable carrier detection Ophthalmological examination for the macular cherry-red spot Neuroimaging to characterise neurodegeneration and exclude alternatives Carrier screening and prenatal or preimplantation testing for at-risk families An autosomal recessive GM2 gangliosidosis caused by deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A due to pathogenic variants in the HEXA gene Carrier frequency is increased in the Ashkenazi Jewish population, making targeted carrier screening and prenatal diagnosis important The classic infantile form presents around 3 to 6 months with loss of milestones, hypotonia progressing to spasticity, and an exaggerated startle response to sound A cherry-red spot at the macula is a hallmark ophthalmological finding Unlike many storage disorders, there is characteristically no hepatosplenomegaly, which helps distinguish it clinically Progressive macrocephaly, seizures, blindness, and neurodegeneration follow, with death usually in early childhood Juvenile and late-onset variants exist and can present with slower motor and psychiatric or cerebellar symptoms No disease-modifying therapy is established, so management is supportive and genetic counselling is central Rapid developmental regression with exaggerated startle in an infant Emerging seizures or loss of vision Progressive swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk Family history in an at-risk population without prior carrier screening Overlooking the diagnosis because hepatosplenomegaly is absent Failing to distinguish it from Sandhoff disease, which additionally involves visceral storage Not offering carrier screening to at-risk populations before conception Attributing the exaggerated startle to a benign cause and delaying evaluation Tay-Sachs disease results from biallelic pathogenic variants in HEXA, which encodes the alpha subunit of the enzyme beta-hexosaminidase A. Deficient enzyme activity prevents degradation of GM2 ganglioside, which accumulates progressively within neuronal lysosomes of the central nervous system. Neuronal engorgement and dysfunction drive relentless neurodegeneration. Because storage is largely confined to neurons, visceral organomegaly is typically absent, distinguishing it from disorders such as Sandhoff disease, in which both hexosaminidase A and B are deficient. The infantile form is progressive and fatal, typically within the first few years of life. Juvenile-onset disease progresses more slowly with death in later childhood or adolescence, while late-onset forms have a more variable and protracted course. Management remains supportive.

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis — ESR / CRP (markedly raised) Temporal artery biopsy Start high-dose steroids if suspected Visual loss is an emergency — do not delay steroids Migraine - common in the elderly (more prevalent than GCA) and may improve with prednisone, so a steroid response does not by itself confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy - associated with a crowded 'disc-at-risk' / small optic cup, in which glucocorticoids should NOT be prescribed, contrasting with the arteritic form (Harrison 22e p.227). Isolated polymyalgia rheumatica without arteritis (Harrison 22e p.2903). Other inflammatory causes of secondary headache such as sarcoidosis and Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.115). Temporal artery biopsy: yield improved by harvesting a long segment (3-5 cm) with serial sectioning because involvement is segmental/patchy; biopsy may still show vasculitis even after about 14 days of glucocorticoids, but prolonged treatment can mask findings (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903). Temporal artery ultrasonography (alone or with axillary arteries) showing a noncompressible 'halo' sign supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2903). Large-vessel imaging by MR or CT angiography to confirm large-vessel disease suggested by diminished pulses or bruits; PET is increasingly studied but its diagnostic/monitoring role remains unclear (Harrison 22e p.2903). Note: in patients treated with an IL-6 inhibitor, CRP and ESR normalize and can no longer be used to monitor disease activity or assess for infection (Harrison 22e p.2902). Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathy mimicking the peripheral arthritis of PMR (Harrison 22e p.2903). Occurs almost exclusively in people over 50; mean age of onset around 70, with women making up roughly two-thirds of cases. Rare in Black patients; higher incidence in Scandinavian populations (Harrison 22e p.115, p.2902). Four phenotypic patterns can occur together, in isolation, or at different times: cranial arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, large-vessel disease, and systemic inflammation (Harrison 22e p.2902). Headache is the dominant cranial symptom; it is usually dull/boring rather than throbbing, may be unilateral or bilateral, is temporally located in only about half of patients, often worse at night, and aggravated by cold (Harrison 22e p.115). Scalp tenderness can be marked - brushing hair or resting the head on a pillow may be intolerable; the temporal (or less often occipital) artery may be tender, thickened, nodular, reddened or have overlying red skin streaks (Harrison 22e p.115). The temporal artery may pulsate early in disease but can become occluded later (Harrison 22e p.2902). Jaw and tongue claudication and scalp pain are recognized cranial-ischemic features; rarer cranial ischemic events include stroke and scalp or tongue infarction (Harrison 22e p.115, p.2902). ESR and/or CRP are elevated in most patients, but a normal ESR does NOT exclude giant cell arteritis (Harrison 22e p.115). Other supportive labs: normochromic or slightly hypochromic anemia, raised alkaline phosphatase (liver function abnormalities common), and increased IgG and complement (Harrison 22e p.2902). Most patients report head or eye complaints before any visual loss, so attention to early cranial symptoms with prompt therapy reduces the risk of blindness (Harrison 22e p.2902). Polymyalgia rheumatica overlaps strongly: PMR is seen in 40-50% of GCA patients, and 10-20% who present with isolated PMR later develop GCA - GCA and PMR are regarded as a spectrum of one disease process (Harrison 22e p.2902). In PMR, creatine kinase is not elevated and rheumatoid factor / anti-CCP should be negative; a worsening peripheral arthritis pattern should prompt reconsideration of seronegative RA or other inflammatory arthropathy (Harrison 22e p.2903). Ischemic optic neuropathy is the dreaded complication; about half of untreated patients develop blindness from ophthalmic-artery involvement, and arteritic AION is the leading cause of rapidly developing bilateral blindness in patients over 60 (Harrison 22e p.115). In suspected arteritic AION / visual loss, start glucocorticoids IMMEDIATELY without waiting for biopsy to protect vision in the fellow eye - a sight-saving principle; do not delay therapy pending diagnostic studies (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903). Sudden visual loss / blindness can be the presenting or emergent feature (Harrison 22e p.2902). Aortic aneurysm: GCA patients are 18 times more likely than the general population to develop thoracic aortic aneurysms, carrying risk of rupture or dissection (Harrison 22e p.2903). Subclavian stenosis presenting as arm claudication signals large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2902). A normal ESR does not rule out GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). A single negative temporal artery biopsy does not exclude the disease because lesions are segmental/patchy - take a long segment and serial sections (Harrison 22e p.2903). Improvement of headache on prednisone is non-specific (migraine also responds), so do not use the steroid response alone to confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). Once an IL-6 inhibitor is started, ESR/CRP can no longer track activity or flag infection (Harrison 22e p.2902). Minor ESR/CRP rises during tapering may reflect other causes (including infection) rather than a true flare, especially in a symptom-free patient (Harrison 22e p.2903). Glucocorticoids should not be given for the nonarteritic form of AION - distinguishing arteritic from nonarteritic AION matters (Harrison 22e p.227). A panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically branches of the carotid (especially the temporal artery) but systemically involving the aorta and its branches. Histology shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall with frequent giant cell formation, intimal proliferation, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina; organ damage results from ischemia of involved vessels. It is considered an antigen-driven process: CD4+ T cells enter via the adventitial vasa vasorum, become activated, and drive macrophage differentiation, with restricted clonal T-cell expansion suggesting an arterial-wall antigen. Lesional T cells produce mainly IL-2 and IFN-gamma; both IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17 lineages contribute and may differ in glucocorticoid responsiveness. Associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04 variants. (Harrison 22e p.2902) Acute mortality directly from GCA is uncommon; when fatal it is usually due to cerebrovascular events or myocardial infarction. The main late mortality risk is rupture or dissection of an aortic aneurysm (18-fold increased thoracic aortic aneurysm risk). Disease is highly glucocorticoid-responsive but relapsing: symptom recurrence during steroid tapering occurs in 60-85% of patients, most require at least 2 years of treatment, and glucocorticoid toxicity affects 35-65% and is a major source of morbidity. (Harrison 22e p.2903)

Tennis elbow — lateral epicondylitis, lateral epicondylalgia, lateral elbow tendinopathy, common extensor origin tendinopathy Radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve entrapment) Radiocapitellar osteoarthritis or a plica Cervical radiculopathy referring pain to the lateral forearm Posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow Referred pain from the shoulder or myofascial trigger points Usually a clinical diagnosis requiring no imaging Ultrasound can confirm tendon thickening, hypoechoic change, or tears and guide injection when the diagnosis is unclear MRI in atypical or refractory cases to characterise the tendon and exclude intra-articular pathology Plain radiographs if bony pathology or calcification is suspected Nerve conduction studies if radial tunnel syndrome or radiculopathy is considered Pain is centred over the lateral epicondyle and the origin of the common wrist extensors, often radiating down the back of the forearm Symptoms are provoked by gripping, lifting with the palm down, and resisted wrist or middle-finger extension Despite the older term epicondylitis, the underlying process is a degenerative tendinopathy rather than acute inflammation It most commonly affects the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin and peaks in middle age, frequently in people doing repetitive forearm work rather than tennis players Diagnosis is clinical; local tenderness just distal to the epicondyle with pain on resisted extension is characteristic First-line management is activity modification, load reduction, and a progressive eccentric or graded strengthening programme, which addresses the underlying tendon problem Counterforce bracing and attention to technique and equipment can offload the tendon during aggravating activities Corticosteroid injection may give short-term relief but is associated with poorer long-term outcomes and higher recurrence than exercise-based rehabilitation Most cases are self-limiting over months to a couple of years, and surgery is reserved for the small minority with refractory symptoms Night pain, systemic symptoms, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour rather than tendinopathy Neurological symptoms pointing to nerve entrapment or cervical radiculopathy History of significant trauma raising the possibility of instability or fracture Failure to improve despite appropriate rehabilitation, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Assuming an inflammatory process and relying on rest and anti-inflammatories rather than progressive loading Repeated corticosteroid injections, which can worsen the tendon and long-term prognosis Overlooking radial tunnel syndrome or cervical radiculopathy in atypical or persistent cases Neglecting kinetic-chain, technique, and workplace factors that perpetuate overload Tennis elbow is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle, most often involving extensor carpi radialis brevis. Repetitive gripping and wrist extension produce microtears and a failed healing response, with angiofibroblastic (mucoid) degeneration, disorganised collagen, and neovascularisation rather than true inflammatory change. The weakened tendon becomes painful and mechanically vulnerable to further load. The natural history is generally favourable, with most patients recovering within a year regardless of specific treatment, though symptoms can persist or recur; structured loading rehabilitation improves long-term outcomes compared with steroid injection.

Tension-type headache — Clinical diagnosis Atypical features warrant imaging Migraine (the main differential, defined by migrainous accompaniments TTH lacks) (Harrison 22e p.3514) Migraine-TTH overlap / mixed phenotype with intercurrent migraine attacks (Harrison 22e p.3514) TTH is a clinical diagnosis; neuroimaging is not routine but CT or MRI of the brain is indicated when the examination is abnormal or the headache is recent-onset, with CT and MRI being comparably sensitive as initial screens (Harrison 22e p.157). Lumbar puncture may be required when a serious secondary cause is suspected and a benign etiology cannot otherwise be established (Harrison 22e p.157). General evaluation of acute headache may add palpation of cranial arteries, cervical spine assessment, blood pressure and urine for cardiovascular/renal status, and ocular examination including funduscopy and intraocular pressure (Harrison 22e p.157). Chronic migraine within the chronic daily headache spectrum (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3) Medication-overuse headache (refractory daily/near-daily headache from analgesic overuse) (Harrison 22e p.158-159) Other secondary causes of chronic daily headache: post-traumatic, inflammatory (e.g., giant cell arteritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet syndrome), and chronic CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3) TTH is recognized as bilateral, tight, band-like discomfort that builds gradually, fluctuates in intensity, and can persist near-continuously for days (Harrison 22e p.3514). The most reliable bedside approach is to reserve the TTH label for headaches entirely lacking accompanying features such as nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing quality, or worsening with movement (Harrison 22e p.3514). Migraine is the principal differential of TTH; the presence of any migrainous accompaniment points away from TTH and toward migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514). Patients who fit the TTH phenotype but also have migraine at other times, a family history of migraine, childhood migrainous syndromes, or typical migraine triggers may be biologically distinct from those with pure featureless TTH (Harrison 22e p.3514). Diagnostic boundaries are genuinely blurred: the International Headache Society main definition permits some nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia, whereas the stricter appendix definition does not, and Harrison favors the appendix (feature-free) definition to separate TTH from migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514). Among primary-care patients with headache lasting 3 months or more and no neurologic symptoms or signs, fewer than 10% actually have TTH and more than 90% have migraine, so a confident TTH label in this setting is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.3514). TTH is the most prevalent primary headache type overall, accounting for roughly 69% of primary headaches in a population series (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-1). Sudden-onset or first severe headache, or the 'worst headache ever' (Harrison 22e p.156-157, Table 17-2) Vomiting preceding the headache (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Subacute worsening over days or weeks (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Pain provoked by bending, lifting, or coughing (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Pain that disturbs sleep or is present immediately on awakening (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Onset after age 55 (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Fever or unexplained systemic signs, or a known systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Abnormal neurologic examination (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Local tenderness, e.g., over the temporal artery region (Harrison 22e p.156, Table 17-2) Serious secondary causes to consider with new severe headache include meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, epidural/subdural hematoma, glaucoma, tumor, and purulent sinusitis (Harrison 22e p.157) Over-applying the TTH label: in chronic headache without neurologic signs, more than 90% of patients actually have migraine, so TTH is frequently overdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.3514). Assuming muscle contraction confirms TTH; it does NOT distinguish TTH from migraine (Harrison 22e p.3514). Overlooking medication overuse, which can convert episodic headache into refractory daily/near-daily headache and blunt the effect of preventive treatment (Harrison 22e p.158-159). Mistaking a serious secondary headache for benign primary headache when an underlying cause has activated or worsened the primary syndrome (Harrison 22e p.158). The mechanism of TTH is incompletely understood. Harrison favors a primary disorder of central nervous system pain modulation alone, contrasting it with migraine, which involves more generalized disturbance of sensory modulation. Despite the name, there is no clear evidence that nervous tension is causative; importantly, muscle contraction does NOT reliably distinguish TTH from migraine, as no difference in contraction is seen between the two headache types. A genetic contribution has been suggested but is unreliable, since current diagnostic criteria likely contaminated those studies with migraine patients (Harrison 22e p.3514). TTH is classified as episodic when infrequent and chronic when occurring on 15 or more days per month; the pain fluctuates and may persist near-continuously for many days. Chronic TTH falls within the chronic daily headache group, which carries considerable disability, and may be complicated by medication overuse (Harrison 22e p.3514, p.158). Pain is characteristically mild to moderate, bilateral, tight and band-like, and non-throbbing. By frequency the IHS scheme distinguishes infrequent episodic, frequent episodic, chronic (>=15 days/month), and probable TTH; Harrison emphasizes the episodic-versus-chronic distinction (Harrison 22e p.3514, p.155 IHS classification).
