Neisseria species are unusually dependent on this direct complement-mediated bacteriolysis for their clearance. When any terminal component is genetically deficient, the classical, lectin and alternative pathways can still opsonise but cannot complete lytic killing, so the host is left disproportionately vulnerable to Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Because early complement functions such as opsonisation and immune-complex handling are preserved, patients typically do not have the encapsulated-organism infection pattern or autoimmune features seen with early classical pathway defects. Individual invasive episodes tend to be less fulminant than in complement-sufficient patients, but the lifelong risk of recurrent neisserial infection persists, and outcome depends heavily on vaccination, patient education, and rapid treatment of febrile illness.

Testicular Cancer — Testicular germ cell tumor, Testicular GCT, Germ cell tumor of the testis Epididymitis Orchitis Testicular atrophy Hereditary persistence of AFP or hepatic disease (false AFP elevation) Non-germ-cell testicular tumors Epididymitis (a trial of antibacterials may be considered, but failure to respond should prompt scrotal ultrasound) Orchitis Scrotal ultrasound of both testicles (GCT typically hypoechoic, possibly multifocal) Serum AFP, hCG, and LDH before and after orchiectomy CT scan of abdomen and pelvis for staging Chest x-ray, with chest CT if retroperitoneal disease or lung nodules are present Pathologic review of the entire orchiectomy specimen by an experienced pathologist Serum microRNA miR-371a-3p (a promising investigational biomarker undergoing validation) Testicular atrophy Hereditary persistence of AFP (mildly elevated baseline AFP) Hepatic disease causing false AFP elevation False hCG elevation from hypogonadism, marijuana use, or assay interference Germ cell tumors (GCTs) account for about 95% of all testicular neoplasms; non-GCTs of the testis are much less common, and roughly 5% of GCTs arise in extragonadal sites such as the mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and pineal gland. Testicular cancer is regarded as a model curable neoplasm: about 95% of newly diagnosed patients are cured, and treatment is dictated by pathology (seminoma vs nonseminoma) and stage. It is the most common malignancy in adolescent and young adult males (age 15-39), most often diagnosed in Caucasians and much less common in African Americans; incidence in those over 50 is rising. Strongest risk factors are a prior history of GCT, cryptorchidism, and germ cell neoplasia in situ; a prior GCT carries a 1-2% risk of a contralateral tumor (usually metachronous), and cryptorchidism raises risk roughly four- to sixfold. Orchidopexy before puberty reduces but does not eliminate the cryptorchidism-associated risk, and the contralateral normally descended testis also remains at risk. A solid mass on scrotal ultrasound (typically hypoechoic, sometimes multifocal) must be considered malignant until proven otherwise; transscrotal aspiration or biopsy must never be performed because it risks seeding the scrotum or inguinal nodes. Tumor marker biology is key: seminomas never secrete AFP, so a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP is managed as a nonseminomatous GCT; hCG can be elevated in both seminoma and nonseminoma, and choriocarcinoma may produce markedly high hCG. Serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH) should be measured before and after orchiectomy; AFP is elevated in roughly 60-70% of nonseminomatous GCTs, while most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation. Lymphatic spread follows a predictable pattern: left-sided tumors drain first to left paraaortic nodes below the left renal vessels, right-sided tumors to aortocaval nodes below the right renal vessels, then to retrocrural, mediastinal, and supraclavicular nodes; the lung is the most common hematogenous site. Genetically, most GCTs show excess copies of isochromosome 12p (i[12p]); the strongest heritable-risk locus identified is KITLG (KIT ligand) on chromosome 12, and overall heritability is nearly 50%. Teratoma is chemotherapy-resistant and must be managed surgically; the other nonseminomatous subtypes (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma) and seminomas are chemosensitive. Sperm banking should be offered before chemotherapy: about 30% of newly diagnosed patients already have severe oligospermia or azoospermia, and treatment-related sterility is common (though ~80% recover spermatogenesis over years). Painless testicular mass (pathognomonic of GCT) or testicular swelling, firmness, or discomfort Back or flank pain suggesting retroperitoneal metastases Cough, dyspnea, or hemoptysis indicating lung metastases Gynecomastia in the setting of elevated hCG Suspected epididymitis/orchitis that fails to respond to antibiotics Rapidly progressive disease with life-threatening symptoms (e.g., hemoptysis) warranting emergent treatment even without tissue diagnosis Performing transscrotal biopsy or aspiration of a testicular mass, which can seed the scrotum or inguinal nodes and should never be done. Misclassifying a histologic seminoma with elevated AFP as a true seminoma, when it must be approached as a nonseminomatous GCT. Over-relying on tumor markers for diagnosis, since most seminomas and up to a third of nonseminomas have no marker elevation. Diagnostic delay (not uncommon) leading to more advanced stage at presentation, including mislabeling a GCT as epididymitis/orchitis. Assuming residual postchemotherapy masses are benign: imaging cannot distinguish necrosis/fibrosis from teratoma or viable tumor, and enlarging cystic retroperitoneal masses with normalized markers may represent growing teratoma syndrome. Forgetting that LDH is a nonspecific marker whose main role is risk classification in metastatic disease, not diagnosis. GCTs originate from the primordial germ cell, and most malignant GCTs arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ; the precise molecular steps driving progression from in situ neoplasia to invasive tumor are not fully defined. Genetic analysis shows excess copy number of isochromosome 12p in most cases, and genome-wide studies implicate several loci, most strongly KITLG on chromosome 12. Tumors are classified as seminoma (must be 100% seminoma; any mixed tumor is treated as nonseminomatous) or nonseminoma. Seminomas may contain syncytiotrophoblastic cells that secrete hCG but never secrete AFP. Nonseminomatous subtypes include embryonal carcinoma (the most undifferentiated, able to differentiate into the others, and may secrete AFP and/or hCG), yolk sac tumor (often AFP-secreting), choriocarcinoma (aggressive, often very high hCG), and teratoma (mature, immature, or malignant somatic tissue derived from two or more germ layers). Outcomes are excellent overall, with about 95% of newly diagnosed patients cured. Nearly all stage I patients (seminoma and nonseminoma) achieve cure. In metastatic (stage III) disease classified by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification, most patients have good-risk disease with >90% cure; intermediate- and poor-risk groups have approximately 80% and 50% five-year survival, respectively. About 20-30% of patients with metastatic GCT treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy do not achieve durable control, with most relapses occurring within 2 years of completing treatment. Three main AJCC TNM-based stages: Stage I limited to the testis; Stage II involving retroperitoneal lymph nodes (subgrouped IIA/IIB/IIC by node size: <=2 cm, >2-5 cm, >5 cm); Stage III with lymph node involvement beyond the retroperitoneum and/or distant metastases. Stage III is further stratified into good-, intermediate-, and poor-risk groups by the International Germ Cell Consensus Classification using histology, primary site, presence of nonpulmonary visceral metastases, and postorchiectomy marker levels (e.g., for NSGCT good-risk: AFP <1000 ng/mL, hCG <5000 mIU/mL, LDH <1.5x ULN; poor-risk: AFP >10,000 ng/mL, hCG >50,000 mIU/mL, LDH >10x ULN, mediastinal primary, or nonpulmonary visceral metastases). Marker half-lives: AFP 5-7 days, hCG 24-36 hours.

salvage depends on detorsion within roughly six hours, so exploration must not be delayed for investigations Sudden severe scrotal pain with a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex until proven otherwise Neonatal torsion, which may present with a firm, discoloured, painless scrotal swelling Progressive testicular ischaemia leading to non-viable testis and need for orchidectomy Attributing acute scrotal pain to epididymo-orchitis and delaying surgical exploration Waiting for or relying on ultrasound when clinical suspicion is high Assuming a normal Doppler study excludes torsion, especially in intermittent or partial torsion Failing to fix the contralateral testis, leaving it at risk of subsequent torsion Dismissing intermittent testicular pain that may represent recurrent torsion-detorsion Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that obstructs venous drainage first and then arterial inflow, producing ischaemia and, if unrelieved, haemorrhagic infarction of the testis. The intravaginal form, most common in adolescents, is facilitated by the bell-clapper deformity where the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis and epididymis completely, allowing the testis to rotate freely within it. Extravaginal torsion occurs in neonates when the entire tunica and its contents twist above the level of attachment. The degree of twisting and the duration of ischaemia determine the likelihood of viability. Testicular viability depends critically on time to detorsion, with excellent salvage within a few hours and progressively poorer outcomes beyond six to twelve hours; a non-viable testis requires orchidectomy, and infarction may later affect fertility.

Wound culture of C. tetani cannot confirm the diagnosis (a positive culture is non-confirmatory). Serum antitetanus IgG measured before antitoxin/immunoglobulin administration: levels >0.1 IU/mL (standard ELISA) are deemed protective and argue against tetanus. Serum tetanus toxin bioassay may help if antibody is below the protective threshold, but a negative result does not exclude tetanus and the assay is not generally performed. PCR and recombinase polymerase amplification to detect the tetanus neurotoxin gene are promising but emerging techniques. Strychnine poisoning Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Dystonic reaction to antidopaminergic drugs Stiff person syndrome Somatic symptom disorder Hypocalcemia Intracranial hemorrhage Trismus (lockjaw) is typically the earliest symptom, progressing to neck and trunk rigidity, dysphagia, and pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm; risus sardonicus and opisthotonos reflect the characteristic sustained muscle rigidity. Generalized tetanus is the most common form, characterized by muscle rigidity with generalized spasms; localized tetanus affects only isolated muscle groups but can progress to the generalized form. Cephalic tetanus is a localized form involving the cranial nerves, which can cause pharyngeal or laryngeal spasm leading to aspiration, airway obstruction, or respiratory failure. Neonatal tetanus classically presents with loss of the ability to suck and cry (a newborn normal in the first 2 days who deteriorates between days 3 and 28), poor feeding, rigidity, and generalized spasms. Laryngeal spasm causing apnea or respiratory failure is a life-threatening event and, without immediate respiratory support, is the most common cause of death. Autonomic nervous system disturbance characteristically emerges in the second week of severe disease, with fluctuating heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, gastrointestinal stasis, and increased tracheal secretions; cardiovascular events then become the major threat. Disease severity is graded with the Ablett classification (Grades I-IV), where Grade IV is Grade III plus autonomic dysfunction. Abdominal rigidity in tetanus is characteristically continuous, distinguishing it from the rigidity of peritonitis or an acute abdomen. Roughly 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry wound; superficial limb abrasions are the most common portal of entry in adults, while deeper injuries (open fractures, drug injection) are linked to more severe disease. Natural infection does not confer protective immunity because tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course. Laryngeal spasm with apnea or respiratory failure - life-threatening and the most common cause of death. Autonomic nervous system disturbance (labile heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, GI stasis, increased tracheal secretions), typically in the second week, marking high cardiovascular mortality risk. Short incubation period (wound to first symptom) and short period of onset (first symptom to first generalized/pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm) - rapid progression predicts worse outcome. Dysphagia with laryngeal hyperactivity, which makes airway management difficult and raises aspiration risk. Diagnosis is clinical - waiting for laboratory confirmation is misguided; a positive wound culture does not confirm and a protective antitetanus IgG (>0.1 IU/mL) argues against the diagnosis. Treatment should not be delayed once tetanus is clinically diagnosed. Assuming natural infection confers immunity: tetanus toxin is poorly immunogenic, so survivors still require a full primary immunization course. Overlooking absence of a wound: about 20-30% of cases have no identifiable entry site, so a negative wound history does not exclude tetanus. Failure to identify and debride the entry wound (to remove anaerobic foci) can lead to recurrent or prolonged disease. Long-term ICU care with deep sedation predisposes to hospital-acquired infections (ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream and urinary tract infection, sepsis), venous thromboembolism, and other complications - prognosis depends on controlling these. Tetanus is caused by tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, gram-positive, spore-forming rod whose resilient environmental spores enter through wounds, abrasions, or the umbilical stump and germinate in anaerobic tissue. Only toxin-producing organisms cause disease. The toxin is a 150-kDa protein cleaved into a heavy (100-kDa) and light (50-kDa) chain joined by a disulfide bond; the heavy-chain carboxy terminal binds presynaptic motor nerve terminals, leading to internalization and retrograde intra-axonal transport to motor nuclei of cranial nerves and spinal cord ventral horns. The toxin then crosses the synapse into GABA-ergic presynaptic inhibitory interneurons, where the light chain (a zinc-dependent endopeptidase) cleaves VAMP2 (synaptobrevin), blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release. Loss of inhibition produces unregulated motor activity (muscle rigidity and spasms), and similar disinhibition in the autonomic system produces autonomic instability; elevated circulating catecholamines in severe disease drive cardiovascular complications. Tetanus has a high survival rate when complications are controlled and interventions are prompt, though recovery is prolonged, typically taking about 4-6 weeks. Rapid onset predicts more severe disease: the shorter the incubation period (wound to first symptom) and the period of onset (first symptom to first generalized or pharyngeal/laryngeal spasm), the worse the prognosis. The Tetanus Severity Score (TSS) outperforms the Dakar and Philips scores for predicting severity and outcome (sensitivity ~66%, specificity ~91%; a cutoff score of >=8 predicts death). Surviving adults, especially the elderly, may have reduced long-term functional outcomes, while affected children and neonates have a higher incidence of neurologic sequelae (neonates may face increased risk of learning disabilities, behavioral problems, cerebral palsy, and deafness). Ablett classification of tetanus severity: Grade I (mild) - mild trismus, general spasticity, no respiratory compromise, no spasms, no dysphagia; Grade II (moderate) - moderate trismus and rigidity, short spasms, mild dysphagia, moderate respiratory involvement, respiratory rate >30/min; Grade III (severe) - severe trismus, generalized rigidity, prolonged spasms, severe dysphagia, apneic spells, pulse >120/min, respiratory rate >40/min; Grade IV (very severe) - Grade III features plus autonomic dysfunction. Prognostic scoring is provided by the Tetanus Severity Score (TSS), which is superior to the Dakar and Philips scores.

Tetralogy of Fallot — TOF, ToF Transposition of the great arteries Tricuspid atresia Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect Truncus arteriosus Severe isolated pulmonary stenosis Double-outlet right ventricle Echocardiography to define the outflow tract, septal defect, aortic override, and pulmonary artery anatomy Chest radiograph looking for a boot-shaped heart and pulmonary vascularity Electrocardiogram showing right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy Pulse oximetry and, in spells, assessment of acidosis Cardiac catheterisation or CT/MR angiography when coronary or pulmonary artery anatomy is unclear Genetic evaluation for 22q11.2 deletion when associated features are present The most common cyanotic congenital heart lesion beyond infancy, comprising four features: a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy. The degree of cyanosis reflects the severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction; some infants are minimally cyanotic (so-called pink Fallot) while others present with marked desaturation. A harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border arises from the outflow obstruction, not from the septal defect itself; the murmur softens during a hypercyanotic spell as flow across the outflow tract falls. Hypercyanotic (tet) spells are episodes of sudden, worsening cyanosis with agitation and deep breathing, often on waking or after feeding or crying, and can be life-threatening. Calming manoeuvres for a spell aim to increase systemic vascular resistance and outflow through the lungs: comforting the child, bringing the knees to the chest, and giving oxygen, with pharmacological support as needed. The chest radiograph classically shows a boot-shaped heart with a concave main pulmonary artery segment and normal or reduced pulmonary vascularity. Echocardiography confirms the anatomy and defines the outflow tract, pulmonary arteries, and coronary artery course before surgery. Older, unrepaired children may adopt squatting to relieve exertional cyanosis by transiently raising systemic resistance and pulmonary blood flow. Complete surgical repair, involving closure of the septal defect and relief of outflow obstruction, is the definitive treatment and is usually performed in infancy. Hypercyanotic (tet) spell with deepening cyanosis, agitation, and a disappearing murmur Loss of consciousness, seizures, or limpness during a spell Duct-dependent presentation with severe outflow obstruction and cardiovascular collapse as the ductus closes Profound or worsening hypoxaemia unresponsive to calming measures Metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate pulmonary blood flow Interpreting a softening or absent murmur reassuringly when it actually signals a severe hypercyanotic spell Aggressively sedating or agitating an infant in a spell rather than using calming, resistance-raising manoeuvres Overlooking a duct-dependent lesion in a neonate whose cyanosis worsens as the ductus arteriosus closes Attributing exertional symptoms or squatting in an older child to behaviour rather than underlying cyanotic heart disease Failing to screen for associated 22q11.2 deletion and other anomalies Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum during development produces right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, a malaligned ventricular septal defect, and an aorta that overrides the defect. Obstruction to pulmonary outflow, combined with the large communication between the ventricles, allows deoxygenated right ventricular blood to shunt right-to-left into the aorta, producing systemic desaturation. The volume of pulmonary blood flow and the resulting cyanosis depend dynamically on the balance between the fixed and dynamic outflow obstruction and systemic vascular resistance; a fall in systemic resistance or a spasm of the infundibulum increases right-to-left shunting and precipitates a hypercyanotic spell. With timely complete surgical repair the long-term outlook is generally good, though survivors need lifelong cardiology follow-up for pulmonary regurgitation, residual outflow obstruction, arrhythmia, and possible need for pulmonary valve replacement. Untreated disease carries high morbidity and mortality from progressive cyanosis, spells, and complications.

achondroplasia or homozygous achondroplasia without molecular confirmation Underestimating the lethality and delaying appropriate counselling and palliative planning Missing the distinction between type I and type II femoral and skull morphology Failing to offer autopsy and genetic counselling to inform recurrence risk Thanatophoric dysplasia is caused by strongly activating variants in FGFR3. The resulting profound constitutive receptor signalling severely disrupts growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, producing extreme limb shortening and a markedly hypoplastic thoracic cage. The small thorax restricts lung development, and the consequent pulmonary hypoplasia is the usual cause of neonatal death. The same signalling excess also affects cortical brain development in some cases, contributing to the cloverleaf skull and neurological abnormalities seen particularly in type II. Thanatophoric dysplasia is almost universally lethal in the perinatal period, with most affected infants dying shortly after birth from respiratory failure. Rare survivors with intensive respiratory support have severe disability and profound growth restriction.

vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, exercise, atropine, isoproterenol - to localize the level of block Invasive electrophysiologic study with His bundle electrogram (AH and HV interval measurement) in syncope with suspected high-grade or infranodal block Evaluation for ischemia when clinical suspicion is present Senile degenerative fibrosis/calcification of the conduction system (Lev disease) Lenegre disease (sclerodegenerative distal bundle branch disease in younger patients) Aortic (and less commonly mitral) valve annular calcification encroaching on the conduction system Cardiac sarcoidosis and amyloidosis Autoimmune/rheumatologic disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, mixed connective tissue disease, scleroderma) Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy, Kearns-Sayre syndrome, muscular dystrophies) Iatrogenic injury (valve/cardiac surgery, TAVR, septal myectomy/alcohol septal ablation, catheter ablation) Hereditary progressive familial heart block (e.g., SCN5A mutations) and lamin A/C cardiomyopathy The AV node is specialized for slow conduction, creating a delay between atrial and ventricular activation and acting as the electrical gatekeeper to the ventricle; its intrinsic backup pacemaker (escape) rate is roughly 20-60 beats/min, normally overridden by the faster sinus node (60-100 beats/min). First-degree AV block means every atrial impulse still conducts but with an abnormally prolonged PR interval (>200 ms); the term block is a misnomer since conduction is delayed, not interrupted. Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree block shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat with grouped beating and progressive RR shortening; it is typically within the AV node, hemodynamically stable, and usually does not warrant pacing when asymptomatic. Mobitz II second-degree block shows a fixed PR interval before a dropped beat, is usually infranodal with a wider QRS, carries a risk of sudden death from an unreliable escape rhythm, and warrants permanent pacing even without symptoms. In 2:1 AV block the ECG cannot reliably distinguish type I from type II; a PR <160 ms with a wide QRS before the conducted beat favors infranodal (type II) block. QRS width of the escape rhythm localizes the block: a narrow QRS escape implies block in the AV node or proximal His with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape (without preexisting bundle branch block) implies distal His or bundle branch block and a slower, less reliable rhythm. Vagal maneuvers and carotid sinus massage slow AV nodal conduction but may paradoxically improve infranodal conduction, while atropine, isoproterenol, and exercise improve AV nodal conduction but may worsen infranodal conduction - useful for localizing the level of block. On the His bundle electrogram, the AH interval (AV nodal conduction) is normally <130 ms and the HV interval (His-Purkinje conduction) is normally <=55 ms; a markedly prolonged HV interval predicts progression to higher-grade block. Functional causes of AV block (autonomic, metabolic/endocrine, drug-related) tend to be reversible, whereas most structural causes producing fibrosis are permanent. Congenital complete heart block with a narrow QRS typically increases heart rate with exercise, whereas acquired complete heart block (especially wide QRS) does not respond to exercise. Acquired persistent AV conduction failure is rare in healthy adults (estimated incidence about 1 per 5000 per year in the U.S.), but becomes much more common with ischemia, aging/fibrosis, or infiltrative disease. Idiopathic progressive fibrosis/sclerosis of the conduction system is the most common acquired cause, accounting for roughly 50% of AV block; it often begins in the fourth decade and is accelerated by atherosclerosis, hypertension, and diabetes. Weak electrical coupling from sparse gap junctions (predominantly connexin-40) plus increased extracellular volume slows conduction and protects the ventricle. The AV junction comprises a transitional (atrionodal) cell zone showing decremental conduction, the compact node, and the penetrating His bundle; conduction continues through the His, right and left bundle branches, and the fast-conducting Purkinje network (1-3 m/s). Bradycardia and block arise when conduction across this axis is compromised by fibrosis/sclerosis, calcification (Lev, Lenegre disease), ischemia/infarction, infiltrative or inflammatory disease, drugs, heightened vagal tone, or congenital/genetic abnormalities; consequences range from fatigue and syncope to asystolic death if no reliable escape emerges. Functional (autonomic/metabolic/drug) causes are often reversible while structural fibrosis is typically permanent. Prognosis depends heavily on the level of block. AV-nodal (proximal) block - including Mobitz I and most inferior-MI-related block - tends to have a faster, stable narrow-complex escape and is often reversible with a favorable outcome. Infranodal (distal His-Purkinje) block, Mobitz II, and high-grade block in anterior MI carry unstable wide-complex escape rhythms, higher mortality, and a risk of sudden asystolic death, so pacing is indicated even when asymptomatic. Functional/reversible causes generally resolve; structural fibrotic disease is usually permanent and progressive. Electrocardiographic grading: First-degree AV block - all atrial impulses conduct but PR is prolonged (>200 ms), delay usually within the AV node. Second-degree AV block - intermittent failure of AV conduction; Type I/Mobitz I/Wenckebach (progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat, usually AV-nodal) and Type II/Mobitz II (fixed PR before a dropped beat, usually infranodal, often with wide QRS). Third-degree (complete) AV block - complete AV dissociation with a ventricular (escape) rate slower than the atrial rate.

The Hyperbilirubinemias — Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome, Dubin-Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, inherited hyperbilirubinemias Hemolytic anemias (hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, beta-thalassemia) causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia Ineffective erythropoiesis (thalassemia major, megaloblastic anemia, congenital dyserythropoietic anemias, lead poisoning) Drug-induced unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (rifampin, novobiocin, atazanavir, indinavir, chloramphenicol, gentamicin) Physiologic, breast-milk, and Lucey-Driscoll neonatal jaundice Acquired hepatocellular or cholestatic liver disease (acute viral hepatitis, common bile duct stone) with mixed hyperbilirubinemia Benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis (BRIC) and progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC types 1-3) Acute viral hepatitis, which the first cholestatic episodes of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis may mimic Fractionation of serum bilirubin into conjugated (direct) and unconjugated (indirect) components Urinalysis for bilirubinuria (present in conjugated, absent in unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) Standard liver biochemistries (aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, prothrombin time) and hemolysis workup (reticulocytes, haptoglobin) Urinary coproporphyrin isomer analysis to distinguish Dubin-Johnson (>=80% isomer I, normal total) from Rotor (markedly increased total, isomer I usually <70%) Phenobarbital challenge to separate Crigler-Najjar type II (>25% fall) from type I (no response) UGT1A1 genotyping (e.g., A[TA]7TAA promoter for Gilbert syndrome); oral cholecystography (gallbladder non-visualized in Dubin-Johnson, visualized in Rotor) Extrahepatic biliary obstruction (e.g., choledocholithiasis) presenting with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia Intrahepatic cholestatic injury Resorbing large hematoma or massive tissue infarction causing transient unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia Bilirubin is the terminal product of heme catabolism, with roughly 70-90% derived from breakdown of hemoglobin in senescent red cells; hepatic handling involves four linked steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases (ligandins), conjugation by UGT1A1, and canalicular excretion (Harrison 22e p.2637-2638). Conjugation by UGT1A1 adds one or two glucuronic acid moieties, disrupting internal hydrogen bonding so the resulting glucuronides become water-soluble; conjugation is obligatory for biliary excretion (Harrison 22e p.2638). Unconjugated bilirubin is too tightly albumin-bound to be filtered and does not appear in urine, whereas conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin is readily filtered, so bilirubinuria indicates a conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia; the kidney acts as an overflow valve so renal failure can amplify jaundice in conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Harrison 22e p.2638). Isolated hemolysis in an otherwise healthy person produces a purely unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with direct fraction <=15% of total; because marrow erythropoiesis can rise only about eightfold, hemolysis alone rarely sustains a bilirubin above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL), so higher values imply concomitant hepatic dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2638-2639). Gilbert syndrome is a common, benign cause of mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (usually <51 micromol/L, <3 mg/dL) with normal liver tests and histology; levels rise with fasting, stress, fatigue, alcohol, and intercurrent illness and fall with caloric intake or enzyme inducers (Harrison 22e p.2640). Crigler-Najjar type I shows extreme lifelong unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL) with essentially absent UGT1A1 activity, no response to phenobarbital, and high kernicterus risk; type II has lower levels, detectable enzyme, pigmented bile, and a >25% bilirubin fall with phenobarbital (Harrison 22e p.2639-2640). Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign, autosomal recessive predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (typically 34-85 micromol/L) caused by mutation of the canalicular transporter MRP2 (ABCC2); the liver is grossly black from lysosomal pigment and urinary coproporphyrin is >=80% isomer I despite a normal total (Harrison 22e p.2640-2641). Rotor syndrome resembles Dubin-Johnson clinically (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubinuria) but the liver is normal in color, the gallbladder is visualized on oral cholecystography, and total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly increased with isomer I usually <70%; it results from combined deficiency of OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 (Harrison 22e p.2641-2642). Most neonates develop mild physiologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia between days 2 and 5 (peak typically <85-170 micromol/L, 5-10 mg/dL) due to low UGT1A1 and enterohepatic recycling, resolving within about 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2639). A rapidly rising neonatal unconjugated bilirubin, or absolute levels above ~340 micromol/L (20 mg/dL), risks bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) as pigment crosses an immature blood-brain barrier and deposits in the basal ganglia (Harrison 22e p.2639). Acquired liver disease (acute hepatitis, common bile duct stone) generally produces a mixed conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and serum levels or fractions cannot reliably distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2640). Gilbert syndrome impairs glucuronidation of the irinotecan (CPT-11) active metabolite SN-38, predisposing to severe diarrhea and myelosuppression; the HIV protease inhibitors indinavir and atazanavir inhibit UGT1A1 and worsen hyperbilirubinemia, most markedly in preexisting Gilbert syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2640). Rapidly rising neonatal unconjugated bilirubin or absolute level above ~340 micromol/L (20 mg/dL) signaling risk of kernicterus Sustained unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL) attributed to hemolysis, implying additional hepatic dysfunction Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with bilirubinuria, prompting evaluation for hepatocellular or obstructive disease Intercurrent febrile illness in Crigler-Najjar that can precipitate late-onset bilirubin encephalopathy Prolonged, debilitating cholestatic attacks in BRIC and progression of PFIC to end-stage liver disease Assuming hemolysis alone explains a markedly elevated bilirubin; sustained levels above ~68 micromol/L (4 mg/dL) imply coexisting hepatic dysfunction Using serum bilirubin levels or conjugated/unconjugated proportions to differentiate intrahepatic from extrahepatic causes of jaundice, which is not reliable Overdiagnosing Gilbert syndrome from a single value, since levels fluctuate widely and at least 25% of patients show transiently normal bilirubin on follow-up Male predominance in Gilbert syndrome may be artifactual, reflecting use of male-derived reference ranges Mistaking the first episodes of benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis for acute viral hepatitis Prescribing drugs cleared by glucuronidation (notably irinotecan) without caution in Gilbert syndrome given risk of severe toxicity Bilirubin, the end product of heme degradation (chiefly from senescent erythrocyte hemoglobin), circulates tightly bound to albumin and is processed by hepatocytes in four steps: carrier-mediated uptake, intracellular binding to glutathione-S-transferases, conjugation with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1 (the physiologically critical isoform encoded by exon A1 plus shared exons 2-5 of the UGT1 gene complex on chromosome 2), and ATP-dependent canalicular excretion of mono- and diglucuronides via MRP2. A portion of glucuronides is also exported into the portal circulation by MRP3 and recaptured by sinusoidal OATP1B1/OATP1B3. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia arises from overproduction (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, resorption of large hematomas/infarcts), decreased hepatic uptake (drugs such as rifampin, novobiocin; contributory in Gilbert syndrome), or impaired conjugation (neonatal immaturity, breast-milk jaundice, drug inhibition of UGT1A1, and hereditary UGT1A1 defects of Crigler-Najjar I/II and Gilbert syndrome). Gilbert syndrome most often reflects a homozygous extra TA insertion (A[TA]7TAA rather than A[TA]6TAA) in the UGT1A1 promoter reducing enzyme expression; Crigler-Najjar reflects coding/structural UGT1 mutations causing absent (type I) or markedly reduced (type II) activity. Predominantly conjugated familial hyperbilirubinemias result from defective canalicular excretion: Dubin-Johnson from MRP2 (ABCC2) mutation and Rotor from combined OATP1B1/OATP1B3 deficiency impairing reuptake of refluxed conjugated bilirubin. Gilbert, Dubin-Johnson, and Rotor syndromes are benign with normal life expectancy and no progression to chronic liver disease. Crigler-Najjar type I carries a grave prognosis: before phototherapy most patients died of kernicterus in infancy or early childhood, and even survivors developed bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction, with early liver transplantation the best means to prevent brain injury and death. Crigler-Najjar type II is far less often complicated by kernicterus and is generally compatible with normal life, though intercurrent illness, fasting, or low albumin can precipitate dangerous bilirubin elevations. BRIC is benign and does not cause cirrhosis, whereas PFIC progresses to end-stage liver disease in childhood. Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia forms a severity continuum by residual UGT1A1 activity: Crigler-Najjar type I (activity absent; bilirubin ~340-765 micromol/L, 20-45 mg/dL; no phenobarbital response; usual kernicterus), Crigler-Najjar type II (reduced activity, typically <=10% of normal; bilirubin ~100-430 micromol/L, 6-25 mg/dL; >25% phenobarbital response; rare kernicterus), and Gilbert syndrome (activity ~10-35% of normal; bilirubin usually <=70 micromol/L, 4 mg/dL absent fasting/hemolysis; normal histology). Familial conjugated hyperbilirubinemias of canalicular function (Dubin-Johnson, Rotor) are benign, distinguished from the progressive cholestatic disorders BRIC (episodic, non-progressive) and PFIC (progressive to end-stage liver disease).

The Metabolic Syndrome — Syndrome X, Insulin resistance syndrome, MetS Type 2 diabetes mellitus / impaired glucose tolerance Genetic lipodystrophies (e.g., Berardinelli-Seip congenital, Dunnigan familial partial lipodystrophy) Acquired lipodystrophy (e.g., HIV-related and antiretroviral-associated) Polycystic ovary syndrome Cushing's syndrome / other endocrine causes of central obesity and hypertension Primary dyslipidemias Fasting lipid panel (triglycerides, HDL cholesterol) and fasting glucose are required for diagnosis Waist circumference measurement and blood pressure Optional insulin-resistance biomarkers individualized to the patient: apoB, hsCRP, fibrinogen, uric acid, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio, liver function tests Sleep study if symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea are present If PCOS suspected (clinical features and anovulation): testosterone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone MAFLD assessment via FIB-4 fibrosis score or elastography DEXA, CT, or MRI if discrimination of visceral versus subcutaneous fat is needed Lipodystrophy syndromes (severe insulin resistance with many overlapping components) Cushing's syndrome (central adiposity, hypertension, hyperglycemia) Polycystic ovary syndrome with insulin resistance Metabolic syndrome is a clustering of metabolic abnormalities (central obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL cholesterol, hyperglycemia, and hypertension) that together raise the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Diagnosis under NCEP:ATPIII (2001) requires three or more of: waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women; triglycerides >=150 mg/dL; HDL <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women); BP >=130/85 mmHg; fasting glucose >=100 mg/dL (or specific medication for, or prior diagnosis of, the relevant condition). The Harmonizing definition uses ethnicity-specific waist circumference cutoffs (e.g., for South Asian and Chinese men >=90 cm, Europid men >=94 cm, Japanese men >=85 cm), reflecting that risk at a given waist circumference differs between populations. Visceral (intra-abdominal) adipose tissue is more strongly linked to insulin resistance, diabetes, and CVD than subcutaneous fat, but waist circumference alone cannot reliably distinguish the two depots; DEXA, CT, or MRI is needed for that distinction. Normal-weight individuals can still be insulin-resistant and meet criteria for metabolic syndrome, a phenotype that is particularly evident in populations from India, Southeast Asia, and Central America. The syndrome is typically asymptomatic; physical examination often shows only elevated waist circumference and blood pressure, which should trigger a search for the other biochemical components. Lipoatrophy and acanthosis nigricans, when present, signal severe insulin resistance, though they are far less common than the standard components. Hypertriglyceridemia is an excellent marker of the insulin-resistant state; fasting triglycerides above roughly 180 mg/dL (~2.0 mM) are typically accompanied by a predominance of small, dense, more atherogenic LDL particles. Most patients (~75%) with type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance have metabolic syndrome, and its presence in these groups marks a higher CVD burden than in those without the syndrome. Conditions strongly associated with insulin resistance and the syndrome include metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD/MASH), polycystic ovary syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea, which should be screened for during evaluation. Obstructive sleep apnea can predict metabolic syndrome even without excess adiposity, and insulin resistance tends to be more severe in apnea patients than in weight-matched controls. Hyperuricemia reflects insulin-resistance-related defects in renal tubular handling of uric acid and may itself contribute to hypertension via effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Acanthosis nigricans or lipoatrophy indicating severe insulin resistance Established type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance (markedly elevated diabetes and CVD risk) Coexisting metabolic syndrome and elevated hsCRP (associated with increased all-cause mortality) Features suggesting MASH/advanced liver fibrosis (precursor of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma) Symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea Waist circumference does not reliably separate subcutaneous from visceral fat, so it can misestimate true metabolic risk without imaging. A single ethnicity-blind waist cutoff under- or over-estimates risk across populations; ethnicity-specific thresholds are needed. Normal body weight does not exclude the syndrome, so insulin resistance can be missed in lean individuals. Whether metabolic syndrome adds CVD or diabetes risk beyond the simple sum of its individual components remains debated, so it should not be over-interpreted as an independent diagnosis. Fasting insulin levels or HOMA capture only part of insulin resistance, so they inadequately quantify the contribution of resistance to hypertension. Obstructive sleep apnea and PCOS are commonly overlooked associated conditions if not actively screened for. Insulin resistance is the most widely accepted unifying mechanism. Early insulin resistance manifests as postprandial then fasting hyperinsulinemia, eventually progressing to hyperglycemia as compensatory beta-cell secretion fails. An overabundance of circulating free fatty acids (FFAs), released from expanded adipose tissue and from lipoprotein-lipase-mediated lipolysis, drives the process: FFAs impair insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle, promote intramuscular and cardiac triglyceride accumulation, and increase hepatic glucose and triglyceride production with VLDL secretion. Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis (its most sensitive action), so resistance amplifies FFA release in a self-perpetuating loop. Increased VLDL/apoB and elevated apoC-III inhibit lipoprotein lipase, raising triglyceride-rich remnants; HDL becomes small, dense, and cleared faster, lowering HDL cholesterol. Loss of insulin-mediated vasodilation (nitric oxide) with preserved renal sodium reabsorption and sympathetic activation, plus adipose angiotensinogen expression, contributes to hypertension. Contributing/associated mechanisms include leptin resistance, reduced anti-inflammatory adiponectin, increased proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, resistin) from adipose-derived macrophages, a prothrombotic state (fibrinogen, PAI-1), oxidative stress with mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in the gut microbiome (increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio). Metabolic syndrome roughly doubles the risk of cardiovascular death and confers about a threefold higher risk of acute myocardial infarction or stroke; the risk for type 2 diabetes is increased three- to fivefold (fasting glucose explaining most of this). In the REGARDS cohort, metabolic syndrome carried a relative risk of about 1.34 for all-cause mortality, with the relationship to hsCRP and mortality stronger in white than in black participants. Prevalence among patients with coronary heart disease may reach up to 60% in those over 75. Risk and prevalence are modifiable: cardiac rehabilitation and lifestyle change (improved nutrition, physical activity, weight reduction) can reduce the prevalence of the syndrome. There is no graded severity scale; the syndrome is defined categorically by meeting three or more of the five diagnostic components (NCEP:ATPIII 2001 or the ethnicity-adjusted Harmonizing definition, Table 420-1). Risk rises with the number of components present and with associated markers such as elevated hsCRP.

The Vasculitis Syndromes — Vasculitis, Systemic vasculitis, ANCA-associated vasculitis, Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Microscopic polyangiitis, Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), Polyarteritis nodosa, Giant cell (temporal) arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein), Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, Polymyalgia rheumatica Other primary vasculitides when the full classic syndrome is incomplete Anti-glomerular basement membrane (Goodpasture's) disease Relapsing polychondritis IgG4-related disease (aortitis/periaortitis mimicking Takayasu) Connective tissue disease-associated (lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid) vasculitis Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthropathy (vs polymyalgia rheumatica) Lymphomatoid granulomatosis and extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (vs GPA midline destructive disease) Bacterial endocarditis Disseminated gonococcal infection Pulmonary histoplasmosis Coccidioidomycosis Syphilis Lyme disease Rocky Mountain spotted fever Whipple's disease Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and rhinoscleroma (midline destructive mimics of GPA) Tissue biopsy of clinically involved organ (highest yield: lung for GPA; symptomatic skin nodules, painful testes, or nerve/muscle for PAN) ANCA testing (anti-PR3 / cANCA and anti-MPO / pANCA) with awareness of variable predictive value by presentation Catheter-directed (dye) arteriography for suspected PAN; MR or CT arteriography of aorta and branches for Takayasu and large-vessel GCA Temporal artery biopsy (3-5 cm with serial sections) and/or temporal +/- axillary artery ultrasound 'halo' sign for GCA ESR and/or CRP, complete blood count (anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, eosinophilia in EGPA) Urinalysis for hematuria, proteinuria, and red-cell casts; serum creatinine Hepatitis B and C serologies/RNA (PAN, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis) Serum cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, and complement levels for cryoglobulinemic vasculitis Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence (IgA and C3 deposition in IgA vasculitis; leukocytoclastic vasculitis in cutaneous vasculitis) Echocardiography at diagnosis in EGPA given cardiac mortality risk Consider DADA2 (adenosine deaminase type 2 deficiency) evaluation in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis Antiphospholipid syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / thrombotic microangiopathies Atrial myxoma Lymphoma and carcinomatosis Drug toxicity (cocaine, levamisole-adulterated cocaine, amphetamines, ergot alkaloids, methysergide, arsenic) Sarcoidosis Atheroembolic disease Amyloidosis Migraine Fibromuscular dysplasia Heritable connective tissue disorders Segmental arterial mediolysis Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls that typically narrows the lumen and produces downstream tissue ischemia; it may be the sole disease, may be secondary to another disease, and may be single-organ or multisystem. Suspect vasculitis in any unexplained systemic illness; clinical clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease. Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs without subjective or objective involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Catheter-directed arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected. ANCA subtypes: cANCA targets proteinase-3 (>90% positive in active granulomatosis with polyangiitis); pANCA most relevantly targets myeloperoxidase (variably positive in microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA, and isolated necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis). Only anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are convincingly vasculitis-associated. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically combines granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower respiratory tracts with glomerulonephritis; upper airway involvement occurs in ~95% and renal disease (~77% over course) dominates prognosis. Renal lesion is pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition). Microscopic polyangiitis resembles GPA but lacks granulomatous inflammation; it favors small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), with glomerulonephritis in at least 79% and alveolar hemorrhage in ~12%. Upper airway disease and lung nodules are atypical and, if present, point instead to GPA. ANCA (usually anti-MPO) in ~75%. EGPA (Churg-Strauss) is defined by asthma, blood and tissue eosinophilia, and vasculitis; eosinophilia exceeds 1000 cells/uL in >80% and ANCA (usually anti-MPO) is present in ~48%. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death, so echocardiography is advised at diagnosis. Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries that spares pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; renal involvement is arteritis (microaneurysms, hypertension), not glomerular. ANCA are rarely found; screen all patients for hepatitis B and C. Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively after age 50, presents with fever, anemia, high ESR/CRP, and headache; ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness is the dreaded complication, and patients carry an ~18-fold increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm. Treatment should not be delayed for biopsy. Polymyalgia rheumatica (aching/stiffness of neck, shoulder and hip girdles with raised ESR/CRP) coexists with GCA in 40-50% of GCA patients; creatine kinase is normal and RF/anti-CCP should be negative. ~10-20% with isolated PMR later develop GCA. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel panarteritis with strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches, classically in adolescent girls and young women; suspect it in a young woman with diminished or absent pulses, an interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) is a small-vessel, immune-complex (IgA) vasculitis most common in children 4-7 years, with palpable purpura over buttocks/lower limbs, arthralgias, colicky GI symptoms (intussusception risk), and usually mild self-limited glomerulonephritis; serum complement is normal and IgA is elevated in about half. Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is most often associated with hepatitis C (estimated in ~5% of chronic HCV); rheumatoid factor is almost always present, hypocomplementemia occurs in ~90%, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis accounts for ~80% of renal lesions. Temporal artery biopsy yield improves with a 3-5 cm segment and serial sectioning because involvement is segmental; biopsy may still show arteritis after about 14 days of glucocorticoid therapy, so starting treatment promptly does not preclude later diagnosis. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or rising creatinine (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis) Hemoptysis / diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (microscopic polyangiitis, GPA) New or worsening headache, jaw or tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or any visual symptom in a patient over 50 (impending GCA-related blindness) Subglottic stenosis or progressive airway obstruction in GPA Mononeuritis multiplex Abdominal pain with GI bleeding suggesting bowel infarction/perforation (PAN, EGPA, IgA vasculitis with intussusception) Cardiac involvement (myocarditis/coronary vasculitis) in EGPA or PAN Interarm blood-pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or aortic aneurysm/dissection in large-vessel disease Concurrent anti-GBM antibody positivity in ANCA-associated vasculitis Do NOT treat a rise in ANCA titer alone as evidence of relapse; only ~43% of patients relapsed within a year of an ANCA rise, and many remain ANCA-positive for years in remission. ANCA predictive value falls sharply when renal disease is absent (~30-60% with sinus/lung-only disease vs ~90% with active glomerulonephritis), so biopsy is needed to exclude infection or malignancy that can cause false-positive ANCA. Upper airway lesions in GPA should NEVER be irradiated; midline destructive disease mimics include NK/T-cell lymphoma and cocaine/levamisole injury (anti-neutrophil-elastase ANCA, granulocytopenia point to levamisole). Eosinophilia is rare in PAN; when markedly elevated it should redirect toward EGPA. In PAN, MR and CT arteriography lack the resolution to visualize the small/medium aneurysms, so catheter-directed dye arteriography is required. When tocilizumab or other IL-6 blockade is used in GCA, ESR and CRP normalize and can no longer be used to gauge disease activity or detect infection. TMP-SMX should never be used alone to treat active GPA involving organs beyond the sinonasal tissue. Failure to exclude infection (especially endocarditis) before starting empirical immunosuppression in a rapidly deteriorating patient can be catastrophic. Glucocorticoids do not reliably benefit the skin or renal disease of IgA vasculitis and do not shorten its course or reduce recurrence. Most vasculitic syndromes are thought to be at least partly immune-mediated responses to antigenic stimuli, with the precise mechanism varying by disease. Three principal hypothesized mechanisms are recognized. (1) Pathogenic immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum-sickness/cutaneous syndromes, HCV-associated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, HBV-associated vasculitis): antigen-antibody complexes formed in antigen excess deposit in vessel walls whose permeability has been raised by vasoactive amines, activate complement (notably chemotactic C5a), recruit neutrophils that phagocytose complexes and release intracytoplasmic enzymes damaging the wall, with later mononuclear infiltration and luminal compromise. (2) ANCA production (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA): when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha or IL-1 or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8; however, some patients have active GPA without ANCA and titers correlate poorly with activity, so a primary pathogenic role remains debated. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, GPA, EGPA): cytokine-activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and secretes IL-1, enabling CD4+ T-cell interactions; IL-1 and TNF-alpha upregulate ELAM-1 and VCAM-1 to enhance leukocyte adhesion. In GCA the disease is antigen-driven, with clonally restricted T cells suggesting an arterial-wall antigen, and both TH1 (IFN-gamma) and TH17 (IL-17) CD4 lineages contribute. The size, type, and location of affected vessels, host genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, reticuloendothelial clearance of complexes, hemodynamic factors, and endothelial integrity all influence the ultimate phenotype. Outcome varies markedly by syndrome and by treatment. Untreated granulomatosis with polyangiitis was once uniformly fatal within months; modern cyclophosphamide- or rituximab-based regimens with glucocorticoids achieve improvement in >90% and remission in ~75%, with 5-year survival >80%, though 50-70% of remissions are followed by relapse and many patients accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity). Treated microscopic polyangiitis has ~74% 5-year survival with relapse in at least 34%, mortality from alveolar hemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease. Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; with treatment about 72% survive at 78 months, and myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths. Untreated PAN carries a 10-20% 5-year survival (death from bowel infarction/perforation and cardiovascular causes); combination immunosuppression markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20%. GCA seldom causes acute death but carries late risk of aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection; PMR generally responds well. Takayasu is usually chronic and relapsing with widely variable reported survival. IgA vasculitis prognosis is excellent (mortality exceedingly rare; 1-5% of children reach end-stage renal disease, possibly higher in adults; recurrences in 10-40%). In cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, glomerulonephritis is a poor prognostic sign (~15% progress to end-stage renal disease, 40% of whom later die of cardiovascular disease, infection, or liver failure). For ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA/microscopic polyangiitis), Harrison frames management by severe vs nonsevere disease. Severe disease involves life- or organ-threatening manifestations and is judged by both extent and the specific organ affected: pulmonary disease may be nonsevere (nodules without respiratory compromise) or severe (alveolar hemorrhage), whereas active glomerulonephritis is ALWAYS considered severe even when renal function is normal. Treatment is conceptually divided into a remission-induction phase followed by a maintenance phase, with regimen choice stratified by this severity assessment along with relapse history and comorbidities.

of the Alport type IV collagen spectrum Overlooking a urological cause when haematuria is non-glomerular or visible Not screening the family or offering genetic counselling Missing early extrarenal features that would reclassify the patient as having Alport syndrome Thin basement membrane nephropathy is a disorder of the type IV collagen network that forms the glomerular basement membrane. Heterozygous variants in COL4A3 or COL4A4, which encode alpha chains of type IV collagen, produce a structurally thinner but largely functional basement membrane. The attenuated membrane is more permeable to red cells, giving rise to persistent glomerular (dysmorphic) microscopic haematuria, but in most people the filtration barrier otherwise functions normally so proteinuria, hypertension and renal impairment are absent or minimal. Because the same genes, when affected biallelically or with certain variants, cause autosomal recessive or dominant Alport syndrome, the condition represents the mild end of a continuous type IV collagen disease spectrum, and a minority of carriers show slow progression over decades. The great majority of individuals maintain normal renal function lifelong with isolated haematuria, but because COL4A3/COL4A4 carriers occasionally progress, ongoing surveillance for proteinuria, hypertension and renal decline is warranted.

thresholds Dismissing incidental thoracic aortic dilatation without arranging appropriate surveillance Applying general size thresholds to patients with connective tissue disease who warrant earlier repair Attributing acute chest and back pain solely to cardiac causes and missing dissection Neglecting family screening in heritable aortopathies Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a permanent localised dilatation of the thoracic aorta resulting from weakening of the aortic wall. Degeneration of medial elastin and smooth muscle, driven by genetic connective tissue disorders, bicuspid valve-associated aortopathy, atherosclerosis, or ageing, reduces wall integrity. According to the law of Laplace, increasing diameter raises wall tension, promoting further expansion in a self-perpetuating cycle. As the wall weakens it becomes vulnerable to acute dissection, in which an intimal tear allows blood to track within the media, and ultimately to rupture. Prognosis depends on aneurysm size, growth rate, and aetiology; small aneurysms often remain stable under surveillance, whereas large or rapidly expanding lesions carry a high risk of dissection or rupture. Elective repair markedly improves survival compared with the very high mortality of rupture, though operative risk varies with aneurysm extent and comorbidity.

Disruption impairs normal cellular growth signalling from before birth, producing severe primordial short stature with characteristic skeletal changes, while sparing cognitive development. Cognition and life expectancy are normal; the main issue is marked short stature, which responds poorly to growth hormone, so management focuses on accurate diagnosis, realistic counselling and monitoring for skeletal and endocrine issues.

the neonatal assessment TAR syndrome is a disorder of megakaryopoiesis and limb development linked to reduced function of RBM8A, a gene encoding a core component of the exon junction complex that regulates messenger RNA processing. Affected individuals typically inherit a rare loss-of-function allele on one chromosome and a common low-expressing regulatory variant on the other, so the gene product is insufficient in the tissues that depend most on it. The resulting deficiency impairs megakaryocyte production and maturation, producing a hypomegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, while parallel effects on limb morphogenesis cause bilateral radial aplasia with sparing of the thumbs. Unlike the classic inherited bone-marrow failure syndromes, the thrombocytopenia is usually isolated and tends to remit over the first years of life rather than progressing to pancytopenia. The thrombocytopenia is typically most dangerous in infancy and generally improves toward near-normal platelet counts in later childhood, so with careful support through the early high-risk period the long-term haematological outlook is good.

Thrombophilia — hypercoagulable state, inherited thrombophilia, prothrombotic state Antiphospholipid syndrome Occult malignancy Myeloproliferative neoplasm including JAK2-associated disease Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria Provoked thrombosis from surgery, immobility, or hormonal therapy Genetic testing for factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A Functional antithrombin, protein C, and protein S assays timed away from acute events and anticoagulation Antiphospholipid antibody panel including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I Full blood count and JAK2 testing where a myeloproliferative disorder is suspected Age-appropriate malignancy evaluation in unprovoked events Thrombophilia denotes an inherited or acquired tendency to venous, and less often arterial, thrombosis Common inherited causes include factor V Leiden and the prothrombin G20210A variant; deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S are rarer but more strongly prothrombotic Acquired causes include the antiphospholipid syndrome, malignancy, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy, nephrotic syndrome, and immobility Clinical features that suggest an underlying thrombophilia include venous thromboembolism at a young age, recurrent events, unusual sites such as cerebral or splanchnic veins, a strong family history, and warfarin-induced skin necrosis Testing rarely changes acute management and is confounded by the acute event, anticoagulation, and pregnancy, so it should be timed carefully and directed by whether the result will alter decisions Antithrombin, protein C, and protein S levels are unreliable during acute thrombosis and while on anticoagulation, whereas genetic tests for factor V Leiden and prothrombin variants are unaffected Management centres on anticoagulation for events and on risk assessment for prophylaxis during high-risk periods rather than on the laboratory label itself Extensive or life-threatening thrombosis such as massive pulmonary embolism or cerebral venous thrombosis Thrombosis at unusual sites suggesting an underlying myeloproliferative disorder or malignancy Skin necrosis after starting a vitamin K antagonist, suggesting protein C or S deficiency Recurrent pregnancy loss or arterial events raising concern for antiphospholipid syndrome Testing during the acute event or while on anticoagulation, producing misleading levels Allowing a positive result to prolong anticoagulation unnecessarily when clinical risk is low Overlooking acquired causes such as malignancy or antiphospholipid syndrome by focusing only on inherited defects Testing asymptomatic relatives without clear benefit or counselling Thrombosis arises when the balance of Virchow's triad shifts toward clot formation through hypercoagulability, stasis, or endothelial injury. Inherited thrombophilias tilt this balance by either increasing procoagulant activity or reducing natural anticoagulant function: factor V Leiden and prothrombin variants enhance clotting, while deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C, and protein S remove restraints on thrombin generation. Acquired states add further procoagulant stimuli, such as antiphospholipid antibodies, tumour-derived tissue factor, or oestrogen effects. Most thrombotic events reflect the interaction of one or more of these predispositions with a transient provoking factor. Prognosis depends on the specific defect and on whether events are provoked; many people with common low-risk variants never have a thrombosis, whereas antithrombin deficiency and antiphospholipid syndrome carry higher recurrence risk and may warrant extended anticoagulation.
