reduced only 30-60% in HELLP) Platelet count and serial monitoring LDH (elevated in hemolysis/TMA), haptoglobin (decreased), bilirubin Direct and indirect Coombs test (negative in microangiopathic hemolysis) Complement studies including C3 and C4 (low C3 with normal C4 suggests alternative pathway activation in aHUS); complement-regulatory gene mutation testing Stool studies for Shiga toxin / E. coli O157:H7 in suspected STEC HUS Antiphospholipid antibody panel: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies Antinuclear antibody pattern and anti-RNA polymerase I/III, anti-U3-RNP for scleroderma renal crisis Doppler ultrasonography, CT angiography (nearly 100% sensitive), or MR angiography for renal vein thrombosis Renal biopsy when diagnosis is uncertain (required for HIV-related TMA; recommended in atypical APLS or scleroderma renal involvement without hypertension) Urinalysis and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (screening in sickle cell nephropathy) LDH-to-AST ratio (about 13:1 in HELLP/preeclampsia vs about 29:1 without preeclampsia), antithrombin III (decreased in HELLP not TTP), D-dimer (elevated in HELLP not TTP) Malignant hypertension (histologically indistinguishable from scleroderma renal crisis) Preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome Cancer-associated TMA (tumor microvascular obstruction) Drug-induced TMA Acute tubular necrosis (contributes to renal failure in HELLP) Thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) is a pathologic lesion of endothelial injury in terminal arterioles and capillaries, with platelet and hyaline thrombi causing partial or complete occlusion; it is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) featuring thrombocytopenia and schistocytes. Renal histology of TMA shows swollen endocapillary cells (endotheliosis), fibrin thrombi, platelet plugs, arterial intimal fibrosis, and a membranoproliferative glomerular pattern; fibrin thrombi may extend into the arteriolar pole producing glomerular collapse and at times cortical necrosis, and recovered kidneys may develop secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. The classic TTP pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurologic symptoms, fever, renal failure) is rare: fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases show the full pentad, so do not wait for all five to act. TTP is defined as MAHA associated with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10%; ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers accumulate, form clots, and shear erythrocytes, but loss of ADAMTS13 alone may need an additional trigger (infection, surgery, pancreatitis, pregnancy) to provoke clinical disease. Atypical (complement-mediated) HUS reflects alternative complement pathway dysregulation; affected patients often have low C3 with normal C4, and factor H deficiency is the most common defect, with more than 70 factor H gene mutations described. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) HUS, classically D+ (diarrhea-associated) HUS, mostly affects children under 5 but can affect adults; bloody diarrhea precedes MAHA within one week in over 80% of cases, fever is typically absent, and neurologic involvement is common, especially in adults. Scleroderma renal crisis presents with acute kidney injury, abrupt-onset hypertension, and a normal urine sediment (though none is strictly required); it occurs in about 12% of diffuse but only ~2% of limited systemic sclerosis, and its renal histology of 'onion-skinning' arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation is indistinguishable from malignant hypertension. Antiphospholipid syndrome produces a predisposition to arterial and venous thrombosis and recurrent fetal loss; 'triple positivity' (lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I, and anticardiolipin antibodies) carries the highest thrombosis risk, and APLS is the leading cause of stroke in patients under 45. HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a microvascular pregnancy complication; the defining organ is the liver (subcapsular hematoma with potential rupture), renal failure occurs in about half of patients, and proteinuria is present in 86-100%. Renal vein thrombosis can present with flank pain, tenderness, hematuria, rapid renal decline, and proteinuria, or be silent and discovered during a pulmonary embolism workup; the left renal vein is more commonly involved and two-thirds of cases are bilateral. Sickle cell nephropathy arises from occlusion of the vasa recta in the renal medulla, where low oxygen tension and high osmolarity favor hemoglobin S polymerization and sickling; sequelae include hyposthenuria, hematuria, and papillary necrosis (which can also occur in sickle trait). Drug-induced TMA occurs via two mechanisms: dose-dependent toxic/endothelial damage (chemotherapeutics such as proteasome inhibitors, mitomycin C, gemcitabine; immunosuppressives such as calcineurin inhibitors, interferon, sirolimus) or non-dose-dependent drug-induced autoantibodies (e.g., quinine, which can react even after a single re-exposure). Neurologic deterioration (seizures, encephalopathy, cerebral infarction) in HUS/TTP, especially in adults Untreated immune-mediated TTP carries a mortality exceeding 90%, and 20% die within the first month even with modern therapy Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome: rapid onset, multiorgan failure, and severe thrombotic events Scleroderma renal crisis with cardiac involvement (myocarditis, pericarditis, arrhythmias) indicating an especially poor prognosis, or with pulmonary edema HELLP syndrome with subcapsular hepatic hematoma/spontaneous liver rupture, cerebral infarction/hemorrhage/edema, or placental abruption HSCT-associated TMA, which carries a 75% mortality within 3 months Bilateral renal vein thrombosis with rapid decline in renal function or life-threatening complications Waiting for the full TTP pentad before acting is a mistake, since fewer than 5% of immune-mediated TTP cases display all five features. Assuming TMA always shows MAHA can mislead: TMA is usually but not always accompanied by microangiopathic hemolysis, and in antiphospholipid syndrome renal TMA is common while signs of MAHA and platelet consumption are usually absent. Scleroderma renal crisis is histologically indistinguishable from malignant hypertension and the two can coexist, so renal biopsy is recommended for atypical renal involvement, especially when hypertension is absent. ADAMTS13 reduction in HELLP (30-60%) is milder than in TTP (below ~10%), so interpreting modest reductions as diagnostic of TTP can mislead during pregnancy when aHUS and TTP can also be triggered. Thrombocytopenia in HIV-related TMA may prohibit renal biopsy, yet biopsy is required for diagnosis because other HIV-associated renal diseases mimic it; ADAMTS13 activity is not reduced in HIV-related TMA. In drug-induced autoantibody TMA (e.g., quinine), disease can recur after even a single re-exposure in a previously sensitized patient, so it is not strictly dose-dependent. Distinguishing HSCT-associated TMA is difficult because thrombocytopenia, anemia, and renal insufficiency are common after transplantation for other reasons. Thrombotic renovascular disorders share endothelial injury of the renal microvasculature (terminal arterioles and capillaries) leading to platelet/hyaline thrombi and microangiopathic hemolysis. In TTP, deficient ADAMTS13 activity (below ~5-10%, from congenital mutation in cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman syndrome or acquired autoantibody in iTTP) allows ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers to accumulate, forming platelet-rich thrombi that shear red cells; an inflammatory trigger is often required to manifest disease. In atypical HUS, dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway (commonly factor H deficiency, or defects in factor I, factor B, CD46/membrane cofactor protein, C3, CFHR1/3/5, thrombomodulin, or autoantibody to factor H in DEAP HUS) causes complement-mediated endothelial damage. STEC HUS results from Shiga toxins (Stx1/Stx2, verotoxins) binding the glycolipid receptor Gb3 on renal microvascular cells, inducing inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, MCP-1, SDF-1) and chemokine receptors (CXCR4/CXCR7) with platelet aggregation; Streptococcus pneumoniae neuraminidase can expose the cryptic Thomsen-Friedenreich antigen so preformed IgM triggers MAHA. Scleroderma renal crisis features arcuate artery intimal/medial proliferation with onion-skinning, fibrinoid necrosis, and thrombosis. Antiphospholipid syndrome causes intralobular fibrous intimal hyperplasia and arterial/arteriolar occlusion. Renal vein thrombosis results from endothelial damage, venous stasis, or hypercoagulability (notably nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy). Prognosis varies by subtype. Untreated immune-mediated TTP has a mortality exceeding 90%, and even with modern therapy about 20% die within the first month from microvascular thrombosis. HSCT-associated TMA is highly lethal, with roughly 75% mortality within 3 months. Scleroderma renal crisis historically had over 90% mortality at 1 month, reduced to about 30% at 3 years with renin-angiotensin system blockade; nearly two-thirds of patients may require dialysis, with renal recovery in about half (median ~1 year). HELLP syndrome carries a mortality of about 7.4-34% and usually resolves spontaneously after delivery. POEMS syndrome rarely progresses to end-stage renal disease. Renal injury in aHUS can be severe and progress to end-stage renal disease, with recurrence risk after transplant depending on the complement-regulatory protein involved. Chronic kidney disease develops in roughly 25-33% of sickle cell nephropathy patients, and nephrotic-range proteinuria predicts progression to renal failure. No single unified severity scale; classification is by etiologic subtype and laboratory criteria. TTP is defined as MAHA with ADAMTS13 activity below 5-10% and subdivided into congenital (cTTP/Upshaw-Schulman) and immune (iTTP) forms. HUS variants include STEC/D+ HUS, pneumococcal neuraminidase-associated HUS, atypical complement-mediated HUS (aHUS), and DEAP HUS. HSCT-associated TMA has formal diagnostic criteria (Harrison Table 329-1): the International Working Group requires schistocytes (over 4% in one set, or RBC fragmentation with at least 2 schistocytes per high-power field), de novo/progressive thrombocytopenia, rising LDH, falling hemoglobin or increased transfusion need, negative Coombs, falling haptoglobin, and concurrent renal/neurologic dysfunction without other explanation. Antiphospholipid syndrome severity is stratified by antibody profile, with 'triple positivity' conferring the highest thrombosis risk and a catastrophic variant defined by rapid multiorgan failure.

Thymoma — thymic epithelial tumour, thymic carcinoma, thymoma Lymphoma involving the anterior mediastinum Germ cell tumour of the mediastinum Retrosternal or ectopic thyroid mass Thymic cyst or thymic hyperplasia Metastatic disease to the mediastinum Parathyroid adenoma or other mediastinal masses Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to characterise the anterior mediastinal mass and local invasion MRI to clarify cystic versus solid components and vascular involvement Testing for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies and evaluation for myasthenia gravis Full blood count and immunoglobulin levels to detect associated red cell aplasia or hypogammaglobulinaemia Biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or the tumour appears unresectable, and PET-CT for suspected thymic carcinoma Thymomas are the most common tumours of the anterior mediastinum in adults and are frequently discovered incidentally on chest imaging There is a strong association with myasthenia gravis, and a proportion of patients present first with neuromuscular symptoms; other paraneoplastic syndromes include pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia Local symptoms, when present, arise from mass effect and include chest pain, cough, dyspnoea, and features of superior vena cava obstruction Thymic carcinoma is a distinct and more aggressive entity than thymoma, with greater invasiveness, higher metastatic potential, and worse prognosis Staging emphasises the degree of local invasion beyond the capsule and into surrounding structures, which is the main determinant of behaviour and treatment Complete surgical resection is the cornerstone of treatment for resectable disease, and completeness of resection strongly influences outcome Radiotherapy is used adjuvantly for invasive or incompletely resected tumours, and chemotherapy, often platinum-based, is used for advanced or unresectable disease Patients with associated myasthenia gravis require optimisation of neuromuscular status before surgery to reduce perioperative respiratory risk Superior vena cava obstruction with facial swelling and distended neck veins Respiratory compromise or myasthenic crisis in a patient with a mediastinal mass Rapidly enlarging or invasive anterior mediastinal mass suggesting thymic carcinoma New pleural or pericardial effusion indicating advanced spread Overlooking underlying myasthenia gravis and precipitating perioperative respiratory failure Failing to distinguish aggressive thymic carcinoma from indolent thymoma Biopsying a potentially resectable encapsulated tumour when upfront resection is preferable Missing associated paraneoplastic cytopenias or immunodeficiency Thymomas are neoplasms of the thymic epithelial cells, typically accompanied by variable numbers of non-neoplastic immature T lymphocytes. They are classified histologically by epithelial morphology and lymphocyte content, while thymic carcinoma shows overt cytological malignancy and loss of organotypic features. The abnormal thymic microenvironment can disrupt immune tolerance, accounting for the frequent paraneoplastic autoimmune phenomena, most notably myasthenia gravis mediated by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Tumours may remain encapsulated or invade the capsule, mediastinal fat, pleura, pericardium, and adjacent great vessels. Encapsulated, completely resected thymomas have an excellent long-term prognosis, whereas invasive tumours and especially thymic carcinoma carry higher recurrence and mortality; degree of invasion and completeness of resection are the key prognostic factors.

on swallowing and on protrusion of the tongue, reflecting its attachment to the tract from the foramen caecum It arises from remnants of the thyroglossal duct along the path of embryological descent of the thyroid gland Cysts may present acutely when they become infected, appearing as a tender, red, sometimes discharging midline mass Before excision it is important to confirm the presence of location Definitive treatment is the Sistrunk operation, which removes the cyst together with the central portion of the hyoid bone and the tract up to the tongue base to minimise recurrence Simple incision or local excision without removing the tract and mid-hyoid leads to high recurrence rates Acute infection with abscess formation requiring drainage and antibiotic treatment A solid or rapidly enlarging component, or the presence of a suspicious nodule, raising the rare possibility of malignancy Evidence that the cyst represents the only functioning thyroid tissue, which contraindicates simple excision Airway compromise from a large lingual or tongue-base lesion Excising the cyst alone without the mid-hyoid and tract, leading to recurrence Operating without first confirming a normally located, functioning thyroid gland Attempting definitive surgery during acute infection rather than controlling infection first Mistaking a midline dermoid or ectopic thyroid for a simple thyroglossal cyst During development the thyroid gland descends from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to its final pretracheal position, leaving behind the thyroglossal duct, which normally involutes. Persistence of epithelial remnants along this tract allows a fluid-filled cyst to form anywhere from the tongue base to the thyroid, but most commonly at or near the hyoid bone. Its intimate relationship with the hyoid explains the movement with swallowing and tongue protrusion, and retained secretions or infection cause enlargement and inflammation. Following a properly performed Sistrunk procedure the outlook is excellent with low recurrence. Recurrence is more likely after inadequate surgery or when a preceding infection has distorted the tissue planes, and malignant change within the cyst is rare.

Thyroid Nodular Disease and Cancer — thyroid nodule, thyroid carcinoma, papillary thyroid cancer, medullary thyroid cancer Benign hyperplastic (colloid) nodule Follicular adenoma Oncocytic (Hurthle cell) adenoma Thyroid cyst (colloid cyst) Multinodular goiter (nodule within an MNG) Toxic adenoma / hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule Noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) - no longer considered malignant Thyroglossal duct cyst / developmental abnormality Thyroid lymphoma Metastasis to the thyroid from another primary Serum TSH (first test in nodule evaluation) Radionuclide (I-123) scan if TSH suppressed, to identify hyperfunctioning 'hot' nodule Thyroid and cervical lymph node ultrasound with risk-stratification (ACR TI-RADS / ATA / EU-TIRADS) Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) with Bethesda System cytology reporting Molecular testing of indeterminate FNA samples (next-generation sequencing, microRNA, gene-expression panels) Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) for surveillance of differentiated cancer after thyroidectomy/ablation Serum calcitonin (and RET mutation testing) for medullary thyroid carcinoma Whole-body radioiodine scan (WBS) for iodine-avid metastases or elevated Tg with negative imaging Neck/chest cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) and PET-CT (18FDG or Ga-68 Dotatate avidity raises malignancy suspicion) Hashimoto's thyroiditis (background for thyroid lymphoma; may produce a goitrous, nodular-feeling gland) Subclinical thyrotoxicosis from autonomous nodule (mimics need for cancer workup but reflects functioning, benign nodule) Hoarseness from gastroesophageal reflux rather than laryngeal nerve invasion by tumor Thyroid nodules are common: ~3-7% of adults by palpation, but up to 50% have nodules on ultrasound, with the majority <1 cm. The vast majority of nodules are benign (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3044, p.3048). Initial workup of a nodule begins with a TSH level. If TSH is suppressed, a radionuclide scan is done; a hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule is almost never malignant, so FNA is unnecessary. Otherwise proceed to thyroid ultrasound (Harrison 22e p.3048). Thyroid ultrasound with a validated risk-stratification system (e.g., ACR TI-RADS, TR1-TR5) is used to decide which nodules need fine-needle aspiration (FNA), combining sonographic pattern with nodule size; more suspicious patterns warrant FNA at lower size cutoffs (Harrison 22e p.3042, p.3048). FNA, ideally ultrasound-guided, is the diagnostic procedure of choice for nodules. Cytology is reported with the six-tier Bethesda System (version 3): benign ~4% malignancy risk, AUS ~22%, follicular neoplasm ~30%, suspicious for malignancy ~74%, malignant ~97% (Harrison 22e p.3044, p.3049). Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) is the most common type (80-85% of well-differentiated cancers); classic and follicular variants are usually indolent, spread mainly via lymphatics, and have an excellent prognosis (>95% present at stage I or II) (Harrison 22e p.3046). Follicular thyroid cancer (FTC) accounts for ~5% of US thyroid cancers and cannot be distinguished from benign follicular lesions by FNA cytology alone; diagnosis requires histologic evidence of capsular and/or vascular invasion (Harrison 22e p.3046-3047, p.3048). Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from calcitonin-producing C cells, accounts for ~5% of thyroid cancers, and can be sporadic or familial (MEN 2A, MEN 2B, familial MTC); elevated serum calcitonin is a marker of residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.3048). All patients with MTC should be tested for RET mutations so that genetic counseling and family testing can be offered; pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery in any patient with a RET mutation (Harrison 22e p.3048). Anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC) is poorly differentiated and aggressive with a bleak prognosis; most patients die within 6 months of diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3040, p.3048). Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a sensitive marker of residual/recurrent disease for PTC, FTC, and oncocytic carcinoma after total thyroidectomy and radioablation, while calcitonin serves this role for MTC (Harrison 22e p.3045, p.3047). Molecular diagnostic panels (next-generation sequencing, microRNA, gene expression) are increasingly used on FNA samples with indeterminate cytology (AUS, follicular neoplasm) to distinguish benign from malignant lesions and reduce unnecessary diagnostic surgery; current validated tests have negative predictive values >95% (Harrison 22e p.3046, p.3050). Nodule fixed to adjacent structures (firm/hard, immobile) Vocal cord paralysis or hoarse voice (suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) Lateral cervical lymphadenopathy ipsilateral to the nodule Rapidly enlarging neck mass Prior head/neck irradiation before age 18 (e.g., mantle radiation for Hodgkin's, cranial radiation for childhood leukemia) Childhood/adolescent exposure to ionizing radiation from fallout Age <20 or >65 years Male gender Family history of PTC in two or more first-degree relatives, MEN 2, or syndromes (Cowden's, familial adenomatous polyposis, Carney complex, PTEN hamartoma) 18FDG or Ga-68 Dotatate PET avidity of the nodule Thyroid cancer is being overdiagnosed: rising incidence is driven by small T1 papillary tumors while disease-specific mortality has not changed in 40 years; routine FNA is not recommended for nodules <1 cm unless metastatic cervical nodes are present. A hyperfunctioning ('hot') nodule on radionuclide scan is almost never malignant; FNA is unnecessary and should not be performed for these. FNA cytology cannot reliably distinguish benign follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma because nuclear features do not differ; the distinction requires histologic evidence of capsular/vascular invasion. LT4 (TSH-suppression) therapy does NOT shrink nodules in iodine-replete (iodine-sufficient) populations and should not be used for that purpose; if it has not reduced nodule size after 6-12 months it should be stopped. Spongiform nodules (TR1) have <3% cancer risk and warrant observation rather than FNA. Iodine-containing contrast agents should be avoided in nodular goiter due to the risk of the Jod-Basedow effect (iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis from autonomous nodules). NIFTP can only be diagnosed on surgical pathology, so it is still included within Bethesda malignancy risk estimates. Hoarseness more commonly reflects benign causes (e.g., reflux) than malignancy, but new vocal cord paralysis is a genuine red flag. In MTC, surgery should not proceed until pheochromocytoma has been excluded in any patient with a RET mutation. For thyroid lymphoma, initial surgical resection should be avoided because it may spread otherwise localized disease. Thyroid nodular disease reflects disordered growth of thyroid cells that may be hyperplastic or neoplastic. Thyroid neoplasms can arise from follicular cells (papillary, follicular, oncocytic, poorly differentiated, anaplastic carcinomas), calcitonin-producing C cells (medullary carcinoma), lymphocytes (lymphoma), or stromal/vascular elements. Cancers are monoclonal, arising from mutations conferring a growth advantage or resistance to cell death. Activation of the RET-RAS-BRAF (MAPK) signaling pathway is seen in up to 70% of PTCs; BRAF V600E mutations occur in up to 60% of PTC, RET rearrangements in ~15% (more frequent after Chernobyl fallout), and RAS mutations in ~15%. FTCs harbor BRAF/RAS mutations plus PAX8-PPARgamma rearrangements (~70% have a mutation/rearrangement). Anaplastic cancers accumulate additional TERT promoter, BRAF, CTNNB1 (beta-catenin), and TP53 mutations driving dedifferentiation and genetic instability. MEN 2-associated MTC carries inherited activating RET point mutations and is preceded by C-cell hyperplasia. External and fallout radiation predispose to chromosomal breaks and increase risk of benign and malignant nodules, especially in children. Most differentiated cancers retain TSH receptor expression and respond to TSH, the basis for both LT4 suppression and radioiodine uptake. Prognosis spans a wide range by histologic type. Differentiated cancers (PTC and FTC) are often curable with good prognosis in early-stage disease; the 20-year disease-specific mortality for low-risk thyroid cancer is ~1%, and most PTC present at stage I/II with survival similar to expected. Mortality rises markedly in stage IV disease, especially with distant metastases (stage IVB, ~1% of patients). FTC, particularly angioinvasive, carries less favorable outcomes than PTC partly due to more stage IV presentation; poor features include distant metastases, age >55, tumor >4 cm, and marked vascular invasion. MTC is more aggressive in MEN 2B than MEN 2A, and familial MTC more aggressive than sporadic. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is aggressive with a bleak prognosis, most patients dying within 6 months. Older age (>65) and male gender are associated with worse outcomes overall. Histologic classification (WHO/Table 397-1): follicular cell-derived (benign follicular/oncocytic adenoma; low-risk neoplasms including NIFTP; malignant - papillary, follicular, oncocytic, differentiated/poorly differentiated high-grade, anaplastic), C-cell-derived medullary carcinoma, mixed medullary-follicular, lymphoma, and others. Staging uses the AJCC/UICC 8th-edition TNM system (tumor size and extrathyroidal invasion, regional nodal metastases, distant metastases) for differentiated and anaplastic cancers. Sonographic risk stratification uses ACR TI-RADS levels TR1 (benign) to TR5 (highly suspicious). FNA cytology uses the six-tier Bethesda System v3 (I nondiagnostic ~13%, II benign ~4%, III AUS ~22%, IV follicular neoplasm ~30%, V suspicious for malignancy ~74%, VI malignant ~97% malignancy risk). MTC risk in MEN 2 is further stratified by specific RET mutation.

syndrome A cause of congenital hypothyroidism in which the thyroid gland is present, often enlarged (goitre), but cannot make hormone normally Usually autosomal recessive, arising from defects in steps of hormone synthesis such as iodide transport, organification (thyroid peroxidase), thyroglobulin, or hydrogen peroxide generation (DUOX2) Detected in many countries through newborn screening impairment A rapidly enlarging or compressive goitre Associated sensorineural hearing loss suggesting Pendred syndrome Severe hypothyroid features such as feeding difficulty and hypotonia in infancy Assuming a present gland excludes a hormone synthesis defect Missing associated deafness in Pendred syndrome Delaying replacement while awaiting confirmatory imaging or genetics in a neonate Under-dosing replacement and allowing persistent goitre or hypothyroidism Thyroid dyshormonogenesis is caused by inherited defects in the enzymatic machinery the thyroid uses to synthesise hormone. Depending on the gene involved, iodide may not be trapped or organified, thyroglobulin may be abnormal, or the hydrogen peroxide needed for organification may be deficient. Impaired hormone output lowers circulating thyroid hormone and, through loss of negative feedback, raises thyroid-stimulating hormone. The resulting chronic stimulation causes the gland to enlarge into a goitre, while the hormone deficiency itself threatens growth and, critically in infancy, neurodevelopment. When congenital hypothyroidism is detected by screening and treated promptly with adequate replacement, growth and neurodevelopment are usually normal; delayed treatment risks permanent cognitive impairment, and the goitre generally regresses once hormone levels are restored.

Thyroid eye disease — thyroid-associated orbitopathy, Graves ophthalmopathy, thyroid orbitopathy, TED, TAO Orbital cellulitis Orbital inflammatory syndrome (orbital pseudotumour) Orbital tumour or lymphoma Carotid-cavernous fistula IgG4-related orbital disease Myasthenia gravis (as a cause of diplopia and lid signs, and a recognised association) Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies including TSH-receptor antibodies Assessment of clinical activity score and disease severity grading Exophthalmometry to quantify proptosis Orbital CT or MRI to assess muscle enlargement and apical crowding Visual acuity, colour vision, visual fields, and pupillary assessment to detect optic neuropathy Ocular motility and diplopia assessment An autoimmune orbitopathy most often associated with Graves disease, though patients may be hyperthyroid, euthyroid, or hypothyroid at presentation Cardinal features include eyelid retraction, lid lag on downgaze, proptosis, restrictive strabismus with diplopia, and ocular surface exposure It follows an active inflammatory phase lasting months to a couple of years, followed by a quiescent fibrotic phase; treatment strategy depends on which phase the patient is in Smoking strongly worsens the disease and its response to treatment, so cessation is a key intervention Disease activity and severity are assessed separately, for example using a clinical activity score and grading of soft tissue, proptosis, motility, corneal, and optic nerve findings Active moderate-to-severe disease is managed with immunosuppression and orbital measures, while stable disease may require rehabilitative surgery in the sequence of orbital decompression, then squint, then eyelid surgery The most feared complication is dysthyroid optic neuropathy from apical crowding, which threatens sight and needs urgent treatment Dysthyroid optic neuropathy with reduced acuity, impaired colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, or disc swelling requiring urgent treatment Corneal exposure or ulceration from severe proptosis and lagophthalmos Rapidly progressive proptosis or globe subluxation Marked orbital congestion with raised intraocular pressure Assuming euthyroid patients cannot have thyroid eye disease and delaying diagnosis Missing early optic neuropathy because central acuity can be preserved while colour vision and fields deteriorate Performing rehabilitative surgery during the active inflammatory phase Neglecting smoking cessation and ocular surface protection Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune inflammatory disorder of the orbit linked to Graves disease. Autoantibodies against the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, expressed on orbital fibroblasts, drive activation and differentiation of these cells. The resulting inflammation causes accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, oedema, and enlargement of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. The expanded orbital contents within a fixed bony cavity produce proptosis, restrictive myopathy, and, when the crowded orbital apex compresses the optic nerve, dysthyroid optic neuropathy. Over time inflammation gives way to fibrosis, leaving fixed muscle restriction and lid changes. Many patients have mild, self-limiting disease, but moderate-to-severe cases can leave lasting proptosis, diplopia, and disfigurement; optic neuropathy risks permanent visual loss if not treated promptly, and smoking cessation improves the overall outlook.

Thyroid Gland Physiology and Testing — Thyroid axis physiology, Thyroid function testing, HPT axis Euthyroid hyperthyroxinemia (familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia, TBG excess, transthyretin variants) with elevated total but normal free T4/T3 Resistance to thyroid hormone (TRbeta mutation) with high free T4/T3 and inappropriately normal/elevated TSH TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma causing inappropriate TSH with high thyroid hormones Sick euthyroid (nonthyroidal illness) syndrome altering TSH and T4-to-T3 conversion MCT8 transporter mutation (X-linked) with low T4, high T3, high TSH and psychomotor retardation Sensitive third-generation TSH immunoradiometric assay (detects to <=0.01 mIU/L) as the screening test Free (unbound) T4 by immunoassay or equilibrium dialysis; free T3 when TSH is suppressed but free T4 is normal (to detect T3 toxicosis) Anti-TPO (and anti-thyroglobulin) antibodies for autoimmune thyroid disease TRAb / thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin assay for Graves' disease and to predict fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis Serum thyroglobulin for thyroiditis and post-thyroidectomy cancer surveillance Radioiodine (123I/131I) uptake and thyroid scan, or 99mTc pertechnetate imaging, to define etiology of thyrotoxicosis Thyroid ultrasound (10-12 MHz) with risk-stratification systems (TI-RADS) and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration for nodules TBG excess from estrogen (pregnancy, oral contraceptives, tamoxifen) raising total T4/T3 while free hormone stays normal TBG deficiency (X-linked) lowering total T4/T3 with normal free levels and euthyroid state Biotin supplement interference falsely lowering TSH and falsely raising T4/T3 in biotinylated assays Drugs displacing hormone from binding proteins (salicylates, salsalate) or impairing T4-to-T3 conversion (propranolol, amiodarone, glucocorticoids, propylthiouracil, oral contrast agents) TSH is the single most useful physiologic marker of thyroid hormone action; because of its long plasma half-life (~50 min) a single measurement reliably reflects circulating levels (p.3021). A normal TSH essentially excludes a primary thyroid abnormality, so the logical first step in evaluation is to determine whether TSH is suppressed, normal, or elevated (p.3026). Primary hyperthyroidism produces a low/suppressed TSH and primary hypothyroidism produces an elevated TSH because thyroid hormone exerts dominant negative feedback on TSH gene expression (p.3021, p.3026). TSH is a glycoprotein with an alpha subunit shared with LH, FSH, and hCG and a unique beta subunit; the structurally similar hCG weakly stimulates the TSH-R, lowering TSH in the first trimester of pregnancy (p.3021, p.3024). T4 is secreted in roughly 15-fold excess over T3 and acts largely as a prohormone, being converted peripherally to the more potent T3 by deiodinases (p.3023-3024). Nuclear thyroid hormone receptors silence target genes when unliganded by binding co-repressors, so hormone deficiency causes both loss of stimulation and active gene repression, giving deficiency a more profound effect than receptor gene deletion (p.3025). About 5-15% of euthyroid women and up to 2% of euthyroid men carry thyroid (anti-TPO) antibodies and are at increased risk of future thyroid dysfunction; nearly all autoimmune hypothyroid patients and up to 80% of Graves' patients have TPO antibodies (p.3026). Functioning (hot) thyroid nodules are almost never malignant and do not require fine-needle aspiration, whereas non-functioning (cold) nodules carry a ~5-10% malignancy risk (p.3026-3027). Serum thyroglobulin is elevated in all forms of thyrotoxicosis except factitious thyrotoxicosis (exogenous hormone), and its principal clinical use is surveillance after thyroidectomy/radioablation for thyroid cancer (p.3026). After total thyroidectomy and radioablation for thyroid cancer, thyroglobulin should be <0.2 ng/mL in the absence of anti-Tg antibodies; a measurable level suggests incomplete ablation or recurrence (p.3026). Retrosternal goiter causing venous distention and dyspnea on raising the arms (Pemberton's sign) Suspicious sonographic nodule features (hypoechoic solid nodule, irregular margins, punctate echogenic microcalcifications) with >90% cancer risk Cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy on thyroid examination suggesting malignancy High maternal TRAb/TSI (>3x upper limit of normal) in the third trimester predicting fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis Untreated maternal/neonatal hypothyroidism in iodine-deficient regions risking cretinism (intellectual disability, growth retardation) Treating low total T4 in TBG deficiency: attempts to normalize total T4 cause thyrotoxicosis and are futile due to rapid clearance. Relying on TSH alone in suspected hypothalamic-pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism, where TSH is inappropriately low-to-normal for a low T4; free T4 must also be measured. Failing to stop biotin supplements >=2 days before testing, leading to falsely low TSH and falsely high T4/T3. Missing T3 toxicosis (2-5% of cases) if only free T4 is checked when TSH is suppressed. Misinterpreting transiently low TSH (0.01-0.1 mIU/L) of early pregnancy, recent hyperthyroidism treatment, or glucocorticoid/dopamine therapy as true thyrotoxicosis. Performing fine-needle aspiration on a hot/functioning nodule, which is almost never malignant; scintigraphy should precede biopsy when TSH is subnormal. Confusing thyroid hormone resistance or a TSH-secreting adenoma with simple primary hyperthyroidism because of elevated hormones with non-suppressed TSH. The hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis is a classic endocrine feedback loop. Hypothalamic TRH stimulates pituitary thyrotrope production of TSH, which binds the TSH-R (a Gs-coupled seven-transmembrane GPCR) on the basolateral surface of thyroid follicular cells, activating adenylyl cyclase/cAMP and phospholipase C to drive gland growth and hormone synthesis. Iodide is actively trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), transported apically via pendrin, and oxidized/organified onto tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase using DUOX-generated hydrogen peroxide; iodotyrosines are coupled to form T4 and T3, which are released after lysosomal proteolysis of reabsorbed thyroglobulin. Circulating hormone is largely protein-bound (TBG, transthyretin, albumin) with only the small unbound fraction biologically available; deiodinases (types I, II, III) regulate peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3 or inactivating reverse T3. T3 acts mainly through nuclear receptors TRalpha and TRbeta, which heterodimerize with RXR on thyroid response elements, exchanging co-repressors for co-activators upon ligand binding. Thyroid hormones feed back, predominantly via TRbeta2 in hypothalamus and pituitary, to suppress TRH and TSH, establishing the axis set point. Most physiologic and binding-protein variants (TBG abnormalities, familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia, classic TRbeta resistance) are benign and require no treatment once recognized, the main goal being avoidance of inappropriate therapy. Early thyroid hormone replacement in congenital hypothyroidism prevents severe developmental abnormality, whereas untreated iodine deficiency in early life causes irreversible cretinism and even mild deficiency can subtly reduce IQ. Not applicable as a discrete disease; thyroid status is categorized biochemically by TSH and free hormone levels into euthyroid, subclinical hypo-/hyperthyroidism (abnormal TSH with normal free hormones), and overt hypo-/hyperthyroidism (abnormal TSH with abnormal free hormones), with trimester-specific reference ranges applied in pregnancy.

the transporter needed to deliver hormone to neurones is defective Diagnosis should be considered in any boy with unexplained developmental delay and this distinctive thyroid function profile Failure to thrive with a hypermetabolic state despite apparent hypothyroid features Progressive spasticity and loss of developmental milestones Recurrent aspiration or feeding difficulty from severe hypotonia Misdiagnosis leading to inappropriate high-dose thyroxine that worsens thyrotoxic effects Mistaking the raised triiodothyronine for ordinary thyrotoxicosis and treating with antithyroid drugs Giving standard levothyroxine and expecting neurological improvement Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy labelled as cerebral palsy Failing to recognise and manage the peripheral hypermetabolic state MCT8, encoded by SLC16A2 on the X chromosome, is a transmembrane transporter that moves thyroid hormone into cells, and it is critical for delivering hormone across the blood-brain barrier and into neurones. When it is defective, thyroid hormone cannot reach the developing brain, producing a state of cerebral hypothyroidism and severe neurodevelopmental impairment. At the same time excess hormone circulates and enters tissues that rely on other transporters, and increased peripheral conversion generates high triiodothyronine, giving a thyrotoxic effect on tissues such as muscle and driving the paradoxical thyroid function tests. The neurodevelopmental impairment is severe and largely irreversible, and most affected boys have profound disability; management is supportive, and experimental thyroid hormone analogues aim mainly to reduce the peripheral thyrotoxic burden rather than restore neurological function.

Thyroid nodule — thyroid lump, solitary thyroid nodule, thyroid mass, nodular goitre Benign colloid or hyperplastic nodule Follicular adenoma Differentiated thyroid carcinoma (papillary or follicular) Medullary or anaplastic thyroid carcinoma Thyroid cyst or focal thyroiditis Parathyroid or other neck mass mimicking a thyroid nodule Serum TSH as the first-line test Thyroid ultrasound to characterise the nodule and assess cervical lymph nodes Radionuclide thyroid scan when TSH is suppressed Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology Molecular marker testing for indeterminate cytology Serum calcitonin when medullary carcinoma is suspected Thyroid nodules are common and usually benign, but the central task is to identify the minority that are malignant Initial evaluation begins with a serum TSH; a suppressed value points towards an autonomously functioning (usually benign) nodule and warrants a radionuclide scan Ultrasound characterises nodules and stratifies malignancy risk, with features such as marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, and a taller-than-wide shape raising concern Fine-needle aspiration is the key diagnostic test, with results reported using standardised cytology categories that guide management Hot (functioning) nodules on scanning rarely harbour malignancy, so aspiration is generally directed at non-functioning nodules History of childhood neck irradiation, family history of thyroid cancer, rapid growth, hoarseness, or fixed hard nodules increase suspicion of cancer Molecular testing of indeterminate cytology samples can refine the risk of malignancy and help avoid unnecessary surgery Rapidly enlarging, hard, or fixed nodule New hoarseness or vocal cord palsy suggesting recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement Cervical lymphadenopathy History of head and neck irradiation or family history of thyroid cancer or MEN syndromes Compressive symptoms such as dysphagia or stridor Proceeding to biopsy before checking TSH and missing an autonomous nodule that does not need aspiration Relying on nodule size alone rather than sonographic risk features to decide on aspiration Falsely reassuring the patient after a non-diagnostic aspirate without repeating sampling Overlooking calcitonin measurement when clinical features suggest medullary carcinoma Thyroid nodules arise from focal proliferation of follicular cells and may be colloid nodules, adenomas, cysts, areas of thyroiditis, or carcinomas. Autonomously functioning nodules develop constitutive activation of thyroid hormone production, often through activating mutations of the TSH-receptor or G-protein signalling pathway, suppressing TSH and appearing 'hot' on scanning. Malignant nodules result from oncogenic alterations (for example in the MAPK pathway) driving unregulated growth, and their behaviour ranges from indolent differentiated cancers to aggressive anaplastic disease. Most nodules are benign and can be followed conservatively, and even most malignant nodules are differentiated cancers with an excellent prognosis after treatment, though anaplastic and some medullary cancers carry a poor outlook.

Thyroid storm — TFTs (TSH↓, free T4/T3↑) ECG Burch-Wartofsky score Life-threatening — beta-blockade, antithyroid drugs Other causes of thyrotoxicosis besides Graves' disease must be considered (e.g. toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre, destructive thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis); radionuclide scan/uptake or color-flow Doppler ultrasonography helps distinguish hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.3078). Suppressed TSH with elevated total and unbound (free) T4 and T3 (Harrison 22e p.3078). T3 toxicosis (only T3 raised) in 2-5% of patients, more in areas of borderline iodine intake; T4 toxicosis (raised T4, normal T3) is occasionally seen when hyperthyroidism is iodine-induced (Harrison 22e p.3078). TRAb (TSH receptor antibody) measurement to support a diagnosis of Graves' disease (Harrison 22e p.3078). Watch for confounding biochemistry: elevated bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, plus microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, may accompany thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3078). Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm) is a rare, life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3080). Characteristic features include fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea and jaundice (Harrison 22e p.3080). Often precipitated by an acute intercurrent illness (e.g. stroke, infection, trauma, diabetic ketoacidosis), by surgery (especially thyroid surgery), or by radioiodine treatment given to a patient whose hyperthyroidism is only partially treated or untreated (Harrison 22e p.3080). Apathetic thyrotoxicosis: in the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss, and can be mistaken for depression (Harrison 22e p.3076). Thyrotoxicosis may be complicated by a form of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, particularly common in Asian males (Harrison 22e p.3076). Treatment of the thyrotoxic state alone restores sinus rhythm in up to 75% of patients with thyrotoxicosis-associated atrial fibrillation who have no underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3077). Fever, delirium, seizures or coma in a thyrotoxic patient indicate thyroid storm (Harrison 22e p.3080). Death is most often due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080). Radioiodine therapy in a patient with partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism can itself precipitate thyrotoxic crisis (Harrison 22e p.3080). In the elderly, thyrotoxicosis may be masked (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), delaying recognition (Harrison 22e p.3076). Thyroid storm represents a severe, decompensated form of thyroid hormone excess (thyrotoxicosis), typically arising when an acute stressor is superimposed on partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism. Excess circulating thyroid hormone drives a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic state; high cardiac output produces a bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and may precipitate or worsen heart failure or angina, particularly in the elderly or those with pre-existing heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3077, p.3080). Mortality remains high (4-17%) even with treatment, usually from cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).

Transient ischaemic attack — Urgent CT/MRI + carotid imaging ECG (AF) ABCD² risk; start antiplatelet/statin High early stroke risk — urgent TIA clinic / admission Seizure (esp. ongoing focal seizure without convulsive activity) — positive symptoms and a marching spread over seconds favour seizure (p.3378, p.3428) Migraine, including acephalgic migraine even in older first-time patients — slower march over minutes with headache, nausea or scintillating visual symptoms (p.3428) Intracranial tumour presenting acutely via haemorrhage, seizure or hydrocephalus (p.3428) Metabolic encephalopathy — fluctuating mental status without focal findings (p.3428) Stroke recrudescence — fever/sepsis unmasking a prior deficit that clears as infection is treated (p.3428) CT- or MRI-based angiography of neck and intracranial vessels to assess large-vessel stenosis/occlusion (MRA is highly sensitive for extracranial carotid stenosis but tends to overestimate severity) (p.3445, p.3430) Echocardiography (transthoracic or transoesophageal), with bubble-contrast/agitated-saline study to detect right-to-left shunt (PFO/ASD) for suspected paradoxical embolism (p.3445) Cardiac telemetry following the initial ECG; ambulatory/prolonged ECG monitoring to detect intermittent atrial fibrillation if none is found in hospital (p.3445) Retinal/funduscopic exam for cholesterol (Hollenhorst) plaques and examination of cervical/peripheral vessels and heart (p.3445) Baseline labs: CBC, ESR, electrolytes, glucose, lipid profile, creatinine/BUN, PT/PTT, urinalysis, chest x-ray (p.3445) Seizure (focal, may mimic transient deficit) (p.3378, p.3428) Migraine / acephalgic migraine with transient aura (p.3428) Syncope from systemic hypotension (cardiac arrhythmia, sepsis, haemorrhagic shock) (p.3428) Metabolic encephalopathy (p.3428) TIA classically produces 'negative' symptoms (transient loss of function); positive sensory symptoms or involuntary movements point instead to seizure (p.3378). Most TIAs last under 1 hour, well within the historical 24-hour window (p.3448). About 25% of symptomatic internal carotid disease is heralded by recurrent transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), typically described as a horizontal shade sweeping down or up across one eye, lasting a few minutes (p.3430). A high-pitched carotid bruit fading into diastole suggests a tight stenosis; paradoxically the bruit may fade or vanish as occlusion becomes imminent and flow drops (p.3430). Causes of TIA and ischaemic stroke are identical, so the diagnostic evaluation of a TIA should parallel that of a completed stroke (p.3448). Most strokes after a TIA occur within the first 2 days — the early window is the highest-risk period and warrants urgent (not deferred) workup (p.3448) Stuttering or crescendo course of small-vessel TIAs heralding lacunar infarct can progress to severe permanent disability (p.3447) Amaurosis fugax indicates a symptomatic internal carotid source needing prompt carotid evaluation (p.3430) A TIA is a clinical diagnosis: a normal brain imaging study does NOT rule it out (p.3448). If a relevant infarction is seen on imaging, the event is reclassified as a stroke regardless of how briefly symptoms lasted — the modern definition is tissue-based, not purely time-based (p.3428, p.3448). Patients with carotid/vertebrobasilar TIA may report symptoms 'in one eye' when the deficit is actually a homonymous hemifield loss affecting both eyes (p.3430-equivalent / cortical visual TIA). Acephalgic migraine can mimic TIA even with no prior migraine history and even after age 65 (p.3428). A TIA results from transient focal cerebral ischaemia when blood flow falls for longer than several seconds; neurons lack glycogen so deficits appear within seconds, but because the occluded vessel reopens and flow is restored before infarction occurs, symptoms resolve completely. Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: emboli to the brain (cardiac or proximal arterial source) or in-situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel. Small-vessel (lacunar) TIAs may recur several times a day and last only minutes (Harrison 22e p.3428, 3448, 3447). Stroke risk after a TIA is approximately 10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 2 days; this early risk is well predicted by the ABCD2 score, so urgent evaluation and treatment are justified (Harrison 22e p.3448). ABCD2 score (Harrison 22e p.3448) stratifies early stroke risk after TIA: 1 point each for Age >=60, BP (SBP >140 or DBP >90 mmHg), and Diabetes; for Clinical features 2 points for unilateral weakness or 1 for speech disturbance without weakness; for Duration 2 points for >=60 min or 1 for 10-59 min. The 3-month stroke rate rises with the total: ~0% at score 0-1, ~3% at 2-3, ~8% at 4, ~12% at 5, ~17% at 6, and ~22% at 7.

Timothy syndrome — CACNA1C-related disorder, long QT syndrome type 8, LQT8, Timothy syndrome type 1 Other genetic long QT syndrome subtypes Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome Andersen-Tawil syndrome Other syndromic causes of syndactyly with cardiac disease Congenital heart block from other causes 12-lead ECG demonstrating marked QT prolongation and any functional 2:1 atrioventricular block Ambulatory monitoring for ventricular arrhythmia Echocardiography for associated congenital heart defects Genetic testing for CACNA1C variants Developmental and neurological assessment Evaluation of immune function, glucose homeostasis and dental health as indicated A rare multisystem disorder caused by gain-of-function variants in the L-type calcium channel gene CACNA1C, classified as long QT syndrome type 8 Marked QT prolongation predisposes to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, often in infancy or early childhood Extracardiac features commonly include cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and toes, facial dysmorphism, and neurodevelopmental problems such as autism spectrum features Congenital heart defects, immune dysfunction, hypoglycaemia and dental abnormalities can also occur The classic form usually arises from de novo variants, so a negative family history does not exclude it Management focuses on preventing arrhythmia with beta-blockers, careful avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and an implantable cardioverter defibrillator in high-risk children Functional 2:1 atrioventricular block can occur because the very long ventricular repolarisation leaves the ventricle refractory to alternate atrial beats Care is multidisciplinary given the cardiac, developmental and systemic involvement Marked QT prolongation with syncope or documented ventricular arrhythmia Functional 2:1 atrioventricular block in an infant Aborted cardiac arrest Syndactyly with cardiac and neurodevelopmental features prompting urgent cardiac evaluation Assuming a negative family history excludes the diagnosis, when most cases are de novo Attributing an infant's QT prolongation to reversible causes and missing the genetic syndrome Focusing on the cardiac problem and overlooking the syndactyly and developmental clues Using QT-prolonging medications that can precipitate torsades Underestimating the systemic and immune complications Timothy syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants in CACNA1C, which encodes the pore-forming subunit of the L-type calcium channel (CaV1.2). The variants impair voltage-dependent inactivation of the channel, so calcium entry into cells is prolonged. In cardiomyocytes this lengthens the action potential and markedly prolongs the QT interval, promoting early afterdepolarisations and torsades-de-pointes ventricular arrhythmia. Because CaV1.2 is expressed widely, the same channel dysfunction disrupts development and function of other tissues, producing the syndactyly, neurodevelopmental, immune and other systemic features that distinguish the syndrome from isolated long QT syndrome. Timothy syndrome carries a high risk of early sudden death from malignant ventricular arrhythmia, and survivors face substantial neurodevelopmental and systemic morbidity; multidisciplinary care and arrhythmia prevention improve but do not eliminate the risk.

Tinea Versicolor — pityriasis versicolor, PV, Malassezia infection Vitiligo (complete depigmentation without scale) Pityriasis alba Post-inflammatory hypo- or hyperpigmentation Seborrhoeic dermatitis Tinea corporis due to a true dermatophyte Erythrasma or, when hypopigmented patches are extensive, early indeterminate leprosy in endemic areas Usually clinical, confirmed by microscopy of skin scrapings showing hyphae and spores Wood's lamp examination for characteristic fluorescence Culture is generally unnecessary because the organism is a normal commensal Consideration of underlying immunosuppression or endocrine factors in extensive or recalcitrant disease Presents as multiple well-defined oval macules and patches on the upper trunk, shoulders, and neck, which coalesce and carry a fine, powdery scale revealed by gently stretching or scratching the skin Lesions vary in colour, appearing hypopigmented on tanned or darker skin and pink-brown on paler skin, which explains the name versicolor It is caused by an overgrowth of commensal Malassezia yeast rather than a true dermatophyte, so despite the name it is not classic ringworm Warmth, humidity, sweating, oily skin, and immunosuppression favour the shift from yeast to the pathogenic filamentous form Microscopy of scale shows the typical spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern of short hyphae and spores, confirming the diagnosis Treatment relies on topical antifungal or keratolytic agents, with systemic antifungals reserved for extensive or recurrent disease; recurrence is common and prophylactic regimens may be needed Warn patients that pigmentary changes can persist for weeks to months after successful treatment, as this does not indicate treatment failure A Wood's lamp may show a coppery-orange or pale fluorescence, aiding assessment Widespread or unusually treatment-resistant disease prompting evaluation for immunosuppression Persistent hypopigmented patches that lack scale and could represent another disorder such as vitiligo or, in endemic settings, leprosy Signs of deeper Malassezia infection such as folliculitis with pustules in an immunocompromised patient Interpreting residual hypopigmentation after treatment as treatment failure Confusing hypopigmented patches with vitiligo and omitting to examine for scale Failing to counsel about the high recurrence rate and the role of maintenance therapy Overlooking predisposing factors such as heat, humidity, or immunosuppression that drive relapse Tinea versicolor results from overgrowth of lipophilic Malassezia yeasts that are normal residents of sebum-rich skin. Under predisposing conditions such as heat, humidity, occlusion, and increased sebum, the yeast converts to its hyphal, pathogenic form and proliferates within the stratum corneum. The organism produces dicarboxylic acids, notably azelaic acid, that inhibit melanocyte tyrosinase and cause the hypopigmented patches, while an associated low-grade inflammatory and hyperkeratotic response produces the scale and, in some, hyperpigmentation. Because the yeast is part of the normal flora, the condition is more a disturbance of host-commensal balance than a transmissible infection, and it readily recurs. The condition is benign and responds well to antifungal therapy, but recurrence is frequent because the causative yeast is part of the normal skin flora and predisposing conditions persist; residual pigmentary change resolves gradually over weeks to months once treated.

Tinnitus — ringing in the ears, subjective tinnitus, objective tinnitus Noise-induced or age-related sensorineural hearing loss Meniere disease Ototoxicity from drugs Otosclerosis or middle ear effusion Acoustic neuroma or other retrocochlear lesion Vascular causes (glomus tumour, arteriovenous malformation, carotid or dural sinus disease) Palatal or middle ear myoclonus and patulous Eustachian tube Otoscopy and pure tone audiometry to characterise associated hearing loss Tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing where middle ear or myoclonic causes are suspected Tinnitus pitch and loudness matching for assessment and rehabilitation MRI of the internal auditory meatus for unilateral or asymmetrical tinnitus CT/MR angiography or venography for pulsatile tinnitus Blood tests for anaemia, thyroid dysfunction or vascular risk factors where clinically indicated Tinnitus is the perception of sound in the absence of an external source and is a symptom rather than a disease in itself It is usefully divided into subjective tinnitus, heard only by the patient, and the much rarer objective tinnitus, which can also be detected by the examiner Most subjective tinnitus accompanies sensorineural hearing loss from noise exposure, presbycusis, ototoxic drugs or Meniere disease Pulsatile tinnitus that is synchronous with the heartbeat suggests a vascular cause such as a glomus tumour, an arteriovenous malformation or a dural sinus abnormality and needs vascular imaging Rhythmic clicking that is not pulse-synchronous may be due to palatal or middle ear muscle myoclonus or a patulous Eustachian tube Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetrical hearing loss should prompt evaluation for a retrocochlear lesion such as an acoustic neuroma Aggravating factors such as ototoxic and other implicated medications, caffeine, stress and poor sleep should be reviewed Because there is often no curative treatment, management centres on treating any underlying cause, hearing aids or sound therapy for masking, and cognitive and habituation-based approaches such as tinnitus retraining therapy Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetrical hearing loss suggesting a retrocochlear tumour Pulsatile tinnitus requiring vascular imaging to exclude a treatable vascular lesion Associated neurological signs, facial numbness or weakness Sudden hearing loss accompanying the tinnitus, which is an emergency Tinnitus with severe distress, depression or suicidal ideation needing urgent mental health support Missing an acoustic neuroma behind unilateral tinnitus Failing to image pulsatile tinnitus for a vascular source Dismissing the symptom without exploring its psychological impact and sleep disturbance Overlooking ototoxic medication or reversible contributors Promising a cure rather than framing management around control and habituation Subjective tinnitus is thought to arise from aberrant neural activity generated when the cochlea or auditory nerve is damaged; loss of input leads to maladaptive changes and increased spontaneous firing and reorganisation in the central auditory pathways, so the brain perceives sound that is not present. Emotional and attentional networks amplify and sustain the perception, which explains why distress and the loudness of tinnitus are only loosely related. Objective tinnitus, in contrast, has a genuine internal acoustic source: turbulent or pulsatile blood flow in vascular lesions, or repetitive contraction of palatal, tensor tympani or stapedius muscles, generates a real sound transmitted to the ear. Many patients habituate over time and cope well with reassurance, sound enrichment and psychological approaches, and tinnitus linked to a treatable cause may improve when that cause is addressed; however, some individuals have persistent, distressing tinnitus that requires ongoing support.

Temporomandibular joint disorder — TMD, temporomandibular disorder, TMJ dysfunction, myofascial pain dysfunction Odontogenic pain from pulpal or periapical disease Otitis or other ear pathology Trigeminal neuralgia or other neuropathic facial pain Giant cell (temporal) arteritis in older patients Salivary gland disease Referred pain from cervical spine or headache disorders Clinical assessment of jaw movement, joint sounds, and muscle tenderness Evaluation of occlusion and parafunctional habits MRI for suspected internal derangement when symptoms persist CT or cone-beam imaging for bony or degenerative joint changes Inflammatory markers if temporal arteritis is a concern in older patients Temporomandibular disorders are a group of musculoskeletal conditions affecting the jaw joints, the muscles of mastication, or both Typical features are jaw pain, joint sounds such as clicking or crepitus, limited or deviated mouth opening, and pain on chewing Pain is often localised to the preauricular region and may radiate to the temple, ear, or face, and can mimic ear or dental pathology Most cases are muscular (myofascial) rather than intra-articular, and parafunctional habits like clenching and grinding are common contributors Disc displacement with reduction typically produces reciprocal clicking, whereas displacement without reduction causes locking and restricted opening It is largely a clinical diagnosis; imaging is reserved for atypical, persistent, or red-flag presentations Initial management is conservative, including reassurance, jaw rest, soft diet, physiotherapy, occlusal splints, and stress and habit control Psychological factors, stress, and chronic pain behaviours strongly influence symptoms and treatment response New onset facial pain with headache, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms in an older patient suggesting giant cell arteritis Progressive limitation of opening, a hard end-feel, or a mass suggesting joint ankylosis or neoplasia Unilateral worsening symptoms with cranial nerve signs pointing to a sinister cause Recent significant trauma raising the possibility of condylar fracture Proceeding to irreversible occlusal or surgical treatment before trying conservative care Missing giant cell arteritis in an older patient with jaw and temporal symptoms Attributing all facial pain to the joint and overlooking dental or neuropathic causes Neglecting parafunctional habits and psychosocial factors that drive symptoms Temporomandibular disorders arise from a multifactorial interplay of biomechanical overload, parafunctional habits, trauma, and psychosocial stress acting on the masticatory system. Sustained muscle hyperactivity from clenching or grinding produces myofascial pain and fatigue, while abnormal loading and internal derangement of the joint can disturb the normal disc-condyle relationship, causing clicking, locking, or degenerative change. Central sensitisation and psychological factors can amplify and perpetuate pain. The result is a spectrum ranging from purely muscular pain to intra-articular disc displacement and degenerative joint disease. Most patients improve with conservative, reversible measures and the condition often follows a self-limiting or fluctuating course, though a minority develop chronic pain or progressive degenerative joint change.

fever Hyper-IgD syndrome / mevalonate kinase deficiency Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult-onset Still disease Cyclical or infective causes of recurrent fever Inflammatory bowel disease presenting with recurrent abdominal pain and fever Acute phase reactants (C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A) during and between attacks Genetic testing of TNFRSF1A Full blood count showing neutrophilia during attacks Urinalysis for proteinuria as an early marker of AA amyloidosis Serum immunoglobulins including IgD to help distinguish related syndromes Tissue biopsy with amyloid staining where amyloidosis is suspected An autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in TNFRSF1A, encoding the type 1 tumour necrosis factor receptor Fever episodes are characteristically prolonged, often lasting one to three weeks, distinguishing it from the shorter attacks of other periodic fever syndromes A migratory, tender erythematous rash overlying underlying myalgia, typically moving distally along a limb, is a suggestive feature Periorbital oedema with conjunctivitis or periorbital pain is a classic ocular manifestation Attacks commonly include serositis (abdominal and chest pain), arthralgia and monocytic fasciitis AA (secondary) amyloidosis is the major long-term complication, driven by chronic inflammation, and warrants surveillance Therapy is directed at the interleukin-1 axis and, in some cases, interleukin-6 blockade, whereas continuous tumour necrosis factor inhibition has been less reliably effective New or increasing proteinuria suggesting evolving AA amyloidosis Persistently elevated inflammatory markers between attacks indicating uncontrolled subclinical inflammation Severe serositis mimicking an acute surgical abdomen Progressive renal impairment Expecting brief attacks and dismissing TRAPS because fevers are unusually prolonged Failing to monitor for proteinuria and missing early amyloidosis Assuming tumour necrosis factor blockade is always effective, when interleukin-1 targeting is often preferred Repeated surgery for recurrent serositis mistaken for a surgical abdomen TRAPS is an autosomal dominant autoinflammatory syndrome caused by mutations in TNFRSF1A, the gene for the 55-kDa tumour necrosis factor receptor 1. Rather than a simple loss of receptor shedding, the mutant receptor misfolds and is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum, provoking a cellular stress response, enhanced production of reactive oxygen species, and ligand-independent, exaggerated pro-inflammatory signalling. This drives excess innate cytokine output, particularly along the interleukin-1 pathway, producing recurrent systemic inflammation. Persistent elevation of acute phase proteins over years predisposes to deposition of serum amyloid A protein in tissues and the development of AA amyloidosis. With effective anti-inflammatory therapy attacks can be controlled and quality of life preserved, but untreated or poorly controlled disease carries a meaningful risk of AA amyloidosis and consequent renal failure, which is the principal determinant of long-term outcome.

Tourette syndrome — Tourette's disorder, Gilles de la Tourette syndrome, TS Provisional (transient) tic disorder or persistent motor or vocal tic disorder Stereotypic movement disorder Myoclonus, dystonia, or chorea from a neurological cause Obsessive-compulsive disorder with compulsions resembling tics Medication-induced or substance-induced movement disorder Functional (psychogenic) movement disorder Detailed clinical history and observation of tics over time Screening for comorbid ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety, and mood disorders Standardised tic severity rating scales to monitor course Neurological examination to exclude other movement disorders Further neurological workup only if atypical features suggest a secondary cause The diagnosis requires both multiple motor tics and one or more vocal (phonic) tics, present at some time during the illness, with onset before age 18 and persistence for more than a year Tics are sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic movements or vocalisations that wax and wane in severity and often shift in type over time Many patients experience premonitory urges, an uncomfortable sensation relieved by performing the tic, and can suppress tics temporarily at the cost of rising inner tension Coprolalia, the involuntary utterance of obscenities, is popularly associated with the condition but actually occurs in only a minority of patients Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, particularly attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder, which often cause more impairment than the tics Behavioural treatment, especially comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics including habit reversal training, is first-line; medication is reserved for troublesome tics Pharmacological options for severe tics include agents acting on dopaminergic transmission and certain alpha-adrenergic agents, chosen by symptom burden and comorbidity Psychoeducation, school liaison, and treating comorbid conditions usually improve function more than suppressing the tics themselves Self-injurious tics causing physical harm Abrupt, explosive onset or neurological signs suggesting a secondary or acquired cause Severe comorbid depression with suicidal ideation Marked functional deterioration from comorbid ADHD or obsessive-compulsive symptoms Focusing on tic suppression while neglecting more impairing comorbid ADHD or obsessive-compulsive disorder Assuming coprolalia is required for diagnosis when it is uncommon Overmedicating mild tics that do not warrant pharmacotherapy Misinterpreting suppressible tics as voluntary or attention-seeking Missing an atypical presentation that points to a secondary movement disorder Tourette syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder involving dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, with abnormalities in dopaminergic neurotransmission within the basal ganglia thought to underlie the generation of tics. It is highly heritable with a complex polygenic basis, and environmental and possibly immune-mediated factors may modulate expression, while overlapping circuitry accounts for the frequent association with obsessive-compulsive and attentional symptoms. Tics typically emerge in childhood, peak in severity in early adolescence, and then decline in many patients, with a substantial proportion experiencing marked improvement or near-resolution by adulthood. Prognosis for overall function depends heavily on comorbid conditions, which often persist and drive impairment, so their recognition and treatment strongly influence outcome.

Toxic and Drug-Induced Hepatitis — Drug-induced liver injury, DILI, Hepatotoxicity, Toxic hepatitis Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C) - idiosyncratic hepatocellular DILI can be clinically and histologically indistinguishable Autoimmune hepatitis (especially with nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) Alcoholic hepatitis (amiodarone produces a pseudoalcoholic picture) Ischemic hepatitis / shock liver Biliary obstruction and primary sclerosing cholangitis (DILI can mimic sclerosing cholangitis after floxuridine or long-term ketamine) Cholestasis of pregnancy (shares genetic canalicular transporter defects with estrogen-induced cholestasis) Acute viral hepatitis A, B, and C Serial ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin to define pattern and compute the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of upper limit of normal) Serum acetaminophen level timed 4-8 h after ingestion, interpreted against the treatment nomogram (levels above 300 mcg/mL at 4 h predict severe injury; below 150 mcg/mL injury unlikely) Acetaminophen-protein (acetaminophen-Cys) adduct measurement by HPLC as an investigational diagnostic marker Arterial blood lactate in acute liver failure (above 3.5 mmol/L suggests likely need for transplantation) Autoantibodies (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-LKM2, anti-mitochondrial) when an autoimmune-pattern or checkpoint-inhibitor injury is suspected Liver biopsy when the pattern is uncertain (may show centrilobular necrosis, microvesicular steatosis, granulomas, phospholipid-laden lamellar bodies in amiodarone, or vanishing bile ducts) Exclusion of viral, autoimmune and biliary causes; structured causality assessment (DILIN expert opinion, RUCAM, or newer RECAM) Autoimmune hepatitis Alcoholic / nonalcoholic steatohepatitis Ischemic hepatopathy Mechanical biliary obstruction Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is the single most common cause of acute liver failure, and hepatotoxicity signals are the leading reason candidate compounds fail to gain approval during drug development; a meticulous history covering prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, dietary, occupational and household chemical exposures is essential (Harrison 22e p.2665). Two broad categories are recognized: direct (intrinsic) toxic injury, which is predictable, dose-dependent and has a short latency (often hours), and idiosyncratic injury, which is infrequent (roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100,000 exposures), less clearly dose-related and typically appears 5-90 days after starting the drug (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666). The R value, the ratio of ALT to alkaline phosphatase (each as a multiple of the upper limit of normal), classifies the injury pattern: R greater than 5 indicates hepatocellular injury, R less than 2 indicates cholestatic injury, and R of 2-5 indicates a mixed pattern (Harrison 22e p.2667). Hy's Law, named for Hyman Zimmerman, holds that drug-induced jaundice during a trial predicts serious liver injury, with roughly a 10-to-1 ratio of jaundiced cases to cases of acute liver failure; such cases often portend failure of drug approval (Harrison 22e p.2667). Acetaminophen is the prototypic direct hepatotoxin and the most prevalent cause of acute liver failure in the Western world; it produces dose-related centrilobular necrosis, and aminotransferases can exceed 10,000 IU/L, far above levels seen in viral hepatitis, often with a relatively low bilirubin in this hyperacute injury (Harrison 22e p.2668). A characteristic biochemical clue to acetaminophen toxicity is the combination of extremely high aminotransferases with low bilirubin; clinical suspicion should prompt empiric N-acetylcysteine even before history is confirmed, since denial or altered mentation can obscure the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2668). Isoniazid causes transient mild aminotransferase elevation in about 10% of recipients early in therapy (an 'adaptive' response that usually resolves despite continued use); clinically significant hepatocellular injury can appear over a latency of up to 6 months and rises sharply with age, being highest in those over 50 and lowest in those under 20 (Harrison 22e p.2670). Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the most commonly implicated single agent in DILI in the United States and Europe, producing a fairly specific mixed or predominantly cholestatic injury that may begin after the drug has already been stopped owing to a long latency (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671). Complementary and alternative medicines, including herbal and dietary weight-loss and body-building products, now account for more than 20% of DILI cases in the United States; implicated agents include green tea extract (Camellia sinensis), kava, germander, chaparral, comfrey (pyrrolizidine alkaloids), Hydroxycut and OxyElite Pro (Harrison 22e p.2671). Certain drugs produce an autoimmune-hepatitis-like phenotype with positive antinuclear antibodies, classically nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine and alpha-methyldopa (Harrison 22e p.2667, 2670-2671). Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab; anti-PD-1 pembrolizumab and nivolumab) cause an immune-mediated hepatitis within weeks, often ANA-positive, mediated predominantly by CD8+ lymphocytes and responsive to glucocorticoids; concurrent immune injury to thyroid, muscle and colon may occur (Harrison 22e p.2671-2672). Withdrawal of the suspected agent at the first sign of an adverse reaction, or when aminotransferases reach five times the upper limit of normal, is critical, because continued use despite symptoms and signs is associated with lethal outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2668).
