causality is hard to prove and many disorders produce an identical clinicopathologic picture Mild transient aminotransferase elevations that resolve during continued therapy ('adaptation,' seen with isoniazid, valproate, phenytoin and statins) can be mistaken for significant toxicity Long latency drugs (notably amoxicillin-clavulanate and nitrofurantoin) may cause injury that manifests only after the drug has been stopped Idiosyncratic reactions occurring in under 1 in 10,000 recipients are missed by clinical trials and only detected through postmarketing surveillance (e.g., troglitazone) In chronic alcohol users, glutathione depletion and CYP2E1 induction can make the toxic acetaminophen dose as low as 2 g Activated charcoal or cholestyramine are ineffective if given more than 30 minutes after acetaminophen ingestion Routine liver test monitoring during statin therapy is not recommended, and asymptomatic isolated aminotransferase elevations need not prompt discontinuation Herbal/dietary supplements may contain undeclared pharmaceuticals (e.g., diclofenac in antirheumatic 'herbs'), so the history must specifically probe alternative-medicine use Hepatotoxicity arises from direct hepatocyte injury (free radicals or reactive metabolites causing membrane lipid peroxidation) or from drug/metabolite activation of innate or adaptive immune pathways, apoptotic signaling, and disruption of bile excretory transport. Interference with canalicular pumps allows injurious endogenous bile acids to accumulate, producing cholestasis; other mechanisms inhibit protein synthesis or impair mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, leading to lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Most drugs are metabolized via phase I cytochrome P450 (oxidation) followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation; most toxicity reflects formation of a reactive phase I metabolite, with glutathione depletion removing a protective pathway. For acetaminophen, phase II conjugation yields harmless metabolites, but a fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the toxic intermediate NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione; when glutathione is overwhelmed or depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive necrosis. Susceptibility to idiosyncratic injury is influenced by HLA haplotypes (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, flucloxacillin), polymorphisms in metabolizing pathways and protective cytokines, and activation of nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR. Factors potentiating acetaminophen injury include enzyme induction (alcohol via CYP2E1, phenobarbital, isoniazid), fasting/starvation and other states that lower hepatic glutathione (Harrison 22e p.2665-2666, 2668-2670). Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after withdrawal of the offending agent. Acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and over 40% of those patients undergo liver transplantation. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have lasting liver injury, though the associated acute kidney injury (seen in nearly 75% of severe cases) is almost always self-limited. Anabolic steroid cholestasis typically resolves over weeks to months with prolonged jaundice. Some agents cause chronic injury: methotrexate, tamoxifen and amiodarone can lead to cirrhosis, and several drugs cause chronic autoimmune-like hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.2668-2670). Injury pattern is graded by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): hepatocellular (R > 5), cholestatic (R < 2), or mixed (R 2-5). Severity is judged clinically by progression to acute liver failure (coagulopathy plus encephalopathy). Causality likelihood is assessed by structured tools including the DILIN expert-opinion scale (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely), RUCAM, and the newer RECAM. Hy's Law identifies high-risk hepatocellular injury when jaundice accompanies hepatocellular enzyme elevation (Harrison 22e p.2667-2668).

pyrrolizidine alkaloids; pre-transplant chemotherapy) (p.2667, p.2670, p.2671) DILI is the most common cause of acute liver failure, and signals of hepatotoxicity in clinical trials are the leading reason candidate drugs fail to reach approval (p.2665). Two broad mechanisms are recognised: direct (intrinsic) toxicity that is predictable and dose-dependent with a short latency, versus idiosyncratic reactions that are infrequent (roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100,000), unpredictable, and may appear at any time but typically 5-90 days after starting the drug (p.2665, p.2667). Although idiosyncratic injury is regarded as not dose-related, most implicated drugs are given at relatively high daily doses (often >100 mg); high-potency drugs given in milligram amounts rarely cause hepatotoxicity (p.2665). The hepatocellular-versus-cholestatic pattern is defined by the R value, the ratio of ALT to alkaline phosphatase (each as multiples of the upper limit of normal): R >5.0 = hepatocellular, R <2.0 = cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 = mixed (p.2667). Hy's Law (named for Hyman Zimmerman): the appearance of jaundice during drug therapy predicts more serious injury, with roughly a 10:1 ratio of jaundiced cases to acute liver failure (about 1 in 10 jaundiced patients progresses to liver failure) (p.2667). Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) is the most frequently implicated single antibiotic/agent causing DILI in the US and Europe, typically producing mixed or predominantly cholestatic injury that may begin after the drug has already been stopped (p.2667, p.2670). Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is the prototype direct hepatotoxin and the most prevalent cause of acute liver failure in the Western world (p.2667, p.2668). A characteristic biochemical signature of acetaminophen injury is very high aminotransferases (often >10,000 IU/L, far above viral hepatitis) with relatively low bilirubin in the hyperacute phase; this should prompt focused questioning even without a clear overdose history (p.2668). Complementary and alternative (herbal/dietary) medicines now account for over 20% of DILI in the US; weight-loss products and anabolic steroids are common culprits and are often unregulated (p.2671). Acetaminophen toxicity is potentiated by chronic alcohol use (CYP2E1 induction plus glutathione depletion), so the toxic dose may be as low as ~2 g in chronic alcoholics; starvation/fasting and enzyme-inducing drugs (phenobarbital, isoniazid) also increase susceptibility (p.2668-2670). Four agents are notable for causing a chronic, autoimmune-hepatitis-like picture with positive ANA: nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, and alpha-methyldopa (p.2667, p.2670). DILI is nearly always a presumptive diagnosis of exclusion; causality assessment relies on temporal association, injury pattern, the drug's prior record, and ruling out other causes (scoring tools: RUCAM, DILIN expert opinion, newer RECAM) (p.2667-2668). Drug hepatotoxicity is generally not more frequent in those with pre-existing chronic liver disease, although the severity of outcome may be greater; statins specifically can be used safely in chronic hepatitis C and steatosis (p.2668, p.2671-2672). Missing the acetaminophen diagnosis because of denial, altered mentation, or staggered/unintentional overdose - very high transaminases with low bilirubin should raise suspicion even without a clear history (p.2668). Forgetting herbal/dietary supplements and OTC products in the drug history - they now cause >20% of US DILI and may contain undeclared chemicals (e.g., diclofenac in 'antirheumatic herbs') (p.2671). Assuming standard acetaminophen doses are safe in chronic alcohol users - the toxic threshold can fall to ~2 g (p.2670). Attributing cholestatic jaundice in a young male body-builder to hepatitis rather than anabolic/androgenic steroid use (p.2670). Expecting injury only early in therapy - amoxicillin-clavulanate and nitrofurantoin can have long latency and may declare after the drug is stopped (p.2670). In direct toxins, focusing on the liver while missing concurrent renal or other organ involvement that may threaten survival (p.2668). Liver injury can follow ingestion of essentially any xenobiotic (industrial toxins, drugs, herbal/dietary supplements). Most drugs are lipophilic and undergo phase I oxidation/methylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation to a water-soluble form for renal/biliary excretion; most hepatotoxicity arises from a reactive phase I metabolite, and glutathione depletion compounds the injury. Damage occurs through several overlapping routes: direct hepatocyte injury via free radicals/reactive intermediates causing membrane lipid peroxidation; activation of innate or adaptive immune responses (HLA-haplotype-dependent hapten binding, cytotoxic lymphocytes, antibody-mediated cytotoxicity); triggering of apoptosis via TNF-alpha/Fas pathways; disruption of bile canalicular transport pumps (e.g., MRP3) leading to toxic bile-acid accumulation and cholestasis; and inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation/respiration producing lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR can also induce hepatotoxicity. For acetaminophen specifically, a minor fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with hepatoprotective glutathione; when NAPQI overwhelms or glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive centrilobular necrosis. Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after the offending agent is withdrawn. However, acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and liver transplantation is undertaken in more than 40% of these patients (p.2668). For acetaminophen, up to 72% of poisoned patients in some Scandinavian series progress to encephalopathy and coagulopathy (lower in the UK/US); a single dose of 10-15 g can cause clinical injury and fulminant fatal disease is usually associated with >=25 g; the N-acetylcysteine antidote markedly reduces severity and is most effective given early (within ~8-12 h), though it retains some benefit up to 24-36 h. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have ongoing liver injury (p.2668, p.2670). Several agents cause chronic injury or progression to cirrhosis (methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and the autoimmune-pattern agents (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) can lead to cirrhosis if not recognised early (p.2668-2670). Injury pattern is classified by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): R >5.0 hepatocellular, R <2.0 cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 mixed (p.2667). Hy's Law serves as a severity/prognostic marker: jaundice (significant bilirubin rise) accompanying hepatocellular DILI predicts a markedly higher risk of acute liver failure (about a 10:1 jaundice-to-failure ratio) (p.2667). The aminotransferase threshold of >5x ULN (or >3x ULN with symptoms) marks the point at which the offending agent should be withdrawn (p.2668). Causality (not severity) is graded on a five-point likelihood scale by DILIN (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely) (p.2668). The clinical endpoint of severity is acute liver failure, defined by coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy (p.2668).

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome — STSS, streptococcal TSS, group A streptococcal toxic shock, invasive GAS toxic shock Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome Septic shock from other Gram-positive or Gram-negative organisms Meningococcaemia Necrotising fasciitis without established shock Severe drug reaction with systemic features Anaphylaxis with distributive shock Heat stroke with multi-organ dysfunction Adrenal crisis Severe acute pancreatitis with systemic inflammatory response Blood cultures and cultures from any surgical or wound specimen Serial lactate, renal and liver function, coagulation profile and creatine kinase to track organ involvement Imaging (CT or MRI) of a suspected deep soft-tissue focus, without delaying surgery when necrotising infection is likely Surgical exploration for tissue diagnosis when necrotising fasciitis is suspected Assessment for disseminated intravascular coagulation Driven by invasive group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) whose exotoxins act as superantigens, provoking massive cytokine release and rapid-onset shock Frequently arises from a soft-tissue focus such as necrotising fasciitis or cellulitis, though a portal of entry is not always evident Pain out of proportion to visible skin findings is an early warning sign and should prompt urgent surgical assessment Hypotension progresses quickly to multi-organ dysfunction, with renal impairment often preceding the drop in blood pressure A generalised erythematous rash may be subtle or absent compared with staphylococcal toxic shock; desquamation can occur late Management combines aggressive fluid resuscitation, prompt source control, and antibiotic principles pairing a beta-lactam with a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin to switch off toxin production Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered as an adjunct to neutralise circulating superantigens in severe disease Mortality is high, so early recognition, critical-care support, and surgical debridement of any necrotising focus are decisive Pain disproportionate to examination findings suggesting underlying necrotising infection requiring urgent debridement Rapidly progressing hypotension and organ failure indicating established septic shock Skin crepitus, bullae, dusky discolouration or rapidly advancing erythema pointing to deep tissue necrosis Falling urine output and rising creatinine signalling early multi-organ dysfunction Attributing severe limb pain to a minor injury and missing early necrotising infection Relying on antibiotics alone without urgent surgical source control Omitting a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin, forgoing its anti-toxin effect Underestimating fluid requirements and delaying critical-care escalation Invasive strains of Streptococcus pyogenes release pyrogenic exotoxins and other superantigens that bind directly to MHC class II molecules and T-cell receptors outside the normal antigen groove. This triggers polyclonal T-cell activation and an overwhelming release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (a cytokine storm), producing capillary leak, vasodilatation, hypotension, and multi-organ failure. Bacteraemia and deep tissue invasion, often within necrotising soft-tissue infection, amplify the toxin load and accelerate the shock state. Even with intensive treatment, mortality remains substantial and is highest when there is an associated necrotising soft-tissue infection or delayed source control; survival depends on early recognition, rapid surgery, and organ support.

Toxoplasmosis — Toxoplasma gondii infection Mononucleosis-like syndrome from acute toxoplasmic lymphadenopathy: EBV infection, CMV infection, HIV infection, Bartonella (cat-scratch disease), and lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1800-1801). CNS mass lesions in an AIDS patient: primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic tumor, brain abscess, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus), fungal infection, and mycobacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Chorioretinitis in an immunocompetent individual: tuberculosis, syphilis, and histoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1801). Chorioretinitis in an AIDS patient: CMV, syphilis, HSV, VZV, and fungal infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Cerebral toxoplasmosis must also be differentiated from herpes simplex encephalitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) (Harrison 22e p.1800). Congenital infection: CMV, HSV, rubella, syphilis, and listeriosis (Harrison 22e p.1801). Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV-associated) presenting as ring-enhancing brain lesion(s) in AIDS Cytomegalovirus infection Epstein-Barr virus infection (infectious mononucleosis) Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus) Cryptococcal meningitis Herpes simplex encephalitis Tuberculous, fungal, or bacterial brain abscess Pneumocystis pneumonia (Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with it) Serology: combined IgG and IgM antibody to Toxoplasma; circulating IgA favors acute infection; Sabin-Feldman dye test, indirect fluorescent antibody test, and ELISA measure IgG; double-sandwich IgM-ELISA or IgM-ISAGA preferred for IgM (Harrison 22e p.1801). IgG avidity testing to help time infection, particularly useful in pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.1801). PCR amplification of T. gondii DNA from blood, CSF, ocular fluid, bronchoalveolar lavage, or amniotic fluid; PCR is the mainstay for detecting organisms but a negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1801). Double-dose contrast CT and contrast MRI of the brain (standard imaging for Toxoplasma encephalitis); MRI is more sensitive for monitoring response (Harrison 22e p.1802). CSF analysis in suspected CNS disease (modest pleocytosis and protein elevation without glucose change; CSF PCR specific but not sensitive) (Harrison 22e p.1800-1801). Lymph node biopsy / histology showing follicular hyperplasia and clusters of epithelioid macrophages; demonstration of tachyzoites establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801). Dilated ophthalmologic examination for chorioretinitis; ocular fluid PCR, Western blot, or Goldmann-Witmer coefficient for ocular disease (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802). In HIV-infected persons, screening for IgG antibody to Toxoplasma at the time of HIV diagnosis to identify latent infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Weekly blood PCR screening after allogeneic HSCT in patients seropositive before transplant; pre-transplant donor and recipient serologies (Harrison 22e p.1800). Next-generation sequencing (metagenomics) of blood or body fluids, especially in immunocompromised individuals (Harrison 22e p.1801). Primary CNS lymphoma Metastatic brain tumor / other CNS malignancy Lymphoma (as a cause of lymphadenopathy) Caused by the obligate intracellular parasite Toxoplasma gondii; up to a third of the world's population is latently infected (Harrison 22e p.1797). Two transmissible stages reach humans: tissue cysts containing bradyzoites in undercooked meat (e.g., lamb, pork, venison, ground beef), and sporulated oocysts shed in cat feces that contaminate soil, food, or water; sporulated oocysts are environmentally hardy and highly infectious (Harrison 22e p.1797). In the immunocompetent host, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, going unrecognized in 80-90% of acquired infections (Harrison 22e p.1799). The most common manifestation of symptomatic acute toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent patients is cervical lymphadenopathy; nodes are usually nontender and discrete, with associated headache, malaise, fatigue, and low-grade fever (temperature usually <40 degrees C) (Harrison 22e p.1799). The classic severe presentation is reactivation encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts (especially HIV-positive individuals or transplant recipients) in whom latent infection has reactivated (Harrison 22e p.1797). In AIDS, >95% of Toxoplasma encephalitis cases are due to recrudescent infection, typically developing when the CD4+ T-cell count falls below 100/microL; encephalitis is the predominant manifestation while meningeal involvement is uncommon (Harrison 22e p.1800). On MRI/CT, Toxoplasma encephalitis classically produces multiple ring-enhancing lesions, most often in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction; a single lesion increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1801-1802). T. gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in immunocompetent individuals and is estimated to cause about 35% of all chorioretinitis cases in the US and Europe (Harrison 22e p.1799, p.1801). Congenital toxoplasmosis results from transplacental passage during primary maternal infection; infants may be asymptomatic at birth but later manifest chorioretinitis, strabismus, epilepsy, hydrocephalus, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and psychomotor retardation (Harrison 22e p.1797, p.1799). Antibody titers are NOT useful for establishing reactivation or following infection activity in immunocompromised patients; however, an absence of positive serology suggests an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800). Diagnosis rests on serology (combined IgG and IgM, with circulating IgA favoring acute infection) and PCR; PCR of body fluids is specific but its sensitivity may be low (Harrison 22e p.1801). A therapeutic trial of anti-Toxoplasma medications is frequently used in AIDS patients with CNS mass lesions: >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, whereas worsening by day 7 (or lymphoma) prompts brain biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802). Focal neurologic deficits, seizures, altered mental status, or ring-enhancing CNS mass lesion(s) in an HIV/AIDS patient (especially CD4+ <100/microL) - reactivation Toxoplasma encephalitis, which is rapidly fatal if untreated (Harrison 22e p.1800). A solitary ring-enhancing CNS lesion - increases the likelihood of primary CNS lymphoma over toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1802). Failure to improve clinically by day 7 of empiric anti-Toxoplasma therapy - prompts brain biopsy and consideration of lymphoma or alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1802). Fulminant sepsis, fever of unknown origin, or pneumonia in an immunocompetent person with travel to or residence in South/Central America - virulent atypical genotypes (Harrison 22e p.1797-1799). Toxoplasma pneumonia / disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts may progress to acute respiratory failure with hemoptysis, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (Harrison 22e p.1800). Acute maternal infection in pregnancy (risk of transplacental transmission; severity highest with first-trimester infection) (Harrison 22e p.1798). Acute toxoplasmosis is asymptomatic and self-limited in 80-90% of immunocompetent adults and children, so the diagnosis is easily missed (in one epidemic, toxoplasmosis was correctly diagnosed in only 3 of 25 patients who sought care) (Harrison 22e p.1799). Antibody titers do not establish reactivation or track infection activity in immunocompromised patients; do not rely on serial titers to gauge active disease (Harrison 22e p.1800). A negative PCR does not rule out toxoplasmosis - PCR is specific but may be of low sensitivity depending on the body fluid (Harrison 22e p.1801). Isolation/demonstration of tissue cysts (bradyzoites) from biopsied tissue indicates only the presence of cysts and should NOT be misinterpreted as evidence of acute toxoplasmosis; only demonstration of tachyzoites (e.g., in lymph nodes) establishes acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). IgM can persist for >1 year, so a positive IgM with positive IgG should not necessarily be interpreted as acute disease; a negative IgM with positive IgG indicates distant infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). MRI/CT findings are not pathognomonic - 40% of CNS lymphomas are multifocal and 50% are ring-enhancing, and the false-negative rate for both MRI and CT is ~10% (Harrison 22e p.1802). In AIDS patients with TE, IgM is usually undetectable and titers may be borderline/low (or transplant patients on B-cell-targeted immunosuppression may become seronegative); fewer than 3% have no demonstrable antibody at diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1800, p.1801). Up to 25% of congenitally infected newborns may be seronegative with normal routine physical examinations, so eye, brain, CSF, and radiologic assessment are needed (Harrison 22e p.1802). Toxoplasma pneumonia can be confused with Pneumocystis pneumonia, and organisms may also be found in healthy tissue, complicating interpretation (Harrison 22e p.1800). If a patient is seronegative for T. gondii, the likelihood that a CNS mass lesion is due to toxoplasmosis is <10%, favoring earlier biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1802). T. gondii is an intracellular coccidian. Ingested tissue cysts (bradyzoites) or oocysts (sporozoites) release organisms that invade gut epithelium and transform into rapidly dividing tachyzoites, which can infect and replicate in all nucleated mammalian cells via a parasitophorous vacuole, causing cell death and focal necrosis with an acute mononuclear inflammatory response. Parasites disseminate as free tachyzoites or within phagocytic 'Trojan horse' cells through blood and lymphatics to lymphatic tissue, skeletal muscle, myocardium, retina, placenta, and CNS. In the immunocompetent host, humoral and cell-mediated immunity (parasiticidal antibody, macrophage activation, IFN-gamma, IL-12-driven TH1 response, CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes) controls infection; tissue cysts containing bradyzoites then form 7-10 days after systemic infection and persist principally in the CNS and muscle, completing the asexual cycle and establishing lifelong chronic infection. Subclinical cycles of cyst rupture and reformation are the probable source of recrudescent infection. Immunocompromised or fetal hosts lack the immune factors (notably CD8+ T cells; reactivating T cells fail to secrete IFN-gamma and IL-2) needed to contain tachyzoite spread, allowing progressive focal destruction (necrotizing encephalitis, pneumonia, myocarditis). The sexual stage occurs only in the cat (definitive host), producing oocysts shed in feces (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800). In immunocompetent individuals, acute infection is usually asymptomatic and self-limited, resolving within several weeks though lymphadenopathy may persist for months; chronic infection persists lifelong with little consequence. Ocular disease can be self-limited but episodic chorioretinitis flares progressively destroy retinal tissue and may lead to glaucoma. In immunocompromised hosts, disease may be rapidly fatal if untreated, mandating prompt diagnosis and therapy; with treatment of Toxoplasma encephalitis, >50% improve by day 3 and >90% by day 7, but relapses are common and maintenance/secondary prophylaxis is needed while CD4+ counts remain low. For congenital toxoplasmosis, factors associated with severe disability include delayed diagnosis/treatment, neonatal hypoxia and hypoglycemia, profound visual impairment, uncorrected hydrocephalus, and raised intracranial pressure; with appropriate treatment upward of 70% of children have normal developmental, neurologic, and ophthalmologic findings at follow-up. Infected infants normal at birth may still have higher rates of learning disabilities and chronic neurologic sequelae (Harrison 22e p.1797-1801). Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system for toxoplasmosis. Clinical stratification is by host immune status and syndrome: (1) immunocompetent acute infection - usually asymptomatic/self-limited (most commonly cervical lymphadenopathy); (2) ocular toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis); (3) reactivation disease in the immunocompromised host - most importantly Toxoplasma encephalitis in AIDS (typically CD4+ <100/microL), which is rapidly fatal if untreated, plus pneumonitis, myocarditis, and disseminated disease; and (4) congenital toxoplasmosis, with severity inversely related to gestational age at maternal infection (earliest infection = lowest transmission but most severe fetal disease) (Harrison 22e p.1797-1800).

Tracheoesophageal Fistula — TEF, TOF/TEF, esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula, EA/TEF Isolated oesophageal atresia without fistula Laryngeal cleft Choanal atresia Severe gastro-oesophageal reflux with aspiration Vascular ring causing feeding difficulty Swallowing dysfunction of neurological origin Attempted passage of a nasogastric tube with radiograph showing tube coiling in the upper pouch Chest and abdominal radiograph to assess the pouch and bowel gas pattern Echocardiography to identify cardiac anomalies and aortic arch side before surgery Renal ultrasound and spinal and limb assessment for VACTERL anomalies Bronchoscopy or contrast study to define an H-type fistula when suspected An abnormal congenital communication between the trachea and oesophagus, most often occurring together with oesophageal atresia; the commonest anatomical type is proximal oesophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula. Typical newborn features include excessive drooling and frothy secretions, choking, coughing, and cyanosis with feeds, and inability to pass a nasogastric tube into the stomach. A characteristic radiographic clue is a feeding tube coiling in the upper oesophageal pouch; gas in the stomach and bowel indicates a distal fistula, while a gasless abdomen suggests atresia without a distal fistula. Aspiration of saliva and, via the fistula, gastric contents into the airway causes respiratory compromise and pneumonitis. An isolated H-type fistula without atresia may present later with recurrent coughing during feeds, cyanotic spells, and recurrent respiratory infections. Initial management protects the airway and lungs: keep the infant nil by mouth, apply continuous suction to the upper pouch, and position to reduce aspiration and reflux through the fistula. It is frequently part of the VACTERL association, so evaluation for vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, renal, and limb anomalies is important. Definitive treatment is surgical division of the fistula and repair of the oesophageal atresia, timed according to the infant's stability and anatomy. Long-term issues can include anastomotic stricture, gastro-oesophageal reflux, tracheomalacia, and dysphagia requiring ongoing follow-up. Choking, cyanosis, and respiratory distress with attempted feeding Aspiration pneumonitis from overflow of secretions or reflux through the fistula Progressive gastric and bowel distension impairing ventilation via a large distal fistula Recurrent respiratory infections and cyanotic spells suggesting a missed H-type fistula Associated critical cardiac or other major anomalies within the VACTERL spectrum Feeding a newborn with excessive drooling before excluding oesophageal atresia, precipitating aspiration Missing a delayed-presenting H-type fistula in a child with recurrent feeding-related respiratory symptoms Failing to search for associated VACTERL anomalies, especially cardiac lesions, before surgery Overlooking that a gasless abdomen indicates atresia without a distal fistula Underestimating long-term reflux, stricture, and tracheomalacia complications requiring follow-up Abnormal separation of the primitive foregut into trachea and oesophagus during embryogenesis leaves an abnormal connection between the two and, commonly, a discontinuous oesophagus (atresia). In the common configuration, the upper oesophagus ends in a blind pouch while the lower oesophagus connects to the trachea. Swallowed secretions collect in and overflow from the upper pouch into the airway, and the distal fistula allows gastric contents to reflux into the trachea and air to distend the stomach. These mechanisms produce aspiration, chemical pneumonitis, and, with a large distal fistula, gaseous abdominal distension that further impairs ventilation. With early diagnosis and surgical repair the outlook is generally favourable, and prognosis is influenced strongly by prematurity, birth weight, and associated anomalies, particularly cardiac lesions. Many children require management of later complications such as strictures, reflux, and tracheomalacia but achieve good long-term function.

Transfusion-related acute lung injury — TRALI, transfusion-related acute lung injury Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) Acute respiratory distress syndrome from other causes Anaphylactic transfusion reaction Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema Bacterial contamination of a component with sepsis Chest radiograph or CT showing bilateral infiltrates Arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia Natriuretic peptide levels and echocardiography to help exclude circulatory overload Investigation of implicated donors for anti-HLA and anti-neutrophil antibodies via the transfusion service Exclusion of infective and cardiac causes Presents as acute hypoxaemia and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema developing during or within about six hours of transfusion Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates appear on chest imaging without evidence of left atrial hypertension or fluid overload A key distinction from TACO is the absence of features of circulatory overload; jugular venous pressure and natriuretic peptides are typically not elevated Often mediated by donor anti-leukocyte (anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil) antibodies, so plasma-rich components from multiparous or previously transfused donors carry higher risk Historically a leading cause of transfusion-related mortality, which fell substantially after mitigation strategies such as using predominantly male-donor plasma Management is supportive with oxygen and lung-protective ventilation as needed; diuretics are unhelpful and the picture is one of capillary leak rather than volume excess Most patients improve within one to three days, distinguishing it from other causes of ARDS Acute severe hypoxaemia and respiratory distress during or shortly after transfusion requiring urgent oxygen and possible ventilatory support Rapid clinical deterioration necessitating critical care Diagnostic uncertainty with concurrent features of overload or sepsis Recurrence on re-exposure to a component from an implicated donor Misattributing the picture to fluid overload and giving diuretics, delaying appropriate supportive care Failing to stop the transfusion and report the reaction to the transfusion service Not investigating and deferring implicated donors, risking further cases Overlooking TRALI in ventilated critically ill patients where hypoxaemia is attributed solely to underlying illness TRALI reflects acute injury to the pulmonary capillary endothelium leading to increased permeability and protein-rich alveolar oedema. A widely used two-hit model proposes that a predisposing condition (such as sepsis, surgery, or inflammation) primes and sequesters neutrophils in the lung; a second hit from transfused antibodies against recipient leukocyte antigens, or from biologically active lipids and cytokines accumulated in stored components, then activates these neutrophils. The resulting release of reactive oxygen species and proteases damages the endothelium and produces non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Most cases resolve within one to three days with supportive care and hypoxaemia improves, but severe episodes can be fatal; identification and deferral of implicated donors prevents further cases.

Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease — TA-GVHD, transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or other drug eruptions Viral infection with rash and cytopenias Marrow failure or aplastic anaemia from other causes Post-transplant graft-versus-host disease Sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction Skin biopsy showing characteristic histology of graft-versus-host disease Full blood count documenting progressive pancytopenia Liver function tests reflecting hepatitis HLA typing and detection of donor lymphocyte chimerism in blood or affected tissue Bone marrow examination showing hypoplasia or aplasia A rare but almost uniformly fatal complication caused by viable donor T lymphocytes engrafting and attacking recipient tissues Typically appears one to six weeks after transfusion with fever, a maculopapular rash, diarrhoea, hepatitis, and progressive pancytopenia Marrow aplasia distinguishes it from graft-versus-host disease after stem cell transplant, where the graft spares recipient marrow Highest risk in severely immunocompromised recipients and when donor and recipient share an HLA haplotype, as with directed donations from blood relatives Gamma or X-ray irradiation of cellular components to inactivate donor lymphocytes is the cornerstone of prevention; leukoreduction alone is insufficient Diagnosis is supported by skin biopsy and by demonstrating donor-derived lymphocytes or chimerism in the recipient Established disease responds poorly to immunosuppression, so prevention through irradiation of at-risk transfusions is paramount Fever, rash, diarrhoea, and falling blood counts within weeks of transfusion in an at-risk patient Progressive pancytopenia signalling marrow aplasia Any cellular transfusion given without irradiation to a severely immunocompromised recipient or from a first-degree relative Rapid multi-organ deterioration requiring urgent haematology involvement Failing to irradiate cellular components for immunocompromised recipients or directed family donations Assuming leukoreduction alone prevents the disease Attributing the rash, diarrhoea, and cytopenias to drugs or infection and delaying recognition Not flagging patients who require lifelong irradiated components in their transfusion records TA-GVHD occurs when immunologically competent donor T lymphocytes contained in a cellular blood component are not eliminated by the recipient's immune system and instead engraft, proliferate, and mount an immune attack against host tissues bearing foreign HLA antigens. This happens when the recipient is profoundly immunosuppressed or when the donor is homozygous for an HLA haplotype shared with the recipient, so the recipient fails to recognise the donor cells as foreign. The activated donor lymphocytes target skin, gut, liver, and bone marrow, with marrow involvement producing the aplasia that drives the high mortality. The prognosis is extremely poor once established, with mortality generally exceeding ninety per cent largely from marrow aplasia and infection; the emphasis therefore lies entirely on prevention by irradiating cellular components for at-risk patients.

Transfusion Reactions — hemolytic transfusion reaction, TRALI, TACO Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction (diagnosis of exclusion once infection and haemolysis excluded) Acute immune-mediated haemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO/clerical error) Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction (anamnestic alloantibody response) Hyperhaemolytic transfusion reaction in haemoglobinopathy/sickle cell disease (bystander haemolysis) Allergic / anaphylactic transfusion reaction TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection / septic transfusion reaction Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease Posttransfusion purpura Acute hypotensive transfusion reaction (bradykinin-related, ACE inhibitor) Transfusion-transmitted bacterial contamination/sepsis presenting with abrupt fever, chills, septic shock and DIC can mimic an acute haemolytic reaction (fever over 2 degrees C is a warning sign favouring bacterial contamination/haemolysis) Septic shock from a contaminated component can mimic anaphylactic or haemolytic shock Direct antiglobulin test (DAT / direct Coombs) detecting immunoglobulin and possibly complement (C3d) on recipient RBCs Indirect antiglobulin test (IAT / indirect Coombs) detecting anti-RBC alloantibody in serum, with antibody elution to identify the culprit alloantibody Plasma haptoglobin (depleted), LDH and unconjugated bilirubin (elevated), haemoglobinemia and haemoglobinuria Repeat ABO determination and thorough clerical check; alloantibody screen and crossmatch Bacterial culture of the component and recipient before starting broad-spectrum antibiotics when bacterial contamination suspected Chest x-ray (bilateral interstitial infiltrates in TRALI; predominantly alveolar infiltrates in TACO) and brain natriuretic peptide (elevated in TACO) Serum ferritin, MRI and liver biopsy to assess iron overload in frequently transfused patients Test for IgA deficiency in patients with anaphylactic or repeated allergic reactions TRALI may be difficult to distinguish from other causes of hypoxia, particularly circulatory overload (TACO) G6PD/enzymatic RBC defects and underlying haemolytic conditions exacerbated by transfusion can mimic immune-mediated haemolytic transfusion reaction Hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease can mimic and be exacerbated by transfusion Acute immune-mediated haemolytic reactions occur when recipient preformed antibodies lyse transfused donor RBCs, during or up to 24 h after transfusion; anti-A/anti-B antibodies cause most of the most severe (potentially fatal) reactions, though alloantibodies against Rh, Kell, and Duffy antigens can also cause severe haemolysis (Harrison 22e p.906). The most dramatic acute haemolytic reactions are usually caused by a failure in product or patient identification, erroneous blood grouping, or unidentified recipient anti-RBC alloimmunisation - i.e. a clerical/identification error (Harrison 22e p.906). Acute haemolytic reactions may present with hypotension, tachypnoea, tachycardia, fever (rise of 1-2 degrees C), chills, chest and back/flank pain, haemoglobinuria, and haemoglobinemia; in the most severe cases DIC, acute renal failure, shock, and death may occur (Harrison 22e p.906). RED FLAG: when an adverse reaction is suspected the transfusion must be STOPPED, the recipient's clinical status assessed, and supportive care initiated; a thorough clerical check is crucial to prevent a possible second misidentified transfusion (Harrison 22e p.908). Management of acute immune haemolytic reaction is mainly supportive: prompt interruption of transfusion, biological workup, vigorous isotonic saline hydration with diuretics to maintain urine output; may require forced alkaline diuresis, electrolyte correction, and pressor support, and in DIC with bleeding, platelet/plasma/cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen (Harrison 22e p.908). Diagnosis of transfusion-associated haemolysis relies on persistent/worsening anaemia, depleted haptoglobin, haemoglobinemia and haemoglobinuria, and elevated LDH and unconjugated bilirubin; the direct antiglobulin test (DAT/direct Coombs) is most often positive, as is the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) (Harrison 22e p.908). Delayed haemolytic reactions present with icterus and persisting or worsening anaemia and result from an anamnestic response in previously sensitised patients who had a negative alloantibody screen at transfusion (low antibody levels); the alloantibody becomes detectable 1-2 weeks after transfusion (Harrison 22e p.906). FNHTR (febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction) is the most frequent reaction to cellular components (up to 300 per 100,000), characterised by chills, rigors and a rise of at least 1 degree C, caused by proinflammatory cytokines in the component or recipient antibodies against donor antigens; it is a diagnosis of exclusion once infection and haemolysis are ruled out (Harrison 22e p.911). Leukocyte reduction (especially prestorage) can prevent FNHTR; premedication with antipyretics has generally proven ineffective and may mask relevant clinical symptoms (Harrison 22e p.911). Most allergic transfusion reactions are mild (rash, pruritus, urticaria, localised oedema) and relate to plasma proteins; rarely they are severe/anaphylactic with bronchospasm, respiratory distress, hypotension, nausea, vomiting and shock - anaphylaxis can occur after only a few millilitres of component (Harrison 22e p.911). TRALI is characterised by occurrence or worsening of hypoxia and NONcardiogenic pulmonary oedema with bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray during or within 6 h of transfusion (delayed cases up to 72 h); it is among the most common causes of transfusion-related fatalities and treatment is supportive only (Harrison 22e p.911). TRALI usually results from donor plasma containing high-titre anti-HLA class II antibodies binding recipient cognate antigen (anti-HLA class I and anti-HNA antibodies may also be involved); a cytokine/chemokine-mediated mechanism without HLA interaction can also occur (Harrison 22e p.911). TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload) is common and underrecognised and is now the main cause of transfusion-related death since TRALI risk was mitigated; it presents with dyspnoea, hypoxia, bilateral and predominantly ALVEOLAR infiltrates on chest x-ray, frequent systolic hypertension, and elevated BNP (fever may also occur) (Harrison 22e p.912). TRALI vs TACO distinction: TRALI gives noncardiogenic oedema with predominantly interstitial infiltrates within 6 h, whereas TACO is volume overload with predominantly alveolar infiltrates (within 12 h), systolic hypertension and elevated BNP; TACO risk factors include older age, renal failure, preexisting fluid overload, cardiac dysfunction, large transfusion volume and excessive transfusion rate (Harrison 22e p.911-912). Transfusion-related GVHD is extremely rare but fatal in over 90% of cases; mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes in a recipient unable to reject them, it presents 5-10 days post-transfusion with cytopenia, fever, characteristic skin rash, diarrhoea and liver function abnormalities, and is prevented by irradiation (minimum 25 Gy) of cellular components in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.911). Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection remains a significant concern, notably with platelet concentrates stored at room temperature; some gram-negatives such as Yersinia grow at 4 degrees C and can contaminate RBC units - recipients may develop abrupt fever and chills deteriorating to septic shock, DIC and death, and after culture sampling broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started promptly (Harrison 22e p.913). Iron overload: each RBC concentrate contains 200-250 mg of iron; in frequently transfused recipients untreated accumulation impairs endocrine, hepatic and cardiac function (death may occur from cardiac failure or arrhythmia), assessed by serum ferritin, MRI and liver biopsy, and prevented/treated by monitoring and iron chelation (Harrison 22e p.912). Acute hypotensive transfusion reactions are an abrupt drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 30 mmHg early after starting transfusion that resolves once transfusion is stopped; they are more likely in patients taking ACE inhibitors (impaired bradykinin metabolism) and the same product should NOT be restarted (Harrison 22e p.912). STOP the transfusion immediately when any adverse reaction is suspected Fever, flank/back pain and haemoglobinuria suggesting acute haemolytic (ABO-incompatible) reaction - perform an urgent clerical/identification check to prevent a second misidentified transfusion Hypotension (systolic drop of at least 30 mmHg) - haemolytic, anaphylactic or septic shock Dyspnoea within 6 h (TRALI) or within 12 h (TACO) of transfusion Temperature rise over 2 degrees C - favours transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection or haemolysis Rash over two-thirds of body within 5 minutes with dyspnoea and shock - anaphylaxis Development of DIC, acute renal failure or shock during/after transfusion Premedication with antipyretics for FNHTR is generally ineffective and may mask relevant clinical warning symptoms FNHTR must not be diagnosed until infection and haemolysis are excluded Failing to perform a clerical/identification check risks a second misidentified (incompatible) transfusion TRALI and TACO are easily confused; both cause hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates - TACO is now the leading cause of transfusion death and is underrecognised In acute hypotensive reactions the same blood product should not be restarted; consider switching ACE inhibitor for patients needing further transfusion Delayed haemolytic reactions occur despite a negative pretransfusion alloantibody screen (low antibody levels) - icterus and worsening anaemia 1-2 weeks later Iron overload is frequently underreported in chronically transfused patients Further RBC transfusion in hyperhaemolytic reaction (sickle cell disease) typically exacerbates ongoing haemolysis Adverse reactions to blood components arise via immune or nonimmune mechanisms. Immune-mediated acute haemolysis occurs when recipient preformed antibodies (anti-A/anti-B IgM/IgG, or alloantibodies to Rh, Kell, Duffy) lyse transfused donor RBCs, with complement activation; ABO incompatibility classically results from clerical/identification error. Delayed haemolysis reflects an anamnestic alloantibody response (neoformed allogeneic IgG, C3b-mediated opsonisation and ADCC-mediated phagocytosis) detectable 1-2 weeks later. FNHTR is driven by proinflammatory cytokines accumulated in the component or recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte antigens. Allergic/anaphylactic reactions relate to plasma proteins and soluble mediators triggering histamine/serotonin release (IgA-deficient recipients may react to IgA). TRALI results from donor anti-HLA (class II, also class I) or anti-HNA antibodies binding recipient antigen, or cytokine/chemokine priming, causing neutrophil aggregation in pulmonary vasculature and release of inflammatory mediators producing noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema. TACO is hydrostatic circulatory overload from excessive volume/rate relative to cardiac/renal reserve. Transfusion-associated GVHD is mediated by engrafted donor T lymphocytes attacking host HLA antigens. (Harrison 22e p.906-912) Most adverse reactions are non-life-threatening, though serious reactions can present with mild symptoms. An average of ~37 transfusion-associated fatalities (possible-to-definite imputability) were reported yearly to the FDA between 2017-2021 among ~15 million transfused components, with leading causes of death being TACO (32%), TRALI (21%), haemolysis (21%) and microbial contamination (13%). Acute haemolysis is often self-limiting but can be fatal (DIC, acute renal failure, shock). Transfusion-associated GVHD is fatal in over 90% of cases and highly resistant to treatment. (Harrison 22e p.906-911) Warning-sign based recognition of transfusion adverse reactions (Harrison Table 118-5): fever of at least 38 degrees C (rise of 1-2 degrees C within 4 h favours FNHTR or TRALI; rise over 2 degrees C favours bacterial infection/haemolysis); hypotension (systolic drop of at least 30 mmHg) suggesting haemolytic, anaphylactic or septic shock; dyspnoea (TRALI within 6 h, TACO within 12 h, severe allergy within 4 h); haemoglobinuria (intravascular haemolysis); rash (minor allergy if under two-thirds body, severe if over two-thirds, anaphylaxis if with dyspnoea/shock within 5 min); icterus (delayed haemolysis); rash/diarrhoea/fever 2 days-6 weeks (GVHD); gum bleeding/purpura 5-12 days (posttransfusion purpura). Reactions are also categorised as immune-mediated vs nonimmunologic, and by timing (acute vs delayed). (Harrison 22e p.908)

Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn — TTN, transient tachypnoea of the newborn, wet lung, retained fetal lung fluid Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome Early-onset neonatal pneumonia or sepsis Meconium aspiration syndrome Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Congenital heart disease Air-leak syndromes Chest radiograph showing wet-lung features Pulse oximetry and monitoring of oxygen requirement Blood gas if distress is significant Sepsis screen and consideration of antibiotics when infection cannot be excluded Blood glucose monitoring A common, benign, self-limited cause of respiratory distress in term and late-preterm newborns caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. It typically presents soon after birth with tachypnoea, mild grunting, nasal flaring, and mild recession, usually without severe distress. Delivery by caesarean section (especially without labour), maternal diabetes, and rapid or precipitous delivery are recognised risk factors. The chest radiograph classically shows prominent perihilar vascular markings, fluid in the interlobar fissures, hyperinflation, and sometimes small pleural effusions. It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion, and sepsis and pneumonia should be considered, particularly if distress is marked or prolonged. Management is supportive with oxygen as required and attention to feeding; the condition usually resolves within the first day or two of life. Oxygen requirement is generally modest, and the need for high oxygen or escalating support should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. Distress persisting well beyond 2-3 days argues against transient tachypnoea and warrants further evaluation. High or rising oxygen requirement Distress persisting beyond the first few days of life Marked recession, grunting, or signs of respiratory failure Features suggesting sepsis or pneumonia Differential pre- and post-ductal saturations suggesting pulmonary hypertension or cardiac disease Anchoring on transient tachypnoea and missing early sepsis or pneumonia Overlooking congenital heart disease presenting with tachypnoea Failing to reconsider the diagnosis when oxygen needs are high or distress is prolonged Unnecessarily delaying feeding or investigation in a stable infant Attributing every caesarean-born tachypnoeic infant to TTN without appropriate observation During fetal life the lungs are filled with fluid that is normally cleared around birth by labour-associated catecholamine and hormonal surges that switch alveolar epithelial cells from fluid secretion to sodium-driven absorption, aided by mechanical squeeze during vaginal delivery. When this clearance is delayed or incomplete, residual fluid remains in the interstitium and air spaces, reducing lung compliance and causing tachypnoea and mild hypoxaemia until the fluid is reabsorbed. The condition is benign and self-limited, resolving within hours to a few days with supportive care and no long-term respiratory sequelae in the great majority of infants.

Transposition of the Great Arteries — TGA, d-TGA, transposition of great vessels Tetralogy of Fallot Total anomalous pulmonary venous return Tricuspid atresia Truncus arteriosus Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn Severe respiratory disease causing cyanosis Echocardiography to confirm ventriculoarterial discordance, mixing sites, and coronary anatomy Hyperoxia test showing little rise in oxygenation with supplemental oxygen (suggesting a cardiac cause) Chest radiograph looking for an egg-on-a-string silhouette Blood gas to assess hypoxaemia and acidosis Pulse oximetry, including pre- and post-ductal comparison In d-transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, so the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel rather than in series. It is a leading cause of cyanosis presenting in the newborn period, often in an otherwise well-grown, term infant. Survival depends on mixing between the two parallel circuits through a patent foramen ovale, atrial or ventricular septal defect, or the ductus arteriosus. Cyanosis is typically profound and, unlike many respiratory causes, does not improve substantially with supplemental oxygen. A prostaglandin infusion is started to maintain ductal patency and improve intercirculatory mixing while the infant is stabilised. Balloon atrial septostomy may be performed to enlarge the atrial communication and improve mixing when cyanosis is severe. Chest radiograph may show an egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette with a narrow mediastinum, though this is not always present. Echocardiography confirms the discordant great-artery connections, defines associated defects, and maps the coronary arteries before surgery. The arterial switch operation, restoring normal ventriculoarterial connections, is the definitive repair and is performed in the neonatal period. Severe cyanosis in a newborn that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen Rapid deterioration and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close, restricting mixing Duct-dependent collapse before prostaglandin is established Worsening metabolic acidosis indicating inadequate systemic oxygen delivery Inadequate intercirculatory mixing requiring urgent septostomy Attributing severe neonatal cyanosis to lung disease and delaying cardiac evaluation because oxygen does not help Failing to start prostaglandin promptly, allowing the ductus to close and mixing to fail Overlooking the need to enhance mixing (septostomy) in a critically hypoxaemic infant Assuming a normal chest radiograph excludes the diagnosis Not mapping coronary anatomy before surgical planning Abnormal division of the truncus arteriosus results in the aorta connecting to the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to the left ventricle. As a consequence, deoxygenated systemic venous blood is pumped back to the body and oxygenated pulmonary venous blood is returned to the lungs, forming two separate parallel circuits. Life is only possible if oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix through a communication at the atrial, ventricular, or ductal level. Inadequate mixing produces severe systemic hypoxaemia and progressive metabolic acidosis, which worsens as the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale close after birth. With prompt stabilisation and an arterial switch operation in the neonatal period, most children do well with good long-term function, though follow-up is required for coronary, valve, and great-artery complications. Without intervention the condition is rapidly fatal.

compressive lesion that requires emergency decompression Failing to test for aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies and misclassifying the disorder Attributing the presentation to a peripheral cause and overlooking the sensory level and cord signs Not investigating for an infective cause before or alongside immunosuppression when indicated Transverse myelitis is focal inflammation of the spinal cord causing demyelination and axonal injury across one or more segments, disrupting ascending sensory and descending motor tracts as well as autonomic pathways. It may follow infection or vaccination as a para- or post-infectious immune response, arise from autoimmune demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, or MOG antibody disease, or occur with systemic autoimmune conditions. Breakdown of the blood-cord barrier and inflammatory cell infiltration produce cord swelling and dysfunction. Outcome is variable and depends on cause, severity, and rapidity of onset. Some patients recover substantially, while others are left with significant residual deficits. Recurrent disease and poorer recovery are more typical of NMOSD and longitudinally extensive lesions, underscoring the importance of accurate aetiological diagnosis and timely immunotherapy.

hypercarbia Falling GCS or a drop of two or more points indicating deterioration Unequal, dilated, or unreactive pupil suggesting uncal herniation from a mass lesion needing urgent decompression immediately to limit secondary injury Attributing hypotension to the brain injury and overlooking extracranial haemorrhage Allowing hypoxia, hypercarbia, or hypotension that aggravate secondary injury Missing an expanding haematoma by not repeating imaging after clinical deterioration Over-sedating so that neurological reassessment becomes impossible Failing to reverse anticoagulation promptly in a bleeding head injury The primary injury is the mechanical damage sustained at impact, which cannot be reversed. Secondary injury develops over hours to days from hypoxia, hypotension, oedema, haematoma expansion, seizures, and disturbed autoregulation. Because the skull is a fixed compartment, expanding blood or oedema raises intracranial pressure; once compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, small volume increases cause steep pressure rises. Rising intracranial pressure reduces cerebral perfusion pressure and drives ischaemia, and pressure gradients can force brain tissue across dural folds or the foramen magnum, producing herniation and brainstem compression. Outcome ranges from full recovery in mild injury to death or severe disability in severe injury. Prevention of secondary insults, timely evacuation of surgical lesions, and control of intracranial pressure improve results, whereas sustained raised pressure and low cerebral perfusion predict poor recovery.

be mistaken for a functional bowel disorder Dehydration during acute diarrhoeal episodes, particularly in young children Weight loss or failure to thrive suggesting a broader malabsorptive process Persistent symptoms despite trehalose avoidance indicating another diagnosis New alarm features prompting evaluation for mucosal disease Attributing recurrent post-meal symptoms to a functional disorder without taking a focused dietary history Overlooking trehalose as a hidden ingredient in some processed foods Failing to include trehalase in the disaccharidase assay panel Assuming symptoms reflect a more common sugar intolerance without confirmatory testing Trehalase deficiency is an osmotic malabsorption disorder of the intestinal brush border. Trehalase, encoded by TREH, hydrolyses the disaccharide trehalose into two glucose molecules for absorption. When trehalase activity is deficient, ingested trehalose, present mainly in mushrooms and certain processed foods, is not digested and remains in the lumen. The unabsorbed sugar draws water osmotically into the bowel and is fermented by colonic bacteria into gas and short-chain acids, producing diarrhoea, bloating and flatulence after trehalose-containing meals. Because exposure is intermittent and food-specific, symptoms occur only after relevant ingestions. Prognosis is excellent, as symptoms are entirely controlled by avoiding trehalose-rich foods and there are no systemic consequences. Recognition prevents unnecessary investigation for functional disorders.

Trichinellosis — trichinosis, Trichinella spiralis infection, trichiniasis Dermatomyositis or polymyositis Other causes of eosinophilia with myalgia (eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome) Influenza or other viral myositis Leptospirosis Angioedema or allergic reaction (periorbital swelling) Other tissue-invasive helminth infections Systemic vasculitis Full blood count and blood film for eosinophilia Serum creatine kinase and other muscle enzymes Trichinella serology (antibody testing) Detailed dietary history for raw or undercooked pork or game Muscle biopsy for encysted larvae in uncertain cases ECG and cardiac assessment, and neurological evaluation, when complications are suspected A zoonotic tissue nematode infection acquired by eating raw or undercooked meat containing Trichinella larvae, classically pork but also wild game such as bear and boar The early intestinal phase causes diarrhoea, abdominal pain and nausea within days of ingestion The later muscle-invasion phase produces fever, myalgia, weakness and the characteristic periorbital and facial oedema Marked peripheral eosinophilia and raised muscle enzymes (creatine kinase) are typical laboratory findings Splinter haemorrhages, conjunctival and subungual haemorrhages, and a rash may be seen Serology becomes positive over the first weeks; muscle biopsy showing encysted larvae is diagnostic when needed Treatment combines anthelmintics such as albendazole or mebendazole with corticosteroids to control the inflammatory reaction in severe disease Serious complications include myocarditis, encephalitis and respiratory muscle involvement, which are the main causes of death Chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure suggesting myocarditis Headache, confusion or focal deficits suggesting encephalitis Breathlessness from respiratory muscle involvement Severe systemic illness with very high eosinophilia and muscle enzyme elevation Missing the dietary history of undercooked pork or wild game Mistaking the myositis and periorbital oedema for dermatomyositis or an allergic reaction Relying on early serology, which may be negative in the first days of illness Failing to give anthelmintics early, before larvae encyst in muscle, when the diagnosis is suspected Overlooking cardiac or neurological complications that determine prognosis Trichinellosis begins when a person eats raw or undercooked meat containing encysted Trichinella larvae. Gastric digestion frees the larvae, which mature into adult worms in the small intestine; the females release newborn larvae that penetrate the mucosa and disseminate through the bloodstream and lymphatics. These larvae preferentially invade striated skeletal muscle, where they encyst within modified muscle cells (nurse cells), provoking an intense eosinophilic and inflammatory response. This muscle invasion accounts for the myositis, myalgia and periorbital oedema, while migration through other tissues can inflame the myocardium, central nervous system and respiratory muscles, explaining the potentially fatal complications. Most cases are mild and self-limiting with a good outcome, but heavy infections with myocardial, neurological or respiratory involvement can be life-threatening; prompt treatment shortens illness and reduces complications.

A. cantonensis PCR on CSF/tissue (available via CDC and Hawaii Dept of Public Health) Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis, dermatomyositis) Retinoblastoma (versus ocular larva migrans) Allergic/angioedematous periorbital swelling Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome Trichinellosis follows ingestion of meat (classically pork, but increasingly wild game such as bear and walrus) containing encysted Trichinella larvae; most infections are mild or asymptomatic, but heavy burdens can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1810). Disease severity tracks larval burden: light infections (<10 larvae/g muscle) tend to be asymptomatic, whereas heavy infections (>50 larvae/g muscle) can be life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.1811). Clinical course is biphasic: an early enteric phase (diarrhea, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea) in the first weeks, followed in the second week by larval-migration symptoms (fever, periorbital/facial edema, eosinophilia) and then a myositis phase as larvae encyst (Harrison 22e p.1811). Periorbital and facial edema with subconjunctival, retinal, and nail-bed (splinter) hemorrhages are characteristic of the migratory phase of trichinellosis (Harrison 22e p.1811). Most deaths in trichinellosis result from myocarditis (with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure) and, less commonly, encephalitis or pneumonitis (Harrison 22e p.1811). Muscle involvement preferentially affects the extraocular muscles, biceps, and the jaw, neck, lower back, and diaphragm muscles, with symptoms peaking around 3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1811). Visceral larva migrans (most often Toxocara canis) chiefly affects preschool children who ingest soil contaminated with embryonated eggs, producing fever, hepatosplenomegaly, wheezing, and extraordinary eosinophilia that can approach 90% (Harrison 22e p.1812). Ocular larva migrans typically occurs in older children/young adults without pica and usually lacks eosinophilia or visceral signs; the retinal granuloma can mimic retinoblastoma and lead to unnecessary enucleation if misdiagnosed (Harrison 22e p.1812). Cutaneous larva migrans ('creeping eruption'), usually from the dog/cat hookworm Ancylostoma braziliense, produces an intensely pruritic serpiginous track that advances several centimeters per day; the larvae cannot mature in humans and self-resolve over weeks to a couple of months (Harrison 22e p.1812). Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) is the most common cause of human eosinophilic meningitis; CSF shows elevated opening pressure, pleocytosis (150-2000 cells/uL) with eosinophilic pleocytosis >20%, elevated protein, and normal glucose (Harrison 22e p.1813). Gnathostomiasis is acquired from raw fish/poultry (e.g., som fak, sashimi) and causes migratory, recurrent pruritic cutaneous swellings; CNS invasion produces eosinophilic myeloencephalitis with agonizing radicular pain followed by paraplegia, and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1813). Stool examination is worthless in toxocariasis because the larvae never develop into egg-producing adults in the human host (Harrison 22e p.1812). Myocarditis with tachyarrhythmias or heart failure (leading cause of death in trichinellosis) Encephalitis or pneumonitis in trichinellosis Dysphagia, dyspnea, or diaphragmatic muscle involvement Severe neurologic, pneumonic, or myocardial involvement in visceral larva migrans (rare deaths) Ascending radicular pain and paresthesias followed by paraplegia in gnathostomiasis (myeloencephalitis) Cerebral involvement with focal hemorrhages in gnathostomiasis (often fatal) Permanent neurologic sequelae from heavy CNS angiostrongyliasis Most mild trichinellosis cases remain undiagnosed; a high index of suspicion and a careful dietary/exposure history are needed. Trichinella serology is typically negative until after the third week, so a presumptive clinical diagnosis (fever, eosinophilia, periorbital edema, myalgia after a suspect meal) may be required early. Stool examination is useless in toxocariasis because larvae do not mature into egg-producing adults in humans. Ocular toxocariasis can be mistaken for retinoblastoma, risking unnecessary enucleation; it often lacks eosinophilia and visceral signs. In angiostrongyliasis, A. cantonensis larvae are only rarely seen in CSF and serologic tests are unstandardized and may be negative at symptom onset. Arctic T. nativa larvae in walrus or bear meat are relatively freeze-resistant and may remain viable despite freezing, so usual freezing prevention may fail. Gnathostomiasis may present with ocular or CNS involvement without antecedent cutaneous swellings. These are zoonotic tissue-dwelling nematode infections arising from incidental human exposure; symptoms derive largely from invasive larval stages that (except for Trichinella) do not mature in humans. In trichinellosis, ingested encysted larvae are freed by gastric acid and proteases, invade small-bowel mucosa, mature to adults, and after about one week females release newborn larvae that migrate via the circulation to striated muscle, where most species encyst by radically transforming muscle-cell architecture into a 'nurse cell'; host immune responses help expel adult intestinal worms but have little effect on muscle larvae. Migrating larvae provoke a marked local and systemic hypersensitivity reaction with eosinophilia. In visceral larva migrans, ingested Toxocara eggs hatch, penetrate the gut, and disseminate to liver, lungs, CNS, and other tissues, eliciting intense eosinophilic granulomatous inflammation. In cutaneous larva migrans, animal hookworm larvae penetrate skin and burrow along the dermal-epidermal junction. In angiostrongyliasis, ingested infective larvae migrate to the brain and die there, inciting eosinophilic inflammation, hemorrhage, necrosis, and granuloma formation. In gnathostomiasis, aberrant migration of a single larva into cutaneous, visceral, neural, or ocular tissue causes local inflammation, including ascending migration along nerve tracts producing myeloencephalitis (Harrison 22e p.1810-1813). Most lightly infected trichinellosis patients recover uneventfully, with symptoms peaking near 3 weeks and subsiding gradually over a prolonged convalescence; heavy infections can be life-threatening, with death usually due to myocarditis. Most visceral larva migrans infections are self-limited (rare deaths from severe organ involvement). Cutaneous larva migrans self-resolves over weeks to a couple of months as the larvae die. Cerebral angiostrongyliasis is usually self-limited with complete recovery, though heavy infections can leave permanent neurologic sequelae or cause death. Gnathostomiasis cutaneous swellings can recur intermittently over years; CNS gnathostomiasis is a serious complication and cerebral involvement is often fatal (Harrison 22e p.1811-1813). Trichinellosis severity correlates with muscle larval burden: light/asymptomatic infection <10 larvae per gram of muscle; heavy, potentially life-threatening infection >50 larvae per gram of muscle. Clinically graded as mild, moderate, and severe (severe = significant myositis/myocarditis) per Harrison's tissue nematode framework (Harrison 22e p.1811-1812).

partners should be treated simultaneously and intercourse avoided until both complete therapy Infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, and it increases susceptibility to HIV acquisition and transmission Infection during pregnancy given the association with preterm delivery and low birth weight Persistent symptoms after treatment suggesting reinfection or nitroimidazole resistance Coexisting HIV infection or features suggesting other serious sexually transmitted disease Signs of pelvic inflammatory disease indicating an alternative or additional pathogen Relying on wet-mount microscopy alone, which misses many infections because of its limited sensitivity Treating the index patient without treating sexual partners, leading to reinfection Overlooking asymptomatic infection, particularly in men, who sustain transmission Failing to screen for coexisting sexually transmitted infections and HIV Trichomonas vaginalis is an anaerobic, flagellated protozoan that adheres to and damages squamous epithelium of the urogenital tract. Cytoadherence and release of proteinases and other virulence factors trigger a local inflammatory response with neutrophil infiltration, producing the characteristic discharge and mucosal microhaemorrhages. The resulting disruption of the epithelial barrier and mucosal inflammation facilitates acquisition and shedding of HIV and other pathogens. The organism cannot survive long outside a moist environment, which underlies its predominantly sexual mode of transmission. With appropriate nitroimidazole therapy and simultaneous partner treatment the cure rate is high; recurrence usually reflects reinfection or non-adherence rather than true drug resistance, which is uncommon but increasingly recognised.
