Tricuspid Valve Disease — Tricuspid stenosis, Tricuspid regurgitation, TS, TR Mitral stenosis (frequently coexists and dominates the picture) Mitral regurgitation (murmur can be confused with TR without attention to respiratory variation) Constrictive pericarditis / restrictive cardiomyopathy as a cause of right-sided venous congestion Other causes of right heart failure with hepatic congestion and ascites Infective endocarditis of the tricuspid valve causing primary regurgitation Transthoracic echocardiography (Doppler) - assesses leaflet thickening/doming, transvalvular gradient, RA and IVC size, associated TR severity, mitral and LV/RV function, and PA pressure Continuous-wave Doppler of the TR jet velocity to estimate PA systolic pressure (may be blunted when TR is very severe) ECG for right atrial enlargement, RVH, prior inferior/RV MI pattern, atrial fibrillation, or preexcitation in Ebstein's anomaly Chest x-ray - RA and superior vena cava prominence with azygos engorgement in combined TS/MS; RA/RV enlargement in TR Real-time three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MR for difficult assessment of TR severity, PA pressures, and RV size/function Exercise testing to assess functional capacity in asymptomatic severe TR Cardiac catheterization - not routinely needed for TS assessment Carcinoid heart disease causing tricuspid leaflet retraction and regurgitation Ebstein's malformation and other congenital tricuspid deformities Myxomatous tricuspid valve prolapse Radiation-induced valve disease Endomyocardial fibrosis Tricuspid stenosis is far less common than mitral stenosis in North America and Western Europe, is usually rheumatic in origin, occurs more often in women, and essentially never appears as an isolated lesion (it is typically combined with mitral stenosis) (Harrison 22e p.2059). Hemodynamically significant tricuspid stenosis is seen in roughly 5-10% of patients with severe mitral stenosis, and rheumatic tricuspid stenosis is commonly accompanied by some tricuspid regurgitation; nonrheumatic causes of stenosis are rare (Harrison 22e p.2059). More than 85% of tricuspid regurgitation encountered clinically is secondary (functional), arising from tricuspid annular dilation and leaflet tethering in the setting of RV remodeling from pressure/volume overload, MI, or trauma rather than from intrinsic valve disease (Harrison 22e p.2060). New-onset atrial fibrillation, especially in older patients, can produce 'atrial functional' tricuspid regurgitation through atrial and annular remodeling (Harrison 22e p.2060-2061). Patients with severe tricuspid stenosis characteristically complain of relatively little dyspnea given the marked hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema present, because the right-sided obstruction limits pulmonary congestion (Harrison 22e p.2059). Tricuspid regurgitation is more often detected by inspecting the neck veins (prominent c-v waves with rapid y descent) than by cardiac auscultation (Harrison 22e p.2061). Carvallo's sign - inspiratory accentuation of the holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border - helps distinguish the murmur of tricuspid regurgitation from that of mitral regurgitation; it diminishes on expiration or during the Valsalva strain phase (Harrison 22e p.2061). The murmur of tricuspid stenosis resembles that of mitral stenosis but is best heard at the lower left sternal border/xiphoid, is most prominent in presystole during sinus rhythm, and increases with inspiration while decreasing during expiration and Valsalva strain (Harrison 22e p.2060). In tricuspid stenosis with sinus rhythm, the right atrial a wave can be enormous (approaching RV systolic pressure) and the y descent is prolonged; presystolic pulsations of an enlarged liver may also be palpable (Harrison 22e p.2059). On ECG, absence of right ventricular hypertrophy in a patient with right-sided heart failure who is presumed to have mitral stenosis should raise suspicion for coexisting tricuspid valve disease; right atrial enlargement gives tall peaked P waves in lead II and prominent upright P waves in V1 (Harrison 22e p.2060). A distinct category of tricuspid regurgitation is caused by cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) leads crossing the valve, producing leaflet entrapment or perforation; right ventricular apical pacing can additionally cause dyssynchronous contraction and functional TR (Harrison 22e p.2060-2061). Coexisting tricuspid stenosis can mask the hemodynamic and clinical features of associated mitral stenosis by lowering cardiac output and keeping left atrial, pulmonary artery, and RV systolic pressures only normal or mildly elevated (Harrison 22e p.2059). Severe hepatic congestion progressing to cirrhosis, jaundice, serious malnutrition, anasarca, and ascites in severe tricuspid valve disease Persistent right-sided failure after an adequate mitral commissurotomy, suggesting unrecognized tricuspid stenosis Progressive RV dilation and declining systolic function in severe TR Marked reduction in cardiac output with prominent c-v wave and rapid y descent and loss of the x descent in severe TR Tricuspid stenosis is easily overlooked because it almost always occurs alongside obvious mitral disease and its diastolic murmur resembles that of mitral stenosis - the diagnosis must be deliberately considered (Harrison 22e p.2059-2060). The TR murmur may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation unless its inspiratory accentuation and the degree of RV enlargement are appreciated (Harrison 22e p.2061). Accurate echocardiographic quantification of TR severity, PA pressure, and RV size/function is genuinely difficult in many patients (Harrison 22e p.2062). Continuous-wave Doppler estimation of PA systolic pressure can be falsely low when TR is very severe because the jet velocity is blunted by rapidly rising RA pressure (Harrison 22e p.2062). Tricuspid stenosis is defined by a diastolic pressure gradient between the right atrium and right ventricle that increases with inspiration (greater transvalvular flow) and falls with expiration. A mean diastolic gradient of about 4 mmHg is usually enough to raise mean right atrial pressure to levels causing systemic venous congestion - hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema. Resting cardiac output is typically depressed and fails to rise with exercise. In tricuspid regurgitation, the incompetent valve allows backward flow from RV to RA, with the regurgitant volume governed by RV systolic driving pressure and the size of the regurgitant orifice; severity is modulated by pulmonary artery systolic pressure, annular dimensions, respiratory changes in RV preload, and RA compliance. Significant TR enlarges the right atrium, raises RA and jugular venous pressures with prominent c-v waves, can 'ventricularize' the RA waveform, and leads to RV volume overload, dilation, and eventual systolic dysfunction - accelerated by any added pressure load from pulmonary hypertension or prior myocardial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2059-2061). Mild-to-moderate tricuspid regurgitation is generally well tolerated when there is no other hemodynamic disturbance. Because TR commonly coexists with left-sided valve lesions, LV dysfunction, or pulmonary hypertension, those conditions often dominate the clinical course. As isolated severe TR progresses, reduced forward cardiac output causes fatigue and exertional dyspnea, and declining RV function leads to cervical pulsations, abdominal fullness, anorexia, muscle wasting, weight gain, and painful lower-extremity swelling. Severe TR is associated with markedly reduced cardiac output and elevated mean RA and RV end-diastolic pressures (Harrison 22e p.2061-2062). Severe tricuspid stenosis is defined echocardiographically by a tricuspid valve area of 1 cm2 or less, or a pressure half-time of 190 ms or more; a mean diastolic gradient around 4 mmHg is hemodynamically significant. For tricuspid regurgitation, severity is staged (progressive Stage B, asymptomatic severe Stage C, symptomatic severe Stage D); annular dilation is defined as >40 mm (>21 mm/m2) on transthoracic echocardiography or >70 mm on direct intraoperative measurement, and severe TR is accompanied by hepatic vein systolic flow reversal (Harrison 22e p.2060-2062).

a broad QRS is the key marker of cardiotoxicity and predicts arrhythmia and seizures A prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR is a supportive ECG sign of sodium-channel blockade Life-threatening features include ventricular arrhythmias, hypotension from myocardial depression and vasodilatation, seizures, and rapid deterioration in conscious level Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone treatment for a widening QRS, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension, working by sodium loading and alkalinisation Deterioration can be abrupt; a patient who looks well early can rapidly progress to coma, seizures, and cardiac arrest, so early cardiac monitoring is essential Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated as they aggravate sodium-channel blockade; refractory arrhythmia may be treated with additional bicarbonate and supportive measures Intravenous lipid emulsion may be considered as a rescue therapy in refractory cardiovascular collapse QRS widening on the ECG indicating significant cardiotoxicity Ventricular arrhythmia or haemodynamic instability Seizures or rapidly declining conscious level Refractory hypotension unresponsive to fluids Rapid clinical deterioration in a patient who initially appeared stable Being reassured by an initially well-appearing patient and delaying continuous cardiac monitoring Using class Ia or Ic antiarrhythmics, which worsen sodium-channel blockade Failing to give sodium bicarbonate promptly for a widening QRS or arrhythmia Allowing acidosis from seizures or hypoventilation to persist and aggravate cardiotoxicity Tricyclic antidepressants exert several toxic actions. Blockade of fast cardiac sodium channels slows myocardial depolarisation, widening the QRS and predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia and myocardial depression; this effect is worsened by acidosis. Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity produces the classic peripheral and central anticholinergic features. Antagonism of peripheral alpha-adrenergic receptors causes vasodilatation and hypotension, and central effects plus GABA and other receptor actions lower the seizure threshold. Seizures worsen acidosis, which in turn intensifies sodium-channel blockade in a dangerous positive-feedback loop. Most deaths occur early from arrhythmia, refractory hypotension, or seizures, often before or soon after arrival; patients who reach hospital and receive prompt bicarbonate and supportive care and survive the first day generally recover well.

cause of multiple cranial neuropathy) Tolosa-Hunt syndrome and other idiopathic granulomatous orbital/cavernous inflammation IgG4-related disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and other vasculitides Lymphoma and metastatic/locally infiltrating tumors (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, neurofibroma, meningioma, chordoma, cholesteatoma) Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (recurrent facial palsy, recurrent facial/labial edema, fissured tongue) Diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, and connective-tissue/collagen-vascular disease (e.g., Sjögren’s, SLE, scleroderma, MCTD) Skull-base and posterior-fossa structural lesions (acoustic neuroma, platybasia, basilar invagination, Paget’s disease, Chiari malformation) Carotid-cavernous fistula or carotid aneurysm Temporal bone fracture or blunt head injury Iatrogenic/traumatic injury (neck surgery, jugular vein cannulation, carotid endarterectomy/dissection, post-intubation Tapia syndrome) Trigeminal neuralgia produces brief (seconds to a minute or two) paroxysms of excruciating, superficial, stabbing pain usually in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin (V2/V3); ophthalmic-division (V1) involvement is rare. Attacks may be triggered by light tactile stimuli at facial, lip, or tongue trigger zones (washing, brushing teeth, a draft of air) and by speaking, chewing, or smiling. An essential diagnostic feature of classic trigeminal neuralgia is the ABSENCE of demonstrable objective sensory loss on examination; demonstrable trigeminal sensory or motor deficit instead points to a structural trigeminal neuropathy or secondary cause. Trigeminal neuralgia is relatively common (incidence ~4–8 per 100,000/year), affects mainly middle-aged and elderly persons, and roughly 60% of cases occur in women; bouts persist for weeks to months and tend to remit then recur. When trigeminal neuralgia occurs in a young adult or is bilateral, suspect multiple sclerosis (demyelinating plaque near the trigeminal root entry zone in the pons), especially if subtle facial sensory loss is present. Bell’s palsy is the most common form of facial paralysis (annual incidence ~25 per 100,000; lifetime risk ~1 in 60); onset is abrupt with maximal weakness by 48 h, often preceded by retroauricular pain for a day or two, and may include loss of taste and hyperacusis. A peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy weakens the whole hemiface including the forehead and eyelid closure, whereas a supranuclear (central) lesion relatively spares the forehead and orbicularis oculi because upper-face muscles receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation. Localizing the seventh-nerve lesion: loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue points to a middle-ear-segment lesion; hyperacusis indicates involvement of the nerve to stapedius; accompanying deafness, tinnitus, or vertigo suggests an internal auditory meatus lesion affecting the eighth nerve. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia resembles trigeminal neuralgia but is much less common; pain is paroxysmal and intense, arises in the tonsillar fossa/throat, may radiate to the ear, and is provoked by swallowing or coughing; rarely it triggers bradycardia/asystole, hypotension, and syncope. Anatomic clustering of cranial nerves yields recognizable syndromes: jugular foramen (IX, X, XI), cavernous sinus (III, IV, V1, VI), pontocerebellar angle (V, VI, VII, VIII), and retroparotid space (IX, X, XI, XII plus Horner’s). Cavernous sinus syndrome is frequently life-threatening: orbital/facial pain, orbital swelling, chemosis, fever, ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), and V1 (±V2) trigeminal involvement—cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial/orbital/sinus infection (including mucormycosis in diabetics) is the most common cause and demands early diagnosis. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous cavernous-sinus/orbital inflammation) causes painful ophthalmoparesis with V1/V2 numbness and shows a dramatic response to glucocorticoids, but its picture can be mimicked by sarcoid, vasculitis, IgG4-related disease, lymphoma, and fungal infection—so confirm before attributing to it. An eleventh-nerve (spinal accessory) palsy causes little overt neck weakness because other muscles assist head turning; detection relies on palpating absent sternocleidomastoid contraction during head turning and on noting a lower shoulder, scapular winging, and inability to abduct the arm beyond 90 degrees. Overlooking multiple sclerosis as the cause of trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult or when symptoms are bilateral. Mistaking a central (supranuclear) forehead-sparing facial weakness for peripheral Bell’s palsy and missing a stroke or hemispheric lesion. Failing to examine the eighth and other cranial nerves in a patient with facial palsy—the eighth nerve runs close to the facial nerve at the pontomedullary junction and in the temporal bone. Attributing an insidious, progressive facial weakness to Bell’s palsy when it actually reflects a temporal bone or pontine tumor. Missing Ramsay Hunt syndrome by not inspecting the external auditory canal and palate for zoster vesicles. Misdiagnosing vagal/laryngeal or pharyngeal muscle disease (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, myotonic dystrophy) as a primary vagus nerve lesion in dysphagia/dysphonia. Searching intracranially for an isolated vocal cord palsy when intrathoracic disease (aortic aneurysm, enlarged left atrium, mediastinal/bronchial tumor) is the far more common cause. Delaying recognition and treatment of cavernous sinus thrombosis, an early-diagnosis emergency. The cranial nerves are 12 paired nerves with mixed motor, sensory, and autonomic functions linked by their close brainstem relationships; nine connect directly to brainstem nuclei, while CN I and II are effectively brain fiber tracts and CN XI arises largely from upper cervical cord. In trigeminal neuralgia, symptoms arise from ectopic action-potential generation in pain-sensitive afferents of the fifth-nerve root just proximal to its entry at the lateral pons; demyelination of large myelinated (non-nociceptive) fibers renders them hyperexcitable and electrically coupled to adjacent small unmyelinated/poorly myelinated pain fibers, so tactile input can ignite paroxysms of pain. Compression of the root by a blood vessel—most often the superior cerebellar artery (or a tortuous vein)—is implicated in most cases; age-related brain sagging and increased vascular tortuosity may explain its predilection for later life. The trigeminal nerve carries oligodendrocyte-derived (central-type) myelin for up to ~7 mm beyond the brainstem, which may underlie trigeminal neuralgia in MS. In Bell’s palsy there is inflammation of the facial nerve with mononuclear cell infiltration suggesting an infectious/immune mechanism; reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 in the geniculate ganglion is thought to cause most cases, with varicella-zoster reactivation implicated in up to one-third (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). The vagus and other lower cranial nerves can be injured along their medullary, meningeal, foraminal, or extracranial courses; the recurrent laryngeal nerve (especially the left) is most often damaged by intrathoracic disease. Trigeminal neuralgia characteristically remits spontaneously after bouts lasting weeks to months, and remissions can be long-lasting, though the disorder ultimately recurs in most patients. In Bell’s palsy, about 80% of patients recover within a few weeks to months; incomplete paralysis during the first week is the most favorable prognostic sign, whereas EMG evidence of denervation after 10 days predicts axonal degeneration with delayed (typically ~3 months) and possibly incomplete recovery, and recurrences occur in roughly 7% of cases. Idiopathic trigeminal neuropathy usually recovers gradually. Most patients with isolated spinal accessory neuropathy recover. Post-intubation Tapia syndrome (vagal plus hypoglossal palsy) usually resolves within a few months. No formal grading scale is presented in this chapter. In Bell’s palsy, clinical severity is gauged by completeness of paralysis, with incomplete paralysis in the first week being the most favorable prognostic indicator and electromyographic denervation after 10 days indicating axonal degeneration and a worse, more prolonged recovery. The diagnosis of Bell’s palsy is supported clinically by a typical presentation, absence of other risk factors/symptoms, no zoster lesions in the ear canal, and a normal neurologic examination apart from the facial nerve.

to fibrosis Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is an immunological hyperresponsiveness to lymphatic filarial worms rather than a direct tissue infection by adult worms in the lung. Microfilariae released into the circulation are rapidly cleared from the blood by an exuberant immune response and become trapped in the pulmonary vasculature and interstitium. There they trigger intense eosinophil recruitment and release of eosinophil granule proteins and inflammatory mediators, driven by a strong immunoglobulin E and antifilarial antibody response. This causes bronchospasm, alveolar and interstitial inflammation, and, if untreated, progressive interstitial fibrosis. With prompt antifilarial treatment most patients recover fully, but diagnostic delay or recurrent untreated episodes can result in chronic interstitial lung disease and irreversible pulmonary fibrosis.

abnormal results point toward DIC (Harrison 22e p.967) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — negative in MAHA (Harrison 22e p.638) Full blood count with platelet count and peripheral smear for schistocytes (Harrison 22e p.968) Reticulocyte count (reticulocytosis supports haemolysis) (Harrison 22e p.638) Renal function / serum creatinine and urinalysis (haematuria, proteinuria, granular or hyaline casts in HUS) (Harrison 22e p.638) Complement-regulatory gene testing (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46, CFI, THBD) and anti-factor-H antibody for suspected atypical HUS — though assigning pathogenicity to variants is difficult and no functional diagnostic assay is established (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801) Disseminated intravascular coagulation (distinguished by abnormal PT/aPTT and clotting-factor/fibrinogen consumption) (Harrison 22e p.967) Drug-induced microangiopathy — immune-mediated (ticlopidine, possibly clopidogrel, quinine) or by direct endothelial toxicity (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, gemcitabine, mitomycin C) (Harrison 22e p.968) Chemotherapy-/cancer-associated HUS (mitomycin and gemcitabine most often; also cisplatin, bleomycin, proteasome and VEGF inhibitors) (Harrison 22e p.638) Malignancy-induced HUS from microvascular metastases or extensive marrow invasion (Harrison 22e p.638) Bone-marrow / haematopoietic stem cell transplant-associated microangiopathy (Harrison 22e pp.638, 967) Pregnancy/postpartum-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (including HELLP in the obstetric context) (Harrison 22e pp.967-968) Systemic vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.967) The thrombotic microangiopathies are unified by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA): thrombocytopenia plus fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear, biochemical haemolysis (high LDH, high unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin) and microvascular thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.967). TTP was classically described as a pentad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal failure, neurologic changes and fever; the full pentad is now seen less often because earlier diagnosis and treatment intervene before it evolves (Harrison 22e pp.967-968). ADAMTS13 activity below 10% is diagnostic of TTP; the assay (activity level plus anti-ADAMTS13 antibody) is central to working up any MAHA (Harrison 22e p.968). ADAMTS13 levels are generally normal in HUS, although they have occasionally been reported as decreased — so a normal ADAMTS13 does not exclude a thrombotic microangiopathy other than TTP (Harrison 22e p.968). Schistocytes are red-cell fragments produced by physical disruption against intravascular platelet/fibrin strands or external forces, and are the morphologic hallmark of MAHA (Harrison 22e p.~640). The Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is negative in microangiopathic haemolysis, helping separate it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Harrison 22e p.638). TTP is more common in women than men, and is over-represented in HIV infection and in pregnancy; congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency (Upshaw-Schulman) may first declare itself during a first pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.968). In a classic HUS presentation, a preceding episode of diarrhoea (often bloody) in a child points to Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 as the commonest, though not the only, cause (Harrison 22e p.968). Atypical HUS is essentially a complement-alternative-pathway disease — driven by mutations in complement components/regulators (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46/MCP, CFI, THBD) or anti-factor-H antibodies — and clinical disease usually requires a trigger such as infection, so penetrance is incomplete (Harrison 22e pp.800-801). New unexplained thrombocytopenia with MAHA is a haematologic emergency — TTP is devastating if not recognised and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.968) Plasma exchange should be initiated urgently on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory ADAMTS13 results, and likewise re-initiated promptly on suspected relapse (Harrison 22e p.968) Fluctuating neurologic abnormalities (especially headache and confusion) in the setting of MAHA suggest TTP (Harrison 22e p.450) Persistently low ADAMTS13 carries a greater risk of ongoing sequelae including stroke (Harrison 22e p.968) In cancer-/transfusion-associated HUS, severe hypertension, pulmonary oedema and rapid worsening of haemolysis and renal function can follow a blood or blood-product transfusion (Harrison 22e p.638) Do not reflexively transfuse platelets in TTP — platelet transfusion may fuel further microvascular thrombosis and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding (principle, Harrison 22e Chap. 120). Do not assume normal coagulation excludes a thrombotic microangiopathy: PT and aPTT are characteristically normal in TTP/HUS, whereas they are abnormal in DIC — use them to discriminate, not to exclude (Harrison 22e p.967). A normal ADAMTS13 does not point to TTP; ADAMTS13 is usually normal in HUS, so the diagnosis there rests on the clinical picture and complement work-up (Harrison 22e p.968). Atypical HUS is a diagnosis of exclusion; patients may be started on plasma exchange until ADAMTS13 returns and the diagnosis clarifies, even though plasma exchange has not been shown to change clinical outcomes in aHUS (Harrison 22e p.968). Plasma infusion/exchange does not alter the course of typical HUS or aHUS except in the subgroup with anti-factor-H antibodies (Harrison 22e p.968). Drug-induced microangiopathy may improve simply on withdrawing or reducing the offending endothelial-toxic agent, so reflexive long-term plasma exchange may be unnecessary (Harrison 22e p.968). Cancer-associated HUS can present without an evident malignancy — in one series 35% had no apparent cancer when the syndrome appeared, and it may surface weeks to months after the last chemotherapy dose (Harrison 22e p.638). TTP arises from deficient or antibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is secreted by endothelium as ultra-large multimers; when these are not cleaved they persist and drive pathological platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing microvascular thrombi. ADAMTS13 deficiency alone is not sufficient — congenitally ADAMTS13-deficient individuals develop TTP only episodically, implying a second trigger. In HUS the dominant lesion is endothelial injury with deposition of fibrin in capillary/arteriolar walls, predominantly in the kidney; typical (diarrhoea-associated) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7, while atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the complement alternative pathway with consequent endothelial damage. The shared downstream picture is microvascular platelet/fibrin thrombi causing red-cell fragmentation (MAHA), consumption thrombocytopenia and end-organ ischaemia (Harrison 22e pp.967-968, 800-801). Plasma exchange transformed TTP outcomes, reducing mortality from roughly 85-100% to about 10-30%. Relapse is common: 25-45% of plasma-exchange-treated patients relapse within 30 days of apparent remission and 12-40% relapse late, with relapse more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at presentation. In diarrhoea-associated HUS roughly 40% of children need some dialysis but overall mortality is <5%; non-diarrhoeal HUS carries higher mortality (~26%). Untreated atypical HUS had acute-phase mortality up to ~15% with up to 50% progressing to end-stage renal disease, though spontaneous remission occurs and relapse is likely with re-exposure to a trigger. Cancer-/chemotherapy-associated HUS has a high case-fatality rate, with most patients dying within months (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801, 638). Harrison does not give a formal TTP/HUS severity score in this material. Functional stratification used: ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic of TTP and severe deficiency at presentation predicts relapse and worse sequelae. HUS is grouped clinically into diarrhoea-associated (typical, Shiga-toxin) HUS versus non-diarrhoea-associated/atypical (complement-mediated) HUS, which carries higher mortality. (No PLASMIC score is described in the source and none is asserted here.) (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801).

Within the node, a cell-mediated immune response forms granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells and central caseous necrosis. With the standard multidrug regimen the outlook is excellent, though nodes may enlarge paradoxically during treatment and residual firm nodes or scarring can persist; relapse is uncommon with adherence, and drug resistance worsens outcomes.

Tuberculous meningitis usually develops when a subependymal or subpial focus (a Rich focus), seeded during earlier haematogenous dissemination, ruptures into the subarachnoid space. The released mycobacterial antigens provoke an intense inflammatory exudate that is most marked at the base of the brain. This basal exudate entraps cranial nerves, obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow to cause hydrocephalus, and induces a vasculitis of perforating arteries leading to ischaemic infarction. The combination of inflammation, raised intracranial pressure and vascular compromise underlies the cranial neuropathies, strokes and depressed consciousness that characterise severe disease. Outcome depends heavily on the neurological stage at which treatment begins; early treatment offers good recovery, whereas presentation with coma, deficits or advanced stage carries high mortality and frequent long-term sequelae such as cognitive impairment, hydrocephalus and paresis.

life-threatening haemorrhage Cardiac rhabdomyomas causing outflow obstruction or arrhythmia in infancy Overlooking subtle skin signs such as hypomelanotic macules that aid early diagnosis Failing to arrange surveillance for growing subependymal giant cell astrocytomas and renal lesions Delaying treatment of infantile spasms with consequences for development Not recognising the neuropsychiatric spectrum and its impact on quality of life Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by inactivating mutations in either TSC1, encoding hamartin, or TSC2, encoding tuberin. Together these proteins form a complex that inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway, which controls cell growth and proliferation. Loss of function releases this inhibition, leading to constitutive mTOR activation and the growth of benign hamartomatous lesions across multiple organs. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, though many cases are de novo, and lesion formation is consistent with a second somatic hit inactivating the remaining allele. The mechanistic understanding underpins the therapeutic use of mTOR inhibitors. Outcome is highly variable; many individuals live full lives, but epilepsy severity, cognitive impairment, and organ complications such as giant cell astrocytomas and renal or pulmonary disease determine morbidity and mortality.

under-assessed and undertreated Tuberous sclerosis complex is caused by loss-of-function variants in TSC1 (encoding hamartin) or TSC2 (encoding tuberin), whose protein product forms a complex that inhibits the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signalling pathway. Loss of this inhibitory brake leads to constitutive mTOR activation, driving unregulated cell growth and proliferation and the formation of hamartomas in multiple organs. Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the burden of neurological, renal and pulmonary disease; epilepsy and neuropsychiatric disorders drive childhood morbidity, while renal and pulmonary complications dominate in adults. Targeted mTOR-inhibitor therapy and structured surveillance have improved outcomes, and many individuals live into adulthood.

A group of disorders that primarily affect the renal tubules and interstitium with relative sparing of the glomeruli and vessels, divided into acute and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute TIN causes AKI either via aggressive inflammatory infiltrates producing tissue edema, tubular cell injury, and compromised tubular flow, or via frank tubular obstruction by casts, cellular debris, or crystals; flank pain may arise from renal capsule distention (Harrison 22e p.2437). Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is most commonly an allergic, immune-mediated drug reaction (antibiotics such as beta-lactams/sulfonamides/quinolones/vancomycin/rifampin, NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, proton pump inhibitors, diuretics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, immune checkpoint inhibitors), but may also be immune-mediated within autoimmune syndromes (Sjogren's, SLE, TINU, granulomatous/sarcoid, IgG4-related disease) or infection-associated (Harrison 22e p.2437-2438). Chronic TIN produces interstitial fibrosis with patchy mononuclear cell infiltration, widespread tubular atrophy, luminal dilation, and thickened tubular basement membranes, manifesting as tubular dysfunction (nephrogenic DI, Fanconi's syndrome, RTA) and progressive azotemia (Harrison 22e p.2437). Because the chronic histopathology is nonspecific, biopsy rarely yields a specific diagnosis, so diagnosis relies on history, drug/toxin exposure, associated symptoms, and imaging (Harrison 22e p.2437). In allergic/drug-induced AIN, discontinuation of the offending agent often reverses the kidney injury, though recovery may be incomplete depending on duration of exposure and degree of tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2438). Granulomatous, idiopathic, TINU, and Sjogren's-related interstitial nephritis generally respond to glucocorticoids, especially when treated early before significant fibrosis, but may relapse and require maintenance immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2438-2439). Chronic TIN damage that has already occurred is impossible to reverse, but further deterioration may be slowed by treating glomerular hypertension (Harrison 22e p.2440). Reflux nephropathy affecting both kidneys often progresses inexorably to ESRD over years even without ongoing infection or reflux (Harrison 22e p.2441). Lithium-associated CKD is often irreversible and slowly progresses to ESRD even after lithium is stopped (Harrison 22e p.2443). AKI from acute hypercalcemia may be fully reversible, whereas chronic hypercalcemic kidney dysfunction may not improve even after correcting the calcium disorder (Harrison 22e p.2443). Harrison classifies tubulointerstitial diseases into Acute Tubulointerstitial Disorders - acute interstitial nephritis (therapeutic agents/drugs, infection, autoimmune including TINU, Sjogren's, SLE, granulomatous, IgG4-related) and acute obstructive disorders (light chain cast nephropathy, acute phosphate nephropathy, acute urate nephropathy) - versus Chronic Tubulointerstitial Disorders (reflux nephropathy, sickle cell disease, chronic toxin/drug exposure such as analgesics, lithium, heavy metals, aristolochic acid, calcineurin inhibitors), metabolic disturbances (hypercalcemia/nephrocalcinosis, hyperuricemia, hypokalemia, hyperoxaluria, cystinosis), cystic/hereditary disorders, and miscellaneous causes (aging, chronic glomerulonephritis, obstruction, ischemia, radiation) (Harrison 22e p.2437).

Loss-of-function variants in EPCAM disrupt the epithelial cell adhesion molecule, impairing cell-cell contacts and the normal architecture of the intestinal epithelium. Enterocytes crowd and pile into focal tufts at the villus surface, with associated villus atrophy and crypt changes, so the absorptive surface is compromised. The syndromic SPINT2-associated form involves a serine protease inhibitor and additional developmental anomalies. The net effect is failure of fluid and nutrient absorption producing chronic diarrhoea from early infancy. Most patients require prolonged or indefinite parenteral nutrition; some achieve partial enteral tolerance while severe refractory disease may progress to intestinal transplantation. Outcome is influenced by nutritional complications and any associated anomalies.

for ulcer specimens it is comparable to culture in sensitivity and specificity (Harrison 22e p.1339) Appropriate specimens for direct detection or culture: ulcer specimens (sampled from the wound edge), lower respiratory tract specimens (sputum, tracheal washing, bronchoalveolar lavage), lymph node biopsies or aspirates, and blood cultures (Harrison 22e p.1339) Blood culture: F. tularensis is slow-growing and a 10-day incubation is recommended for optimal sensitivity; MALDI-TOF identification from blood cultures is an increasingly common, sometimes unexpected, finding (Harrison 22e p.1339) Serology (ELISA or microagglutination) is the mainstay in many laboratories and is especially useful when tularemia is suspected at a later stage; antibodies are generally detectable 10-20 days post-infection (Harrison 22e p.1339) Chest imaging in respiratory tularemia: single or multifocal consolidation, pleural effusion, and hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy; CT may show rounded subpleural consolidations and necrotic lymph nodes; pathology resolution on imaging can be slow and take months (Harrison 22e p.1339) Lung cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339) Head and neck cancer (Harrison 22e p.1337) Lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.1337) Suspected tumor with lymphoid tissue engagement (Harrison 22e p.1337) Zoonosis caused by Francisella tularensis, a small facultatively intracellular aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus; humans are infected via arthropod bites (ticks, tabanid/deer flies, mosquitoes), inhalation of infectious aerosols, handling infected animals, or ingestion of contaminated water/food (Harrison 22e p.1335-1336). Take a deliberate exposure history: wild animal contact (rodents, rabbits, hares), inhalation of dust contaminated with their urine or feces, recent tick/fly/mosquito bites, brush-cutting or grass-trimming, handling wood or hay, and walking or hunting in wildlife habitats; cluster cases sharing the same exposure are a clue (Harrison 22e p.1337). The most common initial manifestation is an influenza-like illness with high fever (acute onset, myalgia, headache, constitutional symptoms); fever may be persistent or intermittent. Incubation is usually 3-5 days but may range from 1 to 21 days (Harrison 22e p.1337). Inflamed, swollen, tender regional lymph nodes are typical; the initial infection route determines which lymphoid tissue is engaged (skin or pharyngeal entry gives regional nodes; inhalation gives mediastinal/hilar nodes) (Harrison 22e p.1337). Ulceroglandular form (most common, ~47% of US cases): skin inoculation by a blood-feeding arthropod or direct contact with an infected animal/contaminated material produces a primary ulcer plus tender regional lymphadenopathy; the primary ulcer is often a small skin break with limited inflammation that requires careful examination to detect (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338). Glandular form (~18% of US cases): regional lymphadenopathy without a detectable primary skin ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1338). Oculoglandular form (~2% of US cases): conjunctivitis with pronounced local inflammation plus regional (e.g., preauricular) lymphadenopathy, acquired by touching the eye with contaminated fingers or by contaminated aerosol (Harrison 22e p.1338). Oropharyngeal form (~2% of US cases): acute pharyngitis with pronounced local inflammation following ingestion of contaminated water or food, with cervical/tonsillar lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.1338). Respiratory/pneumonic form (~17% of US cases): acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosol; more often bacteremic and more likely to progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities. Onset of a dry cough may occur more than 7 days after the influenza-like illness; engaged lymphoid tissue is in the mediastinum or lung hila (Harrison 22e p.1338). Typhoidal form (~14% of US cases): an older term for a typhoid-like syndrome with prolonged high fever, fatigue, headache, and nausea; Harrison recommends avoiding the term because most historic typhoidal cases were in fact respiratory/pneumonic tularemia acquired by inhalation (Harrison 22e p.1338). Routine blood biochemistry is generally unhelpful; findings are nonspecific and may or may not show elevated liver enzymes or hematuria. In a Swedish type B outpatient series, white-cell counts stayed within normal limits in 70% of patients and CRP was only moderately elevated (Harrison 22e p.1338). When tularemia is clinically suspected, communicate the suspicion to the microbiology laboratory in advance so that cultures are handled safely, because F. tularensis causes laboratory-acquired infection and culture requires BSL-3 containment; it is also a US HHS Tier 1 Select Agent (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339). For ulcer sampling, swab the edge of the wound (remove any scab first) and rub firmly so the specimen is slightly blood-tinged to maximize yield (Harrison 22e p.1339). Respiratory/pneumonic form, which is more often bacteremic and may progress to severe disease requiring inpatient care, particularly in patients aged 65 and over and those with comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1338) Multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability, indicating need for inpatient care (Harrison 22e p.1337) Host factors increasing risk of severe infection: geriatric frailty, immunosuppression, severe lung and/or heart impairment, and other significant comorbidities (Harrison 22e p.1337) Lymph node abscess formation, which occurs in about one-third of patients and is associated with antibiotic treatment delay of more than 2-3 weeks after disease onset (Harrison 22e p.1340) Severe complications reported: adult respiratory distress syndrome, myocarditis, pericarditis, endocarditis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, hepatitis, and renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1340) Clinical recognition is challenging, especially if the patient does not spontaneously report fever; tularemia may not be suspected until after extensive and costly investigations, and even in high-endemic areas patients are often initially mistreated for other conditions. A high index of suspicion is critical (Harrison 22e p.1337). If care is sought several weeks after symptom onset, the acute fever onset may not be reported spontaneously and must be actively elicited (Harrison 22e p.1337). The primary ulcer can be a small, minimally inflamed skin break that is easily missed or may be undetectable, in which case the disease is classified as glandular rather than ulceroglandular (Harrison 22e p.1338). Failure to alert the microbiology laboratory to suspected tularemia risks laboratory-acquired infection, as F. tularensis is highly virulent and requires BSL-3 culture conditions (Harrison 22e p.1335, 1339). Acute-phase serology can be misleading because F. tularensis antibodies persist (single titers can remain above the diagnostic cutoff for at least 1 year), so reliable acute diagnosis should rely on a significant rise between paired sera taken 2-4 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.1339). Culture specimens taken from an established lymph node abscess are typically F. tularensis negative (Harrison 22e p.1340). Tularemia patients do not require isolation because there is no human-to-human transmission (Harrison 22e p.1340). Natural transmission is usually through the skin or by inhalation of aerosols, but ingestion of contaminated food/water can also infect. An extremely low dose of about 10-50 organisms inoculated through skin microtrauma or inhaled suffices to cause disease, whereas roughly 10^6-10^8 organisms are required by the oral route. Tissue-resident macrophages (alveolar macrophages in lung, Langerhans cells in skin) transport the organism via blood and lymphatics to lymph nodes, spleen, and bone marrow; in skin, neutrophils phagocytose F. tularensis early. After uptake, the bacterium escapes the phagosome into the cytosol, replicates, exits the cell, and disseminates. F. tularensis is a 'stealth pathogen' that manipulates host-cell signaling, delaying the immune response and permitting rapid systemic spread. Characteristic tissue reactions are granuloma formation and necrotic foci surrounded by macrophages, lymphocytes, and giant cells in lymph nodes, lung, spleen, kidney, and liver; pulmonary autopsy findings show necrotizing pneumonia with fibrin, cellular debris, and neutrophils. Effective protective immunity requires both B and T cells, and antigen-specific recall T-cell responses can persist 25-30 years after infection or vaccination (Harrison 22e p.1337, 1339). Before antibiotics, US case-fatality rates were typically 5-15% and could reach as high as 60% in respiratory/pneumonic tularemia. Recent US surveillance (2006-2021) showed 27 of 903 patients (3.0%) with available outcome data died; treatment with at least one high-efficacy antimicrobial class was independently associated with greatly increased odds of survival. Type A is generally more lethal than type B, though there is heterogeneity among type A genetic varieties. Overall type B fatality is estimated at less than 1% in Sweden, where severe respiratory type B tularemia carried about 1.5% fatality. Recovery (and resolution of imaging abnormalities) may be slow, and some patients report postinfectious persisting fatigue and disability of uncertain cause (Harrison 22e p.1339-1340). Harrison does not provide a formal severity score. Clinically, management level is decided by physical examination of the anatomic site and extent of inflammation (pneumonitis, lymph node inflammation, skin ulcers/pustules, pharyngitis), the rate of progression, and host risk factors: localized symptoms are generally suitable for outpatient care, whereas multiorgan involvement or hemodynamic instability suggests inpatient care. The recognized clinical forms (ulceroglandular, glandular, oropharyngeal, oculoglandular, respiratory/pneumonic, typhoidal) are classified by F. tularensis infection route rather than by severity (Harrison 22e p.1337-1338).

a drug-associated trigger in treated multiple sclerosis Tumefactive demyelination is a focal region of intense inflammatory demyelination large enough to produce a space-occupying appearance. Macrophage-rich inflammation strips myelin while relatively sparing axons, and the advancing inflammatory edge produces the characteristic open-ring pattern of contrast enhancement. Because the pathology is inflammatory rather than neoplastic, restricted diffusion at the rim, relative lack of mass effect for size, and the open-ring sign help distinguish it from tumour, although overlap with the multiple sclerosis spectrum and with Balo and Marburg variants exists. Many patients recover well with corticosteroids, and lesions typically shrink over time; long-term outcome depends on whether the disorder declares itself as multiple sclerosis or remains a solitary event.

hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) makes up about 85% of primary liver cancers, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma about 10%, with rarer entities including fibrolamellar HCC, mixed HCC-iCCA, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, and pediatric hepatoblastoma (Harrison 22e p.659). Cirrhosis of any cause is the dominant risk factor for HCC; about one-third of cirrhotic patients develop HCC over their lifetime, with an annual risk of roughly 3-8% in HBV- or HCV-related cirrhosis and a lower 1-2% per year in cirrhosis from alcohol, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, and cholestatic disorders (Harrison 22e p.659-660). HBV accounts for roughly 50% of HCC cases globally (about 60% in Asia and Africa, about 20% in the West) and can cause tumors via insertional mutagenesis; importantly, 25-30% of MASH-associated HCCs arise in the absence of cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.660). HCC has a strong male preponderance (male-to-female ratio about 2.5:1) and incidence peaks at 65-70 years, though it presents earlier (40-50 years) in populations with vertical HBV transmission (Harrison 22e p.659). The radiologic hallmark of HCC on four-phase CT or dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI is arterial-phase contrast uptake with washout in the portal venous or delayed phase, a pattern with about 95-100% specificity that can make biopsy unnecessary in cirrhotic patients (Harrison 22e p.661). The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system is the most accepted staging scheme; the TNM staging system is NOT used in HCC because it does not capture liver function and performance status, the key prognostic variables (Harrison 22e p.662-664). Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary liver cancer and is classified by location into intrahepatic (iCCA, ~20-30%), perihilar (pCCA, ~50-60%), and distal (dCCA, ~20-30%); perihilar and distal forms together are termed extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (Harrison 22e p.667). FGFR2 fusions and IDH1/2 mutations occur mostly in iCCA, whereas ERBB2/3 amplifications and SMAD4 aberrations characterize extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; up to about 40% of iCCAs carry a targetable mutation (Harrison 22e p.667). Acute painless jaundice occurs in about 90% of perihilar cholangiocarcinoma patients, while roughly 10% present with cholangitis; distal cholangiocarcinoma can be hard to distinguish from early pancreatic cancer (Harrison 22e p.668-669). Gallbladder cancer is the most common biliary tract malignancy worldwide, has a female-to-male ratio of about 3:1, and cholelithiasis is the major risk factor though fewer than 1% of patients with gallstones develop it; gallbladder polyps 10 mm or larger carry transformation risk (Harrison 22e p.669-670). Fibrolamellar HCC typically affects children and young adults (10-30 years) without underlying liver disease, carries the PRKACA-DNAJB1 fusion oncogene in 80-100% of cases, and has a better prognosis than conventional HCC (Harrison 22e p.670). Hepatic (hepatocellular) adenomas occur predominantly in women aged 35-40 (female-to-male ratio ~10:1), are linked to oral contraceptive use in women and anabolic androgenic steroid use in male bodybuilders, and carry risk of hemorrhage and malignant transformation, particularly when larger than 5 cm (Harrison 22e p.670). Symptomatic HCC (malaise, weight loss, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, or signs of liver dysfunction) indicates advanced disease with median survival under 1 year Macrovascular (portal, hepatic, or branch vein) invasion, lymph node involvement, or extrahepatic spread denotes advanced BCLC C disease Child-Pugh class C / severe liver dysfunction (BCLC D) Rising or markedly elevated AFP (>=20 ng/mL prompting imaging; >=400 ng/dL highly suspicious but not diagnostic) Painless jaundice or cholangitis suggesting biliary tract malignancy Hepatic adenoma larger than 5 cm (hemorrhage and malignant transformation risk); active adenoma bleeding A negative liver biopsy does NOT exclude HCC; sensitivity falls below 50% for tumors 1-2 cm, and a second biopsy is advised if findings are inconclusive or the lesion grows/changes enhancement Nodules under 1 cm are unlikely to be HCC and are difficult to diagnose; short-interval ultrasound follow-up (every 3-4 months) is recommended rather than immediate biopsy PET and contrast-enhanced ultrasound perform poorly for early HCC diagnosis and are not recommended as primary diagnostic tools An AFP of >=400 ng/dL is highly suspicious but NOT diagnostic of HCC by guidelines TNM staging should NOT be applied to HCC because it omits liver function and performance status About 25-30% of MASH-related HCCs occur without cirrhosis, so absence of cirrhosis does not exclude HCC in this group Surveillance is generally NOT recommended in advanced (Child-Pugh C) cirrhosis since curative therapy is precluded, except for liver transplant waiting-list patients Liver biopsy carries a ~2-3% risk of complications including tumor seeding and bleeding HCC develops through a multistep process beginning with precancerous low-grade dysplastic nodules that progress to high-grade dysplastic nodules and then early HCC; adult hepatocytes are the principal cell of origin, either transforming directly or de-differentiating into precursor cells, with progenitor cells contributing in a subset. It is a prototypical inflammation-associated cancer in which oxidative stress and the immune microenvironment of chronically damaged liver drive mutation. Tumors accumulate roughly 40-60 somatic alterations, of which 4-8 are driver genes; the leading drivers are TERT promoter mutations (~56%), TP53 (~27%), and CTNNB1 (~26%), all currently non-actionable. Aflatoxin B1 produces a characteristic TP53 R249S hotspot mutation. Only about 20-25% of HCCs carry an actionable mutation. Two molecular subclasses exist: a proliferative class (poor outcome, HBV-related, AFP overexpression, Ras/mTOR/IGF activation) and a nonproliferative class (often CTNNB1-mutated, better outcome). Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from adult cholangiocytes, transdifferentiated hepatocytes, or progenitor-cholangiocyte precursors, whereas extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma arises from biliary epithelium and peribiliary glands. Hepatic adenomas are clonal proliferations from single-gene driver mutations (e.g., CTNNB1, HNF1A inactivation, inflammatory or Hedgehog pathway activation), and focal nodular hyperplasia is a polyclonal hepatocellular proliferation secondary to an arterial malformation (Harrison 22e p.660-670). Prognosis depends on stage, tumor burden, liver function, and performance status. About 40% of HCC patients are diagnosed at BCLC stage 0 or A and are eligible for potentially curative resection, transplantation, or ablation, with median overall survival beyond 5 years (up to ~10 years after transplantation). Optimal surgical resection candidates have 5-year survival of 60-70% (35-55% in suboptimal candidates); RFA achieves ~60% 5-year survival; liver transplantation within Milan criteria yields 70-80% 5-year survival with ~10-15% recurrence at 5 years. Intermediate-stage (BCLC B) untreated natural history is about 16 months, improved to ~25-30 months with TACE. Symptomatic/advanced disease has median survival under 1 year; end-stage (BCLC D) survival is about 3-6 months. Cholangiocarcinoma overall carries a 5-year survival of about 10%; resectable iCCA single tumors have median survival ~40-50 months. Gallbladder cancer 5-year survival ranges 60-90% in resected localized disease but only ~10-12 months median in advanced disease. Fibrolamellar HCC has better prognosis (median ~70 months after resection). Hepatoblastoma overall 5-year survival is ~70% (50-90% by PRETEXT stage); notably, low AFP (<100 ng/mL) indicates poor prognosis in hepatoblastoma, opposite to HCC. Hepatocellular carcinoma is staged by the Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system into five stages: very early (BCLC 0, single nodule <=2 cm, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0), early (BCLC A, single or up to three nodules <=3 cm, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), intermediate (BCLC B, multinodular, Child-Pugh A-B, ECOG 0), advanced (BCLC C, portal/macrovascular invasion, N1 or M1, or ECOG 1-2), and terminal (BCLC D, Child-Pugh C or ECOG >2). Liver function is graded by the Child-Pugh score (classes A-C) and performance by ECOG. Milan criteria (single tumor <=5 cm, or up to three nodules each <=3 cm, no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread) define transplant eligibility. Cholangiocarcinoma is classified anatomically into intrahepatic, perihilar, and distal subtypes; hepatoblastoma uses the PRETEXT (Pretreatment Extent of Tumor) classification (Harrison 22e p.661-669).

Tungiasis — Tunga penetrans, jigger flea infestation, sand flea disease, chigoe flea, pique Plantar wart (verruca) Foreign body granuloma or splinter reaction Myiasis (furuncular) Paronychia or bacterial abscess Scabies or other pruritic dermatoses of the feet Melanoma or pigmented lesion (when the black dot is prominent) Clinical and epidemiological assessment (travel/residence, barefoot exposure) Dermoscopy to visualise the embedded flea and its pore Examination for multiple lesions and secondary infection Assessment of tetanus immunisation status Swab and culture if secondary bacterial infection is suspected Caused by penetration of the skin by the gravid female sand flea Tunga penetrans, endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean Affects impoverished communities where people walk barefoot on sandy or dusty soil; lesions concentrate on the feet, especially the toes, periungual folds and soles The classic lesion is a white papule with a central black dot (the flea's posterior/exsanguination pore) that enlarges into a painful, itchy nodule as eggs develop Lesions can be staged (Fortaleza classification) from penetration through to involution and residual skin changes Diagnosis is clinical, based on typical lesions in an epidemiological context; dermoscopy can confirm the embedded flea Secondary bacterial infection is common and can lead to abscess, ulceration, lymphangitis, and in neglected cases tetanus or gangrene Treatment is careful surgical extraction of the flea under sterile conditions, wound care, and ensuring tetanus immunisation; occlusive topical agents may kill the embedded flea Spreading cellulitis, lymphangitis or abscess formation Signs suggestive of tetanus in an unimmunised patient Gangrene or deep tissue destruction from heavy or neglected infestation Widespread multiple lesions causing difficulty walking and disability Incomplete extraction leaving flea parts that provoke persistent inflammation and infection Performing non-sterile 'home' extraction, introducing secondary infection or tetanus risk Overlooking tetanus prophylaxis Mistaking a solitary lesion for a wart and applying inappropriate destructive treatment Failing to advise on footwear and environmental measures, allowing reinfestation The impregnated female flea burrows head-first into the epidermis, usually of the foot, leaving its posterior end at the skin surface for respiration, defecation and egg expulsion. Over one to two weeks the flea's abdomen swells enormously as eggs mature, producing the characteristic expanding nodule with a central pore. Local inflammation, pain and pruritus result from the parasite and its by-products. Once eggs are shed the flea dies and the lesion involutes, but the breach in the skin and retained flea remnants predispose to secondary bacterial infection. Isolated lesions resolve well after extraction and wound care, but heavy or repeated infestation in endemic settings causes chronic morbidity, deformity and disability, and secondary infection can be limb- or life-threatening if neglected.

Turner Syndrome — 45,X, monosomy X, Ullrich-Turner syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis (45,X) Noonan syndrome (overlapping webbed neck and short stature, normal karyotype) Other causes of short stature (growth hormone deficiency, constitutional delay) Other causes of primary ovarian insufficiency or delayed puberty Mixed gonadal dysgenesis Skeletal dysplasias Karyotype to confirm monosomy X or mosaicism (with additional cells if mosaicism suspected) Echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess aortic valve, arch, and aortic dimensions Renal ultrasound for structural anomalies Gonadotrophins (FSH, LH) and thyroid function testing Audiological assessment Bone age and growth monitoring; screening for coeliac disease A chromosomal disorder affecting females caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, most commonly a 45,X karyotype, with mosaic forms also occurring. The two most consistent features are short stature and gonadal dysgenesis leading to ovarian failure. Newborns may show puffiness of the hands and feet (lymphoedema) and redundant nuchal skin; a fetal cystic hygroma may be detected antenatally. Characteristic features can include a webbed neck, low posterior hairline, widely spaced nipples on a broad chest, and a wide carrying angle at the elbows. Congenital cardiovascular anomalies, particularly bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, carry a risk of aortic dilatation and dissection and require ongoing surveillance. Renal anomalies such as a horseshoe kidney are common, as are recurrent otitis media and hearing loss. Most girls have normal intelligence but may have specific difficulties with visuospatial and mathematical tasks. Growth hormone therapy is used to improve final height, and oestrogen replacement is used to induce puberty and maintain bone and uterine health. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, and lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up addresses cardiac, endocrine, and reproductive needs. Aortic dilatation or symptoms suggesting aortic dissection Severe coarctation or critical cardiac lesions in infancy Progressive hearing loss Features suggesting Y-chromosome material, which raises gonadoblastoma risk Signs of untreated hypothyroidism or coeliac disease Not considering the diagnosis in a girl with unexplained short stature or delayed puberty Missing mosaicism when only a limited number of cells are analysed Overlooking the need for lifelong aortic surveillance Failing to screen for associated hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, and hearing loss Loss of all or part of the second sex chromosome causes haploinsufficiency of genes that normally escape X-inactivation and are needed in two copies. Deficiency of the SHOX gene contributes to short stature and skeletal features, while accelerated loss of ovarian follicles leads to gonadal dysgenesis and oestrogen deficiency. Abnormal fetal lymphatic development produces the lymphoedema, nuchal changes, and associated features such as the webbed neck, and disrupted development contributes to the cardiovascular and renal malformations. With appropriate hormone therapy and surveillance most girls achieve improved height, undergo induced puberty, and have a good quality of life; long-term outlook is influenced chiefly by cardiovascular complications, and fertility is usually impaired though assisted reproduction may be possible.

ossicles Marginal or attic perforation with foul discharge or crusting suggesting cholesteatoma Vertigo, sensorineural loss or facial weakness indicating inner ear or facial nerve involvement Perforation following head trauma with cerebrospinal fluid otorrhoea or associated fracture Persistent bloody discharge or granulations raising concern for neoplasm Failing to distinguish a dangerous marginal or attic perforation from a safe central one Allowing water to enter the ear and precipitate recurrent infection Assuming all perforations need surgery when many heal with conservative care Overlooking ossicular discontinuity as an additional cause of hearing loss The tympanic membrane can be breached when middle ear pressure rises from suppurative infection until necrosis of the drum produces a perforation, or when external forces (direct trauma, sudden pressure change, or a foreign body) tear it mechanically. Loss of an intact vibrating surface and of the round window sound-shielding effect reduces the efficiency of sound transfer to the cochlea, producing conductive hearing loss proportional to the area lost and its position. Small tears usually re-epithelialise and heal, but persistent perforation, ongoing infection, or ingrowth of squamous epithelium through a marginal or attic defect can prevent closure and predispose to cholesteatoma and chronic disease. Small, uncomplicated and traumatic perforations often heal spontaneously with good recovery of hearing, and surgical repair of dry persistent defects has a high success rate; outcomes are worse when there is ongoing infection, ossicular damage or an underlying cholesteatoma.

Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Child) — T1DM, type 1 diabetes, insulin-dependent diabetes, juvenile diabetes, paediatric type 1 diabetes Type 2 diabetes mellitus Monogenic diabetes (MODY) and neonatal diabetes Secondary diabetes (e.g. cystic fibrosis-related, steroid-induced) Diabetes insipidus (for polyuria and polydipsia) Transient stress hyperglycaemia during acute illness Urinary tract infection (for enuresis or dysuria) Blood glucose and HbA1c Blood and/or urine ketones Venous blood gas and electrolytes to assess for ketoacidosis Pancreatic autoantibodies (e.g. GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, islet cell) Thyroid function and coeliac screening at diagnosis and during follow-up C-peptide where the diabetes type is uncertain The most common form of diabetes in children, caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Classic presenting features are polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue, often over a few weeks; new secondary enuresis in a previously dry child is a useful clue. A substantial proportion of children present in diabetic ketoacidosis, which can be the first manifestation of the disease. Lifelong insulin replacement is essential; unlike type 2 diabetes, it cannot be managed by lifestyle measures or oral agents alone. A 'honeymoon' period of partial remission with reduced insulin needs may follow initial stabilisation but is temporary. Management is multidisciplinary, combining insulin, carbohydrate awareness, glucose monitoring, and structured education for the child and family. Careful attention to preventing and recognising hypoglycaemia is central to safe day-to-day care. Long-term care includes screening for associated autoimmune conditions (such as thyroid disease and coeliac disease) and for microvascular complications over time. New-onset type 1 diabetes presenting in diabetic ketoacidosis (vomiting, abdominal pain, deep sighing breathing, dehydration, drowsiness) is a medical emergency Reduced consciousness or focal neurological signs suggesting cerebral oedema during DKA management Severe hypoglycaemia with seizures or loss of consciousness Signs of significant dehydration or shock Persistent vomiting in a known diabetic child, which may signal evolving ketoacidosis Mistaking early symptoms for a urinary tract infection or behavioural enuresis and delaying diagnosis Failing to check ketones and acid-base status in a hyperglycaemic, unwell child Correcting fluids and glucose too aggressively in DKA and precipitating cerebral oedema Assuming the honeymoon phase means resolution and reducing vigilance Overlooking associated autoimmune conditions during follow-up Type 1 diabetes results from T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells in genetically predisposed children, often triggered by environmental factors. Progressive beta-cell loss produces absolute insulin deficiency, so glucose cannot enter cells and hyperglycaemia develops. Without insulin the body shifts to lipolysis and ketogenesis; unrestrained ketone production causes metabolic acidosis, while osmotic diuresis from glycosuria leads to dehydration and electrolyte loss, culminating in diabetic ketoacidosis if untreated. With modern insulin regimens, glucose monitoring, and multidisciplinary support most children live full lives; long-term outcome depends heavily on sustained glycaemic control, which reduces the risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications. Acute risks include ketoacidosis and severe hypoglycaemia.

FAH molecular testing Type 1 (hepatorenal) is the most severe form and stems from deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase in the tyrosine degradation pathway Acute infantile presentation features liver failure, coagulopathy, ascites and a cabbage-like or boiled-cabbage odour Chronic disease produces cirrhosis, renal tubular dysfunction with hypophosphataemic rickets (renal Fanconi syndrome), and a very high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma Painful neurological crises resembling acute porphyria can occur due to accumulated succinylacetone inhibiting porphyrin synthesis Succinylacetone in blood or urine is the key diagnostic marker and is now used in newborn screening Type 2 causes eye and skin lesions with keratitis, and type 3 is a rare neurological form Management is centred on nitisinone (NTBC), which blocks tyrosine degradation upstream, combined with dietary restriction of phenylalanine and tyrosine Nitisinone therapy has transformed outcomes and reduced the need for liver transplantation, though HCC surveillance is still required Acute liver failure with coagulopathy in an infant is a metabolic emergency Porphyria-like neurological crises with pain, weakness and possible respiratory compromise Rising or persistently elevated alpha-fetoprotein or hepatic nodules suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma Severe electrolyte and phosphate loss from renal tubulopathy Relying on plasma tyrosine alone, which is non-specific, rather than measuring succinylacetone Attributing infantile liver failure to infection or sepsis and missing the treatable metabolic cause Assuming nitisinone eliminates hepatocellular carcinoma risk and stopping surveillance Neglecting phenylalanine and tyrosine dietary control while on nitisinone, risking corneal and skin complications Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 is an autosomal recessive defect of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the final enzyme of tyrosine catabolism. Its deficiency causes accumulation of the upstream intermediates maleylacetoacetate and fumarylacetoacetate, which are converted to the toxic metabolites succinylacetone and succinylacetoacetate. These compounds are highly reactive and injure hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, driving hepatic failure, cirrhosis, malignant transformation and renal Fanconi syndrome. Succinylacetone also inhibits delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase, causing porphyrin precursor accumulation and porphyria-like neurological crises. Nitisinone works by inhibiting 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase upstream, preventing formation of the toxic distal metabolites. Untreated type 1 disease historically carried a poor prognosis with death from liver failure in infancy or later hepatocellular carcinoma, but early newborn detection with nitisinone and dietary therapy markedly improves survival and reduces cancer risk; lifelong monitoring remains essential.

considered in end-stage disease Progressive right heart failure in infancy or childhood Ventricular arrhythmia or syncope Signs suggesting risk of sudden cardiac death Severe right ventricular dilatation with haemodynamic compromise Confusing it with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, which has different genetics and management Overlooking the arrhythmic and sudden-death risk while focusing on heart failure Misattributing right heart failure to pulmonary or valvular causes Underestimating disease severity from a preserved left ventricle early in the course Uhl anomaly is a congenital cardiomyopathy in which the right ventricular myocardium is almost entirely absent, so the free wall consists of directly apposed endocardium and epicardium with little or no intervening muscle. This is thought to arise from an excessive developmental loss of right ventricular myocytes, in contrast to the progressive fibrofatty myocardial replacement of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. The resulting parchment-thin wall cannot generate contractile force, leading to a dilated, akinetic right ventricle, progressive right heart failure, and a substrate for ventricular arrhythmia. The outlook is generally poor, with many patients developing progressive right heart failure and arrhythmia; survival varies with severity, and advanced disease may ultimately require cardiac transplantation.

walking Rapidly progressive scoliosis compromising respiratory function Feeding difficulty and failure to thrive in infancy Loss of ambulation requiring orthopaedic and rehabilitation planning Delaying respiratory surveillance because motor function seems relatively preserved Overlooking the diagnostic combination of proximal contractures with distal hyperlaxity in a hypotonic infant Assuming normal collagen VI immunostaining excludes the diagnosis, as staining can be only partially reduced Not recognising that dominant de novo mutations can cause the disorder in a child with no family history Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the collagen VI genes COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3, which more severely disrupt the assembly or function of the collagen VI microfibrillar network than the milder variants causing Bethlem myopathy. Collagen VI links the muscle-fibre basement membrane to the surrounding interstitial matrix, and its severe deficiency impairs the structural and signalling relationship between fibres and their environment, with dysregulated mitochondrial function and increased apoptosis contributing to early and profound muscle degeneration. Because collagen VI is widespread in connective tissue, the disorder also produces the characteristic joint contractures and hyperlaxity, skeletal deformity and skin abnormalities, and the early respiratory failure that dominates its natural history. Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy is more severe than Bethlem myopathy, with many affected children losing ambulation in the first or second decade and developing progressive respiratory insufficiency that determines survival, although proactive respiratory and orthopaedic care can substantially prolong and improve life.

persist beyond a few years, are large, or become complicated Skin changes over a large tense hernia, such as thinning or ulceration, warrant urgent assessment Irreducible, tense, tender umbilical swelling indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency) Features of bowel obstruction with an irreducible hernia Overlying skin ischaemia, ulceration, or impending rupture over a large hernia Systemic sepsis or peritonism suggesting strangulated bowel Assuming an adult paraumbilical hernia will behave like a self-resolving infantile hernia Underestimating strangulation risk because of the narrow neck Overlooking uncontrolled ascites, which increases recurrence and complicates repair Missing a Sister Mary Joseph nodule by attributing all umbilical lumps to hernia Umbilical and paraumbilical hernias arise from a defect at or adjacent to the umbilical cicatrix. In infants the umbilical ring fails to close fully after cord separation. In adults, weakening and separation of the linea alba fibres around the umbilicus, combined with sustained raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy, or ascites, allows protrusion of preperitoneal fat, omentum, or bowel through a paraumbilical defect. The characteristically narrow, fibrous neck restricts reduction and readily compromises the vascular supply of trapped contents, predisposing to incarceration and strangulation. Most infantile umbilical hernias close spontaneously. Adult paraumbilical hernias do not resolve and carry a meaningful risk of incarceration and strangulation; elective mesh repair gives good results, whereas emergency surgery, especially in obese or comorbid patients, is associated with higher complication rates.

identification to mold phase is often required because yeast/hyphal tissue forms can be misidentified (e.g., Emergomyces resembling Histoplasma; Fusarium/Scedosporium resembling Aspergillus) Histopathology with special stains, including Fontana-Masson for melanized (dematiaceous) molds Blood cultures (positive in up to ~50% of disseminated fusariosis and can grow Lomentospora prolificans; S. apiospermum usually negative) Serology for Paracoccidioides (with the caveat that some assays miss P. lutzii) PCR-based molecular identification (including 28S rDNA and rRNA ITS) through fungal reference laboratories, useful in culture-negative or difficult cases Awareness of cross-reactivity: Histoplasma antigen test cross-reacts with Emergomyces; cryptococcal antigen can be positive in Trichosporon asahii infection Species-level identification and susceptibility testing in a reference laboratory to guide management of resistant molds Squamous cell carcinoma (mucocutaneous lesions of paracoccidioidomycosis; rarely arises in chronic chromoblastomycosis) Necrotic/embolic skin lesions of other causes (mimicked by painful necrotic lesions of fusariosis) This group spans endemic dimorphic fungi (paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis, adiaspiromycosis), hyaline and dematiaceous molds (fusariosis, scedosporiosis/lomentosporiosis, phaeohyphomycoses), and the yeast-like Trichosporon; the more common invasive mycoses (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, aspergillosis, mucormycosis) are covered separately (Harrison 22e p.1725). Dimorphic fungi exist as conidia-producing molds in the environment (the infectious form) and convert to yeast (or spherules/adiaspores) at temperatures above about 35 degrees C in tissue; infection generally begins with inhalation of conidia (Harrison 22e p.1725). Paracoccidioidomycosis (Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex, P. lutzii) is acquired by inhalation in humid Central/South American forests, with highest incidence in Brazil; chronic disease shows a striking male predominance (reported male-to-female ratios from 14:1 up to ~70:1) (Harrison 22e p.1726). The acute/juvenile form of paracoccidioidomycosis is uncommon, occurs typically in those under 30, primarily disseminates through the reticuloendothelial system, and often shows peripheral eosinophilia; the chronic/adult form accounts for ~90% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1726). On tissue, Paracoccidioides yeast classically appears as a central yeast ringed by narrow-necked daughter buds (the 'mariner's wheel'); some commercial serologic tests may fail to detect P. lutzii (Harrison 22e p.1726). Talaromycosis (Talaromyces marneffei, formerly Penicillium marneffei) is endemic in Vietnam, Thailand, and other Southeast Asian countries, is epidemiologically linked to bamboo rats, and occurs mostly in advanced AIDS; its presentation mimics disseminated histoplasmosis with umbilicated molluscum-like skin papules (Harrison 22e p.1727). In culture T. marneffei produces a distinctive diffusible red pigment, and tissue/blood smears show yeast-like organisms reproducing by bipolar fission (two ellipses with a central septum) (Harrison 22e p.1727). Emergomycosis (Emergomyces, several formerly Emmonsia) is an emerging dimorphic-fungus infection of patients with impaired cellular immunity; cutaneous involvement (disseminated ulcers, papules, nodules) accompanies pulmonary disease in most patients, while CNS spread is rare (Harrison 22e p.1727). Fusariosis is angioinvasive and mimics aspergillosis, but is distinguished by very common, often painful, nodular or necrotic skin lesions appearing around the onset of fever and by frequently positive blood cultures (~50%); banana-shaped macroconidia are characteristic on culture (Harrison 22e p.1728). Phaeohyphomycoses are caused by melanin-producing (dematiaceous/brown-black) molds; melanin is a virulence factor, certain species (Cladophialophora bantiana, Rhinocladiella mackenziei) are neurotropic, and golden-brown hyphae are highlighted by the Fontana-Masson melanin stain (Harrison 22e p.1728). Trichosporonosis (most often Trichosporon asahii) resembles invasive candidiasis with fungemia, but the presence of arthroconidia helps distinguish it from candidemia, and the serum cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test can be falsely positive because T. asahii shares polysaccharide antigens with Cryptococcus neoformans (Harrison 22e p.1729). Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium apiospermum complex) and lomentosporiosis (Lomentospora prolificans) mimic aspergillosis radiographically and histologically; L. prolificans can grow in blood cultures whereas S. apiospermum usually does not (Harrison 22e p.1729).
