neutropenia or transplantation Missing the diagnosis in 'immunocompetent' patients with disseminated/brain phaeohyphomycosis who may carry CLEC7A/CARD9 pathway defects Most of these fungi enter through inhalation of environmental conidia, with a smaller number introduced by traumatic skin or corneal inoculation or by injection of contaminated material. Dimorphic fungi (Paracoccidioides, Talaromyces, Emergomyces, Emmonsia crescens) convert from mold to invasive yeast/adiaspore form under thermal pressure in the lungs and then disseminate hematogenously to the reticuloendothelial system and other organs; granulomatous inflammation is typical. Disease frequently reflects host immune deficits: inborn errors affecting the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis predispose to severe paracoccidioidomycosis and talaromycosis, and IFN-gamma-primed monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils control Talaromyces. Molds such as Fusarium, Scedosporium, and Lomentospora are angioinvasive, and protection against Fusarium and Trichosporon depends heavily on neutrophils and their oxidative burst, explaining the strong link with profound prolonged neutropenia and with chronic granulomatous disease (defective NADPH oxidase). Dematiaceous molds use melanin as a virulence factor; defense against disseminated phaeohyphomycosis involves Dectin-1 (CLEC7A) and the adaptor CARD9, and deficiencies in this pathway predispose to disseminated and brain infection even in otherwise immunocompetent hosts. In adiaspiromycosis, inhaled E. crescens conidia enlarge into nonreplicating thick-walled adiaspores (up to ~500 micrometers) that drive a granulomatous inflammatory response. Outcomes vary widely by organism and host immune status. Paracoccidioidomycosis generally responds well, though pulmonary fibrosis can progress in chronic disease. Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is usually fatal, but treated mortality is about 10%. Disseminated fusariosis carries high mortality (historically up to ~85%, now around 50% with better therapy) and approaches 100% if neutropenia persists; survival hinges on neutrophil recovery. Invasive S. apiospermum infection has roughly 50% mortality, whereas L. prolificans remains about 85-100% lethal. Disseminated trichosporonosis mortality has been as high as 70% and remains very high with persistent neutropenia. Disseminated and visceral phaeohyphomycoses, particularly with CNS involvement, have high mortality. No single formal staging applies across this heterogeneous group. Practically, infections are stratified by extent and host status: localized cutaneous/keratitis/onychomycosis or pulmonary-limited disease versus disseminated/angioinvasive infection; presence of CNS involvement marks the most severe end (associated with the highest mortality). For dimorphic fungi (e.g., paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis), disease is broadly described as mild/moderate versus severe, and as acute (juvenile) versus chronic (adult) forms for paracoccidioidomycosis.

Unstable angina — UA, crescendo angina, acute coronary syndrome without ST elevation, rest angina NSTEMI and STEMI Aortic dissection Acute pericarditis or myopericarditis Pulmonary embolism Oesophageal spasm or reflux Musculoskeletal chest pain Coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina) Immediate and serial 12-lead ECGs to detect dynamic ischaemic changes Serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin to distinguish from NSTEMI Continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and recurrent ischaemia Risk stratification with validated scoring tools to guide invasive strategy timing Coronary angiography when an early invasive approach is indicated Echocardiography to assess wall motion and ventricular function Defined by angina that is new in onset, occurs at rest or with minimal exertion, or is more frequent, severe, or prolonged than a patient's previous stable pattern It sits on the acute coronary syndrome spectrum and is distinguished from NSTEMI by the absence of a rise in cardiac troponin The ECG may show transient ST depression or T-wave changes, but can also be normal; serial tracings are important High-sensitivity troponin measured serially is required to separate unstable angina from NSTEMI, since myocardial necrosis defines the latter Early risk stratification using validated scores guides the timing of an invasive versus a conservative strategy Initial management centres on antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy, anti-ischaemic measures, and admission for monitoring Because it reflects an unstable coronary plaque, it can progress rapidly to infarction and warrants urgent evaluation rather than outpatient workup MEDICAL EMERGENCY: presentation is an acute coronary syndrome requiring urgent assessment and monitoring because of the risk of progression to myocardial infarction Ongoing or recurrent rest pain despite initial therapy indicating refractory ischaemia Haemodynamic instability, new heart failure, or malignant arrhythmia Dynamic ST-segment shifts or a rising troponin signalling evolving infarction Discharging a patient with rest or crescendo chest pain because a single troponin or ECG is normal Failing to obtain serial ECGs and biomarkers to capture dynamic change Underestimating risk in atypical presentations, particularly in women, older adults, and those with diabetes Delaying antithrombotic therapy or admission while awaiting definitive imaging Unstable angina is usually precipitated by rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed non-occlusive or intermittent thrombus formation, causing an acute reduction in coronary blood flow. Dynamic vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation further limit supply. Unlike infarction, the ischaemia is severe but does not persist long enough or completely enough to produce detectable myocardial necrosis, so cardiac biomarkers remain normal. The same unstable plaque can progress to complete occlusion, linking unstable angina pathophysiologically to NSTEMI and STEMI. With prompt recognition, antithrombotic therapy, and appropriate risk-based revascularisation most patients stabilise, but delayed treatment or high-risk features carry a substantial early risk of infarction, arrhythmia, and death.

benign tumors (lipoma, leiomyoma, neurofibroma, lymphoid nodular hyperplasia) Two biologically distinct esophageal cancers arise in the same organ: squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), favoring the upper and mid esophagus, and adenocarcinoma, almost always in the lower esophagus and at the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ); globally SCC predominates while adenocarcinoma now accounts for over 75% of incident U.S./Western European cases. Because dysphagia and odynophagia are typically not noticed until the lumen is substantially obstructed, most esophageal cancers are locally advanced or metastatic at diagnosis; any patient with these symptoms warrants upper endoscopy with biopsy. Helicobacter pylori is a major chronic-inflammation driver of gastric cancer, but cancer develops in only a small subset of the roughly half of humans infected; eradication has been shown in prospective trials to lower subsequent gastric cancer risk, supporting treatment of asymptomatic H. pylori in those with a first-degree relative with gastric cancer or a prior early-stage gastric cancer. Physical findings suggesting advanced/metastatic gastric cancer include left supraclavicular adenopathy (Virchow's node), a periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule), a palpable rectal-shelf mass (Blumer's shelf), ascites, and an ovarian mass (Krukenberg tumor); more commonly the exam is unrevealing. Diffuse (signet-cell) gastric cancer may not form a discrete mass or ulcer, instead producing thickened gastric rugae and tracking beneath an intact mucosal surface, so initial superficial biopsies can be falsely negative and EUS-guided deeper biopsy may be required. Germline CDH1 (e-cadherin) mutation markedly increases risk of the diffuse/signet-cell gastric cancer subtype and also raises lobular breast cancer risk; prophylactic gastrectomy is an option in CDH1 carriers. Molecular profiling is therapeutically decisive: roughly 20-25% of esophageal/GEJ and about 20% of gastric adenocarcinomas overexpress or amplify HER2/ERBB2, and MSI-high/mismatch-repair-deficient and PD-L1-high (high combined positive score) tumors identify candidates for immune-modulating therapy; NGS plus PD-L1 IHC should be routine in metastatic disease. Gastric lymphomas (about 3% of gastric malignancies) are extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphomas; the GI tract is the most common extranodal NHL site and the stomach is the most common GI site, with MALT (~40%) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (~55%) being the dominant subtypes. MALT lymphoma of the stomach is strongly H. pylori-associated, and the stomach accounts for about 35% of all MALT lymphomas; the t(11;18) translocation marks tumors less likely to respond to H. pylori eradication. GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal and are driven by activating cKIT (~majority) or PDGFRA mutations; the stomach is the most frequent primary site (~60%), followed by small bowel (~25%); spindle-cell histology predominates (~70%) and KIT expression is found in ~95%. Small-bowel neoplasms account for only about 3% of GI tumors; in the U.S., neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors (40-45%) slightly outnumber adenocarcinomas (30-40%), and the duodenum is the most common site (~50%). EBV is associated with a distinct gastric cancer subtype (identified in roughly 8-10% of gastric cancer patients) and is described as a driver in some esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinomas; current EBV positivity does not by itself change therapeutic options. Relying on FDG-PET to exclude disease in diffuse-type gastric cancer, which is often not FDG-avid (PET may be non-informative). Using tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) for diagnosis; they are nonspecific and elevated in many cancers, and are better for monitoring response/progression. Attributing alarm symptoms in patients under 50 to benign illness and delaying diagnostic workup, given rising early-onset upper GI cancer incidence. Missing tracheobronchial invasion in mid/upper esophageal tumors, which precludes curative surgery, by omitting bronchoscopy. Treating gastric lymphoma like adenocarcinoma; surgical resection has no role in primary gastric lymphoma and MALT may respond to H. pylori eradication alone, so accurate subtyping is critical. Assuming a t(11;18)-positive MALT lymphoma will respond to H. pylori eradication; this subgroup is less likely to respond. Forgetting HBV testing before initiating lymphoma therapy (risk of reactivation). Esophageal SCC is linked to mucosal injury from alcohol and tobacco (synergistic), ingestion of very hot beverages, areca/betel-nut chewing, chronic achalasia, prior radiation, lye-induced strictures, and Plummer-Vinson (Patterson-Kelly) syndrome; genomically it resembles SCCs of other sites (e.g., head and neck) more than esophageal adenocarcinoma, and HPV is not implicated. Esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinoma arises in the setting of chronic gastroesophageal reflux producing inflammation and Barrett's metaplasia (glandular gastric-type mucosa extending into the esophagus); progression through dysplasia accumulates TP53 mutations and aneuploidy, with annual risk of progression of Barrett's to cancer about 0.4-0.5%. Gastric adenocarcinoma is predominantly an inflammation-driven malignancy: H. pylori (and the broader gastric microbiome) and ingestion of nitrate-rich smoked/salted/dried foods generate carcinogenic nitrites; the intestinal Lauren subtype associates with H. pylori and atrophic gastritis, while the diffuse subtype (~20%) associates with germline or somatic CDH1 loss. TCGA defines four molecular subtypes (EBV-positive, microsatellite-unstable/hypermutated, genomically stable [diffuse], and chromosomally unstable). The proximal esophagus-GEJ-gastric cardia adenocarcinomas share a similar genomic profile suggesting common driving factors. Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by chronic antigenic stimulation from H. pylori, with the t(11;18) API1-MALT1 fusion activating NF-kB signaling. GISTs originate from Cajal cells via gain-of-function KIT or PDGFRA mutations. Esophageal cancer prognosis remains poor overall but is slowly improving; by clinical (pretreatment) AJCC staging, 5-year survival ranges from about 75-82% for stage 0-I down to roughly 5-18% for metastatic (stage IVB) disease, and most U.S. patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. For gastric cancer, surgery alone yields about 25% overall 5-year survival, with stage-dependent rates falling from about 90% (stage 0) to roughly 3% for stage IV; multimodality therapy (perioperative chemotherapy plus surgery) improves 5-year survival by about 10-15% over surgery alone (e.g., MAGIC trial 36% vs 23%). Even with modern systemic and immune-modulating therapy, overall survival for stage IV gastric cancer is still only about 12-15 months. Gastric MSI-high tumors had the best outcomes and genomically stable (diffuse)/mesenchymal subtypes the worst in genomic series. Lynch-syndrome-associated small-bowel cancers probably have a better prognosis. For nonmetastatic gastric GIST, resected tumors 2 cm or smaller with a mitotic index of 5% or less carry near-zero progression risk, whereas tumors 10 cm or larger with mitotic index above 5% are moderate-to-high risk. Esophageal and gastric cancers are staged with the AJCC TNM system (eighth edition; ninth edition expected 2024), with separate clinical (cTNM, pretreatment), pathologic (pTNM, for patients undergoing initial surgery), and post-neoadjuvant (ypTNM) classifications. The esophageal T stage reflects depth of penetration through the wall (which over most of its course lacks serosa); regional nodal disease is still potentially curable while metastatic disease is generally treated palliatively. Gastric staging similarly progresses from Tis (mucosa-confined, stage 0) through wall penetration and increasing nodal involvement to distant metastasis (stage IV). Gastric lymphomas are NOT staged by TNM; the Lugano system (an Ann Arbor modification) is used: stage I confined to the gastric wall, stage II regional nodal or local-structure involvement, stage III nodes on both sides of the diaphragm, stage IV more extensive nodal or distant/extranodal (including marrow) disease. GIST recurrence risk is stratified by primary tumor size, mitotic index, and GI location. Neuroendocrine tumors are graded 1-3 by Ki-67 positivity, distinct from fully malignant small-/large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomas.

severe neonatal cases may present before results return Severe hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy is a medical emergency requiring immediate ammonia-lowering and often dialysis Rapidly declining level of consciousness, seizures, or signs of raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema Neonate deteriorating after an initially normal period, mistaken for sepsis Recurrent unexplained encephalopathy or coma triggered by high protein intake, infection, or surgery in older patients Failing to measure ammonia in an encephalopathic neonate or child and attributing symptoms to sepsis Allowing sample delay or poor technique to give falsely elevated or unreliable ammonia results Continuing protein intake or under-treating catabolism during acute decompensation Not recognising milder late-onset presentations, especially in females with ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency The urea cycle detoxifies waste nitrogen by converting ammonia derived from amino acid metabolism into urea for renal excretion. Deficiency of any of its enzymes (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, ornithine transcarbamylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, arginase) or of the N-acetylglutamate synthase activator or transporters interrupts this flux, causing ammonia to accumulate. Ammonia is neurotoxic, producing astrocyte swelling, cerebral oedema and glutamine accumulation, leading to encephalopathy and, if untreated, irreversible brain injury or death. The pattern of accumulated intermediates (citrulline, argininosuccinate) and urine orotic acid reflects the position of the block. Outcome correlates strongly with the peak and duration of hyperammonaemia; prolonged severe neonatal hyperammonaemia carries a high risk of death or permanent neurodevelopmental impairment, whereas early recognition, prompt ammonia control and liver transplantation in selected cases improve survival and reduce disability.

examination is difficult Urethral prolapse is circumferential eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the external meatus, forming a doughnut-shaped ring of tissue around the urethral opening It has a characteristic bimodal distribution, occurring in prepubertal girls and in postmenopausal women, both low-oestrogen states Typical presentations are painless vaginal or vulval bleeding or or non-resolving cases, or when the diagnosis is uncertain and tissue is needed A strangulated, thrombosed, or necrotic prolapse causing pain or urinary retention warrants prompt urological assessment Strangulated, thrombosed, or necrotic prolapsed mucosa Acute urinary retention from the prolapse Suspicion of malignancy in a postmenopausal woman with an atypical or firm periurethral lesion Uncertain diagnosis where abuse or trauma is being wrongly considered in a child, or genuine trauma is missed Heavy or persistent bleeding Mistaking benign prolapse in a child for signs of trauma or abuse, or vice versa Confusing it with a urethral caruncle or, in older women, with malignancy Overlooking a strangulated or necrotic prolapse needing surgical intervention Failing to address straining and constipation, allowing recurrence Not obtaining histology when the lesion is atypical in a postmenopausal woman Urethral prolapse results from eversion of the distal urethral mucosa through the meatus. A relative deficiency of oestrogen, as in prepubertal girls and postmenopausal women, weakens the periurethral supporting tissues and the attachments between the inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers of the urethra. Poor cohesion between these layers, combined with raised intra-abdominal pressure from straining, coughing, or constipation, allows the redundant mucosa to protrude and evert around the meatus. The exposed mucosa becomes congested, oedematous, and friable, and if venous drainage is compromised it may thrombose, strangulate, or necrose. Urethral prolapse is benign and generally responds well to conservative measures, particularly topical oestrogen, with a good prognosis and low recurrence when precipitating factors such as straining are addressed. Surgical excision is curative for complicated or refractory cases. Prompt recognition in children avoids unnecessary distress and investigation, while vigilance in older women ensures malignancy is not overlooked.

obstruction A urethral stricture is the result of scarring within the corpus spongiosum (spongiofibrosis) and urethral epithelium following injury or inflammation. Trauma, infection, instrumentation, or inflammatory disease such as lichen sclerosus provokes healing by fibrosis, which contracts and narrows the lumen. The narrowed segment increases outflow resistance, causing high-pressure voiding, turbulent flow, and incomplete emptying. Persistent obstruction leads to proximal urethral dilatation, bladder wall changes, stasis with infection and stone formation, and in severe cases upper tract dilatation and retention. Short strictures may respond to dilatation or urethrotomy but recurrence is common; urethroplasty provides high long-term success for suitable strictures, whereas complex, recurrent, or lichen sclerosus-associated disease can require staged or repeated reconstruction.

for gonorrhoea and chlamydia Urethral Gram-stain smear for leucocytes and Gram-negative intracellular diplococci Culture and antimicrobial sensitivities for Neisseria gonorrhoeae given resistance concerns Testing for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas where indicated Full sexually transmitted infection screen including HIV and syphilis serology Urinalysis to help exclude urinary tract infection Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra presenting with urethral discharge, dysuria, and urethral itch or discomfort, most often sexually transmitted It is broadly divided into gonococcal urethritis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) and non-gonococcal urethritis, of which Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause, along with Mycoplasma genitalium and others Gonococcal urethritis classically produces a profuse purulent discharge, whereas non-gonococcal urethritis tends to cause a scantier, more mucoid discharge, though overlap is common and co-infection frequent Diagnosis rests on demonstrating urethral inflammation (urethral smear with leucocytes or a positive leucocyte esterase on first-void urine) together with nucleic acid amplification testing for the causative organisms Management principles include empirical antibiotic therapy covering both gonococcal and chlamydial infection, guided by local resistance patterns, plus abstinence until treatment is complete Partner notification, treatment of sexual contacts, and a full sexually transmitted infection screen (including HIV and syphilis) are essential components of care Persistent or recurrent urethritis after treatment may reflect reinfection, non-adherence, or organisms such as Mycoplasma genitalium with antimicrobial resistance Reactive arthritis (urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis) may follow chlamydial urethritis, particularly in HLA-B27-positive individuals Features of disseminated gonococcal infection (fever, skin lesions, arthritis) Ascending infection causing epididymo-orchitis or prostatitis Persistent or recurrent urethritis suggesting resistant organism or reinfection Systemic sexually transmitted co-infection such as HIV requiring identification Reactive arthritis with ocular or joint involvement Treating for chlamydia alone and missing co-existing gonococcal infection (or vice versa) Neglecting partner notification and treatment, leading to reinfection Failing to perform a full STI screen including HIV and syphilis Overlooking Mycoplasma genitalium in persistent non-gonococcal urethritis Not counselling on abstinence until treatment and partner therapy are complete Urethritis is inflammation of the urethral mucosa, usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms ascending the urethra. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are the principal pathogens, with Mycoplasma genitalium, Trichomonas vaginalis, and other organisms also implicated. Infection provokes a neutrophilic inflammatory response in the urethral epithelium, producing discharge and dysuria. Non-infective urethritis can follow trauma or instrumentation. Untreated infection may ascend or spread, causing epididymo-orchitis, prostatitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, or, historically, inflammatory urethral stricture, and in women pelvic inflammatory disease. Uncomplicated urethritis usually resolves rapidly with appropriate antibiotics and partner treatment; outcomes are worsened by reinfection, non-adherence, resistant organisms, and complications such as epididymo-orchitis or reactive arthritis.

obstruction or detrusor underactivity Neurogenic bladder Urinary tract infection Vesicovaginal or other urinary fistula (continuous leakage) Urinalysis to exclude infection and haematuria Bladder (frequency-volume) diary Post-void residual volume measurement Cough stress test and pelvic examination (assessing prolapse and pelvic floor) Urodynamic studies in complex, mixed, or pre-surgical stress, urgency, mixed, overflow, and functional (continuous) incontinence Stress incontinence is leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, laughing, exertion) due to sphincter or pelvic floor weakness, common after childbirth and in men after prostatectomy Urgency incontinence is leakage accompanied by a sudden compelling desire to void, usually from detrusor overactivity, and is part of the overactive bladder syndrome Overflow incontinence is dribbling from a chronically distended, poorly emptying bladder, often due to outlet obstruction or an underactive detrusor, and must not be missed A focused history, examination (including pelvic and neurological), a bladder (frequency-volume) diary, and post-void residual measurement usually clarify the type First-line management of stress incontinence is pelvic floor muscle training, while urgency incontinence is treated with bladder training and antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist therapy Reversible contributors summarised by the DIAPPERS concept (delirium, infection, atrophic changes, pharmaceuticals, psychological, excess output, restricted mobility, stool impaction) should be sought and corrected Surgical options such as mid-urethral slings or colposuspension are considered for stress incontinence, and intravesical botulinum toxin or neuromodulation for refractory urgency incontinence Associated haematuria requiring exclusion of urinary tract malignancy New incontinence with neurological signs suggesting cord compression or cauda equina syndrome Overflow incontinence from unrecognised chronic retention with risk of renal impairment Continuous leakage suggesting a urinary fistula Recurrent urinary infection or significant post-void residual Mislabelling overflow incontinence as urgency and prescribing antimuscarinics that worsen retention Failing to measure post-void residual before treating Overlooking reversible causes such as infection, medications, or stool impaction Missing haematuria or a neurological cause behind new incontinence Recommending surgery without adequate assessment of the incontinence type Continence requires coordinated bladder storage at low pressure with a competent, closed outlet, governed by autonomic and somatic innervation. Stress incontinence arises from a weakened pelvic floor and urethral sphincter (from childbirth, ageing, or prostatic surgery) so that raised abdominal pressure overcomes closure. Urgency incontinence results from involuntary detrusor contractions (detrusor overactivity), which may be idiopathic or neurogenic. Overflow incontinence occurs when a chronically overdistended bladder leaks around an obstruction or fails to contract effectively, as in outlet obstruction or an underactive/neurogenic detrusor. Mixed incontinence combines these mechanisms. Many patients improve substantially with conservative measures and correction of reversible factors; stress and urgency incontinence respond well to targeted therapy, and surgery offers durable benefit for refractory stress incontinence, though outcomes vary with cause and comorbidity.

Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis — UTI, Acute cystitis, Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP), Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP), Pyelonephritis, Catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) Asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing symptoms) Sexually transmitted infections - urethritis/cervicitis from Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma genitalium Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) Herpetic urethritis Interstitial cystitis Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (in men) Noninfectious vulvar/vaginal irritation Cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae Vaginitis (Trichomonas vaginalis, Candida albicans) Herpetic urethritis Urethritis from Mycoplasma genitalium Urine dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase (best used to help rule out UTI; only Enterobacterales convert nitrate to nitrite, so non-Enterobacterales and dilute frequently-voided urine can be falsely negative) Microscopic urinalysis for pyuria and hematuria Urine culture with susceptibilities - warranted in pregnancy, suspected resistant organisms, recurrent or complicated UTI, and all male UTI; ASB screening in pregnancy must use culture because dipstick is not sufficiently sensitive Blood cultures when fever or systemic signs suggest infection beyond the bladder Imaging (CT or ultrasound) in men with febrile UTI (even first episode) to evaluate for obstruction or anatomic abnormality; suspect intraparenchymal abscess with persistent fever/bacteremia despite therapy Urologic consultation for unclear diagnosis or recurrent UTI in men Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (noninfectious prostatic pain without bacteriuria) Noninfectious vaginal or vulvar irritation Delirium from non-urinary causes mislabeled as UTI in older adults with incidental ASB UTI denotes symptomatic infection somewhere along the urinary tract; bacteria in urine WITHOUT related symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), not UTI, and generally should NOT be treated (Harrison 22e p.1086). Treatment of ASB is discouraged except in two settings: pregnancy (untreated ASB is linked to pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight) and before urologic procedures causing mucosal injury such as lithotripsy or transurethral prostate resection (Harrison 22e p.1086). Cystitis presents with dysuria, frequency, and urgency, often with suprapubic discomfort, new nocturia, hesitancy, or gross hematuria; fever, rigors, and unilateral flank/back pain are INCONSISTENT with uncomplicated cystitis and point to infection beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1088). Fever is a key feature distinguishing cystitis from pyelonephritis; mild pyelonephritis may show only low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, while severe disease brings high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain (Harrison 22e p.1089). E. coli is the predominant uropathogen across UTI syndromes, accounting for roughly 75-90% of acute cystitis isolates; Staphylococcus saprophyticus causes about 5-15% (more in younger women) (Harrison 22e p.1087). Isolation of S. aureus or Salmonella from urine should raise suspicion of concomitant bacteremia, since hematogenous seeding (<2% of UTIs) typically involves these more virulent organisms (Harrison 22e p.1088). Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is a typically severe illness with dysuria, frequency, and prostatic/pelvic/perineal pain, sometimes with fever, rigors, or bladder outlet obstruction; chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis episodes, often without systemic signs (Harrison 22e p.1088). Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) is far more common than bacterial prostatitis, is NOT associated with bacteriuria, and does NOT improve with antibiotics; obtaining urine cultures in male UTI helps distinguish these entities (Harrison 22e p.1088). Diagnostic stewardship - not culturing urine in patients lacking UTI signs/symptoms (except pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure screening) - is the key intervention to reduce misdiagnosis and overtreatment of ASB (Harrison 22e p.1088). In catheterized patients bacteriuria and pyuria are essentially inevitable, so an abnormal urinalysis alone cannot diagnose CAUTI; localizing or systemic symptoms must be present and other causes excluded (Harrison 22e p.1090). Recurrent UTI is not automatically 'complicated' - individual episodes can be uncomplicated; early recurrence (within 2 weeks) is usually relapse rather than reinfection and should prompt a search for a sequestered focus (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1087). Fever, rigors, or unilateral flank/back pain in a patient with urinary symptoms (suggests pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or bloodstream involvement) Severe pyelonephritis with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in renal/perinephric tissue), occurring almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes Acute papillary necrosis causing obstructive uropathy; bilateral papillary necrosis may present with rapidly rising serum creatinine Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibiotics (suggests intraparenchymal renal abscess) Signs of sepsis in an older patient with altered mentation S. aureus or Salmonella in urine (consider concomitant bacteremia and metastatic prostatic focus) Bladder outlet obstruction with acute bacterial prostatitis Diagnosing UTI from pyuria/bacteriuria alone without requiring symptoms - this conflates ASB with true UTI; degree of pyuria in an asymptomatic patient should not drive the diagnosis (very high pyuria is common with urinary stasis, ESRD, or obstructed catheters). Treating ASB outside pregnancy or pre-urologic-procedure settings - it does not reduce future UTIs and may even increase infection risk (e.g., in renal transplant recipients). Premature diagnostic closure: attributing an older patient's isolated altered mentation to 'UTI' without excluding sepsis and other time-sensitive causes of delirium; a reported history of recurrent UTIs may actually reflect persistent ASB. Relying on a negative dipstick to rule out UTI - false negatives occur with non-Enterobacterales organisms, dilute frequently-voided urine, and it is insufficiently sensitive to exclude bacteriuria in pregnancy. Mistaking an STI (especially C. trachomatis) for UTI, or treating dysuria due to vaginitis/cervicitis as UTI; vaginal discharge should prompt STI evaluation. Assuming all male UTI is 'complicated' or that complicated-UTI guidelines apply to prostatitis; not all men with UTI have urinary tract abnormalities, especially those 45 years or younger. Misinterpreting a mixed-flora culture as infection - usually contamination except in long-term catheterization, chronic retention, or urinary-enteric/genital fistula. The urinary tract behaves as a continuous column of urine from kidney to urethra. Most UTIs arise by ascending infection: periurethral and vaginal-introital colonization by intestinal flora (usually E. coli) is the critical first step, followed by ascent up the urethra to the bladder and, in renal infection, up the ureter to the kidney. Hematogenous seeding accounts for less than 2% of UTIs and usually involves virulent organisms (e.g., S. aureus, Salmonella). Outcome depends on the interplay of host, pathogen, and environmental factors. The flushing action of normal voiding clears bacteria; urinary stasis, obstruction, foreign bodies (stones, catheters), and biofilm formation favor infection. Uropathogenic E. coli express virulence factors: type 1 pili bind mannose on bladder uroepithelium to initiate cystitis, while P fimbriae bind the P blood-group antigen on renal epithelium and are important in pyelonephritis and bloodstream invasion; toxins, iron-acquisition systems, biofilms, and capsules also contribute. Host susceptibility has a hereditary component (familial/maternal history; non-secretor blood-group phenotypes increasing E. coli adherence; Toll-like receptor and IL-8 receptor gene variants). Disruption of vaginal lactobacilli (spermicide/nonoxynol-9, menopausal atrophy) promotes E. coli colonization (Harrison 22e pp.1087-1088). UTI is common and patients typically respond favorably and rapidly to appropriately chosen modern antimicrobials. Uncomplicated cystitis in low-risk women carries a low risk of serious complications and can often be managed remotely. About 20-30% of women with one UTI develop recurrences (average ~2.6 reinfections/year; rate 0.3-7.6 per patient-year), with likelihood of recurrence decreasing as time since the last infection lengthens. Up to 80% of women have at least one UTI in their lifetime; lifetime prevalence in U.S. men is about 14%. Untreated ASB in pregnancy carries risk of pyelonephritis, preterm delivery, and low birth weight. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis causes suppurative destruction of renal tissue and its mass effect can mimic renal malignancy (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1089). Clinical syndrome-based: asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) vs symptomatic UTI. Uncomplicated UTI = infection confined to the bladder (cystitis) in a woman or man without a urinary catheter. Complicated UTI = infection extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or in the setting of catheterization (CAUTI). Pyelonephritis is graded clinically from mild (low-grade fever +/- back/CVA pain) to severe (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Severe/special forms: emphysematous pyelonephritis and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Lab/diagnostic thresholds: pyuria conventionally >10 WBCs/HPF (poor specificity ~36%; a cutoff nearer 250 WBCs/HPF correlates better with symptoms in older women); for women with cystitis symptoms a colony count >10^2 bacteria/mL is more sensitive (95%) than the classic 10^5/mL; CAUTI bacteriuria threshold is >=10^3 CFU/mL (Harrison 22e pp.1086-1092).

UTO must always be considered with UTIs) Generalized sepsis from an infected obstructed system Bladder catheter insertion and postvoid residual measurement Bedside bladder ultrasound to assess bladder volume Abdominal ultrasonography (~90% sensitive and specific for hydronephrosis) Noncontrast multidetector CT (test of choice for acute flank pain; visualizes retroperitoneum and intrinsic/extrinsic sites of obstruction; characterizes stones by Hounsfield units) Duplex Doppler ultrasonography (increased resistive index) Retrograde or antegrade urography (no contrast-induced AKI risk in renal insufficiency) Voiding cystourethrography (vesicoureteral reflux, bladder neck and urethral obstruction; postvoid residual urine) Cystourethroscopy and urodynamic studies (cystometry, pressure-flow analysis) Radionuclide (renal) scan for differential renal function and to predict reversibility after prolonged decompression Abdominal scout film/KUB (insensitive; may show nephrocalcinosis or radiopaque stone) Furosemide-augmented imaging to distinguish functional from anatomic obstruction Prerenal azotemia (acute partial bilateral obstruction may mimic it with high BUN-to-creatinine ratio, concentrated urine, and sodium retention) Renal cystic disease (congenital UPJ obstruction may be mistaken for it; extrarenal pelvis is a normal variant causing false-positive hydronephrosis) Other causes of polyuria/nocturia and concentrating defects ADPKD and other ciliopathies (cystic compression of normal nephrons leading to fibrosis) Urinary tract obstruction (UTO) is a common and potentially reversible cause of both acute and chronic kidney disease (obstructive nephropathy); early recognition and prompt relief can prevent or reverse devastating effects on kidney structure and function (p.2453). Any patient with otherwise unexplained renal failure, or with a history of nephrolithiasis, hematuria, diabetes mellitus, prostatic enlargement, pelvic surgery, trauma, or tumor should be evaluated for UTO (p.2455-2456). When suspected, a bladder catheter should be inserted and abdominal ultrasonography performed to assess renal/bladder size and pyelocalyceal contour; bladder volume can be readily assessed at the bedside by ultrasound (p.2454-2455). Flank pain is the most common presenting symptom and is due to distention of the collecting system or renal capsule; its severity is influenced more by the rate at which distention develops than by the degree of distention (p.2454). Complete bilateral obstruction should be suspected when acute renal failure is accompanied by anuria (p.2455). Wide fluctuations in urine output in an azotemic patient should always raise the possibility of intermittent or partial UTO (p.2455). Azotemia with hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis (acquired distal renal tubular acidosis pattern) should prompt consideration of UTO (p.2455). Flank pain that occurs only with micturition is pathognomonic of vesicoureteral reflux (p.2455). Lower obstruction above the bladder causes unilateral hydroureter and hydronephrosis, whereas lesions at or below the bladder cause bilateral involvement (p.2454). Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of bilateral hydronephrosis in boys; in adults UTO is usually due to acquired defects, with pelvic tumors, calculi, and urethral stricture predominating (p.2454). As many as 50% of men aged >40 years may have lower urinary tract symptoms associated with benign prostatic hypertrophy, but these symptoms may occur without bladder outlet obstruction (p.2454). Noncontrast CT is the imaging test of choice for acute flank pain and improves visualization of the urinary tract in renal impairment; retrograde/antegrade urography carry no risk of contrast-induced AKI in patients with renal insufficiency (p.2455-2456). UTO complicated by infection (infected obstructed system) requires immediate relief of obstruction to prevent generalized sepsis and progressive renal damage; sepsis necessitates prompt urologic intervention with drainage (nephrostomy, ureterostomy, or catheterization) Acute renal failure with anuria suggesting complete bilateral obstruction Overflow incontinence with sudden-onset fecal incontinence, severe lower back pain, and saddle anesthesia requires emergency evaluation for cauda equina syndrome Complete obstruction with infection can lead to total destruction of the kidney within days Fetal LUTO with maternal oligohydramnios or anhydramnios (risk of pulmonary hypoplasia and infant death if untreated) UTO is a reversible cause of AKI that must be actively excluded in any unexplained AKI (insert bladder catheter and perform bladder scan/ultrasound) - the urine sediment is often normal even with marked azotemia and extensive structural damage. Hydronephrosis may be ABSENT on ultrasound when obstruction is <48 h in duration, or associated with volume contraction, staghorn calculi, retroperitoneal fibrosis, or infiltrative renal disease - a negative ultrasound does not exclude obstruction when suspicion remains high. False-positive hydronephrosis can occur with diuresis, renal cysts, or a normal extrarenal pelvis. Insidious obstruction (e.g., chronic UPJ narrowing) may cause little or no pain yet result in total destruction of the affected kidney; unilateral ureteric injury during surgery may remain undetected. After relief, anticipate postobstructive diuresis (see below) - iatrogenic over-replacement of fluids can sustain the diuresis, while under-recognition can lead to profound dehydration and vascular collapse. NSAIDs for renal colic must account for potential renal harm, and opiates in patients with decreased renal function may be dangerous and used with caution. Alpha-adrenergic blockers for BPH carry a risk of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery. Obstruction to urine flow produces stasis and a rise in hydrostatic pressure proximal to the blockade; this pressure is transmitted to the glomerular urinary space, decreasing or stopping filtration. Acutely, bilateral obstruction increases renal blood flow with rising ureteral/tubule pressures (mediated by vasodilator prostaglandins and nitric oxide), then renal blood flow and GFR fall with chronicity as vasoconstrictor prostaglandins and renin-angiotensin production increase. Tubular dysfunction develops: loss of medullary hypertonicity and concentrating ability (AVP-insensitive polyuria, a form of acquired nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from dysregulation of aquaporin-2 water channels), natriuresis from downregulation of proximal salt reabsorption and transporters (Na+/K+-ATPase, NKCC2, ENaC), and partial bilateral UTO causing acquired distal RTA with hyperkalemia and renal salt wasting (disrupted H+-ATPase trafficking in alpha-intercalated cells, reduced ENaC-driven Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion, impaired ammonium excretion). The renal interstitium becomes edematous with mononuclear infiltrate early; later interstitial fibrosis and atrophy of papillae and medulla precede cortical involvement. Increased angiotensin II drives inflammation and fibroblast accumulation via profibrotic cytokines, progressing to chronic kidney damage and permanent loss of renal mass (renal atrophy). Obstruction can be mechanical (intrinsic or extrinsic) at any level from the renal tubules to the urethral meatus, or functional from abnormal pontine/sacral micturition control (e.g., neurogenic bladder). Genetic/fetal causes (CAKUT, LUTO) reflect reduced nephron number, as there is no nephrogenesis after birth (p.2453-2456). With relief of obstruction, return of renal function depends largely on whether irreversible renal damage has occurred. If obstruction is not relieved, course depends on whether it is complete or incomplete, bilateral or unilateral, and whether infection coexists. Complete obstruction with infection can destroy the kidney within days. Partial return of GFR may follow relief of complete obstruction of 1-2 weeks' duration, but after 8 weeks of obstruction recovery is unlikely. In the absence of definitive evidence of irreversibility, every effort should be made to decompress; a renal radionuclide scan after a prolonged period of decompression may predict reversibility. Chronic fibrotic progression to a failing kidney has no demonstrated reversal of scarring to date (p.2453, 2456-2457). No formal severity grade; characterized along clinically meaningful axes per Tables 331-1 and 331-2: by level (upper tract/ureter vs bladder outlet vs urethra), laterality (unilateral hydroureter/hydronephrosis vs bilateral involvement at/below the bladder), completeness (complete vs partial/incomplete), acuity (acute vs chronic vs release/postobstructive phase), and presence of superimposed infection. Postobstructive diuresis follows relief of bilateral, but not unilateral, complete obstruction.

small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis) Mastocytosis (cutaneous or systemic; urticaria pigmentosa) Hereditary angioedema (C1INH type 1/2; type 3 with normal C1INH e.g. factor XII mutation) Acquired C1INH deficiency (lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease) ACE inhibitor-induced (bradykinin-mediated) angioedema CIAS1/NLRP3-associated periodic fever syndromes (familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome) Schnitzler's syndrome, Gleich's syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome Serum sickness and hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis Allergic rhinitis: nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia (NARES), vasomotor/perennial nonallergic rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, gustatory rhinitis, hormonal (pregnancy) rhinitis, drug-induced rhinitis, hypothyroidism, anatomic/structural nasal defects, nasal foreign body Viral infection-associated acute urticaria (a common trigger of new-onset acute urticaria) Bacterial or parasitic infection-associated urticaria (travel history should prompt parasite evaluation) Hepatitis B or C and SARS-CoV-2 infection associated with urticaria/urticarial vasculitis Upper respiratory tract infection mimicking rhinitis; secondary bacterial sinusitis/otitis from mucosal swelling History-directed skin testing (puncture/prick) or serum allergen-specific IgE for suspected allergen triggers Provocation/threshold testing for inducible urticaria (e.g. ice-cube test for cold urticaria; stroking for dermatographism) Limited labs in unrevealing chronic urticaria: CBC with eosinophil assessment, ESR or CRP (most chronic urticaria has no lab abnormality) Skin biopsy for lesions lasting >36 h, scarring, or painful/non-pruritic - to assess for urticarial vasculitis (cellular infiltrate, nuclear debris, fibrinoid venular necrosis) For isolated angioedema: basic chemistries with liver function tests and complement levels C1INH antigen level and functional (catalytic inhibition) assay, with C4 and C2 levels, for suspected HAE; C1q and C1 function additionally reduced in acquired C1INH deficiency Evaluation for paraproteinemia/lymphoproliferative disease where presentation suggests acquired C1INH deficiency Autologous serum skin test and basophil activation markers (CD63/CD203) for autoimmune chronic urticaria; antithyroid antibodies Nasal secretion eosinophils and serum/skin specific IgE for allergic rhinitis (skin test more sensitive; serum specific IgE less sensitive but highly specific) Urticarial vasculitis (lesions >24 h, painful/burning rather than pruritic, residual petechiae/bruising) Mastocytosis presenting with flushing and hyperpigmented papules that urticate on stroking (Darier's sign) Thyroid disease (hypo-/hyperthyroidism) and autoimmune thyroiditis Serum sickness / serum sickness-like reactions Vasomotor (nonallergic) rhinitis and NARES mimicking allergic rhinitis Urticaria (hives) are well-circumscribed wheals (dilation of superficial dermal vessels) that are intensely pruritic, often migrate, individually last <24 h, and resolve without bruising or scarring; angioedema arises from deeper dermis/subcutaneous tissue with more pain than pruritus and minimal erythema, taking hours to days to resolve (p.2807). Urticaria and angioedema reflect similar pathophysiology at different skin levels and often co-occur, with roughly 40% of patients reporting both; together they affect >20% of the population at some point in life (p.2807). Acute urticaria/angioedema are episodes lasting <6 weeks (usually food, environmental, or drug allergen, or viral infection); attacks persisting >6 weeks are termed chronic and are often spontaneous/idiopathic with no identifiable cause. More than two-thirds of new-onset cases are ultimately diagnosed as acute (p.2807). Inducible (physical) urticarias are identified by the precipitating stimulus: dermatographism (linear wheal after brisk stroke, affects 2-5%), cholinergic urticaria (small 1-2 mm pruritic wheals with large surrounding erythema triggered by a rise in core body temperature such as fever, hot bath, or exercise), cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, and contact urticaria; most inducible-urticaria lesions individually last <2 h (p.2807-2808). Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder from SERPING1 mutation causing C1 inhibitor (C1INH) deficiency (type 1, ~85%) or dysfunctional protein (type 2); presentation in childhood/adolescence and a family history of angioedema are distinguishing features (p.2808). HAE diagnosis is suggested by family history, early age of onset, lack of pruritus and urticarial lesions, recurrent gastrointestinal colic, episodes of laryngeal edema, and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines; laboratory confirmation shows low C1INH antigen (type 1) or nonfunctional protein (type 2), with chronically depleted C4 and C2 that fall further during attacks (p.2808-2809). Cold urticaria can be confirmed by ice-cube placement on the volar forearm provoking a wheal within minutes; cryoglobulins or cold agglutinins are present in up to 5% of these patients, and immersion in cold water (swimming) can progress to vascular collapse (p.2807-2808). Up to 45% of chronic urticaria has an autoimmune basis, including autoantibodies to IgE or to the alpha chain of FcepsilonRI, and may be associated with antithyroid antibodies (antimicrosomal peroxidase/thyroglobulin) in both Hashimoto's thyroiditis and a euthyroid state (p.2808). Allergic rhinitis is characterized by sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, lacrimation, and itching of the conjunctiva/nasal mucosa/oropharynx; the nasal mucosa is classically pale and boggy. It requires a temporal relationship to allergen exposure plus documented IgE sensitization (p.2808-2809). Allergic rhinitis usually occurs in atopic individuals and overlaps strongly with other atopic disease: up to 50% of allergic rhinitis patients have asthma, while 70-80% of asthmatics and 80% of those with chronic bilateral sinusitis have allergic rhinitis (p.2809). Seasonal allergic rhinitis is elicited by wind-pollinated tree, grass, and weed pollens (in temperate North America: trees Mar-May, grasses Jun-early Jul, weeds mid-Aug-early Oct); perennial rhinitis is driven by year-round allergens such as dust mites (Dermatophagoides), animal dander, cockroach proteins, and mold spores (p.2809). Pollen-associated (oral allergy) food syndrome causes oropharyngeal pruritus and/or mild swelling after ingesting plant foods cross-reactive with the offending tree, grass, or weed pollen (p.2809). Angioedema of the upper respiratory tract / larynx may be life-threatening due to transient laryngeal obstruction - airway emergency Gastrointestinal angioedema with abdominal colic can mimic an acute abdomen and lead to unnecessary surgical intervention Cold urticaria with cold-water immersion may progress to vascular collapse Progression of urticaria/angioedema to anaphylaxis with vascular collapse (e.g. exercise-induced anaphylaxis, food/drug triggers) Urticarial lesions lasting >24-36 h with bruising/petechiae, scarring, or burning/pain rather than pruritus suggest urticarial vasculitis and warrant biopsy Failing to distinguish histaminergic from bradykinin-mediated angioedema: bradykinin-mediated angioedema (hereditary angioedema from C1INH deficiency, and ACE inhibitor-induced) is conspicuously WITHOUT concomitant urticaria or pruritus, frequently involves the GI tract, lasts >24 h, and characteristically does NOT respond to H1 antihistamines (nor to adrenaline) - treat with C1INH replacement, bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist (icatibant), or kallikrein inhibitor rather than antihistamines. Mistaking urticarial vasculitis for simple urticaria: individual lesions persist >24 h, may leave bruising/petechiae and scarring, and cause burning rather than pruritus - biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis and may signal underlying SLE, Sjogren's, or complement deficiency. Overlooking laryngeal angioedema as an airway emergency, or mistaking GI angioedema for a surgical abdomen. Topical glucocorticoids are of no value in urticaria, and systemic glucocorticoids are generally avoided in idiopathic, allergen-induced, or inducible urticaria due to long-term toxicity. Prolonged use of topical alpha-adrenergic nasal decongestants (7-14 days) causes rebound rhinitis medicamentosa. Concomitant beta-adrenergic blocker therapy increases the risk of severe/refractory anaphylaxis during allergen immunotherapy; immunotherapy is contraindicated in significant cardiovascular disease or unstable asthma. Atopy is a tendency to manifest asthma, rhinitis, urticaria, food allergy, and atopic dermatitis in association with allergen-specific IgE, though urticaria and anaphylaxis can also occur in non-atopic individuals. Mast cells are the key effector cells: IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonRI (sensitization), and antigen-driven receptor aggregation triggers Lyn/Syk/Fyn tyrosine-kinase signaling, calcium influx, and degranulation. This releases preformed granule mediators (histamine, tryptase, chymase, carboxypeptidase A, proteoglycans), newly generated lipid mediators (PGD2 via cyclooxygenase; LTB4 and cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4 via 5-lipoxygenase/FLAP; PAF), and cytokines/chemokines (TNF-alpha, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, GM-CSF). Mast cells can also be activated IgE-independently via C5a/C3a anaphylatoxin receptors, TLRs, alarmin (TSLP, IL-33) receptors, and MRGPRX2 (a target of small-molecule drugs such as ciprofloxacin and rocuronium and of neuropeptides). Histamine and lipid mediators increase venular permeability producing dermal edema (urticaria) or deeper subcutaneous/dermal edema (angioedema). Cold urticaria provides the best evidence for IgE/mast-cell involvement, with documented mast cell degranulation and elevated lesional histamine. In contrast, bradykinin-mediated angioedema (HAE from C1INH deficiency, or ACE inhibitor-induced) results from excess bradykinin: C1INH normally inhibits activated factor XII, kallikrein, and C1r/C1s, and its deficiency leads to bradykinin accumulation with falling C4/C2. Allergic rhinitis arises from sensitized intraepithelial and perivenular nasal mast cells that, on allergen exposure, release histamine, PGD2, and leukotrienes, producing submucosal edema and eosinophilic infiltration. More than two-thirds of new-onset urticaria cases are ultimately acute and self-limited. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is most common in the third to fifth decades and the vast majority shows no laboratory abnormality. Dermatographism generally has a duration of <5 years. Allergic rhinitis prevalence in North America is 10-30% (peak >30% in the fifth decade). Allergen immunotherapy (SCIT/SLIT) for allergic rhinitis provides durable symptom benefit and can reduce asthma symptoms; guidelines recommend 3-5 years of SCIT with discontinuation after minimal symptoms over two consecutive allergen seasons. Urticaria/angioedema classified by duration: acute = episodes lasting <6 weeks; chronic = attacks persisting >6 weeks (Table 363-1 further classifies by precipitating factor into acute vs chronic categories, including drug, food, infection, physical/inducible, autoimmune, vasculitic, mastocytosis, and hereditary forms). Hereditary angioedema typed as: type 1 (low C1INH antigen, ~85%), type 2 (dysfunctional C1INH protein), and type 3 (normal C1INH/complement, often identifiable gene mutation e.g. factor XII). Allergic rhinitis classified as seasonal vs perennial, and managed by severity (mild vs moderate-to-severe).

pigmentosa, producing dual sensory (deaf-blind) impairment Inheritance is autosomal recessive, with many causative genes encoding proteins of the hair-cell and photoreceptor cilium (the 'Usher interactome'), including MYO7A, USH2A and CDH23 Type 1 features profound congenital deafness with absent vestibular function and delayed motor milestones from balance impairment Type 2 features moderate-to-severe hearing loss with preserved vestibular function, and is the commonest subtype Type 3 is characterised by progressive, later-onset hearing loss and variable vestibular findings Night blindness and constricting peripheral (tunnel) vision from retinitis pigmentosa often appear later than the hearing loss, so early audiology cases may be missed as isolated deafness Suspect Usher in any child with congenital sensorineural hearing loss, and arrange ophthalmology and electroretinography follow-up to detect retinal disease early Congenital deafness with delayed independent walking, suggesting vestibular involvement and type 1 disease Progressive night blindness or narrowing visual field in a deaf child Family history of combined hearing and visual loss Deterioration in mobility and orientation from combined sensory decline Attributing congenital hearing loss to an isolated cause and not screening for retinal disease Mislabelling early balance and motor delay as global developmental delay rather than vestibular loss Assuming normal vision excludes Usher, as retinopathy often manifests later Failing to arrange genetic counselling for an autosomal recessive condition with recurrence risk Usher syndrome is a group of autosomal recessive disorders caused by mutations in genes whose protein products are needed for the structure and function of stereocilia in cochlear hair cells and of the connecting cilium in retinal photoreceptors. Loss of these shared proteins impairs mechanotransduction in the inner ear and progressive degeneration of rod and cone photoreceptors, giving the characteristic combination of sensorineural hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa. In some subtypes vestibular hair cells are also affected, producing balance disturbance. The clinical subtype reflects which gene is involved and the severity of the resulting protein defect. Hearing loss is generally stable or slowly progressive depending on subtype, while retinitis pigmentosa is progressive and can lead to severe visual impairment in adulthood; early cochlear implantation and low-vision support substantially improve communication and independence.

Uterine fibroids — leiomyoma, myoma, fibromyoma, uterine leiomyomata Adenomyosis Endometrial polyp Ovarian mass Uterine leiomyosarcoma Pregnancy Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma as a cause of abnormal bleeding Transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound to characterise number, size, and location Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy to define submucosal fibroids and the cavity MRI for detailed mapping before myomectomy or embolisation and to help distinguish adenomyosis Full blood count to detect iron-deficiency anaemia from heavy bleeding Endometrial sampling when there is abnormal bleeding with risk factors for endometrial pathology Fibroids are benign monoclonal tumours of uterine smooth muscle and are the most common pelvic tumour in women Many are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, they commonly cause heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, bulk-related urinary or bowel symptoms, and sometimes subfertility Location matters more than size: submucosal fibroids are most associated with abnormal bleeding and reproductive problems, while subserosal fibroids tend to cause pressure symptoms They are oestrogen and progesterone dependent, so they typically grow during the reproductive years and regress after the menopause Treatment is guided by symptoms, fibroid characteristics, and the woman's fertility wishes, ranging from expectant management to medical therapy, uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy, or hysterectomy Medical options aim to reduce bleeding and shrink fibroids, including hormonal treatments and agents that suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis Rapid growth, particularly after the menopause, should raise suspicion of the rare leiomyosarcoma In pregnancy fibroids may undergo red (carneous) degeneration causing acute pain, and can be associated with malpresentation and obstructed labour Rapidly enlarging uterine mass or postmenopausal growth suggesting leiomyosarcoma Severe anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding Acute severe pain from fibroid degeneration or torsion of a pedunculated fibroid Hydronephrosis from ureteric compression by a large mass Acute urinary retention from a large or cervical fibroid Assuming all abnormal bleeding in a woman with fibroids is due to the fibroids and missing coexisting endometrial pathology Overlooking submucosal fibroids as a cause of infertility or recurrent bleeding when only transabdominal imaging is used Attributing a rapidly growing mass to a benign fibroid without considering sarcoma Neglecting to treat iron-deficiency anaemia Failing to consider fibroid degeneration as a cause of acute pain in pregnancy Fibroids arise from a single transformed myometrial smooth muscle cell that proliferates under the influence of ovarian sex steroids to form a well-circumscribed, pseudo-encapsulated mass of smooth muscle and extracellular matrix. Oestrogen and progesterone, along with local growth factors, drive their growth, which is why they enlarge in the reproductive years and shrink after menopause. Heavy bleeding results from an increased and distorted endometrial surface, altered local vasculature and prostaglandins, and impaired uterine contraction. As fibroids outgrow their blood supply they can undergo hyaline, cystic, calcific, or red degeneration. Fibroids are benign and most women have a good outcome; malignant transformation is very rare. Symptoms often stabilise or regress after the menopause. Recurrence after uterine-conserving treatments such as myomectomy is possible, whereas hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility.

Uterine Prolapse — pelvic organ prolapse, uterovaginal prolapse, descent of the uterus, genital prolapse Cystocele or rectocele without significant uterine descent Vaginal vault prolapse after hysterectomy Enterocele Large vaginal or cervical cyst or fibroid Chronic uterine inversion Urethral diverticulum or other vaginal mass Pelvic examination in different positions and with straining to define the compartments and stage Assessment of pelvic floor muscle strength Urinary assessment including post-void residual and urodynamics where incontinence complicates management Consideration of imaging for large or atypical masses Evaluation and treatment of contributing factors such as constipation, chronic cough, and atrophy Uterine prolapse is descent of the uterus and cervix into or beyond the vagina due to weakening of the pelvic floor supports, and it often coexists with prolapse of the vaginal walls, bladder, and rectum Typical symptoms include a sensation of vaginal bulge or something coming down, pelvic heaviness or dragging, and symptoms that worsen through the day and with standing or straining Associated urinary, bowel, and sexual dysfunction are common and should be assessed directly, as women may not volunteer them Major risk factors include vaginal childbirth, increasing age and menopause, chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, chronic cough or constipation, and connective tissue laxity Severity is graded by how far the leading part of the prolapse descends relative to the hymen, using a standardised staging system Conservative management with pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessaries is appropriate for many women, particularly if surgery is undesirable or unsafe Surgical options range from uterine-preserving procedures to hysterectomy with vault support, and the choice depends on symptoms, fertility wishes, and fitness Vaginal oestrogen can improve atrophic tissue and support pessary use in postmenopausal women Ulceration, bleeding, or infection of exposed prolapsed tissue Urinary retention or obstructed voiding from advanced prolapse Hydronephrosis or renal impairment from ureteric kinking in severe procidentia New abnormal bleeding requiring exclusion of malignancy Complete procidentia that cannot be reduced, needing prompt specialist assessment Failing to ask about associated urinary, bowel, and sexual symptoms Overlooking coexisting prolapse in other vaginal compartments Missing occult stress incontinence unmasked after prolapse correction Neglecting to exclude malignancy in a woman with abnormal bleeding Not treating vaginal atrophy or constipation that undermines pessary use and surgical outcomes The uterus and vagina are held in position by the levator ani muscles and the endopelvic fascia and ligaments, including the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments. Damage to these supports, most often from stretching and denervation during vaginal delivery, together with age-related and oestrogen-deficiency-related weakening of connective tissue and muscle, allows the pelvic organs to descend. Sustained increases in intra-abdominal pressure accelerate this process. As support fails, the uterus and cervix prolapse downward, frequently dragging the vaginal walls and adjacent bladder and rectum with them. Uterine prolapse is a benign but often progressive quality-of-life condition; conservative measures relieve symptoms in many women, and surgery provides good results though prolapse can recur in other compartments over time. Prognosis is favourable overall, and attention to modifiable risk factors such as weight, constipation, and chronic cough helps limit progression and recurrence.

Vaginismus — genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, vaginal muscle spasm, penetration disorder Dyspareunia from other causes Vulvodynia or provoked vestibulodynia Vaginal atrophy from oestrogen deficiency Pelvic infection or inflammation Congenital anatomical abnormality such as a vaginal septum Endometriosis or other pelvic pathology Sensitive sexual and psychological history including any trauma or triggering event Gentle, patient-controlled genital and pelvic examination as tolerated Exclusion of infection, atrophy, or dermatological vulval conditions Assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone, often with physiotherapy input Evaluation for structural anomalies when penetration has never been possible Vaginismus is characterised by involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor and perivaginal muscles that makes vaginal penetration painful, difficult, or impossible It is now grouped with dyspareunia under the umbrella of genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder, reflecting their frequent overlap It may be primary, present from the first attempts at penetration, or secondary, developing after a period of pain-free intercourse Fear and anticipatory anxiety about pain are central, producing a self-reinforcing cycle of muscle guarding, avoidance, and further distress The muscle spasm is involuntary and not under conscious control, a point patients need reassured of to reduce shame and self-blame Examination should be gentle and patient-led, and marked distress or guarding on attempted examination itself supports the diagnosis Organic causes of pain such as infection, atrophy, or structural abnormality should be excluded, since untreated dyspareunia can trigger secondary vaginismus Treatment combines education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, graded desensitisation often using vaginal trainers, and psychological or psychosexual therapy addressing anxiety History of sexual trauma or abuse requiring sensitive, specialised care Findings suggesting an organic structural or gynaecological cause of pain Signs of infection or inflammation needing directed treatment Severe psychological distress or relationship breakdown Attempting a forceful examination, which worsens pain, fear, and guarding Treating it as purely psychological and neglecting pelvic floor physiotherapy Missing an organic cause of dyspareunia that precipitated secondary vaginismus Failing to involve the partner and address relationship and anxiety factors Vaginismus reflects a conditioned, involuntary reflex contraction of the pelvic floor musculature in anticipation of, or response to, attempted vaginal penetration. A trigger, which may be an initial painful experience, infection, trauma, negative sexual conditioning, or fear, leads to protective muscle tightening; the resulting pain reinforces the expectation of pain, so anxiety and guarding become self-perpetuating. Over time the response can be provoked by anticipation alone, independent of any ongoing organic cause. Because the mechanism is largely a learned protective reflex intertwined with anxiety, both the physical muscle response and the psychological component must be addressed for resolution. Vaginismus generally has a good prognosis, with high success rates when treated by a combined approach of education, pelvic floor physiotherapy, graded desensitisation, and psychological support tailored to the individual.
