element that controls SOST expression, reducing sclerostin production Closely related to sclerosteosis but generally milder, and importantly it lacks the syndactyly and overgrowth of stature seen in sclerosteosis Reduced sclerostin releases the brake on Wnt-mediated bone formation, producing generalised osteosclerosis with prominent mandibular enlargement Cranial and skull-base thickening entraps cranial nerves, causing facial palsy, hearing loss, and sometimes optic compromise Patients typically have raised alkaline phosphatase reflecting increased bone formation, with normal calcium and phosphate Radiographs show endosteal cortical thickening of long bones and dense sclerotic skull and jaw Care centres on surgical decompression of entrapped nerves and surveillance for raised intracranial pressure rather than pharmacological bone reduction Progressive facial-nerve weakness or deteriorating hearing or vision Signs of raised intracranial pressure Brainstem compression from posterior skull-base overgrowth Acute neurological decline requiring urgent surgical decompression Assuming a coding SOST mutation when the underlying lesion is a regulatory-region deletion Confusing it with sclerosteosis and expecting syndactyly or gigantism, which are absent here Overlooking treatable cranial nerve entrapment presenting as isolated facial palsy or deafness Failing to monitor for raised intracranial pressure over time Van Buchem disease is caused by homozygous deletion of a conserved regulatory region located downstream of the SOST gene. This element normally drives SOST transcription in bone, so its loss markedly reduces sclerostin expression while leaving the coding sequence intact. Diminished sclerostin fails to inhibit the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, resulting in increased osteoblastic bone formation and progressive generalised hyperostosis. Because sclerostin is reduced rather than completely absent as in coding-mutation sclerosteosis, the phenotype is usually less severe, but skull and jaw overgrowth still narrows cranial foramina and can compress cranial nerves. Generally milder and more indolent than sclerosteosis, with a normal lifespan in most patients, but progressive cranial nerve entrapment can cause facial palsy and sensory loss that may require surgical relief.

Vanishing white matter disease — VWM, childhood ataxia with central hypomyelination, CACH, leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter, EIF2B1, EIF2B2, EIF2B3, EIF2B4, EIF2B5 Metachromatic leukodystrophy and other lysosomal leukodystrophies Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or post-infectious demyelination Alexander disease Cerebral folate deficiency and other treatable metabolic leukoencephalopathies Brain MRI with FLAIR and T2 sequences to demonstrate diffuse white-matter rarefaction with progressive CSF-like signal Molecular genetic testing of EIF2B1-5 to confirm the diagnosis Metabolic screen to exclude other leukodystrophies (arylsulfatase A, very-long-chain fatty acids, lactate) Serial neuroimaging to document progression and cavitation of white matter Endocrine assessment of ovarian function in affected females (ovarioleukodystrophy variant) Autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by biallelic variants in any of the five genes encoding subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (EIF2B1-5) Hallmark clinical feature is episodic, stepwise neurological deterioration provoked by febrile illness, minor head trauma, or acute fright, often with marked lethargy or coma out of proportion to the trigger Cerebellar ataxia and spasticity dominate the motor picture, whereas cognitive function is relatively spared until late Classic childhood-onset form is most common, but the phenotype spans an antenatal/infantile severe end through to adult-onset and an ovarioleukodystrophy variant with premature ovarian failure in females MRI shows diffuse, symmetrical white-matter abnormality that progressively rarefies and takes on cerebrospinal-fluid-like signal on all sequences, with a radiating stripe pattern of relatively preserved tissue FLAIR sequences are especially useful, showing the affected white matter becoming suppressed (dark) as it liquefies, distinguishing it from simple demyelination Confirmation is by molecular genetic testing of the EIF2B genes; there is no curative treatment, and management centres on avoiding known triggers Families should be counselled to seek early care and antipyresis during infections and to minimise head injury, as these precipitate crises Rapid decline into stupor or coma following a febrile illness or minor head injury Acute loss of previously acquired motor milestones after a trigger event Status epilepticus or intractable seizures during an episode of deterioration Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem dysfunction during a crisis Attributing a post-febrile collapse to encephalitis or sepsis alone and missing the underlying leukodystrophy Misreading early MRI as ordinary demyelination and failing to recognise the FLAIR suppression that signals white-matter liquefaction Overlooking premature ovarian failure as a clue in adolescent or adult females Failing to counsel families about trigger avoidance, prompt antipyresis, and head-injury prevention Vanishing white matter disease results from loss-of-function variants in the genes encoding the five subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor central to the regulation of protein synthesis, particularly under cellular stress. Impaired eIF2B activity deranges the integrated stress response, leaving glial cells (especially astrocytes and oligodendrocytes) unable to adapt to metabolic stresses such as fever, inflammation, or trauma. The result is progressive cerebral white-matter breakdown with abnormal, immature astrocytes and dysmyelination, so that the white matter gradually rarefies and cavitates into a fluid-like state while grey matter is comparatively preserved. The disorder is progressive and currently incurable; the classic childhood form typically causes stepwise decline with death within a few years of onset, whereas later-onset forms progress more slowly. Prognosis is strongly influenced by age at onset, with the earliest-onset presentations carrying the worst outlook.

Variceal bleeding — Urgent upper GI endoscopy Crossmatch, coagulation Vasoactive (terlipressin) + antibiotic prophylaxis Major haemorrhage — resuscitate; antibiotics reduce mortality in cirrhotic GI bleed Peptic ulcer disease — the most common cause of upper GI bleeding (~50% of UGIB hospitalisations) (p.360) Mallory-Weiss tear — ~2-10% of UGIB, classically preceded by vomiting/retching/coughing, usually on the gastric side of the gastro-oesophageal junction; stops spontaneously in ~80-90% (p.360) Bleeding gastric varices, intestinal varices, and portal hypertensive gastropathy/enterocolopathy — other portal-hypertension-related sources distinct from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714) Erosive disease — erosive oesophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis (up to ~30% of UGIB), commonly NSAID-related (p.361) Stress-related gastric mucosal injury in the critically ill (p.361) Less common: neoplasm, vascular ectasias (including hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, gastric antral vascular ectasia), Dieulafoy's lesion, aortoenteric fistula, haemobilia/haemosuccus pancreaticus (p.361) Upper endoscopy within 24 h is first-line both to diagnose the bleeding source and to treat acutely; more urgent endoscopy (6-12 h) does not improve outcomes and may worsen them in high-risk patients (p.362, p.2714) Endoscopic surveillance for varices: recommended at diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis, then every 2 years (active liver disease) or every 3 years (inactive); also at the time of hepatic decompensation (p.2714) Liver stiffness by transient elastography — if <20 kPa and no thrombocytopenia, high-risk varices are rare and screening endoscopy may be deferred (p.2714) HVPG measurement by interventional radiology (hepatic vein cannulation) in selected cases to confirm/quantify portal hypertension (p.371, p.2714) Complete blood count (thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism is often the first marker of portal hypertension), liver biochemistry, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR to assess hepatic function and severity (p.371, p.2714) Endoscopic stigmata predicting bleeding risk: red wale signs, hematocystic spots, diffuse erythema, bluish colour, cherry-red spots, white-nipple spots; larger varices and worse Child-Pugh/MELD also predict bleeding (p.2713) Portal hypertensive gastropathy — snakeskin-like mosaic mucosal pattern on endoscopy; can cause acute or chronic (iron-deficiency) GI bleeding and mimics variceal bleeding as a cause of haematemesis/melaena in the same cirrhotic patient (p.2714) Gastric varices — also driven by portal hypertension but managed differently from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714) Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; compensated cirrhosis typically has an HVPG of 5-10 mmHg, while clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), defined as HVPG ≥10 mmHg, carries substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy). Patients with a gradient >12 mmHg are at risk for variceal haemorrhage (p.2713-2714). Each episode of variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate, making it an immediate life-threatening complication of portal hypertension (p.2713). In cirrhotic patients presenting with upper GI bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics (typically ceftriaxone) started before endoscopy reduce bacterial infections, recurrent bleeding AND mortality — this is a mortality-altering intervention, not merely supportive (p.362, p.2714). A vasoactive/vasoconstricting agent (somatostatin, octreotide, terlipressin, vapreotide) improves initial bleeding control, reduces transfusion needs and reduces all-cause mortality; combined endoscopic plus pharmacologic therapy is superior to either alone (p.360, p.2714). A restrictive transfusion strategy (transfuse when haemoglobin <7 g/dL, target 7-9 g/dL) reduced early rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal threshold in randomised trial; haemoglobin may be normal at initial presentation because plasma and red-cell volumes fall proportionately ("people bleed whole blood") and may take up to 72 h to fall (p.362, p.2714). Roughly one-third of patients with histologically confirmed cirrhosis have varices; about 5-15% of cirrhotics develop varices per year, and roughly one-third of patients with varices will bleed (p.2713). IV erythromycin given shortly before endoscopy is suggested as a promotility agent to improve endoscopic visualisation in UGI bleeding, reducing the need for repeat endoscopy (p.362, p.2713). Routine correction of an elevated prothrombin time with fresh frozen plasma is NOT recommended in acute variceal bleeding unless there is evidence of coagulopathy such as bleeding at other sites (e.g. IV-line sites) (p.2714). Bleeding gastric varices, especially when entirely within the stomach or extending into the proximal stomach, are often not amenable to band ligation; tissue-adhesive injection (e.g. cyanoacrylate), TIPS, or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) are alternative principles (p.361, p.2714). Variceal haemorrhage is immediately life-threatening with 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode — treat as a major haemorrhage with airway/haemodynamic priority (p.2713) Hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension), increasing age and comorbidities predict rebleeding and death (p.362) Increased frequency of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with variceal haemorrhage — SBP prophylaxis is recommended at presentation with upper GI bleeding (p.2715) Persistent or recurrent bleeding despite endoscopic and medical therapy, and advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh B score 8-9 with active bleeding, or Child-Pugh C score 10-13), mark patients who benefit from early/salvage TIPS (p.360-361) Assuming a normal initial haemoglobin excludes severe bleeding — haemoglobin may be normal or only minimally reduced at presentation and can take up to 72 h to fall as extravascular fluid re-equilibrates (p.362) Reflexively correcting a prolonged prothrombin time with FFP — not recommended in variceal bleeding without evidence of true coagulopathy, and FFP can raise portal pressure and cause volume overload (p.2714) Over-liberal transfusion — a liberal threshold (Hb 9 g/dL) increased early rebleeding and mortality versus a restrictive (<7 g/dL) threshold (p.362, p.2714) Omitting antibiotics in a cirrhotic UGI bleed — prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality and are a core, not optional, intervention (p.362, p.2714) Attempting band ligation on gastric or proximal-stomach varices, where it is often unsuccessful — consider tissue adhesive, TIPS or BRTO (p.2714) Forgetting that TIPS causes new or worsened hepatic encephalopathy in as many as 20% of patients, especially the elderly and those with pre-existing encephalopathy (p.2714) Oesophageal varices are a consequence of portal hypertension, defined as an HVPG >5 mmHg. Portal hypertension arises from two simultaneous haemodynamic processes: (1) increased intrahepatic resistance to portal blood flow (from cirrhosis, regenerative nodules and microthrombi) and (2) increased splanchnic blood flow secondary to splanchnic vasodilation. Cirrhosis is associated with decreased intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase and nitric oxide, causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction, while systemically nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF rise, driving splanchnic vasodilation. In advanced stages, neurohumoral and vasoconstrictor activation causes sodium/water retention, increased blood volume and a hyperdynamic circulation that further raises portal pressure. Intrahepatic causes (mainly cirrhosis) account for >95% of portal hypertension; pre-hepatic (portal/splenic vein thrombosis) and post-hepatic (Budd-Chiari, right-heart congestion) causes also occur. Elevated portal pressure decompresses into portosystemic collaterals, producing gastro-oesophageal varices that can rupture and bleed. (p.2713-2714) Variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate with each bleeding episode and patients with variceal haemorrhage have poorer outcomes than those with other UGIB sources. Control of acute bleeding is achievable in the vast majority of cases, but bleeding recurs in the majority of patients unless definitive endoscopic therapy is instituted; oesophageal varices reflect clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mmHg), and once cirrhosis decompensates the median survival is <2 years. Prophylactic antibiotics, vasoactive drugs and a restrictive transfusion strategy each independently reduce mortality. (p.360, p.2713-2714) Bleeding/decompensation risk is stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, by HVPG/wedged-hepatic-vein pressure (CSPH ≥10 mmHg; variceal bleeding risk at >12 mmHg), by varix size and location, and by endoscopic high-risk stigmata (red wale signs, cherry-red spots, etc.). For triage of UGIB generally, the Glasgow-Blatchford score (0-23) identifies very-low-risk patients (score 0-1) suitable for outpatient management. Advanced-disease thresholds favouring early TIPS: Child-Pugh B 8-9 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or Child-Pugh C 10-13. (p.362, p.2713-2714)

Varicella-Zoster Virus Infection — chickenpox, shingles, VZV, herpes zoster For chickenpox: disseminated HSV infection in patients with atopic dermatitis; disseminated vesiculopapular lesions of coxsackievirus or echovirus infection; atypical measles (these rashes are more often morbilliform/hemorrhagic than vesicular) (p.1506) Rickettsialpox - distinguished by the 'herald spot' (eschar) at the mite-bite site and a more pronounced headache; serology helps differentiate it from varicella (p.1506) Mpox - consider in travelers from endemic areas and in HIV-infected individuals (p.1506) Smallpox - bioterrorism concern; smallpox lesions are larger than chickenpox lesions and all at the same stage of evolution at any given time (p.1506) For herpes zoster: both HSV and coxsackievirus infections can cause dermatomal vesicular lesions (p.1506) Disseminated HSV infection (notably in atopic dermatitis) (p.1506) Coxsackievirus infection (p.1506) Echovirus infection (p.1506) Atypical measles (p.1506) Rickettsialpox (p.1506) Mpox (p.1506) Smallpox (p.1506) HSV and coxsackievirus causing dermatomal vesicular lesions (mimicking zoster) (p.1506) PCR for VZV DNA in vesicular fluid - diagnostic method of choice; also performed on lesions, blood, and saliva (p.1507) Tzanck smear (scraping of lesion base for multinucleated giant cells) - rapid but low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507) Viral isolation in susceptible tissue-culture cell lines (unequivocal confirmation) (p.1507) Direct immunofluorescent staining of cells from the lesion base or immunoperoxidase detection of viral antigens (p.1507) Serology: seroconversion or fourfold rise in antibody titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; FAMA (fluorescent antibody to membrane antigen) test and ELISA are the most sensitive serologic tools (p.1507) VZV causes two distinct clinical syndromes: primary infection (varicella/chickenpox), usually a benign childhood exanthematous vesicular illness, and reactivation of latent virus (herpes zoster/shingles), a dermatomal vesicular rash usually associated with severe pain (p.1504). In chickenpox, skin lesions appear in successive crops over a 2-4 day period and are present in various stages of evolution simultaneously (maculopapules, vesicles, and scabs) on a given body region - the classic small vesicle on an erythematous base ('dewdrop on a rose petal') (p.1505). Chickenpox is highly contagious (attack rate >=90% in seronegatives); patients are infectious ~48 h before the rash appears, throughout vesicle formation, and until all vesicles are crusted. Incubation is usually 14-17 days (range 10-21) (p.1505). Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent VZV in dorsal root ganglia; most patients have no recent exposure to others with VZV. Incidence is highest in the sixth decade of life and beyond; recurrent zoster is exceedingly rare except in immunocompromised hosts, especially those with AIDS (p.1505). Zoster pain (dermatomal) may precede visible lesions by 48-72 h; in the prodromal stage before the rash appears, the diagnosis can be exceedingly difficult (p.1505-1506). Dermatomes T3 to L3 are most frequently involved in herpes zoster (p.1505). PCR detection of VZV DNA in vesicular fluid is the diagnostic method of choice; specimens for PCR include lesions, blood, and saliva. The Tzanck smear gives a rapid impression but has low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507). Patients with herpes zoster can transmit infection to seronegative individuals, resulting in chickenpox (not zoster) in the contact (p.1506). Zoster ophthalmicus - involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve; a debilitating condition that can result in blindness in the absence of antiviral therapy. Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) signal likely ocular involvement; refer immediately to an ophthalmologist (p.1505-1507) Ramsay Hunt syndrome - geniculate ganglion (sensory branch of facial nerve) involvement causing pain and vesicles in the external auditory canal, loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and ipsilateral facial palsy (p.1506) Disseminated/progressive herpes zoster in immunocompromised hosts - patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma are at greatest risk; cutaneous dissemination occurs in ~40% untreated, raising the risk of pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, and hepatitis by 5-10% (p.1506) Varicella pneumonia - the most serious complication of chickenpox; more common in adults (up to 20%) than children and particularly severe in pregnant women; typically requires ventilatory support (p.1505, 1507) Visceral dissemination in immunocompromised patients - occurs in 30-50% of cases and is fatal 15% of the time without antiviral therapy (p.1505) Perinatal varicella - mortality as high as 30% when maternal disease begins within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1505) CNS involvement: encephalitis (0.1-0.2% of children with chickenpox), aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome; in zoster, symptomatic meningoencephalitis and rare granulomatous angiitis with contralateral hemiplegia (p.1505-1506) Aspirin should never be given to children with chickenpox because of its association with Reye syndrome; aspirin is no longer used for this reason (p.1505, 1507) Zoster sine herpetica: dermatomal pain with serologic evidence of zoster can occur in the absence of any skin lesions - shingles without a rash has been reported, making diagnosis difficult (p.1506) In the prodromal stage of herpes zoster (before lesions appear), diagnosis may be possible only after lesions emerge or by retrospective serology (p.1506) Glucocorticoids for zoster should not be used without concomitant antiviral therapy, and steroid use is appropriate only for relatively healthy elderly patients with moderate/severe pain; patients with osteoporosis, diabetes mellitus, glycosuria, or hypertension may not be appropriate candidates (p.1507) VZIG is NOT indicated for a newborn if the mother has zoster (as opposed to varicella); it is indicated when maternal varicella onsets within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1507-1508) VZV is a member of the Herpesviridae with double-stranded DNA (~125,000 bp), a lipid envelope, and an icosahedral nucleocapsid (~180-200 nm). Primary transmission is by the respiratory route, with localized replication (presumably nasopharynx) seeding the lymphatic/reticuloendothelial system and producing viremia, which manifests as diffuse, scattered skin lesions. Vesicles involve the corium/dermis with ballooning degeneration, multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions; localized skin blood-vessel involvement can cause necrosis and epidermal hemorrhage. During chickenpox the virus infects dorsal root ganglia and remains latent (in sensory dorsal, cranial, and enteric ganglia) until an unknown trigger causes reactivation, producing herpes zoster; active zoster ganglia show hemorrhage, edema, and lymphocytic infiltration. Pulmonary involvement shows interstitial pneumonitis with giant cells, intranuclear inclusions, and hemorrhage; CNS infection produces perivascular cuffing similar to other viral encephalitides, while focal hemorrhagic necrosis (characteristic of HSV encephalitis) develops infrequently in VZV infection (p.1504). In the immunocompetent host chickenpox is usually benign and self-limited (total duration ~7-10 days; skin may take 2-4 weeks to fully normalize). Childhood acute cerebellar ataxia is generally benign and does not require hospitalization. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most debilitating complication of zoster: uncommon in the young but affects at least 50% of patients over age 50, who report dermatomal pain for months after cutaneous healing. Even in immunocompromised patients, disseminated zoster is rarely fatal. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients are at particularly high risk, with a mortality rate of ~10% for posttransplantation VZV infection. The Shingrix subunit vaccine showed 97.2% efficacy in adults >=50 years, although vaccine immunity wanes over time (p.1505-1507).

Varicocele — varicocoele, scrotal varicocele, pampiniform plexus varicosity Spermatocele or epididymal cyst Hydrocele Inguinal hernia (indirect) Testicular tumour Epididymo-orchitis Retroperitoneal or renal mass obstructing venous drainage (secondary varicocele) Scrotal examination in both standing and supine positions with Valsalva Scrotal colour Doppler ultrasound to confirm venous reflux and grade the varicocele Measurement of testicular volume to detect growth arrest, especially in adolescents Semen analysis in men presenting with subfertility Abdominal/renal imaging when a right-sided, isolated, or non-reducing varicocele suggests a retroperitoneal cause A varicocele is an abnormal dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus, classically described as feeling like a bag of worms on scrotal palpation The great majority occur on the left side, attributed to the left testicular vein draining at a right angle into the left renal vein and having a longer course It is more prominent on standing and with Valsalva and typically decompresses on lying down; a varicocele that does not empty when supine should raise concern for a retroperitoneal or renal mass A sudden new right-sided or non-reducing varicocele in an older patient warrants imaging to exclude a renal tumour obstructing venous drainage Clinical grading ranges from subclinical (detectable only on imaging) to visible through the scrotal skin, with intermediate grades palpable with or without Valsalva Varicoceles are a common and potentially reversible factor in male subfertility, associated with impaired sperm count, motility, and morphology, and sometimes with testicular growth arrest in adolescents Most are asymptomatic or cause a dull dragging ache; treatment (surgical varicocelectomy or radiological embolisation) is considered for pain, infertility with abnormal semen analysis, or testicular growth failure in adolescents Semen analysis and assessment of testicular volume guide management decisions in the fertility and adolescent contexts New-onset right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele suggesting a renal or retroperitoneal tumour Progressive ipsilateral testicular atrophy or growth arrest in an adolescent Acute painful scrotal swelling raising alternative diagnoses that require exclusion Significant deterioration in semen parameters in a man seeking fertility Failing to examine the patient standing and with Valsalva, missing a lower-grade varicocele Overlooking a secondary varicocele from a renal tumour in an isolated right-sided or non-reducible case Recommending repair for asymptomatic subclinical varicoceles without a clear indication Neglecting testicular volume assessment in adolescents Attributing subfertility solely to the varicocele without full evaluation of both partners A varicocele results from incompetent or absent valves in the internal spermatic (testicular) veins, leading to retrograde flow and dilatation of the pampiniform plexus. The predominance on the left relates to the anatomy of left testicular venous drainage into the left renal vein at a right angle with a longer, higher-pressure course. The resulting venous stasis is thought to impair testicular function through elevated scrotal temperature, venous hypertension, hypoxia, and reflux of adrenal or renal metabolites, contributing to defective spermatogenesis and, in some cases, testicular atrophy. Many varicoceles are asymptomatic and require no intervention; when treated for pain, subfertility, or adolescent growth arrest, repair often improves semen parameters and testicular growth, though not all men achieve improved fertility.

varicosity is controlled by elevation and direct compression, not by a tourniquet Torrential haemorrhage from a ruptured surface varicosity requiring elevation and direct pressure Non-healing venous ulcer, especially with atypical features suggesting malignant change (Marjolin's ulcer) Signs of deep vein thrombosis or coexisting significant arterial disease before compression Rapidly progressive skin changes or superficial thrombophlebitis extending toward the saphenofemoral junction Applying compression without first excluding significant arterial disease Overlooking underlying deep venous disease or previous DVT causing secondary varicosities Attempting to control variceal bleeding with a tourniquet rather than elevation and compression Missing malignant change in a chronic non-healing venous ulcer Varicose veins develop when incompetent valves in the superficial venous system, or at the saphenofemoral or saphenopopliteal junctions, permit reflux of blood back down the leg. The resulting venous hypertension dilates and elongates the superficial veins, making them tortuous. Sustained ambulatory venous hypertension is transmitted to the skin microcirculation, causing capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, inflammation, and progressive skin changes that culminate in venous ulceration. Contributing factors include heredity, prolonged standing, pregnancy, obesity, and previous deep vein thrombosis, the last causing secondary varicosities through deep venous obstruction or valvular damage. Symptoms and skin changes usually improve with compression and, where appropriate, ablation or surgery, and venous ulcers can heal with effective compression, but recurrence of varicosities and ulcers is common, particularly with deep venous disease or poor compliance.

measures effective in porphyria cutanea tarda Progressive motor neuropathy or respiratory compromise during an acute attack Seizures with hyponatraemia during an attack Severe photocutaneous ulceration with secondary infection Exposure to a known porphyrinogenic drug in a symptomatic patient Mistaking the skin disease for porphyria cutanea tarda and applying inappropriate therapy Prescribing porphyrinogenic drugs that precipitate acute attacks Relying on urinary studies alone and missing the diagnosis between attacks when they may be near normal Failing to protect skin from sunlight and trauma Not screening at-risk relatives, particularly in founder populations Variegate porphyria arises from reduced activity of protoporphyrinogen oxidase, the seventh enzyme of the haem pathway, which oxidises protoporphyrinogen to protoporphyrin. Deficiency causes accumulation of protoporphyrinogen and back-up of upstream intermediates. The photoreactive porphyrins deposited in the skin generate reactive oxygen species on light exposure, causing the blistering photodermatosis, while induction of hepatic ALA synthase during metabolic stress raises the neurotoxic precursors ALA and PBG that drive acute neurovisceral attacks. The dual accumulation explains the mixed acute and cutaneous phenotype. Cutaneous manifestations tend to persist while acute attacks are usually preventable with trigger avoidance; most patients maintain a good quality of life, though severe attacks carry the same neurological risks as other acute porphyrias.

Vascular Dementia — vascular cognitive impairment, multi-infarct dementia Alzheimer's disease (most common dementia; mixed AD-vascular pathology very common) Dementia with Lewy bodies / PDD spectrum Frontotemporal dementia Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) Normal pressure hydrocephalus Delirium Brain MRI is the mainstay for detection and subtyping of cerebrovascular disease; should include FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, and T2*-weighted sequences to detect large and small chronic infarcts, acute microinfarcts, microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities (p.3491) Diffusion tensor MRI (e.g., peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity, PSMD) detects white matter disconnection (largely research use) (p.3490) Vessel imaging (CT or MR angiography) is not required for initial cognitive evaluation but may help determine the cause of identified macroscopic infarcts (p.3491) Screening for atrial fibrillation in individuals with asymptomatic infarcts; prolonged cardiac monitoring for embolic-appearing infarcts (p.3491) Genetic testing for hereditary VCID (CADASIL, hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy) when young onset, positive family history, or suggestive imaging—otherwise unnecessary (p.3491) Alzheimer's disease (frequently coexists as mixed dementia—a key pitfall) Normal pressure hydrocephalus (shares gait disturbance) Delirium (prominent attention/executive deficits) Traditionally defined as dementia due primarily to one or more symptomatic strokes; ranked the second most frequent cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, and especially common where vascular risk factors are undertreated (p.3489). The concept has been broadened to vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), reflecting that cerebrovascular pathology is highly prevalent in the elderly and contributes to cognitive impairment, whether in isolation or—more commonly—combined with neurodegenerative processes (p.3489). Clinical evaluation focuses on identifying vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease), prior stroke/TIA, and family history of early stroke or vascular disease (p.3491). Although stepwise progression and deficits such as loss of executive function are particularly suggestive, most individuals with VCID follow the more typical pattern of gradual progression of impaired episodic memory (p.3491). Patients often show a mixture of executive and visuospatial deficits with prominent psychomotor slowing, and may present with psychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety, delusions, disinhibition, or apathy (p.196). Gait disturbance is common in vascular dementia (as well as PD/DLB and NPH) (p.195). Strategic single infarcts in locations such as thalamus, medial temporal cortex, anterior corpus callosum, or dominant-side angular gyrus can sufficiently impair episodic memory and function to meet memory-based dementia criteria (p.3489). At least some cognitive impairment is present in approximately half of stroke survivors and increases with longer follow-up; even patients with good cognitive recovery show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline (p.3489). One late-onset community autopsy cohort attributed 25% of dementia risk to cerebrovascular disease (vs 39% Alzheimer's, 17% LATE, 12% Lewy body), and most late-onset dementia involves multiple coexisting pathologies (p.195). Young onset, positive family history, or suggestive neuroimaging—consider hereditary forms such as CADASIL or hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3491) Lobar intracerebral hemorrhage or convexity subarachnoid blood, suggesting cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3490) Rapid progression with motor rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than vascular dementia (p.195) Mixed dementia is the rule rather than the exception—cerebrovascular disease commonly co-occurs with Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative pathologies, so attributing cognitive impairment to a single etiology is often incorrect (p.3489). Most individuals with VCID do not show classic stepwise decline but instead a gradual progression of impaired episodic memory resembling Alzheimer's (p.3491). White matter hyperintensities are an almost ubiquitous, nonspecific feature of aging (gliosis, demyelination, or increased water content) and should not be over-interpreted (p.3490). Many chronic lacunar infarcts and microinfarcts cannot be readily identified on routine imaging, so absence of visible lesions does not exclude small-vessel disease (p.3490). Vascular dementia results from the cumulative impact of cerebrovascular disease on age-related cognitive decline. Symptomatic strokes (ischemic or hemorrhagic) produce irreversible injury whose cognitive effect depends on size and location. Cerebral small-vessel disease—principally arteriolosclerosis (thickening of arterioles from plasma-protein infiltration; risk factors age, hypertension, diabetes; centered on deep penetrating territories such as thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (beta-amyloid deposition in walls of small cortical arteries/arterioles/capillaries; main risk factor advancing age; favoring lobar cortex and subcortical white matter)—is often clinically asymptomatic and produces lacunar infarcts, microinfarcts, cerebral microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities. These small distributed injuries disconnect nodes within distributed brain networks. Mixed pathology is the rule: cerebrovascular lesions frequently co-occur with neurodegenerative disease (most commonly Alzheimer's), producing greater impairment than either mechanism alone, possibly via loss of blood-brain barrier integrity and impaired perivascular clearance of beta-amyloid (p.3489-3491). Stroke survivors show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline even after good initial recovery; in one longitudinal study trajectory shifted from a prestroke cognitive gain to poststroke loss. Multiple strokes and larger infarcted volumes raise the likelihood of poststroke cognitive dysfunction. Epidemiologic data show declining age-adjusted dementia incidence paralleling improved hypertension control and stroke prevention, and the SPRINT-MIND trial showed intensive systolic blood pressure lowering reduced rates of mild cognitive impairment and combined MCI/probable dementia, underscoring VCID as a target for prevention (p.3489).

never irradiate true GPA airway lesions (Harrison 22e p.2941) Drug toxicity - cocaine (cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions can show anti-human-neutrophil-elastase ANCA), levamisole (cocaine adulterant; causes cutaneous infarction, granulocytopenia, vasculitis-mimicking serology), amphetamines, ergot alkaloids, methysergide, arsenic (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941) Sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.2937) Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture's) (Harrison 22e p.2937) Amyloidosis (Harrison 22e p.2937) Migraine (Harrison 22e p.2937) Fibromuscular dysplasia (Harrison 22e p.2937) Heritable disorders of connective tissue (Harrison 22e p.2937) Segmental arterial mediolysis (SAM) (Harrison 22e p.2937) Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2937) IgG4-related disease - cause of aortitis/periaortitis distinguished histologically from Takayasu (IgG4+ plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis) (Harrison 22e p.2947) Suspect vasculitis in any patient with an unexplained multisystem illness; specific clues include palpable purpura, pulmonary infiltrates with microscopic hematuria, chronic sinusitis, mononeuritis multiplex, unexplained ischemic events, and glomerulonephritis with multisystem disease (Harrison 22e p.2937). The first step in suspected vasculitis is to exclude conditions that mimic it - especially infections - particularly before starting empirical immunosuppression in a deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937). Definitive diagnosis usually rests on biopsy of clinically involved tissue; 'blind' biopsy of organs with no clinical evidence of involvement has very low yield and should be avoided. Arteriography is used when PAN, Takayasu, or primary CNS vasculitis is suspected (Harrison 22e p.2937-2938). ANCA-associated vasculitides (GPA, MPA, EGPA) share small-vessel involvement and ANCA positivity but have distinct clinical phenotypes and should be regarded as separate entities (Harrison 22e p.2937). cANCA targets proteinase-3 (PR3) - present in >90% of active GPA; pANCA targets myeloperoxidase (MPO) - only anti-MPO antibodies are convincingly linked to vasculitis (MPA, EGPA, GPA, isolated necrotizing crescentic GN) (Harrison 22e p.2937). A pANCA pattern NOT due to anti-MPO can occur in nonvasculitic conditions: rheumatic/nonrheumatic autoimmune disease, inflammatory bowel disease, certain drugs, and infections including endocarditis and bacterial airway infection in cystic fibrosis (Harrison 22e p.2937). ANCA titres do not reliably track disease activity - GPA can be active despite negative ANCA, titres correlate poorly with activity, and patients in remission may keep high ANCA for years (Harrison 22e p.2937, p.2941). Predictive value of a positive ANCA in GPA is ~90% with active glomerulonephritis but falls to 30-60% in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement; tissue biopsy is then needed to exclude infection or malignancy that may give a false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941). In GPA the renal lesion is a pauci-immune (no immune-complex deposition) focal segmental glomerulitis that can evolve into rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940). Saddle-nose deformity (from nasal septal perforation) and subglottic stenosis (~16% of GPA, may cause severe airway obstruction) are characteristic upper-airway sequelae of GPA (Harrison 22e p.2940). Mononeuritis multiplex is a recurring vasculitic clue - common in EGPA (up to ~72%) and PAN (~51%), and also seen in GPA and MPA (Harrison 22e p.2940, p.2943, p.2944). EGPA (Churg-Strauss) requires asthma, peripheral blood eosinophilia (>1000 cells/uL in >80%), and clinical features of vasculitis; eosinophilic tissue infiltration and extravascular granulomas are characteristic (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944). Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, pericarditis, coronary vasculitis) is the leading cause of death in EGPA, accounting for ~39% of mortality; echocardiography is advised in all newly diagnosed patients (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944). PAN does NOT involve pulmonary arteries and does NOT cause glomerulonephritis, granuloma, or significant eosinophilia; venule involvement points away from PAN and toward microscopic polyangiitis (Harrison 22e p.2944). PAN classically causes microaneurysms of small- and medium-sized renal, hepatic, and visceral arteries; catheter-directed dye arteriography (MR/CT lack resolution) can be diagnostic when accessible tissue is unavailable (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). Giant cell arteritis occurs almost exclusively in those over 50; jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, and headache precede the dreaded complication of ischemic optic neuropathy with sudden blindness - therapy should not be delayed for diagnostic testing (Harrison 22e p.2945). GCA and polymyalgia rheumatica are considered spectrums of one disease - PMR occurs in 40-50% of GCA, and 10-20% of isolated PMR later develop GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945). Takayasu arteritis should be strongly suspected in a young woman with diminished/absent peripheral pulses, an inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, or arterial bruits (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947). Hemoptysis may be the first sign of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (~12%); upper-airway disease and pulmonary nodules are atypical for MPA and instead suggest GPA (Harrison 22e p.2942). GPA carries an increased risk of venous thrombotic events (DVT/PE); maintain a heightened awareness even though routine anticoagulation is not recommended (Harrison 22e p.2940). Active glomerulonephritis is always classed as severe disease even with normal renal function (Harrison 22e p.2941) Alveolar/pulmonary haemorrhage - severe manifestation of GPA/MPA; hemoptysis may be the first symptom of alveolar haemorrhage in MPA (Harrison 22e p.2941, p.2942) Visual symptoms in a patient over 50 with headache - ischemic optic neuropathy in GCA can cause sudden, irreversible blindness; do not delay treatment for diagnostic workup (Harrison 22e p.2945, p.2946) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine in ANCA-associated vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940, p.2942) Jaw/tongue claudication, scalp tenderness, or a tender/nodular temporal artery - cranial ischaemic features of GCA (Harrison 22e p.2945) Inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy, absent pulses, or bruits in a young woman - suggests Takayasu large-vessel involvement (Harrison 22e p.2947) Bowel infarction/perforation and GI bleeding in PAN - leading causes of death (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945) Cardiac involvement in EGPA - the chief cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2944) Signs of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism in GPA given the increased venous thrombotic risk (Harrison 22e p.2940) Treating a rise in ANCA titre as a relapse - only ~43% relapse within 1 year of an ANCA increase, so a rising ANCA alone should not prompt reinstitution or escalation of immunosuppression (Harrison 22e p.2941). Relying on ANCA to diagnose vasculitis in sinus/lung disease without renal involvement, where positive predictive value is only 30-60% and biopsy is needed to exclude infection/malignancy with false-positive ANCA (Harrison 22e p.2941). Performing 'blind' biopsies of clinically uninvolved organs - yield is very low (Harrison 22e p.2937). Starting immunosuppression before excluding infectious mimics, especially in a rapidly deteriorating patient (Harrison 22e p.2937). Irradiating upper-airway lesions assuming GPA when the diagnosis is actually NK/T-cell lymphoma - GPA airway lesions should never be irradiated (Harrison 22e p.2941). Overlooking cocaine/levamisole-induced midline destruction, which can produce vasculitis-mimicking serology (anti-elastase ANCA) and granulocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2941). Using CRP/ESR to monitor disease activity or assess infection in GCA patients on IL-6 inhibitors, which suppress these acute-phase reactants (Harrison 22e p.2946). Attributing every minor ESR/CRP rise during a GCA prednisone taper to a flare - small increases may not reflect arteritis, and can also be caused by infection (Harrison 22e p.2946). Mislabelling a necrotizing vasculitis with venule involvement as PAN - venule involvement indicates microscopic polyangiitis, not PAN (Harrison 22e p.2944). Missing DADA2 (adenosine deaminase 2 deficiency) in early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, which responds to TNF inhibitors rather than standard PAN therapy (Harrison 22e p.2944). Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls, usually compromising the lumen and causing ischaemia of supplied tissues; any size, type, or location of vessel may be affected, and disease may be primary/single-organ or secondary to another illness. Most syndromes are at least partly immune-mediated through three broad mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2936): (1) Immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum sickness, hepatitis-B-associated vasculitis, hepatitis-C cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) - resembling serum sickness, complexes deposit in vessel walls, activate complement (notably C5a, chemotactic for neutrophils), and neutrophils infiltrate and release enzymes that damage the wall. (2) ANCA production (GPA, MPA, EGPA) - when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha, IL-1, or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (GCA, Takayasu, GPA, EGPA) - cytokine (IFN-gamma) activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and interacts with CD4+ T cells, with IL-1/TNF-alpha inducing adhesion molecules (ELAM-1, VCAM-1). The 1992/2012 Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature underpins the classification of these syndromes by predominant vessel size (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942). Untreated GPA was historically fatal within months; with cyclophosphamide-based therapy >90% improve, ~75% achieve complete remission, and 5-year survival exceeds 80%, but 50-70% of remissions later relapse and many accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity, chronic sinus dysfunction) (Harrison 22e p.2941). Treated MPA has a ~74% 5-year survival, with deaths from alveolar haemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease, and relapse in at least ~34% (Harrison 22e p.2942). Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; treated, prognosis is favourable (~72% at 78 months), but myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2944). Untreated PAN has a poor 5-year survival of 10-20% (deaths from GI and cardiovascular causes); prednisone plus cyclophosphamide markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20% (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). In GCA acute death is uncommon, but patients face late mortality from aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection (18x more likely to develop thoracic aortic aneurysm than the general population) (Harrison 22e p.2946). Takayasu outcomes vary widely (overall survival >=94% in some North American series; 5-year mortality 0-35% elsewhere), and the disease is usually chronic and relapsing (Harrison 22e p.2947). IgA vasculitis has an excellent prognosis with rare mortality and only 1-5% of children progressing to end-stage renal disease (Harrison 22e p.2948). Vasculitides are classified by predominant vessel size per the Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942): LARGE-VESSEL (giant cell/temporal arteritis, Takayasu arteritis); MEDIUM-VESSEL (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease); SMALL-VESSEL, which splits into ANCA-associated (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and immune-complex (IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schonlein, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis). The chapter also separates PRIMARY syndromes from SECONDARY vasculitis (associated with probable etiology e.g. drug-induced, hepatitis-B/C-related, cancer-associated; or with systemic disease e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid vasculitis), and single-organ vasculitis (cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis, isolated aortitis) (Harrison 22e p.2936). For management stratification, ANCA-associated vasculitis is divided into SEVERE (life- or organ-threatening; e.g., alveolar haemorrhage, and active glomerulonephritis is severe even with normal renal function) versus NONSEVERE/limited disease - severity depends on both extent and the specific organ involved (e.g., nodular pulmonary disease without respiratory compromise is nonsevere, whereas alveolar haemorrhage is severe) (Harrison 22e p.2941).

Vasovagal / orthostatic syncope — Lying/standing BP ECG (exclude arrhythmia) Exertional or cardiac syncope needs cardiac workup Generalized and partial/partial-complex seizures (with secondary generalization, usually preceded by an aura such as an unpleasant smell, fear, anxiety, or abdominal/visceral sensation). Autonomic seizures (autonomic epilepsy), whose cardiovascular, GI, pulmonary, urogenital, pupillary, and cutaneous manifestations mimic syncopal prodrome; accompanying non-autonomic auras help distinguish them. Hypoglycemia, typically in insulin-treated type 1 or type 2 diabetes (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias; hunger is not a typical syncope prodrome). Cataplexy (abrupt loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter or anger; consciousness is preserved, lasts 30 s to 2 min, no prodrome; occurs in 60-75% of narcolepsy). Vertebrobasilar ischemia and hypoxemia as other causes of transient loss of consciousness. Falls due to vestibular dysfunction, cerebellar disease, extrapyramidal/gait disorders, and falls with head trauma (especially difficult in patients with dementia and repeated falls). Psychogenic apparent loss of consciousness from psychiatric disorders (generalized anxiety, panic disorder, major depression, somatization), suggested by frequent fainting without prodrome and rare injury despite numerous falls, with no significant hemodynamic change. 12-lead ECG when arrhythmia or underlying cardiac disease is suspected; look for brady-/tachyarrhythmias, AV block, acute or old myocardial ischemia/infarction, long QT, and bundle branch block. Supine and standing (3 min) blood pressure and heart rate to detect orthostatic hypotension. Tilt-table testing (autonomic testing) to distinguish autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension from the hypotensive-bradycardic response of neurally mediated syncope, and to identify immediate or delayed orthostatic hypotension; may also reproduce psychogenic syncope when symptoms occur without hemodynamic change. Autonomic function testing in specialized centers: heart rate variability to deep breathing and Valsalva (parasympathetic), thermoregulatory sweat test and quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (sympathetic cholinergic), and BP response to Valsalva/tilt (sympathetic adrenergic). Carotid sinus massage (under continuous ECG and BP monitoring) for suspected carotid sinus syncope and in patients >40 years with recurrent unexplained syncope; avoid with carotid bruits, plaque, or stenosis. Inpatient ECG monitoring for high arrhythmia risk; ambulatory Holter monitoring for frequent (near-daily) episodes; external or implantable loop recorders for less frequent episodes (monitor for at least twice the interspell interval). Echocardiography for patients with cardiac history or abnormal exam/ECG (may reveal aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, cardiac tumors, aortic dissection, pericardial tamponade; also stratifies sudden-death risk by ejection fraction). Treadmill exercise testing with ECG and BP monitoring for syncope during or shortly after exercise. Invasive electrophysiologic studies (low sensitivity/specificity, rarely used) only when pretest probability is high in structural heart disease with ECG abnormalities. Baseline blood tests are rarely helpful and should be reserved for suspected specific disorders (e.g., myocardial infarction, anemia, secondary autonomic failure); psychiatric screening for recurrent unexplained syncope. Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness from acute global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, brief duration, and spontaneous complete recovery; reorientation is almost immediate after a syncopal event. Causes fall into three categories: neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac syncope; clinical features, mechanisms, and prognosis differ markedly among them. Neurally mediated syncope is the most common cause overall in population-based studies and accounts for the vast majority of syncope in the young (peak incidence ~age 15); incidence is higher in women, and a first-degree family history is common in young patients. Vasovagal syncope (the common faint) is provoked by intense emotion, pain, the sight of blood, venipuncture, and/or orthostatic stress; situational reflex syncopes have specific localized triggers (cough, micturition, swallow, defecation, carotid sinus pressure). Premonitory (prodromal) features of autonomic activation in neurally mediated syncope include diaphoresis, pallor, palpitations, nausea, lightheadedness, hyperventilation, and yawning. A functioning autonomic nervous system is required to develop neurally mediated syncope, in contrast to syncope from autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension). Neurally mediated syncope can be subdivided by efferent pathway: vasodepressor (sympathetic vasoconstrictor failure), cardioinhibitory (bradycardia/asystole from vagal outflow), or mixed. Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing or head-up tilt; supine and standing BP/HR at 3 min should be measured in every initial evaluation. Initial clinical assessment plus ECG identifies a cause in about 50% of patients and stratifies cardiac mortality risk. A clinically meaningful syncope usually corresponds to a fall in systolic BP to roughly 50 mmHg or lower; cessation of cerebral blood flow for 6-8 s produces loss of consciousness. Syncope during exertion, or while seated or supine. Sudden onset of palpitations immediately followed by syncope, or palpitations at the time of syncope. Chest pain suggesting coronary ischemia, or features of congestive heart failure. Moderate or severe valvular or structural cardiac disease, or known severe coronary artery disease. ECG features: ischemia, history of ventricular arrhythmias, prolonged QT (>500 ms), repetitive SA block or sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, preexcitation, or a Brugada pattern. Family history of sudden death. New chest discomfort, abdominal pain, shortness of breath, or headache associated with the episode. Exam: unexplained systolic BP <90 mmHg, signs of GI hemorrhage, persistent bradycardia <40 beats/min, or an undiagnosed systolic murmur. Convulsive syncope mimics seizure: myoclonic and other movements occur in up to ~90% of syncopal episodes, but syncope-related jerks are typically arrhythmic, multifocal/generalized, and brief (<30 s), with mild flexor/extensor posturing; EEG seizure discharges are absent during syncope. Distinguishing features from seizure: seizure loss of consciousness usually lasts >5 min with prolonged postictal drowsiness/disorientation, whereas reorientation after syncope is almost immediate; muscle aches are longer and more severe after seizures; seizures are rarely provoked by emotion or pain. Urinary incontinence can occur in both syncope and seizure and does not distinguish them; fecal incontinence is very rare in syncope and postictal confusion is rare after syncope. During neurally mediated syncope the eyes typically remain open and deviate upward with dilated pupils, and grunting/moaning/stertorous breathing may occur, which can be mistaken for a seizure. Orthostatic hypotension syncope is usually preceded by warning symptoms but may occur suddenly, mimicking a seizure or cardiac cause. Supine hypertension is common (>50%) in autonomic-failure orthostatic hypotension; treating one condition can unmask or worsen the other. Initial orthostatic hypotension (BP fall within 15 s, resolving by 45 s) and delayed orthostatic hypotension (beyond 3 min) can be missed by a single 3-min standing measurement; initial orthostatic hypotension does not represent autonomic failure. Standing pools 500-1000 mL of blood in the lower extremities, buttocks, and splanchnic circulation, reducing venous return, ventricular filling, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Normally baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch trigger a compensatory reflex that raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal activity, increasing peripheral resistance, venous return, and cardiac output. In neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope this reflex transiently fails: there is a paroxysmal shift in autonomic efferent activity with increased parasympathetic outflow plus sympathoinhibition, producing bradycardia, vasodilation/loss of vasoconstrictor tone (vasodepressor response), and reduced cardiac output. The resulting fall in systemic blood pressure drops cerebral blood flow below the limits of autoregulation, causing transient global cerebral hypoperfusion and loss of consciousness. Multiple afferent triggers (orthostatic stress, carotid sinus, gastrointestinal tract, bladder) converge on the central autonomic network in the medulla. Hyperventilation-induced hypocarbia (cerebral vasoconstriction) and raised intrathoracic pressure (impaired venous return) contribute to many situational reflex syncopes. By contrast, orthostatic hypotension reflects chronic impairment of these homeostatic reflexes (autonomic failure), and cardiac syncope results from arrhythmias or structural disease reducing cardiac output. Syncope of noncardiac and unexplained origin in younger individuals carries an excellent prognosis with unaffected life expectancy. In contrast, cardiac syncope (structural heart disease or primary arrhythmia) is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death and overall mortality, and mortality is also increased with orthostatic hypotension related to age and comorbidities. Hospitalization and mortality risk are higher in older adults. Harrison categorizes syncope by mechanism rather than a graded severity score: (1) neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, (2) orthostatic hypotension, and (3) cardiac syncope. For risk stratification, Table 23-1 lists high-risk features indicating hospitalization or intensive evaluation (e.g., ischemic chest pain, heart failure, significant valvular/structural disease, ECG ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia history, QT >500 ms, SA block/sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, family history of sudden death, preexcitation, Brugada pattern, palpitations at syncope, syncope at rest or during exercise). Neurally mediated efferent subtypes are vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory, and mixed.

Micro-aspiration of contaminated oropharyngeal and gastric secretions pooling above the cuff delivers pathogens to the lower airways. Ventricular Septal Defect — VSD, ventricular septal defects Atrioventricular septal defect Patent ductus arteriosus Atrial septal defect Tetralogy of Fallot with a dominant VSD murmur Innocent (functional) murmur Aortic or pulmonary stenosis Echocardiography to localise the defect and quantify shunt and chamber size Chest radiograph for cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora in large shunts Electrocardiogram for left or biventricular hypertrophy Assessment of growth and feeding as markers of shunt significance Cardiac catheterisation to measure pulmonary vascular resistance when pulmonary hypertension is suspected The most common congenital heart malformation, an opening in the interventricular septum that permits shunting between the ventricles; most are membranous or muscular in location. The direction and size of the shunt depend on the defect size and the relative resistances of the pulmonary and systemic circulations, so many defects become clinically apparent only as pulmonary resistance falls in the first weeks of life. Small defects produce a loud, often harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border but little haemodynamic burden, and many close spontaneously. Large defects cause a significant left-to-right shunt with excessive pulmonary blood flow, leading to heart failure signs such as tachypnoea, poor feeding, sweating, and failure to thrive in infancy. A large shunt may generate a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex from increased flow across the mitral valve. Untreated large defects risk progressive pulmonary vascular disease that can eventually reverse the shunt (Eisenmenger physiology), a late and largely irreversible complication. Echocardiography defines the defect location and size, estimates shunt magnitude, and assesses chamber enlargement and pulmonary pressures. Management of a haemodynamically significant defect focuses on treating heart failure and supporting growth, with surgical or catheter closure for defects that do not shrink or that cause failure or pulmonary hypertension. Many small muscular and membranous defects close on their own during early childhood. Signs of congestive heart failure in infancy: tachypnoea, feeding difficulty, sweating, and failure to thrive Development of pulmonary hypertension or a shrinking left-to-right shunt suggesting rising pulmonary resistance New cyanosis or a diminishing murmur indicating shunt reversal (Eisenmenger physiology) Poor weight gain despite medical therapy Signs of infective endocarditis in a child with a known defect Assuming a loud murmur means a large, dangerous defect when small defects are often the loudest Missing a large defect in the newborn period before pulmonary resistance falls and the murmur becomes apparent Overlooking progression to pulmonary vascular disease by delaying closure of a significant shunt Attributing poor growth to feeding problems rather than an underlying significant shunt Failing to recognise shunt reversal when cyanosis appears in a previously acyanotic child A communication in the ventricular septum allows blood to shunt according to the pressure and resistance gradient between the ventricles. After birth, as pulmonary vascular resistance declines, left-to-right shunting increases, raising pulmonary blood flow and volume-loading the left atrium and left ventricle. A large, sustained shunt increases pulmonary artery pressure and flow, and over time medial hypertrophy and intimal changes in the pulmonary vasculature raise resistance irreversibly; when pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic, the shunt reverses and produces cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome). Small defects have an excellent outlook and often close spontaneously. Large defects, if repaired before irreversible pulmonary vascular disease develops, generally have a good outcome; delayed closure risks fixed pulmonary hypertension and a markedly worse prognosis.

recurrent episodes MEDICAL EMERGENCY: pulseless VT or degeneration into ventricular fibrillation is cardiac arrest requiring immediate defibrillation and resuscitation Haemodynamically unstable sustained VT with hypotension, ischaemia, or reduced consciousness requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion Polymorphic VT with a prolonged QT (torsades) requiring correction of the QT and specific measures Incessant or recurrent VT (electrical storm) requiring intensive management Treating a wide-complex tachycardia as SVT with aberrancy when it is VT, potentially with hazardous AV nodal blocking drugs Delaying cardioversion in an unstable patient in favour of drug therapy Missing a reversible cause such as ischaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, or QT-prolonging drugs Overlooking the need for defibrillator evaluation in secondary prevention after sustained VT with structural disease Most sustained monomorphic VT is due to reentry around regions of myocardial scar, typically after prior infarction, where slow conduction through surviving fibres embedded in fibrosis creates a stable circuit. Polymorphic VT commonly arises from acute ischaemia producing heterogeneous repolarisation, or from delayed repolarisation in long QT syndromes, generating triggered activity that degenerates into torsades de pointes. Abnormal automaticity and triggered activity from afterdepolarisations also contribute, particularly with electrolyte disturbance, drug effects, or catecholamine excess. Sustained rapid ventricular rates impair filling and cardiac output and can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Prognosis is strongly tied to the underlying substrate and left ventricular function; VT in structurally normal hearts is often benign, whereas sustained VT with impaired ventricular function or scar carries a high risk of sudden death that is mitigated by defibrillator therapy and substrate-targeted treatment.

Vertebral osteomyelitis — spinal osteomyelitis, spondylodiscitis, discitis-osteomyelitis, pyogenic spondylitis Mechanical or degenerative back pain Vertebral compression fracture Metastatic or primary bone tumour Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) Modic degenerative end-plate changes Malignant infiltration of the vertebral body Osteoporotic compression fracture Erosive degenerative disc disease Inflammatory spondyloarthropathy MRI of the spine with contrast as the primary imaging test Blood cultures and inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP) which are useful for diagnosis and monitoring Image-guided or open biopsy for microbiological and, where relevant, histological diagnosis Echocardiography to exclude endocarditis when S. aureus or other typical organisms are isolated Investigations for tuberculosis or brucellosis when the clinical picture is subacute or endemic Usually arises from haematogenous seeding of the vertebral body, with the lumbar spine most commonly affected New or worsening back pain, often unremitting and worse at night, with or without fever should prompt consideration, especially with a recent bacteraemia Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent pathogen; consider Gram-negatives with urinary sources and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pott's disease) in endemic or chronic presentations Risk factors include diabetes, injecting drug use, indwelling vascular catheters, recent bacteraemia, endocarditis, and immunosuppression MRI with contrast is the imaging investigation of choice for early and accurate diagnosis and for detecting epidural extension Obtaining a microbiological diagnosis, by blood cultures or image-guided biopsy, before starting antibiotics is important unless the patient is septic Management principles are prolonged targeted antibiotic therapy guided by culture, with surgery reserved for neurological compromise, instability, or failure of medical treatment Screen for infective endocarditis and other seeding foci when S. aureus bacteraemia is present New neurological deficit, radicular weakness, or bladder or bowel dysfunction suggesting epidural abscess with cord or cauda equina compression requiring emergency imaging and surgery Signs of spinal instability or progressive vertebral collapse Sepsis or endocarditis complicating the infection Rapidly progressive, unremitting, or nocturnal back pain in an at-risk patient Starting antibiotics before securing a microbiological diagnosis in a stable patient, obscuring the causative organism Attributing persistent back pain to mechanical causes and delaying MRI Missing an associated epidural abscess or endocarditis Treating for too short a duration and precipitating relapse Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis typically begins when bacteria lodge in the vascular end-plate region of a vertebral body via haematogenous spread from a distant focus. Infection then spreads across the relatively avascular intervertebral disc to involve the adjacent vertebra, producing the characteristic pattern of spondylodiscitis. Progressive infection can form paravertebral or epidural abscesses, erode bone leading to vertebral collapse and deformity, and compress neural structures. Less commonly infection reaches the spine by contiguous spread or direct inoculation from surgery or trauma. With early diagnosis and appropriate prolonged antibiotics most patients recover, but delayed treatment or epidural abscess with cord compression can leave permanent neurological deficits; relapse is more likely with inadequate therapy duration or unaddressed source.

emergency requiring prompt drainage and antibiotics Progressive renal scarring or reduced differential renal function New or worsening hypertension or proteinuria indicating reflux nephropathy High-grade reflux with breakthrough infections despite prophylaxis Bilateral high-grade reflux with impaired renal function Failing to investigate recurrent febrile UTIs in a child for underlying reflux Overlooking bladder and bowel dysfunction, which perpetuates reflux and infection Missing secondary reflux from obstruction such as posterior urethral valves Neglecting long-term monitoring of blood pressure and renal function in children with scarring Delaying treatment of a febrile infection in an obstructed, refluxing system Vesicoureteric reflux occurs when the valve-like mechanism of the vesicoureteric junction fails, allowing urine to reflux from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis. Normally an adequate length of submucosal ureter within the bladder wall is compressed during bladder filling and voiding, preventing reflux; in primary VUR this tunnel is congenitally short or laterally placed. Secondary VUR develops when high intravesical pressures from bladder outlet obstruction or neurogenic/dysfunctional voiding overcome the junction. Reflux of infected urine and elevated pressures transmitted to the kidney cause pyelonephritis and scarring (reflux nephropathy), which underlies later hypertension and renal impairment. Many children with low-grade primary reflux resolve spontaneously as they grow and do well with infection prevention; high-grade reflux, recurrent pyelonephritis, and established scarring carry a greater risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease, making surveillance important.

or neck pain raising concern for vertebral artery dissection Sudden hearing loss accompanying vertigo, which may indicate a vascular or other serious cause Misdiagnosing a cerebellar stroke as vestibular neuritis by relying on imaging that can be falsely reassuring early Prescribing prolonged vestibular suppressants, which impair central compensation Assuming any acute vertigo is peripheral without performing the HINTS examination Overlooking associated hearing loss that changes the differential Delaying vestibular rehabilitation and prolonging disability Vestibular neuritis is attributed to inflammation of the vestibular nerve, possibly from reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus in the vestibular ganglion, causing acute unilateral loss of peripheral vestibular input. The superior vestibular division is most often affected. The sudden asymmetry between the two vestibular systems generates a strong sense of rotational vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus. Over subsequent days to weeks, central adaptive mechanisms recalibrate the vestibular imbalance (central compensation), which underlies clinical recovery even if peripheral function does not fully return. Most patients recover over days to weeks as central compensation develops, though some have persistent unsteadiness or motion sensitivity; early vestibular rehabilitation improves recovery and reduces chronic dizziness.

and features of myelodysplasia Full blood count and blood film demonstrating macrocytic anaemia and evolving cytopenias Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, ferritin) which are typically markedly elevated Skin or cartilage biopsy showing neutrophilic infiltration or chondritis Cross-sectional imaging and vascular studies to assess thromboembolism and organ involvement Almost exclusively affects men over 50 years, reflecting an acquired somatic mutation on the X chromosome Presents as treatment-refractory systemic inflammation with recurrent fevers, neutrophilic dermatosis, chondritis of the ears or nose, and inflammatory ocular disease Frequently overlaps clinically with relapsing polychondritis, Sweet syndrome, polyarteritis nodosa, or giant cell arteritis, but responds poorly to cytoplasmic vacuoles are seen in myeloid and erythroid precursors on bone marrow aspirate Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating a somatic UBA1 mutation (typically affecting methionine-41) in haematopoietic cells Venous and arterial thromboembolism is common and adds substantially to morbidity Inflammation is often corticosteroid-dependent, with high relapse rates on tapering Progressive cytopenias or transfusion dependence signalling evolution to myelodysplastic syndrome Refractory systemic inflammation despite escalating immunosuppression Venous or arterial thromboembolic events Weight loss and constitutional decline suggesting an underlying haematological malignancy Attributing refractory relapsing polychondritis or Sweet syndrome in an older man to the classic diagnosis alone and missing the underlying UBA1 clone Overlooking macrocytosis and early cytopenias as clues to a marrow-based process Failing to send UBA1 sequencing because the phenotype mimics a well-known rheumatological disease Under-recognising the high thrombotic risk and not considering prophylaxis Escalating immunosuppression without haematology involvement despite marrow dysplasia VEXAS syndrome arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the UBA1 gene within haematopoietic stem cells. UBA1 encodes the principal E1 enzyme that initiates cellular ubiquitylation. The mutation, usually at the p.Met41 site, impairs production of the cytoplasmic UBA1 isoform, disrupting ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover and triggering unchecked activation of innate immune and inflammatory pathways. The affected clone expands within the myeloid lineage, producing the diagnostic cytoplasmic vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursors and driving both the systemic autoinflammatory phenotype and a predisposition to myelodysplasia. VEXAS syndrome is a serious, progressive disorder with substantial mortality driven by uncontrolled inflammation, thromboembolism, and haematological progression to myelodysplasia. Many patients remain corticosteroid-dependent; allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only potentially curative option, while hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine and JAK inhibition are used to control disease.

and liver for localisation and staging Somatostatin-receptor functional imaging for occult or metastatic disease Screening for other endocrine tumours where MEN1 is suspected A rare pancreatic
