to preserve function and reduce the extent of surgery Precursor vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and lichen sclerosus warrant surveillance because of their malignant potential A persistent vulvar lump, ulcer, or plaque that does not resolve with treatment Chronic vulvar itching or bleeding in an older woman with lichen sclerosus Palpable or fixed inguinal lymph nodes Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating vulvar lesion Repeatedly treating a persistent vulvar lesion as dermatitis or thrush without biopsy Failing to assess and manage inguinal lymph nodes appropriately Neglecting surveillance of lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia Underestimating the psychosexual and functional impact when planning surgery Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma develops from the vulvar epithelium by two principal mechanisms. In younger women, persistent high-risk human papillomavirus infection drives usual-type vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia that can progress to invasive cancer. In older women, chronic dermatological conditions such as lichen sclerosus produce differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and HPV-independent carcinoma. Invasive tumour infiltrates local structures and spreads first to superficial and deep inguinofemoral nodes and subsequently to pelvic nodes, with distant metastasis occurring late. Prognosis is largely determined by inguinofemoral nodal status and tumour stage; node-negative localised disease has good survival after surgery, whereas nodal involvement or advanced local spread substantially reduces outcomes.

Vulvovaginal Candidiasis — vaginal thrush, candidal vaginitis, yeast infection, monilial vaginitis Bacterial vaginosis Trichomonas vaginalis infection Contact or irritant vulvar dermatitis Lichen sclerosus or lichen planus Genital herpes Physiological discharge Vaginal pH measurement, typically normal in candidiasis Saline and potassium hydroxide wet-mount microscopy for yeasts and pseudohyphae Fungal culture in recurrent, severe, or treatment-resistant cases to speciate Blood glucose or HbA1c testing where recurrent infection suggests diabetes Consideration of HIV or immunosuppression assessment in refractory disease Most infections are caused by Candida albicans, a commensal yeast that becomes symptomatic when the vaginal environment or host defences change Typical features are intense vulval itching, soreness, and a thick, white, non-malodorous discharge often likened to cottage cheese, with vulval erythema and sometimes fissuring The vaginal pH usually remains normal and acidic, which helps distinguish it from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis Predisposing factors include recent antibiotic use, pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression, and high oestrogen states Diagnosis is clinical, supported by microscopy showing budding yeasts and pseudohyphae, and culture is useful in recurrent or treatment-resistant cases to identify non-albicans species Uncomplicated disease responds well to topical or oral antifungal therapy, whereas recurrent disease often needs a longer induction and maintenance approach Recurrent or resistant infection should prompt evaluation for diabetes, immunosuppression, and non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata, which are less responsive to standard azoles It is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, and routine treatment of asymptomatic male partners is not indicated Recurrent or refractory infection suggesting undiagnosed diabetes or immunosuppression Severe vulval swelling, fissuring, or ulceration prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Systemic candidiasis in significantly immunocompromised patients Failure to respond to standard azole therapy suggesting a non-albicans species Coexisting symptoms pointing to another sexually transmitted infection Diagnosing thrush on symptoms alone and missing bacterial vaginosis or dermatoses Repeatedly treating recurrent infection without investigating for diabetes or immunosuppression Assuming all cases are Candida albicans and overlooking azole-resistant species Unnecessarily treating asymptomatic partners Attributing chronic vulval symptoms to candidiasis when a dermatological condition is responsible Candida species colonise the vagina asymptomatically in many women, kept in check by the resident lactobacillus-dominant flora and local immunity. Disturbance of this balance, for example by antibiotics, or increased glycogen availability from high oestrogen states and hyperglycaemia, allows the yeast to proliferate and transform into an invasive hyphal form. Adherence to and penetration of the vaginal epithelium triggers a brisk inflammatory response, producing the pruritus, erythema, and discharge characteristic of symptomatic infection. Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis responds rapidly to antifungal treatment with an excellent outlook. A minority of women develop recurrent disease that is troublesome and requires prolonged maintenance therapy, and outcomes in these cases improve when underlying predisposing factors and non-albicans species are identified and addressed.

Waardenburg syndrome — PAX3, MITF, SOX10, auditory-pigmentary syndrome, WS Other syndromic sensorineural hearing loss such as Pendred or branchio-oto-renal syndrome Piebaldism (KIT mutation) with depigmentation but without hearing loss Vitiligo and other acquired pigmentary disorders Tietz syndrome with generalised hypopigmentation and deafness Isolated congenital sensorineural hearing loss Hirschsprung disease from non-syndromic causes in type 4 presentations Audiometry with age-appropriate testing to characterise hearing loss Detailed dermatological and ophthalmic examination for pigmentary features and iris colour Measurement of inner canthal and interpupillary distances to assess dystopia canthorum Assessment for constipation or bowel obstruction and Hirschsprung disease in suspected type 4 Molecular genetic testing (PAX3, MITF, SOX10 and related genes) to confirm subtype An auditory-pigmentary syndrome combining sensorineural hearing loss with pigmentary anomalies of the eyes, hair and skin Characteristic features include heterochromia or brilliant blue irides, a white forelock, patchy skin depigmentation, and early greying Dystopia canthorum (lateral displacement of the inner canthi) distinguishes type 1 from type 2, in which it is absent Most commonly autosomal dominant with variable expressivity; PAX3 underlies types 1 and 3, and MITF and SOX10 are associated with type 2 Type 3 (Klein-Waardenburg) adds musculoskeletal limb abnormalities, and type 4 (Waardenburg-Shah) is associated with Hirschsprung disease via SOX10, EDN3 or EDNRB Hearing loss is congenital, non-progressive and may be unilateral or bilateral, reflecting absence of melanocytes in the stria vascularis Family examination frequently reveals affected relatives with subtle pigmentary signs Neonatal bowel obstruction or severe constipation suggesting associated Hirschsprung disease Bilateral profound hearing loss affecting speech development in an infant Progressive rather than static hearing loss, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis Family history of combined pigmentary and hearing anomalies indicating dominant inheritance Overlooking subtle pigmentary signs when hearing loss is the presenting problem Confusing dystopia canthorum with true hypertelorism and misclassifying the subtype Assuming normal hearing in one ear excludes the syndrome, as loss may be unilateral Failing to consider Hirschsprung disease in a neonate with pigmentary features Waardenburg syndrome arises from mutations affecting the development, migration or survival of neural-crest-derived melanocytes. Melanocytes contribute pigment to the skin, hair and iris and are also essential within the stria vascularis of the cochlea for maintaining the endolymphatic environment needed for normal hearing. Genes such as PAX3, MITF and SOX10 encode transcription factors within this developmental pathway, so their disruption produces both the pigmentary abnormalities and the sensorineural hearing loss. In type 4 the same neural-crest defect also affects enteric ganglion cells, causing aganglionic megacolon (Hirschsprung disease). Hearing loss is congenital and generally non-progressive, and prognosis is favourable with hearing aids or cochlear implantation and early language support; the pigmentary features are cosmetic, though associated Hirschsprung disease in type 4 requires surgical management.

at-risk pregnancies The most severe congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy, defined by the triad of a brain malformation (cobblestone lissencephaly), eye anomalies, and congenital muscular dystrophy Cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly results from over-migration of neurons beyond the pial surface, producing a bumpy, disorganised cortex distinct from classic lissencephaly Neuroimaging typically shows cobblestone cortex, hydrocephalus, a kinked or hypoplastic brainstem (the Z-shaped brainstem), and cerebellar hypoplasia or cysts Ocular malformations are prominent and may include microphthalmia, cataract, retinal dysplasia or detachment, persistent foetal vasculature, and anterior chamber anomalies The congenital muscular dystrophy causes marked hypotonia and weakness from birth with a raised serum creatine kinase It is autosomal recessive, caused by variants in genes for O-glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan such as POMT1, POMT2, and FKTN, disrupting the dystroglycan-extracellular matrix link Diagnosis integrates the characteristic MRI, ophthalmological findings, raised creatine kinase, and molecular testing of dystroglycanopathy genes Progressive hydrocephalus requiring neurosurgical assessment Severe respiratory and feeding difficulty from profound muscle weakness Refractory seizures Rapidly progressive visual loss from retinal detachment Confusing cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly with classic (type I) lissencephaly, which has different genetics and no primary muscle or eye disease Overlooking the raised creatine kinase and muscle involvement when focused on the brain malformation Missing treatable ocular complications such as retinal detachment Failing to place the child on the dystroglycanopathy spectrum, affecting prognosis and counselling Walker-Warburg syndrome is a dystroglycanopathy caused by biallelic variants in genes required for O-linked glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan. Defective glycosylation prevents alpha-dystroglycan from binding extracellular matrix ligands such as laminin, disrupting the integrity of basement membranes. In the developing brain, breaches of the pial-glial limiting membrane allow neurons to over-migrate beyond the cortex, producing cobblestone lissencephaly, brainstem and cerebellar malformation, and hydrocephalus. The same defect impairs the muscle basement membrane, causing congenital muscular dystrophy, and disrupts ocular development, causing the retinal and anterior segment anomalies. Walker-Warburg syndrome carries the worst prognosis of the dystroglycanopathies, with most affected children dying within the first years of life from neurological, respiratory, and feeding complications. Care is largely supportive alongside genetic counselling.

Airway or feeding compromise in infancy from hypotonia Neurological deterioration requiring imaging Mislabelling Weaver as Sotos syndrome given shared overgrowth, delaying correct EZH2 testing Assuming a benign course and overlooking the reported association with neoplasia Interpreting markedly advanced bone age as a puberty disorder rather than a syndromic feature Missing camptodactyly and joint contractures that need orthopaedic and physiotherapy input Weaver syndrome is caused by germline variants in EZH2, the catalytic subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 2, which trimethylates histone H3 lysine 27 to silence target genes controlling growth and differentiation. Disruption of EZH2 activity dysregulates these developmental programmes, producing accelerated skeletal maturation, generalised overgrowth, and the characteristic craniofacial and limb features. Because EZH2 and NSD1 act on overlapping chromatin pathways, Weaver and Sotos syndromes share overgrowth but differ in facial gestalt and specific complications. Growth acceleration tends to slow after childhood and adult height is often at the upper end of normal, while developmental outcome is variable but frequently better than in Sotos syndrome. The reported tumour risk is modest, and overall life expectancy is generally good.

biallelic WRN variants Slit-lamp ophthalmological assessment for premature bilateral cataract Fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile to detect diabetes and dyslipidaemia Bone densitometry for is absent and short stature becomes apparent Characteristic features emerge in the twenties to thirties: premature greying and hair loss, scleroderma-like tight skin, a beaked nose and a high-pitched There is a markedly raised risk of malignancy, with an unusual predominance of sarcomas (soft-tissue and osteosarcoma) alongside melanoma and thyroid cancer Chronic, poorly healing skin ulcers around the ankles and over the Achilles tendon are typical and difficult to manage Diagnosis rests on the combination of cardinal clinical features supported by molecular confirmation of biallelic WRN variants New or enlarging soft-tissue or bony mass suggesting sarcoma Non-healing lower-limb ulcer with signs of secondary infection or malignant transformation Symptoms of premature myocardial infarction or stroke Rapid visual deterioration from advancing cataract Attributing the scleroderma-like skin changes to systemic sclerosis and missing the progeroid diagnosis Overlooking the characteristically young age of cataract onset Failing to maintain vigilant malignancy surveillance, particularly for sarcomas Underestimating premature cardiovascular and diabetic complications in a relatively young patient Werner syndrome arises from biallelic loss-of-function variants in WRN, which encodes a member of the RecQ family of DNA helicases with additional exonuclease activity. The protein participates in DNA replication, repair, recombination and telomere maintenance. Its loss produces genomic instability, accelerated telomere attrition and premature cellular senescence, which underlie the segmental (partial) acceleration of ageing phenotypes and the predisposition to cancer seen in affected individuals. Life expectancy is shortened, with most affected individuals dying in the fifth to sixth decade, predominantly from malignancy or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Careful metabolic control, cardiovascular risk reduction and cancer surveillance may improve outcomes.

Wernicke encephalopathy — Clinical triad (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) Give IV thiamine BEFORE glucose Reversible — treat empirically with thiamine, do not delay Supranuclear gaze disorder mimicking combined abducens and oculomotor nerve palsy (Wernicke can itself cause this pattern) Other metabolic encephalopathies (hepatic, hypercarbic, hyper-/hyponatremic, hyper-/hypoglycemic) Sepsis-associated encephalopathy Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) Marchiafava-Bignami disease (corpus callosum degeneration in chronic alcoholism) Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration Encephalitis (including herpes simplex encephalitis as a cause of an amnestic state) Whipple's disease (cause of supranuclear gaze palsy) MRI may show changes including abnormal enhancement of the mammillary bodies (coronal T1 postcontrast), typical of acute Wernicke Erythrocyte transketolase activity assay measured before and after adding thiamine pyrophosphate; >25% stimulation (activity coefficient >=1.25) is abnormal Serum/blood thiamine or its phosphorylated esters by high-performance liquid chromatography Serum magnesium (required cofactor for thiamine activation) Autoimmune limbic encephalitis (e.g., AMPAR, LGI1 antibodies) causing amnesia Paraneoplastic encephalitis (e.g., Ma antibodies) Thalamic, medial temporal, or posterior corpus callosum tumor causing amnesia Anterior/posterior cerebral artery territory infarction causing amnesia Stroke (infarct/hemorrhage), multiple sclerosis, vasculitis, or tumor causing supranuclear gaze palsy The classic triad (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, global confusion) is present in only about one-third of acute cases, so a complete triad should not be required to make the diagnosis. Most patients are profoundly disoriented, apathetic/indifferent, and inattentive rather than agitated; agitated delirium, when present, is usually from coexisting alcohol withdrawal. Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke is not confined to alcohol use; non-alcoholic risk groups include hyperemesis, starvation/malnutrition, renal dialysis, cancer, HIV/AIDS, gastric/bariatric surgery, and chronic diuretic therapy (increased urinary thiamine loss). Certain drugs (e.g., metformin, verapamil) can inhibit intestinal thiamine transporters (ThTR-2) and add to deficiency risk. Ocular signs include horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, bilateral lateral rectus (abducens) palsy, conjugate gaze palsies, and rarely ptosis; pupils are usually spared but may become miotic in advanced disease. Gait ataxia is multifactorial, arising from a combination of peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar involvement, and vestibular paresis. Treat on clinical suspicion as a medical emergency: it is common, preventable, and reversible if thiamine is given early. Korsakoff amnestic state may only become apparent as the acute confusion recedes, characterized by recent-memory/learning impairment, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing. The amnestic deficit correlates with lesions of the dorsomedial (dorsal medial) thalamic nuclei. Untreated disease can progress to stupor, coma, and death Giving glucose (parenteral dextrose) before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke in a previously unaffected at-risk patient or rapidly worsen an early form New amnestic state emerging as confusion clears signals evolution to Korsakoff syndrome Waiting for the full classic triad before treating, when only about one-third of patients show all three features. Attributing the quiet, indifferent, inattentive confusional state to depression, sedation, or simple intoxication and missing the diagnosis. Assuming Wernicke occurs only in alcoholics and overlooking it in hyperemesis, malnutrition, dialysis, bariatric surgery, cancer, or HIV patients. Administering glucose-containing fluids before thiamine in an at-risk patient, which can trigger or worsen Wernicke. Thiamine deficiency being overlooked in the setting of head injury (and possibly contributing to motor vehicle accidents). Wernicke disease results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Thiamine is a cofactor for several enzymes including transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency causes a diffuse fall in cerebral glucose utilization and mitochondrial damage; impaired alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase leads to glutamate accumulation, which together with the energy deficit may produce excitotoxic neuronal injury. Lesions are periventricular, surrounding the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle, with predilection for midline structures (dorsomedial thalamus, mammillary bodies, midline cerebellum, periaqueductal gray, and trochlear/abducens nuclei). Acute cases may show petechial hemorrhages; chronic cases show mammillary body atrophy. Outcome depends on early thiamine administration. Ocular palsies improve within hours of thiamine; horizontal nystagmus may persist. Ataxia improves more slowly than ocular signs, and roughly half of patients recover incompletely, left with a slow, wide-based, shuffling gait and inability to tandem walk. Apathy, drowsiness, and confusion resolve gradually. Korsakoff psychosis is frequently persistent, with permanent gaps in memory, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing; prolonged untreated deficiency can cause an irreversible profound amnestic syndrome or death. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is underdiagnosed despite a typical history and picture.

West Nile virus infection — West Nile fever, WNV, West Nile neuroinvasive disease Other arboviral encephalitides (Japanese encephalitis, St Louis encephalitis) Herpes simplex encephalitis Enteroviral meningitis or encephalitis Bacterial meningitis Guillain-Barre syndrome (for the flaccid paralysis presentation) Dengue or other acute febrile arboviral illness Japanese encephalitis Herpes simplex encephalitis Enteroviral CNS infection Poliomyelitis and other causes of acute flaccid paralysis CSF examination showing a lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein in neuroinvasive disease WNV-specific IgM in serum and CSF (mainstay of diagnosis), with paired serology for confirmation Nucleic acid testing in early infection or in immunocompromised or transfusion/transplant-associated settings MRI of the brain and spinal cord to evaluate encephalitis and anterior horn involvement Testing to exclude treatable causes such as herpes simplex and bacterial meningitis A mosquito-borne flavivirus maintained in a bird reservoir with Culex mosquitoes as the main vector; humans are incidental dead-end hosts The large majority of infections are asymptomatic, and most symptomatic cases present as a self-limiting febrile illness (West Nile fever) with headache, myalgia, and sometimes a transient rash A small proportion develop neuroinvasive disease: meningitis, encephalitis, or an acute flaccid paralysis resembling poliomyelitis Advancing age and immunosuppression are the strongest risk factors for severe neuroinvasive disease Acute flaccid paralysis from anterior horn cell involvement is an important clue that distinguishes WNV from many other causes of encephalitis Transmission can also occur through blood transfusion and organ transplantation, so donor screening is relevant in endemic areas Management is supportive; there is no specific licensed antiviral therapy, and prevention centres on mosquito control and personal protection Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal neurological signs indicating encephalitis Acute flaccid limb weakness suggesting anterior horn cell involvement Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem dysfunction Severe disease in an elderly or immunocompromised patient with rapid deterioration Assuming a benign viral illness and missing early neuroinvasive features in an older patient Failing to distinguish WNV flaccid paralysis from Guillain-Barre syndrome, which has different management Not considering transfusion- or transplant-associated transmission in a recently exposed patient Delaying empirical treatment for herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting WNV confirmation West Nile virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus circulating between birds and Culex mosquitoes. After a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing viraemia. In a minority of hosts it crosses into the central nervous system, where it infects neurons, particularly in the brainstem, deep grey matter, and anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, producing encephalitis and flaccid paralysis. Host factors such as age and immune status strongly influence whether infection stays confined to a febrile illness or becomes neuroinvasive. Uncomplicated West Nile fever resolves fully, but neuroinvasive disease carries substantial morbidity and mortality, and survivors of encephalitis or flaccid paralysis may be left with long-lasting neurological and functional deficits, particularly older patients.

hyperextension followed by flexion (or the reverse) of the cervical spine during rapid acceleration-deceleration. This strains and may partially tear the cervical muscles, ligaments, facet joint capsules, and intervertebral discs, and can injure nerve roots or, in severe cases, cause fracture or cord injury. Peripheral tissue injury combined with central pain sensitisation and psychosocial factors contributes to chronic symptoms in some patients. Most people recover within weeks to a few months, but a substantial minority develop chronic neck pain and disability, more likely with high initial pain, neurological signs, and psychological distress.

Whipple Disease — Tropheryma whipplei infection Seronegative inflammatory arthritis / rheumatoid arthritis (initial arthralgic phase is often confused with rheumatologic disorders; RF and ANA usually negative) (p.1368) Lymphoma (mesenteric/retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy on CT commonly raises this concern) (p.1368) Sarcoidosis or granulomatous vasculitis (noncaseating granulomas from lymphatic/hepatic involvement; ocular disease may also be misdiagnosed as sarcoid) (p.1368) Behcet's disease (in patients with ocular/uveitic disease) (p.1368) Mycobacterial infection (PAS positivity is nonspecific and also occurs with mycobacteria and other microorganisms) (p.1369) Giardia lamblia co-infection, occasionally identified, can cause diagnostic misdirection (p.1368) Other causes of culture-negative endocarditis (T. whipplei causes 2.6-6.3% of culture-negative endocarditis) (p.1368) Postbulbar (more distal) duodenal biopsies with PAS staining for diastase-resistant inclusions in lamina propria macrophages plus PCR for T. whipplei (tissue yield exceeds body-fluid yield) (p.1369) PCR of duodenal biopsy: a cycle threshold of <=30 can help confirm the diagnosis even when PAS staining is negative (p.1369) Immunohistochemistry (greater specificity and sensitivity than PAS, usable on archived fixed tissue) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) as complementary tools (p.1369) Electron microscopy to identify the trilaminar cell wall of T. whipplei (p.1369) CSF examination and PCR for T. whipplei (collect even when asymptomatic); CSF may be normal or show lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis and elevated protein, with low glucose reported (p.1369) Brain MRI (lesions usually T2/FLAIR hyperintense, may enhance with gadolinium; may be normal) (p.1368) Echocardiography for suspected endocarditis (vegetations seen in 50-75%) (p.1368) FDG-PET may show uptake at affected sites and can guide tissue sampling (p.1368, p.1369) Biopsy of normal-appearing skin may detect T. whipplei as a minimally invasive diagnostic route in classic WD (p.1369) Video-capsule endoscopy to identify more distal small-bowel lesions when initial duodenal biopsy is nondiagnostic (p.1368) Urine PCR as a potential noninvasive test and therapeutic-monitoring tool (positive in ~75% of cases pretreatment in one small study); plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing for endocarditis (p.1369, p.1370) Crohn disease (intestinal phase confusion) (p.1368) Celiac disease (intestinal phase confusion; small-bowel biopsy differential) (p.1368, p.2546) Other rheumatologic disorders during the early arthralgic stage (p.1368) Whipple disease is a rare chronic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei; because it is uncommon, mimics many other conditions, and needs nonroutine tests, years typically pass between symptom onset and diagnosis (p.1367). "Classic" Whipple disease presents as some combination of migratory arthralgias/seronegative arthritis, weight loss, chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever, with the duodenum and/or jejunum involved over years (p.1367, p.1368). Migratory oligo- or polyarthralgia (knees, wrists, ankles, MCP joints) typically precedes gastrointestinal symptoms by an average of 6-8 years; joint disease is present in >80% of patients (p.1368, p.2546). CNS disease (detected by CSF PCR for T. whipplei) develops in roughly 50% of patients and many are asymptomatic; manifestations include cognitive decline progressing to dementia, personality/mood change, and hypothalamic involvement, and portend a poor prognosis (p.1368). Oculomasticatory and oculofacial myorhythmia are highly suggestive of Whipple disease; supranuclear gaze palsy (usually vertical) is another neuro-ophthalmologic clue (p.1368). Diagnosis rests on small-bowel (postbulbar duodenal) biopsy showing lamina propria infiltration by foamy macrophages with diastase-resistant PAS-positive inclusions, combined with PCR for T. whipplei; PCR has substantially improved sensitivity and specificity (p.1368, p.1369). It is prudent to collect CSF even without CNS symptoms, because asymptomatic CNS disease is common and the CNS is the most common site of relapse, informing treatment duration (p.1369). Treatment requires prolonged therapy; clinical response is often rapid, but eradication and durable cure are challenged by relapse and host predisposition to reinfection, which can occur years to decades later (p.1369, p.1370). WD should be considered in any chronic multisystemic process, especially the combination of rheumatologic and intestinal disease with weight loss, with or without neurologic and cardiac involvement (p.1368, p.1369). CNS involvement (cognitive decline/dementia, personality change, hypothalamic dysfunction such as polyuria/polydipsia or sleep-cycle disorder, supranuclear gaze palsy, oculomasticatory myorhythmia) portends a poor prognosis with significant mortality risk and neurologic sequelae (p.1368) Endocarditis (often afebrile, Duke criteria rarely met) may be complicated by congestive heart failure (~40%), embolic events, arrhythmias, or mycotic aneurysm (p.1368) Progressive weight loss with chronic diarrhea and malabsorption (p.1367, p.1368) Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) after treatment, with recurrent fever, arthritis, skin lesions, pleuritis, uveitis, and periorbital inflammation; some cases have been fatal (p.1369) Serology is of little value: patients with active infection mount a poor IgM/IgG response, and a positive result most likely reflects prior exposure and clearance (p.1369) A normal macroscopic duodenal appearance is common, and a negative test does not exclude WD; pretest probability must be considered (p.1369) Histology/PAS alone is not optimally sensitive and is nonspecific (also positive with mycobacteria and other organisms); anti-TNF-alpha therapy may decrease PAS sensitivity (p.1369) Saliva and fecal PCR are inappropriate as sole diagnostic tools because of low positive predictive value (more often reflecting colonization than disease); a positive result needs confirmation from end-organ tissue or body fluid (p.1370) Treating presumed inflammatory arthritis or uveitis with glucocorticoids or anti-TNF-alpha agents can accelerate disease progression and unmask/precipitate disease; consider screening for WD before immunosuppression (p.1368) Oral tetracycline or TMP-SMX monotherapy has unacceptable relapse rates, particularly for CNS disease; sequence data indicate TMP is not active against T. whipplei (no dihydrofolate reductase) (p.1369, p.1370) Detection of T. whipplei sequence in BALF of asymptomatic individuals does not establish disease; caution is needed before diagnosing isolated pneumonia on sequence alone (p.1368) Culture is not practical for diagnosis as it takes months to turn positive (p.1370) T. whipplei is a weakly staining gram-positive, non-acid-fast bacillus with a small (<1-megabase) genome and incomplete biosynthetic pathways, consistent with an intracellular/nutritionally dependent pathogen; it is one of the slowest-growing human pathogens (doubling time ~18 days). Exposure is far more common than disease, and chronic infection (WD) is a rare outcome (<0.01% of those exposed). Establishing chronic infection involves both an impaired host inflammatory response and pathogen-driven immune modulation: HLA alleles DRB1*13 and DQB1*06 (favoring humoral over cell-mediated responses) raise risk, an impaired TH1 response with increased anti-inflammatory cytokines and regulatory T-cell activity, M2 macrophage polarization with impaired phagosome-lysosome fusion, and blunted T. whipplei-specific T-cell development occur. The organism has tropism for myeloid cells, which it invades and within which it avoids killing; affected tissue is infiltrated by foamy macrophages containing PAS-staining inclusions (ingested bacteria). In the small intestine, villus atrophy, lymphangiectasia, crypt hyperplasia, and surface epithelial apoptosis lead to malabsorptive diarrhea. (p.1367, p.1368) Untreated Whipple disease is often fatal, and delayed diagnosis can lead to irreparable organ damage, particularly in the CNS. With appropriate treatment, clinical response is often rapid and at times remarkable, and timely recognition may yield cure with medical management alone; however, eradication requires prolonged therapy and a durable response is challenged by relapse (especially CNS relapse) and host predisposition to reinfection occurring years to decades later. CNS disease carries a significant mortality risk and may leave neurologic sequelae. (p.1367, p.1368, p.1369, p.1370) Harrison frames the disease by clinical syndrome rather than a graded severity score: asymptomatic colonization/carriage (PCR-detectable T. whipplei in stool, saliva, or duodenal tissue without symptoms); acute infection (e.g., gastroenteritis in children, febrile bacteremia, acute pneumonia); chronic infection comprising "classic" Whipple disease (intestinal involvement with multisystem disease) and "isolated" infection (organ disease such as endocarditis, neurologic, ocular, or pulmonary disease without intestinal symptoms); and reinfection/relapsing disease, including treatment-associated IRIS. (p.1367, p.1368, p.1369)

for cardiovascular involvement Serum and urinary calcium studies to detect hypercalcaemia Renal ultrasound and assessment for renal artery stenosis Developmental, hearing, and ophthalmological evaluation Distinctive personality with an overly friendly, socially engaging manner and characteristic hypersociability Recognisable elfin facies including a broad forehead, short nose with full nasal tip, wide mouth, full lips, and a small chin Supravalvular aortic stenosis is the hallmark cardiovascular lesion, and other arteries including renal arteries may also narrow Idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia may occur and requires attention to dietary calcium and vitamin D intake Cognitive profile shows relative strength in language and social skills but marked weakness in visuospatial tasks Caused by a microdeletion at 7q11.23 that includes the elastin (ELN) gene, explaining the arteriopathy Connective tissue involvement contributes to hernias, joint problems, and a hoarse voice Hypertension may develop over time and requires monitoring given the diffuse arteriopathy Severe or progressive supravalvular aortic stenosis with risk of sudden cardiac events, especially under anaesthesia Symptomatic hypercalcaemia in infancy Hypertension from renal or diffuse arterial narrowing Increased anaesthetic risk due to coronary and aortic involvement requiring specialist planning Mistaking the friendly, verbal manner for higher overall cognitive ability than is present Overlooking cardiovascular disease and the heightened anaesthetic risk Failing to screen for and manage hypercalcaemia Not monitoring for later hypertension and arterial complications Williams syndrome results from a recurrent hemizygous microdeletion of a contiguous set of genes at chromosome 7q11.23. Loss of one copy of the elastin gene (ELN) reduces elastin in arterial walls, producing the generalised arteriopathy and characteristic supravalvular aortic stenosis. Deletion of adjacent genes, including those involved in neurodevelopment such as GTF2I, contributes to the distinctive cognitive and behavioural profile. The deletion usually arises de novo through misalignment of low-copy repeats flanking the region during meiosis. Disturbed calcium regulation of uncertain mechanism accounts for the infantile hypercalcaemia. Many individuals live into adulthood with support, but life expectancy and quality depend on the severity of cardiovascular disease; intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate and social strengths aid functioning.

Wilms Tumour — nephroblastoma, Wilms tumor Neuroblastoma Mesoblastic nephroma (in infants) Renal cell carcinoma (older children) Clear cell sarcoma or rhabdoid tumour of the kidney Multicystic dysplastic kidney or hydronephrosis Hepatoblastoma or other abdominal masses Abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging test Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of the abdomen to define the mass and the contralateral kidney Chest imaging to assess pulmonary metastases Full blood count, renal and liver function, urinalysis Blood pressure measurement Assessment for inferior vena cava or renal vein tumour thrombus The most common primary renal malignancy of childhood, typically presenting in preschool children around 2-5 years of age. The usual presentation is an asymptomatic, smooth abdominal mass discovered by a parent or on routine examination, sometimes with abdominal pain, haematuria, or hypertension. The mass characteristically does not cross the midline, in contrast to neuroblastoma. Associated with syndromes and anomalies such as WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann, and Denys-Drash, and with hemihypertrophy and aniridia; these children warrant surveillance. Examination should be gentle, avoiding vigorous palpation of the mass because of the risk of tumour rupture. Staging and histology (favourable versus anaplastic) guide a multimodal approach combining surgery, chemotherapy, and sometimes radiotherapy. Bilateral disease occurs in a minority and requires nephron-sparing strategies to preserve renal function. The lungs are the most common site of metastatic spread, so chest imaging is part of staging. Overall survival is high, making Wilms tumour one of the success stories of paediatric oncology. Rapidly enlarging abdominal mass Gross haematuria or significant hypertension Features of tumour rupture (acute abdominal pain, distension, haemodynamic instability) Respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases Signs of vascular (caval) extension Aggressive palpation of the abdominal mass, risking rupture Confusing it with neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and has different markers Missing hypertension as an associated finding Failing to screen children with predisposing syndromes Overlooking the contralateral kidney for bilateral disease Wilms tumour arises from embryonal nephrogenic (metanephric) blastema, often showing a classic triphasic pattern of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal elements. It is linked to abnormalities of genes involved in kidney development, including WT1, and to epigenetic changes at chromosome 11p; persistent nephrogenic rests are precursor lesions. Anaplastic histology confers a worse prognosis and greater treatment resistance. With risk-adapted multimodal therapy, most children with favourable-histology disease are cured; prognosis is worse with anaplastic histology, advanced stage, or unfavourable biological features.

Wilson's Disease — hepatolenticular degeneration Viral hepatitis and cirrhosis (often the initial diagnostic considerations in patients who actually have WD) (p.3338) Autoimmune hepatitis / chronic hepatitis (WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear) (p.3026-area AIH text, ch.355/427) Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (WD may be mistakenly diagnosed as these) (p.3338, p.3518) Substance abuse (a competing consideration in late-teen/early-twenties patients presenting with psychiatric features) (p.3339) Viral hepatitis (a frequent initial misdiagnosis in patients with the hepatic presentation of WD) (p.3338) Serum ceruloplasmin (initial screening test; characteristically low) and serum copper (low) (p.3339) 24-h urinary copper excretion (elevated, >100 ug/24 h; use acid-washed copper-free containers); penicillamine challenge with serial urine copper as a variation (p.3339) Percutaneous needle liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper (gold standard; >200 ug/g dry weight characteristic) by ICP-MS or atomic absorption spectrometry; histochemical copper staining is less reliable (p.3339) Slit-lamp or optical coherence tomography ophthalmologic examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings (required to detect early rings) (p.3339) Radiolabeled 64Cu incorporation into ceruloplasmin (highly specific; WD patients incorporate very little) (p.3339) ATP7B molecular/genetic testing (>650 pathogenic variants catalogued; common missense variants H1069Q, M645R, R778L) (p.3339) T2-weighted brain MRI in neurologic disease may show generalized atrophy and signal hypointensity in caudate head, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra, and red nucleus (~50%), though imaging correlates poorly with clinical features (p.3518) Cirrhosis of other cause (p.3338) Autoimmune/chronic hepatitis (p.3338, ch.355/427) Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (p.3338, p.3518) Primary psychiatric illness or substance abuse in adolescents/young adults (p.3339) Autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B (a P-type copper-transporting ATPase), which normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation (p.3338). Typically affects adolescents and young adults; presenting features include nonspecific liver disease, neurologic abnormalities, psychiatric illness, hemolytic anemia, renal tubular Fanconi syndrome, and skeletal abnormalities (p.3338). Age influences presentation: nearly all individuals presenting with liver disease are <30 years, whereas neurologic or psychiatric presentations may range from the first to the fifth decade; regardless of presentation, some degree of liver disease is invariably present (p.3338). Neurologic presentation reflects basal ganglia (caudate, putamen) involvement: dysarthria, dystonia (including facial grimacing/risus sardonicus), rigidity, tremor (classically 'wing-beating'), choreiform movements, abnormal gait, and uncoordinated handwriting; WD can properly be classified as a movement disorder (p.3338, p.3518). Kayser-Fleischer ring (golden to greenish-brown band in the peripheral cornea, from copper deposition in Descemet's membrane) is pathognomonic; present in ~95% of patients with neurologic signs but only about two-thirds of those with hepatic presentations (p.3339). Supportive biochemistry: low serum copper, low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-h urinary copper excretion (>100 ug/24 h), elevated transaminases, aminoaciduria, and hemolytic anemia (p.3339). Hepatic copper >200 ug per gram dry weight (normal 20-50) on percutaneous needle liver biopsy is a gold-standard biochemical diagnostic finding (p.3339). Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features; the Leipzig scoring system (2001), endorsed by EASL, weights and collates these features as a valuable diagnostic guide (p.3339). One of the best-characterized and most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism; prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase plus lifelong treatment are needed to prevent premature mortality (p.3338). Hemolytic anemia from sudden, massive release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly toxic to red cell membranes can be sudden and catastrophic (p.3339). Any teenager or young adult with new-onset psychiatric signs should have WD formally excluded (p.3339). WD should always be considered in the differential of a movement disorder, particularly when arising in the first decades of life (p.3518). WD is treatable and progression is preventable, so it is critical to test for it in any young patient with liver disease and/or a movement disorder or new psychiatric illness; missed diagnoses are tragic (p.3338, p.3518). Normal blood copper, ceruloplasmin, or urinary copper levels do NOT exclude the diagnosis (p.3518). WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic manifestations or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear (p.427/355). Kayser-Fleischer rings are absent in about one-third of patients with hepatic presentations, so their absence does not rule out WD (p.3339). In patients with neurologic presentations, penicillamine treatment can induce paradoxical worsening of neurologic status (p.3340). Autosomal recessive disease caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP7B, a highly conserved P-type copper-transporting ATPase expressed primarily in liver and kidney. ATP7B normally mediates copper removal from the liver via biliary excretion and prevents brain copper accumulation; its loss leads to pathologic copper accumulation, primarily impacting the liver and brain. Neurologic disease reflects copper toxicity in the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, striatum) with neurodegeneration and astrogliosis. Copper also deposits in the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer ring) and lens (sunflower cataract), and renal copper toxicity produces tubular (Fanconi) dysfunction. Massive sudden release of hepatic copper into the circulation directly damages red cell membranes, causing hemolytic anemia (p.3338-3339). In the absence of treatment, the course is progressive, leading to severe neurologic dysfunction and early/premature death in most patients, although a small proportion experience a relatively benign course. WD is one of the most effectively managed inborn errors of metabolism: prompt diagnosis in the presymptomatic or early symptomatic phase and lifelong treatment prevent premature mortality. Liver transplantation, generally needed only when delayed diagnosis or poor compliance has caused irreversible hepatic damage, can correct both hepatic failure and crippling neurologic impairment (p.3338, p.3340, p.3518). No single graded severity scale is given in the source; diagnosis is formalized using a combination of clinical, biochemical, and molecular features, collated by the Leipzig scoring system (2001, endorsed by EASL). Disease is broadly staged as presymptomatic/early symptomatic versus advanced; advanced or medically unresponsive hepatic disease is the indication for liver transplantation (p.3339-3340).

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome — WAS, eczema-thrombocytopenia-immunodeficiency syndrome Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) Atopic dermatitis with recurrent infection Severe combined immunodeficiency and other combined immunodeficiencies X-linked thrombocytopenia (milder WAS spectrum) Hyper-IgE syndrome Congenital thrombocytopenias with normal platelet size Full blood count and blood film assessing platelet number and platelet size (mean platelet volume) WAS gene sequencing and analysis of WAS protein expression Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses Lymphocyte subsets and functional T-cell testing Autoimmune and haemolysis screens where indicated Surveillance for lymphoma in older patients Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder classically presenting in boys with the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and recurrent infections It is caused by mutations in the WAS gene encoding the WAS protein, which regulates the actin cytoskeleton in haematopoietic cells The thrombocytopenia is distinctive for producing microthrombocytes (abnormally small platelets), unlike most other causes of low platelets Bleeding, ranging from petechiae and bruising to serious intracranial haemorrhage, is often the earliest and most dangerous manifestation The infection pattern reflects combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency, with encapsulated bacteria, opportunistic organisms, and viruses all contributing There is a marked predisposition to autoimmune disease (such as haemolytic anaemia and vasculitis) and to malignancy, particularly lymphoma Milder allelic conditions include X-linked thrombocytopenia, while certain mutations cause X-linked neutropenia Definitive treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with gene therapy an emerging option; supportive care includes immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis, and careful bleeding management Significant bleeding, especially intracranial haemorrhage, as an emergency Recurrent or opportunistic infections requiring urgent immunological workup New lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms suggesting lymphoma Live vaccines must be avoided because of the combined immunodeficiency Blood products should be irradiated and leucodepleted to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease Diagnosing isolated ITP and giving immunosuppression or splenectomy without recognising the underlying syndrome Overlooking the diagnostic clue of small platelet size on the blood film Administering live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products Underestimating the lifelong risks of autoimmunity and malignancy after immune reconstitution Delaying referral for transplantation in a child with classic severe disease Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the WAS gene on the X chromosome, which encodes a protein that links cell-surface signalling to reorganisation of the actin cytoskeleton in blood cells. Defective cytoskeletal dynamics impair the formation of immune synapses, the motility and function of T cells, dendritic cells, and phagocytes, and the normal production and structure of platelets, yielding small, poorly functioning platelets and combined immunodeficiency. Disturbed regulatory T-cell function and abnormal B-cell responses drive the high rate of autoimmunity, while impaired immune surveillance and chronic immune dysregulation predispose to lymphoid malignancy. Untreated classic disease carries a poor prognosis owing to bleeding, infection, autoimmunity, and malignancy, but successful haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally performed early, can be curative; milder phenotypes such as X-linked thrombocytopenia have a better outlook though still require monitoring.

karyotyping Midline defects such as cleft lip/palate, coloboma, cardiac septal defects and genitourinary anomalies are frequent Prolonged or clustered seizures and status epilepticus requiring urgent management Failure to thrive and dehydration from severe feeding difficulty Undiagnosed congenital heart disease causing cardiorespiratory compromise Recurrent aspiration pneumonia Relying on a normal karyotype when microarray is needed to detect small deletions Neglecting parental karyotyping and misjudging recurrence risk with a translocation Under-treating a seizure disorder that is central to morbidity Attributing poor growth to behaviour rather than oromotor dysfunction, delaying tube feeding Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of contiguous genes within the distal 4p16.3 region, notably the WHS critical regions containing candidate genes such as WHSC1/NSD2 and LETM1. Reduced dosage of these genes, which influence chromatin regulation, calcium/ion homeostasis and neuronal function, disrupts craniofacial, cardiac and central nervous system development. Loss of LETM1 in particular is implicated in the prominent seizure phenotype. Larger deletions generally produce a more severe clinical picture, and unbalanced familial translocations can also cause the condition. Survival is variable; many infants with larger deletions have high early mortality from malformations and infection, while those surviving infancy live into adulthood with severe intellectual disability. Seizure control and nutritional support strongly influence outcome.

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome — WPW, WPW syndrome, ventricular pre-excitation, accessory pathway syndrome AV nodal reentrant tachycardia without an accessory pathway Atrial fibrillation or flutter with aberrant conduction Ventricular tachycardia Other causes of a short PR interval Bundle branch block mimicking a broad QRS 12-lead ECG to identify pre-excitation and characterise arrhythmia reentrant tachycardia, a regular narrow-complex tachycardia using the AV node antegrade and the accessory pathway retrograde The dangerous arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation conducted rapidly down the accessory pathway, producing an irregular, broad, bizarre, and very fast ventricular response that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, AV nodal blocking curative, and is preferred in symptomatic patients Risk stratification assesses how rapidly the pathway can conduct, since a short refractory period predicts higher risk during atrial fibrillation MEDICAL EMERGENCY: pre-excited atrial fibrillation with a rapid, irregular, broad-complex response that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation Haemodynamic instability during any pre-excited tachyarrhythmia requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion Syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death indicating a high-risk pathway Use of AV nodal blocking agents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which can precipitate deterioration Administering AV nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited atrial fibrillation Assuming an asymptomatic WPW pattern requires no assessment when risk stratification may be warranted Mistaking pre-excited atrial fibrillation for ventricular tachycardia or ordinary atrial fibrillation Delaying cardioversion in an unstable pre-excited tachyarrhythmia In WPW an accessory atrioventricular pathway bypasses the normal AV nodal delay, allowing early activation of ventricular myocardium and producing the delta wave and short PR interval. This creates the substrate for reentry: in orthodromic AVRT the impulse travels down the AV node and back up the accessory pathway, while in the less common antidromic form the direction is reversed, giving a wide-complex tachycardia. The gravest scenario occurs when atrial fibrillation develops and the accessory pathway, lacking the rate-limiting properties of the AV node, conducts rapid atrial impulses to the ventricles, risking degeneration to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. Most patients have an excellent prognosis, and catheter ablation is curative in the great majority; the principal risk is sudden death from rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation in the minority with a short-refractory-period pathway, which risk stratification and ablation substantially reduce.

the enzyme lysosomal acid lipase, leading to accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides within lysosomes Wolman disease is the severe infantile end of the spectrum, presenting in the first weeks of life with vomiting, diarrhoea, and failure to thrive Marked hepatosplenomegaly with progressive liver dysfunction is a prominent feature Bilateral adrenal enlargement with calcification is a Profound failure to thrive with vomiting and diarrhoea in early infancy Progressive liver dysfunction or hepatic failure Adrenal insufficiency associated with adrenal involvement Severe malabsorption with rapid clinical deterioration Overlooking the diagnosis in a neonate with failure to thrive and hepatosplenomegaly Missing adrenal calcification on imaging as a diagnostic pointer Failing to recognise the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease as the same enzyme deficiency Delaying enzyme replacement therapy, which is most beneficial when started early Wolman disease is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in LIPA, encoding lysosomal acid lipase, the enzyme that hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides delivered to the lysosome. Deficient activity causes these lipids to accumulate within lysosomes of the liver, spleen, intestine, adrenal glands, and macrophages throughout the body. Massive lipid storage produces hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic dysfunction, adrenal infiltration with calcification, and intestinal involvement causing malabsorption. Disrupted intracellular cholesterol sensing also drives a proatherogenic dyslipidaemia. The severe infantile phenotype reflects near-absent enzyme activity, whereas residual activity underlies the milder cholesteryl ester storage disease. Untreated infantile Wolman disease is rapidly progressive and usually fatal within the first months of life. Enzyme replacement therapy has substantially improved survival in this severe form, and the later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease has a more chronic course dominated by liver disease and dyslipidaemia with associated cardiovascular risk.

The same gene is required for normal gonadotropin regulation and gonadal function, so affected males also develop hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, typically becoming apparent around the age of expected puberty. The X-linked inheritance explains the predominance of affected males. With lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement and induction of puberty when required, survival and development are generally good, although impaired fertility commonly persists and adrenal crises remain a lifelong risk if replacement lapses.

agammaglobulinemia is caused by mutations in the BTK gene, which encodes Bruton tyrosine kinase, a signalling molecule essential for B-cell maturation The block in B-cell development leads to and lymphoid tissue because germinal centres do not form Cellular (T-cell) immunity is intact, so most viral and fungal infections are handled normally, distinguishing it from combined immunodeficiencies The cornerstone of treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement together with prompt antibiotic treatment of infections Recurrent or severe sinopulmonary infection or sepsis warranting urgent immunological assessment Chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis presenting with progressive neurological decline Live vaccines, especially oral polio, must be avoided because of the antibody defect Progressive bronchiectasis from repeated or inadequately treated respiratory infection Failure to thrive with recurrent infection in an infant boy after 6 months of age Attributing recurrent childhood infections to ordinary illness and delaying immunoglobulin measurement Overlooking the physical clue of absent tonsils and lymph nodes Giving live vaccines, particularly oral poliovirus vaccine Assuming normal viral immunity fully protects, thereby missing enteroviral complications Under-dosing or interrupting immunoglobulin replacement, allowing breakthrough infection and lung damage X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from loss-of-function mutations in BTK, a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that transmits signals from the pre-B-cell and B-cell receptors. Without functional BTK, developing B cells arrest at the pre-B stage in the bone marrow and fail to mature, so mature B cells and plasma cells are largely absent from the periphery and lymphoid tissue. The consequence is a profound deficiency of all antibody classes, leaving the patient unable to opsonise and clear encapsulated bacteria and unable to neutralise certain viruses, notably enteroviruses. Because T-cell and innate immunity are preserved, the clinical picture is dominated by pyogenic bacterial and enteroviral infection rather than opportunistic disease. With early diagnosis and consistent immunoglobulin replacement plus prompt antibiotic therapy, most patients have a good long-term outlook, though chronic lung disease from recurrent respiratory infection and rare enteroviral central nervous system infection remain important causes of morbidity.

carrier detection and genetic counselling are important Hyperthermia or febrile seizures from impaired heat dissipation, especially in infants Recurrent unexplained high fevers mistaken for infection Failure to thrive with recurrent respiratory or ear infections Heat-related collapse during hot weather or exertion Repeatedly investigating recurrent fevers for infection while overlooking impaired sweating Missing subtle or patchy features in carrier females Underestimating the risk of dangerous overheating in infancy Neglecting early dental planning and psychological support X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the EDA gene, which encodes ectodysplasin A. This ligand signals through its receptor during embryonic development to direct formation of ectodermal appendages, including sweat and other exocrine glands, hair follicles, and tooth germs. Without functional signalling these structures fail to develop normally, producing absent or reduced eccrine sweat glands, sparse hair, and missing or malformed teeth. Loss of sweating removes a key route of heat dissipation, so affected individuals overheat readily and are prone to hyperthermia. Intelligence and lifespan are usually normal with appropriate care; the main morbidity comes from heat intolerance and recurrent infections in early childhood and from the dental and cosmetic effects, which can be substantially improved with multidisciplinary and dental management.

X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets — XLH, PHEX-related hypophosphataemia, familial hypophosphataemic rickets Nutritional vitamin-D-deficiency rickets Vitamin-D-dependent rickets (1-alpha-hydroxylase or receptor defects) Autosomal dominant/recessive hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23, DMP1, ENPP1) Tumour-induced osteomalacia (acquired FGF23 excess) Fanconi syndrome with renal phosphate wasting Hypophosphatasia (low alkaline phosphatase, opposite pattern) Serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone Renal tubular phosphate handling (tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per glomerular filtration rate) Serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, characteristically inappropriately low or normal, and FGF23 where available Molecular testing of PHEX to confirm the diagnosis Radiographs of the wrists, knees and lower limbs to document rickets and bowing Renal ultrasound to monitor for nephrocalcinosis, especially during treatment The commonest heritable form of rickets, caused by loss-of-function mutations in PHEX and inherited as an X-linked dominant trait The biochemical signature is hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting with an inappropriately normal or low serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D despite the low phosphate, driven by excess circulating FGF23 Alkaline phosphatase is typically raised and serum calcium is usually normal, which helps distinguish it from calcium-deficiency rickets Children present with progressive lower-limb bowing, a waddling gait, short stature and dental abscesses from poor dentine mineralisation Renal phosphate wasting is confirmed by a low tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate relative to glomerular filtration rate Conventional treatment is oral phosphate combined with active vitamin D (calcitriol/alfacalcidol); the FGF23-targeted monoclonal antibody burosumab is now used for eligible patients Monitoring for treatment complications, including nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism, is essential on conventional therapy In adults the disease causes osteomalacia, enthesopathy, pseudofractures and dental problems Progressive limb deformity or fractures despite treatment Nephrocalcinosis or declining renal function on conventional phosphate and vitamin D therapy Development of tertiary hyperparathyroidism during long-term treatment Recurrent dental abscesses or spinal stenosis and cord compression from enthesopathy in adults Treating as ordinary nutritional rickets with vitamin D alone, which does not correct phosphate wasting Failing to recognise that a normal 1,25-vitamin D is inappropriate in the face of hypophosphataemia Overtreating with phosphate and active vitamin D and causing nephrocalcinosis or hyperparathyroidism Missing the diagnosis in adults presenting with osteomalacia, enthesopathy or dental abscesses X-linked hypophosphataemia is caused by inactivating mutations in PHEX, a membrane endopeptidase expressed in bone and teeth. Loss of PHEX function leads, through incompletely defined mechanisms, to excessive circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). FGF23 reduces expression of renal sodium-phosphate cotransporters, causing phosphate to be lost in the urine, and it also suppresses the enzyme that generates active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The result is chronic hypophosphataemia with an inappropriately low or normal active vitamin D level, impairing mineralisation of the growth plate and osteoid and producing rickets and osteomalacia. With early and sustained treatment, rickets heals and growth and deformity improve, though short stature and dental problems may persist; FGF23-targeted therapy has improved outcomes, but lifelong monitoring for skeletal, renal and dental complications is required.

fetuses Features suggesting a contiguous gene deletion syndrome (e.g. anosmia and hypogonadism, developmental delay) Cryptorchidism requiring urological evaluation Failure of scaling to respond to standard care, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis Confusing it with ichthyosis vulgaris, which spares extremities less consistently and is associated with atopy and keratosis pilaris Overlooking unrelated ocular disease X-linked ichthyosis is caused by deficiency of steroid sulfatase, an enzyme that hydrolyses cholesterol sulfate and sulfated steroid precursors. In the epidermis, accumulation of cholesterol sulfate destabilises the intercellular lipid lamellae of the stratum corneum and inhibits proteases responsible for corneodesmosome breakdown, so desquamation is impaired and corneocytes are retained. This produces the characteristic retention hyperkeratosis with large adherent scales. Because the STS gene lies in a region of the X chromosome that partly escapes inactivation and is prone to deletion, larger deletions may remove neighbouring genes and cause a contiguous gene syndrome. It is a benign, lifelong condition confined largely to the skin in the isolated form, with scaling that persists but is manageable with regular emollient and keratolytic care; prognosis depends on any associated features in patients with larger deletions.

X-linked lymphoproliferative disease — XLP, Duncan disease, SH2D1A, SAP deficiency, XIAP, BIRC4, XLP1, XLP2 Familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis from other genetic causes Other primary EBV-susceptibility disorders (e.g. ITK, CD27, MAGT1 defects) Common variable immunodeficiency presenting with dysgammaglobulinaemia Sporadic EBV-associated lymphoma Very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease (for the XIAP phenotype) Severe primary infectious mononucleosis without underlying defect Flow cytometry for intracellular SAP and XIAP protein expression Molecular genetic testing of SH2D1A and XIAP/BIRC4 Quantitative immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses Natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell function assays EBV viral load and HLH markers including ferritin and soluble interleukin-2 receptor Enumeration of natural killer T cells (typically reduced or absent in XLP1) An X-linked disorder of boys defined by an extreme and often fatal immune dysregulation triggered by Epstein-Barr virus infection XLP1 results from SH2D1A mutation causing loss of the signalling adaptor SAP; XLP2 results from XIAP (BIRC4) mutation The three classic manifestations of XLP1 are fulminant EBV-driven haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, dysgammaglobulinaemia, and B-cell lymphoma XIAP deficiency more often presents with recurrent haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, splenomegaly and inflammatory-bowel-disease-like colitis, and lymphoma is uncommon SAP is required for normal function of natural killer T cells and for cytotoxic control of EBV-infected B cells, explaining the catastrophic response to primary EBV Any boy with fulminant or fatal infectious mononucleosis, or EBV-associated HLH, should prompt evaluation for XLP Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapy and is best undertaken before or after control of an HLH episode Fulminant or progressive infectious mononucleosis with cytopenias and organ dysfunction Ferritin and inflammatory markers rising in keeping with evolving HLH Rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma Recurrent HLH episodes or refractory colitis in a boy (XIAP phenotype) Dismissing severe mononucleosis in a boy as an ordinary viral illness without considering XLP Attributing hypogammaglobulinaemia to common variable immunodeficiency and missing an X-linked cause Failing to test both SAP and XIAP, since their phenotypes overlap but differ in lymphoma risk Delaying definitive transplant planning until after a life-threatening HLH episode X-linked lymphoproliferative disease is a genetic failure to regulate the immune response, classically unmasked by Epstein-Barr virus. In XLP1 the SH2D1A gene encodes the SLAM-associated protein SAP, an intracellular adaptor essential for signalling through the SLAM family of receptors on T cells and natural killer cells; its loss cripples cytotoxic killing of EBV-infected B cells and impairs natural killer T-cell development. In XLP2 the affected gene XIAP encodes an inhibitor-of-apoptosis protein important for inflammasome signalling and lymphocyte survival. In both, uncontrolled activation and expansion of T cells and macrophages during viral challenge drives a hyperinflammatory, cytokine-rich state that produces haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, together with a spectrum of antibody deficiency and, in XLP1, lymphoma. The natural history is severe, with EBV-triggered HLH carrying high mortality, but early recognition, control of hyperinflammation, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation markedly improve survival, particularly when transplantation is undertaken before the onset of fulminant disease.

history to gauge photosensitivity Autosomal recessive disorder of DNA repair, caused by variants in nucleotide excision repair genes (complementation groups XPA-XPG) or in POLH (XP variant) Defective repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage causes extreme photosensitivity and a very high risk of skin cancers at a young age Early signs include severe sunburn from minimal exposure and, later, freckling and poikilodermatous change on sun-exposed skin in early childhood Cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas and melanoma arise decades earlier than in the general population Ocular involvement is prominent: photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, and periocular tumours Some complementation groups develop progressive neurological degeneration (the neurological form) Rigorous, lifelong photoprotection and surveillance are the cornerstone of management New, changing, or non-healing skin lesion requiring urgent biopsy for malignancy Ocular surface deterioration, corneal scarring, or periocular tumour Progressive neurological decline (hearing loss, ataxia, cognitive regression) Evidence of inadequate photoprotection with escalating actinic damage Attributing childhood 'freckling' and severe sunburns to ordinary sun sensitivity and missing the diagnosis Under-recognising the lifelong intensity of photoprotection required, including indoor ultraviolet sources Neglecting ophthalmic and neurological surveillance in favour of skin monitoring alone Delaying biopsy of new lesions given the accelerated pace of malignant change Xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by variant form instead reflects loss of DNA polymerase eta, needed for accurate translesion synthesis.
